“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
Your salvation is not purchased by perfect compliance with every family expectation.
It is God's gift through faith in Christ.
And if you belong to Christ, your identity is not ultimately defined by the cruelest thing someone called you.
Not “worthless.”
Not “ungrateful.”
Not “a disappointment.”
Not “impossible to love.”
Not “a curse upon this family.”
Those labels may have echoed through your childhood.
But they are not the Gospel.
In Christ, believers are adopted into God's family.
Romans 8:15 speaks of receiving “the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.” (KJV)
The Greek text preserves the Aramaic address:
Ἀββᾶ ὁ πατήρ — Abba ho Patēr
“Abba, Father.”
Abba is an Aramaic word for father, carried into the Greek text alongside Patēr, the Greek word for father.
It communicates a real familial address to God, not a magical word and not merely a childish nickname.
And for someone whose earthly father made the word “father” feel frightening, this passage may be both beautiful and difficult.
Perhaps you struggle to imagine fatherly love without conditions.
Perhaps the word itself brings memories you wish you could forget.
If that is you, you do not have to pretend that trust comes easily.
The character of God is not defined by the failures of your earthly parents.
God is not a larger version of the person who terrified you.
His holiness is not cruelty.
His authority is not manipulation.
His correction is not sadism.
His love is not a trap.
Psalm 27:10 says:
“When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.” (KJV)
That verse does not promise that every painful family relationship will be repaired in this lifetime.
But it does testify that abandonment by earthly parents does not place someone beyond God's care.
And maybe you have been carrying a question for years.
“If my own parents could not love me well, why would God?”
Look at Jesus.
Look at the One who welcomed the vulnerable.
Look at the One who warned against causing little ones to stumble.
Look at the One who confronted religious hypocrisy.
Look at the One who suffered injustice without becoming unjust.
Look at the cross, where God's love and holiness are revealed in the saving work of His Son.
Jesus was not crucified to preserve the reputation of abusive families.
He died for sinners and rose again, so that all who repent and believe in Him may receive forgiveness and new life.
That includes wounded children who have grown into exhausted adults.
And it also includes parents who have committed terrible wrongs, if they genuinely turn to Christ.
But we must be careful here.
The possibility of redemption does not eliminate accountability.
A parent who has abused a child cannot demand immediate trust simply because they say, “God forgave me.”
A confession may be a beginning.
It is not a substitute for changed behavior.
True repentance bears fruit.
John the Baptist said in Matthew 3:8:
“Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.” (KJV)
The Greek expression καρπὸν ἄξιον τῆς μετανοίας (karpon axion tēs metanoias) speaks of fruit appropriate to repentance.
Repentance is not merely sorrow at being exposed.
It involves a genuine turning away from sin.

For an abusive parent, that may include acknowledging specific wrongdoing without excuses, stopping harmful conduct, accepting appropriate consequences, seeking qualified help, making restitution where possible, and respecting the boundaries of those harmed.
It may involve cooperating with lawful investigations.
It may involve accepting that the relationship will never return to what it once was.
And it certainly does not entitle the person who caused harm to control the healing process of the person they wounded.
Grace is free.
Trust is not automatic.
Forgiveness is commanded as part of Christian life, but restored access is not owed on demand.
And even when reconciliation is possible, it must not come at the expense of safety or truth.
Perhaps you are reading this and feeling guilty because you have not spoken to a parent in months.
Maybe years.
You see Mother's Day posts.
Father's Day celebrations.
Photographs of families laughing around dinner tables.
And something inside you aches.
You wonder why you cannot have what everyone else seems to have.
You wonder whether you should call.
You wonder whether your boundaries are too harsh.
You wonder whether God is disappointed.
And sometimes, the hardest part is that you still love them.
You miss the parent you needed.
You remember the good moments.
The birthday cake.
The occasional embrace.
The rare words of encouragement.
The times they seemed almost like the parent you had prayed for.
And that makes everything more confusing.
Because abuse does not always erase affection.
Sometimes affection and fear become tangled together so tightly that a person no longer knows what healthy love feels like.
You can grieve someone who is still alive.
You can love a parent and recognize that being near them is harmful.
You can wish for reconciliation and acknowledge that reconciliation is not currently possible.
You can remember moments of kindness without allowing those moments to erase patterns of abuse.
The existence of good memories does not cancel the reality of serious harm.
And protecting yourself does not mean you have stopped caring.
For some people, healthy boundaries may look like limiting phone calls.
For others, refusing conversations that become threatening or degrading.
For others, declining financial demands or preventing a parent from using children as instruments of control.
For some, contact may need to happen only through a trusted intermediary.
And for others, especially where serious danger, coercion, or repeated abuse is involved, no contact may be necessary.
The Bible does not give one universal contact schedule for every adult child and every abusive parent.
Wisdom requires attention to the actual situation.
Proverbs 22:3 says:
“A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.” (KJV)
The proverb commends prudence in the face of danger.
It should not be treated as a simplistic command to sever every difficult relationship.
But neither should Christians dismiss the wisdom of taking protective action when harm is foreseeable.
And if you are a minor experiencing abuse, the burden should not fall on you to negotiate the situation alone.
Tell a trustworthy adult who can help protect you, such as a safe relative, teacher, counselor, safeguarding officer, or appropriate authority.
If you are in immediate danger, seek emergency assistance.
If sexual abuse, serious violence, or threats are involved, seeking protection and reporting to appropriate authorities can be necessary.
Please do not interpret any teaching about forgiveness as a reason to remain in immediate danger.
A church should never pressure someone to conceal abuse for the sake of its reputation.
The reputation of Christ is not protected by hiding wickedness.
It is honored by truth, justice, compassion, and integrity.
And now I want to speak to a different person.
The parent reading this who is beginning to feel uncomfortable.
Perhaps your adult child has pulled away.
Perhaps they no longer answer every call.
Perhaps they have told you that certain words or behaviors hurt them.
And your first reaction has been anger.
“How dare they?”
“I raised them.”
“I paid for everything.”
“They owe me respect.”
But what if, instead of beginning with what they owe you, you asked what your conduct has taught them to expect from you?
What if their silence is not necessarily arrogance?
What if their distance is not necessarily hatred?
What if they have tried to explain their pain, and every attempt became another argument they could not win?
Not every accusation is accurate.
Not every disagreement is abuse.
Parents can be unfairly blamed, and children can behave wrongly too.
But a parent's authority is never a reason to dismiss a serious allegation without examination.
If your child says they were harmed, listen carefully.
Do not begin by defending your intentions.
Ask whether your actions were wrong.
Ask whether you have used fear, humiliation, intimidation, or Scripture to maintain control.
Ask whether your apologies have required your child to comfort you instead of allowing them to speak.
Ask whether you have confused obedience with love.
And if you discover that you have sinned against your child, repent.
Not theatrically.
Not as a strategy to regain access.
Not by saying, “I'm sorry you feel that way.”
Repent with humility.
Tell the truth.
Take responsibility.
Seek help.
Accept consequences.
And do not demand that your child's healing happen according to your timetable.
Because your child is not your property.
Your child is a human being made in the image of God.
Parenthood is a stewardship.
It is not ownership.
And the God who calls children to honor their parents also calls parents to answer for how they treat their children.
There is still grace for the repentant parent.
There is still mercy at the cross.
There is still the possibility of transformation through Jesus Christ.
But grace does not make confession unnecessary.
It makes genuine repentance possible.
And now, perhaps, we are reaching the deepest part of this conversation.
Because for many wounded Christians, the question is no longer simply, “Must I endure abuse?”
The question beneath it is:
“Can I belong to Jesus without betraying myself?”
Can I tell the truth?
Can I protect my children?
Can I stop pretending?
Can I acknowledge that my childhood was not what it should have been?
Can I grieve the mother who was physically present but emotionally absent?
Can I mourn the father whose approval I spent my entire life trying to earn?
Can I admit that I am angry?
Can I bring that anger before God without pretending to be spiritually mature?
The Psalms give us a language for anguish.
They contain tears, protest, lament, fear, and desperate cries for help.
Biblical faith is not the absence of pain.
It is bringing our pain into the presence of the God who hears.
Psalm 34:18 declares:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.” (KJV)
That does not mean every emotional wound disappears immediately after prayer.
Healing can take time.
Some people need trauma-informed counseling, medical care, pastoral support, practical protection, and patient community.
Seeking that help does not demonstrate a lack of faith.
It can be part of wise and faithful stewardship of the life God has given you.
And please remember this.
You do not have to become emotionally numb to prove that you have forgiven.
You do not have to stop grieving to prove that you trust God.
You do not have to rush reconciliation to prove that you are a Christian.
You do not have to turn every painful memory into a testimony before you are ready to speak about it.
There is a difference between surrendering bitterness to God and suppressing the truth of what happened.
Romans 12:19 says:
“Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.” (KJV)
The command is against personal vengeance.
It is not a command to abandon lawful protection, accountability, or justice.
You can refuse revenge while seeking justice.
You can pray for someone while maintaining distance.
You can desire their repentance without exposing yourself to another cycle of harm.
And you can entrust what you cannot control to God.
This is not easy.
Sometimes obedience to Jesus requires courage that nobody sees.
The courage to say, “I will not lie about what happened.”
The courage to say, “I cannot allow you to speak to me this way.”
The courage to say, “My children will not be exposed to the same danger.”
The courage to say, “I hope you repent, but I cannot pretend that trust has been restored.”
The courage to say, “I am willing to seek peace, but I cannot manufacture reconciliation alone.”
Romans 12:18 says:
“If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.” (KJV)
Those words matter.
“If it be possible.”
“As much as lieth in you.”
Scripture recognizes that peace is not always within one person's power.
You are responsible for your conduct.
You are not able to control another person's repentance.
You cannot create mutual trust by yourself.
You cannot make someone safe simply by loving them harder.
And you cannot carry both sides of a relationship indefinitely while calling the exhaustion holiness.
That may be the sentence someone needs to hear today.
Because you have tried.
You have explained.
You have cried.
You have apologized.
You have prayed.
You have gone back again and again, hoping that this time the conversation would be different.
And perhaps it never was.
If that is your story, I will not promise that your parent will change.
I will not promise that the next phone call will bring an apology.
I will not promise that every family relationship will be restored before heaven.
The Bible does not give us permission to make those guarantees.
But it gives us something greater than a false promise.
It gives us Jesus Christ.
The Savior who knows what rejection feels like.
The Savior who was betrayed.
The Savior who was falsely accused.
The Savior who suffered at the hands of sinful people.
And yet the Savior who did not surrender His righteousness to the evil surrounding Him.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that our High Priest is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
Jesus understands suffering without approving of sin.
He understands betrayal without calling betrayal love.
He understands injustice without declaring injustice holy.
And through His resurrection, He has conquered sin and death.
That is why the Christian hope is more than learning to manage painful relationships.
It is the promise of redemption through Christ.
The Gospel does not say your wounds are insignificant.
It says your wounds do not have the final authority over your life.
It does not say your past was acceptable.
It says your past does not have to become your eternal identity.
It does not say that everyone who harmed you will repent.
It says that Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust, even when people have betrayed it.
And for the one who has spent years believing that love must always hurt, that truth may take time to receive.
But it is worth holding onto.
Because honoring your father and mother must never become an excuse for dishonoring the God whose image you bear.
You are not greater than your parents.
You are not called to despise them.
You are not authorized to return evil for evil.
But neither are you a disposable object whose suffering becomes righteous whenever a parent demands it.
You are a person accountable to God.
And so are they.
Maybe this article has exposed something you have never said out loud.
Maybe you have been using the word “honor” to justify staying in a destructive situation.
Maybe you have been using the word “forgiveness” to avoid admitting how deeply you were wounded.
Maybe you have spent years protecting your family's public image while privately wondering why your soul feels exhausted.
Or perhaps you are a parent who now realizes that you have used a commandment meant to cultivate honor as a tool for demanding unquestioning control.
Wherever you find yourself, the invitation of Jesus is not to hide.
It is to come into the light.
To repent where you have sinned.
To seek help where you have been harmed.
To forgive without lying.
To pursue peace without surrendering truth.
To practice honor without enabling evil.
And to trust that the grace of God is powerful enough to transform lives without requiring us to deny reality.
This is why the message of Gospel Warrior matters.
Not because we have every answer.
Not because every wound can be healed through a single article.
But because people desperately need to encounter the whole counsel of Scripture, centered on Jesus Christ, rather than isolated verses used to manipulate the vulnerable.
Some people need to hear about repentance.
Others need to hear that God's grace is not beyond their reach.
Some need the courage to confess.
Others need the courage to seek protection.
Some need to forgive.
Others need to understand that forgiveness and reconciliation are not interchangeable.
And all of us need Jesus.
Not merely to increase the reach of a post, but because someone in your circle may be silently asking the same question.
Someone who has never told anyone why they dread going home.
Someone who thinks setting a boundary will send them to hell.
Someone who has confused parental authority with divine authority.
Someone who needs to know that God does not require them to conceal abuse.
Where someone's safety or privacy could be affected, send the article privately rather than publicly identifying them as a survivor.
There may come a day when guilt returns and you need to read these Scriptures again.
Not the details of trauma you are not ready to share.
Not anything that could compromise your safety.
Just one honest response.

If you have a testimony of repentance, restored relationships, healthy boundaries, or God's faithfulness through a difficult family situation, your words may encourage someone who feels completely alone.

And if you disagree with something in this article, you are welcome to engage respectfully with Scripture. We should be willing to examine our understanding carefully, because truth matters more than winning an argument.
There is also something deeper I want to invite you into.
Not because a payment can purchase His favor.
Not because giving to this particular ministry is a condition of obedience or salvation.
It is not.
But because voluntary, faithful generosity can help make Gospel-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to more people.
Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their work (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that believers should give willingly rather than under pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
If you already support your local church, care for your family, or have financial obligations that must come first, please honor those responsibilities.
It can help turn the message you just read into an ongoing mission.
Because the greatest gift of the Gospel cannot be bought.
And it cannot be sold.
It is the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
Keep reading.
Keep learning.
Keep opening your Bible.
Keep sharing truth.
And keep following Jesus.
Because there are people suffering behind closed doors who do not need another verse used against them.
They need the truth of Scripture rightly understood.
They need safe people who will listen.
They need repentance where there has been wrongdoing.
They need wisdom about boundaries.
They need the hope of redemption.
And above all, they need Jesus Christ.
Before you leave, I want to return to that daughter sitting in her car.
The phone is still on the seat beside her.
The messages have not disappeared.
Her childhood has not suddenly become beautiful.
Her mother has not necessarily repented.
Nothing about the past has been magically undone.
But perhaps something has changed.
For the first time, she is beginning to understand that she does not have to answer every threatening message to prove she loves God.
She can pray.
She can seek wise counsel.
She can take appropriate steps toward safety.
She can refuse cruelty without becoming cruel.
She can grieve what she never received.
She can leave room for genuine repentance without pretending that repentance has already happened.
And she can follow Jesus without surrendering her conscience to another person's control.
Maybe she places the phone down.
Maybe she cries.
Maybe she whispers a prayer she has been too afraid to pray.

“Lord Jesus, help me know what is right. Keep me from hatred. Give me courage to tell the truth. Teach me to forgive without enabling sin. Protect those who are vulnerable. And please heal what I cannot heal on my own.”
It is not a dramatic speech.
It does not solve everything.
But it is honest.
And sometimes honesty before God is where a new chapter begins.
If you recognize yourself in her story, remember that the Savior who calls you to honor your parents also calls you to walk in truth.
He is not asking you to worship your family.
He is asking you to follow Him.
And His grace is sufficient to meet you even in the complicated, unfinished places of your life.
You may never receive the apology your childhood deserved, but the cross declares that your future does not have to remain imprisoned by the sins of your past.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ARE TONGUES AND PROPHECY STILL REAL TODAY—OR HAVE WE BEEN MISTAKING EMOTION FOR THE HOLY SPIRIT?
paragraphs: ARE TONGUES AND PROPHECY STILL REAL TODAY—OR HAVE WE BEEN MISTAKING EMOTION FOR THE HOLY SPIRIT?

Some Christians say the gifts of the Spirit have ceased. Others say every believer should speak in tongues and prophesy. But what if the greatest danger isn't being on the wrong side of the debate—it's being so consumed by spiritual power that we forget the Savior who gives it?
There is a kind of silence that can break a Christian's heart.
Not the silence of an empty church.
Not the silence after the final worship song.
But the silence of someone who has begged God for years to experience what everyone else seems to have experienced.
You watched people fall to their knees. You heard voices rise in languages you couldn't understand. You listened as someone declared, "The Lord told me..."
And somewhere beneath the music, the tears, and the trembling hands, you whispered something you were almost ashamed to admit.
"Jesus... why not me?"
Maybe you have spent years wondering whether something is missing from your relationship with God.
Maybe someone told you that unless you speak in tongues, you haven't truly received the Holy Spirit.
Maybe you grew up in a church where prophecy was treated as ordinary, until someone supposedly speaking for God wounded you with words that never came true.
Or maybe you come from the opposite side.

You were taught that tongues and prophecy disappeared when the apostles died. Every modern claim made you suspicious. Every emotional worship service seemed dangerous. And every testimony of the supernatural sounded like something that needed to be exposed.
Then one day, someone you trusted told you about an experience you couldn't easily dismiss.
And suddenly the question became personal.
Are tongues and prophecy still active today?
Can the Holy Spirit still distribute these gifts?
Or are Christians chasing experiences that God never promised to continue?
And perhaps the question that should trouble us most...
If the Holy Spirit truly is at work, would we recognize Him—or would we be too busy defending our traditions to listen to Scripture?
Before we answer, we need to go somewhere more reliable than testimonies, denominations, viral videos, or the loudest preacher in the room.
We need to return to the Word of God.
Because the Holy Spirit never needs us to abandon the Scriptures in order to experience His presence.
And Jesus never asked His Church to choose between truth and the Spirit who inspired it.
When the apostle Paul wrote to the believers in Corinth, he was addressing a church overflowing with spiritual activity—and deeply troubled by spiritual immaturity.
Think about that.
They were not lacking religious experiences.
They were lacking love, order, humility, and discernment.
Paul acknowledged that they were not lacking in any spiritual gift as they waited for the revealing of Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 1:7).
Yet the same church was divided, proud, morally compromised, and confused about worship.
They had gifts.
But gifts did not automatically mean maturity.
They had knowledge.
But knowledge had become a reason for boasting.
They had extraordinary spiritual experiences.
But ordinary Christian love was being neglected.
Does that sound painfully familiar?
A person can speak beautifully about the supernatural and still speak cruelly to their family.
Someone can claim to prophesy over nations and still refuse to repent of private sin.
A preacher can fill a room with excitement and still fail to care for the wounded people sitting in the back row.
And a Christian can be so determined to expose false spiritual experiences that they forget to demonstrate the gentleness of Christ.
The Corinthian church reminds us of a truth that should humble every side of this conversation.
The presence of a spiritual gift is not proof of spiritual maturity. And the absence of a particular gift is not proof of spiritual inferiority.
Paul makes that unmistakably clear in 1 Corinthians 12.
He writes:
—1 Corinthians 12:4, King James Version
The Greek word translated "gifts" is χαρισμάτων (charismatōn), the plural of χάρισμα (charisma).
It comes from the same word family as χάρις (charis), meaning grace or favor.
This matters.
Because spiritual gifts are not medals awarded to the most impressive Christians.
They are gracious gifts distributed by God.
You cannot earn them through spiritual performance.
You cannot manufacture them through emotional intensity.
And you cannot turn them into a ranking system without contradicting the very grace from which they come.
Paul continues:
"But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal."
—1 Corinthians 12:7, KJV
The phrase "to profit withal" means for the common good.
The Greek expression is πρὸς τὸ συμφέρον (pros to sympheron).
The point is not personal celebrity.
Not religious superiority.
Not the ability to impress a congregation.
The Spirit's gifts are given for the benefit of Christ's body.
Then Paul names gifts including wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment of spirits, various kinds of tongues, and interpretation of tongues.
But notice what happens in verse 11.
Paul says the Spirit distributes these gifts "to every man severally as he will."
The Greek phrase καθὼς βούλεται (kathōs bouletai) means "as He wills."
Not as the preacher demands.
Not as the congregation expects.
Not as religious pressure dictates.
As the Holy Spirit wills.
And this immediately corrects one of the most painful teachings some Christians have encountered.
The Bible does not teach that every Christian must speak in tongues to prove that the Holy Spirit lives within them.
Paul asks in 1 Corinthians 12:30:
"Do all speak with tongues? do all interpret?"
The expected answer in the Greek construction is no.
Different members receive different gifts.
The body needs all its members.
And the believer who does not speak in tongues is not therefore a second-class Christian.
Romans 8:9 teaches that belonging to Christ and having the Spirit are inseparable.
Ephesians 1:13 describes believers as sealed with the promised Holy Spirit when they believed the Gospel.
Your salvation is not secured by producing a particular spiritual manifestation.
Your salvation rests in Jesus Christ.
His death.
His resurrection.
His grace received through faith.
And if someone has made you feel that Jesus is insufficient unless you can reproduce their experience, you need to hear this clearly.
Christ is not incomplete because your spiritual experience looks different from someone else's.
But does that mean tongues and prophecy have ceased?
To understand the question, we must return to the day the Church was born.
Jerusalem.
Pentecost.
A gathering of disciples waiting as Jesus commanded.
Then a sound like a mighty rushing wind.
Tongues resembling fire.
And people speaking in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance.
Acts 2:4 says:
"And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance."
The Greek word translated "tongues" is γλώσσαις (glōssais), from γλῶσσα (glōssa), which can refer to the physical tongue or to a language.
And Acts 2 gives us a crucial detail.
The crowd heard the disciples speaking in their own languages.
Acts 2:8 uses διαλέκτῳ (dialektō), referring to a language or dialect.
People from different regions heard the mighty works of God proclaimed in words they could understand.
This was not a performance designed to glorify the disciples.
It was a sign that the Gospel of Jesus Christ was breaking through human boundaries.
The message that began in Jerusalem was destined for the nations.
And Peter explained what was happening by quoting the prophet Joel.
"And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy..."
—Acts 2:17, KJV
In Joel 2:28, the Hebrew expression for "I will pour out my Spirit" is:
אֶשְׁפּוֹךְ אֶת־רוּחִי
'eshpokh 'et-ruchi
The image is of God pouring out His Spirit.
Not a trickle reserved for an elite religious class.
Not a privilege determined by social status.
Peter announces that the promised age of the Spirit has arrived through the exalted Jesus Christ.
Sons and daughters.
Young and old.
Servants, men and women.
God's promise was reaching people the world might have overlooked.
But Peter did not conclude his sermon by telling everyone to pursue spectacular experiences.
He proclaimed Jesus.
Jesus crucified.
Jesus raised from the dead.
Jesus exalted at the right hand of God.
And when the people were pierced to the heart, they asked what they should do.
Peter called them to repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.
The supernatural event pointed to the crucified and risen Savior.
That is the pattern we must never lose.
The Holy Spirit does not compete with Jesus for attention. He glorifies Jesus.
Christ Himself taught this in John 16:14:
"He shall glorify me: for he shall receive of mine, and shall shew it unto you."
So whenever someone claims to be operating in the power of the Holy Spirit, a question must be asked.
Where is Jesus in all of this?
Is Christ being exalted?
Is Scripture being honored?
Are sinners being called to repentance?
Are believers being strengthened in truth and love?
Or has the experience itself become the object of worship?
Because even a genuinely extraordinary experience becomes spiritually dangerous when it displaces the Lord it should honor.
Now we come to the passage that has divided sincere Christians for generations.
First Corinthians 13.
Paul writes:
—1 Corinthians 13:8, KJV
Some Christians read this and conclude that prophecy and tongues were temporary gifts intended for the apostolic age.
They argue that these gifts served a foundational purpose as the Church was established and the apostolic message was confirmed.
This position is commonly called cessationism.
Its defenders often appeal to passages such as Ephesians 2:20, which describes the Church as built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Jesus Christ as the chief cornerstone.
They also emphasize the unique authority of the apostles and the sufficiency of the completed Scriptures.
Their concern deserves to be heard seriously.
God's people must not be governed by new claims of revelation that rival the Bible.
No modern prophet possesses the authority to rewrite the Gospel.
No spiritual experience can overturn apostolic teaching.
No supposed message from heaven can correct the Word God has already given.
But other faithful Christians read the same passages and reach a different conclusion.
They believe the New Testament gifts may continue until Christ returns, while insisting that every claim must be tested by Scripture.
This position is commonly called continuationism.
They point out that 1 Corinthians 13:8 does not, by itself, tell us exactly when tongues and prophecy cease.
Paul continues:
"For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away."
—1 Corinthians 13:9–10, KJV
The Greek phrase translated "that which is perfect" is τὸ τέλειον (to teleion).
The word teleion can mean complete, mature, or brought to its intended end, depending on context.
Some interpret this completion as the arrival of the completed New Testament canon or the maturity of the apostolic Church.
Others argue that Paul's following words point beyond the present age.
He writes:
—1 Corinthians 13:12, KJV
The Greek phrase πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον (prosōpon pros prosōpon) means "face to face."

Continuationists argue that this language most naturally describes the fullness of knowledge and direct encounter associated with Christ's return, rather than merely the completion of the biblical canon.
That is a substantial contextual argument.
But we must also acknowledge something important.
Christians who affirm the authority of Scripture and the lordship of Jesus have genuinely disagreed about this passage.
The Bible does not explicitly state, "All miraculous gifts will end immediately upon the death of the last apostle."
Neither does it explicitly guarantee that every manifestation reported in every generation is authentic.
We must distinguish what Scripture clearly teaches from conclusions that require interpretation.
And we must be careful not to confuse confidence with infallibility.
There is a difference between defending biblical truth and pretending that our interpretation of every difficult passage is beyond examination.
Consider another instruction Paul gives.
"Wherefore, brethren, covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues."
—1 Corinthians 14:39, KJV
That is a real apostolic command to the Corinthian church.
Continuationists reasonably ask why Christians today should assume it no longer applies without compelling biblical evidence.
Cessationists respond that instructions concerning particular gifts may belong to the period in which those gifts were operative.
This is precisely where the debate lies.
Not between people who love the Bible and people who hate it.
Not automatically between Spirit-filled believers and spiritually dead believers.
But between different understandings of how the New Testament describes the purpose and duration of certain gifts.
We should be willing to examine those arguments without caricaturing our brothers and sisters.
Yet whatever position we hold, we cannot escape the instructions Paul gives concerning spiritual activity.
"Let all things be done unto edifying."
—1 Corinthians 14:26, KJV
"Let all things be done decently and in order."
—1 Corinthians 14:40, KJV
These are not optional decorations.
They reveal the character of Christian worship.
Paul does not celebrate confusion for its own sake.
He does not treat disorder as proof of divine power.
He does not encourage believers to abandon understanding.
In fact, he repeatedly emphasizes intelligibility, interpretation, and the strengthening of the congregation.

In 1 Corinthians 14:27–28, Paul instructs that public speaking in tongues should be limited, orderly, and interpreted. Without an interpreter, the speaker is to remain silent in the church and speak to himself and to God.
That alone should challenge much of what is casually defended as biblical worship.
If someone insists that every uncontrolled public manifestation must be accepted without examination, Paul does not agree.
If someone claims that interpretation is unnecessary because the experience feels powerful, Paul does not agree.
And if someone suggests that spiritual authenticity is measured by the volume of the room, Paul does not agree.
The Holy Spirit is not honored by ignoring the instructions He inspired.
There is also a necessary distinction between the clearly identifiable human languages spoken at Pentecost and the more difficult discussion of tongues in 1 Corinthians 12–14.

Christians disagree about whether all biblical tongues were recognizable human languages or whether Paul's discussion may also encompass speech not understood by ordinary hearers without interpretation.

First Corinthians 13:1 mentions "tongues of men and of angels," but the verse is part of Paul's rhetorical argument about the supremacy of love; it should not be treated by itself as conclusive proof of a separate angelic prayer language.
We must not claim certainty where the text requires careful interpretation.
And now we need to talk about prophecy.
Because for some readers, this is where the deepest wounds are hiding.
Perhaps someone once looked into your eyes and said, "God told me you are going to marry this person."
You believed them.
You rearranged your hopes around their words.
You ignored warning signs.
And when everything collapsed, you wondered whether you had somehow failed God.
Perhaps someone prophesied healing over a sick loved one.
They spoke with confidence.
They promised a miracle.
But the healing did not come.
And when you were already drowning in grief, someone suggested your family simply hadn't possessed enough faith.
Or maybe a leader used the words "God told me" to control your decisions, silence your questions, or keep you from leaving a harmful environment.
If that happened, the problem was not that you asked too many questions.
The problem was that a human claim to divine authority was used in a way that demanded more trust than Scripture permits.
The Bible never tells Christians to accept every spiritual claim unquestioningly.
First Thessalonians 5:20–21 says:
"Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good."
And 1 John 4:1 warns:
"Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world."
The Greek word δοκιμάζετε (dokimazete), used in 1 John 4:1 for testing, carries the idea of examining or evaluating.
Not blindly accepting.
Not automatically rejecting.
Testing.
This is not unbelief.
This is obedience.
In 1 Corinthians 14:29, Paul says:
"Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge."
The Greek verb translated "judge" is related to διακρίνω (diakrinō), which can mean to distinguish, evaluate, or discern.
Even in a congregation where prophecy was operating, prophetic speech was not to escape evaluation.
Think about the implications.
A person saying "God told me" does not remove the responsibility to examine what was said.
A dramatic delivery does not establish truth.
Tears do not establish truth.
A large following does not establish truth.
And a message that contradicts the Gospel does not become holy because someone spoke it while trembling.
Scripture gives severe warnings against false prophecy.
Deuteronomy 18:20–22 warns against speaking presumptuously in God's name, and Deuteronomy 13:1–3 teaches that even an impressive sign must not lead God's people away from Him.
The New Testament likewise warns against false prophets and deceptive signs.
Christians disagree about the precise relationship between Old Testament prophecy, foundational apostolic revelation, and any noncanonical prophetic activity claimed today.
But there is no biblical permission to excuse manipulation, false doctrine, or careless predictions merely because someone claims a spiritual gift.
And we should be especially cautious about those who repeatedly make predictions, refuse accountability, and then blame the wounded when their words fail.
God's name is too holy to be used as a shield against correction.
If you have been harmed by spiritual manipulation, you do not have to abandon Jesus to reject what was done in His name.
The Shepherd is not the same as the person who misrepresented Him.
You can grieve what happened.
You can seek wise pastoral counsel.
You can examine Scripture again.
And you can rediscover that Christ does not need fear, coercion, or manufactured certainty to lead His people.
But there is another danger on the opposite side.
We can become so afraid of deception that we begin to treat every testimony of God's extraordinary work with contempt.
We can become proud of our skepticism.
We can mistake emotional distance for theological maturity.
We can speak accurately about doctrine while refusing to pray with expectancy.
And we can forget that the living God is not confined by our inability to explain everything He may choose to do.
God is sovereign.
He hears prayer.
He heals according to His wisdom.
He acts in providence.
He can do what human strength cannot accomplish.
Believing that certain revelatory gifts have ceased does not require believing that God has become inactive.
And believing that the gifts may continue does not require believing every modern claim.
Both sides should be able to confess that Jesus Christ is alive, that the Holy Spirit indwells believers, and that God remains free to act according to His will.
What we must never do is reduce the Holy Spirit to a religious technique.
He is not a force we activate by repeating a phrase.
He is not an atmosphere we manufacture through music.
He is not a reward for emotional intensity.
He is the divine Person who gives life, glorifies Christ, convicts of sin, strengthens believers, and works according to the will of God.
And this brings us to the most devastating part of Paul's teaching.
Because immediately after discussing spiritual gifts, Paul writes words that should make every gifted person tremble.
"Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal."
—1 Corinthians 13:1, KJV
Then he goes further.
"And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing."
—1 Corinthians 13:2, KJV
Nothing.
Not merely less effective.
Not simply immature.
Nothing.
The Greek word for love here is ἀγάπη (agapē).
In this chapter, Paul describes love through patience, kindness, humility, truthfulness, endurance, and the refusal to seek selfish advantage.
Imagine possessing extraordinary religious abilities and yet failing at the very love those gifts were supposed to serve.
Imagine having a voice that moves thousands but a heart that refuses to forgive one person.
Imagine being celebrated for your prophetic insight while your own children are starving for your kindness.
Imagine winning every theological argument and losing your compassion for the people Jesus died to redeem.
That is the tragedy Paul is confronting.
And it is a tragedy that can happen in charismatic churches and non-charismatic churches alike.
One congregation may idolize manifestations.
Another may idolize intellectual superiority.
One may confuse excitement with holiness.
Another may confuse emotional restraint with holiness.
One may excuse false claims because they sound supernatural.
Another may dismiss sincere believers because their experiences do not fit its expectations.
But Jesus calls all of us to something deeper.
He calls us to Himself.
Remember the words of Jesus in Matthew 7:22–23.
Many will say to Him, "Lord, Lord," and appeal to prophecy, exorcisms, and mighty works performed in His name.
Yet Jesus warns that some will hear the dreadful words:
"I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity."
This passage is not teaching that spiritual gifts are inherently false.
It is teaching something far more frightening.
Religious activity—even activity that appears extraordinary—is not a substitute for truly belonging to Christ.
The question is not merely whether people are impressed by what you do.
The question is whether you know the Lord.
And whether your life is being brought under His authority.
You may have an unforgettable testimony.
You may have witnessed something you cannot explain.
You may be able to defend every detail of your denomination's position.
But have you repented of your sins?
Are you trusting in the crucified and risen Jesus?
Are you learning to love the people around you?
Are you submitting to the truth of Scripture?
Are you becoming more humble, more truthful, more merciful?
Because Galatians 5:22–23 describes the fruit of the Spirit as love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faithfulness, meekness, and self-control.
And although spiritual gifts and spiritual fruit are not the same thing, the fruit of the Spirit matters profoundly when evaluating spiritual life.
A person may claim to possess a remarkable gift.
But no claim of giftedness excuses a life of unrepentant cruelty.
No prophecy makes pride holy.
No tongue makes dishonesty acceptable.
No miracle gives anyone permission to exploit God's people.
And no theological position makes lovelessness a virtue.
Perhaps you came into this article expecting a simple verdict.
Yes, the gifts continue.
Or no, the gifts have ceased.
But Scripture is pressing us toward a larger and more searching question.
What are we doing with the Jesus whom the Holy Spirit came to glorify?
Here is where I stand in approaching this question from the biblical text.

I do not believe Scripture gives us sufficient grounds to declare that God is incapable of granting tongues or prophecy today, or that every modern claim must be false simply because the apostolic era has ended.

The language of 1 Corinthians 13, particularly its movement toward knowing fully and seeing face to face, provides a serious reason to question the claim that the completion of the biblical canon is the clearly stated moment when all such gifts ceased.

At the same time, Scripture gives us no permission to assume that every modern manifestation is genuine, that every believer must possess the same gift, or that contemporary prophecy carries authority equal to the inspired words of the apostles and prophets preserved in Scripture.
The safest biblical posture is neither reckless acceptance nor automatic dismissal.
It is humble openness to God's sovereign work, firm submission to the Scriptures, careful testing of claims, and unwavering devotion to Jesus Christ.
This is a continuationist-leaning conclusion, not a declaration that every faithful Christian must agree with it.
Faithful cessationist Christians offer serious biblical arguments, especially concerning the foundational role of the apostles and prophets and the final authority of Scripture.
They deserve a fair hearing.
But whichever position we hold, we must not make agreement on the continuation of every spiritual gift the test of whether someone belongs to Christ.
The Gospel is too precious to be displaced by that debate.
And now I want to speak to the person who has quietly felt spiritually inadequate.
You have been comparing your prayer life to someone else's.
You have been wondering why your hands don't tremble the way theirs do.
Why you haven't received a vision.
Why you don't speak in tongues.
Why God seems to answer other people's prayers with extraordinary stories while your own life feels painfully ordinary.
You get up early.
You work.
You struggle with bills.
You try to forgive.
You battle temptation.
You pray over your children.
You open your Bible when you're exhausted.
You keep trusting Jesus even when nothing spectacular happens.
And somewhere along the way, you started believing that your quiet faithfulness wasn't enough.
Please hear what Scripture actually says.
The Spirit distributes gifts according to His will.
The body has many members.
The eye cannot say to the hand, "I have no need of thee" (1 Corinthians 12:21).
And the parts that seem weaker are indispensable to the life of the body (1 Corinthians 12:22).
Your place in Christ's body is not determined by how impressive you appear.
The believer quietly caring for a sick parent may be demonstrating extraordinary Christlike love.
The Christian resisting a secret temptation may be fighting a battle no congregation will ever applaud.
The exhausted mother praying over her sleeping children may be exercising a faith that heaven sees even when nobody else does.
The wounded believer who chooses to forgive may be displaying the transforming grace of God.
And the person who continues trusting Christ through unanswered questions is not necessarily less spiritual than the person with a dramatic testimony.
Do not despise the ordinary means by which God shapes His people.
Prayer.
Scripture.
Repentance.
Worship.
Fellowship.
Service.
Faithfulness.
Love.
These are not consolation prizes for Christians who lack spectacular experiences.
They are central to the life of discipleship.
And to the person who believes God has genuinely worked through an extraordinary gift in your life, hear this with equal tenderness.
You do not need to exaggerate what happened to make God look powerful.
You do not need to defend every questionable manifestation to prove you believe in the Holy Spirit.
You do not need to turn your experience into a universal requirement for everyone else.
If God has entrusted you with a gift, use it with humility.
Submit it to Scripture.
Welcome wise examination.
Serve the Church.
Refuse personal glory.
And remember that the Giver is infinitely greater than the gift.
The Holy Spirit does not need your exaggeration.
Jesus does not need your performance.
And God's glory is not strengthened by claims that are untrue.
Sometimes the holiest words a believer can say are, "I believe God can do this, but I need to test whether this particular claim is true."
Sometimes the most courageous words are, "I was wrong."
And sometimes the most Christlike response is to embrace a brother or sister who disagrees with you while remaining faithful to your biblical convictions.
That is not compromise.
That is maturity.
And perhaps the deepest scandal in this entire conversation is that Christians can spend decades debating the gifts of the Spirit while neglecting the Gospel that brought them into God's family.
We argue over tongues while refusing to control our own tongues.
We debate prophecy while ignoring the clear commands of Scripture.
We pursue healing while withholding forgiveness.
We speak about revival while resisting repentance.
We seek signs of divine power while overlooking the cross, where the power and wisdom of God were displayed in a crucified Messiah.
But the cross is where our boasting dies.
The cross tells the charismatic believer, "Your experiences cannot save you."
The cross tells the cessationist believer, "Your theological precision cannot save you."
The cross tells the wounded believer, "Your suffering has not placed you beyond My grace."
And the cross tells every sinner, "You cannot redeem yourself."
Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, entered our broken world.
He lived without sin.
He welcomed the weary.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He healed the afflicted.
He proclaimed the Kingdom.
He was betrayed, mocked, condemned, and crucified.
And on that cross, He bore the penalty of sin as the righteous Savior of the unrighteous.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
This is not a spiritual manifestation competing for our attention.
This is the Gospel itself.
The foundation of Christian hope.
The message Paul declared to be of first importance in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
And it is through this Jesus that sinners receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
The greatest need of the human heart is not to have a more impressive testimony than the person beside us.
It is to be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
What good would it do to speak in every language on earth if your heart remained far from Him?
What good would it do to correctly predict tomorrow if you refused to surrender today?
What good would it do to win a thousand debates about spiritual gifts while rejecting the grace that alone can save you?
And what a beautiful thing it is when someone who once chased religious approval finally rests in Christ.
When someone manipulated by false spiritual authority discovers the gentleness of the true Shepherd.
When someone proud of spiritual experiences bows in repentance.
When someone proud of theological knowledge learns to love.
When someone who believed they were spiritually worthless discovers that they are welcomed by grace through faith in Jesus.
That is transformation.
That is redemption.
That is the story of scandal meeting grace.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because deception didn't matter.
Not because truth was optional.
But because Jesus Christ is mighty to save, forgive, restore, and transform those who turn to Him.
And maybe this is the moment you need to stop asking whether you have experienced enough to impress other Christians.
Maybe you need to ask whether you have surrendered your life to the Savior.
Maybe you need to repent of spiritual pride.
Maybe you need to repent of judging believers whose experiences differ from yours.
Maybe you need to walk away from a ministry that uses God's name to control people.
Maybe you need to stop using past disappointment as a reason to avoid prayer.
Maybe you need to open your Bible again, not to win an argument, but to hear the truth of the God who loves His people.
And maybe, for the first time in a long time, you need to pray something simple.

"Lord Jesus, I don't want to chase power and miss Your presence. I don't want to defend doctrine without love. I don't want to mistake emotion for truth, or fear for discernment. Forgive my pride. Heal what deception has wounded. Teach me to honor Your Word. Fill my life with the fruit of Your Spirit. Give me whatever gifts You desire, and help me use everything You give for Your glory. Above all, make me more like You. Amen."
If this article has exposed something you have been afraid to admit, you do not have to pretend.
Maybe you have felt rejected because you don't speak in tongues.
Maybe you have been wounded by a false prophecy.
Maybe you have been too quick to judge.
Maybe you have witnessed something you still cannot explain.
Or maybe your heart simply longs to know Jesus more deeply.

And if you are comfortable, tell us where you are in this journey. Do you believe the gifts continue, have they ceased, or are you still studying the Scriptures? Have you experienced something that changed your understanding?
You do not have to reveal painful details publicly. Your honesty can be as simple as "I'm still learning" or "Pray for me."
Let the conversation be marked by Scripture, humility, and love rather than accusations.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, don't ignore that thought.
Perhaps it is the friend who has been told they aren't spiritual enough.
Perhaps it is a family member who was hurt by a religious leader.
Perhaps it is someone who has become cynical about everything supernatural.
Or perhaps it is a believer who loves the gifts of the Spirit but needs a reminder that love, holiness, and biblical accountability must never be abandoned.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
Not because an algorithm can produce revival.
But because a thoughtful, Scripture-rooted conversation may reach someone who would never walk into a church or ask a pastor these questions.
Return to 1 Corinthians 12–14.
Read Acts 2.
Study Joel 2.
Examine 1 Thessalonians 5 and 1 John 4.
Don't simply remember what this article said.
Test it against Scripture.
That is how mature disciples grow.
Invite your family.
Your friends.
The Christian who is struggling.
The believer who has become lukewarm.
The seeker who is asking difficult questions.
Even the person who does not yet believe in Jesus.
There is room to hear the Gospel, wrestle honestly with Scripture, and discover why Christ remains our only Savior and ultimate hope.
And we want to do more than create posts that people read once and forget.
We want to help people become serious students of Scripture and faithful followers of Jesus.
These resources are part of our commitment to making biblical encouragement and discipleship accessible.
But sustaining and expanding this work requires real support.
Writing, research, resource development, distribution, and ongoing ministry efforts all involve time, labor, and expenses.
And this is where you can become more than a reader.
Scripture teaches us in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That means your decision must be free.
No pressure.
No guilt.
You can glorify God through generosity, but you cannot purchase His approval.
Jesus already paid the price of our redemption.
What we are inviting you into is not a transaction for spiritual favor.
It is an opportunity for partnership.
These products are simply practical resources and reminders that can encourage faith-filled living. They are not substitutes for the Bible, the local church, or genuine discipleship.
Pray for the ministry.
Save these Scriptures for deeper study.
Because the mission is not to build an audience that admires Gospel Warrior.
The mission is to point people to Jesus.
And when all the debates have ended, when every microphone has gone silent, when every earthly ministry has completed its work, one truth will remain.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
Our spiritual gifts will never be greater than Him.
Our experiences will never outrank His Word.
Our traditions will never replace His Gospel.
And our greatest hope will never rest in what we can do for God, but in what Jesus Christ has accomplished for sinners.
One day, faith will become sight.
We will no longer see dimly.
The questions that have troubled us will find their proper place before the glory of God.
And every redeemed voice will have one infinitely worthy object of worship.
Not the gift.
Not the experience.
Not the preacher.
Not the denomination.
The Lamb who was slain.
The Savior who rose.
The King who reigns forever.
So yes, study the gifts.
Ask the hard questions.
Test the claims.
Honor the Scriptures.
Pray with expectancy.
Exercise discernment.
Love the Church.
But never become so consumed with asking whether tongues and prophecy are still active that you neglect the far greater question of whether your own heart is surrendered to the living Christ.
Because the deepest evidence of grace is not that you have become impressive in the eyes of people.
It is that a sinner who once lived far from God is being transformed by the mercy of Jesus.
And when every extraordinary voice has fallen silent, the nail-scarred hands of Jesus will still be enough to tell you how deeply you are loved.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “TELL IT TO THE CHURCH”: THE WORDS OF JESUS THAT MANY CHRISTIANS QUOTE—BUT FEW ARE PREPARED TO OBEY
paragraphs: “TELL IT TO THE CHURCH”: THE WORDS OF JESUS THAT MANY CHRISTIANS QUOTE—BUT FEW ARE PREPARED TO OBEY

When a brother sins, when trust is shattered, and when silence begins to destroy what love was meant to protect, Matthew 18 reveals a difficult truth: Jesus never commanded His Church to cover up sin, weaponize correction, or abandon the wounded. He commanded something far more costly.
There is a kind of pain that only happens inside the Church.
It is not the pain of being rejected by strangers.
It is the pain of being wounded by people who know your prayers.
People who have heard you worship.
People who have called you brother. Sister. Family.
People who have stood beside you with their hands lifted toward heaven, only to leave you wondering how someone who speaks so beautifully about Jesus could treat another human being so cruelly.
And sometimes the wound goes even deeper.
You finally find the courage to speak.
You explain what happened.
You tell someone you trust.
And instead of asking whether you are safe, whether the truth has been established, or whether the wrong can be corrected, someone opens a Bible and says:
“Matthew 18.”
Three words.
And suddenly, the person who was wounded feels as though they are the one standing trial.
But there is another side to this story.
Somewhere, a Christian has sinned against someone they love.
They know what they did.
They have rehearsed excuses in their mind.
They have prayed for the guilt to disappear without ever making things right.
They still attend church. Still sing. Still serve. Still post Scriptures.
But there is a conversation they are avoiding.
An apology they have not offered.
A truth they have not confessed.
And every time Matthew 18 is mentioned, something inside them becomes uncomfortable.
Because deep down, they know.
Jesus is not merely speaking to the wounded.
He is also speaking to the one who caused the wound.

And perhaps the most frightening possibility is that both people can be sitting in the same congregation, listening to the same sermon, while carrying entirely different reasons to fear the words of Christ.
Now listen carefully.
What if the passage that has been used to silence wounded Christians was actually given to protect the holiness of Christ's people?
What if the passage that has been used to justify harsh public humiliation was actually designed to make restoration possible?
And what if the words “tell it to the church” reveal something much deeper than a procedure for resolving disagreements?
Something about the heart of Jesus.
Something about the seriousness of sin.
Something about the danger of pride.
And something about the kind of love that refuses to surrender a soul to destruction.
Because before Jesus ever said, “Tell it to the church,” He told a story about a sheep.
And unless we understand that sheep, we may completely misunderstand the Church.
In Matthew 18:12–14, Jesus describes a shepherd who has one hundred sheep. One wanders away, and the shepherd goes looking for the one that has strayed.
The point is not that the other ninety-nine have become worthless.
The point is that the wandering one has not become disposable.
Then Jesus says:
“Even so it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.” — Matthew 18:14, WEB
Read that again.
Before confrontation, there is concern.
Before discipline, there is a shepherd's heart.
Before the difficult conversation, there is a Savior who does not treat wandering souls as worthless.
This is the atmosphere in which Matthew 18:15–20 must be understood.
Not revenge.
Not institutional image management.
Not a competition to prove who is more righteous.
But a holy concern for truth, repentance, protection, and the recovery of a brother or sister whenever restoration is possible.
Then Jesus says something that confronts both our fear of conflict and our appetite for gossip.
“If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.” — Matthew 18:15, WEB
The Greek text contains a remarkable expression.
ἐκέρδησας τὸν ἀδελφόν σου
ekerdēsas ton adelphon sou
“You have gained your brother.”
The verb ἐκέρδησας comes from κερδαίνω (kerdainō), meaning to gain or win.
Jesus does not describe the goal as winning the argument.
He describes it as gaining the brother.
There is a difference.
A devastating difference.
One person confronts because they want someone humiliated.
Another confronts because they want the truth acknowledged, the wrong addressed, and a relationship restored if genuine repentance makes that possible.
One wants to say, “I told you so.”
The other longs to say, “Thank God we did not allow this sin to destroy us.”
That is not weakness.
That is love governed by truth.
But notice something equally important.
Jesus does not say, “Pretend nothing happened.”
He does not say, “Call evil good because you are supposed to forgive.”
He does not say, “Protect the reputation of the person who harmed you at the expense of justice.”
He says to address the wrong.
The Greek verb commonly translated “show him his fault” is ἔλεγξον (elenxon), from ἐλέγχω (elenchō).
It carries the sense of exposing, correcting, or bringing a wrong to light.
Not inventing accusations.
Not assuming guilt without evidence.
Not turning suspicion into certainty.
But bringing a genuine wrong into the light where it can be confronted truthfully.
And that matters because a Church that refuses to confront sin is not necessarily a loving Church.
Sometimes it is simply a frightened Church.
Frightened of uncomfortable conversations.
Frightened of losing influential people.
Frightened of financial consequences.
Frightened of discovering that someone admired has been living dishonestly.
Frightened of what will happen when the truth becomes impossible to ignore.
But Jesus did not die to create a community where appearances matter more than righteousness.
He died to redeem sinners and make a people holy.
There is also a textual detail worth understanding.

Some Greek manuscripts of Matthew 18:15 include the words εἰς σέ (eis se), meaning “against you,” while others omit them. That is why some Bible translations read, “If your brother sins against you,” while others read more broadly, “If your brother sins.”
This variation should not be hidden from readers.
It reminds us to interpret the passage carefully rather than building an entire doctrine upon a disputed phrase.

The immediate context certainly includes personal wrongdoing and relationships within the community of believers. Yet the wider New Testament also teaches that serious sin must be addressed appropriately, even when it is not merely a private offense against one individual.
And here is where many people misunderstand Jesus.
They turn the first step into an absolute rule that every injured person must privately confront every offender before seeking help.
But Matthew 18 was never intended to prohibit victims from seeking protection, reporting crimes, involving responsible authorities, or obtaining necessary support.
If someone is being abused, threatened, coerced, or placed in danger, they do not have to meet privately with the person harming them.
If a child has been harmed, the priority is protection, not arranging a private conversation with the alleged offender.
If there is a credible allegation of criminal conduct, reporting it to the appropriate authorities is not disobedience to Jesus.
Romans 13:1–4 recognizes the legitimate role of governing authorities in restraining wrongdoing.
Matthew 18 does not cancel that responsibility.
And when allegations concern a church leader, other biblical passages, including 1 Timothy 5:19–20, provide additional guidance about evidence, accountability, and public correction when warranted.
Biblical confrontation is not a weapon for forcing vulnerable people into unsafe situations.
It is a call to deal with sin faithfully.
Jesus never asked His people to confuse secrecy with holiness.
The first private conversation in Matthew 18 serves a meaningful purpose when it is appropriate and safe.
It prevents unnecessary public exposure.
It creates an opportunity for repentance without needless humiliation.
It protects against careless gossip.
It gives someone a chance to acknowledge wrong before an entire community becomes involved.
Imagine how many relationships could be spared unnecessary damage if Christians stopped discussing someone else's failure with ten people before speaking truthfully to the person concerned.
Imagine how many church divisions begin with a conversation that never should have happened.
A whisper after worship.
A screenshot forwarded to a friend.
A prayer request that is actually disguised gossip.
A private disagreement turned into a public campaign.
Someone says, “I am only telling you so you can pray.”
But sometimes what we call a prayer request is simply gossip wearing religious clothing.
And the Lord sees the difference.
Proverbs 16:28 warns that a whisperer separates close friends.
James 1:19 calls believers to be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.
The Bible does not treat words as harmless.
A reputation can be damaged in minutes.
A friendship can be fractured by half a story.
An entire congregation can become divided because people were more interested in choosing sides than discovering what was true.
And yet, the opposite mistake is just as dangerous.
Some people hear “go privately” and conclude that serious wrongdoing must remain hidden indefinitely.
No.
Privacy is not the same as concealment.
Discretion is not the same as complicity.
And forgiveness is not the same as pretending a person is safe when their behavior demonstrates otherwise.
If the person listens, Jesus says, you have gained your brother.
But what if they do not listen?
What if they deny what is established?
What if they refuse to acknowledge the wrong?
What if they continue causing harm?
Jesus continues:
“But if he doesn't listen, take one or two more with you, that at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.” — Matthew 18:16, WEB
The language recalls Deuteronomy 19:15, where the testimony of two or three witnesses is connected to establishing a matter.
The principle is not that Christians should recruit supporters who will automatically agree with them.
It is that accusations and responses should be handled with care, corroboration, and fairness.
A witness is not supposed to be a cheerleader.
A witness is supposed to help establish the truth.
This is why a faithful church should not be satisfied with hearing only the most influential person's version of events.
It should not assume the wealthiest donor is innocent.
It should not assume the longest-serving volunteer is always right.
It should not assume the person who cries most convincingly is necessarily telling the whole story.
It should not assume the quieter person is lying.
And it should never mistake someone's spiritual vocabulary for evidence of spiritual integrity.
Truth must matter more than status.
Evidence must matter more than popularity.
And justice must matter more than preserving the appearance of peace.
Because a congregation can look peaceful while people inside it are being crushed.
It can sing about freedom while silencing those who need help.
It can preach about holiness while protecting unrepentant wrongdoing.
It can talk about grace while demanding that the wounded bear consequences the offender refuses to face.
That is not the beautiful unity Jesus prayed for.
That is a counterfeit peace purchased with someone else's suffering.
Then comes the sentence that many Christians would rather avoid.
“If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly.” — Matthew 18:17, WEB
In the Greek:
εἰπὲ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ
eipe tē ekklēsia
“Tell it to the church.”
The noun ἐκκλησία (ekklēsia) refers to an assembly or congregation. In this context, it points to the community of believers.
This does not mean that every dispute should immediately become a public spectacle, a social-media post, or an announcement before a congregation.

The precise way a church responsibly involves its recognized leadership and, when necessary, its gathered membership will depend upon the nature of the matter and its biblical understanding of church governance.
But the central point is unmistakable.
When serious, established wrongdoing remains unresolved after appropriate efforts at correction, the matter cannot always remain a private dispute.
The community has responsibilities.
Not merely to the person who sinned.
Not merely to the person who was harmed.
But to the truth, to the holiness of the Church, and to the honor of Christ.
This is where the teaching becomes uncomfortable.
Because we live in a world that often treats correction as hatred.
Yet the Bible says:
“Faithful are the wounds of a friend; although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.” — Proverbs 27:6, WEB
A friend who tells you the truth may hurt your pride.
But a friend who flatters you while you destroy your life is not helping you.
There are moments when love speaks gently.
There are moments when love listens patiently.
And there are moments when love must say:
“This cannot continue.”
Not because love has disappeared.
But because love refuses to cooperate with destruction.
Think of the person who has been hiding an addiction while telling everyone they are fine.
Think of the husband or wife whose secret dishonesty is tearing apart a family.
Think of the church member who continually manipulates others but calls every correction persecution.
Think of the believer who has been confronted repeatedly, not over a difference of opinion or a harmless mistake, but over genuine wrongdoing they refuse to abandon.
At some point, silence stops being kindness.
At some point, avoidance becomes participation.
At some point, the fear of offending someone begins to outweigh the fear of dishonoring God.
But there is a warning here for those who enjoy confronting others.
If the possibility of church discipline excites you because you finally have an opportunity to expose someone you dislike, examine your heart.
If you secretly hope the person refuses to repent because their downfall would satisfy you, examine your heart.
If you use biblical language to humiliate someone rather than pursue truth and godliness, examine your heart.
Galatians 6:1 says that those who are spiritual should restore someone caught in a trespass in a spirit of gentleness, while watching themselves lest they also be tempted.
The word translated “restore” comes from καταρτίζω (katartizō), a verb associated with putting something into proper condition or order.
Restoration is not casual approval of sin.
But neither is it the delight of watching another person collapse.
It is a sober, humble pursuit of what is right.
Because the person being corrected is not the only sinner in the room.
Every one of us stands in need of mercy.
Every one of us has blind spots.
Every one of us has said something we wish we could take back.
Every one of us has failed to love perfectly.
And if we forget that while confronting someone else, our own pride may become another sin demanding repentance.
Then Jesus says something even harder.
“And if he refuses to hear the assembly also, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector.” — Matthew 18:17, WEB
Those words can sound devastating.
And they are serious.
Within the covenant community, persistent refusal to repent may eventually require the Church to stop treating someone as a member in good standing.
Other passages, including 1 Corinthians 5:1–13 and Titus 3:10–11, reinforce the reality that the Church must sometimes draw boundaries in response to grave and persistent wrongdoing.
But notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not command hatred.
He does not authorize cruelty.
He does not give believers permission to threaten, harass, mock, or dehumanize anyone.
And here is the detail that should make us stop.
How did Jesus treat tax collectors?
He called Matthew, a tax collector, to follow Him.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He entered the home of Zacchaeus, whose encounter with Jesus was accompanied by a transformed response to his wrongdoing.
Jesus did not pretend sin was harmless.
But He did not declare sinners beyond the reach of grace.
So when Matthew 18 describes treating an unrepentant person as a Gentile or tax collector, it must be understood alongside the rest of Scripture.
The person may no longer be affirmed as a faithful member of the believing community.
But that does not mean they cease to be a human being worthy of truthful witness, appropriate compassion, and a genuine call to repentance.
Church discipline is not a declaration that someone is beyond salvation.
It is a recognition that persistent, unrepentant conduct cannot simply be affirmed as Christian faithfulness.
And when repentance becomes evident, the Church must not become so attached to punishment that it forgets the possibility of restoration.
Second Corinthians 2:6–8 describes a situation in which Paul urges the believers to forgive, comfort, and reaffirm love toward a person who had received sufficient correction.
Christians debate the precise relationship of that passage to the case in 1 Corinthians 5, but its instruction about reaffirming love is unmistakable.
Correction must never become an excuse for endless cruelty.
And restoration must never be reduced to a rushed declaration that everything is normal again.
Because repentance has fruit.
John the Baptist said:
“Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance!” — Matthew 3:8, WEB
In Greek, the word for repentance is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It speaks of a change of mind and heart that turns a person away from sin toward God.
It is not merely embarrassment at being discovered.
It is not simply sadness over consequences.
It is not an emotional performance designed to regain trust without changing behavior.
True repentance involves acknowledging wrong, turning from it, and pursuing obedience.
Where harm has occurred, repentance may also require restitution, transparency, accountability, and acceptance of consequences.
Zacchaeus did not merely tell Jesus that he felt sorry.
He responded with concrete commitments to generosity and restitution in Luke 19:8.
And that distinction matters.
Because someone can cry during an apology and still refuse to change.
Someone can quote Scripture while continuing to manipulate others.
Someone can say, “God has forgiven me,” while refusing to take responsibility for the damage they caused.
God's forgiveness is not a license to evade accountability.
And the fact that a victim chooses to forgive does not automatically mean trust has been rebuilt.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are related, but they are not identical.
Forgiveness does not require pretending that the danger has ended.
Reconciliation requires truth, and restored trust ordinarily requires credible evidence of change over time.
A person may be forgiven and still face legal consequences.
A leader may repent and still be unqualified to return to leadership.
A relationship may be released from bitterness without becoming safe to resume.
That is not a failure of grace.
It is an acknowledgment that grace does not abolish wisdom.
Now consider the words that follow.
“Most certainly I tell you, whatever things you bind on earth will have been bound in heaven, and whatever things you release on earth will have been released in heaven.” — Matthew 18:18, WEB
The Greek includes the expressions ἔσται δεδεμένα (estai dedemena) and ἔσται λελυμένα (estai lelymena).
These are future forms of “to be” combined with perfect passive participles, often understood as emphasizing a state already established.
The passage concerns the serious responsibility of the Church to make judgments consistent with God's revealed will.
It does not give a congregation the power to force heaven to approve whatever it decides.
A church cannot turn injustice into righteousness by voting for it.
A pastor cannot transform personal preference into divine law by declaring it from a pulpit.
A leadership team cannot call something holy merely because its members agree.
The Church is accountable to Christ.
Not the other way around.
And that should make every person exercising spiritual authority tremble with humility.
Because spiritual authority is never permission to become spiritually unaccountable.
Jesus continues with His teaching about agreement in prayer and then says:
“For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there I am in the middle of them.” — Matthew 18:20, WEB
Many Christians know that verse.
We quote it during small prayer meetings.
We use it when attendance is low.
We remind ourselves that Jesus is present even when only a few believers gather.
That encouragement is consistent with the broader truth of Christ's presence with His people.
But in Matthew 18, the immediate context is not simply the size of a prayer gathering.
It is the solemn responsibility of believers dealing with sin, truth, agreement, and accountability under Christ's authority.
