Because the goal is not to become fearless through sheer determination.
The goal is to become increasingly faithful through dependence on Jesus.
Now consider another encounter.
In Mark 10, a wealthy man came running to Jesus.
He knelt and asked what he must do to inherit eternal life.
He appeared sincere.
Respectful.
Religious.
Morally serious.
He was exactly the kind of person many religious communities would be delighted to welcome.
And then Jesus confronted the thing that held his heart.
Mark 10:21 contains one of the most revealing statements in the entire account.
"Then Jesus beholding him loved him..."
Loved him.
Before Jesus challenged him.
Before the man walked away.
Before the uncomfortable conversation unfolded.
Jesus loved him.
And because Jesus loved him, He did not conceal the truth about the man's attachment to wealth.
He called him to relinquish what stood between him and wholehearted discipleship.
The man went away grieving because he had great possessions.
Think about what Jesus did not do.
He did not run after the man and announce that surrender no longer mattered.
He did not revise His teaching to make the invitation more attractive.
He did not treat the man's sorrow as proof that He had spoken without love.
He loved him.
He told him the truth.
And He allowed the man to respond.
There is an important distinction here.
Jesus' specific instruction to this man must be understood within the encounter; it is not a blanket declaration that every believer must sell every possession to be saved.
But the account exposes a universal spiritual danger.
Anything we treasure more than Christ can become a rival to our obedience.
For that man, wealth was the revealing issue.
For someone else, it might be sexual sin.
For another, bitterness.
For another, status.
For another, control.
And for some of us, the thing we are most reluctant to surrender is the approval of other people.
We want Jesus.
But we also want everyone to approve of our decision to follow Him.
We want biblical conviction.
But we don't want anyone to think we're narrow-minded.
We want to speak about salvation.
But we would rather avoid the subjects of sin, judgment, repentance, and the necessity of faith in Christ.
We want the cross.
But we would prefer a cross that never causes anyone to question the direction of their life.
And perhaps that is why the words of Jesus in Luke 9:23 remain so challenging.
"If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." (KJV)
Daily.
Not merely when Christianity is socially acceptable.
Not merely when faith costs us nothing.
Not merely when the people around us agree.
Daily.
Yet we must not turn this into a demand for constant conflict.
The New Testament also instructs believers to pursue peace.
Romans 12:18 says, "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men."
And 1 Peter 3:15 teaches us to be prepared to explain our hope with meekness and fear—understood in context as gentleness and reverence.
The Christian calling is not to seek offense.
It is to remain faithful even when faithfulness is unwelcome.
Sometimes that means speaking.
Sometimes it means listening carefully before speaking.
Sometimes it means asking a thoughtful question.
Sometimes it means admitting that we were wrong.
Sometimes it means apologizing for the way we communicated something true.
And sometimes it means accepting that even the gentlest explanation of the Gospel will not be received.
We cannot control every response.
We are responsible for faithfulness, not for forcing someone to believe.
The Gospel itself confronts human pride.
In 1 Corinthians 1:23, Paul says that Christ crucified was a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles.
The Greek word σκάνδαλον (skandalon) carries the sense of a stumbling block or cause of offense.
It is a striking word.
The cross was not merely an inspiring religious symbol in the first century.
Crucifixion was associated with shame, suffering, and Roman execution.
To proclaim a crucified Messiah challenged many expectations about power, victory, and salvation.
Yet Paul did not replace the crucified Christ with a more socially appealing message.
He proclaimed Jesus Christ crucified.
Because what appeared foolish to the world was central to God's saving work.
Here is the scandal at the heart of grace.
The sinless Son of God was crucified.
The One who deserved honor endured shame.
The One who committed no sin bore our sins in His body on the tree, as 1 Peter 2:24 teaches.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again, according to the Scriptures, as Paul summarizes in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
This is not a message about how impressive Christians are.
It is a message about what Jesus has done.
We were not rescued by our ability to appear righteous.
We were rescued through the death and resurrection of Christ.
And because He lives, forgiveness and new life are proclaimed in His name.
That is why we cannot afford to misrepresent the Gospel.
If we remove sin, we obscure why forgiveness is needed.
If we remove the cross, we obscure the cost of redemption.
If we remove the resurrection, we abandon the victorious foundation of Christian hope.
If we remove repentance and faith, we obscure the response to which the Gospel calls us.
If we remove grace, we turn Christianity into a crushing attempt at self-salvation.
If we remove the lordship of Christ, we reduce discipleship to religious decoration.
The Gospel must remain the Gospel.
Not because we enjoy difficult conversations.
But because Jesus is worthy of being represented truthfully.
And because the people we love deserve to hear who He truly is.
Maybe this is where you need to stop pretending.
Perhaps you are a Christian who has been living two different lives.
One at church.
Another at work.
One in your Bible study.
Another in your private conversations.
One in your social media posts.
Another when nobody who knows you from church is watching.
You believe in Jesus.
But you have been carefully managing how much of your faith the world is allowed to see.
Not because you hate Him.
But because you fear rejection.
You remember what happened the last time you spoke openly.
Someone mocked you.
Someone called you self-righteous.
Someone you respected became distant.
And you decided that being a quiet Christian was safer.
There may have been genuine wounds behind that decision.
And Jesus is not indifferent to them.
But perhaps today He is inviting you to trust Him with the consequences of faithful obedience.
Not to become reckless.
Not to turn every conversation into a sermon.
Not to treat people as projects.
But to stop being ashamed of the Savior who was not ashamed to bear your sin.
Paul wrote in Romans 1:16:
"For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth..." (KJV)
The Greek expression οὐ γὰρ ἐπαισχύνομαι (ou gar epaischynomai) means "for I am not ashamed."
Paul's confidence was not rooted in his personal eloquence.
It was rooted in the Gospel's divine power.
And this matters because some of us are exhausted from trying to make Christianity appealing through our own personalities.
We think we need the perfect argument.
The perfect words.
The perfect delivery.
The perfect moment.
But salvation belongs to the Lord.
Our responsibility is to bear truthful witness, pray, love people, and remain faithful.
We cannot regenerate a human heart.
We cannot argue someone into the kingdom through pressure.
We cannot manufacture repentance through guilt.
And we certainly cannot replace the work of the Holy Spirit with emotional manipulation.
But we can tell the truth.
We can live what we proclaim.
We can confess our own sins instead of pretending to be spiritually flawless.
We can extend patience to people who struggle.
We can refuse to compromise Scripture merely to preserve our reputation.
And we can trust God with what happens next.
Perhaps the most difficult person to confront with the truth is not your unbelieving friend.
Perhaps it is yourself.
Because it is possible to defend biblical morality publicly while privately resisting the commands of Jesus.
It is possible to condemn compromise in others while excusing our own.
It is possible to demand repentance from the world while refusing to forgive someone who hurt us.
It is possible to speak loudly about holiness while neglecting humility, mercy, justice, and love.
And it is possible to become so concerned with the errors of other Christians that we stop examining our own hearts.
Jesus warned against hypocrisy in Matthew 7:3–5.
Before attempting to remove the speck from our brother's eye, we must address the beam in our own.
That does not mean Christians must become sinless before offering correction.
It means correction should come from humility, repentance, and honest self-examination.
The Gospel confronts the preacher before it confronts the audience.
It confronts the writer before it confronts the reader.
It confronts me before I dare use it to challenge you.
And if this article has exposed something uncomfortable in your heart, perhaps that discomfort is not something to run from.
Bring it before God.
Ask Him whether your desire to be accepted has begun to shape your obedience.
Ask Him whether your commitment to truth has become separated from compassion.
Ask Him whether you have been using grace to excuse sin.
Ask Him whether you have been using holiness to excuse harshness.
Ask Him to make you more like Jesus.
Because the answer to a compromised Gospel is not a cruel Gospel.
The answer is the true Gospel.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ reigning.
Christ calling sinners to repentance and faith.
Christ forgiving those who come to Him.
Christ transforming His people through grace.
And Christ promising to return.
That is the message worth living for.
And yes, worth being misunderstood for.
But before we finish, I want you to imagine something.
Imagine standing before Jesus.
Not before your followers.
Not before your critics.
Not before your relatives who thought you were too religious.
Not before the people whose approval you spent years trying to earn.
Before Jesus.
The One who knew every secret compromise.
Every fearful silence.
Every act of courage.
Every careless word.
Every hidden motive.
Every time you spoke truth with compassion.
Every time you used truth as an excuse to wound.
Every time you chose obedience when nobody applauded.
And every time you needed His mercy again.
What will matter most in that moment?
The number of people who liked you?
The number of arguments you won?
The number of people who never felt uncomfortable around you?
Or whether your life was surrendered to the Savior who gave Himself for you?
We should be careful not to invent a conversation that Scripture does not record.
But Scripture does tell us that believers will give an account to God, as Romans 14:12 teaches.
And it calls us to live in a manner worthy of the Gospel.
So perhaps the question we need to carry into tomorrow is not simply, "Will people be offended if I speak?"
Perhaps it is this:
"Will I represent Jesus faithfully, even when doing so costs me the approval I have been trying so desperately to protect?"
If the answer exposes fear, do not despair.
Remember Peter.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that failure is not beyond the reach of Christ's forgiveness.
And remember that courage is not the absence of trembling.
Sometimes courage is a trembling voice telling the truth with love.
Sometimes it is a quiet apology.
Sometimes it is refusing to laugh along.
Sometimes it is gently telling someone, "I love you too much to pretend that Jesus never spoke about this."
Sometimes it is choosing not to publish an angry response because your pride, not the Holy Spirit, is driving your words.
And sometimes it is simply saying:
"Lord Jesus, I have been more concerned about what people think of me than whether I am faithfully representing You. Please forgive me. Teach me to love people without compromising Your truth."
That prayer may be the beginning of something beautiful.
Not a louder version of your old self.
A more surrendered one.
A Christian whose courage is softened by compassion.
Whose compassion is strengthened by conviction.
Whose confidence rests in Scripture.
Whose identity rests in Christ.
And whose deepest desire is not to be celebrated by the world, but to be faithful to the Lord.
This is what Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim.
Not a Christianity built around outrage.
Not a faith designed to entertain people while leaving their souls untouched.
Not a message that uses fear, guilt, or shame to force people into religious performance.
But the unchanging Gospel of Jesus Christ—His holiness, His mercy, His cross, His resurrection, His call to repentance, and His power to redeem lives that once seemed beyond hope.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And if this message has touched a place in your heart that you have kept hidden, I want to invite you to do something more meaningful than simply reacting to an article.
Be honest before God.
You don't have to expose private details publicly.
You don't have to perform your repentance for an audience.
Not because a comment earns God's favor.
It doesn't.
But because sometimes a few sincere words can open the door to prayer, encouragement, accountability, and a conversation someone else desperately needs.
Perhaps someone who has been hiding behind religious appearances will finally find the courage to seek help.
Perhaps someone who has been wounded by harsh Christianity will see that biblical conviction and genuine compassion can exist together.
And perhaps your testimony will remind another person that the grace of Jesus is still powerful enough to restore a fallen disciple.
If someone came to mind while you were reading, consider sharing this article with them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to win an argument.
Not to publicly expose their struggles.
There is room here for questions.
There is room for honest struggles.
There is room for those who are learning, those who have fallen, and those who are trying to find their way back to the truth.
But we will never pretend that the answer to the human condition is anything less than Jesus Christ.
And if you believe this ministry is worth helping sustain, I want to invite you into something deeper.

Not merely as someone who enjoys Christian content, but as someone who wants to participate in the continued work of making Scripture-centered teaching, encouragement, and discipleship resources available to more people.
Every article takes time to study, write, examine, and prepare.
Every resource represents an opportunity to encourage a struggling believer, help someone understand Scripture, or introduce a searching soul to the message of Christ.
But let us be clear about something important.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing and cheerful, not forced by guilt or pressure.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us, God loves a cheerful giver.

You can glorify Him by obeying His Word, loving your family, serving your church, helping those in need, praying for others, sharing the Gospel, and living faithfully in the ordinary places where He has put you.
We want those resources to continue helping people learn, pray, study, heal, and mature in faith.
Those items are simply expressions of gratitude and opportunities to carry encouraging messages into everyday life.
They are not the Gospel.
They do not make anyone more holy.
They do not purchase spiritual blessings.
Jesus Christ remains the treasure.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read, learn, pray, share, and grow.
You can still encourage a struggling Christian, pray for a family member, or point a searching friend toward the Scriptures.
And no financial contribution can ever replace the saving work of Jesus Christ.
We are simply grateful for every person who helps the message reach farther, whether through prayer, encouragement, sharing, practical service, or voluntary financial support.
Because the mission is bigger than a page.
Bigger than a platform.
Bigger than a writer.
Bigger than any one ministry.
It is about making much of Jesus.
And that brings us back to the question that started everything.
Are we more afraid of offending people than we are of misrepresenting the Gospel?
Maybe today the answer has been uncomfortable.
Maybe you recognized your own silence.
Maybe you recognized your own harshness.
Maybe you realized you have been more concerned with defending your image than reflecting Christ.
Maybe you have been calling compromise compassion.
Or calling cruelty courage.
But the beautiful news is that Jesus does not merely expose what is wrong.
He calls us to Himself.
He forgives.
He restores.
He teaches.
He transforms.
The same Lord who restored Peter can restore a believer who has lost their courage.
The same Savior who welcomed sinners can teach us to welcome people without denying the truth.
The same Christ who confronted hypocrisy can purify our motives.
And the same risen King who commissioned His disciples continues to be worthy of faithful witness today.
So speak the truth.
But let your voice carry the tenderness of someone who knows what it means to be forgiven.
Stand firm.
But never forget that you stand only by grace.
Refuse to distort Scripture.
But be willing to admit when you have misunderstood it.
Love people deeply.
But do not confuse love with the refusal to tell them what Jesus actually said.
And when fear whispers that it would be easier to remain silent, remember the One who endured the cross for you.
You do not need to become everyone's enemy to be faithful to Jesus.
But you must be willing to follow Jesus even when not everyone approves.
Because the goal was never to make people admire our courage.
The goal is to help people see our Savior.
One day, the applause you were afraid to lose will be silent—but the truth about Jesus will still matter.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PRINCIPALITIES AND POWERS: THE INVISIBLE WAR PAUL WARNED YOU ABOUT—AND WHY SATAN DOESN’T WANT YOU TO UNDERSTAND EPHESIANS 6
paragraphs: PRINCIPALITIES AND POWERS: THE INVISIBLE WAR PAUL WARNED YOU ABOUT—AND WHY SATAN DOESN’T WANT YOU TO UNDERSTAND EPHESIANS 6

Not every battle you are fighting began with another person. Not every wound is merely physical. And not every enemy can be seen. But before you blame the devil for everything going wrong in your life, you need to understand what Paul actually meant when he said, “We wrestle not against flesh and blood.” Because the truth is far more sobering—and far more hopeful—than you may have been taught.
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot fix.
You know what it feels like.
You wake up in the morning, reach for your phone, and before your feet even touch the floor, your mind is already fighting.
Yesterday's mistakes.
Tomorrow's uncertainties.
The temptation you promised God you would never return to.
The conversation that keeps replaying in your head.
The bitterness you thought you had forgiven.
The secret nobody at church knows about.
And somewhere beneath all that noise is a quiet, frightening question.
Why am I still struggling like this when I genuinely love Jesus?
You pray.
You read Scripture.
You worship.
You try to do better.

Yet some days, it feels as though something is pressing against your soul, trying to convince you that your faith is useless, your repentance is meaningless, and your future will never be different from your past.
Maybe you've even wondered whether God has abandoned you.
But what if the battle is not evidence that God has abandoned you?
What if Scripture has been telling us all along that following Jesus does not mean the absence of conflict?
And what if the most dangerous thing about spiritual warfare is not merely that evil exists—but that Christians can misunderstand the battle so badly that they begin fighting the wrong enemy?
That is where the apostle Paul takes us.
Not into a fantasy world where every inconvenience is a demon.
Not into a life dominated by fear of invisible beings.

But into a breathtaking revelation about the powers of darkness, the authority of Jesus Christ, and the kind of strength that can keep a wounded believer standing when everything around them is shaking.
Listen carefully to what Paul wrote:

“For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.” — Ephesians 6:12, KJV
Read that again.
We wrestle not against flesh and blood.
Paul did not say that human beings never hurt us.
He did not say that injustice, abuse, betrayal, corruption, or persecution are imaginary.
He was saying something more profound.
Behind the visible conflicts of a fallen world, there is a spiritual dimension of evil that cannot be defeated by treating other human beings as our ultimate enemies.
And that changes everything.
Because the person who betrayed you is not beyond the reach of God's grace.
The family member who wounded you is not the final source of all evil.
The unbeliever who mocks your faith is not someone you have been commanded to hate.
Even the person who has made your life difficult is still a human being made in God's image.
You may need boundaries. You may need justice. You may need to confront wrongdoing or remove yourself from danger.
But you are not called to surrender your heart to hatred.
Paul is warning us that there is a greater battle than the argument happening in front of us.
And to understand that battle, we must understand his words.
When Paul wrote Ephesians, he wrote in Greek.
The phrase translated “principalities” is ἀρχάς (archas), the accusative plural of archē.
The word can refer to beginnings, rulers, or authorities, depending on its context.
Here, it refers to ruling powers or authorities within the spiritual opposition Paul is describing.
The word translated “powers” is ἐξουσίας (exousias), from exousia, meaning authority, right, or delegated power.
These words are important because Paul was not simply describing spooky figures hiding in dark corners.
He was describing a real and organized opposition to God's purposes, using language associated with rule, authority, and dominion.
Then he continues with an even more striking expression:
πρὸς τοὺς κοσμοκράτορας τοῦ σκότους τούτου
pros tous kosmokratoras tou skotous toutou
Against the world-rulers of this darkness.
The unusual Greek word kosmokratoras carries the idea of rulers exercising dominion over the world-order associated here with darkness.
But we must be careful.
Paul is not teaching that Satan owns the universe or possesses authority equal to God.
The devil is not God's opposite in power.
God has no equal.
Paul is describing the influence of evil within the present fallen order—not declaring that darkness is sovereign over creation.
Then comes the final expression:
πρὸς τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις
pros ta pneumatika tēs ponērias en tois epouraniois
Against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.
Notice what Paul is doing.
He is directing the attention of believers beyond merely human conflict toward spiritual opposition.
Yet he does not provide a detailed chart of demonic ranks.
He does not tell Christians to memorize the names of territorial spirits.
He does not command believers to spend their lives investigating invisible hierarchies.
Scripture does not give us enough information to build a complete organizational diagram of the demonic realm from this verse.
And we should never pretend to know more than God has revealed.
Paul's purpose is not to make us fascinated with demons.
His purpose is to make us faithful to Christ.
That distinction matters more than many Christians realize.
Because it is possible to talk about Satan constantly while speaking very little about Jesus.

It is possible to become so obsessed with spiritual warfare that every sickness becomes a curse, every disagreement becomes a demonic attack, and every difficult season becomes evidence that some invisible enemy has gained control.
But Paul never tells believers to live that way.
He begins his instructions with a command that is often overlooked.
“Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might.” — Ephesians 6:10, KJV
Not strong in your ability to identify demons.
Not strong in your volume when you pray.
Not strong in your knowledge of hidden spiritual mysteries.
Strong in the Lord.
The Greek expression is ἐνδυναμοῦσθε ἐν κυρίῳ (endynamousthe en kyriō).
It means, in this context, to be strengthened in the Lord.
The command points believers toward strength found in their relationship with Christ and dependence upon His mighty power.
And perhaps this is exactly where some of us need to stop pretending.
Because you have been trying to fight battles that you were never meant to fight in your own strength.
You have been carrying guilt as though suffering enough could purchase forgiveness.
You have been trying to defeat temptation through promises you repeatedly break.
You have been fighting resentment with forced smiles.
You have been trying to heal wounds by refusing to acknowledge that they exist.
And then, when you fall, you assume that Jesus must be disgusted with you.
But the Gospel tells a different story.
The Gospel says that our hope does not begin with how strong we are.
It begins with what Christ has accomplished.
And to see that clearly, we must go back to an earlier chapter of the same letter.
Paul writes that God raised Christ from the dead and seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly places:
“Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this world, but also in that which is to come.” — Ephesians 1:21, KJV
There it is again.
Principality.
Power.
Dominion.
But this time, the emphasis is not on the enemy.
It is on the exalted Christ.
Jesus is above them all.
Not struggling to become victorious.
Not anxiously waiting to discover whether darkness will defeat Him.
Not negotiating with the powers of evil over who possesses ultimate authority.
He is enthroned above every rule and authority.
The same letter that warns us about spiritual opposition begins by declaring the supremacy of Jesus Christ over every power.
That is not a coincidence.
That is the foundation of Paul's entire teaching about spiritual warfare.
And it gets even more beautiful.
In Ephesians 2, Paul describes humanity's former condition apart from Christ.
He speaks of people walking according to the course of this world, under the influence of the ruler of the authority of the air, and living in disobedience.
But he does not stop there.
Two words interrupt the darkness.
“But God.”
“But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us...” — Ephesians 2:4, KJV
Those two words carry enough hope to reach into the deepest scandal of your life.
But God.
You were lost.
But God.
You were enslaved to sin.
But God.
You had no righteousness of your own to offer Him.
But God.
You had a history that you could not undo.
But God.
And because of His mercy, Paul says that God made us alive together with Christ.
Not because we earned resurrection.
Not because we finally became respectable.
Not because we successfully hid everything shameful about ourselves.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
Do you see the connection?
Paul does not teach spiritual warfare as a separate fascination disconnected from salvation.
He places it within the great story of God's redemption.
The same Christ who rescues sinners is the Christ who strengthens His people against evil.
The same grace that saves us is the grace that teaches us to stand.
And this is where the enemy's accusations become so cruel.
Because one of the most painful battles a believer can experience is the battle over identity.
You know what you did.
You know what you said.
You remember the choices that nearly destroyed your marriage, your family, your reputation, or your relationship with God.
Maybe nobody else knows.
Maybe you have spent years carrying the consequences.
Maybe you still remember the night you crossed a line you swore you would never cross.
And sometimes the memory comes back without warning.
In the middle of worship.
During prayer.
When you are finally beginning to feel peace.
A thought rises:
Who do you think you are?
After what you did?
You think God really wants you?
Now, not every condemning thought is necessarily a direct demonic communication. Human memory, guilt, trauma, temptation, and patterns of thinking also matter.
But Scripture does identify Satan as an accuser.
Revelation 12:10 calls him the accuser of God's people.
And this accusation is answered not by pretending sin is harmless, but by the victory of Christ.
Because the Gospel never says your sin was insignificant.
It says Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
The cross is not God overlooking evil.
It is the place where the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Repentance is not denial.
Forgiveness is not permission to continue harming others.
Grace is not the cancellation of accountability.
But neither is your worst moment the final authority over your identity when you belong to Jesus Christ.
Paul writes:
The Greek word translated “redemption” is ἀπολύτρωσιν (apolytrōsin).
It speaks of release or liberation, a term associated with redemption.
In Ephesians 1:7, Paul connects this redemption directly with the blood of Christ and the forgiveness of sins.
You cannot purchase that redemption with religious performance.
You cannot earn it by punishing yourself emotionally for the rest of your life.
And no spiritual power can overturn what God has accomplished through His Son.
This does not mean a Christian will never struggle again.
It means the struggle takes place under the lordship of a victorious Savior.
And now Paul's command in Ephesians 6 begins to make sense.
“Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.” — Ephesians 6:11, KJV
The word translated “wiles” is μεθοδείας (methodeias).
It refers to schemes or crafty methods.
Paul uses the same Greek noun in Ephesians 4:14 when warning against the craftiness of deception.
That connection is worth noticing.
Because the enemy's schemes are not limited to dramatic displays of evil.
Deception matters.
False teaching matters.
Distorted desires matter.
A lie believed long enough can reshape the way a person lives.
Consider how temptation often works.
It rarely begins by announcing the full cost.
It begins with a suggestion.
You deserve this.
Just this once.
Nobody will find out.
You can repent afterward.
God understands.
And when the sin has done its damage, the message changes.
You are disgusting.
You will never change.
God is finished with you.
First, sin is made to look harmless.
Then grace is made to look impossible.
That is a devastating pattern of deception.
And whether we are confronting spiritual temptation, our own sinful desires, or the pressures of a broken world, the answer is not to negotiate with lies.
It is to return to the truth of God.
This is why Paul describes the armor of God in terms of truth, righteousness, readiness associated with the Gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the Word of God, and prayer.
These are not magical objects.
They are not formulas for controlling spiritual forces.
They describe the resources God provides for His people to remain faithful.
Think about the first piece.
“Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth...” — Ephesians 6:14, KJV
Truth.
Not speculation.
Not fear.
Not rumors about demons.
Truth.
The truth of God's character.
The truth of His Word.
The truth of what Christ has accomplished.
The truth about our sin and our need for repentance.
The truth about the forgiveness available through Jesus.
The truth that we do not need to invent a false version of ourselves to be loved by God.
Some of you are exhausted because you have been trying to maintain an image.
At church, you are the strong one.
At home, you are falling apart.
Online, you post verses about peace.
At night, you cry because your heart is full of anxiety.
People call you faithful.
But privately, you feel like a fraud.
And you have become so accustomed to saying, “I'm okay,” that you no longer know how to tell someone the truth.
But listen.
God does not ask you to defeat darkness by becoming a better actor.
He calls you to walk in the light.
That may mean confessing sin.
It may mean asking someone to pray with you.
It may mean seeking wise pastoral counsel.
It may mean receiving professional help for emotional or psychological suffering.
It may mean admitting that you need protection from someone who has been harming you.
None of those things makes you less spiritual.
Truth is not the enemy of faith.
And a church that understands spiritual warfare should never make suffering people afraid to seek appropriate care.
Then Paul speaks of the breastplate of righteousness.
And we must remember the larger message of Ephesians.
Our standing before God is rooted in His saving grace through Christ, not in our ability to make ourselves righteous.
Yet the life of a redeemed believer must also reflect that grace through genuine obedience.
God does not save us by good works.
He saves us for good works.
Ephesians 2:10 says we are created in Christ Jesus unto good works.
So when temptation invites you back into darkness, remember that grace is not merely the forgiveness of your past.
Grace also calls you into a transformed way of living.
You do not have to keep feeding the sin that once enslaved you.
You can confess.
You can turn away.
You can seek accountability.
You can remove access to the things that repeatedly lead you into temptation.
And when you stumble, you can return to Christ in repentance rather than running deeper into secrecy.
This is not effortless.
Sometimes obedience feels like losing something you desperately want.
Sometimes forgiveness requires surrendering the fantasy of revenge.
Sometimes faithfulness means walking away from a relationship you wanted to keep.
Sometimes repentance means making restitution and accepting consequences.
But the call of Jesus is not to decorate the old life with religious language.
It is to follow Him.
And following Him changes how we fight.
Paul speaks next about having our feet prepared with the Gospel of peace.
Peace.
What an unexpected word in a passage about warfare.
Yet it fits the whole letter.
In Ephesians 2:14, Paul declares concerning Christ:
“For he is our peace...”
He is speaking particularly about how Christ has broken down the dividing wall between Jews and Gentiles, creating one reconciled people through His cross.
That context matters.
Because one of the great works of darkness is division.
Hatred.
Hostility.
Pride.
The conviction that certain people are beyond the reach of mercy.
But Jesus came to reconcile sinners to God and to create peace among those who belong to Him.
So how tragic would it be if Christians used Ephesians 6 as an excuse to hate the very people they are called to love?
Your battle is not against flesh and blood.
That includes the people who disagree with you.
That includes the people who do not yet believe.
That includes the family member who has wandered far from God.
You may confront lies without despising the person deceived by them.
You may oppose injustice without becoming consumed by vengeance.
You may defend the truth without abandoning the character of Christ.
The Gospel does not call us to become cruel in the name of spiritual warfare.
It calls us to stand firm in a world that desperately needs the truth and love of Jesus.
Then Paul writes:
Imagine those flaming arrows.
Fear.
Doubt.
Temptation.
Accusation.
Despair.
The sudden thought that God cannot be trusted.
The whisper that obedience is pointless.
The crushing belief that your prayers no longer matter.
Faith does not mean pretending those arrows are not painful.
Faith means entrusting yourself to the God who remains faithful when your emotions are trembling.
Sometimes faith sounds triumphant.
Sometimes faith sounds like a broken person whispering:
Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.
Those words come from Mark 9:24.
And they remind us that a person can bring an imperfect, struggling faith to Jesus.
You do not need to manufacture an impressive spiritual performance before approaching Him.
You need Him.
Perhaps tonight your faith feels smaller than it did five years ago.
Perhaps grief has shaken you.
Perhaps you prayed for someone who died.
Perhaps you believed your marriage would survive, but it did not.
Perhaps you have begged God for healing, and the pain remains.
I will not insult your suffering by promising that every hardship will disappear if you simply believe hard enough.
Paul himself knew suffering.
He knew persecution.
He knew weakness.
He knew what it meant to depend upon the grace of God in circumstances he could not control.
And Scripture never promises that every faithful believer will experience immediate deliverance from every earthly difficulty.
But it does promise that nothing can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Him.
The shield of faith is not confidence that life will always go your way.
It is confidence in the God who remains worthy of trust when life does not.
And then comes the helmet of salvation.
Imagine a believer who has spent years hearing the voice of shame.
You are what you did.
You will always be that person.
Your past has already decided your future.
But salvation announces that the final word over the redeemed does not belong to shame.
It belongs to Jesus Christ.
Not because we are innocent of every accusation.
But because our Savior is merciful, righteous, and mighty to save.
The Christian hope is not self-reinvention.
It is redemption.
It is being brought from death to life by the grace of God.
It is having a new identity in Christ that produces a new direction of life.
And that is the heart of Gospel Warrior's message.
Not because scandal is glamorous.
Not because sin is something to celebrate.
Not because the consequences of our choices disappear.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem people whose stories seem hopelessly ruined.
Consider the apostle Paul himself.
Before he became a missionary proclaiming Christ, he persecuted the church.
He approved of violence against believers.
He tried to destroy the very movement he would later serve.
If you had known him before his encounter with Jesus, you might have concluded that he was the last person God would use to proclaim the Gospel.
Yet the risen Christ confronted him.
Paul's past was real.
The harm he had caused was real.
But God's mercy was real too.
And the man who once persecuted Christians became a witness to the grace of the Savior he had opposed.
That is not a story about how good Paul was.
It is a story about how merciful Jesus is.
And if you are reading this while carrying the weight of a shameful past, do not confuse the seriousness of your sin with the impossibility of forgiveness.
Come to Christ.
Confess what is true.
Turn away from what is evil.
Receive His mercy by faith.
And begin walking in the new life He gives.
Then Paul describes the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God.
Notice that the armor passage gives believers one weapon explicitly described as a sword.
And it is not anger.
It is not political power.
It is not intimidation.
It is the Word of God.
When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, He answered with Scripture.
He did not need to invent spectacular rituals.
He responded to temptation with the truth of what God had spoken.
And Christians today need that same deep familiarity with Scripture.
Not isolated verses twisted into promises God never made.
Not sensational interpretations that turn every headline into a secret prophecy.
Not teachings that make believers dependent upon personalities who claim exclusive knowledge of invisible spiritual realms.
We need the Word of God understood in context.
We need the whole counsel of Scripture.
We need to know who Jesus is, what He has accomplished, what He commands, and what He promises.
Because a Bible sitting unopened on a shelf will not shape your thinking the way a Bible faithfully read, believed, and obeyed can.
And perhaps one of the quietest tragedies of modern Christianity is that some believers know more about the latest controversy than they know about the words of Christ.
They can recognize the language of spiritual warfare.
But they are unfamiliar with the Sermon on the Mount.
They can discuss demons for hours.
But they struggle to explain the Gospel.
They are quick to identify darkness in the world.
But slow to confess pride, greed, lust, dishonesty, and bitterness in their own hearts.
Yet Paul does not call us merely to recognize evil.
He calls us to stand in God's strength.
And then, almost as though he refuses to let us mistake spiritual warfare for self-reliance, he tells us to pray.
“Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit...” — Ephesians 6:18, KJV
Prayer is not an afterthought.
It runs through the believer's life of dependence upon God.
And there is something deeply moving about what Paul says next.
He asks believers to pray for him.
For boldness.
For the ability to proclaim the mystery of the Gospel.
Think about that.
The man writing about principalities and powers does not ask the church to help him become famous for defeating demons.
He asks for prayer so that he can faithfully proclaim Jesus Christ.
At the time of writing, he describes himself as an ambassador in chains.
His circumstances are painful.
His freedom is restricted.
Yet his concern is that the Gospel would be declared boldly.
That should reshape the way we understand spiritual warfare.
The battle is not about making ourselves appear powerful.
It is about remaining faithful to Jesus in the face of evil, temptation, suffering, deception, and opposition.
And there is another passage that brings the entire picture into sharper focus.
Colossians 2:15 says that through Christ's triumph, the rulers and authorities were disarmed and publicly exposed.
Christ's victory over the powers is connected to His saving work.
The cross, which looked like defeat to those watching, became the place where God's redemptive purpose was accomplished.
The One who was mocked as King is the risen and exalted Lord.
The One who wore a crown of thorns is worthy of every crown.
The One who was nailed to a Roman cross is the One before whom every knee will ultimately bow.
This is the great reversal at the center of Christianity.
The apparent triumph of darkness did not prevent the resurrection.
The grave did not hold Jesus.
And the powers of evil do not possess ultimate authority over those who belong to Him.
But be careful not to misunderstand what that means.
The New Testament still calls believers to resist the devil.
It still warns about temptation.
It still teaches vigilance.
It still acknowledges suffering and persecution.
Christ's decisive victory does not mean that the present conflict has already disappeared.
It means the outcome of God's redemptive purpose is secure in Him.
And this is why Paul repeatedly uses the language of standing.
Stand.
Withstand.
Stand firm.
Not because Christians are invulnerable.
Not because we are incapable of failure.
But because God has supplied what His people need to remain faithful in the conflict.
Sometimes standing looks like refusing a temptation when nobody would have discovered your compromise.
Sometimes it looks like telling the truth when lying would protect your reputation.
Sometimes it looks like forgiving someone while still maintaining necessary boundaries.
Sometimes it looks like getting out of bed after grief has made ordinary life feel impossible.
Sometimes it looks like opening your Bible again after months of spiritual dryness.
Sometimes it looks like saying, “Jesus, I need You,” when you have no eloquent prayer left.
And sometimes standing looks like returning to the Savior after you have fallen.
Not excusing the fall.
Not pretending it did not matter.
But refusing to let shame drive you farther away from the only One who can restore you.
There is a reason the Gospel is such good news.
Jesus did not come merely to give strong people a few additional religious tools.
He came to save sinners.
He came to seek and to save the lost.
He died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures.
And He calls people everywhere to repent and believe the Gospel.
That is the message at the center of everything.
Not demons.
Not fear.
Not human personalities.
Not spiritual sensationalism.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
And perhaps you have reached this point in the article realizing that the greatest battle in your life right now is not the one you have been talking about publicly.
It is the one you have been hiding.
The addiction you keep returning to.
The bitterness you keep feeding.
The compromise you keep justifying.
The secret dishonesty.
The spiritual numbness.
The resentment toward God because life has not turned out the way you expected.
Or perhaps your struggle is simply that you are tired.
So tired.
You still believe.
But the joy feels distant.
You still pray.
But your words feel empty.
You still attend church.
But you wonder whether anyone would notice how much you are hurting if you stopped pretending to be strong.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
Your exhaustion does not surprise Jesus.
Your tears do not embarrass Him.
Your questions do not make Him less sovereign.
And your need for help is not proof that you have failed as a Christian.
Bring your struggles into the light.
Seek the support of trustworthy believers.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Receive the help you need.
And keep turning toward Christ.
Because the answer to spiritual warfare is not a life controlled by fear of darkness.
It is a life increasingly rooted in the Lord who has overcome it.
And that brings us to one final truth from Ephesians that we cannot afford to miss.
Paul's letter is not addressed merely to isolated individuals fighting private battles.
It is addressed to the church.
A people joined together in Christ.
A people called to unity.
A people instructed to speak truth, put away bitterness, forgive one another, walk in love, reject darkness, and live as children of light.
Spiritual warfare is not meant to turn Christians into lonely warriors who distrust everyone around them.
It should drive us toward deeper dependence on Christ and faithful life together as His people.
We need Scripture.
We need prayer.
We need sound teaching.
We need accountability.
We need fellowship.
We need the encouragement of believers who will remind us of God's truth when our own hearts are weary.
And that is one reason Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell the grace of God.
Not to make anyone feel that spiritual growth can be purchased.
But to help put Christ-centered biblical teaching, encouragement, and discipleship resources within reach of people who genuinely want to grow.
These resources are intended to help you read, reflect, learn, and strengthen your understanding of Scripture.
And if this article has helped you see Ephesians 6 more clearly, please do not let it end as another post you read and forget.

Not because a saved article possesses spiritual power, but because there may come a day when fear returns, temptation presses harder, or shame begins speaking again, and you need to remember what Scripture actually says.
Somebody who follows you may be fighting a battle they have never had the courage to discuss.
Someone may be blaming every hardship on demons while overlooking the hope of the Gospel.
Someone may have stopped praying because they believe their past has made them unworthy of God's mercy.
And I want to ask you something more personal.
Not for a performance.
Not to pressure you into making a public confession.
But because sometimes the beginning of change is the moment we stop pretending.
What battle has been hardest for you lately?
Fear?
Temptation?
Shame?
Bitterness?
Spiritual exhaustion?
You can simply write, “I'm still fighting, but I'm holding on to Jesus.”
You do not need to disclose private details or expose wounds you are not ready to discuss publicly.
But if you need encouragement, let the community know.
Someone reading may need to be reminded that God's grace is not just a doctrine written on a page.
It is the grace that saves and transforms real people.
There is also another way to stand with this ministry.
And it should not be presented as a mandatory biblical tithe.
The New Testament teaches generosity that is willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
As Paul wrote:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience, love, service, and faithful stewardship of what He has entrusted to you.
These items are not spiritual necessities.
They are simply practical resources and expressions of appreciation for those who choose to stand with the ministry.
And the free resources are there because the truth of God's Word should never be treated as a privilege reserved only for people who can afford a monthly payment.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical teaching with someone who needs it matters.
Your faithfulness to Jesus matters.
Because this entire message began with one frightening reality.
We are not wrestling merely against flesh and blood.
There are principalities and powers.
There is spiritual opposition.
There is deception.
There is a real enemy who opposes God's purposes.
But the letter that warns us about the powers of darkness also announces something infinitely greater.
Jesus Christ has been raised from the dead.
He is seated above every principality and authority.
Through His blood, sinners receive redemption and forgiveness.
Through grace, the spiritually dead are made alive.
Through His Spirit, believers are strengthened.
Through His Word, they are equipped.
And through His mighty power, they are called to stand.
So tonight, if you are afraid, look to Christ.
If you are tempted, turn to Christ.
If you have sinned, repent and come to Christ.
If you are wounded, bring your pain to Christ and seek the help and care you need.
If you are exhausted, do not mistake your weakness for the absence of His strength.
And if you have spent years believing that your story ended when your life fell apart, remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember the persecutor who became an apostle.
Remember the sinners who were welcomed by the Savior.
Remember that Jesus Christ is still mighty to save.
The powers of darkness are real.
But they are not ultimate.
Your past is real.
But it does not have to be your master.
Your wounds are real.
But they do not make you unreachable.
Your battle is real.
But Jesus Christ is Lord.

And one day, the conflict that has exhausted God's people for generations will finally give way to the fullness of His kingdom, when evil is judged, death is defeated, and God's redeemed people dwell with Him.
Until that day, we do not live in terror.
We stand in the Lord.
We cling to His truth.
We walk in His grace.
We proclaim His Gospel.
And we remember that the One who calls us to stand is the same Savior who gave Himself to bring us home.
The darkness may know the scandal of your past, but it cannot rewrite the grace of the Savior who redeemed you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “TREAT THEM AS A PAGAN OR TAX COLLECTOR” — DID JESUS REALLY TELL US TO CUT PEOPLE OFF?
paragraphs: “TREAT THEM AS A PAGAN OR TAX COLLECTOR” — DID JESUS REALLY TELL US TO CUT PEOPLE OFF?

One of Jesus’ most misunderstood commands has been used to justify rejection, silence, and spiritual abandonment. But when you discover how Jesus actually treated pagans and tax collectors, His words become both more confronting and more beautiful than you ever imagined.
There is a kind of pain that only another Christian can give you.
Not because unbelievers cannot wound you. They can.

But there is something uniquely devastating about being hurt by someone who knows the same Scriptures you know. Someone who sings about grace on Sunday and then treats you like you are beyond its reach on Monday.
Maybe you have experienced it.
You made a mistake. Perhaps a terrible one.
People found out.
The conversations changed. The invitations stopped. The smiles became uncomfortable. Suddenly, people who once called you brother or sister began treating you like a stranger.
And somewhere in the middle of your shame, somebody opened a Bible and said:
“Well, Jesus told us to treat them like a pagan or a tax collector.”
And just like that, rejection sounded holy.
But what if we have been reading those words without paying attention to the Man who spoke them?
What if the same Jesus who commanded the Church to confront sin also showed us something extraordinary about how to treat sinners?
And what if His command was never permission to become cruel, but a call to take sin seriously without forgetting the heart of God?
Stay with me, because the answer is not as comfortable as either side might hope.
It will challenge those who use grace to excuse unrepentant sin.
And it will confront those who use holiness as an excuse to stop loving people.
Most importantly, it may change the way you see someone you have already decided is beyond restoration.
Jesus said:
“Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.”
— Matthew 18:15, KJV
Read those final words again.
“Thou hast gained thy brother.”
Not, “You have won the argument.”
Not, “You have exposed the sinner.”
Not, “You have proven yourself spiritually superior.”
You have gained your brother.
That is the heartbeat of the passage.
Restoration.
Jesus begins with a person who has sinned and another person who must decide what to do about it.
And His first instruction is surprisingly private.
Go to the person.
Alone.
Before you gather an audience. Before you tell the prayer group every detail. Before you post something mysterious on Facebook that everyone knows is about them.
Go privately.
Why?
Because biblical correction is not supposed to become public humiliation.
Jesus is protecting the possibility of repentance without unnecessary shame.
He is giving the person an opportunity to listen, acknowledge the wrong, and turn back.
In the Greek text, the phrase translated “thou hast gained thy brother” is:
ἐκέρδησας τὸν ἀδελφόν σου
ekerdēsas ton adelphon sou
Literally, “you have gained your brother.”
The verb kerdainō carries the idea of gaining or winning something.
Jesus describes a restored relationship as a gain.
Think about that.
In a world where people compete to win arguments, Jesus is concerned about winning back a brother.
And notice something else.
Jesus does not say that love means pretending the offense never happened.
He says to confront it.
Because genuine love does not celebrate the destruction of the person it claims to care about.
Sometimes love has to say, “What you did was wrong.”
Sometimes love has to say, “This cannot continue.”
Sometimes love must speak a truth that risks being rejected.
But love never needs to enjoy another person's disgrace.
And this is where the passage becomes difficult.
Jesus continues:
“But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.”
— Matthew 18:16, KJV
If private correction fails, Jesus instructs us to involve one or two others.
Not a mob.
Not an online audience.
Not people recruited to destroy somebody's reputation.
One or two.
The language echoes Deuteronomy 19:15, where multiple witnesses establish a matter.
The principle is serious: accusations must be handled responsibly.
Truth matters.
Evidence matters.
Fairness matters.
The accused person must not be condemned simply because someone tells a persuasive story.
And the person bringing the concern must also be accountable.
That should make every Christian careful.
Because not every accusation is true.
Not every disagreement is sin.
Not every person who questions a leader is rebellious.
And not every person who refuses an unjust demand is refusing to obey Jesus.
Church discipline must never become a weapon for silencing legitimate concerns, protecting abusive leadership, or demanding loyalty to human authority over God's Word.
If someone is being abused, threatened, manipulated, or harmed, Matthew 18 must not be twisted into a requirement that they privately confront a dangerous person or remain in an unsafe situation.
Protecting the vulnerable, seeking appropriate outside help, and reporting criminal conduct to the proper authorities are not betrayals of Christian forgiveness.
They can be expressions of truth, justice, and love.
Jesus did not give His Church permission to hide evil.
He gave His people responsibility to deal truthfully with it.
Then comes the sentence that has troubled believers for generations.
“And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.”
— Matthew 18:17, KJV
There it is.
The phrase that has ended friendships.
The phrase that has been quoted in church meetings.
The phrase that has sometimes been used to justify complete social rejection.
“Let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.”
But before we decide what Jesus meant, we need to understand what His original hearers would have heard.
The Greek reads:
ἔστω σοι ὥσπερ ὁ ἐθνικὸς καὶ ὁ τελώνης
estō soi hōsper ho ethnikos kai ho telōnēs
A careful translation is:
“Let him be to you as the Gentile and the tax collector.”
The word ethnikos refers here to someone belonging to the nations outside the Jewish covenant community—a Gentile or outsider.
The word telōnēs refers to a tax collector.
In first-century Jewish society, tax collectors were often despised because of their association with Roman taxation and the opportunities their work created for exploitation and corruption.
For many Jewish listeners, Gentiles and tax collectors represented people outside the recognized religious community.
So Jesus' statement was not a small matter.
He was describing a real change in how an unrepentant person should be regarded within the community of disciples.
But here is the question we cannot afford to ignore.
How did Jesus Himself treat Gentiles and tax collectors?
Because if we interpret His command in a way that contradicts His character, we have probably misunderstood something.
Consider Matthew.
Before Matthew became a disciple, he was a tax collector.
The kind of person religious society often despised.
The kind of person people avoided.
The kind of person whose occupation made him a symbol of compromise and corruption.
And one day, Jesus approached his tax booth.
Imagine Matthew sitting there.
Coins on the table.
People passing by with disgust in their eyes.
Perhaps accustomed to being judged before he even opened his mouth.
Then Jesus looked at him.
And said two words.
Matthew 9:9 records that Matthew arose and followed Him.
Jesus did not pretend Matthew's former life was irrelevant.
He called him into an entirely new life.
But He did not treat Matthew as someone incapable of receiving mercy.
And what happened next?
Jesus sat at a meal with tax collectors and sinners.
The Pharisees were offended.
They asked why He ate with such people.
Jesus answered:
“They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick.”
— Matthew 9:12, KJV
Then He said:
“But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice: for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”
— Matthew 9:13, KJV
Did you catch that?
Mercy. And repentance.
Not mercy instead of repentance.
Not repentance without mercy.
Both.
Jesus welcomed sinners without blessing their sin.
He approached the spiritually sick as a physician, not as someone who enjoyed watching them die.
That changes the conversation.
When Jesus tells His disciples to regard an obstinately unrepentant person as a Gentile or tax collector, He is not commanding them to pretend that person remains in good standing within the Church.
The context requires a genuine boundary.
But neither does the wider Gospel permit us to interpret that boundary as permission for hatred, humiliation, revenge, or indifference.
Jesus treated outsiders as people who needed truth, repentance, and the invitation of grace.
The Church must never confuse removing the recognition of fellowship with removing the obligation to love.
Those are not the same thing.
And we must be careful here.
Some people read Matthew 18 and conclude that Jesus was simply saying, “Keep treating them exactly as before.”
But that does not adequately account for the escalating process He described.
Private correction failed.
Witnesses were involved.
The matter was brought before the church.
The person still refused to listen.
Jesus was describing a serious rupture in recognized fellowship.
The New Testament confirms that church discipline can involve the removal of an unrepentant person from the community's fellowship.
In 1 Corinthians 5, Paul addresses a scandalous situation of sexual immorality being tolerated within the Corinthian church.
He does not tell the believers to celebrate their tolerance.
He calls them to act.
In verse 5, he describes a severe disciplinary action with a redemptive purpose:
“That the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.”
Even there, the stated ultimate concern is salvation.
Not entertainment.
Not humiliation.
Not revenge.
And Paul distinguishes between judging those who profess to belong to the Church and judging outsiders.
In 1 Corinthians 5:12–13, he makes clear that the Church has a responsibility to address serious sin within its own fellowship.
This is not a license to police the entire world.
It is a call for integrity among those who claim to follow Christ.
But the story does not end with exclusion.
In 2 Corinthians 2:6–8, Paul speaks about a disciplined individual who should now be forgiven, comforted, and reassured of love, lest he be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
We should not automatically assume that this is the same individual described in 1 Corinthians 5; scholars differ on that identification.
Nevertheless, the passage reveals an essential apostolic principle.
Discipline must not become permanent punishment when repentance and restoration are appropriate.
Paul says:
“Wherefore I beseech you that ye would confirm your love toward him.”
— 2 Corinthians 2:8, KJV
Confirm your love.
Not merely tolerate his presence.
Not keep reminding him of the worst thing he ever did.
Confirm your love.
Can you imagine how different some churches would be if they took both sides of Scripture seriously?
What if we stopped calling everything grace when we are actually afraid to confront sin?
And what if we stopped calling everything holiness when we are actually enjoying someone's downfall?
Because there are two dangerous distortions of the Gospel.
One says, “God loves you, so repentance does not matter.”
The other says, “You sinned, so God's people should never love you again.”
Neither reflects the fullness of Jesus Christ.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
And holiness is not permission to become heartless.
Now think about the woman caught in adultery in John 8.

The account appears in John 7:53–8:11 in many Bibles, though responsible study must acknowledge that the passage is absent from the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John and is marked as textually disputed in many modern translations.
That textual issue matters.
We should never conceal it when claiming to handle Scripture faithfully.
The account nevertheless reflects a pattern consistent with the mercy and moral seriousness seen elsewhere in Jesus' ministry.
The accusers wanted condemnation.
Jesus exposed their hypocrisy.
And the woman heard words that hold mercy and moral transformation together:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
— John 8:11, KJV
Do not miss either half.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
And:
“Sin no more.”
Some of us want the first sentence without the second.
Others seem to love the second sentence while forgetting the first.
But Jesus speaks both.
And the Gospel is diminished whenever we separate what Christ holds together.
Now perhaps you are reading this as someone who has been disciplined, rejected, or publicly shamed.
Perhaps you genuinely sinned.
Perhaps you hurt someone.
Perhaps you lied, betrayed trust, fell into sexual sin, became consumed by pride, or allowed a hidden habit to grow until it damaged your life.
And maybe you have spent years convincing yourself that because people stopped believing in you, God must have stopped calling you.
Listen carefully.
Human rejection is not proof that divine mercy has run out.
But neither is divine mercy an excuse to avoid accountability.
If you have sinned, confess it.
If you have harmed someone, acknowledge the harm.
Where restitution is possible and appropriate, pursue it.
If trust has been broken, understand that rebuilding it may take time.
And if the person you harmed needs distance or protection, respect that boundary.
Forgiveness does not automatically erase consequences.
Repentance does not entitle anyone to immediate access to another person's life.
Reconciliation, especially after serious harm, may require safety, time, demonstrated change, and the willing participation of those involved.
But hear this:
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
There was another disciple whose failure became painfully public.
Peter.
He promised loyalty.
He insisted that even if others abandoned Jesus, he would remain faithful.
Then the pressure came.
The questions.
The fear.
The danger of being associated with a condemned Man.
And Peter denied knowing Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 tells us that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The eyes of the One he loved.
The memory of his promises.
The crushing realization of what he had done.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Have you ever cried because you finally understood what your sin had cost?
Not because you were caught.
Not because your reputation suffered.
But because you realized you had grieved the One who loved you?
Peter knew that kind of sorrow.
And after the resurrection, Jesus met him again.
In John 21, Jesus questioned Peter three times about his love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
The man who had denied Jesus was not beyond the reach of restoration.
But notice what restoration involved.
Peter was not simply told to forget the past.
He was called again to love Christ and serve His people.
Grace did not leave Peter where failure had found him.
Grace brought him into renewed obedience.
That is what Jesus does.
And perhaps that is why the phrase “tax collector” carries such extraordinary meaning when we read it through the whole Gospel.
Because Matthew was a tax collector.
And Jesus called him.
Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector.
And Jesus entered his house.
In Luke 19, Zacchaeus responded with a commitment to generosity and restitution.
Jesus declared:
“This day is salvation come to this house.”
— Luke 19:9, KJV
Then He explained His mission:
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.”
— Luke 19:10, KJV
Seek.
And save.
Not seek and shame.
Not seek and exploit.
Not seek and publicly destroy.
Seek and save.
But notice that Zacchaeus' encounter with Jesus produced visible change.
The Gospel did not merely comfort his conscience.
It transformed his relationship with money, wrongdoing, and his neighbors.
This is the kind of grace that rewrites lives.
Not cheap grace that leaves sin untouched.
Not harsh religion that leaves wounded people without hope.
The grace of Jesus Christ that forgives, confronts, restores, and transforms.
And this brings us back to Matthew 18.
Because there is something remarkable about the surrounding context.
Before Jesus gives instructions about confronting a sinning brother, He tells the parable of the lost sheep.
In Matthew 18:12–14, the shepherd seeks the one sheep that has gone astray.
And Jesus concludes:
“Even so it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish.”
— Matthew 18:14, KJV
Immediately afterward comes the instruction to confront a sinning brother.
That literary context matters.
Jesus is not suddenly changing from a Shepherd who seeks the lost into a religious official who enjoys expelling people.
The concern for those who wander helps us understand the purpose of correction.
And immediately after the teaching on church discipline, Peter asks how often he must forgive his brother.
Seven times?
Jesus responds:
“I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.”
— Matthew 18:22, KJV
The expression communicates forgiveness that is not governed by a petty numerical limit.
So look at the movement of the chapter.
A sheep wanders.
A brother sins.
A community must respond.
And forgiveness remains central.
This does not cancel the need for boundaries.
It explains the heart with which boundaries should be maintained.
The Church must be holy.
But it must also remember whose Church it is.
We belong to the One who carried a cross for sinners.
And there is another Greek word worth considering.
In Matthew 18:15, Jesus uses the word:
ἁμαρτήσῃ
hamartēsē
A form of the verb hamartanō, meaning “to sin.”
Jesus is addressing sin, not simply an unpleasant personality, a disagreement over preferences, or a person's failure to satisfy our expectations.
That distinction is crucial.
Church discipline must not become a method for punishing people who disagree with leadership about nonessential matters.
Nor should Christians confuse personal offense with demonstrated wrongdoing.

Some ancient manuscripts of Matthew 18:15 include the words “against you,” while others do not. That textual variation affects whether the opening statement is understood specifically as a personal offense or more broadly as a brother's sin.
Either way, the passage calls for truthful, proportionate, and restorative action—not impulsive condemnation.
And now we must face an uncomfortable question.
What if you are not the wounded person in this story?
What if you are the one holding the stone?
What if someone sinned years ago, repented, sought help, and began rebuilding their life, but you still introduce them by what they used to be?
What if you say you believe in the transforming power of Christ but refuse to believe that Christ can transform someone you personally dislike?
What if you have been calling bitterness discernment?
What if you have been calling gossip a prayer request?
What if you have been calling humiliation accountability?
That is a painful question.
Because sometimes the person most resistant to grace is not the sinner who needs correction.
Sometimes it is the religious person who cannot bear to see mercy extended.
Think about the older brother in Luke 15.
The younger son had wasted his inheritance in reckless living.
He returned broken.
His father welcomed him.
But the older brother became angry.
He could not celebrate the restoration of someone whose failure he remembered so clearly.
He had stayed.
He had worked.
He had obeyed.
And now the one who had disgraced the family was being welcomed home.
His resentment revealed something sobering.
It is possible to remain close to the father's house while being far from the father's heart.
The father did not deny the younger son's wrongdoing.
He celebrated his return.
“For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.”
— Luke 15:24, KJV
That is the sound of restoration.
And it should make us examine our hearts.
When someone genuinely repents, are we glad?
Or are we disappointed that their story did not end in disgrace?
Do we want people to become holy?
Or do we secretly want them to remain permanently identified by the sin that once made us feel superior?
Jesus did not die so that forgiven sinners could build little kingdoms of condemnation.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
And that reconciliation cost more than any of us could ever pay.
The cross is where this entire conversation must lead.
Because the deepest scandal of Christianity is not that sinners are confronted.
It is that the sinless Son of God willingly bore the judgment sinners deserved.
Jesus was rejected.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Condemned.
Crucified.
And the One who had no sin gave Himself for those who did.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
— Isaiah 53:5, KJV
The Hebrew word translated “transgressions” is:
פְּשָׁעֵנוּ
peshaʿenu
“Our transgressions.”
It speaks of our rebellious wrongs.
Not merely unfortunate mistakes.
Not merely imperfections.
Our transgressions.
The Hebrew phrase translated “our iniquities” is:
עֲוֹנֹתֵינוּ
ʿavonotenu
Our iniquities—our guilt and moral wrongdoing.
Isaiah does not minimize sin.
He magnifies the astonishing reality of the Servant's suffering on behalf of sinners.
And the New Testament identifies Jesus Christ as the fulfillment of the suffering Servant's saving work, as seen, for example, in Acts 8:32–35 and 1 Peter 2:24.
That is why Christians cannot afford to become casual about sin.
Sin is serious enough that Christ suffered and died to save us.
But that is also why Christians cannot afford to become casual about mercy.
Grace is precious because of what it cost Him.
At Calvary, God's holiness and His saving love are not competing truths.
They meet in Jesus Christ.
And no one who truly understands the cross should be eager to make another person's shame into entertainment.
Now consider what Paul writes in Galatians 6:1:
The Greek verb translated “restore” is:
καταρτίζετε
katartizete
From katartizō, meaning to restore, put in order, or make fit.
The word can be used for repairing or preparing something so it can serve its intended purpose.
Paul's instruction is not to destroy the fallen person.
It is to seek restoration with gentleness.
And then he adds a warning.
Consider yourself.
Why?
Because the person correcting someone else is not immune to temptation.
Today you may be helping someone stand.
Tomorrow you may desperately need someone to help you.
That is not an argument against correction.
It is an argument for humility.
A mature Christian can confront sin without forgetting their own dependence on grace.
And perhaps that is what we need to recover.
Churches where truth is not sacrificed for popularity.
Where victims are protected.
Where allegations are examined fairly.
Where serious wrongdoing has real consequences.
Where repentance is more than a public apology.
Where leaders are accountable.
Where discipline is never confused with cruelty.
And where genuinely repentant people are not treated as permanently beyond the possibility of spiritual restoration.
Because the Church is not a museum of flawless people.
It is a community called to holiness by a Savior who rescues sinners.
That does not mean everyone who claims to be repentant is safe to trust.
Words alone do not prove transformation.
Jesus Himself taught that people are known by their fruits (Matthew 7:16–20).
A person may say, “I am sorry,” while continuing to manipulate, deceive, exploit, or harm others.
Biblical restoration must not ignore patterns of behavior.
And reconciliation is not always possible, even where forgiveness is sincerely offered.
Some relationships require permanent protective boundaries.
But no boundary requires hatred.
No act of accountability requires cruelty.
And no Christian should confuse someone's exclusion from fellowship with a declaration that God is powerless to save them.
That final judgment belongs to God.
Our responsibility is to be faithful.
Faithful to truth.
Faithful to holiness.
Faithful to justice.
Faithful to mercy.
Faithful to Jesus.
So when someone asks, “Did Jesus really say to treat them as a pagan or tax collector?” the answer is yes.
He did.
And we should not soften His words until they mean nothing.
He taught that persistent, unrepentant sin among professing believers can require a serious change in recognized fellowship.

But when we ask what kind of heart should govern that response, we must look at the same Jesus who called Matthew, sought Zacchaeus, restored Peter, welcomed repentant sinners, and died for the ungodly.
Treating someone as an outsider to the Church's fellowship does not mean treating them as an outsider to the reach of Christian love.
That is the distinction.
Do not affirm what God calls sin.
Do not pretend repentance is unnecessary.
Do not compromise truth to keep the peace.
But do not close your heart to the possibility that the person who has fallen may one day rise by the grace of God.
And if they genuinely repent, do not make your pride an obstacle to the mercy Christ has commanded His people to show.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying the shame of your own failure.
Maybe the church doors still open for everyone else, but you feel too ashamed to walk through them.
Maybe your family knows what happened.
Maybe your children saw you fall.
Maybe your marriage was wounded.
Maybe your testimony became a warning story.
Maybe you have spent years thinking, “If people really knew everything about me, they would never look at me the same way.”
But Jesus already knows.
He knows the truth without needing a rumor.
He sees the heart without needing an audience.
He knows the sin you confessed and the sin you are still trying to hide.
And His call is not, “Keep pretending.”
His call is to repent and believe the Gospel.
The Greek word often translated “repent” is:
μετανοεῖτε
metanoeite
From metanoeō, meaning to repent—to change one's mind and direction in response to God's truth.
Biblical repentance is more than a passing emotion.
It involves a genuine turning from sin toward God, with a changed life bearing fruit consistent with that turning.
You do not have to manufacture a flawless past.
You cannot.
You do not have to convince God that your sin was harmless.
It was not.
You are called to come to Christ in truth.
And if you belong to Him, His grace is not merely a covering for your reputation.
It is the power of God at work in a life being transformed.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not faithful and just to humiliate us forever.
Faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
Because forgiveness is grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And if you are the person who has been wronged, perhaps your next step is different.
Maybe you need to stop carrying vengeance.
Maybe you need to forgive without denying what happened.
Maybe you need to maintain a necessary boundary without wishing destruction upon the person who harmed you.
Maybe you need to acknowledge that forgiveness and restored trust are not identical.
You can entrust justice to God while still pursuing appropriate accountability.
