You can release personal vengeance without returning to an unsafe relationship.
You can pray for someone's repentance without granting them access to harm you again.
That, too, can be a faithful response to Jesus.
And if you are a pastor, elder, ministry leader, or someone responsible for confronting wrongdoing, remember this:
You are dealing with people for whom Christ died.
Do not trivialize their sin.
Do not trivialize their dignity.
Do not sacrifice the vulnerable to protect an institution.
Do not allow a person's influence, money, popularity, or position to exempt them from accountability.
And do not make discipline a performance designed to demonstrate your authority.
The authority belongs to Christ.
The Church is His.
The sheep are His.
The truth is His.
And the grace is His.
Perhaps this article has brought someone's face to your mind.
Someone who walked away.
Someone who fell.
Someone who hurt you.
Someone your church no longer knows how to approach.
Or perhaps the face you see is your own.
If that is you, I want to ask something deeper than whether you agree with this article.
What is Jesus asking you to do with the truth you have just heard?
To repent?
To forgive?
To seek wise counsel?
To tell the truth?
To stop gossiping?
To protect someone who is being harmed?
To take responsibility for something you have spent years excusing?
To reach out appropriately to someone who is isolated and hurting?
To stop using another person's past as a permanent identity?
Whatever it is, do not let this become another Christian message that moves you emotionally but leaves your life unchanged.
The Word of God is not given merely to make us feel something.
It calls us to respond.
And maybe someone else desperately needs to read this.
Someone who believes their failure disqualified them forever.
Someone who thinks accountability means God has abandoned them.
Someone who has been using Scripture to justify bitterness.
Someone who has confused acceptance with approval.
Someone who is one painful experience away from walking away from the Church entirely.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because truth worth receiving is also worth passing on.
A simple share could help someone reconsider how they understand repentance, church discipline, forgiveness, and the heart of Jesus.
And please, do not leave without joining this conversation.
Or have you witnessed biblical correction lead to genuine repentance and restoration?
You do not need to reveal anyone's private story.
You can simply comment, “Christ is still healing me,” if you are learning what grace and repentance truly mean.
Or comment, “Pray for me,” if you are trying to find your way back to God after a painful season.
We want this to be more than a comment section filled with religious slogans.
We want it to be a place where believers can speak truthfully, encourage one another, and point each other back to Jesus.
There may come a day when you are the one who needs to remember the difference between biblical discipline and religious rejection.
Or when someone you love falls, and you need to remember that truth and compassion are not enemies.
And if you have not yet followed Gospel Warrior, I invite you to stay connected.
Bring your family, your friends, the believer struggling quietly, the Christian who has grown spiritually cold, and even the seeker who is still trying to understand who Jesus really is.
We want people to encounter Scripture that does more than inspire them for a moment.
We want them to know Christ, understand His Word, repent of sin, grow in faith, and experience the transforming power of His Gospel.
Not because financial support makes someone a better Christian.
And certainly not because the grace of Jesus Christ can be bought.
It never could be.
Salvation is God's gift, received by grace through faith, not earned through financial contributions or religious works (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Paul taught that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support for their ministry (1 Corinthians 9:14), and he commended generous giving that comes from a willing heart rather than pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
It should never be represented as a mandatory biblical tithe, a substitute for your responsibilities to your local church, or a condition for God's blessing.
Rather, it is an opportunity to help sustain and expand this work, so more people can encounter Scripture, receive encouragement, be challenged toward repentance, and grow deeper in Jesus Christ.
If these messages have helped you, perhaps you can help make it possible for someone else to receive them.
These are expressions of appreciation, not spiritual rewards.
The greater purpose remains the same: to keep pointing people to Christ.
That free library is part of the mission, too.
Keep reading.
Keep growing.
Keep opening your Bible.
Keep sharing the Gospel.
Because the goal is not merely to build a larger audience.
It is to help people meet the Savior who changes lives.
The same Jesus who called Matthew out of his tax booth.
The same Jesus who brought salvation to Zacchaeus' house.
The same Jesus who restored Peter after his denial.
The same Jesus who commanded His Church to confront sin and taught His disciples to forgive.
The same Jesus who went to the cross, rose from the grave, and still calls sinners to repentance and faith.
So the next time you hear someone quote, “Treat them as a pagan or tax collector,” remember the whole counsel of Scripture.
Remember the necessary seriousness of church discipline.
Remember the dignity of people made in God's image.
Remember that repentance matters.
Remember that accountability matters.
Remember that protecting the vulnerable matters.
And remember how Jesus treated the people religious society considered hopeless.
He did not affirm their sin.
He called them to Himself.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Jesus does not need to rewrite history to redeem a human life.
He tells the truth about our sin.
He bears the cost of our salvation.
He calls us to repentance.
And He gives us a future that our past could never have earned.
So do not use the Bible to excuse the sin Jesus came to save us from.
And do not use the Bible to deny the mercy Jesus died to give.
Because one day, the person standing in need of correction, forgiveness, patience, and restoration may be you.
And on that day, you will understand why the Church must never choose between truth and love.
Christ commands us to walk in both.
Never forget: the hands that were pierced for sinners are the same hands calling the fallen to rise, the wandering to return, and the forgiven to become new.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF OBEDIENCE PROVES YOU’RE SAVED… WHY DID JESUS SAVE A THIEF WHO COULDN’T OBEY ANOTHER COMMAND?
paragraphs: IF OBEDIENCE PROVES YOU’RE SAVED… WHY DID JESUS SAVE A THIEF WHO COULDN’T OBEY ANOTHER COMMAND?

The terrifying difference between following Jesus because you are saved and trying to obey Him so He will save you. One leads to freedom. The other can leave you religious, exhausted, and dangerously far from grace.
There was a man dying beside Jesus who had no time left to become a better Christian.
No time to attend church.
No time to be baptized.
No time to give an offering, repair his reputation, restore everything he had stolen, or build a beautiful testimony of years spent faithfully serving God.
His hands were nailed to a cross.
His past was stained.
His future, humanly speaking, was finished.
And yet, before the sun went down, Jesus promised him paradise.
If obedience is evidence of salvation, what evidence did that dying criminal have?
And if obedience doesn't matter, why did Jesus repeatedly command His followers to obey Him?
Because somewhere between the cross of Christ and the expectations of religious people, a dangerous confusion has entered the church.
Some believers are terrified that one more failure will make God abandon them.
Others are so comfortable talking about grace that they have stopped taking sin seriously.
One group lives as though Jesus didn't finish enough.
The other lives as though His sacrifice didn't cost anything.
And somewhere in the middle stands a bloodstained Savior who refuses to let us turn either obedience or grace into something He never intended.
This is not merely a theological argument.
This is about the woman who cried last night because she promised God she would never fall into that sin again.
It's about the man who has attended church for twenty years, faithfully serves in ministry, and secretly wonders whether God loves him or merely tolerates him.
It's about the young believer who genuinely wants to follow Jesus but feels crushed by Christians who seem more interested in measuring his failures than helping him grow.
And it's about the person who keeps saying, "God knows my heart," while deliberately protecting the very sin Christ is calling him to surrender.
All four need the Gospel.
Not a softer Gospel.
Not a harsher Gospel.
The real Gospel.
Because the question isn't simply whether Christians should obey.
The question is whether our obedience is the fruit of salvation, the price of salvation, or a counterfeit we have mistaken for salvation itself.
And Scripture answers that question with extraordinary clarity.
Paul writes in Ephesians 2:8–9:
The Greek word translated "grace" is χάρις (charis), commonly referring to grace, favor, or gift. In this passage, God's saving grace is not presented as wages earned by religious performance.
It is a gift.
And a gift ceases to be a gift when we imagine we can purchase it with enough moral improvement.
Notice the order.
Grace.
Faith.
Salvation.
Not obedience first, then acceptance.
Not perfection first, then forgiveness.
Not religious achievement first, then eternal life.
God saves sinners through Jesus Christ, not through their successful attempts to become worthy of Him.
But something remarkable happens when we keep reading.
Ephesians 2:10 says:
"For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them."
Did you see it?
The very passage that declares we are not saved by works also declares that we are saved for good works.
The Greek word ποίημα (poiēma), translated "workmanship," describes something made or produced. Believers are God's workmanship, created anew in Christ.
And the Greek expression ἐπὶ ἔργοις ἀγαθοῖς (epi ergois agathois) points to the good works for which this new creation is intended.
In other words, obedience does not manufacture the new birth.
It belongs to the life that flows from it.
We are not saved because we obey. We are called to obey because God has saved us.
That difference is not a theological technicality.
It is the difference between a child obeying because he belongs to a loving father and an orphan desperately working to earn a place at the family table.
And some of you have been living like spiritual orphans for years.
You pray, but not always because you delight in speaking with God.
Sometimes you pray because you're frightened that missing a day will make Him angry.
You read Scripture, but not always because you hunger for His truth.
Sometimes you read because you imagine your spiritual worth depends on completing a religious checklist.
You serve, give, fast, and attend church.
And none of those things is wrong.
They can be beautiful expressions of genuine faith.
But somewhere along the journey, your heart quietly exchanged intimacy for performance.
You stopped asking, "Lord, how can I love You more?"
And started asking, "Lord, have I done enough for You to love me?"
Listen carefully.
If Jesus had waited until you were worthy of His love, Calvary would never have happened.
Romans 5:8 declares that God demonstrated His love toward us while we were still sinners.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we achieved spiritual consistency.
Not after we learned how to look holy in front of other Christians.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
That is grace.
But grace has been terribly misunderstood by some people who want the comfort of forgiveness without the inconvenience of surrender.
And that brings us to the other side of this conversation.
Jesus said in John 14:15:
"If ye love me, keep my commandments."
The Greek text reads:
Ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολὰς τὰς ἐμὰς τηρήσετε.
A faithful rendering is:
"If you love me, you will keep my commandments."
The verb τηρήσετε (tērēsete) is future indicative, describing what those who love Jesus will do. The statement connects love for Christ with obedience to His commands.
Jesus was not describing a relationship in which our works purchase His affection.
He was describing the natural expression of genuine love.
Think about it.

If someone repeatedly tells you they love you while knowingly betraying you, dismissing your words, and refusing every invitation to change, eventually you begin questioning what that person means by love.
Not because love requires flawless performance.
But because real love cannot remain permanently indifferent to the beloved.
The same principle confronts our relationship with Jesus.
A person may stumble while sincerely loving Christ.
A believer may struggle for years against a deeply rooted sin.
A wounded Christian may experience seasons of spiritual exhaustion, confusion, and painful weakness.
But there is a difference between fighting sin and making peace with it.
There is a difference between falling and declaring that repentance is unnecessary.
There is a difference between saying, "Lord, help me overcome this," and saying, "Lord, accept this because I have no intention of changing."
Grace does not make rebellion holy.
Grace calls rebels home.
Paul confronts this directly in Romans 6:1–2:
"What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid."
The Greek response begins:
μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito).
It is a forceful rejection, often rendered "By no means!" or "Absolutely not!"
Paul is not entertaining the idea that God's forgiveness gives Christians permission to embrace sin.
He rejects it.
Why?
Because union with Christ changes our relationship to sin.
The believer has not merely received a religious pardon while remaining untouched by the Savior.
The believer has been brought into a new relationship with the crucified and risen Christ.
That is why repentance matters.
That is why holiness matters.
That is why obedience matters.
Not because Jesus needs our performance to complete His sacrifice.
But because the One who died to rescue us from sin did not die so that we could celebrate remaining enslaved to it.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's saving grace also trains us to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace is not the enemy of holiness.
Grace is the very power that teaches us to pursue it.
And yet, here is where many sincere Christians are wounded.
They hear the word "obedience," and immediately remember the religious environment that nearly destroyed them.
A church where every mistake became public humiliation.
A family where spiritual maturity was measured by appearances.
A ministry where questions were treated as rebellion.
A community where people were quick to condemn visible sins while quietly excusing pride, greed, cruelty, and hypocrisy.
They were taught that a faithful Christian never struggles.
Never doubts.
Never feels depressed.
Never admits weakness.
Never needs help.
And when their humanity eventually became impossible to hide, they were made to feel as though they had disappointed God beyond repair.
Some stopped praying.
Some stopped attending church.
Some began hiding their struggles behind carefully rehearsed smiles.
And some walked away from Christianity altogether, believing that the merciless religion they experienced accurately represented Jesus Christ.
But consider the Savior revealed in Scripture.
Jesus did not approve of sin.
He also did not treat broken sinners as disposable.
In John 8:11, within the traditional account of the woman caught in adultery, Jesus says:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more."
Both parts matter.
"Neither do I condemn thee."
"Go, and sin no more."
Mercy and a call to change.
Compassion and holiness.
Grace and truth.

A textual note is important here: John 7:53–8:11 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts and is marked or bracketed in many modern Bibles. The account should therefore be handled with appropriate textual caution. Nevertheless, the combination of mercy toward sinners and a call to repentance is firmly established elsewhere in the New Testament.
Jesus did not tell sinners that their sins were imaginary.
Neither did He teach that their sins placed them beyond the reach of His mercy.
And we must not separate what Christ holds together.
When churches preach holiness without grace, they can produce fear, hypocrisy, and despair.
When churches preach grace without repentance, they can produce complacency and spiritual self-deception.
But when churches faithfully proclaim Jesus Christ, they call sinners to repentance while pointing them toward the mercy and transforming power found in Him.
Now return to the criminal on the cross.
Luke 23 records two criminals crucified alongside Jesus.
One mocked Him.
The other acknowledged their guilt and the innocence of Christ.
Then he turned toward the dying Savior and pleaded:
"Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." (Luke 23:42, KJV)
The Greek text preserves the heart of his request:
μνήσθητί μου (mnēsthēti mou).
"Remember me."
Two words.
No impressive testimony.
No long history of religious service.
No opportunity to prove himself through years of obedience.
Just a guilty man turning toward Jesus in faith.
And Jesus answered:
"Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." (Luke 23:43, KJV)
The Greek includes:
σήμερον μετ’ ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ.
"Today you will be with me in paradise."
The promise centers on being with Jesus.
Not on the criminal's religious achievements.
Not on his ability to compensate for his crimes.
Not on a future opportunity to accumulate good works.
Christ Himself was his hope.
But we should not overlook something extraordinary.
Although the criminal could not demonstrate a lifetime of obedience, his response was not spiritually empty.
He acknowledged his guilt.
He recognized Jesus' innocence.
He rebuked the other criminal.
He appealed to Jesus as the One whose kingdom extended beyond their approaching deaths.
These were meaningful expressions of faith and repentance.
His actions did not purchase salvation.
They revealed the direction of a heart turning toward Christ.
The thief was not saved by a record of good works.
Yet his faith was not indifferent to truth.
That is the distinction we must understand.
The absence of time for a lifetime of obedience is not the same as the absence of a changed response to Jesus.
The dying criminal teaches us that salvation rests on Christ, not accumulated religious merit.
He does not teach us that someone who has years to follow Jesus may deliberately reject His lordship without concern.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part of this account is that the criminal who received paradise had no opportunity to build the kind of Christian résumé that impresses religious people.
But he had Jesus.
And Jesus was enough.
Now imagine that same dying man somehow being taken down from the cross, miraculously healed, and given another thirty years to live.
Would we expect him to return to his former life with complete indifference toward the Savior who rescued him?
Would we imagine that genuine gratitude for Christ would have no effect on his choices?
Of course not.
His obedience would not be payment for paradise.
It would be a response to mercy.
And that is where James enters the conversation.
James 2:17 says:
"Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone."
James is not contradicting Paul.
Paul rejects works as the basis of justification before God.
James challenges the claim that a merely verbal profession, disconnected from any meaningful response to God, constitutes living faith.
James asks us to consider the difference between saying we believe and possessing a faith that actually moves us.
The Greek phrase πίστις νεκρά (pistis nekra) means "dead faith."
A faith that exists only as an empty claim is not the vibrant trust in Christ that Scripture commends.
And this should make us examine ourselves.
Not obsessively count every failure.
Not compare our spiritual progress with everyone else's.
Not assume that every painful struggle proves we are unsaved.
But honestly ask whether our profession of faith is shaping the direction of our lives.
Are we becoming more willing to confess our sins?
More willing to forgive?
More willing to speak truthfully?
More willing to resist what dishonors Christ?
More willing to love people who cannot repay us?
More willing to admit when we are wrong?
More willing to surrender the parts of our lives we once insisted God could never touch?
Spiritual growth is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like a man finally apologizing to his wife without blaming her for his behavior.
Sometimes it looks like a young woman refusing to return to a destructive relationship, even while crying because leaving hurts.
Sometimes it looks like someone quietly closing a browser window and choosing to pray instead.
Sometimes it looks like a believer confessing an addiction and asking for help rather than pretending the struggle does not exist.
Sometimes it looks like returning to Scripture after months of spiritual numbness.
Sometimes it looks like forgiving someone while still maintaining necessary boundaries.
Sometimes it looks like a Christian saying, "I was wrong," without adding excuses.
And sometimes obedience is simply getting up after another failure, turning back toward Christ, and refusing to call sin your home.
None of those actions earns the love of God.
But they can reflect the transforming work of His grace.
And no, this does not mean every believer grows at the same speed.
Jesus' parable of the soils in Matthew 13 reminds us that spiritual responses differ.
Paul's letters reveal churches filled with real believers who still needed serious correction.
The New Testament repeatedly calls Christians to grow, repent, persevere, and mature.
That would make little sense if conversion immediately removed every weakness.
Sanctification is not the claim that Christians never stumble.
It is God's ongoing work of making His people more like Christ.
And that work can be painful.
Especially when the Holy Spirit begins confronting sins we have spent years defending.
But here is a truth that deserves to be written across the walls of every church where wounded believers are afraid to confess their struggles.
Conviction invites you to return to Christ. Condemnation tells you there is no hope in returning.
Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus."
In the Greek, the central declaration is:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα τοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
"So then, there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus."
The word κατάκριμα (katakrima) refers to condemnation or an adverse judicial sentence.
Paul's declaration is not that sin becomes harmless.
It is that those who belong to Christ are no longer under the condemnation from which He has delivered them.
That freedom does not make holiness unnecessary.
Read the rest of Romans 8.
Paul describes life in the Spirit, the putting to death of sinful deeds, adoption as God's children, suffering, hope, and the inseparable love of God in Christ.
No condemnation is the beginning of a Spirit-led life.
Not permission to abandon it.
And perhaps this is exactly what someone reading needs to hear.
You have been measuring God's love by the quality of your most recent week.
When you prayed consistently, you felt accepted.
When you resisted temptation, you felt secure.
When you failed, you imagined heaven closing its doors.
You confessed the same sin again and wondered whether Jesus had finally grown tired of hearing your voice.
You looked at Christians who seemed stronger and wondered why transformation appeared easier for everyone else.
But your assurance cannot rest on the illusion that you will never struggle again.
It must rest on the faithful Savior who died and rose again, whose promises call you to trust Him and whose Spirit leads His people into holiness.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Notice whose faithfulness is emphasized.
His.
Not the perfection of your confession.
Not the eloquence of your prayer.
Not the intensity of your tears.
His faithfulness.
That does not make repentance a meaningless ritual.
Genuine confession agrees with God about sin and turns toward His mercy.
But the hope of forgiveness is grounded in the character and saving work of God.
So when you fall, do not run from the only One who can restore you.
Run to Him.
Confess honestly.
Seek help when needed.
Make restitution where appropriate and possible.
Remove opportunities for repeated temptation.
Receive the correction of Scripture.
Keep walking in the light.
And when someone tries to convince you that grace means you should never feel concerned about deliberate, ongoing rebellion, remember that Scripture speaks differently.
First John 2:3 says:
"And hereby we do know that we know him, if we keep his commandments."
That verse should not be twisted into a demand for sinless perfection.
John himself has already acknowledged that believers need forgiveness.
But it should not be emptied of its meaning either.
Our relationship with Jesus has moral consequences.
A profession of faith that persistently rejects His commands deserves serious examination.
Not because human obedience can replace the cross.
But because saving faith does not regard the Savior's authority as irrelevant.
And this is where legalism must be named accurately.
Legalism is not simply taking obedience seriously.
A Christian is not automatically legalistic because he believes sexual purity matters, dishonesty is sinful, repentance is necessary, or Jesus' commands should be followed.
Jesus Himself called His disciples to costly obedience.
The apostles taught holiness.
The New Testament contains numerous moral commands.
Calling people to obey Scripture is not inherently legalism.

Legalism appears when we make human obedience the basis of our acceptance before God, impose human rules as though they were divine commands, or elevate outward religious performance while neglecting the deeper demands of faith, mercy, and love.
It can also appear when people use their apparent righteousness to despise others.
Remember the Pharisee and the tax collector in Luke 18?
The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other sinners.
He pointed to his fasting and giving.
The tax collector stood at a distance, acknowledged his sin, and pleaded for mercy.
Jesus said the tax collector went home justified rather than the Pharisee.
The problem was not that fasting and giving were inherently wrong.
The problem was a self-righteous heart trusting in its own religious superiority.
And that danger has not disappeared.
It still walks into churches carrying Bibles.
It still speaks confidently about holiness.
It still notices everyone else's failures while carefully protecting its own.
It still mistakes being stricter than other Christians for being closer to Jesus.
It can even turn good biblical practices into trophies of spiritual superiority.
But the cross leaves no room for boasting in ourselves.
At Calvary, every believer stands as someone who needed mercy.
The pastor.
The worship leader.
The new convert.
The person recovering from addiction.
The faithful grandmother.
The former criminal.
The person who grew up in church.
The person who arrived yesterday.
Every one of us needs the same Savior.
And the ground at the foot of the cross is no place for pretending we rescued ourselves.
There is another uncomfortable truth we must face.
Some Christians are so afraid of legalism that they hesitate to call anyone to repentance.
They fear that confronting sin will sound judgmental.
They worry that preaching holiness will drive people away.
They have watched religious abuse hurt people and sincerely want to avoid repeating it.
That concern can come from genuine compassion.
But withholding what Jesus actually taught is not the answer.
A doctor who refuses to discuss a serious illness because the patient might become upset is not necessarily showing kindness.
Likewise, a church that never speaks about repentance may leave people comfortable in spiritual danger.
Love tells the truth.
But love also cares how that truth is delivered.
Galatians 6:1 calls spiritually mature believers to restore someone caught in wrongdoing with gentleness, while watching themselves.
Restoration.
Gentleness.
Humility.
Those words belong together.
Biblical correction is not an opportunity to humiliate someone.
It is an act intended to help restore them.
If our correction delights in exposing another person's shame, something is wrong with our hearts.
If our preaching produces admiration for our own strictness rather than reverence for Christ, something is wrong with our emphasis.
And if our version of holiness makes struggling people afraid to tell the truth, we should examine whether we have represented the gentleness of Jesus faithfully.
Christ is holy.
Christ is merciful.
Christ is truthful.
Christ is compassionate.
We do not honor Him by sacrificing one part of His character to defend another.
So what does real obedience look like?
It looks like loving Jesus enough to take His words seriously.
It looks like repentance that begins in the heart and becomes visible in the life.
It looks like faith working through love, as Galatians 5:6 teaches.
It looks like dependence on the Holy Spirit rather than confidence in human strength.
It looks like a willingness to obey even when obedience costs something.
It looks like humility when corrected.
It looks like gratitude rather than spiritual entitlement.
It looks like refusing to use grace as an excuse for sin.
And it looks like refusing to use obedience as a weapon against those who are still growing.
Most importantly, it keeps returning to Jesus.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about becoming impressive at religious behavior.
It is about being reconciled to God through His Son and being transformed into His likeness.
Jesus did not come merely to produce better-behaved people who could congratulate themselves on their moral accomplishments.
He came to save sinners.
He lived the righteous life we could not live.
He bore our sins on the cross.
He rose from the dead.
He calls people everywhere to repent and believe the Gospel.
And those who belong to Him are called to follow Him.
Not to improve upon His finished sacrifice.
But because His sacrifice has changed everything.
That is why Philippians 2:12–13 is so beautiful.

Paul urges believers to work out their salvation with fear and trembling, then immediately explains that God is at work in them, producing both the willing and the doing according to His good pleasure.
He does not say to work for salvation as though Christ had left the payment unfinished.
He speaks of living out the salvation God is working within His people.
God's grace does not make our participation meaningless.
Our participation does not make God's grace unnecessary.
We obey because God is at work in us.
And even our growth becomes a reason to praise Him.
Now, before you move on, I want to ask you something personal.
Not a question for the person sitting beside you.
Not a question for the Christian you secretly think needs this article.
A question for you.
Are you using obedience to earn a love Jesus already demonstrated at the cross?
Or are you using grace to excuse a sin He is calling you to surrender?
Perhaps you have been living in the first prison.
You are exhausted.
You love Jesus, but you constantly feel like a disappointment.
You believe the Gospel is true for other people, yet struggle to believe His mercy can reach your repeated failures.
You have mistaken spiritual growth for never needing forgiveness again.
Hear this.
The answer is not to stop pursuing holiness.
The answer is to stop treating holiness as the purchase price of God's grace.
Come back to Christ.
Let His love produce obedience rather than allowing fear to counterfeit it.
Or perhaps you have been living in the second prison.
You know what Scripture says.
You know the habit is destroying you.
You know the relationship is drawing you away from Christ.
You know the bitterness has hardened your heart.
You know the dishonesty must end.
But you have convinced yourself that because salvation is by grace, surrender can wait indefinitely.
Hear this too.
The answer is not to abandon grace.
The answer is to receive grace for what Scripture says it is: God's saving favor that also trains and transforms His people.
Do not confuse God's patience with His approval of sin.
Do not treat the wounds of Christ as permission to remain in what He died to redeem.
Today is a good day to repent.
Not because Jesus is reluctant to receive you.
But because He is worthy of your surrender.
And if you have spent years swinging between fear and compromise, perhaps today is the day to stop looking at yourself as the center of the story.
Look at Jesus.
Look at the crown of thorns.
Look at the nails.
Look at the innocent Son of God bearing the sins of the guilty.
Look at the empty tomb.
Look at the risen Savior who calls His sheep to hear His voice and follow Him.
There is your hope.
Not your flawless record.
Not your religious reputation.
Not your ability to impress other believers.
Christ.
Always Christ.
And the closer you draw to Him, the less attractive both self-righteousness and careless rebellion should become.
Because genuine grace humbles the proud and gives hope to the broken.
It tells the religious performer, "You cannot save yourself."
It tells the careless sinner, "You cannot make peace with what Christ calls you to leave behind."
It tells the repentant believer, "Keep following Jesus."
And it tells the exhausted Christian, "Your Savior is greater than your weakness."
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Not that sin was insignificant.
But that Jesus was willing to bear its terrible cost.
Not that obedience is irrelevant.
But that obedience finds its rightful place as the grateful response of a redeemed life.
Not that Christians become perfect overnight.
But that the One who begins a good work in His people is faithful to carry it forward, as Philippians 1:6 assures us.
And this is where our Gospel Warrior message becomes more than a phrase.
Think of Peter.
He promised loyalty.
He denied Jesus three times.
He wept bitterly.
And after the resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Peter's denial was not harmless.
His restoration was not cheap.
But his worst failure was not the final chapter of his life.
Think of Paul.
A persecutor of Christians.
A man whose former actions caused suffering among the very people he later served.
Yet the risen Christ confronted him, and the persecutor became a preacher of the Gospel.
Paul did not earn that calling by being a good man beforehand.
He received mercy.
And that mercy transformed the direction of his life.
Think of the criminal on the cross.
His story ended in earthly shame.
Yet Christ promised him paradise.
Three men.
Three different histories.
Three powerful reminders that Jesus Christ is able to save sinners.
But notice something.
Peter was restored to faithful service.
Paul's life was redirected toward Christ.
The dying criminal turned to Jesus with the little time he had remaining.
Different circumstances.
The same saving Savior.
And faith was never presented as a license to despise the One who saved them.
This is the message a hurting generation needs.
Not a Christianity that makes people terrified of admitting weakness.
Not a Christianity that congratulates people for remaining in rebellion.
But the Gospel of Jesus Christ, who receives repentant sinners and calls them into a new life.
A Savior holy enough to confront our sin.
Merciful enough to forgive it.
Powerful enough to transform us.
And faithful enough to sustain those who belong to Him.
If this article exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to pretend.
You can begin with an honest prayer.

"Lord Jesus, I have tried to earn what only Your grace can give. Or I have used Your grace to excuse what You are calling me to surrender. Forgive me. Teach me to trust Your finished work, turn from my sin, and follow You through the power of Your Spirit. Make my obedience an expression of love, not a performance driven by fear. Keep my eyes on You. Amen."
You do not need to expose private details to strangers to be honest about needing God's help.
And if God has been restoring you from a season of spiritual failure, your testimony may encourage someone who believes their story is already over.
Not to prove your spirituality to anyone.
But because sometimes an honest confession of our need for grace becomes the encouragement another wounded believer has been praying to find.
And please, don't let this message end with you.
We want this community to become a place where people are not simply moved by a message for a moment, but are continually directed back to the Word of God and the Savior it reveals.
That is also why I want to invite you to consider something deeper than reading, reacting, or sharing.
And certainly not because a payment can purchase His favor.
But Christian generosity can be a meaningful expression of worship when it is offered freely, responsibly, and with a sincere desire to serve others.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And Philippians 4:15–18 gives us a beautiful example of believers supporting Gospel ministry through their material generosity.
But freely given support can still be a sincere offering of gratitude to God.
It can help sustain the time, effort, resources, and continued work involved in creating, developing, and sharing Gospel-centered content.
It can help us pursue the mission of reaching more people with the message that forgiveness, repentance, and transformation are found in Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to help believers move beyond occasional inspiration into a more consistent life of biblical learning and spiritual growth.
The library's free resources remain a gift to the community, not something you must purchase to earn access to God's truth.
Those items are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply another way we can express appreciation to those who choose to stand alongside the ministry.
You are no less welcome.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share the Gospel matters.
Your presence in a community seeking to honor Jesus matters.
Our purpose is not to build a community where financial supporters are treated as more spiritually valuable than everyone else.
Our purpose is to keep pointing people to Jesus.
It is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
And that brings us back to the question that started everything.
Is obedience evidence of salvation?
Scripture teaches that genuine saving faith bears fruit, and obedience is one important expression of that fruit.
Does that mean Christians should measure their worth by flawless performance?
No.
Does grace mean we can deliberately embrace sin without concern?
No.
Does every struggling believer need to live in terror that one failure has erased the work of Christ?
No.
And does a confident profession of faith make repentance and discipleship irrelevant?
Again, no.
Obedience is not the root of our salvation. Christ is our Savior, and obedience is among the fruits of a life being transformed by His grace.
The fruit matters.
But the fruit cannot replace the Savior.

And one day, when every earthly title, ministry achievement, religious reputation, and public accomplishment has faded, none of us will stand before God boasting that we were good enough to save ourselves.
Our only hope will be the mercy of God in Jesus Christ.
So follow Him.
Not to make Him die for you again.
He already gave Himself.
Not to earn a place at a table that His grace alone can provide.
But because the Savior who calls you is worthy of your trust, your love, your repentance, and your life.
When you stumble, return to Him.
When you grow proud, remember the cross.
When you become discouraged, remember the empty tomb.
When you are tempted to compromise, remember the price of your redemption.
And when religious fear whispers that you must become perfect before Jesus will receive you, remember the criminal who turned toward a dying King and heard the promise of paradise.
He had no lifetime of good works to present.
He had a Savior to trust.
And the same Jesus who received that dying man still calls sinners to repent, believe, and follow Him today.
You do not obey to make Jesus your Savior; you obey because the Savior who rescued you is rewriting the story sin once controlled.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “IF YOUR BROTHER SINS AGAINST YOU…” — JESUS GAVE INSTRUCTIONS MOST CHRISTIANS SKIP
paragraphs: “IF YOUR BROTHER SINS AGAINST YOU…” — JESUS GAVE INSTRUCTIONS MOST CHRISTIANS SKIP

Before you expose their sin, tell your friends what happened, post about their betrayal, or decide they are dead to you… Jesus has something to say. And what He commanded in Matthew 18 may confront the way you have been handling the people who hurt you.
There is a conversation you have probably rehearsed a hundred times in your head.
You know exactly what they did.
You remember the words. The look on their face. The moment something inside you changed.
Maybe it was a friend you trusted with something you had never told anyone else.
Maybe it was someone in your church who smiled at you on Sunday, then spoke against you on Monday.
Maybe it was a brother or sister in Christ who knew your weaknesses and used them against you.
Or maybe it was someone you loved so deeply that you never imagined you would have to recover from what they did.
And now, whenever their name comes up, something happens inside your chest.
You tell yourself you have forgiven them.
You tell yourself you have moved on.
But you still remember.
You still replay the conversation.
You still imagine what you would say if you finally had the opportunity to tell everyone what really happened.
And perhaps the most painful part is that they seem perfectly fine while you are still carrying the damage.
So you talk to someone.
Then someone else.
You explain what happened. You defend yourself. You show the messages. You share the screenshots.
You want somebody to understand.
You want somebody to say, "You were right. They were wrong."
And sometimes you genuinely need help, protection, or wise counsel.
But sometimes, without realizing it, the search for understanding becomes an audience for our resentment.
The wound becomes a story.
The story becomes a reputation.
And before we have even spoken honestly to the person who hurt us, half the congregation knows what happened.
Then, somewhere in the middle of all that pain, Jesus speaks.
Not with a slogan.
Not with a motivational quotation about cutting people off.
Not with permission to pretend the offense never happened.
He gives instructions.
And the uncomfortable truth is that many of us have memorized the part of Christianity that tells us to forgive, while overlooking the part that tells us how to confront.
Listen carefully.
"Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother." — Matthew 18:15, KJV
Read those words again.
Not because they are complicated.
But because they are painfully clear.
"If thy brother shall trespass against thee..."
Jesus begins by acknowledging something many wounded Christians need to hear.
Your brother can actually sin against you.
A fellow believer can betray your trust.
A church member can lie.
A ministry leader can mistreat someone.
Someone who knows Scripture can still behave in a way that contradicts it.
Jesus does not require you to rename wrongdoing as a misunderstanding just to keep the peace.
He does not say the wound is imaginary.
He does not command you to smile while pretending that nothing happened.
He calls the offense what it is.
Sin.
But then He gives a command that cuts directly across our instincts.
"Go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone."
Go.
Not immediately to the congregation.
Not first to the group chat.
Not straight to Facebook.
Go to the person.
And here is where we need to understand the original language.
In the Greek text of Matthew 18:15, Jesus says:
ὕπαγε ἔλεγξον αὐτὸν μεταξὺ σοῦ καὶ αὐτοῦ μόνου
Hypage elenxon auton metaxy sou kai autou monou.
A faithful rendering is:
"Go, show him his fault between you and him alone."
The word ἔλεγξον (elenxon) comes from a verb meaning to expose, reprove, or bring a fault to light.
It does not mean to humiliate someone publicly for emotional satisfaction.
It is a call to confront wrongdoing truthfully.
And notice the expression μεταξὺ σοῦ καὶ αὐτοῦ μόνου — "between you and him alone."
Jesus deliberately describes a private encounter.
Why?
Because the goal is not to win an audience.
The goal is to gain a brother.
That is the part many of us have missed.
We approach conflict wanting vindication.
Jesus teaches us to pursue restoration.
We want the other person to admit we were right.
Jesus wants truth to produce repentance and, where possible, reconciliation.
We want to prove how badly someone failed us.
Jesus wants sin confronted without unnecessarily destroying the person who committed it.
And no, that does not mean every situation is safe for a private meeting.

If someone has abused, threatened, assaulted, coerced, or endangered you, you are not required to meet that person alone. Seek protection, involve appropriate authorities, and obtain trustworthy help. Criminal conduct should not be concealed under the language of church reconciliation. Matthew 18 is not a command to place yourself or others in danger.
But for ordinary interpersonal offenses where a private conversation is appropriate and safe, the instruction is astonishingly practical.
Before you make their failure public, give truth an opportunity to work privately.
Before you recruit people to your side, consider whether you have genuinely attempted to reach their conscience.
Before you assume they will never listen, ask whether you have actually spoken to them.
That last question may hurt.
Because sometimes we have had ten conversations about someone without having one honest conversation with them.
And sometimes we call it seeking prayer when, deep down, we are hoping others will share our anger.
There is a difference between seeking wise counsel and spreading damaging information unnecessarily.
There is a difference between reporting serious misconduct and broadcasting a personal offense.
There is a difference between telling the truth for protection and telling the truth as a weapon.
Truth can be spoken with sinful motives.
And being genuinely wounded does not make every response to that wound righteous.
I know.
That is difficult to receive when you are the one who was hurt.
Because pain has a way of convincing us that whatever we do next must be justified.
But Jesus loves us too much to let another person's sin become permission for our own.
And then comes one of the most beautiful phrases in the entire passage.
"If he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother."
The Greek reads:
ἐκέρδησας τὸν ἀδελφόν σου
Ekerdēsas ton adelphon sou.
"You have gained your brother."
The verb ἐκέρδησας (ekerdēsas) carries the sense of gaining or winning.
Think about that.
Jesus does not say, "You have won the argument."
He does not say, "You have defeated your enemy."
He says you have gained your brother.
What a different vision of victory.
Imagine two believers sitting across from one another.
One is trembling because speaking honestly is difficult.
The other is uncomfortable because the truth is exposing something they would rather deny.
There is no audience.
No applause.
No public humiliation.
Just truth, humility, and the possibility of repentance.
Then perhaps the offender says words that seemed impossible only yesterday.
"I was wrong."
"I should never have said that."
"I hurt you."
"Will you forgive me?"
And suddenly, what could have become years of bitterness begins moving toward healing.
Not because the sin was small.
Not because the wound was imaginary.
But because someone obeyed Jesus when retaliation would have been easier.
This is what restoration can look like.
Not always.
Not automatically.
But sometimes.
And those moments matter.
Because there are friendships that might still exist if someone had spoken privately before speaking publicly.
There are families that might have avoided years of unnecessary division.
There are churches where conflicts might have been addressed before rumors multiplied.
Not every relationship can or should be restored to its previous level of closeness. Trust may require time, accountability, changed behavior, and appropriate boundaries.
But where genuine repentance and safe reconciliation are possible, Christians should not treat restoration as an embarrassing defeat.
It is something worth pursuing.
Now perhaps you are thinking:
"But what if I go to them and they refuse to listen?"
Jesus anticipated that.
"But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established." — Matthew 18:16, KJV
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say, "If they refuse, tell everybody."
He introduces another measured step.
Bring one or two others.
Why?
Not to assemble a cheering section.
Not to intimidate the offender.
Not to make the confrontation feel like an ambush.
The witnesses help establish what is said, clarify the facts, and support a just and accountable process.
Jesus echoes the principle found in Deuteronomy 19:15, where matters are established through adequate testimony.
In other words, righteousness requires more than strong feelings.
It requires truth.
It requires fairness.
It requires listening.
It requires the humility to recognize that even when we have been hurt, our understanding of every detail may not be complete.
That is hard to admit.
Especially when the pain feels undeniable.
But Scripture does not teach that emotional certainty is the same as complete knowledge.
Proverbs 18:17 says:
"He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him."
The first account may sound convincing until further examination.
That does not mean every accusation is false.
It means justice must be careful.
And Christians, of all people, should understand why.
We serve a Savior who was falsely accused.
A Savior whose enemies twisted His words.
A Savior who stood before people determined to condemn Him.
We should never be careless with another person's reputation.
Even when confrontation is necessary.
Even when wrongdoing is real.
Then Jesus continues.
"And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church..." — Matthew 18:17, KJV
Only now does the process reach the wider church community.
Not as entertainment.
Not as an invitation to gossip.
Not as a social media spectacle.
But as a serious matter requiring responsible spiritual oversight and accountability.
And if the offender refuses even the church's correction, Jesus describes a change in how that person is to be regarded.
This is sobering.
Church discipline is not supposed to be a performance of superiority. It is a serious response to persistent, unrepentant sin, carried out with justice, humility, and a desire for repentance.
The apostle Paul expresses that restorative concern in Galatians 6:1:
"Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted."
Restore.
In meekness.
While remembering your own vulnerability.
That is not the language of a spiritual mob.
That is the language of a family that understands both the seriousness of sin and the necessity of grace.
And this is where the passage becomes even more uncomfortable.
Because some of us are reading this while thinking about the person who wronged us.
But what if the Holy Spirit is also showing us how we have wronged someone else?
What if we have been the one who refused correction?
What if someone tried to speak to us privately, and we became defensive?
What if they told us we had hurt them, and instead of listening, we immediately began explaining why their feelings were unreasonable?
What if we apologized with words that sounded like repentance but actually shifted the blame?
"I'm sorry you felt that way."
"I'm sorry you misunderstood."
"I'm sorry, but you made me angry."
What if the hardest sentence for us to say is simply:
"I sinned against you, and I was wrong."
There is a particular kind of pride that hides behind religious language.
It quotes verses.
It serves in ministry.
It knows how to pray in public.
But it cannot bear to be corrected in private.
And Scripture confronts that pride.
"He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy." — Proverbs 28:13, KJV
Confession without forsaking sin is incomplete.
An apology without genuine change may be nothing more than an attempt to end an uncomfortable conversation.
And repentance is more than feeling bad because someone discovered what we did.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) is commonly translated "repentance." It speaks of a change of mind or heart that, in biblical teaching, is expressed through a changed direction of life.
Real repentance does not merely ask, "How can I make this problem disappear?"
It asks, "How have I sinned before God, and what must change?"
Sometimes repentance includes restitution.
Sometimes it requires admitting the truth to people we misled.
Sometimes it means accepting consequences.
Sometimes it means understanding that forgiveness does not automatically restore the trust we damaged.
And sometimes it means giving the person we hurt the time and space they need.
Because grace is not permission to escape accountability.
Grace teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly.
That is transforming grace.
Not grace that protects our pride.
Grace that changes us.
But now we must look at what happens immediately after Jesus gives these instructions.
Because Matthew 18 does not end with confrontation.
Peter approaches Jesus with a question that sounds very familiar to anyone who has ever grown tired of forgiving.
"Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?" — Matthew 18:21, KJV
You can almost hear the exhaustion.
How many times, Lord?
How many times do I have to deal with this?
How many times must I release my desire for revenge?
How many times can somebody hurt me before I am finally allowed to stop forgiving?
Peter suggests seven times.
That probably sounded generous.
But Jesus responds:
"I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." — Matthew 18:22, KJV
Jesus is not giving Peter a literal quota of 490 offenses.
He is overturning the idea that forgiveness should be managed with a scorecard.
Then He tells the parable of the unforgiving servant.
A man owes his king an enormous debt.
He cannot pay.
Judgment is approaching.
He begs for mercy.
And the king, moved with compassion, releases him and forgives the debt.
Imagine the relief.
Imagine walking out of that room knowing the burden you could never repay has been lifted.
But then the forgiven servant finds another servant who owes him a much smaller amount.
He grabs him.
Demands payment.
Refuses mercy.
The man who had just received extraordinary forgiveness becomes merciless toward someone else.
And Jesus exposes the contradiction.
How can a person receive such great mercy and then refuse to extend mercy?
This is where the story stops being about the person who offended you.
And starts being about your heart before God.
Because the Gospel begins with a debt we could never pay.
Not a financial debt.
A moral and spiritual debt created by our sin.
We have not merely been misunderstood.
We have sinned against a holy God.
We have loved things more than Him.
We have spoken words we should never have spoken.
We have concealed motives.
We have entertained bitterness.
We have justified pride.
We have failed to love our neighbors as ourselves.
And the frightening truth is that no amount of religious activity can erase our guilt.
We cannot purchase forgiveness.
We cannot earn salvation through good behavior.
We cannot make ourselves righteous by comparing our sins with somebody else's.
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." — Romans 3:23, KJV
All.
The person who hurt you.
And you.
The person who betrayed your trust.
And you.
The person whose sin became public.
And the person whose sin remained hidden.
All of us need mercy.
And then comes Jesus Christ.
The sinless Son of God.
The One who never lied.
Never betrayed.
Never acted from selfish pride.
Never sinned against His Father.
Yet He willingly gave Himself for sinners.
At the cross, Jesus did not pretend sin was harmless.
He bore its judgment.
He did not dismiss evil as insignificant.
He gave His life to redeem people from it.
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." — Romans 5:8, KJV
While we were still sinners.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we became worthy.
Not after we finally learned how to behave.
Christ died for us while we were guilty.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are proclaimed to everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith.
This is why Christian forgiveness is so different from pretending nothing happened.
God's forgiveness is not denial.
It is mercy grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And when we understand how much mercy we have received, it begins to change how we treat those who sin against us.
Not by making evil acceptable.
Not by removing appropriate consequences.
Not by requiring victims to remain in harmful situations.
But by loosening the grip of vengeance on our hearts.
Romans 12:19 reminds believers not to avenge themselves, but to leave vengeance to God.
And Ephesians 4:32 says:
"And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you."
For Christ's sake.
There it is.
The center of everything.
We do not forgive because the offense was insignificant.
We forgive because Christ has shown us mercy beyond anything we could earn.
And we do not confront because we enjoy exposing people.
We confront because truth matters, sin destroys, and love must sometimes say difficult things.
Jesus Himself holds grace and truth together.
John 1:14 describes Him as "full of grace and truth."
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Both.
And this is the balance so many Christians desperately need.
Some people use forgiveness to avoid necessary confrontation.
They remain silent while resentment grows.
They say, "I forgive you," but never address patterns that continue damaging the relationship.
Others use confrontation as an excuse to punish.
They expose, embarrass, and condemn, then call it biblical accountability.
But Jesus calls us to something better.
Truth without cruelty.
Mercy without denial.
Courage without arrogance.
Forgiveness without pretending that repentance, accountability, and trust are meaningless.
And perhaps the most searching question is this:
Do you actually want your brother or sister restored, or do you only want them exposed?
Think carefully before answering.
Because sometimes we become so attached to being the injured person that the possibility of reconciliation almost feels threatening.
We have told the story so many times.
We have received sympathy.
We have built our understanding of the relationship around what they did.
And now, if they genuinely repent, we may have to release the version of the story in which they are only the villain and we are only the victim.
That does not mean the harm disappears.
It does not mean reconciliation is always possible.
It does not mean trust should be restored without evidence of change.
But it does mean we must examine whether bitterness has become part of our identity.
Hebrews 12:15 warns believers about a root of bitterness that can spring up and trouble many.
Notice that bitterness rarely remains private.
It spreads.
It influences how we interpret people.
It changes how we speak.
It teaches us to expect betrayal everywhere.
And sometimes it makes us suspicious of people who never harmed us.
One wound begins shaping an entire life.
Perhaps that is where you are today.
You still attend church.
You still listen to sermons.
You still post Scripture.
You still tell people that God is good.
But there is a name you cannot hear without anger rising inside you.
And you are tired.
Tired of remembering.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of carrying a conversation that never happened.
You may not be ready to speak to that person today.
You may need counsel.
You may need distance.
You may need protection.
You may need to grieve what was lost.
But you can begin by bringing the truth of your heart before Jesus.
Not the polished version.
The real one.
"Lord, I am angry."
"Lord, I feel betrayed."
"Lord, I want them to understand what they did."
"Lord, I don't know how to forgive."
"Lord, I am afraid that if I let go of this bitterness, nobody will ever acknowledge what happened."
God is not confused by your pain.
Psalm 62:8 invites His people to pour out their hearts before Him.
You do not have to manufacture an emotion you do not feel.
But you can surrender your desire for revenge.
You can ask God for wisdom.
You can refuse to turn your wound into a weapon.
You can choose to pursue truth in a way that honors Christ.
And if the person who hurt you never repents?
That is a painful possibility.
Matthew 18 itself recognizes that some people refuse correction.
You cannot force repentance.
You cannot make another person acknowledge what they did.
You cannot single-handedly restore a relationship that requires honesty and willingness from both sides.
Romans 12:18 says:
"If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men."
Those words matter.
"If it be possible."
"As much as lieth in you."
Scripture recognizes that peace is not always achievable through one person's efforts.
You are responsible for your obedience.
You are not responsible for controlling another person's heart.
And sometimes the most faithful response is to forgive while maintaining necessary boundaries, seeking appropriate accountability, and entrusting the unresolved matter to God.
But there is another side of this message.
Maybe you are not the wounded person in the story.
Maybe you are the one who caused the wound.
Maybe somebody tried to tell you.
Maybe they said, "What you did hurt me."
And you dismissed them.
Maybe you accused them of being too sensitive.
Maybe you brought up their past mistakes to avoid discussing your own.
Maybe you recruited friends to defend you.
Maybe you have spent years telling your version of events because you are terrified of what admitting the truth might cost.
Listen.
There is still mercy in Christ for repentant sinners.
You do not have to keep defending what God is calling you to confess.
You do not have to spend the rest of your life protecting a false image of yourself.
You can humble yourself.
You can tell the truth.
You can apologize without excuses.
You can make restitution where appropriate.
You can accept accountability.
And you can ask Jesus to transform the heart that produced the sin.
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — 1 John 1:9, KJV
What a promise.
Not that confession removes every earthly consequence.
Not that every broken relationship will immediately be restored.
But that God is faithful to forgive and cleanse those who come to Him according to His promise.
This is the beauty of the Gospel.
It does not merely tell wounded people to become stronger.
It offers them a Savior.
It does not merely tell guilty people to become better.
It offers them forgiveness and a new life through Jesus Christ.
It does not merely expose sin.
It announces redemption.
And that brings us to something we cannot afford to miss.
The same chapter that teaches us how to confront a sinning brother also reveals the heart of a Father who cares for the wandering.
In Matthew 18:12–14, Jesus speaks of a shepherd who seeks a sheep that has gone astray.
The surrounding context reminds us that God's concern is not merely procedural correctness.
He cares about people.
About those who wander.
About those who need to be brought back.
About those who must be protected.
About those whose souls are in danger.
That does not erase the need for discernment or accountability.
It reveals why those things matter.
Biblical correction should never become an excuse to enjoy someone's downfall.
And biblical compassion should never become an excuse to ignore serious sin.
The church belongs to Jesus.
Its purpose is not to protect appearances at the expense of truth.
Its calling is to honor Christ through holiness, justice, mercy, love, and faithfulness.
Imagine what would change if believers began taking Matthew 18 seriously.
Imagine Christians who refused to spread rumors simply because they were angry.
Imagine leaders who listened carefully rather than automatically defending their friends.
Imagine people who admitted wrongdoing without blaming those they hurt.
Imagine churches that protected vulnerable people while pursuing fair and responsible accountability.
Imagine friendships where difficult conversations happened before resentment became hatred.
Imagine families where the words "I was wrong" were no longer treated as humiliation.
Imagine a community where grace was not confused with secrecy and truth was not confused with cruelty.
Would every relationship be repaired?
No.
Would every offender repent?
No.
Would every wound disappear?
No.
But Christ would be honored through obedience.
And that matters more than winning an argument.
Perhaps you are reading this with tears in your eyes because someone came to mind.
Perhaps it is a person you need to approach.
Perhaps it is someone you need to forgive.
Perhaps it is someone you need to stop speaking against.
Perhaps it is someone you owe a genuine apology.
Or perhaps you need to seek help because what happened was too serious to handle alone.
Whatever your situation, do not turn this passage into another weapon against someone else.
Let it examine your own heart first.
Ask yourself:
Have I pursued truth or merely sympathy?
Have I sought restoration or retaliation?
Have I spoken with humility?
Have I listened when corrected?
Have I confused forgiveness with the absence of boundaries?
Have I allowed bitterness to become a permanent residence in my heart?
And most importantly:
Am I willing to obey Jesus even when His instructions challenge what I feel entitled to do?
Because following Christ is not merely agreeing with His words when they comfort us.
It is submitting to His authority when they confront us.
Jesus said in Luke 6:46:
"And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?"
That question should stop us.
We cannot claim that Jesus is Lord while treating His commands as optional whenever obedience becomes inconvenient.
But remember this too.
Our obedience does not purchase God's love.
We obey because He first loved us.
We pursue holiness because His grace has reached us.
We forgive because we have been forgiven.
We confront sin because Christ is worthy of truth.
We pursue reconciliation where possible because Jesus has reconciled sinners to God through His cross.
And when we fail, we return to Him in repentance.
Again.
And again.
Not because grace is cheap.
But because Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
That is why the theme of Gospel Warrior is more than a memorable phrase.
Think of Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
Not privately in the safety of his own thoughts.
Openly.
Under pressure.
He denied knowing the Lord he had promised never to abandon.
Then the rooster crowed.
And Peter wept bitterly.
Imagine the shame.
The memory of his own voice.
The knowledge that he had failed the One who loved him.
But Peter's failure was not the final chapter.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter and, in John 21, lovingly recommissioned him to care for His sheep.
Peter was not restored because denial was harmless.
He was restored by the grace of the risen Christ.
The same Peter who once denied his Lord later boldly proclaimed Him.
That is not a story about human perfection.
It is a testimony to the power of Jesus.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to know that their worst chapter does not have to become their final chapter.
If you are the one who sinned, repent and come to Christ.
If you are the one who was wounded, bring your pain to Christ.
If you are caught in bitterness, ask Christ to free your heart.
If you are afraid to tell the truth, ask Christ for courage.
If you have been hiding behind a religious appearance, stop running from the Savior who already knows the truth.
Jesus is not asking you to save yourself.
He is calling you to follow Him.
And that changes everything.
Before you leave this article, I want to ask you something personal.
Not for appearances.
Not to make yourself look spiritual.
But because there may be another believer reading the comments who thinks they are the only one struggling.
If you are exhausted from carrying a wound, you can comment, "Pray for me."
If you recognize that you have been avoiding a necessary apology, you can comment, "Lord, humble my heart."
If this message has challenged how you handle conflict, you can comment, "Teach me to obey, Jesus."
And if you have experienced genuine restoration through repentance and forgiveness, consider sharing a brief testimony. Your experience may encourage someone who has almost given up hope.
You do not have to reveal names, private details, or traumatic experiences publicly. God knows the prayers you cannot safely put into a comment.
And please, do not let this message stop with you.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be one angry conversation away from destroying a relationship that could still be repaired.
Someone may be carrying resentment that has quietly consumed years of their life.
Someone may be using Christian language to avoid admitting wrongdoing.
Someone may desperately need to hear that forgiveness is possible without surrendering safety or accountability.
Because a single article can challenge a heart.
But growing as a disciple requires continuing in the Word.
And that is why we are building something deeper than a collection of inspirational posts.
Our desire is to make biblical nourishment accessible, to help people understand Scripture in context, to encourage genuine repentance, and to point wounded and wandering hearts toward the Savior.
But producing, maintaining, and expanding this ministry takes ongoing support.
Not because you can purchase God's favor.
And certainly not because paying a ministry is a requirement for glorifying God.
You glorify God by trusting and obeying Jesus Christ, and one meaningful way you may choose to express that devotion is by generously supporting faithful Gospel ministry.
In Philippians 4:15–17, Paul acknowledges the generosity of believers who supported his ministry, describing their partnership as fruit credited to their account.
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That last phrase matters.
Not grudgingly.
Not under compulsion.
Christian generosity should come from a willing heart.
Think about the person scrolling through Facebook late at night.
The believer who feels ashamed after falling into sin again.
The husband and wife who have stopped speaking.
The young person who is questioning whether God still cares.
The wounded Christian who has nearly abandoned church altogether.
The person who has never understood the Gospel clearly.
We cannot know in advance who will encounter a message or how God may use it.
But we can faithfully continue sowing the seed of His Word.
These items are simply expressions of appreciation. They are not spiritual rewards, and the discount is not a substitute for the eternal treasure found in Christ.
It is the opportunity to participate in making the message of Jesus Christ more widely known.
Pray for this ministry.
Sometimes a simple act of sharing brings Scripture to a person who might never have searched for it.
Your participation matters, even when you cannot contribute financially.
Because the mission has never been to build an audience around a personality.
It is to point people toward Jesus Christ.
And that brings us back to the words with which we began.
"If thy brother shall trespass against thee..."
Maybe the person who came to mind at the beginning of this article is still on your heart.
Maybe you now understand that you need to have a difficult conversation.
Maybe you need to repent before expecting someone else to repent.
Maybe you need to stop repeating a story that no longer needs another audience.
Maybe you need to tell a trusted leader about serious wrongdoing that must not remain hidden.
Maybe you need to forgive while accepting that reconciliation is not presently safe or possible.
Or maybe, for the first time in a long time, you need to stop looking at everybody else's sin and bring your own heart before the cross.
Whatever the next faithful step looks like, take it with Jesus.
Not with pride.
Not with revenge.
Not with fear disguised as wisdom.
With truth.
With humility.
With courage.
With grace.
Because the goal is not simply to have the last word.
The goal is to honor the One who gave His life to reconcile sinners to God.

And one day, when the arguments are over, when the posts have disappeared, when the people who applauded our anger have moved on, and when every hidden motive stands before the Lord, what will matter is not how successfully we defended our pride.
What will matter is whether we belonged to Jesus and followed Him in faith.
So before you expose your brother's sin, remember Matthew 18.
Before you excuse your own sin, remember the cross.
Before you surrender to bitterness, remember the mercy you have received.
And before you decide that a broken story can never be redeemed, remember the empty tomb.
The wound may explain why you are hurting, but it does not have to become the author of who you are becoming. Jesus can write the next chapter.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF POLYGAMY IS WRONG, WHY DID GOD ALLOW ABRAHAM, JACOB, DAVID, AND SOLOMON TO HAVE MULTIPLE WIVES?
paragraphs: IF POLYGAMY IS WRONG, WHY DID GOD ALLOW ABRAHAM, JACOB, DAVID, AND SOLOMON TO HAVE MULTIPLE WIVES?

The Bible records men with many wives. Some were called righteous. Some were kings chosen by God. So was polygamy ever God's plan—or have we misunderstood the difference between what Scripture records, what God permits, and what He actually desires?
There is a question that has troubled believers, fascinated skeptics, and left more than a few Christians struggling to explain their own Bible.
And the uncomfortable part?
It's a fair question.

If marriage is supposed to be between one man and one woman, why did Abraham have Sarah and Hagar? Why did Jacob marry Leah and Rachel? Why did David have multiple wives? And why did Solomon, a king blessed with extraordinary wisdom, end up with seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines?
These weren't merely obscure men hiding in the shadows of biblical history.
Abraham was called God's friend (James 2:23).
Jacob became Israel, the father of the twelve tribes.
David was described as a man after God's own heart (Acts 13:22).
Solomon was entrusted with extraordinary wisdom.
Yet their households tell stories that would break the hearts of almost anyone who has ever loved someone, feared being replaced, experienced jealousy, or wondered whether they were enough.
So here is the question we cannot afford to avoid.
If God is holy, why does His Word contain so many stories of men practicing something Christians generally teach is contrary to His design for marriage?
Was God changing His standards?
Was He making exceptions for powerful men?

Or is there something much deeper happening in these ancient accounts—something that exposes not a contradiction in God's character, but the terrifying human tendency to confuse God's patience with God's approval?
Because once you see what is happening from Genesis to the words of Jesus Christ, you may never read these stories the same way again.
And you may discover that this question is not ultimately about how many wives a man could have.
It is about what happens when human beings take something God created to be beautiful and attempt to improve it by following their own desires.
It begins in a garden.
Not in a palace.
Not in a king's bedroom.
Not with Abraham.
Not with David.
Not with Solomon.

In a garden, before sin entered the world, before jealousy poisoned relationships, before women competed for affection, and before powerful men began treating marriage as an instrument of wealth, political influence, or personal gratification.
Genesis 2:24 declares:
"Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh." (KJV)
The Hebrew reads:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Al-ken ya'azov ish et-aviv ve'et-immo, vedavaq be'ishto, vehayu levasar echad.
The final words matter enormously.
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד — vehayu levasar echad.
"And they shall become one flesh."
The Hebrew word echad means "one." In this passage, the expression describes the profound union formed through marriage.
But we must be careful here.

The Hebrew word echad by itself does not prove monogamy. Scripture uses the word "one" in different contexts, and forcing it to carry an argument it was never intended to carry would weaken rather than strengthen biblical interpretation.
The force of Genesis 2:24 comes from the entire creation narrative.
God creates the man.
God creates the woman.
God brings them together.
And Scripture presents their union as the foundational pattern of marriage.
One man.
One woman.
A covenantal union described as becoming one flesh.
There is no rivalry for Adam's affection.
No second wife standing outside the garden.
No woman wondering whether she will be loved tomorrow.
No household divided into competing mothers and children.
The picture is not of a man collecting wives.
It is of two people joined together.
And centuries later, when religious leaders questioned Jesus about marriage and divorce, He did something extraordinary.
He did not begin with the customs of Abraham.
