He did not appeal to the royal household of David.
He did not point to Solomon's wealth or wisdom.
He went back to creation.
Jesus said:
"Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female,
And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder." (Matthew 19:4–6, KJV)
Notice what Jesus did.
He interpreted marriage by returning to what God established "at the beginning."
The Greek of Matthew 19:5 includes the words:
καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
Kai esontai hoi dyo eis sarka mian.
"And the two shall become one flesh."
There is a word in Jesus' quotation that deserves our attention.
δύο — dyo.
"Two."
Jesus explicitly speaks of the two becoming one flesh.
His immediate subject is divorce, not a direct debate over polygamy. We should not pretend otherwise.
But His appeal to the original creation pattern is foundational to the Christian understanding of marriage as an exclusive union between one man and one woman.
When Jesus was asked to explain what marriage should be, He pointed beyond the complicated arrangements tolerated throughout Israel's history.
He pointed back to God's beginning.
And that distinction changes everything.
The Bible can truthfully describe what people did without declaring that everything they did was righteous.
Read that again.
Because much of the confusion disappears when we learn to distinguish between biblical description and biblical prescription.
Description tells us what happened.
Prescription tells us what ought to happen.
Scripture records murder.
That does not make murder holy.
It records adultery.
That does not make adultery acceptable.
It records deception, slavery, idolatry, betrayal, drunkenness, violence, and the exploitation of vulnerable people.
But recording these things is not the same as commanding or celebrating them.
The Bible is remarkably honest about the people God worked through.
And that honesty is one reason its stories can be so unsettling.
It does not airbrush its heroes.
It does not conceal their moral failures to protect their reputations.
It tells us that Abraham believed God—and also acted out of fear.
It tells us that David worshiped God—and also committed terrible sins.
It tells us that Solomon received wisdom—and later allowed his heart to turn away.
The Bible is not a collection of perfect people demonstrating their perfection.
It is the unfolding revelation of a holy God working in a world profoundly damaged by sin.
And when we examine the earliest biblical account of polygamy, the setting should make us uncomfortable.
The first man explicitly described as taking two wives is not Abraham.
It is Lamech.
Genesis 4:19 says:
"And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah." (KJV)
Lamech appears in the line of Cain, in a narrative that also records his boast about killing a man and his escalating language of vengeance (Genesis 4:23–24).
This does not mean the text explicitly says his two marriages caused his violence.
It does not.
But it is significant that the Bible first introduces plural marriage in a morally troubled context rather than in the original creation account.
And as the biblical story unfolds, the repeated household conflicts become difficult to ignore.
Consider Abraham.
God promised him descendants.
God promised that his offspring would become a great nation.
But years passed.
Sarah remained unable to conceive.
And waiting became painful.
Genesis 16 tells us that Sarah gave her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abraham as a wife so that they might obtain a child through her.
This arrangement reflected a recognizable ancient social practice.
But the fact that something was culturally practiced did not make its consequences harmless.
Hagar conceived.
And almost immediately, the household began to fracture.
Genesis 16:4 records that after Hagar conceived, Sarah was despised in her eyes, as the KJV renders it.
Sarah responded with anger.
Abraham failed to resolve the conflict justly.
Hagar was treated harshly.
And she fled.
Imagine the scene.
One woman desperate for a child.
Another woman placed into a situation shaped by her mistress's expectations and her master's authority.
A husband caught in a conflict that should never be reduced to a simple love triangle.
And an unborn child whose future was entangled in adult decisions he did not make.
This is not a romantic celebration of plural marriage.
It is a deeply painful account of impatience, power, vulnerability, and broken relationships.
Yet something beautiful happens in the middle of that tragedy.
God sees Hagar.
Not merely Sarah.
Not merely Abraham.
Hagar.
A foreign woman.
A servant.
A person whose suffering could easily have been overlooked.
Genesis 16:13 records her response to the Lord who spoke to her.
She identifies Him as the God who sees her.
The Hebrew expression associated with this passage is:
אֵל רֳאִי — El Ro'i.
Commonly understood as "God who sees me," although the precise nuance of the Hebrew phrase has been discussed by interpreters.
Do not miss the beauty of this.
God's care for Hagar does not mean He approved every decision that placed her in that situation.
It means human failure did not place her beyond His compassion.
The God of Scripture was not blind to the woman suffering inside the household of a man of faith.
And perhaps someone reading this knows what that feels like.
To be caught in somebody else's decisions.
To suffer because someone with greater power chose what benefited them.
To feel like the overlooked person in a story where everyone else seems more important.
Hagar's account reminds us that God sees people whom society may ignore.
But the consequences within Abraham's household did not simply disappear.
Years later, the tensions surrounding Isaac and Ishmael resulted in another heartbreaking separation (Genesis 21:8–21).
God continued to care for Hagar and Ishmael.
But the family still experienced pain.
That is an important biblical distinction.
God's faithfulness to people living with the consequences of human decisions is not the same as God's approval of those decisions.
Now consider Jacob.
If Abraham's household makes you uncomfortable, Jacob's household may leave you heartbroken.
Jacob loved Rachel.
He worked seven years to marry her.
Genesis 29:20 says those years seemed like only a few days because of his love for her.
There is something deeply moving about that description.
Seven years of labor.
Seven years of anticipation.
Seven years of looking forward to building a life with the woman he loved.
Then came the wedding.
And the deception.
Laban gave Leah to Jacob instead.
Jacob later married Rachel as well.
And what followed was not the beautiful family arrangement that romanticized portrayals of polygamy might lead us to expect.
It was a household filled with painful comparison.
Genesis 29:30 says Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
Imagine being Leah.
Married.
Present.
Giving your life to a family.
Yet knowing your husband loved another woman more.
Imagine waking up beside a man whose heart was elsewhere.
Imagine bearing children while hoping that each birth might finally make him love you.
Genesis 29:32 records Leah saying:
"Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me." (KJV)
There is an entire lifetime of emotional longing inside that sentence.
"Now therefore my husband will love me."
Not simply, "I have a son."
Not simply, "God has blessed me."
But perhaps now...
Perhaps after this child...
Perhaps after I give him something valuable...
He will love me.
How many people today are still living with that same aching question?
What more must I do to be chosen?
What more must I give to be enough?
How much of myself must I surrender before someone finally loves me without comparison?
Leah's pain was real.
Rachel's pain was real too.
Rachel struggled with infertility while watching her sister bear children.
Genesis 30:1 records Rachel saying to Jacob:
"Give me children, or else I die." (KJV)
That is not the language of a peaceful household.
It is the cry of a woman overwhelmed by grief and desperation.
Eventually, the family arrangement expanded through Bilhah and Zilpah, the servants of Rachel and Leah.
The women and children became caught in a complicated struggle over fertility, status, and affection.
The text does not invite us to celebrate this rivalry.
It invites us to see the suffering.
And yet God continued working through that deeply imperfect family.
The sons born within it became the ancestors of Israel's tribes.
Does that mean God endorsed every part of the arrangement?
No.
It means God's redemptive purposes were not defeated by the failures of the people through whom He worked.
That distinction is essential.
God can bring redemption out of a broken situation without calling the brokenness good.
Then we come to David.
A man who loved God.
A musician.
A shepherd.
A warrior.
A king.
A man who wrote psalms that still comfort suffering believers thousands of years later.
And a man whose personal failures caused extraordinary devastation.
David had multiple wives, as passages such as 2 Samuel 3:2–5 and 5:13 make clear.
But Scripture never tells us that his accumulation of wives was the reason God loved him.
In fact, Deuteronomy 17:17 had already warned Israel's future kings:
"Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away." (KJV)
This matters because some people argue that the Old Testament simply treated unlimited polygamy as a divine ideal.
It did not.
The law contained restrictions that acknowledged plural marriages within Israelite society.
Exodus 21:10, for example, protected a wife's rights to food, clothing, and marital obligations if another wife was taken.
Deuteronomy 21:15–17 regulated inheritance in a household with two wives, preventing a father from unjustly depriving his firstborn son because he preferred another wife.
These laws are important because they show that the issue is more complicated than saying the Old Testament explicitly prohibited every instance of polygamy.
It did not.
Plural marriage was tolerated and regulated in ancient Israel.
But regulation is not necessarily endorsement as an ideal.
Laws addressing difficult social realities can restrain injustice without presenting those realities as the fullest expression of God's intention.
Jesus Himself gives us a vital interpretive principle in Matthew 19:8.
When discussing Moses' permission concerning divorce, He explains that this concession was related to hardness of heart.
Then He says:
"But from the beginning it was not so." (KJV)
Jesus is speaking specifically about divorce.
We should not claim that He explicitly applied that statement to every Old Testament plural marriage.

Nevertheless, His distinction between an accommodated practice and God's original intention helps us understand why Christians look to creation and Christ's teaching when discerning the design of marriage.
Now return to David.
His story contains an especially devastating example of what happens when power is used to take what belongs to another.
In 2 Samuel 11, David saw Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah.
He sent for her.
He slept with her.
She became pregnant.
And David eventually arranged circumstances that led to Uriah's death.
This was not simply another episode of polygamy.
It was an abuse of royal power, adultery, and a grave act of injustice.
The prophet Nathan confronted David.
And the consequences were severe.
The biblical narrative does not treat David's status as king as permission to escape moral accountability.
He was chosen.
He was gifted.
He was powerful.
And he was still answerable to God.
The lesson is uncomfortable because it exposes something that religious people sometimes forget.
Being used by God does not mean every choice you make is approved by God.
Spiritual gifts are not proof of moral perfection.
Public ministry is not a substitute for private obedience.
A beautiful worship song does not erase an act of injustice.
And a title, a platform, or a reputation for faith cannot make sin righteous.
David's life teaches us that a person can genuinely love God and still commit grievous evil.
That does not excuse the evil.
It makes repentance necessary.
Psalm 51, traditionally associated with David's repentance after Nathan confronted him, gives us words that reveal the proper response to sin.
"Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." (Psalm 51:10, KJV)
Not, "God, explain why my position makes this acceptable."
Not, "Everyone else was doing it."
Not, "I have done too much for You to be judged."
But:
"Create in me a clean heart."
And this brings us to Solomon.
Perhaps no biblical figure illustrates the danger of multiplied wives more explicitly.
Solomon began with extraordinary privileges.
God gave him wisdom.
He built the temple.
He possessed wealth and influence.
Yet 1 Kings 11:3 records:
"And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines: and his wives turned away his heart." (KJV)
The passage is painfully direct.
His wives turned away his heart.
The surrounding verses explain that his marriages to foreign women were connected with his participation in the worship of other gods, contrary to God's commands.
The point is not that foreign women as an ethnic group were inherently corrupt.
The text's concern is covenant unfaithfulness and idolatry.
Nor does the passage teach that every woman Solomon married was personally responsible for his sin.
Solomon himself was accountable for his decisions.
He multiplied wives despite the warning given to Israel's kings.
He allowed competing loyalties to draw his heart away from the Lord.
The man who possessed extraordinary wisdom still needed obedience.
The man who built the temple still needed faithfulness.
The man who understood so much still failed to guard his own heart.
And there is something deeply sobering about that.
You can know Scripture and still disobey it.
You can understand theology and still justify your desires.
You can speak beautifully about God while quietly making compromises that are destroying your spiritual life.
Solomon's tragedy was not a lack of information.
It was a failure of faithfulness.
And perhaps this is where the question about polygamy begins to reach beyond ancient marriage customs.
Because human beings still do this.
We search Scripture for permission to keep what we do not want to surrender.
We find a flawed biblical character and say, "But he did it."
We point to someone's blessing and assume everything in that person's life must have God's approval.
We confuse God's mercy with His endorsement.
And sometimes we are less interested in what God actually desires than in how much of our own desire we can keep while still calling ourselves obedient.
That is not merely an ancient problem.
It is a human problem.
But someone may still raise a difficult objection.
"What about 2 Samuel 12:8? Doesn't God say He gave David his master's wives?"
That question deserves a serious answer.
In Nathan's confrontation with David, God speaks of giving him his master's house and his master's wives into his bosom, as the KJV renders the passage.
This language cannot simply be ignored.
It is part of Scripture.
The verse occurs in a royal context, where the transfer of a predecessor's household could symbolize the transfer of royal status and authority.

Interpreters differ over whether the statement should be understood as a literal transfer of Saul's wives to David or as language representing the royal household and privileges associated with kingship.
The passage does not independently establish that every royal marriage was God's original ideal.
But neither should we pretend the verse is absent or easy.
A faithful interpretation must hold it alongside Genesis 2:24, Deuteronomy 17:17, the regulations of Mosaic law, the prophetic warnings, and Jesus' teaching about marriage.
And we should acknowledge another important distinction.
The Old Testament does not consistently describe every plural marriage as a personal sin in the same way it explicitly condemns adultery.
Its legal treatment of polygamy is more nuanced than that.

The Christian conclusion that monogamy expresses God's design for marriage is drawn from the broader canonical witness, especially creation and the teaching of Christ, rather than from pretending there is a single Old Testament verse that simply says, "Every man with more than one wife is guilty of adultery."
Biblical faithfulness requires honesty about what the text says—and what it does not say.
We do not honor God by making Scripture appear simpler than it is.
We honor Him by handling it truthfully.
And that includes another challenging observation.
God did not abandon Abraham.
He did not erase Jacob.
He did not remove David's psalms from Scripture.
He did not pretend Solomon never existed.
But neither did He conceal their failures.
Why?
Because God's redemptive story is not built on the moral perfection of Abraham, Jacob, David, or Solomon.
It is ultimately fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
And this is where everything changes.
Jesus did not come merely to settle an ancient argument about marriage arrangements.
He came to redeem sinners and restore people to God.
The apostle Paul describes marriage in Ephesians 5:31–32 by quoting the one-flesh language of Genesis and then connecting it to Christ and the church.
He writes:
This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church." (KJV)
Notice the pattern.
The two become one flesh.
And Paul sees in marriage a profound relationship to the covenantal union between Christ and His people.
Christian marriage is therefore not merely a private arrangement for fulfilling personal desires.
It is called to reflect faithful, sacrificial, covenantal love.
That is why the New Testament repeatedly places such emphasis on marital faithfulness.
In 1 Corinthians 7:2, Paul speaks of each man having his own wife and each woman her own husband.

In 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:6, church overseers are described using the expression commonly translated "the husband of one wife," with interpretive discussion about the full implications of that qualification.
These passages belong to the wider New Testament picture of marital fidelity, self-control, and covenant responsibility.
And when we look at Jesus Himself, we encounter something more beautiful than the accumulation of relationships for personal advantage.
We encounter the Bridegroom who gives Himself for His bride.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
That is the opposite of using another person merely to satisfy one's own desires.
Christ does not exploit His bride.
He sacrifices Himself for her.
He does not treat her as disposable.
He loves her with covenantal faithfulness.
He does not seek power over her for selfish gain.
He gives Himself for her good.
And that changes the question.
Instead of asking, "How many wives did ancient men manage to have?"
We should be asking, "What kind of love does God call us to practice?"
Instead of searching for loopholes in the stories of flawed men, we should be looking to the character of the sinless Savior.
Because Abraham was not our perfect example.
Jacob was not our perfect example.
David was not our perfect example.
Solomon was not our perfect example.
Jesus is.
And Jesus did not come to teach us how to justify our selfishness.
He came to save us from sin and transform the way we live.
Perhaps you are reading this because someone challenged your faith with this very question.
Perhaps a skeptic asked you why the Bible seems to tolerate something Christians now reject, and you did not know how to answer.
You do not have to be ashamed of asking difficult questions.
Christian faith does not require pretending the hard passages are not there.
It requires approaching them with honesty, humility, and a willingness to let Scripture speak in its full context.
Perhaps you are not struggling with a theological question at all.
Perhaps you know what it means to be Leah.
To love someone who keeps comparing you to somebody else.
To feel invisible inside a relationship.
To give and give while wondering whether you will ever be enough.
Perhaps you know what it means to be Hagar.
To live with the consequences of decisions you did not control.
To feel pushed aside when your presence becomes inconvenient.
Perhaps you know what it means to be Rachel.
To carry an ache that others do not understand.
To watch someone else receive what you have desperately prayed for.
Or perhaps, if you are willing to be painfully honest, you recognize something of David or Solomon in yourself.
Not necessarily their particular sins.
But their capacity to know what is right while choosing what is wrong.
Their temptation to mistake privilege for permission.
Their ability to justify what they should have surrendered.
And maybe the most important question today is not whether Abraham had more than one wife.
Maybe it is whether you have been using somebody else's broken story to excuse what God is asking you to confront in your own.
That question reaches all of us.
Because none of us comes to Christ with a flawless record.
We come carrying pride.
Fear.
Regret.
Compromise.
Wounds.
Secret failures.
Sometimes the consequences of our own choices.
Sometimes the consequences of someone else's.
But the Gospel tells us that sin does not have to be the final word over a repentant sinner's life.
Jesus Christ died for our sins and rose again.
His grace is not permission to continue in rebellion.
It is the mercy that calls us out of rebellion and into new life.
And forgiveness does not mean that every earthly consequence disappears.
Abraham's family still experienced division.
Jacob's household still experienced rivalry.
David's sins still brought suffering.
Solomon's choices still had consequences.
But the Bible's message does not end with the failures of these men.
It moves toward the faithfulness of Christ.
The One who never sinned.
The One who never exploited another person.
The One who never betrayed His Father's will.
The One who offered Himself to redeem those who could never redeem themselves.
That is why the theme of Scripture is not simply the scandal of human failure.
It is the grace of God revealed most fully in Jesus Christ.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by rewriting history to protect the reputations of biblical heroes.
But by entering a world filled with sin and offering redemption through His own death and resurrection.
And here is something I hope you never forget.
The Bible's honesty about the failures of its most celebrated figures is not a weakness that needs to be hidden.
It is part of the testimony that no human hero can take the place of Jesus.
If the Bible were simply trying to manufacture flawless legends, its portraits of the patriarchs and kings would be very different.
Instead, it shows us their failures with startling candor.
And it keeps directing our attention beyond them.
To the God who remains faithful.
To the Savior who is without sin.
To the grace that calls sinners to repentance.
To the transformation that begins when we stop defending our darkness and bring it into His light.
So if someone asks you again, "If polygamy is wrong, why did so many men in the Bible have multiple wives?" you can answer without evasion.
The Old Testament records plural marriages because they were part of the real social and historical world in which God's redemptive purposes unfolded.
The Mosaic law regulated such marriages and sought to restrain certain injustices within them.
Scripture also repeatedly portrays painful rivalry, family division, and spiritual danger within these households.
God's original creation account presents the union of man and woman as one flesh, and Jesus explicitly returns to that beginning as the foundation of His teaching on marriage.
The Bible does not demand that we imitate every action of every person God used.
It calls us to understand those people in light of God's revealed purposes—and ultimately in light of Jesus Christ.
And if you are married, let this truth challenge you beyond the argument.
Do not use another person's failure as permission to become unfaithful.
Do not make your spouse compete for the love and loyalty that your covenant requires.
Do not confuse being desired with being loved.
Do not treat another human being as a possession.
Love with integrity.
Practice faithfulness.
Repent when you have done wrong.
Seek help when a relationship is being damaged.
And remember that forgiveness never requires someone to remain in abuse or danger.
If you are single, your worth is not measured by whether someone has chosen you.
If you are divorced, widowed, abandoned, or carrying the grief of a broken relationship, your life is not beyond God's compassion or His redemptive work.
If you have failed sexually or relationally, do not turn God's mercy into an excuse.
Bring your sin to Christ.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Receive the forgiveness He offers.
And begin walking in obedience, one faithful step at a time.
Because the deepest miracle of the Gospel is not that God found a world filled with perfect people.
It is that Christ came to save sinners.
And that includes people whose stories are complicated.
People whose families are fractured.
People whose past is embarrassing.
People whose questions are difficult.
People who have been wounded by others.
And people who must finally admit that they have wounded others too.
There is room at the foot of the cross for honest repentance.
There is grace for the sinner who turns to Christ.
There is hope for the person who has spent years believing that the worst chapter of their life must be the final chapter.
But do not confuse grace with a license to remain unchanged.
The same Jesus who receives repentant sinners calls them to follow Him.
And following Him means allowing His truth to challenge even the things we have spent years defending.
So let me ask you something personal.
When you read the stories of Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon, what speaks most deeply to you?
Is it the courage to ask difficult questions about Scripture?
The pain of the women whose stories are often overlooked?
The warning that spiritual privilege does not excuse disobedience?
Or the hope that God can still work redemptively through a life marked by failure?
Not simply to win an argument.
Not to shame someone who sees the passage differently.
But because thoughtful, honest conversations about Scripture can help people grow in their understanding of Christ.
And if you are wrestling with a painful question about the Bible, write that question. You do not have to pretend that faith means never struggling to understand.
Someone else may be carrying the same question in silence.
And perhaps your willingness to ask it will help them seek the truth too.
You may need to return to these passages when the question comes up again.
Our desire is not to produce content that merely wins attention.
It is to help people open their Bibles, understand the Gospel, grow in discernment, repent where necessary, and walk more faithfully with Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help believers move beyond occasional inspiration into deeper biblical understanding, prayer, spiritual growth, and daily discipleship.
It is one practical way to partner with the work.
Scripture teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
That is the spirit in which we invite support.
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
But the deepest value of supporting Gospel ministry is not a discount or a product.
It is the opportunity to participate in helping biblical truth reach people who are hungry for it.
Some are believers seeking maturity.
Some are exhausted Christians trying to find their way back to prayer.
Some are skeptics who have never heard a careful answer to their questions.
Some are carrying shame and need to understand what repentance and forgiveness really mean.
And some may be one honest conversation away from opening the Scriptures for themselves.
Keep reading.
Keep learning.
Keep asking questions.
Keep growing in Christ.
No one has to pay to be worthy of God's love.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And the reason we labor to share that message is precisely because no human being can purchase what Christ accomplished through His sacrifice.
So come back to the question that started this entire conversation.
Why did so many men in the Bible have multiple wives?
Because Scripture tells the truth about a fallen world, including the complicated practices of the people through whom God's redemptive history unfolded.
Why does Jesus return to the beginning?
Because God's design is not finally determined by the compromises people make along the way.
And why does any of this matter to you and me?
Because every generation faces the same temptation.
To look at what God has tolerated and call it what God desires.
To look at what someone else got away with and call it permission.
To look at a blessed person's life and assume every choice they made was holy.
But the cross confronts our excuses.
The resurrection announces our hope.
And the words of Jesus call us back to truth.
You do not have to defend Abraham's every decision to believe in Abraham's God.
You do not have to justify David's every action to treasure David's psalms.
You do not have to excuse Solomon's failures to learn from his wisdom.
And you do not have to pretend your own past was righteous in order to receive the mercy of Jesus Christ.
The Bible does not hide the scandals of its heroes.
It reveals the Savior who is greater than every one of them.
And perhaps that is the truth someone needs to hear tonight.
God did not preserve their broken stories so we would have permission to repeat their sins, but so we would learn to place our hope in the Savior who never sinned.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN A GENUINE CHRISTIAN LIVE IN UNREPENTANT SIN FOR YEARS? THE ANSWER MAY TERRIFY THOSE WHO FEEL SAFE—AND BRING HOPE TO THOSE WHO ARE BROKEN.
paragraphs: CAN A GENUINE CHRISTIAN LIVE IN UNREPENTANT SIN FOR YEARS? THE ANSWER MAY TERRIFY THOSE WHO FEEL SAFE—AND BRING HOPE TO THOSE WHO ARE BROKEN.

What if the greatest danger to your soul is not the sin you are struggling to overcome, but the sin you have learned to defend? And what if the very conviction you are trying to silence is evidence that God is still calling you home?
There is a kind of silence that happens when a person reads a Bible verse and suddenly realizes the verse is reading them.
Not their neighbor.
Not their spouse.
Not the hypocrite at church.
Them.
Perhaps you know that silence.

You are sitting alone, scrolling through your phone, when something about Jesus appears on your screen. You almost keep scrolling. You have responsibilities, problems, messages waiting, bills to pay, and a thousand reasons not to think too deeply about eternity.
But something makes you stop.
And suddenly, a question you have avoided for years rises from somewhere deep inside your heart.
“What if I have been calling myself a Christian while refusing to surrender the very thing Jesus has been asking me to leave behind?”
That question is uncomfortable.
It should be.
Because there is a difference between a believer who falls into sin and a person who has made peace with sin.
There is a difference between someone who hates the chains around their wrists and someone who has started decorating those chains.
And there is a difference between trusting the grace of Jesus Christ and using the language of grace to excuse rebellion against Him.
The question is not whether a genuine Christian can sin.
Scripture settles that immediately.
The question is far more serious.
Can someone truly belong to Jesus Christ, remain knowingly and defiantly unrepentant for years, and still confidently claim that nothing is wrong with their relationship with God?
Before answering, we need to walk into a moment from the life of Jesus.
Because the answer is not found in how religious we appear.
It is found in who Jesus is, what He saves us from, and what His grace actually does to a human heart.
Imagine a courtyard in Jerusalem.
The morning air is cool. Dust rises beneath hurried footsteps. Religious leaders have gathered around a woman whose private sin has become a public spectacle.
She has been caught in adultery.
Her reputation is collapsing in front of strangers.
There is nowhere to hide.
The men standing around her are holding something more dangerous than accusations.
They are holding stones.
And standing before them is Jesus.

In John 8:1–11, a passage whose manuscript history deserves careful attention because it is absent from some of the earliest surviving manuscripts of John, the familiar account reaches its unforgettable conclusion.
Jesus says:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
The traditional Greek text records His command:
πορεύου, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε
Poreuou, kai apo tou nyn mēketi hamartane.
“Go, and from now on sin no more.”
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say, “Your sin never mattered.”
He does not say, “Continue living however you want.”
He does not say, “Since I have shown you mercy, obedience is unnecessary.”
But neither does He join the crowd in destroying her.
He extends mercy.
And then He calls her into a different life.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Jesus does not offer forgiveness because sin is harmless.
He offers forgiveness because sin is deadly, and sinners cannot rescue themselves.
Grace does not pretend the prison is a palace.
Grace opens the prison door.
And repentance means we stop insisting that captivity is freedom.

Now imagine that woman returning to the same destructive life, defending the same choices, rejecting every warning, and announcing that Jesus had approved of everything because He had refused to condemn her.
Would that be a faithful understanding of His mercy?
Of course not.
Yet this is precisely the misunderstanding that has quietly entered many modern conversations about Christianity.
We have sometimes reduced salvation to a sentence spoken years ago.
A prayer at an altar.
A baptism certificate.
A childhood memory.
A raised hand during a worship service.
A social media biography that says “Follower of Christ.”
Those things may be connected to genuine faith.
But none of them can replace genuine faith.
You can remember the day you walked down a church aisle and still need to ask whether you are walking with Christ today.
You can know the language of worship without surrendering the direction of your life.
You can sing about the cross while protecting the very rebellion that nailed your Savior there.
And that is why the apostle John wrote words that should make every professing Christian examine their heart.
“Whosoever abideth in him sinneth not: whosoever sinneth hath not seen him, neither known him.” — 1 John 3:6, KJV
Read that carefully.
Because if we misunderstand it, we will either crush struggling believers with despair or comfort unrepentant sinners with false assurance.
The Greek text says:
πᾶς ὁ ἐν αὐτῷ μένων οὐχ ἁμαρτάνει
Pas ho en autō menōn ouch hamartanei.
A close rendering is:
“Everyone who abides in Him does not sin.”
The word μένων (menōn) comes from menō, meaning to remain, continue, or abide.
The word ἁμαρτάνει (hamartanei) comes from hamartanō, meaning to sin.

John uses present-tense language, which, together with the surrounding argument, points to the incompatibility between abiding in Christ and a life characterized by sin. We must be careful, however: Greek present tense alone does not automatically mean “continually” or “habitually.” The context, not a grammatical shortcut, guides our interpretation.
And that context is crucial.
Because earlier in the same letter, John says:
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” — 1 John 1:8, KJV
He also writes:
John is not contradicting himself.
He is confronting two different lies.
The first lie says, “A real Christian never sins.”
The second says, “A real Christian can embrace sin without concern.”
Both are spiritually dangerous.
The Christian life is not sinless perfection.
But neither is it comfortable surrender to sin.
A genuine believer may fall terribly.
A genuine believer may struggle with the same temptation for years.
A genuine believer may experience seasons of spiritual coldness, confusion, disobedience, and even grievous failure.
But Scripture never encourages someone to treat settled, defended, unrepentant sin as harmless evidence of a healthy relationship with Christ.
The presence of a struggle does not prove the absence of salvation. But the absence of repentance should never be treated as proof of its presence.
Think about Peter.
He walked with Jesus.
He witnessed miracles.
He heard teachings that generations of believers would later treasure.
And when the pressure became unbearable, he denied knowing the Lord.
Not once.
Three times.
Imagine the sound of that rooster.
Imagine the memory of Peter's own voice.
“I know not the man.” — Matthew 26:74, KJV
And then Luke records that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
What followed was devastating.
“And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.” — Luke 22:62, KJV
He had failed the One he loved.
But his failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter, as recorded in John 21:15–19.
Peter's tears did not purchase forgiveness.
Christ's mercy was not earned by emotional intensity.
But his grief belonged to the story of a man who could no longer pretend that his denial was acceptable.
Now compare that with Judas.
Judas also followed Jesus outwardly.
He also heard His teachings.
He also lived among the disciples.
He even expressed remorse after betraying Christ.
Yet Matthew 27:3–5 tells us that his remorse ended in tragedy.
The contrast must not be oversimplified. Peter's tears were not a magic formula, and Judas's story is not a reason to despair over anyone who has sinned terribly.
But together their stories force us to consider a vital distinction.
Feeling bad about consequences is not necessarily the same as turning toward God.
The apostle Paul writes:
The Greek word for repentance is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It refers to repentance, a change of mind and heart that involves turning away from sin and toward God.
It is more than feeling embarrassed.
More than fearing exposure.
More than crying because someone discovered what you did.
Biblical repentance is a genuine turning toward God that bears fruit in changed attitudes and actions.
That does not mean the struggle instantly disappears.
It means sin is no longer something you want to enthrone as your master.
Consider the person who has been battling pornography for years.
They hate what it is doing to their mind, their marriage, their integrity, and their communion with God.
They confess. They seek help. They establish boundaries. They sometimes fall again, and each fall brings renewed grief and a desire to return to Christ.
They need the Gospel, wise discipleship, accountability, and perhaps professional help for deeply entrenched patterns.
Now consider another person who indulges the same sin, refuses correction, deliberately hides it, justifies it, and says, “God understands. I am saved by grace. Nobody can tell me how to live.”
The outward sin may look similar.
But the heart's posture toward that sin is profoundly different.
We cannot see either person's heart perfectly.
Only God can.
But Scripture gives us no permission to reassure the second person that deliberate rebellion is spiritually safe.
And the same principle applies beyond sexual sin.
A husband may quote Bible verses every Sunday while emotionally terrorizing his wife throughout the week.
A business owner may donate generously to ministry while deliberately cheating employees.
A church leader may preach repentance publicly while exploiting people privately.
A believer may maintain a polished Christian image while nurturing bitterness, racism, cruelty, greed, dishonesty, or unforgiveness.
And perhaps the most frightening part is how easily we can become skilled at explaining away what we refuse to surrender.
We stop calling it pride.
We call it confidence.
We stop calling it greed.
We call it ambition.
We stop calling it gossip.
We call it concern.
We stop calling it bitterness.
We call it protecting our peace.
We stop calling it lust.
We call it human nature.
We stop calling it rebellion.
We call it freedom.
Until one day, we have constructed a version of Christianity in which Jesus is welcome as Savior but unwelcome as Lord.
And then the words of Jesus confront us.
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” — Luke 6:46, KJV
That question is not aimed only at the obviously immoral.
It reaches the respectable.
The religious.
The churchgoing.
The generous.
The person who knows all the correct answers but has quietly stopped allowing those answers to correct their life.
Jesus also warned:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven.” — Matthew 7:21, KJV
Those are among the most sobering words in Scripture.
Not because Jesus delights in terrifying wounded people.
But because false assurance is a terrible thing.
A doctor who discovers a dangerous illness does not demonstrate compassion by hiding the diagnosis.
Love tells the truth.
And the truth is that a profession of faith without a corresponding life of repentance deserves serious examination.
Yet here is where we must be extraordinarily careful.
We must never confuse salvation by grace with salvation earned by moral performance.
The Gospel does not say that God accepts us because we have finally become sufficiently obedient.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that we are saved by grace through faith, not by our works.
Then verse 10 says we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The order matters.
We do not obey in order to purchase salvation.
We are called to obey because God's saving grace creates a new relationship with Him.
Good works are the fruit of salvation, not the price of admission.
Paul says something astonishing in Romans 6.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” — Romans 6:1–2, KJV
The Greek response is:
μὴ γένοιτο
Mē genoito.
An emphatic rejection often translated “By no means!”
Paul anticipated the argument that if grace increases where sin increases, perhaps Christians should simply keep sinning.
He rejects it decisively.
Why?
Because union with Christ changes our relationship to sin.
The Christian is not merely someone who has received a heavenly exemption from punishment.
The Christian is someone who belongs to the crucified and risen Savior.
And belonging to Jesus means that sin no longer has a rightful claim to rule our lives.
Not because we are strong enough.
But because Christ is alive.
Because the Holy Spirit works within His people.
Because grace does more than pardon.
Grace teaches.
Titus 2:11–12 describes the grace of God as teaching us to deny ungodliness and worldly desires and to live godly lives.
Grace is not God's permission slip for spiritual destruction.
Grace is God's undeserved favor bringing us into a new life.
And that raises the question many people are afraid to ask.
What about someone who has lived in unrepentant sin for ten years?
Twenty years?
An entire adult lifetime?
Can that person still be a genuine Christian?
The most biblically responsible answer requires both seriousness and humility.
Scripture does not give us a precise number of months or years after which we can infallibly declare that someone was never saved.
God alone knows the heart.
Christians also differ in how they understand the relationship between perseverance, assurance, and the possibility of falling away.

Many Reformed and other perseverance-oriented Christians understand prolonged, final unrepentance as evidence that a person's profession of faith was never genuine, drawing on passages such as 1 John 2:19.

Many Wesleyan, Arminian, and other Christian traditions warn that a genuine believer can turn away from faith through persistent, willful rebellion, drawing on warnings such as Hebrews 3:12–14 and Hebrews 10:26–29.
Those are meaningful theological differences.
But neither perspective makes comfortable, defiant, unrepentant sin something to celebrate.
And neither should be used to issue a confident final verdict about a particular person's eternal destiny.
The practical biblical warning remains urgent.
If you have spent years refusing God's correction, do not use a past religious experience to silence the warnings of Scripture.
Do not say, “I prayed the prayer, so nothing else matters.”
Do not say, “I was baptized, so I can live however I choose.”
Do not say, “Once saved, always saved,” as though a theological phrase were permission to disregard Jesus.
And do not assume that because God has not immediately exposed or disciplined you, He has approved your behavior.
Romans 2:4 asks whether we despise the riches of God's goodness, forbearance, and longsuffering, not knowing that His goodness leads us to repentance.
Sometimes what we interpret as permission is actually patience.
And patience should never be mistaken for indifference.
Picture a father standing at the doorway of his home late at night.
His child has wandered into danger.
The father keeps the porch light burning.
He watches the road.
He longs for his child to return.
The light is not an endorsement of the dangerous road.
It is an invitation to come home.
And this is where the story of the prodigal son becomes almost unbearable in its beauty.
In Luke 15, a younger son demands his inheritance, leaves his father's house, and wastes everything.
He exchanges belonging for independence.
Security for pleasure.
Home for a distant country.
And eventually he finds himself hungry, humiliated, and desperate.
Then Scripture says:
“And when he came to himself...” — Luke 15:17, KJV
What a remarkable phrase.
He came to himself.
Sin had promised him freedom but had left him barely recognizing the person he had become.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You remember when prayer came naturally.
You remember when worship could bring tears to your eyes.
You remember when your conscience was tender.
You remember when the thought of disappointing Jesus actually grieved you.
But somewhere along the way, compromise became routine.
One secret became another.
One excuse became a lifestyle.
And what once disturbed you now barely registers.
You still believe in God.
You still know the songs.
You might even be serving in church.
But privately, you know there is something you have been refusing to bring into the light.
Perhaps nobody else knows.
Perhaps everybody thinks you are spiritually strong.
Perhaps the people who admire your faith would be shocked to discover the things you have learned to conceal.
And the worst part is not simply the secret.
It is the exhaustion of maintaining two versions of yourself.
One for Sunday.
One for the rest of the week.
One for public worship.
One for private indulgence.
One who talks about holiness.
One who keeps negotiating with temptation.
You have become tired of hiding.
But you are terrified of being found out.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not call you to continue pretending.
It calls you to Jesus.
The prodigal son did not return home with a presentation explaining why his rebellion had been reasonable.
He came back acknowledging his sin.
And before he could finish his prepared speech, his father welcomed him.
Luke 15:20 says the father saw him while he was still a great way off, had compassion, ran, embraced him, and kissed him.
That is not a picture of sin being declared harmless.
It is a picture of mercy welcoming a repentant sinner.
The son returned from rebellion.
The father responded with compassion.
And the celebration was not because the son had successfully defended his sinful choices.
It was because the lost had been found.
The dead was alive again.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that your past never happened.
Not that your choices have no consequences.
Not that repentance magically repairs every wounded relationship overnight.
But that through Jesus Christ, forgiveness and new life are genuinely offered to sinners who cannot save themselves.
And there is something even more powerful than the story of a father running toward his returning son.
There is the historical reality of the Son of God going to a cross for sinners.
Jesus Christ lived without sin.
He was betrayed, condemned, mocked, beaten, and crucified.
He bore our sins, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again on the third day, according to the Scriptures.
The cross tells us two things that must never be separated.
Our sin is more serious than we want to admit.
And God's mercy in Christ is greater than we could ever deserve.
Look at the cross before you call sin harmless.
Look at the empty tomb before you call yourself hopeless.
The Savior who died for sinners did not remain in the grave.
And that means the person you have become does not have to be the person you remain.
But we must also talk about a passage that has frightened many sincere believers.
Hebrews 10:26 says:
“For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins.”
Those words deserve reverence, not careless interpretation.
The surrounding passage warns against a deliberate rejection of Christ and His sacrifice after receiving knowledge of the truth.
It is not teaching that every Christian who knowingly commits a sin has automatically passed beyond forgiveness.
If that were the meaning, Peter's restoration, the call to confession in 1 John 1:9, and the many biblical appeals to repent would become difficult to reconcile.
The warning is about something profoundly serious: treating the sacrifice of Christ with contempt and turning away from the only Savior who can cleanse us.
There is no alternative sacrifice waiting somewhere beyond Jesus.
No second Messiah.
No better cross.
No other Savior.
That is why deliberate rejection of Him is so dangerous.
And that is also why the answer to spiritual fear is not to run farther away.
It is to turn toward Him.
If you are frightened because you have sinned, the answer is not to declare yourself permanently abandoned.
If you are grieving because you have wandered, the answer is not to surrender to despair.
If you are asking whether you can still come back, hear the invitation of Jesus:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
What a promise.
Not “I will receive only those who have never failed.”
Not “I will welcome only those who can prove they will never struggle again.”
But the one who comes to Him will not be cast out.
And yet coming to Jesus cannot honestly mean demanding that He leave our rebellion untouched.
We cannot cling to the Savior while insisting that our sin must remain our master.
Repentance is not a payment offered in exchange for forgiveness.
It is the fitting response of faith to the mercy of God.
It is turning away from the lies that have been destroying us and turning toward the One who gives life.
And sometimes repentance is not dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like a trembling confession whispered in a dark bedroom.
Sometimes it looks like deleting the secret account.
Sometimes it looks like telling the truth after years of dishonesty.
Sometimes it looks like returning stolen money.
Sometimes it looks like asking for help with an addiction you can no longer manage alone.
Sometimes it looks like confessing a hidden pattern to a mature, trustworthy believer.
Sometimes it looks like accepting church discipline instead of attacking everyone who confronts you.
Sometimes it means leaving an abusive or exploitative situation safely, seeking protection, and refusing to confuse forgiveness with remaining exposed to harm.
And sometimes repentance begins with the smallest, most difficult sentence a proud human heart can speak.
“Lord, I was wrong.”
Not “Lord, they made me do it.”
Not “Lord, everyone else is doing it.”
Not “Lord, You know how difficult my life has been, so my behavior should not matter.”
Just the truth.
“Lord, I have sinned. Have mercy on me.”
And if that prayer is genuine, do not despise its small beginning.
A bruised reed He will not break, as Matthew 12:20 teaches.
But neither should we confuse the beginning of repentance with permission to avoid its fruit.
Real repentance seeks change.
It receives correction.
It makes restitution where appropriate.
It pursues reconciliation where possible and safe.
It seeks accountability.
And it keeps coming back to the grace of Christ, not as an excuse to remain enslaved but as the only hope of freedom.
There is another distinction that matters deeply.
A believer struggling against sin may experience repeated failures without being characterized by settled, unrepentant rebellion.
Duration alone does not tell the whole story.
Someone may spend years battling an entrenched sinful habit while sincerely seeking Christ, receiving help, and learning to walk in obedience.
Someone else may commit fewer outwardly visible sins while harboring a proud, hardened refusal to repent.
God sees what human observers cannot.
This is why we must be slow to pronounce eternal judgments over other people and quick to examine ourselves.
Paul writes:
Notice the invitation.
Examine yourselves.
Not obsessively measure every emotional fluctuation until you lose all peace.
Not make your spiritual confidence depend on perfect performance.
Not compare yourself with someone whose struggles are different.
Examine whether your confidence is rooted in the real Christ of Scripture and whether your life shows the transforming work of His grace.
Ask yourself whether you are bringing your sin into the light or constructing better hiding places.
Ask whether you receive biblical correction or immediately attack the messenger.
Ask whether you desire holiness, even when you stumble.
Ask whether your view of grace makes you love Jesus more or simply makes disobedience easier to justify.
And above all, ask whether you are trusting in Jesus Christ Himself or merely in the memory of something religious you once did.
Because one day, every earthly title will fall silent.
Pastor.
Deacon.
Worship leader.
Ministry founder.
Church member.
Christian content creator.
Longtime believer.
None of those labels can take the place of knowing Christ.
And none of those labels can make unrepentant rebellion spiritually safe.
There is no amount of religious visibility that can compensate for a heart determined to remain hidden from God.
But here is the beautiful interruption of grace.
You are reading this now.
Not yesterday.
Not after another decade of excuses.
Now.
And the call of Scripture is not to wait until you feel sufficiently worthy.
It is to respond to God today.
Hebrews 3:15 says:
“To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.”
Perhaps that is the sentence you needed.
Not another argument.
Not another explanation of why your situation is complicated.
Not another promise to change someday.
Today.
Because every time we justify what God calls us to forsake, we practice resisting the truth.
And every time we surrender to Christ, we acknowledge that His wisdom is greater than our excuses.
This is not about earning a place in heaven through sheer willpower.
It is about the living Savior who calls sinners to Himself and transforms them by His grace.
The same Jesus who restored Peter.
The same Jesus who received tax collectors and sinners.
The same Jesus who spoke truth to the rich young ruler.
The same Jesus who told people to repent and believe the Gospel.
The same Jesus who promised rest to the weary.
The same Jesus who died for the ungodly.
The same Jesus who rose victorious over death.
He has not changed.
His holiness has not diminished.
His mercy has not expired.
His invitation is not empty.
And His grace is not powerless.
If you have been hiding behind religious activity, come into the light.
If you have been using grace as permission to sin, stop misrepresenting the gift that cost Christ His blood.
If you have been crushed by repeated failure while sincerely longing to obey Him, do not mistake your battle for proof that He has abandoned you.
If you have harmed someone, take responsibility and seek to make things right without demanding immediate forgiveness or trust.
If you have wandered far, do not spend another year rehearsing why you cannot return.
Come to Jesus.
You may need pastoral care.
You may need trusted Christian accountability.
You may need professional support for addiction, trauma, or destructive behavioral patterns.
You may need to confess something that will have real consequences.
Following Christ does not guarantee that every earthly consequence disappears.
But no consequence makes His grace less precious.
And no genuine act of repentance is wasted.
Perhaps right now, you are asking the question with which we began.
Can a genuine Christian live in unrepentant sin for years?
Here is what you must not miss.
Scripture does not authorize us to determine a person's eternal state merely by counting the years of their failure.
But it also does not authorize us to offer comfortable assurance to someone who persistently, knowingly, and defiantly rejects repentance.
A Christian can fall.
A Christian can struggle.
A Christian can experience grievous seasons of disobedience.
But a life settled in rebellion is a grave spiritual warning, not a condition to be casually explained away.
And if that warning exposes something in your heart, the answer is not to manufacture enough fear to change yourself.
The answer is to bring your whole life to Jesus Christ.
Because the purpose of biblical conviction is not merely to make you feel terrible.
It is to call you away from sin and toward the Savior.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
And Romans 8 continues by describing the Spirit's work in those who belong to Christ.
Freedom from condemnation is not freedom to worship sin.
It is freedom to belong to Jesus.
And perhaps the most astonishing thing about this entire question is that Christ already knows the truth about you.
Every hidden compromise.
Every failed promise.
Every excuse.
Every tear.
Every secret you have worked so hard to keep.
Nothing surprises Him.
Yet the Gospel still announces forgiveness and new life through His death and resurrection.
Not because your sin is small.
But because His saving work is sufficient.
Not because you deserve another chance.
But because grace is undeserved.
Not because transformation is easy.
But because the risen Christ is mighty to save.
So stop asking only how much sin a Christian can get away with.
Start asking what it means to belong to the One who loved you and gave Himself for you.
Stop measuring the boundaries of permissible rebellion.
Start looking at the beauty of holiness.
Stop treating repentance as a threat to your happiness.
Start recognizing that the sin you defend may be the very thing destroying the joy you are desperate to recover.
And when you fall, do not build a house where you fell.
Confess.
Seek help.
Get up.
Return to Christ.
Walk in the light.
Again and again, depend on His grace.
Not because repentance makes you your own savior.
But because Jesus is the Savior, and His people are called to follow Him.
If this message has uncovered something you have been afraid to acknowledge, you do not need to expose private details publicly. But perhaps you can take one honest step today.
You do not owe strangers your secrets to prove that your repentance is real.

And if this has reminded you of God's faithfulness through your own failures, consider sharing a brief testimony. Someone who believes they have wandered too far may need to hear that the grace of Jesus Christ is not exhausted.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who has stopped attending church because shame convinced them they could never return.
Someone who still quotes Scripture but has secretly surrendered to a destructive habit.
Someone who thinks Christianity is nothing but condemnation.
Someone who believes that grace means they never need to change.
Someone who is one honest prayer away from beginning a difficult journey home.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to prove how righteous you are.
But because biblical truth, spoken with compassion, can reach places our personal conversations sometimes cannot.
There is also something deeply meaningful about helping make resources like these available to more people.
These resources are intended to help people study Scripture, strengthen their understanding of the Gospel, develop consistent devotional habits, and grow in spiritual maturity.
We glorify God by trusting Christ, obeying His Word, loving others, serving faithfully, and giving willingly according to our ability and conviction.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us, giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you to participate.
Not out of guilt.
Not out of fear.
Not because your salvation or God's favor can be purchased.
But because you may believe this ministry is worth helping to sustain.
These products can serve as reminders of Scripture, encouragement in daily life, and opportunities to share conversations about faith.
It is the opportunity to help keep biblical encouragement and discipleship resources reaching people who need them.
Pray for those struggling with sin.
Encourage someone who is trying to return to Christ.
Speak truth with gentleness.
Point people to the Bible.
And above all, point them to Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
A ministry cannot forgive sin.
A Christian product cannot make anyone holy.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
Only His sacrifice is sufficient.
Only His resurrection secures the hope of eternal life.
And every faithful ministry must remain a servant of that Gospel, never a replacement for it.
So before you leave this article, return to the question one final time.
Can a genuine Christian live in unrepentant sin for years?
Do not use the uncertainty of another person's spiritual condition to avoid examining your own.
Do not use your struggles as a reason to despair.
And do not use God's patience as a reason to postpone repentance.
Instead, listen to the invitation of the One who gave His life for sinners.
Come to Him with your failures.
Come to Him with your pride.
Come to Him with the truth you have been hiding.
Come to Him without pretending that your chains are beautiful.
Because the cross is not a celebration of our rebellion.
It is the place where the holiness and love of God meet in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And the empty tomb declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
If you are ready, you can pray:

“Lord Jesus, I have spent too much time explaining away things I should have confessed. I have called some of my compromises harmless when Your Word has called me to repentance. Forgive me for the ways I have resisted Your truth. I cannot save myself, and I cannot transform my own heart through determination alone. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me to trust You, to turn from what dishonors You, and to walk in the light. Give me courage to confess, wisdom to seek help, humility to accept correction, and strength through Your Spirit to follow You. Where I have harmed others, help me take responsibility. Where I have fallen, lead me back to Your grace. I do not want merely to look Christian. I want to belong to You and live for Your glory. In Your name, Jesus. Amen.”
And remember this when the screen goes dark, the room grows quiet, and you are alone again with the truth about your life.
The most dangerous place is not where your sin has brought you low, but where your heart has learned to call its chains freedom—while Jesus is still calling you into the light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES GOD REALLY GIVE HIS TOUGHEST BATTLES TO HIS STRONGEST SOLDIERS? WHAT IF THE PHRASE YOU'VE BEEN CLINGING TO ISN'T WHAT THE BIBLE ACTUALLY TEACHES?
paragraphs: DOES GOD REALLY GIVE HIS TOUGHEST BATTLES TO HIS STRONGEST SOLDIERS? WHAT IF THE PHRASE YOU'VE BEEN CLINGING TO ISN'T WHAT THE BIBLE ACTUALLY TEACHES?

You've been told that your suffering proves how strong you are. But what happens when you're not strong anymore? What if Jesus never asked you to be the strongest soldier in the first place? The truth hidden in Scripture may change how you see your pain, your weakness, and the God who has never abandoned you.
There is a sentence that sounds so beautiful when you're not the one bleeding.
“God gives His toughest battles to His strongest soldiers.”
You've probably heard it in church. Seen it on Facebook. Read it beneath a photograph of someone standing against a storm.
Maybe somebody whispered it to you when your marriage was falling apart.
When the doctor delivered the diagnosis.
When the funeral ended, everyone went home, and you were left staring at a chair that would never be occupied by the same person again.
Maybe they said it when you lost your job, when your child walked away from God, when betrayal shattered your trust, or when you were fighting a temptation you were too ashamed to confess.
And perhaps, for a moment, those words made you feel brave.
God must think I'm strong.
God must have chosen me because He knows I can handle this.
But then came another night.
Another unanswered prayer.
Another bill you couldn't pay.
Another relapse into the sin you promised God you would never touch again.
Another morning when getting out of bed felt like carrying a mountain on your chest.
And suddenly, that comforting sentence became something else.
A burden.
Because if God gives His toughest battles to His strongest soldiers, what does it mean when His soldier is falling apart?
What happens when you don't feel strong?
What happens when you are exhausted from fighting?
What happens when you look toward heaven and whisper something you would never dare say in front of your church friends?
“Lord, I don't think I'm strong enough for this.”
I want you to stay with me, because what Scripture actually says may be far more comforting—and far more challenging—than the popular phrase we've been repeating.
And it begins with a truth some of us desperately need to hear.
God never promised that your strength would be enough. He promised that His grace would be sufficient.
That difference changes everything.
The expression “God gives His toughest battles to His strongest soldiers” is not a Bible verse.
You will not find Jesus teaching it in the Gospels.
You will not find Paul presenting it as a principle of Christian suffering.
You will not find a promise anywhere in Scripture that God measures the difficulty of every trial according to how spiritually strong a believer has become.
And while someone may use the phrase with sincere intentions, sincerity does not automatically make a statement biblically accurate.
Sometimes the words we use to encourage suffering people unintentionally place a weight upon them that God never intended them to carry.
Because underneath that familiar saying is an assumption.
If your battle is enormous, your strength must be enormous too.
But what if the Bible tells a different story?
What if some of the people God used most powerfully were not the strongest people in the room?
What if they were trembling, exhausted, frightened, overwhelmed, and painfully aware of their limitations?
And what if that was precisely where they discovered something about God they could never have learned through self-sufficiency?
Consider the apostle Paul.
This was a man who preached Christ despite persecution, endured imprisonment, suffered beatings, faced dangerous journeys, and carried the burden of concern for the churches.
If anyone might qualify for the modern title of a “strong soldier,” surely Paul would be among them.
Yet listen carefully to what he admitted.
In 2 Corinthians 1:8–9, Paul described an affliction in Asia that was so severe he and his companions were burdened beyond their strength and despaired even of life.
Let those words settle.
Beyond their strength.
The Greek expression is kath’ hyperbolēn hyper dynamin (καθ’ ὑπερβολὴν ὑπὲρ δύναμιν), communicating that the pressure they experienced was exceedingly great, beyond their capacity.
Paul did not say, “We discovered that we were stronger than the suffering.”
He did not say, “God knew we could handle everything ourselves.”
He confessed that the suffering exceeded their strength.
And then he explained what that experience taught them.
It was so that they would not rely on themselves, but on God who raises the dead.
Read that again.
Not rely on themselves.
But on God.
The man who endured extraordinary suffering did not present his personal toughness as the foundation of his survival.
He pointed to the God who raises the dead.
That is not motivational self-confidence dressed in religious language.
That is resurrection-centered faith.
Paul's testimony exposes something important.
A trial can exceed your strength without exceeding God's power.
And perhaps that is where someone reading this needs to stop pretending.
You have spent so much time trying to be the strong one.
The strong parent.
The strong spouse.
The strong ministry worker.
The strong believer who never questions, never struggles, never admits that the pressure is becoming unbearable.
People keep telling you how courageous you are.
They admire how you keep showing up.
They see your Bible verses, your Sunday smile, your encouraging posts.
But they don't see you sitting alone in the dark, trying to find words for a prayer that has become nothing more than tears.
And maybe the hardest part is that you've begun to believe God expects you to maintain the same appearance of strength.
But the God revealed in Scripture does not require you to pretend that you are invincible.
He invites you to trust Him because you are not.
There is another passage frequently attached to this discussion, and misunderstanding it has caused unnecessary guilt for many struggling Christians.
First Corinthians 10:13 says that God is faithful and will not allow believers to be tempted beyond what they can bear, but will provide a way to endure or escape the temptation.
Notice the actual subject.
Temptation.
The Greek word peirasmos (πειρασμός) can refer to a test or trial, and in this context Paul is warning believers against sin, particularly the dangers surrounding idolatry and unfaithfulness.

The passage assures Christians of God's faithfulness in temptation. It does not promise that every tragedy, illness, loss, or painful circumstance will remain within their unaided emotional or physical capacity.
That distinction matters.
God's promise of help in temptation should never be twisted into an accusation against someone who is overwhelmed by suffering.
The grieving mother who cannot stop crying has not disproved God's faithfulness.
The father struggling under financial pressure has not necessarily failed a divine strength test.
The Christian battling depression, exhaustion, or fear is not automatically demonstrating a lack of faith.
And the believer who needs counseling, medical care, rest, or help from the church is not betraying the Gospel by admitting a need.
Sometimes God's provision comes through other people carrying burdens alongside us.
Galatians 6:2 commands believers to bear one another's burdens.
Why would Scripture command us to carry one another's burdens if every burden were designed to be handled alone?
Even more striking is what Paul wrote about his own weakness.
In 2 Corinthians 12, he describes a painful affliction he calls a thorn in the flesh.
Scripture does not identify the thorn precisely, and we should resist claiming certainty where the text does not provide it.
But we know Paul pleaded with the Lord three times for it to depart.
He prayed for relief.
And the Lord answered him.
Not with the removal Paul requested, but with a revelation of sustaining grace.
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
The Greek word translated “sufficient” is arkei (ἀρκεῖ), from arkeō, meaning to be enough or sufficient.
The word for weakness is astheneia (ἀσθένεια), a term that can describe weakness, frailty, or lack of strength.
And the Greek verb teleitai (τελεῖται), translated “is made perfect,” carries the sense of being brought to completion or reaching its intended fulfillment.
In context, Christ's power finds its full expression not through Paul's illusion of self-sufficiency, but in the reality of his dependence upon the Lord.
Jesus was not telling Paul that weakness was imaginary.
He was not demanding that Paul call pain pleasant.
He was declaring that divine grace was enough to sustain him even when the affliction remained.
Think about the tenderness and the power of that answer.
Paul asked for the thorn to leave.
Christ promised His grace would remain.
And sometimes that is the answer that carries us through a season we never would have chosen.
Not because pain is good in itself.
Not because suffering should be romanticized.
Not because every tragedy has an explanation we can confidently announce.
But because the presence of suffering does not mean the absence of Christ.
God's grace does not always remove the battlefield. Sometimes it sustains the wounded believer who can barely stand upon it.
And there is something else we must confront.
The phrase about strongest soldiers can quietly turn the Christian life into a competition of spiritual toughness.
It can make suffering sound like a badge of superiority.
As though those who hurt most must be God's most impressive warriors.
But Scripture does not invite us to rank wounded people by the severity of their wounds.
Jesus Himself rejected simplistic explanations that connected suffering directly with personal spiritual standing.
In John 9, when the disciples encountered a man born blind, they asked whether his condition resulted from his sin or his parents' sin.
Jesus rejected that proposed explanation.
In Luke 13:1–5, He also challenged the assumption that people who suffered terrible deaths were necessarily worse sinners than others.
These passages do not explain every instance of suffering, but they warn us against pretending that we can read God's hidden purposes directly from someone's circumstances.
We must be careful.
Not every battle is a special assignment.
Not every painful event is a divine compliment.
Not every loss means God is preparing you for a public platform.
And not every unanswered prayer should be explained with a confident sentence about what God is supposedly doing behind the scenes.
We live in a fallen world where disease, injustice, human sin, death, and brokenness are painfully real.
Sometimes we suffer because others have sinned against us.
Sometimes we suffer because we have made destructive choices.
Sometimes we suffer for doing what is right.
And sometimes, like Job, we suffer without being given a full explanation.
Yet Scripture repeatedly teaches that God remains sovereign, righteous, and faithful, even when His purposes are hidden from us.
Romans 8:28 assures those who love God and are called according to His purpose that God works all things together for good.
But the next verse matters.
Romans 8:29 identifies conformity to the image of His Son as central to that purpose.
The promise is not that every event will feel good.
Nor that every tragedy will eventually become a financial blessing, a successful ministry, or a dramatic testimony that impresses the world.
The promise is rooted in God's saving purpose in Christ.
And the final hope of believers is greater than merely surviving the present trial.
It is belonging to Jesus, being transformed into His likeness, and sharing in the glory He has promised.
But perhaps the most revealing moment in this entire discussion does not come from Paul.
It comes from a garden.
Gethsemane.
Imagine the darkness.
The silence between the trees.
The approaching betrayal.
The disciples struggling to stay awake.
And Jesus, the sinless Son of God, knowing what awaits Him.
Matthew 26:38 records Him saying that His soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even unto death.
Then He falls on His face and prays.
“O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.” — Matthew 26:39, KJV
In Mark 14:36, Jesus addresses the Father with the Aramaic expression Abba (ἀββᾶ), preserved in the Greek New Testament.

Abba is an intimate familial address meaning “Father.” It expresses a genuine filial relationship, but it should not be simplistically translated as “Daddy,” as though that captures its full historical meaning.
What matters is the relationship revealed in that prayer.
Jesus approaches the Father in perfect trust while facing profound anguish.
The Savior did not pretend the cup was painless.
He did not conceal the horror of what lay ahead.
He prayed with honesty and submitted Himself to the Father's will.

And in Luke 22:43, according to the text preserved in many manuscript traditions, an angel appears to strengthen Him. Scholars note that Luke 22:43–44 has a significant textual history, so it is wise to acknowledge that when discussing the passage.
Now consider what this means.
If the sinless Christ expressed profound sorrow in Gethsemane, why have we sometimes made emotional anguish sound like evidence of spiritual failure?
Of course, Jesus is not merely an example of a courageous sufferer.
He is infinitely more.
He is the obedient Son who went willingly to the cross to accomplish our redemption.
His suffering is unique in its saving purpose.
He bore our sins, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
He died for our sins according to the Scriptures and rose again on the third day, as proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
No believer's suffering can accomplish what His suffering accomplished.
We do not save ourselves through endurance.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And this is where the entire message turns.
Because the center of Christianity is not the story of humanity's strongest soldiers winning the hardest battles.
It is the story of the victorious Savior who entered our broken world to rescue people who could never save themselves.
At Calvary, human pride had nothing to boast about.
Our religious achievements could not remove our guilt.
Our determination could not erase our sin.
Our courage could not defeat death.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of our rebellion and the astonishing mercy of God.
Romans 5:8 declares that God demonstrated His love toward us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not when we had finally become strong enough.
Not when we had overcome every addiction.
Not when our marriages were repaired.
Not when we had cleaned up our reputations.
While we were still sinners.
