They are exhausted believers.
People who have prayed through the night.
People fighting recurring temptations.
People carrying childhood trauma.
People struggling with intrusive thoughts.
People suffering from anxiety, depression, addiction, grief, or shame.
People who already believe something must be terribly wrong with them.
And when every struggle is immediately attributed to a demon, those people may begin to interpret their suffering as proof that Jesus has not truly received them.
That is not a small theological mistake.
It can wound the very people the Church is commanded to shepherd.
Now consider the Apostle Paul's words in Ephesians 6:12.
In the Greek text, he writes:
ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν ἡμῖν ἡ πάλη πρὸς αἷμα καὶ σάρκα
Hoti ouk estin hēmin hē palē pros haima kai sarka.
“For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood.”
Paul continues by describing rulers, authorities, cosmic powers of darkness, and spiritual forces of evil.
The Greek word πάλη (palē) refers to wrestling or struggle.
Paul was not describing an imaginary conflict.
He understood that Christians face genuine spiritual opposition.
But what does he tell believers to do?
Put on the whole armor of God.
Stand firm.
Hold to truth.
Live in righteousness.
Be prepared with the Gospel of peace.
Take up faith.
Receive the helmet of salvation.
Use the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God.
Pray at all times in the Spirit.
This is striking.
In one of the New Testament's clearest passages on spiritual warfare, Paul does not instruct every believer to schedule recurring deliverance sessions.
He does not provide a catalog of demons supposedly assigned to every emotion or personality trait.
He does not teach that every hardship must be traced to an ancestral curse.
He tells the Church to stand in the strength of the Lord.
Biblical spiritual warfare is deeply supernatural, but it is also deeply rooted in ordinary faithfulness to Christ.
Sometimes the most spiritually significant thing a believer can do is not shout at the darkness.
It is refuse a lie.
Confess a sin.
Forgive an enemy.
Resist temptation.
Open Scripture.
Ask for help.
Continue praying.
And trust Jesus when feelings offer no immediate reassurance.
James 4:7 declares:
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (ESV)
The order matters.
Submit to God.
Resist the devil.
The foundation is not fascination with evil.
It is allegiance to the Lord.
And that brings us to one of the most misunderstood questions surrounding modern deliverance ministry.
Can a Christian be demon-possessed?
Christians who take the Bible seriously do not all answer every aspect of this question in exactly the same way.
Some distinguish between demonic possession and varying forms of oppression or influence. Others question whether those categories are sufficiently defined in Scripture.

The New Testament Greek often uses forms of δαιμονίζομαι (daimonizomai) to describe people afflicted by demons. English translations commonly render this as “demon-possessed” or “demon-oppressed,” depending on the translation and context.
The word itself does not settle every modern debate about degrees of demonic influence or whether an indwelt believer can experience a particular kind of affliction.
We must not pretend that a single Greek word resolves a theological question that requires careful consideration of the whole biblical witness.
What Scripture does clearly teach is that those who belong to Christ have been brought into His kingdom.
Colossians 1:13–14 says:
“He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins.” (ESV)
The Greek verb translated “delivered” is ἐρρύσατο (errysato), from rhyomai, meaning to rescue or deliver.
Paul describes a decisive rescue accomplished by God.
Not a rescue that must be purchased repeatedly.
Not a salvation that remains perpetually hostage to the next spiritual specialist.
Christians may still be tempted, deceived, attacked, and called to resist the devil. Scripture does not promise an absence of suffering or spiritual conflict.
But the believer's deepest identity is not determined by darkness.
It is determined by union with Jesus Christ.
First Corinthians 6:19 teaches that the believer's body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.
Romans 8:9 teaches that those who belong to Christ have His Spirit.
First John 4:4 reminds believers that the One who is in them is greater than the one who is in the world.
These passages give profound assurance, although Christians differ in how they apply them to specific claims about demonic affliction.
We should not force Scripture to say more than it says.
And we should never tell a suffering Christian that an ongoing struggle automatically proves a demon is living inside them.
Imagine telling someone who has battled depression for years that their suffering means they have failed to achieve sufficient spiritual freedom.
Imagine telling a grieving mother that her anguish is evidence of a spirit of death.
Imagine telling a survivor of abuse that their trauma symptoms prove they have opened a demonic doorway.
Such claims can deepen shame, delay appropriate treatment, and distort the person's understanding of God's character.
Jesus did not teach that every illness is caused by a demon.
In Matthew 4:24, the Gospel distinguishes various forms of sickness, severe pain, demonic affliction, seizures, and paralysis.
That distinction matters.
Scripture acknowledges human suffering without reducing every condition to the same explanation.

A person experiencing hallucinations, seizures, severe psychological distress, or suicidal thoughts deserves compassionate support and appropriate medical or mental-health evaluation. Prayer and pastoral care can accompany treatment; they should not replace urgently needed care.
Seeking a doctor is not an act of unbelief.
Receiving mental-health treatment is not a betrayal of Christ.
And taking prescribed medication is not proof that someone trusts science more than God.
Luke, Paul's companion, was identified as a physician in Colossians 4:14.
Paul also gave Timothy practical advice concerning his physical ailments in 1 Timothy 5:23.
God's ordinary provisions for human care need not compete with our dependence on Him.
A mature Church should know how to pray fervently while recognizing the limits of its own diagnosis.
But what about generational curses?
What about the frightening claim that Christians remain spiritually imprisoned because of sins committed by their parents, grandparents, or ancestors?
This teaching deserves particular care because it can produce enormous fear.
Exodus 20:5 speaks of the consequences of iniquity extending through generations among those who hate God.
That text must be read within its covenantal context and alongside the rest of Scripture.
Ezekiel 18:20 states:
“The soul who sins shall die. The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father, nor the father suffer for the iniquity of the son.” (ESV)
Ezekiel emphasizes personal moral accountability.
Galatians 3:13 declares that Christ redeemed His people from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for them.
That verse concerns redemption from the law's curse; it should not be casually treated as a mechanical formula covering every proposed ancestral spiritual mechanism.
Families can certainly pass down destructive patterns.
Violence.
Addiction.
Deception.
Abuse.
Idolatry.
Unhealthy ways of responding to pain.
The consequences of sin can affect generations.

But inherited consequences are not identical to inherited personal guilt, and Scripture does not establish that every Christian must undergo specialized rituals to cancel undiscovered ancestral demons.
Sometimes what a family needs is repentance.
Sometimes it needs counseling.
Sometimes it needs protection from an abusive person.
Sometimes it needs patient discipleship across years.
And sometimes the most beautiful evidence of God's grace is a son who refuses to repeat his father's cruelty, or a daughter who learns to raise her children with the tenderness she never received.
That is not a lesser testimony.
That is transformation.
That is the Gospel entering a broken family and changing what comes next.
And if you have ever been frightened into believing that your family history is stronger than your Savior, hear this carefully.
Your ancestry may explain some of your wounds. It does not have the final authority to define your future in Christ.
The cross of Jesus Christ is not an unfinished transaction waiting for a minister to complete it.
When Jesus cried out from the cross in John 19:30, He said:
Τετέλεσται.
Tetelestai.
“It is finished.”
This Greek verb, from teleō, conveys that something has been brought to completion or accomplished.
In John's Gospel, the declaration belongs to the climactic completion of Jesus' earthly mission and suffering.
It is not a promise that Christians will never again experience temptation, illness, grief, or spiritual attack.
But it does announce something that no Christian ministry may improve upon.
Jesus accomplished the saving work entrusted to Him.
His sacrifice is sufficient.
His authority is not borrowed.
His victory does not depend on a minister's charisma.
And His people must never be taught to trust an elaborate deliverance system more than the Savior who redeemed them.
Hebrews 10:14 says:
“For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.” (ESV)
Notice the astonishing relationship between what Christ has accomplished and what God continues to work out in His people.
There is a definitive saving achievement.
And there is an ongoing process of sanctification.
This is why a Christian can genuinely belong to Jesus and still struggle.
A believer may have received forgiveness and still need to learn how to forgive.
A believer may have been reconciled to God and still need years of healing from trauma.
A believer may have turned from sin and still need accountability to resist familiar temptations.
Not every struggle proves that deliverance failed.
Sometimes it means sanctification is still underway.
And that is not evidence that Jesus has abandoned you.
It is an invitation to continue following Him.
But we must also confront the other side of the conversation.
Some Christians have reacted to questionable deliverance practices by dismissing every account of demonic activity as superstition.
That response also goes beyond Scripture.
The Gospels repeatedly portray Jesus confronting unclean spirits.
Mark 5 describes the restoration of a man who had been living among tombs, isolated and tormented.
Luke 8:35 records the man afterward, clothed and in his right mind, sitting at Jesus' feet.
What a picture.
A man once known for his torment is now sitting peacefully with his Deliverer.
The crowd had known him by his condition.
Jesus restored his dignity.
The people had feared him.
Jesus approached him.
His suffering had become his public identity.
Jesus gave him a new story.
And when the restored man wanted to accompany Jesus, the Lord told him to return home and declare what God had done for him.
The result was testimony.
Not a lifetime of obsession with the demons that had afflicted him.
Not a ministry built around endlessly revisiting the darkness.
The man was sent to speak about mercy.
That is the difference between a Christ-centered testimony and a demon-centered spectacle.
One keeps returning to what evil did.
The other cannot stop speaking about what Jesus has done.
And here is where the modern Church must exercise extraordinary discernment.
When someone falls, shakes, cries, screams, vomits, or becomes emotionally overwhelmed during prayer, those reactions alone do not establish demonic possession or prove that a spirit has departed.
The same outward behavior can have different explanations.
A responsible minister should never treat distress as permission to humiliate someone.
Never restrain or physically harm a person under the assumption that violence will drive out a demon.
Never pressure someone to stop medication.
Never force someone to disclose private trauma in front of a congregation.
Never threaten a vulnerable person with spiritual consequences for refusing a session.
Never exploit fear to demand money.
And never turn someone's most painful moment into online content without meaningful, informed consent.
Even consent requires special care when someone is distressed, frightened, or under intense social pressure.
First Corinthians 14:40 teaches that things in the gathered church should be done decently and in order.
First Peter 5:2–3 calls shepherds to care willingly and eagerly, not for shameful gain or by domineering over those entrusted to them.
The Church is not exempt from accountability because it invokes spiritual authority.
In fact, claiming to act in Jesus' name should make accountability more serious.
And yes, the Bible also records extraordinary events surrounding deliverance.
Mark 9 describes a boy whose affliction involved convulsions.
Acts 16 records Paul's command to a spirit in the name of Jesus Christ.
Acts 19 describes extraordinary miracles through Paul.
We must allow those texts to speak without editing out their supernatural character.
But descriptive accounts of what happened in particular circumstances do not automatically authorize every technique that modern ministries may invent.
We must distinguish what Scripture records, what Scripture commands, and what people merely assume.

This is especially important with Mark 9:29, where Jesus teaches the importance of prayer in a difficult case. Some manuscripts also include the words “and fasting,” a textual variation reflected in Bible translation notes.
Prayer is unquestionably central to Christian dependence upon God.
Fasting is a biblical spiritual discipline.
But neither should be presented as a guaranteed technique that forces supernatural outcomes.
God is not controlled by spiritual formulas.
And people should not be blamed for a lack of faith when the outcome they hoped for does not occur.
Think of the father in Mark 9 who brought his suffering son to Jesus.
He was desperate.
He had already experienced disappointment.
And when Jesus spoke to him about faith, the father cried:
“I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24, ESV)
What an astonishing confession.
Not polished.
Not impressive.
Not the kind of sentence someone would ordinarily put on a church banner celebrating victorious faith.
It was the cry of a frightened father who wanted to believe but knew his own weakness.
And Jesus did not reject him for that honesty.
Perhaps someone reading this has been carrying that same prayer.
You believe.
But you're tired.
You love Jesus.
But you're afraid.
You want freedom.
But you're exhausted from being told that your ongoing struggle must mean you are hiding a demon, lacking faith, or refusing to surrender.
Listen.
Your weakness does not surprise Jesus.
Your tears do not disqualify you from His mercy.
Your questions do not place you beyond His reach.
And your need for help does not make you a failure as a Christian.
The Gospel is not the announcement that strong people have finally discovered how to defeat every darkness in their lives.
It is the announcement that the Son of God came to save sinners who could never save themselves.
Romans 5:8 declares that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches salvation by grace through faith, not as a result of works.
And Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” (ESV)
No condemnation.
Not because your spiritual performance is flawless.
Not because you have attended enough deliverance sessions.
Not because you have identified every possible spiritual attack.
But because you are in Christ Jesus.
This is not permission to tolerate sin.
The same grace that forgives also teaches us to renounce ungodliness, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
Repentance matters.
Holiness matters.
Obedience matters.
Confession matters.
But none of these things purchases what only Christ's blood can provide.
The Christian life is not a journey from dependence on Jesus toward dependence on a powerful human deliverer.
It is a lifelong deepening of dependence upon Christ Himself.
And we must remember something else.
Not everyone who says “Lord” speaks with the Lord's approval.
Matthew 7:22–23 records people claiming to have prophesied, cast out demons, and performed mighty works in Jesus' name.
Yet Jesus warns that outwardly impressive ministry claims are not sufficient proof of a genuine relationship with Him.
That passage should humble all of us.
Especially those who lead.
Especially those who teach.
Especially those who build public ministries around extraordinary experiences.
A dramatic manifestation does not authenticate a minister's character.
A viral deliverance video does not prove sound doctrine.
A large audience does not establish God's approval.
And even a genuine supernatural event must never replace the biblical call to know, love, and obey Jesus.
In Matthew 12:43–45, Jesus describes an unclean spirit leaving a person and later returning with other spirits. In context, the warning culminates in a judgment concerning an evil generation.
It is a serious passage, but it should not be turned into a universal prediction that every Christian who struggles after prayer has been repossessed by demons.
Nor should it be used to terrify people into endless paid sessions.
We should interpret Jesus' warning in context rather than transform it into a mechanism for spiritual dependency.
True Christian ministry should help people grow in discernment, maturity, and confidence in God's promises.
It should not make them perpetually dependent on a particular minister to feel safe.
This is one reason Acts 17:11 is so important.
The Bereans examined the Scriptures to see whether Paul's teaching was true.
Think about that.
Even the teaching of an apostle was examined against the Scriptures.
How much more should modern ministries welcome thoughtful biblical scrutiny?
If a leader tells you that questioning their methods is equivalent to questioning the Holy Spirit, be careful.
If they insist that disagreement proves you have a rebellious spirit, be careful.
If they demand money to break a curse, be careful.
If they forbid outside pastoral, medical, or psychological counsel, be careful.
If their teaching causes you to fear leaving their ministry more than you fear departing from Christ, something is profoundly wrong.
The Holy Spirit does not need manipulation to defend the truth.
And the Word of God is not threatened by honest examination.
First John 4:1 tells believers not to believe every spirit but to test the spirits.
First Thessalonians 5:21 says to test everything and hold fast to what is good.
Discernment is not unbelief.
It is obedience.
And perhaps the greatest test of a deliverance ministry is not how loudly it commands demons.
It is how faithfully it represents Jesus.
Does it proclaim His incarnation, death, and resurrection?
Does it call sinners to repentance and faith?
Does it teach the whole counsel of Scripture?
Does it demonstrate compassion toward vulnerable people?
Does it encourage accountability and wise pastoral oversight?
Does it respect human dignity?
Does it acknowledge uncertainty where Scripture does not provide a definitive answer?
Does it point people toward lifelong discipleship rather than dependence upon spiritual personalities?
Does it make the finished work of Christ central?
Because a ministry can talk endlessly about freedom while creating another form of bondage.
The bondage of constant fear.
The bondage of spiritual suspicion.
The bondage of believing every nightmare, illness, intrusive thought, or difficult season is evidence of a hidden demon.
The bondage of thinking you can never be safe unless someone with a special title prays over you again.
That is not the confidence the New Testament calls believers to cultivate.
Second Timothy 1:7 says God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.
That verse should not be misused to condemn people who experience clinical anxiety or other mental-health conditions. In context, Paul is encouraging Timothy toward courage and faithfulness.
But it does remind us that Christian ministry should not deliberately cultivate terror as a means of control.
The Gospel confronts sin.
It exposes deception.
It calls people to repentance.
It warns of judgment.
But it also announces mercy.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
New life.
And hope grounded in a Savior who conquered death.
At the cross, Jesus was publicly humiliated.
Accused.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified between criminals.
To the watching world, it looked like a scandal.
A defeated Messiah.
A crushed hope.
A man whose claims had apparently collapsed under the weight of Roman power.
But what appeared to be defeat was the place where God's saving purpose was being accomplished.
Colossians 2:13–15 describes God forgiving trespasses, canceling the record of debt against us, and disarming the rulers and authorities through Christ's triumph.
The cross was not a desperate improvisation.
It was the place where grace confronted the guilt of sinners and where the victory of Christ was displayed.
And the resurrection declared that death would not have the final word.
This is why our message must never end with demons.
It must end with Jesus.
Not merely Jesus as a name shouted during a spiritual confrontation.
But Jesus the crucified and risen Lord.
Jesus who forgives sinners.
Jesus who restores the ashamed.
Jesus who calls the wandering home.
Jesus who receives the weary.
Jesus who commands repentance.
Jesus who gives eternal life.
Jesus who will one day make all things new.
And if you've spent years terrified that darkness has a stronger claim on you than Christ, I want you to consider the words of John 10:28.
Jesus says of His sheep:
“I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand.” (ESV)
The assurance of that promise rests in the Good Shepherd.
Not in a minister's performance.
Not in your ability to remember every possible sin.
Not in your ability to interpret every frightening dream.
But in the One who lays down His life for the sheep.
Do you belong to Him?
Have you turned from sin and placed your trust in His death and resurrection?
Are you following His voice?
Those are far more important questions than whether you have discovered the name of a supposed spirit.
And if you have not yet surrendered your life to Jesus, the invitation of the Gospel is not to begin by becoming obsessed with the devil.
It is to come to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive His forgiveness.
Follow Him.
And become part of a faithful local church where you can grow in Scripture, prayer, worship, fellowship, and obedience.
If you need prayer, seek mature and trustworthy Christians who will treat you with dignity.
If you need medical or psychological care, receive it without shame.
If you need to confess hidden sin, bring it into the light with appropriate pastoral support and accountability.
If you need to leave a coercive or abusive ministry environment, seek safe, independent help.
And if you have been wounded by people who claimed to represent Jesus, do not confuse their failures with the character of the Savior.
He is not made more holy by their harshness.
He is not made more powerful by their theatrics.
He is not made more glorious by their ability to frighten people.
His glory is already revealed in His truth, righteousness, mercy, and saving work.
Now I want to speak to the person who has been reading this with tears in their eyes.
Maybe you were told that your anxiety was a demon.
Maybe someone publicly exposed your private pain.
Maybe you were pressured to confess things you did not do.
Maybe you were told that a family curse explained every disappointment in your life.
Maybe you spent money you could barely afford because someone promised that one more session would finally make you free.
Or maybe you witnessed something you still cannot explain, and now you are struggling to know what was biblical and what was not.
You do not have to pretend that every experience was false.
And you do not have to accept every interpretation someone attached to it.
You can take your questions to Scripture.
You can seek wise counsel.
You can acknowledge uncertainty.
You can pursue healing.
You can repent where repentance is needed.
And you can continue trusting Jesus.
Because your hope is not in having a perfect explanation for every frightening thing that happened to you.
Your hope is in the Savior whose mercy is greater than your confusion.
If this article has exposed a fear you've been carrying in silence, I want to invite you to respond with honesty.
You do not owe anyone a public disclosure of your trauma. Your honesty matters even when it remains private.
But your perspective may help someone else recognize that they are not alone in seeking biblical truth.
And if you know someone who has become terrified of demons, trapped in spiritual confusion, or wounded by manipulative religious practices, consider sharing this article directly with them.
Not to create hostility toward Christians who disagree.
Not to mock people who sincerely believe they have experienced deliverance.
But to call all of us back to the Word of God and the centrality of Jesus Christ.
Invite your family, your Christian friends, the believer who is quietly struggling, the seeker who has questions, and even the person who no longer trusts the Church to follow along.
Our prayer is that Gospel Warrior will be a place where truth is not sacrificed for popularity, grace is not confused with compromise, and Jesus remains greater than every controversy we examine.
Those resources are part of our commitment to make biblical nourishment accessible.
And if this ministry has helped you grow, I want to extend a personal invitation.
There is a real cost to producing and sustaining ministry resources, even when many of them are offered freely.
Monthly supporters help make that possible.
For Christians who are able and willing, supporting faithful Gospel work can be one expression of generosity and stewardship.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be decided in the heart, not done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And Philippians 4:15–18 shows the Apostle Paul acknowledging the financial partnership of believers who supported his Gospel ministry.
These passages provide a biblical basis for voluntary generosity toward Gospel work.
But we must be equally clear about something important.
Your first responsibility is to honor Christ faithfully, care for those entrusted to you, and exercise wise stewardship.
If you already support your local church, that commitment deserves serious consideration.
If your financial circumstances are difficult, please do not feel pressured to give.
The deeper reason to support is the mission.
More people opening their Bibles.
More believers learning to distinguish truth from error.
More wounded hearts encountering the compassion of Christ.
More free resources reaching people who may never be able to purchase Christian books.
More conversations that lead beyond religious excitement into lasting discipleship.
Because the greatest success of a Christian ministry is not the size of its audience.
It is faithfulness to the Lord whose name it bears.
One day, every viral video will be forgotten.
Every platform will fade.
Every earthly ministry will come to an end.
The applause will stop.
The arguments will cease.
The controversies that consumed so much of our attention will no longer seem nearly as important as they once did.
But Jesus Christ will remain.
And when we stand before Him, the question will not be whether we produced the most dramatic spiritual experiences.
It will be whether we truly belonged to Him.
Whether we trusted His Gospel.
Whether we obeyed His Word.
Whether we loved those He entrusted to our care.
Whether we used His name to serve people—or used people to magnify our own names.
So, are deliverance ministries biblical?

The ministry of Jesus and His apostles clearly demonstrates that deliverance from demonic affliction is biblical. But not every practice performed under the modern label of deliverance ministry is therefore biblical, necessary, wise, or safe.
We must neither deny what Scripture affirms nor invent what Scripture does not teach.
We must not dismiss spiritual warfare.
And we must not make spiritual warfare the center of Christianity.
We must not ridicule sincere testimonies.
And we must not allow testimonies to outrank Scripture.
We must not shame people who need help.
And we must not use their vulnerability to build ministries around fear.
Above all, we must never preach a version of deliverance that makes Jesus seem insufficient.
Because the heart of Christianity is not that darkness is powerful.
It is that Jesus Christ is Lord.
And for the repentant sinner who trusts Him, the most important freedom is not the ability to name every enemy.
It is to know the Savior who has reconciled us to God.
Perhaps that is the truth someone needs to hear tonight.
You are not called to spend your life trembling before every shadow.
You are called to walk in the light of Christ.
And even if your healing is slow, your questions remain, and your journey includes seasons of painful struggle, you can continue coming to the One who does not despise a broken and contrite heart.
The greatest deliverance story is not about how loudly darkness screamed when it left—but about how completely Jesus loved the sinner He came to save.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE’S SEXUAL SCANDALS WERE NEVER JUST ABOUT “BAD WOMEN”—SO WHY HAVE WE BEEN LETTING THE MEN WALK AWAY?
paragraphs: THE BIBLE’S SEXUAL SCANDALS WERE NEVER JUST ABOUT “BAD WOMEN”—SO WHY HAVE WE BEEN LETTING THE MEN WALK AWAY?

The stories we thought exposed sinful women also expose powerful men, hidden lust, religious hypocrisy, sexual exploitation, and the devastating consequences of unchecked desire. And when Jesus enters the story, nobody gets to hide behind someone else’s shame.
There is something deeply disturbing about the way some of us have learned to tell the Bible’s most uncomfortable stories.
We remember the woman caught in adultery.
But we rarely ask where the man was.
We remember Bathsheba bathing.
But we sometimes forget David was watching.
We remember Tamar’s pregnancy.
But we forget Judah was the man who propositioned her.
We remember Samson falling because of Delilah.
But we forget that Samson had been making reckless decisions long before Delilah entered the story.
We remember the Samaritan woman’s five husbands.
But we often speak as though Jesus told us why those marriages ended.
He didn't.
And perhaps one of the most dangerous things we can do with Scripture is become so confident in the shame we assign to someone else that we stop hearing what God is exposing in us.
Because the Bible does not tell these stories so men can congratulate themselves for being righteous while women carry the weight of sexual shame.
It tells the truth about human sin.
Even when that truth embarrasses kings.
Even when it exposes patriarchs.
Even when it confronts religious leaders.
Even when it shatters the reputation of men we have admired since childhood.
And if we read carefully, we discover something breathtaking.
God is not afraid to tell the truth about the people He used.
Not because their sins were acceptable.
But because His grace was never dependent upon pretending those sins never happened.
Before you continue, consider one question.
What if the person you have spent years condemning in a Bible story was never the only person God wanted you to examine?
What if you have been looking at the scandal...
while missing the mirror?
There is a Hebrew word that appears in the Bible's account of David and Bathsheba: שָׁלַח (shalach).
It means “to send.”
A simple word.
Until you notice how David uses the power to send people in 2 Samuel 11.
He sends to inquire about Bathsheba.
He sends messengers to bring her.
He sends word to Joab.
He sends Uriah back toward a battlefield where death awaits him.
And suddenly the story becomes more than an account of forbidden desire.
It becomes a terrifying picture of what happens when a man with authority begins treating other human beings as instruments of his own appetite.
David was not an ordinary man looking for love.
He was Israel's king.
He had armies.
He had servants.
He had influence.
He had power.
Bathsheba was identified as the wife of Uriah the Hittite.
David knew she was married.
And still, he sent for her.

The biblical text tells us that David took her and lay with her (2 Samuel 11:4). It does not describe Bathsheba's internal thoughts or establish that she freely consented. The enormous imbalance of power matters, and we must not invent consent where Scripture does not give it.
Yet how many times have people turned this account into a warning about a woman's clothing, beauty, or bathing?
Scripture does not say Bathsheba was attempting to seduce the king.
It says David saw her.
David inquired.
David sent.
David took.
And when the prophet Nathan finally confronted the scandal, he did not approach Bathsheba with an accusation.
He approached David.
“You are the man,” Nathan declared (2 Samuel 12:7, KJV).
Four words.
Enough to tear the disguise off a king.
Imagine the silence.
David had tried to bury the evidence beneath military orders and a carefully arranged death.
Uriah, a faithful soldier, had refused the comforts of home while his fellow soldiers remained in battle.
And David, the king who should have protected him, arranged his destruction.
The man who had written songs about God had committed adultery, abused royal power, and orchestrated a killing.
Nathan did not soften the truth because David was anointed.
He did not excuse the crime because David had once defeated Goliath.
He did not say the king's ministry was too important to be questioned.
He exposed him.
And David finally said, “I have sinned against the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:13, KJV).
That confession mattered.
But it did not bring Uriah back.
It did not erase the harm Bathsheba had experienced.
It did not prevent the consequences that followed.
And this is something we desperately need to recover in the Church.
Forgiveness is real. But forgiveness is not the same thing as pretending the damage never happened.
God's mercy does not make a victim's suffering insignificant.
Repentance is not a public-relations strategy.
A man cannot use the language of grace to escape the responsibility of telling the truth.
And a leader cannot demand silence from the wounded simply because his reputation is at stake.
If Nathan could confront a king, the Church should never become a hiding place for powerful men who refuse accountability.
But David is not the only man Scripture exposes.
Travel backward into Genesis 38.
There you will find Tamar.
A woman whose story has sometimes been reduced to sexual scandal without sufficient attention to the injustice that preceded it.
Tamar was Judah's daughter-in-law.
After the deaths of her first two husbands, Judah promised that she would eventually be given to his younger son, Shelah, according to the family obligations of that time.
But the promise was not fulfilled.
Tamar was left waiting.
Her future was suspended by a man who possessed authority over the family arrangement.
Then Judah encountered a veiled woman whom he believed to be a prostitute.
He approached her and negotiated a sexual encounter.
He did not recognize that she was Tamar.
Later, when Judah learned that Tamar was pregnant, he demanded severe punishment.
“Bring her forth, and let her be burnt” (Genesis 38:24, KJV).
Can you feel the hypocrisy?
The man who participated in the encounter was ready to condemn the woman for the pregnancy that resulted from it.
He wanted judgment.
Until the evidence reached him.
Tamar produced the personal items Judah had given her as a pledge.
And suddenly the man who was prepared to pronounce judgment had to confront his own conduct.
Judah acknowledged, “She hath been more righteous than I” (Genesis 38:26, KJV).
The Hebrew expression is צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי (tsadeqah mimmeni).
In context, Judah is acknowledging that Tamar was more in the right than he was, because he had failed to give her his son Shelah as promised.
That does not mean every detail of Tamar's actions becomes a universal moral example.
It means the biblical narrative refuses to allow Judah's hypocrisy to stand.
He was prepared to punish someone while refusing to acknowledge his own responsibility.
And isn't that frighteningly familiar?
A woman becomes pregnant, and everyone wants to know what she did.
A man fathers a child, and people sometimes rush to protect his future.
A woman confesses a sexual mistake, and her reputation can follow her for years.
A man confesses the same kind of wrongdoing, and someone may call him a promising leader who simply stumbled.
These double standards are not the righteousness of God.
They are human favoritism dressed in religious language.
And the story becomes even more astonishing when we turn to Matthew 1:3.
Tamar appears in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Read that again.
The woman whose story involved family injustice, deception, and public disgrace is named in the recorded ancestry of the Messiah.
Not because God approved of every action in the story.
But because human brokenness did not prevent God from accomplishing His redemptive purposes.
The genealogy of Jesus does not conceal the complicated history of His human family line.
It tells us that the Savior entered a world already stained by the very sins He came to confront.
Not by calling evil good.
But by bringing redemption into a history where evil had done terrible damage.
Then there is Samson.
How many sermons have reduced his downfall to one message?
Beware of Delilah.
Certainly, Delilah betrayed him.
Judges 16 makes that clear.
But Samson's spiritual collapse did not begin the day Delilah learned the secret of his strength.
Long before that, Samson had repeatedly pursued his desires without the wisdom and self-control his calling required.
Judges 14 records his insistence on marrying a Philistine woman despite his parents' objections.
Judges 16:1 records his visit to a prostitute in Gaza.
Later, his relationship with Delilah becomes the setting of his betrayal and capture.
Delilah was responsible for her deception.
But Samson was responsible for his own choices.
We must stop treating women as though they possess mysterious powers that remove men's responsibility for their decisions.
A man's desire does not become someone else's moral responsibility simply because he finds that person attractive.
James 1:14 teaches that each person is tempted when drawn away by their own desire.
The Greek word ἐπιθυμία (epithymia) refers to desire or longing; in this context, desire that entices toward sin.
Notice where James places responsibility.
Not automatically on the person being desired.
But on the person being drawn away by their own desire.
That truth confronts everyone.
Men and women alike.
We cannot outsource repentance.
We cannot blame another person's appearance for the choices we willingly make.
We cannot build a theology of holiness that requires women to carry responsibility for men's thoughts while men remain unaccountable for their own hearts.
Jesus Himself made this painfully clear.
In Matthew 5:28, He warned against looking at another person with lustful intent.
The Greek expression πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn) concerns looking at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her.
Jesus was addressing the moral responsibility of the person doing the looking.
He was not teaching that the person being looked at automatically bears the guilt.
And the solution Jesus demanded was not to blame the woman.
It was to deal radically with the sin in one's own life.
Not through literal self-mutilation, but through the uncompromising rejection of what leads us into sin.
That is a far more uncomfortable sermon.
Because it removes our favorite excuse.
And perhaps that is why we do not always want to preach it.
Then the story takes us into a room filled with religious accusation.
A woman is brought before Jesus.
She has been caught in adultery, according to her accusers.
The scribes and Pharisees place her in the center.
Not gently.
Not privately.
Publicly.
They ask Jesus whether she should be stoned.
And here is the question that has troubled countless careful readers.
Where is the man?
Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22 address both parties in adultery.
Yet in this scene, only the woman is presented.
The passage does not tell us what happened to the man.
We should not invent an answer.
But his absence from the accusation is conspicuous.
The accusers were not simply seeking justice.
John 8:6 explicitly says they were testing Jesus, seeking grounds to accuse Him.
The woman had become a weapon in someone else's religious confrontation.
And Jesus refused to play their game.
He stooped and wrote on the ground.
We are not told what He wrote.
Theories abound, but Scripture does not identify the words.
Then Jesus spoke.
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her” (John 8:7, KJV).
One sentence.
And the atmosphere changed.
The men who had arrived ready to expose someone else's sin were suddenly confronted with their own.
One by one, they left.
Jesus then said to the woman, “Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more” (John 8:11, KJV).
There is something essential we must preserve here.
Jesus did not declare adultery harmless.
He called her away from sin.
But He also refused to let religious hypocrisy have the final word over her life.
Mercy did not abolish holiness.
Holiness did not extinguish mercy.
They met in Jesus Christ.

An important textual note belongs here: the account of the woman caught in adultery, traditionally placed in John 7:53–8:11, is absent from several of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel and appears in different locations in some manuscript traditions. Many modern Bible translations identify this textual issue. Christians who teach this passage should acknowledge that history rather than conceal it. Its familiar portrait of mercy and repentance is consistent with themes clearly established elsewhere in the New Testament, but its textual status should be handled carefully.
And even with that qualification, the questions raised by this traditional account are worth examining alongside the rest of Scripture.
Why are we sometimes more eager to expose a sinner than to restore a human being?
Why can public shame feel more satisfying than private repentance?
Why do we sometimes enjoy the downfall of someone whose struggles resemble our own?
The Gospel does not invite us to become spectators at someone else's humiliation.
It calls us to face our own need for mercy.
And now consider the woman at the well.
John 4.
Jesus meets a Samaritan woman and asks her for water.
Their conversation moves from ordinary thirst to living water.
Then Jesus tells her to call her husband.
She answers that she has no husband.
Jesus responds that she has had five husbands and that the man she currently has is not her husband.
For generations, this woman has frequently been described as sexually promiscuous.
But the text does not explain how those five marriages ended.
She may have experienced divorce, widowhood, abandonment, or circumstances the narrative simply does not reveal.
We are not told.
And when Scripture does not tell us something, humility requires that we stop pretending it does.
Jesus identifies the truth about her situation.
But He does not give us permission to invent a detailed history of her sexual conduct.
What He does reveal is something much greater.
He speaks to her about worship.
He reveals Himself as Messiah.
And she becomes a witness to her community.
The woman who came to draw water leaves her water jar and goes to tell others about Jesus.
The encounter moves from exposure to revelation.
From personal history to living water.
From being known by Jesus to inviting others to know Him.
And that should make every one of us examine the way we speak about people whose histories we do not fully understand.
Someone may have been divorced several times.
You do not know every betrayal they survived.
Someone may be raising a child alone.
You do not know the circumstances that brought them there.
Someone may carry a sexual history they deeply regret.
You do not know how much manipulation, coercion, loneliness, fear, or personal failure is involved.
This does not mean sin is imaginary.
It means human stories are often more complicated than the labels we assign.
Jesus knew the truth about the Samaritan woman without reducing her to a caricature.
We should learn from Him.
But perhaps the most devastating evidence that Scripture exposes men's sexual wrongdoing comes from stories we would sometimes rather skip entirely.
Genesis 34 tells of Dinah and Shechem.
The narrative describes Shechem taking Dinah and violating her.
Whatever complexities appear in the subsequent negotiations, the original violation is not something to romanticize.
Then there is 2 Samuel 13.
Amnon desires his half-sister Tamar.
He manipulates circumstances to isolate her.
She pleads with him.
She resists.
He refuses to listen.
And he rapes her.
Afterward, the text describes his hatred toward her.
The same man who claimed to desire her now wants her removed from his presence.
Tamar is left devastated.
The biblical narrative does not portray her as the seductress.
It shows the terrible destruction caused by Amnon's violence and the failure of those around her to provide justice.
And there is an especially painful detail.
Tamar asks, “Whither shall I cause my shame to go?” (2 Samuel 13:13, KJV).
She is speaking from within a culture in which the consequences of sexual violence could devastate a woman's social standing.
But the fact that Tamar experiences shame does not mean she is morally guilty for what Amnon did.
The shame imposed upon a victim is not proof of the victim's sin.
Someone needs to hear that.
Perhaps someone reading this has spent years carrying guilt for an act of violence committed against them.
Perhaps someone has been told to remain silent because the person who harmed them was respected.
Perhaps someone has been pressured to forgive before anyone was willing to acknowledge what happened.
Listen carefully.
What another person did to violate you is not your moral failure.
God does not require you to rename abuse as love.
He does not require you to call exploitation a misunderstanding.
He does not require you to surrender your safety to prove that you have forgiven.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are not identical.
Forgiveness does not remove the need for truth, protection, accountability, or lawful justice.
And the Church must never use spiritual language to shield those who harm the vulnerable.
Jesus warned severely against causing the vulnerable to stumble (Matthew 18:6).
The God of Scripture is not indifferent to the suffering of those who have been violated.
Psalm 34:18 tells us, “The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart” (KJV).
Not every wound heals quickly.
Not every story receives earthly justice.
Not every survivor is ready to speak publicly.
And no one should be forced to turn their trauma into a testimony for the comfort of an audience.
But the wounded are not invisible to God.
He sees.
He knows.
And His justice is not canceled by another person's status, title, or religious reputation.
Now we must turn the mirror toward ourselves.
Because it would be easy to read all of this and simply conclude that men are the problem.
That would miss the Gospel too.
Scripture does not teach that women are morally innocent and men are morally corrupt.
Women also make sinful choices.
Men also experience exploitation and violence.
Both men and women are accountable before God.
Both are capable of deception, lust, pride, selfishness, and cruelty.
Both can be wounded.
Both need grace.
Romans 3:23 does not divide humanity into one guilty sex and one innocent sex.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (KJV).
All.
The problem is not that Scripture refuses to confront women's sin.
The problem is that readers sometimes confront women's sin selectively while minimizing the sins of men, especially when those men possess authority.
And selective righteousness is not righteousness.
It is partiality.
The Gospel leaves no room for the man who thinks his private pornography habit is less serious than a woman's public sexual history simply because no one knows about it.
It leaves no room for the husband who demands fidelity while maintaining secret affairs.
It leaves no room for the pastor who preaches purity while exploiting someone under his spiritual care.
It leaves no room for the woman who uses manipulation, deceit, or sexual betrayal and then refuses responsibility.
It leaves no room for the person who delights in exposing someone else's past while carefully concealing their own.
The cross confronts all of us.
And here is where the story becomes personal.
Maybe you have never been a king like David.
But you know what it feels like to hide something.
Maybe you have never stood where Judah stood.
But you remember a time when you judged someone for a sin you secretly excused in yourself.
Maybe you have never lived Samson's life.
But you recognize the slow erosion of conviction when desire repeatedly wins the argument.
Maybe you have never stood among the accusers in John 8.
But you have held someone else's failure in your mind like a stone.
Maybe you have been the one publicly judged.
Maybe you have been the one privately wounded.
Maybe you have been both the sinner and the person sinned against in different chapters of your life.
And somewhere beneath all the defenses, there is a question you cannot quite escape.
What does Jesus do with someone who knows the truth about their own life and cannot rewrite the past?
This is where the Gospel becomes more than a moral lecture.
Because Christianity does not announce that good people have finally found a way to separate themselves from bad people.
It announces that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
The apostle Paul wrote in 1 Timothy 1:15:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief” (KJV).
Paul did not say that Christ came to save people who could successfully manage their reputations.
He came for sinners.
People whose guilt is real.
People whose excuses have run out.
People whose histories contain things they cannot undo.
But we must understand grace correctly.
Grace is not permission to continue abusing others.
Grace is not a spiritual escape hatch for powerful offenders.
Grace is not a demand that wounded people immediately trust the people who hurt them.
Grace is God's undeserved favor, revealed supremely in Jesus Christ, that forgives and transforms those who turn to Him in faith.
The Greek word χάρις (charis) is commonly translated “grace.”
In the New Testament, it can refer to favor, gift, or gracious generosity, depending on context.
And Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that salvation is by grace through faith, not the achievement of human works.
But the passage does not stop there.
Ephesians 2:10 teaches that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace saves us.
And grace begins changing the way we live.
That is why genuine repentance matters.

The Greek noun μετάνοια (metanoia) means repentance, involving a change of mind or orientation; in the biblical call to repentance, it is not merely feeling sorry but turning toward God in a way that bears fruit.
The person who has sinned cannot purchase innocence with a dramatic apology.
The person who has harmed someone cannot demand that the wounded person immediately restore the relationship.
The person who has hidden behind religious respectability cannot substitute ministry activity for integrity.
Real repentance tells the truth.
Real repentance stops defending what God condemns.
Real repentance accepts responsibility.
Real repentance seeks to repair harm where possible, without treating restitution as a purchase of forgiveness.
And real repentance begins with surrender to Jesus Christ.
Not because we can repair ourselves perfectly.
But because the One who died for our sins and rose again is able to make us new.
Consider the woman Luke describes in Luke 7:36–50.
She enters a Pharisee's house while Jesus is reclining at a meal.
Luke identifies her as a woman known in the city as a sinner, but does not specify that her sin was sexual.
That detail matters.
We should not add sexual accusations to a person's story simply because the text uses the word “sinner.”
She weeps at Jesus' feet.
Her tears fall.
She wipes His feet with her hair.
She kisses them and anoints them.
Simon the Pharisee watches.
And in his heart, he judges.
If Jesus were truly a prophet, Simon thinks, He would know what kind of woman this is.
But Jesus does know.
He knows the woman.
And He knows Simon.
That is the part we sometimes forget.
The Lord who sees the tears of the publicly disgraced also sees the pride of the privately respectable.
Jesus tells a parable about two debtors who are forgiven.
Then He turns toward the woman while speaking to Simon.
“Seest thou this woman?” (Luke 7:44, KJV).
What a question.
Simon had seen her.
But only through the lens of her reputation.
He saw a category.
A scandal.
A reason to feel superior.
Jesus saw a person.
And then Jesus declared to her, “Thy sins are forgiven” (Luke 7:48, KJV).
The story does not deny that she was a sinner.
It reveals that her sin was not beyond the reach of divine mercy.
Her faith was directed toward the One who could forgive.
And perhaps that is the invitation this entire article has been moving toward.
Not merely to change how we discuss women in the Bible.
Not merely to confront male hypocrisy.
Not merely to expose religious double standards.
But to recognize that every human being must ultimately stand before Jesus Christ without a disguise.
The abused person does not need to accept blame for the abuse.
The guilty person does need to acknowledge guilt.
The self-righteous person needs to repent of pride.
The broken person needs the hope of God's mercy.
And every one of us needs the Savior.
Because the Gospel is not the story of Jesus choosing a morally superior group of people.
It is the story of the sinless Son of God giving Himself for sinners.
At the cross, we see how seriously God takes evil.
Sin is not dismissed as harmless.
And we see how astonishingly far divine love goes to redeem.
Christ bore our sins.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again, as proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
The resurrection is not a sentimental ending added to a tragic story.
It is the announcement that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
And that changes everything.
David's sin was not made righteous.
Judah's hypocrisy was not made admirable.
Samson's recklessness was not made wise.
Amnon's violence was not made excusable.
The religious accusers' cruelty was not made holy.
But none of these stories can overturn the central truth of the Gospel.
God is holy.
Humanity is fallen.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
And His grace calls us into truth, repentance, forgiveness, and transformation.
Maybe you are reading this with tears in your eyes because someone once used the Bible to shame you for what another person did.
Maybe you have quietly believed that your sexual history disqualifies you from ever being loved by God.
Maybe you are a man who has excused lust, deception, or betrayal for years while judging women more harshly than yourself.
Maybe you are a woman who has hidden destructive choices behind the assumption that only men should be confronted.
Maybe you are a Christian leader who needs to stop protecting an image and start telling the truth.
Or maybe you are simply exhausted from pretending to be cleaner, stronger, and more spiritually stable than you really are.
Hear this.
You do not have to manufacture an innocent past to come to Jesus.
You do have to come honestly.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But through Christ, yesterday does not have to be the master of tomorrow.
And that is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not built around the fantasy that Christians never fall.
It is built around the truth that Jesus Christ saves, restores, disciplines, and transforms people who turn to Him.
Not by denying the scandal.
Not by hiding the victims.
Not by protecting the guilty from consequences.
Not by reducing grace to a slogan.
But by bringing sinners into the light of truth and offering redemption through the crucified and risen Christ.
If this article has exposed something you need to surrender, do not rush past that conviction.
Sit with it.
Open the Scriptures.
Pray honestly.
If you have sinned against someone, stop justifying it. Seek godly accountability, make appropriate restitution, and respect the other person's boundaries.

If you have been harmed, remember that another person's sin does not define your worth. Seek safety, wise support, and appropriate professional or pastoral care from people who will protect rather than silence you.

And if you have been living beneath the crushing weight of shame, remember that Jesus calls people out of darkness not to entertain an audience with their humiliation, but to bring them into His light.
There may be someone in your family who needs to read this.
A son who has been taught that masculine desire is uncontrollable.
A daughter who has been made to feel responsible for someone else's choices.
A husband who needs to confront his double standards.
A wife who needs to hear that God sees her suffering.
A church leader who needs to remember that authority increases responsibility.
A young believer who has confused purity with public reputation.
Or someone who has abandoned church because religious people seemed more interested in scandal than restoration.
Not merely because it may reach more people, but because biblical truth deserves to be discussed beyond the safety of familiar circles.
And I want to ask you something personal.
When you look at these biblical accounts, which truth confronts you most deeply?
That men must be held accountable for their own choices?
That victims should never be blamed for the harm committed against them?
That religious hypocrisy can hide beneath the appearance of holiness?
Or that Jesus still offers forgiveness to repentant sinners whose past cannot be undone?
You can simply write, “Jesus, search my heart.”
Or “No more hiding.”
Or “Christ is still healing me.”
You do not have to reveal private trauma, name anyone, or disclose details you are not ready to share.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to begin a meaningful conversation.
And sometimes someone else reading the comments discovers that they are not the only person trying to find their way back to God.
We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, Jesus Christ remains central, and difficult truths are approached with both courage and compassion.
And if you have been receiving encouragement, conviction, or spiritual nourishment through Gospel Warrior, I want to invite you to consider something deeper.
Our mission is not simply to publish articles that people read for a few minutes and forget.
We want to help people keep opening their Bibles after the emotional moment has passed.
We want struggling believers to find biblical encouragement.
We want seekers to encounter the message of Jesus.
We want families to have resources that help them grow in faith.
We want discipleship to continue beyond a single post.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning and spiritual nourishment more accessible.
But continuing and expanding this work also requires practical support.
Writing, preparing resources, maintaining a growing library, and reaching more people all involve time, effort, and expense.
But I want to be biblically careful here.

Scripture teaches us to give willingly, not under pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7). Supporting your local church, caring for your household, and helping those in need remain important responsibilities.
These items are not substitutes for Scripture or spiritual growth, and the discount is not the reason to pursue Christ.
They are simply one way we can express gratitude to those who help sustain the ministry.
Perhaps someone who has silently carried shame for years will read it.
Perhaps someone who has used spiritual authority irresponsibly will finally begin to confront their conduct.
Perhaps a believer who has been drifting will return to the Scriptures.
Perhaps someone who has never understood the Gospel will begin asking who Jesus really is.
We cannot promise what any particular post will accomplish.
But we can faithfully proclaim Christ and trust God with the fruit.
Because ultimately, Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
A social media page is not the Church.
And no amount of engagement can replace repentance, faith, obedience, and genuine fellowship with other believers.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
And the mission is worth supporting only insofar as it faithfully points people toward Him.
Before you leave, return with me to the question that began this story.
Where was the man?
It was a question about a woman brought before religious accusers.
But perhaps, after everything we have read, we should ask another question.
Where are we standing?
Beside David, hoping no one discovers what we have done?
Beside Judah, condemning someone for a sin in which we share responsibility?
Beside Samson, blaming another person for choices we refuse to confront?
Beside Simon the Pharisee, examining someone else's reputation while ignoring our own pride?
Or at the feet of Jesus, finally willing to tell the truth?
Because the most important question is not whether you can identify the worst sinner in the room.
It is whether you are willing to come to the only One in the room who has never sinned.
And receive the mercy you could never earn.
The Bible's sexual scandals are not invitations to despise women.
They are not invitations to despise men.
They are warnings about what sin can do to human beings, relationships, families, and communities.
They are reminders that power without integrity becomes dangerous.
That desire without self-control can become destructive.
That religious language without humility can become cruel.
And that grace without truth becomes a counterfeit of the Gospel.
But above all, they lead us toward the Savior who is both full of grace and truth (John 1:14).
So put down the stone you were never qualified to throw.
Confess the sin you have been trying to conceal.
Protect the person whose suffering others have tried to minimize.
Tell the truth, even when the truth is costly.
And come to Jesus.
Not as the hero of your own carefully edited story.
But as a human being who needs the mercy of God.
Because one day, when all the excuses have fallen silent, the question will not be how successfully you exposed another person's darkness.
It will be whether you responded to the Light when He called you out of your own.
The hands that were pierced for sinners are still the reason our darkest chapters do not have to be our final ones.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD NEVER PROMISED TO MAKE YOU RICH. HE PROMISED SOMETHING MONEY COULD NEVER BUY.
paragraphs: GOD NEVER PROMISED TO MAKE YOU RICH. HE PROMISED SOMETHING MONEY COULD NEVER BUY.
“Godliness With Contentment Is Great Gain” — Paul’s Devastating Answer to Prosperity Obsession, and the Freedom of Discovering That Jesus Is Enough.
What if the blessing you've been begging God to give you is the very thing that could eventually pull your heart away from Him?
Read that again.
Because somewhere tonight, a Christian is lying awake, staring at a ceiling, wondering why God seems to be blessing everyone else.
Someone just watched another believer celebrate a new house while their own rent is overdue.
Someone saw a testimony about a financial breakthrough and quietly whispered, “Lord, when will it be my turn?”
Someone is faithfully praying, serving, giving, working, and trying to obey God, yet the bills keep coming, the debts keep growing, and the breakthrough never seems to arrive.
And perhaps that someone is you.
You love Jesus. You really do.
But there are moments when you look at your life and wonder whether you're doing something wrong.

Because somewhere along the way, you heard that faithfulness produces financial abundance. That giving guarantees a financial return. That if you declare enough, believe enough, sow enough, and refuse to speak negatively, prosperity will eventually come knocking.
And when it doesn't?
The questions begin.
Is my faith too weak?
Did I offend God?
Have I failed to unlock some spiritual principle?
Why does it seem as though people who barely acknowledge God are flourishing while I'm struggling just to survive?
But what if the problem isn't that God has forgotten you?
What if the problem is that we've allowed the world's definition of blessing to become the measuring stick for God's goodness?
What if Jesus is not withholding the good life from you?
What if He's rescuing you from a counterfeit version of it?
There is a sentence buried in Paul's first letter to Timothy that confronts one of the most seductive lies ever to enter the Christian imagination.
It doesn't need a stage, flashing lights, or a preacher promising seven financial breakthroughs.
It needs only a heart willing to hear the truth.
“But godliness with contentment is great gain.” — 1 Timothy 6:6, KJV
Nine English words.
Enough to dismantle an entire theology built around the worship of more.
And perhaps enough to begin healing the restless place inside you that keeps whispering, “I'll finally be happy when…”
Paul wrote these words in Greek:
ἔστιν δὲ πορισμὸς μέγας ἡ εὐσέβεια μετὰ αὐταρκείας.
Estin de porismos megas hē eusebeia meta autarkeias.
A close translation is: “But godliness with contentment is great gain.”
The word πορισμός (porismos) refers to gain or a means of profit.
εὐσέβεια (eusebeia) refers to godliness, a life marked by reverence toward God.
And αὐτάρκεια (autarkeia) describes contentment or sufficiency.
That last word matters.
In the wider Greek-speaking world, autarkeia could describe self-sufficiency. But when we read Paul alongside his other letters, we discover something remarkable.
Christian contentment is not the proud declaration, “I don't need anybody.”
It is the humble confession, “Whatever my circumstances, Christ will not abandon me.”
Paul was not telling Christians to stop working, abandon responsibility, or pretend that poverty doesn't hurt.
He was confronting the dangerous belief that material wealth is the ultimate evidence of spiritual success.
And the context makes his warning impossible to misunderstand.
Immediately before this verse, Paul describes people who imagine that godliness is a means of financial gain (1 Timothy 6:5).
Then he turns their reasoning upside down.
True gain is not godliness used as a tool for getting rich.
True gain is godliness accompanied by contentment.
Do you see the difference?
One approach says, “I'll follow Jesus because of what He can give me.”
The other says, “I'll follow Jesus because He is worthy, whether I have much or little.”
One makes Christ the means to an earthly treasure.
The other recognizes Christ as the treasure.
And that difference can determine the direction of an entire life.
Imagine a man who spent twenty years chasing success.

He worked overtime. Missed family dinners. Postponed vacations. Told his wife they would spend more time together when business improved. Promised his children that one day he would finally be available.
Every financial milestone produced another milestone.
The first house wasn't enough.
The better car wasn't enough.
The larger savings account wasn't enough.
There was always somebody wealthier, somebody more successful, somebody living a life that looked better through the glass of a smartphone screen.
Then one evening, he came home to a quiet house.
His children had grown older.
His marriage had become distant.
His Bible sat beneath a pile of unopened paperwork.
And the man who had spent his life trying to gain everything realized that he had neglected some of the things he could never purchase back.
This is not an argument against hard work or responsible financial planning.
It is a warning against allowing the pursuit of provision to become the master of your existence.
Jesus asked a question that still echoes across centuries:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” — Mark 8:36, KJV
The terrifying possibility is not merely that you might fail to become wealthy.
It is that you might become wealthy and still lose sight of what matters eternally.
You can have a beautiful house and a restless heart.
You can have thousands of followers and nobody who truly knows you.
You can have a full bank account and an empty prayer life.
You can receive the applause of an entire generation while slowly losing your hunger for the presence of God.
And because the world celebrates visible success, nobody may recognize the spiritual poverty developing beneath the surface.
Not even you.
Paul continues:
“For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out.” — 1 Timothy 6:7, KJV
There is something deeply unsettling about that sentence.
You entered this world without possessions.
You will leave it without taking your possessions with you.
The clothes, the property, the investments, the awards, the devices, the carefully accumulated symbols of achievement…
None of them can cross the boundary of death in your hands.
That doesn't make them automatically evil.
It makes them temporary.
And temporary things become dangerous when we ask them to provide eternal security.
Paul then writes:
Food.
Clothing.
The basic provisions of life.
Paul is not forbidding gratitude for anything beyond these necessities. Nor is he suggesting that Christians must ignore injustice, refuse opportunities, or stop improving their circumstances.
He is teaching us that a heart can learn to rest without demanding an endless accumulation of possessions.
This is especially difficult when life itself feels financially suffocating.
And Scripture does not dismiss that suffering.
There is a difference between the person who is obsessed with becoming richer and the parent who is praying desperately for enough money to buy medicine.
There is a difference between greed and the desire to feed your family.
There is a difference between covetousness and the responsible pursuit of financial stability.
God knows those differences.
Jesus taught His disciples to pray, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11).
He did not shame them for having needs.
He taught them to bring those needs to their Father.
Contentment does not mean you must smile while your children go hungry or pretend that unpaid bills do not exist.
It means that even while you work, ask for help, pursue opportunities, and pray for provision, your identity and ultimate hope do not depend upon the amount of money you possess.
You are not worth less because you earn less.
You are not spiritually inferior because you rent instead of own.
You are not forgotten because your prayers have not produced the lifestyle you once imagined.
And you are not automatically closer to God because your financial circumstances improve.
Listen carefully.
A bigger bank account is not proof of greater holiness. And an empty wallet is not proof of weaker faith.
If wealth were the ultimate evidence of God's approval, how would we explain the apostle Paul?
He knew hunger.
He knew deprivation.
He knew imprisonment.
He knew what it meant to serve Christ without earthly comfort.
Yet this same man wrote:
“I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.” — Philippians 4:12, KJV
And then comes one of the most quoted verses in Christianity:
“I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.” — Philippians 4:13, KJV
How often have we heard that verse presented as a guarantee of extraordinary achievement?
As though Paul were saying, “I can become rich, famous, successful, and unstoppable because Christ empowers my ambitions.”
But read the verses together.
Paul was talking about enduring both abundance and need.
His confidence was not that Jesus would always remove uncomfortable circumstances.
His confidence was that Jesus would strengthen him within them.
The Greek expression in Philippians 4:13 is:
πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με.
Panta ischyō en tō endynamounti me.
In context, Paul is expressing his ability to face all these changing circumstances through the One who strengthens him.
That is not a blank check for every personal ambition.
It is a testimony of Christ-given endurance.
Paul had discovered something that prosperity obsession cannot understand.
He could have plenty without making plenty his god.
He could have little without concluding that God had abandoned him.
He could rejoice in provision without worshiping provision.
And he could suffer loss without losing the One who mattered most.
That is freedom.
Not the freedom of possessing everything you desire.
The freedom of no longer being controlled by everything you desire.
But there is another verse in 1 Timothy 6 that should make every Christian examine their heart.
“But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.” — 1 Timothy 6:9, KJV
Notice Paul's concern.
He is warning about those who are determined to become rich.
The issue is not merely possessing money.
It is what happens when the desire for riches begins to possess us.
Then comes verse 10:
“For the love of money is the root of all evil…” — 1 Timothy 6:10, KJV
The familiar King James wording can be misunderstood if we treat it as though every evil action in history must originate in money.
The Greek reads:
ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία.
Rhiza gar pantōn tōn kakōn estin hē philargyria.
The key word φιλαργυρία (philargyria) means love of money.
The Greek construction is commonly understood as describing the love of money as a root of all kinds of evils, not claiming that money itself is the single cause of every evil.
And Paul immediately explains the danger: some, through craving money, have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.
Money is not inherently sinful.
Scripture includes faithful people who possessed substantial resources.
Abraham had great wealth.
Job possessed considerable material blessings.
Joseph of Arimathea was a rich man who honored Jesus.
And in 1 Timothy 6:17–19, Paul instructs wealthy believers to avoid arrogance, place their hope in God rather than uncertain riches, and be generous.
He does not command every wealthy Christian to become destitute.
He commands them to understand where their security belongs.
The Bible does not teach that poverty automatically produces holiness.
Neither does it teach that wealth automatically proves God's favor.
The central question is deeper.
Who owns your heart?
Because you can worship money while having very little of it.
And you can possess money without making it your god.
The danger begins when financial success becomes your source of identity, your measure of spiritual maturity, or the condition upon which you are willing to trust God.
Perhaps the most heartbreaking form of this deception occurs when people are taught to treat giving as a guaranteed financial transaction.
Give this amount, and God will multiply it.
Sow this seed, and your breakthrough will arrive.
But the Lord is not a machine into which we deposit offerings to withdraw miracles.
God is not indebted to us because we gave money.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
And the suffering Christian should never be made to feel that financial hardship proves a failure to give enough.
Yes, Scripture teaches generosity.
Yes, giving is a meaningful expression of worship.
Yes, God is able to provide abundantly.
But 2 Corinthians 9:7 tells believers to give as they have purposed in their hearts, not grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
The surrounding passage connects God's provision with generosity and good works, not with a guaranteed promise of personal luxury.
Christian giving is not a spiritual investment scheme.
It is a response of gratitude to the God who has already given us the greatest gift.
Jesus Christ.
And if we forget that, even religious language can become a disguise for greed.
This is why Paul's words are so painfully relevant.
We live in a culture where almost everything encourages comparison.
Your phone can show you, within seconds, a thousand reasons to feel dissatisfied with your life.
Someone has a better house.
Someone has a more attractive spouse.
Someone has a more successful business.
Someone has a dream vacation.
Someone has a testimony that sounds far more dramatic than yours.
And before you realize it, gratitude has been replaced by comparison.
Yesterday's answered prayer becomes today's forgotten blessing.
The very thing you once begged God to provide becomes ordinary the moment someone else has more.
You prayed for a job.
God opened a door.
You rejoiced.
Then you saw someone earning twice your salary.
And suddenly, the job that once brought you to tears of thanksgiving no longer seemed sufficient.
You prayed for a home.
You finally had a place to sleep safely.
Then you saw somebody's beautiful house online.
And the walls that once felt like an answer to prayer began to feel like a disappointment.
Isn't it strange how quickly comparison can steal the joy of provision?
We can become so obsessed with what God has not given us that we stop recognizing what He already has.
But contentment is not the denial of desire.
It is the refusal to let desire become a dictator.
It is the ability to say, “Lord, I have needs. I have hopes. I have dreams. I will work faithfully and pray honestly. But I refuse to make these things more important than You.”
And that prayer may be one of the most difficult acts of surrender a modern Christian can make.
Because sometimes the idol is not something obviously wicked.
Sometimes it is a good thing that has become an ultimate thing.
A career.
A business.
A dream house.
A better future for your children.
Financial freedom.
Even ministry success.
All good desires can become spiritually dangerous when they take the place that belongs to Christ alone.
Jesus said:
“No man can serve two masters… Ye cannot serve God and mammon.” — Matthew 6:24, KJV
The word translated “mammon” refers to wealth or riches.
Jesus did not say that money and God cannot exist in the same person's life.
He said they cannot both be masters.
One must be subordinate.
One must surrender its claim to ultimate loyalty.
And here is where the Gospel becomes both deeply comforting and deeply confrontational.
Because our greatest problem is not merely that we desire too much money.
