Seven days outside the camp.
Seven days unable to resume her ordinary place among the people.
Seven days living with the seriousness of what had happened.
And then...
She was received again.
The story does not tell us everything she thought during those days.
We do not know every prayer she prayed.
We do not know every tear she shed.
We do not know precisely what she said when she returned.
But we know she was not left outside forever.
And that is the image I want you to carry.
Not merely the image of Miriam afflicted.
But the image of Miriam being brought back.
Not because her words had been harmless.
Not because her sin had never mattered.
But because judgment was not the final event recorded in her story.
Her failure was real. Her correction was painful. But she was received again.
And for those who belong to Jesus Christ, that truth opens the door to an even greater hope.
Your sin does not have to become your final identity.
Your past does not have to be your permanent prison.
Your shame does not have to be the voice that defines your future.
In Christ, forgiveness is real.
Repentance is possible.
Transformation is possible.
Restoration is possible, even though its earthly form and timing may differ from what we hope.
The Gospel never promises that every consequence will vanish.
But it offers something greater than the illusion of a consequence-free life.
It offers reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community of people who pretend they have never failed.
Not to create another religious platform where appearances matter more than truth.
But to keep pointing struggling, growing, repenting people back to Scripture and the saving grace of Jesus.
Because there are people scrolling through Facebook tonight who are carrying battles nobody knows about.
A father who feels spiritually exhausted.
A mother who prays quietly while holding her family together.
A young believer fighting temptation and wondering whether genuine change is possible.
A person who has not entered a church in years because shame keeps whispering that they do not belong.
A Christian who still loves Jesus but has grown cold, bitter, distracted, or weary.
And sometimes one Scripture-centered article reaches a person at the exact moment they are ready to listen.
That is why sharing matters.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
But because the truth that helped you may also help someone you know.
Our desire is to keep offering daily Scripture-centered encouragement, biblical truth, conviction, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment.
These resources are offered freely because access to biblical encouragement should not depend on someone's ability to pay.
But keeping a ministry active, creating resources, and reaching more people also requires practical support.
And this is where I want to invite you into something meaningful.
And it allows those who believe in this mission to participate in sustaining it.

Scripture teaches that believers may support those who labor in teaching and proclaiming the Gospel (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14), and that giving should be voluntary, generous, and free from compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But it should not be presented as a mandatory biblical tithe, a replacement for responsibilities to one's local church, or a requirement for glorifying God.
You glorify God through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, and faithful stewardship of what He has entrusted to you.
These products are simply another way to keep biblical encouragement present in everyday life.
It is the opportunity to help keep Christ-centered resources available and help this message reach more people.
And your salvation is not purchased by giving money to a ministry.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But gratitude for that grace can move us to serve, give, encourage, and help others encounter the truth.
Perhaps it is a conversation you need to have.
An apology you have been postponing.
A bitter thought you need to surrender.
A person you need to stop comparing yourself with.
A private prayer you need to pray.
Perhaps your heart has become more like Miriam's than you realized.
And perhaps today is the day you stop defending what God is asking you to surrender.
If God played back every private conversation you have had about someone else, would you be comfortable listening to it in His presence?
That question is not meant to drive you into hopelessness.
It is meant to drive you toward honesty.
And honesty can become the doorway to repentance.
The same God who heard Miriam's words also heard Moses' prayer.
He is not deaf to your confession.
He is not indifferent to your struggle.
And through Jesus Christ, He calls sinners to turn from darkness and come into His marvelous light.
If you have been wounded by someone else's words, ask Jesus to help you pursue truth without becoming consumed by bitterness.
If you have wounded someone with your words, ask Him for the courage to repent and seek to make things right.
If you have been jealous, confess it.
If you have been proud, surrender it.
If you have been hiding, come into the light.
And if you are spiritually exhausted, remember that Christ welcomes those who come to Him for rest (Matthew 11:28).
You do not have to manufacture a perfect prayer.
You can begin where Moses began.
With a cry for mercy.
"God, please..."
Please forgive me.
Please change my heart.
Please teach me to love without competing.
Please teach me to speak truth without cruelty.
Please help me celebrate the blessings You give others.
Please make me more like Jesus.
If this passage has brought you to genuine repentance, you may simply write "Jesus, have mercy on me."
You do not need to share details that should remain private. What matters is not how much you reveal online, but whether you respond honestly to God.
And as you go, remember the woman who once stood beside the Red Sea singing about God's victory.
She fell.
She was corrected.
She needed mercy.
And she was received again.
Miriam's story is not permission to treat sin lightly.
It is a warning against pride, a call to humility, and a reminder that mercy is precious.
But the greater story is the Gospel.
Because Moses could pray for his sister's healing.
Jesus Christ can save sinners, reconcile them to God, and transform the hearts that once rebelled against Him.
That is the hope worth sharing.
That is the truth worth living.
And that is the grace none of us could ever earn.

The God who heard the words that exposed Miriam's heart also heard the prayer that pleaded for her healing—and through Jesus Christ, the door of mercy is still open to every sinner who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHOULD CHRISTIAN PARENTS CUT OFF AN ADULT CHILD WHO REJECTS JESUS? THE BIBLICAL ANSWER MAY BREAK YOUR HEART BEFORE IT HEALS IT.
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIAN PARENTS CUT OFF AN ADULT CHILD WHO REJECTS JESUS? THE BIBLICAL ANSWER MAY BREAK YOUR HEART BEFORE IT HEALS IT.

When the child you raised to love God walks away from everything you taught them, should you close the door to protect your faith—or leave it open because Jesus never stopped loving the lost? What Scripture actually teaches about rebellion, boundaries, repentance, parental heartbreak, and the kind of grace that refuses to surrender the truth.
There is a particular kind of heartbreak that only a Christian parent understands.
It is hearing your grown child say, “I don't believe in God anymore.”
And suddenly, the room feels different.
This is the same child whose tiny hands you once folded together in prayer.
The same child you carried into church before they could walk.
The same child you taught to say, “Jesus loves me,” before they understood what those words meant.
You remember their first Bible.
Their first Sunday school lesson.
Maybe even the day they were baptized.
And now?
They tell you Christianity is not for them.
They question the Bible you taught them to trust. They reject the Savior you have spent your life following. Perhaps they mock the faith that carried you through your darkest nights.
And somewhere between your disappointment and your fear, a terrible question begins forming.
Should I cut my own child out of my life because they have rejected Jesus?
Before you answer, I want you to picture something.
A father standing outside his house.
Looking down a road.
Waiting for someone who has broken his heart.
Someone who has dishonored his family.
Someone who has taken what was given to him and wasted it.
The father has every reason to be angry.
Every reason to close the door.
Every reason to say, “You made your choice. Now live with it.”
But when he finally sees his son approaching in the distance, something happens that changes the entire story.
He runs.
And if you are a Christian parent wrestling with whether to cut off your adult child, you need to understand why Jesus told that story.
Because the answer is deeper than simply saying, “Always welcome them,” or “Cut them off until they repent.”
And getting it wrong can wound a family for generations.
Jesus tells us in Luke 15:11–32 about a younger son who demands his inheritance before his father dies.
In that culture, the request was deeply insulting. The son wanted the benefits of his father's possessions without remaining under his father's household.
He wanted the inheritance.
But not the relationship as it had been.
He wanted freedom.
But not the responsibility that came with it.
So the father divided his property.
And the son left.
Notice what the father did not do.
He did not chase his son into the distant country and force him to return.
He did not pretend the son's decisions were wise.
He did not finance an endless rebellion.
But neither does Jesus describe the father declaring that his son was permanently dead to him and forbidden ever to return.
The son eventually squandered everything.
He became desperate.
Hungry.
Humiliated.
And in his misery, he remembered his father's house.
Luke 15:17 says, in the King James Version, “And when he came to himself.”
The Greek expression is εἰς ἑαυτὸν δὲ ἐλθὼν (eis heauton de elthōn).
Literally, the wording conveys the idea of coming to himself.
It is a powerful picture of a man beginning to recognize the reality of his condition.

But we must be careful here. The expression does not mean every struggling or unbelieving adult child is irrational, mentally unwell, or incapable of thoughtful disagreement. Jesus is describing this particular son's awakening within the parable.
And then comes the moment that should stop every wounded parent in their tracks.
Luke 15:20 says:
“But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.”
The Greek word translated “had compassion” is ἐσπλαγχνίσθη (esplanchnisthē), from a verb describing deep, inward compassion.
Not reluctant tolerance.
Not cold permission to enter the house.
Compassion.
The father saw his son before the son reached him.
And he ran.
But do not miss something equally important.
The son returned acknowledging his sin.
The father did not need to call evil good in order to welcome his child home.
Grace did not erase the truth.
And truth did not extinguish grace.
That is the tension Christian parents must learn to carry.
Because some parents believe loving their child means approving every decision that child makes.
Others believe standing for biblical truth requires withdrawing affection until the child changes.
Scripture gives us a more demanding way.
A way that requires conviction without cruelty.
Love without compromise.
Boundaries without revenge.
And faithfulness without pretending we control another person's soul.
Consider this carefully.
Your adult child may reject Christianity.
But does that mean you must reject your child?
No. Scripture does not establish a universal command requiring Christian parents to sever relationships with adult children simply because those children no longer profess faith in Christ.
That distinction matters enormously.
In 1 Corinthians 5, Paul addresses a serious case of public, unrepentant sexual immorality within the Corinthian church.
He instructs the congregation to exercise discipline toward someone who claims membership among believers while persisting in such conduct.
But in verses 9–13, Paul explicitly distinguishes those inside the church from those outside it.
In 1 Corinthians 5:12, he asks:
“For what have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within?”
The context concerns church discipline, not a blanket rule for parents to abandon unbelieving relatives.
A professing Christian living in open, serious, unrepentant sin presents a different pastoral question from an adult child who openly says they are no longer a believer.
Even then, the nature of the relationship matters.
Church membership is not identical to parenthood.
And the authority of a local congregation is not the same as a parent's authority over an independent adult.
We must never turn a passage about church discipline into a weapon Scripture itself has not authorized.
Some will point to Matthew 10:34–37, where Jesus warns that allegiance to Him may divide even the closest families.
And yes, those words are serious.
Christ must come first.
A parent must never deny Jesus to preserve a relationship.
But putting Christ first does not automatically mean refusing to speak to an unbelieving son or daughter.
Jesus warns that following Him may bring division. He does not command parents to manufacture that division whenever a child disagrees with their faith.
There is a difference between suffering rejection because you follow Christ and deliberately rejecting someone to prove that you follow Christ.
Please read that again.
There is a difference between suffering rejection because you follow Christ and deliberately rejecting someone to prove that you follow Christ.
And if that sentence makes you uncomfortable, perhaps it is worth sitting with that discomfort before making a decision that cannot easily be undone.
Because your child is not your enemy.
Ephesians 6:12 reminds believers that our struggle is not ultimately against flesh and blood.
That does not mean your child's decisions have no consequences.
It means your child is not the ultimate enemy to be defeated.
You can disagree with their beliefs.
You can refuse to participate in conduct that violates your conscience.
You can maintain your Christian convictions.
And you can still say:
“You are my child. I love you. I cannot agree with everything you believe or do, but my love for you is not something you have to earn by pretending to believe what I believe.”
Imagine what that kind of sentence might mean to someone who expects nothing but rejection.
Not because it guarantees they will return to Christianity.
It does not.
But because love that is not used as leverage can make honest conversation possible.
And honest conversation matters.
Perhaps your adult child did not walk away because they wanted to live recklessly.
Perhaps they encountered questions they did not know how to answer.
Perhaps they witnessed hypocrisy among Christians.
Perhaps they were hurt by someone who used the Bible to control or shame them.
Perhaps they struggled with suffering, unanswered prayer, or difficult passages of Scripture.
Or perhaps, after serious reflection, they genuinely no longer believe Christianity is true.
You may disagree with their conclusions.
You may believe they are profoundly mistaken.
But if you refuse to listen, how will you understand what they are actually rejecting?
A parent who listens is not necessarily compromising.
Sometimes listening is the beginning of speaking truth wisely.
James 1:19 says:
“Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.”
The Greek phrase ταχὺς εἰς τὸ ἀκοῦσαι (tachys eis to akousai) means “quick to hear.”
Notice that Scripture does not say, “Be quick to win every argument.”
It calls us to hear.
And hearing requires more than waiting for your turn to correct someone.
Some parents have spent years preparing answers to questions their children never actually asked.
Meanwhile, their children have been carrying wounds nobody noticed.
What if, instead of beginning another argument, you asked:
“Can you help me understand what changed?”
“What has your experience of Christianity been like?”
“Did something happen that made trusting God difficult?”
“Have I ever made you feel that you could not be honest with me?”
That last question may be the hardest.
Because it opens the possibility that a parent who sincerely loved Jesus may still have made mistakes.
And Christian parents are not exempt from repentance.
Ephesians 6:4 warns fathers not to provoke their children to wrath, but to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
The Greek verb παροργίζετε (parorgizete) refers to provoking or exasperating.
Paul's instruction does not mean parents must avoid every disagreement or difficult correction.
It does mean that the manner in which parents exercise authority matters to God.
A parent can teach true doctrine in a harsh way.
A parent can defend biblical morality while speaking with contempt.
A parent can insist on outward religious behavior while neglecting the child's inner life.
And a parent can be right about an important biblical principle while being wrong in the way they treat another human being.
If that has happened, repentance is not surrendering your faith.
It is practicing it.
You can say:
“I still believe Jesus Christ is Lord. I still believe the gospel is true. But I recognize that I have sometimes spoken to you with anger instead of patience. I am sorry. Will you forgive me?”
There is no contradiction between confessing Christ and confessing your own failures.
In fact, the gospel gives us a reason to do both.
But what about boundaries?
What if your adult child mocks Jesus in your home?
What if they become verbally abusive?
What if they steal from you, threaten your safety, manipulate you financially, or repeatedly violate reasonable household expectations?
Must you tolerate all of that to prove Christian love?
Absolutely not.
Christian love is not permission for abuse.
Forgiveness is not the same as unrestricted access.
Reconciliation is not the same as the immediate restoration of trust.
And a relationship does not become healthy merely because two people share DNA.
Proverbs 22:3 describes the prudent person as one who foresees danger and takes refuge.
Romans 12:18 says:
“If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.”
Notice the realism of that verse.
If it be possible.
As much as lieth in you.
Peace requires more than one person's willingness.
You can be responsible for your conduct without being able to control another person's response.
If an adult child is abusive, threatening, or dangerous, a parent may need distance, firm restrictions, professional support, or even complete separation for safety.
That is not the same as cutting someone off merely because they no longer believe in Jesus.
A parent can refuse to fund destructive behavior.
A parent can establish conditions for living in their home.
A parent can end conversations that become abusive.
A parent can say, “I will speak with you when we can treat each other respectfully.”
And in genuinely dangerous situations, a parent can prioritize safety without waiting for the other person to agree.
Love does not require remaining available for harm.
But boundaries should serve truth, safety, and responsibility—not become disguised punishments for unbelief.
That is a crucial difference.
“I cannot allow you to threaten me” is a boundary.
“I will never speak to you again unless you become a Christian” makes affection conditional on religious profession.
Those are not the same thing.
And we should never confuse them.
There is another passage many parents need to hear.
Colossians 4:5–6 instructs believers to walk wisely toward outsiders and let their speech be gracious, seasoned with salt.
The Greek expression ἐν χάριτι (en chariti) means “with grace” or “in grace.”
Paul does not tell Christians to abandon conviction.
He tells them to communicate with grace and wisdom.
If we are called to speak graciously to outsiders, why would we assume that our unbelieving adult children should receive less gracious speech simply because their unbelief hurts us personally?
The pain is real.
But pain does not give us permission to become cruel.
And perhaps this is where the deepest issue begins to surface.
Some Christian parents are not only grieving their child's unbelief.
They are grieving the future they imagined.
The family praying together.
The grandchildren raised in church.
The shared worship.
The familiar traditions.
The certainty that the next generation would carry the same faith.
And when that future begins to disappear, fear can masquerade as righteous anger.
We may say, “I am defending God.”
But underneath, we may also be saying, “I am terrified of losing my child.”
If that is you, God already knows.
You do not have to disguise grief as certainty.
You can bring it to Him.
You can weep.
You can pray.
You can ask for wisdom.
You can admit that you are afraid.
But do not let fear convince you that you must become the Holy Spirit in your child's life.
You cannot manufacture saving faith.
You cannot argue someone into regeneration.
You cannot threaten someone into genuine repentance.
Jesus says in John 6:44:
“No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him.”

That statement comes within Jesus' teaching about the Father's work in bringing people to the Son. Christians have long discussed aspects of its theological implications, but the passage clearly directs attention to God's initiative rather than human coercion.
And Romans 10:17 reminds us that faith comes through hearing the message of Christ.
That is why we bear witness.
Why we teach.
Why we pray.
Why we speak the truth.
But we are not sovereign over the result.
Your calling is faithfulness.
Not control.
You are a parent.
You are not the Savior.
And that truth can be painful before it becomes freeing.
Because you may have to surrender something you never realized you were holding so tightly.
The belief that if you prayed enough, taught enough, disciplined enough, or modeled Christianity well enough, your child would certainly become a lifelong believer.

Proverbs 22:6 speaks of training a child in the way he should go, but this wisdom proverb should not be turned into an unconditional guarantee that every faithfully raised child will profess saving faith as an adult.
The Bible itself shows us that people make real moral and spiritual choices.
Parents bear responsibility for their own faithfulness.
But adult children bear responsibility for their own responses to God.
Your child's unbelief is not, by itself, proof that you failed as a parent.
Nor does your sincerity as a parent prove you made no mistakes.
Both truths can stand together.
And perhaps that is where humility begins.
Now consider Jesus Himself.
John 1:11 says:
“He came unto his own, and his own received him not.”
The Son of God knows rejection.
He knows what it means to extend truth and mercy and still be refused.
In Matthew 23:37, Jesus laments over Jerusalem, expressing His desire to gather its children as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, while confronting their unwillingness.
There is tenderness in that lament.
There is also judgment and seriousness.
Jesus does not pretend rejection is harmless.
But His grief is not cold.
His heart is not indifferent.
And at the cross, the gospel reveals something even greater.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
The Greek word συνίστησιν (synistēsin) conveys God's demonstration or commendation of His love.
God's love was demonstrated while we were still sinners.
Not after we had cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we had earned His attention.
Not after we had become spiritually impressive.
Christ died for the ungodly.
And that is the center of Christianity.
Not parental control.
Not religious appearances.
Not the preservation of a perfect-looking family.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen, offering forgiveness and reconciliation with God to sinners who cannot save themselves.
This does not mean every person is automatically reconciled to God regardless of faith or repentance.
Scripture calls people to repent and believe the gospel.
Mark 1:15 records Jesus saying:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
The Greek words μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε (metanoeite kai pisteuete) express the call to repent and believe.
Grace is not permission to remain indifferent to sin.
It is God's undeserved favor revealed supremely in Christ, who calls sinners to turn to Him.
And because salvation is so serious, we must not reduce it to outward compliance.
An adult child who attends church merely to keep parental affection has not necessarily embraced Jesus.
An adult child who says a prayer to stop a family argument has not necessarily experienced genuine conversion.
A child who hides doubts out of fear may look obedient while becoming increasingly isolated.
Would you rather have a child who pretends to believe in order to keep you happy?
Or a child who knows they can speak honestly with you, even when the truth breaks your heart?
Honesty does not guarantee salvation.
But forced religious performance is not the same as saving faith.
And Christian parents should desire genuine faith, not merely the appearance of it.
There is something else we must remember about the father in Luke 15.
He did not run into the distant country and declare the son's rebellion righteous.
He did not rewrite morality to make the relationship comfortable.
But when the son returned, the father did not stand on the porch rehearsing every failure.
He received him with compassion.
He called for a robe.
A ring.
Sandals.
A celebration.
And the father said in Luke 15:24:
“For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.”
The Greek word ἀπολωλώς (apolōlōs) means “lost,” and εὑρέθη (heurethē) means “was found.”
The language belongs to the great movement of Luke 15, where Jesus responds to criticism that He welcomes sinners and eats with them.
The lost sheep.
The lost coin.
The lost son.
And the joy associated with finding what was lost.
The parable is ultimately revealing God's mercy toward repentant sinners and confronting the resentment of those who object to that mercy.
It is not a step-by-step parenting manual.
We should not force every detail into a rule about adult children.
But its picture of mercy, repentance, and welcome should deeply shape how Christians understand the heart of God.
And there is another person in the story.
The older brother.
He stayed home.
He obeyed.
He worked.
And when his younger brother returned, he was furious.
He could not understand why someone who had behaved so badly should be received so generously.
Sometimes, Christian parents can begin to resemble that older brother.
We become so focused on the offense that we lose sight of the person.
So determined to uphold righteousness that we begin to resent mercy.
So concerned with what others will think that we forget what grace looks like.
But the father goes out to the older son, too.
He appeals to him.
He does not treat resentment as righteousness.
And the story ends without telling us whether the older brother entered the celebration.
That unfinished ending leaves a question hanging over the listener.
Will you rejoice in mercy?
Or will you remain outside, convinced that someone else's failure has made them unworthy of love?
Perhaps today, that question is not only for your adult child.
Perhaps it is for you.
Because your son or daughter may need to repent of unbelief or sin.
But you may also need to repent of bitterness.
Of pride.
Of contempt.
Of using silence as punishment.
Of caring more about your family's reputation than your child's soul.
Of turning conversations into interrogations.
Of making every birthday, holiday, or family gathering another opportunity for confrontation.
Of confusing the desire to be right with the calling to love.
And before anyone misunderstands me, let me say this clearly.
You should not compromise the gospel to keep peace.
You should not deny Christ.
You should not celebrate what Scripture identifies as sin merely to avoid disagreement.
You should not abandon wise boundaries.
But you also should not make rejection your first response when Christ has called you to love your neighbor, bear witness with gentleness, and entrust judgment to God.
First Peter 3:15 tells believers to be ready to give an answer for their hope, with meekness and fear—that is, gentleness and reverence.
The Greek word πραΰτητος (prautētos) points to gentleness.
Gentleness is not weakness.
It is strength governed by humility.
And sometimes the strongest thing a Christian parent can do is sit across from a grown child, hear something heartbreaking, and refuse to retaliate.
To say:

“I don't agree with you. My faith in Jesus has not changed. But I still want to understand you. I still want to be part of your life where we can have a healthy relationship. And I will never stop praying for you.”
Not as a rehearsed tactic.
Not as emotional pressure.
Not as a promise that everything will turn out the way you want.
But as a sincere expression of love.
Because there may come a day when your child faces a crisis.
A marriage collapses.
A job disappears.
A friendship betrays them.
A grief arrives that no argument can explain away.
And when that day comes, you do not want their first thought to be:
“I cannot call my parents. They only love the version of me that agrees with them.”
You want them to know that you will tell them the truth, but you will not delight in their pain.
That you will not exploit their suffering to win a theological argument.
That they can come to you without being humiliated.
Not because you can guarantee they will return to Jesus.
But because you are determined not to let your own conduct become an unnecessary obstacle to hearing about Him.
And if you are the adult child reading this, perhaps you have been on the other side of that closed door.
Perhaps you told your parents you no longer believed.
And instead of a conversation, you received an ultimatum.
Perhaps they stopped calling.
Perhaps family gatherings became painful.
Perhaps you have spent years wondering whether your parents love you or only the faith they hoped you would share.
I cannot know everything that happened in your family.
And I will not pretend every disagreement is abuse or every parent who sets boundaries is unloving.
But I can tell you this.
Your questions deserve to be heard respectfully.
Your dignity does not disappear because your beliefs have changed.
And whatever human beings have done in the name of Christianity, their failures should not be mistaken for a complete picture of Jesus Christ.
If you are willing, read the Gospels for yourself.
Look at how Jesus treated the proud.
The broken.
The doubting.
The outcast.
The religious hypocrite.
The sinner who knew he needed mercy.
Do not merely examine what people have said about Him.
Examine Him.
And if you have rejected a distorted picture of Christianity, be willing to consider whether the real Jesus is different from the one you were shown.
He does not call you to pretend.
He calls you to truth.
And the gospel announces that forgiveness and new life are found through His death and resurrection.
For the parent who has already cut off an adult child solely because that child rejected Christianity, perhaps this article is stirring something painful.
You may have believed you were being faithful.
You may have been advised to do it.
You may have feared that maintaining contact would communicate approval.
But perhaps you now see that there is room to reconsider.
You do not have to settle every theological disagreement before making a phone call.
You do not have to promise to affirm everything your child believes.
You can begin with humility.

“I've been thinking about how we've handled things. I still love Jesus, and my convictions remain. But I regret making you feel that you had to share my beliefs to have a relationship with me. If you're willing, I would like us to talk.”
Your child may not respond.
They may need time.
They may have wounds you do not yet understand.
They may decline contact.
Respect that.
Reconciliation cannot be demanded.
And an apology is not a transaction that guarantees immediate access to another person's life.
But you can take responsibility for your part.
You can leave room for an honest response.
You can seek counsel from mature believers who understand Scripture and family relationships.
You can pray without using prayer as a substitute for the difficult work of listening.
And where abuse or serious danger exists, you can pursue wisdom and safety rather than rushing into unsafe contact.
This is not about making every family look perfect.
It is about becoming more faithful to Christ within the family you actually have.
And now I want to speak to the parent who is quietly crying while reading this.
The one who has prayed for years.
The one who still remembers their child's little voice singing worship songs.
The one who sees an empty seat at church and feels the ache all over again.
The one who wonders whether God hears the prayers whispered late at night.
I cannot promise you that your child will return to faith.
No faithful reading of Scripture gives me the right to guarantee the conversion of a particular person.
And I will not use your pain to offer a promise God has not made.
But I can remind you that God is worthy of trust even when the outcome remains uncertain.
He is not limited by your ability to persuade.
He is not confused by your child's questions.
He is not intimidated by unbelief.
And He does not need you to become harsh in order to defend His holiness.
Keep praying.
Keep speaking truth when there is an appropriate opportunity.
Keep living the gospel you proclaim.
Keep your boundaries wise.
Keep your conscience clear.
And when fear rises, remember that your child's eternal destiny does not rest upon your ability to control every conversation.
You are called to be faithful.
God remains God.
Maybe tonight, instead of composing another argument, you need to pray a different prayer.

“Father, I love my child, and I am afraid. Forgive me where fear has made me controlling. Forgive me where anger has made me unkind. Show me where I need to repent. Give me courage to stand for Your truth without using it as a weapon. Protect my child. Open doors for honest conversation. Draw them to Jesus according to Your mercy. And teach me to love faithfully even when I cannot control the outcome. In Jesus' name, amen.”
And perhaps the next step is not a sermon.
Perhaps it is a simple message.
“Thinking of you today. I love you. I hope you're doing well.”
No hidden argument.
No trap.
No condition attached.
Just an open door, where an open door is safe and appropriate.
Because sometimes a child who has stopped listening to your sermons is still watching your life.
They notice whether your faith makes you patient.
Whether your convictions make you humble.
Whether you apologize.
Whether you tell the truth.
Whether you love people who cannot give you what you want.
They are watching whether the Jesus you proclaim is reflected in the way you treat them.
And while your behavior cannot save anyone, your conduct can either support or undermine the credibility of your witness.
So here is the answer to the question that brought us here.
Should Christian parents cut off an adult child who rejects their faith?
Not simply because that child no longer believes.
The Bible does not command such a blanket cutoff.
There may be circumstances requiring firm boundaries, restricted contact, or separation because of abuse, danger, or persistent destructive behavior.
There may be painful disagreements that cannot be resolved.
There may be relationships where peace is not presently possible.
But unbelief alone is not a biblical command to withdraw parental love.
You can remain faithful to Jesus without making your child earn your affection through religious agreement.
You can refuse to compromise without refusing to care.
You can grieve without condemning every conversation to conflict.
You can hold the truth firmly while holding your own pride loosely.
And you can remember that the gospel is not the story of people who earned God's love by becoming acceptable first.
It is the story of Jesus Christ, who came to save sinners.
The cross does not minimize sin.
It reveals how serious sin is.
And it reveals how extraordinary God's mercy is.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not simply about winning arguments or defending religious identity.
It is about Jesus.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who died for our sins.
The One who rose again.
The One in whom forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life are found.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because truth is negotiable.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
And that includes the way we respond when the people we love disappoint us.
If this article has exposed something in your heart, do not rush past it.
Maybe you are the parent who needs to apologize.
Maybe you are the adult child who needs healing.
Maybe you are still trying to understand how to love someone without compromising your faith.
Maybe you have been carrying a prayer request for so long that you no longer know how to put it into words.
And if you have a testimony of reconciliation, repentance, or renewed faith, consider sharing it. Someone else may need the encouragement that God has not finished working in human hearts.
There is also something important I want to share with those who believe this ministry should continue reaching more people.
That kind of work takes time, resources, and consistent support.
Not because you owe this ministry a payment for receiving the gospel.
But because voluntary generosity can be one practical way of helping gospel-centered resources reach more people.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which I want to invite you.
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
These items are not the reason the gospel matters.
They are simply practical resources and expressions of appreciation for those helping the ministry continue.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Make use of the free resources.
Your worth in Christ is not measured by what you can give to a ministry.
And the gospel must never become something available only to those who can afford it.
What matters is that Jesus Christ is proclaimed faithfully, Scripture is handled responsibly, and people are encouraged toward genuine repentance, grace, forgiveness, and transformation through Him.
Before you leave, I want you to return to that road in Luke 15.
Picture the father again.
Looking into the distance.
The son who left has returned.
His clothes are worn.
His plans have collapsed.
His confession is beginning.
And the father runs.
The story does not tell us how long he waited.
It does not promise every wandering child will return.
It does not teach us to tolerate abuse or abandon boundaries.
But it does show us a father whose mercy is greater than his desire to humiliate a repentant son.
And it invites us to consider the mercy of God.
So, Christian parent, stand for Jesus.
Do not surrender the truth.
Do not pretend unbelief does not matter.
But do not confuse cruelty with courage.
Do not confuse silence used as punishment with holiness.
Do not confuse your ability to control a relationship with your ability to save a soul.
And if the road between you and your child has become painfully long, ask God for wisdom about what faithfulness looks like today.
Maybe it means a boundary.
Maybe it means an apology.
Maybe it means listening.
Maybe it means speaking truth gently.
Maybe it means allowing time.
And maybe, where it is safe and welcome, it means keeping a light on without demanding that your child pretend to believe before they can come home.
Because the child who no longer shares your faith should never have to wonder whether your love was real.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS FORGIVE THE PARALYZED MAN BEFORE HEALING HIM? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE THE WOUND YOU'VE BEEN HIDING FROM GOD.
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS FORGIVE THE PARALYZED MAN BEFORE HEALING HIM? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE THE WOUND YOU'VE BEEN HIDING FROM GOD.

Four men carried a broken man to Jesus, hoping he would walk again. But the first words Jesus spoke were not about his legs. They were about his sins. And what happened next reveals a truth that could change the way you see your suffering, your past, your forgiveness, and the Savior who refuses to leave you where He found you.
Imagine being carried into a room where everyone can see what is wrong with you.
You cannot hide your condition.
You cannot stand on your own.
You cannot pretend everything is fine.
Your weakness is visible. Your dependence is undeniable. Your dignity feels as though it is resting in the hands of the people carrying you.
And somewhere inside, perhaps you are wondering whether you will ever live a normal life again.
Then you hear that Jesus is nearby.
The One people say has touched lepers without becoming unclean.
The One who has commanded demons to leave.
The One whose authority has astonished crowds.
The One who has made the impossible happen.
And suddenly, hope begins to breathe again.
Maybe today will be different.
Maybe today you will finally stand.
Maybe today you will walk home on the same feet that have failed you for so long.
Your friends carry you through the streets. They approach the house where Jesus is teaching.
But there is a problem.
The doorway is blocked.
The house is overflowing.
People are packed so tightly around Jesus that there is no room for one more person.
Not even a desperate man lying on a mat.
And this is where the story begins to feel painfully familiar.
Because sometimes the hardest part of suffering is not merely what is happening to you.
It is watching other people stand in places you cannot reach.
Watching others walk through doors that seem closed to you.
Watching others receive what you have spent years praying for.
Watching life continue while you feel trapped in the same condition.
You believe Jesus has power.
You believe He is good.
But you cannot understand why reaching Him seems so difficult.
And perhaps the most exhausting prayer you have ever whispered sounds something like this:
"Lord, I know You can. I just don't understand why You haven't."
If you have ever prayed that prayer, stay with this story.
Because the most astonishing moment is not when the man gets up.
It is what Jesus says while the man is still lying down.
Mark 2:1–12 records the event.
Jesus is in Capernaum, teaching inside a house. Four men arrive carrying a paralyzed man. Unable to bring him through the crowd, they open the roof above Jesus and lower the man on his mat.
Picture the moment.
Dust falling.
Pieces of roofing material being moved aside.
People looking upward.
The teaching interrupted.
A man descending through the ceiling because his friends refuse to let a crowded doorway become the end of his story.
The Gospel does not tell us what the man was thinking.
It does not reveal whether he felt embarrassed, terrified, hopeful, or overwhelmed.
But imagine what it would be like to find yourself lying in the middle of a crowded room, completely exposed before the One person you believe can change your life.
Every eye is on you.
You have nowhere to hide.
And Jesus sees you.
Surely this is the moment.
Surely Jesus will look at his legs.
Surely He will command the paralysis to disappear.
Surely the miracle will begin with the thing everyone can see.
But Scripture records something completely unexpected.
"When Jesus saw their faith, he said unto the sick of the palsy, Son, thy sins be forgiven thee." — Mark 2:5, KJV
Read those words again.
"Son, thy sins be forgiven thee."
Not, "Stand up."
Not, "Your suffering is over."
Not even, "You are healed."
Forgiveness.
Before healing.
And here is the question that should stop us in our tracks.
Why would Jesus address the man's sins when everyone had brought him there because of his paralysis?
Was Jesus overlooking his physical suffering?
Was He suggesting that the man's disability was punishment for a particular sin?
Was He saying spiritual forgiveness matters so much that physical pain does not?
No.
And understanding why is essential.
Because if we misunderstand this passage, we can turn one of the most beautiful demonstrations of Christ's authority into a cruel message that Jesus never intended to preach.
The Bible does not say this man's paralysis was caused by his personal sins.
It does not tell us that he became paralyzed because he had done something terrible.
And we must never invent a hidden scandal where Scripture reveals none.
In John 9:1–3, when the disciples encounter a man blind from birth, they ask Jesus whether the man's blindness resulted from his own sin or his parents' sin.
Jesus rejects that explanation for his blindness.

The fallen condition of our world means suffering and sin are connected in a broad theological sense, but that does not mean every illness, disability, tragedy, or unanswered prayer is punishment for a particular personal offense.
Some of the most faithful people in Scripture suffered deeply.
Job suffered.
Paul suffered.
And Jesus Christ Himself, though entirely without sin, suffered beyond anything we can adequately describe.
So do not let anyone use this story to tell you that your disease proves God is angry with you.
Do not let anyone convince you that your disability reveals some secret wickedness.
Do not let anyone turn the Gospel into a weapon against people who are already hurting.
That is not what Jesus is doing here.
Something far greater is unfolding.
Something the religious teachers in the room are about to recognize, even while they resist its implications.
To understand it, we need to listen carefully to the words Jesus actually spoke.
Mark's Gospel was written in Greek, and the wording of Mark 2:5 is profoundly revealing.
Τέκνον, ἀφίενταί σου αἱ ἁμαρτίαι.
Teknon, aphientai sou hai hamartiai.
A faithful translation is:
"Child, your sins are forgiven."
The Greek word τέκνον (teknon) means "child."
It is a form of address that can communicate tenderness and personal regard.
Jesus does not begin by identifying the man through his disability.
He does not address him as a problem.
He calls him "child."
Think about that.
The crowd sees a man who cannot walk.
His friends see someone they desperately want to help.
The religious teachers will soon see a theological controversy.
But Jesus addresses the man personally.
"Child."
There is something profoundly comforting about being addressed with care when you have become accustomed to being defined by your limitations.
Maybe people know you by your failure.
The marriage that collapsed.
The addiction you are fighting.
The family you disappointed.
The mistake everyone remembers.
The diagnosis you never wanted.
The season when your faith nearly disappeared.
Maybe you have lived so long beneath the weight of what happened to you, or what you did, that you no longer remember who you are apart from it.
But notice what Jesus does.
He speaks to the person before demonstrating His power over the condition.
And then comes the declaration.
"Your sins are forgiven."
The Greek verb ἀφίενταί (aphientai) comes from ἀφίημι (aphiēmi), a word that can mean to send away, release, let go, or forgive, depending on context.
Here it speaks of the forgiveness of sins.
The man has been brought to Jesus because his body needs help.
Jesus declares forgiveness, addressing a need that cannot be seen simply by looking at his mat.
But there is another detail we cannot afford to miss.
Jesus does not explicitly say that the man confessed his sins.
The passage does not describe a lengthy conversation about his past.
It does not identify his particular transgressions.
It simply tells us that Jesus saw their faith and made this astonishing declaration.
That should make us careful about adding details the Gospel does not provide.
And it should make us marvel at the authority of Christ.
Because Jesus is not merely offering encouragement.
He is making a declaration that belongs to the very heart of humanity's relationship with God.
In the Hebrew Scriptures, forgiveness is not a small religious formality.
Psalm 103:12 declares:
"As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us." — KJV
The Hebrew word translated "transgressions" is פְּשָׁעֵינוּ (pesha'einu), referring to our transgressions or acts of rebellion.
And the Hebrew verb used for removing them, הִרְחִיק (hirchiq), communicates the idea of putting something far away.
The psalm celebrates the mercy of God, who removes the guilt of His people.
Not because sin is imaginary.
Not because rebellion does not matter.
But because God is merciful.
And now, in a crowded house in Capernaum, Jesus speaks words of forgiveness to a man lying helplessly before Him.
The scribes understand that this is no ordinary statement.
They begin reasoning within themselves.
"Why doth this man thus speak blasphemies? who can forgive sins but God only?" — Mark 2:7, KJV
There is an important truth inside their objection.
Ultimately, forgiveness of sins belongs to God.
Human beings may forgive wrongs committed against themselves. Priests in Israel could announce forgiveness in connection with the sacrifices God had appointed.
But Jesus is claiming an extraordinary authority.
He is not merely saying, "I hope God forgives you."
He speaks as One authorized to declare forgiveness directly.
The religious teachers recognize the significance.
And Jesus knows what they are thinking.
He asks them a question that cuts through the room.
Which is easier to say to the paralyzed man: "Your sins are forgiven," or "Rise, take up your mat, and walk"?
At first, the question sounds strange.
Surely making a paralyzed man walk is harder.
But consider what Jesus is exposing.
A declaration of forgiveness cannot be verified by looking at someone's body.
Anyone could pronounce the words.
The invisible reality is not something the crowd can measure.
But commanding a paralyzed man to stand?
That claim will immediately be tested.
Either the man will rise, or he will remain on the mat.
Jesus is about to make His invisible authority unmistakable through a visible miracle.
And here is the turning point of the entire passage.
"But that ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins..." — Mark 2:10, KJV
There it is.
The reason Jesus connects forgiveness and healing.
Not because the man's paralysis must have resulted from his personal sin.
Not because Jesus has forgotten his physical need.
But because Jesus intends to reveal His authority to forgive sins.
The healing will serve as a visible sign pointing to a greater truth about who He is.
The Greek word translated "power" in the KJV is ἐξουσία (exousia).
It means authority, right, or jurisdiction.
This is not merely a display of supernatural strength.
Jesus is demonstrating that He possesses authority on earth to forgive sins.
And He identifies Himself as the Son of Man.
That title deserves our attention.
In Daniel 7:13–14, the prophet sees one "like the Son of man" coming with the clouds of heaven and receiving dominion, glory, and a kingdom.
The Aramaic expression in Daniel 7:13 is כְּבַר אֱנָשׁ (kevar enash), meaning "like a son of man" or "like a human being."
Daniel's vision presents a figure receiving extraordinary authority from the Ancient of Days.
When Jesus calls Himself the Son of Man, His words belong to a rich biblical context involving His humanity, mission, suffering, and divine authority.
Mark 2 does not provide every dimension of that title, but it clearly emphasizes His authority to forgive sins.
Now watch what happens.
Jesus turns to the paralyzed man.
"I say unto thee, Arise, and take up thy bed, and go thy way into thine house." — Mark 2:11, KJV
And the man rises.
Immediately.
He takes up the mat.
He walks out before them all.
The same man who entered the house carried by others leaves carrying the very thing on which he had been lying.
Imagine the silence before the astonishment.
Imagine the friends looking down through the opening in the roof.
Imagine the people moving aside as he walks.
Imagine the sound of footsteps where there had been no footsteps before.
Mark tells us the people were amazed and glorified God, saying they had never seen anything like it.
But do not miss what the miracle is meant to reveal.
Jesus did not heal the man to prove that forgiveness was less important. He healed him so the people would know that His authority to forgive was real.
The visible miracle confirmed the invisible declaration.
The man needed physical restoration, and Jesus compassionately gave it.
But Jesus also revealed something that no physician, friend, or human religious authority could accomplish by personal power.
The Son of Man had authority to forgive sins.
And this is where the story begins to reach beyond the roof in Capernaum and into our own lives.
Because some of us have spent years asking Jesus to change our circumstances without seriously considering what it means to be reconciled to God.
We pray for the financial breakthrough.
We pray for the relationship to be restored.
We pray for the medical report to change.
We pray for the opportunity to open.
We pray for the pain to stop.
And none of those prayers is wrong.
God invites His children to bring their needs to Him.
Jesus Himself taught us to ask for daily bread.
Scripture encourages prayer for the sick.
The Lord is not indifferent to suffering.
But there is a danger when we begin to see Jesus only as the solution to the crisis we want removed.
We can become so focused on what we want Him to change around us that we neglect what He came to accomplish for us through His death and resurrection.
We want relief.
He offers reconciliation.
We want the immediate burden lifted.
He calls us into an eternal relationship with the Father.
We want a better chapter.
He offers new life.
And here is a question worth sitting with.
If Jesus changed the circumstances you are praying about, but you continued living far from Him, would you really have received the greatest gift He came to give?
That question is not meant to belittle your pain.
Your pain matters.
Your tears matter.
Your unanswered prayers matter.
But your soul matters too.
Jesus did not come merely to make difficult lives more comfortable.
He came to save sinners.
Matthew 1:21 says:
"Thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins." — KJV
Notice the promise.
From their sins.
Not merely from embarrassment.
Not merely from financial hardship.
Not merely from painful circumstances.
From their sins.
This is the scandalous beauty of the Gospel.
The God who is perfectly holy has not ignored our rebellion.
The God who is perfectly just has not pretended evil is harmless.
Instead, in His astonishing love, He sent His Son.
Jesus lived without sin.
He welcomed sinners without approving of sin.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called people to repentance.
He touched the unclean.
He showed compassion to the rejected.
He carried the cross.
He died for our sins.
And He rose again.
The forgiveness Jesus declared in Capernaum points us toward the saving work that would be accomplished through His cross and resurrection.
Colossians 2:13–14 speaks of God forgiving our trespasses and canceling the record of debt that stood against us, taking it away through the cross.
Forgiveness is not God pretending nothing happened.
It is mercy made possible through the redemptive work of Jesus Christ.
And that means grace is never permission to continue embracing the darkness that destroys us.
Grace calls us out.
Grace teaches us to turn away from sin.
Grace brings us to repentance.
Grace does not simply tell us that our past can be forgiven.
Grace begins transforming the way we live.
Maybe that is the part you have been avoiding.
Not because you do not believe in Jesus.
But because you know that truly following Him will mean surrendering something you have been protecting.
The bitterness you keep rehearsing.
The secret habit you keep excusing.
The dishonesty you have learned to live with.
The relationship you know is leading you away from obedience.
The pride that refuses to apologize.
The resentment you have mistaken for strength.
The hidden compromise you have convinced yourself nobody will ever discover.
You have asked Jesus to make you feel better.
But have you invited Him to change you?
You have asked Him to open doors.
But have you surrendered the places in your heart that you keep locked?
You have asked Him to remove consequences.
But have you come to Him in genuine repentance?
There is no need to pretend before the Savior who already knows the truth.
And there is no need to despair when the Gospel announces that forgiveness is available through Him.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — KJV
That is not a promise that confession will immediately erase every earthly consequence.
It is not a guarantee that all broken relationships will instantly recover.
It is not a promise that every illness will disappear.
It is a promise grounded in the faithfulness and righteousness of God.
And for the person carrying the weight of guilt, that promise is life-changing.
Because some wounds are not visible to anyone else.
Some people are not lying on a physical mat.
They are walking, working, smiling, posting pictures, attending church, raising children, paying bills, and telling everyone they are fine.
Yet inside, they are carrying a memory they wish they could erase.
A betrayal.
A decision.
A secret.
A season of rebellion.
A failure that keeps returning in the quiet hours of the night.
And they wonder whether God could still receive someone who has done what they have done.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe you know how to lift your hands in worship while feeling ashamed of what those same hands have done.
Maybe you know how to encourage everyone else while quietly believing your own story is beyond repair.
Maybe you have become skilled at appearing spiritually strong while feeling desperately weak.
If that is you, hear the Gospel.
Your sin is serious. But Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
You cannot earn forgiveness by punishing yourself long enough.
You cannot purchase it with religious activity.
You cannot make your past disappear through sheer determination.
But you can turn to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
You can confess what you have hidden.
You can stop defending what God calls sin.
You can receive the mercy that comes through His finished work.
And you can begin walking in the newness of life He gives.
Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus." — KJV
Not because their past was imaginary.
Not because their sins were harmless.
But because they are in Christ Jesus.
This is the difference between worldly reassurance and biblical grace.
Worldly reassurance often says, "You did nothing wrong."
The Gospel says, "You have sinned, but Christ came to save sinners."
Worldly reassurance says, "Just believe in yourself."
The Gospel says, "Repent and believe in Jesus Christ."
Worldly reassurance says, "Your past does not matter."
The Gospel says, "Your past can be forgiven, and your future can be transformed through Christ."
And perhaps one of the most moving details in Mark 2 is something we have not yet considered deeply enough.
The man did not arrive alone.
Four people carried him.
Four people refused to abandon him outside.
Four people climbed onto a roof because they believed bringing him to Jesus mattered more than the obstacles in their way.
Mark says Jesus saw their faith.
The narrative emphasizes the faith demonstrated through their extraordinary actions.
It does not tell us everything about the individual spiritual condition of each person involved.
But it gives us a powerful picture of what compassionate, determined faith can look like.
They could not heal their friend.
They could not forgive his sins.
They could not manufacture a miracle.
But they could bring him to Jesus.
And they did.
That should challenge the way we think about the people God has placed in our lives.
Who is struggling quietly while we are too busy to notice?
Who has stopped attending church because they are ashamed?
Who has begun drifting from Christ while everyone assumes they are fine?
Who is battling addiction, grief, depression, loneliness, or spiritual exhaustion and desperately needs someone to walk beside them?
You cannot save another person's soul.
Only Christ saves.
You cannot force someone to believe.
But you can pray.
You can listen.
You can speak the truth with love.
You can share Scripture.
You can offer practical help.
You can remind someone that the invitation of Jesus is still open.
You can refuse to treat a struggling person as disposable.
And sometimes the most Christlike thing you can do is help carry someone toward the Savior when they are too weary to find the way alone.
Maybe that is why this story has reached you today.
Perhaps you needed to be reminded that you can come to Jesus in your weakness.
Or perhaps someone in your life needs you to become one of the friends who refuses to walk away.
Think of the person whose name keeps returning to your heart.
A son.
A daughter.
A husband.
A wife.
A parent.
A friend.
Someone who used to pray but no longer does.
Someone who believes they have gone too far to return.
Someone who smiles in public but is falling apart in private.
Do not assume they already know they are loved.
Do not assume they have heard the Gospel clearly.
Do not assume another person will reach out.
Send them this message if you believe it could help them encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
And if this article has touched something personal, I want to invite you to do something more meaningful than leaving a reaction.
If you are tired of pretending you have everything together, you can comment, "No more hiding."
If you are struggling but still holding on to Christ, comment, "I'm still fighting."
And if you have experienced the mercy of Jesus, consider sharing a short testimony of what His forgiveness has meant in your life.
You do not need to publicly reveal private sins, traumatic experiences, or details that could harm you or others.
A sincere sentence of faith can encourage someone who has nearly lost hope.
Because the Christian life was never meant to be lived as a performance.
We need truth.
We need grace.
We need repentance.
We need Scripture.
We need fellowship.
We need one another.
And above all, we need Jesus Christ.
But there is still one part of the story that deserves our attention.
The man walks out of the house carrying his mat.
The Gospel does not tell us what happened to him afterward.
We are not told his name.
We are not told how many years he lived.
We are not told whether he later faced other hardships.
And we should not pretend Scripture tells us what it does not.
But Mark does tell us enough to understand the point.
The man who had been carried into Jesus' presence walked out because Jesus commanded him to rise.
The healing demonstrated the authority of the One who had already declared his sins forgiven.
And the crowd glorified God.
That is where the miracle directs our attention.
Not merely to a man who could walk.
But to the identity and authority of Jesus.
And this matters enormously for those who have prayed for healing but are still waiting.
Because some faithful Christians do not experience physical healing in this life.
Some remain disabled.
Some continue medical treatment.
Some bury people they prayed desperately would recover.
Some live with chronic pain while sincerely loving Jesus.
Their suffering is not proof that Christ has rejected them.
Their continuing illness is not proof that they lack genuine faith.
The miracle in Mark 2 is a real historical event presented in the Gospel, but it is not a blanket promise that every believer will receive immediate physical healing.
The New Testament teaches us to pray, to seek help, to trust God's wisdom, and to look toward the final resurrection when God will make all things new.
Revelation 21:4 promises a future in which God will wipe away every tear and death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
That hope does not make present suffering insignificant.
It tells us suffering will not have the final word.
And here is something worth remembering when the answer to your prayer has not yet come.
The authority of Jesus to forgive your sins does not disappear when your circumstances remain painful.
You can be deeply loved by God and still face hardship.
You can belong to Christ and still need medical care.
You can be forgiven and still have consequences to work through.
You can be growing spiritually while still grieving.
You can trust Jesus without pretending that everything feels okay.
The Gospel does not demand that you deny your pain.
It invites you to bring your pain to the Savior.
And it reminds you that your greatest hope rests not in the absence of suffering today, but in the crucified and risen Christ.
Maybe you came to this article looking for an explanation of one unusual moment in the ministry of Jesus.
But perhaps you have discovered something more personal.
The question is no longer only, "Why did Jesus forgive before healing?"
The question has become, "Have I truly understood what His forgiveness means for me?"
Because it is possible to admire Jesus as a miracle worker without surrendering to Him as Lord.
It is possible to enjoy Christian inspiration without embracing biblical repentance.
It is possible to love stories about grace while resisting the transformation grace demands.
And it is possible to be surrounded by Christian content while rarely opening the Scriptures for yourself.
That is one reason Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a following around human personalities.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to turn faith into merchandise or spiritual entertainment.
But to keep pointing people toward the Word of God, the Gospel of Jesus Christ, and the daily pursuit of biblical discipleship.
There are people who need more than another motivational quote.
They need to understand who Jesus is.
They need to understand why the cross matters.
They need to understand repentance, forgiveness, grace, obedience, and the hope of eternal life.
They need truth that does not change every time culture changes.
And they need encouragement that does not hide the difficult parts of following Christ.
These resources are intended to help readers study Scripture, strengthen their understanding of the Gospel, develop consistent devotional habits, and become better equipped to encourage others.
Not because you must pay to glorify God.
You do not.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." — KJV
Notice those words.
"Not grudgingly, or of necessity."
Christian generosity should be willing, thoughtful, and sincere.
Supporting Gospel ministry can be a meaningful act of stewardship and worship when it flows from love for God and a desire to serve others.
Your contribution can help this ministry reach more people and continue developing resources for readers who may never be able to pay for them.

If you are already faithfully giving to your local church, caring for your household, or facing financial difficulty, please do not feel pressured to redirect money you need for those responsibilities.
Your local church, family obligations, and wise stewardship matter.
For those who are able and willing, even modest recurring support can help provide a more stable foundation for continued ministry work.
It is the opportunity to participate in making Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources more accessible to others.
Saving it may give you something to return to when guilt, doubt, or spiritual exhaustion becomes overwhelming.
Following Gospel Warrior may help you stay connected to regular Scripture-based encouragement.
Tagging a friend who needs hope may open the door to a conversation that matters far beyond social media.
And commenting with a testimony, prayer request, or honest reflection may remind another believer that they are not walking through their struggle alone.
But please remember what all of this is meant to serve.
Not an algorithm.
Not a personality.
Not a brand.
Jesus Christ.
Because the ultimate purpose of Christian ministry is not merely to gather an audience.
It is to bear witness to the Savior.
And the Savior is still calling sinners to repentance and faith.
So before you leave this story, return with me one final time to that crowded house.
The roof is open.
The crowd is watching.
The religious teachers are questioning.
Four friends are waiting.
And a man is lying on his mat before Jesus.
Everyone knows what they want to see.
They want the man to walk.
And Jesus does make him walk.
But first, He declares forgiveness.
Because the miracle is not simply about the restoration of physical movement.
It is a revelation of the One who possesses authority to forgive sins.
The man came before Jesus unable to stand.
He left carrying his mat.
And the people glorified God.
Now imagine bringing your own life before Christ.
Not pretending you are stronger than you are.
Not hiding behind religious language.
Not explaining away your sin.
Not believing that your wounds make you worthless.
Just coming honestly.
With the regrets.
With the questions.
With the failures.
With the grief.
With the prayers that still seem unanswered.
And instead of demanding that Jesus become the Savior you have designed around your preferences, you surrender to the Savior Scripture reveals.
The holy Son of God.
The friend of repentant sinners.
The One who died for our sins and rose again.
The One whose authority extends beyond sickness, beyond guilt, beyond death, and beyond every human attempt to save ourselves.
Maybe your circumstances will change quickly.
Maybe healing will come through treatment, time, or an extraordinary act of God's mercy.
Maybe the road ahead will be longer than you hoped.
But the invitation of the Gospel remains.
Repent.
Believe in Jesus Christ.
Receive the forgiveness found in Him.
Follow Him.
And trust that the God who raised Jesus from the dead will fulfill His promises.
If you have never truly turned to Christ, you can speak to Him now.
Not with a magical formula.
Not with words designed to impress anyone.
But with genuine repentance and faith.

"Lord Jesus, I confess that I have sinned and need Your mercy. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me, turn my heart away from sin, and teach me to follow You. I surrender my life to You. Help me trust You even when I do not understand what You are doing. Amen."
The words themselves do not save.
Jesus saves.
And genuine faith is not merely a moment of emotion. It begins a life of trusting, obeying, and following Him.
If you are returning to Christ after a season of wandering, do not mistake shame for repentance.
Shame may make you want to disappear.
Repentance brings you honestly before God.
And if you are still suffering while trying to remain faithful, do not measure Christ's love by how quickly your circumstances change.
Look to the cross.
Look to the empty tomb.
Look to the promises of God.
Then keep walking with Him, even if today that walking looks like one trembling step of faith.
If Jesus knows everything about your past, what is keeping you from bringing your whole life to Him today?
And if you have a testimony of forgiveness, consider sharing it so that someone else may find courage to seek Christ.
Invite someone you love to read it.
Because there are still people outside crowded doorways.
Still people carrying burdens they cannot lift alone.
Still people convinced their past has placed them beyond mercy.
And they need to hear that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
The story of the paralyzed man does not teach that every person who comes to Jesus will immediately rise from every physical affliction.
It teaches something far more specific, and gloriously certain.
The Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.
And that same Jesus went to the cross, rose from the grave, and remains the only Savior through whom we can be reconciled to God.
Your past may explain some of your scars.
Your suffering may shape parts of your journey.
Your failures may carry consequences that require humility, restitution, patience, and time.
But none of those things has to be the final word over a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
Because the Gospel is not the story of sinners becoming good enough to deserve a Savior.
It is the story of the Savior who came for sinners and transforms those who belong to Him.
The greatest miracle was not that a man carried his mat home. It was that the One who forgave him would one day carry the cross for sinners like us.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES GOD STILL SPEAK THROUGH DREAMS—OR ARE WE CALLING SOMETHING “GOD” THAT HE NEVER SAID?
paragraphs: DOES GOD STILL SPEAK THROUGH DREAMS—OR ARE WE CALLING SOMETHING “GOD” THAT HE NEVER SAID?

Some dreams leave you trembling. Some seem to reveal things you could never have known. Others are being used to frighten believers, control decisions, and claim authority from heaven. But what if the greatest danger isn't that God has stopped speaking—it's that we've stopped testing what we think we're hearing?
You wake up at 3:17 in the morning.
Your heart is racing.
The room is dark. Everyone else is asleep. But you can't shake what you just saw.
It felt too real.

A face. A warning. A voice. Maybe someone you haven't spoken to in years. Maybe a scene that seemed to reveal something about your future. Maybe something so disturbing that you immediately reached for your phone and searched, “What does this dream mean spiritually?”
And somewhere between fear and fascination, a thought enters your mind.
Was that God?
Now imagine something even more unsettling.
What if it wasn't?
What if it was simply a dream produced by an exhausted mind, a wounded heart, or yesterday's anxieties?
Or what if God, in His sovereignty, really did use a dream to awaken your attention—but you misunderstood what it meant?
Because here's the question many Christians are afraid to ask:
If God spoke through dreams in the Bible, does that mean every powerful dream today deserves to be treated as a message from heaven?
And if we get the answer wrong, the consequences can be devastating.
A marriage can be destroyed because someone dreamed their spouse was unfaithful.
A family can be divided because someone claims God revealed a secret betrayal.
A believer can abandon wise counsel, biblical responsibility, and even medical treatment because a stranger announces, “The Lord showed me something about you.”
A frightened Christian can spend months trying to decode symbols while neglecting the clear instructions God has already given in Scripture.
And sometimes the person saying, “God told me,” may be completely sincere.
That is what makes this conversation so important.
Because sincerity does not guarantee accuracy.
And spiritual intensity does not automatically establish divine authority.
Yet we must be equally careful not to swing to the opposite extreme and declare that God could never use a dream today.
The Bible does not permit us to dismiss what God Himself has done.
But neither does it permit us to baptize every unusual experience with His name.
Somewhere between gullibility and cynicism stands something the modern Church desperately needs to recover.
Biblical discernment.
And it begins with a truth that might change the way you understand every dream, every prophecy, every spiritual impression, and every person who claims to have heard from God.
God has never asked His children to surrender their discernment in order to demonstrate their faith.
He has commanded them to exercise it.

Long before social media was filled with prophetic dream interpretations, before viral videos warned of approaching disasters, before people built entire ministries around visions of angels and mysterious encounters, God spoke through a young man who had been betrayed by his own brothers.
His name was Joseph.
His brothers stripped him of his special robe, threw him into a pit, and sold him into slavery.
The boy who had dreamed of greatness found himself dragged into humiliation.
And perhaps the cruelest part was that the very dreams associated with his future became part of the reason his brothers hated him.

Genesis 37 records Joseph's dreams of sheaves bowing before his sheaf and heavenly bodies bowing before him. His family understood these images as suggesting future authority, and his brothers resented him for them.
But notice something.
Joseph did not control the fulfillment.
He could not force the timing.
He could not escape the pit by repeating what he had dreamed.
He could not avoid slavery, false accusation, or imprisonment merely because God had a purpose for his life.
Years passed.
And the dreamer suffered.
Then, in Egypt, Joseph encountered two prisoners who had experienced troubling dreams. Later, Pharaoh himself had dreams that none of his advisers could satisfactorily interpret.
When Pharaoh called Joseph, Joseph made a statement that should humble every Christian who claims spiritual insight.
In Genesis 41:16, Joseph answered Pharaoh:
בִּלְעָדָי אֱלֹהִים יַעֲנֶה אֶת־שְׁלוֹם פַּרְעֹה
Bil‘adai, Elohim ya‘aneh et-shelom Par‘oh.
The sense of the Hebrew is:
“It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace.”
Joseph did not present himself as a supernatural celebrity.
He did not claim that his personal ability made him indispensable.
He directed attention away from himself and toward God.
And that distinction matters.
Because a genuine servant of God should never become more impressive to you than the God he serves.
Joseph's story also teaches something uncomfortable: even a genuinely God-given dream does not exempt a person from suffering, patience, responsibility, or the ordinary process of obedience.
God's purposes unfolded over years, not according to Joseph's preferred schedule.
Eventually, the brothers who sold him came before him in Egypt, and the significance of his earlier dreams became clear.
But Joseph's greatest testimony was not merely that his dreams came true.
It was what he said to the men who had wounded him.
Genesis 50:20 records his remarkable confession:
“Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.”
What his brothers intended for evil, God had worked through for preservation and deliverance.
That does not make their betrayal righteous.
It reveals God's power to accomplish His purposes even through human wickedness.
And isn't that already a picture pointing us toward something greater?
