And picture the daughter of Pharaoh looking down at a child whose life has been condemned by the authority of her own father.
In that moment, the princess could not see the burning bush.
She could not see the confrontation with Pharaoh.
She could not see the night of the Passover.
She could not see the Israelites walking out of Egypt.
She could not see the sea opening before them.
And she certainly could not see the full unfolding of God's redemptive plan that would ultimately find its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
She saw a child.
She heard him cry.
And she had compassion.
That is what the text tells us.
We do not know what became of her spiritually.
We do not know whether she ever came to worship the God of Israel.
We do not know whether she lived long enough to witness the confrontation between Moses and Pharaoh.
Scripture leaves those questions unanswered.
But it preserves her act of mercy within the story of God's deliverance.
And perhaps that is enough to confront our hearts.
Because while we are often fascinated by the great things God might accomplish tomorrow, we can overlook the simple obedience he requires of us today.
A person needs kindness.
Someone needs truth spoken in love.
A wounded heart needs compassion.
A vulnerable neighbor needs protection.
A sinner needs to hear the Gospel.
A believer needs encouragement to remain faithful.
And somewhere in the middle of an ordinary day, you may face a choice between what is comfortable and what is right.
Do not assume that a faithful act is insignificant simply because it seems small.
Do not assume that your background must determine your future.
Do not assume that the failures of those who came before you require you to repeat their sins.
And above all, do not mistake the instrument of God's providence for the God who deserves the glory.
Pharaoh's daughter showed compassion.
Moses became a deliverer.
But the Lord was faithful to his covenant.
And through the unfolding history of redemption, he has revealed the fullness of his saving grace in Jesus Christ.
So here is my final question.
When you stand before the suffering of another person, what will govern your response?
Fear?
Convenience?
The expectations of others?
Or the mercy and truth of the God you claim to follow?
What is one area of your life where you need the courage to obey God rather than surrender to fear?
Your answer may encourage someone else to take a faithful step they have been postponing.
And if you remember nothing else from this story, remember this:

Pharaoh saw a generation of children as a threat to his throne. His daughter saw one crying child as a life worth saving. But God was already preparing a deliverance greater than either of them could imagine.
May we never become so loyal to the voices of this world that we lose the courage to obey the voice of Christ.
May we never become so familiar with suffering that we stop responding with compassion.
And may we never forget that the God who preserved Moses has now made known his greatest salvation through Jesus Christ, who died and rose again so that sinners might be forgiven and made new.
The baby Pharaoh wanted erased from history became the man God used to confront him—and the Savior to whom Moses' story ultimately points is still calling broken people out of darkness into grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE MOMENT YOU QUESTION YOUR PASTOR, ARE YOU REBELLING AGAINST GOD? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH SOME CHURCHES ARE AFRAID TO CONFRONT
paragraphs: THE MOMENT YOU QUESTION YOUR PASTOR, ARE YOU REBELLING AGAINST GOD? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH SOME CHURCHES ARE AFRAID TO CONFRONT

What if the question you have been terrified to ask is not evidence of rebellion, but evidence that your conscience is still listening to God? A Scripture-anchored confrontation with spiritual authority, wounded believers, blind obedience, and the freedom Jesus never intended His Church to lose.
There is a kind of silence that sounds like holiness.
It sits quietly in church pews.
It smiles when something feels wrong.
It says “Amen” when the heart is troubled.
It raises its hands during worship while carrying questions it has been warned never to ask.
And sometimes, behind that silence, there is a Christian who is slowly falling apart.
Not because they have stopped loving Jesus.
But because they have been taught that questioning the person preaching about Jesus might mean questioning Jesus Himself.
Imagine a young woman sitting in the back of a church she once called home.
She has served faithfully for years. She has given offerings when money was tight. She has volunteered when she was exhausted. She has defended her pastor when others criticized him.
She genuinely loves her church.
But something happened.
Perhaps a teaching did not agree with Scripture.
Perhaps someone was publicly humiliated.
Perhaps financial questions were dismissed.
Perhaps a leader's behavior contradicted what he preached.
Or perhaps she simply opened her Bible one evening and discovered that a passage she had heard explained for years did not seem to mean what she had been told.
So she gathered her courage.
She asked a question.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to divide the congregation.
Not to destroy the ministry.
She just wanted to understand.
And the response shattered something inside her.
“Be careful. You're touching God's anointed.”
“Don't question spiritual authority.”
“You have a rebellious spirit.”
“Remember what happened to those who came against Moses.”
Suddenly, the issue was no longer whether her question had a biblical answer.
The issue was whether she was spiritually dangerous for asking it.
And now she sits in her car after Sunday service, gripping the steering wheel, fighting tears.
Because she cannot understand how wanting to obey God's Word somehow became an accusation of disobeying God.
Maybe you know that feeling.
Maybe you have been that person.
Or perhaps you are a pastor who has been deeply wounded by people who questioned you without kindness, spread accusations, and disguised personal ambition as spiritual discernment.
Both wounds are real.
And both deserve to be brought beneath the authority of Scripture.
Because there is a truth we desperately need to recover.
A pastor is called to shepherd God's people, not replace God's voice in their lives.
And a Christian is called to honor spiritual leadership, not surrender their conscience to another human being.
Those are not contradictory commands.
They are biblical responsibilities that belong together.
But to understand why, we need to go somewhere uncomfortable.
We need to open the Bible and allow it to confront not only abusive leadership, but also the pride, suspicion, and rebelliousness that can exist in our own hearts.
Because the Gospel does not exist to make pastors untouchable.
And it does not exist to make congregations unteachable.
It exists to bring all of us under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And that changes everything.
Consider what happened in Acts 17.
The apostle Paul was preaching the Gospel in Berea.
This was not an inexperienced teacher struggling to understand Christian doctrine.
This was Paul.
A man personally called by the risen Christ.
A man whose apostolic writings would become part of the New Testament.
If anyone could have demanded that people accept his teaching without examination, human reasoning might suggest it was him.
But Scripture tells a very different story.
Acts 17:11 says in the King James Version:
“These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.”
Read that again.
They searched the Scriptures to determine whether Paul's message was true.
And the Bible calls them noble.
Not rebellious.
Not divisive.
Not dishonoring.
Noble.
The Greek text describes them as εὐγενέστεροι (eugenesteroi), meaning more noble-minded or noble in character.
And the word translated “searched” is ἀνακρίνοντες (anakrinontes), from anakrinō, a verb that can describe examining, investigating, or carefully evaluating something.
These believers were not casually hunting for faults.
They were examining what they heard against the Scriptures they already possessed.
Their hearts were receptive, but their minds were not switched off.
And notice something beautiful.
They did not reject Paul's message simply because it challenged them.
They received it eagerly.
They investigated it carefully.
Then many believed.
Biblical discernment and spiritual openness were working together.
That is not rebellion.
That is maturity.
Now consider the implication.
If the Bereans were commended for examining the teaching of an apostle, why should any modern pastor expect his teaching to be exempt from biblical examination?
That question should not frighten a faithful shepherd.
It should encourage him.
Because a pastor who genuinely loves God's Word should rejoice when people become serious students of it.
He may need to correct misunderstandings.
He may need to explain difficult passages.
He may occasionally have to tell someone that their interpretation is mistaken.
But the goal is not to win a contest of authority.
The goal is to help people understand and obey Christ.
A faithful pastor does not need to be infallible to be respected.
He needs to be faithful, teachable, and accountable to the Lord who called him.
And a faithful congregation does not need to agree with every pastoral decision to demonstrate love.
It needs humility, discernment, and a willingness to pursue truth without cruelty.
But perhaps someone has already raised the objection.
“What about Hebrews 13:17?”
That verse matters.
We must not pretend it does not exist simply because it has sometimes been misused.
The King James Version says:
“Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account...”
Those are serious words.
Spiritual leadership is not an optional invention of organized religion.
God genuinely appoints shepherds to teach, guide, protect, and care for His people.
Hebrews 13:17 calls believers to cooperate with their leaders rather than making faithful pastoral work unnecessarily difficult.
The Greek verb πείθεσθε (peithesthe), translated “obey,” comes from peithō, which can carry the sense of being persuaded, trusting, or yielding to someone.
The word does not eliminate the obligation to heed legitimate leadership. But it helps us recognize that the relationship envisioned is not merely one of intimidation and unquestioning compliance.
The verse also uses ὑπείκετε (hypeikete), meaning to yield or give way.
There is a genuine call to humble cooperation.
Yet the verse itself contains something that should make every pastor tremble.
“They watch for your souls, as they that must give account.”
Account to whom?
Not merely a denomination.
Not merely a board.
Not merely the congregation.
Ultimately, to God.
A pastor's authority is a stewardship.
It is not personal ownership of the people entrusted to his care.
And stewardship always comes with accountability.
The passage does not teach that pastors are incapable of error, that their personal preferences are divine commands, or that questioning them is automatically sinful.
Those ideas have to be imported into the text.
They are not what the text says.
And when someone uses Hebrews 13:17 to demand obedience that contradicts God's Word, another passage becomes unavoidable.
Acts 5:29.
“We ought to obey God rather than men.”
Peter and the other apostles spoke those words while facing authorities who commanded them to stop proclaiming Jesus.
The immediate setting concerns obedience to God in the face of human prohibition.
It is not a license to dismiss every instruction we dislike.
But it establishes a principle no Christian authority can erase.
Human authority is never ultimate.
God is.
Not your favorite preacher.
Not your denomination.
Not your church's founder.
Not the person who baptized you.
Not the leader who helped you through your darkest season.
Jesus Christ alone is Lord.
And honoring those who serve Him must never become a substitute for obeying Him.
There is another passage often invoked whenever someone questions a pastor.
“Touch not mine anointed.”
Those words appear in Psalm 105:15, echoing the account of God's protection over the patriarchs.
In the King James Version, the verse says:
“Saying, Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.”
The Hebrew expression אַל־תִּגְּעוּ בִמְשִׁיחָי (ʾal-tiggeʿu vimshiḥai) carries the sense of “Do not touch my anointed ones.”
The verb נגע (nagaʿ) can mean to touch, strike, or come into contact with, depending on context.
But here is the crucial question.
Was God forbidding believers from respectfully examining a pastor's interpretation of Scripture?
No.
The psalm recalls God's protection of His people during the patriarchal period, when they were vulnerable among nations and rulers.
It is not a blanket prohibition against asking spiritual leaders questions.
And even when we consider David's refusal to harm Saul, the distinction remains important.
David would not kill Saul to seize the throne.
Yet David did not pretend Saul's conduct was righteous.
He confronted Saul's wrongdoing while refusing to take vengeance into his own hands.
Respect did not require pretending evil was good.
Restraint did not require denying the truth.
And honoring God's authority did not mean declaring every action of a human leader beyond examination.
We must be careful not to turn a passage about God's protection into a weapon that prevents accountability.
Because when Scripture is used to silence legitimate concerns, the problem is no longer merely poor leadership.
It becomes a distortion of the very Word that was given to protect and guide God's people.
And perhaps this is where the subject becomes painfully personal.
Some people are not afraid to ask questions because they lack courage.
They are afraid because they have already learned what happens when they do.
They have watched others become the subject of sermons after raising concerns.
They have seen friendships disappear.
They have been told that leaving a particular congregation means abandoning God's will.
They have heard that their family will suffer if they withdraw financial support.
They have been made to feel that disagreement with a pastor is equivalent to grieving the Holy Spirit.
And over time, something happens.
They stop asking.
Then they stop thinking aloud.
Then they stop trusting their own ability to read Scripture.
Eventually, they may begin confusing fear of a leader with reverence for God.
But Scripture never commands Christians to worship their shepherds.
It commands shepherds to care for the flock.
Listen to the apostle Peter.
In 1 Peter 5:2–3, he instructs elders to shepherd God's flock willingly and faithfully, concluding with these words:
“Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.”
The Greek expression κατακυριεύοντες (katakyrieuontes) describes exercising mastery or domineering over others.
Peter explicitly warns against that posture.
This is remarkable.
Peter himself was an apostle.
Yet he did not tell church elders to establish unquestionable personal control.
He told them not to domineer.
Instead, they were to become examples.
And a few verses earlier, he reminds them that the flock belongs to God.
Not to them.
A congregation is not a pastor's possession.
It is Christ's Church.
And the Chief Shepherd will appear.
That means every sermon, every counseling conversation, every disciplinary decision, every financial appeal, and every exercise of spiritual influence takes place beneath the gaze of Jesus.
Pastors are not merely managing an organization.
They are handling souls.
Souls Christ purchased with His own blood.
That reality should produce tenderness, not entitlement.
Humility, not intimidation.
A willingness to explain, not a demand to be unquestioned.
But we must also confront the other side of this issue.
Because not every question is innocent.
Not every disagreement is righteous.
And not everyone who says, “I'm just seeking truth,” is actually seeking truth.
Sometimes people question pastors because they are unwilling to receive correction.
Sometimes they want a leader who will affirm what Scripture condemns.
Sometimes they spread private suspicions publicly before seeking clarification.
Sometimes they interpret every difficult sermon as a personal attack.
Sometimes they demand perfection from a pastor while excusing bitterness in themselves.
And sometimes what begins as a legitimate concern becomes a campaign of humiliation, gossip, or revenge.
That is not biblical discernment.
That is sin wearing the language of accountability.
Scripture warns against it.
Numbers 16 records the rebellion of Korah and those who challenged Moses and Aaron.
Their rebellion was not simply that they asked a sincere question.
It involved a direct challenge to the leadership God had appointed, driven by a dispute over authority and position.
The account should make us cautious about prideful attempts to seize spiritual authority.
But it must not be stretched into a claim that every question directed toward a pastor is another Korah rebellion.
That would ignore both the actual context of Numbers 16 and the Bereans' example in Acts 17.
We need the whole counsel of God.
Not isolated verses selected to protect whichever side we already favor.
Proverbs 18:13 warns against answering a matter before hearing it.
Proverbs 18:17 reminds us that the first account of a dispute can appear convincing until another person examines it.
Those principles matter whether you are the pastor being accused or the church member raising a concern.
Truth deserves patience.
People deserve fairness.
And reputations should not be destroyed by rumors.
First Timothy 5:19 also provides an important safeguard regarding accusations against elders, requiring two or three witnesses before an accusation is received.
This is not a command to ignore credible reports of abuse, silence victims, or prevent appropriate investigation.
It is a warning against treating unsupported allegations as established guilt.

When abuse, exploitation, or criminal conduct is alleged, churches should take safety seriously, preserve evidence, involve appropriate independent authorities, and comply with applicable reporting laws.
A private meeting with an accused leader is not always safe or appropriate.
Biblical accountability must never become a system that protects the powerful at the expense of the vulnerable.
And genuine justice does not require abandoning fairness.
Both truths matter.
Now, imagine a different conversation.
A church member approaches a pastor after service.
“Pastor, may I ask you something? I was studying the passage you preached, and I struggled to understand how you reached that conclusion.”
The pastor could respond defensively.
“How dare you question me?”
Or he could say:
“Of course. Let's look at the passage together.”
Those responses reveal very different understandings of spiritual leadership.
The second response does not mean the pastor must agree with the member.
It means he recognizes that the Bible is not threatened by honest examination.
And perhaps, during that conversation, the member discovers they misunderstood the passage.
What a blessing.
They grow.
Or perhaps the pastor realizes he expressed something poorly.
What a blessing.
He grows.
Or perhaps they still disagree on a secondary theological issue, but they part with mutual respect and a shared commitment to Christ.
What a blessing.
Because Christian maturity is not demonstrated by never having difficult conversations.
It is demonstrated by learning to have them truthfully and lovingly.
Ephesians 4:15 calls believers to speak the truth in love.
Not truth without love.
Not love without truth.
Both.
And if your pastor corrects you from Scripture, receive that correction humbly.
You may discover that the problem was not his teaching but your interpretation.
Yet if a pastor refuses all examination, repeatedly manipulates Scripture, or uses spiritual threats to prevent legitimate accountability, do not assume your conscience must remain silent.
Seek wise, biblically grounded counsel.
Examine the evidence carefully.
And remember that faithfulness to Christ sometimes requires difficult decisions.
There is a striking example in Galatians 2.
Paul recounts confronting Peter at Antioch.
Peter had withdrawn from eating with Gentile believers under pressure from certain people.
His behavior compromised the truth expressed in the Gospel.
And Paul says in Galatians 2:11:
“I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.”
Think about that.
Peter.
The apostle who preached at Pentecost.
The man who had walked with Jesus.
The disciple who had witnessed the empty tomb.
He was corrected publicly by another apostle because his conduct was inconsistent with the Gospel.
The issue was serious and had public consequences, which helps explain the public correction.
This passage is not permission to publicly shame every pastor over every disagreement.
But it proves that prominent spiritual authority does not place someone beyond correction.
Peter's apostolic standing did not make his behavior automatically right.
And Paul's confrontation was not presented as rebellion against Christ.
It was a defense of Gospel truth.
That distinction matters more than many people realize.
The Church becomes spiritually dangerous when protecting a leader's image becomes more important than protecting the truth of the Gospel.
And yet there is something equally dangerous about a Christian who becomes so consumed with exposing flawed leaders that they stop loving the Church Christ died for.
Jesus did not shed His blood so that we could build our identities around suspicion.
He came to save sinners.
Including sinful pastors.
Including wounded church members.
Including proud critics.
Including fearful followers.
Including you.
Including me.
Every one of us stands in need of grace.
And this is where the entire conversation must move away from personalities and return to the cross.
Because the central question is not simply, “Can I question my pastor?”
The deeper question is, “Who ultimately owns my allegiance?”
When Jesus stood before religious authorities, He did not treat religious position as proof of righteousness.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He exposed those who placed burdens on others while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
In Matthew 23, His words are severe.
But His confrontation was not rooted in petty resentment.
It flowed from truth and from His holy concern for people being misled.
And in Matthew 20:25–28, Jesus taught His disciples that leadership in His kingdom must not imitate the domineering patterns of worldly rulers.
He said:
“Whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister.”
The word translated “minister” is διάκονος (diakonos), commonly associated with a servant or one who serves.
Jesus then pointed to Himself.
“The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.”
There is the model.
Not a throne built upon people's fear.
A Savior kneeling in service.
Not authority used to extract unquestioning loyalty.
Authority expressed through sacrificial love.
Not a shepherd demanding that sheep protect his reputation at all costs.
The Good Shepherd laying down His life for the sheep.
Jesus did not merely teach servant leadership.
He embodied it.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed the despised.
He washed His disciples' feet.
He endured betrayal.
He carried a cross.
And when sinful humanity displayed its ugliest violence against Him, He accomplished redemption through His death and resurrection.
That is the Gospel.
The sinless Son of God died for sinners, was buried, and rose again.
Our hope is not that we can find a flawless pastor.
Our hope is that we have a flawless Savior.
Our salvation does not rest upon the reputation of a ministry.
It rests upon the finished work of Jesus Christ.
And when we repent and trust in Him, we are not merely recruited into a religious institution.
We are reconciled to God.
Forgiven.
Adopted.
Given new life.
Called to walk in truth.
This is why spiritual authority must always remain accountable to Scripture.
Because the moment we make a human leader functionally untouchable, we risk giving that leader a place that belongs to Christ alone.
And the moment we reject all spiritual authority because some leaders have failed us, we risk refusing a gift God intended for our growth.
The answer is neither blind obedience nor permanent distrust.
The answer is Christ-centered discernment.
Honor your pastor.
Pray for him.
Encourage him.
Remember that he may be carrying burdens you cannot see.
He may be counseling marriages that are collapsing.
He may be praying over a dying church member.
He may be trying to provide for his family while carrying the expectations of an entire congregation.
He may be exhausted.
He may be lonely.
He may have made mistakes he deeply regrets.
Do not treat him as disposable simply because he is imperfect.
But do not treat him as divine because he is gifted.
A powerful sermon does not make a person incapable of error.
A large congregation does not guarantee sound doctrine.
Miraculous claims do not remove the need for biblical testing.
A respected title does not erase the need for integrity.
And years of faithful ministry do not grant immunity from accountability.
First Thessalonians 5:21 says:
“Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.”
In context, Paul is addressing the congregation's response to prophetic activity and the need for discernment.
The Greek verb δοκιμάζετε (dokimazete) means to test, examine, or assess something to determine its genuineness.
The principle is clear.
Christians should not be gullible.
Nor should they be cynical.
We are to test carefully and hold on to what is good.
That includes our own motives.
Before challenging a pastor, ask yourself whether you have understood his teaching fairly.
Have you studied the passage in context?
Are you seeking clarification or merely trying to win?
Are you willing to be corrected?
Are you motivated by love for Christ and His people?
Have you distinguished a biblical command from a personal preference?
And before dismissing a member's question, pastors should ask themselves equally searching questions.
Have I explained the Scripture faithfully?
Am I confusing my authority with God's authority?
Am I responding to a sincere concern as though it were a personal attack?
Am I willing to acknowledge an error?
Have I created an environment where people can tell the truth without fearing retaliation?
Do I care more about shepherding this person than protecting my image?
These are uncomfortable questions.
But sometimes uncomfortable questions become instruments of grace.
Sometimes repentance begins when we finally stop defending ourselves long enough to hear what God is exposing.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking possibility is this.
Somewhere today, a believer is considering walking away from Jesus because someone claiming to represent Jesus wounded them.
They were not simply disappointed by a sermon.
They were spiritually crushed.
They were told that their questions made them unfaithful.
Their sincere concerns were dismissed.
Their trust was broken.
And now, every time they hear the word “church,” their stomach tightens.
Every time someone says “submit,” they remember being controlled.
Every time a pastor speaks about honor, they hear the voice of someone who demanded loyalty but refused accountability.
If that describes you, please hear this.
What happened in a church does not determine who Jesus is.
A leader's failure does not invalidate Christ's faithfulness.
A distorted interpretation of Scripture does not make Scripture itself untrustworthy.
And the sins of people who carry God's name do not erase the holiness of the God whose name they carry.
You do not have to call evil good in order to forgive.
You do not have to return to an unsafe environment to prove that you trust Jesus.
You do not have to deny what happened to demonstrate grace.
Forgiveness, reconciliation, restored trust, and restored leadership are related but distinct matters.
Repentance matters.
Accountability matters.
Safety matters.
And genuine restoration cannot be manufactured by demanding that wounded people pretend nothing happened.
But please do not let a false picture of Jesus steal your desire to know the real Jesus.
Open the Gospels again.
Watch how He treats the broken.
Watch how He responds to sincere seekers.
Watch Him confront hypocrisy.
Watch Him welcome repentant sinners.
Watch Him restore Peter after Peter's devastating denial.
Watch Him call people out of darkness without exploiting their shame.
There is no Savior like Him.
And there is something else you need to remember.
The same Peter whom Paul later confronted was the Peter whom Jesus had already restored.
Failure did not have to be the end of Peter's story.
And correction did not have to mean rejection.
In John 21, the risen Jesus asked Peter whether he loved Him.
Then He entrusted Peter with the care of His sheep.
“Feed my sheep.”
Not “Own my sheep.”
Not “Control my sheep.”
Not “Make my sheep afraid to question you.”
Feed them.
Love them.
Care for them.
That is the heartbeat of Christian shepherding.
And it is why pastors themselves need the Gospel every day.
They need grace when they fail.
They need courage when they must confront sin.
They need humility when corrected.
They need wisdom when criticized unfairly.
They need brothers and sisters who will pray for them rather than flatter them.
And they need to remember that they are sheep before they are shepherds.
They belong to Jesus too.
Maybe you are reading this as a pastor.
And perhaps something in these words has unsettled you.
Maybe you remember a member you dismissed too quickly.
Maybe you used your position to win an argument when you should have opened your Bible.
Maybe you have been so wounded by criticism that you now interpret every question as an attack.
There is grace for repentance.
You can apologize.
You can correct a teaching.
You can invite accountability.
You can seek help.
You can become a safer, wiser, more Christlike shepherd.
Not by pretending you have never failed.
But by refusing to let pride keep you from the transforming work of Jesus.
Or maybe you are reading this as someone who has spent years criticizing pastors.
You know every controversy.
You can identify every doctrinal weakness.
You have become skilled at exposing what is wrong.
But somewhere along the way, compassion disappeared.
You no longer pray for the people you criticize.
You no longer grieve over sin.
You enjoy the downfall of leaders you dislike.
If that is true, you also need to return to the cross.
Because discernment without love can become cruelty.
And truth used as a weapon of personal vengeance does not reflect the heart of Christ.
The Gospel calls us to something deeper than being right in an argument.
It calls us to become like Jesus.
And perhaps you are the quiet believer who started reading this article with tears already close to the surface.
You have been wondering whether God is angry with you for asking questions.
You have been replaying conversations in your head.
You have been frightened that your doubts mean you are losing your faith.
You have even wondered whether your desire to understand Scripture is evidence that your heart is rebellious.
Please understand the distinction.
A question asked in humility is not automatically rebellion.
A concern raised in love is not automatically dishonor.
A request for biblical explanation is not automatically an attack on authority.
And refusing a command that contradicts God's Word is not disobedience to God.
But your questions must still be brought before Him.
Let Scripture examine your motives as carefully as you examine another person's teaching.
Be willing to repent if you have acted pridefully.
Be willing to forgive where forgiveness is needed.
Be willing to receive correction.
Be willing to pursue peace where peace is possible.
And be willing to stand for truth when standing becomes costly.
Because following Jesus has never meant avoiding every difficult conversation.
Sometimes faithfulness sounds like a respectful question.
Sometimes it sounds like an apology.
Sometimes it sounds like a courageous correction.
Sometimes it sounds like refusing to participate in wrongdoing.
And sometimes it sounds like a wounded believer whispering a prayer they have not had the strength to pray in months.
“Lord Jesus, I still want to trust You. Please help me see You clearly again.”
That prayer matters.
Not because the words are impressive.
But because Christ is merciful.
He does not despise the brokenhearted who come to Him.
And He does not require you to understand every mystery before you can cling to His grace.
So should Christians question their pastors?
Yes, when there is a genuine need to seek understanding, test teaching against Scripture, or address legitimate concerns.
But they should do so with humility, fairness, love, and a willingness to be corrected themselves.
Should Christians honor and submit to faithful pastoral leadership?
Yes.
Scripture teaches that too.
And can questioning a pastor become rebellion?
Certainly.
When it grows from pride, contempt, dishonest accusation, divisiveness, or refusal to heed sound biblical correction, it can become sinful.
But asking a question is not itself the sin.
The heart, the truth of the concern, the manner of the approach, and the response to God's Word all matter.
The Church does not need fewer people who think carefully about Scripture.
It needs more people who love Scripture enough to obey it.
It does not need pastors who are terrified of accountability.
It needs shepherds who welcome the refining work of truth.
It does not need congregations that celebrate rebellion.
It needs disciples who understand the difference between godly submission and blind loyalty.
And above everything, it needs Jesus Christ at the center.
Not celebrity.
Not personality.
Not institutional pride.
Not religious intimidation.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The Chief Shepherd.
The One whose authority is perfect because His character is perfect.
The One who never manipulates His sheep to preserve a fragile ego.
The One who speaks truth because He is truth.
The One who corrects those He loves.
The One who welcomes sinners who repent.
The One who can redeem even the most painful chapters of our spiritual history.
From fear to truth.
From manipulation to freedom in Christ.
From wounded faith to renewed trust in the Savior who has never failed.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not to win an argument.
Not to expose your pastor.
Not to encourage public accusations.
But because someone reading your words may be silently carrying the same struggle.
Have you ever been afraid to ask a sincere biblical question because you thought it would be called rebellion?
Or have you been a pastor who was deeply hurt by questions asked without love?
You might simply comment, “Lord, teach me to honor without blindly following.”
Or, if your faith has been wounded, “Jesus, help me trust You again.”
And if you are a pastor seeking to lead more faithfully, perhaps your prayer is, “Lord, make me a shepherd after Your heart.”
Your honesty may encourage someone who thought they were the only one.
Return to the Scriptures. Study them in context. Let God's Word continue the conversation long after you have finished reading.
If you have been strengthened by this message, I also want to invite you into something deeper.
Our desire is to build a community that continues growing in Scripture, repentance, healing, discipleship, and the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our commitment to make biblical encouragement and discipleship more accessible.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Not because you must pay to prove your faith.
Not because grace, biblical truth, or spiritual growth can be purchased.
But because voluntary generosity can help a ministry continue serving people.
If you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel-centered teaching, this is one meaningful opportunity to do so.
Because the ultimate goal is not to build a platform around a human personality.
It is to point people to the One whose name is above every name.
Jesus Christ.
And maybe the greatest thing you take away from this article is not a new argument about church authority.
Maybe it is the courage to open your Bible again.
To ask a sincere question without hatred.
To honor a faithful pastor without idolizing him.
To receive correction without humiliation.
To forgive without pretending wrongdoing was harmless.
To stand for truth without losing love.
To return to Christian fellowship with wisdom rather than fear.
And to remember that your relationship with God was never meant to depend upon another human being's perfection.
Because on the day you stand before Christ, the question will not be whether you protected every decision your pastor ever made.
The question will be whether you belonged to Jesus, trusted His grace, and followed Him faithfully.
So hold your Bible close.
Keep your heart humble.
Love the Church.
Pray for your shepherds.
Test what you hear.
Repent when you are wrong.
Speak when truth requires courage.
And never forget whose sheep you are.
The voice that was meant to lead you to Jesus must never become the voice that keeps you afraid to follow Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE PERSON YOU MARRIED STILL SLEEPS BESIDE YOU… BUT NO LONGER BELIEVES IN THE GOD WHO BROUGHT YOU TOGETHER
paragraphs: THE PERSON YOU MARRIED STILL SLEEPS BESIDE YOU… BUT NO LONGER BELIEVES IN THE GOD WHO BROUGHT YOU TOGETHER

When one spouse loses faith in God, does the marriage have to fall apart? A heartbreaking, Scripture-rooted journey through spiritual loneliness, difficult love, unanswered prayers, and the grace of Jesus Christ that can reach even the places where faith seems to have died.
There is a kind of heartbreak that happens without anyone leaving the house.
No packed suitcase.
No divorce papers.
No affair.
No dramatic goodbye.
Just two people lying in the same bed, staring into the darkness, separated by something neither of them ever imagined could come between them.
One still believes in God.
The other doesn't anymore.
And somewhere between the whispered prayers and the uncomfortable silence, the believing spouse begins to wonder something they are almost afraid to say aloud.
"Lord, how do I stay married to someone who no longer believes in You?"
Perhaps the hardest part isn't even that your spouse stopped attending church.
It isn't that the Bible sits unopened on the nightstand.
It isn't that the person who once held your hand during worship now looks uncomfortable when you mention Jesus.
It's remembering who you used to be together.
You remember praying before meals.
You remember discussing sermons on the way home.
You remember those nights when life was falling apart, but somehow you both found comfort in the same promise.
You remember believing that no matter what happened, you would always have God at the center of your marriage.
And now?
You pray alone.
You worship alone.
Sometimes you even cry alone.
Your spouse is still physically present, but the spiritual companionship you treasured feels like it has disappeared.
And perhaps the most painful question of all is this:
"If the person I love no longer believes in the God I love, can our marriage still survive?"
The answer may surprise you.
Because the Bible addresses this painful situation more directly than many Christians realize.
And what Scripture says is not only challenging.
It is astonishingly gracious.
The apostle Paul wrote to believers in Corinth who were navigating complicated marriages in a culture where Christianity was still spreading through households.
Some people had come to faith while their spouses remained unbelievers.
They were not necessarily married to cruel people.
They were not necessarily living in loveless homes.
But they were experiencing a spiritual division that could have raised frightening questions about whether their marriages should continue.
Paul addressed them directly.
In 1 Corinthians 7:12–13, he wrote:

"If any brother hath a wife that believeth not, and she be pleased to dwell with him, let him not put her away. And the woman which hath an husband that believeth not, and if he be pleased to dwell with her, let her not leave him."
Read that again.
Not quickly.
Not through the pain of your present situation.
Read it as someone who needs to know whether God has forgotten the marriage they are fighting to preserve.
If the unbelieving spouse is willing to remain in the marriage, the believing spouse is not instructed to leave simply because of that unbelief.
That is remarkable.
Paul does not say, "Your spouse no longer shares your faith, so your marriage has become meaningless."
He does not say, "Their unbelief has made your vows worthless."
He does not tell believers to abandon their marriages to protect their spiritual identity.
Instead, he recognizes that a marriage can remain a genuine marriage even when husband and wife no longer share the same convictions about God.
In the original Greek, Paul uses the expression:
συνευδοκεῖ οἰκεῖν — syneudokei oikein
It conveys the idea of being willing or consenting to live together.
That detail matters.
Paul is not describing a spouse who must be forced into remaining.
He is speaking about a spouse who is willing to continue sharing married life.
And that changes how we understand the passage.
The biblical instruction is not to manufacture agreement where none exists.
It is not to pretend spiritual differences are insignificant.
It is to recognize that unbelief alone does not automatically dissolve a marriage covenant.
But there is something else you need to understand.
You can remain faithful to Jesus without demanding that your spouse pretend to believe.
That sentence may be difficult for some Christians to accept.
Especially those who have spent years praying for a husband or wife to return to God.
You want them to believe.
Of course you do.
You love them.
You believe Christ is the way, the truth, and the life, just as He declared in John 14:6.
You believe salvation is found in Him.
You believe eternity matters.
And because you love your spouse, their relationship with God is not a small concern.
It reaches into the deepest part of your heart.
But there is a difference between loving someone toward Christ and trying to control their response to Christ.
There is a difference between witnessing and pressuring.
Between praying and interrogating.
Between speaking truth and turning every conversation into an argument.
Your spouse is not a project.
Your marriage is not a conversion campaign.
And your love should not become something your spouse receives only when they agree with your theology.
Think about how Jesus encountered people.
He spoke truth without surrendering it.
He called sinners to repentance.
He exposed hypocrisy.
He confronted unbelief.
But He also showed extraordinary patience toward people who struggled to understand Him.
Consider the father in Mark 9:24 who cried:
"Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief."
In Greek, the heart of that confession is:
Πιστεύω· βοήθει μου τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ — Pisteuō; boēthei mou tē apistia.
"I believe; help my unbelief."
What an extraordinary confession.
Faith and struggle existing in the same trembling human heart.
That father was not speaking about marriage. The passage concerns his desperate appeal to Jesus for his child.
But his words reveal something profoundly important about human faith.
People can struggle.
People can become confused.
People can find themselves standing between what they once believed and what they can presently understand.
And Jesus did not respond to that father's desperate cry by mocking his weakness.
He responded with power and compassion.
Perhaps your spouse's unbelief began with an intellectual question.
Perhaps it began with suffering.
Perhaps someone they trusted in church betrayed them.
Perhaps they watched a loved one die after years of prayer.
Perhaps they encountered hypocrisy from people who loudly proclaimed Jesus but quietly practiced cruelty.
Perhaps they have questions nobody has answered convincingly.
Or perhaps they have simply concluded that they no longer believe Christianity is true.
Those possibilities are not identical.
And they should not be treated as though they are.
Some people are wounded.
Some are questioning.
Some are angry.
Some are unconvinced.
Some have deliberately rejected the Christian faith.
You cannot understand your spouse's journey if you refuse to listen to their actual reasons.
And you cannot love someone well while constantly replacing their real story with the explanation you would prefer to believe.
Imagine a wife sitting across from her husband one evening.
For months, she has noticed the changes.
He no longer prays.
He avoids church.
He grows quiet whenever she talks about Scripture.
Finally, she asks him:
"Do you still believe in God?"
He looks down.
For a long moment, he says nothing.
Then he whispers:
"I don't think I do anymore."
Her chest tightens.
Her eyes fill.
She wants to ask a hundred questions.
She wants to tell him he is wrong.
She wants to remind him of every answered prayer, every testimony, every moment they once called a miracle.
But underneath all those thoughts is one terrifying fear.
"If he can stop believing in God, what else can he stop believing in? What if one day he stops believing in us?"
That fear is real.
But it is not a prophecy.
Losing religious belief does not automatically mean someone has stopped loving their spouse.
And continuing to profess faith does not automatically make someone a loving partner.
The evidence of marital faithfulness is not found in religious language alone.
It is found in truthfulness.
In commitment.
In tenderness.
In repentance when wrong.
In keeping promises.
In showing up when life becomes difficult.
Jesus warned in Matthew 7:21 that not everyone who says "Lord, Lord" truly belongs to Him.
Words matter.
But words without genuine obedience are not enough.
And this is where some Christian marriages encounter a painful truth.
A spouse who no longer professes Christianity may still behave with more marital integrity than someone who loudly claims to be Christian.
That does not make unbelief spiritually insignificant.
It means we must not confuse religious appearance with Christlike character.
Your spouse's relationship with God matters deeply.
But so does how you treat each other when you disagree.
And sometimes the first thing a struggling marriage needs is not another argument about religion.
Sometimes it needs an honest conversation in which both people feel safe enough to tell the truth.
"Tell me what changed."
"Was there something that hurt you?"
"What questions are you carrying?"
"Have I made it harder for you to speak honestly?"
"I still believe in Jesus. I cannot pretend otherwise. But I want to understand you."
Those words will not resolve every disagreement.
They may not produce immediate reconciliation.
But they can open a door that accusation would have slammed shut.
And Scripture offers another powerful perspective.
In 1 Peter 3:1–2, Peter addresses Christian wives whose husbands do not obey the word, encouraging conduct that may bear witness even without repeated verbal persuasion.
The Greek expression:
ἄνευ λόγου — aneu logou
means "without a word."
In context, Peter is emphasizing the persuasive witness of a wife's conduct rather than suggesting that the Gospel should never be spoken.
Nor is the passage permission for a husband to dominate his wife, demand silence, or abuse her.
The broader Christian call is to holiness, honor, and love.
And Ephesians 5:25 places an extraordinary responsibility upon husbands:
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it."
Christlike love is sacrificial.
It is not coercive.
It does not use Scripture as a weapon to humiliate someone into agreement.
The believing husband or wife must ask a difficult question:
"Does the way I treat my spouse make the character of Jesus more visible—or does it make His name harder for them to hear?"
That question can expose things we would rather leave untouched.
Perhaps you have been so frightened of your spouse's unbelief that you have begun treating them as an enemy.
Perhaps every dinner conversation becomes a theological confrontation.
Perhaps you correct them publicly.
Perhaps you have started withholding affection because they no longer attend church.
Perhaps you speak about their spiritual condition to everyone except the person who most needs your compassion.
Your concern may be sincere.
Your theology may be deeply held.
But fear can sometimes disguise itself as righteousness.
And the Holy Spirit may be calling you to repent—not of loving biblical truth, but of the harshness with which you have sometimes defended it.
Remember Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 13:4:
"Charity suffereth long, and is kind."
The Greek word translated "charity" in the King James Version is:
ἀγάπη — agapē
Love.
Not a shallow feeling that ignores truth.
Not unlimited tolerance of wrongdoing.
Not the surrender of convictions.
But a love that seeks another person's good.
A love marked by patience and kindness.
A love that refuses to rejoice in wrongdoing.
A love that remains anchored in truth.
And here is something that deserves to be said clearly.
Loving your unbelieving spouse does not require you to stop following Jesus.
You do not have to abandon prayer.
You do not have to deny Scripture.
You do not have to pretend that your faith is merely a personal hobby.
You can respectfully maintain your Christian convictions while giving your spouse room to be honest about theirs.
A healthy marriage can make space for disagreement without turning every difference into a threat.
That may mean negotiating how children are taught about faith.
It may mean discussing church attendance without threats or resentment.
It may mean agreeing not to ridicule each other's convictions.
It may mean seeking wise pastoral care or marriage counseling when conversations repeatedly become painful.
And when children are involved, the stakes can feel even higher.
One parent wants to teach them to pray.
The other may question whether they should be raised within Christianity at all.
Those disagreements deserve careful, respectful conversations—not a competition for the children's loyalty.
Children should never become weapons in their parents' spiritual conflict.
They need to know they are loved.
They need permission to ask sincere questions.
They need to see that disagreement does not excuse contempt.
And Christian parents can faithfully teach Scripture without teaching their children to despise the parent who does not believe.
Because your children are watching something more than what you say about God.
They are watching how you treat someone who disagrees with you about Him.
But what if you have tried?
What if you have listened?
What if you have prayed for years?
What if your spouse still says, "I don't believe"?
Then you need to hear something that may release a burden you were never meant to carry.
You cannot save your spouse.
Not with enough tears.
Not with enough arguments.
Not with perfect behavior.
Not by becoming the ideal husband or wife.
Salvation belongs to the Lord.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."
In the Greek New Testament, the word for grace is:
χάρις — charis
Grace.
God's unmerited favor.
Salvation is not a prize you can earn on your spouse's behalf through flawless marital performance.
And it is not something you can force into another person's heart.
You can bear witness.
You can pray.
You can love.
You can speak the Gospel.
You can answer questions honestly.
But you cannot manufacture repentance or saving faith.
That belongs to the work of God, not to human control.
And perhaps that is where your own faith is being tested.
Not simply in whether you believe God can change your spouse.
But in whether you will continue trusting Christ even when the outcome remains uncertain.
Can you remain faithful without a guarantee?
Can you love without controlling?
Can you hope without pretending?
Can you grieve without becoming bitter?
Can you surrender the person you love into God's hands without emotionally abandoning them?
These are not easy questions.
They may take years to work through.
And there may be days when you answer them imperfectly.
But Christian maturity is not measured by never struggling.
It is revealed, in part, by repeatedly returning to Christ in the middle of the struggle.
Now consider something even more surprising in Paul's teaching.
In 1 Corinthians 7:14, he writes that the unbelieving spouse is "sanctified" in relation to the believing spouse.
The Greek word is:
ἡγίασται — hēgiastai
It is a form of the verb meaning "to sanctify" or "to set apart."
This verse has sometimes been misunderstood.
It does not mean that an unbelieving husband or wife is automatically saved because their spouse is a Christian.
That would contradict Paul's broader teaching that salvation is by God's grace through faith.
In context, Paul is affirming that the marriage is not made spiritually illegitimate or unclean simply because one spouse is an unbeliever.
The relationship remains a genuine marital union.
The children are not rendered unclean by their parents' differing religious commitments.
The believing spouse does not need to regard the marriage itself as defiled.
Think about what that means.
The God you worship has not commanded you to despise your marriage simply because your spouse no longer shares your faith.
The covenant you entered is not automatically erased by a change in religious conviction.
There is still room for faithfulness.
Still room for tenderness.
Still room for honest companionship.
Still room for peace.
And perhaps still room for a spiritual story whose ending neither of you can presently imagine.
But we must also be careful not to turn hope into a promise God has not made.
The Bible does not guarantee that every unbelieving spouse will eventually become a Christian.
In fact, Paul asks in 1 Corinthians 7:16:
"For what knowest thou, O wife, whether thou shalt save thy husband? or how knowest thou, O man, whether thou shalt save thy wife?"
His question does not grant the believing spouse the power to save anyone.
Rather, it underscores the uncertainty of the other spouse's eventual response.
You do not know what the future holds.
Your spouse may return to faith.
They may remain unconvinced.
They may become willing to explore Christianity again.
Or they may never share your beliefs.
Faithfulness to Christ must not depend on pretending you know which outcome God will bring.
And the marriage itself may have different possible outcomes.
Some couples learn to live with deep religious differences while maintaining affection, trust, and mutual respect.
Others discover that unresolved conflict, contempt, or incompatible expectations make the relationship increasingly difficult.
Some find reconciliation through patient conversations and wise counseling.
Others face abandonment or serious harm.
Paul recognizes in 1 Corinthians 7:15 that an unbelieving spouse may choose to depart, and he teaches that God has called believers to peace.

Christians differ on some questions concerning divorce and remarriage, but this passage plainly shows that the believing spouse is not instructed to maintain the marriage through coercion when the unbelieving spouse insists on leaving.
And nothing in these passages should ever be used to demand that someone remain exposed to violence, intimidation, sexual coercion, or abuse.
God's call to marital faithfulness is not a command to enable cruelty.
If you are in danger, seek safety and trustworthy help.
If you are being manipulated through threats or religious control, you deserve support.
The Gospel does not require you to confuse suffering abuse with demonstrating godliness.
But for the couple who still loves each other, who still wants the marriage, and who is trying to understand how to live with radically different beliefs, Scripture offers a serious invitation.
Do not abandon one another merely because the journey has become harder than expected.
Do not make faith a weapon.
Do not make unbelief an excuse for contempt.
And do not forget that marriage involves daily choices long after the wedding emotions have faded.
There is something profoundly moving about a believing spouse who continues to pray quietly—not to manipulate, not to perform, but because they genuinely entrust the person they love to God.
There is something beautiful about a spouse who says:
"I don't share your faith anymore, but I respect that it matters deeply to you."
There is something courageous about two people choosing honesty over pretense.
And there is something Christlike about refusing to repay spiritual disagreement with cruelty.
But perhaps you are reading this from the other side.
Perhaps you are the spouse who stopped believing.
Maybe your husband still attends church.
Maybe your wife still prays every morning.
Maybe you feel like a disappointment because you cannot honestly say the words you once said with confidence.
Perhaps you are exhausted from being treated as though every question you ask is rebellion.
Perhaps you wish your spouse understood that you did not necessarily choose this uncertainty.
You may have searched.
Read.
Wrestled.
Prayed.
Waited.
And still found yourself unable to believe.
If that is your story, you do not need to fake faith to deserve basic dignity and compassion.
And you do not have to pretend that the questions are insignificant.
Christianity makes real claims about God, history, sin, resurrection, and salvation.
Those claims can be examined seriously.
You are allowed to ask hard questions.
But I also want to invite you to consider something.
Do not assume that every failure of a Christian is a failure of Christ.
Do not assume that hypocrisy in a church disproves the Gospel.
Those experiences may raise serious and legitimate questions about the credibility of Christian witness, but the truth of Jesus must ultimately be examined on its own grounds.
And do not confuse the people who wounded you with the Savior they claimed to represent.
Jesus Himself confronted religious hypocrisy.
He rebuked those who placed crushing burdens on others while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
The Christ revealed in the Gospels is not indifferent to spiritual abuse or religious pretense.
And at the center of Christianity is not the claim that Christians are morally impressive.
It is the claim that sinners need a Savior.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that we climbed high enough to reach God.
But that God, in His mercy, acted through Jesus Christ to rescue sinners.
Jesus lived in obedience to the Father.
He was crucified.
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
And He rose again, according to the Scriptures, as proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
Christian hope rests on Him.
Not on perfect marriages.
Not on flawless churches.
Not on the emotional certainty of every believer.
On Christ.
And if you have walked away from faith, the invitation to consider Jesus remains.
Not because your spouse can argue you into believing.
Not because you owe a church a performance.
But because the claims of Christ are worth examining with intellectual honesty and an open heart.
Now, to the believer who has been silently crying through this article.
There is something I want you to remember.
Your spouse's unbelief does not mean Jesus has abandoned you.
You may feel spiritually lonely.
You may miss the companionship you once had.
You may grieve the shared worship, the mutual prayers, and the future you imagined.
That grief deserves to be acknowledged.
You do not have to call it insignificant.
You do not have to smile through every church service.
You do not have to tell everyone your marriage is wonderful when you are privately struggling.
There is room in the Christian life for lament.
The Psalms are filled with it.
David cried out to God from places of fear, sorrow, and confusion.
Psalm 13:1 begins:
"How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?"
That is not the language of someone pretending everything is fine.
It is the cry of a believer bringing anguish into the presence of God.
And perhaps tonight, your prayer does not need to sound impressive.
Perhaps it sounds like this:
"Jesus, I don't know how to do this."
"I love my spouse."
"I love You."
"And I feel torn in ways I never expected."
"Please keep my heart from bitterness."
"Teach me to speak truth without cruelty."
"Teach me to listen without surrendering my convictions."
"Give me wisdom for our marriage."
"And Lord, whatever happens, don't let this pain pull me away from You."
That is a prayer you can bring to Christ.
Not because you have earned His attention.
But because Hebrews 4:16 invites believers to approach the throne of grace for mercy and help in time of need.
And the Greek expression translated "throne of grace" is:
θρόνῳ τῆς χάριτος — thronō tēs charitos
A throne of grace.
What an extraordinary place to bring a broken heart.
Not a throne of humiliation.
Not a throne where the exhausted are mocked.
A throne of grace.
A place where believers are invited to seek mercy and help.
You may not know how your marriage will look five years from now.
You may not know whether your spouse will ever pray beside you again.
You may not know whether the conversations you are having will bring you closer together or reveal differences that require painful decisions.
But you can know this:
Christ remains worthy of your trust even when your marriage feels uncertain.
And there is another truth that may be difficult but necessary.
Sometimes the believing spouse must stop trying to win every theological argument and begin asking whether the marriage is still a place of genuine love.
Are we kind to each other?
Do we tell the truth?
Can we disagree without humiliation?
Do we still care about each other's suffering?
Are we willing to seek help?
Can we respect each other's conscience?
Are we protecting our children from hostility?
Can we make room for difficult conversations without treating disagreement as betrayal?
These questions do not replace biblical faith.
They help reveal whether love is being practiced in the ordinary, demanding places where marriage actually happens.
Because marriage is not sustained by wedding photographs.
It is not sustained by public declarations alone.
It is sustained through thousands of small acts of faithfulness.
Through apologies.
Through listening.
Through restraint.
Through difficult conversations.
Through choosing not to use another person's vulnerability against them.
Through remembering that the person across the table is someone you promised to love.
And when you fail, as every imperfect spouse eventually does, the Christian response is not self-righteousness.
It is repentance.
That word matters.
In Greek, the New Testament often uses:
μετάνοια — metanoia
Repentance.
A change of mind and heart expressed in turning from sin toward God.
And perhaps repentance is needed on both sides of a painful marriage.
The believer may need to repent of pride, manipulation, contempt, or harsh speech.
The unbeliever may need to acknowledge dishonesty, mockery, cruelty, or broken promises where those have occurred.
Neither spouse should use the other's religious position to escape responsibility for their own conduct.
And this is where grace becomes more than a beautiful religious word.
Grace confronts us.
Grace humbles us.
Grace exposes the illusion that we can save ourselves through moral superiority.
Grace leads us back to Jesus.
There is a reason the Gospel Warrior message is:
The scandal may be that the marriage everyone admired is struggling behind closed doors.
The scandal may be that the couple who once served together in church no longer knows how to pray together.
The scandal may be that the person who taught Sunday school now says they no longer believe.
Or perhaps the scandal is the pride, resentment, and fear that have quietly taken root in the believing spouse's heart.
But grace reminds us that the present chapter is not the whole story.
Jesus can redeem sinners.
Jesus can transform hearts.
Jesus can restore what human pride has damaged.
Jesus can teach people to love with patience and truth.
And yes, God can bring someone who has rejected the faith to genuine repentance and renewed belief.
But we must never turn the possibility of restoration into a guaranteed outcome for every marriage.
Jesus rewrites lives according to His wisdom and grace, not according to a script we control.
Sometimes His transforming work is visible in reconciliation.
Sometimes it is visible in the believer becoming gentler, wiser, and more faithful.
Sometimes it is visible in the courage to establish necessary boundaries.
Sometimes it is visible in a person who finally stops pretending and begins asking sincere questions about Christ.
And sometimes His grace sustains someone through a sorrow that has not yet been resolved.
The Gospel is not a promise that every marriage will become easy.
It is the good news that Jesus Christ saves sinners and remains faithful to His people.
That is a hope deeper than circumstances.
And it is a hope worth sharing.
Someone in your family, your church, or your circle of friends may be lying awake tonight wondering whether anyone understands what is happening in their marriage.
And I want to ask you something.
Not for a polished answer.
Not for a religious performance.
But for an honest one.
If your spouse stopped believing in God tomorrow, would your love become a weapon—or would your life still bear witness to the grace of Jesus Christ?
That question is not meant to shame you.
It is meant to make us examine our hearts.
Because the way we respond to spiritual disagreement may reveal where we ourselves still need the transforming work of Christ.
If you have experienced a marriage marked by different beliefs, your honest testimony may help someone who feels completely alone.
You do not have to disclose private details. And if your situation involves danger or abuse, please seek confidential support rather than feeling obligated to share publicly.
Your story matters.
Your questions matter.
And your marriage deserves more than shallow slogans and careless advice.

And if Gospel-centered writing like this has helped you, consider following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who no longer believe to follow as well.
We want this to be a place where people can encounter Scripture seriously, wrestle with difficult questions honestly, receive encouragement, and be continually pointed back to Jesus Christ.
Not toward a personality.
Not toward religious performance.
Toward Christ.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One who calls us to repentance and faith.
The One whose grace is greater than our ability to repair ourselves.
Others are able to pray.
Others can help financially.
All of those can be meaningful expressions of Christian love and service.
But if this ministry has nourished your faith, and you believe in helping its message reach others, your voluntary support can become one practical way to participate in that work.
These items are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
But they can serve as reminders of faith, encouragement, and conversations that point others toward Him.
Our desire is not merely to create something people read and forget.
It is to encourage genuine discipleship.
To help believers understand Scripture.
To equip people to endure suffering without abandoning hope.
To challenge complacency.
To proclaim repentance and forgiveness through Christ.
And to remind wounded people that the Gospel still speaks into the darkest rooms of human experience.
Because the goal is not simply a larger audience.
The goal is more people hearing the truth about Jesus Christ.
More struggling believers receiving encouragement.
More marriages receiving wise, compassionate, Scripture-grounded counsel.
More wounded hearts encountering the Gospel.
More people understanding that grace does not mean ignoring sin, and truth does not mean abandoning love.
And before you leave, I want you to picture something.
A quiet bedroom.
A husband and wife lying beside each other.
One believes.
One does not.
There are questions neither knows how to answer.
There are memories that still hurt.
There are prayers that have not been answered the way one of them hoped.
But tonight, instead of beginning another argument, the believing spouse reaches across the bed and gently takes the other's hand.
No sermon.
No ultimatum.
No demand for a confession of faith.
Just a small act of tenderness.
Perhaps the other spouse holds that hand.
Perhaps they do not.
We cannot know.
But the believer quietly prays in their own heart:
"Lord Jesus, help me love truthfully. Help me love wisely. Help me remain faithful to You. And whatever happens, keep me from forgetting Your grace."
That prayer may not instantly change the marriage.
It may not restore shared faith.
It may not answer every question.
But it is a beginning.
A return to the One who teaches us that love is patient, truth matters, repentance is necessary, and grace is never something we can manufacture by human strength.
So can a marriage survive when one spouse stops believing in God?
Yes. It can.
Not every such marriage will survive, and Scripture does not promise that it will.
But a difference in belief does not, by itself, make marital faithfulness impossible.
And for the Christian who is living through this sorrow, there is hope—not in the certainty of controlling another person's future, but in the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
You may no longer kneel together in prayer.
You may no longer sing the same worship songs.
You may not even agree about whether God exists.
But if there is still willingness, honesty, safety, respect, and love, your marriage may still have a future worth tending with patience and wisdom.
And whether your spouse returns to faith or not, Christ calls you to remain His.
Do not trade truth for peace.
Do not trade compassion for the satisfaction of winning an argument.
Do not make another person's unbelief an excuse for your own disobedience.
And never forget that the Savior who calls sinners to repentance is also the Savior who welcomes weary people to come to Him.

Because sometimes the most heartbreaking distance in a marriage is not the space between two pillows, but the silence where two voices once whispered "Amen"—and even there, Jesus has not stopped being Lord.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HANNAH HAD TO WATCH ANOTHER WOMAN GIVE HER HUSBAND THE CHILDREN SHE COULDN’T GIVE HIM… AND STILL FIND THE STRENGTH TO PRAY
paragraphs: HANNAH HAD TO WATCH ANOTHER WOMAN GIVE HER HUSBAND THE CHILDREN SHE COULDN’T GIVE HIM… AND STILL FIND THE STRENGTH TO PRAY

Two wives. One husband. Children in the arms of one woman. Tears in the eyes of the other. And a God who heard the prayer nobody else could understand. The heartbreaking story of Hannah in 1 Samuel 1 reveals what happens when the world mistakes your unanswered prayers for a life God has forgotten.
Imagine sitting at a dinner table with your husband, watching another woman hold the children you have spent years begging God to give you.
She is not a stranger.
She is not someone you can simply avoid.
She is your husband's other wife.
Her children are running through the house. Their laughter fills the rooms. Their little hands reach for their father. They call him by the name you have dreamed of hearing your own child call him.
And you?
You sit there trying to swallow food past a lump in your throat.
You smile when someone looks in your direction.
You pretend the sound of those children doesn't break something inside you.
And perhaps the most painful part is that the woman holding everything you desperately want knows exactly where your heart is wounded.
And she keeps pressing on that wound.
This is not a fictional drama written to make you cry.
This is the world Scripture invites us into in 1 Samuel 1.
And before this story ends, we need to confront a question that may be painfully familiar.
What do you do when someone else is living the answer to the prayer you have been praying for years?
Because Hannah knew what it felt like to love God while carrying a heartbreak that seemed to have no expiration date.
She knew what it felt like to be loved by someone and still feel terribly alone.
She knew what it felt like to worship while wounded.
And she knew something many of us are still learning.
Sometimes the people who appear to have everything are not the people whose hearts are closest to peace.
The Bible introduces us to a man named Elkanah, who had two wives.
One was named Hannah.
The other was named Peninnah.
Peninnah had children.
Hannah had none.
That is how 1 Samuel 1:2 introduces their circumstances, with a simplicity that almost conceals the emotional devastation behind those words.

But anyone who has waited for a child, suffered infertility, experienced repeated disappointment, or watched another person's life unfold in ways they desperately wanted for their own will recognize the grief hidden in that sentence.
Peninnah had children.
Hannah had none.
Six words in the familiar English telling.
An entire world of sorrow.
And Scripture does not tell us Hannah chose this marriage arrangement, wanted to share her husband, or agreed to it because she could not conceive. We must not invent what God has not revealed.
What Scripture does tell us is that she lived within a polygamous household, a reality described in the Old Testament without being presented as God's ideal for marriage.
Jesus later pointed back to God's design from creation, where a man and woman become one flesh (Matthew 19:4–6).
The Bible's honesty about broken households should never be mistaken for an endorsement of everything that happened inside them.
And Hannah's household was deeply broken.
Every year, Elkanah traveled with his family to Shiloh to worship and sacrifice to the LORD.
Imagine the journey.
The preparations.
The children.
The conversations.
The anticipation of worship.
For Peninnah, the journey included her sons and daughters.
For Hannah, it included the painful awareness of the children she did not have.
During the sacrificial meal, Elkanah gave portions to Peninnah and her children. He also gave Hannah a special portion because he loved her.
But here is where the story becomes almost unbearable.
Hannah was loved by her husband, yet his love could not remove her grief.
Someone needs to hear that.
You can be loved and still be hurting.
You can have a good thing in your life and still grieve something missing.
You can be genuinely grateful for what God has given you without pretending you are unaffected by what you have lost or are still waiting to receive.
Gratitude and grief can occupy the same heart.
Faith and tears can exist in the same prayer.
And being surrounded by blessings does not automatically silence the ache of an unanswered longing.
Elkanah tried to comfort Hannah.
He asked why she was crying, why she would not eat, and why her heart was troubled.
Then he asked a question recorded in 1 Samuel 1:8:
"Am not I better to thee than ten sons?"
He loved her.
But love does not always understand the particular shape of another person's suffering.
Perhaps you have experienced something similar.
Someone tells you to be thankful because other people have it worse.
Someone reminds you of all the blessings you already possess.
Someone says you should stop thinking about the one thing that keeps you awake at night.
They may mean well.
They may genuinely love you.
But their words do not necessarily reach the place where you are bleeding.
Hannah's husband could give her affection.
He could give her a special portion.
He could remind her of his love.
But he could not give her the child she longed to hold.
And then there was Peninnah.
The Bible describes her as Hannah's rival.
Not merely another woman living in the same household.
A rival who deliberately provoked her.
The Hebrew of 1 Samuel 1:6 contains a striking expression:
כַּעֲסָהּ צָרָתָהּ גַּם־כַּעַס
Ka'asah tsaratah gam-ka'as.
The wording describes Hannah's rival provoking her severely, causing distress and irritation.
The Hebrew word tsarah can refer to a rival wife in this context, while the related language of provocation emphasizes the intentional distress Peninnah caused.
This was not an innocent misunderstanding.
Scripture presents deliberate cruelty.
Peninnah had the children Hannah desperately wanted, yet she used Hannah's childlessness as a reason to torment her.
Think about that.
The woman who possessed what Hannah longed for was not satisfied simply to enjoy her own blessing.
She turned Hannah's sorrow into a weapon.
And Scripture tells us this happened year after year.
Not once.
Not during one unfortunate argument.
Year after year.
Every return to the house of the LORD could reopen the same wound.
Until Hannah wept and would not eat.
There is something especially painful about being wounded in a place where you came seeking God.
You arrive hoping for comfort.
You expect worship to strengthen you.
You want to lay your burdens before the LORD.
Yet the person who makes your life miserable is sitting nearby.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
Maybe your Peninnah is not another wife.
Maybe it is the relative who keeps asking why you are still unmarried.
The friend who repeatedly compares your children with hers.
The coworker who makes jokes about your failures.
The person who reminds you of the mistake you have spent years trying to move beyond.
The voice that says your life is behind schedule.
Or perhaps the cruelest voice is the one inside your own mind.
The one that whispers:
"Look at everyone else."
"They're moving forward."
"You're still here."
"Maybe God loves them more."
"Maybe something is wrong with you."
And after enough disappointment, you begin to wonder whether those lies might be true.
But listen carefully.
Someone else's blessing is not proof of God's rejection of you.
Peninnah had children.
Hannah did not.
But Peninnah's motherhood did not make her cruelty righteous, and Hannah's infertility did not make her spiritually inferior.
In the ancient world, childlessness could carry profound social pain and stigma.
Yet Scripture refuses to reduce Hannah's worth to her ability to bear a child.
Her suffering was real.
Her longing was real.
But her value before God was never determined by the contents of her womb.
That truth matters today.
Especially for the woman who has endured miscarriage.
For the couple who have spent years pursuing treatment.
For the person who has buried a dream no one else knew existed.
For the believer who has quietly wondered whether an unanswered prayer is evidence of divine displeasure.
