Imagine how differently the people might have responded to the raised serpent.
Some may have been near it.
Others far away.
Some may have been strong enough to stand.
Others may have barely been able to lift their heads.
The passage does not give us those individual stories.
But it does tell us that the promise extended to those who had been bitten and looked at what God had provided.
And that makes me think about how differently people arrive at the foot of the cross.
Some come with years of religious knowledge.
Others come knowing almost nothing about the Bible.
Some come after a lifetime of obvious rebellion.
Others come after years of respectable, hidden pride.
Some arrive with tears.
Others are so emotionally exhausted they can barely feel anything.
But none of us comes with a righteousness sufficient to save ourselves.
We come needing Christ.
And He is sufficient.
That is why the invitation of the Gospel must never be reduced to a demand for money, an emotional performance, or an attempt to impress other Christians.
Yet when grace genuinely takes hold of a person's heart, it often changes how that person thinks about generosity, service, and the spread of God's Word.
We begin to ask a different question.
Not, “How little can I give and still feel religious?”
But, “Lord, how can I faithfully use what You have entrusted to me?”
For some, that means sharing the Gospel with a neighbor.

For others, it means encouraging a struggling believer, discipling a younger Christian, serving in a local church, helping someone in need, or supporting trustworthy ministries that teach Scripture faithfully.

And if Gospel Warrior has helped you understand God's Word, strengthened you during a difficult season, or encouraged you to return to Christ, you can help us continue making these resources available.
Not because every share guarantees someone will be saved.
Salvation belongs to the Lord.
But because sharing biblical truth creates another opportunity for someone to hear about Jesus.
You may never know who is silently reading your posts.
Someone in your family may be struggling with guilt.
An old friend may have stopped attending church.
A coworker may be wondering whether God still cares.
Someone who has never told you about their pain may read a single paragraph that encourages them to open the Bible and seek Christ.
And if one particular person comes to mind as you read this, consider tagging them with kindness or sending the article privately.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose their struggles.
But to remind them that they are not beyond the reach of God's mercy.
What part of this story confronted your heart the most—the complaining, the consequences of sin, the confession, or the invitation to look to Christ?
You can share your testimony, a Scripture that has strengthened you, or simply write “Christ is still healing me” if you are learning to walk in repentance and grace.
You do not need to reveal anything too private to be welcomed into a conversation about God's faithfulness.
And if someone else shares a struggle, respond with compassion. Pray for them. Point them toward Scripture. Let the comments become a place where truth and grace are both taken seriously.
We want to keep opening Scripture together.
Not merely collecting inspiring quotes.
Not merely chasing emotional moments.
But learning what God's Word actually says, understanding it in context, and allowing the truth of Christ to reshape how we live.
These free resources are part of our desire to make biblical encouragement and discipleship accessible to more people.
And for those who are able and willing to help sustain and expand this work, there is another opportunity.
Your monthly contribution can be part of your intentional Christian giving—an offering toward Gospel-centered ministry work.
But it is important to keep our giving biblical.
Scripture calls believers to generosity that is willing, thoughtful, and sincere.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That means giving should never be driven by guilt or spiritual intimidation.
It is an additional opportunity to participate in ministry support as God provides and as you freely choose.
Every ministry needs people who pray.
People who share.
People who encourage.
People who serve.
And, when possible, people who give.
These products are not what make anyone more spiritual.
They are simply additional resources and expressions of encouragement for those who find them useful.
The greater purpose remains the same.
To keep the Gospel visible.
To make Scripture accessible.
To encourage repentance, faith, discipleship, and spiritual growth.
To help people move from knowing about Jesus to faithfully following Him.
Pray that Scripture will never be twisted merely to attract attention.
Pray that truth will never be compromised for popularity.
Pray that people will not simply become followers of a page but genuine disciples of Jesus.
Because the ultimate goal is not to build an audience around Gospel Warrior.
It is to point people to the Savior who is worthy of every heart.
Now, before you leave, I want you to return with me one final time to that wilderness.
Imagine the camp.
The fear.
The cries.
The dying.
The serpent raised on a pole.
And the astonishing mercy of God, who provided a way for bitten people to live.
Then look beyond the wilderness.
Look toward Calvary.
See the Son of God, innocent and holy, willingly enduring the cross.
Hear the words of Jesus in John 19:30:
“It is finished.”
The Greek word is τετέλεσται (tetelestai).
It conveys completion or accomplishment.
Jesus was declaring that His work had reached its appointed fulfillment.
And although the story of the bronze serpent and the crucifixion are not identical in every detail, Jesus Himself gave us the connection we must not miss.
The Son of Man was lifted up so that those who believe in Him may have eternal life.
The wilderness healing was temporary.
The salvation Christ gives is eternal.
The bronze serpent could never forgive sins.
Jesus can.
The bronze serpent could never conquer death.
Jesus rose victorious over the grave.
The bronze serpent was eventually destroyed because people had turned it into an idol.
But Jesus Christ is the risen Lord, worthy of worship forever.
And now the question is no longer simply why God told Moses to make a bronze serpent.
The deeper question is this.
If God has revealed His Son as the only Savior, why would we keep looking everywhere else for the life that only He can give?
Why keep hiding behind pride?
Why keep defending what Scripture calls sin?
Why keep treating the cross as an interesting religious story instead of facing what it means for your own life?
Why keep postponing repentance as though tomorrow has been promised?
The same Jesus who spoke to Nicodemus still calls people to believe.
The same Lord who forgave sinners still calls us to turn from sin.
The same Savior who died at Calvary is alive.
And His invitation is not limited to people whose stories look beautiful.
It reaches into shame.
Into failure.
Into rebellion.
Into regret.
Into the parts of our lives we would rather nobody ever discover.
Not to tell us that sin never mattered.
But to show us just how much His mercy cost.
So if this message has stirred something in you, do not let the emotion be the end of it.
Open your Bible.
Read Numbers 21:4–9.
Read John 3:1–21.
Read Romans 5.
Ask God to expose what needs to change.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Trust the Christ who died and rose again.
And take the next faithful step.
Maybe that means returning to prayer tonight.
Maybe it means finally telling someone the truth.
Maybe it means asking forgiveness.
Maybe it means finding a faithful local church where you can grow in Scripture and Christian fellowship.
Maybe it means sharing this article with someone you love because you want them to hear the Gospel too.
And maybe, for the first time in a very long time, it means letting go of the exhausting attempt to save yourself.
Because you were never meant to be your own savior.
Christ has already accomplished what you never could.
I pray that when you remember this story, you will not remember only the snakes.
You will remember the mercy.
You will remember the cross.
You will remember the Savior.
And you will remember that no sinner is rescued by pretending the poison is harmless.
We are rescued by the grace of God through faith in Jesus Christ.
The poison revealed how desperately they needed to live. The cross reveals how deeply we need the One who died so that sinners could live forever.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE SANG ABOUT GOD’S GOODNESS ON SUNDAY… THEN CRIED HERSELF TO SLEEP THAT NIGHT.
paragraphs: SHE SANG ABOUT GOD’S GOODNESS ON SUNDAY… THEN CRIED HERSELF TO SLEEP THAT NIGHT.

The congregation heard her worship. Heaven heard her weeping. And what Jesus does with the pain we hide behind our praise might change the way you understand faith, suffering, and the God who refuses to abandon His wounded children.
She was still wearing her Sunday dress when she finally broke down.
The same dress she had worn just hours earlier while standing beneath the church lights, holding a microphone, singing about the goodness of God.
People had raised their hands.
Some had closed their eyes.
Others had wiped away tears as her voice filled the sanctuary.
After the service, someone hugged her and said, “You are so anointed.”
Another whispered, “I wish I had faith like yours.”
She smiled.
She thanked them.
She even encouraged someone who had been struggling.
But nobody knew what was waiting for her when she got home.
Nobody knew how much strength it had taken just to stand on that platform.
Nobody knew that the woman singing about God's faithfulness was quietly wondering why her own life seemed to be falling apart.
And nobody knew that before midnight, the same voice that had led an entire congregation in worship would be trembling through a prayer she could barely finish.
“Lord… I know You're good.”
Silence.
“But why does everything hurt so much?”
If you have ever worshiped God publicly while privately wondering how much more pain you could endure, please keep reading.
Because there is something about Jesus that suffering people desperately need to understand.
And it may be the very thing you have been too exhausted to believe.
The woman in this story is a fictional portrait, but the struggle she represents is painfully real.
Perhaps her marriage was unraveling.
Perhaps bills were piling up on a kitchen table already covered with unanswered prayers.
Perhaps she had lost someone she loved, and everyone assumed she had recovered because she had stopped talking about it.
Perhaps depression had made ordinary mornings feel unbearably heavy.
Or perhaps there was no single catastrophe.
Just years of carrying everybody else's burdens while quietly neglecting her own wounds.
She was the dependable one.
The prayer warrior.
The woman who remembered birthdays, checked on sick church members, encouraged discouraged friends, and always seemed to have a Scripture ready.
She knew how to tell other people that God would make a way.
What she didn't know was how to admit that she was struggling to see one herself.
And that night, sitting on the edge of her bed, she finally whispered something she had been afraid to say aloud.
“God, I'm tired.”
Not tired from singing.
Not tired from church.
Tired from pretending that because she believed in God's goodness, she was never supposed to feel devastated.
Tired from answering “I'm blessed” when someone asked how she was doing.
Tired from being praised for her strength while secretly wishing someone would notice her exhaustion.
Tired from thinking that admitting her pain might somehow dishonor the God she loved.
And here is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because sometimes the very communities that proclaim God's healing can become places where wounded people feel pressured to hide their wounds.
Not necessarily because anyone intends to hurt them.
Sometimes because we have confused spiritual maturity with emotional invulnerability.
We celebrate the testimony after the breakthrough.
But what about the believer who is still waiting?
We applaud the person who declares victory.
But what about the Christian who can barely whisper, “Help me”?
We know what to do when someone says, “God answered my prayer!”
But do we know how to sit beside someone who says, “I have prayed for years, and I still don't understand”?
Somewhere along the way, many sincere believers began treating tears as evidence that faith was weakening.
Yet Scripture tells a remarkably different story.
And the difference matters.
In Psalm 13:1, David cries:
“How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?” (KJV)
The Hebrew opening is:
עַד־אָנָה יְהוָה
ʿAd-ʾānah YHWH
“How long, O LORD?”
These are not the words of an unbeliever mocking God.
They are the words of a man who knows God and is suffering deeply.
David does not conceal his anguish beneath religious language.
He brings it directly into the presence of the Lord.
He asks difficult questions.
He describes his sorrow.
And then, within the same psalm, he remembers God's steadfast love.
This is biblical lament.
Not the abandonment of faith, but suffering brought honestly before the One in whom faith rests.
The Hebrew Scriptures do not require hurting believers to pretend that their pain is imaginary.
They teach us to take our pain to God.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years believing that honest sorrow and genuine worship cannot exist in the same heart.
But David's psalms show us otherwise.
A trembling voice can still pray.
A grieving heart can still trust.
A believer can have unanswered questions without surrendering the truth of God's character.
And a woman can sing about God's goodness on Sunday and cry herself to sleep that night without becoming a hypocrite.
Read that again.
Her tears did not automatically make her worship dishonest.
Her suffering did not prove that her faith was counterfeit.
Her exhaustion did not place her beyond the reach of God's mercy.
She might have been genuinely worshiping the Lord while desperately needing His comfort.
And if that sounds like you, there is something even more astonishing waiting in the Gospel of John.
Two sisters once sent word to Jesus that their brother was sick.
Mary and Martha loved Jesus.
Their brother Lazarus was loved by Jesus.
Yet Lazarus died.
When Jesus finally arrived, Martha spoke words that have echoed through centuries of grief.
“Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.” (John 11:21, KJV)
Mary would later say essentially the same thing.
Think about the weight of that sentence.
They believed Jesus had power.
They knew He could heal.
But their brother was dead, and they were standing in the terrible space between what they believed Jesus could do and what He had allowed to happen.
Have you ever lived there?
Between God's power and your unanswered prayer?
Between what Scripture says about His goodness and what your circumstances seem to be screaming?
Between knowing He loves you and wondering why He has not changed what is breaking your heart?
Then notice what happens when Jesus sees Mary weeping.
John 11:35 records two words in English:
“Jesus wept.”
The Greek text reads:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς
Edakrysen ho Iēsous.
“Jesus wept.”
The verb edakrysen describes Jesus shedding tears.
It is an extraordinary moment.
Jesus knows that He is about to raise Lazarus.
Yet He still weeps.
His knowledge of the coming resurrection does not make the present grief meaningless.
His divine authority does not make Him indifferent to human sorrow.
And His tears reveal something that suffering believers must never forget.
The Savior who has power over death is not emotionally detached from the people wounded by it.
Jesus does not stand at the tomb and rebuke Mary for crying.
He does not tell Martha that her sadness proves insufficient faith.
He enters the scene of their grief.
He is deeply moved.
He weeps.
Then He calls Lazarus from the grave.
This passage does not promise that every funeral will end with an immediate resurrection or that every tragedy will be reversed in this life.
It reveals Jesus as the resurrection and the life, the One whose victory over death reaches its fulfillment in the hope He gives to those who believe in Him.
But before the miracle at the tomb, there are tears.
And those tears matter.
Because the woman who sang on Sunday needs to know that her Savior understands what it means to weep.
So do you.
There is another moment in Scripture that takes this truth even deeper.
On the night before His crucifixion, Jesus enters Gethsemane.
The name Gethsemane is commonly connected with the idea of an oil press, a striking setting for the anguish that unfolds there.
Matthew 26:38 records Jesus saying:
“My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death.”
The Greek expression includes:
περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου
Perilypos estin hē psychē mou.
“My soul is deeply sorrowful.”
The word perilypos conveys profound grief or distress.
Jesus is not pretending.
He is not performing sorrow to make a theological point.
He is facing the horror of what lies ahead.
He prays.
He submits Himself to the Father's will.
And He asks His disciples to remain with Him and watch.
Yet they fall asleep.
The disciples who had walked with Him, listened to Him, and witnessed His miracles could not remain awake in His hour of anguish.
Consider that for a moment.
The sinless Son of God experienced sorrow so deep that He described it as overwhelming.
Therefore, deep sorrow cannot, by itself, be evidence of personal sin or spiritual failure.
Jesus never sinned.
Yet Jesus grieved.
Jesus never lacked faith.
Yet Jesus experienced anguish.
And His submission to the Father was not the absence of pain.
It was obedience in the midst of it.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that we have a high priest who can sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
That does not mean Jesus experienced every circumstance exactly as we do.
It means our Savior is not distant, ignorant, or incapable of compassion.
He knows human suffering from within a truly human life.
And He is able to receive those who come to Him for mercy.
So perhaps the question is not, “Why am I crying if I really believe?”
Perhaps a better question is, “Why have I been so afraid to bring my tears to the Savior who wept?”
That Sunday night, our imagined worship leader sat with her Bible open.
Her makeup had been washed away.
Her phone was full of messages thanking her for the worship service.
She could barely bring herself to answer them.
She remembered someone saying, “You always seem so strong.”
And for the first time, she wished they had said something different.
“Are you okay?”
Not because she wanted attention.
Not because she wanted everyone to know her private struggles.
But because she was beginning to understand how lonely it can feel to be admired for a strength you are no longer sure you possess.
Maybe you know that loneliness.
Maybe you are the father who leads family prayer but secretly fears losing his job.
Maybe you are the mother who tells her children that Jesus loves them while struggling with grief no one else sees.
Maybe you are the pastor who has preached hope while carrying private exhaustion.
Maybe you are the young believer who sings with the worship team and then goes home to a house where there is more shouting than peace.
Maybe you are the person who keeps serving because you genuinely love Jesus, even though your heart has become dangerously weary.
And maybe, just maybe, you have mistaken your ability to keep functioning for evidence that you are healing.
They are not always the same thing.
You can fulfill your responsibilities while still needing help.
You can encourage other people while needing encouragement yourself.
You can know Scripture while struggling to apply its promises to your own suffering.
And you can love Christ sincerely while needing someone trustworthy to walk beside you.
God did not design the church to be a stage where everyone performs invulnerability.
The church is the body of Christ.
Galatians 6:2 says:
“Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.”
Notice what this assumes.
Believers will have burdens.
And those burdens are not always meant to be carried alone.
Sometimes the next faithful step is not accepting another ministry assignment.
Sometimes it is admitting to a mature Christian friend, “I need prayer.”
Sometimes it is asking a pastor or counselor for help.
Sometimes it is seeking professional care for persistent depression, anxiety, trauma, or emotional distress.
Receiving appropriate care does not mean abandoning prayer or Scripture.
Nor should anyone be told to discontinue necessary medical treatment simply because they are seeking spiritual support.
God's people can pray, listen, encourage, provide practical assistance, and help someone access qualified care.
Spiritual maturity is not measured by how successfully we conceal our pain.
And a church that speaks constantly about grace should be a place where people can seek help without being shamed for needing it.
But there is an even deeper danger than hiding our pain.
It is allowing pain to distort what we believe about God.
When suffering continues, the heart begins asking questions.
“Did God forget me?”
“Am I being punished?”
“Does He love everyone else more?”
“Would He be more pleased with me if I were stronger?”
And sometimes those questions become accusations against ourselves.
We start searching for a hidden failure that might explain everything.
We assume that because our circumstances are difficult, God must be displeased.
But Scripture does not permit us to make that automatic conclusion.
Consider the man born blind in John 9.
The disciples asked Jesus whose sin had caused the man's blindness.
Jesus rejected the assumption that his condition could be explained by the personal sin of either the man or his parents.
That passage does not explain every instance of suffering.
But it warns us against confidently assigning blame where God has not revealed it.
Not every painful circumstance is divine punishment.
Not every delay is a spiritual rejection.
Not every illness is evidence of weak faith.
And not every season of sorrow means God has withdrawn His love.
At the same time, Scripture does call us to examine our hearts honestly.
There are wounds caused by other people's sins.
There are hardships that come from living in a fallen world.
And there are consequences of our own disobedience that require confession, repentance, and change.
Grace does not require us to deny these distinctions.
It requires us to bring the truth into the light.
If you have sinned, you do not need to defend it.
If you have been harmed, you do not need to pretend it was harmless.
If you are grieving, you do not need to manufacture a smile.
And if you are exhausted, you do not need to earn permission to seek help.
The Gospel is not an invitation to build a more convincing religious disguise.
It is an invitation to come to Jesus Christ in truth.
And this is where the story moves from sorrow to something far greater than temporary emotional relief.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make wounded people feel better about their circumstances.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to bear our sins and conquer death.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
In the Hebrew text, one central expression is:
וּבַחֲבֻרָתוֹ נִרְפָּא־לָנוּ
Uvaḥavurato nirpa-lanu.
“And by his wound, healing has come to us.”
In context, Isaiah 53 presents the suffering Servant bearing the sins and iniquities of others.
The New Testament explicitly connects this passage to Jesus Christ.
First Peter 2:24 applies this healing language to Christ's sin-bearing death and to believers turning from sin and living in righteousness.
Therefore, we must not reduce this verse to a guarantee that every physical or emotional wound will disappear immediately.
The healing secured through Christ is rooted in His saving work, bringing forgiveness, reconciliation, and ultimately the complete restoration promised in God's future.
That distinction does not weaken the promise.
It protects its true glory.
Jesus did not die merely to improve our circumstances.
He died to redeem us from sin and bring us to God.
And because He rose again, suffering and death do not have the final word for those who belong to Him.
This is why the cross matters to the woman who cries after church.
And to the man who cannot sleep.
And to the believer who feels spiritually numb.
And to the person whose past is full of decisions they wish they could undo.
The cross declares that our greatest hope is not found in pretending we are whole.
It is found in the crucified and risen Savior.
At Calvary, Jesus bore the judgment our sins deserved.
Through faith in Him, sinners receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
His grace does not excuse our rebellion.
It calls us out of it.
His mercy does not tell us that our sins were harmless.
It tells us that the Savior's sacrifice is sufficient for those who repent and trust Him.
And His resurrection assures us that redemption is not merely a beautiful religious idea.
It rests upon the living Christ.
The Greek word often translated “grace” is:
χάρις
Charis.
In passages such as Ephesians 2:8, it refers to God's gracious favor, by which salvation is given rather than earned.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.”
A gift.
Not a wage.
Not a reward for never crying.
Not a prize for maintaining a flawless Christian appearance.
Not a certificate presented to the person who managed to hide every weakness.
Salvation is God's gift through faith in Jesus Christ.
And this truth changes the way we understand spiritual growth.
We do not repent to purchase God's mercy.
We repent because the Gospel summons us to turn from sin and come to the Savior who is merciful.
We do not obey to make Christ's sacrifice sufficient.
We obey because the grace that saves us also teaches us to live differently.
We do not worship to prove that we have no pain.
We worship because Jesus is worthy, even when our hearts are hurting.
And sometimes the most sincere worship is not the song everyone hears.
Sometimes it is the prayer spoken through tears when no one is watching.
“Lord, I still believe. Help me where my faith is struggling.”
That prayer resembles the cry in Mark 9:24:
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”
The father who spoke those words did not present Jesus with a polished spiritual performance.
He brought his desperate need.
And Jesus responded with power.
That does not mean every struggling person will receive the exact outcome they desire.
But it does show that imperfect, dependent faith can bring its need to Christ.
You do not have to wait until you feel spiritually impressive to approach Him.
Come because He is merciful.
Come because He is Lord.
Come because He alone has the words of eternal life.
Come because His grace is greater than your ability to maintain appearances.
And if you have wandered into sin while trying to numb your pain, do not let shame convince you to remain there.
Bring that sin into the light.
Confess it.
Turn away from it.
Seek forgiveness and appropriate accountability.
Receive the mercy Christ promises to those who come to Him.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is no need to confuse emotional suffering with moral guilt.
But where real sin exists, there is no need to hide it either.
Jesus Christ is sufficient for the repentant sinner.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin is unimportant.
But that the holy Son of God willingly gave Himself to rescue people who could never rescue themselves.
And that grace is powerful enough to begin transforming lives that seemed hopelessly tangled.
From hiding to confession.
From self-reliance to surrender.
From guilt to forgiveness.
From spiritual performance to honest dependence upon Christ.
Not because every earthly consequence disappears.
Not because every broken relationship is immediately restored.
Not because Christians are guaranteed an easy life.
But because Jesus changes our standing before God and begins making us new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
The promise is not that believers will never struggle again.
It is that union with Christ brings a genuinely new identity and life.
And the One who begins His good work in His people remains faithful.
Now imagine that woman again.
The church is empty.
The music has stopped.
The microphone has been put away.
No one is applauding.
She is sitting alone in her room.
Her tears have not magically disappeared.
Her financial situation has not necessarily changed.
Her grief has not suddenly vanished.
But something begins to shift as she reads the Scriptures.
She realizes that the Bible never commanded her to pretend.
She realizes that Jesus is not disgusted by the weakness she has been desperately trying to conceal.
She realizes that asking for help may be an act of humility rather than an admission of spiritual defeat.
And perhaps, for the first time in a long time, her prayer changes.
Instead of saying, “Lord, make me strong enough that nobody knows I'm struggling,” she whispers:
“Lord, teach me to trust You enough to stop hiding.”
The next morning, perhaps she sends a message to a trusted sister in Christ.
“I need someone to pray with me. I've been having a really difficult time.”
Maybe her friend calls.
Maybe they cry together.
Maybe they read a psalm.
Maybe they arrange to meet.
Maybe she finally receives the support she has needed for months.
Her story does not have to end with an instant miracle to reveal the faithfulness of God.
Sometimes grace meets us through Scripture.
Sometimes through repentance.
Sometimes through the kindness of another believer.
Sometimes through the courage to seek help.
Sometimes through endurance that would have been impossible without God's sustaining mercy.
And sometimes through the quiet assurance that even when our circumstances remain difficult, Christ has not ceased to be our Savior.
There is a verse that deserves to be remembered by everyone who has ever cried alone.
Psalm 56:8 says:
“Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?”
The Hebrew phrase is:
שִׂימָה דִמְעָתִי בְנֹאדֶךָ
Simah dimʿati venodekha.
“Put my tears in Your bottle.”
This is poetic language.
It is not a biblical claim that we should imagine God literally storing tears in physical bottles in heaven.
It is David's vivid appeal to the God who knows his suffering and does not treat it as insignificant.
His wanderings are known.
His tears are remembered.
His distress is not beyond God's attention.
And that is enough to make a wounded heart stop and consider something beautiful.
The tears you are ashamed of are not hidden from God.
The prayers you struggled to finish are not beyond His hearing.
The nights when you could not find the right words do not make you invisible to Him.
He knows.
And for those who belong to Christ, His love is not dependent upon their ability to maintain an appearance of strength.
Romans 8:38–39 declares that neither death nor life, nor the many powers and hardships named by Paul, can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
That is not a promise of a trouble-free life.
It is a declaration of the security of God's love in Christ.
And perhaps that is the truth you need tonight.
Not that tomorrow will automatically be easier.
Not that every unanswered question will suddenly make sense.
Not that everyone who hurt you will apologize.
But that Jesus Christ remains Lord.
His Gospel remains true.
His grace remains sufficient.
His resurrection remains the foundation of Christian hope.
And your present sorrow does not have authority to rewrite who He is.
One day, according to Revelation 21:4, God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of His redeemed people.
Death will be no more.
Neither will mourning, crying, or pain.
That promise belongs to the final restoration God will bring, not to a guarantee that believers will experience no tears before then.
We still live in a world where Christians bury loved ones.
Where faithful people face illness.
Where families struggle.
Where injustice wounds.
Where grief can last much longer than anyone expected.
But we do not grieve as people whose only horizon is the grave.
Because Jesus Christ has risen.
And the resurrection means that the future of God's people is not ultimately determined by their darkest night.
Now I want to speak to the person who has been reading this while quietly thinking, “This is me.”
You do not have to write your entire story publicly.
You do not owe strangers the details of your trauma, marriage, illness, or private battles.
But perhaps you can take one honest step today.
Tell someone trustworthy that you need support.
Open the Scriptures without feeling pressured to pretend you are cheerful.
Pray, even if all you can say is, “Lord, have mercy.”
And if you are carrying guilt over sin, stop running from the One who calls sinners to repentance.
Jesus is not inviting you to decorate your chains.
He is calling you to Himself.
Or write “I'm still fighting” if, by God's grace, you are refusing to walk away from Christ.
Your experience may encourage someone who cannot yet imagine surviving what they are facing.
And if you are not ready to share anything personal, that is okay too.
You are not required to disclose your pain to prove your faith.
But please do not believe the lie that you must suffer completely alone.
And to the believers who are doing well right now, this message is for you too.
Look around your church.
Notice the person who always serves.
The woman who always smiles.
The man who always says he is fine.
The volunteer who never misses a Sunday.
The friend who has suddenly become quiet.
Do not assume that because someone is spiritually active, they are emotionally supported.
Sometimes the person who encourages everyone else is waiting for someone to ask a sincere question and remain long enough to hear the answer.
Reach out.
Listen without rushing to fix everything.
Pray without using Scripture to silence grief.
Offer practical help where you can.
And remember that kindness is not a substitute for truth, nor is truth an excuse for cruelty.
Jesus Christ is full of grace and truth.
His people should seek to reflect both.
If someone came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them if doing so would encourage rather than embarrass them.
You might instead send this privately with a simple message:
“I thought of you while reading this. You don't have to explain anything, but I'm here if you need someone.”
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
Not because the reach of an article determines its spiritual value.
But because the people who need biblical encouragement are not always the ones who openly ask for it.
Some are quietly scrolling after a difficult day.
Some have stopped attending church because they feel ashamed.
Some have never understood that Christianity is centered on the grace of Jesus Christ rather than the perfection of religious people.
Some may be searching for a reason to open a Bible again.
Return to it on a night when you need to remember that lament is biblical, that Christ understands suffering, and that His grace does not depend upon your emotional performance.
Our desire is not merely to publish words that stir emotions for a moment.
It is to keep pointing people toward the living Word of God, the finished work of Jesus Christ, and the daily obedience of discipleship.
Because a powerful article cannot save a soul.
An emotional response cannot replace repentance and faith.
Jesus Christ alone saves.
And everything we build must remain beneath that truth.
That is also why we want to invite those who are able and willing to help sustain and expand this ministry.
Some believers may choose to make it part of their planned giving, alongside the tithes and offerings they give through their local church.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be purposeful, voluntary, and cheerful, not compelled.
God is not glorified by manipulating people into financial decisions.
He is glorified when His people act in faith, truth, love, and willing generosity.
And if your household is facing financial hardship, please care for your essential responsibilities rather than feeling pressured to give beyond your means.
But if you have been blessed with the ability to support Gospel-centered ministry and believe in what we are doing, your partnership can help us continue and expand this work.
It can help us reach readers who are searching for answers, believers who need encouragement, and people who have never heard the Gospel explained clearly.
Those products are not substitutes for Scripture, the local church, or a living relationship with Christ.
The invitation is simple.
If this ministry is bearing good fruit in your life, consider helping us plant more seeds.
Not for applause.
Not for religious status.
Not because God needs our money.
But because the Gospel is worth proclaiming, Scripture is worth teaching, and people are worth serving in the name of Jesus Christ.
Before you leave, return with me one last time to that woman sitting alone in her Sunday dress.
Hours earlier, people had heard her sing.
They heard confidence in her voice.
They saw her raised hands.
They assumed they understood her story.
But later, behind a closed bedroom door, she was weeping.
And if we were writing a shallow story, this would be the moment when every problem disappeared.
Her phone would ring with miraculous news.
Every bill would be paid.
Every relationship would be healed.
Every prayer would receive the answer she wanted.
She would wake up smiling, and the story would end.
But real discipleship does not depend upon fictional guarantees.
Sometimes Monday arrives, and the hardship is still there.
Sometimes the diagnosis remains.
Sometimes the grief is still heavy.
Sometimes the marriage still needs counseling.
Sometimes the heart still aches.
And sometimes the most meaningful change is that a wounded believer finally stops confusing her pain with God's absence.
She opens her Bible again.
She reaches out for help.
She remembers the cross.
She remembers the empty tomb.
And she whispers:
“Jesus, I don't understand everything I'm going through. But I know You are my Savior. Teach me to follow You through this.”
That is not a promise that every tear will immediately stop.
It is a confession of faith in the One who has conquered sin and death.
And perhaps, next Sunday, she will sing again.
Maybe her voice will still tremble.
Maybe she will need to step away from the platform for a season and receive care.
Maybe she will discover that serving Jesus does not always mean holding a microphone.
Sometimes it means receiving the love and support of His people.
Sometimes it means sitting quietly in the congregation and allowing the words of Scripture to minister to her own soul.
Sometimes it means confessing sin and accepting accountability.
Sometimes it means learning to rest without believing she has failed God.
But whether she sings or sits, whether she smiles or weeps, the center of her hope remains the same.
Jesus Christ crucified.
Jesus Christ risen.
Jesus Christ sufficient.
Jesus Christ worthy.
And the grace of God that does not merely cover a painful past, but calls redeemed sinners into a transformed life.
So if you have been carrying a smile that hides a thousand tears, hear this invitation.
You do not have to keep pretending.
Bring your grief to the Lord.
Bring your sin to the cross.
Bring your questions to Scripture.
Bring your burdens into the care of trustworthy believers.
And place your ultimate hope not in the disappearance of every earthly struggle, but in the Savior who died and rose again.
Because the Christian story does not end at the grave.
And your story, if you belong to Christ, is held by the One who has promised a resurrection future beyond the reach of death.
Perhaps tonight you will still cry.
But your tears do not have to become your verdict on God's love.
The cross has already shown the costliness of that love.
The resurrection has already revealed the victory of your Savior.
And the Gospel is still calling you home.
The congregation heard the song she sang, but Jesus knew the tears she could not sing through.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DAVID CAME HOME TO JERUSALEM… BUT TEN WOMEN WERE NEVER ALLOWED TO COME HOME TO THEIR LIVES AGAIN
paragraphs: DAVID CAME HOME TO JERUSALEM… BUT TEN WOMEN WERE NEVER ALLOWED TO COME HOME TO THEIR LIVES AGAIN

The King Reclaimed His Throne. His Son Was Dead. But Behind the Palace Doors, Ten Women Were Left to Carry the Shame of a Sin They Did Not Choose. And What Happened to Them Reveals a Heartbreaking Truth About Human Failure—and Why We Desperately Need Jesus Christ.
There are Bible verses that make you shout.
There are Bible verses that make you weep.
And then there are Bible verses that make you close your Bible for a moment because what you just read is so disturbing that you almost wish you hadn't seen it.
This is one of them.
A king returned to his palace.
A rebellion had been crushed.
The throne was restored.
The kingdom could finally breathe again.
But somewhere inside that royal residence, ten women were about to discover that the end of a national tragedy did not mean the end of their personal suffering.
They had already endured something terrible.
Something humiliating.
Something they never should have been forced to experience.
And now, instead of being restored to ordinary life, they would spend the remainder of their days in seclusion.
Not because Scripture tells us they had committed a crime.
Not because God had pronounced them guilty.
But because powerful men had made decisions, and these women were left living with the consequences.
Listen carefully.
Sometimes the person who suffers the longest is not the person who committed the sin.
And if that sentence touches something buried inside you, stay with me.
Because this story is not merely about David, Absalom, or ten forgotten women.
It is about the devastating reach of sin, the limitations of even Israel's greatest kings, and the Savior who came into a broken world to do what no earthly throne could accomplish.
It is about what happens when the battle ends, but the wounded are still bleeding.
And it is about the difference between a king who returns to his palace and the King who comes looking for the brokenhearted.
The Bible says:

"So David came to his house at Jerusalem; and the king took the ten women his concubines, whom he had left to keep the house, and put them in ward, and fed them, but went not in unto them. So they were shut up unto the day of their death, living in widowhood."
— 2 Samuel 20:3, KJV
Read that last sentence again.
"So they were shut up unto the day of their death, living in widowhood."
Until the day of their death.
Not for a week.
Not until the political crisis passed.
Not until Jerusalem recovered.
For the rest of their lives.
And the most haunting detail?
Scripture never tells us their names.
Ten women.
Ten human lives.
Ten stories of suffering.
And not one name preserved in this account.
Yet God allowed their suffering to remain recorded in Scripture, where generations of readers would encounter it.
Perhaps the most important question is not simply what happened to them.
Perhaps it is what this passage reveals about the terrible consequences of sin—and whether we have learned to see the people those consequences leave behind.
To understand the tragedy, we must return to the rebellion that nearly destroyed David's kingdom.
Absalom was David's son.
Handsome. Charismatic. Ambitious.
He knew how to win the hearts of people.
He stood near the city gate, listened to grievances, criticized the administration of justice, and presented himself as the leader Israel needed.
Second Samuel 15:6 describes the result:
"So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel."
What a terrifying description.
He did not begin by seizing the throne with a sword.
He began by capturing public affection.
And eventually, he moved against his own father.
David fled Jerusalem.
The king who had defeated Goliath was now running from his own son.
The warrior who had survived Saul's pursuit was escaping a rebellion from inside his family.
The man who once sang of God's deliverance was walking toward the wilderness while his kingdom fractured behind him.
And before leaving, David made a decision that would have devastating consequences for ten women.
Second Samuel 15:16 tells us that David left ten concubines behind to keep the palace.

In the ancient royal household, a concubine was a woman in a recognized but lower-status relationship with the king than a principal wife. Such women often had far less power to determine their own circumstances.
They were left in Jerusalem.
The king departed.
The rebellion advanced.
And Absalom entered the city.
Then came one of the most disturbing scenes in David's family history.
Ahithophel, Absalom's adviser, gave him counsel designed to make reconciliation with David politically impossible.
He urged Absalom to have sexual relations with the concubines his father had left behind.
The purpose was public humiliation.
A declaration of dominance.
A calculated announcement that the son had taken what belonged to his father's royal household.
Second Samuel 16:21 records the counsel.
Then verse 22 tells us:
"So they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel."
— 2 Samuel 16:22, KJV
Imagine the horror of that moment.
A rooftop.
A tent.
A rebellious prince.
A nation watching a public assertion of power.
And ten women caught in the middle of a struggle they did not create.

The passage does not describe their individual responses or establish that they consented. Given the circumstances of royal power and political coercion, we must not casually assume that they had meaningful freedom to refuse.
Nor should we turn their suffering into spectacle.
The text emphasizes Absalom's deliberate public act of humiliation against his father. The women were placed at the center of that act.
They were not political advisers plotting a rebellion.
They were not generals commanding an army.
They were not the ones who conceived the plan.
Yet their bodies became instruments in a war between powerful men.
And here is where the story becomes even more painful.
The rooftop was not an accidental location.
Years earlier, David had walked upon the roof of his palace and seen Bathsheba bathing.
That encounter led to David taking Bathsheba, committing adultery, and arranging the death of her husband, Uriah.
The prophet Nathan confronted David and announced that the consequences of his sin would reach into his own household.
In 2 Samuel 12:11, Nathan declared:

"Thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will raise up evil against thee out of thine own house, and I will take thy wives before thine eyes, and give them unto thy neighbour, and he shall lie with thy wives in the sight of this sun."
The events involving Absalom deliberately echo that warning.
David's secret wrongdoing was followed by public humiliation within his own household.
But we must understand something crucial.
The fulfillment of a prophetic judgment does not mean that God morally approved of Absalom's wicked actions.
Scripture repeatedly distinguishes God's sovereign purposes from the sinful intentions of human beings.
Absalom was responsible for his conduct.
Ahithophel was responsible for his counsel.
And David was responsible for his earlier sins.
The ten women must not be blamed merely because they suffered within the consequences of those sins.
This distinction matters.
Because wounded people have endured enough without being told that someone else's evil somehow proves their own guilt.
A child who grows up in the wreckage of a parent's betrayal is not automatically guilty of the parent's sin.
A spouse devastated by another person's unfaithfulness does not become morally responsible for the betrayal.
A person who has been abused does not become impure or spiritually worthless because someone violated their dignity.
And someone living with consequences they never chose should never be told that their suffering makes them less worthy of compassion.
There is a Hebrew word worth examining here.

In 2 Samuel 20:3, the Hebrew text describes David placing the women in a guarded or restricted setting using the expression בֵּית־מִשְׁמֶר (bêt-mišmer), meaning a place of custody, confinement, or guarded keeping.
The verse also says:
וַיְכַלְכְּלֵם (vaykhalkelēm)
Meaning, "and he provided for them" or "and he sustained them."
And then comes the devastating conclusion:
צְרֻרוֹת עַד־יוֹם מֻתָן (tserurot ʿad-yom mutan)
A phrase describing their being shut away or confined until the day of their death.
The passage ends by describing them as living in widowhood.
The Hebrew word אַלְמְנוּת (ʾalmenût) refers to widowhood.
They were not literally widows in the ordinary sense, because David was still alive.
Rather, they lived in a widow-like condition, deprived of an ongoing marital relationship with the king.
David continued to provide for them materially.
But he did not resume sexual relations with them.
The text does not explicitly explain every motive behind his decision.

Some interpreters understand his action in relation to the royal household's sexual boundaries and the political disgrace surrounding Absalom's actions. Others emphasize the severe social restrictions imposed on the women.
We should not pretend to know more than Scripture reveals.
What we do know is heartbreaking enough.
They were provided for.
But they remained secluded.
They survived.
But their former lives were not restored.
And the Bible records no later reversal of their circumstances.
Think about that.
It is possible to have food and still be lonely.
It is possible to have shelter and still feel imprisoned.
It is possible to be physically protected and still carry wounds that nobody has addressed.
It is possible for the people around you to say, "At least you're alive," while you are silently grieving the life you once knew.
Somebody reading this understands.
You have survived something that changed you.
People see you working.
Smiling.
Cooking.
Going to church.
Taking care of your family.
Posting photographs.
Answering messages.
And they assume you have recovered.
But they do not see what happens when the house becomes quiet.
They do not know which memories return.
They do not know how often you have wondered whether you will ever feel like yourself again.
And perhaps the hardest part is that the people responsible for the damage seem to have moved forward while you are still carrying the aftermath.
If that describes you, hear this carefully.
What happened to you is not the whole truth about who you are.
The cruelty of another person does not have the authority to define your worth before God.
And the silence surrounding your pain does not mean your suffering is invisible to Him.
But there is another difficult truth in this story.
David was not an unbelieving pagan king.
He was the Lord's anointed.
A man who wrote psalms.
A man who knew repentance.
A man who experienced mercy.
A man whose life contained extraordinary faith and terrible moral failure.
And that should sober every Christian.
Spiritual history does not make someone incapable of causing harm.
Public ministry does not guarantee private righteousness.
Knowing the language of worship does not excuse injustice.
Being used by God does not place a person beyond accountability.
David's life teaches us that genuine faith and serious failure can exist in the same human story.
That is not an excuse for sin.
It is a warning against spiritual pride.
And when we examine David's household, the warning becomes almost unbearable.
Amnon sexually violated his half-sister Tamar.
David became angry, but the biblical narrative does not describe him securing justice for her.
Absalom eventually murdered Amnon.
Then Absalom rebelled against David.
And during that rebellion, the ten concubines were subjected to another act of sexual humiliation within the royal household.
Different events.
Different individuals.
Different responsibilities.
But an unmistakable pattern of family devastation.
Sin does not remain neatly confined to the moment in which it is committed.
It can fracture trust.
Distort relationships.
Corrupt authority.
And leave generations struggling with consequences they never anticipated.
This is why repentance cannot be reduced to feeling bad after being exposed.
The Hebrew word commonly associated with turning or returning is שׁוּב (shuv).
It carries the basic sense of turning back or returning, and in prophetic calls to repentance it describes turning toward the Lord.
True repentance is not merely saying, "I'm sorry."
It means turning away from sin and toward God.
Where possible, it also produces the fruit of responsibility, truthfulness, and making wrongs right.
David himself understood the seriousness of confession.
In Psalm 51:4, he cried:
"Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight."
That statement emphasizes the ultimate offense of sin against God; it does not erase the real human victims of David's actions.
Psalm 51 also says:
"A broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise."
— Psalm 51:17, KJV
And yet the story of the ten women reminds us that even when a sinner receives forgiveness, the earthly consequences of sin may remain painfully real.
Forgiveness does not mean that the damage never happened.
Grace does not make accountability unnecessary.
And reconciliation should never be demanded from someone whose safety is still at risk.
There is a difference between extending forgiveness and returning to an unsafe situation.
There is a difference between trusting God and pretending that abuse did not occur.
There is a difference between Christian compassion and protecting an offender from the consequences of wrongdoing.
The church must never confuse those things.
Because the God of Scripture is not indifferent to the vulnerable.
Psalm 34:18 declares:
"The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit."
And Psalm 147:3 says:
"He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds."
Notice the language.
He binds up wounds.
That is not the language of a God who mocks suffering.
It is the language of compassionate care.
But the story does not end with the brokenness of David's household.
Because centuries later, another Son of David would come.
Not a son who seized the throne through rebellion.
Not a king who used vulnerable people to demonstrate political power.
Not a ruler who sought to protect his glory at the expense of the wounded.
Jesus Christ.
The promised Messiah.
The true and greater Son of David.
The One whose kingdom would not be established through exploitation, but through righteousness, sacrificial love, and the triumph of His resurrection.
When Jesus began His public ministry, He read from the prophet Isaiah.
Luke 4:18 records His words:

"The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised."

This wording follows the KJV. The phrase "to heal the brokenhearted" reflects the traditional textual form behind that translation, while many modern critical Greek editions of Luke omit that particular clause. The theme of God's care for the brokenhearted is nevertheless explicit in Isaiah 61 and elsewhere in Scripture.
The Greek word ἄφεσις (aphesis), used in Luke 4:18, carries the meaning of release, liberation, or forgiveness, depending on context.
And the word τεθραυσμένους (tethrausmenous) describes those who have been crushed or broken.
Jesus announced good news to people who desperately needed it.
He came to bring the saving reign of God into a world filled with sin, oppression, guilt, grief, and death.
His mission was not merely to improve human circumstances.
He came to save sinners and ultimately make all things new.
And this is where the contrast becomes breathtaking.
David returned to Jerusalem after fleeing a rebellion.
Jesus entered Jerusalem knowing He would be rejected.
David reclaimed his royal residence.
Jesus was led outside the city to be crucified.
David's household bore the consequences of sin.
Jesus, though sinless, bore the sins of His people.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
"But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed."
The cross was not another example of an innocent person being forgotten by God.
It was the place where the sinless Son willingly gave Himself to accomplish redemption.
Jesus was not overcome by evil as a helpless victim of circumstances.
He laid down His life.
John 10:18 records His declaration:
"No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself."
And when He rose from the dead, He demonstrated that sin and death would not have the final word.
This is the Gospel.
Not that suffering is imaginary.
Not that consequences disappear.
Not that every earthly injustice is corrected before we die.
But that Jesus Christ has entered our broken world, conquered death, and secured forgiveness and eternal life for those who belong to Him.
The King who died for sinners is alive.
And His resurrection guarantees that God's final restoration will be greater than anything this fallen world can accomplish.
Revelation 21:4 gives this promise:
"And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away."
Can you imagine that?
No more tears.
No more death.
No more sorrow.
No more pain.
No more victims abandoned to the cruelty of a fallen world.
No more graves.
No more nights spent wondering whether God has forgotten.
The Bible does not tell us the eternal destiny of David's ten concubines.
It does not tell us whether they personally experienced healing, freedom, or restored relationships during their remaining earthly years.
We must not invent a happy ending that Scripture does not provide.
But their unfinished story can awaken our longing for the perfect justice and restoration that only God can bring.
And perhaps that is one of the reasons this verse feels so unbearable.
We want someone to open the doors.
We want someone to say, "You have suffered enough."
We want their names to be remembered.
We want the wrongs to be acknowledged.
We want the women to have the final word instead of the men who controlled their circumstances.
But the narrative moves forward.
And their story disappears from view.
That silence should not make us indifferent.
It should make us more attentive to people who are suffering quietly around us.
Because there may be someone sitting beside you in church who has survived a violation they have never spoken about.
Someone whose marriage collapsed because of another person's choices.
Someone carrying childhood wounds into adulthood.
Someone who smiles while silently grieving.
Someone who has been told to forgive but has never been given the space to speak honestly about what happened.
Someone who believes Jesus can forgive the person who hurt them but wonders whether Jesus has any compassion left for them.
If that is you, please hear this.
Jesus does not require you to deny your pain before you come to Him.
You do not have to manufacture a testimony of complete healing when you are still struggling.
You do not have to call evil good.
You do not have to pretend that everything is fine.
And you do not have to earn the compassion of Christ by becoming emotionally strong enough to impress Him.
Come to Him truthfully.
Come with the tears.
Come with the questions.
Come with the confusion.
Come with the anger that needs His wisdom.
Come with the guilt that needs His forgiveness.
Come with the wounds that need His care.
He is not frightened by the truth about your life.
Matthew 11:28 records His invitation:
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."
But we must also be careful not to turn this story into a message only for those who have been wounded.
There is a warning here for those who have wounded others.
Perhaps you have used your authority selfishly.
Perhaps you have betrayed someone's trust.
Perhaps you have minimized another person's pain because acknowledging it would require you to confront your own sin.
Perhaps you have hidden behind religious language while refusing accountability.
Perhaps you have convinced yourself that because God forgives, the people you hurt should simply move on.
Do not confuse God's mercy with permission to remain unchanged.
Romans 2:4 teaches that God's goodness leads us toward repentance.
And 1 John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Confession means bringing sin into the light.
Repentance means turning away from it.
And genuine faith produces a changed direction of life.
If you have harmed someone, do not use the language of grace to demand their silence.
Do not use Scripture to pressure them into restoring access to their life.
Seek forgiveness from God.
Accept appropriate accountability.
Make restitution where possible.
Respect boundaries.
And let the fruit of repentance speak more loudly than religious promises.
Jesus did not shed His blood so that we could become comfortable with the sins that nailed Him to the cross.
He came to save us from sin, not to teach us how to disguise it.
And if you are the person who has been hurt, understand this distinction.
The call for sinners to repent does not place the responsibility for their repentance upon you.
You cannot repent for another person.
You cannot force someone to become honest.
You cannot heal a heart that refuses correction.
But you can bring your own heart before the Lord.
You can seek wise and trustworthy support.
You can pursue safety.
You can receive help without shame.
And you can begin to discover that the worst thing someone did to you does not have to become the final chapter of your identity.
There is something else I cannot ignore.
David's ten concubines were remembered in the biblical account primarily through what happened to them.
We know their number.
We know their status.
We know their seclusion.
But we do not know their names.
And perhaps some of you know exactly what it feels like to have your entire life reduced to one painful event.
The divorced woman.
The abused child.
The betrayed husband.
The abandoned mother.
The recovering addict.
The person who failed publicly.
The one who went through depression.
The one whose family fell apart.
The one everybody whispers about.
But you are more than the worst chapter of your story.
You are not merely the scandal.
You are not merely the wound.
You are not merely the failure.
And if you belong to Jesus Christ, your deepest identity is found in Him.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
This does not promise instant freedom from every traumatic memory or earthly consequence.
It proclaims the transforming reality of belonging to Christ.
His grace gives sinners a new standing before God and begins a life of renewal that will ultimately be completed in glory.
That is why we keep returning to this message.
Not because scandal is harmless.
Not because grace erases history.
Not because every story receives a beautiful earthly resolution.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem sinners, sustain the brokenhearted, and bring His people into a future that sin cannot destroy.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the terrible chapters were never written.
But by refusing to let sin and death write the final sentence for those He redeems.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Who came to mind while you were reading this?
Was it your mother?
Your daughter?
Your sister?
Your husband?
A friend who has stopped attending church?
Someone whose faith has been shaken by betrayal?
Or was it you?
Maybe you have spent years keeping your pain behind a closed door.
Maybe people have called you strong because they never knew how close you were to collapsing.
Maybe you have been serving everyone else while quietly wondering when someone will notice that you are hurting too.
Maybe you have been asking God why the people who caused the damage seem to have escaped while you are still living with the consequences.
I cannot answer every question about why God permits particular suffering.
And I will not insult your pain by pretending that a few comforting sentences can explain everything.
But I can tell you what the Gospel reveals.
God did not remain distant from a suffering world.
In Jesus Christ, the eternal Son entered human history.
He knew rejection.
He knew betrayal.
He knew injustice.
He knew suffering.
He died for sinners.
He rose in victory.
And He will return to judge the world in righteousness.
That means evil does not have ultimate authority.
Human power does not have ultimate authority.
The grave does not have ultimate authority.
Jesus Christ does.
And the hands that were pierced for our redemption belong to the risen King.
So if you are exhausted, do not mistake exhaustion for abandonment.
If you are grieving, do not mistake tears for unbelief.
If you are struggling to trust again, do not confuse your need for wisdom and safety with a lack of faith.
And if you have wandered from Christ because of your own sin, do not imagine that repentance is beneath you or that grace is beyond His power.
Turn to Him.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you have repaired yourself.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Today.
The Gospel does not say, "Become perfect and then come."
It calls sinners to repent and believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.
And it assures those who come to Him that His saving grace is sufficient.
There is room at the feet of Jesus for the ashamed sinner who needs forgiveness.
There is compassion in the heart of Jesus for the wounded person who needs comfort.
And there is hope in the resurrection of Jesus for everyone who wonders whether darkness will last forever.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to publish religious words.
Not merely to collect reactions.
Not merely to build a page.
But to keep pointing people toward the Scriptures, toward repentance, toward the cross, toward the empty tomb, and toward a deeper relationship with Jesus Christ.
Because someone scrolling through Facebook tonight may be one message away from opening a Bible again.
Someone who has stopped praying may be reminded that God hears the brokenhearted.
Someone carrying secret guilt may finally understand the need to repent.
Someone who has been wounded by religious hypocrisy may begin to distinguish the failures of people from the righteousness of Jesus Christ.
And someone who has never understood the Gospel may hear the good news of salvation for the first time.
If this article has touched something deep within you, please do not feel pressured to reveal details you are not ready to share.
You can simply write "Christ is still healing me."
If you are convicted about sin you have been hiding, you can write "Jesus, have mercy on me."
And if you have a testimony of how the Lord carried you through suffering, consider sharing it. Your words may encourage someone who feels completely alone.
You do not have to tell your entire story publicly for your faith to be real.
Sometimes a simple, sincere prayer is enough to begin an honest conversation.
And please think about someone who needs this message.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to confront publicly.
But someone who needs to know that the compassion of Christ has not run out.
Send this article privately if that would be more appropriate.
One thoughtful share may bring Scripture into the life of someone who would never intentionally search for a Christian article.
We want this to be a place where people encounter biblical truth, not empty religious performance.
A place where repentance is preached without forgetting mercy.
Where grace is celebrated without excusing sin.
Where the wounded are treated with compassion.
And where Jesus Christ—not personalities, popularity, or financial success—remains at the center.
Not because every wound will disappear after reading it.
But because there may come another difficult night when you need to remember that the Lord sees what others overlook.
These resources are intended to help believers study the Word of God, grow in prayer, understand the Gospel, strengthen their faith, and continue following Jesus beyond a single emotional moment.
They are free because biblical encouragement and discipleship resources should remain accessible to people who may not have the means to purchase them.
But keeping resources available and expanding this work also requires practical support.
And that is where I want to speak to you sincerely.
Not because you owe us anything.
Jesus Christ has already paid the price for our redemption. No monthly payment can add anything to His finished work.
But believers can glorify God through voluntary generosity when their giving is motivated by love, truth, and a sincere desire to serve others.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
It can help sustain the work and support its expansion.
It is an additional opportunity to give freely toward a ministry whose work you believe is worthwhile.
You are not less faithful.
You are not less valuable.
You are not less welcome.
Your prayers, thoughtful comments, encouragement, and willingness to share biblical truth also matter.
These items can serve as personal reminders of faith, meaningful gifts, and tools for encouraging others.
It is the opportunity to help keep Christ-centered teaching and free discipleship resources reaching people who need them.
Because this mission is bigger than a page.
It is about the Gospel being heard.
The truth being understood.
Sinners being called to repentance.
Believers being strengthened.
The brokenhearted being reminded of God's compassion.
And Jesus Christ being glorified.
Before you leave, return with me one last time to that palace in Jerusalem.
The rebellion was over.
David was home.
The throne had been restored.
The king had returned.
But ten women remained behind closed doors.
The Bible gives us no scene in which those doors are opened again for them.
No record of a celebration.
No account of restored freedom.
No final testimony in their own voices.
Just the haunting words:
"Shut up unto the day of their death, living in widowhood."
And perhaps this is where the story should change the way we look at people.
Because somewhere around us, there are still people living behind invisible doors.
Doors of grief.
Doors of shame.
Doors of betrayal.
Doors of fear.
Doors of consequences they did not choose.
Some of them are sitting in our churches.
Some are living inside our homes.
Some are among our closest friends.
And some are reading these very words.
May we never become so fascinated by the victories of powerful people that we forget the suffering of those left behind.
May we never preach forgiveness in a way that silences victims.
May we never celebrate grace while refusing to confront evil.
May we never confuse outward survival with inward restoration.
And may we never forget that the greatest hope of the wounded is not found in the perfection of earthly kings, religious leaders, or human institutions.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
The righteous King.
The crucified Savior.
The risen Lord.
The One who forgives repentant sinners.
The One who cares for the brokenhearted.
The One who will judge with perfect righteousness.
The One who will make all things new.
So bring Him your guilt.
Bring Him your grief.
Bring Him your unfinished story.
Above all, do not leave this story merely thinking about ten women who suffered in ancient Jerusalem.
Leave thinking about the Savior who entered human history to redeem a people for Himself.
Because the final hope of the Christian faith is not that every earthly palace will eventually become safe.
It is that Jesus Christ will return, evil will be judged, death will be defeated forever, and those who belong to Him will dwell in His presence.

And until that day, may we proclaim His truth, practice His compassion, protect the vulnerable, pursue holiness, and carry the hope of His Gospel into places where people have nearly forgotten what hope feels like.
The world may remember the throne that was restored, but heaven's King teaches us to care about the wounded people the victory left behind.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE MOST DANGEROUS ADVICE YOU MAY HAVE EVER BELIEVED: “JUST FOLLOW YOUR HEART”
paragraphs: THE MOST DANGEROUS ADVICE YOU MAY HAVE EVER BELIEVED: “JUST FOLLOW YOUR HEART”

What if the voice you’ve trusted most is the very voice leading you away from God? The Bible reveals a truth that could break your heart, save your soul, and completely change the direction of your life.
There is a sentence that has destroyed marriages without ever sounding cruel.

It has led people into relationships they knew were wrong, convinced believers to abandon convictions they once held sacred, and persuaded wounded souls to mistake temporary happiness for lasting peace.
And the frightening part?
It sounds beautiful.
It sounds empowering.
Sometimes, it even sounds spiritual.
“Just follow your heart.”
You have heard it in movies. You have seen it written beneath beautiful photographs. You have probably heard it from someone who genuinely loved you and wanted you to be happy.
Perhaps you have even said it to yourself.
“I deserve to be happy.”
“God knows my heart.”
“It feels so right. How could it possibly be wrong?”
But what happens when the thing your heart desperately wants is the very thing God is asking you to surrender?
What happens when your emotions are screaming yes, but Scripture is quietly saying no?
What happens when following your heart means walking away from the One who gave you life?
There is a reason Jesus never made personal feelings the final authority for His disciples.
And there is a reason the Bible speaks about the human heart with both extraordinary tenderness and terrifying honesty.
Because the heart can love deeply.
The heart can grieve sincerely.
The heart can desire beautiful things.
But the heart can also deceive the very person carrying it.

And somewhere between the wounds you never healed, the desires you never questioned, and the decisions you justified because they felt right, you may have begun trusting your heart more than the voice of God.
Please stay with me.
Because this is not an article about learning to hate your emotions.
It is about discovering why Jesus came to give you something far greater than permission to follow them.
He came to give you a new heart.
And understanding that difference could change everything.
Imagine a woman sitting alone in her car outside her home.
The engine is off.
Her phone is glowing in her hand.
A message has just arrived from someone who makes her feel noticed, valued, and understood in ways she has not felt for years.
She is married.
She knows the conversation has crossed boundaries.
She knows the secrecy is growing.
She knows there are things she would never want her husband to discover.
But she is lonely.
And loneliness has a way of making dangerous attention feel like answered prayer.
She stares at the message.
Her heart races.
Then comes the thought.
“Maybe God just wants me to be happy.”
And suddenly, what began as temptation starts looking like destiny.
Now imagine a young man exhausted from trying to do the right thing.
He has watched dishonest people prosper while his integrity seems to cost him opportunities.
One day, someone offers him a shortcut.
Just one compromise.
Just one lie.
Just one decision nobody needs to know about.
His conscience hesitates.
But his heart whispers, “You have suffered enough. You deserve this.”
And he begins negotiating with something God has already made clear.
Different stories.
Different wounds.
Different temptations.
The same dangerous possibility.
A sincere feeling can become a convincing excuse.
Not because every feeling is sinful.
Not because every desire is corrupt.
But because sincerity is not the same as truth.
And the fact that something feels deeply personal does not make it divinely approved.
Thousands of years before motivational speakers began telling the world to trust every inward impulse, the prophet Jeremiah recorded a warning that still confronts the human soul.
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” — Jeremiah 17:9, KJV
That verse is uncomfortable.
Especially in a generation that often treats personal authenticity as the highest form of morality.
But let us look more closely at what Scripture actually says.
In the Hebrew text, the verse begins:
עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא מִי יֵדָעֶנּוּ
ʿĀqōḇ hallēḇ mikkōl wəʾānuš hûʾ mî yēḏāʿennû
A careful rendering is:
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?”
The Hebrew word ʿāqōḇ carries the sense of something deceptive, crooked, or treacherous.
The word lēḇ, translated “heart,” refers to more than emotion. In biblical Hebrew, the heart is the inner center of human thought, desire, intention, and decision-making.
And ʾānuš can describe something desperately sick or incurable.

The King James Version uses “desperately wicked,” while several modern translations use “desperately sick.” The latter reflects the sickness imagery in the Hebrew more directly, without denying the moral seriousness of the passage.
But notice something essential.
Jeremiah was not writing a random insult against human emotions.
The surrounding chapter contrasts those who trust in human strength with those whose confidence rests in the Lord.
Jeremiah 17:5 warns against making flesh one's strength while turning the heart away from God.
Jeremiah 17:7 declares:
“Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is.”
Then comes the warning about the deceitful heart.
The issue is not whether human beings are capable of genuine love, compassion, or joy.
The issue is whether the fallen human heart can safely become its own ultimate authority.
Scripture's answer is no.
And Jeremiah does not leave us guessing about who truly understands the heart.
The very next verse says:
