One Savior whose mercy is greater than the reputation people thought would define them forever.
And maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe you know what it feels like to be remembered for your worst moment.
Maybe someone still introduces you through a mistake you made years ago.
Maybe your family knows the scandal but has never seen the private repentance.
Maybe you have been carrying shame so long that you cannot imagine a life without it.
Listen carefully.
Jesus does not need to pretend your sin was harmless in order to forgive it.
He does not need to rewrite history by calling evil good.
He rewrites the future of those who come to Him by grace.
The cross tells the truth about sin's seriousness.
The resurrection announces the victory of Christ.
And the Gospel invites sinners to stop hiding and come into the light.
You may not be able to change yesterday.
But by God's grace, yesterday does not have to remain the master of your tomorrow.
That does not mean every consequence disappears.
It does not mean broken trust is restored instantly.
It does not mean every relationship will return to what it once was.
But it does mean forgiveness is real.
Redemption is real.
And the transforming power of Jesus Christ is not a religious slogan.
It is the hope at the heart of the Christian faith.
Now return with me, just for a moment, to those four men outside Samaria.
They found food while an entire city was starving.
They could have hidden everything and thought only of themselves.
But eventually they said:
"This is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace."
What a searching picture of responsibility.
They had received good news.
Others needed to hear it.
And silence was no longer something they could comfortably justify.
Christian, what have you done with the good news entrusted to you?
Not the news that your life is perfect.
Not the claim that every prayer will be answered exactly as you desire.
Not a promise that following Jesus guarantees wealth, health, or an easy road.
The real good news.
That Christ died for sinners.
That He rose from the dead.
That forgiveness is offered through Him.
That repentance and faith are not reserved for people with spotless histories.
That the weary can come to Him.
That the ashamed do not need to hide forever.
That the lost can be found.
That the dead in sin can be made alive in Christ.
Someone in your family needs to hear that.
Someone who used to attend church but has quietly disappeared.
Someone who is smiling publicly and unraveling privately.
Someone who has convinced themselves that God would never receive them again.
Someone who thinks Christianity is only for people who have never made a mess of their lives.
Someone who has never opened a Bible but desperately wants to know whether forgiveness is possible.
Maybe sharing this article will not change their life immediately.
Maybe they will read only a paragraph.
But maybe one sentence will make them stop.
Maybe they will remember a Scripture they heard as a child.
Maybe they will open the Bible for themselves.
Maybe they will pray honestly for the first time in years.
We cannot manufacture another person's conversion.
Only God can bring spiritual life.
But we can faithfully bear witness.
Not as a performance of spirituality, and not to prove anything to anyone, but because the Gospel is too precious to be treated as a private possession.
Send it quietly to a friend who needs hope.
Let the message travel farther than your own circle.
And if you have made it this far, I want to ask you something more personal.
Where are you in this story?
Are you like the officer, so convinced that nothing can change that you have stopped taking God's word seriously?
Are you like the four men, exhausted and desperate, wondering whether there is any reason to take another step?
Are you like the starving city, waiting for relief and struggling to imagine how it could come?
Or are you like the criminal beside Jesus, finally recognizing that you cannot save yourself and asking the Savior for mercy?
You do not have to pretend in order to answer.
You do not have to manufacture a dramatic testimony.
You do not have to reveal details that should remain private.
Your testimony may encourage someone who thinks their story is already over.
Let this be more than another article people read and forget.
Let it become a conversation where believers encourage one another, pray for one another, and point one another back to the truth of Scripture.
Not because saving a post earns favor with God.
Save it as a reminder to open 2 Kings 6–7 and read the complete account for yourself.
Because the deepest nourishment will never come merely from reading what someone says about the Bible.
It comes from returning to the Word itself.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to produce emotional stories.
Not simply to gain views, reactions, or followers.
But to help people encounter biblical truth, examine their lives honestly, grow in their understanding of Scripture, and follow Jesus Christ with greater faithfulness.
And if this ministry has helped you, I want to invite you into something deeper than an occasional encounter with an article on your feed.
Invite your family, your Christian friends, those who have drifted from church, and even those who are still exploring what it means to believe in Jesus.
These resources are intended to help believers move beyond a moment of inspiration into a life of learning, prayer, repentance, obedience, and spiritual maturity.
And for those who believe in this mission and are financially able, there is another way to stand with us.
For some, this may be a meaningful part of their regular Christian giving.
It does not purchase His blessing.
It does not replace your responsibility to support your local church or other obligations you have prayerfully made.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing and sincere.
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
The same passage teaches that giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion.
Not through fear.
Not through guilt.
Not by suggesting that God's favor can be purchased.
But through shared conviction that making biblical teaching and discipleship resources available to more people is a worthwhile mission.
These products are simply another way to encourage faith, share a biblical message, or give someone a meaningful gift. They are not measures of spiritual maturity.
And the free Gospel resources remain central to our desire to serve.
Because the purpose is not to build a following around human personalities.
It is to point people to Jesus.
And that brings us back to the gate of Samaria.
I cannot stop thinking about that man.
He heard the prophet.
He mocked the promise.
He saw the provision.
And he died before he could enjoy it.
There is something deeply tragic about seeing a promise fulfilled and realizing that the opportunity to enjoy its provision has passed.
But there is also something wonderfully hopeful about the four desperate men who found the abandoned camp.
They did not create the deliverance.
They discovered it.
Then they carried the news to others.
And there is something even greater about the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
We did not defeat sin and death by our own power.
Christ accomplished what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
We do not come to Him carrying enough good works to pay for salvation.
We come with empty hands, trusting His finished work.
And we do not need to wait until we become impressive, respectable, or publicly admired before calling on His name.
The invitation is for sinners.
For the proud who need to humble themselves.
For the wounded who need hope.
For the religious who have confused familiarity with surrender.
For the ashamed who believe they have gone too far.
For the exhausted who are barely holding on.
For the person reading this who has not prayed sincerely in years.
Jesus says in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV)
What a promise.
Not a promise that life will suddenly become painless.
Not a guarantee that every earthly situation will change tomorrow.
But a declaration from the Savior that those who come to Him will not be cast out.
So come.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come with the truth about your sin.
Come with your unanswered questions.
Come with your broken history.
Come trusting Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, rather than your own ability to make yourself worthy.
If you do not know what to pray, you can begin simply:

"Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Teach me to turn from sin and follow You. I place my trust in You, not in my own goodness. Amen."
Those words are not a magic formula.
Salvation is not produced by reciting a particular prayer.
The invitation of the Gospel is to repent and believe in Jesus Christ.
And if you already belong to Him but have wandered, return.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Seek forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Ask for help where you have become trapped.
Reconnect with a faithful local church.
Open the Scriptures again.
Do not let shame persuade you to stay away from the very Savior whose mercy you need.
And do not let familiarity with holy things replace a living relationship with the Holy One.
The officer in Samaria could not stop God's word from coming true.
But the deeper lesson for us is not that every doubter should expect his fate.
It is that God's truth deserves to be taken seriously, and our lives are too brief to build them on the illusion that we will always have another tomorrow.
If the Lord were to call me to account for my life today, would I be resting in Jesus Christ—or merely in the fact that I have heard about Him?
That question is not meant to drive you into despair.
It is meant to direct you to the Savior.
Because the Gospel does not end at the gate where a man was trampled.
It leads us to the cross where the Son of God gave His life for sinners.
And beyond the cross stands an empty tomb.
The risen Christ is our hope.
The mercy of God is not a rumor.
Forgiveness is not a fantasy.
And the invitation to come to Jesus is not something you have to earn.
But above all, do not leave this story merely impressed by a miracle.
Leave it looking to Jesus.
Because the greatest tragedy is not failing to receive something we wanted in this life.
It is spending our lives near the truth about the Savior without ever turning to Him in faith.
Do not wait until the final page of your life to discover that the grace you kept postponing was the very grace you needed all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE GETS STRANGER THE MORE YOU READ IT—AND THE STRANGEST PART IS HOW EVERY STORY EXPOSES SOMETHING ABOUT YOU
paragraphs: THE BIBLE GETS STRANGER THE MORE YOU READ IT—AND THE STRANGEST PART IS HOW EVERY STORY EXPOSES SOMETHING ABOUT YOU

Talking donkeys. Golden tumors. A man wrestling through the night. A face shining with unbearable glory. A bronze serpent lifted above dying people. These are not embarrassing stories Christians need to explain away. They are ancient testimonies that confront our assumptions about God, sin, judgment, mercy, and the astonishing way Scripture ultimately leads us to Jesus Christ.
There is a moment that happens to people who actually begin reading the Bible for themselves.
Not just opening it to find a comforting verse.
Not just listening to their favorite preacher explain the passages everyone already knows.
Not just reading the parts that look beautiful on a coffee mug.
I mean really reading it.

Page after page. Chapter after chapter. Through the genealogies, the blood, the battles, the laws, the miracles, the betrayals, the strange visions, the uncomfortable judgments, and the moments when God does something so unexpected that you have to stop and stare at the page.
And somewhere along the way, a thought begins forming.
Wait. That's actually in the Bible?
A donkey talks.
People make golden images of tumors.
A man wrestles with a mysterious figure until sunrise and walks away limping.
Another man comes down a mountain with a face so radiant that people are afraid to approach him.
God tells Moses to lift a bronze serpent on a pole so dying Israelites can look at it and live.
And perhaps the most unsettling discovery of all?
The Bible does not always stop to satisfy our curiosity.
Sometimes it leaves us standing in the mystery.
Sometimes it tells us exactly what happened without explaining every detail of how.
And sometimes, hundreds of years later, another passage opens a window into an earlier story so suddenly that everything you thought you understood begins to change.
But here is where this becomes personal.
Because if you stay with Scripture long enough, you begin to realize that its strangest stories are not merely about strange things that happened to other people.
They confront the blindness we refuse to acknowledge.
The pride we have learned to disguise.
The shame we keep carrying.
The wounds we cannot explain.
The idols we have polished until they look respectable.
And the desperate human need for a Savior who can do what no human being can accomplish.
You may open the Bible expecting to examine its stories.
But there will be moments when you feel as though its stories are examining you.
And one of the first places this happens is on a lonely road, where a man who believed he could see spiritually was about to be corrected by an animal.
Yes.
An actual donkey.
In Numbers 22, Balaam is traveling with Moabite officials after being summoned by King Balak, who wants Israel cursed.

Balaam has received permission to go under specific conditions, yet God's anger is kindled as he travels. The passage does not explain every dimension of that tension, but it does make one thing painfully clear: Balaam's journey is not spiritually safe.
The angel of the LORD stands in the road with a drawn sword.
Balaam does not see him.
His donkey does.
The animal turns aside.
Balaam strikes her.
The donkey presses against a wall to avoid the angel, crushing Balaam's foot.
He strikes her again.
Finally, the donkey lies down beneath him.
And Balaam, furious, beats her with his staff.
Then comes one of the most extraordinary sentences in the Old Testament.
Numbers 22:28 says:
וַיִּפְתַּח יְהוָה אֶת־פִּי הָאָתוֹן
Vayyiftaḥ YHWH et-pi ha'aton.
“And the LORD opened the mouth of the donkey.”
The Hebrew does not merely suggest that Balaam imagined the animal speaking. The narrative explicitly attributes the opening of her mouth to the LORD.
And the donkey asks Balaam what she has done to deserve being struck three times.
Even more astonishingly, Balaam answers her.
Think about that.
The man is so consumed with anger that he enters into an argument with a talking donkey.
Then God opens Balaam's eyes.
He sees the angel.
The drawn sword.
The danger he could not perceive.
And suddenly, the entire scene changes.
The animal he was beating had been protecting him.
The creature he considered beneath him had seen what he could not.
The one who believed himself spiritually knowledgeable was exposed as spiritually blind.
And the donkey had been right.
How many times have we mistaken God's interruption for an inconvenience?
How many times have we become angry because something blocked our plans, never considering that the obstacle might be protecting us from a danger we cannot see?
That does not mean every delay, disappointment, or closed door is a supernatural warning. Scripture does not give us permission to interpret every frustration that way.
But Balaam's story does warn us that religious knowledge does not guarantee spiritual discernment.
A person can speak about God and still resist His correction.
A person can be gifted and still be dangerously wrong.
A person can recognize the language of heaven while remaining attached to the rewards of earth.
The New Testament later warns about Balaam's greed and corrupt influence (2 Peter 2:15–16; Jude 11; Revelation 2:14).
So this is not merely a charming story about an animal with a voice.
It is a warning about the human heart.
And if that makes you uncomfortable, keep reading.
Because the next story is even harder to imagine.
In 1 Samuel 4–6, Israel suffers a devastating defeat at the hands of the Philistines.
The ark of the covenant is captured.

The ark was associated with God's covenant presence among His people. But Israel had treated it as though possessing a sacred object could guarantee victory even when their relationship with God was profoundly disordered.
And when the Philistines capture it, they bring it into the temple of their god, Dagon.
The following morning, Dagon's statue is found fallen on its face before the ark.
They set it upright.
The next morning, it has fallen again, this time with its head and hands broken off.
The message is unmistakable.
The LORD cannot be reduced to a captured religious trophy.
The Philistines then experience severe affliction.

The Hebrew text describes the swellings with the word עֳפָלִים (ofalim), commonly translated as tumors or swellings. The exact medical condition is debated, and some textual traditions use a different Hebrew term. We should not pretend to know the precise diagnosis.
But the affliction is serious.
The people are terrified.
And when the Philistines finally decide to return the ark, their priests and diviners advise them to send a guilt offering.
Five golden tumors.
Five golden mice.
Yes, you read that correctly.
Golden representations of their afflictions and of mice associated with the devastation of their land.
First Samuel 6:4–5 records this unusual offering.
And before someone rushes to turn this into a universal spiritual formula, notice something important.
These instructions come from Philistine religious advisers, not from a direct divine command prescribing how God's people should worship.
The narrative reports what they did. It does not establish golden replicas of diseases as a biblical pattern of repentance.
That distinction matters.
Not everything recorded in Scripture is something Scripture commands us to imitate.
The Bible is truthful enough to show us human beings acting with fear, confusion, superstition, arrogance, and partial understanding.
And in this particular account, God's supremacy over Dagon and the Philistines becomes impossible to ignore.
Their idol cannot even stand upright.
Their attempts to control the ark fail.
The God of Israel is not defeated simply because Israel has suffered defeat.
And there is a warning here for every generation.
We can carry religious objects.
Use religious language.
Wear religious clothing.
Display religious symbols.
Attend religious gatherings.
And still misunderstand the living God.
The ark was never meant to replace obedience to the LORD.
And our Christian identity is never meant to replace genuine trust in Jesus Christ.
A cross around your neck is not a substitute for following the One who died upon a cross.
A Bible sitting beside your bed is not the same as allowing its truth to shape your life.
A Christian label cannot save a soul.
Only Christ can.
And now Scripture takes us somewhere quieter.
Not into a pagan temple.
Not onto a dangerous road.
But beside a river, in the darkness, with a frightened man who is about to encounter God in a way he will never forget.
His name is Jacob.
And if you have ever tried to outrun your past, you may recognize something of yourself in him.
Jacob's life has been tangled in conflict, deception, fear, family rivalry, and the consequences of his own choices.
Now, in Genesis 32, he is preparing to meet his brother Esau.
The brother he had wronged.
The brother whose anger he once feared.
Jacob sends his family and possessions across the stream.
And he remains alone.
Genesis 32:24 says:
וַיֵּאָבֵק אִישׁ עִמּוֹ עַד עֲלוֹת הַשָּׁחַר
Vayye'aveq ish immo ad alot hashachar.
“And a man wrestled with him until the breaking of the day.”
A man.
That is how the encounter begins.
But the identity of this mysterious wrestler becomes increasingly profound.
The stranger touches Jacob's hip, dislocating it.
Jacob refuses to release him without a blessing.
And then comes the question.
“What is your name?”
“Jacob.”
The man who had spent so much of his life grasping, maneuvering, and struggling must speak his own name.
Then the stranger gives him another.
Israel.
Genesis 32:28 connects that name with Jacob's struggle with God and with men.
The precise linguistic derivation of the name Israel is discussed by scholars, but the narrative itself clearly emphasizes Jacob's struggle with God.
Jacob names the place Peniel, saying that he has seen God face to face and yet his life has been preserved.
Hosea 12:3–4 later recalls this encounter and refers to the mysterious opponent as an angel.
The biblical texts therefore invite us to recognize a genuine divine encounter while leaving questions about its exact manifestation.
Some Christian interpreters understand the event as a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ. Others understand it as an encounter with God mediated through an angelic figure.
Scripture does not explicitly identify the wrestler as Jesus, and we should not turn a possible interpretation into an unquestionable fact.
But the theological significance remains astonishing.
Jacob receives a blessing.
He receives a new name.
And he walks away limping.
The encounter that changes his identity also changes the way he walks.
There is something deeply moving about that.
We often imagine that if God truly touches our lives, every visible sign of struggle should disappear.
Every consequence erased.
Every scar removed.
Every painful memory forgotten.
But Jacob's story does not give us that simplistic picture.
He is blessed.
And he limps.
He has encountered God.
And his hip still hurts.
He has a new name.
And he still must face Esau.
God's blessing does not remove his responsibility to confront the past.
Perhaps you know what it is like to love God while still carrying the consequences of choices you regret.
Perhaps you have repented, yet there are relationships that remain complicated.
Perhaps forgiveness has been offered, yet trust still needs rebuilding.
Perhaps you have experienced God's mercy without receiving an immediate escape from every painful circumstance.
Jacob's limp reminds us that transformation is not always the absence of weakness.
Sometimes grace changes how we live with weakness.
And in the New Testament, Paul would hear the Lord say, “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV).
That is not a promise that every wound will remain.
It is a promise that Christ's grace is sufficient even when weakness remains.
And that is good news for people who have spent years pretending to be stronger than they are.
But the Bible is not finished surprising us.
Because there is another man who encounters God, and this time the evidence is written across his face.
Moses has been on Mount Sinai in the presence of the LORD.
When he descends carrying the tablets of the testimony, something extraordinary has happened.
His face is shining.
Exodus 34:29 uses a form of the Hebrew verb קָרַן (qaran), describing the radiance of the skin of his face.

The Hebrew wording is striking because the root is related to a word for horn. This linguistic connection contributed to the famous older Latin rendering that influenced artistic depictions of Moses with horns.
But the narrative's context is clear.
Moses' face is radiating because he has been speaking with God.
Aaron and the Israelites are afraid to come near him.
Moses speaks to them and later uses a veil.
Imagine standing before someone whose face visibly bears the effects of an encounter with the holy God.
No stage lighting.
No theatrical performance.
No human technique.
Just a man who has been in God's presence.
Yet the most remarkable explanation comes much later.
In 2 Corinthians 3, Paul reflects on Moses' veil and the glory associated with the old covenant.
He contrasts that glory with the surpassing glory of the ministry of the Spirit under the new covenant.
And then he writes in 2 Corinthians 3:18:
The Greek word translated “changed” is μεταμορφούμεθα (metamorphoumetha).
It describes being transformed.
Not merely appearing different.
Not learning to perform religious behavior more convincingly.
Being transformed.
Paul is not promising that every Christian's face will physically glow.
He is describing the Spirit's transforming work as believers behold the Lord's glory.
And in the next chapter, Paul identifies the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6).
This is where the story reaches into our lives.
We spend enormous amounts of energy trying to change ourselves through image management.
We curate appearances.
Hide weaknesses.
Measure ourselves against other people.
And sometimes even turn Christianity into another exhausting performance.
But the Gospel does not begin with a demand that sinners manufacture their own glory.
It announces Jesus Christ, through whom God gives light to hearts that could never produce it themselves.
The transformation is real.
The Spirit works within us.
And the glory belongs to God.
Yet of all the strange stories we have considered, there is one that Jesus Himself explicitly brings into the center of His explanation of salvation.
And this is where the entire journey becomes almost unbearable in its beauty.
Because it involves dying people.
Deadly serpents.
A bronze image lifted on a pole.
And a Savior who would one day be lifted up on a cross.
In Numbers 21, the Israelites speak against God and Moses.
Their complaint exposes the bitterness and unbelief that have taken root during their wilderness journey.
Then fiery serpents come among the people.
Many are bitten.
Many die.
The people confess their sin and ask Moses to pray.
And the LORD gives an extraordinary instruction.
Moses is to make a fiery serpent and set it upon a pole.
Those who are bitten are to look at it and live.
Numbers 21:9 says:
וְהִבִּיט אֶל־נְחַשׁ הַנְּחֹשֶׁת וָחָי
Vehibbit el-neḥash hanneḥoshet vaḥay.
“And when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived.” (KJV)
The Hebrew contains a memorable wordplay between naḥash (serpent) and neḥoshet (bronze or copper).
But the theological point is not that bronze possesses supernatural healing power.
The healing comes through God's merciful provision, received according to His word.
And this is important because centuries later, in 2 Kings 18:4, King Hezekiah destroys the bronze serpent after the Israelites begin burning incense to it.
They had turned a former instrument of God's provision into an object of idolatrous devotion.
Think about that.
Something God once used for good had become something people worshiped instead of God.
Even a sacred reminder can become an idol when it receives the devotion that belongs to the LORD alone.
But the most important revelation about the bronze serpent does not come from Hezekiah.
It comes from Jesus.
In John 3, Jesus is speaking with Nicodemus, a Pharisee and teacher of Israel.
Nicodemus is trying to understand the necessity of being born again.
And Jesus reaches back into the wilderness.
John 3:14–15 says:
“And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up: That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.” (KJV)
Read that again.
Jesus Himself connects the bronze serpent with His coming crucifixion.
The Israelites were dying and could not heal themselves.
God provided a means by which they could live.
And Jesus uses that historical event to illuminate the salvation He came to accomplish.
The comparison does not mean Jesus was sinful or evil like the serpent imagery might suggest.
Scripture explicitly teaches that Christ was without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
Rather, Jesus identifies a God-given pattern of deliverance: those facing death receive life through the provision God has appointed.
The cross is not an accident.
It is not simply an inspirational example of sacrificial love.
It is the place where the sinless Son of God gives Himself for sinners.
Second Corinthians 5:21 says that God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
Galatians 3:13 declares that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.
And Isaiah 53 speaks of the suffering Servant who bears the iniquities of many.
Now consider the original scene again.
Imagine an Israelite lying in the dust.
The venom has entered his body.
His strength is failing.
He cannot negotiate with the poison.
He cannot reverse the bite through sheer determination.
He cannot earn a cure by promising to become a better person tomorrow.
But God has provided a way to live.
And Jesus says that this event points toward something far greater.
A world wounded by sin.
Human beings unable to rescue themselves.
And the Son of God lifted up so that whoever believes in Him may have eternal life.
Then comes the verse that countless people have memorized, often without remembering the strange wilderness story immediately preceding it.
John 3:16.
“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.” (KJV)
Do you see it now?
The talking donkey exposes spiritual blindness.
The golden tumors appear in a narrative demonstrating that the LORD cannot be controlled or defeated by idols.
Jacob's wrestling reveals the mystery of divine blessing in the life of a deeply flawed man.
Moses' radiant face becomes part of Paul's explanation of the surpassing glory of the new covenant.
And the bronze serpent becomes an image Jesus Himself uses to explain His saving work.
These passages do not all function in exactly the same way.
Not every detail is a hidden prophecy.
Not every unusual event is a coded reference to the crucifixion.
Not every biblical character is a secret symbol of Jesus.
Faithful reading requires us to respect what each passage actually says, its historical setting, its literary context, and the way later Scripture interprets it.
But taken together within the Bible's unfolding story, they reveal a consistent truth.
Human beings are more spiritually needy than we want to admit.
And God is more merciful than we could ever deserve.
There is another detail about the Bible that should change how we read it.
Its stories are not arranged to make its human characters look consistently admirable.
Abraham fears.
Jacob deceives.
Moses disobeys.
David commits adultery and arranges a man's death.
Peter denies knowing Jesus.
The disciples argue about greatness.
And Paul openly remembers that he once persecuted the church.
Scripture does not protect its heroes from the truth about themselves.
Why?
Because the Bible is not ultimately the story of impressive people earning God's approval through flawless lives.
It is the story of the holy God acting in creation, covenant, judgment, mercy, and redemption, culminating in Jesus Christ.
That does not excuse the sins of its characters.
It makes God's grace all the more astonishing.
And perhaps this is why certain biblical stories feel so uncomfortable.
They destroy the illusion that spiritual maturity is the same as maintaining a spotless public image.
They remind us that religious people can be blind.
That gifted people can be greedy.
That wounded people can be changed.
That sacred things can become idols.
And that sinners need more than inspiration.
They need redemption.
Now, perhaps you have been reading all of this with a quiet question rising inside you.
What does any of this have to do with me?
Maybe more than you expected.
Because there are people reading these words who have become very good at looking spiritually healthy while privately struggling.
You know how to say “God is good.”
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know which Bible verses to share.
You know how to encourage everyone else.
But there are things you have not told anyone.
A habit you keep returning to.
A relationship you damaged.
A resentment you keep feeding.
A private compromise you keep defending.
A prayer you have almost stopped praying because the answer has taken so long.
Or a kind of spiritual exhaustion that makes you wonder whether you are still growing at all.
And perhaps you have begun to believe that your failures are the truest thing about you.
But listen carefully.
Your sin must not be minimized.
Your wounds must not be mocked.
Your responsibility must not be denied.
And God's grace must not be reduced to permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus did not come merely to make us feel better about the darkness.
He came to save us from sin and bring us into the light.
The Greek word commonly translated “repentance” is μετάνοια (metanoia), referring to a change of mind or heart that, in biblical usage, involves turning toward God and away from sin.
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness through emotional suffering.
It is not pretending your past never happened.
It is not manufacturing enough tears to convince God that you deserve another chance.
It is turning to God in response to His truth and mercy.
Mark 1:15 records Jesus proclaiming:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)
Repent.
And believe.
Not because your repentance makes the cross effective.
But because the crucified and risen Christ is the Savior in whom forgiveness and new life are found.
And if you have fallen again, the answer is not to hide deeper.
It is to come into the light.
First John 1:9 tells believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
And Ephesians 2:8–10 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not our works, while also affirming that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not mean sin is harmless.
Grace means sin does not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
This is the heart of the Gospel Warrior message.
Not because the scandal was imaginary.
Not because the damage never mattered.
Not because everyone you hurt is required to trust you immediately.
Not because repentance guarantees the removal of every earthly consequence.
But because the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ make forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and genuine transformation possible.
He does not rewrite history by pretending evil was good.
He redeems sinners without calling their sin righteous.
He gives a new future without requiring us to deny the truth about the past.
And He is still changing lives.
Maybe yours is one of them.
There is something else I want you to notice before you leave this article.
When Jesus rose from the dead, He did not tell His disciples to build a movement around the strangest stories in the Bible.
He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.
Luke 24:27 tells us that beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, Jesus explained the things concerning Himself in the Scriptures.
And Luke 24:44–47 connects the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms with His suffering, resurrection, and the proclamation of repentance for the forgiveness of sins in His name.
That is the destination.
Not fascination without faith.
Not mystery without obedience.
Not knowledge without love.
Not biblical trivia that makes us feel intellectually superior to people who have never studied Hebrew or Greek.
The goal is to know the living God through Jesus Christ.
To read His Word carefully.
To receive His truth humbly.
To repent where we have sinned.
To trust His grace.
And to follow Him with lives increasingly shaped by His Spirit.
The original biblical languages are precious because they help us understand what the biblical authors communicated.
But knowing Hebrew does not automatically make a person holy.
Understanding Greek does not guarantee obedience.
And being able to explain a talking donkey is not the same as listening when God corrects your own heart.
The question is not merely whether you can understand the strange passages.
The deeper question is whether you will allow the truth of Scripture to challenge the comfortable stories you have been telling yourself.
Maybe you have been like Balaam, angry at an interruption while refusing to examine your direction.
Maybe you have been like Jacob, afraid of facing the consequences of your past.
Maybe you have become so attached to a religious symbol, personality, tradition, or institution that you have lost sight of the God it was supposed to direct you toward.
Maybe you have been trying to manufacture a spiritual glow while neglecting the quiet work of prayer, repentance, Scripture, and obedience.
Or maybe you feel like one of those dying Israelites.
Exhausted.
Guilty.
Unable to save yourself.
And desperately needing mercy.
If that is you, do not turn this into another moment of religious performance.
Turn to Jesus.
Tell Him the truth.
Confess the sin you have been defending.
Ask for mercy.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And take the next faithful step.
Sometimes that step is apologizing.
Sometimes it is ending a sinful relationship or pattern.
Sometimes it is seeking pastoral counsel or wise Christian support.
Sometimes it is opening your Bible again after months of silence.
Sometimes it is choosing to forgive while still establishing necessary boundaries.
Sometimes it is simply praying, “Lord Jesus, have mercy on me. Teach me to follow You.”
And if your faith feels weak, remember that the strength of salvation is not found in how impressive you can make your faith appear.
It is found in the Savior upon whom faith depends.
Be honest.
Which of these stories reached the part of your heart you have been avoiding?
Was it Balaam's blindness?
Jacob's limp?
The warning against turning sacred things into idols?
Moses' encounter with God's glory?
Or the bronze serpent pointing toward Christ?
If you are still fighting to follow Jesus through a difficult season, you can simply comment, “I'm still fighting.”
If you need encouragement and prayer, comment, “Pray for me.”
And if this article has reminded you that your past does not have to define your future in Christ, comment, “Jesus is still changing me.”
Someone reading the comments may need your testimony more than you realize.
Not merely to increase its reach.
And perhaps, through that unexpected beginning, they will encounter the truth about the crucified and risen Savior.
Because the deeper you go into Scripture, the more you discover how much there is still to learn.
And this is why the Gospel Warrior ministry exists.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to sell you salvation.
Not to make you dependent on a personality.
But to encourage you to grow in biblical understanding, deepen your relationship with Christ, and become more grounded in the truth of God's Word.
These resources are intended to help people study, pray, understand the Gospel, and mature in their walk with God.
And if this ministry has encouraged you, taught you something, or helped you return to Scripture, I want to extend a personal invitation.
You do not have to pay for God's favor.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Not pressure.
These products are not spiritual necessities.
They do not make anyone more saved, more loved by God, or more deserving of His grace.
You can still read.
Still learn.
Still pray.
Still share.
Still make use of the free resources.
And above all, still grow in Christ.
Because the Gospel is not a product.
Jesus Christ is not behind a paywall.
Salvation is the free gift of God through faith in Jesus Christ.
It does not purchase the mercy of God.
That distinction is not a small detail.
It is part of remaining faithful to the very Gospel we are trying to proclaim.
And perhaps that is the most important lesson hidden in plain sight throughout these astonishing biblical accounts.
God does not need our attempts to make Him more marketable.
He does not need us to remove the uncomfortable passages.
He does not need us to exaggerate the miracles.
He does not need us to manufacture secret meanings the biblical authors never intended.
He calls us to receive His Word with reverence, study it faithfully, and proclaim Jesus Christ truthfully.
Because the Bible is already astonishing.
A donkey speaks because God opens its mouth.
A pagan idol falls because it cannot stand before the living God.
A frightened patriarch wrestles through the night and receives a new name.
A prophet's face shines after speaking with the LORD.
A bronze serpent is lifted in the wilderness, and centuries later Jesus declares that the Son of Man must likewise be lifted up.
And at the center of the Christian faith stands the greatest wonder of all.
The eternal Son of God took on human flesh.
He lived without sin.
He welcomed sinners without approving their sin.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He healed the broken.
He bore the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
Not as a metaphor for positive thinking.
Not as a symbol that life sometimes gets better.
But as the risen Lord whose victory over sin and death stands at the heart of the apostolic Gospel (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And because He lives, repentance is not hopeless.
Forgiveness is not imaginary.
Transformation is not merely self-improvement.
And death does not have the final word for those who belong to Him.
So read the strange passages.
Ask the difficult questions.
Study the original languages when you can.
Pay attention to the context.
Refuse interpretations that sound exciting but cannot be supported by Scripture.
Let the difficult stories humble you.
Let the judgments sober you.
Let the promises strengthen you.
Let the cross expose both the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable greatness of divine love.
And let the resurrection remind you that the God who raised Jesus from the dead is not finished accomplishing His purposes.
You may have come here because the Bible contains a talking donkey.
But I pray you leave thinking about the Savior who speaks life to sinners.
You may have come because golden tumors sounded unbelievable.
But I pray you leave with a greater reverence for the God who cannot be controlled by human idols.
You may have come because a man wrestled with God and walked away limping.
But I pray you leave knowing that your weakness does not place you beyond the reach of His grace.
And you may have come because a bronze serpent sounded strange.
But I pray you leave looking to the One who was lifted up for our salvation.
Because one day, the strangest thing about your story may not be what happened to you.

It may be that after everything you did, everything you lost, everything you feared, and everything you thought could never be redeemed, Jesus Christ met you with mercy, called you to repentance, and began making you new.

The miracle is not that God can make a donkey speak, or a man's face shine. The miracle that should bring us to our knees is that the holy God still calls sinners out of darkness and into the life of His beloved Son.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN CHRISTIANS HAVE DEMONS? THE TERRIFYING QUESTION THE CHURCH CANNOT AFFORD TO ANSWER CARELESSLY
paragraphs: CAN CHRISTIANS HAVE DEMONS? THE TERRIFYING QUESTION THE CHURCH CANNOT AFFORD TO ANSWER CARELESSLY

Can a person belong to Jesus Christ and still experience demonic oppression? What does the Bible actually say about possession, spiritual warfare, hidden bondage, and the freedom purchased by the blood of Jesus? The answer may confront your fears, challenge what you have been taught, and lead you back to the One who has already conquered the darkness.
There is a kind of fear that rarely makes it into Sunday morning testimonies.
It is the fear of the Christian who loves Jesus but still struggles with thoughts they cannot seem to silence.
The believer who worships with raised hands on Sunday but wakes up on Monday fighting temptations they thought they had already conquered.
The woman who has prayed for peace but still trembles when memories of her past return.
The man who has confessed the same sin so many times that he has begun wondering whether something darker is living inside him.
And somewhere in the silence, a terrifying question begins to form.
What if I have a demon?
Perhaps someone has already told you that your anxiety is a spirit. Your depression is a demon. Your addiction is evidence of possession. Your nightmares mean the enemy has entered your life.
Perhaps someone even told you that because you are still struggling, the Holy Spirit must not truly be living in you.
And now you are afraid.
Afraid of the darkness.
Afraid of yourself.
Afraid that your prayers are not working.
Afraid that Jesus has somehow lost His grip on you.
But before fear writes another chapter of your story, there is something you need to hear.
Not every struggle is a demon. Not every temptation is possession. And not every battle means that Christ has abandoned you.
There is a difference between being attacked by an enemy and belonging to that enemy.
And that difference matters more than you may realize.
Because the question is not merely whether Christians can have demons.
The deeper question is this:
Can the darkness claim ownership over someone who has been purchased by the blood of Jesus Christ?
To answer that, we must go beyond frightening testimonies, sensational deliverance videos, inherited religious assumptions, and spiritual experiences that cannot be verified.
We must return to Scripture.
Not because spiritual warfare is imaginary.
But because spiritual warfare is too serious to be governed by imagination.

The New Testament does not deny the existence of demons. Jesus confronted them. He commanded them to leave. He demonstrated authority over them. And His apostles understood that the Christian life involves genuine conflict against spiritual evil.
In Mark 1:27, after Jesus commanded an unclean spirit, the astonished witnesses said:
"What thing is this? what new doctrine is this? for with authority commandeth he even the unclean spirits, and they do obey him."
That is not religious mythology dressed up as inspiration.
That is the biblical testimony concerning the authority of Christ.
But notice something essential.
The authority belongs to Jesus.
Not to our shouting.
Not to our spiritual vocabulary.
Not to our ability to identify a demon behind every human difficulty.
And certainly not to a minister's ability to frighten someone into believing they are possessed.
The kingdom of darkness is real.
But the authority of Jesus Christ is greater.
And Scripture never asks believers to become more fascinated with demons than with their Savior.
This brings us to a Greek word that has generated enormous theological discussion.

In the Gospel accounts, the verb δαιμονίζομαι (daimonizomai) describes people afflicted by demonic influence. It is often translated into English using expressions such as "demon-possessed" or "demonized."
The Greek term itself does not precisely define a demon's legal ownership of a person, nor does it establish a complete doctrine of how demonic influence operates.
That distinction is important.
The English word "possessed" can suggest ownership. But the Greek wording does not, by itself, settle every question about ownership, indwelling, oppression, or spiritual influence.
We must therefore be careful not to build an entire doctrine on assumptions that the word alone cannot prove.
And here is where Christians often disagree.
Some believers teach that a genuine, Spirit-indwelt Christian cannot have a demon dwelling within them because they belong to Christ and are indwelt by the Holy Spirit.
Others believe that a Christian can experience certain forms of internal demonic affliction or bondage while still belonging to Jesus, and they distinguish this from being owned by Satan.
Both positions have been defended within Christian communities.
But Scripture does not provide a single explicit statement that settles every modern category used in this debate.
That means we must be humble where the Bible is not as specific as our theological arguments sometimes pretend.
We must never manufacture certainty where God has not given it.
Yet Scripture gives us powerful truths that should anchor every discussion.
Paul writes in Colossians 1:13–14:
Consider the Greek expression behind "delivered us."
ἐρρύσατο (errysato) comes from a verb meaning to rescue or deliver.
And the word ἐξουσία (exousia), translated here as "power," refers to authority or dominion.
Paul is describing a genuine transfer of kingdom allegiance.
A Christian has been rescued from the dominion of darkness and brought into the kingdom of God's beloved Son.
That is not a motivational slogan.
That is redemption.
It means the believer's ultimate identity is no longer defined by Satan's kingdom.
It means the cross accomplished something that no demonic power can reverse.
It means your past does not hold the deed to your soul.
If you are in Christ, you do not belong to the darkness. You belong to Jesus.
But does belonging to Jesus mean you will never experience spiritual attack?
Absolutely not.
And this is where the story becomes more uncomfortable.
Because even people who truly belong to God can experience intense spiritual opposition.
Consider Peter.
A man who walked with Jesus.
A man who witnessed miracles.
A man who confessed that Jesus was the Christ.
And yet, on the night before the crucifixion, Jesus spoke words that must have shaken him.
"Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not." — Luke 22:31–32
Imagine hearing that.
Satan has demanded to sift you.
Not a stranger.
Not an unbeliever standing outside the covenant community.
Peter.
One of the closest disciples of Jesus.
And notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not tell Peter that spiritual attack proved he had never belonged to God.
He did not declare that every coming failure was caused by a demon living inside him.
Instead, Jesus revealed that Peter would face a devastating test.
And then He gave him a promise.
"I have prayed for thee."
Read that again.
The enemy wanted to sift Peter.
But Jesus was interceding for him.
Peter would fail terribly. He would deny the Lord three times. He would weep bitterly.
But Peter's failure would not be the final sentence of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him.
The man who denied Christ would become a courageous witness to Christ.
From cowardice to courage.
From bitter tears to renewed calling.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to understand that being spiritually attacked does not mean you are spiritually abandoned.
But there is another side to this truth.
Not every battle comes directly from Satan.
Sometimes the problem is not a demon.
Sometimes it is the flesh.
Paul writes in Galatians 5:17:
The Greek word σάρξ (sarx), translated as "flesh," can refer to human physical existence, but in this moral context it describes fallen human tendencies opposed to the Spirit.
Paul does not teach that every sinful desire must be explained by a demon.
He teaches that believers experience a genuine conflict between the desires of the flesh and the leading of the Spirit.
This matters because some Christians have been taught to rebuke what Scripture tells them to repent of.
They try to cast out pride when they need humility.
They try to cast out bitterness when they need to forgive.
They try to cast out lust when they need to flee temptation, renew their minds, establish boundaries, and practice obedience.
They try to cast out deception when they need to stop lying.
And sometimes, rather than confronting their choices, they blame an unseen spirit for behavior they are responsible for changing.
But the Gospel does not remove personal responsibility.
Grace does not excuse sin.
Grace teaches us to turn away from it.
Titus 2:11–12 says:

"For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world."
Notice that grace does more than forgive.
Grace trains.
Grace transforms.
Grace teaches us to say no to what once controlled our decisions.
And if you are struggling with recurring sin, you do not necessarily need someone to announce that a demon is inside you.
You may need repentance.
You may need accountability.
You may need to confess what you have been hiding.
You may need to stop returning to the environment that keeps feeding your temptation.
You may need mature Christian counsel.
And in some situations, you may also need professional help for emotional, psychological, or physical conditions that should never be automatically labeled demonic.
There is no shame in receiving appropriate care.
A believer can love Jesus deeply and still experience depression.
A believer can be filled with faith and still suffer from trauma.
A believer can pray sincerely and still require medical treatment.
Even Elijah, after a dramatic victory over the prophets of Baal, became exhausted and despairing.
In 1 Kings 19, God responded to his condition with food, rest, divine presence, and renewed direction.
The passage does not diagnose Elijah with a demon.
And we should not impose a diagnosis Scripture does not give.
Think about how much unnecessary suffering has occurred because someone treated every mental or emotional struggle as evidence of spiritual possession.
Think about the young Christian who became terrified of their own intrusive thoughts.
The exhausted mother who was told that her depression meant she lacked faith.
The grieving father who believed his inability to feel joy meant an evil spirit had taken over.
The teenager who confessed a frightening thought and was told they were demonized instead of being met with patient care.
Jesus never authorized His followers to turn suffering people into spiritual spectacles.
He calls us to truth.
Compassion.
Discernment.
And love.
Yet we must not swing to the opposite extreme and pretend spiritual evil does not exist.
Paul writes in Ephesians 6:12:
The Greek word πάλη (palē), translated "wrestle," evokes close struggle or combat.
Paul was not describing a comfortable religious life without resistance.
He was describing a spiritual conflict.
But look carefully at the instructions surrounding that verse.
Paul does not tell believers to spend their lives obsessively searching for demons.
He tells them to stand.
To put on the whole armor of God.
To embrace truth.
To practice righteousness.
To remain grounded in the Gospel of peace.
To take up faith.
To receive the assurance of salvation.
To wield the Word of God.
To pray.
This is biblical spiritual warfare.
Not paranoia.
Not superstition.
Not endless fear of hidden spirits behind every inconvenience.
It is steadfast dependence on God.
James 4:7 declares:
"Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you."
The order is not accidental.
Submit to God.
Resist the devil.
The Greek verb ὑποτάγητε (hypotagēte) carries the sense of placing oneself under authority.
And ἀντίστητε (antistēte) means to oppose or stand against.
The Christian's defense against Satan is not independent spiritual bravado.
It is humble submission to God and faithful resistance to evil.
You do not become stronger than Satan by making yourself the center of spiritual warfare.
You stand because Jesus Christ is Lord.
And here is a truth that deserves to be written somewhere you will see it on your darkest days:
The devil is not the opposite equal of God. Satan is a creature. Jesus Christ is the eternal Son of God.
There is no cosmic contest between two equally powerful kingdoms.
At the cross, Christ triumphed over the powers of darkness.
Colossians 2:15 says:
"And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it."
The language is victorious.
The cross that appeared to be Christ's humiliation became the place of His triumph.
What looked like defeat was the accomplishment of redemption.
And what Satan intended for destruction became the public declaration that sin, death, and the powers of darkness would not have the final word.
That does not mean every effect of evil has already disappeared from this present world.
We still await the fullness of Christ's final victory at His return.
But it means that believers do not fight for an uncertain Savior.
They trust a risen Lord.
Now consider another passage frequently brought into this debate.
In 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, Paul writes:
The Greek word ναός (naos), translated "temple," refers to the sacred dwelling place.
Paul's point is breathtaking.
The believer's body belongs to God and is the temple of the Holy Spirit.
You are not your own.
You were bought with a price.
For Christians who believe that a genuine believer cannot be indwelt by a demon, this passage provides an important theological foundation.
They reason that the Holy Spirit's indwelling and the believer's belonging to Christ are incompatible with demonic possession understood as ownership or controlling indwelling.
That is a serious argument worthy of respect.
However, the passage does not explicitly discuss every proposed form of demonic affliction.
Therefore, we should distinguish between what Paul directly teaches and the theological conclusions Christians draw from his teaching.
What Paul clearly establishes is that the Christian belongs to God and is called to honor Him with the body.
That truth must never be minimized.
You are not spiritual property waiting to be claimed by whichever power shouts the loudest.
If you are truly in Christ, your life belongs to Him.
But there is a warning here, too.
Belonging to Jesus does not make disobedience harmless.
Paul warns in Ephesians 4:26–27:
"Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath: Neither give place to the devil."
The Greek word τόπος (topos), translated "place," can mean room, place, or opportunity.
In context, Paul warns believers not to give the devil an opportunity through sinful anger.
It is a serious warning.
But the verse does not explicitly say that a demon enters a Christian's body whenever someone sins.
That conclusion goes beyond what the passage states.
What it does tell us is that persistent sin can provide an opportunity for destructive spiritual influence.
And that should make us examine our lives.
Not with panic.
With repentance.
Because there is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction draws you toward the light.
Condemnation tells you to hide forever.
Conviction calls sin what it is and points you toward the mercy of Christ.
Condemnation insists that your failure has become your permanent identity.
Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus."
That is not permission to continue in sin.
It is assurance that Christ has borne the condemnation deserved by those who belong to Him.
And when believers stumble, they are not called to despair.
They are called to confess and return.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Perhaps you have been carrying a secret.
Something you would never admit in a church gathering.
Something you have promised God you would stop doing.
Something that keeps returning, even after your tears have dried.
And perhaps you have begun believing that your struggle is proof you are beyond restoration.
But listen carefully.
The fact that you are struggling does not prove that you are possessed.
The fact that you are tempted does not mean you have already sinned.
And the fact that you have fallen does not mean that repentance is now impossible.
Do not use grace as permission to remain where you are.
But do not let shame convince you that grace is no longer available.
Jesus came for sinners.
Real sinners.
Not imaginary people who have never failed.
Not religious performers who know how to conceal their brokenness.
People with histories.
People with regrets.
People who have made terrible decisions.
People who need mercy they cannot manufacture for themselves.
Remember the man among the tombs in Mark 5.
He lived among graves.
He cried out.
He harmed himself.
He could not be restrained by the chains people placed upon him.
The Gospel describes him as afflicted by an unclean spirit, and Jesus delivered him.
Later, the people saw him sitting, clothed, and in his right mind.
What a transformation.
But we must be careful with this account.
Mark does not present this man as a previously converted, Spirit-indwelt Christian.
Therefore, his story demonstrates Christ's authority over demons, but it does not directly answer whether a born-again Christian can be demonized.
What it does reveal is the compassionate power of Jesus.
The man whom others feared was not beyond the reach of Christ.
The man whom society had isolated was not forgotten by the Savior.
The man associated with tombs would become a witness to mercy.
Jesus told him in Mark 5:19:
"Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee."
Do you see the beauty?
The story did not end with the demon.
It ended with testimony.
The man's identity was no longer reduced to what had tormented him.
He had encountered Jesus.
And Jesus sent him home with a story of mercy.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Now perhaps you are wondering about the biblical distinction between oppression and possession.
Here we must speak carefully.
Modern Christian teaching frequently distinguishes between external demonic oppression, internal demonic influence, and possession understood as domination or ownership.
Those distinctions can be useful in theological discussion.
But Scripture does not provide a complete technical classification using those exact English categories.
First Peter 5:8–9 warns believers:
"Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour: Whom resist stedfast in the faith."
Peter clearly warns Christians about Satan's hostile activity.
The believer is instructed to resist him.
The passage establishes that Christians can be targets of spiritual opposition.
It does not establish that every Christian under attack has a demon dwelling inside them.
Likewise, 2 Corinthians 12:7 describes Paul's thorn in the flesh as "the messenger of Satan to buffet me."
Christians disagree about the exact nature of Paul's thorn.
We should not pretend to know more than the text reveals.
But we do know that Paul experienced severe affliction and pleaded with God for relief.
And God's answer was extraordinary.
"My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." — 2 Corinthians 12:9
Not every battle ends with an immediate removal of suffering.
Sometimes God sustains His people through trials they desperately wish would disappear.
Sometimes healing unfolds gradually.
Sometimes faithful believers continue to need prayer, community, treatment, counsel, and patient support.
And none of those realities automatically means Jesus has failed them.
This is especially important when discussing deliverance ministries.
We should not mock the biblical accounts of Jesus casting out demons.
Nor should we dismiss every claim of spiritual affliction without examination.
But neither should we accept every claimed deliverance as proof that the explanation offered was correct.
Experiences must be tested by Scripture.
Spiritual authority must be exercised with humility and accountability.
And vulnerable people must never be manipulated through fear.
A minister should not demand money in exchange for deliverance.
A struggling person should not be pressured to stop prescribed medication because someone has declared their illness demonic.
No one should be subjected to violence, humiliation, sexual misconduct, forced confinement, or dangerous practices under the label of spiritual warfare.
These things are not expressions of the compassion of Christ.

If someone is experiencing frightening symptoms, hearing voices, having thoughts of self-harm, or losing touch with reality, urgent professional assessment may be necessary alongside appropriate pastoral support.
Seeking such help is not a denial of faith.
It is an act of responsible care.
And there is something else the church must remember.
We cannot diagnose a demon from a social media comment.
We cannot determine possession from a nightmare.
We cannot identify an evil spirit simply because someone is grieving, addicted, anxious, or struggling with unwanted thoughts.
We must never place spiritual labels on people more confidently than Scripture permits.
The shepherding heart of Jesus calls us to protect people, not terrify them.
Now let us return to the question that brought us here.
Can Christians have demons?

If by "have demons" we mean that Satan owns a truly regenerated believer, Scripture teaches that Christians have been redeemed by Christ and transferred from the dominion of darkness into His kingdom.
They belong to Jesus.
If we mean that Christians can face temptation, spiritual harassment, deception, opposition, or attacks from the enemy, Scripture clearly says yes.

If we mean that a demon can dwell within a truly Spirit-indwelt Christian in some distinct sense that does not involve ownership, Christians disagree, and the biblical texts do not explicitly resolve every detail of that claim.
That is the responsible distinction.
It may not be the sensational answer that attracts the loudest headlines.
But truth matters more than sensationalism.
And the goal of Christian discipleship is not to make people terrified of demons.
It is to make disciples who trust, obey, and worship Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest question you will ever answer is not whether a demon is trying to attack you.
It is whether you have been reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
You can become fascinated with spiritual warfare and still neglect the Gospel.
You can memorize the names of demons and remain ignorant of the character of Christ.
You can watch hours of deliverance testimonies and never open your Bible.
You can spend years fearing the devil while refusing to repent of the sin you already know you need to surrender.
And that would be a tragedy.
Because Jesus did not die and rise again merely to make you knowledgeable about darkness.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to destroy the works of the devil.
First John 3:8 declares:
"For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil."
The Greek verb λύσῃ (lysē), translated "destroy," can carry the meaning of undoing, dissolving, or bringing something to an end.
John's statement announces the purpose of Christ's appearing in relation to the devil's works.
It is not a promise that believers will never suffer or struggle in the present age.
It is a declaration that the Son of God has come to overthrow the works of evil.
And at the center of that victory stands the cross.
Jesus took upon Himself the judgment sinners deserved.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day.
And everyone who truly turns to Him in repentance and faith receives forgiveness and new life through His grace.
Not because they are spiritually impressive.
Not because they have performed a flawless deliverance ritual.
Not because they have never experienced another frightening thought.
But because Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
The Greek word τετέλεσται (tetelestai) appears in John 19:30, where Jesus declares:
"It is finished."
The word expresses completion.
In its immediate context, it marks the completion of the work Jesus came to accomplish as He gives up His spirit.
It should not be reduced to the popular but oversimplified claim that the Greek word itself literally means "paid in full."
Nevertheless, the wider New Testament clearly teaches that Christ's death accomplishes redemption.
His saving work is not unfinished business waiting for Satan's permission.
The cross is not a partial victory.
And the resurrection is not an uncertain hope.
Jesus is alive.
And because He lives, the believer's future is not ultimately determined by the enemy's threats.

Perhaps the most heartbreaking part of this entire conversation is that some Christians spend more time asking whether the devil is inside them than remembering that Christ has promised to remain with His people.
Jesus says in John 10:27–28:
"My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand."
Look at those words.
"I know them."
Not merely their public testimonies.
Not merely their Sunday worship.
He knows His sheep.
Their weaknesses.
Their fears.
Their history.
Their need for grace.
And He gives them eternal life.
That is the Shepherd you need to know.
Not a distant religious figure waiting for you to fail.
The Good Shepherd who laid down His life for the sheep.
And perhaps, as you read this, you realize that the greatest bondage in your life is not some mysterious spiritual entity.
Perhaps it is the shame you have refused to bring into the light.
The bitterness you have protected.
The secret sin you keep feeding.
The unforgiveness you have mistaken for strength.
The fear that has convinced you to hide from God instead of running toward Him.
You do not need to pretend those things are harmless.
You need to bring them to Jesus.
Confess your sins.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Seek help where help is needed.
Open your Bible.
Pray.
Walk with mature believers who will tell you the truth without humiliating you.
And when the enemy accuses you, answer not with your perfection, but with the finished work of Jesus Christ.
Because your confidence is not that you have never sinned.
Your confidence is that Christ is mighty to save.
Your hope is not that you will never face another battle.
Your hope is that the Lord who began His good work in His people is faithful.
And when you fall, do not make a home in the dust.
Repent.
Get up.
Return to the Savior.
Keep walking.
You are not called to spend your life staring into the darkness, trying to discover everything the enemy might be doing.
You are called to walk in the light of Christ.
And there is someone reading this who has not told anyone how exhausted they are.
You have been fighting a private battle.
You have wondered whether God is tired of hearing the same prayers.
You have been afraid to admit that you still struggle.
Perhaps this article has confronted something you have kept hidden.
Then do not let fear have the last word.
If you have been confusing every struggle with demonic possession, perhaps your honest response is "Jesus, teach me Your truth."
You do not need to reveal private details to prove your sincerity.
God sees what the comment section cannot.
But sometimes a simple, honest testimony becomes the encouragement another believer desperately needed.
And please, think of the person you know who lives in fear that every difficulty means they are demon-possessed.
The young believer who is afraid of their own mind.
The friend who is caught between religious fear and genuine spiritual hunger.
The family member who has been told that their suffering proves God has abandoned them.
There is a reason this ministry exists.
There are people who cannot afford a library of Christian books but are hungry to understand Scripture.
There are believers who are spiritually exhausted and need sound teaching that does not exploit their pain.
That is why we continue creating and sharing Christ-centered resources.
These resources are part of a larger mission to make biblical encouragement and discipleship more accessible.
And if this work has strengthened your faith, helped you understand Scripture, or encouraged you to return to Jesus, I want to invite you to become part of sustaining it.
It is not.
He does not.
But because voluntary generosity can be one meaningful way to participate in Gospel-centered work.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
Christian generosity must never be driven by manipulation or fear.
If you are already faithfully supporting your local church, caring for your family, or facing financial hardship, please do not feel pressured to give beyond your means.
It can be part of your personal generosity, but it should not automatically be equated with a biblically required tithe or presented as a substitute for your responsibilities to your local church.
What makes the gift meaningful is not religious pressure.
It is a willing heart that wants to help others hear the truth of Jesus Christ.
It is the opportunity to help this ministry continue placing Christ-centered teaching before people who may be one honest encounter with Scripture away from turning back to God.
Tell someone who is struggling with faith that they are welcome to learn, ask questions, and encounter the truth of Scripture.
Pray that every article, every resource, and every testimony will point beyond the ministry itself and toward Jesus Christ.
Because the mission is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The mission is to make Christ known.
And that brings us to the truth I want to leave with you.
The Christian life is not a promise that darkness will never approach you.
It is a life of belonging to the One whom darkness cannot overcome.
There may be temptations you must resist.
Sins you must confess.
Wounds that require time and care.
Spiritual attacks against which you must stand firm.
Questions you cannot immediately answer.
But none of these should replace the central question of the Gospel.
Do you know Jesus Christ?
Have you turned from sin and placed your trust in Him?
Are you learning to follow Him, not merely seeking relief from fear?
Because one day the greatest concern will not be how many spiritual battles you survived.
It will be whether you belonged to the Savior.
And if you are not yet His, the invitation of the Gospel is before you.
Repent and believe in Jesus Christ.
Come to Him with your sin, your questions, your shame, and your need for mercy.
You cannot save yourself.
But Christ is able to save those who come to God through Him.
And if you already belong to Him, do not allow fear of the enemy to become greater in your mind than confidence in your Lord.
Stand in truth.
Walk in repentance.
Remain in prayer.
Cling to Scripture.
Love the people around you.
Seek wise help when you need it.
And keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because the final chapter of the believer's story will not be written by a demon.
It will not be written by shame.
It will not be written by the worst thing you have ever done.
For those redeemed by Christ, the final hope is resurrection, restoration, and everlasting life with the Lord.
And that is a hope worth sharing.
A hope worth living for.
A hope worth carrying into a world that desperately needs more than another frightening headline.
So when someone asks you, "Can Christians have demons?" do not rush to frighten them or dismiss their suffering.
Open the Scriptures.
Explain what God has clearly revealed.
Be humble about what remains disputed.
And above all, tell them about Jesus.
Tell them about the cross.
Tell them about repentance.
Tell them about forgiveness.
Tell them about the empty tomb.
Tell them that the One who has authority over every unclean spirit is also the Savior who welcomes repentant sinners.
Tell them that grace does not leave us where it finds us.
It brings us into the light.
And if there is one truth you carry away from this article, let it be this:
The darkness may have been part of your battle, but through Jesus Christ, it does not have to become the name of your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WHY HAVE YOU DECEIVED ME?” — THE NIGHT JACOB TASTED THE PAIN HE HAD ONCE GIVEN SOMEONE ELSE
paragraphs: “WHY HAVE YOU DECEIVED ME?” — THE NIGHT JACOB TASTED THE PAIN HE HAD ONCE GIVEN SOMEONE ELSE

He stole a blessing through deception. Years later, he woke up beside the wrong bride. But beneath one of Genesis's most shocking betrayals lies a terrifyingly personal question: What happens when God allows us to recognize the very wounds we once inflicted on others? And can His grace still rewrite the story of someone who has spent years running from the truth?
There are moments in life when the most painful thing that happens to you is not simply what somebody did.
It is what their actions suddenly make you remember about yourself.
A lie you once told.
A person you manipulated.
Someone who trusted you until you gave them a reason not to.
A heart you broke and never went back to repair.
You moved on. You convinced yourself that chapter was closed. You buried the memory beneath years of busyness, religious activity, responsibilities, and carefully rehearsed explanations.
And then one day, somebody does something to you that feels painfully familiar.
Suddenly, you understand the tears you never saw.
The betrayal you once minimized.
The damage you once justified.
And somewhere between your anger and your heartbreak, a question begins rising from a place you thought had gone silent.
Have I ever made somebody feel this way?
That is where we find Jacob.
Not in a palace. Not on a battlefield. Not standing before a congregation.
But in the morning after his wedding.
A morning that should have been filled with celebration.
Instead, it became a confrontation with deception.
Genesis 29:25 records one of the most startling awakenings in Scripture:

“And it came to pass, that in the morning, behold, it was Leah: and he said to Laban, What is this thou hast done unto me? did not I serve with thee for Rachel? wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?” (KJV)
Read that final question slowly.
Wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?
In ordinary English:
“Why have you deceived me?”
Jacob was furious.
He had worked seven years for Rachel. Seven years of labor. Seven years of expectation. Seven years of loving someone he believed would become his wife.
Genesis 29:20 tells us those years seemed like only a few days because of his love for her.
Imagine that kind of anticipation.
He could endure the exhausting work because he believed something beautiful was waiting at the end.
Then the wedding arrived.
The celebration took place.
Night fell.
And Laban brought Leah, his older daughter, to Jacob instead of Rachel.
The biblical account does not explain exactly how Laban concealed the substitution. We should not invent details Scripture does not give us.
But it tells us enough.
Jacob did not realize what had happened until morning.
And when daylight exposed the deception, the man who had once deceived his own father found himself crying out against a deceiver.
There is something almost unbearable about that moment.
Because years earlier, another man had been deceived in a deeply personal encounter.
That man was Isaac.
And the deceiver was Jacob.
Before Jacob ever met Laban, he had participated in a scheme with his mother, Rebekah, to obtain the blessing Isaac intended to give Esau.
Isaac was old. His eyesight had failed. He could no longer distinguish his sons by sight.
