Somewhere, a religious person is polishing the stones they intend to throw, forgetting how much mercy they themselves have received.
And somewhere, the Gospel is still announcing the same astonishing invitation.
Come to Christ.
Bring your sin into His light.
Receive His mercy through faith.
Turn from what is destroying you.
Follow the Savior who gave Himself for you.
You do not have to pretend your darkness is light.
And you do not have to believe your darkness is greater than His grace.
Jesus does not love you because your sin is harmless. He loves you so deeply that He gave Himself to save you from it.
That is the love worth proclaiming.
That is the truth worth standing for.
That is the grace worth sharing.
And that is why we will keep pointing people beyond the scandal of their past toward the redeeming power of Jesus Christ.
The stones people remember throwing may tell the story of your shame, but the nail-scarred hands of Jesus proclaim that shame does not have to be the final chapter.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WE WRESTLE NOT AGAINST FLESH AND BLOOD — SO WHY ARE YOU DESTROYING THE PEOPLE YOU WERE CALLED TO LOVE?
paragraphs: WE WRESTLE NOT AGAINST FLESH AND BLOOD — SO WHY ARE YOU DESTROYING THE PEOPLE YOU WERE CALLED TO LOVE?

The enemy has convinced too many Christians to fight their spouses, abandon their families, attack their brothers and sisters, and hate the very people Jesus died to save. But what if the person you have been fighting is not your real enemy—and the battle you keep losing is happening somewhere you have forgotten to look?
There is something heartbreaking happening in Christian homes, churches, friendships, and families.
And the frightening part?
Some of us are calling it spiritual warfare.
A husband walks out of the bedroom after another argument, convinced his wife is the reason he has no peace.
A wife lies awake beside a man she once prayed to marry, silently wondering how someone she loves so deeply can make her feel so alone.
A mother cries because her child no longer wants anything to do with God.
Two believers stop speaking because one misunderstood a message, one refused to apologize, and both are waiting for the other to humble themselves first.
A church splits.
A friendship dies.
A family stops gathering around the same table.
And somewhere in the middle of all that pain, people who carry Bibles in their hands begin carrying bitterness in their hearts.
They still pray.
They still worship.
They still share Scriptures.
But mention a certain person's name, and something inside them changes.
Their voice hardens.
Their compassion disappears.
Their wounds begin speaking louder than their faith.
And perhaps the most dangerous part is that they can explain exactly why their anger is justified.
Because they were hurt.
Because they were betrayed.
Because they were disrespected.
Because somebody lied.
Because somebody who should have protected them became the reason they needed healing.
And maybe that somebody is the very person who came to your mind when you read the title.
Don't rush past that.
Because what comes next may challenge the way you have been looking at your pain.
You can be genuinely wounded by another human being and still be deceived about who your ultimate enemy is.
The hurt may be real.
The betrayal may be real.
The injustice may be real.
But the person responsible for that hurt is still a human being made in the image of God.
And if you forget that, the wound someone gave you can become the place where bitterness begins reshaping you.
The apostle Paul wrote something that many Christians have memorized but far fewer have allowed to govern their relationships.
"For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places."
— Ephesians 6:12, King James Version
Read those first few words again.
We wrestle not against flesh and blood.
Not your husband.
Not your wife.
Not your rebellious child.
Not the friend who betrayed your confidence.
Not the church member who embarrassed you.
Not the person who mocked your faith.
Not even the person who openly hates you.
Paul was not saying that human beings never commit evil or that wrongdoing should go unanswered.
He was revealing something deeper about the nature of the Christian struggle.
Behind the visible conflicts of life, believers face an unseen spiritual opposition that cannot be defeated by hatred, revenge, manipulation, or human strength.
And if you fight a spiritual battle with the weapons of your wounded flesh, you may end up destroying relationships while believing you are defending righteousness.
The original Greek makes Paul's words even more striking.
The expression translated "we wrestle" comes from the Greek word πάλη (palē), meaning wrestling or struggle.
Paul uses the language of close combat.
Not a distant disagreement.
Not a casual inconvenience.
A struggle.
Something exhausting.
Something that demands endurance.
Something that can leave you feeling as though you have nothing left.
But notice the distinction Paul makes.
He writes:
οὐκ ἔστιν ἡμῖν ἡ πάλη πρὸς αἷμα καὶ σάρκα
ouk estin hēmin hē palē pros haima kai sarka
Literally, the wording conveys: "Our wrestling is not against blood and flesh."
The Greek expression αἷμα καὶ σάρκα (haima kai sarka) refers to human beings in their mortal, bodily existence.
Paul is drawing a line between human opponents and the spiritual powers that oppose God's purposes.
He is not denying human responsibility.
He is identifying the deeper nature of the believer's warfare.
That distinction matters.
Because there is a terrible difference between confronting someone's sin and deciding that the person themselves is beyond redemption.
There is a difference between establishing a necessary boundary and allowing hatred to become your identity.
There is a difference between seeking justice and secretly craving revenge.
And there is a difference between discerning evil and treating every difficult person as though they are possessed by it.
Not every argument is a demonic attack.
Not every disagreement is spiritual oppression.
Sometimes people are selfish.
Sometimes people misunderstand each other.
Sometimes trauma affects the way someone responds.
Sometimes pride keeps two people from saying the words that could begin a difficult conversation.
Sometimes we are simply wrong.
And sometimes the person we have spent weeks praying for God to change is not the only person who needs to repent.
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is much easier to pray, "Lord, expose what is wrong with them," than to pray, "Lord, show me what is wrong in me."
It is easier to identify someone else's arrogance than to recognize our own.
It is easier to remember every harsh word they spoke than to admit the cruelty of the words we spoke afterward.
It is easier to ask God to defend us than to surrender our desire to punish them.
And if that sentence made you uncomfortable, perhaps it touched something that deserves prayer rather than another excuse.
Jesus did not call His followers to pretend evil does not exist.
He called them to refuse to become evil in response.
"Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you."
— Matthew 5:44, KJV
Think about how radical that command is.
Jesus did not say, "Love only the people who understand you."
He did not say, "Pray only for the people who apologize."
He did not say, "Show kindness only when the other person deserves it."
He told His disciples to love their enemies.
Not because their enemies were innocent.
Not because their actions were acceptable.
But because the children of God are called to reflect the character of their Father.
And the Father is merciful.
Even when we have been difficult to love.
Even when we have resisted His correction.
Even when we have given Him every reason to judge us.
There is a moment in the Gospel that exposes just how different the kingdom of Jesus is from the instincts of our wounded hearts.
It happened in a garden.
The night Jesus was betrayed.
Judas arrived with the crowd sent to arrest Him.
There were weapons.
There was tension.
There was treachery.
And Peter, watching the situation unfold, drew a sword.
He struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his right ear.
John tells us the servant's name was Malchus.
And then Jesus did something that should make every angry Christian reconsider what it means to fight for God.
He stopped Peter.
"Put up thy sword into the sheath: the cup which my Father hath given me, shall I not drink it?"
— John 18:11, KJV
Luke also records that Jesus touched the wounded man's ear and healed him (Luke 22:51).
Let that scene settle into your heart.
Peter was ready to injure someone in defense of Jesus.
Jesus was willing to heal the person Peter had injured.
Peter saw an enemy standing in front of him.
Jesus saw a human being whose suffering He could relieve.
And here is what makes the moment even more astonishing.
Jesus was not confused about what was happening.
He knew He was being betrayed.
He knew He was being arrested unjustly.
He knew the suffering ahead of Him.
He was not surrendering because He lacked power.
He was submitting to the Father's redemptive purpose.
The Son of God did not need Peter's violence to secure His victory.
And sometimes, neither does the truth need our cruelty to defend it.
That does not mean Christians must remain silent when confronted with evil.
It means our methods must not contradict the Lord we claim to serve.
If defending your faith requires you to abandon the character of Christ, something has gone terribly wrong in the way you are fighting.
Perhaps you need to hear that because you have been fighting for your marriage with insults.
Fighting for your reputation with gossip.
Fighting for your ministry with resentment.
Fighting for your dignity by humiliating someone else.
Fighting for the truth while refusing to speak it in love.
And somewhere along the way, the fight became more important than the people involved.
You began measuring victory by whether the other person suffered.
Whether they were embarrassed.
Whether they finally admitted you were right.
Whether everybody else discovered what they did to you.
But the kingdom of God does not define victory that way.
Romans 12:21 says:
"Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good."
Not surrender to evil.
Not excuse evil.
Not conceal evil.
Overcome it.
And overcome it with good.
That may mean speaking the truth when silence would be easier.
It may mean confronting sin without humiliating the sinner.
It may mean refusing to participate in gossip even when you possess information that could ruin someone's reputation.
It may mean protecting a child from a dangerous person.
It may mean leaving an abusive environment, seeking help, and allowing appropriate authorities to intervene.
It may mean telling someone, "I forgive you, but I cannot trust you with the same access to my life right now."
Because forgiveness and reconciliation are not identical.
Forgiveness releases the claim to personal vengeance.
Reconciliation involves the rebuilding of a relationship, which may require repentance, truth, accountability, and demonstrated change.
Trust is not automatically restored because someone says, "I'm sorry."
And biblical peacemaking does not require victims to return to danger.
When Paul says, "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men" (Romans 12:18), those opening words matter.
If it be possible.
Peace is worth pursuing.
But peace cannot always be established by one person alone.
You can refuse hatred without pretending someone is safe.
You can pray for an enemy while maintaining distance.
You can desire someone's repentance without granting them permission to continue harming you.
And you can love someone without allowing them to control you.
Jesus Himself sometimes withdrew from those who sought to harm Him.
Love is not the absence of discernment.
It is the refusal to surrender your heart to hatred.
But there is another side to this message.
And for some of us, it is the harder side.
What if the person who has become difficult to love is not an abuser or a dangerous enemy?
What if they are simply someone who disappointed you?
Someone who disagreed with you?
Someone who did not respond the way you expected?
Someone who failed to read your mind?
Someone who made a mistake and has been trying to make it right?
What if the relationship is dying not because reconciliation is impossible, but because pride has made humility feel unbearable?
What if you have been calling it discernment when it is actually resentment?
What if you have been calling it protecting your peace when you are really punishing someone with silence?
What if you have been calling it standing for truth when you are simply refusing to listen?
Those questions are not accusations.
They are invitations to examine our hearts before God.
Because the Bible warns us about the destructive power of unresolved anger.
"Neither give place to the devil."
— Ephesians 4:27, KJV
That verse appears in a passage where Paul addresses anger, truthful speech, work, kindness, forgiveness, and the way believers treat one another.
The Greek word translated "place" is τόπος (topos).
It can mean a place, space, or opportunity.
In this context, Paul warns believers not to give the devil an opening through sinful responses to anger.
He is not teaching that every angry emotion is demonic.
In fact, the preceding verse says:
"Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath."
— Ephesians 4:26, KJV
Anger itself can be a response to genuine injustice.
But anger can also become a doorway to sinful behavior when it is cherished, weaponized, or allowed to rule the heart.
And that is where a spiritual battle can quietly become a personal tragedy.
The original injury may have been caused by someone else.
But what you choose to cultivate afterward matters.
Bitterness does not always arrive looking like bitterness.
Sometimes it arrives looking like a perfectly reasonable decision never to forgive.
Sometimes it sounds like rehearsing the same offense every night.
Sometimes it feels like satisfaction when the person who hurt you experiences misfortune.
Sometimes it hides behind a smile at church while silently hoping another believer will fail.
And sometimes it becomes so familiar that you stop noticing how much space it occupies in your life.
You can become so consumed with proving that somebody else was wrong that you stop asking God to make you right before Him.
And the enemy does not need to make you abandon your Bible if he can persuade you to ignore the parts that confront your hatred.
That is why the spiritual armor Paul describes in Ephesians 6 matters so deeply.
Truth.
Righteousness.
The readiness of the gospel of peace.
Faith.
Salvation.
The word of God.
Prayer.
Notice what is missing.
Revenge.
Cruelty.
Character assassination.
Pride.
Contempt.
The weapons Paul describes are not permission to wage war against people.
They are God's provision for standing firm against spiritual evil.
The believer does not overcome darkness by becoming another expression of it.
And nowhere is that truth more clearly displayed than at the cross.
Consider what happened to Jesus.
He was betrayed by a friend.
Denied by a disciple.
Abandoned by many who had followed Him.
Falsely accused.
Mocked.
Struck.
Condemned.
Crucified.
If anyone could have claimed the right to retaliate, it was the sinless Son of God.
And yet, as Luke records His crucifixion, Jesus prayed:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
— Luke 23:34, KJV

A textual note matters here: this prayer appears in the traditional Greek text and many ancient manuscripts, while some early manuscripts omit it. It is preserved in the King James Version and many modern Bibles, sometimes with a manuscript note.
The prayer expresses the mercy that shines throughout the Gospel accounts.
Jesus did not deny the wickedness of what was being done.
He did not call injustice righteousness.
He did not suggest that sin was harmless.
He bore the consequences of human sin while fulfilling the Father's saving purpose.
And the cross reveals something that human pride finds difficult to accept.
We are not merely people who have been wounded by the sins of others.
We are also sinners who need mercy ourselves.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
Not after we became deserving.
Not after we repaired every wrong.
Not after we proved ourselves worthy of forgiveness.
While we were yet sinners.
Christ died for us.
And a few verses later, Paul says that we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son while we were enemies (Romans 5:10).
Enemies.
That word should silence some of our self-righteousness.
Because before we ask how God could expect us to love difficult people, we should remember how merciful He has been to us.
We were not saved because we were easier to love than everyone else.
We were saved by grace.
Through faith.
Because Jesus Christ did what we could never do for ourselves.
He lived without sin.
He gave Himself for sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
That is the Gospel.
Not a message that simply teaches wounded people how to behave better.
Not a religious strategy for maintaining pleasant relationships.
It is the announcement that God has acted in Jesus Christ to rescue sinners, defeat the powers of evil, forgive the repentant, and make new life possible.
And that new life changes how we see other people.
The person who hurt you is not automatically innocent.
But neither are they beyond God's ability to save.
The person you dislike may still be someone Christ is calling to repentance.
The family member who has wandered from faith may still return.
The friend who failed you may still learn humility.
And the person whose name causes your heart to tighten may be someone you need to entrust to God's justice rather than your own revenge.
You do not know every chapter God may yet write in another person's life.
Consider Saul of Tarsus.
Before he became known as the apostle Paul, he persecuted the church.
He approved of Stephen's death.
He entered homes and dragged away believers.
He threatened followers of Jesus.
If you had been among the Christians living in fear of Saul, you would have had very real reasons to regard him as dangerous.
And he was.
The early believers did not invent that danger.
But on the road to Damascus, the risen Jesus confronted Saul.
And the persecutor became a preacher of the Gospel he once tried to destroy.
That transformation did not erase the suffering Saul had caused.
Nor did it mean believers were required to trust him immediately.
Acts 9:26 records that the disciples in Jerusalem were afraid of him and did not believe he was a disciple.
Their caution was understandable.
Barnabas later helped them understand what God had done.
This is what grace looks like when it enters a story marked by scandal.
It does not pretend the past never happened.
It does not call evil good.
It confronts sin and opens the door to transformation.
The same man who once pursued Christians became a servant of the Christ he had opposed.
The same hands associated with persecution would eventually write letters encouraging believers to love one another.
And the same Paul who knew the violence of religious zeal would write:
Do you see it?
The man who once fought people in the name of God learned that the true battle could not be won by destroying human beings.
That is the kind of grace that rewrites a life.
And maybe, just maybe, it is the grace your own story desperately needs.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying years of resentment toward a parent who never apologized.
Perhaps you have been praying for a spouse while quietly becoming bitter toward them.
Perhaps someone in your church betrayed your trust, and you have been unable to separate their actions from your understanding of God.
Perhaps you were wounded by a Christian who spoke beautifully about love but treated you cruelly.
Perhaps you have been so disappointed by people who claim to represent Jesus that you are beginning to pull away from Jesus Himself.
If that is you, please hear this.
The failure of someone who bears Christ's name is not the measure of Christ's character.
Jesus is not the hypocrisy that wounded you.
He is not the cruelty that was justified with Scripture.
He is not the manipulation that was disguised as spiritual authority.
He is not the betrayal that made you afraid to trust again.
Look at Him in the Gospels.
Look at how He treated the broken.
How He confronted the proud.
How He welcomed repentant sinners.
How He defended the vulnerable.
How He spoke truth without surrendering to wickedness.
How He went to the cross for people who could never save themselves.
That is the Savior you are being invited to follow.
Not a perfect religious community.
Not a flawless spiritual leader.
Not a life free from human disappointment.
Jesus Christ.
And He is worthy of your trust even when people have proven unworthy of it.
Maybe you have been waiting for the person who hurt you to change before you allow God to begin changing you.
Maybe you have been telling yourself that healing cannot start until you receive an apology.
Maybe you believe that if you stop rehearsing what happened, the injustice will somehow disappear.
But releasing vengeance does not erase the truth.
God sees what happened.
He sees what was done in secret.
He sees the tears nobody else noticed.
He sees the years you spent trying to understand why someone you loved treated you that way.
And He does not ask you to call darkness light.
He calls you to bring the darkness into His presence.
To seek truth.
To pursue justice where justice is needed.
To establish boundaries where boundaries are necessary.
To repent where you have sinned.
And to surrender the final judgment of souls to Him.
That surrender is not weakness.
It is faith.
Faith that God's justice is greater than your revenge.
Faith that His mercy is greater than your bitterness.
Faith that your future does not have to remain chained to what somebody did in your past.
And faith that Jesus can transform even the parts of your heart that have become hard through suffering.
Perhaps the most important battle you face today is not another argument with the person who wounded you.
Perhaps it is the battle to remain faithful to Christ while carrying a wound that still hurts.
To speak truth without hatred.
To protect yourself without becoming cruel.
To seek reconciliation without compromising safety.
To forgive without denying reality.
To love without surrendering discernment.
To resist the devil without demonizing human beings.
And to remember that you, too, stand in desperate need of grace.
James 4:7 says:
"Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you."
Notice the order.
Submit to God.
Then resist the devil.
We cannot successfully resist evil while proudly refusing the authority of the Lord.
And one of the hardest forms of submission is allowing God to confront the anger we have grown comfortable defending.
So before you send that message...
Before you post that accusation...
Before you tell another person what somebody did...
Before you decide that reconciliation is impossible...
Before you use the Bible to justify the resentment you have been feeding...
Ask yourself something.
Am I trying to honor Jesus?
Or am I trying to make somebody pay?
Am I pursuing truth?
Or am I pursuing humiliation?
Am I protecting what is right?
Or am I protecting my pride?
Am I resisting evil?
Or am I allowing evil to reshape the way I treat people?
And if you discover something in your heart that needs repentance, do not run from God.
Run toward Him.
Because conviction is not an invitation to despair.
It is an invitation to return.
First John 1:9 reminds believers:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
There is mercy for the wounded person who has become bitter.
There is mercy for the proud person who finally admits they were wrong.
There is mercy for the Christian who has been using spiritual language to disguise personal resentment.
There is mercy for the one who needs to apologize.
There is mercy for the one who needs to establish a boundary.
And there is mercy for the person who has been running from God because the failures of people made faith feel unbearable.
That mercy has a name.
Jesus Christ.
And He does not merely offer to improve your behavior.
He calls you to die to the old life and walk in newness of life through Him.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior will never be simply, "Be a better person."
Our message is that sinners need a Savior.
Wounded hearts need the truth of Christ.
Broken relationships need more than religious appearances.
And a world exhausted by hatred needs to encounter the Gospel of reconciliation.
Second Corinthians 5:18 teaches that God reconciled us to Himself through Jesus Christ and entrusted the ministry of reconciliation to His servants.
That ministry does not mean every broken human relationship will be restored.
But it does mean that people who have received reconciliation with God should not treat hatred as their permanent home.
We are ambassadors of Christ.
Not ambassadors of resentment.
Not ambassadors of revenge.
Not ambassadors of endless arguments.
We belong to the One who makes all things new.
And if this message has reached a place in your heart that you have been trying to keep hidden, I want to invite you to do something more meaningful than simply agreeing with it.
Be honest before God.
You do not have to tell strangers every detail of your pain.
You do not have to name the person who hurt you.
You do not have to expose a private family struggle.
There is no shame in admitting that following Jesus can be difficult when the heart is hurting.
Sometimes those few honest words become the beginning of a conversation, a prayer, or an encouragement another believer desperately needs.
Maybe they will discover that repentance is not humiliation.
It is a return to the God whose mercy is greater than our sin.
There is also someone in your life who may need to read this message today.
Perhaps it is a family member caught in an exhausting conflict.
A friend who is slowly losing faith because of what another Christian did.
A couple who have forgotten they are meant to face their problems together rather than treat each other as the problem.
A believer who has confused righteous conviction with personal hatred.
Or someone who has been hurt so deeply that they no longer believe grace can reach their situation.
Not because every sentence will feel comfortable today.

But because the next time anger rises, the next time betrayal stings, or the next time you are tempted to make another human being the ultimate enemy, you may need to remember what Scripture actually says.
We want this community to be a place where people encounter biblical truth, genuine encouragement, repentance, healing, and the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
Not shallow inspiration that disappears when life becomes difficult.
But spiritual nourishment that calls us back to the Savior.
These resources are meant to help believers study Scripture, deepen their faith, strengthen their families, and continue learning long after they finish reading an article.
And if Gospel Warrior has become part of your spiritual journey, I would also like to invite you to consider something prayerfully.
Not because you can purchase God's favor.
Not because a monthly payment makes you more faithful than a believer who cannot afford one.
And certainly not because the grace of Jesus can ever be bought.
The Gospel is a gift.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not by works or financial contributions (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Paul speaks about supporting those who proclaim the Gospel in 1 Corinthians 9:14, and 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should come from the heart, not from pressure or compulsion.
These products can be reminders of the truths we want to carry into ordinary life, but they are never substitutes for Scripture, prayer, fellowship, or obedience to Jesus.
It is an opportunity to help make biblical encouragement and discipleship resources available to more people.
And our prayer is that every resource, every article, every testimony, and every act of generosity would ultimately direct attention away from ourselves and toward Jesus Christ.
Because the mission is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The mission is to make Christ known.
To remind the ashamed that repentance is possible.
To remind the broken that grace is real.
To remind the bitter that freedom does not have to wait for revenge.
To remind the wandering that the Father still calls sinners to return.
And to remind the church that we cannot proclaim the Gospel of reconciliation while celebrating the destruction of the people Christ commands us to love.
Now, before you leave this article, there is one last picture I want you to carry with you.
Imagine standing before Jesus with every wound you have carried.
Every betrayal.
Every unanswered question.
Every cruel word.
Every sleepless night.
Every moment you wondered whether you would ever be whole again.
Imagine bringing Him the names of the people who hurt you.
And imagine also bringing Him the moments when your own heart responded with sin.
Not to deny what happened.
Not to minimize your suffering.
But to place the entire truth before the One who sees perfectly and judges righteously.
You do not need to imagine that Jesus will ask you to pretend evil was good.
He never does.
But Scripture assures us that the final victory belongs to Him.
He will judge evil.
He will make all things new.
And those who belong to Him will not carry the wounds of this fallen world forever.
Revelation 21:4 promises that God will wipe away every tear and that death, sorrow, crying, and pain will finally pass away.
That is where Christian hope leads.
Not to endless conflict.
Not to permanent bitterness.
Not to a life defined by the worst thing somebody did to you.
But to the risen Christ, who will bring His people into the fullness of His kingdom.
Until that day, we wrestle.
We pray.
We resist evil.
We speak truth.
We seek justice.
We forgive as Christ has forgiven us.
We repent when our own hearts go astray.
We love even when love is costly.
And we remember that the person standing in front of us is not the ultimate enemy Scripture tells us to fight.
The devil would gladly see human relationships destroyed by lies, hatred, temptation, and sin.
But Jesus calls His people to stand firm in truth, righteousness, faith, prayer, and the Gospel of peace.
So put down the weapon of personal vengeance.
Not the truth.
Not wisdom.
Not the boundaries that keep you safe.
Not the courage to confront wrongdoing.
Put down the hatred that has begun to poison your own heart.
And take up the armor God has actually given you.
Because the cross of Jesus Christ has already revealed that the greatest victory is not achieved by becoming more ruthless than our enemies.
It is found in the saving work of the One who conquered sin and death through His sacrifice and resurrection.
If you have never surrendered your life to Jesus, come to Him in repentance and faith.
If you have wandered, return.
If you have sinned, confess it.
If you have been wounded, bring your suffering to Him and seek the help you need.
If you have been consumed by bitterness, ask Him to teach you the freedom of entrusting justice to God.
And if there is a relationship where humble, safe, truthful reconciliation is possible, perhaps today is the day to take the first faithful step.
You may not be able to change the other person.
You may not be able to rewrite what happened.
You may not receive the apology you hoped for.
But through Jesus Christ, your story does not have to end where the injury began.
That is our hope.
That is the Gospel we proclaim.
That is why we keep pointing people back to the cross.
Because no scandal is greater than the power of Christ to redeem a repentant sinner.
No human failure can cancel the truth of His resurrection.
And no darkness can finally overcome the kingdom of the risen King.
The person who wounded you may have written one of the darkest chapters of your life—but do not hand them the pen that writes the rest of your soul.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT IF THE CHRISTIANITY YOU INHERITED IS NOT THE CHRISTIANITY JESUS ACTUALLY TAUGHT?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE CHRISTIANITY YOU INHERITED IS NOT THE CHRISTIANITY JESUS ACTUALLY TAUGHT?

You can inherit a Bible, memorize the right prayers, attend church your entire life, and still miss the heart of the Savior you claim to follow. The most frightening deception may not be the faith you rejected—but the faith you never thought to question.
There is a question that can shake a person's entire spiritual foundation.
Not because it attacks Christianity.
But because it forces us to ask whether we have truly understood Christ.
What if some of the things you were taught to call Christianity were never actually taught by Jesus?
What if the faith you inherited was a mixture of biblical truth, family tradition, cultural expectations, human opinions, and religious habits that nobody ever encouraged you to examine?
What if you have spent years defending things Jesus never commanded while quietly neglecting the very things He said mattered most?
And what if, after all those years of attending church, singing worship songs, quoting Scripture, and trying to be a good Christian, you finally opened the Gospels with fresh eyes...
And discovered a Jesus who was far more holy, far more compassionate, far more confronting, and far more beautiful than the version you had been given?
That discovery could break your heart.
It could also save you from spending the rest of your life confusing religious familiarity with genuine discipleship.
Because there is something more dangerous than not knowing what Jesus taught.
It is being so certain that you already know Him that you stop listening to Him.
And before you dismiss this as another criticism of the Church, understand something important.
This is not an invitation to abandon Christianity.
It is an invitation to return to Christ.
Not to a fashionable reinterpretation of Jesus.
Not to a version of Him that approves of everything we want.
Not to a faith without holiness, repentance, obedience, or truth.
But to the Jesus who actually walked the roads of Galilee, touched the untouchable, confronted religious hypocrisy, called sinners to repentance, died for our sins, and rose again.
The Jesus revealed in Scripture.
The Jesus who is still calling people to follow Him.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part of that invitation is this:
He may be asking you to surrender some things you have always called sacred.
Not because they are necessarily evil.
But because they have quietly taken the place that belongs to Him alone.
Imagine a child growing up in a Christian home.
Every Sunday, the family attends church.
The child learns when to stand, when to sit, when to bow, and when to say amen.
They learn which clothes are appropriate, which people are considered respectable, which questions are discouraged, and which behaviors make someone look like a good Christian.
They learn Bible verses.
They learn worship songs.
They learn the language of faith.
But somewhere along the way, they also learn something nobody intended to teach them.
They learn that looking holy can sometimes matter more than being honest.
They learn to hide their struggles because struggling might disappoint the people who admire their faith.
They learn that doubt is dangerous, confession is embarrassing, and asking difficult questions can make others uncomfortable.
So they become skilled at appearing spiritually healthy.
They know how to smile in church while falling apart at home.
They know how to say, "God is good," while secretly wondering whether God still wants anything to do with them.
They know how to encourage everyone else while carrying a shame they have never dared to confess.
And eventually, they begin to wonder:
Is this really what following Jesus is supposed to feel like?
Maybe you know that person.
Maybe you raised that person.
Maybe you married that person.
Maybe you are that person.
And if you are, please keep reading.
Because the Jesus of the Gospels has something to say to people who are exhausted from carrying a religion that has become heavier than the hope it was supposed to proclaim.
In Matthew 11:28, Jesus says:
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." (KJV)
Notice what He does not say.
He does not say, "Come to Me once you have convinced everybody you are spiritually successful."
He does not say, "Come to Me when your reputation is repaired."
He does not say, "Come to Me after you have learned how to hide your weaknesses."
He says, "Come unto me."
The invitation is personal.
The Savior is the destination.
And the rest He promises is not permission to remain enslaved to sin. It is the beginning of learning from the One whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light.
Jesus continues by calling us to take His yoke and learn from Him.
He does not remove discipleship.
He rescues us from trying to carry it without Him.
That distinction changes everything.
Because Christianity was never meant to be a performance in which exhausted sinners compete to look the most redeemed.
It is the life of people who have been rescued by grace and are learning to follow their Redeemer.
And that brings us to a confrontation Jesus Himself made.
In Mark 7, religious leaders questioned why His disciples did not follow certain traditional washing practices.
Jesus did not condemn every tradition.
He confronted something much more serious.
Human traditions had been elevated in ways that displaced God's commandments.
In Mark 7:8, He declares:
"For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men." (KJV)
Let those words settle.
It is possible to be fiercely loyal to a religious tradition while becoming disobedient to the God that tradition claims to honor.
The Greek text uses the word paradosis (παράδοσις), meaning something handed down or transmitted.
A tradition.
An inheritance.
Something received from those who came before us.
Tradition itself is not automatically sinful. The New Testament also speaks positively about faithful apostolic teaching handed down to believers, as in 2 Thessalonians 2:15.
The problem is not that something was inherited.
The problem is what happens when what was inherited contradicts, obscures, or replaces what God has revealed.
That is why the question is not simply, "What did my parents believe?"
Or, "What has my denomination always practiced?"
Or even, "What does my pastor say?"
The deeper question is:
What does Scripture actually teach, and am I willing to obey it even when it challenges what I have always assumed?
This is not rebellion against godly authority.
It is submission to the highest authority.
And the Bereans in Acts 17:11 give us a beautiful example. They received the apostolic message eagerly while examining the Scriptures to see whether what they heard was true.
They were neither blindly gullible nor proudly dismissive.
They listened.
They examined.
They sought the truth.
Imagine what would happen if more Christians approached their faith that way.
Not with arrogance.
Not with a hunger to expose everyone else's errors.
But with an open Bible and a humble prayer:
"Lord, if I have misunderstood You, teach me. If I have defended something You never commanded, correct me. If I have ignored something You clearly said, give me the courage to obey."
That prayer may be more costly than we realize.
Because sometimes the greatest obstacle to spiritual growth is not ignorance.
It is the fear of discovering that we have been wrong.
And Jesus was never afraid to confront that fear.
Consider the people who made Him angry.
Not every religious leader was corrupt. Some sought Him sincerely, and others eventually believed.
But the Gospels repeatedly show Jesus confronting leaders who used religious authority without reflecting God's heart.
In Matthew 23:23, He rebukes those who meticulously tithed small herbs while neglecting the weightier matters of the law: judgment, mercy, and faith.
He does not dismiss obedience.
He exposes selective obedience.
The kind that becomes meticulous about visible details while remaining careless about the condition of the heart.
The kind that can calculate an offering but overlook a wounded neighbor.
The kind that can defend a religious institution while refusing to show mercy to a repentant sinner.
And before we point at the Pharisees, perhaps we should ask whether we have ever done something similar.
Have you ever been more disturbed by someone's clothing than by their suffering?
More concerned about the appearance of your church than the spiritual condition of its people?
More eager to win a theological argument than to speak the truth in love?
More comfortable discussing another person's sin than confessing your own?
These questions are not meant to erase biblical standards.
They are meant to expose how easily we can demand standards from others while avoiding the searching work of God in ourselves.
Jesus never taught that holiness and mercy are enemies.
He embodied both.
He could expose sin without becoming cruel.
He could extend compassion without pretending sin was harmless.
He could welcome the broken without affirming everything that had broken them.
Look at the woman caught in adultery in John 7:53–8:11, a passage whose manuscript history deserves honest acknowledgment because it is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts.

The account has nevertheless been deeply influential in Christian teaching, and its portrayal of mercy alongside a call to leave sin is consistent with themes firmly established elsewhere in the Gospels.
The woman stands exposed.
Accused.
Humiliated.
Surrounded by people who seem more interested in using her situation as a weapon against Jesus than in restoring a human being.
And Jesus refuses to participate in their trap.
He exposes the accusers' own moral vulnerability.
Then He speaks words of mercy and moral seriousness.
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." (John 8:11, KJV)
Do you see it?
No permission to celebrate sin.
No delight in public humiliation.
Mercy.
And a call to transformation.
The Savior does not have to choose between truth and compassion.
He is full of grace and truth.
And perhaps some of us have inherited a Christianity that emphasizes one while treating the other as a threat.
Some have been taught a version of faith so harsh that every mistake feels like the end of their relationship with God.
Others have been taught a version so permissive that repentance is barely mentioned and obedience sounds unnecessary.
Neither distortion does justice to the Gospel.
Grace does not mean sin is insignificant.
The cross reveals how serious sin truly is.
But the cross also reveals how astonishing God's mercy is toward sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
Not after we became impressive.
Not after our reputation was restored.
Not after we learned every correct religious expression.
While we were yet sinners.
Christ died for us.
And if you have been carrying the secret belief that God only loves the polished version of you, you need to hear that again.
Jesus did not go to the cross because humanity had finally become worthy.
He went because we needed a Savior.
That is not a reason to remain unchanged.
It is the reason real change becomes possible.
The Gospel does not merely offer a new religious identity.
It announces the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ and calls us into a new life through Him.
The apostle Paul writes in Ephesians 2:8–10 that we are saved by grace through faith, not by our works, and that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Notice the order.
We do not perform good works to purchase salvation.
We are saved by grace and then called to walk in the good works God has prepared.
Obedience is not the price of being loved by God. It is a fitting response to the grace we have received.
This matters because a Christianity built primarily on fear of human rejection can produce conformity without genuine transformation.
You can change your clothing without surrendering your pride.
You can stop using certain words while continuing to destroy people with your tongue.
You can memorize doctrines while refusing to forgive.
You can donate money while secretly believing your generosity makes you superior.
You can serve in ministry while neglecting the people who live under your own roof.
You can become publicly religious while remaining privately unrepentant.
Jesus knew this.
In Matthew 15:8, He quotes Isaiah:
"This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me." (KJV)
The Hebrew background of this rebuke in Isaiah 29:13 is especially striking.
The word lev (לֵב), commonly translated "heart," carries a rich biblical sense that includes the inner person—thought, intentions, desires, and will.
God is not merely asking whether the right religious words are coming out of our mouths.
He is confronting the inward direction of our lives.
Where is your heart?
What governs your choices when nobody is watching?
What do you love?
What do you excuse?
What do you refuse to surrender?
Who are you becoming?
Because a person can sound devoted to God while remaining deeply resistant to His authority.
And that is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable for all of us.
It is easy to criticize inherited Christianity.
It is much harder to examine the Christianity we are personally practicing.
We can blame our upbringing.
We can blame religious institutions.
We can blame leaders who failed us.
And sometimes those failures were real and serious.
Spiritual abuse, hypocrisy, manipulation, and the misuse of Scripture should never be minimized or excused.
But eventually, we must confront a question that nobody else can answer for us.
Am I actually following Jesus, or am I merely reacting to the people who claimed to represent Him?
Because there is another danger.
Someone wounded by legalism can become so determined never to be controlled again that they begin rejecting every biblical command that feels demanding.
Someone hurt by religious hypocrisy can confuse legitimate criticism of hypocrisy with permission to abandon the Church entirely.
Someone who has suffered under false teaching can become vulnerable to a different false teaching that promises freedom without repentance.
And the enemy of our souls does not care which distortion captures us.
A counterfeit Christianity that crushes people with man-made burdens is dangerous.
A counterfeit Christianity that removes Christ's authority is dangerous too.
Jesus calls us away from both.
Listen to His first recorded proclamation of the kingdom in Mark 1:15:
"The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel." (KJV)
The Greek word translated "repent" is metanoeite (μετανοεῖτε), from the verb metanoeō.
It carries the idea of changing one's mind or understanding, but biblical repentance is not merely adopting a new opinion.
In the context of Jesus' preaching, it involves a genuine turning toward God that bears fruit in a changed life.
And the word translated "believe" is pisteuete (πιστεύετε), from pisteuō, expressing faith or trust.
Jesus calls people to repent and believe.
Not simply to inherit a religious label.
Not merely to repeat words without understanding.
Not to build a personal spirituality that never challenges their desires.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Trust the King.
Follow Him.
And what is this Gospel?
Paul summarizes its central historical message in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4: Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures.
Christianity is not ultimately founded on our emotional experiences, our family customs, or our preferred religious culture.
It is founded on the person and saving work of Jesus Christ.
His life.
His death.
His resurrection.
His lordship.
Everything else must be examined in the light of Him.
This is why Jesus' words in Luke 6:46 are so piercing:
"And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?" (KJV)
There is no comfortable way around that question.
Jesus is not impressed by a title that our lives continually contradict.
Calling Him Lord while deliberately refusing His authority is a contradiction we must take seriously.
But remember the grace of the One asking the question.
He does not confront us because He enjoys destroying sinners.
He confronts us because He calls sinners to life.
He exposes what is false so that we can turn toward what is true.
He brings hidden things into the light so that repentance and healing can begin.
And sometimes the first thing He must dismantle is the religious image we have spent years protecting.
Maybe you have been the person who judges others because you are terrified someone will discover your own failures.
Maybe you have spent years serving in church because you secretly believe God will abandon you if you stop proving your usefulness.
Maybe you have been financially generous but emotionally absent from your family.
Maybe you have defended biblical morality publicly while privately making peace with a sin you refuse to confess.
Maybe you have rejected the Church because people who represented it wounded you, and now even hearing the name of Jesus brings back memories you wish you could forget.
Or maybe you are simply tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of knowing the language but feeling far from God.
Tired of carrying questions you have been afraid to ask.
Tired of wondering whether the Christianity you inherited has room for someone as complicated as you.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not to invent a Jesus who never confronts you.
And the answer is not to return to every human expectation that once crushed you.
The answer is to come to the real Christ.
The One who said in John 6:37:
"...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." (KJV)
What a promise.
Not that every belief we hold will be affirmed.
Not that every choice we make will be excused.
But that the person who truly comes to Him will not be cast away.
You do not have to arrive with a flawless spiritual résumé.
You come as someone who needs grace.
And you come willing to let the Savior tell you the truth.
There is a beautiful moment in Luke 15 that reveals something of God's heart toward repentant sinners.
A son has squandered his inheritance.
He has dishonored his father.
He has made decisions that leave him desperate, hungry, and humiliated.
Eventually, he comes to himself.
He decides to return home.
He rehearses a confession.
He knows he has sinned.
He has no right to demand restoration on his own terms.
But while he is still a great way off, his father sees him.
And runs.
The father embraces him.
The son confesses.
And the father responds with a celebration of restoration.
The parable does not teach that rebellion was harmless.
It teaches the astonishing joy of restoration when the lost return.
And in the larger context of Luke 15, Jesus tells these parables in response to complaints that He receives sinners and eats with them.
That matters.
Because the religious critics saw scandal.
Jesus revealed the joy of grace.
And this is where our Gospel Warrior theme becomes more than a memorable phrase.
The scandal of a son who dishonored his father.
The grace of a father who welcomed him home.
The scandal of Peter denying the Lord he loved.
The grace of the risen Jesus restoring him and calling him to shepherd His sheep.
The scandal of Saul persecuting believers.
The grace of Christ transforming him into an apostle who proclaimed the Gospel he once opposed.
The scandal of a thief dying beside Jesus, admitting his guilt and turning to the crucified King.
The grace of Jesus promising him paradise.
Not one of these stories tells us that sin does not matter.
They tell us that sin does not have the final word when the Savior intervenes.
And perhaps that is the story you need to hear today.
Because you may have inherited a Christianity that taught you to conceal your scandal at all costs.
Jesus calls you to bring your sin into the light through repentance and faith.
You may have inherited a Christianity that made you believe your failures were the end of your usefulness.
Jesus is able to restore the repentant and shape them into faithful servants.
You may have inherited a Christianity that valued your public image more than your private integrity.
Jesus calls you to truth in the inward person.
And you may have inherited a Christianity that made you fear honest questions.
Jesus invites us to examine His words carefully and respond with faith.
But there is something else we must not miss.
Christianity is not merely about what we leave behind.
It is about whom we follow.
When Jesus called His first disciples, He did not simply hand them a list of religious customs.
He said, "Follow me." (Matthew 4:19, KJV)
That invitation would eventually reshape their priorities, relationships, ambitions, and understanding of the world.
Following Jesus meant learning from Him.
Trusting Him.
Obeying Him.
Being corrected by Him.
And ultimately depending on Him.
It was never meant to be reduced to attending a weekly event while living the rest of our lives as though His words were optional.
Nor was it meant to be reduced to isolated spirituality without fellowship, accountability, worship, or service.
The New Testament calls believers into the body of Christ.
Acts 2:42 describes the early believers continuing in the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayers.
Their faith had doctrine.
It had community.
It had worship.
It had generosity.
It had shared life.
And yes, the early Church had struggles too.
Read the letters to Corinth.
Read Galatians.
Read the warnings in Revelation.
The first Christians were not a flawless community we can romanticize as though they never disagreed or sinned.
But the apostolic writings continually called them back to the same center.
Jesus Christ.
His Gospel.
His truth.
His love.
His holiness.
His lordship.
So perhaps the question is not whether we can recover a perfect religious culture from the past.
Perhaps the question is whether we are willing to be continually corrected by the unchanging truth of God's Word.
Because genuine biblical Christianity is not about finding a community where nobody ever fails.
It is about belonging to Christ and growing with other imperfect believers under the authority of His Word.
And this is why love matters so deeply.
In John 13:35, Jesus says:
"By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." (KJV)
Not by how impressive our religious vocabulary sounds.
Not by how loudly we condemn the people we dislike.
Not by how successfully we build our own reputation.
By love for one another.
But do not confuse that love with moral indifference.
The same Jesus who commanded love also commanded obedience.
In John 14:15, He says:
"If ye love me, keep my commandments." (KJV)
Love and obedience belong together.
And the love Jesus commands is not merely a feeling.
It is a life shaped by His truth.
A willingness to forgive.
A commitment to serve.
A refusal to exploit.
A concern for the weak.
A desire for holiness.
A readiness to bear one another's burdens.
A faith that becomes visible in how we treat actual human beings.
Including the people who cannot benefit us.
Including those who have disappointed us.
Including those whose wounds make them difficult to love.
That is a Christianity worth recovering.
Not because it is easier.
In many ways, it is far more demanding than maintaining a religious appearance.
It is easier to look righteous for an hour than to love patiently for a lifetime.
It is easier to quote a verse about forgiveness than to forgive someone who has genuinely wounded you.
It is easier to criticize the world than to confront the pride, envy, bitterness, and secret compromise in your own heart.
It is easier to call yourself a disciple than to deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Jesus.
And yet the life Jesus calls us into is also the life where we discover that His grace is sufficient for our weakness.
We are not saved by becoming impressive disciples.
We are saved by an impressive Savior.
And the grace that saves us also teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live for Him, as Titus 2:11–14 explains.
That is why this message is not about becoming suspicious of every church, pastor, tradition, or Christian family.
There are faithful churches.
There are godly parents.
There are pastors who preach the Word with integrity.
There are traditions that faithfully preserve biblical truth and direct people toward Christ.
Thank God for them.
The goal is not cynicism.
The goal is discernment.
Hold fast to what is good.
Reject what contradicts Scripture.
Remain teachable.
And never mistake your familiarity with Christian culture for the fullness of knowing Christ.
Because one day, the question will not be whether we were impressive defenders of a religious brand.
It will be whether our profession of faith was genuine.
Jesus gives a sobering warning in Matthew 7:21–23 about people who call Him Lord and even appeal to remarkable religious works, yet are exposed as those who practiced lawlessness.
That passage should not be used to torment tenderhearted believers into believing every weakness means they are rejected by God.
But it should awaken anyone who has made peace with hypocrisy while assuming religious activity guarantees salvation.
Christ is not calling us to despair.
He is calling us to examine ourselves honestly and turn to Him.
And if this has exposed something in you, please do not rush past that conviction.
Maybe there is someone you need to forgive.
Maybe there is a sin you need to confess.
Maybe there is a conversation you need to have with your pastor.
Maybe there is a doctrine you need to study more carefully.
Maybe you need to open the Gospel of Mark tonight and read it slowly, asking not merely what you have heard about Jesus, but what the text actually reveals about Him.
Or maybe, for the first time in a long time, you need to stop performing and pray.

"Lord Jesus, I have inherited many things. Some were good. Some may have distorted my understanding of You. Give me discernment to recognize the difference. Forgive my pride, my hypocrisy, my disobedience, and the ways I have used religion to hide from Your truth. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me to trust You, obey You, love what You love, and follow You faithfully. Restore what has been damaged in my understanding of Your Word. Make me more like You. Amen."
And perhaps this is the moment to be honest with someone else too.
If you have been spiritually exhausted, you do not have to turn your struggle into a polished testimony before you are allowed to ask for prayer.
You do not owe the internet your private history. Share only what you are comfortable sharing.
But perhaps your simple, honest words will remind another struggling believer that they are not the only person learning how to return to the heart of the Gospel.
And please, think of one person who needs this message.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to win an argument against.
Someone you genuinely love.
A family member who grew up knowing church but no longer knows whether they can trust it.
A friend who has confused religious disappointment with disappointment in Jesus.
A believer who has become weary under impossible expectations.
A young person asking questions nobody seems willing to answer.
Because this conversation should not end when the scrolling stops.
It should lead us back to the Bible.
Back to prayer.
Back to repentance.
Back to fellowship.
Back to Jesus.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to become another voice demanding unquestioning loyalty.
Not to sell a shortcut to spiritual maturity.
But to encourage people to examine Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in discipleship, and keep Christ at the center of their lives.
And we want those resources to continue reaching people who may never be able to pay for them.
People who are searching for answers.
People rebuilding their faith.
People who cannot afford a shelf full of Christian books.
People who need encouragement to open Scripture again.
This work requires time, resources, and ongoing support.
It is important to be clear about something.
God is glorified through faith in Christ, worship, obedience, love, generosity, and lives transformed by His grace.
Your salvation cannot be purchased, and God's approval is not for sale.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, not under compulsion. As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says, God loves a cheerful giver.
Not because God needs your money.
But because ministry in this world often depends on people who freely choose to give, serve, and share.
These products can be useful reminders of biblical truth and opportunities to share your faith, but the heart of this ministry will always be the Gospel, not merchandise.
You are still welcome here.
The free resources are still here for you.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Not as a payment for grace.
Not as proof that you are a better Christian.
But as a willing partnership in making Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to more people.
Because the purpose of Gospel Warrior is not to build an audience that depends on us.
It is to help point people toward the Savior on whom we all depend.
And now, before you leave, return to the question that brought you here.
What if the Christianity you inherited is not entirely the Christianity Jesus actually taught?
Perhaps some of what you inherited was beautiful and true.
Keep it.
Perhaps some of it was merely cultural.
Examine it.
Perhaps some of it was harmful or contrary to Scripture.
Have the courage to reject it.
But do not throw away Jesus because someone misrepresented Him.
Do not confuse the failures of His followers with the failure of His Gospel.
And do not assume that questioning an inherited practice requires questioning the truth of Christ's death and resurrection.
The answer to distorted Christianity is not a Christless spirituality.
It is a deeper, more faithful understanding of Jesus Christ as revealed in Scripture.
The Jesus who welcomes repentant sinners.
The Jesus who confronts hypocrisy.
The Jesus who commands holiness.
The Jesus who shows mercy.
The Jesus who laid down His life for His sheep.
The Jesus who rose from the dead.
The Jesus who remains Lord even when our traditions, institutions, and personal assumptions must be corrected.
And perhaps the greatest tragedy would not be discovering that you misunderstood something about Christianity.
Perhaps it would be discovering that you misunderstood—and then refusing to let Jesus teach you.
So open the Bible again.
Not merely to confirm what you already believe.
Open it ready to be corrected, comforted, convicted, and changed.
Read the words of Christ.
Examine them in context.
Listen to the whole counsel of Scripture.
Seek wise and faithful teachers.
Pray for discernment.
And follow the Savior rather than the applause of any religious crowd.
Because you do not need a more fashionable Jesus.
You do not need a more convenient Jesus.
You do not need a Jesus redesigned to fit your preferences.
You need the real Jesus.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His blood.
The One who can take the wreckage of a life and make something new.

And if you have spent years defending a version of Christianity that left you afraid to approach Him, perhaps today is the day you stop hiding behind what you inherited and begin listening more closely to the One who calls you by His Word.
The most heartbreaking thing would be to spend your life protecting a picture of Jesus while refusing to follow the Jesus who stands before you in Scripture.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD LET MOSES DIE WHEN HIS BODY WAS STILL STRONG? THE HEARTBREAKING TRUTH MOST CHRISTIANS NEVER NOTICE
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD LET MOSES DIE WHEN HIS BODY WAS STILL STRONG? THE HEARTBREAKING TRUTH MOST CHRISTIANS NEVER NOTICE

He was 120 years old. His eyes had not grown dim. His strength had not disappeared. He could still climb a mountain. But God told him his journey was over. What happened on that mountain reveals a terrifying truth about disobedience, an astonishing truth about grace, and a hope that reaches all the way to Jesus Christ.
There is something deeply unsettling about the death of Moses.
Because Moses did not die the way we might expect a 120-year-old man to die.
His body had not collapsed under the weight of old age.
His eyesight had not failed.
His physical strength had not disappeared.
He was still capable of climbing a mountain.
Still able to see the land he had spent forty years leading an entire nation toward.
And yet...
He would never walk into it.
Imagine standing close enough to see the fulfillment of your life's greatest assignment, only to hear God tell you that someone else would finish the journey.
Imagine spending decades carrying people who complained about you, questioned your leadership, rebelled against your authority, and sometimes wished they had never followed you.
Imagine praying for those same people when God threatened judgment.
Imagine standing between a rebellious nation and the consequences of its sins.
And then imagine watching those people prepare to enter the land you had longed to see.
Without you.
This was not the death of a man whose body had finally given up.
This was the death of a servant whose earthly assignment had reached the boundary God had established.
And the reason behind that boundary is more serious than many of us realize.

Because hidden within the final moments of Moses is a warning about the holiness of God, the danger of misrepresenting Him, and the astonishing mercy of a Savior who can accomplish what even Moses could not.
But before we reach that mountain, we need to go back to a rock.
A rock in the wilderness.
A thirsty nation.
An exhausted leader.
And one moment of anger that changed everything.
The Bible records Moses' final moments in Deuteronomy 34:5–7:

"So Moses the servant of the LORD died there in the land of Moab, according to the word of the LORD. And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day. And Moses was an hundred and twenty years old when he died: his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated."
— Deuteronomy 34:5–7, King James Version
Read that final sentence again.
"His eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated."
In Hebrew, the description is striking:
לֹא־כָהֲתָה עֵינוֹ וְלֹא־נָס לֵחֹה
Lo-kahatah eino, ve-lo-nas lecho.
Literally, the passage describes Moses' eye as not having grown dim and his vitality as not having departed.

The Hebrew word לֵחֹה (lecho) is associated with freshness or vitality. It communicates that Moses had not suffered the ordinary depletion of physical vigor that we might expect at his extraordinary age.
Scripture is emphasizing something remarkable.
Moses was old in years, but he had not been physically reduced to helplessness.
And this matters because the text refuses to let us assume that Moses died simply because his body was worn out.
God had appointed the conclusion of his life.
But why?
Why would God bring such a faithful servant so close to the Promised Land and then refuse to let him enter?
Was Moses not the man who confronted Pharaoh?
Was he not the man through whom God brought the plagues upon Egypt?
Was he not the man who lifted his staff as the Red Sea opened?
Was he not the man who received the commandments on Mount Sinai?
Was he not the man who repeatedly interceded for Israel when the people turned against the Lord?
Yes.
He was all those things.
But he was also a man who needed God's mercy.
And one of the most dangerous assumptions a believer can make is that years of faithful service somehow make personal disobedience insignificant.
That is where this story begins to reach into our own hearts.
Because you can serve God publicly while struggling to surrender privately.
You can know Scripture and still allow anger to control your words.
You can be genuinely called by God and still make decisions that misrepresent His character.
You can do extraordinary things in His name and still need correction.
Moses knew what it meant to carry responsibility.
And responsibility can become exhausting.
The Israelites had complained again.
They were thirsty.
They were frustrated.
They accused Moses and Aaron of bringing them into a wilderness where there was no water.
And God gave Moses a specific instruction.
Numbers 20:8 records the Lord telling him to take the rod, gather the congregation, and speak to the rock before their eyes.
God promised that water would come forth.
Notice the instruction.
Speak.
Not strike.
Speak.
But something happened inside Moses.
The accumulated frustration of leadership erupted.
He gathered the people and said:
"Hear now, ye rebels; must we fetch you water out of this rock?"
— Numbers 20:10, KJV
Then Moses lifted his hand and struck the rock twice with his rod.
Water came out.
The people drank.
Their animals drank.
The immediate crisis was resolved.
But Moses had disobeyed God.
And that is the uncomfortable part.
Water came out of the rock, but the presence of a miracle did not mean Moses' disobedience had God's approval.
Think about that.
Something visibly powerful happened.
The people received what they needed.
Yet God confronted the very leader through whom the miracle occurred.
This should humble anyone who serves in ministry.
Visible results are not always proof that every action, attitude, or decision behind them was right.
A congregation may be helped by a message even when the messenger needs repentance.
A family may receive blessings while a parent still needs to confront destructive anger.
A ministry may grow while its leaders still need correction.
God's faithfulness to His people must never be confused with His endorsement of everything done by His servants.
Then came the words that changed Moses' future.
"Because ye believed me not, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore ye shall not bring this congregation into the land which I have given them."
— Numbers 20:12, KJV
The Hebrew phrase לֹא־הֶאֱמַנְתֶּם בִּי (lo-he'emantem bi) means, in context, "you did not believe in me" or "you did not trust me."
And the phrase לְהַקְדִּישֵׁנִי (lehaqdisheni) means "to sanctify me" or "to show me as holy."
God was not merely addressing the physical act of striking a rock.
He was addressing a failure of trust and a failure to uphold His holiness before the people.
Moses and Aaron had been entrusted with representing God.
But in that moment, Moses' anger and disobedience distorted that representation.
Psalm 106:32–33 also connects the incident with Moses speaking rashly after the people provoked him.
This was not an innocent misunderstanding.
Nor was it merely that Moses used the wrong technique to obtain water.
The Lord Himself explained the deeper issue.
They had failed to trust Him and honor Him as holy.
And because Moses was a leader, his actions carried enormous weight.
James 3:1 later reminds believers that teachers will receive stricter judgment.
Leadership is not a license to become careless with God's character.
It is a calling to greater faithfulness.
Perhaps you have never stood before a rock in the wilderness.
But have you ever been so angry that you spoke in a way that made someone question the God you claim to follow?
Have you ever used the truth of Scripture as a weapon against someone you were supposed to love?
Have you ever allowed your exhaustion to become an excuse for cruelty?
Have you ever insisted that your intentions were good while refusing to acknowledge that your actions were wrong?
That is why this story is so uncomfortable.
Because Moses' failure does not look entirely foreign to us.
It looks painfully human.
And if we are willing to be honest, we can recognize pieces of ourselves in his frustration.
We know what it feels like to carry responsibilities no one else seems to understand.
We know what it feels like to help people who do not appreciate the sacrifice.
We know what it feels like to pray, serve, forgive, and continue showing up while something inside us becomes increasingly tired.
Sometimes we are not angry because we stopped caring.
Sometimes we are angry because we have been carrying more than we know how to surrender.
But exhaustion does not turn disobedience into obedience.
Pain does not give us permission to misrepresent God.
And spiritual responsibility never removes our need for humility.
Moses was not exempt.
Neither are we.
Yet there is something equally important we must not overlook.
God's discipline did not mean that God had stopped loving Moses.
The Lord did not erase Moses from the story of redemption.
He did not declare that the decades of faithful service had been meaningless.
He did not withdraw every expression of His relationship with him.
In fact, the final chapter of Deuteronomy still calls Moses "the servant of the LORD."
The Hebrew expression is:
עֶבֶד־יְהוָה (eved-YHWH)
The servant of the LORD.
What a remarkable description to find in the account of a man who had experienced such a serious consequence for disobedience.
Moses was disciplined.
But he was still remembered as God's servant.
His sin had consequences.
But his entire life was not reduced to that failure.
And someone reading this needs to understand the difference.
There are consequences that repentance does not necessarily remove.
A broken trust may require years to rebuild.
A careless decision may permanently change a relationship.
A destructive habit may leave wounds that take time to heal.
A missed opportunity may never return in the same form.
God's forgiveness is real.
But forgiveness does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
And yet...
Consequences do not have to be the final word about your relationship with God.
That is not permission to minimize sin.
It is an invitation to take both holiness and grace seriously.
Because the God who disciplines His children is also the God who calls sinners to repentance and receives those who come to Him in faith.
And then we arrive at one of the most heartbreaking moments in Moses' life.
Deuteronomy 3:23–26 reveals that Moses pleaded with the Lord to let him cross over and see the good land beyond the Jordan.
He wanted to enter.
After everything, he still wanted to finish the journey.
But the Lord told him:
"Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto me of this matter."
— Deuteronomy 3:26, KJV
Imagine hearing those words.
Not from an enemy.
Not from a king.
Not from the people who had opposed you.
But from the God you had spent your life serving.
Moses had to accept an answer he did not want.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because sometimes the hardest act of faith is not believing that God can open a door.
Sometimes it is trusting Him when He tells you that a particular door will remain closed.
Some of us are still grieving the life we thought we would have.
The marriage we hoped would survive.
The relationship we wanted to repair.
The years we wish we could recover.
The calling we imagined would unfold differently.
The prayer we begged God to answer in one particular way.
We keep looking at the door.
We keep replaying the moment.
We keep wondering whether everything would have changed if we had done something differently.
And sometimes there really are things we must repent of.
Sometimes there are people we need to apologize to.
Sometimes there are consequences we must accept.
But even when God does not reverse a consequence, we are not abandoned to hopelessness.
His grace is greater than the boundary of one earthly opportunity.
Moses would not lead Israel across the Jordan.
Joshua would.
And that transition teaches another difficult lesson.
God's purposes are greater than any one servant, no matter how extraordinary that servant may be.
Moses was indispensable to the role God had assigned him, but God's covenant promises did not depend on Moses living forever.
The mission would continue.
The people would enter.
The promise would stand.
God remained faithful.
And Moses had to entrust the future to the Lord rather than insist on personally completing everything he had begun.
That is a lesson many of us resist.
We want to see every result.
We want to witness every breakthrough.
We want to know that our sacrifices were worth it.
We want to be present when the people we have prayed for finally change.
But sometimes we are called to plant what someone else will harvest.
Sometimes we are called to prepare a generation for a future we will not personally experience.
Sometimes faithfulness means releasing the work into God's hands.
And sometimes the greatest evidence of trust is accepting that God's story will continue without us at the center.
Then Moses climbed Mount Nebo.
Deuteronomy 34:1–4 records that the Lord showed him the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
There it was.
The land of promise.
The destination that had shaped decades of wilderness wandering.
He could see it.
But he would not enter it.
And there, in Moab, Moses died.
Scripture does not describe a prolonged illness.
It does not say his strength finally failed.
It does not tell us that his eyes closed because he had become too weak to continue.
It simply tells us that Moses died according to the word of the Lord.
There is an important Hebrew expression in Deuteronomy 34:5:
עַל־פִּי יְהוָה (al-pi YHWH)
Literally, "upon the mouth of the LORD," an idiom meaning "according to the command" or "at the word of the LORD."

Some Jewish interpretive traditions beautifully associate this wording with a death by divine kiss. That is a traditional interpretation, not an explicit statement that the biblical text describes God physically kissing Moses.
The text itself makes the central point clear.
Moses' death occurred according to God's word.
It was not presented as the unavoidable result of physical deterioration.
And Deuteronomy 34:6 adds another remarkable detail.
Moses was buried in the land of Moab, but the location of his grave remained unknown.
The passage attributes the burial to God, although interpreters differ over whether the Hebrew should be understood as the Lord Himself burying Moses or the burial occurring under His direction.
Either way, the narrative leaves us with a striking picture.
The great leader of Israel is gone.
His grave is unknown.
His body is not the center of Israel's worship.
His legacy is not preserved through a monument that people must visit.
The focus remains on the Lord who called him.
The Lord who sustained him.
The Lord who corrected him.
