It means holding fast to the hope of the resurrection while caring responsibly for the life God has entrusted to us today.
And if you are the person who has been hiding behind a smile because you were terrified that someone would question your faith, please remember this:
You do not need to prove your love for Jesus by suffering in silence.
You can tell the truth.
You can ask for help.
You can receive treatment.
You can rest.
You can cry.
You can pray through tears.
And you can keep following Christ, one difficult day at a time.
The darkness you are walking through is not proof that the Light of the world has stopped loving you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WOMAN, THE SERPENT, AND THE OFFSPRING: THE WAR THAT BEGAN IN EDEN AND EXPLODED IN REVELATION 12
paragraphs: THE WOMAN, THE SERPENT, AND THE OFFSPRING: THE WAR THAT BEGAN IN EDEN AND EXPLODED IN REVELATION 12

Before the serpent pursued the woman in Revelation, before the dragon stood ready to devour her Child, and before the cross stood on Calvary, God had already spoken a promise over humanity's darkest failure. What if the Bible's most terrifying conflict is also the story of the greatest love that ever came looking for you?
There is something deeply unsettling about the first question God asked fallen humanity.
“Where art thou?” (Genesis 3:9, KJV).
Not because God had lost Adam.
But because Adam had lost the innocence of walking openly with God.
Imagine that moment.
The garden was still beautiful. The trees were still standing. The same God who had breathed life into dust was drawing near.
But something had changed.
For the first time, the sound of God's presence did not bring the comfort of fellowship.
It brought fear.
Adam hid.
Eve stood beneath the crushing weight of what had happened.
And somewhere in that garden was the serpent whose deception had helped turn paradise into a place of shame.
Perhaps you know something about hiding.

You can smile in photographs while carrying a secret that keeps you awake at night. You can sing in church while struggling with something you have never confessed. You can encourage everybody else to trust God while quietly wondering whether God could still want someone like you.
You know what Scripture says.
But you also know what you did.
And sometimes the distance between those two realities feels unbearable.
That is why what happened next in Eden matters more than many people realize.

Because before God drove humanity out of the garden, He announced a promise that would echo through the patriarchs, the prophets, Bethlehem, Calvary, the empty tomb, and finally the terrifying vision of Revelation 12.
A woman.
A serpent.
An offspring.
And a conflict that would reach its decisive turning point at the cross of Jesus Christ.
But here is what makes this story extraordinary.
The serpent heard the announcement of his defeat while the guilty humans were still standing in the wreckage of their disobedience.
Grace was already speaking in the place where sin had entered.
And the story was only beginning.
In Genesis 3:14–15, God pronounced judgment upon the serpent. At the heart of that judgment stood these words:
“And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.” (Genesis 3:15, KJV).
In Hebrew, the opening declaration is:
וְאֵיבָה אָשִׁית בֵּינְךָ וּבֵין הָאִשָּׁה
Ve'evah ashit beinekha uvein ha'ishah.
A close translation is:
“And I will put enmity between you and the woman.”
The Hebrew word אֵיבָה ('evah) means enmity or hostility. This is not a passing disagreement. It describes real opposition.
And notice who establishes it.
God says, “I will put.”
Humanity had listened to the serpent, but God would not allow the serpent's rebellion to have the final word over His creation.
The next Hebrew phrase carries the promise forward:
וּבֵין זַרְעֲךָ וּבֵין זַרְעָהּ
Uvein zar'akha uvein zar'ah.
“And between your offspring and her offspring.”
The word זֶרַע (zera') means seed or offspring. Depending on context, it can refer to descendants collectively or to a particular descendant.
That distinction matters.

Genesis 3:15 introduces a conflict extending beyond the immediate encounter in Eden. Yet within the wider biblical story, Christian interpretation sees that promise coming to its decisive fulfillment in one particular descendant: Jesus Christ.
The Hebrew continues:
הוּא יְשׁוּפְךָ רֹאשׁ וְאַתָּה תְּשׁוּפֶנּוּ עָקֵב
Hu yeshufkha rosh, ve'attah teshufennu 'aqev.
“He will strike you at the head, and you will strike him at the heel.”

The Hebrew verb shuf is uncommon, and translations differ between “bruise,” “strike,” and “crush.” The same verb appears in both clauses, so the difference in outcome should not be attributed to two different Hebrew verbs.
The contrast lies in the locations of the blows.
The head.
And the heel.
The promise portrays conflict and injury, but the image of a blow to the head points toward a decisive defeat.
Christian theology has long called Genesis 3:15 the protoevangelium, meaning the first announcement of the Gospel.
That term is theological, not a Hebrew word found in the verse. Genesis does not yet disclose the full details of Bethlehem, the crucifixion, or the resurrection.
But the unfolding canon reveals why Christians read this passage as the beginning of a promise fulfilled in Christ.
And consider where God spoke it.
Not in a sanctuary filled with worshipers.
Not among people celebrating their obedience.
But in the presence of people who had just disobeyed Him.
God's redemptive purpose was announced while humanity stood exposed.
That does not make sin harmless.
Adam and Eve still faced painful consequences. Death entered the human story. They were expelled from Eden.
Grace did not erase the seriousness of rebellion.
It revealed that rebellion would not be the final chapter.
And that is where this ancient story reaches into your life.
The enemy would have you believe that your worst decision is your permanent identity.
That your shame is stronger than God's mercy.
That because you fell, there can be no restoration.
But the God of Genesis 3 was already announcing His purpose to defeat evil before Adam and Eve could do anything to repair what they had broken.
They could not undo their disobedience.
They could not manufacture innocence.
They could not reopen the way to the tree of life.
They needed God to act.
And so do we.
But Genesis 3:15 does not stand alone.
Follow the promise through Scripture, and a pattern begins to emerge.
In Genesis 4, Eve gave birth to Cain and Abel. Yet the first family did not escape the devastation of sin. Cain murdered his brother, and the ground received innocent blood.
Then another son was born.
Seth.
Genesis 4:25 records Eve's recognition that God had appointed another offspring in place of Abel.
The promise continued through a wounded family.
Later, humanity's wickedness filled the earth, but God preserved Noah and his household through the flood.
After Babel, God called Abraham and promised that through his offspring the nations would receive blessing.
Genesis 22:18 declares:
“And in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed; because thou hast obeyed my voice.” (KJV).
The Hebrew word for offspring is again zera'.
Paul later draws attention to this promise in Galatians 3:16 and identifies Christ as its ultimate fulfillment.

This does not mean every occurrence of zera' in Genesis refers exclusively to one person. Abraham's offspring includes his descendants in its historical setting. Paul's inspired argument identifies the promised blessing as reaching its fulfillment in Christ.
The story moves forward.
Through Isaac.
Through Jacob.
Through Judah.
Through David.
Through generations marked by courage and cowardice, faith and failure, repentance and rebellion.
The biblical genealogies are not merely ancient lists of unfamiliar names.
They trace God's faithfulness through human history.
And when Matthew opens his Gospel, he identifies Jesus Christ as the son of David and the son of Abraham.
The promised King had come.
But look closely at the kind of family history Matthew records.
Judah and Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
David and the wife of Uriah.
Stories involving loss, outsider status, moral failure, courage, injustice, and unexpected mercy.
Not every person in these accounts was guilty of the wrong done to them. Scripture does not flatten victims and perpetrators into the same category.
But together these histories show that God's saving purpose moved through a deeply complicated human world.
A world very much like ours.
Some people come from families where faith was nurtured.
Others come from homes where betrayal was normal.
Some carry wounds they caused.
Others carry wounds they never deserved.
And many carry both.
Yet the arrival of Jesus demonstrates that God did not abandon His promise because human history was stained.
He entered that history.
Then, in the fullness of time, an angel came to a young woman named Mary.
Luke 1:31–33 announced that she would conceive a Son named Jesus, who would receive the throne of David and reign forever.
Mary asked how this would happen, since she was a virgin.
The angel answered that the Holy Spirit would come upon her and the power of the Most High would overshadow her.
This was not an ordinary conception.
The New Testament presents it as a miraculous act of God.
And the Son born of Mary was not merely another descendant hoping to overcome the serpent.
He was the eternal Son of God who had taken on true human nature.
John 1:14 says:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.” (KJV).
Think about that.
The One through whom all things were made entered the world He had created.
The One who needed nothing accepted human weakness without sin.
The One who would conquer death came into a world where death seemed to rule everyone.
And He came through the birth of a child.
This is where the story of the woman and the serpent begins to sound strangely familiar.
Because another biblical scene describes a woman, a child, and an enemy determined to destroy Him.
But to see it, we must go to the final book of Scripture.
Revelation 12.
John writes:
She is pregnant, crying out in the pain of childbirth.
Then another sign appears.
A great red dragon.
Seven heads.
Ten horns.
Seven crowns upon his heads.
Its tail sweeps away a third of the stars of heaven.
And the dragon stands before the woman, waiting to devour her Child the moment He is born.
Read that image slowly.
A woman in labor.
A child about to be born.
An enemy waiting to destroy Him.
The scene is terrifying.
But John does not leave us guessing about the dragon's identity.
Revelation 12:9 identifies him as:
“That old serpent, called the Devil, and Satan, which deceiveth the whole world.” (KJV).
That old serpent.
The wording deliberately brings the reader back toward the beginning of the biblical story.
The serpent of Genesis.
The dragon of Revelation.
The adversary is now named explicitly.
The Greek text reads:
ὁ ὄφις ὁ ἀρχαῖος
Ho ophis ho archaios.
“The ancient serpent.”
The noun ὄφις (ophis) means serpent, and ἀρχαῖος (archaios) means ancient or belonging to an earlier time.
John identifies the dragon with the ancient deceiver.
The enemy who appeared in the opening chapters of Scripture is exposed in the Bible's final book.
And the conflict promised in Eden has reached an extraordinary moment.
But who is the woman?
This question deserves careful treatment because faithful Christians have understood the symbolism in different, sometimes overlapping ways.
Revelation is apocalyptic literature. It communicates truth through visions, symbols, and imagery drawn from the Old Testament.
The woman's sun, moon, and twelve stars recall Joseph's dream in Genesis 37:9–11, where heavenly bodies represent members of Jacob's family.
This connection strongly supports understanding the woman as representing the covenant people of God, particularly Israel, from whom the Messiah came according to His human ancestry.
The woman also has an unmistakable connection to Mary, because Mary literally gave birth to Jesus.

In Catholic interpretation, Mary receives particular attention as the woman, while the image also carries ecclesial meaning. Many Protestant interpreters emphasize faithful Israel and the continuing people of God.

The woman should not be reduced carelessly to a single ordinary individual when the vision extends beyond the birth of Christ to the persecution of those who keep God's commandments and hold to the testimony of Jesus.
Revelation 12:17 makes that wider dimension explicit.
The woman is presented symbolically in a way that connects the Messiah's coming with the covenant community and the faithful who belong to God.
This is not a license to invent secret meanings.
It is an invitation to read Revelation through the Scriptures that came before it.
And the identity of the Child is clearer still.
Revelation 12:5 says:
“And she brought forth a man child, who was to rule all nations with a rod of iron: and her child was caught up unto God, and to his throne.” (KJV).
The language of ruling the nations with a rod of iron comes from Psalm 2, a royal psalm that the New Testament applies to the Messiah.
Revelation 19:15 also uses this imagery for Christ.
The Child is Jesus.
The promised King.
The descendant of David.
The offspring through whom God's promises reach their fulfillment.
Revelation 12 compresses the story of His earthly coming and exaltation into a brief symbolic scene. It does not narrate every event of His life in chronological detail.
And that matters, because the dragon's attempt to devour the Child is part of a much larger conflict.
Consider the events surrounding Jesus' birth.
Herod heard that a king had been born and became troubled.
He sought the Child.
When his schemes failed, he ordered the killing of young boys in Bethlehem and its surrounding region, as Matthew 2 records.
Joseph was warned in a dream, and the family fled to Egypt.
Matthew presents these events as part of the Messiah's story, shaped by fulfillment of Scripture.
Revelation 12 does not explicitly identify Herod as the dragon, and we should not pretend that it does.
Yet Herod's murderous hostility illustrates the kind of opposition that the vision portrays on a cosmic scale.
The Child was threatened.
But God's purpose was not defeated.
Years passed.
The Child grew.
He walked among the sick, the forgotten, the religious, the rebellious, the grieving, and the ashamed.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He announced the kingdom of God.
He forgave sins.
And He called people to repent and believe the Gospel.
The serpent had deceived humanity into distrusting God.
Jesus revealed the Father's character through perfect obedience, truth, holiness, and sacrificial love.
Where Adam disobeyed, Christ obeyed.
Where sin brought condemnation, Christ came to save.
Paul develops this contrast in Romans 5:12–21 and 1 Corinthians 15:21–22, 45–49.
Jesus is the last Adam, the representative of a new humanity.
But His victory did not arrive in the way the world expected.
It came through a cross.
And for those watching, the cross looked like the end.
The crowd mocked.
The religious leaders sneered.
Soldiers divided His garments.
His followers scattered.
His body was wounded.
His hands were pierced.
His blood was shed.
And the One who had never sinned was crucified among sinners.
Imagine standing there.
You had heard Him speak of the kingdom.
You had seen His power.
You believed He was the promised One.
And now He was hanging on Roman wood.
What happened to the promise?
What happened to the King?
What happened to the offspring who would defeat the serpent?
Perhaps that is the question the enemy wanted everyone to ask.
Because what looked like defeat was the very place where Christ was accomplishing redemption.
Colossians 2:14–15 describes Christ's victory over hostile powers through the cross.
Hebrews 2:14 teaches that through death Jesus acted to destroy the power of the one who had the power of death, that is, the devil.
The Greek expression in Hebrews 2:14 includes:
καταργήσῃ τὸν τὸ κράτος ἔχοντα τοῦ θανάτου
Katargēsē ton to kratos echonta tou thanatou.
A close rendering is:
“That He might render powerless the one having the power of death.”
The verb καταργέω (katargeō) can mean to nullify, render ineffective, or bring to an end in a particular sense.
This is not a claim that Satan ceased to exist at Calvary.
Revelation itself portrays continued satanic hostility.
Rather, Christ's death and resurrection decisively broke the devil's claim to hold God's redeemed people under the tyranny of death.
The enemy could wound.
But he could not overthrow God's saving purpose.
The crucifixion was not a tragic accident that God struggled to overcome.
Jesus willingly laid down His life.
John 10:18 records His declaration:
“No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.” (KJV).
The serpent's opposition was real.
Human wickedness was real.
The suffering was real.
But Christ was not a helpless victim of forces greater than Himself.
He was the obedient Son, giving Himself for sinners according to the Father's saving purpose.
And then came the third day.
The tomb was empty.
Death had not held Him.
Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead.
The wounds of the crucifixion were not proof that the promise had failed.
They were wounds borne by the victorious Redeemer.
And now the words of Genesis 3:15 can be read in the light of the completed work of Christ.
The promised offspring had come.
The serpent had opposed Him.
Christ had suffered.
And through His death and resurrection, the decisive victory had been won.
But Revelation 12 reveals another truth.
The dragon does not respond to defeat with quiet surrender.
He responds with fury.
Revelation 12 describes war in heaven, Michael and his angels fighting against the dragon and his angels.
The dragon is defeated and cast down.
John then hears a loud voice announcing salvation, strength, the kingdom of God, and the authority of His Christ.

The passage's symbolism and sequence have been interpreted differently among Christians, especially regarding the timing of Satan's expulsion and its relationship to Christ's exaltation and the church's experience.
Yet the central theological declaration is unmistakable.
The accuser is defeated by God's saving work through Christ.
Revelation 12:10 calls Satan:
“The accuser of our brethren.”
The Greek term is κατήγωρ (katēgōr), meaning accuser.
And suddenly this cosmic vision becomes painfully personal.
Because accusation is something many believers know.
Not every painful thought is a direct attack from Satan. Human memory, conscience, trauma, and emotional struggles also affect what we experience.
But Scripture clearly teaches that Satan accuses, deceives, and opposes God's people.
And accusations can sound terribly convincing when they contain pieces of your real history.
“You failed again.”
“You promised God you would change.”
“You know better.”
“You have disappointed everyone.”
“After what you did, how could you call yourself a Christian?”
Some accusations begin with facts.
But they end with a lie.
Because the Gospel never teaches that sin is imaginary.
It teaches that sin is so serious that Jesus Christ gave His life to redeem sinners.
And His mercy is so sufficient that repentant sinners can truly be forgiven.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV).
Not because their past was harmless.
Not because their repentance earned salvation.
Not because they successfully hid every failure.
But because they belong to Christ.
The blood of Jesus does what self-punishment never can.
It cleanses from sin.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
That promise is not permission to cherish sin.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and come into the light.
And Revelation 12:11 gives one of the most powerful declarations in the entire vision:
“And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.” (KJV).
In Greek, the first clause reads:
καὶ αὐτοὶ ἐνίκησαν αὐτὸν διὰ τὸ αἷμα τοῦ ἀρνίου
Kai autoi enikēsan auton dia to haima tou arniou.
“And they conquered him because of the blood of the Lamb.”
The verb νικάω (nikaō) means to conquer or overcome.
And look at the foundation of their victory.
Not their popularity.
Not their wealth.
Not their perfect reputation.
Not the number of people who admired their faith.
The blood of the Lamb.
Their testimony mattered because it bore witness to the One who had redeemed them.
Their willingness to remain faithful even unto death showed that their allegiance to Jesus was greater than their fear.
This passage does not promise that Christians will escape all earthly suffering.
It shows that suffering and even martyrdom cannot ultimately cancel the victory Christ has secured.
And that is a truth some of us desperately need.
Because there are believers who have mistaken exhaustion for abandonment.
They have prayed for years over the same family member.
They have fought private temptations that nobody knows about.
They have buried people they loved.
They have watched marriages collapse.
They have endured injustice.
They have tried to obey God while everything around them seemed to be falling apart.
And somewhere along the way, they began to wonder whether the struggle itself meant God had forgotten them.
But Revelation 12 tells a different story.
The dragon's rage is not evidence that he has won.
His fury appears within a vision that announces his defeat.
Revelation 12:12 says he has great wrath because he knows that his time is short.
The enemy's remaining activity is serious.
But it is not ultimate.
His hostility has a limit.
Christ's kingdom does not.
And the chapter continues with the dragon pursuing the woman.
She is given protection in the wilderness.
The serpent pours water from his mouth like a flood.
The earth helps the woman.
Then the dragon turns his anger toward the rest of her offspring.
Revelation 12:17 describes them as those who keep God's commandments and hold the testimony of Jesus Christ.
There is the pattern again.
The woman.
The serpent.
The offspring.
The hostility first announced in Genesis is echoed in Revelation's portrayal of the conflict surrounding the Messiah and His people.
But we must understand this carefully.
Christians are not independent saviors who repeat Jesus' atoning work.
There is only one Lamb whose blood redeems.
Only one mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, as 1 Timothy 2:5 declares.
Believers participate in His victory because they belong to Him.
Their endurance is the fruit of grace, not a second sacrifice that completes what the cross lacked.
And the church's calling is not to identify every opponent as a serpent or treat every disagreement as demonic warfare.
Ephesians 6:12 reminds believers that their ultimate struggle is not against flesh and blood.
People are not the enemy we have been commanded to hate.
They are neighbors we have been commanded to love, including those who oppose us.
The Gospel does not authorize cruelty in the name of spiritual warfare.
It calls us to stand firm in truth, righteousness, faith, salvation, God's Word, and prayer.
To resist evil without becoming evil.
To speak truth without abandoning love.
To proclaim Christ without pretending that human beings are beyond redemption.
And perhaps the most astonishing part of this entire biblical pattern is what it reveals about the heart of God.
The first woman stood in a garden after disobedience.
The promised offspring entered the world through a woman.
The dragon pursued the woman and her Child.
And the final vision announces the ultimate triumph of the Lamb.
But this is not merely a story about an ancient enemy.
It is a story about the God who refuses to abandon His redemptive purpose.
A God who keeps His promises across centuries.
A God who brings hope into families marked by failure.
A God who sends His Son into a world that rejects Him.
A Savior who carries sin to the cross.
A risen King who will bring evil to its final end.
And a people called to endure by His grace.
Maybe you have spent years believing your story is too scandalous to be redeemed.
Maybe your childhood left scars that still ache.
Maybe you are ashamed of the person you used to be.
Maybe you are still struggling with the consequences of decisions you wish you could reverse.
Maybe you know the language of faith but have not surrendered your life to Jesus Christ.
Or maybe you once walked closely with God, and somewhere along the way, your heart grew cold.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not promise that every earthly consequence will disappear when you repent.
It does not guarantee instant emotional healing or the immediate restoration of every broken relationship.
It does not say that forgiveness removes the need for accountability, restitution, or patient rebuilding of trust.
But it does proclaim something infinitely greater than denial.
Through Jesus Christ, guilty sinners can be forgiven.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
The alienated can be reconciled to God.
The enslaved can begin walking in new obedience.
The ashamed can come into the light.
And those who belong to Christ have a future that death itself cannot destroy.
That is grace.
Not God pretending the scandal never happened.
But God providing redemption through the crucified and risen Jesus.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you recognize yourself in the hiding, the accusing, or the exhaustion, there is something you need to know.
You do not have to make yourself worthy before coming to Christ.
You come because you need His mercy.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV).
Come honestly.
Confess your sin.
Turn from what is destroying you.
Trust in the Lord Jesus Christ, who died for sins and rose again.
Ask Him to teach you to follow Him.
And when you stumble, do not make hiding your home.
Return to the Savior.
The same Gospel that calls you to repentance also calls you to hope.
Because the final word over those who belong to Jesus is not the accusation of the serpent.
It is the saving authority of the risen Christ.
And the story does not end in Revelation 12.
The dragon still rages in the vision, but Revelation continues toward the final judgment of evil.
Revelation 20:10 portrays the devil's final defeat.
Revelation 21 announces a new heaven and a new earth.
God dwells with His people.
Death is no more.
Mourning, crying, and pain pass away.
And Revelation 22 brings us to something breathtaking.
The tree of life.
The very tree from which fallen humanity was barred in Genesis 3 appears again in the final vision of God's restored creation.
The Bible begins with humanity losing access to the tree of life.
It ends with God's redeemed people receiving life in His presence.
That is not a coincidence of storytelling.
It is part of the Bible's profound movement from creation, through fall and redemption, to new creation.
From a garden stained by disobedience to a renewed creation where the curse is no more.
From humanity hiding from God to His servants seeing His face.
From the serpent's deception to the Lamb's eternal triumph.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by changing the historical facts of what happened.
Not by calling evil good.
But by redeeming sinners, transforming lives, and securing a future that sin and death cannot finally steal.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
If Jesus has shown you mercy, who in your life still believes their past has made them unreachable?
A brother who has stopped attending church.
A daughter who thinks God hates her.
A friend who smiles publicly but is privately unraveling.
A husband who carries years of regret.
A mother who prays through tears.
Someone who has never truly understood why Jesus died.
Someone who believes Christianity is only for people who have their lives together.
They may not open a Bible today.
But they might read something you share.
They might pause over a sentence.
They might recognize their own pain in the story of Adam hiding.
They might discover that the Gospel is not about good people congratulating themselves.
It is about the holy God saving sinners through His Son.
Not to prove how spiritual you are.
Not to collect reactions.
But because someone within your reach may need to hear about Jesus.
And I want to invite you into a conversation deeper than a simple reaction.
If you have experienced the mercy of Christ, consider sharing a few words of your testimony. You do not need to disclose anything that would put your privacy, safety, or healing at risk.
Your testimony does not have to be dramatic to glorify Jesus.
Sometimes the most powerful words are simply, “I was lost, and Christ found me.”
Not because typing those words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But because honest testimony can encourage another person who is struggling to believe that restoration is possible.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
We want people to encounter more than an emotional moment online.
We want them to open Scripture.
To understand the Gospel.
To grow in prayer.
To recognize false teaching.
To repent where repentance is needed.
To find encouragement in suffering.
To be strengthened in biblical discipleship.
And to keep looking to Jesus Christ long after the emotions of a single article have faded.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible to people who are hungry for truth, including those who cannot afford to pay.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
I will tell you that supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be a meaningful way to serve others and honor God when it is done willingly, wisely, and with the right heart.
Those products may be useful reminders of Scripture and opportunities to share encouragement, but they are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
The Gospel is.
People encountering biblical truth is.
Your prayers matter.
Your sharing helps the message travel.
And your faithfulness to Christ matters far more than any number on a screen.
Because this ministry is not about building an audience that worships a page.
It is about pointing people to the Savior who alone is worthy of worship.
And that brings us back to Eden.
Can you see Adam now?
Hiding among the trees.
Ashamed.
Afraid.
Unable to undo what he had done.
Can you hear the footsteps of the Lord?
Can you hear the question?
“Where art thou?”
Now look toward Calvary.
See the Son of God bearing sin.
Hear Him declare:
“It is finished.” (John 19:30, KJV).
In Greek:
Τετέλεσται
Tetelestai.
“It is finished.”
The verb expresses completion. In John's Gospel, Jesus is declaring the completion of the work entrusted to Him as He gives up His spirit.
It is not a magical word that erases every difficulty from a believer's life.
It is the declaration of the Savior who has fulfilled His mission through obedient, sacrificial death.
And now look toward the end of Revelation.
The serpent does not reign forever.
Death does not reign forever.
The curse does not reign forever.
The Lamb reigns.
The One who was crucified is alive.
The One who was rejected is enthroned.
The One who bore the sins of His people will bring them into everlasting fellowship with God.
So when the enemy reminds you of your past, do not pretend your sins never happened.
Remember the cross where Jesus paid for sin.
When shame tells you to hide, remember the Savior who welcomes repentant sinners.
When suffering tempts you to despair, remember that the dragon's rage is not greater than the Lamb's victory.
And when you wonder whether your life can still become a testimony of grace, remember the promise spoken in the ruins of Eden.
God had not finished His story.
And for those who belong to Christ, the final chapter is not written by the serpent.
It belongs to the Lamb.
The serpent may know the scandal of your past, but he cannot overturn the grace of the Savior who holds your eternity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WE TAUGHT THEM HOW TO GET TO HEAVEN… BUT DID WE FORGET TO TEACH THEM HOW TO FOLLOW JESUS ON EARTH?
paragraphs: WE TAUGHT THEM HOW TO GET TO HEAVEN… BUT DID WE FORGET TO TEACH THEM HOW TO FOLLOW JESUS ON EARTH?
What if one of the greatest tragedies in modern Christianity is that we have convinced people to prepare for eternity while leaving them unprepared to live as disciples of Jesus Christ today?
There is a question haunting me.
Not because I have lost faith in the Church.
But because I believe in Jesus too much to pretend that everything we call Christianity actually looks like Him.

What if someone can spend twenty years attending church, memorize the language of salvation, know exactly what to say when someone asks whether they are going to heaven… and still have almost no idea how to follow Jesus when life becomes unbearable?
What if we have taught people how to raise their hands during an altar call, but not how to surrender their pride when they get home?
What if we have taught them to sing about forgiveness on Sunday, but not how to forgive the person whose betrayal still keeps them awake on Tuesday night?
What if we have taught them to anticipate streets of gold while ignoring the brokenhearted people walking beside them on streets of concrete?
And what if the most frightening part is that we have become so accustomed to this contradiction that we barely notice it anymore?
Before you assume this is another article criticizing churches, please hear me.
This is not an attack on the Bride of Christ.
This is a plea for her to remember the voice of her Bridegroom.
Because Jesus never invited us merely to admire the destination.
He called us to follow Him along the way.
And somewhere between our sermons about heaven and our struggles here on earth, we may have forgotten how deeply those two realities belong together.
I think about the person who sits in the back of the church every Sunday.
They know when to stand. When to sit. When to say amen.
They know the songs.
They know the Scriptures printed on the screen.
But nobody knows that they cried in their car before walking into the building.
Nobody knows they are struggling with pornography, resentment, loneliness, secret debt, or a marriage that feels like two strangers sharing an address.
Nobody knows that sometimes they open their Bible, stare at the pages, and quietly wonder why following Jesus seems so much harder than everyone makes it look.
They have been told that heaven is their home.
And that is a glorious promise for those who belong to Christ.
But tonight they are still living in a house full of conflict.
Tomorrow they must return to a workplace where integrity costs something.
Next week they must face someone who wounded them.
And right now they desperately need to know what it means to walk with Jesus through all of it.
Not merely someday.
Today.
This is where the words of Jesus become almost impossible to ignore.
In Matthew 28:19–20, the risen Christ commissions His followers to make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to observe everything He commanded.
The Greek text contains the word μαθητεύσατε (mathēteusate), meaning "make disciples."
Not simply gather audiences.
Not merely produce religious admirers.
Make disciples.
And the command to teach them is joined to τηρεῖν (tērein), meaning to keep, observe, or obey.
Jesus did not command His Church merely to distribute information about Him.
He commanded His Church to form people who would learn to live under His teaching.
And this matters because a person can know a great deal about Jesus without actually walking closely with Him.
You can explain the doctrine of forgiveness while nursing a grudge.
You can defend biblical marriage while neglecting your spouse.
You can argue about holiness while humiliating people online.
You can preach generosity while treating struggling people with contempt.
You can know the correct answers and still resist the Lord who gave them.
James confronts this very danger.
"But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves." (James 1:22, KJV)
That last phrase should make us uncomfortable.
Deceiving your own selves.
Not necessarily deceiving the pastor.
Not necessarily deceiving the congregation.
Yourself.
There is a kind of religious familiarity that can convince a person they are spiritually mature simply because they have heard the truth repeatedly.
But hearing about obedience is not the same as obeying.
Knowing that Jesus washed feet is not the same as humbling yourself to serve.
Knowing that Jesus loved His enemies is not the same as praying for someone who has treated you cruelly.
Knowing that Jesus trusted His Father is not the same as trusting God when your prayers seem unanswered.
And knowing that Jesus died for sinners is not the same as admitting that you still desperately need His mercy.
Perhaps this is why some of the most unsettling words in Scripture were spoken not to atheists, but to people who openly acknowledged Jesus as Lord.
"Why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?" (Luke 6:46, KJV)
Imagine hearing that question without the protection of religious familiarity.
Why do you call Me Lord?
Why do you sing to Me?
Why do you defend My name?
Why do you publicly identify yourself with Me?
But resist My words when they confront the things you refuse to surrender?
This is not a call to earn salvation through flawless performance.
That would contradict the Gospel.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of works.
And the very next verse tells us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared for us to walk in.
Notice the order.
We are not saved because we have successfully followed Jesus.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Christ, and that grace brings us into a new life in which we learn to follow Him.
Obedience is not the price we pay to purchase God's love.
It is the fruit of a life being transformed by His love.
That distinction is everything.
Because without grace, discipleship becomes religious exhaustion.
And without discipleship, our profession of grace can become an excuse for refusing transformation.
Jesus did not shed His blood merely to improve our religious vocabulary.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
To forgive.
To redeem.
To make us new.
And to teach us to walk in the freedom His sacrifice has secured.
The apostle Paul writes in Titus 2:11–12 that the grace of God brings salvation and teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives in this present world.
Did you catch that?
Grace teaches us.
Not just how to die with hope.
How to live with Christ now.
The Greek word translated "teaching" in Titus 2:12 is παιδεύουσα (paideuousa), carrying the sense of training, educating, and disciplining.
Grace is not merely a declaration that our sins can be forgiven.
Grace also trains those who belong to Christ to turn away from sin and grow in godliness.
And that training happens in the ordinary, uncomfortable places where our true character is revealed.
It happens when your child disobeys you for the fifth time and you must choose whether to respond with patience or anger.
It happens when your spouse disappoints you and you must decide whether to seek reconciliation or punish them with silence.
It happens when someone else's success exposes the envy you thought you had overcome.
It happens when nobody is watching and you must decide whether integrity is still worth practicing.
It happens when you are exhausted, misunderstood, tempted, afraid, or carrying a grief that nobody else seems to recognize.
Following Jesus is not reserved for the extraordinary moments when the worship music swells and tears fall down our faces.
It is often revealed in the quiet decisions nobody applauds.
The apology.
The confession.
The refusal to retaliate.
The honest conversation.
The unseen act of generosity.
The prayer whispered through clenched teeth.
The choice to turn away from a familiar sin and seek help instead of hiding again.
These moments may never make anyone famous.
But they matter to the Lord.
And perhaps some of us need to admit something painful.
We have become very good at celebrating Christian identity while sometimes neglecting Christian formation.
We ask people whether they have accepted Jesus.
That is an important question.
But do we also teach them how to abide in Him?
How to read Scripture faithfully rather than merely collect inspirational verses?
How to pray when they feel nothing?
How to resist temptation without pretending temptation does not exist?
How to confess sin without surrendering to despair?
How to practice justice and mercy?
How to endure suffering without assuming God has abandoned them?
How to love their neighbors when their neighbors are difficult to love?
How to handle money, power, relationships, sexuality, ambition, disappointment, and conflict under the lordship of Christ?
How to remain faithful when following Jesus costs them approval?
Because discipleship is not an optional advanced course for unusually serious Christians.
It is the life to which Jesus calls His people.
In Luke 9:23, Jesus says:
"If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." (KJV)
Daily.
That word changes the conversation.
The Greek text uses καθ’ ἡμέραν (kath’ hēmeran), meaning "day by day" or "daily."
Not only at conversion.
Not only during revival meetings.
Not only when circumstances are favorable.
Daily.
When faith feels strong.
When faith feels fragile.
When obedience brings joy.
When obedience involves sacrifice.
When you wake up grateful.
And when you wake up wondering how you will survive another day.
Jesus calls His disciples to follow Him through the ordinary rhythm of life.
But please understand something.

Taking up your cross does not mean remaining in abuse, accepting exploitation, refusing medical treatment, or believing that every form of suffering is something God requires you to endure without help.
Jesus' call is to self-denial and costly allegiance to Him, not permission for others to harm you.
And following Christ does not mean pretending to be strong when you are wounded.
Sometimes faithfulness looks like asking for help.
Sometimes it looks like telling the truth about what happened.
Sometimes it looks like seeking wise pastoral care, professional support, or safety.
Sometimes it looks like finally admitting that the image you have been maintaining is crushing the person underneath.
The Jesus who calls us to deny ourselves is also the Jesus who invites the weary and burdened to come to Him for rest (Matthew 11:28–30).
He is not a cruel taskmaster demanding that broken people manufacture perfection.
He is the Savior who receives sinners, gives rest, and transforms His people by grace.
And this is where I think about Peter.
Not the polished version we sometimes imagine.
The real Peter.
The disciple who boldly promised loyalty.
The man who believed he would stand even if everyone else fell.
The follower who drew a sword in one moment and denied knowing Jesus in another.
Imagine the sound of the rooster.
Imagine the terrible realization that you have done exactly what you insisted you would never do.
Luke 22:61 tells us that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Then Peter remembered.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
Scripture does not tell us everything that passed through Peter's mind.
But anyone who has betrayed their own convictions can recognize something of that moment.
The shame of knowing better.
The weight of having failed.
The awful question of whether your failure has become your identity.
And perhaps that is where some of you are living right now.
You have heard sermons about victory.
But you feel defeated.
You have heard testimonies about freedom.
But you are still fighting a familiar temptation.
You have heard people talk about spiritual maturity.
But you are ashamed of how easily anger, fear, envy, or bitterness still rises inside you.
You love Jesus.
And you are painfully aware of how much in your life still needs to change.
Please do not mistake conviction for the absence of hope.
Peter's story did not end beside that charcoal fire of denial.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, the risen Lord questioned Peter about his love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
The man who had denied Jesus was not beyond the reach of restoring grace.
But notice what Jesus did not do.
He did not teach Peter that failure was harmless.
He did not pretend the denial never happened.
And He did not reduce restoration to a moment of emotional relief.
He called Peter back into love, service, and faithful following.
"Follow me." (John 21:19, KJV)
Two words.
Spoken by the risen Savior to a man who knew the bitterness of failure.
Not, "Prove that you have never fallen."
Not, "Rebuild your reputation before you come near Me."
Not, "Your worst moment must define the rest of your life."
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not that sin does not matter.
Sin matters so profoundly that Christ died for our sins.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
Jesus Himself called people to repent and believe the Gospel (Mark 1:15).
But that failure does not have to be the final chapter for the person who turns to Christ.
There is forgiveness in Him.
There is reconciliation with God through Him.
There is power for a transformed life by His Spirit.
And there is a future that our past cannot purchase, destroy, or deserve.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Yet here is the part we cannot afford to miss.
Jesus did not restore Peter merely so Peter could feel better about himself.
He restored him to a life of following and serving.
The grace that lifted Peter from shame also called him forward into responsibility.
And that is what genuine discipleship does.
It does not leave people imprisoned in guilt.
But neither does it leave them comfortably unchanged.
It brings them to Jesus, again and again, until His truth begins to reshape how they live.
Perhaps the Church needs to recover this kind of patient, truthful, grace-filled discipleship.
Not just bigger crowds.
Deeper roots.
Not just powerful moments.
Faithful lives.
Not just people who can repeat the promise of eternal life.
People who are learning to embody the love of Christ in the world around them.
And please, do not misunderstand me.
We must never stop preaching heaven.
The hope of resurrection is not a distraction from Christian discipleship.
It is one of its greatest sources of courage.
Jesus promised His disciples that He was going to prepare a place for them (John 14:1–3).
Paul reminded believers that their citizenship is in heaven and that they await the Savior (Philippians 3:20).
Revelation 21 gives us a breathtaking vision of God's dwelling with His people, where death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
We need that hope.
The grieving widow needs it.
The believer enduring persecution needs it.
The parent standing beside a grave needs it.
The exhausted Christian who wonders whether suffering will ever end needs it.
Christianity without the resurrection and the promise of eternal life would not be the Gospel proclaimed by the apostles.
But biblical hope does not teach us to abandon the present.
It teaches us to live faithfully within it.
In 1 Corinthians 15, Paul spends an entire chapter defending the resurrection.
Then he concludes by urging believers to remain steadfast and abound in the work of the Lord, knowing that their labor is not in vain.
Do you see the connection?
Because resurrection is real, what we do for Christ now matters.
Because eternity is real, faithfulness today is not wasted.
Because Jesus is coming again, we have every reason to love, serve, endure, and obey while we wait.
Heaven is not an excuse to neglect the earth.
It is a promise that strengthens us to live for Christ here.
Even the prayer Jesus taught His disciples holds these realities together.
"Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven." (Matthew 6:10, KJV)
In the Greek text, the petition includes γενηθήτω τὸ θέλημά σου (genēthētō to thelēma sou) — "let Your will be done."
That prayer is not a demand that we create heaven through human effort.
God alone brings His kingdom to its promised fullness.
But it is a prayer of surrendered allegiance.
We ask for God's will to be done, and we offer ourselves as people willing to obey it.
Not just when we die.
While we live.
So imagine what might happen if we taught discipleship with the same seriousness with which we teach the hope of heaven.
Imagine a church where a newly converted believer is not simply congratulated and then left alone to figure out the Christian life.
Imagine someone walking beside them.
Opening Scripture with them.
Teaching them to pray.
Helping them understand repentance.
Showing them how to face temptation.
Encouraging them when they stumble.
Correcting them gently when they wander.
Reminding them that salvation rests on Christ, not on their ability to maintain an impressive religious image.
Imagine children growing up seeing parents who do not merely quote Scripture, but apologize when they are wrong.
Imagine marriages where the language of grace becomes a daily practice of honesty, humility, fidelity, and forgiveness.
Imagine Christians who are known not only for the positions they defend, but for the mercy, truthfulness, courage, and love with which they live.
Imagine congregations where struggling believers can confess sin and seek help without fear of being turned into gossip.
Where the wounded are protected.
Where the poor are not forgotten.
Where leaders are accountable.
Where the Gospel is not diluted to make everyone comfortable, but neither is truth weaponized to crush the repentant.
Where holiness is pursued with humility.
Where grace is celebrated without excusing evil.
Where the name of Jesus is not merely displayed on a building but honored through the lives of His people.
Wouldn't that be a beautiful witness?
Not a perfect church.
There has never been a congregation of sinless people.
But a church continually returning to its perfect Savior.
A church willing to repent.
A church willing to learn.
A church willing to follow.
Jesus said in John 13:35 that people would recognize His disciples by their love for one another.
That is a remarkable statement.
He did not say the world would recognize us primarily by the size of our platforms, the sophistication of our arguments, or the number of religious events on our calendars.
Love.
Not sentimental approval of everything.
Not avoidance of difficult truth.
But the kind of love that flows from Christ and reflects His character.
The love that serves.
The love that speaks truth.
The love that bears burdens.
The love that refuses to turn wounded people into disposable people.
The love that remembers we were all desperate for mercy before we had anything to offer.
And perhaps this is where the question becomes deeply personal.
Because it is easy to criticize the modern Church.
It is much harder to ask whether we ourselves have been following Jesus.
So I want to ask you something.
Not as a judge standing above you.
As someone who must stand beneath the same Word.
When was the last time Scripture corrected something in your life, and you actually changed direction?
When was the last time you apologized without defending yourself?
When was the last time you prayed for someone who could do absolutely nothing for you?
When was the last time you resisted the temptation to turn someone else's failure into entertainment?
When was the last time you chose obedience over convenience?
When was the last time you opened the Bible not merely looking for reassurance, but ready to be confronted, comforted, and transformed by God's truth?
And perhaps the hardest question of all:
If someone learned what following Jesus means by watching the way you live, what would they learn about Him?
That question reaches me too.
Because I do not want to become so skilled at speaking about Jesus that I forget to sit at His feet.
I do not want to know the language of surrender while protecting the very things He is asking me to release.
I do not want to spend my life inviting people into a faith I am unwilling to practice.
And I do not want anyone reading this to confuse spiritual performance with the real Christian life.
Some days following Jesus will look like courageous public witness.
Other days it will look like quiet repentance in your bedroom.
Some days it will look like serving hundreds of people.
Other days it will look like faithfully caring for one difficult person.
Some days it will look like victory over a temptation.
Other days it will look like refusing to surrender to despair after you have fallen, confessing your sin, receiving God's mercy, and taking the next faithful step.
The Christian life is not sustained by pretending we no longer need grace.
It is sustained by remaining dependent on Christ.
Jesus says in John 15:5:
"I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing." (KJV)
Without Me.
Not without a religious reputation.
Not without an impressive testimony.
Not without a perfect social media image.
Without Me.
That is the difference between merely appearing Christian and actually abiding in Christ.
And it is why we cannot disciple people into dependence on personalities, platforms, or programs.
We must continually point them to Jesus.
Pastors are not the Vine.
Ministries are not the Vine.
Christian influencers are not the Vine.
Even the most helpful discipleship resources are not the Vine.
Christ is the Vine.
Everything else must serve the purpose of helping people know Him, trust Him, obey Him, and grow in His grace.
That conviction is also at the heart of why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a following that revolves around a human personality.
Not to replace the local church.
But to keep placing biblical truth, encouragement, conviction, and discipleship resources before people who need to hear that Jesus is still calling them.
Some of those people are believers who have grown weary.
Some are new Christians who have no idea where to begin.
Some have been wounded by religious hypocrisy and are struggling to trust again.
Some are seekers who have questions they are afraid to ask.
Some are people who have been away from church for years, quietly wondering whether the door back to God is still open.
And some are simply trying to make it through another ordinary day without losing their grip on hope.
They need more than another religious slogan.
They need the Gospel.
They need Scripture handled faithfully.
They need reminders of grace that do not erase repentance.
They need teaching that connects eternal truth with real-life obedience.
And they need to know that the invitation of Jesus is still open.
Those resources are not a substitute for Scripture, prayer, Christian fellowship, or faithful participation in a local church.
They are tools intended to help nourish those practices.
And they are available freely because spiritual growth should never be presented as something only people with money can pursue.
But making resources available, maintaining the ministry, developing new materials, and expanding its reach also involve real work and real costs.
Not because you owe this ministry a payment for God's grace.
You do not.
Those responsibilities deserve their own prayerful consideration.
But because voluntary, generous support can be one practical way of serving others for the glory of God.
The New Testament teaches that giving should be willing rather than coerced. Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver, not someone pressured into giving reluctantly.
For some, that may be an expression of generosity alongside their regular giving.
For others, sharing these resources may be the more appropriate way to help.
Both can be meaningful.
Neither purchases God's favor.
And no one should neglect essential family needs, debt obligations, or the care of others to support an online ministry.
But for those who have been looking for a tangible way to help more people encounter Scripture and grow as disciples, this is an invitation worth prayerfully considering.
The greater purpose is the work we can help sustain together.
More biblical encouragement.
More discipleship materials.
More opportunities to reach people who are searching, struggling, doubting, or learning to follow Christ.
Not merely to increase a number on a screen.
Someone who is exhausted by pretending.
Someone who thinks their repeated failures mean God is finished with them.
Someone who has mistaken church attendance for discipleship.
Someone who needs to discover that following Jesus is neither empty religious performance nor a hopeless attempt to earn salvation.
It is a life of grace, repentance, faith, obedience, and dependence on the living Christ.
Or send this privately to a person who may need encouragement but would not want their struggles discussed publicly.
Not with a polished religious answer.
With something real.
Or share one area where God is teaching you obedience right now.
Perhaps it is forgiveness.
Perhaps it is patience.
Perhaps it is honesty.
Perhaps it is learning to pray again.
Perhaps it is returning to Christ after a season of wandering.
You do not need to reveal private wounds or details you are not ready to share.
But your honest testimony may encourage someone who believes they are the only person still struggling.
And if you are exhausted, a simple "pray for me" is enough.
There is no shame in asking other believers to carry you in prayer.
Return to these Scriptures.
Examine them in context.
Pray over them.
Invite your family, your friends, the believers who feel spiritually distant, and even the people who are still exploring Christianity to follow along.
Not because a social media page can save anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But because a faithful word of Scripture, encountered at the right moment, can direct someone toward the Savior who can.
And perhaps that is how a simple act of sharing becomes an act of love.
One person reads.
One person begins asking questions.
One person opens a Bible that has been gathering dust.
One person seeks forgiveness.
One person returns to Christian fellowship.
One person realizes that they cannot continue calling Jesus Lord while refusing to listen to His words.
And one person discovers that the grace of Christ is not exhausted by the failures they have been hiding.
We cannot manufacture those outcomes.
The Holy Spirit is the One who convicts and transforms.
But we can faithfully plant and water, trusting God for the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).
And that is enough reason to keep going.
Because the goal was never simply to produce more religious content.
The goal is to make much of Jesus.
To proclaim His death and resurrection.
To call people to repentance and faith.
To help believers grow in the knowledge of His Word.
To encourage them to live as His disciples in their homes, workplaces, churches, and communities.
To remind the ashamed that forgiveness is found in Christ.
To remind the proud that they still need mercy.
To remind the weary that Jesus gives rest.
And to remind the Church that the Great Commission was never merely a command to collect decisions.
It was a command to make disciples.
There is one final image I cannot shake.
Imagine standing before Jesus after a lifetime of talking about Him.
Not before an audience.
Not before a congregation.
Not before people impressed by your biblical knowledge.
Before Him.
The One who knew your thoughts when nobody else did.
The One who saw every secret act of kindness.
The One who witnessed every hidden compromise.
The One who knew how often you stumbled and how often you returned to Him for mercy.
The One whose blood alone is sufficient to cleanse sinners.
What would matter in that moment?
Not the number of people who applauded your faith.
Not the image you maintained.
Not the religious arguments you won.
But whether your confidence was truly in Christ — the Savior whose grace calls His people into a life of following Him.
Matthew 7:21–23 contains a sobering warning that merely calling Jesus "Lord" and pointing to impressive religious activity does not guarantee that a person truly belongs to Him.
Those words are not an invitation to despair or to search for assurance in personal perfection.
They are an invitation to reject false confidence and come honestly to the real Jesus.
The Jesus who said, "Come unto me" (Matthew 11:28).
The Jesus who said, "Follow me" (Matthew 4:19).
The Jesus who said, "If ye love me, keep my commandments" (John 14:15).
The Jesus who died for our sins and rose again.
The Jesus who remains the only Savior.
And perhaps that is where this entire question finally leads us.
Are we preparing people for heaven while forgetting to teach them how to follow Jesus today?
We must not choose between those two callings.
We must preach the eternal hope secured by Christ.
And we must teach the present life of discipleship that flows from His grace.
We must proclaim justification by faith.
And we must teach sanctification by the Spirit.
We must tell people that salvation cannot be earned.
And we must tell them that saving grace is never permission to make peace with sin.
We must comfort the brokenhearted.
And we must confront the comfortable.
We must teach believers how to face death with hope.
And how to face tomorrow with faithfulness.
Because the same Jesus who promises resurrection life also calls His people to follow Him today.
So before you close this article, consider one simple question.
What is one thing Jesus has already shown you through His Word that you need to begin obeying today?
Not ten dramatic promises.
Not another temporary emotional high.
One honest step.
One conversation you have been avoiding.
One sin you need to confess.
One person you need to forgive.
One boundary you need to establish.
One act of service you have been postponing.
One decision to seek help.
One return to Scripture.
One prayer of surrender.
Not to earn His love.
But because His grace has met you, and you want your life to reflect the One who saved you.
If you have never truly trusted Christ, begin there. Turn to Him in repentance and faith. His death and resurrection, not your religious achievements, are the foundation of salvation.
If you already belong to Him but have wandered, return to Him.
If you are weary, come to Him.
If you have fallen, confess your sin and seek His mercy.
If you are growing, remain humble.
If you are teaching others, teach them to obey everything Jesus commanded.
And if you are helping build a ministry, a family, a church, or a community, never forget whose name must remain at the center.
Not ours.
His.
Because at the end of everything, the most important question is not simply whether we spent our lives talking about going to heaven.
It is whether we truly knew and followed the Savior who brings His people home.
May we never become so occupied with telling people where Jesus will take them someday that we forget to show them how to walk with Him today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE’S MOST UNCOMFORTABLE SEXUAL LAWS REQUIRE CONTEXT—NOT EMBARRASSMENT, NOT EXCUSES.
paragraphs: THE BIBLE’S MOST UNCOMFORTABLE SEXUAL LAWS REQUIRE CONTEXT—NOT EMBARRASSMENT, NOT EXCUSES.

Some passages sound so disturbing that Christians avoid reading them aloud. Critics use them to accuse God. Believers sometimes rush to defend what they have never studied. But what happens when we stop hiding from the difficult verses, open the ancient Hebrew Scriptures, and discover that understanding the Bible honestly may lead us straight to the heart of Jesus Christ?
There is a moment that can shake a Christian's faith without warning.
Someone opens the Bible, reads a verse about sexual violence, marriage, virginity, or a woman's place in ancient Israel, and asks a question that suddenly makes the entire room uncomfortable.
“Wait. Did God really command that?”
The confident believer goes quiet.
The skeptic leans forward.
The person who has survived sexual abuse feels something tighten inside their chest.
And somewhere in the conversation, somebody says the words Christians should never be afraid to hear:
“Can you explain this without making excuses?”
That question deserves more than a rehearsed answer.
Because if the Bible really is God's Word, we should not have to protect it by pretending its hardest passages are easy.
And if Jesus Christ really is the truth, then honest examination is not His enemy.
But before we go any further, understand something.

This article will not pretend that ancient Israel operated under modern laws. It will not claim every Old Testament regulation represents God's ideal for human relationships. It will not excuse sexual violence, erase women's suffering, or turn difficult Hebrew words into convenient translations.
We are going to open the passages people often avoid.
And we are going to ask what they actually say.
Not what a viral screenshot claims.
Not what an embarrassed Christian wishes they said.
Not what an angry critic assumes they must mean.
What the text says. What the language means. What the historical setting reveals. And how Christians should understand these passages in the light of Jesus Christ.
Because sometimes the most dangerous thing you can do with Scripture is not question it.
It is quote it without understanding it.
Consider Deuteronomy 22.

Within a relatively short section, we encounter laws about accusations of premarital sexual activity, adultery, sexual assault, betrothal, and a man who has sexual relations with an unbetrothed virgin.
These are not comfortable verses.
They were never intended to become inspirational wall decorations.
They belong to an ancient legal collection addressing real disputes in a society radically different from ours.
And the first mistake readers make is treating every law in that collection as though it were a direct instruction to every Christian living today.
That is not how biblical interpretation works.
The Hebrew word תּוֹרָה (torah) can mean instruction, teaching, or law, depending on context. The Torah contains commands, narratives, covenant obligations, and legal provisions given to Israel.
Those laws operated within Israel's particular covenant and social world.
They must be read according to their literary context, their historical setting, and their place in the unfolding biblical story.
This matters because a law regulating a damaged human situation does not automatically mean God delights in the situation being regulated.
Jesus Himself established this distinction.
When religious leaders questioned Him about divorce, He answered:
“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.” — Matthew 19:8, KJV
Read that again.
“From the beginning it was not so.”
Jesus distinguished between a legal concession made in response to human hardness and God's original intention for marriage.
That does not mean every difficult Old Testament law can simply be dismissed as a concession. Each passage still requires careful interpretation.
But it establishes something enormously important.
A biblical law may address human brokenness without presenting that brokenness as God's perfect design.
And suddenly, we have a better question to ask.
Not merely, “Why does this law exist?”
But, “What problem was this law addressing, what did it require in its original setting, and how does it relate to God's larger purposes?”
Now consider one of the most disturbing accusations made against the Bible.
“Doesn't the Bible command a rape victim to marry her rapist?”
The passage usually cited is Deuteronomy 22:28–29.

In the King James Version, it describes a man who finds an unbetrothed virgin, lays hold of her, and has sexual relations with her. The man must pay fifty shekels of silver to her father, and the text says she becomes his wife and that he may not divorce her.
That is what the passage says.
And we must not pretend it says something softer.
The Hebrew wording deserves close attention.
In Deuteronomy 22:25, describing a man who sexually assaults a betrothed woman in the countryside, the verb is וְהֶחֱזִיק (vehecheziq), from a root associated with taking hold of or overpowering.
But in Deuteronomy 22:28, the expression is וּתְפָשָׂהּ (utefasah), from תָּפַשׂ (taphas), meaning to seize, grasp, or take hold of.
These are different Hebrew verbs.
That difference matters.
But here is where honesty becomes essential.
The difference alone does not prove that the second encounter was consensual.

The verb taphas can describe forceful taking, and interpreters disagree about whether Deuteronomy 22:28–29 addresses rape, another form of coercive sexual misconduct, or illicit intercourse in a setting where the woman's consent is not specified.
We should not claim that Hebrew grammar settles a question it does not settle.
And we should not erase the troubling fact that the law is framed within a patriarchal social and legal system.
Exodus 22:16–17 provides a related law involving a man who seduces an unbetrothed virgin. There, the woman's father can refuse to give her in marriage.
That related passage is important context.
But it does not explicitly resolve every question about Deuteronomy 22:28–29, and we should not automatically import every provision from Exodus into Deuteronomy as though the texts were identical.

Some Christian interpreters understand the Deuteronomy law as imposing lifelong financial and marital responsibility on a man who has seriously wronged a woman in a society where marriage strongly affected her economic security.
Others argue that the passage reflects an ancient legal framework that does not adequately address the woman's consent or autonomy by modern standards.
Those concerns cannot be brushed aside.
The text imposes a penalty and an obligation on the man. It does not explicitly say the woman is free to refuse the marriage.
We cannot honestly claim that it does.
But neither should we confuse an ancient legal provision with a universal Christian command that victims of sexual assault must marry their attackers.
No Christian pastor, parent, or church should use this passage to pressure a sexual assault survivor into marrying or remaining with an abuser.
That would be a grievous misuse of Scripture.
And if you have ever heard this passage used to silence your pain, please hear this clearly.
Your suffering is not an inconvenience to biblical interpretation.
You are a human being made in the image of God.
What happened to you matters.
And the Gospel never requires you to call evil good.
Now look at the immediately preceding law.
Deuteronomy 22:25–27 addresses a betrothed woman assaulted in the countryside.
The law holds the attacker responsible and explicitly says that the woman has committed no offense deserving death.
The passage compares the assault to a man rising against his neighbor and killing him.
That comparison is astonishingly serious.
The Hebrew text in verse 26 says:
וְלַנַּעֲרָ לֹא־תַעֲשֶׂה דָבָר
Vela-na'arah lo-ta'aseh davar.
“Do nothing to the young woman.”
The passage continues by stating that she has no sin deserving death.
In its ancient legal context, the law recognizes her innocence and treats the assault as a grave act of violence.
Notice what the text does not say.
It does not blame her for being attacked.
It does not declare her morally contaminated by another person's violence.
It does not say that the crime becomes less serious because the attacker desired her.
It places guilt upon the offender.
That is a vital distinction.

Yet we should also recognize that Deuteronomy 22:23–24, dealing with an assault or sexual encounter involving a betrothed woman in a city, raises serious questions about assumptions concerning whether she could have cried out or obtained help.
We must not turn those ancient assumptions into modern tests of whether someone has been assaulted.
Survivors may freeze, become unable to speak, comply out of fear, or be physically prevented from resisting.
The absence of a scream does not establish consent.
A faithful Christian reading must never weaponize an ancient evidentiary assumption against a person seeking protection today.
And perhaps this is where some of us need to repent.
Not because we asked difficult questions about the Bible.
But because we sometimes answered them without compassion.
We were so desperate to win an argument that we forgot there might be a wounded person listening.
Someone who has spent years wondering whether God cared about what happened behind a locked door.
Someone whose attacker used religious language.
Someone who was told to remain silent to protect a family's reputation.
Someone who heard more concern for a ministry's image than for their own safety.
If that is you, I want you to know that defending the Bible does not require defending the person who harmed you.
And protecting the reputation of a religious institution is not the same thing as honoring Jesus Christ.
There is another passage that demands this same honesty.
Numbers 5:11–31 describes the ordeal of a woman whose husband suspects her of adultery but lacks evidence.
The passage involves a priest, an oath, and a ritual using water mixed with dust from the tabernacle floor.
Some modern readers describe this as a biblical abortion ritual.
Others insist it has nothing whatsoever to do with reproductive consequences.
Both claims can oversimplify a difficult text.
The Hebrew passage includes the expression וְנָפְלָה יְרֵכָהּ (venafelah yerekhah), literally involving her thigh falling or wasting, alongside language concerning her abdomen swelling.
The word יָרֵךְ (yarekh) ordinarily means thigh, but can function euphemistically in contexts involving reproduction or descendants.
Scholars debate the precise physical consequence envisioned.
Some understand the language as referring to reproductive injury, infertility, or miscarriage. Others interpret it differently.
The text does not describe a physician performing a modern medical abortion procedure. Nor does it provide a straightforward basis for claiming that the passage settles contemporary abortion ethics.
Its ancient setting is a ritual ordeal addressing suspected infidelity where ordinary evidence was absent.
The ritual places the outcome under divine judgment rather than authorizing the husband to impose punishment on his own suspicion.
That distinction matters.
So does the fact that the passage centers on a husband's suspicion and does not provide an equivalent ritual for a wife suspecting her husband.
We do not need to conceal that asymmetry.
Context should make our reading more truthful, not more convenient.
And then there is Leviticus 18.
A chapter filled with prohibitions involving incestuous relationships, adultery, same-sex intercourse between males, and sexual relations with animals.
Some readers treat it as though every command can be applied directly without examining the covenantal setting.
Others dismiss the entire chapter as irrelevant ancient material.
Neither approach adequately accounts for the Bible's complexity.
Leviticus 18 belongs to Israel's holiness legislation.
Its concern is not merely individual desire but the identity and conduct of a people called to live differently from the surrounding nations.
Leviticus 18:6 begins with a prohibition against approaching close relatives to uncover their nakedness.
The Hebrew expression לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה (legalot ervah) means “to uncover nakedness,” a legal idiom frequently referring to prohibited sexual relations.
Understanding that expression helps us recognize that the passage is not simply about accidental exposure or ordinary nudity.
It is addressing sexual boundaries.
Leviticus 18:22, meanwhile, prohibits a male lying with another male in the manner described as lying with a woman.
The Hebrew reads:
וְאֶת־זָכָר לֹא תִשְׁכַּב מִשְׁכְּבֵי אִשָּׁה
Ve'et-zakhar lo tishkav mishkevei ishah.
A close rendering is:
“You shall not lie with a male as with the lyings of a woman.”
Christians disagree about how this prohibition should be related to modern understandings of sexual orientation, committed same-sex relationships, and New Testament teaching.
Traditional Christian interpreters generally understand the prohibition as part of a continuing biblical sexual ethic reserving sexual intercourse for marriage between a man and a woman.
Other interpreters argue that the ancient social setting, the nature of the acts envisioned, and the relationship between Israel's holiness laws and Christian ethics require a different conclusion.
We should state those disagreements accurately rather than pretending they do not exist.
And whatever conclusions Christians reach, no one is given permission to humiliate, assault, threaten, or dehumanize another person.
Every person bears the image of God.
Biblical conviction does not cancel the command to love one's neighbor.
And love does not require dishonesty about what we believe Scripture teaches.
The challenge is to hold truth and compassion together without turning either into a weapon.
Now consider another passage that can make modern readers recoil.
Deuteronomy 21:10–14 describes an Israelite man who desires to marry a woman taken captive during war.
The woman is permitted a period of mourning. The man is instructed to follow a prescribed process before marriage, and if he later rejects her, he must let her go freely rather than sell her.
Some defend this passage by pointing out that it places restrictions upon the treatment of a captive woman.
And it does.
But the woman is still a captive.
The circumstances are shaped by war, defeat, and an enormous imbalance of power.
The passage does not explicitly describe her free consent to the marriage.
That is morally troubling.
Acknowledging it is not rebellion against God.
It is taking the words seriously enough to refuse to invent protections the passage never explicitly states.
We can recognize that the law restrains certain abuses within its ancient context without presenting the whole arrangement as the ideal of Christian marriage.
The biblical story does not end with ancient warfare or the legal structures of Israel.
It moves toward Jesus Christ.
And that changes how Christians must approach the whole conversation.
Because when Jesus speaks about marriage in Matthew 19, He reaches behind the Mosaic divorce regulation to Genesis.
To creation.
To the beginning.
Before conquest.
Before monarchy.
Before the accumulated damage of generations of human sin.
Genesis 1:27 declares that God created humanity in His image, male and female.
Genesis 2:24 describes the man and woman becoming one flesh.
Jesus cites this creation account in Matthew 19:4–6.
And in doing so, He points to a vision of marriage grounded in God's creative intention rather than merely the management of human brokenness.
But even here, we must be careful.
Jesus does not invite us to romanticize marriage while ignoring violence inside it.
A marriage certificate does not make cruelty holy.
A wedding vow does not transform sexual coercion into love.
