They survived the Red Sea, escaped Pharaoh, and witnessed the impossible. But just three days later, they discovered something terrifying: Sometimes God leads you to the very place that breaks your heart before He reveals what He can heal.
“When they came to Marah, they could not drink its water because it was bitter.” — Exodus 15:23
Imagine watching the sea split open before your eyes.
Not in a dream. Not in a story someone told you. You were there.

You heard the screams of Egyptian soldiers behind you. You felt the ground trembling beneath the wheels of Pharaoh's chariots. You saw the impossible wall of water rising on either side as you walked through a place where human beings were never supposed to walk.
And when you reached the other side, you watched the waters return.
The army that had terrified your family for generations was gone.
You were free.
For the first time in your life, nobody owned you.
Nobody could whip your back.
Nobody could force your children into slavery.
You had seen what the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob could do.
And then...
Three days later, you were desperately thirsty.
No water.
No wells.
No rivers.
Nothing but heat, sand, exhaustion, and the frightening realization that freedom had brought you into a wilderness where you could die.
Then someone shouted.
“WATER!”
Imagine the relief.
Mothers grabbing their children. Fathers stumbling toward the pools. Elderly people gathering what little strength remained in their bodies.
Finally.
An answer.
A place to drink.
A reason to believe everything would be okay.
But the moment the water touched their lips...
Something was terribly wrong.
It was bitter.
Undrinkable.
And suddenly, the people who had just witnessed one of the greatest miracles in biblical history were standing beside the very thing they needed to survive...
Unable to receive it.
And here is the question that should make every believer uncomfortable: What do you do when God has brought you out of something terrible, but the place you reach next is still painful?
Because some of you know exactly what that feels like.
You prayed for the marriage to survive, but the relationship remains strained.
You begged God to open a door, but the opportunity that finally came carried difficulties you never expected.
You escaped a destructive relationship, only to discover that the wounds followed you into freedom.
You surrendered your life to Jesus, but the anxiety did not disappear overnight.
You believed God was leading you somewhere better.
And now you are standing beside your own Marah.
Looking at something you thought would satisfy you.
Wondering why it tastes so bitter.
And somewhere deep inside, where you rarely allow anyone to look, a question has been growing.
“Lord, after everything You brought me through... why am I here?”
Stay with this story.
Because what happened at Marah was not merely about water.
It was about the hearts of people learning to trust the God who had already delivered them.
And the answer God gave them points us toward a truth that reaches far beyond the wilderness.
A truth we desperately need to hear when the miracle behind us seems greater than the trouble in front of us.
Exodus 15:22 tells us that Moses led Israel away from the Red Sea into the wilderness of Shur.
They traveled three days without finding water.
Three days.
It is easy to read those words from the comfort of a chair with a glass of water nearby.
It is something entirely different to imagine thousands of people, including children and the elderly, moving through an unforgiving landscape with no dependable supply of drinking water.
Their need was real.
Their exhaustion was real.
Their fear was understandable.
Scripture does not ask us to pretend that thirst was imaginary.
But then comes the sentence that changes the entire scene.
In the original Hebrew, Exodus 15:23 reads:
וַיָּבֹאוּ מָרָתָה וְלֹא יָכְלוּ לִשְׁתֹּת מַיִם מִמָּרָה כִּי מָרִים הֵם
Vayyavo'u Maratah, velo yakhelu lishtot mayim miMarah, ki marim hem.
A close English rendering is:
“They came to Marah, but they could not drink water from Marah, because it was bitter.”
The Hebrew word מָרִים (marim) means “bitter,” while מָרָה (Marah) is the place-name associated with that bitterness.
The connection is deliberate.
The place was called Marah because of the bitterness of its water.
But notice something.
The text does not say God had abandoned them.
It does not say Pharaoh had returned.
It does not say the covenant had been canceled.
They had encountered a bitter circumstance while still traveling on the journey that followed God's deliverance.
That distinction matters.
Because too many believers interpret every painful season as proof that God has left them.
We think that if God truly loves us, the road should become easier.
If we have repented, everything should immediately improve.
If we have prayed, the answer should arrive exactly as we imagined.
If God has opened the sea, surely He will never allow us to face thirst.
But the Bible refuses to offer that kind of shallow faith.
Israel's journey teaches us that deliverance from bondage does not mean the immediate disappearance of every difficulty.
And perhaps that is where this story begins to expose something in us.
We celebrate the God who opens the sea.
But do we trust Him when the water is bitter?
We worship when the answer is yes.
But what happens when His providence leads us into a season we do not understand?
We testify when the miracle is visible.
But what happens when all we can see is another problem?
The Israelites had seen God's power.
Now they were being confronted with the question of whether they would trust His character.
Exodus 15:24 says:
“And the people murmured against Moses, saying, What shall we drink?” (KJV)
The Hebrew verb behind “murmured” is וַיִּלֹּנוּ (vayyillonu), from a verb meaning to grumble or complain.
Their question was not unreasonable.
They needed water.
But the narrative identifies their response as grumbling against Moses rather than a faithful appeal to the Lord.
And before we condemn them too quickly, perhaps we should examine ourselves.
How many times have we done something similar?
We have watched God provide before.
We have experienced mercy we did not deserve.
We have survived things that once seemed impossible.
Yet one unexpected disappointment can make us speak as though He has never been faithful.
One unanswered prayer.
One medical report.
One financial crisis.
One betrayal.
One child who walks away from the faith.
One marriage that becomes painfully quiet.
And suddenly, the memory of yesterday's mercy struggles against the weight of today's suffering.
We do not always say, “God has abandoned me.”
Sometimes it sounds more respectable.
“I just don't understand why He would allow this.”
“I've tried to do everything right.”
“I've prayed for years.”
“Maybe God hears other people, but not me.”
Sometimes those words come from genuine grief.
Sometimes they reveal a heart beginning to accuse God.
And sometimes both are tangled together so tightly that we barely know the difference.
That is why this passage deserves more than a quick religious slogan.
Because God does not respond to Marah by telling us that human pain is insignificant.
He shows us what faithful dependence looks like in the middle of genuine need.
While the people grumbled, Moses did something different.
Exodus 15:25 begins:
“And he cried unto the LORD; and the LORD shewed him a tree...”
The Hebrew says:
וַיִּצְעַק אֶל־יְהוָה
Vayyits'aq el-YHWH.
“And he cried out to the LORD.”
That word for crying out, וַיִּצְעַק (vayyits'aq), comes from a verb used for urgent calling or crying for help.
Moses did not pretend the water was sweet.
He did not deny the danger.
He did not deliver a motivational speech about positive thinking.
He cried out to God.
There is something profoundly comforting about that.
Faith does not require you to deny your suffering.
Faith brings your suffering before the One who is able to help.
There is a difference between pouring out your grief to God and allowing grief to become an accusation against Him.
The Psalms are filled with anguished prayers.
David wept.
Job lamented.
Jeremiah grieved.
Even Jesus, in Gethsemane, expressed the terrible weight of the suffering before Him while submitting Himself to the Father's will.
Biblical faith is not emotional numbness.
It is dependence.
And some of us have spent so much energy trying to appear spiritually strong that we have forgotten how to cry out honestly to the Lord.
We know how to post a Bible verse.
We know how to say, “God is good.”
We know how to smile when someone asks whether everything is okay.
But behind closed doors...
The tears come.
The questions return.
The loneliness grows.
And the heart whispers things the mouth is afraid to confess.
What if God is inviting you to stop performing strength and start seeking Him with sincerity?
Not because He does not already know your pain.
But because prayer is one of the ways He teaches His children to depend upon Him.
And then the story takes a remarkable turn.
The Lord shows Moses a tree, or piece of wood, and Moses throws it into the water.
The Hebrew of Exodus 15:25 says:
וַיּוֹרֵהוּ יְהוָה עֵץ וַיַּשְׁלֵךְ אֶל־הַמַּיִם וַיִּמְתְּקוּ הַמָּיִם
Vayyorehu YHWH ets, vayyashlekh el-hammayim, vayimtequ hammayim.
A close translation is:
“And the LORD showed him a tree; he threw it into the water, and the waters became sweet.”
Look closely at that last phrase.
וַיִּמְתְּקוּ הַמָּיִם
Vayimtequ hammayim.
“The waters became sweet.”
The verb comes from the Hebrew root מתק (m-t-q), associated with sweetness.
The water that could not be drunk became suitable for the people to drink.
But Scripture does not identify the species of tree.
It does not explain a chemical process.
It does not suggest that Moses discovered a universal natural remedy for contaminated water.
The emphasis falls on God's intervention.
The Lord showed Moses what to do.
Moses obeyed.
And the water changed.
What had been undrinkable became a provision.
What had been a source of distress became a place where God's power was revealed.
And perhaps the most striking detail is this:
God did not need to take Israel back to Egypt to provide what they needed.
He met them in the wilderness.
At the very place where their need had become undeniable.
Now, we must be careful with what we say next.
Because some sermons turn the tree at Marah into a direct prediction of the cross of Jesus Christ.
The resemblance can certainly invite Christian reflection.

Wood enters bitter water, and the water becomes sweet. Centuries later, Christ bears our sins upon the cross, and through His death and resurrection, sinners receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
But Exodus 15 does not explicitly identify the tree as a prophecy of Calvary.
We should not pretend it does.
The historical meaning of the passage concerns God's provision for Israel and His instruction of His redeemed people.
Yet when we read the whole Bible in light of Jesus Christ, we discover something even greater than a symbolic resemblance.
The God who provided for Israel at Marah is the God who has accomplished our redemption through His Son.
And the cross addresses a problem far deeper than bitter drinking water.
Because our greatest need is not simply for our circumstances to improve.
Our greatest need is to be reconciled to the holy God against whom we have sinned.
That is where the Gospel becomes intensely personal.
You may be able to hide your bitterness from everyone around you.
You may be able to conceal your resentment behind religious language.
You may know how to serve in church while quietly nursing unforgiveness.
You may even speak passionately about Jesus while refusing to surrender the sin you have been protecting.
But the Lord sees the heart.
He knows the anger you have rehearsed.
The envy you have justified.
The pride you have disguised as righteousness.
The secret compromises.
The prayers you stopped praying because you no longer wanted His answer to challenge your desires.
And still, the invitation of the Gospel is not to manufacture your own righteousness.
It is to repent and come to Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired every broken part of our lives.
Not after we earned the right to be loved.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And 1 Peter 2:24 says of Jesus:
“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree...” (KJV)
The Greek expression includes:
ἐπὶ τὸ ξύλον
Epi to xylon.
“Upon the tree,” or “upon the wood.”
Here, the New Testament explicitly speaks of Christ bearing our sins in connection with the wood of His crucifixion.
This does not prove that the tree at Marah was a direct prophecy of the cross.
But it reminds us that the Christian's deepest hope rests not in a mysterious object placed into water, but in the crucified and risen Savior.
Jesus did not come merely to make difficult circumstances more comfortable.
He came to save sinners.
To bear our guilt.
To reconcile us to God.
To give us new life.
And that changes how we understand healing.
Because sometimes the Lord changes the circumstances around us.
Sometimes He provides an unexpected answer.
Sometimes He restores what appeared impossible to repair.
But sometimes the situation remains difficult while He works deeply within us.
The apostle Paul pleaded with the Lord concerning his thorn in the flesh.
Yet the answer he received was:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” (2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV)
God's faithfulness is not measured by how quickly every bitter experience disappears.
And no Christian should be told that prolonged suffering automatically proves weak faith.
The cross itself destroys that assumption.
Jesus, the perfectly obedient Son of God, suffered terribly.
Yet His suffering was not evidence of the Father's abandonment of His saving purpose.
Through the death and resurrection of Christ, God accomplished redemption.
So when you stand at Marah, do not assume that pain has the final word.
But do not assume, either, that God has promised to make every earthly circumstance sweet on your timetable.
He has promised something greater to those who belong to Christ.
His presence.
His grace.
His faithfulness.
And a future in which sin, death, and suffering will not reign forever.
Revelation 21:4 speaks of the day when God will wipe away every tear, and death, sorrow, crying, and pain will be no more.
That promise is not sentimental optimism.
It is anchored in the victory of Jesus Christ.
And until that day, we learn to trust Him in the wilderness.
But there is another detail at Marah that we must not overlook.
After the waters became sweet, Exodus 15:25 says:
“There he made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there he proved them.” (KJV)
The Hebrew word associated with this testing is נִסָּהוּ (nissahu), from the root נסה (n-s-h), meaning to test or prove.
The wilderness was not merely a place where Israel needed provision.
It was also a place where their trust and obedience would be tested.
God was teaching a newly delivered people how to live in covenant dependence upon Him.
They had been rescued from slavery.
But they still needed to learn what it meant to listen to the Lord.
That should make us examine our own understanding of grace.
Because grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
The Jesus who forgives sinners also calls sinners to repentance.
The Savior who receives the broken also teaches His people to walk in holiness.
We are not saved by our obedience.
We are saved by grace through faith in Christ.
But the grace that saves us does not leave us indifferent to God's will.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds these truths together: salvation is God's gift, not the result of our works, and believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
So perhaps the question at your Marah is not merely:
“When will God change this situation?”
Perhaps another question needs to be asked.
“Lord, what are You teaching me about trusting and obeying You here?”
Not every painful event is a punishment.
Not every tragedy contains a hidden lesson we can confidently identify.
We must never use the story of Marah to blame suffering people for their suffering.
But every season can become an occasion to seek the Lord faithfully.
And there are moments when hardship exposes what prosperity has allowed us to ignore.
We discover how quickly we become impatient.
How deeply we crave control.
How easily disappointment becomes resentment.
How much we have confused God's gifts with God Himself.
And perhaps that is why the story of Marah remains so unsettling.
Because the bitter water was not the only thing being revealed.
The hearts of the people were being revealed too.
Some of you are reading this while carrying a bitterness that has lasted for years.
Someone betrayed you.
Someone abandoned you.
Someone made a promise they never intended to keep.
Someone you trusted used your vulnerability against you.
You have replayed the conversation a thousand times.
You know exactly what you wish you had said.
You have imagined the apology that never came.
And even though the person may have moved on, part of your heart is still standing in that painful moment.
You are exhausted.
Not only by what happened.
But by what remembering it continues to do to you.
Listen carefully.
Forgiveness does not mean calling evil good.
It does not mean pretending abuse never happened.
It does not require returning to an unsafe relationship or removing wise boundaries.
It does not mean that justice no longer matters.
But for those who have received mercy in Christ, forgiveness becomes part of the costly journey of refusing to let vengeance rule the heart.
Ephesians 4:31–32 calls believers to put away bitterness, wrath, and malice, and to forgive one another as God in Christ has forgiven them.
That command may confront something you have been protecting.
And it may take time, prayer, wise counsel, and difficult decisions to walk it out.
But do not confuse the difficulty of obedience with the absence of God's grace.
Christ is able to sustain you while you learn to obey Him.
And perhaps today the first honest prayer is not a dramatic declaration of victory.
Perhaps it is simply:
“Jesus, I know I need to forgive, but I am still hurting. Please help me.”
That is not a glamorous prayer.
It may never receive thousands of reactions on social media.
But it can be the beginning of genuine surrender.
And there is something else.
Sometimes we are not merely wounded by what others have done.
Sometimes we are ashamed of what we ourselves have done.
That is a different kind of bitterness.
The memory of a decision you cannot undo.
The relationship you damaged.
The lie you told.
The years you wasted.
The person you became when you thought nobody was watching.
Perhaps you still attend church.
You still know the songs.
You still recognize the verses.
But whenever someone speaks about God's holiness, something inside you tightens.
Because you know.
You remember.
And you wonder whether grace can truly reach someone who knew better and sinned anyway.
If that is you, hear the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not shed His blood only for people with respectable histories.
He came to save sinners.
Peter denied Him.
Paul had persecuted His people.
The thief beside Him had no lifetime of religious achievement to offer.
Their stories are not permission to treat sin lightly.
They are testimonies that God's mercy is greater than our ability to earn it.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Confession is not an attempt to inform God of something He does not know.
It is the honest acknowledgment of sin before Him.
And genuine repentance turns away from sin toward the Savior.
You do not need to decorate your failure before bringing it to Jesus.
You do not need to rewrite your history to make yourself worthy.
You need the mercy of the One who died and rose again.
And if you are in Christ, your past does not have the authority to cancel what His grace has accomplished.
This is why our message at Gospel Warrior has always mattered so deeply:
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because the consequences of sin magically disappear.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
But because Christ can redeem people who cannot redeem themselves.
He can forgive real guilt.
He can give new life to real sinners.
He can teach wounded hearts to trust again.
He can take a person who once lived in rebellion and make that person a witness to His mercy.
And no failure is more powerful than the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Now return with me to the wilderness.
Return to the thirsty families.
Return to the bitter water.
Return to the moment Moses cried out.
The Lord showed him what to do.
The water became sweet.
And the people who had feared they would have nothing to drink received provision.
But the story does not end with the transformation of the water.
In Exodus 15:26, God calls Israel to listen diligently to His voice, do what is right in His sight, and heed His commandments.
Then He declares:
“For I am the LORD that healeth thee.” (KJV)
The Hebrew is:
כִּי אֲנִי יְהוָה רֹפְאֶךָ
Ki ani YHWH rof'ekha.
“For I am the LORD, your healer.”
The word רֹפְאֶךָ (rof'ekha) means “the one who heals you,” from the Hebrew verb רפא (r-f-ʾ), meaning to heal.
This declaration appears within God's covenant instruction to Israel, including a warning concerning the diseases brought upon Egypt.
It must not be twisted into a blanket guarantee that every faithful Christian will experience immediate physical healing.
Nor should it be used to accuse sick people of disobedience.
But it does reveal something essential about the Lord's character.
He is not indifferent to the condition of His people.
He is the God who provides, instructs, restores, and heals according to His wisdom and covenant purposes.
And in Jesus Christ, we see the fullest revelation of God's saving mercy.
Jesus healed the sick.
He welcomed the outcast.
He forgave sins.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called people to repentance.
And He gave His life as a ransom for many.
The healing we need most begins with reconciliation to God.
And through Christ's resurrection, we have the hope of complete restoration in the age to come.
But there is one final detail in Israel's journey that I do not want you to miss.
It appears immediately after Marah.
Exodus 15:27 says:
“And they came to Elim, where were twelve wells of water, and threescore and ten palm trees: and they encamped there by the waters.” (KJV)
Twelve springs.
Seventy palm trees.
Water.
Shade.
Rest.
After Marah came Elim.
After the bitter water came a place where the people could camp beside abundant water.
And I can almost imagine the silence.
The children drinking without fear.
The weary sitting beneath the palms.
The families realizing they had survived another day.
The people discovering that the wilderness contained more than the bitterness they had encountered.
But we must read this faithfully.
Elim does not establish a universal promise that every Christian will receive a comfortable earthly season immediately after suffering.
The Bible contains faithful believers who endured hardship for years, and some who died without receiving earthly deliverance.
Yet Elim reminds us that Marah was not the whole story of Israel's journey.
And if you belong to Christ, your present suffering is not the whole story of your redemption either.
There is a resurrection.
There is a coming kingdom.
There is a Savior who has conquered death.
There is a future secured not by your ability to remain strong, but by the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
So do not make permanent conclusions about God's character from a temporary view of your circumstances.
Do not let one bitter season erase the truth of the cross.
Do not let disappointment become your final theology.
And do not confuse God's silence with proof that He is absent.
He has spoken decisively in His Son.
Perhaps you are at Marah today.
Perhaps you have been there longer than anyone knows.
Perhaps your friends see the smiling photographs, but they do not see the tears after midnight.
Perhaps you have grown tired of telling people you are okay.
Perhaps your prayers have become shorter because you are afraid of hoping again.
I cannot promise that tomorrow your situation will change.
I cannot promise that the person who hurt you will apologize.
I cannot promise that the diagnosis will disappear or that the financial burden will lift.
The Bible does not authorize me to make those promises.
But I can tell you that Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust.
That His grace is sufficient.
That His mercy is real.
That His resurrection is not a metaphor.
And that everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith finds a Savior who is able to save.
If you have been running from God, come home.
If you have been hiding sin, confess it.
If you have been trusting your own righteousness, surrender it.
If you have been crushed by shame, look to the cross.
If you have been wounded by others, ask the Lord for the grace to walk in truth, wisdom, and forgiveness.
And if you are simply exhausted, cry out to Him.
Like Moses did.
Not with polished religious language.
But with an honest heart.
“Lord, I need You.”
That prayer may be the most sincere thing you have said in months.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to know that they are not the only one struggling.
You do not need to reveal private details.
You do not need to expose wounds that are not safe to share publicly.
But your simple words may remind another believer that they are not walking through the wilderness alone.
And if God has already carried you through a bitter season, consider sharing a brief testimony.
Not to make your story look impressive.
But to point someone else toward the faithfulness of Jesus.
There may be a person reading these comments who desperately needs that encouragement.
And please do not let this message end with you.
Not merely because you agree with it.
But because somewhere among your family, friends, coworkers, and acquaintances, there may be someone standing at Marah right now.
Someone whose marriage is barely holding together.
Someone whose faith has grown weak.
Someone silently grieving.
Someone who has stopped praying.
Someone who thinks their past has disqualified them from receiving mercy.
Because spiritual encouragement is not something we outgrow.
We need the Word of God when we are rejoicing.
And we need it when the water is bitter.

We want this community to be a place where believers are strengthened by Scripture, struggling Christians are encouraged to return to the Lord, seekers can encounter the truth of the Gospel, and those who have grown spiritually complacent are challenged to repent and walk faithfully with Jesus.
And for those who want to go deeper, there is another invitation.
These resources are offered freely because spiritual nourishment should never be treated as something that only paying supporters deserve to receive.
But making resources available, preparing biblical content, and continuing to reach people with the message of Jesus Christ also requires faithful support.
It is an opportunity to help sustain and expand a ministry devoted to proclaiming Christ, sharing Scripture, encouraging repentance, and helping people grow in their faith.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful, not pressured or coerced.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
And Philippians 4:15–18 reminds us that believers can participate in Gospel work through material support.
That is the spirit of this invitation.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
But an opportunity to participate willingly in work you believe is faithful to the Gospel.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, strengthened your faith, encouraged you through a difficult season, or pointed you toward Jesus Christ, you may wish to help make that same encouragement available to others.
These items are not the reason we proclaim the Gospel.
They are simply practical resources and reminders that can accompany a life of discipleship.
The real purpose remains unchanged.
To glorify Jesus Christ.
To make His Word known.
To encourage genuine repentance and faith.
To remind the broken that grace is real.
To help believers grow deeper in the truth.
And to reach people who may never walk through the doors of a church but may encounter a Scripture-filled message on their phone.
Read the Scriptures with us.
Pray for this work.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Faithful service to Christ takes many forms, and the Gospel is not for sale.
What matters eternally is whether your hope rests in Jesus Christ.
And now, before you leave this story, I want you to return one last time to that scene in the wilderness.
The sun is still burning.
The desert is still vast.
The people are still far from the Promised Land.
But the water at Marah is no longer bitter.
The same place that exposed their desperate need has become a place where they have witnessed God's provision.
And they are about to continue their journey.
They do not know every trial waiting ahead.
They do not know how many times they will need mercy.
They do not know how much they still have to learn.
But the Lord has not finished dealing with His people.
And perhaps that is the word you need today.
Your story is not finished.
Not because every earthly chapter will have the ending you want.
But because, for those who belong to Christ, death itself cannot overturn the promise of resurrection.
The bitterness you are experiencing is real.
The grief is real.
The struggle is real.
But so is the cross.
So is the empty tomb.
So is the mercy of God.
And so is the invitation to trust the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
The Israelites needed water.
We need living hope.
And Jesus says in John 7:37:
“If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink.” (KJV)
Do you hear the invitation?
Come to Him.
Not to a formula.
Not to a personality.
Not to a religious performance.
To Jesus.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who calls the weary to Himself.
The One who can forgive what you cannot undo and give you a future you could never earn.
And when you remember Marah, remember this:
The bitter water was real. But it was never greater than the God who met His people there.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: KARMA SAYS YOU WILL GET WHAT YOU DESERVE. JESUS SAYS SOMETHING THAT COULD CHANGE YOUR ETERNITY.
paragraphs: KARMA SAYS YOU WILL GET WHAT YOU DESERVE. JESUS SAYS SOMETHING THAT COULD CHANGE YOUR ETERNITY.

You have heard people say, “What goes around comes around.” But what if that familiar saying has quietly distorted the way you understand God's justice, your suffering, other people's failures, and the grace that saved your own soul? The difference between karma and biblical sowing and reaping is not a small theological detail. It leads us straight to the cross, where the sinless Savior suffered what He did not deserve so that guilty sinners could receive the mercy they could never earn.
There is something frighteningly satisfying about watching someone who hurt you finally experience pain.
You may never admit it out loud.

But somewhere deep inside, when the person who betrayed you loses the relationship they thought would last forever, when the person who humiliated you is publicly embarrassed, when the person who lied about you suddenly finds nobody believing them anymore, something whispers inside your heart.
“That's karma.”
And for a moment, it feels good.
Almost like justice.
Almost like heaven finally noticed what they did to you.
But there is a question most people never stop long enough to ask.
What happens when the person who deserves judgment is you?
What happens when the secrets being exposed are yours?
When the lies being remembered are yours?
When the broken promises, hidden compromises, unholy thoughts, selfish decisions, and wounds inflicted on other people are traced back to your own hands?
Do you still want everyone to receive exactly what they deserve?
Or do you suddenly find yourself desperate for something greater than consequences?
Something called mercy.
Stay with me, because what Scripture reveals about sowing, reaping, justice, and grace may confront the way you have been looking at your enemies.
And it may completely change the way you look at yourself.
The Bible does teach that our choices have consequences.
But the Bible does not teach karma.
And confusing the two can quietly turn the Christian life into a system of spiritual transactions instead of a relationship with the living God.
In Galatians 6:7, the apostle Paul writes:
The original Greek makes the agricultural imagery unmistakable:
ὃ γὰρ ἐὰν σπείρῃ ἄνθρωπος, τοῦτο καὶ θερίσει.
Ho gar ean speirē anthrōpos, touto kai therisei.
Literally, the sense is: “For whatever a person sows, this also he will reap.”
The Greek verb σπείρῃ (speirē) refers to sowing, while θερίσει (therisei) refers to reaping or harvesting.
Paul is not introducing an impersonal cosmic mechanism that automatically pays people back.
He is teaching moral accountability before the personal, holy, living God.
And the context matters.
In Galatians 6:8, Paul continues:
“For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.” (KJV)
Notice where Paul directs our attention.
Not toward calculating how soon our enemies will suffer.
Not toward celebrating another person's downfall.
Not toward believing that every painful experience must be repayment for a previous wrong.
He directs our attention toward the flesh and the Spirit.
Toward the direction of our lives.
Toward what we cultivate in the heart.
Toward the eternal significance of living in rebellion against God or walking by His Spirit.
And immediately afterward, Paul tells believers not to grow weary in doing good (Galatians 6:9) and to do good to all people, especially the household of faith (Galatians 6:10).
That is a radically different message from the revenge-centered way people often use the word karma.

Karma, as understood in major Indian religious traditions, concerns the moral consequences of intentional actions, often understood within a larger framework of rebirth or continued existence. Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain understandings differ significantly, and none should be reduced simply to the popular phrase “what goes around comes around.”
Biblical sowing and reaping, however, belongs to a different theological framework.
There is one sovereign Creator.
There is moral responsibility.
There is divine judgment.
There is repentance.
There is forgiveness.
There is resurrection.
And at the center of everything stands Jesus Christ.
Christianity does not teach that the universe is an impersonal moral accountant.
It teaches that the Lord is righteous, merciful, patient, and just.
And this distinction becomes painfully important when suffering enters your life.
Because imagine sitting beside a hospital bed, holding the hand of someone you love, watching their strength disappear.
Imagine a mother burying her child.
Imagine a faithful believer losing everything in a disaster.
Imagine a young woman who has prayed, obeyed, served, forgiven, and still finds herself abandoned by someone who promised never to leave.
Now imagine somebody looking at that suffering and saying:
“You must have done something to deserve this.”
Can you feel how cruel that sounds?
Yet when we turn sowing and reaping into a rigid formula, we can end up treating suffering people exactly that way.
We assume blessing always proves righteousness.
We assume suffering always exposes hidden sin.
We assume the successful must have sown well, and the broken must have sown badly.
But Jesus confronted this way of thinking.
In John 9, the disciples encountered a man who had been blind from birth.
They asked Jesus:
“Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?” (John 9:2, KJV)
They were looking for someone to blame.
They assumed the suffering had to be explained by a particular person's sin.
But Jesus answered:
“Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.” (John 9:3, KJV)
Jesus was not claiming that the man and his parents were sinless.
He was rejecting the assumption that this man's blindness resulted from the particular sins the disciples were trying to identify.
His suffering was not permission for others to pronounce him guilty.
And that should make us careful.
Very careful.
Because sometimes the person you think God is punishing is the very person God is about to meet with extraordinary compassion.
Sometimes the one you are judging is carrying a burden you know nothing about.
Sometimes what looks like a ruined life is the setting in which Christ is about to reveal His glory.
Remember Job.
A man described as upright, who feared God and turned away from evil.
Yet he lost his possessions, his children, and his health.
His friends were convinced that his suffering must reveal some hidden wickedness.
They defended a simple formula: good people prosper, bad people suffer.
But the book of Job exposes the inadequacy of that formula.
God eventually rebuked Job's friends for failing to speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).
Their confident explanations did not make them wise.
Their certainty did not make them compassionate.
And their religious language did not make their accusations true.
There is a warning here for every Christian who has ever looked at someone else's pain and immediately called it divine punishment.
Not every wound is a harvest of personal wrongdoing.
Some suffering comes from living in a fallen world.
Some comes from the sinful actions of others.
Some comes through persecution for righteousness.
Some remains mysterious to us.
And sometimes, even when sin has contributed to suffering, we do not possess the knowledge to pronounce God's exact purpose in another person's circumstances.
Jesus Himself warned against assuming that people who suffer tragedy are worse sinners than those who escape it (Luke 13:1–5).
Instead, He turned the conversation toward a truth that concerned everyone.
Repentance.
Not because every tragedy proves exceptional guilt.
But because every human being needs to be reconciled to God.
And this brings us to something even more uncomfortable.
You may have spent years waiting for someone else to reap what they sowed.
But have you ever considered what you have been sowing while you wait?
The resentment you keep feeding.
The conversations where you quietly destroy another person's reputation.
The bitterness you have begun calling discernment.
The pride you disguise as spiritual maturity.
The refusal to forgive that you justify because your pain was real.
Your pain may indeed be real.
What happened to you may have been deeply wrong.
Forgiveness does not require pretending otherwise.
It does not mean abandoning wisdom, removing necessary boundaries, or allowing an abusive person continued access to your life.
But Scripture still calls us to guard our hearts.
Because bitterness can grow even in the soil of genuine injustice.
And if we are not careful, the person who wounded us will continue shaping the person we are becoming.
That is why Romans 12:19 says:
“Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.” (KJV)
The Greek expression behind “vengeance is mine” is:
ἐμοὶ ἐκδίκησις
Emoi ekdikēsis.
“Vengeance belongs to Me.”
This does not mean injustice is unimportant.
It means ultimate judgment belongs to God, not to our private desire for revenge.
And immediately after this instruction, Paul tells believers to feed a hungry enemy and give drink to a thirsty one (Romans 12:20).
Then he writes:
Do you see how different this is?
The world says, “Wait until they get what is coming to them.”
Jesus calls us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us (Matthew 5:44).
The world tells us to enjoy another person's downfall.
Proverbs 24:17 warns us not to rejoice when our enemy falls.
The world says, “Make them suffer the way they made you suffer.”
The Gospel says, “Leave final judgment with God, pursue what is right, and refuse to let evil conquer your heart.”
And that does not come naturally.
Sometimes it feels impossible.
Especially when the betrayal was personal.
Especially when the apology never came.
Especially when the person who damaged your life appears to be sleeping peacefully while you are still trying to recover.
But hear this carefully.
God's patience with a sinner is not proof that God approves of their sin.
Romans 2:4 teaches that God's goodness, forbearance, and longsuffering are meant to lead people toward repentance.
The Lord's patience is not moral indifference.
And delayed judgment is not the absence of judgment.
The apostle Peter explains that God's patience is connected to His merciful desire for repentance (2 Peter 3:9).
That means the person you desperately want God to destroy may still be someone God is calling to repent.
Someone Christ commands you to pray for.
Someone whose salvation would glorify Jesus far more than their humiliation ever could.
And perhaps that is where this message becomes hardest to accept.
Because we often want grace for ourselves.
But consequences for everyone who hurt us.
We want God to remember our tears.
But forget our sins.
We want our failures understood in context.
But our enemies judged by their worst moments.
We want mercy when we stand before God.
And immediate punishment when someone stands against us.
Yet Jesus tells a story that exposes this contradiction.
In Matthew 18:21–35, a servant owed his master an enormous debt that he could not repay.
When judgment approached, he pleaded for patience.
And the master, moved with compassion, forgave the debt.
Imagine the relief.
Imagine walking away knowing that the burden that threatened to destroy your future had been lifted.
But then that same servant found a fellow servant who owed him a much smaller amount.
He seized him.
Demanded payment.
And refused to show the mercy he had just received.
The parable ends with a severe warning about refusing forgiveness from the heart.
Jesus was not teaching that wrongdoing does not matter.
He was exposing the spiritual contradiction of receiving mercy while refusing to extend it.
And now the question moves from the page into our own lives.
Who are you still holding by the throat in your heart?
Whose name still awakens your anger?
Whose downfall have you secretly imagined?
Whose repentance would disappoint you because you would rather see them punished?
Those questions are not easy.
They were never meant to be.
Because the Gospel does not merely comfort the wounded parts of us.
It also confronts the sinful parts of us.
And no one understood the scandal of undeserved mercy more dramatically than the apostle Paul.
Before he became a preacher of Christ, he persecuted the church.
Acts 8 describes his involvement in the persecution of believers, and Acts 9 records his journey toward Damascus with authority to arrest followers of Jesus.
Paul was not simply someone who had made a few regrettable decisions.
He had actively opposed the people of God.
He had caused real suffering.
There were families who had reason to fear him.
Believers who knew his name not as a source of encouragement, but as a threat.
And then something happened on the road to Damascus.
Jesus confronted him.
“Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?” (Acts 9:4, KJV)
The risen Christ did not pretend Paul's evil was harmless.
He exposed it.
He stopped him.
He humbled him.
And then, astonishingly, He called him.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The enemy of the church became a servant of the Gospel.
The man who had sought to silence the name of Jesus began suffering to proclaim that very name.
That is not a story of sin having no consequences.
Paul's conversion did not erase the pain his persecution had caused, and his ministry included immense hardship.
It is a story of grace transforming a guilty man into a witness for Christ.
Paul later wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” (1 Timothy 1:15, KJV)
And he explained that mercy had been shown to him so that Jesus Christ might display His longsuffering as an example to those who would believe in Him for everlasting life (1 Timothy 1:16).
Think about that.
Someone could have looked at Saul and said:
“I hope he gets exactly what he deserves.”
But Jesus had a redemptive purpose that no one watching Saul's earlier life could have predicted.
This is why Christians must be careful about turning another person's past into their permanent identity.
We should never minimize evil.
We should never silence victims.
We should never confuse a claim of repentance with proof of lasting change.
Real repentance bears fruit, and trust may need to be rebuilt slowly.
But we must also never speak as though the grace of Jesus Christ is too weak to transform a sinner.
Because if that were true, what hope would any of us have?
And now we arrive at the heart of the entire matter.
The cross.
The place where every shallow slogan about people getting what they deserve collapses beneath the weight of divine holiness and divine mercy.
Jesus Christ was sinless.
He never deceived anyone.
Never betrayed the Father.
Never committed injustice.
Never harbored wickedness.
Never needed repentance.
Yet He was rejected, falsely accused, mocked, scourged, and crucified.
If earthly suffering always revealed personal wrongdoing, how would we explain Calvary?
The most righteous man who ever lived endured the most profound injustice.
And He did so willingly, in obedience to the Father, for the salvation of sinners.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” (KJV)
In the Hebrew text, the phrase translated “for our transgressions” is:
מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ
Mippeshaʿenu.
It conveys the sense of “because of our transgressions” or “on account of our rebellions.”
And the phrase:
מֵעֲוֹנֹתֵינוּ
Meʿavonotenu.
Means “because of our iniquities” or “on account of our guilt.”
The passage identifies the suffering Servant's affliction in relation to the sins of others.
Christians understand this prophecy in light of the suffering and saving work of Jesus Christ, as reflected in 1 Peter 2:24–25.
Jesus was not suffering for sins He had committed.
He was bearing the sins of His people.
And Scripture says something astonishing in 2 Corinthians 5:21:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” (KJV)
Christ did not become morally sinful.
He remained the spotless Savior.
But in His sacrificial work, He bore our sin so that those united to Him by faith might receive righteousness before God.
This is not karma.
This is the Gospel.
The guilty cannot save themselves by balancing good actions against bad ones.
And the innocent Son of God was not trapped in an impersonal cycle of moral repayment.
He willingly gave Himself as the sacrifice for sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again, just as the Scriptures proclaimed (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Justice was not dismissed as meaningless.
Sin was not called harmless.
Grace did not arrive because God suddenly stopped caring about holiness.
At the cross, God demonstrated His righteousness while providing justification for sinners who believe in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26).
And that is why the cross is both terrifying and beautiful.
Terrifying, because our sin is far more serious than we like to admit.
Beautiful, because God's mercy is far greater than we could ever deserve.
The Christian hope is not that every wrong action will be offset by enough good behavior.
Our hope is Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
And here is something you need to hear if you have spent years punishing yourself for the person you used to be.
Repentance is necessary.
Confession matters.
Restitution, where possible and appropriate, matters.
Accountability matters.
Consequences may remain.
A marriage may need years of rebuilding.
A reputation may not recover quickly.
A criminal act may still require legal punishment.
A broken relationship may never return to what it once was.
Grace does not magically erase every earthly consequence of sin.
But for those who belong to Jesus Christ, condemnation does not have the final word.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV)
In the Greek, the expression οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα (ouden ara nyn katakrima) carries the force of “there is therefore now no condemnation.”
The word κατάκριμα (katakrima) refers to condemnation or the adverse judicial sentence.
Paul is speaking of the saving standing of those who are in Christ Jesus.
He is not promising that Christians will never experience discipline, suffering, or earthly consequences.
He is declaring something infinitely greater.
Those who are in Christ are no longer under the final condemnation their sins deserve.
Do you understand what that means?
Your past may explain some of your scars.
But it does not have the authority to overrule the saving work of Jesus.
Your mistakes may have consequences.
But they do not have to remain your identity.
Your failures may be remembered by people.
But forgiveness in Christ is not dependent on their willingness to forget.
And the enemy's accusations do not possess greater authority than God's Word.
If you have repented and placed your faith in Christ, do not keep treating your guilt as though the cross were insufficient.
At the same time, do not mistake the invitation of grace for permission to continue in deliberate sin.
Paul confronted that distortion directly.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” (Romans 6:1–2, KJV)
Grace does not make holiness unnecessary.
Grace brings us into a new life where holiness becomes the fruit of belonging to Christ.
We are not saved by good works.
We are saved by grace through faith, and created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:8–10).
That order matters.
We do not obey so that Jesus will finally decide to love us.
We obey because His grace has brought us into a new relationship with Him.
We do not give so that God will forgive our sins.
We give because His generosity has transformed our hearts.
We do not sow righteousness to purchase salvation.
We walk by the Spirit because salvation is God's gift in Christ.
And if you miss that distinction, you may spend your entire Christian life trying to earn what Jesus freely gives.
You will become exhausted.
Afraid.
Obsessed with whether you have done enough.
Terrified that every setback means God is angry with you.
And suspicious that every blessing means you must be spiritually superior to someone else.
But that is not the freedom of the Gospel.
That is spiritual bondage wearing religious clothing.
The Bible's teaching about sowing and reaping is serious.
It warns us that what we cultivate matters.
A life surrendered to sinful desires is not harmless.
A pattern of dishonesty damages trust.
Unrepentant cruelty wounds people.
Neglecting prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and obedience can leave us spiritually vulnerable.
And walking by the Spirit bears fruit that reflects His work in us.
But biblical sowing and reaping is not a promise that every obedient believer will become wealthy, healthy, admired, and comfortable.
Nor is it a guarantee that every wicked person will face visible punishment before death.
Psalm 73 wrestles with the prosperity of the wicked.

Ecclesiastes acknowledges that righteous people sometimes experience what seems fitting for the wicked, while wicked people sometimes experience what seems fitting for the righteous (Ecclesiastes 8:14).
Scripture does not hide these painful realities.
It teaches us to look beyond appearances and trust the final justice of God.
And one day, every person will stand accountable before Him.
Hebrews 9:27 reminds us that death is followed by judgment.
Revelation 20:11–15 portrays the final judgment.
Our hope is not that we can manipulate the harvest.
Our hope is that the Judge of all the earth will do what is right, and that salvation is found in His Son.
So perhaps the question is no longer, “When will the people who hurt me get their karma?”
Perhaps the better question is:
“Lord, what are You asking me to surrender while I wait for Your justice?”
Maybe it is the hatred you have carried for years.
Maybe it is the need to see someone humiliated before you can feel peace.
Maybe it is the pride that keeps you from apologizing to the person you wounded.
Maybe it is a secret sin you keep excusing because someone else has done worse.
Maybe it is the fear that God could never forgive what you have done.
Or maybe you are reading this while struggling beneath consequences you genuinely brought upon yourself.
You made the decision.
You crossed the boundary.
You told the lie.
You betrayed the trust.
And now you are living with the aftermath.
You cannot rewind the conversation.
You cannot retrieve the wasted years.
You cannot force someone to trust you again.
And sometimes the most painful sentence in the world is:
“I did this to myself.”
But listen.
Even there, repentance is not pointless.
Even there, prayer is not useless.
Even there, obedience is not too late.
Even there, the invitation of Jesus still matters.
Consider the criminal crucified beside Christ in Luke 23.
He acknowledged his guilt.
He admitted that he and the other criminal were receiving the consequences of their deeds.
He also declared that Jesus had done nothing wrong.
Then he turned to the crucified Savior and said:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” (Luke 23:42, KJV)
He could not climb down from his cross.
He could not spend the next twenty years repairing his reputation.
He could not produce a lifetime of religious achievements.
He had no opportunity to build an impressive public testimony.
He had only his guilt, his approaching death, and the King beside him.
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43, KJV)
Do not misunderstand that moment.
The criminal was not innocent.
His earthly sentence did not disappear.
His suffering did not suddenly stop.
But he received a promise from the Savior.
A promise that his guilt could not earn.
A promise that his past could not purchase.
A promise made possible by the grace of Jesus Christ.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin is insignificant.
But that Christ is mighty to save sinners who cannot save themselves.
And perhaps there is someone reading these words who has never truly understood that.
You know how to talk about consequences.
You know how to quote Galatians 6:7.
You know how to warn people that they will reap what they sow.
But you have never personally surrendered to the Lord who died and rose again to save sinners.
You have been watching everyone else's harvest while neglecting the condition of your own soul.
Today, stop hiding behind religious language.
Come honestly before God.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust in the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
Ask Him to forgive you, cleanse you, and teach you to walk in obedience.
Not because a particular prayer formula has magical power.
Not because tears can purchase salvation.
But because Jesus Christ is the Savior, and everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13).
And if you already belong to Him, perhaps today is the day to stop treating every hardship as proof that God has abandoned you.
Perhaps today is the day to stop interpreting every blessing as evidence that you are better than someone else.
Perhaps today is the day to forgive someone without pretending their actions were acceptable.
Perhaps today is the day to repent of something you have been defending.
Perhaps today is the day to stop asking God to crush your enemy and begin praying that Christ will bring them to genuine repentance.
There is no shame in admitting that this is difficult.
Some wounds take time to heal.
Some acts of forgiveness must be reaffirmed through long seasons of grief.
Some situations require protection, wise counsel, and appropriate accountability.
But none of that places you beyond the reach of God's sustaining grace.
And if this message has touched a place you rarely allow anyone to see, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
Not to impress anyone.
Not to pretend you have everything figured out.
But to take one honest step into the light.
You do not have to disclose private wounds or name the people involved.
Sometimes a few sincere words become the beginning of a conversation that reminds another struggling believer they are not walking alone.
And think about the people in your life who may need to hear this truth.
The friend who cannot forgive themselves.
The brother still consumed by bitterness.
The sister who believes every hardship means God is punishing her.
The young believer who thinks Christianity is nothing more than behaving well enough to earn blessings.
The person who has walked away from church because they were told their suffering proved they lacked faith.
Not as a religious performance, but as a way of making the truth of Scripture accessible to someone who may never ask you directly for help.
There may come a day when the old bitterness returns, when guilt begins speaking loudly again, or when you are tempted to measure God's love by your circumstances.
On that day, return to the Scriptures we have considered.
Let the Word of God, not the slogans of the world, shape your understanding of justice and grace.

And if you believe that Christ-centered teaching should reach more homes, more struggling believers, more families, and more people who have not yet understood the Gospel, I want to invite you to become part of what we are building through Gospel Warrior.
Following Gospel Warrior is a simple way to stay connected to daily Scripture, biblical encouragement, honest conviction, repentance, healing, and discipleship centered on Jesus Christ.

Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, those who have grown spiritually indifferent, and even those who do not yet believe in Jesus to follow along and examine the message of the Gospel.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, including to people who may not have the means to purchase Christian books or study materials.
But if the Lord has provided you with the means and you believe this ministry is worth supporting, your partnership can help make its work possible.
Paul wrote in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we extend this invitation.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
But an opportunity for willing partnership in work that seeks to honor Jesus Christ.
These products can serve as everyday reminders of Scripture, opportunities for Gospel conversations, and thoughtful gifts for people you love.
Send a free devotional to a struggling believer.
Pray that the Word of God will reach people who need to hear about repentance, forgiveness, and new life in Christ.
Because the mission is not to build admiration for a page.
It is to direct attention to Jesus.
It is to encourage people to become deeply rooted in the Scriptures, connected to a faithful local church, and increasingly obedient to Christ.
And that brings us back to where we began.
The person who hurt you.
The person whose downfall you wanted to witness.
The person whose name still stirs something painful in your heart.
You may never receive the apology you deserved.
You may never see the justice you hoped to see in this life.
You may never fully understand why God allowed certain things to happen.
But you can entrust judgment to Him.
You can pursue what is right.
You can seek safety where it is needed.
You can refuse to celebrate evil.
And you can ask the Holy Spirit to cultivate in you a heart that increasingly resembles Jesus.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that everyone will receive an immediate earthly repayment for everything they have done.
It is the announcement that God is holy, humanity is sinful, judgment is real, and Jesus Christ has died and risen to save all who turn to Him in faith.
Karma and biblical sowing and reaping are not the same thing.
And neither should be confused with the saving grace of Christ.
At the cross, Jesus did not deny the seriousness of sin.
He confronted it through His sacrifice.
At the empty tomb, He did not merely offer a motivational lesson about second chances.
He conquered death and established the certainty of His victory.
And through the Gospel, He does not merely promise to improve your circumstances.
He calls you to repentance, grants forgiveness, and brings you into new life with Him.
So stop measuring your hope by whether your enemies have suffered enough.
Stop measuring God's love by whether your life has become comfortable enough.
And stop measuring the possibility of redemption by how shameful your past has been.
Look to Jesus.
The One who bore sin though He was sinless.
The One who prayed for His executioners.
The One who welcomed a repentant criminal.
The One who transformed a persecutor into an apostle.
The One who still calls sinners out of darkness into His marvelous light.
And remember this whenever the language of karma begins to sound more satisfying than the message of the cross:

If all you wanted was for everyone to receive what they deserved, you would have no Gospel to celebrate—because the mercy that saved you is the very mercy you must never resent God for offering someone else.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS HELL REALLY ETERNAL TORMENT—OR HAVE MILLIONS OF CHRISTIANS MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT JESUS ACTUALLY SAID?
paragraphs: IS HELL REALLY ETERNAL TORMENT—OR HAVE MILLIONS OF CHRISTIANS MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT JESUS ACTUALLY SAID?

The terrifying truth about Gehenna, eternal punishment, the second death, and the Greek words behind Jesus’ warnings—and why the answer may change how you understand God's holiness, His justice, His mercy, and the Cross of Jesus Christ.
There is a question many Christians are afraid to ask.
Not because they don't believe in God.
Not because they want permission to sin.
But because somewhere deep inside, they have been carrying an image they cannot reconcile with the Jesus they have come to love.
A child dies without understanding the Gospel.
A father spends his entire life resisting God.
A woman grows old in bitterness, never finding the courage to surrender.
And someone whispers the question that makes the entire room uncomfortable.
Will they be consciously suffering in fire, without relief, without end, forever and ever?
Some believers answer immediately.
Others go silent.
And some secretly wonder whether asking the question itself is a sin.
But what if the most dangerous thing we could do is not ask the question?
What if it is to become so confident in our inherited explanations that we stop examining the Scriptures themselves?
Because there is something you need to understand before we go any further.

Jesus warned about judgment more seriously than most modern preachers dare to. But understanding precisely what He meant requires us to listen to His words—not merely repeat the frightening pictures we inherited.
And the deeper we go, the more we will discover that this is not simply a debate about what happens after death.
It is a confrontation with the holiness of God, the seriousness of sin, the meaning of eternal life, and the astonishing cost of our redemption.
It is also a question that has divided sincere, Bible-believing Christians for centuries.
Some believe the unredeemed will experience eternal conscious punishment.
Others believe the final judgment results in irreversible destruction, sometimes called conditional immortality or annihilationism.
Still others believe God's judgment will ultimately accomplish the restoration of all people, a position often called Christian universalism.
These positions cannot all be correct in the same sense.
But they deserve to be examined honestly.
Because truth does not become less true when we ask difficult questions.
And the God who commands us to love Him with all our minds is not threatened by a Bible opened with trembling hands.
Perhaps you grew up hearing that hell was a gigantic underground furnace where demons tortured human beings forever.
Perhaps you watched a preacher describe people screaming in flames while God watched from heaven.
Perhaps those images frightened you into saying a prayer when you were young.
And perhaps, years later, you began wondering whether you had come to Jesus because you loved Him—or simply because you were terrified of what would happen if you didn't.
Listen carefully.
The Bible gives us terrifying warnings about judgment. We have no right to erase them.
But neither do we have the right to add details Scripture never gives us.
For example, the popular image of demons ruling hell and torturing condemned humans is not the picture Revelation presents. Revelation 20:10 portrays the devil himself as receiving judgment.
The enemy is not the king of hell.
He is not sovereign over the destiny of humanity.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And that distinction matters more than we realize.
When Jesus spoke about hell in the Gospels, one of the words He used was γέεννα (Gehenna).
Gehenna comes from the Hebrew geographical name גֵּי הִנֹּם (Gê Hinnom), meaning the Valley of Hinnom, associated with the area south of Jerusalem.
This was not an imaginary place.
It carried a horrifying history.

Jeremiah 7:31 condemns the people of Judah for building the high places of Topheth in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, where they burned their sons and daughters in the fire—something God declared He had not commanded.
Imagine the weight of that history.
A valley associated with human sacrifice.
A place of covenant betrayal.
A landscape stained by the consequences of idolatry.
When Jesus used Gehenna as a warning of divine judgment, His Jewish hearers encountered a word carrying biblical memories of shame, defilement, destruction, and God's righteous opposition to evil.
That background matters.
But here is where we must be especially careful.
You may have heard that Gehenna was simply Jerusalem's continually burning garbage dump.
That explanation appears frequently in sermons and Christian literature.
Yet the historical evidence for a perpetually burning municipal garbage dump there during Jesus' lifetime is insufficient to treat that claim as established fact.
We should not build our theology on a story merely because it is memorable.
The Valley of Hinnom is historically real.
Its association with judgment is biblically significant.
But its connection to Jesus' warnings cannot be reduced to a convenient garbage-dump illustration.
And neither can we automatically conclude that because Gehenna referred to a physical valley, Jesus was speaking only about earthly consequences.
In Matthew 10:28, Jesus says:
"Fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell." — Matthew 10:28, KJV
The Greek word translated "destroy" is ἀπολέσαι (apolesai), from the verb apollymi.
It can mean to destroy, ruin, kill, or cause to perish, depending on the context.
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not describe God as merely injuring the body.
He speaks of the destruction of both soul and body in Gehenna.
For Christians who hold to conditional immortality, this verse is central.
They argue that the final punishment of the wicked is not everlasting conscious existence in agony, but the complete and irreversible destruction of the person.
They point out that destruction is not the same ordinary concept as preservation in torment.
And that is a serious argument.
But defenders of eternal conscious punishment respond that apollymi does not always mean cessation of existence.
In Luke 15, for example, the lost sheep is described using a form of the same Greek verb. The sheep has not ceased to exist; it is lost.
Therefore, the word alone cannot settle the debate.
Its meaning must be determined by its context.
And that is precisely why we must continue reading.
Because Jesus said something in Matthew 25 that has troubled theologians, pastors, and ordinary believers for generations.
"And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal." — Matthew 25:46, KJV
In Greek, the key expressions are:
κόλασιν αἰώνιον (kolasin aiōnion) — eternal punishment.
ζωὴν αἰώνιον (zōēn aiōnion) — eternal life.
The same adjective, aiōnion, describes both punishment and life.
That is not a minor detail.
It is one of the strongest arguments for the traditional understanding of eternal punishment.
If the life of the redeemed is eternal, why would the punishment of the wicked not also be eternal?
Christians who affirm eternal conscious punishment argue that the parallel naturally points toward an everlasting punishment corresponding to everlasting life.
And their argument deserves to be taken seriously.
But here is the question raised by conditionalists.
Does an eternal punishment necessarily require an eternally ongoing experience of being punished?
Consider the difference between a punishment that continues to be inflicted forever and a punishment whose consequences can never be reversed.
Both may be described as eternal in different contexts.
Hebrews 6:2 refers to "eternal judgment."
Hebrews 9:12 speaks of "eternal redemption."
Neither expression, by itself, requires the action of judging or redeeming to be continuously repeated forever.
The adjective can describe the enduring result of an act.
Conditionalists therefore argue that Matthew 25:46 could refer to a punishment that is everlasting in consequence, even if the conscious experience of punishment is not everlasting.
Traditionalists respond that the parallel between punishment and life, together with other judgment passages, makes an ongoing punishment the more natural interpretation.
And here is the responsible conclusion.
The Greek expression kolasin aiōnion does not, by itself, conclusively resolve whether the punishment consists of endless conscious suffering or irreversible destruction.
The wider biblical witness must be considered.
We cannot responsibly claim that the original Greek secretly proves one position beyond all reasonable dispute.
It does not.
But then we arrive at another passage.
One that seems almost impossible to read without feeling its weight.
In Mark 9:47–48, Jesus warns about being cast into Gehenna, where:
"their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched." — Mark 9:48, KJV
Those words are frightening.
They are supposed to be.
But Jesus is drawing from Isaiah 66:24, where the prophet describes the corpses of those who rebelled against God.
Corpses.
That detail matters.
Isaiah's picture involves dead bodies subjected to shame and destruction, with worms and fire symbolizing a judgment that cannot be successfully resisted or escaped.
The phrase "unquenchable fire" does not necessarily mean fire that must burn forever without consuming anything.
In Jeremiah 17:27, God warns of a fire that will devour Jerusalem's palaces and will not be quenched.
The language emphasizes the certainty and irresistibility of judgment.
Yet traditionalists argue that Jesus' use of Isaiah in an eschatological warning may extend beyond the original image of corpses to the final fate of the wicked.
Again, the biblical imagery is powerful.
But the precise nature of its fulfillment is debated.
And we should not pretend otherwise.
Now consider Revelation.
Because if Matthew 25 is central to the traditional position, Revelation 14:9–11 and Revelation 20:10 are among its most formidable supporting texts.
Revelation 14 describes those who worship the beast and receive its mark.
The passage speaks of torment, fire and sulfur, smoke ascending forever, and no rest day or night.
Revelation 20:10 declares that the devil, the beast, and the false prophet are tormented day and night forever and ever.
The Greek phrase is extraordinarily emphatic:
εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων (eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn).
It is conventionally rendered "forever and ever."
We should not weaken that expression merely because its implications make us uncomfortable.
For the devil, beast, and false prophet, Revelation 20:10 explicitly describes unending torment.
And Revelation 14:11 gives strong grounds for the traditional understanding of the punishment of the beast's worshipers.
But the interpretation still requires attention to Revelation's literary genre.
Revelation is apocalyptic literature.
It communicates through visions, symbols, prophetic echoes, and dramatic imagery.
The smoke rising forever recalls passages such as Isaiah 34:9–10, where Edom's judgment is portrayed in language of unquenchable fire and ascending smoke.
Edom is not literally still producing a visible column of smoke today.
The imagery communicates devastating, irreversible judgment.
That observation is important.
But it does not automatically prove that Revelation's descriptions of torment are symbolic of annihilation.
Revelation 14 specifically speaks of torment and of having no rest day or night.
That language must be taken seriously.
The traditional interpretation cannot simply be dismissed as a medieval invention.
It has substantial biblical arguments.
At the same time, Revelation 20:14–15 calls the lake of fire "the second death."
In Greek:
ὁ θάνατος ὁ δεύτερος (ho thanatos ho deuteros).
The second death.
Not the second life.
Not eternal life in a different location.
Death.
And this is where conditionalists press their question.
Why does Scripture repeatedly contrast life and death, salvation and destruction, immortality and perishing, if the ultimate fate of every human being is endless conscious existence?
Romans 6:23 says:
"For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord."
John 3:16 says that whoever believes in Christ should not perish but have everlasting life.
Second Thessalonians 1:9 speaks of "everlasting destruction."
Matthew 7:13 speaks of the broad way leading to destruction.
First Timothy 6:16 says that God alone possesses immortality, while 2 Timothy 1:10 declares that Christ has brought life and immortality to light through the Gospel.
Conditionalists understand these passages to teach that immortality is a gift granted through Christ rather than an inherent possession guaranteeing endless conscious existence for everyone.
Traditionalists respond that death and destruction can also describe separation from God, ruin, and the loss of blessed life without requiring the cessation of consciousness.
Both sides seek to account for the language of Scripture.
Neither should be represented by a caricature.
But there is another interpretation that must be addressed.
Some Christians believe that divine judgment, however severe, will ultimately lead to the reconciliation of every person to God.
They point to passages such as Colossians 1:20, which speaks of God reconciling all things through Christ, and 1 Corinthians 15:28, which anticipates God being "all in all."
They also appeal to Philippians 2:10–11, where every knee bows and every tongue confesses Jesus Christ as Lord.
Their central question is whether God's redemptive purpose will ultimately overcome every rebellion.
That hope has appeared in various forms throughout Christian history.
But it faces serious biblical difficulties.
Jesus speaks of an exclusion that is final in Matthew 25.
Revelation depicts the second death.
Hebrews 9:27 connects death with judgment.
And passages about universal acknowledgment of Christ do not necessarily teach universal salvation.
A person may acknowledge a king's authority without entering into a reconciled relationship with him.
Nor does the language of reconciliation automatically settle how every individual responds to God's grace.
Christian universalism therefore cannot simply be assumed from the declaration that God is love.
God's love must be understood together with His holiness, justice, truth, and the warnings He has actually given.
And perhaps that is where the deeper problem begins.
We keep trying to resolve the doctrine of hell by starting with what we think God ought to be like.
One person says, "A loving God could never punish anyone forever."
Another says, "A holy God must punish every sin with endless torment."
But neither human intuition is the final authority.
The question is not whether we can construct a version of God that feels emotionally acceptable. The question is whether we will allow the whole testimony of Scripture to correct us.
God is love.
First John 4:8 declares it.
God is also holy.
Isaiah 6:3 proclaims it.
God is just.
Deuteronomy 32:4 affirms it.
And God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but calls them to turn from their ways and live.
Ezekiel 33:11 makes that clear.
We cannot sacrifice one truth to defend another.
A God without justice would not be good.
A God without mercy would not be the God revealed in Jesus Christ.
And a Gospel without judgment would leave us asking what, exactly, Christ came to save us from.
This brings us to something many discussions about hell completely overlook.
The Bible does not present eternal life as merely living forever. It presents eternal life as knowing God through Jesus Christ.
In John 17:3, Jesus prays:
"And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent."
Read that again.
Eternal life is not simply an endless extension of earthly existence.
It is the gift of knowing the Father through the Son.
It is reconciliation.
Communion.
Restoration.
Life in the presence of the One who created us.
And this changes the emotional center of the entire discussion.
Because the greatest tragedy of judgment is not merely that someone experiences something dreadful.
It is that someone stands condemned before the God who made them, who commands repentance, and who has offered salvation through His Son.
Whether one understands final punishment as eternal conscious torment or irreversible destruction, the warning is not trivial.
The stakes are eternal.
And the Cross tells us that sin is not trivial either.
Think about Gethsemane.
Jesus kneeling in anguish.
The disciples sleeping nearby.
The approaching footsteps.
The betrayal.
The arrest.
The trial.
The mocking.
The crown of thorns.
The nails.
The darkness.
And the cry:
"My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" — Matthew 27:46, KJV
Jesus was quoting Psalm 22:1.
The Gospel of Matthew preserves His cry in a Semitic transliteration:
Ἠλί Ἠλί λεμὰ σαβαχθανί (Ēli Ēli lema sabachthani).
Mark records the opening as "Eloi, Eloi," reflecting a related Semitic form.
The cry carries the anguish of the suffering Messiah and directs us to a psalm that moves from abandonment and suffering toward vindication and praise.
