We want this ministry to be a place where biblical truth is not watered down, where wounded people are treated with compassion, and where Jesus Christ remains at the center of everything.
And if this article has strengthened your faith, I would also like to invite you into something deeper.
Not because you need to pay to receive God's love.
And certainly not because financial support can purchase forgiveness, answered prayers, or spiritual blessing.
The Gospel is the free gift of God's grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
Paul himself thanked the Philippian believers for their partnership and material support, describing their generosity in Philippians 4:10–19.
Their giving was an expression of love and Gospel fellowship.
It was not a transaction that purchased God's favor.
That distinction matters.
It can help us devote more time and resources to producing Christ-centered articles, devotionals, teaching materials, and discipleship resources that people can read and share.
Some believers faithfully give tithes and offerings through their local churches. Others also support additional Gospel ministries as they are able.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Giving should come from a willing heart, not pressure, guilt, or fear.
You can still read.
You can still learn.
You can still share.
You can still pray for this ministry.
Your value before God is not measured by a monthly payment.
These items can serve as reminders of Scripture, opportunities for conversation, and meaningful gifts for people you love.
It is the opportunity to participate in making biblically grounded encouragement and discipleship resources available to more people.
We want people to have access to resources that encourage prayer, repentance, sound doctrine, spiritual maturity, and a life shaped by the Gospel.
Because the goal is not merely to produce more content.
The goal is to point more people toward Christ.
To encourage those who are weary.
To call wandering hearts to repentance.
To remind struggling believers of the promises of God.
And to keep lifting up the name of Jesus in a world filled with confusion and fear.
May every resource we create and every opportunity we receive be used for the glory of God rather than the glory of any human ministry.
And now, before you leave, I want to bring you back to the place where we began.
A prisoner.
An uncertain future.
A letter.
A command that has comforted and challenged generations of believers.
“Be anxious for nothing.”
Paul did not write those words because he had escaped uncertainty.
He wrote them while living within it.
And the next words were not, “Because nothing bad will ever happen to you.”
They were an invitation to pray.
To bring everything before God.
To give thanks.
To trust the Lord who is near.
And to receive the peace that guards hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.
Maybe the answer you have been begging for has not arrived.
Maybe the situation has not changed.
Maybe you still have a difficult conversation tomorrow.
Maybe the hospital appointment is still on the calendar.
Maybe the bills are still waiting.
Maybe there are tears on your face even now.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your life is not outside His sovereign care.
Your suffering is not proof that He has forgotten you.
Your uncertainty is not stronger than His lordship.
And your tomorrow is not beyond the reach of the Savior who conquered death.
So take the next faithful step.
Pray again.
Ask for help when you need it.
Repent where the Spirit convicts you.
Give thanks for the mercies you can see.
Trust God with the things you cannot control.
And when the fear returns, return to Christ.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Until the truth you have been reading becomes a truth you are learning to live.
Not that you will never feel afraid.
Not that you will always understand.
Not that every chapter will unfold the way you hoped.
But that Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust in every chapter.
Because the greatest security a human being can possess is not the ability to predict tomorrow.
It is reconciliation with God through the Lord Jesus Christ.
And the One who gave His life to redeem you is not asking you to face tomorrow without Him.
Paul did not know what tomorrow would bring. But he knew the Christ who would be Lord over it—and that was enough to keep trusting.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS CHOOSE JUDAS… WHEN HE ALREADY KNEW JUDAS WOULD BETRAY HIM?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS CHOOSE JUDAS… WHEN HE ALREADY KNEW JUDAS WOULD BETRAY HIM?

He knew about the thirty pieces of silver. He knew about the kiss. He knew the darkness growing inside the man He had personally chosen. Yet Jesus still called Judas closer. And the reason may reveal something about your own heart that you have spent years trying not to face.
There is something deeply unsettling about the story of Judas Iscariot.
Not because a man betrayed Jesus.
Human beings betray one another every day.

Husbands betray wives. Friends betray friends. Children abandon parents who sacrificed everything for them. People make promises with tears in their eyes and break them when temptation offers something more attractive.
Betrayal is painfully familiar.
But Judas was different.
Jesus knew.
Before the betrayal happened. Before the silver changed hands. Before the torches appeared in Gethsemane. Before Judas leaned forward and pressed his lips against the face of the Son of God.
Jesus knew.
And still, He chose him.
Think about that.

The Lord who could see through the religious hypocrisy of the Pharisees, who knew the private thoughts of His opponents, who understood what was inside the human heart, deliberately included Judas among the Twelve.
He allowed Judas to walk beside Him.
To hear His teachings.
To witness His miracles.
To eat at His table.
To live close enough to see what countless prophets and kings had longed to see.
And that raises a question more disturbing than simply asking why Judas betrayed Jesus.
Why would Jesus choose someone He knew would betray Him?
Was Judas merely a necessary villain in a divine plan?
Was he born without hope?
Was he forced to become a traitor so that prophecy could be fulfilled?
Or is there something about the holiness of Christ, the mystery of human responsibility, and the terrible danger of an unguarded heart that we have failed to understand?
Because if we read this story carefully, we may discover that the most frightening thing about Judas is not how different he was from us.
It is how much of ourselves we might recognize in him.
And yet, somewhere in this tragedy, the Gospel is shining.
Not because Judas's betrayal was good.
But because Jesus Christ is so glorious that even humanity's darkest betrayal could not overthrow God's purpose of redemption.
The story begins with a choice.
Luke 6:12–16 tells us that Jesus spent the night praying to God before selecting twelve men from among His disciples.
Judas Iscariot was one of them.
Luke identifies him as the one who became a traitor.
Notice the weight of that moment.
Jesus did not accidentally acquire Judas as a disciple.
Judas was deliberately chosen to belong to the apostolic circle.
And John 6:70–71 records words that make the mystery even more serious:
"Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?" (John 6:70, KJV).
John explains that Jesus was speaking about Judas Iscariot, who would betray Him.
Jesus was not surprised by what Judas would become.
But here is where we must be careful.
The Bible teaches that Jesus chose Judas, but it does not teach that Judas was an innocent puppet forced against his will to commit evil.
God's foreknowledge is not the same thing as moral coercion.
Scripture holds two truths together, even when our minds struggle to comprehend their relationship.
God's redemptive purpose would be accomplished.
And Judas was responsible for his betrayal.
Jesus Himself declared:
"The Son of man goeth as it is written of him: but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed!" (Matthew 26:24, KJV).
Those words should stop us.
The betrayal was within the scope of God's foretold purpose, yet the betrayer remained morally accountable.
God's sovereignty did not turn Judas's sin into righteousness.
And Judas's wickedness did not make God's plan uncertain.
The cross was not God's emergency response to a disciple who ruined everything.
Acts 2:23 declares that Jesus was delivered according to God's determined counsel and foreknowledge, while those who crucified Him remained guilty of their actions.
God accomplished redemption through events involving real human wickedness without becoming the author of that wickedness.
That distinction matters.
Because there are people who read Judas's story and quietly wonder whether they, too, are simply trapped inside a destiny they cannot escape.
Perhaps you have made terrible decisions.
Perhaps you have betrayed someone who trusted you.
Perhaps you have repeatedly promised God that you would change, only to return to the very sin you claimed to hate.
And somewhere inside, a thought has begun whispering:
Maybe this is just who I am.
Maybe I was always going to fail.
Maybe God already knows I will never become anything better.
Listen carefully.

The fact that God knows the truth about your heart does not give you permission to surrender to sin. And the fact that you have sinned does not mean you are beyond the reach of Christ's invitation to repent.
Judas's story is a warning.
But it is not permission to despair.
There is another detail we cannot overlook.
Judas did not begin his public ministry by openly announcing that he wanted to destroy Jesus.
He belonged to the Twelve.
He traveled with the disciples.
He was present in a community that heard the words of eternal life.

Matthew 10:1–4 places Judas among the apostles to whom Jesus gave authority over unclean spirits and diseases. Scripture does not tell us which particular works Judas personally performed, and we should not pretend it does.
But it does tell us that he occupied a position of extraordinary spiritual privilege.
He was close to Jesus outwardly.
And that is where the story becomes terrifying.
Because proximity to holy things is not the same as a surrendered heart.
You can know the language of Christianity without knowing the Lord in saving faith.
You can memorize Scripture while secretly negotiating with sin.
You can serve in ministry while feeding an appetite you refuse to confront.
You can lift your hands in worship while your private life tells a different story.
You can be surrounded by believers and still be hiding from God.
Judas reminds us that religious association cannot substitute for genuine repentance and faith.
John 12:4–6 gives us a glimpse into his concealed character.
When Mary anointed Jesus with costly perfume, Judas objected, asking why it had not been sold and the money given to the poor.
It sounded compassionate.
It sounded responsible.
It sounded like concern for people in need.
But John exposes what lay beneath the words.
Judas did not say this because he cared for the poor.
He was a thief.
He kept the moneybag and stole from what was placed in it.
Imagine the contrast.
Mary poured out something costly because she treasured Jesus.
Judas objected while secretly treasuring what could be taken for himself.
One heart was moving toward worship.
The other was being consumed by greed.
And both were standing in the presence of Christ.
That should disturb every one of us.
Because sin does not always arrive wearing an obviously wicked face.
Sometimes it arrives disguised as practicality.
Sometimes it borrows the language of compassion.
Sometimes it sounds like wisdom.
Sometimes it even uses religious arguments to protect an unholy desire.
And the longer we excuse it, the easier it becomes to mistake our excuses for the truth.
Perhaps your struggle is not money.
Perhaps it is bitterness.
Pride.
Sexual temptation.
Jealousy.
A secret relationship.
An addiction.
A craving for admiration.
An unwillingness to forgive.
Perhaps it is the need to appear spiritually strong while your inner life is collapsing.
Nobody else may know.
Your family may not know.
Your pastor may not know.
The people who admire your faith may not know.
But Christ knows.
And His knowledge should move you toward honesty, not deeper hiding.
Because the same Jesus who exposes sin is the Savior who calls sinners to repentance.
The tragedy of Judas is not that he encountered a Christ unwilling to receive repentant sinners.
It is that the biblical account never shows Judas turning to Christ in the repentant faith that receives His mercy.
Then comes one of the most astonishing scenes in the entire Gospel.
The night before the crucifixion.
An upper room.
A meal.
Twelve disciples.
And a Savior who knows His hour has come.
John 13:1 tells us that Jesus loved His own to the end.
The Greek expression is εἰς τέλος (eis telos).
In context, it conveys the completeness and enduring character of His love. It can carry the sense of loving to the very end or to the fullest extent.
And what does Jesus do as that love is displayed?
He rises from supper.
Lays aside His outer garments.
Takes a towel.
Pours water into a basin.
And begins washing His disciples' feet.
The eternal Son of God takes the posture of a servant.
Hands that would soon be pierced are washing dusty feet.
The Lord before whom angels worship is kneeling before men who do not yet understand the depth of what He is about to suffer.
And Judas is there.

John 13 presents the foot-washing before Judas leaves the gathering. Although it does not individually describe each disciple's feet being washed, the narrative strongly places Judas among those receiving this extraordinary act of humility.
Think about the moral weight of that scene.
Jesus knows the betrayal is approaching.
Yet He does not abandon His humble service.
He does not allow the coming treachery to make Him cease being holy, loving, and obedient to the Father.
This does not mean that love approves evil.
It means that evil cannot corrupt the character of Christ.
And that is a truth worth holding onto when somebody has wounded you.
You may have been betrayed by someone you loved.
Perhaps they used your generosity.
Perhaps they exposed something you trusted them to protect.
Perhaps they smiled while hiding intentions that would eventually break your heart.
The pain of betrayal can make a person want to become hard.
Suspicious.
Cruel.
Unreachable.
But Jesus shows us that another person's sin does not have to determine the kind of person we become.
That does not mean remaining in abuse or refusing necessary boundaries.
It does not mean restoring trust without repentance or evidence of change.
It means that by God's grace, we can refuse to let another person's darkness become the master of our own hearts.
Then the atmosphere in the upper room changes.
Jesus announces that one of them will betray Him.
The disciples are troubled.
They begin asking who it could be.
Matthew 26:22 records their anguished question:
"Lord, is it I?"
There is something spiritually healthy about that question when it comes from genuine humility.
Not the assumption that everyone else is capable of falling while we are immune.
Not the confidence that our religious history guarantees tomorrow's faithfulness.
But a trembling awareness that we need God's sustaining grace.
Lord, search me.
Lord, expose what I have been defending.
Lord, show me where I am drifting.
Lord, do not let me become comfortable with what is destroying my soul.
And then Judas asks his own question.
"Master, is it I?" (Matthew 26:25, KJV).
Jesus answers:
"Thou hast said."
We should not invent a hidden emotional tone for Judas that the text does not supply.
But the moment is devastating enough without embellishment.
The betrayer sits before the One he intends to betray.
The truth is no longer hidden from Jesus.
It never was.
And yet Judas continues down the road toward his terrible decision.
John 13:27 records that after Judas received the morsel, Satan entered into him.
Jesus then said:
"That thou doest, do quickly."
The text does not mean that Satan's involvement excused Judas.
Nor does it mean Judas's choices were morally meaningless.
Luke 22:3–6 also describes Satan's involvement and Judas's agreement with the religious leaders.
The biblical picture is profoundly serious: spiritual evil was at work, and Judas willingly participated in betrayal.
Then John writes one of the shortest and most haunting sentences in the Gospel:
"And it was night." (John 13:30, KJV).
In Greek:
ἦν δὲ νύξ — ēn de nyx.
Literally, "And it was night."
It was a statement about the time of day.
But in a Gospel that repeatedly contrasts light and darkness, its placement is deeply evocative.
Judas walks away from the table.
Away from the fellowship.
Away from the immediate presence of the One who had called him.
And into the night.
How many people have done something spiritually similar without physically leaving a church?
Still attending.
Still singing.
Still posting Bible verses.
Still saying, "God is good."
But inwardly moving farther and farther from obedience.
A compromise here.
A concealed lie there.
A sin excused because it seems small.
A conviction ignored because repentance would be costly.
Until one day the darkness that once frightened us begins to feel normal.
That is why Scripture warns us not to harden our hearts.
Not because Christ is unwilling to forgive repentant sinners.
But because cherished sin can deceive us until we no longer want to surrender it.
And now we reach the garden.
Gethsemane.
Jesus has prayed in agony.
The disciples have struggled to remain awake.
The hour has come.
And Judas arrives with an armed crowd.
Not as a stranger.
Not as an outsider who never heard the Gospel.
But as one of the Twelve.
He has arranged a signal.
A kiss.
In Matthew 26:48–49, Judas identifies Jesus through this act of greeting.
A sign normally associated with affection becomes the instrument of betrayal.
The Greek verb connected with the kiss in Matthew 26:49 is κατεφίλησεν (katephilēsen), a form of a verb that can convey kissing warmly or earnestly.
The horror is not merely that Judas betrayed Jesus.
It is that he used a gesture of affection to identify Him to His enemies.
How often does sin borrow the appearance of something good?
How often does selfishness disguise itself as love?
How often do we use words of devotion while resisting the very Lord we claim to honor?
And then Jesus speaks.
Matthew 26:50 records:
"Friend, wherefore art thou come?"
The Greek word translated "friend" here is ἑταῖρε (hetaire), a form of hetairos.

It can mean companion or associate. We should not confuse it with every other Greek term for intimate friendship, nor should we force the word to prove an emotional meaning the passage does not explicitly state.
The significance is already overwhelming.
Jesus addresses the man betraying Him without losing control, dignity, or obedience.
Luke 22:48 preserves another piercing question:
"Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?"
The betrayal is exposed.
The sin is named.
Jesus does not pretend evil is harmless.
But neither does He abandon the Father's saving purpose.
Here is the astonishing truth.
Judas handed Jesus over to His enemies, but Judas did not have the power to overthrow Jesus's mission.
In John 10:18, Jesus had already declared that no one took His life from Him in the ultimate sense; He laid it down of His own accord.
The betrayal was real.
The arrest was real.
The injustice was real.
The suffering would be real.
Yet Christ was not a helpless victim of circumstances beyond God's control.
He was the obedient Son moving toward the cross to accomplish redemption.
And the cross would reveal something Judas's silver could never purchase.
Forgiveness for sinners.
Peace with God.
Reconciliation through the blood of Christ.
The defeat of sin and death through the crucified and risen Savior.
But before we celebrate the resurrection, we must face what happened to Judas.
Matthew 27:3–5 says that when Judas saw Jesus condemned, he experienced remorse and returned the thirty pieces of silver.
He confessed:
"I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood."
Those words are heartbreaking.
Judas recognized the innocence of Jesus.
He recognized the wickedness of his own act.
He returned the money.
But he did not find peace.
He departed and hanged himself.
Acts 1:18–19 also describes his dreadful end, emphasizing the terrible aftermath of his betrayal.
We must approach this with reverence, not sensationalism.
The Bible does not invite us to mock Judas's death.
Nor should his suicide be used to shame people struggling with despair or to claim that every person who dies by suicide shares Judas's spiritual condition.
Judas's story concerns a particular betrayal of Christ and its tragic outcome.
It is not a license to pronounce God's final judgment over every suffering person who has died in that way.
But Scripture does place Judas's remorse beside another disciple's failure.
And the comparison is extraordinary.
Peter.
The outspoken disciple.
The man who insisted that even if everyone else abandoned Jesus, he would remain faithful.
Yet when the pressure came, Peter denied his Lord three times.
He denied knowing Him.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
And when the rooster crowed, Peter remembered Jesus's words.
Luke 22:61 tells us that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Two disciples.
Two devastating failures.
Two men who had walked with Jesus.
Both confronted by the reality of what they had done.
But their stories did not end the same way.
Judas experienced remorse and met a tragic end.
Peter wept, and after the resurrection, Jesus restored him to service.
John 21 records that restoration.
Three times Jesus asks Peter about his love.
Three times Peter answers.
And Jesus commissions him to care for His sheep.
We should be careful not to reduce these accounts to a simplistic formula about who cried correctly or who felt sufficiently sorry.
The biblical accounts do not reveal every private movement of either man's heart.
But together they confront us with a life-changing distinction.
Feeling terrible about sin is not the same as turning to Jesus Christ for mercy.
The New Testament calls us to repentance and faith, not merely regret.
Second Corinthians 7:10 says:
"For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death." (KJV).
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) means repentance—a genuine turning of mind and life in response to God's truth.
Biblical repentance is more than emotional pain.
It involves acknowledging sin and turning toward God rather than continuing to protect rebellion.
And salvation is not earned by the intensity of our tears.
It is received through the grace of God in Jesus Christ.
Peter's restoration does not teach that denial was insignificant.
It teaches that Christ's mercy is greater than the failure of those who return to Him in faith.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this desperately needs to hear.
You have failed.
You know it.
You have replayed the moment a thousand times.
The words you said.
The relationship you destroyed.
The temptation you embraced.
The trust you violated.
The secret nobody knows.
You have wondered whether God is tired of hearing you ask for forgiveness.
You have wondered whether the door of mercy has finally closed.
But listen to the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not come into the world to save people who could prove they had never sinned.
He came to save sinners.
First Timothy 1:15 declares:
"Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners."
And Romans 5:8 announces:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
Not after we made ourselves worthy.
Not after we repaired every consequence.
Not after we established a perfect record.
While we were still sinners.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain in darkness.
But God's undeserved favor that brings us to the Savior who forgives and transforms.
Now we can return to the original question.
Why did Jesus choose Judas?
The fullest answer belongs to the wisdom of God.
Scripture does not give us permission to invent every hidden reason in the mind of Christ.
But it does reveal several essential truths within the story.
Jesus chose Judas knowingly, not accidentally.
The betrayal fulfilled Scripture without making Judas innocent of his actions.
Jesus identified the betrayal in connection with Psalm 41:9 in John 13:18, where the language of a trusted companion turning against another finds a profound fulfillment in Christ's suffering.
Judas's presence among the Twelve exposes the danger of outward religious privilege without inward faithfulness.
His greed warns us about cherished sin.
His betrayal displays the terrible reality of human evil.
And through the events that followed, God's redemptive purpose in Jesus Christ was accomplished.
But we must never say that Jesus needed evil because evil itself was good.
The glory belongs to God, who can accomplish His holy purposes despite the wickedness of human beings.
The cross does not make Judas's betrayal righteous.
The cross reveals the righteousness, love, justice, and mercy of God in the face of human sin.
And perhaps the most humbling lesson is this:
Being chosen for a position of spiritual privilege is not the same as possessing saving faith.
Judas was chosen as an apostle.
That does not mean Scripture portrays him as a genuinely redeemed man who simply lost salvation through one unfortunate mistake.
John 6:64 says Jesus knew from the beginning who did not believe and who would betray Him.
The issue was deeper than one terrible evening.
And that should move us away from superficial religion and toward sincere self-examination.
Not obsession with whether we are secretly Judas.
Not endless fear that every weakness proves we are beyond hope.
But a humble response to Paul's instruction in 2 Corinthians 13:5:
"Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith."
The purpose of examining our hearts is not to become trapped in despair.
It is to bring our lives honestly before God and rest our hope in Christ rather than religious appearances.
Because there is a difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
There is a difference between falling and refusing to return.
There is a difference between confessing weakness and building an identity around secret rebellion.
And the invitation of the Gospel remains:
Come to Christ.
Not because you have a spotless history.
But because He is the Savior sinners need.
There is one more detail that makes this story impossible to forget.
Thirty pieces of silver.
Matthew 26:15 records the amount agreed upon for Judas's betrayal.

Matthew 27:9–10 later connects the events surrounding that money with prophetic Scripture, particularly the imagery found in Zechariah 11:12–13, while naming Jeremiah in the fulfillment citation. The relationship between these prophetic references has been discussed by biblical interpreters for centuries, and it deserves careful treatment rather than careless certainty.
What is unmistakable is the awful contrast.
Judas accepted money to hand over Jesus.
But the worth of Jesus Christ cannot be measured in silver.
First Peter 1:18–19 tells believers that they were not redeemed with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
Do you see it?
One man received silver in connection with the betrayal of the Savior.
And the Savior gave His blood to redeem sinners.
Humanity's greed met divine generosity.
Human treachery met perfect obedience.
Our guilt met the sacrifice of the spotless Lamb.
And on the third day, the grave could not hold Him.
Jesus rose.
The betrayal did not win.
The religious conspiracy did not win.
The Roman execution did not win.
Death did not win.
Christ is risen.
And because He lives, repentance is not a journey into hopelessness.
It is a turning toward the living Savior.
That is why the message of Gospel Warrior is not simply a beautiful phrase.
But understand what that means biblically.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending sin never happened.
He does not call betrayal loyalty.
He does not call greed generosity.
He does not call rebellion holiness.
He confronts sin truthfully.
He bears the penalty for sinners who are united to Him by faith.
He forgives.
He restores.
He makes people new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares that if anyone is in Christ, that person is a new creation.
And that is the miracle.
Not that your past suddenly becomes imaginary.
But that your past no longer has to be the final word over your identity and future in Christ.
The enemy wants your failure to become your name.
Jesus calls sinners to Himself and gives them a new life.
The enemy wants shame to keep you silent.
Jesus invites you to confess and receive mercy.
The enemy wants you to believe that because you fell yesterday, you must remain fallen tomorrow.
But the risen Christ is still saving, sanctifying, and restoring people today.
Maybe you are reading this while sitting alone.
Maybe your family thinks everything is fine.
Maybe you are exhausted from being the person everyone expects to be strong.
Maybe you have not told anyone how far you have drifted.
Maybe your prayers have become shorter because guilt makes it difficult to speak.
Maybe you still believe in Jesus, but you have allowed something else to occupy the place of greatest affection in your heart.
Then do not merely admire this story.
Respond to the Savior it reveals.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Turn from what is destroying you.
Seek help from mature, trustworthy believers where you need accountability.
Make restitution where it is appropriate and possible.
And remember that forgiveness is not purchased through self-punishment.
It is grounded in the finished work of Jesus Christ.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
That promise is not an excuse to treat sin casually.
It is a reason to stop running from the God who tells the truth about sin and provides forgiveness through His Son.
And if this message has uncovered something you have been trying to ignore, I want to invite you into a moment of honesty.
Not a performance.
Not a public display of spiritual superiority.
Just an honest response.
And if your struggle is too private to describe publicly, you do not owe the internet your confession.
There are people reading these words who think they are the only ones fighting a hidden battle.
Your honest response may remind another believer that they are not alone in needing the mercy of Christ.
And please, do not allow this message to end with you.
Not merely because you agree with it.
Someone may be drifting into compromise.
Someone may be carrying unbearable shame.
Someone may have decided that their failure has disqualified them forever from seeking Jesus.
Someone may need to hear, today, that the answer is not to run farther into darkness but to turn toward the Savior.
Because there may come a day when your own heart needs to remember the warning of Judas, the restoration of Peter, and the triumph of Christ.
There is also something important I want to share with those who believe this ministry should continue reaching more people.

Every Gospel-centered article takes time, care, study, and commitment. Behind every message is a desire to keep pointing wounded hearts, struggling believers, and searching souls toward Jesus Christ and the truth of His Word.
And this work can grow through the generosity of people who believe in that mission.
Not because paying for ministry is proof that someone loves Jesus more than a person who cannot afford to give.
It is not.
And certainly not because salvation, forgiveness, or spiritual blessing can be bought.
They cannot.
But supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one meaningful expression of Christian generosity and stewardship.
Philippians 4:15–18 shows believers financially partnering with Paul's ministry, and 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be willing and cheerful, not reluctant or compelled.
But if you are looking for another way to honor God through generosity and help Gospel-centered resources reach more people, this is an opportunity to participate.
These resources are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply another way to encourage faith, study, reflection, and Gospel-centered conversations in everyday life.
The heart of this ministry is not merchandise.
It is not popularity.
It is the Gospel.
And every resource, every article, every act of generosity, and every invitation should ultimately serve that purpose.
There should never be shame attached to what someone cannot afford.
Christ's grace is freely offered, and the message of salvation must never be placed behind a financial barrier.
What matters most is that Jesus Christ is proclaimed faithfully.
Because when everything else fades, the question will not be whether we built an impressive religious appearance.
It will be whether our hope was truly in Christ.
And that brings us back to Judas.
The man who walked with Jesus.
Heard His voice.
Saw His works.
Shared His table.
And betrayed Him.
His story is not in Scripture so that we can stand above him in self-righteousness.
It is there, in part, to warn us how dangerous a divided heart can become.
But the Gospel also gives us Peter.
A broken disciple who denied his Lord.
A risen Savior who restored him.
And a testimony that failure does not have to be the end for those who return to Jesus in repentance and faith.
So do not walk away from this article merely asking why Jesus chose Judas.
Ask something closer to home.
What am I choosing while Jesus is calling me to follow Him?
What am I protecting that He is calling me to surrender?
Am I trusting my religious reputation, or am I trusting the crucified and risen Christ?
And if my heart has grown cold, will I keep walking into the night, or will I turn toward the Light of the world?
Jesus said in John 8:12:
"I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life."
That is where hope is found.
Not in pretending we are stronger than Judas.
Not in assuming we could never fail like Peter.
But in trusting the One who remained faithful all the way to the cross.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who rose again.
The One who calls us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
And if you remember only one thing from this entire story, remember this:

Judas reminds us how close a person can stand to Jesus while remaining far from Him in heart. Peter reminds us that a fallen disciple can be restored by the risen Lord. But the greatest hope in both stories is Jesus Christ Himself.
So come to Him while the invitation of the Gospel is before you.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come in faith.
Do not wait until you have made yourself worthy.
You cannot.
Look to the Savior who is worthy.
And let your next step be toward Him.
The darkest tragedy is not that Jesus knows every hidden sin in your heart. It is to keep running from the only Savior who can forgive it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS SAID THE FIRST WILL BE LAST—AND THE REASON SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY CHRISTIAN WHO THINKS THEY'RE ALREADY SAFE
paragraphs: JESUS SAID THE FIRST WILL BE LAST—AND THE REASON SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY CHRISTIAN WHO THINKS THEY'RE ALREADY SAFE

What if the people we expect to see standing closest to Jesus are the very people who have misunderstood His heart? A shocking warning about pride, a scandalous story about grace, and the Kingdom where everything we thought made us important is turned upside down.
Not because He was threatening everyone who had faithfully followed Him.
Not because He wanted His disciples to live in fear.
But because He knew something terrifying about the human heart.
We can spend years doing things for God while quietly beginning to believe that God owes us something.
We can serve until our bodies are exhausted, give until our wallets feel empty, pray until our knees ache, and still carry a secret question we would never dare say aloud:
“Lord, after everything I've done for You… don't I deserve more than this?”
And then Jesus speaks words that dismantle the entire way we measure spiritual greatness.
“But many that are first shall be last; and the last shall be first.” — Matthew 19:30 (KJV)
Read that again.
The first will be last.
The last will be first.
Not necessarily the richest becoming poor or the poorest becoming rich. Not merely the famous becoming forgotten or the forgotten becoming famous.
Something much deeper is happening.
Jesus is exposing the dangerous difference between being impressive in the eyes of people and being humble before the heart of God.
And the most unsettling part?
He said these words while speaking to people who had sacrificed to follow Him.
People like Peter.
People who had left their livelihoods, their security, and their familiar lives behind.
People who were not pretending to be disciples.
They really were disciples.
Which means this warning is not something we can comfortably throw at unbelievers while congratulating ourselves for being Christians.
It reaches right into the church.
Right into the ministry.
Right into the worship team.
Right into the heart of the person reading this article.
And perhaps… right into yours.
To understand what Jesus meant, we have to return to the moment when a wealthy young man approached Him.
The man had everything society admired.
Possessions. Status. Religious discipline. A respectable reputation.
And yet, something was missing.
He approached Jesus asking what good thing he must do to have eternal life.
Jesus eventually confronted the attachment that ruled his heart, telling him to sell his possessions, give to the poor, and follow Him.
The young man walked away sorrowful.
Matthew tells us why.
He had great possessions.
But perhaps the more revealing truth is that his possessions had a great hold on him.
He wanted eternal life.
He wanted the blessing of God.
He wanted the assurance that everything would be all right.
But when Jesus confronted the thing he could not bear to surrender, his feet carried him away from the very Savior he had approached.
Imagine that moment.
The dust beneath his sandals.
The silence after Jesus' words.
The disciples watching him disappear.
A man who appeared to possess everything walked away from the One who offered the life he could never purchase.
And Jesus turned to His disciples and taught them how difficult it is for the rich to enter the Kingdom of Heaven.
Not because wealth itself makes salvation impossible.
Not because every wealthy person is condemned.
But because riches can become a rival master, convincing the heart that it is secure, self-sufficient, and in control.
The disciples were astonished.
“Who then can be saved?” they asked.
Jesus answered with one of the most beautiful declarations in Scripture.
“With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.” — Matthew 19:26 (KJV)
There it is.
Before Jesus ever tells the parable of the workers in the vineyard, He establishes the foundation.
Salvation is not a human achievement.
It is a divine miracle.
No amount of wealth can buy it.
No record of religious activity can manufacture it.
No impressive spiritual résumé can force heaven's doors open.
What human beings cannot accomplish through their own power, God accomplishes through His grace.
But Peter had a question.
A deeply human question.
A question that sounds remarkably familiar when we are tired, disappointed, or secretly comparing our sacrifices with someone else's blessings.
“Behold, we have forsaken all, and followed thee; what shall we have therefore?” — Matthew 19:27 (KJV)
In other words:
“Lord, we stayed when that rich young man walked away.”
“We surrendered what he refused to surrender.”
“We left everything to follow You.”
“So what will we receive?”
Peter was not wrong to recognize that following Jesus involved sacrifice. Nor was Jesus offended by the idea that God rewards faithfulness.
In fact, Jesus answered Peter with remarkable promises.

He spoke of the future renewal, when the Son of Man would sit upon His glorious throne. He promised the apostles a significant role in that coming kingdom, and He assured those who sacrificed for His name that their surrender would not be forgotten.
Jesus does not despise faithful service.
He does not overlook hidden obedience.
He does not forget the sacrifices no one else sees.
But He also knows how quickly gratitude can turn into entitlement.
How easily obedience can become a transaction.
How subtly a servant can begin thinking like a creditor.
And so He adds the warning:
“The first shall be last; and the last shall be first.”
Then, in Matthew 20, Jesus tells a story that would have sounded almost offensive to people who believed reward must always be calculated according to visible effort.
A landowner goes out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard.
They agree to work for a denarius, a normal day's wage.
The workers begin at dawn.
The sun rises.
The hours stretch.
Their backs bend.
Their hands grow tired.
Dust clings to their skin.
They labor through the heat of the day.
Later, the landowner goes out again and hires more workers.
Then more.
And more.
Finally, near the eleventh hour, when the working day is almost finished, he finds others still standing idle.
“Why stand ye here all the day idle?” he asks.
They answer:
“Because no man hath hired us.” — Matthew 20:7 (KJV)
Don't rush past that sentence.
Because no one hired us.
Not necessarily because they were lazy.
Not necessarily because they refused to work.
The story does not tell us everything about their circumstances.
It simply reveals that, until that moment, nobody had brought them into the vineyard.
Can you imagine standing there as the day fades?
Watching other men chosen.
Watching other workers leave with purpose.
Watching the opportunities disappear.
Wondering whether your family would have enough to eat.
Wondering whether tomorrow would be any different.
Perhaps you know something about that feeling.
Being overlooked.
Being the last person considered.
Watching others receive opportunities you prayed for.
Watching someone younger advance while you remain stuck.
Watching people who seem less faithful enjoy blessings you have begged God to provide.
Or perhaps you know the deeper shame of believing you have arrived too late.
Too many wasted years.
Too many broken promises.
Too many nights you wish you could erase.
Too much damage done.
Too many chances squandered.
And somewhere inside, a voice whispers:
“God might forgive you, but you will never matter as much as the people who got everything right from the beginning.”
Then the landowner speaks.
“Go ye also into the vineyard.”
They are invited in.
Even at the eleventh hour.
Even when the day is nearly finished.
Even when everyone else seems to have had a head start.
And when evening comes, the landowner tells his steward to pay the workers, beginning with those who arrived last.
Then something astonishing happens.
The men who worked only one hour receive a full denarius.
The same amount promised to those who had labored since morning.
Imagine their faces.
The surprise.
The relief.
Perhaps the thought of returning home with enough to provide for their families.
They had expected so little.
Yet they received more than they had reason to anticipate.
But the workers who arrived first began doing calculations.
If those men received a denarius for one hour, surely we will receive more.
We carried the burden.
We endured the heat.
We were here when the vineyard was nearly empty.
We deserve more.
But when their turn came, they also received a denarius.
Exactly what had been promised.
And suddenly, what had been a fair agreement in the morning felt unfair in the evening.
Not because the landowner had taken anything from them.
But because he had been generous to someone else.
That is where Jesus' story becomes painfully personal.
Sometimes the blessing that exposes our hearts is not the blessing we failed to receive.
It is the blessing God gave someone else.
You prayed for years to see a family member come to Christ.
Someone else shares a testimony of an unexpected conversion, and instead of rejoicing, you feel a quiet bitterness.
You have served faithfully in the background.
Someone new receives public recognition, and suddenly your hidden obedience feels worthless.
You have walked with Jesus for decades.
A person with a scandalous past repents, finds forgiveness, and is warmly welcomed into the Christian community.
And something inside you whispers:
“After everything they did… why should they be celebrated?”
That whisper is dangerous.
Not because justice does not matter.
Not because repentance is optional.
Not because wrongdoing should be ignored.
But because envy can make us resent the mercy that rescued us.
The first workers complained.
The landowner answered:
“Friend, I do thee no wrong: didst not thou agree with me for a penny?” — Matthew 20:13 (KJV)
The word “penny” in this older English translation refers to a denarius, not a modern one-cent coin.
The landowner had kept his agreement.
Then he asked:
“Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?” — Matthew 20:15 (KJV)
In the original Greek, the final question reads:
ἢ ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου πονηρός ἐστιν ὅτι ἐγὼ ἀγαθός εἰμι;
A close translation is:
“Or is your eye evil because I am good?”
The phrase “evil eye” is an ancient idiom associated with envy, resentment, or a begrudging attitude.
Jesus is not talking about a supernatural curse cast through someone's eyes.
He is confronting a heart that looks upon generosity and responds with bitterness.
The landowner's goodness had become offensive to the workers who believed they deserved special treatment.
Think about that.
They were not angry because they received nothing.
They were angry because someone else received generosity.
And if we are willing to be painfully honest, there are moments when that same ugliness lives inside us.
We celebrate grace when it rescues us.
But sometimes we question grace when it reaches someone we think deserves less.
We rejoice when Jesus forgives our sins.
But we struggle when He forgives the person who hurt us.
We are thankful that God has been patient with our failures.
But we become impatient when He shows mercy to someone whose failures are more public.
We want grace to cover our history.
But we want strict accounting for theirs.
And Jesus confronts us with a question that cannot be answered through religious performance.
Have you begun to resent God's goodness because it refuses to follow your personal ranking system?
The Greek expression Jesus uses at the conclusion of the parable is equally important.
Οὕτως ἔσονται οἱ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι καὶ οἱ πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι.
“So the last will be first, and the first last.” — Matthew 20:16
The Greek words eschatoi and prōtoi mean “last” and “first.”
Jesus is describing a reversal of expected order.
He is challenging the assumption that human status, seniority, and visible achievement automatically determine one's place in God's Kingdom.
And notice the word “so.”
The conclusion is tied directly to the story.
The landowner's generosity exposes the workers' expectations.
The final payment reveals the difference between receiving a promised wage and demanding superiority over others.
The point is not that laziness is better than faithfulness.
It is not that someone should deliberately postpone repentance until the end of life.
It is not that every Christian will receive precisely the same heavenly responsibilities or rewards regardless of faithfulness.
Scripture teaches that God sees and evaluates our works. Paul speaks of believers' work being tested in 1 Corinthians 3:12–15, and Jesus repeatedly teaches the importance of faithful stewardship.
Nor should we treat this parable as a complete economic blueprint for earthly employment contracts.
Its central subject is the Kingdom of Heaven.
The point is that God's generosity cannot be reduced to the calculations of human entitlement.
His grace does not become unjust simply because it is more generous than someone expected.
His Kingdom does not operate according to our obsession with being more important than the next person.
And this truth becomes even more beautiful when we understand the larger biblical picture.
In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word חֵן (ḥēn) often carries the sense of favor or grace.
Genesis 6:8 says:
“But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.” — KJV
The Hebrew expression is:
וְנֹחַ מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה
VeNoaḥ matza ḥēn be'enei Adonai — commonly expressed in English as, “But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.”
The divine name is represented in the Hebrew text by the four letters יהוה, traditionally read as Adonai in Jewish liturgical practice.
This does not mean the Hebrew ḥēn and the Greek word for grace are identical in every usage.
But it does show that divine favor is not a New Testament invention.
God's gracious character runs throughout the biblical story.
And when we arrive at the New Testament, we encounter the Greek word:
χάρις (charis) — grace, favor, or gift, depending on context.
Paul writes:
Read those words slowly.
Not of yourselves.
The gift of God.
Not of works.
Lest any man should boast.
The cross leaves no room for spiritual arrogance.
No one will stand before Jesus and truthfully declare:
“I earned my salvation.”
No one will look at the wounds of the crucified Savior and say:
“My righteousness made Your sacrifice unnecessary.”
The Christian who has walked faithfully with God for sixty years and the repentant sinner who turns to Christ near the end of life must both depend on the same Savior.
Both need mercy.
Both need forgiveness.
Both need the righteousness that comes through Christ.
And neither has the right to boast as though salvation were a personal accomplishment.
This does not make sixty years of faithfulness meaningless.
Far from it.
Those years may be filled with the joy of knowing Christ, the fruit of obedience, the blessing of serving others, and the deepening transformation of the Holy Spirit.
But they do not turn salvation into a debt that God owes.
That distinction changes everything.
And perhaps no scene illustrates it more vividly than the crucifixion.
There, beside Jesus, hung a condemned criminal.
A man facing the consequences of his crimes.
A man with no remaining lifetime in which to build a respectable religious reputation.
No opportunity to spend decades serving in ministry.
No chance to demonstrate years of visible spiritual growth.
No impressive record of good works to present.
Only a dying body.
A guilty past.
And a desperate appeal.
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” — Luke 23:42 (KJV)
What could this man offer Jesus?
He could not climb down from the cross and repair every wrong he had committed.
He could not undo the damage of his past.
He could not promise fifty years of service.
He had nothing with which to bargain.
But he turned toward the crucified King in faith.
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:43 (KJV)
Pause there.
Let the weight of that moment settle.
A condemned man, whose earthly story was almost over, received a promise from the Savior of the world.
Not because his crimes were insignificant.
Not because repentance was unnecessary.
Not because holiness did not matter.
But because Jesus Christ has authority to save those who turn to Him.
The criminal's faith was not an excuse for his wrongdoing.
It was a turning toward the only One who could save him.
And while the thief on the cross is not himself one of the workers in Matthew 20, his story beautifully illustrates a related truth:
The mercy of Christ is not reserved for people who had an early start.
Perhaps you are reading this with a history you cannot erase.
A marriage damaged by your choices.
Children who remember your anger.
Parents whose trust you betrayed.
Years lost to addiction.
Promises broken.
Secret sins.
A faith that once burned brightly but has become buried beneath disappointment.
Perhaps you are not proud of the person you have become.
Perhaps you avoid certain worship songs because they remind you of the person you used to be.
And maybe you have been telling yourself:
“I should have come back to God years ago.”
Maybe you should have.
But hear this carefully.
The fact that you should have returned yesterday is not a reason to refuse His call today.
The vineyard is not yours to control.
The mercy is not yours to purchase.
The Savior is not waiting for you to manufacture a perfect history before you approach Him.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance.
He does not promise that repentance erases every earthly consequence.
Some relationships require rebuilding.
Some wounds take years to heal.
Some wrongs demand confession, restitution, accountability, and a changed life.
Grace is not permission to continue destroying what God calls holy.
But grace means your past does not have to be the final authority over your future.
And that is why the Gospel is not merely inspiring.
It is scandalous.
Not scandalous because God ignores justice.
But because the One who is perfectly just has made a way to justify sinners through the saving work of His Son.
At the cross, God did not pretend sin was harmless.
Christ bore sin's judgment.
The innocent Savior suffered for the guilty.
As Peter writes:
The just for the unjust.
That is the heart of redemption.
Jesus did not come merely to rearrange the social rankings of religious people.
He came to save sinners, reconcile them to God, and create a people transformed by His grace.
And those who have received such mercy are called to become merciful themselves.
But there is another side to this teaching.
A side that should unsettle those of us who have been in church for years.
Because the first workers in Jesus' parable were not outsiders.
They were already inside the vineyard.
Already working.
Already participating.
Their problem was not that they refused to enter.
Their problem was the resentment that surfaced when generosity was shown to others.
It is possible to be active in religious service while becoming spiritually cold.
Possible to defend sound doctrine while speaking cruelly to wounded people.
Possible to give generously while secretly craving applause.
Possible to know Scripture while refusing to forgive.
Possible to preach humility while demanding special treatment.
Possible to celebrate testimonies publicly while privately resenting the attention someone else receives.
And yes, possible to build a ministry around the name of Jesus while slowly making the ministry's success more important than the Jesus it claims to serve.
That is a warning I believe every Christian leader, writer, preacher, and content creator must take seriously.
Including those of us serving through Gospel Warrior.
If people remember our name but never encounter the truth of Christ, we have missed the purpose.
If we gain followers but fail to make disciples, something essential has been lost.
If our words move people emotionally but never lead them toward repentance, grace, biblical truth, and obedience, emotion alone is not enough.
Jesus must remain the center.
Not our platform.
Not our numbers.
Not our reputation.
Not our ability to make people cry.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Because there is a terrible possibility that a person could appear first in the eyes of a religious crowd while being dangerously far from the humility of Christ.
And there is a beautiful possibility that someone the world barely notices may be living a life of profound faithfulness before God.
The elderly widow praying alone.
The exhausted father resisting temptation when no one would ever know.
The mother quietly teaching her children Scripture.
The young believer choosing honesty when dishonesty would be profitable.
The former addict walking away from old companions because following Jesus now matters more than belonging to the crowd.
The struggling Christian who falls, repents, seeks help, and keeps turning back to Christ.
The unknown servant who cleans the church after everyone else goes home.
Heaven sees what the world overlooks.
Jesus taught:
“Whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant.” — Matthew 20:27 (KJV)
And immediately after that, He pointed to Himself.
“Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” — Matthew 20:28 (KJV)
Do you see how the pieces come together?
The first and the last.
The vineyard workers.
The warning against entitlement.
The call to humble service.
The Son of Man giving His life as a ransom.
Jesus is not merely teaching us how to become last so we can secretly manipulate our way into first place.
That would turn humility into another strategy for self-promotion.
He is teaching us to abandon our obsession with superiority and follow the King who humbled Himself for our salvation.
Paul describes Christ's humility in Philippians 2.
Though Christ existed in the form of God, He did not use His divine status for selfish advantage. He took the form of a servant, humbled Himself, and became obedient unto death—even death on a cross.
Then God highly exalted Him.
The way of Christ overturns the world's definition of greatness.
The world says, “Make them serve you.”
Jesus says, “Serve one another.”
The world says, “Protect your image at all costs.”
Jesus calls us to walk in truth.
The world says, “You are only valuable when you are ahead.”
Jesus reveals a Kingdom where the humble are honored and the proud are warned.
The world says, “Never let anyone forget what they did.”
Jesus commands forgiveness, without requiring us to deny wrongdoing or abandon wise boundaries.
The world says, “Your past is your identity.”
The Gospel announces that those who belong to Christ are made new.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
That is not a promise that every consequence disappears overnight.
It is the declaration that union with Christ changes who we are and the direction of our lives.
And now I want to ask you something that may be uncomfortable.
When was the last time you genuinely rejoiced because God blessed someone who had not worked as long as you?
When was the last time you celebrated a repentant sinner without quietly reminding yourself how much better your own record looked?
When was the last time you served without hoping someone would notice?
When was the last time you thanked God simply for allowing you to belong to Him?
Not for a platform.
Not for a title.
Not for an audience.
Not for a promotion.
Not for a miracle.
Just for Him.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy is not that we sometimes fail to receive the recognition we desire.
Perhaps it is that we become so consumed with recognition that we stop enjoying the grace we already have.
The first workers began the day with an agreement.
They ended it with resentment.
The last workers began with uncertainty.
They ended it with unexpected generosity.
And the same goodness that brought joy to one group exposed envy in the other.
That is what grace does.
It comforts the broken.
And it confronts the proud.
It lifts the repentant sinner.
And it dismantles the illusion that any of us can save ourselves.
It invites the weary to come to Christ.
And it warns the religious heart against turning faithfulness into superiority.
So when Jesus says the first will be last and the last first, do not reduce His words to a promise that every overlooked person will eventually become famous.
That is far too small.
Do not twist them into a claim that obedience is worthless.
That is unbiblical.
Do not use them to excuse delayed repentance.
Tomorrow is not promised.
And do not assume they mean God treats every act of faithfulness as though it has no significance.
He is a righteous Judge who sees everything.
Instead, hear the warning and the invitation together.
Stop measuring your worth by where you stand compared with someone else. Start measuring your life by whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
If you have followed Him for decades, remain grateful.
If you have just come to faith, remain humble.
If you are serving in obscurity, do not despise your calling.
If you have received responsibility and influence, do not mistake them for proof of spiritual superiority.
If you have wandered, repent and return.
If you are hiding sin, bring it into the light.
If you have wounded others, take responsibility.
If you have been wounded, seek the healing, truth, and wise support you need.
And if you have been looking at someone else's restoration with resentment, ask God to give you a heart that rejoices when mercy triumphs over a sinner's past.
Because the Kingdom of Heaven is not a competition to see which forgiven sinner can feel most superior.
It is a Kingdom ruled by the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
And one day, when everything hidden is brought into the light, the applause of this world will not determine what matters.
Jesus will.
There is a prayer I hope you will carry away from this article.

“Lord Jesus, forgive me for every moment I treated Your grace like something I had earned. Forgive me for comparing my journey with others. Forgive my pride, my envy, and my secret resentment. Teach me to rejoice when You restore the broken. Teach me to serve without demanding recognition. Give me a repentant heart, a humble spirit, and a love that reflects Yours. Keep me close to Your Word. And let my life glorify You, whether anyone notices me or not. Amen.”
If that prayer exposed something you have been carrying, please do not bury the conviction under another scroll.
You do not have to publish the details of your deepest wounds to ask for prayer.
Sometimes three honest words are enough to let another believer know you need encouragement.
This is also why I want to invite you to become part of what we are building through Gospel Warrior.
It doesn't.
Not because paying for ministry support counts as purchasing forgiveness, securing a blessing, or proving that you are a better Christian.
It doesn't.
And certainly not because anyone should feel guilty for being unable to give.
The Gospel is freely offered, and salvation is never for sale.
But when the Lord places a genuine desire in our hearts to help spread biblical truth, one practical expression of Christian generosity can be supporting trustworthy Gospel-centered work.
Scripture says:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Paul's teaching emphasizes giving that is willing rather than reluctant or compelled.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
We encourage you to remain faithful to your local church and to give responsibly, prayerfully, and willingly.
These items are simply a practical expression of appreciation. They are not the reason we preach Christ.
The reason is that people need the Gospel.
The person quietly questioning whether God still loves them.
The parent crying after everyone has gone to sleep.
The young adult who has confused worldly success with spiritual security.
The longtime church member whose heart has grown cold.
The person with a scandalous past who believes that redemption belongs to everyone except them.
They need to know that Jesus still calls sinners to repentance and faith.
That His grace is sufficient to save.
That His Word is trustworthy.
That holiness matters.
That forgiveness is real.
That transformation is possible through Him.
And that no human being is beyond the reach of Christ simply because the world has already written them off.
Because the mission is not to make the Gospel a luxury.
The mission is to help more people know the Savior.
Not simply to increase a number on a screen, but because someone among your family, friends, or acquaintances may be silently struggling with the very things Jesus has confronted here.
Someone may be comparing their life with everyone else's.
Someone may have spent years serving God and grown bitter.
Someone may be convinced that their past disqualifies them from receiving mercy.
Someone may need to hear that being last in the world's eyes does not make them worthless before God.

Return to Matthew 19:16–30 and Matthew 20:1–28. Read the passages in their full context. Test these reflections against Scripture. Let God's Word, not merely the emotions of this moment, shape your understanding.
You do not need to have every question answered before you begin seeking Jesus.
And you do not need to pretend your life is perfect before you open His Word.
Because we are not gathering around the idea that we are better than everyone else.
We are gathering around the truth that Jesus Christ is the Savior we all desperately need.
And perhaps that is the most important thing to remember about the first and the last.
At the end of the day, the greatest blessing was never merely the denarius.
The workers had been invited into the vineyard.
And for us, the greater wonder is not that we might someday stand ahead of someone else.
It is that through Jesus Christ, sinners who could never save themselves may be forgiven, reconciled to God, and welcomed into His Kingdom.
That is worth more than recognition.
More than status.
More than the applause of a thousand people.
So stop asking whether you are ahead of everyone else.
Ask whether you are following Jesus.
Stop looking at another person's grace as though it diminishes your own.
Look again at the cross.
And if you have been standing outside, convinced that your hour has passed, hear the Gospel's invitation today.
Repent.
Believe in Jesus Christ.
Come to Him.
Not because you deserve salvation.
But because He is merciful, mighty to save, and worthy of your trust.
The greatest tragedy is not arriving last. It is standing so close to grace that you can see others receiving it, while pride keeps your own heart from rejoicing in the Savior.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A HUSBAND’S BED BECAME PART OF A BARGAIN BETWEEN TWO RIVAL SISTERS—AND GOD SAW THE PAIN NEITHER WOMAN COULD HIDE
paragraphs: A HUSBAND’S BED BECAME PART OF A BARGAIN BETWEEN TWO RIVAL SISTERS—AND GOD SAW THE PAIN NEITHER WOMAN COULD HIDE

Two sisters. One husband. A handful of mandrakes. One desperate bargain. But beneath one of the Bible’s strangest family scandals lies a devastating truth about jealousy, rejection, the hunger to be loved, and the God who refuses to abandon broken people.

“And Leah said, A little thing is it that thou hast taken my husband? and wouldest thou take away my son's mandrakes also? And Rachel said, Therefore he shall lie with thee to night for thy son's mandrakes.” — Genesis 30:15, KJV
Imagine being married to a man who comes home to you…
But whose heart belongs to someone else.
Imagine sharing his name, bearing his children, managing his household, and waking up every morning knowing that if he could choose all over again, he would choose your sister.
Now imagine being that sister.
The one he loves.
The one he worked seven years to marry.
The one everyone assumes must be happy because she possesses the affection the other woman desperately wants.
Except every time you hear a baby cry in the next room, something inside you breaks.
Because the child belongs to her.
And your arms are empty.
One woman had children but longed to be loved.
The other was loved but longed to have children.
And one evening, in a household already poisoned by comparison, a few plants gathered from a field became the price of a night in their husband’s bed.
Yes. That actually happened in the Bible.
But before you shake your head at these women, you may want to look carefully at what drove them there.
Because their story is not merely about an ancient family behaving scandalously.
It is about what happens when wounded people begin bargaining for things they were never meant to purchase.
Love.
Worth.
Acceptance.
Security.
The assurance that they matter.
And somewhere inside this uncomfortable story, you may recognize a version of yourself.
Not because you have ever traded mandrakes.
But because perhaps you, too, have spent years trying to earn what your heart desperately needed someone to give freely.
The story begins long before the strange exchange recorded in Genesis 30.
Jacob loved Rachel.
Genesis 29:18 tells us plainly, “And Jacob loved Rachel.”
He agreed to serve her father, Laban, for seven years in order to marry her. Scripture says those years seemed to him like only a few days because of his love for her.
It sounds like the beginning of a beautiful romance.
Until the wedding night.
Laban deceived Jacob and gave him Leah, Rachel’s older sister, instead. When morning came, Jacob discovered the deception.
The deceiver had been deceived.
Jacob, who had previously deceived his own father in the matter of the blessing, now experienced betrayal within his own family.
But Leah was not merely a detail in someone else’s lesson.
She was a woman.
A daughter.
A sister.
A wife whose marriage began under circumstances she had not been shown freely choosing.
And the morning Jacob discovered that the woman beside him was not Rachel, Leah entered a marriage already overshadowed by another woman's place in his heart.
Jacob eventually married Rachel as well, agreeing to additional years of service.
Then Scripture delivers a sentence that reveals the emotional tragedy inside that household.
“And he loved also Rachel more than Leah.” — Genesis 29:30, KJV
More than Leah.
Those three words carry a lifetime of sorrow.
Leah did not have to wonder whether her husband preferred her sister.
Scripture tells us he did.
And God saw it.
Genesis 29:31 says:
“And when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren.”
The Hebrew word translated “hated” is שְׂנוּאָה (senu'ah), from the root שׂנא (sana').

In this context, the language describes Leah’s painful position as the less-loved wife. It does not require us to conclude that Jacob expressed active hostility toward her every day. Genesis 29:30 explicitly establishes the comparison: Rachel was loved more.
That distinction matters.
Because sometimes the deepest wounds do not come from someone openly declaring hatred.
Sometimes they come from being tolerated when you ache to be cherished.
Being included but never preferred.
Being present but feeling invisible.
And if you have ever lived in the shadow of someone else's affection, you understand why those words hurt.
God saw Leah.
Notice what the text does not say.
It does not say Leah became valuable when she gave Jacob children.
It does not say she earned God’s attention by becoming useful.
It says the LORD saw her condition.
Before the rivalry reached its strangest moment, God was already aware of the wounded woman inside the marriage.
Leah conceived and gave birth to Reuben.
She said, “Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me.” — Genesis 29:32, KJV
There it is.
The hope underneath the childbirth.
Now he will love me.
Not simply, “I have a son.”
Not merely, “My family is growing.”
But perhaps now, after giving him something precious, she would finally become precious to him.
Then Simeon was born.
Leah said the LORD had heard that she was hated.
Then Levi.
And her words revealed the same aching hope:
“Now this time will my husband be joined unto me.” — Genesis 29:34, KJV
Can you hear her?
Perhaps this child will change everything.
Perhaps now he will stay.
Perhaps now he will look at me the way he looks at Rachel.
Perhaps now I will be enough.
But a child cannot heal every wound in a marriage.
And no human being, not even a beloved son or daughter, should be forced to carry the burden of proving that a parent deserves love.
Then Leah gave birth to Judah.
This time, her recorded words changed.
“Now will I praise the LORD.” — Genesis 29:35, KJV
The name Judah is associated with praise, from the Hebrew root ידה (yadah), meaning to praise or give thanks.
For a moment, the focus of Leah’s words moves from her husband’s affection to the LORD.
It is a beautiful moment.
But Scripture does not pretend that one declaration of praise instantly erased every insecurity Leah had ever carried.
Her story continued.
Her wounds were real.
And soon, the rivalry intensified.
Rachel, meanwhile, was suffering in a different way.
Genesis 30:1 records her anguish:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
She spoke those words to Jacob.
The woman who had his love was overwhelmed by what she did not have.
And Jacob became angry.
“Am I in God's stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?” — Genesis 30:2, KJV
Jacob could not give Rachel the thing she demanded.
And his angry response did not heal her grief.
So Rachel gave her servant Bilhah to Jacob, and children were born through that arrangement. Leah later gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob as well.
The women were not merely competing emotionally anymore.
Their rivalry had drawn other people into the struggle.
Bilhah and Zilpah were servants living in a deeply unequal household. Scripture records their involvement without inviting us to romanticize the lack of power they had in these arrangements.
This was a family marked by deception, favoritism, polygamy, competition, and wounded relationships.
The Bible reports these realities.
It does not command believers to reproduce them.
And then came the mandrakes.
Genesis 30:14 tells us that Reuben, Leah’s son, went into the field during wheat harvest and found mandrakes.
The Hebrew word is דּוּדָאִים (duda'im).
Mandrakes were plants associated in the ancient world with love and fertility. Their appearance in the story is especially significant because Rachel was struggling with infertility.
But the biblical text never teaches that mandrakes can overcome infertility, nor does it attribute Rachel’s eventual conception to their power.
That distinction is crucial.
Rachel saw what Reuben had brought to Leah.
And she wanted some.
“Give me, I pray thee, of thy son's mandrakes.” — Genesis 30:14, KJV
It sounds like a small request.
A few plants.
Something gathered from a field.
But Leah’s response exposed the wound that had been festering beneath the surface.
“Is it a small matter that thou hast taken my husband? and wouldest thou take away my son's mandrakes also?” — Genesis 30:15, KJV, with modernized punctuation
Stop there.
Read that again.
“Thou hast taken my husband.”
Leah was speaking to the woman Jacob loved more.
Rachel was not a stranger.
She was her sister.
They had grown up in the same family.
And now the relationship that should have offered companionship had become a source of bitterness.
Leah saw Rachel as someone who had taken the affection she longed for.
Rachel saw Leah living the motherhood she desperately desired.
Both women looked across the same household and saw something they believed would finally make them whole.
And neither seemed able to enjoy what she possessed without being tormented by what the other had.
Isn't that what comparison does?
It convinces you that your life cannot be meaningful while someone else possesses something you lack.
You see another person's marriage and question your own worth.
You see someone else's children and quietly grieve the family you hoped to have.
You see another person's success, ministry, beauty, opportunities, or relationships, and suddenly your blessings feel smaller.
You may genuinely love God.
You may sincerely rejoice with others.
And still find yourself asking in the privacy of your heart:
Lord, why them and not me?
That question does not always come from arrogance.
Sometimes it comes from grief.
Sometimes it comes from waiting.
Sometimes it comes from the exhaustion of watching another person receive what you have prayed for through years of tears.
But if grief is allowed to become resentment, it can turn another person's blessing into an accusation against God.
Rachel wanted the mandrakes.
Leah wanted time with Jacob.
And Rachel made an offer.
“Therefore he shall lie with thee to night for thy son's mandrakes.” — Genesis 30:15, KJV
There it was.
A bargain.
Rachel offered Leah a night with their husband in exchange for the plants.
Genesis 30:16 records what happened when Jacob returned from the field.
“And Leah went out to meet him, and said, Thou must come in unto me; for surely I have hired thee with my son's mandrakes.”
The Hebrew expression behind “I have hired thee” is שָׂכֹר שְׂכַרְתִּיךָ (sakhor sekhartikha), an emphatic construction from the root שׂכר (sakhar), associated with hiring or wages.
The language is startling.
Leah spoke as though she had secured Jacob’s company through a transaction.
And the verse ends:
“And he lay with her that night.”
No romantic speech.
No tender reconciliation recorded.
No evidence that Jacob suddenly loved Leah as she had always hoped.
Only the painful fact that a night with her husband had become something negotiated between sisters.
The text does not tell us everything Jacob thought or felt that evening, and we should not invent details Scripture does not reveal.
But what Scripture does reveal is heartbreaking enough.
A wife had come to speak of her husband’s companionship in the language of hiring.
And another wife had treated access to that companionship as something she could exchange.
A relationship had become a transaction.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story reaches into the modern world with uncomfortable precision.
Because many people are still bargaining for affection.
They just use different currencies.
Some bargain with money.
Some with physical intimacy.
Some with constant agreement.
Some with silence.
Some with relentless achievement.
Some with service so exhausting that they no longer know who they are apart from what they do for others.
They keep giving because they are afraid that if they stop being useful, they will stop being wanted.
They keep apologizing even when they have done nothing wrong because peace feels safer than honesty.
They keep hiding their pain because they believe being difficult to love is the same as being unworthy of love.
And some carry that same pattern into their relationship with God.
They begin treating prayer like payment.
Obedience like a negotiation.
Generosity like a way to purchase divine attention.
Religious activity like evidence that God now owes them an answer.
Lord, I have served You. Why am I still waiting?
Lord, I have given so much. Why does my family still hurt?
Lord, I have tried to do everything right. Why do I still feel forgotten?
But the living God is not a merchant selling His mercy to the highest bidder.
And His grace is not merchandise that can be purchased through spiritual performance.
Listen carefully to what happens next in Genesis.
After the exchange, Leah conceived again.
Genesis 30:17 says:
“And God hearkened unto Leah, and she conceived, and bare Jacob the fifth son.”
The Hebrew wording begins וַיִּשְׁמַע אֱלֹהִים אֶל־לֵאָה (vayyishma Elohim el-Le'ah), meaning that God listened to Leah.
The text does not say the mandrakes caused the conception.
It does not say the bargain compelled God to act.
It says God listened.
Later, Leah named her son Issachar, connecting his birth to the language of wages or reward in Genesis 30:18.
Her interpretation of events reflected her own understanding of her circumstances. The narrator, however, had already directed the reader to God's action.
