But because genuine faith in Jesus Christ is never meant to remain a lifeless claim.
James 2:17 says:
"Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone." (KJV)
James is not teaching that our good deeds purchase forgiveness. He is confronting a profession of faith that produces no living evidence of obedience.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9). Yet the very next verse teaches that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
Grace is not the reward for a transformed life.
Grace is the gift that makes a transformed life possible.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because some of us are reading this while remembering things we desperately wish we could undo.
Words spoken in anger.
Promises broken.
A marriage wounded by selfishness.
Children hurt by our impatience.
Friendships destroyed by pride.
Private compromises hidden behind a public image of spiritual strength.
Perhaps you have led worship while your heart was far from God.
Perhaps you have posted Bible verses while secretly feeding bitterness.
Perhaps you have condemned someone else's sin while protecting your own.
Perhaps you have been so busy defending Christianity online that you have neglected to demonstrate Christlike love to the people sitting across from you.
And perhaps the hardest truth is this:
You have become skilled at explaining what Jesus can do for other people while resisting what He wants to do in you.
That realization hurts.
It should.
But conviction is not the same as condemnation.
The Holy Spirit does not expose sin so that we will conclude that Jesus is incapable of saving us.
He brings sin into the light so that we may repent, confess, and return to the Savior whose mercy is greater than our failures.
Consider Peter.
He was not an outsider who had never heard the truth.
He walked with Jesus.
He witnessed miracles.
He heard teachings that generations would treasure.
He boldly declared his loyalty.
And when the hour of testing came, he denied knowing the Lord.
Not once.
Three times.
Luke 22:61 records that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The face of the One Peter loved.
The face of the One he had promised never to abandon.
And suddenly, every confident declaration collapsed beneath the weight of what he had done.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
There are tears that come because we have been caught.
And there are tears that come because we finally recognize whom we have wounded.
Peter knew the difference between his promises and his actions.
But his failure was not the final chapter.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter, confronting him with the question of love and entrusting him with responsibility to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
Jesus did not pretend the denial never happened.
He did not call betrayal faithfulness.
But neither did He leave Peter imprisoned in the worst moment of his life.
This is the glory of the Gospel.
Jesus does not need to rewrite history to redeem a sinner. He changes what happens next.
And that is why the message of Gospel Warrior is not merely a beautiful phrase.
It is a declaration of what Christ's redeeming mercy can do in the life of a repentant sinner.
The scandal of Peter's denial was real.
The grace of his restoration was real.
And the power of the risen Christ was greater than Peter's collapse.
Maybe your story has a chapter you are ashamed to read aloud.
Maybe someone knows you by your worst mistake.
Maybe people remember who you were before you encountered Christ.
Maybe you are still fighting a sin you once believed you had conquered.
Do not confuse God's patience with permission to continue in sin.
But do not confuse the seriousness of your sin with the absence of God's mercy.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
The Greek verb translated "confess" is ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), from homologeō, meaning to acknowledge or confess.
In context, John contrasts honest confession with the false claim that we have no sin.
Real confession does not negotiate with God.
It stops hiding.
It agrees with the truth about our sin and comes to the One who can forgive and cleanse.
That is why you do not need to manufacture an impressive Christian image.
You need to walk honestly with Jesus.
Because a life that refuses to admit sin can make the Gospel appear unnecessary.
But a life that repents, receives grace, and grows in obedience can show why the Gospel is beautiful.
Now consider something else.
What if the people around you are not merely listening for the truth of your words?
What if they are looking for the cost of your love?
Jesus said:
"By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." (John 13:35, KJV)
The Greek word translated "love" is ἀγάπη (agapē).
In this passage, Jesus is speaking specifically about the love His disciples are to have for one another.
And He had just commanded them to love one another as He had loved them (John 13:34).
This is not permission to reduce Christianity to pleasant feelings or to avoid speaking difficult truths.
Christ's love is holy, truthful, sacrificial, and obedient to the Father.
He loved people enough to serve them.
Enough to confront sin.
Enough to welcome the repentant.
Enough to lay down His life.
So when we ask whether people can see Jesus in us, we are not simply asking whether we are friendly.
We are asking whether His character is becoming visible in the way we live.
Can people see His compassion in how we treat the vulnerable?
Can they see His truthfulness when dishonesty would benefit us?
Can they see His humility when we are corrected?
Can they see His mercy when someone genuinely repents?
Can they see His holiness in what we refuse to celebrate?
Can they see His patience in how we respond to difficult people?
And can they see His love when loving someone requires sacrifice rather than applause?
Because it is possible to win an argument about Christianity and lose an opportunity to demonstrate Christian character.
It is possible to defend sound doctrine while behaving in ways that contradict the very doctrine we defend.
And it is possible to become so consumed with exposing the darkness in others that we neglect the sin hiding in ourselves.
Jesus addressed this danger in Matthew 7:3–5 when He warned against noticing the speck in a brother's eye while ignoring the beam in our own.
He was not forbidding all moral discernment.
He was exposing hypocrisy and commanding self-examination before attempting to correct another.
Some of us need to hear that today.
The world does not need Christians who pretend sin does not matter.
But neither does it need Christians who speak about holiness as though repentance is only for other people.
We must be willing to stand under the same truth we proclaim.
And sometimes that means closing the comment section, putting down the phone, walking into the next room, and asking forgiveness from the person we have been treating poorly.
Sometimes the most urgent mission field is not across the ocean.
It is across the dinner table.
Sometimes the person who needs to hear about Jesus is not waiting for another public declaration of faith.
They are waiting for us to stop using religion to justify our pride.
And sometimes the most convincing testimony begins when we stop defending our reputation and begin telling the truth.
But there is another danger here.
We can become so frightened of representing Jesus imperfectly that we stop speaking about Him altogether.
That is not the answer.
The Gospel is not, "Be a good enough person and others will discover salvation by observing you."
The Gospel is the good news that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
People need that message.
They need to know who Jesus is.
They need to hear about sin, repentance, forgiveness, faith, the cross, and the resurrection.
Romans 10:17 teaches that faith comes by hearing the word of Christ.
Our conduct does not replace the proclamation of the Gospel.
Our conduct should make our proclamation more credible, while the Gospel itself remains the power of God unto salvation.
This distinction matters.
Because you cannot save your family by being a flawless parent.
You cannot redeem your marriage by performing religious perfection.
You cannot carry another person's eternal destiny on your shoulders.
Only Jesus saves.
But by God's grace, you can become a more faithful witness to the Savior who saved you.
And that begins with abiding in Him.
Jesus said in John 15:5:
"I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing." (KJV)
In the Greek, the word μένω (menō) means to remain, stay, or abide.
The passage does not present spiritual fruitfulness as the achievement of independent human effort.
The branch bears fruit through its living connection to the vine.
That means the Christian life is not sustained by trying harder to look like Jesus while remaining distant from Him.
It is sustained by depending upon Christ, receiving His Word, obeying His commands, praying, repenting, and walking by the Spirit.
The fruit of the Spirit described in Galatians 5:22–23 includes love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.
Not religious performance.
Not public popularity.
Not a perfectly curated Christian identity.
Fruit.
And fruit takes time to grow.
There may be areas of your life where God has already produced a change that would have seemed impossible years ago.
You no longer respond to every insult with revenge.
You have learned to apologize.
You have begun resisting temptations you once welcomed.
You have started listening before speaking.
You are learning to forgive.
You are beginning to treat people with greater dignity.
Do not despise that growth.
Thank God for it.
And do not use the progress you have made as an excuse to ignore the areas where repentance is still needed.
The goal is not to become a person who can say, "Look how righteous I am."
The goal is to become a person whose life increasingly says, "Look what Jesus is doing in me."
There is a beautiful prayer in Psalm 139:23–24:
"Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting." (KJV)
The Hebrew begins with חָקְרֵנִי אֵל (ḥoqreni El)—"Search me, O God."
The verb comes from the Hebrew root חקר (ḥ-q-r), conveying the idea of searching or examining thoroughly.
The psalmist is inviting God's examination, not merely seeking reassurance that everything is already right.
What a dangerous and beautiful prayer.
Search me, Lord.
Not just my public behavior.
My motives.
My resentments.
My secret habits.
My hidden pride.
My treatment of the people who cannot see the version of me that appears in church.
Search the things I defend because I am afraid to surrender them.
Search the things I call weaknesses when Your Word calls them sin.
Search the places where I have learned to sound spiritual without becoming obedient.
And then lead me.
Not into despair.
Not into a lifetime of self-hatred.
But into Your everlasting way.
Perhaps that is the prayer someone needs to whisper tonight.
Not because they have stopped loving Jesus.
But because they realize how much they still need Him.
And perhaps someone reading this is not a Christian at all.
Perhaps you were wounded by someone who claimed to follow Christ.
Perhaps the people who taught you about God's love were the very people who made you feel unloved.
Perhaps you were shamed, manipulated, betrayed, or treated cruelly under the language of faith.
Your pain should not be dismissed.
Religious language does not make cruelty holy.
And no Christian's misconduct should be excused simply because they claim to represent God.
But I want to ask you something.
Would you be willing to look beyond the failures of those who claim to follow Jesus and examine Jesus Himself?
Read the Gospels.
Look at how He treated the broken.
How He confronted hypocrites.
How He welcomed repentant sinners.
How He spoke truth without corruption.
How He willingly went to the cross.
Do not judge the perfection of Christ by the imperfections of those who follow Him.
Measure us by Him.
Because even the most faithful Christian is still a witness.
Jesus is the Savior.
And there is a difference.
A Christian may disappoint you.
Christ remains faithful.
A church member may betray your trust.
Christ remains worthy of your trust.
Someone may have used the name of Jesus to conceal terrible behavior.
But the Jesus revealed in Scripture does not approve of hypocrisy, exploitation, or unrepentant evil.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He offers forgiveness.
And He makes all things new according to His redemptive purpose.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." (KJV)
That does not mean every consequence of past sin disappears immediately.
It does not mean damaged relationships are automatically repaired.
It does not mean a person becomes incapable of failing again.
It means that union with Christ brings a new identity and a new reality of life under His saving grace.
The old life no longer has the right to define our ultimate identity.
Christ does.
And that is where scandal can become a testimony of grace.
Not because the scandal was good.
Not because the sin was harmless.
Not because consequences no longer matter.
But because Jesus is able to redeem people who could never redeem themselves.
And if He has been merciful to us, how can we refuse to extend mercy to others?
How can we celebrate our own forgiveness while delighting in another person's humiliation?
How can we sing about the patience of God while refusing to show patience to those who are struggling?
How can we proclaim the cross while living as though pride, vengeance, and selfish ambition are acceptable?
These are not questions designed to crush the believer.
They are invitations to return to the One who first loved us.
And now I want you to imagine something.
Imagine that years from now, someone is asked what they remember most about your life.
They might not remember your favorite Bible verse.
They might not remember how many Christian posts you shared.
They might not remember how many services you attended, how many debates you won, or how many people applauded your faith.
But perhaps they will remember that you told the truth when lying would have been easier.
That you prayed with them when they felt alone.
That you brought food when they were hungry.
That you listened when nobody else wanted to hear their pain.
That you asked forgiveness when you were wrong.
That you remained faithful through suffering.
That you refused to abandon them when their life became complicated.
And when they asked why you lived differently, you did not point to your own goodness.
You told them about Jesus.
Imagine your child saying one day:

"My parent wasn't perfect. But when they failed, they repented. When life became difficult, they prayed. When they hurt us, they learned to ask forgiveness. And I knew Jesus mattered to them because I watched them keep returning to Him."
Imagine a friend saying:
"I didn't believe everything they believed at first. But I couldn't ignore the way they treated me when I had nothing to offer."
Imagine someone saying:
"I first became curious about Jesus because I saw what His grace was doing in a person who used to be so different."
Not everyone will respond this way.
Even Jesus Himself was rejected.
Faithful Christian living does not guarantee that others will believe.
But that does not make our witness meaningless.
We are called to faithfulness, not control over another person's response.
And perhaps that is the freedom some of us desperately need.
You do not have to become the world's savior.
You already have one.
His name is Jesus Christ.
You do not have to be the light's source.
You are called to reflect the One who said, "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12).
You do not have to pretend you have never fallen.
You need to keep returning in repentance and faith to the One who can lift you up.
And you do not have to make your life a monument to your own goodness.
Let it become a testimony to His mercy.
If this message has uncovered something you have been hiding from God, don't rush past it.
Stay there for a moment.
Be honest.
What part of your life has been telling a different story from the Gospel you profess?
Your anger?
Your bitterness?
Your dishonesty?
Your private compromises?
Your unwillingness to forgive?
Your neglect of those closest to you?
Do not answer for someone else.
Answer before God.
Not as a public performance of repentance. You do not need to expose private sins or painful details to strangers.
But as a simple acknowledgment that you want your private life and your public faith to belong to the same Lord.
Or perhaps your heart is exhausted because you have been fighting a long spiritual battle.
Let this be a place where believers can encourage one another with grace and truth, not shame.

And if Christ has been restoring you after a season of failure, consider sharing a brief testimony. Someone who thinks their story is beyond redemption may need to hear that God has not finished His work in you.
There is another way this message can become more than something you simply read.
Think of one person who needs to hear it.
Perhaps a Christian who has become discouraged.
Perhaps a friend who has been wounded by hypocrisy.
Perhaps someone struggling with shame.
Perhaps a believer who has slowly drifted into spiritual complacency.

Not because the words of this article have authority equal to Scripture—they do not—but because you may want to return to the biblical passages and questions when you need to examine your walk with Christ.
Because discipleship is not a single emotional moment.
It is a lifelong journey of following Jesus.
That is also why the Gospel Warrior ministry exists.
Not merely to publish content people read once and forget.
But to help people keep opening the Word of God, keep learning the Gospel, keep growing in biblical understanding, and keep walking toward maturity in Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning and spiritual encouragement more accessible.
And if this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, return to prayer, confront sin, find encouragement, or grow in your relationship with Jesus, I want to extend a personal invitation.
Not because you must pay to prove that you love God.
But Scripture does teach that believers may voluntarily support faithful Gospel ministry.

In Philippians 4:15–18, Paul speaks appreciatively of the Philippian believers' financial partnership in his ministry. In 2 Corinthians 9:7, he teaches that giving should be willing rather than reluctant or compelled.
And in 1 Corinthians 9:14, Paul explains the principle that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support through Gospel ministry.
It should not be confused with a mandatory biblical tithe, nor should it replace your responsibilities to your local church, family, or those in genuine need.
You are not less faithful.
You are not less loved by God.
And your prayers, encouragement, sharing, and participation can still be meaningful ways to help this ministry reach others.
These items are simply expressions of appreciation and ways to share encouraging messages. They are not spiritual rewards or measures of faithfulness.
A single share is not a guarantee of someone's conversion.
But it can place Scripture and a Gospel-centered conversation before someone who might not otherwise encounter them that day.
You may never know who reads it quietly.
Who saves it.
Who returns to the Bible because of it.
Who begins asking questions about Jesus.
Or who finally realizes that repentance and forgiveness are still possible.
God alone knows the full reach of a faithful witness.
And He alone receives the glory.
But before you leave this article, I want to bring you back to the question we began with.
If your life were the only Bible someone ever encountered, what would they learn about Jesus?
Would they learn that He is harsh and impossible to please?
Would they learn that Christianity is mostly about judging others?
Would they learn that religion is a performance?
Would they learn that grace is something we celebrate for ourselves but withhold from those who disappoint us?
Or would they see a sinner who has been forgiven?
A person who is still growing.
Someone who loves truth enough to repent.
Someone who loves people enough to serve.
Someone who takes sin seriously without forgetting mercy.
Someone whose hope rests not in personal perfection, but in a perfect Savior.
And if the answer today is not what you wish it were, then hear the good news.
Your story is not finished.
You can repent today.
You can ask forgiveness today.
You can make restitution where appropriate.
You can return to Scripture.
You can pray.
You can take the next step of obedience.
You can stop using yesterday's failures as an excuse for tomorrow's disobedience.
And you can trust the risen Christ to continue His sanctifying work in you.
Not because you are strong enough to transform yourself.
But because His grace is sufficient, His Word is true, and His Spirit is at work in those who belong to Him.
The most powerful testimony is not always the one with the most dramatic past.
Sometimes it is the quiet life of a believer who continues to repent, forgive, love, serve, and remain faithful when nobody is applauding.
So tonight, before you ask God to use your life to reach the world, ask Him to make you faithful to the people He has already placed in front of you.
Before you post another verse about love, ask whether you have been loving.
Before you defend the truth in another argument, ask whether you have been obeying it.
Before you pray for someone else to change, ask the Lord to search your own heart.
And before you give up because of what you have done, remember Peter.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that the Savior who calls sinners to repentance is also the Savior who forgives and restores.
Then go and live—not as someone trying to earn the love of Jesus, but as someone learning to walk in the love already revealed through His death and resurrection.
Let your words tell the truth about Christ.
Let your conduct agree with those words.
Let your repentance be genuine.
Let your love be costly.
Let your hope be visible.
And when someone sees something good in you, may you have the humility to say:
"It is Jesus. Everything good you see is His grace at work in me."
Because one day, the most important thing people remember about you may not be what you said about Jesus.
It may be whether your life helped them recognize the beauty of the Jesus you proclaimed.
May no one have to look past the person we pretend to be to discover the Savior we claim to follow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE DAY JESUS STOPPED EVERYTHING FOR THE PEOPLE EVERYONE ELSE THOUGHT WERE TOO SMALL
paragraphs: THE DAY JESUS STOPPED EVERYTHING FOR THE PEOPLE EVERYONE ELSE THOUGHT WERE TOO SMALL
Why Did Jesus Welcome Children? The Shocking Kingdom Truth Hidden in His Embrace—and Why the Savior Who Made Room for Them Has Not Forgotten You.
Imagine being told you are not important enough to approach Jesus.
Not because you committed some terrible sin.
Not because you rejected God.
But because you were too small. Too young. Too insignificant to deserve His attention.
Now imagine standing there as someone tries to push you away from the very Person you desperately need.
And then suddenly…
Jesus stops.
His expression changes.
The disciples fall silent.
And the Son of God says something that will forever change the way humanity understands greatness, belonging, and the kingdom of heaven.
“Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.” — Mark 10:14, KJV
We have heard this verse so many times that we may have forgotten how astonishing it really is.
But there is something buried beneath this familiar scene that deserves our attention.
Because Jesus was not simply being kind to children.
He was confronting a deeply rooted human instinct: the tendency to measure someone's worth by their importance, accomplishments, influence, strength, or ability to contribute.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part of this story is that the people trying to keep the children away were not enemies of Jesus.
They were His own disciples.
Think about that.
The very people who walked with Christ were standing between vulnerable people and the Savior who had come to receive them.
And before we judge those disciples too quickly, perhaps we should ask ourselves a painful question.
How many times have we done something similar?
How many times have we treated someone as an interruption because they were not important to our plans?
How many times have we overlooked a child, dismissed a struggling parent, ignored a quiet believer, or made someone feel that they needed to become more impressive before they could belong?
And how many times have we secretly believed that about ourselves?
That we need to become stronger before Jesus will receive us.
That we need to stop struggling before we can approach Him.
That we need to have something extraordinary to offer before heaven will notice us.
If that thought has ever lived inside your heart, stay with this story.
Because the hands that reached for those children reveal something extraordinary about the heart of God.
And the ending is far more personal than you might expect.
The Gospel of Mark tells us:
“And they brought young children to him, that he should touch them: and his disciples rebuked those that brought them.” — Mark 10:13, KJV
Picture the scene.
Parents and caregivers are bringing children to Jesus.
Some may have been walking beside their families. Others may have been carried in loving arms.
We do not know their names.
We do not know their backgrounds.
We do not know how far they traveled.
But we know what they wanted.
They wanted Jesus to touch their children.
Matthew's account adds that people brought children so Jesus could lay His hands on them and pray (Matthew 19:13).
Luke tells us that even infants were being brought to Him (Luke 18:15).
These families were not seeking political influence.
They were not asking for positions of authority.
They simply wanted their little ones near Jesus.
And the disciples rebuked them.

Scripture does not explicitly tell us why the disciples acted this way. Perhaps they believed they were protecting Jesus from interruptions. Perhaps they assumed His time should be reserved for matters they considered more important.
Whatever their reasoning, the result was unmistakable.
They were preventing children from coming to Christ.
And Jesus did not remain silent.
Mark records a remarkable detail:
“But when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased.” — Mark 10:14, KJV
Do not rush past those words.
Jesus was much displeased.
The original Greek uses the verb ἠγανάκτησεν (ēganaktēsen), from aganakteō, expressing strong indignation or displeasure.
This was not casual irritation.
Mark deliberately shows us that Jesus reacted strongly to what His disciples were doing.
The same Savior who showed extraordinary patience toward sinners would not quietly approve when His followers obstructed those coming to Him.
And here is something every church, every ministry, every parent, and every believer should remember.
You can believe you are defending the work of Jesus while actually standing in the way of people who need Him.
You can be so occupied with maintaining religious order that you forget the people for whom ministry exists.
You can become so concerned with appearances that you overlook wounded hearts.
You can become so accustomed to religious language that you forget what grace looks like when it kneels down to receive someone who has nothing impressive to offer.
Jesus exposed that danger in a single moment.
But He did not stop with correcting the disciples.
He revealed something about the kingdom itself.
“Verily I say unto you, Whosoever shall not receive the kingdom of God as a little child, he shall not enter therein.” — Mark 10:15, KJV
Now the story becomes even more astonishing.
Jesus was not merely saying that children should be allowed near Him.
He was saying that adults had something essential to learn from them.
The original Greek reads:
ὃς ἂν μὴ δέξηται τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ ὡς παιδίον, οὐ μὴ εἰσέλθῃ εἰς αὐτήν.
Hos an mē dexētai tēn basileian tou theou hōs paidion, ou mē eiselthē eis autēn.
A faithful translation is:
“Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall certainly not enter it.”
Notice the word δέξηται (dexētai).
It comes from the Greek verb dechomai, meaning to receive, welcome, or accept.
Jesus did not say that we must purchase the kingdom.
He did not say we must earn it through religious achievements.
He said we must receive it.
And that distinction changes everything.
Children in the ancient world were loved within their families, but they generally lacked the social status, authority, and independence enjoyed by adults.
Jesus chose people with little worldly standing to illustrate the posture required to receive God's reign.
He was not teaching that children are morally perfect.
Anyone who has raised a child knows that children, like adults, need correction, forgiveness, and grace.
Nor was Jesus suggesting that spiritual maturity means refusing to grow in wisdom.
He was confronting the illusion of self-sufficiency.
The kingdom is not something we can seize through our own greatness.
It is received through humble dependence upon God.
And that truth becomes uncomfortable when we examine our own hearts.
Because most of us have spent our lives learning how not to appear needy.
We learn to hide our weakness.
We learn to protect our reputation.
We learn to smile when our hearts are breaking.
We learn to say, “I'm fine,” even when we are barely holding ourselves together.
We become experts at looking strong.
And sometimes we bring that same performance into our relationship with God.
We pray as though we must impress Him.
We worship as though we must conceal our failures.
We imagine that if He saw the full extent of our fear, jealousy, pride, addiction, bitterness, or secret shame, He might finally decide we are too much trouble.
But Jesus did not point to the most accomplished person in the crowd and say, “Become like this.”
He pointed to a child.
Not because helplessness is a virtue in itself.
But because God's kingdom cannot be received by a heart that insists it has no need of God.
There is a difference between becoming childish and becoming childlike.
Childishness refuses correction.
Childlike faith receives what it cannot manufacture.
Childishness demands its own way.
Childlike faith learns to trust the goodness of the Father.
Childishness avoids responsibility.
Childlike faith admits dependence upon the One who gives life.
And perhaps that is why this passage can pierce the heart of a person who has spent years trying to prove they are worthy of love.
Because somewhere along the way, you may have started believing that your value depended on how useful you were.
Maybe you grew up in a home where affection seemed connected to achievement.
When you performed well, people celebrated you.
When you failed, disappointment filled the room.
Maybe you learned that being quiet kept you safe.
Maybe you were the child who was constantly compared to someone else.
The child who tried harder but never felt good enough.
The child who needed comfort but was told to stop crying.
Or perhaps you had a loving childhood, but adulthood taught you a different kind of pain.
You became the parent who feels guilty for not having all the answers.
The believer who still wrestles with the same temptation.
The spouse who feels invisible.
The worker who wonders whether anyone would notice if they stopped producing.
The Christian who serves everyone else but quietly wonders whether God still sees them.
And somewhere beneath all that exhaustion is a question you may never have spoken aloud.
“Jesus, would You still want me near You if I had nothing left to offer?”
Look again at the children.
They brought no impressive résumés.
They made no theological speeches.
They presented no record of religious accomplishments.
They simply came.
And Jesus welcomed them.
But we must be careful to understand the Gospel correctly.
Jesus does not welcome sinners because sin is harmless.
He does not call us to remain unchanged.
He welcomes us in order to bring us into the life-changing grace of His kingdom.
His invitation is not permission to cling to rebellion.
It is an invitation to repent, believe, and receive the mercy we could never earn.
The same Jesus who welcomed children also proclaimed:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15, KJV
Grace and repentance are not enemies.
Grace is the undeserved mercy of God that makes our return possible.
Repentance is the turning of our hearts away from sin and toward the Savior.
And genuine faith does not merely admire Jesus from a distance.
It comes to Him.
It trusts Him.
It learns to follow Him.
This is where the story becomes bigger than childhood.
Because Mark places this account immediately before the encounter with a wealthy man who asks Jesus about inheriting eternal life.
The contrast is striking.
First, Jesus teaches that the kingdom must be received like a child.
Then a man approaches whose wealth becomes a profound obstacle to following Him.
The problem is not that having possessions automatically excludes someone from God's kingdom.
The problem is that the man's attachment to his wealth prevents him from responding to Jesus' call.
He cannot bear to surrender what holds his heart.
And suddenly the teaching about children becomes sharper.
The child illustrates humble reception.
The wealthy man illustrates the danger of clinging to what we cannot bear to surrender.
One scene speaks of receiving.
The next exposes the tragedy of refusing to let go.
And now we must ask ourselves something difficult.
What are we holding so tightly that we cannot freely follow Jesus?
Is it pride?
Is it the need to control everything?
Is it an image we have carefully constructed?
Is it a relationship we know is leading us away from obedience?
Is it bitterness we have justified for years?
Is it a secret sin we keep promising to abandon tomorrow?
Or is it the exhausting belief that we must somehow save ourselves?
There is no amount of religious performance that can substitute for surrender to Christ.
And there is no human achievement that can purchase the mercy of God.
The apostle Paul later wrote:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
A gift is not a wage.
Mercy is not a trophy.
Salvation is not a prize awarded to the people who successfully convince heaven that they are impressive.
It is God's gracious work through Jesus Christ, received by faith.
And faith that truly receives Christ begins to transform the life that follows Him.
Now consider the final verse of the scene.
It may be one of the most tender descriptions of Jesus in the Gospels.
“And he took them up in his arms, put his hands upon them, and blessed them.” — Mark 10:16, KJV
Read it slowly.
He took them in His arms.
He laid His hands on them.
He blessed them.
The Greek text says:
καὶ ἐναγκαλισάμενος αὐτὰ κατευλόγει τιθεὶς τὰς χεῖρας ἐπ’ αὐτά.
Kai enankalisamenos auta kateulogei titheis tas cheiras ep’ auta.
The verb ἐναγκαλισάμενος (enankalisamenos) describes taking someone into one's arms or embracing them.
And κατευλόγει (kateulogei) expresses the act of blessing.
This was not merely a distant acknowledgment.
Jesus gave these children His attention and His affectionate care.
The disciples had treated their arrival as something to stop.
Jesus treated their presence as something to welcome.
The disciples had rebuked those bringing them.
Jesus rebuked the exclusion.
The disciples saw an interruption.
Jesus revealed the kingdom.
And here is the part that should make every parent, grandparent, guardian, teacher, and church leader examine the way we live.
Children are not merely the church of tomorrow.
They are people who matter to Christ today.
Their questions matter.
Their fears matter.
Their spiritual formation matters.
Their need for protection, patience, truth, and loving guidance matters.
They should not have to become adults before the people of God take their souls seriously.
A child who asks a difficult question about God should not be mocked.
A child who struggles to sit quietly should not be made to believe that Jesus finds them irritating.
A child who has been wounded should never be taught that silence is more important than safety.
A child who needs correction should receive correction shaped by truth, patience, and love rather than humiliation.
And no child should ever be made to feel that their worth depends upon how much money their family has, how successful their parents are, or how perfectly they behave.
Jesus welcomed children as people worthy of His attention.
That does not mean abandoning biblical discipline.
It means remembering that discipline should seek their good rather than satisfy an adult's anger.
It means teaching them Scripture without crushing their spirits.
It means modeling repentance when we ourselves have sinned against them.
Yes, even parents need to say, “I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
Sometimes one of the most powerful lessons a child can receive about grace is watching a parent humbly ask forgiveness.
Because children do not merely learn what we say about Jesus.
They also learn from how we treat people when we are tired, disappointed, inconvenienced, or angry.
And perhaps one of the most sobering questions we can ask is this:
If a child formed their understanding of Jesus entirely from the way I treat them, what kind of Savior would they imagine?
A Savior who is constantly irritated?
A Savior who only notices success?
A Savior who withdraws affection whenever they fail?
Or a Savior who speaks truth, corrects with love, welcomes the humble, and never treats a human soul as worthless?
That question is not meant to drive faithful parents into despair.
Every parent fails.
Every family needs grace.
The good news is that repentance and restoration are possible through Christ.
And sometimes the healing of a family begins when an adult stops defending their pride and starts telling the truth.
“I should not have spoken to you that way.”
“I was wrong to ignore you.”
“I love you, and I want to do better.”
“I need Jesus' help too.”
Those words cannot undo every wound, and some situations require deeper help, protection, and healing.
But humble repentance can begin to rebuild what pride has damaged.
This is the kind of Gospel that must move beyond inspirational quotations and enter our homes.
Because the welcome of Jesus is not simply a beautiful scene to admire.
It is a truth that must reshape the way we live.
And yet there is another dimension to this story that reaches beyond parenting.
What about the grown child who never received that kind of welcome?
What about the adult who still carries the memory of being unwanted?
What about the person who grew up believing love had to be earned?
What about the believer who knows the Bible but still struggles to believe that God cares?
The Gospel does not promise that every painful childhood memory will immediately disappear.
It does not pretend that abuse, abandonment, or rejection are small things.
It does not demand that wounded people deny what happened to them.
But it announces something greater than the verdict spoken over us by other human beings.
Our ultimate worth is not determined by those who failed to recognize it.
We are creatures made in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27).
And the depth of God's redeeming love is revealed in Jesus Christ.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8, KJV
Do you see the connection?
The Jesus who welcomed children did not merely come to offer humanity a few moments of kindness.
He came to accomplish our redemption.
The hands that blessed those children would later be nailed to a Roman cross.
The One who welcomed the overlooked would Himself be rejected.
The One who spoke of receiving the kingdom would give His life so that sinners could be reconciled to God.
He bore our sins.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
This is not merely a message about becoming kinder people.
It is the Gospel of the crucified and risen Christ.
Without the cross, we might admire Jesus as an extraordinary teacher.
Without the resurrection, we would have no victorious Savior.
But because He died and rose again, forgiveness is not wishful thinking.
It rests upon what Christ has accomplished.
And through faith in Him, sinners can receive reconciliation with God and new life.
The same Jesus who said, “Let the little children come unto me,” also declared:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
These passages occur in different contexts, and we should not pretend they say precisely the same thing.
Yet together they reveal the welcoming heart of the Savior toward those who come to Him.
He does not call us to manufacture our own righteousness.
He calls us to trust Him.
He does not tell us to disguise our sin.
He calls us to repentance.
He does not promise a life without suffering.
He promises that those who belong to Him are held by a faithfulness greater than their circumstances.
And maybe that is what you needed to remember today.
You are not too insignificant to pray.
You are not too ordinary to be loved by God.
You are not too far gone to turn toward Christ while His invitation is before you.
Your past does not possess greater saving power than the blood of Jesus.
Your failures are serious, but they are not stronger than the Savior.
And your shame does not have the authority to rewrite what God has revealed in His Word.
Perhaps you have spent years believing that Jesus is always disappointed in you.
Perhaps you have confused conviction with condemnation.
Conviction calls us to acknowledge sin and turn toward God.
Condemnation tells us there is no hope.
But Scripture says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1, KJV
Notice the words in Christ Jesus.
This is not a declaration that sin no longer matters.
It is the glorious assurance that those united to Christ by faith are no longer under sin's condemnation.
The answer to our guilt is not pretending we are innocent.
The answer is the Savior who died for the guilty and rose again.
And this is why the welcome of Jesus matters so deeply.
Because the kingdom belongs neither to the self-righteous nor to those who think they have outgrown their need for mercy.
It is received through faith in the King.
You may have a lifetime of biblical knowledge and still need to surrender your pride.
You may have served in church for decades and still need to learn humility.
You may be respected by everyone around you and still be hiding a heart that desperately needs repentance.
Or you may be someone who has never understood the Gospel until this very moment.
Wherever you are, the question is not whether you can impress Jesus.
The question is whether you will come to Him on His terms.
Not bargaining.
Not pretending.
Not offering excuses for what you know is wrong.
But trusting the One who is mighty to save.
And perhaps today that surrender begins with a prayer as simple as this:

“Lord Jesus, I have spent too long trying to prove myself, hide my failures, and carry burdens I was never meant to carry without You. I confess that I have sinned and need Your mercy. Forgive me. Teach me to trust You rather than my own goodness. Heal what is wounded, correct what is sinful, and transform what needs to change. Help me welcome others with the same compassion You have shown. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I surrender my life to You. Amen.”
There are no magic words that automatically save someone.
Our hope rests in Jesus Christ, not in the mere repetition of a prayer.
But if those words express the genuine repentance and faith of your heart, do not dismiss the significance of turning toward Him.
And if you have been following Jesus for years, perhaps this story is calling you to another kind of repentance.
Maybe you have become one of the disciples at the edge of the crowd.
Not intentionally cruel.
Not openly hostile.
Just too busy to notice the little ones.
Too concerned with your schedule to listen.
Too impressed by important people to recognize those who have no influence.
Too distracted by ministry activity to remember the heart of the Master.
Jesus' response to His disciples reminds us that following Him requires more than being physically near Him.
We must learn to love what He loves.
We must learn to notice those whom the world overlooks.
We must never mistake a person's lack of worldly status for a lack of eternal significance.
And if you are a parent reading this, perhaps your greatest ministry today will not happen on a stage.
It may happen when you put down your phone and listen to your child.
When you pray beside a bed.
When you patiently explain why Jesus died and rose again.
When you refuse to use shame as a substitute for loving correction.
When you teach a child that repentance is not the end of hope, because God's mercy is real.
When you remind them that following Jesus matters more than appearing impressive to the world.
These moments may never become famous.
They may never earn applause.
But faithfulness does not become meaningless simply because the world does not notice it.
And if you have no children of your own, the lesson still belongs to you.
There are younger believers who need encouragement.
There are struggling families who need support.
There are lonely people who need someone to listen.
There are wounded adults who need to see Christians embody the truth they proclaim.
There are people outside the church who have been treated as though they were interruptions rather than neighbors.
We cannot personally solve every problem.
But we can refuse to become obstacles between people and the truth of Jesus Christ.
This is part of what we mean when we say:
The scandal is not that Jesus welcomed children.
The scandal is that human beings so often decide who deserves to be welcomed.
The scandal is that we sometimes turn faith into a competition for importance.
The scandal is that we can stand close to holy things while forgetting the mercy of the Holy One.
But grace interrupts that story.
Grace confronts our pride.
Grace exposes our sin.
Grace calls us to repentance.
Grace brings the undeserving to the feet of the Savior.
And through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, grace opens the way to reconciliation with God.
That is the transformation we proclaim.
Not that every earthly consequence disappears.
Not that every broken relationship is automatically restored.
Not that believing in Jesus makes suffering impossible.
But that Christ redeems sinners, creates new life, and calls His people to walk in truth and love.
And that message is too precious to keep confined to a single page.
Someone in your family may need to read this today.
Perhaps a parent who feels they have failed.
Perhaps an adult still wrestling with childhood rejection.
Perhaps a Christian who has grown harsh without realizing it.
Perhaps a friend who thinks they are too sinful to approach Jesus.
Perhaps someone who has never heard the Gospel explained as an invitation to repent and receive grace rather than a demand to perform for acceptance.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because someone in your circle may be carrying a burden they have never told you about.
And if this message has exposed something personal, I want to invite you into a moment of spiritual honesty.
If you are a parent asking God for wisdom, you can comment, “Lord, help me lead them to You.”
You do not have to reveal private wounds or painful details to strangers. God already knows what you are carrying.
But sometimes a simple, honest response can encourage another believer to stop hiding and seek the help they need.
Because our purpose is not to build a community around a personality.
Our purpose is to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, return to prayer, confront sin, or grow in your walk with Christ, there is another meaningful way you can help.
It can help us keep creating Scripture-centered articles, devotionals, teaching materials, and resources designed to encourage believers and reach people who need to hear the Gospel.
It can also help us expand this work so that more people, including parents, families, and new believers, can access biblical encouragement.
The Bible teaches that generosity can glorify God and support faithful Gospel ministry.
Paul wrote:
“For the administration of this service not only supplieth the want of the saints, but is abundant also by many thanksgivings unto God.” — 2 Corinthians 9:12, KJV
He also taught:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That matters.
Because supporting Gospel ministry should never become a test of whether God loves you.
It does not purchase God's favor.
And it should not be presented as a mandatory biblical tithe or as a replacement for the giving responsibilities you prayerfully recognize toward your local church and those in need.
It is an opportunity to give freely, according to your means and convictions, toward work you believe is faithfully serving Christ.
You can pray, read, learn, share, and encourage others.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And the Word of God must never be held hostage to someone's financial ability.
These resources can serve as reminders of biblical truth, opportunities for encouragement, and meaningful gifts for people you love.
It is the opportunity to participate in making Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources more widely available.
Your prayers are valuable.
Your willingness to share biblical truth is valuable.
But above all, Jesus Christ is worthy of our obedience, worship, and wholehearted devotion.
We are not asking you to glorify a ministry.
We are inviting you to glorify God through whatever faithful response He leads you to make.
And now, before you leave this story, return with me to that moment in the Gospel of Mark.
The crowd is gathered.
The disciples have tried to stop the children.
Jesus has spoken.
And then He takes those little ones into His arms and blesses them.
We do not know what became of those children.
Scripture does not tell us whether they later became disciples, parents, servants, or leaders.
It does not give us their names.
And we should not invent stories about their futures.
But we know what happened that day.
They were brought to Jesus.
He received them.
And He blessed them.
That was enough for the Gospel writer to preserve the moment for generations.
Perhaps that is the final lesson.
The world constantly asks what you have accomplished.
How much you own.
How many people recognize your name.
How successful you have become.
How useful you are.
How impressive your life appears.
But Jesus teaches us to ask a deeper question.
Have you received the kingdom of God with humble faith?
Have you turned from sin and trusted the Savior?
Have you allowed His grace to reshape how you treat others?
Have you stopped trying to earn what only Christ can give?
Because one day, the achievements that seem so important now will no longer command our attention.
Our reputations will fade.
Our possessions will pass to someone else.
Our earthly influence will come to an end.
But the question of whether we belong to Jesus Christ will matter eternally.
So bring Him your repentance.
Bring Him your trust.
Bring Him the pride you need to surrender.
Bring Him the fears you have been hiding.
Bring Him your brokenness without pretending it is righteousness.
Come to the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
And when you see someone whom the world considers small, remember the day Jesus stopped everything to welcome children.
Because perhaps the person you are tempted to overlook is precisely the person you are being called to love.
And perhaps the truth your weary heart most needs to hear is this:
You were never meant to become impressive enough to deserve the arms of Jesus. You were meant to come to Him in faith and discover that His grace is greater than anything you could ever earn.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN YOU TRULY REPENT WHILE ALREADY PLANNING TO COMMIT THE SAME SIN AGAIN?
paragraphs: CAN YOU TRULY REPENT WHILE ALREADY PLANNING TO COMMIT THE SAME SIN AGAIN?
The Terrifying Difference Between Falling Into Sin and Secretly Making Room for It—And Why Jesus Still Offers Grace to the Person Who Is Tired of Living a Double Life.
There is a kind of prayer that sounds like repentance but hides a terrible secret.
“Lord, please forgive me.”

The words are sincere enough to bring tears. Your chest feels heavy. Your conscience is screaming. You know what you did was wrong. You know it wounded your relationship with God. You know you crossed a line you promised yourself you would never cross again.
But somewhere beneath those tears, another conversation is already happening.
Maybe just one more time.
Maybe after this weekend.
Maybe I'll stop when things settle down.
Maybe God will understand.
And suddenly, the most frightening question is not whether God can forgive your sin.
It is whether you have actually decided to leave it.
Because what happens when your mouth is asking Jesus for forgiveness while your heart is quietly reserving a place for the very thing that nailed Him to the cross?
What happens when you kneel before God in the morning but have already made arrangements to disobey Him that night?
And what if the reason you keep returning to the same sin is not simply that you are weak—but that a part of you still loves what you keep asking God to remove?
Read that again.
Not because I want to condemn you.
But because somewhere, someone is exhausted from living two lives.
The life everyone sees.
And the life only God knows.
Perhaps that someone is you.
You love Jesus. At least, you believe you do. You listen to worship music. You share Bible verses. You know how to pray. You know what is right.
But there is a particular sin that keeps finding its way back into your life.

Maybe it is pornography. A secret relationship. Dishonesty. Sexual immorality. Gambling. Bitterness. A hidden addiction. An unforgiving heart. A habit of manipulating people. A pattern of gossip. A relationship you know is leading you away from obedience.
Perhaps nobody suspects anything.
You still smile in church.
You still say, “God is good.”
You still encourage other people to trust Him.
But when the room becomes quiet and the phone is in your hand, when temptation whispers your name, when the opportunity presents itself again, something inside you begins negotiating.
And you know exactly where that negotiation usually ends.
Afterward comes the familiar silence.
The shame.
The promise.
The prayer.
“Jesus, I'm sorry. I won't do it again.”
Until the next time.
But here is where we must be extraordinarily careful.
Struggling with a sin you desperately want to overcome is not the same as deliberately planning a sin you have no intention of surrendering.
Those two conditions may look similar from the outside.
But spiritually, they are not the same.
And confusing them can destroy a person's understanding of repentance, grace, and the Gospel itself.
The Bible does not teach that a genuinely repentant Christian will never stumble again. If that were true, the apostle John would never have written:
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” — 1 John 1:8, KJV
And he continues:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Notice what John does not say.
He does not say that Christians never sin.
He does not say that forgiveness is available only to those who have achieved perfect obedience.
He points us toward confession, God's faithfulness, and the cleansing made possible through Jesus Christ.
Yet this same apostle also writes:
Do you see the beauty and seriousness of those words?
That ye sin not.
And then:
If any man sin.
God's grace is not permission to pursue sin.
It is hope for the sinner who needs a Savior.
Jesus is our Advocate, not our accomplice.
He does not stand beside us to bless our rebellion. He stands for those who come to Him because His righteousness and atoning sacrifice are their only hope.
And this brings us to the word that changes everything.
Repentance.
In the Greek New Testament, the noun commonly translated “repentance” is μετάνοια (metanoia), and the related verb is μετανοέω (metanoeō).
The language speaks of a change of mind or understanding that, in biblical calls to repentance, involves a fundamental turning toward God.
Not merely feeling bad.
Not simply being embarrassed because someone discovered your secret.
Not crying because your actions produced painful consequences.
Biblical repentance involves a changed response to God, sin, and the truth.
Jesus proclaimed:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” — Mark 1:15, KJV
In the Greek text, the command includes:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
Metanoeite kai pisteuete en tō euangeliō.
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
Two commands that belong together.
Turn from your rebellion toward God.
Believe the good news of what Jesus Christ has accomplished.
Repentance is not an attempt to purchase salvation through better behavior. Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Christ, not earned by works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But the grace that saves us does not leave sin unchallenged.
Ephesians 2:10 reminds us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself up so Jesus will finally love you.”
It announces that Jesus Christ came to save sinners—and calls those who trust Him into a new life.
This is where the difference between regret and repentance becomes painfully personal.
Regret says, “I hate what happened to me because of my sin.”
Repentance says, “Lord, I have sinned against You, and I want to turn from it.”
Regret may mourn the consequences.
Repentance recognizes the offense against God.
Regret may wish the evidence would disappear.
Repentance becomes willing to bring what is hidden into the light.
And sometimes both feelings exist in the same broken heart.
That is why we must never pretend to know every person's spiritual condition from a single failure.
God sees what human eyes cannot.
But Scripture gives us a serious warning about sorrow that never becomes surrender.
“For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.” — 2 Corinthians 7:10, KJV
The Greek expression translated “godly sorrow” is ἡ κατὰ θεὸν λύπη (hē kata theon lypē)—sorrow according to God.
Paul's point is not that tears automatically prove repentance.
He describes sorrow that produces repentance.
A grief that leads somewhere.
A sorrow that stops making excuses.
A conviction that begins changing the direction of a life.
And that distinction matters because you can be genuinely emotional without being genuinely willing to change.
You can cry because you lost a relationship while still refusing to abandon the behavior that destroyed it.
You can feel ashamed after watching pornography while already deciding when you will return to it.
You can apologize for lying while secretly preparing your next deception.
You can ask God to forgive an affair while continuing to arrange private meetings with the person involved.
And you can feel miserable about all of it.
But misery alone is not repentance.
Now comes the question many people are afraid to ask.
If I already know I am going to commit the same sin again, can my repentance still be genuine?
The answer depends on what you mean by know.
If you mean, “I am afraid I might fall again because I know how weak I am,” that fear does not automatically make your repentance false.
A believer may sincerely turn from sin and still struggle with temptation, ingrained habits, addiction, or patterns that require sustained spiritual and practical help.
But if you mean, “I have already decided to do it again, and I am asking forgiveness now because I expect God to excuse my future disobedience,” that is something entirely different.
That is not simply weakness.
It is a deliberate intention to continue in what you acknowledge as sin.
And that intention contradicts the turning of heart that repentance requires.
You cannot sincerely say, “Lord, I am turning away from this,” while deliberately planning to keep walking toward it.
You may be beginning to feel conviction.
You may be experiencing the first painful signs of spiritual awakening.
You may even be wrestling with the desire to surrender.
But you should not call a settled plan to continue sinning the same thing as repentance.
This does not mean God's mercy has become unreachable.
It means you need to stop disguising your refusal as surrender.
And the astonishing thing is that you can bring even that divided heart to Jesus.
You can pray:

“Lord, I know this is wrong. Part of me still wants it. I have made excuses. I am afraid of losing what this sin gives me. I cannot honestly tell You that all my desires are pure. But I do not want to keep hiding. Expose what I have been protecting. Teach me to hate what is destroying me. Help me turn to You.”
That is not a polished religious performance.
That is spiritual honesty.
And honesty is a far better beginning than another promise you are not prepared to keep.
There is an ancient Hebrew word that helps us understand this turning.
שׁוּב (shuv).
It commonly means “to turn” or “to return.”
In the Old Testament, it is frequently used when God calls His people to turn away from evil and return to Him.
Through the prophet Isaiah, the Lord declares:

“Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the LORD, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.” — Isaiah 55:7, KJV
Look at the movement of the verse.
Forsake.
Return.
Mercy.
Pardon.
The command is not merely to feel differently about the road.
It is to leave the road and return to the Lord.
And notice that God calls the wicked to return because mercy is available.
Not because the wicked have somehow made themselves worthy.
Not because they have accumulated enough good deeds.
But because the Lord is merciful.
This is the heartbeat of biblical repentance.
Turning from sin and returning to God.
Yet some people hear this and immediately begin drowning in fear.
“What if I repented yesterday and sinned again today?”
“What if I have confessed the same thing a hundred times?”
“What if I am fighting an addiction and keep relapsing?”
“What if I genuinely want to change, but I still experience sinful desires?”
Listen carefully.
The presence of temptation does not prove the absence of repentance.
And a repeated failure does not, by itself, prove that every previous confession was a lie.
The Bible does not teach that repentance means temptation instantly disappears.
Jesus Himself was tempted, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
Temptation and sin are not identical.
Nor does Scripture teach that the Christian life is sustained by human willpower alone.
Galatians 5:16 calls believers to walk in the Spirit.
Romans 8:13 teaches that by the Spirit we put to death the deeds of the body.
The battle is real.
The responsibility is real.
And the help of God is real.
There is a difference between a person who falls while resisting temptation and a person who deliberately builds a comfortable home for sin.
One may cry, “Lord, help me stand.”
The other may quietly whisper, “Lord, forgive me, but do not interfere with my plans.”
And sometimes the most frightening reality is that we can move from one condition toward the other without noticing.
The first time, we tremble.
The second time, we rationalize.
The third time, we prepare.
Eventually, what once troubled our conscience begins to feel ordinary.
That is why Hebrews 3:13 warns about being hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
Sin rarely introduces itself by saying, “I am here to destroy your relationship with God.”
It says, “You deserve this.”
“It is not that serious.”
“Everybody struggles.”
“You can repent later.”
“God understands.”
And the most dangerous lie of all:
“Because God is gracious, you do not need to change.”
But Paul confronts that exact distortion.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” — Romans 6:1–2, KJV
The Greek response translated “God forbid” is μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito).
It is an emphatic rejection, expressing something like, “Absolutely not!”
Paul refuses the idea that grace should become an excuse for continuing in sin.
Why?
Because believers have been united with Christ in His death and resurrection.
Grace does not simply change the consequences of sin.
It establishes a new relationship to sin through Jesus Christ.
The Christian may still struggle.
But sin is no longer to be embraced as master.
And perhaps this is where the article has become uncomfortable.
Because you are remembering something.
A conversation you should not have continued.
A website you keep revisiting.
A message you deleted.
A financial decision you have been concealing.
A person you keep contacting even though you know the relationship is pulling you toward disobedience.
A private habit you have learned to justify with public spirituality.
You have prayed about it.
You have cried about it.
You have promised to stop.
But have you actually begun removing the things that keep leading you back?
Jesus said:
“And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee.” — Matthew 5:29, KJV
Jesus uses deliberately shocking imagery to communicate the seriousness of dealing with sin. This is not a command to physically injure yourself.
It is a call to take radical, decisive action against what leads you into sin.
Sometimes that means deleting an app.
Sometimes it means ending a secret relationship.
Sometimes it means surrendering access to something you repeatedly misuse.
Sometimes it means confessing the truth to a trustworthy, mature Christian who can help you walk in accountability.
Sometimes it means seeking qualified counseling or addiction treatment alongside prayer and pastoral support.
Sometimes it means making restitution for what you have stolen or correcting a lie that harmed someone.
Not because those actions earn forgiveness.
But because repentance is not merely something we claim with our lips.
It bears fruit in the way we respond to sin.
John the Baptist said:
“Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.” — Matthew 3:8, KJV
The Greek expression includes καρπὸν ἄξιον τῆς μετανοίας (karpon axion tēs metanoias)—fruit worthy of repentance.
Fruit is not the root of salvation.
But genuine repentance is not indifferent to fruit.
And if you are unwilling to change anything that makes your sin easier, you should seriously examine whether you have surrendered that sin at all.
Now I want to take you somewhere.
Not to a theological classroom.
Not to a church platform.
But to a courtyard.
A cold night.
A fire burning.
A frightened disciple trying to survive.
His name was Peter.
He had walked with Jesus.
He had seen miracles.
He had heard the voice of the Son of God.
He had confidently declared that he would remain faithful.
Yet when the pressure came, Peter denied even knowing Him.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
And Luke records one of the most devastating moments in the Gospels.
“And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.” — Luke 22:61, KJV
Imagine that look.
Peter had just denied the One he loved.
And Jesus turned toward him.
We are not told every expression that crossed the Savior's face. Scripture does not give us permission to invent His thoughts.
But it tells us what happened next.
“And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.” — Luke 22:62, KJV
Peter broke.
The confident disciple who had insisted he would never fall now had to face what he had done.
But here is something essential.
Peter's failure was not the end of his story.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, Jesus questioned him about his love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Peter did not restore himself by pretending the denial never happened.
And Jesus did not treat Peter's failure as proof that restoration was impossible.
The risen Christ graciously restored a fallen disciple.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
The same Jesus who knows your worst failure is the Savior who calls sinners to Himself.
But do not confuse Peter's restoration with permission to plan your own denial.
Peter's story is not an invitation to betray Jesus because you expect forgiveness afterward.
It is a testimony that even grievous failure need not have the final word when Christ restores a repentant sinner.
And then there is Judas.
Another disciple.
Another betrayal.
Another man who experienced devastating remorse.
Matthew 27:3 tells us that Judas regretted what he had done and returned the thirty pieces of silver.
He acknowledged that he had betrayed innocent blood.
Yet the biblical account does not portray Judas turning in saving faith to the risen Christ.
His story ends in tragedy.
We should not reduce the contrast between Peter and Judas to a simplistic claim that one cried the right kind of tears while the other cried the wrong kind.
The accounts are more profound than that.
Peter's story includes Christ's gracious restoration.
Judas's story demonstrates the terrible seriousness of betrayal and remorse without the restoration we see in Peter.
The lesson is not that you must manufacture a certain emotional intensity to be forgiven.
It is that remorse alone is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
And you must come to Him.
Not simply to your guilt.
Not merely to your shame.
Not to a performance of religious sorrow.
To Christ Himself.
Because the cross is not a place where sin is treated lightly.
It is the place where the seriousness of sin and the mercy of God meet in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
He was not crucified because sin was harmless.
He gave Himself for sinners because sin is deadly, and we could not rescue ourselves.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8, KJV
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired every broken thing.
Not after we had earned the right to approach Him.
While we were sinners.
And because Christ died and rose again, forgiveness is not an empty religious wish.
It is grounded in the finished work of the Savior.
Still, someone reading this may be asking:
“But what if I keep falling?”
Then do not make peace with falling.
Keep bringing your sin into the light.
Keep returning to Scripture.
Keep praying.
Keep seeking the help you need.
Keep taking concrete steps to remove temptation.
And when you fall, do not use the fall as an excuse to abandon the fight.
Confess your sin.
Turn again to Christ.
Remember that your hope is not in the perfection of your repentance but in the sufficiency of your Savior.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It keeps repentance from becoming another attempt to save yourself.
Jesus does not tell us to trust in the emotional strength of our sorrow.
He tells us to believe the Gospel.
And perhaps the most hopeful picture of repentance appears in the story of the prodigal son.
He had demanded his inheritance.
Left his father's house.
Wasted his wealth.
And eventually found himself hungry, humiliated, and desperate.
Then Luke 15:17 says:
“And when he came to himself...”
What a sentence.
He came to himself.
He stopped pretending.
He saw where his choices had taken him.
He recognized what he had lost.
And he decided to return.
But notice what happened next.
He did not merely sit among the pigs feeling guilty.
He got up.
He went home.
And while he was still a great way off, his father saw him, had compassion, ran to him, embraced him, and kissed him.
That is the picture Jesus gave.
Not of a father who approved of rebellion.
Not of a father who pretended the son had done nothing wrong.
But of a father whose mercy welcomed a returning son.
And perhaps today you have been sitting in the same spiritual pigpen, rehearsing apologies while refusing to stand up.
You keep saying you miss the Father's house.
But you keep making plans to stay in the far country.
The invitation is not to become worthy before returning.
It is to get up and come home.
And if your heart is divided, tell Him.
If you are afraid to surrender, tell Him.
If you still feel attracted to the sin, tell Him.
If you have spent years performing Christianity while hiding a secret life, stop pretending that God is surprised.
He already knows.
And still, through the Gospel, the call to repent and believe goes out.
This is what makes grace so astonishing.
God's mercy is not reserved for people with impressive spiritual histories.
Christ came to save sinners.
But His grace must never be turned into an excuse to remain deliberately enslaved to the very sins from which He calls us.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly.
Grace is not merely pardon.
It also trains us.
It reshapes us.
It teaches us to say no to what once ruled us.
Not instantly in every struggle.
Not without painful battles.
But genuinely.
And here is a question worth sitting with tonight.
If Jesus removed every consequence you feared from your favorite sin, would you still want to stop doing it because you love Him?
Do not rush past that.
Would you still want to obey if nobody could discover your secret?
Would you still want purity if there were no embarrassment?
Would you still want honesty if the lie could never be exposed?
Would you still want holiness if disobedience brought you temporary pleasure without immediate earthly consequences?
That question may reveal something about what you love.
But if your answer frightens you, do not despair.
Bring that answer to God.
Ask Him to change not only your behavior but your desires.
David prayed after his grievous sin:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10, KJV
In Hebrew:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים וְרוּחַ נָכוֹן חַדֵּשׁ בְּקִרְבִּי
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim, veruach nakhon chaddesh beqirbi.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.”
David did not merely ask for his reputation to be restored.
He asked for a clean heart.
A renewed spirit.
Something deeper than damage control.
And perhaps that is what you need to ask for today.
Not simply, “Lord, make the consequences disappear.”
But, “Lord, change the heart that keeps choosing this.”
Not simply, “Lord, forgive me so I can feel better.”
But, “Lord, teach me to love You more than I love this sin.”
Not simply, “Lord, let me escape being exposed.”
But, “Lord, lead me into the truth, even when truth requires painful obedience.”
That is a prayer worth praying.
And it may be the beginning of a very different story.
A story in which the person who once concealed an addiction finally asks for help.
The husband who lived dishonestly begins telling the truth.
The woman who kept returning to a destructive relationship finally establishes boundaries.
The believer who has been consumed by bitterness begins the difficult journey toward forgiveness.
The person who has been using grace as an excuse finally recognizes that grace is calling them into freedom.
Not every story resolves overnight.
Some battles require years of faithful perseverance, wise support, and ongoing dependence on the Holy Spirit.
Some broken relationships cannot be repaired simply because we apologize.
Some consequences remain even after God forgives.
And repentance does not guarantee that other people must immediately trust us again.
But none of that makes transformation meaningless.
Jesus is not offering a cosmetic improvement to a religious image.
He calls us to a new life in Him.
“If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
That new identity is grounded in being united to Christ.
It does not mean every temptation instantly vanishes.
It means that your past sin does not have the authority to define who you are in Him.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
And that is why we keep proclaiming the message at the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because He erases the need for repentance.
Not because His forgiveness makes deliberate rebellion harmless.
But because His death and resurrection provide the only foundation for forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and genuine transformation.
He rewrites lives by redeeming sinners, not by renaming sin as righteousness.
And if this message has exposed something you have been hiding, I want to invite you into a moment of honesty.
You do not need to tell strangers the details of your private struggles.
You do not need to expose another person's sin.
But perhaps you need to stop pretending that everything is fine.
And if you have experienced the mercy of Jesus after a season of wandering, consider sharing a testimony of His faithfulness.
Not to impress anyone.
Not to make your spiritual life a performance.
But because someone else may be sitting alone tonight, believing they are beyond the reach of grace.
Your testimony might remind them to turn to Christ.
And if you know someone who is struggling with the difference between conviction and condemnation, send them this article privately.
If someone came to mind while reading, consider tagging them only if doing so would encourage them without exposing or embarrassing them.
One conversation may encourage someone to seek help.
One biblical reminder may interrupt a dangerous decision.
One testimony may point a wandering heart back toward Jesus.
Not as a substitute for opening your Bible.
But as a reminder to return to the Word, resist sin, and remember the mercy of Christ.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have grown spiritually indifferent, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along.
Because the Gospel is not merely for people who already look religious.
It is good news for sinners who need a Savior.
There is also another way to help this ministry continue reaching people.

Scripture teaches that supporting faithful ministry is a worthy use of our resources. Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach the Word, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds believers that giving should be willing and cheerful, not reluctant or compelled.
