And from the line of that fourth son came the Savior who reveals God's love through the cross.
From a home wounded by favoritism, Scripture leads us toward the One who welcomes repentant sinners by grace.
From a woman's longing for affection, we are pointed toward the Messiah whose love is demonstrated not by empty promises, but by His sacrificial death and victorious resurrection.
Not because the scandal was harmless.
Not because the pain was imaginary.
Not because every earthly relationship was repaired.
But because Jesus Christ is greater than the sin, rejection, and brokenness that mark our fallen world.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the old chapters never happened.
But by giving forgiven sinners a new life in Him and an eternal hope that suffering cannot destroy.
And I want to speak personally to the person who has quietly been crying while reading this.
You do not need to pretend anymore.
You do not need to convince everyone that the rejection never hurt.
You do not need to manufacture a testimony that sounds more victorious than your actual experience.
You can tell the truth.
You can say, “I'm still healing.”
You can say, “I still struggle with feeling unwanted.”
You can say, “I have forgiven, but some days the memories still hurt.”
You can say, “I know God is faithful, but I need help trusting Him again.”
And you can bring every one of those honest confessions before Jesus.
You can simply write “Christ is still healing me.”
Not because commenting earns God's favor.
Not because you owe strangers an explanation of your pain.
But because sometimes a few honest words become the beginning of a conversation that reminds another wounded believer they are not alone.
You do not have to share anything you are not comfortable revealing.
Someone else reading the comments may have walked through a similar valley. Your testimony, your prayer request, or even your quiet encouragement could help another person turn toward Christ.
And please think of one person who needs to hear this.
A wife who feels unseen.
A husband who feels unwanted.
A daughter still trying to earn her father's approval.
A son carrying the ache of never being enough.
A single mother exhausted from holding everything together.
A young believer who thinks rejection means God has forgotten them.
Not merely because it may reach more people, but because you never know who is silently carrying the exact burden this passage addresses.
Because there may come another night when old insecurities return and you need to remember that the Lord saw Leah's affliction long before anyone could see the full significance of her story.
And if this message has strengthened your faith, I want to invite you to walk with us more deeply at Gospel Warrior.
We are not here to build a following around human personalities.
Our desire is to point people to the Lord Jesus Christ, to proclaim His Gospel faithfully, and to help believers grow in the truth of God's Word.
That mission takes time, prayer, labor, resources, and the faithful support of people who believe that biblical encouragement should continue reaching those who need it.
And this is where I want to make a sincere invitation.
Keep teaching.
Keep sharing Scripture.
Keep reaching the person who may be reading alone at midnight, wondering whether God has forgotten them.
We also want to be biblically careful about how we speak of giving.

Scripture teaches generosity, cheerful giving, and faithful support for Gospel ministry. Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver, not one who gives under pressure or compulsion.
The Gospel is free.
Salvation is by grace.
And God's love cannot be bought with a monthly payment.
These are small ways of expressing our gratitude for those helping us carry this work forward.
We want people to read the Bible.
Understand the Gospel.
Know Christ.
Grow in discernment.
Turn away from sin.
Learn to pray.
And become rooted in the truth, rather than merely collecting emotional moments online.
Pray for this ministry.
And above all, live out the truth of the Gospel in your own home, church, relationships, and daily life.
Because the greatest testimony is not the size of a ministry's audience.
It is the transforming work of Jesus Christ in the lives of people who hear His Word and follow Him.
Before you leave, return with me one last time to Leah.
Picture her holding Reuben.
A newborn son.
A mother's tenderness.
A heart filled with hope.
“Now therefore my husband will love me.”
She could not see the generations ahead.
She could not see David's throne.
She could not see Bethlehem.
She could not see the cross.
She could not see the empty tomb.
She did not know the full story that God was unfolding through her family.
All she knew in that moment was that the Lord had seen her affliction, and she desperately hoped her husband would finally love her.
And yet, centuries later, we are still reading her words.
Not because Jacob's love was the greatest thing about her life.
But because God's Word has preserved her story within the unfolding history of redemption that leads us to Jesus Christ.

So if you are still waiting to be appreciated, still grieving a rejection, still trying to understand why someone you loved could not love you as you hoped, do not make their response the final verdict on your life.
Bring your heart to Jesus.
Let His Word correct the lies you have believed.
Let His grace lead you to repentance.
Let His promises steady you when emotions rise and fall.
And let the cross remind you that the deepest love you will ever need is not something you can earn through desperate striving.
It is found in the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
You may never receive the apology you deserve.
You may never hear the words you waited years to hear.
Some relationships may never become what you hoped.
But if you belong to Christ, your story does not end with human rejection.
It is held within the greater promise of redemption and resurrection.
And when you finally understand that, you can begin to stop living every day as another attempt to prove you deserve to be loved.
You can begin living as someone called to love God, love others, walk in truth, and rest in the sufficiency of Jesus Christ.
Leah wanted Jacob to look at her and see someone worth loving.
But the Lord had already seen her affliction.
And through the line of Judah, the world would one day behold the Savior.
The woman who cried, “Maybe now he will love me,” became part of the family story that led to the cross, where Jesus demonstrated a love no sinner could ever earn.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES LUST ALWAYS WANT SOMETHING? THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT WHAT YOUR HEART IS REALLY HUNGRY FOR
paragraphs: DOES LUST ALWAYS WANT SOMETHING? THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT WHAT YOUR HEART IS REALLY HUNGRY FOR

Sometimes lust isn't just craving another body. Sometimes it's a wounded heart searching for comfort, a lonely soul begging to feel wanted, and a spiritual battle you keep losing because you've been fighting the symptom while ignoring the wound. But what if Jesus wants to heal something deeper than the desire you've been ashamed to confess?
There is a kind of hunger that doesn't disappear after you feed it.
You know what I'm talking about.
You promised yourself you wouldn't go back.
Not tonight.
Not after everything God has brought you through.
Not after that prayer you prayed with tears running down your face.
But then the room became quiet.
Your phone was within reach.
Your thoughts started wandering.
And somewhere between loneliness, curiosity, exhaustion, and temptation, you found yourself standing at the same door you swore you would never open again.
Maybe you opened it.
Maybe you didn't.
Maybe nobody knows how close you came.
But you know.
And God knows.
And here's the question that might change how you understand your struggle:
What if the thing you're lusting after isn't the only thing you're hungry for?
What if you're reaching for pleasure because you don't know what to do with pain?
What if you're craving attention because somewhere inside, you're terrified of being forgotten?
What if you keep wanting someone to desire you because you've never really believed you were valuable without being desired?
And what if the enemy has learned to exploit legitimate human longings by offering you something that can never truly satisfy them?
Stay with me.
Because this isn't another article telling you to simply stop looking, stop thinking, stop feeling, and somehow become holy through sheer determination.
This is about the difference between a desire that belongs to our humanity and a desire that has begun ruling our hearts.
It's about the moment a longing becomes a master.
It's about the scandal of what we sometimes do in secret.
And the astonishing grace of a Savior who already knows the truth and still calls sinners to come into the light.
But before we go any further, we need to answer the question.
Does lust always want something?
Yes. But what lust consciously wants and what may be driving it beneath the surface are not always the same thing.
And misunderstanding that difference can leave someone fighting the same battle for years.
In the Greek New Testament, one important word translated as lust or desire is ἐπιθυμία (epithymia).
It refers to desire, longing, or craving.
Here is something many people overlook.
The word itself does not always describe sinful desire.
In Luke 22:15, Jesus uses the related verb ἐπεθύμησα (epethymēsa) when He tells His disciples that He has earnestly desired to eat the Passover with them before His suffering.
Jesus desired.
And Jesus never sinned.
That matters.
Because desire itself is not automatically evil.
The desire for intimacy is not evil.
The longing to be loved is not evil.
Sexual attraction is not automatically lust.
Wanting companionship does not make you impure.
And feeling lonely does not mean you have failed God.

The problem begins when desire turns away from God's good purposes and seeks satisfaction through what He forbids, when another person becomes an object to consume, or when a craving begins demanding obedience that belongs to God alone.
James 1:14–15 says:
"But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death." (KJV)
James is not describing every human longing as sinful.
He is describing the deadly progression of desire when it entices a person toward evil.
Notice the movement.
Desire.
Enticement.
Sin.
Death.
Something begins inside before it becomes visible outside.
And sometimes the most dangerous moment isn't when you commit the sin.
It's when you begin negotiating with it.
When you tell yourself one glance won't matter.
One conversation is harmless.
One private message isn't betrayal.
One fantasy isn't hurting anybody.
One more time, and then you'll repent.
But sin has a way of making tomorrow sound like a wonderful day to obey God while convincing you that tonight belongs to your appetite.
And suddenly, what began as a passing temptation becomes a carefully protected secret.
A secret that starts shaping your habits.
Your relationships.
Your prayer life.
Your conscience.
Even the way you see other people.
Jesus addresses this with unsettling clarity in Matthew 5:28:
"But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." (KJV)
The Greek phrase πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn) expresses looking with the purpose of lusting after her.
Jesus is confronting more than involuntary awareness of someone's beauty.
He is exposing the deliberate cultivation of a covetous, sexually possessive gaze.
He is telling us that righteousness cannot be reduced to what our hands have or haven't done.
God cares about what our hearts are choosing.
And that truth is uncomfortable.
Because many people have never physically crossed a boundary while repeatedly crossing it in their imagination.
Some have remained outwardly faithful while inwardly feeding fantasies of someone who isn't their spouse.
Some have never touched pornography but have learned to consume people through social media, imagination, or flirtation.
And some have spent years convincing themselves that because nobody else knows, nothing serious is happening.
But secrecy doesn't turn sin into innocence.
It only hides the evidence from other people.
Not from God.
Yet here is where we must be careful.
Not every unwanted sexual thought is a chosen sin.
Not every intrusive image represents the true desire of your heart.
Not every experience of attraction is rebellion against God.
Temptation and surrender are not the same thing.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that Jesus was tempted, yet without sin.
If temptation itself were identical to sin, that verse would make no sense.
So don't confuse the arrival of temptation with the decision to welcome it.
The battle is not necessarily lost because a thought appeared.
What matters is what you choose to do with it.
Do you entertain it?
Feed it?
Return to it?
Arrange opportunities for it?
Or do you bring it before Christ and turn away?
And now we come to something even more personal.
Sometimes lust is not merely pursuing pleasure. Sometimes it is trying to escape something painful.
For one person, the struggle intensifies after rejection.
For another, it appears after a stressful day.
For another, it grows during seasons of loneliness.
For someone else, it becomes a way to feel powerful after spending the day feeling insignificant.
Sometimes the underlying experience is boredom.
Sometimes insecurity.
Sometimes anger.
Sometimes grief.
Sometimes a desire for reassurance.
And sometimes lust is exactly what it appears to be: a sinful appetite seeking forbidden gratification, without any deeper psychological explanation required.
We must not romanticize sin by assuming every sinful choice is secretly an untreated wound.
The Bible holds us responsible for our choices.
But Scripture also recognizes the complexity of the human heart.
Proverbs 20:5 says:
"Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water; but a man of understanding will draw it out." (KJV)
Human motives are not always obvious, even to the person experiencing them.
And this is why someone can genuinely hate a pattern of sin while continuing to return to it.
They may understand that the behavior is wrong without understanding all the situations, beliefs, habits, and emotional triggers that make it so attractive.
Picture someone sitting alone at 1:17 in the morning.
They've spent the whole day being strong.
Strong for their family.
Strong at work.
Strong at church.
Strong for everyone who needed them.
But nobody asked how they were doing.
Nobody noticed their exhaustion.
Nobody saw the disappointment they swallowed.
And now the silence feels unbearable.
So they reach for their phone.
Not necessarily because they woke up that morning determined to rebel against God.
Perhaps they want relief.
A distraction.
A moment of excitement.
A temporary escape from feeling invisible.
But instead of bringing their exhaustion into the presence of God, they turn toward something that promises immediate comfort without requiring vulnerability.
For a moment, it works.
The mind becomes occupied.
The body responds.
The loneliness seems quieter.
Then the moment passes.
And the original pain is still there.
Only now, guilt may have joined it.
And the cycle begins again.
If that sounds familiar, I want you to understand something.
Recognizing the emotional circumstances surrounding sin does not excuse the sin.
It helps reveal where repentance, healing, wisdom, and practical change may all be necessary.
You cannot heal a wound by pretending it isn't there.
And you cannot overcome sin by pretending it isn't sin.
Both truths matter.
This is where the story of the Samaritan woman becomes so powerful.
In John 4, Jesus meets a woman at Jacob's well.
She comes to draw water.
A completely ordinary activity.
But this encounter becomes one of the most extraordinary conversations in the Gospel of John.
Jesus asks her for a drink.
Then He begins speaking about living water.
In John 4:13–14, He says:

"Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again: But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life." (KJV)
In the Greek text, the phrase ὕδωρ ζῶν (hydōr zōn) means "living water."
In ordinary usage, it could describe flowing or fresh water.
But Jesus uses the image to reveal something far greater: the life He gives, ultimately understood in John's Gospel in connection with the Holy Spirit.
He is not offering a temporary emotional high.
He is speaking of eternal life that comes through Him.
Then the conversation becomes painfully personal.
Jesus tells her to call her husband.
She says she has no husband.
Jesus reveals that she has had five husbands and that the man she currently has is not her husband.
Now, we must not add details Scripture never gives us.
The text does not tell us that she was sexually addicted.
It does not tell us why her marriages ended.
It does not tell us that every relationship was the result of lust.
It does not even tell us that she came to the well at that hour because the community had rejected her.
Those are common assumptions, not established facts.
What Scripture does show is that Jesus knew the complicated truth of her relational life.
And He did not walk away.
He exposed what was true without reducing her identity to her history.
He spoke about worship.
He revealed Himself as the Messiah.
And the woman went back to her community declaring:
"Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" (John 4:29, KJV)
Think about that.
The very things Jesus knew about her did not prevent her from inviting others to meet Him.
Her encounter with truth became the beginning of her testimony.
And many Samaritans believed through her witness.
This is what grace can do.
Grace does not need to falsify your history to give you a future.
It doesn't need to call darkness light.
It doesn't need to pretend your choices never mattered.
Grace brings you to the One who knows everything and can still make you new.
And perhaps that is what frightens us most.
Not merely that God knows our sin.
But that coming to Him means surrendering our right to keep protecting it.
Because sometimes we say we want freedom when what we really want is relief from consequences.
We want peace without confession.
Forgiveness without repentance.
Intimacy with God without surrendering our favorite escape.
We want Jesus to remove the shame while allowing the secret to remain untouched.
But Jesus loves us too much to become the guardian of our hidden chains.
He came to save us from sin, not to help us become comfortable living under its power.
Listen to what He says in John 8:34–36:
"Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin... If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed." (KJV)
The freedom Jesus gives is not merely the ability to feel less guilty.
It is freedom from sin's dominion.
Freedom to obey.
Freedom to love without consuming.
Freedom to see people as image-bearers rather than objects.
Freedom to tell the truth when hiding would be easier.
Freedom to stop worshiping a craving that has never been able to save you.
And that brings us to a painful question.
Have you ever noticed how lust can promise intimacy while training your heart to avoid it?
Real intimacy requires honesty.
Patience.
Respect.
Commitment.
Self-giving love.
It requires recognizing another person as a whole human being, with a soul, a history, boundaries, fears, and dignity.
Lust, by contrast, can reduce someone to the role they play in satisfying your appetite.
It asks, "What can I get?"
Love asks, "How can I honor?"
Lust can become impatient when gratification is delayed.
Love knows how to wait.
Lust can flourish in secrecy and fantasy.
Love seeks truth and faithfulness.
This does not mean genuine love has no physical desire.
God created human sexuality, and Scripture honors its rightful expression within marriage.
The Song of Songs openly celebrates marital desire.
But biblical love refuses to separate desire from holiness, dignity, and faithfulness.
First Corinthians 13:5 says that love "seeketh not her own."
That doesn't mean love never experiences personal longing.
It means love is not governed by selfish insistence.
And if your desire requires you to betray someone, deceive someone, objectify someone, manipulate someone, or violate God's commands, it is not made righteous simply because the feelings are intense.
Intensity is not proof of love.
Chemistry is not proof of God's approval.
And an open door is not always a door God wants you to walk through.
Sometimes the strongest act of love is refusing to take what you have no right to possess.
Sometimes the most courageous thing a person can do is close the conversation.
Delete the secret account.
End the inappropriate relationship.
Confess the hidden pattern.
Ask for accountability.
Seek pastoral help or qualified counseling when the struggle has become deeply entrenched.
Not because any of those actions earn salvation.
But because repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning toward God in a way that changes what you choose today.
The Hebrew word שׁוּב (shuv) carries the sense of turning or returning.
It appears in many Old Testament passages calling people to return to the Lord.
And the Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated "repentance," speaks of a change of mind or heart that, in biblical context, calls for a changed direction.
Repentance is more than an emotional breakdown.
It is more than crying after getting caught.
It is more than promising never to do it again.
It is a turning from sin toward the living God.
And that turning may require difficult, practical decisions.
Because you cannot keep arranging your life around temptation and then act surprised when temptation keeps finding you.
You may need to stop following accounts that deliberately feed your fantasies.
You may need to establish boundaries with someone whose attention has become an emotional addiction.
You may need to stop bringing your phone into the same private situations where you repeatedly compromise.
You may need to admit to a mature, trustworthy believer that your struggle has become more serious than you've allowed anyone to know.
And if pornography or compulsive sexual behavior has become difficult to control, professional support can be part of wise, responsible care alongside spiritual discipleship.
None of this means that every believer will experience immediate victory.
Growth can be difficult.
Old habits may take time to dismantle.
But difficulty does not make obedience meaningless.
And repeated failure should never become an excuse to stop pursuing Christ.
First Corinthians 10:13 reminds believers that God is faithful and provides a way to endure temptation.
That promise is not a guarantee that temptation will feel easy.
It is a call to depend upon God's faithfulness rather than surrendering to the claim that sin is inevitable.
Now let me speak to the person who has already fallen.
The person reading this with a tightness in their chest.
The person who has confessed the same sin so many times that the words "Lord, forgive me" have started to feel painfully familiar.
You might be thinking:
How many times can I ask for forgiveness before God gets tired of hearing my voice?
How can I call myself a Christian when I still struggle with this?
What if I'm only pretending?
What if I've gone too far?
Please hear what Scripture actually says.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
And Romans 8:1 says:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus." (KJV)
These promises are not permission to continue deliberately in sin.
Romans 6:1–2 explicitly rejects that idea.
They are assurances that the grace of God is greater than the accusation that repentant sinners are beyond His mercy.
The foundation of forgiveness is not the emotional intensity of your apology.
It is the finished work of Jesus Christ.
At Calvary, Jesus did not merely offer humanity motivational advice.
He bore sin.
He suffered.
He died.
And He rose again.
The sinless Savior accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
First Peter 2:24 says He "bare our sins in his own body on the tree."
And 2 Corinthians 5:21 tells us that God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
This is the Gospel.
Not that your sin is insignificant.
But that Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Not that holiness doesn't matter.
But that holiness grows from belonging to Christ, not from purchasing His acceptance through your performance.
Not that repentance is optional.
But that the mercy of God calls us to repentance and gives us hope when we turn to Him.
And perhaps one of the most beautiful pictures of that mercy is found in Luke 15.
Jesus tells the story of a son who demands his inheritance, leaves home, and wastes his possessions in reckless living.
Eventually, he is hungry.
Desperate.
Humiliated.
And alone.
The boy who once believed freedom meant escaping his father's house now finds himself longing for food given to pigs.
Then Scripture says something extraordinary.
"He came to himself." (Luke 15:17, KJV)
There is a moment when sin's promises begin to collapse.
When the excitement wears off.
When the pleasure stops distracting you.
When you finally see what your choices have been costing.
And you realize you have been starving while running away from the very place where you could have been fed.
So the son decides to return.
He prepares a confession.
He knows he has sinned.
He does not demand restoration as something he deserves.
But while he is still a great way off, his father sees him.
And runs.
And embraces him.
And welcomes him home.
The father does not celebrate the son's rebellion.
He celebrates his return.
"This my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found." (Luke 15:24, KJV)
That is not a picture of cheap grace.
That is a picture of undeserved mercy.
And while this parable must be understood in its own context, its message speaks powerfully to every sinner who has begun believing that coming home is no longer possible.
Maybe you've wasted years.
Maybe you've betrayed trust.
Maybe you've become someone you never imagined you could become.
Maybe you have been hiding behind church attendance, ministry involvement, and carefully chosen Bible verses while privately feeding a habit that is slowly hardening your heart.
Then stop pretending.
Not because you are beyond hope.
But because you don't have to keep hiding from the One who calls sinners to repentance.
Come into the light.
Tell the truth.
Turn around.
Receive the mercy of Christ.
And begin walking in the freedom He commands and supplies.
But there is one more thing we need to understand about lust.
Even when a person has addressed loneliness, stress, rejection, or insecurity, the struggle may not simply disappear.
Why?
Because lust is not always a symptom of emotional pain.
It can also be an expression of the sinful desires Scripture calls us to put to death.
Colossians 3:5 commands believers to put to death what belongs to their earthly nature, including sexual immorality, impurity, passion, and evil desire.
The Christian life is not simply a journey of self-discovery.
It is a life of self-denial, Spirit-enabled obedience, and transformation into the likeness of Christ.
Jesus says in Luke 9:23:
"If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me." (KJV)
Daily.
Not just on the day you got baptized.
Not just when you first believed.
Not just after a powerful worship service.
Daily.
Some days, following Jesus means refusing something your body strongly wants.
Some days, it means surrendering a fantasy you have secretly treasured.
Some days, it means accepting that a relationship must end because it is drawing you away from obedience.
Some days, it means sitting with loneliness instead of numbing it.
Some days, it means praying through tears because your emotions haven't caught up with your convictions.
And some days, faithfulness looks very ordinary.
Going to bed.
Putting the phone away.
Opening your Bible.
Calling someone you trust.
Leaving the room.
Refusing to answer the message.
Choosing not to look again.
No dramatic music.
No visible miracle.
No applause.
Just a believer, strengthened by grace, choosing obedience when disobedience is available.
And heaven's approval is not measured by how spectacular that moment appears to other people.
Your secret obedience matters.
Not because God loves you more when you succeed.
But because the God who loves you is worthy of your obedience.
Galatians 5:16 says:
"Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh." (KJV)
The instruction is not merely to stare at sin until you become strong enough to defeat it.
It is to walk in the Spirit.
To cultivate a life increasingly shaped by God's Word, prayer, fellowship, worship, confession, and obedience.
To stop feeding the flesh while starving the soul.
To recognize that lasting Christian transformation is not accomplished through shame alone.
It is the work of God's grace as we actively respond in faith.
And here is the question I want you to carry beyond this article:
When lust comes knocking, what is it asking you to give up in exchange for what it promises?
Your integrity?
Your peace?
Your marriage?
Your honesty?
Your ability to see another person with dignity?
Your willingness to trust God?
Your spiritual sensitivity?
Your freedom?
Because lust often advertises what it can give you while concealing what surrendering to it may cost.
It offers a moment.
Then asks for another.
And another.
And another.
Until the thing you once called a choice begins to feel like a chain.
But Jesus offers something radically different.
He does not promise that every desire will vanish the moment you pray.
He does not promise that the Christian life will be free from temptation.
He promises Himself.
His grace.
His truth.
His Spirit.
His presence.
And eternal life through faith in Him.
The One who said "I thirst" while hanging on the cross (John 19:28) is the same Savior who invites the thirsty to come to Him (John 7:37).
Those passages have distinct contexts, but together they draw our attention to the suffering Savior and His gracious invitation.
Jesus knows what it is to suffer.
He knows what it is to be tempted.
He knows what it is to be rejected.
And unlike every false savior you have ever chased, He does not exploit your need.
He gives Himself for sinners.
So perhaps tonight your most important prayer is not simply, "God, take away this feeling."
Perhaps it is:

"Lord, show me what I've been seeking apart from You. Expose what is sinful. Heal what is wounded. Correct what is false. Teach me to desire what is good. And give me the courage to obey You even when my feelings resist."
That is a prayer worth praying.
Not because it guarantees an instant transformation.
But because it expresses a heart turning toward the only Savior who can truly redeem it.
And if you are struggling right now, please don't turn this article into another weapon against yourself.
Let it become an invitation to honesty.
You do not need to announce the details of your private struggle to strangers online.
You do not need to expose another person's sins.
You do not need to manufacture a dramatic testimony.
But you can acknowledge that you need Christ.
You can ask for prayer.
You can reach out to someone trustworthy.
You can take the next faithful step.
Or, if you're still in the middle of the battle, simply write:
Not as a performance.
Not as proof of salvation.
But as a small, honest acknowledgment that you don't want to keep fighting alone.
Someone reading silently may need to know that repentance is possible, that growth can happen, and that the grace of Jesus Christ is not an empty religious slogan.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who looks completely fine.
They post family photos.
They laugh at jokes.
They share inspirational quotes.
They attend church.
And yet, when everyone goes to sleep, they're fighting a battle nobody sees.
And if someone specific comes to mind, consider tagging them with care, or sending the article privately if that would better honor their dignity.
Don't use the message to embarrass someone.
Not because these words have power in themselves, but because the Scriptures we've considered deserve to be revisited when temptation feels louder than truth.
Return to Matthew 5.
Read John 4.
Meditate on Luke 15.
Pray through Romans 8.
Remember 1 John 1:9.
And keep coming back to Christ.
It's about following the real Jesus.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who feel spiritually exhausted, those who have drifted from the faith, and even those who are still searching for truth.
Because the Gospel is not merely for people who already know how to sound religious.
It is good news for sinners who need a Savior.
It does not purchase forgiveness, spiritual favor, salvation, or a blessing.
But Scripture does encourage believers to support faithful Gospel ministry voluntarily, generously, and with discernment.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
It can help us reach people who may be silently wrestling with the very struggles discussed here.
There is no pressure to give what you cannot afford.
Those free resources reflect an important conviction behind this ministry:
The Word of God should never be treated as merchandise that only paying supporters deserve to encounter.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Our mission is to keep pointing people to it.
Send it to a struggling believer.
Pray for the people who will read it.
Because sometimes a message about a hidden struggle reaches someone at the very moment they're considering surrendering to it again.
And sometimes the reminder that Jesus still receives repentant sinners becomes the beginning of a very different decision.
Does lust always want something?
Yes.
Lust reaches for something it believes will satisfy.
Sometimes that desire is intensified by loneliness, fear, insecurity, pain, or exhaustion.
Sometimes it is driven by an appetite that has been repeatedly indulged.
Sometimes several of those things are happening at once.
But whatever the circumstances, sinful lust must be confronted with truth, repentance, and the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest answer to our sin is not simply finding a more effective distraction.
It is being reconciled to God through His Son and learning to live as someone who belongs to Him.
Maybe you've spent years trying to prove that you're strong enough.
Strong enough not to look.
Strong enough not to fantasize.
Strong enough not to fall.
Strong enough to keep your secrets hidden.
But salvation has never depended on proving that you are strong enough to save yourself.
It depends on Jesus Christ, who is mighty to save.
You may still have difficult days ahead.
You may need to rebuild trust.
You may need to make painful changes.
You may need help.
You will need to keep choosing repentance and faith.
But your story does not have to remain trapped in the chapter where your sin became visible.
Peter denied Jesus.
And the risen Christ restored him.
The Samaritan woman had a complicated relational history.
And Jesus revealed Himself to her.
The prodigal son wasted what he had been given.
And his father welcomed him home when he returned.
These are not identical stories.
But each reminds us that failure does not place repentant sinners beyond the reach of God's mercy.
And at the center of our hope stands something greater than every testimony.
The cross.
The empty tomb.
The living Christ.
So tonight, if the old hunger returns, remember that you are not required to obey every desire that demands your attention.
You can stop.
You can pray.
You can seek help.
You can flee temptation.
You can choose the light.
And if you have fallen, you can repent and come to Christ without pretending your sin was harmless or believing His mercy is exhausted.
Because the most beautiful transformation isn't merely when someone stops pursuing what was destroying them.
It's when they begin loving the Savior who gave Himself to redeem them.
The desire that once led you into hiding does not have to write the final sentence of your story. Jesus Christ is still calling sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CHRISTIAN WOMEN WATCH PORN TOO. SO WHY DOES THE CHURCH KEEP ACTING LIKE ONLY MEN NEED DELIVERANCE?
paragraphs: CHRISTIAN WOMEN WATCH PORN TOO. SO WHY DOES THE CHURCH KEEP ACTING LIKE ONLY MEN NEED DELIVERANCE?

Behind some of the most faithful-looking women in church are secret battles with pornography, sexual temptation, and shame that nobody ever taught them how to confess. And the silence may be hurting them more than we realize.
She loves Jesus.
That is the part of her story nobody seems to understand.
She isn't mocking Christianity. She isn't secretly planning to abandon her faith. She isn't sitting in church waiting for an opportunity to rebel against God.
She genuinely loves Jesus.
She prays. She worships. She listens to sermons. Sometimes she even encourages other women to remain strong in their faith.
But there is another part of her life that almost nobody knows exists.
It happens when the house becomes quiet.
When everyone else is asleep.
When loneliness begins to feel heavier than usual.
When her phone is within reach and the temptation she promised herself she would never entertain again starts whispering.
Just this once.
You've had a difficult day.
Nobody will know.
And sometimes, she gives in.
Then comes the silence.
The screen goes dark.
The temporary excitement disappears.
And she is left staring at her reflection, wondering how someone who loves God could keep returning to something she believes dishonors Him.
She whispers another apology.
"Lord, I'm sorry."
Maybe she cries.
Maybe she doesn't anymore.
Maybe that frightens her even more.
Because she remembers when this sin used to break her heart, and now she is terrified that her heart might be getting used to it.
Sunday comes.
She gets dressed.
She opens her Bible.
She walks into church.
And when the pastor begins speaking about pornography, he says something like:
"Men, you need to guard your eyes."
The men shift uncomfortably.
Some look down.
Others laugh nervously.
But she remains completely still.
Because once again, the conversation has passed right over her.
Nobody imagines that the woman quietly holding her Bible might be fighting the very same battle.
Nobody thinks to ask.
And she has become very good at not telling.
But what if the most dangerous part of her struggle is not simply what she has been watching, but the lie that she is the only Christian woman struggling with it?

What if the silence surrounding female sexual temptation has convinced countless women that their struggle is too disgusting to confess, too embarrassing to discuss, and too shameful to bring into the light?
And what if the Church has unintentionally made that silence deeper by speaking as though sexual temptation belongs almost exclusively to men?
We need to talk about this.
Not to normalize pornography.
Not to excuse sin.
Not to embarrass women.
But because Jesus Christ did not shed His blood so that His daughters would spend their lives pretending they have no wounds.
And Scripture has already given us a warning that should make every believer, male or female, pay attention.
"Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall." — 1 Corinthians 10:12, KJV
Read that again.
The warning is not directed only toward men.
It is directed toward anyone who believes they are beyond falling.
The apostle Paul continues:

"There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it." — 1 Corinthians 10:13, KJV
There is something profoundly important in the original Greek.
Paul uses the word πειρασμός (peirasmos), commonly translated as "temptation" or "testing," depending on context.
It does not describe a temptation reserved for one gender.
And when Paul writes ἀνθρώπινος (anthrōpinos), translated in the KJV as "common to man," the meaning concerns what is human or belongs to ordinary human experience.
Paul is not telling women that their temptations are masculine.
He is telling believers that temptation is part of the human condition.
And in the surrounding passage, Paul has been warning the Corinthian Christians through the example of Israel's failures, including idolatry, sexual immorality, and presumption.
The message is sobering.
Do not become so confident in your own spirituality that you stop guarding your heart.
And do not become so ashamed of your temptation that you forget God's faithfulness.
Because the same verse that warns against falling also declares something extraordinary.
πιστὸς δὲ ὁ θεός (pistos de ho Theos).
"But God is faithful."
Not "but you are strong enough on your own."
Not "but your reputation will protect you."
Not "but you will never struggle again if you pray hard enough."
But God is faithful.
That is where hope begins.
Not with the perfection of the tempted believer.
With the faithfulness of the Savior.
And perhaps someone reading this desperately needs to hear that distinction tonight.
Because you have spent months, maybe years, measuring God's willingness to receive you by how successfully you have resisted temptation.
When you resist, you feel worthy of prayer.
When you fall, you hide from the very One whose mercy you need.
But the Gospel does not teach us to earn the right to approach Jesus by achieving a flawless record.
It calls sinners to repent, trust Christ, and come to Him for mercy and transforming grace.
That does not make pornography harmless.
It makes the Savior indispensable.
And we must understand why this battle is not as simple as the stereotypes we have inherited.
For years, pornography has often been discussed in Christian settings as though it were primarily a male problem.
Men are warned about lust.
Men are told to install accountability software.
Men are urged to protect their marriages.
Men are encouraged to find brothers who will confront them when they stumble.
Those conversations are necessary.
But somewhere along the way, too many women were left without an equally honest conversation.
What happens when a Christian woman struggles with sexual imagery?
What happens when a young woman encounters pornography before she has even developed a mature understanding of intimacy?
What happens when a married woman feels emotionally disconnected, spiritually exhausted, or sexually dissatisfied and begins looking for an escape she knows cannot truly satisfy her?
What happens when an unmarried woman wrestles with loneliness, curiosity, desire, and the longing to be wanted?
What happens when someone who experienced unwanted sexual exposure or abuse finds that her relationship with sexuality has become confusing and painful?
These situations are not identical.
And none of them automatically explains every woman's struggle.
But they remind us of something important.
Women are human beings, not spiritual decorations expected to remain untouched by temptation.
Some women encounter pornography through curiosity.
Some through repeated exposure.
Some use it as an escape from stress, loneliness, or difficult emotions.
Some experience compulsive patterns that they find increasingly difficult to interrupt.
And some carry deep shame because they have never heard another Christian woman acknowledge the possibility of this struggle.
None of these realities means every woman who watches pornography is addicted.
Nor does it mean every struggle has the same cause.
It means discipleship must be honest enough to address the actual person in front of us.
Because a church that speaks about sexual purity without making room for truthful confession may unintentionally teach struggling people how to conceal their sin rather than how to seek help.
And concealment can become its own prison.
Think about the woman who has promised God a hundred times that she will never watch pornography again.
She deletes the browser history.
She blocks a website.
She makes it through several days.
Perhaps several weeks.
Then something happens.
An argument.
A rejection.
A lonely evening.
A moment of exhaustion.
An image she didn't expect.
And the old pattern begins again.
She feels the pull.
She knows where it leads.
Part of her wants to turn away.
Another part wants relief.
And after she falls, she doesn't merely think, "I did something wrong."
She begins thinking, "There must be something wrong with me."
That is a devastating difference.
Conviction says, "This is sin. Turn back to God."
Destructive shame says, "You are disgusting. Stay away from everyone."
Conviction directs us toward repentance.
Shame, when it becomes an identity, can drive us deeper into secrecy.
And the enemy of our souls does not need to persuade a believer that sin is good if he can persuade her that returning to Jesus is pointless.
But listen carefully.
You are responsible for your choices, but your worst choice is not the final authority over your identity.
For those who belong to Christ, the final authority belongs to the One who purchased them with His blood.
Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus."
That is not permission to continue deliberately in sin.
Paul has already rejected that distortion of grace in Romans 6:1–2.
It is the glorious announcement that those united to Jesus Christ are no longer under God's condemning judgment.
And that same grace calls us into a new way of living.
Grace does not whisper, "Stay exactly where you are."
Grace says, "Come out of hiding. Christ has not finished His work in you."
Perhaps one of the most moving examples of how Jesus confronts sexual sin is found in John 4.
A woman comes to a well.
At first, the conversation appears ordinary.
Water.
Thirst.
A stranger asking for a drink.
But Jesus knows the deeper story.
He knows her marital history.
He knows the man she is living with is not her husband.
And He brings the truth into the conversation.
Yet notice what He does not do.
He does not pretend her situation is irrelevant.
He does not humiliate her for the entertainment of the crowd.
He does not treat her as a worthless person.
He speaks truth.
And He offers living water.

We should be careful not to invent details Scripture does not give us. John does not say that this woman was a prostitute, nor does it explicitly explain why she came to the well at that particular hour.
Her story is powerful enough without adding accusations to it.
What Scripture actually shows is astonishing.
A woman whose personal life Jesus knows becomes someone who speaks to others about Him.
She says:
"Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" — John 4:29, KJV
Think about that.
The very area of her life that could have made her retreat in embarrassment becomes part of her testimony about the One who knows her.
Jesus does not redeem people by pretending their histories never happened.
He redeems them by bringing truth, mercy, and new life into places they thought could never change.
And this is where the Gospel becomes deeply personal for the Christian woman secretly struggling with pornography.
Jesus already knows.
He knows what you watched.
He knows the thoughts you entertained.
He knows the moments when you resisted.
He knows the moments when you surrendered to temptation.
He knows whether you have been minimizing sin.
He also knows the loneliness you have not explained, the grief you have not processed, and the questions you have been afraid to ask.
Nothing about your life surprises Him.
But His perfect knowledge is not an invitation to become comfortable with sin.
It is an invitation to stop pretending.
You cannot deceive the One who sees everything.
And you do not need to.
The Gospel offers something infinitely better than managing appearances.
It offers forgiveness through Christ and the transforming work of His Spirit.
This is why 1 John 1:9 is so precious:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
The Greek verb ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), translated "we confess," carries the sense of acknowledging or admitting.
Confession is not an elaborate performance designed to impress God with how terrible we feel.
It is honest agreement with the truth about our sin before Him.
No disguises.
No bargaining.
No religious vocabulary intended to make disobedience sound less serious.
Just honesty.
"Lord, I sinned."
"I have been hiding."
"I have tried to manage this alone."
"I need Your forgiveness."
"I need Your help to walk differently."
And the promise of 1 John is not that God forgives because our emotional breakdown was sufficiently dramatic.
He forgives on the righteous foundation of Christ's saving work.
That is why forgiveness is not cheap.
It was purchased at Calvary.
But there is another part of this conversation that cannot be ignored.
Repentance is more than feeling terrible after watching pornography.
A person can feel intense remorse and still refuse to change the conditions that repeatedly lead to temptation.
Biblical repentance involves turning toward God in a way that bears fruit.
That may mean removing access to material that repeatedly draws you into sin.
It may mean changing nighttime routines.
It may mean refusing to carry your phone into the bedroom when you know that isolation and unrestricted access have become a dangerous combination.
It may mean recognizing emotional patterns that often precede a relapse.
It may mean admitting that what you have called "just stress relief" has become a destructive habit.
And for some, it may mean seeking help from a qualified mental health professional, particularly when the behavior feels compulsive or is connected to trauma, anxiety, or other significant distress.
Seeking appropriate professional care does not require abandoning prayer or Scripture.
It can be one responsible part of pursuing healing and wise stewardship of your life.
But there is something else.
You may need another trustworthy person to know.
Not the entire congregation.
Not strangers on the internet.
Not someone who will turn your confession into gossip.
Someone mature.
Someone discreet.
Someone grounded in Scripture.
Perhaps a trusted Christian woman, a wise mentor, or a qualified counselor.
James 5:16 calls believers to confess their faults to one another and pray for one another.
That does not mean every intimate struggle must be announced publicly.
It means Christian life was never intended to be a performance of self-sufficiency.
There is a kind of isolation that makes temptation more powerful.
And there is a kind of loving accountability that helps expose the lies secrecy has protected.
Imagine what could change if a young Christian woman approached an older believer and whispered:
"I'm struggling with pornography, and I don't know how to stop."
And instead of shock, disgust, or gossip, she heard:
"Thank you for trusting me. This is serious, but you are not beyond God's mercy. We can pray, speak honestly, and find the support you need."
Imagine if that conversation became normal enough that women no longer had to choose between appearing spiritually respectable and receiving meaningful discipleship.
Imagine if churches taught sexual holiness with equal seriousness and compassion toward men and women.
Imagine if pastors spoke about temptation without assuming they knew which faces in the congregation were struggling.
Imagine if Christian mothers could talk to their daughters about pornography without treating female sexual curiosity as an unimaginable disgrace.
Imagine if married couples could have difficult conversations about sexual temptation without immediately surrendering to contempt, blame, or denial.
Imagine if single women were discipled as whole human beings, with minds, bodies, desires, vulnerabilities, and a genuine calling to holiness.
This would not weaken the Church's commitment to purity.
It would strengthen it.
Because truth becomes more powerful, not less, when it reaches the people who have been overlooked.
And perhaps we should also be honest about the way Christians sometimes discuss sexual sin.
We can be extraordinarily harsh toward the person whose temptation looks different from ours.
A woman struggling with pornography may condemn someone else's sexual failure while privately battling her own.
A man may assume women are immune to the images that have enslaved his attention.
A married believer may look down on a single person's struggles while neglecting serious problems within their own marriage.
A church leader may preach loudly about visible sins while ignoring pride, dishonesty, cruelty, or secret compromise.
But the cross leaves no room for spiritual superiority.
Every one of us needs grace.
Every one of us needs repentance.
Every one of us needs the righteousness of Christ.
And every one of us must take seriously the warning:
"Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall."
The moment we start treating another person's temptation as proof of our own superiority, we have already misunderstood the humility the Gospel requires.
Now, some readers may be wondering whether Scripture actually condemns pornography when the Bible does not use that modern term.
That is a fair question.
We should not pretend the biblical writers were describing smartphones, streaming platforms, or the modern pornography industry.
They were not.
But Scripture does address the moral realities involved.
Jesus teaches in Matthew 5:27–28 that lustful looking can violate God's intention for sexual faithfulness at the level of the heart.
Paul commands believers in 1 Corinthians 6:18 to flee sexual immorality.
And in 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5, he connects sanctification with abstaining from sexual immorality and learning to live in holiness and honor rather than lustful passion.
These passages require careful application rather than careless proof-texting.
They also make it difficult to defend deliberately seeking sexually explicit material for the purpose of cultivating lust.
Pornography can train us to look at people as instruments of gratification rather than persons made in the image of God.
It may also involve serious concerns about exploitation, coercion, and the dignity of those depicted.
Not every circumstance surrounding pornography is identical, but the Christian calling to sexual holiness, self-control, and love for our neighbors remains relevant.
And that calling applies to women as surely as it applies to men.
Yet we must make another distinction.
Temptation itself is not the same as consenting to sin.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that Jesus was tempted, yet without sin.
A Christian woman who experiences an unwanted sexual thought has not automatically committed the same moral act as someone who deliberately cultivates lust.
A person who accidentally encounters explicit material is not in the same situation as someone who intentionally seeks it out.
And a survivor experiencing intrusive memories or unwanted sexual responses should not be carelessly accused of choosing those experiences.
These distinctions matter.
Because vague condemnation can wound consciences without producing holiness.
The goal is not to make women terrified of having bodies, emotions, or desires.
The goal is to bring those realities under the loving lordship of Jesus Christ.
God did not create women as disembodied spiritual beings.
He created them as human beings.
Sexual desire is not inherently shameful.
But like every human desire, it must be ordered according to God's wisdom.
And that is why the answer to pornography is not learning to hate your body.
It is learning to honor God with your body.
It is not becoming frightened of intimacy.
It is learning to distinguish genuine intimacy from an imitation that can leave the soul feeling increasingly empty.
It is not pretending temptation will never return.
It is learning, through the grace of God, how to respond when it does.
Remember Paul's words:
"But God is faithful."
Then remember the rest.
God provides a way to endure temptation without surrendering to it.
That does not mean every struggle will disappear instantly.
It does not guarantee that the path of obedience will feel easy.
It does not mean a believer will never need accountability, counseling, practical boundaries, or patient support.
It means temptation does not have the authority to overrule God's faithfulness.
And the believer is called to look for the path of obedience rather than surrendering to the lie of inevitability.
Sometimes that path begins with something as ordinary as putting the phone down.
Sometimes it begins with getting out of bed and praying.
Sometimes it begins with calling someone instead of remaining isolated.
Sometimes it begins with grieving honestly rather than numbing the pain.
Sometimes it begins with the courage to say:
"I cannot keep pretending this isn't happening."
And if you have fallen again, do not turn that fall into permission to remain there.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive the mercy Christ promises to those who come to Him.
And take the next faithful step.
Do not confuse the repetition of a struggle with proof that repentance is meaningless.
But do not confuse repeated apologies with a willingness to change, either.
Both grace and truth matter.
Both forgiveness and transformation matter.
And Jesus Christ offers more than the temporary relief of feeling less guilty.
He calls us into a new life.
There is a beautiful phrase in 2 Corinthians 5:17:
καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis).
"A new creation."
Paul writes:
The Greek expression concerns a new creation, not merely a polished version of the old self.
This is not a promise that every harmful habit disappears the moment someone believes.
It is a declaration that union with Christ changes the fundamental reality of a believer's life.
The old life no longer has the final word.
Sin no longer has the rightful claim of a master.
And the future is no longer confined to the pattern of the past.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message is not simply a slogan.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal was harmless.
Not because He erases responsibility.
Not because He tells us that holiness no longer matters.
But because His death and resurrection make forgiveness, reconciliation, and genuine transformation possible.
And perhaps the woman in our opening story is reading this right now.
Perhaps she is holding her phone with tears in her eyes.
Perhaps she is remembering the last time she promised God she would stop.
Perhaps she has become convinced that her private struggle makes every prayer she has ever prayed a lie.
Perhaps she has started avoiding communion, Scripture, or Christian fellowship because she cannot bear the thought of being seen.
If that is you, please hear this.
You do not have to pretend that your sin is small.
But you do not have to pretend that Christ's mercy is small, either.
You do not have to publish your private history to prove you are repentant.
But you do need to stop treating secrecy as your only protection.
You do not have to call yourself disgusting to demonstrate that you take holiness seriously.
But you do need to call sin what it is.
And you do not have to earn your way back to Jesus through weeks of flawless behavior.
You are called to turn to Him in repentance and faith.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners is not shocked by the truth you have been afraid to tell.
He is holy enough to confront it.
And merciful enough to forgive.
Maybe tonight the prayer is not complicated.
Maybe it sounds like this:

"Jesus, I have been hiding something that You already know. I have made promises I could not keep in my own strength. I have looked for comfort in places that cannot give me life. Please forgive me. Teach me to hate what destroys me without hating the person You created. Give me courage to seek help. Give me wisdom to flee temptation. Change my desires. Renew my mind. Help me walk in the light. I cannot save myself. I need You. Amen."
And to the pastors, teachers, parents, husbands, mentors, and ministry leaders reading this:
Please do not miss the other half of the message.
When you speak about pornography, remember that women may be listening with hidden wounds.
When someone confesses, do not mistake humiliation for holiness.
When someone struggles, do not reduce her entire identity to that struggle.
When someone needs professional help, do not shame her for seeking it.
When someone repents, do not make permanent suspicion the price of her honesty.
And when you preach the Gospel, preach the whole Gospel.
The seriousness of sin.
The necessity of repentance.
The sufficiency of Christ.
The power of grace.
The call to holiness.
The hope of restoration.
Because the Church should never become a place where people feel safer pretending to be healed than admitting they need the Great Physician.
I want to ask you something, and I hope you will answer from the heart.
How many Christian women have sat through sermons about purity, silently begging God for help, while everyone around them assumed the message was meant for somebody else?
How many have mistaken their secrecy for uniqueness?
How many have thought, "If they knew, they would never look at me the same way again"?
And how many might finally find the courage to seek help if we stopped speaking as though female sexual temptation were an impossible contradiction?
We may never know every hidden story.
But we can change how we respond to the stories entrusted to us.
If this article has exposed a struggle you have been carrying, you do not need to reveal intimate details in a public comment.
Not as a claim that your journey is already complete.
As a confession that your hope is still in Jesus.
And if you have seen God's grace bring you through a season of secret struggle, consider sharing a testimony that protects your privacy while pointing others toward Christ.
Someone may read your words and realize that asking for help is not the end of her Christian life.
It may be the beginning of a more honest walk with God.
Not because every friend needs to know your personal struggles.
But because there may be a woman among your friends who would never search for this conversation herself.
A daughter.
A sister.
A wife.
A single mother.
A young believer.
A church volunteer.
Someone who loves Jesus but is exhausted from pretending.
Not because these paragraphs can deliver you.
They cannot.
Only Christ saves.
But save it for the day when shame tries to convince you that God's Word has nothing left to say to your situation.
Return to 1 Corinthians 10:12–13.
Return to 1 John 1:9.
Return to Romans 8:1.
Return to the cross.
And remember that the God who calls you to holiness is also the God who supplies grace to His people.
We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, repentance is never treated casually, and grace is never reduced to a religious catchphrase.
Where believers are encouraged to grow deeper.
Where difficult questions can be faced honestly.
Where wounded people are pointed toward Christ rather than toward the illusion of perfect Christians.
And if this ministry has strengthened your faith, challenged your compromises, or helped you return to God's Word, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Not because giving money proves that you love Jesus more than someone who cannot afford to give.
And certainly not because a monthly payment can replace the faithful stewardship, generosity, and giving you practice in your local church.
Biblical giving must remain voluntary and sincere.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us, God loves a cheerful giver, not one pressured into giving.
You are not buying grace.
You are helping make Gospel-centered resources available to others.
And there is another blessing we want you to know about.
We want people to keep learning, praying, examining Scripture, and growing in the faith even after they finish reading an article.
Those items are not the heart of this ministry.
Jesus is.
But they can serve as reminders, conversation starters, and ways to support the ongoing work.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And the people who need to hear it should never be made to feel that God's love is available only to those who can pay.
Because somewhere tonight, a woman may be holding a Bible in one hand and hiding a struggle she has never dared to speak about.
Somewhere, a young believer may be wondering whether she has already ruined her relationship with God.
Somewhere, a married woman may be carrying guilt she cannot explain to her husband.
Somewhere, a church volunteer may be singing worship songs while secretly wondering whether Jesus has grown tired of forgiving her.
Perhaps that will become the moment she stops believing that secrecy is her only option.
Perhaps she will open her Bible again.
Perhaps she will contact someone trustworthy.
Perhaps she will begin taking repentance seriously in a way she has avoided for years.
Perhaps she will remember that Christ came to save sinners.
And perhaps the next time she hears someone speak about pornography as though only men struggle, she will have the courage to say, with humility and wisdom:
"Women need this conversation too."
Because we do.
Our daughters need it.
Our sisters need it.
Our wives need it.
Our single women need it.
Our churches need it.
Not so we can make peace with sin.
But so we can stop making peace with silence.
And above all, so that women who have been hiding in shame can hear the call of Jesus Christ to repent, believe, and walk in the light.
The woman at the well did not have to pretend that Jesus knew nothing about her past.
She discovered that being fully known by Him did not make His invitation to living water disappear.
And the woman struggling with pornography today does not need a Savior who is ignorant of her secret.
She needs the Savior who knows the truth and is mighty to save.
So, dear sister, do not build a home in the darkness simply because you are embarrassed to step into the light.
Do not let your struggle become the name by which you define your entire existence.
Do not mistake the voice of condemnation for the voice of the Shepherd.
Take sin seriously.
Take repentance seriously.
Take accountability seriously.
But take the finished work of Jesus Christ seriously, too.
Because the cross was not erected for people who could prove they had never fallen.
It was where the sinless Savior gave Himself for sinners.
And the empty tomb declares that death and sin do not have the final victory over those who belong to Him.
You may have spent years hiding the pages of your story, but Jesus is still able to write a future that your shame never imagined.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: MANY WILL SAY, “LORD, LORD”… BUT JESUS WILL SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU.”
paragraphs: MANY WILL SAY, “LORD, LORD”… BUT JESUS WILL SAY, “I NEVER KNEW YOU.”

The Most Terrifying Words in the Sermon on the Mount—And the Heartbreaking Truth About Religious People Who Look Saved, Sound Saved, and Even Do Things in Jesus’ Name, Yet Miss the One Person Who Can Save Them.
Imagine spending your entire life believing you were on your way to heaven…
Only to discover, when you finally stand before Jesus Christ, that you never truly belonged to Him.
Not because you had never heard His name.
Not because you had never opened a Bible.
Not because you were an atheist, an unbeliever, or someone who openly mocked God.
But because you had learned how to live around Jesus without ever surrendering your life to Jesus.
You knew the songs.
You knew when to say “Amen.”
You knew how to raise your hands during worship, how to quote Scripture when someone needed encouragement, how to speak about faith when life was going well.
Perhaps you even served in ministry.
Perhaps people looked up to you.
Perhaps someone once told you, “You are such a strong Christian.”
And you believed them.
But there was something happening beneath the surface that nobody could see.
A private compromise.
A cherished sin.
A heart growing comfortable with disobedience.
A religious identity that had slowly become a substitute for genuine fellowship with God.
And then comes the day when appearances no longer matter.
The crowd is gone.
The applause is silent.
The religious titles have lost their meaning.
There is only you…
And Jesus.
Then you hear the words you never imagined could be spoken to someone like you.
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.”
Matthew 7:23, KJV.
Read that again.
Not “I knew you once, but I forgot you.”
Not “You were too weak for Me.”
Not “You struggled too much.”
“I never knew you.”
Those words should disturb every person who has ever mistaken being familiar with Christianity for actually belonging to Christ.
But before fear drives you into despair, you need to understand something.
Jesus did not speak these words to destroy the hope of every struggling believer.
He spoke them to expose a deadly deception.
And buried inside this frightening warning is a truth so beautiful that it can change the way you understand salvation, repentance, obedience, and the grace of God.
Because the question is not simply whether you know enough about Jesus.
The question is whether you have truly come to Him.
And there is a difference.
A difference that eternity makes impossible to ignore.
In Matthew 7:21–23, Jesus declares:
“Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.
Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?
And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.”
Matthew 7:21–23, KJV.
Notice something that makes this passage especially unsettling.
Jesus does not say a few will be surprised.
He says many.
And these people are not presented as strangers to religious activity.
They call Him “Lord.”
Twice.
They appeal to prophecy, deliverance, and mighty works performed in His name.
Their defense is not that they rejected Christianity.
Their defense is that they were deeply involved in things associated with Christianity.
Yet Jesus rejects their claim.
Why?
To understand that, we must listen carefully to what He actually said—not merely what generations of frightened Christians have assumed He meant.
In the original Greek of Matthew 7:21, the words translated “Lord, Lord” are:
Κύριε κύριε — Kyrie, kyrie.
Kyrie is the form of kyrios used when addressing someone as “Lord” or “Master.”
The repeated address communicates an urgent, emphatic appeal.
These people are not approaching Jesus casually.
They recognize Him as the One before whom they must answer.
But acknowledging His authority with their lips does not establish that they have lived under His authority.
That is the first uncomfortable truth.
A person can speak the language of surrender while continuing to live in rebellion.
You can call Jesus Lord on Sunday and spend the rest of the week acting as though He has no authority over your choices.
You can worship publicly while secretly protecting the very things His Word calls you to abandon.
You can defend biblical truth in arguments while refusing to let that same truth confront your own pride.
You can become skilled at recognizing sin in other people while remaining remarkably patient with your own.
And perhaps the most dangerous part?
You can become so accustomed to this divided life that eventually it stops bothering you.
What once convicted you becomes normal.
What once drove you to prayer becomes something you explain away.
What once made you weep before God becomes something you hide behind a smile.
And little by little, you learn to look spiritually alive while your heart drifts further from the One who gives life.
But Jesus sees what the crowd cannot.
He sees the private conversations.
The unspoken motives.
The bitterness you have dressed up as discernment.
The unforgiveness you have justified because somebody really did hurt you.
The secret compromises you keep promising to abandon tomorrow.
He also sees the wounds you never asked for, the battles you are exhausted from fighting, and the tears you have shed while begging Him to help you change.
That distinction matters.
Because there is a difference between someone who struggles against sin and someone who makes peace with it.
There is a difference between falling and refusing to repent.
There is a difference between being wounded and deliberately cultivating wickedness.
And Jesus knows the difference perfectly.
When He says, “I never knew you,” the original Greek reads:
οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς — oudepote egnōn hymas.
Literally, “I never knew you.”
The verb egnōn comes from ginōskō, meaning “to know.”
In Scripture, knowing someone can mean more than possessing information about them. Depending on the context, it can describe personal recognition and relationship.
Jesus is not confessing ignorance.
He is not saying that He lacked information about these people.
The One who knows what is in humanity, as John 2:24–25 teaches, is not suddenly discovering unfamiliar faces.
His declaration is a rejection of their claim to belong to Him.
They may have claimed His name.
But He does not acknowledge them as His own.
And here is what should make us examine our hearts:
Their confidence was built on what they had done in His name—not on the saving mercy of the Christ they claimed to serve.
Listen to their defense.
“Have we not prophesied?”
“Have we not cast out devils?”
“Have we not done many wonderful works?”
Again and again, the emphasis falls on their accomplishments.
Their spiritual résumé.
Their visible achievements.
Their impressive religious history.
They are standing before the Savior, and their defense is a list of their works.
But no amount of religious achievement can substitute for reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Salvation is not a trophy awarded to the most religious person in the room.
It is a gift of grace received through faith in Jesus Christ.
Not church attendance.
Not a ministry title.
Not an impressive testimony.
Not the number of people who admire your spirituality.
Not even extraordinary works performed under a religious banner.
And certainly not the amount of money you have given.
Christ alone saves.
But then someone asks the question that makes this passage difficult.
“If salvation is by grace through faith, why does Jesus say that the one who enters the kingdom is the one who does the will of His Father?”
That question deserves a biblical answer, not a comforting slogan.
Because Jesus never taught that grace gives us permission to remain comfortably enslaved to sin.
He also never taught that imperfect human obedience purchases eternal life.
The same passage in Ephesians that declares salvation to be a gift continues:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.”
Ephesians 2:10, KJV.
Do you see the order?
We are not saved by good works.
We are saved for good works.
Obedience does not purchase salvation.
Genuine saving faith produces a changed direction of life.
Not sinless perfection.
Not a flawless spiritual record.
But repentance, growing trust, and a heart increasingly willing to submit to Jesus.
The grace that forgives us is also the grace that begins transforming us.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God instructs believers to reject ungodliness and live in a way that honors Him.
Grace is not God's permission slip for rebellion.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy bringing sinners into a new life.
And this is where Matthew 7 becomes deeply personal.
Because many of us have spent years asking God to bless the life we have built without ever seriously asking whether that life belongs to Him.
We ask Him to protect our plans.
To increase our income.
To restore our relationships.
To open doors.
To silence our enemies.
To make our ministries successful.
But when His Word confronts something we do not want to surrender…
Suddenly, we become very quiet.
We want His comfort.
But sometimes resist His correction.
We want His promises.
But hesitate before His commands.
We want Him to heal the consequences of our choices while remaining unwilling to turn from the choices themselves.
And still, Jesus calls.
Not because He enjoys exposing our hypocrisy.
But because He loves truth too much to leave us trusting a counterfeit.
In Matthew 7:23, Jesus describes those He rejects as people who “work iniquity.”
The Greek expression is:
οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν — hoi ergazomenoi tēn anomian.
The word anomia refers to lawlessness or disregard for God's law.
The participle ergazomenoi describes those engaged in or practicing such conduct.
This is not a declaration that every believer who commits a sin is immediately condemned.
If that were the meaning, no human being could stand.
First John 1:8 plainly says:
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
But the very next verse gives hope:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
First John 1:9, KJV.
The distinction is not between people who have ever sinned and people who have never sinned.
All have sinned.
The distinction is between trusting Christ with a repentant heart and hiding behind religious claims while refusing His authority.
That is why this warning is not an invitation to obsess over whether you have achieved enough spiritual perfection.
It is an invitation to stop pretending.
To come into the light.
To stop treating repentance as something you will eventually get around to.
To stop confusing religious activity with spiritual life.
And to come to Jesus Himself.
Perhaps you are reading this with a heavy heart because you know there are things you have been hiding.
Maybe nobody knows about the addiction you keep returning to.
Maybe your marriage looks beautiful in photographs, but inside your home there are wounds you refuse to address.
Maybe you have learned how to encourage everyone else while privately growing cold toward God.
Maybe you have preached forgiveness while carrying resentment for years.
Maybe you have been living a double life, terrified that if people discovered the truth, everything you built would collapse.
Or maybe your struggle is different.
You genuinely love Jesus.
You hate the sin you keep fighting.
You repent, you pray, you stumble, you rise, and sometimes you wonder whether your repeated weakness means He has finally rejected you.
