Every article, biblical resource, teaching, and discipleship effort requires time, labor, and practical support.
It does not purchase forgiveness, increase your standing before Christ, or make you more faithful than someone who cannot afford to give.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ, never something bought through financial support.
But voluntary support for sound Gospel ministry can be a meaningful act of generosity and partnership.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should come from the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Philippians 4:15–17 also shows the beauty of believers supporting Gospel work through generous partnership.
It can help us reach more readers, develop more discipleship resources, and keep publishing messages centered on biblical truth, repentance, grace, and transformation through Jesus Christ.
Keep praying.
Keep pursuing the truth.
Keep bringing your struggles to Jesus.
Keep encouraging others to follow Him.
Because the purpose of Gospel Warrior is not merely to build an audience.
It is to point people toward the Savior.
The One who sees what has been hidden.
The One who confronts what has been excused.
The One who comforts those who have been betrayed.
The One who calls the unfaithful to repentance.
The One who forgives sinners through His cross.
The One who rose again and gives new life.
And now, before you leave, return with me to that heartbreaking sentence in Proverbs.
She abandoned the companion of her youth.
There is no need to invent her name.
No need to speculate about the details Scripture does not provide.
No need to turn her into a symbol of every woman or to forget the many men whom Scripture also confronts for marital treachery.
The warning is sufficient.
A covenant was treated as something forgettable.
A relationship was forsaken.
A path of death was chosen over the way of wisdom.
And centuries later, we are still living in a world where people are tempted to make the same exchange.
But the final word of the Gospel is not that every sinner must remain trapped in the worst thing they have done.
Nor is it that every wounded person must forever be defined by what someone else did to them.
The final word belongs to Jesus Christ.
And in Him there is forgiveness for the repentant, strength for the obedient, comfort for the brokenhearted, and hope that reaches beyond the wreckage of human failure.
Maybe you cannot return to the beginning of your marriage.
Maybe you cannot recover the innocence of a trust that was shattered.
Maybe the person you once loved has become someone you no longer recognize.
Maybe you are the one who made choices you would give anything to undo.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But you can surrender today to the Savior who makes all things new.
And that is where the scandal meets grace.
Not in pretending that betrayal never happened.
Not in demanding that every broken marriage be restored.
Not in confusing consequences with condemnation.
But in discovering that Jesus Christ is greater than our sin, greater than our shame, and faithful to everyone who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
The covenant someone abandoned may still leave scars—but the Savior who was wounded for sinners has not abandoned His power to redeem.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN YOU LOVE GOD WITH ALL YOUR HEART… AND STILL WAKE UP WISHING YOU DIDN’T HAVE TO FACE ANOTHER DAY?
paragraphs: CAN YOU LOVE GOD WITH ALL YOUR HEART… AND STILL WAKE UP WISHING YOU DIDN’T HAVE TO FACE ANOTHER DAY?
The Silent Battle of Christians Who Worship on Sunday, Cry in Secret on Monday, and Wonder Whether God Is Disappointed in Them — And the Gospel Truth That Could Change Everything.
There is a kind of suffering that doesn't leave bruises.
Nobody sees it when you walk into church.
Nobody hears it when you say, “I'm blessed.”
Nobody notices it when you lift your hands during worship, even though it took everything inside you just to get out of bed that morning.
You know the songs. You believe the Scriptures. You love Jesus.
But somewhere between the final Amen and the quiet drive home, that familiar heaviness returns.
And when the house finally goes silent, the question you've been afraid to ask begins whispering again.
“If I really love God, why am I still this depressed?”
Maybe you've prayed until you ran out of words.
Maybe you've fasted, confessed every sin you could remember, listened to sermons about joy, and begged God to remove the darkness.
And yet, tomorrow morning, you might wake up feeling exactly the same.
What makes it worse isn't always the depression itself.
Sometimes it's the shame of believing that a genuine Christian shouldn't feel this way.
You've heard people say, “Just have more faith.”
“Stop thinking negatively.”
“Claim your victory.”
“A real believer should be full of joy.”
So you smile harder.
You serve more.
You quote another Bible verse.
And slowly, without realizing it, you begin hiding your pain from the very people who should be helping you carry it.
But what if the Bible tells a more compassionate, more challenging, and far more beautiful story than the one you've been hearing?
What if loving God deeply and battling depression are not mutually exclusive?
And what if the Savior you've been afraid to disappoint is not standing over your suffering with condemnation, but drawing near to you in the middle of it?
Before you answer, come with me to a wilderness.
There is a prophet sitting beneath a tree.
He has witnessed the power of God.
He has seen fire fall from heaven.
And now he is asking God to let him die.
His name is Elijah.
And his story may change the way you understand your own.

In 1 Kings 18, Elijah stands on Mount Carmel against the prophets of Baal. He prays, and the Lord answers with fire. The people witness God's power and fall on their faces, acknowledging that the LORD is God.
It is one of the most extraordinary moments in the Old Testament.
But turn the page.
In 1 Kings 19, after Queen Jezebel threatens his life, Elijah runs into the wilderness.
The man who stood boldly before hundreds is now overwhelmed, frightened, exhausted, and alone.
And beneath a broom tree, he prays:
“It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.” — 1 Kings 19:4, KJV
Read that again.
This is not a pagan rejecting God.
This is not a man who has never experienced God's faithfulness.
This is Elijah.
A prophet who had just witnessed a breathtaking demonstration of divine power.
And now he cannot bear the weight of another day.
Scripture does not diagnose Elijah with clinical depression. It would be irresponsible to impose a modern medical diagnosis on an ancient biblical account.
But Scripture unmistakably shows us a faithful servant of God experiencing profound emotional distress, fear, exhaustion, isolation, and a desire for death.
And what does God do?
Does He immediately rebuke Elijah for not having enough faith?
Does He tell him to stop being negative?
Does He threaten to remove his calling?
No.
God sends an angel.
And the angel gives Elijah food.
Then Elijah sleeps.
And the angel comes again.
“Arise and eat; because the journey is too great for thee.” — 1 Kings 19:7, KJV
The journey is too great for thee.
There is something breathtakingly tender about those words.
God does not pretend Elijah's exhaustion is imaginary.
He acknowledges the weight of the journey.
He provides nourishment and rest before giving further direction.
Later, the Lord meets Elijah at Horeb, questions him, corrects his mistaken belief that he is the only faithful one remaining, and gives him renewed direction and companionship.
God does not leave Elijah in his despair.
But neither does He treat his distress as proof that he never belonged to Him.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear something they have not heard in a very long time.
Your exhaustion is not automatically evidence of spiritual failure.
Sometimes you need prayer.
Sometimes you need sleep.
Sometimes you need someone trustworthy to listen.
Sometimes you need professional treatment.
And sometimes you need all of those things together.
Because you are not merely a soul floating through life.
You are a human being, created by God, living in a body that can become exhausted, ill, overwhelmed, and wounded.
And the God who made you knows that.
Psalm 103:14 says:
“For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust.” — KJV
The Hebrew word translated “frame” is יֵצֶר (yetser), referring here to our formation or constitution.
The word translated “dust” is עָפָר (aphar).
The psalmist is reminding us that God's compassion is not disconnected from our human limitations.
He knows how we were formed.
He remembers our frailty.
He does not discover your limitations with surprise.
And He does not cease being merciful because you have them.
Maybe you've spent years believing you must become emotionally invincible before God can be pleased with you.
But that was never the Gospel.
The Gospel begins with our desperate need for grace.
And grace is not reserved for people who have managed to make themselves strong.
Think about David.
The shepherd who became a king.
The worshiper who wrote songs that have comforted generations.
The man Scripture describes as someone after God's own heart.
Yet the Psalms contain cries of anguish so raw that many modern churches would hardly know what to do with them.
In Psalm 42:5, the psalmist asks:
“Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance.” — KJV
The Hebrew expression מַה־תִּשְׁתּוֹחֲחִי (mah-tishtochachi) conveys the sense of being bowed down or brought low.
The psalmist is not pretending his inner world is peaceful.
He is speaking directly to his troubled soul.
He acknowledges his distress while calling himself to hope in God.
Notice what he does not say.
He does not say, “Because I feel sorrow, I must not love God.”
He does not say, “Because I am struggling, God must have abandoned me.”
Instead, he brings his suffering into conversation with what he knows about the Lord.
That is not hypocrisy.
That is a struggling believer practicing faith.
And sometimes faith looks less like shouting victory from a mountaintop and more like whispering, “Lord, help me,” through tears.
There is another biblical voice we need to hear.
One that refuses to give us a convenient, tidy ending.
Psalm 88 is among the darkest prayers in all of Scripture.
Its writer, Heman the Ezrahite, cries out under the weight of suffering, loneliness, and what feels like divine distance.
The psalm ends:
“Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness.” — Psalm 88:18, KJV
The Hebrew text closes with the word מְיֻדָּעָי (meyudda'ai), meaning “my acquaintances” or “those known to me,” joined in the final expression to darkness.
Unlike many other lament psalms, Psalm 88 does not conclude with an obvious emotional breakthrough.
The darkness is still there when the poem ends.
Yet the prayer itself has been preserved in Holy Scripture.
Think about that.
God has given His people an inspired prayer that does not end with the sufferer saying, “Everything is fine now.”
Why?
The text does not tell us every reason.
But it certainly teaches us that anguish can be brought honestly before God without first being transformed into a cheerful testimony.
Some Christians have been made to feel that every prayer must end in visible triumph.
That every testimony must resolve before the microphone is handed back.
That every tear must be followed immediately by a smile.
But the Bible is more honest about human suffering than that.
Sometimes healing unfolds slowly.
Sometimes faithful people endure seasons they cannot explain.
Sometimes the prayer is simply, “How long, O LORD?”
And the Lord does not forbid that prayer.
Now consider something even more astonishing.
Jesus Christ Himself knew profound sorrow.
In Gethsemane, on the night before His crucifixion, He told His disciples:
“My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: tarry ye here, and watch with me.” — Matthew 26:38, KJV
The Greek phrase περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου (perilypos estin hē psychē mou) means “my soul is deeply sorrowful” or “overwhelmed with sorrow.”
The word περίλυπος (perilypos) communicates intense grief.
We must handle this passage carefully.

Jesus' anguish in Gethsemane should not be casually equated with a clinical diagnosis of depression. His suffering was bound to His unique mission, His approaching crucifixion, and the cup He was about to drink.
But His sorrow matters profoundly.
The sinless Son of God experienced genuine human anguish.
He did not pretend that pain was painless.
He prayed.
He submitted Himself to the Father's will.
And He asked His closest disciples to remain with Him.
If the sinless Savior could express overwhelming sorrow, why have we taught struggling Christians that admitting sorrow is automatically shameful?
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that we do not have a High Priest unable to sympathize with our weaknesses.
Jesus understands human suffering from within the reality of His incarnation.
He is not indifferent to your tears.
And when you cannot find the words to explain what is happening inside you, you are not approaching a Savior unfamiliar with anguish.
You are approaching the Man of Sorrows.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The One whose love was demonstrated not through sentimental promises, but through the cross.
And this is where we must confront a dangerous misunderstanding.
Depression is not automatically a sin, a demon, a punishment from God, or evidence that a person lacks genuine faith.
Clinical depression is a serious health condition that can affect mood, thinking, sleep, energy, concentration, appetite, and the ability to function.
It can involve biological, psychological, social, and environmental factors.
Grief, trauma, chronic illness, isolation, and overwhelming stress can also contribute to depressive symptoms.
Not every season of sadness is clinical depression, and not every experience of depression has the same cause.
But reducing all depression to spiritual failure is neither medically responsible nor biblically justified.
Yes, Scripture calls us to repentance.
Yes, sinful patterns can damage our lives and relationships.
Yes, spiritual struggles can accompany emotional suffering.
But it is wrong to assume that every depressed believer is hiding an unconfessed sin.
Remember the man born blind in John 9.
The disciples asked Jesus whose sin had caused the man's blindness.
Jesus rejected the premise that his condition was the result of his own sin or his parents' sin.
The passage concerns blindness, not depression, but it warns us against automatically assigning personal guilt to someone's suffering.
And if we are not careful, we can wound people in the name of defending God.
Imagine a young mother sitting in the back of a church.
She loves Jesus.
She reads Scripture to her children.
She tries to pray every morning.
But after months of sleepless nights, relentless anxiety, and a crushing sadness she cannot explain, she finally gathers the courage to tell someone she is struggling.
And the response she receives is:
“You just need to pray harder.”
So she goes home.
And she stops talking.
Not because she has stopped believing.
But because she is afraid that telling the truth will make people question her salvation.
Or imagine the father who works long hours, pays the bills, leads family devotions, and laughs at church.
Nobody knows that some evenings he sits alone in his parked car because he cannot bear to walk inside and pretend to be okay.
He wonders whether his family would understand.
He wonders whether his pastor would judge him.
He wonders whether God is tired of hearing the same exhausted prayers.
Or perhaps it is the teenager who loves worship music, highlights Bible verses, and keeps telling friends that God is good.
But privately, that teenager feels numb.
Not rebellious.
Not deliberately rejecting Christ.
Just empty.
And terrified to admit it.
If that sounds familiar, please hear this carefully.
You do not have to conceal your suffering to prove your devotion to Jesus.
Truthfulness is not the enemy of faith.
The church should be a place where suffering people can receive prayer, companionship, wise pastoral care, and encouragement to seek appropriate treatment.
Galatians 6:2 says:
“Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.” — KJV
The Greek verb βαστάζετε (bastazete) means “bear,” “carry,” or “take up.”
Paul is commanding believers to help carry one another's burdens.
Not to shame one another for having them.
Not to compete over who appears strongest.
Not to turn every struggle into a public interrogation.
To carry.
And carrying a burden sometimes means sitting quietly beside someone who has no energy to explain.
It means bringing a meal.
Checking in again after the first conversation.
Helping someone arrange an appointment.
Accompanying them when they are afraid.
Listening without rushing to offer an explanation.
It means refusing to make their suffering about our need to appear spiritually knowledgeable.
Because compassion is not weakness.
It is part of obedience to Christ.
And seeking help is not necessarily evidence that prayer has failed.
A Christian can pray and see a doctor.
A Christian can study Scripture and attend therapy.
A Christian can trust God's providence and take appropriately prescribed medication.
These things are not inherently in competition.
Just as receiving treatment for diabetes does not mean someone has abandoned faith, receiving care for depression does not mean someone has stopped trusting Jesus.
Treatment decisions should be made with qualified healthcare professionals, and medication should not be started, changed, or stopped without appropriate medical guidance.
Spiritual care and professional mental-health care can work alongside one another.
And if you have been struggling for weeks, especially if your symptoms are affecting daily life, please do not interpret seeking an assessment as surrendering your faith.
You may be taking a wise and courageous step toward healing.

If your suffering has brought you to thoughts of ending your life or harming yourself, please tell someone you trust immediately and seek urgent help from local emergency services or a crisis service. Do not remain alone with an immediate danger.
Your life is precious.
You deserve care.
And there are people who can help you through this moment.
Now, I want to speak to the Christian who feels spiritually numb.
The one who opens the Bible and feels nothing.
The one who hears a beautiful worship song and remembers when it used to move them to tears.
The one who kneels to pray but can barely concentrate.
You remember when following Jesus felt vibrant.
You remember the hunger.
The excitement.
The sense of closeness.
And now you are afraid that because the feeling has faded, the relationship must be gone.
But listen.
Your feelings are real, yet they are not the final authority on God's faithfulness.
Depression can affect your ability to experience pleasure, connection, motivation, and emotional responsiveness.
That can include the way you experience prayer, worship, and fellowship.
It does not automatically mean that the Holy Spirit has abandoned you.
It does not mean Christ's promises have expired.
And it does not mean that every prayer spoken through numbness is meaningless.
Romans 8:38–39 declares that neither death nor life, nor any other created thing, can separate God's people from His love in Christ Jesus our Lord.
The Greek expression οὔτε θάνατος οὔτε ζωή (oute thanatos oute zōē) means “neither death nor life.”
Paul is describing the extraordinary security of God's love in Christ.
Depression is not named as a separate item in the passage, but it is not a power greater than Christ.
The assurance of the believer rests ultimately on Jesus Christ and His saving work, not on maintaining a particular emotional state.
This does not mean we ignore sin, abandon spiritual disciplines, or dismiss the call to persevere.
It means we stop confusing emotional intensity with the foundation of salvation.
You are not saved because you can always feel joy.
You are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that unmistakably clear.
And the grace that saves us also teaches us to walk in truth, seek help, repent when needed, love one another, and continue trusting the Lord through seasons we do not understand.
There is an enormous difference between saying, “I do not feel God's presence,” and concluding, “Therefore God has abandoned me.”
The first is an honest description of experience.
The second is a conclusion that must be tested against Scripture.
And Scripture repeatedly calls God's people to remember His faithfulness even when their circumstances feel unbearable.
But perhaps your deepest wound is not merely depression.
Perhaps it is what people have said about your depression.
Maybe someone told you that you were spiritually weak.
Maybe you were accused of being ungrateful.
Maybe your tears were treated as an embarrassment.
Maybe you were told that a Christian who truly trusted God would never need counseling.
And after hearing those words enough times, you began believing that your suffering made you a second-class believer.
Please do not confuse another person's misunderstanding with the voice of Jesus.
Christ never commanded His church to despise the brokenhearted.
Psalm 34:18 declares:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.” — KJV
The Hebrew phrase קָרוֹב יְהוָה (qarov YHWH) means “the LORD is near.”
Near.
Not necessarily removing every symptom instantly.
Not promising that every circumstance will change by morning.
But near to the brokenhearted.
And sometimes the most faithful thing a suffering Christian can do is stop pretending and say:
“I need help.”
Three words.
No dramatic speech.
No polished testimony.
No attempt to impress anybody.
Just the truth.
And maybe those three words become the beginning of a conversation that saves a life.
There is another truth we cannot afford to overlook.
The Gospel is bigger than relief from depression.
Jesus did not come merely to make difficult days feel easier.
He came to save sinners.
We have all sinned and fallen short of God's glory.
Our deepest need is reconciliation with the holy God who made us.
And Jesus Christ, fully God and fully man, lived without sin, died for our sins, was buried, and rose again.
He bore the judgment sinners deserve so that everyone who repents and believes in Him may receive forgiveness and eternal life.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not self-improvement.
Not emotional performance.
Not the promise of a painless life.
But redemption through the crucified and risen Savior.
And this matters because a person can experience genuine salvation while still needing care for a serious mental-health condition.
Likewise, treatment for depression is valuable, but it is not a substitute for reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
We need not force these truths to compete.
We can proclaim Christ faithfully while caring responsibly for the whole person.
We can call people to repentance without accusing every sufferer of secret sin.
We can preach joy in the Lord without demanding that every believer display constant happiness.
We can celebrate answered prayers without shaming those whose recovery is slow.
And we can confess that God is powerful without pretending that we understand every mystery of His providence.
Consider the apostle Paul.
In 2 Corinthians 12, he describes a painful affliction he calls a thorn in the flesh.
The precise nature of that affliction is not identified, and we should not claim that it was depression.
Paul pleaded with the Lord three times for its removal.
But the answer he received was:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
The Greek phrase ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου (arkei soi hē charis mou) means “My grace is sufficient for you.”
Notice what the verse does not promise.
It does not say that faithful people will never experience ongoing weakness.
It does not guarantee immediate removal of every affliction.
It does not teach us to refuse medical care.
It declares the sufficiency of Christ's grace in Paul's weakness.
And that is a profoundly different message from telling someone that suffering proves God has rejected them.
Maybe your testimony will include a dramatic recovery.
Maybe treatment will bring significant improvement.
Maybe healing will involve years of steady progress, setbacks, prayer, professional support, and the loving presence of people who refuse to abandon you.
And maybe there will still be difficult days.
None of those possibilities places you beyond the reach of Christ's grace.
Your story does not have to follow somebody else's timeline to be meaningful.
You do not need to manufacture a miracle story to prove that Jesus is Lord.
He is Lord already.
The empty tomb has settled that question.
And because He lives, the Christian's hope extends beyond the limitations of this present world.
Revelation 21:4 speaks of the coming day when God will wipe away every tear, and death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
That is not a guarantee that every believer will be free from depression in this present life.
It is a promise pointing toward the final restoration God will accomplish.
And sometimes that future hope is what helps us endure a present day we cannot yet understand.
Perhaps tonight you are reading this with tears in your eyes.
Perhaps nobody in your family knows how much you are struggling.
Perhaps you have become so skilled at saying “I'm okay” that even you have stopped asking whether it is true.
And perhaps a part of you is wondering whether Jesus still wants someone who feels as broken as you do.
Look at the cross.
Not at your ability to smile.
Not at your ability to maintain perfect concentration during prayer.
Not at your emotional strength.
Look at the cross.
There, the love of God is revealed in the sacrifice of His Son.
There, our sin is confronted with perfect justice and astonishing mercy.
There, forgiveness is offered through the blood of Jesus Christ.
And in His resurrection, we see that suffering and death do not have the final word.
Your depression is not your identity.
Your diagnosis, if you have one, is not your Savior.
Your darkest season is not the complete story of your life.
And your need for help does not make you less worthy of being treated with dignity and compassion.
You may be struggling.
You may need treatment.
You may need rest.
You may need to ask your church family to walk with you.
You may need to rebuild routines slowly, one small act of faithfulness at a time.
But you do not need to earn the right to come to Jesus by first becoming emotionally well.
He calls the weary and burdened to Himself.
And His invitation is not limited to people who can hide their pain convincingly.
Maybe this is where the hiding ends.
Not because one article can cure depression.
It cannot.
Not because a few Bible verses automatically remove every symptom.
They do not.
But because the truth can begin dismantling the shame that has kept you silent.
You can love Jesus and admit that you are suffering.
You can trust God and accept help.
You can be spiritually sincere and emotionally exhausted.
You can seek treatment while continuing to pray.
You can belong to Christ while walking through a season you would never have chosen.
And if you are part of a church, you can help make it a place where such honesty is met with compassion rather than suspicion.
Because somebody in your congregation may be fighting a battle you cannot see.
Somebody who serves faithfully may be barely holding on.
Somebody who encourages everyone else may desperately need encouragement.
Somebody who says, “God is good,” may be quietly pleading, “Lord, please help me survive today.”
Do not wait for that person to collapse before you show them kindness.
Be the friend who notices.
The believer who listens.
The brother or sister who carries a burden.
The Christian who remembers that speaking truth and showing tenderness are not opposites.
And if you are the one who needs that kindness, let someone know.
Please.
You were never commanded to fight every battle alone.
I also want to invite you to do something that could matter more than you realize.
You don't need to reveal personal details you aren't comfortable sharing.
You can simply write, “I'm still fighting, and I'm still trusting Jesus.”
Not because a comment proves your faith.
Not because public confession of private medical suffering is required.
But because your honest words may help another person realize they are not alone.
And if God has carried you through a season of depression, consider sharing a little of your testimony. Your story does not have to be completely resolved to offer someone encouragement.
Someone needs to know that seeking help is not spiritual defeat.
Someone needs to know that recovery can take time.
Someone needs to know that Jesus Christ remains worthy of trust even when life is painfully difficult.
You may never know who reads it silently.
A friend who stopped attending church because they felt ashamed.
A mother who has been crying after her children fall asleep.
A father who has been carrying more than he knows how to express.
A young believer who thinks depression means God no longer loves them.
Sometimes sending an article privately is the more loving choice.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, those who have drifted from the faith, and even those who are still searching for answers.
We do not want to build a community where people merely look religious.
We want to encourage a community where people know the Scriptures, love Christ, confess their sins, seek wise help, carry one another's burdens, and grow in grace.
Not out of guilt.
Not because a monthly payment can replace obedience, generosity toward your local church, or the biblical responsibility of giving according to conscience and ability.
You can glorify God through countless acts of faithful love and obedience, whether or not you ever spend money on this ministry.
And there is something else worth knowing.
The purpose of that library is not merely to collect information.
It is to encourage believers to open the Scriptures, examine their hearts, deepen their understanding of the Gospel, and grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your thoughtful comments matter.
Your willingness to share a biblically faithful message with someone who needs it matters.
We are grateful for every sincere act of support.

It is that Jesus Christ would be known, His Word would be faithfully proclaimed, the brokenhearted would be treated with compassion, sinners would be called to repentance, and believers would grow into mature disciples who love God and one another.
And now, before you leave, I want you to remember the question that brought us here.
Can a Christian love God deeply and still battle depression?
Yes.
Not because depression is something to celebrate.
Not because suffering is spiritually superior.
Not because Christians should accept despair without seeking help.
But because Scripture never teaches that the absence of emotional suffering is the measure of genuine saving faith.
Elijah knew exhaustion.
The psalmists knew anguish.
Paul knew weakness.
And Jesus Christ Himself knew profound sorrow, though without sin.
The Bible does not flatten their experiences into a single medical diagnosis.
But it does show us that suffering and faithfulness can exist in the same life.
And the answer to our deepest need remains Jesus Christ.
The Savior who died for sinners.
The Lord who rose from the grave.
The Shepherd who calls His people to Himself.
The King who will one day make all things new.
So if tomorrow morning is difficult again, do not assume that today was a spiritual failure.
If you still need treatment, keep seeking appropriate care.
If you need someone to listen, reach out.
If you need to rest, rest.
If you need to repent of sin, come honestly before the Lord and receive the forgiveness promised in Christ.
And if all you can pray tonight is, “Jesus, help me,” then bring that prayer to Him.
You do not have to turn your suffering into a performance.
You do not have to pretend you have already reached the other side.
You do not have to become someone else's definition of strong.
Come to Christ truthfully.
Walk in the light.
Receive the help you need.
And remember that His grace is not measured by the intensity of your emotions.
There may be people who know your smile but have never seen your tears.
There may be people who know your testimony but do not know your present battle.
And there may be days when your faith feels so small that you wonder whether it is even there.
But the hope of the Gospel is not that your grip on Jesus will always feel strong.
It is that Jesus Christ is a faithful Savior.
And your story is not beyond His power to redeem.
You may have cried through the night, but your tears have not erased the cross, your struggle has not canceled His grace, and your unfinished story is still held before the risen Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JESUS SAY, “BLESSED ARE THE POOR IN SPIRIT”? THE ANSWER MAY BREAK YOUR HEART BEFORE IT HEALS YOUR SOUL
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS SAY, “BLESSED ARE THE POOR IN SPIRIT”? THE ANSWER MAY BREAK YOUR HEART BEFORE IT HEALS YOUR SOUL

The first words of Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount reveal a shocking truth: the Kingdom of Heaven does not open to those who have everything together, but to those who finally recognize how desperately they need Him.
There is a kind of poverty that no bank account can measure.
You can have money and still suffer from it.
You can have a beautiful home, a loving family, a respectable reputation, and a Bible sitting beside your bed—and still carry an emptiness that nobody knows exists.
You can worship on Sunday, encourage everyone around you, post Scriptures on Facebook, and tell people that God is good.
And yet, when the lights go out and the room becomes quiet, there is something inside you that whispers:
“Lord, why do I still feel so empty?”
Maybe you have spent years trying to become the kind of Christian who never struggles.
The one who always has faith.
The one who never doubts.
The one who never falls back into an old temptation.
The one who prays without distraction, forgives without hesitation, and trusts God without fear.
But you know the truth.
There are days when your faith feels smaller than your fears.
There are nights when your prayers feel like they barely reach the ceiling.
There are moments when you look at your own heart and wonder how someone who loves Jesus can still wrestle with so much darkness.
And perhaps the most exhausting part is pretending you are stronger than you really are.
But what if the very weakness you have been ashamed to admit is the place where Jesus is inviting you to stop pretending?
What if the confession you have been avoiding is the beginning of something beautiful?
And what if one of the most misunderstood statements Jesus ever made contains the answer?
Because when Jesus opened His mouth on a mountainside in Galilee, He said something that overturned humanity's understanding of blessing.
“Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” — Matthew 5:3 (KJV)
Read that again.
Not blessed are the spiritually impressive.
Not blessed are those who have never failed.
Not blessed are those who can quote the most Scriptures, pray the longest prayers, or convince everyone that their lives are perfectly holy.
Blessed are the poor in spirit.
Why?
Why would the Son of God begin one of His greatest teachings by blessing people who recognize their spiritual poverty?
And why would He promise the Kingdom of Heaven to them?
The answer is more unsettling—and more beautiful—than many of us realize.
Because before grace becomes precious to us, we must recognize why we need it.
And before we understand what Jesus meant, we need to hear His words as His first listeners would have understood them.
Matthew recorded His statement in Greek:
Μακάριοι οἱ πτωχοὶ τῷ πνεύματι, ὅτι αὐτῶν ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν.
Makarioi hoi ptōchoi tō pneumati, hoti autōn estin hē basileia tōn ouranōn.
A careful English rendering is:
“Blessed are the poor in spirit, because the kingdom of heaven belongs to them.”
The Greek word μακάριοι (makarioi) means “blessed,” describing people who are truly fortunate or favored in the light of God's Kingdom.
This is not simply the happiness that comes when life is comfortable.
It is a deeper blessedness grounded in God's gracious favor.
The word πτωχοὶ (ptōchoi) means “poor.” It can describe someone in extreme poverty, a person who lacks the resources to sustain himself.
But Jesus adds two crucial words.
τῷ πνεύματι (tō pneumati) — “in spirit.”
He is not merely praising material poverty, nor is He declaring that people become holy simply by having little money.
He is speaking about the spiritual condition of those who recognize their need before God.
People who know they cannot purchase righteousness.
People who understand that religious activity cannot erase their sins.
People who have stopped imagining that their good deeds can place God in their debt.
People who come before Him with empty hands.
And here is where the words of Jesus begin to confront us.
You can be materially wealthy and poor in spirit. You can also be materially poor and still be consumed by spiritual pride.
The issue is not the size of your possessions.
It is the posture of your heart before God.
And that raises a painful question.
What if some of us have spent our entire Christian lives trying to look spiritually rich while refusing to admit how desperately we need the Savior?
We know how to say, “God is good.”
But do we know how to say, “God, have mercy on me”?
We know how to encourage others to repent.
But when was the last time we allowed the Word of God to expose something in us?
We know how to defend Christianity in public.
But do we know how to humble ourselves before Christ in private?
There is a dangerous kind of spiritual confidence that can grow inside religious people.
It does not always look arrogant.
Sometimes it looks respectable.
It attends church.
It gives offerings.
It serves in ministry.
It knows the right language.
But slowly, almost imperceptibly, it begins to measure righteousness by comparison.
At least I am not like that person.
At least I do not commit that sin.
At least I still go to church.
At least I am better than I used to be.
And before long, the heart begins to depend more on its religious record than on the mercy of God.
Jesus told a story about exactly this.
In Luke 18:9–14, He described two men who went to the temple to pray.
One was a Pharisee.
The other was a tax collector.
In the world of Jesus' listeners, the Pharisee would have appeared religiously respectable, while tax collectors were often despised because of their association with Roman taxation and exploitation.
The Pharisee stood and spoke about his religious accomplishments.
He fasted.
He gave tithes.
He was confident that he was not like other sinners.
But the tax collector stood at a distance.
He would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He struck his chest and prayed:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.” — Luke 18:13 (KJV)
In Greek, his plea reads:
Ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ.
Ho Theos, hilasthēti moi tō hamartōlō.
“God, be merciful to me, the sinner.”
There was no impressive spiritual résumé.
No attempt to explain away his wrongdoing.
No comparison with someone worse.
Only a guilty man appealing to the mercy of God.
And Jesus declared that this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified.
Think about that.
The man who could list his religious accomplishments was not the one Jesus declared justified.
The man who acknowledged his sin and pleaded for mercy was.
Not because confessing sin earns salvation.
Not because humility becomes a substitute for Christ.
But because the tax collector's prayer expressed the dependence that self-righteousness refuses.
He had stopped defending himself.
He was asking for mercy.
And perhaps that is the moment when this teaching becomes painfully personal.
Because we would all like to believe we are the tax collector in the story.
But sometimes, if we are willing to be truthful, we recognize the Pharisee in ourselves.
The quiet judgment.
The hidden pride.
The satisfaction when someone else's failure makes us feel more righteous.
The resentment when God shows mercy to someone we think deserves condemnation.
The way we sometimes want grace for ourselves but consequences for everyone else.
And suddenly, the question is no longer, “Why did Jesus bless the poor in spirit?”
It becomes:
“Lord, have I been too proud to admit how poor I really am?”
That is not a comfortable question.
But it can become a life-changing one.
Because Jesus did not come to congratulate sinners for being sufficient without Him.
He came to save those who could never save themselves.
In Mark 2:17, Jesus said:
“I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” (KJV)
He was not teaching that some people are so righteous they have no need of salvation.
He was confronting the blindness of those who could not recognize their need.
And this truth did not begin in the New Testament.
Centuries before Jesus preached the Sermon on the Mount, the prophet Isaiah recorded these words from God:
“But to this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word.” — Isaiah 66:2 (KJV)
In the Hebrew text, the expression includes:
עָנִי וּנְכֵה־רוּחַ
ʿani u-nekeh-ruaḥ
“Poor and stricken [or contrite] in spirit.”
The Hebrew wording emphasizes humility, affliction, and a deeply humbled spirit before God.
The language is not identical to Matthew's Greek, but the biblical connection is profound.
God is not impressed by the outward grandeur of human religion while the heart remains proud.
He looks with favor upon the person who approaches Him with humility and reverence.
And this is where something extraordinary begins to emerge.
The poor in spirit are not blessed because spiritual poverty itself has the power to save.
They are blessed because God's Kingdom belongs to those who depend upon His grace rather than their own sufficiency.
They know they need the King.
They know they need forgiveness.
They know they need a righteousness they cannot manufacture.
And Jesus Christ is the Savior who provides what they could never obtain for themselves.
But there is another misunderstanding we need to confront.
Being poor in spirit does not mean hating yourself.
It does not mean constantly telling yourself that you are worthless.
It does not mean allowing others to abuse you because you think humility requires silence.
And it certainly does not mean denying the dignity of being made in God's image.
Biblical humility is not pretending that you have no value.
It is recognizing that your greatest hope is not found in your own goodness, but in the goodness and mercy of Jesus Christ.
There is a difference between being broken by despair and being humbled into dependence upon God.
Despair says, “I am beyond hope.”
Repentant faith says, “I cannot rescue myself, but Christ is mighty to save.”
Shame says, “My sin is the end of my story.”
The Gospel declares that Jesus died for sinners and rose again, so forgiveness and new life are offered through Him.
Humility does not require you to deny the grace God has already given.
It teaches you to receive that grace with gratitude.
And perhaps the most beautiful illustration of this truth is found in a moment when one of Jesus' closest disciples was confronted by his own sinfulness.
Peter had been fishing through the night.
He was exhausted.
His nets were empty.
Then Jesus instructed him to let down the nets.
Peter obeyed.
And suddenly the catch was so enormous that the nets began to break.
But notice what happened next.
Peter did not simply celebrate the miracle.
He fell at Jesus' knees and said:
“Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord.” — Luke 5:8 (KJV)
Something about encountering the authority and holiness of Jesus exposed Peter's own unworthiness.
The miracle revealed more than abundance.
It revealed who was standing in his boat.
And Peter could no longer pretend he was simply dealing with an ordinary teacher.
But listen carefully to what Jesus did.
He did not abandon Peter.
He did not say, “You are right. You are too sinful for Me.”
He did not walk away from the trembling fisherman.
Instead, Jesus said:
“Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men.” — Luke 5:10 (KJV)
The man who confessed his sinfulness was called into a new purpose.
What a picture of grace.
Peter's awareness of his sin did not make Jesus less willing to call him.
It revealed the kind of dependence Peter would need to follow Him.
And yet, Peter's story would become even more painful.
Because the same disciple who once fell before Jesus would later insist that he was ready to die for Him.
Then, in the darkness of the night when Jesus was arrested, Peter denied knowing Him.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
The rooster crowed.
And Luke tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Peter remembered His words.
Then he went out and wept bitterly.
Imagine that moment.
The shame.
The regret.
The terrible realization that his confidence had collapsed when tested.
Perhaps you know something about that kind of failure.
You promised God you would never return to that sin.
But you did.
You said you would never let bitterness take root again.
But it returned.
You promised to trust Him through the storm.
But fear overwhelmed you.
You thought you had become stronger.
Then life exposed a weakness you believed was behind you.
And now, whenever you try to pray, your failures seem to speak louder than your faith.
But Peter's story did not end beside that fire of denial.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, Jesus asked him three times whether he loved Him and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
The man who had failed publicly was not discarded.
He was restored to service.
Not because denial was insignificant.
Not because sin had no consequences.
But because the risen Christ is greater than Peter's failure.
And here is something we must never forget:
Jesus did not restore Peter by pretending his sin never happened. He restored him through a love powerful enough to confront his failure and call him forward.
That is the difference between cheap reassurance and Gospel grace.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace does not tell us repentance is unnecessary.
Grace does not invite us to remain comfortably enslaved to sin.
Grace meets sinners with forgiveness and calls them into a transformed life.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains us to renounce ungodliness and live in a way that honors Him.
The grace that saves us also begins to change us.
And that is why being poor in spirit is not a passing emotion that we experience once at conversion.
It is a posture of dependence that remains essential throughout the Christian life.
The longer we walk with Christ, the more deeply we should understand that every breath, every act of obedience, every victory over temptation, and every step toward holiness depends upon His grace.
We do not graduate from needing Jesus.
We grow in understanding how much we need Him.
And now we come to the astonishing promise at the end of Matthew 5:3.
“For theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”
Notice that Jesus does not merely say that the Kingdom might someday belong to the poor in spirit.
The Greek wording is present tense:
αὐτῶν ἐστιν
autōn estin
“Theirs is.”
This does not mean that the fullness of God's Kingdom has already arrived in every respect.
The New Testament speaks both of the Kingdom's present reality and its future consummation.
But Jesus announces that those who belong to His Kingdom are blessed even now.
Their circumstances may still be difficult.
Their struggles may not disappear overnight.
Their tears may not immediately stop.
Yet their deepest security rests in the reign and promises of God.
And consider the extraordinary reversal.
The spiritually bankrupt cannot buy their way into the Kingdom.
The guilty cannot erase their own record.
The proud cannot boast themselves into eternal life.
But the humble sinner who comes to Jesus in repentance and faith discovers that salvation is God's gift.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
The Gospel is not the announcement that human beings can finally become good enough to deserve heaven.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to rescue sinners.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He died for our sins.
He rose bodily from the dead.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who repent and believe.
That is why the Cross stands at the center of this Beatitude.
Because spiritual poverty reveals our need.
But Jesus is the answer to that need.
And the Cross exposes both the seriousness of our sin and the astonishing depth of God's love.
Think about the thief crucified beside Jesus.
Luke 23 records that one of the criminals acknowledged that he and the other criminal were receiving the just consequences of their deeds, while Jesus had done nothing wrong.
Then he turned to Christ and pleaded:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” — Luke 23:42 (KJV)
He had no time to rebuild his reputation.
No opportunity to accumulate years of religious achievements.
No impressive record of ministry service to present.
He could not climb down from the cross and begin proving himself worthy.
He could only turn to Jesus.
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:43 (KJV)
Do not miss the wonder of that moment.
The criminal was not saved by the suffering of his crucifixion.
He was not saved because his crimes suddenly became unimportant.
He was saved by the grace of Christ, received through faith.
He had nothing with which to purchase eternal life.
But he was speaking to the One who could give it.
And perhaps someone reading these words needs to hear that truth more than anything else today.
You may have spent years running from God.
You may have made decisions that wounded people you love.
You may carry memories that still make you ashamed.
You may have fallen into sin so many times that you wonder whether genuine change is possible.
But do not confuse the seriousness of your sin with the limits of Christ's power to save.
Jesus does not invite you to hide your sin.
He calls you to repent.
He does not ask you to manufacture a perfect past.
He calls you to trust Him with your present and future.
He does not promise that following Him will be painless.
He promises that those who come to Him will not be cast out.
John 6:37 records His words:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV)
That promise is not an excuse to cherish the sin that nailed our Savior to the Cross.
It is an invitation to come to Him rather than run away.
To confess rather than conceal.
To surrender rather than perform.
To trust rather than despair.
And there is a reason this matters so much in the world we live in.
We are surrounded by voices telling us to be self-sufficient.
Be stronger.
Be more successful.
Build your image.
Protect your reputation.
Never let anyone see your weakness.
Even in Christian communities, we can become afraid to admit that we are struggling.
We fear judgment.
We fear gossip.
We fear disappointing the people who look up to us.
So we learn to smile while silently collapsing.
We learn to say “Amen” when our hearts are breaking.
We learn to look spiritually healthy while neglecting the very confession, repentance, prayer, and fellowship that could help us grow.
And sometimes the most dangerous place for a struggling believer is behind a religious appearance that nobody is allowed to question.
But Jesus never said, “Blessed are those who successfully convince everyone they are spiritually strong.”
He said:
Blessed are the poor in spirit.
The people who know they need mercy.
The people who stop treating repentance as humiliation and begin recognizing it as a response to grace.
The people who can say, “Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief,” as the father cried out in Mark 9:24.
The people who do not pretend that following Jesus means they never struggle.
And the people who keep turning toward Christ because they know no one else can save them.
Maybe that describes you today.
Maybe you are exhausted from carrying a reputation that no longer reflects the condition of your heart.
Maybe you are tired of hiding behind spiritual language.
Maybe you have been telling everyone that you are fine while secretly fighting a battle that seems to grow heavier every week.
You do not need to confess every private struggle to the entire internet.
You do not need to expose intimate wounds to strangers to prove your sincerity.
But you do need to bring your true self before God.
And when appropriate, you may need the prayer, counsel, accountability, and care of mature believers who can walk with you in truth and love.
Because spiritual poverty is not an invitation to isolation.
It is an invitation to dependence upon God.
And dependence upon God teaches us to stop pretending we were created to carry everything alone.
Perhaps the prayer you need tonight is not complicated.
Perhaps it is simply:

“Lord Jesus, I have spent so much time trying to look strong that I have forgotten how to be honest with You. Forgive my pride. Forgive my hidden sins. Forgive the ways I have trusted my own goodness more than Your mercy. I cannot save myself. I need Your grace. Teach me to repent sincerely, believe Your promises, and walk in obedience to You. Change what I cannot change through my own strength. Make my life a testimony of Your redeeming love. Amen.”
And if that prayer reflects the cry of your heart, do not rush past this moment.
Sometimes the most significant spiritual turning points do not happen in crowded churches or during emotional gatherings.
Sometimes they happen in a quiet room.
Beside an unmade bed.
At a kitchen table after everyone has gone to sleep.
Inside a parked car while tears fall down your face.
In the middle of an ordinary evening when the Holy Spirit uses the Word of God to expose what you have been avoiding.
And suddenly, instead of defending yourself, you surrender.
Instead of hiding, you confess.
Instead of running from Jesus, you turn toward Him.
Not because tears themselves save.
Not because emotional intensity proves repentance.
But because God's Word has confronted your heart, and you are responding to His mercy.
That is where the message of Matthew 5:3 becomes more than a beautiful quotation.
It becomes an invitation to live.
To live without the exhausting illusion that you are your own savior.
To live without building your identity upon the approval of other people.
To live with gratitude for the righteousness of Christ.
To live in repentance when you fall.
To live in faith when you are weak.
To live with compassion toward other sinners because you know how much mercy you have received.
And to live with the quiet confidence that your hope is anchored not in the perfection of your performance, but in the finished work of Jesus Christ.
This is why the first Beatitude is so powerful.
It empties the hands that have been clinging to self-righteousness.
And it directs those empty hands toward the Savior.
It destroys the illusion that we can earn God's Kingdom.
And it announces the blessedness of those who depend upon His grace.
It humbles the proud.
It comforts the repentant.
It confronts the religious pretender.
And it gives hope to the sinner who has finally stopped running.
The poor in spirit are not celebrating their emptiness. They are blessed because their hope is in the fullness of Christ.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
And that is the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
Not a community of people pretending they have never fallen.
Not a gathering of spiritually superior Christians looking down on everyone else.
But a place where the Word of God confronts our sin, magnifies our Savior, and reminds us that grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
It is God's undeserved favor that brings salvation and teaches us to walk in newness of life.
And if this message has reached a place in your heart that you have been afraid to acknowledge, I want to invite you into something more meaningful than simply reading another inspirational post.
You do not have to explain everything.
And if God has brought you through a season of pride, failure, repentance, or restoration, consider sharing a testimony of His faithfulness. Your words may encourage someone who has almost given up.
There may be another Peter reading the comments.
Someone who loves Jesus but feels crushed by failure.
Someone who needs to be reminded that repentance is possible, that Christ is merciful, and that the Savior who restored Peter is still worthy of our trust today.
And perhaps you know someone like that personally.
A friend who has quietly drifted away from church.
A family member who thinks God could never forgive what they have done.
A Christian who has become exhausted trying to appear spiritually perfect.
A young believer who thinks every struggle means their faith is worthless.
A person who has never understood why Christianity speaks so much about grace.
Not simply to spread another post.
We want people to encounter Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in discipleship, and learn what it means to follow Jesus beyond the excitement of a single emotional moment.
Because there is something beautiful about Christians using the resources God has entrusted to them to help make His Word known.

Behind every article, every devotional, every teaching, and every discipleship resource is a mission we hope to continue and expand: pointing people away from self-sufficiency and toward Jesus Christ.
It can help support the ongoing work of producing and sharing biblical encouragement, discipleship content, and resources for people who are hungry to know Christ.
Scripture encourages believers to give willingly, thoughtfully, and cheerfully.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
But I also want to make something unmistakably clear.
You do not have to pay for God's favor.
Your generosity does not purchase salvation, forgiveness, spiritual status, or a greater claim upon God's love.
Your responsibilities to your family, your local church, and other commitments matter.
Giving must never become a transaction in which we imagine we can buy grace.
Christ has already paid the price for our redemption.
We support Gospel ministry not to earn God's love, but because His love has already been revealed to us in Jesus Christ.
That is the kind of generosity we want to encourage.
Freely given.
Prayerfully considered.
Rooted in gratitude.
Directed toward helping others hear the truth.
These products can serve as reminders of Scripture, encouragement in daily life, and opportunities to begin conversations about Jesus.
It is the opportunity to help sustain and expand a ministry committed to proclaiming Christ and encouraging people to grow in His Word.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible.
We want believers to study.
We want seekers to discover who Jesus is.
We want wounded hearts to encounter truth and hope.
We want families to grow in Scripture.
And a sincere comment may remind another person that they are not the only one learning to surrender their pride and depend upon Christ.
We cannot know exactly whose life a particular message will touch.
But we can faithfully share the truth and entrust the results to God.
And now, before you leave, return with me one last time to that mountainside.
Imagine the crowd.
The ordinary people.
The tired people.
The people carrying burdens nobody else could see.
The religious people who thought they understood righteousness.
The sinners who knew they had failed.
And there, before them, stood Jesus.
The One who would carry our sins to the Cross.
The One who would rise victorious over death.
The One through whom sinners could be forgiven and reconciled to God.
And His opening declaration was not an invitation to boast.
It was an invitation to recognize our need.
“Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”
Perhaps you began reading this article believing that your weakness was the greatest obstacle between you and God.
But the deeper danger may be the pride that convinces you to live without depending upon Him.
Your weakness is not your savior.
Your tears are not your righteousness.
Your confession does not pay for your sins.
Jesus Christ is your only Savior.
And when you come to Him in repentance and faith, you are not bringing Him a perfect life.
You are entrusting your broken life to the perfect Savior.
That is why the Gospel is so different from every attempt to earn our way into God's favor.
It does not begin with the declaration that we are sufficient.
It begins with the truth that we need mercy.
And it leads us to the Savior who is sufficient.
So stop trying to impress the God who already knows your heart.
Stop hiding the sins He calls you to confess.
Stop confusing religious appearances with genuine spiritual life.
Stop measuring the possibility of redemption by the size of your failures.
Look to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Follow Him.
And when you fall, do not make peace with sin or surrender to despair.
Return to the Savior.
Because the Kingdom of Heaven is not the reward of those who successfully pretend they need nothing.
It belongs to those who recognize their need and receive the grace of the King.
And perhaps the most beautiful prayer you can pray tonight is also one of the simplest:
“Jesus, I have nothing with which to earn Your mercy. But I believe You are enough.”
Not as a public performance.
Not as a formula for blessing.
But as a simple testimony of where your hope rests.
And remember this when the night is long, when the past accuses you, and when your strength seems to disappear:
The hands you finally stop using to prove your worth are the hands you can open to receive His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE KING WHO TRUSTED GOD FOR VICTORY… BUT COULDN’T TRUST HIM WITH HIS PAIN
paragraphs: THE KING WHO TRUSTED GOD FOR VICTORY… BUT COULDN’T TRUST HIM WITH HIS PAIN

Why did King Asa develop a severe disease in his feet? The disturbing truth behind 2 Chronicles 16:12–13—and the warning every Christian needs to hear before a heart that once trusted God learns to live without seeking Him.
He had watched God deliver an entire nation.
He had seen an impossible battle turn into a miraculous victory.
He had once stood before the Lord and confessed that human strength was nothing compared to the power of the Almighty.
But years later, when disease began consuming his feet, something was terribly wrong.
The man who once ran to God in desperation would not seek Him in his suffering.
And perhaps the most frightening part of King Asa's story is not that his feet became diseased.
It is that his heart had already begun walking away from the very God who had carried him.
Read that again.
Because this is not merely a story about an ancient king who became sick.

It is about what can happen when a believer experiences God's faithfulness, enjoys His blessings, survives impossible battles… and slowly begins trusting something else more than the One who delivered them.
And before we finish, there is a question buried inside this account that every one of us must answer.
What happens when the person who once depended on God begins treating God as a last resort?
The Bible records these chilling words:

"And Asa in the thirty and ninth year of his reign was diseased in his feet, until his disease was exceeding great: yet in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians. And Asa slept with his fathers, and died in the one and fortieth year of his reign." — 2 Chronicles 16:12–13 (KJV)
At first glance, it sounds like a warning against doctors.
But that is not what Scripture teaches.
And if we misunderstand this passage, we risk missing the deeper tragedy entirely.
To understand why this faithful king ended his life under such a troubling shadow, we must return to the days when Asa was still a man who knew where his help came from.
Long before his feet became diseased, Asa was one of Judah's most remarkable reforming kings.
He removed foreign altars, destroyed places of idolatrous worship, and called the people to seek the Lord.
He was not perfect, but his early reign was marked by an extraordinary determination to turn Judah back toward the God of their fathers.
Then came a crisis.
A massive army marched against Judah.
According to 2 Chronicles 14:9, Zerah the Ethiopian advanced with an army described as a thousand thousand men and three hundred chariots.
The biblical account presents Judah facing an overwhelming military threat.
Asa could have surrendered to fear.
He could have placed his confidence in weapons, military calculations, or the strength of his soldiers.
Instead, he prayed.
And the words of his prayer reveal the heart of the man he once was.

"LORD, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power: help us, O LORD our God; for we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude." — 2 Chronicles 14:11 (KJV)
"For we rest on thee."
What a confession.
Not "We have enough soldiers."
Not "Our strategy is unbeatable."
Not "We have everything under control."
We rest on You.
The Hebrew text includes the words:
כִּי־עָלֶיךָ נִשְׁעַנּוּ
Ki 'alekha nish'annu.
Meaning, in context, "For we rely on You."
The verb comes from the Hebrew root שׁען (sha'an), expressing the idea of leaning upon or depending on someone for support.
Picture that.
A king standing before an overwhelming enemy, confessing that his nation was leaning upon God.
Not merely believing God existed.
Not merely respecting God's commandments.
Actually depending on Him.
And Scripture tells us that the Lord struck the enemy before Asa and Judah (2 Chronicles 14:12).
The victory was God's.
The deliverance was God's.
The glory belonged to God.
But here is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Sometimes the greatest danger to our faith does not come before the miracle.
Sometimes it comes after we have survived it.
When we are desperate, we pray.
When the diagnosis frightens us, we cry out.
When our finances collapse, we seek the Lord.
When our family is falling apart, we open our Bibles with trembling hands.
But when life becomes manageable again…
When the income stabilizes…
When the relationship improves…
When the emergency passes…
When our reputation is restored…
We can gradually begin living as though the God who rescued us is no longer necessary for the ordinary decisions of life.
We still attend church.
We still know the worship songs.
We still say, "God is good."
But somewhere beneath the religious language, our dependence has shifted.
And sometimes we do not recognize that shift until another crisis exposes it.
That is what makes Asa's later years so heartbreaking.
In the thirty-sixth year of his reign, according to 2 Chronicles 16:1, King Baasha of Israel came against Judah and fortified Ramah, threatening Asa's kingdom.
Once again, Asa faced a serious political and military crisis.
But this time, his response was different.

Instead of the prayer recorded in chapter 14, we read that Asa took silver and gold from the treasures of the house of the Lord and the king's house and sent them to Ben-hadad, king of Syria, seeking an alliance against Israel.
The plan worked in an immediate political sense.
Ben-hadad attacked Israelite cities.
Baasha stopped building Ramah.
Asa removed the building materials and used them to fortify other cities.
From a purely human perspective, Asa's strategy looked successful.
The threat had been neutralized.
The kingdom had gained relief.
The king could have congratulated himself.
But heaven saw something that political success could not reveal.
God sent Hanani the seer to confront him.
And Hanani's message exposed the problem.
"Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God…" — 2 Chronicles 16:7 (KJV)
There it is.
The same issue that had once defined Asa's faith now exposed his decline.
Reliance.
The king who once leaned upon God had begun leaning upon another source of security instead.
And God reminded him of the earlier deliverance.
Had the Lord not rescued him when the Ethiopian and Libyan forces came against him?
Had Asa forgotten what God had already done?
Then came one of the most beautiful and searching declarations in the Old Testament.
"For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him." — 2 Chronicles 16:9 (KJV)
In Hebrew, the description of the heart includes:
לְבָבָם שָׁלֵם אֵלָיו
Levavam shalem elav.
Their heart is whole, complete, or fully devoted toward Him.
The Hebrew word שָׁלֵם (shalem) carries the sense of wholeness or completeness.
This does not mean that God only helps people who have never sinned.
If that were true, none of us could stand before Him.
The emphasis is on a heart whose loyalty is undivided toward God.
A heart that truly belongs to Him.
A heart that does not merely acknowledge Him publicly while secretly placing its ultimate confidence somewhere else.
And suddenly Asa's story becomes a mirror.
Because it is possible to have a Christian reputation while developing a divided heart.
Possible to defend biblical truth in public while refusing God's correction in private.
Possible to remember the miracles of yesterday while no longer seeking the Lord today.
Possible to appear spiritually strong while becoming inwardly resistant to the very voice of God.
And here is the terrible turning point.
When Hanani confronted Asa, the king did not respond like David when Nathan exposed his sin.
He did not confess.
He did not humble himself.
He did not ask God for mercy.
Instead, Scripture says Asa became angry with the seer and put him in prison.
He also oppressed some of the people at that time (2 Chronicles 16:10).
The man who had once led his nation toward God was now punishing the messenger who called him back to God.
How does a person reach that point?
Not necessarily overnight.
Sometimes it happens through a thousand small refusals to repent.
A warning ignored.
A conviction suppressed.
An apology never offered.
A secret sin defended.
A Scripture passage avoided because it touches something we do not want to surrender.
Until eventually, correction begins to feel like an attack.
And the voice that could have helped us return to God becomes the voice we most want to silence.
Have you ever experienced that?
Someone lovingly confronts something in your life, and your first response is not repentance but defensiveness.
A sermon touches your pride, and instead of asking God to search your heart, you begin criticizing the preacher.
A friend points out a destructive pattern, and instead of listening, you withdraw.
You tell yourself they do not understand.
You convince yourself they are judging you.
But deep inside, there is a quieter possibility you do not want to face.
What if God is using that uncomfortable truth to call you back?
What if the wound you are trying to protect is the very place where repentance needs to begin?
And then, three years after the confrontation recorded in chapter 16, the Bible tells us something devastating.
Asa became diseased in his feet.
His condition grew exceedingly severe.
And in his illness, he did not seek the Lord.
He sought physicians.
The Hebrew of 2 Chronicles 16:12 reads, in part:
וַיֶּחֱלֶא אָסָא ... בְּרַגְלָיו
Vayyechele Asa ... beraglav.
"Asa became ill ... in his feet."
The verse describes the disease as:
עַד־לְמַעְלָה חָלְיוֹ
Ad-lema'lah cholyō.
An expression describing the severity of his illness, rendered in the KJV as "his disease was exceeding great."
But we must be careful here.
The Bible does not identify the exact medical condition.
It does not say Asa had gout, gangrene, diabetes, or any particular modern diagnosis.
Those suggestions sometimes appear in discussions of the passage, but they remain speculation.
We also cannot confidently claim that God directly inflicted this disease as a specific punishment.
The text does not explicitly say that.
What the inspired writer does emphasize is Asa's spiritual response to his suffering.
And that response is deeply troubling.
"Yet in his disease he sought not to the LORD, but to the physicians."
Notice what the passage does not say.
It does not say seeking medical care is sinful.
It does not command believers to reject physicians.
It does not teach that prayer and medical treatment are enemies.
Scripture presents a more complete picture.
Jesus said, "They that are whole need not a physician, but they that are sick" (Luke 5:31, KJV), using the ordinary role of physicians as an illustration.
Paul referred to Luke as "the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14).
And Paul advised Timothy to use a little wine for his stomach and frequent ailments (1 Timothy 5:23), demonstrating that practical remedies were not inherently opposed to faith.
The problem with Asa was not simply that he consulted doctors.
The problem was that, in the chronicler's account, he sought them instead of seeking the Lord.
He repeated the same pattern that had appeared in his political decisions.
When threatened, he depended on Syria rather than God.
When afflicted, he turned to physicians without seeking God.
The repeated spiritual failure was misplaced ultimate dependence.
There is nothing unspiritual about receiving appropriate medical care.
Pray, and seek qualified medical help.
Take prescribed treatment responsibly.
Ask God for wisdom, strength, and healing.
Trust Him whether recovery comes quickly, slowly, or not in the way you hoped.
Faith does not require neglecting the means of care available to us.
But neither should those means replace our relationship with the One who holds our lives.
A hospital can treat a body.
Medicine can address disease.
A skilled physician can provide life-saving care.
But no physician can take the place of God as the ultimate source of our hope.
And now we come to the question that makes Asa's story so haunting.
Why did he refuse to seek the Lord?
Scripture does not reveal his private thoughts.
We cannot know whether he was driven by pride, bitterness, spiritual exhaustion, fear, or some combination of motives.
But the surrounding narrative shows a man who had resisted God's correction and failed to return to the dependence that marked his earlier years.
That is the tragedy.
Not that he became sick.
Not that he needed physicians.
Not even that his physical strength was failing.
The tragedy is that Scripture records his severe suffering without recording a return to the God he had once trusted so completely.
And then comes the final sentence.
"And Asa slept with his fathers, and died in the one and fortieth year of his reign." — 2 Chronicles 16:13 (KJV)
That is how the chapter records the end of his life.
Forty-one years on the throne.
A remarkable beginning.
Important religious reforms.
A miraculous military deliverance.
A public testimony of God's power.
And a final chapter marked by stubbornness and misplaced dependence.
Yet we should not distort his entire legacy.
First Kings 15:14 says that Asa's heart was devoted to the Lord throughout his days, while Chronicles also faithfully records his later failures.
The Bible gives us both truths.
A life can contain genuine faithfulness and serious spiritual failure.
A believer can have a meaningful history with God and still need urgent repentance today.
We must also resist pretending that Asa's final illness gives us complete knowledge of his eternal destiny.
Scripture does not authorize us to pronounce that verdict.
The warning is serious enough without adding what God has not revealed.
And perhaps that makes this story even more piercing.
Because the question is not whether Asa's name appeared in the history books.
It did.
The question is what his final decisions reveal about the danger of allowing yesterday's faithfulness to replace today's surrender.
There are people reading this who once prayed with tears streaming down their faces.
You remember when worship was not a performance.
When opening the Bible felt like coming home.
When you could barely finish a prayer because you were overwhelmed by God's mercy.
When you had nothing to offer Him except a broken heart, and somehow that was enough to bring you to your knees.
You remember the night you begged Jesus to forgive you.
The season when He carried you through grief.
The moment you realized that your sins were greater than you could repair, but His grace was greater still.
And now?
You are not necessarily denying Christ.
You are simply tired.
Distracted.
Guarded.
Maybe disappointed.
You still believe, but you no longer seek Him as you once did.
You have learned how to survive without praying much.
How to make decisions without asking for wisdom.
How to hide your pain behind spiritual language.
How to keep functioning while your soul grows quiet.
And sometimes you wonder why you feel so far from God.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not always that you have committed some dramatic scandal.
Sometimes the distance grows through ordinary self-reliance.
Through the slow habit of carrying burdens God has invited you to bring to Him.
Through becoming so accustomed to handling everything that you forget what it means to surrender anything.
And yet, the Gospel gives us a hope that Asa's tragic final chapter makes us long to hear.
There is another King.
A King greater than Asa.
A King who did not abandon His Father's will when suffering became unbearable.
A King who entered a garden called Gethsemane and faced anguish beyond anything we can fully comprehend.
Jesus Christ.
On the night before His crucifixion, He prayed:
"Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." — Luke 22:42 (KJV)
Where human kings failed, the Son of God remained obedient.
Where sinful humanity has repeatedly chosen self-reliance, Jesus entrusted Himself to the Father's will.
Where we have resisted correction, defended our pride, and pursued our own way, Christ humbled Himself even unto death on the cross (Philippians 2:8).
And here is the breathtaking difference.
Asa's story shows us the tragedy of a heart that would not seek the Lord in suffering.
Jesus' story shows us the Savior who entered suffering in perfect obedience so that sinners could be reconciled to God.
The feet of King Asa became severely diseased.
The feet of Jesus were pierced in the crucifixion.
But we must not confuse the two.
The Bible does not present Asa's disease as a prophetic symbol of Christ's wounds.
Their connection is not an invented prophecy.
It is a Gospel contrast.
The failing king reminds us of humanity's need.
The crucified and risen King reveals God's provision.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
