"But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed." (KJV)
This is not a promise that every faithful Christian will be physically cured in this present life.
Isaiah's prophecy, understood in the light of Christ's saving work, centers on the suffering Servant bearing sin and bringing restoration to His people.
First Peter 2:24 connects this healing with dying to sin and living unto righteousness.
The deepest human disease is not located in our feet.
It is the sin that separates us from a holy God.
And the greatest healing Christ provides is reconciliation with the Father through His death and resurrection.
That is why the Gospel is not merely an invitation to become a better person.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He did what we could never do for ourselves.
He bore the judgment our sins deserved.
He offers forgiveness to those who repent and believe in Him.
He does not simply improve our reputation.
He makes reconciliation with God possible.
He does not merely teach us how to conceal our scandals.
He calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And this is where our Gospel Warrior declaration becomes more than a memorable phrase.
Not because Jesus pretends our sins never happened.
Not because repentance is optional.
Not because consequences always disappear.
But because His mercy can reach the guilty, His forgiveness can cleanse the repentant, and His transforming grace can give a new direction to lives that once seemed hopeless.
Maybe your scandal is public.
People know what you did.
Your family remembers.
Your reputation has suffered.
Maybe your scandal is hidden.
The bitterness you feed.
The pornography you keep returning to.
The pride you refuse to confess.
The resentment you have carried for years.
The spiritual indifference nobody notices because you still look like a committed Christian.
Or maybe your deepest struggle is not a scandal anyone else can see.
Maybe it is the private exhaustion of someone who has been trying to remain strong for everyone else.
You are the one people call when they need prayer.
The one who encourages others.
The one who shares Scripture.
The one who says, "God is faithful," while silently wondering why your own heart feels so empty.
You have become so practiced at being the strong believer that you are afraid to admit you need help.
But Jesus never called you to pretend you were self-sufficient.
He said:
"Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." — Matthew 11:28 (KJV)
Come unto Me.
Not come when you have repaired everything.
Not come when your emotions are under control.
Not come when you can explain why you have drifted.
Come.
With the confusion.
With the shame.
With the stubbornness.
With the questions.
With the tears you have been holding back.
Come to Christ in repentance and faith.
The Savior who receives sinners is not surprised by your weakness.
And His invitation is not permission to continue in rebellion.
His grace calls us to turn from sin and follow Him.
Perhaps you have spent years asking God to remove the pain while resisting what His Word has been exposing in your heart.
Perhaps you have been asking for peace without surrendering the bitterness.
Asking for restoration without admitting the wrong.
Asking for spiritual strength while neglecting the very Word that nourishes faith.
If so, do not use Asa's story to condemn yourself beyond hope.
Use it as a warning that leads you back to Jesus.
Because conviction is not the same as condemnation.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.
And 1 John 1:9 assures us that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
Do not turn these promises into an excuse for sin.
Receive them as an invitation to stop hiding.
And if you are suffering from illness right now, please hear this clearly.
Your disease is not proof that God is punishing you.
Your pain does not automatically mean your faith is weak.
Your need for medicine does not mean you have failed spiritually.
Jesus rejected the assumption that a man's blindness must have been caused by his own sin or his parents' sin (John 9:1–3).
Paul lived with an affliction he asked the Lord to remove, and God's answer emphasized the sufficiency of divine grace (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).
Faithful believers can become seriously ill.
Some recover.
Some continue living with chronic conditions.
Some die while trusting Christ.
Our hope is not that believers will never suffer.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ has conquered sin and death, and that those who belong to Him will share in the resurrection life He has promised.
So seek appropriate treatment.
Receive help.
Let others pray with you.
And do not measure God's love by whether your body is healed on the timetable you desire.
The cross has already revealed the depth of His love.
The empty tomb has already declared the victory of His Son.
And His promise of eternal life is greater than the temporary strength of our mortal bodies.
There is another truth here that we desperately need to recover.
Not every successful decision is a spiritually faithful decision.
Asa's alliance with Syria produced immediate results.
But God rebuked the reliance behind it.
That should make us examine the way we measure success.
A business can grow while its owner becomes spiritually cold.
A ministry can attract attention while its leaders neglect prayer and accountability.
A person can gain influence while losing humility.
A family can appear respectable while unforgiveness quietly destroys relationships behind closed doors.
Visible results cannot replace obedience.
Public approval cannot replace faithfulness.
And religious activity cannot substitute for a heart surrendered to Christ.
This is why Gospel-centered discipleship matters so deeply.
We do not merely need another inspirational quote to carry us through the morning.
We need the whole counsel of God's Word.
We need truth that comforts us when we are wounded and confronts us when we are wandering.
We need believers who will pray with us, encourage us, and lovingly call us to repentance when we begin trusting ourselves more than God.
We need to keep returning to Scripture, not to earn salvation, but because the Savior who saves us also calls us to grow in His grace and knowledge.
And that is the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
Not to build a platform around human personalities.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to turn the Gospel into a product.

But to use the opportunities available to us to proclaim Jesus Christ, encourage believers, reach people who are searching for truth, and provide resources that help Christians become more deeply rooted in Scripture.
These resources are intended to help people study God's Word, strengthen their understanding of biblical truth, and grow in their walk with Jesus Christ.
And here is something important.
You do not need to pay for God's love.
You cannot purchase forgiveness, salvation, or the favor of Jesus Christ.
Those gifts are received by grace through faith, not bought with money.
Not out of guilt.
But because freely chosen generosity can be one meaningful way of supporting the spread of biblical teaching and discipleship resources.
The Bible teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we make this invitation.
It is not a required biblical tithe, and it should not replace the responsibilities of generosity, stewardship, and support you have toward your local church and those in genuine need.
But for those who desire to partner with this work, it is a practical opportunity to participate in making more Scripture-centered resources available.
These items are not the Gospel itself.
But because someone connected to you may be carrying a spiritual burden you know nothing about.
A former church member who has quietly drifted away.
A father struggling to lead his family.
A mother praying through exhaustion.
A young believer afraid to admit they are losing their way.
A person who has convinced themselves that Jesus would never receive someone with their history.
You may never know who reads it.
But you can share the truth faithfully and trust God with the results.
There may come a season when the Lord's faithfulness feels distant and you need to remember the difference between trusting God and merely remembering that you once trusted Him.
When was the last time you truly sought the Lord?
Not simply asked Him to bless a decision you had already made.
Not merely repeated a familiar prayer.
Not opened your Bible just to find a verse to post.
When was the last time you came before God with no excuses, no performance, and no attempt to hide what was happening inside you?
When was the last time you said:
"Lord, search me."
"Correct me."
"Forgive me."
"Teach me to trust You again."
Maybe this article has exposed a place where you have become too dependent on your own strength.
Maybe you have been resisting a truth you know you need to face.
Maybe you have been physically suffering and have misunderstood your pain as evidence that God has abandoned you.
Maybe you are simply tired of pretending your spiritual life is healthier than it really is.
Whatever the case, you do not have to turn the comments into a public confession of private details.
You can also share a testimony of a time God taught you to depend on Him, if you feel comfortable doing so.
Someone reading your words may discover that they are not the only person learning how to surrender.
Because the Christian life is not sustained by pretending we never struggle.
It is sustained by the grace of God, through faith in Jesus Christ, as the Holy Spirit works in us to produce repentance, obedience, perseverance, and love.
And now, as we return to Asa's story one final time, notice something.
The Bible tells us that his feet became diseased.
But it does not tell us that his physical condition was his greatest problem.
His greatest documented failure was that he did not seek the Lord.
And that is the question his life leaves behind.
Not merely, "What happened to Asa's feet?"
But, "What happens to us when we stop seeking the God who once delivered us?"
Do not wait until your circumstances become unbearable before returning to prayer.
Do not wait until pride has hardened into bitterness.
Do not wait until years of spiritual neglect have made surrender feel unfamiliar.
And do not confuse God's patience with permission to keep drifting.
Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your heart (Hebrews 3:15).
Turn to Jesus.
If you have never trusted Him as Savior, repent and believe the Gospel.
If you belong to Him but have wandered, confess your sin and return to walking in obedience.
If you are suffering, seek Him honestly and receive the help you need.
If you are strong today, remain humble enough to remember that every breath is a gift.
And if you are standing in the aftermath of decisions you deeply regret, remember that the grace of Christ is greater than the disgrace of a repentant sinner's past.
The King of kings did not come to save people who could prove they had never fallen.
He came to save sinners.
And the One who died on the cross and rose from the grave is worthy of more than the memory of our former devotion.
He is worthy of our trust today.
So here is my final prayer for you.
May God keep your heart tender when correction comes.
May He give you wisdom when decisions become difficult.
May He surround you with people who love you enough to tell you the truth.
May He strengthen you in suffering without allowing suffering to define your identity.
May He guard you from the quiet pride that forgets yesterday's deliverance.
And may He continually draw your eyes back to Jesus Christ, the author and finisher of our faith.
Because one day, every earthly achievement will fade.
Every title will lose its importance.
Every possession will pass into other hands.
Even the strongest body will eventually fail.
But the promise of eternal life in Jesus Christ will remain.
And when that day comes, the greatest treasure will not be the reputation we built, the victories we won, or the strength we once possessed.
It will be the Savior who loved us, redeemed us, and brought us home.
The saddest thing about Asa was not that his feet could no longer carry him—it was that, in his suffering, he would not turn to the God who had carried him before.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU CALL YOURSELF A CHRISTIAN… BUT WOULD JESUS RECOGNIZE THE LIFE YOU’RE LIVING?
paragraphs: YOU CALL YOURSELF A CHRISTIAN… BUT WOULD JESUS RECOGNIZE THE LIFE YOU’RE LIVING?
The Most Terrifying Thing Isn't That the World Might Discover Who You Really Are. It's That You Could Spend Your Whole Life Calling Jesus “Lord”… Without Ever Truly Surrendering to Him.
Not because it was spoken to atheists.
Not because it was directed at people who openly hated God.
But because Jesus spoke it about people who called Him Lord.
People who believed they belonged to Him.
People who even pointed to extraordinary religious works as evidence of their relationship with Him.
And when the moment came for them to stand before Him, they heard words no human soul should ever want to hear.
“I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.” — Matthew 7:23, KJV
Read that again.
Not, “I knew you once, but forgot you.”
Not, “You didn't attend enough church services.”
Not, “You didn't donate enough money.”
“I never knew you.”
Imagine spending decades speaking His name, posting Bible verses, attending worship services, defending Christianity in arguments, and telling everyone you believe in God…
Only to discover that the faith you displayed publicly was never the surrender Jesus called for privately.
And before you dismiss this as another message about hypocrites, there is something you need to understand.
The most dangerous spiritual deception is not always believing there is no God.
Sometimes it is believing you belong to God while refusing to let Him rule your life.
And the frightening part?
You can become so comfortable with that contradiction that eventually, you stop noticing it.
You know how to raise your hands during worship.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know which Bible verses to post when life becomes difficult.
You know how to look spiritually strong when someone asks how you're doing.
But there are things nobody sees.
The bitterness you've been feeding.
The forgiveness you've been postponing.
The secret habits you've been defending.
The person you keep hurting while insisting you're a good Christian.
The truth you keep avoiding because obedience might cost you something.
And somewhere between Sunday worship and Monday morning, a question quietly waits for you.
If someone removed the Christian label from your life, would the way you live still point them to Jesus?
Not perfectly.
Not flawlessly.
But genuinely.
Would they recognize His love in how you treat people who cannot benefit you?
His mercy in how you respond when someone fails?
His truth in what you do when lying would be easier?
His humility in how you behave when nobody applauds?
His holiness in what you choose when nobody is watching?
Because Christianity was never meant to be a costume we put on when people are looking.
It is a new life received through Jesus Christ.
And sometimes the hardest person to confront with that truth is the one looking back at us in the mirror.
There is something remarkable about the original Greek of Matthew 7:23.
Jesus says:
“Οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς.”
Oudepote egnōn hymas.
“I never knew you.”
The word ἔγνων (egnōn) comes from γινώσκω (ginōskō), meaning “to know.”
In this context, Jesus is not suggesting He lacked information about these people. Scripture presents Him as the One who knows what is in the human heart (John 2:24–25).
The issue is not whether Jesus possessed knowledge of their existence.
The issue is whether they truly belonged to Him.
That distinction should shake us.
You can know facts about Jesus without knowing Jesus.
You can memorize His teachings while resisting His authority.
You can admire His compassion while refusing to show compassion.
You can speak passionately about the cross while refusing to surrender the sins He died to redeem you from.
And you can become so skilled at looking like a Christian that you forget to ask whether you are actually following Christ.
But there is another side to this warning, and you need to hear it before fear convinces you to run away.
Jesus did not speak these words so that every struggling believer would live in constant terror of rejection.
He spoke them as a warning against false confidence, empty profession, and a life that claims His name while practicing lawlessness.
The Christian who hates their sin, grieves over their failures, and keeps returning to Christ in repentance is not the same as the person who has made peace with rebellion.
There is a difference between falling into sin and deciding that sin will remain your master.
There is a difference between struggling to obey Jesus and having no intention of obeying Him.
There is a difference between a wounded sheep who needs the Shepherd and a religious performer who believes the costume is enough.
And perhaps that distinction is exactly what someone reading this desperately needs today.
Because you may be sitting there thinking…
I've failed too many times.
I've made promises to God that I didn't keep.
I've prayed for forgiveness and then found myself struggling with the same temptation again.
What if I'm one of the people Jesus is talking about?
Listen carefully.
The answer is not to pretend your sin is harmless.
But neither is the answer to conclude that Christ's mercy has run out.
The same Jesus who warns against false discipleship also invites weary sinners to come to Him.
He said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
Do not let the enemy use a warning intended to awaken your conscience as an excuse to keep you away from the Savior.
Run toward Christ.
Not away from Him.
Because the purpose of conviction is not merely to make you feel terrible about yourself.
It is to bring you to the One who can forgive, cleanse, and transform you.
And perhaps no story reveals this more powerfully than the night one of Jesus' closest disciples discovered just how weak his own confidence really was.
His name was Peter.
Peter wasn't an outsider.
He wasn't someone who had never heard Jesus preach.
He had walked with Him.
Watched miracles unfold.
Heard the voice that commanded storms.
Seen the glory of Christ revealed.
And when Jesus warned that His disciples would stumble, Peter was convinced that his devotion was stronger than everyone else's.
He said:
“Though all men shall be offended because of thee, yet will I never be offended.” — Matthew 26:33, KJV
In other words…
Other people might abandon You, Lord.
But not me.
I'm different.
I'm loyal.
I'm stronger than that.
How many of us have said something similar?
Maybe not aloud.
But in our hearts.
I would never cheat.
I would never betray someone.
I would never become addicted.
I would never walk away from God.
I would never be like those hypocritical Christians.
Until the day temptation arrived wearing a face we recognized.
Until loneliness made compromise seem comforting.
Until anger became stronger than restraint.
Until fear made honesty feel dangerous.
Until the person we thought we were collided with the person our choices revealed.
That night, Peter denied Jesus.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
And Luke records one detail that makes the entire scene almost unbearable.
“And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.” — Luke 22:61, KJV
Imagine that moment.
The courtyard.
The accusations.
The fear.
The words Peter had just spoken.
And then…
Jesus looked at him.
Scripture does not describe the exact expression on Jesus' face, so we should not pretend to know what Peter saw in His eyes.
But we do know what happened next.
Peter remembered the Lord's warning.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
The man who had confidently declared that he would never abandon Jesus had just discovered the weakness of his own heart.
His public confidence had collapsed under private fear.
And maybe you understand that kind of collapse.
Maybe you remember the moment you realized you were capable of something you once condemned in others.
Maybe you remember sitting alone after an argument, knowing your words had wounded someone you loved.
Maybe you remember deleting messages, hiding evidence, or rehearsing explanations because you were terrified of being exposed.
Maybe you remember the moment after giving in to temptation when the pleasure disappeared and shame remained.
And perhaps the most painful thought wasn't simply, What have I done?
It was…
How could I call myself a Christian and still do this?
But Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.
That is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
After His crucifixion and resurrection, Jesus did not erase Peter from the story.
In John 21, the risen Christ met His disciples by the Sea of Tiberias.
There, Jesus asked Peter three times whether he loved Him.
And He entrusted Peter with the responsibility to care for His sheep.
The man who had denied Jesus three times was not restored by pretending his denial never happened.
He was restored through an encounter with the risen Savior who knew the truth about him.
Peter's failure was real.
His grief was real.
And Christ's grace was real.
Jesus did not call Peter's betrayal good. He proved that betrayal did not have to be the final chapter of Peter's life.
That is what grace does.
Grace does not rename darkness as light.
Grace brings sinners out of darkness.
Grace does not tell you that repentance is unnecessary.
Grace makes repentance possible.
Grace does not teach you to become comfortable with the chains that are destroying you.
Grace leads you to the Savior who breaks their power.
And this is where the message becomes painfully personal.
Because many people want Jesus as their Rescuer while resisting Him as their Lord.
We want Him to calm our anxiety, but we resist His command to trust Him.
We want Him to forgive our sins, but we struggle to forgive those who have sinned against us.
We want Him to bless our relationships, but we refuse to surrender relationships built on deception.
We want Him to heal our hearts, but we keep reopening wounds through bitterness.
We want the comfort of His promises without the inconvenience of His commands.
We want resurrection power without putting the old life to death.
And yet Jesus never presented discipleship as an arrangement where we could keep our old masters and simply add His name to the list.
He said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” — Luke 9:23, KJV
Daily.
Not just when the worship music is playing.
Not just when life is falling apart.
Not just when someone needs prayer.
Daily.
When you're tired.
When you're misunderstood.
When nobody appreciates your sacrifice.
When temptation whispers that one more compromise won't matter.
When forgiveness feels unfair.
When doing what is right costs you comfort, approval, opportunity, or pride.
Following Jesus means learning to say no to the version of ourselves that insists on being its own god.
But please understand something essential.
We do not become Christians by successfully performing enough acts of obedience.
We are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that clear.
And the very next verse tells us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The order matters.
Good works are not the price we pay to purchase salvation. They are the fruit of a life being transformed by the Savior.
A tree does not become alive by attaching fruit to its branches.
A living tree produces fruit because life is already at work within it.
That is why Jesus said:
“Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.” — Matthew 7:20, KJV
He did not say that genuine believers would never struggle.
He did not say that every Christian would mature at the same pace.
He did not say that a single failure automatically proves a person never knew Him.
But He did teach that what grows from our lives matters.
So perhaps the question is not simply whether you have a Christian identity.
Perhaps it is whether your life increasingly bears evidence of Christ's transforming work.
Are you becoming more truthful?
More willing to repent?
More compassionate toward the wounded?
More willing to forgive?
More sensitive to sin?
More hungry for Scripture?
More dependent on prayer?
More concerned with pleasing God than impressing people?
And when you fail, do you return to Christ in humble repentance, or do you continually search for excuses to protect the sin you refuse to surrender?
This is not about achieving perfection before God will love you.
It is about whether the grace you profess is teaching you to walk in a new direction.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves.” — 2 Corinthians 13:5, KJV
The original Greek begins:
“Ἑαυτοὺς πειράζετε εἰ ἐστὲ ἐν τῇ πίστει.”
Heautous peirazete ei este en tē pistei.
“Examine yourselves, whether you are in the faith.”
The verb πειράζετε (peirazete) here carries the sense of testing or examining.
Paul is calling for honest spiritual self-examination, not endless self-torment.
Because there is a kind of self-examination that leads us to Christ.
And there is a kind of self-obsession that keeps our eyes fixed on our failures instead of His sufficiency.
The purpose is not to become consumed with the question, Am I good enough?
The answer to that question, apart from Christ, is no.
The better question is…
Am I truly trusting the Jesus who is enough, and is His grace changing the way I live?
That question reaches beyond religious appearances.
It reaches the person who is admired in church but feared at home.
The person who quotes Scripture online but humiliates strangers in comment sections.
The person who publicly celebrates God's mercy but privately refuses to extend mercy.
The person who speaks about holiness while protecting a hidden pattern of exploitation.
The person who calls for repentance in everyone else but becomes furious when someone lovingly confronts their own sin.
And yes, it reaches the person writing this message as much as the person reading it.
Nobody gets to stand above the Word of God.
We all stand beneath its authority.
We all need grace.
We all need the Savior.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that some of us are morally impressive enough to deserve heaven.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
The apostle Paul, who once persecuted the church, wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” — 1 Timothy 1:15, KJV
Consider who said that.
A man who had once approved of violence against followers of Jesus.
A man whose past was stained with persecution.
A man who could never honestly rewrite his history to make himself look innocent.
And yet that same man became a witness to the mercy of Christ.
Paul did not glorify his former sin.
He glorified the Savior who showed him mercy.
That is the difference between a testimony and an excuse.
A testimony says, Look what Jesus rescued me from.
An excuse says, Because Jesus forgives, I don't need to change.
The first magnifies grace.
The second distorts it.
And Scripture will not allow us to confuse the two.
Romans 6:1–2 confronts the idea that grace gives us permission to continue comfortably in sin.
Paul's answer is unmistakable:
“God forbid.”
Grace is not a license to remain enslaved.
Grace is the gift that brings us into a new relationship with God through Jesus Christ.
And sometimes that transformation begins in the least glamorous places imaginable.
It begins when you apologize without adding an excuse.
When you finally confess what you've been hiding.
When you stop feeding the conversation that is pulling you toward adultery.
When you choose not to retaliate against someone who embarrassed you.
When you return what you dishonestly took.
When you admit you need help.
When you seek accountability instead of pretending you can fight every temptation alone.
When you open the Bible not to find a verse that justifies your anger, but to hear what God actually says.
When you kneel beside your bed and whisper a prayer nobody else will ever hear.
Lord, I cannot keep living like this.
I have called You Lord while fighting to remain in control.
I have wanted Your forgiveness without surrendering what is destroying me.
Please change my heart.
And perhaps the tears come.
Perhaps they don't.
Real repentance is not measured by how dramatically someone cries.
It is a turning of the heart toward God that bears fruit in a changed direction.
The Hebrew Scriptures give us a beautiful word that helps illuminate this.
שׁוּב — shuv
It means “to turn” or “to return,” and in many Old Testament passages it describes turning back to God.
Listen to the invitation in Joel 2:12:
“Turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning.” — KJV
The Hebrew begins:
“שֻׁבוּ עָדַי בְּכָל־לְבַבְכֶם”
Shuvu ʿadai bekhol-levavkhem.
“Return to me with all your heart.”
And in Joel 2:13, the prophet calls the people to rend their hearts and not merely their garments.
That image matters.
In the ancient world, tearing one's garments could express grief or distress.
But God was calling His people beyond outward displays.
He wanted hearts genuinely turned toward Him.
Not religious theater.
Not public performances of sorrow.
Not dramatic words designed to impress an audience.
The heart.
The place where motives hide.
The place where loyalties are revealed.
The place where surrender must become real.
And perhaps that is what Jesus is confronting in your life today.
Not the fact that you have ever failed.
But the fact that you have become skilled at disguising the places where you refuse to yield.
You can fool an audience.
You can fool your family.
You can fool your church friends.
You can even deceive yourself for a season.
But you cannot manufacture a relationship with Christ through appearances.
And that is not meant to leave you hopeless.
It is meant to invite you into honesty.
Because the One who knows the truth about you is also the One who went to the cross for sinners.
Think about that.
Jesus did not enter the world because humanity needed better religious branding.
He came because we needed redemption.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again, according to the Scriptures.
The cross reveals how seriously God takes sin.
The resurrection declares the victory of Jesus Christ over death.
And the Gospel calls us to repent and believe in Him.
Not merely to admire Him.
Not merely to quote Him.
Not merely to wear His name.
To trust Him.
To follow Him.
To belong to Him.
And that means your past, however ugly, does not have to be your future.
The liar can become truthful.
The proud can learn humility.
The bitter can learn forgiveness.
The addicted can seek help, walk in accountability, and experience real change.
The unfaithful can repent and begin the difficult work of rebuilding integrity, even when consequences remain.
The religious hypocrite can stop performing and begin living honestly before God.
Not because human willpower is unlimited.
But because the Holy Spirit is at work in those who belong to Christ.
And that work is often a process.
Some battles are long.
Some wounds require time, prayer, wise counsel, and patient care.
Some consequences do not disappear simply because forgiveness has been received.
But none of that means Jesus has abandoned the believer who continues turning toward Him.
Philippians 1:6 reminds us that the God who begins a good work in His people will bring it to completion.
He is not finished shaping His children.
And there is a remarkable promise in Ezekiel 36:26:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you.” — KJV
Notice what God promises.
Not merely a better reputation.
Not merely improved religious habits.
A new heart.
That is the miracle we need.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about teaching a dead heart to imitate life.
It is about God's power to give new life.
And perhaps, after all these words, the most important question is no longer whether Jesus would recognize the Christian image you've built.
The deeper question is whether you will stop hiding behind that image and come honestly to Him.
Maybe you have been pretending for years.
Maybe you've drifted slowly.
Not through one dramatic decision.
But through a thousand small compromises.
A prayer neglected.
A conviction ignored.
An apology postponed.
A sin justified.
A warning dismissed.
Until one day, the things that once grieved you barely trouble your conscience anymore.
And you cannot remember when your relationship with Jesus became more about maintaining appearances than walking with Him.
If that is you, please hear this.
You do not have to continue pretending.
You can repent today.
You can confess your sins to God today.
You can ask forgiveness from the people you've wronged.
You can seek help for the patterns you've been unable to overcome alone.
You can return to Scripture.
You can begin praying again.
You can stop defending the very things Christ is calling you to surrender.
And if you've never truly placed your faith in Jesus Christ, you can turn to Him now.
You do not need to manufacture a flawless past before coming to the Savior.
You need His mercy.
And His invitation is not reserved for people with impressive spiritual résumés.
It is extended to sinners who come to Him in faith.
Remember the criminal crucified beside Jesus.
He had no opportunity to build a long history of Christian service.
No opportunity to establish a public ministry.
No opportunity to repair every earthly consequence of his crimes.
But he turned to Jesus in faith.
And Jesus said:
“To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:43, KJV
Salvation was not purchased by the man's religious accomplishments.
His hope rested in Christ.
And the same Gospel that offered hope to a dying criminal still calls sinners to repentance and faith today.
So please do not misunderstand this message.
Jesus Christ is the Savior. No ministry can sell what His grace freely gives.
It is also not saying that every genuine Christian must display the same level of maturity.
A new believer learning to walk with Jesus and a mature believer who has followed Him for decades may be at very different stages.
But both need the same Savior.
Both depend on grace.
Both are called to follow Him.
And both must remember that faith is not merely a word on a profile.
It is trust in the living Christ.
Now, before you leave this article, I want to ask you something.
Not as an accusation.
Not as a demand for public confession.
But as an invitation to be honest before God.
What is the one area of your life where you know Jesus is calling you to stop pretending and start surrendering?
Maybe it is your anger.
Your pride.
Your marriage.
Your secret habits.
Your unforgiveness.
Your dishonesty.
Your fear of what others might think.
Or perhaps it is simply that you have been trying to look strong for so long that you have forgotten how to admit you need help.
You do not have to reveal private details that could harm you or someone else.
Not because commenting earns God's approval.
Not because a public declaration automatically proves repentance.
But because sometimes an honest sentence becomes the beginning of a conversation, a prayer, or a connection with another believer who reminds us that we do not have to walk alone.
Not to collect another inspirational post.
For the evening when pride tells you that you don't need to apologize.
For the day when shame whispers that your failure is greater than Christ's mercy.
Return to the Scriptures quoted here.
Read their surrounding passages.
Ask God to teach you not merely to feel convicted for a moment, but to walk faithfully with Him.
And think about one person who might need this message.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to attack.
Someone you love.
Someone who has quietly drifted from faith.
Someone who believes their mistakes have placed them beyond forgiveness.
Someone who attends church but feels spiritually empty.
Someone who has been wounded by religious hypocrisy and needs to see the difference between human failure and the character of Jesus Christ.
Or send this privately with a simple message:
I thought of you while reading this. I hope it reminds you how much Jesus still matters.
One thoughtful share can carry Scripture into the life of someone who may never visit a church page, open a devotional, or search for a sermon.
You may never know who reads it quietly.
Who pauses halfway through.
Who opens their Bible afterward.
Who finally asks for prayer.
Who decides to return to church.
Who begins seeking Jesus again.
The outcome belongs to God.
But sharing the truth with love is one simple way we can serve others.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a following around a personality.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to turn conviction into a business.
But to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ through Scripture, biblical teaching, encouragement, repentance, healing, and practical discipleship.
There are people who need more than another passing motivational quote.
They need biblical truth.
They need patient encouragement.
They need to understand the Gospel.
They need to know that holiness matters, repentance matters, and grace is real.
Resources to help you study Scripture.
Strengthen your understanding of the Christian faith.
Develop a more consistent devotional life.
Grow in prayer.
And continue learning what it means to follow Jesus beyond the emotional moment of a single article.
We want those resources to continue reaching people who are hungry for God's Word.
And we want to keep expanding that work.
God is glorified through faith in Christ and lives of love, obedience, worship, and generosity.
And when believers freely choose to support trustworthy Gospel-centered work, that generosity can become one expression of their desire to serve others for His glory.
These products can be everyday reminders of faith, thoughtful gifts, or useful resources for personal growth.
It is the opportunity to help keep biblical encouragement and discipleship resources available to people who need them.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read, learn, pray, share, comment, and use the free resources.
Your value before God is not determined by what you can afford to give.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And genuine Christian generosity must remain willing, not coerced.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, giving is to be done according to what one has decided in the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the hero of this story.
Jesus is.
And that brings us back to the question that began everything.
You call yourself a Christian… but would Jesus recognize the life you're living?
Perhaps, after reading this, you are afraid of what the answer might reveal.
But don't end here staring at your failures.
Look to Christ.
The One who warned about empty religion is the same One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who exposed hypocrisy is the same One who restored Peter.
The One who commanded us to follow Him is the same One who laid down His life for His sheep.
And the One who calls us to repentance is the same One whose resurrection gives us hope for a genuinely new life.
Do not mistake His patience for permission to remain unchanged.
But do not mistake His holiness for an unwillingness to forgive.
Come to Him.
Tell Him the truth.
Turn from the sin you've been defending.
Trust in His finished work.
Ask the Holy Spirit to transform what you cannot repair through appearances or willpower.
And when you stumble, do not build a home in your failure.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Get up.
Follow Him again.
Not to earn the cross.
But because of what Jesus accomplished there.
If you need words to begin, you can pray something like this:

Lord Jesus, You know the person I show the world, and You know the person I am when nobody is watching. You know my sins, my excuses, my fears, and the things I have tried to hide. I cannot save myself through religious appearances or good works. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. I turn to You for forgiveness and new life. Teach me to repent sincerely, trust Your grace, obey Your Word, and love others as You have loved me. Change the desires I keep protecting. Heal what is wounded. Expose what is false. Strengthen what is weak. And let my life increasingly reflect the truth that I belong to You. Amen.
The prayer itself is not a magic formula.
Its words cannot replace genuine faith.
But the Savior to whom it is directed is real.
And His mercy is greater than the religious image you have been trying so desperately to maintain.
One day, the applause will stop.
The notifications will disappear.
The religious titles will mean nothing.
The carefully managed image will no longer be able to speak for you.
And what will matter is not how convincingly you performed Christianity before the world.
What will matter is whether you truly belong to Jesus Christ.
So don't spend your life polishing a Christian image while neglecting the Savior who came to give you a new heart.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be that people discovered you were a sinner. It would be that you spent your life hiding from the only Savior who could redeem you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PAUL BEGGED GOD THREE TIMES TO TAKE AWAY HIS THORN. GOD SAID NO. AND THE REASON WILL CHANGE HOW YOU SEE YOUR OWN SUFFERING.
paragraphs: PAUL BEGGED GOD THREE TIMES TO TAKE AWAY HIS THORN. GOD SAID NO. AND THE REASON WILL CHANGE HOW YOU SEE YOUR OWN SUFFERING.
What if the prayer God hasn't answered is not proof that He has abandoned you—but the very place where Christ is teaching you that His grace can hold you when your strength cannot?
There is a kind of pain that makes even the strongest believer whisper questions they are afraid to say out loud.
“Lord, how much longer?”
“Have I not suffered enough?”
“Why am I still fighting something I have begged You to remove?”
And perhaps the most heartbreaking question of all…
“God, if You really love me, why won't You take this away?”
You prayed.
You fasted.
You cried until there were no tears left.
You confessed your sins. You searched your heart. You opened your Bible, looking for an answer. You listened to sermons about breakthrough, healing, deliverance, and victory.
And yet, when morning came, the pain was still there.
The diagnosis hadn't changed.
The temptation hadn't disappeared.
The grief still followed you into quiet rooms.
The anxiety still pressed against your chest.
The person you loved was still gone.
The battle you thought would end months ago was still waiting for you when you opened your eyes.
And somewhere between another unanswered prayer and another exhausted night, a terrible thought entered your mind.
“Maybe God is disappointed in me.”
But before you accept that thought as truth, you need to hear what happened to one of the most faithful servants of Jesus Christ.
Because the apostle Paul knew what it meant to pray desperately and not receive the answer he wanted.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
And the Lord's answer was not the removal Paul requested.
It was something Paul would eventually treasure more than the strength he had been asking for.
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Read that again.
God did not tell Paul that his suffering was imaginary.
He did not accuse him of lacking faith because he wanted relief.
He did not tell him to pretend the thorn wasn't painful.
Instead, Christ met him in the very weakness Paul wanted to escape.
And that changes everything.
Because sometimes the greatest testimony is not that God removed what was hurting you.
Sometimes the testimony is that Jesus held you while it was still hurting.
Paul was not an ordinary man living an ordinary Christian life.
He had encountered the risen Christ.

He had preached the Gospel across cities and nations. He had endured persecution, imprisonment, beatings, shipwrecks, betrayal, hunger, sleepless nights, and danger from people who wanted him silenced.
He had witnessed the transforming power of the Gospel.
He had seen doors open where there appeared to be no way forward.
He had experienced extraordinary revelations from God.
And yet, in 2 Corinthians 12, this same apostle reveals something deeply personal.
Something humiliating.
Something painful.
Something he could not overcome by determination, experience, or spiritual maturity.
He called it a thorn.
The Greek text describes it as σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί (skolops tē sarki), commonly translated “a thorn in the flesh.”
The word skolops can refer to a thorn or pointed stake. The expression communicates something painfully piercing or afflicting, not merely a minor inconvenience.
Paul writes:
Notice the tension.
Paul describes the affliction as a messenger of Satan, yet he also recognizes that God was accomplishing a purpose through what he suffered.
This does not mean Satan was good.
It does not mean evil suddenly became holy.
It means that even the adversary's hostility could not place Paul's life outside God's sovereign authority.
What was meant to afflict him would not be permitted to have the final word over him.
And the purpose Paul identifies is astonishing.
To keep him from becoming conceited because of the extraordinary revelations he had received.
Think about that.
The man who had been entrusted with remarkable spiritual experiences still needed the humility of dependence.
Paul had seen things that could have made him proud.
But he was learning that revelation without humility could become dangerous.
A person can know much about God and still need to learn how desperately he depends on God.
A person can preach grace to thousands and still need grace to survive the night.
A person can lead others toward Christ and still carry a private struggle nobody sees.
Perhaps that is the part of Paul's story that touches you most.
Because people may know your ministry but not your misery.
They may admire your faith without understanding your fatigue.
They may see your Sunday worship but never hear your Monday crying.
They may call you strong because they have never watched you collapse when the door closes.
And perhaps you have become so skilled at encouraging everyone else that nobody realizes how desperately you need encouragement yourself.
Paul understood something of that contradiction.
He was an apostle.
And he was afflicted.
He was called.
And he was weak.
He belonged to Christ.
And he still needed help.
Your suffering does not automatically disqualify your calling.
Your weakness does not automatically cancel your usefulness.
Your tears do not make your faith counterfeit.
The Bible never promises that faithful Christians will be spared every painful circumstance in this present life.
In fact, Jesus told His disciples:
“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.” — John 16:33, KJV
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not promise a world without trouble.
He promised that trouble would not overturn His victory.
And sometimes we confuse those two things.
We think victory means never hurting again.
But biblical victory begins with belonging to the risen Christ, who has overcome sin and death, even while we await the fullness of His restoration.
Paul understood suffering.
But he did not enjoy it.
He prayed for relief.
“For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me.” — 2 Corinthians 12:8, KJV
The Greek says:
ὑπὲρ τούτου τρὶς τὸν κύριον παρεκάλεσα ἵνα ἀποστῇ ἀπ᾽ ἐμοῦ
Hyper toutou tris ton kyrion parekalesa hina apostē ap' emou.
A faithful rendering is:
“Concerning this, three times I pleaded with the Lord that it might depart from me.”
The verb parekalesa, from parakaleō, carries the sense of appealing, urging, or earnestly asking.
Paul was not casually mentioning an inconvenience.
He was pleading.
He wanted it gone.
And Scripture records three appeals.
We are not told how far apart those appeals occurred or exactly what each occasion looked like.
But we are told enough to understand that Paul sought relief earnestly.
That matters.
Because there are Christians who have been made to feel ashamed for asking God to end their suffering.
As though requesting healing were a failure of surrender.
As though crying for deliverance meant they had not matured spiritually.
As though genuine faith could only say, “Lord, let it continue.”
But Paul asked for the thorn to leave.
And Jesus Himself, in Gethsemane, prayed:
“O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.” — Matthew 26:39, KJV
The suffering of Jesus was unique. He was approaching the cross, where He would bear the sins of His people. Paul's affliction was not the same as Christ's redemptive suffering.
But Gethsemane teaches us something precious about prayer.
Honest anguish and genuine submission are not enemies.
You can ask God to change your circumstances while trusting Him with the outcome.
You can cry for healing and still love the Healer.
You can pray for deliverance without demanding that God obey your timetable.
You can say, “Father, I do not want this,” and still say, “Your will be done.”
And perhaps somebody reading this needs permission to stop pretending.
You do not have to dress your grief in religious language before bringing it to God.
He already knows.
He knows what you whisper into your pillow.
He knows what you cannot explain to your family.
He knows the struggle behind your smile.
He knows the temptation you are ashamed to confess.
He knows the exhaustion you hide because everybody expects you to be strong.
You can bring all of it into His presence.
Not because every desire of your heart is automatically righteous.
Not because every interpretation you have of your suffering is correct.
But because the throne of grace is open to those who come through Jesus Christ.
“Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.” — Hebrews 4:16, KJV
And then comes the answer that has comforted suffering believers for centuries.
“And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
The original Greek is especially beautiful:
Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου, ἡ γὰρ δύναμις ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελεῖται.
Arkei soi hē charis mou, hē gar dynamis en astheneia teleitai.
“My grace is sufficient for you, for power is brought to its intended fullness in weakness.”
The Greek word ἀρκεῖ (arkei) means “is sufficient” or “is enough.”
χάρις (charis) means “grace.”
δύναμις (dynamis) means “power.”
And ἀσθένεια (astheneia) means “weakness,” a word that can encompass frailty, limitation, or incapacity.
The verb τελεῖται (teleitai) communicates being completed, accomplished, or brought to its intended goal.
Christ's power was not deficient and waiting for Paul's suffering to improve it.
Rather, Christ's already-perfect power would be displayed fully through Paul's weakness.
Do you see the difference?
God was not telling Paul that weakness was stronger than divine power.
He was telling him that divine power did not depend on human strength.
Paul did not have to become invulnerable before Christ could work through him.
He did not have to escape every limitation before his life could glorify God.
The grace of Jesus was enough to sustain him in the calling Christ had given him.
But we must be careful here.
The Bible does not say every illness, trauma, disability, or hardship has been personally assigned by God to teach us humility.
Paul identifies a particular purpose for his particular affliction.
We should not presume to know the hidden reason behind someone else's suffering.
And we should never use Paul's thorn to discourage medical treatment, counseling, practical assistance, protection from abuse, or continued prayer for healing.
God's grace can sustain believers through suffering, and His provision may include physicians, medicine, wise counselors, faithful friends, and the care of the church.
The lesson is not that you must remain in every painful circumstance.
The lesson is that when relief has not yet come, the grace of Christ has not become powerless.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us have been waiting for the wrong evidence that God is near.
We thought His presence would be proven when the problem disappeared.
When the marriage was restored.
When the test results came back clear.
When the bills were paid.
When the nightmares stopped.
When the addiction no longer tempted us.
When the grief no longer interrupted ordinary days.
And we began measuring God's love by how quickly our circumstances improved.
But the cross will not allow us to measure divine love that way.
At Calvary, the beloved Son of God suffered.
Not because the Father had ceased to love Him.
Not because Jesus had failed.
But because, according to God's saving purpose, the sinless Savior was giving His life for sinners.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8, KJV
The clearest proof of God's love is not the absence of suffering.
It is Jesus Christ crucified and risen for our salvation.
That truth does not answer every question about why God permits particular sorrows.
But it tells us where to look when suffering tempts us to doubt His heart.
Look to the cross.
Look to the Savior whose hands were pierced.
Look to the empty tomb.
Look to the One who did not merely speak about suffering from a safe distance but entered our broken world and conquered death.
Paul's thorn points us toward dependence on Christ.
But Christ's wounds point us toward redemption.
And there is an enormous difference between those two things.
Paul could not save himself through suffering.
Neither can you.
Your pain does not purchase forgiveness.
Your endurance does not pay for your sins.
Your tears do not make you worthy of heaven.
Only Jesus saves.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
This is where the Gospel breaks through our obsession with proving ourselves.
You cannot impress God into loving you.
You cannot suffer enough to earn His acceptance.
You cannot manufacture spiritual strength that makes you independent of His mercy.
Salvation is not a reward for the unbroken.
It is God's gift to sinners who trust in Jesus Christ.
And that includes the ashamed.
The exhausted.
The repentant.
The person who fell again after promising never to fall.
The believer who is tired of fighting a hidden battle.
The one who has spent years looking respectable while carrying guilt that feels unbearable.
Consider Paul himself.
Before he became a messenger of Christ, he was Saul, a persecutor of the church.
He approved of Stephen's death.
He pursued believers.
He sought to destroy the very community he would later serve.
His past was not a harmless misunderstanding.
It involved real sin and real harm.
Yet the risen Jesus confronted him.
And the persecutor became a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
Paul later wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” — 1 Timothy 1:15, KJV
And then he explained why mercy had been shown to him: so that Jesus Christ might demonstrate His longsuffering as an example to those who would believe in Him for everlasting life.
What a testimony.
The man who once hunted Christians became a servant of the Christ he had opposed.
But even after his conversion, even after years of ministry, even after extraordinary revelations, Paul still lived by grace.
Not yesterday's grace alone.
Not the grace that first rescued him alone.
Daily grace.
Sustaining grace.
Grace sufficient for the weakness he could not remove.
That is the Gospel.
Grace is not merely the doorway into the Christian life.
It is the ground on which believers continue to stand.
And that means your story is not finished simply because you are still struggling.
Your past does not have to dictate your future.
Your sin must be confronted, not excused.
Your wounds may need care, not concealment.
Your relationships may require repentance, restitution, boundaries, and patient rebuilding.
But none of those realities place a repentant sinner beyond the saving power of Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not promise that every consequence of your past disappears.
It promises something infinitely greater: forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life in Christ.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
And now we arrive at the part of Paul's testimony that is almost impossible to understand until you have lived long enough to know what weakness feels like.
After Christ answered him, Paul wrote:
“Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
And then:
“For when I am weak, then am I strong.” — 2 Corinthians 12:10, KJV
Paul was not celebrating pain for its own sake.
He was celebrating the sufficiency of Christ.
He was not saying that suffering was pleasant.
He was saying that suffering could not separate him from the power of the Savior.
The Greek expression translated “may rest upon me” uses ἐπισκηνώσῃ (episkēnōsē), a verb associated with dwelling or pitching a tent over someone.
It paints a remarkable picture.
Paul's weakness becomes the setting in which Christ's power rests upon him.
Not because Paul has finally become impressive.
But because he has learned that he does not need to be.
Imagine spending your entire life trying to be strong enough that nobody notices you are struggling.
Imagine believing that your value depends on always having the right answer.
Always keeping the family together.
Always paying the bills.
Always encouraging others.
Always winning.
Always appearing spiritually victorious.
And then imagine discovering that Jesus never asked you to become your own savior.
He asked you to follow Him.
To trust Him.
To abide in Him.
To receive what you cannot manufacture.
To obey Him even when obedience costs you.
To depend on His grace when your resources run dry.
Some of us are exhausted not only because life is difficult, but because we have been carrying the impossible burden of pretending we are sufficient without Christ.
And the Gospel confronts that illusion.
Jesus says:
“For without me ye can do nothing.” — John 15:5, KJV
Nothing of lasting spiritual fruit can be produced apart from Him.
Not by charisma.
Not by religious performance.
Not by popularity.
Not by pretending we never struggle.
And this is why Paul's testimony is so liberating.
He did not need the thorn to disappear before he could testify about the faithfulness of Jesus.
His testimony existed in the middle of the struggle.
Perhaps yours does too.
Maybe you cannot yet say, “God healed me.”
But you can truthfully say, “God has sustained me.”
Maybe you cannot say, “My family has been restored.”
But you can say, “Jesus is teaching me to walk in truth, forgiveness, and wisdom.”
Maybe you cannot say, “The temptation is gone.”
But you can say, “By God's grace, I am learning to resist, confess, seek help, and refuse to make peace with sin.”
Maybe you cannot say, “I no longer grieve.”
But you can say, “I grieve with hope because Christ has risen.”
Those are not insignificant testimonies.
They are evidence that the Gospel reaches into real human lives.
But there is something else we need to understand.
Paul's thorn is not permission to remain comfortable in deliberate sin.
Some people use the language of weakness to excuse behavior Scripture commands them to repent of.
They say, “This is just my thorn,” when what they mean is, “I do not want to surrender this sin.”
But a sinful habit we are called to put to death must not be confused with an affliction Paul pleaded for God to remove.
The Bible tells believers to resist temptation, flee sexual immorality, put away falsehood, turn from bitterness, and walk by the Spirit.
God's grace is not a license to keep sinning without repentance.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” — Romans 6:1–2, KJV
Grace forgives.
Grace restores.
Grace also trains us to reject ungodliness.
If your hidden struggle involves sin, the answer is not to rename it as your destiny.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it to God.
Seek trustworthy accountability where needed.
Turn away from what is destroying your soul.
Trust Christ for mercy and transformation.
And if you have fallen, do not turn your failure into a reason to run farther from the Savior.
Run to Him in repentance.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
Not because sin is small.
But because His sacrifice is sufficient.
And if your suffering is not the result of your own wrongdoing, do not allow anyone to burden you with accusations God has not made.
The disciples once encountered a man born blind and asked Jesus whose sin had caused his condition.
Jesus rejected their assumption that his blindness was the direct consequence of his sin or his parents' sin (John 9:1–3).
We must learn the difference between biblical conviction and careless condemnation.
Not every wound is punishment.
Not every unanswered prayer is rejection.
Not every delayed healing reveals deficient faith.
And not every hardship comes with an explanation we can discover in this life.
Sometimes the most faithful sentence we can speak is simply:
“Lord, I do not understand. But I know You are worthy of my trust.”
That is not the absence of faith.
It can be an expression of faith struggling honestly in the presence of God.
And perhaps right now, you are standing in that very place.
Between what you asked for and what God has permitted.
Between the miracle you hoped to see and the endurance you never wanted to need.
Between the person you used to be and the person Christ is shaping you to become.
You have questions.
You have scars.
You may even have anger that you need to bring honestly before God rather than hide behind a religious smile.
And still, the invitation of Jesus remains.
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — Matthew 11:28, KJV
He does not say, “Come only when you are no longer exhausted.”
He does not say, “Come only after you have solved everything.”
He calls the burdened.
He calls the weary.
He calls sinners to repentance and faith.
He calls His people to continue trusting Him.
And He gives rest that is deeper than the illusion of a trouble-free life.
If you have been waiting to return to Jesus until you feel worthy, you have misunderstood grace.
Come because you need Him.
Come confessing your sin.
Come trusting His finished work on the cross and His resurrection from the dead.
Come willing to follow Him.
And if you already belong to Christ but have grown weary, remember that His faithfulness is not exhausted by your limitations.
His grace has not run out because your strength has.
This is why I want to ask you something deeply personal.
What is the thorn you keep praying about?
Not necessarily something you need to reveal publicly in detail.
Some wounds deserve privacy. Some struggles require professional help and the protection of trusted people.
But in your own heart, before God, can you name what has been weighing on you?
Is it grief?
A physical limitation?
A long season of waiting?
A battle with fear?
The shame of your past?
A burden you have been carrying alone?
Or perhaps your deepest struggle is the fear that God has forgotten you.
Not as a performance.
Not as a promise that you will never stumble.
But as a simple confession that you still want to cling to Jesus.
Your words might remind another weary believer that they are not the only person struggling to trust God.
Think about that friend who always says, “I'm fine,” even though you know life has been hard.
Think about the family member who has quietly withdrawn from fellowship.
Think about the believer who is questioning whether God still hears their prayers.
Think about the person who has not yet understood the grace offered through Jesus Christ.
Send this article to them.
You never know who might be reading your post in silence.
Someone may be searching for the courage to pray again.
Someone may need to hear that repentance is still possible.
Someone may be one conversation away from seeking help.
Someone may be ready to hear the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
You do not have to know every detail of their story to share the truth that changed yours.
Not because these words possess any special power.
But because the Scriptures they point toward remain true even when your emotions fluctuate.
Return to 2 Corinthians 12.
Read it in its context.
Remember Paul's plea.
Remember Christ's answer.
Remember that grace is not measured by the absence of pain.
And remember that the Savior who sustained Paul is the same risen Lord believers worship today.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to substitute online content for the preaching of God's Word, fellowship, prayer, pastoral care, and discipleship in a faithful Christian community.
But to serve as another place where people can encounter Scripture, be encouraged toward repentance and faith, grow in biblical understanding, and find resources that point them back to Jesus Christ.
These resources are offered to encourage serious study, spiritual maturity, and a life shaped by the Gospel.
And if these articles and resources have helped you, I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading.
Not because your salvation, spiritual standing, or God's favor depends on financial support.
Christ has already accomplished what money could never purchase.
But because the work of sharing biblical teaching, preparing discipleship resources, and reaching people with the message of Jesus requires real time, effort, and support.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
If you already give tithes or offerings as part of your Christian stewardship, we encourage you to honor those commitments prayerfully.
If you are unable to give financially, you are no less welcome here.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your thoughtful comments matter.
Your willingness to share sound biblical teaching matters.
Jesus is the reason.
There is room here for the person who has walked with Jesus for decades and for the person who is opening the Bible with serious questions for the first time.
Our desire is that every article, every resource, and every conversation will ultimately point beyond Gospel Warrior to the One who alone can save.
Jesus Christ.
Because a ministry is not the Savior.
A library is not the source of eternal life.
Christ is.
And if this ministry ever becomes more important than the Lord it proclaims, it has lost its purpose.
So please hear the heart behind this invitation.
Follow along because growing in biblical truth is worth your time.
But worship Jesus.
Trust Jesus.
Obey Jesus.
Give glory to Jesus.
Always.
Now, before you leave, I want to return to the question that brought you here.
Why did God say no when Paul pleaded three times for his thorn to be removed?
The text does not record the Lord saying the single word “no.” It records something richer: Christ answered Paul by declaring that His grace was sufficient and His power was made perfect in weakness.
The affliction was not removed in the account.
Paul was given something he needed to understand about the power of Christ.
The thorn humbled him.
It kept him dependent.
And it became the setting in which Christ's sufficiency was displayed.
That is what Scripture explicitly teaches.
But here is what we must never forget.
Paul's particular explanation is not a universal formula for diagnosing every unanswered prayer.
We do not always know why a burden remains.
We do not always see what God is doing.
And faith does not require us to invent explanations when Scripture has not given them.
Sometimes God heals.
Sometimes He delivers.
Sometimes He opens a door we thought was permanently closed.
Sometimes He sustains us through a long season we would never have chosen.
And every believer still waits for the final redemption of the body and the day when Christ will make all things new.
The Christian hope is not that pain will always remain.
It is that pain will not remain forever.
Revelation 21:4 promises a day when God will wipe away every tear, and death, sorrow, crying, and pain will be no more.
That is where the story of suffering believers is heading.
Not toward an endless thorn.
Toward resurrection.
Toward the presence of God.
Toward the complete victory of Jesus Christ.
Paul's thorn did not have the last word.
And neither will yours.
So tonight, if you find yourself praying the same prayer again, do not assume that repetition makes you a failure.
Keep coming to the Father through Jesus.
Ask for healing.
Ask for wisdom.
Ask for deliverance.
Seek the help you need.
Confess the sins you must forsake.
Receive the support of faithful believers.
And entrust the outcome to the Lord whose wisdom is greater than yours and whose love has been revealed at the cross.
You may not have the explanation you wanted.
You may not yet have the relief you requested.
But if you belong to Christ, you have a Savior who will not abandon you.
And perhaps your prayer tonight will sound different.
Not because you have stopped asking for the thorn to be removed.
But because you are beginning to understand that your life is held by Someone stronger than the thorn.

“Lord Jesus, You know what I have been carrying. You know the prayers I have repeated and the answers I still do not understand. Forgive my sins. Correct what needs to change in me. Heal what You will, deliver me from evil, and give me wisdom to seek the help I need. Teach me to trust Your Word when my feelings are overwhelmed. Let Your power be seen in my weakness. Keep my heart near You, and let my life bring glory to Your name. Amen.”
Not with a promise that their suffering will disappear tomorrow.
But with the truth that the risen Christ remains worthy of their trust today.
Because the most unforgettable part of Paul's story is not that he had a thorn.
It is that, even with the thorn, he belonged to Jesus.
And that is the truth I want you to carry with you long after you close this page.
The thorn may still be there when you wake up tomorrow—but so will the grace of the Savior who has promised never to leave His own.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS LET LAZARUS DIE… EVEN THOUGH HE COULD HAVE SAVED HIM. WHY?
paragraphs: JESUS LET LAZARUS DIE… EVEN THOUGH HE COULD HAVE SAVED HIM. WHY?

The most disturbing part of Lazarus’ story isn’t that Jesus arrived four days after his burial. It’s that Jesus knew His friend was dying, loved him deeply, and deliberately stayed where He was. What Jesus revealed at that tomb may forever change how you understand God’s silence, unanswered prayers, suffering, and the terrifying moments when heaven seems too late.
There is something about the story of Lazarus that most Christians read too quickly.
Something uncomfortable.
Something that challenges the comforting picture we sometimes carry of how God should respond when the people He loves are suffering.
Because Lazarus did not die because Jesus lacked the power to heal him.
He did not die because his sisters lacked faith.
And according to the Gospel of John, Jesus did not remain where He was because He had forgotten the family.
Jesus knew. Jesus loved them. And Jesus waited.
Read that again.
The same Jesus who opened blind eyes, cleansed lepers, healed the paralyzed, and restored the sick received news that someone He loved was dying.
And instead of immediately rushing to his bedside, He remained where He was for two more days.
Imagine being Mary.
Imagine being Martha.
Imagine watching your brother struggle to breathe while knowing that somewhere out there was the one Person who could save him.
You have seen what Jesus can do.
You have heard the testimonies.
You know His compassion.
You know His power.
And, more importantly, you know He loves your family.
So you send Him a message.
Not a long explanation.
Not a desperate attempt to convince Him.
Just a sentence that carries the weight of everything you are afraid to lose.
“Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick.” (John 11:3, KJV)
Notice what they did not say.
They did not say, “Lord, the man who deserves Your help is sick.”
They appealed to His love.
Surely, they must have thought, that would be enough.
But Jesus did not come immediately.
And Lazarus died.
Before we go any further, there is a question we need to confront.
What do you do when you know Jesus loves you, but what He allows seems impossible to reconcile with that love?
Because perhaps you have been there.
Not beside a tomb in ancient Bethany, but beside a hospital bed.
Perhaps you prayed over a marriage that still collapsed.
Perhaps you begged God to spare someone, only to stand at their funeral.
Perhaps you pleaded for healing, waited for a breakthrough, or cried through another sleepless night while the circumstances grew worse.
And somewhere between your first prayer and your latest disappointment, a question began forming in the quietest part of your heart.
“Lord, if You love me, why didn't You come sooner?”
That is where the story of Lazarus becomes more than a miracle we admire.
It becomes a confrontation with what we believe about Jesus when His timing does not resemble our expectations.
And the answer begins with one of the most startling sentences in the entire account.
John 11:5–6 says:
“Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus. When he had heard therefore that he was sick, he abode two days still in the same place where he was.”
Do you see the connection?
John does not write that Jesus loved them but stayed.
The Greek text uses the conjunction οὖν (oun), commonly meaning “therefore” or “so.”
John is presenting Jesus' love and His decision to remain as connected, not contradictory.
The opening of verse 5 uses ἠγάπα (ēgapa), from the Greek verb agapaō, meaning “to love.”
The point is not that Jesus suddenly stopped caring.
It is that His love was present even in a decision His friends could not understand.
That does not make suffering painless.
It does not make every delay easy to explain.
And it certainly does not mean that whenever someone dies or a prayer seems unanswered, we can confidently announce that God is preparing a spectacular miracle.
We cannot.
John 11 reveals the particular purpose of Jesus in this particular event. Scripture does not give us permission to pretend we know God's hidden reasons for every tragedy.
But it does reveal something breathtaking about Christ.
His love cannot always be measured by how quickly He changes our circumstances.
Sometimes we want a Savior whose love can be verified by immediate rescue.
But the Jesus of Scripture is not controlled by our deadlines.
And in Bethany, something was about to happen that would reveal far more than His ability to heal a dying man.
It would reveal His authority over death itself.
When Jesus first received the message, He declared:
“This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God might be glorified thereby.” (John 11:4, KJV)
At first, those words seem confusing.
Because Lazarus really did die.
His body was buried.
His sisters mourned.
The tomb was sealed.
So what did Jesus mean?
The expression “not unto death” does not mean Lazarus would never physically die. The narrative itself makes that impossible.
Rather, death would not be the final outcome of this illness.
The purpose Jesus identified would reach beyond the grave, revealing the glory of God through the Son.
The Greek phrase ὑπὲρ τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ (hyper tēs doxēs tou theou) expresses that purpose: “for the glory of God.”
But be careful here.
This is not permission to tell grieving people that God killed their loved one just to make a point.
That is not what we are authorized to say.
The passage identifies the divine purpose in Lazarus' extraordinary story. It does not establish a universal explanation for every death.
And there is another detail that makes the account even more remarkable.
When Jesus finally spoke to His disciples about returning to Judea, they were concerned.
The religious authorities had recently attempted to stone Him.
Going back meant danger.
Yet Jesus chose to go.
His waiting was not cowardice.
His arrival was not accidental.
And when He explained that Lazarus had died, He said something almost shocking:
“And I am glad for your sakes that I was not there, to the intent ye may believe.” (John 11:15, KJV)
Imagine hearing that.
Jesus was glad He had not been there?
Was He glad His friend had died?
No.
The verse identifies the object of His gladness: the disciples' opportunity to believe through what He was about to reveal.
He was not celebrating grief.
He was preparing to demonstrate a truth His followers desperately needed to understand.
Because healing a sick man would reveal His authority over sickness.
But raising a man who had been dead for four days would confront them with an even greater reality.
The One standing before them was not merely a healer who could postpone death. He was the Son of God who possessed authority over it.
And that difference changes everything.
By the time Jesus reached Bethany, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days.
John specifically records that detail.
It matters because this was not a momentary collapse mistaken for death.
Lazarus had been buried.
Mourners had gathered.
His sisters had begun living in the unbearable reality of his absence.
The house where his voice once echoed was now filled with grief.
Perhaps his place at the table remained painfully empty.
Perhaps every familiar object reminded them that someone they loved would never walk through the doorway again.
And then Martha heard that Jesus was coming.
She went out to meet Him.
What she said was not polished religious language.
It was grief speaking to the only Person she believed could have prevented her loss.
“Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.” (John 11:21, KJV)
There it is.
The sentence so many believers are afraid to say aloud.
Lord, if You had intervened, my family might still be together.
Lord, if You had answered sooner, perhaps the diagnosis would have been different.
Lord, if You had stopped what happened, I would not be carrying this pain.
Martha did not hide her disappointment behind a spiritual performance.
She brought it to Jesus.
