And through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, He provides forgiveness and reconciliation for those who repent and believe.
The cross does not tell us that our sin was small.
It tells us that God's mercy is astonishingly great.
And this is why Christianity is not merely about becoming a better person.
It is about being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
It is about receiving forgiveness we could never purchase.
It is about being transformed by grace rather than pretending we never needed it.
It is about a Savior who died and rose again.
A living Lord who calls sinners to repentance and faith.
And now, after seeing David's water poured out before God and Christ's blood shed for our salvation, we have to ask something deeply uncomfortable.
What are we doing with the life Jesus has given us?
Not to repay Him.
Because we cannot repay the cross.
Not to purchase His forgiveness.
Because salvation is not for sale.
Not to earn His love.
Because grace cannot be earned by religious performance.
But because those who have received mercy are called to live in grateful surrender.
Paul writes:
Notice the order.
By the mercies of God.
Mercy comes first.
Then surrender.
Grace comes first.
Then transformed living.
We do not offer ourselves so that Christ will finally love us.
We offer ourselves because, in Christ, we have encountered a love that changes everything.
And that surrender reaches into ordinary life.
The way you speak to your family.
The way you treat people who cannot benefit you.
The way you handle money.
The way you respond when nobody is watching.
The way you confess sin instead of defending it.
The way you serve without needing applause.
The way you forgive because you have been forgiven.
The way you use whatever God has entrusted to you.
Your time.
Your opportunities.
Your abilities.
Your resources.
Your influence.
Your voice.
All of it can become an expression of gratitude to the Lord.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
Not because God needs our financial contributions to remain sovereign.
But because the Gospel we have received freely is worth proclaiming faithfully.
Paul reminds us:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
And he specifically teaches that giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion.
That matters.
Christian generosity is not supposed to be manipulated through guilt.
It is a willing response to grace.
When believers prayerfully support sound biblical teaching, discipleship, evangelism, and resources that help people grow in Christ, their generosity can participate in meaningful Gospel work.
But we should also make an important biblical distinction.
Christians hold different convictions about how Old Testament tithing relates to giving under the new covenant.

And yet, if this ministry has strengthened your faith, helped you understand Scripture, or encouraged you to return to Jesus, perhaps you have an opportunity to help that same encouragement reach someone else.
Someone you will never meet.
Someone who is quietly searching for answers.
Someone who is one difficult night away from giving up.
Someone who has never opened a Bible because nobody has helped them understand where to begin.
Someone who thinks their past is too shameful for God to forgive.
Someone who desperately needs to hear that repentance is possible, mercy is real, and Jesus Christ still saves.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the church.
Not to glorify a personality.
Not to build a kingdom around a human name.
But to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ through Scripture, Gospel-centered encouragement, biblical discipleship, and resources that nourish spiritual growth.
And if you believe that work matters, there are meaningful ways to stand with it.
Not merely because sharing increases visibility, but because somebody connected to you may need the truth you just encountered.
You can send it privately to someone who has become weary in serving others.
You can save it for the day you need to remember that God sees what human beings overlook.
It is one practical way to participate in the work, according to your means and convictions.
Not an obligation.
Not a spiritual transaction.
But an opportunity to give willingly toward something you believe honors Christ.
These are not simply items to own. They can become everyday reminders of biblical truth, thoughtful gifts, and opportunities to start conversations about Jesus.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
The Word of God is not a luxury.
And no one should be made to feel that financial support is the price of being welcomed into Christian encouragement.
If you cannot, you are still welcome.
You can still read.
Still learn.
Still pray.
Still share.
Still grow.
Still belong among those seeking to know and follow Christ.
The greatest gift you can give God is not a payment for His grace, but a life surrendered to Jesus Christ because of His grace.
That brings us back to the well in Bethlehem.
Back to those three warriors.
Back to the dangerous journey.
Back to David holding the water.
Think about what would have happened if David had simply drunk it.
The water would have satisfied his thirst for a moment.
And then it would have been gone.
But because David poured it out before the Lord, the moment became a testimony preserved in Scripture.
Thousands of years later, we are still reading about it.
Still examining its meaning.
Still learning about reverence, sacrifice, leadership, and the value of human life.
And there is something worth noticing.
We do not know the names of these three warriors with certainty from this particular episode.
The passage identifies them as three of David's mighty men, but does not explicitly name the three who fetched the water.
Their courage is remembered even though their identities in this event are not fully established.
That is a powerful reminder for anyone who has ever felt invisible.
You do not need to become famous for your faithfulness to matter.
You do not need thousands of followers for your obedience to be significant.
You do not need applause for your service to be seen by God.
And you certainly do not need to risk your life recklessly to prove your worth.
Faithfulness is not measured by how much danger you can endure.
Sometimes faithfulness means serving courageously.
Sometimes it means refusing to exploit another person's devotion.
Sometimes it means acknowledging that what you desire is not worth the harm it could bring to someone else.
Sometimes it means surrendering something good because honoring God matters more than satisfying yourself.
And sometimes…
It means finally admitting that you cannot save yourself.
That your good works cannot erase your sins.
That your religious appearance cannot heal your heart.
That your past cannot be rewritten through denial.
That you need Jesus.
Not simply as an inspiration.
Not merely as a moral example.
But as Savior.
As Lord.
As the crucified and risen Son of God.
The One who can forgive your sin and make you new.
Maybe you have spent years trying to outrun your past.
Maybe you have carried a secret shame so long that you no longer remember what peace feels like.
Maybe you have become skilled at telling everyone, “I'm fine,” while privately falling apart.
Maybe you have been angry with God because your sacrifices seemed unnoticed.
Or maybe you have been the person who took others for granted, and this story has exposed something you would rather not confront.
Whatever brought you here, do not leave this moment with only an emotional reaction.
Bring it to Christ.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Ask forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Extend gratitude where you have overlooked sacrifice.
Seek reconciliation where it is wise and possible.
And place your hope, not in your ability to become perfect overnight, but in the finished work of Jesus Christ.
Because the Christian message is not that broken people can somehow earn a second chance by trying harder.
It is that Jesus Christ died for sinners, rose again, and calls us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
And that grace does not leave us unchanged.
It teaches us to turn from sin.
To pursue holiness.
To love truth.
To walk humbly.
To serve faithfully.
To keep coming back to the Savior who alone can redeem us.
Perhaps that is why this story is so unforgettable.
It begins with thirst.
It moves through danger.
It reaches a moment of astonishing sacrifice.
And it leaves us standing before a question much greater than why David refused a drink.
If David could recognize the value of lives risked for a cup of water, how should we respond to the Savior who willingly gave His life for our salvation?
Not with empty religious performance.
Not with fear-driven giving.
Not with public displays designed to impress others.
But with repentance.
Faith.
Gratitude.
Love.
Obedience.
And a heart that belongs to Him.
If this story has exposed an area of your life that needs surrender, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
You do not need to reveal private details or tell the world everything you are carrying.
Sometimes an honest prayer is enough to begin a conversation that leads someone back to Scripture and to the hope found in Christ.
And if this article reminded you of someone who has sacrificed quietly for your sake, consider telling them.
Do not wait until their funeral to honor what they gave while they were alive.
Thank them now.
Pray for them now.
Show love while you still have the opportunity.
And invite others to join us, not simply to grow an audience, but to help more people encounter the truth of God's Word.
Because at the end of everything, it is not the size of a platform that matters most.
It is faithfulness to Jesus Christ.
It is the Gospel being proclaimed truthfully.
It is sinners hearing the call to repentance.
It is believers being strengthened.
It is the lost being invited to come to the Savior.
And it is every ounce of glory being returned to the One who deserves it.
Now picture David one final time.
The water is in his hands.
The warriors are standing before him.
The well is far away.
The danger is over.
And David pours the water out before the Lord.
The earth receives what his lips will never taste.
He refuses to make their costly devotion an ordinary indulgence.
And centuries later, at Calvary, the greater Son of David gives something infinitely more precious than water.
His own life.
Not for His own thirst.
But for our salvation.
So when you remember the water David refused to drink, remember the blood Jesus willingly shed.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that forgiveness is offered through the risen Christ.
And remember that no matter how stained your past may be, repentance and faith in Jesus Christ open the way to reconciliation with God.
David poured out water because he recognized the cost of another man's life. Jesus poured out His life because He knew the cost of saving yours.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT IF THE DEVIL ISN’T ATTACKING YOU… WHAT IF GOD IS CONFRONTING YOU?
paragraphs: WHAT IF THE DEVIL ISN’T ATTACKING YOU… WHAT IF GOD IS CONFRONTING YOU?

We have become so quick to rebuke the enemy that sometimes we refuse to recognize our own responsibility. But what if the very thing you keep calling spiritual warfare is actually the mercy of God exposing what you have been unwilling to change?
There is a kind of prayer that sounds spiritual but can hide a dangerous refusal to take responsibility.
“Lord, the enemy is attacking my marriage.”
“Lord, Satan is destroying my relationships.”
“Lord, the devil is blocking my blessings.”
“Lord, people are coming against me because of my calling.”
And sometimes, those prayers come from a place of genuine spiritual warfare.

Scripture does not deny the existence of Satan. Jesus Himself was tempted by the devil in the wilderness. Peter warned believers to remain watchful because their adversary prowls like a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8). Paul reminded the church that our struggle is not ultimately against flesh and blood (Ephesians 6:12).
Spiritual warfare is real.
What if the enemy you keep rebuking is not the reason your life keeps falling apart?
What if your marriage is struggling because you have stopped listening?
What if your friendships keep ending because you refuse correction?
What if your finances are suffering because you keep making decisions without wisdom or restraint?
What if the peace you are praying for cannot grow because you keep returning to the very behavior that destroys it?
And what if the people you have labeled enemies are sometimes the very people God has allowed to speak a truth you desperately need to hear?
Read that again.
Because not every uncomfortable conversation is persecution.
Not every closed door is demonic opposition.
Not every consequence is a curse.
And not everyone who confronts you is being used by Satan.
Sometimes the most dangerous thing standing between you and spiritual growth is not an invisible enemy.
Sometimes it is the version of yourself that refuses to be corrected.
And if that sentence stings, please do not leave yet.
Because this is not a story about how terrible you are.
It is about how deeply Jesus loves people He refuses to leave unchanged.
Imagine a man sitting alone in his car outside his house.
The engine is off. The street is quiet. His phone is resting beside him.
Another argument with his wife.
Another evening ending in silence.
Another message from someone he loves saying, “I cannot keep doing this.”
He closes his eyes and whispers, “God, why is the enemy attacking my family?”
And he means it.
He loves God. He attends church. He listens to sermons. He knows how to pray.
But he also knows something else.
He knows how sharply he speaks when he is angry.
He knows how quickly he becomes defensive when his wife expresses pain.
He knows how often he apologizes without actually changing.
He knows that whenever someone confronts him, he finds a way to make himself the victim.
Yet somehow, in every prayer, the devil gets blamed for the damage his own words have caused.
Then, in the quiet of that car, a painful thought crosses his mind.
“What if I have been asking God to remove an attack when I should have been asking Him to change my heart?”
No thunder.
No dramatic vision.
Just a man finally becoming willing to tell the truth.
That is where repentance can begin.
And perhaps someone reading this is closer to that moment than they want to admit.
Because it is possible to love the language of spiritual warfare while avoiding the discipline of spiritual maturity.
It is possible to quote Scripture while refusing to obey the very Scripture we quote.
It is possible to pray against pride in other people while protecting pride in ourselves.
And it is possible to become so convinced that everyone is against us that we stop asking whether anyone might actually be trying to help us.
The Bible gives us a sobering example.
King David was not an unbeliever. He was not a stranger to God's presence. He was a man who had experienced extraordinary victories, divine deliverance, and the mercy of the Lord.
Yet David committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged for her husband Uriah to be killed.
You can read the account in 2 Samuel 11.
For a time, David continued living as king.
He still had authority.
He still had a throne.
He still possessed the outward appearance of someone blessed by God.
But something was terribly wrong beneath the royal garments.
Then God sent the prophet Nathan.
Nathan told David a story about a rich man who took a poor man's only lamb.
David became furious.
He could clearly recognize injustice when someone else was responsible for it.
But he could not yet see the injustice in himself.
And then Nathan spoke four devastating words.
“Thou art the man.” — 2 Samuel 12:7, KJV
Imagine the silence.
The king who could identify another man's sin was suddenly forced to confront his own.
David could have accused Nathan of rebellion.
He could have called the confrontation a spiritual attack.
He could have used his position to silence the prophet.
He could have declared that anyone questioning God's anointed king was opposing God Himself.
But David did something different.
He confessed.
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13, KJV
There was no elaborate defense.
No attempt to blame Bathsheba.
No accusation against Nathan.
No convenient explanation about the pressures of leadership.
Just the truth.
And in that confession, we see something that our generation desperately needs to recover.
Accountability is not always an attack on your calling. Sometimes it is God's mercy protecting you from what your uncorrected character could destroy.
But notice something equally important.
David's confession did not erase every earthly consequence of his actions.
God forgave David, yet the consequences of his sin remained deeply painful.
That distinction matters.
Forgiveness is real.
Grace is real.
Restoration is real.
But grace is not permission to pretend that our decisions have no consequences.
In Psalm 51, David gives us one of Scripture's most profound prayers of repentance.
He cries:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10, KJV
The Hebrew expression translated “create in me” is בְּרָא־לִי (berāʾ-lî), from the verb בָּרָא (bārāʾ), meaning “to create.”
It is the same Hebrew verb used in Genesis 1:1 when Scripture declares that God created the heavens and the earth.
That connection is extraordinary.
David was not merely asking God to improve his public image.
He was pleading for an inward work that only God could accomplish.
The word translated “clean” is טָהוֹר (ṭāhôr), carrying the sense of purity or cleanness.
And the Hebrew word for heart, לֵב (lēb), encompasses the inner person, including thought, desire, and will.
David was asking for something deeper than relief from embarrassment.
He wanted a heart made clean before God.
Not merely a reputation repaired before people.
Not merely consequences removed.
Not merely the discomfort of conviction silenced.
He wanted transformation.
And perhaps that is the prayer some of us have been avoiding.
Because we would rather pray, “Lord, expose my enemies,” than “Lord, expose what is wrong in me.”
We would rather ask God to vindicate our behavior than surrender our behavior to His judgment.
We want victory without examination.
Deliverance without repentance.
Restoration without responsibility.
But Jesus never promised that following Him would mean never being confronted.
In fact, He taught something radically different.
In Matthew 7:3–5, Jesus describes a person who notices a speck in someone else's eye while ignoring a beam in their own.
Think about that picture.
Someone attempting delicate eye surgery while a massive piece of wood obstructs their own vision.
It is almost absurd.
And that is precisely the point.
Jesus was exposing the hypocrisy of people who become experts in identifying everyone else's failures while remaining strangely blind to their own.
The Greek word translated “hypocrite” in Matthew 7:5 is ὑποκριτά (hypokrita), a form of ὑποκριτής (hypokritēs).
In this context, it identifies someone whose outward judgment of another is contradicted by their own unaddressed sin.
Jesus did not tell His followers to ignore every problem in other people.
He told them to deal with their own obstruction first so they could see clearly enough to help.
That is not condemnation.
That is a call to humility.
And humility is difficult when we have built our entire identity around always being the wounded one, the misunderstood one, the betrayed one, the person everyone else has supposedly wronged.
There are people who have genuinely been betrayed.
There are believers who have endured abuse, manipulation, rejection, persecution, and injustice.
Their suffering must never be dismissed.
Accountability does not mean blaming victims for what others did to them.
And no one should be pressured to remain in an abusive or dangerous situation simply to prove that they are humble, forgiving, or spiritually mature.
But there is another reality we must confront.
Sometimes we are not only the people who have been hurt.
Sometimes we have also hurt others.
Sometimes we are not only the ones who need healing.
We are the ones who need to repent.
And both truths can exist in the same person.
You can have wounds that deserve compassion and habits that require correction.
You can have experienced betrayal and still be responsible for the way you treat others.
You can need God's comfort and God's conviction at the same time.
One does not cancel the other.
Consider Peter.
Peter loved Jesus.
He was passionate, outspoken, courageous at moments, and fiercely confident in his loyalty.
When Jesus warned that His disciples would stumble, Peter insisted that even if everyone else fell away, he would not.
Yet before the rooster crowed, Peter denied knowing Jesus three times.
Luke 22:61 records that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The man who had confidently declared his loyalty suddenly realized the depth of his failure.
And Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Jesus did not need to invent a false accusation to humble Peter.
Peter's own actions exposed the gap between his confidence and his character.
But the story did not end beside that fire of denial.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, Jesus asked Peter three times whether he loved Him.
The conversation was painful.
Personal.
Restorative.
Jesus did not pretend Peter had never failed.
Neither did He declare that Peter's failure made him forever useless.
Instead, Jesus recommissioned him to care for His sheep.
That is the beauty of Gospel restoration.
Jesus does not heal us by denying what happened. He heals us through truth, grace, and a restored relationship with Him.
Some of us want the restoration of Peter without the honesty of Peter.
We want Jesus to entrust us with greater responsibility while we refuse to acknowledge how we mishandled the responsibility we already had.
We want the next door opened without examining why the last one closed.
We want new relationships while repeating the patterns that wounded the old ones.
We want a fresh beginning without surrendering the behaviors that made the previous season so destructive.
But what if the greatest miracle God wants to work in your life right now is not changing everyone around you?
What if it is changing you?
Not because everyone else is innocent.
Not because your suffering is imaginary.
Not because the enemy is never active.
But because the Holy Spirit is deeply concerned with the condition of your heart.
James 1:14 teaches:
“But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.” — KJV
James is not denying spiritual opposition.
He is reminding believers that sinful desire within the human heart also matters.
We cannot blame every sinful decision on the devil.
The enemy may tempt.
The world may pressure.
Our flesh may desire.
But we are still called to resist temptation, confess sin, and walk in obedience.
James 4:7 says:
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” — KJV
Notice the order.
Submit to God.
Resist the devil.
We sometimes emphasize the second command while neglecting the first.
We want authority to resist darkness while resisting God's authority over our own decisions.
We want to rebuke the enemy while refusing to surrender our bitterness.
We want to cast out fear while feeding our minds with deception.
We want to defeat division while spreading gossip.
We want the protection of truth while continuing to lie.
But spiritual warfare cannot become a substitute for spiritual obedience.
You cannot repent on behalf of someone else.
You cannot blame your way into holiness.
And you cannot rebuke away a pattern of behavior you are determined to keep practicing.
The apostle Paul makes this deeply practical.
Ephesians 4 calls believers to put away falsehood, speak truthfully, deal with anger without sinning, stop stealing, work honestly, abandon corrupt speech, and forgive one another.
These are not glamorous instructions.
They do not always produce dramatic testimonies.
They rarely look impressive on a stage.
But they reveal what transformed lives actually look like.
A husband who learns to listen.
A wife who chooses truth instead of manipulation.
A parent who apologizes to a child.
A pastor who welcomes appropriate accountability rather than hiding behind spiritual authority.
A ministry leader who handles money transparently.
A Christian who stops spreading rumors disguised as prayer requests.
A believer who finally says, “I was wrong, and I need to make this right.”
That is not weakness.
That is evidence of the Spirit's work.
Proverbs 12:1 says:
“Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish.” — KJV
The Hebrew word translated “reproof” is תּוֹכַחַת (tôkhaḥat), which refers to correction, rebuke, or reproof.
Biblical wisdom does not treat all correction as hostility.
It recognizes that truthful correction can protect us from foolishness.
Of course, not everyone who criticizes you is correct.
Some criticism is unfair.
Some correction is abusive.
Some accusations are false.
Some people use the language of accountability to control others.
That is why discernment matters.
Biblical accountability must be rooted in truth, humility, love, and justice.
Galatians 6:1 tells spiritually mature believers to restore someone caught in wrongdoing with gentleness, while remaining watchful over themselves.
The Greek word translated “restore” is καταρτίζετε (katartizete), from καταρτίζω (katartizō), meaning to restore, put in order, or make fit.
The goal is not humiliation.
It is restoration.
Not public destruction.
Not superiority.
Not revenge disguised as righteousness.
Restoration.
And that means accountability is not a weapon we use to crush people.
It is a responsibility we exercise with humility, care, and reverence for God.
When correction is genuine, we should examine it rather than automatically reject it.
When accusations are false, we can respond truthfully without surrendering to bitterness.
When harm has occurred, repentance may require restitution, changed behavior, appropriate boundaries, and the patient rebuilding of trust.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore trust.
And reconciliation does not always mean returning to the same relationship or situation.
Grace never requires us to abandon wisdom.
Now consider something even more uncomfortable.
Have you ever noticed how quickly we can identify spiritual attacks when our own comfort is threatened?
Someone challenges our behavior.
“That's the enemy trying to discourage me.”
Someone questions our decision.
“That's Satan trying to block my purpose.”
Someone asks us to explain how we handled money, leadership, or responsibility.
“That's persecution against God's work.”
But what if the question is legitimate?
What if the concern is justified?
What if the person speaking is not trying to destroy you but trying to prevent greater damage?
We must be especially careful when spiritual language becomes a shield against examination.
No pastor is above accountability.
No ministry is above accountability.
No Christian influencer is above accountability.
No spiritual gift, testimony, title, or following places a person beyond the authority of God's Word.
Even the apostle Peter was publicly confronted by Paul when his conduct contradicted the truth of the Gospel (Galatians 2:11–14).
Peter was an apostle.
Yet his position did not make his behavior untouchable.
And Paul's confrontation was not evidence that Paul hated Peter.
It was a necessary defense of Gospel truth.
If an apostle could be corrected, why do some of us behave as though correction is an insult to our anointing?
Maybe because accountability threatens the image we have worked so hard to protect.
We want people to see our faith.
Our strength.
Our sacrifice.
Our spiritual maturity.
But we are afraid they might discover our inconsistency.
And so we hide.
We explain.
We deflect.
We blame.
We spiritualize.
We create elaborate stories about enemies and attacks because the simple truth feels unbearable.
“I was selfish.”
“I lied.”
“I was careless.”
“I became proud.”
“I hurt someone who trusted me.”
“I need help.”
“I need to change.”
Those sentences may be difficult to say.
But they can become the beginning of freedom.
Because the Gospel does not require you to maintain a flawless image.
It calls you to come honestly to a flawless Savior.
First John 1:8–9 says:
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
The Greek verb translated “confess” in verse 9 is ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), from ὁμολογέω (homologeō), meaning to confess, acknowledge, or admit.
The word carries the idea of openly acknowledging what is true.
In this passage, confession means honestly acknowledging our sins before God rather than denying them.
And look at the promise.
God is faithful and just to forgive.
He cleanses.
He does not invite us to confess so He can enjoy humiliating us.
He invites us into the light because darkness cannot give us the fellowship, forgiveness, and cleansing we need.
This is where everything changes.
Because Christianity is not a religion of people pretending they have never fallen.
It is the good news of Jesus Christ saving sinners who cannot save themselves.
At the cross, Jesus bore our sins.
He did not excuse evil.
He did not declare rebellion harmless.
He did not redefine sin so that nobody would feel uncomfortable.
He took sin seriously enough to give His life for sinners.
And He loved sinners deeply enough to do it willingly.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
Not while we were already perfect.
Not after we had repaired every relationship.
Not once we had learned to behave respectably.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
And on the third day, He rose again.
That is why repentance is not hopelessness.
That is why confession does not have to become self-destruction.
That is why accountability, rightly practiced, can become part of a believer's journey toward healing.
Because the same Jesus who exposes sin offers forgiveness to the repentant.
The same Savior who calls us to deny ourselves also promises His presence as we follow Him.
The same Lord who confronted Peter restored him.
The same God who heard David's confession remains merciful to sinners who turn to Him.
But do not misunderstand grace.
Grace is not God agreeing to leave us enslaved to the sins that are destroying us.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains believers to reject ungodliness and worldly passions and to live godly lives.
Grace forgives.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
And sometimes the training of grace feels uncomfortable because it challenges something we have been defending for years.
Maybe your anger.
Maybe your dishonesty.
Maybe your jealousy.
Maybe your secret addiction.
Maybe your habit of blaming everyone else.
Maybe the way you treat your spouse behind closed doors.
Maybe the way you handle criticism.
Maybe your refusal to seek help because admitting a problem feels like admitting defeat.
But seeking help is not defeat.
Confessing sin is not defeat.
Making restitution is not defeat.
Learning to listen is not defeat.
Taking responsibility is not defeat.
Sometimes the first visible evidence that pride is losing its grip is a person finally becoming willing to say:
“I need to change.”
And perhaps the most powerful prayer you can pray tonight is not, “God, fight everyone who is against me.”
Perhaps it is:
“Lord, show me where I am wrong.”
“Show me what I have been refusing to see.”
“Show me whom I have hurt.”
“Show me where I have confused conviction with condemnation.”
“Show me where I need boundaries and where I need repentance.”
“Give me courage to receive truthful correction.”
“And teach me to stop using spiritual language to avoid spiritual growth.”
That prayer takes courage.
Because God may bring something to your attention that requires an apology.
He may convict you about a habit you have justified.
He may lead you to seek wise counsel.
He may show you that a relationship needs repair.
He may also reveal that you have accepted blame for harm that was never yours to carry.
True accountability is not automatic self-condemnation.
It is an honest willingness to bring the facts, our actions, and our motives into the light of God's truth.
And sometimes, that truth brings both correction and comfort.
There is a beautiful distinction in 2 Corinthians 7:10:
“For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.” — KJV
The Greek word for repentance here is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It refers to repentance, a genuine turning of heart and mind that bears fruit in changed conduct.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about what happened.
It is not performing tears so people will stop asking questions.
It is not apologizing only because consequences have arrived.
It is a genuine turning toward God that becomes visible in how we live.
A person can cry and remain unrepentant.
A person can feel embarrassed and remain unchanged.
A person can quote a hundred verses and still refuse responsibility.
But when the grace of Christ produces genuine repentance, the direction of a life begins to change.
Not instant perfection.
Not a flawless record.
But a real turning.
A willingness to make things right where possible.
A willingness to learn.
A willingness to be corrected again.
A willingness to walk in the light even when the light reveals something painful.
And that brings us to the question I want you to carry long after this article disappears from your screen.
Are you fighting a spiritual attack, or are you fighting the accountability that could help you grow?
Do not answer too quickly.
Sometimes it really is spiritual warfare.
Sometimes it is the consequences of our choices.
Sometimes it is injustice committed against us.
Sometimes it is a mixture of spiritual struggle, human weakness, relational conflict, and painful circumstances.
Not every hardship has one simple explanation.
That is why we need Scripture, prayer, discernment, honest self-examination, and trustworthy counsel.
But whatever the cause, we should never become so committed to proving that we are under attack that we refuse to ask whether God is calling us to repent.
Because the goal of following Jesus is not to win every argument about who was wrong.
The goal is to become more like Christ.
And Jesus Christ, though sinless, humbled Himself.
Philippians 2:5 calls believers to have the mind of Christ.
The One who had every right to glory took the form of a servant.
The One who was truly righteous never needed to manufacture righteousness through excuses.
The One who could have called legions of angels endured the cross to accomplish our redemption.
If our Savior embraced humility, how can we defend our pride as though it were a spiritual gift?
If our Savior spoke truth, how can we keep building our lives around excuses?
If our Savior gave Himself for us, how can we keep refusing the surrender He calls us to?
Maybe tonight, someone needs to stop composing another message explaining why everyone else is wrong.
Maybe someone needs to call their spouse and listen without interrupting.
Maybe a parent needs to sit beside a child and say, “I should not have spoken to you that way. Will you forgive me?”
Maybe a ministry leader needs to welcome honest questions rather than punish those who ask them.
Maybe a friend needs to admit that the relationship did not end only because the other person was difficult.
Maybe someone who has been mistreated needs to stop accepting false guilt and seek safety, support, and healing.
And maybe someone who has spent years calling every confrontation an attack needs to recognize that truth can be painful without being an enemy.
I do not know which of those stories resembles yours.
But I know this.
Jesus is not asking you to save yourself by becoming better.
He is calling you to come to Him in repentance and faith, receive His grace, and follow Him into a transformed life.
Your past does not have to become your permanent identity.
Your worst decision does not have to become the final chapter.
Your failure does not have to be the end of your story.
But neither does your pain give you permission to keep hurting others.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
At the empty tomb, hope rises.
And in the life of a repentant believer, the Gospel continues to bear fruit.
Not that Jesus makes every consequence disappear.
Not that every damaged relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
Not that repentance earns salvation.
But that through His death and resurrection, sinners can receive forgiveness, be reconciled to God, and begin walking in newness of life.
And that transformation is not merely a beautiful idea.
It reaches into our homes.
Our conversations.
Our finances.
Our habits.
Our relationships.
Our private decisions.
Our public responsibilities.
Even the way we respond when someone tells us we are wrong.
Before you leave, I want to ask something personal.
What is one area of your life where God may be calling you to take responsibility instead of making another excuse?
You do not have to expose private details or confess something publicly that belongs in a safe, appropriate conversation.
There is no shame in asking for prayer.
You may be surprised how many people are quietly wrestling with the same questions.
And if this article reminded you of someone you love, consider sharing it with them gently, not as a weapon or an accusation, but as an invitation to seek Christ together.
Not because every friend needs to be corrected by you.
But because every one of us needs the Gospel, and someone in your circle may be waiting for a reminder that Jesus offers both truth and grace.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, people who have drifted from faith, and even those who are still searching for answers to follow along.
Because our mission is not to create people who merely know how to sound Christian.
It is to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ, who saves, forgives, restores, and transforms.
And if this ministry has been spiritually nourishing you, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is working to continue and expand the reach of Christ-centered articles, Scripture teaching, discipleship materials, and resources that encourage people to grow in biblical truth.

We want those resources and the message of the Gospel to continue reaching people who may never walk into a church building, who may be silently struggling, or who may be only one honest encounter with Scripture away from beginning to seek Jesus.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, faithful stewardship, and generous giving according to your means and convictions.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not fear.
Not guilt.
These items can serve as everyday reminders of faith, encouragement, and the message of Christ.
It is the opportunity to help sustain a ministry committed to making Jesus known and helping people grow in His Word.
Others will share, pray, encourage, and participate in the conversations.
Every form of sincere support is appreciated.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The grace of Jesus Christ cannot be purchased.
And the invitation to repent, believe, and follow Him remains open regardless of anyone's ability to give.
Now, before you go, return to the question that started all of this.
What if the devil is not behind every difficult thing happening in your life?
What if some of the discomfort you feel is the result of truth finally reaching a place you have kept hidden?
What if God is inviting you to stop defending the old version of yourself and begin surrendering more fully to Christ?
You do not need another excuse to remain unchanged.
You need the Savior who died and rose again to redeem you.
And if He is showing you something that needs to change, do not run from the light.
Bring it to Him.
Confess what is yours to confess.
Reject the guilt that is not yours to carry.
Receive His forgiveness.
Make things right where you can.
Seek help where you need it.
And keep following Jesus.
Because the most dangerous prison is not always the one built by your enemies.
Sometimes it is the one built by the excuses you refuse to surrender.
And the moment you stop defending what is destroying you may be the moment you finally begin to experience the freedom Christ has been calling you into.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS GOD STILL DEMANDING 10% OF YOUR MONEY—OR HAVE CHRISTIANS MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT JESUS ACTUALLY REQUIRES?
paragraphs: IS GOD STILL DEMANDING 10% OF YOUR MONEY—OR HAVE CHRISTIANS MISUNDERSTOOD WHAT JESUS ACTUALLY REQUIRES?

The uncomfortable truth about tithing, Malachi's warning, the New Covenant, and the kind of generosity that cannot be measured by a percentage. What if the question was never simply how much you owe God—but whether He truly has your heart?
There is a Christian somewhere right now staring at the last few bills in their wallet.
The electricity bill is overdue. The refrigerator is nearly empty. Their child needs something for school. Payday is still several days away.
And Sunday is coming.
They remember what someone told them from the pulpit.
"If you don't give God His ten percent, you're robbing Him."

They remember Malachi 3:10. They remember hearing about the windows of heaven opening. They remember the warnings about financial curses and the testimonies of people who supposedly became wealthy because they faithfully tithed.
Now they're afraid.
Not because they don't love Jesus.
Not because they want to keep everything for themselves.
But because they're wondering whether feeding their children before putting ten percent into the offering plate means they're failing God.
And perhaps you've been there.

Perhaps you've given faithfully for years, yet still struggled financially. Perhaps you've felt guilty every time you couldn't reach ten percent. Or perhaps you're on the other side—financially comfortable, faithfully giving exactly ten percent, quietly assuming that means you've fulfilled your responsibility to God.
Here is the question that could unsettle both of you.
What if the New Testament never actually commands Christians to give exactly ten percent of their income to the church?
And what if discovering that truth doesn't make generosity less important—but makes it more beautiful, more sacrificial, and more deeply rooted in Jesus Christ?
Before anyone accuses this message of encouraging Christians to stop giving, understand something.
This is not an argument against supporting the church, helping ministers, caring for the poor, or financing the spread of the Gospel.
Scripture clearly teaches those responsibilities.
This is about something far more important.
We must never place a burden on someone's conscience that Jesus and His apostles did not place there.
And we must never use the fear of losing God's favor to extract money from people whom Christ purchased with His blood.
Because the Gospel is not a financial transaction.
And grace is not something you can purchase with ten percent.
To understand this properly, we need to go back—long before modern church buildings, electronic donations, and envelopes marked "Tithes and Offerings."
We need to go back to the Scriptures themselves.
The Hebrew word commonly translated as "tithe" is מַעֲשֵׂר (maʿăśēr), meaning "a tenth" or "tenth part."
That is what the word means.
A tenth.
But understanding a word's meaning is not the same as understanding whether every command involving that word applies to every believer under every covenant.
That distinction changes everything.
In Genesis 14:18–20, Abraham gives Melchizedek a tenth of the spoils following his victory in battle.
This is significant because it occurs before the Law of Moses.
Some Christians therefore argue that tithing is an eternal principle that predates the Mosaic covenant.
And there is a legitimate observation here: giving a tenth was practiced before Sinai.
But notice what the passage does not say.
It does not command Abraham to give ten percent of his regular income for the rest of his life.
It does not establish a recurring requirement for every future believer.
It describes Abraham giving a tenth of the spoils from a particular victory.
Hebrews 7:4 refers to this event and emphasizes the greatness of Melchizedek, to whom Abraham gave a tenth of the choicest spoils.
The argument in Hebrews 7 is about the superiority of Christ's priesthood—not a new command requiring Christians to pay ten percent to their pastors.
That matters.
Because we cannot turn every historical act recorded in Scripture into a universal command.
In Genesis 28:20–22, Jacob also vows to give God a tenth if God will be with him, provide for him, and bring him home in peace.
Again, the passage is important.
But it records a personal vow, not a universal command to the New Covenant church.
Then we arrive at the Law of Moses.
And here, tithing becomes part of Israel's covenant obligations.
Leviticus 27:30 says in the King James Version:
"And all the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land, or of the fruit of the tree, is the LORD'S: it is holy unto the LORD."
Notice the context.
The tithe concerns agricultural produce from the land.
Leviticus 27:32 also refers to the tenth animal passing under the rod from the herd or flock.
Numbers 18:21 explains that the Levites received tithes in Israel because of their service at the tabernacle.
The Levites had a special role in Israel's worship and did not receive a territorial inheritance like the other tribes.
Deuteronomy 14:22–29 describes further instructions involving tithes, worship, rejoicing before God, and provision for Levites and vulnerable people.
Deuteronomy 26:12–13 connects the third-year tithe with provision for Levites, foreigners, fatherless children, and widows.

The exact calculation and relationship of these tithes have been debated by biblical scholars. Some understand them as multiple distinct tithes, while others understand parts of the legislation differently.
But the central point is unmistakable.
Biblical tithing under Moses was embedded in Israel's covenant system of land, agriculture, priesthood, worship, and community provision.
It was not simply an identical version of a modern Christian giving ten percent of a monthly salary to a local church.
And that brings us to one of the most quoted—and frequently misunderstood—passages in the entire conversation.
Malachi 3:8–10.
"Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me."
Those words have frightened generations of Christians.
Some have heard them delivered with such intensity that they began to imagine God standing over their bank accounts, waiting to punish them for every missing percentage.
But who was Malachi addressing?
Malachi 1:1 identifies the message as the word of the Lord to Israel.
Malachi confronts serious covenant unfaithfulness, including corruption in worship and failures among the priests.
In Malachi 3:9, the warning is addressed to the nation.
And Malachi 3:10 says:
"Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house..."
The Hebrew word translated "storehouse" is אוֹצָר (ʾōṣār), a term referring to a treasury or storage place.
In this context, the storehouse was connected to the temple's provision system.
It was not originally a reference to a modern church's bank account.
Nor was Malachi writing to Gentile Christians living under the New Covenant centuries later.
God was confronting covenant violations within Israel.
Does that mean Malachi has nothing to teach Christians?
Absolutely not.
It teaches us that God takes worship, faithfulness, justice, and provision for His servants seriously.
It warns against religious hypocrisy.
It reveals the seriousness of withholding what was required under that covenant.
But applying a passage's enduring moral lessons is different from declaring that its specific covenant penalties automatically apply to Christians today.
This distinction is crucial.
Because Galatians 3:13 declares:
"Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us..."
Read that again.
Christ redeemed us.
The believer's standing before God rests on Jesus Christ, not on successful completion of a financial percentage.
That does not make greed acceptable.
It does not excuse dishonesty.
It does not eliminate the responsibility to give.
But it does mean that a Christian should not be threatened with the Mosaic covenant's curse as though Christ's redeeming work were insufficient.
And please hear this carefully.
You cannot buy your way out of a curse that Christ has already borne for you.
Now someone will ask the obvious question.
"But didn't Jesus Himself command tithing?"
Let's look at what He actually said.
In Matthew 23:23, Jesus confronts the scribes and Pharisees:
"Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith..."
He continues by saying that they should have practiced the weightier matters without neglecting the others.
So yes, Jesus affirmed the obligation of tithing for those He was addressing in that setting.
We should not pretend otherwise.
But the historical and covenant context matters.
Jesus was speaking to Jewish religious leaders operating within the Mosaic Law before His death and resurrection inaugurated the New Covenant.
His central rebuke was that meticulous religious observance had become a cover for neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
They could count tiny herbs while ignoring suffering human beings.
They could be exact about percentages and terribly wrong about the heart of God.
And that should disturb us.
Because it is possible to give ten percent faithfully while treating people cruelly.
It is possible to put money in an offering plate and still be consumed by pride, greed, bitterness, and self-righteousness.
Jesus was not impressed by religious precision without spiritual integrity.
And neither should we be.
The Greek word used for tithing in Matthew 23:23 is ἀποδεκατοῦτε (apodekatoute), meaning "you give a tenth" or "you tithe."
But Jesus' use of that word in a confrontation with Pharisees does not, by itself, establish a ten-percent command for the post-resurrection church.
The decisive question is what the apostles taught believers under the New Covenant.
And here, something remarkable happens.
When Paul gives explicit instructions about Christian giving, he does not prescribe a mandatory ten-percent minimum.
Instead, he writes in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
Look closely at that verse.
The Greek phrase μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης (mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs) means, in context, not out of sorrow or reluctance, nor out of compulsion or constraint.
And the expression ἱλαρὸν δότην (hilaron dotēn) describes a cheerful giver.
Paul is not saying generosity should be accidental, careless, or based only on temporary emotions.
In fact, the passage calls believers to thoughtful, deliberate generosity.
But the motivation is not coercion.
It is grace.
Not terror.
Not public embarrassment.
Not a threat that God will destroy your finances unless you meet a target.
Grace.
And in 2 Corinthians 8:12, Paul adds another essential principle:
"For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not."
According to what a person has.
Not what they do not have.
Think about the struggling parent at the beginning of this story.
The one staring at an overdue bill.
The one wondering whether God is disappointed because their children need food.
Would it be faithful to tell that parent that God will curse them unless they give away money needed for essential family care?
Paul's teaching gives us reason to reject that kind of coercion.
In 1 Timothy 5:8, he speaks strongly about the responsibility to provide for one's household.
And in 2 Corinthians 8:13, he makes clear that giving is not intended to ease others while placing the giver under crushing hardship.
This does not mean that sacrificial generosity is always comfortable.
Sometimes giving costs us deeply.
Sometimes God calls us to surrender comforts, luxuries, and personal ambitions for the sake of others.
But there is a difference between freely chosen sacrifice motivated by love and financially destructive giving extracted through spiritual intimidation.
The difference is not small.
It is the difference between shepherding people and exploiting them.
And the Bible never gives ministers permission to confuse the two.
Peter warns church leaders in 1 Peter 5:2–3 to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for dishonest gain, and not by dominating those entrusted to them.
A faithful pastor should be able to teach generosity without making poor believers afraid of God.
A faithful ministry should be able to invite financial support without suggesting that salvation, forgiveness, or divine affection can be purchased.
And a faithful Christian should be able to ask questions about church finances without being accused of rebellion.
Because biblical stewardship includes accountability on both sides.
Now perhaps you're thinking:
"So does this mean ten percent is wrong?"
No.
Not at all.
A Christian may freely choose to give ten percent as a disciplined expression of gratitude and stewardship.
For some believers, ten percent may be a helpful starting point.
For others with significant resources, ten percent may be far below what love and generosity could reasonably inspire.
And for someone experiencing severe financial hardship, a smaller amount may represent a genuine and costly sacrifice.
The New Testament does not give every Christian one identical percentage.
It gives us something more searching.
A transformed heart.
In 1 Corinthians 16:2, Paul instructs believers to set something aside regularly, in keeping with how they have prospered.
That establishes a principle of intentional and proportionate giving.
In 2 Corinthians 8–9, he encourages willing, generous, and thoughtful contributions.
In Galatians 6:6, believers are taught to share good things with those who instruct them in the Word.
In 1 Corinthians 9:13–14, Paul teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may rightly receive material support from Gospel ministry.
And in 1 Timothy 5:17–18, faithful elders who labor in preaching and teaching are recognized as worthy of support.
So let us be absolutely clear.
The absence of a mandatory New Covenant ten-percent rule does not mean the absence of a New Covenant responsibility to give.
Christians are called to support Gospel ministry.
Christians are called to help people in need.
Christians are called to share their resources.
Christians are called to resist greed.
Christians are called to generosity that reflects the character of Jesus.
But our giving is not the price of belonging to God.
It is one expression of what belonging to God does to a human heart.
And then there is the widow.
The woman whose story should make every church leader tremble before using it in a fundraising appeal.
In Mark 12:41–44, Jesus watches people putting money into the temple treasury.
Many wealthy people contribute large amounts.
Then a poor widow comes forward.
She gives two small copper coins.
Almost nothing by the world's standards.
Yet Jesus tells His disciples that she has given more than the others, because they gave from abundance while she gave out of her poverty.
It is a powerful picture.
But there is a detail we must not ignore.
Immediately before this scene, Jesus condemns scribes who "devour widows' houses" (Mark 12:40).
Immediately afterward, He foretells the temple's destruction (Mark 13:1–2).

Christians have long understood the widow's gift as an example of extraordinary sacrificial devotion. Other interpreters also emphasize the surrounding warning against a corrupt religious system that consumes the resources of vulnerable people.
These observations deserve careful consideration together.
The widow's story should never become a weapon used to pressure struggling people into giving their last money to an institution.
Jesus noticed her.
He valued what the world considered insignificant.
And He also condemned religious leaders who exploited the vulnerable.
We must not celebrate the widow's sacrifice while ignoring Christ's warning against those who devour widows' houses.
That would miss something essential about the heart of Jesus.
Perhaps the most dangerous misunderstanding in this entire debate is the idea that giving guarantees financial prosperity.
Give ten percent, and God will make you rich.
Give more, and your breakthrough will arrive faster.
Send a seed, and expect a multiplied financial harvest.
But the New Testament does not promise that every generous Christian will become wealthy.
Paul experienced hunger, hardship, and material need.
Faithful believers have suffered poverty and persecution throughout church history.
And in 1 Timothy 6:5–10, Paul warns against treating godliness as a means of financial gain and against the destructive love of money.
Second Corinthians 9 does speak about God's provision and the fruitfulness of generosity.
But the purpose is not to turn God into a mechanism for personal enrichment.
God provides so that His people may abound in good works and continue in generosity.
The ultimate harvest is not necessarily a bigger bank balance.
It includes righteousness, thanksgiving, and glory to God.
If your theology tells you that every faithful giver must become rich, what will you tell the generous believer who remains poor?
That they didn't have enough faith?
That God rejected their offering?
That they must give even more?
That is not a burden we have biblical authority to place upon them.
Jesus Christ is not a vending machine.
And the cross is not a business investment.
But now we must confront another danger.
Because some people will read all of this and immediately feel relieved.
"Good. I don't have to give anything."
And that conclusion would miss the Gospel just as seriously as legalistic tithing does.
Because the New Covenant does not free us from greed so that we can become more selfish.
It frees us to love.
Think about the early church.
Acts 2:44–45 describes believers sharing their possessions and distributing resources according to need.
Acts 4:32–35 portrays a community in which generosity helped ensure that needy believers were cared for.
These passages describe remarkable voluntary sharing, not a command that every Christian must surrender all private property.
Acts 5:4 confirms that Ananias had control over his property and the proceeds of its sale; his sin involved deception, not failure to meet a mandatory giving percentage.
Still, the generosity of the early church is breathtaking.
They understood that the Gospel had changed the way they viewed possessions.
Their money was no longer simply a tool for personal comfort.
It had become a means of serving one another.
And that is where this question becomes personal.
Not "How little can I give and still be considered obedient?"
Not "How much do I need to pay so God will bless my business?"
But something much deeper.
"Lord Jesus, everything I have comes from You. How do You want me to use what You have entrusted to me?"
That question can be uncomfortable.
Because sometimes ten percent is easier than surrender.
A person can give ten percent and still worship the remaining ninety.
A wealthy person can give ten percent without ever experiencing meaningful sacrifice.
A struggling person can give a small amount with extraordinary love.
And someone with almost nothing can honor God through generosity expressed in hospitality, service, prayer, encouragement, and faithful care for others.
Money matters.
But money is not the only measure of love.
And giving money is never a substitute for repentance, justice, mercy, or obedience.
Remember the rich young ruler in Mark 10:17–22.
Jesus did not merely tell him to calculate a tithe.
He exposed the possession that had captured his heart.
The man went away sorrowful because he had great wealth.
The problem was not that his percentage was mathematically incorrect.
The problem was that his riches had become a rival master.
And Jesus said in Matthew 6:24:
"Ye cannot serve God and mammon."
The Greek word μαμωνᾷ (mamōna) refers to wealth or riches as a master competing for devotion.
That warning applies to the rich and the poor.
A wealthy person can idolize abundance.
A struggling person can become consumed by the desperate pursuit of money.
A ministry can also fall into the temptation of treating money as its master.
That is why the church must preach both generosity and integrity.
Because when a ministry asks people to give, it carries a sacred responsibility to use those gifts faithfully.
Every offering represents someone's labor.
Someone's sacrifice.
Someone's decision to trust.
And behind some of those gifts are stories no one else can see.
A widow quietly helping others.
A worker setting aside a small amount from an exhausting paycheck.
A young believer giving from their first earnings.
These are not merely financial transactions.
They are acts of worship when offered freely in faith and love.
And they deserve to be handled with reverence.
Now we come to the heart of the matter.
The most important gift in Christianity is not the money we give God.
It is the gift God gave us.
Second Corinthians 8:9 says:
"For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich."
Paul places this truth directly inside his teaching about generosity.
The riches in view are rooted in the grace and saving work of Christ, not a universal guarantee of personal financial wealth.
Jesus gave Himself.
He entered our broken world.
He carried our sin.
He endured the cross.
He rose from the dead.
And He opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
We were spiritually bankrupt.
We could not purchase forgiveness.
We could not earn righteousness.
We could not contribute enough to erase our guilt.
But Christ paid the price we could never pay.
Not with coins.
Not with livestock.
Not with a tenth of His possessions.
With His own life.
First Peter 1:18–19 reminds believers that redemption was not accomplished with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
So when someone asks, "How much do I owe God?" the Gospel takes us somewhere deeper than arithmetic.
We owe Him our worship, our trust, our obedience, our gratitude—our very lives.
Not as payment for salvation.
But because salvation has been given to us by grace.
Romans 12:1 calls believers to present their bodies as living sacrifices to God.
That is the language of a whole life surrendered.
And a surrendered life includes our finances.
But it cannot be reduced to our finances.
Here is where I want to speak to two people.
First, to the person who has been giving faithfully for years.
Please don't hear this article as a dismissal of your sacrifice.
If you have been setting aside ten percent with joy, gratitude, and a desire to honor God, there is no reason to be ashamed of that discipline.
Keep being generous.
Keep supporting sound biblical ministry.
Keep helping those in need.
Keep asking the Lord to make your heart more like His.
But do not imagine that your percentage makes you more loved than the believer who cannot afford the same amount.
And do not look down on someone whose financial circumstances are different from yours.
Now, to the person who has been quietly afraid.
The single mother.
The unemployed father.
The student surviving on almost nothing.
The elderly believer choosing between medication and groceries.
The person whose heart wants to give but whose circumstances are painfully limited.
Please hear this.
Your poverty does not make you a second-class Christian.
Your inability to give ten percent does not mean Christ has abandoned you.
And your salvation is not suspended until your financial situation improves.
Jesus knows your circumstances.
He sees your heart.
He understands the difference between unwillingness and inability.
And the church should be a place where you can receive care, not merely a place where you are pressured to give.
The same Gospel that calls us to generosity also commands us to love our neighbors.
Sometimes that means the congregation should be helping the struggling family rather than demanding more money from them.
That is not weak Christianity.
That is biblical compassion.
And perhaps this is where some of us need to repent.
Not only those who have been selfish with their money.
But those who have used Scripture carelessly.
Those who have confused fundraising with faithfulness.
Those who have implied that financial blessing can be bought.
Those who have made struggling believers feel unwelcome because their offerings were small.
And those of us who have given faithfully while secretly becoming proud of ourselves.
There is grace for all of us at the foot of the cross.
But grace does not leave us unchanged.
It teaches us to repent.
To make things right.
To become generous without becoming boastful.
To become responsible without becoming fearful.
To give without demanding repayment from God.
To serve without turning people into financial opportunities.
And to remember that every Christian ministry, including Gospel Warrior, must remain accountable to the very Scriptures it proclaims.
That brings me to something personal about this mission.

Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim Jesus Christ, encourage biblical discipleship, strengthen struggling believers, and help people move from shame and spiritual confusion toward repentance, grace, and transformation.
Those resources are intended to help believers grow in Scripture, understand the Gospel, and walk more deeply with Jesus Christ.
And we want that work to continue reaching more people.
The exhausted believer scrolling late at night.
The person ashamed to return to church.
The father trying to rebuild his family.
The young Christian confused by competing teachings.
The person who has never truly understood why Jesus died.
This mission takes time, work, resources, and faithful support.
Not because you owe Gospel Warrior ten percent.
But because freely chosen, consistent support can be a meaningful expression of Christian generosity and partnership in Gospel ministry.
It should never be presented as a replacement for every other biblical responsibility, nor as a compulsory payment to God.
But it can be a genuine offering of gratitude and stewardship when given freely, responsibly, and according to your means.
Please do not feel ashamed.
You can still be part of this mission.
Not simply to help an algorithm.
But because somewhere among your friends and family may be a believer who has spent years living under unnecessary guilt about tithing.
Someone may need to discover that grace does not cancel generosity—it transforms its motivation.
It is the opportunity to help more people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
Because this is not just a discussion about money.
It is a discussion about what we believe God is like.
Do we see Him as a Father who loves His children through Christ?
Or as a collector waiting to punish anyone who misses a payment?
Do we give because we have received grace?
Or because we are afraid that grace might disappear?
Do we support ministries because we believe in their faithfulness to Scripture?
Or because someone has convinced us that questioning financial demands is the same as questioning God?
These are questions worth bringing into the light.
So I want to ask you something, and I hope you will answer from your heart.
Have you ever felt afraid that God would punish you financially because you could not give ten percent?
Or have you experienced the joy of giving freely, without fear, because you understood what Christ has already done for you?
And if you believe Christians should still be required to tithe ten percent, you are welcome in this conversation too. Share the Scriptures that have shaped your conviction.
Let us reason together respectfully, test our conclusions against the whole counsel of God, and refuse to make enemies out of fellow believers who are sincerely trying to honor Christ.
Because the goal is not to win an argument about money.
The goal is to know Jesus more faithfully.
To obey His Word more carefully.
To become more generous.
More compassionate.
More honest.
More surrendered.
And more like the Savior who gave Himself for us.
So, is tithing ten percent still a requirement for Christians under the New Covenant?

The strongest reading of the New Testament is that Christians are not placed under a universal, mandatory ten-percent tithe. Instead, believers are instructed to give willingly, intentionally, proportionately, generously, and in love.

Faithful Christians differ on this issue. Some teach ten percent as a continuing obligation or normative minimum, drawing on Abraham, the Mosaic tithe, and Jesus' words about tithing. Others understand the tithe as a covenant-specific command fulfilled in Christ, while affirming the New Testament's strong commands concerning generosity and material support.
Those differences should be acknowledged honestly.

But what is clear is that the New Testament does not present a simple formula in which paying ten percent purchases God's favor, guarantees prosperity, or determines whether someone belongs to Christ.
And that truth should change the way we speak about giving.
Ten percent may be a useful personal discipline.
It is not the price of grace.
Giving is an act of worship.
It is not a substitute for obedience.
Supporting Gospel ministry is a biblical responsibility.
It is not permission for ministries to manipulate people.
And financial generosity should flow from love for Christ, not terror of losing His affection.
So perhaps the question we should carry away from this conversation is not simply, "Have I given God His ten percent?"
Perhaps it is:
"Jesus, now that I know what You have given for me, how can I faithfully honor You with everything You have entrusted to my care?"
That question reaches beyond the offering plate.
Into our homes.
Our spending.
Our savings.
Our debts.
Our generosity.
Our treatment of the poor.
Our support for faithful Gospel work.
And the quiet places of our hearts where money sometimes competes with God.
If you have been selfish, there is room to repent.
If you have been fearful, there is room to rediscover grace.
If you have been manipulated, there is room to seek truth and healing.
If you have been generous, there is room to grow still more.
And if you have been trying to earn God's love through your giving, hear the Gospel one more time.
Christ did not wait for you to become financially worthy before He went to the cross.
He loved us while we were still sinners.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith receives salvation by grace, not by financial achievement.
That is where true Christian generosity begins.
Not with a calculator.
Not with a threat.
Not with an envelope.
But with a crucified and risen Savior.
And when that truth finally settles into the deepest part of your heart, you begin to understand something unforgettable.
Jesus never asked you to purchase the grace He already paid for with His blood.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY MEMORIZED THE SCRIPTURES… THEN STOOD FACE-TO-FACE WITH THE AUTHOR AND WANTED HIM DEAD.
paragraphs: THEY MEMORIZED THE SCRIPTURES… THEN STOOD FACE-TO-FACE WITH THE AUTHOR AND WANTED HIM DEAD.

The Pharisees knew the prophecies, defended God's Law, and waited for the Messiah. But when Jesus finally stood before them, many refused to believe. The terrifying question isn't just how they missed Him. It's whether we could be making the same mistake today.
Imagine spending your entire life waiting for someone.
You study everything written about Him. You memorize the promises. You teach others how to recognize His coming. You build your reputation around being ready.
And then one day…
He stands right in front of you.
He speaks the words of God. He heals people everyone else has abandoned. He opens blind eyes. He forgives sinners. He fulfills prophecies written centuries before His birth.
But instead of falling to your knees…
You begin looking for a way to silence Him.
Not because you have never read the Scriptures.
But because the Messiah standing before you is not the Messiah you have made room for in your heart.
This is one of the most unsettling realities in the Gospels.
Some of the people most familiar with the sacred writings became some of the fiercest opponents of Jesus Christ.
And before we point our fingers at the Pharisees, there is something we desperately need to understand.
It is possible to know what the Bible says and still resist what God is saying to your heart through it.
It is possible to defend religious truth while refusing to surrender to the One who is Truth.
It is possible to be surrounded by holy things and still have a heart that needs repentance.
And that should concern every one of us.
Because this story is not merely about religious leaders who lived two thousand years ago.
It is about the frightening distance that can exist between knowing about God and truly knowing Him.
Jesus once spoke words that should make every serious student of Scripture tremble.

In John 5:39–40, He told His opponents that they searched the Scriptures because they believed they possessed eternal life in them, yet those very Scriptures testified about Him—and they were unwilling to come to Him for life.
Read that again.
They searched the Scriptures.
The Scriptures testified about Jesus.
Yet they refused to come to Jesus.
They possessed the testimony but rejected the One to whom it pointed.
The Greek of John 5:40 makes the tragedy especially personal:
καὶ οὐ θέλετε ἐλθεῖν πρός με ἵνα ζωὴν ἔχητε
Kai ou thelete elthein pros me hina zōēn echēte.
A faithful rendering is:
"And you are unwilling to come to Me so that you may have life."
Notice that expression: οὐ θέλετε — ou thelete.
"You are unwilling."
Jesus was exposing more than a shortage of information. He was confronting a resistance of the will.
The problem was not simply that they needed another Bible study.
They needed to come to Him.
And there is a difference.
A person can study forgiveness while refusing to forgive.
A person can explain humility while secretly worshiping recognition.
A person can preach repentance while carefully protecting the sin they refuse to surrender.
A person can quote the words of Jesus while refusing to obey them when obedience becomes costly.
And perhaps the most dangerous place to be spiritually is not always the place where someone knows nothing about God.
Sometimes it is the place where someone knows enough religious language to stop recognizing their own need for mercy.
But we must be careful here.
Not every Pharisee rejected Jesus.
Not every Jewish religious leader opposed Him.
Nicodemus, a Pharisee, came to Jesus with questions and later participated in His burial (John 3:1–21; 19:39). Acts 15:5 even describes believers who came from the party of the Pharisees.
Jesus Himself was Jewish. His apostles were Jewish. The earliest church was born among the Jewish people.
This is not a story about one people being uniquely blind or wicked.
It is a warning about the human heart.
Our hearts.

The Pharisees emerged from a serious concern for faithfulness to God's Law. They valued Scripture, religious observance, and the preservation of Jewish identity. In a world marked by foreign domination and cultural pressure, those concerns were not inherently evil.
Jesus even acknowledged that the scribes and Pharisees taught from Moses' seat (Matthew 23:2–3), while warning against the hypocrisy of those who failed to practice what they taught.
The problem was never that holiness mattered too much.

The problem arose when outward religious performance replaced inward obedience, when human traditions were elevated above God's commands, and when spiritual authority became something to protect rather than a responsibility to exercise faithfully.
Jesus confronted this in Mark 7:6–8.
He quoted Isaiah's warning about people honoring God with their lips while their hearts remained far from Him.
Think about how devastating that is.
Their mouths were saying the right things.
Their religious practices looked convincing.
Their public reputation could appear spotless.
But Jesus was looking somewhere no crowd could see.
The heart.
And suddenly the question becomes painfully personal.
What if the thing we are most proud of spiritually is the very thing preventing us from recognizing how desperately we need grace?
What if our knowledge has grown faster than our love?
What if we have become skilled at correcting other people's sins while learning to excuse our own?
What if we can identify false teaching in seconds but cannot recognize bitterness growing inside our own homes?
What if we are so busy proving that we are right that we have forgotten how to be humble before the Lord?
There is a reason Jesus' encounters with religious leaders can feel so uncomfortable.
They expose a temptation that still lives inside religious people today.
We can begin treating God as though He exists to affirm the life we have already chosen.
We want Him to bless our plans.
Protect our image.
Defend our opinions.
Reward our sacrifices.
And never challenge the parts of us we have quietly declared untouchable.
But the living Christ does not come merely to decorate the life we refuse to surrender.
He comes as Savior and Lord.
And sometimes the first thing His truth does is expose the very thing we have been hiding.
Consider the day Jesus healed a man with a withered hand.
Mark 3:1–6 describes a synagogue encounter in which some watched Jesus closely, looking for grounds to accuse Him if He healed on the Sabbath.
There stood a man whose hand was withered.
A human being.
Someone carrying a visible burden.
Someone who needed compassion.
And standing nearby were people more concerned with finding an accusation than celebrating the possibility of his restoration.
Jesus asked whether it was lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill.
They remained silent.
Then Mark records something extraordinary.
Jesus looked around at them with anger, grieved at the hardness of their hearts.
The Greek expression in Mark 3:5 includes:
συλλυπούμενος ἐπὶ τῇ πωρώσει τῆς καρδίας αὐτῶν
Syllypoumenos epi tē pōrōsei tēs kardias autōn.
It describes Jesus as being grieved over the hardness of their hearts.
The word πώρωσις — pōrōsis conveys hardness or insensibility.
And that is what makes this scene heartbreaking.
Jesus was not indifferent to the man who suffered.
He was also grieved by the spiritual condition of those who could stand before suffering and remain unmoved.
Then He told the man to stretch out his hand.
The man obeyed.
And his hand was restored.
