Imagine the relief.
Imagine the astonishment.
Imagine what it meant to the man to experience restoration in front of the very people who had watched him suffer.
You might expect everyone to rejoice.
But Mark 3:6 tells us that the Pharisees went out and immediately began conspiring with the Herodians about how to destroy Jesus.
A man had been restored.
And some of the witnesses began planning the death of the Healer.
How does a heart reach that point?
How does someone become so committed to defending a religious position that another person's restoration feels like a threat?
That question is not safely locked away in ancient history.
It reaches into our churches.
Our ministries.
Our families.
Our social media arguments.
Our private conversations.
Have we ever been more concerned about winning an argument than helping a wounded person?
Have we ever judged someone by their past while ignoring the evidence that God was changing their life?
Have we ever felt uncomfortable when grace reached someone we thought did not deserve another chance?
Have we ever cared more about how righteousness looked than about whether we were actually loving our neighbor?
This is where the Gospel stops being a distant historical account.
It becomes a mirror.
And sometimes the reflection hurts.
But Jesus did not expose hardened hearts because He enjoyed humiliating people.
His warnings were calls to repentance.
His truth was not an invitation to despair.
It was an invitation to come into the light.
Another reason many religious leaders struggled to recognize Jesus was that His mission challenged their expectations.
The Scriptures promised a coming King.
Isaiah spoke of a child whose government and peace would have no end (Isaiah 9:6–7).
Micah identified Bethlehem as the place from which a ruler would come (Micah 5:2).
Daniel spoke of a figure like a son of man receiving dominion and an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14).
But Israel's Scriptures also spoke of a servant who would suffer.
Isaiah 53 described one who would bear griefs, be wounded, and make many righteous through His suffering.
Jesus came announcing the kingdom of God.
But He also announced His suffering, rejection, death, and resurrection (Mark 8:31).
He did not arrive merely to overthrow Rome.
He came to confront a deeper bondage.
Sin.
Death.
Separation from God.
The tyranny of evil.
And He would accomplish redemption through a cross.
This was scandalous.
Even His own disciples struggled to understand it.
When Jesus began teaching that He must suffer and be killed, Peter rebuked Him.
Jesus responded with a severe correction because Peter was setting his mind on human concerns rather than the things of God (Mark 8:32–33).
That detail matters.
Misunderstanding the Messiah was not a failure found only among His opponents.
Even those who loved Him needed their expectations corrected.
And perhaps that is one of the most important lessons for us.
We must allow Scripture to correct our expectations of Jesus instead of forcing Jesus to fit our expectations of Scripture.
Sometimes we want a Christ who removes every hardship immediately.
But He calls us to take up our cross and follow Him.
Sometimes we want a Christ who confirms every opinion we already hold.
But He commands us to repent.
Sometimes we want a Christ who promises worldly success.
But He tells us that gaining the whole world is worthless if we lose our soul (Mark 8:36).
Sometimes we want a Christ who never confronts us.
But the Jesus of the Gospels loves people enough to tell them the truth.
And sometimes we want the benefits of His salvation without the surrender of discipleship.
Yet the Gospel never presents Jesus as a Savior who can be reduced to a convenient addition to our lives.
He is Lord.
The Greek New Testament repeatedly uses the word κύριος — kyrios, meaning "lord" or "master," for Jesus.
In Romans 10:9, confessing Jesus as Lord is joined with believing that God raised Him from the dead.
This is not merely religious admiration.
It is allegiance to the risen Christ.
The Messiah did not come simply to make our old lives more comfortable.
He came to give us new life.
And that brings us to another painful moment in John's Gospel.
In John 9, Jesus healed a man who had been blind from birth.
The man's neighbors questioned what had happened.
The Pharisees investigated.
The man's parents were questioned.
And the healed man himself was interrogated.
He could not answer every theological argument.
He did not possess all the explanations.
But he knew what Jesus had done.
John 9:25 records his simple testimony:
"One thing I do know, that though I was blind, now I see." (ESV)
There is something breathtaking about that sentence.
A man who had lived in darkness was now looking at the world.
He could see faces.
Light.
Movement.
The ordinary beauty of things he had never seen before.
And yet his testimony was met with resistance.
Eventually, he was cast out.
But the story did not end with his rejection.
Jesus found him.
Read that slowly.
Jesus found him.
The man had been rejected by religious authorities.
But he was not forgotten by the Savior.
In John 9:35–38, Jesus revealed Himself to him, and the man responded in faith and worship.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that broken people become impressive enough to earn a place with God.
But that Jesus comes to save people who cannot save themselves.
Some of you reading this know what it feels like to be judged by people who know your history but refuse to see what God is doing in your life.
They remember your addiction.
Your failure.
Your divorce.
Your shame.
Your years of wandering.
Your angry words.
Your terrible decisions.
They know the version of you that you are desperately trying to leave behind.
And sometimes they speak as though that version is the only version you will ever be.
But listen carefully.
Your past is real.
Sin has consequences.
Repentance matters.
Restitution and accountability may be necessary.
Grace does not mean pretending the damage never happened.
But your past does not possess greater authority than Jesus Christ.
The One who died and rose again is able to forgive, restore, and transform sinners.
And that includes the sinner who has been hiding behind religion.
It includes the person who has been openly rebellious.
It includes the believer who has grown cold.
It includes the proud.
The ashamed.
The exhausted.
The person who thinks they have gone too far.
And the person who thinks they have never needed much forgiveness.
That is why the Gospel is so offensive to human pride and so beautiful to the repentant heart.
At the foot of the cross, nobody gets to boast about being better than everyone else.
We come as sinners in need of mercy.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.
The Greek word χάρις — charis means grace, favor, or gift, depending on context.
In Ephesians 2, it points to God's saving grace, not something sinners can purchase through religious performance.
You cannot memorize enough verses to buy forgiveness.
You cannot attend enough services to erase your guilt.
You cannot donate enough money to make yourself righteous before God.
You cannot build a ministry impressive enough to replace the finished work of Christ.
Salvation is not for sale.
Jesus paid the price we could never pay.
And when His grace truly reaches us, it does not leave us unchanged.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains us to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace forgives.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
It does not merely cover our scandal with religious language.
It begins rewriting our story through repentance, faith, and the sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit.
And here is where the Pharisees' story becomes even more piercing.
In Luke 18:9–14, Jesus told a parable about two men who went to the temple to pray.
One was a Pharisee.
The other was a tax collector.
The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other sinners and listed his religious accomplishments.
The tax collector stood at a distance.
He would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He beat his breast and pleaded for mercy.
The Greek of Luke 18:13 records his prayer:
Ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ
Ho theos, hilasthēti moi tō hamartōlō.
"O God, be merciful to me, the sinner."
That word ἱλάσθητί — hilasthēti is a plea for mercy with an atoning or propitiatory dimension. It is more than a casual request to overlook wrongdoing.
The man knew he needed mercy before a holy God.
And Jesus said the tax collector went home justified rather than the other man.
Not because sin was insignificant.
Not because religious obedience was worthless.
But because the tax collector came in humility, while the Pharisee trusted in his own righteousness and despised others.
One man came presenting his achievements.
The other came confessing his need.
One compared himself with sinners.
The other pleaded for mercy.
And the man who knew he needed grace went home justified.
Can you imagine the silence when Jesus finished that parable?
Can you imagine how it challenged those who measured spiritual standing by public reputation?
Now imagine what it would sound like if Jesus told that parable in one of our churches today.
One person stands proudly and says:
"Lord, I have served for twenty years. I know the Bible. I never miss church. I give faithfully. I am not like those people whose lives are falling apart."
And another person stands at the back, unable to lift their eyes.
"Lord, I have sinned. I have hurt people. I have hidden things. I have made promises and broken them. I have no excuse. Please have mercy on me."
Which heart resembles yours?
Not which person looks more respectable.
Not which person knows more verses.
Not which person has the cleaner public image.
Which heart resembles yours?
Because the danger is not that Scripture knowledge makes someone a Pharisee.
The danger is that knowledge without humility can become a hiding place for pride.
We need Scripture.
Desperately.
We need sound doctrine.
We need faithful teaching.
We need careful study of Hebrew, Aramaic, Greek, history, literary context, and the whole counsel of God.
We must not replace biblical truth with vague feelings.
But the purpose of understanding Scripture is not to admire our own understanding.
It is to know the God who has revealed Himself and to respond to Jesus Christ in faith and obedience.
In Luke 24:27, the risen Jesus explained to two disciples on the road to Emmaus what the Scriptures said concerning Himself, beginning with Moses and the Prophets.

Later, in Luke 24:44–47, He explained how the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms pointed toward the fulfillment of God's redemptive purposes, including His suffering, resurrection, and the proclamation of repentance for the forgiveness of sins.
The Bible is not merely a collection of religious advice.
It tells the unfolding story of God's redemptive work, fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
And when we read it rightly, we do not simply come away saying, "Look how much I know."
We come away saying, "Lord Jesus, open my eyes. Correct me. Forgive me. Teach me to follow You."
That is why the words of Ezekiel 36:26 are so precious.
God promises:
וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב חָדָשׁ
Venatatti lakhem lev chadash.
"And I will give you a new heart."
The Hebrew expression לֵב חָדָשׁ — lev chadash means "a new heart."

In its original context, this promise concerns God's restoration and renewal of His people Israel. Christians also understand the promised inward renewal in connection with the new covenant and the transforming work of the Holy Spirit.
The hope is not that human beings can polish their religious appearance until their hearts become pure.
The hope is that God can change us from within.
He can soften what has become hard.
He can confront what has become proud.
He can awaken what has become spiritually numb.
He can restore love where bitterness has taken root.
He can teach a person who has spent years hiding behind religion to finally stand before Him in honesty.
And that is where the scandal becomes grace.
Not when we pretend we were never wrong.
Not when we excuse our sins.
Not when we blame everyone else.
But when we stop hiding and come to Christ.
Perhaps you have been reading this with a heavy heart.
Perhaps you have been a Christian for years, but lately your prayers have become mechanical.
You still know the songs.
You still know the verses.
You still know how to sound spiritually strong.
But privately, something has changed.
You are quicker to criticize than to forgive.
Quicker to argue than to pray.
Quicker to notice another person's failure than to confess your own.
And somewhere along the way, your relationship with Jesus began to feel more like a religious routine than a living fellowship with your Savior.
Or perhaps you are on the other side.
You have been wounded by people who claimed to represent God.
They quoted Scripture at you without compassion.
They exposed your failures while hiding their own.
They made you feel as though Jesus would never welcome someone with your story.
If that is you, please do not confuse the failures of religious people with the character of Jesus Christ.
Look at Him in the Gospels.
Watch Him speak to the Samaritan woman in John 4.
Watch Him call Levi, a tax collector, in Mark 2.
Watch Him welcome the repentant sinner in Luke 7.
Watch Him restore Peter after Peter denied Him three times (John 21:15–19).
And above all, look at the cross.
There, the sinless Son of God willingly gave His life for sinners.
There, human cruelty and injustice were displayed in their terrible reality.
There, the love of God was revealed through the sacrificial death of Jesus Christ.
And the cross was not the end.
On the third day, He rose.
The resurrection declares that death did not defeat Him.
The crucified Messiah is the risen Lord.
This is the One the Scriptures were pointing toward.
This is the One who calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
This is the One who can transform a proud religious heart and a broken rebellious heart alike.
And perhaps one of the most extraordinary examples is the apostle Paul.
Before he became known as the apostle who proclaimed Christ among the nations, he was Saul.
A Pharisee.
Educated.
Zealous.
Convinced that he was defending God's truth.
Philippians 3:5–6 records his Pharisaic identity, his zeal, and his confidence in his former religious standing.
But that zeal had led him to persecute the church.
In Acts 9, as Saul traveled toward Damascus, Jesus confronted him.
"Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" (Acts 9:4, ESV)
Think about that moment.
A man convinced that he was serving God discovered that he was persecuting God's Messiah.
His sincerity had not made his actions righteous.
His religious knowledge had not prevented his terrible error.
His zeal had not guaranteed that he understood God's purposes.
He needed Jesus to confront him.
And Jesus did.
But here is the miracle.
Jesus did not leave Saul where He found him.
The persecutor became a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
The man who had tried to silence the church became a witness to the Gospel.
The man who once trusted in his religious credentials came to regard knowing Christ as surpassingly valuable (Philippians 3:7–9).
His story did not erase the suffering he had caused.
But it demonstrated the astonishing power of God's mercy.
The same grace that exposed Saul's sin also transformed his future.
That is the Gospel.
And that is why our message is From Scandal to Grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
Not by making sin harmless.
Not by promising that consequences disappear overnight.
But by forgiving sinners, reconciling them to God, and making them new in Christ.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares that anyone in Christ is a new creation.
The old has passed away.
The new has come.
This does not mean believers instantly become perfect.
It means their identity and future are now bound to the crucified and risen Savior.
The Holy Spirit begins a work of transformation that continues as they follow Him.
And that hope belongs not only to the openly broken.
It belongs to the religiously proud.
To the person who has judged others harshly.
To the person who has used Scripture to win arguments but neglected its call to love.
To the person who has defended doctrine while refusing to confess secret sin.
To the person who has spent years trying to impress God.
You can stop pretending.
You can come to Jesus.
Not with a polished speech.
Not with a list of accomplishments.
Not with an excuse for every failure.
But with repentance and faith.
Like the tax collector:
"God, be merciful to me, the sinner."
And if that prayer expresses what is happening inside your heart right now, do not ignore it.
Take a moment.
Put aside the noise.
Ask yourself whether you have been following Jesus or merely maintaining a religious identity.
Ask whether your Bible knowledge has produced humility, love, holiness, and obedience.
Ask whether you are willing to let Christ confront the very things you have spent years defending.
And if you discover something painful, do not run away from Him.
Run to Him.
First John 1:9 assures believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
There is mercy in Christ.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is hope in Christ.
And there is still a call to surrender.
You do not have to reveal private details or painful experiences you are not ready to share.
But your honest testimony might remind someone else that they are not beyond the reach of Jesus.

And if you know someone who loves Scripture but has been struggling with pride, bitterness, or spiritual exhaustion, consider sharing this article with them privately, with tenderness rather than accusation.
Because our purpose is not simply to collect readers.
It is to help people encounter the truth of God's Word and grow in faithful discipleship to Christ.
These resources are meant to nourish faith, encourage serious study, and help believers become rooted in the Gospel rather than merely inspired for a moment.

You may choose to treat that support as part of your personal Christian giving, according to your convictions and your church's teaching on stewardship. It is not a substitute for any obligation you believe you have to your local church, and it is never a payment for God's favor.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing rather than pressured.
Second Corinthians 9:7 calls believers to give as they have decided in their hearts, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not out of guilt.
Not because God's blessing can be bought.
But because sharing useful biblical teaching and discipleship resources requires real effort, time, and ongoing support.
Those products are simply an added benefit. The deeper purpose is the mission itself: helping more people open their Bibles, hear the Gospel, and grow in Jesus Christ.
A sincere recommendation to one struggling friend may reach someone who desperately needs encouragement.
A thoughtful comment may give another believer the courage to confess their need for prayer.
And a faithful life shaped by the Gospel may speak more powerfully than any post we could ever publish.
The goal is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The goal is to make Jesus Christ known.
Christ alone is our hope.
And that brings us back to the question that began this entire story.
How could people who knew so much Scripture fail to recognize the Messiah?
The Gospels reveal a painful combination of hardened hearts, misplaced expectations, threatened authority, spiritual pride, and unwillingness to receive Jesus on His own terms.
But they also reveal something more hopeful.
Not everyone remained in unbelief.
Nicodemus moved from questioning Jesus at night to publicly assisting with His burial.
Saul the persecutor became Paul the apostle.
Men and women whose understanding had been incomplete came to believe in the crucified and risen Christ.
And the invitation remains open today.
Do not merely admire Jesus.
Come to Him.
Do not merely defend His teachings.
Obey Him.
Do not merely quote His words.
Let His words search your heart.
Do not use your knowledge of Scripture to conceal your need for grace.
Let Scripture lead you to the Savior.
Because the most important question is not whether you can win an argument about Jesus.
It is whether you have truly placed your trust in Him.
Whether you have repented.
Whether you are following Him.
Whether His grace is changing the way you love, forgive, speak, give, and live.
And if you have wandered, return.
If you have grown proud, humble yourself.
If you have become cold, ask Him to renew your love.
If you have sinned, confess it.
If you have never trusted Christ, hear His call to repent and believe the Gospel.
You do not need a perfect religious résumé to come to Jesus.
You need the Savior.
And the Savior who confronted proud hearts also welcomed repentant sinners.
So before you close this article, ask yourself one final question.
If Jesus confronted the parts of my life that I am most determined to protect, would I surrender to Him?
Do not answer too quickly.
Let the question remain with you.
Bring it into prayer.
Bring it into your next reading of Scripture.
Bring it into the way you treat the person you find hardest to love.
And remember the man born blind.
Religious authorities questioned him.
His testimony was challenged.
He was cast out.
But Jesus found him.
That same Jesus is alive today.
And the Gospel still calls us out of darkness into His marvelous light.
The greatest tragedy is not standing far from Jesus and knowing you are lost. It is standing near His words, hearing His voice, and refusing to let Him change your heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE BURIED THE SILVER, THE GOLD, AND THE BEAUTIFUL GARMENT UNDER HIS TENT… BUT HE COULDN’T BURY WHAT GOD ALREADY KNEW.
paragraphs: HE BURIED THE SILVER, THE GOLD, AND THE BEAUTIFUL GARMENT UNDER HIS TENT… BUT HE COULDN’T BURY WHAT GOD ALREADY KNEW.

One man's secret sin brought an entire nation to its knees. And buried beneath the tragedy of Achan is a terrifying question every believer must face: What are you hiding that could be destroying the very life you're praying for God to bless?
Based on Joshua 7:1–26 | Joshua 6:17–19 | Hebrews 4:13 | 1 John 1:9 | Romans 8:1
There was a tent in Israel that looked just like every other tent.
Nothing unusual about the entrance. Nothing suspicious about the ground. Nothing that would make a passing neighbor stop and wonder what was buried underneath.
A family lived there.
People slept there.
Ordinary conversations probably filled the space. Meals were eaten. Days passed.
And beneath the earth, hidden from human eyes, lay silver, gold, and a beautiful garment that should never have been taken.
The man who buried them knew exactly where they were.
His name was Achan.
And perhaps the most frightening part of his story is not that he stole something forbidden.
It is that, for a little while, life may have appeared to continue as normal.
No thunder struck when he buried the treasure.
No voice from heaven publicly exposed him that night.
No soldier immediately came searching through his belongings.
He could have walked among God's people, listened to their conversations, and appeared to be another faithful Israelite who had witnessed the mighty victory at Jericho.
But something was terribly wrong.
And before the story was over, thirty-six men would be dead, an army would be humiliated, a nation would be trembling, and one man's carefully concealed secret would be brought into the light.
Read that again.
Thirty-six men would never return from battle.
And the man whose disobedience had contributed to the disaster was living among the very people mourning them.
This is not merely an ancient story about stolen valuables.
It is a story about what happens when a human heart begins to love something more than obedience to God.
And if we are willing to listen, it may reveal something about our own hearts that we have spent years refusing to confront.
Because not everything buried beneath a tent is made of silver and gold.
Sometimes it is an addiction.
Sometimes it is an affair.
Sometimes it is money obtained dishonestly.
Sometimes it is bitterness that has become so familiar we no longer recognize it as poison.
Sometimes it is a secret conversation, a hidden browser history, an unforgiven offense, or a carefully maintained public image that looks holy while the private life is slowly falling apart.
And sometimes the most dangerous sentence a believer can whisper is this:
"Nobody knows."
But God knows.
And the story of Achan is about to show us why that truth should both terrify the unrepentant heart and awaken hope in the person who is finally ready to come clean.
Israel had just witnessed something extraordinary.
Jericho had fallen.
Not because Israel possessed superior military strength. Not because Joshua had developed an irresistible siege strategy. Not because human hands had accomplished the impossible.
The Lord had given the city into their hands.

For six days, the Israelites marched around Jericho according to God's command. On the seventh day, they marched around the city seven times. The priests blew the trumpets, the people shouted, and the walls collapsed.
Imagine standing there.
Imagine seeing a fortified city fall in a way no human military commander could reasonably claim as his own achievement.
Imagine the trembling in your chest as you realized that the God who parted the Jordan River had once again demonstrated His power.
But victory did not mean Israel could do whatever it pleased.
Before Jericho fell, God had given specific instructions.
The city was devoted to destruction, and its silver, gold, bronze, and iron were to be brought into the treasury of the Lord.
Joshua 6:19 says in the King James Version:
"But all the silver, and gold, and vessels of brass and iron, are consecrated unto the LORD: they shall come into the treasury of the LORD."
Those valuables were not available for personal enrichment.
They belonged to the Lord under the command governing Jericho.
And somewhere amid the destruction, Achan saw something that captured his attention.
A beautiful garment.
Silver.
Gold.
Perhaps his eyes lingered longer than they should have.
Perhaps his mind began calculating what he could gain.
Perhaps he imagined what those possessions could do for his future.
Scripture does not tell us every thought that passed through his mind.
But it tells us something even more revealing.
It tells us the progression of his sin.
When Achan was finally confronted, he confessed.
Joshua 7:20–21, KJV:
"And Achan answered Joshua, and said, Indeed I have sinned against the LORD God of Israel, and thus and thus have I done:

When I saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, and two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels weight, then I coveted them, and took them; and, behold, they are hid in the earth in the midst of my tent, and the silver under it."
There it is.
A confession preserved in Scripture for generations.
Not merely a list of stolen objects.
A description of how temptation became deliberate disobedience.
I saw.
I coveted.
I took.
I hid.
Four movements.
One terrible decision unfolding through the human heart.
The Hebrew text makes this especially vivid.
Achan says:
וָאֵרֶא ... וָאֶחְמְדֵם וָאֶקָּחֵם
Va'ere ... va'echmedem va'eqqachem.
"I saw ... I coveted them, and I took them."
The verb וָאֶחְמְדֵם (va'echmedem) comes from the Hebrew root חמד (chamad), meaning to desire or covet.
That root also appears in the commandment against coveting in Exodus 20:17.
The connection matters.
Achan's sin was not simply that he noticed something beautiful.
Beauty itself was not the enemy.
The problem began when desire crossed the boundary God had established.
He wanted what God had forbidden him to take.
And he acted on that desire.
There is a difference between noticing something and surrendering your heart to it.
There is a difference between temptation and choosing to obey temptation.
Achan did not merely admire the garment.
He coveted it.
Then he took it.
Then he hid it.
And that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because sin often begins with something that seems small enough to manage.
One look.
One conversation.
One compromise.
One transaction.
One decision to keep something that does not belong to us.
One moment when we convince ourselves that God's command is less important than what we want.
Then comes the hiding.
The deleted messages.
The altered explanation.
The carefully rehearsed story.
The smile that conceals the guilt.
The prayer spoken in public while the conscience whispers in private.
And eventually, the person who once trembled at disobedience becomes accustomed to living with it.
Not because the sin has become harmless.
But because the heart has become practiced at concealment.
Achan buried the treasure beneath his tent.
But he could not bury the truth beneath God's knowledge.
The Hebrew phrase describing the hiding place is equally striking:
בְּקֶרֶב הָאֹהֳלִי
Beqerev ha'oholi.
"In the midst of my tent."
The treasure was not somewhere far away.
It was inside the space associated with his everyday life.
The place where he lived.
The place where he rested.
The place where he could return again and again, knowing what lay beneath the ground.
And I wonder how many people reading this understand that feeling.
Not because you have buried stolen gold.
But because there is something in your life you know you have not surrendered to Jesus.
Something you avoid discussing.
Something you hope nobody discovers.
Something you have learned to carry quietly.
You may still attend church.
You may still sing worship songs.
You may still post Bible verses.
You may still encourage other people to trust God.
And some of those expressions of faith may be sincere.
But there is a private struggle you keep postponing.
You tell yourself you will deal with it later.
When life becomes less stressful.
When the temptation becomes weaker.
When the relationship becomes easier.
When you feel stronger.
When you have more time.
But what if the thing you keep postponing is the very thing God is calling you to confront today?
The tragedy of Achan did not end beneath the tent.
Israel moved toward Ai, a smaller city that appeared far less intimidating than Jericho.
After Jericho's astonishing defeat, the next battle might have seemed straightforward.
The spies advised Joshua that only a few thousand men were needed.
But Israel was defeated.
Joshua 7:5 records that approximately thirty-six Israelite men were killed.
The survivors fled.
The people's hearts melted with fear.
Joshua tore his clothes and fell before the ark of the Lord.
The leader who had witnessed the walls of Jericho collapse now lay on the ground, struggling to understand why Israel had suffered such a humiliating defeat.
And God revealed the truth.
Joshua 7:11, KJV:

"Israel hath sinned, and they have also transgressed my covenant which I commanded them: for they have even taken of the accursed thing, and have also stolen, and dissembled also, and they have put it even among their own stuff."
Notice something deeply unsettling.
God said, "Israel hath sinned."
Yet Achan was the individual who had taken the forbidden objects.
Why would the Lord speak about Israel collectively?
Because Israel was a covenant people, and the violation of God's command concerning what was devoted to Him had consequences for the community.
This was not merely a private matter between one man and his possessions.
The stolen valuables had been taken from a city under God's judgment, contrary to His explicit command.
The narrative shows that covenant unfaithfulness could bring devastating consequences beyond the person committing the offense.
But we must be careful here.
The Bible does not teach that every tragedy, defeat, illness, or hardship in someone's life is caused by a hidden personal sin.
Jesus Himself rejected that kind of simplistic conclusion in John 9:1–3 when His disciples asked whether a man's blindness was caused by his sin or his parents' sin.
Achan's story concerns a particular covenant violation in a particular moment of Israel's history.
It is not permission to accuse suffering people of secretly deserving their pain.
Yet it does warn us that sin is rarely as isolated as we imagine.
A lie can fracture a marriage.
Greed can damage an entire family.
An abuse of authority can wound a congregation.
A secret betrayal can leave children struggling with consequences they never chose.
A hidden addiction can gradually consume trust, time, money, and emotional presence.
And sometimes the people most affected are the ones who knew the least.
That is one of the heartbreaking realities of sin.
It promises private pleasure while concealing the possibility of public devastation.
Achan saw treasure.
But he did not see the thirty-six graves that would follow Israel's defeat.
He saw a beautiful garment.
But he did not see Joshua lying facedown in anguish.
He saw silver and gold.
But he did not see the terror that would spread through the camp.
Sin rarely shows us the full price before asking us to pay it.
It shows us what we might gain.
It hides what we might lose.
And by the time the consequences become visible, the decision has already been made.
Maybe that is why someone reading this feels an uncomfortable heaviness right now.
Because you are not merely remembering a Bible story.
You are remembering a choice.
A moment when you knew what was right.
A moment when you crossed the line anyway.
A moment when you told yourself that you could manage the consequences.
And now there is a part of your life you wish you could undo.
But stay with me.
Because this story does not exist simply to make you afraid of being exposed.
It also forces us to ask what we will do when the truth finally confronts us.
God instructed Joshua to consecrate the people and identify the offender.
Tribe by tribe.
Clan by clan.
Household by household.
Man by man.
The circle narrowed.
Until Achan stood before Joshua.
Imagine that moment.
The ground beneath his feet was the same ground he had walked on the day before.
The sky above him was the same sky.
But everything had changed.
The secret he had carried was no longer protected by silence.
Joshua addressed him in Joshua 7:19, KJV:
"My son, give, I pray thee, glory to the LORD God of Israel, and make confession unto him; and tell me now what thou hast done; hide it not from me."
"Hide it not from me."
Those words must have pierced the very place where Achan had been hiding.
And he confessed.
He admitted that he had sinned against the Lord.
He identified the stolen objects.
He described where they were buried.
Joshua sent messengers to the tent.
They ran.
And there, beneath the ground, they found exactly what Achan had described.
The garment.
The silver.
The gold.
The secret had become evidence.
The buried things were brought out before Joshua and the Israelites, and laid before the Lord.
The hiding was over.
Then came the part of the story modern readers often struggle to understand.
Achan faced judgment.
Joshua 7:25–26 describes his execution and the raising of a great heap of stones over him.

The passage also mentions his family, possessions, and livestock being brought to the Valley of Achor. The precise extent of his family's participation and punishment is debated among interpreters, especially in light of biblical laws concerning individual responsibility.
We should not pretend those difficulties do not exist.
Nor should we soften the account into a harmless moral lesson.
Joshua 7 is a severe narrative of divine judgment under Israel's covenant obligations.
It is meant to disturb us.
It reveals that God's holiness is not a decorative religious idea.
His commands matter.
His justice matters.
And sin against Him is not trivial simply because human beings have learned to normalize it.
But here is something equally important.
Achan's confession came after he was identified.
Scripture records his admission, but it does not tell us that he experienced inward repentance or received forgiveness before his death.
We must not invent what the passage does not reveal.
His story is not a promise that a last-minute confession will erase every earthly consequence.
And it is not a model for Christians to imitate by inflicting violence on people who sin.
Rather, it confronts us with the seriousness of rebellion and the danger of treating God's patience as permission to continue.
Yet the Bible does not end in Joshua 7.
And that matters more than you may realize.
Because if all we ever heard was the sound of stones falling in the Valley of Achor, we might forget that the same Scriptures lead us toward the One who came to save sinners.
The story of Achan must be understood within the unfolding revelation of God's redemptive work.
The Valley of Achor became associated with trouble.
The Hebrew word עָכוֹר (Achor) is connected to the idea of trouble or disturbance, reflecting the wordplay in Joshua 7:25–26.
A place remembered for judgment.
A place marked by grief.
A place where the consequences of covenant unfaithfulness could not be ignored.
But centuries later, God spoke through the prophet Hosea.
And He said something astonishing.
Hosea 2:15, KJV:

"And I will give her her vineyards from thence, and the valley of Achor for a door of hope: and she shall sing there, as in the days of her youth, and as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt."
Did you catch that?
The valley of trouble would become a door of hope.
In Hosea, God was speaking about His restoration of unfaithful Israel.
It was a prophetic promise within a specific covenant context, not a statement that Achan's judgment was reversed.
But the image is breathtaking.
The God who judges sin is also the God who promises restoration to His people.
The place associated with trouble becomes, in His redemptive promise, an entrance into hope.
And when we read the whole Bible through the light of Jesus Christ, that pattern finds its deepest fulfillment in the Gospel.
Because Jesus did not come to tell sinners that sin was harmless.
He came because sin was so serious that our redemption required His sacrificial death.
He did not come to celebrate what destroys us.
He came to rescue us from it.
He did not come merely to improve our reputation.
He came to reconcile us to God.
At the cross, the holiness of God and the love of God are not enemies.
God does not overlook evil as though it does not matter.
And He does not abandon His saving purpose toward those who come to Him through Christ.
Romans 5:8, KJV, declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had successfully cleaned up every secret.
Not after we had repaired every broken relationship.
Not after we had learned how to look righteous enough to deserve His attention.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
This does not mean that confession is optional.
It does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
It does not mean that forgiveness removes every earthly consequence of wrongdoing.
It means that salvation rests upon the grace of God in Jesus Christ, not upon our ability to pretend we have never fallen.
And here is the question that changes everything.
What if the thing you are most afraid to bring into the light is the very thing you need to surrender to Christ?
Not because exposure itself saves you.
It does not.
Jesus saves.
But because clinging to deception keeps you resisting the truth you desperately need.
First John 1:9, KJV, says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
The Greek word translated "confess" is ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), a form of ὁμολογέω (homologeō).
In this context, it means to acknowledge or confess our sins.
Not to negotiate their seriousness.
Not to rename them until they sound acceptable.
Not to blame someone else for our choices.
But to acknowledge the truth before God.
And the promise is extraordinary.
He is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
That promise is grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ, whom John identifies as our advocate and the atoning sacrifice for our sins in 1 John 2:1–2.
Forgiveness is not God pretending that evil never happened.
Forgiveness is grace made possible through Christ.
And repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what we did.
It is turning from sin toward God.
It is the heart no longer defending what God has condemned.
It is the willingness to stop calling darkness light.
It is surrender.
Sometimes surrender means telling the truth to someone we have deceived.
Sometimes it means ending a relationship that has become sinful.
Sometimes it means returning money we obtained dishonestly.
Sometimes it means seeking pastoral counsel, professional help, or accountability because a pattern of behavior has become destructive.
Sometimes it means accepting consequences we cannot escape while trusting that God's mercy is still real.
And sometimes it begins in a quiet room, with tears nobody else can see, when a person finally stops making excuses and whispers:
"Lord Jesus, I have sinned. I need Your mercy. I cannot keep living this way."
There is no magic in the wording.
The power is not in a perfectly composed prayer.
The power is in the Savior to whom we turn.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes more than an article you happened to find while scrolling through Facebook.
Perhaps this is the moment you recognize the tent.
Not Achan's tent.
Your own.
The private place.
The hidden burden.
The thing you keep covering.
The sin you have defended so many times that you are beginning to believe your own explanations.
And maybe your heart is exhausted.
Exhausted from keeping appearances.
Exhausted from saying "I'm fine" when you know you are not.
Exhausted from making promises to God and breaking them.
Exhausted from trying to maintain two versions of yourself.
The person everyone sees.
And the person you know you have become.
Listen carefully.
You do not have to earn the right to come to Jesus by first becoming flawless.
But you cannot sincerely seek His mercy while insisting that the sin He calls you to abandon must remain untouched.
His grace welcomes sinners.
His grace also teaches us to renounce ungodliness, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
Jesus is not interested in helping us decorate our hiding places.
He calls us out of darkness into His marvelous light.
And for someone reading this, that invitation may be the beginning of a completely different life.
Not necessarily an easier life.
Repentance can involve difficult conversations.
Restitution can be costly.
Trust may take time to rebuild.
Some consequences may remain.
But there is a freedom in walking honestly before God that deception can never provide.
The freedom of no longer having to protect the lie.
The freedom of no longer pretending that disobedience is harmless.
The freedom of knowing that your standing before God is not secured by a spotless public image but by the righteousness of Jesus Christ.
Romans 8:1, KJV, declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus."
That promise belongs to those who are in Christ.
It is not permission to cherish sin.
It is the astonishing assurance that those who belong to Jesus are no longer under God's condemning verdict.
And that is why the Gospel is not simply a message about becoming a better person.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, according to the Scriptures, as Paul proclaims in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
The resurrection declares that death did not have the final word.
And through faith in the risen Christ, sinners receive the hope of forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life.
Achan's story reminds us of the terrible seriousness of hidden rebellion.
Jesus Christ reveals the astonishing greatness of God's saving grace.
We must never confuse the two accounts or pretend that Achan's fate is identical to the promise given to believers under the new covenant.
But we must also never miss the warning and the invitation that Scripture places before us.
Do not make peace with the sin Christ died to redeem you from.
Do not mistake God's patience for His approval.
Do not confuse religious activity with genuine surrender.
And do not imagine that the deepest problem in your life is merely the possibility of someone discovering your secrets.
The deeper problem is what sin does to your relationship with God and the people you are called to love.
But the deepest hope is greater still.
Jesus Christ receives repentant sinners.
The One who knows the truth about us is also the One who gave Himself to save us.
Hebrews 4:13 says that nothing in creation is hidden from God's sight.
Just a few verses later, Hebrews 4:14–16 calls believers to draw near with confidence to the throne of grace through Jesus, our great High Priest.
Think about that movement.
Nothing hidden.
Everything exposed before God.
And yet, through Christ, an invitation to approach the throne of grace.
Not because God has become indifferent to holiness.
But because Jesus is the merciful and faithful High Priest who opens the way for His people to receive mercy and find grace in time of need.
The God who sees everything is not surprised by the truth you are finally ready to confess.
And the Savior who calls you to repentance is not incapable of restoring a broken life.
That is the hope of the Gospel.
That is why we keep telling these stories.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with shocking Bible accounts while leaving their hearts unchanged.
Not to build a community around fear, religious performance, or spiritual appearances.
But to keep pointing wounded, wandering, struggling, and searching people back to the Word of God and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Because someone who has been hiding for years may encounter a Scripture that finally breaks through the excuses.
Someone who has almost given up on faith may discover that Christ has not ceased to be merciful.
Someone who has never truly understood the Gospel may realize that Christianity is not about pretending to be righteous but about receiving the righteousness and grace found in Jesus.
And perhaps someone reading this article is that person.
Not as a public confession of details you are not ready or safe to share.
Not as proof that you have earned God's forgiveness.
But as a simple expression that you want to walk in the light of Christ.
If you have experienced God's restoring grace, consider sharing a testimony that might encourage someone who believes their failures have placed them beyond hope.
And if this message has challenged you, tell us which Scripture spoke most deeply to your heart.
Your words may help another person realize they are not alone in the struggle to follow Jesus faithfully.
A husband carrying secret guilt.
A wife silently praying for her family.
A young person trapped in a destructive habit.
A believer who has stopped attending church because shame convinced them they could never return.
A friend who smiles in public but feels spiritually empty in private.
Sometimes a message becomes more meaningful the second time we read it.
Sometimes the verse we overlooked yesterday is the very verse we need tomorrow.
Invite your family, your friends, fellow believers, and even those who are still searching for answers about Jesus.
Our desire is to make biblical truth accessible, understandable, and personally meaningful, without compromising the message of Scripture.
These resources are meant to encourage consistent Bible study, strengthen spiritual understanding, and help believers continue growing beyond a single social media post.
And for those who believe in this mission and are able to help sustain it, there is another meaningful way to participate.
Think of it as a voluntary monthly ministry offering—an expression of generosity that can help sustain and expand this work.

Scripture encourages cheerful, willing generosity in 2 Corinthians 9:7. It also recognizes the importance of supporting those who labor in Gospel ministry, as seen in Galatians 6:6 and 1 Corinthians 9:14.
But giving must never be presented as a purchase of God's approval, a substitute for repentance, or a requirement for receiving His blessing.
And it does not replace your responsibility to prayerfully support your local church and its ministry.
It is simply an additional opportunity to give voluntarily toward Gospel Warrior's discipleship and outreach efforts.
And if you cannot contribute financially, please know that you are still welcome here.
Your prayers, encouragement, thoughtful comments, and willingness to share biblical truth are deeply appreciated.
This is a thank-you benefit, not the reason anyone should feel obligated to give.
The goal is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The goal is to make Jesus Christ known.
The goal is not merely to gather more followers.
It is to encourage people to become faithful followers of Christ.
It is to direct them continually to the Savior, His Word, His Church, and the transforming power of His Gospel.
Because one day, the number of reactions on a Facebook post will not matter nearly as much as whether we have truly listened to the Word of God and responded in faith.
And that brings us back to Achan.
Back to the tent.
Back to the buried treasure.
Back to a man who saw, coveted, took, and hid.
Imagine how different his story might have been if he had refused to take what God had forbidden.
Imagine the power of obedience before the secret ever existed.
That is the warning.
But now consider your own life.
You cannot return to yesterday and erase every decision you regret.
You cannot undo every careless word.
You cannot make every consequence disappear.
But today, if you hear God's voice, you do not have to harden your heart.
You can turn to Jesus Christ.
You can confess what is true.
You can seek forgiveness.
You can begin making what is wrong right wherever it is possible.
You can ask for help.
You can stop defending what is destroying you.
You can trust the Savior who died and rose again for sinners.
And you can begin walking in the light.
Not because your past was harmless.
Not because repentance guarantees an easy tomorrow.
But because the grace of Jesus Christ is real.
Because His mercy is not exhausted by the fact that you need it.
Because His resurrection is the foundation of a hope stronger than the shame that has been holding you captive.
And because the Gospel offers something the silver, gold, and beautiful garment could never give Achan.
Reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
A treasure that cannot be stolen.
A mercy that cannot be purchased.
A Savior whose worth exceeds everything this world could place before your eyes.
So before you leave this article, ask yourself one question.
Not, "What would people think if they knew?"
But, "Lord Jesus, what am I still refusing to surrender to You?"
Then answer Him honestly.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that God sees what we hide.
The greatest tragedy would be spending our lives hiding from the very Savior who calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THE OLD HAS PASSED AWAY”… SO WHY ARE YOU STILL FIGHTING THE PERSON YOU USED TO BE?
paragraphs: “THE OLD HAS PASSED AWAY”… SO WHY ARE YOU STILL FIGHTING THE PERSON YOU USED TO BE?

You gave your life to Jesus. You believed you were made new. But then the old temptations returned, the same wounds reopened, and the same sins you thought you had buried came knocking again. Does that mean your transformation wasn't real? Or have you misunderstood what God actually promised when He called you a new creation?
There is a kind of pain Christians rarely talk about.
Not the pain of being rejected by the world.
Not the pain of being misunderstood by unbelievers.
But the pain of kneeling beside your bed, asking God to forgive you for something you promised Him you would never do again.
And the worst part?
You meant that promise.
You weren't pretending when you surrendered your life to Jesus.
You weren't acting when you cried during worship.
You weren't lying when you told God you wanted to change.
You really wanted to become different.
But somehow, here you are.
Again.
The same anger.
The same lust.
The same jealousy.
The same secret compromise.
The same bitterness you thought you had forgiven.
The same anxiety that keeps you awake when everyone else is sleeping.

Maybe you haven't returned to the exact sins of your former life. Maybe your struggle is quieter now. Pride disguised as righteousness. Envy hidden beneath a smile. Resentment buried under years of church attendance.
And somewhere between another confession and another sleepless night, a terrifying question enters your mind.
If Jesus really made me new, why do I still feel so much like the old me?
That question has driven some believers into deeper dependence on Christ.
But it has driven others into despair.
Some stopped praying because they felt too ashamed to approach God.
Some stopped opening their Bibles because every verse seemed to accuse them.
Some continued attending church, singing the songs, lifting their hands, and saying all the right things while privately wondering whether their salvation had ever been genuine.
And some eventually walked away.
Not necessarily because they stopped believing Jesus could save sinners.
But because they began believing He must have grown tired of saving them.
If any of that sounds painfully familiar, stay with me.
Because there is something extraordinary hidden inside one of the most familiar verses in the New Testament.
And understanding it may change the way you see your struggle, your repentance, and the Savior who has not abandoned His people.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17 (KJV)
Beautiful words.
Powerful words.
Words we print on Christian shirts, place on bedroom walls, and celebrate during baptism.
But what happens when the person wearing that shirt still struggles with temptation?
What happens when the person who was baptized last year falls into an old sin this year?
What happens when someone who sincerely loves Jesus discovers that becoming a new creation did not immediately remove every weakness, sinful desire, painful memory, or destructive habit?
Did Paul exaggerate?
Did Jesus fail to finish His work?
Or have we been asking this verse to promise something it never promised?
Look carefully at the original Greek.
ὥστε εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῷ, καινὴ κτίσις· τὰ ἀρχαῖα παρῆλθεν, ἰδοὺ γέγονεν καινά.
Hōste ei tis en Christō, kainē ktisis; ta archaia parēlthen, idou gegonen kaina.
A close rendering is:
“So then, if anyone is in Christ—new creation! The old things have passed away; look, new things have come.”
Notice something important.
Paul does not say, “If anyone tries hard enough, he will eventually become a new creation.”
He does not say, “If anyone never struggles again, that proves he belongs to Christ.”
He says:
ἐν Χριστῷ — en Christō.
In Christ.
That is where everything begins.
Not in your emotional stability.
Not in your record of flawless obedience.
Not in how many consecutive days you have avoided temptation.
In Christ.
The Greek expression καινὴ κτίσις — kainē ktisis means “new creation.”
The word kainē emphasizes newness, and ktisis refers to creation. Paul is speaking of the astonishing reality that belonging to Christ means participating in God's new-creation work.
This is not merely a motivational slogan about improving yourself.
It is the language of divine redemption.
But there is another detail many readers miss.

The Greek verb παρῆλθεν — parēlthen, translated “passed away,” describes the passing of the old. And γέγονεν — gegonen, translated “have come” or “have become,” is a perfect-tense form pointing to a new reality that has come into being.
Paul is announcing something decisive.
Yet the verse does not say that every remaining sinful inclination has already disappeared.
And the surrounding passage tells us why.
In 2 Corinthians 5:14–21, Paul speaks about Christ dying and rising, believers no longer living for themselves, reconciliation with God, and a new way of regarding people.
The old order of alienation and living apart from Christ has been decisively confronted by His saving work.
A new relationship with God has begun.
A new allegiance has been established.
A new creation has broken into the present through Jesus Christ.
And this changes everything.
Being made new in Christ does not mean your battle with sin is imaginary. It means sin no longer has the rightful claim to rule your life.
You may still experience temptation.
You may still need to unlearn habits shaped by years of rebellion, fear, or pain.
You may still need to confess sin, seek forgiveness, repair damage, and walk through difficult processes of healing.
But your struggle must now be understood in light of your union with Christ, not as though His cross never happened.
And before anyone mistakes that for permission to keep sinning, listen to Paul's own words.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” — Romans 6:1–2 (KJV)
Grace is not permission to remain comfortable in darkness.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that brings sinners into a new life with Christ.
And genuine grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
Think about Peter.
Not the stained-glass Peter.
Not the Peter whose name appears in sermons about courage.
The real Peter.
The man who had walked beside Jesus.
The man who had witnessed miracles.
The man who had boldly declared that even if everyone else fell away, he would remain faithful.
Then came the courtyard.
The fire.
The questions.
The fear.
And three denials.
Imagine the sound of that rooster.
Imagine the unbearable weight of realizing that the very mouth which had promised loyalty had now denied knowing the Lord.
Luke tells us that Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Those tears were real.
His failure was real.
And the consequences of his fear could not be dismissed as though nothing had happened.
But his failure was not the final chapter.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter beside the Sea of Galilee.
There, in John 21, the risen Savior confronted the matter of Peter's love and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
Jesus did not call Peter's denial obedience.
He did not pretend the betrayal was harmless.
But neither did He treat Peter's worst night as the only truth about his future.
The man who had denied Jesus would go on to proclaim Him.
Not because Peter discovered some hidden reservoir of human perfection.
But because the risen Christ is merciful, powerful, and faithful.
That is the difference between the Gospel and mere self-improvement.
Self-improvement says, “Repair yourself until you are worthy of another chance.”
The Gospel announces that Christ died for the ungodly and calls sinners to repentance, faith, and a life transformed by His grace.
And sometimes the people who most desperately need to remember that truth are the ones sitting in church every Sunday.
Because there are believers who understand that Jesus forgave their sins before conversion but struggle to believe He remains their Advocate after conversion.
They imagine that God welcomed them when they were lost but now watches their weakness with nothing but disappointment.
Yet Scripture says:
“My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.” — 1 John 2:1 (KJV)
Read that carefully.
John's purpose is that believers do not sin.
There is no celebration of compromise here.
But he also recognizes the possibility that believers will sin.
And where does he direct them?
Not toward hiding.
Not toward pretending.
Not toward earning their way back through religious performance.
Toward Jesus Christ the righteous.
Our Advocate.
The One whose saving work is sufficient.
The One whose righteousness, not ours, is the foundation of our hope.
And here is where the story becomes even more personal.
Some of us have confused conviction with condemnation.
They are not the same.
Conviction, rightly understood, brings sin into the light and calls us toward repentance and obedience.
Condemnation declares a final verdict of guilt and punishment.
Romans 8:1 announces:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV)
That does not mean Christians never face correction, discipline, earthly consequences, or the painful responsibility of making things right.
It means those who belong to Christ are no longer under the condemning verdict from which He has redeemed them.
The enemy of your soul would gladly exploit your guilt to persuade you that returning to God is pointless.
But the Gospel calls you to bring your sin into the light.
The answer to sin is not secrecy.
It is repentance.
It is confession.
It is trusting Christ.
It is walking in the light rather than making peace with darkness.
And yes, sometimes it means telling another mature believer the truth you have been too embarrassed to say aloud.
Sometimes it means ending a relationship that continually draws you into disobedience.
Sometimes it means removing access to something that repeatedly feeds temptation.
Sometimes it means seeking wise pastoral counsel, professional support, or accountability for patterns you cannot responsibly address alone.
None of those actions purchases forgiveness.
They can, however, become part of the obedient response of someone who has received grace.
Because God never called you to use your new identity as a disguise for an unchanged allegiance.
He called you to walk in the life Christ has given you.
Paul describes this tension with remarkable clarity in Galatians 5:17:
“For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other...” (KJV)
The Greek word σάρξ — sarx, often translated “flesh,” does not simply mean your physical body is evil.
In this context, Paul is describing the fallen, sinful orientation that resists the Holy Spirit.
The conflict is real.
The Spirit calls believers toward holiness.
The flesh pulls toward sinful desires.
And Paul is speaking to Christians.
Not merely to people who have never known God.
That matters.
Because the existence of conflict is not, by itself, proof that conversion never happened.
But neither should we assume that every internal conflict proves someone is saved.
Scripture calls us to examine ourselves, repent sincerely, trust Christ, and look for the fruit of His Spirit.
The question is not simply, “Do I still struggle?”
A deeper question is:
What am I doing with that struggle?
Am I defending my sin?
Am I nurturing it secretly?
Am I calling darkness harmless because confronting it would cost me something?
Or am I bringing it before God, turning away from it, and learning to obey Him even when obedience is difficult?
There is an enormous difference between a believer who falls and grieves over sin and someone who deliberately makes peace with sin while refusing Christ's call to repentance.
The difference is not that one person deserves grace more.
It is that saving faith is not indifferent to the Lord who saves.
And this is why another passage deserves your attention.
Philippians 1:6 says:
“Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.” (KJV)
Notice the movement.
God begins.
God continues His work.
And that work moves toward the day of Christ.
Christian transformation is not presented as a self-powered project completed the moment someone first believes.
The New Testament speaks of believers having been sanctified in Christ, being sanctified, and awaiting the final transformation that will accompany Christ's return.
Hebrews 10:14 brings the tension together:
“For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.” (KJV)
Christ's once-for-all sacrifice is sufficient.
And those who belong to Him are being made holy.
There is no contradiction between the completeness of Christ's saving sacrifice and the continuing work of sanctification in the believer.
Your standing before God rests upon Christ.
Your growing obedience flows from your relationship with Him.
Your final hope is the completion of His redemptive work.
And until that day, Christians are called to walk by faith.
Sometimes that walk includes victories that once seemed impossible.
Sometimes it includes painful exposure of pride you did not know was there.
Sometimes it includes discovering that a habit you thought you had conquered still requires vigilance.
Sometimes it includes the difficult work of forgiving someone who never apologized.
And sometimes it includes learning that healing from a wound and repentance from sin are not identical things.
Not every emotional struggle is evidence of rebellion.
Grief is not automatically unbelief.
Trauma is not automatically a moral failure.
An unwanted intrusive thought is not the same as choosing to entertain sin.
Anxiety or depression does not, by itself, mean someone lacks faith.
Jesus Himself wept.
Paul described affliction and weakness.
And Scripture gives us language for lament as well as praise.
We must never turn the promise of new creation into a weapon against wounded people.
Christ does not require His children to pretend they are unhurt in order to prove they belong to Him.
At the same time, suffering does not make every response to suffering righteous.
We can bring both our wounds and our sins honestly before the Lord.
He knows the difference.
And His Word teaches us to take both seriously.
Perhaps you grew up in a home where love had to be earned.
Perhaps you were constantly reminded of your mistakes.
Perhaps the people who were supposed to protect you taught you that failure meant rejection.
And now, without realizing it, you have begun imagining God through the lens of those experiences.
When you fail, you expect abandonment.
When you stumble, you expect humiliation.
When you pray, you imagine Heaven answering with exhausted silence.
But God has revealed His character most clearly in Jesus Christ.
And Jesus told a story about a son who walked away from his father.
The younger son demanded his inheritance, left home, and squandered what he had received.
Eventually, broken and hungry, he came to himself.
He rehearsed a confession.
He knew he had sinned.
He knew he had no right to demand restoration on his own terms.
And when he returned, his father saw him while he was still a long way off.
The father ran.
He embraced him.
He kissed him.
The son confessed.
And the father celebrated his return.
Read Luke 15:11–32.
The son did not discover that rebellion had been harmless.
He discovered that his father's mercy was greater than he had imagined.
That parable is not a license for believers to wander deliberately, assuming there will never be consequences.
It is a revelation of the joy of repentance and the gracious welcome of the Father.
And maybe someone reading this has been standing at a distance for far too long.
You still believe in God.
You still know the verses.
You still remember what it felt like to pray without hiding.
But shame has persuaded you that you should remain far away until you can present a better version of yourself.
Listen.
You do not clean yourself into worthiness before coming to Christ.
You come to Christ because you need the Savior.
And as you come to Him, you do not cling defiantly to the sins He calls you to forsake.
You surrender them.
You confess them.
You trust Him.
You begin again in obedience—not because His sacrifice must be repeated, but because His mercy is sufficient and His Spirit is at work.
There is something profoundly beautiful about a Christian who no longer needs to pretend.
Someone who can say, “I love Jesus, and I am still learning to obey Him.”
Someone who can confess, “I was wrong,” without collapsing into hopelessness.
Someone who can acknowledge progress without becoming proud.
Someone who can acknowledge failure without declaring the Gospel powerless.
Someone who understands that holiness is not a performance staged for an audience.
It is a life increasingly surrendered to God.
And no, that growth will not always look dramatic.
Sometimes transformation is a person who once exploded in rage choosing to remain silent long enough to pray.
Sometimes it is someone who used to lie automatically finally telling the truth, even when the truth costs them.
Sometimes it is a husband confessing his wrongdoing without blaming his wife.
Sometimes it is a wife refusing to let bitterness define the rest of her life.
Sometimes it is a young believer deleting the secret account that continually led them toward temptation.
Sometimes it is an exhausted Christian opening the Bible again after months of spiritual dryness.
Sometimes it is a person who has been hiding for years finally asking, “Will you pray with me? I need help.”
None of these things earns salvation.
But they can be evidence of grace changing the way someone lives.
And there is a passage that captures the beauty of this ongoing transformation.
“But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.” — 2 Corinthians 3:18 (KJV)
The Greek verb μεταμορφούμεθα — metamorphoumetha means “we are being transformed.”
It is a present-tense passive form.
In this context, it speaks of transformation being worked in believers as they behold the Lord's glory.
Not merely trying to manufacture holiness through willpower.
Not becoming obsessed with the old self.
But being changed by the Spirit as we turn toward Christ.
Do you see it?
The Christian life is not fundamentally about staring at your failures until you hate yourself enough to change.
It is about looking to Jesus, believing His Word, repenting of sin, and walking by the Spirit.
You cannot shame yourself into resurrection life.
That life comes through Christ.
And the same Jesus who saves you is the One who calls you to follow Him.
Not casually.
Not halfheartedly.
Not with a secret agreement to keep your favorite sins untouched.
He calls you to deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Him.
That is costly grace.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that confronts.
Grace that restores.
Grace that teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 says:

“For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world.” (KJV)
Grace is not the opposite of holiness.
Grace trains us in holiness.

And if you are waiting for the day when following Jesus requires no struggle, no surrender, no self-denial, and no dependence upon the Holy Spirit, you are waiting for something Scripture does not promise in this present age.
One day, the struggle with sin will end for those who belong to Christ.
One day, what is perishable will put on imperishability.
One day, the people of God will be raised in glory.
One day, the work of redemption will reach its glorious completion.
But until then, we walk by faith.
We confess.
We repent.
We forgive.
We resist temptation.
We pursue righteousness.
We encourage one another.
We get up after falling—not because falling is insignificant, but because Jesus Christ is greater than our failures.
And perhaps the most important question for you tonight is not whether you have ever stumbled since becoming a Christian.
Perhaps it is whether you are still trying to live as though your past has the authority to name you.
Because your past may explain some of your battles.
But it does not have the right to overrule what God declares about those who are in Christ.
Your former sins are not a badge of honor.
Your wounds are not your entire identity.
Your failures are not your savior.
Your achievements are not your righteousness.
Jesus is Lord.
And in Him, a new creation has begun.
This is why the words “the old has passed away” are so much bigger than a promise that you will never have another difficult day.
They announce a new reality established through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
They announce reconciliation with God.
They announce that believers no longer belong to the old order in the same way they once did.
They announce a new direction, a new allegiance, and a new hope.
And they point toward the day when the new creation will be revealed in fullness.
So when the old temptation returns, do not welcome it as your master.
Resist it.
When sin is exposed, do not excuse it.
Confess it.
When you have harmed someone, do not hide behind the language of grace.
Take responsibility and seek to make things right.
When shame tells you to disappear, remember the Advocate who calls you into the light.
And when you cannot see how far you have come, remember that sanctification is not measured only by how impressive you appear to other people.
God sees the hidden acts of obedience.
The prayers nobody hears.
The apologies that cost you your pride.
The temptations resisted when nobody was watching.
The quiet surrender after a long battle with self-will.
But remember this too.
Not every struggle ends quickly.
Not every consequence disappears after repentance.
Not every relationship can be restored to what it once was.
Not every wounded heart heals on the timetable we would choose.
Christian hope does not require us to deny these realities.
It rests on the faithfulness of Jesus Christ in the middle of them.
And that is why I want to speak to the person who almost stopped reading because these words have come too close to home.
The person who has been praying the same prayer for years.
The person who is afraid that another confession will sound meaningless.
The person who has secretly wondered whether God would be better off without them.
Please hear what the Gospel actually says.
Christ did not die because sinners were already worthy.
He died for sinners.
He did not rise from the grave merely to inspire temporary improvement.
He rose in victory over sin and death.
And He does not call His people to make peace with their bondage.
He calls them into the freedom of belonging to Him.
If you are living in unrepentant sin, do not use these words to comfort yourself while refusing to turn.
Repent.
If you are crushed by guilt over confessed sin, do not treat your shame as more authoritative than the promises of God.
Look to Christ.
If you are unsure whether you truly belong to Him, do not settle for an emotional slogan or a religious label.
Turn to Jesus in repentance and faith.
If you are weary from fighting temptation, seek the help of faithful believers who will speak truth to you with love.
And if you have begun to believe that your story is already ruined beyond redemption, remember what God accomplished through the cross.
The greatest scandal in human history was that the sinless Son of God was condemned and crucified.
Yet through that very cross, God accomplished the redemption of sinners.
Human evil did not defeat His saving purpose.
Jesus rose.
And because He lives, the story of everyone who belongs to Him is not finally defined by sin, shame, or death.
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because every earthly consequence will vanish.
But because Jesus Christ redeems sinners and makes all things new according to His perfect purpose.
That is the message we carry at Gospel Warrior.
Not that Christians are perfect.
Not that following Jesus is easy.
Not that faith eliminates every tear.
But that the crucified and risen Christ is worthy of our complete trust, and His Word remains the foundation for genuine transformation.
If this article has uncovered something you have been carrying silently, I want to invite you to respond with honesty.
You do not need to disclose private details publicly. God knows what those words mean.

And if you have a testimony of how Christ brought you out of a destructive pattern, consider sharing it. Not to glorify the darkness you escaped, but to magnify the mercy of the Savior who met you there.
There is someone on your Facebook friends list who may never walk into a church this week.
Someone who still believes in God but has quietly stopped praying.
Someone who thinks becoming a Christian means they should never struggle again.
Someone who has been measuring God's love by the number of times they have failed.
Not merely to increase the reach of a page, but because the Gospel is too important to keep to ourselves.
You may never know whose private prayer is answered through a truth you decided to share.
But I also want to speak about something that matters deeply to this ministry.
A message like this does not have to end when you finish reading.
It can become the beginning of deeper discipleship.
Gospel Warrior is working to continue and expand the reach of biblical articles, Christian books, teaching resources, and encouragement for people who are hungry for the Word of God.
We want people who cannot afford expensive Christian resources to have opportunities to study Scripture, grow in discernment, strengthen their faith, and become better equipped to follow Jesus.
That work takes time, effort, and practical resources.
It is simply one additional opportunity to give generously and intentionally toward work you believe is honoring Christ.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
But willing generosity, motivated by love for Christ and concern for people who need His Word.
These products are not the reason we preach the Gospel.
You can still help meaningfully.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite someone to read Scripture.
Encourage a struggling Christian.
Tell someone what Jesus has done for you.
Use the free resources available to you and grow in the knowledge of Christ.
It is to point people toward the Savior.
But never confuse the means with the mission.
Jesus is the treasure.
Not the platform.
Not the products.
Not the numbers.
Jesus Christ.
The One who entered our broken world.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who died and rose again.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who gives His people new life.
And the One who will complete His redemptive purpose.
So before you leave this article, return with me to the question that brought us here.
If the old has passed away, why am I still struggling?
Because new creation has already begun in Christ, but its full consummation is still ahead.
Because your relationship to sin has changed, even though you must still resist its influence.
Because sanctification is a continuing work of God's grace, not a declaration that you have already become incapable of sin.
Because the Holy Spirit is forming Christlike character in people who still live in a fallen world.
Because the Savior who justifies His people also calls them into a lifelong journey of holiness.
And because the final chapter of your redemption will not be written by your old nature.
