And that misunderstanding can do terrible things to a wounded soul.
It can make the hurting person feel cursed.
It can make the prosperous sinner feel untouchable.
It can turn forgiveness into a weakness.
It can make suffering look like evidence of hidden sin.
And worst of all, it can make the cross of Jesus seem unnecessary.
Because if everyone simply receives exactly what they deserve, what room is left for mercy?
What room is left for forgiveness?
What room is left for the scandalous, undeserved, life-transforming grace of God?
Listen carefully.
The Bible does teach that our choices have consequences.
But the Gospel reveals that consequences are not the whole story.
And Jesus Christ is the reason.
In the original Greek of Galatians 6:7, Paul writes:
Μὴ πλανᾶσθε, θεὸς οὐ μυκτηρίζεται· ὃ γὰρ ἐὰν σπείρῃ ἄνθρωπος, τοῦτο καὶ θερίσει.
Transliterated:
Mē planasthe, theos ou myktērizetai; ho gar ean speirē anthrōpos, touto kai therisei.
A close translation is:
“Do not be deceived; God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, this also he will reap.”
Notice something important.
Paul does not say the universe cannot be mocked.
He says God is not mocked.
The Greek verb myktērizetai carries the sense of being mocked or treated with contempt.
And the agricultural language is deliberate.
Speirē refers to sowing.
Therisei refers to reaping.
Paul is describing a moral and spiritual reality under the authority of the living God, not an impersonal cosmic mechanism operating independently of Him.
And the next verse makes the context unmistakable.
“For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.” — Galatians 6:8, KJV
Paul is addressing the direction of a person's life.
The flesh, in this context, is not simply the physical body. It refers to fallen human nature operating in rebellion against God.
The Spirit is the Holy Spirit, who gives life and transforms those who belong to Christ.
Paul is warning believers not to deceive themselves into thinking they can cultivate rebellion against God without spiritual consequences.
And he is encouraging them to persevere in doing good, as Galatians 6:9–10 makes clear.
This is not a promise that every good deed will produce wealth, that every bad deed will bring immediate disaster, or that every hardship is repayment for some secret wrongdoing.
It is a call to live before God with eternal seriousness.
And that distinction matters more than you might imagine.
Because somewhere in the world, a faithful mother is burying a child she prayed over every night.
A devoted husband is watching his marriage collapse despite his efforts to save it.
A Christian who tried to do what was right is losing a job while a dishonest coworker gets promoted.
And a woman who has spent years serving God is lying awake, wondering why life has been so merciless.
Imagine walking up to any of them and saying:
Well, you reap what you sow.
Do you hear how cruel that can become?
It takes a biblical warning about moral responsibility and turns it into an accusation against the suffering.
Jesus Himself confronted that kind of thinking.
In John 9, His disciples encountered a man who had been blind from birth.
They asked:
“Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?” — John 9:2, KJV
They assumed someone must have done something wrong.
Somebody had to be responsible.
Somebody had to deserve this.
But Jesus answered:
“Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.” — John 9:3, KJV
Jesus was not declaring that the man or his parents had never sinned. He was rejecting the assumption that this particular blindness resulted from their personal sin.
And suddenly, a whole theology of suspicion begins to collapse.
Not every sickness is punishment.
Not every financial struggle is a curse.
Not every broken relationship is divine revenge.
Not every painful season is God collecting an unpaid debt.
Sometimes we suffer because we live in a fallen world.
Sometimes we suffer because other people sin against us.
Sometimes we experience the natural consequences of our own decisions.
Sometimes we endure trials we cannot fully explain.
And sometimes, as with the man born blind, God's work becomes visible in circumstances that human beings have completely misunderstood.
The book of Job makes the same warning painfully clear.
Job's friends were convinced that suffering must prove wrongdoing.
Their reasoning sounded religious.
Their arguments sounded logical.
But God rebuked them for speaking wrongly about Him (Job 42:7).
Be careful when your theology makes you more eager to explain someone's pain than to sit beside them in it.
Because you may be defending a principle while misrepresenting the heart of God.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is easy to reject that kind of judgment when we are the ones suffering.
It is much harder when the person suffering is someone who hurt us.
Think about the person who betrayed you.
The person who humiliated you.
The person who walked away without apologizing.
The person who seemed to destroy something precious in your life and then continued living as though nothing happened.
You may have said, “I leave it to God.”
But privately, you have imagined the day they would finally feel what you felt.
You wanted them to understand.
You wanted them to regret it.
Maybe you wanted them to hurt.
And you called that justice.

The desire for justice is not automatically sinful. God cares deeply about justice, and Scripture does not require victims to deny evil, abandon appropriate boundaries, or avoid lawful accountability.
But there is a difference between trusting God to judge rightly and secretly making another person's destruction the condition of your peace.
Romans 12:19 says:
“Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.”
Those words are not permission to pretend wrongdoing never happened.
They are an invitation to release personal vengeance into the hands of the only Judge who sees everything.
God knows what happened.
He knows what was stolen.
He knows what was said behind closed doors.
He knows the tears you wiped away before anyone entered the room.
And He does not need your hatred to help Him remember.
But here is the question that may expose something in all of us.
What if the person who hurt you genuinely repents and God forgives them?
Would you rejoice?
Or would you feel cheated?
That question leads us to one of the most astonishing scenes in the Bible.
A criminal is dying beside Jesus.
He has no time to rebuild his reputation.
No opportunity to spend decades proving he has changed.
No way to undo the crimes that brought him to his execution.
Luke records that one of the criminals acknowledged the justice of their punishment.
“And we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss.” — Luke 23:41, KJV
The criminal knew something many of us spend our entire lives avoiding.
He was guilty.
He could not save himself.
And the innocent Jesus was suffering beside him.
Then he turned toward Christ.
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” — Luke 23:42, KJV
That was his plea.
Not a speech about his achievements.
Not a promise that he would compensate everyone he had harmed.
Not a list of religious accomplishments.
Just a guilty man turning to a King whose kingdom he somehow recognized through the blood and humiliation of crucifixion.
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” — Luke 23:43, KJV
Read that again.
The criminal did not escape the earthly consequences of his actions.
He still died on that cross.
But he received a promise of paradise from the Savior he had turned to in faith.
His punishment did not disappear.
Yet his guilt did not have the final word over his eternal destiny.
That is not karma.
That is grace.
And if you have never been deeply disturbed by the mercy of Jesus, perhaps you have not yet realized how desperately you need it yourself.
Because there is another man in Scripture whose story is just as scandalous.
His name was Saul.
He persecuted the church.
He approved of Stephen's death and ravaged Christian households.
He pursued believers as enemies.
And then, on the road to Damascus, the risen Jesus confronted him.
Saul did not meet Christ because he had accumulated enough good deeds to deserve a reward.
He met Christ while moving in the wrong direction.
The persecutor was confronted by the One he persecuted.
And the man who had terrorized believers became the apostle Paul, a servant of the Gospel he once tried to destroy.
Did Paul suddenly live a comfortable life?
No.
He suffered imprisonment, beatings, danger, hardship, and rejection.
Grace did not erase the reality of suffering.
It transformed the direction and purpose of his life.
Paul later wrote:
“This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” — 1 Timothy 1:15, KJV
The man who wrote about sowing and reaping also knew what it meant to receive mercy he could never earn.
He understood both moral responsibility and divine grace.
He did not teach that salvation comes through earning enough good outcomes.
He taught:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
And immediately afterward, he explained that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
Do you see the order?
We are not saved because our good works have purchased God's acceptance.
We are saved by grace through faith, and the life of faith bears fruit in obedience.
Good works are not the price of redemption.
They are the fruit of a redeemed life.
This is why the Gospel cannot be reduced to karma with Christian vocabulary.

The popular understanding of karma often imagines a moral cause-and-effect system in which actions bring corresponding consequences. Actual teachings about karma differ among Hindu, Buddhist, and other religious traditions and cannot all be reduced to the slogan “what goes around comes around.”
But biblical sowing and reaping is rooted in the personal, sovereign God of Scripture, His judgment, His patience, His mercy, and His redemptive purposes in Jesus Christ.
It does not operate independently of grace.
And it does not promise that every moral account will be visibly settled before death.
The Bible itself recognizes that wicked people sometimes prosper while righteous people suffer.
Psalm 73 wrestles with that very problem.
The psalmist saw the prosperity of the wicked and nearly stumbled in his faith.
Only when he considered their ultimate end in God's presence did his perspective change.

Ecclesiastes 8:14 likewise acknowledges the disturbing reality that righteous people sometimes experience what seems fitting for the wicked, while wicked people experience what seems fitting for the righteous.
Scripture is not naive about injustice.
It does not pretend that life always looks fair.
Instead, it teaches that God's final judgment is certain even when His present providence is mysterious.
And then the Bible takes us somewhere even more extraordinary.
To a hill outside Jerusalem.
To a wooden cross.
To the place where the only perfectly righteous man who ever lived was condemned as a criminal.
Think about that.
If suffering always proved personal guilt, what would we do with Jesus?
He committed no sin.
Yet He was mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
He was the innocent One suffering for the guilty.
The prophet Isaiah had spoken of this centuries earlier.
In Isaiah 53:5, the Hebrew text includes these words:
וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ מְדֻכָּא מֵעֲוֹנֹתֵינוּ
Transliterated:
Vehu meḥolal mippeshaʿenu, medukka meʿavonotenu.
A close translation is:
“But he was pierced because of our transgressions, crushed because of our iniquities.”
The KJV renders the verse:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
The Hebrew words peshaʿenu and ʿavonotenu refer to our transgressions and our iniquities.
Not His.
Ours.
Christian interpretation understands Isaiah's suffering servant as finding his fulfillment in Jesus Christ, who bore sin and accomplished redemption through His suffering.
And Peter draws that connection explicitly when he writes of Christ bearing our sins in His own body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24).
Now consider the weight of this.
We have sinned.
God is holy.
Sin deserves judgment.
But Jesus, the sinless Savior, willingly gave Himself for sinners.
As 2 Corinthians 5:21 declares:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
That does not mean Jesus became morally sinful.
It means that the sinless Christ stood in our place in God's saving work so that those united to Him by faith might be reconciled to God.
This is where the language of sowing and reaping must be handled carefully.
It would be too simplistic to say that Jesus merely received a mechanical harvest belonging to someone else.
The cross is not an impersonal transfer of cosmic consequences.
It is the deliberate, loving, saving act of God in Christ.
Justice was not treated as meaningless.
Sin was not declared harmless.
Grace was not cheap.
The Savior gave Himself.
And the resurrection declared that death would not hold Him.
At Calvary, the innocent One suffered for the guilty so that the guilty could be forgiven and made new.
That is the scandal.
That is the grace.
That is why Jesus rewrites everything.
But please do not misunderstand.
Grace is not a spiritual loophole that allows you to keep sowing destruction while demanding a painless harvest.
The same Jesus who forgives sinners calls them to repentance.
The same Gospel that offers pardon also calls us to a transformed life.
Romans 6:1–2 asks whether we should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
Paul's answer is emphatic.
“God forbid.”
A person cannot rightly use the mercy of Christ as an excuse to cultivate the very sins from which Christ came to rescue us.
If you have betrayed someone, repentance may require confession, truthfulness, and appropriate efforts to make restitution.
If you have been dishonest, repentance means turning toward honesty.
If you have harmed others, repentance does not erase their right to safety, accountability, or justice.
If you have destroyed trust, forgiveness does not automatically restore that trust overnight.
And if you are suffering because of decisions you made years ago, coming to Christ does not necessarily remove every earthly consequence.
But it does mean those consequences do not have to define your identity forever.
A prison sentence may remain.
A relationship may not be restored.
A reputation may take years to rebuild.
A scar may remain long after the wound has closed.
Yet in Christ, a repentant sinner can become a new creation.
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
That is not permission to deny your past.
It is the promise that your past does not have sovereign authority over your future in Christ.
And maybe that is the word you have needed for years.
You keep looking backward.
Back to the person you used to be.
Back to the decision you wish you could undo.
Back to the season when you were far from God.
You remember the shame so vividly that sometimes you wonder whether the Lord remembers you only as the worst version of yourself.
But when you come to Jesus in repentance and faith, you are not asking Him to pretend your sin never happened.
You are trusting the Savior who died and rose again to forgive it.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
Those words are not spoken over everyone indiscriminately, regardless of their relationship to Christ.
They are the assurance of those who are in Him.
And what a breathtaking assurance that is.
No condemnation.
Not because you were innocent.
Not because your sin was insignificant.
Not because you suffered enough to pay for it.
But because Jesus Christ is sufficient.
Perhaps you have spent years believing that every painful thing happening to you is God's way of making you pay for who you used to be.
You have interpreted every closed door as punishment.
Every disappointment as a sentence.
Every delay as divine anger.
And you have been trying to earn peace through guilt.
But guilt is not a savior.
Self-punishment is not the cross.
And endless shame is not the same thing as repentance.
Godly sorrow leads us toward repentance, as 2 Corinthians 7:10 teaches.
But despair that keeps us hiding from Jesus is not the destination of the Gospel.
Remember Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
He failed publicly, painfully, and personally.
Then he wept bitterly.
But after the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and called him to feed His sheep (John 21:15–19).
The denial was real.
The grief was real.
The restoration was real.
Jesus did not call Peter's failure good.
He called Peter back to Himself.
And perhaps the most moving part is that the Lord knew Peter would fail before Peter ever failed.
Yet He had already spoken of praying for him and of Peter strengthening his brothers after turning back (Luke 22:31–32).
What kind of Savior sees the coming failure and still speaks of restoration?
Jesus.
The One who knows everything about us and still calls sinners to repent and come to Him.
Now, there is another side to this message.
And it is for the person who has been treating grace as though it were permission to keep playing with sin.
You cannot plant bitterness every day and expect love to flourish without repentance.
You cannot cultivate deception and expect trust to grow naturally.
You cannot continually feed lust, pride, cruelty, or greed and pretend those habits are spiritually harmless.
What you repeatedly nurture shapes the direction of your life.
Paul's warning is not imaginary.
It is urgent.
The Greek opening of Galatians 6:7, Mē planasthe, means “Do not be deceived.”
It is a warning against self-deception.
You can fool your audience.
You can fool your friends.
You can fool your family.
You may even fool yourself for a while.
But you cannot mock God.
And yet, if the Holy Spirit is exposing sin in your life today, the answer is not to run farther into hiding.
It is to come into the light.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The invitation is not to negotiate with God over how much guilt you must carry.
It is to confess, repent, and trust His mercy through Christ.
Do not confuse conviction with rejection.
Conviction may be the very means by which God is calling you away from what is destroying you.
And this is where the story of sowing and reaping becomes unexpectedly beautiful.
Because Paul does not only warn us about destructive sowing.
He also calls us to persevere in doing good.
“And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.” — Galatians 6:9, KJV
Maybe you have been sowing prayers nobody hears.
Maybe you have been sowing forgiveness while your heart still aches.
Maybe you have been sowing honesty in a place where dishonesty seems to win.
Maybe you have been sowing kindness while carrying a burden that nobody knows about.
Maybe you have been faithfully teaching your children about Jesus, but you cannot yet see the fruit.
Do not mistake a delayed harvest for an absent God.
Paul does not promise that every prayer will be answered exactly as you imagine or that every faithful act will produce visible success in this life.
But he does encourage believers not to abandon the good they have been called to do.
Faithfulness matters.
Love matters.
Truth matters.
Generosity matters.
Obedience matters.
And no act of genuine faithfulness is hidden from the Lord.
Still, our ultimate hope is not that life will finally reward us with everything we wanted.
Our ultimate hope is Christ Himself.
That distinction protects us from turning Christianity into a transaction.
We do not love God merely so that He will make our lives easier.
We love Him because He first loved us.
We do not give so that heaven will owe us financial prosperity.
We give because we have received grace.
We do not obey to purchase salvation.
We obey because the Savior who redeemed us is worthy.
And that brings us to something very personal.
What are you sowing right now?
Not what are you posting.
Not what do people think about you.
Not what does your church attendance suggest.
What are you cultivating when nobody is watching?
What thoughts are you feeding?
What sins are you excusing?
What grudges are you watering?
What habits are quietly becoming your character?
What truth have you been avoiding because obedience would cost you something?
And what good have you stopped doing because you became tired of waiting?
You do not need to answer publicly to impress anyone.
But you do need to be honest before God.
Because the most dangerous deception is not always believing that sin has no consequences.
Sometimes it is believing that your sin is too great for the mercy of Jesus.
Both lies keep people away from the Savior.
One says, I do not need repentance.
The other says, Repentance will never be enough for someone like me.
The Gospel confronts both.
You need repentance.
And Jesus is a sufficient Savior.
You need grace.
And grace calls you into a new life.
You are responsible for what you sow.
But you are not beyond redemption because of what you have sown.
If this message has touched a place you normally keep hidden, I want to invite you to respond with spiritual honesty.

You do not need to expose private details or confess sensitive sins to strangers. God already knows the full story. But sometimes one honest sentence can open the door to encouragement, prayer, and the reminder that you are not walking alone.
And please, think about the person who needs to hear this.
The friend who believes God has abandoned them because life has become painful.
The brother who has been running from Jesus because of shame.
The sister who is struggling to forgive someone who hurt her.
The parent who feels that years of faithful prayer have been wasted.
The believer who has confused suffering with divine rejection.
Perhaps that day will come sooner than you think.
There is a reason we continue building Gospel Warrior.
Not because we believe another page, ministry, or personality can replace the local church, the Word of God, or the saving work of Jesus Christ.

But because the Gospel deserves to be proclaimed faithfully, and people need continual encouragement to open their Bibles, examine their lives, repent of sin, and grow in the grace and knowledge of the Lord.
Every article takes work.
Every biblical explanation requires care.
Every resource we make available is an opportunity to help someone move beyond a passing emotional moment toward a deeper life of discipleship.
Not out of guilt.
Not because a monthly payment earns God's favor.
And certainly not because financial support is a substitute for the tithes and offerings you prayerfully give through your local church.
You cannot buy grace. You cannot purchase spiritual maturity. And you do not owe a ministry money in order to prove your love for Jesus.
Think of it as becoming a faithful partner in the work, according to your ability and conviction.
Philippians 4:15–18 describes believers supporting Paul's ministry through their giving. Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be willing, not pressured or grudging.
That is the spirit in which this invitation is offered.
Your prayers matter.
Your faithful encouragement matters.
You can help without spending a single peso or dollar.
Those products are not the reason to give.
Those resources are there to encourage serious growth in Jesus Christ through biblical reading, prayer, spiritual reflection, and practical discipleship.
Jesus Christ.
The One who did not come to flatter sinners, but to save them.
The One who did not minimize sin, but bore its cost.
The One who calls us to repent, believe, follow, and become new.
And before you leave this article, I want to return to the question we began with.
What happens when the person who deserves judgment falls at the feet of Jesus?
Sometimes there are still consequences.
Sometimes there are still tears.
Sometimes restitution is necessary.
Sometimes relationships remain broken.
Sometimes healing takes years.
But for the one who truly turns to Christ in repentance and faith, there is forgiveness.
There is reconciliation with God.
There is the gift of the Holy Spirit.
There is a new direction.
There is hope beyond the grave.
And there is a Savior whose resurrection is greater than the power of death.
The world may tell you that your life is nothing more than the sum of what you have done.
Your shame may tell you that you will never escape the person you used to be.
Your bitterness may tell you that peace will only come when the person who hurt you finally suffers enough.
But Jesus calls you to something different.
Repent.
Believe.
Forgive as you have been forgiven.
Pursue justice without becoming consumed by vengeance.
Sow to the Spirit.
Do not grow weary in doing good.
And trust the God who is both perfectly just and astonishingly merciful.
You reap what you sow.
Yes, that is biblical.
But do not stop reading Scripture at the warning.
Keep reading until you reach the cross.
Keep reading until you reach the empty tomb.
Keep reading until you hear the promise that those who belong to Christ are no longer under condemnation.
Keep reading until you understand that Christianity is not about an impersonal universe giving you exactly what you have earned.
It is about the living God calling sinners to repentance and offering eternal life through His Son.
And if you remember nothing else from these words, remember this:
Your sin was serious enough that Jesus went to the cross—but His grace is sufficient to save everyone who comes to Him in faith.
So stop treating karma as your judge.
Stop treating shame as your identity.
Stop treating revenge as your healing.
And stop treating grace as permission to remain unchanged.
Come to Jesus.
The real Jesus.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The Savior who forgives.
The King who transforms.
The One who takes people whose stories seem ruined and makes them living testimonies of His mercy.
Because the most unforgettable part of your story does not have to be what you did, what someone did to you, or what you lost.
It can be what Jesus Christ did to redeem you.
The scars may still tell the story of what happened—but they do not get to write the final sentence when your life belongs to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE CHURCH THAT SILENCED THE WOUNDED TO PROTECT THE ANOINTED
paragraphs: THE CHURCH THAT SILENCED THE WOUNDED TO PROTECT THE ANOINTED
When a pastor's reputation becomes more important than a victim's suffering, something sacred has been betrayed. And the Jesus who overturned tables has something to say about it.
She walked into the church believing it was the safest place she could go.

She had been taught that the church was a family. That pastors were shepherds. That spiritual leaders were called to protect the flock. That when life became unbearable, the house of God was where wounded people could finally breathe.
So when someone she trusted hurt her, she did what she thought a faithful Christian should do.
She told the truth.
And that was when she discovered something more painful than the original betrayal.
The people who had taught her to speak the truth suddenly wanted her to remain silent.
“Are you sure that's what happened?”
“Have you prayed about this?”
“You need to understand how much he's done for this ministry.”
“Think about the people who could lose their faith.”
“Don't let Satan use you to destroy the church.”
And then came the sentence that broke something deep inside her.
“Sometimes we have to forgive and move on for the sake of God's work.”
She had come looking for protection.
Instead, she was being asked to protect the person who hurt her.
Read that again.
The wounded person was being asked to carry the burden of preserving the reputation of the person accused of causing the wound.
And somewhere between the closed-door meetings, carefully worded announcements, and whispered conversations, she began wondering whether telling the truth had made her the enemy.
Perhaps you've never experienced this.
Perhaps you have.
Perhaps you're the person who reported something terrible and watched the church leadership become more concerned about who might find out than about what actually happened.
Perhaps you were told that questioning a pastor was rebellion.
Perhaps someone quoted Scripture to convince you that silence was holiness.
Or perhaps you're a faithful church member who has watched a troubling situation unfold and quietly wondered:
Why does the church sometimes move so quickly to defend a powerful leader, yet so slowly to protect the vulnerable person standing before it?
That question deserves more than a public-relations statement.
It deserves an answer from the Word of God.
Because the greatest scandal is not that sinners can be found inside churches.
We already know that.
The scandal is when a church begins protecting sin while using the name of the Savior who died to redeem sinners from it.
And before this story ends, we need to confront a frightening possibility.
Sometimes what people call protecting the ministry is actually protecting the very thing destroying it.
Jesus never asked His church to sacrifice wounded people on the altar of institutional reputation.
Never.
Not once.
And if we have forgotten that, we have forgotten something essential about the Shepherd we claim to follow.
In Ezekiel 34, God confronts Israel's shepherds because they had cared for themselves while neglecting the flock.
Listen to the accusation.
“The weak have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken...” (Ezekiel 34:4, KJV).
These words were originally spoken against Israel's unfaithful shepherds, not written as a direct description of every modern pastor. But the moral principle is unmistakable.
God sees what happens when those entrusted with care use their position for themselves while the vulnerable suffer.
The Hebrew word for shepherd is רֹעֶה (ro'eh), from the verb רָעָה (ra'ah), meaning to shepherd, pasture, or tend.
A shepherd's calling is not simply to stand above the sheep.
It is to care for them.
To feed them.
To protect them.
To seek the wandering.
To attend to the injured.
Authority in God's design is never permission to consume the people entrusted to your care.
It is a responsibility to serve them.
And when a shepherd becomes more interested in defending his position than tending the wounds of the flock, something has gone terribly wrong.
God does not merely notice the suffering.
He confronts the shepherds.
Later in the chapter, He declares:
“Behold, I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out.” (Ezekiel 34:11, KJV).
Imagine what those words mean to someone who has been abandoned by spiritual authorities.
The leaders may refuse to listen.
The congregation may misunderstand.
The institution may deny responsibility.
But the Lord has not lost sight of His sheep.
And the chapter ultimately points toward God's promised Davidic shepherd, a promise Christians understand as finding its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
The true Shepherd does not exploit His flock.
He gives His life for it.
That is why Jesus says in John 10:11:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.”
Notice the difference.
A corrupt shepherd sacrifices the sheep to preserve himself.
The Good Shepherd sacrifices Himself to save the sheep.
One protects his throne.
The other carries a cross.
One demands silence to preserve his image.
The other declares Himself to be the truth.
And that difference should terrify anyone who claims to lead God's people while knowingly concealing harm.
But how does a church reach the point where protecting an influential leader seems more urgent than protecting a vulnerable member?
It rarely begins with someone openly announcing, “We have decided that reputation matters more than righteousness.”
It often begins with fear.
Fear that the congregation will split.
Fear that donations will decline.
Fear that years of ministry will be questioned.
Fear that outsiders will mock Christianity.
Fear that the pastor's family will suffer.
Fear that everything people have built will collapse.
Some of these fears concern real consequences.
A church scandal can devastate families, divide communities, and wound people who had no involvement in the wrongdoing.
But fear becomes spiritually dangerous when it starts determining what truth may be spoken and whose suffering may be acknowledged.
Proverbs 29:25 warns:
“The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.”
The Hebrew word מוֹקֵשׁ (moqesh), translated “snare,” describes a trap.
That image is painfully appropriate.
A church can become so afraid of losing its reputation that it becomes trapped in decisions that destroy its moral credibility.
First, leaders minimize a complaint.
Then they discourage questions.
Then they frame accountability as disloyalty.
Then they ask the wounded to be quiet.
Eventually, the institution begins treating the exposure of wrongdoing as more dangerous than the wrongdoing itself.
And all the while, people continue singing about holiness.
This is one of the most devastating contradictions a believer can encounter.
Not because Christians are expected to be sinless.
They are not.
But because Christians are called to walk in the light.
The apostle John writes:
The Greek word περιπατῶμεν (peripatōmen), translated “we walk,” describes an ongoing manner of life.
Walking in the light is not a performance of perfection.
It is a life oriented toward God's revealed truth rather than concealed darkness.
And only two verses later, John says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9, KJV).
Do you see the beauty?
The Gospel does not require pretending that sin never happened.
The Gospel invites sinners to bring sin into the light and receive mercy through Jesus Christ.
But where there is deliberate concealment, intimidation, and refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing, we are no longer witnessing the humble confession Scripture commends.
We are witnessing resistance to the very truth through which repentance begins.
And this is where a painful misunderstanding often enters the church.
People say, “But the leader is anointed.”
As though spiritual gifting makes someone immune to correction.
As though a powerful sermon cancels a private act of cruelty.
As though thousands of people being blessed through a ministry means the person leading it cannot be held accountable.
But Scripture never teaches that giftedness is proof of moral innocence.
King David was anointed.
David also committed grievous sin.
He took Bathsheba, arranged Uriah's death, and abused royal power.
And when the prophet Nathan confronted him, Nathan did not say, “Your Majesty, your reputation is too important for us to discuss this.”
He said:
“Thou art the man.” (2 Samuel 12:7, KJV).
Four words.
No flattery.
No institutional damage control.
No suggestion that exposing the king's wrongdoing was a greater offense than the wrongdoing itself.
Nathan spoke the truth.
David's sin was not made righteous by his calling.
His position did not place him above God's judgment.
And although David confessed, the consequences of his actions did not simply disappear.
That matters.
Because genuine repentance is not a magic phrase that erases every earthly consequence.
A leader can receive God's forgiveness and still need to step away from leadership.
A person can repent and still face legal accountability.
A church can extend compassion to someone accused of wrongdoing while taking necessary steps to protect those who may be at risk.
Grace is not the cancellation of justice.
Grace is not permission to keep harming people while everyone else is commanded to forgive.
Some of the most damaging spiritual manipulation happens when biblical words are separated from their biblical meaning.
“Forgive.”
“Submit.”
“Honor.”
“Do not judge.”
“Touch not mine anointed.”
These are serious scriptural themes.
But none gives a church leader unlimited authority or requires a victim to remain exposed to danger.

Psalm 105:15, often quoted as “Touch not mine anointed,” occurs in a passage describing God's protection of His covenant people. It is not a universal prohibition against investigating allegations involving pastors.
Hebrews 13:17 calls believers to respond appropriately to spiritual leaders, but the verse also says those leaders watch for souls as people who must give account.

And Matthew 18 teaches the seriousness of addressing sin within the believing community. It must not be twisted into a requirement that victims of abuse, violence, or criminal wrongdoing privately confront an alleged offender before seeking safety or contacting appropriate authorities.
Scripture must never become a weapon used to keep vulnerable people trapped.
Consider something else.
In 1 Timothy 5:19, Paul instructs Timothy not to receive an accusation against an elder except on the basis of two or three witnesses.
That instruction protects elders from reckless and unsupported accusations.
But the next verse says:
“Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear.” (1 Timothy 5:20, KJV).
Paul did not create a special class of untouchable leaders.
He required fairness in handling accusations and accountability when wrongdoing is established.
Both principles matter.
An allegation must not automatically be treated as a proven fact.
And a respected leader must not automatically be treated as innocent simply because people admire him.
Truth demands careful listening, impartial investigation, appropriate confidentiality, and protection against retaliation.
Where abuse or criminal conduct may be involved, safeguarding and applicable reporting obligations must be taken seriously.
A church is not exempt from civil law because it uses spiritual language.
And a church should never use private spiritual processes to obstruct a lawful investigation.
There is another passage that should make every Christian leader examine his heart.
James 2 confronts favoritism.
A wealthy person enters the assembly wearing fine clothing, and the community gives him preferential treatment while humiliating someone who is poor.
James asks:
“Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts?” (James 2:4, KJV).
The Greek word προσωπολημπτεῖτε (prosōpolēmpteite) in James 2:1 refers to showing favoritism or partiality.
The underlying idea is treating people differently because of outward status rather than judging rightly.
James is directly addressing social and economic favoritism in the assembly.
But the warning reaches into a broader biblical principle.
When wealth, influence, popularity, or position determines whose voice matters, justice is endangered.
Think about how this can happen in a modern congregation.
A famous pastor receives a private meeting with senior leaders.
A frightened member receives a warning about gossip.
A major donor is given the benefit of the doubt.
A volunteer is told not to cause division.
A well-connected leader is described as someone who deserves restoration.
A wounded person is described as someone who needs to learn forgiveness.
The imbalance is heartbreaking.
And it is precisely why churches need processes that do not depend on the popularity of the people involved.
Not every accusation is true.
Not every church handles allegations badly.

Many faithful pastors and congregations quietly do the difficult work of protecting people, investigating concerns fairly, reporting wrongdoing when required, and submitting themselves to accountability.
Their faithfulness matters.
We should not condemn every shepherd because some have betrayed their calling.
But neither should we defend an unfaithful shepherd simply because other shepherds are faithful.
The question is not whether the church contains good people.
The question is whether we will obey Jesus when obedience threatens our comfort.
And perhaps no Gospel scene exposes the danger of religious reputation more powerfully than the trial of Jesus Himself.
In John 11, after Jesus raised Lazarus, the religious authorities discussed the growing public response to His ministry.
Their concern included what Roman intervention might mean for their nation and their position.
John 11:48 records their fear:
“If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him: and the Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation.”
We must read this in its historical context. The passage describes particular leaders and political tensions in first-century Judea; it is not a condemnation of Jewish people as a whole.
But the spiritual danger is unmistakable.
Religious authorities can become so consumed with preserving their place that they resist the truth standing before them.
Think about that.
The One who came to save sinners was treated as a threat to a religious establishment.
The One who healed the broken was rejected by leaders determined to preserve their power.
And eventually, Jesus stood before Pontius Pilate.
He was innocent.
Yet He was condemned.
The crowd demanded His crucifixion.
The powerful protected their interests.
And the Righteous One was led away.
This is not a claim that every mistreated church member is identical to Jesus or that every disputed allegation repeats His trial.
But the Passion of Christ exposes what happens when fear, injustice, and human power prevail over truth.
And it reveals something even greater.
Jesus willingly endured the cross to accomplish the redemption no human institution could provide.
He did not die to make religious organizations look respectable.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
He did not rise from the grave so that Christian leaders could become untouchable.
He rose as Lord.
And every earthly shepherd remains accountable to Him.
Now imagine that wounded church member again.
The one sitting alone after everyone else has gone home.
The one staring at a phone, wondering whether anyone will believe her.
The one whose prayers have become shorter because the words no longer come easily.
The one who still loves Jesus but feels physically sick at the thought of walking into another church building.
Perhaps that person is you.
And perhaps the question you have been afraid to ask is this:
“If people who represented God treated me this way, how can I trust God again?”
That is not a small question.
And it should never receive a careless answer.
I will not tell you that your pain is insignificant.
I will not tell you to return immediately to an unsafe environment.
I will not tell you that forgiving someone means you must trust them again.
And I will not tell you that staying silent about abuse is proof of spiritual maturity.
But I do want you to see something.
The character of Jesus is not defined by the misconduct of someone who claims to represent Him.
The church can fail to resemble Christ.
Christ does not cease to be holy because the church has failed.
A pastor may betray his responsibility.
Jesus remains the Good Shepherd.
A congregation may abandon someone.
Jesus remains faithful.
And if people used God's name to justify cruelty, their misuse of His name does not make their cruelty righteous.
Look at how Jesus treated vulnerable people.
He welcomed children when His disciples tried to turn them away.
He touched those considered unclean.
He received people society despised.
He defended a woman who was being publicly humiliated, while calling her away from sin.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He warned severely against causing vulnerable believers to stumble.
In Mark 9:42, Jesus gives a grave warning concerning those who cause “little ones that believe in me” to stumble.
The Greek verb σκανδαλίσῃ (skandalisē) carries the sense of causing someone to stumble or fall into sin.
The warning is not a license for us to pronounce final judgment on every person who has caused harm.
But it makes one thing unmistakable.
Jesus takes the spiritual endangerment of His people seriously.
He is not indifferent to those whose faith has been damaged by another person's conduct.
He is not impressed by a platform large enough to drown out the cries of the wounded.
And He does not confuse public influence with private righteousness.
Some people will read this and become angry.
They may say articles like this damage the church.
But there is a difference between maliciously attacking Christ's body and lovingly calling Christ's people to repentance.
There is a difference between gossip and a good-faith report of wrongdoing.
There is a difference between spreading unverified accusations and demanding fair, independent examination of serious concerns.
The church should reject slander.
It should also reject cover-ups.
It should protect the rights of the accused.
It should also protect the safety and dignity of those reporting harm.
These responsibilities are not enemies.
They belong together under truth and justice.
And where a church has failed, repentance must become more than a statement read from a pulpit.
It may require acknowledging what happened without minimizing it.
Listening to people who were dismissed.
Providing access to independent safeguarding or investigative processes.
Cooperating with lawful authorities.
Removing dangerous individuals from positions where they can harm others.
Offering meaningful support to those affected.
Correcting policies that allowed misconduct to continue.
Accepting that rebuilding trust may take years.
And refusing to rush wounded people into public reconciliation for the sake of a photograph, a testimony, or a restored institutional image.
Because repentance has fruit.
John the Baptist declared:
“Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance...” (Luke 3:8, KJV).
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), translated “repentance,” refers to a change of mind or disposition, understood in the New Testament as a turning toward God that bears fruit in changed conduct.
Repentance is not merely being sorry that people found out.
It is turning away from sin.
It is telling the truth.
It is accepting responsibility.
It is pursuing what is right even when doing so is costly.
And that applies not only to individual offenders but also to leaders and communities that have enabled wrongdoing.
There is a painful distinction between restoration and reinstatement.
Restoration to fellowship with God through repentance and faith is one matter.
Restoration to a position of spiritual authority is another.
Forgiveness does not automatically establish that someone is qualified to lead.
First Timothy 3 and Titus 1 describe moral qualifications for church overseers.
A person who has violated those qualifications cannot demand an immediate return to leadership simply by invoking grace.
God's mercy is immeasurable.
Leadership remains a sacred trust.
And protecting the flock is not cruelty toward a fallen leader.
It is obedience to the Shepherd who purchased His people with His blood.
Maybe you are a pastor reading this.
Perhaps you have never concealed wrongdoing, but you recognize how easily ministry pressure can distort judgment.
You know what it feels like to carry financial burdens, family expectations, congregational conflict, and the fear that one crisis could undo years of labor.
Hear this with love.
Your calling is not to appear invincible.
Your calling is to be faithful.
You do not need to defend every leader to defend the Gospel.
You do not need to hide every failure to preserve the church.
And you do not need to fear accountability as though it were the enemy of grace.
A shepherd who welcomes correction demonstrates something more valuable than the illusion of perfection.
He demonstrates humility.
Maybe you are a church member who has remained silent because you were afraid of what speaking up might cost.
I understand why fear can be powerful.
Speaking truthfully may strain relationships.
It may expose you to misunderstanding.
It may require courage you do not feel you possess.
But remember that Christian unity is not built on pretending.
Ephesians 4:15 calls believers to speak the truth in love.
Truth without love can become cruelty.
Love without truth can become complicity.
Christ calls His people to something better than either.
And maybe you are the person who was hurt.
The one who lost friends.
The one whose reputation was questioned.
The one who was told to stop talking.
The one who now struggles to open a Bible because the same verses once used to comfort you were later used to control you.
Please hear this.
You do not have to call evil good in order to honor God.
You do not have to deny what happened to prove that you have forgiven.
You do not have to remain in danger to demonstrate submission.
You may seek safety, professional support, pastoral care from trustworthy people, and appropriate legal assistance.
You may take time to grieve.
You may ask difficult questions.
And you may bring your anger, confusion, and sorrow honestly before the Lord.
The Psalms are full of believers who cried out from places of fear, betrayal, and suffering.
God did not erase those prayers from Scripture because they were uncomfortable.
He preserved them.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
The Hebrew phrase קָרוֹב יְהוָה לְנִשְׁבְּרֵי־לֵב (qarov Adonai lenishberei-lev) expresses that the LORD is near to those broken in heart.
Near.
Not necessarily explaining everything immediately.
Not promising that every person will apologize.
Not guaranteeing that every institution will acknowledge its failure.
But near.
And sometimes, when your world has collapsed, that promise becomes the beginning of learning to hope again.
The God who sees you is not waiting for you to manufacture a smile.
He invites you to come to Him truthfully.
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than a message we preach.
It becomes the truth by which we must live.
At the cross, we see the terrible seriousness of sin.
God does not pretend evil is harmless.
At the cross, we also see the astonishing depth of divine love.
Christ, the sinless Savior, willingly gave Himself for sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
This is grace.
Not an excuse for the powerful to escape accountability.
Not a demand that victims suppress their pain.
Not an institutional strategy for surviving scandal.
Grace is God's undeserved favor toward sinners through Jesus Christ.
Grace calls us to repentance.
Grace offers forgiveness.
Grace teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
Grace transforms people who could never save themselves.
And grace never needs a lie to remain beautiful.
There is something profoundly hopeful about this.
A church that has sinned can repent.
A leader who has fallen can humble himself before God and accept the consequences of his actions.
A congregation that has participated in silence can choose truth.
A wounded person can begin healing without pretending the wound never existed.
And a community that once protected its image can learn to protect its people.
Not every story will end with earthly reconciliation.
Not every relationship can safely be restored.
Not every institution will choose repentance.
But the resurrection of Jesus Christ means that sin, injustice, and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
The empty tomb is not permission to minimize suffering.
It is the foundation of Christian hope in the midst of suffering.
And that brings us to the question we can no longer avoid.
What kind of church are we becoming?
One where a powerful person's reputation is protected at the expense of the vulnerable?
Or one where even the most influential leader must submit to the truth?
One where people are told to be quiet because speaking might damage the ministry?
Or one where people can report harm without fear of retaliation?
One where forgiveness is demanded from the wounded while repentance is optional for the offender?
Or one where grace and accountability walk together?
The answer is not found in our branding.
Not in our attendance numbers.
Not in our buildings.
Not in the number of people who follow our livestreams.
It is found in whether we obey Jesus when obedience costs us something.
Because the church belongs to Christ.
Not to its founder.
Not to its most generous donor.
Not to its most charismatic preacher.
Not to the family whose name is on the building.
Christ purchased His people with His own blood.
And no human leader has the right to treat them as disposable.
If this article has brought something painful to the surface, you do not need to share private details publicly to prove your courage.
But perhaps you can leave a few words for someone else who feels alone.
You do not owe strangers your story.
But your words may remind someone that they are not the only person struggling to make sense of what happened.
And if you know someone who has quietly walked away from church because they were mistreated, consider sharing this article with them.
Not to pressure them into returning before they are ready.
Not to dismiss their experience.
But to remind them that the failures of people do not erase the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.
Sometimes a single honest conversation can encourage a church to examine its practices, help a wounded believer feel seen, or challenge a leader to choose righteousness over reputation.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, wrestle honestly with difficult questions, or see the grace of Jesus more clearly, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior exists to point people beyond religious appearances and back to Jesus Christ.
To help believers grow in biblical understanding.
To encourage those who are exhausted.
To challenge spiritual complacency.
To speak about repentance without abandoning grace, and grace without abandoning truth.
We want these resources to keep reaching people who are hungry for Scripture, encouragement, healing, and genuine discipleship.
That mission takes time, effort, resources, and faithful support.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
God's favor is not for sale.
And the Gospel must never become a transaction.
These products are not the reason to give.
They are simply one way of expressing appreciation to those helping sustain the work.
Read.
Pray.
Grow.
Use the free resources.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, those wrestling with their faith, and even people who do not yet know Christ to follow along.
A thoughtful share can bring this message to someone who might never otherwise encounter it.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to speak truth with love matters.
And none of it is insignificant simply because money is not involved.
But before you leave, there is one final thing I want you to remember.
One day, every earthly ministry will have to answer to the Lord of the church.
The crowds will not be able to defend us.
The impressive buildings will not speak for us.
The financial reports will not conceal our motives.
The titles before our names will not exempt us from judgment.
We will stand before the One whose eyes see what human beings can hide.
The One who knows the truth behind every carefully managed statement.
The One who sees the tears that never reached a microphone.
The One who knows the names of people who left quietly because they no longer felt safe.
And the One who knows every faithful shepherd who protected the vulnerable even when it cost him influence, friendship, or position.
That day should humble all of us.
Not because Christians must live in terror of a Savior who has redeemed them.
But because the grace that saves us also teaches us to take holiness seriously.
So let the church repent where it has failed.
Let the innocent be treated fairly.
Let allegations be examined carefully.
Let wrongdoing be confronted.
Let victims and survivors be treated with dignity.
Let shepherds remember whose sheep they are tending.
And let every believer remember that our ultimate allegiance belongs not to a personality, a denomination, a platform, or an institution.
It belongs to Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Lord.
The Good Shepherd.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners.
The King who loves righteousness.
The One who can bring redemption out of the deepest human ruin without ever pretending that evil was good.
This is the Gospel we must defend.
Not a leader's untouchable image.
Not an organization's spotless public appearance.
But the truth of Jesus Christ.
And if the church must choose between protecting its reputation and obeying its Savior, there should never be any confusion about which one matters more.
Because a reputation built on silence can collapse the moment truth emerges.
But a life surrendered to Jesus can be rebuilt through repentance, grace, and the transforming power of God.
The wound they told you to hide was never hidden from the Shepherd who gave His life for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN YOU REALLY LOVE JESUS AND STILL BE ADDICTED TO PORNOGRAPHY? THE ANSWER MAY BREAK YOUR HEART BEFORE IT SETS YOU FREE.
paragraphs: CAN YOU REALLY LOVE JESUS AND STILL BE ADDICTED TO PORNOGRAPHY? THE ANSWER MAY BREAK YOUR HEART BEFORE IT SETS YOU FREE.

You worship on Sunday. You fall into temptation when nobody is watching. You promise God it will never happen again. Then the cycle repeats. But here is the question you have been terrified to ask: Has Jesus given up on you, or is He still fighting for the person you are ashamed to be?
There is a kind of crying that makes no sound.
It happens when the screen goes dark.
When the excitement disappears.
When the room becomes quiet again, and suddenly, the very thing you were chasing for comfort leaves you feeling emptier than before.
You stare at the ceiling.
You feel disgusted with yourself.
And somewhere between the shame and the silence, you whisper something you have whispered a hundred times.
"Lord, I'm sorry."
Again.
You said it last week.
You said it last month.
You said it after that powerful worship service when you lifted your hands, felt the tears running down your face, and genuinely believed that this time would be different.
But here you are.
Again.
And perhaps the most painful part isn't even what you watched.
It's the question that comes afterward.
"If I really love Jesus, why do I keep doing something that breaks His heart?"
Maybe you are a worship leader.
Maybe you teach Sunday school.
Maybe you are a father who prays over his children at night while privately fighting something he has never confessed to his wife.
Maybe you are a mother, a student, a pastor, a new believer, or someone who has followed Christ for decades.
Maybe nobody suspects anything.
They see your Bible verses.
They see your Christian posts.
They see you smiling in church.
They have no idea what happens when you are alone.
And now you are wondering whether your entire relationship with God has become a lie.
Please don't rush past what comes next.
Because Scripture gives us an answer that is more honest than cheap reassurance, more merciful than condemnation, and far more powerful than another empty promise to try harder.

Yes, a person can genuinely love Jesus and still struggle with compulsive pornography use. But loving Jesus does not make pornography harmless, and struggling with sin does not mean we should surrender to it.
There is a difference between fighting sin and making peace with it.
And that difference matters eternally.
The apostle Paul wrote something that has comforted generations of believers who know what it means to struggle against their own desires.
"For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." — Romans 7:19, KJV
Listen to the tension.
He recognizes what is good.
He desires what is good.
Yet he describes doing what he hates.
The original Greek of Romans 7:19 includes the words:
ὃ γὰρ θέλω ἀγαθὸν οὐ ποιῶ, ἀλλὰ ὃ οὐ θέλω κακὸν τοῦτο πράσσω.
A close translation is:
"For the good that I want, I do not do; but the evil that I do not want, this I practice."
The verb πράσσω (prassō) means to do, perform, or practice.
Paul is describing a painful conflict between desire and action.

Christians have understood Romans 7 in different ways. Some interpret it as Paul's description of the ongoing struggle of a believer, while others understand it primarily as the experience of a person confronted by God's law but lacking the liberating power of the Spirit.
We should not pretend that this debated passage settles every question about addiction and salvation.
But Paul's larger message is unmistakable.
Human beings cannot rescue themselves from sin through willpower alone.
And Romans 7 does not end with Paul congratulating himself for trying harder.
It ends with a desperate question.
"O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" — Romans 7:24, KJV
Then comes the answer.
"I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord." — Romans 7:25, KJV
Did you notice?
Paul did not ask, "What technique will make me impressive enough for God?"
He asked, "Who shall deliver me?"
Because the deepest answer to sin is not merely a better system.
It is a Savior.
His name is Jesus Christ.
But before you use that truth to comfort yourself, allow it to confront you.
Because Jesus did not die to make us comfortable remaining enslaved to what destroys us.
He died to redeem us.
And redemption is not permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus said:
"Whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." — Matthew 5:28, KJV
In the Greek text, Jesus uses the expression πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn).
In context, this describes looking at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her.
Jesus is not condemning the mere recognition that someone is attractive or an unwanted thought that enters the mind.
He is confronting deliberate, cultivated lust.
The kind of looking that turns another human being into an object of sexual gratification.
The kind that trains the heart to consume rather than love.
And that is why pornography is not simply a private entertainment preference.

It involves the deliberate pursuit of sexual stimulation through images or videos of other people, frequently in ways that encourage objectification, secrecy, and patterns contrary to the sexual holiness taught in Scripture.

Not every experience of pornography use constitutes a clinical addiction. Some people experience occasional behavior they regret; others develop persistent, difficult-to-control patterns with serious consequences. The moral and spiritual questions are related to, but distinct from, a clinical diagnosis.
And whether your struggle is occasional, habitual, or compulsive, the question remains:
What is this doing to your heart?
Perhaps pornography began long before you understood what you were seeing.
Perhaps you were exposed as a child.
Perhaps somebody introduced you to it.
Perhaps you discovered it during a season when you felt lonely, rejected, curious, or desperate to escape pain.
What began as curiosity became a habit.
What became a habit turned into a hiding place.
And eventually, the hiding place started feeling like a prison.
You didn't wake up one morning and decide, "I want to spend years fighting shame."
You wanted relief.
You wanted comfort.
You wanted to feel something.
And for a moment, pornography seemed to offer what your exhausted heart was searching for.
But afterward, the loneliness was still there.
The rejection was still there.
The wounds were still there.
Only now, shame had joined them.
This does not excuse sin.
But understanding what drives a behavior can help us confront it truthfully rather than simply repeating promises that have already failed.
Because sometimes the question isn't only, "Why do I keep looking?"
Sometimes it is also, "What am I trying not to feel?"
And that question may take courage to answer.
Maybe you are not just fighting lust.
Maybe you are fighting loneliness that nobody knows about.
Maybe you are fighting anxiety, grief, rejection, resentment, or years of emotional pain.
Maybe you have trained yourself to reach for a screen whenever life becomes unbearable.
And now the behavior you once used to escape pain has become another source of pain.
There is no shame in acknowledging that a spiritual struggle may also involve psychological patterns that need professional attention.
Prayer and appropriate therapy are not enemies.
Christian accountability and evidence-informed treatment do not have to compete.
God's truth does not become less powerful when you receive help understanding your behavior.
But there is something even deeper that we must confront.
You cannot heal what you insist on hiding.
In Genesis 3, after Adam and Eve sinned, they hid themselves from the presence of the Lord.
And God called to Adam:
"Where art thou?" — Genesis 3:9, KJV
In Hebrew, the question is:
אַיֶּכָּה (ʾayyekkāh)
"Where are you?"
God was not asking because He lacked information.
The question exposed the distance that sin had created and called Adam to respond.
That ancient question still confronts the human heart.
Where are you?
Not where your church friends think you are.
Not where your social media profile makes you appear to be.
Not where you pretend to be when someone asks how your spiritual life is going.
Where are you really?
Are you hiding behind ministry?
Behind theology?
Behind your reputation?
Behind another promise that nobody will ever find out?
You can fool people who admire you.
You can carefully protect your public image.
But you cannot hide your heart from the God who already sees it.
And here is the astonishing thing.
The God who sees what you are hiding is also the God who calls sinners to come into the light.
Think about Peter.
He loved Jesus.
He had walked with Him.
He had seen miracles.
He had promised loyalty.
Yet when the pressure came, Peter denied knowing Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke records that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Peter remembered the Lord's words.
And he went outside and wept bitterly.
Imagine that moment.
The sound of the rooster.
The realization.
The memory of his own promises.
The unbearable knowledge that he had failed the One he loved.
Perhaps you know something about that kind of weeping.
Not because you deny Jesus with your mouth, but because your actions repeatedly contradict what you confess with your lips.
And perhaps you are convinced that your repeated failure has disqualified you forever.
But Peter's story did not end in the courtyard.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter.
In John 21, Jesus asked him:
"Lovest thou me?" — John 21:17, KJV
Peter answered:
"Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee."
And Jesus entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Notice what Jesus did not do.
He did not pretend the denial never happened.
He did not call betrayal harmless.
He did not tell Peter that repentance was unnecessary.
But neither did He declare Peter beyond restoration.
Jesus confronted the failure and called Peter forward.
That is grace.
Not pretending sin is beautiful.
Not making excuses for what destroys us.
Grace is Jesus meeting a broken person in the truth and calling that person into a different future.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you have failed again, you need to hear something important.
Your tears alone cannot save you.
Your guilt cannot cleanse you.
Your promises cannot purchase forgiveness.
Only Christ can save.
Only His blood can cleanse sin.
Only His grace can reconcile us to God.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
The Greek word translated "confess" is ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), from homologeō, meaning to confess or acknowledge.
It involves agreeing with the truth rather than denying or concealing wrongdoing.
Biblical confession is not simply saying "sorry" because the consequences feel terrible.
It is coming into agreement with God's judgment about sin.
No excuses.
No negotiations.
No disguises.
"Lord, this is wrong."
"Lord, I have been hiding."
"Lord, I need Your mercy."
"Lord, teach me to walk in obedience."
And when confession is genuine, it moves us toward repentance.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) means repentance, a change of mind or heart that involves turning toward God.
It is more than feeling ashamed.
It is more than being frightened of getting caught.
It is more than crying after a relapse.
Repentance involves a changed direction that bears fruit in action.
And this is where some readers may feel uncomfortable.
Because you cannot keep asking God to free you from something while deliberately protecting every doorway that leads back to it.
You cannot sincerely pursue holiness while refusing to examine the habits, devices, relationships, and circumstances that repeatedly pull you toward temptation.
Jesus said in Matthew 5:29 that if the right eye causes someone to sin, it should be plucked out and cast away.
This is forceful figurative language about taking sin seriously, not a command to injure yourself.
Jesus is teaching radical seriousness about removing occasions for sin.
So perhaps repentance looks like installing accountability software.
Perhaps it looks like no longer taking your phone into bed.
Perhaps it means removing certain apps, changing your late-night routine, or ending access to accounts that repeatedly lead you toward pornography.
Perhaps it means confessing to a trustworthy, mature Christian who can help you pursue change without humiliating you.
Perhaps it means speaking with a qualified therapist who understands compulsive sexual behavior.
Perhaps it means finally telling the truth to a spouse who has been affected by secrecy and betrayal, with appropriate pastoral or professional support to navigate that conversation responsibly.
And perhaps it means accepting that healing will require more than one emotional night at the altar.
It may require weeks.
Months.
A long season of rebuilding trust, learning healthier responses to stress, and establishing new patterns.
Not because Jesus is powerless.
But because sanctification is often a process in which the Spirit teaches us to live out the new life we have received in Christ.
There is a difference between the forgiveness God gives and the habits we must learn to change.
Forgiveness is not earned by reaching a certain number of pornography-free days.
And a relapse does not mean every previous step toward obedience was meaningless.
But neither should we use God's patience as an excuse to remain careless.
Romans 6:1–2 asks whether believers should continue in sin so that grace may abound.
Paul's answer is emphatic.
"God forbid."
The Greek expression is μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito).
It conveys strong rejection: "May it never be!"
Grace is not a license to continue sinning.
Grace brings us into a new relationship with Christ, where sin is no longer meant to reign as our master.
And that leads to a question more important than whether you can claim to love Jesus while struggling.
Are you willing to let Jesus confront the very thing you keep protecting?
Because there is a dangerous difference between saying, "Lord, I hate this sin, please help me overcome it," and saying, "Lord, I know this is sin, but I have no intention of surrendering it."
One is the cry of someone seeking deliverance.
The other is an attempt to make peace with rebellion.
Only God knows the heart perfectly.
We cannot determine another person's salvation simply by counting their failures.
But Scripture repeatedly warns against a settled, unrepentant pattern of sin and calls professing believers to examine themselves.
First John 2:1 captures both holiness and hope:
"My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous."
Do you see the balance?
"That ye sin not."
God does not minimize sin.
"And if any man sin, we have an advocate."
God does not leave the repentant sinner without hope.
The Greek word translated "advocate" is παράκλητον (paraklēton).
In this context, it refers to one who comes to another's aid, an advocate.
And John identifies our Advocate.
Jesus Christ the righteous.
Not Jesus Christ the indifferent.
Not Jesus Christ who pretends holiness does not matter.
Jesus Christ the righteous.
The One who never sinned.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who died and rose again.
The One whose righteousness is our hope.
And here is something worth remembering when shame tells you to stay away from Him.
Jesus is not asking you to become clean enough to approach Him. He is calling you to come to Him so that He can cleanse and transform you.
That does not mean hiding your behavior.
It means bringing it into His light.
That does not mean avoiding accountability.
It means embracing the truth.
That does not mean demanding instant freedom on your own timetable.
It means learning daily dependence on Christ.
And if you stumble again, do not let your failure become an excuse to abandon Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Seek help.
Rebuild what needs rebuilding.
Keep walking in the light.
Because despair is not repentance.
And self-hatred is not holiness.
Some people have spent years punishing themselves for sins Christ calls them to confess and forsake.
They believe that if they hate themselves enough, God will finally be satisfied.
But the Gospel does not teach that self-contempt pays for sin.
Jesus paid for sin at Calvary.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
"But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed."
This prophecy points us to the suffering of the Servant, fulfilled in Christ, whose sacrifice addresses our deepest problem of sin and alienation from God.
It should not be turned into a guarantee that every psychological compulsion disappears immediately after prayer.
But it gives us a greater hope.
We are not left to save ourselves.
At the cross, Jesus bore the judgment that sinners deserve.
At the resurrection, He defeated death.
And through union with Him, believers are called into a new life.
That is why Romans 8:1 is so precious.
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus."
The Greek begins:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα (Ouden ara nyn katakrima).
"Therefore, now, no condemnation."
The word katakrima refers to condemnation or an adverse judicial verdict.
Paul is not declaring that sin has stopped mattering.
He is declaring that those who belong to Christ are no longer under the condemning verdict of sin.
And Romans 8 continues by describing life in the Spirit.
Freedom from condemnation is not freedom to embrace darkness.
It is freedom to walk in the light without pretending that you saved yourself.
Maybe you have been measuring God's love by the length of your longest streak.
Thirty days without pornography, and you feel worthy to pray.
Three days after a relapse, and you feel too filthy to open your Bible.
But the cross does not become more powerful on your successful days.
And it does not become less sufficient on the days you confess your failures.
Your obedience matters deeply.
Your choices have consequences.
Your habits can harm you and others.
But your standing before God is not purchased through a flawless personal record.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the grace that saves us also teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 says:

"For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world."
Grace teaches.
Grace corrects.
Grace trains.
Grace transforms.
And that transformation may begin with the sentence you have been most afraid to say aloud.
"I need help."
Not to everyone.
Not publicly if doing so would expose you or someone else to harm.
But to someone trustworthy, mature, and capable of walking with you in truth.
James 5:16 calls believers to confess faults to one another and pray for one another.
Galatians 6:2 calls us to bear one another's burdens.
The Christian life was never designed to be lived in total isolation.
And if you have been trying to fight this battle entirely alone, consider whether secrecy has become part of the problem.
You do not need an audience for your shame.
You need the light of truth, wise support, and a path toward faithful obedience.
And if someone has been harmed by your pornography use, love requires more than private regret.
It may require honesty, changed behavior, accountability, and a willingness to repair what can be repaired.
Grace does not erase responsibility.
It empowers us to face it.
Now imagine something.
Imagine that six months from today, you are no longer living the same way.
Not because you discovered a magical formula.
Not because temptation has vanished from the world.
But because you finally stopped pretending.
You sought help.
You confessed.
You built boundaries.
You learned to recognize the moments when loneliness, exhaustion, stress, or temptation were pulling you toward old habits.
You began reaching for prayer, Scripture, community, and healthier forms of support instead of automatically reaching for the screen.
Some days were difficult.
Some nights you had to walk away.
Some moments required more courage than anyone around you could see.
But you kept turning toward Christ.
And little by little, your life began to reflect a different direction.
Maybe that journey will not be perfectly linear.
Maybe there will be setbacks.
But a setback does not have to become a surrender.
And your story does not have to remain trapped in the chapter that made you ashamed.
Think of the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
Her accusers wanted condemnation.
Jesus exposed their hypocrisy.
And when the confrontation ended, He told her:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." — John 8:11, KJV

These words come from John 7:53–8:11, a passage whose manuscript history is disputed because it is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts. It has nevertheless been treasured in Christian tradition, and its portrayal of mercy joined with a call to holiness is consistent with themes clearly taught elsewhere in Scripture.
Notice the two truths held together.
"Neither do I condemn thee."
"Go, and sin no more."
Mercy.
And transformation.
Compassion.
And holiness.
Jesus does not force us to choose between grace and truth.
He embodies both.
And that is the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not because our sins are insignificant.
Not because every consequence disappears.
