Not because a painful history can simply be erased.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem people whose stories seemed beyond repair.
The adulterer can repent.
The hypocrite can come into the light.
The person trapped in pornography can seek freedom.
The ashamed can receive forgiveness.
The wounded can begin to heal.
The believer who has wandered can return.
And the person who has never truly surrendered to Christ can come to Him today.
Not with a performance.
Not with a religious disguise.
But with repentance and faith.
Put the phone down for a moment if you can.
Be still.
And speak honestly to God.

"Lord Jesus, You know what I have done. You know what I have hidden. You know the promises I have broken and the pain I have tried to escape. I will not excuse my sin anymore. I confess it before You. I believe that You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Change my heart. Teach me to walk in the light. Give me courage to seek help, wisdom to remove temptation, and strength to obey You when nobody is watching. I do not want to keep using Your grace as an excuse. I want to know You, love You, and follow You. In Your name, Jesus. Amen."
And please understand.
Those words are not a magical formula.
Their value is not in reciting them perfectly.
The invitation is to turn to the living Christ in genuine repentance and faith.
If you prayed sincerely, do not make the mistake of thinking that the journey ends here.
This may be where your next faithful step begins.
Perhaps your next step is telling a trusted Christian mentor the truth.
Perhaps it is seeking professional help for compulsive behavior.
Perhaps it is asking someone to pray with you.
Perhaps it is opening your Bible tonight instead of reopening the browser tab that has been pulling you back into darkness.
Do not underestimate a small act of obedience.
And do not underestimate the danger of postponing repentance.
Because "tomorrow" can become the word we use to avoid surrendering today.
You do not need to reveal intimate details, identify anyone else, or disclose anything that could put you at risk.
And if Christ has been restoring your life, consider commenting "Christ is still healing me."
Someone reading the comments may need to know that the struggle is real, but so is the hope we have in Jesus.
Perhaps you are not personally struggling with pornography.
Perhaps you are reading this because you love someone who is.
Please remember that truth and compassion belong together.
Do not mock their struggle.
Do not minimize the harm.
Do not enable secrecy.
But do not forget that the person standing before you is someone Christ calls to repentance and offers mercy.
Your response may help determine whether they seek honest support or retreat further into hiding.
Not to advertise your own righteousness.
Not to expose another person's weakness.
But because somebody in your circle may be sitting alone right now, convinced that their failures have made them unreachable by the grace of God.
You may never know who reads what you share.
You may never know which exhausted believer finds the courage to confess.
You may never know which marriage begins the difficult work of honesty, or which young person finally seeks help.
But it can point someone toward Jesus and encourage that first step into the light.
And sometimes that first step matters more than we realize.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, those who have drifted from faith, and even those who are still searching for truth.
Not everyone needs another argument.
Some people need someone to show them where hope can be found.
These resources are intended to help people engage with Scripture, understand the Gospel, strengthen their faith, and pursue meaningful discipleship.
And there is another way you can help this mission continue.

Your contribution can help sustain the creation and sharing of Gospel-centered articles, discipleship materials, Christian books, devotionals, and resources intended to reach more people with biblical truth.
It can help us continue and, as resources allow, expand this ministry.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, generously, and cheerfully.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That matters.
Your local church, family obligations, and other commitments deserve prayerful consideration.
But if you believe in this work and have the means to support it, your voluntary monthly contribution can be a meaningful ministry offering.
You are not buying God's blessing.
You are helping make Gospel-centered teaching and resources available to others.
These items can serve as reminders of faith, encouragement in daily life, and opportunities to share biblical truth with others.
Read Scripture.
Pray.
Share the Gospel.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Make use of the free discipleship resources.
And above all, remain close to Jesus Christ.
Because the goal has never been to build an audience that admires a ministry.
The goal is to point people toward the Savior who deserves all glory.
And now, before you leave, I want to speak to the person who almost stopped reading halfway through.
The one who felt exposed.
The one who wondered whether this article was somehow describing the very things nobody else knows.
The one who has promised God a thousand times that the next failure would be the last.
I cannot promise you that temptation will disappear tomorrow.
I cannot promise you that recovery will be painless.
I cannot promise you that every damaged relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
But I can tell you what the Gospel declares.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
His death is sufficient.
His resurrection is real.
His call to repentance is serious.
His mercy is not exhausted by the weakness of those who sincerely turn to Him.
And His power is not limited to the chapters of your life you are comfortable showing other people.
So do not confuse your struggle with your identity.
Do not confuse the voice of shame with the voice of God.
Do not confuse religious appearances with spiritual health.
And do not confuse another emotional promise with the daily obedience of following Jesus.
Bring the truth into the light.
Seek help where help is needed.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Trust Christ where fear has ruled.
And remember that the purpose of freedom is not merely to stop watching something on a screen.
It is to love God with an undivided heart.
To learn to see other people with dignity.
To become honest where you once were secretive.
To become faithful where you once compromised.
To walk in the light because you belong to the One who is the Light of the world.
One day, perhaps you will look back on this season and realize that the turning point was not the moment you finally felt strong.
It was the moment you stopped hiding your weakness and began surrendering it to Jesus.
And maybe someone else will hear your testimony and find the courage to begin their own journey of repentance and restoration.
Not because you became perfect.
But because Christ proved faithful.
So here is the question I want to leave with you.
Not merely, "Can someone love Jesus and still be addicted to pornography?"
But something far more personal.
"If I truly love Jesus, what am I willing to bring into His light today?"
Because the answer to that question may change the direction of your life.
And when the screen goes dark tonight, when the room becomes silent, when nobody is watching and you are faced with the choice you have faced so many times before, remember this:
The Savior who sees you in your darkest hour is calling you out of the darkness—not to shame you into hiding, but to lead you into the light where repentance, mercy, and a new life begin.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Nobody Warned You That Watching Everyone Else Move Forward Could Make Waiting Hurt This Much.
paragraphs: Nobody Warned You That Watching Everyone Else Move Forward Could Make Waiting Hurt This Much.

When everybody else seems to be receiving the life you have been praying for, the hardest battle is not always believing God can bless you. Sometimes, it is believing He has not forgotten you while you watch Him bless somebody else.
Nobody tells you how much courage it takes to type “Congratulations!” when your own heart is quietly breaking.

Nobody prepares you for the moment when another engagement announcement appears on your screen, another pregnancy is celebrated, another friend receives the promotion, another family moves into their dream home, another ministry begins to flourish, and another person shares a testimony about the very thing you have been begging God to do for you.
And there you are.
Still waiting.
Still praying.
Still trying to believe.
And maybe you really are happy for them.
That is what makes the pain so confusing.
Because somewhere beneath your genuine happiness for another person is a question you feel almost ashamed to ask.
“Lord, when will it be my turn?”
You would never say it during Sunday worship.
You would never put it in the prayer request group.
You might not even admit it to the people closest to you.
But God has heard the question in the silence of your bedroom.
He has seen the way your smile disappears when you put down your phone.
He knows about the tears you wiped away before anyone entered the room.
And He knows how exhausting it becomes to keep celebrating other people's answered prayers while your own prayers seem to remain unanswered.
There is a particular kind of heartbreak that does not come from losing something you once possessed.
It comes from repeatedly watching other people receive something you have longed for but have never held.
A wedding invitation can reopen the loneliness you thought you had surrendered.
A pregnancy announcement can awaken grief nobody knows you are carrying.
A promotion can remind you of years of effort that still seem invisible.
A photograph of someone's new house can make the walls of your rented room feel smaller.
A ministry testimony can leave you wondering why someone else's calling appears to be flourishing while yours seems buried beneath obscurity.
And sometimes, the worst part is not the announcement itself.
It is what happens afterward.
You begin examining your life as though you are evidence of something gone wrong.
Maybe I am not praying enough.
Maybe I missed God's instructions.
Maybe I am being punished.
Maybe everybody else is more faithful.
Maybe God loves them differently.
And eventually, the question becomes darker.
“What if the life I keep praying for never happens?”
If that thought has ever frightened you, I want you to stay with me.
Not because I can promise that every dream you have will come true.
I cannot.
Scripture does not give me permission to make that promise.
But there is something God says to people who are struggling to remain faithful while the lives around them seem to be advancing.
And it is far more powerful than the shallow reassurance that your breakthrough must be just around the corner.
Psalm 37:7 says:
“Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass.” — Psalm 37:7, KJV
Read that again.
Especially the part about somebody else prospering.
Because God did not overlook the emotional struggle of watching another person advance while you remain in an uncomfortable place.
He addressed it.
And the original Hebrew reveals something deeply important.
The opening words are:
דּוֹם לַיהוָה וְהִתְחוֹלֵל לוֹ
Transliterated: Dōm la-YHWH, wehitḥōlēl lō.
A close rendering is:
“Be still before the LORD, and wait patiently for Him.”

The Hebrew verb דּוֹם (dōm) conveys being silent or still. It is not a command to pretend that pain does not exist. It calls the worshiper away from restless agitation into a posture of reverence before God.

The expression וְהִתְחוֹלֵל לוֹ (wehitḥōlēl lō) carries the sense of waiting for Him. Its underlying Hebrew root can be associated with trembling or writhing in other contexts, although this verse is traditionally understood as an instruction to wait patiently.
That distinction matters.
We should not force a dramatic meaning onto the Hebrew simply because it sounds emotionally powerful.
The verse is powerful enough when we allow it to say what it actually says.
David is calling God's people to quiet their restless hearts before the Lord rather than allowing another person's apparent success to consume them.
And notice something else.
Psalm 37 is not primarily about being unmarried while friends marry, or waiting for children while others announce pregnancies.
Its immediate context concerns the apparent prosperity of evildoers and the temptation to envy those who succeed through wickedness.
The psalm begins:
“Fret not thyself because of evildoers, neither be thou envious against the workers of iniquity.” — Psalm 37:1, KJV
David is addressing a moral and spiritual crisis: Why do people who do wrong sometimes seem to flourish while those who trust God struggle?
That is the original setting.
We must preserve it.

But the underlying warning against envy, fretfulness, and allowing another person's circumstances to destabilize our trust in God also speaks meaningfully to the comparison that can grow inside ordinary seasons of waiting.
There is an important difference, however.
The person getting married is not your enemy.
The friend announcing a pregnancy has not stolen your blessing.
The coworker receiving a promotion has not necessarily taken something God intended for you.
Their good news is not proof of your rejection.
And their happiness does not need to become evidence against God's goodness.
Sometimes, what hurts is not what someone else received.
It is the story you begin telling yourself about what their blessing means for you.
You see someone holding a newborn and think, “I am falling behind.”
You see a couple celebrating their anniversary and think, “Something must be wrong with me.”
You see another ministry reaching thousands and think, “Perhaps my obedience does not matter.”
But whose voice told you that your worth could be measured by someone else's timeline?
Who convinced you that life is a race in which another person's arrival means you have failed?

And where does Scripture teach that God evaluates His children by the age at which they marry, the number of children they have, the size of their house, their salary, or the public visibility of their ministry?
Yet comparison has a cruel way of turning blessings into measurements and people into competitors.
It can even turn prayer into a courtroom.
You begin presenting your sacrifices before God as though He owes you a particular outcome.
“Lord, I have tried to live faithfully.”
“I have served.”
“I have given.”
“I have waited.”
“Why did they receive what I have been asking You for?”
There is something painfully human about that conversation.
And Scripture does not hide such struggles.
Consider Hannah.
Before Samuel was born, Hannah lived with the anguish of childlessness.
First Samuel 1 tells us that Peninnah, the other wife of Elkanah, had children while Hannah did not.
The text also records that Peninnah provoked Hannah severely, intensifying her distress.
Imagine the emotional weight.
The thing Hannah longed for was present in the life of someone who repeatedly reminded her of what she lacked.
Her sorrow was not a passing disappointment.
It followed her into worship.
Scripture says:
“And she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore.” — 1 Samuel 1:10, KJV
She wept.
She prayed.
She was deeply distressed.
And God did not require Hannah to disguise her anguish beneath religious politeness.
When Eli misunderstood her behavior, Hannah explained:
“I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit.” — 1 Samuel 1:15, KJV
There is something sacred about that honesty.
She did not say, “I am perfectly fine.”
She did not claim that waiting was easy.
She did not pretend that her desire had disappeared.
She brought her grief before the Lord.
And perhaps that is where someone reading this needs to begin.
Not with another declaration that everything is wonderful.
Not with another attempt to silence the ache.
But with an honest prayer.
“Father, I love You, but this hurts.”
“Lord, I am thankful for what You have given others, but I am struggling with what I have not received.”
“Jesus, I do not want envy to take root in me.”
“Please help me trust You without pretending that I am not disappointed.”
That is not a performance.
That is prayer.
Hannah eventually received Samuel, and Scripture explicitly presents his birth as an answer to her prayer.
But we must be careful with her testimony.
Her story does not guarantee that every person struggling with infertility will conceive.
It does not guarantee that every unmarried believer will marry.
It does not guarantee that every painful season will end with the specific earthly outcome we desire.
The Bible records Hannah's particular story to reveal God's work in her life and in the unfolding history of Israel, not to establish a universal formula for receiving children.
And that truth may feel uncomfortable.
Because when we are hurting, we desperately want certainty.
We want someone to tell us that our wedding is coming.
That the pregnancy test will become positive.
That the promotion will finally happen.
That the ministry will explode.
That the financial pressure will disappear.
But what happens to faith when we begin trusting God only because we expect Him to deliver a particular result?
What happens when the result is delayed?
Or when it never arrives?
This is where waiting becomes more than an emotional inconvenience.
It exposes what we believe about God.
Do we believe He is good because He gives us everything we want?
Or do we believe He is good because His character has been revealed most fully in Jesus Christ?
That question is not easy.
Especially when the waiting has lasted years.
Especially when you have watched younger people pass milestones you once expected to reach long ago.

Especially when you have prayed over an empty nursery, sat through another family gathering alone, received another rejection letter, or wondered whether your quiet obedience has accomplished anything.
And please hear this carefully.
Your grief does not automatically mean your faith is weak.
Jesus Himself wept at the tomb of Lazarus.
He knew the resurrection He was about to perform, yet He still entered the sorrow surrounding death.
John 11:35 says:
“Jesus wept.”
Two words.
And yet they destroy the idea that deep faith must always appear emotionally untouched.
Christ does not teach us that holiness requires emotional numbness.
He teaches us to bring our sorrow into communion with the Father.
In Gethsemane, Jesus prayed:
“O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.” — Matthew 26:39, KJV
That prayer was not unbelief.
It was perfect obedience expressed amid profound anguish.
And although our disappointments cannot be equated with the unique suffering of Christ, His prayer teaches us something essential.
Surrender is not the absence of desire.
Surrender is bringing our desires before the Father while yielding ourselves to His will.
Sometimes surrender sounds like worship.
Sometimes it sounds like weeping.
Sometimes it sounds like, “Lord, I still want this, but I do not want wanting it to become more important than knowing You.”
And perhaps that is the prayer you have been avoiding.
Because you are afraid that surrender means giving up hope.
But biblical surrender is not the declaration that your desires are worthless.
It is the confession that Jesus is worthy even when your desires remain unfulfilled.
There is a difference.
A profound difference.
And when that difference finally reaches the heart, something begins to change.
Not necessarily your circumstances.
You may still be single tomorrow.
You may still be waiting for medical answers.
Your business may still be struggling.
Your ministry may still be small.
The email you have been waiting for may still not arrive.
But comparison no longer has to be the ruler by which you measure your life.
You can begin learning to rejoice with those who rejoice without condemning yourself for being in a different season.
Romans 12:15 calls believers to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep.
Both commands belong in the same verse.
The Christian community should be a place where someone can celebrate a birth while another person is lovingly supported through infertility.
Where someone can rejoice over an engagement while another person's loneliness is treated with tenderness rather than embarrassment.
Where success is celebrated without treating those who struggle as spiritual failures.
Where people do not have to pretend that every testimony feels easy to hear.
Because love makes room for both joy and tears.
And if you are the person who has been waiting quietly, I want to ask you something.
When was the last time you allowed yourself to be loved without first having something impressive to announce?
When was the last time you believed that your life mattered without a new achievement attached to it?
When was the last time you entered God's presence without treating your unanswered prayer as evidence that you were less valuable?
The world keeps asking, “What have you accomplished?”
Social media keeps asking, “What do you have to show?”
Comparison keeps asking, “Why aren't you there yet?”
But the Gospel directs our attention to a different question.
“What has Jesus Christ already accomplished for you?”
And the answer changes everything.
Before you achieved anything worth celebrating, Christ came for sinners.
Before you earned anyone's admiration, Christ gave Himself for the undeserving.
Before you could prove your worth through marriage, motherhood, fatherhood, financial success, ministry influence, or public recognition, the Son of God went to the cross.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became successful.
Not after our lives looked impressive.
Not after we finally reached the milestones everyone expected.
While we were still sinners.
This is grace.
And grace confronts the deepest lie comparison tells us.
The lie that you must arrive somewhere before you can be loved.
At the cross, Jesus did not merely offer encouragement to disappointed people.
He bore sin.
He suffered in the place of sinners.
He accomplished the redemption that human effort could never purchase.
And through His resurrection, He secured a living hope that reaches beyond every temporary circumstance.
This is why the Gospel is greater than the promise of a better season.
Because even if your circumstances change dramatically, a new season cannot forgive your sins.
A wedding cannot reconcile you to God.
A child cannot become your savior.
A promotion cannot give you eternal life.
A thriving ministry cannot substitute for knowing Christ.
Those things may be wonderful gifts.
But they are not the Redeemer.
Jesus is.
And when a good gift becomes the thing you believe you cannot live without, the heart can quietly begin giving that gift a place that belongs to God alone.
That is not merely a waiting problem.
It can become a worship problem.
And I say that with tenderness, because even beautiful desires can become idols when we begin asking them to provide the identity, security, or ultimate satisfaction that only Christ can give.
The answer is not to hate the desire.
It is to bring the desire under the lordship of Jesus.
To repent where envy has taken root.
To confess where resentment has grown.
To ask forgiveness for the moments when someone else's blessing became an accusation against God.
And to receive the mercy Christ freely offers.
First John 1:9 reminds us that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
You do not need to hide your jealousy behind spiritual language.
You do not need to pretend that bitterness is harmless.
You can bring the truth into the light.
You can say, “Jesus, I have been comparing. I have been resenting. I have been measuring Your love by what I have not received. Forgive me. Change my heart.”
And there is grace for the person who prays that sincerely.
Not because confession earns salvation.
But because the Savior who calls sinners to repentance is rich in mercy.
Perhaps you have been so consumed with the life you do not have that you have stopped noticing the ways God is calling you to faithfulness in the life you do have.
The person who needs encouragement today.
The family member who needs forgiveness.
The neighbor who needs kindness.
The church that needs quiet service.
The Scripture you have neglected.
The prayer you have avoided.
The relationship that needs reconciliation.
The work entrusted to your hands.
Not glamorous things.
Not always things that earn applause.
But meaningful things.
And Jesus sees what other people overlook.
Remember the widow who gave two small coins in Mark 12:41–44.
Her offering appeared insignificant beside the larger gifts of wealthy people.
But Jesus drew attention to her sacrificial generosity.
He saw what others might have dismissed.
That does not mean God values poverty for its own sake or that believers must give beyond their ability.
It means Christ's evaluation is not governed by outward appearance.
And that matters when your own life feels painfully unimpressive.
You may be faithfully caring for an aging parent while others are traveling the world.
You may be working an ordinary job while friends build successful businesses.
You may be serving a small congregation while other ministries attract enormous audiences.
You may be learning to live faithfully with an unanswered prayer that nobody sees.
None of those circumstances automatically makes you more righteous than someone who has prospered.
But neither do they make you spiritually insignificant.
Faithfulness is not measured by applause.
And the kingdom of God is not a competition for the most impressive testimony.
Remember Peter after the resurrection.
In John 21, Jesus spoke to Peter about his future and called him to follow Him.
Peter then turned and asked about another disciple.
Jesus answered:
“If I will that he tarry till I come, what is that to thee? follow thou me.” — John 21:22, KJV
The specific context concerns the different futures of Peter and the beloved disciple.
But the principle is unmistakable.
Peter was not responsible for controlling another disciple's assignment.
He was responsible for following Jesus.
And maybe that is the word your heart needs today.
“Follow thou me.”
Not, “Keep checking how far everyone else has gone.”
Not, “Measure your calling against theirs.”
Not, “Assume I have abandoned you because their story looks different.”
When the announcement appears, follow Me.
When your heart aches, follow Me.
When the door stays closed, follow Me.
When you receive no explanation, follow Me.
When obedience is costly, follow Me.
And when I bless your neighbor, do not stop following Me.
There is freedom in those words.
Because following Christ is something you can do even while waiting.
You cannot force someone to marry you.
You cannot guarantee conception.
You cannot control an employer's decision.
You cannot make a ministry grow by sheer determination.
You cannot command the future to unfold according to your preferred schedule.
But by God's grace, you can continue to follow Jesus today.
You can pray.
You can love.
You can repent.
You can forgive.
You can serve.
You can seek wise counsel.
You can take responsible steps toward legitimate goals.
You can grieve honestly.
You can receive help.
And you can trust the Lord with outcomes that remain outside your control.
This is not passive resignation.
It is active faithfulness without the illusion of control.
And it brings us back to Psalm 37.
The psalm does not invite us to stare at the prosperity of others until envy destroys our peace.
It repeatedly directs us toward the Lord.
Psalm 37:3 says:
“Trust in the LORD, and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land, and verily thou shalt be fed.”
Psalm 37:4 says:
“Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.”
That fourth verse is sometimes presented as though delighting in God guarantees every earthly desire.
But it must be read in the context of the entire psalm.
David is calling God's people to trust, righteousness, patience, and confidence in God's ultimate justice.
Delighting in the Lord is not a technique for controlling Him.
It is the joy of making Him our treasure.
And as we draw near to Him, our desires are brought into deeper relationship with His will.
That does not mean every desire disappears.
It means no earthly desire is permitted to replace the Lord Himself.
Some prayers receive the answer we hoped for.
Some receive an answer we never anticipated.
Some remain unresolved for years.
And some desires will not be fulfilled in this present life.
That last possibility is painful.
But Christian hope is not destroyed by it.
Because our final hope does not rest in the guarantee of earthly milestones.
It rests in the risen Christ and the future He has promised His people.
Revelation 21:4 speaks of the day when God will wipe away every tear and death, sorrow, crying, and pain will be no more.
That promise does not trivialize today's suffering.
It tells us suffering will not have the final word.
Jesus will.
And that is why you do not have to call your life a failure simply because it looks different from the life you imagined.
Your story is not finished simply because a particular chapter has lasted longer than expected.
And even if some of your earthly hopes remain unfulfilled, your life in Christ is not an unfinished mistake.
The Lord has not promised every believer the same circumstances.
He has promised that nothing can separate those who belong to Christ from His love.
Romans 8:38–39 makes that astonishing declaration.
Not even the painful circumstances that make you question your future can sever you from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
So when another announcement appears tomorrow, and that familiar ache rises in your chest, you do not have to pretend it is not there.
You can put your phone down.
You can take your disappointment to the Father.
You can bless the person who received good news.
You can refuse to turn their joy into a verdict against your worth.
You can ask God for help when envy threatens to grow.
And you can remind your soul that Jesus Christ is still worthy of your trust.
Not because tomorrow is guaranteed to bring the answer you want.
But because the One who died and rose again is faithful.
Maybe you have spent years waiting for a moment when you can finally tell everyone, “God answered my prayer.”
But perhaps there is another testimony worth telling even now.
“I am hurting, but I have not stopped coming to Jesus.”
“I do not understand my circumstances, but I am learning to trust His Word.”
“I still have questions, but I know where to bring them.”
“I have struggled with jealousy, but Christ is teaching me to love.”
“I have not received everything I hoped for, but I have received mercy I could never earn.”
Those are not small testimonies.
They are evidence of grace at work in an ordinary, complicated, unfinished human life.
And someone reading this needs to know that they are not the only person who has cried after seeing another person's good news.
Not the only person who has wondered whether God has forgotten them.
Not the only person who has sat in church singing about God's faithfulness while silently wrestling with disappointment.
If that is you, there is room for honesty here.
You do not have to manufacture a triumphant testimony.
You do not have to disclose private pain that you are not ready to share.
Not to prove your faith to strangers.
Not because a comment will unlock a blessing.
But because sometimes the beginning of healing is admitting that you need prayer, and sometimes another weary believer needs to discover they are not struggling alone.
Not just the happy ending, if there was one.
Tell someone about the faithfulness of Christ in the middle.
Because there are people who have heard plenty of stories about spectacular breakthroughs but desperately need to hear that Jesus is still worthy when life remains difficult.

If someone came to mind while you were reading this, consider tagging them gently, especially if you know they would welcome the encouragement. Do not expose their private struggles publicly. A personal message may be even more loving.
Return to it on the days when comparison becomes loud again.
Your willingness to share Scripture-centered encouragement can help that person feel seen and point them toward Christ.
That is part of why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to promise people that Christianity will make every earthly dream come true.
Not to turn pain into entertainment.
Not to offer religious slogans where biblical truth is needed.
But to keep bringing people back to Jesus Christ, to the authority of Scripture, to repentance, to forgiveness, to grace, and to the transformation that comes through the Gospel.
There is so much spiritual noise in the world.
We need more opportunities to open God's Word, examine our hearts, and encourage one another toward faithful discipleship.
It can help us develop more resources for people who are grieving, questioning, struggling, repenting, recovering, or simply trying to follow Jesus one difficult day at a time.
Those free resources matter.
And neither salvation nor spiritual standing can ever be purchased.
Scripture teaches generosity as an expression of worship, love, and stewardship. Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
God is not selling blessings.
Grace is not a transaction.
You can glorify Him through prayer, obedience, service, generosity, faithful witness, and countless acts of love.
Those products can serve as reminders of Scripture, encouragement for daily discipleship, or thoughtful gifts for someone who needs to be pointed back toward Christ.
But the heart of this invitation is not merchandise.
It is ministry.
It is the opportunity to help make biblically faithful encouragement and discipleship resources available to more people.
Your prayers matter.
Your thoughtful comments matter.
And your faithful walk with Christ matters far beyond anything an online platform can measure.
Before you leave, though, I want to return to the person we met at the beginning of this story.
The one holding a phone.
The one who just saw another engagement, another pregnancy, another promotion, another celebration.
The one who typed “Congratulations!” while fighting tears.
Perhaps that person is still you.
Perhaps nothing about your circumstances has changed during the time it took you to read this.
The answer has not arrived.
The loneliness has not vanished.
The opportunity has not opened.
The disappointment is still real.
But perhaps you can begin to see something differently.
The person whose good news hurt you is not your enemy.
Your unanswered prayer is not proof that you are unloved.
Your present circumstances are not a complete account of God's purposes.
And the cross of Jesus Christ is a far more trustworthy revelation of God's love than the milestones appearing on your screen.
You do not have to know how your earthly story will unfold in order to entrust yourself to the Savior who has conquered sin and death.
You do not have to pretend waiting feels beautiful.
You do not have to invent a happy ending.
You can come to Him exactly as you are, with your questions, your tears, your repentance, your longing, and your trembling faith.
Because the greatest story of grace was never about people finally becoming impressive enough for God to notice them.
It was about the holy Son of God coming to rescue sinners who could never save themselves.
That is the scandal of grace.
The undeserving are invited.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The broken can be restored to fellowship with God.
And people whose lives appear unimpressive in the eyes of the world can find their deepest identity in Jesus Christ.
So tonight, if you see another person celebrating the very thing you have been waiting for, you can whisper a different prayer.

“Father, thank You for the good You have given them. You know how much this hurts me. Guard my heart from envy. Teach me to rejoice without pretending I am not grieving. Help me to pursue what is good and surrender what I cannot control. Forgive my bitterness. Keep my heart tender. And above all, teach me to treasure Jesus more than the answer I am waiting for. Amen.”
Maybe your next chapter will contain a beautiful earthly answer.
I hope, where your desires are good and fitting, that you will receive many gifts for which you can thank the Lord.
But whatever comes next, may you never confuse a delayed milestone with a diminished worth.
May you never let another person's celebration convince you that God has abandoned you.
And may you never forget that the greatest gift God has given His people is not a particular outcome in this life.
It is His Son.
You may still be waiting for the life you once imagined, but in Jesus Christ, you are not waiting to become someone God can love.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE WAS PROMISED TO A MAN… BUT SHE WAS STILL SOMEONE ELSE’S PROPERTY. THEN THE BIBLE RECORDS A SEXUAL OFFENSE THAT MOST CHRISTIANS HAVE NEVER HEARD PREACHED.
paragraphs: SHE WAS PROMISED TO A MAN… BUT SHE WAS STILL SOMEONE ELSE’S PROPERTY. THEN THE BIBLE RECORDS A SEXUAL OFFENSE THAT MOST CHRISTIANS HAVE NEVER HEARD PREACHED.

Leviticus 19:20–22 exposes a disturbing intersection of slavery, sexual exploitation, unequal power, and ancient justice. But buried inside this difficult passage is a question that reaches all the way to the Cross: What happens when human beings treat someone as property, but God calls us to recognize their humanity?
There are Bible passages that comfort you.
There are passages that strengthen you.
And then there are passages that make you stop reading because something inside you whispers…
Wait. Did the Bible really say that?
This is one of those passages.
Somewhere in ancient Israel, there was a woman whose name Scripture never records.
We do not know her age.
We do not know her family.
We do not know whether she had ever experienced the freedom to make decisions about her own future.
But we know something deeply troubling about her circumstances.
She was a female slave.
She had been designated for a man.
And she had not yet been freed.
Then another man had sexual relations with her.

What follows is a law that raises uncomfortable questions about consent, responsibility, justice, human dignity, and the difference between what ancient Israel's legal system regulated and what God's ultimate purpose for humanity reveals.
And before you assume this is simply another strange Old Testament law that has nothing to do with your life, consider something.
There are people sitting in churches today who know exactly what it feels like to have their lives controlled by someone else.
People who were used.
People who were violated.
People whose suffering was minimized because someone more powerful controlled the story.
People who were told to remain silent because exposing what happened might embarrass a family, a ministry, or a respected person.
And some of them have spent years wondering whether God noticed.
So we need to read this passage carefully.
Not to sensationalize a woman's suffering.
Not to force modern assumptions onto an ancient text.
And certainly not to defend exploitation in the name of Scripture.
We need to listen to what the passage actually says, understand what it does and does not establish, and allow the whole counsel of Scripture to bring us toward Jesus Christ.
Because sometimes the passages we find most disturbing are the very passages that expose how desperately humanity needs redemption.
Leviticus 19:20–22 reads in the King James Version:

"And whosoever lieth carnally with a woman, that is a bondmaid, betrothed to an husband, and not at all redeemed, nor freedom given her; she shall be scourged; they shall not be put to death, because she was not free.
And he shall bring his trespass offering unto the LORD, unto the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, even a ram for a trespass offering.
And the priest shall make an atonement for him with the ram of the trespass offering before the LORD for his sin which he hath done: and the sin which he hath done shall be forgiven him."
Read those words again.
Slowly.
A woman is enslaved.
She is designated for a man.
Another man has sexual relations with her.
And the law discusses the legal consequences, including an offering made by the man.
If your heart feels unsettled, that discomfort deserves careful examination rather than an easy religious slogan.
But here is where responsible Bible study becomes essential.
The ancient Hebrew text contains details that are easy to misunderstand when we depend entirely on an English translation.
The woman is described as a שִׁפְחָה (shifchah), a female slave or bondwoman.

The passage also uses נֶחֱרֶפֶת לְאִישׁ (necherefet le'ish), a difficult expression traditionally understood as indicating that she had been assigned or designated to a man, often translated as betrothed.
That matters.
Because this was not an ordinary marriage arrangement involving two free individuals.
Her legal condition was fundamentally different.
The Hebrew also says:
וְהָפְדֵּה לֹא נִפְדָּתָה
Ve-hofdeh lo nifdatah.
Meaning, in context, that she had not been redeemed or bought out of her enslaved condition.
The verse continues:
אוֹ חֻפְשָׁה לֹא נִתַּן־לָהּ
O chufshah lo nittan-lah.
Or that freedom had not been granted to her.
There it is.
In the ancient language itself.
She had not been redeemed.
She had not been set free.
Her status mattered so much to the legal case that the text explicitly mentioned it.
And this brings us to one of the most difficult phrases in the entire passage.
The King James Version says, "she shall be scourged."
But the Hebrew expression is:
בִּקֹּרֶת תִּהְיֶה
Biqqoret tihyeh.
This expression is unusually difficult to interpret.

The noun biqqoret occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible, making its precise legal meaning uncertain. The King James Version understands it as a punishment, while many modern translations render it as an inquiry, investigation, or appropriate punishment.
That difference is significant.
We cannot responsibly claim that the Hebrew unambiguously commands the woman to be whipped.
Nor can we confidently reconstruct every legal procedure from these three verses.
And there is another detail we must face.
The passage does not explicitly say whether the woman consented.

It describes sexual intercourse within a deeply unequal social and legal relationship, but it does not supply enough information to determine the circumstances of consent or coercion in this particular case.
That is not a small distinction.
It would be irresponsible to declare, as a proven fact, that this passage describes a specific rape.
It would be equally irresponsible to assume that a woman living under slavery possessed the freedom, security, or bargaining power that a free person might have possessed.
The text leaves questions unanswered.
And sometimes faithfulness to Scripture means refusing to pretend that we know what God has not told us.
But what Scripture does tell us is troubling enough.
The woman's lack of freedom changes how the case is treated.
The law does not apply the death penalty in this situation, unlike the penalties prescribed for certain other sexual offenses involving betrothed free women in Deuteronomy 22.
The man must bring a ram as a guilt offering.
The priest makes atonement for his sin.
And the text says that he will be forgiven.
Now imagine hearing that as someone who has suffered sexual exploitation.
You might ask…
What about her?
Where is her voice?
Where is the account of her pain?
Where is the description of her future?
The passage does not tell us.
And we must not invent an answer merely to make the text feel easier.
But neither should we conclude that because this particular law does not describe her inner experience, her humanity was invisible to God.
A biblical law addressing a particular legal situation is not necessarily a complete statement of God's moral ideal.
That distinction matters enormously.
Ancient Israel's law operated within a society where slavery existed. Some laws restricted conduct, assigned responsibilities, and established penalties within those social conditions.
That does not mean every social arrangement being regulated represented the fullness of God's original design.
Jesus Himself teaches us to distinguish between certain concessions made within fallen human conditions and God's intention from the beginning.
In Matthew 19:8, while discussing divorce, He explains that Moses permitted certain things because of the hardness of human hearts, but that it was not so from the beginning.
We should not simply transfer that explanation mechanically onto every law about slavery.
But Christ's words establish an important principle: permission or regulation within a broken society must not automatically be confused with the highest expression of God's purpose.
So what was God's purpose from the beginning?
Before human beings built systems of ownership…
Before societies divided people according to status…
Before the powerful decided whose voice mattered…
Genesis 1:27 declared:
"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them."
Male and female.
Both bearing the image of God.
Not one made in God's image and the other made to be disposable.
Not the wealthy bearing divine dignity while the enslaved possessed none.
Human worth begins with the Creator.
And that worth is not erased by poverty, captivity, abuse, social status, or another person's exercise of power.
Think about that woman again.
Her name was not preserved.
Her personal story was not recorded.
But the opening chapter of Scripture had already established a truth that no human institution could cancel.
She was a human being made in the image of God.
And that truth should make every believer tremble before treating another person as an object.
Because the moment we begin valuing human beings according to what they can provide us, we have already started moving away from the heart of biblical love.
Sometimes we do not need chains to enslave another person.
Sometimes we use fear.
Sometimes we use money.
Sometimes we use shame.
Sometimes we use religious authority.
Sometimes we manipulate someone's conscience until they believe that resisting mistreatment means resisting God.
And that last form of control is particularly dangerous.
Because when people use God's name to protect their own wrongdoing, they do not make their sin holy.
They add spiritual deception to it.
Maybe you know what that feels like.
Maybe someone once convinced you that your suffering was your responsibility.
Maybe you were pressured to forgive before anyone acknowledged the harm.
Maybe someone demanded your silence and called it submission.
Maybe you were told that protecting a powerful person's reputation was more important than telling the truth.
Hear this carefully.
Biblical forgiveness is not permission for continued abuse.
Repentance is not merely saying religious words while refusing accountability.
And grace does not require victims to pretend that evil never happened.
The same Bible that speaks about forgiveness also commands justice, condemns oppression, and warns those who exploit the vulnerable.
Isaiah 1:17 says:
"Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow."
God does not instruct His people to admire justice from a distance.
He commands them to pursue it.
And when Jesus begins His public ministry in Luke 4, He reads from Isaiah and announces good news to the poor and liberty to the captives.
His mission is not reducible to a political program or a promise that every earthly injustice will disappear immediately.
It is the arrival of God's promised Messiah, bringing salvation and the liberating reign of God.
Yet His words leave no room for the idea that captivity, oppression, and human suffering are unimportant to Him.
Look at the people Jesus encountered.
He touched those society avoided.
He welcomed those religious gatekeepers despised.
He spoke to women whose voices were often disregarded.
He challenged hypocrisy.
He confronted those who burdened others while protecting their own appearance of righteousness.
And then there is the woman in John 8.
A woman brought before Jesus after being accused of adultery.
The religious leaders placed her in the middle of a public confrontation.
She was no longer being treated as a whole human being.
She had become a case.
An accusation.
An instrument in someone else's attempt to trap Jesus.
But Jesus refused to let their manipulation dictate His response.
He exposed the moral hypocrisy of the accusers.
And after they departed, He told her:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." — John 8:11, KJV
Notice both parts.
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin.
Jesus did not announce that sin was imaginary.
He did not say that holiness no longer mattered.
He extended mercy while calling for a transformed life.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Grace does not excuse evil.
Grace calls sinners out of evil.
And if we read Leviticus 19:20–22 through the larger biblical story, we must resist two opposite errors.
We must not pretend the passage is simple, harmless, or identical to modern principles of equal legal standing.
But we must not use its difficulty as an excuse to ignore the Bible's unfolding revelation of God's holiness, justice, mercy, and redemption in Christ.
The text tells us that the man brought an אָשָׁם (asham).
A guilt offering.
An offering associated with guilt and the need for atonement.
The Hebrew says:
וְנִסְלַח לוֹ
Ve-nislach lo.
"And he shall be forgiven."
Those words are important.
Because the law does not treat the man's behavior as morally insignificant.
It explicitly speaks of his sin.
He requires atonement.
He requires forgiveness.
But here we must be very careful.
The guilt offering was not a payment that purchased the woman's silence, nor does the passage say that the offering repaired every harm she may have suffered.
And forgiveness before God must never be twisted into a claim that an offender is automatically free from every human responsibility.
A person can speak about grace and still owe restitution.
A person can seek God's mercy and still need to confess the truth.
A person can claim repentance and still be accountable to lawful authorities.
The Gospel is not a hiding place for unrepentant abusers.
It is a summons to come into the light.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Confession.
Not concealment.
Cleansing.
Not continued corruption.
Forgiveness.
Not a license to repeat the offense.
And now we arrive at the place where this ancient passage begins to point us toward something far greater than the legal system of ancient Israel.
Because Leviticus speaks of a guilt offering.
But the New Testament reveals the One whose sacrifice accomplishes what the old sacrificial system could never finally accomplish.
Jesus Christ.
Hebrews 10:4 declares:
"For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins."
The sacrificial system taught Israel about sin, holiness, guilt, cleansing, and the need for atonement.
But those sacrifices were not the final answer.
They pointed beyond themselves.
To the Lamb of God.
To the spotless Savior.
To the Son of God who entered our broken world, not as a sinner needing forgiveness, but as the righteous One who would bear the sins of His people.
Isaiah 53:10 even uses the Hebrew word asham in describing the suffering servant's life as an offering for guilt.
That connection is profound.
The guilt offering in Leviticus 19 does not mean that Jesus was the offender in that ancient case.
It means the biblical language of guilt and atonement ultimately finds its deepest fulfillment in the saving work of Christ.
He bore what we could not bear.
He accomplished what animal sacrifices could not accomplish permanently.
He opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
But there is something even more astonishing.
The woman in Leviticus 19 had not been redeemed from slavery.
Her condition was described with language of not having been bought out of bondage.
Centuries later, the New Testament uses the language of redemption to describe what Christ has done for His people.
First Peter 1:18–19 declares:
"Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold…
But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot."
The Greek word translated "redeemed" in verse 18 is ἐλυτρώθητε (elytrōthēte), from a verb meaning to release or ransom.
It is not the same original-language word used in Leviticus.
And we should not pretend that Peter was secretly writing a direct commentary on this woman's particular case.
But the biblical theme of redemption creates a powerful theological contrast.
Leviticus describes a woman who had not been freed.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ has paid the price to redeem sinners from bondage to sin and bring them into a new relationship with God.
And this is where the story becomes personal.
Because perhaps you have never experienced literal slavery.
Perhaps you have never been trapped in the ancient legal conditions described in Leviticus.
But you know what bondage feels like.
You know what it means to be trapped in something you cannot seem to escape.
A secret addiction.
A destructive relationship.
A habit you promised God you would abandon.
A bitterness you keep feeding.
A shame that follows you into every quiet room.
A memory you wish you could erase.
An old sin that keeps whispering that you will never change.
Or perhaps you are carrying wounds caused by someone else's choices.
And you have spent years believing that what happened to you permanently reduced your worth.
Listen.
Your suffering is not the same thing as your sin.
What someone did to you is not automatically your guilt to confess.
You do not need to repent for being harmed.
And when Jesus calls sinners to repentance, He is not asking victims to accept blame for another person's wrongdoing.
He calls the guilty to turn away from sin.
He calls the wounded to come to Him for mercy, truth, and healing.
He calls all who trust Him into a life increasingly shaped by His righteousness.
That distinction may sound small.
But for someone who has spent years confusing shame with responsibility, it can change everything.
Because sometimes the deepest wound is not only what happened.
It is what you came to believe about yourself afterward.
That you are dirty.
That you are ruined.
That nobody will want you.
That God must be disappointed whenever He looks at you.
That your past has permanently disqualified you from a future.
But the Cross tells another story.
Not that sin is harmless.
Not that trauma disappears instantly.
Not that consequences are imaginary.
But that Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we made ourselves acceptable.
Not after we repaired every broken thing.
Not after we learned to sound holy in public.
Christ died for us while we were still helpless to save ourselves.
And that grace is not cheap.
It cost the blood of the Son of God.
Think about the Cross.
The One who never exploited anyone was stripped and humiliated.
The One who never abused power was condemned through an unjust process.
The One who never committed sin was treated as a criminal.
The One who possessed all authority chose obedience to the Father, even unto death.
He was not helpless before His enemies in the ultimate sense; He willingly laid down His life, as John 10:18 teaches.
And He did it to accomplish redemption.
Then the stone was rolled away.
The tomb was found empty.
And death itself could not hold Him.
This is not merely a story about a good man who suffered.
This is the Gospel of the crucified and risen Lord.
And His resurrection means that evil, guilt, and death do not get the final word over those who belong to Him.
Perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to hear tonight.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
But it does not have authority to rewrite God's promises.
Your sins may have been real.
But Christ's mercy is real too.
Your suffering may have been severe.
But the Savior has not ceased to be compassionate.
And the story of your life does not have to end at the place where everything went wrong.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling injustice righteousness.
Not by demanding that wounded people smile through their pain.
But by bringing sinners to repentance, offering forgiveness through His sacrifice, restoring what sin has broken according to His wisdom, and giving eternal hope to everyone who trusts Him.
There is another side to this message.
And it may be the side that makes some readers uncomfortable.
Because not everyone reading this identifies with the powerless woman.
Some may recognize themselves in the person who used power selfishly.
Maybe you have controlled someone emotionally.
Maybe you have manipulated another person's vulnerability.
Maybe you have used Scripture to win arguments while refusing to obey it yourself.
Maybe you have wounded someone and then rushed to talk about forgiveness because you did not want to face accountability.
If that is you, do not hide behind religious language.
Come into the light.
Confess your sin.
Stop the harm.
Accept the consequences of your actions.
Make restitution where appropriate and possible.
Seek the help and accountability necessary to change.
And remember that genuine repentance produces fruit.
Grace is not opposed to accountability.
Grace is opposed to the lie that you can save yourself.
There is forgiveness in Christ for sinners who turn to Him in faith.
But there is no biblical promise that a person can deliberately cling to evil, refuse repentance, and use God's mercy as protection from judgment.
The same Savior who welcomed repentant sinners also warned people to turn from sin.
That is why this article is not merely about a difficult passage in Leviticus.
It is about what happens when we finally stop treating the Bible as a collection of comfortable quotations and allow it to confront the world we have built.
A world where the vulnerable are still exploited.
Where power still protects itself.
Where people still confuse legal permission with moral goodness.
Where religion is sometimes used to silence the wounded.
And where sinners still desperately need a Redeemer.
We cannot go back and discover the unnamed woman's complete story.
We cannot tell you what she thought, how she felt, or what happened after the legal proceedings described in Leviticus.
Scripture does not reveal those details.
But we can refuse to erase her humanity.
We can acknowledge the difficulty of her situation.
We can learn to read Scripture with humility rather than pretending every difficult question has a simple answer.
And we can look to Jesus Christ, in whom the righteousness, mercy, and saving purpose of God are revealed.
Galatians 3:28 declares that in Christ Jesus there is neither slave nor free, male nor female, with respect to their shared standing as those who belong to Him.
That does not mean every social distinction disappears overnight.
It means those distinctions do not establish different classes of worthiness before God in Christ.
And Philemon gives us a deeply personal glimpse of how the Gospel challenges relationships shaped by slavery.
Paul urges Philemon to receive Onesimus not merely as a slave but as a beloved brother.
The New Testament's treatment of slavery requires careful historical study, and these passages should not be oversimplified into claims they do not explicitly make.
But the direction of Christian discipleship is unmistakable.
The person standing before you is not merely useful.
Not merely expendable.
Not merely someone whose weakness you can exploit.
If that person is in Christ, you are looking at a brother or sister in the Lord.
And even if that person does not yet believe, you are still looking at a human being made in God's image.
Someone Jesus commands you to love as your neighbor.
Someone whose suffering should matter.
Someone whose dignity should not depend on their ability to defend themselves.
And now I want to ask you something.
Not as a theological exercise.
Not as a debate.
But as a question for your own heart.
Have you ever felt as though the world remembered what happened to you but forgot who you were?
Have you ever been defined by the worst thing someone did to you?
Have you ever looked at your own past and wondered whether God could still write something beautiful from it?
Or have you been the person who needed to stop making excuses and finally repent?
You do not have to tell the internet every detail of your wounds.
You do not owe strangers your private testimony.
But perhaps you can take one honest step today.
A prayer.
A confession to God.
A conversation with a trustworthy pastor or counselor.
A decision to seek safety.
A willingness to stop hiding behind appearances.
Or a simple cry from a weary heart:
"Lord Jesus, I need You."
You do not need to disclose anything unsafe or deeply personal to participate.
And if you see someone asking for prayer, do not treat their vulnerability as content.
Treat them as a person.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Point them toward Christ.
Because Christian community should be a place where truth is spoken with love, not where broken people become spectacles.
And if you know someone who has been told that their past makes them worthless, consider sharing this article directly with them.
Not to force them to talk.
Not to pressure them to forgive an unrepentant offender.
But to remind them that the Gospel is bigger than the lie that their suffering has erased their dignity.
You never know who might read it silently.
Someone who has not prayed in months.
Someone who has been avoiding church.
Someone who has never understood the difference between God's grace and human religious manipulation.
Someone who is quietly searching for a reason to believe that Jesus still welcomes sinners.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, struggling Christians, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along.
Not because following a page makes anyone a Christian.
But because hearing God's Word can lead people to encounter the truth about Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has been helping you understand Scripture, grow in faith, or find encouragement during difficult seasons, I want to invite you to consider something deeper.
Not out of guilt.
Not because God sells blessings.
Those things cannot be bought.
Salvation is the gift of God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But the New Testament also teaches that believers may voluntarily support those who labor in teaching and sharing the Gospel.
Galatians 6:6 speaks about sharing good things with those who teach the Word.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Some believers may prayerfully choose to include such support within their planned Christian giving, alongside their responsibilities to their local church, family, and other worthy needs.
Your giving should be voluntary, thoughtful, and rooted in love for Christ.
More Scripture-centered articles.
More discipleship materials.
More encouragement for believers who feel spiritually exhausted.
More opportunities to reach readers who may never walk through the doors of a church but will encounter a Gospel message on their phones.
Those free resources are part of why this mission matters.
Because not everyone can afford Christian books.
Not everyone has someone patiently helping them understand difficult passages of Scripture.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible.
Those products can be reminders of faith, useful discipleship tools, or meaningful gifts.
But they are not the heart of the invitation.
Jesus is.
The Word of God is.
The work of making disciples is.
You can pray.
You can read.
You can help bring Scripture into conversations that desperately need truth.
But before you leave this article, I want you to remember the woman in Leviticus 19.
The woman whose name we do not know.
The woman whose freedom had not been granted.
The woman whose circumstances became the subject of an ancient legal passage.
We should not pretend we know the rest of her story.
We do not.
But her presence in Scripture should remind us that difficult passages deserve serious study and that the people within those passages must never be reduced to theological props.
They were human beings.
Just as the people sitting beside us in church are human beings.
Just as the people wounded by our words are human beings.
Just as the people we disagree with are human beings.
Just as the people we are tempted to dismiss are human beings.
And every one of us must ultimately reckon with the God who created us.
The God who is holy.
The God who sees injustice.
The God who calls sinners to repentance.
The God who offers forgiveness through His Son.
The God who does not confuse religious appearance with genuine righteousness.
And the God who raised Jesus Christ from the dead.
So if you have been using your power to harm someone, repent.
If you have been hiding sin, come into the light.
If you have been carrying shame for something someone else did to you, do not mistake their guilt for your identity.
If you are weary, come to Christ.
If you are lost, turn to Him.
If you are already His, keep walking with Him.
Because the greatest miracle of grace is not that God calls evil good.
It is that God can forgive the guilty, restore the repentant, comfort the wounded, and make new people through the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And that is why we keep opening the Bible.
Even when its pages confront us.
Even when they disturb us.
Even when they force us to examine our assumptions.
Because we are not searching for a religion that simply tells us what we want to hear.
We are searching the Scriptures to know the living God.
And at the center of His redemptive story stands Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen in victory.
Calling us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
The world may remember the scandal.
People may remember the failure.
Your own heart may remember the shame.
But when Jesus Christ redeems a life, the past no longer has the authority to write its final sentence.
The world may have written your name beside the wound, but Jesus can write your future beneath the word REDEEMED.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABRAHAM GAVE HIS OTHER SONS GIFTS… THEN SENT THEM AWAY FROM ISAAC. WHAT GOD WAS PROTECTING WILL CHANGE HOW YOU SEE REJECTION FOREVER.
paragraphs: ABRAHAM GAVE HIS OTHER SONS GIFTS… THEN SENT THEM AWAY FROM ISAAC. WHAT GOD WAS PROTECTING WILL CHANGE HOW YOU SEE REJECTION FOREVER.
Genesis 25:5–6 reveals a painful family separation, a promise that could not be divided, and a breathtaking Gospel truth: being outside Abraham’s inheritance did not mean being beyond God's mercy.
There is something deeply unsettling about a father giving his children gifts… and then telling them to leave.
Not because they had necessarily done something wrong.
Not because Scripture says they were wicked.
Not because they were worthless.
But because there was one son who would receive an inheritance the others would not.
Imagine standing there.
Your father is Abraham.
The man who heard the voice of God. The man who left his homeland because the Lord called him. The man whose descendants were promised blessings that would reach the nations.
You have grown up under his roof. You carry his blood. You know his stories. You have watched him grow old.
Then comes the day when he places something valuable into your hands.
A gift.
Perhaps something substantial. Perhaps enough to begin a life elsewhere. Scripture does not tell us exactly what each son received.
For a moment, you might feel grateful.
Until you discover what comes next.
You are being sent away.
Away from your father's household.
Away from your brother Isaac.
Away from the place where the promised inheritance will remain.
And perhaps the question burning inside you would be the same question that has haunted wounded hearts for generations.
Why does he get to stay… while I have to go?
Now listen carefully, because this ancient family story contains something far greater than an inheritance dispute.
It exposes the difference between receiving a blessing and inheriting a promise.
Between being connected to a godly family and personally trusting the God of that family.
Between possessing something Abraham could give… and receiving what only God could accomplish.
And before this story ends, we are going to encounter something extraordinary.
The very family separation that might initially make us uncomfortable eventually points us toward a Savior who welcomes people from every nation into God's family through faith.
But to understand that, we must resist the temptation to make Genesis say what it never said.
The Bible tells us:

“And Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac. But unto the sons of the concubines, which Abraham had, Abraham gave gifts, and sent them away from Isaac his son, while he yet lived, eastward, unto the east country.” — Genesis 25:5–6, KJV
Read those words again.
Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac.
But to the other sons, he gave gifts.
Then he sent them away.
There is no recorded argument.
No description of tears.
No conversation between the brothers.
No explanation of how the departing sons felt.
And that silence matters.

We must not invent emotions and present them as biblical history. We can imagine the human weight of such a moment, but Scripture does not tell us whether those sons departed with resentment, acceptance, sorrow, or gratitude.
What Scripture does tell us is enough to confront us with a difficult question.
Why did Abraham distinguish between his sons?
The answer begins long before Genesis 25.
It begins with a promise.

When Abraham was still called Abram, God called him out of his homeland and promised to make him a great nation. God declared that through him all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:1–3).
But the years passed.
And passed.
And passed.
The promised son did not come.
Abraham and Sarah grew old.
Their bodies testified to the limits of human strength, while God's promise continued to demand faith in what human circumstances could not produce.
And then came one of the most painful decisions in their family history.
Sarah gave Hagar, her Egyptian servant, to Abraham, and Hagar bore Ishmael.
Genesis 16 records the conflict that followed.

The household became a place of tension and suffering. Hagar experienced mistreatment. Sarah experienced bitterness. Abraham found himself at the center of consequences that would reach far beyond one generation.
Yet something remarkable happened.
God saw Hagar.
A woman who had been afflicted and who fled into the wilderness was met by the angel of the LORD.
And Hagar responded with a name that still speaks to wounded souls.
אֵל רֳאִי — El Ro'i
Often rendered, “God who sees me,” from Genesis 16:13.
Think about that.
Before Isaac was born, before Abraham's later sons entered the story, God revealed His attention to a suffering woman who could easily have been overlooked by the powerful people around her.
The Lord did not overlook her pain.
He did not treat her as invisible.
And He gave promises concerning Ishmael.
This is crucial.
Because the God who chose Isaac as the covenant heir was not a God who had forgotten Ishmael.
In Genesis 17:19, the Lord explicitly told Abraham that Sarah would bear Isaac and that He would establish His covenant with Isaac.
But in the very next verse, God also answered Abraham's concern for Ishmael.
“And as for Ishmael, I have heard thee: Behold, I have blessed him, and will make him fruitful, and will multiply him exceedingly…” — Genesis 17:20, KJV
Did you catch that?
God chose Isaac for a particular covenant purpose.
And God still promised to bless Ishmael.
Those are not contradictory truths.
They stand together in the biblical account.
Divine election for a particular role did not mean that everyone outside that role was worthless, unseen, or beyond God's concern.
And that distinction is essential for understanding what Abraham later did.
The Hebrew text of Genesis 25:5 says:
וַיִּתֵּן אַבְרָהָם אֶת־כָּל־אֲשֶׁר־לוֹ לְיִצְחָק
Vayyitten Avraham et-kol-asher-lo le-Yitzchaq.
“And Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac.”
The Hebrew verb וַיִּתֵּן (vayyitten) comes from the verb natan, meaning “to give.”
The text emphasizes the comprehensive inheritance assigned to Isaac.
Then verse 6 makes a deliberate distinction.
וְלִבְנֵי הַפִּילַגְשִׁים ... נָתַן אַבְרָהָם מַתָּנֹת
Ve-livnei ha-pilagshim ... natan Avraham mattanot.
“But to the sons of the concubines ... Abraham gave gifts.”
The word מַתָּנֹת (mattanot) means “gifts.”
This was not the same wording as the comprehensive inheritance assigned to Isaac.
And the difference was intentional.
The passage is distinguishing between the principal heir and sons who received other provisions.
There is another detail many readers miss.
Genesis 25:1–4 has just introduced Keturah, who bore Abraham six sons: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.

Genesis 25:6 refers to the sons of Abraham's concubines in the plural. Genesis 25:1 calls Keturah a wife, while 1 Chronicles 1:32 identifies her as Abraham's concubine. These passages help explain her place in Abraham's family history, although Scripture does not individually identify every recipient of the gifts in Genesis 25:6.
We should also be careful not to flatten Ishmael's earlier story into this later scene.
Genesis 21 had already recorded Hagar and Ishmael being sent away, under very different circumstances, while Genesis 25 describes Abraham's arrangements for the other sons during his lifetime.
These distinctions matter because God's Word deserves more than dramatic storytelling.
It deserves faithful handling.
Now notice the end of Genesis 25:6.
Abraham sent the sons away while he was still alive.
The Hebrew expression is:
בְּעוֹדֶנּוּ חַי — be'odennu chai
“While he was yet living.”
The text presents Abraham as making these arrangements before his death.
He was not leaving the entire matter unresolved for the next generation.
He was distinguishing Isaac's inheritance from the gifts given to the other sons.
And he sent them eastward, away from Isaac.
Why?
The passage does not directly state Abraham's private motives.
But within the larger Genesis narrative, the covenant promise was specifically to continue through Isaac.
God had already declared:
“For in Isaac shall thy seed be called.” — Genesis 21:12, KJV
The covenant line was not something Abraham was free to redefine according to preference, birth order, or the number of children he had.
God had spoken.
Isaac was the son through whom the promised covenant line would continue.
And here is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because most of us know what it feels like to stand somewhere in life and watch another person receive something we desperately wanted.
You prayed.
Someone else received the opportunity.
You waited.
Someone else got married.
You worked faithfully.
Someone else was promoted.
You tried to hold your family together.
Someone else seemed to receive the love and approval you had spent your life seeking.
And somewhere inside, a question formed that you were almost ashamed to admit.
God, why them and not me?
Perhaps you never said it aloud.
You kept attending church.
You kept singing worship songs.
You kept telling people you were fine.
But comparison quietly settled into your heart.
And the longer it remained, the more it began to poison things you once enjoyed.
Someone else's blessing started feeling like evidence of your rejection.
Someone else's testimony began sounding like an accusation against your life.
Someone else's open door became a reminder of every door that had closed in your face.
But hear this carefully.
Another person's assignment is not the measurement of your worth before God.
Isaac had a particular role in redemptive history.
That did not make every other son less human.
It did not mean that every other son was condemned.
It did not mean God had no purposes beyond Isaac's household.
In fact, the larger biblical story makes the opposite point beautifully clear.
God's promise through Abraham was always intended to bring blessing to the nations.
The chosen covenant line was not the final destination of God's saving purpose.
It was the historical line through which the promised Messiah would come.
And this is where we must move from Abraham's household to Jesus Christ.
Because without Jesus, Genesis 25 can become merely a story about who received the family estate.
But in the unfolding story of Scripture, Isaac's inheritance belongs to a much greater account.
An account of promise.
An account of grace.
An account of redemption that no human family could accomplish by its own strength.
Centuries later, the apostle Paul wrote:
“Now to Abraham and his seed were the promises made… And to thy seed, which is Christ.” — Galatians 3:16, KJV
Paul is explaining the fulfillment of God's promise in Jesus Christ.
The covenant history that continued through Isaac ultimately leads to the Messiah.
Jesus did not arrive as an unexpected replacement for God's ancient promises.
He came as their fulfillment.
The child born to Sarah in her old age was part of the historical line through which the promised Savior would eventually enter the world.
And when Christ came, He accomplished something far greater than distributing earthly property.
He opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
Think of the contrast.
Abraham could give gifts.
Abraham could distribute property.
Abraham could make decisions concerning his household.
But Abraham could not give any of his sons forgiveness of sins by his own authority.
He could not purchase eternal life for them with livestock, silver, or land.
He could not make anyone righteous before God through inheritance documents.
Only God could provide the salvation humanity needed.
And God did.
Through Jesus Christ.
This is why the Gospel is so much more than an inspirational message about getting another chance.
It is the announcement that the Son of God entered our broken world, lived without sin, died for sinners, and rose from the dead.
Jesus bore the judgment that sinners deserve.
He offers forgiveness through His grace.
He calls people to repent and believe in Him.
And He gives those who belong to Him a new identity that no earthly family history can determine.
