Why do we tell people to stop crying when the Savior we worship cried?
Why do we confuse spiritual maturity with emotional numbness?
The presence of grief does not automatically mean the absence of gratitude.
And the presence of gratitude does not require the absence of grief.
Sometimes both exist in the same trembling heart.
Sometimes thanksgiving sounds like a joyful song in a crowded church.
And sometimes it sounds like a whisper from a hospital bed.
“Jesus, I am afraid. But thank You that You have not left me.”
Sometimes it sounds like a mother praying through tears.
“Lord, I do not understand what happened to my child. But I know You hear me.”
Sometimes it sounds like a husband sitting in his car after another rejection.
“Father, I don't know how I will provide for my family. But thank You that I can still come to You.”
Sometimes it sounds like a believer who has fallen into sin again, finally abandoning excuses.
“Jesus, I have failed You. I have no righteousness of my own to offer. Thank You that Your mercy calls sinners to repentance.”
That is not shallow optimism.
That is faith reaching toward Christ while surrounded by circumstances it cannot control.
And if you have ever prayed like that, even with a shaking voice, you know how costly those words can be.
But we must go deeper.
Because the apostle Paul was not writing these words from a life untouched by suffering.
This was a man who knew persecution.
Who knew physical suffering.
Who knew rejection, danger, and imprisonment.
Who described being beaten, shipwrecked, hungry, sleepless, and exposed to hardship in 2 Corinthians 11.
And the Thessalonian believers themselves had received the Gospel amid affliction, as Paul acknowledged in 1 Thessalonians 1:6.
When Paul commanded them to give thanks in all circumstances, he was not speaking to people whose greatest difficulty was an inconvenient morning.
He was writing to Christians learning to follow Jesus in a hostile world.
And the instruction did not stand alone.
Read the surrounding passage.
“Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all circumstances.” — 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18
Do you see the movement?
Rejoice.
Pray.
Give thanks.
These are not three commands demanding that you deny reality.
They are three expressions of a life continually oriented toward God.
Rejoicing is rooted in the Lord, not in the pleasantness of every event.
Prayer keeps the believer in communion with God.
Thanksgiving remembers His goodness and grace even when circumstances are difficult.
And none of these commands can be separated from the words that follow.
“In Christ Jesus.”
That phrase is not decoration.
It is everything.
Without Christ, gratitude can become a desperate attempt to manufacture happiness.
But in Christ, gratitude becomes a response to grace that suffering cannot erase.
You may lose your income.
You may lose a relationship.
You may lose opportunities you prayed for.
You may even lose your physical life.
But if you belong to Jesus, the forgiveness He purchased through His blood cannot be canceled by an unexpected tragedy.
The resurrection cannot be undone by a medical report.
The promise of eternal life cannot be overturned by another person's betrayal.
And God's steadfast love cannot be measured by the balance in your bank account.
Romans 8:38–39 teaches that neither death nor life, nor anything else in creation, can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Not because suffering is imaginary.
But because Christ's love is real.
And this is where the Gospel confronts something deeper than our circumstances.
Our hearts.
Because suffering is not the only reason we struggle to give thanks.
Sometimes we struggle because we have quietly begun to believe that God owes us a life without disappointment.
We pray.
We serve.
We attend church.
We help others.
We try to obey.
And somewhere along the way, without ever saying it aloud, we begin treating obedience like a contract.
Lord, I did my part. Why didn't You do Yours?
We expected faithfulness to protect us from heartbreak.
We expected generosity to guarantee prosperity.
We expected prayer to produce the answer we wanted.
And when life refused to follow our expectations, resentment began growing in places we did not want anyone to see.
That is a painful thing to admit.
But it may also be the beginning of repentance.
Because Jesus never promised His disciples a trouble-free world.
He said in John 16:33:
“In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.”
Notice what He did not say.
He did not promise that believers would never suffer.
He promised that suffering would never make Him less victorious.
And Christian thanksgiving grows from that victory.
Not from the illusion that everything will happen the way we planned.
There is another Scripture we must handle carefully.
Ephesians 5:20 speaks of “giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”
In Greek, the expression includes ὑπὲρ πάντων (hyper pantōn), commonly translated “for everything” or “for all things.”
So we should not claim that the Bible never calls Christians to thank God for all things.
It does use that language.
But we must read both passages together, within the whole witness of Scripture.
Ephesians does not teach that evil becomes morally good or that God delights in wickedness.
Scripture consistently condemns injustice, cruelty, oppression, and sin.
God does not command His people to approve of evil.
Rather, believers can give thanks to God amid all that He sovereignly permits, trusting His wisdom, His righteous purposes, and His ability to redeem what human beings intended for harm.
We can thank Him for His sustaining grace.
For His presence.
For the good He brings even out of circumstances that are genuinely evil.
For the final restoration He has promised in Christ.
And when we cannot identify any present good in a tragedy, we are not required to invent one.
This distinction is essential.
Because a person who has been abused does not need someone telling them to thank God for the abuse.
They need to know that God condemns evil, that their suffering matters, and that seeking safety, justice, and wise help is not a failure of faith.
A grieving parent does not need someone explaining that the death of a child is secretly wonderful.
They need the compassion of Christ, the hope of resurrection, and a community willing to mourn with those who mourn.
A struggling believer does not need a manufactured explanation for every wound.
Sometimes the most faithful response is simply to sit beside someone and weep.
And perhaps the most powerful biblical picture of this truth is found not in a comfortable room, but in the darkest injustice in human history.
The crucifixion of Jesus Christ.
Think about that Friday.
The innocent Son of God was betrayed.
Falsely accused.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Condemned.
Nailed to a Roman cross.
And as He hung there, suffering beneath the weight of human cruelty, His followers could scarcely comprehend what was happening.
From their perspective, hope itself appeared to be dying.
But Scripture reveals something astonishing.
God was accomplishing redemption through the very event that exposed humanity's sin.
In Acts 2:23, Peter teaches that Jesus was delivered up according to God's definite plan and foreknowledge, while those who crucified Him remained responsible for their lawless actions.
God's sovereign purpose did not make their wickedness righteous.
Their evil was still evil.
Their injustice was still injustice.
Their sin was still sin.
But their sin could not defeat God's saving purpose.
And on the third day, the stone was rolled away.
Jesus rose.
Death was conquered.
The crucified Savior was revealed as the risen Lord.
The cross did not become good because betrayal was good. The cross is our salvation because Jesus, in His perfect love and obedience, accomplished redemption through what sinful humanity did to Him.
That is the difference.
And that is the Gospel.
God does not need evil to become good before He can demonstrate His power over it.
He is able to overcome evil without ever calling evil righteous.
Consider Joseph.
Betrayed by his brothers.
Sold into slavery.
Falsely accused.
Imprisoned.
Forgotten.
Years later, he stood before the very people who had helped destroy his childhood.
And in Genesis 50:20, he said:
“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”
The Hebrew is especially revealing.
אַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
Attem chashavtem alai ra'ah; Elohim chashavah letovah.
A close rendering is:
“You planned evil against me; God planned it for good.”
The Hebrew verb חָשַׁב (chashav), appearing in different grammatical forms in this verse, carries the idea of planning, intending, or devising.
The same underlying verb is used for the brothers' evil intention and God's good purpose.
Joseph did not deny what his brothers had done.
He called it evil.
But he also recognized that their evil intentions had not overthrown God's providence.
And there is a beautiful, necessary caution here.
Joseph was eventually able to see a remarkable way God had worked through his suffering to preserve lives.
Not every suffering believer receives that kind of explanation in this life.
Some prayers remain unanswered in the way we hoped.
Some relationships are never restored.
Some losses leave empty chairs for decades.
Some questions will not be answered until we stand before the Lord.
So the promise is not that every tragedy will become understandable before you die.
The promise is that the God who raised Jesus from the dead will not abandon His redemptive purpose.
Romans 8:28 assures believers that God works all things together for good for those who love Him and are called according to His purpose.
And the following verse identifies the deeper purpose: conformity to the image of His Son.
God's promised good is ultimately greater than earthly comfort.
It is our transformation in Christ and our final glory with Him.
That is why thanksgiving is possible even when explanations are absent.
Not because we know everything.
But because we know the One in whom our hope rests.
And now I want you to think about something personal.
Something you may have spent years avoiding.
What happened to you that made thanksgiving difficult?
Was it the person who abandoned you when you needed them most?
The betrayal that changed the way you trust?
The prayer you prayed for years that still seems unanswered?
The ministry where you were hurt by people who spoke about Jesus but failed to reflect His love?
The season when you were so overwhelmed that even opening your Bible felt exhausting?
Or was it something you did?
A hidden sin.
A decision you regret.
A relationship you damaged.
A season of rebellion you cannot undo.
Maybe you are carrying both wounds and guilt.
You have been hurt.
And you have hurt others.
You need comfort.
And you need repentance.
You need healing.
And you need forgiveness.
And the beautiful truth of the Gospel is that Jesus is sufficient for both.
He is not merely a sympathetic observer of your suffering.
He is the Savior who died for your sins and rose again.
He calls the wounded to come to Him.
He calls sinners to repent and believe.
He does not minimize our wrongdoing.
He does not excuse what destroys us.
He offers forgiveness purchased through His own sacrifice and a new life shaped by His grace.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Not because our tears earn forgiveness.
Not because our gratitude purchases mercy.
But because Jesus Christ is the righteous Savior who has made forgiveness possible.
And this is where thanksgiving becomes something far more beautiful than a religious obligation.
It becomes the response of a rescued sinner.
“Jesus, thank You that my worst decision does not have to define my eternal destiny.”
“Thank You that I can repent instead of hiding.”
“Thank You that Your grace does not give me permission to remain in sin, but power and reason to turn away from it.”
“Thank You that I do not have to pretend I am righteous when I can confess my need for Your righteousness.”
“Thank You that You loved me enough to die for sinners like me.”
And maybe tonight, for the first time in a long time, you can stop trying to perform gratitude.
You can simply be honest before God.
You can tell Him the truth.
“Father, I am angry.”
“Lord, I am confused.”
“Jesus, I miss them.”
“God, I am afraid of what happens next.”
“I want to trust You, but I am struggling.”
There is room in biblical prayer for such honesty.
The Psalms are filled with lament.
Psalm 13 begins with David asking how long the Lord will seem to forget him.
Psalm 22 begins with the agonizing cry, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
And Jesus Himself quoted those opening words from the cross.
Lament is not the opposite of faith.
Biblical lament brings anguish into the presence of God rather than using anguish as a reason to flee from Him.
And sometimes that is where gratitude begins.
Not with a cheerful declaration.
But with a decision to keep praying.
Not with an explanation.
But with surrender.
Not with pretending everything is fine.
But with admitting that everything is not fine, and still turning toward Christ.
There is something else I want you to remember.
Gratitude is not a payment that purchases God's love.
You do not earn His attention by thanking Him enough.
You do not secure His forgiveness through religious performance.
You do not become worthy of salvation by learning to smile through suffering.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works.
And the next verse reminds us that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace comes first.
Transformation follows.
Thanksgiving is fruit, not the price of admission.
That truth matters because some of you have been carrying a secret fear.
You think God is disappointed because you are not handling your suffering well enough.
You compare your tears with someone else's testimony.
You hear another Christian say they praised God immediately after tragedy, and you wonder why you cannot do the same.
You see smiling pictures of people celebrating breakthroughs while you are still waiting for yours.
And you quietly conclude that perhaps your faith is defective.
But spiritual maturity is not measured by how convincingly you conceal your wounds.
The Lord knows your heart.
He knows the difference between rebellion and exhaustion.
He knows when you are resisting His truth.
And He knows when you are desperately reaching for Him through tears.
Remember the father in Mark 9:24 who cried out:
“I believe; help my unbelief!”
What an extraordinary prayer.
Faith and struggle in the same sentence.
Belief and need in the same breath.
And he brought both to Jesus.
Perhaps your prayer tonight is not, “Lord, thank You for everything that happened.”
Perhaps it is:
“Lord, I still believe You are good. Help me trust You with what I cannot understand.”
That is a prayer worth praying.
Again tomorrow, if necessary.
And the next day.
Because the Christian life is not one dramatic moment of surrender followed by a lifetime without struggle.
It is a daily walk of repentance, dependence, obedience, and grace.
There will be mornings when thanksgiving comes easily.
And there will be nights when all you can say is, “Jesus, please help me.”
Keep coming to Him.
Keep opening His Word.
Keep praying.
Keep gathering with faithful believers.
Keep receiving wise help when you need it.
Keep confessing your sins rather than defending them.
Keep remembering the cross.
Because the cross tells you that God's love is not a sentimental promise spoken from a safe distance.
It is a love demonstrated through sacrifice.
And the empty tomb tells you that suffering and death do not get the final word over those who belong to Christ.
That does not erase today's pain.
But it changes the horizon beyond it.
One day, according to Revelation 21:4, God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of His people.
Death will be no more.
Neither will mourning, crying, nor pain.
Do not rush past that promise.
Every tear.
Every grief that made you feel alone.
Every night when you could not explain why you were crying.
Every sorrow that followed you into worship.
God's final restoration will not be a fragile attempt to make suffering more tolerable.
It will be the end of death and the former order of things.
And until that day, we wait with hope.
We pray.
We lament.
We repent.
We endure.
And by God's grace, we give thanks.
Not because every circumstance is good.
But because the God who has reconciled us to Himself through Jesus Christ remains worthy of our trust.
Perhaps that is the truth someone in your life desperately needs today.
Someone who has stopped attending church because they felt judged for grieving.
Someone who believes their suffering means God has rejected them.
Someone who is smiling publicly while privately wondering whether they can keep going.
Someone who needs to hear that the Christian faith does not require them to call evil good.
Someone who needs the Gospel rather than another empty motivational slogan.
Please do not keep this message to yourself if it could help them.
Or send it privately with a simple message:
“I thought of you while reading this. You don't have to pretend you're okay. I'm praying for you.”
Because there may come a night when you need to remember that Jesus never required you to deny your grief in order to trust Him.
And if these words have reached a place in your heart that you usually keep hidden, I want to invite you into something more meaningful than a passing reaction.
It does not have to be a dramatic testimony.
Maybe your answer is simply, “His mercy.”
Maybe it is, “He has not abandoned me.”
Maybe it is, “I am still learning to trust Him.”
Not as a performance.
Not because public words make your faith more genuine.
But because your honest testimony may remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
There is no shame in needing the body of Christ.
We were never meant to carry every burden alone.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious words for a few seconds.
Not to replace the local church, faithful pastors, or the fellowship every believer needs.
But to keep pointing hearts back to Scripture, repentance, the cross, the resurrection, and the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
We want the person who is drifting from God to encounter truth.
The exhausted believer to find biblical encouragement.
The wounded Christian to be reminded of the Savior's compassion.
The unrepentant sinner to hear the loving but urgent call to turn to Christ.
And the growing disciple to find nourishment that reaches beyond a single inspirational post.
We want people to have access to resources that help them study the Bible, deepen their understanding of the Gospel, grow in prayer, pursue holiness, and follow Jesus more faithfully.
And if you believe this mission is worth strengthening, I want to invite you to become part of the people who help sustain it.

It is voluntary financial support that can help us continue producing Scripture-centered messages, developing discipleship resources, maintaining outreach, and expanding the work to reach more people with the Gospel.
But we also want to be biblically clear.
And it is certainly not a payment for God's blessing.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You do not have to pay Gospel Warrior to glorify God.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, worship, generosity, and a life increasingly shaped by His grace.
Not an obligation imposed through guilt.
A partnership offered in faith and love.
These products are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply additional ways to encourage faith, share biblical messages, and express our gratitude to those helping sustain the mission.
You are not less valued.
You are not less faithful.
And the Gospel is not less available to you.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Sharing an article with someone who needs the truth matters.

Following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, curious seekers, and even those who do not yet believe in Christ to encounter daily Scripture and Gospel-centered teaching can help extend the reach of this work.
A single share may place a message of biblical hope before someone we could never reach personally.
A thoughtful comment may encourage someone afraid to speak.
A saved article may become a reminder of God's Word during a difficult night.
Every contribution has its place.
But none of it replaces the One who matters most.
Jesus Christ.
He is the message.
He is the Savior.
He is the reason we speak of grace.
He is the One who calls sinners to repentance, forgives those who come to Him in faith, and transforms lives by His Spirit.
And before you leave, I want you to return to the question we began with.
How am I supposed to thank God for this?
Maybe you still cannot answer it.
Maybe the wound is too fresh.
Maybe the situation has not changed.
Maybe tomorrow will still bring difficult conversations, unpaid bills, unanswered questions, or an empty chair at the dinner table.
I cannot promise that your circumstances will suddenly improve because you finished reading this article.
Scripture does not give me permission to make that promise.
But I can point you to a Savior whose death and resurrection are the foundation of a hope that does not depend on tomorrow being easy.
You can come to Him with the truth.
With your sorrow.
With your sin.
With your fear.
With your gratitude, however small it feels.
You can ask Him to forgive you.
You can ask Him to teach you to trust Him.
You can thank Him for grace while still asking Him for deliverance.
And perhaps your prayer tonight will be something like this.

“Father, I confess that there are things I do not understand. There are wounds I still carry, fears I have not overcome, and sins from which I need to turn. Forgive me for the ways I have doubted Your goodness and resisted Your Word. Thank You for sending Jesus Christ to save sinners. Thank You for His cross, His resurrection, and the promise of eternal life through Him. Teach me to give thanks in every circumstance without pretending that evil is good or that my suffering does not matter. Give me courage to grieve honestly, repent sincerely, obey faithfully, and trust You when I cannot see what You are doing. Let my life glorify Christ, not only when I am rejoicing, but also when I am learning to endure. In Jesus' name, amen.”
And now, one final thought.
The command was never meant to make you grateful for every wound.
It was meant to teach you that even in a wounded world, you have a reason to remain thankful to the God who gave His Son for you.
There is no need to pretend that what happened was good.
There is every reason to remember that Jesus is good.
The scandal of our sin met the astonishing grace of God at the cross.
The tomb that seemed to announce defeat became the place where resurrection victory was revealed.
And the sinner who once stood condemned can now be reconciled to God through faith in the risen Christ.
That is the story worth telling.
That is the grace worth sharing.
That is the Savior worth following.
You may never thank God for the moment your heart shattered, but through Jesus Christ, you can thank Him that your shattered heart is not beyond His redeeming grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THE TWO SHALL BECOME ONE FLESH”—SO WHY DID PAUL USE GOD’S MARRIAGE VERSE TO DESCRIBE SEX WITH A PROSTITUTE?
paragraphs: “THE TWO SHALL BECOME ONE FLESH”—SO WHY DID PAUL USE GOD’S MARRIAGE VERSE TO DESCRIBE SEX WITH A PROSTITUTE?

One of the most disturbing statements in the New Testament reveals something many Christians have never understood about sex, the human body, spiritual union, and the breathtaking mercy of Jesus Christ.
Not because it is difficult to understand.
But because of what it means when we finally do.

The apostle Paul took one of the most beautiful declarations ever spoken about marriage—words first uttered in the Garden of Eden, before sin entered the world—and applied them to a man having sex with a prostitute.
Read that again.
Words God gave to describe the union of husband and wife.
Words Jesus Himself would later affirm when teaching about marriage.
Paul used those very words while warning believers about sexual immorality.
Why?
Was Paul suggesting that sleeping with a prostitute makes someone married to her?
Was he saying every sexual encounter creates an unbreakable spiritual marriage?
Or was he revealing something far more unsettling about what happens when human beings take something God designed for covenant love and separate it from the covenant itself?
Because the answer is not merely about prostitutes in ancient Corinth.
It is about the person who thought a one-night stand meant nothing.
The married person who crossed a line and convinced themselves it was only physical.
The Christian who loves Jesus but keeps returning to pornography.
The believer carrying memories of someone they wish they had never slept with.
The person who feels permanently contaminated by what happened to their body.
And perhaps most painfully, the person who wonders whether God still wants them after everything they have done.
If any of those descriptions touch something you have tried to bury, stay with me.
Because Paul does not end this passage by telling broken people that their bodies are worthless.
He ends by declaring that they were bought with a price.
And that changes everything.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:16:
The original Greek is even more revealing.
ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι ὁ κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνῃ ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν; Ἔσονται γάρ, φησίν, οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν.
A close translation reads:
“Or do you not know that the one joining himself to a prostitute is one body? For, He says, the two shall become one flesh.”
Notice something.
Paul does not merely say that the two people experience pleasure.
He says they become ἓν σῶμα (hen sōma)—“one body.”
Then he supports his argument by quoting Genesis 2:24.
This is where the uncomfortable question begins.
Why would Paul reach all the way back to Eden to explain something happening in the brothels of Corinth?
To understand his warning, we must first understand what God originally said.
Before betrayal.
Before prostitution.
Before pornography.
Before broken marriages, hidden affairs, sexual exploitation, and the countless ways humanity would wound itself through misused intimacy.
There was a garden.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
And there was a God who looked at human loneliness and declared that it was not good for the man to be alone.
Genesis 2 describes God forming the woman and bringing her to the man.
Adam's response is not merely biological recognition.
It is a declaration of shared humanity and intimate belonging.
“This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” (Genesis 2:23, ESV)
Then Scripture declares:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.” (Genesis 2:24, ESV)
In the Hebrew, the final phrase reads:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Ve-hayu le-vasar echad.
“And they shall become one flesh.”
The word בָּשָׂר (basar) means “flesh.”
The word אֶחָד (echad) means “one.”
Together, basar echad expresses the profound bodily and relational unity of husband and wife.
But we must be careful.
The Hebrew phrase does not, by itself, describe a mystical substance passing between two people. Nor does it teach that two individuals lose their separate identities.
Genesis describes a new marital union in which two distinct persons become united in a shared life.
Sexual intimacy belongs within that larger covenant reality.
It is not the whole of marriage, but it is profoundly connected to marriage.
Jesus affirmed this understanding.
When questioned about divorce, He quoted Genesis and declared:
“So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” (Matthew 19:6, ESV)
Jesus was speaking about marriage.
A sacred joining.
A covenant relationship not intended to be casually discarded.
And yet Paul takes that same Genesis language and brings it into a radically different setting.
Not a wedding.
Not a faithful husband and wife.
A prostitute.
Why?
Because the Corinthians were living in a culture where sexual activity could be treated as something detached from moral responsibility.
Corinth was a prosperous Roman city shaped by commerce, social hierarchy, religious diversity, and familiar Greco-Roman sexual double standards.
Sexual exploitation and prostitution were part of that wider ancient world.

We should not exaggerate the evidence by repeating the popular but historically questionable story that Paul's Corinth operated a temple staffed by a thousand sacred prostitutes. That claim is often drawn from descriptions associated with an earlier period and cannot simply be applied to first-century Corinth.
The biblical argument is serious enough without embellishment.
Some believers in Corinth apparently needed to be reminded that freedom in Christ did not make every bodily appetite morally permissible.
Paul addresses the slogan:
“All things are lawful for me.” (1 Corinthians 6:12, ESV)
Then he answers:
“But not all things are helpful.”
And again:
“I will not be dominated by anything.”
That second statement matters.
Because something can begin as a choice and eventually become a master.
A secret habit.
A repeated compromise.
An appetite that demands more while promising satisfaction it cannot finally deliver.
Paul continues by addressing the body itself.
“The body is not meant for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.” (1 Corinthians 6:13, ESV)
That is an astonishing declaration.
Your body is not spiritually irrelevant.
Your body is not disposable.
Your body is not simply a machine that carries around your real self.
Christianity does not teach that God only cares about your soul while ignoring what you do physically.
The Gospel is not an escape from the body.
It includes the redemption of the body.
Paul grounds this in the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
“And God raised the Lord and will also raise us up by his power.” (1 Corinthians 6:14, ESV)
Do you see what he is doing?
Before he speaks about prostitution, Paul speaks about resurrection.
Before he warns against sexual sin, he reminds believers that their bodies have an eternal future in God's redemptive purpose.
The body matters because Christ rose bodily.
The body matters because believers belong to Him.
The body matters because what we do with it cannot be separated from the One who redeemed us.
Then comes the sentence that would have shaken the Corinthian church:
“Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 6:15, ESV)
Imagine hearing that for the first time.
Your body.
With its history.
Its weaknesses.
Its wounds.
Its desires.
Its scars.
Its memories.
A member of Christ.
Paul then asks whether he should take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute.
His answer is emphatic:
“Never!”
The Greek expression is μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito).
It communicates a forceful rejection: “May it never be!” or “Absolutely not!”
Paul is horrified by the contradiction.
Not because he thinks prostitutes are beyond God's mercy.
Not because he considers sexually exploited people less human.
Not because the human body is inherently filthy.
But because a person who belongs to Christ must not treat sexual union as morally meaningless.
The issue is not that sex is too dirty for God.
The issue is that sex is too significant to be treated as nothing.
And this brings us back to the question.
Why did Paul quote Genesis 2:24?
Because even when sexual intercourse occurs outside marriage, its bodily significance does not simply disappear.
Paul's argument depends on recognizing that sexual union is real, even when it occurs in a setting contrary to God's design.
But here we must distinguish what Scripture actually says from what Christians sometimes add to it.
Paul is not teaching that intercourse with a prostitute automatically creates a marriage covenant.
He does not call the prostitute the man's wife.
He does not instruct the man to regard the encounter as a legitimate marriage.
He does not teach that every sexual partner becomes a permanent spouse in God's sight.
Marriage in Scripture involves more than the physical act of intercourse. It is a covenantal union involving faithful commitment and the responsibilities of marriage.
What Paul does teach is that the physical act cannot be dismissed as spiritually or morally insignificant.
Sexual union is not identical to marriage.
But neither is it detached from the one-flesh reality for which God designed sexual intimacy.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because some people have been taught that every sexual encounter creates an indestructible supernatural bond that can only be broken through a special deliverance ceremony.
Others have been told that sexual sin permanently attaches pieces of their souls to previous partners.
Some live terrified that they can never truly belong to a future spouse because too much of themselves has already been given away.
But 1 Corinthians 6:16 does not explicitly teach those claims.
The Greek word translated “joined” is κολλώμενος (kollōmenos), from kollaō, meaning to join, cling, or attach.
It is a strong word.
It emphasizes genuine connection.
But the word itself does not prove the existence of an invisible, permanently binding spiritual chain.
Nor does Paul say that a believer who has sinned sexually must undergo a special ritual to retrieve fragments of their soul.
We should never make Scripture say less than it says.
But we must also refuse to make it say more.
Sexual sin can have profound consequences.
It can wound trust.
It can produce shame.
It can damage marriages.
It can expose people to disease, exploitation, or unwanted pregnancy.
It can shape patterns of attachment and desire.
It can leave memories that take time, wisdom, support, and healing to process.
Those consequences are real.
But they are not evidence that Jesus Christ is powerless to redeem a person's past.
And for someone reading this with tears in their eyes, that difference may be the difference between despair and hope.
Because perhaps you were taught that you were permanently ruined.
Perhaps someone told you that no faithful Christian would ever want you because of your sexual history.
Perhaps you have spent years believing that the worst thing you did is now the truest thing about you.
Or perhaps something was done to you without your consent, and you have been carrying shame that never belonged to you.
Hear this clearly.
Sexual assault is not the victim's sexual sin.
The Bible's call to repentance must never be turned into an accusation against someone who was violated.
The guilt belongs to the perpetrator, not the person who was harmed.
God does not demand that victims repent for violence committed against them.
And no person's worth is erased by what another person did to their body.
If you were violated, you are not spiritually contaminated by someone else's crime.
You deserve protection, compassion, justice, and care.
And if you willingly participated in sexual sin, the Gospel still does not tell you that your story is over.
It calls you to repentance.
And it offers you a Savior.
That is precisely where Paul's argument becomes breathtaking.
After warning against sexual immorality, he writes:
The Greek reads:
ὁ δὲ κολλώμενος τῷ κυρίῳ ἓν πνεῦμά ἐστιν.
Ho de kollōmenos tō kyriō hen pneuma estin.
“But the one joined to the Lord is one spirit.”
Notice the parallel.
The person joined to a prostitute becomes one body.
The person joined to the Lord becomes one spirit.
Paul is contrasting sexual union with the believer's relationship to Christ.
He is not claiming that union with Christ eliminates our personal identity or that believers become divine beings.
He is describing the profound spiritual belonging established through relationship with the Lord.
The believer belongs to Jesus.
And that belonging changes how the believer should live.
Here is the part we cannot afford to miss.
Paul's ultimate answer to sexual immorality is not simply, “Try harder to control yourself.”
It is, “Remember whose you are.”
Remember the Christ who died for you.
Remember the Lord who rose from the grave.
Remember the One who has called you into a new life.
Remember that your body is not an object without purpose.
You belong to Jesus.
And because you belong to Him, you are called to live differently.
This is why Paul commands:
“Flee from sexual immorality.” (1 Corinthians 6:18, ESV)
The Greek verb is φεύγετε (pheugete).
“Flee.”
Run away.
Do not negotiate with it.
Do not build a comfortable home beside temptation and expect yourself never to enter.
Do not keep feeding what you are praying God will help you overcome.
There are moments when spiritual maturity looks less like standing your ground and more like walking out the door.
Closing the browser.
Ending the conversation.
Deleting the secret account.
Refusing the invitation.
Confessing what has been hidden.
Seeking help instead of pretending you have everything under control.
And sometimes it means admitting that you have confused being desired with being loved.
That attention is not necessarily affection.
That physical access is not the same as covenant commitment.
That someone wanting your body does not automatically mean they are willing to honor your heart.
Some of the deepest wounds in people's lives began with the words, “It doesn't mean anything.”
But afterward, it meant something.
Not always in the same way.
Not always with the same emotional consequences.
Yet enough to leave a person asking why something they were told was casual became so difficult to forget.
Paul's teaching challenges the idea that human beings can completely separate physical intimacy from moral responsibility.
But it also challenges another destructive lie.
The lie that once you have sinned, you are no longer worth loving.
Because Paul's warning is not the final word.
Listen to what he says next.
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” (1 Corinthians 6:19, ESV)
A temple.
Think about that.
Not a garbage dump.
Not a disposable object.
Not a ruined building that God has abandoned.
A temple of the Holy Spirit.
Paul is speaking to believers about the indwelling presence of God.
He is not promising that Christians will never struggle again.
He is not denying that sin has consequences.
He is declaring that their bodies now belong to a holy purpose.
Then he gives the reason:
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20, ESV)
Bought with a price.
What price?
The New Testament points us to the sacrificial death of Jesus Christ.
Peter writes that believers were ransomed not with perishable silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19).
Paul himself teaches that Christ died for our sins and was raised on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Not a donation.
Not an offering.
Not a lifetime of religious performance.
It was the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And this is where the Gospel becomes personal.
Because Jesus did not die only for people with respectable histories.
He died for sinners.
People who lied.
People who betrayed.
People who used others.
People who broke promises.
People who worshiped their appetites.
People who lived double lives.
People who needed mercy more than they wanted to admit.
Earlier in the same letter, Paul describes the former lives of some Corinthian believers.
Among the sins he names are sexual immorality, adultery, theft, greed, drunkenness, and other forms of unrighteousness.
Then comes one of the most hope-filled sentences in the entire New Testament:
“And such were some of you.” (1 Corinthians 6:11, ESV)
Were.
One small word.
One enormous testimony.
Paul does not pretend their former sins never happened.
He does not deny the damage sin can cause.
He does not tell them that repentance is unnecessary.
He says something far greater.
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” (1 Corinthians 6:11, ESV)
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
These are not sentimental words.
They describe the saving work of God in people who desperately needed grace.
The Greek word translated “washed” is ἀπελούσασθε (apelousasthe), from apolouō, meaning to wash away or wash clean.
The verse speaks of the decisive change associated with belonging to Christ.
The word “sanctified” points to being set apart for God.
The word “justified” speaks of being declared righteous before God.
And all of this is grounded in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and the work of God's Spirit.
Do you understand the beauty of that?
Paul did not write these words to people who had never sinned sexually.
He wrote them to a church that included people whose former lives had been marked by serious sin.
Their past was real.
But their past was not their final identity.
Jesus had rewritten their story.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by pretending their actions were harmless.
But by saving sinners and bringing them into a new relationship with God.
This is what grace does.
Grace does not excuse sin.
Grace rescues sinners.
Grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace teaches us to turn away from ungodliness and live for Christ (Titus 2:11–12).
Grace does not promise that every consequence will disappear overnight.
Grace promises that sin does not have to be the master of those who belong to Jesus (Romans 6:14).
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
You may still remember what happened.
You may still grieve the choices you made.
You may still need to rebuild trust.
You may still need counseling, accountability, medical care, or time to heal.
Forgiveness does not erase the responsibility to make things right where possible.
But if you are in Christ, you do not have to spend the rest of your life treating your past as more powerful than His cross.
The cross is not fragile.
The resurrection is not weak.
And the mercy of Jesus is not reserved for people who have only made small mistakes.
Consider the woman brought before Jesus in John 8, a passage whose textual history requires care because the account is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel.
The story has been deeply influential in Christian tradition, but we should acknowledge that manuscript question rather than conceal it.
In the familiar account, a woman accused of adultery is placed before Jesus.
Her accusers want judgment.
Jesus exposes their hypocrisy.
And the story ends with His call to leave sin behind.
It is a picture of mercy joined with moral seriousness.
But we do not have to depend on a textually disputed passage to know that Jesus receives repentant sinners.
Luke 7 records Jesus receiving a woman known in the city as a sinner, while a Pharisee silently questions whether Jesus understands what kind of person is touching Him.
Jesus responds with a lesson about forgiveness and love.
He tells the woman:
“Your sins are forgiven.” (Luke 7:48, ESV)
And then:
“Your faith has saved you; go in peace.” (Luke 7:50, ESV)
What a difference between the way the world often labels people and the way Jesus receives those who come to Him in faith.
The world may remember the scandal.
Jesus brings the possibility of redemption.
The world may keep repeating what someone used to be.
The Gospel declares what God's grace can make them.
And that brings us to the heart of the entire passage.
Paul did not quote “the two shall become one flesh” to create hopelessness.
He quoted it to awaken believers to the sacred significance of their bodies and the seriousness of sexual union.
He wanted the Corinthians to understand that sexual behavior matters precisely because they matter.
Their bodies matter.
Their union with Christ matters.
Their obedience matters.
Their future resurrection matters.
And the price paid for their redemption matters.
If you are married, this passage calls you to honor your covenant, guard your fidelity, and treat your spouse as a person to love rather than an appetite to satisfy.
If you are single, it reminds you that your worth is not determined by whether someone desires you sexually.
If you are struggling with pornography, it calls you out of secrecy and toward repentance, accountability, and the freedom of living in the light.
If you have committed adultery, it calls you to stop justifying betrayal, turn from sin, and take responsibility for the harm you have caused.
If you have been sexually exploited or assaulted, it reminds you that another person's wrongdoing does not erase your dignity before God.
If you carry regret over past relationships, it invites you to bring that history honestly before Christ rather than build your entire identity around it.
And if you have fallen again after promising God you never would, do not confuse repentance with pretending your struggle is small.
Bring it into the light.
Confess your sin.
Seek help.
Take concrete steps to turn away.
And remember the promise of 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (ESV)
Not because confession earns salvation.
Not because tears purchase mercy.
But because Jesus Christ is the righteous Savior who has made forgiveness possible.
There is something deeply moving about the fact that Paul uses the language of joining twice.
Joined to a prostitute.
Joined to the Lord.
One speaks of a bodily union outside God's intended covenant.
The other speaks of the believer's spiritual union with Christ.
And the contrast forces a question that reaches far beyond ancient Corinth.
What are you allowing to shape your life when you already belong to Jesus?
What are you returning to when your heart knows it is destroying your peace?
What secret compromise have you been calling harmless because you are afraid to confront it?
What part of your life have you kept away from the Lord who gave His life for you?
These questions are not meant to entertain religious spectators.
They are meant to bring us before God.
Because it is possible to know the right verses and still live with a divided heart.
It is possible to post Scripture publicly while protecting sin privately.
It is possible to condemn the failures of others while hiding our own.
And it is possible to become so accustomed to grace as a theological word that we forget what it cost.
Jesus was crucified.
Not as a symbol of vague religious inspiration.
But as the Savior who bore our sins and rose victorious.
He did not purchase His people so that they could continue treating sin as their rightful master.
He redeemed them so they could belong to Him.
And belonging to Him is not imprisonment.
It is life.
Maybe this is the moment to stop pretending.
Maybe you need to tell your spouse the truth.
Maybe you need to ask a mature believer to pray with you.
Maybe you need to seek pastoral counsel.
Maybe you need to end a relationship that keeps pulling you away from obedience.
Maybe you need to stop punishing yourself for sins you have already confessed and genuinely turned away from.
Maybe you need to understand, for the first time, that holiness is not the price you pay to make Jesus love you.
It is the fruit of a life being transformed by His grace.
And maybe you have never truly surrendered to Christ at all.
You have admired Him.
Quoted Him.
Listened to sermons about Him.
But never turned from sin and trusted Him as Savior and Lord.
The invitation of the Gospel is not to manufacture a respectable past.
It is to come to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
He died for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
He calls people to follow Him.
And He is able to save those who draw near to God through Him (Hebrews 7:25).
If this article has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to perform your confession for strangers on the internet.
But you do need to be honest before God.
If you have experienced the restoring mercy of Christ, consider sharing a testimony of what His grace has changed in your life.
Someone else may need to know that repentance and restoration are possible.
And if you are still fighting to walk faithfully with Jesus, do not mistake the presence of a battle for proof that you must surrender.
Keep bringing your life into the light.
Keep returning to Scripture.
Keep seeking the support of faithful believers.
Keep your eyes on Christ.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to turn people's pain into religious entertainment.
Not to build an audience around shame.
But to help people encounter biblical truth, understand the Gospel, confront sin honestly, and grow in a deeper relationship with Jesus Christ.
There are people who will never enter a church building but may read a Scripture-centered article shared on Facebook.
There are struggling believers who may be one thoughtful message away from asking for help.
There are husbands and wives quietly praying for restoration.
There are young people surrounded by confusing messages about sexuality, identity, and love.
There are people who have been told that their past makes them unreachable.
And they need to hear the truth.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
His Word still exposes darkness.
His grace still calls people into the light.
A single share can place biblical encouragement before someone who would never have searched for it themselves.
And if you believe this kind of ministry is worth sustaining, I want to invite you to consider something more personal.
Some believers may choose to give from the portion of their finances they have set aside for Christian ministry. Others may see this as an additional monthly offering of support.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
“God loves a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, ESV)
You do not have to pay to receive His grace.
And no financial contribution can purchase His favor.
The products are simply an expression of appreciation.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
To help believers open their Bibles again.
To help struggling Christians rediscover hope in Christ.
To help families talk about Scripture.
To encourage repentance without despair and holiness without self-righteousness.
To keep pointing people back to the crucified and risen Savior.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite someone to read the Scriptures.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Speak the truth with love.
Point someone toward Jesus.
The goal is to see more people encounter the Gospel and grow in obedience to Christ.
And now, before you leave, return with me to the question that began this entire conversation.
Why did Paul apply the words “the two shall become one flesh” to sex with a prostitute?
Because what God designed for covenant intimacy cannot be reduced to a meaningless physical transaction.
Because our bodies matter.
Because sexual union carries moral significance even when people try to separate it from God's design.
Because those who belong to Christ are called to honor Him with their bodies.
And because the Gospel is not merely about what Jesus saves us from.
It is also about whom He saves us for.
Himself.
That is why the final command in 1 Corinthians 6 is so beautiful.
“So glorify God in your body.”
Not merely in your songs.
Not merely in your social media posts.
Not merely in your religious conversations.
In your body.
In your private decisions.
In your relationships.
In your integrity.
In the moments when nobody is watching.
In the choices that reveal whether Christ is only someone you admire or truly the Lord you follow.
And when you fail, do not run farther into darkness.
Turn back to Him.
The One who calls you to holiness is the same Savior who gave His blood for your redemption.
The One who exposes sin is the same Lord who offers forgiveness to repentant sinners.
The One who commands you to flee immorality is the same risen Christ who gives His people a new life to walk in.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It may reveal the consequences of choices you regret.
It may contain chapters you wish you could rewrite.
But it does not have the authority to overrule what Jesus Christ has accomplished through His death and resurrection.
The scandal is real.
The sin is serious.
The wounds may be deep.
But the grace of Jesus Christ is not imaginary.
And for those who turn to Him in faith, the story does not have to end where the shame began.
The hands that were pierced for your redemption are not waiting for you to become worthy of being rescued; they belong to the Savior who came because you could never rescue yourself.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “OBEY THE GOVERNMENT”—EVEN WHEN IT TELLS YOU TO DISOBEY GOD? THE TERRIFYING MISUSE OF ROMANS 13
paragraphs: “OBEY THE GOVERNMENT”—EVEN WHEN IT TELLS YOU TO DISOBEY GOD? THE TERRIFYING MISUSE OF ROMANS 13

One of the Bible’s most quoted commands about government has also become one of its most misunderstood. But what happens when obedience to earthly authority demands betrayal of the King of kings? The answer could change how you understand submission, courage, persecution, and what it truly means to follow Jesus Christ.
Imagine standing in a courtroom.
Your hands are trembling. Your family is waiting outside. The judge looks directly at you and gives you one final opportunity to walk away.
All you have to do is deny Jesus.
Just a few words.
No more prison. No more threats. No more uncertainty about whether you will see your children again.
Then someone standing beside you opens a Bible and whispers:
“Romans 13 says you must obey the governing authorities.”
And suddenly, the question becomes unbearable.
If God commands Christians to submit to government, would refusing that judge mean disobeying God Himself?
Would faithfulness to Jesus actually require denying Jesus?
Read that question again.

Because somewhere between a government demanding obedience and a believer trying to remain faithful, a Scripture written to teach Christians how to live responsibly under civil authority can be twisted into something the apostle Paul never intended.
And the consequences are not merely theological.
They can reach into churches, families, courtrooms, prison cells, and the conscience of an ordinary Christian who simply wants to do what is right before God.
Here is the truth we must confront.
Romans 13 commands Christians to submit to governing authorities. It does not command Christians to commit sin whenever governing authorities demand it.
And if we misunderstand that distinction, we can mistake surrendering our conscience for surrendering our lives to Christ.
But before we condemn those who misuse Romans 13, we need to ask a more uncomfortable question.
Have we actually read what Paul wrote?
Not merely the verse someone quoted during an argument.
Not the sentence lifted from its context to defend a politician, silence a Christian, or justify rebellion.
The actual words.
The actual context.
The actual Gospel that shaped the man who wrote them.
Because the truth is more demanding than either blind obedience or reckless defiance.
And it begins with a sentence that leaves no room for casually dismissing civil authority.
“Let every soul be in subjection to the higher powers: for there is no power but of God; and the powers that be are ordained of God.”
— Romans 13:1, American Standard Version (1901)
Paul's original Greek begins:
Πᾶσα ψυχὴ ἐξουσίαις ὑπερεχούσαις ὑποτασσέσθω.
Pasa psychē exousiais hyperechousais hypotassesthō.
A careful rendering is:
“Let every person be subject to the governing authorities.”
Notice the word ὑποτασσέσθω (hypotassesthō).
It comes from hypotassō, meaning to place oneself under an established order or to be subject to authority.
Paul is not encouraging Christians to treat government as irrelevant.
He is commanding a genuine posture of submission.
That matters.
Christians are not automatically more spiritual because they distrust officials, ignore laws, refuse taxes, or oppose every government decision they dislike.
A rebellious spirit does not become holy simply because someone attaches a Bible verse to it.
But neither does a government become morally infallible simply because God permits it to exercise authority.
That is where the deeper question begins.
Paul says governing authority exists under God's sovereign ordering.
He does not say that every decision made by every ruler expresses God's moral approval.
Those are radically different claims.
God can establish the place of civil government in human society without approving the corruption, cruelty, injustice, or idolatry of particular rulers.
The same Bible that commands respect for governing authority also records God confronting kings, judging nations, exposing oppression, and condemning leaders who abuse their power.
God is sovereign over earthly authority.
Earthly authority is not sovereign over God.
And that distinction becomes impossible to ignore when we remember the world in which Paul wrote.
He was not writing from the comfort of a modern democracy with constitutional protections, elections, and broad guarantees of religious freedom.
He was writing to Christians in Rome, the center of an empire ruled by Caesar.
The emperor at the time was Nero.

The early years of Nero's reign preceded the notorious persecution of Christians associated with the aftermath of Rome's great fire in AD 64. Paul was therefore not writing Romans 13 in response to that later persecution. Nevertheless, his readers lived under an imperial system in which political authority was concentrated in rulers who were neither Christian nor morally accountable to Scripture.
Paul knew what unjust power looked like.
And yet he commanded submission.
Why?
Because the Christian life is not a license for disorder.
Because God cares about justice, peace, responsibility, and the protection of human society.
Because the Gospel does not turn every personal grievance into a divine mandate for resistance.
And because the Christian's freedom in Christ must never become an excuse to harm neighbors or despise legitimate authority.
But here is something we cannot afford to overlook.
The same Paul who wrote Romans 13 also endured punishment, imprisonment, and opposition for proclaiming Jesus Christ.
He did not understand submission as permission for the state to silence the Gospel.
He did not believe civil authority could cancel his commission from Christ.
He respected the proper place of government while continuing to obey the Lord who stood above every earthly throne.
And this is where Scripture itself provides the clearest answer.
Picture another courtroom.
Two apostles are standing before religious authorities who have already warned them to stop preaching.
They are not accused of stealing.
They are not plotting violence.
They are not trying to seize political power.
They are preaching Jesus Christ.
And the authorities have commanded them to stop.
Peter and the other apostles respond:
“We must obey God rather than men.”
— Acts 5:29, American Standard Version (1901)
The original Greek is unmistakable:
Πειθαρχεῖν δεῖ θεῷ μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώποις.
Peitharchein dei theō mallon ē anthrōpois.
“We must obey God rather than human beings.”
The word μᾶλλον (mallon) expresses the priority: God rather than people when their demands conflict.
This was not a rejection of all human authority.
It was a declaration that human authority has limits.

Although Acts 5 concerns religious authorities rather than a civil governor, it establishes a principle that applies whenever any human authority commands what God forbids or forbids what God commands.
And Scripture does not leave that principle standing alone.
Remember the three Hebrew men standing before King Nebuchadnezzar.
Shadrach.
Meshach.
Abednego.
The king had commanded worship before a golden image.
The consequences of refusal were terrifying.
A blazing furnace.
Public humiliation.
Death.
They were not given a comfortable option.
They could bow and live, or refuse and face the fire.
Their answer remains one of the most courageous confessions recorded in Scripture.

Daniel 3:17–18, in the Aramaic portion of the book of Daniel, records their confidence that God was able to deliver them, while also declaring that even if He did not, they would not serve the king's gods or worship his image.
The words לָא־פָלְחִין (lāʾ pālḥîn) express their refusal to serve those gods.
They did not deny the king's political position.
They denied his right to command idolatry.
And there is something breathtaking about their faith.
They did not demand that God rescue them before they would obey Him.
They chose obedience even without a guarantee of deliverance.
That is not rebellion for rebellion's sake.
That is worship.
And if we are going to interpret Romans 13 faithfully, we must interpret it alongside Daniel 3.
Alongside the Hebrew midwives in Exodus 1, who feared God and refused Pharaoh's murderous command.
Alongside Daniel 6, where Daniel continued praying to God despite a royal decree designed to prohibit it.
Alongside Acts 4 and 5, where the apostles refused to abandon their witness to Christ.
And alongside Revelation 13, where earthly political power is portrayed as demanding worship and allegiance that belong to God alone.
Think about that last passage.
Romans 13 teaches that governing authority has a God-given role.
Revelation 13 warns that political power can become monstrous when it demands what belongs to God.
These passages are not enemies.
They reveal two truths that must be held together.
Government deserves proper submission because its legitimate authority is accountable to God. Government must never receive worship because only God is worthy of absolute allegiance.
This is not a contradiction.
It is a boundary.
And it is a boundary written into the words of Jesus Himself.
When His opponents tried to trap Him with a question about paying taxes to Caesar, Jesus asked whose image appeared on the coin.
Then He said:
“Render therefore unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.”
— Matthew 22:21, American Standard Version (1901)
Do not miss the brilliance of His answer.
Jesus acknowledged a legitimate claim of civil government.
But He also distinguished that claim from what belongs to God.
Caesar may receive what is properly Caesar's.
He may not receive what belongs to the Creator.
Taxes may belong to the state.
Worship belongs to God.
Civil duties may be owed to rulers.
Ultimate allegiance belongs to Jesus Christ.
Your conscience must be formed by God's Word, not surrendered unconditionally to the commands of human power.
And your soul is not Caesar's property.
Now let us return to Romans 13, because there is another detail that changes how we understand the passage.
Paul does not merely say that authorities possess power.
He describes the purpose of that authority.
“For rulers are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil.”
— Romans 13:3, American Standard Version (1901)
Then he calls the ruler God's servant for good in Romans 13:4.
The Greek expression is:
θεοῦ γὰρ διάκονός ἐστιν σοὶ εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν.
Theou gar diakonos estin soi eis to agathon.
“For he is God's servant to you for good.”
The word διάκονος (diakonos) means servant or minister.
The ruler is not described as a god.
He is described as a servant.
And a servant is accountable to the One he serves.
Paul is explaining the proper function of civil authority: restraining wrongdoing and supporting what is good.
We should be careful here.

Romans 13 does not explicitly provide a complete theory of civil disobedience or a detailed legal procedure for resisting unjust rulers. Christians have differed over how its principles apply to particular governments, forms of resistance, and political systems.
But the wider witness of Scripture makes one point clear: an official's command does not turn an evil action into a righteous one.
When a ruler protects the vulnerable, punishes wrongdoing justly, and maintains public order, that ruler is acting consistently with the purpose Paul describes.
When a ruler commands idolatry, persecution, or murder, the ruler is acting contrary to God's moral will.
And the Christian must distinguish between respecting the office and endorsing every action of the person occupying it.
This matters because there are two dangerous ways to misuse Romans 13.
The first is to make government absolute.
To tell Christians they must obey every command, even if it requires sin.
To demand silence when authorities prohibit the faithful proclamation of Christ.
To excuse cruelty because someone powerful signed a decree.
To treat disagreement with a leader as rebellion against God Himself.
That is not biblical submission.
That is the elevation of human authority beyond its rightful place.
But the second danger is just as real.
It is using the limits of governmental authority as an excuse for pride, contempt, lawlessness, or political fanaticism.
It is declaring every inconvenient regulation an attack on Christianity.
It is refusing ordinary civic responsibilities because we dislike those in office.
It is treating political opponents as enemies to be hated rather than neighbors to be loved.
It is confusing personal preference with divine command.
And it is imagining that because we claim to defend God, every angry reaction must be justified.
Beloved, not every law you dislike violates Scripture.
Not every government policy you oppose is persecution.
Not every political defeat is a spiritual attack.
And not every act of resistance is obedience to Jesus.
Sometimes faithfulness requires standing firm against an unjust command.
Sometimes faithfulness requires paying the tax, following the law, honoring the official, and refusing to let resentment rule your heart.
Romans 13:6–7 specifically addresses paying taxes and giving what is owed, including respect and honor.
That part of the passage is often forgotten by people who enjoy quoting only the verses that support their preferred political position.
But Paul does not allow us to edit Scripture to fit our anger.
And neither does Jesus.
The chapter immediately before Romans 13 gives us a remarkable picture of how Christians should live.
Romans 12 calls believers to bless persecutors, refuse vengeance, pursue peace where possible, and overcome evil with good.
Then Romans 13 speaks about submission to governing authorities.
The chapter numbers were added long after Paul wrote the letter.
His argument flows continuously.
That means Romans 13 should not be separated from the command to overcome evil with good.
Christian resistance, when conscience genuinely requires it, must still be shaped by the character of Christ.
It must not become an excuse for revenge.
It must not be driven by hatred.
It must not confuse cruelty with courage.
And it must not pretend that doing something in Jesus' name automatically makes it righteous.
There may be times when believers must respectfully refuse an unlawful-in-God's-sight demand, accept the consequences, seek lawful remedies, appeal unjust decisions, or protect those being harmed.
But even then, our conduct must reflect the Lord we claim to serve.
Because the Christian is not called merely to win against earthly power. The Christian is called to remain faithful to Christ.
And that brings us to the most searching part of this entire conversation.
What happens when obeying Jesus costs us something?
Not in theory.
Not in a comment section.
Not in a debate where everyone goes home comfortable.
But in real life.
What happens when telling the truth threatens your career?
When refusing corruption costs you an opportunity?
When defending someone vulnerable makes powerful people angry?
When obedience to Christ means losing approval, security, or freedom?
What happens when compromise would make your life easier?
It is one thing to announce that we would stand with Daniel before the lions.
It is another thing to stand for truth when our own comfort is on the line.
It is easy to admire the apostles for saying they must obey God rather than men.
It is harder to obey God when doing so may cost us something we desperately want to keep.
And perhaps that is why this passage should make every one of us examine our hearts.
Because some of us have spent so much time asking whether Christians should obey the government that we have neglected a more personal question.
Are we obeying Jesus in the places where no government is forcing us to do anything?
We argue about religious freedom while refusing to forgive someone who wounded us.
We defend biblical morality publicly while hiding dishonesty privately.
We demand righteous leaders while excusing pride, bitterness, and corruption in ourselves.
We speak passionately about God's authority over nations while resisting His authority over our own desires.
And suddenly Romans 13 is no longer merely about presidents, kings, judges, or lawmakers.
It is about lordship.
Who actually rules your life?
Who has the final word when obedience becomes inconvenient?
Whose approval matters most when faithfulness becomes costly?
There is a profound difference between defending Christianity as an identity and surrendering your life to Jesus as Lord.
You can win a political argument and still lose your tenderness toward people.
You can correctly identify governmental injustice and still be consumed by hatred.
You can quote Acts 5:29 and still refuse to obey the clear commands of Christ in your home.
You can defend the Bible loudly while ignoring what it says quietly.
And if that exposes something in your heart, do not run from the conviction.
Bring it to Jesus.
Because the Gospel is not simply a message about how Christians should respond to political authority.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ is Lord.
And that announcement was never cheap.
When Jesus stood before Pontius Pilate, He faced a Roman governor who possessed real political power.
Pilate reminded Jesus of his authority to release Him or crucify Him.
Jesus answered:
“Thou wouldest have no power against me, except it were given thee from above.”
— John 19:11, American Standard Version (1901)
Think about that.
Jesus acknowledged that Pilate's authority was derivative.
It was not ultimate.
It existed under the sovereignty of God.
Yet Jesus did not pretend that Pilate's actions were morally innocent.
In that same verse, He spoke of sin and differing degrees of responsibility.
Political authority was real.
Moral accountability was also real.
And the Son of God stood before a human judge who did not fully understand Whom he was judging.
The One who formed the world was being questioned by a man whose next breath depended on the Creator's sustaining power.
The One who is perfectly righteous was about to be condemned.
The One who had committed no sin would be crucified.
And here is where everything changes.
Jesus did not go to the cross because earthly government was more powerful than He was.
He went willingly, in obedience to the Father's saving purpose, to give His life for sinners.
The cross exposed the injustice of human hearts.
But it also revealed the immeasurable mercy of God.
Human authorities condemned the innocent Christ.
And through His death and resurrection, God accomplished redemption for the guilty.
That is the scandal of the cross.
The Holy One suffered for sinners.
The righteous One bore our sins.
The rejected Savior became the hope of those who had rejected God.
And grace entered the very place where human wickedness seemed to have won.
Not because injustice is good.
Not because suffering is automatically holy.
Not because every ruler who harms someone is secretly carrying out God's moral will.
But because God is powerful enough to accomplish redemption even through the evil that human beings commit.
The cross never excuses the sin of those who condemned Jesus.
It reveals the mercy of the Savior who came to redeem sinners.

And if Christ could bring salvation through the darkest injustice in human history, then no believer needs to imagine that faithfulness has become meaningless simply because earthly power appears to be winning.
The resurrection declares otherwise.
Caesar does not have the final word.
Pilate does not have the final word.
The crowd does not have the final word.
The grave does not have the final word.
Jesus Christ does.
But we must also be honest about what that means.
The promise of Christ's victory does not guarantee that every faithful believer will escape imprisonment, persecution, poverty, or death in this life.
Some Christians have been delivered from danger.
Others have suffered terribly while remaining faithful.
The difference is not that one group possessed greater faith.
Our hope is not that obedience will always make us safe.
Our hope is that the risen Christ will never cease to be Lord, and that those who belong to Him have an inheritance that earthly rulers cannot destroy.
This is why the Christian response to government cannot be reduced to a slogan.
“Obey every command” is not the full teaching of Scripture.
“Resist every authority” is not the full teaching of Scripture either.
The biblical calling is deeper.
Submit to legitimate civil authority as an act of obedience to God.
Honor people without worshiping them.
Fulfill your responsibilities without surrendering your allegiance to Christ.
Pray for leaders, including those with whom you disagree.
Seek justice without surrendering to vengeance.
Refuse sin when any human authority demands it.
And when obedience becomes costly, remember the One who endured the cross and rose again.
Peter himself, the apostle who declared that God must be obeyed rather than men, later wrote:
“Honor all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the king.”
— 1 Peter 2:17, American Standard Version (1901)
Four brief commands.
And notice the distinctions.
Honor everyone.
Love the family of believers.
Fear God.
Honor the king.
Peter does not say to fear the king as we fear God.
He reserves that ultimate reverence for the Lord.
In the original Greek, the contrast is equally clear:
τὸν θεὸν φοβεῖσθε, τὸν βασιλέα τιμᾶτε.
Ton theon phobeisthe, ton basilea timate.
“Fear God; honor the king.”
Not worship the king.
Not despise the king.
Honor him.
Fear God.
What a powerful correction for our generation.
We live in a world where political loyalty can become almost religious.
People defend leaders as though criticism were blasphemy.
Others despise leaders so deeply that they struggle to pray for them.
Families fracture.
Churches divide.
Christians begin measuring spiritual faithfulness by political affiliation rather than conformity to Jesus Christ.
And somewhere in the noise, the commands to love our neighbors, speak truth, practice humility, and make disciples are pushed aside.
But the church was never called to become the worshiping congregation of an earthly ruler.
Neither was it called to become a community held together by hatred of one.
The church belongs to Jesus Christ.
And His Kingdom is not confined to the rise and fall of governments.
So what should you do when a government command troubles your conscience?
First, make certain that your conscience is being instructed by Scripture rather than merely by fear, anger, political loyalty, or something you read online.
Ask what the law actually requires.
Ask whether it truly commands something God forbids or prohibits something God commands.
Study the relevant passages in context.
Seek counsel from mature believers who are willing to challenge you, not merely agree with you.
Distinguish between a command that is sinful and a policy that is inconvenient, unwise, or open to legitimate disagreement.
Where lawful avenues exist, use them responsibly.
And if a genuine conflict remains between obedience to God and obedience to human authority, remember that faithfulness to Christ comes first.
But do not forget that even righteous conviction must be expressed with integrity, wisdom, and love.
The manner of our witness matters.
The truth we defend must not become an excuse to abandon the character of the One who is Truth.
And perhaps the hardest command of all is this:
Pray for those who govern you.
Paul urges believers in 1 Timothy 2:1–2 to offer prayers and intercessions for all people, including kings and those in authority.
Not only the leaders we voted for.
Not only the officials who protect our interests.
Not only those who speak kindly about Christianity.
All who are in authority.
Pray for their repentance where they are wrong.
Pray for wisdom where they are confused.
Pray for justice where people are suffering.
Pray for restraint where power is being abused.
Pray for peace and for the freedom to live godly lives.
And pray that your own heart will not become so consumed by political anger that you forget the eternal destiny of the people you oppose.
Because Jesus died to save sinners.
Including sinners in positions of power.
Including sinners who have abused power and must be called to repentance and held accountable.
Including sinners who have spent their lives hating those in authority.
Including you.
Including me.
That is the part of the Gospel none of us can afford to forget.
We are not saved because we chose the correct political position.
We are not justified because we understood Romans 13 better than someone else.
We are not made righteous by our courage, patriotism, activism, or religious knowledge.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And that grace does not leave us unchanged.
It teaches us to repent.
To reject sin.
To pursue righteousness.
To love what God loves.
To stand for truth without becoming cruel.
To honor rightful authority without making an idol of it.
To remain faithful when compromise would be easier.
And to remember that our ultimate citizenship is in heaven, as Philippians 3:20 teaches.
Maybe you are reading this while feeling afraid of what is happening in your country.
Maybe you have watched corruption flourish and wondered whether God sees.
Maybe you have seen Scripture used to excuse injustice.
Maybe you have seen other Christians use God's name to justify hatred and rebellion.
Maybe you have been confused about what faithfulness actually requires.
Or maybe the deepest struggle is not with your government at all.
Maybe it is with the authority of Jesus over your own life.
You want Him as Savior, but you have resisted Him as Lord.
You want His protection, but you are afraid of what surrender might cost.
You want to stand courageously in public, but there is something hidden in private that you still refuse to bring into the light.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
Jesus is not calling you to pretend that you are strong.
He is calling you to come to Him.
Bring your fear.
Bring your confusion.
Bring your political anger.
Bring your compromises.
Bring the sins you have excused and the wounds you have carried.
Confess what is wrong.
Turn from what is destroying your soul.
Trust the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
The same Jesus who calls His people to costly obedience is the Jesus who gives grace to those who repent and believe.
You do not have to manufacture your own righteousness.
You need the righteousness and mercy of Christ.
