Not as a clever question designed to produce a quick reaction.
But as something worth taking before God.
What is the field you are being called to steward faithfully right now?
Not the field you wish you had.
Not somebody else's assignment.
Not the life you imagine would be easier.
The responsibility, relationship, act of obedience, or spiritual struggle actually before you.
Is it your marriage?
Your children?
Your integrity?
Your prayer life?
Your repentance?
Your commitment to biblical truth?
Your willingness to forgive?
Your decision to seek help?
Your return to fellowship after a season of isolation?
Or perhaps the field you need to stop defending is the one you have filled with excuses.
Because not every battle is ours to continue.
Some things must be surrendered.
Some situations require leaving.
Some habits must be abandoned.
Some doors must be closed.
And the wisdom to distinguish faithful perseverance from destructive stubbornness is something we should continually seek from God.
James 1:5 invites believers who lack wisdom to ask God.
So ask Him.
Before you make another decision out of fear.
Before you confuse pride with courage.
Before you surrender something good simply because it has become difficult.
Before you continue something harmful simply because you are afraid of what people will say.
Ask the Lord for wisdom.
And then respond to His Word.
Shammah's story is not a command to become fearless.
It is a reminder that the LORD can work through a faithful servant in a place the world considers insignificant.
And for Christians, it is an opportunity to remember the far greater victory accomplished by Jesus Christ.
Because long after Shammah's battlefield fell silent, another declaration would echo through history.
Jesus cried from the cross:
"It is finished."
John 19:30.
The Greek word recorded there is:
τετέλεσται
Tetelestai.
It comes from the verb teleō, meaning to finish, complete, or bring something to its intended end.
In John 19:30, Jesus declares the completion of the work before Him as He gives up His spirit.
We should not reduce that word to a simplistic claim that it always means "paid in full" in every context.
Its meaning here is richer than a slogan.
Jesus had accomplished the work given to Him by the Father.
And His resurrection would publicly vindicate the crucified Messiah and confirm the triumph of God's saving purpose.
This is where our theme becomes more than a memorable phrase.
The cross was an instrument of shame, suffering, and public execution.
To many observers, the crucifixion of Jesus appeared to be humiliation and defeat.
But through that very death, God accomplished redemption.
And through the resurrection, the risen Christ stands revealed as Lord.
The scandal of the cross becomes the proclamation of grace.
Not because sin was insignificant.
But because the Savior is sufficient.
Not because human beings were innocent.
But because Christ died for the ungodly.
Not because we earned a second chance.
But because salvation is the gift of God, received by grace through faith.
Ephesians 2:8–10 makes both truths clear: we are saved by grace through faith, not by our works, and we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace is the foundation.
Faith receives.
Good works follow as the fruit of a transformed life.
Because I want to speak plainly to those who have been encouraged, challenged, or strengthened through Gospel Warrior.
This ministry exists to keep pointing people back to Jesus Christ, the authority of Scripture, repentance, forgiveness, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
Behind every article is a desire to reach someone who may be quietly struggling.
Someone who has drifted from church.
Someone carrying guilt.
Someone searching for answers.
Someone who knows Christian language but has never truly understood grace.
Someone who needs to hear that Jesus Christ is not merely a religious figure from history, but the risen Lord who calls sinners to repentance and faith.
And reaching people consistently requires real work, time, resources, and support.
But please understand something important.
Your salvation cannot be purchased.
God's love is not for sale.
And no Christian ministry has the right to make financial support a condition of spiritual acceptance.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
The biblical tithe belonged to the covenant life of ancient Israel, while New Testament teaching emphasizes willing, generous, proportionate support according to one's means.
So if you prayerfully choose to dedicate a portion of your monthly giving to Gospel Warrior, that can be a meaningful ministry offering.
But it should not be presented as a mandatory replacement for your responsibilities to your local church, your family, or those in need.
Support should come from love, conviction, and freedom in Christ—not guilt.
And if you are struggling financially, please do not feel pressured to give money you need for food, medicine, housing, or your family's basic necessities.
You can still be part of this mission.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
You may not know who among your friends is struggling with guilt, temptation, loneliness, or spiritual exhaustion.
But a single Scripture-centered message, shared with love, can become an invitation for someone to open the Bible and seek the Lord.
These products are not the reason to follow Christ, and they are not substitutes for Scripture, prayer, worship, or life in a faithful local church.
They are simply additional resources and expressions of encouragement connected with the ministry.
The greater invitation is to keep growing in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
You do not have to purchase spiritual growth.
But you do have to make room for it.
Open your Bible.
Pray.
Learn.
Repent when God's Word corrects you.
Remain connected to a faithful Christian community.
Let the truth of Christ shape the way you think, speak, forgive, work, give, and love.
Not to prove your spirituality.
Not to impress anyone.
But because the Gospel is worth sharing.
And if something in this message has touched a place you have been afraid to speak about, I want to invite you into the conversation.
You do not need to share private details or confess sensitive struggles publicly.
If God is bringing you to repentance and a renewed dependence on Christ, you might write:
Your story may encourage someone who feels terribly alone.
Not because every story ends with the outcome we wanted.
But because Christ remains worthy of our trust even in the hardest chapters.
And now, before you leave, I want you to return one last time to that field.
The Philistines are approaching.
The people are fleeing.
The ground is ordinary.
The danger is real.
And one warrior takes his stand.
The Bible does not tell us what Shammah was thinking.
It does not tell us whether his hands trembled.
It does not tell us whether he expected to survive.
So we will not pretend to know.
But we know what he did.
He stood.
He defended the field.
And the LORD accomplished a great victory.
Thousands of years later, his name is still remembered.
Not because lentils are glorious.
Not because a field is greater than a kingdom.
But because the biblical record preserves an extraordinary moment of courage and gives the glory to God.
And now the question reaches across the centuries.
When your moment of obedience comes, what will you do?
Will you cling to sin because repentance is painful?
Will you abandon what is right because faithfulness is difficult?
Will you mistake stubbornness for conviction?
Or will you seek the Lord, receive His grace, follow His wisdom, and obey Him wherever He leads?
You do not have to become another Shammah.
You need Jesus.
You need the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
You need His forgiveness when you fall.
His truth when you are confused.
His grace when you are weak.
His correction when you are wrong.
His presence when you are lonely.
And His promise when the future feels uncertain.
The deepest hope of your life is not that you will always stand perfectly.
It is that Jesus Christ is a faithful Savior.
So if you have been running from God, come to Him in repentance and faith.
If you have fallen, confess your sin and return to Him.
If you are exhausted, bring your burdens to Him.
If you are afraid, ask Him for courage and wisdom.
If you are standing in an ordinary place of costly obedience, remember that your faithfulness is not invisible to your Father.
And if your story has been marked by shame, failure, regret, or brokenness, do not assume that the final chapter has already been written.
Christ does not promise to erase every earthly consequence of our past.
But He truly forgives, redeems, and transforms those who come to Him.
That is the hope we proclaim.
That is the Gospel we refuse to replace with empty inspiration.
And that is why this story of a warrior in a field must ultimately lead us beyond the warrior—to the Lord who saves.
The world may never remember the field where you were faithful, but the Savior who redeemed you will never forget that you are His.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DO WE CALL JESUS “LORD” WHILE NEGOTIATING WHICH OF HIS COMMANDS WE WILL FOLLOW?
paragraphs: WHY DO WE CALL JESUS “LORD” WHILE NEGOTIATING WHICH OF HIS COMMANDS WE WILL FOLLOW?
The Most Dangerous Kind of Disobedience May Be the One We Have Learned to Justify — And the Most Terrifying Words We Could Ever Hear May Come from the Savior We Claimed to Know.

You can sing about Jesus with tears in your eyes, defend His name in public, post Bible verses every morning, attend church faithfully, and still spend much of your life resisting the very One you call Lord.
Not because you openly hate Him.
Not because you have abandoned Christianity.
But because somewhere along the way, you began treating His commandments like suggestions that needed your approval.
You obey when His Word comforts you.
You agree when His teaching supports your decisions.
You celebrate His promises when you need a miracle.
But when His Word confronts your pride, your secret relationships, your bitterness, your dishonesty, your appetite for revenge, your love of money, or the sin you have quietly decided to keep...
Suddenly, you need more time to pray about it.
Suddenly, you want another interpretation.
Suddenly, obedience becomes complicated.
And the question we desperately need to face is not whether we know how to call Jesus Lord.
It is whether we have surrendered the right to tell Him no.
Because one day, every excuse we have carefully rehearsed will stand before the One who sees straight through it.
And there is something Jesus said that should disturb anyone who has learned to sound surrendered while remaining secretly in control.
“Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you?” — Luke 6:46, ESV
Read that again.
Jesus was not speaking to people who had never heard His name.
He was confronting the contradiction between what people confessed with their mouths and what they practiced with their lives.
They knew what to call Him.
But their obedience told another story.
And perhaps that is why this verse feels so uncomfortable.
Because some of us have become remarkably skilled at giving Jesus the title while withholding the throne.
We want a Savior who forgives us.
But we hesitate before a Lord who commands us.
We want His peace without surrendering our grudges.
His blessing without surrendering our idols.
His presence without surrendering our private compromises.
His forgiveness without forgiving the people who wounded us.
His kingdom without allowing His kingship to rearrange our lives.
And the tragedy is not that Jesus has failed to make His will known.
The tragedy is that we sometimes understand exactly what He is asking...
And start negotiating anyway.
In the Greek text of Luke 6:46, Jesus asks:
Τί δέ με καλεῖτε· Κύριε κύριε, καὶ οὐ ποιεῖτε ἃ λέγω;
Ti de me kaleite, Kyrie kyrie, kai ou poieite ha legō?
A close translation is:
“But why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do the things I say?”

The word Κύριε (Kyrie) is the form of Kyrios used when addressing someone. Depending on context, kyrios can mean master, sir, or lord. Here, Jesus is confronting people who address Him as their authority while refusing to act upon His words.
And ποιεῖτε (poieite) comes from poieō, meaning to do, make, or carry out.
Notice what Jesus does not ask.
He does not ask, “Why do you call Me Lord when you are still struggling?”
He does not ask, “Why do you call Me Lord when you have not achieved perfection?”
He asks why they call Him Lord while failing to do what He says.
The issue is not whether a genuine disciple ever falls.
The issue is whether we have made peace with refusing the One we claim to follow.
There is a difference between a believer who stumbles and cries out for mercy and a person who deliberately protects disobedience while demanding that God approve it.
One is fighting sin.
The other is negotiating its continued residence.
And if that distinction makes you uncomfortable, do not rush past it.
Sometimes the mercy of God begins by disturbing the peace we have made with what is destroying us.
Think about the last time Scripture confronted something you did not want to surrender.
Maybe it was a relationship you knew was pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe it was the way you spoke to your spouse when nobody else was listening.
Maybe it was the resentment you kept feeding because forgiving someone felt like allowing them to escape accountability.
Maybe it was a dishonest business practice that had become so normal you no longer called it dishonesty.
Maybe it was the sexual temptation you kept returning to, promising yourself that the next time would be the last.
Or maybe it was something much quieter.
The hunger to be admired.
The refusal to apologize.
The secret satisfaction when someone who hurt you finally suffered.
The pride that made correction feel like persecution.
The habit of being spiritually impressive in public while emotionally cruel at home.
You knew what Scripture said.
You felt the conviction.
And instead of asking, “Lord, how do I obey You?” you began asking, “How far can I go without technically disobeying?”
That is a dangerous question.
Because it reveals that our hearts may be searching for the boundary of rebellion rather than the beauty of holiness.
And before anyone misunderstands, this is not a message declaring that every Christian who struggles with sin is a hypocrite.
If that were true, none of us could stand.
The apostle John wrote to believers:
“If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” — 1 John 1:8, ESV
But he immediately pointed us toward hope:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, ESV
The Gospel does not teach that Christians never sin.
It teaches that sin is no longer something we can comfortably enthrone.
Grace does not mean we stop needing repentance.
Grace brings us back to the Savior who forgives, cleanses, and transforms.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because there was a man who called Jesus Lord, promised extraordinary loyalty, and then failed when it mattered most.
His name was Peter.
Peter was not a stranger to Jesus.
He had walked with Him.
He had witnessed miracles.
He had heard teachings that generations would treasure.
He had seen the sick healed and the impossible become possible.
When Jesus warned His disciples that they would fall away, Peter was certain he would remain faithful.
Even if everyone else failed, Peter believed he would stand.
Yet before the night was over, the man who had promised to remain loyal denied knowing Jesus three times.
Not once.
Three times.
And when the rooster crowed, Luke records a detail that still breaks the heart:
“And the Lord turned and looked at Peter.” — Luke 22:61, ESV
Imagine that moment.
The face of the One who had loved him.
The eyes of the One who had warned him.
The Lord he had promised never to abandon.
Peter remembered.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
There are tears that come because we have been caught.
And there are tears that come because we finally see what our sin has done to a relationship we treasure.
Peter's tears were not the end of his story.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, the risen Christ questioned Peter's love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
The disciple who had publicly denied Jesus was not beyond restoration.
But notice something beautiful.
Jesus did not restore Peter by declaring that denial was harmless.
He restored him through a love that confronted his failure and called him forward into faithful service.
This is the Gospel.
Not pretending that our rebellion was never rebellion.
Not minimizing the commands of Christ.
Not teaching wounded people that they must become flawless before approaching God.
But announcing that the crucified and risen Savior receives repentant sinners and makes new beginnings possible.
Peter's failure was real.
Christ's mercy was greater.
And someone reading this needs to hear that.
You may have denied Jesus through your choices even while professing Him with your words.
You may have compromised in ways that nobody knows.
You may have returned to a sin you promised to abandon.
You may have damaged relationships, wasted opportunities, or carried a secret that makes you feel unworthy even to pray.
But your failure does not have to become your final identity.
The same Jesus who confronted Peter also restored him.
And He has not lost His power to restore those who turn back to Him.
Still, restoration is not permission to continue living as though His words do not matter.
Because Jesus never separated love from obedience.
In John 14:15, He said:
“If you love me, you will keep my commandments.” — ESV
The Greek reads:
Ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολὰς τὰς ἐμὰς τηρήσετε.
Ean agapate me, tas entolas tas emas tērēsete.
The word ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate) comes from agapaō, meaning to love.
The word τηρήσετε (tērēsete) comes from tēreō, meaning to keep, observe, or guard.
The form translated “you will keep” expresses what follows from love. The surrounding passage also connects loving Jesus with keeping His word.
Jesus was not selling salvation in exchange for perfect performance.
He was describing the relationship between genuine love and a life that takes His words seriously.
Obedience is not the price by which we purchase God's love.
It is a fitting response to the love we have received.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not a result of works.
But the very next verse says that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared for them to walk in.
Grace saves us apart from our merit.
And the grace that saves us does not leave us unchanged.
This matters because two terrible misunderstandings have wounded countless souls.
One says, “If you fail, Jesus no longer wants you.”
The other says, “Because Jesus forgives, it does not matter how you live.”
Both distort the Gospel.
The first forgets His mercy.
The second forgets His lordship.
The truth is far more beautiful and far more demanding.
Jesus receives sinners who cannot save themselves.
And He calls those He receives to follow Him.
Not to earn the cross.
But because of the cross.
Not to manufacture righteousness through human effort.
But because the Holy Spirit is at work transforming those who belong to Christ.
Paul addressed this very issue in Romans 6:1–2:
“Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!” — ESV
Grace is not heaven's approval of the sin that enslaves us.
Grace is God's undeserved favor in Christ, bringing forgiveness and new life.
And sometimes that new life begins with the most difficult word a human heart can speak.
Yes.
Yes, Lord, even when obedience costs me.
Yes, Lord, even when I have to admit I was wrong.
Yes, Lord, even when I have to end what I have been secretly defending.
Yes, Lord, even when forgiveness feels impossible without Your help.
Yes, Lord, even when following You means disappointing people whose approval I desperately wanted.
Yes, Lord, even when nobody applauds.
Because calling Jesus Lord is not merely giving Him an honored place in our religious vocabulary.
It is acknowledging that His authority reaches into the places we would rather keep locked.
And here is something that should make us examine our hearts even more carefully.
We can sometimes obey the commands that cost us little while resisting the commands that threaten what we love most.
We can give generously while refusing to reconcile.
We can defend biblical morality while speaking with contempt toward people made in God's image.
We can quote Scripture accurately while using it to crush others instead of speaking truth in love.
We can preach repentance to strangers while refusing to confess our own sin to the people we have hurt.
We can condemn the sins we do not struggle with while carefully excusing the sins we do.
And because our visible obedience looks impressive, we begin believing that the hidden areas no longer matter.
But God sees the whole person.
Jesus rebuked religious leaders who were careful about certain outward duties while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness (Matthew 23:23).
He did not teach that outward obedience was meaningless.
He taught that religious precision cannot excuse a heart that neglects what matters deeply to God.
That should humble all of us.
Because it is possible to be correct about a biblical doctrine and still be disobedient in the way we treat the person sitting across from us.
It is possible to know the language of holiness while refusing the humility holiness requires.
It is possible to win an argument about Christ and fail to reflect His character during the argument.
And perhaps one of the most revealing tests of our discipleship is not how passionately we defend Jesus before people who agree with us.
It is how willingly we obey Him when His words correct us.
Especially when nobody is watching.
Especially when obedience is inconvenient.
Especially when our pride has something to lose.
This is why the warning in Matthew 7:21–23 is so sobering.
Jesus said that not everyone who addresses Him as Lord will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of His Father.
He described people appealing to remarkable religious works done in His name, only to hear Him declare that He never knew them.
This is not a passage inviting anxious believers to despair every time they stumble.
It is a warning against confusing religious activity with a genuine relationship of faith and obedience.
Spiritual accomplishments cannot substitute for knowing Christ.
Public ministry cannot purchase salvation.
Even extraordinary works cannot make a life of lawlessness acceptable to God.
And there is a question worth asking before we ever speak about the sins of the world.
What if the most dangerous deception is not believing that Jesus is unimportant...
But believing that calling Him Lord is the same as following Him?
James gives us another unsettling image.
He compares someone who hears God's Word without acting upon it to a person who looks in a mirror and then walks away, forgetting what he looks like (James 1:22–24).
Think about that.
Scripture exposes what needs attention.
We see it.
We recognize it.
We feel the discomfort.
Then we close the Bible, return to our routines, and behave as though nothing was revealed.
We become collectors of sermons rather than doers of the Word.
We save Christian videos but ignore the truth they contain.
We repost warnings about sin while hiding the habits that are slowly hardening our hearts.
And eventually, even conviction can become familiar.
We feel it, admire the message, perhaps even cry over it...
Then refuse to change.
Tears can be sincere.
But tears alone are not repentance.
Biblical repentance involves turning toward God, a changed mind and heart that bears fruit in a changed direction.
The New Testament often uses the Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance, a word associated with a change of mind and turning from sin toward God.
It is not merely feeling terrible about what we have done.
It is responding to God's truth by turning from sin and trusting Him.
That does not mean transformation is always instant.
Some battles involve years of learning, accountability, confession, and dependence on the Holy Spirit.
Some wounds require time and wise support to heal.
Some patterns must be confronted repeatedly as believers learn to walk in freedom.
But there is a difference between struggling toward obedience and planning to remain disobedient.
A struggling believer says, “Lord, help me surrender what I cannot seem to release.”
A negotiating heart says, “Lord, I will surrender everything except this.”
And Jesus loves us too much to pretend that the difference is unimportant.
Consider the rich young ruler in Mark 10.
He approached Jesus with a serious question about eternal life.
He had an outward record of commandment-keeping.
But Jesus exposed the attachment that held his heart.
Mark 10:21 says something astonishing before describing Jesus' challenge.
Jesus looked at him and loved him.
Then He told the man to sell what he had, give to the poor, and follow Him.
This was a particular command addressed to a particular man, revealing his attachment to wealth. It does not mean every Christian is commanded to sell every possession.
But it reveals a principle none of us can safely ignore.
The thing we refuse to surrender may expose what we are trusting more than Christ.
And the young man went away sorrowful because he had great possessions.
He was close enough to hear the invitation.
But he walked away.
Not because Jesus hated him.
Jesus loved him.
And that love did not prevent Jesus from telling him the truth.
We often want love to mean that God will never confront what we treasure.
But sometimes His love confronts the very thing that threatens to master us.
For one person, it may be money.
For another, reputation.
For another, sexual sin.
For another, bitterness.
For another, control.
For another, the desperate need to be right.
The question is not whether everyone must surrender the same particular possession or circumstance.
The question is whether there is anything we insist must remain beyond the authority of Christ.
Because the moment we declare, “Jesus, You may have everything except this,” we have identified a place where our hearts still need to yield.
And that is not a reason to run away from Him.
It is a reason to come closer.
Look at the cross.
Really look.
The Son of God did not enter our broken world to offer a convenient religious lifestyle.
He came to seek and save the lost.
He lived without sin.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
He died and rose again.
He did what no sinner could do to reconcile us to God.
And when we consider the price of our redemption, how can we treat His words as though they were optional advice from someone who has no claim upon our lives?
We are not saved because our obedience is impressive.
We are saved because Christ is sufficient.
But the One who saves us is also the One who calls us to follow.
The cross is not a bargain in which Jesus gives us forgiveness while we reserve the right to remain our own masters.
It is the place where mercy meets our deepest need and where the old claim of sin upon our lives is decisively challenged.
Paul wrote:
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price.” — 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, ESV
Those words are not meant to erase our human dignity.
They remind believers that redemption changes our belonging.
Our bodies, our choices, our relationships, and our daily lives matter to the Lord who redeemed us.
And if you are feeling convicted right now, please hear this carefully.
The answer is not to perform enough religious activities to make Jesus accept you.
The answer is to come to Jesus.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Stop defending what His Word calls sin.
Ask Him for the grace to obey.
Seek help from mature believers when you need accountability.
Make restitution where appropriate and possible.
Apologize where you have wronged someone.
Forgive as Christ commands, without confusing forgiveness with permission for further abuse or the abandonment of wise boundaries.
And when you stumble, do not turn your failure into an excuse to abandon Him.
Return to the Savior.
Again.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because His mercy is real.
And His transforming grace is stronger than the lie that you can never change.
There is a beautiful promise in Ezekiel 36:26–27.
God promises His people a new heart and a new spirit, and speaks of putting His Spirit within them, causing them to walk in His statutes.
In the Hebrew text, the expression לֵב חָדָשׁ (lev chadash) means “a new heart.”
And רוּחַ חֲדָשָׁה (ruach chadashah) means “a new spirit.”

These words appear in a promise originally addressed to Israel concerning God's cleansing and restoration. Christians understand the promised work of the Spirit in light of the new covenant accomplished through Jesus Christ.
The hope is not simply that people will become better at pretending to be holy.
It is that God Himself changes hearts.
He does not merely demand outward conformity while leaving His people helpless.
He gives His Spirit to those who belong to Christ.
This is why true Christian obedience is not merely willpower wearing religious clothing.
It is the fruit of faith, love, and the Holy Spirit's transforming work.
And that is wonderful news for the person who has tried to change and failed a hundred times.
You do not need another mask.
You need the mercy and power of the living Christ.
You do not need to manufacture a perfect testimony.
You need to tell the truth before God.
You do not need to convince everyone that you are already healed.
You need to keep walking with the One who heals.
And perhaps tonight, that begins with a prayer you have been avoiding.

“Jesus, I have called You Lord while resisting Your Word. I have defended what You have been calling me to surrender. I have wanted Your comfort without always welcoming Your correction. Forgive me. Give me a heart that loves You more than my excuses. Teach me to obey, not to earn Your love, but because You first loved me. By Your Spirit, change what I cannot change on my own. Amen.”
No dramatic music.
No public performance.
Just a heart finally telling the truth.
And maybe that is where the greatest turning point happens.
Not when everybody sees you becoming religious.
But when nobody sees you choosing obedience.
When you delete the message you know you should not send.
When you admit the truth instead of protecting your image.
When you walk away from temptation before it becomes another regret.
When you refuse to feed the bitterness that has been poisoning your soul.
When you choose faithfulness over applause.
When you open Scripture not to find a loophole, but to hear your Lord.
When you whisper, “Jesus, I do not fully understand why this is so hard, but I want to follow You.”
Those moments may never become viral testimonies.
But they matter.
Because discipleship is lived in the ordinary decisions where love becomes action.
And if this message has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to turn your confession into a public spectacle.
But perhaps you can take one honest step.
Not to impress anyone.
Not to pretend you have mastered every struggle.
But as a simple confession that you want Jesus to rule the places you have been reluctant to surrender.
And if you have experienced the restoring mercy of Jesus after a season of compromise, consider sharing a testimony of what His grace has done.
Someone reading the comments may believe they are too far gone.
Your testimony may remind them that repentance is still possible and that Christ has not stopped receiving those who come to Him.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to produce words that stir emotions for a moment.
Not simply to collect reactions, views, or applause.
But to keep pointing people back to Jesus Christ, the authority of Scripture, the necessity of repentance, the wonder of grace, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
We live in a world where distraction is endless and biblical truth can easily become another piece of content that disappears beneath tomorrow's entertainment.
Yet people are still searching.
A father wondering how to rebuild his family after years of spiritual neglect.
A mother praying over a child who has walked away from faith.
A young believer struggling with temptation and afraid to admit it.
A husband and wife trying to learn forgiveness.
A person who has never opened a Bible but secretly wonders whether God could love someone with their past.
And sometimes a single Scripture-centered message, encountered at the right moment, becomes the beginning of a conversation that changes a life.
That is why sharing this article matters.
Not because you owe anyone a performance of faith.
But because someone in your circle may be wrestling with the very question you have just faced.

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to explore Gospel Warrior for daily Scripture, biblical truth, encouragement, conviction, and discipleship.
Not as another religious post to collect.
Return to Luke 6:46.
Return to John 14:15.
Return to the cross.
Remember that the Savior who commands you is the Savior who gave Himself for you.
These resources and gifts can also become opportunities to encourage meaningful conversations about faith in everyday life.
But the deepest value of joining is not the discount.
It is the opportunity to help make more Christ-centered encouragement and biblical discipleship available to others.
Our prayer is that these resources will encourage you to study Scripture, grow in discernment, strengthen your faith, and become more firmly rooted in Christ.
You can still participate in this mission.
Read Scripture.
Pray for this ministry.
Use the free resources.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Love your neighbor.
Remain faithful to your local church.
The Gospel is not for sale, and the grace of Jesus Christ cannot be purchased.
It is to help point a community toward the Lord Jesus Christ.
And that brings us back to the question that started everything.
Why do we call Jesus Lord while negotiating which of His commands we will follow?
Perhaps because surrender frightens us.
Perhaps because we fear what obedience will cost.
Perhaps because we have confused God's patience with His approval.
Perhaps because we have become so familiar with Christian language that we have forgotten how radical the call to follow Jesus really is.
Or perhaps because there is still something we love more than we are willing to admit.
Whatever the reason, the answer is not found in making a more impressive religious promise.
Peter already tried that.
The answer is found in turning back to Christ.
The Christ who knows our failures.
The Christ who speaks truth without compromise.
The Christ who bore our sins.
The Christ who rose victorious over death.
The Christ who receives repentant sinners.
The Christ who sends His Spirit to transform His people.
The Christ who remains worthy of obedience even when obedience is costly.
One day, we will no longer have to choose between the comfort of this world and the commands of our Savior.
Faith will become sight.
But today, we are still walking.
Still learning.
Still being corrected.
Still depending on grace.
And the question is not whether we can promise Jesus a flawless tomorrow.
It is whether we will trust Him enough to obey what He has already shown us today.
Maybe that means confessing a hidden sin.
Maybe it means seeking reconciliation.
Maybe it means leaving something that has been destroying your spiritual life.
Maybe it means returning to prayer after months of silence.
Maybe it means finally opening the Bible you have been quoting but not allowing to correct you.
Maybe it means falling to your knees and admitting that the greatest obstacle in your discipleship has not been a lack of information.
It has been your unwillingness to surrender.
And if that is where you are, there is still hope.
Jesus did not go to the cross to make sin comfortable.
He went to the cross to save sinners.
He did not rise from the grave merely to become an inspiring figure in our stories.
He rose as the living Lord.
And His invitation still stands.
Two words.
No negotiation.
But an invitation full of grace.
So before you leave this article, ask yourself one question that no pastor, writer, friend, or stranger can answer for you.
What has Jesus already told me to surrender that I am still trying to negotiate?
Do not rush to answer publicly.
First, answer Him.
Let it be the beginning of an honest prayer, not a claim of perfection.
Because the goal is not merely that people call Jesus Lord.
It is that people come to know Him, trust Him, love Him, and follow Him.
Your scandal may be real.
Your failure may be painful.
Your compromise may have lasted longer than you ever imagined.
But the final chapter does not have to belong to your sin.
It can belong to the grace of Jesus Christ.
The hands you have been resisting are the very hands that were pierced to bring you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY CALLED VASHTI REBELLIOUS. BUT DID GOD EVER CALL HER THAT?
paragraphs: THEY CALLED VASHTI REBELLIOUS. BUT DID GOD EVER CALL HER THAT?

For years, some pastors have used one queen’s refusal to frighten wives into submission. But what if the real scandal in Esther 1 isn't a woman who said no—but powerful men who were terrified that other women might do the same?
There is a woman sitting in church right now who has learned to fear one particular Bible story.
Not because she hates Scripture.
Not because she refuses to honor her husband.
But because every time the name Vashti is mentioned, she remembers the warning.
“Don't be like Vashti.”
“Don't dishonor your husband.”
“Don't let your pride destroy your marriage.”
And perhaps the most painful one of all:
“If you refuse to submit, God can replace you just like Vashti.”

She hears those words, lowers her eyes, and wonders whether being a godly wife means she must never disagree, never question, never refuse—even when something inside her is screaming that what is being demanded is wrong.
She loves Jesus.
She wants her marriage to honor God.
But she has been taught to confuse obedience to Christ with unquestioning obedience to a man.
And somewhere along the way, the story of a Persian queen became a weapon against her conscience.
But here is the question that may change the way you read Esther forever:
Where, exactly, does God condemn Vashti for refusing the king?
Not where a preacher condemns her.
Not where a cultural tradition condemns her.
Not where an angry husband condemns her.
Where does God condemn her?
Open your Bible.
Read Esther chapter 1 carefully.
Because what the text actually says—and what people sometimes make it say—are not the same thing.
And the difference matters more than you might imagine.
The story begins in the magnificent Persian Empire, under King Ahasuerus, commonly identified with Xerxes I.
This was a ruler surrounded by wealth, military power, political influence, and a royal court designed to display his greatness.
For 180 days, he displayed the riches and splendor of his kingdom. Afterward, he hosted another feast lasting seven days.
The palace was overflowing with luxury.
The wine was abundant.
The atmosphere was extravagant.
And on the seventh day, something happened.

Esther 1:10–11 tells us that the king, whose heart was merry with wine, commanded seven eunuchs to bring Queen Vashti before him wearing her royal crown, so that he could display her beauty to the people and officials.
Notice the wording.
He wanted to show her beauty.
The Hebrew expression in Esther 1:11 is:
לְהַרְאוֹת הָעַמִּים וְהַשָּׂרִים אֶת־יָפְיָהּ
Lehar'ot ha'ammim vehassarim et-yofyah.
“To show the peoples and the officials her beauty.”
That is what the text says.
The king wanted his beautiful queen brought before an assembly of people and officials after days of feasting.
Scripture does not tell us precisely what Vashti was thinking.
It does not tell us whether she feared humiliation, objectification, drunken behavior, or something else.

Some interpreters have suggested that the king demanded she appear naked, wearing only her crown. That interpretation appears in later Jewish tradition, but the biblical Hebrew does not explicitly say she was commanded to appear naked.
We must be careful here.
We cannot defend Vashti by inventing details any more than we should condemn her by inventing sins.
The text gives us enough to ask serious questions without pretending to know what it does not reveal.
Then comes Esther 1:12.
וַתְּמָאֵן הַמַּלְכָּה וַשְׁתִּי
Vatte'ma'en hammalkah Vashti.
“But Queen Vashti refused.”
The Hebrew verb ma'en means to refuse or decline.
That is the action the narrator reports.
She refused.
The king became furious.
But here is something every Christian reading this passage needs to understand.
The king's anger is recorded in Scripture. It is not thereby endorsed by Scripture.
The Bible records many actions without approving them.
It records David's adultery.
It records Pharaoh's oppression.
It records Herod's cruelty.
It records religious leaders who used their authority to burden others.
Recording someone's behavior does not mean God is commanding us to imitate it.
And when Scripture tells us that Ahasuerus became furious with Vashti, it is describing the response of a Persian monarch.
It is not announcing the righteous judgment of God.
Read that again.
A powerful man being angry does not automatically mean the person who displeased him has sinned.
Somebody needed to hear that today.
Because there are marriages where a wife has been made to feel guilty simply because her husband is displeased.
There are homes where disagreement is called rebellion.
Where questions are called disrespect.
Where setting a boundary is called disobedience.
Where the words “God made me the head” are used to silence conversations that desperately need to happen.
And when those women turn to their churches for help, some encounter the same message dressed in religious language.
“Remember Vashti.”
But the question remains.
Who decided Vashti was a model of sinful rebellion?
God?
Or the men who were afraid of what her refusal might inspire?
Because the next part of the story is astonishing.
The king consults his advisers.
One of them, Memucan, argues that Vashti's refusal is not merely an offense against the king.
He claims it threatens husbands throughout the empire.
Esther 1:17 explains his concern: when other women hear what Vashti did, they may begin to despise their husbands.
Think about that.
One woman refuses one royal command.
And suddenly, the palace advisers fear a domestic crisis across an entire empire.
They are not shown examining whether the king's request was wise.
They are not shown asking whether Vashti had a legitimate reason to refuse.
They are concerned about the possibility that women might question their husbands.
So they recommend a royal decree.
Vashti is to lose her position, and another woman is to receive her royal status.
Esther 1:20 expresses the desired outcome: wives throughout the kingdom are to give honor to their husbands.
The Hebrew includes the phrase:
יִתְּנוּ יְקָר לְבַעְלֵיהֶן
Yittenu yeqar leva'aleihen.
“They will give honor to their husbands.”
Honor is not an evil thing.
The Bible certainly teaches that marriage should involve honor.
But look carefully at the source of this particular command.
It comes from the political advisers of a pagan empire, attempting to protect royal authority after a queen refuses a king's demand.
A royal decree in the book of Esther is not automatically a divine command for Christian marriages.
That distinction is essential.
Otherwise, we would be forced to treat every law issued by a biblical king as a model of righteousness.
And Scripture itself will not allow us to do that.
So when someone stands behind a pulpit and declares, “Vashti was removed because she refused to submit, and the same thing can happen to you,” we must ask a question.
Are they explaining the biblical narrative?
Or are they turning the fears of Persian officials into a command from God?
Those are two very different things.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Imagine a wife who has spent years trying to keep peace in her home.
She cooks.
She works.
She raises children.
She prays.
She forgives.
She keeps showing up even when nobody notices how exhausted she has become.
One evening, her husband demands something that violates her conscience.
Perhaps he wants her to lie.
Perhaps he wants her to conceal wrongdoing.
Perhaps he demands intimacy without regard for her willingness or well-being.
Perhaps he uses threats and humiliation to get his way.
And when she refuses, he reaches for Scripture.
“Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands.”
He quotes Ephesians 5:22.
But he never continues reading.
He never reaches Ephesians 5:25.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” (KJV)
He never asks what it means to love like Jesus.
He never considers the terrifying responsibility of being called to imitate a Savior who sacrificed Himself for those He loved.
Instead, he uses one verse as a throne and expects his wife to kneel before it.
That is not the picture of Christian marriage Paul gives us.
The Greek of Ephesians 5:21 says:
Ὑποτασσόμενοι ἀλλήλοις ἐν φόβῳ Χριστοῦ
Hypotassomenoi allēlois en phobō Christou.
“Submitting to one another in the fear of Christ.”
This verse introduces the household instructions that follow.
The Greek word hypotassomenoi comes from hypotassō, meaning to place oneself in an ordered relationship or to submit.
Paul then addresses wives and husbands, parents and children, and enslaved people and masters within the social world of his time.

Christians differ in how they understand the specific roles described in Ephesians 5. Some understand marriage as involving distinct responsibilities of headship and submission. Others emphasize mutual submission without a permanent hierarchy between spouses.
But there is something neither interpretation can faithfully erase.
The husband is commanded to love sacrificially, not to imitate the selfish power of a drunken Persian king.
Paul's model is Christ.
Not Ahasuerus.
Jesus did not use His authority to exploit His bride.
He gave Himself for her.
He did not treat love as permission to humiliate.
He stooped to serve.
He did not command His disciples to imitate the rulers who dominate others.
In Mark 10:42–45, Jesus explicitly contrasted worldly rulers who exercise power over people with the servant-hearted greatness expected among His followers.
And in John 13, the Lord of glory knelt and washed His disciples' feet.
The hands that held all authority took a towel.
The King of kings became a servant.
That changes everything.
Because biblical authority, wherever it is rightly exercised, must answer to the character and commands of Jesus Christ.
A husband's responsibility is not permission to sin against his wife.
A wife's calling to honor her husband is not a command to participate in evil.
And no pastor has authority to require what God forbids.
Acts 5:29 gives a principle that reaches beyond the immediate confrontation between the apostles and the authorities:
“We ought to obey God rather than men.” (KJV)
The apostles were speaking about obedience to God in the face of human commands that contradicted His will.
The passage is not specifically about marriage.
But the principle is unmistakable.
Human authority is not absolute.
Only God deserves unconditional obedience.
That means a wife can respectfully disagree without automatically becoming rebellious.
She can refuse to participate in sin.
She can speak truth when something is wrong.
She can seek help when she is mistreated.
And when abuse or coercion is present, she does not have to remain in danger to prove that she loves Jesus.
Seeking safety is not spiritual failure.
It may be a necessary response to wrongdoing.
Now, we must also be fair to Scripture.
Not every disagreement is righteous.
Not every refusal is wise.
Not every husband who speaks about biblical submission is abusive.
And not every pastor who teaches traditional marriage roles is attempting to control women.
Scripture calls all believers to humility, patience, faithfulness, self-control, repentance, and love.
Wives are not exempt from those commands.
Husbands are not exempt from those commands.
Pastors are not exempt from those commands.
Neither pride nor selfishness becomes holy simply because the person expressing it is a woman.
But neither does domination become holy because the person exercising it is a man.
The issue is not whether Scripture teaches honor in marriage. It does. The issue is whether we are using Scripture faithfully—or using it to protect behavior that Scripture itself condemns.
And that brings us back to Vashti.
Was she a hero?
The text does not explicitly say that.
Was she a sinner for refusing the king?
The text does not explicitly say that either.
Was her refusal motivated by moral conviction?
We are not told.
Was the king's demand necessarily sinful in every detail?
The narrative does not settle that question.

What we do know is that the king was affected by wine, commanded the queen to appear so others could admire her beauty, became furious when she refused, and accepted advice aimed at preventing wives throughout the empire from disregarding their husbands.
Those are the details Scripture provides.
A faithful interpreter must resist the temptation to turn narrative silence into divine certainty.
And perhaps that is one of the most important lessons in this entire discussion.
When the Bible is silent about someone's motives, we should be very careful about preaching as though God has revealed them.
There is another painful irony.
Some preachers contrast Vashti with Esther.
Vashti becomes the disobedient woman.
Esther becomes the submissive woman.
One is supposedly punished.
The other is supposedly rewarded.
But have we forgotten what Esther herself actually did?
Esther approached the king without being summoned.
Under Persian law, this could cost her life.
She acted courageously because her people were facing destruction.
And she said words that still echo through history:
“And if I perish, I perish.” (Esther 4:16, KJV)
Esther did not become an example of faith merely by agreeing with everything the king wanted.
She risked her life to challenge a deadly injustice.
She approached the throne.
She exposed Haman's plot.
She pleaded for her people.
She acted with wisdom, courage, and extraordinary resolve.
Esther's story cannot honestly be reduced to “a good woman always does whatever a powerful man says.”
That is not what makes Esther remarkable.
Her courage becomes especially visible when she acts despite danger.
And the book's larger story is about the preservation of God's people in a world where royal power, political manipulation, and human vulnerability collide.
Remarkably, the Hebrew book of Esther never explicitly mentions God's name.
Yet readers have long recognized the theme of providence running through its events.
The reversals are extraordinary.
The powerful are humbled.
Hidden schemes are exposed.
The threatened are delivered.
And the very instruments designed for destruction become part of an astonishing reversal.
This is why we must read the whole book rather than extracting one woman's refusal and turning it into a universal warning.
Because Esther is not primarily a marriage manual.
It is a narrative about the Jewish people, imperial politics, danger, courage, and deliverance.
And while Vashti's removal creates the circumstances in which Esther becomes queen, that does not mean God approved every action that led to it.
God can work through human wrongdoing without endorsing human wrongdoing.
That truth runs throughout Scripture.
Consider Joseph.
His brothers sold him into slavery.
Years later, Joseph told them:
“Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.” (Genesis 50:20, KJV)
God's providence did not make the brothers' betrayal righteous.
It revealed that human evil could not defeat His greater purposes.
The same distinction matters when reading Esther.
The fact that Esther eventually becomes queen does not prove Vashti deserved what happened to her.
Providence is not the same as moral approval.
And now we arrive at a deeper question.
What happens when a church teaches people to fear authority more than they fear misrepresenting God?
What happens when protecting a leader's reputation becomes more important than protecting someone who has been harmed?
What happens when a woman is told to endure humiliation silently because speaking might embarrass the family, the ministry, or the congregation?
Jesus has already warned us about religious leaders who place burdens on others while failing to live with righteousness themselves.
In Matthew 23:4, He condemns those who bind heavy burdens on people's shoulders but will not lift a finger to help them.
In Ezekiel 34, God rebukes shepherds who fail to care for the flock and instead use their position for themselves.
In 1 Peter 5:2–3, elders are instructed to shepherd God's flock willingly and not as those who dominate those entrusted to their care.
The Greek expression in 1 Peter 5:3 includes:
μηδ᾽ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων
Mēd' hōs katakyrieuontes tōn klērōn.
“Neither as lording it over those entrusted to you.”
The verb katakyrieuō communicates the exercise of dominating authority.
Peter forbids elders from treating God's people as subjects to be controlled.
Instead, they are to be examples.
This is a serious warning for anyone entrusted with spiritual leadership.
A pastor is not the owner of people's consciences.
He is a servant accountable to the Chief Shepherd.
His calling is to teach God's Word faithfully, protect the vulnerable, correct sin with humility, and point people to Jesus.
Not to make them afraid of asking questions.
Not to demand loyalty that belongs to Christ.
Not to use a woman's fear of being called Vashti as a means of enforcing silence.
And certainly not to suggest that enduring abuse is a necessary proof of holiness.
If you are a pastor reading this, please hear the concern beneath these words.
The issue is not whether you believe in biblical marriage.
The issue is whether the people under your care are being taught the whole counsel of God.
Do they hear Ephesians 5:25 as clearly as Ephesians 5:22?
Do they hear that husbands must honor their wives, as 1 Peter 3:7 commands?
Do they hear that love is patient and kind, and does not behave selfishly, as 1 Corinthians 13 teaches?
Do they know that repentance is required of men as well as women?
Do they know that spiritual leadership must never be confused with coercion?
Do they know they can seek help without being immediately accused of rebellion?
Because there is a difference between shepherding someone's soul and controlling someone's life.
And that difference can determine whether a wounded person finds healing in the church—or leaves believing that God Himself has rejected them.
Perhaps you are reading this with tears in your eyes.
Perhaps someone has used Vashti's name against you.
Perhaps you have spent years believing that every time you spoke up, you were disappointing God.
Maybe you learned to apologize even when you had done nothing wrong.
Maybe you learned to keep quiet because the consequences of speaking were too painful.
Maybe you were told that being a godly wife meant you should disappear into the expectations of everyone around you.
And now you are wondering whether Jesus ever wanted that for you.
Look at Him.
Not at the angry Persian king.
Not at the frightened royal advisers.
Look at Jesus.
Look at how He spoke to the Samaritan woman in John 4.
He knew the painful complexity of her history, yet He engaged her in a serious conversation about worship, truth, and living water.
Look at the woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years in Mark 5.
Jesus did not treat her as an inconvenience.
He stopped, listened, and addressed her with dignity.
Look at Mary of Bethany in Luke 10.
She sat at the Lord's feet, learning as a disciple.
And when Martha complained, Jesus defended Mary's choice to receive His teaching.
Look at the women who witnessed His crucifixion and the women who first encountered the news of His resurrection.
The Gospels do not portray women as spiritually insignificant.
They portray women as people Jesus sees, teaches, receives, heals, and calls to faith.
This does not erase the Bible's teaching on marriage, family, or the responsibilities of believers.
It shows us the character of the Savior who must shape how those teachings are understood and practiced.
Jesus never gave His followers permission to weaponize Scripture against the people He calls them to love.
And the Gospel does not simply tell wounded people to endure more pain.
It announces a Savior who enters a world broken by sin, exposes human pride, bears our guilt, dies for sinners, and rises again.
Jesus Christ came not merely to improve human relationships, but to reconcile sinners to God.
That includes the controlling husband who must repent.
That includes the wife whose own heart may need correction.
That includes the pastor who has taught carelessly or abused his authority.
That includes the wounded person who has struggled to believe God still loves them.
None of us stands righteous before God because we have performed our earthly roles perfectly.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
His cross.
His resurrection.
His mercy.
His transforming grace.
And grace never means that sin does not matter.
It means sinners can turn from sin and find forgiveness and new life in Christ.
A man who has controlled his wife must not merely learn gentler religious language.
He must confront his wrongdoing, repent, accept accountability, and demonstrate genuine change.
A pastor who has misused Scripture must not simply say that people misunderstood him.
He must examine what he taught, correct what was wrong, and take responsibility for the harm he caused.
And a woman who has been harmed does not owe immediate reconciliation, restored trust, or continued exposure to danger simply because someone else says the words “I'm sorry.”
Forgiveness, reconciliation, and trust are related, but they are not identical.
Repentance has fruit.
Love does not delight in evil.
Truth matters.
Safety matters.
And God's grace is never a license to continue oppressing someone.
This is where the theme of Gospel Warrior becomes more than a beautiful phrase.
The scandal is not simply that Vashti lost her crown.
The scandal is that, centuries later, some people have used her story to make women afraid of exercising moral judgment.
The scandal is that a narrative about the anxieties of an imperial court can be preached as though it were God's endorsement of male domination.
The scandal is that the name of Jesus—who laid down His life for His people—can be invoked to defend the very selfishness His Gospel calls us to abandon.
But grace enters the story when we stop protecting our assumptions and allow Scripture to correct us.
Grace enters when a husband says, “I have sinned against you. I was wrong to use the Bible to silence you.”
Grace enters when a pastor stands before his congregation and says, “I taught this passage without respecting its context. I need to correct that.”
Grace enters when a wife realizes that her worth is not determined by someone's anger.
Grace enters when a marriage stops revolving around control and begins growing in truth, humility, repentance, and sacrificial love.
Grace enters when wounded people are no longer told to pretend they are healed, but are given room to seek truth, help, and restoration.
And above all, grace is revealed in Jesus Christ, who offers forgiveness and new life to those who repent and believe.
Maybe the most important question in this entire article is not whether Vashti was right or wrong in every aspect of her refusal.
We do not know enough to answer that with certainty.
Maybe the question we urgently need to ask is this:
Why are we so eager to condemn a woman whom the biblical narrator does not explicitly condemn, while being so reluctant to examine the anger and power of the man who punished her?
That question should make us uncomfortable.
Especially if we have ever used Scripture to win an argument rather than to seek God's truth.
Especially if we have ever demanded respect while refusing to show love.
Especially if we have ever called someone rebellious simply because they would not let us control them.
And especially if we have ever stood behind a pulpit and confused our personal preferences with the authority of God.
Because the Bible is not ours to manipulate.
It is God's Word, entrusted to us to handle faithfully.
Second Timothy 2:15 calls believers to rightly handle the word of truth.
And James 3:1 reminds teachers that they will be judged with greater strictness.
That should produce humility in every preacher.
Including those of us who write about difficult biblical subjects.
We must not turn Vashti into a flawless heroine when Scripture does not do so.
But we must not turn her into a divinely condemned villain when Scripture does not do that either.
We must tell the truth.
Even when the truth challenges the sermon we grew up hearing.
Even when it challenges our culture.
Even when it challenges our preferred interpretation.
Even when it requires us to admit that we were wrong.
Because the purpose of studying Scripture is not to make the Bible agree with us.
It is to bring our hearts, beliefs, and lives under the authority of God.
And when we do that, we find ourselves standing before a King utterly unlike Ahasuerus.
One king summoned a woman to display her beauty before his guests.
Jesus, the true King, gave Himself to redeem sinners.
One king reacted to refusal with fury and removal.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance and extends mercy to all who come to Him in faith.
One king's court feared losing control.
Jesus taught His followers that greatness is found in service.
The contrast is not that Jesus approves every human refusal or that His commands may be ignored.
It is that His holy authority is perfectly righteous, and His sacrificial love exposes the selfishness of worldly power.
He is not a King who must be protected from the truth.
He is the Truth.
And if our teaching about marriage makes people more afraid of their spouse than they are devoted to Christ, something has gone terribly wrong.
If our teaching about submission excuses cruelty, we have missed the character of Jesus.
If our teaching about authority protects the powerful while abandoning the wounded, we have forgotten the heart of the Shepherd.
And if our preaching turns a Persian king's anger into God's voice, we need to open the Bible again.
With humility.
With repentance.
With trembling hearts.
And with a willingness to let Jesus correct us.
Before you leave this article, I want to ask something of you.
Not for an argument.
Not for a performance.
For an honest conversation.
Have you ever heard Vashti's story used to frighten, shame, or control wives? And after reading Esther 1 in its context, do you believe that teaching was faithful to Scripture?
Let this become a conversation marked by Scripture, grace, courage, and love rather than hostility.
Somebody reading the comments may discover that they are not alone.
Somebody may finally find the courage to ask for help.
Somebody may return to the Bible with fresh eyes.
And somebody who has been misrepresenting God's Word may begin to reconsider.
Not because every reader will agree.
But because serious biblical conversations should not remain hidden simply because they challenge familiar assumptions.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, people exploring faith, and even those who have become distant from church to follow as well.
Because the answer to distorted Scripture is not to abandon God's Word.
It is to study it more faithfully.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, rediscover the grace of Christ, or find courage to confront a difficult truth, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Some believers support Gospel ministry through prayer.
Some through sharing.
Some through financial giving.
Some through all three.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving is not to be done grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You do not have to purchase anything to glorify God.
And God's favor is not for sale.
But I will tell you this:
It is to help people become more deeply rooted in the Word of God.
To see marriages transformed by repentance and sacrificial love.
To see pastors handle Scripture with reverence.
To see wounded believers rediscover the character of Christ.
To see families open their Bibles again.
To see people who have never truly understood the Gospel encounter the grace of Jesus.
Pray for the ministry.
Keep studying the Scriptures.
There is room in this mission for every sincere believer who wants Christ to be glorified.
Because this ministry is not about building a throne for a human personality.
It is about pointing people to the One who wore a crown of thorns.
The One who was mocked, rejected, and crucified.
The One who rose victorious over sin and death.
The One before whom every earthly king, every pastor, every husband, every wife, and every one of us will ultimately give an account.
Jesus Christ.
The King who never misuses His authority.
The Savior whose grace never excuses sin but transforms sinners.
The Lord who calls His people not into a kingdom of domination, but into lives of truth, holiness, justice, mercy, and sacrificial love.
So the next time somebody tells you, “Don't be like Vashti,” do not respond with hatred.
Open the Bible.
Read the whole chapter.
Ask what the text actually says.
Ask what it does not say.
And then ask whether the teaching reflects the character of Jesus Christ.
Because no earthly ruler's wounded pride should ever be mistaken for the voice of God.
And no person should have to surrender their conscience to someone else's misuse of Scripture in order to prove their devotion to Christ.
The deepest wound was never simply that someone silenced your voice—it was that they taught you to mistake their voice for God's. May the voice of Jesus lead you back to truth.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS YOUR FAITH TRANSFORMING YOUR CHARACTER… OR JUST IMPROVING YOUR PUBLIC IMAGE?
paragraphs: IS YOUR FAITH TRANSFORMING YOUR CHARACTER… OR JUST IMPROVING YOUR PUBLIC IMAGE?
The most frightening kind of spiritual deception is not when the world believes you are holy. It is when you have convinced yourself that looking like Jesus is the same as becoming like Him.
What if the version of you that everyone admires is the very version of you that God is trying to confront?
Read that again.

Because somewhere tonight, a Christian will close their Bible, post an encouraging Scripture, respond to a few comments with “God bless you,” and go to bed without ever confronting the bitterness, pride, lust, jealousy, dishonesty, or unforgiveness quietly ruling their heart.
And tomorrow, they will do it all over again.
Nobody suspects anything.
Their church attendance is consistent. Their social media is filled with Christian content. They know when to say “Amen.” They know how to pray in public. They know which Bible verses sound powerful.
People call them faithful.
People call them anointed.
People might even say, “I wish I had a relationship with God like yours.”
But behind the carefully maintained image is a question that refuses to disappear.
If the people who admire your Christianity could see how you behave when nobody is watching, would they still recognize Jesus in you?
That question is uncomfortable.
It should be.
Not because God enjoys humiliating His children, but because the truth that wounds our pride can become the very truth that opens our hearts to healing.
And before you assume this message is about hypocritical pastors, religious influencers, or someone sitting across the church aisle, consider something far more personal.
What if it is about you?
What if it is about me?
What if the greatest spiritual danger facing some of us is not that we have abandoned Christianity, but that we have learned how to perform Christianity without allowing Christ to transform us?
Jesus addressed something terrifyingly similar.
In Matthew 23:27–28, He confronted religious leaders who appeared righteous outwardly while concealing corruption within.
He compared them to whitewashed tombs.
Beautiful on the outside.
Full of death on the inside.
Imagine standing there.
The religious leaders wore the right clothing. They knew the Scriptures. They occupied respected positions. They were recognized as spiritual authorities.
Yet Jesus looked beyond what everyone else celebrated.
He saw what was underneath.
The Greek text of Matthew 23:28 contains a phrase worth examining:
ἔξωθεν μὲν φαίνεσθε τοῖς ἀνθρώποις δίκαιοι
Exōthen men phainesthe tois anthrōpois dikaioi.
It means, in context, “Outwardly you appear righteous to people.”
Notice the distinction.
Appearing righteous.
Being righteous.
They are not the same thing.
The Greek verb φαίνεσθε (phainesthe) concerns appearing or seeming. Jesus was exposing the tragic difference between public perception and inward reality.
And that distinction should disturb every believer who has ever cared more about protecting a reputation than confessing a sin.
Because it is possible to become exceptionally skilled at managing what people see while neglecting what God sees.
You can learn the vocabulary of holiness without developing the character of holiness.
You can defend biblical marriage publicly while privately treating your spouse with contempt.
You can preach forgiveness and still punish someone emotionally for something they did years ago.
You can post about humility while secretly resenting anyone who receives more recognition than you.
You can quote Scripture about generosity while refusing to help someone because there is nothing to gain from it.
You can condemn the sins that disgust you while quietly protecting the sins that comfort you.
And perhaps most painfully...
You can become so busy proving that you belong to Jesus that you stop asking whether your life is actually becoming more like His.
There is a particular kind of loneliness that comes from maintaining a religious image.
You cannot admit that you are struggling because people expect you to be strong.
You cannot confess your doubts because people expect you to have answers.
You cannot acknowledge your temptations because people have already decided that you are spiritually mature.
So you smile.
You serve.
You encourage.
You keep showing up.
And slowly, without realizing it, you begin protecting a version of yourself that no longer allows you to be honest.
You are surrounded by people who admire your faith.
Yet you feel increasingly afraid that someone might discover your heart.
That is not freedom.
That is a prison decorated with Bible verses.
And Jesus did not shed His blood so you could spend your life trapped inside a religious performance.
He came to save sinners.
Real sinners.
Not imaginary people who have everything together.
Not polished religious personalities who never admit weakness.
People with histories they regret.
People with habits they hate.
People who have promised God they would change and then fallen into the same temptation again.
People who genuinely love Jesus but are painfully aware that parts of their character still resist His authority.
People like Peter.
Think about Peter for a moment.
He was bold.
Passionate.
Loyal in his own estimation.
When Jesus warned that His disciples would stumble, Peter confidently insisted that even if everyone else fell away, he would not.
In Matthew 26:33, Peter essentially declared that others might fail, but he would remain faithful.
Then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The fear.
The denial.
Three times, Peter denied knowing the very Savior he had promised never to abandon.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 records one of the most devastating moments in the Gospels.
“And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.” — Luke 22:61, KJV
Imagine that look.
Peter had built an image of himself as the disciple who would never betray his Master.
But in one terrible night, the distance between his confidence and his actual courage became painfully visible.
He was not the man he thought he was.
And he knew it.
Scripture says he went out and wept bitterly.
Sometimes the most painful moment in your spiritual life is the moment God allows you to see yourself without the excuses you have been using.
Not the version you present in church.
Not the version your friends applaud.
Not the version your social media followers admire.
The real you.
The frightened you.
The prideful you.
The impatient you.
The you who still wants control.
The you who sometimes loves approval more than obedience.
But Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.
And that matters more than you may realize.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, the risen Christ confronted Peter's love and recommissioned him to care for His sheep.
Peter's failure was real.
His denial was serious.
But his failure was not stronger than the grace of Jesus Christ.
The Savior did not pretend Peter had never sinned.
He restored him.
And that is the difference between the Gospel and religious image management.
Religion performed for approval says, “Hide your failures so people will continue respecting you.”
The Gospel says, “Bring your failures into the light because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.”
Religious pride says, “Make sure nobody discovers what you did.”
Repentant faith says, “Lord, You already know. Please change me.”
One protects appearances.
The other surrenders to grace.
And perhaps this is where someone reading needs to stop pretending.
You are exhausted.
Not necessarily because you are doing too much for God.
But because you are spending so much energy trying to appear spiritually healthy while avoiding the places where you desperately need His healing.
You have mastered the Christian smile.
You have not mastered surrender.
You know how to sound gracious.
But your family still walks carefully around your temper.
You know how to encourage strangers.
But the people closest to you rarely receive the patience you show everyone else.
You know how to talk about trusting God.
But when something threatens your comfort, your reputation, or your control, fear takes over.
And perhaps you have begun noticing something that scares you.
Your Christian knowledge has grown.
Your Christian vocabulary has expanded.
Your public ministry may even have increased.
But your private character has not changed nearly as much as you hoped.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not to abandon your faith because you have discovered your inconsistency. The answer is to bring that inconsistency honestly to Jesus.
Because conviction is not the same as condemnation.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1, KJV
And Romans 8:4–13 goes on to describe a life increasingly directed by the Spirit rather than ruled by the flesh.
Grace does not mean sin is harmless.
Grace means sin does not have to remain your master.
Grace does not give you permission to cultivate a double life.
Grace brings you to the Savior who can forgive your sins and begin changing your desires.
Consider the Hebrew prayer of David after his terrible moral failure.
In Psalm 51:10, David cried:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.” — Psalm 51:10, KJV
The Hebrew verb בְּרָא (bera) comes from bara, meaning “to create.”
David was not asking God to help him look innocent.
He was pleading for inward renewal.
He understood that the deepest problem was not simply the public scandal surrounding his sin.
It was the heart from which his sin had emerged.
He needed more than reputation repair.
He needed mercy.
He needed cleansing.
He needed God.
And so do we.
Perhaps you have never committed a scandal that became public.
Perhaps nobody has ever exposed your private messages, confronted your dishonesty, or discovered the secret behavior you have been hiding.
But a sin does not become serious only when somebody finds out.
And a person does not become righteous merely because nobody has discovered what is wrong.
God is not deceived by the absence of public scandal.
He sees the heart.
Yet this is where the beauty of the Gospel becomes almost overwhelming.
The same God who sees everything you have hidden is the God who sent His Son to save sinners.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad people behave better in public.
He came to reconcile sinners to God through His death and resurrection.
He came to redeem.
To forgive.
To cleanse.
To transform.
And the transformation He produces reaches far beyond religious appearances.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — KJV
The Greek expression is:
καινὴ κτίσις
Kainē ktisis.
“New creation.”
Not simply a more impressive religious personality.
Not a better-managed public image.
A new creation in Christ.
That does not mean every sinful habit instantly disappears or that believers never struggle again.
The New Testament repeatedly calls Christians to repentance, perseverance, obedience, and growth.
But it does mean that belonging to Christ is more than adopting a Christian identity.
It means entering a new life in which the Holy Spirit progressively shapes us into the likeness of Jesus.
And this transformation eventually becomes visible in places where applause cannot reach.
In the way you apologize.
In the way you respond when corrected.
In the way you speak about someone who hurt you.
In the way you handle money when nobody is checking.
In the way you treat people who cannot advance your interests.
In the way you behave when your spouse disappoints you.
In the way you respond when someone else receives the recognition you wanted.
In the way you handle temptation when nobody would ever know.
In the way you choose truth even when lying would protect your image.
This is where spiritual maturity becomes painfully practical.
Because character is not merely what you claim to believe.
It is what your beliefs increasingly produce in the ordinary moments of life.
Galatians 5:22–23 describes the fruit of the Spirit:
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Longsuffering.
Gentleness.
Goodness.
Faithfulness.
Meekness.
Temperance.
These are not accessories for a religious personality.
They are qualities the Holy Spirit cultivates in those who walk with Him.
And notice something important.
Paul calls them fruit.
Fruit grows from life.
It cannot be permanently manufactured by appearance.
A tree does not become healthy because someone ties beautiful fruit to its branches.
The fruit must grow from what the tree actually is.
Jesus expressed this principle in John 15 when He taught His disciples to abide in Him.
