Jesus knew the suffering that awaited Him.
Matthew 26:37–38 describes Him as sorrowful and deeply distressed.
He told His disciples:
“My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death.”
—Matthew 26:38, KJV
Then He fell on His face and prayed.
“My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.”
—Matthew 26:39, KJV
Read that slowly.
The sinless Son of God did not face His approaching suffering by pretending it was painless.
He expressed His anguish.
He prayed.
He submitted Himself to the Father's will.
His distress was not unbelief. His obedient surrender was not emotional numbness.

Now, we must not confuse the unique suffering of Christ in Gethsemane with every ordinary experience of anxiety. Jesus was approaching His once-for-all sacrifice for sinners, a work no other person could accomplish.
But His prayer does show us something precious.
Faithful obedience and profound emotional distress are not automatically opposites.
You can experience anguish and still turn toward the Father.
You can cry while surrendering.
You can tremble while obeying.
And you can bring your frightened heart to Jesus because He is not a stranger to human suffering.

Hebrews 4:15–16 tells us that our High Priest is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted as we are, yet without sin, and that we may approach the throne of grace with confidence to receive mercy and help.
Not the throne of humiliation.
Not the throne where struggling believers are mocked for their weakness.
The throne of grace.
There is mercy there.
There is help there.
And there is a Savior whose compassion does not depend on your ability to appear emotionally invincible.
Perhaps you have been hiding your struggle because you believed a good Christian should never feel overwhelmed.
Perhaps you have apologized to God for crying.
Perhaps you have spent years believing that spiritual maturity means never admitting how deeply something hurts.
But Scripture gives us the Psalms.
It gives us David crying out in distress.
It gives us Elijah, exhausted and despairing under a broom tree in 1 Kings 19.
And notice how God dealt with Elijah.
He did not begin by delivering a lecture about how embarrassing Elijah's exhaustion was.
The Lord provided food, water, and rest before continuing to address him.
That does not mean Elijah's every thought was correct.
It means God was attentive to the whole person.
Body.
Mind.
Heart.
Calling.
And when we read the story carefully, we discover that God's care was neither shallow indulgence nor cruel condemnation.
It was patient, purposeful, and restorative.
Some of you need to hear this because you have confused seeking help with betraying your faith.

If your anxiety is persistent, overwhelming, or affecting your sleep, relationships, health, or ability to function, speaking with a qualified mental health professional is not automatically a failure to trust God.
Prayer and appropriate medical or psychological care do not have to compete.
A Christian can trust the Lord while receiving treatment, asking for pastoral support, building healthier habits, and allowing other people to help carry burdens.
Galatians 6:2 tells believers to bear one another's burdens.
That instruction would make little sense if every struggling Christian were expected to carry everything alone.
And this brings us to a part of Philippians 4 that is often overlooked.
Paul did not write his words about anxiety into an emotional vacuum.
Just before Philippians 4:6, he urges two believers, Euodias and Syntyche, to be of the same mind in the Lord.
He calls others to help them.
Then he says:
“Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice.”
—Philippians 4:4, KJV
And:
“The Lord is at hand.”
—Philippians 4:5, KJV
Only then does he speak about anxiety.
The surrounding passage is filled with relationships, rejoicing, gentleness, prayer, and the nearness of the Lord.
This is not an isolated command to manufacture a peaceful emotional state through sheer willpower.
It is an invitation to live consciously before the God who is near, within the fellowship of His people.
And then comes the promise.
Not the promise many of us would have preferred.
Something deeper.
Philippians 4:7 says:
“And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.”
The Greek phrase for “the peace of God” is:
ἡ εἰρήνη τοῦ θεοῦ
Hē eirēnē tou theou.
And the verb translated “shall keep” is:
φρουρήσει
Phrourēsei.
It comes from φρουρέω (phroureō), a word used for guarding or keeping watch.
The imagery is striking.
Paul does not merely describe a pleasant feeling.
He describes God's peace as guarding the hearts and minds of believers in Christ Jesus.
Imagine that.
A prisoner writing about peace standing guard.
A man living under confinement speaking of protection that no prison wall could ultimately provide.
Paul does not promise that prayer will immediately remove every threat.
He does not say every bill will be paid tomorrow.
He does not say every medical result will be favorable.
He does not say every relationship will be restored.
And he does not promise that faithful Christians will never experience another episode of anxiety.
He says God's peace will guard their hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.
The center of the promise is not your power to control tomorrow.
It is your relationship with Christ.
And there is an important distinction here.
God's peace is not a guarantee that you will always feel calm.
It is a divine gift that can sustain believers even when circumstances remain uncertain.
Sometimes that peace is deeply felt.
Sometimes a Christian must cling to God's promises through tears without experiencing immediate emotional relief.
That does not make the promise meaningless.
It reminds us that biblical peace is more profound than a momentary sensation.
It is rooted in the God who has reconciled sinners to Himself through Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:1 declares that, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Before we talk about peace from our circumstances, we must talk about peace with God.
Because our deepest problem is not merely that life is frightening.
Our deepest problem is that sin has separated humanity from the holy God who created us.
We have trusted ourselves.
We have loved things more than Him.
We have rebelled against His commands.
We have attempted to build our identities on money, approval, control, relationships, success, and countless other things that cannot bear the weight of our souls.
And none of us can save ourselves by becoming less anxious.
None of us can earn forgiveness by thinking more positively.
None of us can secure eternal life by becoming emotionally disciplined enough.
That is why the Gospel is such astonishing news.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, entered our broken world.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He bore our sins on the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Through repentance and faith in Him, sinners receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
This is not self-help decorated with Bible verses.
This is redemption purchased by the blood of Christ.
And that changes everything.
Because your greatest hope is not that you will eventually become a person who never feels afraid.
Your greatest hope is that you belong to the Savior who conquered sin and death.
There is a difference.
A life without anxiety would be a wonderful relief.
But reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ is an eternal miracle.
And that miracle is available to people whose lives look nothing like the polished testimonies we sometimes see online.
The mother who has not slept properly in weeks.
The father hiding his financial fear from his children.
The student who feels crushed by expectations.
The believer who fell into sin and now wonders whether God will ever receive them again.
The Christian who knows Scripture but struggles to believe that its promises could still include someone like them.
Listen carefully.
If you have sinned, you need repentance, not excuses.
If you are hiding destructive choices, you need to bring them into the light.
If you have been trusting something more than Christ, you need to turn back to Him.
But if you are suffering, do not automatically mistake your suffering for proof that God has rejected you.
And if your life contains both sin that needs repentance and wounds that need care, do not confuse the two.
Jesus is both holy and compassionate.
He does not flatter our rebellion.
And He does not despise the brokenhearted who come to Him.
Remember Peter.
The disciple who promised loyalty and then denied Jesus three times.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine hearing the rooster crow.
Imagine remembering the warning.
Imagine knowing that when the moment came to stand beside the Lord, fear overcame your courage.
Peter's failure was real.
It was not harmless.
It was not something to excuse.
But it was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and recommissioned him to care for His sheep, as John 21 records.
What Peter could not undo, Christ was able to redeem.
That is the heartbeat of our message.
Not because sin is unimportant.
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because every earthly story ends the way we hoped.
But because the risen Christ can forgive sinners, restore the fallen, transform hearts, and give a future that shame could never manufacture.
And perhaps your scandal is not something the world knows about.
Perhaps it is the private collapse behind your public smile.
Perhaps you have built an entire image of spiritual strength while quietly falling apart.
You lead worship, but you are exhausted.
You encourage everyone else, but you are struggling to find hope for yourself.
You post Bible verses, but sometimes your own heart feels miles away from the comfort you share.
And you are afraid that if people discover how much you are struggling, they will question whether your faith is real.
Dear brother.
Dear sister.
You do not need to build a false testimony to glorify a truthful Savior.
There is no glory in pretending that grace was unnecessary.
The beauty of the Gospel is not that Jesus only welcomes people who already have everything together.
It is that He saves sinners who cannot rescue themselves.
And His work of sanctification continues throughout the Christian life.
That does not make spiritual growth optional.
It makes spiritual growth dependent on grace rather than religious performance.
Now go back to Philippians 4:6.
Read it again.
“Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.”
Notice what Paul includes.
Thanksgiving.
That word can feel almost offensive when life is falling apart.
How do you give thanks when you are grieving?
How do you thank God when the answer has not come?
How do you express gratitude when the future looks terrifying?
The answer is not to pretend that pain is good.
The answer is to remember that God remains good even while pain is real.
Thanksgiving is not denial.
It is remembrance.
It is saying, “Father, I do not understand this season, but I remember Your mercy.”
It is saying, “Lord, I cannot see tomorrow, but I remember the cross.”
It is saying, “Jesus, I am afraid of what may happen, but I thank You that death itself could not defeat You.”
Christian gratitude does not require us to celebrate evil, injustice, sickness, or suffering as though they were inherently beautiful.
It calls us to recognize the faithfulness of God even in a world where those things exist.
And sometimes, thanksgiving begins with the smallest honest sentence.
“Lord, thank You that I can still call on You.”
That may not sound impressive.
But there is something beautiful about a trembling believer turning toward God rather than running away from Him.
And if you are reading this while feeling spiritually exhausted, I want to speak directly to you.
You may have believed that God was waiting for you to stop struggling before He would draw near.
But the Gospel announces that Jesus came to save people who could never make themselves righteous.
You may have believed that the measure of your faith was how little fear you experienced.
But faith is not measured simply by the absence of difficult emotions.
Faith looks to Christ.
Faith receives His Word.
Faith learns to obey.
Faith repents when it sins.
Faith continues to seek Him, even when the heart feels weak.
Sometimes faith sounds like a triumphant declaration.
Sometimes it sounds like the father in Mark 9:24:
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”
What a painfully human prayer.
Belief.
Struggle.
Dependence.
All in one sentence.
And Jesus did not turn the desperate father away for admitting his need.
Perhaps that is the prayer you need tonight.
Not a performance.
Not another promise that you will never feel afraid again.
Just honesty before the Lord.
“Jesus, I believe. Help me where I struggle.”
And perhaps tomorrow, when the worry returns, you will need to pray again.
That does not mean yesterday's prayer was worthless.
Prayer is not a spiritual transaction where one perfect request purchases a lifetime without distress.
It is communion with the living God.
A relationship in which we repeatedly come before our Father with our needs.
Jesus taught His disciples to ask for daily bread.
Daily.
Not a lifetime supply of visible guarantees.
Daily dependence.
And that is especially important for those who have quietly condemned themselves because their anxiety did not disappear after one prayer.
Philippians 4:6–7 should never be used as a weapon to humiliate a suffering believer.
But neither should it be reduced to a comforting slogan that asks nothing of us.
It calls us to pray.
To give thanks.
To bring our needs before God.
To entrust ourselves to Him.

And the next verses continue the call to spiritual discipline, directing our thoughts toward what is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, and worthy of praise, and urging believers to practice what they have learned.
Christian peace is not cultivated through denial.
It is nurtured as we return to truth and walk with the God of peace.
There may be practical steps you need to take.
You may need to ask someone for forgiveness.
You may need to stop feeding a destructive habit.
You may need to speak with a doctor or counselor.
You may need to tell a trusted believer that you have been struggling.
You may need to rest.
You may need to make a difficult decision.
You may need to stop carrying a responsibility God never assigned to you.
And through all of it, you can pray.
Not because prayer guarantees that every outcome will match your preferences.
But because the God who hears you is worthy of your trust.
There is something else I want you to remember.
The Lord's nearness is not dependent on your ability to feel it.
Some nights will still be hard.
Some prayers will be interrupted by tears.
Some fears will need to be confronted repeatedly.
And some seasons of healing will require patience, treatment, support, and time.
But Christ has not ceased to be Lord simply because you are having a difficult night.
He is not less faithful because you are struggling to feel hopeful.
And His resurrection has not become less true because your mind is tired.
If you are in Christ, your identity is not “the anxious one.”
It is not “the failure.”
It is not “the person who should have been stronger.”
You are someone called to belong to Jesus, to repent of sin, to grow in holiness, and to live by His grace.
Your struggle may be part of your story.
It does not have to be the final word over your life.
And this is where the message becomes bigger than your own healing.
Because somewhere on your Facebook friends list, there may be someone who desperately needs to hear this.
Someone who has stopped attending church because they are ashamed of their mental health struggles.
Someone who believes Jesus is disappointed in them because they cannot stop worrying.
Someone who is carrying a burden they have never told anyone about.
Someone who thinks their tears disqualify them from being loved by God.
Not merely because it may reach more people.
But because the person who needs it most might never ask you for help.
They might never comment publicly.
They might never tell you what they are facing.
They might simply read these words alone, in a quiet room, and realize that they can bring their suffering honestly before Jesus.
You can write “Lord, help me trust You” if that is your prayer today.
You can write “I'm still fighting” if you are weary but still seeking Christ.
Or, if God has carried you through a season of fear, share a testimony of His faithfulness.
You do not need to reveal private details or expose wounds you are not ready to discuss.
But your honest words may help another believer realize they are not alone.
We were never meant to make the Christian journey alone.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a platform around human personalities.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to promise instant healing or effortless discipleship.
But to continually point people toward Jesus Christ, the authority of Scripture, repentance, forgiveness, spiritual maturity, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
Our desire is to reach people who are hurting, believers who are drifting, Christians who need deeper biblical understanding, and seekers who have never truly understood the good news of salvation.
If this ministry has helped you grow, please consider following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, fellow believers, and even those who are still searching for truth to follow as well.
These resources are intended to help believers go deeper in Scripture, develop a stronger understanding of their faith, and continue growing in their walk with Jesus Christ.

It is a voluntary way of helping sustain the work of creating biblical teaching, sharing Gospel-centered encouragement, developing discipleship resources, and reaching more people with the message of Christ.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and not compelled.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not out of guilt.
Not out of fear.
Not because your love for Jesus can be measured by a monthly payment.
These items are simply practical expressions of appreciation and ways to share faith-centered messages. They are not spiritual rewards or measures of anyone's devotion to Christ.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
We want people to come to Jesus, not feel pressured to prove their faith through financial support.
Because the Gospel is free to receive, even though our redemption cost our Savior His life.
And that is where I want to bring you back before we finish.
Not to a Facebook page.
Not even to your anxiety.
But to Jesus.
The One who entered Gethsemane.
The One who endured the cross.
The One who rose victorious from the grave.
The One who invites the weary and burdened to come to Him.
Perhaps you have been so focused on finding relief from anxiety that you have forgotten the deeper invitation of the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely offer you a better way to manage your thoughts.
He calls you to Himself.
To repent.
To believe.
To follow.
To surrender your life to the One who gave His life for sinners.
And if you already belong to Him, He calls you to keep coming.
Not because you have earned His attention.
But because you are dependent on His grace.
Tonight, you may still have questions.
The bills may still be waiting.
The diagnosis may still be uncertain.
The relationship may still be broken.
The difficult conversation may still need to happen.
And your heart may still feel afraid.
But you can bring all of that to the Father through Jesus Christ.
You can pray with thanksgiving.
You can ask for wisdom.
You can seek help.
You can take the next faithful step.
You can remember that God's promises do not become false when life becomes difficult.
And you can trust that the Lord who began a good work in His people is faithful to carry His saving purpose forward, as Philippians 1:6 reminds us.
So when someone quotes Philippians 4:6 to you again, remember the whole passage.
Remember the imprisoned apostle.
Remember the invitation to prayer.
Remember the thanksgiving that refuses to forget God's goodness.
Remember the peace that guards hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.
And above all, remember the Savior who makes that peace possible.
If you need a prayer tonight, let it be this:

“Father, I come to You in the name of Jesus Christ. You know what I am carrying, what I am afraid to say aloud, and what I cannot fix by myself. Forgive my sins. Teach me to repent wherever I have turned away from You. Help me trust Your character when I cannot understand my circumstances. Give me wisdom to take the steps I need to take, humility to receive help, and courage to walk in obedience. Guard my heart and mind in Christ Jesus. And when I feel weak, remind me that my hope rests not in my strength, but in my risen Savior. In Jesus' name, amen.”
And if you remember only one thing from everything you have read, remember this:
Philippians 4:6 is not telling you that you must become fearless before you can come to God. It is calling you to bring every fear into the presence of the God who hears you.
The invitation is not to stop being human.
It is to learn dependence on the Lord.
You may not know what tomorrow holds.
But the cross and the empty tomb tell you who Jesus is.
And that is a truth worth holding onto when every other certainty seems to be slipping away.
Your trembling hands can still reach toward the Savior whose nail-scarred hands will never lose their power to save.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE FORBIDS A FATHER FROM SLEEPING WITH HIS SON’S WIFE—AND THE REASON BEHIND THIS COMMANDMENT EXPOSES A DARK REALITY ABOUT ANCIENT FAMILIES
paragraphs: THE BIBLE FORBIDS A FATHER FROM SLEEPING WITH HIS SON’S WIFE—AND THE REASON BEHIND THIS COMMANDMENT EXPOSES A DARK REALITY ABOUT ANCIENT FAMILIES

Leviticus 18:15 reveals something disturbing about sexual sin, family betrayal, and the abuse of power. But behind this ancient prohibition is a truth that reaches into our homes today: God sees what happens behind closed doors, and Jesus Christ came to redeem what sin has destroyed.
There are Bible verses that comfort you.
There are Bible verses that strengthen you.
And then there are verses that make you stop reading, stare at the page, and whisper...
“Wait. Why would God even need to say that?”
Leviticus 18:15 is one of them.
Imagine a young woman living in an ancient household.

She has left the home where she grew up. She has married into another family. Her future, her security, her reputation, and perhaps even her daily survival are closely connected to the household she has entered.
Her husband has a father.
A man whose age, position, wealth, and authority may command considerable respect.
A man everyone expects her to honor.
A man who should be helping protect the family.
But what happens when the person who is supposed to provide security becomes the person who threatens it?
What happens when family authority becomes a weapon?
What happens when the person everyone respects is the person nobody dares to confront?
And what happens when the victim is pressured to remain silent because exposing the truth might bring shame upon the entire household?
Thousands of years ago, God spoke a command that still confronts these questions.
“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy daughter in law: she is thy son's wife; thou shalt not uncover her nakedness.” — Leviticus 18:15, KJV
Read that again.
God did not leave the boundary to family tradition.
He did not leave it to the judgment of the oldest man in the house.
He did not suggest that authority, seniority, or family status could make such a relationship acceptable.
He prohibited it.
And when we examine the original Hebrew, the historical setting, and the wider testimony of Scripture, we discover something far more significant than an unusual ancient rule.
We discover a God who establishes moral boundaries even for people who hold authority.
But there is something important we must understand before going further.
The existence of this command does not prove that every ancient household was filled with sexual exploitation. Scripture does not tell us how frequently this particular offense occurred.
What it does establish is that God explicitly prohibited a sexual relationship between a man and his daughter-in-law.
And the fact that Scripture addresses such relationships should make us consider how deeply sin can invade even the places we call family.
Because sometimes the most dangerous betrayal does not come from a stranger.
Sometimes it comes from someone who knows exactly how much you trust them.
The original Hebrew of Leviticus 18:15 reads:
עֶרְוַת כַּלָּתְךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה אֵשֶׁת בִּנְךָ הִוא לֹא תְגַלֶּה עֶרְוָתָהּ
ʿErwat kallātekhā lōʾ tegallēh; ʾēshet binkhā hīʾ; lōʾ tegalleh ʿerwātāh.
A close English rendering is:
“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your daughter-in-law; she is your son's wife; you shall not uncover her nakedness.”
The expression עֶרְוָה (ʿervāh) means “nakedness,” while גָּלָה (gālāh) means “to uncover” or “to reveal.”
In the legal context of Leviticus 18, the expression “uncover nakedness” is a Hebrew idiom referring to prohibited sexual relations.
This is not merely a command about accidentally seeing someone without clothing.
It concerns a sexual boundary.
And notice how the verse identifies the woman.
“She is your son's wife.”
That relationship matters.
The prohibition is not based on whether the father-in-law feels affection for her, whether she is considered attractive, or whether the family could conceal what happened.
Her place within the family establishes a boundary that must not be crossed.
God does not permit a man to turn his son's marriage into an opportunity for sexual gratification.
But to understand why this command mattered in its ancient setting, we must enter a world very different from our own.
In ancient Israel and its surrounding societies, families often functioned as extended households rather than the smaller, independent households common in many places today.
Land, inheritance, agricultural labor, marriage arrangements, and family identity were deeply interconnected.
Households could include several generations and relatives living together or in close proximity.
Marriage frequently involved much more than two individuals beginning a private life together.
It connected families, property, responsibilities, and future generations.
In many households, senior men exercised considerable social and economic authority.
This did not mean every father-in-law was abusive. Nor does it mean ancient women possessed no agency or influence. The historical reality was more varied than that.
But it does mean that some women, particularly those with limited economic independence, could be vulnerable when family power was misused.
And this is where Leviticus 18:15 becomes especially sobering.
The man addressed by the command could not appeal to his family position to justify sexual access to his son's wife.
The relationship was forbidden.
No amount of household influence could make it righteous.
No private agreement could erase the boundary established in the law.
No family reputation could transform the prohibited relationship into something holy.
And no one should mistake silence for innocence.
Because the fact that wrongdoing remains hidden does not mean God approves of it.
Perhaps you are wondering whether the Bible contains an actual account involving this kind of relationship.
It does.
And the story is painfully complicated.
In Genesis 38, we meet Judah and Tamar.
Tamar was married to Judah's son Er.
After Er died, Judah's second son, Onan, was expected to fulfill a family obligation connected with preserving his deceased brother's line. Onan acted selfishly and was judged by God.
Judah then instructed Tamar to remain a widow in her father's house until his younger son, Shelah, grew older.
But time passed.
Shelah grew up.
And Judah did not give him to Tamar as promised.
Consider what this meant for her.
She was a widow.
Her expected future had been delayed.
The man who held influence over the family's decision had failed to fulfill his promise.
Her circumstances were shaped by decisions she could not simply reverse.
Then the story takes a shocking turn.
Tamar disguised herself and positioned herself where Judah would encounter her.
Judah, not recognizing her, approached her for sexual relations.
Later, when Tamar's pregnancy became known, Judah was told what had happened.
And the man who had participated in sexual wrongdoing initially demanded severe judgment against her.
Do you see the hypocrisy?
The same man who had been involved in the act was ready to condemn the woman.
But Tamar had kept the personal items Judah had given her as a pledge.
When those items were presented, the truth could no longer remain hidden.
Judah recognized them.
And Genesis 38:26 records his confession:
“She hath been more righteous than I; because that I gave her not to Shelah my son.” — KJV
Those words matter.
Judah acknowledged his failure toward Tamar.
He did not simply continue pretending that the entire blame belonged to her.
And the account adds that he did not have sexual relations with her again.
We must read this story carefully.
Genesis 38 describes events in the patriarchal period, long before the giving of the Levitical law at Sinai.
The narrative does not present Judah and Tamar's sexual encounter as an example for believers to imitate.
Nor does Judah's confession mean that every aspect of Tamar's strategy is being held up as a universal moral model.
The passage exposes Judah's wrongdoing, his broken promise, and his hypocritical judgment.
It also reveals how vulnerable someone can become when a powerful family member refuses to fulfill his responsibilities.
And here is something extraordinary.
Tamar later appears in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Matthew 1:3 names her.
Pause there.
The woman whose story includes widowhood, family failure, sexual scandal, and public accusation is named in the earthly family line through which the Messiah came.
God did not erase her from the record because her story was uncomfortable.
Her name remained.
Her story remained.
And centuries later, the Gospel of Matthew placed her within the genealogy leading to Jesus.
That does not mean God approved of every decision made in Genesis 38.
It means human sin and family failure could not ultimately defeat God's redemptive purpose.
The scandal was real. But it did not have the final word.
And that brings us to another disturbing biblical account.
Reuben.
The firstborn son of Jacob.
Genesis 35:22 tells us that Reuben had sexual relations with Bilhah, his father's concubine.
This was not the same relationship described in Leviticus 18:15. Bilhah was Reuben's father's concubine, not his daughter-in-law.
But the incident demonstrates another violation of sexual boundaries within a family.
The account is brief.
Yet its consequences echo years later.
When Jacob addressed his sons before his death, he confronted Reuben's behavior.
Genesis 49:4 declares:
“Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel; because thou wentest up to thy father's bed; then defiledst thou it.” — KJV
Reuben's position as firstborn did not protect him from accountability.
His family status did not make the wrongdoing disappear.
His actions had consequences.
And the Bible refused to conceal the failure simply because it involved one of Israel's founding families.
This is one reason Scripture can be so unsettling.
It does not present its human characters as spotless heroes.
It records betrayal.
Lust.
Deception.
Hypocrisy.
Abuse of privilege.
And the devastating consequences of sin.
Even within families that played important roles in the history of God's people.
Because the Bible is not primarily a collection of stories about how wonderful human beings are.
It is the revelation of a holy God dealing with fallen humanity.
And fallen humanity does not become righteous merely by having a respected family name.
Now consider the larger setting of Leviticus 18.
The chapter begins with God speaking to Israel after their deliverance from Egypt.
In Leviticus 18:3, the Lord warns them not to follow the practices of Egypt, where they had lived, or the practices of Canaan, where they were going.
Israel was not being invited to determine morality solely by observing the surrounding cultures.
They were being called to live according to God's commands.
The chapter then sets out prohibited sexual relationships involving close relatives and other forbidden acts.
These commands were part of Israel's covenant law and its distinctive calling to holiness.
Some readers assume the chapter is merely a collection of ancient social taboos.
But the repeated divine declaration gives the chapter its theological weight.
“I am the LORD.”
In Hebrew:
אֲנִי יְהוָה
ʾAnī YHWH.
“I am the LORD.”
The command rests upon the authority of the covenant God.
The message is not that the strongest person in the household gets to decide what is acceptable.
The message is that human relationships are accountable to God's moral authority.
And this remains a profoundly important truth.
Because there are people who know how to quote Scripture but do not know how to treat others with holiness.
There are people who demand respect while refusing accountability.
There are people who use family loyalty to protect themselves from exposure.
And there are people who mistake being the head of a household for having permission to control everyone inside it.
But biblical authority is never a license for sexual exploitation.
A father's role does not make him the owner of his children's bodies.
A father-in-law's status does not give him sexual rights over his son's wife.
A religious title does not give anyone permission to violate another person.
And the responsibility to honor family members must never be twisted into a command to submit to abuse.
That is not holiness.
That is the corruption of authority.
Yet we must also be careful not to claim more than the biblical text says.
Leviticus 18:15 specifically prohibits the sexual relationship between a man and his daughter-in-law.
It does not provide a historical survey showing how often the offense occurred.
It does not explain every motive that might lead someone to commit it.
And it does not give us permission to assume every ancient family was dangerous.
What the verse does give us is a clear moral boundary.
And when we consider that boundary alongside the rest of Scripture, we see a consistent concern for faithfulness, righteousness, and the rejection of sexual wrongdoing.
But there is another question.
What happens when the damage has already been done?
What happens when someone has been betrayed by a person they were taught to trust?
What happens when the person responsible has died, denied everything, or never faced earthly consequences?
What happens when the family insists that forgiveness means never speaking about the wrongdoing again?
And what happens when the wounded person begins to wonder whether God sees them at all?
This is where we must speak with great care.
If you have experienced sexual abuse, coercion, or exploitation, the wrongdoing committed against you is not your sin.
You are not spiritually contaminated because someone violated you.
You do not have to carry another person's guilt as though it were your own.
And you do not have to remain in danger to prove that you are forgiving.
God's call to forgiveness does not require pretending that evil was good.
It does not erase the need for protection, accountability, or lawful justice.
It does not require immediate reconciliation with someone who remains dangerous or unrepentant.
And it certainly does not require silence.
Psalm 34:18 declares:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.” — KJV
Notice what the verse does not say.
It does not say the Lord is near only to people whose families are respectable.
It does not say He is near only to those whose past contains no scandal.
It does not say He is near only to those who can explain their pain without trembling.
It says He is near to the brokenhearted.
Maybe that is you.
Maybe you have carried a story that nobody in your family wants discussed.
Maybe you have spent years smiling in photographs beside people who know exactly what happened.
Maybe you have been told to move on while the person who wounded you continues living as though nothing occurred.
Or perhaps your struggle is different.
Perhaps you were not the one harmed.
Perhaps you are the one who crossed a boundary.
Perhaps you betrayed your marriage.
Perhaps you abused someone's trust.
Perhaps you used influence, secrecy, or manipulation to pursue something you knew was wrong.
And now you are reading these words with a heaviness you cannot explain.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not give you permission to minimize your sin.
But it does offer a Savior who calls sinners to repentance.
Real repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed because someone discovered the truth.
It is not crying until the consequences disappear.
It is not demanding forgiveness from the person you harmed.
It is not using the name of Jesus to escape responsibility.
The Greek word commonly translated “repent” in the New Testament is μετανοέω (metanoeō), expressing the idea of repenting or changing one's mind.
In the biblical call to repentance, that change is not merely intellectual. It involves turning from sin toward God, with a transformed life bearing appropriate fruit.
John the Baptist said:
“Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.” — Matthew 3:8, KJV
Repentance has consequences for how a person lives.
It calls for truthfulness.
It calls for abandoning wrongdoing.
It calls for accepting accountability.
Where harm has been done, it calls for taking responsibility rather than manipulating the wounded person into offering quick reassurance.
And where a crime has been committed, spiritual language must not be used to obstruct justice.
Because Jesus did not come to make darkness more comfortable.
He came as the light of the world.
John 8:12 records His words:
“I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.” — KJV
Light reveals.
Light exposes.
Light guides.
And sometimes the first mercy of God is that He refuses to let us remain comfortably hidden in the darkness that is destroying us.
But exposure alone cannot save us.
We need something greater.
We need redemption.
And this is where the entire story turns toward Jesus Christ.
Think about His genealogy again.
Judah.
Tamar.
The complicated history of a family marked by failure.
And yet Matthew begins his Gospel by tracing the lineage of Jesus through real human generations.
Not imaginary saints.
Not people with perfect histories.
Real people.
People whose stories included faith, weakness, wrongdoing, grief, and consequences.
Then, in Matthew 1:21, the angel explains the mission of the child Mary will bear:
“Thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.” — KJV
Not merely from embarrassment.
Not merely from a damaged reputation.
Not merely from the discomfort of being exposed.
From their sins.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, entered a fallen world.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He willingly gave His life on the cross.
He bore the judgment of sin.
And He rose from the dead.
Through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who repent and believe.
This is not a promise that every earthly consequence disappears.
It is not a guarantee that every damaged family relationship will be restored in this life.
It is not permission for offenders to demand access to the people they have harmed.
It is something deeper.
Through Jesus Christ, sin does not have to remain your master, and the evil done against you does not have to define your worth.
The cross tells us that sin is serious enough to require the death of the Savior.
The resurrection tells us that death and darkness do not have the final victory.
And grace tells us that God is able to transform people who could never save themselves.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” — 2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
The Greek expression καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis) means “new creation.”
Not merely a person who has learned to manage appearances.
Not merely someone who has become better at hiding shame.
A new creation.
This transformation begins in union with Christ.
It unfolds through a life of faith, repentance, obedience, and dependence upon the Holy Spirit.
It does not mean believers instantly become incapable of sin.
It means their identity and direction are fundamentally changed by God's saving grace.
And perhaps that is the truth someone reading this desperately needs.
Your family history may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have to determine your eternal destiny.
Your past may contain things you cannot undo.
It does not place you beyond the reach of Christ's mercy when you turn to Him.
Your pain may still be real.
Your healing may take time.
Your journey may require wise counsel, trusted support, and protection from people who remain unsafe.
But none of those realities makes the promises of God meaningless.
And none of them makes you invisible to Him.
Remember the woman in the opening of this article?
The woman entering a household where someone powerful might misuse his position?
We do not know her name because she was an imagined picture of a real vulnerability in the ancient world.
But the moral boundary in Leviticus 18:15 was not imaginary.
God spoke.
The prohibition was clear.
And that ancient command still reminds us that no household should become a place where sexual wrongdoing is defended by appeals to authority.
Yet the Gospel takes us beyond the prohibition.
The law exposes sin.
Christ offers salvation.
The law identifies boundaries that must not be violated.
Christ transforms hearts so that holiness becomes more than outward compliance.
And the grace of God teaches us not to celebrate what Jesus came to redeem us from.
Titus 2:11–12 reminds us that God's saving grace teaches believers to reject ungodliness and live in righteousness.
Grace is not permission to continue destroying lives.
Grace trains us to live differently.
That is why the message of Gospel Warrior is not simply about exposing scandals.
It is about pointing wounded people, convicted sinners, struggling believers, and searching souls to the One who can truly save.
From Scandal to Grace. Because Jesus Rewrites Everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by erasing justice.
Not by calling evil good.
But by bringing truth into darkness, mercy to the repentant, dignity to the wounded, and new life through the finished work of Jesus Christ.
And before you leave this article, I want to ask you something personal.
What if the person who most needs to read this is afraid to admit it?
What if someone in your family has spent years believing that God does not care about what happened behind closed doors?
What if someone you know has been confusing forgiveness with silence?
What if someone is secretly trapped in sin and needs to hear that genuine repentance is possible?
If this message has touched something personal, you do not need to reveal private details publicly.
You do not have to explain your story to strangers to be worthy of prayer.
And if this article challenged your understanding of Scripture, tell us what stood out to you.
Was it the Hebrew meaning of the command?
The story of Judah and Tamar?
The distinction between forgiveness and accountability?
Or the realization that Jesus' genealogy includes people whose histories were far from perfect?
And if someone came to mind while you were reading, consider sharing this article directly with them.
Someone who would never search for Leviticus 18:15 might encounter the Gospel because you shared it.
Someone struggling with shame might be reminded of the mercy of Christ.
Someone who has misunderstood biblical forgiveness might discover that grace and accountability belong together.
And someone who has never seriously considered Jesus might begin asking the questions that lead them toward Him.
Return to it when you study Leviticus, Genesis 38, or the genealogy of Christ.
Keep it for those moments when you need to remember that biblical holiness is not about protecting appearances.
It is about belonging to the Lord.
And if you are not yet following Gospel Warrior, I invite you to join us.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have drifted from the faith, and even those who are still searching for truth.
We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, questions are welcomed, sin is not excused, and the grace of Jesus Christ is never treated as something cheap.
There is also something I want you to know about the work happening behind these articles.
Gospel Warrior is more than a page that publishes Christian reflections.
We are working to build a growing library of biblical nourishment and discipleship resources for people who genuinely want to know Jesus Christ more deeply.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, strengthen their faith, deepen their understanding of the Gospel, and continue growing in Christ beyond a single article.
And we want to keep expanding that work.
More resources.
More biblical teaching.
More opportunities to reach people who are hungry for truth.
More encouragement for believers who are trying to remain faithful in a world full of distractions.
But ministry work also involves practical expenses, time, and resources.
Not because you can purchase God's favor.
You cannot.
And not because your financial contribution replaces your responsibility to support your local church or care for your household.
It should not.
But because voluntary generosity can be one meaningful way of participating in the work of sharing the Gospel.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
A willing heart.

In the Old Testament, tithes and offerings had particular roles within Israel's covenant worship and communal life. Christians differ in their understanding of how Old Testament tithing applies under the new covenant.
But it can certainly be an expression of voluntary Christian generosity and partnership in Gospel-centered work.
These products are not the reason we proclaim Christ.
They are simply another way to encourage faith-centered learning and everyday reminders of biblical truth.
The deeper purpose is discipleship.
The deeper purpose is helping people open their Bibles.
The deeper purpose is helping people move from merely recognizing the name of Jesus to genuinely following Him.

And if this ministry has helped you understand a difficult passage, challenged you to repent, strengthened your faith, or reminded you of God's grace, I invite you to consider helping make that same encouragement available to others.
You are welcome here.
The free biblical resources are for you too.
Your prayers matter.
Your thoughtful comments matter.
Your willingness to share sound biblical teaching matters.
And above all, your relationship with Jesus Christ matters infinitely more than any financial contribution you could make.
Because the Gospel is not for sale.
The blood of Jesus cannot be purchased.
And grace is not a product reserved for people who can afford a monthly payment.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.” — Ephesians 2:8, KJV
A gift.
Not a transaction.
Not something earned by giving enough money.
A gift received through faith in Jesus Christ.
And that brings us back to the ancient command that began this entire conversation.
Leviticus 18:15.
A father.
A daughter-in-law.
A boundary that must not be crossed.
A God who refuses to let human authority redefine righteousness.

But now, after walking through the Hebrew text, the ancient household, the failures of Judah, the consequences of Reuben's sin, and the redeeming work of Jesus Christ, perhaps you can see why this verse matters far beyond its immediate subject.
It reminds us that God's Word reaches into places people would rather keep hidden.
It confronts wrongdoing even when it happens inside respected families.
It refuses to excuse sexual sin simply because the offender holds authority.
And when read in the light of the whole Bible, it leads us toward the deeper human need that only Christ can ultimately answer.
We need forgiveness.
We need holiness.
We need hearts transformed by grace.
We need the courage to tell the truth.
We need the humility to repent.
We need the wisdom to protect the vulnerable.
And we need a Savior who is greater than our worst failures and deeper than our most painful wounds.
Maybe tonight you will close this article and return to a family that loves you.
Thank God for that.
Maybe you will return to a home where relationships are strained and conversations are difficult.
Ask God for wisdom.
Maybe you will remember someone who betrayed your trust.
Seek the support and protection you need, and remember that healing does not require pretending the harm was acceptable.
Maybe you will remember something you did that still troubles your conscience.
Do not run from the truth.
Run to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
Because the same Savior who confronted sin also welcomed repentant sinners.
The same Savior who exposed hypocrisy also extended mercy.
The same Savior who died upon the cross rose again in victory.
And He is still calling people out of darkness into His marvelous light.
Am I protecting the appearance of righteousness, or am I truly surrendering my life to Jesus Christ?
There is a difference.
And eternity is too important to ignore it.
May our homes be places of truth rather than secrecy.
May our relationships reflect holiness rather than exploitation.
May our churches protect the vulnerable rather than the reputation of the powerful.
May those who have sinned find the courage to repent.
May those who have been wounded receive compassion, safety, and the support they need.
And may everything we teach, write, share, and support lead people not toward admiration of a ministry, but toward worship of the Lord Jesus Christ.
Because one day, the applause will fade.
The products will wear out.
The articles will stop circulating.
But the Word of the Lord will endure forever.
And the only Savior who can reconcile us to God will still be Jesus Christ.
The deepest tragedy is not that God knows the darkness we tried to hide—it is that we could spend our whole lives hiding from the very Savior who came to bring us into His light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU SAY YOU LOVE JESUS… BUT WHAT IF THE PERSON YOU REFUSE TO FORGIVE IS REVEALING SOMETHING ABOUT YOUR HEART?
paragraphs: YOU SAY YOU LOVE JESUS… BUT WHAT IF THE PERSON YOU REFUSE TO FORGIVE IS REVEALING SOMETHING ABOUT YOUR HEART?

The wound was real. The betrayal was unforgivable in your eyes. But what happens when the Savior who forgave your sins asks you to release the person who sinned against you? This is the uncomfortable truth about forgiveness, grace, justice, and the dangerous difference between loving Jesus with your lips and surrendering your heart to Him.
There is someone whose name can still change the atmosphere inside your chest.
You could be having a perfectly good day.
Laughing. Working. Praying. Worshiping.
Then someone mentions that name.
And suddenly, you're back there.
Back in the conversation that destroyed your trust.
Back in the room where someone made you feel worthless.
Back in the season when you cried yourself to sleep, wondering how someone who claimed to love you could hurt you so deeply.
Maybe it was your father.
Maybe it was your mother.
Maybe it was the spouse who promised forever and then chose someone else.
Maybe it was the friend who knew your deepest secrets and used them against you.
Or maybe, and this is especially painful, it was someone inside the church.
Someone who quoted Scripture.
Someone who lifted their hands during worship.
Someone who called you brother or sister while quietly destroying your reputation.
And now?
You still believe in Jesus.
You still pray.
You still listen to worship music.
You still say, "Lord, I love You."
But there is one sentence you cannot bring yourself to say.
"Lord, I forgive them."
Not because you don't know what the Bible says.
You know.
You've heard the sermons.
You've read the verses.
You've probably even encouraged someone else to forgive.
But they don't know what happened to you.
They didn't hear what was said.
They didn't see what was done.
They weren't there when your entire world collapsed.
And somewhere inside, a question has been quietly growing.
Can I truly love Jesus while deliberately refusing to forgive someone who hurt me?
Before you answer, there's something you need to understand.
Jesus is not asking you to pretend that your wound never happened.
But He is asking you to consider what your refusal to forgive is doing to your heart.
And the answer may be more uncomfortable than you expect.
Because sometimes the greatest spiritual battle isn't against the person who wounded us.
It's against the bitterness that wants to become our permanent home.
And Jesus loves us too much to leave us there.
Think about Peter.
One day, he approached Jesus with what probably sounded like a generous question.
"Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?"
Jesus answered:
"I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven."
— Matthew 18:21–22, KJV
Peter thought seven times was generous.
Jesus shattered the calculation.
In the Greek text, Matthew 18:22 uses the expression ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά (heōs hebdomēkontakis hepta).
It is traditionally rendered "seventy times seven," although the Greek expression can also be understood as "seventy-seven times," echoing the language of Genesis 4:24 in the Greek Old Testament.
But the point is not whether you stop at seventy-seven or four hundred ninety.
Jesus was not giving Peter a forgiveness calculator.
He was confronting the human desire to establish a limit beyond which mercy no longer applies.
And then Jesus told a story.
A king wanted to settle accounts with his servants.
One servant owed him ten thousand talents.
An enormous debt.
So enormous that the amount functions in the parable as an almost unimaginable financial obligation.
The servant couldn't pay.
Judgment was approaching.
He fell down and begged for patience.
But the king did something extraordinary.
He didn't merely extend the deadline.
He forgave the debt.
All of it.
The Greek of Matthew 18:27 says:
καὶ τὸ δάνειον ἀφῆκεν αὐτῷ
And he forgave him the debt.
That verb, ἀφῆκεν (aphēken), comes from aphiēmi, a word that can mean to release, let go, remit, or forgive, depending on context.
The servant walked away owing nothing.
Imagine that.
A debt he could never repay.
A future he thought was destroyed.
A judgment he could not escape.
And suddenly, mercy.
But then something disturbing happened.
That same servant found another servant who owed him one hundred denarii.
A real debt.
Not imaginary.
Not meaningless.
One hundred denarii represented a significant sum, commonly understood as approximately one hundred days of ordinary labor.
The second servant begged for patience.
Almost the same plea the first servant had made before the king.
But instead of remembering the mercy he had received, the forgiven servant seized the other man and demanded payment.
He refused mercy.
He had received forgiveness beyond calculation, yet withheld forgiveness from someone else.
And when the king discovered what had happened, he confronted him.
"Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?"
— Matthew 18:33, KJV
Read that again.
Not quickly.
Not as a verse you've heard a hundred times.
Read it as though Jesus is speaking to the place in your heart you've been protecting.
Shouldn't the mercy you received have changed the mercy you were willing to give?
Jesus concluded the parable with a severe warning about refusing to forgive from the heart.
This was not a harmless disagreement over personality.
It was a warning about the terrifying contradiction of receiving mercy while becoming merciless.
And here is where the story becomes personal.
We want God to consider the circumstances surrounding our sins.
But we often want Him to ignore the circumstances surrounding the sins committed against us.
When we fall, we say, "Lord, You know my heart."
When someone else falls, we say, "They knew exactly what they were doing."
When we need mercy, we remember grace.
When they need mercy, we remember the evidence.
And sometimes, without realizing it, we begin demanding that God treat us according to the cross while treating our enemies according to our anger.
But the Gospel will not allow us to separate those two things so comfortably.
Jesus taught us to pray:
"And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors."
— Matthew 6:12, KJV
Then He made the warning unmistakable:
"For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses."
— Matthew 6:14–15, KJV
These are difficult words.
Especially when your pain is not theoretical.
Especially when the person who hurt you has never apologized.
Especially when they seem perfectly happy while you're still trying to rebuild what they destroyed.
But we must not soften Jesus' warning until it means nothing.
And we must not twist it into something Jesus never taught.
Forgiveness does not purchase salvation.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by earning God's acceptance through our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Yet the grace that saves us also begins transforming us.
Forgiveness toward others is not the price we pay to make God merciful.
It is one of the fruits of a heart being changed by His mercy.
A persistent, hardened refusal to forgive is therefore spiritually serious.
It is not something to celebrate, defend, or excuse.
But neither should we confuse a wounded believer who is struggling to forgive with someone who has defiantly decided that Jesus has no authority over this part of life.
There is a difference between crying, "Lord, I want to forgive, but I don't know how," and declaring, "Lord, I know what You command, but I refuse."
One is a painful struggle toward obedience.
The other is resistance to the Lord we claim to follow.
And if you are struggling right now, listen carefully.
The fact that forgiveness is difficult does not mean your faith is fake.
It may mean the wound was deep.
It may mean the betrayal was devastating.
It may mean healing will require time, prayer, wise counsel, and repeated acts of surrender.
Jesus knows the difference between a heart that is bleeding and a heart that is deliberately hardening.
He is not indifferent to either.
But He does not abandon the wounded heart.
He invites it to come closer.
And perhaps this is where we need to confront one of the most dangerous misunderstandings in Christian life.
Some people hear the word forgiveness and immediately think it means letting an abuser back into their home.
Returning to a dangerous relationship.
Trusting a person who has repeatedly lied.
Remaining silent about criminal behavior.
Pretending that the past never happened.
Or accepting the same destructive treatment over and over again.
That is not what biblical forgiveness requires.
Forgiveness is not the same as reconciliation.
Forgiveness is not the same as restored trust.
Forgiveness is not the same as removing consequences.
Forgiveness is not the same as declaring someone innocent.
You can forgive someone and still establish firm boundaries.
You can forgive someone and still report abuse to the proper authorities.
You can forgive someone and still refuse to return to an unsafe environment.
You can forgive someone and still acknowledge that rebuilding trust requires genuine repentance, accountability, and changed behavior.
Romans 12:18 says:
"If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men."
Notice those words.
If it be possible.
Scripture recognizes that peace is not always achievable through one person's willingness.
You cannot force someone else to repent.
You cannot make someone trustworthy.
You cannot single-handedly restore a relationship that another person continues to destroy.
And forgiveness does not require you to surrender your safety to prove your spirituality.
In fact, Scripture also teaches that governing authorities have a responsibility to address wrongdoing (Romans 13:1–4).
Mercy and justice are not enemies.
The God who commands forgiveness also loves righteousness.
And that matters because someone reading this has been told that being a good Christian means remaining available to the person who keeps hurting them.
No.
Jesus never commanded you to call evil good.
He calls you to release personal vengeance without surrendering truth, wisdom, or justice.
Romans 12:19 says:
"Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord."
Forgiveness does not mean that evil no longer matters.
It means you refuse to make personal revenge the ruler of your life.
You place judgment into hands more righteous than your own.
And sometimes that surrender happens while tears are still falling.
Now imagine something.
Imagine the person who hurt you never apologizes.
Never acknowledges the damage.
Never tells the truth about what happened.
Never returns what was stolen.
Never admits they were wrong.
Would you still be willing to begin forgiving them?
That question hurts because many of us have attached forgiveness to a future moment that may never arrive.
"I'll forgive them when they admit it."
"I'll forgive them when they suffer like I suffered."
"I'll forgive them when they finally understand what they did."
But what if they never do?
Will your obedience to Jesus remain imprisoned inside another person's unwillingness to repent?
Will their silence decide how long bitterness is allowed to govern your heart?
You cannot control whether they repent.
You cannot control whether they apologize.
You cannot control whether they change.
But by God's grace, you can begin surrendering your claim to personal vengeance.
That does not instantly erase the pain.
It does not guarantee that you will never feel angry again.
It does not mean every memory will stop hurting.
Sometimes forgiveness is a decision you must return to when the wound is remembered.
Not because Christ's command has changed.
But because the human heart often needs to bring the same suffering before Him again and again.
And this is where another Scripture becomes deeply important.
"Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath."
— Ephesians 4:26, KJV
The Bible does not pretend that anger itself is always sinful.
Some anger is a morally appropriate response to genuine evil.
Even Jesus displayed righteous anger.
But anger can become destructive when we nurture it into resentment, revenge, contempt, or hatred.
Paul continues:
"And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption."
— Ephesians 4:30, KJV
Then he writes:
— Ephesians 4:31–32, KJV
In the Greek, the expression for forgiving one another uses χαριζόμενοι (charizomenoi), from charizomai.
It carries the sense of showing grace or freely granting forgiveness.
It is related to χάρις (charis), the Greek word commonly translated as grace.
That connection is beautiful.
Paul does not merely tell Christians to suppress their anger and act pleasant.
He calls them to extend grace because they themselves have received grace in Christ.
And notice the order.
God's forgiveness in Christ becomes the foundation for our forgiveness toward others.
We do not manufacture mercy from an empty heart.
We draw upon the mercy that has already met us in Jesus.
And perhaps the reason this feels impossible is because you've been trying to forgive through your own emotional strength.
You've been waiting until you feel ready.
Waiting until the memories stop hurting.
Waiting until your heart becomes soft enough.
But forgiveness is not always born from a sudden change of feeling.
Sometimes it begins with a trembling prayer.
"Jesus, I cannot do this without You."
And that prayer may be the most honest thing you've said in months.
Because the Gospel is not a story about strong people saving themselves.
It is the story of a Savior who comes for people who cannot rescue their own hearts.
Look at the cross.
Not the polished version we place on walls.
Not the beautiful jewelry we wear around our necks.
Look at what actually happened.
Jesus was betrayed.
Abandoned.
Mocked.
Falsely accused.
Stripped.
Beaten.
Humiliated.
Crucified.
The sinless Son of God suffered at the hands of sinners.
And while He hung upon the cross, Luke records these words:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
— Luke 23:34, KJV
There is a textual detail worth understanding here.

This saying appears in the traditional text of Luke and in many ancient manuscripts, but it is absent from some other early witnesses. For that reason, modern translations sometimes include a textual note.
Christians should be honest about such manuscript questions rather than pretending they do not exist.
Yet the portrait of Jesus extending mercy to enemies is consistent with His teaching and with the wider witness of Scripture.
In the Greek text containing this saying, the prayer begins:
Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς
Pater, aphes autois.
"Father, forgive them."
Consider the weight of that prayer.
Jesus did not say that crucifixion was acceptable.
He did not declare the violence righteous.
He did not deny the evil being committed.
He entrusted Himself to His Father.
And He prayed for mercy.
But we must understand something else.
Jesus' prayer does not mean every person involved was automatically reconciled to God without repentance and faith.
The New Testament still calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
At Pentecost, Peter confronted those implicated in Jesus' death and called them to repentance (Acts 2:36–38).
The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the astonishing mercy of God.
Forgiveness is not God's declaration that sin doesn't matter.
Forgiveness is costly precisely because sin matters.
And nowhere is that cost clearer than at Calvary.
Now here is a question that should humble every one of us.
What if Jesus had treated us according to the standard of mercy we sometimes reserve for others?
What if He said:
"I will forgive you only when you've suffered enough."
"I will forgive you only when you can prove you will never fail again."
"I will forgive you only when your repentance becomes impressive enough to deserve My attention."
Where would we be?
Because the truth is, none of us approached the cross as innocent people.
Romans 3:23 says:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God."
All.
The betrayed and the betrayer.
The wounded and the one who wounded.
The religious and the rebellious.
The person who seems respectable and the person whose sins became public.
That does not mean all sins cause equal harm or deserve identical earthly consequences.
It means every human being needs the mercy of God.
And the ground at the foot of the cross leaves no room for spiritual superiority.
Some of us have never committed the particular sin that wounded us.
But none of us can claim we have never needed forgiveness.
This is why Jesus' parable of the unforgiving servant is so devastating.
The servant did not misunderstand the value of mercy.
He had personally experienced it.
His tragedy was that he wanted mercy to stop with him.
And perhaps this is the question Jesus is placing before us today.
Have you allowed the grace of God to reach your heart without allowing it to change how you treat another human being?
Maybe you've been holding on to hatred because it feels like the last evidence that what happened to you mattered.
If you release the anger, you fear the injustice will disappear.
If you forgive, you fear the offender will win.
If you stop replaying the betrayal, you fear you'll be betraying the younger version of yourself who suffered through it.
But forgiveness does not erase your testimony.
It does not rewrite the facts.
It does not make your suffering insignificant.
The wounds of the risen Christ were not proof that the crucifixion had never happened.
They were evidence that evil had not been given the final word.
And this is the heart of our message.
He does not rewrite history by pretending that sin was harmless.
He rewrites the ending through redemption.
He takes what sin intended for destruction and demonstrates that His grace is greater.
Not every broken relationship will be restored.
Not every offender will repent.
Not every injustice will be resolved in this lifetime.
But in Christ, your suffering does not have to become your identity.
Your bitterness does not have to become your future.
And the person who hurt you does not have to remain the central character in the story of your soul.
Jesus is Lord.
Not your offender.
Not your trauma.
Not your anger.
Jesus.
And if He is truly Lord, then even the most painful rooms of your heart belong to Him.
That does not mean He enters them violently.
It means His Word lovingly confronts what we would rather keep hidden.
Perhaps today, the Holy Spirit is exposing something you've been calling protection when it has slowly become bitterness.
Perhaps you've stopped praying for someone's repentance and started secretly wishing for their destruction.
Perhaps you've been rehearsing imaginary conversations where you finally humiliate the person who humiliated you.
Perhaps you smile in church while quietly hoping someone else will suffer.
And perhaps you've become so accustomed to those thoughts that you no longer recognize what they're doing to your soul.
Hebrews 12:15 warns believers to watch carefully lest a root of bitterness spring up and cause trouble, defiling many.
Bitterness rarely stays confined to one memory.
It can influence how we trust.
How we speak.
How we raise our children.
How we respond to correction.
How we interpret the motives of people who never hurt us.
One person's betrayal can become the lens through which we view everyone else.
And before we know it, we're punishing innocent people for wounds they did not create.
But Jesus offers another way.
Not denial.
Not forced reconciliation.
Not pretending to be healed.
Surrender.
The kind of surrender that says:
"Lord, what they did was wrong."
"Lord, I am still hurting."
"Lord, I need wisdom about boundaries."
"Lord, I want justice to be done."
"But Lord, I do not want hatred to become who I am."
That is not weakness.
That is the beginning of a different kind of courage.
The courage to refuse to become what wounded you.
The courage to tell the truth without surrendering to vengeance.
The courage to obey Christ even while your emotions are still catching up.
And if you cannot yet say, "I have forgiven them," perhaps you can begin by saying, "Jesus, make me willing."
Bring that small, trembling willingness to Him.
Do not manufacture a testimony you do not yet possess.
Do not pretend your healing is complete because other Christians expect you to sound victorious.
God does not need your performance.
He calls you to honesty, repentance, faith, and obedience.
If the pain involves abuse or ongoing danger, seek protection and trustworthy help. A faithful response to Christ never requires hiding abuse or placing yourself or someone else in harm's way.
And if you have been the person who hurt someone else, hear this too.
Do not use this article to demand forgiveness from your victim.
Do not quote Matthew 6 to pressure someone into restoring access to their life.
Do not say, "You're a Christian, so you have to forgive me," while refusing to acknowledge what you've done.
Biblical repentance involves truth.
It involves turning from sin.
It may involve restitution, accountability, accepting consequences, and demonstrating genuine change over time.
You are not entitled to immediate trust simply because you requested forgiveness.
And you cannot use God's grace as permission to continue harming people.
The Gospel humbles the wounded and the offender, though their responsibilities are not identical.
To the wounded, Christ calls for a heart that releases vengeance.
To the offender, Christ calls for repentance.
To both, He offers grace that never makes peace with sin.
And to all who come to Him in faith, He offers something greater than self-improvement.
He offers new life.
Maybe this article has brought a face into your mind.
A name you haven't spoken in years.
A conversation you thought you'd buried.
A hurt you told everyone you were already over.
And maybe you feel resistance rising.
"I don't want to forgive."
Be honest with God about that.
He already knows.
But don't stop there.
Ask Him to change what you cannot change by yourself.
You don't need to feel spiritually impressive.
You need the Savior.
You need the One who died for sinners and rose again.
You need the One who can convict without crushing the repentant.
You need the One whose grace is not an excuse to remain unchanged, but the power that teaches us to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God brings salvation and trains us to turn away from ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace is not merely the doorway into the Christian life.
It is the atmosphere in which we learn to obey Christ.
And forgiveness is one of those places where grace must move from something we discuss into something we practice.
Maybe not all at once.
Maybe with tears.
Maybe through many prayers.
Maybe with the support of wise believers, pastors, or qualified counselors.
But genuinely.
And today, perhaps your first step is simply to stop defending the bitterness and start bringing it into the light.
If this message has uncovered a struggle you've been carrying, I want to invite you to respond—not to impress anyone, and not to make a public confession you're uncomfortable sharing.
You don't need to reveal private details or name the person who hurt you. Your story may remind another wounded believer that change is possible through Christ.
And if you have been silently struggling, even a simple prayer shared among fellow believers can become the beginning of an honest conversation.
Because someone reading this needs to know that forgiveness is not always an effortless feeling.
Sometimes it is a long road walked with Jesus.
And nobody should have to pretend that road is easy.
Not because every wound will disappear after one reading.
But because there may come another night when the anger returns, when the memories resurface, and when you need to be reminded of what Scripture actually says.
Not simply to increase its reach, but because someone among your friends may be smiling in public while quietly drowning in resentment, grief, or shame.
Someone may need to discover that Jesus commands forgiveness without commanding them to remain in danger.
Someone may need to hear that repentance is possible.
Someone may need to remember that the cross is still greater than their darkest chapter.
Sometimes a personal message is more appropriate than a public tag.
And there is something else I want to tell you about Gospel Warrior.

Our desire is to help people encounter the truth of Scripture, grow in the knowledge of Jesus Christ, confront sin honestly, discover the riches of grace, and become disciples whose lives are shaped by the Gospel.
These resources are offered to help believers study, pray, mature, and remain grounded in biblical truth.
And we want to keep expanding that work.
More resources.
More Gospel-centered teaching.
More opportunities to reach people who feel too ashamed to enter a church, too wounded to trust again, or too far from God to imagine that grace could still reach them.
Not because you must pay to glorify God.
Jesus Christ is the Savior. Gospel Warrior is only a ministry seeking to point people to Him.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, thoughtfully, and cheerfully—not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Your giving belongs under the Lordship of Christ, with wisdom, prayer, and responsibility toward your family, local church, and other legitimate needs.
They're simply a way of expressing appreciation to those who choose to stand with the ministry.
The deeper purpose is discipleship.
A growing community that takes the Word of God seriously.
A place where conviction leads us toward repentance rather than despair.
Where grace never becomes permission to sin.
Where biblical truth matters more than popularity.
Where people are encouraged to follow Jesus even when obedience is difficult.
Encourage them to explore Scripture for themselves.
Pray for this ministry.
Help us keep pointing people toward Jesus.
Because the goal is not to build admiration for Gospel Warrior.
The goal is to glorify Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry ever becomes more important than the Savior it proclaims, it has lost its purpose.
Now, before you leave, I want to return to the question that brought you here.
Can you truly love Jesus while refusing to forgive someone who hurt you?
The biblical answer requires both tenderness and seriousness.
A Christian may genuinely love Jesus while painfully struggling to forgive a devastating wrong.
The presence of that struggle does not automatically prove the absence of saving faith.
But a settled, defiant refusal to forgive—one that knowingly rejects Christ's command and refuses repentance—cannot be treated as compatible with faithful discipleship.
Jesus calls His followers to forgive because they themselves have been forgiven.
He does not promise that obedience will always feel easy.
He does not require us to deny injustice.
He does not command us to trust untrustworthy people.
But He does call us to surrender revenge, put away bitterness, and walk in the mercy we have received.
And perhaps tonight, you will close your eyes and remember what they did.
Perhaps the tears will come again.
Perhaps your heart will still ache.
But this time, instead of rehearsing what you wish you could do to them, you might whisper something different.
"Father, You saw everything."
"You know what happened."
"You know what it cost me."
"I am not calling evil good."
"I am not pretending that I am healed."
"But I do not want this pain to become my master."
"Teach me to forgive as You have forgiven me."
"Give me wisdom to maintain the boundaries I need."
"Lead me in truth."
"Guard my heart from hatred."
"And where I have sinned through bitterness, pride, or revenge, forgive me too."
"In Jesus' name, amen."
