Scripture teaches that those who receive spiritual instruction may share good things with those who teach, as Galatians 6:6 explains. Paul also affirms the principle of supporting those who proclaim the Gospel in 1 Corinthians 9:14.
Such support is an opportunity for willing generosity, not a compulsory fee for spiritual blessing.
What matters is that generosity be sincere and voluntary.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
But the greatest reason to participate is not a discount.
It is the opportunity to help sustain work that points people toward Christ.
No one should feel pressured to give beyond their means.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Grow.
Invite others to discover the free resources.
Your presence and your prayers matter.
A ministry can offer teaching.
A book can offer guidance.
An article can awaken conviction.
A community can offer encouragement and accountability.
But only Jesus Christ can save.
Only His blood atones for sin.
Only His resurrection secures the Christian's living hope.
Only His grace can bring a sinner into reconciliation with God.
And that brings us back to Jeremiah.
Back to the mountains where Israel chased false gods.
Back to the broken covenant.
Back to the devastating imagery of a certificate of divorce.
Back to Judah's religious pretenses.
Back to the invitation that came after the exposure.
"Return."
What an extraordinary word.
It does not flatter us.
It does not excuse us.
It does not allow us to pretend that our sin has caused no harm.
But it summons us away from the things that cannot save us and toward the God who alone can.
And now, in the light of Jesus Christ, that call carries the full weight of the Gospel.
Turn from sin.
Trust the Savior.
Receive His mercy.
Follow Him.
Not because you have finally become worthy of redemption.
But because the crucified and risen Christ is worthy of your entire life.
Perhaps you began reading this article thinking about Israel's unfaithfulness.
Perhaps somewhere along the way, you began recognizing your own.
And perhaps that is exactly why you needed to hear the invitation.
You are not reading about a God who takes pleasure in religious pretense.
You are reading about the God who tells the truth about sin and calls His people to repentance.
The God whose mercy never requires Him to deny His holiness.
The God whose faithfulness is not defeated by human unfaithfulness.
The God whose redemptive purposes find their fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
So before you close this article, ask yourself one question.
What am I still holding onto that Jesus is calling me to surrender?
Don't answer for the person who hurt you.
Don't answer for the church member who disappointed you.
Don't answer for the relative whose failures are easy to recognize.
Answer for yourself.
Because repentance is not merely something other people need.
It is a call each of us must take seriously.
And if you are ready, you can pray right where you are.

"Lord Jesus, You know everything I have tried to hide. You know where my heart has wandered and where I have chosen my own way instead of Yours. I cannot justify my sin, and I cannot save myself. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Teach me to turn away from what dishonors You. Help me trust in Your finished work, walk in Your truth, and love You with an undivided heart. I surrender myself to You. Lead me in genuine repentance and lasting faith. Amen."
And when the prayer ends, don't let your response end there.
Open the Scriptures.
Seek faithful Christian fellowship.
Make the changes repentance requires.
Ask for help where you need it.
Keep following Jesus.
And stay connected with Gospel Warrior as we continue learning, growing, and pointing one another toward Christ.
Because the most unforgettable part of Jeremiah's shocking marriage imagery is not simply that a covenant was broken.
It is that the holy God who exposed His people's betrayal still called them to return.
And through Jesus Christ, sinners today are summoned to something even greater than a temporary feeling of relief.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
New life.
A future shaped by grace and obedience rather than slavery to sin.
The past does not become good simply because God redeems sinners.
Betrayal remains betrayal.
Sin remains sin.
And the wounds of yesterday may still need healing.
But the Gospel declares that the past does not have to be the final word over the person who belongs to Jesus Christ.
The scars may still tell the story of where you have been, but they do not have to write the ending of who you become in Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABRAHAM LIVED 38 YEARS AFTER SARAH DIED—BUT WHAT HAPPENED IN THOSE YEARS REVEALS SOMETHING MOST BELIEVERS OVERLOOK
paragraphs: ABRAHAM LIVED 38 YEARS AFTER SARAH DIED—BUT WHAT HAPPENED IN THOSE YEARS REVEALS SOMETHING MOST BELIEVERS OVERLOOK

He buried the woman who had walked beside him through decades of waiting, disappointment, miracles, and impossible promises. But God was not finished writing Abraham’s story. And what happened after Sarah's death carries a powerful message for anyone who has ever buried a dream, lost someone they loved, or wondered whether their best days were already behind them.
There is something heartbreaking about realizing that the person who witnessed your greatest miracle may not be there to witness the rest of your journey.
Imagine Abraham standing beside Sarah’s grave.
The woman who had followed him into the unknown was gone.
The woman who had laughed when God promised her a son in her old age was gone.
The woman who had waited through years of barrenness, uncertainty, disappointment, and divine silence was gone.
The woman who finally held Isaac—the child whose very existence testified that God keeps His promises—was gone.
And Abraham was still alive.
Still breathing.
Still carrying promises.
Still walking with the God who had called him out of his homeland so many years earlier.
But now there was an empty place beside him.
And here is the question that makes this story more than a historical curiosity:
How many years did Abraham live after Sarah died—and what did God do with those remaining years?
The answer is 38 years.
But if you stop at the number, you will miss the beauty hidden between two graves.
Because the Bible does not merely tell us when Abraham died.
It shows us something remarkable about what faith looks like when one chapter closes, grief becomes part of your story, and God still has more to accomplish.
And somewhere in those 38 years, there is a message for the person reading this who has quietly wondered:
“Lord, is there still anything left for me?”
Genesis 23:1 records Sarah’s age at death:
“And Sarah was an hundred and seven and twenty years old: these were the years of the life of Sarah.” (KJV)
Sarah died at 127 years old.

Genesis 17:17 establishes that Abraham was ten years older than Sarah. When God spoke of the promised son, Abraham asked whether a child could be born to a man who was a hundred years old and whether Sarah, who was ninety, could bear.
That ten-year difference matters.
When Sarah died at 127, Abraham was approximately 137.
Then Genesis 25:7 tells us:
“And these are the days of the years of Abraham's life which he lived, an hundred threescore and fifteen years.” (KJV)
Abraham died at 175.
Subtract 137 from 175.
Thirty-eight years.
Thirty-eight more years of life after Sarah's death.
Thirty-eight years after the funeral.
Thirty-eight years after the tears.
Thirty-eight years after the woman who shared so much of his extraordinary journey was laid to rest.
And perhaps the most surprising thing is this:
Abraham's story did not end when Sarah's earthly story ended.
But before we explore those remaining years, we need to stand with Abraham at the place where his grief became visible.
Genesis 23:2 says:
“And Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her.”
Do not rush past those words.
Abraham wept.
The man who believed God's promise wept.
The man who left his homeland in obedience to God wept.
The man whose faith would later be celebrated in Hebrews 11 wept.
The man who had seen God do the impossible still knew what it meant to experience unbearable loss.
Faith did not make him incapable of grief.
Trusting God did not make him emotionally untouchable.
Receiving a miracle did not mean he would never experience sorrow again.
He was a man of faith.
And he was a grieving husband.
Both were true.
Some Christians have quietly absorbed the idea that strong faith means never breaking down, never questioning, never feeling devastated.
But Scripture never teaches that godly people are incapable of tears.
Abraham's tears were not evidence that he had abandoned his faith.
They were evidence that he had loved.
And there is something profoundly comforting about a Bible that does not erase the tears of its heroes.
Maybe you understand Abraham more than you expected.
Maybe you have buried someone whose voice you still remember.
Maybe you still reach for your phone before remembering that the person you want to call is no longer there.
Maybe you have walked into a room and felt the weight of an empty chair.
Or perhaps the thing you buried was not a person.
Perhaps it was a marriage you desperately wanted to save.
A relationship that ended despite your prayers.
A business that collapsed after years of sacrifice.
A ministry that never became what you hoped.
A dream that seemed so certain until life turned in another direction.
And somewhere along the way, you began to confuse the death of one chapter with the death of your entire purpose.
But Abraham's remaining 38 years remind us of something important:
The end of a precious season does not necessarily mean the end of God's work in your life.
That does not mean grief is easy.
It does not mean every loss will be replaced.
And it certainly does not mean that God owes us another 38 years or another earthly miracle.
It means that as long as we remain in His hands, our lives are not reduced to the worst thing that has happened to us.
Now look carefully at what Abraham did after Sarah died.
Genesis 23 describes him purchasing a burial place from Ephron the Hittite.
He paid four hundred shekels of silver for the field and the cave of Machpelah.
This was not merely an emotional detail about arranging a funeral.
It carried covenant significance.
God had promised Abraham the land of Canaan.
Yet Abraham spent much of his life living there as a sojourner.
He possessed the promise of an inheritance from God, but he did not personally possess the fullness of that inheritance during his lifetime.
When Sarah died, Abraham purchased a burial place in the very land God had promised to his descendants.
Consider the painful beauty of that moment.
The man who had been promised a land was purchasing a grave in it.
The man who had been promised descendants beyond counting was burying the mother of the promised son.
The man who had received extraordinary promises was still living in a world where death was painfully real.
And yet God's covenant had not failed.
The Hebrew text of Genesis 23:4 records Abraham describing himself as:
גֵּר־וְתוֹשָׁב (gēr wĕtôshāv)
The expression means a resident foreigner or sojourner and settler.
Abraham was acknowledging his position among the people of the land.
He lived there, but he did not yet possess the inheritance in its fullness.
That is not a small detail.
It helps us understand the nature of biblical faith.
Faith is not always standing in the middle of everything God has promised and celebrating its complete fulfillment.
Sometimes faith is standing beside a grave, holding a promise whose final fulfillment you will not see in your earthly lifetime.
Hebrews 11:13 says of the faithful:
“These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them...” (KJV)
Abraham did not see every covenant promise fulfilled before his death.
Yet he trusted the God who had spoken.
And perhaps that is where this story begins to confront us.
Because many of us have been taught to celebrate faith when the doors open, the healing comes, the money arrives, the relationship is restored, and the answer appears.
But what about faith when you are still waiting?
What about faith when the person you prayed for dies?
What about faith when you obey God and still experience disappointment?
What about faith when your hands are empty but His Word remains true?
Abraham's life teaches us that the reliability of God's promises cannot be measured only by how much we personally experience before we die.
The God who made the covenant was faithful even when Abraham's earthly life remained incomplete.
And this is where we must be careful.
God's promises to Abraham were specific covenant promises. We should not turn them into guarantees that every believer will receive land, wealth, children, marriage, or long life.
But through Jesus Christ, believers have something even greater than the assurance of favorable earthly circumstances.
We have the promise of eternal life in Him.
We have forgiveness through His blood.
We have the hope of resurrection.
And we have a Savior whose faithfulness does not expire when our circumstances become painful.
Now notice what Scripture records after Sarah's death.
Genesis 24 tells the remarkable story of Abraham arranging for a wife for Isaac.
Sarah was gone.
But the covenant promise was moving forward through the next generation.
Abraham instructed his servant not to take a wife for Isaac from the daughters of the Canaanites, but to go to his relatives.
The servant's journey led to Rebekah.
And Genesis 24:67 contains one of the tenderest details in the entire account.
Isaac brought Rebekah into Sarah's tent, took her as his wife, loved her, and was comforted after his mother's death.
Read that carefully.
Isaac had lost his mother.
And Scripture does not pretend that the promised son was immune to sorrow.
Even the child born through a miracle experienced grief.
Yet the next generation continued.
The covenant family continued.
God's purposes continued.
Not because Sarah was unimportant.
Not because Abraham could replace her.
But because God's covenant faithfulness was greater than the lifespan of any one human being.
Sarah's death did not cancel the promise God had made concerning Isaac.
That truth is especially powerful for parents and grandparents.
You may not live to see every prayer answered for your children.
You may not witness every spiritual battle they will face.
You may never know the full influence of your obedience.
But your responsibility is not to control the generations after you.
It is to be faithful to God with the time entrusted to you.
The results belong to Him.
And then comes a detail that surprises many readers.
Genesis 25:1 says:
“Then again Abraham took a wife, and her name was Keturah.” (KJV)
Yes.
After Sarah's death, Abraham married again.
And Genesis 25:2 records six sons associated with that marriage: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.
The Bible does not tell us everything about Abraham's relationship with Keturah.
It does not describe his emotional recovery.
It does not reveal exactly when the marriage took place.
It does not tell us that his love for Sarah disappeared.
And we should not invent those details.
What we can say is that Genesis records additional family life in Abraham's later years.
His household's story continued beyond Sarah's death.
This matters because grief can sometimes make people feel guilty for experiencing life again.
A widower may feel guilty for smiling.
A widow may feel guilty for enjoying another season.
Someone who has experienced devastating loss may wonder whether healing means betrayal.
But Scripture does not require the bereaved to remain permanently frozen in the moment of loss.
Love for someone who has died and gratitude for the life still before us are not necessarily enemies.
A new season does not erase the significance of an earlier one.
And yet this passage must not be turned into pressure.
Not every widow or widower needs to remarry.
Not everyone will have children.
Not everyone will experience a dramatic new beginning.
Abraham's later marriage is a historical detail in his life, not a universal command for grieving people.

The deeper truth is that God remains worthy of our trust in every season—whether He leads us into new relationships, quiet service, unexpected responsibilities, or a life that looks different from what we imagined.
There is another important detail in Genesis 25.
Verse 5 says:
“And Abraham gave all that he had unto Isaac.” (KJV)
Verse 6 explains that Abraham also gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them eastward, away from Isaac, while he was still alive.
The distinction matters because Isaac remained the designated heir of the covenant line.
Abraham had other descendants, but God's particular covenant promise would continue through Isaac.
This was not simply a story about an elderly man accumulating possessions or expanding his family.
It was about the unfolding of a promise that ultimately pointed beyond Abraham himself.
And that brings us to the most important part of this entire account.
Because if we only admire Abraham, we have not yet reached the heart of the Gospel.
The story of Abraham is not ultimately about how remarkable Abraham was.
It is about how faithful God is.
Abraham was not a flawless hero.
He had moments of fear.
He had moments of weakness.
He made decisions that caused pain.
Genesis 12 and Genesis 20 record troubling episodes in which Abraham represented Sarah as his sister while withholding the truth about their marriage.
Genesis 16 records the painful consequences surrounding Hagar and Ishmael after Sarah and Abraham attempted to obtain a child through Hagar.
These were not examples of perfect faith.
They were reminders that even the people God uses are capable of serious failure.
And still, God's covenant purposes endured.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because Abraham's mistakes were righteous.
But because God's faithfulness was greater than Abraham's failures.
Here is where the theme of scandal and grace becomes deeply personal.
Abraham's story contains fear, deception, family conflict, painful consequences, and imperfect obedience.
Yet Scripture also remembers him as a man who believed God.
Genesis 15:6 says:
“And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.” (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is especially meaningful:
וְהֶאֱמִן בַּיהוָה (wĕheʾĕmin baYHWH)
“And he believed in the LORD.”
The verse continues with the idea that this faith was reckoned or counted to him as righteousness.
This is foundational to the New Testament's explanation of justification by faith.
Paul returns to Abraham in Romans 4 to show that righteousness is not earned by a perfect record of human achievement.
Romans 4:3 says:
“For what saith the scripture? Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness.” (KJV)
And Romans 4:5 explains that God justifies the ungodly and counts faith for righteousness.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It means that our acceptance before God is not purchased by a lifetime of flawless performance.
It rests upon His grace, received through faith.
And the full revelation of that grace is found in Jesus Christ.
Galatians 3:16 identifies Christ as the ultimate promised offspring through whom the blessing associated with Abraham's covenant reaches its fulfillment.
The promise was always moving toward something greater than Abraham could see.
Toward a Redeemer.
Toward the cross.
Toward the empty tomb.
Toward the One who would confront the deepest enemy facing every descendant of Adam.
Death itself.
Abraham buried Sarah.
Eventually, Abraham himself was buried.
But Jesus Christ entered death and rose again.
That is why Christian hope is not merely the hope of having more years.
It is the hope of belonging to the One who conquered the grave.
Jesus declared in John 11:25:
“I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.” (KJV)
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say believers would never attend funerals.
He did not say faithful families would never experience tragedy.
He did not say everyone who trusts Him would live to 175.
He promised something greater.
Resurrection life in Him.
That is the hope Abraham's story ultimately invites us to consider through the fuller revelation of Scripture.
Not simply how long we live.
But whom we trust with our lives.
And whom we trust when our lives on earth come to an end.
There is a beautiful phrase in Genesis 25:8 describing Abraham's death.
The Hebrew text includes:
בְּשֵׂיבָה טוֹבָה (bĕśêvāh ṭôvāh)
It conveys the idea of a good old age or good old age with gray hair.
The verse says in the King James Version:
“Then Abraham gave up the ghost, and died in a good old age, an old man, and full of years; and was gathered to his people.”
The Hebrew expression translated “full of years” is associated with being full or satisfied; the word “years” is supplied in the English rendering to express the sense.
This description does not mean Abraham had lived without sorrow.
He had known infertility in his household.
He had known displacement.
He had known conflict.
He had known fear.
He had known family pain.
He had buried Sarah.
But at 175, Scripture describes the end of his earthly life as a good old age.
A life does not have to be painless to have been meaningful.
A life does not have to unfold exactly as expected to bear witness to God's faithfulness.
And a person does not need to accomplish everything imaginable to finish the work God entrusted to them.
Then Genesis 25:9 gives us another scene worth remembering.
Isaac and Ishmael buried their father.
Two sons whose family history had been marked by painful separation appeared together in the account of Abraham's burial.
Scripture does not tell us whether all the wounds between them were healed.
It does not record a reconciliation conversation.
We should not claim more than the text reveals.
But their presence together at their father's burial is a striking final detail.
And where was Abraham buried?
In the cave of Machpelah.
The same burial place he had purchased when Sarah died.
Genesis 25:10 says:
“There was Abraham buried, and Sarah his wife.” (KJV)
After 38 years of life beyond Sarah's death, Abraham's earthly remains were laid to rest in the same place.
The narrative that showed us a grieving husband purchasing a grave now closes with the husband buried beside his wife.
Thirty-eight years separated their deaths.
But the biblical account brings us back to the same burial place.
There is something deeply moving about that.
Not because the grave was the fulfillment of every promise.
Not because death had the final word.
But because the same God who had sustained Abraham through decades of waiting remained faithful throughout his life.
And the story of God's covenant did not end at Machpelah.
Isaac lived on.
The promised line continued.
Generations passed.
And in the fullness of time, Jesus Christ came.
The One in whom God's redemptive purposes reach their fulfillment.
Now, consider a question that may be more important than the original question about Abraham's age.
What are you doing with the years God has given you?
Not the years you wish you could recover.
Not the years you imagine you should have had.
Not the years someone else has been given.
The life you have today.
Because none of us knows whether we have 38 more years.
Some will have decades.
Some will have only a little time.
That is not meant to frighten you into desperation.
It is meant to awaken you to the preciousness of the present.
Maybe you have been postponing repentance.
You keep telling yourself you will surrender that hidden sin when life becomes easier.
Maybe you have been delaying forgiveness.
You know bitterness is poisoning your heart, but you keep rehearsing what someone did to you.
Maybe you have been neglecting prayer.
Your Bible sits unopened while your soul grows exhausted.
Maybe you have been living under the weight of shame.
You believe Jesus can forgive other people, but somewhere deep inside you wonder whether your own failures have placed you beyond His mercy.
Listen carefully.
Abraham's righteousness was not grounded in his perfection.
And your hope of salvation is not grounded in yours.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we finally accumulated enough religious achievements to deserve His attention.
Christ died for sinners.
And His resurrection is the declaration that sin and death do not have ultimate authority over those who belong to Him.
That grace is not permission to remain comfortable in rebellion.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God instructs us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly lives.
Real grace does not merely soothe a guilty conscience.
It transforms the person who receives it.
It calls us out of hiding.
It brings our sin into the light.
It teaches us to turn from what is destroying us.
It leads us back to Christ.
And if you have been telling yourself that your story is too scandalous, your past too dirty, your mistakes too public, or your failures too deeply rooted, remember this:
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people have earned a reward.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ died and rose again to save sinners who could never save themselves.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
It is the proper response to the mercy of God.
And perhaps this article found you in a season when you needed to hear that.
Perhaps you have lost someone.
Perhaps you are growing older and wondering whether your life still matters.
Perhaps you feel embarrassed that your faith has been weaker than you expected.
Perhaps you have been carrying a secret that nobody in your church knows about.
Or perhaps you have become so familiar with Christian language that you have forgotten what it means to be genuinely surrendered to Jesus.
Then do not simply admire Abraham's 38 remaining years.
Examine your own heart.
Are you trusting Christ?
Are you turning from sin?
Are you living in obedience to His Word?
Are you using the time entrusted to you to love God and love others?
Are you passing on truth to the people who will remain when your earthly journey ends?
And if you realize you have wandered far from Him, you do not have to manufacture a dramatic religious performance.
Come to Christ with sincerity.
Confess your sin.
Ask for mercy.
Trust in His finished work.
And follow Him.
You can begin with a simple prayer:

“Lord Jesus, I have spent too much of my life trying to control what only You can hold. I have carried regrets, hidden sins, disappointments, and fears. Forgive me. Teach me to trust You in the seasons I do not understand. Heal what is wounded in me. Correct what is sinful in me. Restore what has grown cold in my relationship with You. And help me live the rest of my days for Your glory, whether they are many or few. My hope is not in the number of years I have left, but in Your death and resurrection. Amen.”
And if this story has brought something painful or honest to the surface, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not have to reveal private details.
Sometimes a few sincere words can open the door to prayer, encouragement, and genuine Christian fellowship.
Someone else may be reading silently, wondering whether they can survive what they are facing.
Your testimony may remind them that they are not alone.
But there is something else I want to ask you.
Think of one person who needs this message.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to condemn.
Someone you genuinely love.
A grieving parent.
A widow.
A struggling father.
A young believer who feels spiritually defeated.
A friend who has quietly stopped praying.
Someone who thinks their best years are gone.
A simple act of sharing cannot replace discipleship, prayer, or personal relationships, but it can place biblical encouragement in front of someone who might not otherwise encounter it.
Not because the words here are more important than Scripture, but because you may want to return to these passages when another difficult season comes.
And if you have been following Gospel Warrior, or have only recently discovered this community, I want you to understand something about why we continue this work.
We want to help people encounter Jesus Christ through the faithful teaching of Scripture.
Not merely collect religious quotations.
Not simply stir emotions for a moment.
But encourage real repentance, deeper biblical understanding, genuine spiritual growth, and lasting faithfulness to Christ.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical encouragement and discipleship accessible to people who need it.
It can become part of your personal giving and generosity as you prayerfully consider how to steward what God has entrusted to you.

Scripture teaches the importance of supporting faithful ministry. Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach the Word, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds believers that giving should be willing and cheerful, not reluctant or forced.
That balance matters.
It is not a payment for God's blessing.
It is not a replacement for your responsibilities to your local church, your family, or people in need.
And it should not be confused with a biblically mandated tithe.
But it can be a meaningful voluntary offering of support toward a ministry whose mission you believe is worth helping sustain.
These items are simply expressions of appreciation. The greater purpose is not merchandise.
It is ministry.
It is the opportunity to keep placing Scripture before people who are hurting, questioning, repenting, searching, or learning to walk faithfully with Jesus.
You can still pray for this ministry.
You can still make use of the free resources.
Your financial situation does not determine your worth before God.
And the Gospel of Jesus Christ is not for sale.
If you are not, we are still grateful that you are here.
What matters most is that Christ is proclaimed faithfully and that people are encouraged to know Him, trust Him, and obey His Word.
Now, before you leave, return with me one last time to the cave of Machpelah.
Imagine the silence.
Sarah was buried there.
Thirty-eight years later, Abraham was buried there too.
Their earthly journeys had ended.
Their struggles were over.
Their years of waiting had passed.
And yet the promises of God continued unfolding long after both of them had died.
Abraham never saw Bethlehem.
He never stood beside the manger.
He never watched Jesus carry the cross.
He never saw the stone rolled away from the empty tomb.
But Jesus declared in John 8:56:
“Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad.” (KJV)
Christ's words reveal that Abraham's hope reached toward the day of the Messiah, though Scripture does not explain every detail of what Abraham understood or saw.
The deepest significance of Abraham's faith was never confined to his lifespan.
It pointed toward Christ.
And that is the final lesson of those 38 years.
You can spend your life chasing a legacy that ends at your grave.
Or you can live by faith in the Savior whose kingdom will never end.
You can spend your remaining years consumed by what you have lost.
Or you can grieve honestly while learning to trust the Lord with what remains.
You can keep hiding behind your failures.
Or you can come into the light of the Gospel, repent, and receive the mercy offered through Jesus Christ.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot guarantee tomorrow.
But today, you can turn to the One who holds eternity.
Abraham lived 38 years after Sarah died.
And those years remind us that God's faithfulness does not depend upon our ability to see the entire story.
The God who sustained Abraham through waiting, grief, weakness, and old age is the same God who has revealed His saving grace through Jesus Christ.
If your earthly story ended sooner than you expected, would your greatest confidence be in what you accomplished—or in the Savior who died and rose again for you?
And remember this:
The most important part of Abraham's final 38 years was not that he kept living after Sarah died, but that the God who held his promises was faithful long after Abraham himself was gone.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE SAYS ADULTERY IS LIKE HOLDING FIRE AGAINST YOUR CHEST—SO WHY DO PEOPLE STILL BELIEVE THEY WON’T GET BURNED?
paragraphs: THE BIBLE SAYS ADULTERY IS LIKE HOLDING FIRE AGAINST YOUR CHEST—SO WHY DO PEOPLE STILL BELIEVE THEY WON’T GET BURNED?

One forbidden touch. One secret conversation. One decision nobody was supposed to discover. Proverbs 6:27–29 exposes the fire that destroys marriages, wounds families, and scars souls. But the Gospel reveals something just as astonishing: the same Jesus who refuses to excuse adultery refuses to abandon the sinner who truly repents.
There is a terrifying moment in almost every story of adultery.
It isn't necessarily the moment someone gets caught.
It isn't when the betrayed spouse discovers the messages, when the children begin asking why everything has changed, or when the person who promised forever suddenly becomes a stranger.
Sometimes the most dangerous moment happens much earlier.
When someone looks at something they know is wrong…
And whispers to themselves:
“I can handle this.”
I can keep it innocent.
I can stop whenever I want.
Nobody needs to know.
My marriage is already struggling.
I deserve to feel loved.
It's only a conversation.
It's only a little attention.
It's only one time.
And somewhere between the first compromise and the final catastrophe, something happens that the human heart rarely anticipates.
The fire begins to feel like warmth.
Until it burns.
Thousands of years ago, before smartphones, disappearing messages, private inboxes, and relationships hidden behind passwords, Scripture exposed this very deception.
And it did so with a question so piercing that every generation must answer it.

“Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned? Can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned? So he that goeth in to his neighbour's wife; whosoever toucheth her shall not be innocent.” — Proverbs 6:27–29 (KJV)
Read those words again.
God does not ask whether the person carrying the fire has good intentions.
He does not ask whether the flames are small.
He does not ask whether the person feels lonely, misunderstood, neglected, or emotionally exhausted.
He asks whether someone can hold fire against their own body and somehow escape its consequences.
The expected answer is devastatingly simple.
No.
And that is where this story becomes uncomfortably personal.
Because not every fire begins in a bedroom.
Some begin with a notification.
A compliment.
A conversation you would rather your spouse never read.
A message you delete, not because it was meaningless, but because you know exactly what it meant.
Sometimes the first betrayal happens long before the first kiss.
It begins when someone starts giving another person the emotional intimacy, romantic attention, and secret affection that should never have been cultivated outside the marriage covenant.
And the frightening thing about temptation is that it rarely introduces itself as destruction.
It often arrives disguised as understanding.
“You deserve someone who listens.”
“You deserve someone who appreciates you.”
“You deserve to be happy.”

There may be real pain beneath those thoughts. A neglected marriage can be deeply lonely. Emotional wounds can be genuine. Betrayal, abandonment, and unresolved conflict can leave a person desperately hungry for tenderness.
But pain does not make betrayal holy.
And being wounded does not give anyone permission to wound another person.
The devil does not have to convince you that adultery is righteous. Sometimes he only has to convince you that your situation is the exception.
This is why Proverbs 6 is more than an ancient warning about sexual misconduct.
It is an exposure of human self-deception.
In the original Hebrew, Proverbs 6:27 begins:
הֲיַחְתֶּה־אִישׁ אֵשׁ בְּחֵיקוֹ
Hayachteh ish esh becheiqo?
Literally, the question asks whether a man can scoop or gather fire into his bosom, the area of his chest or the fold of his garment.
The Hebrew word אֵשׁ (esh) means “fire.”
And חֵיק (cheiq) refers to the bosom, lap, or close fold of one's clothing.
Notice the picture.
This is not someone observing a fire from a safe distance.
This is someone bringing the fire close enough to burn what covers and protects them.
The image is intimate.
Deliberate.
Dangerous.
The next verse intensifies the warning.
אִם־יְהַלֵּךְ אִישׁ עַל־הַגֶּחָלִים
Im-yehallech ish al-haggechalim.
“Can a man walk upon hot coals…?”
The imagery leaves little room for pretending.
Fire burns clothing.
Hot coals burn feet.
And adultery brings consequences that cannot be dismissed simply because the participants believed they could control the situation.

This is wisdom literature, not a promise that every adulterous relationship will be exposed immediately or that every consequence will look identical. Proverbs teaches the predictable moral danger of sin through vivid images.
It tells us what temptation desperately wants us to forget.
You cannot make something spiritually safe merely by keeping it secret.
Think about the person who once loved their spouse sincerely.
They remember the wedding.
The vows.
The trembling voice promising faithfulness.
The photographs.
The prayers.
The plans for children, a home, and a lifetime together.
They never imagined becoming someone who would betray those promises.
But somewhere along the road, the marriage became difficult.
Conversations turned into arguments.
Affection became routine.
Responsibilities became exhausting.
And then somebody else appeared.
Someone who laughed at their jokes.
Someone who noticed their appearance.
Someone who made them feel interesting again.
And suddenly, a person who had promised lifelong faithfulness began entertaining a dangerous question.
“What if I married the wrong person?”
That question can become a doorway to rationalization when it is used to justify dishonesty rather than confront the real problems with integrity.
Because an affair often offers something a struggling marriage cannot offer in the same way.
An illusion.
The secret relationship may not carry the weight of unpaid bills, sick children, sleepless nights, aging parents, daily responsibilities, and years of unresolved conflict.
It may exist in carefully selected moments.
Filtered conversations.
Exciting anticipation.
Attention without ordinary accountability.
And what feels like extraordinary compatibility may partly be the excitement of escaping ordinary reality.
Then comes the comparison.
The spouse who shares the burdens of everyday life is compared with someone encountered mainly in moments of excitement.
And the person carrying the fire begins to mistake the heat for love.
But the Bible refuses to confuse intensity with faithfulness.
Proverbs 5:18–19 celebrates marital delight and enduring affection.
Hebrews 13:4 calls believers to honor marriage and warns against sexual immorality and adultery.
And Jesus takes the matter even deeper.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He teaches that adultery is not merely a matter of outward behavior. A person who deliberately looks at another with lustful intent has already committed adultery in the heart.
The Greek expression πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn) points to looking with the purpose of lusting after someone.
Jesus is not declaring that every involuntary attraction is the same as a completed affair.
He is confronting the deliberate cultivation of sinful desire.
The gaze we choose to prolong.
The fantasy we choose to entertain.
The emotional attachment we choose to nourish.
The secret appetite we refuse to surrender.
Because Jesus knows something we often refuse to admit.
What we repeatedly welcome into the heart can eventually reshape what we are willing to do with our hands.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that means.
You haven't crossed the physical line.
Not yet.
But you are waiting for messages that should not matter so much.
You are disappointed when that person does not respond.
You are comparing your spouse with someone who has never carried the full weight of your life.
You are protecting a connection that would deeply wound your husband or wife if they knew its true nature.
And every time your conscience speaks, you answer it with another excuse.
If that is you, please hear this without mistaking conviction for hatred.
God's warning is not proof that He wants to destroy your happiness. It is evidence that He sees the destruction you may be walking toward.
The Lord does not expose sin because He delights in humiliation.
He exposes darkness because darkness is where deception grows.
And sometimes the mercy of God sounds like an alarm.
Stop.
Turn around.
Tell the truth.
Do not carry this any farther.
But what about the person who already crossed the line?
What about the husband who betrayed his wife?
The wife who shattered her husband's trust?
The person whose secret relationship destroyed a family?
What about someone who cannot undo the messages, the meetings, the lies, the promises, or the nights spent in someone else's arms?
Is there any hope left?
To answer that question, we must enter one of the most painful stories in Scripture.
A story involving a king.
A woman.
A pregnancy.
A cover-up.
And a death.
David was not an ordinary man.
He was Israel's king.
A man who had experienced God's deliverance.
A worshiper who wrote psalms.
A leader entrusted with extraordinary responsibility.
Yet 2 Samuel 11 records a moment when David saw Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and took her into his palace.

The account does not give us permission to turn Bathsheba into the villain or pretend that the king's power was irrelevant. David initiated the encounter from a position of immense authority, and Scripture places the responsibility for the unfolding wrongdoing squarely upon him.
When Bathsheba became pregnant, David attempted to conceal what had happened.
He summoned Uriah from battle.
He tried to arrange circumstances that would make the pregnancy appear legitimate.
When his plan failed, he arranged for Uriah to be placed in deadly combat.
And Uriah was killed.
Consider the horror of that progression.
What began with a king's sinful desire became deception, manipulation, and the deliberate orchestration of another man's death.
The fire had spread.
Not only through David's conscience, but through the lives of people who had trusted him.
Then came one of the most chilling statements in the narrative.
“But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 11:27 (KJV)
David could control what many people around him knew.
He could manage appearances.
He could use royal authority to conceal his actions.
But he could not hide from God.
And neither can we.
Then the prophet Nathan confronted David.
Not with flattery.
Not with a carefully constructed excuse.
But with truth.
Nathan told a story about a rich man who stole a poor man's beloved lamb.
David became furious at the injustice.
And Nathan answered:
“Thou art the man.” — 2 Samuel 12:7 (KJV)
Imagine the silence.
The king who had judged another man's cruelty was suddenly forced to confront his own.
No more hiding behind authority.
No more pretending that secrecy meant innocence.
No more escaping into the appearance of respectability.
Only truth.
And the God before whom every heart stands exposed.
David finally confessed:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13 (KJV)
Those words did not resurrect Uriah.
They did not erase Bathsheba's suffering.
They did not cancel every consequence that followed.
But they marked the beginning of David's acknowledged repentance.
And Psalm 51 gives us a window into the brokenness of a sinner pleading for God's mercy.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10 (KJV)
In Hebrew, the opening plea is:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
The verb בְּרָא (bera), from the Hebrew root bara, means “create.”
David was not merely asking God to help him improve his public image.
He was pleading for inward renewal.
Because genuine repentance is not simply wanting the consequences to disappear.
It is recognizing that sin has corrupted something within us that we cannot repair through appearances alone.
And that brings us to an uncomfortable distinction.
Being sorry that you were caught is not the same as being broken over what you did.
A person can cry because their reputation has collapsed.
Because their spouse discovered the truth.
Because their family is angry.
Because their ministry, friendships, finances, or social standing are threatened.
Those tears may be real.
But they do not automatically prove repentance.
Second Corinthians 7:10 distinguishes godly sorrow that leads to repentance from worldly sorrow that leads to death.
True repentance does more than fear exposure.
It turns away from sin.
It stops defending what God condemns.
It becomes willing to tell the truth, accept accountability, and make appropriate restitution wherever possible.
It does not demand immediate forgiveness as proof that someone else is spiritual.
It does not pressure a betrayed spouse to rebuild trust before safety and honesty have been established.
And it does not use the grace of God as permission to continue deception.
Grace is not a hiding place for unrepentant adultery.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy that calls sinners out of darkness and into a transformed life.
Yet there is another person we must not forget.
The betrayed spouse.
The one who never agreed to carry this fire.
The one who discovered that the person they trusted had been living a second life.
Perhaps you remember the exact moment.
The phone in your hand.
The messages on the screen.
The sudden feeling that the room had lost its air.
Your mind searching for some explanation that would make the evidence mean something else.
The questions that followed.
How long?
Who knew?
Was anything real?
Did they think about me?
What did I do wrong?
And perhaps the most painful question of all:
“Why wasn't I enough?”
If you are carrying that wound, hear this clearly.
Another person's decision to betray their covenant does not establish your worth.
You may have had marital problems.
You may have made mistakes.
You may have contributed to patterns of conflict that needed serious attention.
But those difficulties do not transfer responsibility for someone else's adultery onto you.
Their betrayal was their choice.
You do not have to call evil good in order to demonstrate Christian forgiveness.
You do not have to pretend trust has been restored simply because someone has apologized.
You do not have to silence your grief to protect the reputation of the person who wounded you.
Forgiveness, reconciliation, and restored trust are related, but they are not identical.
Forgiveness does not require denying the truth.
Reconciliation requires genuine repentance and appropriate rebuilding.
Trust grows through consistent honesty over time.

And Scripture itself recognizes the seriousness of sexual immorality within marriage. In Matthew 19:9, Jesus addresses sexual immorality as an exception in His teaching concerning divorce, although Christian traditions differ on some questions of application and remarriage.
The church must never use biblical language to force a betrayed person to remain in danger, conceal abuse, or accept continuing deception.
God sees the wounded as surely as He confronts the guilty.
And He is not indifferent to either.
But now we arrive at the heart of the Gospel.
Because if this article ended with the fire, it would leave us with a warning but not the fullness of Christian hope.
The Bible tells us that sin burns.
It also tells us that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Not by pretending sin is harmless.
Not by rewriting God's moral standards.
But by bearing sin's judgment and opening the way to forgiveness through His death and resurrection.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had cleaned up every consequence.
Not after we had become respectable.
Not after we had earned the right to approach Him.
Christ died for sinners.
And that includes adulterers who truly repent.
It includes the sexually immoral.
The dishonest.
The hypocritical.
The proud.
The people whose hidden lives contradict their public worship.
It includes people who have sinned in ways they are ashamed to name.
But the invitation is not to remain unchanged.
First Corinthians 6:9–11 warns that the sexually immoral and adulterers are among those who will not inherit God's kingdom if they remain characterized by such unrighteousness.
Then Paul gives one of the most beautiful declarations of transformation in the New Testament.
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” — 1 Corinthians 6:11 (KJV)
Such were some of you.
Past tense.
Not because their history never happened.
Not because their victims' pain was imaginary.
Not because consequences magically vanished.
But because their old identity no longer had the final word.
The Greek expression καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε (kai tauta tines ēte) means, in context, “And such were some of you.”
The apostle is describing people whose former lives had been marked by serious sin, but who had now been washed, sanctified, and justified through Christ.
That is not self-improvement dressed in religious language.
That is the astonishing announcement of the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely offer sinners a better reputation. He offers forgiveness, a new standing before God, and a transformed life.
And perhaps nowhere do we see the tension between mercy and holiness more memorably than in John 8.
A woman accused of adultery is brought before Jesus.
Her accusers are ready to condemn her.
The woman stands publicly exposed.
And Jesus confronts the hypocrisy of those who seek to use her as a trap.
Eventually, her accusers depart.
Then Jesus says:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11 (KJV)

There is an important textual detail worth knowing. The account in John 7:53–8:11 is absent from several of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel, and modern translations commonly mark its disputed textual status. Christians should be honest about that history rather than conceal it.
Even so, the scene's combination of mercy and the command to abandon sin reflects truths firmly taught elsewhere in Scripture.
Jesus offers forgiveness.
Jesus calls people to repentance.
Jesus refuses to treat sin as righteousness.
And the message is unmistakable.
Mercy does not mean your sin was acceptable. Mercy means your sin does not have to be the end of your story.
Maybe you have been living with a secret for years.
Maybe you have already confessed, but the damage is still painfully visible.
Maybe the person you betrayed has not forgiven you.
Maybe your marriage ended.
Maybe your children are still struggling.
Maybe you genuinely love Jesus but cannot stop grieving what your decisions cost.
Please understand something.
The Gospel does not promise that repentance will restore every relationship.
It does not promise that every spouse will reconcile.
It does not promise that consequences will disappear.
But it does promise that everyone who truly comes to Christ in repentance and faith will find a Savior sufficient to forgive.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That is not a cheap promise.
The cross tells us exactly how serious sin is.
And how extraordinary God's mercy is.
The Savior who hung upon the cross was not minimizing evil.
He was bearing the cost of redemption.
The empty tomb announces that sin and death do not possess ultimate authority over those who belong to Him.
This is why the Gospel Warrior message is not simply about exposing scandal.
It is about proclaiming grace through Jesus Christ.
Not grace that excuses rebellion.
Grace that calls us home.
Not grace that silences victims.
Grace that honors truth and justice.
Not grace that makes repentance unnecessary.
Grace that teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live differently, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
And if you are reading this while standing dangerously close to an affair, perhaps this is the moment to stop.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one last conversation.
Not after one final meeting to explain your feelings.
Now.
End the romantic or sexual relationship that violates your covenant.
Stop protecting the secrecy.
Seek wise, trustworthy pastoral counsel and, where appropriate, qualified professional help.
Tell the truth responsibly, without using confession merely to unload guilt onto someone else.
Accept the consequences of your actions.
Do not demand trust you have not rebuilt.
And surrender to Jesus Christ the desires you have been allowing to rule you.
If you are the person who has been betrayed, you do not have to rush your healing to make someone else comfortable.
Bring your grief before God.
Seek support from people who will protect your dignity, safety, and ability to make informed decisions.
You are not spiritually defective because forgiveness is difficult.
You are not faithless because the wound still hurts.
Healing is not always immediate.
And reconciliation, where possible, must be built on truth rather than pressure.
Perhaps someone reading this is neither the adulterer nor the betrayed spouse.
Perhaps you are single, watching a relationship become emotionally dangerous.
Perhaps you are entertaining an attachment to someone who is married.
Perhaps you are married and have been feeding fantasies that are slowly changing your affections.
Perhaps your greatest struggle is not sexual temptation but the belief that hidden sin is harmless as long as nobody discovers it.
The principle of Proverbs still reaches you.
Do not embrace what God warns will burn you.
And do not confuse God's patience with His approval.
There is a reason this warning has survived thousands of years.
Human technology has changed.
Our language has changed.
Our methods of hiding have changed.
But the human heart still knows how to justify what it desperately wants.
And the Word of God still knows how to expose it.
Yet there is something even more astonishing than the endurance of temptation.
The endurance of God's mercy.
The same Lord who warned us about the fire invites us to come into the light.
He calls us to confession.
To repentance.
To faith.
To forgiveness.
To holiness.
To restoration wherever restoration is possible.
To a life no longer governed by secrecy and shame.
And this is where I want to ask you something deeply personal.
Not as a performance.
Not because you owe strangers the details of your pain.
But because somebody else reading these words may need to know they are not the only one struggling.
What has God been teaching you about faithfulness, temptation, forgiveness, or rebuilding trust?
You do not need to disclose private details or expose another person to make your response meaningful.
Sometimes a few honest words can become the encouragement another struggling believer needed to see.
And please do not allow this message to end with you.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a married person who has been quietly entertaining temptation.
Someone whose home is breaking apart.
Someone who has been betrayed and wonders whether God still sees their tears.
Someone who believes their past has made them permanently unworthy of love.
Not to shame anyone.
Not to start speculation about somebody's marriage.
But to place a biblical warning and a Gospel invitation where someone might encounter them at the very moment they need them.
If one person turns away from an affair, if one wounded spouse finds comfort in Christ, or if one sinner begins to seek genuine repentance, that matters far more than any number on a screen.
Not because reading it once makes anyone immune to temptation.
But because the heart sometimes needs to hear again what it already knows is true.
And if this message has stirred something in you, I want to invite you into something deeper than a single article.
Gospel Warrior exists to keep proclaiming the truth of Scripture, the seriousness of sin, the beauty of repentance, and the life-transforming grace of Jesus Christ.

These resources are intended to help people open their Bibles, strengthen their understanding, nourish their faith, and keep walking with Christ when the excitement of a single inspirational post has faded.
But continuing and expanding this work takes real support.
Research, writing, biblical teaching, discipleship materials, outreach, and the development of new resources require time, effort, and ongoing financial provision.
It is a voluntary way to stand beside this ministry and help make more Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources available to people who need them.
If God has used Gospel Warrior to encourage your faith, challenge your conscience, or draw you closer to Scripture, please prayerfully consider helping sustain and expand that mission.

Supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be a meaningful expression of Christian generosity and stewardship. Scripture encourages believers to share materially with those who teach God's Word (Galatians 6:6) and to give willingly and cheerfully (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But I also want to be biblically clear.
Your giving belongs before the Lord, guided by Scripture, prayer, your responsibilities, and your conscience.
These products are simply another way to encourage biblical reflection, share faith-centered messages, and help sustain the work.
The greatest gift, however, is not a discount.
It is the opportunity to participate in making biblical encouragement and Gospel-centered teaching available to more people.
You can still make a meaningful difference.
Pray for this ministry.
Tell a friend about the free library.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your value to God, and the Gospel is never for sale.
The goal is to see more people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ, grow in His Word, abandon destructive sin, and discover the transforming power of His grace.
And that brings us back to the fire.
Back to the warning.
Back to the question that began this entire journey.
Can a man carry fire against his chest without being burned?
No.
The fire of adultery is not made harmless by secrecy.
The damage is not made imaginary by excuses.
The consequences are not erased by religious language.
But listen carefully.
The fact that sin can destroy what you once held precious does not mean Jesus Christ is powerless to redeem a repentant sinner.
David's failure was real.
Uriah's death was real.
Bathsheba's suffering was real.
The consequences were real.
And God's mercy was real.
That is the tension we must never remove from the Christian message.
We do not glorify the scandal.
We glorify the Savior.
We do not celebrate the sin.
We celebrate the grace that calls sinners to repentance.
We do not pretend the ashes are beautiful.
We proclaim that Jesus Christ can bring genuine new life even to people whose choices have left terrible ashes behind.
So before you close this article, ask yourself one final question.
What am I carrying close to my heart that God has already warned me to put down?
Maybe it is a secret relationship.
Maybe it is a fantasy.
Maybe it is bitterness that has hardened into revenge.
Maybe it is shame that keeps telling you forgiveness is impossible.
Maybe it is the pride that refuses to confess.
Whatever it is, do not wait until the fire consumes more of your life.
Come to Jesus.
Tell Him the truth.
Turn from sin.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Walk in the light.
And where you have harmed others, pursue honesty, accountability, and whatever repair is rightly possible.
Because the most important question is not whether you can keep hiding the fire.
It is whether you will finally surrender your heart to the Savior who calls you out of darkness.
If these words have reached somewhere you have been afraid to let God touch, consider making this your prayer:

“Lord Jesus, You know everything about me. You know the temptations I have entertained, the wounds I have carried, the truths I have avoided, and the sins I cannot undo. Forgive me for the ways I have turned away from You. Give me courage to confess what is wrong, turn away from what destroys, and walk in Your truth. Heal what can be healed. Teach me to accept responsibility for what I have done and to extend grace without denying justice. Create in me a clean heart. Strengthen my faithfulness. Help me love what You love and reject what leads me away from You. I place my life in Your hands. In Your holy name, Jesus. Amen.”
And remember this, especially if your past has convinced you that your story is already over.
The fire may have changed your story forever—but if you surrender to Jesus Christ, the ashes do not get to write its final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN YOU LOVE JESUS AND STILL LIVE COMFORTABLY IN SIN?
paragraphs: CAN YOU LOVE JESUS AND STILL LIVE COMFORTABLY IN SIN?
The Most Dangerous Place for a Christian Is Not Where You Fall Into Sin… It’s Where You No Longer Feel the Need to Get Up.
There is something more frightening than a Christian falling into sin.
It is a Christian who has learned how to live there.

Someone who can worship on Sunday, entertain darkness on Monday, quote Scripture on Tuesday, return to a secret addiction on Wednesday, ask God for blessings on Thursday, ignore conviction on Friday, and walk into church on Saturday as though nothing is wrong.
And the most terrifying part?
They no longer feel the contradiction.
Not because God has stopped being holy.
Not because sin has become harmless.
But because a heart can become so accustomed to compromise that what once brought tears of repentance now barely produces a moment of discomfort.
Read that again.
The sin that once broke your heart can eventually become the sin you defend, if you keep silencing the conviction that was meant to bring you home.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question you will face today is not whether you believe in Jesus.
It is whether the Jesus you claim to love has permission to confront the life you have chosen to protect.
Because there is a difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
A difference between falling into darkness and furnishing a room there.
A difference between crying out, "Lord, deliver me," and quietly deciding, "Lord, understand me."
One is the desperate struggle of a person who needs grace.
The other may reveal a heart that wants the benefits of a Savior without surrendering to His lordship.
And before you assume this article is about somebody else, consider something.
Judas walked with Jesus.
He heard the sermons. Witnessed the miracles. Shared meals with the disciples. Saw compassion that could silence a crowd and authority that could command a storm.
Yet proximity to Jesus did not mean his heart was surrendered to Jesus.
That should make every one of us examine ourselves.
Because you can be close to Christian things while remaining dangerously distant from Christ.
You can know worship songs without knowing surrender.
You can defend biblical truth online while privately refusing to obey it.
You can be surrounded by people who call you a strong Christian while carrying secrets you have convinced yourself God will never confront.
And you can become so skilled at appearing spiritually healthy that even you begin believing the performance.
But Jesus is not deceived by the version of ourselves we present to the world.
He sees the heart.
He sees what happens after the worship music stops.
He sees what you search for when nobody is watching.
He hears the words you say when anger takes control.

He knows the bitterness you keep feeding, the dishonest choices you keep excusing, the sexual temptation you keep entertaining, the pride you refuse to confess, and the forgiveness you keep withholding.
And still, He calls sinners to come to Him.
Not because sin is acceptable.
But because His mercy is greater than the darkness from which He came to rescue us.
Listen carefully to what Jesus actually said.
In John 14:15, the Greek text reads:
«Ἐὰν ἀγαπᾶτέ με, τὰς ἐντολὰς τὰς ἐμὰς τηρήσετε.»
A faithful translation is:
"If you love me, you will keep my commandments."
The word ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate) comes from the verb agapaō, meaning to love. The word τηρήσετε (tērēsete) comes from tēreō, meaning to keep, observe, or guard.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say, "If you love Me, you will never struggle."
He did not say, "If you love Me, you will achieve sinless perfection before you can come near Me."
He connected genuine love with obedience.
In the immediate context, Jesus was comforting His disciples before His departure, promising the Holy Spirit and preparing them for a life of faithful discipleship.
His words were not a formula for earning salvation through flawless behavior.
They described the relationship between love for Christ and a life increasingly shaped by His commands.
Obedience is not the price we pay to purchase His love. It is a fruit that grows from a life transformed by His grace.
And this is where the question becomes deeply personal.
If Jesus says, "Follow Me," but we continually answer, "Only where it is convenient," what exactly are we following?
If He says, "Forgive," but we treasure revenge, what are we protecting?
If He says, "Flee sexual immorality," but we deliberately arrange opportunities to indulge it, what are we choosing?
If He says, "Repent," but we insist that nothing needs to change, have we truly listened?
There is a kind of Christianity that wants Jesus to remove guilt without confronting the sin that produces it.
It wants peace without repentance.
Forgiveness without confession.
Blessing without surrender.
Heaven without holiness.
A Savior who comforts, but never corrects.
But the Jesus revealed in Scripture cannot be reduced to a comforting accessory for a life we refuse to surrender.
He is the crucified and risen Lord.
And His grace does not merely pardon sinners.
It teaches us to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 declares that the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation, and training believers to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.
Think about that.
Grace trains us.
Grace does not give us permission to remain enslaved to what Christ died to redeem us from.
Grace meets us in our brokenness, forgives us through Christ, and begins transforming our desires, decisions, and direction.
This is why the apostle Paul asked a question that still cuts through centuries of religious excuses.
Romans 6:1–2, in the original Greek, begins:
«Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; ἐπιμένωμεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσῃ; μὴ γένοιτο.»
Translated:
"What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? Certainly not!"
The phrase μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito) is an emphatic rejection.
Paul is not mildly suggesting that continuing in sin might be unwise.
He is forcefully rejecting the idea that God's grace should be used as an excuse to continue in sin.
And the context matters.
Romans 6 explains that believers have been united with Christ in His death and resurrection. Because they belong to Him, sin is no longer to reign over their mortal bodies.
Paul does not teach that Christians become incapable of sinning.
He teaches that sin must no longer be treated as their rightful master.
Jesus did not die so you could become comfortable in your chains. He died and rose again so sin would no longer have the final claim over your life.
Imagine a prisoner sitting in a dark cell.
For years, he has begged for freedom.
He has wept over the iron bars, the locked door, the hopelessness of captivity.
Then one day, someone comes.
The debt is paid.
The door is opened.
The chains fall.
The prisoner is invited to walk into the light.
But instead of leaving, he begins decorating the cell.
He hangs pictures on the walls.
He makes the bed more comfortable.
He tells himself that captivity is not so terrible after all.
And when someone asks why he remains, he says, "Because I know I'm free."
That is the contradiction Paul is confronting.
Freedom in Christ is not freedom to embrace the slavery from which He has delivered us.
It is freedom to belong to Him.
But here is where we must be extraordinarily careful.
Because somewhere, someone reading this is not comfortable in sin at all.
You are exhausted by it.
You have prayed about the same weakness so many times that you are ashamed to pray again.
You have made promises you failed to keep.
You have cried after another relapse.
You have wondered whether God is tired of hearing your apologies.
You have asked yourself whether a genuine Christian could possibly struggle as much as you do.
And perhaps this article has made your chest tighten because you are afraid that your failures prove you never loved Jesus.
Please hear this distinction.
A Christian who hates their sin but continues fighting against it is not in the same spiritual condition as someone who deliberately cherishes sin and refuses repentance.
That does not make repeated sin harmless.
Nor does feeling guilty automatically prove genuine repentance.
But Scripture does not tell broken believers to wait until they become perfect before approaching Christ.
First John 1:8 says that if we claim to have no sin, we deceive ourselves.
And the very next verse offers astonishing hope.
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — 1 John 1:9, KJV
John writes these words to believers.
People who still need confession.
People who still need cleansing.
People whose relationship with God is grounded not in their own perfection, but in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Then, in 1 John 2:1, he explains that he writes so believers will not sin, but if anyone does sin, Jesus Christ the righteous is their advocate with the Father.
Do you see the beauty of that balance?
Do not sin.
But if you sin, do not run away from Jesus.
Run toward Him in repentance and faith.
Because the same Christ who calls you to holiness is the Christ who intercedes for His people.
He is not indifferent to your sin.
And He is not unwilling to receive the repentant sinner.
That is the Gospel.
Not a message that says your sin does not matter.
But the breathtaking announcement that your sin was serious enough to require the cross, and God's love was great enough to give His Son.
Now consider Peter.
A man who genuinely loved Jesus.
A man who had witnessed His glory.
A man who boldly declared his loyalty.
And yet, when fear tightened its grip, Peter denied knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Luke 22:61 records that after Peter's denial, the Lord turned and looked at him.
Imagine that moment.
The courtyard.
The cold night.
The fading echoes of his own denial.
And then the eyes of Jesus.
The One Peter had promised never to abandon.
The One he had just denied.
Scripture does not tell us everything Peter saw in that look.
We should not pretend to know every emotion that passed between them.
But we do know what happened next.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
His failure was real.
His grief was real.
And his story was not over.
After the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, beside the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus questioned Peter about his love and entrusted him with the responsibility to care for His sheep.
The man who had denied Jesus was not beyond restoration.
But notice something crucial.
Jesus did not restore Peter by declaring that denial was acceptable.
He restored him into a life of renewed love, obedience, and service.
Grace did not erase the seriousness of Peter's failure. Grace ensured that Peter's failure would not be the final chapter of his story.
From shame to restoration.
From denial to discipleship.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps that is exactly what someone reading this needs to understand.
Your worst failure does not have to become your permanent identity.
Your hidden sin does not have to remain your secret prison.
Your past does not have the authority to cancel the future Christ is calling you into.
But you cannot embrace His restoration while insisting on protecting the very sin He is calling you to surrender.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible after being caught.
It is not simply crying because consequences have arrived.
And it is not promising change just long enough for the guilt to disappear.
The New Testament commonly uses the Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance, associated with a change of mind and understanding that involves turning toward God.
Biblical repentance is not merely a passing emotion.
It is a real reorientation of the heart and life toward God, producing fruit consistent with that change.
That does not mean every sinful habit disappears instantly.
Some battles involve years of growth, accountability, wise counsel, prayer, practical boundaries, and persistent dependence on the Holy Spirit.
But repentance stops defending the enemy.
It stops calling darkness light.
It stops treating God's patience as permission.
And when it falls, it returns to the Savior instead of building a theology to excuse the fall.
There is an Old Testament passage that beautifully captures the seriousness of this surrender.
Ezekiel 36:26 contains God's promise:
וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב חָדָשׁ
Ve-natatti lakhem lev chadash.
"And I will give you a new heart."
In its original context, this promise was given to Israel as part of God's promised restoration, including cleansing, a new heart, and the gift of His Spirit.
It must not be stripped from that covenant setting.
Yet the wider biblical story reveals the significance of God's transforming work, fulfilled through the new covenant established by Jesus Christ.
God does not merely demand external improvement.
He acts to renew His people from within.
And that is something human willpower alone cannot accomplish.
You can delete an app and still desire the sin.
You can avoid a person and still nurture bitterness.
You can stop saying certain words while pride continues ruling your heart.
You can change your surroundings without surrendering your affections.
External boundaries are valuable.
Sometimes they are absolutely necessary.
But the deepest transformation is not merely behavioral management.
It is the work of God renewing a human heart.
That is why you need more than motivation.
You need Christ.
You need the Holy Spirit.
You need the Word of God to confront the lies you have believed.
You need a community of faithful believers who will love you enough to encourage you and tell you the truth.
And sometimes you need to make a painful decision that your old self would never have made.
End the relationship that continually draws you into disobedience.
Confess the deception.
Return what you dishonestly took.
Seek forgiveness from the person you wounded.
Get help for the addiction you keep hiding.
Put boundaries around the temptations you have been deliberately feeding.
Not because these actions earn God's forgiveness.
But because repentance bears fruit.
And because loving Jesus involves learning to say no to the things that pull your heart away from Him.
Jesus used startling language in Matthew 5:29–30 about removing whatever causes one to sin.
In context, He was emphasizing the radical seriousness with which sin must be addressed, not commanding literal self-injury.
The point is unmistakable.
Do not make comfortable arrangements with what is destroying you.
Some doors need to be closed.
Some habits need to be abandoned.
Some secrets need to be brought into the light.
And some excuses need to die before the life you keep praying for can begin taking shape.
But perhaps the greatest danger is not that you have committed a terrible sin.
Perhaps it is that you have become so accustomed to it that you no longer want to change.
Hebrews 3:13 warns believers about being hardened through the deceitfulness of sin.
That word deceitfulness matters.
Sin does not usually introduce itself by announcing that it intends to destroy your fellowship with God, damage your relationships, and dull your conscience.
It whispers.
"Just this once."
"Everyone does it."
"You deserve this."
"God knows your heart."
"You can repent tomorrow."
And tomorrow becomes next week.
Next week becomes next year.
The conscience grows quieter.
The excuses grow louder.
And eventually the person who once trembled at the thought of dishonoring Christ begins defending the very things they once begged Him to remove.
That is why a comfortable relationship with unrepentant sin is spiritually dangerous.
Not because one failure places a repentant believer beyond God's mercy.
But because persistent, willing rebellion against Christ contradicts the profession that He is Lord.
First John 3:6–10 speaks forcefully about the incompatibility between abiding in Christ and an ongoing pattern of lawlessness.
These verses must be read alongside 1 John 1:8–2:2, where the same apostle acknowledges believers' continuing need for forgiveness and Christ's advocacy.
John is not contradicting himself.
He is distinguishing the life characterized by fellowship with God from a life characterized by persistent, unrepentant rebellion.
And we should not use those passages to make final judgments about every struggling person's salvation.
God knows the heart.
But neither should we soften John's warning until it loses its force.
A faith that continually makes peace with what Jesus calls sin deserves serious examination, not automatic reassurance.
Second Corinthians 13:5 tells believers to examine themselves to see whether they are in the faith.
That is not an invitation to endless despair.
It is an invitation to spiritual honesty.
So ask yourself.
When was the last time God's Word changed a decision you were determined to make?
When was the last time you confessed something without waiting to be exposed?
When was the last time you chose obedience even though disobedience promised immediate pleasure?
When was the last time you stopped explaining away a sin and simply admitted, "Lord, You are right, and I am wrong"?
And perhaps the hardest question of all:
Is there something in your life you are asking Jesus to bless that He is actually calling you to leave behind?
Stay with that question for a moment.
Do not rush to another notification.
Do not immediately search your mind for someone who needs to read this more than you.
Allow the Word of God to examine you first.
Because this is not about winning an argument over whether a Christian can sin.
Every Christian still needs grace.
This is about whether we are willing to let the grace of God change us.
And the answer to the title's question must be given carefully.
Can you love Jesus and still struggle with sin?
Yes.
Peter did.
The apostle John acknowledged that believers still sin.
