In Proverbs 5:22, the Hebrew text reads:
עֲוֹנוֹתָיו יִלְכְּדֻנוֹ אֶת־הָרָשָׁע וּבְחַבְלֵי חַטָּאתוֹ יִתָּמֵךְ
Transliterated:
ʿAvonotav yilkkeduno et-harashaʿ, uveḥavlei ḥattaʾto yittamekh.
The Hebrew verb יִלְכְּדֻנוֹ (yilkkeduno) comes from a root associated with catching, capturing, or trapping.
The word חַבְלֵי (ḥavlei) means cords or ropes.
And חַטָּאתוֹ (ḥattaʾto) refers to his sin.
The picture is vivid.
A man caught by his own wrongdoing.
Held by the ropes of his own sin.
Not because desire itself is always evil, but because desire, when welcomed into disobedience and repeatedly indulged, can become a powerful instrument of bondage.
This is not a description of every struggle, addiction, or hardship. Nor does it mean every person who suffers has brought suffering upon himself.
It is a specific biblical warning about the destructive power of persistent, unrepentant sin.
And the context matters.
Proverbs 5 is a father's warning to his son about sexual temptation, especially the danger of adultery and the seductive invitation of forbidden intimacy.
The chapter begins by calling the son to wisdom and discernment.
It describes the tempting words of the forbidden woman as sweet as honey, yet warns that the consequences of pursuing her can become bitter.

The passage is not teaching that women are inherently dangerous or that men alone struggle with temptation. It warns against the path of sexual unfaithfulness, while celebrating faithfulness within marriage.
That distinction matters because Scripture is not condemning the existence of human desire.
God created human beings with desires.
Hunger is not evil.
The longing for love is not evil.
Sexual desire within God's design is not evil.
Wanting companionship, affection, intimacy, and belonging is not evil.
But a good desire can become destructive when we demand its satisfaction outside God's wisdom.
And sometimes the thing that destroys a person does not initially look like something terrible.
Sometimes it looks like attention.
Someone finally notices you.
Someone listens to your frustrations.
Someone makes you feel attractive again.
Someone seems to understand what your spouse does not.
At first, it feels innocent.
You tell yourself it is just conversation.
Then you begin looking forward to their messages.
Then you start hiding the conversations.
Then you find yourself sharing things with them that you no longer share with your spouse.
Then the relationship begins to occupy your imagination.
And one day, the person who once insisted, "I would never cross that line," discovers that the line has already been crossed.
Not in one dramatic moment.
But through a hundred smaller permissions.
That is how many forms of temptation work.
The first compromise does not always feel like captivity.
It can feel like freedom.
The first lie feels manageable.
The first secret feels containable.
The first forbidden indulgence feels temporary.
And because the consequences do not immediately arrive, we begin mistaking God's patience for His approval.
But delayed consequences are not proof that a decision is harmless.
And God's mercy is never permission to keep destroying ourselves.
Imagine a man standing beside a cliff.
The warning sign is visible.
The ground is unstable.
He knows the danger.
But he takes one step closer because he wants a better view.
Nothing happens.
So he takes another.
Still nothing.
Soon he begins to believe the warning was exaggerated.
Until the ground beneath him finally gives way.
The tragedy is not that he was never warned.
The tragedy is that every step without immediate disaster made him less willing to believe the warning.
That is why Proverbs 5:23 is so sobering.
The Hebrew text says:
הוּא יָמוּת בְּאֵין מוּסָר וּבְרֹב אִוַּלְתּוֹ יִשְׁגֶּה
Transliterated:
Hu yamut beʾein musar, uverov ʾivvalto yishgeh.
The word מוּסָר (musar) carries the sense of discipline, correction, or instruction.
And יִשְׁגֶּה (yishgeh) comes from a verb that can mean to stray, wander, or go astray.
The verse portrays a man whose refusal of correction and abundance of folly lead him toward ruin.
He does not merely make a mistake.
He refuses the wisdom that could have redirected his steps.
That is the deeper danger.
Sometimes the greatest threat to your future is not the temptation you feel, but the correction you keep refusing.
Consider how often God may confront us through His Word, through a troubled conscience, through the counsel of a faithful friend, or through circumstances that expose what we would rather conceal.
And yet we say:
"I can stop whenever I want."
"It isn't hurting anyone."
"God knows my heart."
"Everyone struggles with something."
"I'll repent when I'm ready."
Some of those statements contain fragments of truth.
God does know your heart.
Everyone does struggle.
And God's mercy is greater than we can measure.
But those truths become dangerous when we use them to excuse what God calls us to surrender.
God's knowledge of your heart is not a reason to hide your sin.
It is a reason to come honestly before the One who already sees you and still calls you to repentance.
And there is something even more unsettling in the wider context of Proverbs 5.
Verse 21 says:
"For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD, and he pondereth all his goings."
Before the passage describes the cords of sin, it reminds us that God sees the path we are walking.
Not merely the final act.
The path.
The messages.
The motives.
The rationalizations.
The hidden decisions.
The moments when we could have turned around.
This is not meant to portray God as a cruel observer waiting for an opportunity to humiliate us.
It reveals that we live before the eyes of a holy God whose wisdom cannot be deceived by the stories we tell ourselves.
You may successfully hide a conversation from your spouse.
You may erase your browsing history.
You may convince your friends that everything is fine.
You may even become so practiced at pretending that you almost believe your own performance.
But you cannot hide the direction of your heart from God.
And the reason that should shake us is also the reason it should give us hope.
The God who sees the sin you have hidden is also the God before whom you can finally stop pretending.
Perhaps you are reading this with a heavy conscience.
Perhaps there is a habit you have tried to abandon repeatedly.
You prayed.
You cried.
You made promises.
You deleted the app.
You blocked the number.
You told yourself this would be the last time.
And then, somehow, you found yourself back in the same place.
The shame became heavier.
Your prayers became shorter.
Your Bible remained closed longer.
You began avoiding Christian conversations because they reminded you of the distance between your confession and your conduct.
And eventually, the enemy's accusation began to sound convincing.
"You're a hypocrite."
"God must be tired of you."
"You've failed too many times."
"You might as well stop trying."
But listen carefully.
Those accusations are not the voice of the Gospel.
Sin is serious.
Repentance is necessary.
And grace is not a license to continue in rebellion.
Yet the Gospel does not announce that sinners are beyond redemption.
It announces that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
The apostle Paul wrote:
"This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief." — 1 Timothy 1:15, KJV
Paul did not minimize his past.
He had persecuted the church.
He knew what it meant to look backward and see things he could never undo.
Yet his testimony was not that his past had become harmless.
It was that the mercy of Christ was greater than his guilt.
And that brings us to something extraordinary.
Proverbs 5 describes a man held by the cords of his own sin.
But Jesus came to accomplish what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He came to rescue us from sin's guilt and dominion.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to give us new life.
The Gospel is not merely advice about managing desire.
It is the announcement of a Savior who died for our sins and rose again.
Jesus did not go to the cross because sin was insignificant.
He went because sin was so serious that reconciliation required His sacrificial death.
And because His love was so great that He willingly gave Himself.
In John 8:34, Jesus says:
"Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin."
The Greek text uses the expression:
δοῦλός ἐστιν τῆς ἁμαρτίας
Doulos estin tēs hamartias.
It means "is a slave of sin."
The language is strikingly consistent with the warning of Proverbs.
Sin promises independence.
Then it demands obedience.
It promises pleasure.
Then it begins setting the terms.
It promises that you are in control.
Then it exposes how little control you actually possess.
But Jesus does not end His teaching with the diagnosis.
In John 8:36, He declares:
"If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed."
In Greek:
ἐὰν οὖν ὁ υἱὸς ὑμᾶς ἐλευθερώσῃ, ὄντως ἐλεύθεροι ἔσεσθε.
Ean oun ho huios hymas eleutherōsē, ontōs eleutheroi esesthe.
The freedom Jesus describes is not permission to pursue every craving.
It is liberation from slavery to sin through the Son of God.
And that changes everything.
Because the answer to uncontrolled sinful desire is not simply to develop stronger willpower.
Wisdom, discipline, boundaries, accountability, and wise choices matter enormously.
But at the center of Christian transformation is something deeper.
A new relationship with God through Jesus Christ.
A new heart.
A new allegiance.
A new direction.
The Holy Spirit's ongoing work of sanctification.
The grace to confess, turn away, resist temptation, and walk in obedience.
Not instant perfection.
Not a life without struggle.
But a real transformation that begins in Christ and continues as we follow Him.
This is why the apostle James describes temptation with such clarity.
James 1:14–15 says:
"But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death."

The Greek word translated "lust" in the KJV is ἐπιθυμία (epithymia), meaning desire or longing. The word itself can refer to desires of different kinds depending on context, but here James is speaking of desire that entices a person toward sin.
Notice the progression.
Desire draws.
Temptation entices.
Sin develops.
And sin, left to its destructive course, brings death.
James is not saying that experiencing temptation is itself identical to committing sin.
Even Jesus was tempted, yet without sin, as Hebrews 4:15 teaches.
The danger is what happens when temptation is welcomed, nurtured, justified, and acted upon.
You cannot always prevent a tempting thought from appearing.
But you can refuse to make a home for it.
You cannot always prevent someone from offering forbidden intimacy.
But you can choose not to cultivate secrecy with them.
You cannot always control the first impulse.
But through God's grace, you can learn to respond to it differently.
Sometimes faithfulness looks like closing the screen.
Sometimes it looks like ending a relationship you know is leading you away from Christ.
Sometimes it looks like confessing a hidden struggle to a mature, trustworthy believer.
Sometimes it looks like seeking qualified professional help when compulsive behavior has become difficult to manage.
Sometimes it means accepting consequences, making restitution, rebuilding trust slowly, and allowing those you have hurt the space and safety they need.
And sometimes it means admitting something your pride has fought desperately to avoid.
"I need help."
There is no spiritual honor in pretending you are stronger than you are.
There is wisdom in bringing darkness into the light.
Proverbs 28:13 says:
"He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy."
Notice that biblical repentance is more than feeling terrible afterward.
It involves confession and forsaking sin.
The Hebrew idea of turning away from evil runs throughout Scripture.
Repentance is not simply regretting consequences.
It is turning toward God and away from the sin that has dishonored Him.
And the grace of Jesus makes that return possible.
Perhaps one of the most moving examples of this is Peter.
He was not a stranger to Jesus.
He had walked with Him.
He had witnessed miracles.
He had heard teachings that changed human history.
And he confidently declared that he would remain faithful.
But when the pressure came, Peter denied knowing Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine the weight of that failure.
Imagine hearing the rooster crow.
Imagine remembering the warning.
Imagine realizing that the courage you believed you possessed had collapsed in the moment you needed it most.
Luke 22:61–62 records that the Lord turned and looked upon Peter, and Peter remembered His words.
Then Peter went out and wept bitterly.
What happened next matters.
Peter's failure was real.
His tears were real.
His need for repentance was real.
But his story did not end in the courtyard.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, Jesus questioned Peter's love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
The man who had denied Him was not told that denial was acceptable.
He was restored and called to faithful service.
That is the beauty of grace.
Jesus does not need to pretend your failure never happened in order to redeem what comes after it.
He can confront the truth and still offer mercy.
He can expose sin and still restore a repentant sinner.
He can call you out of the life that is destroying you without abandoning you to despair.
And this is where the message becomes deeply personal.
What desire have you been defending that God has been asking you to surrender?
What secret have you been protecting at the expense of your peace?
What relationship has begun pulling your heart away from obedience?
What appetite keeps demanding more, even after you promised it would be the last time?
What warning have you heard so often that it no longer frightens you?
Do not answer for someone else.
Not your spouse.
Not your pastor.
Not the people whose failures you can easily identify.
You.
Because it is possible to recognize the sins of an entire generation while refusing to confront the one sin quietly governing your own decisions.
Jesus asked in Mark 8:36:
"For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?"
What if you finally get the attention you wanted, but lose the trust of the people who loved you?
What if you experience the forbidden pleasure, but spend years repairing what it shattered?
What if you protect your reputation so carefully that you never allow yourself to be honest enough to seek help?
What if the desire you keep feeding is slowly making you indifferent to the Savior you claim to follow?
Those are difficult questions.
But Scripture asks difficult questions because eternity matters.
And love sometimes tells us the truth we would rather avoid.
Still, there is another question.
What if you turned around today?
Not when you feel stronger.
Not after one more indulgence.
Not after the consequences become unbearable.
Today.
What if you finally confessed what you have been hiding?
What if you stopped calling it harmless?
What if you surrendered the relationship, habit, fantasy, or secret compromise you have been protecting?
What if you believed that obedience to Christ is better than the temporary comfort of disobedience?
You may still have consequences to face.
You may need to repair damaged relationships.
Some people may need time before they can trust you again.
And forgiveness from God does not erase every earthly consequence.
But you do not need to remain on the same destructive path.
There is a difference between the pain of repentance and the devastation of refusing to repent.
One leads you toward truth and life.
The other keeps you running from both.
And when shame tells you that you have gone too far, remember the promise of 1 John 1:9:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
The foundation of that forgiveness is not your emotional intensity.
It is the faithfulness of God and the saving work of Jesus Christ.
You do not purchase forgiveness through tears.
You do not earn redemption by making enough promises.
You come to Christ in repentance and faith, trusting the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
And when you belong to Him, you are called to walk in the newness of life He gives.
Romans 6:12 says:
"Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, that ye should obey it in the lusts thereof."
That word "reign" matters.
The Christian may still experience temptation.
But temptation must not be treated as king.
Your cravings are not your lord.
Your past is not your savior.
Your shame is not your identity.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And His lordship reaches into the places we most desperately want to keep private.
The phone nobody checks.
The conversations nobody hears.
The thoughts nobody knows.
The choices made when applause is absent and accountability seems far away.
Real discipleship is not simply looking Christian in public.
It is learning to follow Jesus when nobody is watching.
Not to earn His love.
But because His grace has changed whom you belong to.
And perhaps that is the sentence someone needs to carry into tonight:
You do not defeat sin by convincing yourself that you are incapable of falling. You resist sin by recognizing your weakness and depending upon the strength and grace of Jesus Christ.
If this message has uncovered something in your heart, do not rush past that conviction.
Sit with it.
Pray honestly.
Speak to God without rehearsing an impressive religious speech.
You might begin with something as simple as:

"Lord Jesus, You know what I have hidden. You know the desires I have excused, the warnings I have ignored, and the compromises I have made. I cannot save myself. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Forgive me, cleanse me, and teach me to turn from what dishonors You. Give me courage to confess what needs to be confessed, seek the help I need, and obey You even when obedience is costly. Change my heart. Teach me to love what is good. I surrender myself to You. Amen."
And if you prayed that sincerely, remember that the prayer is not a magical formula.
The call of the Gospel is to repent and believe in Jesus Christ, trusting Him as Savior and following Him as Lord.
Faith does not mean that every struggle disappears by tomorrow.
It means you no longer have to face the struggle apart from Him.
If you are exhausted from fighting a hidden battle, I want you to know something.
You do not have to publish the details of your private sins to prove that your repentance is real.
But you should not let shame isolate you from the trustworthy, godly help you need.
You do not owe strangers your private story.
But you are not the only person who needs the mercy of Jesus.
Someone reading the comments may realize for the first time that other believers are struggling, repenting, seeking help, and refusing to surrender their lives to sin.
And that realization may encourage them to reach out to someone trustworthy rather than continue suffering in silence.
This is one reason Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious language.
Not to build a community that merely applauds emotional stories.
But to keep pointing wounded, struggling, growing, and sometimes wandering people back to Jesus Christ and the truth of His Word.

Because a person can consume hundreds of inspirational messages and still remain spiritually malnourished if those messages never lead to Scripture, repentance, prayer, obedience, and a deeper relationship with God.
We need more than another moment of emotion.
We need discipleship.
We need truth that remains after the screen goes dark.
We need believers who are willing to study the Bible, confront their own hearts, encourage one another, and keep growing when the initial excitement has faded.

These resources are intended to help believers go deeper into Scripture, strengthen their understanding of the Gospel, grow in spiritual maturity, and continue learning long after a single article ends.
And I want to invite you to consider something beyond simply reading and moving on.

If this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, encouraged you through a difficult season, or challenged you to take your relationship with Christ more seriously, you can become part of helping that work continue.
For those who choose to give from their resources, that support can be an expression of Christian generosity and partnership in Gospel-centered work.
Some believers may choose to include such support in their personal giving budget, alongside their tithes and offerings according to their convictions and local church commitments.
You do not need to give money to earn His blessing.
And you should never feel that the grace of Jesus Christ is being offered for sale.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing rather than pressured.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not guilt.
Not spiritual pressure.
But an opportunity to participate voluntarily in work you believe is worth supporting.
These items are not the reason we proclaim the Gospel.
There are meaningful ways to help that cost nothing.
Not merely to increase the number of views, but because someone in your circle may be facing a private battle that they are too ashamed to discuss.
Someone may be one decision away from damaging their marriage.
Someone may be losing hope that genuine change is possible.
Someone may have mistaken the repetition of their failures for proof that Jesus no longer wants them.
A thoughtful share could place a timely biblical warning—and the hope of the Gospel—in front of that person.
Be gentle. Do not publicly identify another person's hidden struggles or use this article to embarrass anyone.
Sometimes the most loving thing you can do is send a quiet message that says, "This reminded me how much we all need God's grace."

And invite your family, friends, struggling believers, people who have drifted from their faith, those exploring Christianity, and even those who do not yet believe to encounter the truth of Jesus Christ through this community.
Bigger than a page.
Bigger than a single article.
It is about proclaiming the Savior who rescues sinners and transforms lives.
And before you leave, I want you to think about the person in Proverbs 5 one final time.
He is not described as a man who never encountered wisdom.
He is described as someone who failed to receive the correction that could have redirected him.
His downfall is a warning.
But you are reading that warning now.
You are hearing it before the next decision.
Before the next message.
Before the next secret meeting.
Before the next compromise.
Before the next excuse.
What will you do with it?
Will you continue feeding what is destroying your peace?
Will you keep calling bondage freedom?
Will you wait until the cords become tighter?
Or will you turn to the One who came to set captives free?
There is no need to pretend that surrender is easy.
Sometimes obedience means grieving the loss of something your flesh still wants.
Sometimes it means choosing truth when a lie would protect your reputation.
Sometimes it means accepting the painful work of rebuilding what sin has damaged.
But Christ is worthy of that surrender.
Not because obedience guarantees an easy life.
Not because repentance erases every consequence.
But because Jesus is better than the sin that promises to satisfy you while leading you away from Him.
Remember the warning of Proverbs 5:22–23.
Sin can capture.
Folly can destroy.
Refusing correction can lead to ruin.
But do not read those verses without also remembering the Gospel.
The Son of God entered our broken world, lived without sin, bore the penalty of sin through His death, and rose victoriously from the grave.
Through Him there is forgiveness.
Through Him there is reconciliation with God.
Through Him there is the gift of new life.
Through Him there is hope for genuine transformation.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
Your choices may have created real consequences.
Your struggle may require patience, accountability, and sustained effort.
But none of those things makes Jesus powerless to save a repentant sinner.
So come into the light.
Tell the truth.
Turn from sin.
Trust Christ.
And keep walking with Him.
Because the greatest testimony is not always the person who never fell into a scandal.
Sometimes it is the person who finally stopped hiding, surrendered to Jesus, and discovered that the grace of God was not permission to remain the same—but power to begin living differently.
The sin you keep defending may become the chain that breaks you—but the Savior you surrender to is able to give you a new life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “HIS LEFT HAND IS UNDER MY HEAD, AND HIS RIGHT HAND EMBRACES ME”—THE BIBLE’S UNEMBARRASSED LANGUAGE OF AFFECTION
paragraphs: “HIS LEFT HAND IS UNDER MY HEAD, AND HIS RIGHT HAND EMBRACES ME”—THE BIBLE’S UNEMBARRASSED LANGUAGE OF AFFECTION

What if the tenderness you have been ashamed to desire is something God Himself was never ashamed to put in Scripture? A breathtaking journey through Song of Songs 8:3, the sacred beauty of human affection, the wounds of misplaced love, and the Savior who teaches broken hearts what love was always meant to be.
There is a sentence in the Bible that sounds almost too intimate to be read aloud in church.
Not because it is sinful.
Not because it is inappropriate.

But because somewhere along the way, many of us became more comfortable talking about spiritual warfare than tenderness. More comfortable discussing obedience than affection. More comfortable preaching against lust than explaining the beauty of love that is patient, faithful, gentle, and unashamed.
And then, right there in the sacred pages of Scripture, a woman speaks.
“His left hand should be under my head, and his right hand should embrace me.” — Song of Solomon 8:3, KJV
Read that again.
There is no embarrassment in her voice.
No apology for wanting to be held.
No suggestion that affection itself is dirty.
Just the language of a woman who longs for the closeness of the one she loves.
One hand supporting her head.
The other drawing her near.
And God, in His wisdom, allowed those words to stand in the Bible.

But before we turn this verse into a romantic slogan, before we use it to justify whatever our hearts desire, and before we rush to make every embrace a direct promise from Jesus, we need to understand something extraordinary.
The God who commands holiness is not the enemy of tenderness.
And the God who created human affection also knows how deeply human affection can wound us when it is separated from truth.
Because some of us are not reading this verse with butterflies in our stomachs.
Some of us are reading it with tears behind our eyes.
You remember what it felt like to be held by someone who eventually walked away.
You remember the arms that once felt safe but later became a place of uncertainty.
You remember believing someone's promises because, at the time, their embrace felt more convincing than their character.
And perhaps the most painful memory is not the person who left.
It is the version of yourself who believed you had finally found a place to rest.
That is why this little verse deserves more than a beautiful photograph and a sentimental caption.
It deserves to be understood.
And its meaning is even richer when we allow Scripture to speak for itself.
In the original Hebrew, Song of Songs 8:3 reads:
שְׂמֹאלוֹ תַּחַת רֹאשִׁי וִימִינוֹ תְּחַבְּקֵנִי
Semolo tachat roshi, vimino techabbeqeni.
A close English rendering is:
“His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand embraces me.”
The Hebrew word תְּחַבְּקֵנִי (techabbeqeni) comes from the verb חָבַק (chavaq), meaning “to embrace” or “to clasp.”
It is not merely a word for looking at someone with admiration from a distance.
It describes physical closeness.
An embrace.
The kind of nearness that cannot be reduced to an abstract idea.
The left hand is described as being beneath the woman's head, while the right hand embraces her. The picture is one of intimate, bodily affection between lovers.
There is also a small but meaningful translation detail.
The King James Version says, “His left hand should be under my head,” while many modern translations render the statement in the present tense: “His left hand is under my head.”
The Hebrew poetic line does not contain an explicit English-style verb for “is” or “should be.” Translators must interpret the relationship between the words and the surrounding context.
This means we should be careful not to build an entire doctrine upon one English auxiliary verb.
The central image remains clear.
A woman speaks of being embraced by her beloved.
And the biblical text does not treat that desire as shameful.
But here is where the story becomes even more beautiful.
Song of Songs 8:3 is not an isolated sentence.
A nearly identical declaration appears earlier in Song of Songs 2:6.
The repetition matters.
Throughout the book, we encounter longing, admiration, delight, anticipation, separation, searching, reunion, and the deep desire for mutual belonging.
These are not the emotions of lifeless religious machinery.
They are recognizably human.
And Scripture gives them poetic expression.

The Song of Songs is a collection of love poetry celebrating the beauty and intensity of human love. Jewish and Christian interpreters have also historically explored spiritual readings involving God's covenant relationship with His people and Christ's love for the Church.
Those spiritual reflections can be meaningful when handled carefully.
But we must not erase the poem's human subject.
The woman is speaking about her beloved.
The verse is not originally a direct quotation from Jesus promising to physically embrace every believer.
And that distinction does not diminish its spiritual importance.
It protects the integrity of God's Word.
Because we do not honor Scripture by making it say whatever comforts us most.
We honor Scripture by receiving what God actually gave us.
And what He gave us here is astonishing.
A sacred poem that speaks openly about the beauty of affection.
Think about that.
The same Bible that calls us to flee sexual immorality also celebrates the goodness of love within its proper boundaries.
The same God who warns against lust created human beings with the capacity for tenderness, desire, attachment, and delight.
The same Creator who said, “Be ye holy; for I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16) also declared, before sin entered the world, that it was not good for the man to be alone (Genesis 2:18).
Human companionship was not invented by the fall.
It belonged to God's good creation.
And marriage, as presented in Genesis 2:24, establishes a covenantal union in which a man and woman become one flesh.
That is why biblical holiness must never be confused with contempt for the human body.
God did not create affection and then become embarrassed by His own creation.
Sin corrupts what God made good.
But corruption is not the same thing as creation.
And this is a distinction many wounded hearts desperately need to hear.
Your longing to be loved is not automatically evidence that something is wrong with you.
But your longing, like every other human desire, must be guided by God's truth.
Because not every embrace is love.
Not every expression of affection is faithful.
Not every person who knows how to hold you knows how to honor you.
And not everyone who whispers, “I love you,” understands what love demands.
There are people who can make you feel cherished for an evening and abandoned by morning.
People who want the privileges of intimacy without the responsibilities of commitment.
People who enjoy your vulnerability but refuse to protect it.
People who say all the right things while their actions quietly contradict every promise.
And perhaps you have known that kind of affection.
Perhaps you mistook attention for devotion.
Chemistry for character.
Possession for protection.
Desire for covenant love.
Perhaps you gave someone access to the most vulnerable parts of your life because you thought being wanted meant being valued.
And when everything collapsed, you did not merely lose a relationship.
You began questioning your worth.
You wondered whether you had been too much.
Too emotional.
Too needy.
Too difficult to love.
Or perhaps you began believing that tenderness itself was dangerous.
So you hardened your heart.
You learned to smile without trusting.
To communicate without revealing.
To stand close to people while keeping your soul far away.
You told yourself you were becoming stronger.
But sometimes what we call strength is simply pain that has learned how to hide.
And then Song of Songs 8:3 appears.
A woman resting in the embrace of her beloved.
No performance.
No competition.
No frantic attempt to prove she deserves affection.
Just closeness.
And suddenly you realize how exhausting it has been to spend your life trying to earn what you were created to receive as a gift.
But there is another truth we must face.
A beautiful embrace cannot make an unhealthy relationship holy.
Tenderness does not excuse manipulation.
Passion does not excuse betrayal.
Romantic intensity does not erase the need for faithfulness, integrity, self-control, and mutual honor.
A relationship can feel emotionally powerful and still lead you away from God.
And a person can speak the language of love while refusing to practice its character.
That is why Scripture never asks us to judge love by emotion alone.
First Corinthians 13:4–6 tells us that love is patient and kind, is not self-seeking, and does not rejoice in wrongdoing but rejoices with the truth.
Notice what that means.
Biblical love is not merely concerned with how intensely someone desires you.
It is concerned with how faithfully they treat you.
Love does not become more authentic when it demands that you violate your conscience.
It does not become deeper when it isolates you from wise counsel.
It does not become sacred because someone uses Bible verses to pressure you into intimacy.
And it does not become Christlike when forgiveness is used to silence accountability.
If someone has used the language of love to control, threaten, exploit, or abuse you, their behavior should not be confused with the tenderness celebrated in Scripture.
God's Word does not require you to remain exposed to harm in order to prove that you understand grace.
You can forgive without pretending evil was good.
You can desire reconciliation without ignoring the need for genuine repentance.
And you can seek safety while trusting the Lord.
Because the embrace described in Song of Songs is not an invitation to surrender your discernment.
It is a poetic celebration of affection that belongs within the larger biblical vision of faithful love.
And that vision reaches its deepest theological meaning when we turn our eyes toward Jesus Christ.
Not because Song of Songs 8:3 secretly contains a prediction about His arms.
But because the whole witness of Scripture reveals the God whose love is holy, truthful, sacrificial, and redeeming.
Look at Jesus.
Look at the way He approached people whom society had learned to avoid.
A leper came to Him in desperate need.
According to Mark 1:40–42, the man pleaded for cleansing.
Jesus did something remarkable.
He stretched out His hand and touched him.
He could have healed the man without touching him.
He had authority to do so.
Yet the Gospel records His touch.
For a man living with the burden of his disease and its social consequences, that moment was more than an impressive display of power.
It revealed the compassion of the Savior.
Jesus was not made unclean by showing mercy.
His holiness was not threatened by the suffering person before Him.
His touch accompanied the restoration He brought.
And then consider the children.
In Mark 10:13–16, people brought little children to Jesus, and the disciples rebuked them.
But Jesus welcomed them.
He took them in His arms, laid His hands upon them, and blessed them.
The Son of God was not too important to hold a child.
Not too occupied to offer tenderness.
Not too holy to show affection.
Yet we must also remember that Christ's love is greater than physical touch.
He loves with perfect righteousness.
He confronts sin.
He calls people to repentance.
He gives Himself for sinners.
He does not simply affirm everything we desire.
He transforms us.
And nowhere is that love more clearly revealed than at the cross.
Because the greatest demonstration of divine love was not a romantic embrace.
It was the crucifixion of Jesus Christ for sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired our reputations.
Not after we convinced everyone that our past was spotless.
While we were still guilty and in need of mercy, Christ died for us.
That is the scandal of grace.
The Holy One gave Himself for the unholy.
The righteous Savior suffered for the unrighteous.
The One who had no sin bore the judgment that sinners deserved.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are proclaimed to everyone who repents and believes in Him.
This is where our story becomes more than a reflection on romance.
Because some people reading these words have never struggled with a lack of affection.
They have struggled with the consequences of seeking affection in places where God never called them to find their identity.
You may have crossed boundaries you once promised yourself you would never cross.
You may have betrayed someone's trust.
You may have confused sexual intimacy with covenant faithfulness.
You may have been unfaithful.
You may have built a secret life around desires you were unwilling to surrender.
Or perhaps you were the one betrayed, discarded, or deeply wounded by someone else's sin.
The circumstances are different.
The responsibility is different.
But every one of us needs a love that is greater than our ability to repair ourselves.
And the Gospel does not say that sin is harmless.
It says that Christ is mighty to save.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
That promise is not permission to continue deliberately in darkness.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
To stop defending what God calls sin.
To stop allowing shame to convince you that repentance is pointless.
To stop pretending that outward religious activity can replace inward surrender.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make your past feel less painful.
He came to save sinners and make them new.
And perhaps that is the part you have been avoiding.
You want the comfort of His presence.
But you have resisted the authority of His Word.
You want reassurance that you are loved.
But you do not want to release the relationship, habit, bitterness, or secret compromise that is pulling your heart away from Him.
You want grace to cover your wounds.
But you have not wanted grace to confront your rebellion.
And yet Christ's mercy is not opposed to His holiness.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners is the same Lord who calls them to follow Him.
He does not heal us by declaring that darkness is light.
He brings us out of darkness.
He does not redeem us so that we can remain enslaved to everything that destroyed us.
He redeems us so that we may belong to Him.
And there is something profoundly tender about that truth.
You do not need to disguise your sin to come to Christ.
You need to confess it.
You do not need to manufacture a spotless history.
You need the Savior whose blood cleanses sinners.
You do not need to convince Him that you have never been broken.
You need to trust that His grace is sufficient for those who turn to Him.
Maybe the most courageous prayer you can pray today is not a long, polished prayer.
Maybe it is simply:

“Lord Jesus, I have been looking for love in ways that have pulled me away from You. Forgive me. Teach me to love what is good. Heal what has been wounded. Expose what I have hidden. Give me the courage to obey You, even when obedience costs me something.”
And if that prayer reflects the struggle of your heart, do not rush past it.
Because sometimes the most important moment in an article is not the sentence that makes you emotional.
It is the moment you stop resisting what God is showing you.
There is another extraordinary passage near the conclusion of Song of Songs.
In Song of Songs 8:6, the woman speaks of love as strong as death and jealousy as fierce as the grave.
The Hebrew text includes the striking phrase:
כִּי־עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה
Ki-azzah khammavet ahavah.
“For love is strong as death.”
Here, אַהֲבָה (ahavah) means “love,” and עַזָּה (azzah) expresses strength or fierceness.
The verse celebrates the extraordinary power and exclusivity of devoted human love.
Then Song of Songs 8:7 declares that many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods drown it.
This is not a claim that every romantic attachment is indestructible.
Nor is it a promise that every relationship will survive regardless of betrayal or disobedience.
It is poetic language describing the strength and pricelessness of genuine love.
The passage goes on to declare that even immense wealth cannot simply purchase it.
Think about that in a world where affection is so often treated like a transaction.
Where people measure their desirability by likes, messages, attention, physical appearance, or financial status.
Where some believe they must give more of themselves than they should just to keep someone interested.
Where others mistake being pursued for being treasured.
The Song reminds us that love cannot be reduced to something bought and sold.
And the Gospel takes us to an even deeper truth.
Your standing before God cannot be purchased with money, earned through religious performance, or secured by becoming desirable in the eyes of others.
Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works, so that no one may boast.
That means your greatest hope is not that someone will finally choose you romantically.
Your greatest hope is that, through Jesus Christ, sinners can be reconciled to the living God.
Human marriage is a beautiful gift, but it is not the ultimate purpose of human existence.
Not everyone will marry.
Not every believer will experience the affection described in Song of Songs 8:3.
Some are single.
Some are widowed.
Some have endured painful separations.
Some live with loneliness that no one around them seems to notice.
And some have spent years asking God why a desire that seems so natural has remained unfulfilled.
If that is you, please hear this carefully.
Your life is not an unfinished story because you do not have someone holding you tonight.
Jesus Himself lived a fully human, holy, and complete life without marriage.
The apostle Paul affirmed the value of singleness and marriage as different circumstances in which believers can serve the Lord (1 Corinthians 7).
Your dignity does not depend on being someone's spouse.
Your spiritual maturity is not measured by romantic attention.
And your belonging to Christ is not diminished by the absence of human romance.
God has not promised every Christian a husband or wife.
But He has promised His people something greater than earthly companionship can ultimately provide.
His faithful presence.
Hebrews 13:5 records God's assurance:
“I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.”
That promise should not be turned into a guarantee that loneliness will immediately disappear.
Christians still grieve.
They still long for companionship.
They still experience nights when faith is real and tears are real too.
But the promise means that God's covenant faithfulness is not dependent on whether another human being stays.
And sometimes that truth becomes most precious when the house is quiet.
When the phone does not ring.
When the person you expected to grow old with is no longer there.
When memories return without warning.
When you are tired of being told that everything happens for a reason, because what you really need is someone willing to sit beside you while you grieve.
The Lord is not indifferent to those tears.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
He is near.
Not because every loss will be reversed in this life.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored.
But because the God who saves His people is compassionate toward their suffering.
And through Jesus Christ, the brokenhearted are not left without hope.
Perhaps you are married, but you have forgotten how to be tender.
You still share a home.
You still manage responsibilities.
You still discuss bills, children, appointments, and everything that must be done before tomorrow.
But somewhere between surviving and providing, you stopped making room for affection.
You no longer reach for your spouse's hand.
You no longer speak with the gentleness you once offered so freely.
You have become efficient partners in managing life while slowly becoming strangers in expressing love.
Song of Songs reminds married couples that affection need not be treated as an embarrassing extra.
Tenderness can be part of the faithful cultivation of covenant love.
Not as a demand.
Not as an entitlement to another person's body.
Not as a substitute for addressing unresolved harm.
But as a gift expressed with mutual care, respect, and delight.
Perhaps tonight the most meaningful thing you can do is not buy something expensive.
Perhaps it is to listen without defensiveness.
To apologize without excuses.
To hold a hand without expecting anything in return.
To tell your spouse, “I know I have been distant. I want to learn how to love you better.”
And perhaps you are the person who needs to hear those words.
Perhaps you have been waiting for years.
If so, do not confuse patience with a requirement to tolerate cruelty or abuse.
Love seeks truth.
Love takes responsibility.
Love protects rather than exploits.
And restoration, when possible, requires more than beautiful promises.
It requires changed behavior.
There is no biblical virtue in pretending a relationship is healthy simply because two people occasionally embrace.
But there is great beauty when affection grows in the soil of faithfulness.
When tenderness is supported by character.
When forgiveness is accompanied by repentance.
When a husband and wife learn, over time, to treat one another not as possessions but as people entrusted to their care.
That kind of love may not always look dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like an elderly couple sitting quietly together after decades of ordinary faithfulness.
One reaches for the other's hand.
No audience.
No applause.
No carefully arranged photograph.
Just a gesture so familiar that neither needs to explain it.
And perhaps that is one of the quiet lessons hidden inside the poetry.
Love does not have to be loud to be real.
Sometimes it is simply faithful.
And now we come back to the woman in Song of Songs.
“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.”
One hand beneath.
One hand around.
Support and nearness.
A simple image.
Yet it has carried us through the beauty of creation, the danger of counterfeit love, the pain of betrayal, the call to holiness, and the mercy of Jesus Christ.
But we must not leave without asking the question that matters most.
What are you allowing to define your worth?
Is it the person who chose you?
The person who rejected you?
The relationship you lost?
The affection you never received?
The mistake you cannot forget?
The shame you have carried for years?
Or the Lord Jesus Christ, who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His finished work?
Because the Gospel does not promise that every person who walks away will return.
It does not promise that every romantic longing will be fulfilled.
It does not promise that every wound will disappear on the schedule we prefer.
But it proclaims something gloriously certain.
Jesus Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He is alive.
He is Lord.
And those who turn to Him in repentance and faith receive forgiveness and new life.
That is a stronger foundation than any human embrace could ever provide.
And one day, for all who belong to Christ, the brokenness of this present world will give way to the fullness of His promised restoration.
Revelation 21:4 tells us that God will wipe away every tear from His people's eyes, and that death, sorrow, crying, and pain will pass away.
That promise is not about finding the perfect earthly romance.
It is about the final victory of God through Christ.
The end of sin's devastation.
The end of death.
The end of all that has made this world groan.
And until that day, we are called to love faithfully, walk humbly, repent sincerely, and receive every good gift with gratitude.
Maybe that is why this verse is so unforgettable.
It reminds us that God is not embarrassed by the tenderness He created.
And the wider story of Scripture reminds us that He is also unwilling to leave us enslaved to the sin that corrupts it.
He created us with the capacity to love.
He teaches us to distinguish love from selfishness.
He calls us to honor Him with our bodies and our relationships.
And in Jesus Christ, He offers redemption to those who have failed.
Not because scandal was secretly harmless.
Not because grace makes repentance unnecessary.
But because the cross of Jesus Christ is sufficient to save sinners, and His resurrection announces that sin and death do not have the final word.
Perhaps someone you know needs this message.
A wife who feels invisible.
A husband who has forgotten how to express tenderness.
A single believer wondering whether something is wrong with them.
A young person confusing attention with love.
A wounded Christian who thinks a painful past has permanently disqualified them from grace.
Or a friend who has never understood that the God of the Bible is both perfectly holy and abundantly merciful.

Has this passage changed how you understand biblical affection? Have you been learning to distinguish genuine love from attention that only looked like love? Or is God teaching you to trust His faithfulness in a season of loneliness?
You do not need to disclose private wounds to participate.
And if this article has convicted you of something you need to surrender, let that conviction lead you beyond a public comment into sincere prayer, repentance, and obedience to Christ.
Your testimony may help someone else realize that grace is not just a word Christians use.
It is the undeserved mercy of God revealed through Jesus Christ.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.

Not simply to publish emotionally moving articles, but to keep bringing people back to Scripture, to the Gospel, to repentance, to discipleship, and to the hope of transformation through Jesus Christ.
There are people in your circle who may never open a Christian book on their own, but who might stop long enough to read a Scripture-centered article you shared.
One faithful conversation can become the beginning of a deeper search for truth.
Our desire is that you would not merely read something that moves you for five minutes, but become more firmly rooted in God's Word for a lifetime.
It is helping another soul encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
And now, before you leave, remember the woman whose words began this journey.
“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.”
The Bible did not blush.
It did not apologize for the beauty of affection.
But neither did it make human affection our savior.
It pointed us toward the goodness of God's creation, and the rest of Scripture leads us to the One who can redeem what sin has broken.
So cherish tenderness.
Practice faithfulness.
Reject counterfeit love.
Honor the Lord with your relationships.
And when your heart is wounded, do not make another human being carry the weight that belongs to God alone.
Come to Jesus.
Not because you have never failed.
But because He is the Savior of sinners.
Not because you can promise never to stumble again.
But because His mercy calls you to rise, repent, and walk in newness of life.
And not because every person who once held you will remain.
But because the Lord who saves His people will never abandon those who belong to Him.
The arms you once trusted may have let you go, but the cross still declares that your broken story is not beyond the redeeming love of Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY TOLD YOU THAT IF YOU DON'T SPEAK IN TONGUES, YOU DON'T HAVE THE HOLY SPIRIT. BUT IS THAT WHAT JESUS ACTUALLY SAID?
paragraphs: THEY TOLD YOU THAT IF YOU DON'T SPEAK IN TONGUES, YOU DON'T HAVE THE HOLY SPIRIT. BUT IS THAT WHAT JESUS ACTUALLY SAID?
The painful question dividing Christians, the misunderstood miracle of Pentecost, and the biblical truth that could finally set a wounded believer free.
Imagine standing in a church filled with people worshiping God.
Hands are raised. Tears are falling. Voices are rising in languages you cannot understand.
Someone beside you begins speaking in tongues. Another person falls to their knees, overwhelmed with emotion. The preacher declares that the Holy Spirit is moving.
And you believe Him.
You love Jesus. You believe He died for your sins. You have confessed Him as Lord. You have cried out to Him in the darkest moments of your life. You have repented of things nobody else knows about.
But then someone places a hand on your shoulder and asks a question that quietly tears through your confidence.
"Have you received the Holy Spirit? Have you spoken in tongues yet?"
You hesitate.
"No."
Their expression changes.
"Then you need to keep praying until you receive Him."
And suddenly, something happens inside you that nobody in the room can see.
You begin questioning everything.
Was my salvation real?
Did God reject me?
Why can everyone else experience something I cannot?
Is there something wrong with my faith?
You return home that evening, carrying a burden you never expected to bring out of a worship service.
And perhaps the most painful thought comes when you finally lie down to sleep.
"Jesus, if You really live inside me, why can't I do what they do?"
If you have ever asked that question, please stay with me.
Because the answer is not found in the loudest voice in the sanctuary.
It is found in the Word of God.
And the truth may challenge both those who insist every Christian must speak in tongues and those who dismiss the gift altogether.
This is not an attack against Pentecostal Christians, charismatic believers, or anyone who sincerely practices spiritual gifts.
Nor is it an attempt to explain away the supernatural power of the Holy Spirit.
This is about something infinitely more important.
We must never require as proof of belonging to Jesus what Scripture does not require of every believer.
And we must never reject what God has genuinely given simply because we have seen people misuse it.
The Bible gives us a much more beautiful, challenging, and Christ-centered picture.
Let's begin in Jerusalem.
Not in a modern worship service.
Not in a theological debate.
But in an upstairs room where frightened disciples were waiting for a promise that would change the world.
Jesus had been crucified.
The One they followed had been publicly humiliated, nailed to a cross, and buried in a borrowed tomb.
But death had not held Him.
The risen Christ appeared to His followers, restored their hope, and commanded them to wait for the promised Holy Spirit.
In Acts 1:8, Jesus declared:
"But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me..." (KJV)
Notice what Jesus emphasized.
Power to be His witnesses.
Not spiritual superiority.
Not an opportunity to divide believers into first-class and second-class Christians.
Not a performance to prove who was closer to heaven.
The promised power was for the mission of Christ.
Then came Pentecost.
Acts 2 describes a sound like a mighty rushing wind, tongues appearing like fire, and believers being filled with the Holy Spirit.
They began speaking in other tongues as the Spirit enabled them.
The Greek expression in Acts 2:4 is:
ἑτέραις γλώσσαις — heterais glōssais
It means "other tongues" or "different languages."
The word glōssa can refer to the physical tongue or to a language, depending on context.
And the context of Acts 2 is extraordinary.
People from different nations heard the disciples declaring the wonderful works of God in their own languages.
The crowd was astonished.
These were Galileans.
How were they speaking languages they had not learned?
It was a miracle.
Not a manufactured religious experience.
Not something the disciples rehearsed.
Not a technique taught by an enthusiastic leader.
The Holy Spirit empowered ordinary people to proclaim God's mighty works across linguistic boundaries.
And Peter explained that this event fulfilled the promise associated with Joel's prophecy: God would pour out His Spirit, and His people would prophesy.
Young and old.
Men and women.
Servants and free.
The message was astonishing.
God was pouring out His Spirit in fulfillment of His redemptive promise.
And the exalted Jesus was the One pouring Him out.
But here is where we must ask a question that many believers are afraid to ask.
Does the fact that believers spoke in tongues at Pentecost mean that every Christian in every generation must speak in tongues to prove they have received the Holy Spirit?
We cannot answer that question with emotion alone.
We must examine the whole counsel of Scripture.
Because Acts records several remarkable occasions when people received the Holy Spirit.
And those occasions are not all described identically.
In Acts 10, Peter preached the Gospel to Cornelius and his household.
These were Gentiles.
People whom many Jewish believers would not have expected to receive the same covenant blessing in the same way.
While Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon those who heard the message.
The Jewish believers accompanying Peter were astonished.
Why?
Because the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even upon the Gentiles.
And they heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying God.
This was significant.
God was demonstrating that Gentile believers were not outsiders to the Gospel.
They were being welcomed through Jesus Christ.
The miracle confirmed their inclusion.
In Acts 19, Paul encountered certain disciples in Ephesus who knew John's baptism but needed to hear more fully about Jesus.
After they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus and Paul laid hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them.
They spoke in tongues and prophesied.
Again, a remarkable manifestation.
Again, a real work of God.
Again, something we must not dismiss.
But there is another account that deserves our attention.
Acts 8 describes the Samaritans receiving the Holy Spirit through the ministry of Peter and John.
Simon the magician observed that something happened when the apostles laid hands on people.
But the text does not explicitly identify speaking in tongues as that manifestation.
Some Christians infer that tongues occurred.
Others caution that Scripture does not tell us.
The honest response is simple.
We must not turn an inference into an explicit biblical statement.
And there are other conversion accounts in Acts where speaking in tongues is not reported at all.
That does not prove it never occurred.
But it does mean the narrative does not consistently present tongues as a recorded requirement for every individual conversion.
Now consider the Apostle Paul.
This is where the question becomes impossible to avoid.
Paul was not hostile to speaking in tongues.
Quite the opposite.
In 1 Corinthians 14:18, he wrote:
"I thank my God, I speak with tongues more than ye all." (KJV)
Paul valued the gift.
He practiced it.
He did not treat genuine spiritual manifestations as something embarrassing or spiritually inferior.
And in 1 Corinthians 14:39, he explicitly instructed believers not to forbid speaking in tongues.
But the same apostle wrote something that should stop every Christian from making tongues a universal test of salvation.
In 1 Corinthians 12, Paul described the Church as one body with many members.
Different gifts.
Different functions.
One Spirit.
Then he asked a series of rhetorical questions.
"Are all apostles? are all prophets? are all teachers? are all workers of miracles? Have all the gifts of healing? do all speak with tongues? do all interpret?" (1 Corinthians 12:29–30, KJV)
Look closely at the Greek question concerning tongues:
μὴ πάντες γλώσσαις λαλοῦσιν;
Mē pantes glōssais lalousin?
Literally, "Do all speak in tongues?"
The Greek particle μή (mē) introduces a question that expects a negative answer.
In the flow of Paul's argument, the answer is no.
Not everyone has the same gift.
Not everyone has the same function.
Not everyone speaks in tongues.

Now, to represent the theological discussion fairly, some Pentecostal Christians distinguish between tongues as an initial sign accompanying baptism in the Holy Spirit and tongues as an ongoing congregational gift.
They argue that Paul's questions in 1 Corinthians 12 concern the distribution of ministry gifts, not necessarily the initial experience described in Acts.
That distinction deserves to be understood rather than caricatured.
However, Scripture does not explicitly establish that distinction as a universal rule requiring every Spirit-baptized Christian to speak in tongues.
And Paul's teaching gives us strong reason to be cautious about making one particular gift the defining evidence of the Spirit's presence in every believer.
Especially when we read what he says elsewhere.
Romans 8:9 contains a statement that every Christian needs to understand.
"Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his." (KJV)
Paul identifies the Spirit's presence as essential to belonging to Christ.
But he does not say that every person who belongs to Christ must demonstrate that reality through tongues.
In Ephesians 1:13, Paul teaches that believers, having heard the Gospel and believed in Christ, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.
And 1 Corinthians 12:13 declares:
"For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body..." (KJV)
The language is about the Spirit's work in uniting believers to Christ and His body.
Christians differ on how Spirit baptism, conversion, and subsequent experiences of empowerment should be understood in relation to one another.
Those differences should be discussed carefully.
But the New Testament does not authorize us to tell a person who truly trusts in Jesus Christ that they necessarily lack the Holy Spirit simply because they have never spoken in tongues.
And if you have been living under that accusation, please hear this.
Your inability to produce a particular spiritual manifestation is not proof that Jesus has abandoned you.
You may have been measuring your relationship with God by the wrong standard.
But we need to go even deeper.
Because there is another danger.
It is possible to become so obsessed with the manifestation of spiritual power that we lose sight of the purpose of spiritual power.
Think about the Corinthian church.
They were spiritually gifted.
They had tongues.
They had prophecy.
They had knowledge.
They had extraordinary experiences.
Yet Paul had to confront their divisions, pride, immaturity, sexual sin, and disorder.
Imagine that.
A church could be rich in spiritual manifestations and still desperately need spiritual correction.
And right between Paul's discussion of spiritual gifts in 1 Corinthians 12 and his instructions for worship in chapter 14, he placed one of the most penetrating chapters in the entire Bible.
First Corinthians 13.
"Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal." (1 Corinthians 13:1, KJV)
The word translated "charity" in the King James Version is:
ἀγάπη — agapē
Love.
Not merely affection.
Not religious excitement.
But the kind of love that reflects God's character and seeks the good of others.
Paul's point is devastating.
A person may possess extraordinary gifts and still fail in the very thing that gives Christian service its proper character.
Without love, even the most impressive spiritual expression becomes empty noise.
Now picture two people sitting in the same church.
One speaks in tongues frequently but humiliates others, refuses correction, spreads gossip, and treats struggling Christians with contempt.
The other has never spoken in tongues but quietly cares for a sick parent, confesses sin, forgives an enemy, serves the poor, and keeps trusting Jesus through suffering.
Which person is demonstrating the character of Christ?
We cannot judge their entire spiritual condition from a brief description.
God knows the heart.
But Scripture makes one thing unmistakable.
Spiritual gifts must never become an excuse to neglect spiritual fruit.
Galatians 5:22–23 describes the fruit of the Spirit:
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Longsuffering.
Gentleness.
Goodness.
Faithfulness.
Meekness.
Self-control.
These are not merely personality traits.
They are characteristics the Spirit cultivates in believers as they walk with Him.
And the most striking evidence of His transforming work may not be what happens during an emotionally charged worship service.
It may be what happens when nobody is watching.
When you could retaliate, but you choose forgiveness.
When temptation knocks, and you turn to Christ.
When pride rises, and you humble yourself.
When you fall into sin, and instead of hiding behind religious appearances, you confess and return to God.
When you are wounded, but you refuse to stop loving.
Not because these works earn salvation.
They do not.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But because the grace that saves us also begins to transform us.
And that transformation matters.
Now perhaps someone reading this is thinking:
"But I speak in tongues, and I know God genuinely touched my life."
I am not here to tell you that your experience was false.
Scripture does not command Christians to reject every supernatural gift.
In fact, Paul wrote:
"Wherefore, brethren, covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues." (1 Corinthians 14:39, KJV)
If God has genuinely given you this gift, receive it with gratitude and humility.
Use it according to Scripture.
Do not be ashamed of it.
But please, do not turn your gift into a weapon against another believer.
Do not make someone feel spiritually worthless because their experience differs from yours.
And do not forget that every gift is given for God's glory, not our superiority.
Paul's instruction in 1 Corinthians 14 is particularly important.
He teaches that when tongues are exercised publicly in the gathered church, their use must be orderly and directed toward the building up of the congregation.
Where a tongue is addressed to the congregation, interpretation is necessary for the church to understand and benefit.

In 1 Corinthians 14:27–28, Paul limits public tongue-speaking to two or at most three speakers, each in turn, with interpretation. Without an interpreter, the speaker is to remain silent in the church and speak to himself and to God.
That instruction is not a rejection of tongues.
It is a safeguard against confusion.
Paul also acknowledges prayer in tongues and distinguishes between speaking with the spirit and speaking with understanding (1 Corinthians 14:14–15).
Christians interpret some details of these passages differently, including the relationship between private prayer and public ministry.
But the governing principles are clear.
Love.
Edification.
Understanding.
Order.
And the glory of God.
"For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace..." (1 Corinthians 14:33, KJV)

If a spiritual practice becomes a way of intimidating people, manufacturing emotional pressure, or ranking Christians according to visible experiences, we have reason to examine whether that practice is being conducted according to the apostolic instructions.
And here is something else we must face.
Some believers have been pressured to imitate sounds they did not genuinely receive.
Some have been told to repeat syllables until something happens.
Some have feared disappointing their pastors or appearing spiritually deficient.
Others have encountered genuine spiritual experiences but were never taught how to evaluate them biblically.
The answer is not to mock those people.
The answer is to bring everything back under the authority of Scripture.
First Thessalonians 5:19–21 tells believers not to quench the Spirit, not to despise prophecies, but to test everything and hold fast to what is good.
That is a remarkable balance.
Do not extinguish genuine spiritual activity.
But do not accept every claim without discernment.
The Holy Spirit never needs deception to prove that He is real.
And no Christian should feel compelled to manufacture a spiritual gift to earn acceptance.
Now I want to speak directly to the person who has been silently carrying shame.
Maybe you have attended prayer meetings where everyone around you seemed to receive something you did not.
Maybe you have watched people weep, tremble, and speak in tongues while you stood there wondering why heaven felt silent.
Maybe you have questioned your salvation for years.
You love Christ.
You believe the Gospel.
You want to obey Him.
You are fighting sins that once controlled you.
You are learning to forgive.
You are growing in prayer.
But a voice keeps whispering:
"You're not a real Spirit-filled Christian."
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not begin with your ability to demonstrate a gift.
It begins with what Jesus Christ accomplished on the cross.
Jesus did not die so that Christians could compete over spiritual experiences.
He died to redeem sinners.
He rose again so that those who trust in Him could receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life.
And He gives the Holy Spirit to His people.
In John 14:16–17, Jesus promised another Comforter, the Spirit of truth, who would dwell with His disciples.
The Greek word translated "Comforter" is:
παράκλητος — paraklētos
A term often rendered Helper, Advocate, or Comforter, describing one called alongside to help.
What a beautiful promise.
The Spirit is not presented merely as a force that produces impressive moments.
He is the divine Helper who dwells with God's people.
He glorifies Christ (John 16:14).
He convicts the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment (John 16:8).
He helps believers in their weakness (Romans 8:26).
He bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:16).
He transforms believers increasingly into Christlikeness (2 Corinthians 3:18).
He empowers witness.
He distributes gifts according to His will (1 Corinthians 12:11).
And He leads us toward Jesus.
That is why we must be careful not to reduce His presence to one outward manifestation.
The Holy Spirit is not a spiritual trophy.
He is God.
And His work is much greater than any single gift.
But perhaps we also need to speak to those who have dismissed tongues entirely.
Some Christians have seen disorderly worship and concluded that every contemporary claim of tongues must be false.
Others hold a cessationist understanding, believing that certain miraculous gifts served a foundational role in the apostolic era and are no longer ordinarily given today.
Still others believe all the gifts described in the New Testament remain available as the Spirit wills.
Faithful Christians disagree on these questions.
Those disagreements should be examined through careful biblical interpretation rather than ridicule or fear.
Scripture commands us to test claims.
It also commands us not to despise what is genuinely from God.
And whatever our position, we should be able to agree on this:
No spiritual experience should become more important to us than the Lord Jesus Christ Himself.
Now consider a scene from Luke 10.
Jesus had sent out seventy disciples, and they returned rejoicing because even demons were subject to them through His name.
They were excited.
They had witnessed spiritual authority.
They had experienced remarkable things.
But Jesus redirected their joy.
"Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven." (Luke 10:20, KJV)
Do you see it?
Jesus did not deny that something extraordinary had happened.
He redirected their attention toward a deeper reason for rejoicing.
Their belonging to God.
That should humble every one of us.
Whether we speak in tongues or do not.
Whether we have experienced miraculous healing or have spent years praying through sickness.
Whether our worship is outwardly expressive or quietly reverent.
Our deepest confidence must never rest in our spiritual achievements or experiences.
It must rest in Christ.
And here is the question that matters far more than whether you can speak in a language you never learned.
Have you truly surrendered your life to Jesus Christ?
Have you acknowledged your sin?
Have you trusted in His death and resurrection?
Are you turning away from sin and learning to follow Him?
Do you love His Word?
Are you willing to be corrected by Scripture, even when it challenges your traditions?
Are you seeking to love God and your neighbor?
These questions do not invite us to earn God's acceptance through flawless behavior.
They invite us to examine whether our profession of faith is sincere and whether our lives are being shaped by the One we claim to follow.
Because a person can speak in tongues and still need repentance.
And a person who has never spoken in tongues may genuinely belong to Jesus.
The decisive issue is not whether we have duplicated another person's experience.
It is whether we belong to Christ through faith.
There is a heartbreaking irony in the way Christians sometimes handle this subject.
We proclaim a Savior who welcomes repentant sinners by grace.
Then we sometimes create environments where wounded believers feel they must prove themselves worthy of belonging.
We preach the cross.
Then we measure people by outward manifestations.
We celebrate the Holy Spirit.
Then we grieve one another through pride, suspicion, and condemnation.
It should not be this way.
Jesus prayed for the unity of His people in John 17.
Not unity at the expense of truth.
But unity grounded in the truth and in our shared relationship with Him.
We can discuss spiritual gifts seriously without treating fellow believers as enemies.
We can disagree without humiliating one another.
We can seek the Spirit's power without abandoning biblical discernment.
And we can honor genuine spiritual gifts without making them a requirement that Scripture does not clearly impose upon every Christian.
Perhaps that is where some of us need to repent.
Not necessarily for believing that tongues are a gift.
Not necessarily for believing that tongues have ceased.
But for the arrogance with which we have treated people who disagree.
For confusing our interpretation with unquestionable authority.
For making wounded Christians feel unwelcome.
For allowing a debate about the Holy Spirit to produce behavior contrary to the fruit of the Holy Spirit.
Imagine if the next conversation about tongues sounded different.
Instead of asking someone, "Why haven't you spoken in tongues?"
We asked, "How can I help you grow closer to Jesus?"
Instead of saying, "You don't have the Spirit because you haven't had my experience,"
We said, "Let's open the Scriptures together and seek to understand what God has promised."
Instead of mocking a believer's spiritual experience,
We listened carefully and tested it with humility.
Instead of making the church a stage for religious performance,
We made it a place where truth and love meet.
A place where the broken can find restoration.
Where the proud are called to repentance.
Where the confused are taught patiently.
Where sinners encounter the grace of Jesus Christ.
Because the Church was never meant to be a competition over who appears most anointed.
It is the body of Christ.
And every member needs the others.
Now let me bring this back to the question that began our journey.
Should Christians speak in tongues as evidence of receiving the Holy Spirit?
The New Testament clearly teaches that speaking in tongues is a genuine spiritual gift and that tongues accompanied the Spirit's coming upon believers on significant occasions in Acts.
Christians should not automatically condemn or forbid the genuine exercise of this gift.
But the New Testament does not clearly teach that every Christian must speak in tongues to prove they have received the Holy Spirit.
Paul explicitly teaches that the Spirit distributes gifts according to His will, and his rhetorical question in 1 Corinthians 12:30 expects that not everyone speaks in tongues.
Scripture places our belonging to Christ in the context of faith in Him and the Spirit's saving work, not a universal requirement to demonstrate one particular gift.
And while the fruit of the Spirit is not a substitute for the Gospel or a way of earning salvation, a transformed life provides meaningful evidence of the Spirit's sanctifying work.
So seek the Holy Spirit.
Pray for His empowering.
Be open to whatever gifts He chooses to give according to His Word.
Do not despise genuine gifts.
Do not imitate what you have not received.
Do not judge another Christian's salvation by a manifestation that Scripture does not universally require.
And above all, do not allow the pursuit of spiritual experiences to replace your pursuit of Jesus.
Because the Spirit who descended at Pentecost is the same Spirit who glorifies the crucified and risen Christ.
He is not competing with Jesus for our attention.
He is leading us to Him.
And maybe this is the moment when you finally stop asking:
"Why am I not like that other Christian?"
And begin praying:
"Lord Jesus, make me more like You."
More faithful.
More humble.
More loving.
More obedient.
More willing to repent.
More courageous in witnessing.
More sensitive to the truth.
More surrendered to the Spirit's work.
That prayer may not attract a crowd.
It may not produce a dramatic video.
It may not impress the person standing beside you.
But a life increasingly conformed to Christ is never insignificant in the sight of God.
And if you have spent years feeling spiritually inferior because you have never spoken in tongues, I want you to remember something.
Jesus did not purchase your redemption with His blood only to leave your assurance dependent upon reproducing someone else's spiritual experience.
Look to Him.
Trust His Gospel.
Receive what His Word teaches.
And walk with Him in faith.
If this article exposed a hidden fear, healed a misunderstanding, or challenged something you have believed for years, I would love to hear your story.
Let's make the conversation a place of biblical truth, humility, and love, not another battlefield where Christians wound one another.
