וְאַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
Ve'attem chashavtem alai ra'ah; Elohim chashavah letovah.
“But as for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” — Genesis 50:20, WEB
The Hebrew verb חָשַׁב (chashav) can express thinking, planning, or intending.
Joseph's brothers intended evil.
God intended good through the very history they had tried to use for destruction.
The brothers were still responsible for their wickedness.
God did not excuse them.
But their intentions did not ultimately control Joseph's story.
And notice what Joseph did not say.
He did not say, “What you did was actually wonderful.”
He acknowledged the evil.
Then he acknowledged God's greater purpose.
That distinction matters when your pain was caused by another person's choices.
You do not have to defend the person who betrayed you in order to defend the goodness of God.
You do not have to return to an abusive situation to demonstrate forgiveness.
You do not have to pretend you were never wounded to testify that Christ is healing you.
The God who redeemed Joseph's story is not glorified by dishonesty about suffering.
He is glorified by truth.
But there is another part of Romans 8:28 that we often overlook.
And without it, we can misunderstand the entire promise.
Paul says all things work together “for good.”
What good?
Our first instinct is to define that word ourselves.
A better job.
A restored relationship.
A successful business.
A healed body.
A public vindication.
A sudden financial breakthrough.
And yes, God may graciously provide any of those things.
We should pray for healing, seek reconciliation where appropriate, work faithfully, pursue justice, and thank Him for every earthly blessing.
But Romans 8:28 does not promise those particular outcomes.
The meaning of “good” is clarified by the very next verse.
“For whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.” — Romans 8:29, WEB
Read that again.
“To be conformed to the image of his Son.”
There it is.
The Greek phrase is:
συμμόρφους τῆς εἰκόνος τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ
Symmorphous tēs eikonos tou huiou autou.
“Conformed to the image of His Son.”
The word σύμμορφος (symmorphos) carries the idea of sharing the same form or being conformed to a likeness.
Paul is revealing the purpose toward which God's saving work is directed.
Christlikeness.
Not merely comfort.
Not merely success.
Not merely relief.
The good God is accomplishing includes making His people like Jesus Christ and bringing them into the fullness of the salvation He has promised.
And that changes everything.
Because you can become more like Jesus while your circumstances remain difficult.
You can grow in patience without receiving an immediate answer.
You can learn compassion because you know what it feels like to be overlooked.
You can become courageous while still feeling afraid.
You can discover the sufficiency of Christ in a season when nearly everything else has been stripped away.
This does not mean God must inflict every wound in order to teach every lesson.
It means no wound is beyond His ability to redeem within His eternal purpose.
And even when you cannot identify a lesson, a blessing, or an explanation, His promise has not expired.
Some suffering remains mysterious in this life.
Some losses never become understandable.
Some graves remain graves until the resurrection.
And Romans 8:28 is still true.
Because the ultimate good promised in Romans 8 is not a painless earthly life.
It is the completed redemption of those who belong to Jesus Christ.
Perhaps you need to hear that today.
Especially if you have been blaming yourself because your circumstances have not improved.
You may have thought, “If I had stronger faith, I would already see the good.”
But Paul never made your ability to recognize God's purpose the condition of God's faithfulness.
In fact, just two verses before Romans 8:28, he acknowledges our weakness in prayer.
“Likewise the Spirit also helps our weaknesses, for we don't know how to pray as we ought. But the Spirit himself makes intercession for us with groanings which can't be uttered.” — Romans 8:26, WEB
Did you catch that?
We don't know how to pray as we ought.
Not just unbelievers.
Not just immature Christians.
Paul says we.
Sometimes faith looks like confident praise.
Sometimes it looks like falling to your knees and whispering, “Lord, I don't even know what to ask anymore.”
Sometimes your prayer is not a beautiful paragraph.
It is a trembling breath.
A tear falling onto your pillow.
A desperate, “Jesus, help me.”
And Scripture says the Spirit helps us in our weakness.
The Greek verb συναντιλαμβάνεται (synantilambanetai) in Romans 8:26 conveys the idea of coming alongside to help bear a burden.
What a tender picture.
The Holy Spirit does not stand at a distance, disgusted by your inability to find the right words.
He helps you.
Even when your prayers are tangled.
Even when grief has exhausted your vocabulary.
Even when you are too overwhelmed to explain what is happening inside you.
You are not abandoned because you are struggling.
Your weakness is not evidence that God has withdrawn.
The same chapter that promises God's purpose also tells us that the Spirit helps us when we do not know how to pray.
And perhaps that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because there are believers reading this who have been carrying something they have never told anyone.
You still attend church.
You still share Bible verses.
You still encourage other people.
You still say, “God is good.”
And you believe it.
But when everyone goes home and the room becomes quiet, there is a heaviness you cannot explain.
You are tired of being strong.
Tired of saying you are fine.
Tired of watching other people receive answers while you keep waiting.
You are not asking for a luxurious life.
You just want peace.
You want to sleep without replaying the past.
You want to stop wondering whether the worst thing that happened to you will define the rest of your life.
And maybe, beneath all those questions, you are afraid to admit something.
You are disappointed.
Not necessarily with God's character.
But with how your life has unfolded.
You imagined something different.
And now you are grieving a future that never arrived.
Friend, the Bible gives us room to lament.
The Psalms contain cries of confusion, sorrow, and desperation.
Jesus Himself wept at Lazarus's tomb.
And in Gethsemane, our Savior prayed in anguish before His crucifixion.
Biblical faith is not emotional numbness.
It is bringing our real hearts before the real God.
But now we must go even deeper.
Because the most breathtaking demonstration of Romans 8:28 is not Joseph's story.
It is the cross of Jesus Christ.
Think about what happened on that hill outside Jerusalem.
The only truly sinless man who ever lived was betrayed.
False witnesses testified against Him.
Religious leaders condemned Him.
A crowd demanded His execution.
Roman soldiers mocked Him, beat Him, and nailed Him to a cross.
His disciples scattered.
His mother watched Him suffer.
And the Son of God died under the weight of human sin.
If you had stood there on that Friday, what would you have seen?
Injustice.
Cruelty.
Humiliation.
Apparent defeat.
The Messiah was dead.
Hope seemed buried.
The disciples could not yet see what God was accomplishing.
But Scripture reveals something astonishing.
Peter later declared:
“Him, being delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you have taken by the hand of lawless men, crucified and killed.” — Acts 2:23, WEB
Do you see both truths standing together?
God's determined purpose.
Human wickedness.
The crucifixion was not a moral good because innocent suffering is good.
It was a wicked act committed by responsible human beings.
Yet through the death of Jesus Christ, God accomplished the greatest act of redemption in human history.
The Lamb of God bore our sins.
The righteous One suffered for the unrighteous.
The Savior died.
And on the third day, He rose.
The darkest Friday in human history became the doorway to resurrection Sunday.
Not because evil won.
But because Jesus conquered sin and death.
That is why Romans 8:28 cannot be reduced to motivational optimism.
Its foundation is the crucified and risen Christ.
The cross proves that God's redemptive purpose can triumph through circumstances that appear utterly hopeless.
But there is something else we must understand.
Romans 8:28 is not an isolated slogan addressed indiscriminately to every person regardless of their relationship with God.
Paul identifies the recipients of this promise.
“Those who love God.”
“Those who are called according to his purpose.”
The Greek expression τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν τὸν θεόν (tois agapōsin ton theon) means “to those who love God.”
And τοῖς κατὰ πρόθεσιν κλητοῖς οὖσιν (tois kata prothesin klētois ousin) describes those who are called according to His purpose.
This is covenant language, rooted in God's saving work.
It does not mean believers earn God's care by loving Him perfectly.
If perfect love were the requirement, none of us could stand.
We love because He first loved us, as 1 John 4:19 teaches.
Our hope rests not in the perfection of our devotion but in the faithfulness of the Savior who calls us to Himself.
And if you are reading this while feeling far from God, this is not an invitation to despair.
It is an invitation to Christ.
Because the Gospel is not merely that God can improve the circumstances of your life.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
He lived the righteous life we could not live.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And He calls us to repent and believe in Him.
Not to purchase His favor.
Not to pretend we have no past.
Not to become respectable enough to deserve mercy.
But to receive the grace we could never earn.
Maybe you have spent years trying to convince everyone that you are a good Christian while privately carrying guilt over things you have done.
Maybe the scandal in your story was not something done to you.
Maybe it was something you did.
A betrayal.
A hidden addiction.
A season of dishonesty.
A destructive decision.
A relationship you knew was wrong.
A choice that hurt someone you loved.
And now every time you hear Romans 8:28, you wonder whether God can possibly bring good out of a story you helped damage.
Listen carefully.
God's forgiveness does not erase the reality of consequences.
Repentance does not mean the people you hurt must immediately trust you again.
Grace does not excuse ongoing sin.
But the blood of Jesus Christ is sufficient to cleanse the repentant sinner.
Your past may require confession.
Restitution.
Accountability.
Difficult conversations.
Years of rebuilding trust.
Yet your sin does not have to remain the ruler of your future.
In Christ, forgiveness is real.
Transformation is possible.
And your identity need not remain chained to the worst chapter of your life.
That is why we proclaim:
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
But because His mercy is greater than the sinner's past, His truth is stronger than our excuses, and His resurrection power brings new life where sin once ruled.
Still, we must be careful.
There is a dangerous way to misuse Romans 8:28.
It happens when we tell grieving people that their suffering is automatically a punishment for something they did.
Or when we suggest that every tragedy is a secret blessing they should immediately celebrate.
Or when we insist that true believers never struggle with depression, grief, anxiety, disappointment, or unanswered questions.
That is not Paul's message.
Remember the context of Romans 8.
Creation is groaning.
Believers are groaning.
The Spirit helps us in our weakness.
Paul speaks of suffering, persecution, famine, danger, and the sword.
He is not writing from a world where Christians never experience pain.
He is proclaiming hope in the middle of a world still awaiting final redemption.
Romans 8:18 says:
“For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which will be revealed toward us.” — WEB
Paul does not deny present suffering.
He compares it with coming glory.
And that distinction is everything.
Christian hope does not require us to believe that our pain is imaginary.
It requires us to believe that our pain is not ultimate.
The final chapter belongs to Christ.
The resurrection is coming.
God will judge evil.
He will make all things new.
And those united to Jesus will share in His glory.
This is why Romans 8:28 is such a powerful promise.
It reaches further than the boundaries of your lifetime.
Some things will not be resolved before you die.
Some apologies will never arrive.
Some questions will remain unanswered.
Some dreams will never take the shape you once imagined.
Yet God's eternal purpose will not fail.
Paul continues in Romans 8:30:
“Whom he predestined, those he also called. Whom he called, those he also justified. Whom he justified, those he also glorified.” — WEB
Notice that final word.
Glorified.
Paul speaks of the completion of God's saving purpose with such confidence that he uses the past tense even for the glory believers still await.
His assurance is rooted in God's faithfulness from beginning to end.
And then, near the close of the chapter, Paul asks one of the most astonishing questions in all of Scripture.
“Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” — Romans 8:35, WEB
Trouble?
Distress?
Persecution?
Hunger?
Danger?
Death?
Paul's answer is that none of these can separate those who belong to Christ from His love.
That means the deepest assurance of Romans 8:28 is not that you will always understand what God is doing.
It is that you are held by the God whose love has been revealed in Jesus Christ.
You may lose things you never expected to lose.
You may walk through seasons you never would have chosen.
You may spend years waiting for an answer that never comes in the form you hoped for.
But if you belong to Jesus, your suffering cannot overturn His promise to bring you into the fullness of His redemption.
And maybe this is the moment to stop asking only, “Lord, when will You make my life easier?”
And begin asking:
“Lord, how can I remain faithful to You here?”
“How can I become more like Jesus in this season?”
“What do I need to surrender?”
“Where do I need to repent?”
“Whom do I need to forgive?”
“What truth have I forgotten?”
And sometimes the most faithful prayer will simply be:
“Father, I cannot see what You are doing. But help me trust the character You revealed through Your Son.”
That is not surrendering your mind.
It is anchoring your hope in the God who raised Jesus from the dead.
And please understand this.
You do not need to manufacture a beautiful testimony while you are still grieving.
You do not have to turn every heartbreak into an inspirational social media post.
You do not have to explain why God permitted every painful event.
There is a time to speak.
A time to weep.
A time to seek help.
A time to confront wrongdoing.
A time to rest.
And through it all, there is a Savior who remains faithful.
Perhaps your testimony today is not, “God restored everything I lost.”
Perhaps it is simply:
“I am still here, and Jesus is still holding me.”
That is not a small testimony.
For someone who almost abandoned their faith, it may be a miracle of perseverance.
For someone who has been silently grieving, it may be the beginning of hope.
For someone trapped in shame, it may be the courage to confess and return to God.
For someone who thought their life was beyond redemption, it may be the first glimpse of grace.
And this is why we cannot keep the Gospel to ourselves.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who is smiling in photographs while quietly falling apart.
Someone is wondering whether God has forgotten them.
Someone is carrying guilt they have never confessed.
Someone has been using Romans 8:28 to silence their own grief because they thought faithful Christians were not allowed to hurt.
They may never tell you.
But a single Scripture-centered message, shared at the right moment, can point them toward the Savior they desperately need.
And think of one person who needs this today.
A friend who has been grieving.
A family member who feels defeated.
A believer who is struggling with unanswered prayers.
A person who has walked away from church because suffering made them question God's goodness.
You do not have to reveal private details.
You do not have to pretend everything is fine.
But perhaps you can write:
Or, if you are struggling to say those words right now:
“Pray for me. I'm still fighting.”
There is room for both the strong and the weary in the family of God.
Someone may need to hear that faith can survive a season of darkness.
Not because it contains a magical formula for eliminating suffering, but because there may come another night when your circumstances feel louder than God's promises.
On that night, return to Romans 8.
Read the whole chapter.
Remember the Spirit who helps your weakness.
Remember the Father whose saving purpose does not fail.
Remember the Son who died and rose again.
Remember that nothing can separate those who belong to Christ from His love.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, new Christians, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to follow as well.
Our desire is to keep pointing people toward Jesus through biblical teaching, conviction, repentance, grace, encouragement, and discipleship.
Because people do not need another religious performance.
They need the truth of God's Word.
They need the Gospel.
They need Jesus Christ.
And there is another way you can help this mission reach further.
Gospel Warrior is committed to sharing Scripture-centered content and discipleship resources with people who are hungry to know Christ more deeply.
We want these resources to continue reaching people who may not have the financial means to purchase Christian books or structured study materials.
And we want to keep developing more resources that help believers move beyond inspirational quotations into a deeper understanding of God's Word.
This takes time, effort, creativity, and practical support.
Not simply to receive more content.
But to help sustain and expand the work of making biblical truth accessible to more people.
You may prayerfully consider it part of your personal generosity toward Gospel work, alongside your responsibilities to your local church and those in need.
But I want to make something very clear.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
Spiritual blessings are not merchandise.
And no financial contribution can earn the favor that Jesus Christ has already secured for His people.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.” — WEB
If you are not able, you are still welcome here.
Keep reading.
Keep learning.
Keep sharing the Gospel.
Keep growing in Christ.
Your presence matters.
These items are simply ways to encourage faith, share biblical messages, and support the continuing work. They are not substitutes for Scripture, the local church, or genuine discipleship.
You may never know whose life is being touched through a message you shared.
You may never meet the person who opens a Bible again because something they read reminded them of Christ.
You may never hear the prayer whispered by someone who finally realizes that suffering has not placed them beyond God's love.
But the Gospel is worth proclaiming.
And every opportunity to point someone toward Jesus is precious.
Now, before you leave, I want to bring you back to the place where we began.
That painful question.
“If all things work together for good, why does this hurt so much?”
Maybe you are still waiting for an answer.
Maybe the wound is still fresh.
Maybe the person who betrayed you has moved on while you are still rebuilding your life.
Maybe you have prayed for years and nothing seems to change.
I will not promise that tomorrow everything will suddenly make sense.
Paul did not promise that.
I will not tell you that every loss will be replaced with something bigger in this lifetime.
Scripture does not guarantee that either.
But I can point you to the cross.
To the empty tomb.
To the Savior who understands suffering.
To the Holy Spirit who helps us in weakness.
To the Father whose purpose is to conform His people to the image of His Son.
And to the promise that death itself will not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
Romans 8:28 is not God saying:
“Everything that happens to you is good.”
It is the assurance that:
Even what is not good cannot finally defeat the good God has purposed for those who are His in Christ.
Your scars may remain.
Your story may still have unanswered questions.
Your circumstances may not look anything like the future you once imagined.
But Jesus Christ has not surrendered His authority to your suffering.
And if you have never truly entrusted your life to Him, you can turn to Him today.
Come honestly.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Believe the Gospel.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And if you already belong to Him but have been struggling, return to His Word.
You do not need to pretend that the storm is over.
You can ask Him for grace to remain faithful while it continues.
Because the Christian's greatest hope is not that every chapter will be pleasant.
It is that the Author of our salvation is faithful.
And when the final chapter of redemption is revealed, it will not be sin, betrayal, shame, suffering, or death that stands victorious.
It will be Jesus Christ.
So tonight, if you find yourself staring at the ceiling with tears you cannot explain, remember this:
The God who raised Jesus from the dead is not limited by what you can see from where you are standing.
You may not understand the road.
You may not know how the pieces fit.
You may not even have the strength to take more than one small step.
But bring that step to Jesus.
And if all you can pray is, “Lord, hold me,” then pray it.
He is worthy of your trust even before you understand.
The wound may still be part of your story, but through Jesus Christ, it does not get to write your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN YOU REALLY FOLLOW JESUS WITHOUT BELONGING TO A CHURCH? THE ANSWER MAY BREAK YOUR HEART BEFORE IT HEALS IT.
paragraphs: CAN YOU REALLY FOLLOW JESUS WITHOUT BELONGING TO A CHURCH? THE ANSWER MAY BREAK YOUR HEART BEFORE IT HEALS IT.

You can be saved without a church membership card. But can you keep calling yourself a follower of Christ while deliberately rejecting the people He calls His body? Somewhere between church wounds, spiritual isolation, and the longing to belong, there is a biblical truth we desperately need to recover.
There is someone reading this who still loves Jesus.

You still believe He died on the cross. You still believe the tomb is empty. Sometimes you pray when nobody is watching. Sometimes you open your Bible in the middle of the night because life has become too heavy to carry alone.
But on Sunday morning, you stay home.
Not necessarily because you hate God.
Maybe because the last time you walked into a church, you walked out carrying wounds nobody apologized for.

Maybe you trusted a pastor who betrayed your confidence. Maybe people who preached forgiveness showed you cruelty. Maybe you watched church members sing about love while destroying someone with their words.
Or maybe nothing dramatic happened.
You simply drifted.
One missed Sunday became a month. One month became a year. Eventually, watching sermons online felt easier than being known by real people.
And somewhere along the way, you began telling yourself something that sounded perfectly reasonable:
“I don't need church. I have Jesus.”
But here is the question that deserves more than a convenient answer.
What if Jesus never intended you to choose between loving Him and belonging to His people?
And what if the real issue is not whether God can save someone outside a church building, but what happens to a heart that slowly learns to live without the body Christ loves?
Stay with me.
Because the answer is not as simple as some churches have made it sound. And it is not as comfortable as our wounded hearts sometimes want it to be.
First, we must establish something that should never be negotiable.
A church cannot save you. Jesus Christ can.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
The Greek text begins with a beautiful declaration:
Τῇ γὰρ χάριτί ἐστε σεσῳσμένοι διὰ πίστεως
Tē gar chariti este sesōsmenoi dia pisteōs.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith.”

The expression este sesōsmenoi emphasizes a salvation accomplished with an abiding result. Paul is not presenting salvation as something purchased by religious attendance, church dues, or human performance.
Salvation is God's gift, received through faith.
And the foundation of that salvation is Jesus Christ—His sinless life, His sacrificial death for sinners, and His victorious resurrection.
A person is not made righteous before God because their name appears on a church membership roll.
A person is justified by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Consider the criminal crucified beside Jesus.
He had no opportunity to attend a membership class.
No opportunity to join a local congregation.
No opportunity to participate in a church ministry.
Yet when he turned to the crucified Savior, Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43, KJV)
That dying man was not saved by a church institution.
He was saved by Christ.
And that matters deeply.

Because someone may be confined to a hospital bed. Someone may live in a region where Christians face persecution. Someone may be physically unable to gather. Someone may have only recently believed and not yet found a faithful congregation.
God's grace is not imprisoned by circumstances.

A genuine Christian can exist without formal membership in a local church. But that does not mean a genuine Christian should consider permanent isolation from Christ's people the normal Christian life.
Those are two very different claims.
And confusing them has wounded people on both sides.
Some have been frightened into believing that missing church automatically means losing salvation.
Others have convinced themselves that because church attendance cannot save them, Christian fellowship is spiritually unnecessary.
Neither conclusion accurately represents the whole counsel of Scripture.
Because the same Jesus who saves individuals also gathers them into a people.
And this is where the conversation becomes personal.
When Jesus spoke of building His church in Matthew 16:18, the Greek word was ἐκκλησία (ekklēsia).

The word refers to an assembly or congregation. In the New Testament, it describes the community Christ calls to Himself, sometimes in a local gathering and sometimes in the wider sense of His people.
It does not simply mean a religious building.
The earliest Christians often gathered in homes.
The church is not fundamentally brick walls, expensive lighting, a stage, or a denomination's name.
The church is the people who belong to Jesus Christ.
But notice something.
An assembly is not merely a collection of disconnected individuals who happen to agree about God.
The New Testament pictures believers worshiping together, learning together, praying together, serving together, correcting one another, bearing burdens, and growing under faithful spiritual care.
Acts 2:42 describes the early believers:
“And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.” (KJV)
The Greek word translated “fellowship” is κοινωνία (koinōnia).
It speaks of participation, sharing, and communion.
Not merely standing near someone.
Not merely watching the same preacher.
Not merely liking the same Christian content.
But sharing life in Christ.
And perhaps this is where some of us need to be gently confronted.
You can listen to a hundred sermons and still have nobody who knows when your faith is collapsing.
You can post Bible verses every morning and still have nobody who can lovingly challenge the sin you keep hiding.
You can know the language of Christianity while remaining unknown to the people who are supposed to help you grow.
A sermon can instruct you.
A devotional can encourage you.
A Christian video can strengthen you.
But none of these, by themselves, can fully replace the mutual relationships and responsibilities of a faithful Christian community.
Christianity is personal, but it was never meant to be solitary.
And maybe that sentence hurts.
Because being alone sometimes feels safer.
Nobody can disappoint you if you never let them close.
Nobody can correct you if you never allow yourself to be known.
Nobody can reject you if you leave before anyone gets the chance.
But safety built entirely on isolation can eventually become a prison.
I wonder how many believers have mistaken the absence of conflict for the presence of spiritual peace.
How many have stopped gathering not because they stopped loving Jesus, but because they stopped believing His people could be trusted?
If that is you, please hear this carefully.
Your pain deserves to be taken seriously.
Spiritual abuse is real. Manipulation is real. Financial exploitation, hypocrisy, coercive leadership, and the misuse of Scripture are real.
Jesus never commanded His followers to pretend evil is holy because it happens inside a church.
In Matthew 23, He openly rebuked religious hypocrisy.
In Ezekiel 34, God condemned shepherds who exploited and neglected His flock.
In Acts 20:29–30, Paul warned that destructive teachers could arise even among professing believers.
The Bible does not ask you to surrender discernment at the church door.
It does not require you to remain under abusive leadership.
It does not demand that you return to an unsafe congregation to prove your loyalty to Christ.
Sometimes leaving a particular church is necessary.
Sometimes reporting misconduct, establishing boundaries, and seeking trustworthy help are acts of wisdom and truthfulness.
Leaving an unhealthy church is not the same as rejecting the church Jesus loves.
Please don't confuse the two.
You may need time to heal.
You may need to rebuild trust slowly.
You may need to find a congregation where Scripture is handled faithfully, leaders are accountable, questions are welcomed, and vulnerable people are protected.
And while you are healing, Jesus has not forgotten where you are.
But there is a danger we must also confront.
A wound can explain why we withdraw.
It cannot automatically justify every decision we make afterward.
At some point, healing may require us to ask whether we are protecting ourselves from harm—or protecting ourselves from ever having to trust, forgive, serve, or be accountable again.
That question is uncomfortable.
I know.
But sometimes the truth that heals us first exposes the places where fear has quietly taken control.
Hebrews 10:24–25 says:

“And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.” (KJV)
The Greek expression μὴ ἐγκαταλείποντες τὴν ἐπισυναγωγὴν ἑαυτῶν (mē enkataleipontes tēn episynagōgēn heautōn) speaks of not abandoning our gathering together.
The word enkataleipontes carries the sense of forsaking or abandoning.
This passage is not declaring that one missed Sunday cancels salvation.
Nor does it mean every believer must attend one particular congregation regardless of circumstances.
The surrounding verses call Christians to draw near to God, hold firmly to their hope, and encourage one another toward love and good works.
The emphasis is mutual perseverance.
Why?
Because following Jesus is not always easy.
There will be seasons when your prayers feel unanswered.
Seasons when temptation seems louder than conviction.
Seasons when grief makes worship difficult.
Seasons when you know what Scripture says but struggle to believe it applies to you.
And in those seasons, God often strengthens His people through other believers.
Someone reminds you of the promises you have forgotten.
Someone sits beside you when words are no longer enough.
Someone lovingly tells you the truth when you are drifting toward destruction.
Someone prays when you can barely find the strength to whisper.
And sometimes you become that person for somebody else.
That is part of the beauty of the church.
Not a gathering of people who never struggle.
But a redeemed people learning to carry one another toward Christ.
Paul describes this beautifully in 1 Corinthians 12.
He does not picture Christians as isolated spiritual consumers.
He pictures them as members of one body.
“For the body is not one member, but many.” (1 Corinthians 12:14, KJV)
And later:
“And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it.” (1 Corinthians 12:26, KJV)
Think about that.
If a part of your physical body becomes injured, you do not celebrate its separation from the rest.
You seek its healing.
You protect it.
You want it restored to healthy functioning.
In the same way, believers are not interchangeable customers in a religious marketplace.
We belong to Christ, and therefore we have responsibilities toward one another.
That is why the statement “I only need Jesus” can become misleading.
Yes, Jesus is completely sufficient as Savior.
No pastor can replace Him.
No congregation can add to His finished work.
But the Jesus who is sufficient is also the Jesus who commands His people to love one another.
In John 13:34–35, He says:

“A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.” (KJV)
How do we meaningfully practice that command while permanently refusing relationships with other believers?
How do we bear one another's burdens, as Galatians 6:2 commands, if we insist that nobody is allowed close enough to know what we carry?
How do we receive correction, extend forgiveness, exercise spiritual gifts, and practice sacrificial love if our faith never moves beyond ourselves?
These are not arguments that every church is healthy.
They are reasons to seek a healthy church rather than abandon Christian community altogether.
And there is another truth that may surprise you.
Being inside a church does not necessarily mean being inside Christ.
Some people attend every Sunday and have never truly repented.
Some serve in ministries while hiding unrepentant sin.
Some know the vocabulary of grace but have never surrendered to the Savior who gives it.
Jesus warns in Matthew 7:21 that not everyone who calls Him “Lord” will enter the kingdom of heaven.
That should sober every one of us.
The question is not merely, “Do you attend church?”
The deeper question is, “Do you belong to Jesus?”
Have you trusted Him as Savior and Lord?
Have you turned from sin toward God?
Is His grace transforming the direction of your life?
Do you love the truth of His Word, even when it confronts you?
Do you desire to obey Him, however imperfectly?
Because a genuine Christian is not someone who never struggles.
A genuine Christian is someone whose hope rests in Jesus Christ, whose life is being transformed by God's grace, and whose faith bears fruit over time.
We are not saved by the fruit.
But living faith does not remain fruitless forever.
And one of the fruits of God's work in us is a growing love for His people.
First John 3:14 speaks of love for fellow believers as evidence of spiritual life.
Not flawless love.
Not instant emotional comfort with every Christian.
But a real, Spirit-shaped movement away from selfishness and toward love.
This brings us to an important distinction.
A believer who cannot presently gather is not necessarily disobedient.
A believer searching for a faithful congregation is not necessarily rebellious.
A believer recovering from serious spiritual harm is not automatically rejecting Christ.

But someone who understands Christ's call to fellowship and persistently rejects every form of meaningful Christian community simply because they refuse accountability should examine that decision honestly before God.
Not because church membership purchases salvation.
But because genuine faith learns to take the commands of Jesus seriously.
And if you have been telling yourself that you are spiritually strong enough to walk alone forever, I want you to consider something.
Even the apostle Paul desired the encouragement of fellow believers.
In Romans 1:11–12, he expressed his longing to visit Christians in Rome so that they might be mutually encouraged by one another's faith.
Paul.
A man used by God to write much of the New Testament.
A man who endured persecution, imprisonment, and extraordinary hardship.
He still valued mutual encouragement.
If Paul did not treat Christian fellowship as unnecessary, why should we?
And if you are a church leader reading this, there is something you need to hear too.
Do not use passages about gathering to intimidate wounded people into returning to environments where they are being harmed.
Do not mistake attendance statistics for spiritual maturity.
Do not confuse unquestioning loyalty to leadership with obedience to Jesus.
The sheep belong to Christ.
Not to your brand.
Not to your platform.
Not to your institution.
First Peter 5:2–3 calls elders to shepherd God's flock willingly and without domineering over those entrusted to their care.
A faithful church should not make people feel that leaving its organization means leaving God.
Its calling is to point people toward Christ, teach the Scriptures faithfully, practice the ordinances He commanded, cultivate genuine fellowship, and help believers grow in holiness and love.
And yes, churches will still contain imperfect people.
There will be misunderstandings.
Disagreements.
Awkward conversations.
Moments requiring patience, confession, repentance, and forgiveness.
But imperfection is not the same as abuse.
A congregation does not need to be flawless to be faithful.
It needs to be submitted to the authority of God's Word and willing to repent when it falls short.
So where does that leave the person who loves Jesus but has no local church?
It leaves you with hope.
Not condemnation.
Not an excuse to remain spiritually disconnected forever.
Hope.
You can begin again.
Perhaps the first step is praying honestly:

“Lord Jesus, You know what happened to me. You know why I pulled away. You know the anger I still carry and the fear I don't know how to explain. Please heal what has been wounded, expose what I need to repent of, and lead me toward believers who will help me follow You faithfully.”

Then begin looking for a congregation where the gospel is clearly proclaimed, Scripture is faithfully taught in context, Christ is exalted above personalities, and leaders demonstrate humility and accountability.
Look for a community where love is more than a slogan.
Where people can ask difficult questions.
Where repentance is practiced, not merely preached.
Where spiritual gifts are used to serve rather than impress.
Where the vulnerable are protected.
Where people care whether you are growing in Jesus, not merely whether you are filling a seat.

If physical limitations or genuine danger prevent you from gathering, seek whatever faithful Christian connection is safely and realistically available. Personal visits, calls, prayer partnerships, and online fellowship can offer meaningful support, even though digital content alone does not reproduce every aspect of congregational life.
If you are able to gather safely, take a step toward real community.
Not because you need to earn God's acceptance.
But because the One who accepted you by grace is teaching you to love as He loves.
And perhaps you are reading this from the opposite side.
You attend church faithfully.
You serve.
You give.
You know everyone in the congregation.
But there is someone you have not seen in months.
Someone who used to sit near you.
Someone whose absence gradually became normal.
Have you checked on them?
Not to ask why they stopped attending.
Not to shame them.
Not to send them another announcement about the next event.
But simply to say:
“I noticed you've been gone. Are you okay? I care about you.”
Maybe the person who disappeared did not need another lecture about attendance.
Maybe they needed someone to notice they were hurting.
Maybe they were waiting for one person to remind them that they were more than a number on a church register.
And maybe God is asking you to be that person.
Because Christian community is not merely about asking who is present.
It is also about loving those who are missing.
Remember the parable of the lost sheep in Luke 15.
Its central message is God's joy over the repentance of a sinner, not a numerical church-attendance strategy.
But it also reveals something beautiful about the heart of God.
The lost are not insignificant to Him.
He does not celebrate their disappearance.
He seeks and saves the lost.
And ultimately, this entire conversation must lead us back to Jesus.
Not to a building.
Not to a religious organization.
Not to a pastor's reputation.
To Jesus Christ.
The One who entered our broken world.
The One who ate with sinners.
The One who confronted religious hypocrisy.
The One who welcomed the repentant.
The One who carried our sins to Calvary.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
The One who does not merely forgive isolated individuals, but creates a redeemed people for His glory.
Ephesians 2:19 says believers are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household.
The Greek word οἰκεῖοι (oikeioi) communicates the idea of household members.
Family.
Think about that.
In Christ, you are not merely given a religious obligation.
You are welcomed into God's household.
And although every earthly church is imperfect, the household of God is meant to reflect the grace, truth, holiness, and love of its Lord.
That does not mean every Christian gathering will feel like family immediately.
Trust takes time.
Relationships require patience.
Sometimes restoration begins with small, trembling steps.
But Jesus is worthy of those steps.
And He is worthy of the surrender that makes them possible.
Maybe you need to repent of pride that refuses correction.
Maybe you need to release bitterness that has begun to control your life.
Maybe you need to stop excusing a pattern of isolation that is slowly weakening your faith.
Or maybe you need to stop blaming yourself for the sins of people who misrepresented Christ.
Maybe you need to hear that what happened in that church was wrong.
That the abuse was not God's will for you.
That seeking safety was not a betrayal of Jesus.
And that your story is not over.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not because grace makes evil acceptable.
Not because forgiveness erases accountability.
Not because every broken relationship must be restored.
But because Jesus can redeem what sin has devastated.
He can bring truth into places where lies once ruled.
He can teach a wounded heart to trust wisely again.
He can transform a proud heart into a humble one.
He can restore fellowship where repentance and reconciliation are genuinely possible.
And He can give you courage to move forward even when the past cannot be undone.
From scandal to grace does not mean pretending the scandal never happened. It means the scandal does not get the final word over a life surrendered to Christ.
Perhaps the most important question is no longer simply, “Can I be a Christian without belonging to a local church?”
Perhaps it is this:
“Jesus, if I truly belong to You, what are You calling me to do with the people who belong to You?”
That is a question worth praying over.
A question worth opening your Bible for.
A question worth bringing before God with honesty rather than defensiveness.
You do not have to reveal private trauma or details you are not ready to share.
But your honest words may encourage someone who feels completely alone.
Not as an accusation.
As an open door.
The biblical answer is worth remembering:
Jesus alone saves. And the Jesus who saves calls His people into loving, accountable fellowship.
And if you want to continue growing in Scripture, following Gospel Warrior can be one way to receive regular biblical encouragement, teaching, conviction, and reminders of the grace of Jesus Christ.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, Christians who have grown spiritually indifferent, and even those who are still searching for truth.
Not because following a Facebook page makes anyone a disciple.
But because biblical truth is worth sharing, and a message may become an invitation for someone to open the Scriptures and seek Christ.
There is also something personal I want to share with those who believe in this ministry's mission.
Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim Jesus Christ, call people to repentance and faith, encourage wounded believers, and help Christians grow deeper in the Word of God.
Making biblical resources available freely is part of the heart behind this work.
But producing, maintaining, improving, and expanding ministry resources also requires time, effort, and financial support.
Scripture does, however, affirm generous and willing support for gospel ministry.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
And Philippians 4:15–18 shows how believers supported Paul's ministry through material gifts.
That is the spirit in which we invite your partnership.
Not through guilt.
Not through promises that a financial contribution will purchase blessings.
But through willing generosity, gratitude, and shared commitment to making biblical truth accessible.
If you already give faithfully to your local congregation, please continue to take those responsibilities seriously. Gospel Warrior is intended to support your discipleship, not replace your church.
These products can also serve as personal reminders of Scripture and opportunities to start meaningful conversations about Jesus.
You can still read.
Still learn.
Still share.
Still pray for this ministry.
Still invite someone to discover biblical truth.
Christ is the treasure.
The gospel is the message.
And our purpose is to keep pointing people to Him.
So before you close this article, return with me to the person we met at the beginning.
The one sitting alone on Sunday morning.
The one who still believes in Jesus but no longer knows where they belong.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe your Bible is still open beside your bed.
Maybe you still remember the songs you once sang with other believers.
Maybe there is a part of you that misses worshiping with people who know your name.
And maybe you are afraid to try again.
I cannot promise that every congregation will treat you well.
I cannot promise that rebuilding trust will be easy.
But I can point you to the Savior whose faithfulness does not depend on human perfection.
The One who was betrayed.
The One who was rejected.
The One who suffered at the hands of sinful people.
The One who understands grief and pain.
And the One who, even after His resurrection, continued gathering, restoring, and commissioning His followers.
Look at Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
Imagine the shame.
The memories.
The unbearable knowledge that when the pressure came, he had failed the Lord he loved.
Yet in John 21, the risen Christ confronted Peter's failure and restored him to a calling of love and service.
Jesus did not pretend the denial never happened.
He addressed Peter's love and entrusted him with the responsibility to care for His sheep.
That is grace.
Not grace that ignores sin.
Grace that restores the repentant and calls them forward.
Perhaps your story is different from Peter's.
Perhaps you were not the one who betrayed.
Perhaps you were betrayed.
But the same risen Christ remains worthy of your trust.
And His grace is sufficient to lead you into whatever faithful obedience comes next.
So do not put your faith in the perfection of a congregation.
Do not build your identity around the approval of a pastor.
Do not confuse religious activity with spiritual life.
And do not allow the failures of human beings to become your final definition of Jesus Christ.
Come to Him.
If you have never truly trusted Him, repent and believe the gospel.
If you have wandered, return to Him.
If you have been wounded, bring Him the truth of your pain.
If you have isolated yourself out of pride or fear, ask Him for the courage to obey.
And if you have been blessed with a faithful church family, love them well.
Serve them.
Pray for them.
Encourage the weak.
Welcome the lonely.
Protect the vulnerable.
Restore the repentant with gentleness.
And never forget that the church is not a stage for the impressive.
It is a people redeemed by a crucified and risen Savior.
So, can someone be a genuine Christian without belonging to a local church?
Yes. A person can genuinely belong to Christ without formal local church membership. Salvation is by grace through faith, not by enrollment in a congregation.
But no, we should not treat deliberate, permanent rejection of Christian fellowship as the biblical ideal for someone who is able to participate faithfully.
Christ saves us by grace, and that same grace teaches us to love, serve, and walk alongside His people.
Not perfectly.
Not without difficulty.
But faithfully.
And perhaps today, the next chapter of your story begins with one simple prayer:
“Jesus, I belong to You. Teach me how to love the people who belong to You, too.”
Because one day, every wound will be answered by the perfect justice and mercy of God, and all who belong to Christ will be gathered before Him.
No more hypocrisy.
No more betrayal.
No more division.
No more tears.
Only the redeemed, worshiping the Lamb who was slain.
Until then, may we refuse both empty religion and lonely, self-sufficient Christianity.
May we cling to Jesus.
May we pursue truth.
May we love His people.
And may our broken stories become testimonies of His redeeming grace.
The people who wounded you may have changed how you see the church, but they do not have to write the ending of your story with Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY WAS JEZEBEL THROWN FROM A WINDOW? THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT THE WOMAN WHO THOUGHT GOD WOULD NEVER CALL HER TO ACCOUNT
paragraphs: WHY WAS JEZEBEL THROWN FROM A WINDOW? THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT THE WOMAN WHO THOUGHT GOD WOULD NEVER CALL HER TO ACCOUNT

She wore a crown, commanded a kingdom, silenced God's prophets, and believed her power could protect her. But when judgment finally arrived, the very people standing beside her became the ones who threw her down. Her story contains a warning every Christian needs to hear—and a revelation about Jesus Christ that could change how you see your own life forever.
There is something deeply unsettling about the final moments of Jezebel's life.
Not merely because she died violently.
Not because her body fell from a palace window.
Not even because dogs eventually consumed her remains.
The most disturbing part is what happened before she fell.
She heard that someone was coming.
She knew the kingdom was changing.
She knew the man approaching had already killed her son, King Joram.
And instead of fleeing, pleading, or showing repentance, she prepared herself to meet him.
She painted her eyes.
She arranged her hair.
And she positioned herself at a window.
Imagine that scene.

A palace filled with the echoes of approaching horses. Servants watching nervously. The sound of a chariot coming closer. A powerful woman standing above the courtyard, looking down upon the man who had come to overthrow her world.
For years, people had trembled at her name.
But now the question was no longer whether people feared Jezebel.
The question was whether Jezebel feared God.
And that question should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because it is possible to spend so much time defending the life we have built that we stop asking whether God is pleased with the person we are becoming.
It is possible to look confident while standing on the edge of disaster.
And it is possible to know that judgment is coming and still refuse to surrender.
But before we examine that window, we need to understand the woman standing behind it.
Jezebel was not simply a woman with a bad reputation.
She was a queen whose actions helped turn a nation away from the worship of the living God.
First Kings 16:31 identifies her as the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and the wife of Ahab, king of Israel.
Her marriage carried political significance. But Scripture's concern is much deeper than politics.
Ahab married Jezebel and went on to serve Baal.
Under their reign, the worship of Baal gained royal support, and the covenant faithfulness God required of Israel was openly violated.
This was not merely a disagreement about religious preferences.
Israel belonged to the LORD.
The Hebrew Scriptures use the divine name יהוה (YHWH), commonly represented in English translations as LORD.
And the first commandment had already declared:
"Thou shalt have no other gods before me." — Exodus 20:3, KJV
Jezebel's influence was not limited to her personal worship.
First Kings 18:4 records that she was killing the prophets of the LORD, while Obadiah secretly hid one hundred prophets in caves and supplied them with bread and water.
Think about that.
While God's servants were hiding to stay alive, the palace was supporting the very religious system that opposed their message.
Truth had become dangerous.
Faithfulness carried a cost.
And a queen who should have understood the responsibility of authority used her position to persecute those who served God.
Yet Jezebel's story becomes even more disturbing when we encounter a man named Naboth.
Naboth owned a vineyard near Ahab's palace.
Ahab wanted it.
Naboth refused to surrender it because it was his ancestral inheritance.
His refusal was not simply stubbornness. It reflected Israel's understanding of inherited land under God's covenant.
Ahab returned home resentful.
He lay on his bed, turned away, and refused to eat.
And Jezebel stepped in.
She arranged for false accusations to be brought against Naboth. She used royal authority, manipulated a public proceeding, and secured the testimony of dishonest witnesses.
Naboth was executed.
Then Ahab went to take possession of the vineyard.
Read 1 Kings 21 carefully.
An innocent man was killed because someone with power wanted what belonged to him.
A family inheritance was seized.
Justice was corrupted.
And religious language was used to disguise wickedness.
Does that sound ancient to you?
Or does it sound painfully familiar?
How many people have been crushed because someone influential refused to hear the truth?
How many families have suffered because greed was dressed up as leadership?
How many reputations have been destroyed by accusations that were never true?
How many people have smiled in public while quietly arranging someone else's downfall?
And perhaps the harder question is this:
Have we ever justified a smaller version of the same sin because admitting the truth would cost us something?
Not everyone has stolen a vineyard.
But some have stolen another person's peace.
Not everyone has arranged false testimony.
But some have repeated accusations without knowing whether they were true.
Not everyone has ordered an innocent person killed.
But some have used words to wound people they were commanded to love.
We must not pretend that these sins are identical in severity.
They are not.
Yet the same human heart that can excuse small acts of dishonesty can become increasingly hardened when it refuses correction.
That is why Jezebel's story is not an invitation to point at a wicked queen and congratulate ourselves for being different.
It is an invitation to examine what happens when sin is protected instead of confessed.
And God did not remain silent.
He sent Elijah.
The prophet confronted Ahab with the truth about Naboth's murder and the stolen vineyard.
Then came a judgment that would echo beyond Ahab's lifetime.
In 1 Kings 21:23, Elijah declared:
"And of Jezebel also spake the LORD, saying, The dogs shall eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel." — KJV
Those words were not a random curse uttered in anger.
Scripture presents them as a divine announcement of judgment against grave wickedness.
God had seen Naboth's blood.
God had seen the lies.
God had seen the persecution.
God had seen what powerful people believed they could hide.
And He had not forgotten.
There is something profoundly important here for anyone who has ever suffered injustice.
The silence of heaven is not proof that God is indifferent.
The delay of judgment is not evidence that evil has won.
And the apparent success of a wicked person does not mean that the LORD has surrendered His throne.
Sometimes justice does not arrive when we expect it.
Sometimes the person who harmed us appears to prosper.
Sometimes the truth remains buried for years.
But Scripture repeatedly teaches that God is righteous and that evil will ultimately be brought into judgment.
Still, we need to be careful.
The story of Jezebel does not give Christians permission to announce that every tragedy is God's punishment for a particular sin.
Jesus Himself challenged that kind of assumption in Luke 13:1–5.
Nor does Jezebel's death authorize anyone to take revenge into their own hands.
"Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord." — Romans 12:19, KJV
The God who judges evil is also the God who commands His people to reject personal vengeance.
And this is where Jezebel's story becomes more surprising than many people realize.
Because before the judgment fell, God had already demonstrated His willingness to show mercy to someone deeply guilty.
That person was Ahab.
Yes. Ahab.
The king who participated in Israel's corruption.
The husband who benefited from Naboth's death.
The ruler whom Scripture describes as having sold himself to do evil.
When Ahab heard Elijah's words, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, fasted, and humbled himself.
And God noticed.
First Kings 21:29 records the LORD saying:
"Seest thou how Ahab humbleth himself before me?"
God then announced that the foretold disaster upon Ahab's house would not occur during Ahab's own days.
This was a postponement of judgment, not a declaration that Ahab's entire life had become righteous.
But do not miss what it reveals.
God took notice of a guilty man's humiliation before Him.
The God who sees wickedness also sees humility.
The God who judges rebellion does not despise genuine repentance.
And now the tragedy of Jezebel becomes even more sobering.
The biblical narrative records no comparable repentance from her.
We are not told everything that passed through her mind or every private opportunity she may have had.
But the final scene Scripture gives us contains no confession, no appeal for mercy, and no turning toward the LORD.
Instead, we find her at the window.
Years had passed since Elijah's prophecy.
Ahab had died.
Joram, Jezebel's son, was ruling Israel.
And Jehu had been commissioned to carry out judgment against Ahab's house, as described in 2 Kings 9.
Jehu drove toward Jezreel.
Joram went out to meet him.
The confrontation ended with Joram's death.
Then Jehu approached the city where Jezebel remained.
Second Kings 9:30 tells us:
"And when Jehu was come to Jezreel, Jezebel heard of it; and she painted her face, and tired her head, and looked out at a window." — KJV
The Hebrew wording deserves attention.
The expression וַתָּשֶׂם בַּפּוּךְ עֵינֶיהָ (vattāśem bappūkh ʿênêhā) describes Jezebel applying eye paint.
The verse also describes her arranging or adorning her head.
The Hebrew term פּוּךְ (pūkh) refers to a cosmetic substance used around the eyes, commonly understood as dark eye paint.
But here is an important distinction.
The Bible does not say Jezebel was judged because she wore makeup.
Cosmetics were not the central offense.
Her idolatry, persecution, manipulation, and involvement in injustice were.
Some readers interpret her final preparation as an act of royal defiance. Others see a deliberate attempt to preserve her dignity or intimidate Jehu.
The text does not explicitly explain her private motive.
What it does show is that she deliberately prepared herself and confronted Jehu from the window.
And what she said next was extraordinary.
"Had Zimri peace, who slew his master?" — 2 Kings 9:31, KJV
To understand that sentence, we need to remember Zimri.
In 1 Kings 16, Zimri assassinated King Elah, seized the throne, and reigned for only seven days before his rule collapsed.
By calling Jehu to mind of Zimri, Jezebel was invoking the example of a royal assassin whose violent seizure of power ended disastrously.
It was a pointed political accusation.
A warning.
Perhaps even an attempt to challenge Jehu's legitimacy.
The woman who had lived at the center of royal power was now speaking to the man who had come to destroy the dynasty she represented.
Then Jehu looked toward the window.
And he asked a question that changed everything.
"Who is on my side? who?" — 2 Kings 9:32, KJV
A few eunuchs looked out toward him.
And Jehu gave the command:
"Throw her down." — 2 Kings 9:33, KJV
The Hebrew is even more abrupt:
שִׁמְטוּהָ (shimṭūhā).
A short imperative meaning, in this context, "Throw her down."
And they did.
The servants who were physically near Jezebel did not protect her.
They threw her from the window.
Her blood struck the wall and the horses, and Jehu trampled her underfoot.
It is a brutal scene.
Scripture does not soften it.
But neither should we turn it into entertainment.
A human being died violently, and the biblical narrator places that death within the fulfillment of an earlier prophetic judgment.
This is not a passage to celebrate cruelty.
It is a passage to take seriously the holiness of God, the consequences of persistent evil, and the terrifying fragility of earthly power.
Jezebel had occupied a palace.
She had influenced kings.
She had persecuted prophets.
She had helped destroy an innocent man.
Yet when the hour of judgment arrived, her title could not protect her.
Her position could not protect her.
Her wealth could not protect her.
And the window from which she looked down upon Jehu became the place from which she fell.
Why was Jezebel thrown from a window?
At the immediate historical level, because Jehu commanded the palace eunuchs to throw her down, and they obeyed.
At the larger biblical level, her death formed part of the judgment pronounced against Ahab's house and against Jezebel herself.
The window was the setting of her death, not a special theological symbol that Scripture explicitly defines.
But the scene still confronts us with an unmistakable truth.
Earthly power cannot place anyone beyond God's judgment.
And there is one detail many people overlook.
After Jezebel's death, Jehu entered the palace, ate, and drank.
Then he ordered that her body be buried, acknowledging that she was a king's daughter.
But when the servants went to bury her, they found only portions of her remains.
Second Kings 9:35 records that they found her skull, feet, and palms of her hands.
The prophecy concerning the dogs had been fulfilled.
And Jehu recognized the connection to the word spoken through Elijah.
Jezebel had spent years in the center of royal life.
Yet her final story was not about the splendor of her palace.
It was about the truthfulness of God's word.
Now I want to speak to the person who has been reading this and feeling an uncomfortable stirring inside.
Perhaps you are not thinking about Jezebel anymore.
Perhaps you are thinking about yourself.
About the secret you have kept.
The bitterness you have fed.
The person you have refused to forgive.
The truth you have twisted.
The relationship you have damaged.
The warning you have ignored.
The spiritual life you have learned to perform in front of others while quietly growing distant from God.
Maybe you still attend church.
Maybe you still know the worship songs.
Maybe you still post Bible verses.
Maybe everyone around you believes you are spiritually strong.
But you know there is an area of your life where you have been resisting the Lord.
And the frightening thing about a hardened heart is that it rarely announces itself.
It usually begins with one compromise.
Then one excuse.
Then another.
Eventually, what once disturbed your conscience begins to feel normal.
You stop calling bitterness bitterness.
You call it discernment.
You stop calling pride pride.
You call it confidence.
You stop calling disobedience disobedience.
You call it freedom.
And you stop asking whether God approves because you have become skilled at explaining why you approve.
But the Gospel does not invite you to live in fear of becoming another Jezebel.
It invites you to come to Jesus Christ before your heart becomes hardened against His voice.
And here is where the story turns.
Because there is another biblical scene involving a guilty person facing death.
Not a queen standing at a palace window.
A criminal hanging beside Jesus on a cross.
He had no royal clothing.
No palace.
No earthly authority.
No impressive record of righteousness to present before God.
He was dying under the consequences of his crimes.
And unlike Jezebel's final recorded confrontation, this man's final recorded words included an acknowledgment of guilt and an appeal to Jesus.
He said:
"Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom." — Luke 23:42, KJV
And Jesus answered:
"Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." — Luke 23:43, KJV
Do you see the contrast?
One scene shows a powerful person confronted by judgment.
The other shows a powerless sinner appealing to a crucified King.
One ends in the fulfillment of a judgment prophecy.
The other reveals the astonishing mercy of the Savior.
The difference is not that one person had committed serious sins while the other was innocent.
The criminal himself admitted that he was receiving the consequences of his actions.
The difference is that he turned toward Jesus in faith.
And Jesus received him.
The Greek word commonly translated "grace" in the New Testament is χάρις (charis).
It speaks of favor and gift, and in the Gospel it directs us toward God's undeserved generosity toward sinners.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." — KJV
That is why the Gospel is not merely a warning that sin has consequences.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
The innocent Son of God bore sin's judgment so that those who repent and believe in Him might receive forgiveness and eternal life.
The cross does not tell us that evil is insignificant.
It tells us that sin is so serious that redemption required the sacrifice of Christ.
And it tells us that God's love is so great that He gave His Son for a world that could never save itself.
This is why you must never confuse God's patience with His approval.
Second Peter 3:9 describes the Lord as patient, "not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance."
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), translated "repentance," expresses a change of mind and turning from sin toward God.
Biblical repentance is more than embarrassment after being exposed.
It is more than crying because consequences have arrived.
It is a genuine turning to God that bears fruit in a changed life.
And this is where the message becomes deeply personal.
You do not have to wait until everything collapses to tell God the truth.
You do not have to lose your family before admitting that pride has damaged your relationships.
You do not have to destroy your testimony before confessing the compromise you have been hiding.
You do not have to reach the end of your strength before acknowledging that you need a Savior.
You can come to Jesus now.
Not because you have made yourself worthy.
Not because you have finally become impressive.
But because the blood of Jesus Christ is sufficient to cleanse those who come to Him in faith.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — KJV
Read that again.
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That promise is not permission to continue deliberately in sin.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and walk in the light.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear something else.
You may have been harmed by someone whose behavior reminds you of Jezebel's cruelty.
Someone controlling.
Someone dishonest.
Someone who used authority to silence you.
Someone who used religious language to justify abuse.
Someone who made you question your worth.
Please understand this.
The biblical account of Jezebel does not authorize us to label every difficult woman, outspoken person, or someone we disagree with as having a "Jezebel spirit."

In Revelation 2:20, the risen Christ rebukes a figure called Jezebel for teaching and seducing His servants into idolatry and sexual immorality. The passage addresses concrete spiritual corruption. It does not establish a universal label for women with strong personalities or people who challenge authority.
We must be faithful to what Scripture actually says.
And if you have been wounded by manipulation or spiritual abuse, forgiveness does not require you to return to an unsafe situation.
You can release vengeance to God while maintaining wise boundaries and seeking justice.
Christ does not ask the wounded to pretend that evil never happened.
He calls us to truth.
He calls us to righteousness.
And He offers healing that does not depend on denying our pain.
Perhaps that is why this story still matters.
Because there are people living behind invisible palace walls.
Some are trapped by their own pride.
Others are trapped by the cruelty of someone else's pride.
Some need to repent.
Others need to stop blaming themselves for another person's wickedness.
And all of us need the Savior who sees what human beings cannot see.
Jesus knows the difference.
He knows the difference between rebellion and suffering.
Between repentance and performance.
Between the person who wounds and the person who has been wounded.
Between someone using Scripture as a weapon and someone desperately searching Scripture for hope.
He is not confused by appearances.
He sees the heart.
And when we look at Jezebel's final window, we should remember another truth.
None of us knows how much time we have.
That is not a reason to live in constant panic.
It is a reason to stop postponing what matters most.
Make peace where you can.
Confess what you have hidden.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Seek forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Offer forgiveness where God is leading you, without confusing forgiveness with the removal of necessary boundaries.
And above everything, come to Christ.
Because the deepest tragedy is not that Jezebel lost her crown.
It is that the biblical account of her final moments gives us no evidence of a heart turning to the God she had resisted.
Her story ends with judgment.
But your story does not have to end with rebellion.
You are reading this while there is still breath in your lungs.
There is still an opportunity to hear the Gospel.
There is still an invitation to repent and believe.
And the invitation does not come from a powerless religious philosophy.
It comes from the risen Jesus Christ.
The One who said:
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." — John 6:37, KJV
What a promise.
The person who comes to Jesus will not be rejected because their past is too shameful.
The sinner who genuinely turns to Him does not have to purchase mercy with good deeds.
The broken person does not have to pretend to be whole before asking for help.
The cross is where justice and mercy meet, not because God ignores evil, but because Christ has accomplished the work of redemption.
And the empty tomb declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because Jesus changes the historical facts of what we have done.
Not because repentance erases every earthly consequence.
Not because grace makes holiness unnecessary.
But because Jesus forgives sinners, gives new life, and begins transforming those who surrender to Him.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It may reveal some of your failures.
It may contain decisions you wish you could undo.
But it does not have to be the final authority over your future in Christ.
And maybe right now, as you read these words, you are tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of fighting the same secret battle.
Tired of carrying guilt.
Tired of looking spiritually strong while feeling spiritually empty.
Then stop performing for a moment.
You do not have to impress God with beautiful words.
You can speak to Him truthfully.

"Lord Jesus, I have sinned. I have tried to justify things You have called me to surrender. I have hidden behind excuses. I need Your forgiveness. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Turn my heart away from sin. Teach me to trust You, obey You, and walk in Your truth. Heal what is broken in me, and help me make right what I can. I surrender myself to You. Amen."
Open your Bible.
Read the Gospel of John.
Find a faithful local church where Scripture is taught and where you can grow in Christian community.
Seek mature believers who will pray with you, encourage you, and lovingly hold you accountable.
Real discipleship is not sustained by emotion alone.
It grows through God's Word, prayer, obedience, fellowship, and the work of the Holy Spirit.
And if this article exposed something you have been hiding, I want to invite you to respond.
You do not have to disclose private details or painful experiences publicly. God knows the burden even when all you can manage is a few words.
Your words may encourage someone who has begun to believe that forgiveness is no longer possible for them.
Think, too, about the person who might need this message.
A brother who has wandered from faith.
A sister who is struggling with bitterness.
A friend who has been deeply wounded.
A family member who believes their past has made them unworthy of God's love.
Someone who does not yet know Jesus.
Not simply to increase a number on a screen, but because a message grounded in Scripture may reach someone you could never reach through a private conversation.
There is also something important I want to share with those who believe in this ministry and want to help it continue.
Gospel Warrior is not intended to be merely another page people visit for a few emotional words before moving on.
Our desire is to help people know Jesus Christ, understand Scripture faithfully, grow in holiness, and find encouragement to persevere in faith.
We want biblical resources to reach people who may not be able to afford shelves full of Christian books.
We want struggling believers to have access to material that helps them study God's Word.
We want families to grow together in faith.
We want seekers to encounter the Gospel clearly.
And we want people who have fallen to know that restoration through Jesus Christ is possible.
But sustaining and expanding a ministry requires real work, time, resources, and faithful support.
Scripture teaches:
"God loveth a cheerful giver." — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Giving should arise from a willing heart, not fear, pressure, or the belief that God's forgiveness can be purchased.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, obedience, love, generosity, and a life surrendered to His will.
These products are simply an additional expression of appreciation. They are not the reason to give, and no purchase can make anyone more acceptable to God.
The greatest gift we can share is the Gospel itself.
Pray for the ministry.
Point people toward the free library resources.
Speak about Jesus with someone who needs hope.
A person who cannot contribute financially can still serve the Lord faithfully and meaningfully.
The mission is not about building an audience around a personality.
It is about directing people to the Savior.
And now, before you leave, I want you to return in your mind to that window in Jezreel.
The approaching chariot.
The queen looking down.
The servants standing nearby.
The sudden command.
The fall.
The fulfillment of a word spoken years earlier.
It is a difficult picture.
But remember the other picture.
A hill outside Jerusalem.
A crucified Savior.
A guilty criminal turning toward Him.
A simple plea for mercy.
And a promise of paradise.
One story warns us not to harden our hearts against the living God.
The other assures us that the mercy of Jesus is available even to a sinner with no opportunity left to rebuild an impressive life.
Do not use Jezebel's story to feel superior to someone else.
Let it lead you to humility.
Do not use the violence of her death to justify cruelty.
Let it deepen your reverence for God's justice.
Do not use the warning of judgment to forget the beauty of grace.
Let it drive you toward the cross.
And do not allow shame to convince you that repentance is pointless.
The Savior who received the dying criminal is still mighty to save.
Today, the question is not whether you have ever sinned.
We all have.
The question is what you will do with the truth when God brings it into the light.
Will you defend what is destroying you?
Or will you surrender it to the One who died to redeem you?
Will you cling to an image of yourself that cannot save you?
Or will you come honestly to Jesus?
Jezebel's final recorded scene was at a window.
The Christian's hope rests in an empty tomb.
And that changes everything.
Never become so determined to protect the crown you built for yourself that you refuse the mercy of the King who wore thorns to save you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY WERE UNCLEAN… BUT HAD THEY SINNED? THE SHOCKING TRUTH ABOUT LEVITICUS 15 THAT MANY CHRISTIANS HAVE NEVER BEEN TAUGHT
paragraphs: THEY WERE UNCLEAN… BUT HAD THEY SINNED? THE SHOCKING TRUTH ABOUT LEVITICUS 15 THAT MANY CHRISTIANS HAVE NEVER BEEN TAUGHT

Not everyone declared unclean was guilty of sin. Not every person kept away from God's sanctuary had rebelled against Him. And when you discover why this distinction matters, you may never read the Law of Moses—or the healing touch of Jesus Christ—the same way again.
Imagine waking up one morning and discovering that something happening naturally inside your own body has made you ceremonially unclean.
You haven't stolen anything.
You haven't lied.
You haven't betrayed your spouse.
You haven't deliberately disobeyed God.
Yet according to the Law given to ancient Israel, you must wash, wait, and temporarily observe restrictions concerning sacred things.
Now imagine someone standing nearby, looking at you as though your condition proves that God is angry with you.
You want to explain.
You want to defend yourself.
