"For the land is full of adulterers; for because of swearing the land mourneth; the pleasant places of the wilderness are dried up, and their course is evil, and their force is not right.
For both prophet and priest are profane; yea, in my house have I found their wickedness, saith the LORD."
Read that last sentence again.
"In my house have I found their wickedness."
Not merely in the streets.
Not merely among those who openly rejected God's covenant.
Even in the place associated with His worship.
The people entrusted with sacred responsibilities were not automatically innocent because they occupied sacred positions.
Their titles could not sanctify their rebellion.
Their religious activities could not conceal their hearts from the Lord.
And their public authority could not make their private wickedness righteous.
The Hebrew language makes the accusation even more striking.
In Jeremiah 23:10, the word translated "adulterers" is מְנָאֲפִים (mena'afim), from the Hebrew root נאף (na'af), meaning "to commit adultery."
This is not a harmless word for ordinary imperfection.
It carries the weight of violated faithfulness.
Throughout the prophetic writings, adultery can describe actual marital unfaithfulness, while the imagery of adultery is also used for covenant betrayal through idolatry and spiritual unfaithfulness.

In this passage, Jeremiah's accusation belongs within that wider world of moral and covenant corruption. The language is serious, but we must not claim that every individual prophet or priest was personally guilty of sexual adultery. The passage does not establish that.
God was exposing a society saturated with unfaithfulness, including the wickedness of those who should have been guiding His people toward righteousness.
And that distinction matters.
Because Scripture must never be twisted merely to make a scandal sound bigger.
The truth is already devastating enough.

Jeremiah 23:11 uses another important Hebrew word: חָנֵף (chanef), translated "profane" in the King James Version. In this context, it communicates moral and religious corruption—conduct that is godless rather than faithful to the Lord.
The priest could perform religious duties.
The prophet could speak religious words.
But neither activity could erase the reality of an unfaithful heart.
And suddenly, Jeremiah's ancient world begins to look painfully familiar.
A person can know the vocabulary of repentance without actually repenting.
A preacher can speak about humility while refusing correction.
A worshiper can lift both hands during a song while refusing to release the bitterness consuming their heart.
A husband can speak publicly about biblical marriage while secretly betraying his wife.
A wife can appear devoted to Christ while nurturing deception she refuses to bring into the light.
A Christian can share Bible verses every morning and still spend every night returning to a hidden habit that is slowly mastering them.
And none of us should read those examples with the comfortable assumption that Jeremiah must be talking about somebody else.
Because the moment we use Scripture only to expose other people's sins while protecting our own, we have already missed part of its warning.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You have learned how to appear strong when you are spiritually exhausted.
You know how to answer "I'm blessed" even when you have not honestly prayed in days.
You know which Bible verses to post.
You know what to say when somebody asks how your walk with God is going.
You know how to make everything appear normal.
But there is something you have been hiding.
Perhaps it is an addiction.
Perhaps it is a relationship that has crossed boundaries you once promised God you would never cross.
Perhaps it is the bitterness you have justified for years.
Perhaps it is the secret pleasure you take in somebody else's failure.
Or perhaps it is something quieter.
You have not abandoned Christianity.
You have simply learned how to practice enough of it to avoid confronting the areas of your life that remain unsurrendered.
And somewhere beneath the religious routine, your conscience has been whispering that something is wrong.
Jeremiah's message reaches directly into that uncomfortable place.
Because God does not measure faithfulness by how convincingly we can perform it.
He sees what is true.
Then the prophecy becomes even more severe.
In Jeremiah 23:13–14, the Lord declares:
"And I have seen folly in the prophets of Samaria; they prophesied in Baal, and caused my people Israel to err.

I have seen also in the prophets of Jerusalem an horrible thing: they commit adultery, and walk in lies: they strengthen also the hands of evildoers, that none doth return from his wickedness: they are all of them unto me as Sodom, and the inhabitants thereof as Gomorrah."
These words were not spoken casually.

The reference to Samaria recalls the corruption associated with the northern kingdom of Israel, while the accusation against Jerusalem's prophets exposes the terrible condition of Judah's own religious leadership.
The Hebrew expression translated "an horrible thing" is שַׁעֲרוּרָה (sha'arurah), describing something appalling or shocking.
And the expression וְהָלֹךְ בַּשָּׁקֶר (vehalok bashaqer) conveys the idea of walking in falsehood.
This was more than an isolated mistake.
It described a pattern of life shaped by lies.
But the most frightening accusation is what came next.
"They strengthen also the hands of evildoers, that none doth return from his wickedness."
Stop there.
God was not only confronting leaders who sinned.
He was confronting leaders whose influence made it easier for other people to continue sinning.
Instead of calling people back to the Lord, they reinforced their rebellion.
Instead of exposing the danger, they made it seem acceptable.
Instead of helping sinners turn away from destruction, they offered messages that allowed them to remain where they were.
And this is where the passage becomes particularly relevant to every generation.
A message can sound comforting and still be spiritually dangerous.
A religious leader can be charismatic and still be unfaithful to Scripture.
A congregation can be large and still need repentance.
A sermon can make everybody feel wonderful and still fail to tell the truth they desperately need to hear.
But we must be equally careful not to confuse biblical courage with cruelty.
Not every gentle sermon is compromise.
Not every strong rebuke is godly.
Not every struggling pastor is a false prophet.
And not every accusation against a religious leader is true.
The standard is not whether a message sounds harsh enough.
The standard is whether it faithfully communicates God's Word, honors Jesus Christ, and bears the fruit of truth and godliness.
That is why Jeremiah's accusation is so devastating.
These prophets were not merely failing to condemn evil loudly enough.
They were actively strengthening those who practiced it.
They were helping people resist the very repentance that could have brought them back into covenant faithfulness.
And that raises a question worth asking ourselves.
Have we ever called something "grace" when what we really wanted was permission to remain unchanged?
Have we ever looked for a teacher who would reassure us rather than challenge us?
Have we ever avoided a passage of Scripture because we already knew what obedience would require?
Have we ever prayed for God to bless a decision we were unwilling to submit to His Word?
There is a difference between a wounded sinner crying out for mercy and a hardened heart demanding divine approval.
Jesus welcomes the repentant sinner.
He does not redefine sin to make repentance unnecessary.
And that truth should humble every one of us.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that sin no longer matters.
It is the glorious announcement that sin was so serious, and God's love so astonishing, that Jesus Christ gave Himself to save sinners.
But before we reach the cross, we need to understand something else about Jeremiah.
He was not a man who delighted in announcing judgment.
He was a prophet whose ministry was marked by grief.
In Jeremiah 9:1, he longs for tears enough to mourn the destruction of his people.
His confrontation flowed from a burden, not from the thrill of humiliating others.
That is a lesson the modern Church desperately needs.
It is possible to become so excited about exposing somebody else's scandal that we forget the person involved is a human being in need of truth, justice, and, where there is repentance, mercy.
It is possible to speak correctly about sin while carrying a heart full of pride.
It is possible to defend biblical holiness while becoming cruel toward the people Christ calls us to love.
Jeremiah gives us no permission for that.
His message reminds us that genuine spiritual concern does not rejoice in corruption.
It grieves over it.
It confronts evil because evil destroys.
It protects the vulnerable.
It refuses to cover up abuse.
It does not demand that victims remain silent to preserve the reputation of a ministry.
And it does not treat public religious influence as an exemption from accountability.
The name of Jesus must never become a shield for wrongdoing.
Nor should forgiveness be used to bypass justice, appropriate boundaries, or the responsibility to make restitution where possible.
If a spiritual leader has harmed someone, biblical repentance does not mean asking everyone to pretend the harm never happened.
Grace does not require dishonesty.
And reconciliation is not the same thing as automatically restoring someone to a position of trust.
That is not a rejection of the Gospel.
It is part of taking truth, holiness, and human dignity seriously.
Yet Jeremiah's warning is not intended only for the powerful.
It also reaches those of us who have been hurt by religious hypocrisy.
Perhaps you trusted somebody who represented God.
You believed their counsel.
You defended them when others questioned their behavior.
You gave them the benefit of the doubt because you could not imagine that somebody who spoke so passionately about Scripture could be living so differently.
And then the truth came out.
The disappointment was not merely personal.
It shook something inside your faith.
You began asking questions you never expected to ask.
Was any of it real?
Can I trust the Church again?
Did God see what happened?
Why did He allow somebody who spoke in His name to cause so much damage?
Those are not small questions.
And they should not be dismissed with religious slogans.
But there is something in Jeremiah 23 that wounded believers need to hear.
God saw.
Before the public knew.
Before the lies were uncovered.
Before the reputation collapsed.
God saw.
The same Lord who said, "In my house have I found their wickedness," was not deceived by the religious appearance surrounding that wickedness.
He did not mistake influence for integrity.
He did not confuse spiritual language with spiritual faithfulness.
And He did not approve of evil simply because someone committed it while claiming to represent Him.
If you have been wounded by hypocrisy, please understand this distinction.
The failure of someone who claims to follow Christ is not the failure of Christ Himself.
Jesus is not the corruption committed in His name.
He is the righteous Lord before whom all corruption will ultimately be judged.
And He is also the Savior who calls wounded, guilty, and weary people to Himself.
The people who betrayed your trust do not get to define who Jesus is.
Look at Him.
Look at the way He treated the vulnerable.
Look at the way He confronted hypocrisy.
Look at the way He welcomed repentant sinners.
Look at the way He refused to turn God's house into a marketplace for exploitation.
Look at the way He gave His life for people who could never earn salvation.
There is no contradiction between the holiness of Jesus and the mercy of Jesus.
His mercy is holy.
His holiness is never separated from His perfect righteousness and love.
And this is where Jeremiah's prophecy opens into something breathtaking.
Because the chapter does not end with the corruption of the prophets.
It moves toward a promise.
Jeremiah 23:5 declares:
"Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth."
After exposing leaders who walked in lies, God promised a righteous King.
After confronting shepherds who scattered and harmed His people, God spoke of a ruler who would execute justice.
After revealing the failure of human leadership, God pointed toward the hope of a coming Davidic King.
The Hebrew expression צֶמַח צַדִּיק (tsemach tsaddiq) means "a righteous Branch" or "righteous Shoot."
The image communicates new growth, hope, and the continuation of God's promise to David.
Christians understand this promised righteous Branch as finding its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, the Son of David.
And the contrast is extraordinary.
Jeremiah exposed leaders whose lives contradicted their message.
Jesus came as the One whose life perfectly embodied the righteousness He proclaimed.
Jeremiah condemned shepherds who led people astray.
Jesus declared in John 10:11:
"I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep."
Do you see the difference?
False shepherds use the sheep for themselves.
The Good Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.
Corrupt leaders protect their position.
Jesus humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross, as Philippians 2:8 declares.
Unfaithful leaders may conceal their wrongdoing.
Jesus, who committed no sin, willingly bore the suffering of the cross for sinners.
The religious corruption Jeremiah condemned could not be healed merely by replacing one imperfect leader with another.
Humanity needed something far greater.
We needed a Savior.
And God did not leave us without one.
Jesus Christ entered a world filled with the very sins Jeremiah had exposed.
Adultery.
Deception.
Religious pride.
Hypocrisy.
Greed.
Abuse of authority.
Self-righteousness.
Hardness of heart.
He did not participate in those sins.
He confronted them.
He exposed them.
And He offered forgiveness to those willing to repent and believe.
Consider the woman caught in adultery in John 8:1–11.
The religious authorities brought her before Jesus, seeking to use her situation as a trap.
Jesus refused to join their attempt to weaponize her shame.
He confronted the accusers.
And when the confrontation ended, He spoke words that revealed both mercy and moral clarity.
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more."
He did not tell her that adultery was harmless.
He did not announce that her past defined her forever.
He extended mercy while calling her away from sin.
That is the beauty of Jesus.
He does not need to lie about our condition to love us.
He knows exactly what we have done.
He knows the sins we confess and the ones we are still afraid to name.
He knows what happened behind closed doors.
He knows the moments when we chose rebellion even while knowing better.
And still, the Gospel announces that forgiveness is available through His death and resurrection.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because His sacrifice is sufficient.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we perfected our religious appearance.
Not after we convinced everybody we had changed.
Not after we accumulated enough good works to cancel our guilt.
Christ died for sinners.
And He rose again.
This is where the scandal of human sin meets the greater wonder of divine grace.
The cross exposes how seriously God takes evil.
The cross also reveals how deeply God loves those He came to save.
And the resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
Perhaps that is why this story matters so much.
Because some people reading it are angry at religious hypocrisy.
Others have been wounded by it.
Some are afraid they have become part of it.
And others are carrying secrets they have never told another living soul.
But the invitation of Jesus is not to build a more convincing disguise.
It is to come into the light.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say God forgives only those whose sins were socially acceptable.
It does not say cleansing is reserved for people who have never failed publicly.
It does not say the door of mercy closes the moment someone realizes how far they have wandered.
It calls us to confession.
And it points us to God's faithfulness.
Yet biblical confession is more than a carefully worded apology designed to protect a reputation.
Real repentance involves turning toward God and away from sin.
It means ceasing to defend what He condemns.
It means being willing to tell the truth.
It means accepting responsibility.
It means making necessary changes, seeking help, and refusing to use grace as an excuse to continue harming others.
And when we fall, it means returning to Christ rather than surrendering to despair.
Perhaps you have failed so many times that you are afraid to believe restoration is possible.
You promised God you would stop.
Then you returned to the same sin.
You cried.
You prayed.
You felt conviction.
And eventually, you began wondering whether your repentance could ever be sincere again.
Please hear this carefully.
Do not make peace with the sin that is destroying you.
But do not mistake the depth of your struggle for proof that Christ is unable to save.
Bring the truth into the light.
Seek wise, trustworthy help.
Take the steps necessary to turn away from what has enslaved you.
And place your confidence not in your ability to manufacture a perfect spiritual record, but in the crucified and risen Savior.
There is no need to pretend before the One who already knows.
The most hopeful thing about being fully known by God is that He calls us to approach Him through Jesus Christ.
And that is why the message of Jeremiah 23 should not end with outrage against corrupt religious leaders.
It should end with all of us asking a more personal question.
Lord, is there any falsehood in me?
Am I more concerned about appearing holy than becoming obedient?
Do I demand accountability from others while making excuses for myself?
Do I prefer messages that flatter me over Scripture that corrects me?
Am I helping people follow Christ, or am I encouraging them to remain comfortable in disobedience?
Those are painful questions.
But sometimes the questions that disturb us most are the very ones that awaken us to our need for grace.
And perhaps tonight, somebody who has spent years hiding behind a religious appearance will finally whisper a prayer that is painfully simple.
"Jesus, I am tired of pretending."
No performance.
No impressive vocabulary.
No attempt to negotiate with God.
Just the truth.

"Lord, You know what I have done. You know what I have hidden. You know how many times I have made excuses. I cannot save myself. Forgive me through Jesus Christ. Teach me to repent sincerely. Give me courage to obey You, to tell the truth, and to walk in the light. Change what I cannot change by pretending. Make me faithful to You."
That prayer is not a magical formula.
It is an expression of the surrender to which the Gospel calls us.
And if you are coming to Christ in repentance and faith, you do not have to wait until you look respectable enough to approach Him.
Come to Him because you need Him.
Come with your guilt.
Come with your grief.
Come with your questions.
Come with the truth you have been afraid to face.
Because the Gospel is not about sinful people successfully hiding their scandals from a holy God.
It is about a holy Savior who came to redeem sinners and transform their lives.
And there is something else we must not overlook.
When Jeremiah confronted the religious leaders of his day, he was not building a platform around himself.
He was delivering a message entrusted to him.
The goal was faithfulness to God.
That same principle should govern every Christian ministry today, including Gospel Warrior.
Our mission must never be to gather attention merely for the sake of attention.
It must be to point people toward Jesus Christ, faithfully explain Scripture, encourage genuine repentance, strengthen struggling believers, and help people grow in biblical truth.
That is why your participation matters.
Somewhere on Facebook, there may be a person who has quietly stopped attending church because of spiritual betrayal.
Someone who has been battling a secret sin and believes they are beyond forgiveness.
Someone who has confused religious performance with a relationship with Christ.
Someone who has never heard the Gospel explained without manipulation, shame, or condemnation masquerading as holiness.
A friend may read it without reacting.
A relative may return to it late at night.
A struggling believer may save it because they are not ready to talk about what they are facing.
Someone who has spent years avoiding God may encounter a passage of Scripture that finally makes them willing to seek Him again.
You cannot control how someone responds.
But you can faithfully place biblical truth where it may be heard.
Not to make yourself appear religious.
Not to win an argument.
But because the truth about Jesus is worth sharing.
And please, do not leave without reflecting honestly on what this passage has stirred in your heart.
You do not need to disclose private details, identify someone who harmed you, or confess sensitive matters publicly. A simple expression of faith or a request for prayer is enough.
Your honesty may encourage someone who has been silently carrying a similar burden.
Because the Church does not become healthier by pretending nobody struggles.
It grows healthier when believers walk in truth, practice repentance, protect one another, and point one another back to Jesus Christ.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, those who have grown spiritually cold, and even those who are still searching for answers to follow along.
Our desire is to provide daily biblical encouragement, honest discipleship, Gospel-centered teaching, and reminders that transformation is possible through Jesus Christ.
We also want to place helpful Christian resources within reach of people who are serious about growing deeper in their faith.

These resources are intended to help readers move beyond inspirational moments into a more sustained life of studying Scripture, growing in prayer, understanding biblical doctrine, and following Christ.
And for those who believe in this mission and have the ability to help sustain it, there is another meaningful way to participate.
It is a voluntary act of support for a Christian ministry whose work you believe is worth sustaining.
These products are simply additional ways to encourage faith, reflection, and Gospel-centered conversations in everyday life.
The greater purpose remains the same.
Jesus Christ must be at the center.
You are still welcome here.
You can still read, pray, learn, share, comment, and grow with this community.
The free resources remain part of our commitment to helping people encounter biblical truth.
Because this mission is not about building a monument to Gospel Warrior.
It is about pointing people to the Savior.
The same Jesus who confronted religious hypocrisy.
The same Jesus who welcomed repentant sinners.
The same Jesus who gave His life for the ungodly.
The same Jesus who rose from the dead.
The same Jesus who calls His people to holiness without denying them the hope of grace.
And when all the excitement of this article has faded, when the comments have stopped appearing, when the notifications have gone silent, there is one truth I pray you will remember.
Jeremiah did not expose religious corruption so that people could become better at judging everybody else.
His words revealed how desperately God's people needed faithfulness, righteousness, and a true Shepherd.
And that need ultimately directs our eyes toward Jesus Christ.
The righteous Branch.
The Good Shepherd.
The crucified Savior.
The risen King.
The One who does not merely teach us how to appear different.
The One who saves and transforms those who belong to Him.
So do not walk away from Jeremiah 23 merely asking which religious leader deserves to be exposed next.
Ask whether your own heart is surrendered to Christ.
Ask whether your life is becoming more truthful.
Ask whether you are willing to repent when God's Word confronts you.
Ask whether you have placed your hope in Jesus Himself rather than in the reputation of those who speak about Him.
And if you discover something painful in your own heart, do not run deeper into hiding.
Run to the Savior.
Because the answer to religious hypocrisy is not another mask.
It is truth.
It is repentance.
It is grace.
It is Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the most unforgettable part of Jeremiah's warning is this:
God was not fooled by the holiness they performed—and the same God who sees through every disguise is the One who invites repentant sinners to come into the light of His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PAUL TOLD TIMOTHY TO DRINK WINE—BUT THE REASON MAY EXPOSE SOMETHING THE CHURCH HAS FORGOTTEN
paragraphs: PAUL TOLD TIMOTHY TO DRINK WINE—BUT THE REASON MAY EXPOSE SOMETHING THE CHURCH HAS FORGOTTEN
One sentence. One troubled stomach. One surprising instruction from an apostle. And a powerful lesson about holiness, healing, grace, and the God who cares for the body while transforming the soul.
“Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for thy stomach's sake and thine often infirmities.” — 1 Timothy 5:23 (KJV)
Imagine spending your life trying to honor God.
You pray when nobody sees you. You resist temptations other people surrender to without a second thought. You study Scripture. You serve the church. You fight to keep your conscience clean.
And yet, your body keeps failing you.
You wake up tired. Your stomach hurts. Your strength disappears when you need it most. You ask God for healing, but tomorrow arrives with the same weakness.
Then a letter comes from someone who loves you deeply.
Someone who knows your faith.
Someone who has witnessed miracles, endured persecution, and encountered the risen Jesus Christ.
The apostle Paul.
And instead of telling you to pray harder, fast longer, or prove your faith by enduring more pain, he writes something so ordinary that generations of Christians would eventually argue over it.
“Use a little wine.”
Wait.
Wine?
From Paul?
To Timothy?
In a letter containing serious instructions about holiness, church leadership, purity, and godly conduct?
Why would an apostle who warned believers against drunkenness recommend wine to a young pastor?
Was Paul permitting alcohol? Was he prescribing medicine? Was Timothy practicing complete abstinence? And what does any of this have to do with the Gospel?
The answer is more profound than the controversy.
Because hidden inside this easily misunderstood verse is a beautiful reminder that God never asked His children to confuse unnecessary suffering with spiritual maturity.
And to understand why, we must first meet the man receiving the instruction.
Timothy was not an ordinary young believer.
He was Paul's beloved coworker, a man shaped by sincere faith and entrusted with enormous responsibility.

His grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice had helped establish his spiritual foundation (2 Timothy 1:5). From childhood, he had known the sacred Scriptures that could make him wise for salvation through faith in Jesus Christ (2 Timothy 3:15).
Paul regarded him with extraordinary affection.
In 1 Timothy 1:2, he called him his own son in the faith.
Not because Timothy was Paul's biological child, but because their relationship had been formed through discipleship, spiritual responsibility, and shared devotion to Christ.
Timothy had witnessed the cost of following Jesus.
He knew that ministry was not a platform for applause.
It was a calling that demanded courage.
He had to confront false teaching, model godliness, care for believers, and lead faithfully in circumstances that could easily overwhelm a young minister.
And somewhere in the middle of those responsibilities, Timothy was frequently sick.
Scripture does not tell us exactly what illness he suffered from.
It does not identify an ulcer, infection, digestive disorder, or any other specific medical diagnosis.
What it does tell us is enough.
Timothy had stomach problems and recurring ailments.
And Paul knew about them.
That detail matters.
Because the apostle who cared about Timothy's doctrine also cared about Timothy's health.
The man who instructed him to guard the Gospel did not ignore the pain in his stomach.
Timothy was more than a worker in God's kingdom. He was a person worth caring for.
Now look closely at the original Greek.
Paul writes:
Μηκέτι ὑδροπότει, ἀλλὰ οἴνῳ ὀλίγῳ χρῶ διὰ τὸν στόμαχον καὶ τὰς πυκνάς σου ἀσθενείας.
A careful translation is:
“No longer drink only water, but use a little wine because of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.”
Several Greek expressions help us understand what Paul was actually saying.

The word ὑδροπότει (hydropotei) refers to drinking water. Combined with μηκέτι (mēketi), meaning “no longer,” the instruction indicates that Timothy should stop relying exclusively on water as his drink.
Paul was not commanding him to abandon water altogether.
The contrast is between drinking only water and making limited use of wine.
Then comes the phrase that should silence much of the careless debate.
οἴνῳ ὀλίγῳ (oinō oligō).
“A little wine.”
The Greek word oinos ordinarily refers to wine, and oligos emphasizes a small quantity.
The text does not say, “Drink as much as you want.”
It does not say, “Use wine to escape your troubles.”
It does not say, “Your ministry is stressful, so intoxication is understandable.”
Paul's instruction is deliberately limited.
Then he gives the reason.
διὰ τὸν στόμαχον (dia ton stomachon).
“Because of your stomach.”
And finally:
τὰς πυκνάς σου ἀσθενείας (tas pyknas sou astheneias).
“Your frequent illnesses.”
The Greek adjective pyknas indicates recurring or frequent occurrences. Astheneias refers here to illnesses or bodily weaknesses.
Paul was addressing a real physical concern.
Not a social occasion.
Not an invitation to indulgence.
Not a new religious ritual.
A suffering believer needed practical care.
And the apostle gave him practical advice.
But here is where we must be especially careful.
Some Christians have claimed that the wine Paul recommended was definitely nonalcoholic grape juice.
Others have insisted that this verse proves every Christian should drink alcoholic beverages.
Neither conclusion follows from the text.
In ordinary first-century Greek usage, oinos could refer to fermented wine, and there is no clear indication in this verse that Paul meant unfermented juice.
At the same time, Paul's recommendation was specific to Timothy's condition and explicitly restricted to a little wine.
It was not a universal command requiring Christians to drink alcohol.
Nor does it establish that alcohol is a necessary or medically appropriate treatment for digestive illnesses today.
Modern medicine recognizes that alcohol can irritate the stomach, aggravate certain conditions, interact dangerously with medications, and contribute to serious health problems.
The ancient medical context must not be confused with present-day clinical advice.
Paul was speaking to Timothy in his historical circumstances, not writing a modern prescription for every believer with stomach pain.
That distinction protects us from forcing Scripture to say what it never intended to say.
But there is another question.
Why was Timothy apparently drinking only water?
Was he avoiding wine because of personal conviction?
Was he practicing unusually strict self-denial?
Was he concerned about his testimony?
Was he following an ascetic practice?
We are not told.
And faithful Bible interpretation requires the humility to admit what Scripture leaves unanswered.
It is possible that Timothy's abstinence reflected a personal discipline or concern for purity, but the passage does not explicitly reveal his motive.
What we know is that Paul considered a limited change appropriate for Timothy's health.
And that opens a much larger conversation.
Because sometimes believers begin to treat their own self-imposed restrictions as though they were commands from God.
They assume that if something is difficult, it must be holy.
If something is uncomfortable, it must be spiritually superior.
If they refuse every form of relief, perhaps God will be more pleased with them.
But Scripture never teaches that pain itself makes a person righteous.
Holiness is not measured by how much avoidable suffering we can accumulate.
And righteousness is not earned through the unnecessary neglect of our bodies.
Consider Paul's words in Colossians 2:23.

He warns about religious practices that possess an appearance of wisdom through self-imposed worship, false humility, and severe treatment of the body, yet lack genuine power against sinful indulgence.
That does not mean fasting is wrong.
It does not mean discipline is unnecessary.
Jesus Himself fasted.
Paul taught self-control.
The Christian life requires sacrifice.
But biblical self-denial is not the same as treating every physical need as an enemy of faith.
There is a difference between carrying the cross Christ calls us to carry and creating burdens Christ never commanded.
And perhaps someone reading this knows that difference all too painfully.
You have been exhausted for months.
But you keep telling yourself that rest is laziness.
You have been struggling emotionally.
But you feel ashamed to ask for help.
You have been sick.
But somewhere along the way, you began to believe that seeking treatment might reveal a lack of faith.
You love Jesus.
You truly do.
Yet you have started treating yourself with a harshness you would never impose upon someone you love.
Listen carefully.
Needing help does not make you less faithful.
Timothy was a devoted servant of Christ.
And Timothy was frequently ill.
Both statements were true at the same time.
His sickness did not erase his calling.
His weakness did not invalidate his faith.
His physical condition did not make him a spiritual failure.
And Paul's response was not condemnation.
It was care.
Think about that for a moment.
Paul had seen extraordinary works of God.
Acts 19:11–12 describes unusual miracles associated with his ministry, including healings.
Yet when addressing Timothy's recurring illnesses, Paul did not simply command him to demonstrate greater faith.
He offered practical counsel.
Why?
Scripture does not tell us why Timothy's illnesses persisted or why Paul chose this particular recommendation instead of describing a miraculous healing.
But the passage does show that practical measures and trust in God are not necessarily enemies.
We can pray for healing and seek appropriate medical care.
We can trust God's power while acknowledging our physical limitations.
We can believe in miracles without pretending every illness will disappear immediately.
Remember what Paul himself experienced.
In 2 Corinthians 12:7–9, he described a painful affliction he called a thorn in the flesh.
He pleaded with the Lord three times that it might depart.
And the Lord answered:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” — 2 Corinthians 12:9 (KJV)
We should not assume Paul's thorn was the same kind of illness Timothy experienced. Scripture does not identify it with certainty.
But the spiritual principle remains powerful.
God's grace does not depend upon the disappearance of every weakness.
Sometimes God delivers.
Sometimes He sustains.
Sometimes He works through ordinary means.
And sometimes, while we wait for answers, He reminds us that our value was never determined by our physical strength.
Now consider another detail that many people overlook.
Paul's advice appears in a letter that also warns against drunkenness.
In 1 Timothy 3:2–3, overseers are instructed to be temperate and not given to wine.
In 1 Timothy 3:8, deacons are warned against being devoted to much wine.
And in Ephesians 5:18, Paul writes:
There is no contradiction.
Paul could warn against drunkenness while recommending a small amount of wine for a particular physical problem.
The distinction is between limited use in a specific circumstance and the misuse of alcohol.
And that distinction matters because Christians sometimes approach Scripture looking for permission to do what they already want.
One person reads 1 Timothy 5:23 and announces, “See? The Bible says drinking is fine.”
Another reads the same verse and insists that Paul could not possibly have meant fermented wine.
But neither person's preferences should determine the meaning of Scripture.
We must allow the Word of God to correct us rather than forcing it to confirm us.
Proverbs 20:1 warns about wine's power to deceive.
Proverbs 23:29–35 vividly portrays the suffering associated with excessive drinking.
Romans 14 teaches believers to consider the consciences and spiritual welfare of others.
And 1 Corinthians 6:12 reminds us that even when something may be permissible, we must not allow ourselves to be mastered by it.
Therefore, 1 Timothy 5:23 cannot reasonably be used to defend drunkenness, addiction, reckless drinking, or disregard for another person's spiritual vulnerability.
Nor should it be used to shame Christians who choose complete abstinence.
Some believers abstain because of conscience.
Some because of family history.
Some because of addiction recovery.
Some because of health concerns or medications.
Some because they believe abstinence best serves their witness and responsibilities.
Such decisions deserve serious respect.
And anyone who struggles with alcohol dependence should never feel pressured to drink because Paul gave Timothy this instruction.
Christian freedom is never a command to become enslaved.
But there is an even deeper lesson here.
One that reaches far beyond wine.
What kind of God do we imagine when we think about holiness?
A God who watches us suffer and demands that we prove our devotion by refusing help?
Or the God revealed in Jesus Christ, who calls sinners to repentance, confronts destructive behavior, and also shows extraordinary compassion toward human weakness?
Look at Jesus.
When He encountered the sick, He did not treat their suffering as an inconvenience.
When a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years approached Him, He received her with compassion and restored her (Mark 5:25–34).
When a blind man cried out for mercy, Jesus did not silence him. He responded to his need (Mark 10:46–52).
When the crowds were hungry, Jesus cared about their physical condition (Mark 8:1–9).
And when His disciples returned from demanding ministry, He told them:
“Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while.” — Mark 6:31 (KJV)
Rest.
From Jesus.
To people serving Him.
How many believers need to hear those words today?
You can love God deeply and still need sleep.
You can serve faithfully and still need nourishment.
You can be spiritually mature and still need medical attention.
You can be filled with the Holy Spirit and still experience physical weakness.
Your body is not an obstacle to your salvation.
It is part of your created humanity, and God calls you to honor Him with it.
First Corinthians 6:19–20 teaches believers that their bodies belong to God and that they are to glorify Him in their bodies.
The immediate context concerns sexual immorality, so we should not pretend Paul was specifically discussing diet, medicine, or alcohol in those verses.
Nevertheless, the passage reminds us that our physical lives matter to the Lord.
Our bodies are not disposable instruments for religious productivity.
They are part of the lives we have been entrusted to steward.
And this brings us to something deeply personal.
There are Christians who have spent years serving everyone except themselves.
They visit the sick while ignoring their own symptoms.
They comfort the grieving while refusing to acknowledge their own sorrow.
They pray for struggling families while silently watching their own relationships deteriorate.
They encourage others to seek help while believing they must handle everything alone.
And eventually, something gives way.
Sometimes it is their health.
Sometimes it is their emotional endurance.
Sometimes it is their ability to keep serving with joy.
They are not necessarily rebellious.
They may simply be exhausted.
And perhaps the most compassionate thing they need to hear is not another demand to do more.
Perhaps they need to remember that even Timothy, a trusted minister of the Gospel, received permission to address a physical problem.
Paul did not tell Timothy to abandon his calling.
He told him to care for his stomach.
There is something beautifully human about that.
The Christian life is not an endless performance of invincibility.
We follow a Savior who entered human history in real flesh.
Jesus knew hunger.
He knew thirst.
He knew exhaustion.
John 4:6 describes Him sitting by Jacob's well, wearied from His journey.
John 19:28 records Him saying, “I thirst,” during His crucifixion.
And Hebrews 4:15 tells us that our great High Priest can sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin.
Jesus is not distant from the reality of human frailty.
He understands what it means to inhabit a vulnerable human body.
But His mission went infinitely beyond showing sympathy.
He came to save sinners.
That is where this entire conversation must ultimately lead.
Because our deepest problem is not merely that our bodies become sick.
It is that our hearts are corrupted by sin.
We can receive excellent medical treatment and still remain spiritually lost.
We can practice perfect self-discipline and still be separated from God.
We can avoid alcohol, maintain strict religious habits, and appear respectable before others while secretly carrying pride, bitterness, lust, dishonesty, unforgiveness, or unbelief.
Outward discipline cannot cleanse a guilty conscience.
And physical health cannot reconcile a sinner to a holy God.
Only Jesus Christ can do that.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” (KJV)
But the story does not end with our guilt.
Romans 5:8 announces:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
This is the Gospel.
Not that we made ourselves acceptable through perfect performance.
Not that we earned forgiveness by suffering enough.
Not that we became righteous through strict religious routines.
But that Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, bore our sins, died upon the cross, and rose again.
He did what we could never do.
He accomplished what our discipline could never achieve.
And He offers forgiveness and reconciliation to those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
That is grace.
Not permission to continue comfortably in sin.
But God's undeserved favor that saves us and teaches us to live transformed lives.
Titus 2:11–12 reminds us that the grace of God trains believers to reject ungodliness and worldly desires and to live self-controlled, upright, godly lives.
Grace does not make holiness unnecessary.
Grace makes genuine holiness possible.
And this is why the theme of Gospel Warrior matters so deeply.
Because Jesus Rewrites Everything.
The scandal is not merely what other people discovered about your past.
It is what God already knows about every human heart.
The hidden sins.
The excuses.
The failures.
The compromises.
The years spent trying to appear spiritually healthy while remaining inwardly wounded by guilt.
Yet the grace of Jesus Christ reaches people who cannot rescue themselves.
He does not excuse their sin.
He calls them to turn from it.
He does not leave them imprisoned in shame.
He offers forgiveness.
He does not promise that following Him will remove every earthly hardship.
He promises that those who belong to Him will never be abandoned.
And His resurrection assures us that suffering, sin, and death will not have the final word.
Perhaps your scandal was public.
Perhaps nobody knows what happened.
Perhaps you have been living with the consequences of a decision you wish you could undo.
Or perhaps your struggle is quieter.
You have become so committed to appearing strong that you no longer know how to admit you are weak.
You can explain theology to others.
But you struggle to believe that God's mercy still reaches you.
You can quote verses about grace.
But you punish yourself for failures Christ calls you to bring into the light.
Listen.
Repentance is necessary.
Confession matters.
Obedience matters.
But self-punishment cannot accomplish what Christ's sacrifice has already accomplished.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
You do not need to pretend your sin was harmless.
You need to bring it honestly before the Savior.
You do not need to manufacture your own righteousness.
You need the righteousness that comes through faith in Christ.
And you do not need to prove that you are spiritually strong enough to deserve God's attention.
You need to come to Him in humility.
Even with your weakness.
Even with your trembling faith.
Even with the questions you have been afraid to ask.
Now return to that small instruction in 1 Timothy 5:23.
“Use a little wine.”
It is easy to become so distracted by the word wine that we miss the tenderness of the moment.
An apostle was concerned about a younger minister's recurring illness.
The letter was filled with matters of enormous spiritual significance.
False teachers had to be confronted.
The church needed order.
Leaders needed integrity.
The Gospel had to be guarded.
Yet Paul's attention did not become so consumed with the mission that he forgot the person carrying it.
He remembered Timothy's stomach.
He remembered his frequent illnesses.
He cared enough to say something practical.
That should challenge the way we practice discipleship.
Do we only ask people how their ministry is going?
Or do we ask how they are actually doing?
Do we celebrate their service while overlooking their suffering?
Do we admire their strength while making it impossible for them to admit weakness?
Do we encourage prayer while also helping people access appropriate care?
A healthy Christian community should be a place where truth is proclaimed, sin is confronted, grace is extended, and suffering people are not treated as failures.
James 5:14–16 calls the church to pray for the sick.
Galatians 6:2 calls believers to bear one another's burdens.
And Romans 12:15 tells us to weep with those who weep.
The church is not supposed to be a gathering of people pretending they never struggle.
It is a redeemed family learning to follow Christ together.
Some need correction.
Some need encouragement.
Some need rest.
Some need medical care.
Some need help escaping destructive habits.
Some need to hear the Gospel clearly for the first time.
And all of us need Jesus.
That is why this passage should never become merely an argument about whether Christians may drink wine.
The question is important, and Scripture deserves careful interpretation.
But the verse also teaches us to distinguish God's actual commands from human assumptions.
It teaches us to value truth over convenience.
It teaches us that practical care can coexist with deep faith.
And it reminds us that Christian maturity is not demonstrated by pretending we have no limitations.
Maybe you have spent years trying to impress God with your strength.
But what if today you finally stopped pretending?
What if you confessed the sin you have been hiding?
What if you sought help for the suffering you have been minimizing?
What if you stopped using religious activity to avoid confronting what is happening inside your heart?
What if you discovered that surrender is not the end of your story, but the beginning of a transformed life in Christ?
Jesus said in Matthew 11:28:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (KJV)
Notice whom He invited.
The weary.
The burdened.
The people who could no longer carry everything themselves.
And His invitation still stands.
Not as a promise that every problem will disappear overnight.
But as a call to come under His gracious lordship and find rest for the soul.
If this article has touched a struggle you rarely speak about, you do not have to tell the whole world your private story.
But perhaps you can take one honest step today.
Someone reading may desperately need to know they are not alone.
Your honesty may encourage a believer who has been suffering in silence.
And your testimony may direct someone toward the Savior who sustained you.
If a particular person came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them gently, or sending this article to them privately.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to diagnose their spiritual condition.
But to remind them that their worth is not measured by how successfully they hide their pain.
Your family may read it.
A friend who has stopped attending church may encounter it.
Someone quietly wrestling with guilt may discover a reminder of Christ's mercy.
Even a person who does not yet believe may begin asking serious questions about Jesus.
You cannot control what another person does with the message.
But you can faithfully help make it available.
Not because every sentence is equally important, but because the Scripture behind it deserves to be revisited.
Come back to 1 Timothy 5:23 when you are tempted to confuse unnecessary suffering with holiness.
Come back to 2 Corinthians 12:9 when weakness makes you feel ashamed.
Come back to Matthew 11:28 when your soul is exhausted.
And come back to the cross when your conscience reminds you of sins you cannot undo.
Our desire is to keep opening the Scriptures, confronting difficult questions, encouraging repentance, and pointing people toward Jesus Christ.
Not merely toward emotional inspiration that fades by tomorrow.
But toward truth that forms disciples.
These resources are intended to help believers grow in biblical knowledge, prayer, spiritual maturity, and faithful Christian living.
But keeping Gospel-centered resources available and continuing to develop new teaching takes time, work, and financial support.
That is why I want to extend a personal invitation.
For believers who choose to make this part of their regular Christian giving, it can be an expression of generosity toward Gospel ministry, much like other voluntary offerings.
But it is important to be biblically clear.
Christians glorify God through faith, obedience, love, generosity, service, and lives surrendered to Him.

Scripture encourages believers to support worthwhile Gospel work (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14; Philippians 4:15–17), while 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be willing rather than compelled.
I will not suggest that a monthly payment purchases divine favor.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by financial contributions (Ephesians 2:8–9).
Think of the people who may encounter a Scripture explanation because someone helped make it possible.
Think of the believer searching for encouragement late at night.
The parent looking for a devotional.
The young Christian trying to understand a difficult Bible passage.
The person who has wandered from church and is cautiously beginning to seek God again.
We cannot promise how many lives will be changed.
Only God knows the full fruit of faithful ministry.
But we can work together to keep sharing the truth.
These items can serve as reminders of biblical truth, personal encouragement, or meaningful gifts for others.
It is not the reason anyone must give.
The greater purpose is to support the continuing work of sharing Scripture, strengthening disciples, and proclaiming Jesus Christ.
Now, before you leave, remember Timothy.
A faithful servant.
A young minister.
A man carrying serious responsibilities.
A believer whose body was not always cooperating with his calling.
And Paul, the great apostle, took time to care about something as ordinary as his stomach.
It is almost startling how much tenderness can fit inside one verse.
Maybe that is what someone needed to see today.
God is not honored by our prideful refusal to acknowledge that we are human.
He is honored when we trust Him enough to obey His Word, acknowledge our need, receive appropriate help, and walk faithfully in the strength He provides.
The Gospel does not promise a life without weakness.
It promises a Savior whose grace is sufficient.
It does not promise that faithful Christians will never suffer.
It reveals a risen Lord who will one day make all things new.
And it does not teach that the strongest believer is the one who never needs help.
It teaches us to depend upon Jesus Christ.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Seek forgiveness where you have sinned.
Ask for help where you are struggling.
Care for the body God has entrusted to you.
Love the people He has placed around you.
And never allow an argument about one small cup of wine to distract you from the immeasurably greater gift of salvation through the blood of Jesus Christ.
Because the most important thing Paul offered Timothy was not advice about a beverage.
It was a life devoted to the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
And the most important thing you can receive today is not a temporary remedy for an earthly problem.
It is the grace of the Savior who died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God.
You may be carrying a weakness that has not disappeared, but you do not have to carry your life without the Savior who knows your name, sees your suffering, and calls you to Himself.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “ALL THINGS WORK TOGETHER FOR GOOD” — PAUL NEVER SAID YOU WOULD CALL EVERYTHING GOOD
paragraphs: “ALL THINGS WORK TOGETHER FOR GOOD” — PAUL NEVER SAID YOU WOULD CALL EVERYTHING GOOD
Romans 8:28 Was Never God's Command to Pretend Your Pain Was Beautiful. It Was His Promise That Even What Nearly Destroyed You Cannot Defeat His Purpose in Christ.
There is a kind of pain that makes you question everything you thought you knew about God.
Not because you stopped believing in Him.
But because you believed Him when you prayed. You believed Him when you waited. You believed Him when you obeyed. You believed Him when you surrendered something you desperately wanted to keep.
And still, everything fell apart.
The marriage you prayed over collapsed.
The person you trusted betrayed you.
The diagnosis came back worse than expected.
The child you raised in church walked away from the faith.
The door you were certain God would open remained painfully closed.
And somewhere in the middle of your heartbreak, someone looked you in the eyes and said:
"Don't worry. All things work together for good."
You smiled because you didn't know what else to do.
But inside, something broke a little deeper.
Because how could this be good?
How could betrayal be good? How could burying someone you love be good? How could years of abuse, humiliation, unanswered prayers, and sleepless nights possibly be good?
And perhaps the question you were too ashamed to ask was this:
"God, if You are working everything for good, why does this feel like it is destroying me?"
Stay with me, because there is something in Romans 8:28 that many Christians have heard their entire lives but have never been taught to see.
Something that doesn't erase your suffering.
Something that doesn't excuse the people who wounded you.
Something that doesn't require you to call evil good just to prove you have faith.
And when you finally understand what Paul was actually saying, you may never read this familiar verse the same way again.
Because Paul never said everything that happens to you is good.
He said something far more powerful.
He said God is at work even when what happens to you is not good.
And those are not the same thing.
The apostle Paul wrote:
"And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose." — Romans 8:28, KJV
Those words have comforted millions.
But they have also been used carelessly.
Sometimes they are spoken to people who are still bleeding emotionally, as though faith requires them to stop grieving before the wound has even begun to heal.
Sometimes they are used to silence honest questions.

Sometimes they are repeated as though the Bible promises that every disappointment will eventually become a promotion, every broken relationship will be restored, every financial loss will be recovered, and every tragedy will receive an explanation before we die.
But Paul never promised any of those things.
And the original Greek helps us understand why.
Romans 8:28 begins:
Οἴδαμεν δὲ ὅτι τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν τὸν θεὸν πάντα συνεργεῖ εἰς ἀγαθόν
Oidamen de hoti tois agapōsin ton theon panta synergei eis agathon.
A careful rendering of this portion is:
"And we know that, for those who love God, all things work together toward good."
The Greek verb συνεργεῖ (synergei) carries the sense of working together or cooperating toward a result.
The expression εἰς ἀγαθόν (eis agathon) means "toward good" or "for good."
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say that every event is morally good.
He does not say every human decision is righteous.
He does not say every painful experience comes with an immediately recognizable blessing.
The verse speaks about the outcome toward which things are being worked, not the moral goodness of everything that happens.

Some Greek manuscripts explicitly identify God as the one who works in all things, reflected in translations such as the NIV. Other manuscripts preserve the shorter wording familiar from the KJV. The difference matters for careful translation, but neither reading requires us to believe that evil becomes good simply because God can overcome it.
And the surrounding passage makes God's involvement unmistakable.
Paul is not describing a universe where suffering magically organizes itself into a happy ending.
He is describing the sovereign faithfulness of God toward those who belong to Jesus Christ.
That distinction changes everything.
Because the God who can bring good out of evil does not need to approve of evil to accomplish His purpose.
Think about that.
God's power to redeem what happened does not mean He delighted in what happened.
Somebody needs that truth today.
Especially the person who has spent years wondering whether God somehow approved of the cruelty they experienced.
No.
Scripture never gives us permission to rename wickedness as righteousness.
Isaiah 5:20 warns against calling evil good and good evil.
James 1:13 teaches that God does not tempt anyone with evil.
And Jesus Himself wept at the tomb of Lazarus, even though He knew resurrection was moments away.
John 11:35 contains two of the shortest and most devastating words in Scripture:
"Jesus wept."
He knew what He was about to do.
He knew death would not have the final word over Lazarus that day.
And still, He wept.
Do you understand what that means?
Knowing God has the power to redeem a tragedy does not make grief an act of unbelief.
Jesus did not stand outside that tomb and shame Mary for crying.
He did not tell Martha that her brother's death was beautiful.
He entered their sorrow.
And then He confronted the grave.
So why have we sometimes made grieving Christians feel guilty for behaving more like Jesus than like the cheerful religious image we expect them to maintain?
You can love God and still cry.
You can trust His sovereignty and still acknowledge that what happened was terribly wrong.
You can believe Romans 8:28 and still need counseling, medical care, protection, justice, and time to recover.
You can forgive someone and still establish boundaries.
You can surrender vengeance to God without returning to an unsafe relationship.
And you can confess that God is good without pretending the people who harmed you were good.
Faith is not emotional dishonesty.
Faith is bringing your honest pain before a faithful God.
But there is another truth hidden in the way we often quote Romans 8:28.
We love verse 28 because it contains the word "good."
We rarely continue to verse 29 because it tells us what that good is ultimately moving toward.
Paul writes:
There it is.
The good God promises is inseparably connected to making His people more like Jesus.
Not merely making us comfortable.
Not guaranteeing wealth.
Not ensuring that everyone who rejected us will one day regret it.
Not promising that every closed door will reopen.
Not promising that our enemies will watch us become famous.
God's eternal purpose is deeper than the temporary outcomes we desperately want.
He is forming a people who belong to His Son.
A people who will ultimately share in Christ's glory.
And sometimes that work happens in circumstances we would never have chosen.
But be careful here.
This does not mean every tragedy was specifically sent to teach you a lesson.
It does not mean someone had to abuse you so you could become spiritually mature.
It does not mean God needed your child to die, your spouse to betray you, or your family to abandon you in order to accomplish His will.
Those claims go beyond what Romans 8:28 teaches.
The promise is not that every evil was necessary.
The promise is that no evil can finally overthrow God's saving purpose for those who are in Christ.
There is a difference between saying God can redeem suffering and claiming that suffering itself is sacred.
And that difference matters enormously to someone who is trying to heal.
Consider Joseph.
His own brothers hated him.
They stripped him of his special robe.
They threw him into a pit.
They sold him into slavery.
He was taken away from his father, his home, and everything familiar.
Later, he was falsely accused and imprisoned.
Years passed.
Not days.
Years.
Imagine being Joseph on an ordinary night in prison.
No angel explaining the entire plan.
No written promise that Pharaoh would eventually summon him.
No assurance that his brothers would one day stand before him.
Just another night behind walls he had done nothing to deserve.
What would you have prayed?
"Lord, I tried to do what was right. Why am I here?"
And yet the story did not end in that prison.
God eventually raised Joseph to a position of authority in Egypt, where he helped preserve lives during a devastating famine.
Years later, when Joseph confronted the brothers who had betrayed him, he said something astonishing:
"But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good..." — Genesis 50:20, KJV
The Hebrew makes the contrast striking.
אַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה
Attem chashavtem alai ra'ah.
"You intended evil against me."
And then:
אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
Elohim chashavah letovah.
"God intended it for good."
The Hebrew verb chashav is used in both statements, conveying intention or purpose.
But the intentions are radically different.
Joseph's brothers intended רָעָה (ra'ah) — evil or harm.
God intended טוֹבָה (tovah) — good.
Joseph did not say, "What you did was actually good."
He identified their actions as evil.
He did not rewrite their guilt to make his testimony more inspiring.
He recognized that God's purpose had prevailed over their wicked intentions.
That is biblical redemption.
Not pretending the pit was pleasant.
Not calling slavery a blessing.
Not praising false accusations.
But recognizing that God remained faithful through circumstances that human beings had made cruel.
And even here, we must remember something.
Joseph's story is not a guarantee that every betrayed believer will eventually become wealthy, powerful, or publicly vindicated.
His life reveals what God is capable of doing.
Romans 8 reveals the deeper promise that stands even when our earthly stories do not end like Joseph's.
Because sometimes the prison doors do not open when we expect.
Sometimes the diagnosis does not change.
Sometimes the apology never comes.
Sometimes the person we prayed would return never returns.
Sometimes the faithful Christian dies without seeing the earthly answer they longed for.
Does that mean Romans 8:28 failed?
No.
It means we have to read Romans 8 as Paul actually wrote it.
Listen to what he says earlier in the same chapter:
"For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us." — Romans 8:18, KJV
Paul acknowledges suffering.
Then he describes creation groaning under its brokenness.
He speaks about believers groaning as they await the redemption of their bodies.
He even admits that there are moments when we do not know what we should pray for.
And then comes this extraordinary promise:
"Likewise the Spirit also helpeth our infirmities: for we know not what we should pray for as we ought..." — Romans 8:26, KJV
Read that slowly.
Sometimes you are so overwhelmed that you cannot even form the right prayer.
You sit on the edge of your bed.
Your phone is silent.
Your chest feels heavy.
You have already cried so much that you wonder whether there is anything left.
You want to pray, but the words will not come.
And perhaps all you can whisper is:
"Jesus... please."
Paul does not describe that moment as spiritual failure.
He tells us that the Spirit helps us in our weakness.
The same chapter that declares all things work together for good also acknowledges groaning, weakness, suffering, and prayers too deep for words.
Romans 8:28 was never written to silence the wounded.
It was written within a message of hope for people who were suffering.
And Paul knew suffering personally.
He had been beaten.
Imprisoned.
Rejected.
Threatened.
He had endured hunger, danger, exhaustion, and persecution.
He was not writing from a luxurious room where everything had gone according to plan.
He was writing as someone who understood what it meant to follow Jesus when obedience was costly.
So when Paul said, "We know," he was not offering shallow optimism.
He was expressing confidence in the God whose saving purpose reaches beyond the worst that this present world can do.
And perhaps nowhere is that truth more clearly revealed than at the cross.
Because if you want to understand how God can bring good out of something truly evil, look at Calvary.
Look at Jesus.
The sinless Son of God was betrayed by someone close to Him.
He was abandoned by His disciples.
He was falsely accused.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Spat upon.
Condemned.
Nailed to a Roman cross.
And left to die in public humiliation.
Nothing about the betrayal was righteous.
Nothing about the false accusations was holy.
Nothing about the cruelty of the executioners was morally good.
Human sin was on full display.
And yet Scripture declares that God was accomplishing His saving purpose through the death of Christ.

Peter proclaimed that Jesus was delivered according to God's determined counsel and foreknowledge, while also holding those responsible for His crucifixion accountable for their wicked actions (Acts 2:23).
Do not miss that.
God's sovereign purpose did not make the perpetrators innocent.
Their evil remained evil.
But their evil could not defeat God's plan of redemption.
The cross was not good because betrayal suddenly became beautiful.
The cross is the supreme revelation of God's redeeming love because Jesus willingly gave Himself for sinners, bearing our sins and accomplishing salvation through His death.
And then came the resurrection.
The stone was rolled away.
The tomb was empty.
Death had not won.
Sin had not won.
The powers of darkness had not won.
Jesus Christ was risen.
And suddenly, the darkest event in human history stood at the center of the greatest news humanity has ever received.
Not because evil became good.
But because God overcame evil through the crucified and risen Christ.
That is the Gospel.
And that is why Romans 8:28 must never be separated from Jesus.
Without Christ, the verse becomes a vague promise that everything will somehow turn out the way we want.
With Christ, it becomes an assurance that the God who raised His Son from the dead will not abandon His people or fail to complete His saving purpose.
Now perhaps you are thinking about something that happened years ago.
Something you rarely discuss.
Maybe the people around you believe you have already moved on.
You go to church.
You sing.
You serve.
You post encouraging Bible verses.
You tell everyone you are fine.
But there are nights when the memory still returns.
A particular smell.
A familiar song.
A name appearing unexpectedly on your screen.
And suddenly, you are back in the moment you thought you had survived.
You wonder why healing has taken so long.
You wonder whether you are failing God because the pain still hurts.
Please hear this.
The fact that something still hurts does not prove that God has stopped working.
Healing is not always immediate.
Sanctification is not always visible.
And spiritual maturity is not measured by how convincingly you hide your wounds.
The Psalms are filled with lament.
Job wrestled with questions he could not answer.
Jeremiah wept.
Paul pleaded with the Lord about his thorn in the flesh.
And Jesus prayed in Gethsemane with such anguish that Luke describes His sweat becoming like great drops of blood falling to the ground.
He prayed:
"Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." — Luke 22:42, KJV
Jesus did not teach us to pretend that suffering is painless.
He demonstrated perfect obedience in the midst of real anguish.
So perhaps your next act of faith is not forcing yourself to say, "Everything is good."
Perhaps it is kneeling before the Lord and finally admitting:
"Father, this was not good. I am still hurting. I do not understand why You allowed it. But I believe You are good, and I am placing what I cannot understand into Your hands."
That is not a weak prayer.
That is a prayer of surrender.
And surrender does not mean surrendering your ability to recognize wrong.
It means entrusting yourself to the God who judges rightly.
It means refusing to let bitterness become your master.
It means seeking help where help is needed.
It means allowing truth, grace, repentance, forgiveness, and wise boundaries to shape your next steps.
And sometimes it means accepting that you may never receive every answer you wanted in this life.
There is another part of Romans 8 that we cannot ignore.
Paul says this promise belongs "to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose."
This is not a universal guarantee that every person will automatically receive a happy ending regardless of their relationship with Christ.
Paul is speaking about God's saving faithfulness toward those who belong to Him.
And that brings us to a question far more important than whether your circumstances will improve tomorrow.
Do you belong to Jesus Christ?
Not merely, "Have you heard about Him?"
Not merely, "Did you grow up in a Christian family?"
Not merely, "Do you share Bible verses online?"
But have you turned from sin and placed your trust in the crucified and risen Savior?
Because the greatest good God offers is not the recovery of everything you lost on earth.
It is reconciliation with Himself through Jesus Christ.
Forgiveness of sins.
A new heart.
Adoption into His family.
The presence of His Spirit.
The promise of resurrection.
And eternal life with Him.
You may have experienced betrayal, but you also need the Savior who forgives your own sins.
You may have been wounded by others, but you also need grace for the ways you have wounded others.
You may have spent years searching for an explanation for your suffering while overlooking the invitation of the One who suffered to redeem you.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your circumstances.
He came to save sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were sinners.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we repaired every broken relationship.
Not after we became worthy of His attention.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
And that is where scandal becomes grace.
The scandal of human rebellion.
The scandal of betrayal.
The scandal of religious hypocrisy.
The scandal of the innocent Savior condemned by sinful people.
And then the astonishing grace of God, who offers forgiveness through the very Savior humanity rejected.
This does not mean every earthly scandal will end in public restoration.
It means no sinner is beyond the saving reach of Christ while the invitation to repent and believe remains open.
It means your past does not have to be your master.
It means shame does not have to be your identity.
It means the cross has the final word over the guilt of those who come to Jesus in faith.
And it means the resurrection guarantees that suffering and death will not have the final word over God's redeemed people.
That is why we say:
Not because Jesus changes the historical facts of what happened.
But because He changes the eternal destiny of those He saves, redeems what sin has broken, and brings His people into a future that suffering cannot destroy.
Perhaps you have spent years asking God to change your story.
And perhaps today He is inviting you first to surrender your life to the Savior at the center of the story.
You do not need to manufacture perfect faith.
You need Christ.
You do not need to understand every chapter.
You need the One who holds the future.
You do not need to call your wounds beautiful.
You need the Savior whose wounds secured your redemption.
And if you are ready to turn toward Him, you can pray sincerely:

"Lord Jesus, I confess that I am a sinner in need of Your mercy. I have carried wounds I cannot heal by myself, and I have committed sins I cannot erase. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me. Teach me to repent, trust You, and follow You. Help me surrender what I cannot control. Guard me from bitterness and from false hope. Make me more like You, even while I am still healing. I place my past, my present, and my future into Your hands. Amen."
The prayer itself is not a magic formula.
Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ, not earned by words, religious performance, or financial contributions (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And if you already belong to Jesus but have been spiritually exhausted, perhaps this is the moment to stop pretending you are stronger than you are.
You are allowed to ask for prayer.
You are allowed to admit that you are struggling.
You are allowed to say that you believe God is faithful even though you cannot yet see what He is doing.
You do not have to share details that are too personal or unsafe to disclose.

And if God has carried you through a season you once thought would destroy you, consider sharing a little of your testimony. Someone reading quietly may need to know that they are not the only one still learning how to trust.
There may also be someone on your Facebook friends list who has been silently struggling with this exact verse.
Someone who was told to stop crying.
Someone who was pressured to forgive without being protected.
Someone who believes God is disappointed because they cannot yet see the good.
Not because sharing a post proves your faith.
But because a carefully shared truth can reach someone who would never walk into a church building or admit that they need help.
Our mission is not merely to publish something that makes people emotional for a few minutes.
We want to help people open their Bibles again.
We want struggling believers to rediscover the promises of God in their proper context.
We want families to grow in biblical understanding.
We want seekers to encounter the Gospel clearly.
We want those who have wandered to hear Christ's call to repentance and faith.
And we want people who have been hurt by distorted teachings to discover that the truth of Scripture is stronger, deeper, and more beautiful than the slogans sometimes spoken in its name.
We want that biblical nourishment to continue reaching people, including those who cannot afford to pay for it.
And that work takes time, resources, consistency, and faithful support.

For those who choose to give from their resources as an expression of Christian generosity, that support can be part of their broader stewardship and offering to the Lord. Scripture teaches generous, willing giving, not giving under pressure (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But it can be a meaningful way to help a ministry continue serving others.
These items are simply additional resources and expressions of appreciation. They are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus is.
The Word of God is.
The Gospel is.
The people who have not yet heard, the believers who need strengthening, and the families longing for biblical nourishment are why this work matters.
Keep reading Scripture.
Keep growing in Christ.
Make use of the free resources.
Pray for this ministry.
We are grateful for every person who helps spread the truth, whether through giving, praying, encouraging others, or simply living faithfully for Jesus in the place God has entrusted to them.
But before you leave, I want to bring you back to where we began.
To that hospital room.
That betrayal.
That unanswered prayer.
That grave.
That closed door.
That memory you wish you could erase.
Perhaps you came into this article expecting someone to tell you that everything that happened was good.
I cannot tell you that.
Scripture does not ask me to.
Some things were evil.
Some losses were devastating.
Some wounds were inflicted by people who should have protected you.
Some consequences may remain for the rest of your earthly life.
And some questions may not be answered until you stand in the presence of Christ.
But I can tell you what the Gospel declares.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
Jesus Christ reigns.
And those who belong to Him are held by a love that suffering cannot finally sever.
Listen to the way Paul ends Romans 8.
He speaks of tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, and sword.
He does not pretend those things are imaginary.
He does not say believers will never experience them.
Instead, he declares:
"Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us." — Romans 8:37, KJV
Notice those words.
In all these things.
Not necessarily after all these things disappear.
Not because all these things are good.
But in them, through the love of Christ.
And then Paul reaches his magnificent conclusion:

"For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord." — Romans 8:38–39, KJV
That is the promise.
Not that you will never enter the valley.
Not that the people you love will never disappoint you.
Not that your body will never suffer.
Not that you will understand every tragedy.
But that nothing in all creation can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Him.
And one day, the promise will reach its glorious fulfillment.
Revelation 21:4 speaks of the day when God will wipe away every tear, when death, sorrow, crying, and pain will be no more.
