Genesis 30:14–16 describes an exchange involving mandrakes, plants associated in the ancient world with fertility.
Rachel asked for some of the mandrakes Reuben had found.
Leah agreed to give them in exchange for spending the night with Jacob.
Pause and consider how sorrowful that scene is.
The sisters were negotiating over access to their own husband.
The longing for affection and children had become so entangled with rivalry that even intimate family relationships were treated as bargaining arrangements.
And still, the story continued.
Leah bore Issachar and Zebulun, and later a daughter named Dinah.
The text does not identify Dinah as Leah's only daughter or establish that no other daughters were born in the wider family.
Then, at last, the narrative returned to Rachel.
Genesis 30:22 says:
“And God remembered Rachel, and God hearkened to her, and opened her womb.”
The Hebrew expression וַיִּזְכֹּר אֱלֹהִים (vayyizkor Elohim) means “And God remembered.”
In biblical language, God's remembering does not imply that He had forgotten Rachel and suddenly recalled her existence.
It describes God's purposeful attention and action toward her.
Rachel conceived and gave birth to Joseph.
She declared that God had taken away her reproach.
And she named him Joseph, saying, “The LORD shall add to me another son.”
The name יוֹסֵף (Yosef) is connected with the Hebrew verb יָסַף (yasaf), meaning “to add.”
Rachel finally held the child she had long desired.
But even here, the naming reveals that her longing was not finished.
She asked for another son.
Later, in Genesis 35, Rachel would give birth to Benjamin and die following the difficult delivery.
The Bible does not allow us to turn her story into a simple promise that every long season of waiting ends exactly as we hope.
That would be unfair to Rachel.
And unfair to every person still praying through infertility, loss, loneliness, or unanswered longing.
God's compassion is real.
But His faithfulness cannot be measured by whether every desire is fulfilled according to our timetable.
Now look at the larger picture.
Genesis 29–30 records the births of eleven sons of Jacob, along with Dinah. Benjamin's birth comes later in Genesis 35.
Together, Jacob's twelve sons became the ancestral foundation of the twelve tribes of Israel.
The eventual tribal arrangement has important distinctions: Levi received a priestly role and no ordinary tribal land inheritance, while Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh received tribal portions.
But the family origin remains unmistakable.
Reuben.
Simeon.
Levi.
Judah.
Dan.
Naphtali.
Gad.
Asher.
Issachar.
Zebulun.
Joseph.
Benjamin.
Names that would echo through Israel's history.
Names connected with wilderness journeys, covenant promises, territorial inheritances, kings, prophets, worship, judgment, exile, and restoration.
And the beginnings of those names were found in a household full of wounds.
That does not mean God approved of every choice made there.
It means human sin and weakness did not overthrow His covenant faithfulness.
God had promised Abraham that his descendants would become a great nation and that through him all the families of the earth would be blessed.
That promise passed through Isaac and Jacob.
And despite deception, rivalry, jealousy, and human failure, God continued to accomplish His purposes.
This is one of the most astonishing truths in Scripture.
God's faithfulness does not depend on human beings having flawless family histories.
But we need to go deeper.
Because the greatest revelation of this story is not merely that God brought twelve tribes out of a fractured household.
It is that the story ultimately directs us toward Jesus Christ.
The tribe of Judah would produce Israel's royal line.
The promised Messiah would come through that lineage.
And Jesus would enter a world just as wounded by rejection, betrayal, envy, and sin as the household of Jacob.
He was not born into a humanity that had finally learned how to love perfectly.
He came to save sinners.
John 1:11 tells us:
“He came unto his own, and his own received him not.”
Isaiah 53:3 describes the suffering Servant as:
“despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.”
Jesus understands rejection.
But He is more than someone who understands our pain.
He is the Savior who came to deal with the sin beneath humanity's brokenness.
Leah needed more than Jacob's approval.
Rachel needed more than children.
Jacob needed more than a peaceful household.
They needed the same ultimate redemption that every human heart needs.
Reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness.
Grace.
A transformed heart.
And that is why the Gospel matters.
Jesus Christ lived in perfect obedience to the Father, died for our sins, and rose again.
His sacrifice is not simply an inspiring example of love.
It is the foundation of our salvation.
The Greek New Testament describes God's grace using the word χάρις (charis), meaning grace or favor.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Grace is not something we earn by becoming impressive enough.
It is God's undeserved favor, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
And repentance is not an attempt to purchase His love.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can save us.
That means the person who has been rejected can come to Christ.
The person consumed by jealousy can come to Christ.
The person who has manipulated others can come to Christ.
The person whose marriage is broken, whose family is complicated, whose heart is bitter, whose past is shameful, whose faith is weak, can come to Christ.
Not because their sin is harmless.
But because His mercy is greater than their ability to repair themselves.
And genuine grace does not leave us comfortably enslaved to sin.
It calls us to repentance and begins transforming how we live.
Maybe you recognize yourself in Leah.
You have been trying to earn love by being useful.
By giving more.
By sacrificing more.
By becoming whatever someone else needed you to be.
And somewhere along the way, you forgot that your worth was never supposed to be decided by another person's affection.
Or maybe you recognize yourself in Rachel.
You have something beautiful in your life, but you cannot stop grieving what you do not have.
Every announcement of someone else's blessing feels like a reminder of your own unanswered prayer.
You want to rejoice.
But sometimes you can barely breathe.
Or perhaps you recognize yourself in Jacob.
You have made choices that wounded people.
You have favored one person while neglecting another.
You have allowed your desires to govern decisions that should have been shaped by righteousness.
And now the consequences are living in the same house as you.
Whoever you recognize, Scripture is not inviting you merely to identify your pain.
It is inviting you to bring your whole heart before God.
To confess the envy.
To acknowledge the bitterness.
To repent of the favoritism.
To stop treating another human being as the source of an identity only God can securely establish.
And to trust Jesus Christ.
Because the Gospel does not promise that everyone who rejected you will return.
It does not guarantee that every marriage will be restored.
It does not promise that every infertile couple will conceive.
It does not assure us that every fractured family will be healed in this life.
But it does proclaim that everyone who comes to Christ in faith can receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
And it promises that God's people are not abandoned to a future without hope.
One day, in Christ, every tear will be wiped away.
Until then, grace teaches us how to live faithfully even when the story remains unfinished.
Think about Leah one more time.
She named her fourth son Judah.
“I will praise the LORD.”
She could not have known how far that name would travel.
From a troubled family.
Through generations of Israel's history.
Through the royal line of David.
Until the birth of Jesus Christ.
And through His death and resurrection, the blessing promised to Abraham would reach people from every nation who believe in Him.
This is not a claim that Leah's suffering was good in itself.
It is a testimony that God was not defeated by it.
And that is a distinction every wounded heart needs to remember.
God does not need to call evil good in order to accomplish good despite evil.
He does not need to approve of betrayal to remain faithful through betrayal.
He does not need to celebrate human rivalry to bring His redemptive promises to fulfillment.
From scandal to grace does not mean the scandal was holy. It means the grace of God is powerful enough to meet sinners in the wreckage.
And maybe that is the sentence you needed today.
Your family history may be complicated.
Your childhood may contain wounds nobody knows about.
Your marriage may be carrying conversations you are afraid to have.
Your heart may be exhausted from trying to be chosen.
But your history is not greater than Christ.
Your shame is not greater than His cross.
And your need for mercy is not greater than His willingness to receive those who turn to Him.
You do not have to pretend you are healed when you are still hurting.
You do not have to manufacture a testimony before you have learned how to pray honestly.
You can begin with the truth.
“Lord, I am jealous.”
“Lord, I feel unwanted.”
“Lord, I have hurt people.”
“Lord, I have been measuring my worth by someone else's attention.”
“Lord, forgive me.”
“Lord, teach me to love what is right.”
“Lord, help me trust You when I cannot understand what You are doing.”
That is not weakness.
That is the beginning of honesty before God.
And sometimes the first step toward healing is not a dramatic moment.
It is finally telling the truth in the presence of the One who already sees.
If Leah's story has touched a place you rarely speak about, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not need to reveal private details or expose your family's pain publicly.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to let another believer know they are not alone.

And if you have experienced the grace of Jesus in the middle of rejection, share a little of your testimony. Someone reading silently may need to hear that the Lord has been faithful to another wounded heart.
There is also someone in your life who may need this story.
A friend who feels unwanted.
A sister quietly struggling with comparison.
A husband who needs to confront favoritism.
A mother who has been grieving.
A believer who has been measuring God's love by unanswered prayers.
Because we all need to be reminded that our circumstances do not have the final authority to tell us who God is.
This ministry exists to keep pointing people beyond religious performance and toward the living Christ.
And for those who want to help us continue and expand this work, there is a deeper way to stand with us.

Scripture teaches generous, willing support for Gospel ministry. Philippians 4:15–18 records believers partnering financially in Paul's ministry, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be reluctant or compelled.
Your giving to your local church, care for your household, and other biblical responsibilities remain important.
God's grace cannot be bought.
These resources and products are not the heart of the ministry.
Christ is.
They are simply additional ways to encourage faith, keep biblical truth close, and support the ongoing work.
You do not have to pay to begin growing in God's Word.
The free resources are there to help you.
A Facebook share can introduce someone to a Scripture passage they have never considered.
A thoughtful comment can open a conversation about repentance.
A private message can remind a struggling believer that someone cares.
And a life genuinely transformed by Christ can bear witness far beyond anything a social media page can accomplish.
Before you leave, return with me to that house in Genesis.
Leah still wanted to be loved.
Rachel still wanted children.
Jacob's family was still deeply imperfect.
And no one inside that home could see the full story.
But God was keeping His covenant promises.
Centuries later, the descendants of Judah would lead us to a manger in Bethlehem.
And the child born there would go to a cross.
Not to teach us how to compete more successfully for human affection.
But to save us from sin and reconcile us to God.
That is the center of the story.
Not Jacob's preferences.
Not Leah's rejection.
Not Rachel's envy.
Not even the twelve tribes themselves.
Jesus Christ.
The promised Savior.
The Lion of Judah.
The Lamb who was slain.
The risen Lord who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His grace.
So if you are still waiting to be loved, do not make another person's affection your savior.
If you are still grieving what you lack, do not let comparison steal your ability to see God's goodness.
If you have sinned, do not hide behind your wounds.
Come to Christ.
And if your family story is complicated, remember that the Bible never needed to hide the brokenness of Jacob's household in order to reveal the faithfulness of God.
Maybe the world has already decided what to call you.
Unwanted.
Second choice.
Failure.
Barren.
Forgotten.
Too damaged.
Too late.
But those labels do not have the authority to cancel the promises of God in Jesus Christ.
And when you stand before the cross, you discover something greater than being chosen by the person who rejected you.
You discover the grace of the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
So tonight, if all you can manage is one honest prayer, let it be this:

“Lord Jesus, I have spent too long looking to people and circumstances for what only You can ultimately give. Forgive my sin. Heal what is wounded in me. Teach me to repent where I have done wrong, to forgive as You have forgiven me, and to trust Your Word even when my life is painful. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Help me follow You faithfully. Let my life bring glory to Your name. Amen.”
And remember this, long after you close this article:

Leah spent years longing to be chosen by Jacob, never knowing that through her son Judah, God was preparing the lineage of the Savior who would call the rejected, the broken, and the sinful to Himself.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE ANGEL WHO SPOKE AS GOD: WAS JESUS WALKING THROUGH THE OLD TESTAMENT BEFORE BETHLEHEM?
paragraphs: THE ANGEL WHO SPOKE AS GOD: WAS JESUS WALKING THROUGH THE OLD TESTAMENT BEFORE BETHLEHEM?

The burning bush. The terrified warrior. The mysterious Messenger who accepted God's name, spoke with God's authority, and left men trembling in His presence. What if these ancient encounters were pointing toward the greatest revelation in human history—Jesus Christ Himself?
There is something deeply unsettling about the burning bush.
Not because it was burning.
But because Someone was speaking from inside the fire.
And the man standing before it had absolutely no idea how dramatically his life was about to change.
Moses wasn't standing inside a temple. He wasn't leading a worship service. He wasn't expecting a supernatural visitation.
He was tending sheep.
A former prince of Egypt, now living in the wilderness, carrying a past stained by bloodshed, failure, fear, and exile.
Forty years earlier, Moses had killed an Egyptian and fled for his life (Exodus 2:11–15; Acts 7:23–30).
Perhaps he thought the most significant chapter of his life was already behind him.
Then he saw something that should have been impossible.
A bush engulfed in flames.
Yet the branches weren't turning to ashes.
The fire burned, but the bush was not consumed.
Moses moved closer.
And then a voice called his name.
"Moses, Moses."
He answered, "Here am I."
But what happened next reveals one of the most astonishing mysteries woven throughout the Old Testament.
Because Exodus doesn't initially say that God appeared in the bush.
It says something far more intriguing.
"And the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush." — Exodus 3:2, KJV
The Angel of the LORD.
But just two verses later, the same passage declares:
"God called unto him out of the midst of the bush." — Exodus 3:4, KJV
And then the voice identifies Himself:
"I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." — Exodus 3:6, KJV
Read that carefully.
The Angel of the LORD appears.
God speaks.
And the One speaking identifies Himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
Moses doesn't respond as though he has encountered an ordinary angel delivering a heavenly message.
Scripture says he hides his face because he is afraid to look upon God.
Who was this mysterious Messenger?
And why does His identity matter so profoundly for understanding Jesus Christ?
Because this question takes us beyond a burning bush, beyond a frightened man hiding in a winepress, and into the astonishing unity of God's redemptive story.
A story that begins long before Bethlehem.
A story that reaches its climax at Calvary.
A story in which the God who calls sinners out of hiding is the same God who provides their salvation.
And perhaps, before we reach the end, you'll recognize something painfully familiar about the people He chose to visit.
Because Moses wasn't looking for a second chance.
Gideon wasn't looking for a confrontation with heaven.
And many of us aren't prepared for what happens when God's Word exposes the places where we've been hiding.
But first, we need to understand who this Angel actually was.
In the Hebrew text of Exodus 3:2, the expression is:
מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה — malʾakh YHWH
It means "messenger of the LORD" or "angel of the LORD."
The Hebrew word malʾakh describes a messenger. Depending on the context, that messenger may be human or heavenly.
The word itself does not automatically tell us the messenger's nature.
It describes the messenger's function.
That distinction is enormously important.
Because when modern readers hear "angel," they often immediately picture a created heavenly being.
But the Hebrew term does not, by itself, establish that conclusion.
We have to examine what the Messenger says, what He does, how Scripture describes Him, and how the passage fits within the Bible's wider revelation.
And this is where the mystery deepens.
In Exodus 3, the Messenger is introduced as the Angel of the LORD, yet the narrative identifies the speaker as God.
When Moses asks for His name, the answer comes:
אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה — ʾehyeh ʾasher ʾehyeh
Traditionally rendered:
"I AM THAT I AM." — Exodus 3:14, KJV
The Hebrew expression can also be understood as "I AM WHO I AM" or "I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE," reflecting the richness of the Hebrew verb for being.
This is no ordinary introduction.
The One speaking reveals Himself as the covenant God who will be faithful to His promises and present with His people.
And notice what He does not say.
He doesn't say Moses has become too old.
He doesn't say his previous failure has permanently disqualified him.
He doesn't pretend Moses' past never happened, either.
Instead, He calls Moses into a mission far greater than Moses' confidence or ability.
When Moses objects, "Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh?" God's answer is not a speech about Moses' hidden greatness.
It is a promise.
"Certainly I will be with thee." — Exodus 3:12, KJV
There it is.
The foundation of Moses' calling was never Moses' worthiness.
It was God's presence.
And someone reading this needs to understand the difference.
Your failures are real.
Your sins cannot be excused.
Your past may have consequences you still carry.
But your history does not place you beyond the reach of God's mercy.
Repentance is not pretending the past never happened.
Grace is not God declaring evil harmless.
Grace is God doing for sinners what they could never accomplish through their own righteousness.
And ultimately, that grace is revealed through Jesus Christ.
But the burning bush isn't the only place where this mysterious Angel appears.
Centuries later, another man encounters Him.
And this time, the man isn't standing before a burning bush.
He's hiding.
His name is Gideon.
Israel has fallen into a devastating cycle of disobedience, oppression, desperation, and crying out to God.
The Midianites have ravaged the land.
Israel's crops have been destroyed or seized.
The people have been driven into hiding.
And Gideon is threshing wheat in a winepress, trying to conceal what little food he can preserve.
Then Scripture says:
"And the angel of the LORD came, and sat under an oak which was in Ophrah." — Judges 6:11, KJV
Imagine that scene.
A frightened man trying to survive.
Dust on his clothes.
An uncertain future.
The crushing weight of an occupied nation.
And a heavenly Messenger sitting beneath a tree.
Then comes a greeting that must have sounded almost absurd.
"The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour." — Judges 6:12, KJV
Mighty man of valor?
Gideon is hiding from his enemies.
He isn't standing on a battlefield.
He isn't commanding an army.
He isn't demonstrating heroic courage.
He is trying not to be discovered.
And yet the Messenger addresses him in terms of the calling God is placing upon him.
But Gideon doesn't immediately respond with triumphant faith.
He responds with a question that sounds painfully human.
"If the LORD be with us, why then is all this befallen us?" — Judges 6:13, KJV
Have you ever prayed something similar?
If God is with me, why is my family falling apart?
If God hears me, why does this suffering continue?
If God is faithful, why do I feel abandoned?
Gideon's question comes from a nation experiencing genuine suffering, though Judges also explains that Israel's covenant unfaithfulness contributed to its condition.
The text does not dismiss the suffering.
Neither does it excuse the sin.
It brings both into the presence of God.
And then something extraordinary happens.
Judges 6:14 says:
"And the LORD looked upon him, and said, Go in this thy might." — KJV
Did you notice the transition?
The Angel of the LORD appears in verse 11.
The Angel speaks in verse 12.
But in verse 14, the narrative says the LORD Himself looks at Gideon and speaks.
The Hebrew uses the divine name YHWH.
The same covenant name associated with the God who called Moses.
And when Gideon protests that his family is poor and that he is the least in his father's house, the answer echoes the burning bush.
"Surely I will be with thee." — Judges 6:16, KJV
Different man.
Different generation.
Different crisis.
The same divine assurance.
God's presence is greater than the weakness of the person He calls.
But Gideon's encounter becomes even more startling.
He prepares an offering of meat, unleavened cakes, and broth.
The Angel instructs him to place the meat and bread upon a rock and pour out the broth.
Then the Angel touches the offering with the end of His staff.
Fire rises from the rock and consumes it.
And the Angel of the LORD disappears.
Gideon suddenly understands the terrifying significance of what he has witnessed.
"Alas, O Lord GOD! for because I have seen an angel of the LORD face to face." — Judges 6:22, KJV
Gideon fears death.
Yet the LORD answers:
"Peace be unto thee; fear not: thou shalt not die." — Judges 6:23, KJV
So Gideon builds an altar and calls it Jehovah-shalom.
The LORD is peace.
And now the question becomes impossible to ignore.
Why do these encounters repeatedly move between the Angel of the LORD and the LORD Himself?
Why does the Messenger sometimes speak as God, rather than merely delivering a message from God?
And could these appearances have anything to do with Jesus?
Here we must be careful.
Not because the question is unimportant.
But because Scripture deserves more than sensational conclusions.
Many Christians throughout church history have understood certain appearances of the Angel of the LORD as preincarnate appearances of the Son of God.
The theological term is Christophany—an appearance of Christ before His incarnation.
This interpretation is especially associated with passages in which the Angel of the LORD speaks with divine authority, bears the divine name, or is identified with God in the surrounding narrative.
It is a serious, historically influential Christian interpretation.
But it is important to state something clearly.
Exodus 3 and Judges 6 do not explicitly identify the Angel of the LORD as Jesus Christ.

Other interpreters understand these passages through the biblical principle of divine agency: God's messenger may speak on God's behalf so fully that the narrative moves between the messenger and the God who sent him.
That explanation also deserves consideration.
And the New Testament does not provide a single, unambiguous statement saying, "The Angel of the LORD in Exodus 3 and Judges 6 was Jesus."
We should not claim that it does.
Faithfulness to Scripture means distinguishing between what the Bible explicitly teaches and what Christians reasonably infer from its wider testimony.
But there are powerful reasons why Christians have connected these mysterious appearances with the eternal Son.
John's Gospel opens with words that take us back before creation itself.
"In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." — John 1:1, KJV
The Greek reads:
Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ λόγος — En archē ēn ho logos
"In the beginning was the Word."
And later:
καὶ θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος — kai theos ēn ho logos
"And the Word was God."
John does not present Jesus as a created being who began existing in Bethlehem.
He presents the Word as eternally existing, personally distinct from the Father, and truly divine.
Then John 1:14 announces:
"And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." — KJV
The eternal Son entered human history by taking on human nature.
Bethlehem was not the beginning of His existence.
It was the beginning of His incarnate earthly life.
And that distinction changes how Christians read the Old Testament.
Because the Son did not begin to exist when Mary gave birth.
He was already eternal.
He was already divine.
He was already active in God's works.
Colossians 1:16–17 teaches that all things were created through Christ and for Him, and that He is before all things.
Hebrews 1:1–3 presents the Son as the One through whom God made the worlds and as the radiance of God's glory.
And John 1:18 describes the unique role of the Son in making God known.
These passages establish the eternal identity and divine activity of Christ.
They make the possibility of preincarnate appearances theologically coherent.
They do not, by themselves, prove that every Old Testament appearance of the Angel of the LORD was Christ.
But they reveal why the question matters.
The Jesus revealed in the New Testament is not an afterthought in God's plan.
He is the eternal Son through whom God's saving purposes reach their fulfillment.
And then we come to another extraordinary connection.
In John 8, Jesus confronts religious opponents who challenge His claims.
The conversation turns to Abraham.
And Jesus declares:
"Before Abraham was, I am." — John 8:58, KJV
In Greek:
πρὶν Ἀβραὰμ γενέσθαι ἐγὼ εἰμί — prin Abraam genesthai egō eimi
Notice the contrast.
Abraham came into existence.
Jesus says, "I am."
The wording is striking.
Many Christian interpreters understand this as an assertion of Christ's eternal existence and divine identity, with an important theological connection to God's self-revelation in Exodus.
The surrounding narrative shows how seriously His opponents took the statement: they picked up stones to throw at Him.
We should also recognize that the Greek expression egō eimi does not always function as a divine-name declaration in every context.
And the Greek translation of Exodus 3:14 has its own distinctive wording.
The connection between these passages is therefore theological and contextual, not simply a claim that the Hebrew and Greek phrases are identical.
But the larger testimony of John's Gospel is unmistakable.
Jesus is not merely a prophet telling people about God.
He is the eternal Word who became flesh.
He is the Son who reveals the Father.
He is worthy of the honor due to God.
And He is the One through whom salvation comes.
Now think again about Moses.
A man burdened by failure, standing barefoot before holy ground.
Think about Gideon.
A frightened man hiding from his enemies, overwhelmed by the weakness of his own circumstances.
Neither man could save his people by personal strength.
Both needed God's presence.
Both needed God's promise.
Both were confronted by the holiness of the One who called them.
And both stories ultimately belong to the larger biblical account of God's faithfulness.
But there is another truth we must not miss.
The Angel of the LORD is not always presented in exactly the same way in every Old Testament passage.
Sometimes the language strongly identifies the Messenger with God.
Elsewhere the distinction between God and His messenger is more apparent.
The term itself does not guarantee that every occurrence refers to the same kind of manifestation.
That is why careful interpretation examines each passage rather than forcing every reference into a single conclusion.
Consider another important encounter.
In Genesis 16, Hagar is fleeing into the wilderness.
She is an Egyptian servant who has suffered mistreatment and finds herself vulnerable and alone.
The Angel of the LORD meets her.
The narrative describes the encounter in language that leads Hagar to speak of the LORD who has seen her.
She calls Him El Roi, commonly understood as "the God who sees me."
Here again, God's revelation reaches someone living at the margins.
Someone whose pain others might have ignored.
Someone whose future seemed uncertain.
And whether one understands this appearance as a Christophany or as God speaking through His messenger, the passage reveals something precious and undeniable.
The living God sees the afflicted.
He is not indifferent to suffering.
He is not unaware of the wilderness.
But the full revelation of God's mercy does not stop with Hagar, Moses, or Gideon.
It leads us to Jesus.
And here the mystery becomes personal.
Because there is a danger in becoming so fascinated by the identity of the Angel of the LORD that we miss the central message of Scripture.
We can study Hebrew vocabulary.
We can compare Greek expressions.
We can debate ancient appearances.
We can learn the vocabulary of theology.
And still avoid the question that matters most.
Have you actually surrendered your life to the Jesus whom Scripture reveals?
Not merely admired Him.
Not simply agreed that He exists.
Not merely shared Christian posts or attended church.
Have you turned to Him in repentance and faith?
Because the God who spoke from the burning bush is holy.
And holiness is not something sinful humanity can casually approach on its own terms.
When Moses draws near, he is commanded to remove his shoes.
The ground is holy because God has manifested His presence there.
Moses hides his face.
Gideon fears that he will die.
These are not scenes designed to make God appear harmless.
They confront us with the majesty of the Creator.
And yet, in the fullness of time, the eternal Son truly became man.
He entered a world filled with rebellion, violence, hypocrisy, grief, and shame.
He walked among sinners.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed the repentant.
He confronted religious pride.
He called people out of darkness.
He exposed sin without becoming a sinner.
He loved without compromising truth.
And then He went to the cross.
Not because humanity was innocent.
But because humanity was guilty.
Not because sin was insignificant.
But because sin was so serious that our redemption required the sacrifice of the spotless Lamb of God.
At Calvary, Jesus bore the judgment due to sinners, fulfilling God's saving purpose through His atoning death.
And on the third day, He rose bodily from the dead.
This is the Gospel.
Not a motivational speech about becoming a better version of yourself.
Not a promise that following Jesus will eliminate every hardship.
Not a religious system in which you purchase God's acceptance through good deeds.
It is the good news that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And salvation is received by God's grace through faith, not earned through human achievement (Ephesians 2:8–9).
That means you cannot buy forgiveness.
You cannot earn redemption through donations.
And no financial contribution, however generous, can replace repentance and faith in Christ.
Jesus has already accomplished what money could never purchase.
But those who have received His grace are called to respond with grateful obedience, love, generosity, and a desire to make the Gospel known.
And that is where this message reaches beyond ancient history.
Maybe you're reading this while carrying a secret nobody knows.
Maybe your family thinks you're spiritually strong, but you know how exhausted you've become.
Maybe you've been hiding behind church attendance while privately wrestling with sin.
Maybe you love Jesus, but lately your prayers have felt empty.
Maybe you once walked closely with God, but compromise slowly became comfortable.
Or perhaps you don't yet believe, and you're wondering whether the God of the Bible could possibly care about someone like you.
Look again at Moses.
Look again at Gideon.
Their stories are not identical to yours.
And their specific callings were not promises that every believer will experience a burning bush or receive an extraordinary military commission.
But they reveal the character of a God who acts in history, confronts human weakness, calls people to trust Him, and remains faithful to His purposes.
And through Jesus Christ, we are invited to something even greater than witnessing a mysterious flame.
We are invited to be reconciled to God.
Not because we deserve it.
But because Christ is sufficient.
There is a line in Hebrews 1:1–2 that brings the entire discussion into focus.
God spoke in various ways through the prophets in former times.
But in these last days, He has spoken to us by His Son.
That is the decisive revelation.
Whatever conclusions Christians reach about particular appearances of the Angel of the LORD, we do not need to search for an uncertain manifestation to know what God is like.
We look to Jesus Christ.
He is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15).
He is the exact representation of God's nature (Hebrews 1:3).
He is the One who said, "He that hath seen me hath seen the Father" (John 14:9).
And He is the only mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5).
The burning bush makes us wonder.
The encounter with Gideon makes us tremble.
The Hebrew text makes us examine.
The New Testament makes us behold the eternal Son.
And the cross brings us to the point of decision.
What will you do with Jesus?
Because one day, the most important question will not be whether you correctly identified every mysterious Messenger in the Old Testament.
It will be whether you have placed your trust in the Savior whom the Scriptures proclaim.
And that question is too important to hide behind religious familiarity.
Maybe you've been saying, "I'll come back to God when I fix myself."
But you cannot cleanse your own heart by waiting.
Maybe you've been saying, "I've gone too far."
But the mercy of Christ is greater than the guilt of every sinner who truly comes to Him.
Maybe you've been saying, "I believe in God, so I'm fine."
But the Gospel calls us beyond vague belief into repentance and personal trust in Jesus Christ.
Hear His invitation:
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." — John 6:37, KJV
That promise is not reserved for people with respectable histories.
It is for those who come to Christ.
Bring your guilt.
Bring your shame.
Bring the sins you've been defending.
Bring the fears you've been concealing.
Bring the questions you still struggle to answer.
You do not have to pretend to be righteous before coming to the Savior.
But you must not cling to sin as though it were more precious than Him.
Turn to Christ.
Trust His finished work.
Receive His mercy.
And follow Him.
If this message has exposed something you've been hiding, you can begin with a simple, sincere prayer:

"Lord Jesus, I confess that I have sinned against You. I cannot save myself. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising from the dead. Forgive me, change my heart, and teach me to follow You in truth. I surrender my life to You. Amen."
The prayer itself is not a magical formula.
It is the repentance and faith expressed from the heart that matter.
And if you're already a believer but have grown weary, remember this:
The Christian life is not sustained by pretending you are strong.
It is sustained by the grace of the Savior who remains faithful.
Now I want to ask you something personal.
When you read about Moses hiding his face and Gideon hiding in a winepress, which man did you recognize in yourself?
The person ashamed of the past?
Or the person frightened of the future?
Perhaps both.
You don't have to reveal private details or expose wounds you're not ready to discuss.
And if you've experienced God's restoration after a season of failure, consider sharing a little of your testimony. Your words may encourage someone who believes their story is already over.
Because sometimes a testimony becomes the reminder another believer desperately needed.

Return to Exodus 3:2–6, Judges 6:11–24, John 1:1–18, and Hebrews 1:1–3. Read them carefully. Examine the context. Let God's Word shape your convictions rather than relying on an emotional experience alone.
Not merely to increase a number on a screen.
But because someone in your circle may be wrestling with the very questions we have explored.
Someone may be spiritually exhausted.
Someone may have quietly walked away from church.
Someone may believe their past has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone may never have understood that Jesus Christ existed before Bethlehem.
One thoughtful share can place the Scriptures before a person you may never have known was searching.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture more deeply, understand the Gospel more clearly, and become more firmly rooted in Jesus Christ.
They are also part of a ministry mission that requires time, labor, resources, and ongoing support.
And that brings me to something I want to share with you openly.
And not because we can claim that God requires you to support this particular ministry.
Scripture makes no such demand.
But the Bible does encourage believers to support faithful Gospel ministry willingly, generously, and according to their means.
Paul teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." — KJV
And Philippians 4:15–18 shows believers participating in Gospel ministry through practical financial support.
It should never be treated as a compulsory tithe, a substitute for responsibilities to your local church, or a requirement for spiritual blessing.
Rather, it can be a voluntary expression of generosity and partnership in the Gospel.
Those items are simply expressions of appreciation.
They are not the heart of the mission.
The mission is Jesus Christ.
The mission is biblical truth.
The mission is helping people move beyond religious appearances into genuine repentance, faith, spiritual maturity, and transformation through the Gospel.
Pray for the ministry.
Read and share the Scriptures.
Encourage others to grow in Christ.
And if you have the desire and means to help sustain this work monthly, we would be grateful to have you stand with us.
There is no pressure to give beyond your ability.
No promise that a payment will unlock a miracle.
Just an invitation to participate willingly in a ministry that desires to lift up the name of Jesus Christ.
Only Jesus saves.
And the greatest thing Gospel Warrior could ever accomplish is to help one more person hear His Word, understand His Gospel, and turn to Him in faith.
Picture Moses.
The sheep are nearby.
The desert is silent.
The bush is burning.
A voice calls his name.
He removes his sandals.
He hides his face.
And the God who remembers His covenant prepares to deliver His people.
Then picture Gideon.
A frightened man in a winepress.
A nation crushed by oppression.
A Messenger beneath an oak tree.
A promise of divine presence.
Fire rising from a rock.
And a trembling man hearing the words:
"Peace be unto thee."
We may continue studying the precise identity of these mysterious appearances, and faithful Christians may reach different conclusions about the Angel of the LORD.
But the greatest revelation is no longer hidden in a question about an ancient Messenger.
It has been made known in Jesus Christ.
The eternal Son came in the flesh.
The sinless Savior died for sinners.
The crucified Lord rose from the grave.
And everyone who truly trusts in Him receives the promise of salvation.
That is the hope Moses and Gideon could only anticipate within their own place in redemptive history.
That is the Gospel we now proclaim openly.
And that is the grace capable of rewriting a human story—not by erasing its history, but by redeeming the sinner and making all things new in Christ.
So if your life has become a wilderness, don't mistake the silence for proof that God has forgotten you.
If your heart has become a hiding place, don't confuse concealment with safety.
And if your past feels like a scandal that can never be overcome, remember that the cross declares both the seriousness of your sin and the astonishing sufficiency of your Savior.
The greatest wonder was never that God spoke from a burning bush—but that the eternal Son came into our broken world to bring sinners home to God.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD SENT THUNDER DURING THE HARVEST—AND WHAT HAPPENED NEXT SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY HEART THAT HAS GROWN COMFORTABLE WITHOUT HIM
paragraphs: GOD SENT THUNDER DURING THE HARVEST—AND WHAT HAPPENED NEXT SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY HEART THAT HAS GROWN COMFORTABLE WITHOUT HIM

Why did God interrupt Israel’s wheat harvest with thunder and rain? The answer in 1 Samuel 12:16–18 exposes a frightening truth about human rebellion, reveals the mercy hidden inside divine warnings, and points us to the only King who can rescue a heart that has rejected Him.
Imagine standing in the middle of the greatest harvest of your life.
The fields are golden. The grain is ready. The work of your hands is finally producing something beautiful.
You have waited for this season.
You have prayed for provision, labored through uncertainty, endured the heat, and watched the wheat grow.
Everything looks promising.
And then…
Thunder.
Not the distant rumbling of an ordinary passing storm.
Thunder that makes you stop working.
Thunder that turns every face toward heaven.
Rain begins falling over the wheat.
And suddenly, the harvest you thought you controlled reminds you how little control you actually possess.
Now imagine discovering that the storm was not an accident.
God had sent it.
Not because the wheat had sinned.
Not because the farmers had failed to work hard enough.
But because an entire nation had made a decision that revealed something terribly wrong with its relationship with God.
And the most frightening part?
The people had not fully understood how serious their decision was until heaven answered.
That is what happened in 1 Samuel 12.
And before you dismiss this as an ancient story about Israel, consider something uncomfortable.
What if the greatest danger in your life is not that God has stopped blessing you, but that you have become so comfortable with His blessings that you no longer recognize how much you need Him?
Because Israel was about to discover that a full harvest could never compensate for an empty relationship with God.
And the thunder was only the beginning of the story.
The real miracle would come afterward.
Israel had asked for a king.
That might not sound like a terrible request.
After all, nations need leadership. Communities need order. People need protection.

And kingship itself was not inherently forbidden in Israel. Deuteronomy 17:14–20 had already given instructions concerning a future king, and God's promises concerning His people included royal expectations.
The deeper problem was not simply that Israel wanted a human ruler.
It was why they wanted one.
In 1 Samuel 8, Israel's elders approached Samuel and demanded a king to judge them like the surrounding nations.
They wanted something visible.
Something politically impressive.
Something they could point to when enemies approached.
Something that made them feel secure.
And beneath their request was a rejection they did not want to acknowledge.
God told Samuel:
"They have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them." — 1 Samuel 8:7, KJV
Read that again.
They had not merely requested a change in government.
They had rejected God's kingship over them.
They wanted the security of a throne they could see while neglecting the sovereignty of the King they could not see.
And isn't that painfully familiar?
We say we trust God.
But sometimes we feel safer when the bank account is full.
We say Jesus is Lord.
But sometimes we allow public approval to determine our decisions.
We say God is our refuge.
But when uncertainty arrives, we desperately search for something we can control.
A relationship.
A position.
A business.
A person.
A reputation.
A plan that leaves no room for surrender.
None of these things is automatically sinful.
But even good things become spiritually dangerous when we demand that they provide the security, identity, or ultimate confidence that belongs to God alone.
Israel wanted a king like the nations.
And God allowed them to have one.
That should make us think.
Because receiving what we insist upon is not always evidence that God approves of the motives behind our insistence.
Sometimes God allows us to experience the limitations of the very things we thought would save us.
And sometimes the moment of greatest spiritual danger is the moment we finally get what we wanted.
Israel had received Saul as king.
The people had their visible ruler.
The nation had its political structure.
The wheat harvest had arrived.
And Samuel, the aging prophet who had faithfully served Israel, stood before them to deliver a final public warning.
He reminded them of God's faithfulness.
He rehearsed their history.
He exposed their repeated pattern of forgetting the Lord, suffering under oppression, crying for deliverance, and receiving mercy.
Then he confronted their demand for a king.
And suddenly, the atmosphere changed.
Samuel said:
"Now therefore stand and see this great thing, which the LORD will do before your eyes." — 1 Samuel 12:16, KJV
Stand.
Watch.
Pay attention.
Because God was about to make visible what Israel had refused to recognize spiritually.
Then Samuel asked:

"Is it not wheat harvest to day? I will call unto the LORD, and he shall send thunder and rain; that ye may perceive and see that your wickedness is great, which ye have done in the sight of the LORD, in asking you a king." — 1 Samuel 12:17, KJV
There it is.
The reason for the thunder.
The reason for the rain.
The reason heaven interrupted the harvest.
God was exposing the seriousness of Israel's rebellion.
But to appreciate the force of this moment, we need to understand something about the season.
In ancient Israel, the wheat harvest generally occurred around late spring to early summer, during the transition into the dry season.
Rainfall at that time was unusual, especially compared with the normal winter rainy season.
It was not that rain could never fall during wheat harvest.
It was that a sudden thunderstorm, arriving precisely in response to Samuel's prayer, would be an extraordinary and unmistakable sign.
And rain during the harvest could threaten grain that needed dry conditions for gathering and processing.
The timing mattered.
The prayer mattered.
The storm mattered.
God did not simply produce impressive weather.
He gave Israel a sign that confronted its conscience.
The Hebrew text makes this even more striking.
In 1 Samuel 12:17, Samuel declares:
וּדְעוּ וּרְאוּ כִּי־רָעַתְכֶם רַבָּה
Ude'u ure'u ki-ra'atkhem rabbah.
Meaning:
“Know and see that your wickedness is great.”
The two opening verbs are commands.
Know.
See.
This was not merely an invitation to observe an unusual event.
It was a summons to recognize moral reality.
The Hebrew word רָעָה (ra'ah) can refer to evil, wrongdoing, harm, or calamity depending on context.
Here, with the expression referring to what Israel had done in asking for a king, it describes the evil of their action.
And רַבָּה (rabbah) emphasizes its greatness or seriousness.
Samuel was not minimizing their rebellion.
He was telling them that what they had treated as a reasonable national demand was, in God's sight, a grave spiritual offense.
They had underestimated the seriousness of rejecting the Lord's rule.
Then comes verse 18.
"So Samuel called unto the LORD; and the LORD sent thunder and rain that day: and all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel." — 1 Samuel 12:18, KJV
Notice the sequence.
Samuel prayed.
The Lord answered.
Thunder and rain came that very day.
And the people feared.
The Hebrew expression for the thunder is especially vivid:
קֹלוֹת וּמָטָר
Qolot u-matar.
Literally, “sounds/voices and rain,” with qolot functioning in this context as thunderclaps.
The Hebrew word קוֹל (qol) can mean a voice, sound, or thunder depending on its setting.
That does not mean the text records God speaking audible sentences through the storm.
It means the thunder was a powerful manifestation accompanying His divine warning.
The people could no longer treat Samuel's message as merely the opinion of an aging prophet.
The Lord had confirmed it.
And now something remarkable happened.
The same people who had confidently demanded a king suddenly recognized the danger of their rebellion.
They pleaded:
"Pray for thy servants unto the LORD thy God, that we die not: for we have added unto all our sins this evil, to ask us a king." — 1 Samuel 12:19, KJV
There is something heartbreaking about those words.
They were no longer celebrating their new king.
They were asking for mercy.
They were no longer insisting that they knew what was best.
They were confessing that they had sinned.
The storm had exposed what their prosperity had concealed.
And perhaps that is where this ancient passage begins to touch our lives.
Not because every storm we experience is a punishment from God.
Scripture does not permit us to make that assumption.
Jesus explicitly rejected simplistic conclusions about suffering and personal guilt in Luke 13:1–5, and John 9:1–3 warns against automatically attributing suffering to someone's particular sin.
We must never tell a grieving family that their tragedy proves God is punishing them.
We must never assume that sickness, financial hardship, or natural disaster is a divine verdict against a particular person.
The thunder in 1 Samuel 12 was a specifically announced sign, confirmed through Samuel's prayer. It was not a universal formula for interpreting every hardship.
But this passage does ask a searching question.
When God confronts us through His Word, do we listen?
Or do we wait until the consequences of our choices become impossible to ignore?
Think about the things we sometimes protect from God's authority.
The bitterness we refuse to release.
The secret sin we keep explaining away.
The pride that makes repentance feel humiliating.
The relationship we know is drawing us away from obedience.
The dishonesty we call survival.
The unforgiveness we have carried for so long that it feels like part of our personality.
The public appearance of faithfulness that hides a private life of spiritual exhaustion.
We can become so skilled at appearing strong that we forget how desperately we need grace.
And perhaps the hardest words to say are not “God, bless me.”
Perhaps they are:
“Lord, I was wrong.”
Because those words require surrender.
They require us to stop defending what God has already exposed.
They require us to admit that the problem is not always outside us.
Sometimes the problem is the throne we have built inside our own hearts.
And we have been sitting on it.
But here is where the story takes a turn that should bring hope to anyone who has ever failed God.
After the people confessed their sin and begged Samuel to pray for them, Samuel answered:
"Fear not: ye have done all this wickedness: yet turn not aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart." — 1 Samuel 12:20, KJV
Wait.
Did you catch that?
Samuel did not say their wickedness was imaginary.
He did not tell them that their motives had been misunderstood.
He did not soften the seriousness of their rebellion.
He said, in effect:
Yes, you have done this evil.
But do not turn away from the Lord.
What astonishing mercy.
The very God they had rejected was still calling them to return.
Their sin was real.
Their guilt was real.
Their need for repentance was real.
But their failure did not mean they should abandon all hope of walking with God.
And this is where many struggling believers need to listen carefully.
There is a kind of guilt that brings us to repentance.
And there is a kind of despair that whispers that repentance is useless.
The first leads us toward God.
The second tempts us to run farther away.
Samuel did not invite Israel to pretend nothing had happened.
He called them to renewed obedience.
He continued:
"And turn ye not aside: for then should ye go after vain things, which cannot profit nor deliver; for they are vain." — 1 Samuel 12:21, KJV
The Hebrew word תֹּהוּ (tohu), used here for what is vain or worthless, carries the idea of emptiness or futility.
The same Hebrew word appears in Genesis 1:2 in the description of the earth as “without form,” though the contexts differ.
Here it describes the uselessness of false objects of trust.
Things that cannot ultimately profit.
Things that cannot deliver.
Things that promise security but cannot save.
And suddenly, Israel's story becomes a mirror.
How many empty things have we trusted to give us peace?
How many temporary comforts have we asked to heal eternal wounds?
How many times have we run toward something that promised freedom, only to discover that it had become another chain?
Approval cannot forgive sin.
Money cannot reconcile a soul to God.
Pleasure cannot erase guilt.
Religious appearance cannot replace a transformed heart.
Even the best human leader cannot do what only the Lord can do.
Israel needed more than a better political system.
They needed a restored relationship with God.
And so do we.
But the most beautiful words in this entire chapter may be the ones Samuel spoke next.
"For the LORD will not forsake his people for his great name's sake: because it hath pleased the LORD to make you his people." — 1 Samuel 12:22, KJV
Read that slowly.
The Lord will not forsake His people for His great name's sake.
Their hope did not rest on the perfection of their obedience.
It rested on the faithfulness of the God who had graciously chosen them.
This was not permission to continue rebelling.
Samuel immediately called them to fear the Lord, serve Him faithfully, and consider the great things He had done.
And he warned in verse 25 that persistent wickedness would bring judgment upon both people and king.
The promise of God's faithfulness did not cancel the necessity of repentance.
But neither did their failure erase His covenant mercy.
That tension matters.
God is holy.
God is merciful.
God does not call evil good.
And God does not delight in the destruction of those who turn to Him.
The thunder was not the end of the conversation.
Mercy followed the warning.
And the warning itself gave the people an opportunity to recognize their sin and return.
Now look ahead through the unfolding story of Scripture.
Israel wanted a king.
They wanted someone strong enough to lead them.
Someone powerful enough to defeat their enemies.
Someone who could establish their security.
But Saul would prove deeply flawed.
David, though chosen and greatly used by God, would also sin grievously.
And the generations of kings that followed would repeatedly demonstrate the limitations of human rule.
The Old Testament story would leave God's people longing for a righteous King whose reign would not be corrupted by sin.
Then, centuries later, Jesus Christ came.
Not merely as another ruler in Israel's troubled history.
But as the promised Son of David.
The Messiah.
The righteous King.
The One whose kingdom would never end.
Luke 1:32–33 declares that He would receive the throne of His father David and reign forever.
And unlike every sinful human king, Jesus would be perfectly faithful.
He would not exploit His people to preserve His own comfort.
He would give Himself for them.
He would not use power to escape suffering.
He would willingly suffer to save sinners.
And here is the breathtaking contrast.
In Samuel's day, thunder accompanied the exposure of Israel's sin.
At Calvary, darkness fell as the sinless Son of God gave His life for sinners.
Matthew 27:45 records darkness over the land during the crucifixion.
Matthew 27:51 records the tearing of the temple curtain and an earthquake following Jesus' death.
These are distinct events with distinct meanings, and Scripture does not tell us that the thunder of 1 Samuel 12 directly predicted the darkness at Calvary.
But together they reveal something central to the biblical story.
The God who takes sin seriously is also the God who has provided salvation through His Son.
At the cross, Jesus bore our sins.
Not because He had rebelled.
Not because He needed forgiveness.
But because we did.
As 1 Peter 2:24 says:
"Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed." — KJV
The One who had every right to condemn sinners willingly laid down His life to redeem them.
And He rose again.
Death did not hold Him.
The grave did not defeat Him.
The crucified King is the risen Lord.
That is the Gospel.
Not that sin does not matter.
But that Christ has done what sinners could never do for themselves.
Not that repentance is unnecessary.
But that through Jesus, forgiveness and new life are genuinely offered.
Not that our past was harmless.
But that our past does not have to be the final word over our future.
Think about that.
Israel's scandal was not simply that they asked for a king.
It was that they wanted the benefits of God's care while rejecting His rightful rule.
And our scandal is not merely that we have made mistakes.
It is that we have sinned against the holy God who made us.
Yet the Gospel announces that sinners can be reconciled to Him through Jesus Christ.
Not by pretending to be innocent.
Not by purchasing forgiveness.
Not by earning enough religious credit.
But by grace, through faith in Christ, a grace that calls us into repentance and a transformed life.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes clear that salvation is God's gift, not the result of our works.
And verse 10 reminds us that those saved by grace are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not leave us where it found us.
It changes the direction of our lives.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years believing that God could never welcome them back.
Maybe you once walked closely with Him.
You prayed.
You worshiped.
You loved opening your Bible.
You remember when His Word felt alive in your heart.
But somewhere along the way, something changed.
A disappointment.
An unanswered prayer.
A relationship that shattered.
A temptation you thought you could manage.
A private compromise that slowly became a habit.
And now you still know the language of faith, but inside, you feel distant.
You know how to say “God is good” while quietly wondering why your soul feels so empty.
You know how to encourage others while struggling to believe there is hope for yourself.
And the frightening thing is that nobody around you may know.
You look fine.
You sound fine.
You have learned how to keep functioning.
But you know.
And God knows.
The question is not whether you can maintain the appearance of a harvest.
The question is whether your heart still belongs to the Lord of the harvest.
Because a person can appear successful and still be spiritually lost.
A person can be surrounded by religious activity and still be resisting God.
A person can know Bible verses and still refuse the truth those verses reveal.
And yet…
There is still an invitation.
Turn to Christ.
Not after you have made yourself impressive.
Not after you have somehow erased your past.
Not after you have convinced everyone that you never struggled.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Forsake what needs to be forsaken.
Seek forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Receive the mercy that Jesus purchased through His death and resurrection.
And begin walking in obedience.
It may not be easy.
There may be consequences to face.
There may be relationships to repair.
There may be habits that require serious accountability and patient perseverance.
But the Gospel does not promise that genuine repentance will always be comfortable.
It promises that Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
And that is better than temporary comfort.
Perhaps this is why Samuel's words still matter thousands of years later.
He did not tell the people to spend the rest of their lives staring at the storm.
He told them to return to the Lord.
And he promised something else.
"Moreover as for me, God forbid that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you: but I will teach you the good and the right way." — 1 Samuel 12:23, KJV
What a picture of faithful spiritual leadership.
Samuel had been rejected as Israel demanded a king.
He had witnessed their stubbornness.
He had confronted their sin.
Yet he refused to abandon them in prayer.
He would continue interceding.
He would continue teaching them the right way.
And if Samuel's faithful intercession is moving, consider the greater hope believers have in Jesus Christ.
Hebrews 7:25 teaches that Christ is able to save completely those who come to God through Him, because He always lives to intercede for them.
Samuel was a faithful prophet.
Jesus is our perfect and eternal High Priest.
Samuel prayed for a rebellious people.
Jesus gave Himself for sinners and now intercedes for those who belong to Him.
Samuel called Israel back to the Lord.
Jesus is the way through whom we come to the Father.
This is why we cannot leave this story with the thunder.
Because the deepest answer to human rebellion is not a dramatic weather event.
It is the crucified and risen Savior.
And that changes how we read the harvest.
The wheat was not the real treasure.
The king was not the ultimate answer.
The storm was not the final message.
God was calling His people to recognize His holiness, remember His faithfulness, and return to wholehearted obedience.
And today, through the Gospel, He calls sinners to repent and believe in His Son.
Maybe you have been asking God to remove every uncomfortable thing from your life.
But what if the more important prayer is:
“Lord, whatever happens around me, do not let me become deaf to Your Word.”
Not every hardship is a divine rebuke.
Not every loss is a punishment.
Not every storm carries a secret message that we must decode.
But every day is an opportunity to humble ourselves before God, examine our hearts in the light of Scripture, and place our confidence in Jesus Christ.
The harvest will not last forever.
Our possessions will not last forever.
Human applause will not last forever.
The earthly things we cling to so desperately cannot carry the weight of eternity.
But Christ is risen.
His Word endures.
And His grace is sufficient for all who come to Him in faith.
So here is the question I want to leave with you.
If God exposed the one thing you have been trusting more than Him, would you surrender it—or would you defend it?
Don't rush past that.
Don't answer merely because you know what a Christian is supposed to say.
Bring the question before the Lord.
Perhaps the answer will lead you to confess pride.
Perhaps it will lead you to forgive someone.
Perhaps it will lead you to stop hiding a destructive habit.
Perhaps it will lead you to seek wise pastoral counsel and accountability.
Perhaps it will lead you, for the first time, to truly place your faith in Jesus Christ.
Whatever the Lord's Word is exposing, do not confuse conviction with hopelessness.
The people in Samuel's day feared when the thunder came.
But Samuel called them to keep following the Lord.
And the Gospel now announces the fullness of God's saving grace in Jesus Christ.
You do not need to make peace with the sin that is destroying you.
And you do not need to believe that your sin is greater than the Savior's power to redeem.
Come to Christ.
Not because you deserve His mercy.
But because He is merciful.
Not because you have never fallen.
But because He is mighty to save.
Not because your story has been clean.
But because Jesus Christ can make sinners new.
And if you have experienced the restoring grace of God, consider sharing a little of your testimony. Someone reading your words may be quietly wondering whether there is still hope for them.
You do not have to disclose private wounds or personal sins publicly to prove that your repentance is genuine. God sees the heart.
But there is something beautiful about believers encouraging one another with humility, truth, and hope.
Not merely to increase the reach of a page.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, people who have grown spiritually indifferent, and those who are still seeking the truth about Jesus.
Because discipleship is not meant to end with one emotional moment.
We need to keep learning.
Keep praying.
Keep studying Scripture.
Keep growing in holiness.
Keep pointing one another back to Christ.
This ministry is committed to sharing the Word of God, strengthening believers, encouraging repentance, and helping people grow in their understanding of the Gospel.
It can be an intentional expression of Christian generosity—an offering of support toward the ministry's ongoing mission.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, cheerfully, and according to their ability, not under pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And supporting Gospel ministry is a biblical principle (Philippians 4:15–18; Galatians 6:6).
These products are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply another way to encourage believers, share biblical truth, and express appreciation to those helping sustain the ministry.
The greater purpose is spiritual.
We want people to know Jesus.
We want believers to understand Scripture.
We want wounded hearts to encounter biblical hope.
We want those trapped in sin to hear the call to repentance and the promise of forgiveness in Christ.
And we want those who are serious about growing in the faith to have access to resources that can help them continue learning.
These resources are offered to help believers go deeper in God's Word, grow in spiritual maturity, and remain grounded in biblical truth.
Because the mission is bigger than any single article.
It is about people.
Real people.
The father who has forgotten how to pray.
The mother who cries after everyone else has fallen asleep.
The young person who thinks their mistakes have ruined their future.
The believer who feels ashamed of falling into the same sin again.
The person who has never truly understood why Jesus died on the cross.
The soul who appears to have everything together but desperately needs to hear that repentance and forgiveness are possible through Christ.
Somewhere, someone may read this article at exactly the moment they are tempted to give up on their faith.
And perhaps a simple act of sharing will place the truth of God's Word before them.
We cannot manufacture conversion.
We cannot purchase the work of the Holy Spirit.
Only Jesus saves.
But we can faithfully proclaim His Gospel.
We can pray.
We can teach.
We can give.
We can encourage.
We can make the truth available.
And we can trust God with the results.
So before you leave, remember the field.
Remember the wheat.
Remember the people who thought they had secured their future because they finally had a king.
Remember the thunder that exposed their rebellion.
Remember their confession.
But above all, remember what came after the storm.
A call to return.
A promise rooted in God's faithfulness.
And, in the fullness of God's redemptive plan, a Savior greater than every earthly king.
Jesus Christ.
The King who wore a crown of thorns.
The King who carried a cross.
The King who died for sinners.
The King who rose from the grave.
The King before whom every knee will bow.
And the King whose grace can transform even the most broken story.
The thunder exposed what Israel had done—but God's mercy revealed that their sin did not have to be the end of their story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE BROKE OPEN A FORTUNE AT THE FEET OF JESUS—AND WHAT HE SAID NEXT STILL EXPOSES THE HUMAN HEART
paragraphs: SHE BROKE OPEN A FORTUNE AT THE FEET OF JESUS—AND WHAT HE SAID NEXT STILL EXPOSES THE HUMAN HEART

Why did Mary of Bethany pour perfume worth nearly a year's wages on Jesus? The answer is more than a beautiful act of worship. It is a story of extravagant love, hidden betrayal, misunderstood devotion, and a Savior walking toward the cross. And somewhere between Mary's tears, Judas's objection, and the fragrance that filled the house, we may discover what our own hearts truly treasure.
There are moments in Scripture that are so quiet, so deeply human, that you can almost hear the breathing in the room.
A family gathered around a table.
The sound of people talking.
Food being served.
A man who had recently been dead, now sitting alive among the guests.
And a woman carrying something so expensive that breaking it open would cause everyone to notice.
Nobody in that room could have imagined how long her act would be remembered.
But Jesus knew.
He knew the cross was approaching.
He knew betrayal was already growing in a heart sitting near Him.
He knew the suffering waiting for Him in Jerusalem.
And while others were occupied with the dinner, Mary of Bethany approached Him with something she could never recover once it was poured out.
A costly perfume.
A possession worth almost a year's wages.
Perhaps one of the most valuable things she owned.
And then she did something that made people question her judgment.
She poured it on Jesus.
Not a drop.
Not a cautious little offering.
She anointed His feet and wiped them with her hair.
And John records one extraordinary detail.
“And the house was filled with the odour of the ointment.” — John 12:3, KJV
The whole house.
Think about that.
One woman's worship became impossible for everyone else to ignore.
But what makes this account so powerful is not simply the price of the perfume.
It is the fact that Jesus was about to die.
And Mary gave Him something precious while He was still there to receive it.
There is a question hidden in that moment that every believer eventually has to confront.
What is Jesus worth to you when loving Him costs you something?
Not when worship is convenient.
Not when obedience makes you look spiritual.
Not when following Him brings applause, comfort, or recognition.
But when surrender costs you something you genuinely treasure.
Because that evening in Bethany, one woman poured out what was precious.
And another disciple looked at the same act and saw only wasted money.
The difference between those two hearts should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Six days before the Passover, Jesus arrived in Bethany.
John 12:1 places the event near the final Passover before Christ's crucifixion. Jesus had already raised Lazarus from the dead, and the consequences of that miracle were still unfolding.
Imagine being Lazarus.
Imagine remembering the darkness of death, then hearing the voice of Jesus calling you out of the tomb.
Imagine sitting at dinner, eating ordinary food, surrounded by familiar faces, knowing that you were alive because the Son of God had spoken your name.
John tells us Lazarus was among those reclining at the table.
Martha was serving.
Mary was about to worship.
There is something beautiful about these details.
The family was together again.
The brother they had buried was alive.
The grief that had overwhelmed their home had been interrupted by the resurrection power of Christ.
But the miracle had not removed every shadow.
Jesus was moving toward His own death.
And the One who had called Lazarus out of the grave would soon enter a tomb Himself.
That is the breathtaking tension of this story.
A resurrected man was sitting at the table.
And the Resurrection and the Life was preparing to die.
Before we go further, we need to remember something about Mary.
This was not the first time Scripture placed her at the feet of Jesus.
In Luke 10:39, Mary sat at His feet and listened to His teaching while Martha was occupied with serving.
In John 11:32, Mary fell at His feet in grief after Lazarus died.
And now, in John 12:3, Mary is once again at His feet.
Listening.
Grieving.
Worshiping.
Three scenes.
Three profoundly different moments.
One consistent posture.
Mary knew where to bring her attention, her sorrow, and her devotion.
But we must be careful not to invent details Scripture never gives us.
The Bible does not identify Mary of Bethany as Mary Magdalene. Neither does it identify her as the unnamed sinful woman in Luke 7. Those women should not be automatically treated as the same person.
Mary of Bethany was the sister of Martha and Lazarus.
And the extraordinary thing about her is that John does not need to give us a dramatic history of scandal to show us the power of grace.
Her devotion is powerful precisely because she recognized something about Jesus that others were failing to appreciate.
She had listened to Him.
She had grieved before Him.
She had witnessed His power over death.
And now she would honor Him as He approached His burial.
John tells us:
“Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair.” — John 12:3, KJV
The original Greek adds richness to this scene.
John describes the perfume as:
μύρου νάρδου πιστικῆς πολυτίμου
myrou nardou pistikēs polytimou
This refers to costly perfume made from nard.
The word πολυτίμου (polytimou) means “very costly” or “of great value.”

The term πιστικῆς (pistikēs) has been interpreted in different ways, often understood as indicating genuine or pure nard. Its exact nuance is debated, so we should not build an entire spiritual doctrine on that one word.
What is unmistakable is the expense.
Judas later estimated its value at three hundred denarii.
A denarius was commonly associated with a day's wage for a laborer, as illustrated in Matthew 20:2.
Three hundred denarii, therefore, represented roughly the earnings of hundreds of working days.
This was no ordinary bottle of perfume.
It represented enormous economic value.
We do not know how Mary acquired it.
We do not know whether it was an inheritance, a gift, a family possession, or something purchased with years of savings.
Scripture does not tell us.
But we know it was precious.
And Mary chose to use it to honor Jesus.
Pause there.
Because we live in a world that teaches us to calculate the value of nearly everything.
How much does it cost?
What will I get in return?
Will people appreciate it?
Will this benefit me?
Will it be worth the sacrifice?
There is a place for wise stewardship. Scripture never praises carelessness merely because it is expensive.
But Mary was not trying to impress an audience.
She was honoring her Lord.
And that is what makes her act so searching.
She did not appear to be negotiating with Jesus.
She was not purchasing a miracle.
She was not buying forgiveness.
She was not giving in order to make God owe her something.
She was responding to the One who had already shown her family extraordinary mercy.
True worship is not a transaction through which we purchase God's love. It is a response to the love and grace we have received.
That distinction matters.
Because some people have spent their entire Christian lives believing that if they pray enough, give enough, serve enough, or sacrifice enough, perhaps God will finally accept them.
But the Gospel tells a different story.
We are not saved because our offerings are impressive.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that clear.
And the next verse reminds us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace comes first.
A transformed life follows.
Mary's perfume did not purchase Christ's approval.
Her act expressed devotion to the Christ she loved.
And then came the moment that turned the dinner into a confrontation.
Judas Iscariot spoke.
“Why was not this ointment sold for three hundred pence, and given to the poor?” — John 12:5, KJV
At first, his objection sounded reasonable.
Three hundred denarii.
Think how many hungry people that money could help.
Think how much practical good it could accomplish.
Why pour something so valuable on someone's feet?
Why not use it for a cause everyone could recognize as worthwhile?
It sounded compassionate.
Responsible.
Even righteous.
But John exposes what was happening beneath the words.
“This he said, not that he cared for the poor; but because he was a thief.” — John 12:6, KJV
Judas kept the common moneybag and stole from what was placed in it.
His objection was not an honest disagreement over charitable priorities.
According to John's testimony, it was hypocrisy.
He used concern for the poor to conceal his own greed.
And here is where this account becomes painfully personal.
Because it is possible to speak the language of righteousness while hiding an entirely different motive.
It is possible to sound deeply spiritual while resisting the very Lord we claim to serve.
It is possible to criticize another person's devotion while neglecting our own obedience.
But this passage does not give us permission to accuse everyone who questions a ministry's spending of being like Judas.
Accountability is biblical.
Generosity toward the poor is biblical.
Financial integrity is biblical.
Jesus Himself affirmed the continuing presence and needs of the poor in John 12:8, echoing the concern of Deuteronomy 15:11.
The problem was not that Judas mentioned the poor.
The problem was that he did not genuinely care about them.
His words concealed a heart that wanted to take.
Mary's actions revealed a heart that wanted to honor Christ.
And the contrast could hardly be greater.
One disciple was calculating the price of the perfume.
One woman was expressing the worth of Jesus.
Judas saw what could have been placed in the moneybag.
Mary saw the Savior before her.
And before anyone could reduce her act to foolishness, Jesus spoke.
“Let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this.” — John 12:7, KJV
These words deserve careful attention.
The Greek text includes the expression:
εἰς τὴν ἡμέραν τοῦ ἐνταφιασμοῦ μου
eis tēn hēmeran tou entaphiasmou mou
It means “for the day of my burial.”
The word ἐνταφιασμοῦ (entaphiasmou) refers to burial or preparation for burial.
Jesus connected Mary's anointing to His approaching death.
There is a textual and translational difficulty in the full sentence of John 12:7, which is why English translations differ in how they express Mary's keeping of the perfume.
But the central point remains clear.
