Some of you have been confusing spiritual maturity with never struggling.
You think that because temptation still visits, something must be wrong with your salvation.
But being tempted is not identical to consenting to sin.
Jesus Himself was tempted, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
The presence of a battle does not automatically prove the absence of the Holy Spirit.
What matters is how we respond to that battle.
Do we surrender to sin and defend it?
Or do we bring our weakness into the light, seek God's help, and continue learning to walk by the Spirit?
A hardened heart says, “God understands, so I do not need to change.”
A repentant heart says, “God is merciful, so I can come honestly and ask Him to change me.”
Those are not the same thing.
And maybe you needed to hear that tonight.
Because there is someone reading this who has almost given up praying.
Not because you stopped believing God exists.
But because you have become ashamed of how often you disappoint yourself.
You remember when following Jesus felt new.
When Scripture stirred your heart.
When worship was not just another song.
When you were eager to obey, quick to confess, and grateful for every opportunity to grow.
Now you feel distracted.
Numb.
Spiritually tired.
And you wonder where that tenderness went.
But spiritual numbness is not always proof of a specific sin. Exhaustion, grief, trauma, depression, and other human struggles can also affect how someone experiences prayer and worship.
Do not mistake every difficult emotion or season of dryness for God's displeasure.
Still, if you know you have been deliberately protecting something Scripture calls you to surrender, do not silence that truth.
Bring it before the Lord.
Because the solution to spiritual compromise is not pretending.
It is repentance.
And repentance is far more than feeling terrible about yourself.

The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated “repentance,” refers to a change of mind or turning, understood in the New Testament as a response to God that involves a changed direction of life.
Biblical repentance does not mean purchasing forgiveness with tears.
It means turning from sin toward God, trusting His mercy and seeking to live in obedience.
The prophet Isaiah declared:
“But they rebelled, and vexed his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he fought against them.” — Isaiah 63:10, KJV
The Hebrew text uses the expression וְעִצְּבוּ אֶת־רוּחַ קָדְשׁוֹ (veʿitstsevu et-ruaḥ qodsho), meaning that they grieved His Holy Spirit.
The Hebrew verb here conveys causing grief or pain.
Centuries before Paul wrote to the Ephesians, Isaiah described Israel's rebellion against the God who had shown His people extraordinary mercy.
Read the larger passage in Isaiah 63:7–14.
It recalls God's lovingkindness, His compassion, His saving presence, and His care for His people.
Then comes the tragedy.
They rebelled.
They grieved His Holy Spirit.
Their rebellion was not merely the violation of a distant law.
It was faithlessness in the face of extraordinary covenant mercy.
Isaiah 63:10 also reminds us that God's holiness must not be trivialized. Persistent rebellion is serious, and divine judgment is real.

We should not flatten the historical covenant setting of Isaiah into a claim that every Christian failure produces the identical judgment Israel experienced. But the passage does reveal a consistent biblical truth.
God's gracious dealings with His people never make rebellion harmless.
And now think about the cross.
Think about Jesus in Gethsemane.
The anguish.
The surrender.
The words:
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42, KJV
Think about the mockery.
The crown of thorns.
The nails.
The public humiliation.
The innocent Son of God bearing the judgment of sin.
Not because He had committed evil.
But because He came to save sinners.
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21, KJV
And then ask yourself something that cannot be answered casually.
If Jesus loved me enough to bear my sin, why am I working so hard to defend the sin He came to deliver me from?
That question is not meant to crush you.
It is meant to awaken you.
Because the Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself up, and perhaps Christ will accept you.”
The Gospel says that Jesus Christ died for sinners, rose again, and calls us to repent and believe.
And those who belong to Him are not left unchanged.
The same grace that forgives also teaches us to deny ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).
The same Savior who welcomes the weary also calls His disciples to follow Him.
The same Spirit who assures believers of their adoption also works to produce holiness in their lives.
This is why grieving the Holy Spirit matters.
Not because God is trying to make Christians live in constant terror.
But because He has called us into a life that reflects His Son.
And this reaches far beyond private behavior.
It reaches into your marriage.
Your parenting.
Your workplace.
Your conversations.
Your online comments.
Your response when someone disagrees with you.
Your willingness to admit that you were wrong.
Your treatment of the person who cannot do anything for you.
Your conduct when there is no audience to impress.
Some of the deepest evidence of spiritual transformation appears in places where nobody applauds.
A husband choosing gentleness instead of intimidation.
A wife choosing truthful, gracious speech instead of contempt.
A parent admitting wrongdoing to a child.
A believer returning money that was taken dishonestly.
A Christian refusing to spread a damaging rumor.
Someone seeking help to break a destructive habit instead of continuing to hide it.
Someone choosing to establish wise boundaries without surrendering to hatred.
These things may not go viral.
But they matter before God.
And perhaps this is where the message becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is possible to become so occupied with looking spiritually alive that we neglect the ordinary obedience through which genuine faith becomes visible.
We can argue theology while refusing to apologize.
Defend biblical truth while treating people with cruelty.
Speak passionately about revival while resisting personal repentance.
Call ourselves defenders of the faith while allowing pride to govern our words.
And Paul is standing before the church, through the words of Scripture, saying:
Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God.
Not just in the sanctuary.
In the kitchen.
In the office.
In the car.
In the comment section.
In the private conversations nobody else will ever hear.
Especially there.
Because Jesus is not interested in merely decorating your public identity with religious language.
He is transforming your life.
And transformation often begins where our excuses end.
Maybe your next act of obedience is not dramatic.
Maybe it is deleting something you know is feeding temptation.
Maybe it is confessing a lie.
Maybe it is asking someone to forgive you without adding an explanation that shifts the blame.
Maybe it is finally seeking pastoral counsel, accountability, or professional help for a struggle you cannot wisely navigate alone.
Maybe it is opening your Bible again.
Not to search for a verse that excuses your choices.
But to hear the voice of the Lord through His Word.
And maybe, for the first time in a long time, your prayer needs to be very simple.

“Lord Jesus, I have been hiding behind excuses. I have called things small that Your Word calls sin. I have cared more about appearing faithful than becoming obedient. Please forgive me. Search my heart. Teach me to walk by Your Spirit. Help me make right what I can, surrender what I have been protecting, and trust the mercy You purchased at the cross. Amen.”
You do not need impressive words to begin confessing honestly.
You need the Savior.
John wrote:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Notice the foundation of that promise.
God is faithful and just.
Forgiveness is not offered because God has decided that sin does not matter.
It is offered in the context of the saving work of Jesus Christ, whom John identifies as our advocate with the Father and the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:1–2).
The cross does not make sin insignificant.
The cross reveals both how serious sin is and how astonishing God's mercy truly is.
And perhaps that is why the story of Peter is so unforgettable.
Peter loved Jesus.
He was bold.
He made promises.
He believed he would remain faithful even if others fell away.
Then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The fear.
The denial.
Three times, Peter denied knowing his Lord.
Luke tells us that after the rooster crowed, the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
And Peter went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:60–62).
Imagine carrying that memory.
The sound of the rooster.
The face of Jesus.
The realization that you had denied the One you promised never to abandon.
But Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter in a deeply personal encounter recorded in John 21:15–19.
Three times, Jesus asked Peter about his love.
And He entrusted Peter with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
Peter's denial was real.
His grief was real.
His restoration was real.
And the grace of Jesus was greater than the failure that had shattered his confidence.
That is not permission to sin.
That is hope for the repentant sinner.
And perhaps you are closer to Peter than you want to admit.
You made promises.
You failed.
You wept.
You wondered whether you could ever be useful to God again.
But do not confuse your worst moment with the final chapter Christ is writing in your life.
If you are willing to turn to Him, the invitation of the Gospel remains.
Come to Christ.
Confess what is true.
Receive His mercy.
Follow Him.
Not because your past never happened.
But because His resurrection means your past does not have to be your master.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because Jesus pretends scandal never occurred.
Not because grace erases accountability.
Not because forgiveness removes every earthly consequence of our decisions.
But because Jesus redeems sinners, restores the repentant, and makes new lives possible through His death and resurrection.
He does not merely improve the appearance of a broken life.
He gives new life.
And that is why we keep returning to Scripture.
Not to entertain ourselves with religious content.
Not to win arguments.
Not to accumulate inspiring quotations while our hearts remain unchanged.
But to know Jesus Christ more deeply, grow in obedience, and help others encounter the truth that saves.
If this message has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to disclose private details publicly.
But perhaps you can take one small, honest step.
Someone else may need to know that repentance is possible, that grace is real, and that the Lord is still at work in the lives of imperfect people.
Please do not let your response end with a comment, though.
Bring whatever God has shown you into prayer, confession, and practical obedience.
Because a public declaration is not a substitute for a surrendered life.

And if one person came to mind while reading this, someone quietly struggling with guilt, someone drifting from the faith, someone who thinks they have failed Jesus too many times, consider tagging them with kindness or sending this article to them privately.
Not to shame them.
Not to expose them.
But to remind them that the door of repentance and mercy is not closed to those who come to Christ.

There may come a night when your conscience is troubled, when old habits are calling, or when you need to remember the difference between conviction that leads you toward Jesus and despair that tempts you to run from Him.
You may never know who is reading in silence.
A struggling believer.
A discouraged pastor.
A parent who feels spiritually exhausted.
A young person trapped in secrecy.
Someone who has not prayed in months.
Someone who needs to hear that holiness matters and that Christ's mercy is greater than the shame they have been carrying.
A simple share can place the Word of God before someone who would never have searched for it.
That is one reason Gospel Warrior exists.
To keep proclaiming Christ.
To keep opening Scripture.
To keep encouraging repentance, healing, biblical discipleship, and genuine spiritual growth.
Not because a payment proves your love for God.
The grace of God cannot be bought.
But Scripture does affirm the value of freely and generously supporting faithful Gospel ministry.
Paul wrote:
“Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel.” — 1 Corinthians 9:14, KJV
He also taught:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Those words matter.
Christian giving is meant to be willing, thoughtful, and joyful.
Not pressured.
Not manipulated.
Not extracted through guilt.
It can help us keep producing Christ-centered teaching, biblical encouragement, devotional material, and discipleship resources intended to reach more people with the Gospel.
It is not simply about sustaining a page.
It is about helping sustain a mission of sharing God's Word.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible.
We want struggling believers to have resources that point them back to Christ.
We want seekers to discover the Gospel.
We want families to have material they can read, discuss, and grow through together.
And we want believers who have been living on spiritual leftovers to rediscover the richness of God's Word.
These products can be practical reminders of faith, useful discipleship tools, and opportunities to begin meaningful conversations about Jesus.
But the greatest value of joining this mission is not a discount or a physical product.
It is the opportunity to participate in making Christ-centered teaching and resources more widely available.
Keep reading.
Keep learning.
Keep seeking the Lord.
Because our mission is not to gather people around a personality.
It is to point people to the Savior.
And before you leave, I want you to return to the question that brought you here.
Can God really be grieved by a Christian?
Scripture says yes.
The Holy Spirit is holy, personal, and fully divine. Sin among God's people is not something to celebrate, excuse, or ignore.
But here is the part I hope stays with you long after you close this article.
The same passage that tells believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit also reminds them that they have been sealed by Him unto the day of redemption.
A warning to take holiness seriously.
And a reason to trust God's faithful work.
Both truths belong together.
Do not use grace to defend the sin that Christ died to forgive.
And do not use your sin as an excuse to run from the Christ who calls you to repent.
If you have wounded someone, seek to make it right.
If you have been dishonest, tell the truth.
If you have been feeding a destructive habit, bring it into the light and seek wise help.
If you have been withholding forgiveness, ask God to begin changing your heart.
If you have been pretending, stop pretending.
Come honestly.
Come humbly.
Come to Jesus.
The Christian life was never meant to be a performance of perfection.
It is a life of faith, repentance, obedience, and dependence upon the grace of God.
And if the Holy Spirit is bringing a particular truth from Scripture to your attention today, do not harden your heart against it.
Respond.
Not tomorrow, when life becomes easier.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Today.
Because the One who calls you to holiness is the same Savior who gave Himself to redeem you.
And there is still grace for the sinner who comes to Him.
The sin you are afraid to bring into the light is not hidden from Jesus—and His mercy is still calling you out of the darkness.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE WAS SLEEPING WITH HIS FATHER’S WIFE… AND THE CHURCH WAS PROUD OF IT.
paragraphs: HE WAS SLEEPING WITH HIS FATHER’S WIFE… AND THE CHURCH WAS PROUD OF IT.

One forbidden relationship. One shocking scandal. One ancient commandment that exposed a church’s dangerous misunderstanding of grace. And one question that still confronts Christianity today: What happens when the people who proclaim Jesus stop taking His holiness seriously?
There are sins people commit in darkness because they are terrified of being discovered.
And then there are sins so openly tolerated that nobody even bothers to hide them anymore.
The second kind may be more dangerous than we realize.
Because when a person sins and trembles, there may still be a conscience crying out for mercy.
But when an entire church learns to celebrate what God has forbidden, something has gone terribly wrong.
Imagine walking into a gathering of believers in the ancient city of Corinth.
People are praying. Someone is speaking about spiritual gifts. Others are discussing the wisdom of God. The name of Jesus Christ is being proclaimed.
Everything sounds spiritual.
Until you discover something happening among them.
A man is having a sexual relationship with his father's wife.
Not merely an accusation whispered by an enemy.
Not a private suspicion circulating through the congregation.
The apostle Paul has received a report about it.
And what makes the situation even more disturbing is not simply the man's behavior.
It is the church's response.
They are arrogant when they should be grieving.
They are boasting when they should be mourning.
They are acting as though their spiritual confidence somehow excuses their moral blindness.
And Paul writes words that must have landed like thunder.
"It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father's wife." — 1 Corinthians 5:1, KJV
Read that again.
His father's wife.
Not his own wife.
His father's.
And suddenly, an ancient commandment from Leviticus becomes impossible to ignore.
"Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's wife: it is thy father's nakedness." — Leviticus 18:8, KJV
Why would God forbid this relationship so explicitly?
Why describe sexual relations with a father's wife as uncovering the father's nakedness?
Why did Paul treat this Corinthian scandal with such severity?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all...
What does a scandal from nearly two thousand years ago reveal about the compromises we sometimes defend in the name of grace?
Because this story is not merely about a man who crossed a sexual boundary.
It is about a church that forgot the difference between welcoming sinners and approving sin.
And if we read it carefully, we may discover that the warning is closer to our own lives than we want to admit.
To understand the commandment, we need to enter the world in which it was first spoken.
Israel had been delivered from Egypt. God was forming a covenant people who were not to imitate every practice of the surrounding nations.
Their worship, justice, relationships, and sexual conduct were all to reflect their belonging to Him.
Leviticus 18 addresses forbidden sexual relationships, including relationships within the family.
The Hebrew of Leviticus 18:8 reads:
עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָבִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה עֶרְוַת אָבִיךָ הִוא
ʿErvat ʾeshet-ʾavikha lo tegalleh; ʿervat ʾavikha hi.
A close translation is:
"You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's wife; it is your father's nakedness."

The expression עֶרְוָה (ʿervah), translated "nakedness," can refer to bodily nakedness or sexual exposure. In the prohibitions of Leviticus 18, the phrase "uncover nakedness" functions as a way of describing prohibited sexual intimacy.
This is not merely a command about accidentally seeing someone unclothed.
The context concerns sexual boundaries.
And the Hebrew phrase אֵשֶׁת־אָבִיךָ (ʾeshet-ʾavikha) means "your father's wife."
That distinction matters.
The text does not restrict the prohibition to a man's biological mother. It includes a woman married to his father, such as a stepmother.
Leviticus 18:7 separately addresses the nakedness of one's father and mother. Verse 8 specifically addresses the father's wife.
The law protects a boundary within the family that must not be crossed.
And the final words are striking.
"It is your father's nakedness."

The language connects the father's wife to the father's marital relationship. Sexual access to her is not presented as an isolated private decision. It violates a relationship that the law treats as belonging within the father's marriage.
It is a violation of family boundaries, marital fidelity, and the order God established for His covenant people.
This does not mean a woman is merely her husband's property, or that her dignity depends on him.
Scripture presents human beings as created in God's image (Genesis 1:27), and marriage as a union involving both husband and wife (Genesis 2:24).
The command concerns the seriousness of sexual relationships within the family, not permission to diminish the woman involved.
And the prohibition is repeated elsewhere.
Deuteronomy 22:30 declares that a man must not take his father's wife.
Leviticus 20:11 treats sexual intercourse with a father's wife as a grave offense under Israel's covenant law.
These were not casual cultural preferences.
They were solemn moral boundaries within the life of ancient Israel.
But here is where the story becomes even more revealing.
Centuries later, the apostle Paul confronts essentially the same kind of relationship in a Christian congregation.
Not in Israel's wilderness.
Not under the administration of ancient Israel's civil penalties.
But inside a church that confesses Jesus Christ as Lord.
The Greek of 1 Corinthians 5:1 contains the phrase:
γυναῖκά τινα τοῦ πατρὸς ἔχειν
gynaika tina tou patros echein
Literally, in context, it means "for someone to have his father's wife."
The verb ἔχειν (echein), "to have," appears here in a context describing an ongoing illicit sexual relationship.
Paul does not tell us every detail.
He does not explicitly identify the woman as the man's biological mother, nor does he establish whether the man's father was alive or whether the woman was still married to him.
The most natural reading is that she was his father's wife or stepmother.
But we should not invent details Scripture does not provide.
We do not know the man's name.
We do not know the woman's name.
We do not know how the relationship began.
We do not know what excuses were offered.
What we do know is that Paul regarded the situation as unmistakably immoral.
And we know that the congregation's response deeply troubled him.
"And ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned..." — 1 Corinthians 5:2, KJV
That word "puffed up" is devastating.
In Greek, Paul uses a form of φυσιόω (physioō), meaning to become inflated or arrogant.
They were spiritually swollen with pride.
Their problem was not merely that someone among them had sinned.
Their problem was that they had failed to respond with appropriate grief.
Think about that.
A church can possess spiritual language and still lack spiritual discernment.
A congregation can celebrate its knowledge and overlook its disobedience.
People can become so impressed with their freedom that they forget the One who freed them.
And we need to be careful here.
Paul does not say the church should hate the man.
He does not command them to humiliate him publicly for entertainment.
He does not encourage gossip, cruelty, or self-righteousness.
He calls them to take sin seriously.
There is an enormous difference.
Because biblical holiness is not permission to become merciless.
And biblical mercy is not permission to call evil good.
Both errors can destroy people.
One crushes sinners beneath condemnation.
The other leaves sinners trapped in what is destroying them.
Jesus came to rescue us from both.
Perhaps you know what it feels like to live between those two extremes.
Maybe you grew up around religious people who knew how to condemn but never learned how to restore.
You made a mistake, and suddenly you were treated as though your entire life could be reduced to your worst decision.
You learned to hide your struggles.
To smile while breaking.
To say "I'm blessed" when you were barely surviving.
Or perhaps your experience was different.
Maybe you encountered people who told you that because God loves you, nothing in your life really needs to change.
They called every correction judgment.
Every boundary oppression.
Every call to repentance an attack on your freedom.
And for a while, that message felt comforting.
Until the thing you were defending began destroying your peace.
Because sometimes what we call freedom is simply bondage that has learned to speak beautifully.
And sometimes the most loving words God gives us are the ones that interrupt the direction we are heading.
Leviticus 18:8 is one of those interruptions.
It tells us that desire does not automatically make a relationship righteous.
That mutual attraction does not erase every moral boundary.
That secrecy does not transform wrongdoing into innocence.
And that something can feel powerful, intimate, and emotionally convincing while still violating God's design.
This is not an invitation to suspect every relationship or to shame people for their histories.
It is a reminder that God's commands are not rewritten by the intensity of our feelings.
And then Paul takes the matter further.
In 1 Corinthians 5:6, he asks:
"Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump?"
In the immediate context, leaven illustrates the spreading influence of tolerated wrongdoing and the congregation's boasting.
Paul is concerned not only for the individual but for the spiritual integrity of the church.
A community teaches through what it celebrates.
It teaches through what it confronts.
And it teaches through what it knowingly refuses to address.
A church does not become loving by pretending that sin has no consequences.
Neither does it become holy by treating wounded people as disposable.
This is why Paul's instructions must be read carefully.
He directs the Corinthian congregation to remove the unrepentant man from its fellowship.
That is a serious act of church discipline.
But it is not a license for violence, harassment, public humiliation, or the abandonment of compassion.
Nor does Paul command Christians to impose the civil penalties of ancient Israel upon people.
He is addressing the responsibility of a Christian congregation toward a professing believer openly persisting in serious wrongdoing.
He even distinguishes between judging those within the church's fellowship and attempting to police everyone outside it (1 Corinthians 5:12–13).
And in 1 Corinthians 5:5, the purpose of the severe disciplinary action includes the hope that the man's spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.
Even in correction, the ultimate concern is not revenge.
It is salvation.
Not the satisfaction of exposing someone.
But the possibility of bringing someone back to truth.
That is a distinction the modern church desperately needs to remember.
Because we live in a world where exposing a person's failure can become entertainment.
A scandal appears online.
Screenshots circulate.
Names are dragged through conversations.
People who have never met the individuals involved become judges, prosecutors, and executioners.
And somewhere in the noise, the actual human soul disappears.
Paul's words do not justify that behavior.
Biblical correction must be governed by truth, justice, humility, and the hope of restoration.
And when abuse, coercion, or exploitation is involved, protecting victims and pursuing appropriate accountability must never be sacrificed to preserve a religious institution's reputation.
Grace does not require silence in the face of harm.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending consequences no longer exist.
Restoration does not mean automatically restoring someone to a position of trust or authority.
The Gospel calls us to truth and mercy together.
But there is another detail in this Corinthian scandal that we cannot overlook.
Paul does not stop at condemning the sin.
He points the congregation to Christ.
"For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us." — 1 Corinthians 5:7, KJV
There it is.
The center of everything.
Jesus Christ.
Paul moves from the corruption of the congregation to the sacrifice of the Savior.
Why?
Because holiness without Christ becomes an impossible attempt at self-salvation.
And grace without Christ's transforming lordship becomes an empty excuse for remaining unchanged.
The Christian life begins and continues through Jesus.
His death is not permission to cherish the very sins from which He came to redeem us.
His resurrection is not merely a promise that we can survive death.
It is also the foundation of a new life in which sin no longer has the final claim upon us.
Paul expresses this truth elsewhere:
"Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid." — Romans 6:1–2, KJV
Grace is not God's declaration that sin never mattered.
The cross reveals how seriously sin matters.
And how immeasurably God loves sinners.
At Calvary, we see both truths.
The holiness of God is not dismissed.
The mercy of God is not withheld.
Jesus gives Himself for the ungodly.
He bears our sins.
He opens the way for forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life.
Not because we were already clean.
But because we could never cleanse ourselves.
And that changes how we read the Corinthian scandal.
The man's sin was serious.
The congregation's arrogance was serious.
But neither reality placed the situation beyond the need for the Gospel.
The answer was not to redefine the sin until it became acceptable.
The answer was to return to the Savior whose grace calls sinners to repentance.
And here is something that should make every believer examine their heart.
It is possible to condemn the Corinthian man while quietly protecting a different sin in ourselves.
We may never enter the relationship described in Leviticus 18:8.
But we may become skilled at defending our own disobedience.
We call bitterness discernment.
We call revenge justice.
We call greed ambition.
We call pride confidence.
We call dishonesty survival.
We call lust harmless entertainment.
We call spiritual indifference a busy season.
And then we wonder why our hearts feel increasingly distant from God.

Not every struggle is evidence of rebellion. Temptation is not the same as consenting to sin. A believer who is fighting, confessing, seeking help, and returning to Christ is not in the same position as someone defiantly celebrating wrongdoing.
But we must be willing to ask ourselves a difficult question.
Am I bringing my struggles into the light, or am I demanding that God bless what I refuse to surrender?
That question can hurt.
Especially when the thing we are holding on to has become part of our identity.
Especially when repentance may cost us a relationship, an opportunity, an image, or a comfortable way of living.
Especially when we know what Scripture says but are afraid of what obedience might require.
And yet Jesus never calls us to surrender something sinful because He delights in our pain.
He calls us away from sin because He is Lord, because He loves us, and because life apart from His truth cannot give us the freedom we were created to enjoy.
There is another scene in the New Testament that helps us understand the heart of Christ.
In John 8, a woman accused of adultery is brought before Jesus.
Her accusers want to use her as a weapon in their confrontation with Him.
But Jesus refuses to turn her into a spectacle.
He exposes the hypocrisy of those who seek to condemn her.
And when the accusers have departed, He tells her:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." — John 8:11, KJV
Those two statements belong together.
"Neither do I condemn thee."
"Go, and sin no more."
Mercy.
And a call to change.
Compassion.
And holiness.
Jesus does not deny the moral seriousness of adultery.
Neither does He allow the woman to be reduced to her accusation.

We should note that the account in John 7:53–8:11 has a well-known textual history: the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John do not contain it, and modern Bibles commonly mark the passage. Its themes should therefore be considered alongside securely attested passages about Jesus' mercy and His call to repentance.
And those themes are unmistakably present throughout the New Testament.
Jesus came to call sinners to repentance (Luke 5:32).
He came to seek and save the lost (Luke 19:10).
And those who belong to Him are called to walk in newness of life (Romans 6:4).
This is why the Gospel is greater than mere moral improvement.
Jesus does not simply hand us a list of rules and leave us alone to repair ourselves.
He offers reconciliation with God through His death and resurrection.
He calls us to repent and believe.
He gives His Spirit to His people.
He teaches us to walk in truth, even when the process is difficult and unfinished.
And sometimes that process begins with one sentence we have been terrified to say.
"Lord, I was wrong."
No excuse.
No performance.
No blaming everyone else.
Just truth.
Perhaps that is where someone reading this article is standing right now.
You love Jesus.
Or at least you want to.
But there is something you have been hiding.
A relationship you know is not right.
A secret habit you keep promising to abandon.
A lie that has grown so large you no longer know how to confess it.
A compromise you once resisted but now barely notice.
And the worst part is not that you have stopped hearing God's Word.
It is that you have become very good at explaining why it does not apply to you.
If that describes you, do not mistake conviction for hopelessness.
The fact that God's Word confronts you does not mean His mercy is unavailable.
Scripture says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Notice what the promise does not say.
It does not say we must pretend.
It does not say we must become perfect before approaching God.
It does not say we can purchase forgiveness through religious performance.
It calls us to confession and directs us to God's faithfulness.
The cleansing is His work.
The mercy is His gift.
And our response is to stop hiding and come into the light.
But what happened to the man in Corinth?
Did he repent?
Was he restored?
Did the church finally learn to mourn what it had previously tolerated?
Paul's later correspondence offers a possible glimpse of hope.
In 2 Corinthians 2:6–8, he speaks about a person who has experienced discipline and urges the church to forgive, comfort, and reaffirm love toward him, lest he be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
Some interpreters have connected this individual with the man in 1 Corinthians 5.
Others believe Paul is discussing a different offender and a separate incident.
The text does not identify the person clearly enough to settle the question.
We should not claim certainty where Scripture does not give it.
But one truth remains unmistakable.
Paul understood that discipline must not become endless punishment when repentance calls for forgiveness and comfort.
A church that refuses to confront serious wrongdoing fails in its responsibility.
A church that refuses to show mercy to the repentant also fails.
The Gospel demands more of us than either extreme.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes most personal.
Because some people reading this are not the person hiding the sin.
You are the person who has already confessed.
You have already walked away.
You have already suffered the consequences.
You have already cried over what you did.
But there are people who still introduce you by your worst chapter.
They remember the scandal.
They remember the failure.
They remember the version of you that existed before repentance.
And no matter how sincerely you seek Christ, they keep returning you to the place where you fell.
Hear this carefully.
Repentance does not erase every earthly consequence.
Trust may need to be rebuilt.
Relationships may not return to what they were.
Some wounds require years of healing, and some responsibilities may never appropriately be restored.
But your past does not possess greater authority than the redeeming work of Jesus Christ.
Paul wrote to the Corinthians about people whose former lives included serious sins.
Then he declared:
"And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God." — 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV
And such were some of you.
Not because their past had never happened.
Not because their wrongdoing was imaginary.
But because the grace of God had changed their standing and called them into a new way of life.
Those words carry astonishing hope.
The Gospel does not say that sin is harmless.
It says that Jesus Christ is a mighty Savior.
It does not say that consequences are meaningless.
It says that consequences do not have the power to cancel God's promises.
It does not say that Christians will never struggle again.
It says that those who belong to Christ are no longer defined solely by the bondage from which He is delivering them.
And this is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because the scandal was good.
Not because the damage was small.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus can redeem a life that sin has devastated.
He can bring truth into a house built on secrecy.
He can teach humility to a heart inflated with pride.
He can lead a compromised believer back to obedience.
He can comfort the wounded.
He can forgive the repentant.
He can form a new future where shame once seemed to have written the final sentence.
And this is why we must never preach grace as though it means God has stopped caring about holiness.
Real grace is more beautiful than that.
Grace welcomes us when we have nothing to boast about.
Grace tells the truth when we would rather hide.
Grace leads us to repentance when our hearts have wandered.
Grace sustains us when obedience feels costly.
And grace reminds us that the blood of Jesus is sufficient for every sinner who comes to Him in faith.
The Corinthian church needed that grace.
The man at the center of the scandal needed that grace.
And so do we.
Before you move on, ask yourself something.
If the Lord were to expose the one area of your life you most desperately want to keep hidden, would you run farther into darkness?
Or would you finally come to Him?

You do not have to publish your private sins for strangers to examine. You do not have to expose sensitive details in a public comment section. Genuine confession should be made wisely, with appropriate accountability, and with the safety of those affected in mind.
But you can stop pretending before God.
You can seek help from a trustworthy pastor, mature believer, or qualified professional where needed.
You can take the next honest step.
And you can remember that the Savior who calls you to repentance is the same Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
You do not need to share the details of your struggle. Those simple words may encourage someone else who thought they were fighting alone.
Someone reading quietly may need to know that repentance is possible.
That healing takes time.
That grace is real.
That Jesus has not stopped calling people home.
And if this article helped you understand why Leviticus 18:8 mattered, and why Paul's response in 1 Corinthians 5 was so serious, please save it.
Not merely because it is a powerful story.
But because there may come a day when you need to remember that God's holiness and God's mercy are not enemies.
One thoughtful share can bring Scripture into the life of someone who would never think to search for a Bible study.
Someone may be wrestling with a forbidden relationship.
Someone may be drowning in guilt.
Someone may have confused God's patience with His approval.
Someone may have been wounded by religious cruelty and needs to encounter the truth of Christ's compassion.
And someone may simply need to hear that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Never use Scripture as a weapon to embarrass someone.
Let it become an invitation to encounter Jesus.
We are here to keep pointing people back to Jesus Christ through biblical truth, repentance, grace, forgiveness, spiritual growth, and discipleship.
Not just through messages that comfort.
But also through passages that challenge us.
Because sometimes the verse we would rather avoid is the very passage God uses to bring us back to truth.
And for those who want to help this ministry continue and reach more people, there is another meaningful way to stand with us.
But we want to be clear about something important.
Biblical giving is meant to be willing, thoughtful, and sincere—not compelled by guilt.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, God loves a cheerful giver.
But if this ministry has helped you understand Scripture more deeply, return to prayer, confront a hidden compromise, or draw nearer to Christ, consider helping us continue that work.
These items are simply expressions of gratitude and tools that may encourage faith-centered living. The real value of discipleship is never measured by merchandise or discounts.
These resources are intended to help believers deepen their understanding of Scripture, strengthen their prayer lives, and continue growing in Jesus Christ.
Your prayers matter.
Your comments matter.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
And when you are able to give financially, that support can also help make the ministry's continued work possible.
Our goal is not to build a community impressed with Gospel Warrior.
It is to build a community increasingly devoted to Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest testimony of any Christian ministry is not how many people admire its content.
It is whether people are being faithfully directed toward the Savior.
And that brings us back to the man in Corinth.
A man who crossed a forbidden boundary.
A congregation that responded with pride instead of grief.
An apostle who refused to pretend that sin was harmless.
And a Savior whose sacrifice stood at the center of Paul's appeal.
The ancient commandment was not meaningless.
The scandal was not trivial.
The call to holiness was not optional.
But neither was the message of redemption absent.
The same Gospel that exposes sin announces forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
The same Lord who commands repentance welcomes those who turn to Him.
And the same grace that rescues us from condemnation teaches us to walk in a different direction.
Maybe that is the message you needed today.
Not that your past was harmless.
Not that every choice you made was right.
Not that the wounds you caused or suffered can be dismissed with a religious phrase.
But that your story does not have to end in the darkness where sin brought you.
Come to Jesus.
Tell Him the truth.
Turn from what He calls sin.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Receive His mercy.
And keep walking with Him, one faithful step at a time.
Because the most astonishing part of the Gospel is not that God found people who had never fallen.
It is that the holy Son of God came to save sinners.
The scandal may explain how you fell, but it does not have the authority to decide who you become in Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PETER BEGGED JESUS TO LEAVE HIM—BUT WHAT JESUS DID NEXT CHANGED EVERYTHING
paragraphs: PETER BEGGED JESUS TO LEAVE HIM—BUT WHAT JESUS DID NEXT CHANGED EVERYTHING

Why did a fisherman fall at the feet of Jesus and cry, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man”? The answer in Luke 5:4–11 reveals something terrifying about encountering God's holiness—and something breathtaking about the grace that refuses to abandon the broken.
There is a moment in a person's life when the greatest fear is no longer that God might not hear their prayers.
It is that God might come close enough to see everything they have been hiding.
Every secret.
Every compromise.
Every promise they made to God and quietly broke.
Every sin they thought they had buried deeply enough that nobody would ever find it.
And then comes the unbearable question.
What if Jesus sees all of it?

Not the version of you that smiles at church. Not the version that posts Bible verses online. Not the version that tells everyone, “I'm doing fine,” while privately fighting battles nobody knows exist.
The real you.
The exhausted you.
The ashamed you.
The person who sometimes wonders whether God has finally had enough.

Now imagine that Jesus steps into your ordinary, complicated life, reveals something extraordinary about Himself, and suddenly you realize you are standing before someone far holier than you ever understood.
What would you say?
Would you ask Him to bless you?
Would you beg Him to fix your circumstances?
Or would you fall to your knees and whisper something you never imagined yourself saying?
“Lord, please leave me. You don't know what kind of person I am.”
That is remarkably close to what happened to Simon Peter.
And what makes this story unforgettable is not merely what Peter said.
It is what Jesus refused to do.
Luke takes us to the shore of the Lake of Gennesaret, another name for the Sea of Galilee.
The morning should have been ordinary.
Fishermen were washing their nets after a long, unsuccessful night. The boats were there. The equipment was there. The experience was there.
But the fish were not.
And for men whose livelihood depended on the catch, an empty net meant more than disappointment.
It meant another day of uncertainty.
Another reminder that hard work does not always produce the results you desperately need.
Perhaps you understand that kind of exhaustion.
You have prayed.
You have worked.
You have sacrificed.
You have tried to do what you believed was right.
And still, your nets seem empty.
Your marriage remains strained.
Your finances remain uncertain.
Your family remains divided.
Your prayers seem unanswered.
Your heart is tired of hoping because hoping has started to hurt.
Peter was not standing on that shoreline celebrating a breakthrough.
He was washing the evidence of another fruitless night.
Then Jesus came.
And notice something beautiful.
Jesus did not wait for Peter to have a successful day before stepping into his boat.
He entered the setting of Peter's disappointment.
Luke 5:3 tells us that Jesus got into Simon's boat and asked him to move a little way from shore. From there, Jesus taught the crowds.
Think about that.
The very boat associated with Peter's failure became the place from which the words of Christ were proclaimed.
The circumstances had not yet changed.
The nets were still empty.
But Jesus was already present.
Sometimes we become so consumed with asking God to change our situation that we overlook the greater gift of His presence in the middle of it.
And then Jesus said something that must have sounded unreasonable to an exhausted professional fisherman.
In Luke 5:4, Jesus instructed Simon to move into deeper water and lower the nets for a catch.
The Greek text records His command:
Ἐπανάγαγε εἰς τὸ βάθος
Epanagage eis to bathos.
“Put out into the deep.”
Then came the instruction to lower the nets.
To someone reading the passage casually, this may sound like a simple fishing suggestion.
But Peter knew the lake.
He knew his equipment.
He knew what had happened throughout the night.
He had already tried.
And he had caught nothing.
His answer in Luke 5:5 is one of the most painfully relatable statements in Scripture:
“Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net.” (KJV)
Listen to the tension in those words.
We have worked all night.
That is experience speaking.
We have caught nothing.
That is disappointment speaking.
Nevertheless, at Your word...
That is faith beginning to speak.
The Greek expression is especially meaningful:
ἐπὶ δὲ τῷ ῥήματί σου
Epi de tō rhēmati sou.
“But at Your word.”
Peter was not claiming that he understood the situation.
He was not pretending the previous night had been successful.
He was not denying his exhaustion.
He was placing the authority of Jesus' word above the discouragement of his circumstances.
And that distinction matters.
Biblical faith is not pretending the net is full when it is empty.
It is trusting the Lord enough to obey Him even when the net is empty.
Perhaps that is where this story finds you today.
You have reasons to be discouraged.
You have memories that make obedience frightening.
You have already tried to forgive someone.
You have already tried to rebuild your life.
You have already tried to return to prayer after months of spiritual silence.
And somewhere deep inside, you are wondering whether another act of obedience will only lead to another disappointment.
But Peter's words offer a different response.
“Nevertheless, at Your word.”
Not because everything makes sense.
Not because the outcome is guaranteed to look the way you want.
But because the One speaking is worthy of trust.
Then the impossible happened.

Luke 5:6–7 describes such an enormous catch of fish that the nets began to break. Peter and his companions signaled to their partners in another boat for help. Both boats became so full that they began to sink.
Imagine the scene.
The splashing water.
The shouting fishermen.
The frantic movement between boats.
The nets stretched under the weight of an astonishing catch.
Men who had worked all night without success were suddenly struggling to contain what Jesus had provided.
But here is where the story takes a turn many people miss.
The miracle was not the moment Peter became most interested in the fish. It was the moment he became overwhelmed by Jesus.
Think about that.
Peter had just witnessed what could have been an extraordinary financial blessing for a working fisherman.
The boats were full.
The business opportunity was enormous.
The night's disappointment had been overturned.
If the story were only about material prosperity, this would be the moment to celebrate the catch.
But Peter did something completely unexpected.
He fell at Jesus' knees.
And he said:
“Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord.” (Luke 5:8, KJV)
Why?
Why would a man who had just received an astonishing blessing ask the One who gave it to leave?
Why did abundance produce confession?
Why did a miracle lead to trembling?
Because Peter was beginning to see that the greatest reality in the boat was not the fish.
It was the identity of the Man standing before him.
Luke tells us that Peter and his companions were astonished at the catch. But Peter's own words reveal something deeper than amazement.
He became painfully conscious of his sinfulness in the presence of extraordinary divine power and authority.
The Greek text of Luke 5:8 reads:
Ἔξελθε ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ, ὅτι ἀνὴρ ἁμαρτωλός εἰμι, κύριε.
Exelthe ap' emou, hoti anēr hamartōlos eimi, kyrie.
A faithful translation is:
“Depart from me, because I am a sinful man, Lord.”
Notice the word:
ἁμαρτωλός — hamartōlos.
It means “sinful” or “a sinner.”
Peter did not say, “I made a small mistake.”
He did not say, “I have a few areas to improve.”
He identified himself as a sinful man.
And he did not respond by comparing himself to the other fishermen.
He did not point toward someone whose life was more scandalous than his own.
He did not offer Jesus a list of his accomplishments.
He simply confessed.
I am sinful.
That is what happens when a human being begins to recognize the holiness of God.
The excuses that once sounded convincing suddenly lose their power.
The comparisons stop working.
The carefully constructed image begins to collapse.
And the heart is confronted with the truth.
God is holy.
I am not.
This is not the first time Scripture shows such a response.
When the prophet Isaiah saw a vision of the Lord's glory, he cried:
“Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips.” (Isaiah 6:5, KJV)
When Job encountered God's overwhelming majesty, he was brought to humility and repentance (Job 42:5–6).
When John saw the glorified Christ in Revelation 1:17, he fell at His feet as though dead.
There is a recurring biblical pattern.
When sinful humanity encounters the overwhelming majesty of God, casual confidence gives way to reverence.
But we must be careful here.
Luke does not say Peter fully understood everything about Jesus' divine identity at that moment. His understanding would continue to develop throughout the Gospel story.
What Luke does show is that Peter recognized an extraordinary authority in Jesus and became deeply aware of his own unworthiness.
And that is more than enough to explain why he fell.
Peter had expected fish.
He encountered a revelation of who Jesus was.
And suddenly the man who knew how to handle nets did not know how to handle his own heart.
Maybe you know that feeling.
There are moments when a sermon stops sounding like a message for somebody else.
A Scripture you have read a hundred times suddenly exposes something you have spent years avoiding.
A quiet prayer brings to the surface a bitterness you thought you had overcome.
A moment of conviction reveals that you have become comfortable with something God is calling you to surrender.
And your first instinct is not always to run toward Him.
Sometimes it is to hide.
That instinct is ancient.
After Adam and Eve sinned, they hid from the presence of the Lord among the trees of the garden (Genesis 3:8).
Sin does not merely produce guilt.
It can also produce a desperate desire for distance.
We fear being known because we fear being rejected.
We imagine that if God truly sees what we have done, His response must be to turn away.
But here is the tragedy.
The very One we fear approaching is the only One who can save us.
Peter said, “Depart from me.”
Jesus did not depart.
Read that again.
Peter asked Jesus to leave, but Jesus answered his fear instead.
Luke 5:10 records Jesus' response:
“Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men.” (KJV)
In Greek, Jesus begins with two beautiful words:
Μὴ φοβοῦ
Mē phobou.
“Do not be afraid.”
Not, “You are exaggerating your sin.”
Not, “Your past doesn't matter.”
Not, “Holiness is unimportant.”
Jesus did not deny the seriousness of sin.
But neither did He treat Peter's confession as a reason to abandon him.
He addressed his fear.
And then He called him into a new future.
There is a profound Gospel truth here.
Jesus does not save us by pretending we are righteous.
He saves sinners through His grace.
He does not need us to hide the truth about ourselves before we approach Him.
He already knows.
And He is able to forgive, cleanse, and transform those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
This is why the Gospel is so much greater than a message of self-improvement.
Self-improvement says, “Make yourself worthy, then come.”
The Gospel says that Christ came to save the unworthy.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired every broken relationship.
Not after we had finally managed to appear holy enough.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not mean repentance is optional.
It means repentance is possible because the Savior has come near.
And the same Jesus who stood before Peter would eventually go to the cross, bearing the judgment our sins deserve, and rise again in victory over death.
His grace is not cheap permission to continue in rebellion.
It is costly mercy purchased through His sacrifice.
It forgives.
It cleanses.
It calls us out of darkness.
It teaches us to follow Him.
And it gives us a future that our past could never have earned.
But perhaps the most moving part of Peter's story is what happened after this encounter.
Because Peter's confession beside the fishing boats was not the last time he would discover how weak he really was.
Years of following Jesus lay ahead.
He would witness miracles.
He would hear teachings that changed history.
He would confess Jesus as the Christ.
He would boldly declare his loyalty.
And then, on one terrible night, Peter would deny knowing Jesus three times.
Three times.
The same man who once fell before Jesus because he knew he was sinful would later face the horrifying reality of his own failure.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that after Peter's denial, the Lord turned and looked at him.
Peter remembered Jesus' warning.
Then he went outside and wept bitterly.
Try to imagine those tears.
The shame.
The regret.
The unbearable memory of promises made with confidence and broken under pressure.
Have you ever been there?
Not necessarily denying Christ with your lips before a hostile crowd.
But denying Him through choices you knew were wrong.
Staying silent when you should have stood for truth.
Returning to a sin you had promised to abandon.
Choosing approval over obedience.
Allowing fear to become stronger than conviction.
And afterward, when the noise faded, realizing what you had done.
Perhaps you have asked yourself:
How could God still want someone like me?
Peter's story does not end with his tears.
After Jesus' resurrection, John 21 records another extraordinary encounter beside the Sea of Galilee.
There were fishermen.
There was a boat.
There was another remarkable catch.
And there was Jesus.
The parallels are striking.
The disciple who once cried, “Depart from me,” was about to encounter the risen Savior after the greatest failure of his life.
Jesus asked Peter about his love.
Three times, Jesus questioned him.
Three times, Peter answered.
And Jesus entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
We should not flatten that encounter into a sentimental scene.
Peter's denial was serious.
His restoration was not a declaration that his failure had been harmless.
Jesus called him back to love, service, and discipleship.
And in John 21:19, the command came again:
Consider the beauty of that.
At the beginning, Peter felt too sinful to remain near Jesus.
Later, Peter proved just how weak he could be.
Yet the risen Christ still called him to follow.
The Savior who knew Peter's sin also knew what His grace could make of Peter's life.
That is the difference between worldly shame and Gospel repentance.
Worldly shame can leave a person trapped in the belief that failure is their final identity.
But godly sorrow leads toward repentance and salvation (2 Corinthians 7:10).
The Gospel does not tell you that your sin is imaginary.
It tells you that Jesus Christ is a real Savior.
Your guilt matters.
Your choices matter.
The people you have hurt matter.
Repentance matters.
But your worst moment does not have to become the final chapter of your life.
Not when Jesus Christ is able to forgive and restore.
This is the heart of what we mean when we say:
It does not mean scandal is glamorous.
It does not mean sin should be celebrated.
It does not mean consequences disappear or broken trust is automatically repaired.
It means that even a life marked by shame can become a testimony to the mercy of Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not erase the seriousness of the past.
It announces that the past does not have ultimate authority over those redeemed by Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this right now desperately needs that truth.
You have been hiding behind religious activity.
You know the worship songs.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know how to sound spiritually mature.
But there is a private battle you have never surrendered.
Maybe it is lust.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe dishonesty.
Maybe a secret addiction.
Maybe a hardened heart that no longer feels sorrow over sin.
Or perhaps your struggle is different.
You have repented, but you continue living as though Christ's forgiveness cannot possibly reach you.
You keep replaying what you did.
You keep punishing yourself.
You keep allowing your past to speak louder than God's promises.
Listen carefully.
You cannot heal yourself by pretending sin is harmless.
But neither can you purchase forgiveness by refusing to receive the grace Christ offers.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise is not an invitation to manipulate grace.
It is an invitation to walk in the light.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn from what needs abandoning.
Seek reconciliation where you have caused harm.
Make restitution where appropriate and possible.
Ask for help when you cannot fight alone.
And trust the sufficiency of Jesus Christ rather than the strength of your own religious performance.
Peter's encounter also reveals something about calling.
Jesus did not merely tell him, “Do not be afraid.”
He said:
“From henceforth thou shalt catch men.”
The Greek phrase is:
ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν ἀνθρώπους ἔσῃ ζωγρῶν
Apo tou nyn anthrōpous esē zōgrōn.
A close rendering is:
“From now on you will be catching people alive.”
The verb ζωγρέω (zōgreō) carries the sense of capturing alive.
In this context, Jesus was calling Peter away from his former occupation into a mission of gathering people through the proclamation of the kingdom and the Gospel.
This was not a promise that Peter would become a manipulator of human souls.
It was a call to participate in Christ's life-giving mission.
The fisherman who had spent his days drawing fish out of the water would now become a disciple through whom people would hear the message of salvation.
And look at Luke 5:11.
“When they had brought their ships to land, they forsook all, and followed him.” (KJV)
They left everything.
Not because fish were evil.
Not because honest work was meaningless.
But because the call of Jesus was greater than the life they had previously known.
The miracle had filled their boats.
The Savior had captured their hearts.
And following Him became more important than keeping the catch.
That is a searching question for us.
Do we want Jesus Himself, or do we only want what Jesus can provide?
Would we still follow Him if obedience cost us something?
Would we still trust Him if the nets remained empty?
Would we still worship Him if the breakthrough took longer than we hoped?
Would we surrender the sin we secretly love if He called us to leave it behind?
Because true discipleship is not simply receiving blessings.
It is belonging to Christ.
And that is where this story becomes personal.
Peter did not say, “Depart from me,” because Jesus had mistreated him.
He said it because the presence of Jesus exposed how unworthy he felt.
Yet Jesus did not respond by making distance the answer.
He invited Peter into discipleship.
Perhaps you have been doing the opposite.
You have been keeping your distance from prayer because you feel unworthy.
Avoiding Scripture because it exposes your compromises.
Avoiding fellowship because you fear being known.
Avoiding repentance because you are afraid of what surrender will cost.
And all the while, the Gospel is calling you to stop hiding and come to Christ.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV)
What an astonishing promise.
The One who has every right to judge sinners offers mercy to those who come to Him.
Not because sin is small.
But because His saving work is sufficient.
If you have never truly entrusted your life to Jesus Christ, do not confuse admiration for Him with surrender to Him.
You can admire His miracles and still resist His lordship.
You can know Bible stories and still need reconciliation with God.
You can participate in religious activities and still refuse repentance.
The call is not merely to be impressed by Jesus.
It is to repent and believe the Gospel.
And if you belong to Christ but have wandered far from Him, do not let shame become another excuse for remaining distant.
Return.
Not with theatrical promises about how strong you will be tomorrow.
Come with honesty about how desperately you need His grace today.
You do not need to manufacture a spectacular testimony.
You need a real Savior.
And Jesus Christ is enough.

If these words have exposed something you have been carrying in silence, you do not have to describe your private sins publicly. But perhaps this is the moment to stop pretending that everything is fine.
Your words may encourage someone who believes they are beyond forgiveness.
There may be another Peter reading quietly, convinced that failure has disqualified them forever.
Let them hear that Jesus still saves sinners.
Let them hear that repentance is not the end of hope.
Let them hear that grace is greater than the shame they have been carrying.
And if someone came to mind while you were reading this, do not ignore that thought.
Not merely to increase the number of people who see it, but because the message of Christ deserves to be heard beyond the walls of our churches and the boundaries of our friendships.
Sometimes one shared Scripture becomes the beginning of a conversation someone has been afraid to start.
Sometimes one honest testimony helps another believer find the courage to ask for prayer.
Sometimes the reminder that Jesus did not abandon Peter becomes exactly what a discouraged soul needs to hear.
There may come a night when your own failures seem louder than God's promises.
When the enemy's accusations feel relentless.
When you struggle to remember that the Christian life is sustained by grace, not by pretending to be perfect.
Return to Luke 5.
Read the passage again.
Remember the fisherman who fell at Jesus' knees.
Remember the words, “Depart from me.”
And remember the Savior who answered, “Do not be afraid.”
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.

Not to build a personality around religious content, but to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ, the authority of Scripture, genuine repentance, the hope of forgiveness, and a life of faithful discipleship.

If these messages have helped you return to Scripture, confront sin, find encouragement, or grow in your walk with Christ, consider following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, fellow believers, and even those who are still exploring the Christian faith to follow along.
There is so much noise competing for our attention.
So many voices telling us to pursue success, image, comfort, and approval.
But our souls need something deeper.
We need truth.
We need sound biblical teaching.
We need reminders that holiness matters, grace is real, and Jesus Christ is worthy of our lives.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, including to people who cannot afford paid materials.
We believe supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one meaningful way to honor God with the resources He has entrusted to us.
Scripture teaches the importance of generosity and supporting those who labor in the ministry of the Word (Galatians 6:6; 1 Corinthians 9:14).
But we also want to be clear about something essential.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
Your worth before God is not measured by a monthly payment.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ.
Our hope is simply that those who have been blessed through this ministry and are able to help will prayerfully consider partnering with us to reach more people.
These items can serve as everyday reminders of Scripture, opportunities for meaningful conversations, and thoughtful gifts for people you love.
It is the opportunity to help make Christ-centered teaching, biblical encouragement, and discipleship resources available to more people.
A sincere comment can encourage someone who feels alone.
A prayer can express our dependence on the Lord who alone changes hearts.
And the Gospel itself remains the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes (Romans 1:16).
Now, before you leave, I want you to return to that boat one last time.
Picture Peter on his knees.
The boats are heavy with fish.
The nets have been stretched.
The other fishermen are astonished.
But Peter is not celebrating.
His eyes are fixed on Jesus.
And from somewhere deep inside his trembling heart come the words:
“Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord.”
Perhaps that is the sentence you have been carrying for years.
You may never have spoken it aloud.
But you have lived as though it were true.
You have believed that your failures make you too damaged for God's mercy.
That your past makes you unfit for His presence.
That the things you have done have placed you beyond His willingness to forgive.
But listen to the answer Jesus gave Peter.
“Fear not.”
Two words.
No denial of Peter's sin.
No compromise of holiness.
No suggestion that following Jesus would be easy.
Just the voice of the Lord, calling a frightened sinner into a life he could never have imagined.
And years later, after Peter's denial, after his bitter tears, after the resurrection, that same Savior would still say:
That is the wonder of grace.
Not that Peter was secretly good enough all along.
Not that his failures were insignificant.
But that Jesus Christ was merciful enough to call him, powerful enough to restore him, and worthy enough to be followed to the end.
So come to Christ.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come trusting His finished work on the cross and His victory over the grave.
Do not turn your shame into a hiding place.
Do not turn His mercy into permission to remain in sin.
Let His grace bring you into the light.
Because the greatest miracle in Luke 5 was not simply that empty nets became full.
It was that a sinful fisherman encountered the Lord Jesus, heard His call, and began a life of following Him.
And the deepest hope of that story is not that Jesus will fill every earthly net you cast.
It is that the Savior who called Peter is still worthy of your trust, your repentance, your love, and your life.
Peter begged Jesus to leave because he saw his sin. But Jesus called Peter to follow because the Savior already knew the grace that would carry him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE STOOD BESIDE DAVID WHEN DEATH WAS NEAR—SO WHY DID SOLOMON STRIP HIM OF THE PRIESTHOOD?
paragraphs: HE STOOD BESIDE DAVID WHEN DEATH WAS NEAR—SO WHY DID SOLOMON STRIP HIM OF THE PRIESTHOOD?
The heartbreaking downfall of Abiathar reveals a terrifying truth about misplaced loyalty, the consequences of compromise, and the mercy of God that can still reach us after everything falls apart.
Imagine surviving the massacre of your entire family.
Imagine watching the people you love die because a powerful king believes they have helped his enemy.

You escape with your life. You carry the weight of everything you have lost. And somehow, in the middle of that unimaginable grief, you find yourself serving alongside a man who will one day become Israel's greatest king.
You stand with him when he has no throne.
You suffer with him when he has no palace.
You remain with him when being his friend could cost you your life.
Years pass. Battles are fought. Prayers are offered. A kingdom is established.
And then, near the end of your life, the son of that very king looks you in the eyes and tells you that you are no longer worthy to serve as priest.
Not because you abandoned the God of Israel.
Not because you had spent your life worshiping idols.
But because, at a moment when loyalty mattered more than ever, you supported the wrong man.
This is the story of Abiathar.
And before you dismiss it as an ancient political conflict involving kings and priests, understand something.
You can have a remarkable history of faithfulness and still make a devastating decision in the present.
That is what makes this account so unsettling.
Because somewhere between Abiathar's suffering, his years of service, his compromise, and his removal from the priesthood, we may recognize something painfully familiar about ourselves.
The question is not simply why Solomon removed Abiathar.
The deeper question is what happens when someone who has walked with God for years begins trusting something other than God's revealed will.
And the answer takes us from a blood-soaked priestly city to a royal judgment, from an ancient prophecy to the cross of Jesus Christ.
Stay with this story.
Because the most surprising thing about Abiathar's downfall may not be the judgment he received.
It may be the mercy he was shown.
Abiathar's story began with a tragedy almost too terrible to imagine.
In 1 Samuel 21–22, David was fleeing from King Saul. Hungry and desperate, he came to Nob, where Ahimelech the priest gave him bread and the sword of Goliath.
Ahimelech did not realize the full danger surrounding David's visit.
But Doeg the Edomite reported what had happened to Saul.
Saul interpreted the assistance as treason.
What followed was horrifying.
Eighty-five priests wearing the linen ephod were killed, and the city of Nob was struck with the sword, including its inhabitants and livestock (1 Samuel 22:18–19).
One man escaped.
Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech.
He fled to David and told him what had happened.
And David said something that must have pierced both their hearts:
"I have occasioned the death of all the persons of thy father's house." — 1 Samuel 22:22, KJV
Then David told Abiathar to remain with him, promising that he would be safe under David's protection (1 Samuel 22:23).
Think about that moment.
A grieving priest who had lost his family.
A fugitive who knew his actions had contributed to the danger.
Two men bound together by suffering, danger, and the uncertain future of a kingdom not yet established.
Abiathar did not join David when David was sitting comfortably on a throne.
He joined him when association with David could be a death sentence.
That matters.
Because Abiathar was not some shallow opportunist who had never sacrificed anything.
He had endured real suffering.
He had remained with David through extraordinary danger.
He had served in a sacred office during one of Israel's most turbulent generations.
And this is precisely why his later decision is so tragic.
Sometimes the people who fall are not people who never stood for anything. Sometimes they are people who stood faithfully for years but stopped watching where their hearts were going.
Perhaps you know something about that.
There was a season when your prayers were desperate and sincere.
You opened your Bible because you genuinely needed to hear from God.
You walked away from relationships, habits, or opportunities because you believed obedience mattered more than comfort.
You remember what God brought you through.
But somewhere along the way, something changed.
Maybe your confidence quietly shifted from God's Word to your own experience.
Maybe you began believing that because you had suffered for the Lord in the past, your present decisions did not require the same humility.
Maybe you became so accustomed to being near holy things that you stopped examining the condition of your heart.
Abiathar's story confronts that danger.
Not because every mistake is identical to his.
But because yesterday's faithfulness cannot replace today's obedience.
And then came the succession crisis.
David was old.
His reign was nearing its end.
And the question of who would sit on Israel's throne had become urgent.
Adonijah, another son of David, declared himself king.
First Kings 1:5 records his ambition:
"I will be king." — 1 Kings 1:5, KJV
Those four words expose something deeply human.
Not, "What has God commanded?"
Not, "Whom has the Lord appointed?"
But, "I will."
Adonijah gathered powerful supporters, including Joab, David's military commander.
And among those who supported him was Abiathar the priest.
First Kings 1:7 says that Adonijah consulted with Joab and Abiathar, and they followed and helped him.
Yet the same chapter identifies Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and others who did not support Adonijah.
This was no harmless disagreement about administrative arrangements.
The throne was at stake.
David had sworn that Solomon would succeed him (1 Kings 1:13, 17, 30). First Chronicles 22:9–10 also presents Solomon as the son designated by God to succeed David and build the temple.
Adonijah's attempt to seize royal authority therefore stood against the succession David had committed himself to establish.
Abiathar had once risked his life by standing beside God's chosen king.
Now he was supporting a rival to the son appointed to succeed that king.
Scripture does not explicitly tell us what motivated Abiathar.
Perhaps he thought Adonijah had the stronger claim because of his age.
Perhaps longstanding relationships influenced him.
Perhaps he misjudged the political situation.
We should not pretend to know what the Bible does not reveal.
But we do know his decision.
He supported Adonijah.
And that decision carried consequences.
Here is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
You do not have to hate God to make a decision that conflicts with His will.
You do not have to publicly renounce your faith to become spiritually careless.
Sometimes compromise begins with a calculation that seems reasonable.
A relationship you do not want to lose.
An opportunity you cannot imagine passing up.
A position you have spent years trying to secure.
A fear that obedience will cost too much.
And suddenly the question becomes less about what God has said and more about what you stand to gain or lose.
Not every difficult choice is a rebellion against God. Scripture calls us to discern carefully rather than invent divine commands where none have been given.
But when God's Word is clear, personal advantage is never a sufficient reason to disobey.
The most dangerous compromise is often the one we have learned to explain to ourselves.
Then David acted.
Bathsheba and Nathan brought the succession crisis before him, and David ordered Solomon to be anointed king.
Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet participated in Solomon's public anointing (1 Kings 1:32–40).
The people rejoiced.
The city erupted with celebration.
Adonijah's attempt collapsed.
His supporters scattered.
And Abiathar, who had survived Saul's slaughter and served through David's reign, now faced the consequences of having supported a rival claimant.
When David died and Solomon began securing his kingdom, the reckoning came.
First Kings 2:26 records Solomon's words to Abiathar:

"Get thee to Anathoth, unto thine own fields; for thou art worthy of death: but I will not at this time put thee to death, because thou barest the ark of the Lord GOD before David my father, and because thou hast been afflicted in all wherein my father was afflicted." — 1 Kings 2:26, KJV
Read that carefully.
Solomon did not pretend Abiathar's betrayal was insignificant.
He regarded Abiathar as deserving death for his involvement in the rebellion.
But he did not execute him.
Why?
Because Solomon remembered.
He remembered that Abiathar had carried the ark before David.
He remembered that Abiathar had shared David's afflictions.
He remembered the years of costly service.
The king who had the power to execute him instead sent him away to his fields in Anathoth.
That is not the same as forgiveness through the Gospel. The passage describes Solomon's royal decision, not Abiathar's personal repentance or eternal standing before God.
But it does reveal a remarkable restraint.
Abiathar's wrongdoing was not ignored.
Yet his past suffering and service were not forgotten.
He lost his priestly position.
But his life was spared.
