I am a servant who needs grace, correction, discernment, and the truth of God's Word just as much as anyone reading my articles.
The Holy Spirit never needs me to exaggerate His work to make Him appear powerful.
His Word is already powerful.
And that brings me to a passage that has shaped how I understand this responsibility.
In John 16:13, Jesus describes the Holy Spirit as:
τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας
to pneuma tēs alētheias
"The Spirit of truth."
That Greek expression matters.
Jesus did not describe the Holy Spirit as the Spirit of emotional excitement, religious popularity, or impressive storytelling.
He called Him the Spirit of truth.

In the same passage, Jesus explains that the Spirit will guide His disciples into the truth. And in John 16:14, He says something that I believe every Christian writer, preacher, teacher, and content creator needs to remember.
"He shall glorify me." — John 16:14, KJV
Read that again.
He shall glorify Me.
Jesus.
Not the writer.
Not the ministry.
Not the person holding the microphone.
Not the number of followers.
Not the name printed at the bottom of an article.
Jesus Christ.
If my writing makes people admire my words but never leads them to consider the Savior, I have missed the very purpose of Gospel Warrior.
If people remember my name but forget the cross, something has gone terribly wrong.
If my articles stir emotions but never point toward repentance, forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and transformation through Christ, then beautiful writing is not enough.
Because the Holy Spirit does not exist to build my reputation.
He glorifies Jesus.
And that is why, whatever subject I write about, I want the message to find its way back to Christ.
A broken marriage?
Jesus must remain at the center.
A hidden addiction?
Jesus must remain at the center.
A painful betrayal?
Jesus must remain at the center.
A warning against hypocrisy?
Jesus must remain at the center.
A testimony of restoration?
Jesus must remain at the center.

Even when the subject is uncomfortable, even when the truth exposes something we would rather hide, even when the article makes someone angry before it makes them think, my desire is not to win an argument.
It is to remain faithful to the Gospel.
Because without Jesus, Gospel Warrior would become just another page filled with inspirational words.
And the world already has enough inspiration that cannot save a soul.
There is a difference between feeling better for five minutes and being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
One can happen through an encouraging sentence.
The other happens only through the Savior who died for our sins and rose again.
And I never want to confuse the two.
Sometimes I think about the person who almost scrolls past one of my articles.
Maybe they see the length and think, "That's too much to read."
I understand.
Life is busy.
People are tired.
Our minds are constantly pulled in a hundred directions.
But somewhere inside that long message may be a Scripture they have never understood, a truth they have avoided, or a reminder of God's mercy they desperately need.
I cannot promise that every article will be for every person.
I cannot promise that the Holy Spirit personally dictated every word.
But I can pray that God will use whatever is true, faithful, and helpful in the writing to accomplish good beyond anything I could plan.
And I can trust Him with what happens after I publish.
That trust is rooted in Scripture.
Isaiah 55:11 says:
"So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it." — KJV
The Hebrew word translated "void" is רֵיקָם (rēqām), carrying the sense of emptiness or without accomplishing its intended purpose.
Notice whose word God is speaking about.
His Word.
Not every thought that enters my mind.
Not every emotional sentence I write.
Not every article simply because I attach a Bible verse to it.
God's Word accomplishes His purposes.
That is precisely why I want Scripture to shape my writing rather than merely decorate it.
I want to understand what a passage meant in its original context before applying it to someone's present struggle.
I want to handle Hebrew and Greek carefully, not use ancient words to create an impression of spiritual authority.
I want to distinguish what the Bible actually promises from what I personally hope will happen.
Because the person reading may be holding on to every word.
And when someone is spiritually wounded, careless words can do real harm.
I think about that often.
Imagine a woman sitting alone after midnight.
She has spent years trying to keep her family together.
She smiles at church.
She tells everyone she is blessed.
But behind closed doors, she feels invisible.
She opens Facebook, not because she is looking for a sermon, but because she wants a few minutes of distraction.
Then she sees an article about the Samaritan woman at the well.
She reads how Jesus knew the complicated details of that woman's life and still chose to speak with her.
For the first time in months, she remembers that being fully known by Christ does not mean being beyond His reach.
Or imagine a man who has spent years pretending that his secret sin is under control.
He has made promises.
Broken them.
Made them again.
He has become skilled at hiding his struggle from everyone except himself.
Then he reads about Peter.
The disciple who insisted he would never deny Jesus.
The disciple who failed so publicly.
The disciple who wept bitterly.
And later, the disciple whom the risen Christ restored and commissioned.
Perhaps that man finally realizes that repentance is not the same as hopelessness.
That his sin must not be excused.
But neither must he conclude that his failure is greater than the mercy of Christ.
These are examples, not stories I claim to have personally witnessed.
But they represent the kinds of human struggles that lead me to pray over every message.
Because behind every profile picture is a real person.
Behind every reaction is a life we cannot fully see.
Behind some of the loudest smiles are prayers nobody has heard.
And behind some of the quietest accounts are people desperately trying to survive another day.
That is why I refuse to think of Gospel Warrior as merely a content page.
To me, it is a responsibility.
A place where the Scriptures must be handled with reverence.
A place where broken people should hear both the seriousness of sin and the greatness of God's grace.
A place where the comfortable can be challenged without being treated with contempt.
A place where the wounded can find compassion without being given false promises.
A place where seekers can ask difficult questions without being mocked.
And a place where every road leads back to the Person at the center of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ.
Paul expressed this priority in 1 Corinthians 2:2:
"For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified." — KJV
Paul was not saying that Christians should never discuss other subjects.
He was declaring the central importance of the crucified Christ in his ministry.
The Greek phrase Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν καὶ τοῦτον ἐσταυρωμένον (Iēsoun Christon kai touton estaurōmenon) emphasizes Jesus Christ as the One crucified.
That is the center.
Not motivational slogans.
Not religious performance.
Not a personality cult built around a Christian creator.
The crucified and risen Savior.
And this is where my heart becomes especially burdened.
Because I know how easy it is for Christian content to become another form of entertainment.
We read something powerful.
We feel convicted.
We react with a heart emoji.
We say, "Amen."
Then we continue living exactly as before.
But the Gospel calls us to more than momentary emotion.
It calls us to repentance and faith.
To surrender.
To obedience.
To loving God and our neighbor.
To forgiving because we have been forgiven.
To turning away from sin, not merely feeling guilty about it.
To becoming disciples who follow Jesus even when nobody is watching.
James 1:22 says:
"But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves." — KJV
That verse confronts me as a writer too.
Because I can write about forgiveness and still need to forgive someone.
I can write about humility and still need to repent of pride.
I can write about trusting God and still struggle with fear.
I can write about surrender and discover another area of my life I have been trying to control.
I am not standing above the people who read Gospel Warrior.
I am standing with them beneath the authority of the same Word.
And I need Jesus every single day.
That is something I never want you to forget.
The Gospel Warrior is not the hero of these stories.
Jesus is.
The Gospel Warrior is not the one who can forgive your sins.
Jesus is.
The Gospel Warrior cannot heal every wound, restore every relationship, or guarantee that your suffering will end tomorrow.
But I can keep pointing you to the One who conquered sin and death, who receives repentant sinners, and who will ultimately make all things new.
That is why our theme means so much to me.
Think about the people whose lives appear in Scripture.
David, whose adultery and abuse of royal power led to terrible consequences.
Peter, who denied the Lord he loved.
The Samaritan woman, whose personal history became part of a conversation that led her to speak about Jesus.
Paul, who once persecuted the church before becoming a servant of Christ.
Their stories are not identical.
Their sins, circumstances, and consequences are different.
And God's grace did not erase the historical reality of what happened.
But their failures did not have the final word over what God could do in their lives.
That is what I mean when I say Jesus rewrites everything.
Not that He makes the past imaginary.
Not that every earthly consequence disappears.
Not that repentance becomes optional.
But that through His death and resurrection, the future of a repentant sinner is no longer defined only by the shame of yesterday.
Listen to 2 Corinthians 5:17:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." — KJV
The Greek expression καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis) means "new creation."
This is deeper than a temporary improvement in mood.
It speaks of the transforming reality of belonging to Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that today.
Your worst decision does not have to become your permanent identity.
Your secret sin does not have to remain your master.
Your history does not place you beyond the reach of God's mercy.
But neither can you simply rename your sin and call it grace.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness.
He does not ask us to pretend darkness is light.
He calls us out of darkness.
And if you are reading this while carrying something you have never told anyone, I want you to know why I keep writing.
Not because I have all the answers.
Not because I have reached some level of spiritual perfection.
Not because I believe my articles are indispensable.
I keep writing because the Gospel is too precious to remain unspoken.
Because Christ is worthy of being proclaimed.
Because people need more than shallow religious encouragement.
And because I believe God can use ordinary believers, ordinary words, and ordinary acts of obedience in ways we may never fully see.
Paul reminds us in 1 Corinthians 3:6:
"I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase." — KJV
That verse protects my heart from something dangerous.
The temptation to believe that the results depend entirely on me.
They don't.
I can write.
I can study.
I can pray.
I can share.
I can correct my mistakes.
I can do everything possible to communicate the truth clearly and compassionately.
But I cannot manufacture spiritual transformation.
I cannot force someone to repent.
I cannot make a hardened heart believe.
I cannot convert a soul through emotional language, clever writing, or a perfect publishing schedule.
God gives the growth.
And that is freedom.
It means I do not need to manipulate your emotions to make my ministry look successful.
I do not need to claim that God told me you must read every word.
And I certainly do not need to turn financial support into a test of whether you truly love God.
The Gospel deserves better than that.
You deserve to hear the truth without pressure disguised as spiritual authority.
But I also want to speak openly about something important.
Gospel Warrior is not sustained by words alone.
There is work behind every article.
Time spent studying Scripture.
Time spent writing and editing.
Time spent preparing Christian resources.
Time spent maintaining a growing library and making discipleship materials available to people who may not have the money to purchase them.
Time spent trying to reach more readers with messages centered on Christ.
And as this work grows, so do the practical needs involved in sustaining and expanding it.
Not because God needs your money.
He doesn't.
Absolutely not.
I am inviting you because supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be a meaningful expression of Christian generosity and partnership.
In Philippians 1:5, Paul thanks believers for their fellowship, or partnership, in the Gospel.
The Greek word κοινωνία (koinōnia) speaks of sharing or participation.
In context, Paul is grateful for the Philippians' continuing partnership in the work of the Gospel.
Later, in Philippians 4:15–18, he specifically acknowledges their material support.
That gives us a biblical foundation for voluntary financial partnership in Gospel work.
Your local church, your family responsibilities, and other genuine needs deserve prayerful consideration.
Not simply because it helps with expenses.
But because it allows this work to continue and, God willing, reach farther.
Perhaps to someone in another country.
Perhaps to someone who cannot afford a Christian book.
Perhaps to someone who has never opened a Bible but is willing to read a testimony.
Perhaps to a believer who has grown spiritually cold and needs to be reminded of the truth.
Only God knows what fruit may come.
But I can promise that the purpose of this ministry will remain the same.
To proclaim Jesus Christ.
To handle Scripture responsibly.
To call people toward repentance, faith, and spiritual growth.
To offer encouragement rooted in biblical truth.
And to continue making discipleship resources accessible.
And I want that word to remain meaningful.
FREE.
I know there are people who genuinely want to grow spiritually but are already struggling to provide for their families.
I see no reason to place unnecessary financial barriers between them and the biblical nourishment we can offer.
But I want to be clear about something.
It is not the Gospel.
Jesus is the reason this ministry exists.
Not because you are obligated to prove your faith publicly.
Not because sharing a post earns spiritual rewards.
But because someone among your friends or family may need to hear the truth of the Gospel.
You may not know who.
Maybe the person who always reacts to your posts but never talks about their problems.
Maybe an old friend who has quietly walked away from church.
Maybe a relative who is carrying shame.
Maybe someone who thinks Christians have no room for people with a complicated past.
Sharing this article may give them an opportunity to encounter Scripture and consider Jesus.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose their struggles.
But because you care about them.
You can even send it privately if that would be more thoughtful.
Not because my words deserve a permanent place in your heart.
But because the Scriptures discussed here deserve more than a hurried glance.
Return to them.
Read their surrounding chapters.
Examine what they mean.
Pray over what God is teaching you through His Word.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who do not yet believe in Christ to follow as well.
They do not need to pretend to have everything figured out before they can begin learning about Jesus.
And there is one more thing I want to ask of you.
Not for an algorithm.
Not for another impressive engagement statistic.
But because I believe honest conversations can encourage people who think they are fighting their spiritual battles alone.
Not a polished religious answer.
Not something you think other Christians want to hear.
Just something true.
Perhaps your faith has been tired lately.
Perhaps you have been running from a conviction you know you need to face.
Perhaps you are grateful because Christ has carried you through a season you thought would destroy you.
Perhaps you are still learning how to pray again.
Or, if you need prayer, write:
You do not need to disclose anything private or painful that you are not ready to share publicly.
Someone else may be encouraged by hearing that another believer has struggled, repented, persevered, and continued following Christ.
Because the Christian life is not a performance in which everyone pretends to be strong.
It is a life of dependence on the Savior.
And that includes me.
There are days when I sit down to write and the words come slowly.
Days when I have to stop and search the Scriptures again.
Days when I realize that a sentence I thought was profound needs to be rewritten because it does not communicate the passage accurately.
Days when I have to surrender a topic I wanted to pursue and give attention to another concern that has become pressing through prayer, study, or the needs I see around me.
That is what I mean when I say I let the Holy Spirit guide my writing.
Not that I become unconscious of my choices.
Not that my judgment becomes infallible.
Not that careful study is unnecessary.
But that I want my decisions, including what to write about and when to stop, to be governed by prayerful submission to God and the authority of Scripture.
I am responsible for the words I publish.
And I remain accountable for correcting them when necessary.
That is part of honoring the Lord too.
Because spiritual sincerity without biblical accuracy can mislead people.
And biblical knowledge without love can wound people.
I want neither.
I want truth spoken in love.
I want grace that never excuses sin.
I want conviction that never hides the mercy of Christ.
I want writing that helps people open their Bibles rather than become dependent on my articles.
And I want every person who encounters Gospel Warrior to know that the invitation is ultimately not to follow me.
It is to follow Jesus.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who confronted hypocrisy.
The One who showed compassion to the broken.
The One who obeyed the Father perfectly.
The One who bore our sins upon the cross.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One through whom forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered.
That Jesus.
Not a version of Him shaped to flatter our preferences.
Not a Jesus who exists merely to make our dreams come true.
The Jesus revealed in Scripture.
The Savior who calls us to deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him.
And perhaps that is why this article became longer than I initially expected.
Because I began by wanting to explain how I write.
But I cannot explain why I write without explaining whom I serve.
And I cannot explain whom I serve without telling you about the Gospel.
Because this ministry was never meant to be about the length of an article.
It was never meant to be about how many people recognize the Gospel Warrior name.
It was never meant to be about building a following large enough to impress the world.
I want to be faithful with what God has entrusted to me.
If one article is short, may it be faithful.
If another is long, may it be faithful.
If thousands read it, may Christ be glorified.
If only a few read it, may Christ still be glorified.
If someone is encouraged, may they thank the Lord.
If someone is convicted, may they turn toward Him.
If someone questions what I have written, may they search the Scriptures carefully.
And if someone finds an error, may I have the humility to receive correction.
Because this is not about defending my reputation.
It is about honoring the truth.
Before I finish, I want to return to the person I mentioned at the beginning.
The person I may never meet.
The person whose name I do not know.
The person I pray will encounter whatever truth from Scripture they need to hear.
Perhaps you are that person today.
I don't know.
I would never claim to know God's hidden purposes for your life simply because you encountered this article.
But I do know that the Gospel invitation is real.
You do not have to clean up your entire life before coming to Christ.
You come to Him in repentance and faith, trusting in His mercy and His finished work.
And the grace that receives sinners is also the grace that begins transforming them.
You may have a scandal in your past.
You may have wounds that still ache.
You may have consequences you cannot undo.
You may have years you wish you could recover.
But if you are in Christ, your story is not ultimately held together by your ability to repair every broken chapter.
It is held together by the Savior who redeems sinners.
If Jesus is calling you to stop hiding, to repent, to trust Him, or to return to a life of faithful obedience, what are you waiting for?
Don't answer that for me.
Answer it before God.

You can also help this message reach others by sharing it, tagging someone who would appreciate its encouragement, saving it for deeper reflection, and following Gospel Warrior for more Christ-centered teaching.
May you know Jesus Christ.
May you grow in the truth of His Word.
May you experience the freedom of repentance and forgiveness.
May you learn to recognize His grace without taking His holiness lightly.
And may your life become a testimony that points others toward Him.
Tomorrow, I may sit down to write again.
I may have a subject already on my heart.
Or I may discover, through prayer, study, and the needs before me, that I need to write about something entirely different.
I may write a few paragraphs.
I may write several pages.
But before I begin, I hope to offer the same prayer I have offered so many times.

"Lord, please guide my words. Keep me faithful to Scripture. Guard me from pride and error. Let Jesus be glorified. And if someone needs to encounter Your truth through this message, please open the door for it to reach them."
Then I will write.
And when the article is finished, I will place the outcome in God's hands.
Because the greatest thing that could ever happen through Gospel Warrior is not that someone becomes a fan of my writing.
It is that someone comes to know and follow Jesus Christ.
If you remember nothing else about the person behind these articles, remember the Savior I have spent every word trying to point you toward.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: MOSES ASKED GOD, “WHO AM I?” — BUT GOD’S ANSWER REVEALS SOMETHING THAT COULD CHANGE YOUR LIFE FOREVER
paragraphs: MOSES ASKED GOD, “WHO AM I?” — BUT GOD’S ANSWER REVEALS SOMETHING THAT COULD CHANGE YOUR LIFE FOREVER

He was a fugitive with a painful past, a shattered identity, and forty years of silence behind him. Then God called his name from a burning bush. What happened next reveals why your failures, fears, and feelings of inadequacy do not have the final word over your future.
There is a question people sometimes carry for years without ever having the courage to say it aloud.
Who am I?
Who am I to believe God could use someone like me?
Who am I to speak about holiness when I remember the sins I committed?
Who am I to pray for my family when I can barely hold myself together?
Who am I to believe there is still a purpose for my life after everything I have ruined?
And perhaps the most painful question of all...
Who am I to think God would still want me?
You might be surprised to discover that one of the greatest leaders in biblical history once stood before God with a question remarkably similar to yours.
His name was Moses.

And when God called him to deliver an entire nation from slavery, Moses did not immediately celebrate. He did not confidently announce that he was ready. He did not begin describing his qualifications.
He asked a question that exposed something deeply human.
“Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh, and that I should bring forth the children of Israel out of Egypt?” — Exodus 3:11 (KJV)
Read those words again.
Who am I?
Not, “How powerful is Pharaoh?”
Not, “How many soldiers will I need?”
Not even, “How will this mission succeed?”
His first recorded objection was about himself.
And what God said next is one of the most beautiful answers ever given to a person who feels inadequate.
But to understand why it matters, you need to know what Moses had been carrying long before he ever encountered the burning bush.
Because the man standing on that mountain was not the confident prince people sometimes imagine.
He was a man whose past had followed him into the wilderness.
Moses had been born during a terrifying season in Israel's history.
Pharaoh had commanded that Hebrew baby boys be killed. Yet through the courage of his mother, the compassion of Pharaoh's daughter, and God's providential care, Moses survived.
He was raised in Pharaoh's household, surrounded by privileges his own people could scarcely imagine.
But luxury could not erase his identity.
He belonged to the Hebrews, a people suffering under Egyptian oppression.
And one day, everything changed.
Exodus 2:11–12 records that Moses saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. After looking around, Moses killed the Egyptian and hid his body in the sand.
It was a devastating turning point.
The following day, when Moses confronted two Hebrews who were fighting, one challenged him:
“Who made thee a prince and a judge over us?” — Exodus 2:14 (KJV)
Do you see the terrible irony?
Long before Moses asked God, “Who am I?” someone had already challenged his authority to lead.
Who made you a ruler over us?
Moses knew he had been discovered.
Pharaoh sought to kill him, and Moses fled Egypt.
The man who had grown up in a palace became a fugitive in Midian.
He eventually married, had a family, and tended the flock of his father-in-law, Jethro.
The years passed.
The palace became a memory.
Egypt continued suffering under the weight of its own cruelty, while Israel groaned beneath oppression.
And Moses lived far from the place where his story had begun.
Acts 7:23 and 7:30 place approximately forty years between Moses' decision to visit his people and the appearance of the angel in the burning bush.
Forty years.
Think about that.
Long enough for youthful confidence to fade.
Long enough for the memory of Egypt to become painful.
Long enough for a man once associated with royal privilege to become accustomed to an ordinary shepherd's life.
Scripture does not tell us everything Moses thought during those years. We should not pretend to know every emotion he carried.
But his later words reveal that he struggled to understand how someone like him could fulfill the assignment God was giving.
And that is where his story begins to touch ours.
Because some people reading this know what it means to live with a past they cannot change.
You once imagined your life would become something beautiful.
You had plans.
You had convictions.
You had dreams you believed God might bless.
Then something happened.
Perhaps you made a decision you deeply regret.
Perhaps your marriage collapsed.
Perhaps you betrayed someone's trust.
Perhaps you wandered so far from God that returning now feels almost impossible.
Or perhaps there was no dramatic scandal at all.
Just years of disappointment.
Years of unanswered questions.
Years of feeling ordinary, overlooked, and spiritually exhausted.
You still believe God is powerful.
You simply struggle to believe He could do anything meaningful through you.
And then comes the whisper that can paralyze a person's faith.
Look at your history. Look at your weakness. Who do you think you are?
Moses knew something about that question.
But here is where the story becomes extraordinary.
One day, while Moses was tending Jethro's flock near Horeb, the mountain of God, he saw something that refused to behave normally.
A bush was burning.
Yet it was not consumed.
The flames were real.
But the bush remained.
Moses turned aside to investigate.
And when the LORD saw that he had turned aside, God called to him from the bush.
“Moses, Moses.” — Exodus 3:4 (KJV)
And Moses answered:
“Here am I.”
Before Moses could explain his inadequacy, God had already called him by name.
Before Moses could present his objections, God had already taken the initiative.
Before Moses could describe what he could not do, God had already revealed that He was present.
That matters.
Because the burning bush was not Moses' discovery of a God who had forgotten Israel.
Exodus 2:23–25 tells us that God heard the Israelites' groaning, remembered His covenant, saw their suffering, and knew their condition.
When Exodus says God “remembered” His covenant, it does not mean He had previously forgotten it. The language emphasizes His faithful regard for the promises He had made.
And now, at the burning bush, God declared:
“I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows.” — Exodus 3:7 (KJV)
Those words deserve to be heard slowly.
I have seen.
I have heard.
I know.
God was not indifferent to His people's suffering.
He was not ignorant of their tears.
He was not absent from their history.

And although this passage concerns God's particular covenant relationship with Israel, it also reveals something consistent with the wider testimony of Scripture: the LORD is not blind to human suffering.
Psalm 34:18 declares that the LORD is near to the brokenhearted.
And in Jesus Christ, we see the compassion of God revealed with astonishing clarity.
If you have spent nights wondering whether anyone understands what you are carrying, remember this:
The God who heard Israel's cries has not become less compassionate.
But the story does not stop with God's compassion.
It moves toward His calling.
God told Moses that He would send him to Pharaoh to bring the Israelites out of Egypt.
Imagine hearing that.
Moses had escaped Pharaoh's reach.
Now God was sending him back.
He had fled the land where his past was known.
Now God was commanding him to return.
The shepherd was being called to confront the throne.
And Moses answered with the question at the heart of this entire story.
“Who am I?”
In the original Hebrew, Exodus 3:11 begins:
מִי אָנֹכִי
Mi anokhi.
Literally:
“Who am I?”
The Hebrew word mi means “who,” and anokhi is an emphatic form of the first-person pronoun, “I.”
The full Hebrew verse reads:
וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֶל־הָאֱלֹהִים מִי אָנֹכִי כִּי אֵלֵךְ אֶל־פַּרְעֹה וְכִי אוֹצִיא אֶת־בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִמִּצְרָיִם
A faithful rendering is:
“And Moses said to God, ‘Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh, and that I should bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?’”
There is no need to invent a secret meaning hidden inside the Hebrew.
The plain meaning is already powerful.
Moses was questioning his suitability for the mission.
He looked at the assignment and saw an overwhelming gap between what God was commanding and what he believed himself capable of accomplishing.
And now comes the part that can change the way you understand your own calling.
God did not answer Moses by listing his accomplishments.
He did not remind Moses of his education in Egypt.
He did not tell Moses to improve his self-esteem.
He did not say, “Moses, you are more talented than you realize.”
Instead, God answered:
“Certainly I will be with thee.” — Exodus 3:12 (KJV)
In Hebrew:
כִּי־אֶהְיֶה עִמָּךְ
Ki ehyeh immakh.
“For I will be with you.”
Notice the movement.
Moses asked about his identity.
God answered with His presence.
Moses was focused on the insufficiency of the messenger.
God directed his attention toward the sufficiency of the One sending him.
This is the theological heartbeat of Exodus 3:11–12.
God did not promise Moses that the mission would be easy.
He did not deny that Pharaoh was powerful.
He did not pretend Moses had no weaknesses.
He promised something greater than self-confidence.
His presence.
And that distinction matters more than many people realize.
Because the Gospel does not teach that you are secretly powerful enough to save yourself.
It teaches that Jesus Christ is mighty to save sinners who cannot rescue themselves.
Christian faith is not ultimately about discovering how impressive you are.
It is about discovering how gracious, holy, faithful, and sufficient God is.
And perhaps that is why some of us remain spiritually exhausted.
We keep asking God to prove that we are enough.
When Scripture is calling us to trust that He is enough.
We measure ourselves against our past.
Against our failures.
Against other people's achievements.
Against the expectations we have never managed to fulfill.
We look in the mirror and see every reason we should be disqualified.
But when God called Moses, the decisive answer was not found in Moses' personal greatness.
It was found in God's faithful presence.
Now, we must be careful here.
This passage does not mean that every ambition we have is automatically a calling from God.
It does not mean that every difficult situation will end with a spectacular miracle.
And it certainly does not mean that our failures carry no consequences.
Moses' story is not permission to ignore sin, reject accountability, or baptize our personal desires as divine assignments.
The point is deeper.
When God truly calls someone to obey Him, human inadequacy cannot overturn God's ability to accomplish His purposes.
That does not remove the need for repentance.
It makes humble obedience possible.
And Moses still had much to learn.
In Exodus 3:13, he asked what he should tell the Israelites if they questioned the name of the God who sent him.
God answered in Exodus 3:14:
“I AM THAT I AM.” — Exodus 3:14 (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is:
אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה
Ehyeh asher ehyeh.
It is traditionally translated “I AM THAT I AM,” though the Hebrew verbal form can also carry the sense “I WILL BE WHAT I WILL BE.”
The phrase is profound, and interpreters have discussed its nuances for centuries.
What is clear in context is that God is revealing Himself as the One whose identity, faithfulness, and presence do not depend upon Moses.
The word ehyeh, “I am” or “I will be,” also appears in God's promise in Exodus 3:12:
I will be with you.
Do you see the connection?
Moses asks, “Who am I?”
God promises, “I will be with you.”
Then God reveals Himself as “I AM.”
The mission rests not upon Moses' independent greatness, but upon the God who sends him.
That is not a motivational slogan.
That is biblical theology.
And it is far more enduring than any speech about believing in yourself.
But the narrative becomes even more honest when we continue reading.
Moses did not suddenly become fearless after hearing God's promise.
He raised further objections.
What if the people did not believe him?
What if they refused to listen?
What if he could not speak effectively?
In Exodus 4:10, Moses described himself as slow of speech and tongue.
God answered by reminding him who made the human mouth.
Then, in Exodus 4:13, Moses asked God to send someone else.
And Exodus 4:14 records that the LORD's anger was kindled against him.
That detail is important.
Because Scripture does not romanticize every hesitation as humility.
There is a difference between honestly acknowledging weakness and persistently resisting what God has clearly commanded.
Sometimes our question, “Who am I?” is a sincere confession of inadequacy.
Sometimes it becomes an excuse to avoid obedience.
And sometimes, if we are willing to be painfully honest, it is both.
We want God to use us.
But we do not want to be uncomfortable.
We want spiritual transformation.
But we resist surrendering the sin that has become familiar.
We want forgiveness.
But we hesitate to confess what we have done.
We want to follow Jesus.
But we are afraid of what following Him might cost.
And that is where this story stops being merely about Moses.
It begins confronting us.
Because what if the deepest problem in your spiritual life is not that God has failed to make Himself known?
What if you already know something He has commanded, but fear has convinced you to keep postponing obedience?
You know you need to forgive.
You know you need to tell the truth.
You know you need to turn away from that hidden sin.
You know you need to stop pretending everything is fine.
You know you need to return to prayer, open Scripture, and seek the Lord with sincerity.
But you keep waiting to feel strong enough.
You keep waiting for the fear to disappear.
You keep waiting until you believe you have become worthy.
And perhaps the question that needs to change is not simply, “Who am I?”
Perhaps it is:
Lord, if You have spoken, why am I still allowing my fear to have the final word?
There is another detail in Moses' story that makes this even more remarkable.
God did not abandon him after his objections.
He provided Aaron to assist him.
He gave Moses signs to confirm his commission.
He continued unfolding His purposes through a reluctant servant.
This was mercy.
Not because Moses deserved endless accommodation, but because God remained faithful to His covenant purpose.
And that is where we begin to see the larger biblical story moving toward Jesus Christ.
Moses would eventually confront Pharaoh.
God would bring judgment upon Egypt.
The Passover would mark a decisive moment in Israel's deliverance.
The Israelites would leave the land of bondage.
And through the Red Sea, God would demonstrate that salvation belonged to Him.
Yet Moses himself was not the final deliverer humanity needed.
Israel's rescue from Egypt was real and historically central to the biblical narrative.
But humanity's deepest bondage goes beyond political oppression.
Scripture teaches that sin enslaves, separates us from God, and brings death.
And no human leader, however faithful, can finally remove our guilt before a holy God.
That is why the story of Moses must ultimately lead our attention beyond Moses.
Toward Jesus.
In Deuteronomy 18:15, Moses spoke of a prophet whom God would raise up from among the people.
The New Testament identifies Jesus as the fulfillment of this prophetic expectation, as seen in Acts 3:22–23.
And Hebrews 3:1–6 compares Moses and Christ.
Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house.
But Christ is faithful as the Son over God's house.
The distinction is breathtaking.
Moses was sent to lead Israel out of Egypt.
Jesus came to save His people from their sins.
Moses was a servant through whom God brought deliverance.
Jesus is the Son of God, who gave Himself for sinners and rose again.
Moses confronted an earthly Pharaoh.
Jesus conquered sin and death through His crucifixion and resurrection.
And here is where the words “From Scandal to Grace” become more than a beautiful phrase.
Because the Gospel is not the story of God discovering that sinful people were secretly innocent.
It is the story of a holy God extending mercy to people who desperately need forgiveness.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we erased every consequence of our mistakes.
Not after we convinced everyone that we had changed.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not make sin small.
The cross reveals how serious sin truly is.
But it also reveals the extraordinary depth of God's love.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our public image.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He lived in perfect obedience, died for our sins, and rose from the dead.
And through repentance and faith in Him, we receive forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life.
This is why your past must never be allowed to become more authoritative than the Gospel.
Your failures may be real.
Your consequences may be painful.
The people you hurt may need time, truth, and evidence of genuine change.
Repentance does not demand that wounded people immediately trust you again.
But neither does your past possess the power to cancel the mercy God offers through Jesus Christ.
Listen to the promise of 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise is not an invitation to conceal wrongdoing.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
And perhaps someone reading this has been hiding for a very long time.
You have learned how to smile while carrying shame.
You have learned how to worship while avoiding the one area of your life you do not want God to confront.
You know how to say “God is good” while secretly wondering whether His goodness could still reach someone like you.
You have become skilled at appearing spiritually healthy.
But behind the appearance, something is exhausted.
Something is wounded.
Something is desperate for mercy.
And perhaps tonight, for the first time in a long time, you are ready to stop running.
Not because you have finally become worthy.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy of your trust.
You do not need to manufacture a spotless history before coming to Him.
You need to repent, believe the Gospel, and surrender yourself to the Savior who receives those who come to Him.
Jesus said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
That is not a small promise.
That is a refuge for the ashamed.
A welcome for the repentant.
A reason for the weary sinner to stop hiding.
And it changes how we hear Moses' question.
Who am I?
Perhaps you are a person who has failed.
Perhaps you are someone who has been rejected.
Perhaps you are still dealing with the consequences of decisions you wish you could undo.
Perhaps you have spent years convinced that your most meaningful days are behind you.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your failures are not your ultimate identity.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (KJV)
This does not mean your memories disappear.
It does not mean consequences instantly vanish.
It means that in Christ, a genuinely new life has begun.
A life marked by repentance.
A life shaped by grace.
A life increasingly transformed through the work of the Holy Spirit.
And unlike shallow promises of effortless success, the Gospel gives us hope strong enough to face the truth.
You may still struggle.
You may still grieve.
You may still have difficult conversations ahead.
You may need to make restitution, seek wise counsel, rebuild trust, and endure a long season of healing.
But none of those realities makes God's grace less glorious.
Sometimes the evidence of transformation is not a dramatic public testimony.
Sometimes it is a quiet confession.
An honest apology.
A decision to abandon a secret sin.
A husband learning to love faithfully.
A mother praying through exhaustion.
A young person choosing obedience when no one is watching.
A wounded believer opening the Bible again after months of silence.
A person who once ran from God finally whispering:
Lord Jesus, I am coming home.
And maybe that is the moment this article has been leading toward.
Not a moment when you admire Moses.
A moment when you stop hiding from Christ.
Because the God who called Moses from the wilderness is the same God whose redemptive purpose is revealed fully in Jesus Christ.
And the Savior who died and rose again still calls sinners to repent and believe.
You do not have to pretend you are strong.
You do not have to call your sin a mistake when Scripture calls it sin.
You do not have to deny the damage your choices have caused.
You can tell the truth.
And you can bring that truth to Jesus.
There is no spiritual victory in protecting a false image while your heart remains far from God.
There is freedom in confession.
There is mercy in Christ.
There is hope in His resurrection.
And there is a new way of living for those who follow Him.
Your story might encourage someone who is afraid to take their first step toward repentance.
There is no shame in asking for prayer.
You do not need to perform spiritual strength to belong among believers.
We are a people who need grace.
Every one of us.
Not to collect attention.
Not to prove how religious you are.
But because there may be someone silently asking the same question Moses asked.
Who am I?
Someone you know may be convinced that God could never forgive them.
Someone may be one honest conversation away from seeking help, confessing sin, or returning to Christian fellowship.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, and those who are still searching for truth to join us.
Because this mission is not about building an audience around a personality.
It is about pointing people toward the Savior.
And there is something else I want to share with you.
Gospel Warrior is working to make biblical teaching, discipleship, encouragement, and Christian resources accessible to more people.
These resources are part of our desire to help believers move beyond occasional inspiration into genuine spiritual growth.
But creating, maintaining, and expanding a ministry of encouragement and biblical resources requires faithful support.
Not because God needs your money.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not through financial contributions or religious performance (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But Scripture also teaches that generosity can be a meaningful expression of worship and partnership in Gospel ministry.
Philippians 4:15–18 describes believers supporting Paul's ministry, and Paul speaks of their gifts as a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
This is the spirit in which I invite you.
Give freely, thoughtfully, and according to your ability.
It is the opportunity to participate in a continuing work of Scripture-centered encouragement, discipleship, and Gospel outreach.
Because a ministry that gains attention but loses biblical truth has lost something far more important than an audience.
We want people to encounter the Gospel.
To understand the Word.
To turn away from sin.
To know the mercy of Christ.
And to follow Him with genuine faith.
Now, before you leave, I want you to return to that mountain in Exodus.
Picture Moses standing before the burning bush.
A shepherd.
A fugitive.
A man with a complicated past.
He has been given a task far greater than anything he believes he can accomplish.
And he asks:
Who am I?
God does not answer by making Moses the center of the story.
He answers by promising His presence.
“Certainly I will be with thee.”
There is a reason those words still matter.
Because when you come to the end of your confidence in yourself, you have not necessarily come to the end of hope.
You may be standing at the beginning of a deeper dependence upon God.
But do not confuse dependence with passivity.
Moses still had to obey.
He still had to return to Egypt.
He still had to confront Pharaoh.
He still had to learn, stumble, persevere, and trust the LORD.
And you, too, may have steps of obedience ahead.
A confession you have delayed.
A relationship in which you need to take responsibility.
A habit you need to abandon.
A wound for which you need help.
A prayer you need to begin praying again.
A truth you need to stop running from.
Do not wait until you feel impressive enough to obey God.
Do not turn your inadequacy into an excuse for unbelief.
And do not imagine that your past is stronger than the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Look to Him.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and faith.
The One who promises His people that He will be with them always, even to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20).
That promise does not make you the hero.
It reminds you who the Savior is.
So perhaps the next time your heart whispers, Who am I?, you can answer with something more faithful than either self-hatred or self-exaltation.
I am someone who needs God's mercy.
I am someone who cannot save myself.
I am someone who must trust and obey Jesus Christ.
And if I belong to Him, I am someone whose life is no longer defined by condemnation, but by the grace of my Redeemer.
That is not arrogance.
That is gratitude.
That is not pretending the past never happened.
That is believing that Jesus Christ truly saves and transforms sinners.
And that is the hope behind every story we share here.
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because the consequences disappear.
But because Jesus Christ is greater than the sin and shame from which He redeems His people.
What if the thing you have been using to convince yourself that God could never receive you is the very thing you need to bring honestly before Jesus today?
Do not keep hiding.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe.
And follow Him.
Because the most beautiful part of your story is not that you were never broken by sin—it is that Jesus Christ can redeem what sin could never restore.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD CHOOSE 70 ELDERS? THE HIDDEN LESSON IN NUMBERS 11 THAT EVERY EXHAUSTED CHRISTIAN NEEDS TO HEAR
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD CHOOSE 70 ELDERS? THE HIDDEN LESSON IN NUMBERS 11 THAT EVERY EXHAUSTED CHRISTIAN NEEDS TO HEAR

Seventy men. One overwhelmed leader. A nation drowning in complaints. And a God who answered a desperate cry in a way that reveals something extraordinary about spiritual leadership, human weakness, the Holy Spirit, and the grace we desperately need today.
There is a kind of exhaustion that sleep cannot cure.
You can close your eyes for eight hours and still wake up tired.
You can smile in church, raise your hands during worship, encourage somebody else to trust God, and then go home carrying a weight you are almost ashamed to admit is crushing you.
You love God.
You believe His promises.
You know He has been faithful.
But somewhere between the responsibilities, the disappointments, the unanswered prayers, and the people depending on you, something inside you has started whispering…
“Lord, I don't know how much longer I can carry this.”
Perhaps you have never said those words aloud.
Moses did.
And what happened next reveals something about God that many believers desperately need to understand.
Because when Moses reached the breaking point, God did not simply tell him to become stronger.
He called seventy elders.
But why seventy?
Why not twelve, representing Israel's tribes?
Why not forty, a number repeatedly associated with periods of testing in Scripture?
Why seventy men, and why did God take from the Spirit resting upon Moses and place that same Spirit upon them?
The answer begins with a scandal of the human heart.
And it ends by pointing us toward a Savior greater than Moses.
But before we reach that moment, we need to walk into the wilderness.
Not as spectators.
As people who recognize ourselves in the story.
Israel had already witnessed miracles that generations would talk about for centuries.
They had seen the plagues in Egypt.
They had walked through the Red Sea.
They had watched Pharaoh's army disappear beneath the waters.
They had eaten bread from heaven.
They had seen God's presence manifested in the cloud and the fire.
They had every reason to trust Him.
And yet, in Numbers 11, they were complaining again.
This time, about food.
The people were tired of manna.
Imagine that.
Every morning, God provided nourishment in a wilderness where survival should have been impossible.
And eventually, the miracle became something they resented.
They remembered the fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic of Egypt.
They remembered the menu.
But somehow, they had forgotten the chains.
Sometimes the most dangerous thing about spiritual bondage is that distance makes it look beautiful.
Egypt had enslaved them.
Egypt had oppressed them.
Egypt had been the place from which they cried out for deliverance.
Yet now, under the pressure of the wilderness, they were romanticizing the very place God had rescued them from.
Does that sound familiar?
You prayed for God to deliver you from a destructive relationship, but loneliness makes you remember only the good moments.
You begged God to free you from an addiction, but suffering makes the old escape look comforting.
You cried for a new beginning, but the difficulties of obedience make your former life seem easier.
And slowly, the heart begins negotiating with the bondage Jesus came to break.
This is not merely Israel's story.
It is a mirror.
The wilderness exposed something that the Red Sea crossing had not removed.
A person can experience deliverance from slavery while still needing God to transform the desires of the heart.
That is why redemption must reach deeper than circumstances.
We do not simply need a change of location.
We need a change of heart.
And this brings us to Moses.
The man who confronted Pharaoh.
The man who stretched out his staff over the sea.
The man who stood before God on Sinai.
The man through whom the Lord had performed astonishing signs.
That same Moses was now emotionally collapsing under the burden of leading the people.
Listen to his words in Numbers 11:14, from the King James Version:
“I am not able to bear all this people alone, because it is too heavy for me.”
Read that again.
Not because it sounds impressive.
Because it sounds human.
“I am not able…”
Moses was not pretending anymore.
He had reached the end of what he could carry.
And in the following verse, his anguish became even more disturbing.
He pleaded with God to take his life rather than leave him facing such misery.
That was not the voice of a man enjoying leadership.
It was the cry of someone overwhelmed beyond his strength.
Scripture does not conceal this moment.
It allows us to see a great servant of God at his lowest.
And perhaps that is exactly what somebody reading this needs to know.
You can love God deeply and still become exhausted.
You can be called to serve and still need help.
You can have genuine faith and still experience moments when your emotions feel unbearable.
The Bible does not present Moses as a flawless spiritual machine.
It shows us a dependent human being.
And when God answered him, His response was remarkable.
Numbers 11:16 records the Lord saying:
“Gather unto me seventy men of the elders of Israel…”
God instructed Moses to bring recognized elders and officers of the people to the tabernacle of the congregation.
These were not seventy random strangers chosen for their appearance, charisma, or popularity.
They were men already known among the people as elders and officers.
And God intended to share the burden of leadership with them.
Numbers 11:17 explains His purpose:
“And they shall bear the burden of the people with thee, that thou bear it not thyself alone.”
There it is.
One of the most beautiful truths in this passage.
God did not design Moses to carry the entire nation alone.
And the Lord was not asking him to prove his faithfulness by destroying himself under responsibilities that could be shared.
Notice something important.
God did not remove Moses from his calling.
He provided others to help him fulfill it.
There is a difference.
Sometimes we assume that if God truly called us, we should never need assistance.
We tell ourselves that needing help means our faith is weak.
That asking someone to share the load means we are failing.
That a real leader should be able to endure everything without breaking.
But Numbers 11 challenges that assumption.
God Himself established a shared responsibility.
And the Hebrew language makes this even more meaningful.
In Numbers 11:17, the expression translated “the burden of the people” includes the Hebrew word מַשָּׂא (massaʾ).
It refers to a load, burden, or something carried.
The verse also uses the verb נָשָׂא (nasaʾ), meaning to lift, bear, or carry.
These words belong to the same Hebrew root family.
The language emphasizes the reality of the weight and the act of carrying it.
God was addressing an actual burden.
Not an imaginary weakness.
Not an excuse.
Not an embarrassment.
A burden.
And He was making provision for that burden to be shared.
Think about how many believers are silently breaking because they have confused faithfulness with carrying everything themselves.
The pastor who cannot admit he is struggling.
The mother who feels guilty whenever she rests.
The father who believes he must solve every financial problem without telling anyone he is afraid.
The ministry worker who keeps serving while his spiritual life becomes increasingly dry.
The young Christian who is trying to overcome temptation alone because confession feels too humiliating.
And the person who encourages everyone else but has no one to call when the darkness comes.
We have become skilled at saying, “God is enough,” while sometimes refusing the very help God provides through His people.
Yes, God is sufficient.
But His sufficiency does not mean He never works through human relationships.
The same Lord who sustained Moses also appointed seventy elders to help him.
Receiving help is not necessarily a failure of faith. Sometimes it is obedience to God's provision.
But there is still the question.
Why seventy?
And here we must be careful.
Because Scripture deserves more than impressive-sounding speculation.
The Bible does not explicitly state that God chose seventy elders because seventy represented a particular spiritual mystery.
We should not pretend that it does.
Yet the number seventy appears elsewhere in significant biblical settings.
Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 associate seventy persons with Jacob's household entering Egypt, according to the Hebrew textual tradition reflected in the Masoretic Text.
Genesis 10 also contains a traditional count of seventy nations in the Hebrew text, although textual traditions and methods of counting differ.
And Exodus 24:1, 9 describes seventy elders of Israel who accompanied Moses, Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu in a remarkable covenant setting.
That earlier appearance is especially important.
The seventy elders in Numbers 11 did not emerge in a biblical vacuum.
Israel already had a recognized pattern of elder leadership.
However, Scripture does not explicitly establish that the seventy elders of Exodus 24 were the identical individuals appointed in Numbers 11.
Nor does it tell us that each elder represented one nation or one particular family.
These connections can help us appreciate the broader biblical setting, but they must not be confused with explanations God has not given.
What the passage clearly tells us is more important than any hidden numerical theory.
God appointed seventy recognized leaders so they could share Moses' burden, and He empowered them by His Spirit for that responsibility.
That is the central answer.
Not numerology.
Not a secret code.
Not an invitation to build doctrine on speculation.
God was establishing Spirit-enabled, shared leadership among His covenant people.
And then something extraordinary happened.
Numbers 11:25 says:
“And the LORD came down in a cloud, and spake unto him, and took of the spirit that was upon him, and gave it unto the seventy elders…”
Imagine that moment.
The wilderness stretching in every direction.
The tabernacle standing among the tents of Israel.
Moses, exhausted and burdened, standing before the God who had called him.
Seventy elders gathered in obedience.
Then the Lord descended in the cloud.
And the Spirit who had empowered Moses was placed upon the elders.
The Hebrew phrase in this verse is especially significant:
מִן־הָרוּחַ אֲשֶׁר עָלָיו
Min-ha-ruach asher alav.
Literally, “from the spirit that was upon him.”
The Hebrew word רוּחַ (ruach) can mean wind, breath, or spirit, depending on its context.
Here, the passage concerns the divine empowerment given to Moses and shared with the elders.
The text does not teach that God's Spirit was physically divided into seventy pieces.
Nor does it require us to imagine Moses losing spiritual power every time another leader received it.
The emphasis is that the same divine empowerment associated with Moses' leadership was now given to others.
The elders were not being told to imitate Moses through sheer human determination.
They were being equipped by God.
And when the Spirit rested upon them, they prophesied.
The Hebrew verb is וַיִּתְנַבְּאוּ (vayyitnabbeʾu), meaning “and they prophesied.”
This prophetic manifestation served as a visible sign of the Spirit's activity among them.

The closing Hebrew phrase of Numbers 11:25, וְלֹא יָסָפוּ (velo yasafu), is commonly understood to mean that they did not continue or repeat that prophetic manifestation, although the expression has been interpreted differently in translation traditions.
The passage does not say that the Spirit immediately abandoned them.
The prophetic event and their continuing responsibility as elders should not be confused.
And here is the breathtaking reality.
The same God who called Moses was capable of empowering others to serve alongside him.
God's work was never dependent upon Moses being everywhere, doing everything, and carrying everyone.
And God's work today is not dependent upon any one pastor, evangelist, ministry founder, or spiritual leader becoming indispensable.
The Lord is indispensable.
His servants are not.
That truth can humble the proud.
And heal the exhausted.
Because there are people who secretly believe everything will collapse if they stop moving.
They cannot rest because they feel guilty.
They cannot delegate because they fear losing control.
They cannot ask for help because they have built their identity around being needed.
But what happens when the ministry becomes more important than the Master?
What happens when the calling becomes the source of our identity instead of the Christ who called us?
What happens when we become so consumed with serving God that we forget how to depend upon Him?
Moses needed to learn that the burden was not his alone.
And perhaps we do too.
But the story becomes even more surprising.
Two men named Eldad and Medad were among those registered, yet they had remained in the camp rather than going out to the tabernacle with the others.
Nevertheless, the Spirit rested upon them.
And they prophesied in the camp.
A young man ran to tell Moses.
Joshua, Moses' assistant, became concerned and asked Moses to stop them.
And Moses responded with words that reveal the heart of a leader who understood something greater than personal influence.
Numbers 11:29 says:
“Enviest thou for my sake? would God that all the LORD'S people were prophets, and that the LORD would put his spirit upon them!”
That statement deserves to be heard slowly.
Moses was not threatened by the Spirit's work through other people.
He was not desperate to monopolize spiritual authority.
He did not demand that every manifestation of God's power revolve around his own reputation.
He expressed a longing for the Lord's Spirit to be upon all His people.
A godly leader does not need to be the only person God uses.
And those words reach beyond the wilderness.
Centuries later, the prophet Joel announced that God would pour out His Spirit upon all flesh, with sons and daughters prophesying, and old and young participating in the promised outpouring.
Then came Pentecost.
Acts 2 records the Holy Spirit being poured out upon the gathered believers.
Peter explained the event by quoting Joel's prophecy.
What Moses had longed for anticipated, in a meaningful way, the broader outpouring of the Spirit under the new covenant.
But we must understand the distinction.
Numbers 11 describes a particular empowerment of Israel's elders for leadership.
Acts 2 announces a decisive moment in the fulfillment of God's promises through the risen and exalted Jesus Christ.
The two events are connected within the unfolding story of Scripture, but they are not identical.
And the center of that unfolding story is Jesus.
Not Moses.
Not the seventy.
Not the experience of prophesying.
Jesus Christ.
Because Moses could help lead Israel through the wilderness.
But he could not remove the sin that kept corrupting their hearts.
Moses could intercede for the people.
But he could not become the final sacrifice that would reconcile sinners to God.
Moses could receive God's instructions.
But he could not give humanity the new heart promised through God's saving work.
Israel's deepest problem was never merely the absence of enough leaders.
It was the presence of sin.
And that is our deepest problem too.
We can organize better.
We can establish stronger ministries.
We can develop leadership teams.
We can distribute responsibilities.
And these can be wise, biblical things.
But none of them can wash away guilt.
None can make a rebellious heart holy.
None can raise the spiritually dead.
Only God can save.
And that is why the story must lead us to the greater Mediator.
Hebrews 3:3 declares that Jesus is worthy of greater glory than Moses.
Hebrews 3:5–6 explains that Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house, while Christ is faithful as Son over God's house.
Moses was a servant.
Jesus is the Son.
Moses needed help carrying the burdens of Israel.
Jesus willingly carried the burden of our sin to the cross.
Isaiah 53:6 says:
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
Do you see the difference?
The seventy elders shared Moses' leadership burden.
But Jesus bore the judgment our sins deserved in a way no human leader ever could.
He did not merely come to improve our circumstances.
He came to redeem us.
He did not simply come to teach exhausted people better time management.
He came to reconcile sinners to the Father through His death and resurrection.
And the cross reveals a grace more astonishing than anything we could manufacture.
The One who was without sin was treated as a sinner for our sake.
The One who deserved honor endured humiliation.
The One who possessed all authority submitted Himself to death.
And the One who was crucified rose again.
So that guilty people could be forgiven.
So that rebellious hearts could be transformed.
So that people who have spent years running from God could come home through faith in Jesus Christ.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not because God pretends sin is harmless.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because our choices have no consequences.
But because Jesus Christ has accomplished what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
The scandal is that we were sinners who could not save ourselves. The grace is that Christ came to save sinners.
And if you have been reading this while quietly carrying something you are afraid to confess, I want you to hear something.
God knows.
He knows the resentment you have been hiding.
He knows the temptation you keep returning to.
He knows the bitterness behind your smile.
He knows the prayers you stopped praying because you felt ashamed.
He knows the exhaustion you have disguised as strength.
He knows the moments when you looked back toward your own Egypt and wondered whether obedience was worth the struggle.
And He calls sinners to repentance and faith in His Son.
Not to make peace with sin.
Not to remain enslaved.
But to receive mercy and begin walking in newness of life.
First John 1:9 reminds believers:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
And Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus…”
The gospel is not permission to remain in darkness.
It is God's gracious invitation to come into the light.
Perhaps you are the exhausted Moses in this story.
You have been carrying people, responsibilities, expectations, and private grief for so long that you no longer remember what it feels like to breathe freely.
Perhaps you are like the Israelites.
God has delivered you from something, yet your heart keeps looking backward.
Perhaps you are like Joshua.
You have become so protective of the way God worked yesterday that you struggle to recognize His work through someone else today.
Or perhaps you are like Eldad and Medad.
You feel overlooked.
You are not standing where everyone expects the important people to stand.
And you wonder whether God can still use someone like you.
The details of your life may be different.
But the call remains.
Return to the Lord.
Trust His Word.
Submit to His will.
Receive His grace.
And stop treating your limitations as though they are a surprise to the God who created you.
Jesus Himself said in Matthew 11:28:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
That invitation does not promise a life without suffering or responsibility.
It promises rest found in coming to Christ and learning from Him.
There is a burden only Jesus can remove: the guilt of sin through His redeeming work.
And there are burdens He teaches us to carry faithfully, often through the strength, wisdom, and care He provides within His people.
Galatians 6:2 tells believers to bear one another's burdens and so fulfill the law of Christ.
Do not miss how beautifully that connects with Numbers 11.
The Lord who provided seventy elders to help Moses also calls His people to care for one another.
Christianity was never intended to be a performance in which everybody pretends to be strong.
It is a redeemed community learning to walk together under the lordship of Jesus.
Sometimes the most spiritual sentence you can speak is not, “I can handle everything.”
Sometimes it is:
“I need prayer.”
“I need help.”
“I have sinned.”
“I am struggling.”
“I need to come back to Jesus.”
And sometimes the most Christlike thing you can do is listen when another believer finally finds the courage to say those words.
Not condemn them.
Not gossip about them.
Not turn their pain into entertainment.
But point them to the truth, extend compassion, encourage repentance where needed, and walk with them toward Christ.
Because spiritual maturity is not measured by how convincingly we hide our wounds.
It is revealed in growing dependence upon the Lord and obedience to His Word.
And if this message has touched something you have kept hidden, I want to invite you into a moment of honesty.
Not for appearances.
Not to impress anyone.
But because sometimes another believer needs to know they are not the only one struggling.
And if God has already brought you through a season when you thought you could not endure another day, consider sharing a little of your testimony.
Your words may encourage someone who is struggling to believe that tomorrow is worth facing.
You do not have to disclose anything private or unsafe.
Even a simple, sincere expression of faith can become an encouragement to another person.
Because somewhere, somebody is reading this with tears they have not allowed anyone to see.
Somebody is serving in church while quietly wondering whether they have anything left to give.
Somebody is fighting a temptation they thought they had already conquered.
Somebody is carrying a family crisis, a financial burden, a broken relationship, or grief that refuses to disappear.
And perhaps they need to encounter the same truth Moses learned.
God never asked you to become God.
He calls you to trust Him.
And to receive the help He provides.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to replace the Scriptures.
Not to create dependence upon a personality, a page, or a ministry brand.
But to help point people continually back to Jesus Christ through biblical teaching, encouragement, discipleship, and accessible Christian resources.

Our prayer is that the exhausted will find encouragement in God's Word, the wandering will be called to repentance, the wounded will discover the hope of the gospel, and believers will grow in their understanding of Scripture.
And there is something important I want to share with those who believe this work is worth continuing.
Gospel-centered ministry takes prayer, time, effort, resources, and faithful people who are willing to help.
It does not purchase salvation, forgiveness, spiritual favor, or a higher place in the kingdom.
And it should never replace the financial responsibilities you believe God has entrusted to you, including your obligations to your family and your local church.
But it can be a voluntary expression of generosity toward a ministry whose biblical mission you want to support.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which we invite support.
Not through guilt.
Not through pressure.
But through willing partnership in the work of making Christ known.
It can help us keep reaching those who are quietly searching for answers about God, forgiveness, repentance, suffering, and eternal life.
These products are not the gospel.
They are simply resources and reminders that can encourage faith, conversation, and daily reflection on God's Word.
The greater purpose remains the same.
Jesus must be proclaimed.
Scripture must be understood.
And people must be encouraged to follow Christ.
Explore those resources.
Read Scripture for yourself.
Test what you hear against the Bible.
Grow in prayer.
Remain connected to a faithful local church.
And share what you are learning with others.
Not simply to increase the reach of a page.
But because you may have a friend who needs to hear that God sees the weight they are carrying.
Send it privately to someone who is struggling.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have drifted from the faith, and even those who do not yet believe to explore the message of Jesus with us.
Because this is not about building an audience around ourselves.
It is about directing attention to the Savior.
And before we finish, I want to bring you back to the wilderness one last time.
Imagine Moses standing there.
The man who had once faced Pharaoh now faced something he could not overcome through his own strength.
He had reached the limits of his endurance.
He had confessed that the burden was too heavy.
And God answered.
Not by declaring that Moses was worthless.
Not by telling him to pretend he was fine.
But by giving him help and empowering others for the work.
The seventy elders remind us that God's people need shared responsibility and divine strength.
Eldad and Medad remind us that God's work cannot be reduced to one person's prestige.

Moses' longing for the Spirit upon all God's people directs our attention toward the unfolding promise that finds its climactic fulfillment in Christ's redemptive work and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.
And Jesus reminds us that the deepest burden of all—our sin—could never be removed by seventy elders, seventy thousand leaders, or all the strength humanity could gather.
It required a Redeemer.
It required the cross.
It required the risen Christ.
So perhaps the most important question is not merely why Israel had seventy elders.
Perhaps the question is whether we have learned what Moses' weakness, Israel's rebellion, and God's provision reveal.
We need God.
We need His mercy.
We need His truth.
We need the grace that saves and transforms us.
And we need to stop mistaking self-sufficiency for spiritual maturity.
If you have wandered, repent and return to Christ.
If you are exhausted, bring your burdens to Him and seek wise support.
If you have been forgiven, walk in gratitude and obedience.
If God has given you gifts to serve others, use them humbly.
And if you are tempted to look back toward Egypt, remember what it cost to set you free.
Not merely from earthly bondage.
But from the dominion of sin through the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Before you leave, I would love to hear your answer to one question.
What burden have you been trying to carry alone that you need to surrender to God and, perhaps, allow trustworthy people to help you bear?
You may never know how much they needed that reminder.
Because the God who saw Moses in the wilderness still sees His people in their weakness.
And the Savior who died for sinners still calls the weary to come to Him.
You were never meant to be everyone's savior. You were meant to know the One who is.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE PROVERBS 31 WOMAN IS FAMOUS—BUT THE WARNING ABOUT SEXUAL DESTRUCTION BEFORE HER STORY IS ALMOST NEVER PREACHED.
paragraphs: THE PROVERBS 31 WOMAN IS FAMOUS—BUT THE WARNING ABOUT SEXUAL DESTRUCTION BEFORE HER STORY IS ALMOST NEVER PREACHED.

Before the Bible describes a woman worth more than rubies, a mother warns her son about the kind of desire that can destroy a king. And what she says may expose something our generation desperately needs to confront.
Everybody wants to talk about the Proverbs 31 woman.
Her virtue. Her beauty. Her strength. Her wisdom. Her business. Her marriage. Her children. Her faith.

Churches preach about her. Christian women aspire to become like her. Men are encouraged to look for her. Social media turns her into inspirational captions, marriage advice, and standards for godly womanhood.
But there is something deeply uncomfortable about the chapter that made her famous.
Before Proverbs 31 ever celebrates a virtuous woman, it warns a man not to destroy himself through sexual recklessness.
Read that again.
Before the description of a faithful wife, there is a warning about destructive desire.
Before the praise of noble character, there is a call to self-control.
Before the chapter tells us what kind of woman is worthy of honor, it confronts what kind of man is capable of ruining his own life.
And perhaps that is why so many people begin reading Proverbs 31 at verse 10.
Because verse 10 inspires us.
But verse 3 confronts us.
And sometimes the Scriptures we skip are the very Scriptures our souls need most.
Imagine a mother looking into the eyes of her son.
Not an ordinary son, but a king. A man with influence, authority, resources, and the power to make decisions that could affect an entire nation.
She knows the dangers surrounding him.
She knows power attracts attention.
She knows that admiration can become temptation, temptation can become entitlement, and entitlement can eventually become destruction.
And she knows something every parent eventually discovers.
You can give your child a crown, but you cannot give him character.
You can prepare him for leadership, but you cannot make his heart love righteousness.
So she speaks.
Not as a politician.
Not as a palace adviser.
But as a mother who refuses to remain silent while her son stands near the edge of a dangerous cliff.

Proverbs 31:1 introduces her words as the teaching King Lemuel received from his mother. The passage does not identify Lemuel with certainty, nor does it name his mother. We should not pretend to know what Scripture has not revealed.
But we know what she said.
And her words still speak.
In Proverbs 31:3, the Hebrew reads:
אַל־תִּתֵּן לַנָּשִׁים חֵילֶךָ וּדְרָכֶיךָ לַמְחוֹת מְלָכִין
ʾAl-titten lanashim ḥeilekha, uderakhekha limḥot melakhin.
A close rendering is:
“Do not give your strength to women, or your ways to that which destroys kings.”
The Hebrew word ḥayil (חַיִל), appearing here as ḥeilekha, carries meanings associated with strength, capability, wealth, or resources.
And the warning is not merely about physical energy.
It concerns what a man gives away.
His strength.
