His attention.
His resources.
His integrity.
His capacity to lead wisely.
His ability to remain faithful to the responsibilities entrusted to him.
The language about women must also be understood carefully. This is not a declaration that women are dangerous or that female sexuality is inherently corrupt.
That interpretation would contradict the chapter itself, which goes on to honor a woman of wisdom, dignity, strength, and godly character.
The warning concerns a king surrendering himself to destructive sexual relationships and conduct that undermine his responsibilities.
The problem is not womanhood.
The problem is desire without wisdom, power without restraint, and pleasure pursued at the expense of faithfulness.
And that warning is not limited to men.
Because the human heart has never needed a crown to become intoxicated with what God has forbidden.
Some people are destroying their marriages for a moment of attention.
Some are sacrificing their integrity for a relationship they know they should leave.
Some are carrying secret conversations that would devastate their spouses if the messages were exposed.
Some have learned to quote Scripture publicly while privately negotiating with temptations they refuse to surrender.
Some are not physically unfaithful, but they are cultivating emotional intimacy with someone who is not their husband or wife.
And some have been wounded so deeply by betrayal that merely reading these words brings back memories they have spent years trying to bury.
Perhaps you know that pain.
Perhaps you are the person who was betrayed.
Perhaps you are the one who betrayed someone.
Perhaps nobody knows what you are fighting.
But God does.
And He is not exposing sin in His Word because He delights in humiliation.
He calls sinners into the light because darkness is a terrible place to build a life.
The tragedy of sexual sin is not simply that it breaks a rule.
It can break trust.
It can destroy families.
It can corrupt judgment.
It can turn people into objects to be consumed rather than neighbors to be loved.
It can teach a person to defend deception until lying feels normal.
And it can slowly persuade someone that temporary satisfaction is worth more than lasting faithfulness.
That is the danger King Lemuel's mother wanted him to recognize.
A person may possess tremendous authority over others and still lack authority over his own impulses.
A king may govern a nation while failing to govern himself.
And a Christian may know the language of holiness while resisting the surrender holiness requires.
Think about David.
A man who loved God.
A man who wrote psalms.
A man who experienced divine deliverance and received extraordinary responsibility.
Yet in 2 Samuel 11, David saw Bathsheba, sent for her, and took her while she was married to Uriah.
We must not soften the abuse of royal power in that account or place the blame upon Bathsheba.
David was the king.
David initiated the wrongdoing.
David orchestrated the attempt to conceal it.
And David arranged circumstances that led to Uriah's death.
The consequences were devastating.
David's story is not a warning about the seductive power of women.
It is a warning about what happens when a powerful man treats his desires as more important than God's commands and other people's dignity.
And when the prophet Nathan confronted him, David eventually confessed:
“I have sinned against the LORD.” — 2 Samuel 12:13, KJV
Those words matter.
Because repentance begins when we stop explaining away what God calls sin.
Not when we blame loneliness.
Not when we blame our spouse.
Not when we blame temptation.
Not when we say everybody does it.
But when we come before God without pretending.
“I have sinned.”
Three words in English that can mark the beginning of a changed life.
And yet the story does not end with David.
Consider Solomon.
A king associated with extraordinary wisdom, yet whose later life became marked by serious spiritual compromise.
According to 1 Kings 11:1–4, Solomon loved many foreign women, and his wives turned his heart toward other gods.
The passage condemns his disobedience and idolatry, not the inherent worth of women from other nations.
The warning is sobering.
You can possess wisdom and still refuse to obey it.
You can recognize danger and still walk toward it.
You can know what God says and still persuade yourself that your situation is somehow an exception.
And perhaps that is one of the most frightening forms of spiritual deception.
Not ignorance.
But knowing the truth while quietly arranging your life around a lie.
Yet Proverbs 31 does not stop at sexual warning.
The mother continues.
In verses 4–5, she warns Lemuel about intoxicating drink and the danger of impaired judgment.
In verses 8–9, she commands him to speak for those who cannot speak for themselves, to judge righteously, and to defend the rights of the poor and needy.
Do you see the connection?
The king must not become enslaved to his appetites because other people depend upon his judgment.
His moral choices are not isolated.
His private conduct can affect public justice.
His self-control is connected to his responsibility toward the vulnerable.
And then comes verse 10.
The passage everyone recognizes.
“Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies.” — Proverbs 31:10, KJV
But even here, something beautiful is hidden beneath the familiarity of the English words.
The Hebrew expression is:
אֵשֶׁת־חַיִל
ʾEshet ḥayil.
Often rendered “virtuous woman,” it can also communicate the idea of a woman of strength, excellence, capability, or noble character.
Notice that word again.
Ḥayil.
The same Hebrew noun family associated with the king's strength in verse 3 is used to describe the excellent woman in verse 10.
The connection is striking, even though we should be careful not to claim that the entire chapter rests upon this single repeated word.
The king is warned against giving away his strength in destructive relationships.
Then the poem celebrates a woman characterized by strength and excellence.
One passage warns against moral ruin.
The other honors faithful character.
And together they challenge the shallow way we sometimes talk about relationships.
Because Proverbs 31 is not teaching men to demand perfection from women while excusing their own lack of discipline.
Nor is it teaching women that their worth depends upon becoming exhausted, endlessly productive, or flawless.
The woman described in Proverbs 31:10–31 is not a social media performance.
She is a poetic portrait of wisdom expressed through faithful living.
The passage is an alphabetic acrostic in Hebrew, with its twenty-two verses beginning successively with the letters of the Hebrew alphabet.
It presents a comprehensive literary celebration of excellent character, not a checklist by which every woman must be measured every morning.
She works diligently.
She acts wisely.
She cares for her household.
She engages in productive enterprise.
She extends her hands to the needy.
She speaks with wisdom and kindness.
And above all, she fears the LORD.
Proverbs 31:30 declares:
“Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.” — KJV
That is the foundation.
Not appearance.
Not popularity.
Not wealth.
Not an impressive online image.
The fear of the LORD.
And that is not a principle reserved for women.
It is the foundation of biblical wisdom for everyone.
A man who fears the LORD cannot justify exploiting women.
A woman who fears the LORD is not called to excuse betrayal or abuse in the name of submission.
A husband who fears the LORD must learn to love sacrificially.
A wife who fears the LORD is worthy of dignity and honor.
And a single believer who fears the LORD is not spiritually incomplete because marriage has not happened.
The Gospel does not divide humanity into the married people who matter and the unmarried people who are waiting to matter.
Our deepest identity is not found in our relationship status.
It is found in our relationship with Jesus Christ.
And this is where the message becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us have spent years searching for a Proverbs 31 spouse while refusing to become a person of Proverbs-shaped character.
We want someone faithful while entertaining secret unfaithfulness.
We want someone honest while concealing our own compromises.
We want someone prayerful while neglecting prayer.
We want someone who fears God while keeping certain parts of our lives outside His authority.
We ask God to send someone trustworthy.
But have we become trustworthy?
We ask God to protect our future marriage.
But are we protecting our present integrity?
We ask God for a relationship that honors Christ.
But do our private decisions honor Him now?
These are uncomfortable questions.
They should be.
Because biblical wisdom does not exist merely to make us admire righteousness from a distance.
It calls us to live differently.
And yet there is another danger here.
The danger of turning this chapter into a weapon.
A weapon against women who are already exhausted.
A weapon against husbands who are struggling to grow.
A weapon against people carrying shame from sexual sins they have already confessed and abandoned.
A weapon against those whose marriages collapsed despite their sincere efforts to remain faithful.
A weapon against survivors of exploitation who were never responsible for the wrongdoing committed against them.
That is not what this passage was given to accomplish.
Scripture confronts sin.
But Scripture must never be twisted to excuse cruelty.
Jesus Christ never treated sexual sin as harmless.
Yet He also refused to reduce human beings to their worst moments.
Remember the woman at the well in John 4.
Jesus knew the complicated truth about her relationships.
He did not need her to perform innocence.
He did not pretend her circumstances were irrelevant.
But neither did He treat her as a disposable person.
He spoke to her about living water.
He revealed Himself to her.
And the woman who had come to draw water left with news she could not keep to herself.
She went back to her community and told people about Jesus.
The story is not merely about a woman with a difficult relational history.
It is about the Messiah revealing Himself and offering life.
That is the center of the Gospel.
Not that sinners are impressive.
Not that our past is harmless.
Not that repentance is optional.
But that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
And when we turn to Him, we discover that grace is neither permission to remain in bondage nor a reward for pretending we were never broken.
Grace meets us in truth.
And grace calls us into transformation.
Listen to the words of the apostle Paul.
In 1 Corinthians 6:18, he commands believers to flee sexual immorality.
The Greek phrase is:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
The verb pheugete is an imperative, a command to flee.
Not entertain it.
Not test how close you can get.
Not keep the conversation going because you think you are spiritually strong enough.
Flee.
Sometimes fleeing means ending the private conversation.
Sometimes it means deleting the secret account.
Sometimes it means confessing deception and seeking accountability.
Sometimes it means leaving a relationship that continually pulls you away from obedience to Christ.
Sometimes it means seeking pastoral guidance or professional help for entrenched patterns of sexual behavior.
And sometimes it means finally admitting that what you have been calling a harmless friendship has become an emotional betrayal.
But do not misunderstand.
Fleeing sin is not the same as fleeing a person who has been victimized.
If someone has been coerced, assaulted, manipulated, or abused, the responsibility belongs to the perpetrator. Seeking safety and trustworthy support is not a failure of faith.
God's call to holiness must never be used to silence those who have suffered injustice.
And for the person who knows they have sinned, there is still hope.
Real hope.
Not the cheap hope of pretending nothing happened.
Not the false hope of avoiding consequences.
But the costly hope purchased by Jesus Christ.
Because the same chapter of 1 Corinthians that warns about sexual immorality also reminds believers of the transforming work of God.
After naming various patterns of sinful living, Paul writes:
Such were some of you.
Not because their past never existed.
Not because sin suddenly became righteous.
But because the grace of God had reached them.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Not by their own moral résumé.
But in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God.
Perhaps you need to hear that tonight.
You are not beyond the reach of Christ because you have fallen.
You are not beyond His mercy because you have failed more than once.
You are not beyond forgiveness because your sin became public.
And you do not have to invent a spotless past before approaching the Savior who already knows the truth.
But neither should you confuse forgiveness with an excuse to keep returning deliberately to the same destructive choices.
Jesus calls us to repentance.
To turn away from sin and toward Him.
To bring our secrets into His light.
To surrender what has been controlling us.
And to learn obedience through the power of His Spirit.
Some consequences may remain.
Some relationships may require years of rebuilding.
Some trust may never be restored in the way we hoped.
Grace does not guarantee that every person we wounded will reconcile with us.
But grace does mean that our failure does not have to be the final authority over who we become.
And that brings us back to the mother in Proverbs 31.
I wonder how many tears were behind her instruction.
The text does not tell us.
We do not know whether she spoke from personal grief, observed tragedy, prophetic wisdom, or ordinary maternal concern.
We should not invent a biography for her.
But we can recognize the love expressed in the warning.
Because genuine love does not always sound like applause.
Sometimes love says, “Do not go there.”
Sometimes love says, “That relationship is destroying you.”
Sometimes love says, “Your family needs your faithfulness more than your reputation needs protecting.”
Sometimes love says, “Stop hiding.”
Sometimes love says, “Come back to God.”
And perhaps someone reading this has been resisting such a warning for months.
You know the conversation you need to end.
You know the confession you have been postponing.
You know the boundary you keep crossing.
You know the spiritual compromise you have dressed up with religious language.
And the Holy Spirit may be using the plain truth of Scripture to confront you right now.
Do not harden your heart.
Not because God is waiting for an opportunity to crush you.
But because the Savior who died for sinners is worthy of your surrender.
You do not need another inspirational quote that leaves your life unchanged.
You need Jesus.
Not merely as a religious symbol.
Not merely as someone you mention when life becomes difficult.
But as Lord.
As Savior.
As the One who has authority over your relationships, your body, your decisions, your money, your words, your ambitions, and the secret places of your heart.
Because Christianity is not about looking respectable while quietly making peace with sin.
It is about being reconciled to God through Jesus Christ and learning to walk in newness of life.
And here is something the Proverbs 31 conversation desperately needs.
The virtuous woman is not the savior of an undisciplined man.
A godly wife cannot repent on behalf of her husband.
A faithful husband cannot manufacture holiness inside his wife.
Marriage cannot do what only Christ can do.
You can marry someone beautiful and remain spiritually empty.
You can marry someone hardworking and remain unfaithful.
You can marry someone deeply devoted to God and still resist His Word yourself.
A spouse is not a substitute for surrender.
And if you are unmarried, you do not have to wait for a wedding to begin living faithfully.
Your calling to holiness is already real.
Your dignity is already real.
Your responsibility before God is already real.
And your worth in Christ is not postponed until someone chooses you.
The deepest question of Proverbs 31 is not simply, “Where can I find a virtuous woman?”
It is also, “Am I becoming a person shaped by the wisdom and fear of the LORD?”

Because when the chapter is read from beginning to end, it challenges the desires of the powerful, defends the vulnerable, honors excellent character, and directs our attention toward reverence for God.
And when we read it in the light of the whole Bible, it ultimately exposes our need for someone greater than Lemuel.
Greater than Solomon.
Greater than David.
Someone who never surrendered His righteousness to temptation.
Someone who used His authority not to exploit the vulnerable but to serve and save.
Someone who did not take advantage of the weak but gave Himself for sinners.
Jesus Christ.
The true King.
The faithful Son.
The sinless Savior.
The One who was tempted, yet without sin, as Hebrews 4:15 teaches.
The One who gave His life as a ransom for many, as Mark 10:45 declares.
The One who rose again so that those who trust in Him might receive forgiveness and new life.
This is why the Gospel is greater than self-improvement.
Because our greatest problem is not that we have failed to become the perfect Proverbs 31 man or woman.
Our greatest problem is sin.
And our greatest hope is Christ.
We do not earn salvation by achieving flawless moral discipline.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
Yet Ephesians 2:10 immediately reminds us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace saves us.
And the grace that saves us also begins changing how we live.
That is why repentance matters.
That is why holiness matters.
That is why faithfulness matters.
Not because we are trying to purchase God's love.
But because, in Christ, we have received a love that changes everything.
Maybe you are reading this with tears in your eyes.
Maybe you are thinking about the marriage you damaged.
The trust you broke.
The person you used.
The temptation you entertained.
The warning you ignored.
Or perhaps you are remembering how someone else's sin shattered your sense of safety.
If that is you, please hear this carefully.
The cross of Jesus Christ is not a declaration that your suffering was insignificant.
It is the place where God's justice and mercy are revealed with breathtaking seriousness.
Sin is so serious that Christ bore its judgment.
Grace is so extraordinary that Christ willingly gave Himself for sinners.
And resurrection means death and darkness do not have the final word.
You may not be able to rewrite yesterday.
But in Christ, yesterday does not have to dictate every tomorrow.
So pray.
Not with polished religious language.
Not with a performance designed to impress other believers.
Just speak to Him.

“Lord Jesus, You know the truth about me. You know what I have hidden, what I have justified, what I have suffered, and what I have done. Forgive my sins. Heal what is broken. Give me courage to repent, wisdom to make things right where I can, and strength to walk in obedience. Teach me to love what You love and turn away from what dishonors You. I cannot save myself. I need Your mercy, Your truth, and Your transforming grace. Amen.”
And if this message exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to reveal private details publicly to prove your repentance.
But you can take one honest step.
Not as a performance.
Not to earn approval.
But as a reminder that nobody should have to pretend they are spiritually invincible.
We need one another.
We need prayer.
We need biblical truth.
We need repentance.
We need encouragement.
And above everything else, we need Jesus Christ.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious content for a few seconds before they return to the same spiritual emptiness.
But to keep placing Scripture, conviction, encouragement, and the hope of the Gospel before people who desperately need truth.
There are believers who are hungry for God's Word but do not know where to begin.
There are families struggling to raise their children in the faith.
There are Christians trying to rebuild their lives after failure.
There are seekers asking whether Jesus could really forgive someone like them.
And there are people who may never walk into a church building today but might encounter a Scripture-centered message on their Facebook feed.
That is why your sharing matters.
Not merely because you agree with it.
But because someone connected to you may be standing at the very crossroads this passage describes.
Someone may be about to sacrifice a marriage for a secret relationship.
Someone may be wondering whether forgiveness is still possible.
Someone may be blaming themselves for betrayal they never deserved.
Someone may be searching for a reason to return to Christ.
You do not know who might read it.
And you do not know what God may do through His Word.
Because temptation rarely announces itself as destruction.
Sometimes it arrives as flattery.
Sometimes as loneliness.
Sometimes as a seemingly innocent conversation.
Sometimes as the comforting lie that nobody will ever know.
And when those moments come, you may need to remember the warning that stood before the famous Proverbs 31 woman.
And for those who believe in this mission and have the means to help it continue, I want to extend a personal invitation.
But let us keep something biblically clear.
The Bible teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Your salvation cannot be purchased.
God's favor cannot be bought.
And financial hardship does not make anyone less faithful.
You can honor Christ by praying, serving, sharing His Word, caring for people in need, and supporting sound ministry in ways appropriate to your circumstances.
These products can be reminders of faith, conversation starters, and resources for encouragement, but the real purpose of this ministry will always be greater than merchandise.
It is about pointing people to Jesus.
It is about helping believers grow.
It is about bringing biblical truth into places where confusion, compromise, shame, and spiritual exhaustion have taken root.
And it is about remembering that every person who encounters the Gospel is more important than any number on a screen.
Because the ultimate goal is not to build a following around a page.
It is to point people toward the Savior.
And that brings us to the question we began with.
Why does the famous chapter about the virtuous woman begin with a warning about destructive desire?
Because wisdom is not merely about recognizing the beauty of godly character in someone else.
It is about allowing God's truth to confront the desires within ourselves.
Because a beautiful relationship without faithfulness is fragile.
Because authority without self-control is dangerous.
Because religious knowledge without obedience can become a mask.
Because outward admiration of virtue is not the same as inward surrender to God.
And because the God who calls us to holiness is also the God who provides forgiveness and transforming grace through His Son.
So the next time someone quotes Proverbs 31:10, remember Proverbs 31:3.
Remember the mother who warned her son.
Remember the king who needed wisdom.
Remember the vulnerable people whose well-being depended upon righteous leadership.
Remember the woman whose true excellence was rooted in the fear of the LORD.
And above all, remember Jesus Christ.
The King who never failed.
The Savior who died for those who have.
The Lord who calls us to repent.
The Redeemer who makes new life possible.
The Proverbs 31 woman deserves to be honored.
But the warning before her description deserves to be heard.
And the Christ to whom all Scripture ultimately directs us deserves more than our admiration.
He deserves our faith.
Our repentance.
Our obedience.
Our worship.
Our lives.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that you once fell into sin—it is to hear the voice of grace calling you home and choose to remain where sin left you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU KEEP TELLING THE DEVIL TO FLEE… BUT HAVE YOU SURRENDERED TO GOD?
paragraphs: YOU KEEP TELLING THE DEVIL TO FLEE… BUT HAVE YOU SURRENDERED TO GOD?
The Forgotten Beginning of James 4:7 — Why the Enemy You Keep Fighting May Not Be Your Greatest Problem, and Why the Victory You Desperately Want Begins With the Surrender You Keep Avoiding.
There is something deeply unsettling about a Christian who knows how to rebuke the devil but has forgotten how to obey God.
Read that again.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is exhausted from fighting spiritual battles they cannot seem to win.
They have prayed. They have cried. They have declared Scripture over their circumstances. They have commanded the enemy to leave their home, their mind, their marriage, their finances, their future.
And yet, behind closed doors, there is still a conversation they know they should end.
A bitterness they refuse to release.
A secret they keep protecting.
A habit they keep excusing.
A command of Jesus they keep postponing.
They want the devil to leave.
But there are parts of their lives they still will not surrender to God.
And what makes this so heartbreaking is that they may have memorized the very verse that exposes the problem.
“Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
James 4:7.
Powerful words.
Biblical words.
Words that have strengthened countless believers in moments of temptation.
But those words are not the beginning of the verse.
And sometimes, what we leave out of Scripture is precisely what our hearts most desperately need to hear.

Because before James ever tells you to resist the devil, he gives you a command that confronts your pride, challenges your independence, and calls your entire life back under the authority of Jesus Christ.
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” — James 4:7, KJV
There it is.
The beginning we keep forgetting.
Submit yourselves therefore to God.
Not after you win.
Not when your circumstances improve.
Not when you finally understand everything God is doing.
Not when obedience becomes comfortable.
Submit.
And if those words make something inside you uncomfortable, please do not run from that discomfort too quickly.
Because sometimes the most merciful thing God does is confront the very thing that is quietly destroying us.
You may have been fighting the wrong battle.
Or, more precisely, you may have been trying to fight the right battle while refusing the surrender that belongs at its beginning.
And that changes everything.
The original Greek makes this even more striking.
James writes:
Hypotagēte oun tō theō; antistēte de tō diabolō, kai pheuxetai aph’ hymōn.
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
The word translated “submit” is ὑποτάγητε — hypotagēte, from the verb hypotassō, meaning to place under, subject oneself, or come under rightful authority.
It is an imperative.
A command.
Not a suggestion for unusually devoted Christians.
Not an optional spiritual exercise for people who have already mastered their emotions.
James is calling believers to yield themselves to God.
And notice the word immediately following it.
οὖν — oun.
“Therefore.”
Such a small word.
Such enormous significance.
Because “therefore” tells us that James is not beginning a new, disconnected thought.
He is drawing a conclusion from what he has already said.
And what he has already said should make every one of us examine our hearts.
In James 4:1, he asks where conflicts and quarrels come from.
His answer is painfully personal.
He points to desires waging war within us.
Not merely to the difficult people surrounding us.
Not merely to circumstances beyond our control.
Not merely to spiritual opposition.
He looks beneath the arguments, the envy, the frustrated ambitions, and the wounded pride.
He looks into the human heart.
James goes on to confront selfish desires, worldly loyalties, and the kind of friendship with the world that puts us in opposition to God.
Then comes James 4:6:
“God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.”
And only then:
“Submit yourselves therefore to God.”
Do you see it?
The command to submit grows directly out of the promise of grace to the humble.
James is not teaching that surrender earns God's love.
He is teaching that proud resistance to God must give way to humble dependence upon Him.
The tragedy is that we can become so focused on the devil's resistance against us that we fail to recognize our own resistance against God.
We notice every temptation.
Every attack.
Every disappointment.
Every closed door.
But we become strangely quiet when the Holy Spirit confronts our unforgiveness.
Our arrogance.
Our dishonesty.
Our compromise.
Our refusal to repent.
And perhaps the hardest question in this entire passage is not, “Why won't the devil leave me alone?”
Perhaps it is this:
What am I still refusing to place in God's hands?
That question followed me into the silence.
Because surrender sounds beautiful when it is written on a church banner.
It sounds inspiring when someone sings about it with tears in their eyes.
It sounds holy when we pray, “Lord, have Your way.”
Until having His way means forgiving someone who never apologized.
Until it means telling the truth when a lie would protect your reputation.
Until it means ending a relationship that repeatedly pulls you away from Christ.
Until it means surrendering the dream you have turned into an idol.
Until it means admitting that the person everyone thinks is spiritually strong is privately struggling.
Then surrender stops being a beautiful Christian expression.
It becomes a costly act of trust.
And suddenly we discover how much we love the idea of Jesus being our Savior while struggling with the reality of Jesus being our Lord.
We want His peace.
But sometimes we resist His correction.
We want His promises.
But sometimes we negotiate with His commands.
We want the comfort of His presence.
But we hesitate when His Word exposes something we have grown comfortable hiding.
And yet the Lord does not confront us because He delights in humiliating us.
He confronts us because He loves us too much to leave us enslaved to what is destroying us.
There is a difference between condemnation that drives you away from Christ and godly conviction that calls you back to Him.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
And Romans 2:4 teaches that the goodness of God leads us toward repentance.
That is the heart of this message.
Not that God is waiting for you to become flawless before He welcomes you.
But that His grace is far too precious to be reduced to permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus did not shed His blood so that we could make peace with the sin that enslaves us.
He came to redeem sinners.
To forgive.
To cleanse.
To reconcile us to the Father.
To make us new.
And sometimes the first evidence of that transforming grace is the painful honesty of a prayer we have avoided for years:
“Lord, I have been asking You to change everything around me while resisting what You want to change inside me.”
Maybe you know that prayer.
Maybe you are living inside it right now.
Maybe you are the husband who keeps praying for peace in his marriage but refuses to apologize for the words that wounded his wife.
Maybe you are the wife who asks God to restore tenderness while quietly allowing resentment to harden her heart.
Maybe you are the parent who wants children who love Jesus but has never learned to admit when you were wrong.
Maybe you are the young believer who posts verses about holiness while privately returning to something you know is pulling your heart away from Christ.
Maybe you are the church worker who serves faithfully in public but is slowly becoming bitter in private.
Maybe you are the person who can explain spiritual warfare to everyone else but cannot remember the last time you sat alone before God and said:
“Search me.”
Not my enemies.
Not my critics.
Not the people who hurt me.
Me.
“Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts.” — Psalm 139:23, KJV
That prayer requires courage.
Because the Lord may reveal something we have spent years explaining away.
But He does not expose our sin merely to leave us ashamed.
He calls us out of darkness and toward the light of His mercy.
And there is a scene in Scripture that captures this beautifully.
A woman stands before Jesus.
Her life has become a public scandal.
Her sin is no longer hidden.
Her accusers are ready to make her disgrace the final word over her existence.
John 8 tells us that she was brought before Jesus after being caught in adultery.
The people surrounding her wanted judgment.
They wanted to use her situation to trap Jesus.
But Jesus refused to play their cruel game.
One by one, her accusers departed.
Then Jesus spoke to the woman.
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Look carefully at those words.
He did not excuse her sin.
And He did not reduce her to her sin.
He extended mercy while calling her to leave her sinful way of life.
That is the breathtaking beauty of Christ.
He does not need to pretend your darkness is light in order to love you.
He can tell you the truth about your sin while offering you the grace you could never deserve.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
It is the fitting response of a heart being drawn back to the God of grace.
And that is why submission is not spiritual defeat.
It is the proper response of a redeemed person to the Lord who saved them.
But we need to be careful here.
James 4:7 is not a formula that guarantees every hardship, intrusive thought, illness, or painful circumstance will disappear the moment you surrender.
The promise that the devil will flee is not a promise that Christians will never again experience temptation or spiritual conflict.
Scripture itself shows faithful believers enduring trials.
Even Jesus was tempted by the devil in the wilderness.
And the apostle Paul experienced suffering while remaining devoted to Christ.
So we must never use this passage to accuse suffering believers of secretly refusing to submit to God.
That would wound people whom Scripture calls us to encourage.
James is speaking about humble allegiance to God and steadfast opposition to the devil.
The command translated “resist” comes from ἀντίστητε — antistēte, from anthistēmi, meaning to stand against or oppose.
It too is an imperative.
James calls believers to take a definite stand against the devil.
But he places that command alongside submission to God.
The two belong together.
Resistance is not presented as a display of independent spiritual power.
It is the stand of someone whose allegiance belongs to God.
And that matters.
Because the authority we desperately need does not originate in our volume, our confidence, or our ability to sound powerful in prayer.
Our hope rests in Jesus Christ.
The One who resisted Satan's temptations in the wilderness.
The One who obeyed the Father where we have failed.
The One who bore our sins on the cross.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One whose victory over sin and death is not dependent on our emotional strength.
Colossians 2:15 speaks of Christ's triumph over the hostile powers through the cross.
Hebrews 2:14 teaches that through death Jesus defeated the one who held the power of death, that is, the devil.
And 1 John 3:8 declares that the Son of God was manifested to destroy the works of the devil.
Our confidence is not that we have finally become strong enough to save ourselves.
Our confidence is that Jesus is the victorious Savior.
This is why Christian submission is so different from surrendering to a cruel master.
You are yielding yourself to the One who gave Himself for you.
The One who washed His disciples' feet.
The One who welcomed the repentant.
The One who wept at a friend's tomb.
The One who prayed in Gethsemane:
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42, KJV
Think about that.
The sinless Son submitted Himself to the Father's will, even as the cross approached.
He did not need to repent.
He had no rebellion to confess.
Yet in perfect obedience, He embraced the Father's redemptive purpose.
And because He obeyed, suffered, died, and rose again, sinners like us can be forgiven and reconciled to God.
Philippians 2:8 says that Christ “humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.”
We do not submit to God in order to complete what Jesus failed to accomplish.
We submit because the Savior who accomplished our redemption is worthy of our whole lives.
That is where everything changes.
Because surrender is no longer merely about what you must give up.
It becomes about the One you are finally learning to trust.
Perhaps you have been holding onto control because control makes you feel safe.
Perhaps your heart learned long ago that trusting someone could lead to disappointment.
Perhaps you have been betrayed, abandoned, manipulated, or wounded by people who claimed to love you.
And now, even when you pray, a part of you whispers:
“What if I surrender and everything falls apart?”
That fear deserves compassion.
But it also deserves the truth.
God is not another broken human being asking for your trust while hiding selfish intentions.
His character is revealed supremely in Jesus Christ.
The cross is not proof that following Him will always be comfortable.
It is proof of the depth of His sacrificial love.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Before we could repair our reputations.
Before we could undo our mistakes.
Before we could offer Him a life worthy of His holiness.
Christ died for us.
So when God calls you to surrender, He is not asking you to purchase His mercy with your obedience.
He is calling you to respond to mercy with faith.
To stop pretending that your wisdom is greater than His.
To stop defending the sin that Christ died to redeem you from.
To stop treating His commands as obstacles to your happiness when they are expressions of His holy wisdom.
And to trust Him even when obedience costs something.
But perhaps the most overlooked beauty of James 4 is what comes immediately after the command to resist the devil.
James 4:8 says:
“Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.”
Do not rush past that.
The passage does not merely call you away from the devil.
It calls you toward God.
That is the destination.
Not spiritual pride.
Not a life consumed with fear of demons.
Not an endless obsession with detecting attacks.
God Himself.
The God who gives grace to the humble.
The God who calls sinners to repentance.
The God who welcomes those who draw near through Christ.
The God who is not impressed by religious performance but sees the truth of the heart.
James continues by calling for cleansing, purity of heart, mourning over sin, and humility before the Lord.
Then comes another promise.
“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.” — James 4:10, KJV
The chapter begins with conflicts born from disordered desires.
It confronts pride.
It commands submission.
It calls for repentance.
And it promises grace to the humble.
That is the movement of the passage.
From pride to humility.
From divided loyalties to renewed allegiance.
From resistance against God to submission before Him.
From sin toward repentance.
From spiritual self-sufficiency toward dependence upon divine grace.
And at the center of our hope stands Jesus Christ.
Not a motivational slogan.
Not a spiritual technique.
A Savior.
And perhaps this is the moment when the words finally become personal.
Because it is possible to read an article about surrender and still avoid surrendering.
It is possible to feel convicted and then distract yourself until the feeling fades.
It is possible to share a powerful Scripture and never allow that Scripture to confront your own heart.
It is possible to agree with everything you have read and still refuse the one act of obedience God has already made clear.
What have I been calling a struggle that I am actually choosing to protect?
Not every struggle is willful rebellion. Some involve deep wounds, persistent temptation, illness, or circumstances beyond our control.
But sometimes we know the difference.
We know when we are fighting temptation.
And we know when we are making arrangements to return to it.
We know when forgiveness is difficult.
And we know when we have decided to nourish resentment.
We know when we are seeking God's will.
And we know when we are asking Him to approve a decision we have already made.
That recognition can hurt.
But it can also become the beginning of repentance.
You do not have to perform your brokenness for an audience.
You do not have to tell strangers every private detail.
You do not have to manufacture tears to prove that you are sincere.
You can simply come to Jesus.
Confess what is true.
Receive His mercy.
And take the next faithful step.
First John 1:9 offers this assurance:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Those are not small words.
They are the language of hope for people who know they cannot save themselves.
Maybe you have fallen so many times that you are embarrassed to pray again.
Maybe you promised God you would never return to that sin, only to find yourself grieving another failure.
Maybe you have been hiding behind ministry, work, family responsibilities, or religious activity because silence makes it harder to avoid the truth.
Hear this carefully.
Your repeated failure is not a reason to abandon Christ.
It is a reason to stop trusting your own strength and return to Him with humility.
Repentance is not pretending that sin has no consequences.
Forgiveness does not erase every earthly consequence or instantly repair every damaged relationship.
And grace does not mean that difficult patterns disappear without patient obedience, wise counsel, accountability, and sometimes professional help.
But no failure is greater than the sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice for those who turn to Him in faith.
You can come out of hiding.
You can confess.
You can seek reconciliation where it is right and safe to do so.
You can ask for help.
You can begin walking in the light.
And when you stumble, you can return to the Savior rather than surrendering to despair.
This is the Gospel.
Not that good people finally become good enough for God.
But that Jesus Christ saves sinners by grace through faith, and His grace begins transforming the lives of those who belong to Him.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds these truths together.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works.
And we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Salvation is God's gift.
Obedience is the fruit of His transforming grace, not the price of admission into His family.
That distinction matters more than we sometimes realize.
Because without it, surrender becomes another desperate attempt to earn the love that Christ has already demonstrated at the cross.
But with it, surrender becomes worship.
The response of a heart that can finally say:
“Jesus, You gave Yourself for me. I do not want to keep withholding my life from You.”
And now I want to ask you something that goes beyond this article.
If these words have exposed a hidden battle, would you be willing to stop hiding behind the appearance of strength?
You do not need to share the details publicly.
Not because a comment earns God's attention.
Not because public words replace private repentance.
But because sometimes a simple, honest response helps us stop pretending we are the only ones who struggle.
Your story may encourage someone who is afraid they have wandered too far to return.
There is another reason I hope you will not simply read this and move on.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be carrying a battle they have never told anyone about.
The father who feels he has failed his family.
The young woman quietly wondering whether God still wants her.
The believer who has not prayed honestly in months.
The friend who once loved Jesus passionately but has slowly drifted away.
The person who thinks the church has no room for someone with their past.
You may never know who needs to encounter James 4:7 in its proper context.
Not as a way of proving your spirituality.
Not to collect reactions.
But as a simple act of pointing people toward Scripture and the Savior it reveals.
It is to submit yourself to God.
Because following Jesus was never meant to be reduced to a moment of emotional inspiration.
We need His Word tomorrow.
And the day after.
We need truth when feelings change.
We need encouragement when obedience becomes difficult.
We need reminders of grace when shame tries to speak louder than the cross.
That is also why we are continuing to build and expand Gospel Warrior as a place for biblical encouragement and discipleship.
These resources are intended to help people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, understand the Gospel, and continue growing beyond a single post.
And if Gospel Warrior has become part of your spiritual encouragement, I want to extend a personal invitation.
But we must honor what those passages actually teach.
It is a voluntary way to support this particular ministry.
You do not have to give money to prove your love for Jesus.
And you do not have to purchase access to His grace.
Christ has already paid the price of our redemption.
But if you believe this work is helping people encounter biblical truth, and you have the means and desire to support it, your partnership can help us continue and expand that work.

Even a modest monthly commitment, given freely and responsibly, can become part of a larger effort to encourage believers, reach people who are searching, and point hurting hearts toward Jesus Christ.
Some will be able to give.
Some will be able to share.
Some will be able to pray.
And all of us can seek to honor Christ faithfully with what God has entrusted to us.
Because the mission is not to build a platform around a personality.
It is to keep pointing people toward the Person who changes everything.
Jesus Christ.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who gives grace to the humble.
The One who calls His people out of darkness.
The One who never asks us to find salvation in our own strength.
The One who loved us enough to die and rose again so that those who trust Him might have life.
And now, as we return to the words that began this journey, I hope you hear them differently.
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
James 4:7.
Perhaps you came here looking for another way to fight the enemy.
And instead, Scripture has invited you to examine your allegiance.
Perhaps you came wanting a stronger declaration.
And instead, you have discovered the need for a humbler prayer.
Perhaps you came hoping God would change your circumstances.
And He has reminded you that His grace is also at work changing your heart.
Do not misunderstand.
You may still face battles tomorrow.
Temptation may still come.
Grief may still hurt.
Healing may still take time.
And obedience may still be costly.
But you do not have to face those things as someone trying to manufacture victory apart from Christ.
You can stand in faith, clothed in the armor of God described in Ephesians 6, depending upon the strength of the Lord.
You can resist the devil while submitting to God.
You can confess your sin without surrendering to hopelessness.
You can grieve your failures without believing they are the final word over your life.
You can stop pretending.
And you can come home to the Father through Jesus Christ.
So perhaps tonight, your most important prayer will not be long.
Perhaps it will not sound impressive.
Perhaps nobody else will hear it.
Perhaps it will be spoken through tears beside a bed, behind a closed door, in a parked car, or in the silence after everyone else has fallen asleep.
“Father, I have been trying to control what belongs in Your hands.
I have called myself surrendered while protecting things You have told me to release.
I have sometimes been quicker to recognize the enemy's temptations than to acknowledge my own pride.
Forgive me.
Thank You for sending Jesus Christ to save sinners like me.
Thank You that His sacrifice is sufficient and His mercy is greater than my failures.
Teach me to submit to You.
Give me courage to resist temptation.
Help me obey Your Word even when obedience is uncomfortable.
Cleanse what I have hidden.
Heal what is wounded.
Restore what can be restored.
Give me wisdom to seek help where I need it.
And make my life a testimony, not of how strong I am, but of how faithful You are.
In the name of Jesus Christ.
Amen.”
And before you leave, remember the woman standing before Jesus with her scandal exposed.
Remember Peter, who denied the Lord and was later restored to serve Him.
Remember the prodigal son, who came home with nothing to boast about and found a father ready to welcome him.
Remember the thief on the cross, who had no lifetime of good works left to offer, yet turned to Jesus in faith and received His promise.
Different people.
Different failures.
Different stories.
But the same astonishing truth.
Human sin does not have to be the final chapter when the grace of Jesus Christ enters the story.
The cross is not a denial of how serious sin is.
It is the greatest demonstration of both God's holiness and His redeeming love.
And the empty tomb declares that death itself does not get the last word over those who belong to Christ.
So do not walk away merely remembering a Greek word.
Remember the Savior to whom that word calls you to surrender.
Do not merely admire the beauty of repentance.
Repent.
Do not merely speak about grace.
Receive it by faith.
Do not merely quote the promise that the devil will flee.
Begin where James begins.
Submit yourself to God.
Because the greatest transformation in your story may begin at the very moment you stop insisting on writing every chapter yourself.
The scandal may explain where you have been, but through Jesus Christ, it does not have to decide who you become.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE SERPENT BRUISED HIS HEEL… BUT HE NEVER SAW HIS OWN HEAD ABOUT TO BE CRUSHED
paragraphs: THE SERPENT BRUISED HIS HEEL… BUT HE NEVER SAW HIS OWN HEAD ABOUT TO BE CRUSHED

The first promise of Jesus Christ was spoken in the middle of humanity’s greatest scandal. Before the nails, before the crown of thorns, before the empty tomb, God had already announced that the serpent’s victory would become his defeat. And buried inside that ancient promise is a truth that could change the way you see your sin, your suffering, your battles, and the Savior who refused to abandon you.
There was a moment in human history when everything beautiful broke.
No armies marched. No cities burned. No nails pierced a Savior’s hands.
There was only a garden.
A man. A woman. A serpent.
And a question that sounded innocent enough to destroy the world.
“Yea, hath God said…?” (Genesis 3:1, KJV).
That was how the serpent began.
Not with a sword.
With suspicion.
He did not need to convince Eve that God did not exist. He only needed her to question whether God could be trusted.
And isn't that still how so many of our darkest battles begin?
A quiet thought that God is withholding something good. A temptation that promises relief. A compromise that seems harmless. A secret decision nobody else will ever know about.
Until everything changes.
Adam and Eve ate the forbidden fruit.
Their eyes were opened.
But instead of becoming what the serpent had promised, they discovered something terrifying.
They were naked.
They were ashamed.
And for the first time, the people who had walked in fellowship with God wanted to hide from Him.
Imagine that.
The hands that had never trembled with guilt were suddenly reaching for leaves to cover their shame.
The hearts that had known no fear were now racing at the sound of their Creator approaching.
And when God called, “Where art thou?” (Genesis 3:9), Adam did not run toward the voice that had given him life.
He hid.
That is the tragedy of sin.
It does not merely lead us into disobedience.
It teaches us to fear the very God whose presence we were created to enjoy.
Maybe you know something about that.
Maybe you still pray, but there are things you cannot bring yourself to confess.
Maybe you worship on Sunday while carrying a secret you hope nobody discovers on Monday.
Maybe people see your Bible verses, your church attendance, your smiling photographs, and your encouraging words.
But they do not see what happens when the room becomes quiet.
The regret.
The temptation.
The memories.
The private battles.
The shame that whispers, If they knew everything about you, they would never look at you the same way again.
And perhaps the most painful thought of all:
How could God still want someone like me?
If that question has ever kept you awake at night, you need to hear what happened next in Eden.
Because before Adam and Eve could repair anything, before they could offer a sacrifice, before they could prove that they deserved another opportunity, God spoke a promise.
Not first to Adam.
Not first to Eve.
But to the serpent.
And that promise would eventually lead to a bloodstained cross outside Jerusalem.
Genesis 3:15 records these words:
“And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.” (KJV)
Read those words again.
The serpent would strike.
But the serpent would not have the final victory.
Hidden in the judgment pronounced in Eden was the first announcement of a conflict that would reach its decisive turning point at Calvary.
Christian theology has long called this verse the protoevangelium, a Latin term meaning “first gospel.”
It is the first glimpse of the good news within the unfolding biblical story.
And to understand how astonishing that is, we need to look carefully at what the Hebrew actually says.
The Hebrew text of Genesis 3:15 includes this extraordinary declaration:
הוּא יְשׁוּפְךָ רֹאשׁ וְאַתָּה תְּשׁוּפֶנּוּ עָקֵב
Hu yeshufkha rosh, ve'attah teshufennu aqev.
A close translation is:
“He will strike you at the head, and you will strike him at the heel.”
The Hebrew verb שׁוּף (shuf) is used for both actions. Depending on its context, it can convey striking, bruising, or crushing.
That matters.
Because some Christians have heard this passage explained as though the original Hebrew uses two completely different verbs, one for a minor injury and another for a fatal blow.
It does not.
The same verb appears in both clauses.
The contrast is found especially in the location of the blows.
The head.
And the heel.
A serpent striking a heel can cause terrible injury, even death.
A blow to a serpent’s head, however, points toward the destruction of its power.

The ancient Greek Septuagint renders the decisive clause with language meaning that he will watch for or strike at the serpent’s head, while the serpent will watch for or strike at his heel. This reminds us not to build the entire doctrine on a single English word.
The victory is understood through the whole testimony of Scripture.
And that testimony leads us to Jesus Christ.
But notice something else.
Genesis 3:15 speaks of the woman’s “seed,” or offspring.
The Hebrew word זֶרַע (zeraʿ) can refer collectively to descendants or to an individual descendant, depending on context.
The verse begins with hostility between two lines of offspring, yet its language also allows the reader to focus on a particular representative.
Genesis itself does not yet identify that descendant by name.
The promise unfolds through the rest of the Bible.
Through Abraham.
Through Judah.
Through David.
Through the prophets.
Until, in the fullness of time, a child is born in Bethlehem.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of God.
Born of a woman (Galatians 4:4).
The promised Messiah.
The One who came not merely to improve human behavior, but to confront the ruin sin had brought into the world.
Think about the wonder of that.
The first humans had fallen.
The garden had been corrupted.
The relationship had been broken.
And before the story had even left Eden, God had already revealed that evil would face an enemy it could not ultimately overcome.
Humanity had rebelled.
Yet God was not finished with humanity.
That does not mean sin was harmless.
It does not mean judgment disappeared.
Adam and Eve were expelled from Eden. Suffering and death entered the human story. The consequences of their rebellion were real.
But judgment was not the only word spoken that day.
There was also promise.
And that promise was greater than Adam and Eve could possibly have understood.
Centuries passed.
Generations were born and buried.
Kingdoms rose and collapsed.
God’s people repeatedly wandered into idolatry, injustice, unbelief, and rebellion.
Still, the promise continued.
Then one night, in the humility of Bethlehem, the promised Redeemer entered the world.
Not with the appearance of an earthly conqueror.
But as a baby laid in a manger.
The One through whom all things were made had taken on human flesh.
The eternal Son had entered the very world wounded by human rebellion.
And from the beginning, His earthly life was marked by opposition.
Herod sought to destroy Him.
Satan tempted Him in the wilderness.
Religious leaders plotted against Him.
His own disciple betrayed Him.
His friends abandoned Him.
And eventually, the crowds that had heard His teaching and witnessed His works would see Him condemned to death.
It looked as though darkness was winning.
But darkness had misunderstood the mission of Jesus.
He had not come to avoid suffering at all costs.
He had come to save sinners through His obedient life, sacrificial death, and victorious resurrection.
Listen to the words of 1 John 3:8:
“For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil.” (KJV)
Not negotiate with them.
Not surrender to them.
Destroy them.
And Hebrews 2:14 explains that through death, Christ would destroy the devil’s power over death.
Through death.
Do you see the astonishing reversal?
The very weapon that appeared to secure Satan’s victory became the means by which Christ accomplished redemption.
The cross was not an interruption of God's saving purpose.
It was central to that purpose.
Now imagine Jerusalem.
The morning air heavy with dust.
Roman soldiers moving through the streets.
A crowd gathering around a condemned man.
His back torn by scourging.
His face disfigured by violence.
A crown of thorns pressed into His head.
The hands that had touched lepers and restored the broken were about to be fastened to wood.
The feet that had walked toward the rejected and the forgotten were about to be pierced.
And the Son of God would hang between criminals.
To the watching world, it looked like humiliation.
To His enemies, it looked like defeat.
To His frightened disciples, it looked like the end of everything they had hoped for.
But Scripture reveals something the crowd could not see.
The suffering of Jesus was not merely the cruelty of men.
It was also the fulfillment of God's redemptive purpose.
Isaiah had foretold:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” (Isaiah 53:5, KJV)
And Peter would later write:
Jesus was not suffering for His own sins.
He had none.
He was bearing the sins of others.
Our pride.
Our rebellion.
Our dishonesty.
Our lust.
Our selfishness.
Our bitterness.
Our refusal to trust God.
Every sin that we are tempted to minimize was serious enough that our redemption required the death of the sinless Son of God.
That truth should humble us.
Because the cross tells us something about sin that our culture rarely wants to admit.
Sin is not merely a mistake.
It is rebellion against a holy God.
And yet the same cross tells us something about divine love that shame struggles to believe.
God did not wait for sinners to make themselves worthy before sending His Son.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had cleaned up every secret.
Not after we had mastered every temptation.
Not after we had repaired every broken relationship.
Christ died for sinners.
This does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible without pretending that we can save ourselves.
And then came the moment.
Jesus cried out:
“It is finished.” (John 19:30, KJV)
The Greek word recorded in John's Gospel is τετέλεσται (tetelestai).
It comes from the verb teleō, meaning to finish, accomplish, or bring something to completion.
It is a perfect-tense form, expressing an action brought to completion with an abiding result.
The word itself does not automatically mean “paid in full” in every context, even though related forms could appear in financial settings.
Here, its meaning is anchored in the mission Jesus had come to accomplish.
He had completed the work entrusted to Him.
His obedient sacrifice was not a failed rescue attempt.
It was the fulfillment of His saving mission.
John tells us that after saying these words, Jesus bowed His head and gave up His spirit.
The soldiers saw a dead man.
The disciples faced overwhelming grief.
His body was placed in a tomb.
A stone was rolled across the entrance.
And silence settled over Jerusalem.
But the serpent had not won.
Because on the third day, the tomb was empty.
Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead.
Death could not hold Him.
The grave could not keep Him.
And the resurrection publicly vindicated the One who had been condemned.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15:54–57 that death is swallowed up in victory and that God gives us victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
The resurrection is not simply an inspirational ending to a tragic story.
It is God's declaration that the crucified Jesus is the victorious Lord.
The heel had been struck.
But the promised victory belonged to Christ.
Colossians 2:14–15 describes how Christ dealt with the record of debt against us and triumphed over the hostile powers through the cross.
And Romans 16:20 gives believers an extraordinary promise:
“And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly.” (KJV)
There is the language of Genesis again.
The serpent.
The crushing.
The victory.
Only now the people of God are included in the triumph of their Lord.
Not because believers possess independent power over Satan.
Not because Christians are incapable of being tempted.
Not because the battle against evil has already disappeared from our daily experience.
But because the risen Christ has secured the decisive victory, and those who belong to Him will share in its final fulfillment.
Revelation 20:10 looks ahead to the ultimate judgment of the devil.
The enemy's final defeat is certain in the biblical story.
Yet until that final judgment, Christians still live in a world where temptation, suffering, persecution, and death remain painfully real.
That is why this promise matters so deeply.
Because perhaps you are reading this while facing something you thought you would have overcome by now.
Maybe you have repented of the same sin more times than you can count.
Maybe your marriage is strained.
Maybe your family is broken.
Maybe you have buried someone you love, and the silence of their absence feels unbearable.
Maybe you have served in church while secretly wondering why your own heart feels so far from God.
Or maybe your greatest battle is the voice that keeps telling you your past has permanently disqualified you from being loved.
Hear this carefully.
The victory of Jesus does not mean your wounds are imaginary. It means your wounds do not have the authority to overturn His promises.
You may still need to confess what you have hidden.
You may still need to seek forgiveness from someone you have hurt.
You may need to walk away from a relationship that keeps drawing you into sin.
You may need pastoral counsel, accountability, professional help, or the patient support of people who will tell you the truth in love.
Grace does not excuse what destroys us.
Grace teaches us to turn away from it.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God teaches believers to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live soberly, righteously, and godly.
That is one of the most beautiful and challenging truths of the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely forgive us so that we can remain comfortable in the darkness.
He saves us to bring us into the light.
And sometimes coming into the light hurts.
It hurts to admit that the person you have blamed for years is not responsible for every decision you have made.
It hurts to acknowledge that the addiction you keep defending is enslaving you.
It hurts to confess that your religious appearance has become more important to you than your private obedience.
It hurts to admit that you have been asking God to bless a life you have refused to surrender to Him.
But there is mercy in that exposure.
Because the Savior who calls you to repentance is the same Savior who stretched out His arms on the cross for sinners.
Remember Adam in the garden.
He hid among the trees.
And God called to him.
Now remember Jesus at Calvary.
He was nailed to a tree.
And through His sacrifice, guilty sinners can be reconciled to God.
In Eden, human beings grasped at what God had forbidden.
At Calvary, the obedient Son submitted to the Father's will.
In Eden, shame led humanity into hiding.
Through Christ, forgiven sinners are invited to approach God with confidence.
In Eden, sin brought death into the human story.
Through the risen Christ, eternal life is promised to all who believe in Him.
Paul draws the great comparison between Adam and Christ in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15.
Through Adam came sin and death.
Through Christ come righteousness, resurrection, and life for those who belong to Him.
The Bible is not a collection of disconnected moral lessons.
It is the unfolding story of God's holiness, humanity's rebellion, and His saving purpose fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
From the garden to the cross.
From the cross to the empty tomb.
From the empty tomb to the promised restoration of all things.
And in Revelation 22, the Bible's closing vision brings us back to the imagery of life, the tree of life, and the removal of the curse.
What humanity lost through rebellion cannot be recovered by human effort.
But God has acted in Christ to bring His people into the life they could never earn.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior is more than a memorable phrase.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because every earthly story receives the ending we wanted.
But because Christ can redeem sinners, reconcile them to God, transform their lives, and give them a future that sin and death cannot finally destroy.
Think about Peter.
He promised that he would never abandon Jesus.
Then, under pressure, he denied knowing Him three times.
Imagine the sound of the rooster.
Imagine Peter remembering the words of Jesus.
Imagine the unbearable realization that his courage had collapsed when it mattered most.
Luke 22:62 tells us that Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Yet the risen Jesus did not leave Peter's story at that courtyard.
In John 21, Jesus restored Peter and called him again to serve.
Peter's denial was real.
His grief was real.
His restoration was real.
And the grace of Christ was greater than his failure.
Perhaps you needed to remember that today.
Not because your failure is unimportant.
But because your failure is not more powerful than the Savior.
Peter could not undo his denial.
But Jesus could restore him.
The thief on the cross could not go back and live a different life.
But Jesus could promise him paradise (Luke 23:43).
Paul could not erase his history of persecuting Christians.
But the risen Christ could show him mercy and transform him into a servant of the Gospel (1 Timothy 1:12–16).
And you cannot travel backward through time to undo every word, every choice, or every betrayal.
But you can turn to the Savior who died and rose again.
You can repent.
You can believe.
You can begin walking in obedience today.
You can seek reconciliation where possible.
You can tell the truth.
You can stop hiding behind religious language and finally bring your actual heart before God.
And if you have already placed your faith in Jesus, you can remember that your standing before God rests on Christ, not on your ability to maintain the appearance of perfection.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus…” (KJV)
That promise is not a license to cherish sin.
It is freedom from condemnation for those who belong to Christ.
And when believers stumble, 1 John 1:9 calls them to confess their sins, trusting God's faithfulness and righteousness to forgive and cleanse.
Maybe the enemy has been reminding you of everything you used to be.
But the Gospel invites you to remember who Jesus is.
The serpent is not your savior.
Your shame is not your judge.
Your past is not your redeemer.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And His resurrection is not dependent on whether you feel victorious this morning.
He is risen whether your hands are trembling.
He is risen whether your prayers come through tears.
He is risen whether your healing takes longer than you expected.
He is risen whether the people who wounded you ever apologize.
And because He lives, those who trust in Him have a living hope.
There is something deeply personal about this.
Somewhere, someone is reading these words while sitting beside a hospital bed.
Someone is reading while wondering how to pay the next bill.
Someone is reading after a night of fighting temptation.
Someone is reading with a Bible open and tears falling onto the pages.
Someone is reading after being told that their life will never amount to anything.
And someone is reading who has not prayed sincerely in years.
If that someone is you, please understand what the promise in Genesis 3:15 is ultimately pointing toward.
Not a secret technique for making every problem disappear.
Not a guarantee that faithful Christians will never suffer.
Not a declaration that you can defeat the devil through your own strength.
It points toward Jesus Christ, the promised Redeemer, whose death and resurrection have decisively confronted sin, death, and the devil.
And He calls you to Himself.
Not to an image you have carefully constructed.
Not to a religious performance.
To Himself.
Jesus said:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Matthew 11:28, KJV)
That invitation is still beautiful.
Still urgent.
Still true.
If you have never trusted Christ, do not confuse admiration for Jesus with surrender to Jesus.
The Gospel calls us to repent and believe (Mark 1:15).
Acknowledge your sin before God.
Stop treating His mercy as something you can earn.
Trust in the crucified and risen Savior.
And follow Him.
If you are a believer who has wandered, do not make peace with the darkness.
Come back into the light.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Seek help where help is needed.
Return to Scripture.
Return to prayer.
Return to fellowship with faithful believers.
And remember that the One who began a good work in His people is faithful to carry it forward (Philippians 1:6).
Perhaps you need words to begin.
You can pray something like this, not as a formula that earns salvation, but as an honest expression of repentance and faith:

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I have tried to hide what You already know. I cannot save myself, and I cannot undo my past. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising from the dead. I turn away from my sin and place my trust in You. Forgive me, change my heart, teach me to obey You, and help me walk in Your truth. I belong to You. Amen.”
And if that prayer reflects the sincere cry of your heart, do not keep your journey isolated.
Find a faithful, Bible-teaching local church.
Seek baptism and discipleship.
Open the Scriptures.
Learn to follow Jesus in ordinary, costly, beautiful obedience.
Because the Christian life is not only about the moment you first believe.
It is about a lifetime of being shaped by the grace and truth of Christ.
And that brings me to something I want to ask you personally.
If this message has uncovered a battle you have been fighting in silence, would you be willing to speak honestly?
You do not need to reveal private details or expose wounds you are not ready to share.
Or, if you are struggling to hold on:
“I'm still fighting.”
And if you need prayer:
“Pray for me.”
Not because a comment saves you.
Not because public confession is a substitute for repentance before God.
But because someone else reading may be convinced that they are the only person who is struggling.
Your few words might remind them that they are not alone, and that hope is found in Jesus Christ.
Not to glorify the past.
But to glorify the Savior.
There may also be someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this message.
Someone who used to be active in church but has quietly disappeared.
Someone who keeps posting that everything is fine while privately falling apart.
Someone in your family who has been carrying guilt for years.
Someone who does not yet know Christ.
Not as another piece of content to fill a feed.
But as a way of placing the truth of Scripture where someone might encounter it at the right moment.
Send it privately to someone who needs compassion more than public attention.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who need strengthening, those who have grown spiritually cold, and those who are still seeking answers to follow as well.
We are building a community that wants more than momentary inspiration.
We want to know Christ more deeply.
To understand His Word faithfully.
To repent sincerely.
To love one another.
And to grow into mature disciples who can stand firm when life becomes difficult.
These resources are intended to help people grow deeper in Scripture, strengthen their faith, and develop a more Christ-centered life.
And if this ministry has been a blessing to you, I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading, liking, or sharing.
For some, supporting Gospel ministry financially is a meaningful expression of generosity and worship.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not from pressure or compulsion.
And that matters deeply to us.
You are not purchasing God's favor.
You are not paying for grace.
You are helping make freely accessible Gospel resources possible for others.
The deeper purpose is to help this ministry continue reaching people with the truth of Jesus Christ.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Invite others.
Use the free resources.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God, and the Gospel must never become something only paying supporters can access.
Our prayer is that every resource, every article, every testimony, and every act of support would ultimately direct attention away from ourselves and toward Jesus Christ.
Because He is the reason this message exists.
He is the promised offspring.
He is the obedient Son.
He is the crucified Savior.
He is the risen King.
He is the One who will bring the serpent's defeat to its final fulfillment.
And when we return to Genesis 3:15, something becomes impossible to ignore.
God announced the promise while Adam and Eve were still standing in the wreckage of their disobedience.
They had no achievements to offer.
No righteousness of their own to present.
No way to restore Eden by human strength.
Yet the Lord revealed that evil would not have the final word.
That is the wonder of redemption.
The first human scandal did not defeat God's saving purpose.
The cross did not defeat His Son.
The tomb did not hold Him.
And the final future of those who belong to Jesus is not determined by the serpent's accusations, but by the victory of the Lamb.
So the next time shame tells you to hide, remember the garden.
The next time suffering makes you question whether God has abandoned you, remember the cross.
The next time death seems stronger than hope, remember the empty tomb.
And the next time the enemy whispers that your story is already over, remember the promise God spoke at the beginning.
The serpent struck the heel.
But Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
And the serpent's final defeat is certain.
The wound was real. The blood was real. The grave was real. But so was the resurrection—and the serpent never gets to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SAUL WAS READY TO KILL HIS OWN SON—AND THE REASON SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY CHRISTIAN
paragraphs: SAUL WAS READY TO KILL HIS OWN SON—AND THE REASON SHOULD TERRIFY EVERY CHRISTIAN

Jonathan had just helped save Israel. But instead of receiving his father's blessing, he was sentenced to death. What happened in 1 Samuel 14 exposes the frightening difference between defending God's honor and defending our own pride—and reveals why we desperately need Jesus Christ.
Imagine risking your life to save your people.
Imagine walking toward an enemy army with almost no chance of surviving, trusting God when everyone else is afraid.
Imagine watching the Lord turn an impossible situation into a victory.
Then imagine coming home and discovering that the person who wants you dead is your own father.
Not because you betrayed him.
Not because you joined the enemy.
Not because you rejected God.
But because you unknowingly broke a command you never heard.
And the man who gave that command would rather see you die than admit that he was wrong.
This is not a fictional tragedy.
This happened in the household of Israel's first king.
And the most disturbing part of the story is not simply that Saul threatened Jonathan's life.
It is that Saul was prepared to use the name of God to justify what he was about to do.
Read that again.
A man can speak passionately about God's honor while being dangerously protective of his own pride.
And before we condemn Saul too quickly, there is a question we need to confront.
Have we ever been so determined to prove ourselves right that we stopped caring whom we were hurting?
Because this story is not only about a king, a son, and a battlefield thousands of years ago.

It is about what happens when spiritual authority becomes entangled with insecurity, when religious zeal outruns obedience, and when someone mistakes the preservation of his reputation for the preservation of God's glory.
And somewhere in this ancient tragedy, there is a wounded son who deserved to be heard.
His name was Jonathan.
Before we reach the moment when Saul demanded his son's death, we need to understand what Jonathan had actually done.
Israel was facing the Philistines, an enemy whose military strength had left God's people in a frightening position.
Saul was king, but Jonathan was the one who stepped forward with extraordinary faith.
In 1 Samuel 14:6, Jonathan said to his armor-bearer:
"Come, and let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised: it may be that the LORD will work for us: for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few." (KJV)
There is something breathtaking about that confession.
