“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9, KJV).
And Jesus Himself said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (John 6:37, KJV).
These are not promises that excuse deliberate rebellion.
They are invitations to genuine repentance and faith.
You do not have to manufacture a perfect spiritual record before coming to Christ.
You come because you need the Savior.
You confess because He is merciful.
You turn from sin because His grace is too precious to treat casually.
And you follow because the One who died for you is worthy of your entire life.
Joshua did not become stronger than Jericho by falling on his face.
He acknowledged the authority of the One who was greater than Jericho.
And maybe that is what you need today.
Not another motivational speech telling you how powerful you are.
Not another promise that everything will work out exactly as you want.
Not another religious performance designed to convince people you have everything together.
Maybe you need to kneel before the Lord and tell Him the truth.
“Jesus, I have been trying to control everything.”
“I have been defending things You are calling me to surrender.”
“I have been asking You to bless decisions I made without seeking You.”
“I have been more concerned about winning arguments than reflecting Your character.”
“I have wanted Your help, but I have resisted Your correction.”
“Lord, forgive me.”
That kind of prayer may not impress the world.
But Scripture tells us:
“God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.” (James 4:6, KJV).
And there is something beautiful about a person who finally stops pretending.
A father admitting he needs to apologize to his children.
A wife or husband choosing honesty instead of another season of hidden resentment.
A young believer confessing a secret sin and seeking trustworthy spiritual accountability.
A church leader remembering that ministry is not a personal kingdom.
A Christian who has wandered far from prayer opening the Bible again with trembling hands.
A person who has never truly trusted Christ finally calling upon Him for salvation.
These moments may never trend online.
But they matter before God.
Because repentance is not spiritual humiliation for its own sake.
It is the turning of a sinner toward the mercy and authority of Jesus Christ.
And the most remarkable thing about Joshua's encounter is what happened afterward.
The LORD gave Joshua instructions that would have sounded absurd according to ordinary military strategy.
March around the city.
Carry the ark.
Have the priests blow trumpets.
Follow the appointed pattern.
Then, at the appointed time, shout.
Read Joshua 6 carefully.
Israel was not instructed to trust in superior weapons or human ingenuity.
The victory was presented as the LORD's gift, received through obedient faith.
Hebrews 11:30 later declares:
“By faith the walls of Jericho fell down, after they were compassed about seven days.”
By faith.
Not by arrogance.
Not by spiritual showmanship.
Not by treating God like a tool for accomplishing personal ambitions.
By faith.
And faith in Scripture is not merely believing that something good will happen.
It is trusting the God who has spoken.
Even when obedience does not look impressive.
Even when the waiting feels unbearable.
Even when the outcome is beyond our control.
That is why the lesson of Joshua's encounter is not simply, “God will knock down every wall in your life.”
That would be a comforting slogan, but it would go beyond what this passage promises.
Some obstacles are removed.
Some trials endure.
Some prayers are answered differently than we hoped.
Some faithful believers suffer deeply and never receive the earthly outcome they longed for.
Yet Christ remains Lord.
His resurrection remains true.
His grace remains sufficient.
And His promise never to abandon His people remains secure.
The greatest victory God offers us is not a life without trouble.
It is reconciliation with Himself through Jesus Christ and the certain hope of eternal life.
So perhaps the question is not whether your Jericho will fall tomorrow.
Perhaps the question is whether you will trust Jesus today.
Will you obey Him when no one is watching?
Will you forgive when bitterness feels more satisfying?
Will you confess when hiding seems safer?
Will you make things right where repentance requires restitution or an apology?
Will you remain faithful when obedience costs you something?
Will you follow Christ even when He refuses to become a servant of your personal agenda?
Because Joshua's question still echoes across the centuries.
“Are You for us, or for our enemies?”
And the Lord's authority still confronts every generation.
We do not get to recruit God into our pride, prejudice, selfish ambition, or self-righteousness.
We are called to surrender to Him.
Even our religious pride.
Even our desire to appear victorious.
Even our tendency to confuse our personal preferences with the will of God.
Especially those things.
And before you move on, I want to ask you something that deserves more than a casual answer.
What is the Jericho standing in front of you right now?
Not necessarily the problem you want God to remove.
But the place where you are struggling to trust and obey Him.
Is it fear?
Unforgiveness?
A hidden sin?
The need to control everything?
The shame of your past?
The exhaustion of trying to appear spiritually strong?
Someone may need to hear that Jesus has not stopped working in the lives of imperfect people.
Not because your story makes you the hero.
But because His mercy deserves the glory.
There is also someone in your life who may need this message more than you realize.
The friend who has quietly stopped attending church.
The parent carrying the pain of a wandering child.
The brother or sister who feels defeated by recurring temptation.
The person who believes their past is too scandalous for grace.
The unbeliever who thinks Christianity is only for people who already have their lives together.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because the Gospel is worth making known.
And if you have not yet followed Gospel Warrior, I invite you to become part of this growing community of believers and seekers who want more than inspirational religious content.
We want to open Scripture.
We want to understand what it actually says.
We want to confront the uncomfortable truths we would rather avoid.
We want to grow in repentance, faith, holiness, grace, and love.
We want our families and friends to know Jesus Christ.
And we want every story of redemption to point back to the Savior, not to ourselves.
That is also why I want to invite you to consider something deeper than simply reading another article.
There is a real difference between consuming Christian content and choosing to help make faithful Christian teaching available to others.
Every article requires time, study, writing, and care.
Every resource made available freely represents an opportunity for someone to encounter biblical truth.
We cannot know how God will use any particular article.
But we can be faithful with the opportunities He places before us.

For Christians who are prayerfully considering their giving, such support can be a voluntary ministry offering. It should not, however, be confused with a mandatory biblical tithe or treated as a replacement for responsibilities to one's local church, family, or other commitments.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and joyful:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV).
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
Not by suggesting that God's approval can be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift through faith in Jesus Christ, not a reward for financial support (Ephesians 2:8–9).

But if this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, drawn you closer to Christ, encouraged you through difficult seasons, or equipped you to share the Gospel with others, consider becoming one of the people who help sustain it.
These products are not the reason we proclaim the Gospel.
These free resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment and spiritual growth accessible to more people.
Read.
Pray.
Grow.
Share the Gospel.
Your prayers, thoughtful comments, testimonies, and willingness to share biblical truth also matter.
Jesus Christ is worthy.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not any writer.
Not any ministry platform.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who forgives repentant sinners.
The One who calls His people to holiness.
The One who turns the ashamed toward grace, the wandering toward repentance, and the spiritually dead toward new life.
And now, before you close this article, I want you to return one last time to that scene outside Jericho.
Imagine the dust beneath Joshua's feet.
The silent city walls in the distance.
The weight of thousands of lives resting upon his leadership.
The armed Stranger standing before him.
The drawn sword.
The question.
“Are You for us, or for our enemies?”
And then that unexpected answer.
“No.”
Joshua had approached with the mindset of a commander.
He ended the encounter facedown as a servant.
And that is the image I want you to remember.
Not a powerful leader standing proudly with his sword.
But a surrendered man bowing before the authority of the LORD.
Because before Joshua could lead Israel into battle, he needed to remember who truly commanded the army.
And before we can faithfully follow Jesus, we must stop treating Him as an accessory to the lives we have already decided to live.
He is not a mascot for our ambitions.
He is not a weapon for our personal arguments.
He is not obligated to endorse every decision we make.
He is Lord.
And the astonishing beauty of the Gospel is that this holy Lord did not abandon sinners to their rebellion.
He came to save.
He bore our sins.
He rose victorious.
And He still calls people to repent, believe, and follow Him.
So if your life feels like a battlefield right now, do not mistake surrender to Christ for defeat.
You may still have difficult conversations ahead.
You may still need to seek forgiveness.
You may still need to rebuild what sin has damaged.
You may still face a tomorrow that frightens you.
But you do not have to face it while pretending you are your own savior.
Bow before Jesus.
Trust His Word.
Receive His grace.
Walk in obedience.
And remember that the God who met Joshua before Jericho is not limited by the walls that terrify human beings.
The same Scriptures that tell us of Joshua's encounter also lead us to the greater hope of Christ's finished work.
That is where our confidence belongs.
Not in the strength of our grip on God.
But in the faithfulness of the Savior who holds His people fast.
So tonight, when the noise fades and no one is watching, perhaps your most important prayer will not be, “Jesus, please take my side.”
Perhaps it will be:
“Jesus, I surrender. Teach me to stand where You want me to stand.”
And if this message has brought something hidden into the light, do not let the moment disappear into another scroll.
Respond to the Lord in prayer.
Return to His Word.
Seek the help of faithful believers where you need it.
And remember that the invitation to grace is not the end of discipleship.
It is the beginning of a life transformed by Jesus Christ.
The walls of Jericho were not Joshua's greatest lesson; before the walls ever fell, a warrior had to learn how to kneel.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE FIRST MAN IN THE BIBLE TO HAVE TWO WIVES—AND THE TERRIFYING WORDS HE SPOKE AFTERWARD
paragraphs: THE FIRST MAN IN THE BIBLE TO HAVE TWO WIVES—AND THE TERRIFYING WORDS HE SPOKE AFTERWARD

Before the flood, before the kings of Israel, and long before David and Solomon, one man took two wives. But the most disturbing part of his story isn't how many women he married. It's what happened to his heart—and how his story reveals humanity's desperate need for Jesus Christ.
There is a man in the Bible whose name most Christians have heard but whose story many have never truly examined.
He was not a king.
He was not a prophet.
He was not remembered for building an altar to God.
Yet in just a handful of verses, his life reveals something frightening about the human heart.
He had two wives.
He became the father of children whose contributions would help shape human civilization.
And then, one day, he spoke words so chilling that they exposed how far a human heart could drift from God while still living in a world full of remarkable achievements.
His name was Lamech.
And what makes his story unsettling is not merely that he was the first man explicitly recorded in Scripture as having two wives.
It's that his story appears in the same chapter where the Bible first tells us about murder.
Read that again.
The first recorded murder.
The first recorded polygamous marriage.
And a man who would eventually boast about taking a life.
All within the fourth chapter of Genesis.
Coincidence?
Scripture does not tell us that Lamech's marriages caused his violence. But the placement of these events invites us to look carefully at the world developing outside Eden.
Because sometimes the most frightening thing about sin is not how suddenly it destroys a person.
It's how gradually a person can become comfortable living with it.
And before we judge Lamech too quickly, there is something in his story that every one of us needs to confront.
Something that might be closer to home than we want to admit.
Genesis 4:19 records:
"And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah." — Genesis 4:19, KJV
There it is.
One sentence.
Two women.
One man.
A moment that marks the Bible's first explicit record of a man having multiple wives.
But the original Hebrew makes this account even more interesting.
The verse begins:
וַיִּקַּח־לוֹ לֶמֶךְ שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים
Vayyiqqaḥ-lo Lemeḵ shtei nashim.
Literally, the phrase communicates:
"And Lamech took for himself two wives."
The Hebrew expression shtei nashim means "two women" or "two wives," with the marital context making "wives" the appropriate translation.
And the phrase vayyiqqaḥ-lo, "he took for himself," describes Lamech's action. The wording alone does not prove his motives were selfish, abusive, or lustful.
That distinction matters.
We must never force Scripture to say more than God has revealed.
Yet the contrast with the creation account is difficult to overlook.
In Genesis 2:24, before sin entered the world, Scripture declared:
"Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh."
In Hebrew, the closing words are:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Vehayu levasar echad.
"And they shall become one flesh."
One flesh.
A covenant union.
A relationship established in God's good creation before shame, blame, jealousy, and violence entered human experience.
Jesus Himself later returned to this passage when teaching about marriage.
In Matthew 19:4–6, He appealed to God's creation of male and female and the two becoming one flesh, emphasizing the permanence and sacredness of the marriage bond.
So when Genesis 4 introduces Lamech with two wives, we are encountering the first recorded departure from the one-man, one-woman marriage pattern presented in Eden.
But we must be careful here.
The Bible does not say that Lamech was the first man in all human history to practice polygamy. It identifies him as the first person whose multiple marriages are explicitly recorded.
Nor does Genesis 4:19 pause to issue a direct command about his marriages.
It simply tells us what happened.
And that raises a question every serious Bible reader must learn to ask:
When Scripture records someone's behavior, does that automatically mean God approves of it?
Of course not.
The Bible records adultery, deception, murder, idolatry, betrayal, and countless other human failures.
Not because God celebrates them.
But because the Bible tells the truth about humanity.
Even when that truth is uncomfortable.
Even when the people involved are important.
Even when their lives contain remarkable achievements.
And Lamech's household was remarkable.
His first wife, Adah, gave birth to Jabal and Jubal.
Genesis 4:20 describes Jabal as the father of those who dwell in tents and keep livestock.
Genesis 4:21 identifies Jubal as the father of those who play the lyre and pipe.
His second wife, Zillah, gave birth to Tubal-cain, who worked with bronze and iron. The passage also names Tubal-cain's sister, Naamah.
Think about that.
Animal husbandry.
Music.
Metalworking.
Skills that would become deeply connected with human society and culture.
These were not insignificant people.
Their family was associated with developments that mattered.
And here is where the story becomes painfully relevant.
A person can contribute something valuable to the world and still have a heart that desperately needs God.
You can be gifted and spiritually lost.
Successful and inwardly empty.
Admired and privately cruel.
Talented enough to build something extraordinary while neglecting the condition of your own soul.
You can have a beautiful house and a broken marriage.
A growing business and a shrinking prayer life.
A respected name and a conscience you keep trying to silence.
You can even be deeply involved in Christian activities while quietly resisting the very Lord whose name you speak.
Not every outward success is evidence of God's approval of everything happening behind the scenes.
And not every outward struggle means God has abandoned someone.
The human heart is more complicated than appearances.
Maybe that is why Lamech's story is so unsettling.
His household was connected with remarkable human abilities.
But when the Bible finally lets us hear Lamech speak, we do not hear a prayer.
We do not hear gratitude.
We do not hear repentance.
We hear a song about violence.
And suddenly the atmosphere changes.
Genesis 4:23 says:
"And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech: for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt." — KJV
Imagine the scene.
Adah and Zillah are listening.
The man who shares their household demands their attention.
But instead of words of affection, humility, or confession, he announces that he has killed someone.
The Hebrew text reads:
כִּי אִישׁ הָרַגְתִּי לְפִצְעִי וְיֶלֶד לְחַבֻּרָתִי
Ki ish haragti lefitsi, veyeled lechabburati.
A close rendering is:
"For I have killed a man for wounding me, and a young man for striking me."

The precise circumstances remain uncertain. The parallel lines may describe one killing poetically rather than two separate victims. The text does not give us enough information to reconstruct the incident or determine every detail of Lamech's responsibility.
But the tone of his declaration is unmistakably alarming.
There is no recorded appeal for God's mercy.
No recorded confession of guilt.
No expression of sorrow for the dead.
Instead, the speech moves toward an extraordinary claim.
Genesis 4:24:
"If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold."
Seventy-sevenfold.
Consider the arrogance of that declaration.
Earlier in Genesis 4, Cain murdered his brother Abel.
When God confronted Cain, the consequences were severe.
Cain feared that someone would kill him, and God placed a protective sign upon him, warning against vengeance.
That protection was not a divine celebration of Cain's crime.
It was God's restraint upon further bloodshed.
But now Lamech invokes Cain's protection and declares an even greater measure of vengeance for himself.
The text does not record God granting Lamech that claim.
It is Lamech speaking.
And the difference matters enormously.
Cain feared being killed. Lamech spoke as though vengeance itself were his security.
One man trembled under the consequences of sin.
Another proclaimed his own terrible measure of retaliation.
And somewhere between those two generations, we see how violence can become something a person not only commits but also defends and celebrates.
That is a warning worth hearing.
Because sin does not always begin with someone proudly announcing rebellion against God.
Sometimes it begins with a small compromise.
A bitterness we refuse to surrender.
A secret we justify.
A boundary we keep moving.
A relationship we know is wrong but refuse to release.
A lie we repeat so often that eventually it feels like the truth.
At first, our conscience protests.
Then we explain ourselves.
Then we become defensive.
Then, if we continue resisting correction, we may begin defending the very thing that once troubled us.
And perhaps the most dangerous moment is not when we fall.
It is when we no longer believe we need to repent.
Have you ever been there?
Not necessarily in the dramatic sins of Lamech.
But in the quieter rebellion that hides behind ordinary routines?
You know you should forgive someone.
But you keep replaying the injury.
You know you should apologize.
But your pride insists they should apologize first.
You know something in your life needs to change.
But you have become skilled at explaining why it can wait.
You still believe in God.
You still know the language of faith.
You may even continue attending church.
But somewhere inside, surrender has been replaced with negotiation.
And the frightening thing is how normal it can begin to feel.
That is why Lamech's story cannot remain merely an ancient lesson about marriage.
It reaches into our homes.
Our private conversations.
Our wounded pride.
Our excuses.
Our relationships.
Our refusal to be corrected.
And it asks a question that is difficult to escape.
Are you allowing God's Word to change you, or are you trying to make God's Word excuse you?
There is another important truth we must not overlook.
Lamech's two wives were named Adah and Zillah.
They were real women within the biblical narrative, not merely symbols for a sermon.
Scripture does not tell us whether they willingly entered these marriages, how they felt about their circumstances, or what their daily relationships were like.
We should not invent their suffering, rivalry, or personal histories to make the account more dramatic.
But we can recognize that they lived in a household where a man openly spoke of killing and multiplied vengeance.
And that should make us think seriously about the people affected by our choices.
Because sin rarely stays as private as we imagine.
A father's unchecked anger can frighten an entire household.
A mother's unresolved bitterness can shape the atmosphere in which children grow.
A husband's dishonesty can wound his wife.
A wife's betrayal can devastate her husband.
A leader's pride can injure people who trusted him.
A believer's hypocrisy can discourage someone who was beginning to seek Christ.
Our decisions have consequences beyond ourselves.
And this is precisely why God's design for marriage must never be reduced to an argument about how many spouses someone may have.
Biblical marriage is about covenant faithfulness, sacrificial love, truth, holiness, and responsibility before God.
It is not a license for domination.
It is not permission to mistreat someone in the name of spiritual authority.
It is not a competition for control.
And it is certainly not a place where cruelty should be excused by quoting Scripture.
Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
That is the opposite of selfish power.
Jesus did not love His bride by exploiting her.
He gave Himself for her.
He laid down His life.
He showed that godly love is measured not by how much control someone possesses but by how faithfully that person loves in obedience to God.
And this is where we must confront another difficult question.
If Lamech was the first recorded polygamist, why do later biblical figures such as Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon also have multiple wives?
Doesn't that mean God approved of polygamy?
Not necessarily.
We must distinguish between what God permits or tolerates within fallen human history and what He presents as His original design.
Genesis describes multiple marriages without treating every action of the patriarchs as exemplary.
Abraham's household experienced painful conflict involving Sarah and Hagar.
Jacob's family was marked by rivalry, favoritism, and deep relational wounds.
David's household suffered devastating consequences amid his many moral failures.
Solomon's many wives turned his heart toward other gods, as recorded in 1 Kings 11.
These accounts differ in their circumstances, and we should not claim that every family tragedy was caused solely by polygamy.
But neither should we turn the Bible's descriptions of these marriages into a blanket endorsement.
Deuteronomy 17:17 specifically warned Israel's future king against multiplying wives.
And when Jesus taught about marriage, He did not point to Solomon's household as the ideal.
He returned to Genesis.
To the beginning.
To God's design.
That is what makes biblical interpretation so important.
We cannot simply ask, "Did someone in the Bible do this?"
We must also ask, "What does the whole counsel of Scripture reveal about God's will?"
Because the Bible is not merely a collection of stories about people we should imitate.
It is the unfolding revelation of God's work in a world shattered by sin.
And ultimately, it leads us to Jesus.
But before we reach the beauty of grace, there is one more connection in Lamech's story that deserves our attention.
One that many readers miss.
Lamech declared vengeance seventy-sevenfold.
Centuries later, Jesus spoke about forgiveness using strikingly similar language.
In Matthew 18:21, Peter approached Jesus and asked how often he should forgive someone who sinned against him.
Would seven times be enough?
Jesus answered in Matthew 18:22:
"I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." — KJV
The Greek phrase is:
ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά
Heōs hebdomēkontakis hepta.
This expression can be understood as "seventy-seven times" or "seventy times seven," depending on how the construction is interpreted. The familiar King James rendering is "seventy times seven."
The Greek wording also echoes the numerical expression found in the Greek Old Testament's rendering of Genesis 4:24.
We should not claim with absolute certainty that Jesus was deliberately quoting Lamech.
Matthew does not explicitly say that.
But the contrast is profound.
Lamech's words magnified vengeance.
Jesus' words magnified forgiveness.
Lamech spoke of retaliation.
Jesus taught His disciples to forgive repeatedly.
Lamech's declaration displayed the human desire to answer injury with greater injury.
Jesus revealed a kingdom where mercy breaks the endless cycle of revenge.
Do you see the beauty?
Humanity had learned to multiply vengeance.
Jesus taught His followers to multiply forgiveness.
And He did not merely teach it.
He lived it.
When Jesus was crucified, He suffered mockery, injustice, humiliation, and unimaginable pain.
Yet Luke 23:34 records His prayer:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
The One who had every right to judge was praying for mercy.
The sinless Son of God was giving His life for sinners.
And suddenly, the story of Lamech becomes part of something much larger.
Not because Lamech secretly represents Christ.
Not because Genesis 4 directly predicts the crucifixion.
But because the Bible's unfolding story reveals the depth of humanity's sin and the greatness of the Savior we need.
Lamech's world was marked by vengeance.
Our world still is.
Look around.
Families destroyed by pride.
Marriages wounded by betrayal.
Friendships abandoned over unforgiven offenses.
Churches divided by bitterness.
People who would rather win an argument than restore a relationship.
People who carry wounds for decades because nobody ever taught them how to surrender their pain to God.
And then Jesus enters the story of humanity.
Not as another violent man demanding revenge.
But as the righteous Savior who willingly bears the punishment of sin.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were still sinners.
Not after we cleaned up our lives.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired every broken relationship.
Not after we proved ourselves worthy.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
That is grace.
But grace is not permission to remain in rebellion.
The same Jesus who welcomes sinners also calls them to repentance.
Mark 1:15 records His proclamation:
"The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel."
Repent.
Believe.
Turn from sin and trust in Christ.
The Gospel does not tell us that our wrongdoing was harmless.
It tells us that our wrongdoing was so serious that we needed a Savior—and that God's love was so great that He gave His Son.
That is why we must never confuse forgiveness with pretending evil did not happen.
Forgiveness does not mean remaining in danger.
It does not require an abused person to return to an unsafe relationship.
It does not erase accountability or the need for justice.
Biblical forgiveness releases personal vengeance into God's hands while pursuing truth, wisdom, and righteousness.
And reconciliation, where possible, requires more than sentimental words.
It requires truth, repentance, and a rebuilding of trust.
Jesus never calls us to make peace with sin.
He calls us to surrender it.
Perhaps someone reading this is carrying a secret.
Something you have hidden for years.
A decision you regret.
A relationship you damaged.
A marriage you betrayed.
A child you failed.
A parent you dishonored.
A season of your life that still fills you with shame.
And you have wondered whether God could ever receive someone like you.
Listen carefully.
The Bible does not tell us whether Lamech ever repented.
We do not know how his earthly story ended.
We must not invent an ending Scripture never gives.
But we do know what the Gospel promises to sinners who turn to Jesus Christ.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
The forgiveness Christ offers is not earned by impressive religious performance.
It is received through faith in Him, the crucified and risen Lord.
And genuine faith does not leave us indifferent to sin.
God's grace begins transforming the heart.
That transformation may involve painful honesty.
Confession.
Apologies.
Restitution where appropriate.
Accountability.
Learning new patterns.
Walking away from what once controlled us.
And sometimes accepting that people we wounded will need time to heal.
Grace does not erase every earthly consequence.
But it does mean your past does not have to remain the master of your future.
Because Jesus Christ is not merely interested in making you feel better about who you used to be.
He is making His people new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
That is not a promise that every struggle disappears overnight.
It is a declaration of a new identity and a new life in Christ.
And perhaps that is the word someone needs tonight.
You have spent years defining yourself by your worst chapter.
The affair.
The addiction.
The anger.
The divorce.
The lies.
The years you wasted.
The people you disappointed.
The prayers you stopped praying.
You have been living as though the most shameful thing you ever did must become the final description of who you are.
But if you are in Christ, your identity is not ultimately determined by your worst sin.
It is determined by the Savior who redeemed you.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have to become your god.
Your failures may require confession and consequences.
They do not place you beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
And your brokenness does not disqualify you from coming to the One who came to save sinners.
Not because sin is small.
But because Christ is greater.
Not because every broken relationship will automatically be restored.
But because God can restore sinners to Himself and teach them to walk in truth.
Not because the past never happened.
But because the cross and resurrection of Jesus Christ have opened the way to forgiveness, redemption, and new life.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not as someone looking for a perfect religious answer.
But as someone who understands that we all need mercy.
What is one area of your life where you need Jesus to replace pride with surrender, bitterness with forgiveness, or hiding with honesty?
You do not have to expose private details or name anyone.
And if God has already brought you through a season of repentance, healing, or restoration, consider sharing a brief testimony.
Your words may remind another person that they are not the only one seeking God's mercy.
Sometimes the testimony someone needs to hear is not from a famous preacher.
Sometimes it is from an ordinary believer who can say:
"I was wrong. I needed Jesus. And by His grace, I am learning to walk differently."
Not as another piece of content to forget tomorrow.
For the moment pride tells you not to apologize.
For the night when shame whispers that God could never forgive you.
Return to the Scriptures.
Read Genesis 4.
Read Matthew 18.
Read Romans 5.
And remember that the God who exposes sin also calls sinners to receive His mercy through Jesus Christ.
If someone came to mind while you were reading, consider sharing this article with them.
Not to shame them.
Not to send a hidden accusation.
But because you genuinely care about their soul.

Whether they are mature believers, struggling Christians, people who have grown cold in faith, or seekers still asking questions about Jesus, there is room to begin a serious conversation about the truth of God's Word.
Because the goal is not merely to gather an audience.
It is to help people open their Bibles, understand the Gospel, repent of sin, trust Christ, and grow in faithful discipleship.
And if this ministry has been helping you grow, there is another meaningful way to stand with the mission.
But it is important to understand something.
The New Testament teaches generous, willing, and cheerful giving—not financial pressure as a condition of spiritual acceptance.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
You do not have to pay to receive God's grace.
It can help us continue publishing biblical teaching, reaching more readers, and developing resources that encourage people to grow deeper in Christ.
Those products are not the heart of the mission.
They are simply another way to share encouragement and Scripture-centered messages in everyday life.
The heart of the mission remains Jesus Christ.
His Word.
His Gospel.
His transforming grace.
And the people who still need to hear about Him.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, develop a deeper prayer life, strengthen their understanding of the Gospel, and grow in their walk with Jesus.
But if you want to go beyond reading and become a regular supporter of this ongoing work, we warmly invite you to join us.
Read.
Pray.
Invite others.
Encourage someone to open the Bible.
A sincere conversation about Christ can matter more than you realize.
Every believer has opportunities to serve the Lord, whether through giving, teaching, prayer, hospitality, encouragement, or faithful witness.
What matters is that we serve from love and obedience to Christ, not from guilt or the desire to earn His approval.
And now, before you leave, return with me to the beginning.
To a man named Lamech.
To two wives named Adah and Zillah.
To a household remembered for music, livestock, and metalworking.
To a voice that proclaimed vengeance instead of repentance.
And to a chapter of Scripture that shows how deeply human life had been affected by sin.
We cannot change what Lamech said.
We cannot rewrite his recorded actions.
We cannot pretend the violence of Genesis 4 never happened.
But we can listen to the warning.
We can examine our own hearts.
We can refuse to make peace with the sins that are destroying us.
And we can turn to Jesus Christ.
Because the final word over the repentant believer is not the arrogance of Lamech.
It is not the violence of Cain.
It is not the shame of Eden.
It is the saving work of Jesus Christ—the One who died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, just as the Scriptures proclaim in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
Lamech's song declared the multiplication of vengeance.
Christ's Gospel announces forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
And that leaves every one of us with a decision.
Will we continue defending the things God is calling us to surrender?
Or will we come to Christ with empty hands and an honest heart?
Maybe tonight is the night you stop hiding.
Maybe it is the night you finally confess what you have been justifying.
Maybe it is the night you ask forgiveness from someone you have wounded.
Maybe it is the night you open your Bible again after years of silence.
Maybe it is the night you stop believing that your worst chapter must become your final chapter.
If that is you, pray sincerely:

"Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I have defended things I should have confessed. I have carried pride, bitterness, and shame. I cannot save myself. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Forgive me, change my heart, and teach me to follow You in truth. Help me turn away from sin and trust Your grace. Amen."
And remember, the power is not in repeating a particular prayer.
Salvation is found in Jesus Christ, received by grace through faith.
If this is the beginning of your return to Him, tell a trusted, biblically grounded Christian who can pray with you and help you grow.
You do not have to pretend you have everything figured out.
But you do need to take seriously the One who calls you to follow Him.

The most tragic thing about Lamech's story is not that we remember his sin. It is that Scripture never tells us he laid down his pride—and you still have the opportunity to lay down yours at the feet of Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE MOST DANGEROUS LIE ABOUT GOD’S GRACE IS THE ONE THAT MAKES YOU COMFORTABLE IN YOUR SIN
paragraphs: THE MOST DANGEROUS LIE ABOUT GOD’S GRACE IS THE ONE THAT MAKES YOU COMFORTABLE IN YOUR SIN

Jude warned about people who turned the mercy of Jesus Christ into permission to live however they pleased. Nearly 2,000 years later, that warning may be more urgent than ever. Because the greatest danger isn't always someone telling you to abandon Jesus. Sometimes it's someone convincing you that you can keep Jesus while refusing to surrender the very sin He died to save you from.
There is a kind of preaching that makes people feel safe while their souls are drifting further from God.
It sounds compassionate.
It sounds liberating.
It uses beautiful words like grace, freedom, acceptance, love, and forgiveness.
And some of those words are among the most precious truths in the entire Bible.
But something terrible happens when those truths are separated from repentance, holiness, and the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Grace becomes an excuse.
Freedom becomes a disguise.
And the cross becomes something people celebrate with their mouths while refusing to let its message confront their lives.
The frightening part?
A person can become comfortable with that kind of Christianity without ever realizing what has happened.
They can sing worship songs on Sunday, quote Scripture on Monday, encourage someone else on Tuesday, and return to the same deliberately protected sin by Wednesday.
And whenever conviction begins to rise, they whisper something that sounds spiritual enough to silence it.
“God understands.”
“I'm only human.”
“Nobody is perfect.”
“Jesus already forgave me.”
But what happens when the truth of God's forgiveness becomes the excuse we use to avoid His call to repentance?
What happens when we begin treating the blood of Jesus as permission to continue doing what nailed Him to the cross?
That is not a new question.
Nearly two thousand years ago, a servant of Jesus Christ named Jude confronted this very danger.
And his warning was so serious that it deserves more than a quick reading.
It deserves an examination of our hearts.
Jude wrote:

“For certain men crept in privily, even they who were of old written of beforehand unto this condemnation, ungodly men, turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness, and denying our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.”
— Jude 4, American Standard Version (1901)
Read that again.
Not people who openly announced that they hated God.
Not necessarily people who entered the church carrying obvious signs of rebellion.
People who crept in unnoticed.
People who could move among believers while corrupting the meaning of grace.
People who took something holy and used it to justify something unholy.
And Jude wanted the church to recognize the danger before it spread.
In the original Greek, the expression translated “turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness” includes these words:
τὴν τοῦ θεοῦ ἡμῶν χάριτα μετατιθέντες εἰς ἀσέλγειαν
Tēn tou theou hēmōn charita metatithentes eis aselgeian.
The word χάρις (charis) means grace, favor, or a gift of kindness. In this passage, it refers to God's grace, which these ungodly people were misusing.

The participle μετατιθέντες (metatithentes) comes from a verb meaning to change, transfer, or alter. Jude is describing people who were perverting grace by turning it toward a purpose completely opposed to its true meaning.
And the word ἀσέλγεια (aselgeia) refers to sensuality, licentiousness, or shameless conduct. It is a term associated with behavior that disregards moral restraint, often including sexual immorality.
Jude was not merely warning about people who struggled with temptation.
He was confronting people who twisted God's grace into a justification for ungodliness.
That distinction matters.
Because there is an enormous difference between a believer who hates the sin they keep falling into and someone who has decided that grace means they no longer need to fight it.
One is wounded and needs restoration.
The other is defending the very thing from which Christ calls us to turn.
And sometimes, if we are painfully honest, we have stood somewhere between those two realities.
We knew something was wrong.
We felt conviction.
We promised God we would change.
Then temptation came again.
The private conversation.
The hidden relationship.
The pornography nobody knew about.
The dishonest transaction.
The bitterness we kept feeding.
The gossip we disguised as concern.
The addiction we insisted we could control.
The secret life that looked nothing like the person everyone saw at church.
And after everything, we told ourselves that grace would cover it.
Now hear this carefully.
God's grace truly is sufficient for the sinner who comes to Christ. But His grace was never given to make peace with the sin that is destroying us.
The apostle Paul confronted the same distortion.
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. We who died to sin, how shall we any longer live therein?”
— Romans 6:1–2, ASV
In Greek, Paul's rejection begins with:
μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito).
An emphatic expression meaning, in this context, “Absolutely not!” or “May it never be!”
Paul was not uncertain.
He did not suggest that continued sin was simply an unfortunate but acceptable consequence of abundant grace.
He rejected the entire idea.
Why?
Because grace does not merely change our standing before God.
Grace also changes our relationship with sin.
The gospel announces forgiveness through Jesus Christ, and it calls forgiven people into a new life.
Not a life of instant perfection.
Not a life without temptation.
Not a life where believers never stumble.
But a life in which sin is no longer defended as our rightful master.
This is where the message becomes deeply personal.
Because some of us are not struggling to understand what the Bible says.
We are struggling to surrender what we already know God is asking us to leave behind.
We want forgiveness without confession.
Comfort without correction.
Resurrection without the death of our old ways.
A Savior who rescues us from judgment, but not a Lord who has authority over our choices.
And yet Jesus never presented discipleship that way.
He said:
“If any man would come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.”
— Luke 9:23, ASV
Daily.
Not just when worship music makes us emotional.
Not just when the sermon speaks directly to our circumstances.
Not just when life falls apart and we suddenly remember how desperately we need God.
Daily.
There is a cross-shaped surrender that belongs to following Jesus.
And it is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like deleting a number you keep returning to.
Sometimes it looks like confessing the truth after months of pretending.
Sometimes it looks like walking away from money you could have gained dishonestly.
Sometimes it means asking forgiveness from someone you have spent years blaming.
Sometimes it means admitting that the thing you call a harmless habit has become a master.
Sometimes it means closing the door to a relationship you know is pulling your heart away from Christ.
And sometimes it means kneeling beside your bed with tears in your eyes, finally saying:
“Lord, I don't want to keep defending this anymore. I need You to change me.”
That is not the death of grace.
That is what grace can begin to produce in a surrendered heart.
But perhaps someone reading this has already begun to feel afraid.
Because you know your own failures.
You know how many times you have made promises.
You remember the prayers you prayed with trembling sincerity, only to find yourself battling the same temptation again.
And now a question is rising inside you.
Have I gone too far?
Have I abused God's grace too many times?
Is Jesus tired of me?
Before fear convinces you to run from Him, remember something essential.
Jude's warning was not written to teach broken sinners that Jesus refuses to receive the repentant.
It was written to protect the church from those who corrupt the truth about God's grace.
And the same Bible that warns against turning grace into license also reveals the breathtaking mercy of Christ toward those who return to Him.
Consider Peter.
He had walked with Jesus.
He had witnessed miracles.
He had heard the teachings.
He had promised loyalty.
And when the moment of testing came, Peter denied knowing the Lord.
Not once.
Three times.
Imagine the weight of that memory.
The sound of his own voice.
The fear.
The shame.
The terrible realization that the courage he thought he possessed had collapsed when it mattered.
Luke records that Peter went out and wept bitterly.
But Peter's failure was not the final chapter of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him.
In John 21, the risen Christ confronted Peter not to destroy him, but to call him again into love and service.
“Feed my sheep.”
Those words were not permission for Peter to keep denying Jesus.
They were a commission from the Savior who had not finished working in him.
That is the difference between grace and permission.
Permission says, “Stay where you are. Nothing needs to change.”
Grace says, “Come to Christ. Your failure does not have to be the end.”
And perhaps that is exactly what someone needs to hear today.
Your past does not have to write your future.
Your worst decision does not have to become your permanent identity.
Your shame does not have to become your home.
But neither does the mercy of Jesus give you a reason to remain chained to what He calls you to abandon.
Jesus does not forgive us because sin is harmless. He forgives us because His mercy is greater than the guilt of those who turn to Him.
And that mercy came at a cost beyond anything we could ever repay.
Think about Calvary.
Not as a religious symbol you have seen so many times that it no longer moves you.
Think about the real suffering of the Son of God.
The betrayal.
The abandonment.
The mocking.
The scourging.
The cross.
The darkness of that hour.
The innocent Christ bearing our sins.
Peter wrote:
“Who his own self bare our sins in his body upon the tree, that we, having died unto sins, might live unto righteousness; by whose stripes ye were healed.”
— 1 Peter 2:24, ASV
Notice both parts.
He bore our sins.
And the purpose includes that we might live unto righteousness.
Forgiveness and transformation belong together in the saving work of Jesus.
We are not made righteous before God by achieving moral perfection through our own strength.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 declares.
But the very next verse says we are created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared for us to walk in.
Grace is the source.
Good works are not the price of salvation.
They are part of the life God prepares for those He saves.
That is why Titus 2:11–12 is so important.

“For the grace of God hath appeared, bringing salvation to all men, instructing us, to the intent that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly and righteously and godly in this present world.”
— Titus 2:11–12, ASV
Do you see it?
Grace instructs us.
Grace trains us.
Grace teaches us to reject ungodliness.
The same grace that welcomes the repentant sinner also teaches that sinner to turn away from the old life.
And that means conviction is not always evidence that God has abandoned you.
Sometimes conviction is the very warning you desperately needed to stop walking toward destruction.
There is a difference between condemnation that drives you into despair and godly sorrow that leads you toward repentance.
Paul wrote in 2 Corinthians 7:10 that godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, while worldly sorrow produces death.
One leaves us trapped in hopelessness.
The other turns us toward God.
So when the Word exposes something in your life, do not automatically mistake that exposure for rejection.
Ask whether the Lord is calling you to bring into the light what you have kept hidden.
Because the enemy would love for you to choose one of two terrible extremes.
Either become so comfortable with sin that you no longer repent.
Or become so consumed by shame that you no longer believe Christ will receive you.
Both can keep a person from coming honestly to Jesus.
But the gospel calls us away from both.
It tells the self-righteous that they need mercy.
It tells the guilty that mercy is available in Christ.
It calls the rebellious to repent.
And it calls the despairing to trust the Savior.
John wrote:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
— 1 John 1:9, ASV
Not because our confession purchases forgiveness.
Not because tears are payment.
Not because we have finally punished ourselves enough.
But because Jesus Christ is the righteous Savior whose sacrifice is sufficient.
And genuine confession does not merely seek relief from consequences.
It agrees with God about the seriousness of sin and turns toward His mercy.
There is a Greek word often associated with repentance in the New Testament:
μετάνοια (metanoia).
It means repentance, involving a change of mind and outlook that turns a person toward God and away from sin.
Biblical repentance is deeper than feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what you did.
It is deeper than regretting the consequences.
It is a changed response to God, expressed in turning from sin and toward Him.
And here is the beautiful truth.
You cannot manufacture a new heart by sheer willpower.
You need the transforming work of God.
That is why the gospel is not merely a message about trying harder.
It is the good news of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, saving sinners and bringing them into new life.
The same Savior who commands repentance also gives His people the Holy Spirit.
And the Spirit produces fruit that human performance alone cannot create.
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Longsuffering.
Kindness.
Goodness.
Faithfulness.
Meekness.
Self-control.
These are not trophies for people who have never struggled.
They are evidence of God's transforming work in the lives of those who belong to Christ.
And transformation often happens through difficult, ordinary obedience.
One honest confession.
One temptation resisted.
One act of reconciliation.
One prayer offered when you feel spiritually dry.
One decision to seek wise pastoral counsel or accountability instead of hiding.
One more day of trusting Jesus when the battle has not yet ended.
Maybe nobody applauds.
Maybe nobody notices.
Maybe you are still healing from damage you caused or suffering consequences that forgiveness does not immediately erase.
But faithfulness is not meaningless simply because it happens in private.
God sees what others cannot.
And the Christian life is not sustained by pretending we are strong.
It is sustained by abiding in Christ.
Jesus said in John 15:5:
“Apart from me ye can do nothing.”
That truth humbles us.
And it gives us hope.
Because if spiritual transformation depended entirely on our ability to repair ourselves, none of us would have reason to boast or confidence to endure.
But our hope rests in the living Christ.
Now return to Jude.
His warning is especially striking because the letter begins by addressing believers as those who are called, beloved in God the Father, and kept for Jesus Christ.
And near the end, Jude urges them to build themselves up in their most holy faith, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God's love, and wait for the mercy of Jesus Christ unto eternal life.
He also commands them to show mercy to those who doubt and to seek the rescue of others in spiritual danger, exercising discernment and caution.
Jude was not promoting a cruel Christianity that delights in humiliating struggling people.
He was calling believers to contend for the faith while showing mercy and taking sin seriously.
Truth and mercy were never meant to become enemies.
A church that speaks of holiness without the mercy of Christ can crush the wounded.
A church that speaks of mercy while refusing to confront sin can leave the wounded in danger.
But a church faithful to Jesus must proclaim both.
The holiness of God.
The seriousness of sin.
The sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice.
The necessity of repentance.
The freedom of forgiveness.
And the transforming power of grace.
This is the message our generation desperately needs.
Not a gospel rewritten to make everyone comfortable.
Not a religion built on fear, performance, and spiritual appearances.
But the real gospel.
The one that exposes sin without denying the possibility of restoration.
The one that humbles the proud and lifts the repentant.
The one that announces that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners.
And the one that never confuses being saved from sin with being granted permission to cherish it.
Perhaps this article found you at a moment when your heart is tired of pretending.
You have become skilled at saying, “I'm fine.”
Your family thinks you're strong.
Your friends see the encouraging posts.
People at church know your smile.
But there is a battle behind that smile.
Something you have not surrendered.
Something you are afraid to confess.
Something you keep promising will be the last time.
And deep down, you wonder whether the person everyone admires would still be loved if the truth came out.
Listen.
Jesus already knows the truth about you.
Nothing hidden in your heart surprises Him.
And the invitation of the gospel is not to become a convincing actor.
It is to come into the light.
Not every struggle should be exposed publicly, and wisdom matters when deciding whom to trust with painful details. But you do not have to keep defending darkness in order to protect an image.
You can confess to God.
You can seek help from a mature and trustworthy believer.
You can pursue accountability.
You can make restitution where appropriate.
You can begin taking real steps away from the sin that has been ruling your decisions.
And when you fall, you do not need to pretend the fall was harmless.
You can return to Christ in repentance, remembering that His mercy is not exhausted by the weakness of those who sincerely seek Him.
This is why I want to ask you something.
Not as a test of how religious you are.
Not to force a public confession.
But because someone else reading the comments may be carrying the same private battle.
Are you fighting a sin you once tried to justify, but now desperately want Jesus to help you overcome?
And if God is teaching you that repentance is not the end of hope but the beginning of restoration, share a little of what He has been teaching you.
You do not need to reveal private details.
You do not need to perform your pain for strangers.
But your honest testimony may remind another struggling believer that they are not alone and that the door of repentance is still open.
This is also why the mission of Gospel Warrior matters to us.
There are people scrolling through Facebook right now who will never voluntarily walk into a church building.
People carrying shame.
People questioning whether God can forgive them.
People who have heard a distorted gospel.
People who have been hurt by religious hypocrisy.
People who believe Christianity is either a list of impossible rules or a promise that nothing they do matters.
And somewhere among them is a person who may encounter the truth of Jesus Christ through an article someone cared enough to share.
Think about that.
Tagging a family member or friend who needs encouragement may open a meaningful conversation.
Saving this article may give you something to revisit when temptation tries to persuade you that grace and holiness have nothing to do with each other.
Following Gospel Warrior means you can continue receiving Scripture-centered encouragement, biblical teaching, and reminders of the hope found in Christ.
Not because a social media page can save anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But because faithful witnesses can point others toward Him.
And that is the heart behind the Gospel Warrior mission.
We want to keep creating resources that bring people back to the Word of God.
We want to help believers grow beyond inspirational quotations into genuine biblical understanding.
We want people to know not only that Jesus forgives, but also what it means to follow Him.

These resources are part of our desire to make biblical encouragement and discipleship accessible to more people, including those who may not have the financial means to purchase books or study materials.
But continuing and expanding this work takes time, labor, and practical resources.
That is why I want to speak openly about something.
The Bible teaches us to give willingly, not under pressure.
“Let each man do according as he hath purposed in his heart: not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7, ASV
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
But through an opportunity to help sustain and expand work that seeks to honor Jesus Christ.
If you want to glorify God through supporting faithful gospel-centered ministry, this is one practical way you can participate.
These products are simply an added thank-you.
The greater purpose is the mission.
The opportunity to help someone encounter the truth.
To encourage a weary believer.
To challenge a heart growing comfortable with compromise.
To remind a broken person that Jesus Christ still saves and restores.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
Your response to Jesus.
Because this message is not ultimately about a ministry.
It is not about a platform.
It is not about building an audience.
It is about the Savior who died and rose again so that sinners could be reconciled to God.
And that brings us back to the question Jude forces every generation to confront.
Have we received God's grace as the gift that saves and transforms us, or have we begun using the language of grace to protect what God is calling us to surrender?
There is no benefit in answering that question for someone else while refusing to answer it for ourselves.
It is easy to see compromise in the world.
It is easy to criticize the hypocrisy of public figures.
It is easy to condemn the sins that do not personally tempt us.
But what about the ones that do?
What about the private compromises?
The carefully managed appearances?
The sins we excuse because they are familiar?
The things we would tell another believer to abandon while quietly making exceptions for ourselves?
The Word of God does not permit us to stand above others as though we have no need of mercy.
We all need Christ.
And that is precisely why the gospel is such good news.
The cross does not tell us that our sin was insignificant.
It tells us that Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
The empty tomb declares that death did not have the final word.
And the invitation to repent reminds us that we do not have to keep living under the dominion of the very things from which Christ came to save us.
Maybe your next step is not another promise made in a moment of emotion.
Maybe it is honest surrender.
Maybe it is confessing the truth to God without excuses.
Maybe it is seeking help.
Maybe it is finally making the difficult decision you have postponed for months.
Maybe it is trusting Jesus again after shame has convinced you that you are beyond His mercy.
Whatever your circumstances, do not confuse grace with permission to remain in rebellion.
And do not confuse repentance with earning salvation.
Come to Jesus.
Not with a polished performance.
Not with a list of reasons your sin should be overlooked.
Not with confidence in your ability to change yourself.
Come with faith in the crucified and risen Lord.
Come acknowledging your need.
Come asking for mercy.
Come willing to follow Him.
And remember how Jude ends his letter.
After warnings about false teachers, corruption, judgment, and spiritual danger, he lifts the eyes of believers toward the One who is able to preserve them.

“Now unto him that is able to guard you from stumbling, and to set you before the presence of his glory without blemish in exceeding joy, to the only God our Saviour, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion and power, before all time, and now, and for evermore. Amen.”
— Jude 24–25, ASV
What an ending.
Jude does not leave believers staring helplessly at the danger.
He points them to the power of God.
The God who calls His people to holiness is also able to keep them.
The Savior who exposes sin is the Savior who offers forgiveness.
The Lord who commands surrender is the Lord who gives grace to those who depend on Him.
And the final hope of the Christian is not that we were strong enough to save ourselves.
It is that Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
So tonight, or whenever these words reach you, perhaps you can make this your prayer:

“Lord Jesus, forgive me for the times I have used Your mercy as an excuse instead of receiving it with gratitude and repentance. Show me what I have been hiding, what I have been defending, and what I need to surrender. I cannot change my heart by my own strength. Teach me to trust You, obey Your Word, and walk by Your Spirit. Restore what sin has damaged, give me courage to make things right where I can, and help me remember that Your grace is not permission to remain in darkness. You are my Savior and my Lord. Lead me in Your truth. Amen.”
Not because typing those words saves you.
Not because a public comment proves repentance.
But because sometimes an honest declaration can encourage someone else to seek the Lord as well.
Above all, let the words become a genuine prayer expressed in a life increasingly surrendered to Christ.
Because the most beautiful story is not the one where a sinner learns to make sin look acceptable.
It is the one where a sinner discovers that the grace of Jesus is powerful enough to forgive, restore, and begin making all things new.
The scandal was never that Jesus welcomed sinners; the scandal is when we use His welcome as a reason to refuse the transformation He offers.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABSALOM SLEPT WITH HIS FATHER’S CONCUBINES ON A ROOFTOP IN FRONT OF ISRAEL—BUT THE MOST TERRIFYING PART OF THIS STORY IS WHAT HAPPENED BEFORE HE EVER CLIMBED THOSE STAIRS
paragraphs: ABSALOM SLEPT WITH HIS FATHER’S CONCUBINES ON A ROOFTOP IN FRONT OF ISRAEL—BUT THE MOST TERRIFYING PART OF THIS STORY IS WHAT HAPPENED BEFORE HE EVER CLIMBED THOSE STAIRS

2 Samuel 16:21–22 | A son publicly humiliates his father. A family collapses beneath the weight of hidden sin. A kingdom watches in disbelief. And behind one of the darkest scandals in Israel’s history stands a warning about unforgiveness, the consequences of sin, and the desperate need for a Savior who can redeem what human rebellion has destroyed.
There are some Bible stories that make you close the book for a moment.
Not because you doubt God.
But because you cannot believe what human beings are capable of doing to one another.
A son climbs onto the roof of his father’s palace.
Below him is Jerusalem.
The city that once celebrated his father’s victories. The city where worship rose toward heaven. The city where a shepherd boy who had once faced Goliath became the king of Israel.
And now that king is running for his life.
Not from the Philistines.
Not from a foreign army.
From his own son.
And what Absalom is about to do on that rooftop is so deliberately humiliating, so calculated, and so morally devastating that Scripture refuses to soften it.
Listen to the words of 2 Samuel 16:21–22 in the King James Version:

“And Ahithophel said unto Absalom, Go in unto thy father's concubines, which he hath left to keep the house; and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father: then shall the hands of all that are with thee be strong.
“So they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.”
Read that last sentence again.
“In the sight of all Israel.”
This was not a private romance.
This was not a misunderstood family dispute.
This was an act of sexual exploitation, political domination, and public humiliation.
Absalom was announcing to the nation that he had taken his father's throne, his household, and his royal authority.
And the women caught in the middle?
They were treated as instruments in a man's war for power.
The Bible does not tell us that they freely consented. We must not pretend that it does. Nor should we turn their suffering into sensational entertainment.
These women were human beings.
They had names, histories, fears, and dignity, even though this passage does not preserve their individual voices.
And there is something deeply disturbing about a society in which powerful men can use vulnerable people to prove who is in control.
But here is the question that should trouble every person reading this.
How does a son become so consumed by bitterness that he is willing to destroy his own father's dignity before an entire nation?
Because Absalom did not wake up one morning and suddenly become this man.
There was a history.
There were wounds.
There was blood.
There was silence.
And there was sin that nobody could undo.
To understand that rooftop, we have to go backward.
Back to another rooftop.
Back to David.
Years earlier, King David had walked upon the roof of his palace and seen Bathsheba bathing.
Second Samuel 11 tells us that David sent for her, took her, and slept with her. Bathsheba was married to Uriah, one of David's soldiers.
David then attempted to conceal what had happened.
When his attempts failed, he arranged for Uriah to be placed in deadly combat and abandoned.
Uriah died.
David took Bathsheba as his wife.
And for a moment, perhaps from the outside, it appeared that the king had managed to bury the scandal.
But the final verse of 2 Samuel 11 declares:
“But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.”
Those words should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because people can applaud what God condemns.
People can overlook what God sees.
People can be impressed by someone's position while remaining completely unaware of the corruption taking place behind closed doors.
David was Israel's king.
He was also a sinner who had grievously abused his power.
And no crown, calling, anointing, ministry, or spiritual reputation could make that evil righteous.
God sent the prophet Nathan to confront him.
Nathan announced consequences that would reach into David's own household.
In 2 Samuel 12:11–12, the Lord declared that calamity would arise against David from within his house and that what David had done secretly would be answered by public humiliation.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 12:12 contains a devastating contrast:
בַסָּתֶר — bassāter, meaning “in secret.”
And:
נֶגֶד כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל — neged kol-Yisra'el, meaning “before all Israel.”
David had tried to conceal his wrongdoing.
But its consequences would become publicly visible.
This does not mean that God approved of Absalom's later actions. God's judgment upon David never turned Absalom's wickedness into righteousness.
It means that the Lord had warned David that his sin would bring consequences far beyond the moment in which he committed it.
And that is a truth our generation desperately needs to recover.
Forgiveness is real.
Grace is real.
But forgiveness does not always erase the earthly consequences of what we have done.
A marriage may be forgiven and still require years of rebuilding trust.
A child may forgive a parent and still carry painful memories.
A leader may genuinely repent and still need to surrender a position of authority.
David confessed his sin.
Psalm 51 reveals the language of a broken man pleading for mercy:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10, KJV
And Nathan assured David that the Lord had put away his sin.
But David's household was not suddenly healed.
There is a difference between receiving God's forgiveness and escaping every consequence of our choices.
Then another terrible event unfolded.
David's son Amnon violated his half-sister Tamar.
Second Samuel 13 records the violence, the shame, and Tamar's devastation.
And Absalom, Tamar's brother, knew what had happened.
Scripture says David became very angry.
But the biblical account does not record David administering justice to Amnon.
Imagine the pain inside that household.
Tamar had suffered a terrible wrong.
Amnon remained alive.
David was angry.
And Absalom watched.
Perhaps you know something about that kind of pain.
Not the details of this royal family.
But the experience of seeing wrongdoing go unaddressed.
Watching someone powerful avoid accountability.
Hearing people tell the wounded to move on while the person responsible never seems to face the truth.
Maybe you have sat at a family gathering where everyone pretended nothing happened.
Maybe you learned to smile while carrying a memory nobody wanted to discuss.
Maybe the person who should have protected you remained silent.
If that is part of your story, hear this clearly.
What happened to you was not made acceptable by someone else's silence.
And God does not require you to call evil good.
Absalom's grief and anger over Tamar's suffering were rooted in a genuine injustice.
But what he eventually chose to do with that anger became another tragedy.
Second Samuel 13:22 says:
“And Absalom spake unto his brother Amnon neither good nor bad: for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had forced his sister Tamar.”
There is something chilling about those words.
Neither good nor bad.
Silence.
Not reconciliation.
Not peace.
Not justice.
Silence.
For two years, Absalom waited.
Then he arranged for Amnon to be killed.
The brother who had violated Tamar was dead.
But murder did not restore Tamar.
It did not heal the family.
It did not bring Absalom peace.
Instead, Absalom fled.
Years passed.

He eventually returned to Jerusalem, but his relationship with David remained fractured. When David finally received him and kissed him, the outward gesture did not mean every underlying wound had been resolved.
And eventually, Absalom began stealing the hearts of Israel.
He stood near the city gate.
He listened to people's grievances.
He presented himself as the leader who would give them justice.
He cultivated loyalty.
He built influence.
He prepared rebellion.
And eventually, he declared himself king.
The wounded son had become a calculating political rival.
That is one of the most sobering movements in this entire narrative.
Absalom had witnessed injustice.
Then he committed injustice.
He had seen the damage caused by the misuse of power.
Then he used power to harm others.
He had watched his family fracture.
Then he helped tear the kingdom apart.
His pain was real.
But his pain did not justify his cruelty.
And that distinction matters enormously.
Because some of us have been hurt so deeply that we are tempted to believe our suffering gives us permission to hurt someone else.
We think, After what they did to me, they deserve whatever happens.
We think, They made me this way.
We think, I am only giving them back what they gave me.
But vengeance does not become holy because the wound behind it is genuine.
Romans 12:19 tells believers not to take vengeance into their own hands.
That does not mean ignoring abuse, avoiding lawful accountability, or pretending that injustice is harmless.
It means refusing to make personal revenge our god.
And now we arrive at that rooftop.
David has fled Jerusalem.
Absalom has entered the city.
His adviser Ahithophel proposes a public act designed to make reconciliation with David politically impossible.
The concubines David left to care for the palace are still there.
In the ancient royal world, taking possession of a king's women could function as a claim to his royal prerogatives.
This is part of the political meaning of Ahithophel's advice.
But there is another detail that should not be overlooked.
In the Hebrew of 2 Samuel 16:22, the phrase translated “in the sight of all Israel” is:
לְעֵינֵי כָּל־יִשְׂרָאֵל — le'enei kol-Yisra'el.
Literally, “before the eyes of all Israel.”
This is the language of public visibility.
The narrative describes a tent being erected on the roof and Absalom going in to his father's concubines.

It does not require us to imagine that every citizen literally witnessed the sexual act itself. The point is that the act was made publicly known and carried out as an unmistakable political declaration.
The rooftop had become a stage.
The women had become victims of a struggle for power.
The son had made himself his father's enemy.
And the nation was being forced to witness the consequences of a collapsing royal household.
Now notice the terrible connection.
David's earlier sin involving Bathsheba began with what he saw from a palace rooftop.
Absalom's public humiliation of David took place on a palace rooftop.
The two scenes are not identical, and the victims must never be treated as interchangeable.
But the narrative echoes are difficult to miss.
The king who once abused his power now suffers humiliation at the hands of a son who is abusing his own.
Sin has consequences that can spread through households and communities.
Yet we must be careful here.
The Bible does not teach that every child is destined to repeat a parent's sins.
It does not teach that a victim of family dysfunction is doomed to become an abuser.
And it does not teach that someone else's wrongdoing removes our personal responsibility.
Ezekiel 18:20 makes that clear:
“The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son.”
David was accountable for David's sin.
Absalom was accountable for Absalom's sin.
And the women harmed by their actions were not responsible for the evil done against them.
This is not a story about an unavoidable family curse.
It is a story about real human choices, real moral responsibility, and devastating consequences.
And perhaps that is what makes it so frightening.
Because somewhere in this story, we may recognize something about ourselves.
Not necessarily in the sexual scandal.
Not necessarily in the political rebellion.
But in the resentment.
The pride.
The secrecy.
The desire to control.
The temptation to punish someone who wounded us.
The desperate effort to make sure nobody ever humiliates us again.
You can carry bitterness so long that it begins to feel like your personality.
You can rehearse an injury so often that revenge starts sounding like justice.
You can become so determined never to be powerless again that you begin controlling everyone around you.
And you can look spiritually respectable while your heart is slowly hardening.
That is why Hebrews 12:15 warns about a “root of bitterness” that springs up and troubles many.
Notice that.
Many.
Bitterness rarely stays confined to the person carrying it.
It affects marriages.
Children.
Friendships.
Churches.
Communities.
Sometimes the people who suffer most from our unhealed anger are people who never caused the original wound.
And still, we have to make another distinction.
Healing is not the same as forced reconciliation.
Forgiveness does not mean giving an unsafe person unrestricted access to your life.
Repentance does not mean avoiding accountability.
Biblical grace never requires us to deny the truth.
The Gospel calls us away from vengeance while also calling evil what it is.
And this is where the story becomes even more heartbreaking.
Absalom's rebellion eventually ends in his death.
Second Samuel 18 records that he was caught in a tree during battle and killed by Joab and his men, despite David's instruction to deal gently with him.
When David heard the news, the king was overcome with grief.
He cried:
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!” — 2 Samuel 18:33, KJV
Think about that cry.
The father whose throne had been stolen.
The father whose household had been publicly humiliated.
The father whose son had sought his downfall.
He is not celebrating.
He is weeping.
And suddenly the story is no longer merely about a scandal on a rooftop.
It is about a father grieving a son who will never come home.
There will be no final conversation.
No opportunity to confront everything that happened.
No reconciliation scene.
No embrace after the rebellion.
Absalom is dead.
And David is crying for him.
We must not romanticize their relationship or pretend David was an innocent father who did everything right.
He did not.
But neither should we ignore the anguish of this moment.
David's lament reveals the unbearable grief of a father facing the death of his son.
And those words—
“Would God I had died for thee”—
lead us toward a greater question.
What if there were a King who did not merely wish to die for His enemies?
What if there were a King who actually did?
This is where we must turn from David's broken household to Jesus Christ.
Not because Absalom's wickedness secretly becomes good.
Not because the abuse of vulnerable women was necessary for salvation.
Not because every disturbing biblical event is a hidden symbol of Jesus.
