“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — World English Bible.
That promise is not an invitation to continue sinning without repentance.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and come honestly before God.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot undo every consequence.
Sometimes repentance requires difficult conversations, rebuilding trust, ending sinful relationships, accepting accountability, and making restitution where possible.
Forgiveness does not guarantee that every damaged relationship will be restored to its former condition.
But your past does not have the authority to cancel the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And your failures do not have to become the final description of your life.
There is a reason Paul began by reminding the Corinthians that some of them had once lived in the very sins he was warning them against.
He wanted them to remember who they had become in Christ.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
These are not casual religious compliments.
They speak of God's saving work, cleansing, consecration, and the believer's right standing before Him through Jesus Christ.
The people Paul called to holiness were people who had received grace.
Obedience was not the price of their redemption. It was the fitting response to the Redeemer.
And that truth is essential.
Because a person can become so obsessed with escaping sexual sin that they begin to imagine Christianity is nothing more than a long struggle against temptation.
But Jesus did not merely come to make you stop doing something.
He came to reconcile you to God.
He came to bring sinners into His kingdom.
He calls you to love God, love your neighbor, deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Him.
Sexual holiness belongs within that greater calling.
The goal is not simply a clean browsing history.
The goal is a heart increasingly surrendered to Jesus Christ.
A life shaped by His Word.
A mind renewed by truth.
Relationships governed by love.
A body offered to God.
A faith that remains when nobody is applauding.
And a hope anchored in the promise that the One who raised Jesus from the dead will also raise those who belong to Him.
So tonight, before you sleep, perhaps there is a conversation you need to have with God.
Not the polished prayer you offer when other people are listening.
Not the carefully edited version of your life.
The truth.
“Lord Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“I have allowed things into my life that do not honor You.”
“I have confused desire with love.”
“I have tried to satisfy my soul with what cannot save me.”
“I need Your forgiveness. I need Your strength. Teach me to turn away from sin and walk in Your truth.”
You do not need eloquent words.
You need a sincere heart turning toward the Savior.
And if you have never placed your trust in Jesus Christ, the invitation of the Gospel is not merely to improve your behavior.
It is to repent and believe in Him.
Believe in the crucified and risen Lord.
Receive the salvation that cannot be purchased by religious performance.
And follow the One who gave Himself for sinners.
Because the deepest answer to sexual brokenness is not simply stronger willpower.
It is Jesus Christ, whose grace saves, whose truth exposes, whose Spirit sanctifies, and whose resurrection secures the believer's hope.
Maybe someone you love needs to read this.
Someone who smiles in public but fights temptation in secret.
Someone who has stopped attending church because shame convinced them they no longer belong.
Someone who believes their sexual past has made them unworthy of being loved.
Someone who needs both the courage to repent and the hope to believe that Christ still receives those who turn to Him.
Not because sharing a post earns spiritual credit, but because the truth of Scripture may reach someone who would never admit they are struggling.
A single act of sharing can place the Gospel before a person you may never know is quietly searching for hope.
And if one particular person comes to mind, consider tagging them with kindness and discretion, or sending the article privately. Never expose someone else's personal struggle publicly.
You do not have to reveal private details. You do not have to turn your pain into a public performance.
But sometimes a sincere confession of our need for God's grace can remind another believer that they are not the only one learning to walk in obedience.
Someone who feels trapped may need to hear that repentance, accountability, and spiritual growth are possible.
Return to 1 Corinthians 6.
Read the passage in context.
Remember that your body belongs to Christ, that His resurrection matters for your future, and that the Holy Spirit calls you to glorify God in the life you live today.
And if you believe this ministry should continue reaching people with the Gospel, there is another meaningful way to participate.
Not to purchase God's favor.
Not to prove you are a better Christian than someone who cannot afford to give.
The Bible teaches that believers should give willingly, thoughtfully, and without compulsion. As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us, God loves a cheerful giver.
But voluntary generosity can become one genuine expression of worship when it is offered in faith and love.
The distinction matters because the Gospel must never become something people feel pressured to purchase.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
The ministry is only a servant.
And the ministry exists to point people to Him.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, not merely available to people who can pay.
Your sharing can help more people encounter it.
Your prayers can strengthen the people serving behind it.
And your own faithful witness can carry the message of Jesus into places an article may never reach.
Your body was made for the Lord.
That was Paul's declaration.
Not because your body is an enemy to destroy.
Not because your past makes you permanently unclean.
Not because sexuality is shameful in itself.
But because Jesus Christ is Lord over the whole person.
The same Lord who died for sinners is the Lord who rose bodily from the grave.
The same Savior who forgives is the Savior who calls us to holiness.
And the same grace that welcomes the repentant sinner teaches us to turn away from the sin that once held us captive.
One day, everything you have tried so desperately to hide will seem very different in the light of eternity.
The secret compromises that once appeared irresistible.
The approval you thought you could not live without.
The temporary pleasures that demanded so much and gave so little.
The nights you thought your failure was the end.
And the moments when God's Word called you back.
What will matter most is not whether you successfully convinced the world that you had never struggled.
It will be whether you truly belonged to Jesus Christ.
So do not wait until you feel worthy to come to Him.
Come in repentance.
Come in faith.
Come ready to surrender what you have been defending.
Come trusting the One whose mercy is greater than your ability to repair yourself.
And then rise to walk in obedience, not to earn the cross, but because the crucified and risen Savior is worthy of your life.
The world may remember your scandal.
Your conscience may remember your failures.
Your scars may remind you of what happened.
But the Gospel declares that the repentant sinner's story does not have to end where sin left it.
The body you once surrendered to sin can become the very place where your life bears witness to the grace of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps, years from now, when someone asks how a person with your history could have become someone who loves God so deeply, your answer will not be a story about how strong you were.
It will be a testimony about how merciful Jesus has been.
Your past may explain the wounds you carry, but it does not have to write the ending of the life Christ has redeemed.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE CHASED OTHER LOVERS FOR BREAD AND WATER… BUT THE GOD SHE BETRAYED WAS THE ONE FEEDING HER ALL ALONG.
paragraphs: SHE CHASED OTHER LOVERS FOR BREAD AND WATER… BUT THE GOD SHE BETRAYED WAS THE ONE FEEDING HER ALL ALONG.
The heartbreaking warning of Hosea 2:5–13: When God's blessings become more precious than God Himself, the very things we chase can become the things that destroy us.
What if the thing you keep running toward for happiness is the very thing keeping you from the God who has never stopped loving you?
Read that again.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is lying awake beside a person who cannot satisfy the emptiness in their soul.
Someone is checking a bank account, hoping another paycheck will finally bring peace.
Someone is scrolling through photographs of other people's happiness, wondering why their own life feels so painfully incomplete.
Someone is working themselves into exhaustion, chasing a future they believe will finally make them feel secure.
And someone who once prayed with tears in their eyes has slowly stopped praying altogether.
Not because they openly decided to abandon God.
But because something else became more important.
Something else became their comfort.
Their security.
Their reason for waking up.
Their source of worth.
And the frightening part?
They may not even realize what has happened.
More than twenty-seven centuries ago, God spoke through a prophet named Hosea about a people who had done something heartbreakingly similar.
They were not necessarily denying that God existed.
They were doing something more subtle.
They were enjoying His gifts while giving their devotion to someone else.
And God described their unfaithfulness with words so painfully intimate that they still expose the human heart today.
In Hosea 2:5, the prophet records the words of an unfaithful wife:

"For their mother hath played the harlot: she that conceived them hath done shamefully: for she said, I will go after my lovers, that give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, mine oil and my drink." (KJV)
Bread.
Water.
Wool.
Flax.
Oil.
Drink.
Notice something unsettling.
She was not talking about stealing kingdoms.
She was not asking for a throne.
She was chasing ordinary things.
Food for survival.
Water for thirst.
Clothing for protection.
Oil for daily life.
Things that, by themselves, were not sinful.
And that is what makes this passage so dangerous to read honestly.
Because sometimes the greatest rival to God in our hearts is not something obviously wicked.
Sometimes it is something perfectly ordinary that we have elevated into something ultimate.
A relationship.
A career.
A comfortable life.
A bank account.
The approval of people.
The fear of losing everything we have worked so hard to build.
The problem was not that Israel needed bread.
The problem was that Israel had forgotten who truly provided it.
And perhaps that is where this story begins to sound uncomfortably familiar.
You can have food on your table and still forget to thank the Lord.
You can receive an answered prayer and slowly stop seeking the One who answered it.
You can enjoy opportunities God has permitted and eventually become so consumed by them that worship becomes an inconvenience.
You can ask God to bless a relationship, then compromise your obedience to Him because you are terrified of losing that relationship.
You can spend years praying for financial stability, then begin trusting your money more than the God who sustains your life.
And without ever saying the words, your heart begins to whisper:
"I will go after my lovers."
Not necessarily another person.
But whatever promises to give you what you have stopped trusting God to provide.
That is the tragedy Hosea was confronting.
And the original Hebrew makes the picture even more piercing.
In Hosea 2:5, the expression translated "my lovers" is מְאַהֲבַי (me'ahavay), meaning "those who love me" or "my lovers."
The Hebrew word אֶתְנָה (etnah) means "I will give" or "let me give," but the form used in this verse for Israel's pursuit is אֵלְכָה (elekhah), meaning "I will go."
It communicates deliberate movement.
A decision.
A direction.
She was not merely being tempted.
She was choosing whom to pursue.
And that distinction matters.
Because spiritual drift often begins long before an outward collapse.
It begins when we repeatedly choose something other than God as the center of our confidence.
One compromise.
One neglected prayer.
One rationalized disobedience.
One decision to protect our comfort instead of honoring Christ.
Until eventually we look around and wonder how we became so far removed from the devotion we once had.
But to understand Hosea properly, we must remember that this was not originally a generic warning about personal ambition or relationships.
It was God's covenant accusation against ancient Israel.
The northern kingdom had become entangled in Baal worship, a religious system that associated false gods with agricultural fertility, rainfall, and prosperity.
The people were attributing their harvests and material abundance to idols rather than to the LORD who had delivered and sustained them.
Hosea's marriage imagery portrayed Israel's covenant unfaithfulness.
The language of adultery was not merely about sexual misconduct.
It exposed spiritual betrayal.
Israel belonged to the LORD by covenant, yet pursued rival gods for the very blessings that ultimately came from Him.
And then comes one of the most devastating statements in the passage.
God declares in Hosea 2:8:
"For she did not know that I gave her corn, and wine, and oil, and multiplied her silver and gold, which they prepared for Baal." (KJV)
Do you see it?
God gave her the grain.
God gave her the wine.
God gave her the oil.
God increased her silver and gold.
And she took what God had provided and used it to honor a false god.
Imagine the heartbreak of that picture.
The Provider was forgotten.
The gift was celebrated.
And the glory was handed to an idol.
The Hebrew text uses the expression וְהִיא לֹא יָדְעָה (vehi lo yade'ah) — "but she did not know."
This was not a statement that Israel had never heard of the LORD.
It exposed her failure to recognize and acknowledge Him as the true source of her blessings.
She had received.
But she had forgotten.
She had prospered.
But she had misplaced her worship.
And perhaps the most frightening spiritual condition is not always having nothing.
Sometimes it is having so much that you begin to imagine you no longer need God.
Think about that.
How many times have we begged God to open a door, only to walk through it and become too busy to seek Him?
How many times have we cried for deliverance, then gradually forgotten the mercy that carried us through?
How many times have we called something a blessing while allowing it to become an excuse for disobedience?
God gives us gifts to receive with gratitude, stewardship, and worship.
But a gift becomes an idol when we demand from it the identity, security, or ultimate satisfaction that belongs to God alone.
And idols are cruel masters.
They promise what they cannot finally deliver.
Money can purchase medicine, but it cannot purchase eternal life.
Human affection can bring extraordinary comfort, but no human being can bear the weight of being your savior.
Success can open doors, but it cannot cleanse a guilty conscience.
Popularity can surround you with attention while leaving your soul painfully lonely.
And pleasure can distract you from emptiness without ever healing its deepest cause.
This is why Hosea's prophecy is more than ancient history.
It reveals a pattern that still lives in the human heart.
We can spend our lives chasing what God created while neglecting the God who created it.
And sometimes, in His mercy, God confronts the very thing we have mistaken for salvation.
Listen to Hosea 2:6:
"Therefore, behold, I will hedge up thy way with thorns, and make a wall, that she shall not find her paths." (KJV)
Thorns.
A wall.
A blocked road.
Not exactly the imagery we usually associate with divine love.
We tend to imagine God's kindness only in open doors, successful plans, comfortable circumstances, and answered requests.
But here, within the specific covenant judgment Hosea announces against Israel, God describes obstructing the path of her unfaithfulness.
Why?
The next verse explains.

"And she shall follow after her lovers, but she shall not overtake them; and she shall seek them, but shall not find them: then shall she say, I will go and return to my first husband; for then was it better with me than now." (Hosea 2:7, KJV)
There it is.
The turning point.
She chased.
She pursued.
She searched.
But the lovers she trusted could not give her what she expected.
And in the emptiness of that pursuit, she began to remember the husband she had abandoned.
"I will go and return."
Those words are almost unbearable.
Because there are people reading this who know exactly what it feels like to reach the end of something they once believed would save them.
You fought to keep a relationship that was drawing you away from obedience to Christ.
You sacrificed your peace to maintain an image of success.
You chased recognition until you barely recognized yourself.
You kept telling yourself that one more achievement, one more purchase, one more promotion, one more person's approval would finally make you whole.
But the emptiness remained.
And now, quietly, perhaps painfully, you are beginning to wonder whether you have been running in the wrong direction.
Please understand this carefully.
Hosea does not give us permission to declare that every failed relationship, financial loss, sickness, or disappointment is God punishing someone for idolatry.
Scripture does not teach that every hardship can be traced to a particular personal sin. Jesus Himself rejected that simplistic assumption in John 9:1–3.
But Hosea does teach us that God takes covenant unfaithfulness seriously.
And the broader witness of Scripture teaches that His discipline can be an expression of fatherly love toward His children (Hebrews 12:5–11).
Sometimes a closed door is simply a closed door.
Sometimes suffering occurs in a fallen world for reasons we do not understand.
And sometimes God's Word uses our disappointments to expose where our confidence has been misplaced.
The question is not whether every painful event is a secret punishment.
The question is whether we will allow God's truth to examine our hearts.
Because an obstacle is not always evidence that God has abandoned you.
And a successful pursuit is not always evidence that God approves of what you are chasing.
Israel had enjoyed prosperity while dishonoring the LORD.
That prosperity did not make her idolatry righteous.
Then God announced something even more sobering.
He would withdraw the agricultural gifts she had credited to false gods.
Hosea 2:9 declares:
"Therefore will I return, and take away my corn in the time thereof, and my wine in the season thereof, and will recover my wool and my flax given to cover her nakedness." (KJV)
The bread she thought her lovers provided?
God claimed it as His.
The wool she credited to them?
It had come from Him.
The harvest she celebrated before Baal?
The LORD was its true giver.
This was not God discovering that Israel had become unfaithful.
He already knew.
This was God exposing the lie that had captured her heart.
And the judgment continues through verses 10–13.
Her shame would be uncovered.
Her festivities would cease.
Her vines and fig trees, which she had regarded as rewards from her lovers, would be devastated.
Her worship of the Baals would be confronted.
Then comes the final accusation of verse 13:
"And she went after her lovers, and forgat me, saith the LORD." (KJV)
"And forgat me."
Four words in the King James translation.
Enough to stop a heart that is still willing to listen.
The Hebrew expression is וְאֹתִי שָׁכְחָה (ve'oti shakhechah) — "but me she forgot."
The contrast is devastating.
She remembered her lovers.
She remembered her celebrations.
She remembered her ornaments.
She remembered the pleasures she was pursuing.
But she forgot the LORD.
And here is the question that should disturb every comfortable heart, including mine:
What if we have become experts at remembering everything except the One who gave us life?
We remember appointments.
Deadlines.
Bills.
Messages.
Birthdays.
Our favorite shows.
Our online accounts.
Our plans for the future.
But when did we last sit quietly before God without asking Him for anything?
When did we last open Scripture because we genuinely wanted to know Him?
When did we last confess a sin without defending it?
When did we last thank Jesus for the cross with the same seriousness we bring to our daily anxieties?
When did we last choose obedience even when it cost us something?
This is not about pretending that every believer must maintain a perfect devotional routine.
It is about something deeper.
The direction of the heart.
The place of our trust.
The object of our worship.
And if these questions are exposing something you would rather keep hidden, please do not rush away from that conviction.
There is a difference between the conviction that leads us to repentance and the despair that tells us there is no way home.
The Gospel does not end with exposure.
It leads us to Jesus Christ.
And that is where Hosea's message becomes breathtaking.
Because the same prophetic book that announces judgment also reveals God's astonishing purpose to restore His people.
Immediately after the judgment passage, Hosea 2:14 declares:
"Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak comfortably unto her." (KJV)
Read the movement of that passage.
Judgment has been announced.
Unfaithfulness has been exposed.
The false lovers have been unmasked.
And then God speaks of drawing His people back.
The Hebrew expression וְדִבַּרְתִּי עַל־לִבָּהּ (ve-dibbarti al-libbah) means, literally, "and I will speak to her heart."
The King James Version beautifully renders it "speak comfortably unto her."
It carries the sense of speaking tenderly and persuasively to the heart.
Not because the sin was insignificant.
Not because idolatry was harmless.
Not because covenant betrayal could simply be ignored.
But because God's redemptive purpose was greater than Israel's rebellion.
The wilderness, which might appear to be a place of abandonment, becomes in this promise a setting for renewed covenant relationship.
The God who exposed her false security would speak to her heart.
And that should make every spiritually exhausted person reading this stop for a moment.
Because perhaps you have been assuming that the only thing God has left to say to you is condemnation.
You remember the promises you broke.
The prayers you abandoned.
The compromises you defended.
The years you wasted.
The times you knew what was right and chose what was easier.
You remember how sincerely you once worshiped.
And you wonder whether you could ever return to that kind of love again.
But the God revealed in Scripture is not a God who delights in the destruction of the repentant.
He calls sinners to turn from their ways and live (Ezekiel 18:23, 30–32).
And in Jesus Christ, the promise of mercy shines with a clarity that changes everything.
Because Hosea's story does not find its deepest Christian significance in the idea that we can simply try harder to become faithful.
It directs us toward the God whose covenant faithfulness accomplishes what sinful human hearts cannot achieve on their own.
Hosea 2:19–20 speaks of a future relationship marked by righteousness, justice, steadfast love, mercy, and faithfulness.
And the New Testament reveals Jesus Christ as the Bridegroom who gives Himself for His people.
Ephesians 5:25 declares:
"Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
Not merely advised Himself for it.
Not merely felt compassion for it.
Gave Himself for it.
At the cross, Jesus did not excuse sin.
He bore its judgment as the sinless Savior.
He did not pretend our rebellion was harmless.
He gave His life to redeem sinners.
He did not come because humanity had finally proven worthy of salvation.
He came in grace.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired everything.
Not after we had made ourselves impressive.
Not after we had earned the right to be loved.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
And this is why the Gospel is not merely a motivational message about starting over.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, saves sinners who repent and believe in Him.
He offers forgiveness that we cannot purchase.
Righteousness that we cannot manufacture.
Reconciliation with God that we cannot achieve through human effort.
And new life that begins not with our greatness, but with His grace.
Maybe you have been chasing lovers for bread and water.
Maybe your particular idol has never had a physical altar.
Maybe it lives in your phone.
Your ambitions.
Your resentment.
Your appetite for approval.
Your secret habits.
Your desperate need to control tomorrow.
Maybe it is something you are afraid to surrender because you cannot imagine life without it.
But hear the words of Jesus in John 6:35:
"I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst." (KJV)
Do you see the beautiful contrast?
Israel pursued false lovers for bread and water.
Jesus declares Himself the Bread of Life.
He is not promising that believers will never experience physical hunger, hardship, or material need.
He is revealing Himself as the One who satisfies the deepest spiritual hunger through the life He gives.
The things we chase cannot reconcile us to God.
Jesus can.
The idols we protect cannot forgive our sins.
Jesus can.
The success we worship cannot defeat death.
Jesus has conquered the grave.
And the love of Christ does not merely make our old idols less interesting.
It calls us into an entirely new allegiance.
A new identity.
A new way of living.
A new relationship with God.
That is what repentance means.
The Greek noun μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance, a change of mind and heart that involves turning from sin toward God.
Biblical repentance is not simply feeling guilty because something went wrong.
It is not merely crying because the consequences hurt.
It is not promising to become better while secretly planning to return to the same idols.
It is turning toward God in faith, acknowledging our sin, and receiving the mercy found in Jesus Christ.
And genuine repentance begins to bear fruit in a changed life.
Not perfection overnight.
But a new direction.
A growing willingness to obey.
A renewed hatred of what separates us from God.
A deepening love for the Savior who gave Himself for us.
Perhaps you are reading this with tears in your eyes.
Perhaps no one knows how spiritually distant you have become.
Your family still thinks you are strong.
Your friends still think you are doing well.
Your social media still looks cheerful.
You still know the worship songs.
You still know how to say "God is good."
But privately, you know how far your heart has wandered.
And perhaps the most painful part is that you remember what it was like when Jesus was not simply part of your life.
He was your joy.
Your refuge.
Your first love.
And somewhere along the way, you began chasing other things.
If that is you, there is no need to manufacture an impressive prayer.
You can come to Christ honestly.

"Lord Jesus, I have loved Your gifts more than I have loved You. I have trusted things that cannot save me. I have defended sins that I should have confessed. Please forgive me. Turn my heart away from what has taken Your place. Teach me to trust You again. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising from the dead. I surrender my life to You. Make me faithful by Your grace. Amen."
There is no magical power in reciting those particular words.
Our confidence rests in Jesus Christ, not in the eloquence of a prayer.
But if your heart is being awakened to repentance, do not ignore that invitation.
Come to Him.
Not because you have earned another chance.
But because He is merciful.
And if you already belong to Christ but have wandered, remember the promise of 1 John 1:9:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
Faithful.
Just.
Forgiving.
Cleansing.
That is the Savior we proclaim.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not as a religious performance.
Not as a way to impress strangers.
But as an invitation to honest reflection.
What is the one thing you have been trusting more than God lately?
You do not have to expose private details publicly.
But perhaps your first act of honesty can be to stop pretending that everything is fine.
Let the comment section become more than a place for reactions.
Let it become a place where believers encourage one another with Scripture, compassion, truth, and prayer.
Someone may be reading these words while feeling completely alone.
Your honest testimony could remind them that repentance is possible, grace is real, and Christ is still at work in the lives of His people.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, consider sending the article to them personally.
Not to accuse them.
Not to embarrass them.
But because love sometimes means reminding someone where living water is found.
A person who would never walk into a church might stop long enough to read a testimony about the mercy of Christ.
A believer who has quietly drifted away might encounter the very Scripture they needed to hear.
A family member who has been carrying secret shame might discover that the Gospel offers a way home.
We cannot control who reads, believes, or responds.
But we can faithfully place biblical truth where people have an opportunity to encounter it.
Not because these words are more important than Scripture.
But because there may come a day when you find yourself chasing something that promises everything and delivers emptiness.
On that day, return to Hosea 2.
Remember the bread.
Remember the water.
Remember the forgotten Provider.
And remember the mercy of the God who calls His people back to Himself.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a personality around a page.
Not to sell the illusion of a trouble-free Christian life.
But to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ through Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, and biblical discipleship.
There are people who need more than another inspirational quotation.
They need Scripture explained faithfully.
They need encouragement rooted in truth.
They need to know that Christianity is not a promise of worldly comfort, but a call to follow the crucified and risen Savior.
And some people need a community that will remind them of God's faithfulness when their own hearts are weary.
We want these resources to continue reaching people who may not have the money to purchase Christian books or access paid discipleship materials.
And this is where I want to speak to those who believe in the mission of spreading the Gospel.
For Christians who choose to give from their resources, such support can be a voluntary expression of generosity and stewardship offered to the glory of God.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
Notice those words.
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
Cheerfully.
That is the spirit in which we invite you to participate.
And your generosity must never be measured by how much money you can give.
You do not have to purchase anything to receive God's favor.
Salvation is God's gift through faith in Jesus Christ, not something purchased through religious donations (Ephesians 2:8–9).
These items are not spiritual necessities.
They are simply resources and everyday products that may encourage reflection, conversation, and a visible witness to your faith.
The greater purpose remains unchanged.
Christ must be proclaimed.
Scripture must be honored.
People must be invited to repent and believe the Gospel.
And discipleship must point beyond a ministry brand to the Lord Jesus Himself.
Pray that we never sacrifice biblical faithfulness for popularity.
Pray that we never confuse emotional excitement with genuine spiritual transformation.
Pray that every resource, article, and message remains accountable to the truth of God's Word.
Pray that the people who encounter this ministry will see more of Jesus and less of us.
Because the greatest success of any Christian ministry is not the number of followers it gathers.
It is faithfulness to the Lord it claims to serve.
And now, before you leave, return with me to that ancient image in Hosea.
A woman chasing lovers.
Bread in her imagination.
Water in her expectations.
Promises of security in her heart.
She thought her lovers were sustaining her.
But the LORD was the true Provider.
She remembered what she wanted.
And forgot the One who had given her everything.
What a terrible tragedy it would be to spend our lives pursuing the blessings of God while remaining indifferent to God Himself.
What a sorrow to gain the admiration of people and neglect the Savior who gave His life for sinners.
What a loss to fill our homes with possessions while our hearts remain empty of worship.
But what extraordinary grace that the story does not have to end in rebellion.
Hosea announces judgment, but the book also proclaims restoration.
The New Testament announces something even greater in its fullness: Jesus Christ has come, died for our sins, and risen again.
And through Him, sinners are called to repentance, faith, forgiveness, and new life.
The question is not whether you have ever wandered.
The question is whether you will continue running from the One who calls you to return.
You may have spent years chasing bread.
You may have exhausted yourself pursuing water.
You may have given your deepest devotion to things that were never capable of saving you.
But Jesus Christ still calls sinners to come to Him.
And no earthly idol can give you what only the risen Savior provides.
You were never meant to spend your whole life chasing the gifts while forgetting the hands that gave them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE FAMILY SECRETS, FORBIDDEN DESIRES, AND SEXUAL SCANDALS GOD REFUSED TO ERASE FROM THE BIBLE
paragraphs: THE FAMILY SECRETS, FORBIDDEN DESIRES, AND SEXUAL SCANDALS GOD REFUSED TO ERASE FROM THE BIBLE

From incest and prostitution to royal concubines, dangerous seduction, and passionate marriage poetry—why would a holy God preserve such uncomfortable stories in His Word? The answer may change how you see your own past, your deepest struggles, and the redeeming power of Jesus Christ.
There are things families refuse to talk about.
Things buried beneath respectable last names. Things whispered behind closed doors. Things that happened years ago but somehow still haunt the people who never even witnessed them.
A pregnancy nobody wants explained.
A betrayal everyone pretends never happened.
A marriage that looks beautiful in photographs but is collapsing behind the walls.
A child carrying shame that never belonged to them.
A secret desire. A forbidden relationship. A moment of weakness that became a lifetime of consequences.
And sometimes, the people carrying these stories are sitting in church every Sunday.
Smiling.
Singing.
Lifting their hands in worship.
While silently wondering whether God could ever look at the whole truth about their lives and still love them.
But here is something that might surprise you.
God already knows the worst chapters of human history. And He deliberately allowed some of them to be recorded in the Bible.
Not because He celebrates wickedness.
Not because He excuses exploitation.
Not because every relationship described in Scripture receives His approval.
But because the God who saves sinners has never needed a sanitized version of humanity to reveal the glory of His grace.
Open your Bible.
You will find incestuous family histories, prostitution, adultery, sexual violence, royal concubines, seduction, polygamy, and marriages devastated by betrayal.
You will also find breathtaking poetry celebrating the beauty of marital love.

And standing above all these complicated human stories is a holy God who refuses to confuse love with lust, desire with entitlement, forgiveness with permission, or grace with the absence of consequences.
The Bible is not embarrassed by the truth.
Perhaps the more uncomfortable question is why we are so determined to hide ours.
Consider Lot.

He had survived the destruction of Sodom. He had witnessed judgment upon a city infamous for its wickedness. He had escaped with his daughters, yet his family was already carrying the devastation of everything they had lost.
Then Genesis 19 records one of the most disturbing family episodes in Scripture.
Lot's daughters made their father drunk and had sexual relations with him while he was unaware of what was happening.
The account connects those pregnancies with the origins of Moab and Ammon.
Read it carefully.
There is no command from God approving what happened. No divine celebration of incest. No suggestion that desperation turns wrongdoing into righteousness.
And the intoxicated father is not presented as knowingly consenting to those encounters.
Scripture records the event without requiring us to defend it.
This distinction matters enormously.
The Bible describing an action is not the same as God endorsing that action.
There are people today who have suffered violations within their own families, sometimes at the hands of people who were supposed to protect them.
If that is part of your history, hear this clearly.
What someone did to you does not make you spiritually contaminated.
Their wrongdoing is not your guilt.
Your worth was never surrendered to the person who violated your trust.
And the God who sees what happened does not demand that you pretend it was harmless.
Healing may require safety, truthful disclosure, wise pastoral care, professional support, and accountability for those responsible.
Forgiveness must never be twisted into permission for abuse to continue.
God's grace does not require victims to deny the truth.
But the story does not end in that cave.
Centuries later, a woman named Ruth appears.
She is a Moabite.
And suddenly, one of the peoples connected to that painful Genesis history becomes part of a much larger redemptive story.
Ruth follows Naomi into Bethlehem. She chooses loyalty over abandonment. She trusts the God of Israel.
And eventually, Ruth marries Boaz.
Their son is Obed.
Obed becomes the father of Jesse.
Jesse becomes the father of David.
And Matthew's Gospel places Ruth within the ancestry leading to Jesus Christ.
Think about that.
A woman from Moab becomes an honored figure in the family history of Israel's greatest king and, ultimately, in the earthly genealogy of the Messiah.
This does not mean God approved the wrongdoing recorded in Genesis 19.
It means that a people's painful origin does not place every future generation beyond the reach of His mercy.
Your family history may explain where you came from. It does not have the authority to decide what God's grace can make of your life.
And if that already challenges the way you see your past, wait until you meet Tamar.
Genesis 38 introduces a woman whose story is filled with bereavement, injustice, withheld responsibility, deception, and a sexual encounter that exposes a powerful man's hypocrisy.
Tamar had been married into Judah's family.
Her first husband died.
Her second husband also died after acting wickedly.
Judah then withheld the remaining son he had promised would eventually become her husband, leaving Tamar in a vulnerable position within the social and family structures of that time.
Eventually, Tamar disguised herself as a prostitute and Judah had relations with her without recognizing her.
When her pregnancy became known, Judah initially demanded punishment.
Then the evidence revealed that he himself was the father.
And Judah said something extraordinary.
In the Hebrew text of Genesis 38:26, he acknowledges:
צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי
Tsadeqah mimmenni.
A close translation is, "She is more righteous than I."
Not because every part of Tamar's strategy should be copied.
Not because sexual deception becomes a universal model of righteousness.
But because Judah recognized his own failure and the injustice he had committed against her.
The man who was ready to condemn a woman had to confront the wrongdoing he had been hiding.
Does that sound familiar?
How quickly people can demand judgment for the sins they can see while protecting the sins they have learned to conceal.
How easily religious language can become a shield for personal hypocrisy.
And yet Tamar's story does not disappear from the biblical record.
Matthew 1:3 explicitly names her in the genealogy of Jesus.
Perez, one of the sons born from that encounter, becomes an ancestor in the line leading to David and ultimately to Christ.
God did not need to rewrite the historical record to make the Messiah's ancestry look more respectable.
He preserved the truth.
Not to glorify the scandal.
But to show that human failure could not overthrow His redemptive purpose.
And then there is Rahab.
A woman introduced in Joshua 2 as a prostitute living in Jericho.
In Hebrew, the word used to describe her is:
זוֹנָה
Zonah.
The word ordinarily means a prostitute.
Scripture does not need to pretend she had a different occupation to make her story acceptable.
Rahab lived in a city facing judgment, yet she recognized that the God of Israel was truly God.
She protected the Israelite spies and asked that her family be spared.
Her confession in Joshua 2:11 is remarkable.
She acknowledges the LORD as God in heaven above and on earth beneath.
Her past is part of her story.
But it is not the final word about her faith.
Hebrews 11:31 remembers Rahab among those who acted by faith.
James 2:25 points to her actions as evidence of living faith.
And Matthew 1:5 names Rahab in the genealogy of Jesus.
Imagine that.
A woman once identified by prostitution is remembered in the New Testament for faith.
Not because prostitution itself was celebrated.
Not because God reclassified every past action as righteous.
But because faith in the living God mattered more than the identity by which society had known her.
Some people spend their entire lives terrified that their worst chapter will become their permanent name.
The adulterer.
The addict.
The abandoned woman.
The person with the ruined marriage.
The one whose past everyone knows.
But Rahab's story asks a question that reaches beyond Jericho.
What happens when God begins writing a future that your old reputation never could have predicted?
Then Scripture takes us into the royal courts of Israel.
And the stories become even more uncomfortable.
Kings had wives.
Kings had concubines.
Kings formed households that reflected the power arrangements of their world.
The Hebrew word often translated "concubine" is פִּילֶגֶשׁ, pilegesh.
It refers to a woman in a recognized but generally secondary marital or household relationship, whose social position and protections could differ from those of a principal wife.
These relationships existed in the ancient world.
But their presence in biblical narratives does not make them God's ideal for marriage.
Genesis 2:24 presents the foundational pattern of a man and his wife becoming one flesh.
Jesus returns to that creation account in Matthew 19:4–6 when teaching about marriage.
The fact that powerful men accumulated women does not mean the Creator commanded them to do so.
In fact, Deuteronomy 17:17 warns Israel's king against multiplying wives for himself.
And when you read the stories of the royal households, you begin to understand why.
David's family became fractured by sexual wrongdoing, violence, rivalry, and devastating grief.
In 2 Samuel 13, Amnon violated his half-sister Tamar despite her resistance.
The account portrays an act of sexual violence, not a romantic encounter.
Tamar's protest and suffering matter.
Her story should never be softened into a tale of forbidden passion.
There is a profound difference between love and possession.
Between affection and coercion.
Between desire and the decision to disregard another person's dignity.
A desire that refuses to respect another person's humanity is not made holy simply because it feels powerful.
Later, Absalom publicly took his father's concubines as part of his rebellion, fulfilling a devastating prophetic judgment recorded in 2 Samuel 12:11–12 and narrated in 2 Samuel 16:21–22.
These women were caught in a struggle for royal power.
Their vulnerability should not be overlooked.
The narrative is not an invitation to admire the spectacle.
It reveals how ambition, humiliation, and the abuse of power can turn human beings into instruments of revenge.
And Solomon?
The king associated with extraordinary wisdom accumulated seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines, according to 1 Kings 11:3.
Yet Scripture explicitly says his wives turned his heart away.
What the world might have interpreted as status and abundance became part of his spiritual downfall.
One thousand women did not produce one thousand measures of faithfulness.
Royal privilege could not protect a divided heart.
And there is a lesson here that reaches directly into modern life.
You can have access to more people, more attention, more opportunities, and more pleasure than previous generations ever imagined.
You can carry an entire world of temptation inside a phone.
You can be admired publicly and spiritually empty privately.
You can be surrounded by people and still be profoundly lonely.
The human heart cannot be healed merely by giving it more of everything it desires.
David himself knew the devastation of desire left unchecked.
He saw Bathsheba bathing.
He sent for her.
He slept with her.
And when she became pregnant, he attempted to conceal what had happened.
Bathsheba was the wife of Uriah, one of David's soldiers.
David was the king.
That imbalance of power must not be ignored.
The text does not give us grounds to treat Bathsheba as the architect of David's wrongdoing.
Scripture places grave responsibility upon David, who used his position, arranged Uriah's death, and took Bathsheba as his wife.
Second Samuel 11:27 declares that what David had done displeased the LORD.
The prophet Nathan confronted him.
David confessed.
And although God showed mercy, the consequences were devastating.
The child born from that pregnancy died.
David's household continued to experience terrible suffering.
Repentance was real.
Forgiveness was real.
But forgiveness did not erase every earthly consequence.
That is a truth many people would rather avoid.
We sometimes want grace to mean that nothing painful follows our choices.
We want repentance without confession.
Restoration without accountability.
Mercy without truth.
But biblical grace is not the art of pretending sin was harmless.
It is the mercy of God meeting sinners in the truth.
Psalm 51 gives voice to David's repentance.
In Psalm 51:10, the Hebrew reads:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
"Create in me a clean heart, O God."
Notice what David asks for.
Not merely a repaired reputation.
Not a more convincing explanation.
Not a way to silence Nathan.
A clean heart.
He knows the problem runs deeper than public exposure.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us are not afraid of being guilty.
We are afraid of being discovered.
We know how to look faithful.
We know which Bible verses to post.
We know how to speak about holiness.
But when nobody is watching, we return to the same habits, the same conversations, the same secret compromises.
And then we wonder why our souls feel exhausted.
The Gospel does not invite us to become better actors.
It invites us to come into the light.
But here is where the Bible surprises us again.
After all these painful accounts of distorted desire, Scripture gives us a book filled with passionate love poetry.
The Song of Songs.
In Hebrew, its title begins:
שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים
Shir haShirim.
Literally, "Song of Songs"—a Hebrew expression conveying the excellence of the song.
And its language is tender, poetic, intimate, and at times strikingly sensual.
The lovers express longing.
They admire one another.
They delight in physical beauty.
They anticipate closeness.
They speak in images drawn from gardens, vineyards, spices, flowers, and the natural world.
Song of Songs 8:7 declares, in a close translation of the Hebrew:
"Many waters cannot extinguish love, and rivers cannot sweep it away."
Think about what this means.
The same Bible that exposes adultery and condemns sexual exploitation also preserves poetry celebrating romantic desire.
Why?
Because human desire itself is not automatically evil.
God created human beings as embodied creatures.
Marriage is not presented in Scripture merely as a legal arrangement without affection.
The biblical vision includes covenant, faithfulness, mutual belonging, and delight.
Desire becomes destructive when it is detached from truth, faithfulness, and love of neighbor.
It becomes dangerous when another person is reduced to an object.
When pleasure becomes more important than integrity.
When secrecy replaces honesty.
When the pursuit of satisfaction tramples the dignity of another human being.
But desire expressed faithfully within God's design for marriage is not something believers need to regard as inherently shameful.
The Song of Songs has also been read by Jewish and Christian interpreters as expressing deeper truths about divine love.
Yet its poetic celebration of human love should not be erased in the process.
God does not need to deny the goodness of creation in order to teach us holiness.
Holiness is not the destruction of everything human. It is the surrender of our humanity to the One who created it.
And now we come to the most astonishing part of all.
Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy.
For many readers, genealogies are the pages they hurry past.
Names.
Generations.
Fathers.
Sons.
History.
But hidden in that list are reminders of some of the stories we have just encountered.
Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
And the wife of Uriah.
Matthew does not even name Bathsheba in that particular reference.
He calls attention to her connection with Uriah, preserving the memory of the marriage David violated.
It is as though the genealogy refuses to let royal history become a polished public-relations campaign.
There are stories here that no human family would choose for its official portrait.
And yet the genealogy moves steadily toward Jesus.
The Christ.
The promised Son of David.
The One whose coming was not prevented by the failures of those who came before Him.
But do not misunderstand this.
Jesus did not come because sin was beautiful.
He came because sinners needed a Savior.
He did not come to baptize human rebellion with religious language.
He came to redeem.
He came to call sinners to repentance.
He came to seek and save the lost.
He came to do what no human being could accomplish through self-improvement alone.
And this is why the Gospel is so much greater than a motivational message about overcoming your past.
Jesus Christ is not merely offering you a better self-image.
He is offering reconciliation with God through His death and resurrection.
The Son of God entered our broken world without participating in its sin.
He was tempted, yet without sin, as Hebrews 4:15 teaches.
He gave Himself for sinners.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree, according to 1 Peter 2:24.
And He rose again.
Not simply to make people feel forgiven.
But to accomplish the salvation that human beings could never earn.
When Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:9–11 about patterns of unrighteousness, he does not pretend sin is unimportant.
He names serious sins and warns against continuing in unrighteousness.
Then he writes something extraordinary:
And he goes on to speak of believers being washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
The Greek of 1 Corinthians 6:11 includes:
ἀλλὰ ἀπελούσασθε
Alla apelousasthe.
"But you were washed."
The verb communicates cleansing, and in this passage it belongs to Paul's description of the decisive change associated with belonging to Christ.
He is not saying that every struggle instantly disappeared.
He is not saying that believers never need repentance again.
He is saying that their former sinful identities no longer have the final authority over who they are in Christ.
That is the difference between religious performance and redemption.
Religion without the Gospel can teach you how to conceal the stain.
Christ offers cleansing.
Religion without grace can make you terrified of exposure.
Christ calls you into truthful repentance and forgiveness.
Religion without transformation can leave you outwardly respectable and inwardly enslaved.
Christ gives His people the Holy Spirit and calls them to walk in newness of life.
And maybe you are reading this while carrying a secret nobody knows.
Maybe your marriage has been wounded by betrayal.
Maybe pornography has become a habit you keep promising to abandon.
Maybe you are wrestling with desires you do not know how to surrender.
Maybe someone exploited you, and you have spent years blaming yourself.
Maybe your family history is filled with abandonment, violence, infidelity, or shame.
Or maybe your greatest struggle is not something the world would call scandalous.
Maybe it is pride.
Self-righteousness.
A judgmental heart.
The quiet pleasure of seeing another person's sin exposed while your own remains hidden.
Whatever brought you here, do not confuse conviction with hopelessness.
The Holy Spirit's work of conviction calls us toward truth and Christ.
It is not an invitation to despair.
There is a difference between saying, "I have sinned," and believing, "I am beyond the reach of God's mercy."
The first can become the beginning of repentance.
The second denies the sufficiency of the Savior.
And for those who have been sinned against, the call is not to confess responsibility for another person's evil.
It is to know that Christ sees your suffering, values your dignity, and offers hope without requiring you to excuse injustice.
The cross speaks both of the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable mercy of God.
At Calvary, grace was not cheap.
Our redemption was purchased at the cost of Christ's own life.
And the empty tomb declares that death did not have the final word.
So why do we keep behaving as though our past is more powerful than the risen Jesus?
Why do we keep hiding from the One who already knows us?
Why do we keep returning to the very things that are destroying our peace?
Why do we sometimes prefer the appearance of holiness to the difficult beauty of actual repentance?
There is a moment in John 8 when a woman accused of adultery stands before Jesus, surrounded by men eager to condemn her.

The passage of John 7:53–8:11 has a well-known textual-history question: it is absent from many of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts and appears in different locations in some manuscript traditions. It has nevertheless been received in many Christian traditions as a treasured account, and its themes accord with Jesus' clearly attested mercy toward sinners and His call to repentance.
In the familiar account, Jesus says:
"Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more."
Notice both parts.
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin behind.
Jesus does not treat the woman as disposable.
Neither does He describe adultery as harmless.
He refuses to make condemnation the end of her story.
And He calls her toward a different life.
This is the Christ-centered balance we desperately need.
Truth without cruelty.
Grace without compromise.
Repentance without despair.
Forgiveness without pretending consequences do not exist.
Love without exploitation.
Holiness without hypocrisy.
And hope grounded not in human perfection, but in the finished work of Jesus Christ.
If this article has touched a place you normally keep hidden, I want to invite you into something more meaningful than another quick reaction on social media.
Be honest before God.
You do not have to disclose private trauma or personal sins publicly to prove your sincerity. But if you want someone to pray with you, you can comment, "Christ is still healing me."
And if your testimony is that Jesus has brought you out of a painful past, consider sharing a few words about His faithfulness. Someone reading the comments may need to know that change is possible.
There may be a person in your family who believes they have already ruined their life.
A friend who has quietly abandoned church because of shame.
A husband or wife struggling to rebuild trust.
A young believer who has never understood the difference between biblical desire and sinful lust.
A survivor who needs to hear that the wrong committed against them does not define their worth.
But I also want to speak to those who believe this ministry should continue reaching more people.
Every article requires time, research, writing, biblical care, and the ongoing work of placing these messages before readers who may never walk into a church building.
Every testimony shared, every biblical truth explained, and every struggling soul encouraged represents an opportunity to serve Christ by serving people.
It is a practical way of helping sustain and expand this work so that more people can encounter biblical teaching, Gospel-centered encouragement, and resources for spiritual growth.
The New Testament teaches that giving should be willing, not coerced.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says that each person should give as they have decided in their heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
It does not replace repentance, worship, fellowship, or obedience.
And you do not have to pay to glorify God.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one meaningful expression of generosity and partnership in ministry.
It is spiritual nourishment.
It is helping make room for more biblical teaching, more encouragement, and more opportunities to point people toward Jesus.
Those free resources are part of our desire to make biblical encouragement and spiritual learning more accessible.
Because the purpose of this ministry is not to build a following around human personalities.
It is to keep pointing people toward the One who died for sinners and rose again.
Why would God preserve so many uncomfortable human stories in His holy Word?
Why leave the record of Lot's family?
Why tell us about Tamar and Judah?
Why identify Rahab as a prostitute?
Why expose David's adultery and abuse of power?
Why show the ruin that followed Solomon's multiplied marriages?
Why preserve both the darkness of sexual wrongdoing and the beauty of faithful marital love?
Because Scripture tells the truth about the human condition.
Because sin is real.
Because desire matters.
Because the vulnerable matter.
Because holiness matters.
Because our choices have consequences.
And because God's redemptive purpose is greater than the human failures that appear throughout the biblical story.
But above all, because these accounts prepare us to recognize how desperately we need Jesus Christ.
The Bible is not a gallery of flawless heroes.
It is the unfolding revelation of a holy God who acts in history to redeem a people for Himself.
Its central hope is not that human beings eventually learn to hide their failures more successfully.
Its central hope is that Jesus Christ has come to save sinners.
And that means the final question is not simply whether your past is scandalous.
It is whether you will bring your life into the light of His truth.
Will you repent where repentance is needed?
Will you seek help where healing is needed?
Will you stop defending what God calls sin?
Will you stop carrying guilt for what someone else did to you?
Will you trust that the blood of Christ is sufficient to cleanse the sinner who comes to Him in faith?
Will you follow Jesus, not merely admire the idea of being forgiven?
The past cannot be undone.
Some consequences must still be faced.
Some relationships may never return to what they once were.
Some wounds require long seasons of care and healing.
But the Gospel declares that no repentant sinner needs to remain separated from God when they come to Christ in faith.
And no survivor of another person's wrongdoing needs to accept shame as their identity.
Jesus does not promise that every earthly story will become painless.
He promises something infinitely greater to those who belong to Him.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
The presence of His Spirit.
The hope of resurrection.
And a future in which sin, death, and sorrow will not reign forever.
So when the enemy of your soul tries to convince you that the worst chapter of your life is the only chapter that matters, remember the testimony of Scripture.
God did not erase the uncomfortable histories.
He revealed His saving purpose through the unfolding story that leads to Christ.
And when you are tempted to believe that your story is already finished, remember the empty tomb.
The scars may remain in your story, but they do not have to become the name by which you live forever.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE NIGHT HEAVEN OPENED OVER A BROKEN WORLD: Why Jesus Said Angels Would Ascend and Descend Upon Him
paragraphs: THE NIGHT HEAVEN OPENED OVER A BROKEN WORLD: Why Jesus Said Angels Would Ascend and Descend Upon Him

One mysterious sentence from Jesus. One ancient dream about a stairway to heaven. And one breathtaking revelation: the distance between a holy God and a sinful humanity was never going to be overcome by our efforts. Heaven had already prepared Someone who would come down for us.
There are moments when you can be surrounded by people and still feel impossibly far from God.
You pray, but the ceiling seems silent.
You worship, but your heart feels strangely empty.
You smile at church, answer messages, go to work, take care of your family, and convince everyone that you're doing fine.
But somewhere beneath all that activity is a question you rarely dare to say aloud.
“After everything I've done… can someone like me still come close to God?”
Maybe you haven't stopped believing in Jesus.
You've simply started wondering whether He still wants you near Him.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part is that you've spent years trying to climb your way back to a God who already came down to find you.

Because hidden inside one of the most astonishing statements Jesus ever made is a truth powerful enough to change how you understand heaven, forgiveness, prayer, salvation, and your entire relationship with God.
Jesus said something to a man named Nathanael that must have sounded almost impossible.
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.” — John 1:51, KJV
Read those words again.
Not angels merely descending from heaven.
Not angels simply returning to heaven.
But angels ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.
Why would Jesus describe Himself this way?
Why would He speak of an opened heaven?
And why did He choose imagery that would have reminded a Jewish listener of one of the strangest dreams in the Old Testament?
To understand what Jesus was revealing, we have to travel backward through Scripture, to a lonely man sleeping on the ground, with a stone beneath his head and a history he could not escape.
His name was Jacob.
And his story was anything but respectable.
Jacob was running.
Not because he had been unjustly accused.
Not because everyone had misunderstood his intentions.
He was fleeing the consequences of a family shattered by deception, rivalry, and betrayal.

Jacob had obtained his brother Esau's birthright through a transaction and, later, deceived his aging father Isaac to receive the blessing intended for Esau. His brother became furious enough to threaten his life.
So Jacob left home.
No grand procession.
No comfortable bed.
No visible sign that his life was heading toward anything beautiful.
Just a frightened man on a difficult journey, carrying a complicated past.
And somewhere along the road, as darkness settled over the land, Jacob stopped to sleep.
Genesis 28:11 tells us he took one of the stones of that place, placed it beneath his head, and lay down.
Imagine that scene.
The cold earth.
The silence.
The uncertainty of tomorrow.
A man who had manipulated his way toward a blessing, now lying in the wilderness with almost nothing.
And then something extraordinary happened.
“And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it.” — Genesis 28:12, KJV
There it is.
The connection.
The very imagery Jesus would later use.
But there is something in the original Hebrew that makes this scene even more fascinating.
The word translated “ladder” is סֻלָּם (sullām).
It refers to a structure connecting different levels, traditionally understood as a ladder or stairway. The precise physical appearance of Jacob's dream is not described in detail.
What matters is what the structure represents.
Earth below.
Heaven above.
And a connection between them that Jacob did not build.
Jacob was asleep when the vision came.
He wasn't constructing a tower.
He wasn't performing a religious ceremony to earn an encounter.
He wasn't proving himself worthy of divine attention.
God took the initiative.

And the LORD stood above the stairway, declaring His covenant promises to Jacob, including the promise that his descendants would become a great people and that through his offspring all the families of the earth would be blessed.
Then came words that must have shaken Jacob more deeply than the dream itself.
“And, behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest…” — Genesis 28:15, KJV
God was not endorsing Jacob's deception.
The rest of Jacob's story would involve painful consequences, difficult lessons, and profound transformation.
But God's covenant faithfulness was greater than Jacob's failures.
When Jacob awoke, he was overwhelmed.
“Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not.” — Genesis 28:16, KJV
Then he said:
“This is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.” — Genesis 28:17, KJV
He called the place Bethel.
In Hebrew, בֵּית־אֵל (Bēṯ-ʾĒl) means “house of God.”
And centuries later, Jesus would take the imagery of Jacob's dream and make a declaration that changed everything.
But first, we need to understand the man standing before Him.
Nathanael.
When Philip told Nathanael that they had found the One Moses and the prophets had written about—Jesus of Nazareth—Nathanael was skeptical.
“Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?” — John 1:46, KJV
Philip did not launch into a long argument.
He simply answered:
“Come and see.”
And sometimes that is where a life-changing encounter with Christ begins.
Not with every question answered.
Not with every doubt resolved.
But with enough willingness to come and see who Jesus really is.
As Nathanael approached, Jesus said:
“Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!” — John 1:47, KJV
The Greek word translated “guile” is δόλος (dolos), meaning deceit, trickery, or cunning.
That detail matters.
Because Jacob, whose name became Israel, had a history deeply marked by deception.
Yet here stood Nathanael, an Israelite Jesus described as being without deceit.
The connection is striking.

John does not explicitly explain every intended association between Nathanael and Jacob, so we should not pretend to know more than Scripture tells us. But the language makes the coming reference to Jacob's dream especially meaningful.
Nathanael was astonished.
“Whence knowest thou me?”
Jesus answered:
“Before that Philip called thee, when thou wast under the fig tree, I saw thee.” — John 1:48, KJV
We are not told exactly what Nathanael was doing beneath that fig tree.
Some have imagined that he was praying or meditating on Scripture, but the text does not say.
What we do know is that Jesus revealed knowledge of Nathanael that Nathanael found extraordinary.
And suddenly, the skeptical man confessed:
“Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel.” — John 1:49, KJV
But Jesus was not finished.
He told Nathanael that he would see greater things.
Then came the breathtaking declaration:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.” — John 1:51, KJV
The Greek is worth hearing:
ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν… τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀνεῳγότα καὶ τοὺς ἀγγέλους τοῦ θεοῦ ἀναβαίνοντας καὶ καταβαίνοντας ἐπὶ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου.
A close translation is:
“Truly, truly, I say to you… heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.”
Notice something easily missed in English.
Jesus begins with λέγω ὑμῖν (legō hymin)—“I say to you,” using the plural form.
Although Jesus is speaking in conversation with Nathanael, His promise reaches beyond Nathanael alone.
And the Greek word ἀνεῳγότα (aneōgota) describes heaven as opened.
Then comes the most astonishing detail.
In Jacob's dream, the angels ascend and descend upon the stairway.
In Jesus' declaration, they ascend and descend upon the Son of Man.
Jesus does not say, “I will show you where the ladder is.”
He places Himself where the ladder stood in Jacob's vision.
The connection between heaven and earth is no longer presented merely as something Jacob saw in a dream. It is revealed in Someone standing before Nathanael.
Jesus Christ.
The eternal Son who became flesh.
The One through whom the Father makes Himself known.
The One who would reconcile sinners to God through His death and resurrection.
The One who could say:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” — John 14:6, KJV
This does not mean Jesus was literally a wooden ladder.
It does not mean believers should seek angelic encounters as proof of salvation.
And it does not mean John 1:51 provides a complete explanation of every movement of angels between heaven and earth.
The imagery is far greater than that.
Jesus is identifying Himself as the decisive meeting place between God and humanity.
The fulfillment toward which Jacob's vision points.
And here is where this ancient passage begins to reach into the most private places of our lives.
Because many of us are still living as though salvation depends upon building our own stairway to heaven.
We think that if we pray enough, God might finally listen.
If we serve enough, perhaps He will accept us.
If we stop failing, maybe He will draw near.
If we hide our worst sins, perhaps we can preserve the appearance of holiness.
So we keep climbing.
One religious performance after another.
One promise to do better.
One exhausting attempt to prove that we deserve the love of God.
And when we fall, we assume we have lost all the ground we gained.
But the Gospel announces something radically different.
We could not climb our way into heaven, so the Son of God came down to rescue us.
John 1:14 declares:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us…”
The Greek expression ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν (eskēnōsen en hēmin) means that He dwelt, or tabernacled, among us.
The language evokes God's dwelling among His people.
Think about that.
The God who revealed His presence to Jacob in the wilderness entered human history in the person of Jesus Christ.
Not as an illusion.
Not as a temporary appearance pretending to be human.
The eternal Word truly became flesh.
He knew hunger.
He experienced weariness.
He wept.
He was rejected.
He was betrayed.
He stood among people who were ashamed, wounded, religiously proud, morally compromised, and desperate for mercy.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called people away from sin without withholding compassion from those who came to Him.
And eventually, He walked toward a cross.
Because the greatest barrier between us and God was not simply emotional distance.
It was sin.
Scripture does not soften that reality.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23, KJV
Not some.
All.
The respectable and the rebellious.
The churchgoer and the skeptic.
The person whose sins became public and the person whose sins remain carefully hidden.
We have all fallen short.
And no amount of spiritual enthusiasm can erase our guilt.
But listen to what Scripture says about Jesus:
“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; Who gave himself a ransom for all…” — 1 Timothy 2:5–6, KJV
One mediator.
Not your religious reputation.
Not your good works.
Not your family history.
Not your financial generosity.
Not even your ability to maintain a perfect Christian appearance.
Jesus Christ.
The One who is fully God and truly man.
The One who alone is sufficient to reconcile us to the Father.
And perhaps you need to hear this more than anything else today:
Jesus did not come to help you finish building a ladder. He came to accomplish the salvation you could never build for yourself.
That is why the cross matters.
At Calvary, Jesus did not merely provide an inspiring example of sacrificial love.
He bore sin.
He suffered for sinners.
He accomplished the work of redemption.
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God…” — 1 Peter 3:18, KJV
Did you catch those final words?
“That he might bring us to God.”
That is the heart of it.
The purpose of reconciliation.
The beauty behind the imagery of an opened heaven.
Jesus brings sinners to God.
And when Christ died, the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom.
Matthew 27:51 records that extraordinary event.
The book of Hebrews helps us understand the significance of Christ's sacrifice: through His blood, believers have confidence to draw near to God.
Hebrews 10:19–22 calls us to approach with a true heart and full assurance of faith.
Not because we have become sinless through our own strength.
But because Christ's sacrifice is sufficient.
And then, on the third day, the crucified Savior rose from the dead.
Death did not defeat Him.
The grave did not hold Him.
The One who came down from heaven accomplished His mission and was exalted in glory.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately about people desperately trying to reach an inaccessible God.
It is about the holy God who acted in Jesus Christ to save people who could never save themselves.
And still, something remarkable remains in Jesus' words to Nathanael.
He specifically mentioned angels.
Why?
In Genesis 28, the angels are part of Jacob's vision of heaven's activity and God's sovereign presence.
In John 1:51, Jesus uses that imagery to reveal His own central place in God's saving purpose.
Throughout the Gospels, angels appear in connection with significant moments in Jesus' earthly ministry.
An angel announces His conception to Mary.
Angels announce His birth to shepherds.
Angels minister to Him after His temptation in the wilderness.
An angel strengthens Him in Gethsemane, according to Luke 22:43, a verse whose textual transmission has been discussed by scholars.
Angels announce the empty tomb.
And at His ascension, heavenly messengers testify that He will return.
Yet notice what Scripture never asks us to do.
It never tells us to make angels the center of our faith.
It never tells us to seek salvation through angels.
It never tells us to worship them.
In Revelation 22:8–9, an angel explicitly rejects worship and directs it toward God.
And Hebrews 1:14 describes angels as ministering spirits sent forth to serve for the sake of those who will inherit salvation.
The angels are servants.
Jesus is the Savior.
The angels testify to God's work.
Jesus accomplishes the work of redemption.
The angels ascend and descend.
Jesus is the One through whom sinners are brought to the Father.
And that distinction matters because we live in a world fascinated with supernatural experiences while often neglecting the Savior Himself.
People want signs.
Visions.
Mysteries.
Secret revelations.
But the greatest revelation of God's saving love has already been given in His Son.
You do not need an angel to tell you whether Jesus is willing to receive repentant sinners.
Jesus has already spoken.
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37, KJV
Read that slowly.
Not “the person with a flawless past.”
Not “the person who has never doubted.”
Not “the person who never fell into the same sin twice.”
“Him that cometh to me…”
Come to Him.
Not to excuse your sin.
Not to negotiate with God.
Not to pretend repentance is unnecessary.
But to confess, turn, trust, and surrender to the One whose grace is sufficient to save.
Repentance is not an attempt to purchase God's mercy.
It is the fitting response of a heart turning away from sin and toward Christ.
And faith is not confidence that you will never struggle again.
It is confidence in the Savior who died and rose again, and whose grace teaches His people to live transformed lives.
Maybe you have been hiding a sin that has slowly hardened your heart.
Maybe your marriage is wounded.
Maybe you have disappointed people who trusted you.
Maybe your secret addiction has made you afraid to pray.
Maybe you have spent years serving in ministry while privately wondering whether you truly know the Lord.
Or maybe you are the person who has never stepped inside a church because you assume God would want nothing to do with you.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not promise that your actions have no consequences.
It does not guarantee that every broken relationship will be restored immediately.
It does not tell you that healing will always be quick.
But it does declare that no repentant sinner is beyond the saving power of Jesus Christ.
“Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound.” — Romans 5:20, KJV
That verse is not permission to continue in sin.
Paul immediately rejects that misunderstanding in Romans 6:1–2.
Grace does not make sin harmless.
Grace brings us under the lordship of the One who breaks sin's dominion.
And perhaps that is the miracle you need most.
Not another temporary emotional high.
Not another promise that everything will become easy.
But a real encounter with Jesus Christ that begins changing the direction of your life.
Jacob's story did not end beside that stone in the wilderness.
He would encounter hardship, experience God's discipline and faithfulness, and eventually receive the name Israel in the context of wrestling with God.
The man who once fled from his past would be brought through a long process of transformation.
And Nathanael's story did not end beneath the fig tree.
The skeptical man was invited into a greater revelation of the Messiah.
One man saw a stairway in a dream.
Another heard the Son of God declare that heaven would be opened upon Him.
And we, reading these Scriptures after the cross and resurrection, can see how profoundly they point us toward Christ.
Not every detail of Jacob's dream is explained in the New Testament.
We should remain humble about what Scripture leaves unexplained.
But the central connection is unmistakable.
Jesus deliberately echoes the vision of ascending and descending angels, and places Himself at the center.
He is not merely another religious teacher pointing upward.
