He does not know that God will use him to preserve many lives.
All he knows is that the people he trusted have betrayed him.
And still, God has not abandoned him.
But the most glorious truth is not that every Joseph will eventually become a ruler in Egypt.
Scripture does not promise that every believer will receive earthly power, financial prosperity, or public vindication.
The greater promise is found in Jesus Christ.
The Savior who was betrayed.
The Savior who suffered.
The Savior who died.
The Savior who rose again.
The Savior who will one day judge all evil and make all things new.
Joseph's brothers received twenty pieces of silver.
Judas received thirty.
But neither transaction could determine the worth of the innocent person betrayed.
And no betrayal you have suffered can cancel the dignity God gave you as His image-bearer.
No sin you have committed is beyond the sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice when you turn to Him in repentance and faith.
No human price tag can measure the riches of God's grace.
So do not leave this story merely admiring Joseph's resilience.
Look to Joseph's God.
Look to the greater Savior to whom Joseph's story points.
Look to Jesus Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Follow Him.
And remember that the greatest transformation is not from poverty to wealth, from obscurity to influence, or from prison to a palace.
It is from condemnation to forgiveness.
From spiritual death to life.
From alienation to reconciliation with God.
From sin to grace through Jesus Christ.

They could sell Joseph for twenty pieces of silver, but they could never sell away the purpose of the God who held his life—and at Calvary, Jesus proved that human betrayal would not have the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN YOUR LOVED ONES IN HEAVEN SEE YOU CRYING? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT MAY CHANGE HOW YOU GRIEVE FOREVER
paragraphs: CAN YOUR LOVED ONES IN HEAVEN SEE YOU CRYING? THE BIBLICAL TRUTH THAT MAY CHANGE HOW YOU GRIEVE FOREVER

When someone you love dies, are they watching you from heaven? Do they know when you're suffering, when you fall into sin, or when you finally surrender your life to Jesus? Scripture reveals something far more profound than the comforting answers we often hear—and the truth leads us to the One who has never taken His eyes off you.
There is a kind of loneliness that only someone who has buried a loved one can understand.
You can be surrounded by people and still feel it.
You can laugh at a family gathering, smile for a photograph, go to church, sing the worship songs, and tell everyone you're doing fine.
Then you come home.
The door closes.
The noise disappears.
And suddenly, the silence becomes unbearable.
You look at the empty chair.
The untouched belongings.
The photograph that somehow carries an entire lifetime inside one frame.
And without warning, you whisper something into the room.
“Mom, can you see me?”
“Dad, are you proud of me?”
“Grandma, do you know how much I miss you?”
Or perhaps the question comes from a wound nobody else knows about.
“If you can see me from heaven, did you see what happened to me?”
Did you see the betrayal?
The divorce?
The diagnosis?
The night I almost gave up?
Did you see me crying when everyone else thought I was strong?
And somewhere between longing and faith, another question rises.
Can people in heaven actually see what is happening here on earth?
Not what Hollywood says.
Not what a sentimental quotation says.
Not what we wish were true because the alternative feels too painful.
What does God actually reveal in His Word?
Because there is something dangerous about building our comfort on something God never promised.
And there is something extraordinarily beautiful about discovering that the comfort He did promise is greater than the answer we were searching for.
Stay with me.
Especially if you have ever stood beside a grave and wished heaven had a window.
Because by the time we reach the cross of Jesus Christ, this question will become much more personal than you might expect.
And the answer may change not only how you think about the dead—but how you live before the living God.
The first passage people often mention is Hebrews 12:1.

“Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us.” (KJV)
That sounds almost unmistakable, doesn't it?
A great cloud of witnesses.
People who have gone before us.
People surrounding us.
Surely that means our departed loved ones are watching us from heaven like spectators in a stadium.
But before we make that conclusion, we need to do something many believers have forgotten how to do.
We need to read the verse in context.
The original Greek describes the cloud of witnesses as:
νέφος μαρτύρων — nephos martyrōn
Literally, “a cloud of witnesses.”
The word martyrōn is the genitive plural of martys, meaning a witness—someone who testifies.
It is the word from which the English word “martyr” eventually developed.
But here is what matters.
Hebrews 11 has just recounted the faith of Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab, and others who trusted God despite suffering, uncertainty, persecution, and death.
These people are witnesses to the faithfulness of God through the testimony of their lives.
Their stories testify that God can be trusted.
Hebrews 12 then calls us to run our own race faithfully.
The image of a surrounding cloud may evoke spectators, but the text does not explicitly say that these believers are continuously observing everything happening on earth.
And notice where the writer directs our attention immediately afterward.
“Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith.” (Hebrews 12:2, KJV)
Not looking toward heaven to see whether Grandma is watching.
Not living for the approval of departed saints.
Looking unto Jesus.
The Greek phrase begins with:
ἀφορῶντες εἰς Ἰησοῦν — aphorōntes eis Iēsoun
It carries the sense of directing our gaze toward Jesus, turning our attention to Him.
The writer's purpose is not to satisfy our curiosity about heavenly observation.
It is to strengthen our endurance through Christ.
And that distinction matters.
Because sometimes we become so desperate to know whether someone in heaven is looking down at us that we forget the One who is looking upon us with perfect knowledge, mercy, and love.
Jesus.
The Savior who knows every hidden tear.
The Shepherd who never loses one of His sheep.
The Lord who does not need a window into your life because nothing about your life has ever been hidden from Him.
But Hebrews is not the only passage that raises this question.
There is another.
And this one is even more fascinating.
In Revelation 6:9–10, the apostle John describes the souls of martyrs crying out to God for justice.
They ask:
“How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?” (Revelation 6:10, KJV)
Think carefully about what is happening.
These martyrs are portrayed as conscious in God's presence.
They remember the injustice they suffered.
They know that God's final judgment has not yet been completed.
They cry out for divine justice.
This gives us a legitimate biblical reason to believe that those in heaven may possess awareness of at least some matters connected with earthly events.
But we must be careful.
The passage does not explain how the martyrs received their knowledge.
It does not tell us whether they are watching earth directly.
It does not say they know every conversation, every tragedy, every private decision, or every moment of their families' lives.
And because Revelation is apocalyptic literature filled with symbolic imagery, we must interpret its visions with humility.
We can affirm what Scripture reveals without pretending it reveals more.
Some heavenly awareness of earthly matters is biblically plausible. Unlimited observation of everything happening on earth is not biblically established.
That is not a disappointing answer.
It is an honest one.
And faith does not become weaker when we refuse to invent details God has not given us.
Faith becomes stronger when we learn to trust Him even where revelation stops.
Now consider something Jesus said in Luke 15:7.
“I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance.” (KJV)
Joy in heaven.
Over a sinner who repents.
Imagine that.
Somewhere tonight, a man who has spent years destroying his marriage may finally fall to his knees and confess his sin.
A young woman who believes she has gone too far may finally understand that the blood of Christ is sufficient to cleanse her.
A hardened unbeliever may open the Bible expecting nothing and encounter the truth of the Gospel.
A churchgoer who has worn a religious mask for decades may finally stop pretending.
And Jesus says there is joy in heaven over repentance.
In the Greek, the word for repentance is:
μετανοοῦντι — metanoounti
It comes from metanoeō, meaning to repent—to change one's mind or understanding in a way that involves turning from sin toward God.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling ashamed.
It is not simply crying because consequences have arrived.
It is a genuine turning toward God, inseparable from faith and expressed in a changed direction of life.
And heaven rejoices over that.
Luke 15:10 further says there is joy “in the presence of the angels of God” over one sinner who repents.
Does this mean departed believers personally witness every conversion?
The passage does not say.
Some Christians understand these verses as allowing for the participation of heaven's inhabitants in such joy.
Others emphasize the joy of God and His angels without drawing conclusions about departed human beings.
Both should acknowledge what the text does and does not explicitly reveal.
But do not miss the unmistakable truth.
Your repentance matters to heaven.
Not your popularity.
Not your bank account.
Not the size of your house.
Not how many people applaud you.
Your repentance.
Your return to the Father.
Your surrender to Jesus Christ.
Heaven's joy is not presented as a celebration of how impressive you have become.
It is a celebration of God's mercy toward sinners who come home.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that more than anything else today.
You have been wondering whether your mother in heaven would be proud of you.
But there is a greater question.
Are you walking with the Savior she taught you about?
You have been wondering whether your father can see how successful you have become.
But what if the most important thing about your life is not what you have accomplished?
What if it is whether you belong to Jesus?
You have been trying to live in a way that would make someone you lost smile.
And there is tenderness in that desire.
But please hear this.
The dead cannot become the center of the life that Christ purchased with His blood.
Honor their memory.
Give thanks for their love.
Remember the lessons they taught you.
But worship Jesus.
Follow Jesus.
Trust Jesus.
Because even the most faithful person who ever loved you could never save your soul.
Only Christ can do that.
And there is another biblical passage we need to face honestly.
Ecclesiastes 9:5 says:
“For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing.” (KJV)
Some readers point to this verse as proof that the dead have absolutely no consciousness or awareness.
Others understand it in the context of Ecclesiastes' repeated observations about life “under the sun.”
The surrounding passage emphasizes that the dead no longer participate in ordinary earthly life and its activities.
Ecclesiastes 9:6 says they no longer have a portion in what is done under the sun.
Christians disagree about how these passages relate to the intermediate state between death and resurrection.
Some understand the dead as unconscious until the resurrection.
Others understand believers as consciously present with Christ while awaiting bodily resurrection.
The wider biblical discussion includes Luke 23:43, Philippians 1:23, 2 Corinthians 5:8, and Revelation 6:9–11.
Those texts must be considered together rather than forcing one verse to answer every question.
For example, Paul speaks of his desire “to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better” (Philippians 1:23, KJV).
Many Christians understand this as teaching conscious fellowship with Christ after death.
Others interpret the experience of death and resurrection differently.
Yet the central Christian hope remains the same.
Our ultimate hope is not becoming invisible spectators of earthly life.
It is resurrection and everlasting life through Jesus Christ.
And here is where the conversation becomes even more serious.
Because not every person who dies automatically enters heaven.
That may be uncomfortable to read.
But if we truly love people, we cannot replace the Gospel with a comforting assumption.
Jesus said:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.” (John 14:6, KJV)
Salvation is not earned by being kind enough, religious enough, wealthy enough, or admired enough.
It is God's gift of grace, received through faith in Jesus Christ, whose death and resurrection provide forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes this clear.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” (KJV)
We cannot know the eternal destiny of every person who has died.
God alone knows every heart and judges with perfect righteousness.
But we can know where Scripture directs the living.
To Christ.
To repentance.
To faith.
To the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
And this leads us to a question that is often hiding beneath the original question.
What if your loved ones could see you?
Would you be comforted?
Or would you be terrified?
Would you want them to see the person you have become?
The anger you hide.
The bitterness you nurse.
The private compromises.
The addictions.
The secret messages.
The moments when you smile in church but have no intention of surrendering the sin you protect behind closed doors.
Would you want them to know?
That question can be sobering.
But listen carefully.
You do not need an audience of departed loved ones to make holiness matter.
You already live before God.
Psalm 139:1–3 declares that the Lord searches and knows us, understanding our thoughts and being acquainted with our ways.
Hebrews 4:13 says that no creature is hidden from His sight.
And that truth is both terrifying and beautiful.
Terrifying because our secrets are not secret to Him.
Beautiful because our suffering is not secret to Him either.
He saw the moment you were betrayed.
He saw you staring at the ceiling at three in the morning.
He saw you sitting in your car, unable to walk into your own house because the grief was too heavy.
He saw the tears you wiped away before your children entered the room.
He saw the prayers you could barely speak.
He saw the moment you almost walked away from your faith.
And He sees you now.
Not as a distant observer.
Not as someone watching your pain for entertainment.
But as the God who entered human suffering through His Son.
Remember the shortest verse in many English Bibles?
“Jesus wept.” (John 11:35, KJV)
Two words.
An ocean of meaning.
The Greek reads:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς — edakrysen ho Iēsous
“Jesus wept.”
He stood near the tomb of Lazarus.
He saw Mary grieving.
He encountered the anguish of people devastated by death.
And He wept.
Think about that.
Jesus knew He was about to raise Lazarus.
He knew death would not have the final word in that moment.
Yet He still wept.
Knowing the power of resurrection did not make Him indifferent to human sorrow.
The One who could call a dead man out of the grave did not refuse to stand beside grieving people and cry.
That is your Savior.
Not cold.
Not detached.
Not irritated by your questions.
Not offended because you still miss someone you lost years ago.
He understands grief.
He understands separation.
He understands tears.
And He understands death more deeply than any of us ever could.
Because He entered it.
At Calvary, Jesus Christ bore our sins, suffered, died, and was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
That resurrection is the foundation of Christian hope.
Not the idea that deceased loved ones become angels.
Not the belief that every butterfly is a message from heaven.
Not the assumption that every dream is a supernatural visitation.
Not the promise that departed relatives are constantly monitoring our lives.
Those ideas may be emotionally meaningful to some people, but Scripture does not establish them as reliable Christian doctrine.
Our hope rests on something infinitely stronger.
Jesus Christ actually conquered death.
And because He lives, those who belong to Him have the promise of resurrection.
In John 11:25, Jesus declares:
“I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live.” (KJV)
In Greek, His declaration begins:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή — egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē
“I am the resurrection and the life.”
Notice what He did not say.
He did not merely say He could explain resurrection.
He did not say He could point people toward life.
He identified Himself as the resurrection and the life.
Our hope is not ultimately an event separated from Him.
Our hope is a Person.
Jesus Christ.
And this changes everything.
Because the Christian promise is not simply that we might somehow be observed by those who have gone before us.
It is that, through Christ, death itself will one day be defeated completely.
Revelation 21:4 declares:
“And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.” (KJV)
Read that again.
No more death.
No more sorrow.
No more crying.
No more pain.
Can you imagine a world where hospitals no longer become places of final goodbyes?
Where children never have to stand beside a parent's coffin?
Where husbands and wives are never separated by death again?
Where grief no longer arrives unexpectedly in the middle of an ordinary afternoon?
Where no one has to whisper into an empty bedroom, “I wish you were still here”?
That is the glorious future God promises His redeemed people.
And the reason it is possible is not human goodness.
It is the victory of Jesus Christ.
But perhaps you're thinking of something else.
Perhaps you lost someone before you could apologize.
You said words you wish you could take back.
You were too busy to visit.
You ignored a phone call.
You thought there would be another birthday.
Another Christmas.
Another conversation.
Another opportunity to say, “I love you.”
And then there wasn't.
Now the guilt follows you everywhere.
You wonder whether they know you're sorry.
Whether they can see how much you've changed.
Whether they know you would give almost anything for five more minutes.
I cannot promise you that your loved one in heaven has heard your apologies.
Scripture does not give me the authority to make that promise.
But I can tell you something God has revealed.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
There is grace for the repentant.
There is mercy for people who cannot go backward and repair every broken moment.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot undo every failure.
You cannot resurrect a lost opportunity through regret.
But you can bring your guilt, grief, and unfinished sorrow to the Savior.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It means sin confessed before God can be forgiven through Christ.
And if your grief is tangled with guilt, you do not have to keep punishing yourself as though your suffering could purchase forgiveness.
Jesus has already paid the price for sin.
Turn to Him.
Trust Him.
And where reconciliation is still possible with the living, pursue it.
Make the phone call.
Speak the apology.
Forgive where forgiveness is needed.
Tell people you love them while they can still hear your voice.
Do not spend your whole life wishing for another conversation with the dead while neglecting the people God has placed beside you today.
And there is one more difficult but necessary truth.
Scripture does not encourage believers to seek contact with the dead.
Deuteronomy 18:10–12 condemns practices involving mediums and attempts to consult the dead.
The biblical response to grief is not to seek secret messages from departed spirits.
It is to seek the living God.
We do not need to chase signs to know we are loved.
We do not need supernatural experiences to validate God's promises.
We have His Word.
We have the Gospel.
We have the risen Christ.
And we have the Holy Spirit, whom Jesus promised to His people.
That is not a lesser comfort.
It is a surer foundation.
So, can people in heaven see what is happening on earth?
Here is the most responsible answer Scripture allows.

The Bible gives indications that heaven is aware of certain earthly realities, including the cry for justice and the joy associated with repentance. But it does not clearly teach that departed believers continuously watch everything happening on earth, nor that our loved ones can see every moment of our lives.
Christians may reach different conclusions about the extent of heavenly awareness.
We should show humility where Scripture has not given exhaustive details.
But on the most important matter, the Bible is unmistakably clear.
Jesus sees.
Jesus knows.
Jesus saves.
Jesus reigns.
And Jesus will return.
Perhaps that is where our hearts need to settle.
Not on whether someone in heaven can see our pain.
But on the certainty that the Savior who defeated death has never been unaware of it.
I want you to imagine one final scene.
A woman stands alone at a cemetery.
Her hands are trembling.
She places flowers beside a gravestone and whispers, “I hope you can see me. I hope you know I'm trying.”
Then she breaks down.
Because life has been harder than she expected.
Because she has made mistakes.
Because she misses the person whose name is carved into that stone.
Because deep inside, she still feels like a little girl who wants someone to tell her everything will be okay.
And maybe, for the first time in years, she stops trying to speak to the person she lost.
She lifts her eyes toward heaven.
And she prays.

“Lord Jesus, I don't know what they can see. I don't know what they know. But You know me. You know what I've done. You know what I've lost. You know how tired I am. Please forgive me. Please heal what grief has broken. Please teach me to trust You.”
Nothing dramatic happens.
No audible voice.
No mysterious sign.
No promise that a departed loved one has been watching.
Just a grieving heart turning toward the living Christ.
And that matters.
Because sometimes the greatest miracle is not receiving an answer to every question about heaven.
Sometimes it is discovering that the God of heaven is enough to carry us through what we cannot understand on earth.
Maybe your story has been marked by scandal.
By addiction.
By betrayal.
By family wounds.
By secret shame.
By grief that nearly destroyed your faith.
Maybe people know you by the worst thing you ever did.
Maybe you know yourself by the worst thing you ever survived.
But the Gospel announces that your past does not have to be the final chapter.
The cross declares that sin is serious.
The empty tomb declares that death is defeated.
And grace declares that those who come to Christ can be forgiven, redeemed, and made new.
That is why we keep saying:
Not because Jesus pretends our sins never mattered.
Not because grief suddenly stops hurting.
Not because every earthly consequence disappears.
But because His mercy can transform sinners, His presence can sustain the brokenhearted, and His resurrection guarantees that death will not have the final victory over those who belong to Him.
If this article has exposed something hidden in your heart, don't bury it beneath another religious smile.
Bring it to Jesus.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Christ, you can begin by turning from sin and trusting the crucified and risen Savior. You do not need perfect words. Come to Him sincerely.
Perhaps you can pray:

“Lord Jesus Christ, I confess that I am a sinner in need of Your mercy. I believe You died for sins and rose again. Forgive me, turn my heart away from sin, and teach me to follow You. Heal what is broken, strengthen my faith, and help me trust Your promises even when I cannot understand Your ways. My hope is not in signs or speculation. My hope is in You. Amen.”
And please, don't keep this message to yourself if someone you know needs it.
And if these messages have been helping you grow in your faith, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is more than a collection of articles.
Our desire is to build a growing ministry of biblical teaching, discipleship, encouragement, spiritual restoration, and practical resources that help people know Jesus and follow Him faithfully.
These resources are offered freely because we believe access to biblical nourishment should not depend on someone's ability to pay.
But continuing this work, developing new materials, reaching more people, and expanding the ministry requires faithful support.
The Bible teaches us to give willingly, not under pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
Keep reading.
Keep growing.
Keep praying.
Keep sharing the truth.
Your presence matters here.
These are simply gifts of appreciation for those helping us continue the work—not spiritual rewards, and certainly not a measure of anyone's faithfulness to God.
Our goal is not merely to grow a page.
It is to see people come to know Christ.
To see sinners repent.
To see broken families encounter grace.
To see grieving hearts discover resurrection hope.
To see believers become rooted in Scripture instead of being carried away by every emotional claim or spiritual trend.
And to keep pointing people back to the only Savior who can redeem what sin has ruined.
Jesus Christ.
Before you leave, I want to ask you something personal.
When you think about the person you miss most, what is the one thing you wish you could tell them?
And then ask yourself a second question.
What would change in my life today if I stopped living only for the approval of people I have lost and started living more faithfully for the Jesus who died and rose again for me?
Because one day, the questions that have haunted us may give way to something far greater.
Not speculation.
Not longing.
Not endless wondering.
But the fulfillment of God's promises in Christ.
Until then, we grieve with hope.
We remember with gratitude.
We repent with humility.
We love while there is time.
And we keep our eyes fixed on Jesus.
You may never know whether the person you miss can see your tears—but you can know that the Savior who conquered their greatest enemy has never missed a single one of yours.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY TRIED TO DESTROY YOU. JESUS SAID TO BLESS THEM.
paragraphs: THEY TRIED TO DESTROY YOU. JESUS SAID TO BLESS THEM.
“Bless Those Who Persecute You” Was Never About Handling a Little Criticism. Paul Was Calling Wounded Believers to Do Something Humanly Impossible.
There is a kind of pain that doesn't leave bruises.
It leaves you staring at the ceiling at 2:17 in the morning, replaying conversations you wish you could forget.
It makes you question people you once trusted. It makes you rehearse arguments in the shower. It makes your stomach tighten when you hear a familiar name.
And sometimes, the person who wounded you is sleeping peacefully while you're still trying to understand how someone could be so cruel.
You didn't start the fight.
You didn't ask to be betrayed.
You weren't looking for enemies.
You were simply trying to live your life, love people, do what was right, and perhaps follow Jesus as faithfully as you knew how.
Then somebody decided to make you suffer for it.
They lied about you.
They twisted your words.
They turned people against you.
They attacked your character, questioned your motives, and made you look like the villain in a story where you were the one bleeding.
And somewhere in the middle of all that pain, you opened your Bible and encountered a sentence that almost felt unbearable.
“Bless them which persecute you: bless, and curse not.” — Romans 12:14 (KJV)
You read it once.
Then again.
And perhaps, for one uncomfortable moment, you wanted to close your Bible.
Because surely Paul couldn't have meant that person.
Surely God understood what they did.
Surely there must be an exception for someone who deliberately humiliated you, betrayed your trust, or made your life miserable.
But here is where the Gospel begins confronting something deeper than the people who hurt us.
What if the person who wounded you never apologizes, but Jesus still refuses to let hatred become the ruler of your heart?
Stay with that question.
Because what Paul wrote in Romans 12 was not advice for surviving an unpleasant comment on social media.
He was describing the supernatural character of people whose lives had been overtaken by the mercy of Jesus Christ.
And once you understand the world behind his words, this command becomes far more disturbing—and far more beautiful—than most of us have ever imagined.
Paul wrote:
εὐλογεῖτε τοὺς διώκοντας ὑμᾶς· εὐλογεῖτε καὶ μὴ καταρᾶσθε.
Eulogeite tous diōkontas hymas; eulogeite kai mē katarasthe.
“Bless them which persecute you: bless, and curse not.” — Romans 12:14 (KJV)
Notice the Greek word διώκοντας (diōkontas).
It comes from the verb diōkō, which can mean to pursue, chase, or persecute. In this context, it describes those who persecute believers.
Paul wasn't merely talking about someone who disagrees with your opinion.
He was speaking about people who actively pursue others with hostility.
People who make faithfulness costly.
People whose opposition can threaten your reputation, livelihood, freedom, relationships, or even your life.
And that matters because the earliest Christians were not living in a world where following Jesus was simply a comfortable religious preference.
They could face rejection, public shame, violence, imprisonment, and death.
Paul himself knew this world intimately.
In Acts 8:3, before his conversion, Saul was entering houses, dragging away men and women, and committing them to prison.
Think about that.
The man who would later command Christians to bless their persecutors had once been one of the persecutors.
He wasn't writing about suffering from a safe distance.
He had caused it.
He had watched the church suffer.
And after encountering the risen Jesus, he would experience persecution himself.
In 2 Corinthians 11:24–25, Paul recounts receiving thirty-nine lashes from Jewish authorities on five occasions, being beaten with rods three times, and being stoned once.
This was not a man who confused persecution with inconvenience.
He knew what human cruelty could do.
He knew what it meant to be opposed.
He knew what it meant to have scars.
Yet he wrote, “Bless, and curse not.”
Why?
Because Paul had encountered a Savior who did not merely teach mercy.
He embodied it.
And that is where this story becomes almost impossible to ignore.
Imagine the road to Damascus.
Saul is traveling with authority to arrest followers of Jesus.
He believes he is defending God.
He is convinced he is righteous.
He is pursuing Christians, not to encourage them, but to bring them into custody.
Then suddenly, everything changes.
A light from heaven.
A voice.
A confrontation that would destroy his old understanding of himself.
“Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?” — Acts 9:4 (KJV)
Not merely, “Why are you persecuting My followers?”
Jesus identifies Himself with His suffering people.
Why are you persecuting Me?
The persecutor discovers that the people he has been attacking belong to the risen Lord.
And what does Jesus do?
He confronts Saul, humbles him, and directs him toward the very community he had tried to destroy.
Jesus does not declare Saul innocent.
He does not pretend his actions were harmless.
But neither does He leave Saul beyond the reach of grace.
The man who once hunted Christians becomes a preacher of the Christ he opposed.
The persecutor becomes a witness.
The enemy becomes a brother.
And the church is confronted with an astonishing reality:
The grace of Jesus can reach the very person you would have considered beyond redemption.
That does not mean every persecutor will repent.
It does not mean every enemy will change.
It does not mean every broken relationship will be restored.
But it means no Christian can honestly look at another sinner and declare that the transforming mercy of Christ is powerless to reach them.
Paul knew this better than almost anyone.
Because he was living proof.
Perhaps that is why his command in Romans 12 sounds so uncompromising.
He remembered who he had been.
He remembered what Jesus had done.
And he understood that the Christian life cannot be built upon receiving mercy while refusing to extend it.
But there is something else in the Greek that deserves our attention.
Paul uses the word εὐλογεῖτε (eulogeite)—“bless.”
It is a command.
And he repeats it.
Bless those who persecute you.
Bless, and do not curse.
The repetition gives the instruction unmistakable force.
This is not a passing suggestion.
It is a deliberate call to respond differently from the world around us.
To bless someone is not to announce that their evil was good.
It is not to call betrayal loyalty.
It is not to describe abuse as love.
It is not to pretend injustice never happened.
Rather, in this setting, blessing means refusing to answer hostility with a desire for another person's destruction, and instead seeking what is truly good under God's righteous authority.
That may include praying for their repentance.
Praying that God will expose their sin.
Praying that they will stop harming people.
Praying that truth will prevail.
Praying that the person who has become an instrument of pain might one day become a testimony of redemption.
And sometimes the most honest prayer you can offer is not eloquent at all.
“Lord, I do not know how to bless this person. I am angry. I am hurt. I want them to understand what they did. Please keep my heart from becoming like the evil that wounded me.”
That is not spiritual failure.
That is bringing your struggle into the presence of God instead of disguising it beneath religious language.
Some people have been taught that forgiveness means never admitting they are angry.
So they smile.
They say they're fine.
They quote Scripture.
They keep serving.
But beneath the surface, something is slowly hardening.
And eventually, bitterness begins shaping how they see everyone.
One betrayal becomes a reason to trust nobody.
One cruel person becomes proof that everyone is dangerous.
One painful church experience becomes a reason to withdraw from every Christian community.
One injustice becomes a permanent identity.
And without realizing it, the person who wounded them begins influencing the way they live long after the original injury.
That is one of bitterness's cruelest consequences.
Someone can be absent from your life and still occupy enormous space in your heart.
Jesus does not command us to bless our enemies because He is indifferent to our wounds.
He commands us to love our enemies because He knows what hatred can do to the wounded.
But we must be careful here.
This teaching has sometimes been misused against people who are already suffering.
A woman experiencing domestic violence may be told to forgive and remain silent.
A child harmed by someone in authority may be pressured to protect the offender's reputation.
A church member may be instructed to endure manipulation because “Christians must turn the other cheek.”
That is not a faithful application of Romans 12:14.
Blessing a persecutor does not require remaining within reach of their abuse.
You can pray for someone's repentance and still report their wrongdoing.
You can refuse revenge and still seek justice.
You can forgive someone without restoring access to your life.
You can love an enemy while maintaining firm boundaries.
You can desire someone's salvation while refusing to trust them with responsibilities they have abused.
Romans 12 itself tells believers, “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” (Romans 12:18, KJV).
Notice those words.
If it be possible.
Paul recognizes that peaceful relationships do not depend on one person alone.
And Romans 13, immediately following this teaching, discusses governing authorities and their responsibility to respond to wrongdoing.
Personal nonretaliation is not the same as abandoning public justice.
God never asks you to rename evil so that someone else can avoid accountability.
Jesus Himself spoke truthfully about sin.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He warned against those who exploited the vulnerable.
And when struck during His questioning, He challenged the injustice of the act (John 18:22–23).
Christlike love is not moral blindness.
It is love governed by truth.
And nowhere is that truth more breathtaking than at the cross.
Picture Calvary.
The sky darkening.
The crowd watching.
The soldiers carrying out the execution.
The religious leaders mocking.
The Son of God hanging between criminals.
The One through whom all things were made is being rejected by the very world He came to save.
And Luke records this extraordinary prayer:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.” — Luke 23:34 (KJV)

There is a textual detail worth knowing: this sentence is present in many ancient manuscripts of Luke but absent from some other early witnesses. That is why certain modern Bible editions mark it with a footnote.
Even with that textual question, the wider New Testament unmistakably teaches Christ's mercy toward sinners and His call for believers to pray for their persecutors.
Jesus had already taught:
“Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.” — Matthew 5:44 (KJV)
The cross reveals the depth of that teaching.
Jesus does not deny the evil being committed against Him.
He does not call His executioners innocent.
He does not suggest that sin carries no consequences.
He bears suffering without surrendering to sinful hatred.
And through His death and resurrection, He accomplishes what no wounded human heart could ever accomplish for itself.
Reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness for sinners.
Victory over sin and death.
The hope of a new creation.
This is why Romans 12 cannot be understood properly if we detach it from Romans 1 through 11.
Paul has spent chapter after chapter unfolding the Gospel.
Humanity's sin.
God's righteousness.
Justification by faith.
Peace with God through Jesus Christ.
Life in the Spirit.
The faithfulness and mercy of God.
Then Romans 12 begins:
“I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.” — Romans 12:1 (KJV)
By the mercies of God.
That phrase changes everything.
Paul does not say, “Bless your persecutors so that God will finally love you.”
He does not say, “Forgive perfectly and you will earn salvation.”
He is calling those who have received mercy to live as people transformed by that mercy.
Grace comes first.
Transformation follows.
The Christian does not bless enemies to purchase God's acceptance.
The Christian learns to bless enemies because Christ has already shown undeserved mercy to sinners.
And if we're being painfully honest, that is where the Gospel exposes all of us.
Because we love to imagine ourselves as the innocent person in every biblical story.
We identify with Joseph in the pit.
David pursued by Saul.
Daniel surrounded by enemies.
Stephen facing stones.
But the Gospel requires us to confront another possibility.
Before grace found us, we were not merely wounded people needing comfort.
We were sinners needing reconciliation with God.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
And Romans 5:10 goes even further, describing our former condition as enemies reconciled to God through the death of His Son.
Enemies.
That word should silence some of our pride.
We want mercy for our failures and justice for everyone else's.
We want God to understand the reasons behind our worst decisions, while demanding that He judge other people's motives without hesitation.
We remember our own wounds in vivid detail.
But sometimes we forget the wounds our own sins have caused.
Perhaps you have never persecuted a church.
Perhaps you have never dragged anyone into prison.
But have you ever damaged someone's reputation?
Have you ever repeated a story you knew you should have kept private?
Have you ever enjoyed hearing that someone who hurt you was finally suffering?
Have you ever disguised revenge as a prayer request?
Have you ever said, “I forgive them,” while quietly hoping their life would fall apart?
This is not written to crush a wounded person with shame.
It is an invitation to bring the entire heart—its pain and its sin—into the light of Christ.
Because Jesus is not only interested in what happened to you.
He is also interested in what is happening inside you.
And sometimes the hardest enemy to confront is the bitterness we have begun to justify.
Maybe you know exactly what that feels like.
You see their name on Facebook, and your chest tightens.
You hear that something good happened to them, and you feel disappointed.
You hear that something bad happened, and for a split second, you feel satisfied.
Then you realize what your heart has become.
You never wanted to be this person.
You just wanted the pain to stop.
But somewhere along the way, your wound began asking for revenge instead of healing.
And the Lord, in His mercy, is calling you to something different.
Not denial.
Not pretending.
Not instant emotional recovery.
But surrender.
“Lord, I cannot make them repent. I cannot rewrite what they did. I cannot force an apology. But I can place my desire for vengeance into Your hands.”
That is where Romans 12:19 becomes essential.
“Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.”
Paul is drawing from Deuteronomy 32:35, where God declares that vengeance and recompense belong to Him.
The Hebrew word נָקָם (naqam) refers to vengeance or retribution.
In the biblical context, the point is not that wrongdoing is unimportant.
It is that final judgment belongs to the righteous God, not to our wounded impulses.
God sees what people conceal.
He knows what happened behind closed doors.
He knows the words spoken when no one else was listening.
He knows the manipulation, the threats, the lies, and the injustice.
He knows the difference between someone who stumbled and someone who deliberately exploited another person.
And His justice is not weakened by your decision to refuse personal revenge.
You do not have to become cruel to prove that cruelty was wrong.
You do not have to destroy someone to demonstrate that they damaged you.
You do not have to spend the rest of your life prosecuting their case inside your imagination.
You can pursue appropriate justice, tell the truth, protect yourself and others, and still leave ultimate judgment with God.
This is not surrendering truth.
It is surrendering vengeance.
And those are two very different things.
Paul continues:
“Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head.” — Romans 12:20 (KJV)
Here Paul quotes Proverbs 25:21–22.
The image of burning coals has been interpreted in different ways, including the possibility of provoking shame that leads to repentance or pointing toward divine judgment.
But the surrounding passage makes one thing unmistakable.
Paul is not teaching believers to perform kindness as a secret method of revenge.
He is commanding genuine acts of good rather than retaliation.
And then comes the conclusion:
“Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.” — Romans 12:21 (KJV)
Read that slowly.
Be not overcome of evil.
There is more than one way for evil to overcome a person.
Sometimes evil overcomes someone through the suffering inflicted upon them.
But sometimes its influence continues when the wounded person begins reproducing the same hatred, dishonesty, or cruelty they once condemned.
The Gospel calls us to resist both.
You may not be able to stop every injustice committed against you.
But by God's grace, you do not have to let that injustice determine the kind of person you become.
This does not happen overnight.
Some wounds require years of healing.
Some situations require counseling, legal protection, wise pastoral care, or sustained support from trustworthy people.
Some relationships cannot safely be restored.
And sometimes obedience begins with nothing more dramatic than refusing to send the angry message you have already typed.
Or choosing not to spread a humiliating story.
Or praying one sentence through tears.
“Jesus, help me want what is right.”
That may seem small.
But small acts of obedience matter.
Not because they make you your own savior.
But because the Savior who redeemed you is patiently transforming you.
Think again about Stephen.
In Acts 7, he is surrounded by people enraged by his testimony.
He is driven outside the city.
Stones begin to fall.
And as he dies, Stephen cries:
“Lord, lay not this sin to their charge.” — Acts 7:60 (KJV)
This was not a man responding to a rude remark.
He was being killed.
And among those connected with that scene was a young man named Saul, who consented to Stephen's death, as Acts 8:1 records.
Scripture does not say Stephen's prayer directly caused Saul's conversion.
We must not invent that connection.
But the sequence is still staggering.
A Christian dies praying for mercy.
A persecutor approves of his death.
And later, that persecutor meets the risen Christ and becomes an apostle.
The story does not promise that every enemy you pray for will become another Paul.
But it reminds us that God's grace can write chapters no human being could have predicted.
And perhaps that is the truth someone reading this desperately needs.
The person who betrayed you may never apologize.
The people who believed the lies may never publicly correct them.
The opportunity you lost may never return.
The relationship may never be what it once was.
You may never receive the earthly closure you wanted.
But your future is not chained to their repentance.
Your obedience is not dependent on their apology.
And your identity in Christ is not determined by their accusations.
They may have written a painful chapter in your life.
But they do not hold the pen that writes your eternity.
Jesus Christ does.
And His Gospel does not merely offer you a better reputation.
It offers you a new life.
A life where the sinner can repent.
Where the ashamed can find forgiveness.
Where the wounded can receive comfort.
Where the bitter can learn mercy.
Where the persecutor can become a brother.
Where the betrayed can be restored without pretending betrayal was harmless.
Where justice and grace are not enemies.
Where the cross tells the truth about sin while revealing the immeasurable mercy of God.
This is what we mean when we say:
Not that every scandal disappears.
Not that every consequence is erased.
Not that the past becomes imaginary.
But that Jesus Christ can redeem sinners, restore what sin has devastated according to His wisdom, and give His people a future no longer ruled by condemnation and despair.
Perhaps right now, one name is sitting heavily on your heart.
You have been thinking about that person since the beginning of this article.
You know what they said.
You remember what they did.
You still feel the cost.
I am not asking you to pretend it was acceptable.
I am not asking you to contact them.
I am not asking you to return to an unsafe situation.
I am asking you to consider whether the Lord is inviting you to place something into His hands that you have been carrying alone.
Maybe it is the desire to retaliate.
Maybe it is the need for everyone to hear your side.
Maybe it is the belief that you cannot move forward until someone finally admits the truth.
Maybe it is the fear that forgiving them would mean what happened did not matter.
But forgiveness does not erase truth.
And blessing does not cancel accountability.
You can entrust someone to God's justice while refusing to become the instrument of personal revenge.
You can pray for their repentance without giving them another opportunity to hurt you.
You can acknowledge the depth of your pain while trusting Christ to begin healing what you cannot repair.
And if you are not ready to pray for them today, begin by telling Jesus the truth about that too.
He already knows.
There is no need to perform strength in front of the One who sees your weakness.
You can say:

“Lord Jesus, You know what happened. You know what I lost. You know how angry I still am. Forgive me for the ways bitterness has taken root in my heart. Give me wisdom to seek truth and justice without revenge. Protect me from further harm. Teach me to pray for repentance where there is sin, healing where there is pain, and mercy where I have become hard. I cannot change another person's heart, but I surrender my own to You. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Help me live as someone who has received Your grace. Amen.”
And maybe, for the first time in a long time, you do not need to have the final word.
You can let God be God.
Or perhaps your prayer is, “Lord, help me forgive without compromising truth.”

You do not have to expose private details or name the person who hurt you. Sometimes a few honest words can become the beginning of a meaningful conversation with other believers who understand the struggle.
Someone who feels trapped in anger may need to hear that healing is possible.
There may also be someone on your Facebook friends list who is silently fighting this battle.
Someone who has been betrayed.
Someone who has stopped trusting people.
Someone who believes their anger is the only thing protecting them from being hurt again.
Not simply to increase its reach, but because a biblical reminder offered at the right moment may help someone turn toward Christ instead of surrendering to despair.
We are not building a community around perfect people.
We are gathering people who know they need a perfect Savior.
And for those who want to help carry this Gospel-centered mission further, I want to invite you into something more personal.
If you have been blessed through Gospel Warrior and desire to glorify God by helping others receive biblical truth, this is one meaningful opportunity to participate.
God's grace is not for sale. Your salvation cannot be purchased. And no monthly payment can replace genuine repentance, faith, obedience, or love.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Our hope is that these resources will help people open their Bibles, examine their lives, grow in sound doctrine, persevere through suffering, and become more faithful disciples of Jesus.
But above everything else, remember why this ministry exists.
Not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
Not to make any writer indispensable.
Not to turn suffering into entertainment or faith into a transaction.
We want people to see Jesus.
The Jesus who confronted Saul on the Damascus road.
The Jesus who forgives sinners without excusing sin.
The Jesus who teaches His followers to love their enemies.
The Jesus who endured the cross and rose victorious from the grave.
The Jesus who still calls wounded, angry, exhausted, imperfect people to repentance, faith, and a new way of life.
What if the person who hurt you never apologizes?
What if they never acknowledge what happened?
What if they continue telling their version of the story?
Will you allow their actions to determine the condition of your soul?
Or will you bring your pain to the Savior who knows what it means to suffer unjustly?
You do not need to deny the wound.
You do not need to rush the healing.
You do not need to call evil good.
But you can begin to release the desire for vengeance into the hands of the One who judges righteously.
Because the greatest miracle in this story may not be that your enemy changes.
It may be that, through the grace of Jesus Christ, you refuse to become the person your suffering was tempting you to be.
And one day, when you remember what they did, perhaps the pain will no longer be the loudest voice in the room.
Perhaps the mercy of Christ will be.
They may never ask you for forgiveness—but through Jesus, their cruelty does not have to become the final chapter of your heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HER NAME WAS NYMPHA. HER HOUSE BECAME A CHURCH. AND ONE VERSE EXPOSES SOMETHING WE MAY HAVE FORGOTTEN ABOUT FOLLOWING JESUS.
paragraphs: HER NAME WAS NYMPHA. HER HOUSE BECAME A CHURCH. AND ONE VERSE EXPOSES SOMETHING WE MAY HAVE FORGOTTEN ABOUT FOLLOWING JESUS.

Before Christianity had grand cathedrals, expensive sound systems, and buildings filled with thousands, a woman opened her home to believers. Paul remembered her by name. Nearly 2,000 years later, her story still asks a question that could change the way we understand church, generosity, women in the early Christian movement, and what it really means to give Jesus everything.
“Greet the brethren which are in Laodicea, and Nymphas, and the church which is in his house.” — Colossians 4:15, KJV
Read that verse again.
Slowly.
Because there is something extraordinary hiding inside what appears to be an ordinary greeting.
A name.
A house.
A church.
And a story that history almost swallowed.
Imagine living in the first century.

There is no church building waiting for you on Sunday morning. No glowing cross above a sanctuary. No worship team rehearsing under colorful lights. No leather-bound Bible resting on the seat beside you.
You live in a world where confessing Jesus as Lord can bring rejection, suspicion, and sometimes persecution.
And somewhere near the ancient city of Laodicea, a group of believers gathers in a home.
Perhaps someone arrives carrying the exhaustion of another difficult week.
Perhaps a widow sits quietly among them.
Perhaps a new believer is still struggling to understand what it means to leave old loyalties behind.
Perhaps someone has lost friends because of faith in Christ.
We do not know their individual stories. Scripture does not tell us.
But we know something remarkable.
They had a place to gather.
And a person named Nympha was remembered in connection with that gathering.
The apostle Paul considered this person and the congregation meeting in that home important enough to mention in his letter.
Not an emperor.
Not a famous philosopher.
Not a wealthy religious celebrity.
A believer whose home had become a gathering place for the people of God.
And before we go any further, there is something important we must understand.
The name is preserved in Scripture. But the details of the life behind that name require careful handling.
Some English Bibles call this person Nympha and refer to a church meeting in her house. Others, including the King James Version, use Nymphas and his house.
Why?
Because ancient Greek manuscripts differ.
And understanding that difference does not weaken Scripture. It helps us read the historical evidence responsibly.
The Greek text of Colossians 4:15, as printed in widely used modern critical editions, reads:
Ἀσπάσασθε τοὺς ἐν Λαοδικείᾳ ἀδελφοὺς καὶ Νύμφαν καὶ τὴν κατ᾽ οἶκον αὐτῆς ἐκκλησίαν.
Transliteration:
Aspasasthe tous en Laodikeia adelphous kai Nymphan kai tēn kat’ oikon autēs ekklēsian.
A faithful English rendering is:
“Greet the brothers and sisters in Laodicea, and Nympha, and the church in her house.”
The Greek word ἐκκλησία (ekklēsia) refers to an assembly or congregation. In the New Testament, it commonly identifies the gathered people of God, not necessarily a religious building.
And the expression κατ᾽ οἶκον (kat’ oikon) means “in a house” or “at home.”
That matters.
Because when Paul refers to the church in Nympha's house, he is not describing a miniature cathedral.
He is describing a congregation associated with a household.

There is also a textual issue worth acknowledging. Some manuscripts read the equivalent of “his house,” while others have “their house.” The personal name itself can be understood differently depending on the textual form and interpretation.
Many modern translations, including the ESV and NIV, follow the feminine reading, “Nympha” and “her house.”
The KJV follows the masculine reading.
We should not pretend that this variation does not exist.
But notice what remains certain across the readings.
An early Christian congregation met in a home, and Paul deliberately recognized the person associated with that home.
That is the historical foundation.
And it is powerful enough without inventing a single detail.
Now imagine what that meant.
When the believers arrived, someone had to make room.
Someone had to welcome them.
Someone had to accept the inconvenience of a private home becoming a gathering place for a spiritual family.
There may have been interruptions.
There may have been additional expenses.
There may have been difficult conversations.
Hospitality in the ancient world could involve real social and material obligations.
And if the feminine reading preserved in many modern translations reflects the original wording, here stands a woman whose home was connected with the life of an early Christian congregation.
Paul did not treat her name as irrelevant.
He included it.
In a letter that Christians would continue reading long after the original congregation had disappeared.
Think about that.
We do not know whether Nympha was married, widowed, wealthy, or living with extended family.
We do not know the size of her home.
We do not know how many people gathered there.
We do not know whether she taught, led the meetings, or simply provided the place where they assembled.
The verse does not settle those questions, and we should never force it to say more than it says.
But we do know that her association with the congregation was worth remembering.
And that reveals something beautiful about the early Christian movement.
The Gospel was not confined to prestigious buildings or powerful institutions.
It moved through ordinary human relationships.
Through households.
Through meals.
Through prayer.
Through teaching.
Through people opening their lives to one another because Jesus Christ had changed them.
Christianity did not begin as a competition to construct the most impressive religious facilities.
It began with the announcement that the crucified and risen Jesus is Lord.
And those who believed that announcement became a new kind of family.
A family purchased not with silver or gold, but through the redeeming work of Christ.
The church was never merely the address where believers assembled.
The church was the people Christ had called to Himself.
And suddenly, a house could become the setting for something eternal.
Not because its walls were holy.
Not because its owner was famous.
But because believers gathered there in the name of the risen Savior.
And this is where Nympha's story begins to reach into our own lives.
Because many of us have spent years asking God to give us something bigger.
A bigger platform.
A bigger income.
A bigger ministry.
A bigger audience.
A bigger opportunity.
And there is nothing inherently wrong with wanting to serve God on a greater scale.
But what if we have become so preoccupied with what we do not have that we have overlooked what we already possess?
What if the place where God wants to begin using you is not somewhere far away?
What if it is your dining table?
Your living room?
Your spare chair?
Your phone?
Your willingness to listen to someone who has nowhere else to turn?
What if the next person who needs to hear about Jesus is not waiting inside a church building?
What if that person is already standing outside your door?
There is a sobering possibility here.
You can spend your whole life waiting for a ministry opportunity while repeatedly walking past the people God has placed within your reach.
And that should make us think.
Because some of the most important acts of Christian faithfulness are not performed before an audience.
They happen when nobody is recording.
When someone makes time for a hurting friend.
When a believer welcomes a lonely person into their home.
When a family prays together after a painful argument.
When someone opens Scripture with a new Christian who is too embarrassed to admit how little they know.
When a person who has been forgiven by Christ decides to show mercy instead of keeping a record of wrongs.
The world may never applaud those moments.
But the Lord sees.
And the New Testament gives us a remarkable pattern.
In Acts 2:46, believers are described as breaking bread in their homes.
In Acts 12:12, believers are gathered in the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where people are praying.
In Romans 16:3–5, Paul greets Priscilla and Aquila and the church meeting in their house.
In 1 Corinthians 16:19, he again refers to a congregation associated with that couple's home.
In Philemon 1–2, Paul addresses Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church in their house.
And then there is Nympha.
Different names.
Different households.
The same extraordinary reality.
The message of Jesus was spreading through communities of people whose faith was becoming visible in the places where they actually lived.
Not merely through religious ceremonies.
Not merely through public declarations.
But through shared lives.
Through costly love.
Through practical hospitality.
Through the ordinary obedience of people who believed that Christ was worthy of everything.
And perhaps that is what makes this verse so uncomfortable.
Because it is easier to admire the faithfulness of early Christians than to examine our own.
We can celebrate a woman opening her home nearly two thousand years ago while refusing to open our hearts to the person sitting beside us.
We can speak passionately about the importance of Christian community while allowing pride, resentment, or indifference to keep us isolated.
We can post Bible verses about loving our neighbors while ignoring the neighbor who is visibly struggling.
We can know the language of discipleship without practicing its demands.
And sometimes the most painful truth is not that we have rejected Jesus openly.
It is that we have learned how to speak about Him without allowing His words to interrupt our comfort.
Jesus said:
“By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.” — John 13:35, KJV
Not by the size of our building.
Not by the popularity of our ministry.
Not by the beauty of our religious vocabulary.
By love.
Real love.
The kind that costs something.
The kind that makes room.
The kind that refuses to reduce people to interruptions.
And the Greek word used for love in John 13:35 is ἀγάπη (agapē), appearing in the form agapēn in the verse.
It is the love that Jesus commands His disciples to show one another.
Not simply warm emotion.
Not merely affectionate words.
But love expressed through genuine concern and faithful action.
And this love finds its greatest revelation in Jesus Himself.
Because the center of Christianity is not Nympha.
It is not hospitality.
It is not generosity.
It is not even the early church.
The center is Jesus Christ, who gave Himself for sinners and rose again so that those who trust in Him might receive forgiveness and new life.
Nympha's story matters because it points toward what the Gospel produces in human lives.
Christ does not save us because we have opened our homes, donated money, or performed enough good deeds.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
And the very next verse tells us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Do you see the order?
Grace comes first.
Transformation follows.
We do not serve to purchase God's acceptance.
We serve because Christ has already shown us a mercy we could never purchase.
We do not give because Jesus needs our money to complete His redemption.
We give because redemption changes what we treasure.
We do not welcome people into our lives to prove that we deserve heaven.
We welcome them because the Savior has welcomed us through grace.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because not everyone reading this has a beautiful home.
Some of you live in a small room.
Some share crowded spaces with relatives.
Some are struggling financially.
Some are working overseas, separated from family, trying to survive one demanding week after another.
Some are raising children alone.
Some are carrying medical bills.
Some are grieving someone whose chair at the table will never be occupied again.
Some have homes filled with people but hearts filled with loneliness.
And when you read about someone opening a house for the church, perhaps your first thought is:
“I could never do that.”
But please hear this.
The point is not that every Christian must own a house or host a congregation.
The point is that whatever Christ has entrusted to us can become an opportunity to love and serve.
You may not have a large home.
But you can offer a prayer.
You may not have financial abundance.
But you can encourage someone who is losing hope.
You may not have a public ministry.
But you can speak truth to one person who desperately needs it.
You may not have all the answers.
But you can sit beside someone who is hurting and remind them that they do not have to face everything alone.
Sometimes hospitality begins with a door.
Sometimes it begins with a conversation.
Sometimes it begins with the willingness to stop pretending that we are too busy to care.
And sometimes the person who needs that love most is sitting inside your own household.
Your spouse.
Your child.
Your parent.
Your sibling.
The family member you have not spoken to in months.
The person you keep promising to forgive someday.
It is possible to become so passionate about reaching strangers that we neglect the people closest to us.
And Nympha's house reminds us that the Gospel must never remain an idea we admire from a distance.
It must enter the spaces where we live.
Where we argue.
Where we forgive.
Where we fail.
Where we begin again.
Where we learn, slowly and imperfectly, what it means to follow Jesus.
There is another detail that deserves our attention.
Nympha appears in a section of Colossians filled with greetings and relationships.
Paul is not writing about isolated spiritual heroes.
He is speaking about interconnected believers.
People who carried messages.
People who encouraged churches.
People who prayed.
People who labored together for the Gospel.
Christianity was never meant to be lived as a solitary performance.
Yes, personal faith matters.
Yes, private prayer matters.
Yes, every believer must respond personally to Christ.
But following Jesus also brings us into relationship with His people.
We need correction.
We need encouragement.
We need sound teaching.
We need brothers and sisters who will tell us the truth when we are tempted to deceive ourselves.
We need people who will pray with us when our faith feels weak.
And sometimes we need to admit that we are not doing as well as we pretend.
Perhaps you have been smiling in church while silently falling apart.
Perhaps you have been encouraging everyone else while your own soul feels exhausted.
Perhaps you have been serving for years, but resentment has slowly replaced joy.
Perhaps you have grown distant from God, and nobody around you knows how far you have drifted.
If that is you, do not confuse spiritual exhaustion with the end of your story.
Come to Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive His mercy.
And allow trustworthy believers to walk beside you.
The same Jesus who called sinners to repentance is the Savior who welcomed the weary and offered rest.
You do not need to manufacture an impressive spiritual image before approaching Him.
You need to come honestly.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that good people have finally become impressive enough for God.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
And that includes people whose lives are far messier than their public appearance suggests.
This is why our theme at Gospel Warrior is more than a memorable phrase.
Consider what grace has already done throughout Scripture.
A persecutor named Saul became an apostle who proclaimed the Christ he once opposed.
A tax collector named Matthew became a follower of Jesus.
Peter denied knowing his Lord, yet the risen Christ restored him and entrusted him with responsibility.
A criminal crucified beside Jesus turned to Him in faith and received a promise of paradise.
These stories are not identical.
And grace does not erase the real consequences of sin.
But they reveal the astonishing mercy of a Savior who calls sinners to repentance and gives them a future they could never earn.
And somewhere in the story of the early church, we find Nympha.
Not because Scripture tells us she had a scandalous past. It does not.
Not because we know she experienced a dramatic public restoration. We do not.
But because her name reminds us that the grace of Christ does not merely change what we believe about eternity.
It changes how we live in the present.
A house can become a place of fellowship.
A meal can become an act of love.
An ordinary believer can become part of an extraordinary story.
And a name that might otherwise have disappeared from human memory can remain preserved in the pages of Scripture.
There is a lesson here for everyone who has ever felt insignificant.
You may never become famous.
You may never preach before thousands.
You may never write a bestselling book.
You may never have your name displayed on a ministry building.
But faithfulness is not measured by public recognition.
The Lord knows His people.
And nothing done sincerely in service to Christ is made worthless simply because the world fails to notice it.
First Corinthians 15:58 reminds believers that their labor in the Lord is not in vain.
That promise should steady us.
Especially when serving feels difficult.
Especially when generosity goes unnoticed.
Especially when the people we love do not seem to appreciate the sacrifices we make.
Especially when we wonder whether any of it matters.
It matters.
Not because every act of service produces immediate visible results.
Not because every person we help will eventually thank us.
But because the risen Christ is worthy of faithful obedience.
And our labor belongs to Him.
Now there is a danger we must address.
People can be pressured.
Guilt can be used as leverage.
Financial support can be presented as a test of whether someone truly loves God.
But Scripture gives us a better way.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — KJV
The Greek expression μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης (mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs) means, in context, not out of grief or reluctance, and not under compulsion.
That is important.
Christian generosity should not be manufactured through shame.
It should arise from a willing heart shaped by grace.
The New Testament also affirms the legitimacy of material support for Gospel ministry.
First Corinthians 9:14 teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from Gospel work.
Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach the Word.
And Philippians 4:15–18 describes the Philippian believers' financial partnership with Paul's ministry.
So supporting Gospel work is biblical.
But purchasing God's favor is not.
That distinction matters because the truth matters.
And Gospel ministry should never have to distort Scripture to invite support.

At Gospel Warrior, our desire is to keep sharing Christ-centered teaching, biblical encouragement, devotionals, discipleship resources, and messages that call people away from spiritual complacency and toward genuine faith in Jesus.
We want to reach the person who has never opened a Bible.
The believer who is quietly struggling.
The family searching for hope.
The Christian who has drifted from prayer.
The wounded person who has mistaken the failures of human beings for the character of Jesus.
And the person who needs to hear, perhaps for the first time, that repentance and forgiveness are still possible through Christ.
This work requires time, effort, resources, and faithful support.
Not because you owe us a payment for God's grace.
You do not.
But because willing partnership can help sustain and expand the work of sharing biblical truth with others.
It should be the conviction that the message of Jesus Christ deserves to be proclaimed faithfully.
Not merely to increase a number on a screen.
But because someone connected to you may need this truth.
You may never know who reads it quietly at two in the morning.
You may never know whose understanding of church begins to change.
You may never know who realizes that serving Jesus does not require fame, wealth, or a public platform.
You may never know whose heart is moved to return to Christian fellowship after years of isolation.
And you may never know who begins asking serious questions about the Savior after reading a passage they had never noticed before.
And if this article has exposed something in your own heart, I want to invite you to do something more personal than simply pressing a reaction button.
You do not have to share private details publicly.
But perhaps your honest response will remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
And if God has used someone else's hospitality, generosity, or quiet faithfulness to strengthen your walk with Christ, tell us about it.
Your testimony might encourage someone who is wondering whether their small acts of obedience have any value.
For the days when you wonder whether your sacrifices matter.
For the days when you are tempted to believe that only prominent people can accomplish meaningful things for God.
Because Christian truth is not something we should reserve only for those who already agree with us.
It is good news to be shared with humility, love, and courage.
These resources are intended to help believers move beyond momentary inspiration and grow in a deeper understanding of Jesus Christ, His Word, and the life of discipleship.
Because the goal is not simply to build an audience.
The goal is to point people toward Jesus.
To encourage repentance where sin has taken root.
To proclaim forgiveness where guilt has become unbearable.
To teach Scripture where confusion has grown.
To strengthen weary believers.
And to remind a wounded world that the Gospel still announces the grace of God through the crucified and risen Christ.
But before you leave, return with me to that ancient house.
Imagine the believers gathering once again.
No elaborate stage.
No impressive religious architecture.
No knowledge that nearly two thousand years later, Christians across the world would still be reading about their congregation.
Only a gathering of people whose hope rested in Jesus Christ.
Someone may have read aloud a letter from an apostle.
Someone may have prayed.
Someone may have wept.
Someone may have found courage to continue following Jesus.
We cannot reconstruct the details of that particular gathering.
But we can recognize the significance of the community Scripture remembers.
A home had become a place where believers assembled.
And the name Nympha was connected with that gathering.
That is enough to challenge our modern assumptions about what makes Christian service meaningful.
Because the church was never supposed to be reduced to a building we visit, a program we attend, or an identity we display.
The church is Christ's people, called to worship Him, hold fast to His Word, love one another, and bear witness to His saving Gospel.
And perhaps the question Nympha's story leaves us with is not whether we can reproduce the first-century house church exactly.
Perhaps the more important question is this:
Has the grace of Jesus changed the way we use the life He has entrusted to us?
Has it changed the way we treat our families?
Has it changed the way we welcome people?
Has it changed the way we think about possessions?
Has it changed the way we respond to suffering?
Has it changed the way we forgive?
Has it changed the way we give?
Has it changed the way we see those whom the world considers unimportant?
Because genuine faith in Christ is not merely an addition to an otherwise unchanged life.
It is the beginning of a new life under a new Lord.
And the Jesus who saves us by grace also calls us to follow Him.
Not perfectly.
Not without struggle.
Not without moments of weakness and repentance.
But sincerely.
Faithfully.
With hearts increasingly surrendered to His will.
So tonight, before you close this article, consider the place where you live.
Consider the people God has placed around you.
Consider the opportunities you have been postponing.
Consider the relationships that need healing.
Consider the person who needs encouragement.
Consider what you can offer without neglecting your genuine responsibilities.
And ask the Lord to show you where obedience begins.
Maybe it begins with an apology.
Maybe it begins with inviting someone to share a meal.
Maybe it begins with praying for your family.
Maybe it begins with returning to a healthy local church.
Maybe it begins with opening your Bible after months of silence.
Maybe it begins with surrendering the pride that has kept you from loving someone well.
And maybe, for some of you, it begins with realizing that God has never required you to become famous before you can become faithful.
Nympha's name survived in a letter.
But our hope is greater than having our names remembered by history.
Our hope is that we belong to Jesus Christ.
The Savior who died for our sins.
The Lord who rose from the grave.
The Redeemer who calls us to repentance and faith.
The King who is making all things new.
And if He has rescued you by His grace, then the question is no longer whether your life is impressive enough to matter.
The question is whether you are willing to place that life in His hands.
Because you do not need a cathedral to begin loving people.
You do not need a platform to begin speaking truth.
You do not need an audience to begin serving.
You need the grace of Christ.
You need His Word.
You need a willing heart.
And you need to take the next faithful step.

History may never remember the doors you opened, the tears you wiped away, or the people you helped find their way back to Jesus—but the Savior who sees in secret will never overlook a life surrendered to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE WENT DOWN INTO A PIT WITH A LION ON A SNOWY DAY—BUT THE MOST SHOCKING PART OF BENAIAH’S STORY IS WHAT HAPPENED AFTER
