“For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.” (KJV)
The Greek reads:
τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν τὸ αἷμά μου τῆς διαθήκης
Touto gar estin to haima mou tēs diathēkēs.
“For this is my blood of the covenant…”
The word διαθήκη (diathēkē) means “covenant” in this biblical context.
The connection with Exodus 24 is profound.
At Sinai, Moses declared the blood of the covenant.
At the Last Supper, Jesus identified His own blood with the covenant.
The Gospels present Jesus' death as the sacrifice through which the promised new covenant is established.
And Hebrews makes the connection between covenant, blood, and Christ's saving work unmistakable.
Hebrews 9:15 calls Jesus the mediator of the new covenant.
Hebrews 9:22 emphasizes the importance of blood in the sacrificial system's treatment of purification and forgiveness.
Hebrews 10:19–22 announces that believers have confidence to enter God's holy presence through the blood of Jesus.
Do not miss the difference.
At Sinai, the elders were granted an extraordinary encounter under the old covenant.
In Christ, believers receive access to God through the perfect and sufficient sacrifice of the new covenant Mediator.
We should not claim that Exodus 24 explicitly describes the Last Supper or that every detail is a direct prediction of it.
But the canonical connection is real.
The blood of the covenant at Sinai prepares us to understand the greater covenant secured by the blood of Jesus Christ.
And the fellowship meal on the mountain helps us appreciate the astonishing grace of being welcomed into communion with God.
Now consider something else.
The elders did not climb the mountain because they were morally flawless.
And Scripture later makes that painfully clear.
Two of the men named in this extraordinary encounter were Nadab and Abihu.
The sons of Aaron.
Men who had witnessed something of God's glory.
Men who had been present at this covenantal meal.
And yet, in Leviticus 10, Nadab and Abihu later offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, contrary to His command.
Fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them.
They died.
Let that sink in.
Two men who once ate in God's presence later died under His judgment.
That detail should silence the dangerous assumption that a powerful spiritual experience automatically guarantees lifelong faithfulness.
You can witness something extraordinary and still need to obey God.
You can have a moving encounter and still be accountable for what you do afterward.
You can know the language of worship and still allow disobedience into your heart.
An unforgettable moment with God is not a substitute for an obedient walk with God.
And this is not written to make tenderhearted believers despair.
It is a warning against presumption.
God's grace should lead us toward reverence, gratitude, repentance, and faithfulness—not careless confidence that our choices no longer matter.
Maybe you remember a season when your faith was alive.
You prayed with tears.
You opened your Bible with hunger.
You worshiped without worrying who was watching.
You wanted nothing more than to honor Jesus.
But somewhere along the way, your heart became distracted.
A compromise seemed small.
A secret habit became familiar.
A bitterness remained unresolved.
A prayer life slowly disappeared.
And now you are living on the memory of a fire that no longer seems to burn the way it once did.
Please hear this.
You do not need to manufacture another emotional experience to impress God.
You need to return to Christ.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Turn away from what needs to be abandoned.
Receive the forgiveness He offers.
And begin walking in obedience again.
First John 1:9 tells us:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
There is hope for the repentant.
There is mercy for the broken.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
And the same Gospel that calls you out of sin also assures you that you do not have to save yourself.
Christ has done what you could never do.
But perhaps you are still troubled by the original question.
How could the elders see God when Exodus 33 says no one can see His face and live?
The New Testament gives us another essential piece of the answer.
John 1:18 declares:
“No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.” (KJV)
John's Gospel emphasizes that God is made known through His Son.
The Greek verb translated “declared” is ἐξηγήσατο (exēgēsato), from a verb meaning to explain, recount, or make known.
Jesus Christ uniquely reveals the Father.
This does not mean that Exodus 24 was imaginary.
Nor does it require us to insist that the elders saw God's essence.
It means that God's self-revelation reaches its supreme clarity in Jesus Christ.

Some Christian interpreters understand Old Testament appearances of God as manifestations of the preincarnate Son. Others interpret Exodus 24 more cautiously as a divinely granted vision or manifestation without identifying the visible form specifically as the Son.
Exodus 24 itself does not explicitly settle that question.
What Scripture does make clear is that Jesus Christ is the definitive revelation of God.
Colossians 1:15 calls Him “the image of the invisible God.”
And Hebrews 1:3 describes Him as “the express image of his person” in the KJV.
So if you want to know what God's saving mercy looks like…
Look to Jesus.
If you want to know whether God takes sin seriously…
Look to the cross.
If you want to know whether forgiveness is possible…
Look to the risen Savior.
And if you want to know whether a broken sinner can be welcomed into fellowship with God…
Listen to what the Gospel announces.
Romans 5:1–2 says:

“Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God.” (KJV)
Peace with God.
Not because we have become sinless through our own efforts.
Not because our religious performance has earned divine approval.
But through our Lord Jesus Christ.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
The holy God who cannot compromise His righteousness has provided salvation through His Son.
Jesus lived without sin.
He died for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
And all who truly turn to Him in repentance and faith receive forgiveness and new life.
This is not permission to continue in rebellion.
It is an invitation to leave rebellion behind.
And now the mountain of Exodus 24 begins to look different.
Because the most astonishing part of the story is no longer simply that the elders survived.
It is that their encounter belongs to a much larger biblical story.
A story that moves from Sinai to Calvary.
From covenant blood to the blood of Christ.
From a mountain where selected representatives were permitted to approach…
To a Savior through whom believers are invited to draw near to God.
Hebrews 4:16 says:
“Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.” (KJV)
Notice the invitation.
Come boldly.
Not arrogantly.
Not carelessly.
Not pretending sin is harmless.
But confidently, because Jesus is our great High Priest.
The confidence belongs to those who trust in Him.
The mercy comes from God.
The access is secured by Christ.
And perhaps that is what your soul has been starving for.
Not another religious performance.
Not another week of pretending you have everything together.
Not another attempt to hide your wounds behind a polished Christian image.
But genuine fellowship with the living God.
The kind of fellowship that changes how you live when nobody is watching.
The kind that makes you honest about sin without leaving you trapped in condemnation.
The kind that teaches you to love what Christ loves and turn away from what grieves Him.
The kind that reminds you that the Christian life is not merely about surviving judgment.
It is about knowing the God who saves.
Think about the elders one final time.
They were on a mountain.
Before them was a manifestation of divine glory.
Beneath God's feet was something like sapphire, clear as the heavens.
And the Bible tells us that He did not stretch out His hand against them.
They ate.
They drank.
They lived.
Now imagine what it means that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, willingly gave His life so that sinners could be reconciled to the Father.
The elders did not deserve to control God's presence.
Neither do we.
They depended upon divine mercy.
So do we.
But we have been given something they could only anticipate within the unfolding history of redemption.
We have the revelation of Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
We know the name of the Savior.
We have heard the announcement of the new covenant.
We have been told that forgiveness is available through Him.
And that changes everything.
The question is no longer merely, “How did Moses and the elders survive seeing God?”
The question becomes deeply personal.
“What will I do with the grace God has offered me through Jesus Christ?”
Will I keep hiding?
Will I keep postponing repentance?
Will I continue treating God's mercy as though it were ordinary?
Or will I finally surrender?
Not because I can earn His love.
But because His love has been revealed so powerfully in Jesus Christ.
If you have wandered, come back to Him.
If you are carrying secret sin, bring it into the light.
If you are exhausted from trying to appear spiritually strong, stop pretending and begin praying honestly.
If you have never trusted Jesus Christ as your Savior, do not confuse admiration for Christianity with saving faith in Christ.
Turn to Him.
Trust Him.
Follow Him.
There is no greater rescue than the salvation He provides.
And there is no greater privilege than being reconciled to God.
Perhaps this article has reminded you of someone.
A brother who no longer attends church.
A daughter who thinks she has gone too far.
A friend who believes their past makes them unacceptable to God.
A believer who has quietly drifted away.
Or someone who has never understood why Jesus had to die.
Not simply to increase its reach.
But because someone scrolling through their feed tonight may be asking a question they have never dared to say out loud:
“Could God still forgive someone like me?”
A single shared message of Scripture cannot save anyone by itself. Salvation belongs to the Lord.
But God can use His Word, shared faithfully, to point someone toward the Savior.
And I want to invite you to do something more than simply react to what you have read.
Have you ever felt unworthy to approach God because of something in your past?
Have you ever confused a powerful spiritual experience with a faithful daily walk?
Have you ever discovered that God's grace was greater than the shame you were carrying?
You do not need to reveal private details to strangers.
Sometimes a simple testimony is enough to encourage someone who thought they were fighting alone.
Return to Exodus 24.
Read the entire chapter.
Compare it with Exodus 33, Matthew 26, John 1, and Hebrews 9–10.
Do not simply take my words as the final authority.
Let Scripture test what you have read.
Because the goal of Gospel Warrior is not to make you dependent upon an article.
It is to help you become more deeply rooted in Jesus Christ and His Word.
That is why I also want to speak openly about the mission behind Gospel Warrior.
Every article, biblical teaching, devotional, and discipleship resource represents an opportunity to encourage believers, reach searching hearts, and proclaim the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
And that mission requires time, dedication, resources, and the faithful support of people who believe that biblical truth should continue reaching others.
It does not purchase blessings, forgiveness, spiritual protection, or a closer relationship with Christ.
Those things cannot be bought.
Scripture teaches us that giving should be willing and sincere.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the spirit in which I want to invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through fear.
But through a shared desire to glorify Christ by helping biblical teaching reach more people.
These are simply thank-you benefits, not spiritual rewards.
The greater purpose is the mission.
To keep pointing people toward Jesus.
To help believers grow in biblical understanding.
To encourage repentance, restoration, and faithful discipleship.
And to make sound Christian resources more accessible.
Because the Word of God is not a commodity to be withheld from people who cannot afford to give.
You can still pray.
You can still share biblical teachings.
You can still help bring the message of Jesus Christ to someone who desperately needs hope.
It is about the Savior.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who died and rose again.
The One who transforms lives through His grace.
The One who alone deserves the glory.
And now, before you leave this story, remember the mountain one last time.
Seventy elders.
Moses.
Aaron.
Nadab.
Abihu.
The God of Israel.
The sapphire-like pavement.
The blood of the covenant.
The extraordinary meal.
And that unforgettable declaration:
“Upon the nobles of the children of Israel he laid not his hand.”
They lived because God mercifully permitted them to remain in His presence.
And today, the Gospel announces that through Jesus Christ, sinners who repent and believe may be reconciled to that same holy God.
Not because holiness has changed.
Not because sin no longer matters.
Not because we have become worthy through our own efforts.
But because Jesus Christ is the sufficient Savior.
The cross does not make God's holiness disappear.
It reveals both His righteousness and His saving love.
The resurrection declares the victory of the One who died for our sins.
And the invitation remains.
Come to Christ.
Turn from sin.
Receive His mercy.
Walk in His truth.
Do not spend your entire life standing at a distance from the grace God has made known in His Son.
Because the greatest wonder of Exodus 24 is not simply that sinful men stood before a holy God and lived.
It is that their encounter helps prepare us to understand the greater mercy revealed in Jesus Christ.
They stood on a mountain and lived to tell of God's mercy. Jesus died on a hill and rose again so that those who trust in Him could live forever in God's presence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HOW OLD WAS ESAU WHEN HE MARRIED HIS FIRST TWO WIVES? THE ANSWER IS 40—BUT THE HEARTBREAK BEHIND GENESIS 26:34 IS SOMETHING EVERY FAMILY NEEDS TO HEAR
paragraphs: HOW OLD WAS ESAU WHEN HE MARRIED HIS FIRST TWO WIVES? THE ANSWER IS 40—BUT THE HEARTBREAK BEHIND GENESIS 26:34 IS SOMETHING EVERY FAMILY NEEDS TO HEAR

He was old enough to marry, old enough to make his own decisions, and old enough to know his family's spiritual heritage. But one decision would bring bitterness into the home of Isaac and Rebekah. Behind this overlooked verse is a devastating warning about choices, spiritual compromise, parental heartbreak, and the grace of God that can reach even the most complicated family.
There is a kind of heartbreak that doesn't come from losing someone to death.
It comes from watching someone you love make decisions that slowly carry them away from everything you prayed they would become.
A father watches his son grow into a man, yet wonders whether the faith he tried to pass down ever truly reached his heart.
A mother remembers holding her child when he was helpless, teaching him what was right, praying over his future, and believing that one day he would walk faithfully with God.
Then the child grows up.
He begins making his own decisions.
And suddenly, the parents discover something painful.
You can raise a child in a home that knows God without being able to guarantee that the child will choose God's ways.
That is part of the sorrow waiting inside Genesis 26:34–35.
And what makes this passage so unsettling is that the Bible does not begin with a dramatic scandal, a violent confrontation, or a public catastrophe.
It begins with a man's age.
Forty.
Just one number.

But behind that number is a family story involving spiritual inheritance, parental grief, divided loyalties, wounded relationships, and choices whose consequences would reach far beyond one household.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part is this:
Before we finish looking at Esau, we may discover something about ourselves.
Scripture says:
"And Esau was forty years old when he took to wife Judith the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Bashemath the daughter of Elon the Hittite: Which were a grief of mind unto Isaac and to Rebekah."
— Genesis 26:34–35, KJV
There is the direct biblical answer.
Esau was forty years old when he married Judith and Bashemath, his first two wives named in Genesis 26:34.
The text identifies Judith as the daughter of Beeri the Hittite and Bashemath as the daughter of Elon the Hittite.
It does not provide two separate wedding dates. It presents both marriages in connection with Esau being forty years old.
That is what Scripture tells us.
But if we stop at the number, we miss the human anguish that the next verse reveals.
Because the real emotional weight of the passage is not simply that Esau married.
It is what those marriages meant within the story of a family entrusted with God's covenant promises.
And to understand that, we need to return to something that happened long before Esau turned forty.
Before there were wives, before there was parental grief, before the family became divided by deception and resentment, there were two brothers struggling inside their mother's womb.
Rebekah was pregnant with twins.
The struggle was so troubling that she sought the LORD.
God answered her:
"Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger."
— Genesis 25:23, KJV
Even before Esau and Jacob were born, God had revealed that their family history would unfold in an extraordinary way.
These were not merely two boys who would grow up with different personalities.
They would become ancestors of peoples whose histories would be intertwined.
Esau would become associated with Edom.
Jacob would receive the name Israel.
But being born into a family connected to God's covenant did not automatically produce a heart that treasured the things of God.
And this is where Esau's story begins to disturb us.
Genesis 25 describes Esau as a skillful hunter, a man of the field, while Jacob was a quieter man who dwelt in tents.
Their father Isaac loved Esau, particularly because he enjoyed the game Esau brought home. Rebekah loved Jacob.
Already, we see a household vulnerable to favoritism.
Already, there are fractures.
And then comes the incident involving the birthright.
Esau returns from the field exhausted and hungry.
Jacob has prepared food.
Esau wants something to eat.
Jacob demands his birthright in exchange.
And Esau agrees.
Genesis 25:34 ends with a devastating statement:
"Thus Esau despised his birthright."
The Hebrew expression is:
וַיִּבֶז עֵשָׂו אֶת־הַבְּכֹרָה
Vayyivez Esav et-habekhorah.
Meaning, in context:
"So Esau despised the birthright."
The verb translated "despised" comes from the Hebrew root בָּזָה (bazah), which conveys treating something as insignificant, holding it in contempt, or failing to give it its proper value.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say Esau had no appetite.
He was hungry.
It does not say his physical need was imaginary.
His exhaustion was real.
The problem was that he treated something of lasting importance as though it were worth surrendering for immediate satisfaction.
And that is a warning that reaches across centuries.
Sometimes the most dangerous decisions are not made when we hate what is holy.
Sometimes they are made when we want something else more urgently.
We know what matters.
We know what we have been taught.
We know what God has said.
But something in front of us begins to feel more important than everything we might lose.
One moment of anger.
One secret relationship.
One dishonest transaction.
One temptation we have been entertaining for too long.
One decision we tell ourselves we can undo later.
And suddenly, we discover that a temporary appetite can produce consequences that last far longer than the satisfaction it promised.
That does not mean every mistake is irreversible.
The Gospel is full of hope for repentant sinners.
But grace does not make wisdom unnecessary.
And forgiveness does not mean our decisions have no earthly consequences.
Now return to Esau at forty.
There is an important detail here that is easy to overlook.
Genesis 25:26 tells us Isaac was sixty years old when Rebekah gave birth to Esau and Jacob.
Therefore, when Esau was forty, Isaac was approximately one hundred years old.
This was not a family without history.
Isaac had lived through decades of God's provision.
He was the son of Abraham, the child whose birth had testified to God's faithfulness to His promise.
And Isaac himself had married Rebekah when he was forty years old, according to Genesis 25:20.
Do you see the striking parallel?
Isaac was forty when he married Rebekah. Esau was forty when he married Judith and Bashemath.
The same age.
But very different marriage narratives.
In Genesis 24, Abraham had been deeply concerned that Isaac should not take a wife from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom he lived.
He sent his servant to seek a wife from his own kin.
That concern belonged to the specific covenant history of Abraham's family. It was not a declaration that one ethnicity was inherently superior to another.
The issue was preserving covenant faithfulness in a world filled with competing religious loyalties.
The servant prayed.
God providentially guided the journey.
Rebekah entered the story.
And the account culminated in a marriage that continued the covenant family line.
Then, one generation later, Genesis tells us that Esau married two Hittite women.
And the immediate result recorded in Scripture is grief.
The Hebrew of Genesis 26:35 reads:
וַתִּהְיֶיןָ מֹרַת רוּחַ לְיִצְחָק וּלְרִבְקָה
Vattihyeyna morat ruach le-Yitzchaq ule-Rivqah.
The expression מֹרַת רוּחַ (morat ruach) communicates bitterness or distress of spirit.
A close English rendering is:
"And they were a bitterness of spirit to Isaac and Rebekah."
The KJV says "a grief of mind."
The Hebrew wording helps us feel the depth of the statement.
This was not presented as a minor family disagreement.
It was deep distress.
Something about these marriages brought real bitterness into the lives of Isaac and Rebekah.
We must be careful here.
Genesis 26:35 does not give us a detailed record of Judith's or Bashemath's personal conduct. It does not quote their conversations or tell us every reason for the parents' distress.
We should not invent accusations against these women that Scripture itself does not make.

What the broader narrative does show is a longstanding concern about marriage alliances with the Canaanite peoples, a concern later made explicit by Isaac when he instructed Jacob not to take a wife from the daughters of Canaan (Genesis 28:1).
Genesis 27:46 also records Rebekah's anguish concerning the Hittite women.
So the passage belongs to a larger biblical concern about covenant identity, household loyalty, and the preservation of faith.
The spiritual danger was not someone's ancestry by itself.
Throughout Scripture, God welcomes people from outside Israel who turn to Him in faith.
Rahab was welcomed.
Ruth the Moabite became part of the ancestry of David and, ultimately, the earthly genealogy of Jesus Christ.
The issue is never that God's mercy belongs to only one ethnic group.
The issue is whether people will honor the true God or turn their hearts toward idols.
And that brings us to a question that every believer should consider.
Are we making decisions that honor God, or are we expecting God to bless decisions we have already made without seeking Him?
Because there is a difference.
We can pray for God's blessing while refusing to submit our desires to His Word.
We can ask God to protect our relationships while ignoring the spiritual direction in which those relationships are carrying us.
We can speak about faith publicly while making our most important decisions as though God's wisdom has nothing to say.
And sometimes the people who see the danger first are those who love us most.
But there is another side to this story.
Perhaps you are not identifying with Esau.
Perhaps you are identifying with Isaac and Rebekah.
You know what it is to pray for someone who keeps choosing a painful path.
You have tried to speak gently.
You have tried to warn them.
You have watched them dismiss advice that came from love.
And there are nights when you wonder whether anything you taught them still matters.
There is a special kind of helplessness in loving someone whose choices you cannot control.
You cannot repent on their behalf.
You cannot manufacture faith inside their heart.
You cannot force spiritual maturity through fear, arguments, or endless reminders.
You can speak truth.
You can pray.
You can love.
You can set appropriate boundaries.
But you cannot become the Holy Spirit in someone else's life.
And if that describes your pain, remember this:
Your inability to control another person's choices does not mean God has lost the ability to reach that person.
The story of Esau, however, also warns parents against imagining that every family wound belongs entirely to the children.
Isaac and Rebekah were not flawless.
Their favoritism toward different sons helped create a deeply divided household.
Later, Jacob would deceive his father, Rebekah would participate in the scheme, and Esau would become furious over the blessing he lost.
Genesis does not present this family as a collection of perfect saints surrounded by one troublesome son.
It presents human beings.
Complicated human beings.
People who had received extraordinary promises from God but still struggled with fear, favoritism, manipulation, appetite, and resentment.
And isn't that what makes the Bible so painfully believable?
It does not pretend that families connected to God's purposes are automatically free from dysfunction.
It does not conceal the failures of patriarchs.
It does not erase the tears.
It does not sanitize the consequences.
It tells the truth.
And then it shows us that God remains faithful even when human beings are not.
That does not mean God approves of deception, compromise, or family cruelty.
It means His redemptive purposes are not dependent upon human perfection.
There is also an important complication in the later genealogical records.
Genesis 28:9 reports that Esau subsequently married Mahalath, a daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebajoth.
Genesis 36:2–3 gives another account of Esau's wives, naming Adah daughter of Elon the Hittite, Oholibamah daughter of Anah, and Basemath daughter of Ishmael, sister of Nebaioth.
These lists do not match the names and family descriptions in Genesis 26:34 in a simple one-to-one way.
Some interpreters have suggested that certain women had multiple names. Others understand the lists differently. Scripture does not explicitly explain every difference.
It would therefore be careless to pretend that all the naming questions are conclusively settled.
But the uncertainty concerning the later lists does not erase the clear statement in Genesis 26:34.
Esau was forty when he took Judith and Bashemath as wives, according to that verse.
And Genesis immediately tells us that these marriages brought grief to his parents.
Now consider what happens next in the larger narrative.
In Genesis 28:8–9, Esau recognizes that the daughters of Canaan were displeasing to his father Isaac.
He then takes another wife from Ishmael's family.
It is a revealing moment.
Esau appears to be responding to his father's displeasure.
But the text does not tell us that this action amounted to spiritual repentance or a complete change of heart.
And that distinction matters.
Because changing an outward decision is not necessarily the same as surrendering the inward person to God.
Someone can change relationships to gain approval.
Someone can begin attending church because of family pressure.
Someone can adopt religious language to repair a reputation.
Those outward actions may be meaningful.
But true repentance goes deeper than appearance.
It is not merely asking, "How do I make people stop being disappointed in me?"
It is asking, "Lord, where have I sinned against You, and how must my heart change?"
The New Testament gives us another sobering perspective on Esau.
Hebrews 12:16–17 warns believers against becoming sexually immoral or profane, using Esau as an example of someone who sold his birthright for a single meal.
The Greek word used to describe Esau is βέβηλος (bebēlos).
It carries the sense of being profane or irreverent toward sacred things.
The writer's concern is not merely that Esau made an unwise bargain.
It is that he treated a sacred privilege as though it were ordinary and expendable.
Hebrews then recalls how Esau later sought the blessing with tears.
The passage is serious and has been interpreted in different ways, particularly concerning the statement that he found no place for repentance.
In its Genesis context, Esau could not reverse Isaac's blessing of Jacob, despite his anguish. Hebrews uses that event as a solemn warning against despising spiritual privilege.
We should not twist it into the claim that every person who has sinned deeply is forever beyond God's mercy.
That would contradict the Gospel's invitation to repent and believe in Jesus Christ.
But we should also refuse to weaken the warning.
Tears over consequences are not automatically the same as repentance toward God.
Regret can say, "I hate what this cost me."
Repentance says, "I have sinned, and I need God's mercy."
Regret may be concerned primarily with what was lost.
Repentance turns toward the Lord.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story becomes intensely personal.
What have you been treating as ordinary that God calls precious?
Your marriage?
Your integrity?
Your purity?
Your calling?
Your responsibility to your children?
Your commitment to truth?
Your time in Scripture?
Your relationship with Jesus Christ?
What have you been willing to exchange for a moment of satisfaction?
And what have you been calling harmless simply because the consequences have not arrived yet?
There is no need to pretend.
God already knows.
He knows the compromise you have been rationalizing.
He knows the prayer you have been avoiding.
He knows the conviction you keep silencing.
He knows the relationship you are afraid to surrender.
He knows the bitterness you have been carrying.
He knows the difference between the person you present publicly and the battles you fight privately.
And yet the Gospel does not begin with the announcement that sinners must somehow repair themselves before approaching God.
It begins with what God has done through His Son.
Jesus Christ entered a world filled with broken families, sinful desires, betrayal, and human grief.
He did not come merely to give people better advice.
He came to save sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
That is the difference between mere moral instruction and the Gospel.
The law exposes our sin.
The Gospel announces the Savior who bore sin.
Jesus lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He died on the cross for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are proclaimed.
We do not receive salvation because our family history is impressive.
We do not receive it because our parents were faithful believers.
We do not receive it because we have never made an Esau-like decision.
We receive salvation by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that unmistakably clear.
And the grace that saves us also calls us to a transformed life.
It teaches us to turn away from sin and walk in obedience.
It does not merely comfort us in our compromises.
It calls us out of them.
There is a beautiful contrast here.
Esau's story warns us about a man who treated his birthright lightly.
But the New Testament points believers toward an inheritance that comes through Jesus Christ.
First Peter 1:3–4 speaks of a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ and an inheritance that is incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading.
Think about that.
Esau's birthright could be sold.
Earthly blessings could become sources of conflict.
Family relationships could fracture.
But the inheritance secured for God's people through the risen Christ rests upon the faithfulness of God.
This is not permission to become careless.
It is a reason to treasure Christ above every temporary appetite.
And if you have already made terrible choices, hear this carefully.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot force people to forget what happened.
You cannot demand that trust return immediately.
You may have to face painful consequences, make restitution, seek forgiveness, and rebuild what your actions damaged.
But your past does not have to become an excuse to reject the Savior today.
The cross does not make sin insignificant. It reveals how serious sin is—and how extraordinary God's mercy is.
This is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not that human beings can somehow rescue themselves through stronger determination.
Our message is Jesus Christ.
His truth.
His holiness.
His sacrifice.
His resurrection.
His mercy toward repentant sinners.
His power to transform lives.
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin deserves applause.
Not because consequences are imaginary.
But because the grace of God in Jesus Christ is greater than any story we could have written for ourselves.
Perhaps you are the son or daughter who walked away.
Perhaps you are the parent still praying.
Perhaps you are the husband who regrets what he allowed into his marriage.
Perhaps you are the wife who feels spiritually alone.
Perhaps you have been following Jesus for years, yet something has slowly begun competing with your love for Him.
Or perhaps you are reading this without knowing whether you truly believe at all.
Whatever brought you here, do not miss the central question.
Not merely, "How old was Esau when he married?"
But, "What am I doing with the spiritual privileges and opportunities God has placed before me?"
Because knowing the answer to a Bible question is not the same as allowing God's Word to examine your heart.
And information alone cannot save your soul.
Jesus Christ can.
If you recognize sin in your life, confess it to God.
Do not hide behind religious appearances.
Do not use someone else's failures to excuse your own.
Turn to Christ in repentance and faith.
If you have wounded people, take responsibility where you can.
If you have been wounded, seek the Lord's wisdom for forgiveness, healing, and healthy boundaries.
If you are praying for a loved one who has wandered, keep bringing that person before God without confusing love with control.
And if your heart has become cold toward Scripture, begin again.
Open the Bible.
Read it carefully.
Pray for understanding.
Listen to what God has actually said, rather than only what you wish He had said.
There is something deeply humbling about realizing that a verse written thousands of years ago can expose a struggle we thought nobody understood.
Forty years old.
Two wives.
One grieving household.
And a warning that still reaches us today.
But I don't want this story to end with Esau's age.
I want it to lead us to the One who is greater than every patriarch, greater than every earthly inheritance, and greater than every failure we have ever committed.
Jesus Christ.
The Savior who calls sinners to repentance.
The Shepherd who seeks the lost.
The Lord who deserves more than the leftovers of our attention.
The King who is worthy of our lives.
And because this truth matters, I want to ask something of you.
Not as a demand.
Not as a way to earn God's favor.
But as an invitation to help carry the message of Christ to people who may never walk into a church, open a Bible, or admit publicly that their hearts are breaking.
One simple share can place Scripture in front of someone who desperately needs it.
You may never know who reads it in silence.
A struggling father.
A grieving mother.
A young person drifting from faith.
A believer wrestling with temptation.
Someone who has been hiding their guilt behind a smile.
And I want to invite you to do something even more personal.
Have you ever watched someone you love make decisions that broke your heart? Or have you been the one who ignored wise counsel and later regretted it?
If you are comfortable sharing, tell us what God has been teaching you.
You do not need to reveal private details or confess sensitive matters publicly. God hears the prayer you cannot put into a comment.
But your testimony, your encouragement, or even a sincere request for prayer may remind another person that they are not alone in their struggle.
We want this community to be a place where Scripture is not reduced to inspirational slogans, where difficult passages are not avoided, and where Jesus Christ remains at the center.
There is also a deeper way you can help sustain this mission.
Some believers may prayerfully choose to make that support part of their regular giving.
But I want to be biblically careful about something important.
It does not purchase forgiveness, salvation, spiritual favor, or a closer relationship with Jesus.
And it should never replace the responsibility to care for your family, fulfill your obligations, or faithfully support your local church.
The Bible teaches that Christian giving should be willing and sincere, not driven by guilt or pressure.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
These items are simply resources and expressions of appreciation. They are not the reason we preach Christ.
The message matters infinitely more than the merchandise.
These resources are intended to help believers who are serious about growing deeper in Jesus Christ, strengthening their understanding of Scripture, and nourishing their daily walk with God.
Your prayers matter.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
And above all, your relationship with Jesus Christ matters.
Our hope must rest in Christ alone.
And the life of genuine faith bears fruit through love, obedience, generosity, repentance, and perseverance.
That is the kind of discipleship we want to encourage.
Now, before you leave, return with me to the beginning.
A man was forty years old.
He married two women.
His parents grieved.
The Bible preserved the account.
And thousands of years later, we are still learning from it.
Why?
Because the human heart has not changed.
We still struggle with appetite.
We still wrestle with family expectations.
We still confuse immediate satisfaction with lasting joy.
We still make decisions without fully considering what they may cost.
And we still need the mercy of God.
But there is something Esau's story cannot give us by itself.
The final answer to human sin.
For that, we must look to Jesus.
The One who did not despise the Father's will.
The One who obeyed where we have failed.
The One who endured the cross.
The One who rose victorious over death.
The One who offers forgiveness and new life to those who repent and believe.
So do not merely remember that Esau was forty.
Remember what his story warns you not to take lightly.
Remember that spiritual privilege is a responsibility, not a decoration.
Remember that decisions have consequences.
Remember that families need truth and grace.
Remember that no earthly relationship should take the place of obedience to God.
And remember that even when your life has become a story of regret, Jesus Christ is still the Savior to whom you are called to turn.
You may not be able to recover every opportunity you wasted.
You may not be able to repair every consequence overnight.
But you can stop running from the truth.
You can repent.
You can believe.
You can take the next faithful step.
And you can trust the Savior who died and rose again.
Esau was forty when he made the marriages recorded in Genesis 26:34—but whatever your age today, don't wait another forty years to give Jesus the place in your heart that has always belonged to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ARE CHRISTIAN INFLUENCERS MAKING DISCIPLES… OR JUST BUILDING PERSONAL BRANDS?
paragraphs: ARE CHRISTIAN INFLUENCERS MAKING DISCIPLES… OR JUST BUILDING PERSONAL BRANDS?

When Jesus becomes the content, followers become the currency, and ministry becomes a business, one terrifying question remains: Are we leading people to the Cross… or teaching them to admire the person holding the microphone?
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ one day.
Not as a content creator. Not as a pastor. Not as an author, worship leader, evangelist, or Christian influencer.
Just you.
No camera. No audience. No verified badge. No impressive ministry statistics.
And imagine having to confront a question you spent your entire online life avoiding.
“You told thousands of people about Me. But did you teach them to follow Me… or to depend on you?”
Now, those are not recorded words of Jesus. Scripture does not give us that exact conversation.
But the question behind them is frighteningly biblical.
Because Jesus once warned that not everyone who calls Him “Lord, Lord” will enter the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 7:21–23).
And that warning was not directed only toward people who openly rejected God.
It included people who claimed to have prophesied, driven out demons, and performed mighty works in His name.
Read that again.
People who could point to impressive religious activity.
People who could say they had done extraordinary things.
Yet Jesus exposed the terrible possibility that public ministry and genuine obedience are not always the same thing.
And perhaps that is where our conversation needs to begin.
Not with another attack on Christian influencers.
Not with another cynical declaration that every online ministry is a scam.
But with something much more uncomfortable.
What if the greatest danger facing Christian influence today is not that people have stopped talking about Jesus?
What if it is that we have become exceptionally good at talking about Jesus while quietly learning how to make everything revolve around ourselves?
And before anyone points a finger at somebody else, there is something we need to admit.
This temptation does not belong exclusively to famous preachers or creators with millions of followers.
It can live inside the person with fifty followers.
Inside the church volunteer who secretly resents not being recognized.
Inside the worship leader who feels disappointed when someone else receives the applause.
Inside the believer who shares Scripture but keeps checking how many people reacted.
And yes, it can live inside a ministry like Gospel Warrior too.
Nobody who speaks publicly about Christ is automatically immune.
Not even the person writing these words.
That is what makes this conversation necessary.
Because sometimes the most dangerous idol in Christian ministry is not money.
It is the version of ourselves that we have convinced people to admire.
And an idol becomes especially difficult to recognize when it is holding a Bible.
Jesus understood the human appetite for recognition long before algorithms existed.
In Matthew 6:1, He warned against practicing righteousness before others in order to be seen by them.
The Greek expression is πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι αὐτοῖς (pros to theathēnai autois).
It conveys the purpose of being seen or observed by others.
Notice what Jesus was exposing.
Not merely the fact that someone performed a good deed publicly.
But the motive behind it.
The desire to turn obedience into a performance.
The desire to make holiness an advertisement for oneself.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because public faithfulness is not inherently hypocrisy.
Jesus also told His disciples to let their light shine before others so that people would see their good works and glorify their Father in heaven (Matthew 5:16).
The difference is not simply whether people see you.
It is who receives the glory when they do.
One person shares a testimony because someone desperately needs hope.
Another shares a testimony because being admired has become emotionally necessary.
One person teaches Scripture because the truth has transformed their life.
Another gradually discovers that controversy, outrage, and dramatic declarations generate more engagement than careful biblical teaching.
And the terrifying thing is that, from the outside, both may look almost identical.
Both may quote Scripture.
Both may pray publicly.
Both may speak passionately about salvation.
Both may attract thousands of followers.
Only God sees the heart perfectly.
And sometimes, by His grace, He allows us to recognize what is happening inside our own hearts before our public success becomes our private destruction.
There is a story in Scripture that should make every Christian communicator tremble.
In John 3, John the Baptist's disciples came to him concerned that people were going to Jesus.
Think about the situation.
John had been preaching repentance.
He had baptized crowds.
He had faithfully prepared people for the coming Messiah.
Now attention was moving away from him.
The very people who once gathered around his ministry were turning toward Someone else.
In the world of modern influence, we might call that a devastating loss of audience.
But John did not panic.
He did not launch a campaign to reclaim attention.
He did not treat Jesus as competition.
Instead, he said something that may be the most important sentence any Christian influencer could ever learn.
ἐκεῖνον δεῖ αὐξάνειν, ἐμὲ δὲ ἐλαττοῦσθαι.
Ekeinon dei auxanein, eme de elattousthai.
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
— John 3:30
The Greek word δεῖ (dei) expresses necessity: something that must happen.
John was not merely expressing a preference.
He understood that the growing prominence of Jesus was the very purpose of his own ministry.
His joy was not threatened when people went to Christ.
His joy was fulfilled.
Can we say the same?

Would we rejoice if someone stopped watching our videos because they had become deeply rooted in Scripture, committed to a healthy local church, and mature enough to walk with Christ without depending on our daily posts?
Would we celebrate if a person we discipled grew beyond us?
Would we be grateful if another ministry reached people we could not reach?
Or would some hidden part of us feel abandoned?
That is a painful question.
Because discipleship is not about creating lifelong dependence on the discipler.
It is about helping people become faithful followers of Jesus.
A true disciple-maker should be able to say, “I am thankful you listened to me. But I am even more thankful that you have learned to listen to Christ through His Word.”
And that brings us to something deeply troubling about the culture we live in.
We have learned to measure influence with numbers.
Views.
Likes.
Shares.
Comments.
Monthly revenue.
Audience growth.
Engagement rates.
And none of those numbers is automatically sinful.
A widely shared Gospel message may reach a person who would never enter a church building.
A Christian author may rightly receive payment for honest labor.
Paul taught that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), even though he sometimes chose not to exercise that right.
Financial support is not the enemy of faithful ministry.
But there is a difference between using resources to serve the Gospel and using the Gospel to acquire resources.
There is a difference between reaching more people because you love them and loving people primarily because reaching them increases your numbers.
And there is a difference between making disciples and manufacturing customers who are afraid to leave.
The Bible does not condemn every form of financial support for Christian ministry.
But it does condemn greed, manipulation, and treating godliness as a means of gain.
In 1 Peter 5:2–3, church elders are instructed to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for shameful gain, and not by domineering over those entrusted to them.
In 2 Corinthians 2:17, Paul distinguishes his ministry from those who peddle God's word for profit.
These passages do not establish that every paid ministry is corrupt.
They establish something far more searching.
The way we handle people, money, and authority reveals something about what we believe ministry is for.
And if a Christian influencer cannot be questioned without immediately accusing the questioner of attacking God's anointed, something has gone wrong.
If every criticism becomes persecution, accountability disappears.
If every disagreement becomes rebellion, the personality becomes untouchable.
If every financial appeal suggests that refusing to give means refusing God, generosity has been replaced with pressure.
Jesus did not commission His followers to build spiritual empires around personalities.
He commanded them to make disciples.
Matthew 28:19 begins with the Greek:
μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη
Mathēteusate panta ta ethnē.
“Make disciples of all nations.”
The key verb, μαθητεύσατε (mathēteusate), means to make disciples.
And Jesus immediately explains what that mission involves: baptizing people in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything He commanded.
That is much deeper than generating religious excitement.
A disciple is not simply someone who enjoyed your message.
Not simply someone who agrees with your opinion.
Not someone who types “Amen” and continues living as though Christ has no authority over their life.
A disciple is a learner and follower of Jesus, called to trust Him, obey Him, and grow in His likeness.
And that transformation cannot be reduced to analytics.
You can have a million followers and still fail to teach people what Jesus commanded.
You can have a small audience and faithfully help people understand the Scriptures, repent of sin, love their neighbors, persevere in suffering, and remain rooted in Christ.
Numbers can tell us how far content travels.
They cannot, by themselves, tell us how deeply the Gospel has taken root.
Think about that lonely believer who has been struggling for months.
The one who smiles at church but cries in the bathroom.
The one who has fallen into the same sin again and is beginning to wonder whether repentance is still possible.
The one who has prayed for healing, watched other people celebrate answered prayers, and quietly asked God why their own suffering continues.
Imagine that person opening Facebook at two in the morning.
They find a Christian video.
The music is beautiful.
The speaker is confident.
The editing is cinematic.
The comments are filled with declarations of victory.
But the message leaves them with one conclusion.
“If I had stronger faith, I would already be successful, healed, wealthy, or free from suffering.”
So they close the app feeling even more ashamed.
That is not what biblical discipleship should produce.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that sufficiently spiritual people will never struggle.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners, that He died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
It is the announcement that salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward for impressive religious performance (Ephesians 2:8–9).
It is the announcement that those who belong to Christ can bring their failures into the light, confess their sins, and find forgiveness and cleansing in Him (1 John 1:9).
And it is the announcement that following Jesus may involve suffering, self-denial, endurance, and a cross.
Jesus never promised that discipleship would make us celebrities.
He said:
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me.”
— Luke 9:23, ESV
Daily.
Not just when the camera is recording.
Not just when the post performs well.
Not just when the ministry receives financial support.
Daily.
When nobody applauds.
When telling the truth costs you followers.
When correcting a mistake damages your image.
When a struggling believer needs compassion instead of a motivational slogan.
When repentance requires admitting publicly that you were wrong.
When obedience is expensive and nobody notices.
That is where the difference between a personal brand and a life surrendered to Jesus begins to become visible.
And there is another biblical story we cannot ignore.
In Acts 8, Simon had amazed people in Samaria with his magic, and people regarded him as someone great.
Then Philip proclaimed Christ, and many believed.
Later, Simon saw the apostles laying hands on believers, who received the Holy Spirit.
And Simon offered money for the power he had witnessed.
Peter rebuked him sharply.
Why?
Because Simon attempted to obtain God's gift through money and revealed a heart that was not right before God.
Its immediate concern is the attempted purchase of spiritual power.
But it reveals a principle that should still disturb us.
Holy things must never become instruments of personal ambition.
The power of God is not merchandise.
The Holy Spirit is not a product.
Spiritual authority is not something we purchase, package, or possess for self-exaltation.
And human souls are not inventory.
There is a reason Paul asked the Corinthians:
“Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?”
— 1 Corinthians 1:13, ESV
The church in Corinth was struggling with divisions around human leaders.
Some identified themselves with Paul.
Others with Apollos.
Others with Cephas.
And Paul redirected their attention to the One who was actually crucified for them.
Christ.
Not Paul.
Not Apollos.
Not the most eloquent speaker.
Not the most admired religious personality.
Christ.
Imagine if we applied that question to our modern Christian culture.
Was your favorite influencer crucified for you?
Did your favorite preacher carry your sins on the Cross?
Did your favorite author rise from the dead?
Can your favorite ministry forgive your sins?
No.
Only Jesus saves.
And every faithful Christian voice, including this one, must remain willing to be measured against that truth.
But perhaps you are reading this as someone who has been hurt by Christian leaders.
Maybe you once trusted a ministry.
You gave.
You served.
You defended its leaders.
You believed their promises.
And then something happened.
Perhaps you discovered dishonesty.
Perhaps your questions were dismissed.
Perhaps you were made to feel guilty for not giving more.
Perhaps someone used Scripture to control you instead of helping you understand it.
And now, every time you see another Christian influencer speaking passionately into a camera, something inside you tightens.
You wonder whether the tears are real.
Whether the compassion is genuine.
Whether the message is simply another carefully constructed strategy to get your attention and eventually your money.
If that is where you are, your questions deserve to be taken seriously.
But please do not confuse the failures of people who represent Jesus with the character of Jesus Himself.
He is not another religious celebrity protecting His reputation.
He is the Savior who confronted hypocrisy, welcomed repentant sinners, washed His disciples' feet, and gave His life for His sheep.
He did not exploit the wounded.
He moved toward them.
He did not need to manufacture a scandal to gain attention.
He entered our broken world and bore the shame of the Cross.
He did not offer forgiveness as a premium benefit for those who could afford it.
He gave Himself for sinners who could never purchase their own redemption.
And here is where the Gospel becomes personal.
Because the Cross does not merely expose corrupt religious influence.
It exposes our own hunger to be important.
Our desire to be seen.
Our need to be affirmed.
Our tendency to turn even good things into ways of proving our worth.
The Gospel confronts that hunger with a Savior who had every right to receive honor yet humbled Himself.
Philippians 2:5–8 describes Christ's humility, culminating in His obedience to death on a cross.
The passage does not teach that Jesus stopped being divine.
It reveals the astonishing humility of the Son who took the form of a servant.
And that changes the way Christian influence should look.
If our Lord served, how can we justify using people?
If our Lord humbled Himself, how can we make self-exaltation our ministry strategy?
If our Lord gave His life, how can we treat wounded people as disposable engagement?
If our Lord told the truth even when people walked away, how can we compromise Scripture simply to preserve our audience?
The answer is not that Christian influencers should stop creating content.
The answer is that every Christian platform must remain under the lordship of Christ.
A camera can become a tool of discipleship.
A Facebook page can become a place where someone first encounters biblical truth.
A book can help a believer understand Scripture.
A video can encourage someone to seek help, confess sin, return to a local church, or begin reading the Bible.
An online ministry can serve people who are isolated, searching, grieving, or spiritually hungry.
These things matter.
But they must lead somewhere beyond themselves.
Toward Scripture.
Toward prayer.
Toward repentance and faith.
Toward fellowship with other believers.
Toward love expressed in real life.
Toward obedience to Jesus.
And toward the recognition that no digital ministry, however helpful, can replace the whole life of the church.
A faithful influencer should not fear a follower becoming spiritually mature enough to disagree with them respectfully.
A faithful ministry should welcome correction when it has misunderstood Scripture.
A faithful teacher should be able to say, “I do not know,” rather than inventing certainty.
A faithful Christian communicator should care more about whether a message is true than whether it is viral.
And a faithful audience should test what it hears.
Acts 17:11 commends the Bereans for examining the Scriptures to see whether Paul's teaching was true.
Think about that.
Even the apostle Paul's preaching was examined against Scripture.
How much more should our favorite online personalities be examined?
Do not surrender your discernment because someone has a large following.
Do not assume that emotional music proves biblical accuracy.
Do not mistake confidence for spiritual maturity.
Do not confuse expensive production with God's approval.
And do not automatically condemn a ministry simply because it has resources, sells books, or receives voluntary support.
Look at its teaching.
Look at its handling of Scripture.
Look at how it treats people.
Look at whether its leaders welcome accountability.
Look at what happens when someone says no.
Look at whether the ministry continually points beyond itself to Jesus.
Because a genuine servant of Christ does not need to become the center of your spiritual universe.
Jesus is enough.
And perhaps this is the question that should stay with every person reading this:
If the name of the influencer disappeared tomorrow, would the people they reached still know how to follow Jesus?
Would they still open their Bibles?
Would they still pray?
Would they still gather with believers?
Would they still seek holiness?
Would they still love their enemies?
Would they still trust Christ when life became painful?
Would they still know that forgiveness comes through Jesus rather than through loyalty to a personality?
If the answer is yes, something beautiful may have happened.
The messenger became less necessary because the message had taken root.
The servant stepped aside because people had learned to follow the Master.
And that is not a failure of influence.
That is one of its greatest possible fruits.
Now, I want to speak directly to the person who feels convicted.
Maybe you are building a ministry, and somewhere along the way, the numbers began controlling your emotions.
You started measuring your worth by the reach of your posts.
You became jealous when someone else succeeded.
You found yourself softening difficult biblical truths because you feared losing support.
You began enjoying the attention more than the responsibility.
Or maybe you are not a creator at all.
Maybe you have become more loyal to a Christian personality than to the Word of God.
Maybe you defend everything your favorite leader says without examining Scripture.
Maybe you spend hours watching Christian content but rarely spend quiet time with Jesus.
Maybe you know the opinions of your favorite preacher better than you know the teachings of Christ.
There is still grace for repentance.
That is the beauty of the Gospel.
Jesus does not expose our sin merely to leave us drowning in shame.
He calls us to turn from it and come to Him.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated “repentance,” refers to a change of mind or heart that, in biblical context, involves turning toward God and away from sin.
Repentance is not simply feeling embarrassed because someone discovered our motives.
It is acknowledging what is wrong and turning to Christ.
It is surrendering what we have been protecting.
It is saying, “Lord, even this ministry belongs to You.”
“Even this platform belongs to You.”
“Even this reputation belongs to You.”
“Even my desire to be remembered must bow before You.”
And if you have fallen, the answer is not to construct a more convincing spiritual image.
The answer is to come honestly to Jesus.
Because He does not need the polished version of your story.
He already knows the truth.
The failures.
The compromises.
The envy.
The hidden pride.
The secret exhaustion.
The prayers you stopped praying.
The motives you have been afraid to examine.
And the same Christ who calls sinners to repentance also offers forgiveness through His finished work.
That is why the words From Scandal to Grace matter so deeply to us at Gospel Warrior.
Not because every scandal should be excused.
Not because repentance removes every earthly consequence.
Not because a disgraced leader must automatically be restored to public ministry.
And certainly not because grace gives anyone permission to exploit people.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem sinners, transform lives, and bring truth and hope into places marked by shame.
Grace does not make accountability unnecessary.
Grace teaches us to stop hiding from the truth.
And genuine restoration must never come at the expense of those who have been harmed.
The Cross tells us both that sin is serious and that God's mercy is astonishing.
That is the Gospel we want to keep proclaiming.
Not a Gospel that makes Gospel Warrior famous.
Not a Gospel that makes any founder, writer, or creator indispensable.
But the Gospel of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen.
And this is also why we want to be transparent about the invitation we are making.
Gospel Warrior is committed to sharing Scripture-centered encouragement, biblical teaching, and discipleship resources.
At the same time, producing, maintaining, and expanding ministry resources involves real work and real costs.
It does not make you a better Christian.
It does not secure forgiveness or spiritual blessing.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing and not compelled.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says, God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we make this invitation.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
The heart remains Jesus.
The Word remains our foundation.
Discipleship remains our calling.
Not because we need another impressive number.
But because someone in your circle may be struggling with disillusionment toward Christian leadership.
Someone may be confusing religious popularity with spiritual authority.
Someone may have walked away from Christian community because a leader failed them.
Someone may be serving God publicly while privately losing the joy of knowing Him.
And someone may need to hear that Jesus is still worthy of their trust, even when the people who speak about Him are imperfect.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to start a public fight.
But to open a conversation that could lead to humility, healing, and renewed faithfulness.
And please, do not leave this article without examining your own heart.
I want to ask you something, and I hope you will answer with spiritual honesty rather than a polished religious response.
Have you ever found yourself admiring a Christian personality more than actually spending time with Jesus?
Or have you ever felt hurt, manipulated, or disappointed by someone who claimed to represent Him?
And if you want to share your experience, your testimony, or a Scripture that has helped you discern faithful Christian teaching, the comments are open for that conversation too.
You do not have to reveal private wounds or name individuals publicly.
But your honest words may help another believer realize they are not alone.
Because pride rarely announces its arrival.
Sometimes it simply begins by making applause feel necessary.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, struggling Christians, and even those who are still searching for truth to follow along.
Not because every question has an easy answer.
But because Jesus deserves to be sought with honesty.
And before we finish, I want to return to that opening image.
Standing before Christ.
No audience.
No camera.
No analytics.
No carefully written biography.
Only the truth of a life laid bare before the Lord.
Scripture teaches that believers will give an account to God, and that our works will be tested (Romans 14:12; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15).
But our hope of salvation does not rest in producing a perfect ministry record.
It rests in Jesus Christ, whose death and resurrection are sufficient for all who trust in Him.
That is why we must not build our identity on how many people know our names.
Our deepest joy is that, through Christ, we may belong to God.
The world may remember a Christian influencer for their charisma.
For their voice.
For their content.
For their success.
For their controversy.
But the greatest legacy any Christian communicator can leave is not an audience that cannot stop talking about them.
It is people who have learned to love, trust, and obey Jesus.
So let the platforms be useful.
Let the books be written.
Let the videos be made.
Let the resources reach people.
Let generous supporters help faithful ministries continue their work.
Jesus Christ is the Savior. We are not.
And when our names are forgotten, when the algorithms have moved on, when the applause has gone silent, may the people we served still be walking with Him.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be losing our audience.
It would be gaining the world's attention while forgetting the One we were supposed to proclaim.
May they forget the sound of our voices long before they forget the Savior we pointed them toward.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HER HUSBAND WAS OLD. HER HOPE WAS BURIED. THEN ELISHA SPOKE SEVEN WORDS THAT CHANGED EVERYTHING.
paragraphs: HER HUSBAND WAS OLD. HER HOPE WAS BURIED. THEN ELISHA SPOKE SEVEN WORDS THAT CHANGED EVERYTHING.
The Shunammite Woman’s Unthinkable Miracle: When God Spoke Life Into a Future She Had Stopped Asking For — 2 Kings 4:8–37
She had a home. She had a husband. She had enough resources to welcome a prophet into her house.
But there was one thing she did not have.
A child.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part of her story was not that she had never held a son.
It was that she had apparently learned how to live without expecting one.
Have you ever wanted something so badly that, after years of disappointment, you stopped mentioning it?
Not because the desire disappeared.
But because hoping had become painful.

You learned to smile when other people received what you had prayed for. You learned to celebrate their blessings while quietly carrying questions about your own. You learned to say, "I'm fine," even when there was a room inside your heart you could no longer bear to enter.
And eventually, you stopped asking.
That is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because in 2 Kings 4, we meet a woman whose generosity was visible, whose hospitality was remarkable, and whose private longing was apparently known to someone else before she ever spoke of it.
And then one day, the prophet Elisha called her to the doorway.
What he said next would reopen a hope she had carefully protected herself from feeling.
But the greatest shock in this story is not simply that an older husband and his wife would have a son.
It is what happened after the promise came true.
Because the child she had never dared to expect would eventually lie dead in her arms.
And the God who had given her a promise would be the very God she would have to trust when that promise seemed to have died.
Stay with this story.
Especially if you have ever wondered how to keep believing when the thing God allowed you to love becomes the thing you are terrified of losing.
The Bible introduces her in 2 Kings 4:8 as a prominent woman living in Shunem.
The Hebrew describes her as an ishah gedolah (אִשָּׁה גְדוֹלָה), literally a "great woman," an expression that can communicate her standing, influence, or substantial means.
She was not presented as helpless or without resources.
She had something to offer.

When Elisha traveled through Shunem, she urged him to stop and eat. What began as hospitality became a regular act of generosity. Whenever the prophet passed through, he could find a meal in her home.
Eventually, she told her husband that she recognized Elisha as a holy man of God.
And she proposed something extraordinary.
They would build him a small upper room, furnished with a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp.
Read that carefully.
Before she ever received the promise of a son, she had already made room for the work of God in her home.
She was not negotiating a miracle.
She was not buying divine favor.
She was not offering hospitality as a spiritual investment that would guarantee a return.
The text gives us no reason to believe she expected a child in exchange for her kindness.
She simply recognized a servant of God and responded with practical generosity.
There is something beautiful about that.
Sometimes the most sincere expressions of faith are not dramatic declarations made before a crowd.
Sometimes faith looks like preparing a meal.
Opening a door.
Providing a place to rest.
Giving something without expecting repayment.
Jesus would later teach that even a cup of cold water given to one of His disciples because that person belongs to Him would not go unnoticed (Matthew 10:42).
But we must be careful here.

The Shunammite woman's story does not teach that generosity purchases miracles. God's grace cannot be bought, and a gift to a ministry cannot obligate God to grant a child, healing, prosperity, or any other desired outcome.
What her story shows is a woman whose generosity was genuine before any extraordinary blessing was announced.
And then, one day, Elisha wanted to express his gratitude.
He instructed his servant Gehazi to call her.
Elisha asked whether she wanted him to speak on her behalf to the king or the commander of the army.
She declined.
Her answer in 2 Kings 4:13 is striking:
"I dwell among mine own people." (KJV)
She did not ask for influence.
She did not request political protection.
She did not use her kindness to obtain a powerful connection.
She appeared content with her place among her people.
But Gehazi noticed something.
Something her outward composure did not reveal.
In 2 Kings 4:14, Elisha asked what could be done for her.
And Gehazi answered:
"Verily she hath no child, and her husband is old." (KJV)
There it was.
One sentence.
A whole history of possible disappointment compressed into a few words.
She had no child.
And her husband was old.
Scripture does not tell us her exact age, how long they had been married, whether she had experienced miscarriages, or how many nights she had prayed for a baby.
We should not invent details God has not revealed.
But the text does establish two realities.
She was childless.
And her husband's advanced age made the prospect of having a child appear increasingly unlikely.
The Hebrew phrase describing her husband is:
וְאִישָׁהּ זָקֵן
Ve'ishah zaqen.
"And her husband is old."
The word zaqen (זָקֵן) means "old" or "aged."

It is not a technical medical diagnosis. It does not specify that he was incapable of fathering a child. But in the narrative, his age helps explain why the announcement of a son would be astonishing.
Then Elisha called her again.
She came and stood at the doorway.
Imagine that moment.
The woman who had helped provide a doorway of hospitality for the prophet was now standing in that doorway, about to hear something she had not requested.
Elisha said:
"About this season, according to the time of life, thou shalt embrace a son." (2 Kings 4:16, KJV)
The Hebrew begins:
לַמּוֹעֵד הַזֶּה כָּעֵת חַיָּה
La-mo'ed hazzeh ka'et chayyah.
A careful rendering is, "At this appointed time, about this time next year."
The wording points toward a corresponding season in the following year, not an indefinite promise that something good might eventually happen.
And what was she promised?
Not merely a pregnancy.
Not merely an improvement in her circumstances.
She would embrace a son.
The Hebrew verb choveqet (חֹבֶקֶת) comes from a root meaning "to embrace" or "to hold close."
The announcement was deeply personal.
The child she did not have would become a child she could hold.
The promise concerned more than an abstract future.
It concerned the warmth and weight of a living son in his mother's arms.
But her response was not the triumphant declaration we might expect.
She said:
"Nay, my lord, thou man of God, do not lie unto thine handmaid." (2 Kings 4:16, KJV)
Do you hear the emotion?
Not, "Finally!"
Not, "I knew this day would come!"
Not even, "How wonderful!"
Instead:
Please do not deceive me.
Please do not give me a hope that will break my heart.
The Hebrew includes the expression:
אַל־תְּכַזֵּב בְּשִׁפְחָתֶךָ
Al-tekazzev be-shifchatek.
"Do not deceive your servant."
Her response suggests that the possibility of a child touched something profoundly sensitive.
We cannot know everything she felt.
But we can recognize the fear of being disappointed again.
There are people reading this who understand that feeling.
You are not necessarily afraid of the miracle.
You are afraid of believing in it.
You have survived by lowering your expectations.
You have learned how to function without the answer you once begged God to give.
You still attend church.
You still worship.
You still encourage other people.
You still tell them that God is faithful.
But when someone speaks about your own deepest longing, something inside you tightens.
Because you remember what happened the last time you hoped.
Perhaps your longing is for a child.
Perhaps it is for reconciliation with someone you love.
Perhaps it is for freedom from an addiction, restoration after betrayal, or healing from a wound nobody else can see.
Perhaps you are asking whether God can still do something meaningful with a life you believe you have wasted.
Listen carefully.
The Shunammite woman's story is not a universal promise that every childless couple will conceive or that every desired outcome will arrive within twelve months.
It is a historical account of a particular word given through God's prophet to a particular woman.
But it reveals something enduring about the character of God.
Our limitations do not limit His power.
And our disappointments do not make us invisible to Him.
Then comes one of the most beautiful verses in the account.
2 Kings 4:17 says:
"And the woman conceived, and bare a son at that season that Elisha had said unto her, according to the time of life." (KJV)
She conceived.
She bore a son.
At the appointed season.
Exactly as the prophet had announced.
The Bible does not tell us about the months between the promise and the birth.
It does not describe every anxious thought or every conversation between husband and wife.
It simply tells us that the word came to pass.
And suddenly the woman who had said, "Do not deceive me," was holding the child she had been told she would embrace.
Imagine how that first embrace might have felt.
The tiny fingers.
The fragile breath.
The realization that the child was no longer merely a promise spoken at a doorway.
He was alive.
He was hers to love.
But if you stop reading at verse 17, you will miss the part of this story that makes it almost unbearable.
Because the same chapter that records the birth of her son also records his death.
Years passed.
The boy grew.
One day, he went out to his father among the reapers.
Suddenly, he cried:
"My head, my head." (2 Kings 4:19, KJV)
His father instructed a servant to carry him to his mother.
The boy sat on her knees until noon.
And then he died.
There is no way to make that sentence comfortable.
The son she had not asked Elisha to promise was now lifeless in her arms.
The miracle had become the source of an unimaginable grief.
What do you do when yesterday's answered prayer becomes today's heartbreak?
What do you do when the very blessing that taught you to hope again seems to have been taken away?
The woman carried her son upstairs and laid him on the bed of the man of God.
Then she shut the door.
And she went to find Elisha.
Her husband questioned why she was going to the prophet when it was neither the new moon nor the Sabbath.
She replied with a Hebrew word that many believers recognize:
שָׁלוֹם
Shalom.
Often translated "peace," the word can also communicate well-being, wholeness, or that things are well.
In this context, her brief answer should not be treated as proof that she felt no grief or possessed absolute certainty about what would happen.
Her son was dead.
Her circumstances were devastating.
Yet she was determined to reach the prophet.
When she arrived, Gehazi came to ask whether all was well with her, her husband, and her child.
Again, she answered that it was well.
But when she reached Elisha, she grasped his feet.
Her distress could no longer remain hidden.
And then she spoke words that expose the wound beneath the miracle:
"Did I desire a son of my lord? did I not say, Do not deceive me?" (2 Kings 4:28, KJV)
That question is devastating.
She was not merely grieving a child.
She was confronting the unbearable tension between a promise she had received and a reality she could not understand.
She had warned Elisha not to raise her hopes.
Now the son who had fulfilled that promise was dead.
And she wanted answers.
Some of us have been taught that genuine faith never asks difficult questions.
That faithful people never weep in confusion.
That trusting God means pretending everything makes sense.
But this woman did not pretend.
She brought her anguish to the place where the promise had been announced.
And Scripture did not erase her protest.
There is a lesson here for every believer who feels ashamed of being wounded.
Grief is not automatically unbelief.
Tears are not proof that faith has disappeared.
