He arrived as property.
His own brothers had betrayed him. The people who should have protected him had sold him. His father was grieving a son he believed was dead.
Imagine being carried into a foreign country with no certainty that you would ever see home again.
Imagine hearing unfamiliar voices, seeing unfamiliar faces, and realizing that the people who sold you were going home while you were being taken farther away.
Joseph had every human reason to become bitter.
He could have decided that integrity was pointless.
He could have argued that God had allowed too much suffering to expect obedience from him.
But Genesis 39:2 records a remarkable truth:
“And the LORD was with Joseph.” (KJV)
Not Joseph was comfortable.
Not Joseph was free.
Not Joseph understood everything.
The LORD was with Joseph.
The Hebrew text says:
וַיְהִי יְהוָה אֶת־יוֹסֵף
Vayehi Adonai et-Yosef.

A faithful rendering is, “And the LORD was with Joseph.” The Hebrew consonants יהוה represent God's covenant name, commonly rendered LORD in English Bibles; Adonai is the traditional Jewish spoken substitute.
That little word “with” changes everything.
God's presence was not proof that Joseph would never suffer.
God's presence meant suffering would not have the final authority over Joseph's life.
Somebody reading this needs to understand that.
You may be in a season you never chose.
You may have been betrayed by someone you trusted.
You may be carrying wounds that nobody in your church knows about.
You may have prayed faithfully and still watched your circumstances become worse.
Do not measure God's faithfulness only by the comfort of your surroundings.
Joseph was enslaved, yet the LORD was with him.
And the same God who sustained Joseph has not become incapable of sustaining His people today.
Joseph eventually served in the household of Potiphar, an Egyptian officer of Pharaoh. God prospered the work entrusted to Joseph, and Potiphar recognized that the LORD was with him.
Joseph gained responsibility.
Trust.
Access.
Influence.
Then the temptation came.
Genesis 39:7 says Potiphar's wife “cast her eyes upon Joseph” and said, “Lie with me.” (KJV)
There was nothing ambiguous about the proposition.
She wanted a sexual relationship with a man who was not her husband.
And Joseph was not dealing with an ordinary situation between two people of equal standing.
He was enslaved in her household. She belonged to the family that controlled his circumstances. Her position gave her power that Joseph did not possess.
The passage does not tell us everything Joseph felt. It does not say he was attracted to her, nor does it describe his private emotional struggle.
We should not invent what Scripture does not reveal.
But Scripture tells us what he chose.
He refused.
And the words he spoke are among the most courageous declarations of moral conviction in the Old Testament.
“How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” — Genesis 39:9 (KJV)
Look carefully at what Joseph did not say.
He did not say, “What if my master finds out?”
He did not say, “What if this ruins my reputation?”
He did not say, “What if somebody sees us?”
His concern reached deeper.
“How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
The original Hebrew is even more striking.
וְאֵיךְ אֶעֱשֶׂה הָרָעָה הַגְּדֹלָה הַזֹּאת וְחָטָאתִי לֵאלֹהִים
Ve'eikh e'eseh hara'ah hagedolah hazzot vechatati l'Elohim?
Literally, the sense is:
“And how could I do this great evil and sin against God?”

The Hebrew word רָעָה (ra'ah) refers here to evil or wrongdoing. הַגְּדֹלָה (hagedolah) means “the great,” emphasizing the seriousness of the act. The expression וְחָטָאתִי לֵאלֹהִים (vechatati l'Elohim) means “and sin against God.”
Joseph was not describing a harmless attraction.
He was identifying the proposed act as grave moral evil.
And that matters because our generation has become extraordinarily skilled at renaming sin until it sounds less offensive.
Adultery becomes “finding happiness.”
Lust becomes “having needs.”
Deception becomes “protecting someone's feelings.”
Secret relationships become “emotional connections.”
Pornography becomes “private entertainment.”
And repentance is sometimes replaced with the comforting idea that God understands everything, so nothing needs to change.
Yes, God understands our weakness.
But His understanding does not transform evil into good.
Grace does not require God to abandon His holiness.
And love does not require Him to pretend that sin cannot destroy what He created to be beautiful.
Joseph understood that adultery would be a betrayal of Potiphar's trust, a violation of the marriage covenant, and ultimately an offense against God.
Genesis 39:9 also records Joseph acknowledging that Potiphar had withheld only his wife from him because she was married to him.
This was not simply a question of whether Joseph could obtain something he desired.
It was a question of whether he would violate a relationship God intended to be honored.
Long before the written Law of Moses was given to Israel, Joseph recognized the moral gravity of adultery.
And centuries later, Jesus would reveal that God's concern reaches beyond outward acts into the desires of the heart.
In Matthew 5:27–28, Jesus teaches that lustful intent itself violates the heart of the commandment against adultery.
That should confront every one of us.
Because some people have never physically committed adultery but have been secretly cultivating desires that dishonor their spouse.
Some have never met the person they are emotionally entangled with, yet they are giving that person affection, secrecy, and attention that belong within their marriage.
Some have convinced themselves that deleting the conversation means erasing the sin.
Others are unmarried but have begun treating people as objects for pleasure rather than neighbors bearing God's image.
And some are carrying profound shame over sexual sins they have already committed.
If that is you, please do not stop reading.
This story is not being told so that you will conclude you are beyond redemption.
It is being told because sin is serious, and the mercy of Jesus Christ is greater than your ability to repair yourself.
But mercy must never become permission to continue destroying what God calls us to surrender.
There is another detail in Joseph's story that deserves our attention.
Genesis 39:10 says that Potiphar's wife spoke to Joseph “day by day.”
Day by day.
Not one unexpected encounter.
Not one isolated invitation.
Repeated pressure.
Repeated opportunity.
Repeated refusal.
And Joseph did not merely refuse to sleep with her. The verse says he would not listen to her “to lie by her, or to be with her.” (KJV)
He was resisting the act and avoiding the compromising proximity.
That is a lesson many Christians desperately need.
You cannot consistently nourish temptation and then be surprised when resisting it becomes harder.
You cannot deliberately cultivate intimacy with someone else's spouse and assume your intentions will remain innocent.
You cannot keep returning to the same secret conversation, the same explicit content, the same dangerous setting, while insisting that you are simply testing your spiritual strength.
There are temptations we must confront by standing firm.
And there are temptations we must confront by getting away.
Joseph did both.
Then came the day that changed everything.
Genesis 39:11–12 describes Joseph entering the house to attend to his work. None of the men of the household were inside.
Potiphar's wife seized him by his garment and demanded that he lie with her.
This was no longer merely a verbal proposition.
She physically grabbed him.
And Joseph ran.
He left the garment in her hand and fled outside.
The Hebrew of Genesis 39:12 says:
וַיָּנָס וַיֵּצֵא הַחוּצָה
Vayyanas vayyetse hachutzah.
“And he fled and went outside.”
No extended negotiation.
No attempt to prove how strong he was by remaining in danger.
He escaped.

We must also recognize something important: Joseph was the person being sexually pressured and physically seized. The responsibility for that wrongdoing belonged to the woman who pursued and grabbed him.
The lesson is not that victims of coercion are guilty if they cannot escape.
The lesson is that Joseph, when he had the opportunity, refused to participate in wrongdoing and fled from the person violating his boundaries.
Sometimes the holiest thing you can do is leave.
Leave the conversation.
End the secret relationship.
Close the browser.
Block the contact.
Step away from the compromising situation.
Tell the truth to someone trustworthy.
Seek help before another decision deepens the damage.
The New Testament reinforces this principle.
“Flee fornication.” — 1 Corinthians 6:18 (KJV)
The Greek begins:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν
Pheugete tēn porneian.
The verb φεύγετε (pheugete) is a present imperative meaning “flee” or “keep fleeing.” The noun πορνεία (porneia) refers broadly to sexual immorality.
Paul was not telling believers to become experts at standing as close to sexual sin as possible without crossing a technical boundary.
He commanded them to flee it.
Not because their bodies are worthless.
But because their bodies matter to God.
In the same chapter, Paul reminds Christians that they belong to Christ and are called to glorify God in their bodies.
That is why holiness is not merely a collection of restrictions.
It is the fitting response of someone redeemed by a Savior who gave Himself for them.
But here is the part of Joseph's story that many people would rather skip.
Joseph ran from sin.
And the consequences were terrible.
Potiphar's wife used the garment Joseph left behind as the centerpiece of a false accusation.
The very thing he abandoned while escaping became evidence she used against him.
Joseph was innocent of the alleged offense.
Yet he was imprisoned.
Can you imagine the questions that might arise in such a situation?
Why did doing the right thing lead to suffering?
Why was the liar believed?
Why did integrity not protect him?
Why did God not immediately expose the truth?
Scripture does not record Joseph asking those particular questions, so we should not place imaginary speeches into his mouth.
But the injustice itself is unmistakable.
And anyone who has ever been falsely accused, misunderstood, betrayed, or punished for doing what is right can recognize the pain of that reality.
Sometimes obedience costs you something.
Sometimes telling the truth damages your popularity.
Sometimes ending a sinful relationship leaves you lonely.
Sometimes refusing corruption closes a professional door.
Sometimes your commitment to Christ will be misunderstood by people who benefited from your compromise.
And sometimes doing what is right does not immediately make life better.
This is where shallow teaching about faithfulness collapses.
If someone tells you that obeying God always produces immediate comfort, Joseph's story stands against that claim.
Joseph obeyed.
Joseph suffered.
And yet Genesis 39:21 says:
“But the LORD was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy.” (KJV)
There it is again.
The LORD was with Joseph.
In the house where he served.
And in the prison where he suffered.
God's presence did not disappear when Joseph's circumstances changed.
The prison was not evidence that Joseph had made the wrong moral choice.
And the delay in his vindication was not evidence that God had forgotten him.
That truth should reach someone who is exhausted from doing the right thing without seeing the outcome they hoped for.
You may be waiting for an apology that has never come.
You may be living with consequences caused by another person's dishonesty.
You may have chosen repentance, only to discover that rebuilding trust takes longer than you imagined.
You may have refused to compromise and watched someone else receive the opportunity you wanted.
Do not confuse delayed justice with divine indifference.
But also do not turn Joseph's eventual rise to power into a guarantee that every faithful Christian will receive wealth, promotion, public vindication, or earthly success.
Joseph's story is a particular account of God's providence within His larger purposes.
Its enduring promise is not that every prison becomes a palace in this lifetime.
Its enduring witness is that God remains sovereign and faithful even when the righteous suffer.
Eventually, Joseph would be brought before Pharaoh, interpret his dreams through God's enabling, and be entrusted with extraordinary responsibility.
Through the events recorded in Genesis 41–50, God used Joseph to preserve many lives during famine, including the family through whom His covenant purposes would continue.
Years later, Joseph spoke to the brothers who had betrayed him.
And Genesis 50:20 gives us one of Scripture's clearest testimonies to God's providence:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good.” (KJV)
Notice what Joseph did not say.
He did not call their evil good.
He did not excuse their betrayal.
He did not pretend that injustice was harmless.
He acknowledged their evil intentions while recognizing God's power to accomplish good through circumstances that human beings had wickedly created.
That is not the same as saying God approves of evil.
It is saying evil does not overthrow His sovereign purposes.
And now we come to the most important part of this entire story.
Because if we stop with Joseph, we may leave thinking Christianity is simply about becoming strong enough to resist temptation.
Be disciplined.
Be courageous.
Run away.
Never fail.
But what happens to the person who already failed?
What happens to the husband who crossed the line?
The wife who concealed the relationship?
The unmarried believer trapped in a cycle of sexual compromise?
The Christian who knows the language of holiness but has been hiding a divided life?
What happens when the garment has already been left behind, the boundary has already been crossed, and the conscience is crying out?
Joseph's example can expose our sin.
But Joseph cannot save us from it.
We need someone greater.
We need Jesus.
Joseph was a faithful servant who resisted a particular temptation.
Jesus Christ is the sinless Son of God who resisted temptation and fulfilled the Father's will completely.
Hebrews 4:15 says Jesus was tempted in every respect as we are, “yet without sin.” (KJV)
The Greek expression is:
χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας
Chōris hamartias.
“Without sin.”
Not without understanding human weakness.
Not without experiencing genuine temptation.
Without sin.
Where we have compromised, Jesus remained obedient.
Where we have hidden, Jesus walked in truth.
Where we have betrayed, Jesus remained faithful.
And unlike Joseph, whose suffering was part of God's providential preservation of lives during famine, Jesus' suffering accomplished redemption through His death and resurrection.
He did not merely show us how to escape temptation.
He came to save sinners.
He bore our sins on the cross.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us to repent, believe the Gospel, and follow Him.
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.” — 1 Peter 3:18 (KJV)
The just for the unjust.
Think about that.
The One who never committed adultery gave Himself for people who have.
The One who never entertained sinful lust came to redeem those enslaved by it.
The One who never lied offered mercy to liars.
The One who never betrayed the Father willingly suffered to reconcile rebellious people to God.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin was insignificant.
But that the sinless Savior paid an immeasurable price to redeem sinners.
And this grace is not a license to return comfortably to the darkness.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's saving grace trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions.
Real grace does not merely comfort us while we cling to sin.
It teaches us to turn from sin toward the One who loves us.
And perhaps that is where this article becomes painfully personal.
Because you might be reading it while protecting something you already know needs to end.
A conversation.
A relationship.
A secret habit.
An arrangement built on deception.
A pattern of behavior you keep promising to stop.
You have prayed about it.
You have cried about it.
You have made promises in the middle of the night.
And yet you keep returning.
Listen carefully.
You do not overcome sin by pretending you are stronger than you are.
You begin by bringing the truth into God's light.
Confess your sin to God.
Stop defending what Scripture condemns.
Take practical steps to remove opportunities for compromise.
Seek appropriate accountability from a mature, trustworthy Christian.
Where you have wronged another person, pursue honest repentance and responsible repair, without demanding instant forgiveness or trust.
If abuse, coercion, or threats are involved, seek safety and qualified help. The call to repentance must never be used to blame victims or pressure anyone to remain in danger.
And when shame tells you that you have gone too far to return to Christ, remember His invitation.
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
That promise is not an invitation to cherish sin.
It is an invitation to come to the Savior.
You do not need to clean yourself up enough to earn the right to approach Him.
You need to come honestly, trusting His mercy and surrendering to His lordship.
First John 1:9 declares that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
And Romans 8:1 proclaims that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Not because their sins were imaginary.
Not because their past never happened.
But because Jesus Christ has accomplished what guilty sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message is not merely “Run like Joseph.”
It is also “Return to Jesus.”
Run from what is destroying you.
Run toward the Savior who can redeem you.
And if you have already fallen, do not make your failure your permanent identity.
Repent.
Believe.
Rise to walk in the newness of life Christ gives.
You are not saved by Joseph's courage.
You are saved by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the same Lord who forgives His people also calls them to holiness.
Perhaps you are the person who needs to end the secret relationship today.
Perhaps you need to confess something you have concealed.
Perhaps you need to stop treating your spouse's trust as something expendable.
Perhaps you need to acknowledge that your private online habits are shaping your heart in ways you have refused to confront.
Or perhaps you are the person who was betrayed, manipulated, falsely accused, or violated.
Then hear this too.
The sin committed against you is not your shame to carry.
Joseph was not guilty of the offense falsely attributed to him.
And you do not need to accept blame for another person's wrongdoing.
Christ sees the wounded as well as the guilty.
His mercy is not reserved only for those who need forgiveness. He also welcomes those who need healing, protection, justice, and restoration.
Some wounds require time, wise counsel, safety, and the support of trustworthy people.
There is no shame in needing that help.
And there is no biblical requirement to pretend that trust has been restored before it actually has.
Jesus Christ is full of grace and truth.
We need both.
Truth without grace can leave a wounded sinner despairing.
A counterfeit grace without truth can leave a sinner comfortable in bondage.
But the Gospel brings us face to face with a holy Savior who loves sinners enough to call them out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And that is why this message must not end as something we simply admire.
It must become something we respond to.
And if you have been falsely accused or suffered for doing what is right, your testimony may encourage someone who is quietly wondering whether obedience is worth the cost.
You do not have to expose private wounds to prove your faith.
But your honest testimony may become the encouragement another believer desperately needs.
Think of someone you love who may be standing at a dangerous crossroads.
A married friend struggling with temptation.
A young believer surrounded by sexual pressure.
Someone carrying shame over a past mistake.
Someone who thinks their hidden choices have nothing to do with their relationship with God.
Someone who has done the right thing and is now suffering because of it.
Because the world does not need another generation that merely knows how to quote Joseph.
It needs Christians who take holiness seriously, acknowledge their own need for grace, and point broken people toward Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has helped you grow closer to Jesus, there is another meaningful way you can participate in the work.
Not because God measures your devotion by the amount you contribute.
And certainly not because the Gospel can be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ. It is not for sale.
But Scripture does teach that believers may voluntarily support faithful Gospel ministry.
Galatians 6:6 speaks of sharing good things with those who teach the Word, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should come from a willing heart, not reluctance or compulsion.
What matters is that any gift be given freely, responsibly, and with a sincere desire to honor God.
And remember, Gospel Warrior is not only about articles.
These resources are part of our desire to encourage a faith that continues beyond a moment of emotional inspiration.
A faith that studies Scripture.
A faith that learns to pray.
A faith that repents.
A faith that grows in wisdom.
A faith that follows Jesus when nobody is watching.
Our deepest desire is that you belong to Jesus Christ.
Because one day, the products will wear out.
The posts will disappear beneath newer posts.
The numbers, reactions, and statistics will fade from memory.
But the Word of God will remain.
And the question Joseph faced will still matter.
How can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?
Maybe the answer you need today is not another excuse.
Maybe it is a confession.
Maybe it is a decision to leave.
Maybe it is a phone call to someone who can help you break a destructive pattern.
Maybe it is finally bringing your shame to the feet of Jesus.
And maybe, for the first time in a long time, you need to stop asking how close you can get to sin without falling and start asking how closely you can walk with the Savior who died to set you free.
Joseph lost his garment, but he refused to surrender his integrity.
He lost his freedom for a season, but God had not abandoned him.
He was falsely accused, but his story did not end with the accusation.
And his life, for all its suffering and remarkable providence, points us toward a far greater Redeemer.
Jesus Christ was condemned though He was without sin.
He endured the cross.
He rose victorious.
And through Him, sinners can be forgiven, the ashamed can find mercy, and the broken can begin a new life.
Do not leave this message merely impressed by Joseph.
Leave it looking to Jesus.
Because Joseph shows us the beauty of faithfulness under temptation.
But Jesus is the Savior who gives hope to those who have failed.
And whether you are standing before temptation, suffering because you refused it, or grieving because you surrendered to it, the call of the Gospel is still before you.
Turn to Christ.
Trust His mercy.
Obey His Word.
Walk in His light.
The door Joseph ran through led away from temptation; the cross of Jesus opens the way home for everyone who has fallen and turns to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DO SOME CHRISTIANS TREAT STRANGERS LIKE JESUS… BUT TREAT THEIR OWN SPOUSES LIKE ENEMIES?
paragraphs: WHY DO SOME CHRISTIANS TREAT STRANGERS LIKE JESUS… BUT TREAT THEIR OWN SPOUSES LIKE ENEMIES?

They can pray for a stranger, forgive a church member, and speak gently to everyone outside their home. But the person they promised to love before God is quietly breaking under the weight of their words. What happens when your public Christianity looks more like Christ than your private marriage?
There is a kind of heartbreak that doesn't leave bruises.
It doesn't make the evening news. It doesn't always end in divorce. Sometimes it sits quietly at the dinner table, wearing a wedding ring, pretending everything is fine.
And perhaps the most painful part?
The person causing that heartbreak might be someone everybody else calls a wonderful Christian.
Someone who serves at church. Someone who knows Scripture. Someone who can spend an hour comforting a struggling friend but cannot spare five minutes to listen to the person sleeping beside them.
Someone who says, “God bless you,” to strangers with genuine warmth, then walks through the front door and speaks to their spouse as though kindness is a privilege they no longer deserve.
And the spouse?
They hear the laughter from the other room.
They watch their husband or wife answer a friend's phone call with enthusiasm after ignoring their own attempts to talk all evening.
They see the patience. The tenderness. The compassion.
They know that person is capable of being gentle.
That is what makes it hurt so much.
Because sometimes the deepest wound in a marriage isn't discovering that your spouse doesn't know how to love.
It's discovering that they know exactly how to show kindness.
They just seem to have stopped showing it to you.
And before you assume this article is about your husband or your wife, there is a question every married Christian needs the courage to ask.
What if the person who needs to repent isn't sitting across from you?
What if that person is reading these words right now?
Somewhere tonight, a woman is lying beside a man who spent Sunday morning lifting his hands in worship, yet hasn't spoken tenderly to her in weeks.
Somewhere else, a husband is sitting alone after another evening of being belittled, wondering why the woman who encourages everybody at church seems to have nothing encouraging left for him.
And somewhere, a couple who once prayed for God to bring them together now barely know how to pray together without feeling the distance between them.
Their marriage didn't necessarily collapse in one terrible moment.
It happened in ordinary moments.
A sarcastic comment.
An apology withheld.
A conversation interrupted.
A private humiliation disguised as a joke.
A tired spouse asking for affection and receiving irritation instead.
One person saying, “Can we please talk?”
And the other answering, “Not this again.”
Little by little, the home that was supposed to be a place of refuge became a place where somebody learned to measure every word before speaking.
And then Sunday comes.
The smiles return.
The greetings become warm.
The Bible opens.
The prayers sound beautiful.
But God sees Monday too.
And the Jesus we worship in public is the same Jesus who sees how we treat one another behind closed doors.
This is where Scripture becomes painfully personal.
In Ephesians 4:32, the apostle Paul writes:
Look carefully at the word translated “kind.”
In the Greek text, Paul uses χρηστοί (chrēstoí), meaning kind, benevolent, or gracious in one's treatment of others.
Then comes εὔσπλαγχνοι (eúsplanchnoi), commonly translated “tenderhearted,” conveying deep compassion.
Paul is not describing a polished public personality.
He is describing the kind of character that should grow in people who have received the mercy of Jesus Christ.
And notice something else.
He does not say, “Be kind to one another, except when you have been married for fifteen years.”
He does not say, “Be tenderhearted toward people who appreciate you.”
He does not say, “Forgive the church members, but keep a permanent record of your spouse's failures.”
The command is not suspended at the front door of your house.
If anything, the intimacy of marriage makes its application even more urgent.
Because the person who sees your weaknesses most closely should not automatically receive the least compassion.
Yet why does this happen?
Why can a Christian show extraordinary patience to a stranger and extraordinary impatience toward the person they married?
Sometimes it is because strangers encounter our presentation, while spouses encounter our patterns.
A stranger may see us for five minutes.
Our spouse sees us when we're exhausted, disappointed, frightened, financially pressured, or struggling with something we haven't surrendered to God.
Strangers rarely confront the unresolved wounds in our character.
Marriage often does.
A stranger doesn't usually remind us of an argument from three years ago.
A stranger doesn't know the promises we broke.
A stranger doesn't ask why we keep avoiding difficult conversations.
But a spouse might.
And when pride is stronger than humility, we may respond to that closeness not with gratitude, but with defensiveness.
Sometimes familiarity becomes an excuse for carelessness.
We begin to assume that the person who has stayed will always stay.
We stop saying thank you.
We stop noticing sacrifices.
We offer strangers the benefit of the doubt while interpreting our spouse's every mistake through the lens of past disappointment.
We become polite where we want approval and careless where we assume acceptance.
But love that only behaves beautifully when people are watching needs serious examination.
Jesus spoke directly to the danger of outward religious appearance without inward transformation.
In Matthew 23:27–28, He rebuked religious leaders who appeared righteous outwardly while concealing corruption within.
That passage was not specifically about marriage, and we should not pretend that it was.
But its warning reaches into every place where outward religious reputation becomes a substitute for genuine obedience.
You can protect your Christian image and still neglect your Christian character.
You can defend biblical marriage in public while failing to practice biblical love in private.
You can know the language of grace and still refuse to extend it.
And if that realization stings, don't rush to defend yourself.
Ask the Holy Spirit to show you what needs to change.
Because conviction is not the enemy of grace.
Sometimes conviction is the doorway through which we finally stop running from the truth.
There is another passage that deserves our attention.
Colossians 3:19 says:
“Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them.” (KJV)
The Greek expression μὴ πικραίνεσθε (mē pikraínesthe) carries the sense of not becoming embittered or harsh toward them.
Think about that.
The Holy Spirit, through Paul, addressed the danger of bitterness entering the marriage relationship.
Not merely adultery.
Not merely abandonment.
Bitterness.
That slow poison that turns ordinary conversations into battles.
That habit of responding sharply because resentment has been rehearsed for too long.
That coldness that grows when offenses are collected instead of honestly addressed.
And husbands, this command is not permission to demand submission while withholding tenderness.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
The Greek verb ἀγαπᾶτε (agapâte) comes from agapaō, meaning to love. In this context, Paul defines that love by pointing to Christ's self-giving sacrifice.
Not domination.
Not intimidation.
Not emotional abandonment.
Not using Scripture to win arguments.
Christlike marital love is sacrificial.
It does not ask, “How much can I demand from this person?”
It asks, “How can I honor Christ in the way I care for this person?”
And wives are not exempt from the call to kindness, respect, and faithful love.
Ephesians 5:21 calls believers to submit to one another in the fear of God, and the surrounding passage gives particular instructions for husbands and wives.
Whatever theological differences Christians may have about the application of marital roles, Scripture gives no spouse permission to be cruel, contemptuous, manipulative, or abusive.
A marriage is not made holy by one person having power over another.
A marriage honors God when His truth shapes how both people live.
And this is where the story becomes even more uncomfortable.
Because some Christians have confused being respected with being feared.
They say, “My spouse needs to respect me.”
But what they actually demand is silence.
They say, “I'm the head of this household.”
But they use that claim to avoid accountability.
They say, “The Bible says to forgive.”
But what they mean is, “Stop bringing up what I did, even though I haven't changed.”
Others use tears, guilt, withdrawal, or public embarrassment to control the person they promised to cherish.
And some hide behind religious language so effectively that their spouses begin to question whether asking for basic dignity is somehow unspiritual.
It is not.
Forgiveness is biblical. So are repentance, truthfulness, accountability, and justice.
Reconciliation is not the same thing as pretending nothing happened.
Trust is not automatically restored because somebody said sorry.
And the call to love your spouse never requires you to accept violence, coercion, threats, or ongoing abuse.
If you are unsafe, seeking protection and qualified help is not a failure of faith.
God's Word must never be turned into a weapon that traps someone in harm.
Now consider a quieter form of marital pain.
Not every wounded marriage is marked by dramatic cruelty.
Sometimes the tragedy is neglect.
Two people who still love each other but have forgotten how to communicate that love.
They pay the bills.
They raise the children.
They attend church.
They fulfill their responsibilities.
But affection has become rare.
Every conversation is about schedules, expenses, responsibilities, or problems.
Nobody asks, “How is your heart?”
Nobody says, “I noticed you've been carrying a lot lately.”
Nobody reaches across the distance because both are waiting for the other to move first.
And perhaps neither person intended to become this way.
Life became exhausting.
Parenthood became overwhelming.
Financial pressure swallowed their attention.
Disappointments accumulated.
Unspoken hurt turned into emotional distance.
Then distance became routine.
And routine began to feel permanent.
But what if permanent is not the word God wants written over your story?
What if this is the moment He is inviting you to stop treating your marriage as something that merely survives and begin treating your spouse as someone worth loving intentionally?
Remember how it began.
There may have been a time when a single message from that person could change your entire day.
You waited for their calls.
You listened to stories you'd already heard because hearing their voice mattered more than the story itself.
You noticed their favorite food.
You remembered the little things.
You prayed about your future.
You imagined growing old together.
And on your wedding day, you made promises before God.
Not promises to feel romantic every morning.
Not promises that neither of you would ever fail.
But promises of covenant faithfulness.
Promises that love would become more than an emotion.
So what happened to the tenderness?
Where did the patience go?
When did the person you once thanked God for become the person you speak to most carelessly?
Perhaps the answer isn't that all love has disappeared.
Perhaps love has been buried beneath pride, exhaustion, resentment, disappointment, or wounds neither of you has learned to address.
And perhaps the next faithful step is not another argument about who started it.
Perhaps it is a moment of humility.
“I know I have hurt you.”
“I have been kinder to other people than I have been to you.”
“I have made you feel alone.”
“I have defended myself when I should have listened.”
“I cannot undo those moments, but I want to repent and begin changing.”
Those words will not instantly heal years of pain.
They are not magic.
And an apology without changed behavior can become another wound.
But genuine repentance has a different sound from self-defense.
Self-defense says, “You made me act this way.”
Repentance says, “I am responsible for how I responded.”
Self-defense says, “Why can't you just move on?”
Repentance says, “I understand why rebuilding trust may take time.”
Self-defense says, “Nobody's perfect.”
Repentance says, “Lord, show me what I need to surrender.”
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than a message we preach.
It becomes the power by which we are called to live.
In Mark 1:15, Jesus proclaims:
“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (KJV)
The Greek word μετανοεῖτε (metanoeîte) means “repent,” calling for a change of mind and direction in response to God's kingdom.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning toward God today.
It is admitting that the old way cannot remain the accepted way.
And the good news is that Jesus does not call sinners to repentance while offering no mercy.
He came to save sinners.
He bore sin at the cross.
He rose again.
He offers forgiveness and new life to those who turn to Him in faith.
That does not mean every marriage will be restored or every wounded relationship will become safe.
But it means no one has to defend sin as though transformation were impossible.
The Gospel gives us a reason to stop hiding.
Because the Savior who knows the truth about us is also the Savior who calls us to come into the light.
Think of the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She stood publicly exposed, surrounded by accusers.
Jesus refused to join their condemnation, and He did not treat her sin as meaningless.
He told her, “Go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV)
Mercy and holiness were not enemies in His response.
That matters for our marriages.
Grace is not permission to keep wounding somebody.
Grace invites us out of the very patterns that have wounded them.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been living under the weight of shame.
You know you've been harsh.
You know you've neglected your spouse.
You know the smile you give the congregation doesn't always match the attitude you bring home.
You love Jesus, but you have been resisting His correction in this part of your life.
Hear this carefully.
Your failure does not need to become your final identity.
But neither should you use God's forgiveness as an excuse to remain unchanged.
Confess what is true.
Seek forgiveness without demanding it.
Listen without immediately correcting your spouse's account of their pain.
Make room for accountability.
If the wounds run deep, seek help from a qualified Christian marriage counselor who understands healthy relationships and safety.
If you have been controlling or abusive, take responsibility and seek specialized intervention; do not pressure your spouse into joint counseling or reconciliation.
Let repentance become visible in consistent actions, not only emotional promises.
And if you're the spouse who has been carrying the hurt, please understand something equally important.
You are not responsible for manufacturing another person's repentance.
You cannot love somebody into taking accountability.
You cannot pray hard enough to make someone else choose honesty.
You can pray.
You can seek wisdom.
You can establish boundaries.
You can ask for support.
You can refuse to repay cruelty with cruelty.
But you do not have to deny reality in order to honor God.
Jesus Christ sees the wounds nobody at church knows about.
And He is not impressed by religious appearances that conceal mistreatment.
One of the most revealing passages about Christian love appears in 1 Corinthians 13:4–5:

“Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil.” (KJV)
The word translated “charity” is ἀγάπη (agápē), love.
And the Greek expression χρηστεύεται (chrēsteúetai) means “is kind” or “acts kindly.”
Love is not merely something we claim to possess.
It expresses itself in how we treat people.
Especially when we're tired.
Especially when we disagree.
Especially when the person standing before us knows our weaknesses.
Especially when there is no audience to applaud our patience.
Imagine what might change if Christian husbands and wives began measuring spiritual maturity not only by how faithfully they attended church, but also by how faithfully they practiced love at home.
Imagine a husband who stops mid-argument and says, “I was speaking harshly. I'm sorry. You deserve to be heard.”
Imagine a wife who recognizes that sarcasm has become her shield and chooses an honest conversation instead.
Imagine two exhausted parents who turn off their phones for fifteen minutes and ask each other how they're really doing.
Imagine a couple who have avoided praying together for months finally sitting side by side, unsure what to say, and beginning with:
“Lord, help us.”
Not an impressive prayer.
Not a performance.
Just two people acknowledging their need for grace.
Sometimes that is where the first honest conversation begins.
Not with a perfect speech.
Not with an instant miracle.
But with humility.
With listening.
With the willingness to stop repeating what has been destroying the relationship.
And if you are single, please don't dismiss this message as something only married people need.
The character you cultivate today is the character you carry into your closest relationships tomorrow.
Kindness is not something you should begin practicing after a wedding.
It is part of following Christ now.
And if you are divorced, widowed, separated, or recovering from a deeply painful marriage, this message is not meant to place shame on your shoulders.
Your life is not spiritually worthless because your marriage ended.
Your identity is not reduced to your relationship status.
The Gospel is larger than marital success.
Jesus is the Savior of sinners, the comforter of the brokenhearted, and the Lord who calls His people to walk in truth.
If your spouse described the way you treat them when nobody is watching, would that description resemble the Jesus you tell other people about?
Not the version of you who shakes hands at church.
Not the version who comments “Amen” under Christian posts.
Not the version who knows the right Bible verses.
The version who comes home exhausted.
The version who responds when challenged.
The version who speaks when frustrated.
The version who handles another person's vulnerability.
Would they say you are gentle?
Would they say you listen?
Would they say your apologies lead to change?
Would they say your faith makes them feel safer, more valued, and more respected?
Or would they quietly admit that the people outside your home receive the kindness they have been longing for?
This question is not about achieving perfection.
Every marriage has difficult moments.
Every Christian still needs grace.
But we must never confuse imperfection with permission to remain unrepentant.
In James 1:22, Scripture says:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.” (KJV)
We can hear sermons about love for years and still resist the daily practice of loving.
We can memorize verses about forgiveness and remain unwilling to acknowledge our own offenses.
We can share inspirational posts while ignoring the person asking us to put down the phone and listen.
And yes, even this article can become another religious message we agree with without allowing it to change us.
Please don't let that happen.
If you recognize yourself in these words, don't simply send the article to your spouse as proof that they are wrong.
Begin by asking what God may be showing you.
If appropriate and safe, go to the person you've hurt.
Not to deliver another sermon.
Not to explain why your behavior was understandable.
But to listen.
To confess.
To make things right where you can.
And to demonstrate change over time.
Because the goal is not to win a biblical argument.
The goal is to become more like Jesus.
You don't have to expose your spouse, reveal private details, or tell the internet something that could put you at risk.
But perhaps you can write:
And if you feel exhausted from fighting for what is right, perhaps your simple response is:
“Pray for me.”
Those few words may become the beginning of an honest conversation with God.
They may also remind another believer reading silently that they are not alone.
And if you have a testimony of how Christ changed the way you love, forgive, communicate, or take responsibility, consider sharing it.
Somebody needs to know that repentance can produce real change.
Not every story ends with reconciliation.
But transformation through Jesus Christ is real, and every testimony of His faithfulness deserves to point back to Him.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to publish another Christian article that makes people emotional for a moment.
Not to gather applause for religious language.
But to keep bringing people back to Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and the transforming Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Because some people have nobody helping them understand the Bible.
Some are struggling in marriages they cannot openly discuss.
Some are trying to rebuild their faith after years of disappointment.
Some are new believers who desperately need sound biblical teaching.
Others have spent decades in church but are only now beginning to recognize the difference between religious activity and genuine discipleship.
They need more than another passing inspirational quote.
They need the Word of God.
They need encouragement rooted in truth.
They need opportunities to grow.
And they need to be reminded, again and again, that Jesus Christ is worthy of following in the ordinary, unseen places of life.
These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, understand the Gospel more clearly, strengthen their faith, and become more intentional disciples of Jesus Christ.
And we want that mission to continue reaching people who may never walk through the doors of our churches.
People scrolling through Facebook at two in the morning because their hearts are heavy.
People questioning whether God can forgive them.
People whose marriages are hurting.
People who need biblical truth presented with both courage and compassion.
But meaningful ministry also requires time, resources, and people willing to stand behind the mission.
Your first responsibility is to give faithfully, wisely, and willingly according to biblical conviction, while caring for the responsibilities God has entrusted to you.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
We want people who genuinely believe in what Gospel Warrior is doing and desire to help that work continue.
These items are simply ways to encourage faith, share meaningful messages, and help sustain the work.
They are not the reason we preach Christ.
Jesus is the reason.
The Gospel is the message.
Changed lives are the prayer.
Not because we need another number on a screen.
But because someone in your circle may be silently living through the very pain we have been discussing.
A husband may need to confront his harshness.
A wife may need to recognize how resentment has shaped her words.
A struggling couple may need encouragement to seek help.
Someone who has been mistreated may need to hear that biblical love never requires them to accept abuse.
And someone who has been hiding behind a Christian reputation may finally need to face the truth about their private character.
Not as a trophy of how much you agree with it.
For the day exhaustion makes gentleness difficult.
For the day you need to remember that Christian maturity is not proven only in public worship.
Sometimes it is revealed in the quiet decisions nobody applauds.
Our prayer is that you will keep opening your Bible, seeking Christ, growing in truth, and allowing His Word to shape the way you live.
Because one day, the applause of strangers will fade.
The compliments from church members will fade.
The public recognition will fade.
But the words you spoke at home may remain in somebody's memory for years.
May those memories increasingly become memories of grace.
Of humility.
Of repentance.
Of tenderness.
Of a husband who learned to listen.
Of a wife who chose honesty over contempt.
Of two imperfect people who stopped pretending and began seeking help.
Of a wounded person who found safety, support, and hope.
Of a home where the name of Jesus was not merely spoken, but honored through the way people treated one another.
And if your marriage is already deeply wounded, don't hear this as a demand to manufacture a beautiful ending.
Hear it as an invitation to bring the truth into the light and take the next faithful step before God.
Some stories need reconciliation.
Some need protection and distance.
Some need professional help.
All need truth.
And every one of us needs the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Perhaps the most unforgettable scandal is not that Christians sometimes fail to love perfectly.
It is that we can become so skilled at looking loving to the world that we forget to love the people closest to us.
But the Gospel calls us to something better.
Not image management.
Not religious performance.
Not pretending.
A life surrendered to Christ.
A heart willing to repent.
A faith that bears fruit.
A love that learns to be kind when nobody is watching.
Because the real test of your Christianity may not be how warmly you greet the stranger after Sunday worship.
It may be how gently you speak to the person waiting for you when you get home.
Don't let the person who knows your love most intimately become the person who has to watch everyone else receive it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF YOU DIED BEFORE YOU REACHED THE WATER… WOULD JESUS STILL SAVE YOU?
paragraphs: IF YOU DIED BEFORE YOU REACHED THE WATER… WOULD JESUS STILL SAVE YOU?

One dying thief never made it to a baptismal pool. Three thousand believers were baptized in a single day. And somewhere between those two stories is a question that has divided Christians, troubled sincere believers, and revealed something extraordinary about the grace of Jesus Christ.
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ.
Your life is over. Every secret is exposed. Every sin you thought you had buried is known. Every good deed you once trusted to make you acceptable before God suddenly seems painfully insufficient.
And then comes the question that has haunted countless believers:
“Lord, I believed in You. I repented. I wanted to follow You. But I died before I could be baptized. Am I lost?”
Now imagine another person standing there.
They were baptized years ago. Their family celebrated. Their church took photographs. Everyone congratulated them.
But afterward, nothing changed.
They continued living without repentance, without surrender, without any real desire to know the Savior whose name had been spoken over them.
They had gone beneath the water.
But had they ever truly come to Christ?
Two people. Two very different stories.
And one question that cannot be answered by religious tradition, emotional preference, or a convenient verse pulled out of context.
Does water baptism save us, or does baptism testify to the salvation we receive through Jesus Christ?
Before you answer, stay with me.

Because Scripture says more about baptism than many Christians realize. And the answer requires us to take seriously both the astonishing generosity of God's grace and the uncompromising call of Jesus to obey Him.
Some people have been terrified into believing that without water, God's mercy cannot reach them.
Others have treated baptism like an optional ceremony that has nothing to do with serious discipleship.
Both deserve a closer examination of the Word of God.
And somewhere in this conversation, you may discover that the question is not merely whether you have been baptized.
It is whether you truly belong to Jesus.
There was a man dying beside Christ who had no opportunity to attend a discipleship class, walk down a church aisle, or enter baptismal waters.
He was a criminal.
Not a misunderstood religious hero. Not a man whose reputation had been unfairly damaged.
A condemned man who admitted that he deserved his punishment.
Luke records his words:
“We indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss.” (Luke 23:41, KJV)
Then, with death approaching and his options disappearing, he turned toward the crucified Jesus.
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” (Luke 23:42, KJV)
Think about that moment.
His hands could not reach for a Bible.
His feet could not carry him toward a river.
His remaining hours could not be spent repairing everything he had destroyed.
He had no religious achievement to present.
Only a guilty past, a dying body, and a desperate appeal to the King hanging beside him.
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43, KJV)
Not after he completed a ceremony.
Not after he proved himself worthy.
Not after someone found a way to remove him from the cross and immerse him in water.
Jesus promised him paradise.
The thief could not come down from the cross to enter the water. But the Savior had already come to the cross to rescue sinners.
That is grace.
But we must handle this account carefully.

The thief's salvation demonstrates that Jesus can save someone who has no opportunity to receive water baptism. It does not prove that Christians who have the opportunity should disregard Christ's command.
The thief was not a model of deliberate disobedience.
He was a dying sinner who turned to the only Savior who could rescue him.
And the Savior did.
Now consider something else.
If salvation depended upon the performance of a religious work, how could the apostle Paul write:
The Greek word translated “grace” is χάρις (charis), meaning grace, favor, or gift.
The word for faith is πίστις (pistis), expressing faith, trust, or reliance.
And the word translated “saved” in Ephesians 2:8 is σεσῳσμένοι (sesōsmenoi), a perfect passive participle from sōzō, meaning to save or rescue.
Paul's language presents salvation as something accomplished for believers, with continuing significance, rather than something they achieve through their own merit.
God is the Savior.
We are the rescued.
And that distinction changes everything.
Yet Paul does not stop at verse 9.
He continues:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” (Ephesians 2:10, KJV)
Do you see the order?
We are not saved by good works.
We are saved for good works.
Obedience does not purchase grace.
Grace produces a new direction of obedience.
This is why we must never turn the free gift of salvation into an excuse for refusing to follow Jesus.
Because the same Savior who saves by grace also commands His disciples to be baptized.
After His resurrection, Jesus declared:
“Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.” (Matthew 28:19, KJV)
The Greek word translated “baptizing” is βαπτίζοντες (baptizontes), from baptizō, a verb commonly associated with dipping, immersing, or washing.
The word itself does not settle every historical disagreement about baptismal mode, but the command is unmistakable.
Baptism belongs to the mission Jesus gave His Church.
It is not a human invention.
It is not a decorative tradition.
It is not something Christians should casually dismiss because they already believe they are saved.
If Jesus is truly your Lord, His commands matter to you.
Not because obeying Him makes Him love you.
But because His love has begun transforming your heart.
And here is where the discussion becomes more challenging.
Some Christians quote Ephesians 2:8–9 and conclude that baptism has no meaningful relationship to salvation.
But other Christians turn to Acts 2:38, Mark 16:16, John 3:5, or 1 Peter 3:21 and conclude that baptism is ordinarily necessary for receiving salvation.
We cannot pretend these passages do not exist.
We cannot build a doctrine by reading only the verses that make us comfortable.
Truth deserves more than that.
On the day of Pentecost, Peter preached Christ crucified and risen.
The crowd was pierced with conviction.
They asked:
“Men and brethren, what shall we do?” (Acts 2:37, KJV)
Peter replied:
“Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.” (Acts 2:38, KJV)
The Greek word for repentance is μετανοήσατε (metanoēsate), an imperative from metanoeō, calling for repentance—a changed mind and turning toward God.
The word translated “for” in “for the remission of sins” is εἰς (eis).
This small Greek preposition has become part of a much larger theological debate.
Some interpret Peter's words as teaching that baptism is the appointed means through which forgiveness is received.
Others understand baptism as the commanded expression of repentance and faith, closely associated with forgiveness without being the independent cause of salvation.
The Greek word alone does not settle the dispute.
What is clear is that Peter did not present baptism as an insignificant afterthought.
He called his hearers to repent and be baptized.
And Acts 2:41 tells us that those who gladly received his word were baptized.
Their response was not, “We believe, so why bother obeying?”
Their response was to embrace the message and act upon it.
Now travel with me to another house recorded in Acts.
A Roman centurion named Cornelius had gathered people to hear Peter proclaim the Gospel.
Peter announced that everyone who believes in Jesus receives forgiveness of sins through His name (Acts 10:43).
Then something remarkable happened.
“While Peter yet spake these words, the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word.” (Acts 10:44, KJV)
The Holy Spirit came upon these Gentile listeners.
And only afterward did Peter ask:
“Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized, which have received the Holy Ghost as well as we?” (Acts 10:47, KJV)
Read that again.
They received the Holy Spirit before their water baptism.
Peter then commanded them to be baptized (Acts 10:48).
For many evangelical and Protestant interpreters, this is powerful evidence that God can grant saving grace before water baptism and that baptism follows as an act of obedience.
Other Christian traditions understand the episode as an extraordinary moment in salvation history, when God visibly demonstrated that Gentiles were fully welcomed into His people.
But both observations matter.
God acted before the water.
And Peter still commanded the water.
Grace was not powerless without the ceremony. And the ceremony was not meaningless because grace had already appeared.
That is a distinction worth remembering.
Now consider the passage that may be the most difficult for those who say baptism is merely an outward symbol.
The apostle Peter writes:
Yes.
The Bible actually says baptism saves.
We should not erase those words.
But we must also read Peter's explanation.
He explicitly distinguishes baptism from the mere removal of physical dirt.
The Greek phrase οὐ σαρκὸς ἀπόθεσις ῥύπου (ou sarkos apothesis rhypou) means “not a removal of dirt from the flesh.”
The word translated “answer” in the KJV is ἐπερώτημα (eperōtēma), which has been understood as an appeal, request, pledge, or response, depending on the interpreter.
This is one reason modern translations and theological traditions differ in explaining the verse.
Some understand Peter to be describing baptism as a sacramental means through which God grants saving grace.
Others understand him to be emphasizing the believer's appeal to God through Christ, expressed in baptism.
But Peter identifies the ultimate saving foundation:
“By the resurrection of Jesus Christ.”
Not the moral perfection of the candidate.
Not the holiness of the person administering the water.
Not the magical power of a physical substance.
The risen Jesus Christ.
This is essential.
Christians may disagree about exactly how baptism participates in salvation, but Christian baptism cannot be understood apart from the death and resurrection of the Savior.
Paul writes:
There is something breathtaking about this picture.
The old life.
The burial.
The resurrection.
The beginning of something new.
Baptism visibly identifies us with the saving work of Jesus Christ.
It announces that our hope is not in the person we used to be, but in the Savior who died and rose again.
And whether one's tradition emphasizes baptism as a means of grace or as the outward testimony of inward faith, no faithful reading of Romans 6 should reduce it to an empty performance.
Baptism points to death and resurrection.
To surrender and new life.
To belonging to Christ.
And it confronts every believer with a deeply personal question.
Have you merely participated in a ceremony?
Or are you walking in the newness of life to which that ceremony points?
Because water can touch your skin while your heart remains far from God.
You can emerge from a baptismal pool and still cling to bitterness.
You can possess a baptism certificate and still refuse repentance.
You can remember the date of your baptism while having no desire to know Jesus today.
And yet the opposite danger is just as real.
You can profess faith in Christ while repeatedly refusing a clear command of Christ.
You can say, “Jesus is my Lord,” while treating His instructions as negotiable.
Neither spiritual pride nor deliberate disobedience belongs at the center of Christian discipleship.
Jesus said:
“If ye love me, keep my commandments.” (John 14:15, KJV)
He did not say, “Keep My commandments so that I will finally become willing to love you.”
His words call those who love Him into obedience.
Love does not make obedience unnecessary.
Love gives obedience its proper meaning.
And perhaps this is where your own story enters.
Maybe you were baptized as a child and have spent years wondering whether it counted.
Maybe you were baptized as an adult, but you know your life afterward did not reflect the repentance you publicly professed.
Maybe you recently surrendered to Jesus and have been afraid to take the next step.
Maybe you belong to a Christian tradition that understands baptism differently from the church down the road, and you have grown tired of believers treating one another like enemies.
Or maybe you have never been baptized at all.
You love Jesus.
You believe He died for your sins.
You believe He rose again.
But somewhere along the way, you began postponing the very thing He commanded.
Not because you cannot obey.
But because you have not decided to.
This is not an invitation to panic.
It is an invitation to take Jesus seriously.
If you have come to faith and have not been baptized, speak with a biblically grounded pastor or church leader about taking that step.

If you were baptized in infancy, understand that historic Christian traditions differ on whether a later believer's baptism is appropriate. Many churches recognize infant baptism as valid, while Baptist and other believer's-baptism traditions teach that baptism should follow personal faith.
Do not pretend these differences are trivial.
But do not allow the controversy to distract you from Christ Himself.
Read Scripture carefully.
Pray humbly.
Seek wise pastoral guidance.
And refuse to let either fear or pride make your decision.
There is another verse we must face.
Mark 16:16 reads:
“He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned.” (KJV)
This passage connects belief, baptism, and salvation.
It also identifies unbelief in its warning of condemnation.

However, responsible interpretation must acknowledge an important textual issue: Mark 16:9–20 is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts, and many modern Bibles identify this longer ending as textually disputed.
Therefore, this verse should not bear the entire weight of a doctrine about baptism.
The wider New Testament must guide our understanding.
And throughout that New Testament, the message of salvation repeatedly centers on Jesus Christ.
Paul tells the Philippian jailer:
“Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house.” (Acts 16:31, KJV)
Then the jailer and his household receive the word, and baptism follows that same night (Acts 16:32–33).
Faith and baptism appear together in the story.
But the saving object of faith is the Lord Jesus Christ.
And when Paul explains the Gospel in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, he places Christ's death for our sins, His burial, and His resurrection at the center.
Not our accomplishments.
Not our religious reputation.
Not our ability to perform perfectly.
Christ.
This is why the question of baptism must never replace the greater question of the Gospel.
Who saves sinners?
Jesus Christ.
What is the foundation of salvation?
His death and resurrection.
How do we receive His saving grace?
The New Testament repeatedly calls us to repentance and faith in Him.
What place does baptism have?
It is commanded by Jesus, intimately connected with conversion and Christian initiation, and understood in different ways across historic Christian traditions.

Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Lutheran, and some other traditions teach that baptism is ordinarily a means through which God grants saving grace, while also recognizing important qualifications about God's mercy and extraordinary circumstances.

Many Baptist, evangelical, and other Protestant traditions teach that justification is received through faith apart from baptism, and that water baptism is the commanded public expression of faith and identification with Christ.
These differences should be represented honestly rather than pretending all Christians have always agreed.
Yet across those differences stands a truth that should humble us all.
No sinner can save himself.
Not with water.
Not with tears.
Not with religious attendance.
Not with charitable giving.
Not with a spotless public reputation.
We need a Savior.
And the Gospel announces that God has given us one.
His name is Jesus.
Perhaps the most heartbreaking thing about religious confusion is that people can spend years debating the water while neglecting the wounded Savior whose blood was shed for them.
They can win arguments and lose tenderness.
They can defend their theological vocabulary while refusing to forgive someone who hurt them.
They can explain Greek verbs but never kneel in repentance.
They can know everything about baptism and still know very little of daily fellowship with Christ.
And that should disturb us.
Because Jesus did not die merely to create people who could argue about Christianity.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
To forgive the guilty.
To rescue the lost.
To make the spiritually dead alive.
To transform people who could never transform themselves.
Consider the woman who thinks her past has disqualified her from grace.
The father who secretly regrets the years he wasted.
The young believer who keeps falling into the same sin and wonders whether repentance is still possible.
The person who looks faithful on Sunday but cries alone at night.
The one who has been baptized and still carries shame.
The one who has not been baptized and fears God has already rejected them.
Hear the Gospel.
Christ does not invite you to save yourself.
He calls you to come to Him.
His sacrifice is sufficient.
His resurrection is real.
His mercy is not a reward for those who have successfully hidden their brokenness.
But grace is also not permission to remain comfortably enslaved to sin.
Jesus receives sinners and transforms them.
Repentance matters.
Faith matters.
Obedience matters.
And baptism matters because the Savior who commands it matters.
The Gospel is neither salvation by human achievement nor a faith that treats Jesus' authority as irrelevant.
It is grace that brings us to Christ and teaches us to follow Him.
Titus 2:11–12 tells us that the grace of God brings salvation and teaches believers to deny ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace does not simply forgive our past.
It begins reshaping our future.
And this brings us back to the criminal on the cross.
He had no opportunity to live decades of Christian discipleship.
No opportunity to join a congregation.
No opportunity to be baptized.
Yet he turned to Jesus, and Jesus promised him paradise.
Now imagine that same man had miraculously survived.
Imagine he had been released.
Imagine he had been given twenty more years to live.
Would it make sense for him to say, “Jesus saved me, so I have no reason to obey Him”?
Of course not.
The mercy that rescued him would give him every reason to follow his Savior.
That imagined future is not recorded in Scripture, and we must not mistake it for biblical history.
But it illustrates the distinction.
Baptism is not something a believer should reject simply because salvation is gracious. And grace is not something we should deny to a repentant believer simply because baptism was impossible.
That is the conclusion many evangelical Christians draw from the combined testimony of Scripture.
Other historic traditions would describe baptism's role in salvation differently, but they too insist that God's saving action is grounded in Christ, not human merit.
The Christian response should be humility before God's Word.
Not careless indifference.
Not manufactured terror.
Not hostility toward every believer who interprets a difficult passage differently.
And certainly not confidence in a ceremony while refusing the Lord to whom it points.
Maybe you need to stop asking whether the water was enough.
Maybe you need to ask whether you have truly surrendered to Jesus.
Maybe you need to stop using grace as an excuse to postpone obedience.
Maybe you need to stop living in fear that God's mercy is too weak to reach someone who dies before baptism is possible.
Maybe you need to return to the simple, devastatingly beautiful center of the Gospel:
“For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.” (Romans 10:13, KJV)
Whosoever.
The ashamed.
The exhausted.
The religiously confused.
The repentant sinner with a past nobody else knows.
The believer who has spent years struggling to understand the Scriptures.
The person who finally realizes that Jesus is not asking them to pretend they are righteous.
He is calling them to trust the One who is.
If you have never truly turned to Christ, do not settle for religious familiarity.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Call upon Jesus.
If you have believed and are postponing baptism, do not let another season pass without seriously considering His command.
And if you have already been baptized, remember what your baptism points toward.
You were not called to live forever as the person you once were.
You were called to follow the crucified and risen Lord.
To forgive because you have been forgiven.
To confess rather than conceal sin.
To resist temptation rather than negotiate with it.
To love when bitterness would be easier.
To remain faithful when the world offers easier paths.
To become, by the grace of God, a living witness that Jesus still transforms people.
This is the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not religious performance.
Not manufactured perfection.
Not a platform built around human personalities.
But the truth that the most scandalous chapters of a human life do not have to be the final chapters when Jesus Christ enters the story.
From the shame of sin to the wonder of forgiveness.
From spiritual death to resurrection life.
From hiding in darkness to walking in truth.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And if this message has reached a place in your heart you have been avoiding, please do not rush past it.
Be honest before God.
Perhaps your prayer today is simply:
“Lord Jesus, I have trusted religious appearances more than I have trusted You. Forgive me. Teach me to obey You from a heart transformed by grace.”
Or perhaps:
“Jesus, I believe You saved me by Your grace. Give me the courage to follow You faithfully, including in baptism.”
Or perhaps:
“Lord, I have lived under fear for too long. Help me understand Your Word and rest in the sufficiency of Your sacrifice.”
You do not need to impress God with eloquent words.
Come to Him sincerely.
And if you are struggling, do not struggle alone.
Because there may be someone reading the comments who has been too afraid to ask these questions in church.
Your thoughtful response might help them begin searching the Scriptures for themselves.
And perhaps you know someone who needs this article today.
A friend who believes they are beyond God's forgiveness.
A family member who has confused baptism with a guarantee of salvation apart from living faith.
A new believer who wants to be baptized but is afraid.
A Christian who has grown careless about obedience.
A person who has walked away from church because religious arguments wounded them.
Not merely to increase the reach of a page, but because the Gospel deserves to be heard beyond the walls of our familiar circles.
We are also building something beyond individual posts.
These resources are intended to help you move beyond a moment of inspiration into a more consistent life of Scripture, prayer, discernment, repentance, and spiritual growth.
Because a powerful article may stir your heart for a moment.
But discipleship is a lifelong journey.
And we want to keep walking that journey with you.
Scripture says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Not the suggestion that money can purchase spiritual blessing.
But a willing decision to help make sound Christian teaching and discipleship resources accessible to more people.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, gifts of encouragement, or practical tools for personal study.
It is the opportunity to participate in a ministry effort that points people back to Jesus Christ.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Share the Gospel.
Use the free resources.
Encourage another believer.
And the saving power of Jesus Christ is never behind a paywall.

We simply believe that when people who have been nourished by biblical teaching voluntarily help sustain that work, more people can be reached, more resources can remain free, and more lives can be encouraged toward faithful discipleship.
Because ultimately, this entire discussion returns to one unforgettable scene.
A dying criminal.
A crucified Savior.
No baptismal pool.
No opportunity to build a religious résumé.
Only a desperate sinner who turned toward Jesus.
And a King who answered him with mercy.
That scene should destroy our pride.
But it should never destroy our willingness to obey.
If you can be baptized, take Christ's command seriously.
If you have been baptized, live in the light of the Gospel it proclaims.

If you are afraid because baptism was impossible for someone you love, remember that the Judge of all the earth is perfectly just and merciful. Entrust that person to Him rather than pretending to know what Scripture has not revealed about their final state.
And if you are still trying to earn what Christ alone can give, hear the invitation of the Gospel again.
Come to Jesus.
Not because you have finally become worthy.
But because He is the worthy Savior of unworthy sinners.
The water matters.
Obedience matters.
Truth matters.
But never forget whose death, whose resurrection, and whose mercy stand at the center of our salvation.
The water can mark the moment you publicly identify with Jesus—but only Jesus can turn a condemned sinner's story into a testimony of redeeming grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD CLOSED EVERY WOMB IN A KING’S HOUSEHOLD—BECAUSE OF ONE WOMAN HE HAD NO RIGHT TO TOUCH.
paragraphs: GOD CLOSED EVERY WOMB IN A KING’S HOUSEHOLD—BECAUSE OF ONE WOMAN HE HAD NO RIGHT TO TOUCH.

One king thought he was innocent. One husband concealed the truth. One woman stood in the middle of a dangerous deception. And before anyone understood what was happening, God had already intervened. The terrifying and beautiful story of Genesis 20 reveals what happens when human failure collides with divine holiness—and why grace is sometimes the only reason judgment does not have the final word.
Imagine waking up one morning and discovering that something is terribly wrong inside your home.
Not because someone has died.
Not because an enemy has invaded.
Not because your wealth has disappeared.
But because life itself has mysteriously stopped moving forward.
The women in your household cannot conceive. Something has happened that no physician can explain, no royal decree can reverse, and no amount of wealth can purchase its way out of.
And somewhere behind the walls of your palace is a woman you never should have taken.
Her name is Sarah.
You do not know the whole truth about her.
But God does.
And heaven is about to interrupt your life.

This is not a fictional tragedy. It is the extraordinary account recorded in Genesis 20, where the Lord intervened in the household of Abimelech, king of Gerar, because Sarah, Abraham's wife, had been taken into the king's household.
The Bible gives us this astonishing conclusion:

“So Abraham prayed unto God: and God healed Abimelech, and his wife, and his maidservants; and they bare children. For the LORD had fast closed up all the wombs of the house of Abimelech, because of Sarah Abraham's wife.” — Genesis 20:17–18, KJV
Read that again.
God had closed the wombs of an entire royal household.
Not because Sarah had committed adultery.
Not because the women of that household were individually identified as guilty.
And not because God had forgotten His mercy.
The judgment was connected to Sarah's presence in Abimelech's household, where she had been taken under a dangerous misunderstanding.
But here is what makes this story even more unsettling.
The king was not the only man who had done something wrong.
The man God had chosen to carry His covenant promise had also failed.
And his failure helped create the crisis.
Abraham, the man of faith, had become a man of fear.
Sarah, the woman through whom God had promised a son, had become vulnerable to another man's claim.
And Abimelech, the king who believed he was acting innocently, was about to discover that ignorance does not make a dangerous situation harmless.
This is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because sometimes the greatest danger in our lives does not begin with open rebellion against God.
Sometimes it begins with fear.
A half-truth.
A decision we justify because we are frightened of what might happen if people know the whole story.
Abraham had traveled into the region of Gerar. There, he told people that Sarah was his sister.
Technically, that statement contained truth.
Later, Abraham explained that Sarah was his half-sister, the daughter of his father but not of his mother (Genesis 20:12).
But Sarah was also his wife.
And that was the truth he concealed.
Why?
Because Abraham feared that the men of that place would kill him to take Sarah.
Think about that.
This was the same Abraham who had received the promises of God.
The same Abraham whom the Lord had called out of his former homeland.
The same Abraham who had been told that nations would come through him.
Yet when fear confronted him, he tried to protect himself through deception.
Have you ever done something similar?
Not necessarily with a lie as dramatic as Abraham's.
