The Bible invites us to understand the world in which these events occurred without assuming that every custom in that world expresses God's ideal.
Now look at the man who captured the city.
His name was Othniel.
The Hebrew text of Joshua 15:17 says:
וַיִּלְכְּדָהּ עָתְנִיאֵל בֶּן־קְנַז
Vayyilkedah Othni'el ben-Qenaz.
"And Othniel son of Kenaz captured it."
The Hebrew verb vayyilkedah comes from the root לָכַד (lakhad), meaning to capture or seize.
This was not merely a man announcing that he was brave.
He acted.
And that distinction matters.
The city was called Kiriath-sepher, also associated with Debir in the biblical account.
Othniel captured it, and Caleb gave him Achsah in marriage, just as he had promised.
But Othniel's story does not end there.
Later, in Judges 3:7–11, Israel falls into disobedience and comes under foreign oppression.
When the people cry out to the Lord, God raises Othniel as a deliverer.
Judges 3:10 declares:
"And the Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and he judged Israel, and went out to war."
Notice the difference.
Joshua records Othniel's military victory.
Judges records the Spirit of the Lord empowering him to deliver Israel.
The later account makes clear that Israel's deliverance was ultimately God's work.
Othniel was the instrument.
God was the Deliverer.
And that distinction leads us to Jesus Christ.
Because Scripture is not ultimately a collection of stories about impressive human beings accomplishing impressive things.
It is the unfolding revelation of God's redemptive purposes, culminating in Jesus.
Othniel was a real deliverer raised up for Israel at a particular moment in history.
But his deliverance was temporary.
Israel would fall into sin again.
Oppression would return.
More judges would be needed.
Human deliverers could rescue Israel from enemies, but they could not permanently remove the sin that continually drew the nation away from God.
That is why we need more than another courageous warrior.
We need a Savior.
Jesus did not merely defeat an earthly enemy.
Through His death and resurrection, He accomplished the redemption sinners could never achieve for themselves.
Colossians 2:13–14 describes God forgiving our trespasses and canceling the record of debt that stood against us.
Hebrews 10:14 speaks of the sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice.
And John 8:36 declares:
"If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed."
Othniel could capture a city.
Jesus can redeem a sinner.
Othniel's victory changed the possession of territory.
Christ's victory changes the eternal destiny of those who belong to Him.
And the glory belongs to Jesus.
But don't leave Achsah behind.
Because after the victory, the narrative shifts.
The warrior who captured the city moves into the background.
And the woman whose marriage had been announced becomes the central figure.
Joshua 15:18–19 records Achsah seeking a field and approaching her father with another request.
The account is also preserved in Judges 1:12–15, with closely corresponding details.
Here is what makes the moment unforgettable.
Achsah has received land.
But the land is in the Negev, a dry southern region where access to water is vital.
Land without adequate water can be difficult to cultivate.
An inheritance may look impressive when its boundaries are described, yet still present serious challenges for the family trying to live on it.
And Achsah recognizes the need.
She approaches Caleb.
And she speaks.
Joshua 15:19 records her words:
"Give me a blessing; for thou hast given me a south land; give me also springs of water."
That sentence deserves more attention than it usually receives.
Because in Hebrew, the opening request is striking.
תְּנָה־לִּי בְרָכָה
Tenah-li verakhah.
"Give me a blessing."
The word berakhah (בְּרָכָה) means blessing, and in this context it introduces a request for a concrete provision.
Achsah is not asking for an abstract feeling.
She is asking for something that will make a real difference to her future.
Water.
And she is specific.
The Hebrew continues:
וְנָתַתָּה לִי גֻּלֹּת מָיִם
Venatattah li gullot mayim.
"Give me springs of water."
She knows what she needs.
She knows whom to approach.
And she asks.
Then comes the father's response.
Joshua 15:19 concludes:
"And he gave her the upper springs and the nether springs."
The Hebrew names them:
גֻּלֹּת עִלִּיּוֹת וְגֻּלֹּת תַּחְתִּיּוֹת
Gullot illiyyot ve-gullot tahtiyyot.
The upper springs and the lower springs.
Not merely a vague promise of help.
Actual water sources.
A tangible answer to a practical need.
And suddenly, the story that began with a father offering his daughter in marriage ends with that daughter making a request and receiving a valuable provision.
That does not erase the difficult questions surrounding the marriage arrangement.
It does not prove that Achsah enjoyed unrestricted freedom in every area of her life.
But it does show her exercising initiative in a significant moment.
She was not merely mentioned as someone's daughter or someone's wife.
She spoke.
She asked.
And her request mattered.
Now I want you to consider something.
How many people are living with what looks like an inheritance but feels like a wilderness?
You have a home, but there is tension inside it.
You have a job, but your soul feels exhausted.
You have a family, but communication has become painfully difficult.
You attend church, but you struggle to pray when nobody is watching.
You know the right Christian words, but you are carrying questions you are afraid to say out loud.
You believe God is good.
Yet some mornings, you wake up feeling spiritually dry.
And the most exhausting part is pretending that everything is fine.
You smile.
You serve.
You encourage everyone else.
You tell people you're blessed.
But when the door closes and the room becomes quiet, there is a prayer you keep swallowing.
"Lord, I need help."
Listen carefully.
Achsah's story is not a promise that every Christian who asks God for something will receive exactly what they requested.
Her conversation with Caleb is a historical account of a daughter asking her father for springs, not a formula guaranteeing prosperity, healing, marriage, or financial increase.
We must not turn a descriptive narrative into a promise God never made.
But her request can remind us of a broader biblical truth that Scripture clearly teaches elsewhere.
God invites His children to bring their needs before Him.
Philippians 4:6 encourages believers to make their requests known to God through prayer and supplication with thanksgiving.
Hebrews 4:16 says:
"Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need."
And Jesus teaches in Matthew 7:11 that our heavenly Father knows how to give good gifts to His children.
Do you see the connection?
Achsah approached her earthly father with a real need.
Through Jesus Christ, believers are invited to approach their heavenly Father with confidence.
Not because the two fathers are identical.
Not because every request will be answered in the same way.
But because Christ has opened the way for sinners to receive mercy and grace from God.
And that is far more astonishing than the springs of Joshua 15.
Because the deepest problem in our lives is not merely that we lack resources.
It is that we are sinners who need reconciliation with a holy God.
We do not simply need better circumstances.
We need forgiveness.
We need a new heart.
We need to be rescued from the power and penalty of sin.
We need Jesus.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Some people have spent years asking God to change their circumstances while resisting the very repentance He is calling them toward.
We want peace, but refuse to release bitterness.
We want restoration, but refuse to admit where we have been wrong.
We want the comfort of God's promises, but avoid the commands that confront our hidden compromises.
We want the blessings of following Jesus without surrendering the throne of our lives to Him.
And that is not discipleship.
Jesus did not come merely to decorate an unchanged life with religious language.
He came to save sinners.
He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
Mark 1:15 records His words:
"Repent ye, and believe the gospel."
Repentance is not simply feeling guilty.
It involves turning from sin toward God.
And genuine faith is not merely agreeing that Jesus exists.
It is trusting in the crucified and risen Christ as Savior and Lord.
That is why the Gospel is such breathtaking news.
God does not demand that we repair our own souls before we may come to Christ.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we finally became impressive.
Not after we successfully concealed every failure.
Not after we convinced the world that our families were perfect.
Not after our private struggles disappeared.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes grace astonishing.
Because the same Savior who receives repentant sinners also calls them into a transformed life.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and live in a godly way.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace is the undeserved favor of God that saves us and teaches us to live differently.
And there is something else in Achsah's story that deserves to be remembered.
She did not merely ask for water in general.
She asked for springs.
A spring is different from a temporary container of water.
A container can be emptied.
A spring is a source.
In its original setting, Achsah's request was about actual water for actual land.
But as we consider the whole witness of Scripture, water also becomes a powerful image in Jesus' teaching.
In John 4, Jesus meets a Samaritan woman at a well.
She arrives looking for ordinary water.
But Jesus speaks to her about something far greater.
John 4:14 records His promise:
"But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life."
The Greek expression includes:
ὕδατος ἁλλομένου εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον
Hydatos hallomenou eis zōēn aiōnion.
"Water springing up into eternal life."
Jesus is not explaining Joshua 15 here, and we should not claim that Achsah's springs were a hidden prophecy about Him.
These are distinct passages with distinct meanings.
But reading them together allows us to appreciate a profound contrast.
Achsah needed physical springs to sustain life on the land she had received.
The Samaritan woman needed something no earthly well could provide.
And Jesus revealed Himself as the giver of living water.
Not a temporary emotional experience.
Not a religious performance.
Not another promise of a trouble-free life.
Eternal life through Him.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years trying to satisfy a spiritual thirst with things that cannot save.
Approval.
Success.
Romantic attention.
Money.
Recognition.
Ministry accomplishments.
The admiration of other Christians.
You have worked so hard to appear full that you have forgotten what it means to admit you are thirsty.
But Jesus sees through the performance.
He knows the secret grief.
He knows the sins you have confessed and the ones you are still trying to excuse.
He knows the wounds that others caused and the damage your own choices have done.
And His invitation is not to keep pretending.
It is to come to Him.
There is a difference between being exposed to condemnation and being convicted unto repentance.
The Gospel exposes our sin so that we may see our need for the Savior.
And for those who are in Christ Jesus, Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus."
That is not a small promise.
That is the difference between living beneath the crushing weight of guilt and standing in the grace of God.
And now I want to return to the daughter whose story began with an uncomfortable announcement.
Achsah could easily have disappeared from the narrative as a detail in the account of Othniel's victory.
Instead, Scripture records her words.
"Give me a blessing."
"Give me also springs of water."
And Caleb gave her the springs.
It is a brief exchange.
But it reminds us not to overlook people whose voices are easy to miss.
Not every significant act of courage happens on a battlefield.
Sometimes courage is found in an honest conversation.
Sometimes it is a daughter speaking up about a genuine need.
Sometimes it is a husband admitting that his pride has been destroying his marriage.
Sometimes it is a wife finally telling the truth about her exhaustion.
Sometimes it is a young believer confessing a hidden sin and seeking accountability.
Sometimes it is someone walking back into church after years away, trembling because they do not know whether they will be welcomed.
Sometimes it is a person quietly praying:
"Jesus, I cannot keep living this way. Please forgive me. Change me."
And sometimes that prayer marks the beginning of a life that will never be the same.
Not because the person suddenly becomes strong enough to save themselves.
But because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
Maybe you have been thinking about someone while reading this.
Someone who has grown distant from God.
Someone who looks successful but is spiritually exhausted.
Someone whose marriage is suffering.
Someone who is ashamed of what they have done.
Someone who believes their scandal is the final chapter of their life.
Not to impress anyone.
Not simply to increase the reach of another Christian page.
But because the truth of Scripture deserves to be heard, and someone in your circle may need to encounter the Gospel today.
And if this article has uncovered something in your own heart, you do not have to pretend.
You do not need to reveal private details or publicly confess something that should be addressed with a trusted pastor, mature believer, or the person you have wronged.
But do not underestimate the encouragement that can come when believers pray for one another.
James 5:16 reminds us of the importance of confession and prayer within the community of faith.
Someone may be wondering whether a life marked by failure can truly change.
Your testimony can point them to the Savior who changed yours.

Not because a saved post possesses spiritual power, but because you may want to return to these Scriptures when your faith feels weak or when you need to remember that God's grace is sufficient for His people.
Invite your family, your friends, believers who are struggling, people who have drifted from church, and even those who are still exploring Christianity.
There is room here for honest questions.
There is room for repentance.
There is room to open the Bible together and seek the truth.
But there is no substitute for Christ Himself.
And there is something important I want to share with those who believe this ministry is worth sustaining.
Gospel Warrior is working to make biblical teaching, encouragement, and discipleship resources accessible to more people.
These resources are intended to help readers move beyond a moment of inspiration into a more consistent life of studying Scripture, praying, learning sound doctrine, and following Christ.
Because one emotional article may stir the heart.
But discipleship is a lifelong journey.
And meaningful ministry requires people who are willing to help carry the work forward.
Scripture teaches that giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from coercion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
You do not have to give money to earn God's favor.
Jesus Christ has already accomplished what no financial contribution could ever purchase.
You can still help.
Recommend the free library to someone who wants to understand the Bible.
Pray that this ministry will remain faithful to Scripture, accountable in its teaching, and focused on the glory of God rather than the praise of people.
Because the mission has never been to build a platform for its own sake.
It is to point people to the One whose name is above every name.
Jesus Christ.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who touched the unclean.
The One who confronted hypocrisy.
The One who laid down His life for His sheep.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One who still calls people out of darkness into His marvelous light.
A father offered his daughter in marriage to the man who could capture a city.
The warrior captured the city.
The marriage took place.
But the daughter recognized something that still mattered.
The land needed water.
So she asked for springs.
And she received them.
That is the historical account.
But the greater question for us is not whether we can claim Achsah's springs as a promise of material blessing.
The greater question is whether we recognize our own need before God.
Have you been trying to live on yesterday's spiritual enthusiasm while neglecting prayer and Scripture?
Have you mistaken religious activity for genuine fellowship with Christ?
Have you been carrying guilt that you need to bring to the Savior in repentance?
Have you become so consumed with what God might give you that you have forgotten the immeasurable gift of knowing Him?
You may have many things and still be spiritually thirsty.
You may have lost many things and yet possess the greatest treasure of all if you belong to Jesus Christ.
Because the Gospel does not promise that every earthly story will end the way we hoped.
It promises something greater.
That sinners can be forgiven.
That the guilty can be justified through faith in Christ.
That those who were far from God can be brought near through His blood.
That the dead in sin can be made alive with Christ.
And that those who belong to Him have an inheritance that cannot perish.
First Peter 1:3–4 describes a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ and an inheritance that is incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading.
That inheritance is not a dry piece of land waiting for a better irrigation system.
It is the eternal hope secured by the risen Savior.
So come to Christ.
Not with a polished performance.
Not with a list of achievements.
Not with the illusion that you have earned His acceptance.
Come in repentance and faith.
Come trusting the grace of God revealed in the cross and resurrection.
Come ready to surrender what you have been defending.
And when you discover that you still need help tomorrow, come to Him again in prayer.
For the Christian life is not sustained by yesterday's emotional experience.
It is lived through ongoing dependence upon the Lord who saves, sanctifies, and keeps His people.
Achsah asked for springs because she needed water to live on the land.
And the Gospel calls us to recognize something infinitely greater.
We need Christ Himself.
Not merely His gifts.
Not merely relief from our circumstances.
Not merely a better version of the life we already wanted.
We need the Savior who forgives our sins and makes us new.
That is the message worth sharing.
That is the truth worth returning to.
That is the Gospel worth supporting, proclaiming, and living.
And if there is one thing I hope you remember long after you have forgotten the names of the ancient city and its conqueror, it is this:
You may have spent your whole life trying to conquer the city, only to discover that your deepest thirst could never be satisfied by anything you won—only by the Savior who gave Himself for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY SOLD WHAT THEY OWNED… BECAUSE SOMEONE ELSE WAS HUNGRY. WHAT DID THE FIRST CHRISTIANS UNDERSTAND THAT WE HAVE FORGOTTEN?
paragraphs: THEY SOLD WHAT THEY OWNED… BECAUSE SOMEONE ELSE WAS HUNGRY. WHAT DID THE FIRST CHRISTIANS UNDERSTAND THAT WE HAVE FORGOTTEN?

They weren't trying to become poor. They had encountered a Savior who made them rich in something money could never buy. And what happened next shook Jerusalem, challenged the meaning of ownership, and revealed a kind of Christianity our generation desperately needs to rediscover.
Scripture: Acts 2:44–45; Acts 4:32–35
Imagine walking into church this Sunday.
You take your usual seat. You sing the familiar songs. You listen to the sermon. You shake a few hands, smile at a few people, and prepare to return to the life waiting outside.
Then someone stands up.
Not to announce another program.
Not to ask for applause.
Not to tell everyone how generous they are.
Just a man with tears in his eyes.

He says a family in the congregation hasn't eaten properly in three days. Their children are hungry. Their father has been searching for work. Their mother has been quietly praying that somebody, somewhere, might notice.
The room becomes silent.
And then something happens.
One believer offers groceries.
Another offers employment.
Someone quietly pays the family's overdue rent.
Another gives money they had been saving for something they wanted.
Nobody asks for recognition.
Nobody reaches for a camera.
Nobody demands that the family prove they deserve compassion.
They simply respond.
Because somewhere between hearing about Jesus and following Jesus, they have learned that another person's suffering is no longer somebody else's problem.
Now imagine an entire community living that way.
Not for a weekend.
Not during a fundraising campaign.
Not because a charismatic leader pressured them into giving.
But because Jesus Christ had so completely transformed their hearts that their possessions no longer possessed them.
That is not a fictional description of what Christianity could become.
It is a glimpse of what happened when the Gospel first began spreading through Jerusalem.
And the most uncomfortable part of this story is not that those believers gave so much.
It is that they seemed to understand something about Jesus that many of us have spent years learning how to avoid.
Acts 2:44–45 records:
“And all that believed were together, and had all things common; And sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all men, as every man had need.” (KJV)
Read that again.
Not as a slogan.
Not as a political argument.
Not as a command to immediately empty your bank account.
Read it as a window into hearts that had been changed by the risen Christ.
These were not people who had simply discovered a new philosophy of economics.
They had encountered the Gospel.
Only weeks earlier, Jerusalem had witnessed the crucifixion of Jesus of Nazareth.
The Messiah had been rejected.
The innocent One had been condemned.
The Son of God had been nailed to a Roman cross.
And yet the grave could not hold Him.
Peter proclaimed that God had raised Jesus from the dead and made Him both Lord and Christ (Acts 2:22–36).
When the crowd heard this, Scripture says they were “pricked in their heart” (Acts 2:37).
The Greek expression is κατενύγησαν τὴν καρδίαν (katenygēsan tēn kardian).
It communicates the piercing conviction that overtook their hearts.
They realized the gravity of what had happened.
The One they had rejected was the very Savior they needed.
And when they asked what they should do, Peter answered:
“Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins...” (Acts 2:38, KJV)
That day, about three thousand people received his word and were baptized.
Then something extraordinary followed.
They devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayers.
And they began sharing what they owned.
Do you see the order?
First came the proclamation of Christ.
Then conviction.
Then repentance and faith.
Then a new life together.
Their generosity was not the price of their salvation. It was evidence of the Savior who had changed them.
This distinction matters more than we might realize.
Because when we misunderstand Acts, we can turn a beautiful testimony of grace into a weapon of guilt.
We can make people feel that God will love them only if they give enough.
We can make struggling families feel spiritually inferior because they have little to contribute.
We can turn generosity into a transaction, as though heaven were selling blessings to the highest bidder.
But that is not the Gospel.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
And verse 10 teaches that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace comes first.
Transformation follows.
The first Christians did not share their possessions to persuade Jesus to accept them.
They shared because, through Jesus, they had already been welcomed into the family of God.
And once you begin seeing other believers as family, the question changes.
It is no longer merely, “How much of my money do I have to give?”
It becomes, “How can I watch my brother suffer when God has placed something in my hands that could help him?”
That is a much more personal question.
And perhaps a much more frightening one.
Because it brings the Gospel out of the sanctuary and into our wallets, our calendars, our kitchens, and our daily decisions.
It asks whether the Jesus we worship on Sunday is truly Lord over what we protect on Monday.
But before anyone uses these passages to demand that Christians surrender everything they own, we need to look carefully at what the Bible actually says.
Acts 4:32 records:
“And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.” (KJV)
In the Greek text, we encounter the remarkable expression καρδία καὶ ψυχὴ μία (kardia kai psychē mia).
Literally, “one heart and one soul.”
This is the heartbeat of the passage.
Their unity was not simply an organizational achievement.
It was a shared spiritual identity centered on Jesus Christ.
They belonged to Him.
And because they belonged to Him, they recognized a responsibility toward one another.
Notice something else.
The passage says that no one regarded their possessions as exclusively their own.
It does not say that every believer had permanently lost the legal right to own property.
In fact, Acts 5:4 helps clarify this.
When Peter confronted Ananias about his deception, he asked whether the property had remained his before it was sold and whether the proceeds had been under his authority afterward.
The sin of Ananias and Sapphira was not that they failed to donate every coin.
It was that they lied about their gift and attempted to deceive the Holy Spirit.
That distinction is essential.
The early church's generosity was not a system of compulsory confiscation.
It was an extraordinary expression of voluntary, Spirit-shaped love.
The Greek word κοινά (koina), translated “common” in Acts 2:44, comes from a word family associated with what is shared or held in common.
It does not, by itself, establish a detailed economic system.
The context shows believers making their resources available to meet real needs.
And Acts 2:45 says the distribution happened according to need.
Not according to popularity.
Not according to influence.
Not according to who could return the favor.
According to need.
Imagine how different our churches would look if we took that seriously.
Imagine the widow who would no longer have to choose between medicine and food.
The single mother who would no longer feel invisible.
The elderly believer whose loneliness would finally be noticed.
The young father ashamed to admit that his paycheck cannot cover the bills.
The new Christian who has lost relationships because of his faith and desperately needs a community that will stand beside him.
Not every need can be solved by money.
Sometimes the greatest gift is a meal.
Sometimes it is time.
Sometimes it is a ride to the hospital.
Sometimes it is helping someone find work.
Sometimes it is sitting beside a grieving person when everybody else has gone home.
And sometimes, yes, it is opening your wallet when every selfish instinct tells you to close it.
Because Christian generosity is not merely about giving away things.
It is about refusing to let things become more important than people.
And there is another detail in Acts 4 that deserves our attention.
Verse 33 says:
“And with great power gave the apostles witness of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus: and great grace was upon them all.” (KJV)
Immediately afterward, the passage describes how those with lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds to the apostles for distribution.
That placement is not accidental to the story Luke is telling.
The resurrection of Jesus stands at the center.
Their compassion was not disconnected from their proclamation.
The church was bearing witness to a living Savior, and its shared life was demonstrating the transforming power of His grace.
The Greek text describes the grace upon them as χάρις τε μεγάλη (charis te megalē) — “great grace.”
Great grace.
Not merely great wealth.
Not merely great enthusiasm.
Not merely great organization.
Great grace.
The same grace that forgives sinners was teaching forgiven sinners to care for one another.
And Acts 4:34 makes a stunning observation:
“Neither was there any among them that lacked...” (KJV)
This does not mean poverty disappeared from every Christian community forever.
The New Testament later records continuing material needs, collections for poor believers, and practical challenges in caring for widows.
Even in Jerusalem, Acts 6 describes a complaint because some widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution.
The early church was not a flawless paradise.
It was a redeemed community still learning how to love faithfully.
But Acts 4 gives us a breathtaking picture of what happened when believers responded to one another's needs with sacrificial generosity.
For that moment in the community Luke describes, their sharing meant that no one among them was left in need.
And I wonder what would happen if we stopped admiring that verse from a distance and began asking what it might require of us.
Not because every Christian must sell a house.
Not because every believer has the same resources.
Not because giving guarantees financial prosperity.
But because the Gospel should change how we view what God has entrusted to us.
There is a reason Jesus warned:
“Ye cannot serve God and mammon.” (Matthew 6:24, KJV)
Mammon refers to wealth or riches.
Jesus was exposing the danger of treating money as a master.
Money can be useful.
Money can provide for a family.
Money can fund good work.
Money can help feed the hungry, distribute Scripture, and support Gospel ministry.
But money makes a terrible god.
It promises security while quietly demanding our trust.
It promises freedom while teaching us to fear losing what we have.
And sometimes the most revealing question is not how much money we possess.
It is how much power money possesses over us.
Perhaps you know that struggle.
You want to be generous.
You really do.
But you remember what it felt like to have nothing.
You remember unpaid bills.
You remember borrowing money.
You remember the embarrassment of telling someone you could not afford something your family needed.
So now that you have a little stability, you hold tightly to it.
Not always because you are greedy.
Sometimes because you are afraid.
And Scripture does not require us to pretend those fears are imaginary.
Providing responsibly for one's household matters. First Timothy 5:8 speaks seriously about family responsibility.
Second Corinthians 8:12 teaches that a gift is accepted according to what a person has, not according to what the person does not have.
Paul also explains that giving should not be arranged so others are relieved while the giver is crushed by hardship (2 Corinthians 8:13).
Christian generosity is not reckless neglect of responsibility.
It is faithful stewardship shaped by love.
And that means the believer with very little is not spiritually worthless.
The widow who gave two small coins was seen by Christ, not because her gift impressed the wealthy, but because He knew the heart and sacrifice behind it (Mark 12:41–44).
God does not measure devotion by the size of a public receipt.
He sees what people cannot.
He sees the sacrifice nobody applauds.
He sees the groceries quietly delivered.
He sees the money sent to a struggling relative.
He sees the hours spent comforting someone who has lost hope.
He sees the believer who has almost nothing but still offers kindness, prayer, and encouragement.
And He sees the wealthy believer who opens his hands rather than allowing riches to harden his heart.
The question is not whether everyone can give the same amount.
The question is whether our lives are becoming more like Jesus.
Because the deepest answer to why the first Christians shared their possessions is found beyond Jerusalem.
It is found at Calvary.
Before there was a church selling property to feed the needy, there was a Savior giving Himself to rescue sinners.
Before believers opened their hands to one another, Jesus stretched out His hands upon a cross.
Before Christians shared earthly resources, Christ had already given something infinitely greater.
His life.
Second Corinthians 8:9 declares:
“For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.” (KJV)
Paul is not promising that every Christian will become financially wealthy.
He is pointing to the astonishing grace of Christ, who humbled Himself for our salvation.
Jesus did not save us by making a comfortable donation from a safe distance.
He entered our broken world.
He bore rejection.
He endured suffering.
He gave Himself for sinners who could never purchase their own redemption.
And at the cross, the greatest scandal of human sin met the greatest revelation of divine grace.
The innocent suffered for the guilty.
The Holy One bore the judgment sinners deserved.
And through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and new life became available to all who turn to Him in faith.
That is not merely a beautiful phrase.
It is the story of redemption.
And when that Gospel takes hold of a human heart, generosity begins to make sense in a completely different way.
We do not give because we believe we can outgive God.
We give because we have already received a gift we could never repay.
We do not love others to earn a place at Christ's table.
We love because Christ has welcomed us by grace.
We support it because God graciously allows His people to participate in making His truth known.
That brings us to a question that cannot remain trapped in the first century.
If the first Christians used what they had to strengthen the church and meet needs, what should that look like for believers living in a digital world?
We may not all have land to sell.
We may never stand in the Jerusalem congregation described in Acts.
But we do have opportunities.
Some have financial resources.
Some have time.
Some have skills.
Some have the ability to teach, encourage, pray, write, translate, design, organize, or share the Gospel with people they may never meet face-to-face.
And in a world where a single message can cross oceans within seconds, even a simple act of sharing biblical truth can become part of someone's journey toward Christ.
Think about the person scrolling through Facebook tonight.
They may look completely fine.
Their profile picture is smiling.
Their recent posts seem normal.
Their friends think everything is going well.
But behind the screen, they are exhausted.
Their marriage is breaking.
Their faith is growing cold.
Their heart is full of guilt.
They have been wondering whether God would still receive them after everything they have done.
And then an article appears.
Not an empty motivational speech.
Not a promise that following Jesus will make life painless.
But the Gospel.
The truth that Christ died for sinners.
The truth that repentance is possible.
The truth that forgiveness is offered through Him.
The truth that grace does not leave us unchanged.
Perhaps they read one paragraph.
Then another.
And for the first time in months, they open their Bible.
They pray.
They reach out to another believer.
They begin returning to the Lord.
Only God can change a heart.
But we can faithfully place biblical truth where people may encounter it.
And that is part of why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to replace pastors, fellowship, or personal Bible study.
Not to sell access to God's favor.
But to help put Christ-centered Scripture, encouragement, discipleship, and Gospel teaching within reach of people who need them.
Free resources matter.
Because the person who cannot afford a book still needs sound biblical teaching.
The new believer with limited resources still deserves opportunities to grow.
The struggling Christian who needs encouragement should not be made to feel that spiritual nourishment is reserved for those who can pay.
That is why freely accessible Christian resources are worth protecting and expanding.
But meaningful ministry also requires practical support.
Writing, preparing, maintaining, distributing, and expanding resources involves real work and real expenses.
And just as the early church participated in meeting practical needs, believers today can voluntarily help sustain ministries that faithfully proclaim Christ.
Not because your name must appear on a supporters' list for God to notice you.
And certainly not because a monthly payment purchases forgiveness, blessing, or salvation.
But because a voluntary, prayerful monthly commitment can be a meaningful expression of Christian generosity and partnership in Gospel work.
It should not be presented as a mandatory biblical tithe, nor as an automatic replacement for the responsibilities of supporting one's local church, household, and people in need.
The New Testament calls us to generous, willing giving.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
Not grudgingly.
Not under compulsion.
But willingly.
That is the spirit in which this invitation is offered.
It can be one practical way to glorify God through the faithful stewardship of what He has entrusted to you.
Those products may serve as reminders of biblical truth, opportunities to begin meaningful conversations, or gifts of encouragement for others.
The heart is the mission.
More biblical nourishment.
More accessible Christian resources.
More opportunities to encourage weary believers.
More Scripture-centered content that points beyond human personalities and back to Jesus Christ.
You are still welcome here.
You can still benefit from the free resources.
You can still pray for this work.
You can still share the Gospel.
You can still be a faithful follower of Jesus.
Your worth in Christ has never depended on your ability to fund a ministry.
In fact, there is another form of support that costs nothing but a little time and intentionality.
Not merely to increase a number on a screen.
Somebody may be holding tightly to bitterness, fear, possessions, or the belief that faith is only about attending services.
Somebody may have been hurt by religious fundraising and needs to hear the difference between grace-filled generosity and spiritual manipulation.
Somebody may be hungry for a Christianity that looks more like Jesus.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to pressure them.
But to encourage them.
Sometimes the people who give the most of themselves receive the least recognition.
A sincere word of gratitude can remind them that their love has not gone unnoticed.
And if this article has stirred something in your own heart, I want to invite you into a more personal conversation.
Or, if you are walking through a season of financial difficulty and need the prayers of fellow believers, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You do not have to explain private circumstances publicly.
You do not have to perform your pain for anyone.
But you do not have to believe you are alone, either.
Someone else may need the encouragement of knowing that Christian love can still be real.
Invite your family, your friends, a struggling believer, someone returning to faith, or even someone who is still searching for answers to follow along.
But please do not miss the most important invitation of all.
The invitation to surrender your life to Jesus Christ.
Because you can donate to every ministry you know and still need forgiveness.
You can give away possessions and still carry a heart full of pride.
You can share a thousand Christian posts and still refuse to repent of the sin you are hiding.
You can wear a shirt with a Bible verse and still live far from the Lord.
Christian generosity matters deeply.
But generosity cannot substitute for regeneration.
The first Christians were not merely people who shared their belongings.
They were people who had responded to the Gospel of the crucified and risen Christ.
Their outward actions flowed from an inward transformation.
And that is what we need today.
Not simply more religious activity.
Not simply more financial contributions.
Not simply more Christian content circulating online.
We need hearts made alive by the grace of God.
We need repentance that is more than temporary regret.
We need faith that clings to Jesus rather than trusting in our own goodness.
We need believers who tell the truth, care for the vulnerable, provide responsibly for their families, support faithful Gospel work, and love one another when nobody is watching.
We need churches where the suffering are noticed.
Where generosity is not exploited.
Where giving is not a competition.
Where the poor are not humiliated.
Where the wealthy are not automatically condemned but are called to faithful stewardship.
Where ministry leaders are accountable.
Where the Gospel is proclaimed without a price tag.
Where Christ receives the glory.
Because that is what makes the account in Acts so unforgettable.
The believers did not simply discover a better way to distribute possessions.
They discovered that, in Jesus, they belonged to one another.
The Gospel had given them a new family.
And in that family, another person's burden mattered.
That is why Barnabas appears at the end of Acts 4.
Joseph, whom the apostles called Barnabas, sold a field and brought the money to the apostles (Acts 4:36–37).
His name was associated with encouragement.
And his action matched the spirit of that name.
He did not merely speak encouragement.
He embodied it.
He used something he possessed to strengthen others.
What a beautiful legacy.
Not simply that he owned a field.
But that he was willing to use it for the good of God's people.
One day, the things we are so afraid to lose will no longer belong to us.
Our bank balances will pass into other hands.
Our homes will be occupied by others.
Our possessions will be sold, donated, discarded, or forgotten.
Even the things we treasure most in this world are temporary.
But the love of Christ is not temporary.
And the fruit of a life surrendered to Him reaches beyond what money can measure.
So perhaps the question we should carry away from Acts 2 and Acts 4 is not, “Why did those Christians sell their possessions?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
“What had Jesus done in their hearts that made loving people more important than holding tightly to things?”
And then comes the question that brings the whole story painfully close to home.
What is Jesus asking me to surrender?
Maybe it is money.
Maybe it is selfishness.
Maybe it is indifference.
Maybe it is the need to be recognized every time you do something good.
Maybe it is the fear that if you open your hands, God will somehow forget your needs.
Or maybe, before any conversation about giving, you need to surrender the sin you have been defending and receive the forgiveness Christ offers.
Whatever the answer, do not confuse the invitation of grace with a demand to purchase God's love.
Jesus has already paid the price of redemption through His own blood.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
And then, as His grace changes you, learn to live with open hands.
Because the church does not become more like Jesus simply by collecting more money.
It becomes more like Jesus when the people who belong to Him increasingly reflect His truth, holiness, mercy, and sacrificial love.
The first Christians shared their possessions because the risen Savior had changed the meaning of everything they possessed.
And perhaps the greatest miracle was not that property was sold.
Perhaps it was that hearts once ruled by self-interest were learning to love like Christ.
That is the Christianity worth recovering.
That is the generosity worth practicing.
That is the Gospel worth sharing.
And that is the Savior worth following.
They opened their hands because Jesus had opened the way to the Father—and the grace that rescued their souls was now reaching through their lives to rescue others from being forgotten.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD CALLED IT WICKEDNESS: THE FORBIDDEN FAMILY RELATIONSHIP THAT LEVITICUS EXPOSED
paragraphs: GOD CALLED IT WICKEDNESS: THE FORBIDDEN FAMILY RELATIONSHIP THAT LEVITICUS EXPOSED

One man. One family. One boundary God refused to let anyone cross. But behind this disturbing command is a truth about sexual sin, broken trust, hidden shame, and the mercy of Jesus Christ that every generation desperately needs to hear.
What if the sin you keep calling a private matter is quietly destroying the people who trusted you most?
There are sins that happen in public.

And there are sins that happen behind locked doors, inside homes where everyone smiles at the dinner table, where family photographs still hang on the walls, and where the people being betrayed have no idea that something sacred has already been violated.
Sometimes the most devastating betrayal doesn't come from an enemy.
It comes from someone who was supposed to protect the family.
Someone who knew the boundaries.
Someone who understood the trust.
Someone who crossed the line anyway.
And thousands of years ago, God spoke into that darkness with a command so direct that it still makes modern readers uncomfortable.
A man was forbidden from having a sexual relationship with a woman and her daughter. The prohibition also extended to her granddaughter.
Listen carefully to the words of Leviticus 18:17 in the King James Version:

“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter, neither shalt thou take her son's daughter, or her daughter's daughter, to uncover her nakedness; for they are her near kinswomen: it is wickedness.”
Read that again.
Not because the language is sensational.
But because God was protecting something that human desire has repeatedly tried to destroy.
The sanctity of family relationships.
The trust between generations.
The dignity of people who must never become objects of another person's sexual appetite.
And the boundaries that protect a household from becoming a place of betrayal.
Here is something important that many people miss when discussing this passage.

Leviticus 18:17 does not specifically name a wife's mother. It forbids sexual relations with a woman and her daughter or granddaughter. The direct prohibition involving a man's mother-in-law appears in Leviticus 20:14 and Deuteronomy 27:23.
That distinction matters.
Because if we are going to speak in God's name, we must handle God's Word faithfully.
We do not need to exaggerate Scripture to make it powerful.
Its truth is already powerful enough.
And when we examine the original Hebrew, the message becomes even more sobering.
The expression translated “uncover the nakedness” comes from the Hebrew phrase לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה — legalot ervah.
In this legal context, it is a Hebrew expression referring to prohibited sexual relations.
It is not simply about accidentally seeing someone unclothed.
The passage concerns sexual conduct and forbidden family relationships.
And near the end of the verse appears another striking Hebrew expression:
זִמָּה הִוא — zimmah hi.
“It is wickedness.”
The Hebrew noun zimmah can describe a morally reprehensible act or scheme. Here, it condemns the sexual violation of the family boundary described in the passage.
God was not merely issuing an arbitrary social preference.
He was identifying behavior that corrupts the relationships a family depends upon.
And the context makes this even clearer.
In Leviticus 18:6, God establishes the broader principle:
“None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their nakedness: I am the LORD.”
Notice how the command ends.
“I am the LORD.”
Not, “This is merely how your ancestors lived.”
Not, “This is only a matter of personal taste.”
Not, “Follow whatever your desires tell you.”
God grounds His instruction in His own authority.
The One who created human beings also has the right to establish moral boundaries for human relationships.
And this is where the passage becomes painfully relevant.
Because we live in a world where people often confuse desire with permission.
Where attraction is treated as justification.
Where secrecy is mistaken for safety.
Where someone can tell themselves that an action is harmless simply because nobody has discovered it.
But secrecy does not make betrayal innocent.
And the absence of witnesses does not mean the absence of consequences.
Imagine a family gathering.
The children are laughing.
The food is being prepared.
A husband sits beside his wife.
Her mother is nearby, helping with the meal.
There is nothing inappropriate about the scene. It is ordinary family life.
But imagine that the husband begins entertaining sexual thoughts about his wife's mother.
He knows the relationship.
He knows the trust.
He knows what it would mean if he pursued those desires.
Yet instead of turning away, he begins feeding the fantasy.
A conversation becomes flirtation.
Flirtation becomes secrecy.
Secrecy becomes rationalization.
And eventually, he faces a decision that could devastate his marriage and fracture an entire family.
This is an illustration, not a story recorded in Leviticus.
But the moral danger is real.
And it reveals why God's boundaries are not enemies of love.
They are meant to protect the relationships that love has a responsibility to honor.
A mother-in-law is not another romantic possibility for a married man.
A daughter is not a sexual alternative to her mother.
A granddaughter is not someone whose family connection can be ignored when desire appears.
These relationships carry obligations that sexual exploitation and betrayal would violate.
And Scripture refuses to treat those obligations as disposable.
Now consider something even more disturbing.
The damage from such wrongdoing would rarely stop with the two people involved.
Think about the wife.
The daughter.
The grandchildren.
The family members who suddenly discover that relationships they believed were safe have been violated.
The people who must live with questions they never wanted to ask.
Was any of it real?
How long was this happening?
Who knew?
Who lied?
Can I trust anyone again?
Sexual betrayal can leave consequences that last long after the secret is exposed.
And when coercion, manipulation, or abuse is involved, the harm can be even more severe.
God's command is not permission to shame those who have been harmed.
The responsibility for abuse belongs to the person who commits it.
A victim is not guilty because someone violated a boundary against them.
And genuine repentance never requires a victim to remain in danger, surrender appropriate boundaries, or conceal wrongdoing.
That is worth saying clearly because some people have used religious language to protect reputations while ignoring wounded people.
But biblical holiness is not a costume worn to hide corruption.
It is a call to walk in truth before God.
And this is where the story becomes more than an ancient prohibition.
Because the question is no longer simply whether a man should pursue his wife's mother.
The question becomes:
What are you allowing into your heart that you already know has no rightful place there?
Maybe you have never faced the particular temptation described in Leviticus.
But perhaps there is a conversation you keep deleting.
A relationship you keep explaining away.
A private attachment that has become emotionally intimate in ways you would never openly acknowledge.
A boundary you have been moving little by little because crossing it all at once would have frightened your conscience.
Or perhaps your struggle has nothing to do with sexual temptation.
Maybe it is dishonesty.
Bitterness.
Envy.
A hidden addiction.
A habit you have defended for years.
Something that has slowly taken control of your decisions while you continue telling everyone that you are fine.
The specific sin may be different.
But the spiritual danger is familiar.
We begin by making room for what we should resist.
Then we become accustomed to what once troubled us.
And eventually, we risk calling normal what God has called us to turn away from.
The Bible warns us about this progression.
James 1:14–15 says:
“But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
Notice the movement.
Desire.
Enticement.
Sin.
Death.
James does not teach that every unwanted temptation makes someone guilty of having committed the act.
Temptation and chosen sin are not identical.
But he does warn that when sinful desire is embraced and allowed to govern our actions, it can produce devastating consequences.
And Jesus takes this warning deeper.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He teaches:

“Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
Jesus was not saying that an involuntary thought is the same as physically committing adultery.
He was exposing the moral seriousness of deliberately cultivating lust.
He was showing that obedience is not merely about avoiding an outward act while privately nurturing the desire to commit it.
God cares about what happens inside us.
The thoughts we entertain.
The intentions we protect.
The choices we make when nobody else can see.
And that truth can be uncomfortable.
Because a person may appear faithful while inwardly becoming consumed by unfaithfulness.
A person may know the language of holiness while repeatedly negotiating with temptation.
A person may attend church, sing worship songs, and quote Bible verses while refusing to confront a hidden pattern of sin.
But here is where we must be careful.
The purpose of exposing sin is not to convince people that they are beyond redemption.
It is to bring what is hidden into the light so that repentance, truth, and transformation become possible.
And no one demonstrates that purpose more clearly than Jesus Christ.
Think about the woman brought before Him in John 8.
She was publicly accused of adultery.
The crowd stood ready to condemn her.
Her shame was no longer private.
Her situation had become a public spectacle.
And Jesus refused to participate in the crowd's hypocrisy.
He confronted the accusers.
Then, when they had gone, He spoke to the woman.
John 8:11 records His words:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
Do not miss either half of that statement.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
Mercy.
“Go, and sin no more.”
A call to repentance.
Jesus did not celebrate adultery.
He did not pretend sin was harmless.
He did not tell the woman that holiness no longer mattered.
But neither did He join a crowd eager to destroy her.
His response revealed a mercy that refused to abandon truth.
And a truth that did not extinguish mercy.
That is the Gospel we desperately need.
Not a message that excuses every desire.
Not a message that humiliates every sinner.
But the good news that Jesus Christ came to save sinners and transform lives.
Consider what Paul wrote to the Corinthians.
In 1 Corinthians 6:9–10, he warns that those who persist in unrighteousness must not presume upon the kingdom of God.
His list includes sexual immorality and other serious sins.
But then comes one of the most beautiful sentences in the New Testament.
1 Corinthians 6:11:
“And such were some of you.”
Pause there.
Were.
Not because their past had never happened.
Not because their actions had no consequences.
Not because everyone they harmed had automatically recovered.
But because their former sins no longer defined their standing before God in Christ.
Paul continues:
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.”
Look at those words.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
The Greek word translated “washed” is ἀπελούσασθε — apelousasthe.
It points to washing or cleansing.
The word translated “sanctified” is ἡγιάσθητε — hēgiasthēte.
It speaks of being made holy or set apart.
And “justified” translates ἐδικαιώθητε — edikaiōthēte.
It refers to being declared righteous or put into right standing.
Paul is describing what God has done for believers through Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit.
He is not claiming that conversion erases every earthly consequence.
He is proclaiming that sin does not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that.
Because you have been carrying something.
Maybe a choice you made years ago.
Maybe a relationship that crossed a boundary.
Maybe a betrayal you deeply regret.
Maybe a past you have tried to bury because you are terrified of what people would think if they knew.
You have learned how to smile.
How to function.
How to keep going.
But sometimes, when everything becomes quiet, the memories return.
And you wonder whether God could still receive someone like you.
Listen carefully.
Jesus Christ did not come because humanity had managed to keep itself clean. He came because sinners needed a Savior.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had repaired every mistake.
Not after we had earned forgiveness.
Not after we had finally become impressive enough to deserve divine attention.
Christ died for sinners.
And that includes people whose sins have left them deeply ashamed.
But grace is not permission to keep harming others.
Grace calls us out of darkness.
If you have betrayed someone, repentance means more than feeling guilty.
It means turning away from the wrongdoing.
Ending the sinful conduct.
Refusing to keep manipulating the truth.
Accepting accountability.
And, where possible and appropriate, taking responsible steps to address the harm without demanding immediate forgiveness or restored trust.
If abuse or criminal conduct has occurred, protecting those at risk and involving appropriate authorities must not be replaced by private religious assurances.
Forgiveness does not eliminate the need for justice.
And reconciliation cannot be forced.
This is not a contradiction of grace.
It is part of taking sin and the dignity of other people seriously.
Now return to Leviticus.
Why would God speak so directly about relationships that many people would rather never discuss?
Because the Lord was teaching His people that sexuality was not a lawless territory where appetite alone determined what was right.
In Leviticus 18:3–5, Israel is instructed not to imitate the practices of Egypt or Canaan, but to walk according to God's statutes.
The chapter establishes boundaries around sexual relationships as part of Israel's covenant life.
Christians must read these commands in their historical and covenantal context, rather than treating every feature of Israel's ancient civil law as directly applicable today.
Yet the New Testament continues to condemn sexual immorality and calls believers to honor marriage, holiness, and the dignity of others.
Hebrews 13:4 declares:
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.”
And 1 Thessalonians 4:3 says:
“For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication.”
The biblical vision is not that human sexuality is inherently dirty.
It is that sexuality matters.
It has moral significance.
And its misuse can wound people in profoundly personal ways.
God's boundaries are not an expression of contempt for human beings.
They reflect His concern for how human beings treat one another.
But perhaps the most challenging question is not whether we agree with the prohibition.
Perhaps it is whether we are willing to let Scripture correct us when our desires disagree with it.
Because everyone enjoys the comforting passages.
The promises of peace.
The assurance of forgiveness.
The beautiful declarations of God's love.
And rightly so.
Those truths are precious.
But what happens when the Bible confronts a relationship we do not want to surrender?
A behavior we do not want to stop?
A secret we do not want exposed?
Will we still listen?
Will we still trust the God whose mercy we gladly receive?
Or will we begin editing His Word to protect what we want?
Jesus said in John 14:15:
“If ye love me, keep my commandments.”
That is not a declaration that obedience purchases salvation.
Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not a reward earned through moral perfection.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that clear.
But genuine faith does not regard obedience as meaningless.
Ephesians 2:10 goes on to say that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace saves us.
And the same grace begins reshaping how we live.
Sometimes that transformation is painful.
Because surrender means letting go of things we have grown attached to.
It means admitting that a desire can be powerful and still be wrong.
It means recognizing that love is not always demonstrated by saying yes.
Sometimes love says no.
No to betrayal.
No to exploitation.
No to the fantasy that another person's dignity is less important than our gratification.
No to the lie that hidden wrongdoing becomes acceptable when it feels emotionally satisfying.
And yes to truth.
Yes to repentance.
Yes to accountability.
Yes to the freedom of living without having to build an entire life around protecting a secret.
There is a particular kind of exhaustion that comes from hiding.
The constant calculations.
The fear of being discovered.
The effort of maintaining appearances.
The way a guilty conscience can turn ordinary conversations into moments of anxiety.
And there is another kind of pain carried by those who have been betrayed.
The confusion.
The grief.
The anger.
The struggle to trust again.
Some people reading this are not the ones who crossed the boundary.
They are the ones who suffered because somebody else did.
If that is you, hear this clearly.
You are not responsible for another person's decision to violate your trust.
You do not have to minimize the harm to prove that you are a Christian.
You do not have to pretend you are healed when you are still hurting.
And you do not have to allow someone continued access to your life simply because they claim to have repented.
God's grace is real.
So is the need for safety, wisdom, support, and time.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.”
The Lord sees the brokenhearted.
He does not despise their pain.
And the Gospel offers hope to both the repentant sinner and the wounded person, without confusing their responsibilities or minimizing what happened.
This is why the cross of Jesus Christ stands at the center of everything we teach at Gospel Warrior.
At Calvary, sin was not dismissed as a small inconvenience.
Its seriousness was revealed in the suffering and death of the Savior.
Yet God's love was also revealed there.
Jesus gave Himself for sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
His resurrection declares that death does not have the final victory.
And through Him, forgiveness and new life are offered to those who repent and believe.
That is not merely an inspirational message.
It is the heart of the Christian Gospel.
And it changes how we read a disturbing passage like Leviticus 18:17.
We no longer read it merely to be shocked by the sins people are capable of committing.
We read it with reverence for the God who establishes moral boundaries.
With compassion for those harmed when those boundaries are violated.
With humility about our own vulnerability to temptation.
And with gratitude that Jesus Christ is able to save and transform sinners.
Perhaps today is the day you stop defending something that has been damaging your soul.
Perhaps it is time to end a secret relationship.
To seek wise pastoral counsel.
To speak truthfully.
To pursue professional help where needed.
To confess to God what you have spent years trying to justify.
Or perhaps today is the day you stop blaming yourself for someone else's betrayal and begin seeking the care and support you deserve.
Whatever your circumstances, do not confuse conviction with hopelessness.
The Holy Spirit's work is not to lead us into endless despair.
He directs us toward Christ, truth, repentance, and the life that follows.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is no need to pretend before a God who already knows the truth.
And there is no need to believe that the worst chapter of your life must be the last.
From scandal to grace is not the story of sin becoming harmless. It is the story of Jesus Christ being powerful enough to redeem sinners without ever calling evil good.
And if these words have confronted something in your heart, do not rush past that moment.
Pray.
Examine yourself before the Lord.
You might simply write, “Lord, teach me to honor Your boundaries.”
You do not need to disclose private sexual details, name anyone who harmed you, or reveal something that would place you or another person at risk.
Sometimes the most meaningful confession begins quietly before God.
And sometimes a simple request for prayer reminds someone else that they are not alone in their struggle.
There is another reason I hope you will not keep this article to yourself.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who may be wrestling with a secret temptation.
Someone whose marriage is under strain.
Someone who has been betrayed.
Someone who believes their past has made them unreachable by grace.
You may not know who they are.
And you do not need to know.
If a particular friend comes to mind, consider tagging them privately and thoughtfully, without implying that they are guilty of the sins discussed here.
Not because following a page makes someone a Christian.
But because regular exposure to Scripture, faithful teaching, encouragement, and Christ-centered discipleship can help people keep returning to the truth.
Not because every sentence will be easy to read.
But because some truths become especially important when temptation returns, when conscience grows quiet, or when someone you love needs encouragement to choose what is right.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, grow in your faith, or return to Jesus during a difficult season, I want to invite you into something deeper.

Our mission is to continue sharing the Gospel, teaching biblical truth, encouraging repentance, helping wounded people discover hope in Christ, and providing discipleship resources to those who are hungry for God's Word.
We want those resources to continue reaching people.
And we want to keep expanding the work.
Scripture teaches us in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
Not because financial support proves the strength of your faith.
But because generosity, when freely offered for a worthy purpose, can help sustain work that points people toward Jesus Christ.
Those products can be meaningful reminders of faith and opportunities to encourage others, but the heart of this invitation is not merchandise.
It is the Gospel.
It is Scripture.
It is the hope that someone who feels lost today may encounter the truth of Jesus Christ tomorrow.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And no one has to pay to come to Jesus.
We simply want to keep making Christ known.
Because at the end of the day, this article is not really about an ancient prohibition that makes modern people uncomfortable.
It is about the God who sees what happens behind closed doors.
The God who cares when families are betrayed.
The God who commands holiness because people matter.
The God who calls sinners to repentance.
And the God who sent His Son to redeem those who could never save themselves.
Maybe you began reading because the title shocked you.
Maybe you stayed because the Scripture challenged you.
Maybe something in these words reminded you of a wound, a regret, or a decision you have been avoiding.
But I pray you leave remembering something far greater than the scandal.
Jesus Christ is still calling people out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
He is still forgiving repentant sinners.
Still teaching His people to walk in holiness.
Still bringing hope to wounded hearts.
Still giving grace to those who come to Him in faith.
And still proving that the darkest truth about a person's past does not have to be the final truth about their future.
Not what someone else needs to repent of.
Not whose life this article reminds you of.
Not which person you think should read it.
Ask yourself:
Lord Jesus, what are You calling me to surrender, and will I trust You enough to obey?
Because the most dangerous secret is not always the one other people might discover.
Sometimes it is the one we keep defending even after God's Word has exposed it.
And the most beautiful turning point is not when we finally convince the world that we are good.
It is when we stop hiding from the Savior who already knows the truth and still calls us to come to Him.
The door you have been afraid to open may be the very place where repentance begins and the healing grace of Jesus Christ meets you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU LOVE JESUS… SO WHY DO YOU KEEP GOING BACK TO MASTURBATION?
paragraphs: YOU LOVE JESUS… SO WHY DO YOU KEEP GOING BACK TO MASTURBATION?

You prayed. You repented. You promised God it would be the last time. But when the loneliness returned and nobody was watching, you found yourself fighting the same battle again. What if the deepest problem isn't simply what you're doing with your body—but what your heart has been desperately searching for?
There is a prayer some Christians have whispered so many times that they almost feel ashamed to pray it again.
"Lord, I'm sorry."
Three words.
Sometimes spoken through tears. Sometimes whispered into a pillow. Sometimes said while staring at a phone screen that has just gone dark.
You told yourself you wouldn't do it again.
Not after that sermon.
Not after that worship service when you felt God's presence so deeply.
Not after the last time you fell to your knees and promised Jesus that things would be different.
But here you are.
Again.
And perhaps the most painful part isn't even what happened.
It's what happens afterward.
That quiet, crushing thought:
How can I say I love Jesus when I keep returning to something I've asked Him to help me leave behind?
You open your Bible, but guilt follows you into the pages.
You try to pray, but shame interrupts every sentence.
You see other Christians worshiping with their hands lifted, and you wonder whether you're the only one hiding a battle like this.
You begin to question everything.
Your sincerity.
Your salvation.
Your love for God.
Maybe even whether Jesus is tired of hearing your apologies.
But before you surrender to another night of self-condemnation, there is something you need to understand.
Jesus already knows the part of your story you're afraid to tell Him. And He is not asking you to pretend it isn't there.
He is calling you into the light.
Not because darkness makes you too disgusting to love.
But because darkness is a terrible place to heal.
And the Gospel is not the story of perfect people proving they deserve God.
It is the story of a holy Savior coming to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Stay with me, because this conversation is not going to end where you think it will.
We need to talk about desire.
We need to talk about loneliness.
We need to talk about what the Bible actually says—and what it does not say.
And we need to talk about the difference between someone who is struggling against sin and someone who has stopped caring about it.
Because confusing those two things has left too many Christians drowning in shame instead of growing in holiness.
Let's begin with a truth that may surprise you.
The Bible never explicitly mentions masturbation by name.
Read that carefully.

Scripture speaks extensively about sexual holiness, lust, self-control, marriage, the body, temptation, and the intentions of the heart. But it does not contain a verse that directly names and universally condemns every instance of masturbation.
That distinction matters.
Not because we should search for loopholes in God's Word.
But because we must never claim that God explicitly said something when Scripture does not explicitly say it.

Some Christians conclude that masturbation is inherently sinful because of its relationship to sexual desire outside marriage. Others distinguish the physical act from the presence of pornography, lust, compulsive behavior, or other sinful motivations.
Faithful Christians disagree about how to apply biblical principles to this specific question.
What Scripture does make clear is that sexual desire must never become an excuse to exploit another person, indulge lust, surrender self-control, or allow anything to master us.
Jesus said in Matthew 5:28:
"But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." (KJV)
The Greek expression translated "to lust after her" includes the phrase πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn).

The verb epithymeō means to desire or long for something. The word itself is not automatically sinful in every biblical context. Here, Jesus is addressing deliberately cultivated sexual desire directed toward someone in a way that violates the faithfulness God requires.
He is confronting the heart behind the outward action.
And that changes the conversation.
Because the question isn't merely, "Did I do something physical?"

It is also, "What was I feeding in my heart? What was I imagining? Was I using another person's body as an object for my gratification? Was I running toward something I knew was drawing me away from obedience to Christ?"
And sometimes, underneath those questions, there is another one.
"What was I trying not to feel?"
Because not every recurring sexual struggle begins with a person waking up determined to rebel against God.
Sometimes it begins with exhaustion.
Sometimes rejection.
Sometimes boredom.
Sometimes anxiety.
Sometimes the aching silence of being alone when everybody else seems to have someone.
You come home after a difficult day.
Nobody asks how you're doing.
Nobody notices the weight you're carrying.
Your mind is restless, your body is tired, and your heart wants relief.
You reach for your phone.
One image becomes another.
One thought becomes a fantasy.
One moment of curiosity becomes a familiar pattern.
And for a little while, the loneliness feels quieter.
But when the moment passes, the pain you were trying to escape may still be waiting.
Only now, shame has joined it.

This doesn't mean every instance of masturbation is caused by emotional pain. Sexual desire is also a normal part of being human. But for some people, repeated sexual behavior becomes a learned way of managing stress, loneliness, or uncomfortable emotions.
And if that is happening to you, simply promising to "try harder" may never address the whole problem.
You may be fighting the behavior while ignoring the wounds and habits that keep feeding it.
You may be asking God to remove the temptation while refusing to confront the environment in which it grows.
You may be praying for purity while leaving pornography one click away every night.
And perhaps you have mistaken intense guilt for genuine transformation.
Because feeling terrible after something is not the same as learning to live differently.
The apostle Paul wrote in 1 Corinthians 6:12:
"All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any." (KJV)
The final Greek phrase is οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος (ouk egō exousiasthēsomai hypo tinos).
In context, Paul is challenging the misuse of freedom and refusing to be dominated by anything.
He is not specifically naming masturbation in this verse.
But the principle reaches deeply into every area of Christian life.
Something can promise you relief while gradually gaining power over your choices.
When you keep returning to a behavior you no longer feel free to refuse, the question of mastery becomes painfully relevant.
Are you choosing freely?
Or are you being pulled by a pattern that increasingly controls your attention, your time, your relationships, and your conscience?
That is a question worth bringing before God without excuses—and without exaggeration.
Because there is another danger here.
Some Christians have been taught to treat every sexual feeling as evidence of spiritual corruption.
They experience attraction and immediately feel dirty.
They experience bodily arousal and assume they have already sinned.
They wake from an involuntary sexual dream and spend the morning begging forgiveness for something they never consciously chose.
But temptation is not identical to sin.
Involuntary bodily responses are not automatically acts of moral rebellion.
And experiencing sexual desire does not make you unworthy of Christ's love.
Hebrews 4:15 says of Jesus:
"For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin." (KJV)
Jesus was truly tempted, yet without sin.

We must not assume this means He experienced every specific modern circumstance or temptation in precisely the same way we do. The verse's central assurance is that our Savior understands human weakness and temptation while remaining sinless.
And the next verse is extraordinary.
"Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need." (Hebrews 4:16, KJV)
Notice what Scripture does not say.
Come boldly when you've been pure for thirty days.
Come boldly when you haven't struggled for six months.
Come boldly after you've finally become someone God can tolerate.
No.
It says to come to the throne of grace in your time of need.
The very moment you feel most desperate for mercy is not the moment to run away from the One who gives it.
And this is where the enemy of your soul would love to confuse you.
Not every feeling of guilt is the same.
There is a kind of sorrow that awakens the conscience and leads a person toward repentance.
And there is a kind of despair that convinces a person repentance is pointless.
Paul wrote:
