"For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death." (2 Corinthians 7:10, KJV)
Godly sorrow does not celebrate sin.
It does not make excuses.
It recognizes wrong, turns toward God, and seeks a changed life.
But hopeless shame says something very different.
"You've done this too many times."
"Your prayers are meaningless."
"Real Christians don't struggle like you."
"God must be finished with you."
Those accusations can sound religious.
They can even sound like humility.
But they are not the Gospel.
Because the Gospel does not teach that Christ's mercy expires when a believer becomes difficult to sanctify.
Nor does it teach that grace gives us permission to remain comfortably enslaved.
Romans 6:1–2 confronts that misunderstanding directly:
"Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. How shall we, that are dead to sin, live any longer therein?" (KJV)
Grace is neither permission to surrender nor a reward for flawless performance.
Grace brings us to Christ, and the Spirit teaches us to walk in newness of life.
Perhaps you need to hear that distinction more than anything else today.
You do not overcome sin so that Jesus will finally love you. You learn to fight sin because, in Christ, you have already encountered a love that calls you into something better.
Remember Peter.
He loved Jesus.
He made bold promises.
He believed he would remain faithful even when others fell away.
Then came the courtyard.
The questioning.
The fear.
The denial.
Three times, Peter denied knowing the very Lord he had sworn to follow.
And when the rooster crowed, the reality of what he had done crushed him.
Luke 22:62 records:
"And Peter went out, and wept bitterly." (KJV)
Imagine those tears.
This was not a stranger who had never known Jesus.
This was a disciple who had walked beside Him.
He had heard the teachings.
Seen the miracles.
Confessed that Jesus was the Christ.
And still, under pressure, he fell.
Does that sound painfully familiar?
You know the truth.
You believe the Gospel.
You genuinely want to honor Jesus.
And yet you have discovered that loving Christ does not make you immune to weakness.
But Peter's story did not end in the courtyard.
After the resurrection, Jesus met him again.
In John 21, the risen Lord questioned Peter about his love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Jesus did not pretend Peter's denial never happened.
He restored him and called him forward.
Peter's failure was real.
But it did not get the final word.
The same Jesus who knew Peter would deny Him also knew Peter's story would continue beyond the denial.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to stop defining their entire Christian life by the last thing they regret.
Your struggle matters.
Your choices matter.
Repentance matters.
But your worst moment is not the full measure of what Christ can accomplish in a surrendered life.
And no, this does not mean you can repeat a harmful pattern indefinitely without concern.
It means your next step should be toward Jesus, not away from Him.
So what does that look like when the temptation comes back?
It may begin with something surprisingly ordinary.
Honesty.
Not the dramatic promise you make when guilt is overwhelming.
Not another emotional declaration that you'll never be tempted again.
Just honesty.
"Lord, I'm lonely."
"Lord, I'm anxious."
"Lord, I want to look at something I know will feed lust."
"Lord, I don't even know whether I'm seeking pleasure, comfort, escape, or control."
"Help me understand what is happening in my heart."
Then take a real step.

If pornography is part of your pattern, remove the easy access that keeps pulling you back. Use content restrictions where helpful. Stop following accounts that deliberately feed your fantasies. Keep your phone away from the bed if late-night scrolling repeatedly leads you somewhere you do not want to go.
If loneliness is the trigger, do not treat isolation as a spiritual achievement.
Build friendships.
Participate in your church community.
Speak with a mature believer who can respond with wisdom and confidentiality rather than humiliation.
If stress is the trigger, develop healthier ways to respond before you reach the breaking point.
Sleep.
Exercise.
Pray.
Take a walk.
Talk to someone.
Learn to sit with difficult feelings without immediately demanding an escape from them.

And if your behavior feels compulsive, causes significant distress, or continues despite serious consequences, speaking with a qualified mental health professional can be a wise step. Seeking appropriate help is not a betrayal of faith.
Sometimes spiritual care and psychological care can work together.
You do not need to choose between taking Scripture seriously and understanding how habits, emotions, and the body function.
And please understand this:
A single lapse does not erase every step of progress.
If you fall, do not turn one failure into a week of surrender because you have convinced yourself everything is ruined.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Receive God's mercy.
Learn what led to the moment.
Make a wiser decision next time.
Keep walking.
The Christian life is not a performance in which one mistake means the curtain falls forever.
It is a life of repentance, faith, obedience, and growth under the grace of Jesus Christ.
Galatians 5:16 says:
"This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh." (KJV)
The Greek expression Πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε (Pneumati peripateite) means "walk by the Spirit."
The language communicates an ongoing manner of life.
Not merely one emotional victory.
Not a temporary burst of religious enthusiasm.
A walk.
Daily dependence.
Daily decisions.
Daily surrender.
And sometimes, after a difficult day, the most meaningful act of obedience may be turning off the phone, refusing to feed a fantasy, and going to sleep.
Nobody applauds.
Nobody sees.
There is no dramatic music.
But God sees the heart that is learning to choose differently.
And when you fail, that same God calls you to repent rather than hide.
This is why Romans 8:1 is so precious:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus." (KJV)

The earliest Greek textual witnesses support the shorter wording reflected in many modern translations, ending the verse with "in Christ Jesus." The longer phrase appearing in the KJV is also found later in Romans 8:4.
The opening Greek words are Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα (Ouden ara nyn katakrima).
The meaning is astonishing.
There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
This does not mean every behavior is acceptable.
It means that the believer's standing before God rests upon Christ's saving work, not upon an imaginary record of perfect self-control.
Conviction still has a place.
Discipline still has a place.
Repentance still has a place.
But condemnation is not the identity of the person who belongs to Christ.
And perhaps that is the deepest battle for someone reading this tonight.
Not simply the battle against lust.
But the battle to believe that Jesus is still worthy of your trust after you've disappointed yourself.
You may know how to confess your sins.
But do you know how to receive forgiveness?
You may know how to identify your weakness.
But do you know how to depend on God's strength?
You may know how to hate the pattern that has trapped you.
But do you know how to live without hating yourself?
Because self-hatred is not holiness.
And shame is not a substitute for repentance.
Jesus does not invite you to despise the person He came to redeem.
He invites you to deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Him.
There is a difference.
One path says, "I am worthless, so why bother?"
The other says, "Christ is worthy, so by His grace I will keep following."
One leads deeper into hiding.
The other leads toward the light.
And the light is where confession becomes possible.
The light is where habits can be confronted.
The light is where genuine accountability can begin.
The light is where someone finally says, "I need help," without believing that those words make them a failure.
Maybe your story has been hidden for years.
Maybe you've served in church while privately battling pornography.
Maybe you've led worship while wrestling with desires you never knew how to discuss.
Maybe you're married and ashamed that certain patterns have continued.
Maybe you're single and exhausted by the assumption that faithful Christians never experience sexual frustration.
Maybe you've been taught that one sexual failure permanently damages your worth.
If so, hear this clearly:
Your worth as a human being is not measured by your sexual history.
You bear the dignity of someone made in God's image.
And the Christian call to holiness is not an invitation to erase that dignity.
It is an invitation to honor the God who gave it.
For some readers, repentance may mean turning away from pornography, deliberate lust, deception, or behavior that has become controlling.
For others, it may mean examining assumptions they've accepted without careful biblical study and learning to distinguish genuine conviction from excessive religious fear.
In either case, do not let a slogan replace an honest conscience informed by Scripture.
Seek truth.
Seek wisdom.
Seek Christ.
And do not confuse the absence of temptation with the presence of spiritual maturity.
Sometimes growth means temptation becomes less frequent.
Sometimes it means recognizing temptation earlier.
Sometimes it means refusing to turn a difficult moment into a destructive pattern.
Sometimes it means finally asking for help.
And sometimes it means learning that God has not abandoned you simply because sanctification is taking longer than you expected.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
Notice where the faithfulness is located.
Not in the perfection of our promises.
In Him.
He is faithful.
He is just.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible without despair.
So tonight, if you find yourself standing in the same place again, don't make another reckless promise merely to silence your guilt.
Come to Jesus with the truth.
Tell Him what happened.
Tell Him what you wanted.
Tell Him what you feared.
Tell Him what you are still struggling to understand.
And ask Him not merely to change what you do when nobody is watching, but to transform what you love, what you pursue, and where you seek comfort.
Pray something like this:

"Lord Jesus, You know me completely. You know my desires, my habits, my loneliness, and the things I hide from others. Forgive what is sinful in me. Expose the excuses I have made. Heal the wounds I have ignored. Teach me to honor You with my body, my thoughts, and my choices. Give me wisdom to recognize temptation, courage to seek help, and humility to keep growing. When I fall, lead me to repentance instead of despair. When I am tempted, remind me that obedience is possible through Your grace. And above everything else, teach me to love You more than the temporary comforts that compete for my heart. Amen."
And if that prayer is painfully close to your own story, I want you to know something.
You do not have to tell strangers the intimate details of your sexual life to prove that you are serious about repentance.
But you also do not have to carry your struggle in total silence.
And if you've experienced the mercy of Christ in a place where you once believed there was no hope, consider sharing a testimony that could encourage someone else.
Your honesty may remind another believer that they are not the only person seeking grace.
Please remember that a public comment section is not a confidential counseling space. Share only what you are comfortable making public.
And if someone comes to mind while you're reading this—someone who seems strong in public but may be silently struggling—consider sharing this article with them privately.
Not as an accusation.
Not as a way to embarrass them.
But as a reminder that the door to repentance and grace is still open.
You never know whose prayer might be answered through a message of biblical truth delivered at the right moment.
Because on that night, you may need to remember that the answer to sin is not to run farther from Christ.
It is to return to Him in repentance and faith.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community of people pretending to have conquered every weakness.
But to keep pointing wounded, struggling, growing people back to the truth of Scripture and the finished work of Jesus Christ.
There are people who need more than another passing inspirational quote.
They need the Word of God.
They need sound teaching.
They need encouragement that does not flatter their sin and conviction that does not crush their hope.
They need to hear about Jesus.
For those who choose to give from a heart of worship, it can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership in Gospel ministry.
But let's be biblically clear.
Christ's grace cannot be purchased, and no believer should be pressured into paying to demonstrate faithfulness.
Scripture says in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." (KJV)
Giving should be willing, thoughtful, and joyful—not driven by fear or guilt.
Your responsibilities to your family, your local church, and those in need remain important.
These are simply practical ways of expressing our appreciation. The real purpose remains unchanged: helping people grow deeper in their knowledge and love of Jesus Christ.
Because biblical nourishment should never be reduced to a financial transaction.
Our mission is to point people toward Christ, encourage spiritual maturity, and make the truth of God's Word accessible to those who hunger for it.
Pray for the people reading.
And most importantly, take the truth of Scripture seriously in your own life.
Because this article was never supposed to be merely about masturbation.
It was about the hidden battles that make people question whether God could still love them.
It was about the loneliness that can turn into temptation.
The temptation that can turn into habit.
The habit that can turn into secrecy.
And the secrecy that can make a believer feel farther from Jesus than they have ever felt before.
But the cross tells a different story.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die for an imaginary humanity that had never experienced moral failure.
He died for sinners.
Real sinners.
People with histories.
People with regrets.
People who needed forgiveness they could never earn.
And on the third day, He rose again.
Not merely to make people feel better about their brokenness.
But to bring salvation, reconciliation with God, and new life to all who repent and believe in Him.
That is the Gospel.
Not that sin is harmless.
Not that repentance is optional.
Not that grace makes obedience irrelevant.
But that Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior, and no repentant sinner needs to pretend to be whole before coming to Him.
So if you love Jesus and you're still fighting this battle, don't let the struggle become your identity.
Do not build your theology on your worst night.
Do not mistake repeated temptation for proof that God has abandoned you.
And do not use grace as a reason to stop pursuing holiness.
Bring your whole life to Christ.
Your desires.
Your habits.
Your loneliness.
Your fears.
Your body.
Your future.
Your unanswered questions.
All of it.
And when tomorrow comes, walk with Him again.
Not because you have finally become strong enough to live without grace.
But because you have finally begun to understand how desperately you need it.
Your last fall does not have to be the final sentence of your story—because the risen Jesus is still calling you out of hiding and into the light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JUDAS LEFT AN EMPTY SEAT… BUT WHY DID GOD ALLOW MATTHIAS TO TAKE HIS PLACE?
paragraphs: JUDAS LEFT AN EMPTY SEAT… BUT WHY DID GOD ALLOW MATTHIAS TO TAKE HIS PLACE?

One disciple betrayed Jesus. Another was chosen in the shadow of that betrayal. But hidden in Acts 1:15–26 is a truth about failure, faithfulness, God's sovereignty, and the grace that can rewrite a story everyone thought was finished.
There was an empty place among the twelve.
And everybody knew why.
It wasn't empty because someone had died faithfully serving Jesus. It wasn't empty because an apostle had been sent to another country to preach the Gospel.
It was empty because someone who had walked with Jesus had betrayed Him.
Judas Iscariot.
A man who had heard the same teachings. Witnessed the same miracles. Sat near the same Savior. Shared the same ministry. And yet, for thirty pieces of silver, handed Jesus over to His enemies.
Imagine being one of the remaining eleven disciples.
Every time you looked around, you remembered who was missing.
Every memory of the Last Supper carried the weight of betrayal.
Every recollection of Jesus washing their feet reminded them that even Judas had been there.
And now, after the crucifixion, after the resurrection, after forty days of the risen Christ teaching them about the kingdom of God, Jesus had ascended into heaven.
The disciples were waiting in Jerusalem for the promised Holy Spirit.
But there was still an empty place.
And that raises a question most Christians have probably never considered deeply enough.
Why did the disciples believe they needed to replace Judas? Why Matthias? And was this truly God's will—or merely a human attempt to repair what betrayal had destroyed?
The answer is more profound than a simple leadership appointment.
Because before Matthias was chosen, something had to be confronted.
The terrible reality that someone could be incredibly close to the ministry of Jesus and still have a heart that was far from Him.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes uncomfortably personal.
You can know the songs.
You can attend the services.
You can quote the verses.
You can even serve in ministry.
But none of those things, by themselves, can substitute for genuine repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
Judas is a sobering reminder that proximity to holy things is not the same as surrender to the Holy One.
Yet Acts 1 is not merely a warning about Judas.
It is also a testimony that human betrayal cannot overthrow the purposes of God.
And that is where the story begins to change.
In Acts 1:15, Peter stood among approximately 120 believers.
These were not people celebrating an easy victory. They had witnessed the arrest and crucifixion of their Lord. They had experienced fear, confusion, and their own failures.
Peter himself knew what it meant to fall.
He had denied Jesus three times.
Three times he had insisted that he did not know the very Savior he had promised never to abandon.
But something remarkable had happened.
The risen Jesus had restored Peter, as John 21:15–19 records.
And now the man who once denied Christ before others stood before the gathered believers to speak about Scripture, betrayal, and the future of their mission.
Think about that.
The man addressing Judas's failure was himself a man who had needed extraordinary mercy.
That distinction matters.
Judas betrayed Jesus and died without the restoration that Peter experienced. Peter denied Jesus, wept bitterly, and was restored by the risen Lord.
The lesson is not that Peter's sin was harmless or that Judas's sin was beyond the power of God's mercy.
The lesson is that sin must never be treated lightly, and that the proper response to failure is to turn toward Christ rather than away from Him.
Somebody reading this knows what it feels like to fail God.
You promised you would never go back to that sin.
But you did.
You said you would never compromise again.
But you compromised.
You told yourself that this time you would remain faithful.
And then came the moment of weakness.
Now shame keeps whispering that you have disqualified yourself forever.
But look at Peter.
The same mouth that denied Jesus was now speaking boldly among His followers.
Your failure does not have to become the final sentence of your story.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because Jesus Christ is a merciful Savior who restores those who return to Him.
Peter then explained why the believers needed to address Judas's vacant apostleship.
He appealed to Scripture.
Acts 1:20 records Peter citing two passages from the Psalms.
In the King James Version, the second quotation reads:
"And his bishoprick let another take." — Acts 1:20
That old English word bishoprick can sound strange to modern readers.
The Greek word behind it is ἐπισκοπή (episkopē), which can refer to oversight, responsibility, or an office of service.
The phrase in Acts 1:20 is:
τὴν ἐπισκοπὴν αὐτοῦ λαβέτω ἕτερος
“Let another take his office.”
Peter was drawing from Psalm 109:8, a passage originally expressed within a psalm of judgment against a wicked adversary.
The Hebrew wording includes:
פְּקֻדָּתוֹ יִקַּח אַחֵר
“Let another take his office.”
The Hebrew noun pequddato concerns an assigned responsibility, charge, or office.
Peter understood this Scripture as applicable to Judas's betrayal and the vacancy he had left among the apostles.
He also cited Psalm 69:25 concerning desolation.
This was not Peter inventing a new ministry position because he was uncomfortable with an empty chair.
He was interpreting what had happened in light of Scripture and seeking to restore the apostolic number.
But why was the number twelve so important?
Because Jesus had not randomly selected twelve disciples.
The number was deeply connected to the history and promises of Israel.
Israel had twelve tribes.
And Jesus had appointed twelve apostles, a symbolic act connected to the restoration and fulfillment of God's purposes for His people.
In Matthew 19:28, Jesus spoke of the twelve apostles sitting on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
The twelve were not merely a leadership committee.
Their number carried covenantal significance.
The betrayal of Judas did not mean God's redemptive purpose had collapsed.
But it left a vacancy within the group Jesus had appointed.
And before the public outpouring of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, the gathered believers sought to fill it.
There is something deeply moving about the timing.
Jesus had told them to wait for the promised Holy Spirit.
They were not instructed to launch a campaign, build an empire, or prove their importance.
They were waiting.
Praying.
Remaining together.
And attending to what they understood Scripture required.
Sometimes faithfulness looks less like spectacular action and more like quiet obedience while you wait for God.
Perhaps you are living in that kind of season.
The opportunity has not opened.
The answer has not arrived.
The healing is taking longer than you expected.
You are tempted to believe that waiting means God has forgotten you.
But the disciples were waiting in Jerusalem, and heaven had not forgotten them.
The promised Spirit would come.
And in the meantime, they had a responsibility to carry out faithfully.
Then Peter stated the qualifications for Judas's replacement.

Acts 1:21–22 explains that the candidate needed to be someone who had accompanied the disciples throughout Jesus's earthly ministry, beginning with John's baptism and continuing until Jesus was taken up from them.
Most importantly, he needed to become a witness with them of Jesus's resurrection.
This was not a popularity contest.
Not a reward for the loudest personality.
Not an appointment based on money, social influence, or public recognition.
The replacement needed firsthand knowledge of the ministry of Jesus and His resurrection.
The central qualification was connected to the central message.
Jesus Christ had risen from the dead.
The apostles were not being appointed to promote themselves.
They were commissioned to testify to Him.
That is why this passage must never be reduced to a motivational story about getting a second chance at a vacant position.
The real center of Acts 1 is not Matthias.
It is the risen Jesus Christ, whose witnesses were being prepared to proclaim the Gospel.
And then something fascinating happened.
The believers presented two men.
Joseph called Barsabbas, also known as Justus.
And Matthias.
Two qualified candidates.
Two men who had apparently remained with the wider circle of Jesus's followers through the events Peter described.
And yet Scripture tells us remarkably little about either man's personal history.
We do not receive a dramatic speech from Matthias.
We do not hear Joseph pleading his case.
There is no record of one attacking the character of the other.
Instead, the gathered believers prayed.
Acts 1:24–25, in the King James Version, records their appeal:

"Thou, Lord, which knowest the hearts of all men, shew whether of these two thou hast chosen, That he may take part of this ministry and apostleship, from which Judas by transgression fell, that he might go to his own place."
Do not miss those words.
“Thou, Lord, which knowest the hearts of all men.”
The Greek expression is:
σὺ κύριε καρδιογνῶστα πάντων
“You, Lord, knower of the hearts of all.”
The word καρδιογνῶστα (kardiognōsta) means knower of hearts.
It combines the idea of the heart with knowledge.
The believers recognized something that every generation of Christians needs to remember.
Human beings can evaluate outward qualifications.
But God knows what is hidden.
He knows the difference between a public performance and private surrender.
He knows the motives behind our ministry.
He knows when our prayers are sincere and when our words are merely religious habits.
He knows what nobody else knows about you.
And that truth should produce both reverence and hope.
Reverence, because nothing is hidden from Him.
Hope, because the God who knows the darkest corners of the human heart is also the God who sent His Son to save sinners.
You do not have to manufacture a flawless image before coming to Jesus.
You must come truthfully.
Confessing your sin.
Trusting His mercy.
Turning from what is destroying you.
And believing that His death and resurrection are sufficient to save.
There is no mask that can fool God.
But there is also no need to wear a mask before the Savior who already knows the truth.
Then came the moment that has puzzled Christians for centuries.
They cast lots.
And the lot fell to Matthias.
Acts 1:26 states:
"And they gave forth their lots; and the lot fell upon Matthias; and he was numbered with the eleven apostles." — KJV
To modern readers, casting lots can sound like gambling or making a spiritual decision through chance.
But within the biblical world, lots were sometimes used in recognized settings to make selections or distribute responsibilities.
Proverbs 16:33 says:
"The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD." — KJV
That proverb expresses God's sovereignty over outcomes that may appear uncertain to human observers.
The disciples had first identified candidates who met the stated qualifications.
Then they prayed.
Then they used lots to make the final selection.
The account presents this as their means of choosing between two eligible men while appealing to the Lord who knows hearts.
It is important, however, not to claim more than the passage actually says.
Acts does not explicitly command Christians in every generation to cast lots when appointing leaders.
Nor does it establish casting lots as the normal pattern for church leadership after Pentecost.
Later in Acts, believers are shown relying on prayer, the Holy Spirit's guidance, spiritual qualifications, and communal discernment.
And what about the popular claim that the disciples made a mistake by choosing Matthias because God actually intended Paul to become the twelfth apostle?
That interpretation has been suggested by some Christians.
But Acts itself never states that Matthias was an illegitimate apostle or that the believers were wrong to select him.
Luke records Matthias being numbered with the eleven.
In Acts 2:14, Peter stands with the eleven at Pentecost, consistent with the restored apostolic group.
Paul would later be called directly by the risen Christ and become an apostle with a remarkable mission to the Gentiles.
But Scripture does not say Paul's calling invalidated Matthias's selection.
We should be careful not to turn an argument from silence into a doctrine.
The most natural reading of Acts 1 is that the community, guided by its understanding of Scripture and prayerful dependence on God, selected Matthias to fill Judas's vacant place.
And here is something else that deserves our attention.
After this event, Matthias virtually disappears from the New Testament narrative.
No extended biography.
No famous sermon recorded under his name.
No detailed account of his later missionary work in the biblical text.
Christian traditions tell various stories about his later ministry and death, but these accounts are not established by the New Testament itself.
We should not confuse later tradition with what Scripture actually reveals.
And yet his limited appearance in the biblical record carries a powerful reminder.
Being faithful to Jesus does not guarantee that your name will become famous.
Some people will preach before thousands.
Others will quietly disciple one struggling believer.
Some will write books that travel across nations.
Others will pray for their children at a kitchen table while the rest of the house sleeps.
Some will be remembered in history.
Others will be known only to the people whose lives they touched.
But visibility is not the measure of faithfulness.
God does not need to make you famous to make your obedience meaningful.
Maybe you have spent years serving without recognition.
You have encouraged people who never thanked you.
You have prayed for someone who never knew.
You have given when nobody noticed.
You have remained faithful while watching others receive opportunities you hoped would come to you.
And sometimes you wonder whether any of it matters.
Matthias's story does not promise that your quiet service will eventually bring public promotion.
It reminds us that a person can have a genuine place in God's work without receiving a long public record of accomplishments.
The Lord knows His servants.
And the mission is greater than the recognition.
But there is another person in this story whom we must not forget.
Joseph Barsabbas.
He was qualified.
He was considered.
He was prayed over.
And he was not selected.
Scripture never tells us that Joseph was less faithful than Matthias.
It never says that his heart was inferior.
It never describes him as rejected by God.
He simply was not chosen for that particular apostolic vacancy.
And that distinction can bring healing to someone reading this.
Because sometimes you can be qualified and still not receive the position.
You can work faithfully and still not be the person selected.
You can love Jesus sincerely and still watch a door open for someone else.
Not every closed door is divine punishment.
Not every disappointment is evidence of spiritual failure.
And not every person who receives a visible assignment is more loved by God than the person who does not.
Our identity in Christ cannot rest on whether people choose us.
It rests on the Savior who gave Himself for us.
The Gospel does not say you become valuable when you are appointed.
It announces that God demonstrated His love for sinners through Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
Before you achieved anything impressive.
Before anyone applauded your ministry.
Before your name appeared on a platform.
Christ died for sinners.
And salvation comes through His grace, not through a title, position, or religious achievement.
That is why the contrast between Judas, Peter, Joseph, and Matthias is so striking.
Judas reminds us that outward association with Jesus does not guarantee inward faithfulness.
Peter reminds us that terrible failure need not be the end when a sinner turns back to Christ.
Joseph reminds us that not receiving a particular assignment does not prove a person is spiritually inferior.
Matthias reminds us that faithfulness may be real even when Scripture records little about the rest of someone's life.
Four lives.
Four different lessons.
One Savior at the center of the story.
And over all of them stands the sovereign purpose of God.
Judas's betrayal was wicked.
It was not made righteous simply because God accomplished redemption through the suffering of Jesus.
Human responsibility remains real.
But human evil could not prevent the crucifixion and resurrection through which God accomplished salvation.
The cross was not the defeat of God's plan.
It was central to the saving work of Christ.
Jesus was not merely the innocent victim of circumstances beyond His control.
He willingly gave His life.
He bore sin.
He rose victorious.
And now His witnesses were preparing to proclaim repentance and forgiveness in His name.
This is the Gospel.
Not that God overlooks sin.
Not that every broken relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
Not that every person who fails will receive the same earthly assignment again.
But that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, as Paul summarizes in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
Through Him, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed.
And that brings us to the most personal question in this entire passage.
What are you doing with the Jesus whom Judas betrayed, Peter denied, and Matthias was chosen to proclaim?
It is possible to spend years discussing biblical characters while avoiding the condition of your own soul.
You can debate whether casting lots was appropriate.
You can study the Greek vocabulary.
You can examine the symbolism of the twelve tribes.
You can memorize every name in Acts 1.
And still avoid the question that matters most.
Have you truly surrendered your life to Jesus Christ?
Not merely admired Him.
Not merely posted about Him.
Not merely defended Christianity in arguments.
Have you repented of your sin and trusted Him as Savior and Lord?
Because there is something more frightening than an empty apostolic seat.
It is a heart filled with religious activity but unwilling to surrender to Christ.
And there is something more beautiful than receiving a prestigious ministry position.
It is being forgiven by the One who knows everything about you.
Every hidden compromise.
Every private tear.
Every shameful memory.
Every promise you failed to keep.
He knows.
And the invitation of the Gospel still stands.
Come to Christ.
Not because you are worthy.
But because He is merciful.
Not because you can erase your past.
But because His grace is sufficient to forgive and transform those who believe.
Not because you can rewrite your own story through willpower.
But because Jesus Christ saves.
Perhaps you have been carrying guilt for years.
Perhaps you have walked away from prayer because you feel ashamed.
Perhaps you are still attending church while privately fighting something that is slowly hardening your heart.
Do not use Judas's story to conclude that you are beyond hope.
Use it as a warning not to continue in hidden sin or presume upon grace.
And look to Peter as a reminder that the risen Christ is able to restore a repentant sinner.
Do not wait until you have cleaned yourself up to approach Jesus.
Come in repentance and faith.
Tell Him the truth.
He already knows it.
And if you are exhausted from pretending, perhaps this is the moment to stop hiding.
You do not need to publish the details of your private struggles. God hears even the prayers you cannot put into words.
But there is still one final detail in Acts 1 that changes how we should understand the entire story.
After Matthias was chosen, the apostles did not suddenly become powerful because the number twelve had been restored.
Their confidence was not supposed to rest in having the perfect organizational structure.
They still needed what Jesus had promised.
The Holy Spirit.
In Acts 2, the Spirit came upon the believers at Pentecost, and the public proclamation of the risen Christ moved forward with extraordinary boldness.
That is the larger movement of the story.
From betrayal to witness.
From fear to proclamation.
From waiting to Spirit-empowered mission.
From the apparent collapse of everything the disciples had hoped for to the announcement that Jesus Christ had risen and was exalted.
The empty place left by Judas was filled.
But the greater miracle was not the appointment of Matthias.
It was that the crucified and risen Savior was continuing His mission through weak, dependent, imperfect human beings.
People who needed grace themselves.
People who could not save the world.
People whose only hope was the One they proclaimed.
And that is still true of the Church today.
We do not save people by building impressive ministries.
We do not transform hearts through clever words.
We do not purchase God's favor through money, influence, or religious performance.
We proclaim Jesus Christ, depend on His Spirit, teach His Word, love our neighbors, and invite people to repent and believe the Gospel.
And when believers support faithful Gospel ministry, they participate in helping that message reach others.
That is why I want to speak to you personally about Gospel Warrior.
If this message has helped you understand Scripture, confronted something in your heart, or reminded you of the grace of Jesus Christ, consider what it would mean to help this ministry continue.
Behind every article is a desire to make biblical truth accessible to people who may be struggling, searching, grieving, repenting, or quietly longing to know Jesus more deeply.
Some readers may never enter a church building before encountering a Scripture-centered message online.
Some may be believers who have grown cold.
Some may be people carrying questions they are afraid to ask.
Some may be one honest conversation away from seeking the Lord.
We cannot know how God will use every article.
But we can remain faithful in sharing His Word.
And you can help.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and joyful—not forced by guilt or pressure.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
"God loveth a cheerful giver."
You cannot purchase God's blessing.
And you never need to pay to earn His grace.
But if you believe in the mission of Gospel Warrior and have the means to support it, your monthly contribution can make a meaningful difference in helping this work continue and grow.
These are practical ways to encourage biblical learning, carry Scripture-centered reminders into daily life, and share faith-inspired gifts with others.
The purpose is not merely to collect Christian material.
It is to grow in the Word.
To understand the Gospel.
To learn obedience.
To deepen prayer.
To become more discerning.
To be shaped increasingly into the likeness of Christ.
Not simply because it might reach more people.
But because someone among your family, friends, or followers may need to hear the truth that Jesus restores repentant sinners and that human failure cannot overthrow God's redemptive purposes.
You may have a friend who feels disqualified.
A relative who has drifted from faith.
A fellow believer who is quietly exhausted.
Someone who knows the name of Jesus but has never seriously considered what it means to follow Him.
If you have read this far, I want to leave you with one final question.
Not about Matthias.
Not about Judas.
Not even about Peter.
About you.
Are you more concerned about being seen as a faithful Christian—or about actually being faithful to Christ when nobody is watching?
That question reaches deeper than a title, a church position, or a public reputation.
Because the God who knows every heart is not impressed by religious appearances.
He calls us to repentance, faith, love, and obedience.
And when we fall, our hope is not in pretending we never failed.
Our hope is in Jesus Christ.
The Savior who died for sinners.
The Lord who rose from the grave.
The King who remains faithful.
The One whose Gospel continues to change lives.
Judas's betrayal did not stop the mission.
Peter's denial did not prevent his restoration.
Joseph's not being selected did not prove he was unworthy.
Matthias's relative obscurity did not make his appointment meaningless.
And your worth before God is not measured by your popularity, your position, or the applause of others.
The question is whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
If you do, remain in Him.
If you have wandered, repent and return.
If you are seeking, come to Him in faith.
If you are weary, remember that your strength is not the foundation of your salvation.
Christ is.
Not as a performance for other people.
But as a simple expression of the prayer you want to live.
Because at the end of the day, the greatest tragedy is not being forgotten by the world.
It is spending your life near the things of God while refusing the Savior Himself.
And the greatest victory is not having your name remembered by generations.
It is knowing the Lord Jesus Christ, who died and rose again.
The world may remember the empty seat Judas left behind, but heaven's greatest invitation is not to take Judas's place—it is to surrender your heart to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY MARKED A DAY FOR THEIR DEATH. GOD TURNED IT INTO A DAY THEY WOULD NEVER FORGET.
paragraphs: THEY MARKED A DAY FOR THEIR DEATH. GOD TURNED IT INTO A DAY THEY WOULD NEVER FORGET.

Why Did the Jews Establish the Feast of Purim? — Esther 9:20–28 | The terrifying story of a death sentence, a hidden deliverance, and the God who can turn the day meant to destroy you into a testimony of His faithfulness.
There was a date on the calendar when an entire people were supposed to die.
Not just the soldiers. Not just the leaders. Not just the people who had offended someone powerful.
The children, too.
The mothers holding their babies. The fathers trying to protect their families. The elderly who had survived wars, exile, and years of uncertainty.
All of them.
One day had been chosen for their destruction.
And somewhere in the Persian Empire, ordinary Jewish families were living with the knowledge that their enemies had been given legal permission to kill them.
Imagine trying to sleep with that knowledge.
Imagine looking at your children and wondering whether you would still be alive to hold them when that day arrived.
Imagine praying while the calendar kept moving.
One day closer.
Another day closer.
And heaven seemed silent.
But here is what makes the story of Purim so unforgettable.
The date that was chosen for their destruction became the date their descendants would celebrate their deliverance.
The very thing intended to erase their future became part of the story their children would remember.
And before you dismiss this as an ancient Jewish festival with little connection to your life, consider something.
Have you ever lived through a season when the future frightened you more than the present?
When something beyond your control threatened everything you loved?
When you prayed, but nothing seemed to change?
When God seemed absent, and you wondered whether He was doing anything at all?
Then you may understand more of Esther's story than you realize.
Because Purim is not merely about people surviving a crisis.
It is about remembering a deliverance so extraordinary that forgetting it would have been another tragedy.
And for Christians reading Esther in the light of the whole Bible, it also invites us to look toward the greater redemption accomplished through Jesus Christ.
But to understand why the Jews established Purim, we must first understand the terror that made the celebration necessary.
The story begins with a man named Haman.
Haman was not an ordinary enemy.

He held tremendous authority under King Ahasuerus, commonly identified with Xerxes I of Persia. He possessed political influence, royal access, and enough personal pride to turn one man's refusal to honor him into a campaign against an entire people.
That man was Mordecai, a Jew living in the Persian Empire.
When Mordecai refused to bow down to Haman, Haman's anger grew beyond personal revenge.
Esther 3:6 explains that Haman sought to destroy all the Jews throughout the kingdom.
Think about the terrifying disproportion.
One man's wounded pride.
An entire people's threatened extinction.
Haman then cast lots to determine the date of his planned destruction.
Esther 3:7 records that the lot was cast in the first month, Nisan, and that the selected date fell in the twelfth month, Adar.
The Hebrew word for the lot is פּוּר — pur.
It refers to a lot used to make a selection or determine an outcome.
This small Hebrew word matters because it eventually becomes the name of the entire celebration.
But at first, it represented something horrifying.
A date selected for death.
Haman obtained royal authorization for a decree permitting the destruction of the Jews on the thirteenth day of Adar.
Esther 3:13 describes the order to destroy, kill, and annihilate the Jews, including young and old, women and children, and to plunder their possessions.
This was not a misunderstanding.
This was not an ordinary disagreement.
It was an empire-wide threat of mass violence.
And the Jews could not simply pretend it would disappear.
The decree bore the authority of the Persian king.
The date was set.
The machinery of destruction had begun moving.
Then something happened that makes Esther one of the most remarkable books in Scripture.
A Jewish woman was already inside the palace.
Her name was Esther.
She had become queen, but her Jewish identity had not initially been disclosed to the king.
Mordecai urged her to intervene.
Yet approaching the king without being summoned could cost her life.
Esther was facing a decision that would expose the difference between possessing influence and being willing to risk it.
Would she remain silent?
Would she protect her position?
Or would she identify herself with a threatened people and accept the danger?
Mordecai confronted her with a question that has echoed through generations.
In Esther 4:14, he asked whether she had come to her royal position for such a time as this.
Notice something important.
Mordecai did not claim to know every detail of God's hidden purposes.
He expressed confidence that deliverance could arise from another place, while warning Esther that her own position would not guarantee her safety.
Esther responded by calling for a fast.
Then she made her decision.
She would approach the king.
And if she perished, she perished.
There is something profoundly moving about that moment.
Courage did not mean Esther had received a guarantee that nothing painful could happen.
Courage meant she would do what was necessary even when the outcome remained uncertain.
Some of the most significant acts of faithfulness happen when people have no certainty of earthly safety.
A mother keeps praying.
A father chooses integrity.
A wounded believer refuses to repay evil with evil.
Someone finally tells the truth.
Someone stands beside the vulnerable, knowing there may be consequences.
Not every courageous decision ends with an earthly rescue.
The Bible never promises that it will.
But Esther reminds us that fear does not have to make the final decision.
And then the story begins to turn.
Haman prepares a structure on which he intends to have Mordecai executed.
But the king experiences a sleepless night.
The royal chronicles are read aloud.
A previously overlooked act of loyalty by Mordecai is brought to the king's attention.
Haman arrives expecting to advance his own plans, only to be instructed to honor the very man he hates.
Eventually, Esther exposes Haman's plot before the king.
The man who sought Mordecai's death is executed on the structure he had prepared for Mordecai.
The reversal is astonishing.
But the danger is not over.
The original royal decree remains a threat.
According to Esther 8, another decree is issued, authorizing the Jews to assemble and defend themselves against those who attack them.
When the appointed day arrives, the Jews prevail over their enemies.

The biblical account does not present this as a harmless celebration or a conflict without bloodshed. Esther 9 records deaths and violent confrontation, and those difficult details must not be erased.
It also repeatedly states that the Jews did not lay hands on the plunder, even though the royal authorization had permitted them to take it.
The account distinguishes their defense against hostile attackers from a campaign of enrichment.
By the time the conflict ends, the people who had expected destruction have experienced deliverance.
Their mourning is turned into gladness.
Their fear gives way to relief.
Their threatened future becomes a future they can pass on to their children.
And this is where Esther 9:20–28 answers the question at the heart of the story.
Why did the Jews establish the Feast of Purim?
Because they refused to let the memory of their deliverance disappear.
Mordecai wrote to the Jews throughout the provinces of the Persian Empire, instructing them to observe the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar annually.
Esther 9:22 describes those days in the King James Version as the time when the Jews rested from their enemies, and the month that had been turned:
“from sorrow to joy, and from mourning into a good day.”
The Hebrew text makes the reversal especially vivid.
מִיָּגוֹן לְשִׂמְחָה וּמֵאֵבֶל לְיוֹם טוֹב
Mi-yagon le-simchah, u-me'evel le-yom tov.
Literally, the expression conveys the movement from grief to joy, and from mourning to a good or festive day.
The Hebrew word yagon means grief or sorrow.
Simchah means joy or gladness.
Evel refers to mourning.
And yom tov means a good day, here describing a festive occasion.
These words are not decorative poetry placed over a pleasant memory.
They describe a complete reversal of the people's circumstances.
The Jews had expected to mourn their dead.
Instead, they were able to celebrate their survival.
They had faced a decree intended to destroy their families.
Instead, they could gather with those families and remember their deliverance.
What had been a month of dread became a month of joy.
And they wanted future generations to know why.
Esther 9:26 explains the festival's name:
“Wherefore they called these days Purim after the name of Pur.”
Purim is the plural form associated with pur, the lot Haman had cast.
Consider the extraordinary irony.
The festival was named after the very instrument Haman had used to select the day of their destruction.
Every time the people spoke the name Purim, they recalled the threat from which they had been delivered.
The name did not hide the darkness of the story.
It remembered that the darkness had not prevailed.
This is one reason Purim has such enduring significance in Jewish life.
It preserves the memory of a people who survived an existential threat, and it celebrates the reversal described in the book of Esther.
But there is another detail many readers overlook.
The celebration was never intended to remain a private feeling.
Esther 9:22 describes feasting, gladness, sending portions of food to one another, and giving gifts to the poor.
Joy was meant to move outward.
Those who had survived together were to celebrate together.
Those with food were to share.
Those who were poor were not to be forgotten.
The people were not simply told to remember what happened.
They were given practices that would carry that remembrance into their communities.
And this confronts something in us.
Sometimes we become so consumed with our own relief that we forget the person who is still suffering.
We thank God for provision but fail to notice the hungry.
We celebrate answered prayers but forget those who are still waiting.
We rejoice that our families are safe while remaining indifferent to families living in fear.
Purim reminds its observers that communal deliverance calls for communal remembrance and generosity.
And Christians can recognize a wider biblical principle here: gratitude should make us more generous, not less.
The God we thank with our lips must not be dishonored by the way we treat our neighbors.
But perhaps the most haunting feature of Esther is something the book never directly says.
In the Hebrew text of Esther, the name of God is not explicitly mentioned.
Not once.
That does not mean the story teaches that God was absent.
It means the book tells its story without an explicit declaration identifying God's action at every turn.
Readers are invited to notice the remarkable convergence of events.
Esther becomes queen.
Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king.
His loyalty is recorded but initially unrewarded.
The king cannot sleep at a decisive moment.
The chronicles are read.
Mordecai's earlier act is discovered.
Haman's plans collapse.
The Jews survive.
The narrative never gives us permission to claim that we can identify God's purpose behind every painful event in our own lives.

Yet its pattern has long led Jewish and Christian readers to reflect on providence: the possibility of divine care operating through circumstances that appear ordinary, uncertain, or even threatening.
And that speaks to the person reading this who has been quietly asking:
Where is God?
Where was He when the diagnosis came?
Where was He when the marriage fell apart?
Where was He when the person you trusted betrayed you?
Where was He when you prayed until you had no more words?
Those questions deserve more than a shallow religious slogan.
Esther does not explain every mystery of suffering.
It does not promise that every believer will escape tragedy.
And it does not teach that every painful chapter will end with the kind of public reversal Esther experienced.
But it challenges the assumption that God's silence in our perception proves His absence.
Sometimes we do not understand what is happening.
Sometimes we cannot see the outcome.
Sometimes obedience must continue without an explanation.
And sometimes the evidence of God's faithfulness becomes clearer only when we look backward.
That is part of why remembrance matters.
Because suffering can distort our perspective.
Fear can make yesterday's mercy feel distant.
Grief can make us forget what once sustained us.
And even after deliverance, human beings are remarkably capable of forgetting.
The Jews established Purim so that the story would not be swallowed by time.
Esther 9:28 declares that these days were to be remembered and kept throughout generations, families, provinces, and cities.
The text specifically emphasizes that the remembrance of Purim should not perish among their descendants.
This was more than a holiday.
It was an intentional act of historical memory.
Parents would tell children.
Communities would gather.
The story would be read.
The threatened destruction and the extraordinary reversal would remain part of the people's identity.
They would remember that their survival had once been in danger.
And they would remember that the danger had not been the end of their story.
Now we must ask an important question.
What does any of this have to do with Jesus Christ?
To answer faithfully, we must first honor what Esther actually says.
Purim is a Jewish festival, not a Christian ordinance.
Esther 9 does not command Christians to observe Purim, nor does it explicitly identify Esther, Mordecai, or the festival as direct prophecies of Jesus.
We should not force Christ's name into verses where the biblical author did not place it.
Yet Christians read the Old Testament as part of the larger biblical story that finds its fulfillment in Christ.
And within that larger story, the preservation of the Jewish people matters profoundly.
God's promises to Abraham included blessing for the nations through his offspring (Genesis 12:3; 22:18).
The Messiah would come through Israel.
The New Testament identifies Jesus as the son of David, the son of Abraham (Matthew 1:1), and Paul writes that Christ came from Israel according to His human ancestry (Romans 9:5).
The preservation celebrated in Esther belongs within that history of God's covenant dealings with Israel.
But the connection becomes even more powerful when we consider the biblical theme of reversal.
At Purim, a day intended for destruction became a time of deliverance.
At the cross, Jesus willingly entered the suffering and death that human sin and evil brought upon Him.
The rulers who crucified Him believed they had brought His mission to an end.
His followers watched Him die.
His body was placed in a tomb.
And for a moment, hope appeared buried.
But the resurrection revealed that death had not defeated Him.
Acts 2:23–24 declares that Jesus was delivered up according to God's definite plan and foreknowledge, crucified by lawless men, and raised by God.
Human wickedness was real.
Christ's suffering was real.
His death was real.
And His resurrection was real.
The cross was not merely an unfortunate event that God later repaired.
According to Scripture, Jesus gave Himself for our sins in accordance with God's saving purpose (Galatians 1:4).
Here we encounter something greater than a reversal of earthly danger.
Through Jesus Christ, sinners are offered forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life.
The threatened Jews in Esther needed deliverance from those who sought to kill them.
Every human being also faces a deeper spiritual problem: sin and separation from a holy God.
Romans 3:23 says that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
Romans 6:23 declares that the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
And Romans 5:8 announces the astonishing heart of the Gospel:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
That is grace.
Not God pretending our sin does not matter.
Not God calling evil good.
Not God offering cheap reassurance without repentance.
Grace is God giving His Son to save people who could never save themselves.
Jesus did not come merely to make difficult lives more comfortable.
He came to save sinners.
He died for our sins.
He rose from the dead.
And He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
That is why the Christian hope is deeper than the promise that every frightening situation will disappear.
Even when earthly circumstances do not change as we desire, the risen Christ remains the believer's hope.
Even when death comes, it does not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
Even when a life has been scarred by sin, forgiveness and transformation are possible through His grace.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to hear.
You may have spent years believing your worst chapter defines you.
The affair.
The addiction.
The secret.
The betrayal.
The years of pretending.
The faith you abandoned.
The family you hurt.
The prayers you stopped praying because you were ashamed to face God.
You remember things other people know nothing about.
You know how to smile while carrying guilt.
You know how to sit through worship while feeling spiritually distant.
You know how to tell people you are fine when your conscience is exhausted.
And somewhere along the way, you may have begun to believe that your story is already decided.
But hear the Gospel clearly.
Your sin is serious. Your shame is not your savior. And your past is not more powerful than the grace of Jesus Christ.
You cannot rewrite history.
You cannot undo every consequence.
You cannot force broken relationships to heal on your timetable.
But you can come to Christ in repentance and faith.
You can confess what you have hidden.
You can turn away from the sin you have defended.
You can receive the forgiveness that Jesus purchased through His death and resurrection.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
That promise is not an invitation to continue in sin without concern.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and come into the light.
The Gospel does not promise that repentance will erase every earthly consequence.
It promises something infinitely precious: forgiveness and reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
And that is where the theme of this ministry becomes more than a memorable phrase.
Not because Jesus changes the facts of what happened.
Not because He makes every painful memory vanish.
Not because the damage caused by sin suddenly becomes insignificant.
But because He can redeem sinners, transform lives, and give an eternal future that human failure could never produce.
The apostle Paul once persecuted the church.
Peter denied knowing Jesus.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left to rebuild his reputation.
Yet the New Testament bears witness to the mercy of God reaching people in profoundly different circumstances.
No sinner should presume upon grace.
And no repentant sinner should conclude that Christ is unwilling to receive those who truly come to Him.
Jesus Himself declared in John 6:37 that whoever comes to Him He will never cast out.
Think about that.
You may have been rejected by people.
You may have destroyed your own reputation.
You may have reached a point where you struggle to believe you could ever change.
But Jesus calls sinners to Himself.
Not to remain enslaved to sin.
Not to celebrate rebellion.
But to be forgiven, reconciled, and transformed.
The story of Purim begins with a people facing a day of destruction.
It ends with a people establishing days of remembrance.
The Christian Gospel tells of a Savior who entered death and rose victorious, opening the way to eternal life for all who trust in Him.
These are distinct biblical events, and we should never confuse them.
Yet both remind us that apparent finality is not always the final word.
And for the believer, the resurrection of Jesus is the decisive reason for hope.
Maybe you are still in the middle of a chapter you do not understand.
Maybe you are praying for a child who has walked away from faith.
Maybe your family is carrying a burden nobody else sees.
Maybe you are trying to rebuild trust after years of failure.
Maybe you are grieving someone you desperately wish you could speak to again.
I will not tell you that every earthly loss will be reversed.
I will not promise that tomorrow will bring the answer you want.
But I will tell you what Scripture allows us to say with confidence.
Jesus Christ is risen.
His grace is sufficient for those who belong to Him.
His call to repentance is still open.
And nothing can separate those who are in Christ from the love of God in Him (Romans 8:38–39).
So do not confuse an unfinished chapter with an abandoned life.
Do not confuse unanswered questions with proof that God does not care.
And do not let shame convince you to run away from the only Savior who can forgive you.
Come to Jesus.
Not after you have repaired yourself.
Not after you have made your life look respectable.
Come with repentance.
Come with faith.
Come with the truth.
Because the One who died and rose again is not asking you to manufacture your own redemption.
He calls you to receive the salvation He alone can give.
And if this article has exposed something you have been hiding, I want to invite you to respond—not for appearance, not for applause, but with sincerity.
If you are exhausted from struggling, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
You do not have to disclose private wounds or painful details publicly. A few honest words are enough to let fellow believers know you desire prayer.
Someone who is still waiting may need the encouragement of hearing how Christ has sustained you.
Before you leave, remember something else from Purim.
The people did not keep their deliverance to themselves.
They passed the memory forward.
They made sure the next generation would know.
And today, you have an opportunity to pass biblical truth forward, too.
There is also a practical way to help this work continue.
Gospel Warrior exists to make biblical truth accessible, to encourage believers toward deeper discipleship, and to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ.
Keeping these resources available, developing new teaching materials, and expanding the reach of this ministry require time, labor, and financial support.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You can glorify Him through obedience, worship, generosity, service, prayer, and faithful love for others.
And whether or not you are able to give financially, your prayers, thoughtful comments, and willingness to share sound biblical teaching are genuinely valuable.
A simple Facebook share can introduce someone to a passage of Scripture they have never considered.
A personal invitation can encourage a discouraged believer to begin reading the Bible again.
A prayer can strengthen someone whose struggle you may never fully know.
And a faithful testimony can point attention away from human achievement and toward the mercy of Christ.
That is worth remembering.
Because Purim was established so that the generations after Esther would not forget the deliverance their ancestors had experienced.
And Christians, above all, have been entrusted with a message that must never be forgotten.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day.
And forgiveness and eternal life are proclaimed in His name.
This is not merely a story about surviving a difficult season.
It is an invitation to remember who God is, to take sin seriously, to trust the risen Savior, and to live in the light of His grace.
The Jews called their celebration Purim because of the lot that had once marked their threatened destruction.
What Haman intended to be remembered as a day of terror became a yearly remembrance of deliverance.
And if you belong to Jesus Christ, your deepest hope does not rest on whether every earthly circumstance turns out the way you desire.
It rests on the Savior who conquered death.
So when you remember Esther, remember the courage.
Remember the threatened people.
Remember the reversal.
Remember the generations who were taught not to forget.
And when you look toward the cross and the empty tomb, remember something greater still.
The Savior who bore our sins is alive.
The door of repentance is open.
The invitation of grace is real.
And the story of every person who comes to Christ is forever changed by Him.
The day you thought your story was over may become the day you finally discover that Jesus, not your past, has the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: TWO WIVES. ONE LOVED. ONE UNLOVED. AND A GOD WHO REFUSED TO LET FAVORITISM HAVE THE FINAL WORD.
paragraphs: TWO WIVES. ONE LOVED. ONE UNLOVED. AND A GOD WHO REFUSED TO LET FAVORITISM HAVE THE FINAL WORD.

He could choose which woman to love. But God would not let him use that love to steal another woman's son's inheritance. Buried in Deuteronomy 21:15–17 is a heartbreaking family story—and a revelation about justice, rejection, and the God who sees those whom others overlook.
Imagine growing up in a house where your father loves your brother's mother more than yours.
You eat at the same table. You carry the same family name. You call the same man Father.
But somehow, you know.
You see it in the way he looks at her.
You hear it in the tenderness of his voice when he speaks to her children.
You notice how quickly he celebrates their accomplishments while yours barely receive a nod.
Nobody has to announce that your mother is the less-loved wife.
The atmosphere tells you.
And perhaps the most painful part is watching your mother pretend she doesn't notice.
Now imagine your father is dying.
The family gathers. The inheritance is about to be divided. And the man who made your mother feel second-best all her life now has one final opportunity to make you feel the same way.
He wants to give the greater inheritance to the son of the woman he loves.
Even though you were born first.
Even though the birthright legally belongs to you.
Even though you have spent your entire life trying to earn the affection that came so naturally to your brother.
Then, in the middle of this painfully human situation, God speaks.
And what He says changes everything.
"He may not make the son of the beloved firstborn before the son of the hated, which is indeed the firstborn." — Deuteronomy 21:16, KJV
Read that again.
God did not say the father had to feel equal affection for both women before justice could be done.
He commanded the father to act justly even when his feelings were unequal.
That distinction matters more than most people realize.
Because the God of Scripture does not permit personal preference to become an excuse for injustice.
And somewhere, someone reading this knows exactly what it feels like to be on the wrong side of someone's preference.
Perhaps you were the child who never seemed good enough.
The spouse who gave everything and received emotional leftovers.
The sibling who watched someone else receive the affection you desperately wanted.
The believer who has quietly wondered why others seem to be celebrated while you remain unseen.
If that is you, stay with this passage.
Because Deuteronomy 21:15–17 is not merely an ancient inheritance regulation.
It is a window into God's concern for justice in a family where love has become painfully unequal.
And its deeper biblical connections lead us toward the grace of Jesus Christ.
The passage begins with words that almost sound like the opening scene of a family tragedy:
"If a man have two wives, one beloved, and another hated..." — Deuteronomy 21:15, KJV
The original Hebrew is especially revealing.
The phrase is:
הָאַחַת אֲהוּבָה וְהָאַחַת שְׂנוּאָה
Ha'achat ahuvah veha'achat senu'ah.
Literally, the one is loved, and the other is hated.
The Hebrew word אֲהוּבָה (ahuvah) describes the loved woman, while שְׂנוּאָה (senu'ah) describes the hated or unloved woman.
But here we must be careful.
The Hebrew verb sane' can communicate hatred, yet in certain relational comparisons it can also describe being loved less, rejected, or disfavored.
That does not mean the word is harmless.
It means we must allow the context to explain the kind of unequal relationship being described.
In this law, the contrast concerns a man's preference between two wives and the danger that his preference will corrupt his treatment of their sons.
The law does not tell us whether the less-loved wife was subjected to open hostility, quiet neglect, or something in between.
It does tell us that God would not allow the father's unequal affection to determine who received the firstborn's legal inheritance.
And there is something else we must understand before going further.
This passage regulates an existing polygamous household. It does not command men to take multiple wives or declare polygamy God's ideal for marriage.
In Genesis 2:24, the foundational marriage pattern is a man joined to his wife, becoming one flesh. Jesus returns to that creation account when teaching about marriage in Matthew 19:4–6.
Throughout the Old Testament, households involving multiple wives frequently reveal painful consequences: rivalry, jealousy, favoritism, and fractured relationships.
God's law here addresses injustice within a social reality that existed in ancient Israel.
It protects a vulnerable son's legal rights rather than endorsing every feature of the household.
That distinction is essential.
Because we cannot understand the mercy and justice of God's Word by confusing what Scripture regulates with what Scripture celebrates.
And now the story becomes even more personal.
Long before Moses delivered this command to Israel, another family had already experienced the agony of one loved wife and one unloved wife.
Her name was Leah.
And her story may be one of the most emotionally devastating portraits of marital rejection in the Bible.
Jacob loved Rachel.
He worked seven years to marry her.
Then, through Laban's deception, he found himself married to Leah first. He subsequently married Rachel as well.
Genesis 29:30 says Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
And the next verse contains words that should make every reader stop:
"And when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren." — Genesis 29:31, KJV
Notice the first movement in that verse.
The LORD saw.
Before the children came.
Before the family became complicated.
Before Leah's longing was expressed through the names she gave her sons.
God saw that she was unloved.
The same Hebrew language of being hated or disfavored appears in Leah's story and in Deuteronomy's law.
That connection does not prove that Deuteronomy 21 was written specifically about Jacob's household. The law addresses a broader situation.
But Leah's life gives us a vivid biblical example of the emotional suffering such a household could contain.
When Leah gave birth to Reuben, she said:
"Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me." — Genesis 29:32, KJV
There it is.
The heartbreak beneath the motherhood.
She was not merely celebrating a son.
She was hoping that becoming a mother might finally make her husband love her.
Can you imagine carrying a child while carrying that kind of loneliness?
Can you imagine looking at your newborn and wondering whether this precious little life might finally make you worthy of affection?
Leah named her firstborn Reuben, a name associated with seeing.
She understood her son's birth in light of the Lord seeing her affliction.
Then came Simeon.
Her explanation again revealed the wound:
"Because the LORD hath heard that I was hated..." — Genesis 29:33, KJV
God saw.
God heard.
The husband whose affection she longed for did not love her as she hoped.
But the Lord was not unaware of her pain.
Then came Levi.
And Leah said:
"Now this time will my husband be joined unto me..." — Genesis 29:34, KJV
Another son.
Another hope.
Another longing for closeness.
And then Judah was born.
Something changes in the words Scripture records.
"Now will I praise the LORD..." — Genesis 29:35, KJV
This time, her words turn explicitly toward praise.
We should not pretend that one verse proves Leah never struggled with rejection again. Scripture does not say that.
But it does record a remarkable moment in which her attention turns from longing for her husband's affection to praising the Lord.
And here is the astonishing part.
Judah, the son born to the less-loved wife, would become an ancestor of Jesus Christ.
Read Matthew 1:2–3.
Read Hebrews 7:14.
The Messiah came from Judah's tribe.
Not because Leah earned God's favor through suffering.
Not because rejection automatically guarantees earthly greatness.
Not because God approved of the injustice she experienced.
But because God's redemptive purposes were not controlled by Jacob's romantic preference.
The woman who longed to be loved became part of the family line through which the Savior entered the world.
The Bible does not invite us to celebrate Leah's rejection.
It invites us to marvel that human rejection could not prevent God's purposes from unfolding.
And that brings us back to the father in Deuteronomy 21.
The law says that if the firstborn son belongs to the unloved wife, the father cannot give the firstborn's status to the son of the loved wife.
He must acknowledge the actual firstborn.
Why?
Because a birthright was not merely a sentimental family title.
It carried recognized legal and economic significance in ancient Israel.
Deuteronomy 21:17 commands:
"But he shall acknowledge the son of the hated for the firstborn, by giving him a double portion of all that he hath..." — KJV
The Hebrew phrase for the double portion is:
פִּי שְׁנַיִם
Pi shenayim.
It refers here to a twofold share of the inheritance.
This did not mean the firstborn received the entire estate.
It meant that, when the inheritance was divided into shares, the firstborn received twice the share of each other eligible son.
Four shares in total.
The firstborn would receive half, and each younger son one-quarter.
The law was not designed to make the less-loved wife's son richer because his mother suffered.
It protected the recognized birthright from being transferred simply because the father preferred another woman and her child.
The verse explains the reason:
"For he is the beginning of his strength; the right of the firstborn is his." — Deuteronomy 21:17, KJV
The Hebrew expression רֵאשִׁית אֹנוֹ (re'shit ono) means the beginning or firstfruits of his strength, referring to his firstborn son.
And the closing expression, מִשְׁפַּט הַבְּכֹרָה (mishpat habbekhorah), concerns the legal right of the firstborn.
This is not a vague encouragement to be kind.
It is a concrete legal restraint on paternal favoritism.
God was placing a boundary around a father's power.
He was saying, in effect, that a man's personal preference could not rewrite the rightful order of inheritance.
Think about how significant that was.
The father had authority.
He controlled property.
He had emotional preferences.
And in a society where household power could easily be misused, God required him to recognize a right that his feelings might tempt him to deny.
That is what makes this passage so relevant beyond its ancient setting.
Not because Christians today are commanded to reproduce Israel's exact inheritance arrangements.
But because the law reveals a moral concern that appears throughout Scripture.
Justice must not be sold to favoritism.
James 2:1 warns believers against holding faith in Jesus Christ while practicing partiality.
James then describes a gathering where a wealthy person receives special treatment while a poor person is dishonored.
Different situation.
Same dangerous human tendency.
We see someone we prefer.
Someone more impressive.
Someone more useful.
Someone who makes us feel important.
And suddenly, fairness becomes negotiable.
It happens in families.
It happens in churches.
It happens in friendships.
It happens in workplaces.
Sometimes it even happens in ministry, when people with influence receive attention while quiet, wounded believers struggle to be noticed.
And we should ask ourselves a question that is uncomfortable precisely because it is necessary.
Have we ever made someone feel less valuable simply because we loved, admired, or preferred someone else?
Have we ever allowed our affection to become an excuse for unfair treatment?
Parents, have you compared your children until one began to believe love must be earned?
Husbands and wives, have you used affection as a reward and emotional distance as punishment?
Church leaders, have you made room for the influential while overlooking the wounded?
And those of us who have experienced rejection—have we allowed our pain to become permission to treat others unjustly?
Deuteronomy 21 does not answer every modern relationship question.
But it confronts a temptation that has survived thousands of years.
The temptation to make our feelings the final authority over what is right.
And then comes a question even more difficult.
What if you are the one who was overlooked?
What if you are the son of the unloved wife?
What if your whole life has felt like standing outside a room where everyone else was invited?
You watched other people receive affection.
You watched them receive opportunities.
You watched doors open for them while you quietly wondered what was wrong with you.
Perhaps nobody ever said you were worthless.
They simply treated you as though you mattered less.
And over time, you began to believe them.
