Are you protecting your children or teaching them fear?
Are you reaching your neighbors or simply trying to appear more spiritual than they are?
These questions are worth asking.
Not because Halloween is the greatest spiritual issue facing the church.
But because ordinary decisions often reveal extraordinary truths about our hearts.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking possibility is this:
We could spend an entire evening arguing about darkness while neglecting the people Jesus commanded us to love.
We could condemn costumes while overlooking cruelty.
We could reject frightening decorations while secretly feeding bitterness, pornography, greed, unforgiveness, or hypocrisy.
We could pride ourselves on avoiding a controversial holiday while refusing to repent of sins that Scripture plainly identifies.
And then we could congratulate ourselves for being holy.
Jesus warned against this kind of spiritual blindness.
In Matthew 23:23, He rebuked religious leaders who were meticulous about certain religious obligations while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
His rebuke was not against obedience.
It was against distorted priorities and hypocrisy.
That warning should humble us.
Because holiness is not a costume we wear to convince others we belong to God.
Holiness is the fruit of a life being transformed by His grace.
The Greek word ἁγιασμός (hagiasmos), often translated “sanctification” or “holiness,” refers to being set apart for God and the process of living in a manner consistent with that belonging.
In 1 Thessalonians 4:3, Paul writes:
Holiness is not merely avoiding certain cultural activities.
It is belonging to God with our bodies, desires, decisions, relationships, and conduct.
It means rejecting genuine sin.
It means loving truth.
It means practicing repentance.
It means extending grace.
It means learning to desire what honors Christ.
And when we fail, it means returning to the Savior who is faithful to forgive.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that we can make ourselves righteous by avoiding Halloween.
Not that our freedom to celebrate proves we are spiritually mature.
But that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
He lived without sin.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And through repentance and faith in Him, we receive forgiveness and new life.
Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast.” — ESV
No one may boast.
Not the Christian who celebrates.
Not the Christian who abstains.
Not the parent who has every household rule carefully arranged.
Not the believer who has never touched a Halloween decoration.
Our confidence is not in our ability to manage a holiday perfectly.
Our confidence is in Jesus Christ.
And His grace does not leave us unchanged.
It teaches us to turn away from sin and live for Him.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives.
Grace is not the enemy of holiness.
Grace is what teaches us to pursue it.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message has always been so much deeper than public appearances.
Think about that.
Some of us have stories we would never want displayed in public.
Some have practiced things Scripture condemns.
Some have lived in spiritual darkness.
Some have been deceived.
Some have judged others mercilessly while hiding their own failures.
Some have been wounded by religious people who knew how to condemn but did not know how to love.
And some are still trying to understand how a holy God could welcome someone with such a complicated past.
But the cross answers that question.
Jesus does not save people because their stories are clean.
He saves sinners by His grace.
He calls us to repentance, forgives us, and begins transforming our lives.
Your past does not have to be your future.
Your failures do not have to be your identity.
And your spiritual growth does not have to end where your understanding is today.
If you have been involved in genuine occult practices, turn away from them and seek Christ.
If you have participated in things that violated your conscience, confess them to God.
If you have condemned fellow believers without understanding Scripture, repent of that too.
If you have used Christian liberty to excuse spiritually destructive choices, bring those choices before the Lord.
And if you have been so afraid of making a mistake that your faith has become dominated by anxiety, remember the Savior who invites His people to trust Him.
Jesus does not call us to careless freedom.
He calls us to faithful freedom.
A freedom that is obedient.
A freedom that loves.
A freedom that refuses idolatry.
A freedom that does not enslave other believers to human rules.
A freedom that asks, again and again:
“Lord Jesus, how can I honor You here?”
So, should Christians participate in Halloween celebrations?
Christians must reject occult practices, idolatry, and activities that glorify genuine evil. But Scripture does not establish a universal prohibition against every modern Halloween custom.
Participation in ordinary, non-occult activities requires discernment concerning conscience, content, motives, influence, and love for others.
Some Christians will reasonably conclude that abstaining is the wisest and most faithful choice for their families.
Others may participate in carefully chosen activities without violating any clear biblical command.
Both should submit their decisions to Christ.
Neither should despise the other over matters Scripture leaves open to conscience.
And no believer should compromise a clear biblical command merely because a cultural tradition has become popular.
That is not a convenient answer.
It requires thought.
Prayer.
Humility.
Scripture.
Self-examination.
And sometimes the courage to disappoint people on either side of the debate.
But that is what following Jesus looks like.
It is not always easy.
It is not always popular.
And it cannot always be reduced to a slogan.

Tonight, when children are laughing in the streets, when families are gathering, when social media is overflowing with arguments, and when Christians are once again debating what should or should not happen on October 31, remember this:
Jesus Christ is Lord.
Not just on Sunday.
Not just during worship.
Not just when we open our Bibles.
He is Lord over our entertainment, traditions, relationships, homes, convictions, and decisions.
And one day, the greatest question will not be whether we won the Halloween argument.
It will be whether we truly belonged to Him.
Whether we trusted His Gospel.
Whether we followed His Word.
Whether we loved the people He placed around us.
Whether we allowed His grace to transform the way we lived.
So before you close this article, I want to ask you something personal.
Has this discussion exposed an area where you have been careless with your faith—or perhaps too quick to judge someone else's?
You don't need to pretend that you have everything figured out.

And if God has been teaching you to balance biblical conviction with Christlike love, share what you have learned. Your testimony might encourage another believer who is wrestling with the same question.
Because our mission is not to win arguments about holidays.
Our mission is to proclaim Christ.
And that mission requires more than one article.
It requires ongoing biblical teaching, discipleship, prayerful preparation, resources, and a community willing to help carry the Gospel message farther.
Scripture teaches:
“Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, ESV
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Not the idea that you must pay to prove your love for Jesus.
But a willing partnership in helping others hear His Word.
Pray for this ministry.
Share the Gospel.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Open your Bible with someone who is searching for truth.
A faithful witness is not measured by the amount of money someone gives.
It is measured by faithfulness to the Lord.
Because ministries are servants.
Christ is the Savior.
And He alone deserves the glory.
Now, before you return to the noise of the world, remember the little girl standing in front of the mirror.
The one who asked whether Jesus becomes sad when Christians celebrate Halloween.
Perhaps the most important thing her mother could teach her is not merely a rule about one evening.
It is how to open the Bible.
How to recognize genuine evil.
How to obey God with a sincere conscience.
How to treat people with kindness.
How to disagree without hatred.
How to repent when she is wrong.
And how to trust Jesus more than she fears the darkness.
Because long after the costumes are put away, the decorations disappear, and the candy is forgotten, that little girl will still need a Savior.
So will her mother.
So will the Christian who celebrates.
So will the Christian who abstains.
And so will you and I.
The greatest danger is not that darkness will own one night of the year, but that we might spend our lives debating the darkness while failing to surrender our hearts to the Light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “TAKE EVERY THOUGHT CAPTIVE”—THE VERSE CHRISTIANS KEEP QUOTING WITHOUT KNOWING WHAT PAUL WAS ACTUALLY FIGHTING
paragraphs: “TAKE EVERY THOUGHT CAPTIVE”—THE VERSE CHRISTIANS KEEP QUOTING WITHOUT KNOWING WHAT PAUL WAS ACTUALLY FIGHTING

You were told this verse was about silencing the thoughts inside your head. But when you discover the battlefield Paul was actually describing, you may never read 2 Corinthians 10:5 the same way again.
There is a kind of exhaustion that nobody sees.
You can be sitting in church, singing about the goodness of God, while your mind is somewhere else entirely.
You remember the sin you promised you would never commit again.
The conversation you keep replaying.
The person who wounded you.
The prayer that still seems unanswered.
The terrible thought that entered your mind while you were trying to worship.
And then, almost automatically, you hear a familiar Christian instruction:
“Take every thought captive.”
So you try.
You fight the thought. You condemn yourself for having it. You pray harder. You try to force your mind into silence.
But the harder you fight, the louder everything seems to become.
Eventually, a frightening question rises inside you.
What if the reason I cannot control my thoughts is that something is wrong with my faith?
And perhaps the most painful part is that you have been using a Bible verse to accuse yourself without ever being shown what that verse was actually saying.
Because when the apostle Paul wrote about taking every thought captive, he was not primarily giving anxious Christians a technique for stopping unwanted thoughts.
He was describing a spiritual conflict involving false claims, human arrogance, resistance to the knowledge of God, and the authority of Jesus Christ.
And that distinction matters.
Not because your private thought life is unimportant.
But because Scripture becomes dangerous in our hands when we turn a passage about the triumph of Christ's truth into another weapon of self-condemnation.
There is something much bigger happening in 2 Corinthians 10.
And once you see it, you may discover that the verse you have been using to fight yourself was actually pointing you toward the One who came to rescue you.
Before we go any further, consider this: What if the greatest stronghold in your life is not the thought you are ashamed of, but the lie you have believed about God because of it?
Paul wrote:

“For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war after the flesh: (For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;) Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ.”
— 2 Corinthians 10:3–5, King James Version
Read those words again, especially the words surrounding the famous command.
Paul speaks about warfare.
Strongholds.
Arguments.
Prideful opposition to the knowledge of God.
Captivity.
Obedience to Christ.
This is not merely a description of someone trying to stop thinking negatively while lying awake at midnight.

Paul is defending his apostolic ministry against opposition in Corinth. Some were challenging his authority, judging by outward appearances, and undermining his message. In the surrounding chapters, he confronts the influence of rival teachers and the danger of being led away from sincere devotion to Christ.
He is explaining that the power of his ministry does not come from worldly intimidation, impressive appearances, or fleshly methods.
It comes from God.
The battle concerns the truth of the Gospel and the claims that rise against it.
Now look at the original Greek.
The expression translated “taking every thought captive” is:
αἰχμαλωτίζοντες πᾶν νόημα
aichmalōtizontes pan noēma*
The participle αἰχμαλωτίζοντες (aichmalōtizontes) comes from a verb meaning to take captive, as one might capture a prisoner in warfare.
The phrase πᾶν νόημα (pan noēma) means “every thought,” “every conception,” or “every design,” depending on context.
And Paul continues:
εἰς τὴν ὑπακοὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ
eis tēn hypakoēn tou Christou
Meaning, “into obedience to Christ.”
This is important.
Paul is not describing thoughts floating helplessly through a person's consciousness as though every unwanted mental event must immediately be treated as a spiritual enemy.
He is using the language of conquest to describe bringing what opposes God's truth under the authority of Christ.
In the immediate context, the focus is on dismantling arguments and pretensions raised against the knowledge of God.
The Greek word λογισμούς (logismous) in verse 5 refers to reasonings, arguments, or calculations.
Paul says these are being torn down.
Why?
Because there are ways of thinking that set themselves against the truth of God.
And those ways of thinking can deceive entire communities.
They can distort the Gospel.
They can elevate human pride above divine revelation.
They can persuade people to trust outward power rather than the crucified and risen Savior.
That was no small matter in Corinth.
And it is no small matter today.
Think about how easily a lie can become a belief.
A belief becomes a conviction.
A conviction shapes decisions.
Decisions become habits.
And eventually, a person can build an entire life around something that was never true.
Someone hurts you, and you begin believing nobody can be trusted.
You fall into sin, and you begin believing you can never change.
You experience unanswered prayer, and you begin believing God has abandoned you.
You see another Christian prosper, and you begin believing God's love must be measured by visible success.
You suffer, and somewhere along the way, you begin treating your suffering as evidence that Christ has stopped caring.
Those conclusions are not necessarily the truth.
But they can begin to feel like truth when they have been repeated long enough.
And this is where Paul's words have a profound application to our personal lives, even though that was not the passage's primary focus.
The Gospel does not merely challenge what we do. It challenges what we believe.
And sometimes the most deeply rooted false belief is not that God is weak.
It is that His grace could never reach someone like you.
Perhaps you have carried that belief for years.
You know the language of Christianity.
You know when to say amen.
You know how to encourage someone else with Scripture.
But privately, you still measure your relationship with God by how well you performed this week.
When you pray consistently, you feel acceptable.
When you fail, you hide.
When you resist temptation, you feel close to God.
When you stumble, you imagine heaven turning its face away.
And without realizing it, you begin living as though Jesus saved you by grace but now keeps you by your flawless performance.
That is not the Gospel Paul preached.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of works.
Romans 8:1 announces:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That does not mean sin is harmless.
It does not mean repentance is optional.
It does not mean obedience is unimportant.
It means that the believer's acceptance before God rests upon Jesus Christ, not upon an imaginary record of uninterrupted perfection.
And when you understand that, something begins to change.
You stop treating every spiritual struggle as proof that you do not belong to God.
You begin learning to distinguish conviction from condemnation.
Conviction exposes sin and calls you back to Christ.
Condemnation tells you that returning is pointless.
Conviction agrees with the holiness of God.
Hopeless condemnation denies the sufficiency of His mercy.
The Holy Spirit does not need to lie about your identity to lead you into repentance.
He reveals the truth.
And the truth always brings us face-to-face with Jesus.
But there is another misunderstanding we need to confront.
Some Christians have been taught that every disturbing, intrusive, fearful, or unwanted thought is a spiritual failure.
That if a blasphemous thought suddenly enters their mind, they have somehow chosen it.
That if they experience anxiety, they must not trust God enough.
That if a frightening image appears without invitation, they are responsible for its arrival.
But Scripture does not teach that every involuntary thought is equivalent to a deliberate act of rebellion.
A thought entering your awareness is not necessarily the same as agreeing with it, cherishing it, or acting upon it.
And 2 Corinthians 10:5 should not be used to erase that distinction.
Jesus Himself was tempted, yet without sin, as Hebrews 4:15 teaches.
His temptation was real.
His holiness was never compromised.
That does not make every kind of mental experience identical to Christ's temptation. But it does establish something essential: experiencing temptation is not, by itself, the same as committing sin.
And if you are someone who struggles with recurring intrusive thoughts, you do not need to interpret every unwanted thought as evidence of spiritual defeat.
Sometimes an anxious mind produces thoughts that are unwanted precisely because they contradict what a person loves and values.
You may need prayer.
You may need wise pastoral support.
You may also benefit from qualified mental-health care, especially if those thoughts become persistent and distressing.
Seeking such help is not a betrayal of faith.
And turning Paul's military metaphor into an endless ritual of monitoring and suppressing every mental event can actually deepen the suffering of someone already overwhelmed.
Christ did not call His people to live in constant terror of their own minds.
He called them to follow Him in truth.
And that brings us to a question that may be uncomfortable.
Are we actually taking thoughts captive to Christ, or have we sometimes taken people captive to religious fear?
Because there is a difference.
A person can quote Scripture accurately and still apply it carelessly.
A person can preach obedience while forgetting mercy.
A person can talk about spiritual warfare while wounding the very people Christ came to restore.
Paul himself warned against distorted teaching.
In 2 Corinthians 11:3, he expressed concern that the Corinthians might be led away from sincere and pure devotion to Christ.
Notice where his concern ultimately points.
Christ.
Not Paul's reputation.
Not a religious personality.
Not the appearance of spiritual superiority.
Christ.
And when Paul defended his authority, he explained that it was given for building believers up, not tearing them down (2 Corinthians 10:8).
That should humble every Christian who teaches, posts, preaches, or shares Scripture.
Including us.
Because the purpose of biblical truth is not to make wounded people more afraid of approaching Jesus.
It is to expose what is false and lead people into faithful submission to the One who is true.
Now consider something even more searching.
What happens when the false argument we must confront is one that makes us feel spiritually superior?
What happens when we believe that our knowledge makes us better than other Christians?
What happens when we begin treating people who struggle as though they are beneath us?
What happens when we know how to defend doctrine but have forgotten how to love our neighbor?
Those, too, are patterns of thinking that must bow before Christ.
The proud imagination is not always found in the unbeliever.
Sometimes it is sitting in a church pew, holding a Bible, and silently thanking God that it is not like everyone else.
Jesus exposed that very attitude in the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector in Luke 18:9–14.
One man boasted about his righteousness.
The other pleaded for mercy.
And Jesus said the repentant tax collector went home justified rather than the self-exalting Pharisee.
Imagine that.
The man who appeared religiously impressive was not the example Jesus wanted His listeners to imitate.
The man who knew he needed mercy was.
There is a scandal in grace that human pride cannot tolerate.
We want to believe that the people who have done the most good deserve the closest place to God.
But the Gospel announces that sinners are reconciled to God through the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Not through the illusion that they were never sinners.
Not through public admiration.
Not through religious performance.
Through Christ.
The cross destroys every argument that says we can save ourselves.
It also destroys every argument that says a repentant sinner is beyond the reach of God's mercy.
At Calvary, our sin was not minimized.
It was confronted with unimaginable seriousness.
And God's love was not merely spoken.
It was demonstrated.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we learned to control every thought perfectly.
While we were yet sinners.
That is grace.
And grace is not permission to remain enslaved to sin.
It is the undeserved mercy that brings us to the Savior who forgives, renews, and teaches us to walk in obedience.
Titus 2:11–12 explains that the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live godly lives.
True grace does not leave us unchanged.
But neither does it demand that we transform ourselves before we are allowed to come to Christ.
Think of Peter.
He had walked with Jesus.
He had heard His teaching.
He had witnessed His miracles.
He had confidently declared his loyalty.
And then, when the pressure came, Peter denied knowing Him.
Three times.
Imagine the shame of remembering your own voice saying you did not know the One you loved.
Imagine hearing the rooster crow.
Imagine realizing that your confidence in yourself had collapsed.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that Peter went out and wept bitterly.
That was not a small failure.
But Peter's story did not end in the courtyard.
After the resurrection, Jesus met him again.
In John 21, the risen Christ questioned Peter about his love and entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
Peter's denial was real.
His grief was real.
His restoration was real.
And the risen Jesus was greater than Peter's worst moment.
This is what makes the Gospel different from a motivational speech.
A motivational speech tells you to believe in yourself.
The Gospel tells you that your hope rests in the crucified and risen Christ.
A motivational speech tells you to become strong enough to overcome your past.
The Gospel tells you that Jesus died for sinners, rose again, and calls them into a new life of repentance and faith.
A motivational speech says your story is yours to rewrite.
The Gospel declares that Jesus Christ is the Redeemer who can transform a life that seemed ruined.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by removing the need for repentance.
But by forgiving sinners and making them new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
And here is the beautiful connection.
The same letter that speaks about taking every thought captive also proclaims reconciliation through Christ.
The same apostle who confronts arrogant arguments also pleads with people to be reconciled to God.
The same Paul who speaks of spiritual warfare declares in 2 Corinthians 12:9 that Christ's grace is sufficient and His strength is made perfect in weakness.
So if you read 2 Corinthians 10:5 and come away believing that Christianity is fundamentally about winning a private battle of perfect mental control, you have missed the greater story.
The passage is about the supremacy of Christ over what opposes the knowledge of God.
And its faithful application to our thought life must remain rooted in that truth.
Yes, examine what you believe.
Yes, reject lies that contradict Scripture.
Yes, repent of thoughts you deliberately nurture that lead toward pride, hatred, lust, deceit, or rebellion.
Yes, renew your mind, as Romans 12:2 teaches.
Yes, direct your attention toward what is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, and praiseworthy, as Philippians 4:8 encourages.
But do not confuse spiritual maturity with the absence of every unwanted thought.
Do not confuse obedience with pretending you never struggle.
And do not confuse the voice of shame with the voice of the Shepherd.
The Christian life is not a performance in which we must convince God that we are worth saving.
It is a life of trusting, following, and being transformed by the Savior who has already accomplished what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
And maybe that is what you need to hear tonight.
Maybe you have spent years trying to defeat a thought when you needed to confront a lie.
The lie that your past has the final word.
The lie that one failure erased every evidence of God's work in you.
The lie that you must hide until you are worthy to pray again.
The lie that Jesus welcomes everyone except the person you see in the mirror.
Bring those claims into the light of Scripture.
Do they agree with the Gospel?
Do they agree with the cross?
Do they agree with the resurrection?
Do they agree with the invitation of Christ, who said in John 6:37:
“...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
That is not an invitation to cherish sin.
It is an invitation to come to the Savior.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come without pretending that your wounds are healed or that your sins were insignificant.
Come because Christ is sufficient.
And if you have been using “take every thought captive” as a reason to hate yourself, perhaps today is the day to stop making your own mind the center of the battlefield.
Turn your eyes toward Jesus.
Study His Word in context.
Test what you hear, including what you hear from Christian pages and ministries.
Let His truth expose your pride and your despair alike.
Let His mercy lead you to repentance.
Let His resurrection remind you that failure and death do not have the final victory over those who belong to Him.
And when a lie rises against the knowledge of God, do not answer it merely with your own willpower.
Answer it with the truth of Christ.
When shame says, “There is no hope for you,” remember the cross.
When pride says, “You do not need mercy,” remember the cross.
When fear says, “God cannot be trusted,” remember the character of the Savior who laid down His life for His sheep.
When sin says, “You can never change,” remember that the risen Christ gives His people new life.
And when religious performance says, “You must earn the right to be loved,” remember that salvation is a gift of grace.
There is no greater stronghold-breaking truth than the Gospel rightly understood and faithfully believed.
And perhaps you are realizing that you have never truly surrendered to Jesus.
You have admired Christianity.
You have quoted verses.
You have shared religious content.
You may even have defended the faith in public.
But deep inside, you know that you have been trusting yourself more than Christ.
You cannot argue your way into salvation.
You cannot donate your way into forgiveness.
You cannot earn eternal life by sharing Christian posts.
Salvation is found in Jesus Christ.
He died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Turn from sin and trust Him.
Not because you have finally become worthy.
But because He is the worthy Savior.
And if your heart is weary, you can pray something as simple as this:

“Lord Jesus, I have believed things about You that were not true. I have trusted my own strength, hidden behind shame, and sometimes confused fear with faith. Forgive my sins. Teach me to understand Your Word faithfully. Expose the lies I have believed, and lead me into obedience through Your grace. I do not want merely to control my thoughts. I want to know You, trust You, and follow You. Have mercy on me, Lord. Make my life a testimony of Your redeeming power. Amen.”
There is no magic in repeating a prayer.
The hope is in the living Christ to whom we turn in repentance and faith.
And if this message has uncovered something you have been carrying silently, I want to invite you into a moment of honesty.
You do not have to reveal private details or explain wounds you are not ready to discuss.
But perhaps your honest words will remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
Perhaps someone reading the comments tonight has been quietly wondering whether there is still room for them at the feet of Jesus.
Let our words point them toward His mercy.
And please, do not allow this truth to end with you.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because someone among your family, friends, or acquaintances may be carrying a burden that this passage has been mistakenly used to intensify.
Someone may be exhausted from fighting thoughts they never chose.
Someone may be living beneath a religious burden Christ never placed upon them.
Someone may be one Scripture passage, rightly explained, away from recognizing that the Gospel is better news than they imagined.
Invite your family, your Christian friends, those who have drifted from church, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along.
Because we do not want to build a community that merely knows how to quote the Bible.
We want to grow into a community that understands Scripture, follows Jesus, and lives the Gospel.
Not because God will love you more.
Not because a paid membership is a biblical requirement for faithful discipleship.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion. Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”

If Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture more faithfully, brought encouragement during a difficult season, or pointed you back to Jesus when you were drifting, you may choose to make this ministry part of your regular Christian giving.
And every supporter matters.
Not because a contribution purchases spiritual blessing, but because faithful ministry requires time, effort, resources, and people willing to help.
We want more people to discover these resources.
More struggling believers to be encouraged.
More seekers to encounter the message of salvation.
More families to open the Scriptures together.
More Christians to move beyond inspirational quotations into a deeper, faithful understanding of God's Word.
It is the opportunity to stand alongside a ministry committed to making much of Jesus Christ.
If you are not able, please do not feel ashamed.
You are welcome here.
Not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to turn biblical truth into a product.
But to proclaim the Savior whose grace is greater than our shame and whose Word deserves to be understood faithfully.
Because somewhere, a person is still reading 2 Corinthians 10:5 and believing they are a failure because their mind will not become quiet.
Somewhere, a believer is still confusing an unwanted thought with a chosen sin.
Somewhere, someone has accepted the lie that one terrible chapter has permanently disqualified them from God's mercy.
And somewhere, another person is beginning to discover that Jesus Christ is far greater than the distorted picture of Him they have carried for years.
That is why context matters.
That is why truth matters.
That is why grace matters.
And that is why we must never settle for using Scripture as a collection of powerful-sounding sentences detached from the Gospel they were given to proclaim.
Paul did not write about taking thoughts captive so that Christians would become prisoners of fear.
He was declaring the power of God to overthrow opposition to divine truth and bring every thought into submission to Christ.
The proper response is not to make ourselves the savior of our own minds.
It is to submit our thinking, our pride, our fears, our beliefs, and our entire lives to Jesus Christ.
The One who was crucified.
The One who rose again.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who forgives.
The One who restores.
The One who transforms.
And the One whose grace can reach into the most shame-filled chapters of a human life and write a future that the past could never have predicted.
So the next time someone tells you to take every thought captive, remember what Paul was actually saying.
Do not simply ask, “How can I make this thought disappear?”
Ask, “Does what I am believing agree with the truth of Jesus Christ?”
And when you discover that it does not, bring that belief before the Lord, open His Word, and learn to walk in His truth.
Because the goal was never to become a person who never struggles.
The goal is to belong to Christ, know His truth, and grow in obedience to Him.

Your darkest thought does not have to become your identity, your worst failure does not have to become your ending, and your deepest shame does not have to be the final word—because the final word belongs to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “HEAP BURNING COALS ON HIS HEAD” — DID GOD REALLY TELL YOU TO HURT YOUR ENEMIES WITH KINDNESS?
paragraphs: “HEAP BURNING COALS ON HIS HEAD” — DID GOD REALLY TELL YOU TO HURT YOUR ENEMIES WITH KINDNESS?

The shocking truth behind Romans 12:20 that exposes the difference between Christian love and disguised revenge—and why the people who wounded you may reveal something about the condition of your own heart.
There is a kind of revenge that looks so holy, even Christians can mistake it for obedience.
You smile at someone who betrayed you.
You speak gently to someone who humiliated you.
You help someone who would never lift a finger to help you.
And somewhere deep inside, where nobody else can hear your thoughts, you whisper:
“Just wait. God will make you regret what you did to me.”
You call it kindness.
You call it taking the high road.
You might even quote Scripture to justify it.
“If thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head.” — Romans 12:20 (KJV)
There it is.
The verse that sounds like heaven has finally given you permission to burn someone without touching them.
Be kind enough to make them suffer.
Love them until they feel guilty.
Bless them so dramatically that they cannot escape the shame of what they did.
And when they finally break under the weight of your goodness, you can quietly congratulate yourself for obeying God.
But what if that is not what Paul meant?
What if the very Scripture you have been using to justify your secret desire for revenge is actually confronting that desire?
What if those burning coals were never meant to become another weapon in your hands?
And what if the most uncomfortable part of Romans 12:20 is not what God might do to your enemy...
But what He is asking to change inside you?
Because sometimes the person we want God to humble is not the only person who needs to repent.
Sometimes the fire reaches our own hearts first.
If anyone could have justified revenge, it was Him.
Yet the cross tells a radically different story.
To understand why, we have to return to the actual words of Scripture.
Paul writes in Romans 12:19:
Notice what Paul says before he mentions the burning coals.
Do not avenge yourselves.
Not with your fists.
Not with your words.
Not through public humiliation.
Not through carefully arranged acts of kindness designed to make someone feel small.
The Greek word translated “avenge” comes from ekdikeō (ἐκδικέω), meaning to exact justice, avenge, or vindicate.
Paul is not saying injustice is imaginary. He is not telling wounded people to pretend their suffering never happened.
He is telling believers that personal vengeance does not belong in their hands.
Then he quotes the Lord's declaration from Deuteronomy 32:35: “To me belongeth vengeance, and recompence” (KJV).
God is not indifferent to evil.
He sees what happened.
He knows what was said behind your back.
He knows the promises that were broken, the money that was stolen, the lies that damaged your reputation, the trust that was exploited, and the tears you wiped away when nobody was watching.
But God's perfect knowledge of injustice does not give us permission to become instruments of personal revenge.
And then Paul continues:
“Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head.” — Romans 12:20 (KJV)
Paul is quoting Proverbs 25:21–22.
This command did not suddenly appear in the New Testament. Its roots reach back into the wisdom literature of ancient Israel.
The Hebrew of Proverbs 25:22 includes these words:
כִּי גֶחָלִים אַתָּה חֹתֶה עַל־רֹאשׁוֹ
Ki geḥalim attah ḥoteh ʿal-rosho.
Literally, the phrase speaks of gathering or heaping burning coals upon his head.
The Hebrew word geḥalim (גֶחָלִים) means burning coals or embers. The verb ḥoteh (חֹתֶה), from ḥātāh, conveys the action of taking up or gathering coals.
In Romans, the corresponding Greek expression is:
ἄνθρακας πυρὸς σωρεύσεις ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ
Anthrakas pyros sōreuseis epi tēn kephalēn autou.
“You will heap burning coals upon his head.”
The Greek verb sōreuō (σωρεύω) means to heap up or pile together.
The image is intense.
Paul does not soften it.
But the crucial question is what the image means within the passage.

Some interpreters understand the burning coals as a picture of painful shame or remorse that may lead an enemy toward repentance. Others emphasize the possibility of divine judgment upon someone who persists in evil despite receiving kindness.

The precise background of the metaphor remains debated. A frequently repeated explanation connects it to an ancient Egyptian repentance ritual involving coals carried on the head, but that specific historical explanation is not firmly established and should not be presented as proven biblical fact.
What we can say with confidence is that neither Proverbs nor Romans authorizes believers to use kindness as a method of psychological torture.
Why?
Because Paul immediately explains the moral direction of his teaching:
“Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.” — Romans 12:21 (KJV)
Overcome evil with good.
Not with disguised evil.
Not with spiritualized cruelty.
Not with a smile concealing the desire to see someone destroyed.
With good.
The Greek word translated “good” is agathos (ἀγαθός), describing what is good in a moral sense.
And the command to overcome evil carries the language of victory.
Paul is calling believers to resist being conquered by evil and to defeat its influence through genuine goodness.
Think about that.
If somebody's hatred turns you into a hateful person, what has happened?
Their evil has begun to shape your character.
If their cruelty teaches you to enjoy cruelty, even when disguised as righteousness, their sin has gained influence over your heart.
If their betrayal makes revenge the organizing purpose of your life, the wound has become a master.
You may have escaped the person.
But have you escaped what their actions are doing inside you?
That is the question Romans 12 refuses to let us avoid.
And it is painful because some of us have been carrying our enemies inside our hearts for years.
You still remember the conversation.
The exact words.
The look on their face.
The moment you realized someone you trusted was capable of hurting you so deeply.
Maybe it was a spouse who shattered your marriage.
A friend who exposed something private.
A church leader who abused spiritual authority.
A relative who treated you like you were disposable.
A business partner who took advantage of your generosity.
Or someone who wounded you and then carried on with life as though nothing happened.
You tried to pray.
You tried to move forward.
You told people you had forgiven them.
But then you saw them smiling in a photograph.
Enjoying success.
Receiving applause.
Being celebrated by people who had no idea what they had done.
And something inside you screamed:
“Lord, how can they be happy after what they did to me?”
That question is more human than many Christians are willing to admit.
Scripture itself contains cries for justice.
The Psalms are filled with wounded people bringing their anguish before God.
Biblical faith does not require emotional dishonesty.
But there is a difference between asking God for justice and demanding that God satisfy our appetite for revenge.
There is a difference between grieving over wickedness and secretly hoping another human being becomes miserable.
And there is a difference between wanting someone to repent and wanting someone to suffer.
Repentance seeks transformation.
Revenge seeks repayment.
The Gospel calls us to surrender vengeance to the only Judge who sees every heart without distortion.
But please understand something equally important.
Forgiveness is not the same as reconciliation.
And kindness does not mean abandoning wisdom.
Romans 12:20 does not require an abused person to return to an unsafe home.
It does not require a victim to conceal a crime.
It does not demand that someone continue lending money to a person who repeatedly exploits them.
It does not mean giving an unrepentant offender unrestricted access to your children, your finances, your home, or your emotional life.
You can forgive while maintaining necessary boundaries.
You can refuse revenge while seeking lawful justice.
You can pray for someone's repentance while reporting wrongdoing to appropriate authorities.
You can love an enemy without pretending that enemy is trustworthy.
Romans 13, immediately following Paul's teaching on overcoming evil, recognizes the legitimate role of governing authorities in restraining and punishing wrongdoing.
The same Bible that commands personal mercy does not erase public justice.
And if you are still in danger, seeking protection is not a failure of Christian love.
It is entirely possible to refuse hatred and still say:
“You cannot keep hurting me.”
That is not revenge.
That is a boundary.
Now consider the greater shock of this passage.
Jesus did not merely command His followers to love enemies.
He lived it.
In Matthew 5:44, He says:
“Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you.” (KJV)
These words are not permission to manipulate enemies into feeling guilty.
They are a call to reflect the character of our heavenly Father.
Jesus continues by reminding His listeners that God causes His sun to rise on the evil and the good and sends rain upon the just and unjust.
God's generosity exposes how narrow our own love can become.
We are often willing to love those who appreciate us.
We are willing to help those who thank us.
We are willing to forgive those who apologize beautifully.
But what happens when the person does not apologize?
What happens when they never acknowledge the damage?
What happens when your kindness is met with indifference?
What happens when obedience brings no satisfying emotional ending?
Will you still obey Jesus?
That is where love stops being a performance.
That is where the Gospel begins to confront our motives.
Because if your kindness only feels worthwhile when your enemy suffers, you may not be seeking their good at all.
You may simply be looking for a more respectable way to retaliate.
And here is where the story becomes deeply personal.
There was a time when you were not merely someone wounded by sin.
You were also someone guilty of sin.
So was I.
The Bible does not divide humanity into innocent people who need kindness and guilty people who deserve only contempt.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” (KJV)
All.
The betrayer and the betrayed.
The offender and the wounded.
That does not make every wrongdoing equally severe. It does not remove the responsibility of those who commit terrible harm.
But it does mean that none of us can stand before a holy God claiming to be righteous through our own merit.
And Romans 5:8 delivers the truth that changes everything:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after we cleaned up our lives.
Not after we became worthy of His affection.
Not after we apologized perfectly.
Christ died for us while we were still guilty.
Then Romans 5:10 goes further:
“For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life.” (KJV)
Did you catch that word?
Enemies.
We were enemies.
And instead of leaving sinners without hope, God acted in love through His Son to make reconciliation possible.
The eternal Son of God took on human flesh.
Jesus lived the righteous life we could never live perfectly.
He bore our sins upon the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
He did not come merely to teach wounded people how to become emotionally stronger.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to break the dominion of sin and death.
He came to give new life to people who could never rescue themselves.
And suddenly Romans 12:20 becomes far more than a lesson about difficult relationships.
It becomes a window into the transforming power of the Gospel.
Because Christians are not called to show mercy in order to earn salvation.
We are called to show mercy because we have received mercy through Jesus Christ.
We do not forgive because sin is harmless.
We forgive because we know what it cost our Savior to deal with sin.
We do not abandon revenge because justice is unimportant.
We abandon personal vengeance because God is perfectly just.
And we do not love enemies because we are naturally better than they are.
We love because Christ first loved us.
Now picture Calvary.
The soldiers have driven nails through the hands and feet of Jesus.
His body is wounded.
His enemies mock Him.
Religious leaders ridicule Him.
People who witnessed His compassion now stand near the cross as He suffers.
The One who healed the sick is being treated as a criminal.
The One who welcomed sinners is being rejected.
The One who never sinned is suffering under the weight of human wickedness.
And Luke 23:34 records Jesus saying:
“Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.” (KJV)
This saying is preserved in many ancient manuscripts, although some early witnesses omit it, a textual detail worth acknowledging when studying the passage carefully.
Yet the prayer itself beautifully accords with the mercy Jesus taught throughout His ministry.
He did not celebrate the evil done to Him.
He did not declare His executioners innocent.
He did not pretend the cross was anything other than an act of terrible injustice.
He prayed.
And His prayer revealed a mercy deeper than human instinct.
That mercy did not make repentance unnecessary.
It revealed the heart of the Savior through whom forgiveness is offered.
And perhaps this is what makes the command to love enemies so difficult.
We want our enemies to feel the weight of their sin.
But Jesus also wants us to remember the weight of ours.
We want God to confront what they have done.
And He may.
But He also confronts what we have become while carrying the wound.
We want their hearts to break.
Yet perhaps our own hearts have become hard in places we no longer notice.
Have you ever replayed someone's failure because remembering it made you feel morally superior?
Have you ever imagined the day they would come crawling back, finally admitting that you were right?
Have you ever offered help while secretly hoping your generosity would humiliate them?
Have you ever prayed, “Lord, bless them,” while quietly hoping the blessing would never arrive?
These are uncomfortable questions.
But grace often begins its deepest work where our carefully managed religious image starts to crack.
And maybe you have just recognized yourself.
Not in the betrayal you suffered.
Not in the wrong someone committed against you.
But in the bitterness you have been protecting ever since.
If that is where you are, do not hide behind another spiritual performance.
Come to Christ honestly.
You do not have to call evil good.
You do not have to manufacture feelings you do not possess.
You do not have to pretend the wound has healed.
You can say:
“Lord Jesus, I am still angry.”
“I still want them to understand what they did.”
“Sometimes I want them to hurt the way I hurt.”
“I know You are calling me away from revenge, but I cannot change my heart by pretending.”
“Have mercy on me. Teach me to love without surrendering truth.”
That is not a polished prayer.
But it is an honest one.
And the God who knows your heart already is not impressed by a mask.
He calls you to come into the light.
The Greek word often translated “repentance” is metanoia (μετάνοια), referring to a change of mind or disposition, and in the New Testament it belongs to the larger call to turn from sin toward God.
Repentance is more than feeling bad.
It involves turning.
Turning away from cherished bitterness.
Turning away from the fantasy of revenge.
Turning away from the belief that your enemy's destruction is necessary for your healing.
And turning toward Jesus Christ, who alone can forgive sin and transform the human heart.
This does not mean emotional pain disappears immediately.
Some wounds take time to process.
Some situations require wise counsel, accountability, protection, and patient recovery.
Forgiveness may be a settled commitment that you must repeatedly bring before God when old memories return.
And sometimes the first evidence of change is not that you suddenly feel affection for someone who harmed you.
It is that you stop feeding the desire to destroy them.
You stop rehearsing imaginary revenge.
You stop arranging your goodness as a public accusation.
You stop measuring your freedom by whether they finally admit they were wrong.
You begin to pray for truth.
For justice.
For repentance.
For protection of those who might otherwise be harmed.
And, where possible, for their genuine restoration through Christ.
That is not weakness.
That is what it looks like when the Gospel begins to loosen sin's grip on a wounded heart.
But there is another danger.
Some Christians hear this teaching and immediately turn it into pressure against wounded people.
They say, “You must forgive,” but never confront the person who committed the evil.
They demand reconciliation without repentance.
They tell victims to be silent in order to preserve a church's reputation.
They use biblical language to protect powerful offenders.
That is not what Romans 12 teaches.
Biblical mercy must never become a shelter for ongoing abuse.
Christian love does not rejoice in unrighteousness.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 13:6 that love “rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth” (KJV).
Truth matters.
Accountability matters.
Justice matters.
And sometimes loving an offender means refusing to enable their continued wrongdoing.
Sometimes the most merciful thing you can do is tell the truth and allow legitimate consequences to follow.
The purpose is not revenge.
It is righteousness, protection, and, where God grants it, repentance.
And now we return to those burning coals.
What if your enemy feels ashamed because you refuse to retaliate?
That may happen.
What if your kindness becomes part of what awakens their conscience?
That may happen too.
What if they repent, seek forgiveness, and begin to change?
Praise God.
But what if they do none of those things?
What if they laugh at your kindness?
What if they interpret your mercy as weakness?
What if they never confess?
What if they die without ever telling you they were sorry?
Does that mean your obedience failed?
No.
Because Romans 12:20 is not a promise that your kindness will force repentance.
It is a command governing how you respond to evil.
You cannot control another person's conscience.
You cannot manufacture another person's repentance.
You cannot save someone by being sufficiently kind.
Only God can change the heart, and salvation comes through Jesus Christ.
Your responsibility is not to become the Holy Spirit in somebody else's life.
Your responsibility is to obey the Lord who has shown you mercy.
And that obedience may be unseen.
It may happen when you choose not to publish the humiliating details you know about someone.
When you refuse to return an insult.
When you give truthful testimony without embellishment.
When you stop encouraging others to hate someone on your behalf.
When you pray for an offender's repentance while still maintaining necessary distance.
When you refuse to let bitterness become the inheritance you pass to your children.
These moments may never go viral.
Nobody may applaud them.
Your enemy may never notice.
But your Father sees.
And sometimes the most significant victory is not that your enemy finally admits defeat.
It is that their sin no longer dictates who you are becoming.
This is why the Gospel Warrior message matters so deeply:
Not because every earthly scandal receives a beautiful public resolution.
Not because every broken relationship is restored.
Not because every offender repents.
But because Jesus can redeem sinners, transform lives, sustain the wounded, and give eternal hope even when earthly circumstances remain painfully unfinished.
The cross was the place where human injustice and divine mercy met in a way no human being could have invented.
And the resurrection declared that sin, death, and the grave would not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
Your past does not have to become your identity.
Your wounds do not have to become your master.
Your bitterness does not have to become your future.
And your enemy does not have to become the center of your story.
Jesus Christ is worthy of that place.
Maybe you came into this article looking for permission to make someone regret hurting you.
But now you realize the Lord is inviting you into something far greater than revenge.
Freedom from being ruled by it.
Not freedom from accountability.
Not freedom from consequences.
Not freedom from grief.
But freedom to belong wholeheartedly to Christ, even while healing.
And if this has exposed something you have kept hidden, I want to invite you to respond with spiritual honesty.
You do not need to describe your trauma publicly or reveal the identity of anyone who harmed you. God knows the details you are not ready to share.
Someone reading may desperately need to know that God's grace is not a theory.
There is also someone on your Facebook friends list who needs this truth.
Perhaps they are angry at a former spouse.
Perhaps they are quietly planning revenge against someone who betrayed them.
Perhaps they have confused forgiveness with returning to danger.
Or perhaps they are the person who has caused harm and desperately needs to repent.
Because the next time anger rises, you may need to remember that overcoming evil with good is not the same as pretending evil never happened.
Every soul matters.
Every opportunity to make the Gospel known matters.
And there is something else I want to share with you.
Gospel Warrior is not meant to be merely another page that fills your feed with religious words.
Our desire is to help people encounter Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in biblical discernment, turn from sin, find encouragement in Christ, and become more deeply rooted in the Word of God.
We want biblical nourishment to reach people who may not be able to afford shelves full of Christian books.
We want believers to have resources they can return to when their faith is tested.
We want families to have teaching they can share.
And we want the message of salvation through Jesus Christ to reach beyond the limits of one post, one page, or one person's voice.
But continuing and expanding this work requires real support.
You do not have to pay to glorify Jesus.
And you should never feel that your financial circumstances make you less valuable to this community.
It is the opportunity to participate in a mission that points people beyond themselves and toward the Savior.
But only Jesus Christ can save a soul.
That distinction must never be lost.
Before you leave, I want you to imagine something.
Imagine standing before the Lord one day.
The memories of those who wounded you no longer rule your heart.
The unfinished arguments no longer demand another hearing.
The hunger for revenge has finally lost its voice.
Not because evil was insignificant.
Not because justice was abandoned.
But because you are standing before the righteous Savior who knows every truth, judges with perfect justice, and makes all things new.
And in His presence, the thing that once seemed impossible to surrender no longer owns you.
Perhaps that work of surrender can begin today.
Not when your enemy apologizes.
Not when they suffer.
Not when they finally understand your pain.
Today.
You can bring the wound to Jesus.
You can repent of the revenge you have cherished.
You can ask for grace to respond truthfully and wisely.
You can take the necessary steps to protect yourself and others.
You can trust that the Lord sees what you cannot resolve.
And you can remember that the One who calls you to overcome evil with good is the very One who has already conquered sin and death through His cross and resurrection.
So no, Romans 12:20 is not Jesus teaching you how to hurt someone through kindness.
It is Scripture calling you away from vengeance and toward the kind of goodness that refuses to become another form of evil.
The burning coals are not yours to weaponize.
The judgment is not yours to control.
The repentance of another person is not yours to manufacture.
But your heart can be surrendered to Christ.
And His grace is sufficient for the journey of obedience that follows.
Because the greatest miracle may not be watching the person who hurt you finally burn with regret—but watching Jesus remove the hatred that was slowly burning you alive.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD COMMANDED AN ENTIRE NATION TO CURSE THESE SINS OUT LOUD—BUT WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE GUILTY PERSON IS SOMEONE YOU LOVE?
paragraphs: GOD COMMANDED AN ENTIRE NATION TO CURSE THESE SINS OUT LOUD—BUT WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE GUILTY PERSON IS SOMEONE YOU LOVE?

The terrifying public declarations of Deuteronomy 27:20–23 reveal why God refuses to call sexual betrayal a private matter—and why the same Bible that exposes hidden sin ultimately leads us to the cross, where Jesus Christ offers forgiveness, justice, and the possibility of a completely different ending.
There are sins people confess.
And there are sins families bury.

Some are hidden behind locked doors. Some behind respected surnames. Some behind Sunday clothes, polished reputations, and photographs of smiling relatives who have learned never to mention what happened.
Sometimes everyone knows.
But nobody speaks.
The victim is told to move on. The offender is protected because of his position. The family reputation becomes more important than the wounded person. And silence is renamed peace.
Then you open the Bible.
And suddenly, you encounter something almost impossible to imagine.
God commanded an entire nation to stand together and publicly pronounce curses against certain sexual violations committed within the family.
Not whisper about them.
Not excuse them because the offender was influential.
Not pretend they were harmless because they happened behind closed doors.
Publicly declare them.
And the people were commanded to answer:
“Amen.”
Think about that.

The very God who would later reveal the fullness of His mercy in Jesus Christ also required His covenant people to acknowledge, in public, that certain hidden acts were utterly unacceptable before Him.
Why?
Why would the God of love demand such a solemn declaration?
And what does that mean for someone who has committed a shameful sin, someone who has been wounded by another person's sin, or someone who has spent years pretending that nothing happened?
Stay with this, because the answer is not simply about ancient Israel.
It is about holiness.
It is about the danger of protecting evil with silence.
And, ultimately, it is about a Savior who does not need to deny the seriousness of sin in order to rescue sinners.
In Deuteronomy 27, Moses instructed Israel concerning a covenant ceremony to take place after the people entered the land God had promised them.

Six tribes were to stand on Mount Gerizim in connection with the blessing, and six on Mount Ebal in connection with the curse. The Levites would pronounce solemn covenant declarations, and the people would respond.
This was not a spectacle invented to humiliate selected individuals. It was a national acknowledgment of the moral obligations of God's covenant.
Israel was being taught that obedience to God could not be separated from the way people treated one another, including those within their own households.
Then came words that should still make us tremble.
Deuteronomy 27:20 declares in the King James Version:
“Cursed be he that lieth with his father's wife; because he uncovereth his father's skirt. And all the people shall say, Amen.”
The Hebrew begins:
אָרוּר שֹׁכֵב עִם־אֵשֶׁת אָבִיו
Arur shokhev im-eshet aviv.
Meaning, in context:
“Cursed is the one who lies with his father's wife.”
The word אָרוּר (arur) means “cursed.” It is a solemn declaration of covenant judgment, not an invitation for the crowd to unleash personal revenge.

The expression translated “his father's wife” is significant. It identifies a woman through her marital relationship to the man's father. This prohibition includes a stepmother and should not be reduced merely to the biological mother-son relationship.
The verse goes further by explaining that the act dishonors the father's marital relationship and violates the boundaries God established.
This is not simply about an ancient society being uncomfortable with an unconventional relationship.
It is about a fundamental betrayal of family boundaries.
And the congregation was required to say, “Amen.”
In Hebrew:
אָמֵן (amen).
The word expresses affirmation—something like “truly,” or “so be it.”
Imagine standing among thousands of people and hearing the declaration.
You could not pretend that God had never spoken.
You could not honestly say that family relationships were morally unimportant.
You were being called to affirm that God's judgment was right.
Then came another declaration.
Deuteronomy 27:22:
“Cursed be he that lieth with his sister, the daughter of his father, or the daughter of his mother. And all the people shall say, Amen.”
The Hebrew expression אֲחֹתוֹ (achoto) means “his sister.”
The wording expressly includes a sister through either parent, covering the relevant half-sibling relationships as well.
This prohibition was not based on whether the relationship could be kept secret.
It was not suspended because two people claimed they had developed feelings.
It was not erased because nobody outside the household knew.
God's moral boundaries were not determined by the likelihood of discovery.
And again, the people answered:
“Amen.”
Then Deuteronomy 27:23:
“Cursed be he that lieth with his mother in law. And all the people shall say, Amen.”
The Hebrew word חֹתַנְתּוֹ (chotanto) refers to his mother-in-law.
Once again, the command addresses sexual conduct that violates an established family relationship.
The passage also includes another prohibition that must not be overlooked.
Deuteronomy 27:21 declares:
“Cursed be he that lieth with any manner of beast. And all the people shall say, Amen.”
This verse concerns bestiality, not incest. It appears within the same sequence of public declarations and shows that the passage addresses more than one category of forbidden sexual behavior.
The Bible is specific.
And when we speak about Scripture, we must be specific too.
Deuteronomy 27:20–23 does not describe a public trial of named offenders, nor does it command Israel to parade victims before a crowd.
It commands a public affirmation of covenant standards.
That distinction matters.
Because God's Word must never be twisted into permission to publicly expose, mock, or retraumatize people who have already suffered abuse.
The purpose of the declarations was to establish that these acts were morally forbidden before God, even when committed in private.
And that raises a painful question.
What happens when the people who should protect a family become the very people who violate its sacred boundaries?
For some readers, this is not an abstract theological discussion.
You remember the room.
The voice.
The threat.
The warning not to tell anybody.
Maybe you were too young to understand what was happening. Maybe you understood enough to feel frightened, but not enough to know how to ask for help.
Maybe the person responsible was someone everyone respected.
A relative.
A trusted adult.
Someone whose public reputation made your private experience almost impossible to explain.
And perhaps, when you finally tried to speak, somebody told you that exposing the truth would destroy the family.
But listen carefully.
The person who reveals abuse is not the person who created it.
The responsibility belongs to the person who committed the wrong.
If you were abused, coerced, threatened, or exploited, the shame of that wrongdoing does not belong to you.
And no appeal to forgiveness, family loyalty, religious reputation, or submission should ever be used to force you back into danger.
God's holiness is not an excuse for cruelty toward victims.
It is one of the reasons wrongdoing must be taken seriously.
That is why the wider context of Deuteronomy matters.
Only a few verses earlier, Deuteronomy 27:19 declares a curse against anyone who perverts justice for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.
The same covenant ceremony that condemned forbidden sexual acts also condemned injustice toward vulnerable people.
God was not merely concerned with maintaining appearances.
He was concerned with righteousness.
And righteousness cannot flourish where the powerful are protected while the wounded are silenced.
But now we must confront another truth.
Not everyone reading this is identifying with the victim.
Some are remembering a sin they committed.
A boundary they crossed.
A relationship they knew was forbidden.
A secret they have defended for years.
Perhaps nobody knows.
Perhaps you have become skilled at keeping your outward life separate from the things you have done.
You still attend church.
You still know the songs.
You still know when to raise your hands.
And yet there is a memory you do not want God to bring into the light.
You may have spent years telling yourself that time has made it less serious.
But time does not transform wrongdoing into righteousness.
And secrecy does not make sin disappear.
Numbers 32:23 warns:
“Be sure your sin will find you out.”

In its original context, Moses was warning certain Israelite tribes about failing to fulfill their covenant responsibilities. The words should not be treated as a promise that every hidden offense will inevitably become publicly known in this life.
Nevertheless, the warning reminds us that wrongdoing cannot be safely dismissed merely because human beings have not discovered it.
God sees what people conceal.
Hebrews 4:13 teaches that nothing in creation is hidden from His sight.
That truth can be terrifying.
But it can also become the beginning of freedom.
Because the God who sees the hidden sin is also the God who calls sinners to repentance.
And the God who sees hidden suffering does not require victims to pretend their wounds never existed.
Here is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
The Old Testament's moral seriousness does not disappear when Jesus enters the story.
Jesus did not arrive to announce that holiness had been a misunderstanding.
He did not tell humanity that sin was harmless.
He did not redefine repentance as simply feeling better about ourselves.
In Matthew 5:17, Jesus said:
“Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.”
Christ fulfills the Law and the Prophets.

That means we must read Deuteronomy through the full unfolding of God's redemptive purposes, rather than treating every command given to ancient Israel as an unchanged legal procedure for the church today.
The church is not instructed to reenact the Mount Ebal ceremony or establish the civil penalties of ancient Israel.
But the New Testament does not treat incest as morally acceptable.
In fact, the apostle Paul confronted a shocking situation in the Corinthian church.
First Corinthians 5:1 says:
“It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father's wife.”
There it is again.
A man involved sexually with his father's wife.
The same family relationship condemned in Deuteronomy 27:20.
Centuries had passed.
The covenantal administration had changed.
Christ had come.
Yet Paul did not celebrate the situation as an expression of freedom.
He confronted it.
The Greek word Paul used for sexual immorality was πορνεία (porneia), a broad term referring to illicit sexual conduct.
And what disturbed Paul was not only the reported wrongdoing.
It was the church's attitude toward it.
Rather than mourning the situation, the community had become arrogant.
Think about the implications.
A church can be spiritually proud while morally compromised.
It can have impressive gatherings and still refuse to confront destructive behavior.
It can talk endlessly about grace while forgetting that grace is never permission to continue exploiting people.
Paul instructed the church to take the matter seriously through church discipline, with the aim of confronting the offender and protecting the integrity of the community.

Later, in 2 Corinthians 2:6–8, Paul urged the Corinthians to forgive and comfort a disciplined person who had experienced sufficient correction. The passage does not explicitly identify that individual as the man from 1 Corinthians 5, so we should not claim with certainty that it records his restoration.
Still, the larger New Testament witness is clear.
Christian correction is not supposed to be an exercise in cruelty.
It is meant to uphold truth and, where genuine repentance occurs, seek restoration consistent with justice and safety.
And that brings us to the most difficult question of all.
Can someone guilty of a deeply shameful sexual sin truly be forgiven?
The Gospel answers with hope.
But not cheap hope.
Not the kind that says, “Just say sorry, and everyone must trust you again.”
Not the kind that tells a wounded person to forget what happened.
Not the kind that confuses forgiveness with avoiding consequences.
Biblical repentance involves turning away from sin.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) means repentance, involving a changed mind and orientation that bears fruit in a changed life.
It is not merely embarrassment after being caught.
It is not sorrow because a reputation has been damaged.
It is not a carefully rehearsed apology designed to regain access to someone who has been harmed.
Genuine repentance acknowledges wrongdoing without shifting blame.
It accepts accountability.
It stops harmful behavior.
It respects boundaries.
It does not demand immediate reconciliation.
And when a crime has been committed, spiritual language must never be used to obstruct lawful reporting, investigation, or protection.
A repentant person cannot purchase forgiveness through secrecy.
Nor can repentance erase another person's right to safety.
Yet even here, in the place where guilt is undeniable, the Gospel announces something astonishing.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Not to pretend sin was insignificant.
But to deal with sin through His death and resurrection.
Galatians 3:13 declares:
“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree.”
The Greek begins:
Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἐξηγόρασεν ἐκ τῆς κατάρας τοῦ νόμου
Christos hēmas exēgorasen ek tēs kataras tou nomou.
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law.”
The word ἐξηγόρασεν (exēgorasen) communicates redemption or release by purchase.
The word κατάρα (katara) means curse.
Paul draws upon Deuteronomy 21:23 to explain the significance of Christ's crucifixion.
Notice what the apostle is saying.
The Law exposed humanity's guilt.
Christ bore the curse on behalf of those He came to redeem.
This does not mean that every specific curse pronounced in Deuteronomy 27 should be mechanically equated with a particular individual's experience.
It means that the larger reality of condemnation under the Law finds its redemptive answer in the crucified and risen Christ.
At the cross, God did not simply shrug at evil.
Sin was taken with immeasurable seriousness.
And grace was revealed with immeasurable beauty.
Imagine that.
The One who had no sin willingly gave Himself for sinners.
The One who was perfectly holy entered a world of betrayal, violence, corruption, and shame.
The One who deserved worship was mocked.
The One who gave life was put to death.
And on the third day, He rose.
Not so that humanity could return comfortably to darkness.
But so that those who believe in Him could receive forgiveness and new life.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired every consequence of our past.
Not after we learned to sound religious.
Christ died for sinners.
But please do not misunderstand what this means.
The Gospel is not a shelter for unrepentant abuse.
It is not a theological loophole for those who refuse accountability.
And it is not a command for victims to surrender their safety so an offender can feel restored.
Christ's grace is free, but it is not trivial.
The Savior who forgives also calls people to follow Him.
And following Him means walking in truth.
Perhaps you are reading this as someone who has carried guilt for years.
You know what you did.
You cannot undo it.
You cannot go back and become the person you should have been.
But you can stop defending the sin.
You can confess it to God.
You can turn away from it.
You can accept appropriate accountability and seek help to ensure the harm is not repeated.
And you can come to Jesus Christ without pretending to be innocent.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is not a promise that earthly consequences vanish.
It is a promise concerning God's forgiveness and cleansing.
And sometimes the most powerful evidence of repentance is a person's willingness to face consequences rather than escape them.
Perhaps, instead, you are reading this as someone who was harmed.
You have spent years asking why God did not stop what happened.
Why someone who claimed to love you crossed a boundary that should never have been crossed.
Why people believed the person who hurt you.
Why healing has taken so long.
I will not pretend that one article can answer every painful question.
And I will not tell you that the mere passage of time should have healed everything.
But I want you to know something.
The sin committed against you does not determine your worth.
You are not spiritually contaminated because another person violated your dignity.
You do not have to carry the offender's guilt.
And you do not have to call injustice good in order to demonstrate Christian forgiveness.
The Lord is near to the brokenhearted, as Psalm 34:18 declares.
Healing may involve prayer, trusted support, qualified counseling, appropriate reporting, and the patient rebuilding of safety.
Seeking that help is not a failure of faith.

And if you are currently being harmed, especially if you are a minor or someone dependent on the person responsible, please reach out to a safe adult, appropriate protection service, or local authorities.
Your safety matters.
Your voice matters.
Your life matters.
Now consider the deeper message of those ancient declarations.
When Israel answered “Amen,” the people were affirming that God's standards were true.
But what happens when a community says “Amen” to God's holiness in public and refuses to practice justice in private?
What happens when we condemn biblical sins on social media but protect those same sins within our circles?
What happens when a church fears scandal more than it fears disobedience?
What happens when we care more about preserving an institution's reputation than protecting someone who has been wounded?
The answer is devastating.
Our public religion becomes a contradiction of our private conduct.
Jesus confronted religious hypocrisy with piercing clarity.
In Matthew 23:27, He compared hypocritical religious leaders to beautiful whitewashed tombs that were inwardly full of uncleanness.
The image is unforgettable.
Beautiful outside.
Corrupt within.
A polished exterior cannot transform what is hidden underneath.
And this is why the Gospel Warrior message must never be reduced to an attractive slogan.
From Scandal to Grace does not mean from exposure to successful damage control.
It does not mean from wrongdoing to a restored public image without repentance.
It does not mean from victimization to enforced silence.
It means bringing what is broken, sinful, and wounded into the light of Jesus Christ.
It means allowing truth to speak.
It means calling evil what God calls evil.
It means seeking justice without surrendering to hatred.
It means offering the hope of forgiveness without excusing the wrong.
It means believing that Jesus can transform lives while recognizing that trust must be rebuilt through truth, safety, and consistent change.
And perhaps that is the word someone desperately needs today.
The Gospel does not require you to keep pretending.
You can stop hiding behind religious appearances.
You can stop defending what Scripture condemns.
You can stop believing that your worst moment is more powerful than the grace of Jesus Christ.
And if someone sinned against you, you can stop believing that their wrongdoing has the authority to define your identity.
At the cross, we encounter both the seriousness of sin and the extraordinary mercy of God.
