Some through resentment.
Some through compromise that began so gradually they barely noticed it.
Some lose their way while chasing approval, money, pleasure, control, or relationships they hoped would finally make them feel loved.
And some, already hurting, make decisions that leave them more wounded than before.
The parable does not tell us why the sheep wandered.
That silence is important.
Jesus does not invite His listeners to spend the story speculating about the sheep's motives.
He directs their attention to the shepherd's response.
Think about that.
The missing sheep does not deliver a speech.
It does not negotiate its rescue.
It does not present an impressive record of obedience.
The shepherd goes looking.
And if you have ever believed that you must first make yourself worthy before you can come to Christ, you need to hear the difference between earning salvation and receiving grace.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired every consequence of our mistakes.
Not after we proved that we would never fail again.
While we were yet sinners.
But do not misunderstand this grace.
Jesus does not search for the lost because sin is harmless.
He searches because sin is deadly, and lost people need salvation.
Grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved to the very thing destroying us.
Grace is God's undeserved kindness bringing us toward repentance, forgiveness, and a transformed life.
The Shepherd does not celebrate the sheep remaining lost.
He celebrates its recovery.
And then Jesus gives us one of the most tender pictures in the entire parable.
Luke 15:5 says:
“And when he hath found it, he layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing.”
Stop there.
The shepherd finds the sheep.
And carries it.
Jesus could have described the shepherd angrily driving the animal back toward the flock.
He could have described punishment.
He could have focused on the inconvenience.
Instead, He describes shoulders.
And rejoicing.
The Greek expression includes:
ἐπιτίθησιν ἐπὶ τοὺς ὤμους αὐτοῦ χαίρων
epitithēsin epi tous ōmous autou chairōn
“He places it upon his shoulders, rejoicing.”
The Greek participle χαίρων (chairōn) means “rejoicing.”
This is not a picture of a shepherd reluctantly accepting an unwanted responsibility.
He is glad the sheep has been found.
And perhaps that is the part some wounded believers struggle most to believe.
You can imagine God tolerating your return.
You can imagine Him allowing you into the back of the room.
You can imagine Him forgiving you while remaining permanently disappointed that you ever needed forgiveness.
But rejoicing?
Could the holy God of heaven truly rejoice over the repentance of somebody whose life has been marked by failure?
Jesus says yes.
Not because the sin was beautiful.
Not because the consequences were imaginary.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because the lost has been found.
And the sinner has turned back toward God.
There is a difference between being rescued and being celebrated.
Jesus deliberately includes both.
Maybe you need to sit with that for a moment.
Because somewhere along the way, you may have begun imagining God through the faces of people who wounded you.
People who kept records of your failures.
People who offered forgiveness but never stopped reminding you of what you had done.
People who made you feel that one terrible season had become your permanent identity.
But the character of God must be understood through His revelation in Scripture, not merely through the behavior of people who claim to represent Him.
And Jesus Christ reveals the Father perfectly.
In John 10:11, Jesus says:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.”
Now the parable becomes even more powerful.
The Shepherd who searches for the lost is not simply a sentimental image.
Jesus Himself is the Good Shepherd.
And His mission leads to the cross.
The rescue of sinners is not cheap.
It is not accomplished by pretending that evil does not matter.
The Son of God enters our broken world, lives without sin, and willingly gives His life to redeem sinners.
At Calvary, the holiness of God and the mercy of God are not enemies.
Jesus bears sin so that those who repent and trust in Him may be forgiven and reconciled to God.
The One who came seeking the lost would eventually be rejected, mocked, wounded, and crucified.
He did not save us because salvation cost Him nothing.
He gave Himself for us.
That is why the cross must never be reduced to a motivational symbol.
It is the place where the seriousness of sin and the greatness of divine love confront us together.
And the resurrection declares that death did not have the final word.
Jesus Christ is alive.
The Good Shepherd who laid down His life took it up again.
This is the Gospel.
Not that you are secretly good enough.
Not that your mistakes do not matter.
Not that you can heal yourself through positive thinking.
But that Jesus Christ saves sinners through His death and resurrection, and calls them to repent, believe, and follow Him.
And if that truth exposes something in your heart, do not rush past it.
Perhaps you have been running from God while convincing everybody around you that you are doing fine.
Perhaps you have been excusing something the Holy Spirit has repeatedly brought to your attention.
Perhaps you have mistaken religious activity for a living relationship with Christ.
Or perhaps shame has persuaded you that the door of mercy has already closed.
It has not closed simply because you have sinned.
Jesus calls sinners to come to Him.
And genuine repentance does not begin with pretending that nothing happened.
It begins with bringing the truth into the light.
There is no need to perform spiritual perfection in front of the One who already knows your heart.
You can confess.
You can turn.
You can ask for mercy.
You can begin making things right where repentance requires it.
And you can trust that forgiveness rests upon the saving work of Jesus, not the strength of your emotional experience.
If you are reading this with tears in your eyes, I want to ask you something.
When was the last time you stopped defending yourself long enough to let God's Word confront you?
Not the person beside you.
Not your spouse.
Not the friend who betrayed you.
Not the church member who disappointed you.
You.
Because it is possible to be so preoccupied with the sins of others that you stop recognizing your own need for grace.
That was part of the tragedy unfolding around Jesus in Luke 15.
The religious leaders were offended that sinners were coming near.
Yet their own hearts needed to understand the mercy of God.
And here is the uncomfortable question.
What if you have spent years identifying yourself with the ninety-nine while treating someone else as the one who should never be welcomed home?
The person who ruined their reputation.
The addict trying to rebuild a life.
The unfaithful spouse who is genuinely repentant.
The former unbeliever who knows almost nothing about church.
The young person whose mistakes became public.
The believer who fell and is trying to stand again.
Can you rejoice when grace reaches someone whose past makes you uncomfortable?
Or do you secretly prefer a Christianity where forgiveness is available to people whose sins are easier for you to tolerate?
Jesus did not tell this story merely to comfort people who feel lost.
He told it in response to people who complained about His welcome of sinners.
The parable exposes both the desperation of the lost and the hardness of hearts that refuse to celebrate their restoration.
And that brings us to the ending.
Luke 15:6 says the shepherd calls together his friends and neighbors:
“Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost.”
The joy does not remain private.
It becomes shared.
Then Jesus explains the meaning.
Luke 15:7:
“I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance.”
Here is the answer to the question that began this entire story.
Why did Jesus describe a shepherd leaving ninety-nine sheep for one?
Because one lost sinner matters enough to be sought, and one sinner's repentance is an occasion for joy in heaven.
The Greek text uses the word:
μετανοοῦντι — metanoounti
Meaning “repenting” or “one who repents.”
It comes from the verb metanoeō, commonly translated “to repent.”
In biblical context, repentance involves a genuine turning of mind and heart toward God, away from sin. It is more than feeling embarrassed after being caught.
It is not simply crying because life has become difficult.
It is not a temporary burst of religious emotion.
It is a response to God that changes the direction of a person's life.
Repentance is not the price paid to purchase grace.
It is inseparable from the response of faith to the God who graciously calls sinners to Himself.
And when Jesus speaks of ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance, we must read His words in the setting of His conversation with the Pharisees and scribes.
He is not teaching that most people are sinless or can enter God's kingdom without grace.
Scripture plainly teaches that all have sinned (Romans 3:23).
His statement highlights the joy over the lost being restored and challenges those who consider themselves righteous while resenting mercy shown to sinners.
The following parables in Luke 15 deepen that challenge, especially the older brother who refuses to celebrate the return of the prodigal son.
There is no biblical basis for claiming that God loves the one lost sheep more than the ninety-nine.
Nor should we use this parable to calculate that ninety-nine percent of believers will be abandoned for the sake of one sinner.
That misses Jesus' point.
The number illustrates the value of the individual who has gone missing.
The search reveals the shepherd's concern.
The carrying reveals the tenderness of the recovery.
The celebration reveals heaven's joy over repentance.
And the entire story reveals the heart of God toward the lost.
There is something astonishing about the way Jesus measures significance.
We live in a world fascinated by crowds.
Numbers.
Popularity.
Influence.
Visible success.
A hundred people can gather, and we may feel satisfied because ninety-nine remain.
But Jesus makes His listeners notice the missing one.
Not because the others are unimportant.
Because the one is not unimportant either.
You are not invisible to God simply because the world has learned to live without noticing you.
You are not beyond the invitation of the Gospel because your story has become complicated.
And you are not too respectable to need the same mercy you hope others will receive.
The ground at the foot of the cross is level.
Every sinner who is saved is saved by grace.
Every forgiven person has reason to worship.
Every restored life is evidence that Jesus Christ is not finished displaying His mercy.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior has always centered on a truth that reaches deeper than religious appearances:
Not because every scandal is automatically redeemed without repentance.
Not because trusting Jesus erases every earthly consequence.
Not because the people we have hurt are obligated to trust us immediately.
But because the Gospel can transform the deepest meaning and ultimate direction of a human life.
A person once defined by rebellion can become a disciple of Christ.
A heart hardened by pride can learn humility.
A sinner enslaved to secret darkness can begin walking in truth.
A person overwhelmed by guilt can receive forgiveness through Jesus Christ.
And a believer who has wandered can return to the Shepherd and learn to follow His voice again.
Redemption does not make evil good.
It reveals the power of God to save sinners despite the evil they have done.
Perhaps somebody reading this has been quietly thinking, I wish I could start again.
You cannot go back and undo yesterday.
You cannot rewrite every conversation.
You cannot retrieve every wasted year.
But in Christ, your past does not have to be the final authority over your future.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That promise is not an invitation to deny your history.
It is the announcement of new life in Christ.
And if you have not yet surrendered your life to Jesus, there is no need to wait until you feel worthy enough to approach Him.
Come honestly.
Acknowledge your sin.
Believe the Gospel.
Turn to Christ.
Ask Him for forgiveness and entrust your life to Him.
If you are a believer who has wandered, stop making peace with the distance.
Return to Him.
Confess what needs confessing.
Seek reconciliation where appropriate.
Find a faithful local church where you can receive biblical teaching, fellowship, prayer, and accountability.
And remember that Christian growth is not meant to happen in isolation.
You need Scripture.
You need prayer.
You need the body of Christ.
You need truth spoken with love.
You need reminders of grace when shame tries to silence you, and loving correction when sin tries to deceive you.
That is one reason Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to turn discipleship into a commercial transaction.
Not to suggest that anyone can buy the favor of God.
But to keep pointing people toward Jesus Christ through Scripture-centered teaching, encouragement, conviction, and resources for spiritual growth.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible, including to people who cannot afford to give.
And for those who are able and genuinely want to help this mission continue, there is another way to participate.
Some believers may prayerfully choose to include such support within their broader personal giving and offerings.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, not under spiritual pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Supporting Gospel ministry can be one beautiful expression of Christian generosity.
So can serving your local church, caring for someone in need, encouraging a discouraged believer, praying faithfully, and sharing the Gospel with someone who has never heard it clearly.
Those products may be meaningful reminders of biblical truth, but they are not the reason anyone should follow Christ or support His work.
The greatest gift remains the Gospel itself.
Not merely to increase its reach.
But because someone among your friends may be carrying a burden you know nothing about.
Someone may be smiling through spiritual exhaustion.
Someone may have stopped praying because they believe God is finished with them.
Someone may be avoiding church because they are afraid of being judged.
Someone may be one honest conversation away from asking what it truly means to repent and believe in Jesus Christ.
And a shared message about the Good Shepherd could become the beginning of that conversation.
Or send this privately to someone whose struggle should not become a public spectacle.
You do not have to expose anybody's pain to show them love.
Sometimes the most compassionate thing you can do is quietly remind someone where hope can be found.
And if this message has reached a place in your own heart that you have been avoiding, I want to invite you to do something more personal.
Not for attention.
Not to prove that you are spiritual.
Not because public confession is required for forgiveness.
But because your testimony or a simple request for prayer may encourage another person to stop pretending.
And if you have experienced God's restoring mercy, consider sharing a few words of testimony without revealing details that could harm you or someone else.
Someone needs to know that repentance is possible.
Someone needs to know that grace does not end where shame begins.
Someone needs to know that the Good Shepherd still calls sinners to Himself.
You are saved by Christ, not by a payment.
You are welcomed through grace, not through a membership.
And you grow as His disciple by following Him in faith, truth, repentance, love, and obedience.
Before you leave, return with me to the scene Jesus painted.
A shepherd notices that one sheep is missing.
He goes looking.
He finds it.
He lifts it onto his shoulders.
And he returns rejoicing.
Then he invites others to celebrate.
What began with absence ends with joy.
What began with wandering ends with recovery.
And Jesus says that heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents.
One.
Not a stadium full of people.
Not a movement with millions of followers.
One sinner turning back to God.
That is how Jesus answers the religious leaders who objected to His fellowship with sinners.
He shows them the joy they have been refusing to share.
And He shows us the mercy we could never deserve.
Perhaps tonight, that truth is calling you to stop running.
Perhaps it is calling you to forgive someone you have refused to see as capable of repentance.
Perhaps it is calling you to abandon the pride that has made you think grace is something other people need more than you do.
Or perhaps it is simply calling you to kneel and pray:

“Lord Jesus, I have wandered. I have sinned. I have tried to hide behind excuses, distractions, and appearances. I cannot save myself. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Forgive me. Turn my heart away from sin. Teach me to hear Your voice and follow You. Help me walk in truth, receive Your grace, and extend mercy to others. Let my life bring glory to You. Amen.”
And when you finish praying, do not measure God's willingness to receive repentant sinners by how intensely you feel something.
Measure it by the truth of His Word and the finished work of Jesus Christ.
Because the most important part of Luke 15 is not that the sheep became extraordinary.
It is that the shepherd was merciful.
And the most important part of your salvation story will never be how impressive you became.
It will be the grace of the Savior who gave Himself to redeem you.
You may have spent years believing you were the mistake everyone remembered, while Jesus was calling you to become a testimony of the mercy no one could earn.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A WIDOW, A BROTHER-IN-LAW, AND A SANDAL REMOVED IN PUBLIC—THE BIBLICAL CEREMONY OF SHAME MOST CHRISTIANS NEVER STUDY
paragraphs: A WIDOW, A BROTHER-IN-LAW, AND A SANDAL REMOVED IN PUBLIC—THE BIBLICAL CEREMONY OF SHAME MOST CHRISTIANS NEVER STUDY

She had already buried her husband. Now, before the elders of Israel, another man would have to decide whether her dead husband's name deserved to survive. What happened next involved a sandal, a public humiliation, and an ancient law that reveals something extraordinary about family responsibility, human dignity, and the redeeming heart of Jesus Christ.
Imagine burying the person you thought you would grow old with.
The funeral is over. The mourners have returned home. The last comforting voice has faded into silence.
And now you are standing inside a house that suddenly feels too large.
His place at the table is empty.
His clothes still carry the memory of his presence.
And every morning, for one terrible moment, you forget that he is gone.
Then reality returns.
Again.
But imagine that your grief is only the beginning.
You have no child. No son to carry your husband's name. No guarantee that the family inheritance will remain connected to his memory.
And in the ancient world, where family identity, land, and survival were deeply intertwined, the death of a husband could threaten far more than a woman's emotional security.
Then you discover something astonishing.
God had already spoken into circumstances like yours.
Not with a vague religious slogan.
Not with a command to simply stop grieving.
But with a law so unusual that many Christians have read past it without realizing what was happening.
A brother-in-law.
A widow.
A marriage obligation.
A sandal pulled from a man's foot.
And a public declaration that would follow his household in Israel.
It sounds like the beginning of a scandal.
But hidden inside this uncomfortable passage is a question that still confronts us today:
What happens when someone has the power to preserve another person's dignity, but chooses personal convenience instead?
And before this story ends, we will discover why a sandal at the city gate can help us appreciate the difference between a reluctant human redeemer and the Savior who willingly came for us.
The passage is Deuteronomy 25:5–10.
And once you understand it, you may never read the story of Ruth—or the genealogy of Jesus Christ—the same way again.
The law begins with these words in the King James Version:

“If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger: her husband's brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of an husband's brother unto her.” — Deuteronomy 25:5, KJV
Read that carefully.

This was not a general command for every widow to marry her brother-in-law. It addressed a particular situation in ancient Israel: brothers belonging to the same family setting, one dying without offspring, and the continuation of his household being placed in jeopardy.
The Hebrew text uses an expression that deserves attention:
יְבָמָהּ יָבֹא עָלֶיהָ
Yevamah yavo aleha.
In context, it describes the deceased husband's brother entering into the marriage relationship with the widow.

The related Hebrew word יָבָם (yavam) means a husband's brother in this particular family role. From this vocabulary comes the designation levirate marriage, derived from the Latin levir, meaning brother-in-law.
This was not simply a family suggestion.
It was a covenant-era legal responsibility.
The purpose becomes clearer in the following verse:
“And it shall be, that the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead, that his name be not put out of Israel.” — Deuteronomy 25:6, KJV
There it is.
“That his name be not put out of Israel.”
The Hebrew says:
וְלֹא־יִמָּחֶה שְׁמוֹ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
Velo-yimmacheh shemo miYisrael.
A faithful rendering is:
“And his name shall not be wiped out from Israel.”
The verb yimmacheh, from the Hebrew root מחה (machah), carries the idea of being wiped away or blotted out.
The concern was not merely sentimental remembrance.
In Israel's covenant society, a household's name, descendants, and inheritance were connected to its continuing place among God's people.
A man could die.
But the law provided a way for his household not to disappear with him.
And the widow, whose future could be precarious, was not supposed to be treated as though her husband's death had made her irrelevant.
That matters.
Because when Scripture speaks about widows, it repeatedly reveals God's concern for people vulnerable to neglect and exploitation.
Deuteronomy 10:18 describes the Lord as the One who executes justice for the fatherless and widow.
Psalm 68:5 calls God a defender of widows.
And James 1:27 reminds believers that pure religion includes caring for orphans and widows in their distress.
Different passages. Different covenant settings.
But a consistent moral concern.
God sees people whom society is tempted to overlook.
Now comes the part that makes this law so startling.
What if the brother-in-law refused?
What if he looked at the responsibility and decided it was too inconvenient?
What if preserving his brother's household meant sacrificing something he did not want to sacrifice?
Deuteronomy 25:7 says:

“And if the man like not to take his brother's wife, then let his brother's wife go up to the gate unto the elders, and say, My husband's brother refuseth to raise up unto his brother a name in Israel, he will not perform the duty of my husband's brother.”
Notice something easily missed.
The widow was given a public voice.
She was not simply told to remain silent.
She could bring the matter before the elders at the city gate, where legal and communal affairs were addressed.
She could identify the refusal.
She could demand that the community recognize what had happened.
The elders would then summon the man and speak with him.
But if he persisted in refusing, the law did not authorize forcing him into the marriage.
Instead, it prescribed a public ceremony.
And that ceremony was unforgettable.

“Then shall his brother's wife come unto him in the presence of the elders, and loose his shoe from off his foot, and spit in his face, and shall answer and say, So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother's house.” — Deuteronomy 25:9, KJV
Imagine the scene.
The elders are assembled.
The man has been called forward.
The widow approaches.
She bends down.
And removes his sandal.

Then comes the act of spitting, rendered in the KJV as “spit in his face.” The Hebrew expression וְיָרְקָה בְּפָנָיו (veyareqah befanav) indicates spitting before or in his presence; the exact physical direction has been discussed by interpreters and later Jewish tradition.
Either way, the ceremony was deliberately humiliating.
It publicly marked his refusal to fulfill the prescribed family duty.
The final verse declares:
“And his name shall be called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.” — Deuteronomy 25:10, KJV
Think about that irony.
The law was concerned with preserving the deceased brother's name.
Yet the refusing brother could acquire a name associated with his own unwillingness.
The man who would not build up his brother's household would be publicly remembered for the sandal removed from his foot.
The Hebrew expression is:
בֵּית חֲלוּץ הַנָּעַל
Beit chalutz ha-na'al.
“The house of the one whose sandal was removed.”
The ceremony is known in Jewish tradition as chalitzah, the release from the levirate marriage obligation.
This is not a ritual Christians are commanded to practice today. It belonged to the specific legal structure of ancient Israel.
And it is important not to romanticize it.

The widow's vulnerability was real. The marriage arrangement was rooted in a patriarchal family system. The text does not invite us to pretend that every woman involved would have experienced the arrangement in the same way.
Nor does Scripture present the public humiliation as a universal Christian method of dealing with someone who refuses a family obligation.
We must understand the law in its historical and covenantal context before drawing moral lessons from it.
But within that context, something significant stands out.
The brother's decision was not treated as purely private.
His refusal affected another household.
And his community was permitted to acknowledge that publicly.
Now consider the question this raises for us.
How many people are quietly carrying burdens because someone else decided responsibility was inconvenient?
A mother raising children without meaningful support.
An elderly parent waiting for a visit that never comes.
A widow whose phone stopped ringing after the funeral.
A struggling relative everyone assumes someone else will help.
A brother or sister in Christ who has become very good at saying, “I'm fine.”
Sometimes abandonment is dramatic.
Sometimes it is simply the slow disappearance of people who promised they would stay.
And perhaps that is why this ancient law still makes us uncomfortable.
It forces us to consider whether we have confused the freedom to walk away with the righteousness of walking away.
But there is another biblical story that brings this entire subject into even sharper focus.
A story involving another widow.
Another family obligation.
Another sandal.
And a woman whose name would eventually appear in the family history of Jesus Christ.
Her name was Ruth.
Ruth was a Moabite widow who chose to remain with her widowed mother-in-law, Naomi, rather than return to her former life.
Her words in Ruth 1:16 are among the most beautiful expressions of loyalty in Scripture:
“Whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God.”
But loyalty did not immediately remove her hardship.
Ruth still had to gather leftover grain to survive.
She still lived with uncertainty.
She still belonged to a vulnerable household.
Then she encountered Boaz.
A man who treated her with unusual kindness.
A man who recognized her faithfulness.
A man who was connected to Naomi's deceased husband's family.
And eventually, the question of redemption reached the city gate.
Now we must be careful with the biblical details.
Boaz was not identified as Ruth's deceased husband's brother. Therefore, Ruth 4 is not simply an exact reenactment of Deuteronomy 25:5–10.
The book of Ruth brings together related concerns about family redemption, inheritance, marriage, and the preservation of a deceased man's name.
It also describes a sandal custom connected with confirming a legal transaction.
Ruth 4:7 explains:

“Now this was the manner in former time in Israel concerning redeeming and concerning changing, for to confirm all things; a man plucked off his shoe, and gave it to his neighbour: and this was a testimony in Israel.”
Notice the distinction.
In Deuteronomy 25, the widow removes the refusing brother-in-law's sandal in a ceremony of public disgrace.
In Ruth 4, the sandal is removed in connection with the confirmation of a redemption transaction.
The ceremonies are related by their ancient legal symbolism, but they are not identical.
And there is no spitting ceremony recorded in Ruth 4.
That distinction matters because a powerful biblical message should never require us to blur what Scripture actually says.
At the city gate, Boaz speaks with a nearer relative who has the first opportunity to redeem the family property.
At first, the man is willing.
But when he learns that the matter also involves Ruth and the responsibility of preserving the deceased man's name in connection with the inheritance, he declines.
He fears damaging his own inheritance.
And then Boaz steps forward.
Not as a man being forced by Deuteronomy 25 to marry his brother's widow.
But as a willing family redeemer who accepts the responsibility before the elders and witnesses.
Boaz declares in Ruth 4:10:

“Moreover Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, have I purchased to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance, that the name of the dead be not cut off from among his brethren.”
That phrase again.
“That the name of the dead be not cut off.”
The same concern that appears in Deuteronomy.
A name.
An inheritance.
A household threatened by death.
And a living person willing to bear a cost for the sake of another.
But the story does not end at the city gate.
Boaz marries Ruth.
They have a son named Obed.
Obed becomes the father of Jesse.
Jesse becomes the father of David.
And generations later, Matthew opens his Gospel by tracing the genealogy of Jesus Christ through David's royal line.
Matthew 1:5 specifically names Boaz and Ruth.
Think about that.
A foreign widow, once gathering grain to survive, becomes part of the recorded ancestry of the Messiah.
The woman who could have been overlooked is remembered in the opening chapter of the New Testament.
Not because she engineered her own destiny.
Not because her suffering was secretly pleasant.
But because the God of Scripture was working through real human faithfulness, costly decisions, and providence that reached far beyond what Ruth could see.
And here is where we must turn our eyes toward Jesus.
Boaz is a beautiful example of a willing family redeemer.
But Boaz was not sinless.
Boaz did not save humanity from death.
And the Bible does not explicitly identify every detail of his actions as a direct prophecy of Christ.
Yet his willingness to bear a cost for another helps illuminate a greater biblical theme.
Redemption is not merely a comforting word. Redemption involves someone acting to bring another out of loss, bondage, or danger.
In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word גֹּאֵל (go'el) refers to a redeemer, often a family member who acts to recover property, protect family interests, or fulfill certain kinship obligations.
The Lord Himself is also called the Redeemer of His people.
And when we reach the New Testament, the language of redemption finds its supreme fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 1:7 declares:
“In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace.”
The Greek word translated “redemption” is ἀπολύτρωσις (apolytrōsis).
It speaks of release or deliverance through redemption.
And in Ephesians, Paul connects that redemption directly to the blood of Christ and the forgiveness of sins.
This is the center of the Gospel.
We were not merely people who needed a little encouragement.
We were sinners who needed reconciliation with a holy God.
We could not erase our guilt through good intentions.
We could not purchase forgiveness through religious performance.
We could not make ourselves righteous by pretending our sins were smaller than they were.
But Jesus came.
He lived without sin.
He gave Himself for sinners.
He died on the cross.
And He rose again.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputations.
Not after we proved ourselves worthy.
Not after we became impressive enough to deserve His attention.
While we were still sinners.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that more than anything else.
Because your life has not been a neat testimony.
There are chapters you do not like remembering.
Words you wish you could take back.
Relationships damaged by decisions you cannot undo.
Private compromises that never appeared in public.
Promises made to God and broken before the week was over.
Maybe you have learned how to smile at church while carrying guilt that follows you home.
Maybe you can quote Scripture and still feel ashamed of what you did last night.
Maybe you believe Jesus forgives sinners, but you struggle to believe that His mercy can reach someone who has repeatedly failed after knowing the truth.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you that sin is harmless.
It tells you that sin is so serious that Christ died for it.
And grace is so astonishing that Christ willingly died for sinners.
You do not need to invent excuses for your past.
You need to bring your sin into the light of His mercy.
You need repentance.
You need forgiveness.
You need the Savior who does not merely improve a public reputation but transforms the heart.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
A forgiven person may still need to repair harm, seek reconciliation, accept accountability, or live with painful consequences.
But forgiveness in Christ is real.
And no scandal is greater than the sufficiency of His sacrifice.
This is why our message is not that everyone will get the earthly ending they wanted.
Ruth received marriage and a child.
But not every widow remarries.
Not every grieving family has another baby.
Not every broken relationship is restored.
Not every financial crisis ends with unexpected wealth.
The Bible does not promise that faithfulness will always produce a Ruth chapter 4 ending in this lifetime.
It promises something greater and more enduring.
That those who belong to Christ are not abandoned by God.
That His grace is sufficient.
That His resurrection has broken the finality of death for His people.
And that one day He will make all things new.
The ultimate hope of the Gospel is not that every earthly story becomes comfortable.
It is that Jesus Christ has conquered sin and death.
Now return to that ancient city gate.
Imagine the sandal being removed.
The elders watching.
The public acknowledgment that a man would not carry the responsibility placed before him.
And then consider Jesus.
The Son of God did not come unwillingly.
He did not approach the cross looking for a convenient escape from the Father's saving purpose.
He said in John 10:18 concerning His life:
“No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself.”
His death was voluntary.
His sacrifice was obedient.
His love was not reluctant.
The contrast is not that Deuteronomy 25 secretly predicts the crucifixion through a sandal. Scripture does not make that claim.
The contrast is moral and theological.
Human beings often shrink back from costly obligations.
Christ willingly accomplished the saving work that no mere human redeemer could perform.
And when Jesus was stripped, mocked, and publicly humiliated before His crucifixion, He bore disgrace not because He had failed in righteousness, but because He was obedient even unto death.
Hebrews 12:2 says He endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of God's throne.
At the ancient gate, shame exposed a man's refusal to fulfill a family duty. At Calvary, the sinless Savior endured shame while fulfilling His Father's saving will.
What a difference.
One man was unwilling to preserve his brother's household.
Jesus willingly gave His life to redeem sinners and bring them into the household of God.
Ephesians 2:19 describes believers as members of God's household.
And Galatians 4:4–5 explains that God sent His Son so that those under the law might be redeemed and receive adoption as sons.
Do you see how much bigger the story becomes?
We began with a widow facing the possible disappearance of her husband's name.
We passed through a city gate where a sandal testified to a man's refusal.
We watched Ruth's family history unfold through the willingness of Boaz.
And now we stand before the cross, where the true and greater Redeemer gave Himself to rescue people who could never save themselves.
This is not merely a story about an ancient marriage custom.
It is an invitation to examine what redemption means, what responsibility costs, and how astonishing the grace of Christ truly is.
And it should change the way we live.
If God cares about widows, we cannot treat lonely people as invisible.
If God calls His people to justice, we cannot use religious language to excuse neglect.
If Christ has forgiven us, we cannot celebrate grace while stubbornly refusing repentance.
If Jesus gave Himself for us, we cannot reduce Christianity to receiving comfort while refusing the call to love our neighbors.
Perhaps there is someone you need to call.
Someone you need to forgive.
Someone to whom you owe an apology.
Someone who needs practical help rather than another promise that you will pray.
And perhaps the person who needs to stop hiding is you.
Not because public confession to strangers is required for forgiveness.
It is not.
But because you are exhausted from maintaining an appearance that no longer reflects what is happening inside your heart.
Jesus already knows.
He knows the secret.
He knows the struggle.
He knows the wound.
He knows the sin you keep minimizing.
And He calls you not to despair, but to repentance and faith.
You do not have to disclose private details to strangers. You do not have to turn your pain into a public performance.
But perhaps your honest words will encourage another believer who thought they were fighting alone.
Someone reading silently may need to know that following Jesus is not the absence of struggle, but a life sustained by His grace.
There is also something I want to ask of you.
Do not let this article end with you.
Not because social media engagement measures spiritual maturity.
But because someone in your circle may have never studied this passage, may be grieving a loss, or may be quietly wondering whether their past has placed them beyond redemption.
Come back to the Hebrew words.
Read Deuteronomy 25:5–10 for yourself.
Read Ruth 4 slowly.
Then read Ephesians 1 and remember what redemption through Christ's blood actually means.
Because the goal is not simply to remember an unusual biblical ceremony.
The goal is to know the Lord more deeply.
And that is why Gospel Warrior exists.
We want to keep bringing Scripture into the places where real life hurts.
Into the questions people are afraid to ask.
Into the biblical passages many believers have never had the opportunity to study.
Into the struggles of people who need more than religious entertainment.
They need the Word of God.
They need sound teaching.
They need encouragement grounded in truth.
Above all, they need Jesus Christ.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be purposeful and willing, not reluctant or under compulsion.
We want that same spirit here.
Your prayers, thoughtful comments, and willingness to share sound biblical teaching also matter.
These are simply ways to express appreciation for those who help sustain the work. They are not spiritual rewards or measures of faithfulness.
We want the Word to be studied.
We want believers to mature.
We want struggling Christians to find biblical encouragement.
We want seekers to hear the Gospel clearly.
And we want every resource, every article, every invitation to point beyond this ministry to the only Savior who can forgive sin and give eternal life.
Because this is bigger than growing a page.
It is about making Christ known.
A widow stands at the city gate.
Her husband is dead.
Her future is uncertain.
The elders are watching.
A sandal is removed.
And an entire community witnesses the consequences of a man's refusal to fulfill his responsibility.
Then the centuries move forward.
Another city.
Another crowd.
Another public humiliation.
This time, outside Jerusalem.
A crown of thorns.
A wooden cross.
A Savior who has done no wrong.
And the One who could have called upon heavenly power remains there, accomplishing the redemption He came to provide.
He does not save us because we deserve to be saved.
He saves by grace.
He does not forgive because our sins were insignificant.
He forgives because His sacrifice is sufficient.
He does not invite us to hide behind our religious appearance.
He calls us to come into the light, repent, believe, and follow Him.
So if you have been running from God, come home.
If you have been excusing sin, repent.
If you have been crushed by guilt, look to Christ.
If you have been abandoned by people, remember that the Lord is near to the brokenhearted.
And if you have received His mercy, do not keep that hope to yourself.
The sandal at the gate reminds us that human beings can refuse costly responsibility.
The cross reminds us that Jesus did not refuse the work of our salvation.
The most unforgettable thing about your past is not how far you fell, but how far the Savior came to redeem you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS SAID THERE WILL BE NO MARRIAGE IN HEAVEN—BUT WHAT HE REVEALED NEXT CHANGES EVERYTHING
paragraphs: JESUS SAID THERE WILL BE NO MARRIAGE IN HEAVEN—BUT WHAT HE REVEALED NEXT CHANGES EVERYTHING

Will you still recognize your husband? Will you still love your wife? What happens to the person you promised forever? The answer Jesus gave in Matthew 22:29–30 is far more astonishing—and far more comforting—than most people realize.
Imagine standing in heaven.
The pain is gone. The sickness is gone. The funeral you never wanted to attend is now a distant memory. Death has finally lost its grip.
And then you see someone.
A face you have missed for years.

Perhaps your husband, whose hand you held as his breathing slowed. Perhaps your wife, whose empty side of the bed still brings tears to your eyes. Perhaps someone you loved so deeply that even after their death, part of your heart never stopped reaching for them.
You run toward them.
But suddenly, a question rises in your heart.
Will they still be mine?
Because Jesus said something that has confused Christians for centuries.
"For in the resurrection they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven." — Matthew 22:30, KJV
Read that again.
Not because Jesus was taking something beautiful away.
But because He was revealing something so glorious that our earthly understanding of love struggles to contain it.

And before you conclude that marriage means nothing in eternity, or that your spouse will somehow become a stranger, you need to understand who asked Jesus this question, why they asked it, and what His answer actually means.
Because this conversation was never merely about marriage.
It was about whether death gets the final word.
The people who confronted Jesus that day were called the Sadducees.
They were influential religious leaders who denied the resurrection. Matthew 22:23 explicitly tells us that they said there was no resurrection.
They were not approaching Jesus as grieving widows or heartbroken husbands seeking comfort.
They were trying to trap Him.
They presented a hypothetical situation based on the law of Moses concerning levirate marriage, described in Deuteronomy 25:5–10.

A woman married a man who died without children. According to the situation they described, his brother married her, but he also died. This happened repeatedly until seven brothers had married the same woman, and eventually she died too.
Then came their question.
"Therefore in the resurrection whose wife shall she be of the seven? for they all had her." — Matthew 22:28, KJV
They thought they had found an impossible problem.
If resurrection were real, they reasoned, wouldn't the woman have seven husbands? Wouldn't eternity become a tangled mess of competing marital claims?
They expected Jesus to struggle.
Instead, He exposed the mistake beneath their entire argument.
"Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God." — Matthew 22:29, KJV
There it is.
One of the most piercing corrections Jesus ever delivered to religious people.
You are mistaken because you do not understand the Scriptures or the power of God.
Imagine hearing that from the Son of God.
These were men who studied sacred writings, debated religious law, and considered themselves qualified to challenge the Messiah.
Yet they had made a devastating assumption.
They assumed that resurrection life must operate according to the limitations of the present world.
They imagined eternity as though God would simply restart earthly life with all its existing arrangements.
But Jesus was telling them that the resurrection is not merely a continuation of the world as we know it.
It is the transformation of human existence through the power of God.
And that changes everything.
In the Greek text of Matthew 22:30, Jesus says:
ἐν γὰρ τῇ ἀναστάσει οὔτε γαμοῦσιν οὔτε γαμίζονται
Transliterated:
en gar tē anastasei oute gamousin oute gamizontai
A close translation is:
"For in the resurrection, they neither marry nor are given in marriage."
The Greek word ἀνάστασις (anastasis) means resurrection—a rising up, especially the raising of the dead.
This matters.
Jesus was not describing believers becoming disembodied spirits floating through eternity.
He was speaking about resurrection.
The future God promises is not the permanent abandonment of the body but its redemption and transformation.
Paul explains this in 1 Corinthians 15:42–44, contrasting the body sown in corruption with the body raised in incorruption.
And in Philippians 3:20–21, he teaches that Christ will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body.
Christian hope is not that death releases us from being human forever.
Christian hope is that Jesus Christ will raise and transform His people.
Now notice the two Greek verbs.
γαμοῦσιν (gamousin) means "they marry."
γαμίζονται (gamizontai) means "they are given in marriage."
Together, they describe the entering into marriage.
Jesus is saying that marriage as an earthly institution will not continue to be established in the resurrection.
He does not say that love disappears.
He does not say that memories are erased.
He does not say that husbands and wives will hate one another, forget one another, or become strangers.
He says they will not marry or be given in marriage.
That is what the text explicitly teaches.
And we must be careful not to make Jesus say more—or less—than He actually said.
This is where the question becomes painfully personal.
Because perhaps you are not studying Matthew 22 out of theological curiosity.
Perhaps you are reading it because you buried someone.
You stood beside a hospital bed and begged God for another day.
You watched the person who knew your favorite food, your private fears, your awkward habits, and your unfinished dreams slowly slip away.
You returned home to a house that still smelled like them.
Their clothes were still there.
Their Bible was still beside the bed.
Their coffee cup had not moved.
And the silence felt unbearable.
Then someone told you that there would be no marriage in heaven.
And instead of feeling hope, you felt another loss.
As though death had already taken your spouse, and eternity might somehow take your relationship too.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
Jesus did not teach that resurrection destroys everything beautiful about human love.
He taught that resurrection transforms the conditions under which human beings live.
There is a difference.
A profound difference.
Marriage is a precious gift from God.
Genesis 2:24 describes a man leaving his father and mother, being joined to his wife, and the two becoming one flesh.
Jesus Himself affirmed this teaching in Matthew 19:4–6.
Marriage is not a human accident.
It is part of God's good creation.
It provides companionship, covenant faithfulness, mutual care, and, in many marriages, the nurturing of children.
But Scripture also reveals that marriage has a purpose beyond itself.
In Ephesians 5:31–32, Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and then says:
"This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church." — KJV
Do not miss that.
Earthly marriage can point beyond itself to the covenant love of Jesus Christ for His people.
The faithful love of a husband.
The sacrificial care of a wife.
The forgiveness that follows a painful argument.
The promise to remain through sickness, poverty, aging, and weakness.
At its best, Christian marriage becomes a living witness to a greater love.
But the witness is not greater than the One to whom it points.
Marriage is a sign. Christ is the fulfillment.
That does not make the sign meaningless.
It makes its purpose glorious.
Think about a photograph of someone you love.
You may treasure that photograph because it reminds you of the person.
You may carry it through years of separation.
You may look at it when loneliness becomes difficult.
But when the person finally stands before you, you do not need to embrace the photograph instead of embracing them.
The photograph was precious.
The presence is greater.
In a far deeper way, earthly marriage points toward the covenant communion between Christ and His redeemed people.
Revelation 19:7–9 describes the marriage supper of the Lamb.
Revelation 21:2 presents the holy city, new Jerusalem, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
These are biblical pictures of the final union of Christ and His people.
The ultimate wedding celebration of eternity is not centered on an earthly husband and wife.
It is centered on the Lamb who was slain and the people He redeemed.
And here is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
The One who promises resurrection is the One who entered death Himself.
Jesus did not stand at a safe distance from human suffering.
He entered a world of betrayal, grief, broken families, disappointed hopes, and funerals.
He knew what it meant to be rejected.
He knew what it meant to weep.
At the tomb of Lazarus, Scripture records two of the shortest and most emotionally powerful words in the Bible:
"Jesus wept." — John 11:35, KJV
The Son of God stood before a grave and wept.
He knew He was about to raise Lazarus.
Yet He still wept.
That means Christian hope does not require pretending that death is painless.
Faith does not mean you never cry.
Resurrection hope does not mean you never miss someone.
And trusting Jesus does not mean every empty chair stops hurting.
But Jesus did not remain at Lazarus's tomb merely to share the sorrow.
He declared:
"I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." — John 11:25, KJV
Notice what He did not say.
He did not merely say, "I can explain resurrection."
He said, "I am the resurrection."
Our hope is not ultimately in an idea about the afterlife.
Our hope is in a Person.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified for sinners.
Buried in a tomb.
Raised bodily on the third day.
And alive forevermore.
That is why the Christian promise of eternity is not wishful thinking about meeting loved ones again.
It is grounded in the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
As Paul writes:
Without Christ's resurrection, our hope collapses.
With His resurrection, death is no longer the ultimate authority over those who belong to Him.
But we still need to answer the question that so many grieving hearts are asking.
Will we recognize our loved ones in the resurrection?
Scripture gives us reasons to hope for meaningful personal continuity, although it does not explain every detail of heavenly recognition.
After His resurrection, Jesus remained recognizably Himself.
His disciples encountered the same Lord who had been crucified, now gloriously raised.
In Luke 24:39, He showed them His hands and feet and affirmed the reality of His risen body.
In Matthew 17:1–3, Moses and Elijah appear at the transfiguration as distinct persons, although that event is not a complete description of the final resurrection.
Paul also writes in 1 Corinthians 13:12:

This verse emphasizes the fullness of knowledge that is to come, especially in relation to knowing God. It should not be treated as a direct promise spelling out exactly how every family relationship will function in eternity.
Nevertheless, Scripture does not portray God's final redemption as the erasure of personal identity.
Our resurrection hope concerns the redemption of the people God has made and saved.

So while we should not claim certainty about every heavenly reunion or every remembered detail, we have no biblical reason to conclude that eternal life requires the destruction of all personal recognition.
But there is another question.
A harder one.
If I recognize my spouse, but we are no longer married, won't that hurt?
That question deserves tenderness, not a careless theological slogan.
Jesus tells us that marriage will not operate in the resurrection as it does now.
Revelation 21:4 tells us that God will wipe away every tear, and that death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more.
We are not told exactly how every earthly relationship will be experienced in the new creation.
But we are promised that God's redeemed people will not live under the tyranny of grief, jealousy, loss, or death.
The love of God will not become smaller in eternity.
His presence will not leave His people emotionally impoverished.
Whatever the transformed relationships of the resurrection involve, they will exist in a creation where sin and death no longer corrupt human life.
That is not permission to invent details Scripture has not revealed.
It is permission to trust the character of the God who has revealed Himself in Jesus Christ.
And there is something else many people overlook.
In Luke's account of the same encounter, Jesus gives additional explanation.
"Neither can they die any more: for they are equal unto the angels; and are the children of God, being the children of the resurrection." — Luke 20:36, KJV
Now we are getting closer to the heart of His answer.
Jesus does not say resurrected human beings become angels.
The Greek word ἰσάγγελοι (isangeloi) means "equal to angels" or "like angels" in the relevant respect.
Luke connects this angel-like condition particularly with the fact that those who share in the resurrection life Jesus describes can no longer die.
They are not transformed into another species of creature.
They remain God's redeemed people, living in a deathless resurrection existence.
Marriage, as we know it, belongs to the conditions of this present age.
But resurrection life is no longer governed by mortality.
No widow will stand beside another grave because death has returned.
No husband will spend sleepless nights wondering how to survive without his wife.
No wife will watch cancer slowly take the man she loves.
No child of the resurrection will live beneath the shadow of another approaching funeral.
Death will not be waiting around the corner anymore.
And perhaps that is why Jesus refused to answer the Sadducees according to their limited assumptions.
They were arguing about which man would possess a marital claim over a woman.
Jesus was revealing a world in which death itself had lost its claim over God's people.
They were thinking about ownership.
Jesus was speaking about resurrection.
They were thinking about the continuation of earthly arrangements.
Jesus was revealing the power of God to bring about an entirely new order of life.
And there is a warning here for us.
Sometimes we become so preoccupied with what eternity might take away that we overlook the One eternity will reveal.
We ask, "Will I still have my husband?"
"Will I still have my wife?"
"Will I still have the relationships that made life worth living?"
These are understandable questions.
But beneath them lies an even greater one.
Will Jesus Christ be enough?
Not because our loved ones are unimportant.
Not because earthly affection is sinful.
Not because grief is weakness.
But because the deepest purpose of redemption is to bring us into everlasting fellowship with God through Jesus Christ.
Revelation 22:4 declares:
"And they shall see his face; and his name shall be in their foreheads." — KJV
Think about that.
The face of the Savior.
The One whose hands were pierced.
The One who carried our sins.
The One who endured the cross.
The One who knew every secret we tried to hide and still called us to repentance and faith.
The One who did not merely promise forgiveness but purchased redemption through His blood.
We will see Him.
And no earthly love, however beautiful, can replace the glory of the Redeemer.
But here is something equally important.
Jesus being enough does not mean the people you love suddenly become worthless.
God is not glorified by teaching us to despise His good gifts.
He is glorified when we receive them gratefully, love others faithfully, and worship the Giver above the gifts.
If you are married, love your spouse today.
Do not use eternity as an excuse to neglect the person beside you.
Pray together.
Forgive quickly.
Repent when you are wrong.
Stop treating your marriage like a battlefield where someone must win every argument.
Remember that the person beside you is not your possession.
They are a human being made in God's image.
And if both of you belong to Christ, you are not merely husband and wife.
You are also brother and sister in the Lord.
Your earthly marriage has a boundary.
But your shared belonging to Jesus Christ rests on a promise stronger than death.
If you are single, hear this too.
Jesus' teaching means that marriage is not the highest possible state of human existence.
You are not an unfinished person because you do not have a wedding ring.
You are not spiritually inferior because no one has chosen you as a spouse.
You do not need to find a husband or wife to become complete in Christ.
Jesus Himself lived without marrying.
Paul honored singleness as a genuine calling in 1 Corinthians 7.
And the resurrection reminds every believer that the fullness of eternal life is not reserved for married people.
The center of heaven is not a wedding ring.
The center of heaven is Jesus Christ.
And if your marriage has ended in divorce, betrayal, abandonment, or heartbreak, there is hope for you too.
Perhaps your story did not unfold the way you prayed.
Perhaps you once stood before God and promised a lifetime, only to watch that promise collapse.
Perhaps you made sinful choices you now deeply regret.
Perhaps you were wounded by another person's unfaithfulness.
Or perhaps you are carrying both responsibility and pain.
The Gospel does not call evil good.
It does not excuse betrayal.
It does not pretend that broken covenants have no consequences.
But neither does it declare that your worst chapter must become your final identity.
There is repentance.
There is forgiveness.
There is grace.
There is a Savior who receives sinners who turn to Him in faith.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) refers to repentance—a change of mind and direction that involves turning from sin toward God.
And grace is not merely permission to remain unchanged.
God's grace brings forgiveness and calls us into a transformed life.
This is the heart of our message.
Not because scandal is harmless.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because the cross of Jesus Christ is greater than the condemnation that sinners could never remove by themselves.
The blood of Jesus is not a decoration for religious people who believe they have never failed.
It is the foundation of salvation for sinners who desperately need mercy.
You may have ruined a relationship.
You may have spent years living far from God.
You may have pretended to be spiritually strong while secretly falling apart.
But if you are still breathing, the call of the Gospel still confronts you.
Turn to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Believe in the risen Lord.
Receive His forgiveness.
And follow Him.
Your past does not have the authority to overrule the grace of God.
But do not misunderstand this either.
Not everyone automatically receives eternal life simply because they die.
Jesus' promise of resurrection life must be understood alongside His call to repentance and faith.
In John 5:28–29, Jesus teaches a future resurrection that includes both life and judgment.
In John 11:25–26, He connects the promise of life with believing in Him.
And in John 14:6, He declares Himself the way, the truth, and the life.
Our hope is not that everyone we love will automatically enter God's kingdom regardless of their response to Christ.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ is mighty to save, merciful toward sinners, and faithful to every promise He has made.
That truth should not make us cold.
It should make us urgent in love.
Pray for your family.
Share the Gospel with your friends.
Speak to your spouse about Jesus.
Let your children hear more than religious arguments; let them see a life being changed by grace.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be discovering that earthly marriage does not continue in its present form.
The greatest tragedy would be spending our lives discussing heaven while refusing the Savior who opens the way to eternal life.
And now, return to that scene where we began.
Imagine the resurrection.
Not as a fantasy we can describe in every detail, but as the real future promised by the risen Christ.
Death has been defeated.
The redeemed are raised.
Sin no longer rules.
God dwells with His people.
The tears that once seemed endless have finally come to an end.
You no longer measure life by how many years remain.
You no longer fear the doctor's next report.
You no longer wonder whether tomorrow will bring another goodbye.
And at the center of it all is Jesus.
The Savior who loved you when you were unworthy.
The Shepherd who pursued you when you wandered.
The Redeemer who paid for your sins.
The King who conquered the grave.
Suddenly, the question is no longer merely, "Will my earthly marriage continue?"
The greater wonder is this:
How glorious must the resurrection be if even the most beautiful earthly marriage is only a sign pointing toward something greater?
That is what Matthew 22:29–30 invites us to consider.
Not that love is abolished.
Not that human identity is erased.
Not that grief is foolish.
But that the power of God reaches beyond everything our present experience can comprehend.
Jesus corrected the Sadducees because they underestimated both Scripture and God's power.
Let us not make the same mistake.
Do not shrink eternity until it fits inside your present understanding.
Do not measure resurrection life only by what you are afraid of losing.
And do not confuse the limits of your imagination with the limits of God's promises.
There is a reason Paul wrote:
"For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain." — Philippians 1:21, KJV
He was not saying earthly life was meaningless.
He was saying that belonging to Christ changes the meaning of both life and death.
So cherish the people God has entrusted to you.
Hold their hands while you can.
Tell them you love them.
Make peace while there is time.
Lead them toward Jesus, not merely toward a comfortable life.
And when grief comes, as it does in this fallen world, do not believe that the grave is more powerful than the Savior.
Jesus has already walked out of a tomb.
And He has promised resurrection to those who belong to Him.
If this message has touched a wound you rarely talk about, I want to invite you to respond with honesty.
You do not need to share private details to be part of a community that prays.
Your testimony may help another believer remember that God's grace is still at work.
Because this ministry is not simply about publishing articles.
It is about pointing people back to Jesus.
Not out of guilt.
And certainly not because God's favor can be purchased.
But because sharing the Gospel and providing faithful discipleship resources is work worth supporting.

In that sense, it can be part of your personal giving and stewardship before God. It should not, however, be confused with a biblically required tithe or replace responsibilities you may have to your local church, family, and others in need.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, giving should be willing, not pressured, because God loves a cheerful giver.
It is the opportunity to help sustain a ministry devoted to Scripture, repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through Jesus Christ.
Your prayers matter.
Your shares matter.
Your encouragement matters.
And before you leave, remember the question that brought us here.
Will there be marriage in the resurrection?
Jesus said that people in the resurrection neither marry nor are given in marriage.
That is His teaching.
But He also revealed that the Sadducees had failed to understand the power of God.
And perhaps that is the truth your heart needs most tonight.
You do not have to understand every detail of eternity to trust the Savior who conquered death.
You do not have to pretend your grief is small.
You do not have to stop loving the people God gave you.
You do not have to manufacture answers to questions Scripture has left unanswered.
You are invited to trust Jesus Christ—the crucified and risen Lord—with everything you cannot yet see.
Because the One who conquered the grave is not powerless before your questions.
And the One who promises to make all things new will not fail to complete His work.
The hands that were pierced to save you are the same hands you can trust with everyone and everything you are afraid to lose.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS FEELING GUILTY THE SAME THING AS REPENTING? THE TERRIFYING DIFFERENCE THAT COULD CHANGE YOUR ETERNITY
paragraphs: IS FEELING GUILTY THE SAME THING AS REPENTING? THE TERRIFYING DIFFERENCE THAT COULD CHANGE YOUR ETERNITY

You can cry over your sin, hate what you have done, promise God you will never do it again—and still walk away unchanged. But there is a difference between a heart crushed by shame and a heart transformed by Jesus Christ.
There is a kind of prayer that sounds like repentance but isn't.
“Lord, I'm sorry. I promise this is the last time.”
You whisper it with tears in your eyes. Your chest feels heavy. You cannot believe you did it again.
Maybe it was the pornography you promised never to watch again.
The secret relationship you knew you should end.
The lie you told to protect your reputation.
The bitterness you keep feeding while telling everyone you have forgiven.
The private compromise nobody at church knows about.
Or perhaps something that happened years ago, something you have already confessed a hundred times, yet the memory still makes you feel unworthy of looking toward heaven.
You kneel. You cry. You ask God to forgive you.
And for a moment, you feel better.
Until the temptation returns.
Until the same door opens.
Until the same decision appears in front of you.
And somehow, despite everything you felt the night before, you walk through it again.
Then comes the guilt.
Again.
And the tears.
Again.
And the promises.
Again.
Eventually, a frightening question begins whispering inside your soul.
“Have I actually repented, or have I just become very good at feeling sorry?”
Stay with that question.
Because Scripture tells us about two men who sinned against Jesus, experienced profound sorrow, and reached very different endings.
One betrayed Him.
The other denied Him.
Both had reason to weep.
But their stories reveal something that every Christian needs to understand before mistaking emotional pain for spiritual transformation.
And somewhere between Judas and Peter, you may recognize your own heart.
Judas Iscariot was not a stranger to Jesus.
He walked with Him. Heard His teaching. Witnessed His miracles. Shared meals with Him. Saw compassion in His eyes and authority in His words.
Imagine that.
The man who betrayed the Son of God had spent years standing close enough to hear His voice.
And yet proximity to Jesus did not mean Judas had surrendered his heart to Jesus.
When Judas realized that Jesus had been condemned, Matthew records something deeply disturbing.

“Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, Saying, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood.” (Matthew 27:3–4, KJV)
Read that again.
Judas admitted his sin.
He acknowledged Jesus' innocence.
He returned the money.
He experienced overwhelming remorse.
He even used words that sounded like confession.
And yet his story ended in tragedy.
There is an important detail hidden in the original Greek.
In Matthew 27:3, the word translated “repented himself” in the King James Version is μεταμεληθεὶς (metamelētheis), from metamelomai, a verb that can express regret, remorse, or a change of mind.
It is not the same word used in Jesus' command to repent in Mark 1:15.
There, Jesus says:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
The Greek verb is μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite), from metanoeō, referring to repentance—a turning of one's mind and life toward God.

We must be careful here. These Greek words are not always mutually exclusive, and metamelomai can describe a positive change of heart in other passages, such as Matthew 21:29. A dictionary distinction alone cannot determine someone's spiritual condition.
But Matthew's account of Judas, considered alongside the wider teaching of Scripture, reveals a sobering reality.
Regretting what sin has done is not necessarily the same as turning from sin to God.
Judas recognized the horror of his actions, but Scripture does not describe him returning to Jesus in trusting surrender.
His remorse became a crushing despair.
And his life ended before he witnessed the risen Christ.
We should not use Judas' tragedy to speculate beyond what Scripture reveals about every detail of his inner thoughts.
But we must not miss the warning.
You can hate the consequences of sin without yet loving the holiness of God.
You can fear exposure without desiring transformation.
You can desperately wish you had never done something while still refusing to surrender the desires that led you there.
And perhaps the most painful possibility of all is this:
You can become so consumed with your failure that you stop looking toward the Savior who alone can redeem you.
Now look at Peter.
Peter loved Jesus.
He was passionate, outspoken, impulsive, and confident.
When Jesus warned that His disciples would stumble, Peter insisted he would remain faithful.
He was certain of his courage.
Until courage became costly.
In the courtyard, while Jesus faced interrogation, Peter was confronted about his connection to Him.
And Peter denied Him.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke records one of the most heartbreaking moments in the Gospels.
“And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.” (Luke 22:61, KJV)
Can you imagine that look?
The face Peter had watched heal the sick.
The eyes that had seen him before he ever understood his calling.
The Lord who had welcomed him, taught him, corrected him, and loved him.
Now looking directly at him after his denial.
Peter remembered Jesus' warning.
And Scripture says:
“And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.” (Luke 22:62, KJV)
Those tears were real.
His failure was real.
His shame was real.
But the tears themselves were not the whole story.
After the resurrection, Jesus came to His disciples.
And in John 21, beside a charcoal fire, the risen Savior addressed Peter personally.
Three times, Jesus asked Peter about his love.
Three times, Peter answered.
Jesus then entrusted him with responsibility for His sheep.
Think about the mercy in that scene.
Peter had denied knowing Jesus beside a fire.
Now, beside another fire, Jesus was restoring a fallen disciple.
The man who had publicly failed was being called to follow again.
Jesus did not pretend the denial had never happened.
He did not tell Peter that sin was harmless.
He did not remove the seriousness of what had occurred.
But neither did He declare that Peter's worst moment had become his permanent identity.
He called him forward.
“Follow me.” (John 21:19, KJV)
And Peter did.
The same man who had trembled before questioning later stood before crowds proclaiming the crucified and risen Christ.
Not because Peter discovered hidden strength within himself.
But because the risen Jesus restored him, and the Holy Spirit empowered him.
That is the difference we must understand.
Guilt can make you stare at your sin. Repentance turns you toward the Savior.
And Scripture explains this distinction with extraordinary clarity.
In 2 Corinthians 7:10, Paul writes:
The original Greek describes λύπη κατὰ θεόν (lypē kata theon)—sorrow according to God, or godly sorrow.
And that sorrow produces μετάνοιαν (metanoian)—repentance.
Notice the order.
Godly sorrow produces repentance.
It is not automatically identical to repentance.
A person can experience intense sadness without surrendering to God.
A person can feel exposed without becoming obedient.
A person can cry during worship, confess during prayer, and feel deeply convicted during a sermon—yet continue protecting the very sin that God is calling them to abandon.
Emotional intensity is not proof of spiritual change.
But neither is the absence of tears proof that repentance is missing.
Some people weep openly.
Others become quiet.
Some feel immediate emotional relief.
Others begin obeying God while still wrestling with fear, grief, or lingering shame.
Repentance is not measured by how dramatically you cry.
It is revealed in the direction your heart is turning.
And that brings us to a question many of us would rather avoid.
Are you grieving because you sinned against God, or because your sin has made your life uncomfortable?
Perhaps you are sorry because your spouse discovered the messages.
Because your reputation suffered.
Because your family no longer trusts you.
Because the consequences became unbearable.
Those consequences matter. The pain you have caused matters. The damage must not be minimized.
But genuine repentance reaches deeper.
It begins to say:
“Lord, even if nobody had discovered this, it would still be wrong because it dishonors You.”
That is a different kind of sorrow.
Not merely embarrassment.
Not merely fear.
Not merely self-disgust.
It is the painful awakening of a heart that begins to see sin in the light of God's holiness and grace.
And this is where the Old Testament gives us another beautiful window into the meaning of repentance.
The Hebrew verb שׁוּב (shuv) means to turn or return, and it is frequently used in calls for God's people to turn back to Him.
In Joel 2:12–13, the Lord calls His people:
“Turn ye even to me with all your heart, and with fasting, and with weeping, and with mourning: And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God.” (KJV)
The Hebrew phrase שׁוּבוּ עָדַי בְּכָל־לְבַבְכֶם (shuvu adai bekhol-levavkhem) means, in context, “Return to Me with all your heart.”
Not merely return to religious activity.
Not merely return to church attendance.
Not merely return to looking respectable.
Return to Me.
God was not impressed by the outward tearing of garments when the heart remained distant.
He wanted the heart itself.
And why could His people return?
Because the same passage declares that He is gracious, merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in steadfast love.
Do you see it?
God's call to repentance is not an invitation to earn His mercy through sufficient misery.
It is an invitation to return to the merciful God.
Some of us have been trying to punish ourselves enough to feel worthy of forgiveness.
We replay what happened.
We revisit old conversations.
We remember the faces we disappointed.
We lie awake wondering whether God has finally grown tired of us.
And somewhere along the way, we begin to believe that continuing to hate ourselves is evidence that we take sin seriously.
But self-condemnation is not the same as holiness.
You cannot suffer enough to become your own savior.
You cannot cry enough tears to purchase forgiveness.
You cannot reverse yesterday by despising yourself today.
The blood of Jesus Christ—not the intensity of your regret—is the foundation of your forgiveness.
Listen to 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
What extraordinary words for a guilty person.
And yet we must not twist that promise into permission to continue deliberately embracing sin.
Grace is not God's approval of rebellion.
Romans 6:1–2 confronts that misunderstanding directly.
“Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” (KJV)
The Gospel does not teach us to become comfortable with the chains from which Christ came to free us.
It announces forgiveness and calls us into a new life.
That new life does not mean Christians suddenly become incapable of stumbling.
It means sin can no longer be treated as a treasured master.
The repentant believer may still struggle.
May still need help.
May still battle deeply rooted habits.
May still experience setbacks while learning to walk in obedience.
But something has changed.
Instead of defending the darkness, they begin bringing it into the light.
Instead of celebrating compromise, they begin resisting it.
Instead of demanding that God accept their sin, they ask Him to transform their desires.
And when they fall, they are called to return to Christ rather than surrender to despair.
Consider the prodigal son.
Jesus tells us in Luke 15 about a younger son who demanded his inheritance, left home, and squandered what he had received.
Eventually, everything collapsed.
The money disappeared.
The pleasure faded.
The friends were gone.
And the young man found himself hungry, humiliated, and longing for food given to pigs.
His consequences were terrible.
But the turning point was not merely that he felt miserable.
Scripture says he came to himself.
