He recognized his condition.
He acknowledged his sin.
And then he made a decision.
“I will arise and go to my father.” (Luke 15:18, KJV)
There it is.
Not simply, “I feel terrible.”
Not simply, “I wish things were different.”
Not simply, “I hate what happened to me.”
I will arise and go to my father.
He moved toward the one he had wronged.
And while he was still a great way off, his father saw him.
The father ran.
He embraced him.
He kissed him.
The son confessed.
And the father welcomed him home.
Do not miss what Jesus is revealing about the Father's heart.
The son did not return with an impressive record of good works.
He returned acknowledging his sin and depending on mercy.
The father's compassion was not purchased by the son's suffering.
And the son's return was not an attempt to prove that rebellion had been harmless.
It was a homecoming made possible by grace.
Perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to hear tonight.
You have spent so long standing in the ruins of your choices that you have forgotten there is a road home.
You keep saying, “I feel guilty.”
But Jesus is calling you beyond guilt.
Come home.
Not because your sin was small.
But because His mercy is greater than you imagined.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because repentance is precisely the response His grace calls forth.
And perhaps your situation is more complicated.
Maybe you genuinely repented years ago.
You confessed.
You turned away.
You made restitution where possible.
You sought forgiveness from the people you harmed.
You began walking differently.
But guilt still visits you.
An old photograph brings back memories.
A familiar place makes your stomach tighten.
Someone mentions the past, and suddenly you feel like the same person you were before Christ began changing your life.
Listen carefully.
The continued feeling of guilt does not necessarily mean you have failed to repent.
Feelings can remain long after genuine forgiveness has been received.
Some consequences remain.
Some relationships require years of rebuilding.
Some wounds need patient healing.
And some memories continue to hurt.
Repentance does not erase history.
Forgiveness does not automatically eliminate earthly consequences.
But neither do lingering emotions cancel the promises of God.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV)
That is not a declaration that sin never matters.
It is the announcement that those who belong to Christ are no longer under the condemning judgment from which He has redeemed them.
And if you are in Christ, you must learn to distinguish the Spirit's conviction from hopeless condemnation.
Conviction calls you to acknowledge sin and return to God.
Condemnation tells you that returning is pointless.
Conviction directs your attention toward truth, confession, faith, and obedience.
Hopeless condemnation insists that your failure is greater than the cross.
But the cross of Jesus Christ is not a fragile offer of forgiveness.
At Calvary, the sinless Son of God bore sin's judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
The resurrection is not merely an inspiring ending to a tragic story.
It is God's triumphant declaration that Jesus Christ has conquered death and that His saving work is sufficient.
That is why repentance and faith belong together.
Jesus did not simply announce, “Feel bad about your sins.”
He proclaimed:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (Mark 1:15, KJV)
Turn from sin.
Believe the good news.
Trust the Savior.
Follow Him.
Not to purchase salvation through your obedience, but because salvation is God's gracious gift received through faith, and genuine faith bears fruit in a transformed life.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds these truths together.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works.
And we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace is the source.
Faith receives.
Obedience follows.
The order matters.
Because if you reverse it, you will spend your life trying to become good enough for Jesus to love you.
And if you remove obedience altogether, you will misunderstand the transforming purpose of His grace.
So what does repentance look like when tomorrow morning arrives?
It may look like telling the truth after months of lying.
Deleting the secret account you used to feed temptation.
Ending an adulterous relationship rather than merely apologizing for it.
Returning what you stole.
Confessing wrongdoing without blaming the person you hurt.
Seeking pastoral counsel and appropriate professional help for patterns you cannot safely or wisely address alone.
Accepting accountability.
Making restitution where possible.
Respecting the boundaries of people you harmed instead of demanding immediate reconciliation.
And choosing, day after day, to walk in the light.
These actions do not purchase forgiveness.
They are ways genuine repentance may bear fruit.
John the Baptist called people to “Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.” (Matthew 3:8, KJV)
Fruit is not the root of salvation.
But a living tree is not meant to remain fruitless forever.
And if you are reading this while struggling with the same temptation you have fought for years, please hear the difference between encouragement and permission.
Do not surrender to despair.
But do not make peace with the sin either.
Do not conclude that every struggle proves you are beyond God's mercy.
But do not use the language of struggle to excuse a deliberate refusal to change.
Bring the truth into the light.
Seek help.
Remove access to what repeatedly draws you into sin.
Pray honestly.
Stay connected to mature believers who will love you enough to tell you the truth.
And remember that the Christian life is not sustained by human willpower alone.
We depend upon the Holy Spirit.
Galatians 5:16 calls believers to walk in the Spirit.
Transformation is not merely behavior management.
It is a life increasingly shaped by communion with Christ.
And now I want to ask you something.
Not as a stranger looking for your secrets.
Not as someone pretending to know the private condition of your soul.
But as a fellow human being who knows how easily we can confuse the pain of consequences with the surrender of repentance.
What have you been calling repentance that God may actually be asking you to bring fully into His light?
Is it the apology you keep repeating while refusing to change?
The relationship you keep justifying?
The bitterness you keep protecting?
The image of yourself you are terrified to lose?
Or is your struggle the opposite?
Have you truly turned to Christ, yet continued treating yourself as though His forgiveness could never be enough?
One person needs to stop excusing sin.
Another needs to stop rejecting grace.
Both need Jesus.
And that is why this message matters so deeply.
Because Christianity is not a story about good people who never failed.
It is the good news of a holy Savior who came to rescue sinners.
It is not the celebration of scandal.
It is the triumph of grace over the sin and shame that scandal exposes.
It is the testimony of Peter, who denied his Lord but was restored by the risen Christ.
It is the homecoming of the prodigal, who returned to a father rich in compassion.
It is the witness of David, who, after terrible sin, cried out:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” (Psalm 51:10, KJV)
Notice what David asked for.
Not merely a cleaner reputation.
Not merely relief from consequences.
A clean heart.
A renewed spirit.
That is a prayer worth making your own.
“Jesus, I do not want to become an expert at apologizing while remaining unchanged.
I do not want to mistake shame for holiness.
I do not want to hide behind religious language while refusing Your truth.
Show me where I have been making excuses.
Give me courage to confess what I have concealed.
Teach me to turn from what dishonors You.
Help me repair what I can, accept what I cannot undo, and walk faithfully in the light.
And where I have genuinely repented but still carry crushing shame, teach me to trust the forgiveness You purchased at the cross.
I cannot save myself.
I need Your mercy.
I need Your Spirit.
I need You.
Amen.”
Maybe you are crying as you read this.
Maybe you feel uncomfortable.
Maybe you feel relieved.
Maybe for the first time you understand why you have spent so many years apologizing without finding freedom.
Or perhaps you finally understand that the shame you have carried for years is not a debt Jesus is asking you to keep paying.
Whatever brought you here, do not allow this moment to become another emotional experience that fades when you close your phone.
Respond to the truth.
If you need to confess, confess.
If you need to turn, turn.
If you need help, reach out.
If you need to trust God's promise of forgiveness, open your Bible and let His Word speak more authoritatively than your feelings.
And if you have never placed your faith in Jesus Christ, today is an opportunity to call upon Him.
Not because reading an article saves you.
Not because repeating a particular prayer earns eternal life.
But because the crucified and risen Savior calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
And His invitation is real.
Before you leave, I want to invite you into a conversation that may help someone else find the courage to stop hiding.
You do not need to reveal private details or expose anyone else's sins publicly. A few honest words may be enough to remind another person that they are not alone.
Not merely to circulate another religious post.
But because someone in your circle may desperately need to understand the difference between feeling condemned and being called to repentance.
There is also a deeper way to stand alongside this mission.

Gospel Warrior exists to help bring Scripture, discipleship, encouragement, and the message of Jesus Christ to people who may never walk into a church building but will encounter a message while scrolling through their phones.
Some are searching.
Some are grieving.
Some are hiding.
Some are one honest conversation away from asking questions about the Gospel they have avoided for years.
Creating and sharing faithful Christian resources takes time, work, and ongoing support.
Scripture says in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
Christian generosity must be willing, never coerced.
You do not have to pay to glorify God.
You can glorify Him through repentance, obedience, love, prayer, generosity, and faithful service.
The products are simply a token of appreciation.
The deeper purpose is to help more people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
The Word of God must never become something people feel they have to purchase before they can grow.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Let this be more than a page people visit.
Let it become a place where people are pointed toward Scripture, challenged to repent, encouraged to believe, and reminded that redemption is found in Christ alone.
Because somewhere tonight, another person is sitting on the edge of a bed, staring at the floor.
They have done something they deeply regret.
They have promised to change more times than they can count.
They are wondering whether God has heard enough apologies from them.
Maybe that person is someone you love.
Maybe that person is you.
And if so, remember Peter.
Remember the prodigal.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
The answer is not to become better at feeling guilty.
The answer is to turn to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith, and to keep walking with Him.
Your sin must never be minimized.
Your need for repentance must never be denied.
But neither should the mercy of the risen Savior be underestimated.
Because the Gospel does not end with the moment you fell.
It announces the Savior who died for sinners, rose victorious, and calls them into newness of life.
You may never be able to rewrite the moment you fell, but by the grace of Jesus Christ, that moment does not have to write the ending of your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHEN HONORING YOUR PASTOR BECOMES IDOLATRY: THE DANGEROUS MOMENT A SERVANT OF GOD TAKES THE PLACE OF GOD
paragraphs: WHEN HONORING YOUR PASTOR BECOMES IDOLATRY: THE DANGEROUS MOMENT A SERVANT OF GOD TAKES THE PLACE OF GOD

You can love your pastor, defend your pastor, give to your church, and serve faithfully for years… yet slowly surrender to a human being the devotion that belongs to Jesus Christ alone. And the most frightening part? You might call it faithfulness while your heart is being led away from the very Savior your pastor was called to preach.
There is a kind of church hurt that does not begin with someone leaving the church.
Sometimes, it begins with someone who refuses to leave.
Someone who sees things they should question but remains silent.
Someone who hears Scripture being twisted but convinces themselves that questioning the preacher would be questioning God.
Someone who watches a struggling family get ignored while an influential leader receives extravagant attention.
Someone who knows something is wrong…
But is terrified to say it.
Because somewhere along the way, they were taught that touching the reputation of a pastor was the same as touching the glory of God.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part is that they genuinely love Jesus.
They pray. They serve. They sacrifice. They give. They volunteer when nobody else shows up.
They are not trying to rebel.
They are trying to be faithful.
But nobody told them that loyalty can become dangerous when it demands the surrender of biblical discernment.
Nobody explained that submission to spiritual leadership is not the same as surrendering your conscience.
And nobody warned them that a church can speak the name of Jesus every Sunday while gradually making one human personality the emotional center of everything.
Read that again.
Because this is not merely about pastors who abuse authority.
It is also about believers who, sometimes without realizing it, give spiritual leaders a place in their hearts that Scripture reserves for Christ.
And before anyone mistakes this for an attack against pastors, understand something important.
Faithful pastors are gifts to the Church.

They carry burdens most congregations never see. They visit hospital rooms, bury loved ones, counsel broken marriages, preach while exhausted, pray for people who never know their names were mentioned before God, and sometimes endure criticism while quietly carrying their own grief.
They deserve love.
They deserve prayer.
They deserve appropriate honor and support.
Scripture is unmistakably clear about that.
But there is a line.
A holy line.
And when that line is crossed, honoring a shepherd becomes worshiping a servant.
And Jesus never died on the cross so that another human being could occupy His throne.
The apostle Paul addressed a disturbing problem in the Corinthian church.
Believers were dividing themselves according to their preferred spiritual leaders.
Some identified with Paul.
Others with Apollos.
Others with Cephas.
Their attachment to human messengers was becoming a source of rivalry within the body of Christ.
Listen to Paul's question in 1 Corinthians 1:13:
“Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?” (KJV)
That question should make every Christian uncomfortable in the right way.
Was your pastor crucified for you?
Did your bishop carry your sins to Calvary?
Did your apostle conquer death?
Did your favorite preacher shed sinless blood for your redemption?
No.
Jesus did.
And that distinction changes everything.
Paul did not deny the importance of spiritual leadership. He corrected the dangerous tendency to build Christian identity around human personalities.
Later, in 1 Corinthians 3:5, he asked:
“Who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed, even as the Lord gave to every man?” (KJV)
The Greek word translated “ministers” is διάκονοι (diakonoi).
It refers to servants or ministers.
Not saviors.
Not spiritual celebrities whose words are beyond examination.
Not human beings who become the final authority over another person's relationship with God.
Servants.
Paul understood something that many churches desperately need to remember.
The messenger matters.
But the message belongs to Christ.
The shepherd matters.
But the sheep belong to Christ.
The preacher may help you find the narrow road.
But the preacher is not the Way.
Jesus is.
And this is where the question becomes painfully personal.
What happens when your pastor says something that contradicts Scripture?
What happens when the person you deeply respect becomes defensive about accountability?
What happens when a church leader begins demanding the kind of unquestioning loyalty that belongs only to God?
What happens when your conscience, informed by Scripture, tells you something is wrong, but everyone around you insists that obedience means silence?
Would you still follow Jesus if following Him meant respectfully disagreeing with your pastor?
Or have you become so attached to the voice behind the pulpit that you can no longer recognize the voice of the Shepherd?
Jesus said in John 10:27:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” (KJV)
Notice whose voice ultimately defines the sheep.
Not the voice of a famous preacher.
Not the voice of a church founder.
Not the voice of a charismatic personality.
His voice.
The voice of Jesus Christ.
That does not mean Christians should reject pastors or imagine they need no teaching. Christ gives shepherds and teachers to equip His people (Ephesians 4:11–13).
But every faithful shepherd must lead people toward the Chief Shepherd, never toward personal dependence that replaces devotion to Christ.
Peter made that distinction remarkably clear.
In 1 Peter 5:2–3, he instructed church elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for dishonest gain, and not as those who dominate the people entrusted to them.
The Greek expression μηδ’ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες (mēd’ hōs katakyrieuontes) conveys the prohibition against domineering rule.
Pastoral leadership is not permission to control souls.
It is a calling to care for them.
And verse 4 identifies Jesus as the ἀρχιποίμενος (archipoimēn)—the Chief Shepherd.
Think about that.
Even the most respected pastor in the world is still an undershepherd.
Still accountable.
Still human.
Still in need of mercy.
Still dependent on the same grace that saves the people sitting in the congregation.
A pastor who understands this will not be threatened when Scripture is opened.
He will welcome the Word of God being honored above his own opinions.
Because a faithful shepherd does not need to compete with Jesus.
He knows whose flock he serves.
But there is another side to this conversation that we cannot ignore.
Sometimes, the congregation helps create the very idol that later wounds it.
We elevate leaders beyond healthy boundaries.
We treat their opinions as unquestionable.
We excuse behavior we would condemn in anyone else.
We defend them before examining the facts.
We confuse charisma with anointing.
We confuse popularity with holiness.
We confuse emotional preaching with biblical faithfulness.
And when someone raises a legitimate concern, we accuse them of rebellion before we even hear their testimony.
That is not spiritual maturity.
That is dangerous partiality.
And Scripture does not support it.
Consider Acts 17:11.
The Bereans were commended because they received the apostolic message eagerly while examining the Scriptures daily to determine whether the teaching was true.
They did not reject Paul.
They listened carefully.
But they also examined what they heard.
If the apostle Paul could be examined against Scripture, why should any modern preacher be considered beyond biblical examination?
Read that slowly.
Paul, whose letters became part of the New Testament, did not demand that people abandon discernment simply because he carried apostolic authority.
Yet today, some Christians feel guilty for opening their Bibles to verify what was preached on Sunday.
Something has gone terribly wrong when biblical discernment is labeled dishonor.
And something has become spiritually unhealthy when asking sincere questions is treated as an attack against God.
But we must also be careful not to turn discernment into suspicion.
Not every disagreement proves spiritual abuse.
Not every pastoral mistake is deliberate deception.
Not every uncomfortable sermon is manipulation.
Not every correction is control.
Pastors are human beings who can misunderstand, grow, repent, and change.
Scripture calls believers to receive legitimate spiritual leadership with humility, not with perpetual hostility.
Hebrews 13:17 teaches the seriousness of responding to those who watch over souls and must give an account.
First Timothy 5:17 speaks of elders who rule well being worthy of double honor, especially those laboring in preaching and teaching.
The Greek word τιμή (timē), used in this passage, carries the sense of honor, value, or esteem.
The passage recognizes genuine pastoral service and the importance of appropriate respect and support.
But honor is not worship.
Accountability is not rebellion.
And biblical submission never requires participating in sin or concealing wrongdoing.
Acts 5:29 gives a principle that remains decisive whenever human authority conflicts with God's commands:
“We ought to obey God rather than men.” (KJV)
Those words were spoken by the apostles in response to authorities who ordered them to stop proclaiming Jesus.
The immediate context concerns obedience to God under persecution, not an ordinary disagreement between church members and pastors.
Nevertheless, the principle is unmistakable.
No human authority is ultimate.
Not political authority.
Not family authority.
Not church authority.
God alone possesses absolute authority.
And this becomes especially important when leaders misuse biblical language to silence those who are hurting.
Perhaps you have heard someone say, “Touch not mine anointed.”
The phrase appears in Psalm 105:15 and 1 Chronicles 16:22.
In its historical setting, Psalm 105 recounts God's protection of the patriarchs and His covenant people.
The Hebrew expression אַל־תִּגְּעוּ בִמְשִׁיחָי (ʾal-tiggeʿu vimshiḥay) means, in context, “Do not touch my anointed ones.”
The passage is not a blanket prohibition against respectfully questioning a pastor's teaching, examining misconduct, or seeking biblical accountability.
Using it that way goes beyond what the text establishes.
And that matters.
Because when Scripture is taken out of context, the people most likely to suffer are often those who are already afraid to speak.
A young believer who notices something troubling.
A woman who has been mistreated.
A volunteer who witnesses financial dishonesty.
A family pressured to give beyond its ability.
A church member who asks a sincere question and suddenly finds themselves treated like an enemy.
Not every accusation is true, and justice requires careful investigation.
First Timothy 5:19 cautions against receiving an accusation against an elder without two or three witnesses, while the following verse calls for public rebuke of elders who persist in sin.
Both principles matter.
Leaders must be protected from reckless accusations.
And congregations must be protected from leaders whose wrongdoing is concealed.
Biblical accountability is neither a license for gossip nor a shield for abuse.
It is a call to truth.
And truth should never be sacrificed to preserve a religious image.
Imagine sitting in a church you have loved for fifteen years.
You were baptized there.
Your children attended Sunday school there.
You learned to pray there.
Your pastor stood beside your family when your father died.
He helped you through a season when you almost abandoned your faith.
You owe him genuine gratitude.
Then one day, something happens.
You discover a serious concern that cannot simply be dismissed.
Your stomach tightens.
You do not want it to be true.
You pray that you misunderstood.
You look for a reasonable explanation.
You speak carefully because you know reputations matter.
But the more you seek clarity, the more you are told to stop asking questions.
And suddenly you are faced with a painful choice.
Protect the relationship you treasure…
Or remain faithful to the truth you believe God has revealed.
That is where many Christians begin to understand the difference between honoring a pastor and idolizing one.
Honoring a pastor means appreciating faithful service while remembering that the pastor is accountable to God.
Idolizing a pastor means treating loyalty to that pastor as more important than truth, righteousness, or obedience to Christ.
Honoring a pastor means praying for him when he is weak.
Idolizing him means pretending he cannot be wrong.
Honoring a pastor means receiving biblical correction with humility.
Idolizing him means accepting every instruction without testing it against Scripture.
Honoring a pastor means supporting faithful ministry.
Idolizing him means believing that giving money to a particular leader or organization proves your devotion to God.
Honoring a pastor means protecting the church from baseless accusations.
Idolizing him means suppressing credible concerns because acknowledging them would threaten the leader's reputation.
And perhaps the clearest distinction is this:
Honor recognizes the servant's calling. Idolatry gives the servant the place that belongs to the Savior.
The Bible contains a remarkable moment that exposes how easily human beings can misdirect spiritual devotion.
In Acts 10:25–26, Cornelius fell at Peter's feet and worshiped him.
Peter immediately lifted him up and said:
“Stand up; I myself also am a man.” (KJV)
What a response.
Peter did not enjoy the moment.
He did not build a theology around his own importance.
He did not tell Cornelius that honoring the apostle meant bowing before him.
He refused the worship.
Because Peter knew something every Christian leader must remember.
The servant must never receive what belongs to the Master.
There is another moment in Acts 14:11–15 when the people of Lystra attempted to treat Paul and Barnabas as gods after a miraculous healing.
The apostles rejected that response and directed the crowd toward the living God.
The pattern is clear.
When human admiration begins turning into religious devotion, faithful servants redirect attention to God.
They do not cultivate worship of themselves.
And if you are a pastor reading this, perhaps this is the question worth carrying into your next sermon.
When people leave your church, are they more impressed with your personality, or more captivated by Jesus?
Do they know your favorite expressions better than they know the teachings of Christ?
Are they afraid to disagree with you?
Can they approach you with legitimate concerns without fearing humiliation or retaliation?
Do you teach them to depend on Scripture, or have they become dependent on your approval?
Do you welcome accountability, including accountability that might be uncomfortable?
These are not questions meant to destroy faithful pastors.
They are questions that can protect a ministry from becoming centered on a human being.
And to the congregation, the questions are just as searching.
If your pastor lost his platform tomorrow, would you still worship Jesus?
If your favorite preacher disappointed you, would the Gospel still be true?
If the church you love failed you, would the cross lose its power?
If the person who taught you about Christ walked away from his own teaching, would you walk away from Christ too?
These are painful questions.
But they reveal where our faith is anchored.
Paul wrote in 1 Corinthians 3:11:
“For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.” (KJV)
Not your denomination.
Not your church's reputation.
Not your pastor's following.
Not a ministry's financial success.
Jesus Christ.
Everything else must be built upon Him.
And there is a deeply personal reason this matters.
When we idolize spiritual leaders, we place impossible expectations upon imperfect human beings.
We expect them never to disappoint us.
Never to struggle.
Never to misunderstand.
Never to fail.
And when they do, our faith can collapse because we have unknowingly attached the reliability of Jesus to the reliability of a person.
But Jesus never asked anyone to place that burden upon a pastor.
Only Christ is without sin.
Only Christ is the perfect High Priest.
Only Christ is the one mediator between God and humanity, as 1 Timothy 2:5 teaches.
The Greek phrase εἷς γὰρ θεός, εἷς καὶ μεσίτης (heis gar theos, heis kai mesitēs) begins with the declaration that there is one God and one mediator.
Paul then identifies that mediator as Christ Jesus.
This does not eliminate the value of pastoral care, intercession, counseling, or Christian fellowship.
It establishes that no spiritual leader occupies Christ's unique position as mediator of redemption.
Your pastor can pray with you.
But Jesus is your Savior.
Your pastor can teach you.
But Jesus is your Lord.
Your pastor can walk beside you through suffering.
But Jesus is the One who conquered sin and death.
Your pastor may help you understand the Scriptures.
But your salvation does not rest upon your pastor's approval.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear those words more than anything else today.
You have spent years trying to be the perfect church member.
You volunteered when you were exhausted.
You gave when finances were difficult.
You stayed quiet when something felt wrong.
You were terrified of disappointing people because you had been taught that their disappointment might mean God's rejection.
And now you feel confused.
Perhaps even ashamed.
You wonder whether questioning something makes you rebellious.
You wonder whether leaving an unsafe situation would mean abandoning God.
You wonder whether the faith you have known is strong enough to survive an honest examination.
Hear this carefully.
Jesus Christ is not threatened by truth.
You do not need to deny reality to remain faithful to Him.
You do not need to defend wrongdoing to prove that you love the Church.
You do not need to surrender your God-given moral responsibility to honor spiritual leadership.
And if you have been harmed by someone who misused spiritual authority, what happened should be taken seriously.
Seek wise, trustworthy support. Where there is abuse, coercion, exploitation, or criminal conduct, appropriate safeguarding and civil authorities may need to be involved.
Forgiveness does not require concealing wrongdoing.
Reconciliation does not require immediate restoration of trust.
And honoring Christ does not mean remaining exposed to harm.
But there is also a warning for those who have been wounded.
Do not allow the failure of an imperfect shepherd to convince you that the Chief Shepherd has failed.
Human betrayal is real.
The pain can be devastating.
The consequences can last for years.
But the Gospel was never built upon the sinlessness of pastors.
It was built upon the sinlessness of Jesus.
Hebrews 13:8 declares:
“Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.” (KJV)
The pastor who once encouraged you may change.
The church you once trusted may change.
Your circumstances may change.
Your understanding of people may change.
But Jesus Christ remains faithful.
And the cross still stands.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not because grace excuses scandal.
Not because repentance is optional.
Not because wrongdoing should be hidden under religious language.
But because the grace of Christ can meet people in the wreckage of human failure and lead them toward truth, repentance, healing, and restoration.
Grace does not ask us to call darkness light.
Grace brings us into the light.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise applies to the proud pastor who needs to repent.
It applies to the congregation that enabled wrongdoing.
It applies to the believer who confused loyalty with worship.
It applies to the Christian who has allowed bitterness to harden the heart.
And it applies to the exhausted soul who wants to return to Jesus but no longer knows how to trust.
The door of repentance is not reserved for those whose sins are socially acceptable.
The mercy of Christ calls every one of us.
Pastor and congregation.
Leader and follower.
The wounded and those who have caused wounds.
All of us must come before the same cross.
All of us need the same Savior.
And no one gets to stand above the Gospel.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build another personality-centered religious platform.
Not to replace your local church or demand the loyalty that belongs to Jesus.
But to keep pointing hearts back to the Word of God, to repentance, to grace, to forgiveness, to spiritual discernment, and to the transforming power of Christ.
Because there are people scrolling through Facebook tonight who are spiritually exhausted.
Some have been hurt by churches.
Some have been disappointed by leaders.
Some have become suspicious of every pastor because one pastor betrayed their trust.
Others are still trapped in unhealthy spiritual dependence and do not know how to distinguish biblical honor from idolatry.
And some faithful pastors are quietly asking God to help them lead without pride.
Every one of these people needs something greater than another religious personality.
They need Jesus.
They need the Scriptures opened faithfully.
They need a place where conviction is not confused with condemnation.
Where grace is not confused with permission to sin.
Where truth is not sacrificed for popularity.
And where spiritual growth is measured by becoming more like Christ, not by becoming more loyal to a platform.
These resources are offered freely because spiritual nourishment should not be reserved only for those who can afford to pay.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, examine your heart, find courage to repent, or remember the grace of Jesus during a difficult season, you have an opportunity to help this ministry reach others.

Scripture affirms the value of supporting Gospel ministry. Galatians 6:6 encourages those who receive instruction in the Word to share good things with those who teach, while 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be willing, not reluctant or compelled.
And that distinction matters especially in an article about spiritual authority.
There is no pressure to give what you cannot afford.
And there is no suggestion that your money can purchase spiritual blessing.
But there is a meaningful invitation.
It is helping make ongoing discipleship resources and Gospel-centered encouragement available to people who may desperately need them.
Not merely because a ministry wants more views.
But because someone you know may be wrestling with the exact questions we have discussed.
A pastor may need a gentle reminder that the flock belongs to Christ.
A church member may need permission to examine teaching against Scripture.
A wounded believer may need to know that the failures of human leaders do not invalidate the faithfulness of Jesus.
A young Christian may need to understand that biblical honor and blind loyalty are not the same thing.
And if this article has brought something to the surface in your own heart, I want to invite you into an honest conversation.
Or, if you are still healing from spiritual disappointment, you can simply comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
You do not owe strangers the details of your pain.
You do not need to expose private experiences publicly to prove that you are sincere.
But your honest words may remind another believer that they are not alone.
Because the goal is not to produce Christians who know how to defend a favorite preacher.
The goal is to grow disciples who know, love, trust, obey, and follow Jesus.
And before you leave, I want to ask you one final question.
A question that reaches beyond church culture, denominations, personalities, and religious traditions.
If Jesus stood beside your pastor this Sunday…
And the two of them gave you conflicting instructions…
Whose voice would you follow?
The answer may reveal more about your spiritual foundation than years of church attendance ever could.
A faithful pastor would want you to follow Jesus.
A faithful church would want you to follow Jesus.
A faithful ministry would want you to follow Jesus.
Because the Church does not belong to the preacher.
The Bride belongs to the Bridegroom.

And one day, when every pulpit is silent, every religious title has faded, every ministry platform has disappeared, and every human reputation has been laid bare before God, the only name worthy of ultimate worship will still be the name of Jesus Christ.
So honor your pastor.
Pray for your pastor.
Encourage your pastor.
Support faithful ministry as God enables you.
Receive biblical teaching with humility.
But never hand a human being the throne of your heart.
That throne belongs to the One who wore a crown of thorns.
The One who carried the cross.
The One who forgave sinners.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who can restore what religious pride, spiritual confusion, human betrayal, and sin have broken.
His name is Jesus.
And He is not asking you to worship His servants.
He is calling you to follow Him.
Never let your love for the person who introduced you to Jesus become the reason you stop listening to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE FATHER LOVED ANOTHER WOMAN MORE—BUT GOD REFUSED TO LET HER SON STEAL THE FIRSTBORN’S INHERITANCE
paragraphs: THE FATHER LOVED ANOTHER WOMAN MORE—BUT GOD REFUSED TO LET HER SON STEAL THE FIRSTBORN’S INHERITANCE

Buried in Deuteronomy 21:15–17 is a law about a wounded son, a divided family, and a God who refuses to let human favoritism decide someone’s worth. But when you follow this truth through Scripture, it leads to something even greater: Jesus Christ, the beloved Son, who brings the undeserving into the Father’s household.
Imagine growing up in a house where you knew your father loved someone else more.
Not because he told you.
Because you could feel it.

You saw it in the way he smiled when the other children entered the room. You heard it in the tenderness of his voice when he spoke to their mother. You noticed how quickly he celebrated their achievements while yours seemed to disappear into silence.
You learned to recognize the difference between being provided for and being cherished.
You had food on the table. A roof over your head. A place to sleep.
But you still wondered why love seemed to come so easily to everyone else.
And then one day, your father dies.
The family gathers. The inheritance is about to be divided. And suddenly, the same favoritism that wounded your childhood threatens to follow you into your future.
Your father had another wife.
He loved her more.
And now her son is about to receive what the law says belongs to you.
You are the firstborn.
But you are not the favorite.
And everyone knows it.
Now imagine discovering that centuries before you were born, God had already spoken about this exact injustice.
Not in a sentimental poem.
Not in a comforting proverb.
But in a law that could prevent a father from using his authority to punish the son of a woman he did not love.
Deuteronomy 21:15–17.
A passage many Christians have probably read without stopping.
A passage that reveals something astonishing about the character of God.
Because sometimes the most powerful evidence of God's justice is not found in a miracle that splits the sea.
Sometimes it is found in a command that stops a powerful man from taking advantage of someone who cannot defend himself.
And if you have ever been the unwanted one, the overlooked one, the child who had to work twice as hard to receive half as much affection, you need to understand what God was protecting here.
The law begins with a painful reality.
In Deuteronomy 21:15, Moses describes a man with two wives, one loved and the other unloved, and both women having sons.
Notice something important.
The passage does not command a man to marry two women. It addresses an existing situation in ancient Israel and regulates the injustice that could arise within it.

The Bible frequently describes polygamous households without presenting their rivalries and suffering as God's ideal for marriage. Genesis 2:24 establishes the foundational picture of a man and his wife becoming one flesh, a passage Jesus later affirms in Matthew 19:4–6.
But God was addressing a society in which such divided households existed.
And He did not ignore the vulnerable people living inside them.
The Hebrew wording makes the situation especially striking.
The loved wife is described with the word הָאֲהוּבָה (ha'ahuvah), meaning the loved one.
The other is described as הַשְּׂנוּאָה (has-senu'ah), commonly translated the hated one or the unloved one.
The underlying Hebrew verb, שָׂנֵא (sane'), can express hatred, but in contexts involving contrasting affections it can also communicate rejection or being loved less.
This distinction matters.
The text does not require us to imagine a husband violently despising one wife. The injustice can exist even when the husband simply favors the other.
And sometimes that is exactly how deep wounds begin.
Not with screaming.
Not with cruelty everyone can recognize.
But with unequal affection that becomes unequal treatment.
The firstborn son belongs to the less-favored wife.
Then comes the day when the father distributes his inheritance.
And God says something that removes the father's power to rewrite his son's legal standing.
Deuteronomy 21:16, in the King James Version, declares:
"He may not make the son of the beloved firstborn before the son of the hated, which is indeed the firstborn."
Read that again.
The father could love one wife more.
He could feel closer to her children.
He could have personal preferences.
But he was not permitted to turn those preferences into a false declaration of birth order.
His feelings did not change the facts.
His affection did not cancel the law.
And his authority did not place him above God's command.
The Hebrew expression behind the prohibition is especially revealing:
לֹא יוּכַל לְבַכֵּר (lo yukhal levakker)
Literally, it communicates that he is not permitted or able, under the law, to treat another son as firstborn in place of the actual firstborn.
The verb לְבַכֵּר (levakker) is related to בְּכוֹר (bekhor), the Hebrew word for firstborn.
This was not merely a family title.
In ancient Israel, firstborn status carried a recognized inheritance right.
And God was protecting that right from manipulation.
Why?
Because the firstborn son's legal position could not be erased simply because his mother had fallen out of favor.
Then verse 17 delivers the command that makes the entire passage unforgettable.
"But he shall acknowledge the son of the hated for the firstborn, by giving him a double portion of all that he hath: for he is the beginning of his strength; the right of the firstborn is his."
— Deuteronomy 21:17, KJV
The words are almost breathtaking.
He shall acknowledge.
The Hebrew expression is כִּי אֶת־הַבְּכֹר בֶּן־הַשְּׂנוּאָה יַכִּיר (ki et-habbekhor ben-has-senu'ah yakkir).
The key verb יַכִּיר (yakkir) comes from נָכַר (nakar), which in this form means to recognize or acknowledge.
The father was commanded to recognize the rightful firstborn.
Not manufacture a new one.
Not pretend the original son did not exist.
Not allow his preference for another woman to determine which son received the firstborn's inheritance.
And the double portion was not a poetic exaggeration.
The Hebrew phrase פִּי שְׁנַיִם (pi shenayim) refers here to a twofold share.
For example, if a father had three sons entitled to share the estate under this rule, the firstborn would receive two shares while each of the other sons received one.
The inheritance would be divided into four shares, with the firstborn receiving two.
This was a legal entitlement, not proof that God considered the firstborn twice as valuable as his brothers.
And that distinction is essential.
God was not commanding the father to feel more love. He was commanding him not to commit an injustice.
There is a difference between regulating someone's conduct and controlling someone's emotions.
The law could not force affection into a father's heart.
But it could forbid him from allowing his unequal affection to rob a son of his recognized inheritance.
And perhaps that is where this ancient passage begins to touch something painfully modern.
Because some of you know what it means to be treated differently because someone loved somebody else more.
You were the child from the first marriage.
The child who reminded someone of a painful relationship.
The sibling who was never quite good enough.
The family member whose accomplishments were expected but whose mistakes were remembered.
The one who quietly learned that fairness and affection do not always arrive together.
Maybe nobody ever stole an inheritance from you.
But something else was taken.
Confidence.
Security.
The ability to believe you were wanted.
And perhaps you spent years trying to earn what other people seemed to receive without asking.
But before we turn this law into a promise that every rejected person will receive a material inheritance, we must remain faithful to what Scripture actually says.
Deuteronomy 21:15–17 is a specific command governing firstborn inheritance in ancient Israel.
It is not a universal promise that every overlooked child will eventually receive more money, greater success, or public vindication.
Its direct concern is justice within a particular legal setting.
Yet the principle it reveals about God's character reaches far beyond that household.
Human favoritism does not make injustice righteous.
And the rest of Scripture gives us painful examples of what happens when families forget that truth.
Consider Jacob.
He knew what it meant to live in a household shaped by unequal love.
Genesis 29:30–31 tells us that Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah and that the LORD saw Leah was unloved.
The family that followed was marked by rivalry, grief, longing, and competition for affection.
Leah bore sons while struggling with the pain of not being loved as Rachel was.
In Genesis 29:32, after the birth of Reuben, she expressed the hope that her husband would now love her.
Imagine that.
A woman holding her newborn son, hoping that his arrival might finally make her husband love her.
And years later, Jacob's own household would be torn by favoritism.
Genesis 37:3 tells us that Israel loved Joseph more than all his other children.
Joseph received a special robe.
His brothers noticed.
And the family fractured.
Envy grew into hatred.
Hatred grew into a conspiracy.
And Joseph was sold into slavery.
One father's favoritism did not merely create hurt feelings.
It became part of a chain of events that devastated an entire household.
Yet God, in His providence, worked through what Joseph's brothers intended for evil.
Joseph would eventually say in Genesis 50:20:
"But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good."
That is not permission to commit evil.
It is testimony that evil human intentions cannot defeat God's ultimate purposes.
But there is another detail that makes the connection with Deuteronomy even more remarkable.
Reuben was Jacob's firstborn.
Yet 1 Chronicles 5:1–2 explains that because Reuben defiled his father's bed, his birthright was given to Joseph's sons, while the royal leadership came through Judah.
This is not a contradiction of Deuteronomy 21.

The Deuteronomic law forbids replacing a rightful firstborn simply because the father prefers another wife. Reuben's loss of birthright is presented in Scripture as connected to his own serious misconduct, not merely his mother's lower standing in Jacob's affections.
The distinction matters because Scripture must interpret Scripture.
God's Word is not honored when we flatten different situations into one emotional slogan.
And the deeper we read, the more we discover that God's justice is not identical to human favoritism, nor is His sovereign grace limited by human customs.
That brings us to another family.
A father.
Two sons.
And an inheritance.
In Luke 15, Jesus tells the story commonly known as the parable of the prodigal son.
The younger son asks for his share of the estate before his father's death.
He leaves home.
He wastes his wealth.
He descends into hunger, humiliation, and desperation.
Eventually, he decides to return.
Not because he believes he deserves restoration.
But because he knows he has sinned.
He plans to confess:
"Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, And am no more worthy to be called thy son."
— Luke 15:18–19, KJV
And then something happens that no exhausted sinner should ever forget.
While the son is still far away, his father sees him.
He runs.
He embraces him.
He kisses him.
The father does not deny the son's sin.
The son does not pretend his rebellion was harmless.
But repentance meets astonishing mercy.
A robe is brought.
A ring is placed on his hand.
A feast begins.
And the father declares that his lost son has been found.
But Jesus does not end the story there.
There is another son.
The elder brother.
He has stayed home.
He has worked.
He hears the celebration and becomes angry.
And suddenly, the parable exposes another wounded heart.
The younger son struggled with rebellion.
The older son struggled with resentment and a sense of entitlement.
The father goes out to him too.
And in Luke 15:31, he says:
"Son, thou art ever with me, and all that I have is thine."
Do you see the beauty of this?
The father's mercy toward the returning younger son does not require him to deny the older son's place in the household.
The celebration is not presented as a legal theft of the elder brother's remaining inheritance.
Jesus is teaching the joy of repentance and the scandal of grace.
And the father extends his appeal to both sons.
One needed forgiveness for leaving.
The other needed his heart corrected while remaining at home.
Both needed the father's grace.
That is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we identify with the rejected firstborn in Deuteronomy.
Sometimes we identify with the wounded elder brother in Luke 15.
And sometimes, if we are willing to tell the truth, we have been the person showing favoritism.
The parent who praises one child more.
The leader who rewards loyalty over integrity.
The Christian who treats wealthy people with greater respect.
The believer who welcomes those who look respectable but keeps struggling sinners at a distance.
James 2:1 warns believers not to hold faith in Jesus Christ with partiality.
James then describes a gathering where a wealthy visitor receives preferential treatment while a poor visitor is dishonored.
The point is unmistakable.
We cannot claim allegiance to the impartial Lord of glory while measuring human worth by wealth, appearance, status, or personal advantage.
And that means Deuteronomy 21 is not merely about what someone else did to you.
It is also an invitation to examine what you might be doing to someone else.
Whose presence do you celebrate?
Whose pain do you minimize?
Whose name do you remember?
Whose dignity have you quietly treated as negotiable?
And whose place have you attempted to give away because you preferred somebody else?
This is where repentance becomes more than an emotional moment.
It becomes a change of direction.
A father who has shown favoritism may need to confess it to his children.
A mother who has compared siblings may need to stop.
A family that has manipulated an inheritance may need to pursue restitution and justice.
A church that has honored influential people while neglecting the vulnerable may need to change its practices.
Grace is never an excuse to continue the injustice from which Christ calls us to turn.
But the Gospel takes us deeper still.
Because the greatest hope in this passage is not that we can all become perfect parents, fair siblings, or faultless people.
We cannot save ourselves through better family behavior.
We need a Savior.
And Scripture introduces Jesus Christ as God's beloved Son.
At His baptism, the Father's voice declares:
"This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."
— Matthew 3:17, KJV
In the Greek New Testament, the expression is:
ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός (ho huios mou ho agapētos)
Meaning:
"My beloved Son."
The Father's love for Jesus is not the sinful favoritism condemned in human relationships.
Jesus is the eternal Son, perfectly righteous, one with the Father, and worthy of the glory that belongs to Him.
And here is the wonder of the Gospel.
The beloved Son came into a world filled with rejected people.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He ate with tax collectors.
He spoke with people society had learned to avoid.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He defended the truth.
And He called the weary and burdened to come to Him.
But He did not come merely to make wounded people feel seen.
He came to save sinners.
He came to do what none of us could accomplish.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He bore our sins on the cross.
He died.
And He rose again.
The sinless Son suffered for the guilty so that those who repent and believe in Him might be reconciled to God.
And this is where the language of inheritance becomes breathtaking.
Romans 8:16–17 teaches that the Spirit bears witness that believers are God's children and that, as children, they are heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ.
Galatians 4:4–7 declares that God sent His Son to redeem those under the law so that believers might receive adoption as sons.
The Greek word υἱοθεσία (huiothesia) means adoption as sons or placement in the status of sons.
In its ancient setting, this language communicated a recognized position within a family, including the standing associated with inheritance.
And the New Testament applies this astonishing privilege to believers in Christ.
Not because we were born into the right earthly family.
Not because our parents loved us properly.
Not because our past was clean.
Not because we earned our way into God's favor.
But because of Jesus.
The inheritance we receive in Christ is not a reward for being the family's favorite. It is a gift of grace secured by the beloved Son.
This does not mean every Christian will become wealthy.
It does not mean believers are promised an easy life.
It does not mean the painful consequences of family injustice will automatically disappear.
Our inheritance in Christ is greater than a bank account or a piece of land.
First Peter 1:3–4 describes the living hope given through the resurrection of Jesus Christ and an inheritance that is incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven.
An inheritance that cannot decay.
An inheritance that sin cannot stain.
An inheritance death cannot destroy.
And it comes through the resurrection of Jesus.
Think about what that means for the person who has spent a lifetime feeling unwanted.
Your earthly father may have failed you.
Your mother may have struggled to love you well.
Your family may have treated you as though you were a mistake.
Those wounds are real.
And the Gospel does not ask you to pretend they never happened.
But your earthly family's failures do not have the final authority to determine your standing before God.
Through faith in Jesus Christ, you are welcomed into God's household.
Not as a tolerated inconvenience.
Not as an unwanted guest.
Not as someone barely allowed through the door.
But as a child of God.
And perhaps you need to hear something else.
Being wronged does not make every response to that wrong righteous.
You may have been overlooked.
You may have been cheated.
You may have been abandoned.
But bitterness can become a prison long after the person who hurt you has walked away.
Forgiveness does not mean declaring evil good.
It does not require abandoning lawful claims, ignoring abuse, or trusting an unrepentant person without wisdom and boundaries.
Biblical forgiveness begins with releasing vengeance into God's hands, while justice, truth, and accountability still matter.
Romans 12:19 reminds us that vengeance belongs to the Lord.
And Romans 12:21 calls us not to be overcome by evil but to overcome evil with good.
That is not weakness.
That is the difficult work of grace.
Sometimes healing begins with tears.
Sometimes it begins with telling the truth.
Sometimes it begins with repentance for the resentment we have secretly fed.
Sometimes it begins with asking forgiveness from the child we favored less.
And sometimes it begins with finally admitting to Jesus that the pain we have carried for years has become too heavy to carry alone.
There may be someone reading this who has never told anyone how deeply their family wounded them.
You became successful.
You learned to smile.
You learned to function.
You even learned to serve in church.
But there is still a little boy or girl inside your memories asking a question you never received an answer to.
"Why wasn't I enough?"
Listen carefully.
Deuteronomy 21 does not say that every rejected child will eventually become the favorite.
It says that a father's preference was not sufficient grounds to deny his firstborn son's lawful inheritance.
And the Gospel says something even greater.
You cannot earn salvation by becoming somebody's favorite.
You must come to Jesus Christ.
The Son of God who died for sinners and rose again is the only Savior who can reconcile you to the Father.
He does not promise to rewrite every earthly relationship exactly as you wish.
But He does offer forgiveness, new life, adoption into God's family, and an eternal inheritance that cannot be taken away.
That is why our message is not simply about overcoming family trauma.
It is about redemption.
It is about the holiness of God.
The seriousness of sin.
The necessity of repentance.
The wonder of mercy.
And the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
Not because scandal is harmless.
Not because injustice should be excused.
Not because suffering automatically makes us holy.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem sinners and bring eternal hope into lives marked by brokenness.
Maybe today you need to repent of favoritism.
Maybe you need to seek forgiveness from someone you hurt.
Maybe you need to stop measuring your worth by the affection someone withheld.
Maybe you need to surrender the anger that has been consuming you.
Or maybe, for the first time, you need to place your faith in Jesus Christ rather than merely admiring His teachings.
Whatever brought you here, do not leave this passage as merely an interesting detail about ancient inheritance law.
Let it examine your heart.
Let it challenge your treatment of others.
And above all, let it lead you to the Savior.
Because the law in Deuteronomy could protect a firstborn son's rightful share of an earthly estate.
But only Jesus Christ can save a sinner and bring that person into the Father's eternal household.
You can write "Christ is still healing me" if you are learning to bring old wounds into the light of His grace.
Or "Pray for me" if family rejection, bitterness, or grief has made your walk with God difficult lately.
And if you have experienced God's restoring grace, consider sharing a part of your testimony. Someone reading the comments may need the courage your story offers.
You do not have to disclose private details to prove your faith. Even a simple, sincere response can remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
And please, do not let this message stop with you.
Not because God needs your money.
Not because a payment can replace your worship, obedience, generosity, or faithful stewardship.
Jesus Christ alone saves. His grace cannot be purchased.
But Scripture does encourage believers to support faithful Gospel ministry through willing and generous giving.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Philippians 4:15–18 gives us an example of believers materially supporting Paul's ministry, and Paul describes their generosity as an offering pleasing to God.
That is the spirit in which we invite you to partner with Gospel Warrior.

It is not a substitute for your responsibility to support your local church or to care for your family. Whether it fits within your personal giving commitments is a matter for prayerful, responsible stewardship.
But for those who are able and willing, it can become a beautiful partnership in the work of making Christ known.
Our desire is not simply to gather an audience.
It is to help people become grounded in the Word of God, strengthened in their faith, and increasingly conformed to the likeness of Jesus Christ.
Pray for those who read it.
Invite someone into a conversation about Jesus.
And no financial contribution is greater than the price Christ has already paid for our redemption.
Somewhere, there is a person who still believes they are worth less because someone they loved chose somebody else.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe it is someone sitting beside you in church.
Maybe it is the adult child who still remembers which sibling was celebrated and which one was ignored.
Maybe it is the parent who now realizes the damage that favoritism caused.
Whoever it is, Deuteronomy 21 reminds us that God took injustice inside the family seriously.
And the Gospel reminds us that our deepest hope is not found in becoming the favorite of another imperfect human being.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
The beloved Son.
The crucified Savior.
The risen Lord.
The One through whom repentant sinners are forgiven, adopted, and made heirs of eternal life.
The people who should have loved you may have failed to recognize your worth—but through Jesus Christ, the Father offers something no human rejection can take away: a place in His eternal family.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD TOLD EZEKIEL TO SHAVE HIS HEAD—THEN BURN HIS HAIR. THE REASON SHOULD MAKE EVERY CHRISTIAN TREMBLE.
paragraphs: GOD TOLD EZEKIEL TO SHAVE HIS HEAD—THEN BURN HIS HAIR. THE REASON SHOULD MAKE EVERY CHRISTIAN TREMBLE.
Three portions of hair. Three terrifying judgments. A handful preserved. And a warning written in Ezekiel 5 that still confronts every heart tempted to mistake God's patience for His approval.

Imagine waking up tomorrow and discovering that God has commanded a prophet to stand before your city, shave his head, cut off his beard, weigh every strand of hair, and then burn one portion, strike another with a sword, and scatter the rest into the wind.
You would probably think the man had lost his mind.
Until you realized...
He wasn't performing a strange religious ritual. He was showing an entire nation what was about to happen to them.
And the most frightening part?
The people watching him were not strangers to God.
They were the people who had received His covenant, His commandments, His promises, and His warnings.
They knew what worship looked like.
They knew the language of holiness.
They had the temple, the priesthood, the sacrifices, and the history of God's deliverance.
But knowing the things of God had not kept their hearts faithful to God.
And perhaps that is where this ancient prophecy begins to become painfully personal.
Because it is possible to know the words of worship while quietly surrendering your heart to something else.
It is possible to appear spiritually alive while slowly becoming comfortable with what God has called you to abandon.
It is possible to stand among God's people and still desperately need to repent.
Before we go any further, remember this:
Ezekiel's shaved head was not a lesson about hairstyles. It was a warning about judgment, covenant unfaithfulness, and the terrifying consequences of refusing to listen to God.
But hidden within that devastating picture was something else.
A few strands of hair.
A small portion that would be preserved.
And a truth about God's mercy that becomes even more astonishing when we follow the story of Scripture all the way to Jesus Christ.
Because the God who warns sinners of judgment is also the God who calls them to turn and live.
And the Gospel reveals just how far His mercy was willing to go.
Ezekiel was not standing in Jerusalem when God gave him this command.
He was among the Judean exiles in Babylon, living in a foreign land after being carried away from home.
Jerusalem still stood, but its destruction was approaching.
Many people continued to believe that their sacred city could never fall completely. Surely the temple meant they were safe. Surely their identity as God's covenant people guaranteed protection.
Yet the prophets had repeatedly warned that possessing the signs of the covenant was no substitute for faithfulness to the Lord.
And now Ezekiel was about to become a living warning.
God commanded him:
"And thou, son of man, take thee a sharp knife, take thee a barber's rasor, and cause it to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard: then take thee balances to weigh, and divide the hair."
— Ezekiel 5:1, King James Version
Read that again.
God did not merely tell Ezekiel to cut his hair.
He told him to weigh it.
To divide it carefully.
To make the destruction of Jerusalem visible through something as ordinary, intimate, and personal as the hair on a man's head.
In the Hebrew text, the command to shave uses the verb וְהַעֲבַרְתָּ (wehaʿavarta), from a root meaning to cause something to pass over or across.
Here it describes passing the cutting instrument over his head and beard.
The instrument is described using the Hebrew חֶרֶב (ḥerev), meaning a sword, followed by language identifying it as a barber's razor.
The imagery is deliberately unsettling.
An instrument associated with cutting and violence becomes the means by which the prophet removes his hair.
Then comes the command to use מֹאזְנֵי מִשְׁקָל (moʾzne mishqal)—weighing balances or scales.
Nothing about the symbolism is casual.
The hair must be divided by weight.
The coming judgment is not portrayed as an uncontrolled accident, an unfortunate coincidence, or evidence that Babylon's gods are stronger than Israel's God.
Ezekiel is announcing that Jerusalem's destruction will take place under the sovereign judgment of the Lord.
And then the command becomes even more disturbing.
God tells Ezekiel to divide the hair into three portions.
One portion must be burned.
Another must be struck with a sword.
The final portion must be scattered into the wind.
And even the scattered hair will not be beyond the reach of judgment.
What could possibly justify such a terrifying message?
The answer comes when God explains the prophecy Himself.
"This is Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations and countries that are round about her."
— Ezekiel 5:5, KJV
The hair represents Jerusalem and its people.
The city had been placed among the nations as a people called to live under God's covenant and bear witness to His holiness.
But instead of reflecting His character, Jerusalem had rebelled against His judgments and statutes.
Ezekiel 5:6–7 describes a people who had turned from God's commands.
Their privilege had not produced obedience.
Their knowledge had not produced humility.
Their religious identity had not produced covenant faithfulness.
And now the consequences were coming.
This is where the prophecy stops feeling like a distant historical curiosity.
Because we can become dangerously skilled at using spiritual language to conceal spiritual compromise.
We can say, "God knows my heart," while refusing to let His Word examine it.
We can ask for blessings while resisting correction.
We can sing about surrender while secretly protecting the one thing we refuse to surrender.
And we can mistake the fact that God has not yet confronted us with visible consequences for evidence that He approves of everything we are doing.
But God's patience is not permission to continue in sin.
Romans 2:4 teaches that God's kindness, forbearance, and patience are meant to lead us toward repentance.
Not complacency.
Not excuses.
Repentance.
And that brings us back to the three portions of Ezekiel's hair.
The first third was to be burned in the midst of the city when the days of the symbolic siege were completed.
God later explains:
"A third part of thee shall die with the pestilence, and with famine shall they be consumed in the midst of thee..."
— Ezekiel 5:12, KJV
The burning hair represented the people who would perish through famine and pestilence during the siege.
Imagine Jerusalem's streets.
Families running out of food.
Parents unable to protect their children from hunger.
The security they had taken for granted disappearing.
The city they believed could never fall becoming a place of unbearable suffering.
This was not an invitation to enjoy imagining the pain of others.
It was a dreadful warning of the consequences of covenant rebellion and the catastrophe of siege warfare.
God was telling His people what was coming before it came.
And that matters.
Because divine warnings are not given merely to satisfy curiosity about the future.
They confront the present.
They expose the direction of a life, a people, or a nation.
They summon hearers to take God's Word seriously.
The second third of the hair was to be struck with the sword around the city.
Ezekiel 5:12 explains that another third would fall by the sword.
Babylon's military assault would bring death.
The defenses of Jerusalem would not save everyone.
Its walls would not guarantee deliverance.
And the sword would reach those who had placed their confidence in what could not ultimately protect them.
There is something deeply sobering here.
The things people trust most can become the very things that reveal how fragile their security really is.
Money can disappear.
Reputation can collapse.
Influence can fade.
Health can change.
Human approval can vanish overnight.
None of these things can reconcile a sinner to God.
And although Ezekiel's specific judgment concerns ancient Jerusalem, the spiritual danger of misplaced confidence remains real.
We may not bow before carved idols, but the human heart still manufactures false saviors.
Some people worship success.
Some worship control.
Some worship the approval of others.
Some cling to secret sins because the thought of surrender feels more frightening than the thought of judgment.
And some have spent years maintaining a Christian appearance while quietly losing their hunger for Christ.
Perhaps nobody knows how exhausted you have become from pretending.
Perhaps you have learned how to smile in church while carrying guilt you cannot explain.
Perhaps you still believe in Jesus, but you know there are areas of your life where you have stopped listening to Him.
If that is you, do not mistake conviction for a declaration that you are beyond hope.
The purpose of bringing hidden things into the light is not to convince you that Christ cannot receive you.
It is to stop you from running away from the One who can forgive, cleanse, and restore you.
Now look at the third portion of Ezekiel's hair.
God commanded the prophet to scatter it into the wind.
Ezekiel 5:12 explains that the surviving third would be scattered, and the sword would pursue them.
The people who escaped the immediate destruction would face dispersion and continuing danger.
Their homeland would be lost.
Their familiar lives would be shattered.
Their world would never be the same.
Burned.
Struck.
Scattered.
Three portions of hair.
Three dimensions of judgment.
And an entire city confronted with the consequences of its rebellion.
But then something extraordinary happens in the prophecy.
God tells Ezekiel:
"Thou shalt also take thereof a few in number, and bind them in thy skirts."
— Ezekiel 5:3, KJV
A few strands.
Not a large bundle.
Not enough to make the scene look hopeful by human standards.
Just a few.
And Ezekiel must gather them and bind them in the folds of his garment.
The Hebrew uses מְעַט בְּמִסְפָּר (meʿat bemispar), meaning a small number or few in number.
The command to bind them comes from the Hebrew root צָרַר (tsarar), which can mean to bind, wrap, or bundle together.
The prophet must keep these few hairs close in his garment.
After all the burning, cutting, and scattering, a small portion is set apart.
It is a striking picture.
Yet we must read it carefully.
Ezekiel 5:4 immediately adds that some of those hairs are also to be taken and thrown into the fire.
The preserved handful is not a simplistic promise that every person initially spared will escape all further judgment.
The passage emphasizes how severe and far-reaching Jerusalem's judgment will be.

Nevertheless, the imagery of a small preserved portion fits within the larger biblical theme of God's preservation of a remnant, a theme that becomes clearer elsewhere in Ezekiel and throughout the prophets.
God's judgment upon Jerusalem did not mean His covenant purposes had failed.
Later, in Ezekiel 11:16–20, the Lord promises to be a sanctuary to His scattered people, to gather them, and to give them a new heart and a new spirit.
And in Ezekiel 36:26–27, He declares:
"A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you..."
— Ezekiel 36:26, KJV
Do you see the movement?
Ezekiel 5 shows the devastating consequences of a rebellious heart.
Ezekiel 36 announces God's promise to give His people a new heart.
The problem was deeper than Jerusalem's walls.
Deeper than its political leaders.
Deeper than its military defenses.
The people needed inward renewal.
They needed more than a repaired city.
They needed hearts transformed by God.
And this is where the story begins to point us toward the astonishing beauty of Jesus Christ.
Not because Ezekiel's three portions of hair are a secret code predicting three events in Jesus' life.
Scripture does not teach that.
And we do not need to force such symbolism onto the text to discover Christ-centered hope.
The connection is greater, deeper, and rooted in the unfolding message of the Bible.
The holy God who judged Jerusalem's rebellion is the same holy God who promises a new covenant, forgiveness, and transformed hearts.
The judgment announced by Ezekiel reveals the seriousness of sin.
The promises that follow reveal the mercy and faithfulness of God.
And the New Testament announces that Jesus Christ is the mediator of the new covenant.
Hebrews 8:6–12 connects that new covenant with God's promise to forgive sins and remember them no more.
At the cross, Jesus did not announce that sin was harmless.
He bore the judgment sinners deserved so that those who trust in Him might be forgiven and reconciled to God.
The apostle Paul writes:
— 2 Corinthians 5:21, KJV
The Greek text includes the phrase ἁμαρτίαν ἐποίησεν (hamartian epoiēsen)—literally, "He made [him] sin."
This does not mean Jesus became morally sinful.
Paul explicitly says that Christ knew no sin.
Rather, the language speaks of the sinless Christ being appointed to bear sin on our behalf, so that through union with Him believers receive righteousness before God.
Consider what that means.
The One who never rebelled against His Father willingly entered the suffering of the cross.
The One who deserved no condemnation endured death for sinners.
The One who had no guilt of His own became the Savior of the guilty.
And the One who was laid in a tomb rose again.
This is not merely an inspiring ending to a tragic story.
It is the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day, as proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
He did not come merely to make religious people feel better about themselves.
He came to save sinners.
To call them to repentance.
To forgive.
To reconcile.
To give new life.
To make people new.
And this is why our message is not simply that scandal can be forgotten.
It is that grace can transform the person whose life has been marked by scandal.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by removing every earthly consequence.
But by forgiving sin, changing hearts, restoring fellowship with God, and giving believers a new identity in Christ.
There is a difference between hiding your past and being redeemed from it.
Hiding says, "I hope nobody ever discovers who I was."
Grace says, "Jesus knows the truth about me, and He is still able to save."
Hiding keeps you imprisoned by the fear of exposure.
Grace invites you to confess, repent, and walk in the light.
Hiding teaches you to perform holiness.
Grace teaches you to depend on Christ for genuine transformation.
And perhaps the most painful thing about Ezekiel's prophecy is realizing how long people can resist God's voice before they finally understand what they have been refusing to hear.
But listen carefully.
You are reading this today.
You are not being asked to reconstruct Jerusalem's siege.
You are being invited to consider the condition of your own heart in the light of Scripture.
Are you walking with Jesus, or have you become comfortable merely looking like someone who does?
Is there a sin you keep excusing because you have not yet experienced its consequences?
Is there someone you need to forgive?
Is there dishonesty you need to confess?
Is there a relationship, habit, or hidden compromise that has been slowly drawing your heart away from Christ?
These are not questions meant to make you despair.
They are questions worth bringing honestly before the Lord.
Because the Gospel does not end with exposure.
It opens the door to repentance, forgiveness, and restoration.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Notice the promise.
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Not because confession earns salvation.
Not because tears can purchase mercy.
Not because we can undo the damage of yesterday through our own efforts.
But because forgiveness rests upon the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And when someone truly comes to Him in repentance and faith, that person is not beyond His power to redeem.
The enemy of your soul would love for you to believe that the worst thing you have done must be the final word over your life.
But Jesus Christ is greater than your worst chapter.
Your sin is serious.
Your choices matter.
Your repentance must be genuine.
Yet your failures do not have greater saving power than the blood of Christ.
There is mercy for the repentant sinner.
There is hope for the believer who has wandered.
There is grace for the person who is finally tired of hiding.
And there is a Savior who does not need you to manufacture a flawless past before you come to Him.
He calls you to come honestly.
To turn from sin.
To trust Him.
To follow Him.
Maybe you have been carrying a secret for years.
Maybe your family knows only the version of you that you allow them to see.
Maybe you have prayed the same prayer a hundred times because you keep returning to the same struggle.
Maybe you are ashamed that your spiritual life has become so cold.
Or maybe you have been hurt by someone who used the name of God while behaving nothing like Christ.
Whatever your story, do not confuse the failures of human beings with the character of Jesus.
Look to Him.
He is holy.
He is merciful.
He is truthful.
He does not excuse sin, and He does not despise the brokenhearted who turn to Him.
Ezekiel himself later records these words from the Lord:
"For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord GOD: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye."
