But because the sinless Son of God willingly gave Himself for sinners.
Isaiah 53:5 declares that He was wounded for our transgressions.
Second Corinthians 5:21 tells us that God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
And Romans 5:8 reminds us that God demonstrated His love toward us while we were still sinners.
Ezekiel carried the baggage of exile as a prophetic sign.
Jesus bore our sins in His body on the tree, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
These are not identical acts, and Ezekiel 12 should not be misrepresented as a direct prophecy of Christ carrying luggage.
But when we read Ezekiel within the whole story of Scripture, we see the same holy God who judges rebellion also revealing His astonishing plan to redeem sinners through Jesus Christ.
The cross does not make sin insignificant.
It reveals how serious sin truly is.
And it reveals how extraordinary God's mercy is.
Jesus did not die to make rebellion comfortable.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
He did not rise from the grave so that we could keep pretending our hearts were healthy.
He rose victorious over death, calling us to repentance, faith, forgiveness, and new life in Him.
That is the Gospel.
Not that we were good enough to deserve another chance.
Not that our religious achievements outweighed our failures.
Not that God simply overlooked our guilt.
But that Jesus Christ, the righteous One, died for the unrighteous to bring us to God.
And He rose again.
Which means your story does not have to end where your sin left you.
Your betrayal does not have to become your identity.
Your secret addiction does not have to become your master.
Your past failure does not have to be the final word spoken over your life.
Your shame does not have to keep you hiding from the Savior who already knows the truth.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is reconciliation through His blood.
There is grace for the repentant sinner.
There is power for a transformed life through the Holy Spirit.
But that grace is not an invitation to remain unchanged.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
And maybe that is why this story feels so personal.
Because somewhere beneath the religious language, the Bible knowledge, and the carefully maintained appearance, there may be something we have been refusing to face.
Perhaps you are still carrying resentment toward someone who wounded you years ago.
Perhaps you have become skilled at hiding a habit you know is destroying your spiritual life.
Perhaps you are exhausted from pretending to be strong while privately feeling far from God.
Perhaps you have been calling something "just a struggle" when you know the Lord has been confronting it as sin.
Or perhaps you have never truly trusted Christ at all.
You know the songs.
You know the Christian expressions.
You know how to look like someone who belongs.
But when you are alone, you wonder whether you have ever genuinely surrendered your life to Jesus.
If that is you, do not turn this moment into another opportunity to perform.
You do not need to impress God with a dramatic confession.
You need to come honestly to Him.
Tell Him the truth.
He already knows.
Confess your sin.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Place your faith in Jesus Christ, who died and rose again.
Ask Him to make you new.
And if you have fallen after beginning to follow Him, do not confuse repentance with hopelessness.
First John 1:9 reminds believers that God is faithful and just to forgive our sins and cleanse us from unrighteousness when we confess them.
The answer to sin is not to hide more carefully.
It is to return to the Savior.
There is a difference between feeling exposed and being restored.
Conviction shows us what is wrong.
Grace leads us to the One who can make us right with God.
And the Holy Spirit does not merely help us manage a religious image.
He works to transform our hearts.
So ask yourself something tonight.
What warning have I been ignoring?
What truth have I heard repeatedly but refused to obey?
What false security am I trusting more than Christ?
And what would genuine repentance look like in my life—not someday, not when everything becomes convenient, but now?
You may not need to dig through a literal wall.
You may need to tell the truth you have been hiding.
You may need to seek forgiveness.
You may need to stop defending the compromise that has been slowly hardening your heart.
You may need to open your Bible again, not merely to find encouragement, but to hear what God actually says.
You may need to ask another mature believer to pray with you and help you walk faithfully.
And perhaps, for the first time in a long time, you need to stop telling God what you want Him to approve and begin asking Him what He wants you to surrender.
Ezekiel obeyed while the people watched.
The tragedy is that seeing the sign did not automatically mean they would heed its warning.
Do not make the same mistake.
Do not become so familiar with the message of repentance that you forget to repent.
Do not admire biblical courage while refusing to practice ordinary obedience.
Do not applaud stories of transformation while quietly resisting the transforming work of Jesus in your own life.
Because one of the saddest possibilities in the Christian life is to be deeply moved by the truth for a moment, then return to the very thing the truth was calling us to leave.

If this message has exposed something you have been carrying in secret, I want to invite you to respond—not for appearances, not to prove anything to strangers, but as a small act of spiritual honesty.
Someone else reading may recognize their own struggle in those few words and realize they are not the only person seeking grace.
There is also a deeper way to help this ministry continue.

Every article, every Scripture-centered message, every devotional, and every resource shared through Gospel Warrior is part of a desire to make the truth of Jesus Christ more accessible to people who need it.
And ministry requires faithful people willing to pray, share, serve, and give.
It can help keep biblical encouragement reaching people who are struggling in silence.
It can help make discipleship resources available to people who cannot afford them.
It can help this ministry continue speaking about repentance, forgiveness, restoration, and the saving grace of Jesus Christ in a world that desperately needs the Gospel.
Those free resources are part of the heart of this ministry.
Because the Gospel is not merchandise.
Grace is not for sale.
And no one should ever feel that they must pay to become worthy of God's love.
Christ has already paid the price for our redemption.
Because the goal is not to make a ministry famous.
The goal is to make Christ known.
And if one person encounters the Gospel, turns from sin, and begins walking with Jesus because someone cared enough to share the truth, that is worth celebrating.
Now return with me to that strange scene one final time.
A prophet stands before a wall.
His belongings are gathered.
The people are watching.
The opening is made.
And as darkness approaches, Ezekiel lifts his baggage and walks out.
He cannot make the people repent.
He cannot force them to believe.
He cannot make them recognize what they are refusing to see.
He can only obey the Lord and deliver the warning entrusted to him.
And centuries later, the question remains.
Will we listen?
Will we recognize the mercy of God in the truth that confronts us?
Will we stop trusting the walls we have built around our own rebellion?
Will we turn to the Savior while the invitation of grace is before us?
You do not know how many tomorrows you have.
Neither do I.
But you have this moment to hear the truth.
And the truth is that Jesus Christ still calls sinners to repentance and faith.
He still receives those who come to Him.
He still forgives.
He still restores.
He still transforms lives through His grace.
The story of Ezekiel's broken wall is a warning about the consequences of refusing God's Word.
But the Gospel announces that through Jesus Christ, ruined sinners can be reconciled to God.
That is the hope we must never lose.
That is the grace we must never cheapen.
That is the Savior we must never stop proclaiming.
The greatest tragedy is not discovering that the wall you trusted could fall—it is refusing the Savior who was calling you to come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE FAMILY SECRET GOD REFUSED TO KEEP: WHY DID GOD FORBID SEX BETWEEN CLOSE RELATIVES WHEN EVEN BIBLICAL FAMILIES HAD PRACTICED IT?
paragraphs: THE FAMILY SECRET GOD REFUSED TO KEEP: WHY DID GOD FORBID SEX BETWEEN CLOSE RELATIVES WHEN EVEN BIBLICAL FAMILIES HAD PRACTICED IT?

Before God gave Israel the laws of Leviticus 18, some of the most important families in Scripture had already crossed boundaries that would later be forbidden. Was God changing His mind? Was He overlooking sin? Or was He revealing something about human intimacy, family betrayal, holiness, and grace that we desperately need to understand today?
“None of you shall approach any one of his close relatives to uncover nakedness. I am the LORD.” — Leviticus 18:6 (ESV)
There is something deeply unsettling hidden in the family histories of the Bible.
Abraham married Sarah, his half-sister.
Jacob married two sisters, Leah and Rachel.
Lot's daughters became pregnant by their own father after getting him drunk.
And then, generations later, God spoke through Moses and declared that sexual relationships between close relatives were forbidden.
Wait.
Read that again.
The same Bible that records those ancient relationships also contains God's unmistakable command against them.
And if you have ever read Scripture carefully enough to notice that tension, you may have wondered something you were afraid to ask out loud.
Why would God forbid something that people in earlier biblical generations had practiced?
Did God's standards change?
Were those relationships acceptable before Moses?

And what about the uncomfortable question people often raise about Adam and Eve's children? If humanity began with one family, how could the earliest generations have multiplied without close relatives marrying?
These are not foolish questions.
They are questions that deserve more than a religious slogan, a frightening warning, or an answer that pretends every difficulty in Scripture disappears when we quote a verse.
Because when we study Leviticus 18 honestly, something extraordinary emerges.
We discover that God's commands concerning sexual boundaries are not simply about restricting desire.

They are also about protecting the vulnerable, preserving the integrity of family relationships, confronting the misuse of power, and teaching His people that love must never become an excuse for violating what is holy.
And underneath this difficult passage is a truth that reaches far beyond ancient Israel.
Not everything that happened in a biblical family was approved by the God who loved that family.
That distinction changes everything.
Imagine growing up in a household where the people who were supposed to protect you were the very people who made you afraid.
Imagine the confusion of discovering that someone could use the language of love while crossing a boundary that love itself should have protected.
Imagine carrying a family secret so heavy that even years later, hearing the word home does not bring comfort.
For some readers, this subject is an intellectual question.
For others, it touches a wound they have spent their entire lives trying to hide.
And that is why we must approach this passage carefully.
Not with sensationalism.
Not with condemnation toward those who have been harmed.
And certainly not with the dangerous assumption that everyone involved in a sexual relationship within a family had equal freedom, equal power, or equal responsibility.
God sees what people conceal.
He sees the difference between willing wrongdoing and exploitation.
He sees the child who could not consent, the vulnerable person who was manipulated, and the survivor who has spent years believing a lie about their own guilt.
The God who speaks in Leviticus is not indifferent to any of them.
But to understand why these commands appear where they do, we must first enter the world in which they were given.
Israel had been delivered from Egypt.
For generations, the Israelites had lived surrounded by a culture whose religious and social practices did not always reflect the holiness of the God who had rescued them.
Now they were being formed into a covenant people.
They were learning that freedom from slavery was not the same thing as freedom to live without moral boundaries.
God had brought them out of Egypt.
But Egypt's ways still had to be confronted.
In Leviticus 18:3, the Lord warned Israel not to imitate the practices of Egypt or Canaan. In verse 4, He commanded them to follow His judgments and statutes.
Then came the solemn declaration in verse 6.
In the Hebrew text, the central prohibition reads:
אִישׁ אִישׁ אֶל־כָּל־שְׁאֵר בְּשָׂרוֹ לֹא תִקְרְבוּ לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה
Ish ish el-kol she'er besaro lo tiqrevu legalot ervah.
In context, this means:
“None of you shall approach any one of his close relatives to uncover nakedness.”
The expression she'er besaro refers to close kinship, literally conveying the idea of one's own flesh or near family relation.
The expression legalot ervah, “to uncover nakedness,” is a Hebrew idiom used in this chapter for prohibited sexual exposure or relations.
This is not merely a warning about accidentally seeing someone without clothing.
The chapter is establishing sexual boundaries within family relationships.
And the command ends with words that appear repeatedly throughout the holiness laws:
אֲנִי יְהוָה — Ani YHWH.
“I am the LORD.”
That ending matters.
God was not presenting these boundaries as a matter of changing fashion, social embarrassment, or personal preference.
He was speaking as Israel's covenant Lord.
His people were not free to define holiness merely by what surrounding societies permitted.
And they were not free to call something righteous simply because their ancestors had done it.
Now comes the difficult part.
What do we do with Abraham?
Genesis 20:12 records Abraham explaining that Sarah was his father's daughter, though not his mother's daughter.
In other words, according to Abraham's own account, Sarah was his half-sister.
Yet Leviticus 18:9 explicitly prohibits sexual relations with a sister, whether she is the daughter of one's father or one's mother.
How do we reconcile that?
First, we must recognize that Abraham lived centuries before the Mosaic covenant and the giving of the Levitical law.
The Bible does not portray him as living under the specific legal code later delivered to Israel at Sinai.
But this does not automatically establish that every action of Abraham was morally ideal or that God approved of every aspect of his marriage.
The Bible's description of an event is not necessarily God's endorsement of it.
That is one of the most important principles for reading biblical narratives responsibly.
Scripture tells us that Abraham lied about his marital relationship out of fear.
It tells us that Jacob's household was torn by jealousy and rivalry.
It tells us that David committed adultery and arranged a man's death.
The fact that God continued working through these people does not transform their every decision into a divine example.
God's faithfulness to His promises is not proof that human beings have lived flawlessly.
Sometimes the most astonishing thing about the Bible is not how righteous its central human characters appear.
It is how honestly their failures are exposed.
Jacob's story is another striking example.
He married Leah and Rachel, two sisters.
Yet Leviticus 18:18 later prohibits taking a woman as a rival wife to her sister while the first sister is alive.
Read Genesis carefully, and the pain within that family becomes impossible to ignore.
Leah longs to be loved.
Rachel struggles with infertility.
Competition and resentment poison relationships that should have been marked by tenderness.
The narrative does not present their household as a peaceful model of family harmony.
It shows the suffering that unfolded within it.
Still, we must be precise: the existence of suffering in a biblical story does not, by itself, prove the precise reason for every later command.
What we can say is that the Bible does not require us to romanticize those arrangements.
It allows us to see their brokenness.
And that brings us to Lot.
Genesis 19:30–38 records one of the most disturbing episodes in the Old Testament.
Lot's daughters, fearing the loss of their family line, made their father drunk and had sexual relations with him without his informed participation.
The account is deeply troubling.
It is not a romance.
It is not an example to imitate.
And it is not presented as a command from God.
It is a narrative of desperation, deception, and a devastating violation of sexual boundaries.
When Leviticus later explicitly forbids such relations, we should not imagine that the earlier account was therefore being celebrated.
The Bible can preserve the truth about human darkness without asking us to admire it.
But perhaps you are still thinking about the question that reaches even further back.
Adam and Eve.
If they were the first human couple, and if their children formed the earliest human families, how did humanity multiply?
Genesis 5:4 tells us that Adam had other sons and daughters.
Under a reading of Genesis in which all humanity descends immediately from a single original couple, marriages among close relatives would appear necessary in the earliest generations.
That is a reasonable inference within that interpretation.
But we must be equally honest about what the text does not say.
Genesis does not provide a detailed marriage register for Adam's children.
It does not explicitly explain the precise relationships of Cain's wife or establish a complete system of early marriage rules.
And it does not directly state that God temporarily authorized incestuous marriages before later withdrawing that authorization.
Some Christians propose that close-relative marriage was initially permitted and later forbidden as human circumstances changed. Others approach the early Genesis genealogies differently.
These interpretations should not be confused with explicit statements of Scripture.
We must never pretend that our explanations are as authoritative as God's written Word.
The Bible gives us enough clarity to understand the command in Leviticus 18, even when it does not answer every historical question about the earliest generations.
And that distinction is not weakness.
It is reverence.
Faith does not require us to manufacture certainty where Scripture has not supplied it.
Now consider what Leviticus 18:6–18 actually does.
It does not merely prohibit one relationship.
It systematically identifies family boundaries.
Relations involving parents, siblings, grandchildren, aunts, certain in-laws, and other specified kinship connections are addressed.
Some prohibitions involve blood relationships.
Others concern relationships created by marriage.
The passage recognizes that family structures carry obligations that sexual desire must not override.
A parent is not merely another possible romantic partner.
A sibling relationship is not simply a friendship that can become sexual if both people desire it.
The family is a place where trust, dependency, authority, affection, and vulnerability intersect.
Sexualizing those relationships can profoundly damage the very bonds through which people are meant to receive security and care.
Modern knowledge also recognizes additional concerns, including the elevated risk of certain recessive genetic disorders among children conceived by close biological relatives.
That is a legitimate medical consideration.
But we should not claim that genetics is the stated reason for God's command in Leviticus.
The chapter does not give a genetic explanation.
Its explicit framework concerns holiness, prohibited sexual relations, and Israel's separation from the practices of surrounding nations.
We can recognize modern biological concerns without forcing scientific claims into a passage that does not make them.
The deeper theological principle remains powerful.
Human desire does not become holy simply because it feels powerful.
And affection does not automatically make a relationship righteous.
Sometimes what people call love is actually possession.
Sometimes what they call intimacy is exploitation.
Sometimes what they call a family secret is a wound that has been passed from one generation to the next.
But biblical love does not demand the surrender of another person's dignity.
Love protects.
Love refuses to exploit vulnerability.
Love does not use authority, dependence, fear, or silence to obtain what should never be taken.
This is why the broader witness of Scripture matters.
Psalm 82:3–4 calls for justice for the weak and the fatherless and for deliverance of the needy from the hand of the wicked.
Jesus Himself warned severely against causing the vulnerable to stumble (Matthew 18:6).
And when the apostle Paul addressed a sexual relationship involving a man and his father's wife in 1 Corinthians 5:1–5, he did not treat it as a harmless matter of private preference.
He called the church to take sexual wrongdoing seriously.
The New Testament does not present the coming of Christ as permission to disregard holiness.
Grace does not turn exploitation into love.
Forgiveness does not make wrongdoing harmless.
And redemption never requires victims to pretend that what happened to them was acceptable.
Perhaps that is where this article becomes painfully personal.
Because some people reading these words have never committed the kind of sin described in Leviticus 18.
But they have been sinned against.
They were children.
They were vulnerable.
They trusted someone.
And someone betrayed that trust.
Maybe the person responsible was respected in the community.
Maybe that person quoted Scripture.
Maybe they prayed in public, served in church, or told everyone that family problems should never leave the home.
And perhaps you were told that speaking about what happened would destroy the family.
So you learned to smile.
You learned to function.
You learned to carry shame that never belonged to you.
If that is part of your story, please hear this clearly.
What someone did to you does not make you morally guilty of their actions.
You are not spiritually defiled because another person violated your boundaries.
You do not need to repent for being abused.
And the Gospel does not require you to return to an unsafe situation, conceal a crime, or offer someone renewed access to you in order to prove that you have forgiven them.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are not identical.
Reconciliation requires truth, accountability, and safety. In some circumstances, restored personal contact may never be wise or possible.
Where abuse has occurred, seeking appropriate protection, professional care, and lawful accountability is not a betrayal of Christian faith.
The God of truth does not need lies to protect His reputation.
And the church must never confuse protecting an institution with protecting the people entrusted to its care.
But there is another reader.
Someone who knowingly crossed a sexual boundary.
Someone who has hidden wrongdoing behind excuses, rationalizations, or years of silence.
For that person, the message is different, but the invitation of Christ is still real.
Do not call darkness light.
Do not use grace as permission to continue harming others.
Do not confuse feeling sorry with genuine repentance.
Biblical repentance involves turning away from sin, telling the truth, accepting appropriate consequences, and taking responsibility for the harm caused.
Where a crime has been committed, spiritual language must never be used to obstruct justice.
And where another person has been harmed, repentance does not entitle the offender to forgiveness on demand, restored trust, or renewed access to that person's life.
Yet even here, the Gospel confronts us with something extraordinary.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Not by pretending sin is harmless.
Not by erasing justice.
Not by calling evil good.
But by bearing sin's judgment through His sacrificial death and opening the way to forgiveness and new life for those who repent and believe.
The cross is not evidence that God takes sin lightly.
It is evidence of how seriously He takes it—and how immeasurably great His mercy is.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (ESV)
Notice the timing.
Christ did not wait until humanity became worthy.
He came while we were sinners.
But His grace does not leave us unchanged.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and live upright, godly lives.
Grace is not a hiding place for unrepentant evil.
It is God's undeserved favor that brings salvation and teaches His people a new way to live.
This is where our Gospel Warrior message becomes more than a memorable phrase.
But understand what that means.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending the scandal never happened.
He does not rewrite a victim's story by demanding silence.
He does not rewrite an offender's story by removing the need for repentance.
He rewrites lives through truth, mercy, justice, forgiveness, and transformation.
He brings what was hidden into the light.
He restores dignity to the wounded.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He gives hope where shame once appeared to have the final word.
And He offers a new identity that is not determined by the worst thing someone suffered or the worst thing a repentant sinner once did.
Think about the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
The crowd wanted a public spectacle.
They wanted judgment.
Jesus exposed the hypocrisy of her accusers, refused to participate in their cruelty, and told the woman to leave her life of sin.

The passage, whose textual history is debated because it is absent from some of the earliest surviving manuscripts of John, has long been cherished by Christians for its portrayal of mercy joined to moral seriousness.
Its message resonates with truths clearly taught throughout the New Testament.
Jesus is neither indifferent to sin nor eager to destroy the repentant.
And in John 4, He speaks with a Samaritan woman whose complicated marital history becomes part of a conversation about living water and true worship.
He does not reduce her entire identity to her relationships.
He directs her attention to the gift of God.
This is the Savior we proclaim.
Holy enough to confront what destroys us.
Merciful enough to receive those who come to Him.
Powerful enough to begin a work of transformation no human being could accomplish alone.
And now return to the question that began this journey.
Why did God forbid sexual relationships with close relatives, even though earlier biblical families sometimes practiced them?
Because the giving of the law to Israel established explicit boundaries for God's covenant people, including boundaries that distinguished them from surrounding nations.
Because Scripture's record of earlier practices is not the same thing as a divine endorsement of those practices.
Because family relationships carry responsibilities that must not be surrendered to sexual desire.
And because God's call to holiness reaches into the places where human beings are most capable of both extraordinary tenderness and devastating betrayal.
We should not claim to know every unstated reason behind each prohibition.
But we can affirm what the text clearly teaches.
God did not leave Israel free to decide that every form of intimacy was acceptable.
He called His people to honor the boundaries He had established.
And through the fuller revelation of Jesus Christ, Christians are called not merely to avoid outward wrongdoing, but to love others with purity, truth, humility, and self-giving care.
The central question is no longer merely, “What did ancient families do?”
It is also, “Will I allow the Word of God to correct what my culture, my history, or my desires have taught me to accept?”
Because sometimes the hardest part of following Jesus is discovering that something familiar is not necessarily faithful.
Sometimes an inherited practice must be rejected.
Sometimes a family secret must be brought into the light.
Sometimes repentance begins with finally admitting, “What I called love was not love.”
And sometimes healing begins with the words, “What happened to me was wrong, and I do not have to carry the shame anymore.”
Maybe this article has answered a question you have carried for years.
Maybe it has challenged an assumption you never examined.
Or maybe it has touched a place in your life that still needs the healing presence of Christ.
Wherever you find yourself, do not run from the truth.
Bring it to Jesus.
If you need to repent, come honestly.
If you need protection, seek it without shame.
If you need help, reach out to safe, trustworthy people who will take your concerns seriously.
If you are struggling to understand Scripture, keep studying.
And if you have been wounded, remember that healing does not have to happen on someone else's timetable.
Jesus is not frightened by difficult questions.
He is not embarrassed by the truth.
And His invitation to come to Him is not reserved for people with uncomplicated stories.
There is a reason Gospel Warrior continues to speak about the passages others sometimes avoid.
Because people are asking questions.
Because families are hurting.
Because believers need more than inspirational quotations.
Because the church needs disciples who can distinguish biblical truth from cultural assumptions, grace from permissiveness, and forgiveness from the concealment of harm.
And because somewhere, someone is one honest encounter with Scripture away from realizing that the Gospel is deeper than they ever imagined.
If this article opened your eyes, please do not allow the conversation to end here.

Some truths deserve more than a hurried reading. Return to Leviticus 18, Genesis 20, Genesis 29, 1 Corinthians 5, and the Gospel passages we have considered. Open your Bible. Examine the context. Let Scripture shape your convictions.
I also want to hear from you.
And if this strengthened your faith, share a Scripture that has helped you understand God's holiness or His mercy. Your testimony may encourage someone else to open the Bible again.
Our mission is to keep pointing people to Jesus Christ through Scripture, conviction, repentance, encouragement, biblical understanding, and the life-changing truth of the Gospel.
We also want to invite you into something deeper.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning and spiritual nourishment accessible to people who are hungry for truth.
For believers who choose to give as part of their worship and stewardship, supporting Gospel ministry can be a meaningful expression of generosity.
But we want to be biblically clear.
Your responsibility to your local church, your family, and those in need should not be neglected.
You can still help.
Your prayers matter.
Your thoughtful comments matter.
Your sharing of sound biblical teaching matters.
Your willingness to help someone encounter Jesus matters.
But the greatest reward of supporting Gospel work is not merchandise.
It is knowing that your generosity is helping sustain a ministry dedicated to proclaiming Christ, encouraging discipleship, and making biblical resources available to others.
Because Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
Jesus Christ has already accomplished what money could never buy.
And no amount of engagement, public support, or religious activity can replace repentance and faith in Him.
That is why we will continue pointing back to the cross.
Back to the empty tomb.
Back to the Word of God.
Back to the Savior who does not excuse evil but can redeem lives devastated by it.
Perhaps you arrived at this article curious about ancient marriage practices.
Perhaps you expected an argument about genetics, history, or biblical law.
But I hope you leave with something more.
A deeper respect for the holiness of God.
A clearer understanding of the difference between biblical history and biblical commands.
A renewed commitment to protect the vulnerable.
And a stronger confidence that the Gospel of Jesus Christ is sufficient to confront the truth without surrendering hope.
The Bible does not hide the scandals of its families.
It exposes them within the unfolding story of God's dealings with humanity.
And through that story, it ultimately directs our eyes toward the One who entered our broken world without becoming part of its sin.
Jesus Christ.
The One who was betrayed but never became a betrayer.
The One who was wounded but never used His power to exploit the weak.
The One who bore the cross and rose again so that sinners could be forgiven, captives could find hope, and those who trust Him could receive new life.
He is not merely the answer to an uncomfortable Bible question.
He is the hope of a world filled with uncomfortable truths.
And when everything hidden is finally brought into the light, the greatest hope of the Gospel will remain:
Your family's darkest chapter does not have to become the final sentence of your story—because the final word belongs to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: LEAH COULDN’T GIVE JACOB ANOTHER CHILD—SO SHE GAVE HIM ANOTHER WOMAN. BUT THE REAL TRAGEDY WASN’T WHAT HAPPENED IN THEIR BEDROOM.
paragraphs: LEAH COULDN’T GIVE JACOB ANOTHER CHILD—SO SHE GAVE HIM ANOTHER WOMAN. BUT THE REAL TRAGEDY WASN’T WHAT HAPPENED IN THEIR BEDROOM.

Genesis 30:9–13 | The heartbreaking story of a woman who had already given her husband four sons but still feared she wasn't enough—and how God was writing a story of redemption through a family drowning in jealousy, rejection, rivalry, and desperate attempts to be loved.
She had already given him four sons.
Four children who carried his blood. Four living reminders of her devotion. Four reasons she might have hoped that, finally, her husband would look at her with tenderness instead of obligation.
But Leah was still fighting for something childbirth could not guarantee.
Her husband's love.
And when the children stopped coming, something happened that reveals just how deeply rejection can wound the human heart.
She gave Jacob another woman.
Not a stranger.
Not someone outside the household.
Her own servant, Zilpah.
And the Bible records the moment with a simplicity that almost makes it more painful.
“When Leah saw that she had left bearing, she took Zilpah her maid, and gave her Jacob to wife.” — Genesis 30:9, KJV
Read that again.
Leah had already become a mother four times.
But somewhere inside her, the woman who had been overlooked was still trying to become the woman who would finally be chosen.
And before you judge her, consider this uncomfortable question.
Have you ever been so desperate to feel loved that you started sacrificing pieces of yourself just to keep someone's attention?
Have you ever done more, given more, tolerated more, or exhausted yourself trying to earn something you believed should have been freely given?
Then Leah's story may be closer to your own than you realize.
Because this is not merely a story about a complicated ancient marriage.
It is a story about what rejection can do to the soul.
And it is also a story about the God who sees people even when the people closest to them do not.
To understand what happened in Genesis 30, we have to return to the night that changed Leah's life.
Jacob loved Rachel.
That was never a secret.
He had worked seven years for the privilege of marrying her, and Scripture tells us those years seemed like only a few days because of his love for her (Genesis 29:20).
But on the wedding night, Rachel's father, Laban, deceived Jacob and gave him Leah instead.
By morning, Jacob discovered the deception.
The man who had once deceived his own father was now experiencing deception himself.
And Leah was caught in the middle.

The Bible does not tell us everything Leah felt that morning. It does not reveal how much freedom she had to refuse her father's arrangement. It does not record a private conversation between her and Jacob.
We should not invent those details.
But Scripture tells us something devastating about the marriage that followed.
Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
And Genesis 29:31 says:
“And when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren.” — KJV
The Hebrew word translated “hated” is שְׂנוּאָה (senu'ah), from the root שָׂנֵא (sane').
The word can communicate being hated, but in a relational comparison such as this one, it can also describe being loved less or disfavored.
That distinction matters.

Genesis 29:30 explicitly says Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah. The text does not require us to imagine that Jacob was constantly cruel to Leah, but it certainly does not minimize her painful position.
She was the less-loved wife.
And God saw her.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say Leah was the most beautiful.
It does not say she was the favorite.
It does not say she had finally convinced Jacob to love her.
It says the LORD saw.
In Hebrew, the verb is related to רָאָה (ra'ah), meaning “to see.”
The God of Israel was not blind to the suffering of a woman whose own household reminded her that she was not first in her husband's affections.
And then Leah began having children.
Her first son was Reuben.
Genesis 29:32 records her explanation:
“Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me.”
Can you hear the longing?
Not simply, “I have a son.”
But, “Now my husband will love me.”
She named her child while looking toward the affection she hoped to receive.
Her second son was Simeon.
And again, her words revealed her pain.
“Because the LORD hath heard that I was hated, he hath therefore given me this son also.” — Genesis 29:33
God had heard.
Yet Leah still lived with the ache of being less loved.
Then came Levi.
And Leah said:
“Now this time will my husband be joined unto me, because I have born him three sons.” — Genesis 29:34
Three sons.
Three moments of hope.
Three opportunities to believe that perhaps this child would finally change her marriage.
Then something remarkable happened.
Her fourth son was born.
And she named him Judah.
“Now will I praise the LORD.” — Genesis 29:35
Judah's name, יְהוּדָה (Yehudah), is associated with the Hebrew verb יָדָה (yadah), meaning to praise or give thanks.
For a moment, the focus of Leah's words shifted.
Instead of saying, “Now my husband will love me,” she said, “Now will I praise the LORD.”
That was significant.
But it did not mean every wound in Leah's heart had instantly disappeared.
And this is where the story becomes painfully human.
Because spiritual breakthroughs do not always mean that old insecurities will never return.
A person can sincerely praise God and still struggle with rejection.
A person can recognize God's goodness and still find themselves tempted to compete for another person's affection.
And Leah's next recorded decision shows that her story was not finished.
Genesis 29:35 says that after Judah's birth, she stopped bearing children.
Meanwhile, Rachel was struggling with her own grief.
Rachel was deeply loved by Jacob, but she had not been able to conceive.
And she envied Leah.
Think about the heartbreaking contrast.
Leah had children and longed for her husband's love.
Rachel had her husband's love and longed for children.
Each woman possessed something the other desperately wanted.
Neither was at peace.
Rachel eventually gave her servant Bilhah to Jacob, and Bilhah bore Dan and Naphtali.
This arrangement belonged to an ancient household world in which enslaved or servant women could be given to men for childbearing, with children counted within the larger family structure.
But we must be careful here.
The Bible's description of a practice is not automatically God's approval of that practice.
Zilpah and Bilhah were not merely instruments in someone else's emotional struggle. They were women whose own experiences, wishes, and suffering are largely left unrecorded.
Scripture does not give us enough information to claim that they freely chose these arrangements.
Their silence in the narrative should make us more attentive, not less, to their humanity.
Then Genesis 30:9 brings us back to Leah.
“When Leah saw that she had left bearing, she took Zilpah her maid, and gave her Jacob to wife.”
The Hebrew begins:
וַתֵּרֶא לֵאָה כִּי עָמְדָה מִלֶּדֶת
Vattere Le'ah ki amedah milledet.
A close rendering is:
“And Leah saw that she had ceased from bearing.”
The wording identifies Leah's recognition that she was no longer giving birth at that point in the story.
It does not establish permanent infertility. In fact, the following verses eventually tell us that Leah conceived again.
Nor does the text directly state every motive behind her decision.
But the surrounding narrative gives us a clear context.
Rivalry.
Childbearing.
Status within the household.
A family in which children had become entangled with the competition between two sisters.
Rachel had already given Bilhah to Jacob.
Now Leah gave Zilpah.
And the consequences were immediate.
Zilpah bore a son.
Leah named him Gad.
Genesis 30:11 records Leah's reaction, traditionally rendered in the KJV as:
“A troop cometh.”

The Hebrew expression here, בָּא גָד (ba gad), is famously difficult to translate with complete certainty. It has been understood in connection with fortune, good luck, or a troop, which explains differences among English translations.
We should not build a doctrine on one disputed rendering.
But the next birth makes the emotional atmosphere unmistakable.
Zilpah bore another son.
And Leah declared:
“Happy am I, for the daughters will call me blessed: and she called his name Asher.” — Genesis 30:13, KJV
The Hebrew includes the expression:
בְּאָשְׁרִי כִּי אִשְּׁרוּנִי בָנוֹת
Be'oshri ki ishsheruni vanot.
A close translation is:
“In my happiness, for women will call me happy.”
The name אָשֵׁר (Asher) is associated with happiness or blessedness.
And here is the tension that makes this passage so compelling.
Leah announced happiness.
But the larger story had already shown us how deeply she longed to be loved.
We cannot claim that her happiness was false. The text does not say that.
But neither should we assume that the birth of another child through Zilpah had healed every wound in Leah's marriage.
That is something many of us understand.
You can celebrate a blessing and still carry an unresolved hurt.
You can smile in a photograph while privately grieving.
You can tell people God has been good—and mean every word—while still praying through something you have never told anyone.
You can be genuinely thankful and still be struggling.

And sometimes the most dangerous mistake we make is believing that the next achievement, the next relationship, the next promotion, the next child, the next compliment, or the next public recognition will finally settle the question of our worth.
But what happens when it doesn't?
What happens when the applause ends?
When the person you tried to impress remains unimpressed?
When you give everything you know how to give, and still feel unseen?
Leah's story confronts that painful possibility.
Because being fruitful is not the same thing as being loved.
And being useful is not the same thing as being cherished.
Perhaps you know what it feels like to be the dependable one.
The person everyone calls when they need something.
The person who keeps the family functioning.
The one who gives, serves, forgives, sacrifices, and stays.
But when your own heart is breaking, you wonder whether anyone notices.
Maybe you have spent years trying to become enough for someone who keeps moving the standard.
Maybe you have confused being needed with being loved.
Maybe you have allowed someone else's approval to become the measure of your value.
And maybe, like Leah, you have repeatedly told yourself:
One more thing.
One more sacrifice.
One more achievement.
Then I will finally matter.
But listen carefully.
You cannot secure your identity by endlessly auditioning for a love that refuses to see you.
And you were never created to make another human being your ultimate source of worth.
That does not mean relationships are unimportant.
Marriage matters.
Affection matters.
Faithfulness matters.
Human love is a genuine gift from God.
But no human being was designed to occupy the throne that belongs to the Lord.
When another person's approval becomes the foundation of your identity, their rejection can begin to feel like the destruction of your entire life.
And that is a burden no human relationship can safely carry.
The tragedy in Jacob's household was not simply that people wanted love or children.
Those desires were not inherently wrong.
The tragedy was the rivalry, manipulation, favoritism, and human brokenness surrounding them.
And yet God did not abandon this family.
That is where grace begins to astonish us.
Because if we were writing the history of God's covenant people, we might choose a spotless household.
A peaceful marriage.
A family without jealousy.
A story without manipulation or sorrow.
But Genesis does not offer us that kind of polished family portrait.
It gives us Jacob.
Rachel.
Leah.
Bilhah.
Zilpah.
Children born into complicated relationships.
A household where blessing and brokenness existed side by side.
And God continued His covenant purposes through people who were far from perfect.
But be careful not to misunderstand that truth.
God's ability to bring redemption out of human sin does not make the sin good.
God's faithfulness does not justify exploitation.
His sovereignty does not excuse favoritism, manipulation, or treating another person as a means to an end.
Grace is not God's declaration that everything we do is acceptable.
Grace is His mercy toward people who desperately need Him.
And here comes the part of Leah's story that reaches far beyond Genesis 30.
Remember Judah?
The fourth son.
The child whose birth moved Leah to say, “Now will I praise the LORD.”
Judah's family line would become central to the unfolding story of biblical redemption.
Genesis 49:10 associates Judah with royal authority.
Centuries later, Matthew 1 traces the genealogy of Jesus Christ through Judah.
And Revelation 5:5 identifies Jesus as:
“The Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David.”
Do you understand what this means?
The woman who was not Jacob's favorite became the mother of Judah, through whose line the promised Messiah would come.
Not because Leah was sinless.
Not because her marriage was ideal.
Not because every choice made in that household was righteous.
But because God's covenant faithfulness was greater than the failures of the people through whom He worked.
And there is an important distinction here.
Jesus did not descend from Zilpah's sons, Gad and Asher. He descended through Leah's son Judah.
Genesis 30:9–13 shows the continuing rivalry within Jacob's household, while the larger biblical story reveals how God's redemptive promise moved through Judah's line.
That connection must not be exaggerated.
But it should not be missed.
The less-loved wife was not overlooked in the unfolding purposes of God.
And this is where the story becomes more than a lesson about emotional insecurity.
It becomes a window into the Gospel.
Because Jesus Christ entered a world filled with the same kinds of human brokenness we see in Genesis.
Rejection.
Betrayal.
Sin.
Shame.
Misused power.
Broken relationships.
And He did not come merely to tell wounded people to think more positively about themselves.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to do what our own striving could never accomplish.
Isaiah 53:3 describes the suffering servant as:
“Despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.”
Jesus knows rejection.
He knows what it is to be misunderstood.
He knows betrayal.
He knows suffering.
But unlike us, He was without sin.
And at the cross, He bore our sins, offering Himself as the perfect sacrifice through whom forgiveness and reconciliation with God are possible.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we proved ourselves worthy.
Not after we repaired every damaged part of our lives.
While we were yet sinners.
That is the difference between the exhausting pursuit of human approval and the astonishing grace revealed in Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
It says your sin is so serious that Christ went to the cross—and God's mercy is so great that He offers forgiveness through the crucified and risen Savior.
The Gospel does not promise that every person who rejected you will eventually apologize.
It does not promise that every marriage will be restored.
It does not promise that every longing for children will be fulfilled.
It does not promise that following Jesus will eliminate grief.
But it does promise something infinitely greater.
That everyone who repents and believes in Jesus Christ receives forgiveness and eternal life through Him.
That our standing before God rests on Christ, not on our ability to impress other people.
That those who belong to Christ are not abandoned by the Father.
And that even suffering cannot separate God's people from His love in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:38–39).
Maybe you are reading this with a wound nobody knows about.
Maybe you have spent years being compared with someone else.
Maybe you have carried the shame of feeling like the unwanted one.
Maybe you have been chasing recognition from someone who never seems satisfied.
Or perhaps the story exposes something even harder.
Maybe you have been the one doing the comparing.
The one who made someone feel second.
The one who used affection as a reward.
The one who treated people as valuable only when they were useful.
If so, the Gospel is not merely inviting you to feel comforted.
It is calling you to repent.
To turn away from sin.
To stop defending what God is calling you to surrender.
To seek forgiveness where you have caused harm.
To pursue restoration where it is possible, wise, and safe.
And to receive the grace that changes how you love other people.
Because Jesus did not die simply to make us feel better about remaining the same.
He died and rose again to save us and make us new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That is not a promise that every painful memory immediately disappears.
It is a declaration that union with Christ brings a new identity and a new life.
You no longer have to build your entire existence around being someone's favorite.
You no longer have to treat another person's rejection as the final verdict on your worth.
You no longer have to believe that your failures have placed you beyond the reach of God's mercy.
You can come to Christ.
Not pretending to be whole.
Not pretending to be innocent.
Not pretending that everything is fine.
But confessing the truth.
Lord, I have tried to find in people what I should have sought first in You.
I have allowed rejection to shape my identity.
I have compared myself with others.
I have sinned in ways I need to confess.
I need Your mercy.
Forgive me.
Teach me to trust You.
Change my heart.
And if that prayer reflects the genuine cry of your heart, do not treat it as merely an emotional moment.
Turn to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith.
Open His Word.
Walk with believers who will help you grow in truth.
Seek wise pastoral counsel when you need it.
And remember that spiritual healing is not measured by how quickly you stop crying.
Sometimes it is revealed in the quiet decision to obey God while the tears are still falling.
Leah's story did not end at Genesis 30:13.
Later in the chapter, God heard Leah, and she conceived again.
She bore Issachar and Zebulun, and later gave birth to Dinah (Genesis 30:17–21).
And even then, Genesis 30:20 records her continuing hope that her husband would honor or dwell with her.
The biblical writer does not pretend that one moment of praise erased every complicated emotion.
That honesty matters.
Because the people of Scripture were not cardboard heroes.
They were human.
And God was faithful in the middle of their humanity.
By Genesis 49:31, Jacob's final instructions reveal that Leah was buried in the family burial place at Machpelah, where Jacob also asked to be buried.
We should not invent an undocumented romantic reconciliation between them.
Scripture does not give us that scene.
But it does give us a testimony to God's faithfulness through generations.
And the greatest testimony is Jesus Christ.
The Savior who came through Judah's line.
The Savior who welcomes repentant sinners.
The Savior who brings hope to people whose lives have become entangled in choices they regret and wounds they cannot easily explain.
So perhaps the question tonight is not merely why Leah gave Zilpah to Jacob.
Perhaps the question is what you have been giving away in your own desperate attempt to feel enough.
Your peace?
Your convictions?
Your boundaries?
Your honesty?
Your time with God?
Your willingness to say no?
Your obedience to Scripture?
What have you sacrificed because you were afraid that being yourself would not be enough to keep someone close?
And what might change if you stopped treating human approval as your savior?
This is not a call to abandon your responsibilities or stop loving people.
It is a call to put love back in its rightful order.
Love God above all.
Love your neighbor as yourself.
Serve without turning service into a transaction for approval.
Give without believing that your gifts can purchase someone's affection.
And when you discover that your heart has wandered, return to Christ.
There is grace for the repentant.
There is forgiveness through His blood.
There is new life in His resurrection.
And there is a Savior whose faithfulness does not depend on the shifting opinions of the crowd.
Sometimes an honest request for prayer is the beginning of a conversation someone has needed for years.
Your words may encourage someone who has begun to believe that their own story is beyond redemption.
There is also someone on your Facebook friends list who may need this message.
Someone who has been silently comparing themselves with others.
Someone who is exhausted from trying to earn affection.
Someone who knows the language of faith but has forgotten what grace feels like.
Because the purpose of this ministry is not merely to collect readers.
It is to point people to Jesus.
And if this kind of Scripture-centered teaching has helped you, there is another meaningful way to participate in the work.
For believers who prayerfully choose to give, supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be a genuine expression of generosity and stewardship.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That matters deeply.
You do not have to purchase God's favor.
And no financial contribution can replace repentance, faith, obedience, or the grace of God.
Your local church and the responsibilities God has entrusted to you should not be neglected.
The products are simply a practical expression of appreciation.
The deeper invitation is to grow in the Word, stay spiritually encouraged, and help make biblical resources available to others.
Those free resources are part of the mission too.
Because biblical nourishment should not be reduced to a transaction.
Read.
Pray.
Grow.
Share the Gospel.
Encourage another believer.
A faithful act of sharing can reach a heart that money alone could never reach.
Jesus Christ.
Leah could not force Jacob to love her the way she longed to be loved.
Zilpah's sons could not resolve every broken relationship in that household.
And the birth of more children could not, by itself, heal the deeper spiritual condition of the human heart.
But God saw Leah.
God continued His covenant purposes.
And through the line of Judah, the promised Savior came.
Not to excuse our sin.
Not to glorify our brokenness.
But to redeem sinners who turn to Him in faith.
So when you remember Leah, do not remember only the woman who gave her servant to her husband.
Remember the God who saw the less-loved wife.
Remember the danger of turning human approval into an idol.
Remember the women whose voices the narrative does not fully preserve.
Remember the grace of God working through a family that could never have saved itself.
And above all, remember Jesus.
Because the final hope of this story is not that every human being will finally choose you.
It is that through Jesus Christ, you can be reconciled to the God who made you.
Leah spent years longing to be chosen by one man—yet through her son Judah came the Savior who calls the rejected, the guilty, and the broken to find redemption in Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “GREAT IS YOUR FAITHFULNESS” WAS WRITTEN WHILE JERUSALEM WAS IN RUINS
paragraphs: “GREAT IS YOUR FAITHFULNESS” WAS WRITTEN WHILE JERUSALEM WAS IN RUINS

Before these words became a song of comfort, they were a confession of faith rising from unbearable grief. And if your life feels like it is falling apart, the story behind Lamentations 3 may change how you understand the faithfulness of God forever.
There is something deeply unsettling about the words “Great is Your faithfulness.”
Not because they are difficult to believe when life is beautiful.
But because of where those words appear in Scripture.
They were not spoken from a palace overflowing with prosperity.
They were not written in the middle of a celebration, after every prayer had been answered and every enemy defeated.
They appear in a book filled with tears.
A book written in the shadow of Jerusalem's destruction.
A book where the streets are devastated, families are grieving, and the people of God are confronting the consequences of their rebellion.
And right there, surrounded by descriptions of suffering, we encounter one of the most breathtaking declarations in the entire Bible.
“Great is thy faithfulness.” — Lamentations 3:23 (KJV)
Read that again.
Not great is my understanding.
Not great is my strength.
Not great is my ability to hold everything together.
Great is Your faithfulness.
Because sometimes the most extraordinary confession of faith is not made by someone who has escaped the fire.
It is made by someone still standing in the ashes.
And perhaps that is why you need to hear this today.
Because there are people reading these words who know exactly what it means to live among ruins.
Your Jerusalem may not be a city destroyed by an invading army.
It may be a marriage that has become painfully distant.
A child you have prayed for until you no longer know what to say.
A diagnosis that changed the way you look at tomorrow.
A betrayal that shattered your ability to trust.
A financial struggle that has quietly stolen your sleep.
Or perhaps something even harder to explain.
You still go to church.
You still smile when people greet you.
You still tell everyone that God is good.
But when the house becomes quiet, and nobody is watching, you wonder why the God you love has allowed your life to become so painful.
And somewhere beneath all the prayers you know how to pray is a question you are almost afraid to ask.
Lord, are You still faithful when everything around me is falling apart?
That is not a modern question.
The book of Lamentations forces us to confront it.
In 586 BC, Jerusalem fell to the Babylonians. The temple was destroyed. The city was devastated. Many were killed, and others were carried into exile.
The place that had represented worship, national identity, and the visible presence of God's covenant promises lay in ruins.
And Scripture does not romanticize what happened.
Lamentations describes hunger, bereavement, humiliation, abandonment, and anguish so intense that the writer struggles to find language for it.
This was not simply an unfortunate historical tragedy.
The biblical prophets had repeatedly warned Judah that persistent idolatry, injustice, and covenant unfaithfulness would bring judgment.
God had not failed to keep His word.
Tragically, His warnings had proven true.
And that makes the declaration in Lamentations 3 even more astonishing.
Because God's faithfulness was not merely the promise that He would bless His people when they obeyed.
His faithfulness also meant that He would remain true to His holy character, even when His people rebelled.
The writer does not deny the devastation.
He does not pretend the suffering is imaginary.
He does not call judgment a blessing.
Instead, he looks directly into the darkness and remembers something the darkness cannot erase.
Listen to the movement of his heart:
“This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope.”
— Lamentations 3:21 (KJV)
Notice what happens.
His circumstances have not suddenly changed.
Jerusalem has not been rebuilt.
The temple has not been restored.
The grief has not disappeared.
But something changes within him.
He remembers.
And what he remembers becomes the foundation of his hope.
“It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.”
— Lamentations 3:22–23 (KJV)
Now we must look beneath the familiar English words, because the original Hebrew makes this confession even richer.
The Hebrew word commonly translated as “mercies” in verse 22 is חַסְדֵי (ḥasdei), from ḥesed (חֶסֶד).
It speaks of steadfast love, covenant loyalty, and faithful kindness.
Not merely a passing feeling of affection.
Not a momentary emotional response.
It describes love that acts faithfully according to God's character and covenant commitments.
The Hebrew word behind “compassions” is רַחֲמָיו (raḥamav), from raḥamim, a word associated with deep tenderness and mercy.
And the declaration “Great is thy faithfulness” comes from the Hebrew:
רַבָּה אֱמוּנָתֶךָ
Rabbah emunatekha.
Literally, “Great is Your faithfulness.”
The word emunah (אֱמוּנָה) carries the sense of firmness, reliability, and faithfulness.
The writer is not saying that God has made his circumstances easy.
He is declaring that God's character remains trustworthy even when his circumstances are devastating.
And there is another detail we must not overlook.

The Hebrew text of Lamentations 3:22 contains a textual and translation question. Many traditional English translations, including the King James Version, read that God's mercies are why “we are not consumed.” Other translations render the verse along the lines that the LORD's steadfast love never ceases.
Both readings direct our attention toward the endurance of God's covenant mercy, but they should not be treated as identical word-for-word translations.
The central confession remains unmistakable.
God's compassion has not reached its end.
Even in judgment, His mercy has not vanished.
Even in national devastation, His covenant purposes have not been extinguished.
Even when His people have lost so much, God has not ceased to be God.
And perhaps this is where the words begin to reach into the places you have been trying to hide.
Because some of us have quietly built our understanding of God's faithfulness around the things He gives us.
When the job is secure, God is faithful.
When the family is healthy, God is faithful.
When the bills are paid, God is faithful.
When the prayer is answered the way we hoped, God is faithful.
But what happens when the job disappears?
When the relationship breaks?
When the test results are frightening?
When the prayer seems to meet silence?
Was God only faithful when life was comfortable?
Or have we confused His faithfulness with our preferred outcomes?
That question hurts.
Especially when you have obeyed God through tears, served Him through exhaustion, and watched someone else receive the very thing you have been begging Him for.
There is a particular kind of spiritual pain that comes when you know the right Bible verses but cannot understand your own life.
You know Romans 8:28.
You know Jeremiah 29:11.
You know that God is good.
Yet your heart still aches.
And sometimes you feel guilty for hurting because you think genuine Christians should be stronger than this.
But Lamentations gives us a different picture.
The Bible does not demand that grieving believers pretend they are happy.
It gives them words for their grief.
It allows lament.
It allows tears.
It allows anguished questions to be brought before the living God.
Faith does not always sound like a victorious shout.
Sometimes faith sounds like a broken whisper:
Lord, I do not understand what You are doing. But I know You have not stopped being who You are.
And that is not weak faith.
That is faith learning to rest on God's character rather than the appearance of immediate circumstances.
But there is something else we need to understand.
The suffering described in Lamentations had a particular historical and covenant context. Jerusalem's destruction was connected to Judah's rebellion and God's announced judgment.
That does not mean every tragedy in your life is punishment for a specific sin.
Scripture itself rejects that simplistic assumption.
In John 9:1–3, Jesus challenged the idea that a man's blindness must have resulted from his sin or his parents' sin.
And in Luke 13:1–5, Jesus refused to portray victims of tragedy as worse sinners than everyone else.
So please do not turn Lamentations into a weapon against every hurting person.
A grieving mother does not need someone casually telling her that her loss must be God's punishment.
A struggling believer does not need every hardship interpreted as evidence that God is angry.
Sometimes suffering exposes our sin and calls us to repentance.
Sometimes suffering comes through the evil actions of others.
Sometimes it reflects the brokenness of a fallen world.
And sometimes we simply do not know why God has permitted a particular trial.
But in every circumstance, we are invited to bring our pain honestly before Him.
Because biblical hope is not built on pretending we know every reason.
It is built on knowing the God who remains faithful.
And this brings us to a line that is often overlooked.
“The LORD is my portion, saith my soul; therefore will I hope in him.”
— Lamentations 3:24 (KJV)
My portion.
Not my possessions.
Not my reputation.
Not my perfect future.
Not even the immediate restoration of everything I have lost.
The LORD Himself is my portion.
Can you feel the weight of that confession?
When almost everything that once gave life stability has been stripped away, the writer remembers that God Himself remains the deepest inheritance of His people.
This does not make the losses insignificant.
It makes the Lord greater than what has been lost.
And that truth becomes even more breathtaking when we follow the story of Scripture toward Jesus Christ.
Because Jerusalem's destruction was not the final chapter of God's redemptive plan.
God preserved His people.
He brought exiles home.
He continued His covenant purposes.
And in the fullness of time, the promised Messiah came.
Jesus Christ.
Not a Savior who stood at a comfortable distance from human suffering.
Not a King who demanded that hurting people become emotionally presentable before approaching Him.
But the Son of God who entered our broken world.
He wept at the tomb of Lazarus.
He was betrayed by someone close to Him.
He was abandoned by His disciples.
He was mocked, scourged, and crucified.
And on the cross, He bore our sins, fulfilling the saving purpose of God.
Isaiah had foretold the suffering Servant:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
— Isaiah 53:5 (KJV)
That healing cannot be reduced to a guarantee that every believer will immediately recover from every disease or escape every earthly hardship.
The passage points fundamentally to the Servant's redemptive suffering, through which God brings reconciliation and restoration to sinners.
At Calvary, the faithfulness of God was revealed in a way that human imagination could never have invented.
The righteous Son suffered for the unrighteous.
The sinless Savior bore the judgment sinners deserved.
The One who had every right to condemn became the sacrifice through whom forgiveness is offered.
And then came the resurrection.
The stone was rolled away.
Death did not have the final word.
Sin did not have the final word.
The grave did not have the final word.
Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
And now the Gospel announces something infinitely greater than the possibility of an easier life.
It announces reconciliation with God through the crucified and risen Savior.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
— Ephesians 2:8–9 (KJV)
This is where the theme of scandal and grace becomes intensely personal.
Because the greatest scandal in your story may not be what someone did to you.
It may be what you have done and cannot undo.
The secret sin.
The compromise.
The lies.
The pride.
The bitterness.
The years of resisting God's voice.
The choices you would never want displayed before the people who respect you.
And perhaps you have wondered whether the Lord could still receive someone who knows the truth and has repeatedly walked away from it.
Listen carefully.
God's mercy is not permission to continue in rebellion.
Grace is not a disguise for unrepentant sin.
The Gospel does not tell us that our sin was never serious.
The cross tells us just how serious it was.
But the cross also reveals how extraordinary God's mercy is toward sinners who come to Christ in repentance and faith.
The same Jesus who said, “Repent ye, and believe the gospel” (Mark 1:15) also declared:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
— John 6:37 (KJV)
Think about that.
You may be ashamed of what you have become.
You may be exhausted from fighting the same temptation.
You may be carrying years of spiritual regret.
But the invitation of Christ is not to clean yourself up so thoroughly that you no longer need a Savior.
It is to come to Him because you desperately do.
To confess.
To turn from sin.
To trust His finished work.
To receive the forgiveness you could never purchase through your own religious performance.
And to follow Him in the new life His grace makes possible.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by erasing every earthly consequence.
Not by promising that repentance will instantly repair every broken relationship.
But by giving forgiven sinners a new standing before God, a new direction for their lives, and a living hope that suffering cannot ultimately destroy.
This is why Lamentations 3:23 is so powerful.
It was not written by someone who could see every beautiful thing God would eventually do.
It was written from within a story that still hurt.
And yet the writer could say:
Not because every morning brings good news.
Not because every morning erases yesterday's grief.
Not because every morning guarantees an unexpected financial breakthrough, a restored marriage, or a miraculous recovery.
But because God's compassion is not exhausted by yesterday.
His faithfulness is not diminished by the darkness of the night.
And His people can seek Him again.
There may be someone reading this who has not prayed sincerely in weeks.
You have been angry.
Disappointed.
Perhaps even numb.
You have opened your Bible, stared at the page, and closed it because you could not bear another promise that seemed so far from your present reality.
And now you are wondering whether God is tired of you.
Whether you have disappointed Him too many times.
Whether your spiritual life has become too damaged to rebuild.
Remember what Lamentations says:
“The LORD is good unto them that wait for him, to the soul that seeketh him.”
— Lamentations 3:25 (KJV)
And later:
“For the Lord will not cast off for ever: But though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion according to the multitude of his mercies.”
— Lamentations 3:31–32 (KJV)
These words do not promise that every earthly situation will turn out as we wish.
They do reveal the compassion of the Lord within the covenant story of His people.
And through Jesus Christ, we have the assurance that everyone who belongs to Him has a hope extending beyond this present age.
The final restoration promised in Scripture is not merely a return to the life we used to have.
It is something greater.
A new heaven and a new earth.
God dwelling with His people.
Death abolished.
Mourning ended.
Sin removed.
And every tear finally wiped away.
Revelation 21:4 says:
“And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.”
That is the future toward which Christian hope ultimately looks.
Not an endless cycle of earthly disappointments interrupted by occasional blessings.
But the final victory of Jesus Christ over sin, death, and all that has corrupted God's creation.
Until then, we walk by faith.
Sometimes with confidence.
Sometimes with trembling hands.
Sometimes singing.
Sometimes crying so hard that the only prayer we can manage is His name.
Jesus.
And that name is enough to begin praying again.
Maybe today you need to stop measuring God's faithfulness by how quickly your circumstances change.
Maybe you need to repent of a sin you have been protecting.
Maybe you need to surrender the bitterness that has slowly become part of your identity.
Maybe you need to forgive someone, even while establishing wise boundaries and acknowledging the damage they caused.
Maybe you need to ask for help because the weight you are carrying has become too heavy to bear alone.
Or maybe you simply need to hear this:
Your present ruins do not prove that God has abandoned you.
And your inability to understand His timing does not make His promises untrue.
There is a beautiful difference between saying, “I know everything will happen exactly as I want,” and saying, “I know the Lord is faithful, whatever happens.”
The first depends on an outcome.
The second depends on God.
And only one of those foundations can hold when the outcome breaks your heart.
Be honest before God.
Not as a performance.
Not because a public comment earns God's attention.
But because sometimes admitting that we need prayer becomes the first honest conversation we have had in a long time.
Let those words become your confession, not that everything is okay, but that the Lord remains worthy of your trust.
Perhaps someone else reading the comments needs to know they are not the only believer struggling to hold on.
And if you see someone asking for prayer, consider taking a moment to pray for them.
We were never meant to carry every burden alone.
That is also why I hope you will not keep this article to yourself.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because somewhere among your friends and family may be someone who is quietly losing hope.
Someone who has stopped attending church.
Someone who feels too ashamed to return to Jesus.
Someone who is wondering whether God still sees them.
You may never know how much a Scripture-filled message means to a person who was barely holding on when they encountered it.
Because spiritual growth is not sustained by one emotional moment.
We need the Word of God repeatedly.
We need prayer.
We need fellowship with faithful believers.
We need sound teaching.
We need correction when we wander.
And above everything else, we need Jesus Christ.
That is the heart behind Gospel Warrior.

We want to help people move beyond simply being inspired by Christian content toward actually knowing Scripture, growing in discernment, confronting sin, understanding grace, and following Jesus more faithfully.
These resources are intended to help believers become more deeply rooted in the Word of God, better equipped to face life's struggles, and more confident in sharing the Gospel.
And I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading and sharing.
It helps sustain a ministry committed to proclaiming Christ in a world where countless people are spiritually hungry.
But please understand something important.
It does not purchase His favor.
It does not make anyone more spiritual than someone who cannot afford to give.
And it should never replace the responsibilities you have toward your family, your local church, or people genuinely in need.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Supporting Gospel ministry can be a beautiful expression of generosity and stewardship.
What matters is that your giving be voluntary, thoughtful, and offered with a sincere desire to honor the Lord.
And perhaps that is the most beautiful part of Christian generosity.
You may never hear the prayer they whisper.
You may never know which Bible passage finally helped them understand the Gospel.
But you can participate in helping the truth reach farther.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The grace of Jesus Christ is not a product.
Salvation is the gift of God, received through faith in the Savior.
Our desire is simply to make the truth of that Gospel known.
And now, before you leave, I want to return to the person we met at the beginning.
The person standing in the ruins.
The person who has been trying to understand why life hurts so much.
The person who still believes in God but feels ashamed to admit how tired they are.
Perhaps that person is you.
I cannot promise that tomorrow will bring the answer you have been waiting for.
I cannot promise that everyone who left will return.
I cannot promise that your illness will disappear, that your finances will immediately recover, or that every broken relationship will be restored.
Scripture does not authorize me to make those promises.
But I can point you to the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
To the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
To the Lord whose mercy is not exhausted.
To the One who has promised never to forsake those who belong to Him.
And I can remind you that the book containing the words “Great is thy faithfulness” did not begin with a happy ending.
It began with a devastated city.
It contained mourning.
It contained confession.
It contained painful questions.
And right in the middle of it all, a wounded voice remembered the character of God.
Perhaps your circumstances have not changed yet.
Perhaps the tears are still there.
Perhaps you are still waiting.
But tonight, you can bring your honest heart before the Lord.
You do not need an impressive prayer.
You do not need to manufacture an emotion.
You can simply say:
Father, I am tired.
I have questions I cannot answer.
I have carried things I should have surrendered.
Forgive my sins. Cleanse my heart. Teach me to trust You.
Help me remember Your mercy when I cannot understand my circumstances.
Keep my eyes on Jesus, who died for sinners and rose again.
And when tomorrow comes, help me seek You again.
Amen.
There is no magic in repeating those words.
The hope is not in the prayer itself.
The hope is in the living God to whom we pray.
