The point is that the God who rules over death is worthy of our trust.
That truth becomes even more powerful when we return to the beginning of Genesis.
In Eden, humanity's rebellion shattered the relationship between human beings and their Creator.
Adam and Eve hid when they heard the presence of God in the garden.
Sin produced shame.
Shame produced hiding.
And hiding became a pattern that humanity has repeated ever since.
We hide behind busyness.
We hide behind religious appearances.
We hide behind carefully edited photographs and confident smiles.
We tell everyone we are doing fine while privately fighting battles we are ashamed to admit.
We know how to attend church without surrendering our hearts.
We know how to quote Scripture while refusing to forgive.
We know how to speak about holiness while secretly negotiating with temptation.
And sometimes the most exhausting thing about being a Christian is not the battle itself.
It is pretending there is no battle.
Perhaps you know that exhaustion.
Perhaps you still believe in Jesus, but your prayer life has become almost silent.
Perhaps you have been carrying guilt over something you promised God you would never do again.
Perhaps you feel far from the Lord and cannot remember when your relationship with Him began to feel mechanical.
Enoch's story does not say, “Become extraordinary so God will notice you.”
It asks a more searching question.
Are you walking with God, or have you become comfortable merely knowing about Him?
There is a difference.
You can know the language of faith without living in dependence upon Christ.
You can be surrounded by Christian content and still neglect personal prayer.
You can defend biblical truth publicly while refusing to obey it privately.
But the answer is not to manufacture an impressive spiritual life.
The answer is to return to the Lord.
To repent honestly.
To confess what you have hidden.
To receive the mercy offered through Jesus Christ.
Because the Christian life is not built on pretending we are sinless.
It is built on the grace of the Savior who came to rescue sinners.
And this is where we must make an important distinction.
Enoch walked with God.
But Enoch was not Jesus.
Enoch was a human being who lived by faith.
Jesus Christ is the eternal Son of God who became truly human, lived without sin, died for sinners, and rose bodily from the grave.
Enoch was taken by God.
Jesus willingly gave Himself for us.
Enoch did not experience ordinary death.
Jesus entered death itself and conquered it through His resurrection.
And that difference changes everything.
The greatest hope of Christianity is not that we might mysteriously disappear like Enoch.
The greatest hope is that Jesus Christ has defeated the power of death and promises resurrection life to those who belong to Him.
Listen to His words in John 11:25–26:
“I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?” (KJV)
Jesus spoke those words in the shadow of a tomb.
Lazarus had died.
His sisters were grieving.
Their questions were painfully human.
Why had Jesus not arrived sooner?
Why had He allowed suffering?
Why had death entered their home?
And Jesus did not respond with a shallow explanation.
He revealed Himself as the resurrection and the life.
Then He went to the tomb and called Lazarus out.
But even Lazarus would eventually face physical death again.
His restoration to earthly life pointed forward to something greater.
The final resurrection promised through Christ.
Enoch's unusual departure demonstrates that God is not helpless before death.
But Jesus' resurrection establishes the foundation of the believer's everlasting hope.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 15:20:
And later, in 1 Corinthians 15:54–55, he celebrates the promised final victory:
“Death is swallowed up in victory.”
“O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?”
That is the Christian hope.
Not immortality achieved through our own spirituality.
Not escape earned through religious performance.
Not secret knowledge available to a privileged few.
Resurrection through the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
There is another detail in Enoch's story that deserves our attention.
Genesis tells us he walked with God for three hundred years after becoming the father of Methuselah.
Three hundred years.
Not three days of emotional excitement.
Not a single extraordinary encounter followed by a lifetime of indifference.
Three centuries.
Scripture does not tell us that becoming a father caused his walk with God, and we should not pretend it does.
But it does tell us that his walk with God continued through the ordinary responsibilities of family life.
He had sons and daughters.
He lived in a fallen world.
He belonged to a generation moving steadily toward the judgment later described in the account of Noah.
His faith was lived in history, not in a world untouched by human corruption.
And the New Testament gives us another glimpse of his witness.
Jude 14–15 presents Enoch as proclaiming the Lord's coming judgment against ungodliness.
That matters because walking with God is not simply a private feeling of spiritual comfort.
True faith does not make holiness irrelevant.
Grace does not turn repentance into an optional extra.
A genuine relationship with God changes the direction of a person's life.
Not because obedience purchases God's love.
But because the God who saves us also calls us to turn from sin.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds these truths together.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works.
And we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace is not the reward for becoming worthy.
Grace is the gift that transforms the unworthy.
That is why the message of Enoch should not leave us obsessing over how he disappeared.
It should leave us examining how we are living.
Because there is something sobering about a man whose story occupies only a few verses but whose testimony has endured for thousands of years.
His life asks questions that our modern distractions cannot silence.
What are you becoming when nobody is applauding?
What is happening to your soul while you pursue everything else?
Are you becoming more dependent on Jesus or merely more familiar with Christian language?
Are you confessing your sins or learning to excuse them?
Are you following Christ when obedience costs you something?
And if your earthly life ended sooner than you expected, what would truly matter about the years you had been given?
Not everyone will leave behind a famous name.
Not everyone will write a book.
Not everyone will lead a ministry.
Not everyone will be remembered by the world.
But every human life is lived before God.
And the Lord does not measure faithfulness by the standards of social media.
Perhaps the mother praying quietly over her children is serving Christ more faithfully than someone receiving thousands of public compliments.
Perhaps the exhausted father choosing honesty over dishonest gain is honoring God in ways nobody else sees.
Perhaps the believer who has fallen into sin but finally comes into the light through repentance is taking a more meaningful step than someone who has perfected the appearance of religious success.
The Lord sees.
And that should both humble and comfort us.
Because He sees the sin we try to conceal.
But He also sees the trembling heart that comes to Him seeking mercy.
First John 1:9 gives us this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise is not permission to cherish sin.
It is an invitation to stop hiding from the Savior who cleanses sinners.
Maybe you need to hear that tonight.
You do not need another week of pretending.
You do not need another carefully constructed excuse.
You do not need to wait until you feel spiritually impressive before returning to Jesus.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Bring the truth.
Bring the shame.
Bring the failures.
Bring the habits you have struggled to surrender.
Bring the questions you are afraid to ask.
Christ does not promise that following Him will remove every earthly sorrow.
But He does promise that those who come to Him will not be cast out.
John 6:37 says:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV)
And there is something else we must understand about Enoch.
Some readers connect his translation with the future gathering of believers to Christ described in 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17.
It is understandable why they see a resemblance.
Enoch was taken by God without experiencing ordinary death, and Paul teaches that believers who are alive at Christ's return will be caught up to meet the Lord.
But Genesis does not explicitly identify Enoch's translation as a prophetic prediction of the rapture.
We should distinguish a possible theological parallel from a claim the text itself makes.
The certain promise is greater than speculation about the timing of future events.
Whether believers die before Christ returns or remain alive at His coming, their ultimate hope rests in belonging to Jesus.
That is what Paul emphasizes when he concludes the passage:
“And so shall we ever be with the Lord.” — 1 Thessalonians 4:17 (KJV)
With the Lord.
Think about those words.
The deepest hope of the Christian faith is not merely escaping suffering.
It is not simply avoiding a grave.
It is not even the wonder of heaven considered apart from its greatest treasure.
It is being with Christ.
The One who loved us.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who rose again.
The One who will make all things new.
And perhaps that is the most beautiful connection between Enoch's story and the Gospel.
Enoch walked with God.
The Christian is called to walk in Christ.
Colossians 2:6 says:
“As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in him.” (KJV)
Notice the language.
Walk.
Not merely admire Him from a distance.
Not simply discuss Him when it is convenient.
Walk in Him.
Daily.
Dependently.
Through ordinary mornings and sleepless nights.
Through repentance after failure.
Through obedience when temptation is strong.
Through grief when prayers seem unanswered.
Through seasons when faith feels joyful and seasons when faith means clinging to God's promises through tears.
And when we stumble, we do not place our confidence in the perfection of our walking.
We place it in the perfection of our Savior.
Because Jesus is not merely the example of someone who walked faithfully with God.
He is the Redeemer who reconciles sinners to God through His blood.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we earned a spotless record.
Not after we became worthy of His attention.
While we were yet sinners.
That is grace.
And it is why our message at Gospel Warrior will always return to the same glorious truth.
He does not erase the historical reality of our sins or pretend their consequences never existed.
He does something greater.
He forgives those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
He reconciles the guilty to God.
He gives new life.
He transforms people who could never save themselves.
And He promises a future in which death itself will finally be destroyed.
Enoch's story began in a genealogy marked by death.
But his entry interrupted the pattern.
And the Gospel announces an even greater interruption.
A tomb outside Jerusalem was occupied by the crucified body of Jesus.
His followers mourned.
His enemies believed the story was finished.
The stone stood before the entrance.
But on the third day, Jesus rose.
Not as a legend created to make people feel better.
Not merely as a metaphor for new beginnings.
The New Testament proclaims His bodily resurrection as a real event and the foundation of Christian hope.
And because He lives, the final word over those who belong to Him is not death.
It is life in Christ.
So here is the question I want to leave with you.
Not whether you could disappear like Enoch.
Not whether you understand every mystery surrounding his translation.
Not whether you can explain every difficult passage about the end times.
But this:
If God examined the direction of your life today, would He find a heart returning to Him in faith—or a heart continually running away?
That question is not meant to drive you into hopelessness.
It is meant to direct you to Jesus.
If you have wandered, return.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you are spiritually weary, come to Christ.
If you have never truly trusted Him, do not confuse religious familiarity with saving faith.
The Gospel calls you to turn from sin and trust in the crucified and risen Lord.
You do not need to become another Enoch.
You need Jesus.
You can simply write “Lord, teach me to walk with You.”

If Christ has been restoring your life after a painful season, share a little of your testimony. Someone reading may need to know that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and God's grace has not run out.
You do not have to reveal private details to be honest about your need for Him.
And perhaps someone on your Facebook friends list needs this message more than you realize.
Someone who has recently buried a loved one.
Someone terrified of death.
Someone who feels too ashamed to return to church.
Someone who has mistaken religious activity for intimacy with God.
Someone who is beginning to wonder whether Jesus still receives broken people.
Not simply to increase its reach, but because the hope of Christ's resurrection deserves to be heard.
Because faith grows through God's Word, not through emotional excitement alone.
And if these messages have helped you understand Scripture, return to Christ, or strengthen your walk with Him, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is not meant to be another page that briefly stirs your emotions before you continue scrolling.
Our desire is to help people open their Bibles, understand the Gospel, recognize error, repent of sin, and grow into mature disciples of Jesus Christ.
These resources are offered to help people learn, pray, study, and become more firmly rooted in biblical truth.
You may prayerfully regard that support as part of your Christian generosity and stewardship.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
These products are not the heart of our mission.
Jesus Christ is.
They are simply another way to encourage biblical reflection, share meaningful messages, and help sustain the work.
Your spiritual worth is not measured by your financial contribution.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The message of Jesus Christ must never become a transaction.
We serve because He first loved us.
We give because we have received grace.
We share because people need the truth.
And we follow because Jesus is Lord.
Now return with me, one final time, to that ancient genealogy.
Adam.
And he died.
Seth.
And he died.
Enosh.
And he died.
The names continue.
The years accumulate.
The grave waits.
Then Enoch appears.
A man whose earthly life is summarized in a few extraordinary words.
He walked with God.
And God took him.
But thousands of years later, another name entered human history.
Jesus.
He walked among sinners.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed the repentant.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He wept beside a tomb.
He carried a cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day…
He rose again.
Enoch's story reminds us that death does not rule over God.
Jesus' resurrection declares that God has provided the victory over death through His Son.
And now the invitation is before you.
Will you keep hiding?
Or will you come to Christ?
Will you spend your life chasing a world that cannot save you?
Or will you follow the Savior who gave His life to redeem you?
You do not know how many mornings remain.
You do not know what tomorrow will bring.
But today, you can repent, believe the Gospel, and begin walking in renewed dependence upon Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest question is not whether your name will be remembered on earth.
It is whether you belong to the Savior who has conquered the grave.
Enoch disappeared from the earth without a recorded death—but Jesus entered the grave and rose again so that death would never have the final word over those who belong to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY WERE STARVING… THEN SOMEONE POISONED THE ONLY FOOD THEY HAD.
paragraphs: THEY WERE STARVING… THEN SOMEONE POISONED THE ONLY FOOD THEY HAD.
Why Did Elisha Throw Flour Into a Deadly Pot? The Forgotten Miracle in 2 Kings 4:38–41 That Reveals What Happens When Death Enters the Place Where Life Was Supposed to Be.
Imagine being so hungry that you can barely stand.

Your stomach is empty. Your strength is fading. There is famine everywhere, and the little food you have managed to find feels like the difference between surviving another day and becoming another victim of the crisis.
Then, finally, someone places a bowl of warm stew in front of you.
You lift it toward your mouth.
You take a bite.
And suddenly, someone screams.
“There is death in the pot, O man of God!”
Not a metaphor.
Not an exaggeration meant to frighten people.
Something had gone terribly wrong with the food.
And what happened next is one of the strangest miracles recorded in the Old Testament.
The prophet Elisha did not throw the entire meal away.
He did not search for an antidote.
He did not order the men to prepare another pot.
He asked for flour.
Ordinary flour.
Then he threw it into the very pot that had become dangerous.
And the Bible says the food was no longer harmful.
But here is the question that should stop every serious reader of Scripture:
Why flour?
Why would God use something so ordinary in a situation so deadly?
And what does this ancient account teach us about trusting God when something we desperately needed has become the very thing that threatens us?
Because sometimes the deepest lessons of faith are discovered not in a palace, a battlefield, or a temple…
But beside a cooking fire, where hungry people are staring at a pot they can no longer trust.
And to understand this miracle, we need to return to the famine.
The Bible tells us:

“And Elisha came again to Gilgal: and there was a dearth in the land; and the sons of the prophets were sitting before him: and he said unto his servant, Set on the great pot, and seethe pottage for the sons of the prophets.”
— 2 Kings 4:38, KJV
Notice something important.
These were not people who had abandoned God.
They were associated with the prophetic community. They were sitting before Elisha, presumably receiving instruction from the man of God.
And yet they were hungry.
They were experiencing famine.
They were living through hardship.
That matters because some people have been taught, directly or indirectly, that if they are faithful enough, obedient enough, or prayerful enough, suffering will somehow avoid their doorstep.
But here were men gathered around a prophet of God…
And there was still famine in the land.
Being close to the things of God does not mean you will never experience the difficulties of living in a fallen world.
Sometimes you can be seeking the Lord sincerely and still find yourself facing a season you never expected.
You can pray and still grieve.
You can obey and still struggle financially.
You can love Jesus and still walk through illness, betrayal, uncertainty, or loss.
The famine was real.
And so was God's presence among His people.
Please do not miss that.
The hardship did not prove that God had forgotten them.
And your hardship, by itself, does not prove that He has forgotten you either.
Then something happened that made their situation worse.
One of the men went out into the field to gather herbs.
He discovered a wild vine and collected its gourds, filling his garment with them. He returned and cut them into the pot of stew.
But there was a problem.
Scripture says:
“For they knew them not.”
— 2 Kings 4:39, KJV
Those four words carry the turning point of the entire story.
They did not know what they had gathered.
The Hebrew expression is כִּי־לֹא יָדָעוּ (ki-lo yada'u), meaning, “for they did not know.”
The text emphasizes ignorance, not deliberate poisoning.
The man was trying to contribute food.
He went searching because people were hungry.
He brought back something that appeared useful.
And without knowing what it was, he introduced danger into the meal.
The Bible does not identify the plant with certainty. Some interpreters have suggested colocynth, a bitter wild gourd, but the exact species is not established by the passage.
What Scripture makes clear is that the gathered plants were unknown to the men, and the resulting stew became harmful.
Now think about how painfully familiar that can feel.
Not every disaster begins with someone trying to hurt you.
Sometimes it begins with a decision made without understanding.
A relationship you entered because you were lonely.
Advice you accepted because the person sounded convincing.
A compromise you justified because you were desperate.
A teaching you believed because it was wrapped in religious language.
A habit you welcomed because it promised relief.
At first, it looked harmless.
Perhaps even helpful.
But eventually, you discovered that something was terribly wrong.
And this is where we must be careful with Scripture.
The wild gourds in 2 Kings 4 were actual plants, and the stew was actual food. The passage is not secretly a code about every toxic relationship, every bad decision, or every spiritual struggle.
But the event does invite a sobering reflection: human beings can introduce danger into their lives and communities without recognizing it.
Sincerity is not the same as wisdom.
Good intentions do not make every choice safe.
And spiritual maturity includes the humility to admit, “I do not know enough to trust this.”
Proverbs 14:12 warns:
“There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.”
How many times have we trusted something because it seemed right?
How many times have we confused familiarity with truth?
How many times have we allowed something into our hearts simply because it promised to satisfy an immediate hunger?
And how many times did we discover the danger only after we had already tasted it?
The men in Gilgal did not recognize the problem while the ingredients were being gathered.
They recognized it when the stew was served.
Scripture says:

“So they poured out for the men to eat. And it came to pass, as they were eating of the pottage, that they cried out, and said, O thou man of God, there is death in the pot. And they could not eat thereof.”
— 2 Kings 4:40, KJV
“There is death in the pot.”
The Hebrew phrase is unforgettable:
מָוֶת בַּסִּיר — mavet ba-sir.
Literally, “Death in the pot.”
The Hebrew word מָוֶת (mavet) means “death,” while סִיר (sir) refers to a cooking pot.
The cry is startlingly direct.
They were not merely complaining that the food tasted unpleasant.
They believed something in the stew threatened their lives.
And suddenly, the thing prepared to nourish them had become something they feared.
There is something deeply human about that moment.
Because some of life's most painful experiences involve discovering danger in places where we expected safety.
A home where love was supposed to live.
A friendship where trust was supposed to grow.
A promise that was supposed to bring stability.
A religious community where people were supposed to encounter compassion and truth.
And when something sacred or precious is mishandled, the pain can reach places that ordinary disappointment never touches.
Maybe you know what that feels like.
Maybe you have sat quietly with the consequences of someone else's carelessness.
Maybe you have carried guilt over a decision you made before you understood its cost.
Maybe you have looked at something you once celebrated and whispered, “How did this become so painful?”
But the story does not end with the men crying out.
And that is where the miracle begins.
Elisha hears their distress.
Then he gives an instruction that would have sounded almost absurd.
“But he said, Then bring meal. And he cast it into the pot; and he said, Pour out for the people, that they may eat. And there was no harm in the pot.”
— 2 Kings 4:41, KJV
Bring meal.
Bring flour.
The Hebrew word is קֶמַח (qemach), meaning flour or meal.
Not an exotic substance.
Not a mysterious medicine.
Not a secret ritual ingredient.
Just flour.
And here is where we need to resist a popular but unsupported interpretation.
Some people claim that the flour represented the body of Jesus Christ, that it chemically absorbed the poison, or that the miracle establishes a formula for spiritual cleansing.
But the passage does not say any of those things.
The text does not explain why flour was chosen.
It does not identify flour as an antidote.
And it does not instruct believers to imitate Elisha's action as a method of neutralizing poisonous food.
The miracle was not that flour possesses supernatural power. The miracle was that God, working through His prophet, removed the harm.
The ordinary material was part of the prophetic action, but the power belonged to God.
This distinction matters.
Because biblical faith is not magic.
God's power cannot be reduced to a recipe, a religious object, or a technique that human beings can control.
Elisha's action points us toward the Lord who has authority over the circumstances that threaten His people.
The same God who provided manna in the wilderness could make a dangerous meal safe.
The same God who sustained Elijah during famine could preserve this community of prophets.
The same God who brought Israel through the Red Sea was not helpless before a pot of poisoned stew.
And the beauty of the scene is that the miracle happened in an ordinary place.
No royal audience.
No magnificent building.
No crowd of thousands.
Just hungry men, a cooking pot, a prophet, and the mercy of God.
Sometimes we become so fascinated with spectacular demonstrations of power that we overlook the quieter ways God has shown His care throughout Scripture.
He is not only the God of the mountain.
He is also the God of the table.
He cares about human need.
He knows that people require bread, water, shelter, and daily provision.
And He is not indifferent to the ordinary burdens that weigh on human lives.
But we must also recognize something else.
Not every poisoned situation in life is miraculously reversed in the way this stew was.
Not every sickness disappears.
Not every relationship is restored.
Not every financial crisis ends overnight.
And no faithful Christian should be made to feel that an unanswered prayer proves a lack of faith.

This account describes a particular miracle in the ministry of Elisha. It reveals God's power and compassion, but it is not an unconditional promise that every dangerous circumstance will be immediately removed.
Our confidence rests in God's character, not in our ability to demand that He repeat every miracle on our preferred timetable.
And that brings us to the most important question.
What does this account have to do with Jesus Christ?
We must not force Christ into every detail of the story by inventing symbols the biblical author never explained.
The flour is not explicitly identified as Jesus.
The pot is not explicitly identified as the human heart.
The wild gourds are not explicitly identified as sin.
Yet this event belongs to the larger biblical story that ultimately finds its fulfillment in Christ.
Throughout Scripture, God reveals Himself as the One who provides, preserves, rescues, and restores.
Elisha was a prophet through whom God displayed His power.
But Jesus is greater than Elisha.
In the Gospels, Jesus did not merely provide food for a small prophetic community. He fed thousands with a few loaves and fish.
He healed the sick.
He welcomed sinners.
He confronted evil.
He forgave sins.
He raised the dead.
And then He did something no prophet could accomplish on humanity's behalf.
He gave His own life for sinners and rose again.
The deepest danger confronting humanity is not poisoned stew.
It is sin and death.
Romans 6:23 declares:
“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
And Romans 5:8 tells us:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Think about those words.
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we cleaned up every failure.
Not after we repaired every broken relationship.
Not after we convinced the world that our lives were respectable.
While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
That is grace.
And grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is God providing, through Jesus Christ, the salvation we could never earn for ourselves.
At the cross, Jesus bore our sins.
In His resurrection, He conquered death.
And through repentance and faith in Him, sinners receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and the promise of eternal life.
That is far greater than the restoration of one meal.
The poisoned pot reminds us of God's power to preserve physical life.
The Gospel announces His power to give eternal life through His Son.
And perhaps that is the truth someone reading this desperately needs to hear.
You may have made choices that brought pain into your life.
You may have trusted people you should not have trusted.
You may have ignored warnings.
You may have sinned knowingly, even after understanding what was right.
You may have spent years trying to cover your shame with achievement, religion, pleasure, or the approval of other people.
But your failure does not place you beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
Do not confuse that mercy with permission to continue in sin.
Jesus does not save us so we can comfortably remain enslaved to what destroys us.
He calls us to repent, believe, and follow Him.
Repentance is not merely feeling bad about consequences.
It is a turning of the heart toward God.
It is acknowledging sin without excuses and coming to Jesus Christ for forgiveness and a changed life.
And here is something that should bring a trembling sinner hope:
The Savior who calls you to repentance is the same Savior who welcomes those who come to Him.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
Read that again.
He will not cast out the one who comes to Him.
Perhaps you have spent so long hiding that you have forgotten what it feels like to be honest before God.
Perhaps everyone around you thinks you are strong.
They see your smile.
They see your church attendance.
They see your Bible verses.
They see your photographs.
But they do not see the nights when you wonder whether your faith has become little more than an appearance.
They do not see the temptation you keep returning to.
They do not see the bitterness you have been feeding.
They do not see the tears you wipe away before anyone enters the room.
And somewhere inside, you are exhausted.
Not necessarily because you have stopped believing in God.
But because you have been trying to carry things you were never meant to hide from Him.
Listen carefully.
You do not have to impress Jesus with a polished version of yourself.
Come to Him truthfully.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Turn away from what needs to be abandoned.
Seek reconciliation where it is appropriate and safe.
Ask for help when the struggle is too heavy to face alone.
And remember that forgiveness is not earned by pretending your wounds are small.
It is received through the mercy of the crucified and risen Christ.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is a reason that verse has comforted generations of believers.
It directs our confidence away from our own perfection and toward God's faithfulness.
And perhaps the most beautiful detail in Elisha's story is found at the very end.
After the flour was thrown into the pot, Elisha did not merely announce that the danger had passed.
He told them to serve the food.
“Pour out for the people, that they may eat.”
The meal that had become dangerous was made fit for its intended purpose.
The people could eat again.
Their immediate need was met.
And the story ends with these words:
“And there was no harm in the pot.”
The Hebrew expression וְלֹא הָיָה דָּבָר רָע בַּסִּיר (ve-lo hayah davar ra ba-sir) communicates that no harmful thing remained in the pot.
What a quiet ending to such a frightening moment.
No extended celebration is recorded.
No speech of triumph.
Just a simple statement that the danger was gone.
The men could receive the food they needed.
And the Lord had shown His power through His prophet.
Now, the Gospel does not promise that every earthly consequence of our mistakes will disappear.
Some wounds take years to heal.
Some choices leave consequences that require patient repentance, responsibility, and rebuilding.
Some losses remain painful even when forgiveness has been received.
But in Christ, sin does not have to be the final word over your eternal destiny.
Shame does not have to become your identity.
Your past does not have to be the master of your future.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
This is not a promise that Christians will never struggle again.
It is the announcement of a new life and a new standing in Christ.
A life that begins with grace.
A life that grows through repentance and obedience.
A life shaped by the Word of God and the work of the Holy Spirit.
And a life sustained by the One who has promised never to abandon His people.
That is why we keep returning to this truth at Gospel Warrior:
Not because every scandal disappears.
Not because every painful memory is erased.
Not because God calls evil good.
But because the Gospel reveals a Savior who redeems sinners, transforms lives, and gives a future that human failure could never purchase.
There is a world full of people who are spiritually hungry.
Some have been wounded by false teaching.
Some have been deceived by empty promises.
Some have grown cold in their love for Christ.
Some have never truly understood the Gospel.
And some are sitting in church every Sunday while quietly wondering whether anyone would still love them if their struggles became known.
They do not need another performance.
They need the truth of God's Word.
They need to hear about Jesus Christ.
They need sound biblical teaching, compassionate discipleship, and a community that points them toward repentance, grace, forgiveness, and spiritual maturity.
That is the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
And we want to make biblical resources accessible to people who may never be able to purchase a shelf full of Christian books.
These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, understand the Gospel more clearly, and continue following Christ beyond a single inspiring article.
If this message has helped you, please do not let it end with the final paragraph.
Return to the Scriptures.
Read 2 Kings 4:38–41 for yourself.
Pray over what God is teaching you.
Perhaps a family member will read it.
Perhaps a friend who has stopped attending church will pause long enough to consider the Gospel again.
Perhaps someone who has been silently wrestling with guilt will encounter the invitation of Jesus Christ to repent and believe.
You cannot control how another person responds.
But you can faithfully place biblical truth where it may be heard.
And I want to ask you something personal.
When you read about the men crying, “There is death in the pot,” did something in your own life come to mind?
A decision you regret?
A spiritual compromise you need to confront?
A season when you were desperate for God's help?
Or perhaps a moment when you discovered that the Lord was merciful to you even though you had made a terrible mistake?
You do not need to reveal private details or expose wounds you are not ready to discuss.
And if the Holy Spirit is convicting you of something you need to surrender, you can write:
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite believers who want to grow stronger in Scripture.
Even invite those who are skeptical or still searching, because the truth of the Gospel is worth examining.
It can also help us invest in the work required to reach more people and strengthen the resources available through Gospel Warrior.
Think of it as a voluntary monthly ministry-support gift—an expression of generosity and partnership in Gospel outreach.
Scripture teaches believers to give willingly, generously, and with sincere hearts.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which we extend this invitation.
And you do not have to give money to receive the grace of Jesus Christ.
Salvation is God's gift, not something purchased through a monthly payment.
But when believers freely support sound biblical ministry, their generosity can help make more teaching and discipleship resources available to others.
Paul expressed gratitude for believers who partnered with him in the work of the Gospel, describing their generosity in Philippians 4:15–18.
That kind of willing partnership is what we hope to cultivate.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not promises of financial miracles in exchange for donations.
But grateful hearts joining together to serve Christ and make His truth known.
These products are not the Gospel itself, and purchasing them is not a measure of anyone's spiritual maturity.
The mission is bigger than a page.
Bigger than any one writer, teacher, or ministry.
It is about Jesus Christ being proclaimed faithfully.
It is about sinners hearing the Gospel.
It is about believers being nourished by Scripture.
It is about wounded people discovering that Christ calls them not into deeper shame, but into repentance, forgiveness, and new life.
And before you leave, I want you to picture that ancient scene one final time.
A famine-stricken land.
A group of hungry men.
A pot that was supposed to feed them.
A sudden cry of terror.
A prophet who turned to the power of God.
And a meal that became safe to eat.
The miracle was never ultimately about the greatness of flour.
It was about the greatness of the Lord.
And the Gospel is not ultimately about the greatness of our ability to repair ourselves.
It is about the greatness of Jesus Christ, who died for our sins and rose again.
So do not put your trust in religious formulas.
Do not place your hope in outward appearances.
Do not try to earn forgiveness through your own efforts.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Follow Him.
And when you fall, do not run farther into darkness. Return to the Savior who calls His people to walk in the light.
Because the God who showed His mercy beside a cooking pot in Gilgal is the same God whose saving purpose is revealed fully and gloriously in Jesus Christ.
And when the world tells you that your worst chapter must define the rest of your story, remember what the cross and the empty tomb declare.
Your past may explain the scars you carry, but only Jesus Christ can give you the new life your soul desperately needs.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE KING’S SISTER. THE REBEL’S MOTHER. THE GENERAL WHO STOOD AGAINST HIS OWN BLOOD.
paragraphs: THE KING’S SISTER. THE REBEL’S MOTHER. THE GENERAL WHO STOOD AGAINST HIS OWN BLOOD.

She belonged to David’s family. Her son commanded the army of the man trying to destroy David’s throne. And buried inside this family scandal is a truth about loyalty, betrayal, mercy, and the greater King who can redeem what rebellion has broken.
There are betrayals that hurt because they come from enemies.
And then there are betrayals that nearly destroy you because they come from family.
Imagine hearing that someone carrying your own blood has joined the people who want to see you fall.
Imagine the whispers spreading through the palace.
Your son has turned against you.
Your trusted adviser has abandoned you.
And now, the man commanding the rebel army is your own nephew.
This was not a fictional royal tragedy.
This was the house of David.
And hidden in the genealogies of Scripture is a woman whose name many Christians have read without ever stopping to consider the family catastrophe surrounding her.
Her name was Abigail.
Not Abigail, the wise woman who married David after Nabal's death.
Another Abigail.
David's own sister.
And her son would become one of the most astonishing figures in a rebellion that almost destroyed Israel's king.
But before we judge this family, there is something we need to understand.
Sometimes the most dangerous battles are not fought between strangers.
Sometimes they begin at the family table.
And sometimes the greatest tragedy is not that someone has turned against a king.
It is that the human heart has turned against God.
The story begins with two verses most people would never think to connect.
First Chronicles 2:16–17 records David's family:
"Their sisters were Zeruiah, and Abigail. And the sons of Zeruiah; Abishai, and Joab, and Asahel, three. And Abigail bare Amasa: and the father of Amasa was Jether the Ishmeelite." (KJV)
There it is.
Almost hidden.
Abigail.
Amasa.
Jether.
Names that could easily disappear into a long genealogy.
But they are not meaningless names.
Abigail was a sister of David. Amasa was her son. And that made Amasa a nephew of the king.
Now look at 2 Samuel 17:25.

"And Absalom made Amasa captain of the host instead of Joab: which Amasa was a man's son, whose name was Ithra an Israelite, that went in to Abigail the daughter of Nahash, sister to Zeruiah Joab's mother." (KJV)
Read the first words again.
"And Absalom made Amasa captain of the host instead of Joab."
Absalom.
The rebellious son of David.
Amasa.
The nephew of David.
Joab.
David's military commander, who was also David's nephew through Zeruiah.
This was more than a struggle for political power.
It was a family tearing itself apart.
Amasa was not an outsider hired to fight Israel's king. He belonged to the extended royal family, and he had been placed in command of the forces supporting Absalom's revolt.
Consider how devastating that must have been.
David had already endured the humiliation of fleeing Jerusalem because his own son was seeking his throne.
Now another member of his family stood on the opposing side.
The Bible does not tell us what Abigail thought when her son joined Absalom's cause.
It does not tell us whether she approved, protested, wept, or remained silent.
We must not invent her private emotions and present them as Scripture.
But we can recognize the terrible reality surrounding her family.
Her brother was the threatened king.
Her son was the rebel commander.
And her sister Zeruiah was the mother of Joab, the commander serving David.
Two sisters.
Two sons.
Two opposing armies.
One wounded family.
And a nation caught in the middle.
If you have ever watched your family divide over pride, money, inheritance, jealousy, loyalty, or bitterness, perhaps this ancient account feels less distant than you expected.
You may never have lived in a palace.
But you know what it means when people who once belonged together begin standing against one another.
You know the silence after an argument.
The familiar voice that suddenly sounds like an enemy.
The painful realization that sharing blood does not guarantee sharing convictions.
And perhaps you know the even harder truth.
Sometimes we are not merely the people wounded by rebellion.
Sometimes we are the ones participating in it.
That is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is easy to condemn Amasa for standing with Absalom.
It is harder to ask where our own hearts have been standing against the rightful King.
Before going further, we need to notice something important about the biblical record.

First Chronicles calls Amasa's father Jether the Ishmaelite, while 2 Samuel 17:25 calls him Ithra the Israelite. The passages also describe Abigail's family relationships differently, with Samuel identifying her as a daughter of Nahash and sister of Zeruiah.

These differences have been discussed by biblical interpreters for centuries. Jether and Ithra may reflect forms of the same name, while the differences in ancestry and family description have received various explanations, including possible textual transmission issues. Scripture does not give us enough information to settle every detail with certainty.
We should not pretend that it does.
The clear historical connection remains: Abigail was David's sister, Amasa was her son, and Amasa became Absalom's commander.
Even the original Hebrew draws our attention to the military appointment.
In 2 Samuel 17:25, the Hebrew expression שַׂר־הַצָּבָא (sar-hatstsava) means "commander of the army" or "chief of the military force."
This was not a ceremonial position.
Amasa was being entrusted with leadership in a real military conflict.
He had become a commander in the rebellion against his uncle.
And the rebellion itself had not appeared overnight.
Absalom had spent time cultivating the hearts of Israel.
Second Samuel 15:6 says that Absalom "stole the hearts of the men of Israel."
Think about that expression.
He did not begin by marching directly into battle.
He began by winning confidence.
He presented himself as someone who would hear the people's complaints and give them justice.
He positioned himself as the answer to their disappointments.
And eventually, people who owed loyalty to David were drawn toward Absalom.
That is often how rebellion works.
It rarely announces itself at first as rebellion.
Sometimes it begins as wounded pride.
A resentment we refuse to surrender.
A desire to be recognized.
A conviction that we deserve what someone else possesses.
A quiet thought that whispers, Why should I submit when I could be in control?
Not every disagreement is rebellion. Not every challenge to human authority is sinful. Scripture itself records righteous resistance to wrongdoing.
But Absalom's revolt was not simply a disagreement over policy.
It was an attempt to seize his father's throne.
And when the moment came, David fled.
The man who had faced Goliath now walked away from Jerusalem under the weight of his own household's disaster.
Second Samuel 15:30 describes him ascending the Mount of Olives, weeping, with his head covered and his feet bare.
Picture that scene.
The king is not sitting on a golden throne.
He is climbing a hill in sorrow.
The warrior who once ran toward a giant now leaves the city to prevent a greater catastrophe.
And while David grieves, Absalom gathers his forces.
Amasa stands among the leaders of the opposing army.
The tragedy is almost unbearable.
But the story does not end with Amasa's appointment.
Absalom's rebellion collapses.
His army is defeated in the forest of Ephraim.
And Absalom dies at the hands of Joab and his men, despite David's command to deal gently with him.
When David hears the news, he does not celebrate the death of his enemy.
He cries out for his son.
"O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!" (2 Samuel 18:33, KJV)
There are few cries in the Old Testament more heartbreaking.
A father has survived a rebellion.
A king has retained his throne.
But a son is dead.
And victory tastes like grief.
Here is a truth we cannot afford to miss.
Winning a conflict does not always mean escaping its wounds.
Some families win arguments and lose relationships.
Some people prove themselves right and discover that pride has cost them years they cannot recover.
Some parents spend decades waiting for a phone call.
Some children carry regrets they never found the courage to confess.
And some of us have built entire walls around wounds that Jesus has been calling us to bring into His light.
But then something extraordinary happens in Amasa's story.
David makes a decision that would have surprised many people.
Instead of permanently treating Amasa as an irredeemable enemy, David offers him leadership.
In 2 Samuel 19:13, David sends this message concerning Amasa:
"Art thou not of my bone, and of my flesh? God do so to me, and more also, if thou be not captain of the host before me continually in the room of Joab." (KJV)
Stop there.
"Of my bone, and of my flesh."
The same family connection that made Amasa's involvement in the rebellion so painful now becomes part of David's appeal.
David offers his former opponent the command of his own army.

We should not romanticize the decision. It had political consequences, and Scripture does not tell us that Amasa had experienced genuine spiritual repentance. David was also dealing with Joab, whose actions had repeatedly created serious problems.
Nevertheless, the reversal is remarkable.
A man who commanded the rebel forces was offered a place in the king's service.
A man associated with the attempt to overthrow David was not automatically excluded from future responsibility.
The king extended an astonishing opportunity.
And this is where the story begins to illuminate something far greater than itself.
Not because David was a perfect picture of Jesus.
He was not.
David sinned. David failed. David's family suffered consequences connected to his own grievous actions.
But the story reminds us that a person's involvement in rebellion does not necessarily have to be the final word over that person's future.
And the Gospel declares something infinitely greater.
We have not merely been caught on the wrong side of human conflicts.
By our sin, we have rebelled against the holy God who created us.
Romans 3:23 says:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God."
All.
Not merely the obviously wicked.
Not merely the publicly disgraced.
Not merely the people whose scandals became known.
All of us.
The respectable believer hiding unforgiveness.
The churchgoer protecting a secret habit.
The father whose anger has wounded his children.
The mother exhausted by guilt.
The young person smiling online while privately struggling with temptation.
The Christian who knows the right words but has quietly drifted from obedience.
The person who once loved Jesus passionately but now barely prays.
The person who feels too ashamed to return.
The person who has been pretending that everything is fine.
All have sinned.
And if the story ended there, we would have no hope.
But it does not.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were still sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we proved ourselves worthy.
Not after we made our past disappear.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
The original Greek emphasizes the wonder of this grace.
Romans 5:8 uses the expression ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν (eti hamartōlōn ontōn hēmōn).
It means "while we were still sinners."
That matters.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that good people finally earned God's acceptance.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for sinners, rose again, and calls us to repentance and faith.
David could offer Amasa a military position.
Jesus offers repentant sinners reconciliation with God.
David could restore a man's opportunity to serve.
Jesus can forgive sin, give new life, and transform the heart.
David was a wounded human king trying to reunite a fractured kingdom.
Jesus is the sinless, risen King who gave His life to redeem those who had rebelled against God.
And His grace is not permission to remain in rebellion.
It is the power and invitation to turn away from sin and come home.

The Greek word often translated "repentance," μετάνοια (metanoia), speaks of a change of mind and orientation. In the New Testament, genuine repentance involves turning toward God and away from sin, not merely feeling sorry because we were exposed.
That distinction matters.
You can regret the consequences of sin without truly repenting.
You can cry because someone discovered your secret without surrendering the secret itself to God.
You can be embarrassed by your scandal and still refuse the grace that would transform you.
Jesus did not come merely to make rebellious people feel better about their rebellion.
He came to save sinners.
And saving grace changes the direction of a life.
But perhaps you are reading this and thinking, You do not know what I have done.
You are right.
I do not.
Perhaps you betrayed someone's trust.
Perhaps you abandoned a relationship you should have protected.
Perhaps you have spent years justifying something the Holy Spirit has been convicting you to confess.
Perhaps you have been wounded by people who used the language of faith while behaving without love.
Perhaps your deepest shame is something no one else knows.
Listen carefully.
Your sin is serious.
But it is not stronger than the blood of Jesus Christ.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That promise is not an excuse to conceal ongoing wrongdoing, avoid necessary accountability, or escape the consequences of our actions.
It is an invitation to come into the light.
To stop defending what God is calling us to surrender.
To stop confusing secrecy with safety.
To stop treating shame as though it were more powerful than the Savior.
And if this has reached a place in your heart that you have kept hidden, you do not have to describe your private struggle publicly.
Not to impress anyone.
Not to prove that you are spiritual.
But as a small, voluntary expression of the prayer you want to live.
Because sometimes the hardest prayer is not "Lord, bless me."
Sometimes it is "Lord, change me."
And now, we must return to Amasa.
Because his story contains one more devastating turn.
After David offers him command, Amasa is given a responsibility during another uprising, this time involving Sheba son of Bichri.
Amasa delays in gathering the men of Judah beyond the time David had appointed.
David then sends Abishai to pursue Sheba.
And in 2 Samuel 20, Amasa encounters Joab.
Remember who Joab was.
Amasa's cousin.
The son of Abigail's sister Zeruiah.
A man whose own hands had already been stained by violence.
When they meet near the great stone at Gibeon, Joab approaches Amasa with the appearance of affection.
Second Samuel 20:9 records his words:
"Art thou in health, my brother?"
He takes Amasa by the beard with his right hand, as though to kiss him.
But Amasa does not recognize the danger of the sword in Joab's hand.
And Joab strikes him.
Amasa falls.
He dies there.
Not on the battlefield fighting David.
Not while leading Absalom's rebellion.
But after David has offered him a place in the royal army.
At the hands of his own cousin.
The story that began with family loyalty divided by rebellion ends with family blood spilled through treachery.
It is a terrible ending.
And Scripture does not ask us to pretend otherwise.
Not every biblical story ends with earthly restoration.
Not every wounded family is reconciled before death.
Not every person who receives a second opportunity lives long enough to see its full promise.
The Bible is too truthful to offer us a sentimental ending where none exists.
But it does point us toward a greater hope.
Because Jesus Christ also encountered betrayal from someone close to Him.
Judas approached Him with a kiss.
An outward sign of affection became the instrument of betrayal.
Yet we must be careful with the comparison.
Amasa was a flawed human being caught in the conflicts of David's kingdom.
Jesus was the righteous and sinless Son of God.
His death was not merely another tragedy of political betrayal.
It was the fulfillment of God's saving purpose.
Jesus willingly gave His life for sinners.
And unlike Amasa, whose story ended in death, Jesus rose bodily from the grave.
Death did not have the final word.
Sin did not have the final word.
Betrayal did not have the final word.
The crucified King is alive.
And that changes everything.
There is a profound reason the Gospel must remain at the center of stories like this.
If we only read about Abigail and Amasa as an ancient family scandal, we might leave with little more than a warning about betrayal.
If we only read it as political history, we might remember the names and forget the condition of the human heart.

But when we read it within the larger biblical story, we see the terrible consequences of sin, the fragility of earthly power, the limits of human reconciliation, and our desperate need for the true King.
Amasa received an opportunity to serve David, but Scripture does not reveal the ultimate condition of his soul.
We cannot declare him saved, condemned, repentant, or unrepentant beyond what the text tells us.
Abigail's personal response to her son's choices also remains unknown.
We must let Scripture speak and respect its silences.
But what Scripture clearly reveals about Jesus is enough to call every one of us to a decision.
Will we continue defending the rebellion in our own hearts?
Or will we surrender to the King who died and rose again?
Maybe your family has been divided for years.
Maybe someone betrayed you, and forgiveness still feels impossible.
Maybe you are the one who caused the wound.
Maybe you cannot undo what happened.

You may not be able to restore every relationship. Reconciliation requires truth, repentance, and, where necessary, appropriate boundaries and accountability. Forgiveness does not require returning to abuse or pretending that harm never happened.
But you can bring your wounded heart to Christ.
You can repent where you have sinned.
You can pursue peace where it is possible.
You can refuse to make bitterness the ruler of your life.
And you can trust that the God who raised Jesus from the dead is not powerless before the ruins of a broken human story.
That is why we say:
Not because every scandal disappears.
Not because every earthly consequence is removed.
Not because every broken family receives a perfect ending in this life.
But because through Jesus Christ, forgiveness, redemption, and genuine transformation are possible.
And because those who belong to Christ have a hope that reaches beyond the grave.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
The Greek expression καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis) means "new creation."
Not merely a person with a better public image.
Not merely a sinner who learned to conceal the evidence.
A new creation.
That is what the grace of Jesus Christ makes possible.
Not cosmetic religion.
Not carefully managed appearances.
New life.
And perhaps this is the moment when you need to stop reading about someone else's rebellion and begin talking to God about your own.
You do not need a dramatic speech.
You do not need perfect words.
You can pray right where you are.

"Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I have carried pride, fear, bitterness, and things I have tried to hide. I cannot save myself. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Forgive me, turn my heart away from sin, and teach me to follow You in truth. Heal what is broken according to Your wisdom, and give me courage to obey You. My life belongs to You. Amen."
And if you are already following Christ but feel exhausted by the battle, remember that discipleship is not sustained by human willpower alone.
We need Scripture.
Prayer.
The fellowship of believers.
Sound teaching.
Correction.
Encouragement.
And the daily grace of God.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to publish moving stories, but to help people encounter the truth of Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in discernment, and continue following Jesus Christ when life becomes difficult.
These resources are offered to encourage Bible reading, spiritual maturity, healing, and faithful Christian living.
And if this article has helped you see a familiar passage in a new light, there are meaningful ways you can help this ministry reach others.

But because someone in your circle may be struggling with betrayal, family division, guilt, or spiritual exhaustion, and a message pointing them back to Jesus could be exactly what they need to encounter today.
And before you leave, I would love to hear something meaningful from you.
What is one thing God has been teaching you about forgiveness, repentance, or family wounds?
Your response may encourage another person who thought they were struggling alone.
For Christians who choose to give, financial support can be one expression of generosity and stewardship before God.
The Bible teaches believers to give willingly, not under pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
The Gospel is not for sale.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
And the invitation to know Jesus Christ remains freely proclaimed.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, encouragement for daily discipleship, or thoughtful gifts for people you love.
Read the Word.
Pray.
Share what encourages you.
Invite others to discover the Gospel.
Use the free resources.
Continue growing in Christ.
Because the mission is not to build an audience that admires Gospel Warrior.
It is to point people toward the Savior who alone is worthy of worship.
And now, one last thought.
Somewhere in the ancient record of Israel stands the name of Abigail, David's sister.
A woman whose son became the commander of a rebellion against her own brother.
We know almost nothing about her personal feelings.
But we know the conflict that surrounded her family.
We know Amasa was appointed by Absalom.
We know David later offered him command.
We know Joab killed him.
And we know that even the greatest human kings could not fully heal the brokenness caused by sin.
That is why we need someone greater than David.
A King who does not merely offer a position in an earthly army.
A King who can reconcile sinners to God.
A King who was betrayed but did not abandon His saving mission.
A King who was crucified but conquered death.
A King whose grace does not deny the truth about our sin, but meets repentant sinners with forgiveness purchased by His own blood.
His name is Jesus.
And whatever your family history, whatever your wounds, whatever shame you carry, His call still stands.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come to Him.
Follow Him.
Because the most important question is not whether your name appears in a story of scandal.
It is whether your life has been surrendered to the Savior.
Your past may explain the wounds you carry, but only Jesus Christ can give you the new life your soul desperately needs.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “EVERYTHING IS PERMISSIBLE”—THE DANGEROUS LIE THAT ALMOST DESTROYED THE CORINTHIAN CHURCH
paragraphs: “EVERYTHING IS PERMISSIBLE”—THE DANGEROUS LIE THAT ALMOST DESTROYED THE CORINTHIAN CHURCH
They believed grace gave them freedom to do whatever they wanted. Paul confronted them with a terrifying question: What if the very thing you call freedom has already made you its slave?
There is a kind of prison that does not have bars.
Its doors are wide open. Its prisoners can go wherever they want. They laugh, worship, post Bible verses, attend church, and tell everyone they are doing just fine.
But when nobody is watching, something else is in control.
An appetite they cannot silence.
A relationship they know they should leave.
A secret they keep promising God they will surrender.
A habit they defend in public but regret in private.
And perhaps the most dangerous part?
They have learned how to use the language of freedom to justify the very thing that is destroying them.
“God knows my heart.”
“I'm under grace, not the law.”
“Nobody is perfect.”
“It's my body. It's my life.”
“As long as I believe in Jesus, what difference does it make?”
If any of those words sound familiar, stay with me.
Because nearly two thousand years ago, the apostle Paul confronted a church that had become dangerously comfortable with this kind of thinking.
And what he wrote was not merely a correction for ancient Corinth.
It is a mirror for the modern Christian.
A mirror that may expose something we have spent years refusing to see.
The most frightening bondage is the one you have convinced yourself is freedom.

The city of Corinth was wealthy, influential, religiously diverse, and notorious for its moral temptations. It was a major commercial center where competing philosophies, social ambitions, and sexual practices shaped everyday life.
And right in the middle of that complicated city, God had established a church.
Real believers.
People who had heard the Gospel, believed in Jesus Christ, and been brought out of their former ways of life.
Yet something was going terribly wrong.
The culture surrounding them was beginning to influence the way some of them understood Christian freedom.
They had received the message of grace, but some appeared to be using freedom as an excuse for indulgence.
Paul confronted their reasoning with words that remain painfully relevant:
“All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any.” — 1 Corinthians 6:12, KJV
Read that last sentence again.
“I will not be brought under the power of any.”
That is where the comfortable Christian life suddenly becomes uncomfortable.
Because Paul was not simply asking whether someone could do something.
He was asking what that thing was doing to them.
Was it helping them follow Christ?
Was it building them up?
Or was it quietly becoming their master?
In the original Greek, the phrase translated “All things are lawful” is:
Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν — Panta moi exestin.
It means, in context, “All things are permissible for me” or “All things are lawful for me.”

Many biblical interpreters understand Paul to be repeating a slogan used by some Corinthians and then correcting its misuse. The text does not explicitly identify the original speaker, so we should be careful not to claim more than Scripture tells us.
But Paul's response is unmistakable.
ἀλλ᾽ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει — all’ ou panta sympherei.
“But not all things are beneficial.”
The Greek verb sympherei carries the idea of something being advantageous, profitable, or beneficial.
In other words, even when an action is not inherently forbidden, that does not automatically make it spiritually wise.
Then Paul goes deeper.
ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος — all’ ouk egō exousiasthēsomai hypo tinos.
“But I will not be mastered by anything.”
The verb exousiasthēsomai comes from a Greek word family associated with authority or power. Here, Paul speaks of being brought under another's control.
Notice the force of his argument.
The Corinthians spoke about what they had permission to do.
Paul spoke about what had power over them.
They were concerned with their rights.
Paul was concerned with their spiritual freedom.
And there is a world of difference between those two things.
Because you can have permission to enjoy something and still become enslaved to it.
You can possess something without being controlled by it.
You can participate in something without allowing it to become your identity.
But when you cannot say no anymore, you need to ask whether you are still the one making the decisions.
That question becomes even more serious when we remember what Paul was actually addressing.
He was not writing a vague motivational speech about productivity, self-discipline, or breaking bad habits.
He was confronting sexual immorality and a distorted understanding of the human body.
The next verse says:
“Meats for the belly, and the belly for meats: but God shall destroy both it and them. Now the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body.” — 1 Corinthians 6:13, KJV
The Corinthians apparently had a way of reasoning about bodily appetites that treated sexual desire as though it were simply another physical need.
Food is for the stomach.
The stomach is for food.
So why should satisfying sexual appetite be any different?
Paul refused that comparison.
Food and sexual intimacy are not morally interchangeable simply because both involve the body.
The human body is not an insignificant container that the soul can use however it pleases.
“The body is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body.”
The Greek word translated “fornication” is porneia (πορνεία), a broad biblical term for sexual immorality.
Paul's concern was not that the body was evil.
Quite the opposite.
The body mattered so much that he reminded believers of its relationship to Jesus Christ.
And then, in verse 14, he wrote something that should change the way every Christian thinks about the physical life:
“And God hath both raised up the Lord, and will also raise up us by his own power.” — 1 Corinthians 6:14, KJV
Do you see it?
The Christian hope is not escape from the body as though the body were worthless.
It is resurrection.
Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead, and believers have the promise of resurrection through Him.
Your body matters because God's redemptive purpose includes it.
Your choices matter because you belong to Christ.
Your sexuality matters because the Lord who redeemed you is also the Lord who calls you to holiness.
And that is where this ancient letter becomes painfully personal.
Because many of us have become very skilled at asking the wrong question.
We ask, “How far can I go before it becomes sin?”
Instead of, “How can I honor Jesus with my life?”
We ask, “Where does the Bible specifically forbid this?”
Instead of, “Is this drawing my heart closer to Christ?”
We ask, “Can I still be saved if I keep doing this?”
Instead of, “Why am I fighting so hard to keep something that is pulling me away from the One who saved me?”
Those are not the same questions.
And the difference matters.
Christian freedom was never intended to become an excuse for making peace with sin.
Paul would later write:
Freedom in Christ is real.
But it is not freedom from Christ's authority.
It is freedom from sin's dominion so that we may belong to Him and walk in love.
And perhaps that is the truth some of us have been avoiding.
We want Jesus to forgive us.
But we resist when He begins changing us.
We want the comfort of His promises.
But we struggle with the demands of discipleship.
We want the cross to remove our guilt.
But sometimes we hesitate to let it confront our idols.
And still, Jesus does not stop calling us.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because His grace is greater than the darkness we are afraid to surrender.
Think about the person reading this at two in the morning.
The one who has just fallen into the same sin they promised God they would never repeat.
Their Bible is nearby.
Their phone is still in their hand.
They know what happened.
They know the excuses.
They know the shame that follows.
And they are tired.
Tired of asking forgiveness.
Tired of starting over.
Tired of feeling spiritually divided.
Tired of appearing strong in church while privately feeling defeated.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe you have begun to wonder whether genuine transformation is even possible.
Listen carefully.
Your repeated struggle is not evidence that Jesus has run out of mercy. But His mercy is never permission to surrender yourself to the sin He came to save you from.
That distinction could change your life.
Because the Gospel does not tell you to pretend your sin is small.
It tells you that Christ is a sufficient Savior.
The Gospel does not say your actions are meaningless.
It announces that forgiveness and a new life are possible through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And the Gospel does not leave the believer alone to manufacture holiness through willpower.
God gives His Spirit to those who belong to Christ.
Paul had already reminded these same Corinthians of the lives some of them once lived.
In 1 Corinthians 6:9–10, he warned that those characterized by persistent unrighteousness would not inherit the kingdom of God.
He did not soften the seriousness of sin.
He did not redefine holiness to make the surrounding culture comfortable.
But then came one of the most beautiful sentences in the entire letter.
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” — 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV
And such were some of you.
Were.
Not because their past never happened.
Not because their wounds instantly disappeared.
Not because every temptation vanished overnight.
But because Jesus Christ had changed their standing before God and brought them into a new life.
They were washed.
They were sanctified.
They were justified.
Those words are not decorations for a religious speech.
They describe the astonishing work of God's grace.
The Greek word translated “washed” is apelousasthe (ἀπελούσασθε), referring here to cleansing.
The word translated “sanctified” is hēgiasthēte (ἡγιάσθητε), describing being made holy or set apart.
The word translated “justified” is edikaiōthēte (ἐδικαιώθητε), speaking of being declared righteous.
And Paul places these realities in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
This is not a story about people rescuing themselves through moral perfection.
It is a story about sinners receiving the grace of God through Jesus Christ.
That is why the phrase “And such were some of you” carries so much hope.
Your past can be real without remaining your identity.
Your sin can be serious without being beyond Christ's power to forgive.
Your repentance can be painful without being pointless.
Your transformation can be ongoing without being imaginary.
And your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
From scandal to grace. Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But we must understand what that means.
Jesus does not rewrite our story by pretending that evil was good.
He does not call darkness light.
He does not erase the need for repentance.
He rewrites our story through redemption.
Through the cross.
Through the empty tomb.
Through forgiveness that we could never earn.
Through the Spirit who continues transforming those who belong to Him.
And sometimes that transformation begins with a deeply uncomfortable admission.
“Lord, I have been calling something freedom when it has actually been controlling me.”
That confession may be the beginning of a different kind of life.
Perhaps you need to end a relationship that continually draws you into sexual sin.
Perhaps you need to confess a hidden addiction to a trustworthy, mature Christian who can help you pursue accountability.
Perhaps you need to stop treating pornography as harmless entertainment.
Perhaps you need to confront dishonesty, pride, bitterness, or a consuming desire for approval.
Perhaps you have allowed social media, money, pleasure, or other people's opinions to exercise authority over your heart.
Not every strong desire is sinful.
Not every pleasure is forbidden.
And not every difficult habit is evidence of spiritual rebellion.
But anything that begins ruling your life deserves serious examination before God.
The issue is not whether you can construct an argument defending it.
The issue is whether you can honestly bring it before Jesus.
Paul's words expose something modern Christianity desperately needs to remember.
A person can win an argument about personal freedom and still lose the battle for self-control.
That is why 1 Corinthians 6:12 is not a command to live in fear of everything enjoyable.
It is a call to refuse slavery to anything that competes with Christ's rightful lordship.
And Paul's argument reaches its climax a few verses later.

“What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.” — 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, KJV
Ye are not your own.
Those words confront the individualism of every generation.
The Christian does not belong to Christ because God has taken away human dignity.
The Christian belongs to Christ because Jesus has redeemed us at immeasurable cost.
And the price was not money.
It was His sacrificial death.
The sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
This is why the call to holiness cannot be separated from the Gospel.
We do not pursue holiness to purchase salvation.
We pursue holiness because the Savior who purchased our redemption is worthy of our lives.
Grace is not the reward for becoming perfect.
Grace is God's undeserved favor in Christ, which teaches and transforms those who receive it.
As Titus 2:11–12 teaches, the grace of God trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
Real grace does more than comfort the guilty conscience.
It begins changing the surrendered heart.
And no, that does not mean every Christian will experience instant victory over every temptation.
Some battles require years of prayer, wise counsel, accountability, practical boundaries, and patient growth.
Some wounds need careful attention.
Some habits require serious intervention.
But none of that makes repentance meaningless.
The believer who falls must not be encouraged to despair.
Nor should they be encouraged to make peace with the fall.
First John 1:9 reminds us that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
And Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
No condemnation in Christ does not mean no conviction.
It means that those who belong to Jesus need not flee from Him in hopelessness when His truth exposes their sin.
They can come into the light.
They can confess.
They can repent.
They can receive mercy.
They can continue learning to walk in obedience.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because something has finally been exposed, please hear this.
You do not have to impress Jesus with a performance of spiritual strength.
Come to Him truthfully.
Tell Him where you are struggling.
Tell Him what you have been hiding.
Tell Him where you have confused liberty with license.
Ask Him to forgive you.
Ask Him to change you.
Then take the next faithful step.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel spiritually impressive.
Today.
Maybe that means opening your Bible again.
Maybe it means deleting something that repeatedly leads you into temptation.
Maybe it means reaching out to a pastor, mentor, or mature believer instead of fighting alone.
Maybe it means making restitution for a wrong.
Maybe it means choosing honesty when hiding would be easier.
The next step may seem small.
But obedience does not become insignificant simply because nobody applauds it.
And the Lord sees the heart that turns toward Him.
There is something else worth remembering.
Paul did not write this letter to a church filled with people who had never failed.
He wrote to a deeply troubled congregation.
There were divisions.
Pride.
Confusion.
Moral compromise.
Misunderstandings about spiritual gifts.
Disorder in worship.
Even serious questions about the resurrection.
Yet Paul continued instructing them in the truth of Christ.
