But biblical knowledge is meant to lead us toward the living God, not merely make us feel clever.
Jesus said in John 5:39–40 that people could search the Scriptures and yet refuse to come to Him for life.
What a terrifying possibility.
To study the words.
To memorize the verses.
To know the names.
And still miss the Savior to whom Scripture bears witness.
Maybe that is the question we need to carry beyond Shem's age.
Not merely, "How old was he?"
But, "What am I doing with the truth God has placed before me?"
Because there is a difference between being interested in Jesus and surrendering to Him.
There is a difference between feeling convicted and repenting.
There is a difference between admiring grace and receiving it by faith.
And there is a difference between appearing religious and being reconciled to God through Christ.
The Gospel does not call you to pretend that your past never happened.
It calls you to bring your sin into the light and trust the Savior who died for sinners.
First John 1:9 tells us:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
That is not permission to keep hiding.
It is an invitation to stop.
To confess.
To turn.
To trust Christ.
And to walk in the new life He gives.
Perhaps the most beautiful thing about Shem's place in Scripture is that his story did not end with the Flood.
He lived beyond the judgment.
He became a father.
His descendants continued.
And centuries later, the genealogical record would point toward the arrival of Jesus Christ.
The age of Shem is a small detail in the Bible.
But it sits inside a story of breathtaking scope.
The God who judged wickedness is also the God who preserved Noah.
The God who called Abraham is the God who kept His covenant promises.
The God who sent His Son is the God who now commands all people everywhere to repent, as Acts 17:30 declares.
And the God who raised Jesus from the dead is the God who offers forgiveness and eternal life through Him.
Not because every scandal disappears.
Not because the consequences of sin suddenly become imaginary.
Not because following Jesus guarantees a comfortable life.
But because in Christ, sin and shame do not have to be the final word over a repentant sinner.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 5:17:
The Greek phrase καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis) means "new creation."
Not merely a polished version of the old self.
Not a better public image.
Not a religious performance designed to impress people.
New creation.
A life brought into a new relationship with God through Jesus Christ.
A life in which forgiveness is real, repentance matters, and transformation begins through the grace of God.
And if you have ever felt that your past has disqualified you from being loved by God, I want you to consider the cross.
Christ did not die for people who could prove they never needed mercy.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were still sinners.
Not after we fixed ourselves.
Not after we earned forgiveness.
Not after we became respectable enough to deserve a second chance.
Christ died for us while we were sinners.
That is grace.
And grace, rightly understood, never makes sin harmless.
It reveals how serious sin is—and how astonishing the mercy of God truly is.
Maybe you came here because you were curious about an ancient man's age.
Maybe you expected a quick calculation.
Maybe you wanted to settle a Bible discussion.
But perhaps something deeper has been stirring in your heart as you've read.
Perhaps you have been surviving for so long that you have forgotten what it feels like to hope.
Perhaps you have been attending church while quietly drifting from Christ.
Perhaps you have convinced everyone around you that you are spiritually strong, while privately struggling with guilt, resentment, temptation, or exhaustion.
I cannot know your circumstances.
But I do know what Scripture calls us to do.
Come to Christ.
Not with a rehearsed performance.
Not with excuses.
Not with the claim that your good deeds outweigh your sins.
Come with repentance and faith.
Tell Him the truth.
Ask for mercy.
Trust the One who died and rose again.
And if you already belong to Him, return to His Word with humility.
Let Scripture correct your assumptions.
Let the Gospel confront your sin.
Let grace teach you to walk in obedience.
Let the truth of Christ shape the way you live when nobody is watching.
And don't try to carry every struggle alone.
Find faithful believers who will pray with you, encourage you, and point you back to the Scriptures.
You might write "Christ is still healing me" if you are learning to trust His grace through a difficult season.
Or "Pray for me" if you need encouragement to turn away from something that has been pulling your heart from God.
You don't have to reveal private details. A simple, sincere response is enough.
And if you have a testimony of how Christ has changed your life, consider sharing it. Someone reading the comments may be facing the very struggle from which God has helped you turn.
There is also someone in your circle who might never search for an article about Shem.
Someone who would never think to open Genesis 11.
Someone who is silently questioning the Bible.
Someone who feels too ashamed to walk back into church.
Someone who has begun to believe that Jesus would never welcome them.
Not merely to increase a number.
But to make the message available to someone who might need to hear it.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, curious seekers, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along.
We want people to encounter the Word of God, examine its claims, and understand the Gospel—not merely consume another religious post and forget it.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture more deeply, I want to invite you to consider something more personal.
There is a real difference between occasionally encountering biblical content and intentionally supporting the ongoing work of making it available.
Writing, researching, preparing, publishing, and expanding discipleship resources require time and resources.
We want that library to continue growing.
We want more people to have access to biblical resources.
We want struggling believers to find encouragement, seekers to encounter Scripture, and families to have material they can read and discuss together.
And we want everything we produce to point beyond Gospel Warrior to Jesus Christ.
It can be part of your voluntary Christian generosity—an offering of support for Gospel-centered teaching and discipleship.
But I also want to be biblically clear.
Christians should honor their responsibilities to their local churches and households, and they should give according to conscience, ability, and biblical conviction.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
But a sincere opportunity to help sustain and expand resources that proclaim His Word.
These items can serve as reminders of Scripture, conversation starters, or thoughtful gifts, but they are never substitutes for knowing Christ and obeying His Word.
The free resources remain an important part of our mission.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
We are not asking you to put your faith in a ministry.
We are asking you to consider helping a ministry point people to the Savior.
And that distinction matters.
Because ministries come and go.
Platforms change.
Algorithms rise and fall.
But the Word of the Lord endures forever.
And Jesus Christ remains the same yesterday, today, and forever.
So before you leave, remember the question that brought us here.
How old was Shem when the Flood happened?
Approximately 98.
That is the answer supported by the ordinary chronology of Genesis 7:6 and Genesis 11:10.
But the greater story is not about a number.
It is about the faithfulness of God across generations.
Shem lived through the Flood.
His family line continued.
God's promise to Abraham followed.
And in the fullness of time, Jesus Christ came.
The One greater than Noah.
The One who does not merely preserve us through earthly danger, but saves sinners from the judgment their sins deserve.
The One who calls us out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
The One whose resurrection assures believers that death itself will not have the final word.
So don't stop at the arithmetic.
Open your Bible.
Read the passages.
Test what you have heard.
And most importantly, consider the Christ to whom the Scriptures bear witness.
Because you can spend your whole life counting the years of those who lived before you and never face the question that matters most for your own eternity.
Have you placed your faith in Jesus Christ?
If not, today is an opportunity to hear His Gospel and respond with repentance and faith.
And if you have, may this small detail in Genesis remind you to treasure every word of Scripture and follow the Savior it reveals.
The world before the Flood was gone.
Shem's life continued.
And God's redemptive purpose moved forward until the promised Christ came.
That is the wonder of the biblical story.
Not that human beings were strong enough to preserve themselves.
But that God remained faithful.
And when we finally understand that, we begin to see why grace is not simply a comforting religious word.
Grace is the mercy sinners could never earn.
Grace is the forgiveness Christ purchased through His blood.
Grace is the new life God gives to those who belong to His Son.
And grace is why a repentant sinner's past does not have to define their eternal future.
The waters may have buried the world Shem once knew, but they could not bury the promise of the Savior who was yet to come.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THERE IS NO FEAR IN LOVE” — THEN WHY ARE YOU STILL TERRIFIED WHEN YOU BELIEVE IN JESUS?
paragraphs: “THERE IS NO FEAR IN LOVE” — THEN WHY ARE YOU STILL TERRIFIED WHEN YOU BELIEVE IN JESUS?

You pray. You believe. You love God. But some nights, your heart still races, your mind imagines the worst, and fear whispers louder than your faith. Does that mean your love for God is incomplete? Or have we misunderstood one of the most beautiful promises in Scripture?
There is a kind of fear that visits people who genuinely love Jesus.
It doesn't always arrive with a scream.
Sometimes it arrives at 2:17 in the morning.

You wake up, stare at the ceiling, and suddenly remember the unpaid bills. The medical results you haven't received. The child who has stopped listening. The marriage that feels increasingly fragile. The mistake you made years ago that still makes you wonder whether God looks at you differently.
You reach for your phone.
You scroll because silence feels unbearable.
You whisper a prayer because you don't know what else to do.
And somewhere between the trembling and the tears, a Bible verse comes back to you.
“There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear.” — 1 John 4:18 (KJV)
And instead of comforting you, it almost breaks you.
Because you are afraid.
Very afraid.
And now you're wondering whether your fear is evidence that something is wrong with your faith.
Maybe you've heard someone say, “If you really trusted God, you wouldn't be afraid.”
Maybe someone told you anxiety is always a sign of weak faith.
Maybe you've smiled in church, lifted your hands during worship, and said, “God is good,” while secretly fighting thoughts you were too ashamed to admit.
You love Jesus.
But you're still scared.
And the question you haven't dared to ask out loud is this:
“Lord, if Your love is supposed to cast out fear, why is fear still living inside me?”
Please don't walk away from this question.
Because the answer is not that Jesus has rejected you.
The answer is hidden in what the apostle John was actually saying.
And when you understand it, you may discover that the verse you've been using to condemn yourself was written to help you become confident in the love of God.
John writes:
Now listen carefully to the original Greek.
“φόβος οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν τῇ ἀγάπῃ, ἀλλ᾽ ἡ τελεία ἀγάπη ἔξω βάλλει τὸν φόβον.”
Phobos ouk estin en tē agapē, all’ hē teleia agapē exō ballei ton phobon.
A close translation is:
“There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts fear outside.”
The word φόβος (phobos) means fear, dread, or alarm. But its meaning here must be understood from the surrounding verses.
The word τελεία (teleia) comes from teleios, conveying what is complete, mature, or brought to its intended goal.
And βάλλει (ballei) means to throw or cast.
John is describing love that drives fear out.
But what kind of fear?
And whose love is doing the casting?
This is where many well-meaning Christians accidentally turn a promise of assurance into a weapon of shame.
Go back one verse.
“Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment.” — 1 John 4:17 (KJV)
There it is.
The day of judgment.
John is not teaching that a Christian will never be startled, grieve, tremble before surgery, feel afraid during persecution, or struggle with anxious thoughts.
He is speaking particularly about the fear of punishment before God.
The Greek word translated “torment” in the King James Version is κόλασις (kolasis), which means punishment or penalty.
The context makes the meaning unmistakable.
John is addressing the terrifying possibility of standing before a holy God and facing condemnation.
And he is telling believers that God's love, brought to its intended maturity in them, produces confidence rather than the dread of punishment.
Why?
Because salvation does not rest on the emotional steadiness of the person being saved.
It rests on Jesus Christ.
John has already explained the foundation:
“Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.” — 1 John 4:10 (KJV)
Read that again.
Not that we loved God.
But that He loved us.
The Gospel does not begin with your ability to love God perfectly.
It begins with God's love demonstrated in sending His Son.
That changes everything.

Because if your assurance depended on never feeling afraid, your salvation would rise and fall with your nervous system, your circumstances, your sleep, your health, and your ability to control every frightening thought.
But the cross of Jesus Christ is not that fragile.
You may wake up shaking.
Christ has not stopped being Savior.
You may cry while praying.
His resurrection has not been undone.
You may struggle to believe tomorrow will be better.
The blood Jesus shed for sinners has not lost its power.
And you may be fighting fear while still genuinely trusting the One who promises never to abandon His people.
Think about the disciples.
They had watched Jesus heal the sick.
They had witnessed His authority.
They had heard His teaching.
And then one night, a storm threatened their boat.
The wind roared. The waves rose. Water entered the vessel.
Experienced fishermen became terrified men.
And Jesus was asleep.
Can you imagine their confusion?
The One who had performed miracles was resting while they believed they were about to die.
They woke Him and cried:
“Lord, save us: we perish.” — Matthew 8:25 (KJV)
They were afraid.
And they called on Jesus.
Notice something beautiful.
Their fear did not prevent them from turning toward Him.
Jesus answered:
“Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith?” — Matthew 8:26 (KJV)
He confronted their fear and exposed their little faith.
Scripture does not pretend their response was spiritually mature.
But neither does the story end with Jesus abandoning them because they were frightened.
He arose and rebuked the winds and the sea.
And there was a great calm.
The same disciples who feared the storm were left marveling at the authority of Christ.
Their fear revealed how much they still needed to learn about the One who was with them.
And perhaps that is where you are.
Not faithless.
Not spiritually finished.
But still learning who Jesus is.
Still discovering that the presence of danger does not mean the absence of God.
Still learning that the Lord who commands the sea is worthy of trust even before the wind becomes quiet.
And then there is Peter.
Bold Peter.
The man who declared loyalty so confidently.
The man who said he was ready to die with Jesus.
But when pressure came, Peter denied knowing Him.
Three times.
And then the rooster crowed.
Luke tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The sound of the rooster.
The realization.
The eyes of the Savior.
And the crushing knowledge that Peter had done exactly what he promised he would never do.
“And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.” — Luke 22:62 (KJV)
Fear had contributed to his collapse.
His courage failed.
His promise failed.
His confidence in himself failed.
But the story of Peter did not end beside that fire.
After His resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, the risen Christ asked Peter three times whether he loved Him.
And Jesus entrusted him with the care of His sheep.
What grace.
The man who denied Jesus was not beyond restoration.
His failure was real.
His repentance mattered.
And Christ's mercy was greater than the scandal of his denial.
This does not mean sin is harmless.
It means the Savior is merciful.
It means that the person who has failed terribly can still find forgiveness and restoration in Jesus Christ.
And somebody reading this needs to hear that.
Because you are not only afraid of tomorrow.
You are afraid of yesterday.
You are afraid that the things you did when nobody was watching have permanently disqualified you from being loved by God.
You remember the lie.
The betrayal.
The secret compromise.
The addiction you promised to leave.
The angry words.
The years of spiritual indifference.
The time you knew what was right and deliberately chose what was wrong.
You have asked God to forgive you, but sometimes you still feel as though heaven is waiting to punish you.
That is why the distinction in 1 John matters so much.
There is a difference between the reverent fear of the Lord and the terror of condemnation.
The Bible does not command us to abandon reverence.
Proverbs 9:10 declares:
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.”
The Hebrew expression is יִרְאַת יְהוָה (yir’at YHWH), the fear of the LORD.
In this wisdom context, it describes reverent recognition of God's holiness, authority, and majesty—a reverence that shapes obedience.
This is not the same as the punishment-centered fear John says mature love casts out.
A child who loves a good father can deeply respect his authority without living in constant terror that every mistake will result in rejection.
In an infinitely greater way, those who belong to Christ are called to approach God with reverence and confidence grounded in His grace.
We must never confuse freedom from condemnation with freedom to sin.
Grace does not make holiness irrelevant.
Grace teaches us to turn away from sin and live for the God who redeemed us.
And repentance is not the price we pay to purchase God's love.
It is part of the response of a heart being turned toward Him.
Now consider another scene.
Not a boat in a storm.
Not a courtyard where Peter denied Jesus.
A garden.
Gethsemane.
The night before the crucifixion.
Jesus knew what was approaching.
Betrayal.
Abandonment.
Mockery.
The cross.
And the Gospel writers do not describe Him as emotionally untouched by the horror ahead.
Mark 14:33 says He began to be deeply distressed and troubled.
Jesus Himself declared:
“My soul is exceeding sorrowful unto death.” — Mark 14:34 (KJV)
Luke records His anguish as He prayed.
Yet Jesus remained perfectly obedient to the Father.
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42 (KJV)
We must be careful here.
Jesus' holy anguish cannot simply be equated with every form of human anxiety. His suffering was unique, and His sinless obedience was perfect.
But Gethsemane destroys the careless assumption that profound emotional distress automatically means spiritual failure.
The sinless Son of God experienced genuine human sorrow and anguish without sinning.
And Hebrews 4:15 tells us that our High Priest is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
So when you approach Jesus trembling, you are not approaching a Savior who is ignorant of suffering.
You are approaching the One who entered human suffering and remained faithful.
The One who understands.
The One who intercedes.
The One who carried our sins to the cross.
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than a comforting sentence.
It becomes your only lasting hope.
Because the deepest problem in our lives is not merely that we feel afraid.
It is that we are sinners who need reconciliation with a holy God.
No amount of positive thinking can remove guilt before God.
No amount of self-improvement can undo sin.
No religious performance can make us our own saviors.
But Jesus Christ lived in perfect obedience, died for sins, and rose again.
The apostle Paul writes:
No condemnation.
Not because sin never mattered.
But because Christ has accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
The Greek word κατάκριμα (katakrima) means condemnation or an adverse judicial sentence.
For those who are in Christ, the verdict of condemnation has been removed.
This is not a blanket declaration that everyone is automatically saved regardless of their relationship to Jesus.
It is a glorious promise for those who belong to Him.
And the invitation of the Gospel is to repent and believe in Christ.
Not to pretend you are innocent.
Not to hide your sins behind religious language.
Not to earn acceptance through impressive spirituality.
But to come to the crucified and risen Savior in faith.
To stop defending what God calls sin.
To confess.
To turn.
To trust Him.
And to receive the grace you could never deserve.
Maybe that is the real battle taking place in your heart.
You have spent so long trying to prove you are a good Christian that you have forgotten the Christian life begins with admitting you need a Savior.
You are exhausted from pretending.
Exhausted from being the strong one.
Exhausted from telling everyone, “I'm blessed,” when you barely made it through the night.
You know the language of faith.
But you're afraid to admit the depth of your struggle.
Listen.
There is a difference between surrendering to fear as your master and admitting that fear is a struggle you need God's help to face.
The Psalms give us language for this.
David wrote:
“What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.” — Psalm 56:3 (KJV)
Not “I have never been afraid.”
Not “I will only trust You once all fear disappears.”
But “When I am afraid, I will trust.”
The Hebrew is striking:
יוֹם אִירָא אֲנִי אֵלֶיךָ אֶבְטָח
Yom ira, ani elekha evtach.
A close rendering is:
“When I am afraid, I will trust in You.”
Fear is acknowledged.
Trust is chosen.
And the trust is directed toward God.
That is not an excuse to nurture unbelief.
It is an invitation to bring our weakness into the presence of the Lord rather than hiding it.
Faith does not require you to lie about your circumstances.
Faith calls you to tell the truth about God in the middle of them.
You may be afraid of losing your job and still trust the Lord to provide.
You may be afraid of a diagnosis and still believe that Christ holds your life.
You may be afraid of grief, rejection, or the unknown and still choose obedience.
You may need pastoral counsel, Christian community, and professional care for persistent anxiety while continuing to walk faithfully with Jesus.
Seeking appropriate help is not automatically a rejection of God's power.
And experiencing symptoms of anxiety is not, by itself, proof that you are living in sin.
Our bodies are vulnerable.
Our minds can become overwhelmed.
Trauma, illness, exhaustion, and prolonged stress can affect how fear is experienced.
The Bible does not authorize us to condemn every frightened believer as spiritually defective.
At the same time, Scripture does call us to grow in trust, bring our concerns to God, and resist allowing fear to govern our obedience.
Paul writes in Philippians 4:6–7 about bringing our requests to God through prayer and thanksgiving, and about the peace of God guarding our hearts and minds in Christ Jesus.
That peace is not a promise that every difficult circumstance will immediately disappear.
It is the peace of belonging to God and depending on Him in the midst of circumstances we cannot control.
Sometimes God calms the storm.
Sometimes He sustains His people through it.
Sometimes the answer comes quickly.
Sometimes endurance is learned over a long and painful season.
But His love is not measured by how quickly your circumstances become comfortable.
It was demonstrated decisively at Calvary.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8 (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Before we could clean ourselves up.
Before we could offer an impressive record of obedience.
Before we could present ourselves as people who deserved His favor.
Christ died for us.
This is why the perfect love of 1 John 4 cannot be reduced to a command to manufacture perfect emotions.
John says:
“We love him, because he first loved us.” — 1 John 4:19 (KJV)
God's initiating love is the foundation.
Our love is the response.
And as His love reaches its intended maturity in us, fear of final punishment gives way to confidence in Christ.
That is a lifelong journey of growth, not a test requiring you to become emotionally invulnerable overnight.
And now I want to speak to the person who almost stopped reading because this feels painfully personal.
The person who has been asking God for a sign.
The mother who lies awake worrying about her children.
The father who feels ashamed because he cannot provide everything his family needs.
The young believer who keeps falling into temptation and wonders whether repentance is still possible.
The Christian who sits in church while quietly battling panic.
The person who is afraid of dying.
The one who wonders whether God is angry every time something goes wrong.
You do not need another performance.
You need the truth.
And the truth is that God's holiness is real, sin is serious, judgment is certain, and Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
Do not use God's love as permission to remain in rebellion.
But do not use your remaining fears as evidence that Christ is unwilling to receive those who come to Him.
Hear His words:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” — John 6:37 (KJV)
What a promise.
Not because we deserve it.
But because He is gracious.
You can come with your guilt.
Come with your trembling.
Come with your confession.
Come with the faith that feels small.
Come ready to surrender the sin you have been defending.
Come believing that the Savior who died and rose again is worthy of your trust.
And if you have already come to Christ, stop treating every frightened moment as a fresh verdict against your salvation.
Look to Him.
Not to the strength of your emotional response.
Not to the absence of every anxious thought.
Not to how impressive your faith appears to other people.
Look to Jesus.
His cross.
His resurrection.
His promises.
His ongoing intercession for His people.
And when fear returns, remember Psalm 56:3.
“When I am afraid, I will trust in thee.”
Maybe you'll need to pray that verse more than once.
Maybe you'll need to repeat it through tears.
Maybe you'll need a brother or sister in Christ to sit beside you while you struggle to believe it.
That is not a reason to disappear from the fellowship of believers.
It is a reason to seek encouragement, prayer, biblical counsel, and the help you need.
And perhaps someone reading your words today is carrying the same secret burden.
You do not have to disclose private details or explain everything that has happened.
A few honest words may become the beginning of a meaningful conversation and an opportunity for others to pray with you.
And if this message has exposed an area where fear has led you away from obedience, don't merely admire the words.
Respond to God.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Ask Him to teach you to trust Him more deeply.
Because the goal of this article is not to make you feel inspired for five minutes.
It is to point you toward a lifetime of following Jesus Christ.
And that is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a following around a personality.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to turn spiritual struggles into entertainment.
But to keep directing people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, biblical discipleship, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
There are people scrolling Facebook tonight who will never enter a church building unless someone first reaches them with the truth of Christ.
There are wounded believers who need encouragement.
There are seekers who have questions they are afraid to ask.
There are Christians who have grown spiritually cold and need to hear the call to return to Jesus.
And sometimes a simple act of sharing can place a message of biblical hope in front of someone who desperately needs it.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
Not because an algorithm determines your faithfulness.
But because the Gospel is worth making known.
Send this privately to someone who has been quietly struggling.
Invite your family, your friends, the believer who has drifted, and the person who has never understood the Gospel to follow along.
One message will never replace the patient work of discipleship, but it can become a doorway into a deeper conversation about Jesus.
And for those who want to help sustain and expand this ministry, I want to invite you into something more personal.
But let us be biblically clear.
Scripture teaches generosity and faithful stewardship. Believers should not neglect the responsibilities of supporting their local church, caring for their families, and helping those in need.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving is to be purposeful, willing, and not under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Not because you fear God will love you less if you don't.
But because you want to help more people encounter biblical truth.
Those products can be useful reminders, gifts, and resources, but they are not the heart of this mission.
Jesus is.
The Word of God is.
The Gospel is.
And the opportunity to help people grow as disciples of Christ is far more important than anything we could sell.
God's love is not merchandise.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is not a membership benefit.
Now return with me, just for a moment, to that room at 2:17 in the morning.
The ceiling has not changed.
The bills may still be waiting.
The diagnosis may still be unknown.
The child may still be far from home.
The marriage may still need difficult conversations and genuine healing.
The storm outside may not have stopped.
But something inside your understanding of God can change.
You no longer have to read “There is no fear in love” as though John were saying, “If you ever feel afraid, you do not belong to Jesus.”
You can read it in the light of the cross.
The love of God revealed in Christ is powerful enough to deliver those who belong to Him from the dread of final condemnation.
And as you grow in that love, you can learn to approach God with increasing confidence.
Not because you are perfect.
Because Jesus is the perfect Savior.
Not because your heart never trembles.
Because your hope rests in the One who conquered sin and death.
Not because you know what tomorrow holds.
Because you know the One to whom you have entrusted your life.
So tonight, if you are afraid, pray.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you are weary, seek help and encouragement.
If you are uncertain of your standing before God, turn to Christ and trust His Gospel.
And if you belong to Jesus, remember that your assurance is not found in proving you can never feel fear again.
It is found in the crucified and risen Lord.
You do not have to pretend the storm is harmless.
You do not have to pretend the tears are not real.
You do not have to pretend you are stronger than you are.
You are invited to trust the Savior who is stronger than you could ever be.
The miracle is not that your hands never tremble again. It is that even with trembling hands, you can reach for the Savior whose hands were pierced for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A MAN MARRIED HIS OWN SISTER—AND GOD STILL CHOSE THEIR SON TO LEAD ISRAEL?
paragraphs: A MAN MARRIED HIS OWN SISTER—AND GOD STILL CHOSE THEIR SON TO LEAD ISRAEL?

The shocking family secret behind Moses’ birth, the uncomfortable truth hidden in Exodus 6:20, and the breathtaking grace of a God who can bring deliverance out of a family history nobody would dare put on display.
What if I told you that one of the greatest deliverers in biblical history was born into a family relationship that God would later explicitly forbid?
Not a rumor.
Not an ancient conspiracy theory.
Not something invented to embarrass Christianity.
It is written in your Bible.
And the most unsettling part?
God did not erase the family record. He preserved it in Scripture.

Before Moses stood before Pharaoh, before the Red Sea opened, before the mountain shook with the presence of God, there was a marriage in his family that would make many modern readers deeply uncomfortable.
His father, Amram, married Jochebed.
And Jochebed was his father's sister.
His aunt.
Yes. You read that correctly.

But before you close your Bible in confusion, before someone uses this passage to mock Christianity, and before you conclude that God somehow approved of everything that happened in Moses' family, there is something extraordinarily important you need to understand.
Because this story is not about God celebrating a forbidden relationship.
It is about the difference between what Scripture records, what God commands, and what His grace can accomplish through deeply imperfect human histories.
And if you have ever looked at your own family, remembered something painful, and wondered whether your past disqualifies you from being used by God...
Stay with me.
There is something here for you.
Something that begins with a disturbing genealogy but leads us all the way to the cross of Jesus Christ.
Exodus 6:20 says:
“And Amram took him Jochebed his father's sister to wife; and she bare him Aaron and Moses: and the years of the life of Amram were an hundred and thirty and seven years.”
— Exodus 6:20, KJV
Read those words again.
“His father's sister.”
The Hebrew is even more revealing.
דֹּדָתוֹ — dodato
This means “his aunt,” specifically referring here to his father's sister.
The relevant Hebrew wording is:
וַיִּקַּח עַמְרָם אֶת־יוֹכֶבֶד דֹּדָתוֹ לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה
Vayyiqqach Amram et-Yokheved dodato lo le'ishah.
“And Amram took Jochebed, his aunt, as his wife.”
The Hebrew does not say that Amram married his biological sister.
It says he married his paternal aunt.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because sensationalism may attract attention, but biblical truth must govern what we teach.
Numbers 26:59 gives us another piece of the family history:
“And the name of Amram's wife was Jochebed, the daughter of Levi, whom her mother bare to Levi in Egypt: and she bare unto Amram Aaron and Moses, and Miriam their sister.”
— Numbers 26:59, KJV
Jochebed belonged to Levi's family. Amram was descended from Levi through Kohath.
Under the straightforward reading of these genealogies, Jochebed was Amram's paternal aunt.
And from this marriage came three names that would become inseparable from Israel's deliverance.
Miriam.
Aaron.
Moses.
A prophetess associated with Israel's song of victory.
A priest who would become Israel's first high priest.
And a man whom God would call to confront the most powerful ruler in Egypt.
But now comes the question that makes this account so difficult.
Didn't God later forbid this exact kind of marriage?
Yes.
And the Bible does not hide that either.
Leviticus 18:12 declares:
“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's sister: she is thy father's near kinswoman.”
— Leviticus 18:12, KJV
Leviticus 20:19 also prohibits sexual relations involving a father's sister or mother's sister.
These are not vague restrictions.
They address the precise degree of family relationship described in Exodus 6:20.
So how do we understand this?
How could Moses come from a marriage involving his father's sister when the Law later delivered through Moses would forbid such a union?
Here is where careful reading becomes essential.
Amram and Jochebed's marriage took place before the Mosaic Law was given at Sinai.
The explicit prohibitions in Leviticus were delivered to Israel later, after the exodus from Egypt.
This chronological difference helps explain why the narrative records the marriage without pausing to apply the later legal penalty to Amram and Jochebed.
But we must be careful.
The fact that a marriage occurred before the giving of a particular command does not automatically prove that God morally approved of it.
Nor does the Bible tell us that God praised their marriage.
Scripture simply records the relationship.
It does not provide a detailed moral evaluation of their union.
And that distinction is crucial.
The Bible's honesty about what happened is not the same as God's endorsement of everything that happened.
Think about that.
Scripture records Abraham's deception.
Jacob's manipulation.
David's adultery.
Solomon's disobedience.
Peter's denial.
And Judas's betrayal.
Yet the presence of those events in Scripture never means God approved of them.
Sometimes the Bible tells us what people did so that we can understand the history of redemption, not so that we can imitate every decision they made.
And there is another important truth.
The Bible does not present Moses as the leader of Israel because his parents' marriage was exceptional.
God called Moses according to His redemptive purpose.
The story is not an invitation to justify incestuous relationships today.
The biblical prohibitions against close-kin sexual unions remain serious moral boundaries.
Grace is never permission to redefine what God calls sin.
But grace does mean that human brokenness cannot automatically defeat God's purposes.
Now imagine the world into which Moses was born.
Egypt.
A nation of towering monuments, magnificent palaces, and merciless oppression.
The Israelites were suffering under forced labor.
Their cries were rising toward heaven.
And Pharaoh had issued a terrifying command.
Hebrew baby boys were to be killed.
Imagine being a mother in that world.
You have just given birth.
You hold your child against your chest.
You study his tiny fingers.
You listen to his breathing.
And somewhere outside your home, soldiers have the authority to take his life.
Every cry could expose him.
Every passing footstep could mean danger.
Every knock at the door could become a nightmare.
That was Jochebed's world.
Exodus 2:2 tells us that she hid her baby for three months.
Three months of fear.
Three months of whispered prayers.
Three months of trying to keep a newborn quiet while an empire hunted children like him.
Can you imagine that?
A mother pressing her baby close, perhaps trembling every time he cried.
A father wondering how much longer they could protect him.
A sister watching everything unfold, too young to change the world but old enough to understand that her little brother's life was in danger.
And then the day came when hiding him was no longer possible.
Jochebed prepared a basket.
She waterproofed it.
She placed her son inside.
And she set it among the reeds by the Nile.
Try to picture her hands.
The same hands that had held him.
Fed him.
Comforted him.
Now carefully releasing the basket that carried everything she desperately wanted to protect.
The Bible does not record her private thoughts or exact prayers.
But it tells us what she did.
And Hebrews 11:23 later remembers the faith and courage of Moses' parents.
They were not simply surrendering their child to chance.
They were resisting a murderous royal command.
And into that terrifying moment, God's providence was already at work.
Pharaoh's daughter came to the river.
She discovered the child.
She recognized him as a Hebrew baby.
And she had compassion.
Then Miriam, watching nearby, approached with a remarkable question.
Could she find a Hebrew woman to nurse the child?
The princess agreed.
And the woman who was summoned was Jochebed herself.
The mother who had released her child into the river was given the opportunity to nurse and care for him.
Read Exodus 2:1–10.
The beauty of that moment is almost overwhelming.
The king had ordered Hebrew sons to die.
Yet a Hebrew son was rescued through the compassion of the king's own daughter.
The mother who could no longer hide him was allowed to care for him.
And the child who should have been killed would one day stand before Pharaoh with God's command:
“Let my people go.”
Do you see it?
The empire believed it controlled the future.
But God was preparing a deliverer right under Pharaoh's roof.
And here is what makes this story deeply personal.
Moses did not enter history with a family background that modern readers would consider uncomplicated.
His ancestry contained a relationship that would later be prohibited under Israel's Law.
His people were enslaved.
His infancy was threatened.
His childhood involved separation and adoption into an Egyptian royal household.
And later, Moses himself would commit a serious act of violence.
Exodus 2:12 records that he killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew man.
Moses then fled.
The man who would eventually confront Pharaoh first became a fugitive.
The future leader spent years away from the place where his calling would unfold.
And when God finally called him from the burning bush, Moses did not respond like a fearless hero.
He questioned his own ability.
“Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh?”
— Exodus 3:11, KJV
Who am I?
Four words.
But perhaps you know what they feel like.
Who am I to serve God after what I have done?
Who am I to speak about Jesus when my own family has so many problems?
Who am I to encourage others when I still struggle?
Who am I to pray when I have failed so many times?
Who am I to believe God could use me when I can barely forgive myself?
Some people carry shame that began long before they made their own decisions.
They grew up in families marked by addiction.
Infidelity.
Abandonment.
Violence.
Secrets.
Broken promises.
Generational conflict.
Some were told they were unwanted.
Some were blamed for circumstances they never created.
Some learned to hide their family history because they feared that if people knew the truth, they would never be accepted.
And perhaps that is why the genealogy of Moses matters more than we first realize.
Because God did not need to rewrite Moses' ancestry into a spotless family history before calling him.
But listen carefully.
That does not mean family trauma is good.
It does not mean harmful relationships should be defended.
It does not mean we should romanticize sin, excuse abuse, or ignore the consequences of destructive choices.
It means that a person's family history is not the final authority over that person's future.
Your parents' failures are not automatically your guilt.
Your family's reputation is not your identity.
And the circumstances surrounding your birth do not determine your worth before God.
Ezekiel 18:20 teaches personal moral responsibility, declaring that the son does not bear the guilt of the father merely because he is his son.
That truth matters.
Especially to someone who has spent years carrying shame that was never theirs to carry.
But there is something even greater than the story of Moses.
Because Moses was never meant to be the final answer.
He was a deliverer.
But he was not the ultimate Deliverer.
He confronted Pharaoh.
But he could not conquer the power of sin and death.
He led Israel out of Egypt.
But he could not, by his own righteousness, bring humanity into eternal reconciliation with God.
He mediated the old covenant.
But another would come who would be greater.
Jesus Christ.
And here is where this entire story turns from uncomfortable genealogy into breathtaking Gospel hope.
God did not save Israel because Moses came from a flawless family. And God does not save us because we come from flawless families either.
Our salvation rests on Jesus Christ.
Not our pedigree.
Not our reputation.
Not our achievements.
Not the absence of scandal in our family tree.
But the finished work of the crucified and risen Savior.
Consider the opening of Matthew's Gospel.
Before Matthew tells us about the birth of Jesus, he presents a genealogy.
And that genealogy contains stories that are anything but sanitized.
Judah and Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
David and the wife of Uriah.
Their circumstances were not identical, and their stories must not be carelessly reduced to the same moral category.
But together they remind us that the biblical history leading to the Messiah was not a parade of morally flawless people.
Matthew 1:6 even identifies Solomon's mother by reference to Uriah, recalling one of David's darkest chapters.
Why preserve such painful history?
The text does not explain every reason.
But it certainly does not hide the past.
And when we reach the end of that genealogy, we encounter the One who changes everything.
Jesus.
The Christ.
The promised Son of David.
The Savior who entered a world already scarred by human sin.
He did not come because humanity had finally cleaned itself up.
He came because sinners needed saving.
Matthew 1:21 declares:
“And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.”
Not merely from embarrassment.
Not merely from public criticism.
Not merely from the consequences of a ruined reputation.
From their sins.
That is the Gospel.
And it is far more powerful than a motivational message about overcoming a difficult past.
Because the Gospel does not simply tell us that we are stronger than our history.
It tells us that Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
The New Testament expresses this beautifully in Ephesians 2:8–9:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
The Greek word translated “grace” is:
χάρις — charis
Grace.
God's undeserved favor.
Not a reward for an impressive family history.
Not a prize for having avoided every mistake.
Not something purchased by religious performance.
A gift.
And the Greek word translated “saved” in Ephesians 2:8 is:
σεσῳσμένοι — sesōsmenoi
A perfect passive participle from the verb sōzō, meaning “to save.”
In this construction, it describes believers as having been saved, with the resulting condition continuing.
The emphasis is not on sinners rescuing themselves.
It is on God's saving action received through faith.
And that changes the way we look at our lives.
Because some of us are still trying to earn what Christ offers by grace.
We think if we pray enough, serve enough, give enough, suffer enough, or prove ourselves enough, God might finally accept us.
But the cross announces something altogether different.
Jesus did not die so that we could purchase forgiveness through good behavior.
He died because we could never make ourselves righteous before God through our own efforts.
And He rose again, demonstrating His victory over sin and death.
This is why the Gospel cannot be reduced to the slogan that God uses imperfect people.
That statement is true, but it is incomplete.
The deeper truth is that God saves guilty sinners through the perfect righteousness, sacrificial death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And the grace that saves us also calls us to change.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains us to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace does not tell us to remain comfortable in sin.
Grace calls us out of darkness.
Grace confronts what destroys us.
Grace leads us toward repentance.
Grace teaches us to forgive.
Grace empowers a new way of living.
And this brings us back to Amram and Jochebed.
Their family relationship is not a model for Christian marriage.
Their genealogy is not permission to ignore biblical sexual boundaries.
And the later prohibitions in Leviticus must not be dismissed simply because Moses came from that family.
But neither should we pretend that the Bible's difficult family histories somehow make God's redemptive work impossible.
God's holiness remains holy.
His commands remain serious.
His mercy remains astonishing.
And His sovereign purposes are not defeated by the imperfections of human ancestry.
Now I want to ask you something.
Not as someone looking for a dramatic reaction.
But as someone who knows that behind every screen is a real person carrying a story.
What part of your history have you allowed to convince you that God could never use your life?
Was it something your parents did?
A broken marriage?
A childhood you rarely talk about?
A decision you regret?
A season when you walked away from God?
A secret that still makes you feel ashamed?
Maybe you have been attending church while quietly believing you are less worthy than everyone sitting beside you.
You sing about forgiveness.
But struggle to believe it applies to you.
You tell others that Jesus changes lives.
But wonder whether yours is too damaged.
You encourage people to trust God's promises.
Then return home and stare at the ceiling, wondering why your own heart still feels so heavy.
Listen.
You do not have to pretend your past was harmless.
You do not have to call evil good.
You do not have to minimize what someone did to you.
And you do not have to manufacture a beautiful testimony before coming to Jesus.
Come truthfully.
Come repentantly where you have sinned.
Come wounded where you have been hurt.
Come weary where life has exhausted you.
Come trusting the Savior who said:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
— Matthew 11:28, KJV
He did not say, “Come when your family tree is perfect.”
He did not say, “Come when nobody remembers your mistakes.”
He did not say, “Come after you have repaired every broken piece of your life.”
He said, “Come unto me.”
And perhaps those are the words you have needed to hear for a very long time.
Not because God overlooks sin.
But because Jesus is the Savior sinners desperately need.
Not because a comment saves anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But because sometimes an honest expression of need opens the door for another believer to encourage you, pray with you, and remind you of the promises of God.
Your story may help someone who feels completely alone.
There may be someone reading quietly who has not prayed in months.
Someone who still believes in God but has stopped believing that mercy is possible for them.
Someone who thinks the failures of their parents have permanently ruined their future.
Someone who needs to know that the Bible does not hide complicated families—and that the Gospel offers something greater than a perfect reputation.
Not merely because it is surprising.
Not because scandal generates attention.
But because biblical truth deserves to travel farther than misinformation, shame, and despair.
Sometimes the most loving thing we can do is make sure someone encounters the truth of Jesus Christ at the moment they need it.
There may come a day when your own past starts speaking louder than God's promises.
Return to the Scriptures.
Remember the difference between God's commands and the human failures recorded in biblical history.
Remember that your identity is not established by your family's worst chapter.
And above all, remember that Jesus Christ is the only sufficient foundation for forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a transformed life.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to turn the Bible into sensational entertainment.
Not to build a following around controversy.
Not to promise that every painful story will end exactly as we wish.
But to help people open Scripture, encounter the truth, repent of sin, grow in faith, and follow Jesus Christ with greater understanding and devotion.
And if this message has strengthened you, I want to invite you into something deeper.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical teaching and spiritual nourishment more accessible to people who are hungry for God's Word.
You can help that work continue.
Think of it as a voluntary monthly ministry offering—a practical expression of generosity toward work you believe is helping others encounter the Gospel.
But I want to make something very clear.
It is not a requirement for salvation.
It does not replace your responsibility to care for your family or the faithful support of your local church.
And it should not be confused with a biblically mandated tithe.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Cheerfully.
Without pressure or guilt.
Jesus is.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Share the Gospel.
Invite others.
Make use of the free resources.
Because the message of salvation must never be treated as something that can be purchased.
There is so much confusion about Scripture.
So much shallow teaching.
So much pain hidden behind smiling faces.
People need more than another religious slogan.
They need the Word of God understood faithfully.
They need the truth about sin and repentance.
They need the hope of forgiveness.
They need to know Jesus Christ.
And now, before we finish, return with me one last time to that little Hebrew baby by the Nile.
A basket.
A river.
A death sentence.
A watching sister.
A grieving, courageous mother.
An Egyptian princess.
And a future that no one standing beside that river could fully see.
The baby would grow.
The fugitive would be called.
The reluctant man would confront Pharaoh.
The sea would part.
The people would walk toward freedom.
And generations later, another Deliverer would come.
Not to rescue Israel from Pharaoh, but to accomplish a redemption far greater than the exodus from Egypt.
Jesus Christ would bear the sins of His people.
He would suffer on the cross.
He would rise from the dead.
And through Him, all who repent and believe receive the forgiveness and life that no human leader could ever provide.
Moses' story was remarkable.
But Moses was not the center of God's final answer to human sin.
Jesus is.
And that is the most important thing to remember when reading any difficult passage in Scripture.
The Bible is not ultimately a collection of stories about perfect people.
It is the unfolding revelation of the holy God who keeps His promises and brings redemption to sinners through His Son.
So when you read Exodus 6:20 again, do not deny the uncomfortable details.
Do not exaggerate them.
Do not turn them into permission for what Scripture forbids.
And do not miss the greater story of God's faithfulness.
The same Bible that honestly records the complicated ancestry of Moses also reveals the spotless Savior who came to redeem sinners.
That is why we can speak about scandal without glorifying it.
That is why we can speak about grace without cheapening it.
That is why we can confront sin without declaring any repentant sinner beyond the reach of Christ.
And that is why your story does not have to end where your shame began.
Because perhaps the most important thing about your life is not what happened before you knew Jesus.
Perhaps it is what Jesus is doing now as you learn to follow Him.
Your family history may explain where your story began, but only Jesus Christ can redeem you—and your past does not get to overrule His promise of grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU SAID, “I CAN STOP ANYTIME.” THEN WHY HAVEN’T YOU?
paragraphs: YOU SAID, “I CAN STOP ANYTIME.” THEN WHY HAVEN’T YOU?

The most dangerous prison may be the one you keep calling freedom. And the most frightening moment isn't when you realize you're trapped—it's when you discover how long you've been defending the chains.
Nobody heard you say it.
Maybe you whispered it while closing another private browser window.
Maybe you thought it while deleting your search history.
Maybe it happened after another night when you promised yourself you would never go back.
“I can stop anytime.”
Four words.
Four words that sounded like confidence.
Four words that helped you sleep when your conscience wouldn't leave you alone.
Four words that allowed you to keep calling something harmless even though it was quietly taking more from you than you ever intended to give.
And perhaps the most disturbing part wasn't that you said them.
It was that you believed them.
Because somewhere between the first compromise and the hundredth excuse, something changed.
What you once considered a choice began to feel like a necessity.
What you once did occasionally became something you anticipated.
What you once could walk away from became something you repeatedly returned to, even when returning left you ashamed, exhausted, distracted, or spiritually numb.
You still had your Bible.
You still knew how to pray.
You could still sing worship songs and say “Amen” when the preacher spoke about holiness.
But there was another version of your life that nobody saw.
A version that waited until the room was empty.
Until the phone was within reach.
Until loneliness grew loud enough.
Until stress, rejection, boredom, or disappointment made the old escape feel attractive again.
And every time you returned, you told yourself the same thing.
“Just this once.”
Then afterward came the familiar silence.
The regret.
The promise.
The bargaining.
The attempt to convince yourself that next time would be different.
And maybe it was different.
For three days.
For a week.
For an entire month.
Until something happened.
A difficult evening. An argument. A memory. A temptation you didn't expect.
And suddenly you were back in the very place you had sworn you would never visit again.
Not because you had forgotten your promise.
But because a promise, by itself, cannot always break a pattern that has been deeply reinforced.
Now here is the question you may have been avoiding.
If you are so certain you can stop whenever you want, why do you keep postponing the moment you actually do?
Don't answer too quickly.
Because the apostle Paul wrote something almost two thousand years ago that cuts straight through the excuses we have become skilled at making.
In 1 Corinthians 6:12, he wrote:
“All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient. All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any.” (KJV)
The original Greek makes the warning especially striking.
ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος
all’ ouk egō exousiasthēsomai hypo tinos
“But I will not be mastered by anything.”
The verb ἐξουσιασθήσομαι (exousiasthēsomai) comes from a word family associated with authority and power. Here it means to be brought under another's authority or control.
Notice the contrast.
Paul is discussing what someone may claim the freedom to do, yet he refuses to allow that supposed freedom to become a new master.
In other words, the question is not merely, “Can I do this?”
It is also, “What is this doing to me?”

And in the surrounding passage, Paul is not giving Christians unlimited permission to indulge whatever they desire. He is confronting a distorted understanding of freedom, specifically in a discussion that leads directly into sexual immorality, the body, and belonging to Christ.
This matters.
Because some people have taken the language of Christian liberty and used it to defend what Scripture calls them to flee.
But Paul does not separate freedom from holiness.
He does not treat the body as spiritually irrelevant.
He goes on to declare:
“Now the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body.” (1 Corinthians 6:13, KJV)
And then, a few verses later:
“Flee fornication.” (1 Corinthians 6:18, KJV)

The Greek word translated “fornication” is πορνεία (porneia), a broad term for sexual immorality. It is not the ancient Greek word for modern internet pornography, but the passage establishes the biblical framework for sexual holiness, bodily obedience, and the rejection of sexual behavior outside God's design.
Paul's argument is not that every desire is evil.
Nor is he saying that experiencing temptation means a person is already defeated.
His warning is that our bodies belong to the Lord, and Christian freedom must never become an excuse for surrendering ourselves to sin.
That brings us to a deeply uncomfortable possibility.
What if the thing you keep defending as your personal freedom is the very thing quietly exercising authority over you?
What if “I can stop anytime” has become the sentence you repeat because admitting the truth would require a change you are afraid to make?
There is a difference between having a struggle and defending a struggle.
There is a difference between falling into temptation and making peace with it.
And there is a difference between being tempted by something and repeatedly arranging your life so you can return to it.

Not every repeated habit is a clinical addiction. Not everyone who struggles with pornography experiences the same degree of compulsivity, and difficulty stopping does not automatically establish a diagnosis.
But repeated loss of control, continued behavior despite serious consequences, and persistent unsuccessful attempts to change can be warning signs that a habit has become deeply entrenched.
You do not need to wait for a diagnosis before taking an honest look at what is happening in your heart and your life.
Because Scripture is asking a question that reaches beyond clinical terminology.
Is this helping you live faithfully before Christ, or are you increasingly organizing your life around it?
And perhaps the answer is more painful than you expected.
Because pornography doesn't always announce its consequences with a dramatic collapse.
Sometimes the damage appears quietly.
You begin hiding things from someone who trusts you.
You become more comfortable with secrecy.
You notice that your private choices no longer reflect your public convictions.
You promise yourself you will pray after one more indulgence.
You postpone repentance until tomorrow.
You find yourself using something sexual to escape emotions you have never learned to bring honestly before God.
Not every person experiences all these consequences. But for some, these are the warning lights they have spent months or years ignoring.
And one of the hardest truths to face is this:
A habit does not have to destroy your entire life before it deserves your serious attention.
Sometimes you know something is wrong long before anyone else discovers it.
You know because you remember the person you wanted to become.
You remember praying for purity.
You remember the sincerity of your early walk with Jesus.
You remember when opening Scripture felt less like facing an accusation and more like coming home.
Now, perhaps, you avoid certain passages.
Not because God's Word has lost its power.
But because you already suspect what it will ask you to surrender.
And surrender feels terrifying when the thing you must release has become your favorite way to cope.
That is why this conversation cannot end with someone shouting, “Try harder!”
You have probably tried harder.
You have made promises.
You have deleted apps.
You have installed filters.
You have counted clean days.
You have experienced genuine progress, and perhaps painful setbacks.
And after enough disappointment, you may have begun wondering whether lasting change is even possible for someone like you.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not begin with the announcement that you are strong enough to save yourself.
It begins with the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Not impressive sinners.
Not sinners who already know how to fix themselves.
Sinners who need mercy.
Sinners who need forgiveness.
Sinners who cannot manufacture a new heart through willpower alone.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had successfully cleaned every hidden corner of our lives.
Not after we had accumulated enough victories to deserve His attention.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
But do not misunderstand that grace.
The grace that welcomes sinners does not encourage them to remain comfortable in sin.
The same Jesus who receives the broken also calls them to repentance.
The same Savior who forgives also transforms.
And the same cross that reveals the seriousness of sin reveals the extraordinary depth of God's mercy.
Perhaps you have spent so long thinking of repentance as punishment that you have forgotten what it really means.
In the New Testament, the Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) means repentance, involving a change of mind and a turning of one's life toward God.
It is more than feeling terrible after doing something wrong.
It is more than crying because you were caught.
It is more than making another emotional promise while secretly leaving the door open for tomorrow's temptation.
True repentance involves turning toward God in faith, agreeing with His truth about sin, and taking real steps away from what dishonors Him.
And even that turning is not something we accomplish apart from His grace.
You may need to confess what you have been hiding.
You may need to stop treating secrecy as protection.
You may need to remove access to material that repeatedly draws you into temptation.
You may need an honest conversation with a mature, trustworthy believer who can pray with you and hold you accountable without humiliating you.
And if your behavior has become persistent, compulsive, or seriously disruptive, professional mental health support may also be appropriate. Seeking help is not a denial of faith.
It may be one of the ways you begin acting on the truth you have finally acknowledged.
But whatever practical steps are needed, never confuse the tools of change with the Savior who gives your life its deepest hope.
A filter cannot forgive your sins.
An accountability partner cannot redeem your soul.
A streak of successful days cannot purchase your righteousness before God.
Only Jesus Christ can reconcile you to the Father.
And the One who saves you also calls you to walk in newness of life.
That is why the words of Jesus in John 8:34–36 are so powerful.
“Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.”
And then:
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.” (KJV)
The Greek word translated “servant” is δοῦλος (doulos), often rendered “slave” or “bondservant.”
Jesus is describing the spiritual bondage of sin, not giving a modern clinical definition of addiction.
And His promise reaches deeper than simply improving our ability to resist an impulse.
He speaks of the freedom that comes through the Son.
Freedom from sin's ultimate claim over those who belong to Him.
Freedom to live in the truth.
Freedom to follow God rather than surrender unquestioningly to every desire.
And this freedom is not a guarantee that temptation will disappear overnight.
Some battles involve long seasons of growth, repeated choices, support, and perseverance.
But the Christian's hope is not that the battle is easy.
It is that sin is no longer the rightful master of someone who belongs to Jesus Christ.
Think about that.
You may have spent years saying, “I can stop anytime.”
But the Gospel invites you to say something entirely different.
“Lord Jesus, I cannot make myself righteous. I need Your mercy, Your truth, and Your transforming grace. Teach me to walk in the freedom You purchased.”
That is not weakness disguised as spirituality.
That is surrender.
And surrender to Christ is not the destruction of your humanity.
It is the beginning of living as someone who belongs to the One who created and redeemed you.
Maybe you are reading this with tears in your eyes.
Maybe your spouse is sleeping beside you, unaware of the struggle you have been hiding.
Maybe you are single, and loneliness has become the excuse you use to return to pornography.
Maybe you are a church leader, a worship team member, a parent, or someone everyone assumes is spiritually strong.
Maybe you are young and frightened by how quickly something you considered harmless has become difficult to resist.
Or maybe you have already begun to change, but the memory of your past still whispers that you are a hypocrite who will never be different.
Whatever your story, hear this.
Your sin must be taken seriously.
But your sin is not greater than the sufficiency of Jesus Christ.
The cross is not a decoration for people who have everything together.
It is the place where the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
And His resurrection declares that death and sin do not have the final word.
First Corinthians 6 contains another extraordinary passage that deserves to be heard alongside its warning about being mastered.
After naming serious patterns of sin, Paul tells the Corinthian believers:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.” (1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV)
And such were some of you.
Were.
That single word carries the testimony of lives changed by the grace of God.
Paul is not claiming that every believer has become incapable of sinning.
He is describing the decisive change of identity and standing that comes through God's saving work.
Their past was real.
Their sins were real.
Their need for repentance was real.
But their former identity did not have the final authority to define who they now were in Christ.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Not because they were morally impressive.
But in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to create a community where people pretend they have no struggles.
Not to entertain religious audiences with stories that make them feel spiritual for a few minutes.
But to keep pointing people to the Word of God, the seriousness of sin, the necessity of repentance, and the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Because there are people who will never walk into a church and admit what they are battling.
People who cannot bring themselves to tell their families.
People who have stopped praying because they believe God must be tired of hearing their apologies.
People who are one honest encounter with Scripture away from finally asking for help.
And sometimes a message shared at the right moment can become the beginning of that conversation.
Not because a Facebook article has the power to save a soul.
Only God saves.
But because God can use His truth, carried through ordinary human faithfulness, to confront, encourage, and draw people toward Christ.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be fighting a battle they have never admitted to anyone.
Someone may have told themselves those same four words this morning.
“I can stop anytime.”
And perhaps seeing this article on your profile will challenge them to ask the question they have avoided for years.
You do not need to expose anyone's private struggle.
You do not need to speculate about who is secretly battling pornography.
If one person begins an honest conversation, opens Scripture, reaches out for help, or turns toward Christ because of something you shared, that is a reason to thank God.
And if a particular friend or family member has already expressed that they are seeking biblical encouragement, consider tagging them with kindness, not embarrassment.
The goal is restoration.
Never public humiliation.
Some people can share.
Some can pray.
Some can encourage another believer.
And some are in a position to help financially sustain and expand this work.
All of these can be meaningful acts of service when offered sincerely to the Lord.
It is a practical way to help this ministry continue and, as resources allow, expand its reach.
Scripture teaches that believers may support those who faithfully minister the Word.
Galatians 6:6 says:
“Let him that is taught in the word communicate unto him that teacheth in all good things.” (KJV)
And 2 Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
These passages matter together.
Financial support for Gospel ministry can be a sincere expression of generosity and stewardship.
God is not selling forgiveness.
Jesus Christ has already paid the price of redemption through His blood.
Not because you have been pressured.
But because you believe helping sound biblical teaching reach more people is a worthy use of what God has entrusted to you.
These products are not the Gospel.
They cannot replace Scripture, prayer, the local church, or personal discipleship.
They are simply additional ways to encourage faith, keep biblical truth close, and support the ongoing work.
The invitation is to keep growing deeper in Jesus Christ.
To study the Bible.
To examine what you believe.
To strengthen your understanding of grace, repentance, forgiveness, holiness, and the Christian life.
To become someone who not only reads the truth but increasingly lives in obedience to it.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, struggling Christians, and even those who are still searching for answers to follow as well.
Not everyone is ready to enter a church building.
But someone may be willing to read a passage of Scripture on a screen.
And that can become an opportunity to begin a deeper conversation about Jesus.
I want to return to the person sitting alone with a phone, a secret, and a promise.
The person who has whispered, “This is the last time,” more times than they can count.
The person who has confused repeated regret with genuine repentance.
The person who fears that if anyone discovered the truth, they would never be looked at the same way again.
I want you to imagine something.
Imagine that tonight, instead of opening the familiar website, you open your Bible.
Instead of preparing another excuse, you tell God the truth.
Instead of making a dramatic promise that depends entirely on your willpower, you begin with a humble confession.

“Father, I have called this freedom, but I have allowed it to influence my choices. I have hidden what I should have brought into the light. I have excused what Your Word calls me to turn away from. Have mercy on me through Jesus Christ. Teach me to repent sincerely, seek wise help, and walk in obedience.”
Then imagine taking one real step.
Not an impressive public announcement.
Not another emotional declaration that you will never struggle again.
One honest step.
Delete what needs to be deleted.
Change the routine that keeps leading you back.
Talk to someone trustworthy.
Seek appropriate help if you need it.
Return to Scripture.
Pray again tomorrow.
And when temptation comes, remember that temptation itself is not the same as surrendering to it.
First Corinthians 10:13 reminds believers that God is faithful and provides a way to endure temptation.
And when you stumble, do not turn your failure into permission to abandon Christ.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Confession is not a technique for making sin harmless.
It is part of living honestly before the God whose mercy we desperately need.
Do not use grace as an excuse to return.
And do not let shame convince you that returning to God is pointless.
The Christian life is not a performance in which one failure automatically erases every evidence of God's work.
It is a life of faith, repentance, obedience, perseverance, and dependence upon Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the most important change begins when you stop asking, “How long can I keep doing this without anyone finding out?”
And begin asking, “Lord, what would faithfulness look like for me today?”
That question changes the direction of your attention.
Away from protecting your secret.
Toward honoring your Savior.
Away from defending your chains.
Toward walking in the light.
Away from pretending you are in control.
Toward submitting yourself to the Lordship of Jesus Christ.
And if this article has confronted something you have been unwilling to admit, I want to invite you to respond.
Not with a confession of private sexual details.
Not with information that could expose you or someone else.
But with a simple expression of where you want to go from here.
You do not have to explain your story to strangers.
You do not have to prove your repentance in a comment section.
But your words may encourage another person who thought they were the only one struggling.
And if you have a testimony of how Jesus has been changing your life, share what is appropriate and helpful.
Someone needs to hear that growth is possible.
Someone needs to know that seeking help is not shameful.
Someone needs to remember that the mercy of Christ is greater than the lies that keep sinners hiding.
The most important question is what you will do with Jesus Christ.
Will you continue defending what He calls you to surrender?
Will you keep hiding behind the language of freedom while ignoring the influence of sin?
Or will you come honestly before the Savior who died and rose again, confess your need, and follow Him?
Because this story was never supposed to end with a person proving how strong they are.
It was always meant to point to the One who is mighty to save.
And perhaps one day, when you look back on this moment, you will remember the four words you used to say.
“I can stop anytime.”
But you will remember something else, too.
The day you finally stopped trusting those words to save you.
The day you stopped defending the darkness.
The day you began telling the truth.
The day you took a real step toward repentance.
The day you remembered that your life was not purchased by your own strength, but by the precious blood of Jesus Christ.
You may still have hard days ahead.
You may still need help.
You may still need to rebuild trust, change habits, and persevere through difficult seasons.
But you do not have to keep calling bondage freedom.
And you do not have to keep treating your worst choices as the final verdict on your life.
Because the Gospel declares that sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed through Jesus Christ.
The scandal is that we have so often loved the darkness.
The grace is that Christ came into this broken world to save sinners and call them into His marvelous light.
And the invitation remains open.
Not to hide more carefully.
Not to make another empty promise.
But to repent, believe, and follow the Savior.
The chains you kept defending were never worth the freedom Christ died to give you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD TOOK EZEKIEL’S WIFE… THEN TOLD HIM NOT TO CRY? THE HEARTBREAKING TRUTH BEHIND ONE OF THE BIBLE’S MOST DISTURBING COMMANDS
paragraphs: GOD TOOK EZEKIEL’S WIFE… THEN TOLD HIM NOT TO CRY? THE HEARTBREAKING TRUTH BEHIND ONE OF THE BIBLE’S MOST DISTURBING COMMANDS

He called her “the delight of your eyes.” By evening, she was dead. And God told her husband not to mourn publicly. But behind this heartbreaking silence was a warning to an entire nation—and a truth about judgment, grief, and the mercy of Jesus Christ that we cannot afford to misunderstand.
Imagine coming home after the longest day of your life.
