You open the door.
Everything is where it should be.
Her belongings are still there. The place where she usually sits is empty. The little things you never thought about suddenly feel unbearable.
You want to hear her voice one more time.
You want to tell her something you forgot to say.
You want just one more ordinary morning.
But there will be no more ordinary mornings.
Now imagine that before she died, God had already told you what was coming.
And then He told you something almost impossible to comprehend.
When she dies, do not mourn the way everyone expects you to mourn.
No public lamentation.
No customary mourning rituals.
No outward demonstration of the devastation tearing through your heart.
You are allowed to groan.
But quietly.
This is not fiction.
This is what happened to the prophet Ezekiel.
And perhaps the most unsettling part of the story is not that his wife died.
It is that God made Ezekiel's personal tragedy a prophetic sign for people who had refused to listen to His warnings.
Why?
Why would the God who declares Himself compassionate ask a grieving husband to carry such an unbearable assignment?
Was Ezekiel's love for his wife somehow less important than his ministry?
Was God teaching believers to suppress their emotions?
Or was something far more devastating unfolding beneath the surface?
Stay with this story.
Because the answer is not found by pretending this passage is easy.
It is found by allowing Scripture to tell us exactly what happened—and by following its painful warning all the way to the cross of Jesus Christ.
Ezekiel was not simply a preacher delivering sermons to comfortable people.
He was a priest and prophet living among Jewish exiles in Babylon.

His people had already experienced national humiliation. Families had been uprooted. Their homeland was far away. Jerusalem still stood, but the kingdom was collapsing under the weight of covenant unfaithfulness, idolatry, injustice, and rebellion against God.
Many continued to place their confidence in the temple.
Surely Jerusalem could not fall completely.
Surely the city containing God's sanctuary would remain secure.
Surely their religious identity would protect them.
But they had confused possessing sacred things with faithfully belonging to the God who made those things sacred.
Then, in Ezekiel 24, the word of the LORD came with a message that would devastate the prophet personally.
God said:
“Son of man, behold, I take away from thee the desire of thine eyes with a stroke: yet neither shalt thou mourn nor weep, neither shall thy tears run down.”
— Ezekiel 24:16, KJV
Read those words again.
“The desire of thine eyes.”
God did not describe Ezekiel's wife as an inconvenience.
He did not reduce her to an anonymous instrument.
He identified her through the language of affection.
In Hebrew, the expression is מַחְמַד עֵינֶיךָ (maḥmad ʿênêkha).
The noun maḥmad refers to something desirable, precious, or treasured. ʿÊnêkha means “your eyes.”
Together, the expression communicates something deeply cherished—the delight of his eyes.
The Lord knew exactly whom Ezekiel loved.
And that makes the passage even harder.
Because the woman about to die was not merely “the prophet's wife.”
She was someone precious to him.
Someone whose absence would change the sound of his home.
Someone he would never again see walking toward him.
Someone he loved.
Scripture does not tell us her name.
It does not tell us how long they had been married.
It does not tell us whether they had children.
And we must not invent those details simply to make the story more dramatic.
What Scripture does tell us is enough.
She was the delight of his eyes.
And she was about to die.
God continued:
“Forbear to cry, make no mourning for the dead, bind the tire of thine head upon thee, and put on thy shoes upon thy feet, and cover not thy lips, and eat not the bread of men.”
— Ezekiel 24:17, KJV
These instructions concerned recognizable mourning customs.
Ezekiel was to keep his head covering in place, retain his sandals, avoid covering the lower part of his face, and refrain from the customary food associated with mourning.
He was not being commanded to celebrate her death.
He was not being told that marriage was unimportant.
He was being instructed not to perform the ordinary public rituals through which his community expressed bereavement.
And there is a crucial distinction here.
God restricted Ezekiel's outward mourning practices. The passage does not say Ezekiel felt no sorrow.
In fact, the Hebrew instruction contains an extraordinary detail.
The opening words of Ezekiel 24:17 include:
הֵאָנֵק דֹּם (hēʾānēq dōm)
The first word concerns groaning or sighing. The second communicates silence or stillness.
The sense is that Ezekiel may groan, but must do so quietly rather than engage in the customary public lamentation.
There is pain in that command.
Real pain.
A grief that has not disappeared simply because its usual expression has been restrained.
And then comes one of the most heartbreaking verses in the entire book.
“So I spake unto the people in the morning: and at even my wife died; and I did in the morning as I was commanded.”
— Ezekiel 24:18, KJV
That is all Ezekiel tells us.
He spoke to the people in the morning.
His wife died in the evening.
The next morning, he obeyed.
No description of the final conversation.
No account of the room where she died.
No record of the tears he may have wanted to shed publicly.
Just one short verse carrying an enormous weight.
And sometimes Scripture's restraint is more devastating than a thousand descriptive sentences.
Because anyone who has buried someone they love knows that grief does not need elaborate language.
Sometimes the worst moment is simply waking up the next morning.
And remembering.
They are gone.
Yet Ezekiel rose and obeyed the instruction he had received.
The people noticed.
They could see that something was profoundly unusual.
So they asked:
“Wilt thou not tell us what these things are to us, that thou doest so?”
— Ezekiel 24:19, KJV
In other words:
Ezekiel, what does this mean for us?
Why are you behaving this way?
What is God trying to tell us?
And suddenly, the meaning of the prophet's terrible assignment began to emerge.
This was not merely about one husband's sorrow.
It was about a nation approaching catastrophe.
God declared:

“Behold, I will profane my sanctuary, the excellency of your strength, the desire of your eyes, and that which your soul pitieth; and your sons and your daughters whom ye have left shall fall by the sword.”
— Ezekiel 24:21, KJV
There it is.
The connection.
The same language of preciousness used for Ezekiel's wife now appears in the warning about God's sanctuary.
For Ezekiel, the delight of his eyes was his beloved wife.
For the exiles, the temple was a cherished source of identity, beauty, security, and national hope.
And God was announcing that the sanctuary in which they had placed such confidence would be desecrated and destroyed.
Jerusalem would fall.
Families would suffer.
The children and relatives left behind would face the violence of war.
What Ezekiel experienced personally was a sign pointing toward a much greater national calamity.
But notice something essential.
The destruction of Jerusalem was not presented as a random divine outburst.
Throughout Ezekiel, God had repeatedly confronted His people about their idolatry, bloodshed, corruption, and covenant unfaithfulness.
The temple had become a place of false security for people who wanted God's protection without submitting to His holiness.
They wanted the benefits of belonging to God while refusing to listen to Him.
And that is where this ancient story begins to confront us.
Because it is possible to love the appearance of Christianity while resisting the lordship of Christ.
It is possible to cherish a Bible without obeying what it says.
It is possible to attend worship, sing passionately, post Scripture online, and still hide a heart unwilling to repent.
It is possible to become attached to the gifts of God while neglecting the God who gives them.
And no religious object, building, tradition, ministry, or public reputation can replace genuine faith and obedience.
The people of Jerusalem had made a deadly mistake.
They assumed that because the temple was sacred, they were safe from judgment.
But God's holiness could not be manipulated.
His presence was never a license for rebellion.
The temple was not a magical shield against the consequences of persistent sin.
And Ezekiel's silent mourning became a living warning that the people would face a disaster so overwhelming that their ordinary expressions of grief would be disrupted.
God said:
“And ye shall do as I have done: ye shall not cover your lips, nor eat the bread of men.”
— Ezekiel 24:22, KJV
Then He explained that they would pine away because of their iniquities and mourn among themselves (Ezekiel 24:23).
This matters tremendously.
God was not teaching that grief is sinful.
He was announcing a particular response to an approaching judgment.
Ezekiel's unusual conduct was a prophetic sign.
It was not a universal command for every bereaved Christian.
Please do not miss that.
Because someone reading this may have recently lost a spouse.
Someone may have buried a parent.
Someone may still be carrying the pain of a child who died.
And perhaps someone has told you that strong faith means you should stop crying.
That tears reveal unbelief.
That if you truly trusted God, you would not grieve so deeply.
But that is not what Ezekiel 24 teaches.
And it is certainly not what the whole counsel of Scripture teaches.
Abraham mourned Sarah (Genesis 23:2).
David lamented the deaths of Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:17–27).
Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus (John 11:35).
And when Stephen was buried, devout men made great lamentation over him (Acts 8:2).
The Bible does not condemn tears.
It gives them language.
The Psalms are filled with cries from wounded hearts.
The apostle Paul tells believers not that they must never grieve, but that they must not grieve as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
There is a difference between hopeless grief and grief sustained by the promises of God.
Christian hope does not make death painless.
It declares that death will not have the final word.
And that brings us to something astonishing.
The God who told Ezekiel not to perform public mourning rituals is the same God who, in the person of Jesus Christ, stood before a grave and wept.
The Greek text of John 11:35 reads:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς (edakrysen ho Iēsous)
“Jesus wept.”
Two words in English.
An ocean of compassion.
Jesus knew He was about to raise Lazarus.
He knew the miracle was coming.
He knew that death would not hold His friend in that tomb.
Yet He wept.
He did not treat the grief of Mary and Martha as embarrassing.
He did not rebuke everyone for having emotions.
He entered their sorrow.
And the tears of Jesus remind us that knowing God's power does not make human suffering insignificant.
But there is an even deeper connection between Ezekiel's story and the Gospel.
Ezekiel's wife was called the delight of his eyes.
Jerusalem's sanctuary was also described as the delight of the people's eyes.
Then, centuries later, Jesus stood in the shadow of Jerusalem's coming judgment and spoke about the temple's destruction.
He also wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41–44).
He knew what was coming.
He knew that judgment was real.
And He grieved over the city.
The God revealed in Jesus Christ is not indifferent to human sorrow.
His holiness is real.
His judgment is real.
And so is His compassion.
We must not erase any of those truths to make the Bible more comfortable.
Yet the Gospel takes us beyond Ezekiel's grief.
It leads us to the cross.
There, the sinless Son of God willingly bore the judgment deserved by sinners.
Isaiah had foretold the suffering Servant:
“Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows.”
— Isaiah 53:4, KJV
And the apostle Peter explained:
“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree.”
— 1 Peter 2:24, KJV
Ezekiel's suffering was a prophetic sign announcing judgment.
Jesus' suffering was the saving sacrifice through which forgiveness and reconciliation are offered to sinners.
Those are not identical assignments.
Ezekiel did not atone for Israel's sins through his wife's death.
His wife was not a sacrifice for the nation.
The text does not say that God needed her death to purchase anyone's redemption.
That belongs to Christ alone.
But Ezekiel's painful sign forces us to reckon with the seriousness of sin and judgment.
And the cross reveals the astonishing depth of God's mercy toward sinners.
At Calvary, Jesus did not merely announce that judgment was serious.
He bore sin's penalty for His people.
He was mocked.
Rejected.
Wounded.
Crucified.
And buried.
But the grave could not hold Him.
On the third day, He rose.
And because Jesus lives, the story of everyone who trusts in Him does not have to end in condemnation.
That is why the Gospel is not simply advice for becoming a better person.
It is good news for people who cannot save themselves.
The person trapped in secret sin.
The believer whose heart has grown cold.
The husband who has failed his family.
The wife carrying wounds nobody sees.
The churchgoer who knows the right words but has drifted far from genuine fellowship with God.
The grieving person who can barely pray.
The one who has made a public mess of life and quietly wonders whether redemption is still possible.
Listen carefully.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot undo every consequence of sin.
You cannot resurrect the years you wasted.
But Jesus Christ can forgive sins, reconcile you to God, and begin transforming the life you thought was beyond redemption.
And He does not do it because you deserve another chance.
He does it by grace.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.”
— Ephesians 2:8, KJV
That is the heart of everything we mean when we say:
Not that every earthly tragedy immediately becomes a happy ending.
Not that repentance erases all consequences.
Not that Christians never suffer.
But that Jesus can bring forgiveness where there was guilt, reconciliation where there was separation from God, and eternal hope where death seemed to have spoken the final word.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question in Ezekiel 24 is not why Ezekiel was forbidden to mourn publicly.
Perhaps it is this:
What have we been trusting instead of God?
The people treasured the temple.
But many had turned away from the Lord of the temple.
They cherished what represented His presence while resisting His commands.
And it is possible for us to repeat the same mistake in different clothing.
We can trust our religious background.
Our ministry position.
Our years of church attendance.
Our reputation for being a good person.
Our knowledge of Scripture.
Even our generosity.
But none of those things can cleanse the human heart.
Only Christ saves.
And true faith does not merely admire Jesus from a distance.
It turns toward Him in repentance and trust.
Maybe you have been hiding something.
Maybe your prayer life has become a performance.
Maybe you are exhausted from pretending that everything is fine.
Maybe you have been carrying guilt so long that you no longer remember what peace feels like.
Or maybe your struggle is not rebellion at all.
Maybe you are simply grieving.
You have lost someone you love.
You are trying to understand why God allowed something that broke your heart.
And this passage has frightened you because you wondered whether God expects you to remain silent about your pain.
Hear this with the tenderness Scripture allows.
Ezekiel 24 does not give anyone permission to shame you for crying.
You are not disobeying God because you miss someone.
You are not spiritually inferior because grief returns unexpectedly.
And you do not need to manufacture happiness to prove your faith.
Bring your sorrow to Christ.
Bring your questions.
Bring the prayers that sound more like groaning than beautiful sentences.
The Savior who wept at Lazarus's tomb is not embarrassed by your tears.
And the Savior who conquered death offers a hope that reaches beyond the cemetery.
Revelation 21:4 promises that God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of His redeemed people, and that death, sorrow, crying, and pain will finally pass away.
That promise does not mean we are spared every loss today.
It means loss does not get the final chapter.
And if you are reading this while feeling far from God, do not wait until you have cleaned up your life to come to Jesus.
Come honestly.
Confess your sins.
Turn from what you know is wrong.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Ask Him for the grace to follow Him.
He does not promise an easy life.
He promises Himself.
And He is enough to sustain His people even when they cannot understand everything He permits.
There is another part of Ezekiel's story that deserves our attention.
God told Ezekiel that he would be a sign to the people, and that when the announced events came to pass, they would know that He is the LORD (Ezekiel 24:24).
The prophet's obedience was not an advertisement for Ezekiel's greatness.
It was meant to direct attention to God.
That should challenge every Christian ministry—including ours.
If a ministry makes people admire its personality more than Jesus, something has gone wrong.
If we build a platform but neglect the Gospel, we have missed our calling.
If we persuade people to give money but fail to teach them the truth of Scripture, we have betrayed their trust.
Our purpose at Gospel Warrior is not to make people dependent on a page.
It is to help people know Jesus Christ more deeply, understand His Word more faithfully, and live out their faith with conviction, humility, courage, and love.
That is why we continue creating and sharing Scripture-centered teaching, devotional reflections, and discipleship resources.
It is a practical way to participate in this ministry's mission.
But we also want to be biblically clear.
It does not purchase salvation, forgiveness, healing, or spiritual blessing.
Scripture teaches:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Giving should flow from gratitude and love, never spiritual pressure.
But if you believe in this mission and have the means to help, your partnership can make a meaningful difference in keeping it going and helping it reach others.
And beyond that, we want you to have opportunities to grow in the Word—not merely consume inspirational content.
These free resources are part of our desire to help equip believers, encourage families, and make sound Christian teaching more accessible.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
But because someone in your circle may be silently wrestling with grief, disappointment, spiritual compromise, or questions about God's character.
Someone may have read Ezekiel 24 and walked away believing God was cruel.
Someone may be grieving a spouse and wondering whether their tears offend Him.
Someone may be hiding behind religious activity while their heart is far from Christ.
And someone may simply need to hear that Jesus still welcomes repentant sinners.

Because there may come a day when you need to return to the reminder that Scripture does not demand emotional numbness from grieving believers—and that God's warnings must never be separated from the mercy revealed in Jesus Christ.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something personal.
Not a question designed to make you look spiritual.
A question that deserves an honest answer.
When you read about Ezekiel losing the delight of his eyes, what moved you most?
Was it his obedience?
Was it the seriousness of God's warning?
Was it the realization that even faithful servants of God can experience terrible grief?
Or was it the comfort of remembering that Jesus Himself wept?
If you are grieving, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.”
If you have been trusting religious appearances more than Christ, you can comment, “Lord, bring me back.”
If you are still holding on to Jesus through a season you do not understand, comment, “I'm still trusting Christ.”
And if you have a testimony of how God's grace met you in grief, repentance, or restoration, consider sharing it. Your story may encourage someone who feels completely alone.
You do not have to reveal private details to be honest.
Sometimes a few sincere words are enough.
Because there is something beautiful about believers carrying one another's burdens rather than pretending none of us have any.
And now, before we close, return with me to that small, devastating sentence in Ezekiel 24:18.
“I spake unto the people in the morning: and at even my wife died.”
The morning began with a prophet delivering God's Word.
The evening ended with a husband losing the delight of his eyes.
And the next morning, he obeyed.
We are not told that he understood everything.
We are not told that obedience removed his pain.
We are not told that he ever stopped missing her.
But his life became a sign that God was speaking, that judgment was approaching, and that His people could no longer treat His warnings lightly.
Centuries later, another morning would arrive after another terrible death.
The body of Jesus had been placed in a tomb.
His followers had watched their hopes collapse.
The One they loved had been crucified.
But that morning was not like any other.
The tomb was empty.
Jesus Christ had risen.
And the resurrection declared that sin and death would not have the final victory over those who belong to Him.
Ezekiel's story reminds us that God's judgment is not something to dismiss.
Jesus' resurrection reminds us that God's grace is not something to underestimate.
So do not harden your heart when Scripture confronts you.
Do not run from Christ because you are ashamed.
Do not assume your tears disqualify you from faith.
And do not confuse the silence of a grieving person with the absence of God's compassion.
Come to Jesus.
Come with repentance.
Come with faith.
Come with the truth about your life.
Because the One who bore our sins is also the risen Savior who will one day make all things new.
And perhaps this is the sentence someone needs to carry into the night:
Ezekiel was told to mourn without public tears, but in Jesus Christ we meet a Savior who wept—and who rose again so that sorrow would never have the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HIS SON TRIED TO KILL HIM. THEN DAVID CRIED THE WORDS THAT BROKE A KING.
paragraphs: HIS SON TRIED TO KILL HIM. THEN DAVID CRIED THE WORDS THAT BROKE A KING.
Why did David mourn Absalom after his rebellion? The heartbreaking truth behind 2 Samuel 18:33—and what a father's grief reveals about sin, love, regret, and the greater grace of Jesus Christ.
He stole his father's throne.
He turned a nation against him.
He forced his own father to flee for his life.
And when the news finally arrived that the rebellion was over, the king should have celebrated.
His enemies were defeated. His kingdom was being restored. His soldiers had won.
But David did not celebrate.
He climbed into a room above the city gate, trembling, and began to weep.
And what came out of his mouth was not the cry of a victorious king.
It was the cry of a broken father.
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!” — 2 Samuel 18:33 (KJV)
Read those words again.
Not as a Bible verse you have heard before.
Hear them as the voice of a father who knows that his son is never coming home.
There is something devastating about those words.
David did not say, “The traitor is dead.”
He did not say, “Justice has been served.”
He did not say, “My throne is finally safe.”
He said, “My son.”
Again.
And again.
And again.
The very son who wanted his crown was the son David wished he could have died for.
Why?
Why would a father mourn someone who had deliberately tried to destroy him?
And why would Scripture preserve this terrible moment instead of simply celebrating David's victory?
Because buried inside this story is a truth many of us would rather avoid.
Sometimes the person who has wounded you most deeply is still someone you desperately wish you could save.
And sometimes the consequences of sin become painfully clear only when it is too late to undo what has happened.
But to understand David's tears, we must go back.
Long before Absalom died in the forest, something was already dying inside his family.
David was a man after God's own heart, as Scripture describes him in 1 Samuel 13:14 and Acts 13:22.
But that did not mean David was a flawless father.
It did not mean his household was healthy.
And it certainly did not mean his decisions were free from devastating consequences.
David had committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged for Uriah's death. When the prophet Nathan confronted him, David confessed his sin, and Nathan declared that the LORD had put away his sin.
David was forgiven.
But forgiveness did not erase every earthly consequence.
Nathan warned that the sword would not depart from David's house (2 Samuel 12:10–13).
That warning did not make Absalom innocent of his own choices. It did, however, reveal that David's household would experience terrible consequences connected to his sin.
And then came another family tragedy.
Amnon, one of David's sons, sexually violated Tamar, Absalom's sister.
Tamar was left devastated.
Absalom was furious.
And David?
Scripture says he was very angry (2 Samuel 13:21).
But the biblical account does not describe David bringing Amnon to justice.
Imagine Tamar's suffering.
Imagine Absalom watching his sister carry the consequences of another man's wickedness while the family remained fractured.
Absalom eventually took revenge by arranging Amnon's murder.
That murder was evil. Tamar's suffering did not justify it.
Yet the family had already become a place where terrible wrongs, unresolved anger, and failed relationships were poisoning everything.
Absalom fled.
Years passed.
And even after he returned to Jerusalem, he was kept from seeing his father's face for two more years.
When father and son finally met, David kissed him (2 Samuel 14:33).
But a kiss is not necessarily reconciliation.
Scripture does not tell us that their deeper wounds were healed.
And soon Absalom began plotting.
He stood near the city gate, listened to people's grievances, and presented himself as the man who would give them justice.
He was charming.
He was calculated.
He knew how to make people feel heard.
And slowly, the Bible says, he “stole the hearts of the men of Israel” (2 Samuel 15:6, KJV).
The Hebrew expression is striking:
וַיְגַנֵּב אַבְשָׁלוֹם אֶת־לֵב אַנְשֵׁי יִשְׂרָאֵל
Vaygannēv Avshalom et-lēv anshei Yisra'el.
Literally, Absalom stole the heart of the men of Israel.
The Hebrew verb comes from the root גנב (ganav), meaning “to steal.”
Absalom was not simply gaining popularity.
He was taking loyalty that belonged to the king and turning it toward himself.
Eventually, his rebellion became open warfare.
David fled Jerusalem.
The father who once ran from Saul was now running from his own son.
Think about that.
David had survived lions and bears.
He had faced Goliath.
He had endured Saul's attempts to kill him.
He had fought battles that terrified entire armies.
But now the danger was coming from someone he had once held as a child.
Someone whose first steps he may have watched.
Someone whose name he had spoken with affection long before that name became associated with betrayal.
The Bible does not record those childhood memories. But it does record enough to show us that David's heart was not untouched by the son who rebelled against him.
And here is where the story becomes almost unbearable.
Before the battle, David gave his commanders an extraordinary order.
“Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom.” — 2 Samuel 18:5 (KJV)
Not “Destroy him.”
Not “Make an example of him.”
Not “Bring me his head.”
Deal gently.
For my sake.
Even with Absalom.
David knew his son was dangerous.
He knew the rebellion had to be stopped.
He knew people had already suffered because of Absalom's ambition.
Yet David wanted his son spared.
That is one of the painful tensions in this account.
David was responsible for protecting a kingdom.
But he was also a father who loved his son.
The king needed the rebellion to end.
The father wanted Absalom to live.
And those two desires were about to collide.
During the battle in the forest of Ephraim, Absalom rode beneath a great oak, and his head became caught in its branches. His mule continued onward, leaving him suspended.
He was helpless.
Joab, David's commander, learned what had happened.
He knew David had commanded the army to deal gently with Absalom.
But Joab chose otherwise.
He thrust three darts into Absalom while he was still alive, and Joab's armor-bearers finished killing him (2 Samuel 18:14–15).
The rebellion was crushed.
The threat to David's throne was removed.
But a son was dead.
And David did not yet know.
When the messengers approached, David asked the question that revealed what mattered most to him.
“Is the young man Absalom safe?” — 2 Samuel 18:32 (KJV)
Not, “How many enemies died?”
Not, “Did we recover the throne?”
Not, “Is my kingdom secure?”
Is Absalom safe?
The messenger's answer made the truth clear.
Absalom was dead.
And then David broke.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 18:33 begins:
וַיִּרְגַּז הַמֶּלֶךְ
Vayyirgaz hammelekh.
“The king was deeply shaken.”
The verb רגז (ragaz) carries the sense of trembling, shaking, or being disturbed. In this context, it conveys David's profound emotional upheaval.
Then comes the cry:
בְּנִי אַבְשָׁלוֹם בְּנִי בְנִי אַבְשָׁלוֹם
Beni Avshalom, beni, beni Avshalom.
“My son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom.”
That repeated word is בְּנִי (beni).
“My son.”
David does not address Absalom as a rebel.
He does not address him as a political enemy.
He calls him his son.
And then comes the sentence that makes this account so unforgettable:
מִי־יִתֵּן מוּתִי אֲנִי תַחְתֶּיךָ
Mi-yitten muti ani tahtekha.
“Oh, that I had died instead of you.”
The Hebrew expression תַחְתֶּיךָ (tahtekha) means “in your place” or “instead of you.”
David wished he could have taken his son's place in death.
Pause there.
Because that is the center of this tragedy.
Absalom wanted David's throne.
David wished he could have taken Absalom's death.
Absalom was willing to destroy his father to become king.
David was willing, at least in the anguish of his grief, to imagine dying instead of the son who betrayed him.
That does not make Absalom's rebellion righteous.
It does not make David's parenting perfect.
It does not mean David's emotional response was beyond criticism.

In fact, the next chapter tells us that David's public grief became so overwhelming that his victorious soldiers felt ashamed. Joab confronted him because the men who had risked their lives for David needed their king to acknowledge their sacrifice (2 Samuel 19:1–8).
Scripture allows us to see both truths.
David's grief was real.
And his grief also affected people who had faithfully defended him.
The Bible does not flatten human beings into heroes who never fail or villains who never suffer.
It shows us people as they are.
Complicated.
Wounded.
Responsible for their choices.
And desperately in need of God's mercy.
Perhaps that is why this story feels so personal.
Because some people reading this know what it is to love someone who has hurt them.
A parent whose child has walked away from the faith.
A mother who prays for a son who no longer answers her calls.
A father who regrets words he cannot take back.
A husband or wife grieving the destruction of a relationship.
A son or daughter carrying wounds from a parent who should have protected them.
Or perhaps you are the Absalom in someone's story.
You know what it means to become angry.
To feel overlooked.
To let resentment grow.
To convince yourself that your pain gives you permission to hurt others.
You have justified things you once knew were wrong.
You have pushed away people who loved you.
You have allowed bitterness to become part of your identity.
And maybe the most frightening thing is that you have become so accustomed to defending yourself that you no longer know how to repent.
Listen carefully.
Your pain may explain some of your choices, but it cannot make sin righteous.
Absalom had real reasons to be distressed by the evil that had taken place in his family.
But he was still accountable for murder, deception, and rebellion.
David had genuine love for his son.
But love did not erase his own failures.
And that is one of the hardest truths Scripture teaches.
We can be wounded and still wound others.
We can love deeply and still fail terribly.
We can be forgiven by God and still need to face the consequences of our actions.
We can be right about the evil someone has done to us and still be wrong about how we respond.
But there is another truth.
One that reaches beyond the tragedy of David's household.
The story of David and Absalom makes us long for a better King.
David cried, “Oh, that I had died instead of you.”
But David could not undo Absalom's death.
He could not go back and rewrite his family's history.
He could not save his son by wishing he had died in his place.
His cry was the cry of a grieving father, not an accomplished act of redemption.
And this is where we must be careful with Scripture.
David is not Jesus.
Absalom is not a direct biblical symbol of every sinner.
And 2 Samuel 18:33 does not explicitly present David's lament as a prophecy of the cross.
Yet when we read this passage within the larger story of Scripture, David's helpless wish reminds us of something extraordinary that God actually accomplished through Jesus Christ.
David wished he could die in the place of his rebellious son.
Jesus Christ willingly died for sinners.
The difference is immeasurable.
David's words were spoken after Absalom had died.
Jesus gave His life in history, according to the Father's saving purpose, to redeem those who would otherwise perish in their sins.
David was a sinful father grieving a sinful son.
Jesus is the sinless Son of God who gave Himself for sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
Not after we made ourselves worthy.
Not after we repaired every relationship.
Not after we cleaned up every secret.
While we were yet sinners.
The Greek text says:
ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανεν
Eti hamartōlōn ontōn hēmōn, Christos hyper hēmōn apethanen.
“While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
The phrase ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν (hyper hēmōn) means “for us” or “on our behalf.”

That phrase alone should not be made to carry every detail of the doctrine of substitution. But within the wider teaching of the New Testament, Christ's death is clearly presented as a saving sacrifice for sinners.
First Peter 3:18 says:
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.” (KJV)
The just for the unjust.
The righteous for the unrighteous.
Not because rebellion is harmless.
Not because sin does not matter.
But because God's grace is greater than anything sinners could earn.
At the cross, God did not pretend evil was good.
He dealt with sin through the sacrifice of His Son.
Jesus bore our sins, died, and rose again.
And because He lives, forgiveness and new life are offered to those who turn to Him in repentance and faith.
This is the Gospel.
Not merely that God feels sorry for broken people.
Not merely that Jesus understands emotional pain.
But that the crucified and risen Christ saves sinners and reconciles them to God.
And suddenly, David's grief points our attention toward an even greater question.
If an imperfect earthly father could feel such anguish over a rebellious son, how seriously should we take the love God has revealed in sending His own Son to save the lost?
Remember the parable Jesus told in Luke 15.
A younger son demanded his inheritance, left his father's house, and wasted his possessions in reckless living.
He ended up hungry, humiliated, and desperate.
Eventually, he came to himself.
He decided to return.
Not with excuses.
Not with demands.
But with confession.
“Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee.” — Luke 15:18 (KJV)
And while he was still a great way off, his father saw him.
He had compassion.
He ran.
He embraced him.
He kissed him.
The son who had disgraced the household was welcomed home.
Not because his rebellion was acceptable.
But because he returned in repentance and received mercy.
Do you see the contrast?
Absalom's story ends with a father mourning a son who died in rebellion.
Jesus' parable shows a father rejoicing over a son who returns.
And the Gospel reveals the Savior through whom repentant sinners can truly be reconciled to God.
One story leaves us hearing a father's cry.
The other invites us to hear a father's welcome.
And Christ makes that welcome possible.
Maybe you have spent years running.
Not necessarily from a church building.
Not necessarily from religious people.
But from God.
You still know the songs.
You still remember the verses.
But there are places in your life you have refused to surrender.
An addiction you keep protecting.
A relationship you know is leading you away from obedience.
A secret sin you have learned to hide.
A bitterness you continue feeding.
A pride that makes confession feel unbearable.
And you tell yourself, “I'll deal with it later.”
Later, when life is less complicated.
Later, when the temptation is weaker.
Later, when you feel more spiritual.
Later, when no one will be disappointed.
But Absalom's story reminds us of something sobering.
We are not promised unlimited tomorrows.
That is not a reason to panic.
It is a reason to stop treating repentance as something that can always wait.
Do not wait for a tragedy to teach you the value of a relationship you could begin repairing today.
And do not wait until your heart grows harder before responding to the grace of God.
If you have wronged someone, confess it.
If restitution is possible and appropriate, pursue it.
If you have wounded your children, do not hide behind your authority.
If you have dishonored your parents, consider what genuine repentance requires.
If someone has abused or endangered you, remember that forgiveness does not require returning to an unsafe situation or abandoning wise boundaries.
Reconciliation, where possible, involves truth, repentance, safety, and restored trust—not pretending that evil never happened.
And if you have wandered from Jesus, come to Him.
Not because you have finally made yourself acceptable.
But because He is merciful and mighty to save.
First John 1:9 reminds believers:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is new life in Christ.
And there is hope even for people whose stories contain chapters they wish had never been written.
This does not mean every broken family will be restored in this life.
It does not mean every estranged child will return.
It does not mean every grieving parent will receive the earthly ending they prayed for.
We must not promise what Scripture has not promised.
But we can proclaim what God has promised.
Jesus Christ is able to save those who come to God through Him (Hebrews 7:25).
He receives those who come to Him (John 6:37).
And nothing in all creation can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Him (Romans 8:38–39).
That is a hope stronger than sentiment.
It is hope anchored in the finished work and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Perhaps tonight, somewhere, a father is awake wondering where he failed.
A mother is staring at a photograph of a child who no longer speaks to her.
A young adult is carrying resentment that has been growing for years.
Someone is grieving a person with whom they never had the chance to make peace.
And someone else is quietly wondering whether God could still receive them after everything they have done.
If that person is you, hear this.
Your story is not beyond the reach of Christ.
Your past cannot be changed.
But your future does not have to remain enslaved to it.
The cross does not make sin insignificant.
It reveals how serious sin is—and how astonishing God's mercy is.
The resurrection declares that death does not have the final word over those who belong to Jesus.
And repentance is not the death of hope.
It is the turning of a sinner toward the Savior who gives life.
Maybe you need to pray right now.

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I have defended what I should have confessed. I have carried wounds that I do not know how to heal. Forgive me. Teach me to repent without excuses, to forgive without denying the truth, and to obey You even when it is difficult. Where relationships can be restored, give me humility and wisdom. Where they cannot, teach me to entrust my grief to You. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. I place my hope in Your mercy, not my own goodness. Make me new. Amen.”
Not as a religious performance.
Not to impress anyone.
But as an honest response before God.
What part of David and Absalom's story touched the place in your heart you rarely talk about?
Was it the pain of a parent?
The regret of a child?
The danger of bitterness?
The ache of unfinished reconciliation?
Or the realization that Jesus Christ loved sinners enough to die for them?
And please do not let this message stop with you.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is someone who needs to remember that rebellion has consequences, that repentance matters, and that the mercy of Jesus Christ is real.
Not to chase attention.
But to place the truth of Scripture where someone might encounter it at the moment they need it.

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have grown distant from their faith, and even those who do not yet believe to follow along. Every person deserves the opportunity to hear the truth of the Gospel.
There is also something I want to share with those who believe in this ministry's mission.
Gospel Warrior exists to help people encounter God's Word, understand the Gospel, and grow in their walk with Jesus Christ.
These resources are intended to help believers go deeper in Scripture, strengthen their faith, and continue learning about Jesus Christ beyond a single article.
Keeping that work going—and reaching more people—requires time, effort, and resources.
It is a voluntary way to help sustain and expand the work, develop more biblical resources, and continue making free discipleship materials available to people who need them.
And biblical giving is to be willing, not pressured.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
If you already give faithfully through your local church or support other ministries, continue exercising wisdom and prayerful stewardship.
These are simply expressions of gratitude for those who choose to walk alongside this ministry.
The greater purpose remains unchanged.
To lift up Jesus Christ.
To proclaim His Word faithfully.
To call sinners to repentance.
To encourage the weary.
To strengthen believers.
Because the mission is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The mission is to make Jesus known.
One more time, return to that room above the city gate.
See David climbing the stairs.
Hear his footsteps.
Imagine the silence before the sobbing begins.
The kingdom has been saved.
The battle has been won.
But David is calling out for a son who will never answer.
“My son Absalom.”
“My son.”
“My son.”
It is one of Scripture's most painful portraits of human love, failure, and loss.
And it leaves us with a question worth carrying into our own lives.
What are we doing with the people God has placed before us while we still have time to love them, tell them the truth, seek forgiveness, and pursue peace?
More importantly, what are we doing with the invitation of Jesus Christ?
David could not bring Absalom back from the dead.
But Jesus Christ rose from the dead.
David could only wish that he had died in his son's place.
But Jesus actually gave His life for sinners and conquered the grave.
And while David's story ends in the sorrow of a father who could not save his son, the Gospel announces a Savior who can bring lost sinners home to God.
So come to Christ.
Come with your regrets.
Come with your confession.
Come with the wounds you cannot explain.
Come with the sins you can no longer justify.
Come in repentance and faith.
Do not confuse His patience with permission to keep running.
And do not confuse your failures with proof that His mercy is beyond your reach.

The most heartbreaking words in David's story were “I wish I had died instead of you.” The most hope-filled truth of the Gospel is that Jesus Christ did die for sinners—and rose again so that those who trust in Him may live.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN YOU LUST AFTER YOUR OWN SPOUSE? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE SOMETHING YOUR WEDDING VOWS NEVER FIXED.
paragraphs: CAN YOU LUST AFTER YOUR OWN SPOUSE? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE SOMETHING YOUR WEDDING VOWS NEVER FIXED.

You can wear a wedding ring, share a marriage bed, and still misunderstand what God intended intimacy to be. Because marriage makes sexual union honorable, but it does not make selfishness holy. And sometimes the deepest betrayal in a marriage begins long before anyone commits adultery.
There is a question many Christians have never dared to ask out loud.
Not because the Bible is silent about sexuality.
But because the answer might force us to examine something we have spent years defending.
Can you actually lust after the person God has given you permission to love?
Think carefully before answering.
Because somewhere tonight, a wife is lying beside her husband, wondering why she feels more like an obligation than someone cherished.
Somewhere else, a husband is quietly struggling with rejection, wondering whether his desire for his wife makes him selfish.
Somewhere, a Christian couple has stopped talking about intimacy because every conversation ends in guilt, frustration, tears, or silence.
And somewhere, a believer is convinced that because the person they desire is their lawful spouse, everything they want must automatically be righteous.
But what if the real question is not simply whether you desire your spouse?
What if the question is what your desire is doing to the person you promised before God to love?
Because there is a difference between wanting to be close to someone and wanting to consume them.
There is a difference between longing for intimacy and demanding access.
There is a difference between a desire that says, "I want to give myself to you," and an appetite that says, "You exist to satisfy me."
And Scripture makes that difference impossible to ignore.
Jesus said in Matthew 5:28:
"But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart." (KJV)
Those words should make us tremble—not because sexual attraction is inherently dirty, but because Jesus refuses to separate the outward act from the inward condition of the heart.
In the original Greek, the expression translated "to lust after her" includes the phrase πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn).
The verb epithymeō means to desire, long for, or covet. Depending on the context, that desire may be good or sinful.
That distinction matters enormously.
The Greek word itself does not mean that every experience of sexual attraction is wicked.
In fact, the same family of Greek words appears in Luke 22:15, where Jesus speaks of His earnest desire to eat the Passover with His disciples.
Desire itself is not automatically sin.
What matters is its object, its intention, and whether it submits to God's will.

In Matthew 5, Jesus is confronting a deliberately cultivated desire that violates faithfulness. He is exposing the heart behind adultery, not declaring that a husband sins whenever he is sexually attracted to his wife.
That would contradict the very Scriptures that celebrate marital desire.
And this is where we must be careful.
Matthew 5:28 does not directly teach that desiring your own spouse is adultery. But the rest of Scripture absolutely challenges selfish, degrading, coercive, and unloving behavior within marriage.
A wedding covenant does not turn every attitude into holiness.
A marriage certificate cannot sanctify cruelty.
And a wedding ring is not a license to disregard another person's dignity.
Now consider something beautiful.
Proverbs 5:18–19 tells a husband to rejoice in the wife of his youth and to be continually satisfied with her love.
The Hebrew text uses the language of delight and deep affection. The word אַהֲבָה (ahavah) means love, and the passage speaks openly and positively about the joy of marital intimacy.
God is not embarrassed by the desire He designed.
He is not standing in heaven condemning a husband for finding his wife beautiful.
He is not shaming a wife for longing for her husband's affection, touch, or closeness.
Read the Song of Solomon.
There is longing.
There is admiration.
There is romantic pursuit.
There is the unmistakable celebration of physical beauty and marital love.
Song of Solomon 7:10 declares:
"I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me." (KJV)
The Hebrew word translated "desire" is תְּשׁוּקָה (teshuqah), a word associated with strong longing or desire.
Here, that desire appears in the setting of mutual romantic affection.
The beloved does not speak as though being desired is automatically degrading.
She delights in being loved.
This is important because some Christians have been taught to feel guilty for experiencing sexual attraction even within marriage.
They have confused purity with the absence of passion.
They have mistaken holiness for emotional distance.
They have carried shame into a relationship where God intended covenant love, tenderness, faithfulness, and joy.
But God did not create marriage so two people could spend their lives apologizing for finding each other attractive.
Hebrews 13:4 says:
"Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge." (KJV)
The marriage bed is not inherently shameful.
Faithful marital intimacy is not spiritual contamination.
And physical affection does not become sinful simply because it is intense.
But now comes the part that may be uncomfortable.
Just because desire belongs in marriage does not mean every expression of desire honors marriage.
Imagine a husband who approaches his wife with affection only when he wants sex.
He barely listens when she speaks.
He dismisses her exhaustion.
He ignores her emotional pain.
He offers tenderness when he expects something in return, but withdraws it when she says she is not ready.
Eventually, she begins to wonder whether he loves her or merely loves what she can provide.
Or imagine a wife who uses intimacy as a tool to punish, manipulate, humiliate, or control her husband.
His vulnerabilities become weapons.
His longing for affection becomes something she exploits.
Neither situation reflects the self-giving love Scripture commands.
The problem is not that either spouse experiences sexual desire.
The problem is that desire has become detached from love.
And when desire becomes a justification for pressure, manipulation, or disregard, something has gone terribly wrong.
Marriage does not erase personhood.
Your spouse is not a possession.
Your spouse is not a reward for your religious performance.
Your spouse is not a machine designed to meet your needs whenever you press the right buttons.
Your spouse is a human being created in the image of God.
Someone with fears.
Someone with wounds.
Someone with a body that can become tired.
Someone with emotions that can become overwhelmed.
Someone who needs to feel safe, respected, and cherished.
Someone Christ calls you to love—not merely someone you are permitted to desire.
Ephesians 5:25 says:
"Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it." (KJV)
Read those words again.
Gave himself.
Not demanded everything.
Not exercised selfish control.
Not insisted that his own desires always come first.
Gave himself.
The Greek verb παρέδωκεν (paredōken), translated "gave," comes from paradidōmi, meaning to hand over or give up. In this verse, it describes Christ's self-giving sacrifice.
That is the model Paul places before husbands.
And it is a model that confronts every selfish instinct within us.
Christ did not love His church by exploiting her vulnerability.
He gave Himself for her good.
That does not mean marriage is devoid of sexual pleasure or that spouses must suppress every personal longing.
It means love must govern how those longings are expressed.
The question becomes painfully personal.
When you approach your spouse, do they experience your desire as affection or pressure?
When they are struggling, do you notice?
When they are hurting, do you listen?
When intimacy is difficult, do you seek understanding or immediately assign blame?
Can your spouse be honest with you without fearing punishment, humiliation, or retaliation?
And when your desires are not fulfilled, does your love remain recognizable?
These questions are not designed to shame married people for having sexual needs.
They are designed to expose the difference between mutual intimacy and selfish entitlement.
Because a person can desire their spouse sexually and still fail to love them sacrificially.
That truth should humble every one of us.
Perhaps you are reading this and realizing that you have sometimes approached your marriage more like a consumer than a covenant partner.
Perhaps your spouse has been trying to explain their pain for years, but you interpreted every conversation as rejection.
Perhaps you have been physically present while emotionally absent.
Or perhaps you are the spouse who has carried silent shame because someone convinced you that marriage meant surrendering your right to speak honestly about your own body.
Listen carefully.
God does not require you to call mistreatment holy.
Marriage is a covenant of faithfulness and love, not permission for sexual coercion or abuse.
First Corinthians 7:3–5 speaks about mutual marital responsibilities and warns against unilateral deprivation. But notice something often overlooked: Paul's instruction is reciprocal.
The husband has responsibilities toward the wife.
The wife has responsibilities toward the husband.
And in verse 5, Paul specifically speaks of abstaining for a time by mutual consent.
The Greek expression ἐκ συμφώνου (ek symphōnou) means by agreement or mutual consent.
That phrase matters.
The passage calls spouses toward mutual consideration, not forced compliance.
It must never be used to justify assault, intimidation, or the idea that a spouse loses bodily dignity after marriage.
Biblical mutuality does not erase the obligation to treat one another with patience, kindness, and honor.
And the call to marital faithfulness never authorizes abuse.
Now consider the other side.
What about the husband who deeply desires his wife but feels ashamed because he has heard that lust is always sinful?
What about the wife who feels drawn to her husband, yet worries that passionate attraction makes her spiritually impure?
They need to hear this too.
You do not have to repent for loving the beauty of the person you married.
You do not have to feel ashamed for longing for mutual physical closeness.
You do not have to treat your God-given capacity for attraction as though it were an enemy of holiness.
What you must surrender is the temptation to turn that attraction into selfishness, fantasy that violates faithfulness, pressure, objectification, or control.
There is a world of difference between saying, "You are beautiful, and I long to be close to you," and communicating, "Your feelings do not matter because I want what I want."
One honors the beloved.
The other reduces the beloved to a means of satisfaction.
And sometimes, that difference is revealed not when your spouse says yes, but when your spouse says no.
Can you still be gentle?
Can you still be affectionate?
Can you still be kind?
Can you remain faithful without turning disappointment into punishment?
Can you talk honestly about unmet needs without demanding, threatening, or manipulating?
Because love is not proven only in the moments when you receive what you desire.
Sometimes love becomes clearest in the moments when you choose another person's well-being over immediate gratification.
First Corinthians 13:5 says that love "seeketh not her own."
That does not mean loving spouses can never express their own needs.
It means biblical love is not ruled by selfish insistence.
And here is something else we must not ignore.
A marriage can suffer from sexual distance without either spouse being the villain.
Illness can change intimacy.
Trauma can affect trust.
Childbirth, exhaustion, grief, medication, disability, depression, unresolved conflict, and other burdens can make physical closeness complicated.
Sometimes couples need patient conversation.
Sometimes they need medical care.
Sometimes they need wise pastoral guidance or qualified marriage counseling.
Sometimes they need to rebuild emotional safety before physical intimacy can become joyful again.
And sometimes a person needs protection from abuse rather than another sermon telling them to try harder.
Not every painful marriage problem can be solved by quoting a verse and demanding immediate change.
God's Word calls us to truth.
And truth requires us to see people as they really are, including the wounds they carry.
But there is another wound this conversation must address.
Pornography.
Because some husbands and wives have unknowingly brought the expectations of pornography into their marriages.
They compare real human bodies to carefully manufactured images.
They expect constant availability.
They mistake performance for intimacy.
They grow dissatisfied with the very person they once prayed to marry.
And slowly, the spouse who was supposed to be cherished begins to feel inadequate.
This is one way sinful lust can corrupt marital intimacy.
Not because the spouse is the wrong person to desire.
But because desire has been trained to consume rather than cherish.
Pornography can cultivate habits of objectification, secrecy, comparison, and discontent that undermine marital trust.
And the solution is not to blame the spouse for failing to compete with fantasy.
The solution begins with truth, repentance, accountability, and renewed faithfulness.
Jesus said in Matthew 5:29–30 that we must deal radically with what leads us into sin.
His graphic language is a serious call to remove occasions of sin, not an instruction to physically injure ourselves.
For someone trapped in pornography, that may mean removing access, seeking accountability, confessing deception, and pursuing competent support.
For someone whose desire has become controlling, it may mean admitting that entitlement has been masquerading as love.
For someone whose marriage has become emotionally cold, it may mean finally listening instead of defending.
For someone who has been mistreated, it may mean seeking safety, trusted support, and appropriate professional help.
Repentance does not look identical in every marriage.
But it always requires honesty before God.
And perhaps this is where the Holy Spirit is speaking to someone reading these words.
You have defended your behavior by saying, "But we are married."
You have assumed that being legally entitled to a relationship means every demand within that relationship is righteous.
You have confused covenant privilege with personal ownership.
And now you are beginning to understand something.
The person you married is not merely someone you have the right to touch. They are someone you have the responsibility to love.
That truth changes everything.
It changes how you speak.
How you listen.
How you respond to vulnerability.
How you handle rejection.
How you pursue reconciliation.
How you confess sin.
How you treat the person who sees you when no one else does.
Because Christian marriage is not ultimately about proving that your desires are legitimate.
It is about learning to bring those desires under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And that is where the Gospel enters this conversation with extraordinary power.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our behavior.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to forgive what we cannot undo and transform what we cannot repair by our own strength.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we perfected our marriages.
Not after we conquered every selfish impulse.
Not after we became worthy of grace.
Christ died for us while we were sinners.
And that matters because some people reading this article are carrying regret.
You remember the night you spoke cruelly.
The time you ignored your spouse's tears.
The seasons when you treated intimacy like a transaction.
The secrecy you allowed to grow.
The bitterness you refused to confront.
The love you withheld.
The trust you broke.
And you wonder whether God can still restore someone like you.
The answer begins at the cross.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ for those who repent and trust in Him.
There is grace for the person who finally stops making excuses.
There is mercy for the believer who confesses sin rather than concealing it.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
But grace is not permission to keep harming someone.
Repentance is more than feeling guilty after reading a powerful article.
It bears fruit.
It tells the truth.
It accepts responsibility.
It stops blaming others.
It seeks help where needed.
It respects boundaries.
It makes restitution where possible.
It understands that broken trust may take time to rebuild.
And it does not demand immediate forgiveness, reconciliation, or renewed intimacy as proof that the injured person has obeyed God.
True repentance refuses to use the language of grace as another instrument of control.
That is how we know the Gospel is doing more than stirring emotion.
It is changing the direction of a life.
And maybe tonight, that transformation begins with one difficult sentence.
"I'm sorry. I have been thinking about what I want more than how you feel."
Or perhaps:
"I have been so afraid of being rejected that I stopped hearing your pain."
Or:
"I have confused physical closeness with emotional safety, and I want to learn how to love you better."
Or even:
"I need help, because what has been happening in our marriage is not healthy."
Those words may not solve everything overnight.
But honest confession can become the beginning of a different story.
A story where tenderness returns.
Where trust is rebuilt patiently.
Where forgiveness is sought without being demanded.
Where desire becomes an expression of love instead of a substitute for it.
Where two imperfect people learn that the marriage covenant was never meant to replace daily obedience to Christ.
And where, if a relationship is unsafe, the wounded person is supported in seeking protection rather than pressured into remaining in danger.
This is the beauty of the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely expose our sin.
He offers forgiveness and calls us into a new way of living.
Ephesians 4:22–24 speaks of putting off the old self, being renewed in the spirit of our minds, and putting on the new self created after God in righteousness and true holiness.
That transformation reaches even the most private places of our lives.
Even our marriages.
Even our desires.
Even the thoughts we have never confessed aloud.
So can you lust after your own spouse?
Here is the answer we must carry carefully.
Sexually desiring your spouse is not inherently sinful. Scripture celebrates faithful marital attraction, delight, and mutual intimacy.

But a person can express sexual desire within marriage in sinful ways—through selfishness, coercion, degrading treatment, objectification, manipulation, or a refusal to love the spouse as a whole person.
The biblical question is not whether passion exists.
It is whether passion is governed by covenant love, faithfulness, holiness, and the dignity of the person being loved.
Your spouse is not your enemy.
Desire is not automatically your enemy.
But sin is never your friend, even when it hides behind something God created good.
And the answer is not less Jesus in your marriage.
It is more surrender to Him.
More truth.
More compassion.
More humility.
More repentance.
More grace.
More love that actually looks like Christ.
If your spouse could describe how your desire makes them feel, what would they say?
Cherished?
Safe?
Beautiful?
Respected?
Or pressured, unseen, and alone?
And if you are the one who has been wounded, what would it look like to begin believing that your dignity matters to God too?
You do not have to answer publicly with details that belong in a safe and private conversation.
But perhaps you can take one honest step today.
Pray.
Listen.
Confess.
Seek help.
Forgive where forgiveness is possible.
Establish boundaries where boundaries are necessary.
And ask the Lord to teach you how to love without using another person.

If God has brought you through a season of brokenness and restoration, your testimony may encourage someone who has nearly given up. Share what you are comfortable sharing, without exposing your spouse's private struggles.
Not to publicly accuse your spouse.
Not to embarrass someone.
But because a biblical conversation about marriage may reach a person who has never heard these truths explained with both conviction and compassion.
Because what we are building is not simply another page filled with religious content.
Our prayer is to help people encounter the truth of God's Word, understand the Gospel, grow in discipleship, and find the courage to surrender what needs to change.
Scripture teaches the importance of cheerful, willing giving. Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver.
And that is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not from fear.
Not from guilt.
Not because God's favor can be purchased.
But if you believe in this mission and have the means to help, your partnership can make a genuine difference in sustaining and expanding the work.
We want the Word of God to reach people.
We want believers to be equipped.
We want marriages to be strengthened by truth rather than religious confusion.
We want the broken to hear about the Savior who forgives sinners and transforms lives.
We want those who are spiritually hungry to have resources that help them grow.
And we want every article, every book, every testimony, and every act of generosity to point beyond Gospel Warrior to Jesus Christ Himself.
A sincere comment may remind another believer that they are not alone in their struggle.
And that matters.
Because this article was never merely about sex.
It was about the human heart.
It was about the difference between possessing and cherishing.
Between taking and giving.
Between religious excuses and genuine repentance.
Between shame that drives people into hiding and grace that calls sinners into the light.
It was about a Savior who does not merely tell us what love should look like.
He showed us.
At the cross.
Where the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Where mercy met our guilt.
Where forgiveness was purchased by His blood.
Where the greatest expression of love was not selfish consumption, but sacrificial giving.
So tonight, when you look at the person you married, remember this.
They are not simply the answer to your longing.
They are a neighbor you are commanded to love.
A person whose dignity matters to God.
A soul whose well-being must never be sacrificed on the altar of your appetite.

And if your marriage has been damaged by sin, remember that Christ can change hearts, empower repentance, and guide people toward what is true and good. Restoration may require time, accountability, professional help, and, where necessary, safety and separation from harm. But no failure is beyond the reach of God's power to forgive the repentant sinner.
May your marriage never become a place where Scripture is used to justify selfishness.
May your desire never become louder than your compassion.
May your wedding vows be reflected not only in the promises you made before an altar, but in the way you treat one another when nobody else is watching.
And may Jesus Christ be glorified in the love you give, the truth you speak, the sins you confess, and the grace you learn to extend.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that your spouse might stop desiring you. It is that they might spend years being desired without ever feeling truly loved.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY WALKED PAST HIM FOR YEARS… UNTIL THE NAME OF JESUS CHANGED EVERYTHING
paragraphs: THEY WALKED PAST HIM FOR YEARS… UNTIL THE NAME OF JESUS CHANGED EVERYTHING
Why Did Peter and John Heal a Man at the Beautiful Gate? The Heartbreaking Truth of Acts 3:1–10—and the Miracle That Reveals What Jesus Really Came to Restore.
He was sitting at a gate called Beautiful.
But there was nothing beautiful about the life he was living.
Every morning, someone had to carry him.
Every evening, someone had to take him home.
He could hear footsteps approaching, watch people disappear into the temple, and listen to the sounds of worship coming from a place he had spent his entire life unable to walk into on his own.
He was surrounded by people going somewhere.
But he could not take a single step.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part of his story was not that he couldn't walk.
It was that he had learned to survive by asking for less than what God was about to give him.
He asked for money.
He received something money could never buy.
And what happened next was so extraordinary that the people who had seen him begging for years could hardly believe their eyes.
But there is something in this story that many of us miss.
Something about the gate.
Something about the hands that reached toward him.
Something about the Name Peter spoke.
And something about the way God sometimes interrupts a life that has become painfully familiar.
Because you can spend years sitting beside something called Beautiful while privately wondering whether anything beautiful will ever happen to you.
And then Jesus changes the story.
Not because you finally became worthy.
But because His grace was never limited by your circumstances.
Acts 3 begins quietly.
No thunder. No dramatic announcement. No crowd waiting for a miracle.
Just two disciples walking toward the temple.
Peter and John.
The same Peter who had denied knowing Jesus three times.
The same John who had stood near the cross while Jesus suffered.
Two men who had witnessed the crucifixion, encountered the risen Christ, and received the Holy Spirit.
Now they were going to pray.
Acts 3:1 tells us:
“Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour.” (KJV)
That was approximately three o'clock in the afternoon.
An ordinary hour of prayer.
An ordinary journey.
Until they encountered a man whose suffering had become part of the daily scenery.
Scripture says he had been lame from his mother's womb.
Not injured yesterday.
Not temporarily weakened.
He had never known what it felt like to stand on his own feet.
Acts 4:22 later reveals that he was more than forty years old.
Think about that.
More than four decades of living with a condition he did not choose.
More than four decades of dependence.
More than four decades of watching other people do what he could not.
And every day, he was carried to the temple gate called Beautiful to ask for alms.
We are not told his name.
We are not told whether he had a family of his own.
We are not told what he thought about God during those long years.
And we must be careful not to invent feelings Scripture never records.
But we do know something painfully human.
A person can become so accustomed to surviving that the possibility of a different tomorrow becomes difficult even to imagine.
Maybe you know something about that.
Perhaps you have prayed about the same problem for years.
Perhaps you have carried a private grief so long that people have stopped asking whether you are okay.
Perhaps you have learned how to smile in public while privately calculating how much more disappointment your heart can endure.
Or perhaps your struggle has nothing to do with physical suffering.
Maybe it is the shame of a sin you keep returning to.
The guilt of a decision you cannot undo.
The loneliness of a marriage that looks healthy in photographs.
The exhaustion of providing for a family while wondering who will ever notice that you are falling apart.
And you have become very good at surviving.
But surviving is not the same thing as being whole.
Then Peter and John approached.
The man did what he had probably done countless times before.
He asked for alms.
He expected a coin.
A little assistance.
Something to help him get through another day.
And Peter said something unusual.
“Look on us.” (Acts 3:4, KJV)
The man gave them his attention, expecting to receive something.
Then came the words that changed everything.
“Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk.” (Acts 3:6, KJV)
Read that again.
“In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk.”
Not in Peter's name.
Not in John's name.
Not through the power of religious reputation.
Not because these apostles possessed some independent supernatural ability.
In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth.
The Greek text of Acts 3:6 contains the extraordinary declaration:
Ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ Ναζωραίου
En tō onomati Iēsou Christou tou Nazōraiou.
“In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene.”
In the biblical context, acting in someone's name means acting under that person's authority, not merely pronouncing a religious formula.
Peter was not presenting himself as the source of the miracle.
He was bearing witness to the authority of the risen Jesus.
And later, when the astonished crowd gathered, Peter made that absolutely clear.
He asked:
“Why look ye so earnestly on us, as though by our own power or holiness we had made this man to walk?” (Acts 3:12, KJV)
There it is.
Peter refused to steal the glory.
He knew the difference between being used by God and being God.
And that difference matters more than ever.
Because we live in a world where people sometimes turn ministry into personal fame, spiritual gifts into entertainment, and suffering people into opportunities for attention.
But Peter pointed away from himself.
Toward Jesus.
The One whom the people had rejected.
The One whom God had raised from the dead.
The One whose name was now being proclaimed in the very city where He had been crucified.
The miracle was not a commercial for Peter's ministry.
It was a witness to the living Christ.
And this is where the story becomes even more powerful.
Peter did not simply speak.
Acts 3:7 says:
“And he took him by the right hand, and lifted him up: and immediately his feet and ankle bones received strength.” (KJV)
The Greek word translated “immediately” is παραχρῆμα (parachrēma).
It emphasizes that the strengthening happened at once.
Not after months of physical rehabilitation.
Not after a long process of learning to walk.
The passage describes an immediate act of divine healing.
And the next verse is breathtaking.
“And he leaping up stood, and walked, and entered with them into the temple, walking, and leaping, and praising God.” (Acts 3:8, KJV)
Walking.
Leaping.
Praising God.
The man who had been carried was now moving under his own strength.
The man who had been asking for alms was now offering praise.
The man who had spent years beside the gate was now entering the temple with Peter and John.
Notice where the story leads.
Not to Peter's personal glory.
Not to a fundraising spectacle.
Not to the man's financial prosperity.
To the worship of God.
And that is part of the answer to the question: Why did Peter and John heal this man?
Because Jesus Christ was continuing His work through His apostles by the power of the Holy Spirit.
The healing demonstrated that the crucified and risen Jesus was alive, powerful, and worthy of faith.
It became a public sign that opened the door for Peter to proclaim the Gospel.
And it showed that the mercy of God was not merely an idea to discuss.
It was something that could transform an actual human life.
But there is a detail here that deserves our attention.
The gate was called Beautiful.
In Greek, Acts 3:2 uses Ὡραίαν (Hōraian), a form of the word meaning “beautiful” or “lovely.”
Scholars differ about precisely which temple gate Luke intended, and the text does not identify its location beyond the name.
But the contrast is unforgettable.
A man whose life was marked by physical limitation sat daily at a gate known for beauty.
He could see a beautiful entrance.
But he could not walk through it unaided.
Then the name of Jesus was proclaimed.
And everything changed.
Not because the gate possessed special power.
Not because Peter discovered a secret technique.
But because the risen Christ was revealing His authority through a miraculous act of mercy.
And something else is worth noticing.
Peter and John were going to the temple at the hour of prayer.
They were not searching for a platform.
They were not staging an event.
They were simply following the rhythm of worship and prayer.
Yet God used that ordinary journey to accomplish something extraordinary.
That should challenge us.
How many opportunities to show the compassion of Christ have we walked past because we were too busy trying to do something important?
How many hurting people have become invisible to us because their suffering has become familiar?
How many times have we entered a place of worship without truly seeing the person suffering outside?
The man was not an interruption to their devotion.
He became the occasion for the power of Jesus to be displayed.
And there is a lesson here for the Church.
We must never become so fascinated with beautiful buildings, impressive programs, polished presentations, and growing audiences that we forget the human beings sitting at our gates.
People are not projects.
The poor are not props.
The suffering are not illustrations.
They are people made in the image of God.
People deserving dignity, compassion, and love.
And the Gospel does not authorize us to ignore their practical needs while offering religious words.
Peter gave what he had, acting in the authority of Christ.
We should give what we genuinely can—prayer, compassion, material assistance, encouragement, and faithful witness—without pretending we possess apostolic power at our command.
Because another truth must be protected.
This miracle does not mean every believer who remains sick lacks faith.
Scripture never teaches that all physical suffering will disappear immediately when someone believes strongly enough.
Paul himself spoke of a thorn in the flesh that was not removed despite repeated prayer (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).
And the final promise of complete restoration belongs to the new creation, when God will wipe away every tear and death, mourning, crying, and pain will be no more (Revelation 21:4).
We can pray boldly for healing.
We can believe God is able.
