I cannot promise you those things.
Scripture does not authorize me to promise you a specific financial outcome.
But I can tell you what the Gospel declares.
Jesus Christ died for sinners.
He rose again.
He calls us to repentance and faith.
He offers forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life to all who truly trust in Him.
And those who belong to Him are not abandoned to a meaningless existence, even when they walk through suffering.
This does not mean every hardship will disappear.
It means suffering does not get the final word over those who are in Christ.
And that is why our message has always been:
The scandal is not simply that people struggle financially.
The deeper scandal is that sinful humanity has rebelled against a holy God and cannot save itself.
The grace is that Jesus Christ willingly entered our broken world, bore our sins on the cross, and rose victorious from the grave.
He did not come merely to rewrite our financial circumstances.
He came to rewrite our eternal destiny.
From guilt to forgiveness.
From rebellion to reconciliation.
From spiritual death to new life.
From the shame of sin to the grace of redemption.
And through the ongoing work of His Spirit, He continues transforming those who belong to Him.
This is the true richness of the Gospel.
It is not a promise that every believer will become financially prosperous.
It is the astonishing reality that spiritually bankrupt sinners can become children of God through Jesus Christ.
And once you understand that, Philippians 4:19 begins to shine with its proper beauty.
“My God shall supply all your need…”
Not because you have earned His attention.
Not because you have given enough money.
Not because your faith is a tool for controlling heaven.
But because the God who cares for His people is rich in glory, wise in His provision, and faithful in Christ Jesus.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not as a test of your spirituality.
Not to make you feel guilty.
But because I believe there are people reading this who have been carrying a burden they have never spoken aloud.
Have you ever secretly wondered whether God had forgotten you because your prayers for provision seemed unanswered?
Have you ever felt ashamed because you were struggling financially while other Christians appeared to be flourishing?
Have you ever confused the absence of abundance with the absence of God's love?
You can simply write:
You do not have to reveal private details or explain your situation publicly.
Someone else may need to remember that God's care often arrives through the love and faithfulness of His people.
Let this become more than a comment section.
Let it become a place where believers encourage one another to trust Christ, practice generosity, and hold firmly to Scripture.
Because truth is worth passing on.
Not to win an argument.
Not to embarrass someone who has been taught differently.
But to help another soul discover the beauty of God's Word in its proper context.
Perhaps tonight, someone will open Philippians 4:19 with trembling hands.
Perhaps their bills will still be unpaid.
Perhaps their circumstances will still be painful.
But perhaps they will finally understand that their heavenly Father has never promised to become their servant.
He has invited them to trust Him as their God.
And perhaps they will stop asking whether they are loved only when life is comfortable.
Perhaps they will look again at the cross.
At the wounded Savior.
At the empty tomb.
And realize that God's greatest declaration of love was never written on a bank statement.
It was demonstrated in the sacrifice of His Son.
So pray for daily bread.
Work with diligence.
Give with wisdom.
Receive help with humility.
Help others when you are able.
Seek first the kingdom of God.
And when fear rises, return to the promise in its proper context.
God's riches are not exhausted by your need.
His wisdom is not defeated by your circumstances.
And His love for His children is not measured by their financial prosperity.
If you are trusting Christ today, remember this:
You may not possess everything you want.
You may still be waiting for what you need.
You may still be walking through a season you do not understand.
But the Savior who redeemed you is infinitely more precious than everything this world can offer.
And when you finally stand before Him, the greatest treasure of heaven will not be its streets of gold.
It will be the Lord Jesus Christ Himself.
You may still be waiting for God to change what is in your hands, while He is teaching your heart to treasure the One whose hands were pierced for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD TOLD ISAIAH TO TAKE OFF HIS CLOTHES—AND WALK INTO PUBLIC VIEW. THE REASON SHOULD TERRIFY EVERYONE WHO TRUSTS IN THE WRONG SAVIOR.
paragraphs: GOD TOLD ISAIAH TO TAKE OFF HIS CLOTHES—AND WALK INTO PUBLIC VIEW. THE REASON SHOULD TERRIFY EVERYONE WHO TRUSTS IN THE WRONG SAVIOR.

For three years, a prophet became a living warning. What God was exposing through Isaiah's humiliation was bigger than a nation's downfall—and the truth still confronts every heart that has mistaken temporary security for salvation.
Imagine waking up tomorrow morning and hearing God command you to do something that would cost you your reputation.
Not your money.
Not your comfort.
Your dignity.
Imagine walking through familiar streets while people stare. Neighbors whisper. Children point. People who once respected you begin questioning whether something has gone terribly wrong.
And you cannot defend yourself by explaining everything away.
Because the very thing making you uncomfortable is the message God has commanded you to carry.
Now imagine that this does not end after one embarrassing afternoon.
It continues for three years.
This is not a fictional story designed to make you emotional.
Something extraordinary happened to the prophet Isaiah.

And buried inside four verses of Scripture is a warning about misplaced trust, the humiliation of human pride, the danger of false security, and the mercy of a God who exposes what cannot save us before it destroys us.
But there is something we must understand before going any further.
God did not command Isaiah to do this because He enjoyed humiliating His servant.
Isaiah was being called to become a living prophecy.
And the people watching him were about to discover that the empire they trusted could not rescue them.
The frightening question is whether we are making the same mistake today.
Isaiah chapter 20 opens during a time of political anxiety.

Assyria was the dominant military power threatening the ancient Near East. Smaller nations were desperately searching for ways to survive. Alliances were being discussed. Rebellions were being encouraged. Egypt and Cush appeared to offer hope against Assyrian expansion.
To frightened people, that hope seemed reasonable.
After all, Egypt had history, resources, military strength, and an established reputation. Cush, the kingdom associated with the region south of Egypt, was also a significant political power.
When an empire threatens your future, another powerful nation can look like salvation.
But God saw something the people were refusing to see.
The help they were looking toward would itself be brought low.
And so God gave Isaiah a command that would make His warning impossible to ignore.
Isaiah 20:2 records:
"Go and loose the sackcloth from off thy loins, and put off thy shoe from thy foot. And he did so, walking naked and barefoot." (KJV)
Read that again.
The prophet was instructed to remove the sackcloth he was wearing and take off his footwear.
The Hebrew description includes the words עָרוֹם וְיָחֵף (ʿārôm wəyāḥēp̄), meaning "naked and barefoot."
But we must be careful not to exaggerate what Scripture does not explicitly settle.

The Hebrew word ʿārôm can describe nakedness, but in certain contexts it can also refer to someone stripped of ordinary outer clothing or insufficiently clothed. Scripture does not give us a detailed description of precisely how much clothing Isaiah retained.
Some interpreters understand Isaiah as completely naked. Others understand him as stripped of his prophetic outer garment, perhaps retaining a basic undergarment.
The text's unmistakable emphasis is not on sensational exposure.
It is on visible humiliation, vulnerability, and the condition of captives.
Isaiah was to look like someone who had lost the protection, status, and dignity that clothing and footwear ordinarily represented.
And that distinction matters.
Because the message was not about attracting attention to a prophet's body.
It was about confronting a nation's misplaced confidence.
Then comes the detail that makes the account even more unsettling.
Isaiah 20:3 says:
"And the LORD said, Like as my servant Isaiah hath walked naked and barefoot three years for a sign and wonder upon Egypt and upon Ethiopia." (KJV)
Three years.
The Hebrew expression is שָׁלֹשׁ שָׁנִים (šālōš šānîm).
Three years.
Not three minutes of embarrassment.
Not a single dramatic performance followed by applause.
A prophetic sign associated with an extraordinary period of time.

Scholars differ over whether Isaiah maintained this appearance continuously throughout the three years or performed the sign repeatedly during that period. The passage does not specify the exact frequency.
But the duration is unmistakably part of God's message.
For three years, the warning remained before the people.
And perhaps that is where the story begins to reach into our own lives.
Because sometimes the truth God is showing us is not something we fail to notice.
It is something we keep refusing to face.
We see the warning.
We hear the Word.
We recognize the danger.
And still we tell ourselves that the thing we are trusting will somehow save us.
The relationship that has become our identity.
The money that has become our peace.
The career that has become our worth.
The approval that has become our oxygen.
The religious appearance that has become our substitute for genuine repentance.
None of these things is necessarily evil in itself. Relationships, work, provision, and community can all be gifts from God.
But a gift becomes a dangerous refuge when we ask it to provide what only God can ultimately give.
And that was the spiritual crisis behind Isaiah's strange assignment.
The people were tempted to place their confidence in Egypt and Cush rather than the Lord.
They were measuring safety by armies, alliances, and political strength.
They could see military power.
They could not see the future.
God could.
And the future He announced was devastating.
Isaiah 20:4 declares:
"So shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptians prisoners, and the Ethiopians captives, young and old, naked and barefoot, even with their buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt." (KJV)
Suddenly, Isaiah's appearance becomes painfully clear.
He was portraying the condition of defeated captives.
People who had once belonged to proud and powerful nations would be marched away in disgrace.
The Hebrew text includes חֲשׂוּפַי שֵׁת (ḥăśūp̄ay šēt), describing exposed buttocks, an image of humiliating captivity.
This was not merely a prediction that a military campaign would go badly.
It was an announcement that the powers people considered impressive would be exposed as vulnerable.
The nations that appeared capable of protecting others would not even be able to protect themselves.
And the people who trusted them would be ashamed.
Isaiah 20:5–6 continues the warning, describing the dismay of those who had looked toward Cush and Egypt for deliverance.
Their question becomes haunting:
"How shall we escape?" (Isaiah 20:6, KJV)
There it is.
The question they should have asked before placing their hope in the wrong refuge.
How shall we escape?
Not when everything is comfortable.
Not when the army looks strong.
Not when the bank account is full.
Not when everyone is applauding.
But when the thing we depended upon can no longer hold us.
How shall we escape?
And if we are willing to be painfully honest, many of us know what it feels like to reach that moment.
You trusted someone who promised never to leave.
Then one day, they did.
You built your identity around a position, only to discover how quickly a title can disappear.
You believed financial stability would finally silence your anxiety, but every increase brought another fear of losing it.
You smiled through church services while quietly carrying sins you were terrified someone would discover.
You learned how to look spiritually strong while becoming increasingly exhausted inside.
You knew how to say, "God is good."
But you were struggling to surrender what you had made more important than God.
And the hardest part was not always losing something.
Sometimes the hardest part was realizing how much of your heart had belonged to it.
The most dangerous idol is not always the thing you openly worship. Sometimes it is the thing you secretly believe you cannot survive without.
That is why Isaiah's story matters.
It is not an invitation to laugh at an ancient prophet doing something unusual.
It is an invitation to examine the places where our own hearts have confused earthly security with divine salvation.
But we also need to be careful here.
Isaiah 20 does not teach that every painful experience is God publicly humiliating someone for hidden sin.
It does not teach that every financial loss, betrayal, illness, or hardship is punishment for misplaced trust.
And it certainly does not authorize anyone to imitate Isaiah's unusual prophetic act simply because they feel spiritually compelled to do something shocking.
Isaiah received a specific prophetic command for a specific historical purpose.
We are not free to turn that command into a universal religious practice.
The passage teaches us to take God's revealed warnings seriously, to recognize the limits of earthly power, and to place our ultimate confidence in Him.
And that brings us to the most important part of this story.
Because if we stop with Isaiah walking barefoot, we may leave with fear but miss the greater hope of Scripture.
Isaiah was a prophet who bore a visible sign of coming shame.
But centuries later, Jesus Christ would enter human history and willingly endure public shame to accomplish something Isaiah could never accomplish.
Not merely to announce judgment.
But to secure redemption.
Think about the contrast.
Isaiah's stripped appearance warned that powerful nations would be humiliated.
Jesus was stripped of His garments by Roman soldiers on the way to the cross.
Matthew 27:28 records that the soldiers stripped Him and placed a scarlet robe on Him.
Matthew 27:35 then records that they crucified Him and divided His garments.
The One who deserved all honor was mocked.
The One who had committed no sin was condemned.
The One through whom all things were created allowed Himself to be treated with contempt by His own creatures.
And unlike Isaiah, who portrayed the shame of coming captivity, Jesus endured the shame of crucifixion as part of His saving work.
Hebrews 12:2 says that Jesus, "for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame."
The Greek word translated "shame" is αἰσχύνη (aischynē).
It refers to disgrace or dishonor.
Jesus did not pretend the shame of the cross was pleasant.
He endured it.
And He endured it for the joy set before Him.
But we must not force Isaiah 20 into a prophecy it does not claim to be.
Isaiah's three-year sign was directly about Egypt, Cush, Assyria, and the danger of trusting political powers that could not deliver.
It was not explicitly written as a prediction of Jesus being stripped at Calvary.
The connection is a broader biblical contrast, not a claim that every detail of Isaiah's action secretly foretold the crucifixion.
Yet when we read Isaiah within the whole testimony of Scripture, the difference between human inability and divine salvation becomes breathtaking.
Isaiah exposed the helplessness of nations.
Jesus reveals the saving power of God.
Isaiah's sign announced that earthly rescuers could themselves become captives.
Jesus came to free sinners from the deeper bondage of sin and death.
Isaiah's message confronted false confidence.
The Gospel calls us to place our confidence in the crucified and risen Christ.
And here is the part that should bring even the proudest heart to silence.
Jesus did not go to the cross because humanity had finally become worthy of Him.
He went because sinners needed a Savior.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we concealed every shameful memory.
Not after we became impressive enough to deserve mercy.
While we were yet sinners.
The Gospel does not say your sin is harmless.
It says your sin is serious enough that Christ died for it, and God's grace is sufficient to forgive those who turn to Him in faith.
That is the scandal.
And that is the grace.
The scandal is that we have repeatedly placed created things where only the Creator belongs.
The grace is that Jesus Christ offers forgiveness and reconciliation to those who repent and believe in Him.
The scandal is that we have tried to cover our guilt with performance, excuses, religious appearances, and human approval.
The grace is that Christ bore our sins and calls us into the freedom of truth.
The scandal is that we are often more afraid of losing people's admiration than losing our intimacy with God.
The grace is that the risen Savior still calls sinners to come into the light.
And maybe that is why this passage feels so uncomfortable.
Because most of us are not standing barefoot in a public street.
We are standing behind carefully maintained images of ourselves.
We know how to appear okay.
We know how to sound spiritual.
We know which struggles to mention and which ones to bury.
We can post a Bible verse while refusing to forgive someone.
We can speak about surrender while secretly clinging to a sin.
We can tell others to trust God while allowing fear to govern every decision.
We can become so skilled at looking faithful that we stop asking whether our hearts are actually following Jesus.
But Scripture does not invite us into a life of pretending.
It calls us to repentance and faith.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated "repentance," refers to a change of mind or heart that involves turning from sin toward God.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what we did.
It is recognizing sin for what it is, turning away from it, and coming to God for mercy.
It is not a performance to earn forgiveness.
It is a response to God's truth and grace.
And when genuine repentance takes root, it bears fruit in a changed life.
You may not be able to undo yesterday.
But in Christ, yesterday does not have to remain the master of your tomorrow.
You may have damaged relationships that require confession, restitution, patience, and accountability.
Grace does not erase every earthly consequence.
But forgiveness in Christ is real, and transformation is possible.
You may still be battling temptation.
You may still be grieving the damage your choices caused.
You may still need help, wise counsel, and the support of faithful believers.
But you do not have to keep defending the very thing Jesus is calling you to surrender.
Listen carefully.
You cannot heal what you insist on hiding from the light of God's truth.
And the God who calls you into that light is not inviting you to earn His love through public humiliation.
He is calling you to come honestly to Christ.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (KJV)
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say He is faithful to forgive only the sins that seem respectable.
It does not say He will cleanse you only if your past is less complicated than someone else's.
It does not say you must first convince the world that you deserve another chance.
It points us to the faithfulness and justice of God, grounded in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And that is why the cross is not merely an inspirational symbol.
It is the place where the seriousness of sin and the greatness of divine love confront us together.
Now return, for one moment, to Isaiah.
Picture the prophet walking through the streets.
Barefoot.
Stripped of his usual outer covering.
His appearance declaring that the nations people admired would not be able to save them.
Imagine someone watching him and quietly wondering, "What if he is right?"
What if Egypt really cannot save us?
What if the alliance we are depending on collapses?
What if we have mistaken strength for safety?
Now bring those questions into your own life.
What if the thing you have been holding most tightly is not strong enough to carry the weight of your soul?
What if the approval you are chasing cannot give you peace?
What if the success you are sacrificing everything to obtain cannot rescue you from death?
What if the sin you keep defending is slowly destroying what you claim to love?
And what if the mercy of Jesus is closer than your shame has allowed you to believe?
There is no need to manufacture an emotional answer.
Just be honest before God.
What has become your Egypt?
What are you trusting to rescue you when you should be trusting the Lord?
What would surrender actually look like today?
For one person, it may mean finally confessing a hidden sin to God and seeking appropriate accountability.
For another, it may mean ending a dishonest practice.
For someone else, it may mean forgiving an offender without pretending the harm was acceptable or abandoning necessary boundaries.
For another, it may mean admitting that religious activity has replaced genuine dependence on Jesus.
And for someone reading this who has never truly trusted Christ, it may mean responding to His call for the first time.
Not because this article has the power to save you.
It does not.
Only Jesus saves.
Acts 4:12 declares that salvation is found in no other name.
And Ephesians 2:8–9 reminds us that salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of our works.
You do not purchase redemption.
You receive it through faith in Jesus Christ.
You do not earn forgiveness by becoming publicly impressive.
You come to the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
And if your heart is convicted right now, do not confuse conviction with hopelessness.
The Holy Spirit's work of exposing sin is not an invitation to despair.
It is a call to turn toward the One who can forgive and transform.
You can begin with a prayer as simple and sincere as this:

"Lord Jesus, I have trusted things that cannot save me. I have hidden sins, defended my pride, and tried to find security apart from You. I cannot rescue myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Teach me to repent, trust You, and follow You in truth. I surrender my life to You. Amen."
Those words are not a formula that automatically produces salvation.
The invitation of the Gospel is to repent and believe in Jesus Christ.
And if you have been following Him for years but have grown spiritually cold, remember that returning to obedience is not beneath you.
It is where renewed fellowship begins.
There is something else Isaiah's story should awaken in us.
A warning was not given so people could admire the prophet's courage and then return unchanged to their ordinary lives.
It was meant to be heard.
Considered.
Remembered.
And acted upon.
That is why, if this message has exposed a place where your confidence has shifted away from Christ, I want to invite you to do something meaningful.
You do not have to disclose private details or confess sensitive struggles publicly. God knows the burdens you cannot yet put into words.
But sometimes a small, sincere admission opens the door to encouragement from other believers.
And perhaps someone reading the comments will realize they are not the only person learning how to surrender.
Not because saving a post makes someone more spiritual.
But because there may come a morning when your confidence is shaken, when fear returns, or when something you once depended upon begins to crumble.
And on that day, you may need to remember what Isaiah's warning teaches:
No earthly power is worthy of the trust that belongs to God alone.
If someone came to mind while you were reading, consider sharing this article directly with them or tagging them with care.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to announce that you think they are living in sin.
But because you love them enough to share the hope of Christ.
A simple share may place Scripture before a family member, a struggling believer, a friend who has drifted from church, or someone who has never seriously considered the Gospel.
You cannot control how another person responds.
But you can faithfully make the message available.
This is part of why Gospel Warrior exists.

Not to build a community around emotional stories alone, but to keep pointing people back to the living Word of God, the finished work of Jesus Christ, and the daily call to repentance, faith, and discipleship.

There is room here for the believer who needs strengthening, the seeker who has difficult questions, the Christian who has become spiritually distracted, and the wounded person learning to trust Jesus again.
We never want to confuse financial support with spiritual worth.

You help make it possible to continue creating and sharing resources. You help strengthen a growing community centered on Scripture. And you help us pursue the mission of bringing biblical truth to more people.
These are resources and reminders intended to encourage a life centered on Christ, not substitutes for Scripture, prayer, or fellowship with a local church.
The Word of God must never become something people feel they can approach only if they can afford a membership.
Your prayers matter.
Your thoughtful comments matter.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
You can join here:

If Gospel Warrior has encouraged you, consider inviting a friend or family member to follow alongside you. Faith grows through hearing God's Word, and discipleship becomes richer when believers encourage one another to obey it.
But before you leave, there is one final thing I want you to remember.
Isaiah walked barefoot and stripped of his usual covering as a warning that the powers people trusted would fail.
And long after Isaiah's ministry, Jesus Christ entered the deepest humiliation of the cross to accomplish the salvation that no earthly kingdom could provide.
The world may teach you to hide your weakness.
Pride may tell you to protect your image.
Fear may persuade you to cling to anything that promises security.
But the Gospel calls you to stop trusting what cannot save you and come to the Savior who can.
Your past may be scandalous.
Your failures may be real.
Your consequences may be painful.
Your repentance may require difficult changes.
But the risen Christ is not defeated by the depth of human sin.
He is mighty to save.
So do not walk away from this story merely remembering a prophet without shoes.
Remember the God who warned His people against false refuge.
Remember the Savior who endured the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
And remember that the final word over a repentant sinner who belongs to Jesus is not condemnation, but grace.
The things you trusted may leave you exposed, but the Savior who bore your shame can give you a future your past could never deserve.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SAUL BUILT AN ALTAR AFTER HIS SOLDIERS SINNED—BUT THE MOST DISTURBING PART IS WHAT HAPPENED BEFORE THEY BROKE GOD’S LAW
paragraphs: SAUL BUILT AN ALTAR AFTER HIS SOLDIERS SINNED—BUT THE MOST DISTURBING PART IS WHAT HAPPENED BEFORE THEY BROKE GOD’S LAW
1 Samuel 14:31–35 | When a leader's reckless spirituality leaves people starving, obedience becomes a struggle, and an altar is built only after the damage is done.
What if the sin you are condemning in someone else was made easier by the burden you placed on them?
That is an uncomfortable question.
Especially when you are the one holding the Bible. The one giving instructions. The one claiming to protect holiness. The one everyone expects to know what God wants.
Because sometimes the greatest danger to God's people does not begin with someone openly rejecting God.
Sometimes it begins with someone speaking in God's name while failing to reflect His heart.
And there is a moment in the life of King Saul that should make every pastor, parent, ministry leader, husband, wife, and believer examine their heart.
His soldiers were exhausted. Their bodies were failing. They had been fighting an enemy all day. And when they finally reached for food, their desperation led them into disobedience.
Then Saul built an altar to the LORD.
But here is the question that makes this story so disturbing.
Why did Saul wait until his soldiers had broken God's law before building an altar?
And what does that reveal about the terrifying difference between religious activity and genuine surrender?
The answer begins before the blood, before the altar, before the soldiers fell upon the animals.
It begins with a king who made a vow that God had never commanded him to make.
In 1 Samuel 14, Israel was fighting the Philistines. The battle had taken a dramatic turn after Jonathan, Saul's son, courageously moved against a Philistine outpost with his armor-bearer.
Jonathan believed that the LORD was able to save whether by many or by few (1 Samuel 14:6).
And God brought about a remarkable deliverance.
Panic spread through the Philistine camp. Their forces were thrown into confusion. Israel's enemies began turning against one another.
Scripture makes the source of the victory unmistakable.
“So the LORD saved Israel that day.” — 1 Samuel 14:23, KJV
Notice those words.
The LORD saved Israel.
Not Saul's leadership genius.
Not Saul's ability to control his soldiers.
Not Saul's religious declarations.
The LORD.
But while God was giving Israel victory, Saul placed a terrible burden upon the very men fighting the battle.
He bound them under an oath, declaring:
“Cursed be the man that eateth any food until evening, that I may be avenged on mine enemies.” — 1 Samuel 14:24, KJV
Read that last part again.
That I may be avenged on mine enemies.
Not simply that the LORD's name would be honored.
Not that Israel would remember God's mercy.
Saul's own desire for vengeance was woven into the command.
We should be careful here. Scripture does not tell us every private motive inside Saul's heart. But it does record his words, and those words expose something deeply troubling about his priorities.
He had turned a military pursuit into an occasion for a self-imposed religious restriction.
And his soldiers paid the price.
They marched through the woods where honey was available, but no one dared eat because of the oath.
Jonathan, who had not heard his father's command, tasted a little honey. His eyes brightened.
When he learned about the oath, he recognized the damage.
“My father hath troubled the land.” — 1 Samuel 14:29, KJV
Jonathan was not saying that obedience to God was the problem.
He was exposing the destructive consequences of his father's command.
The soldiers could have been strengthened. Instead, they were weakened.
The army could have pursued the enemy with renewed energy. Instead, their strength was being drained.
And by the time we reach verse 31, the consequences have become painfully visible.
“And the people were very faint.” — 1 Samuel 14:31, KJV
In Hebrew, the text describes the people as exceedingly weary, using the expression וַיָּעַף הָעָם מְאֹד (vayya'af ha'am me'od).
The sense is unmistakable.
They were not merely inconvenienced.
They were profoundly exhausted.
Imagine those men.
Dust clinging to their faces.
Hands trembling around their weapons.
Feet aching from the pursuit.
Stomachs empty after hours of fighting.
The enemy had been driven back, but the soldiers themselves were nearly collapsing.
Then, finally, the restriction was over.
And the men rushed toward the spoil.
They took sheep, cattle, and calves. They slaughtered them on the ground and began eating.
But there was a serious problem.
“And the people did eat them with the blood.” — 1 Samuel 14:32, KJV
To a modern reader, that detail may seem strange.
Why was eating blood such a serious offense?
Because God had explicitly forbidden His people to consume blood.
Leviticus 17:11 explains:
“For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls.” — KJV
Blood was not to be treated as ordinary food. God had assigned it a sacred significance connected with life and atonement.
The Hebrew word for blood is דָּם (dam).
And in the biblical sacrificial system, blood was closely associated with life given before God.
Israel was not free to disregard that command simply because its soldiers were hungry.
Their exhaustion helps us understand the circumstances of their sin.
It does not make their sin righteous.
That distinction matters.
Because compassion does not require us to call disobedience obedience.
And biblical holiness does not require us to ignore the circumstances that contributed to someone's collapse.
Both truths can stand together.
The soldiers had violated God's command.
And Saul's reckless oath had contributed to the conditions in which that violation occurred.
Then someone brought the news to Saul.
“Behold, the people sin against the LORD, in that they eat with the blood.” — 1 Samuel 14:33, KJV
And Saul responded:
“Ye have transgressed.”
In Hebrew, the rebuke uses בְּגַדְתֶּם (begadtem), from a verb that can express acting treacherously or unfaithfully.
Saul was not wrong to recognize that God's law had been violated.
But the irony is difficult to miss.
The king who had burdened the people was now rebuking them for what happened when they became desperate.
He ordered a large stone to be rolled into place. He instructed the soldiers to bring their animals there and slaughter them properly rather than continue eating with the blood.
That was a necessary correction.
Saul was right to stop the violation.
And this is important: we must not twist the passage into claiming that every action Saul took was wrong.
His instruction to stop eating with the blood was consistent with God's law.
The problem is deeper.
He recognized the people's disobedience without the narrative recording any acknowledgment of his own contribution to their exhaustion.
And then comes the verse that raises the central question.
“And Saul built an altar unto the LORD: the same was the first altar that he built unto the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 14:35, KJV
There it is.
The first altar Scripture records Saul building to the LORD.
After the exhausting oath.
After the desperate rush toward food.
After the violation of God's command.
After the rebuke.
Only then does the altar appear.
Why?
We need to distinguish carefully between what Scripture tells us and what it does not.

The passage does not explicitly say that Saul built the altar as a public-relations strategy. It does not state that the altar was a deliberate attempt to hide his failure. Nor does it reveal every thought behind his decision.
The immediate context shows Saul correcting the improper slaughter and consumption of the animals. The altar belongs to that moment of responding to the people's violation of God's law.
And although this is called his first altar to the LORD, that does not mean Saul had never previously participated in sacrifice or worship. Earlier passages record sacrifices during his reign.
But the placement of this first recorded altar is still spiritually sobering.
Because the story places Saul's religious action beside the consequences of his leadership.
It invites us to consider a question that reaches far beyond ancient Israel.
What happens when we become more concerned with correcting visible sin than confronting the pride, impatience, or foolishness that helped create the crisis?
Perhaps you have lived on the receiving end of that kind of leadership.
You were trying your best.
You were carrying responsibilities nobody noticed.
You were exhausted, overwhelmed, and quietly falling apart.
Then you made a mistake.
And suddenly, the people who had never asked why you were struggling became very interested in telling you what you had done wrong.
They saw the failure.
But they did not see the fatigue.
They saw the reaction.
But they did not see the pressure.
They saw the moment you stumbled.
But they did not see how long you had been trying to remain standing.
Maybe it happened in your family.
Maybe at work.
Maybe even in a church.
And perhaps you still carry the wound of being corrected by someone who never stopped to understand what you were carrying.
But this passage is not only for people who have been hurt by leaders.
It is also for those of us who have hurt others while believing we were doing what was right.
A father can demand respect while making his children afraid to speak honestly.
A mother can insist on obedience while failing to notice that her child is emotionally exhausted.
A ministry leader can demand constant service while neglecting the spiritual and physical well-being of volunteers.
A Christian can quote Scripture accurately while applying it without patience, tenderness, or wisdom.
And any of us can become so focused on the wrongdoing in front of us that we stop examining what is happening inside us.
That does not mean truth should be compromised.
It means truth must never become an excuse for lovelessness.
The Bible does not give us permission to replace God's commands with our personal preferences and then treat every struggle against those preferences as rebellion against God.
Saul's oath was not the same thing as God's law concerning blood.
One came from the king.
The other came from the LORD.
And confusing human demands with divine commands can wound the very people we are supposed to serve.
There is something else we must notice.
Saul's oath was not simply harsh. It was unnecessary to the victory God had already begun to accomplish.
Jonathan's faith had moved him to act because he trusted God's power.
Saul's oath placed the army under a restriction that weakened them.
What a contrast.
One man trusted that God could save with few.
The other tried to intensify the pursuit through a curse that left his soldiers hungry.
And the tragedy became even more personal when Saul's own son was nearly condemned under that oath.
Later in the chapter, Saul was prepared to see Jonathan die because Jonathan had unknowingly eaten the honey.
But the people intervened, recognizing that God had worked through Jonathan that day (1 Samuel 14:43–45).
The same chapter that records God's deliverance also reveals how dangerously Saul's judgment had become entangled with his own declarations.
That is why this is not merely a story about soldiers eating blood.
It is a story about what happens when a leader's will begins to overshadow the well-being of the people entrusted to him.
And it asks a question every Christian should take seriously.
Am I helping people obey God, or am I exhausting them with expectations God never placed upon them?
There is a difference between calling someone to repentance and crushing someone beneath your control.
There is a difference between spiritual discipline and spiritual pride.
There is a difference between honoring God's holiness and using religious language to protect your own authority.
And perhaps the most dangerous moment comes when we can no longer recognize that difference.
Because we can build altars.
We can attend worship.
We can quote Scripture.
We can correct others.
We can serve in ministry.
We can appear deeply religious.
And still need to repent of the way we have treated people.
An altar does not automatically prove a surrendered heart.
Religious activity cannot substitute for obedience.
Later, in 1 Samuel 15, after Saul again failed to obey God's instruction, Samuel confronted him with words that illuminate the larger pattern of his reign.
“Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams.” — 1 Samuel 15:22, KJV
The Hebrew word translated “to obey” is שְׁמֹעַ (shemoa'), related to the verb shama', meaning to hear or listen, often with the implication of responding obediently.
God was not rejecting the sacrificial system He had established.
He was exposing the emptiness of sacrifice offered as a substitute for listening to Him.
And that distinction reaches into our own lives.
You cannot repair a pattern of cruelty simply by singing louder on Sunday.
You cannot justify dishonesty by giving generously.
You cannot replace repentance with public religious performance.
You cannot continually wound people and assume that spiritual activity makes the wounds insignificant.
God desires truth in the inward parts.
He calls us not merely to look holy but to belong to Him.
And that is where this story becomes more than a warning about Saul.
It becomes a mirror.
Because before we point toward the king and say, “How could he do that?” we need to ask whether we have ever done something similar.
Have you ever corrected someone harshly because you were embarrassed by their mistake?
Have you ever demanded patience while refusing to be patient?
Have you ever expected grace for your own failures but immediate consequences for everyone else's?
Have you ever defended your decisions so fiercely that you could no longer hear the pain of those affected by them?
Have you ever been more concerned with appearing right than becoming right before God?
Those questions hurt.
They should.
Not because God delights in humiliating us.
But because conviction can become a doorway to repentance.
And repentance is not the end of hope.
It is where we stop defending what needs to be surrendered.
This is where the Gospel changes the direction of the story.
Because Saul is not the final king we are meant to look toward.
There is another King.
A King who never confused His Father's will with selfish ambition.
A King who did not place needless religious burdens upon the weary.
A King who saw the exhausted, the hungry, the guilty, and the broken.
And instead of exploiting their weakness, He moved toward them with truth and compassion.
His name is Jesus Christ.
In Matthew 11:28, Jesus says:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” — KJV
Look at the difference.
Saul's command left his soldiers faint.
Jesus calls the weary to Himself.
Saul spoke of avenging himself upon his enemies.
Jesus willingly laid down His life for sinners.
Saul's leadership exposed the danger of human pride.
Jesus revealed the perfection of humble obedience.
Philippians 2:8 says that Christ humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.
He did not merely teach obedience.
He embodied it.
He did not merely identify human sin.
He bore the judgment our sin deserved.
And unlike an earthly king who may overlook his own failures while condemning others, Jesus is the sinless Savior who sees every hidden thing and still invites sinners to repent and come to Him.
But do not misunderstand His compassion.
Jesus does not call evil good.
He does not excuse sin because we were tired, wounded, pressured, or afraid.
He tells us the truth about our condition.
And then He offers something no human altar, religious performance, or self-justifying explanation could ever provide.
Forgiveness through His finished work.
The book of Hebrews declares that Christ entered the holy place by His own blood, obtaining eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12).
The blood Israel was forbidden to consume pointed to the sacredness of life and the seriousness of atonement within the old covenant.
The sacrifices of that covenant prepared the way for understanding the greater sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
His blood was not shed because He had sinned.
It was shed because we had.
“In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace.” — Ephesians 1:7, KJV
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that our failures do not matter.
Not that leaders are never accountable.
Not that our wounds give us permission to disobey God.
But that Jesus Christ came to save sinners, including those who have been wounded by others and those who must face the painful truth that they have wounded others.
Some of us need healing from the burdens people placed upon us.
Some of us need repentance for the burdens we placed upon others.
And some of us need both.
Maybe you are reading this as someone who has been spiritually exhausted for years.
You love Jesus.
But you are tired.
Tired of pretending that you never struggle.
Tired of feeling as though every weakness makes you a disappointment.
Tired of being afraid that if people knew what was really happening inside you, they would stop treating you with kindness.
Hear this carefully.
You do not have to pretend that you are strong before coming to Christ.
You must come honestly.
Confess your sin where you have sinned.
Seek help where you are wounded.
Lay down the impossible burden of earning a salvation that only grace can give.
Jesus does not promise a life without obedience, sacrifice, or suffering.
He calls us to take up our cross and follow Him.
But He is not a careless master who invents burdens to satisfy His ego.
He is the Good Shepherd who laid down His life for His sheep.
And maybe you are reading this from the other side.
Maybe you have been the Saul in someone's story.
You had authority.
You had influence.
You believed you were protecting what was right.
But now you are beginning to recognize that your words wounded people.
Your expectations exhausted them.
Your pride made it difficult for you to apologize.
You corrected their failures while refusing to acknowledge your own.
If that is you, do not turn away from the conviction.
Do not rush to defend yourself.
Do not build another outward display of spirituality to avoid dealing with what God is exposing within.
Go to Jesus.
Repent.
Where possible and appropriate, acknowledge the harm you caused.
Ask forgiveness without demanding it.
Make restitution where it is needed.
Change the way you lead.
Let your repentance become visible through humility, truthfulness, and a different way of treating people.
Because genuine repentance is not merely feeling bad that something happened.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And the grace of Christ is not permission to remain unchanged.
It is the power and mercy through which forgiven sinners begin to walk in newness of life.
Perhaps that is the deepest warning in Saul's first recorded altar.
You can recognize the sin around you and still be blind to the repentance needed within you.
And perhaps the deepest hope is this:
Jesus is able to open our eyes before our pride destroys what has been entrusted to us.
So before you finish reading, consider one question.
What altar are you building to avoid an apology you need to make?
What religious activity are you using to distract yourself from an act of obedience God is calling you to?
What burden have you placed upon someone that you need to lift?
Or what burden have you been carrying that was never God's command in the first place?
Do not rush past those questions.
Bring them before the Lord.
Let His Word examine you.
And remember that the purpose of conviction is not to drive the repentant sinner into hopelessness.
It is to lead us toward the Savior whose mercy is greater than our excuses, whose holiness is greater than our self-righteousness, and whose grace is sufficient to transform a surrendered life.
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only person wrestling with these things.
Because one day you may need to return to this passage—not to examine someone else's failures, but to remember the kind of servant Christ is calling you to become.

And if you have not yet followed Gospel Warrior, you are invited to walk with us as we continue sharing Scripture, biblical encouragement, honest conviction, and the transforming hope of Jesus Christ.
Not to build a following around a human personality.
But to keep directing attention toward the Savior who alone can redeem sinners.
There is also something I want to share with those who believe this kind of Gospel-centered work should continue reaching more people.
Writing, publishing, maintaining resources, and making biblical discipleship material accessible requires time, effort, and financial support.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, not under pressure.
“For God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
We honor those responsibilities.
The Gospel is free.
God's grace cannot be bought.
These resources and products are not the foundation of anyone's faith.
Christ is.
They are simply ways to encourage believers, carry biblical reminders into everyday life, and help sustain the ministry's ongoing work.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite your family and friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even people who do not yet believe, to read the Scriptures and consider the claims of Jesus Christ.
Follow along.
Join the conversations.
Encourage someone who is weary.
A single sincere conversation about the Gospel can matter more than we realize.
Because that is what Saul's story should ultimately drive us toward.
Not admiration for religious performance.
Not fear of human authority.
Not a life spent hiding behind spiritual appearances.
But surrender to the true King.
The One who never sinned.
The One who obeyed the Father perfectly.
The One who carried our guilt to the cross.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who calls the proud to repentance and the weary to rest.
Saul built an altar after the damage was done.
But Jesus Christ gave Himself as the perfect sacrifice to deal with the deepest damage sin has done to us all.
And that is why your story does not have to end where your failure began.
Your pride can be confronted.
Your sin can be forgiven.
Your wounds can be brought before the Savior.
Your life can be changed.
Not because you finally learned how to appear holy.
But because Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
The altar Saul built could not undo the wounds his leadership had caused—but the cross of Jesus Christ still calls wounded people and repentant sinners home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THEY THAT WAIT UPON THE LORD SHALL RENEW THEIR STRENGTH” — BIBLICAL WAITING IS NOT DOING NOTHING
paragraphs: “THEY THAT WAIT UPON THE LORD SHALL RENEW THEIR STRENGTH” — BIBLICAL WAITING IS NOT DOING NOTHING
You thought God was making you wait because nothing was happening. But what if the waiting room is actually the workshop where God is rebuilding the person who will walk through the next door?
There is a kind of exhaustion sleep cannot fix.
You can sleep eight hours and wake up tired.
You can take a vacation and still feel something inside you dragging its feet.

You can smile at church, answer “I’m blessed” when somebody asks how you are doing, post a Scripture verse, encourage somebody else, and then sit alone later wondering why God seems so painfully quiet about the one thing you have begged Him to change.
You prayed.
You waited.
You prayed again.
Still nothing.
At least, nothing you can see.
The diagnosis has not changed.
The marriage has not healed.
The child has not come home.
The financial pressure has not disappeared.
The opportunity has not opened.
The loneliness has not lifted.
The temptation has not stopped knocking.
The answer you thought would arrive in weeks has taken months.
Maybe years.
And somewhere between “Lord, I trust You” and “Lord, how much longer?” you became tired.
Not necessarily tired of God.
Just tired of waiting.
That is exactly where one of Scripture’s most beloved promises becomes far more powerful than the inspirational sentence we sometimes make it.
Isaiah wrote:
“But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.”
— Isaiah 40:31
But slow down.
Because there is something hiding inside that word wait.
The Hebrew reads:
וְקוֹיֵי יְהוָה יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ
veqovey YHWH yachalifu koach
The opening expression, וְקוֹיֵי יְהוָה — veqovey YHWH, speaks of those who wait for, hope in, or look expectantly toward the LORD.
The Hebrew verb behind it is קָוָה — qavah.
It carries the biblical idea of waiting with hope and expectation.
That changes everything.
Biblical waiting is not spiritual laziness.
It is not sitting on the floor saying, “Well, I guess God will do everything.”
It is not refusing responsibility.
It is not procrastination dressed in Christian vocabulary.
It is not passivity.
Waiting on God is a posture of dependent expectation.
You continue trusting when you cannot yet see.
You continue obeying when obedience has not yet produced the outcome you wanted.
You continue praying when heaven feels quiet.
You continue walking when your emotions are begging you to quit.
You keep your eyes on the character of God when circumstances seem to contradict the promises of God.
That is waiting.
And sometimes waiting requires more faith than moving.
Because movement can make us feel powerful.
Waiting reminds us that we are not.
Maybe that is why you hate it.
Maybe that is why I hate it.
Waiting exposes us.
When there is something we can fix, we can become the hero.
When there is somebody we can call, a strategy we can execute, money we can spend, a door we can force open, or a problem we can solve, we can maintain the illusion that we are in control.
But eventually life brings you somewhere your hands cannot reach.
A hospital room.
A betrayal.
A closed door.
A prodigal child.
A prayer without an immediate answer.
A season where every plan collapses.
And suddenly your résumé cannot rescue you.
Your intelligence cannot rescue you.
Your followers cannot rescue you.
Your money cannot rescue you.
Your connections cannot rescue you.
Your religious vocabulary cannot rescue you.
You discover something terrifying and liberating at the same time:
You are not God.
And perhaps one of the hidden mercies of waiting is that it slowly kills the illusion that you ever were.
Isaiah 40 was not originally written as a decorative slogan for comfortable people having a difficult Monday.
Its message addresses people confronted with weakness, discouragement, and the overwhelming greatness of God.
Just before the famous promise, Isaiah asks:
“Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, My way is hid from the LORD, and my judgment is passed over from my God?”
Then comes the answer.
God has not become exhausted.
God has not misplaced His people.
God has not fallen asleep.
God has not reached the end of His wisdom.
“Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?”
— Isaiah 40:28
Read that again when you are exhausted.
You become weary. God does not.
You lose perspective. God does not.
You become confused. God does not.
You see today. God sees what you cannot.
You reach the edge of your strength.
God has no edge.
Then Isaiah says something astonishing:
“He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.”
— Isaiah 40:29
Notice who receives strength.
The faint.
The powerless.
The people who have finally stopped pretending they have an unlimited supply.
And then Scripture goes even further:
“Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall.”
— Isaiah 40:30
In other words, even natural strength eventually fails.
Youth fails.
Adrenaline fails.
Talent fails.
Willpower fails.
Human strength has an expiration date.
Then comes verse 31.
“But…”
What a beautiful word.
Human strength fails.
But.
You are exhausted.
But.
You cannot see the answer.
But.
You do not know what tomorrow holds.
But.
“They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength.”
And the Hebrew expression becomes even more fascinating here:
יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ — yachalifu koach
The verb חָלַף — chalaph can carry the sense of changing, passing on, or renewing.
In Isaiah 40:31, the idea is that those hoping in the LORD receive renewed strength.
Do not turn that into a mystical formula.
Isaiah is not promising that believers become physically invincible.
He is revealing the sufficiency of God for people who have reached the end of themselves.
Your strength runs out.
God sustains.
Your ability reaches its limit.
God remains God.
And perhaps the breakthrough you desperately need is not always God immediately changing your circumstances.
Sometimes it is God sustaining and changing you in the middle of them.
That may not be the miracle you requested.
But do not underestimate that miracle.
Because there are prayers God answers by removing the mountain.
And there are seasons in which God teaches His people to walk faithfully while the mountain is still standing.
Paul knew something about that.
He pleaded with the Lord concerning his “thorn in the flesh.”
He wanted it gone.
Instead, Christ answered:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
— 2 Corinthians 12:9
Paul asked for removal.
Christ revealed sufficiency.
That distinction matters.
Christian faith does not teach that every painful circumstance disappears if you pray hard enough.
Sometimes prison doors open.
Ask Peter.
Sometimes faithful servants remain imprisoned.
Ask Paul.
Sometimes God delivers from the fire.
Ask Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.
Sometimes faithful believers die while still trusting God.
Read Hebrews 11 all the way to the end.
Biblical faith is not confidence that God must write the chapter exactly the way we demand.
Biblical faith is confidence that God remains faithful even when we cannot understand the chapter He has permitted us to enter.
And that is where waiting becomes worship.
Waiting says:
“Jesus, I still trust You when I cannot trace You.”
Waiting says:
“I will not manufacture an Ishmael because I am impatient for Isaac.”
Abraham and Sarah knew what happens when human beings become tired of waiting.
God had promised Abraham offspring.
Time passed.
Age advanced.
The promise looked increasingly impossible.
Then human ingenuity entered the story.
Genesis 16 records the painful consequences surrounding Hagar and Ishmael after Abraham and Sarah attempted to solve through human arrangement what God had promised according to His own purpose.
How often do we do the same thing?
God says wait.
We say, “Maybe He needs help.”
God closes a door.
We start looking for a window to crawl through.
God says trust.
We manipulate.
God says obey.
We compromise.
God says remain faithful.
We panic.
And then we ask God to bless the thing our impatience created.
Some of the deepest scars in our lives did not come because God abandoned us.
They came because we became terrified that His timing could not be trusted.
That sentence may hurt.
But grace is not afraid to expose what it intends to heal.
Maybe you are waiting right now.
Waiting for someone to love you.
And loneliness is whispering, “Take whoever will stay, even if they pull you away from Christ.”
Wait.
Maybe you are waiting for financial relief.
And desperation is whispering, “Compromise just this once.”
Wait.
Maybe you are waiting for recognition.
And insecurity is whispering, “Promote yourself. Exaggerate. Make people notice.”
Wait.
Maybe you are waiting for justice.
And anger is whispering, “Destroy them before God deals with it.”
Wait.
Maybe you are waiting for restoration.
And shame is whispering, “God is finished with you.”
That one is a liar.
Because if you belong to Jesus Christ, your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write your ending.
Peter knew that.
One night he was certain he was strong enough.
Jesus warned him.
Peter insisted.
Then pressure came.
And the courageous disciple collapsed.
Not once.
Three times.
“I do not know the man.”
Imagine the silence after the rooster crowed.
Imagine remembering the warning.
Imagine realizing that the Jesus you swore you would never abandon had heard your denial.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Scandal.
Failure.
Shame.
The kind of moment you wish could be deleted from Scripture.
But Jesus did not delete Peter.
After the resurrection, John 21 gives us one of the most tender restoration scenes in the Bible.
Jesus meets Peter.
Jesus speaks to Peter.
Jesus restores Peter.
Jesus recommissions Peter.
“Feed my sheep.”
Peter's failure was real.
So was Christ's grace.
And that is the Gospel.
Christianity is not the announcement that good people finally learned how to become strong enough.
It is the announcement that sinners who could never save themselves have been offered mercy through the crucified and risen Son of God.
Jesus did not wait for us to repair ourselves.
He came for sinners.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is not purchased by our religious performance.
It is received through Christ.
Repentance is not paying Jesus back.
You cannot.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can rescue you.
Maybe the waiting season is exposing something in you right now.
Good.
Not because exposure feels good.
But because whatever grace exposes, we no longer have to keep pretending is not there.
Maybe waiting exposed your anger.
Your pornography.
Your bitterness.
Your jealousy.
Your secret relationship.
Your pride.
Your obsession with approval.
Your addiction to control.
Your resentment toward God.
Your fear that if God does not give you what you want, He cannot possibly love you.
Do not hide it behind church language.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Repent.
Run to Christ.
Not away from Him.
The enemy wants your failure to become a hiding place.
Jesus calls sinners into the light.
And maybe somebody reading this has been hiding for a very long time.
You still attend church.
You still know the songs.
You still know when to say “Amen.”
But spiritually?
You are exhausted.
You have been performing Christianity instead of abiding in Christ.
You have been carrying everyone else while secretly wondering who would carry you.
You have been telling people God is faithful while crying at night because you are struggling to believe those same words for yourself.
Then hear Isaiah again:
“He giveth power to the faint.”
Not merely to the impressive.
Not merely to the successful.
Not merely to the person who has everything together.
To the faint.
There is no shame in admitting:
“Lord, I have no strength left.”
That confession may become the place where dependence begins.
Waiting on the Lord does not mean you stop doing what God has already told you to do.
Pray while you wait.
Work honestly while you wait.
Forgive while you wait.
Repent while you wait.
Seek wise counsel while you wait.
Study Scripture while you wait.
Serve while you wait.
Love your family while you wait.
Show up while you wait.
Take the next faithful step while you wait.
If there is sin to abandon, abandon it.
If there is an apology to make, make it.
If there is work God has placed before you, do it faithfully.
If there is medical, pastoral, financial, or professional help you genuinely need, seeking appropriate help is not necessarily a failure to trust God.
Waiting on the Lord is not refusing every available means while demanding a miracle.
It is refusing to make an idol of the means.
You work, but God is your hope.
You seek counsel, but God is your hope.
You plan, but God is your hope.
You receive treatment, but God is your hope.
You knock on doors, but God is your hope.
You do what faithfulness requires without pretending that your own hands are sovereign.
Then Isaiah paints three pictures.
“They shall mount up with wings as eagles.”
Beautiful.
“They shall run, and not be weary.”
Powerful.
And then:
“They shall walk, and not faint.”
Walk?
After eagles?
After running?
Walking sounds almost disappointing.
Unless you have lived long enough to understand that sometimes walking is the miracle.
Some seasons feel like flying.
Doors open.
Prayers are answered quickly.
You feel the wind beneath your faith.
Other seasons feel like running.
There is momentum.
Purpose.
Movement.
But then there are seasons when getting out of bed and still saying “Jesus, I trust You” is an act of warfare.
You did not fly today.
You did not run.
But you walked.
You prayed even though you cried through half the prayer.
You opened your Bible even though your mind wandered.
You went to church even though you felt numb.
You resisted the temptation one more night.
You did not send the message you knew you should not send.
You apologized.
You stayed sober today.
You chose truth over the lie.
You refused to abandon Christ because your circumstances hurt.
You walked.
Do not despise that.
Some victories do not sound like thunder.
Sometimes victory sounds like exhausted footsteps still moving toward Jesus.
That is why waiting is not doing nothing.
Waiting is where roots grow beneath ground nobody applauds.
Think about Joseph.
He received dreams, but the palace did not arrive the next morning.
There was betrayal.
A pit.
Slavery.
False accusation.
Prison.
Delay.
Genesis even records that the chief cupbearer forgot Joseph for a time.
Forgotten by a man.
Not forgotten by God.
And when the appointed circumstances converged, Joseph was brought before Pharaoh.
Years that might have looked wasted became part of the road God used in preserving many lives.
That does not make betrayal good.
It means evil does not outrank God's sovereignty.
Joseph later told his brothers:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good…”
— Genesis 50:20
Notice Scripture does not call their evil good.
Their intention was evil.
God's purpose was greater.
That is hope for somebody carrying scars.
What happened to you may genuinely have been wrong.
Betrayal is wrong.
Abuse is wrong.
Deception is wrong.
Sin is wrong.
Christian faith does not require you to rename darkness as light.
It tells you that darkness does not get the final word over those held by God.
The cross proves it.
Human betrayal.
False accusation.
Mockery.
Violence.
Crucifixion.
The innocent Christ hanging between criminals.
To the disciples, Friday looked like catastrophe.
Then came Saturday.
Silence.
Imagine that wait.
Jesus had died.
The tomb was sealed.
Hope seemed buried behind stone.
But Saturday was not the ending.
Sunday came.
The tomb was empty.
Christ was risen.
And suddenly the darkest chapter became the doorway into the proclamation that would echo across nations:
Jesus Christ is Lord.
This is why Christians can wait without worshiping despair.
Our hope is ultimately not that every earthly story will become comfortable.
Our hope is a Person.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Reigning.
Coming again.
So perhaps you are living in a Saturday season.
Something died.
Something closed.
Something broke.
And you cannot yet see resurrection on the horizon.
Do not confuse God's silence with God's absence.
Do not confuse delay with abandonment.
Do not confuse waiting with inactivity.
And do not build your theology around one painful afternoon.
The story is not finished.
Maybe your circumstances change tomorrow.
Maybe they take longer than you want.
Scripture does not give us permission to manufacture dates God has not revealed.
But it gives us something deeper than a deadline.
It gives us God Himself.
And if your strength is almost gone, maybe your prayer tonight does not need to sound impressive.
Maybe it can simply be:
“Jesus, I am tired.
I do not understand.
I cannot carry tomorrow yet.
So give me grace to obey You today.
Forgive what needs forgiving.
Expose what needs exposing.
Heal what You desire to heal.
Correct what needs correcting.
Close the doors I keep trying to force open.
Give me courage to walk through the doors You open.
And while I wait…
keep my heart near You.”
That is not weakness.
That is surrender.
And surrender to Christ is not the end of your story.
It may be where the rewriting begins.
There may be another believer reading the comments who knows exactly what that kind of night feels like.

And if God has already carried you through a long waiting season, tell somebody what He taught you. Your testimony may become encouragement for the person who is currently standing where you once stood.
Not because every sentence will solve tomorrow.
The mother still praying for her child.
The husband fighting for his marriage.
The widow learning to wake up alone.
The believer fighting a secret temptation.
The person waiting on medical answers.
The person whose plans collapsed.
The Christian who is beginning to wonder whether God still sees them.
Do not assume they already know you care.
Tell them.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, helping you return to Scripture, pointing you toward repentance, reminding you of grace, and keeping Jesus Christ in front of you when the noise of the world keeps pulling your eyes elsewhere, you can also help this ministry continue and expand.
Following Gospel Warrior costs nothing, and sharing these messages costs nothing. Both genuinely help the message travel farther.
But hear this clearly:
You cannot purchase God's favor.
It does not buy salvation.
It does not replace repentance.
It does not purchase answered prayer.
Scripture says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
— 2 Corinthians 9:7
So support should never be manipulated out of fear or spiritual pressure.
And yes, practical support matters.
Printing matters.
Publishing matters.
Technology matters.
Distribution matters.
Creating biblical resources takes time and resources.
Reaching another exhausted believer matters.
Reaching another person who has never understood grace matters.
Helping someone open Scripture again matters.
Helping someone encounter the Gospel matters.
But the merchandise is not the mission.
Jesus is.
The Gospel is.
Changed lives are.
And the deeper reason to stay connected is spiritual nourishment.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the Christian who has drifted.
Invite the person who is skeptical.
Invite the person who has been wounded by religion and needs to see the difference between human hypocrisy and Jesus Christ.
Invite the person who needs Scripture more than another motivational slogan.
Because perhaps the next article they encounter will reach them on the night they were considering giving up.
Perhaps one verse will send them back to the Bible.
Perhaps one testimony will make them pray again.
Perhaps one Gospel message will remind them that grace is still calling.
We cannot save anybody.
Only Christ saves.
But we can point.
We can share.
We can speak.
We can give.
We can pray.
We can refuse to keep good news to ourselves.
And maybe that is part of what God is teaching you in the waiting.
You thought waiting meant your life was on pause.
But God was teaching you dependence.
You thought nothing was growing.
Roots were going deeper.
You thought your weakness disqualified you.
Christ was teaching you where real strength comes from.
You thought the closed door meant rejection.
Perhaps God was protecting you.
You thought the silence meant absence.
God had not moved from His throne.
You thought you needed an explanation.
God was inviting you to trust His character.
You thought you needed enough strength for the next ten years.
God was giving you enough grace for the next step.
So walk it.
Slowly, if necessary.
With tears, if necessary.
With trembling hands, if necessary.
But walk toward Jesus.
And when you cannot run…
walk.
When you cannot fly…
walk.
When everybody else seems to be passing you…
walk.
When prayers seem unanswered…
walk.
When your heart hurts…
walk.
When you have to repent again…
walk back toward Jesus.
When shame tells you to hide…
walk into the light.
When you do not understand what God is doing…
keep your eyes on who God has revealed Himself to be.
Because the promise was never that those who wait upon the Lord would never become tired.
The promise is that exhausted human beings do not have to make their own strength their final hope.
וְקוֹיֵי יְהוָה יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ
Veqovey YHWH yachalifu koach.
Those who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength.
Maybe you entered this season asking God:
“When will You get me out?”
And perhaps one of the questions worth asking now is:
“Jesus, who are You forming me to become while I am here?”
Do not waste the waiting.
Pray in it.
Repent in it.
Learn in it.
Love in it.
Serve in it.
Heal in it.
Obey in it.
Worship in it.
Hope in it.
And when strength returns, remember where it came from.
Not your greatness.
His grace.
Then share this with somebody whose waiting room has become unbearably quiet.
Not because giving purchases grace.
But because grace, when it captures a heart, teaches us to stop living only for ourselves.
And remember this when the night feels longest:
The waiting room may feel silent, but the Author has not put down the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU ASKED GOD TO OPEN A DOOR. DID YOU ASK WHETHER YOU SHOULD WALK THROUGH IT?
paragraphs: YOU ASKED GOD TO OPEN A DOOR. DID YOU ASK WHETHER YOU SHOULD WALK THROUGH IT?

Not every opportunity is an answered prayer. Some doors lead to blessing. Others lead to the very thing God has been trying to save you from. And sometimes, the most dangerous decision is the one that finally gives you everything you wanted.
What if the door you've been begging God to open is the very door you need the courage to walk away from?
Read that again.
Because somewhere right now, someone is celebrating an opportunity they haven't prayed deeply enough about.
Someone just received the job offer.
Someone's former lover just came back.
Someone was offered a business deal that could change their family's financial future.
Someone finally got the recognition they've spent years chasing.
And someone is standing in front of an open door, smiling through tears, whispering, "Thank You, Lord. I knew You would come through."
But there's a question that can change everything.
Did God actually lead you to that door, or did you assume it was His because it opened?
That question might make you uncomfortable.
Especially if you've already told everyone it was a blessing.
Especially if you've already imagined your new life on the other side.
Especially if walking away would mean disappointing people, losing money, surrendering a dream, or admitting that something you desperately wanted might not be God's will for you.
But what if the greatest act of faith isn't walking through the door?
What if it's trusting Jesus enough to leave it unopened?
There is a warning in Scripture that should make every believer think carefully before confusing opportunity with obedience.
Proverbs 14:12 says:
"There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death." — Proverbs 14:12, KJV
In the original Hebrew, the opening words are:
יֵשׁ דֶּרֶךְ יָשָׁר לִפְנֵי־אִישׁ
Yesh derekh yashar lifnei ish.
A close translation is, "There is a way that is straight [or right] before a man."
The Hebrew word יָשָׁר (yashar) carries the sense of being straight, upright, or right.
Notice the danger.
The path doesn't necessarily look crooked.
It looks straight.
It makes sense.
It appears reasonable.
It might even look like the answer to years of prayer.
But the verse continues:
וְאַחֲרִיתָהּ דַּרְכֵי־מָוֶת
Ve'acharītah darkhei-mavet.
"But its end is the ways of death."
The proverb is not teaching that every opportunity is evil or that every attractive choice ends in disaster. It is warning us that human judgment, even when confident, can be tragically mistaken.
A road can look right from the entrance and still lead somewhere devastating.
And perhaps that's what makes this warning so frightening.
You don't always recognize a dangerous path by how it begins.
Sometimes you recognize it by what you have to compromise to stay on it.
Think about that job you've been praying for.
The salary is better. The title is impressive. Your family is excited. For the first time in years, you can imagine breathing financially.
Then comes the conversation.
Your future employer explains that certain numbers occasionally need to be adjusted. Nothing major, they say. Everyone in the industry does it.
You feel that quiet discomfort in your conscience.
But then you remember your bills.
Your children's needs.
Your exhausted spouse.
The prayers you've whispered at midnight.
And suddenly you begin negotiating with the very conviction you once promised God you would never abandon.
"Lord, You know I need this."
"Lord, maybe this is just how business works."
"Lord, surely You wouldn't open this opportunity if You didn't want me to take it."
But Scripture never says that financial relief makes dishonesty righteous.
An open door does not turn sin into obedience.
Now imagine another person.
She has spent months asking God to heal her loneliness.
Then the message arrives.
"I miss you."
Three words from someone she thought she'd finally forgotten.
He knows how to make her laugh. He remembers her favorite food. He says he's changed.
And perhaps he really has.
But as they begin talking again, the old pressure returns.
The boundaries she fought to rebuild start feeling inconvenient.
Her commitment to Christ becomes something she is expected to soften to keep the relationship.
And because she has been lonely for so long, she begins wondering whether compromise is simply the price of being loved.
But listen carefully.
A relationship that requires you to betray your obedience to Jesus is not made holy by how badly you wanted it.
That doesn't mean every difficult relationship is wrong or that reconciliation is impossible. Christ transforms people, and genuine repentance can bear real fruit.
It means love must be tested by truth, not merely by longing.
Some of the hardest spiritual decisions happen when something is genuinely attractive, genuinely beneficial in certain ways, and still requires a compromise you know you shouldn't make.
And if you're reading this with a particular opportunity in mind, don't rush past that feeling.
You may need to bring it into the light.
Because the question isn't simply, "Can I have this?"
It's, "Can I follow Jesus faithfully if I take it?"
There's a scene in the Bible that reveals just how easily an open door can become a test of the heart.
David was running for his life.
King Saul was hunting him, driven by jealousy and determined to destroy the man God had chosen to succeed him.
David had been anointed, but he wasn't sitting on the throne.
He was hiding in caves.
Sleeping in uncertainty.
Living under the threat of death.
Then, in 1 Samuel 24, something extraordinary happened.
Saul entered a cave, unaware that David and his men were hiding deeper inside.
There he was.
The man who had caused David so much suffering.
Vulnerable.
Within reach.
David's men immediately interpreted the moment as divine opportunity.
They told David that this was the day the LORD had delivered his enemy into his hand.
Can you imagine the temptation?
David could end the chase.
He could escape the fear.
He could move closer to the throne he had already been promised.
And the opportunity was standing right in front of him.
But David refused to kill Saul.
He secretly cut off a corner of Saul's robe, and even that troubled his conscience.
