Someone else may need the encouragement that repentance and restoration are possible.
I also want to hear from married couples, singles, and those who are still healing.
Can a relationship remain deeply loving without sex? And what do you believe distinguishes genuine love from mere physical desire?
Speak honestly. Speak respectfully. And remember that behind every comment is a real person with a story you may not know.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should be a matter of willing conviction, not pressure or compulsion.
We want people to be nourished by God's Word, not merely moved by a single article.
Above everything, keep your eyes on Christ.
Do not merely search for a relationship that makes you feel wanted.
Seek to live a life that honors the One who loved us while we were still sinners.
Do not build your identity on your desirability.
Build your life on the truth of the Gospel.
And do not mistake physical closeness for spiritual unity, emotional safety, or covenantal faithfulness.
Because when beauty changes, health falters, emotions fluctuate, and the excitement of the beginning becomes the ordinary work of remaining faithful, the deeper character of love comes into view.
One day, the question may no longer be whether someone still desires your body—but whether they ever learned to cherish the soul standing before them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE DIED CALLING HIM THE SON OF HER SORROW. HIS FATHER REFUSED TO LET SORROW HAVE THE FINAL WORD.
paragraphs: SHE DIED CALLING HIM THE SON OF HER SORROW. HIS FATHER REFUSED TO LET SORROW HAVE THE FINAL WORD.

Rachel named her last child Ben-Oni with her dying breath. Jacob called him Benjamin. But buried inside Genesis 35:18 is a truth about grief, identity, redemption, and the God who can write a future that pain could never imagine.
There are some names you never chose to carry.
Failure.
Rejected.
Unwanted.
Broken.
Abandoned.
Maybe nobody ever called you those things to your face. Maybe life did something worse.
It made you believe them.

One betrayal convinced you that you were unlovable. One terrible mistake made you feel permanently disqualified. One funeral divided your life into before and after. One season of suffering left you wondering whether joy would ever feel safe again.
And somewhere along the way, you began introducing yourself to the world through what happened to you.
But there is a moment in Scripture that deserves more than a hurried reading.
A woman is dying.
A baby is being born.
A mother speaks a name over her child.
And a father gives him another.
What happened in that moment was not a simple disagreement over what to call a newborn.
It was a collision between unbearable sorrow and the possibility of a future beyond it.
And if you've ever allowed the worst chapter of your life to become the definition of your entire existence, you need to stay with this story.
Because Rachel's final words were heartbreaking.
But they were not the last words spoken over her son.
Genesis 35:18 records:
"And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing, (for she died) that she called his name Benoni: but his father called him Benjamin." (KJV)
Read that again.
As her soul was in departing.
The Bible does not soften the scene.
Rachel was not standing in a peaceful nursery, smiling over a sleeping child.
She was dying in childbirth.
The woman who had once cried out to Jacob, "Give me children, or else I die" (Genesis 30:1), was now losing her life while bringing another child into the world.
There is a terrible irony here.
The longing that once consumed her life had finally been answered again, but this time, the answer arrived through a doorway she would not survive.
To understand how devastating this was, we need to remember who Rachel was.
Jacob had loved her deeply.
Genesis 29 tells us that he served seven years to marry her, and those years seemed to him only a few days because of his love for her.
But their love story was not a fairy tale.
It was tangled in deception, family rivalry, jealousy, infertility, and years of waiting.
Rachel watched her sister Leah bear children while she remained unable to conceive.
Imagine the silent ache.
Watching other women hold babies while your own arms remain empty.
Trying to celebrate someone else's blessing while privately asking God why your prayers seem unanswered.
Smiling in public.
Crying where nobody can see.
Scripture says God remembered Rachel, listened to her, and opened her womb (Genesis 30:22).
She gave birth to Joseph.
And when she named him, she said, "The LORD shall add to me another son" (Genesis 30:24, KJV).
That prayer would eventually be answered.
But not in the way anyone would have wanted.
Years later, while Jacob's family was traveling from Bethel toward Ephrath, Rachel went into difficult labor.
Genesis 35:16 says she had "hard labour."
The Hebrew expression is וַתְּקַשׁ בְּלִדְתָּהּ (vattiqash belidtah), describing the severity of her childbirth.
This was not a mild inconvenience.
This was a dangerous delivery.
Her midwife tried to encourage her.
"Fear not; thou shalt have this son also." (Genesis 35:17, KJV)
What a sentence.
The child she had hoped for was coming.
But Rachel was slipping away.
The midwife could see the baby arriving.
Rachel was facing death.
And then came the name.
בֶּן־אוֹנִי — Ben-Oni.
The Hebrew word ben means "son."
The second element, oni, is understood in this context as referring to sorrow, affliction, or suffering.
So the name is commonly translated "son of my sorrow."
Some linguistic discussions also note possible associations with strength, but the traditional interpretation of sorrow fits the immediate narrative of Rachel's death.
Think about what that means.
A baby entered the world, and his first name became inseparable from the suffering surrounding his birth.
He had done nothing wrong.
He had not chosen the circumstances.
He had not caused his mother's death through any moral failure.
Yet the name given to him carried the anguish of that moment.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story begins to touch something painfully familiar.
Because some of us have been carrying names that came from tragedies we never caused.
You grew up in a home filled with anger, and now you struggle to believe you are worthy of gentleness.
Someone abandoned you, and you started calling yourself unwanted.
A marriage ended, and you began defining yourself as a failure.
You made a sinful decision, repented, and still wake up feeling that your past has permanently ruined your future.
You suffered something you never deserved, and now you wonder whether anything beautiful can still come from your life.
But listen carefully.
What happened to you matters. It may have wounded you deeply. But it does not possess the authority to tell the whole truth about who you are.
Rachel's sorrow was real.
Her pain was not imaginary.
Her death was not a metaphor.
And Scripture never asks us to pretend otherwise.
That is important, because sometimes Christians speak about suffering as though faith requires us to deny how much it hurts.
But the Bible does not teach that.
Jesus wept at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:35).
David poured out his anguish in the Psalms.
Job mourned what he had lost.
Even the apostle Paul described being burdened beyond his own strength (2 Corinthians 1:8).
Grief is not automatically unbelief.
Tears are not proof that your faith has failed.
And healing does not require you to pretend that the wound never existed.
Rachel was a mother facing death, and her last act was to name the son she would never raise.
We should approach her suffering with compassion, not judgment.
But the story does not end with Ben-Oni.
Because Jacob heard the name.
And Genesis says:
"But his father called him Benjamin."
In Hebrew:
בִּנְיָמִין — Binyamin.
The name is traditionally understood as "son of the right hand."

In ancient Hebrew usage, the right hand was associated with strength, honor, favor, and an important place of standing. The Hebrew word yamin can also mean "south" in certain geographical contexts, but "son of the right hand" is the familiar and contextually meaningful rendering here.
Notice what the text actually tells us.
Rachel named him Ben-Oni.
Jacob named him Benjamin.
Scripture does not explicitly reveal every thought in Jacob's mind or say that he consciously intended to deliver a sermon about identity.
We should not pretend to know motives God has not revealed.
But the contrast between the two names is unmistakable.
One name remembered sorrow.
The other spoke of the right hand.
The grief surrounding Benjamin's birth remained part of his history, but it did not remain his name.
And there is something profoundly moving about that.
Jacob did not bring Rachel back from the dead.
He could not undo what had happened.
He could not give his son the childhood he would have had with his mother.
He could not erase the grave that would stand along the road to Ephrath.
But the child would grow up being called Benjamin.
Not Ben-Oni.
Benjamin.
And that is where we must be careful, because the Gospel offers something even greater than a human father changing a child's name.
Jesus Christ does not merely give sinners a more encouraging description of themselves. He reconciles them to God through His death and resurrection.
Our deepest problem is not simply that people have labeled us incorrectly.
Our deepest problem is that sin has separated humanity from a holy God.
We need more than affirmation.
We need forgiveness.
We need repentance.
We need reconciliation.
We need a Savior.
And this is where the story becomes even more powerful when we follow the whole testimony of Scripture.
Benjamin's name points us toward the imagery of the right hand.
But the New Testament reveals someone who truly occupies the place of supreme honor and authority.
Jesus Christ.
Hebrews 1:3 says that after making purification for sins, Christ "sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high."
And in Matthew 26:64, Jesus speaks of the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power.
The Greek expression used in Hebrews 1:3 is:
ἐν δεξιᾷ — en dexia.
It means "at the right hand."
In biblical imagery, this signifies a place of authority and exaltation, not a claim that God the Father possesses a physical right hand like a human being.
Now consider the astonishing contrast.
Benjamin was given a name associated with the right hand after his mother died.
Jesus, the eternal Son of God, suffered death and was raised and exalted to the Father's right hand.
These are not identical events, and Genesis 35 does not explicitly present Benjamin's naming as a prophecy of Christ.
But read through the wider biblical witness, the contrast invites us to contemplate a glorious truth.
The risen Christ has authority to accomplish what no human father could ever accomplish: to rescue sinners from condemnation and bring them into the family of God.
And He did not accomplish that redemption cheaply.
He went to the cross.
He was mocked.
He was rejected.
He was wounded.
He bore our sins.
The One who had never sinned willingly suffered for sinners.
Isaiah 53:3 describes the promised suffering servant as "a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief."
Jesus knew sorrow.
Not from a distance.
Not as an observer.
He entered the suffering of this fallen world.
In Gethsemane, He said, "My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death" (Matthew 26:38, KJV).
At Calvary, He endured the cross.
And on the third day, He rose again.
Death did not have the final victory.
Sin did not defeat Him.
The grave could not hold Him.
That is why Christian hope is not merely the belief that tomorrow might feel better.
Christian hope rests on a living Savior who has conquered death.
And because He lives, those who belong to Him have a future that suffering cannot ultimately destroy.
Maybe that is what someone reading this needs to hear tonight.
You have been calling yourself by the name of your worst season.
You have allowed an old betrayal to speak louder than the promises of God.
You have let a failed relationship become your entire identity.
You have treated a regretted decision as though Christ's mercy could never reach it.
You have been replaying a chapter that God has not asked you to make the title of your life.
But listen to Romans 8:1:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus." (KJV)
Notice those words.
In Christ Jesus.
Not simply everyone who feels positive about themselves.
Not everyone who refuses to acknowledge sin.
Not everyone who claims a new identity while continuing to reject the Savior.
The promise belongs to those who are in Christ.
And this is why repentance is not an enemy of grace.
Repentance is the turning of the heart away from sin and toward God.
Grace does not tell us that our sins never mattered.
Grace tells us that Christ's sacrifice is sufficient to forgive and cleanse those who come to Him in faith.
The Greek word often translated "repentance" is μετάνοια — metanoia, expressing a change of mind and heart that bears fruit in a changed direction of life.
You do not earn salvation by becoming good enough.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that salvation is by grace through faith, not by works.
But the grace that saves us does not leave us comfortably enslaved to the sins from which Christ came to rescue us.
The very next verse says we are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
So when the Gospel speaks of a new identity, it is not offering a superficial motivational slogan.
It is announcing the miracle of new life in Jesus Christ.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." (KJV)
The Greek expression καινὴ κτίσις — kainē ktisis means "new creation."
Not merely a repaired public image.
Not simply a more confident personality.
A new creation.
That does not mean every painful memory disappears when you believe.
It does not mean every consequence of past choices instantly vanishes.
It does not mean Christians will never grieve, struggle, or need help.
It means something deeper.
Through union with Christ, your relationship to God has been transformed.
Your sin no longer has to be your master.
Your condemnation has been answered by the cross.
Your future is anchored in the resurrection.
And the One who began a good work in His people will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying a sorrow you have never told anyone about.
Perhaps your family sees your smile but never sees the tears that come after midnight.
Perhaps you have served in church while quietly wondering whether God is disappointed in you.
Perhaps you have drifted from prayer because shame keeps telling you that you are no longer welcome.
Or perhaps you are not sure you believe in Jesus at all.
You have seen too much hypocrisy.
You have been hurt by people who spoke His name but did not reflect His character.
You have questions that nobody has answered.
If that is you, do not confuse the failures of human beings with the character of Christ.
Look at Him in the Gospels.
Look at how He approached the broken.
Look at how He confronted religious pride.
Look at how He welcomed repentant sinners without pretending their sins were harmless.
Look at the cross.
And ask whether the One who willingly gave His life for sinners might be worthy of your trust.
There is another detail in Rachel's story that makes this passage even more sobering.
Genesis 35:19 tells us that Rachel died and was buried on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem.
Jacob set up a pillar over her grave.
Her death was remembered.
Her grave was not erased.
And much later, in Genesis 48:7, Jacob himself recalled Rachel's death while speaking to Joseph.
Years had passed.
The family had changed.
Benjamin had grown.
But Jacob still remembered where he buried the woman he loved.
That detail matters.
Because giving Benjamin a different name did not require Jacob to forget Rachel.
Hope does not require amnesia.
Some losses remain with us.
Some empty chairs never stop being noticeable.
Some anniversaries always hurt.
Some prayers are answered in ways we do not understand.
And some questions may remain unanswered in this lifetime.
But the Christian hope is not that we will eventually become so strong that we no longer need God.
It is that God will remain faithful even when we are weak.
And one day, through the victory of Jesus Christ, death itself will be destroyed.
Revelation 21:4 promises a future in which God will wipe away every tear and death shall be no more.
That is not a promise that believers will never cry today.
It is a promise that tears will not reign forever.
Rachel's story ended in death.
But God's redemptive story did not end at a grave.
And neither did the story of Jesus.
There is a difference between the grave of Rachel and the tomb of Christ.
Rachel's grave testified to a death that human love could not reverse.
Christ's empty tomb testifies to a resurrection that human power could never accomplish.
That is the foundation of our hope.
Not a changed name by itself.
Not positive thinking.
Not pretending the past never happened.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
And that brings us back to the child.
Ben-Oni.
Benjamin.
A son whose arrival was surrounded by sorrow.
A son whose life continued beyond the tragedy of his birth.
Imagine, without pretending Scripture records the conversation, what it might have meant for Benjamin to grow up learning about his mother.
To discover how dearly she had been loved.
To hear how painfully she had suffered.
To learn the name she had given him.
And to understand that his father had called him Benjamin.
He could not change the day he was born.
He could not rewrite his mother's death.
But he was not required to live as though the tragedy of his beginning exhausted the meaning of his existence.
And neither are you.
If you are in Christ, your wounds may explain parts of your story, but they cannot cancel God's promises.
Your failures may require confession, restitution, and change, but they do not place you beyond the reach of the Savior who welcomed the repentant thief on the cross.
Your grief may remain real, but it is not greater than the resurrection.
Your past may be painful, but it is not more powerful than Jesus.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Him, today you can turn to Him in repentance and faith.
You do not have to manufacture perfect words.
Come truthfully.
Confess your sin.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Ask Him for mercy.
Follow Him.
Not because a story about Benjamin guarantees that every painful circumstance will suddenly change.
But because the Gospel announces that Jesus Christ saves sinners and gives eternal life to those who believe in Him.
And perhaps the most important question is not what people have called you.
It is whether you have heard what God says about those who belong to His Son.
Forgiven.
Reconciled.
Adopted.
Loved in Christ.
Called to holiness.
Given a living hope.
Not because we deserve these gifts.
But because Jesus is merciful.
And if this story has exposed something you have been hiding, I want to invite you into a moment of honesty.
You do not have to reveal private details or pretend you have already healed.
Your words may encourage someone who has been suffering in silence.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who has been living under the weight of a name that pain gave them.
Someone who feels rejected.
Someone grieving a child, a parent, a marriage, or a future they imagined.
Someone who has wandered from God and wonders whether the door is still open.

And if you believe Scripture-centered messages like this are worth keeping alive, consider following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, fellow believers, and those still searching for truth to follow as well.

We want it to be a place where the wounded encounter biblical hope, where believers grow in discernment, where sinners hear the call to repentance, and where Jesus Christ—not a personality, a platform, or a brand—remains at the center.
But sustaining and expanding that work requires people willing to stand alongside it.
And this is where I want to speak to you as a fellow servant of the Gospel, not as someone trying to place a price on God's grace.
Salvation is God's free gift through Jesus Christ.
But if this ministry has encouraged you, helped you return to Scripture, or given you something meaningful to share with another struggling soul, you can choose to help us continue that work.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from pressure or compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Not the suggestion that God will love you more if you pay.
But gratitude expressed through willing partnership.
You can still pray for this ministry.
You can still invite people to read Scripture, seek Christ, and grow in truth.
You can still use the free resources.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God.
What matters most is that Jesus Christ is proclaimed, His Word is handled faithfully, and lives are changed by His grace.
Because in the end, the story of Rachel and Benjamin is not an invitation to worship the power of a name.
It is an invitation to consider how sorrow can mark a beginning without possessing the whole future.
Rachel's death was real.
Jacob's grief was real.
Benjamin's loss was real.
And yet the child lived.
Centuries later, another Son entered our broken world.
He carried our sins to the cross.
He rose victorious from the grave.
And now He reigns at the right hand of the Father.
His name is Jesus.
The only Savior.
The One who can forgive the guilty, welcome the repentant, strengthen the weary, and give eternal life to those who trust in Him.
So when the enemy accuses you with sins that you have confessed and brought to Christ, remember the cross.
When grief whispers that nothing good can ever come again, remember the resurrection.
When shame tells you that your story is already over, remember the Savior who makes all things new.
And when you think about the dying mother who whispered Ben-Oni and the grieving father who called his child Benjamin, remember that the greatest hope of all is not found in what Jacob could change.
It is found in what Jesus has accomplished.
Your sorrow may be written into the story of your life, but in Christ, it does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHEN GIVING TO GOD BECOMES A THREAT: ARE CHRISTIANS BEING TAUGHT GENEROSITY… OR TRAINED TO FEAR THE CURSE?
paragraphs: WHEN GIVING TO GOD BECOMES A THREAT: ARE CHRISTIANS BEING TAUGHT GENEROSITY… OR TRAINED TO FEAR THE CURSE?

What if the offering you gave with trembling hands was never what God demanded? A biblical confrontation with spiritual manipulation, the truth about tithes, and the beautiful difference between giving because you are afraid of God—and giving because you know His heart.
There is a kind of silence that falls over a church when the offering begins.
Not because people have nothing to give.
But because some are terrified of what will happen if they don't.

Somewhere in the congregation, a mother is calculating how much money remains for groceries. A father is thinking about the electricity bill he promised to pay. A young believer is remembering the warning he heard last Sunday: If you withhold your tithe, you are stealing from God.
And then comes the sentence that makes his stomach tighten.
“Don't expect God to bless you if you refuse to give Him what belongs to Him.”
He reaches into his wallet.
Not because his heart is overflowing with gratitude.
Not because he has joyfully decided to participate in the work of the Gospel.
But because he is afraid.
Afraid his children might suffer.
Afraid his business might collapse.
Afraid God might withdraw His protection.
Afraid that the next tragedy in his life will somehow be his fault because he did not put enough money in the offering basket.
And nobody around him knows what is happening inside his heart.
They see a man giving.
God sees a man trembling.
Here is the question that should shake every church that claims to preach the Gospel of Jesus Christ:
When did an invitation to generosity become a threat of divine punishment?
And even more importantly...
If Jesus Christ has redeemed us from the curse of the law, why are some Christians still being threatened with a curse whenever they cannot afford to give?
That question is not rebellion against God.
It is a question that deserves an answer from Scripture.
Because the Bible does not merely tell us to give.
It also tells us what kind of giving pleases God.
And the difference could change the way you understand worship, money, ministry, and the very heart of your heavenly Father.
The apostle Paul wrote something astonishing to the believers in Corinth:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Read those words carefully.
Especially the phrase “or of necessity.”
In the original Greek, Paul uses the expression ἐξ ἀνάγκης (ex anankēs), meaning “out of compulsion” or “under necessity.”
He then describes the giver God loves with the word ἱλαρόν (hilaron), meaning cheerful, glad, or willing.
This is not a command to manufacture a smile while surrendering money you feel forced to give.
It is a revelation about the heart.
Paul is contrasting generosity that flows from a willing decision with giving that is driven by reluctance or pressure.
God is not looking for an offering extracted from a frightened conscience.
He delights in generosity that comes from a willing heart.
And that should make us ask an uncomfortable question.
If God loves a cheerful giver, why would anyone deliberately make Christians afraid to give?
Now, we must be careful.

Not every sermon about tithing is manipulation. Not every pastor who teaches sacrificial giving is exploiting the congregation. Churches have genuine financial needs. Missionaries need support. Gospel workers deserve appropriate provision. Buildings require maintenance. Outreach costs money. The poor need practical help.
Scripture plainly teaches believers to share their resources.
But a biblical responsibility can become spiritually abusive when someone uses God's name to manufacture fear, shame, or financial obedience.
That is where discernment becomes essential.
Consider the passage frequently quoted when churches discuss tithing.
“Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings.” — Malachi 3:8, KJV
The following verse warns of a curse, and verse 10 calls for the tithes to be brought into the storehouse.
These are real words from Scripture.
We must never pretend they are not there.
But we must also refuse to tear them away from their covenant setting.

Malachi was addressing Israel, a people bound to God under the Mosaic covenant. Their tithing system was connected to the Levites, the temple, the land, and provisions for those supported through Israel's covenant worship.
The Hebrew word מַעֲשֵׂר (maʿaser) means “tenth” or “tithe.”

The Old Testament describes tithes particularly in relation to agricultural produce and livestock, with provisions connected to the Levites and the vulnerable (Leviticus 27:30–33; Numbers 18:21–24; Deuteronomy 14:22–29).
Malachi's rebuke was not a fundraising slogan invented for modern churches.
It was a prophetic confrontation within Israel's covenant life.
Does that mean Malachi has nothing to teach Christians?
Of course not.
It teaches us that God takes worship, faithfulness, justice, and the care of those serving Him seriously.
But learning from Malachi is different from automatically transferring every covenant sanction onto a Christian who is struggling to pay rent.
And this distinction matters enormously.
Because Paul writes in Galatians 3:13:
The Greek verb translated “redeemed” is ἐξηγόρασεν (exēgorasen), conveying the idea of buying out or redeeming.
Paul is speaking about Christ's redemptive work and the curse of the law, not issuing a direct statement about modern church budgets.
Nevertheless, his declaration makes one truth impossible to ignore:
A Christian's standing before God rests upon the redeeming work of Jesus Christ, not upon the amount placed in an offering basket.
Christ did not endure the cross so that His redeemed people could live under a perpetual threat that missing a payment would undo His saving grace.
Salvation is not purchased through donations.
Forgiveness is not maintained through a monthly financial transaction.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
Grace is a gift.
And gifts cannot be sold without corrupting their meaning.
Imagine a young widow sitting alone after a Sunday service.
Her husband has died. Her savings are nearly gone. She has two children waiting at home.
She wants to give.
She truly does.
She loves Jesus.
But this week she has barely enough money to buy food.
Then someone tells her that unless she gives her tenth, she is opening the door to a curse.
So she gives.
She goes home with an empty wallet.
Her children ask what they will eat.
And somewhere deep inside, she wonders why loving God feels so much like being punished.
Now ask yourself something.
Would the Savior who welcomed the weary and burdened want His church to ignore her hunger while congratulating itself for collecting her money?
Jesus did commend the poor widow who gave two small coins in Mark 12:41–44 and Luke 21:1–4.
He observed that she gave out of her poverty, while others gave from abundance.
But the context is sobering.
Immediately before that scene, Jesus condemned religious leaders who “devour widows' houses” (Mark 12:40).
Christ's observation of the widow must never become an excuse for modern religious leaders to devour the resources of vulnerable people.
Faithful Christians interpret the widow's offering in different ways—some emphasize her extraordinary devotion, while others also see a tragic exposure of a corrupt religious system.
Either way, Jesus did not command church leaders to pressure impoverished widows into giving away their last money.
That command simply is not there.
And we must never place words in the mouth of Christ that He did not speak.
There is another passage that deserves to be heard.
In 2 Corinthians 8:12, Paul writes:
Do you see it?
According to what a person has.
Not what someone wishes they had.
Not what a preacher demands they produce.
Not what they are frightened into borrowing.
Paul continues in verses 13–14 by explaining that the goal is not to ease the burden of others while creating distress for the giver, but to pursue fairness and mutual care.
This does not eliminate sacrifice.
Christian generosity can be deeply sacrificial.
The Macedonian believers gave generously despite their affliction and poverty (2 Corinthians 8:1–5).
But Paul says they gave “of their own accord” (2 Corinthians 8:3, ESV).
That detail changes everything.
Their sacrifice was voluntary.
It was not extracted by threatening their families with disaster.
And perhaps this is where the real wound begins to surface.
Some Christians have spent years believing that every financial hardship is evidence of spiritual disobedience.
A job disappears.
A child becomes sick.
A business fails.
A family experiences an unexpected expense.
And immediately, the frightened believer begins searching for the offering they missed.
Did I fail God?
Did I give too little?
Is He punishing me?
But Jesus Himself rejected the simplistic assumption that personal suffering always reveals a specific personal sin.
In John 9:1–3, when His disciples questioned whether a man's blindness resulted from his sin or his parents' sin, Jesus refused their explanation.
In Luke 13:1–5, He also rejected the idea that those who suffered terrible tragedies were necessarily worse sinners than others.
This is not a promise that every financial decision has no consequences.
It is a warning against pretending we know God's hidden reasons for another person's suffering.
A Christian facing hardship does not automatically mean a Christian has failed to give enough.
And anyone who confidently tells a grieving family that their tragedy happened because they missed a tithe should tremble at the responsibility of speaking in God's name.
Because that is not a small accusation.
It can crush a conscience.
It can distort a person's understanding of God.
It can turn prayer into panic.
And it can make the cross appear insufficient.
Yet Scripture does not tell us to stop giving.
Far from it.
It calls us to something much more beautiful.
When Zacchaeus encountered Jesus in Luke 19, something extraordinary happened.
Here was a wealthy tax collector whose life had been marked by greed and injustice.
Jesus entered his house.
Grace entered his story.
And Zacchaeus declared that he would give half his possessions to the poor and restore fourfold what he had wrongfully taken.
Notice the order.
Jesus did not first demand a donation as the price of entering Zacchaeus's home.
The encounter with Christ produced repentance.
Repentance produced restitution.
And grace transformed the way Zacchaeus treated money and people.
That is the Gospel's power: not money purchasing acceptance, but grace producing a changed heart.
From greed to generosity.
From exploitation to restoration.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And He still does.
A selfish person can become generous.
A fearful giver can learn to give freely.
A wounded believer can rediscover the Father's goodness.
And a church that has mishandled money can repent, become accountable, and return to the integrity Scripture requires.
But there is another side of this conversation we cannot ignore.
Sometimes Christians rightly reject manipulative fundraising, only to conclude that they have no responsibility to support Gospel ministry.
That is not the biblical answer either.
Paul teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from the Gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14).
Galatians 6:6 encourages those who receive instruction in the Word to share good things with their teachers.
First Timothy 5:17–18 addresses appropriate honor and provision for faithful elders.
And Philippians 4:10–19 celebrates the Philippian believers' financial partnership with Paul's ministry.
So yes, supporting faithful Christian ministry is biblical.
Giving toward evangelism, discipleship, teaching, mercy, and practical service is a meaningful expression of Christian stewardship.
The question is not whether believers should be generous.
The question is whether their generosity is being cultivated through truth and love—or extracted through intimidation.
And that brings us to a necessary distinction.
Giving is worship. But giving is not a payment that forces God to perform.
We cannot purchase miracles.
We cannot buy protection from suffering.
We cannot guarantee prosperity by making a particular donation.
And no ministry has the authority to promise that God will return a fixed financial reward for every contribution.
Yes, 2 Corinthians 9:6 speaks about sowing and reaping.
Yes, Scripture celebrates God's provision.
But the same passage points toward sufficiency, good works, generosity, and thanksgiving to God—not a guaranteed financial investment scheme.

When Paul speaks of God supplying the Philippians' needs in Philippians 4:19, he is encouraging a church that has participated faithfully in his ministry. He is not offering a formula that eliminates every hardship from the lives of donors.
God is not a vending machine.
He is our Father.
And the Gospel is not a business contract.
It is the announcement of salvation through Jesus Christ.
There is something else we need to confront.

A pastor can be sincere and still teach a passage incorrectly. A ministry can do genuine good and still need greater financial accountability. And a Christian can love the church while asking difficult questions about how money is collected and used.
Those things are not contradictions.
They are part of mature discernment.
Paul himself took precautions in handling a financial collection so that his conduct would be honorable before God and people (2 Corinthians 8:20–21).
Transparency is not an enemy of faith.
Accountability is not rebellion.
And asking where an offering goes is not the same as refusing to honor God.
Healthy ministries should welcome responsible stewardship.
They should be willing to explain their mission, their needs, and how financial support is administered.
They should never suggest that their leaders are beyond examination.
Because the church belongs to Jesus Christ.
Not to a personality.
Not to a fundraising department.
Not to an institution's bank account.
To Christ.
And if a ministry truly belongs to Christ, it must be willing to operate in the light.
Perhaps you are reading this with a painful memory.
You remember giving money you could not afford because you feared God's anger.
You remember a sermon that made you feel worthless because you had nothing to offer.
You remember being told that your financial struggle was proof of weak faith.
Or perhaps you are on the other side.
You are a faithful pastor who has spent years serving a congregation, struggling to keep the lights on, helping the needy, and trying to teach generosity without burdening anyone.
You are tired of seeing every appeal for support treated as exploitation.
Both realities deserve to be acknowledged.
There are wounded sheep.
And there are faithful shepherds.
There are ministries that manipulate.
And there are ministries that quietly sacrifice for others.
We must not confuse them.
But we must also remember whose voice should govern them all.
Jesus said:
“Freely ye have received, freely give.” — Matthew 10:8, KJV
In its immediate context, Jesus was instructing the Twelve as He sent them out in ministry. The principle reflects the freely received nature of what they were commissioned to share.
The Gospel begins with a gift we could never afford.
And that gift changes how we give.
Not because we are trying to earn a place at God's table.
But because Jesus has welcomed us through grace.
Not because we are buying His affection.
But because we have already encountered His love.
Not because we are frightened that He will abandon us.
But because He has promised never to forsake His people.
And when that truth finally settles into the heart, something extraordinary happens.
Generosity stops feeling like ransom.
It begins to look like gratitude.
A believer gives because someone needs food.
Because a missionary needs help.
Because a church is faithfully serving its community.
Because biblical teaching is reaching people who have never heard the truth.
Because children need discipleship.
Because the poor should not be forgotten.
Because the Gospel deserves to be proclaimed.
Not to purchase God's favor.
But because God's grace has already changed what the believer treasures.
This is the kind of generosity we want to cultivate at Gospel Warrior.
We believe biblical truth should never be held hostage behind a payment.
We want people who are struggling financially to have access to biblical encouragement.
We want the curious seeker to be able to explore the faith.
We want the exhausted Christian to find sound teaching.
We want families, new believers, and those returning to Christ to discover resources that help them understand Scripture and follow Jesus.
And we want that work to continue and expand.
Not because a payment can replace repentance, obedience, or personal worship.
But because voluntary, consistent support can help sustain the work of creating, sharing, and expanding Christ-centered discipleship resources.
You may choose to regard that support as part of your personal giving budget, according to your convictions, resources, and responsibilities.
What we can say is that supporting faithful Gospel ministry is a legitimate and meaningful expression of generosity.
And if you choose to partner with us, we want you to know that your participation matters.
These products are not the Gospel.
They do not make anyone more spiritual.
They are simply resources and expressions of encouragement that can accompany a life of faith.
But please hear this clearly.
Do not neglect food, medicine, rent, family responsibilities, or necessary care because you are afraid God will be disappointed in you.
The Gospel is not for sale.
The love of Christ is not for sale.
You are welcome to learn, read, grow, and share.
If you are able to support, we are grateful.
If you are not able, we still want you to encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
And if this article has helped you understand the difference between biblical generosity and spiritual pressure, there is another meaningful way to help.
Not as an advertisement.
Not because sharing earns God's approval.
But because someone in your circle may be silently carrying the fear that every financial hardship is divine punishment.
Someone may be thinking of abandoning the church because they have confused religious manipulation with the character of Jesus.
Someone may be a faithful pastor who needs encouragement to teach generosity with compassion and biblical accuracy.
Someone may be using guilt to raise money without realizing how deeply their words are hurting people.
Invite your family, your friends, the believer who has grown distant, and even the person who is still searching for answers about Jesus.
Because the goal is not to build an audience that depends on a personality.
The goal is to help people become disciples who depend on Christ.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something personal.
Not how much money you gave last Sunday.
Not whether you have ever missed a tithe.
I want to ask:
Have you ever given to God because you were afraid of what would happen if you didn't?
You do not have to share an amount, a church name, or a private experience you are not ready to discuss.
But if this message has touched something real in your life, consider leaving a comment.
You might simply write, “Lord, teach me to give with love, not fear.”
Or perhaps your prayer is, “Jesus, heal what fear has done to my faith.”
If you have experienced freedom from financial guilt, your testimony may encourage someone who is still struggling.
Let this be a place where we seek truth with humility.
Where wounded believers are heard.
Where faithful ministry is honored.
Where Scripture is examined carefully.
And where no one is made to feel that their salvation depends on a financial contribution.
Because one day, when we stand before Jesus Christ, the question will not be whether we successfully purchased His favor.
We never could.
The foundation of our hope is that He gave Himself for sinners.
“For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich.” — 2 Corinthians 8:9, KJV
In context, Paul uses the self-giving grace of Christ to inspire the Corinthians' generosity.
He does not turn Christ's sacrifice into a guarantee that every believer will become financially wealthy.
He points to the Lord who gave Himself for us.
And that is where Christian generosity must begin.
At the cross.
Where grace was not sold.
Where mercy was not auctioned.
Where forgiveness was not reserved for the highest bidder.
Where the Son of God willingly gave Himself for people who could never repay Him.
So give when you can.
Give thoughtfully.
Give generously.
Give sacrificially when it is wise and genuinely willing.
Give with discernment.
Support ministries that handle Scripture faithfully and money responsibly.
Care for your family.
Remember the poor.
And never allow someone to convince you that a donation can accomplish what only the blood of Jesus Christ can do.
If you have been using money to bargain for God's love, come back to the cross.
If you have been withholding generosity because greed has taken hold of your heart, come back to the cross.
If you have been manipulating others through fear, repent and come back to the cross.
And if you have been wounded by religious pressure, do not mistake the failures of people for the heart of your Savior.
Jesus still calls sinners to repentance.
He still forgives.
He still restores.
He still transforms.
And He still teaches His people to love, serve, and give.
Not as prisoners trying to purchase their freedom.
But as redeemed people learning to live in the freedom He has already won.
Because the hands that were pierced to redeem you are not reaching toward you with a collection basket demanding payment for His love.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE’S MOST ROMANTIC BOOK CONTAINS A WARNING THAT COULD SAVE YOUR HEART: LOVE CANNOT BE BOUGHT, EVEN WITH ALL THE WEALTH IN THE WORLD.
paragraphs: THE BIBLE’S MOST ROMANTIC BOOK CONTAINS A WARNING THAT COULD SAVE YOUR HEART: LOVE CANNOT BE BOUGHT, EVEN WITH ALL THE WEALTH IN THE WORLD.

Song of Songs 8:7 reveals a truth many people discover only after heartbreak: You can purchase attention, impress someone with riches, and surround a person with luxury. But you cannot buy the one thing your soul desperately longs for—genuine love. And the Gospel reveals a Savior whose love was never for sale.
There is a kind of loneliness that money cannot cure.
It is the loneliness of lying beside someone who no longer looks at you the same way.
The loneliness of paying the bills, buying the gifts, remembering every anniversary, doing everything you thought love required… and still wondering whether you are truly loved.
It is the ache of someone who gave everything to keep a relationship alive, only to discover that everything was still not enough.
And perhaps the most painful part?
You can spend years trying to earn a place in someone's heart without realizing that genuine love was never supposed to be purchased.
Now imagine opening the Bible, expecting another commandment, another warning, another account of kings and prophets…
And discovering a book filled with longing, poetry, kisses, fragrance, gardens, desire, and the extraordinary beauty of two people delighting in one another.
A book so intimate that some readers are surprised it belongs in Scripture.
The Song of Songs.

And near its conclusion, this breathtaking celebration of love delivers a statement that should make every wealthy person, every struggling spouse, every brokenhearted lover, and every believer stop and listen.
“Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it: if a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.” — Song of Solomon 8:7, KJV
Read that last sentence again.
If someone offered everything in his house in exchange for love, his offer would be utterly despised.
Not because money is inherently evil.
Not because gifts are meaningless.
But because real love possesses a dignity that money cannot purchase.
And buried inside the original Hebrew is something even more striking.
The Hebrew text says:
אִם־יִתֵּן אִישׁ אֶת־כָּל־הוֹן בֵּיתוֹ בָּאַהֲבָה בּוֹז יָבוּזוּ לוֹ
Im-yitten ish et-kol-hon beito ba'ahavah, boz yavuzu lo.
A careful rendering is:
“If a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love, he would be utterly despised.”
Notice the Hebrew word הוֹן (hon).
It refers to wealth, substance, or possessions.
The writer is not imagining someone offering a small gift.
He is describing someone offering the accumulated wealth of his household.
Everything.
His possessions. His resources. His material security.
And the expression בּוֹז יָבוּזוּ (boz yavuzu) intensifies the idea of contempt or scorn.
The Hebrew construction emphasizes how thoroughly such an attempt to purchase love would be rejected.
Think about that.
The Bible does not merely suggest that love is expensive.
It declares that authentic love cannot be treated as merchandise.
You may buy a beautiful wedding.
You cannot buy a faithful marriage.
You may purchase an expensive ring.
You cannot purchase devotion.
You may finance a luxurious home.
You cannot purchase peace inside it.
You may shower someone with gifts.
You cannot force that person's heart to love you.
And you may spend your entire life building an impressive image that convinces people to admire you…
While secretly wondering whether anyone would still stay if you had nothing left to offer.
That is where this Scripture becomes painfully personal.
Because some people are not trying to buy love with money.
They are trying to buy it with exhaustion.
They give until they are empty.
They apologize even when they have done nothing wrong.
They silence their convictions because they are terrified of abandonment.
They confuse being needed with being cherished.
They believe that if they become attractive enough, successful enough, generous enough, obedient enough, or useful enough, someone will finally choose them.
And slowly, without noticing, they begin treating their own worth as something another person has the authority to determine.
But listen carefully.
Being loved is not the same as being purchased. And being valuable is not the same as being useful.
You were made in the image of God before you ever earned a salary, entered a relationship, received a compliment, or accomplished anything impressive.
Genesis 1:27 places human dignity in God's creation of humanity in His image.
Not in wealth.
Not in popularity.
Not in romantic desirability.
Not in another person's approval.
Your dignity was never meant to rise and fall with someone's willingness to stay.
And yet the Song of Songs does not stop at the impossibility of buying love.
It says something extraordinary about love's strength.
“Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.”
In Hebrew:
מַיִם רַבִּים לֹא יוּכְלוּ לְכַבּוֹת אֶת־הָאַהֲבָה
Mayim rabbim lo yukhelu lekhabbot et-ha'ahavah.
“Many waters cannot quench love.”
The image is astonishing.
Picture a fire burning so fiercely that enormous waters cannot extinguish it.
Floodwaters rise.
Storms rage.
The currents become violent.
And still the fire refuses to die.
That is the poetic picture.
Not a shallow attraction that disappears when circumstances become inconvenient.
Not an arrangement sustained merely by material benefits.
But love portrayed as powerful, enduring, and resistant to overwhelming opposition.
The preceding verse intensifies the imagery:
“For love is strong as death; jealousy is cruel as the grave: the coals thereof are coals of fire, which hath a most vehement flame.” — Song of Solomon 8:6, KJV
The phrase translated “a most vehement flame” contains the Hebrew expression שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָה (shalhevet-yah).

It is commonly understood as an intensely powerful flame. The ending -yah is also associated with the divine name Yah, and some interpreters understand the expression as “a flame of Yah,” or “the flame of the LORD.”
Scholars differ over whether the expression is explicitly invoking God's name or using an intensified poetic form.
But the central picture is unmistakable.
Love is being described through the language of overwhelming fire.
Powerful.
Dangerous when mishandled.
Beautiful when rightly cherished.
And impossible to reduce to a financial transaction.
But there is something we must not misunderstand.
Song of Songs is first and foremost a celebration of human romantic love, with its beauty, mutual desire, exclusivity, and covenantal implications.
We must not erase that original meaning by pretending every romantic image is secretly a direct reference to Jesus.
The lovers in this poem are not simply coded characters whose every word must be transformed into an allegory.
Scripture deserves better than that.
And so do its readers.
Yet when we read this celebration of love within the whole Bible, we encounter something breathtaking.
The God who created human beings capable of love is also the God who reveals His own steadfast love through His covenant faithfulness and ultimately through Jesus Christ.
And here is where the story becomes more than romantic.
It becomes redemptive.
Because humanity has spent generations trying to buy what only grace can give.
We try to purchase acceptance with religious performance.
We try to silence guilt through charitable acts.
We try to bargain with God through promises.
“Lord, if You forgive me, I will never do it again.”
“Lord, if You bless me, I will finally become faithful.”
“Lord, if I give enough, serve enough, pray enough, suffer enough… perhaps You will love me.”
But the Gospel dismantles that entire system of bargaining.
Listen to the words of the apostle Peter:

“Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold… But with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.” — 1 Peter 1:18–19, KJV
Not redeemed with silver.
Not redeemed with gold.
Not redeemed through the accumulated wealth of the world.
Redeemed through the precious blood of Jesus Christ.
And this distinction matters more than we sometimes realize.
When Scripture speaks of Christ paying the price of redemption, it is not teaching that we purchased God's affection or that money can obtain salvation.
It is teaching that our rescue was accomplished through Christ's sacrificial work, not through our ability to earn it.
The Greek word ἐλυτρώθητε (elytrōthēte) in 1 Peter 1:18 means “you were redeemed” or “you were ransomed.”
It describes deliverance through redemption.
And Peter deliberately contrasts perishable wealth with the immeasurable worth of Christ's sacrifice.
Humanity could not finance its own rescue.
Jesus accomplished what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
Now consider how scandalous that grace really is.
Jesus did not wait until sinners became respectable before extending mercy.
He ate with tax collectors.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He touched those society avoided.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He called people out of darkness without pretending their darkness was harmless.
He offered forgiveness without calling evil good.
He demonstrated a love that was neither sentimental indulgence nor cold condemnation.
It was holy love.
Truthful love.
Merciful love.
Transforming love.
And then He went to the cross.
Not because humanity had finally become deserving.
But because God's saving love moved toward people who could never rescue themselves.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8, KJV
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we repaired our reputations.
Not after we paid off our moral debts.
Not after we learned how to appear religious in public.
While we were still sinners.
And perhaps that is the sentence someone reading this has desperately needed to hear.
Because you know what it means to carry a history you cannot rewrite.
You know what it means to smile at church while privately remembering things you wish had never happened.
You know what it means to look at your reflection and wonder whether the person staring back is still worthy of love.
Perhaps you betrayed someone.
Perhaps someone betrayed you.
Perhaps you made a terrible decision and have been living under the weight of it ever since.
Perhaps you were abandoned by someone who promised to stay.
Perhaps you have mistaken someone's attention for genuine affection because loneliness made almost anything feel like love.
Or perhaps you are surrounded by people, successful by every visible measure, and still carrying a quiet emptiness that no achievement has ever filled.
Hear this.
Jesus does not minimize sin.
He calls us to repentance.
But He also does not tell repentant sinners to purchase their way back into His presence.
He calls them to come.
To believe.
To turn from sin.
To receive the mercy they could never earn.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
A gift.
Not a financial transaction.
Not a reward for religious perfection.
A gift received through faith.
And genuine faith does not leave us content to remain enslaved to the sins Christ came to save us from.
Grace transforms.
It teaches us to turn away from ungodliness, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
It leads us toward obedience, holiness, and a new way of living.
It does not simply comfort us in the ruins.
It begins rebuilding what sin has broken.
And that brings us back to the extraordinary wisdom of Song of Songs.
Because when you understand that love cannot be purchased, you begin seeing relationships differently.
You stop treating generosity as a guarantee of affection.
You stop believing expensive gifts can replace repentance.
You stop confusing jealousy with devotion or control with commitment.
You stop assuming that staying in every destructive situation is proof of biblical love.
The Song celebrates powerful romantic love, but it does not command anyone to tolerate abuse, coercion, betrayal, or danger.
True love cannot be reduced to possession.
Biblical love must also be understood alongside the character described in 1 Corinthians 13.
It is patient.
It is kind.
It does not rejoice in wrongdoing.
It rejoices in the truth.
And if someone repeatedly uses money, gifts, religious language, or emotional pressure to control you, that behavior should not be romanticized as the irresistible fire described in Song of Songs.
Love does not become holy simply because someone calls it love.
Its character matters.
Its fruit matters.
Truth matters.
And sometimes the most faithful thing a person can do is stop calling manipulation devotion.
Somebody reading this knows exactly why that sentence matters.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to prove that you are worth choosing.
You have sacrificed your peace.
You have ignored warning signs.
You have apologized for another person's cruelty.
You have convinced yourself that if you just give a little more, endure a little longer, or become a little better, everything will finally change.
But money cannot create repentance in another person's heart.
Sacrifice cannot force someone to become faithful.
And your willingness to suffer cannot transform another person against their will.
God can change hearts.
You cannot purchase that transformation.
This is why love must be accompanied by wisdom.
Why commitment must be accompanied by truth.
Why forgiveness must not be confused with the automatic restoration of trust.
And why grace must never be used as an excuse to continue harming others.
The Gospel calls both the wounded and the one who has done the wounding to face the truth before God.
For the wounded, there is comfort and hope.
For the guilty, there is a call to repentance and the possibility of forgiveness.
For the proud, there is a warning.
For the humble, there is grace.
And for everyone willing to come to Jesus Christ, there is an invitation to new life.
But perhaps the deepest question is not whether you can buy someone else's love.
Perhaps it is whether you have spent your entire life trying to buy God's.
You give offerings because you fear He will reject you if you do not.
You serve because you believe rest will disappoint Him.
You compare your spiritual life with others and secretly wonder whether you have done enough to deserve His attention.
You treat every unanswered prayer as evidence that God has stopped loving you.
And somewhere along the way, the Father becomes a distant employer whose approval must be earned instead of the gracious God who calls sinners to Himself through His Son.
If that is you, remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that Jesus Christ is not waiting for you to become wealthy enough, impressive enough, or religious enough to make His sacrifice worthwhile.
His invitation is to repent and believe the Gospel.
And if you already belong to Him, your obedience is not a payment for His love.
It is the grateful response of a life being transformed by grace.
There is a world of difference between those two things.
One produces spiritual slavery.
The other produces worship.
One says, “I must earn what Christ has done.”
The other says, “Because Christ has loved me, I want to live for Him.”
And that changes even how we think about money.
Money is not evil in itself.
Scripture warns that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil (1 Timothy 6:10).
Wealth can be used selfishly.
But it can also be used generously.
Money can finance vanity.
But it can also help feed the hungry, support faithful ministry, provide Scripture resources, assist families, and spread the message of Jesus Christ.
The question is not simply how much we possess.
It is what possesses our hearts.
Jesus said:
“For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.” — Matthew 6:21, KJV
Our giving can reveal what we value.
But it must never become an attempt to buy divine approval.
For some supporters, that may be part of their planned Christian giving.
Scripture calls believers to give willingly, thoughtfully, and cheerfully—not under pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
You should never give money you need for essential responsibilities because someone has made you afraid that God will love you less if you do not.
And that is precisely why this invitation matters.
Not because salvation has a price.
But because freely supporting sound biblical teaching and Gospel-centered encouragement can be a meaningful expression of generosity and stewardship.
The greater purpose remains the same.
To lift up Jesus Christ.
To make Scripture understandable.
To call people toward repentance and faith.
To remind struggling believers that spiritual growth requires more than occasional inspiration.
And to help people become rooted in the Word of God.
These resources are available to help believers grow deeper in Jesus Christ, understand Scripture, strengthen their spiritual disciplines, and continue learning beyond a single article.
And even if you cannot contribute financially, you can still help carry this message farther.
Not merely because you enjoyed reading it.
Someone may be trying to earn love from a person who continually humiliates them.
Someone may be using gifts to avoid taking responsibility for the damage they have caused.
Someone may be afraid that their past has placed them beyond the reach of God's mercy.
And someone may be quietly believing that God will only welcome them when they have finally become good enough.
Imagine that person opening Facebook tonight.
Then encountering one sentence:
“Your salvation was never for sale. Jesus Christ has already accomplished what you could never purchase.”
Perhaps that will be the moment they finally open their Bible again.
Perhaps they will pray honestly for the first time in months.
Perhaps they will recognize the need to repent.
Perhaps they will realize they need help leaving a harmful relationship.
Perhaps they will remember that the cross is greater than the shame they have been carrying.
You do not know who needs this message.
But you may know someone who does.
And before you leave, I want to ask you something.
Not about your bank account.
Not about your relationship status.
Not about how impressive your life appears to others.
What have you been trying to purchase with your sacrifices that only genuine love or God's grace can give?
Acceptance?
Security?
Forgiveness?
Someone's loyalty?
God's approval?
You do not have to expose private wounds publicly. But if this message touched something real in your heart, consider leaving a simple, honest comment.
And if you have experienced God's restoring mercy, your testimony may encourage someone who believes their story is already over.
Return to Song of Songs 8:6–7.
Read it in context.
Remember that the beauty of human love is not found in its market value.
And remember that the Gospel points us to a love greater than anything humanity could earn.
Because one day, everything money can purchase will fail.
The expensive clothes will wear out.
The impressive houses will need repairs.
The newest possessions will become old.
The applause will fade.
The titles will disappear.
And every human life will eventually face the reality that no amount of accumulated wealth can purchase eternal life.
But Jesus said:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” — Mark 8:36, KJV
That question reaches beyond romance.
Beyond marriage.
Beyond financial success.
Beyond the desire to be admired.
It reaches the soul.
You can gain the world and still be spiritually lost.
You can lose worldly status and still discover eternal treasure in Christ.
And you can come to the Savior empty-handed, confessing your sin, trusting His death and resurrection, and find that His invitation was never reserved for the wealthy or the impressive.
This is the breathtaking difference between worldly transactions and the grace of God.
The world asks, “What can you offer?”
The Gospel announces what Jesus Christ has accomplished.
The world measures your usefulness.
The Gospel calls you to repent, believe, and receive new life in Christ.
The world may reduce love to appearance, advantage, or wealth.
But the cross reveals a holy and sacrificial love that confronts sin, offers forgiveness, and transforms those who belong to Jesus.
And that brings us back to the most romantic book in the Bible.
A book that celebrates the beauty of love between a man and a woman.
A book that describes love as a powerful flame.
A book that declares many waters cannot quench it.
A book that refuses to place a price tag on what should never be merchandise.
“If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, it would utterly be contemned.” — Song of Solomon 8:7, KJV
All the wealth in the house.
And still, love cannot be bought.
So stop trying to purchase what cannot be purchased.
Stop treating another person's approval as the final verdict on your worth.
Stop trying to pay God for forgiveness that Christ offers through grace.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you have been wounded, seek the truth, wise support, and the healing you need.
If you have been forgiven, live in gratitude and obedience.
If you have resources, use them faithfully and generously.
And if you have never entrusted your life to Jesus Christ, do not wait until you have something impressive to bring Him.
Come in repentance and faith.
Come acknowledging your need for mercy.
Come believing that the crucified and risen Savior is able to save.
Because the greatest treasure is not a person you can persuade to love you with enough money.
It is knowing Jesus Christ, in whom forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life are found.
And perhaps the most beautiful thing you will discover is this:
You could never afford the redemption your soul needed—but Jesus Christ gave Himself to accomplish it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD MAKE EZEKIEL LIE ON HIS LEFT SIDE FOR 390 DAYS? THE TERRIFYING WARNING MOST CHRISTIANS NEVER NOTICE
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD MAKE EZEKIEL LIE ON HIS LEFT SIDE FOR 390 DAYS? THE TERRIFYING WARNING MOST CHRISTIANS NEVER NOTICE

Before Jerusalem fell, God turned one prophet's body into a living warning. But behind those 390 days lies a truth about hidden sin, divine judgment, and the mercy of Jesus Christ that may change the way you look at your own life.
Imagine waking up tomorrow morning and hearing God tell you to lie down.
Not because you are tired.
Not because you are sick.
But because an entire nation has become so comfortable with sin that ordinary warnings no longer seem to reach its heart.
Now imagine being told to lie on your left side for 390 days.
Three hundred and ninety.
Not minutes. Not hours.
Days.
And every time someone walks past, every time someone stares, every time someone wonders whether you have lost your mind, your suffering becomes part of a message they desperately need to hear.
That is what happened to the prophet Ezekiel.
And the most unsettling part of this story is not how long he lay there.
It is why God told him to do it.
Because sometimes the most dangerous spiritual condition is not openly rejecting God.
It is becoming so accustomed to disobeying Him that His warnings no longer disturb you.
And before you decide this is only a strange Old Testament story about ancient Israel, stay with me.

There is something about those 390 days that speaks to the person who still prays but has stopped listening. The person who knows Scripture but keeps negotiating with temptation. The person who looks spiritually alive in public while privately carrying a burden of compromise.
And there is something even more extraordinary waiting at the other end of this story.
Grace.
But first, we must understand the warning.

Ezekiel was not standing in Jerusalem when God gave him this command. He was among the Jewish exiles in Babylon, far from the city many of them still associated with God's presence and covenant promises.
Jerusalem had not yet experienced its final catastrophic destruction at the hands of Babylon.
Some people still believed the city would survive.
After all, the temple stood there.
The religious institutions remained.
The people had a history with God.
Surely that counted for something.
But a sacred history cannot make persistent rebellion harmless.
And God's patience must never be mistaken for His approval.
In Ezekiel chapter 4, God instructed the prophet to take a brick, portray Jerusalem on it, and arrange a miniature siege against it.
Imagine the scene.
A grown man placing a brick before him.
Drawing a city.
Building siegeworks around it.
Setting an iron plate between himself and the model city as a sign of the coming siege.
To the people watching, it must have looked extraordinary.
But this was not street entertainment.
It was a prophetic sign.
God was making visible what the people refused to take seriously.
Then came the command that has puzzled Bible readers for centuries.

“Lie thou also upon thy left side, and lay the iniquity of the house of Israel upon it: according to the number of the days that thou shalt lie upon it thou shalt bear their iniquity.” — Ezekiel 4:4, KJV
The next verse reveals the number.
“For I have laid upon thee the years of their iniquity, according to the number of the days, three hundred and ninety days: so shalt thou bear the iniquity of the house of Israel.” — Ezekiel 4:5, KJV
Read that carefully.
God did not merely tell Ezekiel to lie down.
He commanded him to portray the burden of Israel's iniquity.
The Hebrew text contains a word that makes the message even more serious.
עָוֹן — ʿāwōn
Commonly transliterated avon, this word can refer to iniquity, guilt, and, depending on context, the consequences or punishment associated with wrongdoing.
It is not merely the idea of making an innocent mistake.
It describes the moral seriousness of sin before a holy God.
When Ezekiel was commanded to bear Israel's ʿāwōn, he was acting out a prophetic representation of the nation's guilt and its consequences.
He was not becoming Israel's redeemer.
He was not removing its sins.
He was not making an atoning sacrifice.
He was portraying a burden that the nation could no longer pretend did not exist.
And here is where the story becomes painfully personal.
We are often more concerned about whether our sins are visible to other people than whether they are grieving the heart of God.
We worry about being exposed.
God calls us to repent.
We worry about our reputation.
God calls us to truth.
We worry about losing what we have built.
God calls us to surrender what is destroying us.
Israel had a covenant history, a temple, and religious traditions.
But none of those things could make disobedience righteous.
And neither can ours.
You can attend church and still be resisting God.
You can post Bible verses and still be refusing to forgive.
You can know the language of worship while secretly feeding the very sin Christ calls you to abandon.
That does not mean every struggling Christian is a hypocrite.
There is a difference between fighting sin with repentance and making peace with sin while refusing to turn away.
One is the painful struggle of a heart returning to God.
The other is the dangerous comfort of a heart becoming hardened.
Ezekiel's message confronts that difference.
But why exactly 390 days?
Why not 40?
Why not 70?
Why such a strange number?
The text itself gives the essential explanation: God assigned a symbolic relationship between days and years.
One day represented one year.
In Hebrew, Ezekiel 4:6 expresses this principle with the words:
יוֹם לַשָּׁנָה — yōm laššānāh
Literally, “a day for a year.”
The 390 days represented 390 years associated with the iniquity of the house of Israel.
But there is an important detail that responsible Bible interpretation must not overlook.
Ezekiel chapter 4 also commands the prophet to lie on his right side for 40 days, representing the iniquity of the house of Judah.
The text distinguishes Israel and Judah, though interpreters differ on how the periods relate to their histories.

Some understand the 390 years as representing a long period of Israel's covenant unfaithfulness. Others propose particular historical starting and ending points, including events surrounding the divided monarchy and the exile.
The exact historical calculation is debated.
Scripture does not explicitly identify a universally agreed beginning and ending date for those 390 years.
And while some have proposed that the 390 and 40 years combine into a larger symbolic total, we should not pretend that every proposed chronology has been conclusively established.
The message God actually gives us is already powerful enough.
The nation had accumulated a history of covenant rebellion.
Judgment was approaching.
And God was making the seriousness of that rebellion visible through His prophet.
Think about that.
The people were not being warned about a single bad afternoon.
They were being confronted with a long history of refusing to listen.
Generation after generation had received the testimony of God's covenant, His commands, His prophets, and His warnings.
Yet the nation repeatedly turned toward idolatry, injustice, and unfaithfulness.
And this is where the number 390 becomes more than a historical curiosity.
It forces us to consider how easily a pattern becomes a lifestyle.
Nobody begins by planning to become spiritually numb.
It often starts with something small.
A conviction ignored.
An apology postponed.
A secret defended.
A compromise justified.
A prayer life slowly abandoned.
Then another day passes.
And another.
Until the thing that once troubled your conscience no longer seems particularly serious.
Not because God's holiness has changed.
But because your heart has grown accustomed to what should have driven you to repentance.
That is one reason this passage deserves more than a quick reading.
It shows us that God's warnings are not meaningless interruptions.
They are calls to return before destruction overtakes us.
And Ezekiel's assignment was not comfortable.
The prophet's body became part of the message.
He was commanded to remain on his assigned side during the prophetic sign, with God also speaking of restraining him until the appointed days were completed.
The surrounding passage includes carefully measured food, rationed water, and a portrayal of the hardships associated with Jerusalem's coming siege.
We should be careful not to invent details the Bible does not provide.
The text does not tell us everything about Ezekiel's daily routine, whether the sign occupied every hour without interruption, or how every practical necessity was handled.
But it leaves no doubt about the purpose.
This was an embodied warning.
A public demonstration of the weight of sin and the severity of approaching judgment.
And that makes me wonder how many warnings we dismiss because they do not arrive in the form we expected.
Sometimes God confronts us through Scripture.
Sometimes a faithful friend tells us the truth we have been avoiding.
Sometimes a sermon exposes a compromise we thought nobody knew about.
Sometimes the consequences of our choices reveal just how far we have wandered.
Not every hardship is a punishment for personal sin. Jesus explicitly challenged that assumption in John 9:1–3.
But whenever Scripture exposes our rebellion, the proper response is not to defend it.
It is to repent.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to hear tonight.
You have been carrying something.
Maybe it is guilt over a decision you wish you could undo.
Maybe it is resentment toward someone who hurt you.
Maybe you have been living two different lives, one that people admire and another that you are terrified they might discover.
Maybe you are not running from church.
You are running from the particular truth God has already made clear to you.
And every time conviction rises, you tell yourself you will deal with it later.
Later, when life settles down.
Later, when you feel stronger.
Later, when giving up that relationship, habit, bitterness, or secret does not seem so painful.
But what if later is becoming the very excuse that keeps you from surrendering today?
Listen carefully.
The point of Ezekiel's 390 days is not that God has a secret numerical countdown attached to your personal failures.
Scripture does not teach that.
The point is that sin is serious, God's warnings matter, and His people must not confuse His patience with indifference.
And even in judgment, Ezekiel's book does not leave us without hope.
Because the God who exposes sin is also the God who promises to transform hearts.
Later, in Ezekiel 36:26, God declares:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.” — KJV
Do you see the beauty of that promise?
God does not merely say, “Try harder to make your heart softer.”
He promises to give His people a new heart.
A heart that responds to Him.
A heart no longer ruled by stubborn resistance.
A heart transformed by His gracious work.
The Hebrew expression for a new heart is:
לֵב חָדָשׁ — lēv ḥādāš
A new heart.
Not a polished version of the old rebellion.
Not a religious mask covering unchanged desires.
Something new.
And that promise finds its deepest fulfillment in the saving work of Jesus Christ and the new-covenant life given through the Holy Spirit.
But before we rush to the comfort of that promise, we need to face something.
The gospel is not beautiful because sin is small.
The gospel is beautiful because sin is so serious that we could never rescue ourselves from its guilt, and yet God has acted in Christ to save sinners.
Ezekiel lay on his side as a prophetic sign of Israel's iniquity.
Centuries later, Jesus Christ would bear sin in a way Ezekiel never could.
Not symbolically representing the guilt of one nation in a prophetic performance.
But truly giving Himself as the sinless Savior.
Isaiah 53:6 declares:
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.” — KJV
Notice the connection.
Iniquity.
The burden of sin.
The reality we cannot explain away.
Yet we must also preserve the distinction.
Ezekiel's sign was a warning about covenant judgment.
Christ's sacrifice is the saving work by which sinners are reconciled to God.
Ezekiel did not die for Israel's sins.
Jesus died for our sins.
Ezekiel acted out a burden.
Jesus bore our sins in His body on the cross, as 1 Peter 2:24 teaches.
