This is why we keep returning to the cross.
Not because we enjoy talking about brokenness.
But because Jesus Christ is the only One who can deal with our deepest problem: sin separating us from a holy God.
At the cross, the Son of God bore the judgment our sins deserve.
Through His resurrection, He conquered death.
And through repentance and faith in Him, sinners receive forgiveness and new life.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have to become the master of your future.
Your family history may influence your circumstances.
It does not determine whether Christ can save you.
Your failures may have real consequences.
But they are not stronger than the mercy of the risen Savior.
From Scandal to Grace is not a promise that every earthly consequence disappears. It is the proclamation that Jesus Christ can redeem sinners and transform lives that seemed beyond hope.
And there is one more thing I want you to see.
Elisheba's name is preserved in Scripture, but the biblical narrative does not make her its central hero.
Neither is Aaron the final hero.
Nor Nahshon.
Nor Moses.
The story of Scripture keeps moving toward the One greater than them all.
Jesus.
The Lion of the tribe of Judah.
The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
Our great High Priest.
Our Redeemer.
Our risen King.
That is why a small verse in Exodus can send us searching through Numbers, Ruth, Matthew, and Hebrews until we stand once again in awe of Christ.
Not because every detail is a hidden prophecy.
Not because every marriage conceals a secret code.
But because the Bible presents a unified history of God's dealings with His people, culminating in the person and saving work of Jesus Christ.
And when we read Scripture carefully, even its genealogies can help us understand the world in which God's promises unfolded.
Maybe that is the invitation for you today.
Stop rushing past the Word.
Stop assuming the unfamiliar names have nothing to teach you.
Stop measuring your spiritual life by how much attention you receive.
And stop believing that your failures have placed you beyond the reach of Jesus.
Open your Bible again.
Pray again.
Repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ is calling you to forgive.
Seek help where you need help.
Return to fellowship.
Let the truth of Scripture correct what you have believed wrongly and strengthen what has grown weak.
And if you are reading this while feeling forgotten, remember that the God who sees in secret is not limited by human applause.
You are not saved by becoming important.
You are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And a life surrendered to Him is never meaningless.
Or share what God has been teaching you about serving Him without needing recognition.
Someone else reading your words may discover that they are not alone in their struggle.
And think of one person who needs this message.
A parent who feels unnoticed.
A ministry worker who has grown weary.
A young believer who thinks their past disqualifies them.
A friend who is drifting from the faith.
We want this community to be more than a place where people read inspiring words and keep scrolling.

We want it to be a place where the Gospel is proclaimed, the Scriptures are opened, weary believers are encouraged, sinners are called to repentance, and disciples are equipped to follow Jesus faithfully.
Not because you can purchase God's favor.
And certainly not because your giving can replace your responsibilities to your local church, family, or those in need.
Salvation is God's gift, not a product for sale.
These products are simply an additional benefit. The heart of this invitation is not merchandise.
It is biblical nourishment.
It is encouraging people to keep growing in Christ.
It is making the message of repentance, grace, forgiveness, and redemption accessible to more people.
You can help without spending anything.
Pray that the Lord will use the Scriptures to open hearts.
And keep walking with Jesus.
Because this ministry is not about building a name greater than His.
It is about pointing people to the only Name by which we must be saved.
The name of Jesus Christ.
And before you leave, return with me one last time to that overlooked woman in Exodus.
Elisheba.
A wife.
A daughter.
A sister.
A mother.
A woman whose name appears in a genealogy that many people will never stop to read.
Her husband became Israel's high priest.
Her brother led Judah.
Her sons entered priestly service, and two of them died under God's judgment.
And through her brother's family line, Scripture traces the ancestry that leads to Jesus Christ.
One verse.
So many connections.
Yet the greatest truth is not that she was related to important people.

The greatest truth for us is that importance in the kingdom of God is not measured by public recognition, and that every sinner's deepest need is fulfilled not by family connections or religious positions, but by Jesus Christ alone.
So when you close this article, do not merely remember Elisheba.
Remember the Savior.
The One who sees what others overlook.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who receives those who come to Him in faith.
The One whose blood can cleanse what human effort never could.
The One whose resurrection means death does not have the final word.
And the One who is still transforming lives through the power of His Gospel.
You may spend your whole life unnoticed by the world, but the greatest tragedy would not be that people forgot your name—it would be to hear the name of Jesus and never truly come to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE PROVERBS 31 WOMAN WAS NEVER MEANT TO MAKE CHRISTIAN WOMEN FEEL INADEQUATE
paragraphs: THE PROVERBS 31 WOMAN WAS NEVER MEANT TO MAKE CHRISTIAN WOMEN FEEL INADEQUATE
If reading Proverbs 31 has ever made you feel like you are failing God as a woman, you may have been carrying a burden the passage itself was never written to put on your shoulders.
There is a woman sitting somewhere tonight who loves Jesus…
but she is tired.
Not the kind of tired that disappears after eight hours of sleep.
Soul tired.
She has dishes waiting in the sink. Laundry she meant to fold yesterday. Messages she has not answered. A Bible she wishes she opened more often. Prayers she started and somehow never finished.

She sees another Christian woman online with a spotless kitchen, smiling children, an organized devotional journal, a thriving marriage, a successful business, homemade bread cooling on the counter, and a caption about waking up at 5:00 a.m. to spend two uninterrupted hours with God.
And something inside her quietly whispers:
Why can't you be more like her?
Then somebody mentions Proverbs 31.
And suddenly the whisper gets louder.
She remembers the woman who rises while it is still night.
The woman who works willingly.
The woman who buys fields.
The woman who plants vineyards.
The woman whose children rise and call her blessed.
The woman whose husband praises her.

The woman who seems wise, productive, generous, financially competent, spiritually mature, physically strong, domestically capable, emotionally stable, respected, prepared, disciplined, compassionate, and apparently able to accomplish more before breakfast than some of us accomplish before Thursday.
And the exhausted Christian woman closes her Bible feeling worse than when she opened it.
Maybe that woman is you.
If it is, stay with me.
Because something beautiful has been hiding in this passage…
and once you see it, Proverbs 31 may stop sounding like an accusation and start sounding like what it was always meant to be:
honor.
The famous passage begins with words that deserve to be heard in their original Hebrew:
אֵשֶׁת־חַיִל מִי יִמְצָא
Eshet chayil, mi yimtza?
Proverbs 31:10.
Often translated along the lines of:
“Who can find a virtuous woman?”
But that familiar English word virtuous can sound strangely delicate to modern ears.
The Hebrew is stronger.
אֵשֶׁת — eshet means “woman of” or “wife of.”
And חַיִל — chayil carries ideas associated with strength, ability, valor, capability, wealth, or force depending on its context.
This is not merely a portrait of a woman who remembers to vacuum.
This is a woman of strength.
A woman of substance.
A woman of valor.
An eshet chayil.
And that changes the atmosphere of the passage.
Proverbs 31 is not God standing over an exhausted woman with a clipboard saying,
“You missed three things today.”
It is poetry celebrating the kind of strength produced by wisdom and the fear of the Lord.
Read that again.
Celebration.
Not condemnation.
The passage itself eventually tells us where her true beauty comes from:
“Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.”
Proverbs 31:30.
There it is.
Not perfection.
Not appearance.
Not productivity.
Not spotless floors.
Not flawless motherhood.
Not marriage.
Not entrepreneurship.
Not having children.
Not making bread.
Not owning property.
Not waking up before everybody else every single morning.
Her deepest distinction is that she fears the Lord.
And perhaps somewhere along the way, Christian culture occasionally turned a poem of praise into a performance review.
We took a portrait and made it a checklist.
We took wisdom and turned it into comparison.
We took a celebration of godly womanhood and sometimes handed it to exhausted women as another measuring stick with which to beat themselves.
But look more carefully.
Proverbs 31:10–31 is beautifully constructed Hebrew poetry. The verses move through the Hebrew alphabet as an acrostic poem.
That matters.
It gives the passage the feel of an A-to-Z celebration of a woman shaped by wisdom.
It is as though the poet is saying:
Look at her faithfulness.
Look at her courage.
Look at her wisdom.
Look at her generosity.
Look at her strength.
Look at what reverence for God can produce through the ordinary movements of a human life.
The poem is not saying every godly woman must perform every described activity every day.
And there is another detail we often rush past.
Proverbs 31 does not begin with a man lecturing women about how to become worthy of him.
The chapter opens with:
“The words of king Lemuel, the prophecy that his mother taught him.”
A mother is instructing her son.
Think about that.
Before Proverbs 31 became something women were told to measure themselves against, its surrounding context included a woman teaching a man wisdom.
And when the poem reaches its conclusion, the woman's works are not hidden.
“Give her of the fruit of her hands; and let her own works praise her in the gates.”
Proverbs 31:31.
Honor her.
Recognize her.
Let what God has produced through her life speak.
This passage is not designed to humiliate faithful women.
It dignifies them.
Which means maybe the woman who most needs Proverbs 31 tonight is not the woman who believes she has mastered it.
Maybe it is the woman crying quietly in the bathroom because motherhood has overwhelmed her.
The widow learning how to live in a house that suddenly feels too quiet.
The single woman wondering whether the church sees her as somehow incomplete.
The wife praying for a marriage nobody knows is struggling.
The woman rebuilding after divorce.
The grandmother carrying burdens for children who no longer listen to her.
The young woman fighting temptation in secret.
The woman whose business failed.
The woman working two jobs.
The woman caring for aging parents.
The woman fighting through grief.
The woman who opened Instagram for five minutes and somehow walked away believing everybody else's life is blessed except hers.
The woman who loves Christ deeply but does not feel impressive.
Listen carefully.
Your worth was never supposed to come from successfully impersonating another woman.
And it certainly does not come from outperforming her.
Christian womanhood is not a competition.
The woman beside you is not your measuring stick.
Jesus is not asking you to become her.
He is calling you to follow Him.
And this is where Proverbs 31 becomes even more beautiful when read inside the larger story of Scripture.
Because if you turn every biblical description of righteousness into a ladder you must climb before God will love you, eventually every ladder becomes an instrument of despair.
You will always discover another rung you have not reached.
Another command you have broken.
Another opportunity you wasted.
Another morning you slept too long.
Another conversation where you lost your temper.
Another season where prayer became difficult.
Another failure you wish nobody knew about.
Another version of yourself you promised God you would become by now.
And eventually you have to confront the truth Christianity has been telling us all along:
You cannot save yourself by becoming impressive enough.
That is why Jesus came.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people finally figured out how to become good enough for God.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners who could never make themselves righteous can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ carried what we could not carry.
Christ fulfilled righteousness we could never manufacture.
Christ bore sin at the cross.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
And the woman who comes to Him in repentance and faith does not stand before God desperately waving her spiritual résumé.
She stands clothed in grace.
That does not make obedience irrelevant.
Grace does not tell us sin does not matter.
Grace transforms why we obey.
We do not obey so Jesus will finally love us.
We obey because in Christ we have encountered a love powerful enough to change us.
That distinction can rescue a woman from years of religious exhaustion.
Maybe you have spent years trying to prove that you are a “good Christian woman.”
Maybe nobody knows how tired you are.
You serve.
You smile.
You encourage everybody.
You show up.
You say, “God is good.”
And He is.
But underneath your smile is a frightened question:
Am I enough?
Here is the answer Christianity gives you.
On your own?
No.
Neither am I.
Neither is the woman you keep comparing yourself to.
That is precisely why grace is such astonishing news.
Jesus did not come for people who had finally become enough.
He came for sinners.
For failures.
For the ashamed.
For the spiritually bankrupt.
For people with histories.
For people with wounds.
For people who cannot rewrite yesterday.
For people who need resurrection, not cosmetic improvement.
And perhaps this is where someone needs to stop reading for a moment.
Because you are not merely tired.
You are hiding.
There is something beneath the Christian appearance that nobody knows.
A secret sin.
Bitterness.
Pornography.
An affair.
Jealousy.
Anger.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A private addiction.
A wound you have allowed to become hatred.
A compromise you keep renaming because repentance sounds too painful.
Grace is not permission to remain there.
Jesus loves sinners too much to merely decorate their chains.
He calls us out.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Turn around.
Bring the ugly thing to the Savior who already knows it exists.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is restoration in Christ.
There is no scandal in your past greater than the grace found at His cross.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
Not by telling us consequences are imaginary.
Jesus rewrites everything by taking guilty people, forgiving them through His blood, making them His own, and beginning the long holy work of transforming them.
Maybe Proverbs 31 has hurt because you read it while carrying shame.
So every virtue sounded like an accusation.
“She is strong.”
I'm weak.
“She speaks with wisdom.”
I've said things I regret.
“She watches over her household.”
Mine feels like it is falling apart.
“Her children arise up, and call her blessed.”
My child barely speaks to me anymore.
“The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her.”
My marriage is wounded.
“She shall rejoice in time to come.”
I'm afraid of tomorrow.
And suddenly a poem celebrating wisdom became twenty-two reminders of everything you think you are not.
But beloved woman, hear the Gospel.
Your failures do not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
Repentance can begin today.
Healing can begin today.
Forgiveness can be received today.
Wisdom can grow today.
Character can be formed today.
You do not need to become the finished portrait overnight.
Sanctification is not microwave Christianity.
God forms His people across years of surrender, correction, suffering, Scripture, prayer, obedience, failure, repentance, community, endurance, and grace.
Sometimes becoming a woman of strength looks surprisingly unimpressive.
Sometimes strength is apologizing to your child.
Sometimes strength is admitting your marriage needs help.
Sometimes strength is deleting the number.
Sometimes strength is walking away from the relationship.
Sometimes strength is confessing what you have hidden.
Sometimes strength is asking another believer to pray for you.
Sometimes strength is opening Scripture when you feel nothing.
Sometimes strength is forgiving while your emotions are still catching up with your obedience.
Sometimes strength is saying,
“Jesus, I don't know how to fix this, but I surrender it to You.”
Sometimes an eshet chayil looks less like a perfectly curated Christian influencer and more like a woman on her knees whispering through tears,
“Lord, help me.”
And heaven does not despise that prayer.
There is something else women desperately need to hear.
Proverbs 31:30 does not say the woman who fears the Lord will never struggle.
It says she should be praised.
Faithfulness is not the absence of struggle.
Sometimes faithfulness is what keeps reaching for Christ in the middle of it.
So stop assuming the woman beside you has no battles because she carries herself beautifully.
You do not know what she survived before she arrived at church.
You do not know what she cried about in the car.
You do not know what diagnosis she received.
You do not know what betrayal she forgave.
You do not know what temptation she resisted.
You do not know what memories still wake her at night.
You do not know how many times she almost gave up.
Perhaps instead of competing with women, Christian women should become ferocious defenders of one another.
Pray for her.
Encourage her.
Teach the younger woman.
Honor the older woman.
Sit beside the lonely woman.
Include the single woman.
Comfort the grieving woman.
Welcome the repentant woman.
Protect the vulnerable woman.
Tell the ashamed woman about Jesus.
And when another woman succeeds, resist the temptation to interpret her blessing as evidence of your failure.
Her story is not God's rejection of yours.
There is room at the feet of Jesus for both of you.
Maybe you know a woman who desperately needs to hear that.
Not tomorrow.
Tonight.
Tag her.
Not to embarrass her.
The mother who kept going.
The grandmother who taught you to pray.
The sister who survived something she rarely talks about.
The friend who stayed near Jesus through a brutal season.
Let her know:
I see the grace of God in your life.
And if this exposed something in you that you have been hiding, don't perform.
Be honest.
Pray.
We were never meant to survive Christianity as isolated performers.
We are the body of Christ.
Because comparison has a way of returning.
There may come another night when you feel behind.
Another morning when the mirror is cruel.
Another scroll when somebody else's life makes yours look painfully ordinary.
Come back and remember:
God did not call you to worship the image of the perfect Christian woman.
He called you to Jesus.
And perhaps you are wondering why Gospel Warrior keeps creating messages like this.

Because there are millions of people scrolling through oceans of noise every day while carrying questions about God, shame, marriage, temptation, grief, identity, forgiveness, salvation, and whether Jesus could possibly still want them.
We want to meet them there with Scripture.
Not empty motivation.
Not Christianity stripped of repentance.
Not condemnation disguised as holiness.
Not grace stripped of truth.
Jesus.
The Gospel.
Biblical truth.
Conviction.
Repentance.
Forgiveness.
Healing.
Discipleship.
Hope.
And if God has used Gospel Warrior to strengthen your faith, you can help this mission continue and expand.
It does not purchase blessing.
It does not buy salvation.
And we will never tell you that giving money earns spiritual status before God.
Jesus cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift in Christ.
But Scripture does teach believers to support Gospel work generously and willingly. Paul wrote:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ, μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Hekastos kathōs proērētai tē kardia, mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs…
In other words, giving is to come from what one has purposed in the heart—not reluctantly or under compulsion.
And Paul finishes that thought:
ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεός
“For God loves a cheerful giver.”
—2 Corinthians 9:7
That protects both giver and ministry.
Christian giving should never be spiritual extortion.
You are helping us keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Keep placing Christ-centered truth in front of people who may never walk into a church building before they encounter a Gospel message on their phone.
You are helping this ministry go farther.
And there is another way to support that costs nothing.
Share.
You do not know who is silently watching.
You do not know who has been asking God for a sign of hope.
You do not know who is one conversation away from finally admitting they need Jesus.
Your share may look like a click to you.
God may use it as a doorway for someone else.
It is partnership.
It is helping make more room for Scripture, discipleship, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, and the Gospel in a digital world drowning in everything else.
Follow.
Stay close to truth.
Save what strengthens you.
Share what could reach somebody else.
Pray for this ministry.
Pray for the people reading beside you.
Pray that everything bearing the name Gospel Warrior would ultimately disappear behind the greater Name we exist to proclaim:
Jesus Christ.
Because this article was never really about becoming the Proverbs 31 woman.
It was about finally understanding her.
She was never given to Christian women as a weapon of inadequacy.
She is a celebration of wisdom.
Of strength.
Of faithful labor.
Of generosity.
Of courage.
Of reverence for God.
And none of those things require you to pretend you have already arrived.
Maybe today your house is messy.
Maybe your heart is too.
Maybe you have made mistakes.
Maybe your children are struggling.
Maybe your marriage needs prayer.
Maybe you are single and tired of people talking as though marriage is graduation into complete womanhood.
Maybe your career collapsed.
Maybe motherhood does not look anything like you imagined.
Maybe menopause changed your body.
Maybe grief changed your personality.
Maybe betrayal changed the way you trust.
Maybe sin took you somewhere you swore you would never go.
Maybe you barely recognize the woman in the mirror anymore.
Jesus does.
And He knows the entire story.
Not the Facebook version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version you tell people when they ask how you are doing.
The whole thing.
The chapters you celebrate.
The chapters you hide.
The sentences you wish could be erased.
And this is the breathtaking scandal of grace:
Christ calls sinners to repentance knowing exactly what He is forgiving.
At the cross, Jesus did not die for the imaginary, polished version of you.
He died for sinners.
So come to Him.
Not when the laundry is finished.
Not when your marriage is perfect.
Not when you finally become disciplined enough.
Not when your emotions settle down.
Not when you have memorized enough Scripture.
Not when you have transformed yourself into somebody worthy of being loved.
Come now.
Repent.
Believe.
Surrender.
Let Him teach you wisdom.
Let Him correct you.
Let Him heal what can be healed.
Let Him expose what must be exposed.
Let Him remove what must go.
Let Him strengthen what is weak.
Let Him transform you through His Word and Spirit.
And years from now, perhaps someone will look at your life and see strength.
They may never know how many nights that strength looked like tears.
They may never know how many times courage sounded like,
“Jesus, help me.”
They may never know how many failures were followed by repentance.
How many wounds were followed by forgiveness.
How many scandals were swallowed by grace.
How many broken pieces were placed into the hands of Christ.
But God will know.
And perhaps that is enough.
Woman of God…
you were never commanded to become somebody else's highlight reel.
Fear the Lord.
Walk with Christ.
Receive grace.
Repent when you fall.
Rise again.
Love deeply.
Serve faithfully.
Speak wisdom.
Practice generosity.
Grow in strength.
And let Jesus write the story.
Because the woman you keep criticizing in the mirror may still be standing in the middle of a chapter God has not finished writing.
Do not mistake an unfinished chapter for a finished story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD CURSED THIS SIN BY NAME—BUT WHY? THE DISTURBING SECRET BEHIND DEUTERONOMY 27:23
paragraphs: GOD CURSED THIS SIN BY NAME—BUT WHY? THE DISTURBING SECRET BEHIND DEUTERONOMY 27:23

One forbidden relationship. One terrifying declaration from Mount Ebal. And one uncomfortable truth about family, hidden sin, and the holiness of God that reaches far beyond the ancient world. But the most astonishing part of this story is not the curse. It is what Jesus Christ came to do for people living under the weight of sin.
There are Bible verses that comfort you.
There are Bible verses that strengthen you.
And then there are Bible verses that make you stop reading, stare at the page, and whisper…
“Lord, why is THAT in the Bible?”
Deuteronomy 27:23 is one of them.

Imagine standing among thousands of Israelites in the land God promised their ancestors. Families are gathered. Children are listening. The Levites are speaking with authority. The entire nation is being reminded that their covenant with God is not a religious performance.
It is a matter of life and death.
Then, suddenly, a particular curse is announced.
“Cursed be he that lieth with his mother in law. And all the people shall say, Amen.” — Deuteronomy 27:23, KJV
Read that again.
Not a general warning against sexual immorality.
Not a vague command about inappropriate relationships.
God specifically identifies sexual intercourse with a mother-in-law.
And the entire congregation must answer:
“Amen.”
Why?
Why would the Lord of heaven and earth single out something so disturbing?
Was this happening in ancient Israel? Was there a deeper cultural reason? Was God protecting marriage, family boundaries, or something much greater?
And what does an ancient curse about a mother-in-law have to do with the person reading this article today?
Perhaps more than we would like to admit.
Because before this passage confronts the scandal inside a family, it exposes something far more universal.
The human heart has an astonishing ability to justify what God has forbidden.
And sometimes the most dangerous sins are not committed by strangers.
They happen behind doors that everyone assumes are safe.
The Hebrew text makes the prohibition unmistakable.
אָרוּר שֹׁכֵב עִם־חֹתַנְתּו וְאָמַר כָּל־הָעָם אָמֵן
ʾĀrūr šōkhēḇ ʿim-ḥōṯantō; wəʾāmar kol-hāʿām ʾāmēn.
A close English rendering is:
“Cursed is the one who lies with his mother-in-law. And all the people shall say, Amen.”
The word אָרוּר (ʾārūr) means “cursed,” expressing a solemn declaration of judgment.
The expression שֹׁכֵב עִם (šōkhēḇ ʿim) literally means “lying with,” a biblical expression that in this context refers to sexual intercourse.
And חֹתַנְתּו (ḥōṯantō) identifies his mother-in-law.
There is no mysterious alternate meaning that transforms this into an innocent family disagreement.
There is no hidden Hebrew metaphor about disrespecting your wife's mother.
The verse is addressing a prohibited sexual relationship.
But understanding the Hebrew is only the beginning.
To understand why this curse appears, we must enter the world of the covenant.
In Deuteronomy 27, Moses instructs Israel about a solemn ceremony to take place after entering the promised land.
The people are to stand in relation to Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, with blessings and curses publicly declared.
This is not merely a collection of strange ancient laws.
It is a national confrontation with covenant responsibility.
The people who have experienced God's deliverance must now understand what faithfulness to Him requires.
And notice something fascinating about the curses in Deuteronomy 27.

They address idolatry, dishonoring parents, stealing a neighbor's land, misleading the blind, perverting justice, prohibited sexual relationships, secret violence, bribery, and failure to uphold God's law.
These are not random offenses.
They expose the ways people betray God and harm one another, often while maintaining an appearance of respectability.
Consider Deuteronomy 27:15, which condemns the making of an idol and setting it up “in a secret place.”
Or verse 24, which condemns someone who strikes a neighbor secretly.
The repeated concern with concealed wrongdoing helps us recognize a broader pattern.
God's covenant standards do not stop at the front door.
They enter the private life.
They confront the things a community might never discover.
They reach the places where human witnesses are absent.
And that should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because we know what it feels like to have a public version of ourselves and a private version.
We know how easily a person can appear faithful on Sunday while fighting temptations no one else can see.
We know how families sometimes protect appearances instead of confronting wrongdoing.
And we know that the sentence “Nobody will ever find out” has preceded countless tragedies.
But Scripture refuses to confuse secrecy with innocence.
What is hidden from people is never hidden from God.
Now look at the closely related law in Leviticus.
Leviticus 18:17 forbids sexual relations involving a woman and her daughter, identifying the relationship as a violation of family boundaries.
Leviticus 20:14 addresses a man who takes a woman and her mother, prescribing a severe punishment under Israel's ancient covenant law.
These passages belong to a wider body of legislation defining forbidden sexual relationships and protecting the boundaries of kinship and marriage.
The biblical text does not tell us that Deuteronomy 27:23 was introduced because of one documented incident involving a particular Israelite family.
We should not invent a scandal the Bible never records.
What we can say is that the law explicitly prohibits this relationship, and its placement among the covenant curses communicates its seriousness.
In biblical ethics, marriage does not erase all family boundaries.
A mother-in-law is not simply another unrelated adult available for sexual pursuit.
She belongs to a family relationship that must be honored rather than sexualized.
And violating that boundary can produce betrayal across generations.
Imagine the devastation.
A daughter discovers that the husband she trusted has become sexually involved with her own mother.
A marriage is shattered.
A mother-daughter relationship is deeply wounded.
Trust collapses inside the family.
People who should have protected one another become sources of profound pain.
And the consequences may reach children, relatives, and an entire household.
That is not merely a private romantic choice.
It is a betrayal of relationships that carry moral responsibilities.
This helps explain why the biblical prohibition matters.
God is not treating human sexuality as something dirty.
Scripture presents marital intimacy as good and honorable within its proper covenant setting.
Genesis 2:24 describes a man leaving his father and mother and being joined to his wife, with the two becoming one flesh.
Hebrews 13:4 calls marriage honorable and warns against sexual immorality and adultery.
The problem in Deuteronomy 27:23 is not that sexual intimacy exists.
The problem is that intimacy has crossed a boundary God forbids.
A sacred gift has been misused.
And when something designed for covenant faithfulness becomes an instrument of betrayal, the damage can be devastating.
But there is another detail in this verse that deserves our attention.
The people must respond:
אָמֵן — ʾāmēn.
This Hebrew word communicates affirmation, certainty, and agreement.
In this setting, the people are publicly acknowledging the righteousness and authority of the covenant declaration.
They are not being asked to enjoy the punishment of another human being.
They are being called to affirm that God's standards matter.
Even when those standards expose sins that people might prefer to ignore.
And here is where the passage becomes painfully personal.
It is easy to say “Amen” when the sin being condemned belongs to someone else.
It is easy to agree with God's holiness when the person under examination is a stranger.
It is easy to become outraged by a scandal that does not threaten our own reputation.
But what happens when Scripture turns toward us?
What happens when Jesus confronts our own lust, dishonesty, pride, bitterness, selfishness, or secret compromise?
Do we still say “Amen”?
Or do we begin searching for excuses?
Jesus intensifies this examination in Matthew 5:27–28.
He reminds His listeners of the commandment against adultery and then teaches that looking at someone with lustful intent already exposes adultery in the heart.
That does not mean every temptation is identical to committing a physical act, nor does it erase the different harms and consequences of different sins.
It means God's concern reaches beyond outward behavior into the desires we deliberately entertain.
A person may never violate the specific prohibition in Deuteronomy 27:23 and still desperately need God's mercy.
The ancient verse is not permission to feel morally superior.
It is an invitation to examine our own hearts before the Lord.
And this is where the story takes an unexpected turn.
Because the Bible that announces curses against sin is also the Bible that reveals a Savior who bears the curse for sinners.
Listen carefully.
Deuteronomy does not end with the conclusion that sinful people can save themselves by trying harder.
The larger biblical story moves toward Jesus Christ.
Paul writes in Galatians 3:10 about the curse associated with failure to continue in everything written in the Law.
Then comes one of the most breathtaking declarations in the New Testament.
“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.” — Galatians 3:13, KJV
The Greek text begins:
Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἐξηγόρασεν ἐκ τῆς κατάρας τοῦ νόμου
Christos hēmas exēgorasen ek tēs kataras tou nomou.
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law.”
The verb ἐξηγόρασεν (exēgorasen) expresses the act of redeeming or buying out of bondage.
And κατάρα (katara) means “curse.”
Paul is not teaching that Jesus became morally sinful.
He is declaring that Christ bore the curse on behalf of His people through His crucifixion.
The innocent Savior took upon Himself the judgment that sinners could never overcome through their own righteousness.
Do you see the wonder?
In Deuteronomy 27, the people hear the solemn declaration:
“Cursed.”
In Galatians 3, believers hear the astonishing announcement:
“Christ redeemed us.”
The Gospel does not say that God's holiness was exaggerated.
It does not say sin was harmless after all.
It does not say betrayal no longer matters.
It says something infinitely more costly.
The Son of God gave Himself to redeem sinners.
The cross is not God pretending evil never happened.
It is the revelation of His justice and mercy in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And that changes everything.
Because there are people reading this who carry memories they have never spoken aloud.
Perhaps you crossed a boundary you knew was wrong.
Perhaps you betrayed someone's trust.
Perhaps you were involved in a relationship that wounded your family.
Perhaps you have lived for years with guilt, shame, or the fear of being exposed.
Or perhaps you are the one who was betrayed.
You trusted someone.
You believed your family was safe.
You thought the people closest to you would protect your heart.
And instead, they became part of the reason it broke.
If that is your story, hear this carefully.
The guilt belongs to the person who committed the wrong.
If you were coerced, exploited, or abused, you are not responsible for another person's sin against you.
The commandment condemns wrongdoing; it does not condemn its victims.
And forgiveness must never be twisted into a demand that victims remain in danger, abandon necessary boundaries, or silence the truth.
Jesus does not require us to call evil good.
He calls sinners to repentance, offers grace to the broken, and teaches His people to walk in truth.
For the person who has committed serious sin, repentance is not merely feeling bad because consequences have arrived.
It is turning away from sin and turning toward God.
It means ending the forbidden relationship.
It means refusing to continue the deception.
It means taking responsibility without blaming the person who was harmed.
It means pursuing appropriate accountability and accepting that reconciliation may require time, boundaries, and consequences.
And where abuse or criminal wrongdoing has occurred, repentance does not replace the need for protection or lawful accountability.
Grace is not permission to continue destroying lives.
Grace is the mercy of God that calls us out of darkness and into the light.
Consider the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
Her accusers wanted to use her situation as a trap.
Jesus confronted their self-righteousness without declaring sin acceptable.
And after the accusers departed, He told her:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV
Notice both parts.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
“Go, and sin no more.”
Mercy and holiness.
Forgiveness and transformation.
Grace that receives the sinner without celebrating the sin.
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Jesus does not offer us a new name for our rebellion so that we can remain unchanged.
He offers forgiveness and a new life.
And that is why the words of 1 John 1:9 are so precious.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
The promise is not that confession will erase every earthly consequence.
It is that God's forgiveness and cleansing are available through Jesus Christ.
No human scandal is too complicated for God to understand.
No hidden sin is beyond His knowledge.
And no repentant sinner must conclude that Christ's mercy is insufficient.
That does not make sin small.
It makes the Savior glorious.
Perhaps the most haunting question in Deuteronomy 27:23 is not why God named this particular sin.
Perhaps it is why we are so quick to recognize the ugliness of someone else's wrongdoing while minimizing our own.
We see betrayal and cry for justice.
We see hypocrisy and demand exposure.
We see scandal and wonder how anyone could do such a thing.
But when God examines our own hearts, do we welcome His truth?
Or do we hide?
Remember Adam and Eve in Genesis 3.
After disobeying God, they hid.
Sin had introduced shame, fear, and alienation.
And the Lord called to Adam:
“Where art thou?”
God was not lacking information.
The question confronted Adam with his condition.
And throughout Scripture, that same searching reality remains.
Where are you?
Not geographically.
Spiritually.
Where are you standing before God?
Behind excuses?
Behind religious appearances?
Behind the approval of people who do not know what happens in private?
Behind the sentence, “At least I am not as bad as that person”?
Or are you finally willing to come into the light?
The Gospel invitation is not to pretend you have never fallen.
It is to come to the One who died and rose again to save sinners.
Jesus Christ was crucified for our sins, buried, and raised on the third day, according to the Scriptures, as Paul proclaims in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
Our hope is not in our ability to rewrite our own past.
Our hope is in the crucified and risen Savior.
The same Jesus who calls us to repent is the Jesus who welcomes the weary.
The same Lord who exposes darkness offers the light of life.
And the same Gospel that declares forgiveness also creates a people who learn to honor marriage, protect the vulnerable, tell the truth, and live in holiness.
That is why this difficult passage still deserves to be read.
Not because shocking sexual scandals are entertaining.
Not because the church needs another reason to humiliate broken people.
But because God's Word tells the truth about sin, even when that truth is uncomfortable.
And because the greater story of Scripture leads us to the One who can redeem what sin has devastated.
Maybe someone you love needs to hear this.
Not to be publicly accused.
Not to be embarrassed.
But to be reminded that hidden compromise is dangerous and that genuine repentance is possible.

You do not need to disclose private details, name people who harmed you, or make a public confession to receive God's forgiveness. A simple prayer, a Scripture, or a word of encouragement may be exactly what another reader needs.
Because people do not merely need religious inspiration.
We need the truth that leads us to Jesus.
If this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, confront sin, rediscover grace, or grow closer to Christ, I also want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is working to continue and expand its ministry of biblical teaching, Gospel-centered encouragement, and discipleship resources.
These resources are intended to help believers study the Word, strengthen their faith, grow in spiritual maturity, and remain rooted in the Gospel.
And keeping this work going requires time, resources, and faithful support.
Not because God's love can be purchased.
Not because giving money proves someone is a better Christian.
But because believers are free to support Gospel ministry generously, willingly, and with joy.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
You can glorify God through faithfulness, generosity, service, love, and obedience in countless ways.
No one needs to pay to belong to Christ.
No one needs to purchase access to His mercy.
But when believers freely come together to support sound biblical teaching, they can help bring that message to more people.
Perhaps someone reading the next article will finally open a Bible.
Perhaps someone who has been hiding in shame will find the courage to seek help and repent.
Perhaps a wounded believer will discover that Jesus has not abandoned them.
Perhaps a family will begin rebuilding on truth rather than secrecy.
We cannot manufacture those outcomes.
But we can faithfully proclaim the Gospel and entrust the results to God.
And now, before you leave, return with me one last time to that ancient gathering in Deuteronomy.
The people stand beneath the solemn weight of God's covenant.
A curse is declared against a sin that violates the sacred boundaries of family.
The congregation answers:
“Amen.”
Generations pass.
Israel's story unfolds through faithfulness and rebellion, judgment and mercy, exile and restoration.
Then, outside Jerusalem, the sinless Son of God hangs upon a Roman cross.
The crowd sees suffering.
His enemies see defeat.
But the apostles will proclaim something far greater.
Christ has redeemed His people from the curse of the law.
He has given Himself for sinners.
And through His death and resurrection, the way of forgiveness and reconciliation with God has been opened.
That is the difference between a message that merely exposes scandal and the Gospel that announces grace.
The law reveals the seriousness of sin.
The cross reveals the astonishing cost of redemption.
And the resurrection declares that death does not have the final word.
So do not leave this passage merely thinking about somebody else's forbidden relationship.
Ask what God is teaching you about holiness.
Ask where your own heart needs repentance.
Ask whether you have mistaken secrecy for safety.
Ask whether you have allowed shame to convince you that Jesus could never receive you.
And remember the promise of Romans 8:1:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That is not a declaration that sin does not matter.
It is the glorious announcement that those who belong to Christ are no longer under condemnation.
The curse is real.
The cross is real.
The resurrection is real.
And the grace of God in Jesus Christ is more powerful than the shame of a past that has been brought into His light.
The sin you were afraid to bring into the light may be the very place where you finally discover how desperately you need the Savior who never stopped calling you out of the darkness.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Did God Command the Land to Stop? The Forgotten Sabbath That Exposed Israel’s Heart
paragraphs: Why Did God Command the Land to Stop? The Forgotten Sabbath That Exposed Israel’s Heart

Every seventh year, God told Israel to stop planting, stop harvesting for profit, loosen their grip on what grew, and trust Him. It looked like an agricultural command. It was actually exposing something much deeper: who owned the land, who sustained their lives, how they treated the poor, and whether they truly believed God could be trusted when obedience became costly.
Imagine standing at the edge of your field.
This is not a hobby garden.
This field feeds your children.
It pays what you owe.
It is your security when tomorrow becomes uncertain.
For six years you have awakened before sunrise, pushed seed into stubborn soil, watched clouds, prayed for rain, fought insects, pulled weeds, harvested grain, and stored enough to survive.
Then God says something that sounds almost frightening.
Stop.
Do not sow the field this year.
Do not cultivate it as you normally would.
Do not organize your life around squeezing another harvest from it.
Let the land rest.
And trust Me.
That was the Sabbath year.
And if we read it merely as an ancient agricultural regulation, we may miss the trembling human heart underneath it.
Because the question behind the Sabbath year was never merely, “Will Israel let the soil rest?”
The deeper question was:
Will Israel trust God enough to release what they desperately want to control?
That question is thousands of years old.
But it may be sitting inside your life right now.
The command appears clearly in Exodus 23:10–11. The Hebrew begins:
“וְשֵׁשׁ שָׁנִים תִּזְרַע אֶת־אַרְצֶךָ…”
Ve-shesh shanim tizra et-artzekha…
“For six years you shall sow your land…”
Then comes the seventh year:
“וְהַשְּׁבִיעִת תִּשְׁמְטֶנָּה וּנְטַשְׁתָּהּ…”
Veha-shevi'it tishmetennah u-netashtah…

In context, Israel was commanded in the seventh year to release the land and leave its produce available so that the poor could eat, with what remained available to the animals. The same principle applied to vineyards and olive groves.
That Hebrew verb connected with releasing the land matters.
This seventh-year institution is commonly called Shemittah or Shemitah, from the idea of release or letting go.
And suddenly the command becomes painfully personal.
Because letting go has always been difficult.
We like God providing.
We are less comfortable with God asking us to release control.
We like promises about tomorrow.
We struggle when obedience requires trusting Him today.
We love saying, “God is my Provider.”
But sometimes God allows a moment when those words must stop being lyrics and become faith.
Israel's Sabbath year was one of those moments.
Leviticus 25 makes the command even more striking. Six years Israel could sow the fields, prune the vineyards, and gather produce. But the seventh year was different.
The Hebrew describes it:
“שַׁבַּת שַׁבָּתוֹן יִהְיֶה לָאָרֶץ”
Shabbat shabbaton yihyeh la'aretz.
A Sabbath of solemn rest was to be for the land.
Think about that.
The land itself was placed under Sabbath.
Not because dirt had committed sin.
Not because agriculture was evil.
Not because productivity was sinful.
God was teaching His covenant people that even good things must never become gods.
The field could produce food.
It could not become Israel's ultimate provider.
The vineyard could produce grapes.
It could not become Israel's savior.
Their hands could work.
Their hands could not replace God's hand.
And perhaps this is where the ancient field begins looking uncomfortably like the modern heart.
We have different fields now.
A career.
A business.
A bank account.
A ministry.
A reputation.
A social-media following.
A relationship.
A retirement plan.
A carefully constructed future.
Something that whispers:
“If I can just keep this under control, I will be safe.”
And God keeps reminding His people of a truth human beings repeatedly forget.
You were never God.
You were never holding the universe together.
You were never your own savior.
The Sabbath year was therefore not an invitation to laziness.
For six years God explicitly expected work.
The seventh-year command interrupted that normal rhythm.
Work faithfully.
Then release.
Plant faithfully.
Then trust.
Gather faithfully.
Then remember where everything came from.
That rhythm attacked one of humanity's oldest idols:
the illusion of self-sufficiency.
And God drove the lesson even deeper.
The land Israel cultivated ultimately did not belong to them in an absolute sense.
Leviticus 25:23 gives the theological foundation:
“כִּי־לִי הָאָרֶץ”
Ki li ha'aretz.
“For the land is Mine.”
Those four Hebrew words can dismantle an empire inside the human heart.
The land is Mine.
God was effectively reminding Israel:
You may work it.
You may live on it.
You may receive its abundance.
You may enjoy My gifts.
But never confuse stewardship with ownership.
The earth still belongs to Me.
That changes everything.
Because if everything belongs ultimately to God, then generosity stops looking like God taking something that belongs exclusively to us.
We begin realizing that we are stewards of what first came from Him.
Your breath is borrowed.
Your strength is borrowed.
Your opportunities are borrowed.
Your days are numbered gifts.
The ability to work is a gift.
The next heartbeat is mercy.
The Sabbath year put an entire nation face-to-face with that reality.
But there was another dimension that makes this command even more beautiful.
The poor were watching.
Exodus does not simply say, “Let the land rest.”
It says that what grew could become food for the needy.
Suddenly a field that normally reinforced economic boundaries became a place where vulnerable people could eat.
The Sabbath year was not only about soil.
It was about neighbors.
It confronted greed.
It interrupted accumulation.
It placed limits on exploitation.
It reminded those with land that God's concern extended to people who had little.

And Deuteronomy 15 connects the seventh-year pattern with another extraordinary idea: release from debts among Israelites, alongside repeated commands not to harden the heart or close the hand toward the poor.
That means biblical rest was never merely private relaxation.
God's covenant order confronted the clenched fist.
The seventh year asked the landowner:
Can you trust God when someone else benefits from what you normally call yours?
Can you open your hand?
Can you see the poor person as a human being made under God's sovereign care rather than as an inconvenience?
Can blessing flow through you instead of terminating with you?
Those questions have not become obsolete.
And then the story becomes darker.
Because Israel's Scriptures do not allow us to turn the Sabbath year into a sentimental environmental slogan.
There were consequences attached to covenant rebellion.
Leviticus 26 warned that if Israel persistently rejected God's covenant commands, exile would come and the land would receive the Sabbath rests denied to it.
Centuries later, Jerusalem fell.
Judah went into exile.
The fields became quiet.
The terrible irony is preserved at the end of Chronicles:

the land finally enjoyed its Sabbaths while it lay desolate. Second Chronicles 36:21 explicitly connects the desolation with the land's Sabbath rests and the fulfillment of Jeremiah's word concerning the seventy years.
Read that slowly.
The land rested.
But the people were gone.
What they would not willingly release in obedience was eventually taken from their control in judgment.
There is something haunting about that.
Imagine those abandoned fields.
No farmers shouting.
No sickles cutting grain.
No children running between workers.
No families celebrating harvest.
Just wind.
Dust.
Silence.
The soil finally resting while God's covenant people lived far from home.
And somewhere inside that silence is a warning.
God's commands were never suggestions to be obeyed only when convenient.
Grace does not make rebellion harmless.
God is patient, but His patience should lead us toward repentance rather than teach us to presume upon Him.
Sometimes we become so accustomed to God's mercy that we mistake delayed consequences for divine approval.
Israel's story warns us against doing that.
But if the story ended with judgment, Christianity would have no Gospel to proclaim.
Because Scripture does not ultimately move toward an abandoned field.
It moves toward a Savior.
And this is where the Sabbath theme becomes breathtaking.
Jesus enters a synagogue in Nazareth.
He receives the scroll of Isaiah.
He reads words announcing good news to the poor, liberty to captives, sight to the blind, freedom for the oppressed, and the favorable year of the Lord.
Luke's Greek uses a word loaded with the idea of release:
“ἄφεσιν”
aphesin.
Release.
Liberty.
Forgiveness.
The same Greek noun can carry the sense of release or forgiveness depending upon context. In Luke 4:18, it appears in Jesus' proclamation of release to captives and freedom for the oppressed.
Jesus was announcing something greater than agricultural recovery.
Greater than a debt ledger being cleared.
Greater than a field lying fallow.
Humanity had a deeper captivity.
Sin.
Guilt.
Alienation from God.
A debt we could never erase by moral improvement.
A slavery no political revolution could finally cure.
We needed more than rested soil.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed redemption.
We needed Jesus.
And here is where every attempt to save ourselves finally collapses.
Some of us have spent years spiritually doing what Israel did agriculturally.
Plant.
Harvest.
Control.
Repeat.
Except our field is our own righteousness.
We try to produce enough goodness to silence our guilt.
We promise God we will do better.
We compare ourselves with people who appear worse.
We hide what embarrasses us.
We curate the outside while something inside is starving.
We work harder.
Smile harder.
Pretend harder.
Perform harder.
And somewhere beneath all that religious productivity is an exhausted soul whispering:
“Is it enough yet?”
No.
And that is exactly why the Gospel is good news.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your religious productivity.
He came to save sinners.
The cross announces the end of boasting.
You cannot cultivate enough righteousness to purchase forgiveness.
You cannot harvest enough good deeds to erase yesterday.
You cannot negotiate your way out of sin's verdict.
Christ carried what sinners could not carry.
He died for sins.
He rose again.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not, “Work hard enough until God finally tolerates you.”
It is:
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Receive mercy you could never earn.
There is a reason rest becomes such a profound biblical picture.
Hebrews 4:9 says:
“ἄρα ἀπολείπεται σαββατισμὸς τῷ λαῷ τοῦ θεοῦ”
Ara apoleipetai sabbatismos tō laō tou Theou.
“So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God.”
The unusual Greek word σαββατισμός — sabbatismos carries the idea of Sabbath rest. Hebrews uses it while developing its larger argument about entering God's rest through faith rather than unbelief.
We should not flatten every Old Testament Sabbath command into an identical New Testament command, nor pretend that Israel's land legislation was written directly to the modern church.
But the canonical movement is difficult to miss.
God taught His people that life does not ultimately depend upon endless human production.
God taught them release.
Dependence.
Trust.
Mercy.
And in Christ, exhausted sinners discover the One whom no human labor could replace.
Maybe that is why this ancient command feels unexpectedly personal.
Because perhaps you are exhausted.
Not physically only.
Spiritually.
You have been trying to control everything because somewhere along the way you became terrified of what would happen if you stopped.
You carry everybody.
You solve everything.
You anticipate every disaster.
You replay conversations at 2:00 in the morning.
You calculate tomorrow before today has finished.
You tell everyone, “I'm okay.”
But you know you are not.
Your soul has forgotten how to unclench.
And perhaps the question of the Sabbath year has finally reached your field:
Do you trust God only while you can still control the harvest?
That question hurts.
Because sometimes we do not discover what we worship until God asks us to release it.
Abraham had Isaac.
The rich ruler had possessions.
Peter had his confidence in himself.
Paul had his religious credentials.
And you have something too.
So do I.
Something we instinctively grip when fear enters the room.
Money.
Control.
Approval.
A relationship.
Success.
Our plans.
Our image.
Even ministry.
And Jesus keeps calling His people away from idols and back to Himself.
Not into irresponsible living.
Not into laziness.
Not into financial foolishness.
But into faithful stewardship without worshiping the thing being stewarded.
Work hard.
But your career is not Christ.
Save wisely.
But your bank account is not Christ.
Love your family.
But your family is not Christ.
Serve faithfully.
But your ministry is not Christ.
Use the field.
Do not worship the field.
Because eventually every earthly field goes quiet.
Every bank account changes hands.
Every house belongs to somebody else.
Every title disappears.
Every body returns to dust unless Christ returns first.
And then only one question will finally matter:
What did you do with Jesus Christ?
Not how impressive your harvest looked.
Not how many people applauded you.
Not whether strangers thought you were successful.
Jesus.
The One who was crucified.
The One who rose.
The One before whom every hidden thing is exposed.
The One whose grace is still greater than the scandal you are terrified someone might discover.
Maybe that scandal is why you almost stopped reading.
You know the thing.
The memory.
The addiction.
The secret conversation.
The compromise.
The bitterness.
The pornography.
The affair nobody knows about.
The lie that grew into ten more lies.
The prayerlessness.
The hypocrisy.
The years you wasted.
The person you wounded.
The faith you abandoned.
The version of yourself you hope nobody ever meets.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more terribly than we often admit.
But the cross also proves something else.
Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Real ones.
Guilty ones.
Ashamed ones.
People whose histories cannot be edited.
People whose reputations cannot rescue them.
People who finally stop negotiating and fall before God with empty hands.
That is repentance.
Not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Turning from sin toward God.
Dropping the weapons.
Ending the excuses.
Bringing the hidden thing into His light.
And trusting Christ.
Perhaps your Sabbath moment is not God asking you to stop working a literal farm for a year.
Perhaps it is the moment you finally stop trying to save yourself.
Stop hiding.
Stop pretending.
Stop defending what God is asking you to confess.
Open your hands.
Come home.
Because the hands of Jesus were opened on a cross for sinners like us.
That is where scandal meets grace.
Not because God calls evil good.
Not because holiness stops mattering.
But because at Calvary the Holy One bore the judgment sinners deserved, and the risen Christ now calls sinners into forgiveness, reconciliation, obedience, and transformed life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the old chapter never happened.
But by refusing to let sin have the final word over everyone who truly belongs to Him.
Maybe someone reading this feels like an abandoned field.
Everything you expected to grow has disappeared.
The relationship ended.
The opportunity vanished.
Your plans collapsed.
People walked away.
Prayer feels dry.
You look across your life and see nothing but empty ground.
Do not confuse an empty field with an absent God.
Israel's land became silent under judgment, yes—but exile was not the final chapter of God's redemptive purposes.
God remained faithful to His promises.
And eventually, in the fullness of God's plan, Christ came.
Sometimes Scripture teaches us that what looks like an ending can stand inside a story God has not finished writing.
So if you are exhausted, come to Christ.
If you are guilty, come to Christ.
If you have wandered, return to Christ.
If you are hiding, step into His light.
If you are proud, repent.
If you are broken, do not make brokenness your savior either.
Come to Christ.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding from God, do not manufacture a polished Christian answer.
Be honest.
Not because typing words into a comment saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that we need prayer is the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And somebody else reading those comments may realize they are not the only person fighting.
That matters.
If one person came to mind while you were reading this, send this to them.
Not randomly.
Not because we need another piece of content circulating online.
Send it because you know their field.
You know what they have been carrying.
You know how tired they have become.
Save it too.
Because there may come a night when you are the person who needs to read it again.
We want to say this carefully because biblical truth matters more than fundraising language.
None of those things can be purchased.
But Christians are repeatedly encouraged to give willingly, generously, and purposefully to support Gospel work and meet needs.
And there is another way you can help that costs nothing.
Share.
A Facebook share may seem small to you.
But you do not know whose screen it will reach.
You do not know who is awake at midnight.
You do not know who has been thinking about giving up.
You do not know who has quietly wandered from God.
You do not know whose carefully maintained smile is hiding a collapsing soul.
You do not know who needs to hear, tonight, that repentance is still possible and Christ still receives sinners who come to Him.
Your share can place Gospel truth in front of someone we could never personally reach.
If you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel ministry, prayerfully consider whether supporting this work is one way you can steward what He has entrusted to you.
But the merchandise is not the heart of this.
Jesus is.
The Gospel is.
People meeting Christ is.
People opening Bibles again is.
People repenting instead of hiding is.
Families praying again is.
Wounded believers discovering that failure does not have to become apostasy is.
Lukewarm hearts awakening.
Seekers hearing the Gospel clearly.
Christians growing beyond inspirational quotes into serious discipleship.
That is why we keep building.
The Sabbath year ultimately confronted Israel with a terrifyingly simple question.
Can God be trusted when obedience requires open hands?
Maybe that is the question waiting for us too.
We spend our lives planting.
Building.
Collecting.
Protecting.
Planning.
Trying to guarantee tomorrow.
Then Scripture walks into our carefully managed field and reminds us:
The land belongs to God.
The harvest belongs to God.
Our lives belong to God.
Our salvation belongs to Christ.
And grace cannot be harvested by human effort.
It must be received.
So perhaps tonight the bravest thing you can do is stop pretending you are your own provider, your own redeemer, your own refuge, and your own god.
Open your hands.
Repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Give where God leads you to give.
Release what He tells you to release.
Work faithfully where He tells you to work.
Care for the vulnerable.
Stop hiding.
Trust Him.
And come again to Jesus.
Because one day every field we spent our lives protecting will belong to someone else.
But the soul that belongs to Christ has found a treasure death itself cannot harvest away.
Maybe the field had to become quiet before your heart could finally hear the voice of the One who owned it all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE LOVERS HEAR EACH OTHER, SEARCH FOR EACH OTHER, MISS EACH OTHER, AND LONG FOR EACH OTHER—BIBLICAL ROMANCE IS NOT EMOTIONLESS
paragraphs: THE LOVERS HEAR EACH OTHER, SEARCH FOR EACH OTHER, MISS EACH OTHER, AND LONG FOR EACH OTHER—BIBLICAL ROMANCE IS NOT EMOTIONLESS
Somewhere along the way, some Christians became so afraid of lust that they almost became afraid of love. But Scripture never was.
There is a woman awake at night because the man she loves is absent.
She reaches for him.
He is not there.
She searches.
She cannot find him.
She gets up.
She walks through the city.
She asks the watchmen if they have seen him.
Why?
Because she misses him.
Because love has made absence painful.
And somehow this scene is sitting right there in the Bible.
Not in a secular romance novel.
Not in a Hollywood screenplay.
Not in a forbidden diary somebody hid beneath a mattress.
In Scripture.
The Song of Songs gives us these startling Hebrew words:
עַל־מִשְׁכָּבִי בַּלֵּילוֹת בִּקַּשְׁתִּי אֵת שֶׁאָהֲבָה נַפְשִׁי
ʿal-mishkavi balleilot biqqashti et she’ahavah nafshi…
“On my bed at night, I sought the one whom my soul loves…”
Then comes the ache:
בִּקַּשְׁתִּיו וְלֹא מְצָאתִיו
“I sought him, but I did not find him.”
—Song of Songs 3:1
Read that slowly.
The one whom my soul loves.
She misses him.
She searches for him.
She longs to find him.
And God did not blush and remove those words from His Bible.
Maybe we should stop pretending biblical romance is emotionless.
Because sometimes Christians have been taught a strange version of love.
Be committed—but do not be too emotional.
Be faithful—but do not be too passionate.
Marry—but somehow pretend attraction does not matter.
Love your spouse—but never speak as though you actually ache for their presence.
Desire marriage—but feel vaguely guilty for wanting to be wanted.
We rightly warn people against lust.
We rightly warn against sexual immorality.
We rightly preach holiness.
But holiness does not require emotional anesthesia.
Purity is not the absence of affection.
Biblical self-control is not the death of tenderness.
And godly romance is not two Christians signing a theological contract and then spending fifty years pretending they never desperately wanted to hold each other.
The Bible is far more human than that.
The lovers hear each other.
They search for each other.
They miss each other.
They admire each other.
They delight in each other.
They long for each other.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs permission to understand something:
Wanting to be deeply loved is not automatically carnality.
The problem is not that the human heart longs to love.
The problem is what sin does with that longing.
There is a difference.
Long before Song of Songs, there was another scene.
A man sees a woman.
And something happens inside him.
Genesis says that when God brought the woman to Adam, Adam responded:
זֹאת הַפַּעַם עֶצֶם מֵעֲצָמַי וּבָשָׂר מִבְּשָׂרִי
Zot happaʿam, ʿetsem meʿatsamai uvasar mibbesari.
“This one, at last, is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”
—Genesis 2:23
Do not miss those little words:
“At last.”
There is recognition there.
Wonder.
Arrival.
Someone corresponding to him.
Then Scripture gives us the foundation of marriage:
A man leaves father and mother, clings to his wife, and the two become one flesh.
Before betrayal entered Eden…
before lust distorted desire…
before pornography commercialized bodies…
before adultery shattered homes…
before manipulation turned affection into leverage…
before people learned to use sex without covenant and covenant without tenderness…
God created man and woman.
Marriage was not Satan's invention.
Romantic love was not Hollywood's invention.
Human sexuality was not invented by pornography.
The enemy did not create these gifts.
He corrupted them.
And there is an enormous difference between creation and corruption.
Maybe that is why Song of Songs can sound almost shocking to ears accustomed to treating Christianity as emotionally sterile.
Listen.
The woman hears something.
קוֹל דּוֹדִי
Qol dodi.
“The voice of my beloved!”
—Song of Songs 2:8
You can almost hear the excitement.
He is coming.
The beloved approaches, and then she remembers his voice calling her:
קוּמִי לָךְ רַעְיָתִי יָפָתִי וּלְכִי־לָךְ
Qumi lakh, raʿyati, yafati, uleki-lakh.
“Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.”
—Song of Songs 2:10
That is not cold.
That is not mechanical.
That is not embarrassed affection.
The lovers speak.
They listen.
They notice.
They praise.
They desire presence.
They experience separation.
They experience reunion.
And sometimes they experience pain.
That matters.
Because maybe you know exactly what it means to miss somebody.
Maybe there is a name you still cannot hear casually.
Maybe there is a chair that became painful after someone left.
Maybe there are photographs you avoid because one image can resurrect an entire season.
Maybe you loved somebody who did not stay.
Maybe your marriage has become painfully quiet.
Maybe you sleep beside someone who feels a thousand miles away.
Maybe you are single, and underneath all the Christian language about “waiting on God's timing,” there are nights when you simply wish somebody would choose you.
Not use you.
Not hide you.
Not keep you as an option.
Choose you.
Maybe you are divorced.
Maybe betrayed.
Maybe widowed.
Maybe still recovering from a relationship where the person who said “I love you” slowly taught you to fear love.
And perhaps you have wondered whether your longing itself was shameful.
Scripture gives us a better answer.
Longing can be beautiful.
But longing also needs redemption.
Because we can turn a person into a god.
We can ask another human being to heal wounds only Christ can reach.
We can demand from romance what romance was never designed to provide.
We can call obsession “love.”
We can call possession “protection.”
We can call lust “chemistry.”
We can call emotional dependency “soulmates.”
We can ignore character because somebody makes our heart race.
We can stay where God is being dishonored because loneliness frightens us more than compromise.
And that is where biblical romance confronts modern romance.
The Bible celebrates love without worshiping the lover.
It celebrates desire without making desire sovereign.
It celebrates the body without separating the body from covenant, faithfulness, holiness, and responsibility.
It allows lovers to burn with affection while still insisting that God remains God.
That distinction can save your heart.
Because no husband can be Jesus.
No wife can be Jesus.
No boyfriend can be Jesus.
No girlfriend can be Jesus.
No wedding can resurrect your soul.
No human kiss can permanently silence the deepest cry inside fallen humanity.
You were created for relationship with people, yes.
But beneath every human hunger is a deeper reality:
You were created for God.
And this is where the love story becomes bigger than romance.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to teach lonely people how to find partners.
He came to rescue sinners.
He came for adulterers.
For the sexually broken.
For the abandoned.
For the ashamed.
For the lustful.
For the betrayed.
For the betrayer who repents.
For the person who gave too much away.
For the person who took what was not theirs.
For the person carrying memories they desperately wish they could erase.
For the person whose private search history would humiliate them if exposed.
For the woman who thinks her past made her unlovable.
For the man who thinks his failures permanently disqualified him.
Christ came into the scandal.
And He brought grace.
Not cheap grace that says sin does not matter.
Grace that tells the truth about sin and then pays an unimaginable price to redeem the sinner.
At the cross, Jesus did not pretend our corruption was beautiful.
He bore it.
The Greek New Testament announces the heart of the Gospel with words Christians should never become numb to:
Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανεν
Christos hyper hēmōn apethanen.
“Christ died for us.”
See Romans 5:8.
While we were still sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we became worthy romantic partners.
Not after we finally stopped struggling.
Christ moved toward sinners.
The Gospel is not the story of good people climbing toward God.
It is the story of the holy Son of God coming down to rescue people who could never save themselves.
That changes romance too.
Because when Christ becomes the center, love stops asking only:
“What can you make me feel?”
Love begins asking:
“How can I honor Christ in the way I treat you?”
That changes dating.
That changes marriage.
That changes sexuality.
That changes conflict.
That changes forgiveness.
That changes attraction.
That changes what you tolerate.
That changes what you refuse.
Biblical love is deeply emotional, but it is more than emotion.
Feelings can say, “I want you.”
Covenant says, “I will be faithful.”
Attraction can say, “You are beautiful.”
Love says, “Your soul matters to God.”
Lust asks, “How much of you can I take?”
Love asks, “How faithfully can I seek your good?”
Manipulation says, “Prove that you love me.”
Godly affection says, “I refuse to make you sin in order to keep me.”
That is romance redeemed.
And Song of Songs gives us perhaps its most unforgettable declaration:
כִּי־עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה
Ki ʿazzah khammavet ahavah.
“For love is strong as death.”
—Song of Songs 8:6
The poem continues with imagery of blazing fire and an astonishing declaration:
Many waters cannot extinguish love.
Floods cannot sweep it away.
That is powerful language.
But Scripture never tells us that every intense feeling is therefore holy.
Intensity alone proves nothing.
You can intensely desire the wrong person.
You can intensely desire someone else's spouse.
You can intensely desire what God has forbidden.
You can intensely miss somebody God rescued you from.
Your tears do not automatically make a relationship righteous.
Your chemistry does not rewrite Scripture.
Your loneliness does not turn disobedience into God's will.
That may hurt.
But sometimes grace hurts before it heals.
Sometimes Jesus loves us enough to separate us from the thing we kept calling love because He can see what it is doing to our souls.
And maybe this article found you while you are trying to return to someone you know keeps pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe you keep rereading messages.
Checking whether they are online.
Remembering the nights when everything felt alive.
Missing the person so badly that you have started editing the memories.
You remember the tenderness.
You forget the compromise.
You remember being held.
You forget how often you were spiritually disappearing.
You remember the apology.
You forget the cycle.
You remember what they promised.
You forget what they repeatedly chose.
Listen carefully:
Missing someone does not always mean you are supposed to return to them.
Sometimes grief is simply the price of finally walking away from what was destroying you.
And sometimes the person you need to run toward is not the person you lost.
It is Jesus.
Because there is another voice in Scripture calling.
Christ describes Himself as the Good Shepherd, and He says His sheep hear His voice.
He knows them.
They follow Him.
See John 10:27.
Do you see the deeper beauty?
The lovers hear each other.
But above every human voice, the redeemed learn to recognize the voice of Christ.
The lovers search for each other.
But Jesus spoke of the shepherd who searches for the lost.
The lovers ache in separation.
But sin created the separation no human romance can ultimately repair.
And the Gospel announces that God acted.
Christ came.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ calls.
Christ forgives.
Christ restores.
Christ makes sinners new.
That is why Christian romance cannot ultimately be about finding somebody who “completes” you.
Christ is not the missing decoration around your love story.
He is Lord.
And when two people belong to Him, romance can become something beautiful precisely because it is no longer required to become their god.
You can say, “I miss you,” without saying, “I cannot exist without you.”
You can say, “I desire you,” without saying, “Therefore I am entitled to you.”
You can say, “You are beautiful,” without turning a body into an object.
You can say, “Stay,” while still surrendering the future to God.
You can love fiercely and worship Christ supremely.
That is freedom.
And married couples, perhaps you need to hear this too.
Do not become so familiar with your spouse that you stop pursuing the person you once prayed God would give you.
Speak.
Listen.
Notice.
Flirt with your spouse.
Tell them they are beautiful.
Tell him you appreciate him.
Tell her what you still notice.
Reach for the hand you have held ten thousand times.
Put the phone down.
Look into the face across the table.
Ask what is happening inside their heart.
Pray together even when it feels awkward.
Repent quickly.
Forgive biblically.
Protect your marriage from secret appetites.
And please—do not outsource to strangers on a screen the desire that belongs inside your covenant.
Pornography trains the eyes to consume bodies without covenant.
Jesus teaches us to see people as souls bearing God's image.
Adultery says desire outranks faithfulness.
Christ teaches us that obedience sometimes means crucifying desires that feel overwhelmingly alive.
Christian marriage does not destroy passion.
It gives passion a holy home.
And single believer, your life is not God's waiting room.
You are not half a Christian until somebody puts a ring on your finger.
Jesus was not incomplete.
Paul was not spiritually defective.
Marriage is a gift.
Singleness can also be a gift.
And neither marital status determines your worth before God.
So do not marry simply because silence scares you.
Do not accept spiritual incompatibility because the attention feels intoxicating.
Do not trade conviction for companionship.
Do not hand your future to someone who wants your body but resents your devotion to Jesus.
You are not looking merely for someone who makes your heart beat faster.
You need character.
Truth.
Repentance.
Faithfulness.
Humility.
Someone who understands that love must eventually survive mornings when nobody feels cinematic.
Because real biblical romance is not less emotional than the world's version.
It is deeper.
It has butterflies, but it cannot survive on butterflies.
It has desire, but desire bows to holiness.
