A teenager secretly drowning.
A believer trapped in shame.
A skeptic watching Christians fight and wondering whether Jesus is anything like the people invoking His name.
A prodigal who thinks he has gone too far.
And perhaps God will use something as ordinary as your share to put the name of Jesus in front of that person one more time.
So before we ask God to fix the nation…
before we ask Him to defeat our enemies…
before we ask Him to restore the culture…
before we quote 2 Chronicles 7:14 beneath another flag…
perhaps we should finally hear the words that come before the healing:
“If My people humble themselves…”
His people.
Us.
Me.
You.
Maybe revival begins when the finger we pointed at the world finally curls back toward our own chest…
and then the hand opens in surrender before Jesus.
Because the greatest healing is not winning back a country while losing our souls.
It is sinners coming home to Christ.
And when everything you tried to hide finally stands exposed before Jesus, remember this:
The hands that uncover your sin are the same scarred hands that were pierced to redeem you from it.
The world does not need Christians who have mastered the art of identifying everybody else's wicked ways.
It needs men and women who have looked into the holiness of God, fallen to their knees, turned from their own—and discovered that Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: LEVITICUS 20 GIVES A SERIOUS PENALTY FOR SEX DURING MENSTRUATION—BUT DOES THIS LAW STILL APPLY TO CHRISTIANS?
paragraphs: LEVITICUS 20 GIVES A SERIOUS PENALTY FOR SEX DURING MENSTRUATION—BUT DOES THIS LAW STILL APPLY TO CHRISTIANS?

One disturbing verse. One severe consequence. And one question many Christians are almost afraid to ask: If we believe the whole Bible is the Word of God, what are we supposed to do with Leviticus 20:18?
There are verses in the Bible people underline.
There are verses people frame on walls.
There are verses Christians memorize when life is falling apart.
And then there are verses we quietly pass over because we are not quite sure what to do with them.
Leviticus 20:18 is one of those verses.
Read slowly what the King James Version says:

“And if a man shall lie with a woman having her sickness, and shall uncover her nakedness; he hath discovered her fountain, and she hath uncovered the fountain of her blood: and both of them shall be cut off from among their people.”
—Leviticus 20:18, KJV
That is not a comfortable verse.
And perhaps it should not be.
But discomfort is not permission to distort Scripture.
Some people will read this and immediately conclude, “See? The Old Testament is cruel.”
Others will respond from the opposite direction and say, “God said it, so Christians must still enforce it exactly as ancient Israel did.”
Both reactions can move too quickly.
Because before asking, “Do Christians have to obey this?” we need to ask a more fundamental question:
What exactly did God command, to whom did He give the command, what did the command mean within the covenant God made with Israel, and what changed when Jesus Christ established the New Covenant?
That journey takes us somewhere much deeper than menstruation.
It takes us into holiness.
Covenant.
Sin.
Blood.
Grace.
And ultimately...
Jesus.
The Hebrew text of Leviticus 20:18 begins:
וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר־יִשְׁכַּב אֶת־אִשָּׁה דָּוָה
Ve’ish asher-yishkav et-ishah davah...
In straightforward terms:
“And a man who lies with a menstruating woman...”

The word דָּוָה (davah) describes the woman in connection with her menstrual condition. The verse then says that the man has “uncovered her nakedness” and exposed her מָקוֹר (maqor)—her source or fountain—and that she has uncovered the source of her blood.
Then comes the frightening conclusion:
וְנִכְרְתוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם מִקֶּרֶב עַמָּם
Venikhretu sheneihem miqqerev ‘ammam.
“And both of them shall be cut off from among their people.”
Notice something immediately.
The Hebrew does not say, “Both of them shall be stoned.”
It does not explicitly say, “Execute them.”
It says they are to be “cut off”—from the Hebrew root כרת (karat).
That distinction matters.

The expression translated “cut off” appears elsewhere in the Torah and has generated considerable discussion concerning precisely how the sanction was understood—whether exclusion from the covenant community, divine judgment, premature death, loss of descendants, or some combination depending on context.
So we should not make Leviticus 20:18 say more than it actually says.
But neither should we make it say less.
This was serious.
Very serious.
Within Israel’s covenant life, this was not presented as an insignificant private matter.
And this is where the question becomes uncomfortable for modern Christians.
Why?
Why would God care about something so intimate?
To understand that, you have to walk backward several chapters.

Leviticus 15 discusses bodily discharges and ritual uncleanness. Menstruation made a woman ceremonially unclean for a period of time. Contact with certain things associated with that condition could communicate ritual uncleanness.
That did not mean the woman was morally disgusting.
It did not mean menstruation itself was a personal sin.
That distinction is absolutely essential.
Biblical ritual uncleanness and personal moral guilt are not identical categories.

People could become ceremonially unclean through ordinary realities of embodied human life. The book of Leviticus carefully regulates how Israel approached the holy presence of God, and categories of clean and unclean formed part of that covenant system.
In fact, Leviticus 15:24 says that if a man lies with a menstruating woman and her menstrual impurity comes upon him, he becomes unclean for seven days.
Then Leviticus 18:19 goes further and explicitly commands:
“Also thou shalt not approach unto a woman to uncover her nakedness, as long as she is put apart for her uncleanness.”
Then Leviticus 20:18 gives the corresponding sanction.
So we should not flatten these passages into one sentence.
Leviticus 15 discusses ritual impurity.
Leviticus 18 gives a prohibition.
Leviticus 20 attaches a serious covenant consequence.
The Bible is doing more than saying, “Blood is gross.”
That modern caricature completely misses the theological world of Leviticus.
Blood had enormous significance in Israel’s worship.
“For the life of the flesh is in the blood...”
—Leviticus 17:11
Blood represented life.
Blood belonged profoundly within Israel’s sacrificial symbolism.
Blood was associated with purification, sacrifice, atonement, life, death, and approach to a holy God.
And Leviticus repeatedly teaches Israel something modern humanity desperately wants to forget:
God is holy.
Not casually holy.
Not symbolically holy.
Not holy only when holiness happens to agree with our preferences.
Holy.
The Hebrew word is קָדוֹשׁ—qadosh.
Set apart.
Distinct.
God was teaching Israel that approaching Him was not casual business.
Their bodies mattered.
Their sexuality mattered.
Their worship mattered.
Their relationships mattered.
Their blood mattered.
Their obedience mattered.
Their covenant mattered.
This is where many readers make a mistake.
We open Leviticus as twenty-first-century Christians and instinctively ask, “Which of these rules do I personally have to follow?”
But Leviticus was originally given within the Mosaic covenant to Israel.
It was not dropped out of heaven as an isolated collection of random regulations addressed identically to every nation in every historical covenant setting.
Israel was a covenant people.
God had redeemed them from Egypt.
He had bound Himself to them.
He gave them priesthood, sacrifices, purity regulations, civil judgments, festivals, dietary distinctions, circumcision, tabernacle worship, and laws governing life in the covenant community.
And then Jesus came.
This is where the story turns.
Not because the Old Testament was a mistake.
Not because holiness stopped mattering.
Not because God suddenly changed His personality.
Jesus came because everything toward which the Law was moving finds its ultimate fulfillment in Him.
At the Last Supper, Jesus took the cup and declared:
“This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.”
—Luke 22:20, KJV
There it is again.
Blood.
But now...
His blood.
The book of Hebrews explains the enormous covenantal significance of what Christ accomplished.
“In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old.”
—Hebrews 8:13, KJV
Christians therefore do not live under the Mosaic covenant as ancient Israel lived under it.
That does not mean Christians tear Leviticus out of the Bible.
It means we read Leviticus through the fulfillment brought by Jesus Christ.
This distinction is visible almost immediately in the early Church.
When Gentiles began coming to Christ, the apostles faced an enormous question.
Would Gentile believers have to enter the Mosaic covenant and bear its requirements in the same manner as Jewish Israel?
Acts 15 records the Jerusalem Council wrestling with that very issue.
The apostles did not command Gentile converts to become Israel under the Mosaic covenant.
Yet—and this matters enormously—they did not conclude that grace means moral chaos.
They specifically instructed believers to abstain from idolatry, blood, things strangled, and sexual immorality (Acts 15:28–29).
Grace did not erase holiness.
Grace changed our covenant relationship to the Law.
That is why the Christian response to Leviticus 20:18 cannot simply be:
“That is Old Testament. Ignore it.”
No.
Christians should never be embarrassed by something God chose to reveal.
We should study it.
Understand its covenant setting.
Ask what it reveals about God's holiness.
Recognize how the New Testament treats the Mosaic covenant.
And then bring the entire matter to Christ.
So does Leviticus 20:18 mean Christians today should “cut off” a husband and wife who have sexual intercourse during menstruation?
Christians are not authorized by the New Testament to recreate ancient Israel’s covenant sanctions and impose Leviticus 20:18 as a civil or ecclesiastical penalty.
The Church is not ancient Israel's theocratic civil government.
Jesus established the New Covenant.
The apostolic Church did not simply transfer every Mosaic purity regulation and its associated national sanctions into Christian church discipline.
But that answer should not become an excuse for another dangerous error:
“Then Leviticus has nothing to teach us.”
It has everything to teach us about the God we worship.
It reminds us that God has never treated sexuality as spiritually meaningless.
Our culture often says that what consenting adults do sexually is nobody else's concern.
Scripture never gives sexuality that kind of spiritual independence.
Your body belongs to God.
Your marriage belongs to God.
Your desires belong under the lordship of Christ.
Your sexuality is not a tiny kingdom where Jesus has no throne.
Paul would later write:
—1 Corinthians 6:19–20, KJV
Read those words again.
“You are not your own.”
That sentence collides violently with modern individualism.
We want Jesus as Savior while keeping certain rooms locked.
My money.
My body.
My sexuality.
My relationship.
My entertainment.
My secret habits.
My private messages.
My browser history.
My resentment.
My addiction.
My hidden fantasy.
My life.
And Jesus stands at the door of every room we have labeled “private.”
Not because He wants to destroy us.
Because He purchased us.
The Christian life is not Jesus decorating the parts of your old life you are willing to show Him.
It is death and resurrection.
It is surrender.
And maybe that is why a strange verse in Leviticus can suddenly become painfully personal.
Because perhaps your issue has nothing to do with Leviticus 20:18.
Perhaps your issue is the room you refuse to surrender.
The relationship you know is pulling you from Christ.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The bitterness you have baptized as “boundaries.”
The affair hidden behind deleted messages.
The pride disguised as discernment.
The secret compromise you keep promising God you will abandon “soon.”
The Sunday worship followed by Monday surrender to the same chains.
You came here wondering about menstrual sex.
And somehow Scripture turned the mirror toward you.
That is what the Word of God does.
“For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword...”
—Hebrews 4:12, KJV
It cuts through our performances.
Through religious vocabulary.
Through excuses.
Through carefully edited Christian appearances.
And eventually it reaches the place where we cannot hide.
But please hear what happens next.
Because Christianity does not end with exposure.
If exposure were the end, every one of us would be finished.
The same Bible that reveals God's holiness reveals something even more astonishing.
A holy God came looking for unholy people.
Not with lowered standards.
With pierced hands.
Jesus did not come to announce that sin had stopped mattering.
He came because sin mattered so much that redemption would cost blood.
His blood.
The ancient sacrificial system had trained generations of Israelites to understand that approaching holiness was costly.
Then outside Jerusalem, the Lamb of God was nailed to wood.
Blood ran from His wounds.
The innocent for the guilty.
The righteous for the unrighteous.
The Holy One for sinners.
And suddenly the Bible's long story of holiness, sacrifice, blood, cleansing, covenant, priesthood, and forgiveness converged on a crucified Messiah.
Jesus was not Plan B.
He was the Lamb “foreordained before the foundation of the world” (1 Peter 1:20).
At the cross, God did not pretend sin was harmless.
He dealt with it.
And when Jesus rose from the dead, grace walked out of the tomb alive.
That is why there is hope for the sexually broken.
Hope for the adulterer.
Hope for the porn addict.
Hope for the ashamed.
Hope for the religious hypocrite.
Hope for the person who knew better and did it anyway.
Hope for the person carrying memories they wish they could erase.
Hope for the person reading this quietly thinking:
“If everyone knew what I had done, they would never look at me the same.”
Jesus already knows.
Every chapter.
Every deleted scene.
Every secret.
Every night.
Every compromise.
Every wound.
Every sin.
And the Gospel is not the announcement that those things do not matter.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ is greater.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, KJV
Cleanse.
There is a word Leviticus prepares us to understand.
We spend enormous energy trying to look clean.
Jesus came to make sinners clean.
Not through ritual performance.
Not through pretending.
Not through social-media Christianity.
Through His blood.
Through repentance.
Through faith.
Through grace.
Through a Savior who died and rose again.
Maybe you have spent years hiding.
Maybe people call you strong.
Maybe your family thinks everything is fine.
Maybe you can quote Scripture while carrying a private war nobody sees.
Then stop performing for one moment.
God already knows.
You do not have to impress the One who watched you fall.
You need to surrender to the One who can raise you.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the door through which you stop running from the only One who can actually save you.
Turn to Jesus.
Confess what needs confessing.
Leave what needs leaving.
Repair what can be repaired.
Seek help where help is needed.
Bring darkness into light.
Not because obedience purchases salvation.
Because the Savior who purchased you is worthy of your obedience.
And if you stumbled onto this article because somebody shared it...
Maybe they were not judging you.
Maybe they were thinking about you because they love you.
Maybe this is the conversation you have avoided.
Maybe God is using an uncomfortable verse from Leviticus to remind you that He still wants every part of your life.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to write the details publicly.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become another person's reason not to give up tonight.
Not because every sentence is easy.
Neither honors the whole biblical story.
We need the Law.
We need the prophets.
We need the apostles.
And above all, we need Jesus Christ—the One toward whom the Scriptures lead.
That share matters more than you may realize.
Someone may be drifting from Christianity because nobody ever helped them understand the Bible in context.
Someone may be drowning in secret shame.
Someone may be convinced that what they have done has permanently disqualified them from grace.
Let this reach them.
At the cross, they meet.
Help us keep going.
Christian ministry requires people willing not only to receive but also to participate—to pray, share, serve, give, and help truth travel farther than it could travel without them.
Your giving before God is a matter of faithful Christian stewardship, conscience, and conviction.
Supporting Gospel work can glorify God when it flows from love for Christ rather than pressure, appearance, or manipulation.
Paul described Christian generosity this way:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
—2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Not grudgingly.
Not of necessity.
From the heart.
That is the kind of support we want.
But the deeper reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Invite the friend who is struggling.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the person who is angry with God.
Invite the seeker with questions Christians sometimes seem afraid to answer.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing intelligent to say.
And keep sharing.
Because sometimes evangelism begins with a pulpit.
Sometimes it begins across a kitchen table.
And sometimes it begins when one Christian presses “Share” and a wounded person, alone at 1:37 in the morning, finds exactly the truth they were about to stop searching for.
Leviticus 20:18 is serious.
We should let it be serious.
It belonged to the covenant God made with Israel, and Christians should neither rip it from that covenant setting nor pretend it never existed.
It reminds us that the God of Scripture is holy.
It reminds us that sexuality belongs under His authority.
It reminds us that blood, purity, covenant, and access to God's presence run deeply through the biblical story.
But Leviticus is not the end of that story.
There is another covenant.
Another Priest.
Another sacrifice.
Another blood.
Jesus Christ entered the story.
And for the sinner who comes to Him in repentance and faith, the final word is no longer simply:
Unclean.
Outcast.
Condemned.
The Gospel announces something scandalously beautiful.
Forgiven.
Cleansed.
Redeemed.
Adopted.
Made new.
Maybe that is what you needed to hear more than the answer to the original question.
God's holiness is more terrifying than modern Christianity sometimes admits.
Your sin is more serious than your excuses have allowed you to believe.
But the blood of Jesus is more powerful than the darkest chapter you have ever written.
So stop hiding.
Come home.
And remember this when shame tries to introduce you by your worst moment:
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your story—but when Jesus takes the pen, your scandal does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “HE WHO FINDS A WIFE FINDS A GOOD THING” — BUT WHAT IF WE HAVE BEEN MAKING THIS VERSE PROMISE SOMETHING GOD NEVER SAID?
paragraphs: “HE WHO FINDS A WIFE FINDS A GOOD THING” — BUT WHAT IF WE HAVE BEEN MAKING THIS VERSE PROMISE SOMETHING GOD NEVER SAID?

Proverbs 18:22 is beautiful. It is also one of the easiest verses about marriage to quote, romanticize, weaponize, and misunderstand. What God actually said is better than the fantasy we sometimes attach to it.
“He who finds a wife finds a good thing, and obtains favor from the LORD.”
Proverbs 18:22.
You have probably heard it at weddings.
You have seen it beneath engagement photographs.
You may have watched someone post it after finally meeting the person they had prayed for.
Maybe you have whispered it yourself.
Maybe you are still waiting for it.
Or maybe reading those words hurts.
Because you found a wife... and your marriage has been difficult.
Because you became a wife... and discovered that a wedding ring does not magically turn two wounded human beings into spiritually mature people.
Because you prayed, waited, dated carefully, believed you had found “the one,” and still ended up heartbroken.

Or perhaps you are single, getting older, watching other people announce engagements, pregnancies, anniversaries, and family photographs while quietly wondering whether God somehow passed over your name.
Then this verse appears:
“He who finds a wife finds a good thing...”
And suddenly a beautiful proverb begins sounding like an accusation.
If marriage is favor, does singleness mean I am less favored?
If a wife is a good thing, does that mean every woman I desire is God's choice for me?
If I marry, is happiness guaranteed?
If my marriage is painful, did I marry the wrong person?
If I have not found a spouse, has God withheld something good because something is wrong with me?
Those questions deserve more than Christian clichés.
They deserve Scripture.
And when we slow down long enough to hear what the Bible actually says, Proverbs 18:22 becomes deeper, wiser, and far more beautiful than the slogan we sometimes make it.
The Hebrew reads:
מָצָא אִשָּׁה מָצָא טוֹב וַיָּפֶק רָצוֹן מֵיְהוָה
Matza ishah, matza tov; vayafeq ratzon me-YHWH.
In straightforward sense:
The one who finds a wife finds good and receives favor from YHWH.
The word מָצָא — māṣāʾ means to find, encounter, attain, or come upon.
אִשָּׁה — ʾiššâ can mean woman or wife according to context.
טוֹב — ṭôḇ is one of Scripture's great words for that which is good, beneficial, beautiful, desirable, or fitting.
And רָצוֹן — rāṣôn carries the sense of favor, goodwill, acceptance, or pleasure.
So yes.
Do not explain the verse away.
Marriage is good.
A godly wife is good.
A faithful husband is good.
Covenant companionship is good.
There is something genuinely beautiful about two people standing before God and saying, in effect, “My life is no longer only about me.”
Scripture does not apologize for celebrating marriage.
But notice something equally important.
The verse says a wife is a good thing.
It does not say a wife is the ultimate good thing.
It says marriage may be experienced as favor from the LORD.
It does not say marriage is the only evidence of God's favor.
And it certainly does not say:
“He who finds the person he is attracted to has found God's guaranteed soulmate.”
That verse is not in your Bible.
Neither is:
“He who gets married will never feel lonely again.”
Neither is:
“He who finds a wife will automatically have a peaceful marriage.”
Neither is:
“Every romantic relationship that feels supernatural was sent by God.”
Neither is:
“If you are still single, God is withholding His favor.”
We have to stop making God responsible for promises He never made.
Because sometimes the deepest disappointment in our spiritual lives comes not from God breaking His Word...
but from us attaching our expectations to His Word and calling those expectations promises.
Read Proverbs as Proverbs.
Biblical proverbs ordinarily communicate wisdom about how life works under God's moral order. They are not magical formulas guaranteeing identical outcomes in every circumstance.
“Train up a child in the way he should go...” does not turn parents into sovereign controllers of another human being's future choices.
“A soft answer turns away wrath” does not mean every furious person will immediately become peaceful.

And “he who finds a wife finds a good thing” does not mean putting a wedding ring on someone's finger guarantees fifty years without betrayal, conflict, sickness, grief, financial pressure, temptation, misunderstanding, or tears.
Marriage is good.
Marriage is also lived by sinners.
That changes everything.
Two people do not stop needing grace because they said, “I do.”
In many ways, marriage reveals how desperately they need it.
You can love Jesus and still communicate badly.
You can pray together and still hurt one another.
You can know Bible verses and still carry childhood wounds into your bedroom.
You can worship on Sunday and fight in the car on the way home.
You can genuinely love your spouse and, in a moment of selfishness, behave in ways that do not look much like love.
Marriage does not remove the old nature.
It gives the old nature fewer places to hide.
And perhaps that is part of marriage's severe mercy.
Someone begins seeing you up close.
Not the church version.
Not the Facebook version.
Not the carefully edited version.
The tired version.
The insecure version.
The irritated version.
The version that wants its own way.
The version that sometimes says, “Nothing's wrong,” when almost everything is wrong.
The version that needs forgiveness.
That is why Christian marriage cannot survive spiritually on romance alone.
Romance can bring two people to dinner.
Only covenant teaches them to remain at the table when the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Attraction may begin a relationship.
It cannot crucify pride.
Chemistry can make your heart race.
It cannot make you holy.
A beautiful wedding can gather hundreds of people into a room.
It cannot create the character required for a beautiful marriage.
Only Christ can transform the sinner.
That is where Proverbs 18:22 becomes even more meaningful when read beside Proverbs 19:14:
“House and riches are the inheritance of fathers: and a prudent wife is from the LORD.”
There is a difference between merely finding someone and recognizing godly character.

Proverbs itself refuses to teach that every wife, simply by occupying the marital position, automatically brings peace and wisdom into a household. Elsewhere the same book warns vividly about contentious relationships.
So Proverbs 18:22 cannot reasonably mean, “Any woman you marry will necessarily produce a wonderful marriage.”
The Bible is wiser than that.
The good being celebrated is God's beautiful design of covenant companionship rightly lived.
And that means the verse is not permission to become desperate.
Please hear this if loneliness has been making decisions for you.
You do not need to turn every attractive stranger into a prophecy.
You do not need to call chemistry “confirmation.”
You do not need to ignore character because somebody said they believe in God.
You do not need to overlook manipulation, deception, uncontrolled anger, habitual unfaithfulness, or contempt because you are afraid you will never find anyone else.
And you certainly do not need to marry someone merely because being alone has become painful.
Loneliness can make red flags look pink.
Desperation can make attention feel like love.

And when you have prayed for companionship for years, sometimes simply being wanted can feel so much like being answered that you stop asking whether the relationship actually resembles the wisdom of God.
But God never asks you to abandon wisdom in order to receive His gifts.
A godly marriage is not built merely on finding someone willing to marry you.
It is built through two people continually surrendering themselves to Christ.
And there is another side of this verse that the Church must say clearly.
Single Christian...
Proverbs 18:22 is not an insult to you.
Your unmarried life is not God's waiting room.
You are not half a Christian waiting for your other half to arrive.
Jesus Christ was not incomplete.
Paul was not spiritually defective because of singleness.

In 1 Corinthians 7, Paul speaks positively about both marriage and singleness and recognizes different gifts and callings from God. He even explains that unmarried believers may possess particular freedom to devote themselves to the Lord.
That means the Bible that says marriage is good is the same Bible that can say singleness is good.
There is no contradiction.
There are different gifts under the same Lord.
Your spouse cannot become your savior because you already have One.
And perhaps that is where some marriages quietly begin collapsing.
We ask another human being to carry messianic weight.
“Make me happy.”
“Make me secure.”
“Make me feel valuable.”
“Heal what my father did.”
“Repair what my mother never gave me.”
“Convince me I am attractive.”
“Make my loneliness disappear.”
“Complete me.”
That is too much weight for human shoulders.
Your husband cannot be Jesus.
Your wife cannot be Jesus.
And whenever we demand that a spouse provide what ultimately belongs to Christ, even a good marriage can begin suffocating beneath impossible expectations.
Marriage is a gift.
Christ is the Giver.
Never worship the gift.
Because every human marriage eventually reaches places where romance cannot save it.
There will be moments when forgiveness costs something.
Moments when repentance has to become more than a theological word.
Moments when “I was wrong” becomes harder to say than “I love you.”
Moments when grace stops being something you sing about and becomes something you must give to the person who wounded you.
And suddenly...
the Gospel is standing in your living room.
Because Christian marriage, at its deepest, points beyond itself.
Scripture presents the relationship between husband and wife against the breathtaking backdrop of Christ and His Church.
Jesus does not love His people because His people have always been lovable.
Look at us.
We wander.
We doubt.
We hide.
We make promises and break them.
We sin after swearing we would never do it again.
We bring Him hearts full of contradictions.
Yet Christ went to the cross.
Not because sin did not matter.
Because it mattered so much that blood was required.
Grace is not God pretending our scandal never happened.
Grace is God meeting guilty people inside the scandal and doing what they could never do for themselves.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus paid the debt.
Jesus rose from the grave.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
That is why the Gospel is bigger than marriage.
And this may be the sentence somebody reading this desperately needs tonight:
A spouse cannot rewrite your story.
Jesus can.
Maybe your marriage is beautiful right now.
Thank God.
Do not worship it.
Steward it.
Maybe your marriage is struggling.
Do not hide behind photographs.

Bring what is broken into the light. Seek biblical wisdom, repentance, wise pastoral counsel where appropriate, and qualified professional help when needed. Forgiveness never means calling evil good, and covenant faithfulness should never be twisted into permission for abuse or danger.
Maybe your marriage ended and you carry shame every time Christians talk about “successful families.”
Bring the wreckage to Jesus.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Jesus sees you.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Do not rename your sin, but do not run from the only Savior who can forgive sinners either.
Repent.
Come into the light.
The cross was built for guilty people.
Maybe you are widowed and still instinctively reach toward the other side of the bed.
Maybe you are single and tired of pretending you never ache for companionship.
Maybe everyone keeps telling you, “God is preparing someone,” even though Scripture never promised that every Christian will marry.
You do not need another cliché.
You need Christ.
Because whether married, divorced, widowed, abandoned, betrayed, waiting, healing, or happily single, your deepest identity cannot safely rest in your relationship status.
It must rest in Jesus.
“He who finds a wife finds a good thing.”
Yes.
Believe it.
Celebrate it.
Protect it from distortion.
But never turn “a good thing” into God Himself.
Marriage is not heaven.
Your spouse is not the Holy Spirit.
A wedding is not salvation.
And being chosen romantically is not the same thing as being chosen in Christ.
There is a greater love story running through Scripture.
Humanity ran from God.
We sinned.
We hid.
We rebelled.
And God did not respond by lowering His holiness and pretending rebellion was harmless.
He came for sinners.
The Son of God entered our world.
Jesus lived the righteousness we could not live.
He carried the judgment sinners deserved.
He was crucified.
Buried.
And He rose.
The ultimate answer to human loneliness is therefore not, “Find a spouse.”
It is:
Be reconciled to God.
And when Christ becomes the center, marriage can finally stop carrying the burden of being your god.
Then a husband can love his wife without possessing her.
A wife can love her husband without worshiping him.
Two imperfect people can repent.
Forgive.
Grow.
Fall down.
Get back up.
And keep walking toward Jesus.
Not because marriage magically fixes sinners.
Because Jesus transforms sinners.
Be honest.
Maybe you have idolized marriage.
Maybe you have judged single believers.
Maybe you have stayed desperate because you thought having someone—anyone—was better than being alone with God.
Maybe you are married and have spent years demanding from your spouse what only Christ can give.
Maybe you are the one who needs to repent.
Maybe you are simply tired.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that repentance, grace, forgiveness, wise help, and patient obedience still matter.

Not because you need another post sitting in a folder, but because feelings have short memories. There may come a day when loneliness starts preaching to you again. There may come a night when disappointment begins rewriting what God actually said.
Come back.
Read the verse again.

Following Gospel Warrior also helps you stay connected to daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment. Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the person who is not sure what they believe yet.
It does not.
Not because financial support can buy blessing, forgiveness, salvation, or a better standing before God.
It cannot.

And not because supporting Gospel Warrior should be presented as replacing whatever your conscience and biblical convictions lead you to give through your local church, generosity to people in need, missions, or other faithful Christian work.

But voluntary financial support can be an act of Christian generosity and stewardship when it is given freely, wisely, cheerfully, and for the advancement of work you genuinely believe is bearing good fruit.
It helps us keep reaching the person scrolling alone at two in the morning.
The marriage quietly falling apart.
The believer wrestling with temptation.
The prodigal wondering whether Jesus would still receive them.
The wounded Christian who almost gave up.
The seeker who has never understood grace.
The person who will never comment but reads every word.
And the soul we may never meet on this side of eternity.
That matters because this was never supposed to be about building consumers.
It is about making disciples.
Come to Jesus.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you have wandered, return.
If you have been hiding, step into the light.
If your marriage has become an idol, put Christ back on the throne.
If singleness has become bitterness, bring the bitterness to Him.
If heartbreak has convinced you that God abandoned you, bring Him the questions you are afraid to say aloud.
If shame keeps whispering that your story is already ruined...
look at the cross.
Christianity begins with a scandal human beings could never have invented their way out of:
sinners guilty before a holy God.
And then came grace.
Not cheap grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Cross-shaped grace.
Empty-tomb grace.
The kind of grace that does not merely improve your public image.
The kind that raises dead things.
So yes...
“He who finds a wife finds a good thing.”
Treasure the truth.
But remember the greater truth.
The greatest thing that can happen to a man is not that he finds a wife.
The greatest thing that can happen to a woman is not that she finds a husband.
The greatest thing that can happen to either of them is that, by grace, they belong to Jesus Christ.
Because eventually every earthly marriage reaches its final day.
Every photograph ages.
Every anniversary count eventually stops.
Every hand we hold in this life must someday be released unless Christ returns first.
But the redeemed will never reach the end of Christ.
So love your spouse.
Pray for your future spouse if marriage is something you desire.
Honor marriage.
Honor faithful singleness.
Seek wisdom instead of desperation.
Repent quickly.
Forgive biblically.
Love sacrificially.
And never ask a human being to sit on a throne that belongs to Jesus.
Because sometimes the “good thing” God gives you is not meant to become the center of your story.
It is meant to lead your eyes back to the One who is.
Your wedding ring may tell the world whom you married—but only the scars in the hands of Jesus can tell you how completely you are loved.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS SAID MOSES PERMITTED DIVORCE BECAUSE OF HARDNESS OF HEART—THEN POINTED BACK TO EDEN
paragraphs: JESUS SAID MOSES PERMITTED DIVORCE BECAUSE OF HARDNESS OF HEART—THEN POINTED BACK TO EDEN
They asked Jesus when a marriage could be ended. Jesus answered by taking them back to why marriage existed before sin ever entered the world.
There are questions we ask because we desperately want truth.
And then there are questions we ask because we are hoping truth will give us permission.
The Pharisees came to Jesus carrying one of those questions.
“Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for just any reason?”
It sounded theological.
It sounded like a debate about Moses.
But Jesus heard something underneath the question.
A human heart looking for the boundary.
How far can I go?
When am I allowed to walk away?
What is the minimum God requires of me?
Where is the loophole?
And instead of beginning with divorce...
Jesus began with Eden.
That should stop us.
Because when human beings wanted to discuss how a marriage could be dismantled, Jesus pointed them toward the moment marriage was created.
Matthew records the question this way:
“Εἰ ἔξεστιν ἀνθρώπῳ ἀπολῦσαι τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ κατὰ πᾶσαν αἰτίαν;”
The heart of their question is essentially:
“Is it lawful for a man to release/divorce his wife for every cause?”
The Greek verb ἀπολῦσαι (apolysai) carries the sense of releasing, sending away, or divorcing.
But Jesus refuses to begin where they begin.
He says:
“Οὐκ ἀνέγνωτε...”
“Have you not read...?”
Then He reaches all the way back to creation.
Not merely to Moses.
Not merely to Deuteronomy.
Not merely to what fallen people were permitted to do in a broken world.
Back...
to the beginning.
Jesus recalls Genesis:
“ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐτοὺς”
“Male and female He made them.”
Then:
“ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν”
“The two shall become one flesh.”
And then comes the sentence that changes the entire conversation:
“ὃ οὖν ὁ θεὸς συνέζευξεν ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω.”
“What therefore God has joined together, let no human being separate.”
Matthew 19:4–6.
Notice what Jesus just did.
They asked about permission.
Jesus spoke about purpose.
They asked about divorce.
Jesus spoke about creation.
They asked what a man was legally allowed to do.
Jesus reminded them of what God had done.
That difference matters.
Because the biblical vision of marriage does not begin with two people standing at an altar.
It begins with God.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
A man leaves his father and mother, clings to his wife, and they become “one flesh.”
Basar echad.
בָשָׂר אֶחָד.
“One flesh.”
Not merely two people sharing a house.
Not merely two people sharing bills.
Not merely two people who once felt butterflies.
Not merely two people posting anniversary pictures while quietly becoming strangers behind closed doors.
One flesh.
Marriage, in Jesus’ teaching, reaches deeper than convenience.
Deeper than chemistry.
Deeper than romance.
It is covenantal union under God.
And that is exactly why what happens next is so uncomfortable.
The Pharisees push back.
If that is God's intention, they essentially ask, then why did Moses tell people to give a certificate of divorce?
Jesus answers:
“Μωϋσῆς πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν ἐπέτρεψεν ὑμῖν ἀπολῦσαι τὰς γυναῖκας ὑμῶν...”
“Moses, because of your hardness of heart, permitted you to divorce your wives...”
Then Jesus adds:
“ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως.”
“But from the beginning it has not been this way.”
Matthew 19:8.
Read that again.
Because one word changes everything.
Permitted.
The Greek is ἐπέτρεψεν—epetrepsen.
Permitted.
Jesus does not describe divorce here as the beautiful design God established in Eden.
He points to a concession associated with human brokenness.
And He names the disease beneath it:
σκληροκαρδία.
Sklerokardia.
Hardness of heart.
It is a brutal word because it does not allow us to keep every conversation safely outside ourselves.
We would rather discuss who was technically right.
Who started it.
Who apologized first.
Who failed more.
Who had biblical grounds.
Who said what.
Who signed what.
Who left whom.
Jesus goes deeper.
The heart.
Because before some marriages collapse publicly, something has often been hardening privately.
A heart stops listening.
A heart stops confessing.
A heart stops forgiving.
A heart starts keeping score.
A heart becomes comfortable with contempt.
A heart learns how to punish with silence.
A heart can sit beside someone in church, sing about grace, listen to a sermon about mercy...
and then go home unwilling to say,
“I was wrong.”
Hardness does not always arrive screaming.
Sometimes it arrives quietly.
One ignored wound.
One secret message.
One unconfessed resentment.
One flirtation justified as harmless.
One apology withheld because pride would rather win than reconcile.
One night sleeping back-to-back.
Then another.
Then another.
Until two people who once could not imagine life apart begin imagining peace only if the other person disappears.
And perhaps that is where this article found you.
Maybe your marriage is beautiful.
Guard it.
Do not wait for catastrophe before learning how to repent.
Do not wait for betrayal before establishing boundaries.
Do not wait until affection disappears before becoming intentional about tenderness.
Do not assume a wedding covenant survives automatically because wedding photographs still exist.
Bring your marriage continually under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
But perhaps you are reading this with tears already forming.
Maybe you know what it feels like to watch something sacred fracture.
Maybe you have been divorced.
Maybe someone abandoned you.
Maybe adultery shattered what you thought was safe.
Maybe you were the unfaithful one.
Maybe you were the hard-hearted one.
Maybe you begged someone to stay.
Maybe you were handed papers you never wanted.
Maybe there are children involved.
Maybe years have passed, but hearing the word “divorce” still makes something inside you ache.
Maybe your story is complicated enough that simplistic Christian slogans feel like another wound.
Then hear this carefully:
Jesus' words about the sacredness of marriage were not spoken so Christians could weaponize them against wounded people.
They were spoken because covenant matters to God.
And the same Jesus who tells the truth about sin is the Jesus who receives sinners.

The church must never turn God's high view of marriage into permission to shame every divorced person as though every broken marriage has the same story, the same responsibility, or the same circumstances.
Scripture itself requires more careful pastoral wisdom than that.

Matthew 19 continues into Jesus' teaching concerning sexual immorality. Paul later addresses abandonment by an unbelieving spouse in 1 Corinthians 7. Faithful Christians have debated aspects of divorce and remarriage for centuries, but none of those debates should erase the central force of Jesus' answer here:
God's design must not be reconstructed around the hardness of the human heart.
And neither should Jesus' teaching be twisted into demanding that someone quietly endure violence or immediate danger.
Protecting someone from harm is not the same thing as treating covenant casually.

If you are in danger, getting to safety and seeking trustworthy pastoral, professional, and legal help can be necessary. Reconciliation, where it is biblically and safely possible, requires truth and repentance; it is not pretending evil never happened.
Because biblical reconciliation is not merely returning to the same room.
It involves truth.
Repentance.
Grace.
Transformation.
And this is where Matthew 19 stops being merely an article about divorce.
It becomes an examination of us.
Because sklerokardia does not belong only in divorce court.
Hardness of heart can live inside a marriage that never legally ends.
It can live inside a church pew.
Inside a ministry.
Inside a preacher.
Inside the person sharing Bible verses every morning.
Inside you.
Inside me.
You can remain married and still have a hard heart.
You can know Scripture and have a hard heart.
You can defend biblical marriage while treating your own spouse with cruelty.
You can win theological arguments and lose tenderness.
You can expose everybody else's sin while protecting your own.
You can say “Jesus is Lord” and still have rooms inside your heart where Jesus is not allowed to touch anything.
That is why the deepest question is not merely:
“Have I ever been divorced?”
The deeper question is:
“Where has my heart become hard toward God?”
Where have you stopped listening?
What sin are you defending?
Whom have you refused to forgive?
What secret are you protecting?
What bitterness have you renamed “discernment”?
What pride have you renamed “standards”?
What lust have you renamed “needs”?
What selfishness have you renamed “self-care”?
What disobedience have you renamed “my truth”?
Jesus is not merely trying to improve marriages.
Jesus came to save sinners.
That includes husbands.
That includes wives.
That includes divorced people.
That includes people who have committed adultery.
That includes people who have been betrayed.
That includes people whose marriages survived.
That includes people whose marriages did not.
That includes people carrying consequences they cannot reverse.
That includes the person reading this thinking,
“If people knew what I did, they would never look at me the same way.”
Jesus already knows.
And He went to the cross anyway.
This is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin does not matter.
Grace would be meaningless if sin did not matter.
The scandal is that our sin mattered enough for the Son of God to bleed for it...
and His mercy is greater than the darkest chapter surrendered to Him.
At Calvary, Jesus did not call evil good.
He bore evil's judgment.
He did not pretend sin was harmless.
He was pierced because sin is deadly.
He did not lower God's holiness until sinners could reach it.
He came down to sinners, fulfilled righteousness, carried our guilt, died our death, and rose again.
So repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the grave.
It is the moment you stop defending what is killing you.
It is the moment you stop saying,
“But they did...”
and finally ask,
“Jesus, what has happened to my heart?”
Maybe your spouse needs repentance.
Maybe your former spouse needs repentance.
Maybe somebody who wounded you needs repentance.
But you cannot repent for them.
You can only bring your own heart before Christ.
And sometimes the bravest prayer in a marriage is not,
“Lord, change them.”
Sometimes it is:
“Lord...
start with me.”
Search me.
Break my pride.
Expose my selfishness.
Teach me to listen again.
Teach me to tell the truth.
Teach me to forgive without pretending sin does not matter.
Teach me to seek forgiveness without demanding instant trust.
Teach me to love as someone who has been loved by Christ.
Give me a heart of flesh again.
That language should sound familiar.
God promised in Ezekiel 36:26:
“וַהֲסִרֹתִי אֶת־לֵב הָאֶבֶן מִבְּשַׂרְכֶם וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב בָּשָׂר”
God speaks of removing the “heart of stone” and giving a “heart of flesh.”
Think about that beside Matthew 19.
Jesus identifies hardness of heart.
The Gospel announces a Savior who does not merely command hard hearts to behave better.
He makes people new.
Christianity is not behavior modification with Bible verses attached.
It is resurrection.
It is the Holy Spirit invading places sin has made dead.
It is Christ taking people who have learned to hide, blame, manipulate, betray, lust, hate, withdraw, and destroy...
and teaching them another way to live.
That does not mean every broken marriage will be restored.
Some consequences remain.
Some relationships cannot return to what they were.
Some people will refuse repentance.
Some wounds require enormous time.
Forgiveness does not automatically recreate trust, and reconciliation cannot be manufactured by one person's effort alone.
But no surrendered life is beyond the redeeming reach of Jesus Christ.
Your past may explain scars.
It does not have to become your god.
Your divorce does not have to become your identity.
Your betrayal does not have to become your identity.
Your failure does not have to become your identity.
Your victimization does not have to become the final sentence over your life.
If you belong to Christ, the loudest name over you is not “divorced.”
Not “abandoned.”
Not “adulterer.”
Not “failure.”
Not “damaged.”
Not “unlovable.”
Christ has the final word over those who come to Him in repentant faith.
Forgiven.
Redeemed.
Being made new.
And maybe now we understand why Jesus went back to Eden.
He was doing more than winning an argument with Pharisees.
He was exposing the tragedy of sin.
Look at what God intended.
Then look at what hard hearts have done.
But do not stop there.
Look at Christ.
Because the Bible begins with a marriage in a garden...
and moves toward another wedding.
Christ and His redeemed people.
The Bridegroom who does not abandon His Bride because loving her became inconvenient.
The Bridegroom who loved His people sacrificially.
The Bridegroom who gave Himself for His church.
The Bridegroom whose covenant faithfulness exposes our faithlessness...
and whose grace is the only reason faithless sinners can ever come home.
So if your marriage is healthy, do not become proud.
Stay dependent on Christ.
If your marriage is struggling, do not wait until resentment has eaten everything tender.
Seek help.
Tell the truth.
Pray together.
Confess quickly.
Get wise biblical counsel.
Put the phone down.
Listen.
Repent.
Forgive.
Fight for holiness harder than you fight to be right.
If you have sinned sexually, stop hiding.
If you are emotionally involved with someone who is not your spouse, stop feeding the fantasy.
If pornography has invaded your covenant, drag it into the light.
If bitterness has become your daily bread, stop calling it protection.
If you are manipulating Scripture to control your spouse, repent.
If you have wounded someone, do not use grace as a shortcut around accountability.
And if you are the wounded one, remember that forgiveness does not require you to call evil good.
Bring everything into the light of Jesus.
Everything.
Because Jesus did not die merely to make our scandals less embarrassing.
He died and rose again to make sinners new.
That is our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior.
From scandal...
to grace.
Not because scandals are insignificant.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because Christians never fail spectacularly.
But because Jesus Christ still saves, forgives, restores, sanctifies, heals, disciplines, and transforms people who surrender themselves to Him.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Talk to Jesus.
Right now.
Not as a performance.
Not so strangers will think you are spiritual.
Let it be a confession.
A small public declaration that you are finished pretending you have nothing left for Christ to change.
And if you have been hiding something that needs to come into the light, perhaps today your words are simply:
“No more hiding.”
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not the only person fighting for faith.
Someone may pray for you.
Someone may see your testimony months from now and realize failure does not have to be the final chapter.

Not because every sentence will be easy to hear, but because there may come a night when anger is louder than covenant, temptation is louder than wisdom, shame is louder than grace, or hopelessness tells you nothing can change.
Come back.
Read Matthew 19 again.
Remember Eden.
Remember the hard heart.
Then remember the cross.
But voluntary generosity is biblical.
Keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep putting Scripture in front of people who may never walk into a church but will stop long enough to read something on their phone at 2:00 in the morning.
And sometimes...
that is where Jesus meets them.
The resources are important.
Bigger than numbers.
Bigger than algorithms.
Bigger than us.
We want Jesus Christ proclaimed.
We want Scripture opened.
We want sinners called to repentance.
We want ashamed people shown the cross.
We want wounded believers reminded that grace is not a theory.
We want marriages strengthened where restoration is possible.
We want hard hearts softened.
We want lost people found.
We want believers discipled.
We want Christ glorified.
Pray for the ministry.
Comment and help another person feel less alone.
Save the truth and return to it.
There are many ways to participate in spreading the Gospel, and none of us purchases God's favor.
Jesus already paid the price we never could.
Maybe that is where this entire conversation finally lands.
The Pharisees came asking Jesus about the point at which a person could let someone go.
Jesus took them back to the God who joined them together.
They pointed to paperwork.
Jesus pointed to the heart.
They pointed to Moses.
Jesus pointed to Eden.
And eventually...
the story of Scripture points us to a cross.
Because our deepest problem has never merely been broken marriages.
It is broken hearts.
Hard hearts.
Sinful hearts.
Hearts that need more than advice.
More than rules.
More than religious appearances.
We need resurrection.
We need forgiveness.
We need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
So before you leave this page, ask yourself one question that no Pharisee asked that day:
“Jesus... where has my heart become hard?”
Do not answer quickly.
Let Him search you.
And whatever He reveals...
bring it into the light.
Because the heart that finally stops defending its hardness is the heart grace can begin transforming.
You may not be able to rewrite what happened yesterday—but when you surrender the pen, Jesus can still redeem what your story becomes tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF JESUS FULFILLED THE LAW, WHY DO BIBLICAL SEXUAL LAWS STILL FEEL SO PERSONAL?
paragraphs: IF JESUS FULFILLED THE LAW, WHY DO BIBLICAL SEXUAL LAWS STILL FEEL SO PERSONAL?

The uncomfortable question many Christians quietly ask: If we are under grace, not the Mosaic covenant, what exactly does Jesus expect us to do with the Bible’s sexual boundaries—and what happens when those boundaries reach into the most private room of our lives?
There is a moment when Christianity stops being theoretical.
It usually does not happen while you are sitting comfortably in church.
It happens when Scripture touches something you love.
Something you want.
Something you have already justified.

Something connected to your body, your relationship, your memories, your loneliness, your marriage, your attraction, your secret browser history, your private conversations, your past, your shame—or the person you cannot imagine surrendering.
Suddenly the Bible is no longer an ancient book sitting politely on a shelf.
It is standing in your bedroom.
And that is when one of the most emotionally loaded questions in Christianity comes crawling out of the shadows:
“If Jesus fulfilled the Law, why should Christians still care about biblical sexual laws?”
Maybe you have wondered it.
Maybe somebody you love has asked it.
Maybe you have heard someone say:
“Christians eat pork.”
“Christians wear mixed fabrics.”
“Christians do not offer animal sacrifices.”
“So why do Christians suddenly quote the Old Testament when sex enters the conversation?”
That question deserves more than a slogan.
It deserves more than outrage.
And it certainly deserves more than Christians throwing isolated Bible verses at hurting people as though winning an argument were the same thing as winning a soul.
Because behind many theological questions about sexuality is a human being.
Sometimes frightened.
Sometimes confused.
Sometimes wounded.
Sometimes genuinely searching.
Sometimes desperately hoping God will approve what the heart already wants.
And sometimes quietly terrified that He will not.
So before we go any further, hear this:
Jesus did fulfill the Law.
Completely.
Gloriously.
Perfectly.
But “Jesus fulfilled the Law” does not mean, “Therefore nothing God ever revealed about holiness matters anymore.”
Jesus Himself said:
“Μὴ νομίσητε ὅτι ἦλθον καταλῦσαι τὸν νόμον ἢ τοὺς προφήτας· οὐκ ἦλθον καταλῦσαι ἀλλὰ πληρῶσαι.”
“Do not think that I came to destroy the Law or the Prophets. I didn’t come to destroy, but to fulfill.”
Matthew 5:17.
The crucial Greek word is πληρῶσαι — plērōsai, from plēroō: to fulfill, fill up, bring to completion.
And notice the word Jesus deliberately contrasts it with:
καταλῦσαι — katalysai.
To tear down. Destroy. Demolish. Abolish.
Jesus is not announcing that God's previous revelation was embarrassing and He had arrived to erase it.
He is declaring that it reaches its intended fulfillment in Him.
That distinction changes everything.
Because Christians do not approach Moses as though Jesus never came.
But neither do Christians approach Jesus as though Moses never existed.
We read the whole story through Christ.

The Torah revealed God's holiness, exposed human sin, formed Israel as God's covenant people, anticipated realities ultimately fulfilled in Christ, and carried Israel through a particular covenant administration.
Then Jesus came.
Not as another lamb standing beside the altar.
As the Lamb.
Not as another priest repeating sacrifices.
As the One to whom the sacrifices were pointing.
Not merely as another teacher interpreting God's revelation.
As the Son in whom God's redemptive purposes reach their climax.
That is why the New Testament can say things that initially seem almost contradictory.

Galatians says the Law functioned as a guardian until Christ, and that with the coming of faith God's people are no longer under that guardian. Hebrews speaks explicitly of the new covenant and describes the former covenant as obsolete.
So Christians are not ancient Israelites living under the Sinai covenant.
We do not rebuild the Levitical priesthood.
We do not return to animal sacrifices.
We do not seek justification by keeping Torah.
We do not pretend Calvary never happened.
But here comes the part that makes the question intensely personal.
When the apostles brought the Gospel to Gentiles—people who had never lived as Jews under the Mosaic covenant—they did not conclude:
“Jesus fulfilled the Law, therefore sexual conduct no longer matters.”
Quite the opposite.

At the Jerusalem Council, while explicitly refusing to require Gentile converts to take on the whole Mosaic covenant as the means of belonging to God's people, the apostles still instructed them to abstain from πορνεία — porneia, sexual immorality.
The Greek of Acts 15:20 contains the unmistakable phrase:
“ἀπέχεσθαι … τῆς πορνείας”
—to abstain from sexual immorality.
That should make us stop.
Because these are Gentile Christians.
This is after the resurrection.
After the cross.
After Christ fulfilled the Law.
And sexual holiness did not disappear.
Paul tells the Thessalonian believers:
“τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν, ἀπέχεσθαι ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ τῆς πορνείας”
“For this is the will of God: your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality.”
1 Thessalonians 4:3.
Read that slowly.
Your sanctification.
Not your humiliation.
Not God's attempt to make you miserable.
Not God's embarrassment over the human body.
Sanctification.
Being made holy.
Belonging increasingly and visibly to God.
This is where many modern conversations go wrong.
We ask:
“How close can I get to the boundary without technically sinning?”
The New Testament asks something far more beautiful and far more terrifying:
“How completely can this body belong to Christ?”
That changes the conversation.
Christian sexual ethics are not ultimately built upon disgust for the body.
They are built upon the breathtaking value God gives the body.
Paul does not tell Christians that their bodies are worthless.
He says something almost shocking:
Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.
You are not your own.
You were bought with a price.
Therefore glorify God in your body.
There it is.
The Gospel enters the bedroom.
Not because Jesus is obsessed with catching people doing something dirty.
Because Jesus purchased the whole person.
Your Sunday morning belongs to Him.
Your bank account belongs under His lordship.
Your anger belongs under His lordship.
Your ambitions belong under His lordship.
Your mouth belongs under His lordship.
Your phone belongs under His lordship.
Your sexuality belongs under His lordship.
Your body belongs under His lordship.
Grace never meant:
“Jesus forgave me, therefore my body is irrelevant.”
Grace means something infinitely greater:
“Jesus bought me, therefore even my body can become an instrument of worship.”
And this is why simplistic arguments about “Old Testament sexual laws” often fail.

Leviticus 18 does contain sexual prohibitions. It forbids various incestuous unions, adultery, child sacrifice in connection with Molech, male-male intercourse, and bestiality, among other prohibited practices. The chapter also portrays these practices as defiling and connects them not only with Israel but with the nations occupying the land before Israel.
But Christians should not simply grab Leviticus, ignore the covenantal storyline, and declare the interpretive work finished.
We must ask what happens after Christ comes.
Does the New Testament reaffirm sexual holiness?
Yes.
Does it continue to condemn porneia?
Repeatedly.
Does the apostolic church tell Gentile Christians to abstain from sexual immorality?
Yes.
Does Paul apply an Old Testament sexual boundary involving a man's father's wife directly to a Christian congregation?

Yes. In 1 Corinthians 5, Paul condemns a relationship involving “his father's wife,” showing that at least some sexual boundaries known from Torah remain morally relevant in apostolic Christian instruction.
Does the New Testament teach that keeping Mosaic Law earns salvation?
No.
That is the distinction we desperately need.
A Christian does not refuse sexual sin in order to purchase salvation.
A Christian pursues holiness because salvation has been purchased by Christ.
Those are completely different religions.
One says:
“Obey so God might accept you.”
The Gospel says:
“In Christ, you have been received by grace; now learn to live as someone who belongs to Him.”
One produces pride when you succeed and despair when you fail.
The other produces gratitude, repentance, dependence, and transformation.
And perhaps this is where the conversation stops being theological and becomes painfully personal.
Because maybe you did not click this article because you wanted a lesson about Greek verbs.
Maybe there is a name in your head right now.
A relationship.
A habit.
A night you cannot erase.
A secret.
Maybe you already crossed boundaries you once promised God you never would.
Maybe you have been sleeping beside someone while quietly wondering whether Jesus approves.
Maybe pornography has trained your mind to consume bodies while nobody in church knows.
Maybe your marriage has become sexually cold, and temptation suddenly feels less theoretical.
Maybe somebody used Scripture to shame you so brutally that whenever Christians speak about sexual holiness, you hear condemnation before you hear Jesus.
Maybe you are carrying sexual wounds that were inflicted upon you rather than chosen by you.
Hear this distinction carefully:
Being sinned against is not the same as committing the sin done against you.
Someone else's violation does not make you spiritually contaminated beyond Christ's reach.
And if you were abused, exploited, assaulted, manipulated, or coerced, the Gospel does not ask you to carry the perpetrator's guilt as though it belonged to you.
Jesus is not standing over wounded people saying,
“Disgusting.”
He is the Savior who touched people society would not touch.
The Savior who ate with sinners.
The Savior who confronted hypocrisy.
The Savior who spoke truth without needing cruelty.
The Savior who called people to repentance while opening His arms to repentant sinners.
This is where Christianity becomes scandalous.
Because Jesus neither tells us that sin does not matter nor tells sinners that they are beyond redemption.
He does something far more astonishing.
He takes sin seriously enough to die for it.
And loves sinners deeply enough to die for them.
That is Calvary.
Truth without grace becomes a hammer in human hands.
Grace without truth becomes permission to remain imprisoned.
But in Jesus Christ, grace and truth meet.
He does not save us by pretending darkness is light.
He enters our darkness and leads us out.
That means repentance is not God demanding that you destroy yourself.
Repentance is turning toward the One who came to rescue you.
And yes...
sometimes repentance hurts.
Sometimes following Jesus means surrendering something that feels woven into your identity.
Sometimes obedience means deleting a number.
Ending a relationship.
Confessing to your spouse.
Installing accountability.
Leaving the room.
Closing the browser.
Calling a pastor.
Seeking wise Christian counseling.
Admitting that what you called “freedom” has actually been mastering you.
Sometimes discipleship feels like death because Jesus really does call us to take up a cross.
But Christianity has never taught that every desire inside us automatically possesses moral authority simply because we experience it intensely.
Every disciple eventually discovers desires that must be surrendered.
Sexual desires.
Financial desires.
Desires for revenge.
Desires for status.
Desires for control.
Desires for applause.
Desires for comfort.
Desires to hate.
Desires to hide.
The question is not merely:
“What do I desire?”
The deeper Christian question is:
“Who is Lord of what I desire?”
And the answer cannot be Moses.
It cannot be your pastor.
It cannot be your denomination.
It cannot be your political tribe.
It cannot be social media.
It cannot even be your feelings.
For the Christian, the answer is Jesus Christ.
That does not make biblical interpretation easy.

Sincere Christians and Christian traditions have disagreed over precisely how Old Testament commands should be categorized and applied under the new covenant. The familiar categories of moral, ceremonial, and civil law can be useful theological tools, but the Bible itself does not present Leviticus with modern headings marking every command with those three labels.
So humility matters.
Context matters.
Biblical theology matters.
Jesus matters.
The apostles matter.
We should neither flatten the covenants into one nor cut the Old Testament away from Christian Scripture.
We follow the storyline all the way to Christ.
And when we do, something becomes difficult to escape:
The New Testament does not lower the significance of sexual holiness after Jesus.
It roots holiness more deeply in union with Jesus.
Paul's argument is not merely:
“Moses prohibited something.”
His argument becomes:
You belong to Christ.
Your body matters because Christ redeemed you.
Your sexual conduct matters because your body is for the Lord.
Your holiness matters because the Holy Spirit dwells in God's people.
Suddenly the question changes.
Not:
“Can Christians find a technical exemption?”
But:
“Does this glorify the Jesus who bought me with His blood?”
That question reaches places legalism never can.
Because legalism wants the minimum requirement.
Love asks how much of me belongs to Him.
And the Gospel answers:
All of you.
But perhaps you are thinking:
“You don't know what I've done.”
No.
But Jesus does.
“You don't know how many times I've fallen.”
Jesus does.
“You don't know what I watched.”
He knows.
“You don't know who I slept with.”
He knows.
“You don't know the lies.”
He knows.
“You don't know what happened to me.”
He knows that too.
And still the cross stands.
That is the scandal.
The holy Son of God knew exactly what humanity was—and came anyway.

He did not wait for prostitutes, adulterers, addicts, hypocrites, liars, religious frauds, sexually broken people, sexually wounded people, and self-righteous people to become clean enough to approach Him.
He came looking for sinners.
But He loves us too much to make peace with whatever is destroying us.
Grace says:
“Come as you are.”
Discipleship says:
“You cannot remain exactly as you were.”
The cross says both.
Come.
And die.
Come.
And live.
Come with your shame.
Come with your desires.
Come with your history.
Come with your questions.
Come with your confusion.
Come with the thing you are terrified to surrender.
But come to Jesus.
Not to a Jesus redesigned to agree with us.
To the crucified and risen Christ who loves us enough to forgive us and has authority enough to transform us.
Maybe you have spent years asking God to endorse your desires.
Perhaps tonight the prayer becomes:
“Jesus, teach my desires to bow to You.”
That prayer is dangerous.
Because He may touch something.
But He may also free something.
And perhaps what you thought would be the funeral of your happiness becomes the beginning of your freedom.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sexual history publicly.
If you need prayer, simply write:

And if Christ has already rescued you from sexual bondage, shame, pornography, adultery, destructive relationships, or years of secret compromise, consider sharing what God has done without exposing details that should remain private.
Someone reading the comments may believe they are the only person Jesus could never restore.
Your testimony may become the sentence that keeps them from running away.
Not because everybody needs another religious argument on Facebook.
Someone may be trapped between desire and discipleship.
Someone may believe sexual failure permanently disqualified them from Christ.
Someone may be searching for permission when what their soul actually needs is freedom.
Someone may need to discover that holiness and grace are not enemies.
It does not.
Not because paying Gospel Warrior saves you.
Only Jesus saves.

Christians and churches differ in how they understand tithing under the new covenant, and your responsibility to support your local church and other ministries should be approached prayerfully, faithfully, and according to conscience before God.
But voluntary financial partnership with Gospel ministry is thoroughly compatible with the New Testament pattern of believers generously supporting Gospel work.
If you want your resources to glorify God, prayerfully consider whether supporting this work should become part of your voluntary Christian giving.
Your support helps keep the work moving.
Your share helps this message cross a wall money cannot cross.
Your comment tells another struggling believer, “You are not fighting alone.”
And your prayers matter more than any algorithm ever will.
Pray.
Read.
Grow.
Send it privately to somebody who needs it.
Because ultimately this article was never merely about sex.
It was about lordship.
It was about what happens when Jesus reaches the one room of our lives where we desperately want the final word.
The question is not whether you have a scandal in your story.
Some scandals are public.
Others have passwords.
Some happened because of what we chose.
Others because of what someone did to us.
Some live in bedrooms.
Some live inside memories.
Some are hidden behind wedding photographs and Sunday smiles.
The question is what happens when the scandal meets Jesus.
Because at the cross, Christ does not merely expose sin.
He pays for sin.
He does not merely command repentance.
He makes restoration possible.
He does not merely tell the sexually broken to become clean.
He gives Himself to make sinners clean.
So bring Him the relationship.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the adultery.
Bring Him the fantasy.
Bring Him the confusion.
Bring Him the wounds.
Bring Him the loneliness.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the desires you understand.
Bring Him the desires you do not understand.
Bring Him the past you cannot rewrite.
Then watch what happens when the Author of resurrection takes the pen.
Your past may explain the scars—but it does not get to write the final sentence after Jesus takes hold of the story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Forgave Your Parents for What They Did. Now You Have to Grieve What They Never Gave You.
paragraphs: You Forgave Your Parents for What They Did. Now You Have to Grieve What They Never Gave You.

Some childhood wounds are not memories of what happened. They are memories of what never happened—and forgiving the people who failed you does not mean pretending you were never wounded by what was missing.
Maybe you already forgave them.
Maybe you prayed the prayer.
Maybe you stopped replaying the arguments.
Maybe you stopped demanding an apology you finally realized might never come.
Maybe you surrendered the anger to Jesus because carrying it was poisoning places inside you that your parents could no longer even see.
And perhaps you thought that was supposed to be the end of the story.
So why does something inside you still ache?
Why can a father hugging his grown daughter in an airport make your throat tighten?
Why can watching a mother speak gently to her child awaken something you cannot explain?
Why does hearing someone say, “My parents always believed in me,” sometimes make you genuinely happy for them...
and strangely sad for yourself?
You forgave what they did.
But perhaps nobody ever told you that you may still need to grieve what they never gave you.
The affection that never came.
The protection you needed but did not receive.
The words, “I’m proud of you.”
The apology.
The safety.
The consistency.
The bedtime conversations.
The father who should have shown up.
The mother who should have listened.
The home where you should not have needed to study everybody’s mood before deciding whether it was safe to speak.
The childhood where being a child should have been enough.
There are wounds caused by something terrible happening.
And there are wounds created by something beautiful never happening at all.
Sometimes the second kind is harder to explain because there is no single scene to point toward.
No photograph of absence.
No scar with a date written underneath it.
Only an empty chair inside the heart.
And sometimes that empty chair follows you into adulthood.
It follows you into friendships.
Into marriage.
Into parenting.
Into church.
Sometimes even into prayer.
You wonder why reassurance matters so much to you.
Why silence can feel like rejection.
Why conflict makes something inside you panic.
Why receiving affection feels wonderful and frightening at the same time.
Why you keep trying to prove that you are useful enough, spiritual enough, successful enough, generous enough, strong enough...
to deserve being kept.
And somewhere beneath the adult you became is still the child who learned a devastating question far too early:
“Am I worth staying for?”
Then Psalm 27:10 speaks.
Not with shallow optimism.
Not by pretending parents never fail.
Not by demanding that wounded people call abandonment love.
It says:
כִּי־אָבִי וְאִמִּי עֲזָבוּנִי וַיהוָה יַאַסְפֵנִי
Ki avi ve’immi azavuni, vaYHWH ya’asfeni.
The Hebrew expresses the thought: though father and mother forsake me, the LORD will gather or receive me.
That final word is breathtaking.
יַאַסְפֵנִי — ya’asfeni.

It comes from the Hebrew verb אָסַף — ’asaph, carrying the sense of gathering, collecting, receiving or taking in. In Psalm 27:10, the word has been understood with the beautiful implication of taking someone into care and protection.
Read that again.
The Scripture does not have to deny the abandonment in order to proclaim the faithfulness of God.
The verse contains both realities.
They may forsake me.
The LORD will gather me.
That matters.
Because biblical faith is not pretending the first half never happened so you can celebrate the second half.
David's poetry has room for both.
Human failure is named.
Divine faithfulness is named.
Loss is acknowledged.
God is trusted.
And perhaps that is where your healing has been stuck.
You thought forgiving meant you were no longer allowed to be sad.
It does not.
Forgiveness and grief are not enemies.
Forgiveness says, “I will not make vengeance my god.”
Grief says, “What was lost actually mattered.”
Forgiveness says, “I release judgment into God's hands.”
Grief says, “I wish this had been different.”
Forgiveness refuses to become consumed by the debt.
Grief acknowledges there really was a debt.
Paul tells believers not to avenge themselves but to leave vengeance to God. He does not tell them that evil must therefore be renamed good.
And when Paul describes forgiveness in Ephesians 4:32, the Greek says:
χαριζόμενοι ἑαυτοῖς καθὼς καὶ ὁ Θεὸς ἐν Χριστῷ ἐχαρίσατο ὑμῖν

Believers are called to forgive one another as God in Christ forgave them. The verb is related to grace—χαρίζομαι, charizomai—and Paul places Christian forgiveness squarely in the grace believers themselves have received in Christ.
But forgiveness does not require rewriting history.
Jesus never needed lies in order to produce grace.
And neither do you.
You can forgive your father and still admit that you needed him.
You can forgive your mother and still acknowledge that something important was missing.
You can love your parents and tell the truth about your childhood.
You can honor them without calling every decision they made honorable.
You can release vengeance without surrendering wisdom.
You can pray for someone and still recognize that trust, where it has been deeply damaged, is not identical to forgiveness.
You can stop demanding that yesterday change...
and still cry because it never will.
Some of you need permission to cry over something that happened thirty years ago.
Not because you want to live in the past.
Because you finally became safe enough to tell the truth about it.
You survived by minimizing.
“They did their best.”
“Other people had it worse.”
“At least I had food.”
“At least nobody hit me.”
“At least they stayed married.”
“At least they took me to church.”
Perhaps some of those things are true.
But gratitude for what you received does not require dishonesty about what you did not.
Two things can be true at once.
Your parents may have been wounded people themselves...
and they may have wounded you.
They may have loved you in the only ways they understood...
and those ways may still have been painfully insufficient.
They may have carried trauma they never learned to name...
and you may now be carrying consequences you never volunteered to inherit.
Understanding their story can produce compassion.
