paragraphs: THE BIBLE’S MESSAGE TO SEXUALLY BROKEN PEOPLE ISN’T “PRETEND IT NEVER HAPPENED”—IT IS REPENTANCE AND REDEMPTION

Jesus does not ask you to rename darkness as light, erase your history, or manufacture an innocent past. He does something infinitely greater: He meets you in the truth, calls sin what it is, washes the guilty, receives the repentant, binds the wounded, and gives ruined people a future their past no longer has the authority to write.
There are things people confess out loud.
And then there are things they take to the grave.
The browser history nobody knows about.
The affair that still wakes you up at 2:13 in the morning.
The pornography you promised God you would never watch again.
The relationship you knew crossed boundaries, but loneliness kept whispering, Just one more time.
The body you gave away because you were desperate to feel wanted.
The person you used because desire became stronger than love.
The secret messages.
The hidden fantasies.
The shame after the screen goes dark.
The memory of somebody touching you when you never gave permission.
The childhood wound you still cannot describe without feeling dirty, even though you were the one who was violated.
The marriage damaged by betrayal.
The years of sexual choices you wish you could somehow pull out of your history.
And perhaps the hardest part is Sunday morning.
Because you know how to smile.
You know when to stand.
You know when to sing.
You know how to say, “God is good.”
But somewhere underneath the worship song is a question you are terrified to ask:
If everybody knew the whole story, would they still believe I belonged here?
And beneath even that question is another one.
Does Jesus know everything?
Yes.
Everything.
And that is precisely why what comes next matters.
Because the Bible's message to sexually broken people is not, “Pretend it never happened.”
It is not, “Your choices don't matter.”
It is not, “Your body doesn't matter.”
It is not, “God understands, so keep doing whatever you want.”
But neither is it:
“You are disgusting.”
“You are permanently contaminated.”
“You went too far.”
“You can never become clean again.”
“You will always be what you did.”
The Gospel is far more devastating to sin than that...
and far more merciful to sinners.

Paul writes to a church in Corinth surrounded by sexual immorality and moral confusion, and he refuses to soften the truth. He warns them plainly about unrighteousness and names sexual immorality among the sins incompatible with inheriting the kingdom of God.
Then comes one of the most beautiful turns in the New Testament.
“And such were some of you.”
Not such are you.
Such were some of you.
Then three enormous words fall like thunder over human shame:
ἀπελούσασθε — apelousasthe — you were washed.
ἡγιάσθητε — hēgiasthēte — you were sanctified, made holy, set apart.
ἐδικαιώθητε — edikaiōthēte — you were justified, declared righteous.
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.”
—1 Corinthians 6:11
Do not rush past that.
Paul does not say they imagined their past away.
He does not say their sins were insignificant.
He does not tell them to pretend Corinth never happened.
He says something far more astonishing.
Christ happened.
There is a difference.
Christian redemption does not require historical amnesia.
You may remember what happened.
You may remember what you did.
You may remember who you became.
You may even carry consequences that forgiveness does not instantly erase.
But the Gospel declares that your past does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus Christ.
That is why Christianity can look directly at sexual sin without blinking.
We do not need to pretend sin is harmless in order to prove that God is loving.
The cross proves something much greater.
Sin was serious enough that Christ died.
Grace was powerful enough that He willingly did.
Somebody reading this has spent years trying to solve shame by changing vocabulary.
You called bondage “freedom.”
You called lust “just being human.”
You called adultery “finally finding happiness.”
You called pornography “stress relief.”
You called compromise “love.”
You called what God told you to leave “complicated.”
But changing the label never healed the wound.
Jesus does not redeem the imaginary person you pretend to be.
He redeems the sinner who finally comes into the light.
That is why biblical repentance is beautiful.
The New Testament repeatedly uses the language of μετάνοια — metanoia — repentance, a turning of mind and heart that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
It is not making yourself clean enough for Jesus.
You cannot.
It is not hating yourself until God believes you are sorry.
Self-hatred is not the Gospel.
Repentance is the sinner finally dropping the defense.
No more excuses.
No more hiding.
No more negotiating with what is destroying you.
No more demanding that God call holy what He calls sin.
You turn toward Christ.
You confess.
You surrender.
And you discover that the Savior standing before the repentant sinner is not holding a stone.
He is holding scars.
There is something else that must be said, because careless religious language has wounded people God never accused.
Not every sexually broken person is broken because of sexual sin they chose.
Some were sinned against.
If somebody abused you, assaulted you, exploited you, groomed you, coerced you, manipulated you, or violated you, their sin does not become your guilt.
You do not need to repent for being victimized.
You are not morally contaminated because another person committed evil against you.
What happened matters.
Justice matters.
Truth matters.
Healing matters.
And Jesus is not standing over the wounded asking why they were wounded.
Scripture shows Him drawing near to the crushed and brokenhearted.
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart.”
—Psalm 34:18

There may be wounds requiring patient healing. There may be trauma that needs wise pastoral care and qualified professional help. There may be crimes that need to be reported to appropriate authorities. Forgiveness does not mean calling evil good, abandoning justice, or placing yourself back within reach of an abuser.
Jesus is not glorified by protecting darkness.
He is glorified by truth.
And whether your story is primarily the story of sins you committed, sins committed against you, or a painfully tangled mixture of both, the invitation of Christ remains astonishing:
Come into the light.
Because shame says, Hide.
Jesus says, Come.
Shame says, If people knew, you would be finished.
Jesus says, I already know.
Shame says, This is who you are.
The Gospel says, Such were some of you.
Perhaps that sentence is why you were meant to read this today.
Such were some of you.
The Bible never says, “Such never happened to you.”
It says something better.
Your history may describe where you have been.
It does not get the final word on who you become in Christ.
David committed adultery and arranged the death of Uriah. When Nathan confronted him, David did not receive permission to rename his rebellion. He was brought to confession.
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
—2 Samuel 12:13
Psalm 51 gives us the cry of a man who understood that grace is not pretending.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.”
—Psalm 51:10
The Hebrew plea is breathtaking:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
David does not merely ask God to improve his public image.
He asks God for cleansing at the center of who he is.
That is repentance.
And that is why cheap grace cannot save anyone from bondage.
If the message were merely, “God forgives you, so don't worry about what you're doing,” there would be no rescue in it.
Imagine telling a drowning person:
“The water loves you exactly where you are.”
No.
Love reaches into the water.
Love pulls you toward life.
Grace does not merely comfort us inside slavery.
Grace breaks chains.
Jesus said:
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.”
—John 8:36
Free indeed.
Not free to polish the chains.
Not free to decorate the prison.
Not free to rename captivity.
Free.
Maybe you have prayed after falling into the same sexual sin so many times that even your own apology sounds fake to you.
“God, forgive me.”
Again.
Then again.
Then again.
And eventually the enemy begins preaching his own sermon:
Look at you.
You will never change.
You don't really love God.
Why bother coming back?
Listen carefully.
The fact that repeated sin is serious does not mean repeated return to Christ is pointless.
You do not defeat sin by running away from the only One who can save you from it.
Bring the sin into the light.
Confess it.
Cut off what feeds it.
Seek mature Christian accountability.
Stop arranging private access to the thing you publicly claim you want freedom from.
If an app keeps becoming a doorway, close the doorway.
If a conversation keeps becoming seduction, end the conversation.
If secrecy keeps feeding bondage, break secrecy with trustworthy, mature believers.
Jesus used radical language about removing occasions of sin because holiness is not a hobby.
But hear this carefully:
Your discipline does not purchase God's mercy.
Jesus purchased your redemption.
You fight from grace, not for the right to receive grace.
That difference changes everything.
Because at the center of Christianity is not a sexually flawless person congratulating himself for being better than everybody else.
At the center is a crucified Messiah.
Jesus Christ.
The sinless One.
The Lamb of God.
The One who bore sin He never committed so sinners could receive righteousness they could never earn.
At the cross, God does not pretend sin never happened.
He judges sin.
At the cross, God does not pretend sinners are innocent because their behavior does not matter.
Christ bears judgment.
At the cross, mercy does not defeat justice by ignoring it.
Mercy comes through the sacrifice of Jesus.
And at the empty tomb, we discover that scandal does not have to be the final chapter.
Death itself does not get the final chapter.
This is why there is no Christian redemption without Jesus Christ.
Therapy may help you understand patterns.
Accountability may help you break secrecy.
Boundaries may protect you.
Wise counseling may help heal wounds.
Community may carry you when you are weak.
These can be profound gifts of God's common and providential grace.
But none of them can become your Savior.
Only Jesus reconciles sinners to God.
Only Christ bore our sins.
Only Christ rose from the dead.
Only Christ can say to the guilty who trust Him that condemnation no longer owns their future.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
—Romans 8:1
No condemnation does not mean no conviction.
Conviction says, This must change. Come back to God.
Condemnation says, You can never come back.
Learn the difference.
One leads you toward the Father.
The other makes you hide from Him.
Somebody needs to stop confusing shame with holiness.
Feeling filthy forever is not evidence that you have adequately respected the seriousness of your sin.
If Christ has forgiven you, insisting that your guilt is stronger than His cross is not humility.
Bring your sin to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive His mercy.
Then get up and walk with Him.
Perhaps slowly.
Perhaps with tears.
Perhaps with accountability.

Perhaps with trembling hands deleting numbers, ending relationships, installing safeguards, confessing secrets, seeking counseling, rebuilding a marriage, learning healthy intimacy, grieving what happened to you, or finally telling somebody trustworthy what you have carried alone for years.
But walk.
One obedient step after another.
Because sanctification often looks less like one cinematic moment and more like a thousand quiet decisions to keep saying yes to Jesus.
And if you fall?
Do not make peace with the ground.
Get up.
Run toward Christ.
Confess honestly.
Learn what opened the door.
Strengthen the boundary.
Receive help.
Keep walking.
The goal is not to become somebody who can brag, “I fixed myself.”
The goal is to become somebody whose life says:
“Look what Jesus Christ can redeem.”
That is why the words “such were some of you” should shake the Church.
There should be people sitting in our congregations whose former lives would scandalize us if we knew every detail.
Former adulterers.
Former porn addicts.
Former prostitutes.
Former exploiters.
Formerly promiscuous men and women.
People whose histories are complicated.
People whose scars remain.
People whose families were shattered.
People who once believed they were beyond saving.
And now?
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Not because the Church lowered God's standard.
Because Jesus paid the sinner's debt.
Not because sin became less sinful.
Because grace proved greater than their rebellion.
This is the kind of Church sexually broken people need.
Not a Church afraid to call sin sin.
And not a Church addicted to making sinners feel permanently unclean.
Truth without grace crushes.
Grace without truth deceives.
Jesus Christ brings truth and grace together.
Maybe this article is not primarily about “those people.”
Maybe it is about you.
The secret you have protected while reading every paragraph.
The memory that made your stomach tighten.
The name that came into your mind.
The habit you immediately tried to justify.
The wound you still blame yourself for.
The confession you know you need to make.
The surrender you have postponed.
You do not have to tell the internet every detail of your story.
Wisdom matters.
Privacy matters.
But you do need to stop lying to God.
And perhaps tonight the most spiritual thing you can do is close the door, put the phone down, kneel somewhere nobody can applaud you, and finally tell Jesus the truth.
“Lord, this is what happened.”
“Lord, this is what I did.”
“Lord, this is what was done to me.”
“Lord, this is what I keep returning to.”
“Lord, I cannot free myself.”
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
There is no magic in the wording.
The power is not in an emotional formula.
The power is in Christ.
Turn to Him.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details.
And if Christ has already begun rewriting a chapter you once thought could never be redeemed, tell somebody below:
“Christ is still healing me.”
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needed to survive tonight.
And if you know somebody quietly drowning beneath sexual shame, send this to them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose them.
Send it privately if wisdom requires it.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has wandered.
Invite the believer growing cold.
Invite the person who does not yet believe.
Because the Gospel was never meant to remain trapped inside people who have already heard it.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
God does not owe us blessings because we clicked a button.
Christian giving is worship when it flows freely from a heart that belongs to Christ: “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Jesus is.
The Gospel is.
People are.
Souls matter more than sales.
If God has blessed you through this ministry, prayerfully consider helping us keep going.
Send it personally to the person whose name will not leave your heart.
Comment so another struggling believer sees they are not the only person fighting.
Follow because none of us outgrow our need for Scripture.
And above everything else...
follow Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot wash you.
A comment cannot justify you.
A book cannot redeem you.
A ministry cannot save you.
Jesus Christ can.
Maybe your story really is scandalous.
Maybe some of it was your fault.
Maybe some of it absolutely was not.
Maybe you carry both repentance and wounds.
Maybe you have consequences you cannot reverse.
Maybe people still remember who you used to be.
Maybe you remember too.
But if you belong to Christ, there are three words the enemy desperately hopes you never learn to say with confidence:
“Such. Were. Some.”
Were.
There is an entire Gospel hiding inside that tense.
You were not saved because the scandal never happened.
You were saved because Jesus entered the story.
And when Jesus enters a surrendered story, He does not need to erase yesterday to prove that yesterday no longer owns tomorrow.
Your darkest chapter may remain part of your testimony—but it does not get to hold the pen when Jesus Christ has taken hold of your life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: POLYGAMY IS EVERYWHERE IN PARTS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT—BUT DOES RECORDING IT MEAN GOD APPROVED IT?
paragraphs: POLYGAMY IS EVERYWHERE IN PARTS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT—BUT DOES RECORDING IT MEAN GOD APPROVED IT?

Abraham had more than one woman. Jacob had two wives and two concubines. David had multiple wives. Solomon had hundreds. So why would Christians claim that God’s design for marriage is one man and one woman? The answer is hiding in a distinction we often forget when reading the Bible: Scripture can tell you what happened without telling you to imitate it.
There is a question that can make Christians uncomfortable if they have never seriously wrestled with it.
If God intended marriage to be between one man and one woman…
why is there so much polygamy in the Old Testament?
Not merely among pagan kings.
Among men whose names are woven into the history of God’s people.
Abraham.
Jacob.
David.
Solomon.
Men used by God.
Men remembered in Scripture.
Men standing inside the unfolding story that eventually leads to Jesus Christ.
So someone opens the Bible, sees all of this, and asks a question that sounds devastating:
“If God disapproved of polygamy, why did He allow His servants to practice it?”
That question deserves something better than panic.
It deserves an open Bible.
Because one of the most dangerous mistakes we can make when reading Scripture is assuming that everything the Bible describes is something the Bible prescribes.
The Bible records murder.
That does not make murder holy.
The Bible records adultery.
That does not make adultery righteous.
The Bible records deception, incest, drunkenness, idolatry, betrayal, cowardice, sexual immorality, family dysfunction, political corruption, and even the crucifixion of the sinless Son of God.
Recording an event is not the same thing as endorsing it.
Sometimes Scripture shows us human beings exactly as they were because God refuses to build His story upon sanitized biographies.
And that is where this subject becomes much bigger than polygamy.
Because perhaps the scandal you noticed in Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon is supposed to make you confront something uncomfortable about yourself:
God has always accomplished His purposes through deeply imperfect people without calling their imperfections good.
That distinction changes everything.
Go back before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before Israel.
Before kings.
Before humanity had accumulated centuries of broken customs and complicated households.
Go back to the beginning.
Genesis gives us the pattern.
A man.
A woman.
A covenant union.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew contains the words:
וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ … וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
ve-davaq be-ishto … ve-hayu le-basar echad
He is joined, clings, holds fast to his wife…
and they become one flesh.
Basar echad.
One flesh.
Notice something crucial.
When Jesus was challenged centuries later concerning marriage and divorce, He did not point His listeners toward Solomon’s palace.
He did not say, “Look at what David practiced.”
He did not build His doctrine of marriage upon Jacob’s household.
Jesus went further back.
Back beyond Israel’s kings.
Back beyond patriarchal customs.
Back to creation.
Christ said:
“Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female?”
Then Jesus quoted Genesis:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.”
And then He said:
“So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Matthew 19:4–6.
The Greek expression preserved in Matthew is striking:
οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
hoi dyo eis sarka mian
“The two into one flesh.”
The two.
Jesus does something enormously important here.
When fallen human practice had complicated marriage, Christ interpreted marriage by returning His hearers to God’s creational intention.
Not merely, “What have human beings done?”
But:
“What was it from the beginning?”
That distinction matters.
Because if you determine morality simply by finding someone in Scripture who did something, you can make the Bible justify almost anything.
David committed adultery.
No Christian concludes adultery is therefore righteous.
Noah became drunk.
No Christian concludes drunkenness is therefore God’s ideal.
Peter denied Jesus.
No Christian concludes denying Christ is acceptable discipleship.
Abraham lied about Sarah.
No Christian concludes deception becomes holy because Abraham practiced it.
The existence of sinful or disordered behavior among God’s people does not transform that behavior into God’s design.
And Scripture does not hide the devastation surrounding plural marriages.
Look closely.
Abraham and Sarah received a promise from God, but the waiting became unbearable.
Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham.
A child was conceived.
And almost immediately the household began bleeding.
Genesis tells us that when Hagar conceived, relational contempt entered the picture. Sarah became bitter. Hagar suffered. Eventually a mother and child were sent away into the wilderness.
God saw Hagar.
God heard Ishmael.
God showed compassion to people caught inside the wreckage.
But divine compassion toward wounded people should never be confused with divine endorsement of every human decision that helped produce the wound.
Then comes Jacob.
Jacob loved Rachel.
But through Laban’s deception he received Leah first, then Rachel, and the household expanded further through Bilhah and Zilpah.
Read the story slowly.
It does not read like a romantic advertisement for plural marriage.
It reads like heartbreak.
Leah knows she is unloved.
Rachel knows she is barren.
Sisters become rivals.
Children become entangled in the emotional competition of adults.
Even the naming of children becomes intertwined with longing, pain, rivalry, and the desperate hope of finally being loved.
Imagine Leah.
Sharing a husband with the sister he actually wanted.
Giving birth and wondering whether perhaps this child would finally make her husband love her.
That is not an abstract theological debate.
That is a human heart breaking inside somebody’s home.
The Bible lets you hear it.
And perhaps that is intentional.
Sometimes God does not merely give us a prohibition.
Sometimes Scripture lets us walk through the wreckage.
Then David becomes king.
David accumulates wives.
But his household does not become an advertisement for multiplying them.
His family becomes a tragedy.
Sexual sin.
Violation.
Hatred.
Murder.
Rebellion.
A son turning against his father.
A kingdom shaken.
And then Solomon.
If anyone wants to argue that the Old Testament simply celebrates kings collecting wives, Solomon becomes a devastating problem for that argument.
Long before Solomon’s excesses, Deuteronomy 17:17 instructed Israel’s king that he must not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.
Those words become almost prophetic when you reach Solomon.
The man famous for wisdom ignored a warning already sitting in the Law.
First Kings says Solomon had seven hundred wives of royal birth and three hundred concubines.
And what happened?
Exactly what Deuteronomy warned could happen.
“His wives turned his heart away.”
Do not rush past that.
A thousand women did not give Solomon a thousand times more fulfillment.
His multiplied relationships became part of the story of his divided heart.
The man who possessed extraordinary wisdom still discovered that knowing truth is not the same thing as surrendering to truth.
And suddenly Solomon does not feel so ancient anymore.
Because we do this too.
Maybe not with seven hundred wives.
But we know what God says…
and still convince ourselves that our exception will somehow end differently.
We rename compromise.
We negotiate with conviction.
We search for loopholes.
We point toward somebody else who did something similar and survived.
We whisper:
“God understands.”
And yes…
God understands far more than we realize.
But His understanding is not permission to call darkness light.
This is why another distinction matters.
God sometimes regulates realities within a fallen society without presenting those realities as His original ideal.

Biblical laws addressing complicated family situations should therefore be read carefully. A law protecting people within an existing broken social reality does not automatically mean God is declaring every feature of that reality morally ideal.
God cared about people living inside imperfect systems.
Women mattered.
Children mattered.
Inheritance mattered.
Justice mattered.
The vulnerable could not simply become disposable because powerful men made complicated decisions.
Regulation can restrain evil and protect people without turning every regulated circumstance into the creation ideal.
We see a related principle when Jesus discusses divorce.
When asked why Moses permitted certificates of divorce, Jesus answered that Moses allowed it because of the hardness of human hearts.
Then came the words that should echo through this entire discussion:
“But from the beginning it was not so.”
Matthew 19:8.
There it is.
The difference between what God tolerated within fallen human conditions and what God established in creation.
From the beginning.
That is where Jesus takes us.

And Scripture continues developing marriage as covenant faithfulness. Malachi speaks of “the wife of your youth,” describing her as a companion and a wife by covenant, while condemning marital faithlessness.
Then the New Testament takes marriage somewhere even deeper.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5 that marriage mysteriously points beyond itself.
Beyond husband.
Beyond wife.
Beyond romance.
Beyond sexuality.
Beyond companionship.
Toward Christ and His Church.
Jesus Christ is the Bridegroom.
His people are His bride.
Marriage becomes a living signpost toward covenant love.
Christ does not casually discard His bride.
He gives Himself for her.
He loves.
He sanctifies.
He cleanses.
He remains faithful.
He goes to a cross.
And suddenly the deepest Christian answer to the question of marriage is not merely a rule.
It is a Person.
Jesus.
This is why Christianity cannot build its theology of marriage simply by counting how many wives various Old Testament men possessed.
We must read the entire biblical story.
Creation.
Fall.
Human brokenness.
Covenant.
Law.
Prophets.
Christ.
Cross.
Resurrection.
Church.
New creation.
The Bible is not a collection of disconnected episodes where every character’s behavior carries equal moral authority.
It is the unfolding story of God redeeming sinners and ultimately revealing His saving purposes in Jesus Christ.
And that brings us somewhere unexpectedly personal.
Because perhaps you clicked this expecting an argument about polygamy.
But Scripture has quietly moved the mirror.
You may never have had multiple spouses.
But you have your own chapters you hope nobody reads aloud.
So do I.
The scandal may have a different name.
Pornography.
Adultery.
Pride.
Bitterness.
Secret messages.
A double life.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
An addiction hidden behind a respectable profile picture.
Jealousy.
Lust.
Manipulation.
A marriage quietly dying while everyone online thinks you are happy.
A church face covering a starving soul.
You know what it is.
And perhaps you have made the same mistake people sometimes make when reading these Old Testament stories.
You have confused God’s patience with God’s approval.
You are still breathing.
Therefore you assume everything must be fine.
Nothing collapsed today.
Therefore perhaps God does not care.
You prayed and still received mercy.
Therefore perhaps repentance can wait.
But mercy was never given so we could become comfortable in chains.
Romans asks the piercing question:
Should we continue in sin so grace may increase?
Paul’s answer is emphatic:
By no means.
Grace does not rename your chains.
Grace breaks them.
And this is where the scandals of Scripture become strangely beautiful.
Abraham was flawed.
Jacob was complicated.
David sinned catastrophically.
Solomon compromised despite astonishing wisdom.
Yet human failure could not stop God’s redemptive purpose.
That does not make their sins righteous.
It makes God’s grace astonishing.
Eventually the story reaches Jesus.
Not another compromised patriarch.
Not another king with a divided heart.
Not another sinner requiring forgiveness.
The spotless Lamb.
The faithful Son.
The true King.
Jesus does what every other human being in the story fails to do perfectly.
He obeys.
He remains faithful.
He bears sin.
He goes willingly to the cross.
And there, the Gospel confronts every one of us.
God does not save you by pretending your scandal was never sinful.
He saves you by dealing with sin through Christ.
Jesus did not bleed so that we could learn better ways to excuse ourselves.
He died to reconcile sinners to God.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the invitation to stop running from the One who already knows the truth.
The cross says your sin is serious enough that Christ had to die.
The resurrection says His grace is powerful enough that your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
That is the Gospel.
Maybe your past is ugly.
Maybe your marriage has wounds nobody sees.
Maybe sexual sin has followed you for years.
Maybe you crossed lines you swore you never would.
Maybe you have been betrayed.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Maybe you have wondered whether someone with your history can still become useful to God.
Look at the Bible.
Not superficially.
Look closely.
God never needed spotless human biographies to accomplish His purposes.
He had one spotless Man.
Jesus Christ.
And everyone else comes needing grace.
The message is not:
“Abraham failed, so failure does not matter.”
The message is:
“Abraham failed, David failed, Solomon failed, we fail—and we desperately need a Savior.”
Jesus does not merely edit the public version of your story.
He redeems sinners.
He forgives the repentant.
He restores the broken.
He transforms hearts.
And He calls forgiven people not merely to feel relieved…
but to follow Him.
So perhaps the real question after studying polygamy in the Old Testament is no longer:
“Why did God allow them to do that?”
Perhaps the harder question is:
What have I been asking God to tolerate in me that Jesus is calling me to surrender?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit with it.
Because sometimes we become fascinated with somebody else’s scandal precisely because it keeps us from confronting our own.
Be honest.

And if Jesus has already brought you out of a chapter you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needs tonight.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because someone in your circle may be quietly wrestling with this exact question.
Someone may be using the failures of biblical characters as a reason to reject Scripture.
Someone may be using grace as permission to remain in sin.
Someone may believe their sexual or relational past has disqualified them permanently from Christ.
Let this reach them.
There are truths you understand differently when life finally makes them personal.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you understand Scripture, confront compromise, heal through biblical truth, and grow deeper in Jesus Christ, stay close to this ministry.
There is room here for difficult questions.
But every road must ultimately lead us back to Christ.
Not because Gospel Warrior can replace your local church, your responsibilities to your family, or Spirit-led generosity elsewhere.
We do not.
Give because you have decided before God that this ministry is worth supporting.

Scripture teaches generosity freely given rather than extracted by pressure. Paul wrote that each person should give what he has decided in his heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That is the spirit in which we ask.
Pray.
Read.
Grow.
Encourage someone.
Because the goal was never merely to win an argument about polygamy.
The goal is to read Scripture faithfully enough that eventually Scripture begins reading us.
Abraham’s household cannot save you.
Jacob’s story cannot save you.
David cannot save you.
Solomon’s wisdom cannot save you.
Your morality cannot save you.
Your religious reputation cannot save you.
There is one Savior.
Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is why God allowed the Bible to preserve so many uncomfortable stories.
If Scripture contained only flawless heroes, sinners like us might eventually imagine salvation belonged to flawless people.
Instead, page after page whispers the truth.
Human beings fall.
Human beings complicate what God made good.
Human beings wander.
Human beings hide.
Human beings rationalize.
Human beings desperately need redemption.
And then Jesus enters the story.
The faithful One among the faithless.
The sinless One among sinners.
The Bridegroom who does not abandon His bride.
The King whose heart never turns away from His Father.
The Savior who walks straight toward a cross carrying scandals that were never His.
Including yours.
Including mine.
So no—recording polygamy does not automatically mean God approved of it.
Sometimes the broken households of Scripture are not loopholes inviting us to lower God's design.
Sometimes they are warning lights showing us what happens when fallen humanity wanders from it.
And sometimes the darkest pages exist so that when grace finally appears in all its fullness, we understand just how desperately we needed it.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your life—but once surrendered to Jesus Christ, it does not have the authority to write your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN CHRISTIANS ENJOY ORAL SEX?
paragraphs: CAN CHRISTIANS ENJOY ORAL SEX?
What the Bible Does—and Does NOT—Explicitly Say About Specific Marital Acts
There are questions Christians whisper that almost nobody wants to answer from the pulpit.
This is one of them.
A husband wonders whether something he desires with his wife is sinful.
A wife wonders whether enjoying something intimate makes her dirty.
A newly married couple loves Jesus, wants to honor Scripture, and suddenly discovers that nobody ever taught them how to distinguish biblical holiness from inherited embarrassment.
So they search quietly.
They delete the browser history.
They ask anonymously.
Sometimes they carry guilt for years over something God never actually called sin.
And sometimes, on the opposite extreme, people use the phrase “the Bible doesn't forbid it” as permission to ignore love, conscience, dignity, holiness, or the wishes of their spouse.
Both errors matter.
Because when Christians ask, “Can a married Christian couple engage in oral sex?” the most faithful answer is neither a nervous yes nor a thunderous no.
The first answer must be:
What has God actually said?
That question changes everything.
And before we go any further, understand what this article is not.
This is not an attempt to drag something sacred into vulgarity.
It is an attempt to rescue something sacred from both vulgarity and unnecessary shame.
Because sex did not originate in pornography.
Pornography corrupted something it did not create.
Sex did not originate in Hollywood.
Sex did not originate in hookup culture.
Sex did not originate in human rebellion.
Before there was sexual exploitation, there was Eden.
Before lust commodified bodies, God created bodies.
Before humanity learned to hide in shame, Scripture says of the first husband and wife:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
Genesis 2:25.
That sentence appears before the Fall.
Let that settle into your heart.
Nakedness between husband and wife was not introduced as something filthy.
Shame entered later.
Sin entered later.
Distortion entered later.
God was there first.

That does not mean every imaginable sexual behavior automatically becomes righteous simply because two married people perform it. Scripture still governs Christian sexuality through holiness, faithfulness, love, self-control, conscience, and the command never to exploit another person.
But it does mean Christians must be careful not to call something sinful merely because discussing it makes us uncomfortable.
God alone has the authority to define sin.
And this is where the question becomes surprisingly important.
Search the Bible from Genesis to Revelation and you will not find a verse saying, “A husband and wife shall not engage in oral sex.”
You will not find one saying, “A husband and wife must engage in oral sex,” either.
Scripture simply does not explicitly name the practice.
That fact matters.
It means we should resist two opposite temptations: inventing a divine prohibition Scripture never states, and inventing a divine endorsement Scripture never specifically gives.
The Christian question therefore becomes deeper than:
“Where is the verse about this particular act?”
The question becomes:
What biblical principles govern sexual intimacy inside marriage?
And suddenly the Bible has quite a lot to say.
Consider the Song of Songs.
Some Christians have almost treated this book as though God accidentally left a romantic poem in the middle of the Bible.
He did not.
Its Hebrew poetry is unashamedly affectionate.
The woman opens with longing:
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu.
“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.”
Song of Songs 1:2.
Notice something beautiful.
She speaks.
She desires.
She expresses affection.

Biblical marital love is not portrayed as a cold transaction in which the woman silently tolerates the husband's desires. The Song gives the woman a voice, longing, delight, initiative, and emotional presence.
Later the husband says:
נֹפֶת תִּטֹּפְנָה שִׂפְתוֹתַיִךְ כַּלָּה דְּבַשׁ וְחָלָב תַּחַת לְשׁוֹנֵךְ
Nofet tittopnah siftotayikh kallah; devash vechalav tachat leshonekh.
“Your lips drip sweetness, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue.”
Song of Songs 4:11.
The language is sensual.
It speaks of lips.
Kisses.
Taste.
Fragrance.
Bodies.
Desire.
Delight.
Elsewhere the lovers praise one another physically with imagery that would make many modern churches uncomfortable reading aloud.
But here is where responsible interpretation matters enormously.
Those passages demonstrate that Scripture is capable of speaking positively and poetically about sensual marital desire.
They do not, by themselves, prove that Song of Songs 2:3 or 4:11 is a technical description of oral sex.
That claim goes further than the text allows.

Yes, interpreters have sometimes seen suggestive sexual imagery in the Song. Yes, the book contains unmistakably erotic poetry. But responsible Bible interpretation requires us to distinguish between what a passage clearly says and what someone believes its imagery might imply.
We do not need to exaggerate Scripture to defend the goodness of marital intimacy.
The Bible is already beautiful enough.
So if Song of Songs does not explicitly settle the question, where do we go?
To the broader biblical theology of marriage.
Hebrews 13:4 declares:
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.”
The Greek word translated “bed” is κοίτη — koitē, a word that can refer to the marriage bed and, by extension in various contexts, sexual relations.
Notice the contrast.
Marriage is honored.
The marriage bed is to remain undefiled.
Sexual immorality and adultery stand under judgment.
The biblical vision is therefore neither “sex is dirty” nor “anything sexual is acceptable.”
It is something far more beautiful.
Sexual intimacy belongs within a covenant of faithfulness.
Not exploitation.
Not adultery.
Not pornography.
Not bringing outsiders into the marriage covenant.
Not using another person's body as an object.
Not coercion disguised as marital authority.
Not selfish gratification while the other person's soul quietly disappears.
Marriage does not transform selfishness into holiness.
A wedding ring does not sanctify cruelty.
And perhaps nowhere is this clearer than Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 7.
The Greek of verse 4 is startling:
ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ὁ ἀνήρ· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ἡ γυνή.
Paul says that the wife does not exercise authority over her body independently of her husband—and then immediately gives the husband the same reciprocal statement concerning his wife.
That second half destroys any attempt to turn this passage into male sexual entitlement.
ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ — homoiōs de kai.
“Likewise also.”
Mutuality.
Reciprocity.
Neither spouse is presented as a sexual consumer while the other becomes merchandise.
And Paul continues by warning married couples against depriving one another, while allowing abstinence by mutual agreement for a spiritual purpose.
That means Christian marital intimacy cannot faithfully be built upon coercion.

If your spouse is frightened, humiliated, physically hurting, traumatized, morally distressed, or pleading with you to stop, “But we're married” is not a biblical justification for forcing your desire upon them.
Love does not behave that way.
The Christ-centered pattern of marriage moves toward sacrificial love.
Jesus does not teach husbands to dominate their wives for personal gratification. Ephesians 5 calls a husband toward a terrifyingly high standard:
Love your wife “as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
Christlike love asks:
“How can I give?”
Lust asks:
“What can I take?”
Those two questions can sometimes occur in the same bedroom while looking outwardly similar.
That is why the deepest Christian question about sexual intimacy is not merely:
“Is this technically allowed?”
It is:
“Can we do this together in faithfulness, mutual desire, tenderness, gratitude, holiness, and love before Jesus Christ?”
Now we can finally return to the question people came here asking.
Can a Christian husband and wife enjoy oral sex?
Scripture does not explicitly prohibit oral sex between husband and wife.
Scripture also does not explicitly command or specifically endorse that particular sexual act by name.
Therefore Christians should be very cautious about declaring categorically, “God says oral sex is sinful,” because no biblical text actually says that.
But Christians should be equally cautious about saying, “We're married, therefore anything goes.”
Anything does not go.
Adultery remains sin.
Sexual immorality remains sin.
Pornography does not become holy because a married couple watches it together.
Inviting another person into the sexual union does not become covenant faithfulness because both spouses consent.
Degradation does not magically become Christlike love because it occurs behind a locked bedroom door.
Coercion does not become marital intimacy.
Violence does not become affection.
And deliberately violating your spouse's conscience is not an expression of sacrificial love.
There is another principle Christians sometimes forget.
Romans 14 teaches believers not to violate conscience in morally disputable matters. Although Paul is not discussing sexual practices there, the principle concerning conscience remains important.
That means a spouse should never weaponize an article like this.
Please hear that.
Do not send this article to your husband or wife and say:
“See? You have to do this now.”
No.
That would completely miss the point.
Biblical freedom is not ammunition for pressuring someone you promised to love.
If one spouse desires a particular form of intimacy and the other is deeply uncomfortable, love should create conversation, patience, safety, understanding, and time.
There may be history underneath that discomfort.
There may be trauma.
There may be fear.
There may be physical concerns.
There may simply be a preference.
A Christian spouse is not a sexual vending machine into which marriage vows are inserted so desires can be dispensed on demand.
You married a person.
An image-bearer.
A soul.
Someone Jesus commands you to love.
And perhaps that is where some marriages desperately need healing.
Maybe the real problem was never oral sex.
Maybe the real problem was that nobody taught you how to talk honestly about sex without shame.
Maybe you grew up hearing that sexual desire was filthy, and then expected a wedding ceremony to switch twenty years of shame off overnight.
Maybe your husband has interpreted rejection as proof that he is undesirable.
Maybe your wife has spent years wondering whether you love her or simply what her body can provide.
Maybe pornography quietly trained your expectations before marriage and now reality feels disappointing because a screen discipled your sexuality more than Scripture did.
Maybe something happened to you that you have never told your spouse.
Maybe you learned to smile while uncomfortable because saying no never felt safe.
Maybe you are reading this beside someone you love while carrying a secret ache neither of you knows how to name.
And suddenly this article isn't really about one sexual act anymore.
It is about whether Jesus is Lord of the bedroom too.
Not merely Lord of Sunday morning.
Not merely Lord of worship music.
Not merely Lord of Bible study.
Lord of your eyes.
Lord of your imagination.
Lord of your desires.
Lord of your body.
Lord of your marriage.
Lord of the places nobody else sees.
That is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because some people reading this do not merely carry questions.
They carry history.
Pornography.
Promiscuity.
Adultery.
Sexual selfishness.
Secret fantasies.
Abuse.
Shame.
Things done to you.
Things done by you.
Memories you wish could be erased.
And Christianity does not answer that brokenness by pretending sin doesn't matter.
The cross says sin mattered enough for Christ to die.
But the empty tomb says your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to make sexually broken people behave better.
He came to redeem sinners.
To forgive.
To cleanse.
To restore.
To make new.
Paul writes to believers in Corinth after listing serious forms of unrighteousness and says something astonishing:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because their past never happened.
Not because sin became acceptable.
Because Jesus rewrote their identity.
“But ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus.”
That is Christianity.
Not pretending there was never a scandal.
Grace walking straight into the scandal and declaring that the blood of Jesus is stronger.
Maybe your sexual history is messy.
Bring it to Christ.
Maybe your marriage has wounds.
Bring them to Christ.
Maybe pornography has poisoned intimacy.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Seek help.
Install boundaries.
Stop feeding what is destroying you.
Maybe you have pressured your spouse sexually.
Repent.
Not with excuses.
Not with “But I have needs.”
Repent.
Ask forgiveness.
Become safe again.
Maybe you have lived with unnecessary shame over enjoying your spouse.
You may need to learn that marital desire itself is not something from which Jesus needs to rescue you.
God created covenant intimacy.
Sin corrupts God's gifts.
Grace teaches us how to receive them rightly.
And maybe the sentence someone desperately needs tonight is this:
Holiness is not the absence of desire. Holiness is desire surrendered to Jesus.
So when husband and wife consider any intimate practice Scripture does not specifically name, perhaps they should ask better questions.
Does this remain exclusively between us?
Are we both genuinely willing?
Does either spouse feel pressured?
Does this violate either person's conscience?
Is anyone being physically or emotionally harmed?
Is pornography, fantasy about outsiders, humiliation, or another person being brought into our union?
Can we thank God afterward without hiding from Him?
Does this deepen tenderness or quietly cultivate selfishness?
Are we loving each other—or merely using each other?
Those questions expose far more than a checklist ever could.
Because Christian sexuality was never supposed to be governed merely by finding the outer boundary of what we can get away with.
Christ calls us higher.
Love.
Faithfulness.
Self-control.
Tenderness.
Honor.
Truth.
Mutual care.
A clean conscience.
A marriage where neither person needs to be afraid.
So, can married Christians engage in oral sex?
The most biblically responsible conclusion is this:

The Bible does not explicitly identify oral sex between husband and wife as sinful, nor does it explicitly command or specifically describe it as a required marital practice. Where Scripture has not issued a specific prohibition, Christians should not manufacture one and bind another believer's conscience as though God Himself spoke it. At the same time, every expression of marital sexuality remains accountable to Scripture's commands concerning fidelity, holiness, mutuality, sacrificial love, conscience, and freedom from coercion or exploitation.
That answer may frustrate people who wanted a one-word verdict.
But sometimes biblical faithfulness means refusing to put words into God's mouth.
And maybe that is the greater lesson hiding underneath this uncomfortable question.
We have to stop confusing embarrassment with holiness.
We also have to stop confusing freedom with selfishness.
The marriage bed is neither a dirty place from which God runs nor a lawless place where Christ's lordship disappears.
It belongs to Him too.
And when grace enters that room, shame does not have to control the conversation anymore.
Neither does lust.
Jesus does.
If this exposed shame you have carried silently, you do not have to describe your private life publicly. But you can simply comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
If God is calling you to repentance, you can write, “Jesus, forgive me.”
And if you are married and realizing that your spouse needs tenderness more than demands, perhaps your comment can simply be:
Someone else reading those words may realize they are not the only believer fighting for healing.
And if Gospel Warrior's Scripture-centered work has been feeding your faith, you can help us continue creating and expanding it.
And never because anyone should be manipulated into giving.
Paul wrote:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ… μὴ… ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Let each person give as determined in the heart—not ἐξ ἀνάγκης, “under compulsion.”
That matters to us.
Come to Jesus.
Not polished.
Not pretending.
Not hiding behind religious language.
Come with the questions.
Come with the marriage wounds.
Come with the shame.
Come with the secret history.
Come with the desires that need surrender.
Come with the sins that need repentance.
Come with the places that still hurt when nobody is watching.
The Savior who met sinners at wells, tables, roadsides, graves, and crosses is not intimidated by the room in your heart you are afraid to unlock.
He already knows what is behind the door.
And He is still calling your name.
Because the most intimate question was never merely what a husband and wife may do with their bodies.
The deeper question has always been:
Will every part of us belong to Christ?
Your marriage.
Your sexuality.
Your memories.
Your wounds.
Your desires.
Your future.
Your whole life.
Bring all of it into the light.
Because grace does not merely cover the chapter you wish you could tear out.
Jesus can take the page you thought ruined the whole story—and make it the place where redemption becomes impossible to forget.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BAD COMPANY CORRUPTS GOOD CHARACTER” — THE VERSE WAS NEVER JUST ABOUT CHOOSING BETTER FRIENDS
paragraphs: “BAD COMPANY CORRUPTS GOOD CHARACTER” — THE VERSE WAS NEVER JUST ABOUT CHOOSING BETTER FRIENDS
What if the most dangerous “company” in your life is not the sinner sitting beside you…but the lie you have allowed to sit inside you?
Most Christians have heard the verse.
“Bad company corrupts good character.”
We quote it when a teenager starts hanging around the wrong crowd.
We use it when someone begins dating a person who keeps pulling them away from God.
We say it when a believer starts spending too much time with people whose lives seem to be dragging them toward compromise.
And there is wisdom in recognizing that relationships influence us. Scripture repeatedly warns about the power of companionship, counsel, imitation, and influence.
But there is something much bigger happening when Paul writes those famous words in 1 Corinthians 15:33.
Something more serious.
Something that reaches beyond your friend group.

Because when Paul said, “Bad company corrupts good character,” he was standing in the middle of an argument about something far more consequential than whether Christians should choose respectable friends.
He was defending the resurrection of the dead.
And once you see that context, this familiar verse becomes frighteningly personal.
The Greek reads:
“μὴ πλανᾶσθε· φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί.”
Mē planasthe; phtheirousin ēthē chrēsta homiliai kakai.
A straightforward sense is:
“Do not be deceived: bad associations corrupt good character.”
Notice how Paul begins.
μὴ πλανᾶσθε — mē planasthe.
“Do not be deceived.”
That is the alarm bell.
Paul is not merely saying, “Be careful who your friends are.”
He is saying, in effect:
Do not let yourself be led astray.
Do not swallow a lie.
Do not allow corrupting influence to reshape what you believe and, eventually, how you live.
Because immediately before this warning Paul is talking about people denying the resurrection.
That changes everything.
First Corinthians 15 begins with the Gospel itself.
Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
He was buried.
He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.
He appeared to witnesses.
Paul builds his argument around the historical and theological reality of the risen Christ.
Then comes the crisis.
Some among the Corinthians were saying there was no resurrection of the dead.
Paul refuses to treat that idea as a harmless theological disagreement.
Because follow the lie to its conclusion.
If there is no resurrection of the dead, Paul argues, then Christ has not been raised.
And if Christ has not been raised, Christian preaching collapses.
Faith becomes empty.
The apostles become false witnesses.
And horrifyingly, Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, “you are still in your sins.”
That is how much is at stake.
Christianity does not rest upon the vague idea that Jesus inspires people to become nicer.
It rests upon a crucified Messiah who truly died and a risen Lord who truly conquered death.
No resurrection?
No Christianity.
No risen Christ?
No Gospel.
No victory over death.
No final resurrection.
No Christian hope beyond the grave.
And Paul understands something about human beings that we still desperately need to understand:
What you believe about eternity eventually changes how you live today.
Listen to his reasoning just before the famous warning.
If the dead are not raised, then why suffer?
Why sacrifice?
Why endure?
Why risk everything for Christ?
If death gets the final word, why not simply live for whatever pleasure can be squeezed out of the few years we have?
Paul invokes the chilling logic:
“Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
Then comes the warning.
“Do not be deceived.”
“Bad company corrupts good character.”
Then immediately:
Wake up.
Stop sinning.
Some have no knowledge of God.
Do you see it now?
This is bigger than choosing friends.
Paul is exposing the spiritual chain reaction between corrupt teaching, corrupted belief, and corrupted living.
A lie enters the mind.
The lie settles into the heart.
The heart adjusts its expectations.
The conscience slowly negotiates.
Behavior follows.
And eventually a person can begin living according to a theology they would never openly confess.
That may be where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because you can say that you believe in the resurrection while living as though this life is all there is.

You can sing about heaven on Sunday and spend Monday through Saturday building your entire identity around money, applause, appearance, comfort, possessions, status, sexual gratification, popularity, career advancement, resentment, entertainment, or being admired by strangers.
Your mouth can say,
“Christ is risen.”
While your decisions quietly say,
“Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
That is the danger.
Sometimes it arrives as a sentence repeated often enough that you stop challenging it.
“Everybody does it.”
“God just wants me happy.”
“My truth is my truth.”
“It’s only one time.”
“Nobody will know.”
“I can repent later.”
“I deserve this.”
“My body, my desires, my money, my life.”
“Jesus will forgive me anyway.”
And slowly…
almost invisibly…
what once disturbed your conscience becomes normal.
What once made you pray now makes you shrug.
What once sent you running from temptation now becomes something you negotiate with.
You did not wake up one morning intending to become spiritually numb.
You simply stopped guarding what was discipling you.
That is why “company” cannot be reduced merely to the people whose phone numbers are saved in your contacts.
Ask yourself a harder question.
What keeps company with your mind?
Whose voice lives rent-free inside your thoughts?
What sermons shape you?
What podcasts shape you?
What entertainment shapes you?
What accounts shape you?
What jokes shape you?
What comments shape you?
What private conversations shape you?
What ideology shapes you?
What desires have been preaching to you?
What do you consume so consistently that it has started interpreting reality for you?
Because somebody—or something—is discipling you.
Every day.
And you may not notice the transformation until you begin defending what you once knew was destroying you.
That is how corruption often works.
Not always through open rebellion.
Sometimes through slow familiarity.
One compromise.
One rationalization.
One secret.
One voice telling you that obedience is too extreme.
One relationship where Jesus gradually becomes inconvenient.
One community where holiness becomes embarrassing.
One teacher who makes sin sound sophisticated.
One algorithm that learns exactly which weakness keeps you staring at the screen.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Until something that once shocked you becomes entertainment.
Something you once resisted becomes curiosity.
Curiosity becomes tolerance.
Tolerance becomes participation.
Participation becomes bondage.
And bondage eventually starts demanding that you rename it freedom.
“Do not be deceived.”
Those words feel different now, don’t they?
But we must be careful here.
This verse does not give Christians permission to become self-righteous, suspicious, isolated people who refuse to associate with unbelievers.
Jesus Himself destroys that interpretation.
Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners.
He touched people religious society avoided.
He moved toward the broken.
He spoke with the rejected.
He welcomed the ashamed.
He was called a friend of sinners.
But Jesus could enter a room full of darkness without allowing darkness to redefine Him.
He did not join sinners in order to become like them.
He came to call sinners to repentance.
That distinction matters.
Christian holiness is not hiding from lost people.
It is belonging so completely to Jesus that you can love lost people without needing to imitate what is destroying them.
The question is not merely:
“Do I have unbelieving friends?”
A better question may be:
“Who is influencing whom?”
Are you carrying the light of Christ into that relationship?
Or are you gradually dimming your convictions so the relationship becomes easier?
Can you speak about Jesus without embarrassment?
Can you say no when everyone says yes?
Can you walk away when staying would require compromise?
Can you love someone deeply without allowing that person to become lord over your conscience?
There are people God may send you toward because they desperately need to see Christ.
And there are influences you may need to flee because you are not evangelizing them anymore.
They are discipling you.
Knowing the difference requires humility.
Maybe the hardest “bad company” to leave is not another person.
Maybe it is an old version of yourself.
The person who keeps whispering:
“You’ll never change.”
“You’ve gone too far.”
“You’re still that addict.”
“You’re still that adulterer.”
“You’re still that liar.”
“You’re still what you did in that bedroom.”
“You’re still what happened in that marriage.”
“You’re still the secret nobody knows.”
“You’re still the mistake your family remembers.”
“You’re still the scandal.”
And this is where the Gospel crashes into the story.
Because 1 Corinthians 15 is ultimately not a chapter about bad company.
It is a chapter about a risen King.
Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners.
He was buried.
And He rose.
The tomb did not keep Him.
Death did not defeat Him.
Sin did not win.
Satan did not get the final word.
Jesus is alive.
And because Jesus is alive, repentance is not walking toward a dead religious system hoping you can somehow repair yourself.
Repentance is turning from sin toward a living Savior.
Grace does not say your sin never mattered.
The cross proves that sin mattered more terribly than we often want to admit.
Grace says Jesus Christ paid what guilty people could never pay for themselves.
That is why Christianity does not tell the ashamed person merely:
“Improve your character.”
The Gospel announces something infinitely better:
Come to Christ.
Bring Him the corruption.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the affair.
Bring Him the greed.
Bring Him the hypocrisy.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the theology you distorted because obedience became inconvenient.
Bring Him the person you became when nobody was watching.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Stop calling darkness light.
Stop negotiating with what crucified your Savior.
Stop assuming grace means Jesus is indifferent about whether you change.
The same grace that forgives also begins transforming.
And maybe somebody reading this needs to hear that tonight.
Your scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
Peter's denial did not write his final chapter.
Paul's persecution of the church did not write his final chapter.
The thief's criminal past did not get the final word at the cross.
And your worst chapter does not possess greater authority than the grace of Jesus Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by lowering God's holiness until our sin becomes comfortable.

Jesus rewrites everything by meeting guilty people with truth, calling them to repentance, washing them with grace, and giving them a new identity centered not in what they have done but in what He has done.
That is why the resurrection matters so much.
If Jesus remained in the grave, despair would make sense.
If Jesus remained in the grave, sin would still reign.
If Jesus remained in the grave, death would still be undefeated.
But Christ has been raised.
Therefore your obedience is not meaningless.
Your suffering is not meaningless.
Your fight against temptation is not meaningless.
Your secret prayers are not meaningless.
Your refusal to compromise is not meaningless.
Your tears are not meaningless.
Your repentance is not meaningless.
Your labor for Christ is not meaningless.
That is exactly where Paul takes the chapter.

After defending the resurrection and proclaiming Christ's victory over death, he tells believers to remain steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that their labor in the Lord is not in vain.
That is the opposite of:
“Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
The world says:
You only live once, so satisfy yourself.
The resurrection says:
You will stand before the risen Christ, so live for what survives the grave.
The world says:
Protect your comfort.
Jesus says:
Take up your cross.
The world says:
Follow your desires.
Jesus says:
The world says:
Death ends the story.
The empty tomb says:
Death has already met its Conqueror.
So perhaps the question is not simply whether you have “bad company.”
Perhaps the question is:
What voices have been teaching you how to live?
And are those voices preparing you to meet Jesus?
Some friendships need boundaries.
Some relationships need courage.
Some influences need to be unfollowed.
Some conversations need to end.
Some habits need to die.
Some teachers need to stop having access to your soul.
Some entertainment is costing you more spiritually than you are willing to admit.
And some Christians need to stop blaming “bad company” for choices they themselves keep making.
Your friends can influence you.
They cannot repent for you.
Your culture can tempt you.
It cannot surrender for you.
Your past can explain wounds.
It cannot become permission to remain in sin.
Eventually there comes a moment when you stand before Jesus without excuses and say:
“Lord, this is mine. I did this. I believed this. I tolerated this. I hid this. Have mercy on me.”
And He is not frightened by honest confession.
The cross was built for guilty people.
The Gospel is good news precisely because we needed rescuing.
Maybe this article exposed something.
Maybe you immediately thought of a relationship.
Maybe you thought of a screen.
Maybe you thought of a secret habit.
Maybe you realized that the loudest bad company in your life has been a belief you adopted because it made disobedience easier.
Do not merely feel convicted and keep scrolling.
Talk to God.
Be specific.
Repent specifically.
Ask for help specifically.
And where wisdom requires it, bring another mature believer into the fight.
Not because typing a sentence saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing what has been hiding into the light is the first honest admission that you are finished pretending.
Someone else may desperately need your testimony tonight.
Then think of one person who needs this truth.
Not twenty random names.
One person.
The friend slowly compromising.
The son who thinks Christianity is merely rules.
The daughter surrounded by voices redefining truth.
The believer quietly drifting.
The person who stopped attending church.
The person drowning in shame.
The unbeliever who thinks his past makes him unreachable.
Save it too.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget truths we were certain about yesterday.
Come back when the compromise starts sounding reasonable again.
Come back when sin starts asking to be renamed.
Come back when the crowd gets loud.
Come back and remember:
“Do not be deceived.”
Gospel Warrior exists to keep putting Christ-centered truth in front of people who may never walk into a church building but will stop long enough to read something on a screen.
And if you believe this ministry should continue and expand, there is another way you can stand with it.
Absolutely not.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift in Jesus Christ.
Share the truth.
Pray.
Tell somebody about Jesus.
The kingdom of God is not a marketplace where the wealthy purchase greater access to grace.
The widow's two small coins mattered to Jesus.
So did the people who opened their homes.
So did those who prayed.
So did those who served.
So did those who carried the message.
What matters is faithfulness to Christ with whatever He has entrusted to us.
Because one day the scrolling stops.
One day the notifications stop.
One day nobody will care how many followers knew your name.
One day the possessions change hands.
The trophies collect dust.
The body returns to the earth.
And the question will never be whether the world thought you were impressive.
The question that matters eternally is what you did with Jesus Christ.
The risen Christ changes everything.
So choose your influences carefully.
Guard the truth entrusted to you.
Love sinners without surrendering to sin.
Reject teaching that empties the Gospel of its power.
Refuse to let a dying culture teach you how to prepare for eternity.
Repent quickly.
Forgive freely.
Love courageously.
Give generously.
Stand firmly.
And keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because “bad company corrupts good character” was never merely advice about finding nicer friends.
It was a warning not to let corrupting voices convince you to live as though the resurrection is not real.
Christ is risen.
Therefore your life matters.
Your holiness matters.
Your choices matter.
Your witness matters.
Your repentance matters.
Your faithfulness matters.
And because the tomb is empty, your story does not have to end where your sin left it.
The voice that corrupted yesterday does not have to narrate tomorrow when the risen Jesus has called your name.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “A THOUSAND MAY FALL AT YOUR SIDE…” — DOES PSALM 91 REALLY GUARANTEE THAT NOTHING BAD WILL HAPPEN TO YOU?
paragraphs: “A THOUSAND MAY FALL AT YOUR SIDE…” — DOES PSALM 91 REALLY GUARANTEE THAT NOTHING BAD WILL HAPPEN TO YOU?
What if one of the Bible’s most comforting promises has been misunderstood—not because it promises too much, but because what God actually promises is deeper than merely keeping trouble away?
There is a verse people reach for when the diagnosis comes.
When the plane begins to shake.
When somebody you love is driving through a storm.
When violence erupts.
When disease spreads.
When the phone rings at an hour when good news rarely calls.
When fear crawls into the room and sits beside you.
You know the verse.
Maybe you have whispered it with tears in your eyes.
Maybe your mother prayed it over you.
Maybe your grandmother kept Psalm 91 open beside her bed.
Maybe you have posted it online during a crisis.
Maybe you have spoken it over your children before they walked out the door.
“A thousand may fall at your side, ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not come near you.”
And perhaps you believed those words meant something very specific:
If I trust God enough, the tragedy will hit somebody else.
Then one day...
it came near you.
The disease came near.
The accident came near.
The betrayal came near.
The funeral came near.
The thing you begged God to prevent happened anyway.
And suddenly Psalm 91 became harder to read.
Because nobody prepared you for the question hiding behind your grief:
Did God break His promise?
Or worse...
Was my faith not strong enough?
Before you quietly carry that accusation against yourself—or against God—we need to read Psalm 91 again.
Slowly.
Honestly.
Without reducing its poetry to a Christian good-luck charm.
Because Psalm 91 is true.
Gloriously true.
But it does not say everything people sometimes make it say.
And the difference may completely change the way you understand suffering, protection, faith... and Jesus Christ Himself.
The Hebrew of Psalm 91:7 reads:
יִפֹּ֤ל מִצִּדְּךָ֨׀ אֶ֗לֶף וּרְבָבָ֥ה מִימִינֶ֑ךָ אֵ֝לֶ֗יךָ לֹ֣א יִגָּֽשׁ׃
Yippol mitztiddecha eleph, urevavah miminecha; eleicha lo yiggash.
“A thousand may fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand; it will not come near you.”
Those words really are there.
We do not need to weaken them.
We do not need to apologize for them.
We do not need to explain away God’s power.
God protects.
God rescues.
God intervenes.
God can shut the mouths of lions.
God can open prison doors.
God can preserve a life when every human calculation says that life should be over.
God can command angels.
Psalm 91 itself declares:
כִּ֣י מַ֭לְאָכָיו יְצַוֶּה־לָּ֑ךְ לִ֝שְׁמָרְךָ֗ בְּכָל־דְּרָכֶֽיךָ׃
Ki mal'akhav yetzavveh-lakh, lishmorkha bekhol-derakhekha.
“For He will command His angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways.”
That is not mythology.
That is Scripture.
But now something extraordinary happens.
Centuries after those words were written, someone quoted them directly in the presence of Jesus.
And the person quoting Psalm 91...
was Satan.
Read that again.
When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, the devil took Him to the pinnacle of the temple and essentially said:
If You really are the Son of God, jump.
Why?
Because Scripture says God will command His angels concerning You.
The devil quoted the protection language of Psalm 91 to the very Son of God. Matthew preserves the quotation in Greek:
Τοῖς ἀγγέλοις αὐτοῦ ἐντελεῖται περὶ σοῦ...
“He will command His angels concerning you...”
The temptation was devastatingly subtle.
Satan was not asking Jesus to stop believing Scripture.
He was tempting Jesus to misuse Scripture.
He was effectively saying:
If God promised protection, make Him prove it.
And Jesus refused.
His response was:
Οὐκ ἐκπειράσεις κύριον τὸν θεόν σου.
Ouk ekpeiraseis Kyrion ton Theon sou.
“You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.”
There it is.
One of the clearest warnings against turning Psalm 91 into a guarantee that faithful people can deliberately presume upon physical protection comes from Jesus Himself.
Christ did not deny Psalm 91.
He interpreted faith correctly.
Faith trusts the Father.
Presumption tries to force the Father to prove Himself.
Faith says, “God is my refuge.”
Presumption says, “Because God is my refuge, nothing painful can possibly happen to me.”
Those are not the same confession.
And this is where Psalm 91 becomes far more beautiful than the version of it we sometimes put on coffee mugs.
Because buried near the end of the Psalm is a sentence that changes everything.
God says:
עִמּוֹ־אָנֹכִי בְצָרָה
Immo anokhi vetsarah.
“I am with him in trouble.”
Not merely:
I will make sure trouble never reaches him.
But:
I am with him in trouble.
The Hebrew word צָרָה — tsarah carries the sense of trouble, distress, adversity.
God does promise deliverance in the same verse. But notice where God says He will be.
Inside the trouble.
“With him.”
The Psalm that people sometimes use to promise the absence of suffering explicitly pictures the faithful person experiencing tsarah—distress—and God being there with him.
That changes the question.
The question is no longer merely:
“Will trouble ever reach me?”
The deeper question becomes:
“Who will be with me when it does?”
And suddenly the entire Bible begins to harmonize.
Think about Acts 12.
James and Peter.
Two apostles.
Same Jesus.
Same Gospel.
Same early church.
Same period of persecution.
Herod had James killed with the sword.
Then Herod imprisoned Peter.
The church prayed earnestly for Peter.
And in the middle of the night an angel appeared.
Chains fell.
Doors opened.
Peter walked out alive.
One apostle was killed.
Another apostle was miraculously delivered.
The Bible records both without suggesting that James had inferior faith or that Peter had discovered a superior formula.
That chapter alone should make us very careful about telling suffering Christians:
“If you really trusted God, nothing would have happened to you.”
Tell that to James.
Tell it to Stephen beneath the stones.
Tell it to Paul after beatings, imprisonment and danger.
Tell it to the martyrs.
Tell it to the apostles who followed Christ knowing discipleship might cost them everything.
Better yet...
tell it to Jesus.
Because Christianity does not ultimately point us toward a man who escaped every wound.
It points us toward a Savior with scars.
Jesus trusted His Father perfectly.
No human being has ever possessed purer faith.
And yet Jesus was betrayed.
Arrested.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Scourged.
Nailed to a cross.
And killed.
If Psalm 91 meant, “A person who trusts God sufficiently can never experience physical suffering or death,” then the cross itself would become impossible to explain.
But the cross does not disprove God’s protection.
The cross reveals something infinitely greater about it.
The Father did not abandon the Son to ultimate defeat.
Death touched Jesus...
but death could not keep Jesus.
The grave received Him...
but the grave could not own Him.
Friday looked like destruction.
Sunday exposed the lie.
Jesus Christ rose.
And suddenly biblical protection becomes larger than our heartbeat.
Larger than our circumstances.
Larger than our ability to avoid pain.
Larger even than death.
This is why Jesus could say something that sounds almost contradictory in Luke 21.
He told His disciples that some of them would be put to death.
Then, only moments later, He said that not a hair of their heads would perish.
Some of you will die.
Yet ultimately you will not perish.
Read superficially, those statements collide.
Read through resurrection, they become magnificent.
Jesus was teaching His followers that there are things this world can do to your body that it can never do to the life God has secured for you.
People can wound you.
They cannot erase you from Christ.
Cancer can attack cells.
It cannot cancel the resurrection.
Persecution can imprison a Christian.
It cannot imprison Christ.
A bullet can stop a heartbeat.
It cannot overthrow the kingdom of God.
Death can close your eyes.
It cannot separate a believer from Jesus.
Paul understood this.
That is why Romans 8 does not say believers will never encounter tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, or sword.
Paul actually names those things.
Then he declares that in all these things believers are “more than conquerors” through the One who loved them.
Notice the wording.
Not always away from these things.
Sometimes in these things.
And his conclusion is breathtaking:
neither death nor life nor anything else in creation can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
This is stronger than “nothing bad will ever happen to me.”
Much stronger.
Because that promise would last only until something bad happened.
The Gospel gives you something suffering cannot invalidate.
God may deliver you from the furnace.
God may deliver you through the furnace.
And ultimately, in Christ, God will deliver you beyond the furnace.
That means you can pray Psalm 91 boldly.
Pray for protection.
Ask God to guard your children.
Ask Him to heal the disease.
Ask Him to prevent the accident.
Ask Him to stop the violence.
Ask Him to send angels.
Ask Him to open impossible doors.
Ask Him for miracles.
There is nothing spiritually mature about refusing to ask your Father for rescue.
But do not turn prayer into a contract God never signed.
Do not say:
“God, because I quoted Psalm 91, You are now obligated to arrange every circumstance according to my preferred outcome.”
Jesus would not jump from the temple to force His Father to prove Psalm 91.
Neither should we.
Sometimes faith looks like chains falling from Peter’s wrists.
Sometimes faith looks like Stephen seeing heaven opened while stones are falling.
Sometimes faith looks like Daniel walking out of the lions’ den.
Sometimes faith looks like Paul continuing to preach while carrying scars.
Sometimes faith looks like Jesus sweating blood in Gethsemane and still saying yes to the Father.
And maybe...
sometimes faith looks like you.
Sitting beside a hospital bed.
Holding a medical report you never wanted.
Standing beside a coffin.
Watching a marriage collapse.
Wondering why the prayer you prayed did not receive the answer you expected.
Still whispering...
“Jesus, I trust You.”
