And generations later, through this royal line, Matthew brings us to Jesus Christ.
Think about what that means.
The woman whom many people would have reduced to her sexual history appears in the genealogy Matthew uses to introduce the Messiah.
The scandal did not disappear from history.
Grace overwhelmed its authority to define the ending.
This is our theme because it is written all over the Gospel:
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin should be romanticized.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes sinners and makes them saints.
Enemies can be reconciled to God.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The spiritually dead can be made alive.
The lost can be found.
The ashamed can stop hiding.
And the story people thought had reached its final chapter can become evidence that God is still writing.
Rahab even appears again in James 2:25.
James points to her actions in receiving the messengers and sending them out another way.
Hebrews emphasizes her faith.
James emphasizes the action produced by that faith.
There is no contradiction.
There is transformation.
Real faith moves.
Real faith acts.
Real faith changes allegiance.
Rahab did not merely say, “I believe Israel's God is real,” and then hand the spies over to Jericho.
What she believed changed what she risked.
That should confront us.
Because modern Christianity can become frighteningly comfortable with professions of faith that require almost nothing.
We say we believe Jesus is Lord…
but refuse to surrender the secret sin.
We sing about grace…
but refuse to forgive.
We post Bible verses…
but privately feed addictions.
We call Him Savior…
while resisting Him as Lord.
Rahab reminds us that saving faith is not admiration from a distance.
Faith steps out from behind the walls.
Faith entrusts itself to God.
And perhaps your wall is not made of stone.
Perhaps yours is made of shame.
You built it slowly.
One regret at a time.
One secret at a time.
One betrayal at a time.
One night you promised yourself would never happen again.
One browser history you deleted.
One bottle nobody knows about.
One relationship you cannot explain.
One prayer you stopped praying because you became convinced God must be tired of hearing from you.
Brick.
By brick.
By brick.
Until eventually you were living inside your own Jericho.
And Jesus is calling you out.
Not into denial.
Into repentance.
Not into pretending.
Into truth.
Not into self-salvation.
Into grace.
The Gospel does not tell you to make yourself worthy and then approach Christ.
You cannot.
You come because Christ alone is worthy.
Jesus said He came not to call the righteous, but sinners.
The apostolic Gospel announces that Christ died for our sins and rose again.
And the invitation remains astonishingly open:
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Stop making peace with the very chains from which He calls you to freedom.
You may have been called many things.
But the question is no longer merely what people called you.
The question is:
Who will you trust now?
Rahab heard what God had done.
She believed.
She acted.
And when Jericho fell, faith had already moved her allegiance beyond those walls.
Maybe your moment is now.
Maybe you have been reading Gospel content for months while keeping Jesus at a safe distance.
Maybe you know Christian vocabulary without knowing surrender.
Maybe you know how to say “Amen” while your heart is exhausted from hiding.
Then stop hiding.
Jesus already knows.
He knows the chapter you would delete.
He knows the name.
The bed.
The bottle.
The screen.
The lie.
The betrayal.
The abortion.
The affair.
The bitterness.
The secret.
The relapse.
The years you wasted.
The promises you broke.
And knowing all of it, the Gospel still summons sinners to come to Him in repentance and faith.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Because His grace is astonishing.
If you cannot even find the strength for a long explanation, simply write:
There may be another believer reading the comments who understands exactly what those three words cost you.
And if Jesus has already rescued you from a past that once defined you, tell somebody.
Your testimony may become another person's Jericho moment.
Not because you are the Savior.
You are not.
But because broken people need to see what happens when sinners encounter the Savior who is.
Not merely because sharing helps this ministry reach more people—although it genuinely does.
Someone may believe sexual sin has disqualified them forever.
Someone may think addiction has written the last sentence.
Someone may be one secret away from giving up.
Someone may have spent years believing church is only for people with clean histories.
Put Rahab's story in front of them.
Send this privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they need it.
But understand why.
You cannot buy grace.
And we will not tell you that giving money to us is a requirement for glorifying God.
It isn't.
God is glorified through lives surrendered to Jesus Christ.

But Scripture does teach voluntary, generous support for Gospel work. Paul wrote that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from the Gospel, while Christian giving is to come from the heart rather than manipulation or compulsion.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Keep pointing wounded people away from hopelessness and toward Jesus Christ.
Sometimes the support you can give today is financial. Sometimes it is sharing. Sometimes it is prayer. Sometimes it is all three.
And there is more available even if you never spend a cent.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the person who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the seeker with uncomfortable questions.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing to say to someone with their history.
Because Rahab's story says otherwise.
And ultimately, Rahab's story is not powerful because Rahab was impressive.
It is powerful because God is merciful.
The Bible did not need to hide her past to demonstrate her faith.
Hebrews could say both.
Rahab.
The prostitute.
By faith.
Perhaps that is the sentence someone needed tonight.
Your worst chapter may be true.
But it does not have to become your final chapter.
Your sin may be real.
Your consequences may be real.
Your wounds may be real.
Your shame may feel real enough to suffocate you.
But Jesus Christ is real too.
His cross is real.
His resurrection is real.
His call to repentance is real.
His forgiveness is real.
His grace is real.
And transformation in Him is real.
Rahab entered Scripture carrying a label.
She entered Hebrews remembered for faith.
She entered the genealogy of Matthew on the road that leads the reader toward Christ.
That does not mean God promises every believer earthly prominence.
It means something better:
No repentant sinner who comes to Christ has to remain imprisoned by the identity sin once gave them.
So come out from behind the wall.
Stop negotiating with the darkness.
Stop rehearsing the prosecution's case as though Calvary never happened.
Confess what must be confessed.
Repent of what must be abandoned.
Make restitution where wisdom and righteousness require it.
Seek help where you need help.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Ask forgiveness where you have wounded others.
And place your faith not in your ability to repair yourself, but in Jesus Christ.
Then walk.
One trembling step at a time.
Because the Gospel has never been about pretending there was no scandal.
It is about what Jesus Christ can do with sinners who surrender to Him.
So when your past whispers its old name tonight…
remember Rahab.
Remember Jericho.
Remember the woman in the window.
Remember the faith that acted.
Remember the mercy that rescued.
Remember the genealogy.
Remember Hebrews.
And above all…
remember Jesus.
“Christ is still healing me.”
Four words.
One testimony.
And perhaps the beginning of another person's courage to come home.
Because when Jesus takes hold of a surrendered life, the name shame gave you no longer gets to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WHOM SHALL I SEND?” — THE TERRIFYING PART OF ISAIAH 6 WE RARELY PREACH AFTER “SEND ME”
paragraphs: “WHOM SHALL I SEND?” — THE TERRIFYING PART OF ISAIAH 6 WE RARELY PREACH AFTER “SEND ME”
Everybody loves Isaiah’s “Here am I; send me.” Far fewer people keep reading long enough to discover where God was sending him—and what obedience was going to cost.
There is a version of Isaiah 6 that fits beautifully on a coffee mug.
“Here am I. Send me!”
It sounds courageous.
It sounds adventurous.
It sounds like the beginning of something extraordinary.
And it is.
But there is something almost unsettling about the way we sometimes quote those words.
Because we stop reading.
We celebrate the surrender without reading the assignment.
We preach the availability of Isaiah, but sometimes quietly walk away before hearing what God actually told the available man to do.
And if you have ever told Jesus, “Use me,” while secretly imagining what being used by Him would look like…
Isaiah 6 may disturb you.
Because sometimes God answers, “Send me,” by sending you somewhere you never would have chosen, to people who may not applaud, carrying truth they may not want to hear.
The story begins not with Isaiah volunteering.
It begins with a death.
“In the year that king Uzziah died…”
Isaiah 6:1.
A king was gone.
A throne on earth had become empty.
But Isaiah looked higher and discovered that the ultimate throne had never been vacant.
“I saw also the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up…”
That changes everything.
Before Isaiah becomes a messenger, Isaiah becomes a witness.
Before he sees the mission, he sees the Majesty.
Before he says, “Send me,” he encounters the holiness of the One doing the sending.
Seraphim cry to one another:
“Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory.”
The Hebrew is breathtaking:
קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ קָדוֹשׁ
Qādôš, qādôš, qādôš.
Holy.
Holy.
Holy.
Not “Isaiah, Isaiah, Isaiah.”
Not “calling, calling, calling.”
Not “success, influence, platform.”
Holy.
The center of Isaiah 6 is not the greatness of a willing prophet.
It is the holiness of an incomparable God.
The foundations shake.
The house fills with smoke.
And suddenly Isaiah does something that should make every person who wants to be “used by God” think carefully.
He does not introduce himself.
He does not announce his qualifications.
He does not tell God about his potential.
He falls apart.
“Woe is me! for I am undone…”
The Hebrew begins:
אוֹי־לִי
’Ôy-lî.
“Woe to me.”
Then comes the devastating confession:
כִּי אִישׁ טְמֵא־שְׂפָתַיִם אָנֹכִי
Ki ’ish teme-sefatayim anokhi.
In sense: “For I am a man of unclean lips.”
Isaiah had been speaking prophetic woes over others.
Then he saw God.
And suddenly the sinner he could see most clearly was himself.
That is what genuine encounters with holiness do.
They do not merely make us emotional about everybody else’s sin.
They expose ours.
Maybe that is where this story has to become personal.
It is easy to look at a collapsing culture and say, “Woe to them.”
Easy to point at the addict.
The adulterer.
The hypocrite.
The corrupt leader.
The compromised church.
The rebellious generation.
The person whose sins happen to be more visible than yours.
But then the throne comes into view.
And suddenly you remember the messages you deleted.
The bitterness you renamed “discernment.”
The lust you kept feeding.
The apology you never gave.
The forgiveness you keep withholding.
The secret habit nobody at church knows about.
The pride hidden underneath your theology.
The prayer life that has quietly become almost nonexistent.
The private version of you that would terrify the public version of you if it ever became visible.
And before a holy God, Isaiah does not say, “At least I am better than them.”
He says, essentially:
I am unclean too.
But this is where Isaiah 6 becomes Gospel-shaped long before Bethlehem.
God does not leave the confessed sinner standing there condemned.
A seraph takes a burning coal from the altar.
It touches Isaiah’s lips.
And Isaiah hears words every guilty soul longs to hear:
“Thine iniquity is taken away, and thy sin purged.”
Do not rush past that.
Isaiah did not cleanse himself before volunteering.
Grace touched him first.
The altar came before the assignment.
Cleansing came before commissioning.
Forgiveness came before sending.
That pattern matters because Christianity is not the story of sinful people making themselves impressive enough for God to employ.
It is the story of grace reaching the unclean.
And what Isaiah experiences symbolically around the altar points us toward something infinitely greater revealed fully in Jesus Christ.
At Calvary, our hope is not a coal touching our lips.
Our hope is the crucified and risen Son of God bearing sin and accomplishing redemption.
Peter writes that Christ “bare our sins in his own body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
Paul says that in Christ “we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins” (Ephesians 1:7).
Isaiah needed cleansing.
So do you.
So do I.
And the Gospel declares that forgiveness is not found in pretending we were never dirty.
It is found in Jesus Christ.
Then—and only then—comes the question.
Isaiah hears the voice of the Lord:
אֶת־מִי אֶשְׁלַח וּמִי יֵלֶךְ־לָנוּ
’Et-mi ’eshlach, umi yelekh-lanu?
“Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?”
And Isaiah answers:
הִנְנִי שְׁלָחֵנִי
Hineni, shelacheni.
“Here am I; send me.”
Hineni.
Here I am.
Not merely, “I am standing at this geographical location.”
It is availability.
Presence.
Readiness.
Here I am.
And perhaps you have prayed something like it.
“Jesus, use me.”
“Lord, send me.”
“God, whatever You want.”
Beautiful words.
Dangerous words.
Because God answers Isaiah.
And this is where the coffee-mug version usually ends.
The Bible does not.
God tells him:
“Go.”
But what follows is not a promise that thousands will immediately repent.

Isaiah receives a severe prophetic commission to a spiritually resistant people. He is to proclaim God's word in the midst of hardened hearing and blinded perception, and Isaiah eventually asks the agonizing question:
“Lord, how long?”
Think about that.
Isaiah said, “Send me.”
God did.
And the assignment included rejection.
The man who saw the throne would now speak to people who often would not listen.
The man whose lips had been cleansed would use those lips to proclaim truth that would expose hardened hearts.
His obedience could not be measured merely by applause.
His faithfulness could not be measured merely by visible results.
And suddenly Isaiah 6 becomes painfully relevant.
Because maybe you thought obedience would make everybody understand you.
Maybe you thought following Jesus would automatically repair every relationship.
Maybe you thought sharing biblical truth would guarantee appreciation.
Maybe you thought serving faithfully meant your ministry would explode.
Maybe you thought raising your children in Christ guaranteed they would never wander.
Maybe you thought praying faithfully meant the answer would arrive quickly.
Maybe you thought, “Send me,” meant God would send you somewhere glamorous.
Instead He sent you back into that difficult home.
Into that workplace.
Into that marriage that needs patient faithfulness.
Into conversations nobody applauds.
Into years of praying for someone who still seems far from God.
Into serving when almost nobody notices.
Into telling the truth lovingly when silence would have been easier.
And somewhere inside you a question begins forming.
“Lord… how long?”
How long do I keep praying?
How long do I keep forgiving?
How long do I keep serving?
How long do I keep sharing Christ with someone who keeps rejecting Him?
How long do I remain faithful when faithfulness feels invisible?
Isaiah asked that question too.
And this is one of the truths we desperately need to recover:
Your assignment is obedience.
The results belong to God.
That does not mean results do not matter. Scripture repeatedly cares about fruit.
It means visible success is not the sovereign judge of faithfulness.
Noah preached righteousness in a wicked generation.
Jeremiah spoke while people resisted him.
The apostles suffered for proclaiming Christ.
And Jesus Himself was abandoned by many who had once followed Him.
So perhaps the question is not merely:
“Will God use me?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
“Will I still obey Him when being used by Him looks nothing like what I imagined?”
Will you still say hineni when nobody claps?
Will you still say shelacheni when obedience costs something?
Will you still speak truth with love when truth becomes unpopular?
Will you still follow Christ when Christianity stops being convenient?
Will you still serve when your name is forgotten?
Will you still forgive when your flesh wants revenge?
Will you still pray when heaven seems silent?
Will you still carry the Gospel when the people you love roll their eyes?
That is where “Here am I” becomes more than Christian merchandise.
It becomes surrender.
But there is another astonishing detail.
Isaiah's story does not ultimately terminate in judgment.
The book bearing his name keeps moving.
Through warnings.
Through tears.
Through judgment.
Through promises.
Until the horizon begins glowing with Someone Isaiah could not yet see in Bethlehem but whom God was already revealing through prophecy.
A child would be born.
A Son would be given.
A Servant would suffer.
A wounded Savior would bear the sins of others.
“He was wounded for our transgressions…”
Isaiah 53:5.
Centuries later, Jesus Christ came.

And when the Gospel of John reflects on Isaiah's vision, it makes an astonishing Christ-centered connection: after quoting from Isaiah 6, John says Isaiah “saw his glory, and spake of him” (John 12:41).
The throne of Isaiah 6 and the cross of the Gospel are not competing pictures.
The Holy One we cannot domesticate is the Savior who came to redeem sinners.
The God before whom Isaiah cried “Woe is me” is not indifferent to ruined people.
In Christ, He came for them.
That includes you.
Your scandal is not stronger than His grace.
Your history is not stronger than His blood.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
Your secret sin should be confessed, not protected.
Your guilt should drive you toward Christ, not deeper into hiding.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the mercy of God calling you out of the grave you were decorating.
Jesus does not merely make bad people appear respectable.
He makes spiritually dead people alive.
So maybe your first response today should not be:
“Send me.”
Maybe it should be:
“Woe is me.”
Maybe before asking God for a platform, you need the altar.
Before asking Him to enlarge your influence, you need Him to expose your heart.
Before saying, “Use my mouth,” perhaps you need to surrender what your mouth has been saying.
Before asking for a calling, perhaps you need repentance.
Because God is not looking for actors who know how to appear holy.
He calls sinners.
Cleanses sinners.
Transforms sinners.
And then sends forgiven sinners to tell other sinners where mercy can be found.
That is why your past does not automatically disqualify you from becoming a testimony of grace.
Peter denied Jesus and was restored.
Paul had persecuted the church and became a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The woman of Samaria carried the news of Jesus back toward people who knew her complicated story.
Again and again, Scripture reveals a God whose grace does not pretend the scandal never happened.
Grace does something better.
It redeems.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by pretending sin does not matter.
Not by lowering God's holiness until nobody needs repentance.
Jesus rewrites everything by confronting sin, bearing judgment, offering forgiveness, raising the dead, restoring the broken, and creating new lives that could never have written themselves.
So here is the question Isaiah 6 leaves burning in the room:
If Jesus has forgiven you…
where is He sending you?
Maybe it is not across an ocean.
Maybe it is across the hallway.
Maybe your mission field has your last name.
Maybe it sits beside you at work.
Maybe it is the friend whose jokes hide depression.
Maybe it is the child who stopped going to church.
Maybe it is the spouse you stopped praying for because disappointment became easier than hope.
Yes.
Even there.
What if the article you share becomes the article somebody reads alone at 2:13 in the morning while trying desperately not to collapse?
You cannot save them.
Gospel Warrior cannot save them.
A preacher cannot save them.
Only Jesus saves.
But someone can carry the message.
“Whom shall I send?”
Perhaps tagging that friend is not about engagement at all.
Perhaps it is you saying, “I thought of you, and I refuse to let embarrassment keep me silent.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you have been exhausted but you refuse to abandon your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to remember you in prayer, simply comment, “pray for me.”
And if God is confronting you about something you already know He has been asking you to surrender, comment, “Here am I.”
Not for performance.
Not to impress strangers.
As a small public confession that you do not want to keep running.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding you with Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical teaching, and reminders that continually lead you back to Jesus, you can also help this work continue.
It does not.
It does not.
And not because anyone should be pressured into giving. Scripture says plainly that giving must not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves cheerful giving (2 Corinthians 9:7).

But Scripture also gives us a beautiful picture of believers voluntarily partnering in Gospel work. The Philippians repeatedly supported Paul's ministry, and Paul described their generosity as “an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God” (Philippians 4:16–18).
That is the spirit in which we invite you.

Your support helps us keep creating and distributing Christ-centered content, biblical encouragement, discipleship materials, and resources designed to reach the wounded, the wandering, the curious, the struggling believer, and the person who may be one Gospel encounter away from finally crying out to Jesus.
Send it privately to the person God just brought to your mind.
Because the mission was never supposed to stop with the person who received the message.
Someone carried the Gospel until it reached you.
Now somebody else may be waiting for someone willing to carry it to them.
And perhaps that is the part of Isaiah 6 we have avoided.
“Send me” was never merely a beautiful sentence.
It was permission.
Permission for God to interrupt Isaiah's plans.
Permission to speak through cleansed lips.
Permission to send him toward difficult people.
Permission to remain faithful when visible results were painful.
Permission to keep going long enough to ask:
“Lord, how long?”
Maybe you are standing there now.
Tired.
Disappointed.
Still carrying scars from your own scandal.
Still wondering whether God could possibly use someone with your history.
Look again.
The story did not begin with Isaiah's usefulness.
It began with God's holiness.
Isaiah confessed.
God cleansed.
God called.
Isaiah answered.
And that same Gospel rhythm still destroys our excuses today.
See His holiness.
Confess your sin.
Run to Christ.
Receive the mercy purchased at the cross.
Rise in grace.
Then go wherever your King sends you.
Not because you are spotless.
Because Jesus saves sinners.
Not because you are fearless.
Because Christ is worthy.
Not because everyone will listen.
Because the One who sends you deserves your yes.
So when heaven asks…
“Whom shall I send?”
May your answer no longer be a verse you merely admire.
May it become the surrender by which you live.
And when your voice trembles as you say “Here am I,” remember: the God who sends you already knows every chapter behind you—and through Jesus Christ, grace can still write what comes next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES “LUST” SETTLE THE MASTURBATION QUESTION—or Is the Biblical Discussion More Complicated?
paragraphs: DOES “LUST” SETTLE THE MASTURBATION QUESTION—or Is the Biblical Discussion More Complicated?

Jesus spoke directly about lust. Paul spoke about sexual holiness, self-mastery, conscience, and glorifying God with the body. But the Bible never actually uses the word “masturbation.” So what happens when we stop repeating slogans, open the Scriptures, and allow the text to ask harder questions than the ones we expected?
There are sins people confess at the altar.
And then there are sins—or struggles, questions, habits, wounds, compulsions—that people carry home.
Quietly.
They worship on Sunday.
They raise their hands.
They quote Scripture.
They love Jesus.
Then midnight comes.
The bedroom door closes.
The phone lights up.
The loneliness gets louder.
The body remembers what the conscience has been trying to forget.
And afterward?
Silence.
Sometimes shame.
Sometimes repentance.
Sometimes confusion.
Sometimes the exhausted prayer of a Christian who has promised God for the fiftieth time, “Lord, I will never do this again.”
And sometimes there is another question—one many believers are almost afraid to ask because they assume merely asking it makes them rebellious:
What, precisely, does the Bible actually say about masturbation?
Not what Christian culture says.
Not what pornography says.
Not what secular culture says.
Not what your guilt says.
Not what somebody’s viral video says.
What does Scripture say?
Because there is a dangerous way to become “biblical” that actually requires putting words into the Bible that the Bible never says.
And there is an equally dangerous way to exploit biblical silence as permission to indulge whatever the flesh desires.
Neither is faithful.
So stay with me.
Because this discussion becomes much more uncomfortable before it becomes hopeful.
And somewhere underneath the question about masturbation may be another question entirely:
Who owns your body when nobody else is watching?
Jesus gives us one of the most important texts in this conversation in Matthew 5:28.
The Greek reads:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.
A close rendering is:
“But I say to you that everyone looking at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Pay attention to the expression:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι — pros to epithymēsai
The verb epithymeō can mean to desire, long for, covet, or—depending upon context—lust.
And the construction here matters.
Jesus is not teaching that noticing that another human being is physically attractive is automatically adultery.
He is going after something deeper.
The look that becomes intentional desire.
The gaze that welcomes and cultivates sexual possession in the heart.
The human being standing before you—or appearing on your screen—ceases to be treated as someone bearing God's image and becomes material for your imagination.
Jesus moves the courtroom into the heart.
That changes this entire discussion.

Because if masturbation is being fueled by pornography, deliberately cultivated fantasies about someone who is not your spouse, voyeurism, sexually exploitative imagery, or intentional fantasizing designed to produce lust, then we cannot simply isolate the physical act from what the heart is doing.
The question is no longer merely:
“Did my body experience sexual release?”
The question becomes:
What did I ask my heart to consume in order to get there?
That is harder.
Because nobody else may have been in the room.
But someone may have been in your imagination.
Someone whose body became raw material for your gratification.
Someone who never consented to occupy the sexual world you constructed inside your mind.
And Jesus cares about what happens there.
Not because sexual desire itself is dirty.

God created human beings as embodied creatures. Scripture does not teach that possessing sexual desire makes you filthy. The biblical story affirms marriage, one-flesh union, marital intimacy, desire, embodiment, and the goodness of God's creation.
The problem is not that you possess a body.
The problem is what sin can teach us to do with desire.
Paul puts the matter this way in 1 Thessalonians 4:3:
Τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν, ἀπέχεσθαι ὑμᾶς ἀπὸ τῆς πορνείας.
“This is the will of God—your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality.”
The word ἁγιασμός — hagiasmos speaks of holiness or sanctification.
And πορνεία — porneia refers broadly to sexual immorality.
A few verses later Paul speaks of not living:
ἐν πάθει ἐπιθυμίας — en pathei epithymias
“In passion of lust/desire.”
So yes.
Lust matters enormously.
But here is where Christians must resist saying more than Scripture says.
The Bible never directly names masturbation as an act.
There is no verse that says, “You shall not masturbate.”
That fact should neither frighten us nor become a loophole.
It should make us more careful interpreters.
Some people immediately run to Onan.

Genesis 38 tells how Judah commanded Onan to fulfill his obligation toward his deceased brother's wife and raise offspring for his brother. The Hebrew text speaks of raising זֶרַע — zeraʿ, “seed” or offspring, for his brother.
Onan understood that the offspring would not be reckoned as his.
So during intercourse with his brother's widow, he deliberately prevented conception rather than fulfilling the obligation placed upon him.
Genesis says what he did was wicked before the LORD.
But read the story carefully.
The text describes intercourse and Onan's deliberate refusal to provide offspring for his deceased brother.
It does not describe masturbation.

Whatever broader ethical conclusions Christians may draw from the passage, turning Genesis 38 into a straightforward verse saying “God killed Onan for masturbating” does not accurately represent what the narrative actually says.
And Christians should never need a distorted Bible verse to defend holiness.
Truth does not need our exaggeration.
But now someone may say:
“Then masturbation must be okay.”
Not so fast.
Biblical ethics often works through more than a dictionary of explicitly named behaviors.
Paul gives us a devastating principle in 1 Corinthians 6:12:
Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν, ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει... ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος.
“All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial... I will not be mastered by anything.”
That final idea deserves to sit in the room with us for a moment.
I will not be mastered by anything.
Because perhaps the question you have been asking is:
“Can I do it?”
When another question may expose much more:
“Can I stop?”
That changes things.
Can you walk away for a week?
A month?
Can you sleep without it?
Can you experience stress without running toward it?
Can you feel lonely without immediately needing sexual release?
Can you encounter temptation without opening pornography?
Can you pray when the urge comes instead of automatically obeying it?
Can you say no?
Or has what you once called relief slowly become a master?
There is an enormous difference between having an appetite and being ruled by one.
Paul does not merely ask whether something appears on a forbidden-behavior list.
He asks whether it is beneficial.
Whether it dominates.
Whether it belongs with holiness.
Whether the body is being offered to God.
Then Paul says something staggering:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς· δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν Θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.
“You were bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body.”
There it is.
Perhaps the deepest question in the entire discussion.
Not merely:
“Is masturbation technically forbidden?”
But:
“Can I bring this before Jesus without hiding?”
Can I thank Him for it?
Can I practice it in faith?
Can I say, “Lord Jesus, this body belongs to You. Be glorified in what I am about to do”?
Can I do it without pornography?
Without mentally possessing another person?
Without feeding fantasies that violate Christ's teaching about the heart?
Without being mastered?
Without violating my conscience?
Without using sexual pleasure as anesthesia for wounds Jesus is asking me to bring into His light?
Those questions do not manufacture a commandment Scripture never gives.
They do something much more searching.
They bring the behavior underneath the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And that may expose another uncomfortable truth.
For some people, masturbation is not primarily a sexual problem.
It has become pain medication.
You are lonely.
You do it.
Rejected.
You do it.
Anxious.
You do it.
Depressed.
You do it.
Angry with your spouse.
You do it.
Feeling unwanted.
You do it.
Unable to sleep.
You do it.
Ashamed that you did it yesterday.
And somehow...
you do it again.
The body becomes the place where an emotional wound repeatedly demands anesthesia.
And this is where shouting “STOP LUSTING!” may fail to reach the actual battlefield.
Yes, sinful lust must be resisted.
Yes, pornography must be rejected.
Yes, sexual immorality must be fled.
But sometimes discipleship must also ask:
What are you trying not to feel?
What loneliness keeps returning?
What rejection are you medicating?
What wound keeps asking for relief?
What happened to you?
What are you afraid to tell anyone?
Why does darkness feel safer than being known?
This does not excuse sin.
It helps expose where the battle is actually being fought.
Because Jesus does not merely want to take pornography out of your browser history.
He wants your heart.
He does not merely want cleaner behavior.
He wants freedom.
Paul writes in Galatians 5:16:
Πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε καὶ ἐπιθυμίαν σαρκὸς οὐ μὴ τελέσητε.
“Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desire of the flesh.”
Notice the direction.
Walk by the Spirit.
Christian holiness is not merely spending the rest of your life screaming “NO!” at your body.
It is learning to say a greater “YES” to Christ.
Yes to prayer.
Yes to truth.
Yes to bringing temptation into the light.
Yes to accountability.
Yes to removing pornography rather than negotiating with it.
Yes to getting the phone out of the bedroom if that phone repeatedly becomes a doorway.
Yes to calling a mature Christian when secrecy begins whispering again.
Yes to learning how to suffer loneliness without worshiping relief.
Yes to learning that an urge can exist without becoming your master.
And yes—even after failure—to getting up again.
Somebody reading this failed last night.
Maybe this morning.
Maybe five minutes before finding this article.
And you almost stopped reading because every paragraph felt like someone opening curtains in a room you desperately wanted dark.
Listen carefully.
Conviction says:
“Come into the light.”
Shame says:
“Hide until you become worthy of the light.”
Those voices are not saying the same thing.
The Gospel does not tell sinners to cleanse themselves enough to approach Jesus.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
The cross is not God's declaration that your sin does not matter.
The cross is the terrifying proof that sin matters more than we imagined—and the breathtaking proof that God's grace reaches farther than we deserved.
“If we confess our sins,” Scripture says, “He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
And Romans 8:1 announces:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Do not confuse no condemnation with no transformation.
Grace does not say:
“Stay chained.”
Grace walks into the prison carrying keys.
Jesus did not shed His blood merely so you could become more comfortable hiding.
He died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Confess what needs confessing.
Delete what needs deleting.
Block what needs blocking.
Bring into community what secrecy has protected.
If pornography is involved, stop pretending the masturbation question can be separated from pornography.
If deliberate lustful fantasy is involved, bring the fantasy under Matthew 5:28.
If the behavior controls you, bring it under Paul's refusal to “be mastered by anything.”
If your conscience is continually accusing you, do not repeatedly bulldoze your conscience merely because you found somebody online willing to give you permission.

And if your struggle has become compulsive, entrenched, or connected to trauma, loneliness, anxiety, or other deep wounds, seeking help from a trustworthy pastor, mature Christian mentor, or qualified professional is not spiritual defeat.
Sometimes walking into the light sounds like:
“I need help.”
Perhaps you have spent years asking God:
“Why can't I stop?”
Maybe tonight the prayer needs to change.
“Jesus, show me what I have been running from.”
That prayer can become frightening.
Because He may show you the pornography.
The fantasy.
The loneliness.
The resentment.
The boredom.
The secret entitlement.
The unhealed rejection.
The habit.
The self-pity.
The craving for control.
Maybe even the religious shame that convinced you God was disgusted every time you stumbled and therefore made you hide from the only One who could heal you.
Bring all of it.
Not just the respectable pieces.
Bring the scandal.
That is what grace is for.
And no, this article cannot honestly reduce every circumstance to the simplistic sentence, “Masturbation equals lust, therefore the discussion is over.”
Scripture deserves better than that.
Neither can we say, “The Bible doesn't mention the word, therefore anything goes.”
Scripture deserves better than that too.
The faithful question reaches deeper.
What accompanies the act?
What feeds it?
What does the heart intentionally desire?
Does pornography participate?
Does another person become an object inside the imagination?
Does it strengthen self-control or weaken it?
Is it mastering you?
Can it be brought honestly before Christ?
Does it move you toward holiness or repeatedly into secrecy?
Can you genuinely seek to glorify God in your body while doing it?
Those questions may produce different pastoral complexities, but they refuse both legalistic invention and convenient loopholes.
And perhaps that is why this subject hurts.
Because eventually it stops being about winning an argument concerning masturbation.
It becomes about surrender.
Jesus does not want one sanitized corner of you.
He wants you.
Your sexuality.
Your imagination.
Your loneliness.
Your browser history.
Your memories.
Your wounds.
Your body.
Your desires.
Your failures.
Your future.
All of you.
And the hands of Christ are not the hands of a disgusted Savior reluctantly touching contaminated people.
Those hands were pierced.
For sinners.
For the ashamed.
For people with histories they wish they could erase.
For people who promised “never again” and then did it again.
For people who have become experts at worshiping publicly while bleeding privately.
The Gospel is not that you finally became strong enough to save yourself.
The Gospel is that Christ came when you could not.
Died for sinners.
Rose victorious.
Calls us to repentance.
Forgives those who come to Him.
And begins making His people new.
So if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not have to write the details publicly.
But you can stop pretending.

And please remember: the comment section should never become a confessional booth for graphic details. Protect your privacy. Protect others. Confess specific sins to God and, where appropriate, to trustworthy people who can actually walk with you.

If someone came into your mind while reading this—someone fighting pornography, shame, secret sexual habits, loneliness, or the exhausting cycle of falling and hiding—send this article to them privately.
Not to embarrass them.
To remind them that there is still a door out of darkness.
It does not.
Only Jesus saves.
Christian giving is meant to come willingly from the heart, not through spiritual coercion.
Pray.
Share.
Save the teachings that help you.
Support the spread of biblical truth in whatever faithful way God enables you.
Because ultimately this ministry is not about building an audience around Gospel Warrior.
It is about pointing an audience beyond Gospel Warrior...
to Jesus.
The One who sees what happens after the bedroom door closes.
The One who knows what nobody else knows.
The One who refuses to call darkness light.
And the One whose grace is powerful enough that your darkest chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
You may be ashamed of the chapter you wrote in secret—but the nail-scarred hands of Jesus are still capable of writing redemption across the page.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU STOPPED READING ROMANS ONE VERSE TOO SOON
paragraphs: YOU STOPPED READING ROMANS ONE VERSE TOO SOON

Paul condemns sexual rebellion in Romans 1. Then, without giving the religious reader time to celebrate, he turns around and confronts the person holding the stones. Romans 1–2 is not merely somebody else’s indictment. It is a trapdoor beneath every self-righteous heart—and the only safe place left to fall is at the feet of Jesus.
There is a dangerous way to read Romans 1.
You can read every word Paul says about sexual sin…
nod your head…
underline the verses…
think about somebody else…
and completely miss the moment when Paul turns around and starts talking to you.
That is what makes Romans 1–2 so uncomfortable.
And so brilliant.
Paul allows the morally confident reader to listen while humanity’s rebellion is exposed.
Idolatry.
Lust.
Dishonorable passions.
Sexual disorder.
Greed.
Malice.
Envy.
Murder.
Strife.
Deceit.
Gossip.
Slander.
Pride.
Disobedience.
Heartlessness.
Ruthlessness.
The list keeps growing.
And somewhere in the middle of it, the religious person can begin feeling strangely comfortable.
“Yes, Paul.”
“Tell them.”
“Finally somebody is willing to call sin what it is.”
And then comes Romans 2:1.
One little Greek word changes the direction of the room.
Διό — Dio.
“Therefore.”
Not “meanwhile.”
Not “on an unrelated subject.”
Not “now let us begin an entirely different discussion.”
Therefore.
Paul has been building toward something.
And suddenly the person who thought he was sitting safely in the jury box discovers that Paul has called his name from the witness stand.
The Greek reads:
Διὸ ἀναπολόγητος εἶ, ὦ ἄνθρωπε πᾶς ὁ κρίνων
Dio anapologētos ei, ō anthrōpe pas ho krinōn.
A close rendering is:
“Therefore you are without excuse, O man, every one who judges.”
Read that again.
Slowly.
Because if Romans 1 has ever made you think primarily about “those people,” Romans 2 is coming for you.
Paul is not withdrawing what he has just said about sin.
He is destroying your ability to use what he said as a platform for self-righteous superiority.
That difference matters.
Deeply.

Romans 1:26–27 really does contain strong language about same-sex sexual behavior. Paul writes of women exchanging what he calls the natural use for what is παρὰ φύσιν — para physin, “contrary to nature,” and of men leaving the natural sexual relation with women and burning in desire toward one another.
The Greek is not vague:
αἵ τε γὰρ θήλειαι αὐτῶν μετήλλαξαν τὴν φυσικὴν χρῆσιν εἰς τὴν παρὰ φύσιν
and then:
ἄρσενες ἐν ἄρσεσιν
“males with males.”
We should not make Paul say less than he says because his words make modern ears uncomfortable.
But neither should we make Romans say less than Romans says because the next words make religious ears uncomfortable.
Paul's argument does not end at Romans 1:27.
It does not even end at Romans 1:32.
The chapter number “2” was not written by Paul as a giant spiritual stop sign telling Christians, “You may now close the Bible and go condemn somebody.”
Keep reading.
That may be one of the most important commands for anyone quoting Romans 1.
Keep.
Reading.
Because Paul is doing something devastating.
He first exposes humanity’s rejection of God.
Then he exposes the person who recognizes everyone else’s rebellion while remaining strangely blind to his own.
Romans 1 says sin is real.
Romans 2 says your neighbor's sin does not make you righteous.
Both are true.
And we desperately need both.
Some people want a Christianity that says, “Never judge anything. Sin is whatever you personally decide it is.”
Paul will not give us that Christianity.
Others want a Christianity that says, “Look how disgusting those sinners are. Thank God we aren't like them.”
Paul will not give us that Christianity either.
The Gospel destroys both illusions.
Truth without grace becomes a weapon in proud hands.
Grace without truth becomes permission to remain enslaved.
Jesus brings something infinitely better.
Truth that exposes us.
Grace that receives the repentant.
And power that begins transforming what grace has forgiven.
That is why Romans 2:1 is so frightening.
Paul continues:
ἐν ᾧ γὰρ κρίνεις τὸν ἕτερον, σεαυτὸν κατακρίνεις
“For in that which you judge the other, you condemn yourself.”
There is a difference between recognizing that something is sinful and assuming that recognizing somebody else's sin somehow establishes your righteousness.
Paul is attacking the second.
Biblical discernment is necessary.
Self-righteous condemnation is deadly.
The Christian can say, “That is sin.”
But the Christian can never truthfully add:
“And therefore I don't need mercy.”
Maybe your sexual history looks cleaner.
What about your pride?
Maybe you never committed the sin you condemn most loudly.
What about the sins you learned to hide?
What about the bitterness nobody sees?
The pornography erased from the browser history?
The flirtation you insist “never became physical”?
The fantasies you entertain but would never confess?
The greed dressed up as ambition?
The envy disguised as discernment?
The gossip introduced with, “I'm only telling you so you can pray”?
The hatred you renamed “righteous anger”?
The unforgiveness you have protected for fifteen years because the person who hurt you never apologized?
The secret addiction.
The manipulation.
The lies.
The cold marriage.
The private messages.
The ego.
The double life.
The Sunday smile.
The Monday compromise.
The worship song on your lips while resentment sits enthroned in your heart.
Be careful when somebody else's scandal makes you feel holy.
You may simply have found a sinner whose sins are easier for you to hate than your own.
That is the trap.
And Paul knew exactly how to spring it.
Romans 1:18 begins with the wrath of God being revealed against human ungodliness and unrighteousness.
By Romans 2, Paul is confronting the judging person.
Then the argument keeps tightening.
Gentile.
Jew.
Moralist.
Religious insider.
Possessor of the Law.
Hearer of the Law.
Everybody eventually finds himself standing beneath the same unbearable light.
Paul is not flattening every sin into identical earthly consequences.
Scripture does not require us to pretend every act produces exactly the same damage.
He is establishing something even more fundamental:
No category of sinner can manufacture righteousness by pointing at another category of sinner.
That is why Romans eventually arrives at the devastating conclusion:
“There is none righteous, no, not one.”
And:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
Romans is closing every escape route.
Imagine a courtroom.
You walk inside carrying a folder containing everybody else's failures.
You have screenshots.
Names.
Dates.
Verses.
Evidence.
You know exactly what is wrong with the culture.
You know what is wrong with your neighbor.
You know what is wrong with that denomination.
That politician.
That celebrity.
That gay couple.
That adulterer.
That addict.
That hypocritical pastor.
That rebellious child.
That compromised Christian.
That person who betrayed you.
You walk toward the Judge confident that your evidence will prove something about you.
You place the folder on His desk.
God opens it.
Then He looks at you.
And asks the question you were hoping would never come.
“What about you?”
Suddenly the room becomes quiet.
Because the Gospel does not ask whether you can identify darkness.
It asks what you will do when God's light exposes yours.
This is where Romans 2 becomes astonishingly beautiful.
Because after confronting the judging heart, Paul says something many Christians can quote but sometimes fail to practice.
Romans 2:4:
τὸ χρηστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ εἰς μετάνοιάν σε ἄγει
to chrēston tou theou eis metanoian se agei.
“The kindness of God leads you toward repentance.”
Notice where God's kindness leads.
Not toward pretending sin does not matter.
Toward repentance.
The Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia carries the idea of repentance, a change of mind and direction.
Grace is not God shrugging at our rebellion.
Grace is God meeting rebels with undeserved kindness and calling them home.
Repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is one of grace's miracles.
Jesus does not save us because our sins were insignificant.
He saves us because His mercy is greater.
The cross makes absolutely no sense if sin is trivial.
Why blood?
Why judgment?
Why substitution?
Why a crucified Messiah?
Why would the eternal Son of God enter our world, take flesh, suffer, bleed, and die if humanity merely needed encouragement?
The cross tells the truth about us.
Something is terribly wrong.
And the cross tells an even greater truth about God.
He loved sinners enough to come for us anyway.
That means Romans 1 should never become ammunition for bullying gay people.
Nor should Romans 2 become ammunition for erasing what Romans 1 says about sexual morality.
We do not have to amputate one chapter to protect the other.
We can let Paul speak.
Sexual sin is sin.
Heterosexual sexual sin is sin.
Homosexual sexual behavior is addressed as sin in Paul's argument.
Adultery is sin.
Fornication is sin.
Lust is sin.
And pride is sin.
Hypocrisy is sin.
Malice is sin.
Greed is sin.
Deceit is sin.
Gossip is sin.
Slander is sin.
Disobedience is sin.
Self-righteousness cannot save you.
Religious knowledge cannot save you.
Being heterosexual cannot save you.
Being respectable cannot save you.
Being conservative cannot save you.
Being progressive cannot save you.
Knowing Greek cannot save you.
Knowing Romans cannot save you.
Winning an argument about Romans cannot save you.
Jesus saves sinners.
That is where the entire conversation must eventually go.
Not toward “Which group can we hate?”
But:
Who will repent and come to Christ?
Maybe you are reading this and same-sex desire has been part of your struggle.
You are not beyond the reach of Jesus.
Maybe your battle is pornography.
You are not beyond His reach.
Maybe you committed adultery and destroyed something you once promised God you would protect.
Come to Christ.
Maybe you slept with someone outside marriage last night.
Come to Christ.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been doing.
Come to Christ.
Maybe your sexual history is not your deepest shame at all.
Maybe it is your cruelty.
Your pride.
Your anger.
Your secret drinking.
Your dishonesty.
Your obsession with money.
Your unforgiveness.
Your jealousy.
Your hunger for attention.
Your religious arrogance.
Come to Christ.
And maybe you have spent years looking down at people whose sins look different from yours.
Come to Christ.
There is room at the foot of the cross for the sexually broken person.
There is room for the hypocrite.
There is room for the religious fraud.
There is room for the ashamed.
There is room for the person who knew better.
There is room for the person who promised, “Never again,” and then did it again.
But nobody walks through the door carrying a résumé proving why he deserved admission.
We enter empty-handed.
Repentant.
Dependent.
Desperate for mercy.
And this is where the scandal becomes grace.
The scandal is not merely that sinners sinned.
That story is painfully predictable.
The scandal is that the holy God moved toward guilty people.
The scandal is that Christ died for the ungodly.
The scandal is that the cross has room for people we would have cancelled forever.
The scandal is that Jesus can take the person whose history seems permanently attached to his name and give him another identity.
Forgiven.
Justified.
Adopted.
Redeemed.
Beloved.
Being transformed.
Not because sin suddenly became acceptable.
Because Christ paid for sin and broke its claim upon those who belong to Him.
Christianity is not the announcement:
“Good people, congratulations. You correctly identified the bad people.”
Christianity announces:
The King came for rebels.
And once you understand that, it becomes harder to throw stones.
You can still call sin sin.
You can still hold biblical convictions.
You can still refuse to celebrate what Scripture forbids.
But you cannot stand beneath a blood-stained cross bragging about your superiority.
Look up.
The Man hanging there is innocent.
You are not.
Neither am I.
That changes the tone of everything.
We don't approach sinners as people who never needed rescue.
We approach them as beggars who found Bread.
We don't say, “Become like us and perhaps God will tolerate you.”
We say:
“Come meet the Savior who confronted our sin, carried our guilt, forgave our rebellion, and is still changing us.”
That is Christian witness.
Conviction without contempt.
Truth without cowardice.
Compassion without compromise.
Humility without surrendering Scripture.
Grace without pretending repentance is unnecessary.
And repentance without believing your worst chapter gets the final word.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe this article made you uncomfortable.
Good.
Romans should.
It was never written merely to provide ammunition for arguments.
It was written as part of an apostolic proclamation of the Gospel that strips human beings of boasting and drives sinners toward the righteousness God provides.
So before you share Romans 1 against somebody else, read Romans 2 over yourself.
Then keep reading.
Keep going until Romans 3 closes your mouth.
Keep going until Romans 5 shows Christ dying for the ungodly.
Keep going until Romans 6 tells you grace is not permission to continue comfortably in sin.
Keep going until Romans 8 announces that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Keep going until the question stops being:
“Who is worse?”
And becomes:
“Who needs Jesus?”
The answer is everyone.
The gay man needs Jesus.
The straight man needs Jesus.
The lesbian woman needs Jesus.
The adulterous husband needs Jesus.
The sexually pure but unbearably proud churchgoer needs Jesus.
The addict needs Jesus.
The pastor needs Jesus.
The skeptic needs Jesus.
The person writing this needs Jesus.
The person reading it needs Jesus.
There are no spectators at Calvary.
Only sinners.
And one Savior.
So if this exposed something you have hidden behind religious respectability, don't perform for the comments.
Be honest before God.
Not because typing a sentence saves anyone.
It doesn't.
Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when pride finally stops pretending.
Send it privately to the person who thinks Christians only know how to condemn.
Send it to the believer who has confused biblical conviction with spiritual superiority.
Send it to the struggling Christian who needs to remember that repentance still has a door—and that door has not been nailed shut.
Because there will come a day when somebody quotes Romans 1 as though Romans 2 never happened, or Romans 2 as though Romans 1 suddenly disappeared.
Come back and read them together.
Truth needs the whole text.
This ministry exists to keep putting Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ in front of people who desperately need it.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
If you want to help us glorify God through the continued spread of His Word, this is one practical way you can stand with the mission:
And there is something else we want believers to know.
We want Scripture opened.
Disciples strengthened.
Wounded believers reminded of grace.
Sleeping Christians awakened.
Sinners called to repentance.
And Jesus Christ proclaimed.

And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because there are moments when another believer needs to see that they are not the only one being convicted, fighting temptation, repenting, healing, and learning to live beneath grace.
“Christ is still healing me.”
That may be the testimony somebody else desperately needed tonight.
Because Romans 1 was never permission to hate the sinner.
Romans 2 was never permission to redefine sin.
And the Gospel was never permission for any of us to pretend we did not need the cross.
The finger you pointed at someone else's scandal may be the very thing God uses to lead your eyes back to your own need for grace.
And when you finally have nothing left to prove…
nothing left to hide…
nothing left to boast about…
there is still Jesus.
The Judge who knows your whole story is the Savior who gave His life to redeem sinners—and your worst chapter does not have to be the last chapter when Jesus holds the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN PORN DAMAGE YOUR FUTURE MARRIAGE?
paragraphs: CAN PORN DAMAGE YOUR FUTURE MARRIAGE?
You may delete the history from your phone. But what happens when the images have already followed you into the way you see love, intimacy, your future spouse…and yourself?
There is a person you may not have met yet.
Maybe you know their name already.
Maybe you have been praying for them.
Maybe somewhere tonight, they are praying for you.
They may one day stand across from you with trembling hands, look into your eyes, and promise before God to love you faithfully.
They may become the person who sees you without the filters.
Without the performance.
Without the carefully selected photographs.
Without the version of yourself everyone else gets.
Your spouse will eventually meet the person you have been becoming in secret.
And that is why this conversation matters.
Because pornography rarely introduces itself by saying:
“I want to affect the way you experience your future husband.”
“I want to affect the way you experience your future wife.”
“I want to teach your eyes to wander.”
“I want to train desire to demand novelty.”
“I want secrecy to become normal.”
“I want you to compare covenant intimacy with manufactured fantasy.”
No.
It usually begins much smaller.
Curiosity.
Loneliness.
A late night.
A private browser.
A difficult week.
A relationship that ended.
A body that feels restless.
A heart that feels rejected.
A phone nobody else can see.
One click.
Then another.
And sometimes something that began as a moment slowly becomes a pattern.
A pattern becomes a hiding place.
And the hiding place begins teaching the heart.
That is where Christians must speak carefully.
Not hysterically.
Not dishonestly.
Not with fake statistics.
Not by pretending every person who has ever watched pornography will inevitably destroy a marriage.
That claim would go beyond the evidence.

Research on pornography and relationships is complicated. Some studies have found pornography use to be unassociated with certain relationship outcomes, and findings can differ according to gender, whether use is solitary or shared, whether partners know about it, attitudes toward pornography, and differences between partners. Yet large-scale and longitudinal research has repeatedly found concerning associations between pornography use—particularly certain patterns of solitary or secret use—and lower relationship satisfaction, intimacy, sexual satisfaction, commitment, or other measures of relational well-being. A 2024 meta-analysis covering 41 studies and more than 70,000 participants found a small overall negative correlation between pornography use and sexual satisfaction. Other large studies have similarly found pornography use to be either unrelated or negatively associated with many measures of relationship quality, while emphasizing that association does not automatically prove causation.
So no, pornography does not mathematically guarantee a ruined future marriage.
But yes…
it can matter.
And Scripture takes us deeper than statistics ever could.
Jesus said:
“Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery:
But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
Matthew 5:27–28, KJV.
Look carefully at what Jesus does.
He takes the discussion from the bedroom…
to the heart.
The Greek behind Matthew 5:28 includes the verb ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō — referring here to desiring or lusting after someone.
Jesus is not teaching that merely noticing that another human being is attractive is identical to committing physical adultery.
The construction describes a look joined to lustful desire.
That distinction matters.
Because Christianity is not a religion of pretending human sexuality does not exist.
God created sexuality.
God created marriage.
God created the body.
The Christian answer to pornography is therefore not:
“Sex is dirty.”
The Christian answer is almost the opposite.
Sexuality is too meaningful to reduce people made in God's image to consumable images.
The body matters.
Desire matters.
Faithfulness matters.
The person on the screen matters.
Your future spouse matters.
And your heart matters to Jesus.
Pornography offers something radically different from covenant.
Pornography says:
Look without knowing.
Desire without serving.
Consume without committing.
Leave without grieving.
Change the person when you become bored.
Search again when the image no longer excites you.
Covenant says:
Know me.
Stay.
Serve.
Forgive.
Be known.
Be faithful when life becomes ordinary.
Remain when bodies age.
Love when emotions fluctuate.
Choose the same person again tomorrow.
Do you see the collision?
Pornography can train consumption.
Marriage requires communion.
Pornography can revolve around novelty.
Marriage asks for fidelity.
Pornography can hide behind secrecy.
Marriage needs truth.
Pornography can turn another person's body into something viewed primarily for personal gratification.
Christian marriage calls two people toward self-giving love.
And somewhere between those two visions of sexuality stands a human heart deciding what kind of lover it is becoming.
That may be the uncomfortable question beneath the question.
Not merely:
“Will pornography damage my future marriage?”
But:
“What is pornography teaching me to become before I enter it?”
Because a wedding does not magically erase yesterday's habits.
A ring is not a reset button.
You can wear white and still carry secrets.
You can say vows while carrying expectations your spouse never created.
You can enter a marriage desperately wanting covenant while still having desires shaped by years of private consumption.
And then comes the heartbreak nobody showed you on the screen.
Your spouse is human.
Their body is human.
Their energy changes.
Their appearance changes.
Pregnancy can change bodies.
Age changes bodies.
Illness changes bodies.
Stress changes desire.
Children interrupt schedules.
Work exhausts people.
Sometimes intimacy is beautiful.
Sometimes awkward.
Sometimes hilarious.
Sometimes tender.
Sometimes deeply emotional.
Sometimes one person needs patience more than passion.
Real marital intimacy is not edited.
It does not have a production crew.
It is two vulnerable human beings learning how to give themselves faithfully to one another.
And that vulnerability can be extraordinarily beautiful precisely because it is real.
Pornography cannot teach you that kind of love.
A screen cannot make a covenant with you.
An image cannot know your wounds.
A video cannot forgive you.
A fantasy cannot grow old beside you.
And pixels cannot hold your hand when somebody you love dies.
Pornography may promise intimacy without vulnerability.
But intimacy without vulnerability is not the same thing as being known.
Perhaps that is why this struggle can become so lonely.
You see bodies…
while your soul becomes increasingly hidden.
And eventually you may discover that the deepest hunger was never simply sexual.
Maybe you wanted comfort.
Maybe you wanted escape.
Maybe you wanted to feel wanted.
Maybe rejection left a hole in you.
Maybe abuse distorted the way you understood intimacy.
Maybe loneliness became unbearable.
Maybe anxiety needed somewhere to go.
Maybe pornography became anesthesia.
And anesthesia can numb pain without healing the wound.
Jesus wants the wound too.
Not merely your browser history.
Your heart.
That is why the Gospel must enter this conversation.
Because without the Gospel, an article like this becomes nothing more than:
“Porn is bad. Try harder.”
And some of you have tried harder.
You made promises.
You deleted apps.
You installed filters.
You cried.
You prayed.
You lasted three days.
Three weeks.
Three months.
Then something happened.
Stress.
Loneliness.
Temptation.
Opportunity.
And suddenly you were staring at the same screen again.
Afterward came the familiar voice:
“You are disgusting.”
“You are fake.”
“God is finished with you.”
“You might as well stop praying.”
“You will never change.”
Listen carefully.
Conviction and condemnation are not the same thing.
Conviction brings sin into the light so we can run toward Christ.
Condemnation whispers that because we sinned, we should hide from Him.
The Gospel says something far more devastating to our pride and far more beautiful to our shame:
Your sin is serious enough that Jesus had to die.
And His grace is powerful enough that He willingly came to save sinners.
The cross does not tell you pornography does not matter.
The cross tells you sin mattered so much that redemption cost blood.
Paul wrote to believers in Corinth:
“Flee fornication… What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you… and ye are not your own?
For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body…”
1 Corinthians 6:18–20, KJV.
The Greek command is striking:
φεύγετε — pheugete.
Flee.
Not negotiate.
Not see how close you can stand.
Not prove how strong you are.
Flee.

Paul's larger argument is rooted in identity: believers belong to Christ. They were “bought with a price.” Sexual holiness is therefore not presented merely as fear of consequences. It flows from redemption.
You belong to Jesus.
That changes the question.
Instead of:
“How much can I get away with?”
Grace teaches us to ask:
“How can the body Christ redeemed glorify the One who purchased me?”
That can mean doing something painfully practical.
Deleting access.
Installing accountability software.
Moving the phone out of the bedroom.
Stopping the secret account.
Unfollowing the page.
Refusing the private conversation feeding fantasy.
Telling a mature Christian you trust.
Speaking honestly with your spouse rather than building another layer of deception.
Seeking a qualified counselor when the pattern feels compulsive, traumatic, or deeply entrenched.
Getting pastoral help from someone who understands both holiness and grace.
Not because practical boundaries save you.
Jesus saves you.
But genuine repentance does not merely mourn the chains.
It begins walking away from the prison.
And maybe somebody reading this is thinking:
Too late.
You don't understand what I've watched.
Too late.
You don't know how long this has been happening.
Too late.
I'm already married.
Too late.
My spouse discovered it.
Too late.
Trust is broken.
Too late.
I promised God I would stop and went back again.
Then perhaps these are the two words your shame least wants you to hear:
Not necessarily.
Your past may have consequences.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Healing may be slow.
Your spouse may have legitimate wounds that cannot be rushed away with a Bible verse.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending betrayal did not hurt.
Repentance does not entitle us to immediate restoration of another person's trust.
Some marriages need serious counseling.
Some people need specialized help.
Some conversations will involve tears.
Some consequences cannot simply be deleted.
But Christianity is built around a Savior who walks into places human beings call hopeless.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted His people.
The Corinthian church had a deeply disordered sexual past, yet Paul could say of believers who had lived in serious sin:
“And such were some of you…”
1 Corinthians 6:11.
Were.
That little word is thunder.
Not because Christians become incapable of temptation.
Not because sanctification happens instantly.
But because sin no longer gets the final word over the identity of someone washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of Jesus Christ.
That is Gospel territory.
Scandal becoming testimony.
Shame meeting mercy.
Hiddenness meeting light.
Bondage meeting a Savior.
From scandal to grace…
because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe pornography has written chapters in your story you wish had never existed.
Jesus does not call evil good.
He does something infinitely better.
He redeems sinners.
He teaches eyes to see differently.
He teaches hearts to desire holiness.
He teaches men to see women as image-bearers rather than products.
He teaches women to see men as image-bearers rather than instruments.
He teaches husbands to love.
He teaches wives to love.
He teaches single believers that purity is not wasted waiting.
He teaches married believers that confession can be the beginning of truth rather than the end of hope.
He teaches ashamed people to walk into light.
And He teaches broken people that being tempted is not the same thing as being abandoned by God.
So perhaps your future marriage does not need a “perfect” version of you.
Perhaps it needs the version of you who learned how to repent.
The version who learned how to tell the truth.
The version who stopped protecting the secret and started protecting covenant.
The version who understands that another person's body is not merchandise.
The version who can say:
“I need help.”
The version who knows how to fall at the feet of Jesus and get back up.
The version who discovered that purity is not merely saying no to pornography.
It is learning to say yes to a better vision of people.
Yes to dignity.
Yes to covenant.
Yes to truth.
Yes to sacrificial love.
Yes to a mind increasingly occupied by what Paul calls true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, commendable, excellent, and praiseworthy in Philippians 4:8.
Maybe you are single.
Fight now.
Not because marriage will cure lust.
It won't.
Your future spouse was never designed to become your rehabilitation program.
Fight because Christ is worthy now.
Maybe you are dating.
Do not build engagement photographs over buried secrets.
Truth before vows is better than discovery after them.
Maybe you are married and hiding.

The next faithful step may be difficult, and wisdom matters greatly in how disclosure happens, especially where trauma, coercion, abuse, or serious relational instability exists. Seek mature pastoral and professional guidance when needed.
But stop calling darkness home.
Maybe you are the spouse who discovered the secret.
Your pain matters too.
You are not required to pretend betrayal did not wound you.
Healing cannot be demanded on somebody else's timetable.
Grace and truth belong together.
And if the person you love is genuinely repenting, remember this:
You are not their savior.
Jesus is.
That removes an impossible burden from both of you.
Be honest.
If confession and repentance have already begun changing your life, tell somebody what Jesus is doing.
Your testimony may become the sentence another ashamed believer desperately needed tonight.
And if somebody came to your mind while reading this, don't send this article as a weapon.
Send it as an invitation.
Save it too.
Not merely for yourself.
“I think this is destroying me.”
Then you will have something to send them that says both:
Come into the light.
And…
there is still grace.
It doesn't.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It cannot.
We should never place that burden on Scripture.
Give faithfully to God according to conscience, biblical conviction, and the teaching of your local church.
But voluntary financial support of Gospel work can be a genuine expression of generosity and partnership in ministry.
One share can place the Gospel in front of a person we may never reach ourselves.
One tag can begin a conversation.
One comment can tell another struggling believer, “You are not the only person fighting.”
One saved article can resurface exactly when someone needs it.
One faithful act of generosity can help keep Christian resources moving outward.
Come to Jesus.
Not when you have finally cleaned yourself.
Now.
Bring Him the browser history.
Bring Him the fantasies.
Bring Him the loneliness underneath them.
Bring Him the marriage that is hurting.
Bring Him the engagement you are afraid to jeopardize.
Bring Him the memories you wish you could erase.
Bring Him the relapse.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the tears.
Bring Him the person you became in darkness.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Walk into the light.
Receive forgiveness through Christ.
Then begin, one obedient decision at a time, becoming the person who no longer needs darkness in order to survive.
Because pornography may have trained your eyes.
It may have distorted expectations.
It may have wounded trust.
It may have complicated intimacy.
It may even have followed you farther than you ever intended.
But pornography is not sovereign over your future.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And the hands pierced for sinners are still capable of writing redemption across pages you thought were permanently ruined.
So when your past whispers, “Look what you became,” point to the cross and remember who has the final word.
Your secret may have written yesterday—but it does not get to hold the pen forever. Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ROMANS 1 SAYS WOMEN EXCHANGED “NATURAL RELATIONS”—BUT WHAT ARGUMENT IS PAUL ACTUALLY MAKING?
paragraphs: ROMANS 1 SAYS WOMEN EXCHANGED “NATURAL RELATIONS”—BUT WHAT ARGUMENT IS PAUL ACTUALLY MAKING?
Romans 1:26 Is About Sexual Sin—But If That Is All You See, You Have Missed Something Terrifying About Paul’s Warning
There is a sentence in Romans that people quote in arguments, whisper in uncomfortable conversations, throw across comment sections, and sometimes use like a weapon.
But Paul did not write it as a weapon for respectable sinners to use against people whose sins make them uncomfortable.
He wrote it in the middle of an indictment of the human race.
And if you read Romans 1:26 carefully enough, something unsettling happens.
You eventually realize Paul is not merely talking about “those people.”
He is talking about what happens to human beings when we exchange God for something else.
And sooner or later, that means he is talking about you.
About me.
About all of us.
Here is the line.
In the Greek text of Romans 1:26 we read:
“Διὰ τοῦτο παρέδωκεν αὐτοὺς ὁ θεὸς εἰς πάθη ἀτιμίας· αἵ τε γὰρ θήλειαι αὐτῶν μετήλλαξαν τὴν φυσικὴν χρῆσιν εἰς τὴν παρὰ φύσιν.”
A close rendering is:
“For this reason God gave them over to dishonorable passions; for their females exchanged the natural use for that which is contrary to nature.”
The wording matters.
Paul uses μετήλλαξαν — metēllaxan.
They “exchanged.”
He uses φυσικὴν — physikēn, meaning natural or according to nature.
He speaks of χρῆσιν — chrēsin, “use” or “relations,” a word functioning sexually in this context.
And then comes the phrase that has generated centuries of discussion:
παρὰ φύσιν — para physin.
“Contrary to nature.”

The Greek wording itself is not mysterious. The debate concerns what Paul means by it and how his argument functions within Romans as a whole. The immediate context makes clear that sexual relations are in view, and verse 27 removes much of the ambiguity because Paul immediately parallels the women with males abandoning sexual relations with females and desiring other males.
So we should not make the text say less than it says.
But neither should we make it say something Paul never said.

Paul does not discuss modern psychological categories of sexual orientation in this passage. He does not pause to distinguish every possible circumstance, biography, temptation, relationship, or contemporary identity category.
His language concerns actions within a much larger theological argument.
And that argument begins before Romans 1:26.
That is where things become uncomfortable.
Because before Paul speaks about exchanging sexual relations, he speaks about another exchange.
Romans 1:23 says humanity “exchanged the glory of the immortal God” for created images.
Then Romans 1:25 says they “exchanged the truth of God for a lie” and worshiped creation rather than the Creator.
Then Romans 1:26 uses exchange language again.
Do you see the pattern?
Glory exchanged.
Truth exchanged.
Natural relations exchanged.

Paul is describing disordered human existence flowing from disordered worship. Romans 1:18–32 repeatedly connects humanity’s refusal to honor the Creator with the corruption that follows when created things occupy the Creator’s place.
That means Romans 1 is not fundamentally a chapter about homosexual behavior with a few introductory verses about God.
It is an indictment of idolatry and human rebellion, within which Paul presents same-sex sexual behavior as one manifestation of humanity’s disorder after exchanging the Creator for creation.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because if you read Romans 1:26 and your first response is,
“Finally. A verse about them.”
Keep reading.
Paul is coming for your idols too.
Maybe yours does not involve sexuality.
Maybe your idol wears a suit.
Maybe it lives in your bank account.
Maybe it sleeps beside you.
Maybe people applaud yours.
Maybe yours stands behind a pulpit.
Maybe yours is your reputation.
Your career.
Your body.
Your politics.
Your relationship.
Your ministry.
Your anger.
Your need to be admired.
Your secret pornography.
Your heterosexual lust.
Your bitterness.
Your obsession with money.
Your religious pride.
Your carefully constructed Christian image.
Anything created can become spiritually catastrophic when it receives the trust, obedience, identity, devotion, or worship belonging ultimately to the Creator.
And that is the deeper horror of Romans 1.
Sin does not merely make us break rules.
Sin rearranges worship.
We exchange.
God for pleasure.
Truth for convenience.
Holiness for appetite.
Obedience for autonomy.
The Creator for creation.
And eventually we can become so accustomed to the exchange that what once disturbed our conscience begins to feel normal.
Then comes perhaps one of the most frightening expressions in Romans 1:
παρέδωκεν αὐτοὺς ὁ θεός — paredōken autous ho Theos.
“God gave them over.”
Paul repeats this idea three times—Romans 1:24, 1:26, and 1:28.
God gave them over.
God gave them over.
God gave them over.
Sometimes judgment does not look like lightning falling from heaven.
Sometimes judgment looks like God allowing rebellious humanity to travel farther down the road it demanded.
That should terrify every one of us.
There is a frightening possibility in sin: eventually the person saying, “God, leave me alone,” may experience something resembling the very thing requested.
Yet Romans does not end there.
Thank God.
Because Paul is building an argument larger than Romans 1.
And before the religious reader can become comfortable while watching “those sinners” condemned, Romans 2 turns the spotlight.
“Therefore you are without excuse, O man, every one of you who judges…”
The trap closes.
The person nodding through Romans 1 suddenly finds himself standing in the courtroom.
Then Paul keeps going until Romans 3 delivers the verdict no self-righteous human being wanted:
