The Jesus who went to the cross for sinners.
The Jesus who rose from the grave.
The Jesus who still forgives.
Still restores.
Still confronts.
Still heals.
Still calls sinners home.
And when you open your Bible tomorrow, remember the scene on the temple.
Remember the enemy holding a real verse inside a false invitation.
Remember Jesus refusing to separate one passage from the truth of another.
Then whisper something Satan will never sincerely whisper:
“Lord, Your Word is not here to serve my desires.
I am here to surrender my desires to You.”
Because the most dangerous Bible verse may not be the one you don't know.
It may be the one you know...
but refuse to let God finish explaining.
Don't merely carry Scripture in your mouth—let Christ write it into the places of your heart you have been afraid to surrender.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SARAH REALLY WAS ABRAHAM’S HALF-SISTER—THE FAMILY DETAIL MOST PEOPLE MISS
paragraphs: SARAH REALLY WAS ABRAHAM’S HALF-SISTER—THE FAMILY DETAIL MOST PEOPLE MISS
One sentence Abraham spoke in Genesis 20:12 changes the way many people read his marriage to Sarah—and exposes something even more astonishing about the kind of people God chooses to redeem.
There is a sentence buried in Genesis that many Christians have read dozens of times without realizing what they just read.
It is uncomfortable.
It raises questions.
And once you see exactly what the Hebrew says, you cannot simply pretend the verse is not there.

Abraham—the man Scripture would later call the father of those who believe—was standing before a pagan king trying to explain why he had introduced Sarah as his sister instead of openly identifying her as his wife.
Then Abraham said something startling.
Not merely that Sarah was like a sister.
Not merely that she was a distant relative.
He said:
“וְגַם־אָמְנָה אֲחֹתִי בַת־אָבִי הִוא אַךְ לֹא בַת־אִמִִּי וַתְּהִי־לִי לְאִשָּׁה”
Ve-gam omnah, achoti bat-avi hi, akh lo bat-immi; va-tehi-li le-ishah.
The sense is remarkably direct:
“And moreover, she truly is my sister, the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother; and she became my wife.”
Genesis 20:12.
Read those words again.
“My sister.”
“My father’s daughter.”
“Not my mother’s daughter.”
“She became my wife.”
On the plain reading of Abraham’s own explanation, Sarah was his paternal half-sister.
And suddenly one of the strangest moments in Abraham’s story becomes even stranger.
But stay with this, because the shocking family detail is not actually the deepest thing happening in Genesis 20.
The deepest thing is what God does with deeply complicated human beings.
The ancient Greek Septuagint preserves the same basic sense:
“καὶ γὰρ ἀληθῶς ἀδελφή μού ἐστιν ἐκ πατρός, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐκ μητρός· ἐγενήθη δέ μοι εἰς γυναῖκα.”
The crucial expressions are difficult to miss.
adelphē mou — “my sister.”
ek patros — “from [my] father.”
ouk ek mētros — “not from [my] mother.”
The Hebrew text and the ancient Greek translation therefore point in the same direction.
Yet careful Bible reading requires one qualification.

Genesis 11:29 names Sarai as Abram’s wife, but unlike Milcah, whose father Haran is explicitly identified, that verse does not give Sarai’s parentage. Later Jewish interpreters such as Rashi and Rashbam understood Abraham’s words through the broader biblical use of family terminology and associated Sarah with Abraham’s extended family rather than necessarily reading Genesis 20:12 as a statement of immediate biological half-siblinghood.
So we should not pretend that no interpretive discussion exists.
There is.
But neither should we soften what Genesis 20:12 itself says.

The most straightforward reading of Abraham’s explanation is exactly what makes modern readers uncomfortable: Sarah was his sister through his father but not through his mother, and she became his wife.
And somebody immediately asks:
“Then why would God allow that?”
That is where we have to stop forcing Abraham's world into ours.

Abraham lived centuries before the Mosaic covenant and before Israel received the detailed laws governing prohibited sexual relationships. Later, Leviticus would explicitly prohibit sexual relations with a sister, whether “your father’s daughter or your mother’s daughter” (Leviticus 18:9; compare Leviticus 20:17).
Scripture records history honestly.
That does not mean Scripture commands us to imitate everything it records.
The Bible tells us that Noah became drunk.
It does not command drunkenness.
The Bible tells us that Jacob had multiple wives.
It does not establish his household dysfunction as the Christian model for marriage.
The Bible tells us David committed adultery and arranged Uriah's death.
It certainly does not approve either act.
And the Bible tells us the uncomfortable details surrounding Abraham and Sarah without sanitizing their family story for modern readers.
That distinction matters.
Because the Bible is not propaganda for flawless religious heroes.
It is the revelation of a flawless God working through profoundly flawed humanity.
And maybe that is why this obscure sentence can hit us somewhere much deeper than genealogy.
Because some of us have spent years believing God only uses people with clean histories.
We imagine the people God chooses must have beautiful families, uncomplicated backgrounds, spotless reputations, perfect decisions and testimonies that sound safe enough to tell in church.
Then you actually read the Bible.
Abraham's story is complicated.
Sarah's story is complicated.
Jacob's family becomes painfully complicated.
Judah's story becomes scandalous.
Rahab enters the biblical story carrying a reputation most religious people would rather hide.
David's family history becomes stained with adultery, betrayal, violence and blood.
And eventually Matthew opens his Gospel and refuses to airbrush the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ.
The Bible keeps showing us something religious pride desperately wants to forget:
God does not need a spotless human history to accomplish a holy purpose.
That does not mean God celebrates sin.
It means sin does not get the final word when God enters the story.
And Abraham certainly needed grace.
The immediate context of Genesis 20 proves it.
Abraham and Sarah entered Gerar, territory ruled by Abimelech.
Abraham was afraid.
He believed men might kill him to obtain Sarah.
So once again he relied upon the arrangement he and Sarah had apparently used before:
“She is my sister.”
Technically, according to Abraham's explanation, the statement contained truth.
But it concealed the truth that mattered most.
Sarah was also his wife.
That is terrifyingly relatable.
Because deception does not always require inventing something false.
Sometimes we deceive by telling enough truth to protect ourselves while withholding enough truth to mislead someone else.
We say:
“I didn't lie.”
Maybe not technically.
But did you deliberately create a false impression?
“I didn't tell them anything untrue.”
But did you hide what you knew would change their understanding?
That is the uncomfortable mirror inside Genesis 20.
Abraham's statement could be factually defensible and still function deceptively.
And if we are willing to be spiritually honest, some of us know exactly what that feels like.
The hidden messages.
The deleted conversations.
The addiction described as “just stress.”
The bitterness renamed “discernment.”
The gossip disguised as a prayer request.
The emotional affair defended because “nothing physical happened.”
The pride renamed “standards.”
The greed renamed “ambition.”
The compromise renamed “survival.”
The secret browser history.
The private habit.
The relationship nobody knows about.
The version of ourselves we carefully present at church while praying nobody ever discovers what happens when the doors close.
Half-truths are incredibly useful when we desperately want to remain hidden.
Abraham was afraid he might die.
So fear started writing the strategy.
And fear has written some of our strategies too.
That is where this ancient story suddenly stops feeling ancient.
Maybe you have never stood before Abimelech.
But perhaps you have stood before consequences.
Perhaps you have thought:
“If people knew everything, they wouldn't look at me the same.”
“If my family discovered this, everything would change.”
“If the church knew what I struggle with, they would never trust me again.”
“If God really exposed me…”
And so you learned how to survive behind technically accurate sentences.
But there is Someone you cannot deceive with selective truth.
God.
He already knows.
And strangely, that may be the most comforting sentence in this entire article.
He already knows.
God knew Abraham's fear before Abraham entered Gerar.
God knew the arrangement between Abraham and Sarah.
God knew Abraham's motives.
God knew Sarah's history.
God knew the entire complicated family line.
And God did not discover any of it halfway through His plan and panic.
He knew whom He had called.
That does not excuse Abraham.
It magnifies God.
Because grace is not God discovering that you are better than everyone thought.
Grace is God knowing exactly how desperately you need mercy and moving toward sinners anyway.
That truth reaches its fullness not in Abraham…
but in Jesus Christ.
The Christian Gospel is not:
“Clean up your history so God can finally tolerate you.”
It is:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.”
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending sin never mattered.
He rewrites everything by dealing with sin at the cross.
That distinction is everything.
Christian grace is not divine denial.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace does not rename rebellion obedience.
Grace does not tell us repentance is unnecessary.
Jesus carried the judgment sinners deserved so that those who turn to Him in repentance and faith can receive what they could never earn—mercy, forgiveness, reconciliation and new life.
At Calvary, grace was not cheap.
It bled.
The Son of God was crucified.
Our sins were not brushed aside as insignificant.
Christ bore sin and rose victorious over death.
And that means your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Maybe your scandal looks nothing like Abraham's.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe you have become incredibly skilled at smiling while something inside you is collapsing.
Maybe your scandal isn't public.
Maybe it happened ten years ago.
Maybe it happened last night.
Maybe someone did something terrible to you and you have carried the wound so long that pain has started becoming your identity.
Maybe you are the one who caused the damage.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe you broke promises.
Maybe you walked away from God.
Maybe you are reading Christian articles while secretly wondering whether you even believe anymore.
Maybe you love Jesus, but there is still a battle inside you that you are ashamed to admit exists.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
The Gospel says Jesus is greater.
Repentance means we stop defending what Christ died to save us from.
We bring it into His light.
We confess.
We turn.
We stop negotiating with the darkness.
And we discover that the hands we expected to push us away are the nail-scarred hands of the Savior calling sinners home.
This is why Scripture's uncomfortable details matter.
If the Bible had erased every embarrassing chapter from the lives of the people God used, millions of broken people would eventually conclude there was no place for them.
Instead, Scripture leaves the scars visible.
Not to glorify the scandal.
To glorify the God of grace.
Abraham was not ultimately counted righteous because he possessed an impressive family history.
Genesis 15:6 says Abraham believed the LORD, and it was counted to him as righteousness.
The New Testament returns to that truth again and again.
Paul's argument in Romans 4 is not that Abraham earned salvation by being morally flawless.
His argument is about faith.
And the Gospel carries that story to its glorious fulfillment.
We are not saved because our family tree is clean.
We are not saved because our past is respectable.
We are not saved because nobody ever found out.
We are not saved because our church attendance outweighs our secrets.
We are saved by grace through faith, and salvation rests upon what Jesus Christ has accomplished, not upon our ability to manufacture an impressive religious résumé.
That is why perhaps the question Genesis 20:12 should leave inside your heart is not merely:
“Was Sarah really Abraham's half-sister?”
The text gives us very strong reason to understand Abraham as saying exactly that.
But there is another question waiting underneath it:
What does God do with people whose stories are complicated?
Look at Abraham.
Then keep reading Scripture.
Then look at the cross.
He redeems.
He forgives.
He disciplines.
He restores.
He transforms.
He calls sinners out of darkness.
And He refuses to let human scandal have greater authority than divine grace.
That is the heartbeat behind Gospel Warrior:
Not because every earthly consequence magically disappears.
Not because repentance erases history.
Not because grace gives us permission to continue deliberately in sin.
But because in Christ, your history no longer has the authority to determine your eternal identity.
Jesus does.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail.
But you can take the first honest step.
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need proof that restoration is possible.
And please don't keep this message trapped on this page.
Not because an algorithm deserves it.
Because someone you know may be smiling publicly and drowning privately.
Someone may need to discover tonight that Christianity is not a museum for people with spotless histories.
It is the proclamation that there is a Savior for sinners.
And yes—even share it with the skeptic who thinks the Bible hides its difficult passages.
It doesn't.
Scripture is often brutally honest about the people inside its pages.
One day shame may try to convince you that God only works through people with uncomplicated stories, and you may need to read this again.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding you spiritually, helping you understand Scripture, pointing you toward repentance, strengthening your faith and keeping Jesus Christ before your eyes, consider staying close to this mission.
But hear this clearly because biblical integrity matters:
Scripture teaches generosity, but it also teaches that giving must come from the heart rather than manipulation or compulsion.
That kind of support matters.
So does sharing.
Some people can financially support the work.
Others cannot.
Nobody should be ashamed for that.
Give because you want Christ proclaimed.
Share because somebody needs the Gospel.
Tag because you know people who need truth.
Save because there are truths we forget when shame gets loud.
Follow because none of us outgrows our need for Scripture.
But whatever you do, never confuse supporting Gospel ministry with purchasing God's favor.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot donate enough money to make God owe you salvation.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
That is the Gospel.
And maybe that is why Abraham's uncomfortable family detail matters more than we first realized.
Sarah really was presented in Genesis 20:12 as Abraham's sister through his father and not through his mother.
It is strange to modern ears.
It deserves careful interpretation.
It should never be sensationalized beyond what Scripture actually says.
But hidden inside that uncomfortable verse is a reminder stretching across the entire Bible:
God has never depended upon perfect human beings to accomplish His perfect purposes.
The Bible does not need to clean up Abraham before telling you his story.
And Jesus does not need you to manufacture a fake past before you come to Him.
Come honestly.
Come repentant.
Come believing.
Bring the chapter you wish you could erase.
Bring the secret.
Bring the failure.
Bring the shame.
Bring the questions.
Bring the wounds.
Bring the mess you cannot rewrite.
Then place it before the One who was crucified for sinners and walked out of the grave.
Because your scandal may explain where you have been.
But when Jesus takes hold of a surrendered life, your scandal does not get to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN THE BIBLE ANSWER QUESTIONS ABOUT MASTURBATION WHEN IT NEVER DIRECTLY NAMES THE ACT?
paragraphs: CAN THE BIBLE ANSWER QUESTIONS ABOUT MASTURBATION WHEN IT NEVER DIRECTLY NAMES THE ACT?

The Bible never says the word. Jesus never directly names the act. Yet what Scripture says about lust, desire, self-control, the body, holiness, and grace may reach far deeper than the question most Christians are afraid to ask.
There is a question millions of Christians have probably asked in silence.
Not from a church pew.
Not during Bible study.
Not while the pastor was standing nearby.
But alone.
Behind a locked door.
Late at night.
After everyone else had gone to sleep.
Maybe after deleting the browser history.
Maybe after promising God for the tenth, hundredth, or thousandth time:
“Lord... I won't do it again.”
And then came the shame.
That terrible silence afterward.
The ceiling above you.
The phone beside you.
Your thoughts accusing you.
And one question you were almost afraid to ask God:
“Did I just sin?”
Then perhaps another:
“If masturbation is really sinful, why doesn't the Bible simply say so?”
That is not a foolish question.
And Christians should not be afraid of it.
Because if we have to invent a Bible verse to defend our position, our position is already in trouble.
So before going any further, something needs to be said clearly:
The Bible does not directly name masturbation or give a command that literally says, “You shall not masturbate.”
We should not pretend otherwise.
But that does not mean Scripture has nothing meaningful to say about it.
The Bible does something deeper.
It forces us to examine what is happening not merely with our hands...
but with our hearts.
And that distinction changes everything.
One of the passages sometimes used in discussions about masturbation is Genesis 38 and the story of Onan. But we need to handle Scripture honestly.

Onan was commanded to fulfill his responsibility toward his deceased brother's widow and provide offspring for his brother. Instead, Genesis says that when he went in to her, he deliberately prevented conception because he knew the offspring would not belong to him.
The Hebrew text says:
וְשִׁחֵת אַרְצָה לְבִלְתִּי נְתָן־זֶרַע לְאָחִיו
In context, he wasted or destroyed his seed on the ground “so as not to give offspring to his brother.”
That final phrase matters.

The passage is describing intercourse followed by Onan's deliberate prevention of conception in order to deny his brother offspring. The text does not describe masturbation. Using Genesis 38 as though it were a straightforward prohibition of masturbation goes beyond what the passage actually says.
And Christians should never need to distort Scripture in order to defend holiness.
Truth does not need our help.
So if Genesis 38 is not a direct prohibition, where do we go?
We go to Jesus.
And suddenly the question becomes much more uncomfortable.
Because Jesus moves the conversation away from merely asking:
“What did my body do?”
and toward asking:
“What was my heart doing?”
Jesus said in Matthew 5:28:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ
“But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
The critical expression is:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
—looking in order to desire/lust after her.
Jesus is addressing intentional, cultivated sexual desire toward another person outside the righteous boundaries He is teaching.
He takes sexual holiness beyond external behavior and brings it into the secret courtroom of the heart.
And now the question changes.
Not simply:
“Did masturbation happen?”
But:
What was happening inside me while it happened?
Was pornography involved?
Was someone being mentally undressed?
Was a person who bears God's image being converted into material for private sexual gratification?
Was fantasy deliberately cultivated?
Was I rehearsing in imagination what I would recognize as sinful if acted out physically?
Was this bringing my desires under Christ...
or training my desires to demand whatever they wanted?
Those questions are harder than searching for a verse containing a particular English word.
Because Jesus refuses to let us hide behind technicalities.
You can keep your body away from another person's body and still cultivate a sexual world inside your imagination that Jesus wants to confront.
And yet another distinction matters.
Sexual desire itself is not identical to sinful lust.

God created human beings as embodied, sexual creatures. Temptation is not automatically the same thing as surrender. Bodily arousal is not automatically a moral failure. An unwanted thought appearing in your mind is not the same as deliberately welcoming, feeding, and enjoying that thought.
Otherwise Christians can become trapped in endless self-surveillance, condemning themselves merely for having bodies.
That is not the freedom of the Gospel.
The biblical question is what we do with desire.
Paul writes:
Πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε καὶ ἐπιθυμίαν σαρκὸς οὐ μὴ τελέσητε
“Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.”
And later he names part of the Spirit's fruit:
ἐγκράτεια — enkrateia — self-control.
Then comes the piercing statement:
“Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.”
Christianity is therefore not a religion of pretending desire doesn't exist.
It is the miracle of desire being brought under a new King.
Jesus.
That brings us to one of the most revealing biblical tests of all.
Paul writes:
Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος
“All things are lawful for me... but I will not be dominated by anything.”
Then he says:
τὸ δὲ σῶμα... τῷ Κυρίῳ
“The body... [is] for the Lord.”
And finally:
δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν Θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν
“Glorify God in your body.”
That may be one of the most important biblical principles in this entire discussion.
Because perhaps the question isn't merely:
“Can I get away with this?”
Maybe the better question is:
“Can Christ be Lord here too?”
In my bedroom.
In my imagination.
In my browser.
In my loneliness.
In my hormones.
In my sexual frustration.
In the places nobody sees.
Especially there.
Because Christianity was never supposed to be Jesus owning Sunday morning while secret appetites own Saturday night.
Paul says something similar in 1 Thessalonians 4.
Τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν
“This is the will of God, your sanctification.”
He continues by calling believers away from sexual immorality and toward holiness and honor rather than πάθει ἐπιθυμίας — pathei epithymias, “passion of lust.”
Notice the direction.
Sanctification.
Holiness.
Honor.
Not merely rule keeping.
Transformation.
That means a Christian examining masturbation should probably ask questions like these in the privacy of the heart:
Can I do this without intentionally lusting after someone?
Can I do it without pornography?
Can I do it without fantasies I know dishonor God or another person?
Does it increasingly control me?
Do I run to it whenever I am lonely, rejected, stressed, angry, bored, anxious, or emotionally wounded?
Am I using sexual release as medication for a soul that actually needs something deeper?
Can I freely abstain?
Can I honestly bring this behavior before Christ without hiding?
Is it producing greater self-control...
or less?
Those questions expose something a simple yes-or-no rule sometimes misses.
Because for some people, the real story underneath the sexual behavior isn't primarily pleasure.
It is pain.
Loneliness.
Rejection.
Stress.
A broken relationship.
A marriage starving for intimacy.
A childhood wound nobody knows about.
A pornography habit that started as curiosity and slowly became captivity.
Maybe you weren't searching for sex anymore.
Maybe you were searching for five minutes in which you didn't have to feel what hurt.
And afterward...
the pain was still there.
Except now shame was sitting beside it.
That is where this conversation must become unmistakably Christian.
Because the Gospel is not:
“Clean yourself up so Jesus will finally tolerate you.”
The Gospel is that sinners who cannot rescue themselves are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ did not go to the cross because respectable people needed motivational advice.
He went because sinners needed redemption.
The person secretly fighting sexual sin is not beyond the reach of the blood of Christ.
The pornography addict is not beyond His reach.
The believer who fell again after swearing, “Never again,” is not instructed to run away from Christ until becoming worthy.
Run to Christ.
Repentance is not hiding from Jesus until you become clean enough to approach Him.
Repentance turns around and comes home.
There is an enormous difference between conviction and hopeless condemnation.
Conviction says:
“Bring this into the light.”
Condemnation whispers:
“Hide. God is disgusted with you. You might as well keep going.”
One leads toward Christ.
The other drives you deeper into darkness.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that darkness feels like.
You pray.
You resist.
You fall.
You repent.
You last three days.
Maybe three weeks.
Then one lonely night destroys your confidence again.
And eventually you stop believing freedom is possible.
You begin introducing yourself to yourself by your failure.
“I'm dirty.”
“I'm addicted.”
“I'm fake.”
“I'm disgusting.”
“God must be tired of me.”
Listen carefully.
Your sin should never be trivialized.
But neither should the cross.
Jesus did not shed His blood so that your worst night could become your permanent name.
Repentance means sin is taken seriously precisely because grace is real.
Bring the browser history.
Bring the fantasy.
Bring the relapse.
Bring the loneliness.
Bring the compulsive behavior.
Bring the shame you've been carrying since adolescence.
Bring the secret nobody at church knows.
Bring all of it into the light of Christ.
And if the pattern has become compulsive, don't fight completely alone.
Find a mature, trustworthy Christian.
A pastor.
A mentor.
An accountability partner.
If necessary, a qualified counselor.
Remove easy access to pornography.
Change routines.
Stop negotiating with triggers you already recognize.
Put distance between yourself and whatever repeatedly pulls you toward sin.

Jesus' language immediately after His teaching about lust is intentionally severe: if your eye causes you to stumble, remove the source of stumbling. His point is not casual self-harm; it is radical seriousness toward sin.
Sometimes we pray:
“Jesus, deliver me.”
And Jesus begins showing us doors we need to close.
Apps we need to delete.
Accounts we need to unfollow.
Conversations we need to have.
Secrets we need to confess.
Patterns we need to interrupt.
Hours of the night we need to stop spending alone with a phone.
Freedom can become painfully practical.
But do not confuse fighting with earning salvation.
You do not defeat sin so Jesus will finally love you.
You fight sin because in Christ you are being called out of slavery and into holiness.
The cross is not permission to make peace with bondage.
The cross is where bondage loses its claim to be your master.
So can the Bible answer questions about masturbation when it never directly names the act?
Yes—but we must state carefully how.
Not by pretending there is a verse explicitly naming masturbation.
There isn't.
Not by forcing Genesis 38 to say something it does not say.
But by allowing the whole counsel of Scripture to examine the desires, fantasies, habits, mastery, motives, conscience, and fruit surrounding the behavior.

Where masturbation is joined to pornography, deliberate lust, sexually immoral fantasy, objectification, or an appetite that has become master rather than servant, Scripture gives substantial reason for the Christian to reject what is happening.

Where those factors are claimed to be absent, Christians have disagreed about the moral status of the physical act considered entirely by itself. Scripture's silence about the specific act means we should be cautious about claiming more explicit biblical certainty than the text itself gives.
But biblical silence about a particular word does not mean biblical silence about your heart.
And maybe that is the sentence somebody needed tonight.
Because God is interested in something bigger than whether you can locate a loophole.
He wants you.
Not merely your church attendance.
Not merely your Christian Facebook posts.
Not merely your worship playlist.
You.
Your body.
Your thoughts.
Your desires.
Your wounds.
Your sexuality.
Your secret life.
Your midnight life.
The version of you nobody else sees.
Jesus wants Lordship there too.
And if this article exposed something you've been hiding, you don't need to perform for us.
But you can stop pretending.
Maybe your comment becomes the moment another Christian realizes:
I'm not the only one.
And if someone came into your mind while reading this—someone struggling quietly, someone drowning in pornography, someone convinced God wants nothing more to do with them—send this article to them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose them.
Send it because sometimes love knocks on a locked door.
It doesn't.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior replaces generosity to your local church or automatically constitutes the biblical tithe.
It doesn't.
We will never sell you grace.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
But voluntary Christian generosity can help Gospel-centered ministry continue.
Your support can help the message travel farther.
More articles.
More discipleship resources.
More biblical teaching.
More opportunities for a wounded person scrolling alone at midnight to encounter something that points them away from despair and toward Jesus Christ.
And sharing costs nothing.
Every time you share Gospel Warrior content publicly, you help carry the message beyond the people we could reach alone.
Jesus Christ is the treasure.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not merchandise.
Jesus.
We exist to point toward Him.

And if all this article accomplishes is making one person close the pornography, come out of hiding, confess the truth, seek help, repent, and discover again that the arms of Christ are still open to the repentant sinner...
then praise belongs to God.
Because your scandal does not get the final sentence.
Your secret does not get the final sentence.
Your relapse does not get the final sentence.
Your shame does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
So tonight, when the room becomes quiet again...
when nobody is watching...
when temptation begins negotiating...
remember:
You are not merely deciding what to do with your body.
You are deciding what kind of desire you will feed, what kind of person you are becoming, and whether even this hidden room of your life will be surrendered to the Lord who bought you with a price.
And if you fall?
Don't build a house in the dirt.
Come home.
Repent.
Get up.
Reach for Christ again.
Grace does not tell you that bondage doesn't matter.
Grace tells you bondage doesn't have to be the end of your story.
The secret you thought would make Jesus walk away may become the very place where you finally discover how desperately you need His grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ARE TATTOOS SINFUL FOR CHRISTIANS TODAY?
paragraphs: ARE TATTOOS SINFUL FOR CHRISTIANS TODAY?
The Bible’s Answer May Expose a Much Deeper Question About Your Heart
Maybe the tattoo is already on your skin.
Maybe you're sitting in a tattoo shop scrolling through designs.
Maybe your son came home with one and you're furious.
Maybe your daughter wants a tiny cross on her wrist.
Maybe you've been a Christian for twenty years and somebody looked at the ink covering your arm, looked you straight in the eyes, and said:
“You know the Bible says that's a sin, right?”
And suddenly you weren't discussing ink anymore.
You were discussing whether God was disappointed in you.
That's where this gets personal.

Because somewhere between Leviticus, Christian tradition, personal conviction, modern culture, and our tendency to judge what we can see, a surprisingly complicated biblical question has sometimes been reduced to one sentence:
“Christians aren't supposed to have tattoos.”
But is that actually what Scripture teaches?
Before you answer, stay with me.
Because this article isn't ultimately about tattoos.
It's about something much closer to your heart.
And by the end, you may discover that the most dangerous mark a Christian can carry isn't necessarily the one everybody can see.
The verse almost everyone reaches for is Leviticus 19:28.
The Hebrew reads:
"וְשֶׂרֶט לָנֶפֶשׁ לֹא תִתְּנוּ בִּבְשַׂרְכֶם וּכְתֹבֶת קַעֲקַע לֹא תִתְּנוּ בָּכֶם"
Transliterated in part:
...u-khetovet qa‘aqa lo tittenu bakhem...
The traditional sense is:
You shall not make cuts in your flesh for the dead or put tattoo marks upon yourselves.

The unusual Hebrew expression כְּתֹבֶת קַעֲקַע — ketovet qa‘aqa refers to an inscribed or tattooed mark. Ancient Jewish interpretation likewise understood the prohibition as involving writing or marking impressed into the flesh.
So let's not dodge the uncomfortable part.
Yes.
There really is a biblical verse prohibiting tattoo-like markings.
We don't need to pretend it isn't there.
But responsible Bible reading asks another question:
What covenant is being addressed?
What is happening in the surrounding passage?
And how does a command given to ancient Israel relate to followers of Jesus under the New Covenant?
Leviticus 19 contains commands covering worship, holiness, agriculture, social justice, sexual morality, treatment of neighbors, pagan practices, and Israel's distinct life as God's covenant people.
And notice something easily overlooked in verse 28.
The tattoo prohibition appears alongside:
“cuttings in your flesh for the dead.”
That matters.

The surrounding material is concerned with Israel remaining distinct from practices associated with the nations around them, including practices connected with the dead and forbidden religious customs.
That doesn't make Leviticus irrelevant.
Far from it.
“All Scripture is breathed out by God” (2 Timothy 3:16).
But Christians do not faithfully interpret the Old Testament merely by finding a command and transferring it unchanged into the church.
If we did, consistency would require Christians to observe Israel's entire covenant legislation in precisely the same manner.
The New Testament itself forces us to think more carefully than that.
Jesus fulfilled the Law.
The apostles wrestled explicitly with which requirements were to be imposed upon Gentile believers.
And nowhere in the New Testament do Jesus or the apostles issue a universal command saying:
“You shall never receive a tattoo.”
That distinction is important.
But don't run to the tattoo shop yet.
Because “the New Testament doesn't explicitly prohibit this” is not the same thing as “therefore anything I want is automatically wise and pleasing to God.”
And this is where the question becomes uncomfortable for everybody.
The person with tattoos.
The person without tattoos.
The pastor.
The rebellious teenager.
The conservative grandmother.
The Christian influencer.
You.
Me.
Paul writes:
The Greek contains the striking words:
τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς... ἁγίου πνεύματος
to sōma hymōn naos... hagiou pneumatos
Your σῶμα — sōma, your body, is a ναός — naos, a sanctuary or temple, of the Holy Spirit.
And Paul continues:
“You are not your own.”
Then:
“You were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body.”
That is the principle Christians cannot escape.
But even here we must respect context.
First Corinthians 6 is addressing sexual immorality. Paul did not write this passage as a tattoo regulation.
So using “your body is a temple” as though Paul were specifically saying “therefore tattoos are sinful” goes beyond what the passage itself says.
Yet the underlying truth absolutely matters.
Your body belongs to Christ.
Which means the Christian question isn't merely:
“Am I allowed to tattoo this body?”
It is:
“Jesus, what do You want me to do with the body You redeemed?”
That changes everything.
Christian freedom isn't:
“I can do whatever I want.”
Christian freedom is being liberated from slavery to sin so that your life can belong joyfully to Jesus.
Sometimes we desperately want Christianity to give us a giant list.
Allowed.
Forbidden.
Allowed.
Forbidden.
Because lists can be easier than surrender.
But discipleship often asks a more penetrating question:
Why do you want it?
That's where the ink reaches the heart.
Maybe you want a tattoo commemorating someone you loved.
Maybe it's artistic.
Maybe it's cultural.
Maybe you want Scripture permanently written somewhere you can see it.
Maybe you survived something horrific and the tattoo represents the fact that you're still here.
Maybe you're getting one because everybody around you has one.
Maybe you're trying to prove you're not like your Christian parents.
Maybe you're trying to look dangerous.
Maybe you're desperate for somebody to notice you.
Maybe you're putting something on your body that celebrates darkness, sexual immorality, violence, occult spirituality, hatred, idolatry, or something else clearly contrary to Christ.
Those are not morally identical situations.
The needle can look the same.
The heart beneath it can be completely different.
Scripture repeatedly moves believers beyond mere external appearance toward motives, conscience, love, holiness, witness, and God's glory.
Paul gives another principle:
“Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.”
Whatever you do.
That reaches considerably farther than tattoos.
Can I place this image on my body to the glory of God?
Can I choose it with a clear conscience?
Does it celebrate something Christ calls evil?
Am I acting from faith?
Am I being driven by rebellion?
Am I seeking attention because somewhere inside I desperately need people to tell me I'm valuable?
Could this unnecessarily damage my witness in the community or ministry where God has placed me?
Am I ignoring wise counsel because I have already decided what I want?
And perhaps the most revealing question:
If Jesus told me no, would I still want Jesus more than I want the tattoo?
There it is.
Because now we aren't really talking about ink anymore.
We're talking about lordship.
Romans 14 deals with disputed matters among believers, particularly food and days. It should not simply be turned into a “tattoo chapter.”
But its principles concerning conscience and faith are deeply relevant to decisions where Scripture does not provide the kind of direct New Testament prohibition some Christians wish it did.
Paul concludes:
“Whatever is not from faith is sin.”
The Greek centers upon πίστις — pistis, faith. In its actual context Paul is warning someone against acting while doubting whether the action is right before God.
So if your conscience is screaming,
“Don't do this,”
don't bulldoze your conscience simply because somebody on social media gave you permission.
Stop.
Pray.
Search Scripture.
Seek mature counsel.
Examine your motive.
You don't need to prove your freedom.
And sometimes maturity means having the freedom to do something and choosing not to do it because love, wisdom, witness, or conscience matters more.
But now we need to speak to another person.
The Christian looking at somebody covered in tattoos and quietly deciding:
“They can't really know Jesus.”
Be careful.
You may be committing a much older sin while condemning somebody else's skin.
Humans are remarkably good at measuring spirituality by visible things.
We see the tattoo.
God sees the heart.
We see sleeves of ink.
God sees pride.
We see piercings.
God sees unforgiveness.
We see somebody walk into church looking completely unlike us, and before they've reached their seat we've written a biography about their spiritual condition.
Meanwhile, somebody else walks in wearing a beautiful suit, carrying an expensive Bible, knowing every worship lyric...
and secretly hasn't spoken honestly to God in months.
One person's scars are visible.
Another person's idols wear church clothes.
Jesus reserved some of His strongest rebukes not for people whose brokenness was obvious, but for religious people who polished the outside while corruption remained within.
That should frighten every Christian who has learned how to look holy.
Because a clean arm does not equal a clean heart.
And tattooed skin does not put somebody beyond the blood of Jesus Christ.
Maybe that's exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
Perhaps you got tattoos before Christ.
Maybe some of them represent a life you don't live anymore.
Maybe there's an old symbol on your body connected to addiction, a relationship, a gang, an occult practice, hatred, rebellion, sexuality, or a version of yourself you wish you could bury forever.
And every time you look in the mirror, your past looks back.
Listen carefully.
Jesus is not intimidated by your history.
The Gospel does not say:
“Clean your skin and perhaps God will accept you.”
The Gospel announces that sinners are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ died for our sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
Repentance isn't pretending the past didn't happen.
Grace isn't calling evil good.
Grace is God meeting guilty people with forgiveness through Christ and transforming those who turn to Him.
Maybe the tattoo remains.
But the person wearing it doesn't have to remain the same.
That's Gospel.
Your body can carry evidence of yesterday while your life carries evidence of resurrection.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Corinthian church contained people with deeply sinful histories.
Yet Paul could write of believers who had been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.
Grace does not rewrite history by pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace rewrites what the scandal gets to become.
A testimony.
A warning.
A scar.
A place where someone else sees that Jesus still saves people.

And perhaps that's why this question cannot end with a simplistic universal declaration that every modern tattoo is automatically sinful—or with the equally careless declaration that tattoos never matter spiritually.
Scripture demands something deeper.
If the tattoo itself contains or celebrates what God condemns, the issue is clear.
If your motivation is rebellion against God, the issue is deeper than the ink.
If you cannot proceed in faith and with a clear conscience, don't violate your conscience.
If your choice disregards love, wisdom, stewardship, or your Christian witness, those things deserve serious consideration.
If you're merely asking, “How close can I get to sin without technically sinning?” your question has already exposed something.

But if you're asking whether the Bible explicitly declares every modern tattoo on every Christian inherently sinful simply because pigment has been permanently placed beneath the skin, Scripture does not give us grounds to make that sweeping New Covenant declaration.
And if you already have tattoos?
Don't spend another night imagining that Jesus is standing outside the door of salvation inspecting your skin before deciding whether His blood is sufficient for you.
Come to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Bring Him the beautiful parts.
Bring Him the embarrassing parts.
Bring Him your addictions.
Bring Him your pride.
Bring Him the secret browser history.
Bring Him the religious hypocrisy.
Bring Him the anger nobody knows about.
Bring Him the tattoo you love.
Bring Him the tattoo you regret.
Bring Him the memory attached to it.
Bring Him everything.
Repentance means turning from sin toward God.
Faith means trusting Christ rather than yourself to save you.
Grace means you stop pretending you can erase your own record.
Jesus didn't go to the cross because humanity needed better cosmetics.
He went because humanity needed resurrection.
And maybe you've spent years hiding because Christians saw your appearance before they saw your humanity.
I'm sorry that happened.
But don't confuse Jesus with people who represented Him badly.
Look at Christ Himself.
The crucified Savior knows what it is to have His body wounded.
He knows rejection.
He knows public shame.
He knows what it means to be stared at.
And He willingly bore our sins so sinners could be reconciled to God.
The deepest mark defining the Christian isn't ink.
It is ownership.
“You were bought at a price.”
Christ's.
Redeemed.
Forgiven.
Being transformed.
So perhaps the better question tonight isn't:
“Can Christians get tattoos?”
Perhaps it's:
Does Jesus have all of me?
My body.
My image.
My sexuality.
My money.
My ambition.
My phone.
My relationships.
My hidden habits.
My wounds.
My reputation.
My past.
My future.
Everything.
Because you can have John 3:16 tattooed across your chest and still refuse to surrender your heart to Christ.
And you can have no tattoo anywhere on your body while pride quietly writes its name across your soul.
Jesus wants deeper than skin.
He wants you.
If this exposed something you've been hiding, don't turn the comments into another theological battlefield.
Turn them into testimony.
Someone reading silently may need to discover that there are other people whom grace found in places they thought God would never enter.

Share it not because every Christian must agree on every disputed matter, but because Christians desperately need to learn how to open the Bible, respect its context, examine their hearts, and keep Jesus Christ at the center.
You may need to read it again when this question stops being theoretical and becomes personal.
It doesn't.
Not because supporting this ministry saves you.
Only Jesus saves.
Scripture says Christian giving should come from the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).

If you already give your tithes and offerings through your local church or elsewhere, supporting Gospel Warrior need not replace that stewardship. Consider this simply another opportunity for voluntary generosity toward Gospel work you believe is bearing fruit.
If you feel led to stand with us:
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help tremendously.
Send it privately to someone wrestling with this question.
Pray for the ministry.
Because sometimes the article you almost didn't share becomes the article somebody reads alone at 2:00 in the morning while wondering whether God could possibly still want them.
And perhaps that's the sentence they need tonight:
The marks of your past may remain on your skin, but they do not get the final word over your soul—Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WAS SODOM DESTROYED ONLY BECAUSE OF SEXUAL SIN? EZEKIEL ADDS DETAILS MANY PEOPLE FORGET
paragraphs: WAS SODOM DESTROYED ONLY BECAUSE OF SEXUAL SIN? EZEKIEL ADDS DETAILS MANY PEOPLE FORGET
We remember what happened behind Sodom’s doors. God also remembered what was happening outside them. And Ezekiel’s description may make the story far more uncomfortable than you expected.
There is something frightening about reading a Bible story for years and suddenly realizing you have been standing safely outside of it.
Sodom.
Just hearing the name can make people think they already know the sermon.
Sexual immorality. Perversion. Judgment. Fire.
And Scripture absolutely does speak about Sodom’s sexual wickedness. We should never erase what the Bible refuses to erase.
But then God says something through Ezekiel that many Christians rarely hear when Sodom is discussed.
Something that moves the spotlight.
Something that takes a story we may have used to point at somebody else...
and turns it toward us.
Listen carefully to the Hebrew of Ezekiel 16:49:
הִנֵּה־זֶה הָיָה עֲוֹן סְדֹם אֲחוֹתֵךְ גָּאוֹן שִׂבְעַת־לֶחֶם וְשַׁלְוַת הַשְׁקֵט הָיָה לָהּ וְלִבְנוֹתֶיהָ וְיַד־עָנִי וְאֶבְיוֹן לֹא הֶחֱזִיקָה׃
A faithful rendering is essentially:
“Behold, this was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, fullness of bread, and prosperous ease were hers and her daughters’; yet she did not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy.”
Then verse 50 continues:
וַתִּגְבְּהֶינָה וַתַּעֲשֶׂינָה תוֹעֵבָה לְפָנָי...
“They became haughty and committed abomination before Me...”
Read that again.
Pride.
Fullness of bread.
Comfort.
Neglect of the poor.
Haughtiness.
Abomination.
And judgment.
Suddenly Sodom feels closer.
Because it is easy to condemn a sin you believe belongs to somebody else.
It is much harder when God starts talking about the sins that can live comfortably in respectable houses.
The Hebrew word translated “pride” is גָּאוֹן — ga'on. It carries the sense of exaltation, arrogance, majesty, pride.
Then comes an expression almost painfully vivid:
שִׂבְעַת־לֶחֶם — siv'at-lechem.
Fullness of bread.
They had enough.
More than enough.
Their stomachs were full while someone else's hands were empty.
And God noticed.
Not because possessing food is sinful.
Not because prosperity automatically makes someone wicked.
Abraham himself possessed great wealth.
The problem was what abundance had done to their hearts.
Their blessings had become insulation.
Their comfort had stopped producing gratitude and started producing indifference.
Their abundance had become an excuse not to see suffering.
They had bread...
but no mercy.
They had ease...
but no compassion.
They had resources...
but would not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy.
And perhaps this is where the ancient ruins of Sodom begin appearing uncomfortably close to our own front doors.
We can have refrigerators full of food and hearts empty of compassion.
We can spend without thinking on things we barely need while calculating whether generosity is worth the inconvenience.
We can sing, “Lord, I love You,” on Sunday and spend Monday protecting a lifestyle in which nobody else's pain is allowed to interrupt us.
We can know theology...
quote Scripture...
debate morality...
and still walk past Lazarus at the gate.
That should disturb us.
But we also need to be extremely careful here, because another error has become common.
Some people quote Ezekiel 16:49 and conclude:
“See? Sodom had nothing to do with sexual sin. It was only about pride and neglecting the poor.”
That is not what the whole Bible says either.
We do not honor Scripture by correcting one oversimplification with another.

Genesis 19 presents a horrifying scene in which the men of Sodom surround Lot's house and demand access to his male visitors. The episode involves attempted sexual violence, degrading lust, brutality, and a terrifying collapse of moral restraint.
And the New Testament does not permit us to remove sexual immorality from Sodom's indictment.
Jude 7 says:
ὡς Σόδομα καὶ Γόμορρα... ἐκπορνεύσασαι καὶ ἀπελθοῦσαι ὀπίσω σαρκὸς ἑτέρας...
The crucial word ἐκπορνεύσασαι — ekporneusasai comes from a verb describing giving oneself over to sexual immorality.
Jude therefore explicitly remembers Sodom and Gomorrah in connection with sexual immorality and pursuing “other/strange flesh.”
So was Sodom destroyed only because of sexual sin?
No.
Was sexual wickedness irrelevant to Sodom's judgment?
Also no.
The biblical picture is larger...
and more terrifying.
Sodom had become a culture of rebellion.
Sexual corruption was part of it.
Pride was part of it.
Violence was part of it.
Abundance without compassion was part of it.
Haughtiness before God was part of it.
Neglect of vulnerable people was part of it.
What happened in Genesis 19 was not some isolated accident occurring in an otherwise compassionate society.
It was fruit growing from a diseased tree.
And Ezekiel takes us toward the roots.
Pride.
Self-satisfaction.
Indifference.
Haughtiness.
Abomination.
A society so consumed with itself that other human beings could become objects to exploit rather than neighbors to love.
And now comes the part we would rather avoid.
Ezekiel was not primarily preaching a sermon so Jerusalem could feel morally superior to Sodom.
He was confronting Jerusalem.
God calls Sodom Jerusalem's “sister” in this prophetic indictment and tells His covenant people that their own wickedness had become so terrible that comparison with Sodom should humiliate them.
Think about that.
The name “Sodom” was not handed to Jerusalem as ammunition.
It was handed to Jerusalem as a mirror.
That changes how Christians should read this passage.
Before asking, “Who in today's culture reminds me of Sodom?”
perhaps we should ask:
“Jesus... where is Sodom hiding in me?”
Where has pride survived beneath Christian vocabulary?
Where have I become comfortable enough that somebody else's suffering feels inconvenient?
Where do I secretly believe my morality makes me superior to people trapped in sins different from mine?
Where am I sexually compromising while maintaining a religious appearance?
Where have lust, pornography, fantasy, adultery, fornication, exploitation, or secret impurity been given a locked room inside my life?
Where have money and comfort become masters?
Where do I have fullness of bread while refusing to strengthen the hand of someone in need?
Where do I condemn publicly what I tolerate privately?
That is where this passage stops being an argument.
It becomes an examination.
And maybe somebody reading this just became uncomfortable.
Good.
Not because shame is the destination.
Because sometimes discomfort is mercy knocking before destruction has to.
The Gospel does not begin by telling us that everybody else is worse.
It tells us the truth about us.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
All.
The sexually immoral need Jesus.
The greedy need Jesus.
The proud need Jesus.
The self-righteous need Jesus.
The religious hypocrite needs Jesus.
The person neglecting the poor needs Jesus.
The person drowning in secret lust needs Jesus.
The person who has never committed the scandalous sins everybody whispers about still needs Jesus.
Because the dividing line of the Gospel is not respectable people on one side and scandalous people on the other.
It is sinners...
and a Savior.
And this is where Sodom's warning must lead us—not into smugness, but toward the cross.
Because if we stop at judgment, we have not yet reached the center of Christianity.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to give sinners better behavior.
He came to save sinners.
At Calvary, the holy Son of God bore sin's judgment.
The One who never surrendered to lust...
never exploited the vulnerable...
never ignored the suffering...
never worshiped comfort...
never lied...
never sinned...
was crucified among sinners.
Jesus did not excuse sin.
He carried its penalty.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion does not matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin mattered enough that Christ died.
But look again.
You mattered enough that He came.
That is the scandal of grace.
The Gospel does not tell the sexually broken, “Clean yourself up enough and maybe Jesus will receive you.”
It says come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Bring the darkness into His light.
The Gospel does not tell the proud Christian, “At least you are better than those people.”
It says come down from the throne you built for yourself.
Repent.
The Gospel does not tell the prosperous believer that having possessions automatically condemns them.
It asks something far more searching:
Do your possessions possess you?
Has the mercy God poured into your life begun flowing through you?
Can you see the poor?
Can you see the lonely?
Can you see the hungry?
Can you see the person everybody else avoids?
Can you see the sinner without treating their sin lightly or treating them as less human?
Because Jesus could look at sinners with astonishing tenderness without ever calling darkness light.
That is the balance we desperately need.
Truth without cruelty.
Compassion without compromise.
Holiness without self-righteousness.
Grace without pretending repentance is unnecessary.
Jesus embodied all of it.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years thinking their scandal disqualified them from ever becoming useful to God again.
Maybe your Sodom is not theoretical.
Maybe you have lived through sexual sin.
Maybe adultery destroyed your marriage.
Maybe pornography has chained you in secrecy.
Maybe greed hardened you.
Maybe pride destroyed relationships.
Maybe you ignored people God repeatedly placed in your path.
Maybe you have been the religious person throwing stones while carefully hiding what nobody was allowed to discover.
Maybe you know exactly what it feels like to wonder:
“If people knew everything about me, would anybody still love me?”
Jesus already knows.
Every room.
Every browser history.
Every thought.
Every compromise.
Every selfish decision.
Every tear.
Every excuse.
Every secret.
And the Gospel invitation still stands.
Not an invitation to remain unchanged.
An invitation to repent and be made new.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).
That promise does not belong to people who successfully constructed an innocent past.
It belongs to people who are in Christ.
That means your history does not have to become your identity.
Your worst night does not have to write your final chapter.
Your secret does not have to become your tombstone.
Your sin may explain part of your story...
but Jesus Christ can determine its ending.
This is why repentance is not God's attempt to humiliate you.
Repentance is the doorway out of the burning house.
When Christ says turn, He is not trying to rob you of life.
He is calling you back to it.
And maybe that is what Ezekiel's forgotten description of Sodom was supposed to do all along.
Not give us another weapon for culture wars.
Give us a mirror.
Look into it.
Not at your neighbor.
Not at the politician you despise.
Not at the denomination you criticize.
Not at the person whose sexuality you condemn.
Not at the unbeliever whose lifestyle troubles you.
Look at yourself.
Has pride entered?
Has abundance anesthetized compassion?
Has ease made obedience inconvenient?
Has sexual compromise become normalized?
Have you become better at identifying abomination in others than rebellion in yourself?
Have you been fed spiritually for years while refusing to strengthen somebody weaker?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Tell the truth.
Or simply write:
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Someone else reading those words may realize they are not fighting alone.
And please hear this carefully.
A seeker.
A lukewarm Christian.
Even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing to offer except condemnation.
Let them encounter the Christ who tells the truth about sin and then stretches scarred hands toward sinners.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's conviction disappear tomorrow.
Come back when pride whispers.
Come back when comfort makes you numb.
Come back when lust starts negotiating.
Come back when self-righteousness makes somebody else's sin look enormous and yours look microscopic.
Come back and remember:
Sodom is easier to condemn from a distance than to recognize in a mirror.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, grow deeper in Christ, confront hidden sin, understand difficult passages, and remember the Gospel when your soul is exhausted, stay close.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It never will.
It should not.
Give voluntarily, prayerfully, and cheerfully—not under compulsion (see 2 Corinthians 9:7).
Supporting faithful Gospel work can be one meaningful way to use what God has entrusted to you for His glory—but glorifying God is never something you purchase.
you can still help.
That costs nothing.
You may never know who reads because you shared.
You may never see the person crying behind a phone screen.
You may never know whose secret sin was confronted.
Whose hardened heart softened.
Whose faith awakened.
Whose shame finally drove them toward Christ instead of farther into hiding.
Gospel Warrior cannot save anyone.
An article cannot save anyone.
A church cannot save anyone.
A Christian product cannot save anyone.
Jesus Christ saves.
That is why everything must return to Him.
Sodom reminds us that God takes sexual sin seriously.
Ezekiel reminds us that He also takes pride, abundance without mercy, haughtiness, complacency, and neglect of the poor seriously.
Jude prevents us from rewriting the story as though sexual immorality played no role at all.
And the Gospel prevents us from reading any of this merely to discover whom we are allowed to condemn.
The cross levels us.
At its foot stands the sexually broken.
The greedy.
The arrogant.
The wounded.
The hypocrite.
The addict.
The religious.
The irreligious.
The rich.
The poor.
The ashamed.
The person everyone knows has sinned...
and the person whose scandal has never been discovered.
All empty-handed.
All unable to purchase mercy.
All needing the same Savior.
And there...
where judgment and mercy meet...
Jesus rewrites stories.
Maybe yours is next.
So repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ commands you to forgive.
Make restitution where righteousness requires it.
Break with the secret sin you have been protecting.
Open your hand to the needy.
Come down from pride.
Stop calling comfort peace when it has actually become spiritual sleep.
And run to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you become respectable.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Now.
Because the deepest warning in Sodom's story may not merely be that terrible sinners can face judgment.
It may be that people can become so comfortable with darkness that eventually they stop recognizing darkness at all.
But the breathtaking promise of the Gospel is this:
Christ still calls sinners out of darkness.
And when He calls...
the proper response is not to defend the darkness.
It is to walk toward the Light.
Then send this to somebody whose story looks too broken to be rewritten.
Because somewhere tonight, someone believes their scandal is the end of their story.
May they discover that the ashes do not get the final word when Jesus holds the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES DEUTERONOMY MENTION BOTH A FEMALE PROSTITUTE AND A MALE CULT FIGURE?
paragraphs: WHY DOES DEUTERONOMY MENTION BOTH A FEMALE PROSTITUTE AND A MALE CULT FIGURE?
One Strange Hebrew Verse Exposes a Counterfeit Kind of “Holiness”—and What God Was Protecting Israel From Still Has the Power to Expose Us Today
There are verses you read and immediately understand.
Then there are verses that make you stop.
Deuteronomy 23:17 is one of them.
Hidden inside a section of laws that many Christians hurry past are two ancient Hebrew words—one feminine, one masculine—that have produced radically different English translations.
Some Bibles speak of prostitutes.
Others say “cult prostitutes.”
Others say “shrine prostitutes.”

Older English translations use a word so loaded with later associations that modern readers can easily walk away believing the verse says something much more specific than the Hebrew itself actually says.
But when you slow down...
when you stop forcing a modern argument onto an ancient sentence...
and when you actually look at the Hebrew...
something unsettling appears.
Because the scandal of this verse is not merely sexual.
It is spiritual.
And before we are finished, this obscure command from Moses will ask a question far more uncomfortable than, “What were those people doing thousands of years ago?”
It will ask:
What have you allowed to wear the clothing of holiness while quietly taking the place that belongs to God?
Here is the Hebrew text:
לֹא־תִהְיֶה קְדֵשָׁה מִבְּנוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלֹא־יִהְיֶה קָדֵשׁ מִבְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל׃
Lōʾ tihyeh qĕdēšāh mibbenōt Yiśrāʾēl, wĕlōʾ yihyeh qādēš mibbenê Yiśrāʾēl.
In a deliberately cautious rendering:
“There shall not be a qĕdēšāh among the daughters of Israel, and there shall not be a qādēš among the sons of Israel.”
That may sound frustrating.
Why leave the two important words untranslated?
Because this is precisely where we need enough humility to let Scripture speak before we decide what Scripture must mean.
The Hebrew text really does use קְדֵשָׁה — qĕdēšāh, the feminine term, and קָדֵשׁ — qādēš, its masculine counterpart.
And both belong to the Hebrew q-d-š word-family—the linguistic world of holiness, consecration, sacredness, or being set apart.
That is what makes the verse so disturbing.
These are not ordinary words for “prostitute.”
The ordinary Hebrew term associated with prostitution is זֹנָה — zōnāh.
In fact, the very next verse uses language associated with the wages of a zōnāh.
So Moses has placed before us vocabulary in which sexuality, religious devotion, consecration, and forbidden worship become tangled together.

For centuries, many interpreters untangled that knot by translating qĕdēšāh and qādēš as “cult prostitute,” “shrine prostitute,” or similar expressions. Several major modern translations still do exactly that.
That interpretation is possible.
But here is something serious students of Scripture need to know.
It is not as historically certain as Christians are sometimes told.

Modern scholarship has challenged the old assumption that these Hebrew terms prove the existence of an organized system of “sacred prostitution” in ancient Israel or the surrounding cultures. Scholars continue debating exactly what functions these people performed. Some understand them in connection with prohibited sexual activity associated with pagan worship; others argue that the words more basically identify male and female religious functionaries or persons consecrated to a non-Yahwistic cult, without the word itself necessarily meaning “prostitute.”
That distinction matters.
We should never defend the Bible by making it say more than the Bible says.
Truth does not need exaggeration.
And Scripture does not become stronger when Christians pretend a debated historical reconstruction is an unquestionable translation.
But neither does the uncertainty make the verse meaningless.
Quite the opposite.
What is certain is already devastating.
Israel belonged to Yahweh.
Their sons belonged to Yahweh.
Their daughters belonged to Yahweh.
Their worship belonged to Yahweh.
Their bodies belonged under His covenant.
And God would not permit His covenant people to surrender themselves to religious identities and practices that contradicted exclusive allegiance to Him.
Notice the language surrounding this command.
Only a few verses earlier, Israel is told:
“For the LORD your God walketh in the midst of thy camp...”
The camp must therefore be holy because God Himself is present among His people.
That changes everything.
Holiness in Deuteronomy is not religious cosmetics.
It is not appearing spiritual.
It is not knowing religious vocabulary.
It is not standing near sacred things.
Holiness begins with belonging to the Holy One.
And suddenly the strange vocabulary of verse 17 becomes painfully relevant.
Because one of humanity's oldest temptations is not simply to abandon God.
It is to replace God...
and keep the religious appearance.
That is far more dangerous.
You can reject God loudly.
But you can also betray Him while singing.
You can wander away from Christ while still posting Bible verses.
You can hide lust behind ministry.
You can hide greed behind “blessing.”
You can hide bitterness behind “discernment.”
You can hide pride behind theology.
You can hide an addiction behind a testimony everybody thinks happened years ago.
You can know exactly when to raise your hands in worship while knowing exactly which browser history you have to erase before somebody borrows your phone.
You can call Jesus “Lord” publicly while protecting the one room of your heart where you have already told Him:
You cannot enter here.
And that is where an ancient command suddenly stops feeling ancient.
God was forming a people whose worship could not be absorbed into the religious practices surrounding them.
Male or female, Israelite sons and daughters were not to become devoted to a rival sacred order.
God wasn't interested in merely having another shrine in Israel's collection.
He demanded covenant faithfulness.
And perhaps somebody reading this has finally discovered why this verse makes you uncomfortable.
It isn't because you have become a qādēš or qĕdēšāh in some ancient Canaanite sense.
It is because you know what divided worship feels like.
You know what it is to love Jesus...
and still love something Jesus is asking you to surrender.
You know what it is to pray...
then return to the same secret.
Repent...
then negotiate with the temptation.
Cry...
then hide.
Promise God, “Never again”...
then find yourself staring at the ceiling at 2:13 in the morning wondering how you became the person who broke that promise again.
And shame whispers:
Look at you.
You call yourself a Christian?
That whisper has destroyed people.
Because shame tells you to hide from the only Person who can heal what you are hiding.
But this is where we have to move from Deuteronomy to Jesus.
Not because Jesus cancels God's holiness.
Jesus reveals how terrifyingly serious holiness actually is...
and how unimaginably costly grace became.
Christ did not come to tell sinners that sin wasn't really a problem.
He came because the problem was so deep that nothing less than the blood of the Son of God could reconcile sinners to God.
The cross is not God lowering His standards.
The cross is God satisfying His righteousness while extending mercy to the guilty.
Jesus touched people religious society would not touch.
He ate with people respectable people despised.
He received the broken.
He confronted hypocrites.
He called sinners to repentance.
He forgave.
He restored.
He transformed.
But He never called darkness light in order to make darkness feel welcome.
He brought people into the light.
That is grace.
Grace does not say:
“Stay exactly where sin left you.”
Grace says:
“Come to Christ. You don't have to remain there anymore.”
Paul would later describe the breathtaking transformation of people whose former lives were marked by sexual sin, idolatry, greed, drunkenness and other unrighteousness.
Then comes one of the most beautiful turns in the New Testament:
“And such were some of you...”
Were.
Not because they became morally impressive enough to rescue themselves.
Paul continues by pointing to washing, sanctification, and justification in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
That is Christianity.
Not sinners pretending they were never sinners.
Not religious people polishing their reputations.
Dead people receiving life.
Guilty people receiving justification.
Captives receiving freedom.
Unclean people being washed.
People with histories receiving futures.
People with scandals receiving grace.
And maybe that is exactly what somebody needs tonight.
Your worst chapter is real.
But it does not have to be your final chapter.
Your secret may be ugly.
Your compromise may have lasted years.
Your marriage may be bleeding.
Your prayer life may feel almost nonexistent.
You may have returned to pornography after swearing you never would.
You may be carrying sexual shame nobody knows about.
You may have made money your god.
Approval your god.
A relationship your god.
Ministry itself your god.
You may have learned how to look spiritually alive while privately becoming numb.
But listen carefully.
The Gospel does not require you to edit your past before approaching Jesus.
It requires you to stop defending your sin and come to Him.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who already paid a debt you could never pay.
Jesus was crucified.
Jesus was buried.
Jesus rose.
And the risen Christ is still rewriting human lives.
That is why Deuteronomy 23:17 cannot merely become ammunition for attacking “those people.”
That would be an extraordinarily convenient reading.
Point at somebody else's sexual sin.
Somebody else's confusion.
Somebody else's lifestyle.
Somebody else's idolatry.
Somebody else's scandal.
And never notice your own altar.
But Scripture has a way of turning the mirror around.
Before asking who “they” are...
ask what owns you.
What receives the devotion Christ deserves?
What sin have you renamed so you can keep it?
What compromise have you baptized with Christian vocabulary?
What would terrify you if everybody at church suddenly knew?
What do you defend whenever the Holy Spirit puts His finger on it?
What have you placed on an altar and called sacred...
when God never asked for it?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
If something hidden has been exposed, you don't have to write the details publicly. But you can make a small declaration that you are finished running.
And when somebody else leaves one of those comments, don't treat it like entertainment.
Pray for them.
There is a human soul behind that screen.
Maybe trembling.
Maybe ashamed.
Maybe typing three words because three words are all they have strength to say.
Be the Church.
There is another uncomfortable detail in this passage.
The next verse refuses offerings associated with what God condemns.
The principle is piercing: God is not impressed when we try to finance worship with a life we refuse to surrender to Him.
You cannot purchase God's approval.
You cannot donate your way around repentance.
You cannot give enough money to make God owe you grace.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Jesus already paid.
And Christian giving must never be manipulated by pretending otherwise.
Scripture says God loves a cheerful giver, not someone coerced into giving. Christian generosity flows from grace; it does not purchase grace.

So if Gospel Warrior has strengthened your faith, helped you understand Scripture, encouraged you through darkness, confronted you when you were drifting, or helped bring your attention back to Jesus, there is a way to help this ministry continue.
Not to buy God's favor.
Not to replace repentance.
Not because a monthly payment magically becomes your biblical tithe.
And certainly not because salvation is for sale.
It isn't.
And there is another way to help that costs nothing.
That share matters.
Because you have no idea who is quietly watching your feed.
The friend who jokes about everything may be falling apart.
The cousin who stopped attending church may still read what you post.
The believer who looks strong may be fighting an addiction alone.
The person who says he doesn't believe in God may still stop when he sees the name Jesus.
So share this.
Send it privately to someone who needs grace more than another lecture.
Use them.
Share them.
Put biblical resources into somebody's hands.
Help another believer grow.
Because discipleship was never supposed to terminate with us.
Truth received becomes truth carried.
Grace received becomes grace proclaimed.
And perhaps now we can finally answer the question we started with.
Why does Deuteronomy mention both the female qĕdēšāh and the male qādēš?
At minimum, because God's covenant claim was not restricted to one sex.
Daughters of Israel belonged to Him.
Sons of Israel belonged to Him.
No woman was beyond His claim.
No man was exempt from His holiness.
Israel was not permitted to surrender its people to rival forms of religious devotion incompatible with loyalty to Yahweh.

Whether the disputed historical details behind these terms involved institutionalized cult prostitution exactly as older scholarship reconstructed it should be stated with appropriate caution. The Hebrew vocabulary itself is connected to consecration, and the precise social functions represented by these terms remain debated. Even the ancient Greek Septuagint reflects the interpretive complexity, using language involving prostitution while also adding terminology associated with ritual initiation or cultic status.
That scholarly honesty does not weaken Scripture.
It protects us from making Scripture say what we want it to say.
And underneath the historical debate stands something unmistakable:
The God of Israel would not share the allegiance of His covenant people with counterfeit worship.
Neither will Christ settle for becoming a decorative addition to ours.
Jesus is not asking to become one tab among twenty open tabs in your life.
Not Sunday Jesus.
Not emergency Jesus.
Not motivational-quote Jesus.
Not Jesus beside the idol you refuse to surrender.
Jesus Christ is Lord.

And the same Savior who exposes our counterfeit altars stretched out His hands on a Roman cross for idolaters, adulterers, hypocrites, rebels, religious pretenders, sexually broken people, proud people, greedy people...
people like us.
That is the scandal.
And that is the grace.
God sees what you hide...
and still calls you to come into the light.
Not so your sin can destroy you there.
So Christ can free you from the darkness in which you have been protecting it.
Repent.
Come home.
Receive mercy.
Then get up and follow Jesus.
Not because your money can glorify God while your heart remains His rival's.
Give Him the heart first.
Then let your time, your sharing, your generosity, your testimony, your obedience, and your resources follow.
But above everything else...
give Jesus the thing you have been afraid He would ask you to surrender.
Because one day you may realize the thing you were terrified to place in His hands was the very thing keeping your hands from being free.
Some chains survive only because we keep calling them sacred after Jesus has already called us out of them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ARE THERE SEXUAL ACTS BETWEEN HUSBAND AND WIFE THAT SCRIPTURE EXPLICITLY FORBIDS?
paragraphs: ARE THERE SEXUAL ACTS BETWEEN HUSBAND AND WIFE THAT SCRIPTURE EXPLICITLY FORBIDS?
What the Bible actually says about the marriage bed may confront both the legalist who invented rules God never wrote—and the spouse who has used “we’re married” to excuse what love should never do.
There are questions Christians whisper because they are afraid somebody will hear them.
This is one of them.
Maybe you have wondered about it but never dared ask your pastor.
Maybe you searched online and found two opposite worlds waiting for you.
One says almost everything between husband and wife is sinful.
The other says almost nothing can be sinful once two people are married.
One produces shame.
The other can produce license.
And somewhere between them sits a husband and wife who genuinely love Jesus, genuinely love each other, and simply want to know:
What does God actually say?
Not what somebody's grandmother said.
Not what pornography taught.
Not what secular culture celebrates.
Not what a preacher personally dislikes.
Not what social media normalizes.
What does Scripture say?
And here is where we have to be unusually careful, because Christians should never place words in God's mouth.

The Bible explicitly condemns sexual immorality and adultery. It commands faithfulness, holiness, honor, sacrificial love, and marital responsibility. Yet Scripture does not give married couples an exhaustive catalogue naming every conceivable intimate act and placing each into a column marked “permitted” or “forbidden.”
That distinction matters.
Because calling something sin when God has not called it sin is dangerous.
