Paul uses the word hagiasmos—sanctification, holiness, consecration. It carries the idea of being set apart for God. He is not describing cosmetic Christianity. He is describing a life increasingly brought under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say, “Your body is evil.”
He does not say, “Sexual desire itself makes you filthy.”
He does not say, “If you have ever fallen sexually, God could never want you again.”
He says something far more demanding—and far more beautiful.
Learn.
Learn how to live differently.
Learn how to handle your body in holiness and honor.
That word matters because holiness is not merely something you admire in mature Christians.
It is something the grace of God teaches you to practice.

There is an important translation question here. The Greek word skeuos literally means a “vessel” or “instrument.” Interpreters have historically debated whether Paul means controlling or possessing one’s own body, or whether the expression refers to acquiring or living honorably with one’s wife. The “body” interpretation fits many modern translations and makes strong sense in a passage addressed to believers concerning sexual self-control; the marital interpretation also has historical arguments behind it.
But whichever interpretive question you examine, Paul’s larger point does not become blurry.
Sexuality is not exempt from holiness.
The Christian cannot say, “Jesus has my heart, but my body belongs to me.”
Paul will say elsewhere:

“Flee fornication… What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you… and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body…” — 1 Corinthians 6:18–20, KJV
Read those words again.
“You are not your own.”
That sentence collides violently with the spirit of our age.
Our culture tells us that freedom means obeying whatever desire feels most authentic.
Jesus offers something radically different.
Freedom is no longer being enslaved by what once commanded you.
There is an enormous difference between having a desire and surrendering your throne to it.
You can feel temptation without making temptation your master.
You can experience attraction without turning another human being into an object.
You can have a sexual past without allowing your past to write your future.
You can have fallen last night and still fall before Christ today.
That is where this passage stops being merely uncomfortable and becomes breathtakingly hopeful.
Because Paul is writing to Christians.
People being sanctified.
People learning.
People whose old world had not magically disappeared simply because they believed the Gospel.
Paul does not tell them merely to feel ashamed.
He calls them forward.
Maybe that is exactly what somebody reading this needs to hear.
You hate what you keep doing.
You promised God you would stop.
Then you returned.
You deleted it.
Then downloaded it again.
You blocked the person.
Then searched the name again.
You cried during worship.
Then lost the battle in private.
And now shame has begun preaching its own gospel to you.
“You are disgusting.”
“You are fake.”
“God must be tired of you.”
“You might as well stop trying.”
Listen carefully.
That is not the Gospel.
The Gospel does not call sin harmless.
But neither does the Gospel tell the sinner that Christ is powerless.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could rename our chains “freedom.”
And He did not rise from the grave so repentant sinners would spend the rest of their lives believing their worst moment has more authority than His cross.
This is why holiness matters.
Not because holiness purchases salvation.
Jesus purchases sinners.
Not because controlling your body earns the love of God.
The cross demonstrates a love you could never earn.
Not because Christians become acceptable to God by constructing an impressive record of sexual purity.
We are reconciled to God through Christ.
Holiness is not the entrance fee for grace.
Holiness is what grace begins producing in the person grace has rescued.
That changes everything.
Paul says God’s will is your hagiasmos.
Your sanctification.
Not simply your reputation.
Not simply that nobody catches you.
Not simply that you become better at deleting browser histories.
God wants something deeper than concealed behavior.
He wants transformed desire.
He wants the secret room too.
Because Jesus is not interested in becoming the decorative Savior hanging on the wall of your public life while another master occupies your private life.
He is Lord.
And perhaps that explains why Paul immediately contrasts holiness with people who live “in the passion of lust” and “do not know God.”
Paul connects sexual ethics with knowing God.
That is enormous.
Christian holiness is not merely gritting your teeth harder than everybody else.
It grows from knowing Someone.
When God becomes more than an idea…
when Christ becomes more precious than the appetite…
when you begin seeing another person not as material for your fantasy but as someone bearing God-given dignity…
when your body becomes something entrusted to you rather than something whose impulses must always be obeyed…
the battle begins changing.
Not always instantly.
Sometimes painfully.
Sometimes with tears.
Sometimes through confession.
Sometimes through accountability.
Sometimes by fleeing instead of pretending you are strong enough to stand beside temptation and negotiate.
Sometimes holiness looks surprisingly unspiritual.
Turning the phone off.
Leaving the room.
Ending the conversation.
Blocking the account.
Refusing the second glance.
Confessing to a mature believer.
Installing accountability.
Changing the routine.
Ending a relationship that continually drags you away from Christ.
Jesus Himself spoke radically about removing occasions of sin. Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible after falling.
Repentance turns.
And some of us have been asking God to remove a temptation while continuing to feed it every night.
We pray, “Lord, make me strong.”
Then keep the doorway unlocked.
We pray, “Jesus, deliver me.”
Then preserve the secret access.
We pray for freedom while protecting the chain.
Paul says learn to govern your vessel in holiness and honor.
There is dignity in that word timē—honor.
Biblical sexual holiness is not hatred of the body.
It is honor.
Your body is not garbage.
The body matters so much to Christianity that the Son of God took on flesh.
Christ was bodily crucified.
Christ bodily rose.
And Christians await resurrection.
Christianity is not the story of God rescuing spirits from meaningless bodies.
God cares what we do with them.
That means your eyes matter.
Your hands matter.
Your bed matters.
Your messages matter.
Your search history matters.
Your relationships matter.
What you do with another person’s body matters.
And what you do with your own matters.
But perhaps your chest tightens reading that because your history is already written.
Maybe purity sounds beautiful until you remember yourself.
The affair.
The pornography.
The hookup.
The secret relationship.
The years of compromise.
The messages you hope nobody ever discovers.
The things done to you.
The things you willingly did.
The line you crossed.
Then crossed again.
Maybe you are wondering whether an article about holiness has anything left to say to somebody whose story already contains scandal.
Yes.
It has one Name left to say.
Jesus.
Jesus Christ does not specialize in polishing people who already look clean.
He saves sinners.
The woman exposed in adultery encountered both mercy and a summons away from sin.

The sexually immoral in Corinth were reminded that some of them had once been defined by patterns of sin—but they had been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is Christianity.
Not denial.
Not condemnation without hope.
Not grace without transformation.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Jesus does not look at repentance and say, “Pretend it never happened.”
He says, in effect, “It does not have to own you anymore.”
That is why your scandal does not get the final sentence.
Grace does.
But grace does not merely erase guilt and then return you unchanged to the same prison.
Grace opens the door and says:
Come out.
Maybe you have fallen a hundred times.
Then repentance begins again today.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Stop making peace with what crucified your Savior.
Stop calling bondage a personality trait.
Stop measuring the power of Christ by the number of times you have failed.
Your repeated failure proves your weakness.
It does not prove His weakness.
And do not confuse conviction with condemnation.
Conviction says, “This is killing you. Come back to Christ.”
Condemnation says, “You are beyond Christ. Hide.”
One leads toward Jesus.
The other drives you deeper into darkness.
There is no healing in pretending.
There is no freedom in renaming sin.
But there is astonishing mercy for the person who finally stops hiding.
So be honest.
Has your body been leading your discipleship instead of Christ?
Has an appetite quietly become a master?
Have you learned how to look Christian while protecting something you know is destroying your communion with God?
Talk to Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Ask for help.
If necessary, tell a trustworthy mature Christian today.
If your struggle has become compulsive, seek wise pastoral and professional help rather than fighting indefinitely in isolation.
There is no trophy for hiding successfully.
And there is no shame in needing brothers and sisters to help you walk toward the light.

Paul later says in this same passage that God did not call His people to impurity, but to holiness, and that rejecting this instruction ultimately means rejecting God, who gives believers His Holy Spirit.
Do not miss that final part.
God gives His Holy Spirit.
The command toward holiness comes with the presence of the Holy One.
Christian self-control is therefore not merely self-improvement.
You are not being told to save yourself through discipline.
You are being called to walk by the Spirit because Christ has already accomplished what your moral performance could never accomplish.
The cross deals with guilt.
The resurrection announces a new creation.
The Spirit works transformation.
And sanctification continues.
Sometimes slowly.
Sometimes through brutal battles.
But genuinely.
So when temptation whispers, “This is who you are,” remember your identity is not finally determined by your appetite.
When shame whispers, “After everything you've done, you cannot come home,” remember the cross.
When your flesh whispers, “You need this,” remember the empty tomb.
When the enemy whispers, “Hide,” run into the light.
And when you fall, do not build a house on the ground.
Get up.
Confess.
Repent.
Return to Jesus.
Again.
And keep walking.

And if Christ has already been restoring an area of your life you once thought was hopeless, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to interrupt someone else’s despair.
Not because saving a post makes anyone holy, but because temptation has a strange way of making us forget what conviction sounded like when our minds were clear.
Come back to these words when compromise starts sounding reasonable again.
You may never know who reads it at 2:13 in the morning.
You may never know whose finger stops scrolling.
You may never know who was one decision away from returning to an old bondage when these words reminded them that Jesus is still calling them toward the light.
Some battles deserve privacy, dignity, and compassion.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends who are willing to explore the Gospel.
Let that support be voluntary worship—not pressure.
Scripture says Christian giving should come from what a person has decided in the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
It is not.
It does not.
Your obedience belongs to Christ, not to this ministry.
Do not admire holiness from a distance.
Do not merely share an article about surrender while refusing to surrender.
Do not publicly defend biblical purity while privately feeding what is destroying you.
Go to Christ.
Because Paul’s command was never merely, “Control yourself better.”
It was a summons to become what the Gospel says you now are:
Someone who belongs to God.
Someone whose body matters.
Someone whose desires no longer deserve the throne.
Someone being sanctified.
Someone purchased at a price.
Someone in whom the Holy Spirit is at work.
Someone whose worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
And perhaps tonight, somewhere behind a locked door, with tears nobody else will ever see, the most powerful prayer you can pray is not eloquent at all.
“Jesus… this part too.
You can have this part too.”
Because the secret you surrender to Christ today does not have to become the scandal that destroys you tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THE BIBLE CONTAINS POLYGAMY” IS NOT THE SAME AS “THE BIBLE COMMANDS POLYGAMY”
paragraphs: “THE BIBLE CONTAINS POLYGAMY” IS NOT THE SAME AS “THE BIBLE COMMANDS POLYGAMY”
The Bible Records the Wreckage of Broken People Without Calling the Wreckage Holy—and Jesus Himself Takes Us Back to the Beginning
Someone opens the Bible.
They read about Abraham.
Then Jacob.
Then David.
Then Solomon.
They stop.
They look up.
And with the confidence of someone who thinks they have just discovered Christianity’s fatal contradiction, they say:
“See? The Bible contains polygamy.”
Yes.
It does.
But slow down.
Because you have just stepped into one of the most important distinctions you will ever learn when reading Scripture:
The Bible containing something is not the same as the Bible commanding it.
And if you miss that distinction, you can make the Bible endorse almost anything.
The Bible contains murder.
It does not therefore command murder.
The Bible contains adultery.
It does not therefore bless adultery.
The Bible contains incest, drunkenness, betrayal, prostitution, deception, idolatry, violence, cowardice, greed, abuse of power, spiritual compromise, and horrifying human decisions.
Not because God approves of them.
Because God tells the truth about us.
That may be one of the reasons the Bible feels so painfully human.
It does not airbrush its heroes.
It does not Photoshop the patriarchs.
It does not protect kings from embarrassment.
It does not quietly delete the scandals of people God used.
Abraham can believe God and still make disastrous decisions.
Jacob can encounter God and still carry dysfunction into his home.
David can write psalms that have comforted millions and still commit sins that devastate his family.
Solomon can possess extraordinary wisdom and still become a living warning about what happens when wisdom is known but not obeyed.
The Bible does something religious propaganda almost never does:
It exposes its own people.
And that should tell us something.
Scripture is not trying to convince you that biblical characters were flawless.
It is showing you why humanity desperately needs a Savior.
So when someone says, “But Abraham had more than one woman,” or “Jacob had multiple wives,” or “David had several wives,” or “Solomon had hundreds,” the correct response is not to panic.
The correct response is:
What does the text actually say about it?
Because description is not prescription.
Narrative is not necessarily command.
Permission within a fallen social world is not necessarily the Creator’s original design.
And the consequences written into these stories matter.
Go back before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before David.
Before Solomon.
Before Israel had kings.
Before human civilization became tangled in generations of sin.
Go back to the beginning.
There, Scripture gives us something remarkably simple.
Genesis 2:24 reads in Hebrew:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
‘Al-ken ya‘azov-ish et-aviv ve’et-immo, vedavaq be’ishto, vehayu levasar echad.
In straightforward sense:
Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother, clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.
That final expression is unforgettable:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad — “one flesh.”
One new covenantal union.
One joined life.
And centuries later, when people tried to drag Jesus into a debate about marriage, Jesus did something incredibly important.
He did not begin with Abraham.
He did not say, “Well, Jacob had four women involved in his household, so let us use Jacob as our blueprint.”
He did not point to David's palace.
He certainly did not point to Solomon's enormous household.
Jesus went behind all of them.
Back beyond human accommodation.
Back beyond Israel's failures.
Back to creation.
He said:
“From the beginning…”
Then He quoted Genesis.
The Greek of Matthew 19:5 contains the words:
καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
Kai esontai hoi dyo eis sarka mian.
“And the two shall become one flesh.”
Then Jesus presses the conclusion:
“So they are no longer two, but one flesh.”
Notice the language.
The two.
One flesh.
And then:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Jesus' interpretive move matters enormously.
When human history becomes confusing, He points us toward the Creator's design “from the beginning.”
That is where Christians must begin too.
And suddenly the scandals of the Old Testament start looking very different.
Look at Jacob's household.
It is sometimes presented casually as evidence that Scripture approves of plural marriage.
But actually read the story.
Do not merely count the wives.
Watch the house.
Leah is unloved.
Rachel is jealous.
The sisters compete.
Children become entangled in their mothers' desperate struggle for affection and status.
Handmaids enter the conflict.
Fertility becomes currency.
Mandrakes become bargaining chips.
A home that should have been a place of covenant peace becomes emotionally fractured.
The Bible does not need a narrator standing over every paragraph shouting, “THIS IS DYSFUNCTIONAL!”
The dysfunction is the commentary.
You can hear it in Leah's heartbreak.
You can feel it in Rachel's desperation.
You can watch it spill into the next generation.
That is what careful Bible reading requires.
Do not merely ask:
“What happened?”
Ask:
“What did it produce?”
Then there is David.
A man after God's own heart.
A worshiper.
A warrior.
A king.
And a deeply flawed man.
David's household expanded.
So did its wounds.
Sexual sin.
Jealousy.
Violence.
Sibling hatred.
Murder.
Political rivalry.
Rebellion.
Grief.
The Bible does not hide any of it.
David's greatness does not make every decision David made great.
Being used by God does not mean everything a person does represents the will of God.
That sentence alone could rescue many believers from terrible theology.
God's grace toward a sinner is not God's endorsement of the sinner's every decision.
Then Solomon arrives.
If biblical polygamy were supposed to be a glorious model, Solomon would be a strange place to make the argument.
He had seven hundred wives of royal status and three hundred concubines.
But Scripture does not finish that sentence with:
“And behold, what a wonderful example of biblical marriage.”
It tells us that his wives turned his heart away.
Long before Solomon's collapse, Deuteronomy 17:17 had already warned Israel's future king not to multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.
Then Solomon did exactly that.
And his heart turned away.
The warning.
The violation.
The consequence.
All sitting there in Scripture.
The Bible did not command Solomon's excess.
It warned against it.
And then recorded what happened when the warning was ignored.
That is not endorsement.
That is tragedy.
But there is another layer that Christians need to understand.
Some Old Testament laws address situations that already existed in the fallen ancient world.
Regulating a broken situation does not necessarily mean declaring that situation God's ideal.
Sometimes biblical law restrained harm inside circumstances produced by human sin.
Jesus Himself gives us the interpretive principle when discussing divorce.
Moses permitted certain things because of the hardness of human hearts.
Then Jesus says, in effect:
But it was not that way from the beginning.
Those words are devastating to shallow arguments built merely on what fallen human beings were permitted or recorded as doing.
From the beginning.
That is where Jesus takes us.
Not “What did fallen humanity manage to normalize?”
But:
“What did the Creator intend?”
There is an enormous difference.
And this is where this discussion stops being merely about polygamy.
Because you and I do the same thing.
Maybe not with multiple wives.
But with our own favorite sins.
We search Scripture for somebody who failed like us and then quietly turn their failure into permission.
David did it.
Jacob did it.
Samson did it.
Peter did it.
The Corinthians struggled with it.
Everybody has flaws.
God understands.
And somewhere along the way, grace becomes an excuse for refusing to repent.
But that is not grace.
Grace does not look at the wreckage and call it beautiful.
Grace walks into the wreckage and begins rebuilding.
Jesus did not come merely to make you comfortable while you remain enslaved to everything destroying you.
He came to save.
To forgive.
To cleanse.
To transform.
To restore.
To make dead people live.
And maybe this argument about polygamy exposes something much closer to home.
Because the real question is not simply:
“Did biblical characters sin?”
Of course they did.
The frightening question is:
Why are we so eager to use someone else's failure to justify our own?
Maybe you have done that.
I have to examine my heart too.
We read about somebody's compromise and think, “See? God still used them.”
Yes.
He did.
But perhaps we have misunderstood the lesson.
The lesson is not:
“Sin doesn't matter because God uses sinners.”
The lesson is:
“Grace is astonishing because God can redeem sinners.”
Those are completely different messages.
One protects sin.
The other magnifies Christ.
The Bible's scandals are not embarrassing interruptions in the Gospel story.
They are evidence of why the Gospel is necessary.
Every fractured family.
Every compromised king.
Every jealous heart.
Every adulterous decision.
Every act of betrayal.
Every attempt to manipulate God's promises through human schemes.
Every broken covenant.
Every secret.
Every failure.
They keep whispering the same thing across the centuries:
We need Someone better.
Better than Abraham.
Better than Jacob.
Better than David.
Better than Solomon.
We need Jesus.
Abraham could believe and still stumble.
Jesus remained faithful.
David could conquer armies and still lose battles inside his own desires.
Jesus faced temptation and did not sin.
Solomon possessed wisdom yet allowed his heart to wander.
Jesus is Wisdom incarnate, perfectly faithful to His Father.
The Bible was never ultimately asking you to worship its human heroes.
It was preparing you to recognize the only flawless One when He arrived.
Jesus Christ.
That is why Christianity does not collapse when someone points out the moral failures of biblical characters.
Their failures are part of the case Christianity makes about humanity.
Something has gone terribly wrong inside us.
Education cannot fully cure it.
Power cannot cure it.
Romance cannot cure it.
Money cannot cure it.
Political authority cannot cure it.
Even extraordinary wisdom, by itself, cannot cure it.
Solomon proved that.
The human heart needs redemption.
And that is where the cross enters the story.
Not as decoration.
Not as religious jewelry.
Not as a sentimental ending.
As rescue.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die because humanity was basically fine.
He died because sin is deadly.
He carried our guilt.
He bore judgment.
He opened the way for forgiveness.
And He rose again.
The Gospel does not tell scandalous people to pretend they never had a scandal.
It tells them to bring their scandal to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Then get up and follow Him.
Maybe your story has sexual failure in it.
Maybe divorce.
Maybe betrayal.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe broken relationships.
Maybe choices you would give almost anything to undo.
Maybe you are reading an article about ancient polygamy while carrying a completely different secret.
Jesus already sees it.
And His invitation is not:
“Hide it better.”
His invitation is:
Come.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the door through which you stop running from the One who can heal you.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is restoration for ruined people.
There is a future after failure.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
It means your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final chapter.
Jesus does.
That is the heartbeat behind everything we mean when we say:
The Bible is filled with scandals because humanity is filled with sinners.
But the Bible does not end with scandal.
It moves toward redemption.
Toward a cross.
Toward an empty tomb.
Toward a returning King.
Toward a redeemed people.
Toward Christ.
So the next time someone tells you,
“The Bible contains polygamy,”
you do not have to deny it.
Say:
“Yes. It does.”
Then keep reading.
Read about the jealousy.
Read about the rivalry.
Read about the fractured homes.
Read Deuteronomy's warning to kings not to multiply wives.
Read what happened to Solomon.
Then go back to Genesis.
Then listen to Jesus.
From the beginning.
The question is not merely what broken humanity practiced.
The question is what the Creator intended—and where Christ leads redeemed people.
The New Testament continues to point Christian households toward covenant fidelity. Even the qualifications for an overseer use the striking Greek expression:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα — mias gynaikos andra
Literally, a “one-woman man,” commonly rendered “husband of one wife.”
Whatever interpretive discussions surround the precise pastoral application of that phrase, it certainly does not celebrate a man accumulating wives.
The trajectory is not difficult to see.
Creation.
Covenant faithfulness.
Christ.
And redemption.
So no:
“The Bible contains polygamy” is not the same statement as “the Bible commands polygamy.”
Not even close.
The Bible is brutally honest enough to record what humans did and holy enough not to confuse everything humans did with what God desires.
And perhaps that is why some passages make us uncomfortable.
The Bible refuses to flatter us.
It tells the truth.
About them.
About us.
About sin.
And then—thank God—it tells the truth about grace.
And if this challenged something in you personally, do not disappear quietly.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read.
Because sooner or later someone will ask this question again.
And when they do, you will want more than a clever comeback.
You will want Scripture.
Not because anyone can buy a blessing.
They cannot.
Give freely, prayerfully, and cheerfully before God.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Keep building.
And there is more waiting for believers who are hungry to grow.
Send it privately to someone wrestling with Scripture.
Comment so others know they are not alone.
Follow so we can keep walking through hard passages together.
And above everything else—
Follow Jesus.
Because Christianity was never built on Abraham being perfect.
Or Jacob being perfect.
Or David being perfect.
Or Solomon being perfect.
It stands upon the One who actually is.
Jesus Christ.
The Bible does not hide the scandals of its people.
It reveals the Savior of scandalous people.
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you long after this article disappears from your screen:
God did not preserve their failures so you could imitate their chains; He preserved the truth so you could recognize your need for the One who breaks them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THERE IS A WAY THAT SEEMS RIGHT TO A MAN…” — THE TERRIFYING DANGER OF TRUSTING WHAT FEELS RIGHT
paragraphs: “THERE IS A WAY THAT SEEMS RIGHT TO A MAN…” — THE TERRIFYING DANGER OF TRUSTING WHAT FEELS RIGHT
The most dangerous road may not look evil. It may feel peaceful, reasonable, justified—even blessed. And that is exactly why Scripture warns us about it.
There are decisions you regret because you knew they were wrong when you made them.
And then there are decisions that frighten you years later because, at the time, they felt completely right.
You had peace about it.
You prayed about it.
You talked yourself through it.
Your friends agreed with you.
Your emotions confirmed it.
Every door seemed to be opening.
You told yourself, “Surely God wouldn’t let me feel this strongly if this weren’t His will.”
And then somewhere down the road, everything began falling apart.
Not because God failed you.
Not because Scripture stopped being true.
But because there is something the Bible has been warning humanity about for thousands of years:
You can be completely sincere…
and completely wrong.
That sentence should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because one of the most dangerous lies of our generation is also one of the most comforting:
“Follow your heart.”
It sounds beautiful.
It fits on coffee mugs.
It belongs underneath sunset photographs.
It feels compassionate, empowering, liberating.
But there is a problem.
God never told you that your heart was qualified to be your god.
And the book of Proverbs gives us a warning so serious that Scripture records essentially the same proverb twice, in Proverbs 14:12 and Proverbs 16:25:
“יֵשׁ דֶּרֶךְ יָשָׁר לִפְנֵי־אִישׁ וְאַחֲרִיתָהּ דַּרְכֵי־מָוֶת”
Yesh derekh yashar lifnei-ish, ve’acharitah darkhei-mavet.
There is a way that is right before a man…
but its end is the ways of death.
Look carefully at what God does not say.
He does not merely warn about a way that looks wicked.
He warns about a way that appears יָשָׁר — yashar.
Straight.
Right.
Upright.
Correct.
That is what makes this verse terrifying.
The road does not necessarily have a skull painted on the entrance.
Sometimes it has flowers.
Sometimes it has applause.
Sometimes it has opportunity.
Sometimes it has chemistry.
Sometimes it has money.
Sometimes it has relief.
Sometimes it has religious language.
Sometimes it even feels like peace.
And still…
it can end in death.
Maybe you know that road.
Maybe you stayed in something because leaving felt cruel.
Maybe you entered a relationship because loneliness hurt more than compromise did.
Maybe you walked away from someone because your anger felt justified.
Maybe you withheld forgiveness because what they did really was terrible.
Maybe you kept the secret because telling the truth threatened everything you had built.
Maybe you called lust “love.”
Maybe you called greed “ambition.”
Maybe you called gossip “concern.”
Maybe you called bitterness “discernment.”
Maybe you called cowardice “protecting my peace.”
Maybe you called disobedience “following my heart.”
Maybe you even found people who would agree with you.
That is the frightening thing about deception.
If deception felt like deception, very few people would embrace it.
Deception succeeds because falsehood can feel true.
The first great human rebellion in Genesis did not begin because Eve looked at the forbidden fruit and thought, “I want destruction.”
She saw something desirable.
Something that appeared beneficial.
Something that seemed capable of making her wise.
The serpent did not need to convince humanity to hate goodness.
He only needed humanity to redefine goodness apart from God.
And we have been doing it ever since.
“I feel…”
“I think…”
“I deserve…”
“I don’t see anything wrong with…”
“This makes me happy…”
“This is my truth…”
Listen carefully.
Your feelings are real.
But real feelings are not necessarily reliable authorities.
Pain is real.
Attraction is real.
Anger is real.
Fear is real.
Desire is real.
Loneliness is real.
Confusion is real.
None of that means those feelings should sit on the throne.
Feelings can tell you something is happening inside you.
They cannot, by themselves, tell you what is holy.
That belongs to God.
Jeremiah 17:9 describes the human heart with uncomfortable honesty:
“עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל”
‘Aqov halev mikkol…
The heart is deceitful above all.
That does not mean every emotion you experience is sinful.
It means fallen human beings cannot safely treat inner desire as an infallible compass.
We need revelation.
We need truth outside ourselves.
We need the Word of God.
And ultimately, we need Jesus.
Because Christianity is not the story of good people learning to trust themselves more.
It is the story of lost people being rescued by Someone they desperately needed.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your instincts.
He came to save you.
There is a difference.
And perhaps this is where the knife turns.
Because sometimes what “feels right” is exactly what keeps us from repentance.
Repentance has never depended on whether confession feels comfortable.
Forgiving someone may not feel fair.
Walking away from sin may not feel liberating at first.
Ending an ungodly relationship may feel like your heart is being ripped apart.
Confessing what you have hidden may feel terrifying.
Returning what does not belong to you may feel humiliating.
Apologizing when your pride has built an entire courtroom proving you were justified may feel unbearable.
Obeying God sometimes hurts before it heals.
Ask Peter.
Jesus told His disciples that He would suffer, be killed, and rise again.
Peter did what probably felt loving.
He objected.
Surely protecting Jesus was the right thing.
Surely suffering could not be God's plan.
Surely preventing the cross was compassionate.
Yet Peter's human reasoning collided with the redemptive purpose of God.
Imagine that.
A man could love Jesus…
and in the same moment oppose the road Jesus had come to walk.
That should humble every Christian who has ever said, “But I have peace about it.”
Peace matters.
But “I feel peaceful” is not a replacement for “It is written.”
Circumstances matter.
Counsel matters.
Wisdom matters.
Conscience matters.
But none of them outrank the revealed character and Word of God.
Sometimes an open door is simply an open door.
Jonah found a ship going exactly where he wanted to go while running from what God had commanded him to do.
Availability is not automatically approval.
Convenience is not confirmation.
Difficulty is not automatically prohibition.
And emotional relief is not always the peace of Christ.
There are moments when obedience will cost you the very thing your flesh is begging you to keep.
And then there is Jesus in Gethsemane.
This is where our shallow definition of “follow your heart” collapses.
Jesus knew what was coming.
Betrayal.
Mockery.
Scourging.
Nails.
Suffocation.
Blood.
The cross.
And in the anguish of Gethsemane, He prayed in submission to the Father’s will.
Jesus did not teach us that holiness means doing whatever feels easiest.
He showed us obedience.
And He walked toward Calvary.
For us.
Think about that.
The road that looked like defeat became the road of victory.
The cross looked like scandal.
God turned it into the place where grace was proclaimed to sinners.
The tomb looked final.
Then Sunday morning came.
And suddenly the entire story changed.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely make bad people behave better.
He raises the spiritually dead.
He forgives the guilty.
He cleanses the stained.
He welcomes the repentant.
He restores the broken.
He takes stories people thought were permanently ruined and writes grace across pages soaked in shame.
That is why you cannot build your life on what merely seems right.
You need the One who is right.
Jesus did not say, “Discover whatever path feels true to you.”
He said:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life.”
The Christian faith is radically Christ-centered because salvation is not found by looking deeper into ourselves until we discover our own truth.
We look to Christ.
And perhaps you are reading this with something already burning in your conscience.
You know what it is.
Nobody else needs to know for this moment to matter.
That relationship.
That conversation.
That hidden browser history.
That bitterness.
That habit.
That secret.
That compromise.
That private justification you keep rehearsing because somewhere beneath all the excuses you already know what obedience would require.
Maybe you have been asking God to approve something He has already addressed.
Maybe you have been asking for another sign because you do not like the answer Scripture already gave you.
Maybe you have confused God's patience with God's permission.
Maybe you have spent months trying to make peace with something the Holy Spirit keeps bringing into the light.
Then hear this carefully:
Conviction is not God throwing you away.
Conviction may be mercy calling you home.
Peter failed Jesus spectacularly.
He denied Him.
Not once.
Three times.
The man who had promised loyalty collapsed under pressure.
Imagine the shame when the rooster crowed.
Imagine replaying those words afterward.
“I don’t know Him.”
Again.
“I don’t know Him.”
Again.
“I don’t know Him.”
There are moments when your worst sentence echoes louder than every good thing you have ever done.
Maybe you have one too.
Something you wish you could erase.
A night.
A betrayal.
A lie.
An addiction.
A decision.
A secret.
A season when you hardly recognize the person you became.
But Peter’s failure was not the final chapter.
Jesus rose.
Jesus restored him.
Grace met the man who had failed.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes grace astonishing.
The Gospel never says your rebellion did not matter.
The Gospel says it mattered so much that the Son of God went to the cross—and His grace is so great that repentant sinners can be forgiven, reconciled, cleansed, and made new.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming darkness as light.
Not by telling us to trust ourselves.
But by meeting sinners in truth and mercy and calling us:
Come.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Me.
Maybe this article is not asking you to discover whether you are a “good person.”
Maybe the deeper question is simpler:
Who has the final word in your life?
Your emotions?
Culture?
Your friends?
Your wounds?
Your desires?
Your fear?
Your past?
Or Jesus Christ?
Because sooner or later every disciple reaches a crossroads where feelings and faithfulness stop walking in the same direction.
That moment reveals who sits on the throne.
So before you make that decision…
before you send that message…
before you return to that relationship…
before you walk away from your marriage…
before you retaliate…
before you compromise…
before you call something good merely because it feels good…
stop.
Bring it into the light.
Open Scripture.
Pray without demanding that God agree with the conclusion you have already chosen.
Seek wise, biblically grounded counsel.
Ask the uncomfortable question:
“Lord, am I asking You to lead me—or am I asking You to bless where I already decided to go?”
That question can change a life.
And if something has already been exposed in you while reading this, do not run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
There is mercy at the feet of Christ.
There is forgiveness for the repentant.
There is cleansing for the ashamed.
There is restoration for the fallen.
There is no sin made safe by hiding it, but there is no repentant sinner who needs to fear that Christ's mercy is too small.
Come into the light.
Be honest.
Someone scrolling beneath you may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people without scars.
We are people whose scars no longer get the final word.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody you know may currently be standing on a road that feels absolutely right.
They may be praying for confirmation when what they really need is truth.
They may never tell you they needed this.
Share it anyway.
Because there may come a night when what God says and what you feel seem impossibly far apart, and you will need the reminder again:
Sincerity does not make a road safe.
Jesus does.
But hear this clearly, because biblical integrity matters more than a conversion:
It does not purchase God's favor.
It is not a substitute for obedience to Christ.
And we should not tell you that it automatically replaces whatever convictions you hold concerning tithes, offerings, or giving through your local church.
Scripture teaches generosity, but Scripture also protects believers from religious manipulation.
Paul wrote:
“ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ … μὴ … ἐξ ἀνάγκης”
Each one according as he has purposed in his heart … not under compulsion.
That matters.
Christian generosity is not supposed to be extracted through spiritual pressure.
Do it prayerfully.
Do it because you genuinely believe this work is worth supporting.
Do it as voluntary support for Gospel-centered content, discipleship resources, and the continued expansion of material intended to point people toward Jesus Christ.
Your support helps us keep writing.
Keep publishing.
Keep reaching.
And support is not only financial.
Every share matters.
Every thoughtful comment matters.
Jesus is calling you to follow Him.
The deepest danger was never simply choosing the wrong career, dating the wrong person, sending the wrong message, or taking the wrong opportunity.
The deepest danger is building an entire life around a compass that cannot save you.
Your heart was never meant to be your Savior.
Jesus is.
So when your feelings say one thing and Christ says another…
when culture applauds what Scripture warns against…
when compromise promises immediate relief…
when obedience feels costly…
when everybody around you says, “Do what makes you happy”…
remember the ancient warning:
There is a way that seems right to a man.
And remember the Savior who calls you onto a better road.
The road may be narrow.
It may cost you.
It may expose you.
It may require repentance.
It may break your pride.
It may lead through tears.
But if it leads you deeper into obedience to Jesus, you are not losing your life.
You are learning where life is found.
Because one day, you may look back and realize that the moment God interrupted the road that “felt right”…
was the moment grace kept you from reaching its end.
Sometimes the mercy of God sounds like a roadblock because He can see the grave your feelings cannot.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Can Provide Everything for Your Children Except the Father They Needed
paragraphs: You Can Provide Everything for Your Children Except the Father They Needed
You can pay every bill, fill every refrigerator, buy every birthday gift, and give your children opportunities you never had—and still one day discover that what they were starving for was you.
There is a kind of heartbreak that does not show up on a bank statement.
The mortgage was paid.
There was food on the table.
The school fees were covered.
Christmas came with gifts under the tree. Birthdays had cakes. Shoes were replaced when feet grew. Phones were upgraded. Vacations were photographed. College funds were discussed.
From the outside, it looked like provision.
Maybe even excellent provision.
But somewhere inside that house was a child who would have traded some of it for twenty uninterrupted minutes with Dad.
Not Dad looking at his phone.
Not Dad answering emails.
Not Dad half-listening while the television played.
Not Dad saying, “Later.”
Just Dad.
Present.
Listening.
Looking into their eyes as though what they were saying mattered.
And perhaps the most painful part is that Dad was not necessarily a bad man.
Maybe he was exhausted because he was trying to be a good one.
Maybe nobody ever taught him that a father could be physically inside the house and emotionally miles away.
Maybe his own father never hugged him.
Maybe he learned early that men provide, men endure, men don't cry, men don't talk about fear, and men prove their love by working until there is almost nothing left of them.
So he worked.
And worked.
And worked.
He told himself, I'm doing this for them.
But sometimes the people we are doing everything for quietly begin wondering why they cannot have us.
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because work is not the only thing that can steal a father.
Sometimes it is golf.
Sometimes gaming.
Sometimes endless scrolling.
Sometimes pornography.
Sometimes alcohol.
Sometimes another relationship.
Sometimes ministry itself.
Sometimes it is simply the habit of retreating into a screen because dealing with a child's emotions requires an emotional vocabulary a father was never given.
And sometimes there is no obvious addiction at all.
Just distance.
A thousand tiny moments of, “Not now.”
A thousand opportunities to listen that disappeared.
A thousand nights when the child eventually stopped knocking on the door.
Then one day Dad finally has time...
and the child no longer has anything to say.
That sentence should hurt.
Not because fathers need another person condemning them.
But because some things are too important to soften until they become harmless.
Paul wrote something remarkably direct to fathers:
“Καὶ οἱ πατέρες, μὴ παροργίζετε τὰ τέκνα ὑμῶν, ἀλλὰ ἐκτρέφετε αὐτὰ ἐν παιδείᾳ καὶ νουθεσίᾳ κυρίου.”
Ephesians 6:4.
A careful rendering is:
“And you fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but nourish and raise them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.”
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not merely say, “Feed them.”
It does not merely say, “House them.”
It does not merely say, “Pay for them.”
It says, ἐκτρέφετε αὐτά—ektrephete auta.
Bring them up. Nourish them. Rear them.
The same verb appears in Ephesians 5:29 in the context of nourishing and caring for one's own body. This is not the language of detached financial sponsorship.
Fatherhood in Ephesians 6:4 is personal.
Relational.
Intentional.
Spiritual.
And then comes another uncomfortable word:
παροργίζετε—parorgizete.
“Do not provoke...”
The verb carries the idea of provoking or exasperating to anger.
A father can wound his children not only through what he does, but through the environment his repeated choices create.
Constant criticism can provoke.
Humiliation can provoke.
Hypocrisy can provoke.
Unpredictable rage can provoke.
Promises repeatedly broken can provoke.
Never being good enough for Dad can provoke.
And yes...
chronic emotional absence can leave wounds too.

We should be careful here. Ephesians 6:4 is not saying that every disappointed or angry child has been wronged by a father. Children need boundaries. Loving discipline will sometimes frustrate them. Biblical fatherhood is not permissive parenting.
Paul's alternative to provocation is not indulgence.
It is παιδείᾳ καὶ νουθεσίᾳ κυρίου—paideia kai nouthesia Kyriou—the formative discipline and instruction of the Lord.
In other words, a Christian father is not called merely to make his child comfortable.
He is called to help form a human soul under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And you cannot outsource all of that.
Your child's school cannot replace you.
Your pastor cannot replace you.
The youth leader cannot replace you.
A Christian YouTube channel cannot replace you.
Mom cannot become Dad simply because Dad decided his only responsibility was paying for everything.

Children need mothers and fathers to fulfill their God-given responsibilities faithfully, while remembering that every family also lives in a fallen world where death, abandonment, divorce, hardship, and countless other circumstances can leave homes looking very different.
And if you are a single mother reading this, this article is not an accusation against you for a man's absence.
If you are a grandfather, stepfather, foster father, mentor, or faithful man helping a child whose biological father disappeared, do not underestimate the holy weight of consistent presence.
But fathers...
we need to talk.
Because perhaps you know exactly why you are still reading.
Maybe your son has stopped asking you to play.
Maybe your daughter tells Mom things she used to tell you.
Maybe your teenager's bedroom door stays closed now.
Maybe dinner has become a table full of people staring into separate screens.
Maybe you know more about your team's statistics than your son's fears.
Maybe you know what happened at work today but not what happened inside your daughter's heart.
Maybe you have spent years building a future for children whose present you keep missing.
And maybe something inside you is whispering:
I thought providing was enough.
Providing matters.
Please hear that clearly.

Scripture does not glorify irresponsibility. Paul speaks strongly elsewhere about caring for one's household. Working honestly and meeting legitimate family needs can be an expression of love, stewardship, and obedience.
The problem is not provision.
The problem is believing money can perform the work of presence.
It cannot.
Money can buy your child a bed.
It cannot kneel beside that bed and pray.
Money can buy a phone.
It cannot make the call your grown son wishes you would make.
Money can pay tuition.
It cannot tell your daughter, “I'm proud of the woman of God you are becoming.”
Money can buy a vacation.
It cannot create intimacy between people who have forgotten how to speak honestly to each other.
Money can leave an inheritance.
It cannot guarantee a relationship.
Your children need more than what comes from your hands.
They need something of your heart.
And perhaps that frightens you because your own heart carries wounds you never learned how to name.
Maybe your father was absent too.
Maybe he was present only when you failed.
Maybe affection embarrassed him.
Maybe “I love you” never crossed his lips.
Maybe you promised yourself you would be different.
Then adulthood came.
Bills came.
Pressure came.
Disappointment came.
And slowly, almost invisibly, you became unavailable in a different way.
Your father disappeared physically.
You disappeared emotionally.
Different absence.
Similar ache.
And this is exactly where the Gospel must interrupt the story.
Because Christianity does not tell wounded fathers merely to try harder.
It announces that sinners can become new men through Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not excuse your failures.
It gives you somewhere to take them.
To the cross.
Maybe you missed years.
Bring the years to Jesus.
Maybe you have been harsh.
Confess it.
Maybe you have been distant.
Name it.
Maybe pornography has taken your attention, tenderness, sexual integrity, and spiritual authority.
Bring the darkness into the light.
Maybe alcohol, gambling, gaming, ambition, hobbies, anger, pride, or your phone became easier to love than the complicated human beings God entrusted to your care.
Repent.
Not performatively.
Not with another dramatic promise everyone has heard before.
Repent biblically.
Turn.
Come to Christ.
And then walk down the hallway.
Knock on the door.
Sit beside your child.
And perhaps say the words some fathers believe will make them look weak:
“I was wrong.”
“I have not been there the way I should have been.”
“You deserved more of my attention.”
“I cannot recover yesterday, but by God's grace I want to change how I love you today.”
“Will you forgive me?”
Do not add an excuse.
Do not explain your workload for fifteen minutes.
Do not remind them how expensive their shoes were.
Do not turn your confession into a defense.
Listen.
Your child may cry.
Your child may shrug.
Your child may say, “It's fine.”
It may not be fine.
Your teenager may not suddenly collapse into your arms because you had one sincere conversation.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Presence has to become a pattern.
Repentance has fruit.
So come home when you can.
Put the phone down.
Learn the names of their friends.
Ask questions that cannot be answered with yes or no.
Pray with them.
Open Scripture with them.
Apologize when you sin against them.
Discipline without humiliating.
Correct without crushing.
Listen without immediately lecturing.
Laugh with them.
Tell them you love them while they are still close enough to hear it every day.
Tell your son strength and tenderness can live in the same man.
Tell your daughter her worth is not determined by whether the world notices her beauty.
Let them see you worship.
Let them see you repent.
Let them catch you reading the Word when nobody asked you to perform Christianity for them.
Let them discover that Dad's faith is not merely something he wears on Sunday.
And when you fail again—and you will fail in ways great and small—do not hide behind pride.
Return to grace.
Because your children do not need a father pretending to be Jesus.
They need a father who desperately needs Jesus.
There is only one perfectly faithful Father.
And there is only one perfectly obedient Son.

Jesus Christ entered our broken world, bore sin at the cross, died, and rose again. In Him there is forgiveness for guilty fathers, healing for wounded sons and daughters, and power to begin walking differently.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become the final chapter.
This is what we mean when we say:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming sin.
Not by erasing consequences with religious clichés.
Jesus rewrites lives through repentance, forgiveness, reconciliation, truth, grace, and transformation.
Maybe your children are small.
Then you still have time to create memories they will carry for decades.
Maybe they are teenagers.
Then knock before the door becomes harder to open.
Maybe they are adults.
Call them.
Maybe they have children of their own.
Call them anyway.
Maybe the relationship is badly fractured and wisdom requires patience, boundaries, counseling, pastoral help, or a slow rebuilding of trust.
Start where faithfulness allows you to start.
You cannot force reconciliation.
You cannot demand forgiveness on your timetable.
You cannot use Christianity to pressure a wounded child into pretending everything is healed.
But you can repent.
You can change.
You can pray.
You can become truthful.
You can become present.
You can follow Christ from this day forward.
And if your father is already gone and these words reopened something you buried years ago, hear this carefully:
Jesus sees the child who waited.
He sees the birthdays.
The empty chair.
The conversations that never happened.
The apology that never came.
Forgiveness does not require pretending evil was good or wounds were imaginary. Bring that grief to Christ. Refuse to let another person's absence become the architect of your entire future.
The Gospel can interrupt generational patterns.
The neglected son can become a present father.
The angry boy can become a gentle man.
The daughter who questioned her worth can discover an identity rooted more deeply than a human father's failures.
Grace does not change yesterday.
Grace can change what yesterday produces in you tomorrow.
And father, if this article exposed you, please do not merely feel guilty for five minutes and continue scrolling.
Do something.
Put your phone down after reading this.
Find your child.
Call your grown son.
Sit beside your daughter.
Pray.
Confess.
Listen.
Come home—not merely to your address, but to the people inside it.

And if you are reading this thinking of a father who loves his children but is slowly losing them to overwork, distraction, addiction, or emotional distance, share this with him privately before you judge him publicly.
If this made you think of your own father, your husband, your brother, or a man fighting to become the father he never had, tag him with grace, not humiliation.
He may need someone to remind him that his children need him too.
Not because it was pleasant to read.
Because there may be a night when work is calling, your screen is glowing, your child is standing at the doorway, and you need to remember which invitation matters more.
Someone drowning in regret may need evidence that repentance is not the end of hope.

Scripture calls Christians to generous, willing giving before God; faithful support of your local church, care for people in need, and support for Gospel work should never be reduced to a digital transaction.
Jesus does not primarily want your money.
He wants you.
Your repentance.
Your trust.
Your obedience.
Your life.
And perhaps tonight, one of the first places that surrendered life needs to become visible is not on a platform, in a church building, or in front of an audience.
Maybe it is in a child's bedroom.
Maybe the holiest thing you do tonight is put the phone face down...
walk through the door...
sit beside your child...
and stay.
Because years from now, your children may forget what their shoes cost.
They may forget which model phone you bought them.
They may forget the expensive birthday present.
But they may never forget whether Dad looked up when they walked into the room.
You spent years trying to give them a better life. Don't wake up one day and discover that the one thing missing from that life was you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WOMAN JESUS CALLED “JEZEBEL”: THE SIN THYATIRA TOLERATED UNTIL CHRIST HIMSELF SPOKE
paragraphs: THE WOMAN JESUS CALLED “JEZEBEL”: THE SIN THYATIRA TOLERATED UNTIL CHRIST HIMSELF SPOKE
The terrifying warning of Revelation 2:20 is not merely that sexual immorality entered a church. It is that people who loved Jesus learned to tolerate what Jesus told them to confront.
There are sins that enter the church screaming.
And there are sins that enter smiling.
They know the songs.
They know when to say “Amen.”
They know Christian vocabulary. They know how to sound spiritual. They may speak about revelation, freedom, grace, love, prophecy, destiny, and deeper things of God.
And sometimes the most dangerous deception does not stand outside the church shouting against Jesus.
Sometimes it sits inside the church...
and speaks in His name.
That is what makes the words of Jesus to the church in Thyatira so disturbing.
Christ did not begin His message by calling them worthless.
Quite the opposite.
He told them He knew their works, their love, their faith, their service, and their perseverance. He even acknowledged that their latter works exceeded their first.
This was not a spiritually dead congregation with absolutely nothing commendable about it.
There was love there.
There was faith there.
There was service there.
There was endurance there.
There was growth there.
And then Jesus essentially said:
But I have something against you.
One sentence changed the atmosphere.
Because apparently it is possible for a church to have love...
and tolerate deception.
To have faith...
and tolerate compromise.
To serve...
and still refuse to confront something Christ considers destructive.
Then came the accusation:
“ἀλλὰ ἔχω κατὰ σοῦ ὅτι ἀφεῖς τὴν γυναῖκα Ἰεζάβελ, ἡ λέγουσα ἑαυτὴν προφῆτιν, καὶ διδάσκει καὶ πλανᾷ τοὺς ἐμοὺς δούλους πορνεῦσαι καὶ φαγεῖν εἰδωλόθυτα.”
Revelation 2:20.
The sense of the Greek is devastatingly direct:

“But I have this against you: you tolerate the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, and she teaches and leads My servants astray to commit sexual immorality and to eat things sacrificed to idols.”
Notice the word that should make every Christian leader, parent, teacher, ministry worker, and believer uncomfortable:
ἀφεῖς — apheis.
You tolerate.
You allow.
You permit.
Jesus did not accuse every believer in Thyatira of personally teaching Jezebel’s doctrine.
He confronted them for allowing it.
That distinction matters.
There are moments when silence is patience.
There are moments when silence is wisdom.
There are moments when refusing to argue is Christlike.
But Revelation 2 reminds us that there are also moments when tolerance becomes participation in the damage because destructive teaching is being permitted to continue unchecked.
And before we go any further, we need to rescue the name “Jezebel” from some of the careless ways Christians use it today.
Revelation 2:20 is not permission to call every strong woman a “Jezebel.”

It is not permission to weaponize Scripture against a woman because she disagrees with a pastor, challenges a decision, possesses influence, dresses differently than someone prefers, or has a personality somebody finds intimidating.
Jesus' accusation is specific.
This woman claimed prophetic authority.
She taught.
She deceived Christ's servants.
And her teaching led people toward sexual immorality and participation in idolatrous practices.
That is the biblical accusation.
Anything beyond that needs evidence rather than imagination.

There is even a textual detail worth knowing. Some ancient witnesses contain a reading that can be translated “your wife Jezebel,” while significant witnesses support simply “the woman Jezebel.” Christians should therefore be careful about constructing elaborate theories around the disputed possessive.
The central accusation, however, is unmistakable in either reading.
A woman whom Jesus identifies as “Jezebel” was exercising corrupting religious influence among His people, and the church was tolerating it.
And “Jezebel” almost certainly carries us backward into Israel's history.

The Jezebel of the Old Testament was the Phoenician wife of King Ahab. First Kings presents her in connection with Baal worship, persecution of the LORD's prophets, and the murderous injustice surrounding Naboth's vineyard. Ahab's marriage to Jezebel became part of an extraordinary collapse into idolatry.
So when the risen Christ uses the name “Jezebel” in Revelation, the name arrives carrying centuries of biblical memory.
Idolatry.
Seduction away from covenant faithfulness.
Corrupt influence.
Compromise.
Whether “Jezebel” in Thyatira was this woman's literal name or a symbolic identification comparing her with the infamous queen, the point is unmistakable:
Something poisonous had been given spiritual credibility.
And perhaps that is where this ancient letter becomes frighteningly modern.
Because compromise rarely introduces itself by saying:
“I am here to destroy your relationship with Jesus.”
It usually says:
“It isn't that serious.”
“Everybody struggles.”
“God understands.”
“Don't be so judgmental.”
“Times have changed.”
“Surely grace means this doesn't matter anymore.”
And there is a dangerous half-truth hidden inside some of those statements.
Yes, everybody struggles.
Yes, God understands our weakness.
Yes, Christians can become hypocritically judgmental.
Yes, grace is astonishingly greater than our sin.
But biblical grace never requires pretending that the sin which crucified Christ is harmless.
Grace does not rename darkness so darkness can remain comfortable.
Grace brings sinners into the light.
There is an enormous difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
One person falls and cries, “Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Another falls and eventually says, “There is nothing wrong with this.”
Those are not the same spiritual posture.
The Gospel has room for the broken.
The Gospel has room for the addicted.
The Gospel has room for the sexually fallen.
The Gospel has room for the ashamed.
The Gospel has room for the person who destroyed years of his life.
The Gospel has room for the woman carrying a past she desperately wishes she could erase.
The Gospel has room for adulterers, fornicators, idolaters, liars, hypocrites, prodigals, and religious pretenders.
The cross proves it.
But Jesus does not rescue us by declaring our chains beautiful.
He rescues us by breaking them.
And this is where Revelation 2 becomes unexpectedly tender.
Because after confronting Jezebel's sin, Jesus says something astonishing.
He gave her time to repent.
Read that again.
He gave her time.
The Christ whose eyes are described as being like a flame of fire...
waited.
The One who knew exactly what she had taught...
waited.
The One who saw every person she had influenced...
waited.
The One who knew what happened behind closed doors...
waited.
Why?
Because judgment was not His first invitation.
Repentance was.
That single statement destroys the caricature of Jesus as a Savior who is either too loving to confront sin or too holy to show mercy to sinners.
He is both perfectly holy and astonishingly merciful.
He confronts because He loves.
He warns because He loves.
He calls people to repent because He loves.
The frightening words that follow in Revelation 2:21–23 come after the offer of repentance is resisted.
Jesus is not indifferent to what destroys His people.
And neither should we be.
Maybe your “Jezebel” is not a person.
Maybe it is the compromise you have quietly permitted inside yourself.
The private messages you keep deleting.
The browser history nobody sees.
The relationship you know is dragging you away from Christ.
The fantasy you keep feeding.
The bitterness you have baptized as discernment.
The greed you call ambition.
The gossip you call concern.
The pride you call standards.
The addiction you call stress relief.
The secret life you have become frighteningly good at separating from your public Christianity.
You still worship.
You still post Scripture.
You still attend church.
You still tell people God is good.
And perhaps He is whispering into the room you keep locked:
I know.
Not because He wants to humiliate you.
Because He wants you free.
This is what repentance actually means.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia — carries the idea of a changed mind, a turning of the inner person that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about what happened last night.
You can hate the consequences of sin without hating the sin.
You can cry because you got caught without turning toward Christ.
You can feel shame without surrender.
Repentance says:
“Jesus, You are right about this, and I have been wrong.”
It stops negotiating.
Stops renaming.
Stops hiding.
Stops demanding that Scripture accommodate the secret.
And turns toward Christ.
Maybe this article found you while you are exhausted from hiding.
Then hear something more powerful than condemnation:
You can come home.
Not after you clean yourself.
Not after you become impressive.
Not after you prove that you can go thirty days without falling.
Come to Christ now.
The scandal of Christianity is not that good people earn heaven.
The scandal is that guilty people can be forgiven because the innocent Son of God took the judgment sinners deserved.
Jesus Christ lived without sin.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And the risen Jesus speaking to Thyatira is the same Jesus who still calls sinners to repent and believe.
The cross does not tell you that your sin was small.
The cross tells you that His mercy is enormous.
There is blood for this.
There is forgiveness for this.
There is restoration after this.
There is life beyond this.
Your worst chapter does not possess enough authority to overrule the Author of redemption.
That does not mean earthly consequences magically disappear.
Repentance may require confession.
Relationships may need rebuilding.
Trust may take time.
Some doors may remain closed.
Some wounds require patient healing.
But consequences are not the same thing as condemnation for the person who is in Christ.
Jesus is not asking you to pretend the scandal never happened.
He is asking you to surrender it to the One who can write grace into places you thought could contain nothing except shame.
And there is another side of Thyatira's warning we cannot ignore.
Jesus addressed the church.
Meaning this passage is not only for the person trapped in sexual sin.
It is also for the people watching destructive teaching spread while saying nothing.
Christian love is not cowardice wearing a smile.
But neither is biblical confrontation cruelty wearing a Bible verse.
We are called to truth and love.
If your idea of holiness makes you enjoy humiliating sinners, something is wrong.
If your idea of love requires you to pretend sin cannot destroy people, something is also wrong.
Jesus managed what we repeatedly separate.
Perfect truth.
Perfect holiness.
Perfect compassion.
Perfect justice.
Perfect mercy.
He could look at a sinner and say, in effect, “Repent,” while simultaneously opening the door of mercy.
That is our Savior.
And perhaps the most important detail in this entire letter comes after the warning.
Not everyone in Thyatira had accepted this teaching.
Jesus spoke to those who had not followed it and told them to hold fast until He came.
Hold fast.
When culture moves...
hold fast.
When temptation whispers...
hold fast.
When compromise becomes fashionable...
hold fast.
When obedience costs friendships...
hold fast.
When holiness makes you look strange...
hold fast.
When you are tired of fighting the same temptation...
hold fast.
When you fell yesterday and Satan tells you there is no reason to stand today...
run to Christ...
and hold fast.

And if Christ has already begun restoring something you thought was beyond repair, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to keep another person from surrendering to despair.
Send this to the friend whose silence has been worrying you.
One share can put truth in front of someone we may never meet.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget tomorrow what conviction made painfully clear today.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront compromise, understand the Gospel, and keep your eyes on Jesus, stay close.
And if you believe this work should continue and expand, you can help carry it.
It does not.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior can replace repentance, obedience, generosity toward people in need, or faithful participation in your local church.
It cannot.
Scripture deserves more care than that.

But voluntary financial support can be a genuine expression of Christian generosity when it is given freely, prayerfully, and cheerfully. Scripture says giving should come from what a person has purposed in the heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV).
Let it be support freely given to the work—not money extracted through guilt.
And even if you cannot financially support Gospel Warrior, you can still help.
Pray.
Send it privately to the person God placed on your heart while you were reading.
Speak about Jesus.
Because the mission was never to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The mission is to make Christ known.
Thyatira reminds us that Jesus sees what churches celebrate...
and what churches tolerate.
He sees our love.
He sees our service.
He sees our faith.
He sees our endurance.
And He also sees the room we hoped He would never enter.
But when Jesus opens that door, it is not necessarily the end of your story.
It may finally be the end of your hiding.
There is still time to repent.
There is still mercy at the cross.
There is still cleansing for the guilty.
There is still restoration for the fallen.
There is still a Savior whose scars testify that sin is more serious than we imagined...
and grace is more magnificent than we dared believe.
So don't merely ask whether there was a Jezebel in Thyatira.
Ask the question Revelation 2 forces much closer to home:
What have I learned to tolerate that Jesus is asking me to surrender?
Be honest.
Maybe that question hit harder than you expected.
If it did, don't run from the conviction.
Run toward Christ.
Because perhaps the most dangerous thing about darkness is not that it exists.
It is the day we become comfortable enough to stop calling it darkness.
But Jesus still walks among His churches.
His eyes still see.
His voice still calls.
His grace still reaches.
And for the sinner willing to turn around...
the thing Jesus exposes does not have to become the thing that destroys you. It can become the place where grace finally finds you with the door unlocked.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Grief Is Strange: You Can Laugh at Breakfast and Break Down in the Grocery Store
paragraphs: Grief Is Strange: You Can Laugh at Breakfast and Break Down in the Grocery Store
If you have ever wondered how you could worship God in the morning and cry beside a grocery cart that afternoon, there is something Jesus did beside a grave that you desperately need to see.
You were fine five minutes ago.
That is the part nobody warns you about.
You woke up. You made coffee. Maybe you even laughed at something on your phone. For a few precious minutes, life almost felt normal again.
Then you went to the grocery store.
You weren't looking for a memory.
You were looking for bread.
Milk.
Coffee.
Something for dinner.
And then you saw it.
Their favorite cereal.
The brand of tea they always bought.
A jar of sauce they insisted was better than every other jar on the shelf.
Maybe a song started playing overhead.
Maybe somebody walked past wearing the same perfume.
Maybe you heard a laugh that sounded almost—almost—like theirs.
And suddenly you weren't standing in aisle seven anymore.
You were standing in the ruins of a life that used to include someone who is no longer there.
Your throat tightened.
Your chest hurt.
Your eyes filled.
You stared at a grocery shelf while strangers pushed carts around you, completely unaware that your whole world had just collapsed again between the canned vegetables and the breakfast cereal.
And perhaps the worst part came afterward.
You felt guilty.
Why am I still doing this?
Shouldn't I be stronger by now?
I thought I was healing.
I was laughing this morning.
Why am I crying again?
And if you are a Christian, another question can creep into the darkness.
Does this mean my faith is weak?
Please stay here for a moment.
Because there is a scene in Scripture that refuses to let us treat tears as spiritual failure.
There is a grave.
There are grieving sisters.
There is a crowd trying to make sense of death.
And standing in the middle of it all is Jesus Christ.
John 11 tells us about Lazarus, the brother of Mary and Martha and a man Jesus loved.
Lazarus became sick.
Jesus knew.
Yet Jesus did not arrive before Lazarus died.
By the time Christ came to Bethany, Lazarus had been in the tomb four days.
Martha went out to meet Him.
Mary eventually came too.
And when Mary reached Jesus, she fell at His feet with words that carry the sound of shattered expectation:
“Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.”
Then Mary wept.
The people around her wept.
And John tells us something extraordinary.
The Greek text of John 11:33 says:
“Ἰησοῦς οὖν ὡς εἶδεν αὐτὴν κλαίουσαν…”
Jesus saw her weeping.
Then comes language far stronger than a picture of a detached religious teacher calmly explaining why everything would eventually be okay.
“ἐνεβριμήσατο τῷ πνεύματι καὶ ἐτάραξεν ἑαυτόν.”
He was deeply moved in spirit and troubled.
Those Greek expressions matter.

John does not portray Jesus as emotionally untouched by the scene before Him. The language carries profound inner disturbance. Jesus enters the terrible reality surrounding death rather than standing at a safe emotional distance from it.
Then He asks:
“Where have ye laid him?”
They answer:
“Lord, come and see.”
And then comes one of the shortest verses in the Bible.
Two words in many English translations.
John 11:35.
“Jesus wept.”
The Greek is equally arresting:
“ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς.”
Edakrysen ho Iēsous.
Jesus wept.
Read that again slowly.
Jesus knew what He was about to do.
Jesus knew Lazarus would not remain inside that tomb.
Jesus knew resurrection was only moments away.
And Jesus still wept.
That changes something.
Because we sometimes imagine that if we truly trust God, knowledge of the resurrection should somehow erase the agony of the grave.
But Jesus knew more about resurrection than anybody standing in Bethany that day.
And He cried.
He did not say, “Stop crying. Lazarus is coming back.”
He did not rebuke Mary for grieving.
He did not shame Martha because death had wounded her.
He did not stand outside human sorrow pretending that correct theology makes tears unnecessary.
He wept.
This is Christianity at the graveside.
Not hopelessness.
Not denial.
Hope with tears running down its face.
You can believe Jesus Christ is the resurrection and the life and still miss somebody so much that their empty chair hurts.
You can believe in heaven and still hate funerals.
You can know that death does not have the final word and still wish desperately that you could hear that person's voice one more time.
You can sing on Sunday and cry on Monday.
You can pray with confidence at 7:00 in the morning and feel your knees weaken when you find an old photograph at 3:17 in the afternoon.
You can laugh at breakfast...
and break down in the grocery store.
That does not automatically mean you have abandoned faith.
Sometimes it simply means you loved someone whose absence still has weight.
Grief is strange because grief does not ask permission before entering the room.
It does not check your calendar.
It does not care that today was supposed to be a good day.
It can hide inside birthdays.
Christmas songs.
Hospital corridors.
Empty bedrooms.
Old voicemail recordings.
A particular road.
A familiar smell.
A restaurant table.
A church pew.
A name appearing unexpectedly on an old document.
A phone number you cannot bring yourself to delete.
Sometimes grief screams.
Sometimes it whispers.
Sometimes it waits quietly for six months and then ambushes you because you reached for two coffee cups instead of one.
And there you are again.
Hurting.
Maybe embarrassed by how much you're hurting.
But Scripture never gives us a commandment saying, “Thou shalt finish grieving by Thursday.”
The Bible gives us lament.
David asks, “How long, O LORD?” in Psalm 13.
The Psalms contain cries, questions, anguish, loneliness and tears alongside praise, trust and worship.
Ecclesiastes says there is “a time to weep.”
Paul does not tell believers never to grieve. In 1 Thessalonians 4:13, he distinguishes Christian grief from grief without hope.
That distinction matters.
The Gospel does not turn Christians into people incapable of sorrow.
The Gospel gives sorrow somewhere to go.
Toward Christ.
Toward the One who stood outside Lazarus's tomb.
Toward the One who Himself would soon enter a tomb.
And this is where the story becomes even more astonishing.
Jesus did not merely come to Bethany to sympathize with people devastated by death.
He came to confront death.
He called:
“Lazarus, come forth.”
And the dead man came out.
But Lazarus's resurrection was a sign pointing beyond Lazarus.
Because another tomb was coming.
Another stone.
Another body wrapped for burial.
Another group of devastated followers convinced that everything had ended.
Except this time the dead Man inside the tomb would not need someone standing outside commanding Him to emerge.
Jesus Christ would rise.
The cross and empty tomb are God's declaration that death is an enemy—but it is a defeated enemy.
Sin brought ruin into God's good creation.
And all of us stand guilty before a holy God, needing far more than emotional comfort. We need reconciliation. We need forgiveness. We need redemption.
That is why Jesus did not merely come to make grieving people feel better.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, Christ bore sin.
He suffered.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day He rose.
The Christian hope is therefore not vague optimism that somehow everything eventually works out.
Our hope has a name.
Jesus.
Our hope has an empty tomb.
Our hope has scars in His hands.
And because Christ lives, grief does not get the last sentence.
But notice something beautiful.
Jesus knew the last sentence before everybody else did...
and He still stopped to weep in the middle of the paragraph.
Maybe that is where you are right now.
In the middle.
