Grace rewrote the ending.
And perhaps your story looks scandalous right now.
Maybe there are chapters you would burn if life were a book.
Jesus is not frightened by those pages.
Bring Him the manuscript.
Every page.
The beautiful pages.
The embarrassing pages.
The pages stained by other people’s sins against you.
The pages stained by your own choices.
The chapter you keep rereading.
The chapter you refuse to talk about.
The chapter you wish had never happened.
Give it to Him.
Because Christianity does not proclaim that your past never happened.
Christianity proclaims something infinitely better:
Your past does not have to be your master.
Jesus Christ died.
Jesus Christ was buried.
Jesus Christ rose again.
And resurrection means God specializes in stories everyone else thought were over.
So yes.
Come as you are.
Come exhausted.
Come ashamed.
Come confused.
Come skeptical.
Come angry.
Come wounded.
Come addicted.
Come religious.
Come irreligious.
Come successful and secretly empty.
Come broke.
Come grieving.
Come after the divorce.
Come after the relapse.
Come after the diagnosis.
Come after the betrayal.
Come after what you did.
Come after what they did to you.
Come while your hands are trembling.
Come when you do not have impressive words.
But come to Jesus.
And when you come, do not ask Him merely to make your old life more comfortable.
Lay the old life down.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Him.
Let grace forgive what you cannot undo.
Let truth expose what you keep defending.
Let Christ heal what you keep hiding.
Let the Holy Spirit begin transforming what human determination could never permanently change.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to sell salvation.
Not to place spiritual growth behind a paywall.
And certainly not to suggest that giving money earns favor with God.
We exist because people are scrolling through their phones while silently fighting battles nobody around them can see.
Somebody is contemplating giving up.
Somebody has not opened a Bible in months.
Somebody loves Jesus but feels spiritually exhausted.
Somebody walked away from church after being wounded.
Somebody thinks their sin has made them permanently unwanted.
Somebody is searching tonight for one reason to come home.
We want to keep meeting them there with Scripture.
With conviction.
With hope.
With discipleship.
With the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Think of it not as purchasing God's blessing, and never as a replacement for generosity and responsibility toward your local church, but as a voluntary ministry offering—a practical way of saying:
“Keep reaching people. Keep teaching Scripture. Keep putting Christ into feeds filled with everything except Christ.”
Scripture gives us an important boundary here.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
Each person should give as he has determined in his heart—not reluctantly and not ἐξ ἀνάγκης, out of compulsion or necessity.
Then:
“ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεός.”
God loves a cheerful giver.
He will not.
That would go beyond Scripture.
You can still help.
That costs nothing.
And it may accomplish more than you realize.
You do not know who needs to discover tonight that Jesus still receives sinners.
You do not know who has confused “come as you are” with “God wants me to remain as I am.”
You do not know who thinks they have become too dirty to return.
And before you leave, do something harder than clicking “like.”
Be honest.
If you have been hiding, let those words become your confession.
And if Christ has already rescued you from a chapter you thought would destroy your life, tell us what Jesus did.
Someone reading the comments may need your testimony more than you realize.
Because the comments beneath a Gospel message should be more than reactions.
They can become a room full of people pointing one another toward Christ.
No pretending.
No spiritual performance.
No competition over who looks holiest.
Just sinners and saints admitting the same truth:
We need Jesus.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because somebody you know may need the invitation.
Come.
Not to us.
Not to a brand.
Come to Christ.
Come as you are.
But never confuse His open arms with permission to remain chained.
The hands welcoming you still bear scars.
Those scars are proof that grace was never cheap.
Jesus paid dearly to forgive you.
And the Savior who receives you exactly where you are intends, by His grace, to lead you somewhere you could never reach without Him.
So bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shattered pieces.
Then watch what happens when the Author gets the pen.
You may come to Jesus carrying the chapter you are most ashamed of—but never forget that wounded hands are still holding the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SODOM’S SIN WAS BIGGER THAN YOU WERE TOLD — AND THAT SHOULD TERRIFY ALL OF US
paragraphs: SODOM’S SIN WAS BIGGER THAN YOU WERE TOLD — AND THAT SHOULD TERRIFY ALL OF US

Why does the Bible condemn Sodom for sexual wickedness AND for pride, abundance, complacency, and abandoning the poor—and what happens when Christians only preach the half that condemns somebody else?
There is something deeply uncomfortable about the way the Bible talks about Sodom.
Not because Scripture is unclear.
Because Scripture may be clearer than we want it to be.
We have learned how to say “Sodom” and immediately think about somebody else.
Someone else’s sexuality.
Someone else’s rebellion.
Someone else’s lifestyle.
Someone else’s sin.
And then Ezekiel walks into the room.
And suddenly the finger we were pointing begins to tremble.
Because God says something about Sodom that many Christians have read dozens of times without allowing it to interrogate them.
Listen carefully.
“Behold, this was the iniquity of thy sister Sodom, pride, fulness of bread, and abundance of idleness was in her and in her daughters, neither did she strengthen the hand of the poor and needy.”
That is Ezekiel 16:49 in the KJV.
Now look at the Hebrew:
הִנֵּה־זֶה הָיָה עֲוֹן סְדֹם אֲחוֹתֵךְ גָּאוֹן שִׂבְעַת־לֶחֶם וְשַׁלְוַת הַשְׁקֵט הָיָה לָהּ וְלִבְנוֹתֶיהָ וְיַד־עָנִי וְאֶבְיוֹן לֹא הֶחֱזִיקָה׃
The words are devastating.
עֲוֹן — avon — iniquity, guilt, perversity.
גָּאוֹן — ga'on — pride, arrogance, exaltation.
שִׂבְעַת־לֶחֶם — siv'at-lechem — fullness, abundance, satiety of bread.
עָנִי — ani — poor, afflicted.
אֶבְיוֹן — evyon — needy, destitute.
God looks at Sodom and sees a society swollen with abundance while vulnerable people remain unsupported.
Full tables.
Empty compassion.
Comfort without mercy.
Prosperity without responsibility.
People who had enough to become generous...
and instead became proud.
But do not stop reading.
That would be just as dishonest as ignoring verse 49.
The next verse says:
“And they were haughty, and committed abomination before me: therefore I took them away as I saw good.”
Ezekiel 16:50.
That matters.
The Bible does not permit us to erase Sodom’s sexual wickedness in order to turn the story exclusively into a lesson about poverty.
And it does not permit us to erase Sodom’s arrogance, prosperous self-indulgence, violence, and neglect of the vulnerable in order to turn the story exclusively into a weapon against sexual sin.
God gives us the whole indictment.
We do not have permission to edit His evidence.
Go back to Genesis 19.
Two angelic visitors enter Sodom. Lot receives them into his house. Then the men of the city surround that house and demand that the visitors be brought outside so they can “know” them.
Whatever modern argument someone wants to attach to the chapter, the immediate scene is horrifying.
This is not romance.
It is not mutual affection.
It is threatened sexual violence.
It is domination.
Humiliation.
Predation.
A mob attempting to use human bodies as instruments of power.
And the New Testament refuses to let us pretend sexual rebellion is irrelevant to Sodom.
Jude 7 says:
“Even as Sodom and Gomorrha, and the cities about them in like manner, giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh…”
The Greek is even harder to dodge:
ἐκπορνεύσασαι … ὀπίσω σαρκὸς ἑτέρας
ekporneusasai … opisō sarkos heteras.
The first term describes giving oneself over to sexual immorality. The latter expression literally concerns going after “other” or “different flesh.”
So when somebody says, “Sodom had nothing to do with sexual sin,” Jude will not cooperate.
But when somebody says, “Sodom was only about sexual sin,” Ezekiel will not cooperate either.
Maybe that is the point.
We keep trying to make Sodom small enough to use against our preferred enemies.
God keeps making Sodom large enough to expose us.
Sexual corruption was there.
Pride was there.
Violence was there.
Exploitation was there.
Abundance without compassion was there.
Neglect of the poor was there.
Haughtiness before God was there.
These were not competing explanations.
They were branches growing from a diseased root.
Human beings had rejected God's order so profoundly that other people ceased to be neighbors to love and became objects to consume, ignore, exploit, dominate, or discard.
And suddenly Sodom is not safely buried beneath ancient ruins anymore.
It is standing frighteningly close to us.
Because what happens when a culture becomes sexually unrestrained while simultaneously becoming obsessed with itself?
What happens when bodies become commodities?
What happens when pornography trains human beings to consume one another?
What happens when the powerful exploit the vulnerable?
What happens when churches can thunder about sexual morality while stepping over desperate people?
What happens when Christians defend biblical sexuality but ignore biblical generosity?
What happens when people preach compassion while redefining whatever sexual boundaries God has established?
Different compromises.
Same terrifying instinct.
We want the parts of God's holiness that expose other people and quietly negotiate with the parts that expose us.
That is why Ezekiel 16 should make comfortable Christians uncomfortable.
Imagine sitting at a table overflowing with food while somebody outside cannot eat.
Imagine having three closets of clothes while another human being is shivering.
Imagine knowing someone is drowning financially, emotionally, spiritually—and having the ability to strengthen their hand—but saying, “Someone else will help.”
Then imagine opening your Bible and thanking God that you are not like Sodom.
Ezekiel whispers:
Look again.
This is where Scripture becomes personal.
Perhaps you have never joined a mob outside Lot's door.
But have you become proud?
Perhaps you would never defend sexual violence.
But have you secretly consumed another person's body through pornography?
Perhaps your theology of marriage is completely orthodox.
But does the poor person matter to you?
Perhaps you condemn immorality loudly.
But are you sleeping with someone who is not your spouse?
Perhaps you serve the poor faithfully.
But have you begun using compassion as permission to call something good that God calls sin?
Perhaps you can quote every verse about sexuality.
But when was the last time your abundance became somebody else's answered prayer?
That hurts.
It is supposed to.
Not because Jesus delights in crushing sinners.
Because Jesus loves sinners too much to leave our favorite hiding places undisturbed.
And here is where the story becomes infinitely greater than Sodom.
Because if Scripture only exposed us, every one of us would eventually stand condemned.
The Bible's message is not:
“Find the Sodomites and destroy them.”
The Gospel's message is:
“All have sinned.”
You.
Me.
The sexually broken.
The sexually proud.
The greedy.
The self-righteous.
The adulterer.
The porn addict.
The religious hypocrite.
The wealthy person who has forgotten mercy.
The activist who has forgotten holiness.
The preacher who secretly believes his correct doctrine makes repentance unnecessary.
The church member who knows exactly which sins God hates—as long as they are somebody else's.
We all need the same Savior.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
This is where scandal collides with grace.
Jesus does not rescue us by pretending sin is harmless.
He rescues us by bearing its judgment.
At the cross, Christ does not redefine darkness as light.
He enters the darkness.
He carries guilt.
He bears wrath.
He sheds His blood.
He dies.
And on the third day, He rises.
The Gospel is not God lowering His holiness until sinners can comfortably climb over it.

The Gospel is the holy Son of God coming down to sinners, taking upon Himself the judgment His people deserved, and rising victorious so that those who repent and believe can be forgiven, reconciled, cleansed, and transformed.
That means there is hope for sexual sinners.
Real hope.
Not affirmation that leaves us unchanged.
Grace that transforms us.
There is hope for the greedy.
There is hope for the proud.
There is hope for people enslaved to pornography.
There is hope for adulterers.
There is hope for people carrying sexual histories they cannot bear to remember.
There is hope for people whose desires have become their identity.
There is hope for wealthy hearts that have forgotten the poor.
There is hope for religious people who discovered that their morality had become pride.
There is hope for the person reading this who quietly thought:
“If people knew everything about me, they would never look at me the same way again.”
Jesus already knows.
Every room.
Every search.
Every touch.
Every fantasy.
Every selfish purchase.
Every person you ignored.
Every secret.
Every excuse.
Every night you promised God it was the last time.
He knows the scandal.
And the breathtaking announcement of Christianity is that the scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning from the grave because Christ is calling you into life.
Grace is not permission to remain what sin made you.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy meeting you in the wreckage and beginning to make you new.
Maybe that is why Sodom still matters.
Not so Christians can carry its name around like a stone to throw.
But so all of us can recognize what happens when human beings dethrone God.
Sex becomes detached from holiness.
Prosperity becomes detached from generosity.
Power becomes detached from mercy.
Desire becomes detached from obedience.
Comfort becomes detached from responsibility.
Religion becomes detached from repentance.
Eventually everything becomes about us.
My body.
My money.
My comfort.
My truth.
My appetite.
My life.
My rules.
And Jesus confronts the kingdom of self with two words that sound terrifying until you realize they are the doorway to freedom:
Not your appetite.
Not your bank account.
Not your political tribe.
Not your shame.
Not your sexual history.
Not your self-righteousness.
Me.
Jesus.
This is why Christians must refuse the false choice between holiness and compassion.
We do not have to choose.
Christ commands both.
We can uphold God's design for sexual holiness while loving sexually broken people with extraordinary tenderness.
We can care fiercely for the poor without pretending material generosity cancels rebellion elsewhere.
We can speak truth without cruelty.
We can show mercy without rewriting truth.
We can call sin “sin” because Christ offers forgiveness.
And we can call grace “grace” because forgiveness was purchased at an unimaginable price.
The cross leaves no room for superiority.
Nobody stands beneath it bragging.
Nobody arrives there because his sins were more respectable than his neighbor's.
We arrive empty-handed.
And perhaps that is the question Sodom finally asks us.
Not merely:
“What was their sin?”
But:
“What is mine?”
Where have I become proud?
Where has abundance made me numb?
Whose hand could I strengthen but have refused to strengthen?
Where have I violated God's sexual holiness—in action, imagination, consumption, secrecy, or desire?
Where have I used somebody else's sin to distract myself from my own?
Where am I asking Jesus to be Savior while resisting Him as Lord?
Sit with it.
Because sometimes the verse that makes you most uncomfortable is the verse God uses to open the prison door.
If something hidden was exposed while you read this, you do not have to describe your private sin publicly. But if you want to mark a moment of repentance, comment, “Jesus, have mercy on me.”
If you are exhausted from fighting the same temptation, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If shame has kept you hiding from Christian community, comment, “No more hiding.”

And if Christ has already pulled you from a place you thought you would never escape, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to keep another wounded believer from giving up tonight.
Not because every paragraph was comfortable.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, grow deeper in Christ, repent honestly, heal biblically, and follow Jesus more faithfully, stay close by following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even unbelieving friends who are willing to listen—to follow as well.
There is also a deeper way to help this ministry continue.
Keeping Gospel-centered resources moving outward takes real support.
It does not purchase salvation.
It does not make God love you more.
Christian giving must be voluntary. Paul says giving is not to be done “grudgingly, or of necessity,” because “God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And if financial support is not possible for you, please do not carry shame.
Pray.
Those actions can help truth travel farther than you may ever know.
Because the goal was never to build an audience that merely says, “Amen.”
The goal is to make disciples who look more like Jesus.
People who are sexually holy and radically compassionate.
People who refuse both self-righteousness and moral compromise.
People whose tables are open.
Whose hands strengthen the weak.
Whose bodies belong to Christ.
Whose money belongs to Christ.
Whose sexuality belongs to Christ.
Whose influence belongs to Christ.
Whose wounds are being healed by Christ.
Whose sins are being confessed to Christ.
Whose lives increasingly say:
Jesus is Lord.
Maybe you opened this article expecting to discover what was wrong with Sodom.
Maybe God used it to ask what is happening inside you.
That is not the end of the story.
That may be exactly where grace begins.
Bring Him the sexual sin.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the greed.
Bring Him the secret browser history.
Bring Him the coldness toward the poor.
Bring Him the hypocrisy.
Bring Him the theology you used as camouflage.
Bring Him the years you cannot undo.
Bring Him the part of your story you wish had never happened.
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Because the most terrifying thing about Sodom is not that ancient sinners became exceedingly corrupt.
It is how easily we can recognize their sins everywhere except in ourselves.
And the most beautiful thing about Jesus is that when He finally exposes what we were hiding, He is still mighty enough to save.
The sin you finally stop defending may become the very place where you discover how desperately you needed grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS FLIRTING A SIN—OR IS IT THE DOORWAY TO SOMETHING YOUR HEART IS HIDING?
paragraphs: IS FLIRTING A SIN—OR IS IT THE DOORWAY TO SOMETHING YOUR HEART IS HIDING?
The Bible never says, “Thou shalt not flirt.” But Jesus asks a far more uncomfortable question: What is happening inside your heart while you do it?
It starts so innocently.
A smile held a second longer than necessary.
A playful message.
A compliment with just enough ambiguity to make the other person wonder what you meant.
A late-night conversation you would probably describe as “nothing.”
A heart reaction.
Another message.
Then another.
You tell yourself you are only being friendly.
Maybe you are.
But somewhere between harmless conversation and emotional electricity, something changes.
You start checking whether they have seen your message.
You notice when they are online.
You think about what to say next.
You replay their words.
You enjoy knowing that they are thinking about you.
And perhaps the most revealing thing of all...
you would feel strangely disappointed if they stopped.
So let’s ask the question Christians often ask:
Is flirting a sin?
But before answering it, perhaps we need to ask a more dangerous question.
Why are you flirting?
Because Scripture does not contain a verse that simply says, “Flirting is sinful.”
The Bible does something much more penetrating.
It goes after the heart.
Proverbs 4:23 says:
“Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.”
The Hebrew is striking:
מִֽכָּל־מִ֭שְׁמָר נְצֹ֣ר לִבֶּ֑ךָ כִּֽי־מִ֝מֶּ֗נּוּ תּוֹצְא֥וֹת חַיִּֽים
Mikkol-mishmar netzor libbekha, ki-mimmennu tots'ot chayyim.
The command נְצֹר — netzor means to guard, watch, preserve, keep.
And לִבֶּךָ — libbekha means “your heart.”
The biblical heart is not merely romantic emotion. It is the inner person—the place from which desires, decisions, intentions, and direction emerge.
That is why Scripture does not allow us to evaluate our behavior only by asking, “Technically, did I break a rule?”
God goes deeper.
“What is your heart doing?”
“What are you awakening?”
“What are you trying to receive from this person?”
“What are you encouraging them to feel?”
And...
“Where is this taking both of you?”
That changes the entire conversation.
Because flirting itself can describe many different behaviors.
Two unmarried people who genuinely like each other may smile, joke, tease appropriately, express interest, compliment each other, and slowly discover whether a relationship might develop.
There is nothing inherently sinful about communicating romantic interest.
Attraction is not automatically lust.
Finding someone beautiful is not adultery.
Enjoying someone's company is not sexual immorality.
Wanting marriage is certainly not shameful.
Scripture celebrates romantic attraction within its proper moral setting. The Song of Songs does not pretend men and women are emotionless creatures incapable of delighting in one another.
So Christianity is not asking you to become cold.
The Gospel does not require Christians to pretend nobody is attractive.
But attraction can become something else.
Interest can become manipulation.
Playfulness can become seduction.
Attention can become emotional dependency.
And flirting can become a way of taking something from another person's heart without having any intention of caring for that heart.
That is where the question gets serious.
Because sometimes flirting is not really about love.
Sometimes it is about validation.
You don't actually want them.
You want to know that they want you.
Read that again.
You don't necessarily want a relationship.
You want the feeling produced when someone finds you desirable.
So you send the signal.
Then pull back.
Give attention.
Then disappear.
Show interest.
Then deny that you ever meant anything.
You keep someone emotionally close enough to feed your ego but far enough away that you never have to take responsibility for their heart.
And if they finally ask what this is, you say:
“I was only being friendly.”
Maybe you were.
But sometimes we know better.
Sometimes the scandal is not what happened with our bodies.
It is what we knowingly did with somebody else's heart.
Paul told Timothy how believers should relate to one another, including treating younger women as sisters “with all purity.”
The Greek phrase is beautiful and demanding:
ἐν πάσῃ ἁγνείᾳ — en pasē hagneia
“In all purity.”
Not partial purity.
Not public purity while privately playing games.
Not purity when somebody is watching.
All purity.
That principle reaches far beyond one gender.
The person in front of you is not an emotional vending machine.
They are not there to dispense affirmation whenever your self-esteem feels empty.
They bear the image of God.
Their heart matters to Christ.
Their purity matters.
Their future marriage matters.
Their healing matters.
And if you claim to love Jesus, then how you handle another person's vulnerability matters.
Then Jesus takes us deeper still.
In Matthew 5:28, He says:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.
The crucial expression is:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν — pros to epithymēsai autēn
The construction describes looking directed toward lusting after her.
Jesus is not condemning the biological recognition that another person is attractive.
He is confronting desire deliberately cultivated in the heart.
The issue is not merely seeing.
It is seeing in order to desire sexually.
Suddenly the question “Is flirting sinful?” becomes too small.
Because Jesus asks what your flirting is feeding.
If you flirt because you genuinely want to know an unmarried person with honorable intentions, that is one situation.
If you flirt to manipulate someone into desiring you, that is another.
If you deliberately arouse sexual desire you have no righteous intention of honoring, that is another.
If you are married and giving romantic energy to someone who is not your spouse, the stakes become dramatically different.
If they are married, the same warning applies.

If you know someone is becoming emotionally attached and you continue feeding that attachment simply because you enjoy being wanted, wisdom should tell you something is wrong long before physical boundaries are crossed.
And if your messages must constantly be deleted...
if your spouse cannot see them...
if your boyfriend or girlfriend would feel betrayed reading them...
if you would change your tone immediately if your pastor sat beside you...
if the conversation gets warmer after midnight...
if “just joking” keeps carrying sexual undertones...
if you keep telling yourself nothing is happening while secretly hoping something does...
perhaps the question is no longer:
“Is flirting a sin?”
Perhaps the question is:
How close to the fire can I stand while still calling myself innocent?
Paul writes that God's will is our sanctification: believers are to abstain from sexual immorality and live in holiness and honor rather than lustful passion.
Notice the direction.
Christianity is not merely about discovering the exact border of sin so we can stand one millimeter away from it.
Jesus did not die so we could spend our lives negotiating how much darkness we are permitted to touch.
He died to make us His.
There is a difference between asking:
“How far can I go?”
and asking:
“How beautifully can I honor Christ?”
One question searches for a loophole.
The other searches for Jesus.
And maybe this is where the article stops being about flirting and starts becoming about you.
Because perhaps nobody knows why you need the attention.
Nobody knows how lonely you have been.
Nobody knows how rejected you felt growing up.
Nobody knows how deeply that breakup wounded you.
Nobody knows how invisible you sometimes feel.
So when someone attractive notices you...
something inside you wakes up.
For a few minutes you feel chosen.
Wanted.
Beautiful.
Masculine.
Feminine.
Interesting.
Alive.
And perhaps that is why giving up flirtatious attention feels harder than you expected.
Because you were never merely addicted to conversation.
You were drinking validation.
You were asking another human being to answer a question only God can finally settle:
“Am I worth loving?”
And this is where Jesus does something far more beautiful than merely telling you to behave.
He exposes the thirst beneath the behavior.
Then He offers Himself.
The Gospel says your deepest worth is not established by how many people desire you.
Your identity is not measured by unread messages, heart reactions, compliments, dates, followers, admirers, or the number of people who find you attractive.
At the cross, Christ demonstrated a love deeper than romantic validation could ever provide.
He knew the hidden version of you.
The version nobody sees.
The motives you cleaned up before explaining them.
The conversations you deleted.
The fantasies you never confessed.
The attention you secretly enjoyed.
The boundaries you crossed.
The person you led on.
The relationship you damaged.
The marriage you endangered.
The nights when you knew better...
and did it anyway.
And Christ went to the cross for sinners.
Not polished sinners.
Not people who successfully made themselves desirable to God.
Sinners.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus does not say your sin is insignificant.
He says His blood is sufficient.
Repentance is not pretending nothing happened.
Repentance brings what happened into the light and turns toward Christ.
Grace does not say, “Keep playing with fire because Jesus forgives.”
Grace says:
“You don't have to live beside the fire anymore.”
Maybe you need to end a conversation.
Maybe you need to confess something to your spouse.
Maybe you owe someone an apology because you knowingly played with their emotions.
Maybe you need to stop calling lust “chemistry.”
Maybe you need to stop calling emotional infidelity “friendship.”
Maybe you need to stop calling manipulation “flirting.”
Or maybe your situation is genuinely innocent, and what you need is not guilt but wisdom.
Then walk in wisdom.
Be honest.
Be honorable.
Be clear.
If you like someone and both of you are free to pursue a relationship, you do not need manipulation.
You do not need sexual pressure.
You do not need mind games.
You do not need to manufacture jealousy.
You do not need to keep three other people emotionally interested in case your first choice fails.
Christian romance should increasingly produce clarity, honor, self-control, truthfulness, and love—not confusion deliberately maintained for attention.
And if you are married, guard what belongs to your covenant.
Your spouse should not have to compete with a secret emotional world you built with somebody else.
Marriage rarely collapses because two strangers suddenly wake up one morning and commit adultery without anything preceding it.
Boundaries are often crossed in inches before they are crossed in miles.
A joke.
A private message.
A personal confession.
A compliment you should not have needed from them.
A conversation you begin hiding.
A connection you defend more passionately than you protect your marriage.
Then one day someone says:
“We never meant for this to happen.”
Perhaps not.
But wisdom asks whether we kept walking toward the place where it could.
This is why guarding your heart is not legalism.
It is love.
You guard your heart because Christ purchased you.
You guard another person's heart because Christ loves them.
You guard your marriage because covenant matters.
You guard your sexuality because your body belongs to the Lord.
You guard your intentions because holiness is not merely what people see.
So...
Is flirting a sin?
There is no biblical command that declares every behavior we call “flirting” inherently sinful.

But flirting becomes morally dangerous—and may become sinful—when it cultivates lust, deception, sexual impurity, manipulation, marital unfaithfulness, dishonorable intentions, or knowingly exploits another person's emotions.
The better question is not simply:
“Can a Christian flirt?”
Ask instead:
“Can I do this before Jesus with a clean conscience, truthful intentions, self-control, love for this person's soul, and genuine concern for their holiness as well as mine?”
That question is harder.
It is also safer.
And perhaps tonight there is one name already sitting inside your mind.
You know exactly why.
Don't run from conviction.
Run to Christ.
There is mercy there.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to tell strangers every private detail. But you can make a simple confession of dependence on Christ.
And if you feel spiritually exhausted and need other believers to pray for you, simply write:
Let the comments become more than engagement.
Let them become reminders that Christians do not have to fight hidden battles alone.
Then think of one person who needs this conversation.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Someone you love.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's convictions feel negotiable tomorrow.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends who are willing to listen.
It does not.
Not because anyone should be pressured into giving.
Scripture says giving should come from a heart that has freely decided to give, “not reluctantly or under compulsion.”
But voluntary generosity can be one genuine way believers support Gospel work they believe is bearing fruit.
Pray.
Send it privately to somebody whose heart may need it tonight.
Because sometimes the message you almost didn't share becomes the message somebody desperately needed before making a decision they could regret for years.
And above everything else...
come back to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you clean yourself up.
Now.
Bring Him the flirtation.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the loneliness.
Bring Him the broken marriage.
Bring Him the secret conversation.
Bring Him the hunger to be desired.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the person you have become when nobody is watching.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive grace where grace is offered.
Make restitution where love requires it.
Set boundaries where wisdom demands them.
Then get up and walk with Christ again.
Because your worst conversation does not have to become the final sentence of your story.
Your failure does not have to become your identity.
Your scandal does not have to become your ending.
The heart that once chased attention can become the heart that finally learns it was Christ it was hungry for all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “PRIDE GOES BEFORE A FALL”—THAT’S NOT EXACTLY WHAT PROVERBS 16:18 SAYS
paragraphs: “PRIDE GOES BEFORE A FALL”—THAT’S NOT EXACTLY WHAT PROVERBS 16:18 SAYS
You’ve probably quoted it. But the words we shortened may be warning us about something far more terrifying than embarrassment.
There is a sentence almost everyone knows—even people who rarely open a Bible.
“Pride goes before a fall.”
We say it when someone gets arrogant and loses.
We say it when a celebrity destroys his reputation.
We whisper it when the person who thought he was untouchable suddenly discovers that he wasn’t.
Sometimes we even say it with a little satisfaction.
See?
Pride goes before a fall.
Except that is not exactly what Proverbs 16:18 says.
And when you read what the Hebrew actually says, the warning becomes heavier.
Much heavier.
Because Scripture is not merely warning you that arrogance might eventually embarrass you.
It is warning you that there is a posture of the soul that can quietly walk in front of destruction.
And perhaps the most frightening thing about pride is that you can recognize it immediately in somebody else...
while remaining almost completely blind to it in yourself.
The Hebrew of Proverbs 16:18 reads:
לִפְנֵי־שֶׁבֶר גָּאוֹן וְלִפְנֵי כִשָּׁלוֹן גֹּבַהּ רוּחַ
Lifnei-shever ga'on; velifnei kishalon govah ruach.
A close rendering is:
“Before destruction is pride, and before stumbling, a haughty spirit.”
The familiar English wording “pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” captures the Hebrew parallelism well. But notice what our shortened proverb usually loses.
Destruction.
The Hebrew word is שֶׁבֶר — shever.
It carries the idea of breaking, fracture, ruin, destruction.
Not merely embarrassment.
Not simply losing an argument.
Breaking.
Then comes the second line.
גֹּבַהּ רוּחַ — govah ruach.
Literally, something like “height of spirit”—an elevated, haughty spirit.
And before what?
כִשָּׁלוֹן — kishalon.
Stumbling. Falling. Collapse.
The proverb is Hebrew poetry. The two lines illuminate each other.
Pride.
Haughtiness.
Breaking.
Stumbling.
Do you feel the weight of it now?
The verse is not a clever ancient way of saying, “Don’t get too confident or life might humble you.”
It is exposing something spiritually dangerous.
Sometimes destruction has footsteps.
And pride may be walking just ahead of it.
That should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Because pride does not always look proud.
Sometimes pride walks into church carrying a Bible.
Sometimes it knows theology.
Sometimes it serves.
Sometimes it gives.
Sometimes it posts Scripture.
Sometimes it says, “God told me,” when what it really means is, “Nobody is allowed to question me.”
Sometimes pride does not boast aloud.
It simply refuses correction.
Sometimes pride sounds like:
“I know.”
“I don’t need help.”
“They’re the problem.”
“I already apologized.”
“They should come to me.”
“I deserve better.”
“I would never do what they did.”
And sometimes the most dangerous form of pride is the one wearing religious clothing.
“I’m not like those people.”
Do you hear it?
Jesus did.
He told a story about two men who went to pray.
One was a Pharisee.
One was a tax collector.
The Pharisee was outwardly religious. He fasted. He gave. He could point to visible evidence of moral discipline.
And then came the sentence that exposed him:
“God, I thank you that I am not like other people...” (Luke 18:11).
That is terrifying because his prayer contained the word “God.”
His religion was real enough to get him into the temple...
but his pride was strong enough to make his prayer revolve around himself.
Then, somewhere at a distance, stood the scandalous man.
The tax collector.
The compromised man.
The man respectable religious society had reasons to despise.
He would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He beat his chest.
And his prayer was painfully small.
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
No résumé.
No comparison.
No defense.
No list of people worse than him.
Mercy.
That was all he had left.
And Jesus said that man went home justified rather than the other.
That is the scandal of grace.
The man who arrived with nothing but sin and repentance went home with mercy.
The man who arrived impressed with his own righteousness went home exposed by the very righteousness he thought made him superior.
Maybe this is where Proverbs 16:18 stops being something we quote about other people.
Maybe now it begins reading us.
Because pride does not begin when everyone else notices.
Pride begins in hidden rooms.
It begins when correction feels insulting instead of loving.
It begins when apologizing feels like losing.
It begins when someone else’s success feels like your diminishment.
It begins when you secretly enjoy watching someone who hurt you fail.
It begins when you cannot celebrate another person without comparing yourself.
It begins when you become more concerned about appearing holy than becoming holy.
It begins when confession disappears from your prayers because repentance has slowly been replaced by explanation.
It begins when you stop asking, “Lord, search me,” and start asking, “Lord, deal with them.”
And this is why the next verse matters so much.
Proverbs 16:19 immediately gives us the contrast:
“Better to be of a humble spirit with the lowly than to divide the spoil with the proud.”
Better.
God says there is something better than standing among winners if winning requires becoming proud.
Better to kneel with the humble than celebrate with the arrogant.
Better to lose status and keep your soul tender.
Better to be corrected than celebrated into destruction.
Better to say, “I was wrong.”
Better to confess.
Better to repent.
Better to come home.
And now we arrive at Jesus.
Because if this article ends merely with “Try harder to be humble,” we have missed the Gospel.
Christianity is not self-improvement for arrogant people.
The Gospel is much more devastating...
and much more beautiful.
Scripture does not simply tell us to manufacture humility.
It shows us Humility Himself.
Jesus Christ.
Paul writes of Him in Philippians 2.
Christ did not cling selfishly to status. He humbled Himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient even to death on a cross.
Think about that.
The One who had every legitimate reason to be exalted humbled Himself.
We, who have every reason to humble ourselves, spend our lives trying to be exalted.
He descended.
We climb.
He served.
We demand recognition.
He washed feet.
We protect reputations.
He accepted humiliation.
We can barely survive being corrected.
He carried a cross.
We carry grudges.
And still...
He came for us.
That is grace.
Jesus did not go to Calvary because humble people had finally made themselves worthy of salvation.
He went because sinners could not save themselves.
The cross destroys human boasting because nobody stands at Calvary and says, “Jesus needed to do this, but only a little. I handled the rest.”
No.
At the cross, every résumé falls from our hands.
Our morality cannot purchase forgiveness.
Our church attendance cannot erase sin.
Our theological knowledge cannot reconcile us to God.
Our ministry cannot save us.
Our generosity cannot save us.
Our reputation cannot save us.
Our followers cannot save us.
Our accomplishments cannot save us.
Jesus saves.
This is why pride hates grace.
Grace says you need rescue.
Pride says you can manage.
Grace says confess.
Pride says explain.
Grace says surrender.
Pride says control.
Grace says receive.
Pride says earn.
Grace says, “Come empty.”
Pride whispers, “Make sure everybody thinks you're full.”
Maybe your fall has already happened.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe something broke.
A marriage.
A friendship.
A ministry.
A reputation.
A career.
Trust.
Maybe you made choices you once swore you would never make.
Maybe you became someone you barely recognize.
Maybe your secret finally became public.
Or perhaps nobody knows yet.
Perhaps the collapse has happened entirely inside you.
You still smile.
Still work.
Still post.
Still say, “I’m okay.”
But somewhere underneath the performance, you know.
Something is cracking.
Listen carefully.
Being broken is not the same thing as being beyond redemption.
Peter learned that.
Hours before Jesus' crucifixion, Peter sounded extraordinarily confident.
Even if others fell away...
he would not.
Even if dying became necessary...
he was ready.
Then a servant girl asked him a question.
And the fearless disciple started collapsing.
Denial.
Again.
Again.
Then the rooster.
Imagine that moment.
The man who thought he would die beside Jesus discovered that he could not even admit knowing Jesus.
Peter fell.
Hard.
But Peter's failure was not the final sentence of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus went after him.
Not to pretend the denial never happened.
Not to rename sin as harmless.
Not to tell Peter that repentance was unnecessary.
Jesus restored him.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”
Three denials.
Three questions.
A disgraced disciple sitting beside the risen Christ.
Scandal meeting grace.
Failure meeting mercy.
A broken man discovering that Jesus can write another chapter.
That is the Gospel.
Maybe pride brought you somewhere you never intended to go.
Maybe you refused counsel.
Maybe you hurt people.
Maybe you thought you could control the temptation.
Maybe you were certain you would never become addicted.
Never cheat.
Never lie.
Never compromise.
Never walk away.
Never become cold.
Never become bitter.
Never become “one of those people.”
And then you did.
What now?
You stop hiding.
You stop blaming.
You stop polishing the story.
You stop trying to make your sin sound respectable.
You come to Christ.
Repentance is not God humiliating you for entertainment.
Repentance is surrendering the lie so grace can meet you in the truth.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Notice who is faithful.
He is.
Your hope is not the perfection of your repentance.
Your hope is the perfection of your Savior.
And maybe somebody needs to hear this before another night passes:
Your scandal does not have to become the last word over your life.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still breaks chains.
Jesus still receives prodigals.
Jesus still transforms hearts.
Jesus still takes people whose stories look ruined and turns their scars into testimonies of mercy.
But grace is not permission to remain proud.
Grace brings us to our knees.
So ask yourself the question most of us would rather ask about somebody else:
Where is pride hiding in me?
Not them.
Me.
Where have I become unteachable?
Whose correction have I automatically dismissed?
Who am I refusing to forgive because forgiving them feels like letting them “win”?
Where am I defending something God is asking me to confess?
Where am I more concerned about looking right than becoming right?
Where have I confused influence with spiritual maturity?
Where have I secretly believed that because God uses me, God must approve of everything in me?
Where have I begun needing applause?
Where have I stopped trembling at His Word?
Where have I started looking down on the very sinners Jesus died to save?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Talk to Jesus.
Right now.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary necessary.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Sometimes revival begins with four honest words.
Not to perform repentance publicly.
Not to prove anything to strangers.
But if you are willing, let those words become your small declaration that you are finished pretending you have nothing to surrender.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not fighting alone.
Let the people of God do what pride so often prevents us from doing:
carry one another.
And send this article to the person you love enough not to flatter.
Because pride has a strange way of returning after the tears dry.
You may need these words again.

Scripture gives real grounds for supporting Gospel ministry. Paul taught that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support from Gospel work (1 Corinthians 9:14). But Scripture also guards the heart of giving: “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7).
So this is not a spiritual tax.
It is not a payment for God's favor.
It does not purchase blessing, salvation, answered prayer, or a higher place in God's kingdom.
It is simply an opportunity for willing partnership.
But the deepest reason to support Gospel work should never be merchandise.
It should be love.
Love for Christ.
Love for truth.
Love for souls.
Love for the person you may never meet who encounters one Gospel message on the night they desperately need it.
Pray.
Share.
Save the message.
Follow.
A share costs nothing, but it can place the truth of Jesus Christ in front of someone Gospel Warrior could never reach alone.
The goal is not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
The goal is to make Jesus known.
Because one day, every platform disappears.
Every follower count becomes meaningless.
Every possession changes hands.
Every human reputation fades.
Every proud empire falls.
And only what belongs to Christ will ultimately matter.
So perhaps the old saying needs to become personal.
Not:
“Pride goes before their fall.”
But:
“Lord, expose the pride in me before it carries me somewhere I never wanted to go.”
Because the safest place for a sinner is not standing tall while pretending to have no weakness.
It is kneeling before Jesus with nothing left to defend.
Peter fell...
and Jesus restored him.
The tax collector confessed...
and Jesus said he went home justified.
The proud can humble themselves.
The wandering can return.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The broken can be restored.
The scandal does not have to have the final word.
Christ does.
And perhaps the very place where your pride finally breaks will become the place where you discover just how breathtaking His grace has always been.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PAUL SAYS SEXUAL IMMORALITY CAN WRONG ANOTHER PERSON—Sexual Sin Isn’t Always “Just Between Two Adults”
paragraphs: PAUL SAYS SEXUAL IMMORALITY CAN WRONG ANOTHER PERSON—Sexual Sin Isn’t Always “Just Between Two Adults”
We call it private. Paul calls it something that can cross a boundary, take advantage of another human being, and bring God Himself into the matter.
There is a sentence our culture has learned to say almost automatically whenever sexual morality becomes uncomfortable:
“What two consenting adults do in private is nobody else’s business.”
It sounds reasonable.
It sounds compassionate.
It sounds like the perfect way to end an argument.
Nobody was forced.
Nobody was physically attacked.
Both people agreed.
So what could possibly be wrong?
Then the apostle Paul writes one sentence that refuses to let the conversation remain that simple.
In the middle of one of the New Testament’s clearest passages about sexual holiness, Paul says:
“that no one transgress and wrong his brother in this matter…”
—1 Thessalonians 4:6
Read that again.
Not merely:
“Do not hurt yourself.”
Not merely:
“Do not break a religious rule.”
Not merely:
“Try to avoid feeling guilty afterward.”
Paul introduces another person.
Someone can be wronged.
And suddenly sexual sin is no longer only about what two people wanted in a moment.
It becomes a question of what one human being may have taken from another.
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because some of us have spent years calling something “love” that Scripture may force us to examine as something much more complicated.
Paul originally wrote these words in Greek:
“τὸ μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν καὶ πλεονεκτεῖν ἐν τῷ πράγματι τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ…”
The words deserve our attention.
ὑπερβαίνειν — hyperbainein
It carries the idea of stepping beyond, going beyond a boundary, transgressing.
Then comes:
πλεονεκτεῖν — pleonektein
To overreach.
To gain an advantage.
To exploit.
To take advantage of another.
Paul is describing conduct that does not merely happen with another person.
It can happen against another person.
And that changes the question.
The modern question is often:
“Did we both want it?”
Paul forces a deeper question:
“Did I honor this person before God?”
Those are not necessarily the same question.
Because two people can mutually agree to something and still mutually participate in something destructive.
Two people can consent to bitterness.
Two people can cooperate in dishonesty.
Two people can encourage one another toward drunkenness.
Two people can participate willingly in adultery.
Mutual willingness does not automatically transform everything people choose into righteousness.
Biblical love asks something deeper than:
“Will you let me?”
Biblical love asks:
“Will this help me honor you as someone who belongs to God?”
And perhaps that is the question many of us never asked.
We asked whether they wanted us.
We asked whether there was chemistry.
We asked whether anyone would discover it.
We asked whether we were technically dating.
We asked whether everybody else was doing it.
We asked how far was “too far.”
We asked whether God would really care.
But we rarely stopped in the heat of desire and asked:
“Am I helping this person become holy?”
Because lust does not naturally ask that question.
Love does.
And Paul refuses to separate sexuality from holiness.
Listen to the entire movement of his argument:
“For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality…”
—1 Thessalonians 4:3
The Greek word translated “sexual immorality” is:
πορνεία — porneia
It is a broad New Testament term for sexual immorality—sexual behavior outside the boundaries God establishes for sexual faithfulness.
Paul continues by telling believers to live in holiness and honor rather than being ruled by “the passion of lust.”
Then comes verse 6.
Do not cross the boundary.
Do not take advantage of your brother or sister “in this matter.”
Then Paul says something even heavier:
“because the Lord is an avenger in all these things…”
This is not casual language.
And yet we need to read it carefully.

There has been interpretive discussion over precisely how Paul’s wording in verse 6 should be understood, particularly the expression ἐν τῷ πράγματι — en tō pragmati, “in the matter.” But the immediate passage unmistakably moves through sanctification, sexual immorality, bodily holiness, lust, wrongdoing toward another person, impurity, holiness, and the Holy Spirit.
So whatever excuses we bring to the text, we cannot honestly pretend Paul thinks sexual conduct is spiritually insignificant.
He does not.
Sex matters because people matter.
Bodies matter because people bearing God’s image matter.
Holiness matters because God matters.
And suddenly another uncomfortable possibility emerges.
Maybe sexual sin sometimes takes something even when the other person willingly gives it.
Maybe you can receive someone’s body while refusing them covenant.
Maybe you can awaken intimacy without accepting responsibility.
Maybe you can whisper permanence while intending something temporary.
Maybe you can enjoy somebody’s vulnerability and disappear when vulnerability becomes inconvenient.
Maybe you can tell yourself, “They wanted it too,” while never asking whether you were leading someone God loves toward holiness or away from it.
And maybe sometimes both people are doing that to each other.
That is what makes sexual sin so deceptive.
It can feel extraordinarily intimate while producing extraordinarily deep loneliness.
Two bodies can be close while two souls remain terrified of being truly known.
Someone reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You thought giving more of yourself would finally make them stay.
So you crossed another boundary.
Then another.
You told yourself this was what love required.
You were afraid that saying no would mean losing them.
Maybe nobody physically forced you.
But fear was sitting in the room.
Loneliness was sitting in the room.
Insecurity was sitting in the room.
The desperate need to be chosen was sitting in the room.
And afterward…
they still left.
Or perhaps you stayed together, but something changed inside you.
What promised closeness created anxiety.
What promised freedom produced secrecy.
What promised affirmation made you wonder whether you were loved…
or merely desired.
And perhaps you have carried the shame ever since.
But there is another person who needs to keep reading.
The person who did the using.
Maybe you never called it that.
You said:
“We both knew what this was.”
You said:
“They could have said no.”
You said:
“We weren't married.”
You said:
“It was consensual.”
You said:
“I never promised anything.”
Maybe technically, according to the rules you created for yourself, you can construct a defense.
But stand before Jesus for a moment and ask a different question.
Did you love them?
Not:
Did you desire them?
Not:
Did they desire you?
Did you love them with a love that sought their holiness, dignity, spiritual good, and eternal good?
Because Scripture’s definition of love is far more demanding than desire with permission.
Love “does no wrong to a neighbor.”
—Romans 13:10
Love does not ask:
“How much can I take without technically becoming the villain?”
Love asks:
“How can I honor you because Christ died for sinners like both of us?”
That changes everything.
And before anyone turns this article into ammunition against someone else, hear this carefully.
Paul is not giving religious people permission to stand over sexually broken people with stones in their hands.
Christianity begins with the devastating realization that we are the sinners who need mercy.
Sexual sin is real.
But so is sexual shame.
And shame has convinced millions of people that their worst night became their permanent name.
Adulterer.
Porn addict.
Used.
Dirty.
Unfaithful.
Promiscuous.
Unworthy.
Damaged.
Hypocrite.
Maybe nobody knows.
You sing worship songs.
You post Bible verses.
You go to church.
You smile when people ask how you are.
But somewhere underneath the Christian vocabulary is a memory you desperately hope never becomes public.
A browser history.
A hotel room.
A message thread.
A relationship nobody knew about.
Someone else's husband.
Someone else's wife.
A secret addiction.
A compromise you promised God would happen only once.
Then twice.
Then again.
And perhaps the hardest part is not merely remembering what someone did to you.
It is remembering what you did to someone else.
That is where the Gospel becomes more than inspirational language.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make respectable people feel spiritually encouraged.
Jesus came for sinners.
Real sinners.
Guilty sinners.
Ashamed sinners.
People who were wronged.
And people who did the wronging.
People whose sexuality was exploited.
And people who selfishly exploited others.
People who crossed boundaries.
People who broke vows.
People who hid.
People who lied.
People who cannot rewind what happened.
The Gospel does not say your sin was harmless.
The Gospel says something infinitely better:
your sin does not have to have the final word.
At the cross, Jesus does not rename darkness as light so we can avoid repentance.
He brings darkness into the light so sinners can be forgiven and transformed.
Grace is not God pretending nothing happened.
Grace is God doing for guilty people what guilty people could never do for themselves.
Jesus bears sin.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus restores.
Jesus changes hearts.
And Jesus calls us out of the darkness we once defended.
That is why Paul does not stop at prohibition.
Just one verse later he says:
“For God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness.”
—1 Thessalonians 4:7
Called.
Do you see it?
Christian sexual ethics are not merely about what God tells you to run from.
They are about what God is calling you into.
Holiness.
Freedom.
Integrity.
A life where your body no longer controls your master.
A life where another person's body is not something to consume.
A life where desire learns to bow before Jesus.
A life where you stop asking how close you can walk to the cliff and start asking how closely you can walk with Christ.
And then Paul writes:
—1 Thessalonians 4:8
Notice that final phrase.
God gives His Holy Spirit.
Paul does not leave struggling believers standing before an impossible command with nothing but willpower.
God gives Himself.
The Spirit who convicts is also the Spirit who empowers.
So if you have fallen sexually, the answer is not pretending it never mattered.
And the answer is not spending the rest of your life believing you are too filthy for Jesus.
The answer is repentance.
Come into the light.
Confess what needs confessing.
End what needs ending.
Block what needs blocking.
Flee what needs fleeing.
Seek pastoral or mature Christian accountability where needed.

If you have seriously wronged someone, repentance may involve accepting consequences and seeking wise counsel about appropriate restitution rather than demanding immediate forgiveness or renewed access to the person you hurt.

And where abuse, coercion, assault, exploitation, or criminal conduct has occurred, do not hide it behind vague religious language about “mutual sin.” Victims are not morally responsible for another person's abuse against them, and serious wrongdoing may require professional, pastoral, safeguarding, and legal intervention.
Biblical grace never requires calling evil good.
Grace tells the truth…
and then opens the door home.
Perhaps that is why this message hurts.
You did not expect 1 Thessalonians 4:6 to expose that memory.
You did not expect one Greek verb to make you reconsider a relationship you have spent years justifying.
You did not expect to wonder whether something you called “consensual” was nevertheless selfish.
But conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Condemnation whispers:
“Hide from God.”
Conviction says:
“Come back to God.”
Condemnation says:
“You are what you did.”
The Gospel says:
“There is redemption in Jesus Christ.”
The woman caught in adultery encountered a Savior who neither celebrated her sin nor abandoned her to her accusers.
Grace did not say sin was meaningless.
Grace gave the sinner somewhere to go.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Maybe you have been carrying sexual shame for ten years.
Maybe twenty.
Maybe what happened was last night.
Maybe you are still inside the relationship you know you need to surrender.
Maybe you are reading this beside the person with whom you keep compromising.
Maybe you have confessed the same sin so many times that you are embarrassed to pray again.
Pray anyway.
Run to Christ again.
Not because sin is small.
Because His mercy is greater.
Repentance means turning.
And sometimes turning begins with one trembling sentence:
“Jesus, I cannot keep living like this.”
If that is you, do not perform for the comments.

And if Christ has already been restoring an area of your life you once believed could never be healed, tell someone what grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to give another wounded person enough courage to seek help.
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Not because you need another saved post buried in your phone, but because temptation has an extraordinary ability to make us forget what conviction once made painfully clear.
Not to publicly shame anyone. Not to throw stones.
Truth should be carried with love.
We want this community to remain a place for daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Give because you freely want to help the work continue.
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help enormously.
Leave a meaningful comment.
Invite someone to follow.
Send it privately to the person whose name came into your heart while reading.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is calling bondage freedom.
Someone is calling lust love.
Someone is calling shame their identity.
Someone is convinced they have gone too far for Jesus to want them anymore.
And they need to discover what the Gospel has been saying all along.
Sin may explain part of your story.
It does not have the authority to write the ending.
The night you thought permanently stained your name may become the very place where the mercy of Jesus teaches you what it means to be made new.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WOMAN HE COULD NEVER TAKE BACK
paragraphs: THE WOMAN HE COULD NEVER TAKE BACK

Deuteronomy 24:1–4 sounds like a scandal about divorce. But buried inside this difficult law is a warning about covenant, human hardness, irreversible choices—and our desperate need for the Redeemer who does what the law could never do.
There is a moment when some doors close.
Not because God has stopped being merciful.
Not because grace has run out.
But because choices have consequences, covenant is not a toy, and human beings were never meant to pass one another back and forth as though hearts were property.
Deuteronomy 24:1–4 takes us into one of those uncomfortable places in Scripture.
A man marries a woman.
Something fractures.
He sends her away with a certificate of divorce.
She leaves his house.
She becomes another man's wife.
Then the second marriage ends—whether through divorce or death.
And suddenly the first husband wants her back.
Perhaps that sounds romantic to modern ears.
Maybe he finally realized what he lost.
Maybe years have passed.
Maybe regret has been eating him alive.
Maybe he remembers the woman who once sat across from him at the table, the woman whose presence he once took for granted.
Maybe he wants to undo everything.
But God says no.
And that “no” has troubled readers for centuries.
Why would reconciliation be forbidden?
Why couldn't they simply begin again?
Why would the God of restoration close this particular door?
Before answering that, we need to read carefully, because careless reading can turn this passage into something it never intended to be.
The Hebrew begins:
“כִּי־יִקַּח אִישׁ אִשָּׁה וּבְעָלָהּ…”
Ki-yiqqaḥ ish ishah uve‘alah…
“When a man takes a woman and becomes her husband…”
Then comes the difficult expression:
“עֶרְוַת דָּבָר”
‘ervat davar.

The expression is notoriously difficult to capture with a single English phrase. It carries the idea of something indecent, shameful, or objectionable. Later Jewish interpretation debated its scope intensely.
Then the husband gives her:
“סֵפֶר כְּרִיתֻת”
sefer keritut.
Literally, a document of cutting off—a certificate of divorce.
She leaves.
And Scripture says:
“וְהָלְכָה וְהָיְתָה לְאִישׁ־אַחֵר”
Vehalkhah vehayetah le’ish-aḥer.
She goes and becomes another man's wife.
Notice something important.
The command at the heart of this passage is not simply, “Divorce your wife.”
Moses is addressing a situation in which divorce has occurred, the woman has subsequently married another man, and that later marriage has also ended.
Then comes the prohibition.
“לֹא־יוּכַל בַּעְלָהּ הָרִאשׁוֹן… לָשׁוּב לְקַחְתָּהּ”
Lo-yukhal ba‘alah harishon… lashuv leqaḥtah.
Her former husband “may not… take her again.”
That is the boundary.
Deuteronomy 24:1–4 is therefore not permission for a man to casually discard a woman and then retrieve her whenever his emotions change.
Quite the opposite.
There is something chilling about the scenario.
He cannot simply say:
“I changed my mind.”
“I want her back.”
“She used to be mine.”
Because she is not merchandise.
Covenant is not a revolving door.
Human beings are not possessions to be exchanged, reclaimed, discarded, and reclaimed again according to someone's appetite.
And this matters because people still do something remarkably similar today.
Maybe not with ancient divorce documents.
But with hearts.
We leave when things become inconvenient.
We return when loneliness becomes unbearable.
We call lust love.
We call control reconciliation.
We call nostalgia repentance.
We want people back because we miss what they gave us, while never asking whether we have actually become safe enough to hold their heart again.
We want yesterday restored without becoming different people today.
And Scripture refuses to romanticize human instability.
There are consequences.
There are boundaries.
There are decisions that cannot simply be rewound because regret finally arrived.
That truth hurts.
Especially if you have lived long enough to have something you desperately wish you could undo.
A marriage.
An affair.
A betrayal.
A night you wish had never happened.
Words screamed across a room.
A signature placed on a document.
A child who watched two parents become strangers.
A relationship you destroyed because you were proud.
Someone you lost because you would not change until losing them finally changed you.
There are people reading this who would give almost anything for one more conversation.
One more embrace.
One opportunity to go back.
But the Bible does not lie to us.
Sometimes repentance changes you without changing yesterday.
Sometimes forgiveness cleanses the sinner without erasing every earthly consequence of the sin.
David was forgiven, yet consequences remained.
Peter was restored, yet he could never unsay his three denials.
The thief beside Jesus received paradise, yet he still died on the cross beside Him.
Grace is not pretending the wound never happened.
Grace is God meeting sinners in the wreckage and refusing to let the wreckage have the final word.
And this is where Deuteronomy 24 becomes even more important when we listen to Jesus.
Centuries later, religious leaders approached Christ with questions about divorce.
Jesus brought them farther back than Moses.
Back beyond the certificates.
Beyond the arguments.
Beyond the loopholes.
Back to creation.
“Haven't you read,” He asked, before pointing them toward God's design in Genesis: male and female, joined together, becoming one flesh.
Then came the words that still confront every generation:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Matthew 19:6.
When they asked why Moses had permitted certificates of divorce, Jesus exposed the disease beneath the legislation:
“Because of your hardness of heart…”
Matthew 19:8.
There it is.
Hardness.
The problem was never merely paperwork.
It was the human heart.
A heart that can promise forever on Saturday and start looking for an escape on Monday.
A heart that can stand before God saying, “Until death,” and later begin calculating how cheaply covenant can be abandoned.
A heart that can demand mercy for itself while withholding mercy from everyone else.
Jesus did not treat marriage casually.
Neither should we.
But neither did Jesus build His ministry around finding wounded people and crushing them underneath their histories.
Think about the people He moved toward.
The sexually broken.
The publicly ashamed.
The morally compromised.
The religiously despised.
The people everybody else whispered about.
Jesus never renamed sin so sinners could remain comfortable.
But He also never treated repentant sinners as though their worst chapter were their permanent name.
That is the Gospel tension we desperately need.
Truth without grace can become cruelty.
Grace without truth becomes permission.
Jesus gives us both.
“Neither do I condemn you.”
And:
“Go, and from now on sin no more.”
John 8:11.
Maybe divorce is part of your story.
Maybe remarriage is part of your story.
Maybe adultery is.
Maybe abandonment is.
Maybe you were the one who walked away.
Maybe someone walked away from you.
Maybe you fought desperately to save something the other person had already decided to destroy.
Maybe your situation is complicated enough that a social-media paragraph cannot responsibly adjudicate it.
Hear this carefully:

Deuteronomy 24:1–4 should never be used as a club to declare that every divorced person carries the same guilt, that every divorce happened for the same reason, or that every broken marriage can be reduced to one simplistic formula.
Scripture itself requires more care than that.

Jesus speaks about sexual immorality in Matthew 19. Paul addresses abandonment by an unbelieving spouse in 1 Corinthians 7. Pastoral situations involving abuse, danger, coercion, abandonment, adultery, repentance, reconciliation, divorce, and remarriage require serious biblical wisdom rather than slogans.
But neither should we run to exceptions because we are frightened of conviction.
Jesus calls us to holiness.
Marriage matters.
Faithfulness matters.
Sexual purity matters.
Promises matter.
Repentance matters.
And if you have sinned, repentance does not mean explaining your sin until it no longer sounds sinful.
It means bringing it into the light.
Maybe that is what God is doing in you right now.
Not humiliating you.
Calling you.
There is a difference.
Conviction says, “Come out of hiding.”
Condemnation says, “Stay there because there is no hope for you.”
The Gospel says something radically different.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Romans 8:1.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
Because the cross proves exactly how much it matters.
Look at Jesus.
The nails were real.
The blood was real.
The judgment was real.
The cost was real.
The Son of God did not bleed because our rebellion was insignificant.
He bled because sin destroys—and because His love determined to rescue sinners at unimaginable cost.
This is where the story becomes bigger than the divorced woman of Deuteronomy.
Because somewhere beneath all our religious respectability is another broken covenant story.
Ours.
Humanity has been unfaithful to God.
We have chased idols.
We have worshiped ourselves.
We have broken His commandments.
We have loved creation more than the Creator.
We have sinned publicly and secretly.
We have promised God things in desperate moments and forgotten those promises when life became comfortable again.
We have returned to sins we once cried over.
We have hidden things in browser histories, private messages, hotel rooms, bank accounts, fantasies, resentments, addictions, and memories.
And still Christ came.
That does not mean Deuteronomy's marriage law disappears or that its prohibition somehow secretly means the opposite of what it says.
It means something greater.
Jesus entered our ruined human story to accomplish the redemption sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
He did not come merely to make bad people respectable.
He came to make the dead alive.
He came for sinners.
He came for adulterers who repent.
He came for the divorced.
He came for the abandoned.
He came for the betrayed.
He came for betrayers who finally stop defending themselves.
He came for the sexually broken.
He came for religious hypocrites willing to admit they need mercy.
He came for the person staring at a past that cannot be rewritten by human hands.
And this is why our message is not:
“Pretend it never happened.”
Our message is:
Bring what happened to Jesus.
Repent where you sinned.
Forgive where Christ commands you to forgive.
Seek wise counsel where your circumstances are complicated.
Make restitution where possible.
Protect the vulnerable.
Stop hiding.
Stop performing.
Stop building theological loopholes around the thing God is asking you to surrender.
And then believe the Gospel.
Because your past may explain some of your scars.
It does not have authority to become your savior.
Your divorce papers do not outrank the blood of Christ.
Your sexual history does not outrank the blood of Christ.
Your adultery does not outrank the blood of Christ.
Your abandonment does not outrank the blood of Christ.
Your shame does not outrank the blood of Christ.
But neither should anyone use the blood of Christ as an excuse to continue deliberately in rebellion.
Grace does not say, “Sin doesn't matter.”
Grace says, “Sin mattered so much that Jesus died—and you are loved so deeply that He calls you out of it.”
That is repentance.
Not merely feeling terrible.
Turning.
Coming home.
Surrendering the keys.
Dropping the excuses.
And saying:
“Jesus, I cannot rewrite what I did.
But You can rewrite what I become.”
Perhaps that is the sentence somebody reading this has needed for years.
You cannot always return to the life you had before the wreckage.
But you can return to God.
You cannot make every consequence disappear.
But you can kneel at the cross.
You cannot force another human being to restore a relationship.
But you can allow Christ to restore your soul.
You cannot edit yesterday.
But in Jesus Christ, yesterday does not have to own tomorrow.
Be honest.
There are moments when three honest words are more sacred than three paragraphs pretending everything is fine.
And if someone came into your mind while reading this, send this to them.
Not as an accusation.
Not as ammunition.
As an invitation.
Because conviction has a strange way of becoming inconvenient tomorrow.
Come back when your emotions settle.
Read the Scriptures yourself.
Test what you have read.
Stay close to Christ.
We want this ministry to keep placing Christ-centered truth in front of people who might otherwise never walk into a church building.
It doesn't.
Only Jesus saves.
Support should therefore come from worship, gratitude, conviction, and generosity—not spiritual pressure.
If you have been reading quietly for months, saving the articles, sharing them, growing through them, and wondering how you can stand with the mission, this is one way.
Pray.
Share the Gospel.
Keep opening Scripture.
Keep pointing wounded people toward Jesus.
Because this was never supposed to be about building an audience.
It is about reaching souls.
It is about people discovering that holiness is more beautiful than compromise, repentance is better than hiding, forgiveness is stronger than shame, and Jesus Christ is still mighty to save.
Deuteronomy 24 reminds us that human decisions can create consequences we cannot simply reverse.
The cross tells us something even greater.
Consequences do not get to decide whether Christ can redeem a human life.
Some pages cannot be erased.
Some relationships cannot simply be returned to their former state.
Some scars will remain until resurrection.
But scars are not the same thing as chains.
And your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Because when Jesus takes hold of a surrendered life, He does not need to pretend the scandal never happened.
He turns the scandal into a testimony of grace.
So bring Him the marriage.
Bring Him the divorce.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the regret.
Bring Him the part of your history you still cannot say aloud without your voice trembling.
Bring Him all of it.
Then watch what the Redeemer does with a life finally willing to stop hiding.
You may never be able to return to yesterday—but at the feet of Jesus, yesterday can finally lose the right to imprison tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “PAUL SAID HE WASN’T TELLING CHRISTIANS TO AVOID EVERY SEXUALLY IMMORAL PERSON IN THE WORLD”
paragraphs: “PAUL SAID HE WASN’T TELLING CHRISTIANS TO AVOID EVERY SEXUALLY IMMORAL PERSON IN THE WORLD”
We may have spent years avoiding the very people Jesus sent us to reach—while becoming strangely comfortable with unrepentant sin inside the church.
There is a sentence in the Bible that can make religious people uncomfortable.
Not because it excuses sin.
Not because it lowers God's standard.
But because it exposes how easily we can apply God's standard to everybody except the people Paul was actually confronting.
Read this slowly.
Paul was dealing with sexual immorality so serious that he refused to soften his words. Yet in the middle of that confrontation, he stopped to make something unmistakably clear:
When he told Christians not to associate with sexually immoral people...
he was not talking about every sexually immoral person in the world.
That changes the conversation.
Because some of us learned Christianity as though holiness meant staying as far away as possible from sinners.
Don't sit with them.
Don't befriend them.
Don't eat with them.
Don't let people see you around them.
Don't enter their world.
Don't get too close.
And somewhere along the way, separation from sin quietly became separation from sinners.
But then you open 1 Corinthians 5.
And Paul says, essentially:
That isn't what I meant.
The original Greek is painfully clear:
Ἔγραψα ὑμῖν ἐν τῇ ἐπιστολῇ μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι πόρνοις, οὐ πάντως τοῖς πόρνοις τοῦ κόσμου τούτου...
Egrapsa hymin en tē epistolē mē synanamignysthai pornois, ou pantōs tois pornois tou kosmou toutou...
“I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people—not at all meaning the sexually immoral people of this world...”
Then Paul says something almost startling in its simplicity.
If that were what he meant...
you would have to leave the world.
Think about that.
You would have to leave the world.
Paul knew Christians would encounter sexually broken people.
Greedy people.
Idolaters.
Swindlers.
People whose lives were nowhere near God's design.
And his solution was not:
“Disappear.”
It wasn't:
“Build walls high enough that sinners can never reach you.”
It wasn't:
“Only associate with people whose lives already look Christian.”
Because if Christians disappear from the lives of sinners...
who is going to tell sinners about Christ?
This is where the passage becomes uncomfortable in another direction.
Because Paul wasn't becoming permissive.
He wasn't saying sexual immorality doesn't matter.
He wasn't saying, “Who are we to judge?” as though holiness were irrelevant.
Actually, the rest of the chapter destroys that interpretation.
Paul's concern was so serious that he demanded church discipline against a professing believer openly persisting in scandalous sexual sin.
The distinction is everything.
Paul writes:
ἐάν τις ἀδελφὸς ὀνομαζόμενος ᾖ πόρνος...
ean tis adelphos onomazomenos ē pornos...
The force of the words is roughly:
