So perhaps the most important response to Amos 2:7 is not:
“Look how corrupt those people were.”
Perhaps it is:
“Jesus, search me.”
Talk to God.
Tell the truth.
Repent.
Seek wise pastoral or Christian accountability where needed.
If another person's abuse or exploitation is involved, bringing darkness into the light does not mean placing yourself back into danger; seek safe, trustworthy help.
Not because typing a comment saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes a small public confession becomes the moment somebody finally stops pretending.
And if Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, do not hide the testimony forever.
“Christ is still healing me.”
Somebody reading beneath you may desperately need evidence that grace still reaches ruined places.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because somebody you know may be smiling publicly while collapsing privately.
Send it privately to the person God puts on your heart.
There may come a night when temptation starts negotiating again.
There may come a morning when shame starts preaching again.
Come back and remember:
Jesus did not shed His blood so you could become comfortable in chains.
He came to set captives free.
It cannot.
The Gospel is grace.
But Gospel ministry requires people willing to participate in carrying truth farther.

We should be careful with the word tithe. Give first as Scripture and conscience direct you, support your local church and faithful ministry, care for people in need, and never confuse financial support with salvation.
But if you have been asking, “How can I help this ministry continue?”
This is one tangible way.
Your support can help us keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Keep placing Scripture in front of people who may never walk through a church door before they encounter truth on a screen.
And comment.
Be honest.
Maybe this hit harder than you expected.
Maybe Amos exposed something.
Maybe Jesus is calling something out of hiding.
Maybe today is finally the day you stop protecting the thing that has been destroying you.
Because the most frightening part of Amos 2:7 is not that Israel became scandalous.
It is that people could become comfortable with corruption while remaining close to religious things.
And the most beautiful part of the Gospel is that Jesus still walks directly into the wreckage and calls sinners home.
So come home.
Not when you have cleaned yourself enough.
Not when your history becomes less embarrassing.
Not after you manufacture a respectable testimony.
Come to Christ in repentance and faith.
Let Him expose what needs exposing.
Forgive what He commands you to forgive.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repair what can rightly be repaired.
Leave what needs leaving.
Seek help where you need help.
And follow Jesus.
Because there is something greater than having a spotless history.
There is having a Redeemer.
The scandal may explain how you arrived here. It does not have the authority to decide where Jesus will take you next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “LOVE ALWAYS TRUSTS”—SO WHY DOES LOVING THEM KEEP DESTROYING YOU?
paragraphs: “LOVE ALWAYS TRUSTS”—SO WHY DOES LOVING THEM KEEP DESTROYING YOU?
Does Christianity Require You to Trust Someone Who Keeps Hurting You? What 1 Corinthians 13:7 Actually Says May Set Someone Free Tonight.
There is a sentence in the Bible that has comforted millions of people.
And wounded some of them.
Not because the Bible was wrong.
Because somebody used it wrong.
“Love always trusts.”
Maybe those words were handed to you while your heart was still bleeding.

Maybe someone lied to you, betrayed you, manipulated you, humiliated you, cheated on you, abandoned you, controlled you, or repeatedly broke promises—and when you finally became afraid to trust them again, somebody reached for 1 Corinthians 13.
“Love always trusts.”
So you stayed.
You believed another promise.
You ignored another warning.
You silenced another question.
You wondered whether protecting yourself meant you were bitter.
You wondered whether asking for accountability meant you were unforgiving.
You wondered whether noticing the pattern meant you lacked faith.
And perhaps the most painful part was this:
You started wondering whether God Himself expected you to keep handing someone the weapon they kept using to wound you.
If that is where you are, please keep reading.
Because Scripture does command Christians to love.
Scripture does command Christians to forgive.
Scripture does command us to reject bitterness, vengeance, hatred, and unforgiveness.
But Scripture never commands you to call darkness light.
Jesus never taught that forgiveness requires pretending nothing happened.
And biblical love is not the same thing as unlimited interpersonal trust.
Those distinctions matter.
Especially when somebody has repeatedly hurt you.
Paul's actual words in 1 Corinthians 13:7 are:
πάντα στέγει, πάντα πιστεύει, πάντα ἐλπίζει, πάντα ὑπομένει.
Panta stegei, panta pisteuei, panta elpizei, panta hypomenei.
Literally, the verse carries the repeated force of:
Love bears all things.
Believes all things.
Hopes all things.
Endures all things.
The phrase commonly translated “believes all things” is:
πάντα πιστεύει — panta pisteuei.
The crucial verb is πιστεύει — pisteuei, from pisteuō.
It can carry the sense of believing, trusting, having faith, or placing confidence in something.
But here is where context becomes everything.
Paul cannot mean that Christian love requires believing every statement another human being makes regardless of evidence.
Why?
Because only one verse earlier Paul tells us:
“Love does not delight in evil but rejoices with the truth.”
Love and truth are not enemies.
Biblical love does not require abandoning discernment.
Love does not demand that you believe a lie simply because the liar says, “If you loved me, you would trust me.”
That is not 1 Corinthians 13.
That is manipulation wearing a Bible verse.
Imagine someone has lied to you ten times.
They come back an eleventh time.
“I promise.”
You want desperately to believe them.
Your heart remembers who they used to be—or perhaps who you hoped they would become.
But something inside you hesitates.
Then guilt whispers:
Love always trusts.
And suddenly discernment begins feeling like sin.
But listen carefully.
The same Jesus who commanded extraordinary forgiveness also said:
“Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.”
He did not say:
Be innocent and therefore naïve.
He joined innocence with wisdom.
A Christian heart can remain tender without becoming gullible.
You can refuse hatred without refusing reality.
You can forgive somebody while recognizing that their character has not yet become trustworthy.
You can pray for somebody while refusing to participate in their destructive behavior.
You can desire their restoration while requiring evidence of change before restoring the same level of access.
Because forgiveness and trust are related...
but they are not identical.
Forgiveness is something Christians are commanded to extend.
Trust is relational confidence.
And relational confidence can be shattered.
Jesus Himself gives us a breathtaking picture in Luke 17:3:
“If thy brother trespass against thee, rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him.”
Notice what Jesus did not say.
“If your brother sins, pretend it didn't happen.”
He said:
Rebuke him.
That means biblical love can confront.
Biblical love can name wrongdoing.
Biblical love can say:
“This hurt me.”
“This was wrong.”
“This cannot continue.”
“I forgive you, but something must change.”
The Jesus who teaches forgiveness is the same Jesus who makes room for confrontation.
That should free somebody from years of unnecessary guilt.
Because perhaps you were taught that a loving Christian never confronts.
Jesus disagrees.
Perhaps you were taught that boundaries automatically mean bitterness.
Scripture does not say that.
Perhaps somebody told you that forgiveness means immediately returning a relationship to exactly what it was before betrayal.
Scripture does not say that either.
And perhaps somebody keeps demanding your trust while refusing the very repentance that could begin rebuilding it.
That is not reconciliation.
That is entitlement.
Real repentance does not merely say:
“Why can't you get over it?”
Real repentance begins saying:
“I understand why what I did damaged your trust.”
It does not demand instant restoration.
It accepts accountability.
It stops blaming the wounded person for bleeding.
It begins producing fruit.
Because biblical repentance is more than regret over consequences.
It is a turning.
And this is where grace becomes astonishing.
Christianity does not teach us to permanently imprison people inside their worst moment.
The Gospel exists precisely because sinners can change.
Liars can become truthful.
Adulterers can repent.
Addicts can be transformed.
Abusers of power can surrender.
Prodigals can come home.
Hard hearts can become flesh again.
People who destroyed trust can, through genuine repentance and the transforming work of Christ, become different people.
That is grace.
But grace is not pretending transformation has happened when it hasn't.
Grace tells the truth about sin precisely because grace believes Jesus can redeem the sinner.
Think about Peter.
He denied Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
Imagine hearing Peter swear that he did not know the Man he had promised never to abandon.
What a scandal.
Yet Peter's failure was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus met him again.
Not to pretend the denial never happened.
Not to tell Peter betrayal was harmless.
Jesus restored him.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”
The man who denied Jesus became a man commissioned to feed His sheep.
That is not cheap grace.
That is transforming grace.
Jesus did not merely erase Peter's scandal.
He rewrote Peter's future.
And perhaps that is what somebody reading this desperately needs to hear.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Maybe you are not the person who was betrayed.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Maybe you lied.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe you manipulated somebody.
Maybe you repeatedly broke someone's trust and then became angry because they could no longer believe you.
Maybe you have been quoting “love always trusts” because facing what you did feels unbearable.
Then hear this with hope:
Jesus Christ is not asking you to manipulate someone into trusting you.
He is inviting you to repent.
There is a difference.
You do not need to defend the old you.
You need Christ to crucify it.
Stop demanding that someone ignore the fruit of your past behavior.
Start asking Jesus to produce new fruit in your life.
Confess what you did.
Stop minimizing it.
Stop blaming the person you wounded for responding like someone who was wounded.
Accept consequences where consequences remain.
Seek forgiveness without demanding control over the response.
Then walk faithfully.
Tomorrow.
And the next day.
And the day after that.
Let integrity become ordinary.
Let truth become your language.
Let humility become visible.
Let repentance become more than an emotional speech.
Trust may return slowly.
Perhaps painfully slowly.
But genuine change does not need manipulation to prove itself.
Fruit eventually speaks.
And to the person who has been hurt...
there is another danger you must guard against.
Pain can teach discernment.
But pain can also become a prison.
Someone betrayed you, so now nobody gets close.
Someone lied, so everybody becomes suspicious.
Someone abandoned you, so you leave first.
Someone weaponized your vulnerability, so you buried tenderness somewhere so deep that even people who genuinely love you cannot reach it.
That is not healing either.
The person who hurt you should not be allowed to become the architect of every relationship you have afterward.
Jesus wants more for you than that.
Christian wisdom does not say, “Trust everybody.”
But neither does Christian healing say, “Trust nobody.”
It says something infinitely safer:
Trust Christ completely.
Let Him teach you how to love people truthfully.
Humans can fail.
Jesus does not.
People can change overnight.
Christ is faithful.
People can promise forever and disappear tomorrow.
Jesus said He would never leave nor forsake His people.
Your deepest trust was never meant to rest upon the flawless performance of another sinner.
It belongs to God.
And when that foundation is restored, something beautiful happens.
You can forgive without becoming foolish.
You can love without enabling.
You can hope without denying evidence.
You can establish boundaries without hatred.
You can say “no” without becoming cruel.
You can leave room for restoration without manufacturing reconciliation.
You can pray:
“Jesus, I forgive them. I refuse revenge. I refuse hatred. I refuse to let bitterness become my master. But give me wisdom about what access this person should have to my life.”
Sometimes love opens the door.
Sometimes love waits to see fruit.
Sometimes love confronts.
Sometimes love says, “You need help.”
Sometimes love creates distance.
Sometimes love refuses to participate in another person's sin.
Sometimes love welcomes the genuinely repentant person home.
And sometimes love continues praying from somewhere safer.
None of those decisions should be made merely from fear, anger, pressure, or a single slogan pulled out of context.
They should be brought before Jesus.
Because Christ is not merely interested in saving relationships.
He is interested in saving people.
Sometimes preserving the illusion of peace allows sin to continue unchecked.
Sometimes the most loving thing somebody can hear is:
“No more.”
No more lying.
No more manipulation.
No more hiding behind Scripture.
No more demanding forgiveness while rejecting repentance.
No more calling consequences “unloving.”
No more using God's grace as permission to remain unchanged.
The Gospel is not Jesus helping us become comfortable versions of the same people.
The Gospel announces death and resurrection.
The old life dies.
A new life begins.
Christ forgives sinners—and Christ transforms sinners.
At the cross, Jesus did not minimize our sin.
Look at Calvary and you discover how seriously God takes evil.
Our rebellion was not brushed aside.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to the cross.
And yet look again.
Because Calvary simultaneously reveals how fiercely God loves sinners.
Jesus took what guilty people deserved.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Justice and mercy met.
Truth and grace kissed.
The scandalous were offered redemption.
The guilty were offered forgiveness.
The spiritually dead were offered life.
That is why Christianity can look directly at betrayal without surrendering hope.
Jesus specializes in resurrection.
But resurrection requires something to die.
Maybe tonight it is your bitterness.
Maybe your denial.
Maybe your manipulation.
Maybe your obsession with getting revenge.
Maybe your insistence that somebody trust you before you've become trustworthy.
Maybe your belief that forgiveness means becoming available for another wound.
Maybe your fear that boundaries make Jesus disappointed in you.
Bring it to Christ.
All of it.
You don't need another inspirational slogan.
You need Jesus.
And perhaps somebody else needs this truth tonight too.
Someone is sitting alone wondering whether Christianity requires them to walk back into the same cycle because “love always trusts.”
Send this privately to someone who would never admit publicly what they are going through.
Because emotions become confusing when old wounds reopen, and you may need to return to this truth:
Forgiveness does not require pretending evil was trustworthy.
If this exposed something hidden in you, don't disappear quietly.
You do not owe strangers the details of your pain.
But sometimes three honest words become the moment someone stops pretending.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, challenging your compromises, pointing you back to Scripture, helping wounded believers find their way toward Jesus, and reaching people who desperately need the Gospel, consider becoming one of the people who helps keep this mission moving.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Pray.
Then act according to your conscience before God.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the seeker.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing meaningful to say about real wounds and complicated lives.
But whether you ever give one cent or not, never confuse the messenger with the Savior.
Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A church cannot save you.
Religious performance cannot save you.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive His grace.
Follow Jesus.
And let Him begin rewriting what you thought could never be redeemed.
Because maybe the deepest question was never:
“Do I have to trust the person who keeps hurting me?”
Maybe the question beneath the question has always been:
“After everything that happened...is there still Someone I can trust completely?”
Yes.
His name is Jesus.
People may break promises.
People may break hearts.
People may even misuse Scripture while doing it.
But Christ remains faithful.
And when human betrayal leaves you afraid to trust again, remember this:
You don't have to reopen every door to prove you have forgiven—but never let the person who broke your trust convince you that Jesus will break His too.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IBZAN HAD THIRTY SONS AND THIRTY DAUGHTERS—Then Arranged Sixty Marriages Outside His Clan
paragraphs: IBZAN HAD THIRTY SONS AND THIRTY DAUGHTERS—Then Arranged Sixty Marriages Outside His Clan

Sixty children. Sixty marriages reaching beyond his household. Seven years judging Israel. Then one quiet sentence: “Ibzan died.” Hidden inside three easily skipped verses is a disturbing question for every person building a life, a family, a reputation, or even a ministry: When everything you worked so hard to build is finally counted…what will actually remain?
Most people have probably never heard a sermon about Ibzan.
There is no Red Sea opening beside his name.
No walls collapse.
No giant falls.
No fire descends from heaven.
No famous speech survives him.
There are only three verses.
And somehow, that makes his story even harder to forget.
Judges records:

“After him, Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel. He had thirty sons, and he married off thirty daughters outside the clan and likewise brought in thirty from outside the clan for his sons. He led Israel seven years. Then Ibzan died and was buried in Bethlehem.”
Read it again slowly.
Thirty sons.
Thirty daughters.
Thirty daughters sent outward in marriage.
Thirty women brought from outside for his sons.
Seven years of leadership.
Then death.
The Hebrew is striking:
"וַֽיְהִי־ל֞וֹ שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים בָּנִ֗ים וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֤ים בָּנוֹת֙ שִׁלַּ֣ח הַח֔וּצָה וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים בָּנ֔וֹת הֵבִ֥יא לְבָנָ֖יו מִן־הַח֑וּץ"
Vayehi-lo sheloshim banim, usheloshim banot shillach hachutzah, usheloshim banot hevi levanav min-hachutz…
The repeated language is impossible to miss.
הַחוּצָה — hachutzah — outward, outside.
מִן־הַחוּץ — min-hachutz — from outside.
His daughters went outward.
Women came inward for his sons.

Some English translations understandably make the relational implication explicit by rendering this as marriage “outside the clan.” The Hebrew itself emphasizes the movement outward and inward, while the context makes clear that marriages are being described. Ancient commentators likewise understood the daughters as being given away in marriage and women being brought home as wives for Ibzan’s sons.
That distinction matters.
Because we should never make Scripture say more than Scripture says.
The text does not tell us that Ibzan married his children to pagan idolaters.
It does not tell us that these marriages violated the Law of Moses.
It does not explicitly condemn the marriages.
It does not tell us the names of the sixty spouses, their tribes, their motives, or what happened inside those marriages.
And although later Jewish tradition identified Ibzan with Boaz, that is a later rabbinic identification, not something Judges itself states.
So we must resist the temptation to manufacture a scandal where God did not reveal one.
But what Scripture does tell us is remarkable enough.
Ibzan possessed a household of extraordinary size.
Sixty children.
Think about that.
Sixty voices calling one man father.
Sixty childhoods.
Sixty futures.
Sixty marriages connecting his household outward.

For an ancient leader, such a family represented far more than photographs around a fireplace. Marriage could enlarge kinship networks, relationships, influence, security, and social reach. Whatever Ibzan's personal motives were—and Scripture does not reveal them—the narrator clearly considers the extraordinary size and marital reach of his household important enough to preserve.
And then comes the sentence that levels kings and peasants alike:
"וַיָּ֣מׇת אִבְצָ֔ן"
Vayamot Ibzan.
“And Ibzan died.”
Four words in English.
An entire lifetime disappears behind them.
That is where this ancient story suddenly stops feeling ancient.
Because you and I are building too.
Maybe not sixty marriages.
But something.
A career.
A business.
A house.
A family.
A reputation.
A Facebook page.
A ministry.
A bank account.
A name.
A future.
We collect connections.
Followers.
Achievements.
Contacts.
Properties.
Degrees.
Titles.
Photos.
Possessions.
People who know our name.
And somewhere beneath all that activity lives a terrifying question we are very good at avoiding:
What happens when the sentence after everything I built is simply, “And then he died”?
Ibzan judged Israel for seven years.
Seven years.
Then another judge came.
That is how quickly this world learns to continue without us.
One day somebody else sits at your desk.
Somebody else owns your house.
Somebody else drives the car you washed every weekend.
Your clothes are placed in bags.
Your passwords become somebody else's problem.
Your photographs become memories.
The people who once could not imagine life without you slowly learn how to live it.
And the world keeps moving.
That sounds depressing until you realize the Bible is not trying to make you despair.
It is trying to wake you up.
Because death does not make life meaningless.
Death exposes what kind of meaning can survive it.
Jesus asked the question even more sharply:
“What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?” — Mark 8:36.
Imagine gaining almost everything people spend their lives chasing…
and losing the one thing you could never replace.
Your soul.
That is the scandal beneath human success.
We know we are mortal, yet we live as though accumulation can save us.
We know money cannot forgive sin, yet we sacrifice our families to acquire it.
We know applause cannot resurrect us, yet we become addicted to being noticed.
We know followers cannot stand before God's judgment in our place, yet we measure our worth by how many people watch us.

We know our children need Christ more than they need our accomplishments, yet sometimes we spend more energy preparing them to succeed in this world than preparing them to stand faithfully before God.
And some of us are doing something even more painful.
We are building Christian-looking lives while hiding Christless rooms inside our hearts.
Bible verses in our profiles.
Worship music in our playlists.
Church on Sunday.
Secret bondage on Monday.
Smiling family photographs.
A marriage quietly bleeding.
A respectable reputation.
An exhausted soul.
A public “God is good.”
A private “God, where are You?”
You can be surrounded by people and still be spiritually starving.
You can build an impressive family and still wonder whether your children truly know Jesus.
You can be admired by hundreds and secretly hate the person you have become.
You can know Christian language so well that nobody realizes you have forgotten how to pray honestly.
And maybe the most dangerous sentence a Christian can learn to say is:
“I’m fine.”
When you are not.
Maybe you have been carrying something nobody sees.
A sin you promised God you would stop.
A bitterness you keep feeding.
Pornography hidden behind deleted history.
An affair living first in your imagination.
Jealousy disguised as discernment.
Greed disguised as ambition.
Pride disguised as standards.
Unforgiveness disguised as boundaries.
Religious performance disguised as holiness.
Fear disguised as wisdom.
You have learned how to survive while spiritually bleeding.
And Jesus already knows.
Not the edited you.
Not the church you.
Not the version of you your family sees.
You.
The frightening thing about Christ is that nothing is hidden from Him.
The beautiful thing about Christ is exactly the same.
Nothing is hidden from Him…
and He still calls sinners to come.
That is the Gospel.
Christianity is not the announcement that respectable people can become slightly better.
It is the announcement that guilty people can be forgiven.
Dead people can live.
Prodigals can come home.
Enemies can become children.
The ashamed can be clothed.
The condemned can be justified.
The enslaved can become free.
Not because we finally became impressive enough for God.
Because Jesus Christ stepped into the place of sinners.
At the cross, Christ did not merely demonstrate love.
He bore sin.
The innocent One stood where the guilty should have stood.
The sinless Son of God received judgment so that everyone who repents and trusts in Him can receive mercy.
Then the grave received Him.
And the grave could not keep Him.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
That is why failure does not have to have the last word.
That is why addiction does not own the copyright to your future.
That is why your family's dysfunction does not get to name your destiny.
That is why the sin you are ashamed to confess does not have greater saving power than the blood of Jesus.
The Gospel does not say your scandal never happened.
Grace does something infinitely better.
Grace says your scandal does not have to be the end of the story.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending sin is harmless.
By paying for it.
Not by calling darkness light.
By bringing sinners into the Light.
Not by helping us decorate our chains.
By breaking them.
Repentance therefore is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you out of the burning house.
Turn around.
Come home.
Stop defending what is destroying you.
Stop negotiating with the sin Christ died to free you from.
Stop waiting until you feel worthy to approach the Savior whose entire mission was to rescue the unworthy.
You may have wasted years.
Come.
You may have destroyed trust.
Come.
You may have failed your children.
Come.
You may have wandered so far that the person you once were feels like somebody you used to know.
Come.
Jesus did not say, “Clean yourself completely, then perhaps I will receive you.”
He calls sinners to repent and believe.
And when a sinner comes to Christ, the story changes.
Not always instantly in circumstances.
Consequences can remain.
Relationships may need rebuilding.
Trust can take time.
Wounds may require patient healing.
Restitution may be necessary.
Temptation may still knock tomorrow morning.
But something deeper has happened.
The sinner belongs to Christ.
Forgiven.
Reconciled.
Being transformed.
No longer condemned for those who are in Christ Jesus.
And suddenly Ibzan's tiny obituary becomes a mirror.
Because one day your earthly biography will close too.
The question is not whether people will remember how many things you accumulated.
The question is whether you belonged to Jesus.
Your children do not ultimately need you to leave them an impressive surname.
They need to see what repentance looks like.
Your spouse does not need a flawless Christian performance.
They need truth, faithfulness, humility, forgiveness, and Christ.
Your friends do not merely need the entertaining version of you.
They need someone courageous enough to say:
“I needed mercy too.”
Maybe that is why you were meant to read this today.
Not so you could learn an obscure fact about a minor judge and scroll to the next post.
Maybe you needed three forgotten verses to remind you that your days are numbered.
And numbered days are not worthless days.
They are precious days.
There is still time to apologize.
Still time to forgive.
Still time to confess.
Still time to open Scripture again.
Still time to kneel beside your bed.
Still time to tell your children about Jesus.
Still time to repair what pride has kept broken.
Still time to stop pretending.
Still time to surrender.
Still time to come home.
But none of us has been promised unlimited tomorrows.
So if this exposed something you have been hiding, don't perform for us.
Bring it first to Christ.
And if Christ has already begun restoring something in your life that you once believed was beyond repair, tell someone below.
Your testimony might become the sentence God uses to keep another wounded person from giving up tonight.
Then think of one person who needs this.
Not fifty random people.
One.
The brother who has grown cold.
The daughter who stopped believing she could come home.
The friend whose marriage is quietly collapsing.
The Christian who keeps smiling while drowning.
The unbeliever who thinks Christianity is only for clean people.
One share can become one conversation.
One conversation can lead someone back to Scripture.
And God can use Scripture to bring someone face-to-face with Christ.
Save this too.
There will be a day when achievement starts whispering that success is everything.
There will be a night when shame starts telling you your story cannot be redeemed.
Come back and remember:
The world counts what you accumulated.
Jesus asks who owns your heart.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, challenging your compromise, helping you understand Scripture in context, or repeatedly pointing you back to Jesus Christ, consider staying close to this work.

We want this community to remain a place for daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, repentance, grace, and spiritual nourishment centered unapologetically on Jesus Christ.
That support matters.
But hear this carefully, because biblical integrity matters more than conversion statistics:
It cannot buy a blessing.
It cannot replace obedience.
The New Testament says giving should come from the heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
We will tell you something simpler and truer.
Your sharing helps us reach farther.
Your prayers matter even more.
Give Christ your life.
Because eventually every biography reaches its final earthly sentence.
Ibzan had sixty children.
He arranged sixty marriages.
He judged Israel seven years.
Then Ibzan died.
Your résumé will end too.
Your possessions will change hands.
Your influence will fade.
Your body will return to dust.
But Jesus Christ is risen.
And the person whose life is hidden in Him possesses a hope that death cannot repossess.
If everything I have built disappeared tonight, would I still have Christ?
Be honest.
But above everything else…
Follow Jesus.
Because the most terrifying tragedy is not reaching the end with too little.
It is reaching the end with everything—
except the One you were created for.
And perhaps that is the sentence worth carrying with you tonight:
When death closes the book the world wrote about you, make sure your name is resting in the grace of the Savior who conquered the grave.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS SAYING “THE UNIVERSE WILL PROVIDE” HARMLESS—OR ARE WE QUIETLY REPLACING GOD?
paragraphs: IS SAYING “THE UNIVERSE WILL PROVIDE” HARMLESS—OR ARE WE QUIETLY REPLACING GOD?

It sounds positive. It feels spiritual. Millions say it without thinking twice. But there is one uncomfortable question every Christian needs to ask: When did the thing God created become the one we thank for what only God can give?
“The universe will provide.”
Maybe you have said it.
Maybe someone said it to you when you were scared about money.
“The universe has your back.”
Maybe you heard it after a relationship ended.
“Trust the universe.”
Maybe you saw it printed across a beautiful sunset on social media and, because nothing about it looked evil, you kept scrolling.
No pentagram.
No obvious rejection of Jesus.
No angry declaration against God.
Just a peaceful sentence wrapped in stars, sunsets, manifestation language, and reassurance.
And that is precisely why this conversation matters.
Because not everything that moves your emotions deserves your worship.
Not everything that sounds spiritual comes from Scripture.
And sometimes the most dangerous replacement for God is not something that openly declares war against Him.
Sometimes it is something beautiful enough to borrow His attributes while quietly erasing His name.
So before you dismiss this as Christians arguing over words, stay with me.
Because this is not really an article about a phrase.
It is about something much closer to your heart.
It is about whom you trust when the bank account gets low.
Whom you thank when the door unexpectedly opens.
Whom you call upon when the doctor gives you news you never wanted to hear.
Whom you believe controls tomorrow when tonight has left you terrified.
And ultimately...
who gets the glory when provision finally comes.
Go all the way back to the first sentence of Scripture.
In Hebrew, Genesis begins:
בְּרֵאשִׁית בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים
Bereshit bara Elohim.
“In the beginning, God created...”
Notice the direction.
God creates.
Creation is created.
That distinction runs through the entire biblical story.
The stars are magnificent.
But they are not God.
The oceans are terrifyingly beautiful.
But they are not God.
The galaxies can leave you speechless.
But they are not God.
Nature can display God's craftsmanship, power, wisdom, and glory.
But creation never becomes the Creator simply because creation is breathtaking.
The universe did not invent God.
God created the universe.
That means the universe is not an independent intelligence sitting above your life deciding which opportunities to send you.
It is not your heavenly Father.
It does not forgive sins.
It does not hear prayer because it possesses divine omniscience.
It did not send its Son to Calvary.
It did not bleed for you.
It did not rise from the grave.
It cannot reconcile you to God.
It cannot write your name in the Book of Life.
And it cannot save your soul.
Yet somehow, in modern spirituality, we have taken characteristics belonging to a personal God and begun assigning them to an impersonal creation.
“The universe knows.”
“The universe heard me.”
“The universe wanted this for me.”
“The universe removed that person.”
“The universe will provide.”
Listen carefully to what happened.
Knowledge.
Purpose.
Providence.
Wisdom.
Provision.
Attributes and works Scripture associates with God are being transferred to creation.
And Scripture has a category for what happens when creation receives what belongs to the Creator.
Paul writes in Romans 1:25 that people exchanged God's truth for falsehood and “worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.”
The Greek contrast is striking:
τῇ κτίσει παρὰ τὸν κτίσαντα
tē ktisei para ton ktisanta
The creation...
rather than the One who created.
There is the line.
Creation.
Creator.
Gift.
Giver.
Stars.
The One who spoke stars into existence.
And maybe the uncomfortable question is not merely whether saying “the universe will provide” makes someone an idolater.
Words can be used carelessly. People sometimes repeat expressions without intending the worldview behind them. God alone perfectly knows the heart.
The deeper question is this:
What do I actually mean when I say it?
That question reaches somewhere uncomfortable.
Because maybe you never consciously rejected God.
Maybe you simply stopped naming Him.
God blessed you...
and you called it luck.
God opened a door...
and you called it “the universe aligning.”
God carried you through a season that should have destroyed you...
and you called it good energy.
God answered a prayer...
and you called it manifestation.
God placed people around you...
and you thanked destiny.
And slowly, almost invisibly, the Giver disappeared behind His gifts.
James 1:17 gives us a radically different picture:
πᾶσα δόσις ἀγαθὴ καὶ πᾶν δώρημα τέλειον ἄνωθέν ἐστιν
Pasa dosis agathē kai pan dōrēma teleion anōthen estin.
Every good giving and every perfect gift is from above.
James does not leave “above” as an anonymous cosmic force.
He identifies the source:
ἀπὸ τοῦ πατρὸς τῶν φώτων
apo tou patros tōn phōtōn
“from the Father of lights.”
Do you see the beauty?
The lights are not your Father.
The Father made the lights.
The stars do not provide for you.
The Father who made the stars does.
Creation can be an instrument in God's providence.
People can be instruments.
Jobs can be instruments.
Doctors can be instruments.
Businesses can be instruments.
Unexpected opportunities can be instruments.
Rain can be an instrument.
So can soil, governments, communities, churches, friends, strangers, technology, and circumstances.
But Christians do not confuse the instrument with the Source.
Imagine someone desperately needed money for medicine.
A friend heard about it and secretly placed cash inside an envelope.
Another person delivered the envelope.
The suffering person opens it, begins crying, embraces the delivery person and says:
“You saved me. You knew exactly what I needed. You provided this.”
But the messenger knows something the recipient does not.
The messenger did not provide it.
Someone else did.
The messenger merely carried what another person supplied.
Now imagine the giver standing nearby...
completely ignored.
That is the tragedy hidden inside so much vague spirituality.
We receive something through creation...
then worship, thank, trust, or glorify creation...
while the Creator stands forgotten.
And before Christians become self-righteous, we should admit something.
We do this too.
Maybe we don't call it “the universe.”
Maybe our version is money.
Connections.
A career.
A spouse.
A politician.
A pastor.
Our intelligence.
Our savings account.
Our ability to control everything.
Anything created can become the place where we seek the security, identity, hope, and confidence that belong ultimately to God.
Idolatry does not always look like kneeling before a statue.
Sometimes it looks like panic when your bank balance falls because money had quietly become your functional provider.
Sometimes it looks like emotional collapse when someone leaves because that person had quietly become your savior.
Sometimes it looks like believing everything will be okay because you can control it.
Then one day the thing you trusted fails.
The money disappears.
The relationship ends.
The diagnosis comes.
The plan collapses.
The person you thought would never abandon you walks away.
And suddenly you discover what your heart had actually been worshiping.
Jesus speaks directly into this fear.
In Matthew 6, He talks about food.
Drink.
Clothing.
Tomorrow.
The ordinary anxieties that keep human beings awake at 2:13 in the morning staring into darkness while mentally calculating bills.
Jesus does not tell frightened people:
“Ask the universe.”
He points them toward their heavenly Father.
Then comes the command that rearranges our priorities:
ζητεῖτε δὲ πρῶτον τὴν βασιλείαν
zēteite de prōton tēn basileian
Seek first the kingdom.
Not first your manifestation.
Not first cosmic alignment.
Not first your preferred outcome.
God's kingdom.
God's righteousness.
God's will.
And that changes everything.
Because biblical faith is not believing that God is obligated to give you everything you visualize.
Christian prayer is not manifestation with Jesus' name attached.
God is not a cosmic vending machine.
Faith does not mean, “I believe strongly enough, therefore reality must obey me.”
Faith means trusting God even when His answer is different from the answer you desperately wanted.
Ask Jesus in Gethsemane.
His prayer was not an exercise in forcing circumstances to conform to personal desire.
It was surrender:
“Not my will, but yours.”
That is Christianity.
Not controlling reality.
Surrendering to the Father.
And maybe that is why “the universe will provide” can feel easier.
The universe never tells you to repent.
The universe does not confront your pornography.
The universe does not challenge your bitterness.
The universe does not tell you to forgive your enemy.
The universe does not expose your pride.
The universe does not command you to deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow Christ.
An impersonal spiritual force can comfort you without having authority over you.
But Jesus does something far more loving.
He calls you out of darkness.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He commands.
He transforms.
He becomes Lord.
And that is where the Gospel enters this conversation.
Because perhaps you have spent years looking everywhere for signs that somebody—or something—was watching over you.
Perhaps your attraction to “the universe” was never really rebellion.
Maybe underneath it was loneliness.
You desperately wanted to believe you were not alone.
That your suffering had meaning.
That somebody knew.
That somebody saw you.
That somehow things could still work together when your life looked shattered beyond repair.
There is something heartbreaking about that search.
Because Christianity says you do not have to send desperate wishes into an impersonal cosmos hoping something hears you.
You are known.
Not by the universe.
By the God who made it.
You are seen.
You are heard.
And the astonishing claim of the Gospel is not that the universe loved you so much that it sent positive energy.
It is that God entered His own creation.
Jesus Christ came.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed sinners.
He confronted hypocrites.
He wept beside a grave.
He carried a cross.
And there, outside Jerusalem, the Creator allowed created hands to drive nails through His flesh.
Think about that.
The One through whom creation came into being entered creation to rescue rebels who had loved created things more than their Creator.
That is grace.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin.
Not because humanity had manifested salvation.
Not because our vibrations finally became high enough.
Not because we had attracted forgiveness.
Grace came looking for sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Then came the tomb.
Sealed.
Silent.
Final, everyone thought.
Until Sunday morning.
Jesus rose.
Not as positive energy.
Not as a metaphor for personal reinvention.
Not as “the universe reminding us to keep going.”
The Christian proclamation is far more explosive:
Christ is risen.
Death did not get the final word.
Sin does not have to get the final word.
Your past does not have to get the final word.
Your worst night does not have to become the title of your entire life.
This is why we keep saying it:
Maybe your scandal was unbelief.
Maybe addiction.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe pride.
Maybe secret sin nobody knows about.
Maybe you have been spiritually numb for years while maintaining a Christian appearance.
Maybe you love Jesus, but without realizing it you began borrowing beliefs from a culture that talks constantly about spirituality while avoiding the lordship of Christ.
Then this is not your invitation to panic.
It is your invitation to come home.
Repentance is not God standing at the door waiting to humiliate you.
Repentance is turning away from false gods and running back to the God who has been worthy all along.
So perhaps today your prayer becomes painfully simple:

“Father, forgive me for giving creation the glory that belongs to You. Forgive me for trusting gifts more than the Giver. Forgive me for trying to control what You asked me to surrender. Jesus, I belong to You. Teach me to recognize Your hand without worshiping the instruments You use. You alone are my God.”
And when provision comes...
thank God.
When the doctor helps...
thank God for the doctor and thank the doctor too.
When someone gives generously...
honor that person, but remember the ultimate Giver.
When an impossible door opens...
do not merely say, “The universe did it.”
Look higher than the stars.
Look beyond creation.
Say His name.
Thank You, Father.
Because gratitude becomes worship when it reaches the rightful destination.
And if this article exposed something you have never examined before, don't hide behind embarrassment.
Be honest.
No performance.
No pretending.
Just honesty.
Then think about one person you love who constantly says, “The universe will provide.”
Do not send this article as a weapon.
Send it as an invitation.
It never could.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
If this ministry is producing spiritual fruit in your life, do not underestimate what consistent support can make possible.
If you believe this work should continue reaching people who are scrolling through darkness looking for one sentence that might point them home, you can stand with us.
Sometimes support provides the resources.
Sometimes sharing provides the reach.
at exactly the moment they were thinking about giving up.
And perhaps that is the final irony.
People keep saying,
“The universe will provide.”
But the universe itself is pointing beyond itself.
The heavens declare glory...
but they are not the One receiving it.
The stars shine...
but they are not your Savior.
Creation is breathtaking...
but creation never climbed onto a cross for you.
Never become so fascinated with the stars that you forget the hands that made them—and never thank the universe for what cost your Savior His blood.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD ALLOW THE PATRIARCHS TO HAVE MULTIPLE WIVES—IF THAT WAS NEVER HIS DESIGN?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD ALLOW THE PATRIARCHS TO HAVE MULTIPLE WIVES—IF THAT WAS NEVER HIS DESIGN?

Abraham had Sarah and Hagar. Jacob married Leah and Rachel and fathered children through their servants. David had multiple wives. Solomon had hundreds. So why didn’t God stop them? The answer is more uncomfortable—and more beautiful—than simply saying, “That was the Old Testament.”
There is a question many Christians have quietly carried but were afraid to ask out loud.
Maybe you have carried it too.
You read Genesis.
You meet Abraham—the man Scripture calls the father of all who believe.
Then Hagar enters the story.
You meet Jacob—the man whose name becomes Israel.
Then there is Leah.
Rachel.
Bilhah.
Zilpah.
You keep reading.
David appears.
A man after God's own heart...yet surrounded by multiple wives.
Then Solomon arrives with a household so enormous that modern readers almost cannot comprehend it.
And somewhere between Sunday school and serious Bible reading, an uncomfortable question begins scratching at the door of your faith:
“If God designed marriage to be between one man and one woman...why did He allow His own patriarchs and kings to practice polygamy?”
And beneath that question is another one.
A more dangerous one.
“Did God change His mind?”
No.
But to understand why, we have to stop confusing something the Bible records with something God recommends.
That distinction changes everything.
Because the Bible is brutally honest about its heroes.
It does not airbrush Abraham.
It does not sanitize Jacob.
It does not protect David's reputation.
It does not edit Solomon's failures out of the story.
Scripture does something far more astonishing.
It shows us sinful human beings as they really were...
and then shows us a holy God continuing His redemptive work in spite of them.
That is not divine approval of everything they did.
That is grace.
And perhaps that is why this question matters far more than polygamy.
Because sooner or later, you are going to discover that the Bible is filled with people God used despite things in their lives God never intended as His ideal.
And then...
if you are courageous enough...
you will realize you are one of them.
Before Abraham ever took Hagar...
before Jacob ever found himself caught between two sisters...
before David built a complicated household...
before Solomon accumulated wives until his heart wandered...
God had already shown humanity what marriage was meant to be.
You have to go back before the patriarchs.
Before Israel.
Before Moses.
Before kings.
Before human civilization learned how to normalize its brokenness.
Go back to Eden.
Genesis 2:24 says:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
‘Al-kēn ya‘ăzāḇ-’îš ’eṯ-’āḇîw wə’eṯ-’immōw, wəḏāḇaq bə’ištōw, wəhāyū ləḇāśār ’eḥāḏ.
“For this reason a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
Listen carefully to the language.
בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ — bə’ištōw
“His wife.”
And then:
לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד — ləḇāśār ’eḥāḏ
“One flesh.”
One covenant union.
Before sin distorted human relationships, God presented Adam and Eve.
Not Adam, Eve, and several additional wives.
The pattern appears before the fall.
And that matters.
Then Genesis does something fascinating.
The first explicit polygamist mentioned in Scripture is not Abraham.
It is Lamech.
Genesis 4:19 tells us that Lamech “took two wives.”
Read the surrounding story carefully and the atmosphere is not one of spiritual advancement.
Humanity is descending deeper into violence, pride, vengeance, domination, and rebellion.
Lamech eventually boasts about killing a man.
Polygamy enters the biblical narrative not as a new command from heaven but within a world increasingly fractured by sin.
Then Abraham comes.
God promises Abraham descendants.
But years pass.
Sarah remains barren.
The promise seems impossible.
And human beings do what human beings have been doing ever since Eden:
they attempt to accomplish God's purposes through human control.
Sarah gives Hagar to Abraham.
Hagar conceives.
And almost immediately...
the house begins to bleed.
Genesis does not need to insert a sentence saying, “Polygamy causes problems.”
The story shows you.
Jealousy.
Contempt.
Humiliation.
Conflict.
A vulnerable woman running into the wilderness.
A child eventually separated from his father.
Sarah hurts.
Hagar hurts.
Abraham hurts.
Ishmael hurts.
And generations feel the consequences of people trying to manufacture what God had promised to provide.
That is one of Scripture's most sobering methods of teaching.
Sometimes God gives a command.
Sometimes He lets the consequences preach.
Then comes Jacob.
And if anyone tries to use Jacob's household as an advertisement for polygamy, they have not read the story slowly enough.
Jacob loves Rachel.
He is deceived into marrying Leah.
Then Rachel becomes his wife as well.
Then Bilhah enters.
Then Zilpah.
And suddenly the home becomes a battlefield of comparison.
One woman desperate to be loved.
Another desperate to have children.
Servants brought into reproductive rivalry.
Children becoming symbols in their mothers' struggle for affection and status.
Even the naming of children sometimes carries the emotional scars of women trying to be seen.
This is not paradise.
This is heartbreak with a family tree.
God works through that family.
But do not confuse God's ability to redeem dysfunction with God's endorsement of dysfunction.
That distinction is absolutely essential.
God can bring holiness out of wreckage without calling the wreckage holy.
God can fulfill His promises through broken people without declaring their broken choices righteous.
God can write redemption through a dysfunctional family without pretending the dysfunction was His original design.
That is grace.
And then the Law comes.
Here the question becomes even more difficult.
Because instead of immediately abolishing every existing manifestation of polygamy in Israelite society, Mosaic law contains regulations addressing situations in which multiple wives existed.
Why?
Because biblical law sometimes regulates life in a fallen society without presenting every regulated condition as God's creational ideal.
Jesus Himself gives us the interpretive key when discussing another marital issue—divorce.
In Matthew 19, religious leaders question Him about divorce.
Jesus does something remarkable.
He does not begin with Moses.
He goes farther back.
Back to creation.
He quotes Genesis.
The Greek of Matthew 19:5 says:
καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
kai esontai hoi dyo eis sarka mian
“The two shall become one flesh.”
Notice that word:
δύο — dyo
Two.
And:
μίαν — mian
One.
Jesus continues:
ὥστε οὐκέτι εἰσὶν δύο ἀλλὰ σὰρξ μία
“So they are no longer two, but one flesh.”
Then He says:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
When challenged about Moses permitting divorce, Jesus explains that Moses permitted it because of the hardness of human hearts, but adds:
“from the beginning it was not so.”
Those words give us a crucial biblical principle.
Permission within human brokenness is not necessarily the same thing as God's original design.
Read that again.
Because it reaches far beyond ancient marriage customs.
There are things God confronts immediately.
There are things He restrains.
There are things He regulates amid fallen social realities.
There are consequences He allows human beings to experience.
And through the unfolding story of redemption, He continually draws His people toward His holiness.
Even Israel's kings were explicitly warned about multiplying wives.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
Wəlō yarbeh-lō nāšîm, wəlō yāsūr ləḇāḇō.
“He shall not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.”
That warning becomes almost terrifying when you reach Solomon.
Because Solomon eventually becomes a living demonstration of the warning.
The king famous for wisdom became foolish precisely where God had warned Israel's kings.
First Kings 11 describes Solomon's many foreign wives and tells us that they turned his heart toward other gods.
The tragedy was not merely romantic excess.
It became spiritual adultery.
The man who built the temple allowed idols into his heart.
Think about that.
You can build something for God while quietly allowing something else to take God's place inside you.
You can know Scripture and still negotiate with desire.
You can possess extraordinary wisdom and still rationalize the one compromise that eventually conquers you.
Solomon is not merely an ancient warning about marriage.
He is a mirror.
Because every generation has its own version of multiplying wives.
Something God warned us about...
something culture normalizes...
something our flesh desires...
something we tell ourselves we can control.
Until one day...
it controls us.
And maybe this article stopped being about Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon several paragraphs ago.
Maybe now it is about you.
Maybe there is something in your life you have been defending simply because God has not struck you down for it.
Something you tolerate because judgment has not arrived.
Something you keep calling “grace” when grace has actually been calling you to repentance.
Be careful.
God's patience is not proof of God's approval.
That sentence can save someone's soul from years of unnecessary pain.
The patriarchs demonstrate something profoundly important about Scripture:
God's redemptive plan does not depend upon morally flawless human beings.
If it did...
Genesis would have ended very quickly.
Abraham lied.
Jacob deceived.
Judah fell into sexual scandal.
Moses failed.
David committed devastating sins.
Solomon compromised.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul once persecuted Christians.
Yet God's promise kept moving.
Not because sin did not matter.
But because grace was greater than the sinners through whom God chose to work.
And all those fractured stories eventually move toward One who was not fractured.
Jesus Christ.
The faithful Son.
The spotless Lamb.
The true Bridegroom.
This is where the biblical picture of marriage becomes even more beautiful.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5 that the union of husband and wife points beyond itself toward Christ and His Church.
Marriage was never merely about human companionship.
It carries a Gospel-shaped mystery.
Christ loves His Bride.
Christ gives Himself for His Bride.
Christ sanctifies His Bride.
Christ does not exploit His Bride.
He dies for her.
The ultimate answer to humanity's broken relationships is therefore not merely better relationship rules.
It is Christ.
Because our deepest problem has never simply been polygamy, divorce, lust, jealousy, adultery, or dysfunctional families.
Those are branches.
The root goes deeper.
The human heart departed from God.
And Jesus came to bring sinners home.
That is why Christianity is not the story of good people proving themselves worthy of God.
It is the story of sinners discovering they never were.
And then discovering something even more astonishing:
Jesus knew...
and came anyway.
Maybe your scandal looks nothing like Abraham's.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe your marriage is struggling.
Maybe pornography has been eating your soul in secret.
Maybe you crossed a boundary you promised yourself you never would.
Maybe resentment has turned your bedroom cold.
Maybe jealousy is poisoning you.
Maybe your family history is complicated.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Maybe your children know a version of you that your church never sees.
Maybe you have been reading about dysfunctional biblical families because your own family feels painfully familiar.
Hear this clearly.
The Bible does not hide broken families because God does not need perfect backgrounds to create redeemed futures.
But grace is not permission to remain where sin left you.
Jesus does not merely forgive.
He transforms.
He calls adulterers to purity.
Liars to truth.
The proud to humility.
The sexually broken to holiness.
The bitter to forgiveness.
The hidden sinner into the light.
The dead...
to life.
This is the Gospel.
Not “God doesn't care how you live.”
And not “Fix yourself so God will love you.”
The Gospel says:
You could not rescue yourself.
So Christ came for you.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died the death sinners deserved.
He rose victorious.
And now forgiveness is offered not because your scandal was small...
but because His sacrifice was enough.
Repent.
Come home.
Stop hiding.
Stop using biblical characters' failures to justify what Jesus is asking you to surrender.
Abraham's failures cannot save you.
David's failures cannot excuse you.
Solomon's compromises cannot defend you.
Only Jesus can redeem you.
And perhaps that is why God allowed Scripture to show us these men exactly as they were.
Because if the Bible contained nothing but flawless heroes, people like us might eventually conclude there was no place in God's story for people like us.
But Scripture leaves the scars visible.
Then grace walks straight through them.
Be honest.

And if God has already brought you through relational wreckage, betrayal, sexual sin, family dysfunction, or a season you thought would destroy you, share what Christ has done. Someone reading your testimony may desperately need proof that failure does not have to write the final chapter.
Not because every sentence is easy.
Not merely to help an algorithm.
Somebody is wondering whether the Bible contradicts itself.
Somebody thinks their family is too broken for God.
Somebody has mistaken God's patience for permission.
Somebody needs Jesus.
But voluntary generosity can glorify God when it flows from faith, gratitude, love, and a sincere desire to help Gospel ministry continue.
Pray.
Because somewhere tonight, another Abraham is discovering the cost of taking matters into his own hands.
Another Leah is wondering why she never feels chosen.
Another Hagar feels abandoned in the wilderness.
Another David is hiding a scandal.
Another Solomon thinks he can manage his compromise.
And another broken sinner is wondering whether God could possibly still want them.
The answer is standing at a cross with wounded hands.
Yes.
But He loves you too much to leave you unchanged.
The Bible never needed perfect patriarchs to prove that God was faithful. It needed a perfect Savior—and His name is Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: REHOBOAM HAD EIGHTEEN WIVES AND SIXTY CONCUBINES—But Loved One Woman More Than All the Others
paragraphs: REHOBOAM HAD EIGHTEEN WIVES AND SIXTY CONCUBINES—But Loved One Woman More Than All the Others

He had access to more women than most men could imagine. Yet Scripture quietly records that one woman held a place the others did not—and hidden inside that uncomfortable story is a warning about desire, favoritism, legacy, and the things we think will finally satisfy us.
Eighteen wives.
Sixty concubines.
Twenty-eight sons.
Sixty daughters.
A palace filled with people.
A kingdom beneath his feet.
And still, in the middle of all those staggering numbers, Scripture suddenly slows down and tells us something painfully human about King Rehoboam.
One woman was different.
Her name was Maacah.
And the Bible says:
“וַיֶּאֱהַב רְחַבְעָם אֶת־מַעֲכָה בַת־אַבְשָׁלוֹם מִכָּל־נָשָׁיו וּפִילַגְשָׁיו”
Vayye’ehav Rechav‘am et-Ma‘akhah bat-Avshalom mikol-nashav ufilagshav…
“Rehoboam loved Maacah the daughter of Absalom above all his wives and his concubines.”
—2 Chronicles 11:21
Read that again.
Not because this is some ancient royal romance we are supposed to imitate.
It isn’t.
And not because Scripture is celebrating a king collecting women as though human beings were trophies.
It isn’t.
In fact, centuries before Rehoboam sat upon the throne, God had already warned Israel’s kings against multiplying wives to themselves.
So the shocking number in this passage is not evidence of Rehoboam’s greatness.
It is part of the tragedy.
Because sometimes the Bible tells you what happened without telling you to copy what happened.
And that distinction matters.
Rehoboam had eighteen wives and sixty concubines, yet the inspired writer still pauses to tell us that he loved Maacah more than the others.
Think about the haunting irony.
Seventy-eight women could not make seventy-eight hearts equally precious to him.
Quantity could not manufacture intimacy.
Access could not guarantee love.
Abundance could not eliminate preference.
Possession could not create satisfaction.
And suddenly this ancient king does not feel quite so ancient anymore.
Because we may not have Rehoboam’s palace…
but we understand his disease.
More.
One more relationship.
One more purchase.
One more promotion.
One more follower.
One more compliment.
One more achievement.
One more person telling us we matter.
One more secret pleasure.
One more night scrolling.
One more thing added to the collection of things we once believed would finally make us whole.
We keep adding.
And adding.
And adding.
Yet somehow the human heart can remain painfully hungry.
Maybe that is why this verse feels so uncomfortable.
It exposes something we would rather not admit:
You can possess more and still not love better.
You can be surrounded and still be empty.
You can have options and still have no peace.
You can live in a palace and still carry a wilderness inside your chest.
Rehoboam knew something about palaces.
He was Solomon’s son.
Think about the shadow under which this man grew up.
His father was Solomon—the king associated with extraordinary wisdom, wealth, construction, international influence, and staggering excess.
Yet Solomon himself had multiplied wives on an enormous scale, and Scripture records the devastating spiritual consequence: his wives turned his heart after other gods.
Then comes Rehoboam.
Another generation.
Another throne.
Another man surrounded by women.
Different numbers.
Same human heart.
That should make every parent tremble.
Because children can inherit more than our eyes, our surnames, our property, or our mannerisms.
They watch what we normalize.
They learn what we excuse.
They absorb what we worship.
And sometimes what one generation tolerates, the next generation learns to call normal.
That is why grace must do more than improve our behavior.
Jesus must transform our hearts.
Because if Christ does not interrupt the cycle, yesterday’s compromise can become tomorrow’s inheritance.
But there is something else buried in this story.
Maacah was not merely Rehoboam’s favorite.
Her position appears to have affected the future of the kingdom.
Immediately after telling us Rehoboam loved Maacah above his other wives and concubines, Scripture tells us:
“And Rehoboam made Abijah the son of Maachah the chief, to be ruler among his brethren: for he thought to make him king.”
—2 Chronicles 11:22
Do you see it?
What occupied the king’s affection reached into the king’s decisions.
His private preference touched public succession.
The heart never stays completely hidden.
Eventually, what rules inside us starts influencing what happens around us.
What you love shapes what you choose.
What you treasure shapes what you protect.
What you worship shapes what you sacrifice.
That is why Jesus went deeper than behavior.
He went after the heart.
We often want Christianity to become a divine renovation project.
Jesus, fix my finances.
Fix my marriage.
Fix my anxiety.
Fix my children.
Fix my reputation.
Fix my circumstances.
Fix the consequences.
And Christ certainly cares about every wounded place we carry.
But Jesus did not come merely to rearrange the furniture inside the old life.
He came to make us new.
The Gospel does not say, “Try harder until God can tolerate you.”
The Gospel announces something infinitely more beautiful:
You were a sinner who could not rescue yourself.
Christ came for you.
Jesus lived the righteousness you could never perfectly live.
He went to the cross willingly.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The answer to the restless human heart is ultimately not another relationship.
Not another possession.
Not another experience.
Not another secret indulgence.
Not another person telling you that you are enough.
The answer is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
And perhaps somebody reading this knows exactly why those words hurt.
Because your life looks full from the outside.
But God knows about the empty room inside you.
People see your photos.
God sees your loneliness.
People see your marriage.
God sees the distance.
People see your Bible verses.
God sees the compromise you keep deleting from your history.
People hear you say, “I’m okay.”
Jesus knows you cried when nobody was watching.
People think you have moved on.
God knows you are still bleeding from something that happened years ago.
And maybe you have been trying to solve a spiritual hunger with earthly multiplication.
More attention.
More pornography.
More money.
More relationships.
More entertainment.
More alcohol.
More approval.
More work.
More religious activity.
Even more ministry.
Anything…
as long as you never have to sit quietly before Jesus and admit:
“Lord, I am still empty.”
That confession may be closer to freedom than you realize.
Because grace begins where pretending ends.
Look again at Rehoboam.
Eighteen wives.
Sixty concubines.
And Scripture still had to distinguish one love from another.
There is no number large enough to heal a heart that is looking to creation for what only the Creator can ultimately provide.
But before we turn Rehoboam into the villain and ourselves into the jury, remember who his story is really exposing.
Us.
We multiply things too.
Our idols simply fit inside our pockets now.
Some of them have screens.
Some have bank accounts.
Some have bodies.
Some have job titles.
Some have church titles.
Some look respectable enough that nobody realizes we are worshiping them.
And that may be the most dangerous idol of all:
the one you can carry into church without anybody noticing.
Jesus does not merely ask what you own.
He exposes what owns you.
That is where this ancient scandal suddenly becomes painfully personal.
What has your heart?
Not what do you say has your heart.
What actually has it?
What could you not imagine surrendering if Christ asked you to lay it down?
Whose approval can destroy your entire day?
What do you run toward when you feel unwanted?
What secret habit becomes your counterfeit comfort?
What are you terrified of losing?
There may be your answer.
And here is the breathtaking difference between Rehoboam’s palace and Christ’s kingdom.
Rehoboam surrounded himself with many.
Jesus gave Himself for His people.
Rehoboam accumulated.
Jesus emptied Himself.
Earthly kings often use people to build kingdoms.
Jesus gave His life to redeem people for His Kingdom.
At Calvary, Christ was not collecting trophies.
He was shedding His blood for sinners.
The crown placed upon His head was made of thorns.
The throne men gave Him was a cross.
The royal robe became mockery.
The crowd did not shout affection but rejection.
And the King stayed.
Nails did not ultimately keep Jesus there.
Love did.
That is the love your restless heart has been searching for.
Not indulgence.
Not possession.
Not endless romantic validation.
Covenant love.
Holy love.
Crucified love.
Resurrected love.
A love strong enough to confront your sin without abandoning you to it.
A love gracious enough to forgive what you are ashamed to confess.
A love powerful enough to rewrite a life everyone else has already written off.
That is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the mercy of God calling you out of the grave before the grave becomes home.
Maybe you have failed sexually.
Come to Jesus.
Maybe your marriage carries wounds nobody knows about.
Come to Jesus.
Maybe you became emotionally attached to somebody who was never yours to have.
Come to Jesus.
Maybe pornography has quietly trained your heart to consume people instead of love them.
Come to Jesus.
Maybe success became your mistress.
Come to Jesus.
Maybe you have been sleeping beside someone every night while your heart has been somewhere else.
Come to Jesus.
Maybe your scandal is public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Come anyway.
The cross was built for guilty people.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace is the power and mercy of God meeting sinners where they are and refusing to leave them there.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
And sometimes He begins by tearing away the lie that the next thing will finally satisfy us.
The next woman.
The next man.
The next paycheck.
The next purchase.
The next achievement.
The next dopamine hit.
The next secret.
The next escape.
Eventually you discover what generations before us discovered:
A human soul is too deep to be filled by created things.
You were made for God.
And perhaps that is the real reason this strange little verse survived thousands of years and found its way onto your screen today.
Not so we could gossip about an ancient king.
So an ancient king could become a mirror.
Rehoboam had more than most people could dream of possessing.
Yet Scripture still makes us look beneath the numbers and toward the heart.
So forget his seventy-eight women for a moment.
What are your seventy-eight substitutes?
What have you been multiplying because one surrendered relationship with Jesus feels too costly?
What have you accumulated because silence with God terrifies you?
What are you using to anesthetize the ache?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need your testimony tonight.
Do not underestimate what one honest sentence can do.
And think of one person who needs this message.
Not twenty strangers.
One person.
The friend quietly destroying a marriage.
The brother drowning in lust.
The woman convinced another relationship will finally make her whole.
The successful person nobody realizes is empty.
The believer who loves Jesus but has wandered far from Him.
Sometimes evangelism begins with something as simple as refusing to keep a life-giving message to yourself.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget what conviction taught us yesterday.
You may need these words again.
There is another way you can help this work continue.
Gospel ministry requires people who pray, people who share, people who serve, and people who voluntarily give.
But hear this clearly:
It does not.
It cannot.
Scripture says giving should come from a heart that has decided freely, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
And if Gospel Warrior is one of the ministries you choose to support financially, we receive that support with gratitude, not entitlement.
And whether you are able to give financially or not, you can still help.
Pray.
Share.
Invite people to follow.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
That distinction matters.
Use them.
Share them.
Study Scripture.
Test what you read against the Word of God.
Grow.
And keep Jesus at the center.
Because eventually every earthly collection becomes dust.
Palaces disappear.
Crowns pass to another head.
Possessions find another owner.
Beauty fades.
Applause stops.
Bodies age.
Numbers that once impressed everybody become forgotten statistics in somebody else’s history book.
Rehoboam once had eighteen wives and sixty concubines.
Today we remember him through a few lines of ancient Scripture.
But Jesus Christ still reigns.
And that leaves you with one question far more important than how many wives Rehoboam possessed or which woman he preferred:
Who possesses your heart?
If the answer exposes something painful, do not run.
The Savior already knows.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the affair.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the loneliness.
Bring Him the greed.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the secret messages.
Bring Him the broken marriage.
Bring Him the wasted years.
Bring Him the version of yourself you desperately hope nobody ever discovers.
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
Because the most beautiful thing about Jesus is not that He pretends your scandal never happened.
It is that He can meet you in the wreckage, forgive the repentant sinner, and begin writing something your failure never had the authority to finish.
Your scandal may explain a chapter of your life—but because of Jesus, it does not have to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JOASH HAD TWO WIVES CHOSEN FOR HIM BY THE PRIEST WHO SAVED HIS LIFE — But That Is Not the Most Shocking Part of His Story
paragraphs: JOASH HAD TWO WIVES CHOSEN FOR HIM BY THE PRIEST WHO SAVED HIS LIFE — But That Is Not the Most Shocking Part of His Story

He survived a massacre. He was hidden inside the house of God. A priest risked everything to save him, helped put a crown on his head, guided his life, and even chose his wives. Then something happened after that priest died that should terrify every Christian who has ever confused being surrounded by godly people with actually knowing God.
There is one sentence in 2 Chronicles that sounds almost like a passing family detail.
Read too quickly, and you will miss the tragedy already gathering behind it.
Joash was king.
Jehoiada was priest.
And Scripture tells us:
“And Jehoiada took for him two wives; and he begat sons and daughters.” — 2 Chronicles 24:3, KJV
The Hebrew is striking:
וַיִּשָּׂא־לוֹ יְהוֹיָדָע נָשִׁים שְׁתָּיִם וַיּוֹלֶד בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת
Vayyissa-lo Yehoyada nashim shetayim, vayyōled banim uvanot.
In straightforward sense: Jehoiada took—or obtained—two wives for him, and he fathered sons and daughters.
Some English translations therefore say Jehoiada “chose two wives for him.”
That detail is genuinely in the text.
But we need to be careful with what we make it say.

The Chronicler reports that Joash had two wives. The passage does not command polygamy, celebrate it as God’s ideal, or tell believers to imitate it. Description is not automatically prescription. From Genesis onward, Scripture's foundational picture of marriage is the man and his wife becoming “one flesh,” a pattern Jesus Himself later reaffirmed.
So why does Chronicles tell us this?
Because these two verses are painting a picture of something much bigger.
Joash's life was being built.
A kingdom.
A family.
Children.
A future.
And standing beside him through it all was an old priest named Jehoiada.
But you cannot understand how painful that becomes until you remember where Joash came from.
He was never supposed to grow up.
He was never supposed to sit on a throne.
He was barely supposed to survive childhood.
His grandmother Athaliah attempted to destroy the royal heirs.
Imagine the terror.
Royal blood being hunted.
A dynasty apparently collapsing.
A little boy surrounded by death before he was old enough to understand why people wanted him dead.
Yet Joash escaped.
He was hidden for six years in the house of God while Athaliah ruled the land.
Six years.
Think about that.
While other children could run outside, this child carried a secret he probably could not fully comprehend.
His existence was dangerous.
His identity could get him killed.
His future was hidden behind temple walls.
And there was Jehoiada.
The priest.
The protector.
The man who would eventually bring the young heir out, place the crown upon his head, overthrow Athaliah's murderous regime, renew covenant faithfulness, and help establish Joash as king.
Joash did not merely know Jehoiada.
In a profound human sense, he owed much of his earthly life to him.
Jehoiada had stood between the child and destruction.
Then comes one of the most revealing statements in the entire story:
“Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest.”
Read it again.
“All the days of Jehoiada.”
That qualification should make your heart uneasy.
Because sometimes a sentence that sounds like praise is also quietly exposing a weakness.
Joash looked faithful.
Joash acted faithful.
Joash even became passionate about repairing the temple.
The boy who had once been hidden in God's house grew into a king determined to restore God's house.
It sounds beautiful.
It almost sounds like the perfect testimony.
Saved from death.
Raised around the things of God.
Guided by a faithful spiritual mentor.
Established with a family.
Restoring the temple.
Doing what was right.
If the story stopped there, Joash would look like one of Judah's great redemption stories.
But the Bible refuses to give us sanitized biographies.
It tells us what happened when the godly voice beside Joash disappeared.
Jehoiada grew old.
He died.
And suddenly the scaffolding around Joash's faith was gone.
Then came other voices.
The officials of Judah approached the king.
Joash listened.
And the man who had spent his childhood inside the house of God abandoned the house of God.
Let that sink in.
You can grow up around holy things and still have an unsurrendered heart.
You can know worship songs and not know surrender.
You can quote Scripture and still resist the God who wrote it.
You can have a praying mother, a faithful father, a godly pastor, a Bible-believing spouse, a Christian friend group, and years inside a church...
and still discover that much of your spiritual life was leaning on somebody else's conviction.
That is where Joash stops being an ancient king and starts becoming a mirror.
Maybe your “Jehoiada” was your grandmother.
She prayed with you.
She brought you to church.
She told you about Jesus.
When she was alive, somehow you stayed close.
Then she died.
And slowly...
quietly...
you drifted.
Maybe it was your parents.
Maybe it was your pastor.
Maybe it was the spouse who kept asking you to pray.
Maybe it was the friend who kept checking on your soul.
Maybe you behaved like a disciple because someone you loved was watching.
