Grace will forgive the sinner who falls—but grace was never given to make peace with the sin that keeps pulling us back.
There is a sentence we use when the truth gets too close.
When the guilt becomes uncomfortable.
When somebody confronts what we did.
When our conscience starts whispering the thing we desperately do not want to hear.
“Everybody makes mistakes.”
And it is true.
Painfully true.
Every one of us has failed.
Every one of us has said something we wish we could pull back into our mouths.
Every one of us has entertained thoughts we would never want projected onto a screen.
Every one of us has disappointed someone.
Every one of us has looked into the mirror and seen a version of ourselves we promised we would never become.
Scripture does not flatter humanity.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
Not some.
All.
The religious person.
The addict.
The pastor.
The skeptic.
The person reading this while quietly carrying something nobody knows.
Me.
You.
Everybody.
But here is where one of the most dangerous lies can quietly enter the Christian life.
Because “everybody makes mistakes” can begin as an admission of human weakness…
and slowly become permission to keep choosing what Jesus died to free us from.
There is a difference between falling into sin and making a home there.
There is a difference between weakness that drives you toward Christ and rebellion that uses Christ as an excuse.
There is a difference between saying, “Jesus, I fell again. Please help me,” and saying, “Jesus will forgive me anyway, so why stop?”
And that difference matters.
More than we may want to admit.
Imagine someone standing at the edge of the same hole for the hundredth time.
The first time, he fell.
The second time, perhaps he stumbled.
But eventually he memorized the road.
He knows where the hole is.
He knows what leads there.
He knows what happens afterward.
He knows the shame.
He knows the tears.
He knows the promises he will make at 2:00 in the morning.
He knows the prayer he will pray.
And still…
he keeps walking toward it.
At some point we have to ask the terrifying question:
Am I merely making a mistake…
or have I started protecting the sin I keep asking God to forgive?
Paul anticipated almost exactly this distortion of grace.
After explaining the astonishing abundance of God's grace, he asks in Romans 6:1:
“Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; ἐπιμένωμεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσῃ;”
In plain English:
“What then shall we say? Should we continue in sin so that grace may increase?”
The crucial word is ἐπιμένωμεν — epimenōmen, from epimenō.
It carries the idea of remaining, continuing, persisting.
Paul is not asking whether a Christian will ever stumble again.
He is confronting the idea of continuing in sin because grace is available.
And his answer is explosive:
“μὴ γένοιτο.”
Absolutely not.
May it never be.
Then Paul asks how those who died to sin can still live in it (Romans 6:2). The Greek text itself makes the contrast unmistakable: grace is not Paul's permission slip for remaining under sin's rule.
Grace is not God's way of saying sin does not matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin mattered enough that Christ bled.
Grace is God's astonishing answer to sin.
And that means grace does not merely say,
“You are forgiven.”
Grace begins teaching the forgiven sinner,
“You don't have to remain who you were.”
That distinction changes everything.
Because someone reading this has probably been fighting the same battle for years.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe lust.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe drunkenness.
Maybe gossip.
Maybe dishonesty.
Maybe rage behind closed doors.
Maybe greed dressed up as ambition.
Maybe pride disguised as discernment.
Maybe jealousy you would never admit publicly.
Maybe you keep returning to someone you know is pulling your heart away from Christ.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your church friends don't know.
Your family doesn't know.
Your spouse doesn't know.
Your followers certainly don't know.
Your Sunday face looks fine.
But God has seen every midnight.
Every deleted message.
Every secret search.
Every rationalization.
Every “last time.”
Every promise.
Every relapse.
Every tear.
And here is where this message could become cruel if we stopped too soon.
Because conviction without the Gospel would leave us staring at our filth.
But Jesus does not expose darkness merely to humiliate people.
He brings darkness into the light so captives can become free.
Listen carefully to the balance Scripture gives us.
John writes:
“My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin.”
Then immediately:
“καὶ ἐάν τις ἁμάρτῃ, παράκλητον ἔχομεν πρὸς τὸν πατέρα Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν δίκαιον.”
“But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.” (1 John 2:1)
Do you see it?
That single verse destroys two lies at once.
The first lie says:
“Sin doesn't matter because grace exists.”
John says no.
“I write… so that you may not sin.”
The second lie says:
“You sinned again. God must be finished with you.”
John says no again.
“If anyone does sin, we have an Advocate.”
Jesus Christ the righteous.
This is Christianity.
Not permission.
Not perfectionism.
Not pretending.
Christ.
The goal is holiness.
The reality is that believers can still fall.
And the hope of the fallen believer is not his flawless performance.
His hope is Jesus Christ.
That means your failure does not have to become your identity.
But neither should grace become your alibi.
There is a devastating difference between struggling against sin and surrendering to it.
A struggling believer may fall repeatedly and hate that he keeps falling.
He confesses.
He seeks help.
He cuts off access.
He gets back up.
He cries.
He prays.
He asks trusted believers to walk with him.
Sometimes his progress feels painfully slow.
But somewhere inside him there is still war.
The person making peace with sin begins doing something different.
He stops fighting and starts defending.
“It isn't really hurting anybody.”
“God knows my heart.”
“Nobody is perfect.”
“Everybody does it.”
“I can repent later.”
“Jesus forgives.”
And suddenly grace—the very grace purchased at immeasurable cost—has been turned into camouflage for rebellion.
Please hear this without running into the opposite ditch.
Repeated failure does not automatically prove that your repentance is fake.
Some battles are long.
Some habits have roots that reach deep into wounds, patterns, environments, relationships, and years of practiced behavior.
Sanctification is real, but Christians do not mature at identical speeds.
The answer to repeated failure is therefore not hopelessness.
It is deeper surrender.
Bring the sin into the light.
Confess it to God.
Stop romanticizing it.
Stop renaming it.
Stop protecting the doorway through which it keeps entering.
Seek wise Christian accountability.
Remove access where necessary.
Repair what your sin has damaged where possible.
Run toward Christ instead of hiding from Him.
Because repentance is more than feeling horrible after sin.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a changed mind and turning that produces a changed direction.
Repentance does not mean you will never stumble again.
It means you can no longer comfortably call darkness home.
Think about Peter.
He did not merely make an embarrassing mistake.
He denied Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
He had walked with Christ.
He had heard His teaching.
He had seen miracles.
He had sworn loyalty.
And when pressure came, Peter collapsed.
Imagine the moment the rooster crowed.
Imagine realizing that the warning you thought you were strong enough to overcome had just become reality.
Luke tells us Peter went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).
That could have been the final chapter.
Failure.
Coward.
Hypocrite.
Finished.
But Jesus was not finished writing Peter's story.
After the resurrection, Christ met the disciple who had denied Him.
Jesus restored him.
“Feed my sheep.”
Peter's scandal was real.
His failure was real.
His tears were real.
But so was grace.
And grace did not restore Peter so Peter could return comfortably to denying Jesus.
Grace restored Peter so he could follow Jesus.
That is the part we sometimes miss.
Restoration has a direction.
Jesus does not rescue us so we can lovingly carry our chains back into the prison.
He calls us out.
And maybe that is why this hurts.
Because perhaps the Holy Spirit has already put something in your mind while you have been reading.
You know what it is.
You didn't need me to name it.
The relationship.
The website.
The substance.
The resentment.
The secret conversation.
The dishonest money.
The hidden appetite.
The unforgiveness.
The private compromise.
The habit you keep calling “a mistake” even though you have been planning when you will do it again.
Be honest.
Not with Facebook.
Not with me.
With God.
What are you asking Jesus to forgive that you are still arranging your life to repeat?
That question is uncomfortable.
But perhaps uncomfortable is exactly where healing begins.
There is no Gospel in pretending you never sinned.
There is also no Gospel in deciding sin owns you forever.
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He lived the righteousness we could not produce.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin's judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is not offered because you finally became impressive enough for God.
Forgiveness is offered through Christ.
So stop trying to clean yourself enough to approach Him.
Come.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
And when you fall, do not run away from the only One who can restore you.
Run toward Him.
But don't crawl toward Jesus asking Him to forgive the chain while your other hand refuses to let it go.
Open your hand.
Even if it shakes.
This is where scandal meets grace.
This is where the person you became collides with the Savior who already knows what you did.
This is where Satan whispers, “You're finished,” while the Gospel declares that Christ still saves sinners.
This is where shame says, “Hide.”
Jesus says, “Come.”
Sin says, “One more time.”
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
And maybe today you need to stop saying, “Everybody makes mistakes.”
Maybe today the prayer becomes:
“Jesus, I have sinned.
I don't want to defend it anymore.
I don't want to hide it anymore.
I don't want to use Your grace as permission to remain unchanged.
Have mercy on me.
Forgive me.
Change me.
Teach me to hate what is destroying me and love what draws me closer to You.
When I fall, bring me back.
When I am tempted, give me strength.
When I begin making excuses, expose them.
I belong to You.
Jesus, rewrite everything.”
Be honest.
You do not have to publish the details of private sin. God does not require public oversharing to prove repentance. But sometimes three honest words can become the moment someone stops pretending.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, don't weaponize this article against them.
Love them.
Pray for them.
Not because you expect to fail, but because temptation has a way of making us forget what we knew clearly yesterday.
Come back when “just once more” begins sounding reasonable.
Come back when shame tells you not to pray.
Come back when you need to remember:
Grace is not permission to remain in chains.
Grace opens the prison door.
It does not.
It cannot.
And not because somebody who truly loves God must prove that love by paying us.
The Gospel cannot be bought.

But voluntary financial support can help Gospel-centered work continue, reach more people, develop more resources, and put biblical encouragement in front of people who may never walk voluntarily through a church door.
Give freely, prayerfully, and never from manipulation or guilt. As Paul teaches concerning Christian generosity, giving is not to be done reluctantly or under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Jesus Christ is still the message.
His Gospel is still the hope.
Repentance is still necessary.
Grace is still astonishing.
Forgiveness is still available.
The cross is still enough.
The tomb is still empty.
So share if it may reach somebody.
Follow if you want to keep walking through Scripture with us.
But above everything else…
follow Jesus.
Because the most dangerous thing about repeated sin is not that you made another mistake.
It is that, little by little, you may stop calling darkness darkness.
And the most beautiful thing about grace is not that Jesus gives you permission to keep returning to the grave.
It is that the risen Christ calls you out of it.
You may have returned to the same sin a hundred times—but today does not have to become one hundred and one.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: BEFORE HE COULD TOUCH HER, GOD MADE HIM WAIT
paragraphs: BEFORE HE COULD TOUCH HER, GOD MADE HIM WAIT

A captive woman had lost her home, perhaps her family, and almost everything familiar to her. Then, in a brutal world where victorious men possessed extraordinary power over defeated women, God put something between a soldier’s desire and this grieving captive: time. Deuteronomy 21:10–14 is uncomfortable. It should be. But hidden inside this difficult law is a truth about the character of God that becomes breathtaking when we finally see where the whole biblical story is going.
Imagine her.
Not as a theological problem.
Not as a verse you are trying to defend.
As a woman.
The battle is over.
Smoke hangs over what used to be home.
The voices she knew are disappearing behind her.
She does not know what tomorrow looks like.
She does not know whether the people she loves are alive.
She does not know whether she will ever see her homeland again.
And now she is a captive.
Then an Israelite soldier sees her.
Scripture does not romanticize what happens next.
It says:
"וְרָאִיתָ בַּשִּׁבְיָה אֵשֶׁת יְפַת־תֹּאַר וְחָשַׁקְתָּ בָהּ"
Vera'ita bashivyah eshet yefat-to'ar, vechashaqta vah...

“You see among the captives a beautiful woman, and you desire her...”
—Deuteronomy 21:11
That Hebrew word is important.
וְחָשַׁקְתָּ — vechashaqta.
You desire her.
The text begins with the desire of the powerful man.
But then something happens.
He does not simply get everything his desire wants immediately.
God interrupts him.
The woman is brought into the household, and the text describes her tending to her hair and nails, removing the clothing of her captivity, remaining in the house...
and grieving.
Listen to the Hebrew:
"וּבָכְתָה אֶת־אָבִיהָ וְאֶת־אִמָּהּ יֶרַח יָמִים"
Uvakhtah et-aviha ve'et-immah yerach yamim.
“And she shall weep for her father and her mother a month of days.”
A month.
Thirty days, approximately, depending upon the lunar month.
Before the relationship described by the law could proceed, her grief occupied the house.
Think about that.
The victorious soldier had power.
He had desire.
He had opportunity.
But desire was not allowed to erase mourning.
For an entire month, this woman’s tears became part of his world.
He would know she was crying.
He would know she had a father.
He would know she had a mother.
He would know that the woman he found beautiful was also somebody’s daughter.
That matters.
And yet we must be careful here.
We should not turn Deuteronomy 21 into something sentimental that it is not.
This woman was still a captive.
There was an enormous imbalance of power.
The passage does not describe modern courtship between two free people meeting on equal terms, and Christians should not pretend otherwise.
Nor should we use this passage to justify sexual coercion, wartime abuse, trafficking, forced marriage, or the exploitation of vulnerable women.
The law addresses an ancient wartime reality and places restrictions upon the victorious Israelite man within that reality.
The text makes him wait.
The text acknowledges her mourning.
The text moves the relationship into the category of wife rather than disposable sexual property.
And the following verse adds another startling restriction.
If the man later ceases to want her, Scripture says:
Veshillachtah lenafshah.
He must let her go free.
Then comes the prohibition:
"וּמָכֹר לֹא־תִמְכְּרֶנָּה בַּכָּסֶף"
Umachor lo-timkerennah bakasef.
“You shall certainly not sell her for money.”
He could not decide:
I don't want her anymore, so perhaps I can make money from her.
No.
She was not merchandise.
She could not simply be converted into cash.
The man who once saw a beautiful captive was being forced to confront something lust and power constantly try to forget:
she was a human being.
And suddenly this ancient passage becomes painfully modern.
Because we still live in a world that sees people before it knows people.
We see a beautiful body before we see a wounded soul.
We see somebody’s usefulness before we see their humanity.
We swipe.
Scroll.
Desire.
Consume.
Discard.
Sometimes we do it sexually.
Sometimes emotionally.
Sometimes financially.
Sometimes even spiritually.
We can become so accustomed to asking, “What can this person give me?” that we forget to ask, “What has this person survived?”
Maybe that is where this passage finds you.
Because perhaps you have been the person who desired without understanding.
Or perhaps...
you have been the person nobody bothered to understand.
Maybe somebody loved your appearance but never learned your pain.
Maybe somebody wanted your body but had no interest in your tears.
Maybe somebody enjoyed what you could provide until providing became difficult.
Maybe somebody promised permanence and treated you as disposable.
Maybe you were abandoned when you were no longer convenient.
And somewhere inside you there is still a person mourning what was taken.
A childhood.
A marriage.
A parent.
A relationship.
Trust.
Safety.
Innocence.
Years you cannot recover.
Perhaps everyone around you thinks you should have moved on by now.
But God knows grief cannot always be commanded to disappear.
There is something astonishing about those words:
"וּבָכְתָה... יֶרַח יָמִים"
She shall weep... a month of days.
Scripture makes room for tears.
Not because thirty days magically cures grief.
It doesn't.
But because biblical faith is not built upon pretending pain never happened.
God repeatedly encounters people in Scripture inside their sorrow.
Hagar cries in the wilderness.
Hannah weeps before the Lord.
David drenches his bed with tears.
Jeremiah becomes known as the weeping prophet.
Jesus Himself stands before Lazarus' tomb and weeps.
The shortest verse many Christians memorized as children contains one of Christianity's deepest revelations:
“Jesus wept.”
The Son of God did not consider tears beneath holiness.
And that changes the way we read this captive woman's month.
Her grief was not an inconvenience to be edited out of the story.
She was allowed to mourn.
Somebody reading this needs permission to hear that.
You can love Jesus and still cry.
You can trust God and still miss somebody.
You can believe in resurrection and still ache beside a grave.
You can forgive and still need healing.
You can worship while carrying questions you cannot answer.
Faith is not the absence of grief.
Sometimes faith is bringing your grief into the presence of God instead of allowing grief to drive you away from Him.
But there is an even deeper confrontation waiting inside this passage.
The law restrains what a powerful person may do to someone vulnerable.
That pattern matters profoundly for followers of Jesus.
Because the Gospel does not teach us to ask how much power we are permitted to exercise over another person.
Jesus teaches us what love does with power.
Look at Christ.
The One possessing all authority does not exploit the weak.
He receives them.
He touches lepers others avoided.
He welcomes children others considered interruptions.
He speaks publicly with women others dismissed.
He eats with sinners religious society despised.
He sees the overlooked.
He restores the disgraced.
He defends the vulnerable.
And then the One with all authority does something almost incomprehensible.
He kneels.
He washes feet.
Then He goes to a cross.
The Gospel turns the world's understanding of power upside down.
Human sin says:
I have power, therefore I can take.
Jesus says:
I have power, therefore I can serve.
Human lust says:
I desire you, therefore you owe me.
Christlike love says:
I love you, therefore I seek your good.
Human cruelty says:
You are no longer useful, therefore you are disposable.
The Gospel announces:
You bear the image of God, therefore you possess a dignity your usefulness never created and your weakness cannot erase.
This is why Christianity can never use Deuteronomy 21 to excuse abuse.
The Bible's story is moving somewhere.
Toward Jesus Christ.
Toward the King who refuses to treat broken people like conquered property.
Toward the Bridegroom who gives Himself for His bride.
Toward the Savior who does not purchase us in order to exploit us but gives His own blood to redeem us from slavery to sin.
And there is an uncomfortable question waiting for every one of us.
Have you been treating people as people...
or as things?
Your spouse.
Your boyfriend.
Your girlfriend.
Your employees.
Your children.
Your parents.
The attractive stranger on your screen.
The person whose body became entertainment.
The person whose weakness became gossip.
The person whose scandal became content.
The person you stopped calling when they stopped benefiting you.
Christianity is not merely about avoiding obvious cruelty.
Jesus goes after the heart.
The same human heart capable of turning another person into an object is the heart Christ came to transform.
And that means this story cannot end with us pointing at an ancient soldier.
Eventually the finger turns around.
Toward us.
What has your desire made you justify?
What has your anger made you dehumanize?
Who became disposable when they disappointed you?
Whose tears did you ignore because their pain interrupted what you wanted?
Those are difficult questions.
But grace does not become beautiful until sin becomes honest.
The Gospel does not say, “Pretend you never sinned.”
The Gospel says:
Repent.
Turn around.
Bring the ugliness into the light.
Because Jesus Christ did not die for the imaginary version of you who never failed.
He died for sinners.
That is the scandal.
And that is the grace.
At the cross, humanity did the unthinkable.
We rejected the Holy One.
Mocked the innocent One.
Stripped Him.
Humiliated Him.
Nailed Him to wood.
And Jesus answered human sin with an offer of mercy.
Not cheap mercy.
Blood-bought mercy.
The cross does not tell us sin does not matter.
The cross tells us sin mattered enough that redemption cost Christ His life.
And resurrection tells us sin does not get the final sentence.
That is why your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
The adulterer can repent.
The porn addict can repent.
The abusive person can repent and must stop abusing.
The bitter person can repent.
The manipulator can repent.
The person drowning in shame can come home.
The wounded can begin healing.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The captive can become free.
Not because evil suddenly becomes acceptable.
Because Jesus Christ rewrites human lives through repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and transforming grace.
Maybe this article exposed something you have kept hidden.
Don't perform spirituality here.
Be honest.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the light.
That is what Christian community should do.
Not celebrate sin.
Not weaponize shame.
Lead one another toward Jesus.
Send this privately to someone who has been treated as disposable.
Grace cannot be purchased.
But voluntary generosity can glorify God when it flows from a willing heart and is used faithfully for Gospel work.
Pray.
Tell another wounded person where you found encouragement.
Because somewhere tonight there may be another person sitting alone with a phone glowing in a dark room, believing the lie that what happened to them made them worthless.
Maybe your tag interrupts the worst night of their year.
And maybe a difficult law about an unnamed captive woman becomes the doorway through which they encounter something they desperately needed to remember:
God sees human beings where sinful people see objects.
God hears mourning others find inconvenient.
And Jesus receives sinners whom shame tells to stay away.
That woman in Deuteronomy 21 is never given a name.
We don't know what her voice sounded like.
We don't know what memories made her cry hardest during that month.
We don't know what happened every night when the house became quiet and memories returned.
But Scripture did not erase her tears.
Thousands of years later...
we are still reading about them.
Perhaps that is the line you need to carry with you tonight.

What the world tried to reduce to someone's possession, Scripture still forces us to remember as someone's daughter—and what sin has tried to reduce to your worst chapter, Jesus can still redeem into a testimony of grace.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the grief.
Bring Him the hidden thing.
Bring Him the years you wish you could recover.
Bring Him the sin you cannot excuse.
Bring Him the wound you cannot erase.
Come honestly.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive as Christ teaches you to forgive.
Seek safety where abuse exists.
Make restitution where you have harmed others.
Receive mercy where shame has convinced you mercy is impossible.
And keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because the deepest message of Scripture is not that human beings never make ruins of things.
We do.
The message is that ruins do not frighten the Redeemer.
Your tears may belong to a chapter you never would have chosen—but they do not get to write the last sentence when the pen is surrendered to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HOSEA EXPOSED THE MEN TOO: While Their Daughters Bore the Shame, God Revealed What the Fathers Were Doing in Secret
paragraphs: HOSEA EXPOSED THE MEN TOO: While Their Daughters Bore the Shame, God Revealed What the Fathers Were Doing in Secret

Hosea 4:13–14 is not merely a warning about sexual sin. It is a terrifying exposure of religious hypocrisy—and a reminder that before we condemn the scandal in somebody else’s life, God may first uncover the altar we have hidden in our own.
There is something almost unbearable about Hosea 4.
Not because the Bible mentions prostitution.
Not because it talks openly about adultery.
Not even because an entire nation had become spiritually unfaithful.
What makes the passage so uncomfortable is where God turns the light.
Toward the men.
Toward the people who could have looked at the younger generation and shaken their heads.
Toward people who could see sexual corruption spreading through their families while somehow failing to recognize their own participation in the darkness.
And suddenly Hosea stops sounding like an ancient prophet shouting at ancient Israel.
He sounds frighteningly close.
Because human beings have always been remarkably skilled at being disgusted by sins that look uglier on somebody else.
We can condemn publicly what we entertain privately.
We can grieve over what our children are becoming while refusing to examine what they learned from the world we helped create.
We can speak about morality while secretly negotiating with temptation.
We can worship on Sunday and feed an addiction on Monday.
We can quote Scripture while hiding messages.
Preach purity while nurturing fantasy.
Demand repentance while refusing to repent.
And then God speaks.

Hosea 4:13 describes Israel sacrificing on mountaintops and burning offerings beneath trees. This is not merely a story about sexual misconduct. The chapter is describing covenant unfaithfulness, idolatry, corrupted worship, and a people abandoning the knowledge of God.
Then come the devastating words:
“Therefore your daughters play the whore, and your brides commit adultery.”
But God does not stop there.
The next verse changes the direction of the accusation.
The Hebrew says:
לֹא־אֶפְקוֹד עַל־בְּנוֹתֵיכֶם כִּי תִזְנֶינָה וְעַל־כַּלּוֹתֵיכֶם כִּי תְנָאַפְנָה כִּי־הֵם עִם־הַזֹּנוֹת יְפָרֵדוּ וְעִם־הַקְּדֵשׁוֹת יְזַבֵּחוּ וְעָם לֹא־יָבִין יִלָּבֵט
In context, the force of the verse is devastating:

God says He will not single out the daughters for their prostitution or the daughters-in-law for adultery, because the men themselves are going aside with prostitutes and sacrificing with women associated with the corrupted worship.
Read that again.
The women were not being presented as the only problem.
The men themselves were involved.

Different English translations describe the women in the latter part of verse 14 as “cult prostitutes,” “shrine prostitutes,” “temple women,” or “ritual harlot.” We should be careful not to pretend every historical detail is beyond scholarly discussion.
But Hosea’s central accusation is not difficult to see.
The men were participants in the corruption they could so easily have blamed on the women.
And that is where this ancient passage walks through the front door of the modern church.
Imagine a father discovering sexual content on his daughter’s phone...
while pornography sits hidden behind the password on his own.
Imagine a husband raging about adultery in society...
while maintaining conversations his wife would be devastated to read.
Imagine parents horrified by the sexual confusion surrounding their children...

while those same children have spent years watching marriages without tenderness, apologies without repentance, Christianity without transformation, and church attendance without Christlike character.
Imagine condemning the generation beneath us for wandering...
while refusing to ask who showed them the road.
That does not remove anyone’s personal responsibility before God.
Children are responsible for their choices.
Parents are responsible for theirs.
Women are responsible for theirs.
Men are responsible for theirs.
Hosea is not exchanging one form of partiality for another.
God does not excuse sexual sin.
He exposes hypocrisy.
And there is a difference.
The frightening thing about hypocrisy is that eventually you become better at seeing everyone else than seeing yourself.
Jesus confronted exactly that instinct centuries later.
Why notice the speck in another person’s eye while ignoring the log in your own?
That question is devastating because the hypocrite is not necessarily blind to sin.
Sometimes he sees sin extremely well.
Just selectively.
He can identify it across the room.
In another denomination.
In another political tribe.
In another family.
In another generation.
In another gender.
In his spouse.
In his children.
But somehow the flashlight never turns around.
Hosea turns it around.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to stop here.
Not because you need another theological argument.
Because there is something you already know.
A browser history.
A relationship.
A conversation.
A habit.
A second account.
A secret meeting.
A fantasy you keep feeding.
A compromise you keep renaming.
Something you promised God would happen “only once.”
Something you have confessed repeatedly without actually fleeing from it.
Something you desperately hope nobody discovers.
Maybe everybody thinks you are strong.
Maybe your children think you are strong.
Maybe your spouse thinks you are strong.
Maybe people at church ask you for prayer.
And somewhere behind the public version of you is another person fighting desperately to remain undiscovered.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not require you to remain undiscovered.
It invites you to become forgiven.
There is an enormous difference.
Satan says, “Hide it.”
Jesus says, “Come into the light.”
Shame says, “If they knew everything, you would be finished.”
Grace says, “Christ already knew everything when He went to the cross.”
Religion teaches people how to manage appearances.
Jesus raises dead people.
This is why Hosea cannot ultimately be reduced to a sensational story about sex.
The deepest prostitution in Hosea is spiritual.
Israel belonged to Yahweh and chased other gods.
The bedroom scandal exposed an altar scandal.
Their bodies revealed what had already happened in their hearts.
They had exchanged faithfulness for idols.
And before modern Christians distance ourselves from them, we should remember that idols no longer require carved statues.
Anything can become an altar when we give it what belongs to God.
Sex can.
Money can.
Success can.
Attention can.
Pornography can.
Approval can.
A career can.
A relationship can.
A ministry can.
Even religious reputation can.
You can spend your entire life protecting the appearance of being a Christian while slowly losing intimacy with Christ.
That may be the most frightening scandal of all.
Not that someone falls publicly.
But that someone can decay privately while appearing spiritually alive.
You can know worship songs and not worship.
Know Bible verses and not obey.
Know Christian vocabulary and not know surrender.
Know how to say “God bless you” while your secret life is destroying you.
And Hosea refuses to let us hide behind somebody else’s scandal.
Your daughter’s sin cannot repent for yours.
Your husband’s failure cannot justify yours.
Your wife’s failure cannot excuse yours.
Your pastor’s hypocrisy cannot cleanse yours.
The corruption of society cannot become camouflage for the corruption of your heart.
Eventually every one of us stands before God without another sinner available to use as a shield.
Just us.
And Him.
That sounds terrifying.
Until you remember who stands between guilty sinners and holy judgment.
Jesus Christ.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Because Christianity does not announce that good people can repair themselves.
It announces that guilty people can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
The cross destroys both pride and despair.
Pride cannot survive there because our sin was serious enough that the Son of God had to die.
Despair cannot have the final word there because His sacrifice was sufficient to save sinners who come to Him.
At Calvary, nobody gets to boast.
And nobody who truly comes to Christ needs to believe his scandal is stronger than Christ’s grace.
Jesus did not shed His blood only for respectable sins.
He died for adulterers.
Liars.
The sexually broken.
The religious hypocrite.
The ashamed.
The addicted.
The person who has spent years pretending.
The father who failed.
The mother who wandered.
The son who rebelled.
The daughter carrying a history she wishes she could erase.
The churchgoer whose public Christianity and private life have become almost unrecognizable from each other.
But grace is not permission to keep hiding.
Grace calls us out.
Repentance is not saying, “I feel terrible.”
Repentance turns.
It stops negotiating.
It stops blaming.
It stops saying, “Everybody does it.”
It stops asking how close to darkness we can walk while still calling ourselves children of light.
Sometimes repentance means deleting something.
Ending something.
Confessing something.
Returning something.
Seeking accountability.
Asking forgiveness.
Accepting consequences.
Getting away from the environment feeding the sin.
And sometimes the most spiritual sentence a person can finally say is:
“I have been blaming everyone except myself.”
Maybe that is why Hosea 4:14 hurts.
God will not permit us to build moral platforms on top of secret altars.
Imagine what could happen in families if fathers stopped merely demanding purity and started modeling repentance.
Imagine a father looking his children in the eyes and saying:
“I have failed too. I need Jesus too. I have sinned. I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
Imagine mothers who do not need to maintain the illusion of perfection.
Imagine husbands confessing before being caught.
Imagine wives choosing truth before secrecy hardens into bondage.
Imagine churches where testimony is not merely a performance about what God delivered us from twenty years ago, but where believers can say:
“I need prayer today.”
Imagine Christians who become known not because they never fail, but because when they fail they run toward Christ instead of deeper into darkness.
That kind of Christianity would confuse a world built on image management.
Because the Gospel gives us something the world cannot manufacture:
the freedom to tell the truth about ourselves because our hope is no longer ourselves.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Then stop running.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
You do not need to clean yourself enough to approach Jesus.
You approach Jesus because you cannot cleanse yourself.
Confess your sin to God.
Turn from it.
Trust Christ.
Where appropriate and safe, seek mature Christian accountability and make right what your sin has damaged.
There may still be consequences.
Grace does not magically erase every earthly consequence of our choices.
But consequences are not the same thing as condemnation.
For those who belong to Christ, shame no longer gets to write the final chapter.
Jesus does.
That is the heartbeat behind Gospel Warrior:
Not because scandal is entertaining.
Because grace is astonishing.
We are not building a community of people pretending they have never fallen.
We want a community of people continually being brought back to Jesus—back to Scripture, repentance, forgiveness, holiness, healing, discipleship, and the transforming truth of the Gospel.
Not performative.
Not religious.
Honest.
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only person fighting.
Someone may finally confess.
Someone may finally pray.
Someone may finally come home.
Not because an algorithm needs another post.
Because somebody in your circle may be smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
There may come a night when temptation returns and you need to remember:
being exposed by God can become the beginning of being restored by God.
It does not.
Not because anyone should pressure you into giving.
Scripture teaches that Christian generosity should come from a willing heart, not compulsion.
But voluntary, regular generosity can absolutely become one practical way of supporting Gospel work you believe is bearing fruit.
And even if you cannot financially support Gospel Warrior, you can still help.
Pray.
Share.
Save the message.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that perfect people found God.
It is the announcement that while sinners were lost, God came looking for them.
Hosea exposed a nation whose worship had become corrupted and whose private compromises were producing public devastation.
And perhaps that is the question left hanging over us now:
What are we condemning in the next generation while quietly feeding its roots in ourselves?
Fathers, come home.
Mothers, come home.
Husbands, come home.
Wives, come home.
Sons and daughters, come home.
Pastors, leaders, wounded believers, secret strugglers...
come home.
Not to religion.
Not to appearances.
Not to another mask.
To Jesus.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the adultery.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the hypocrisy.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the person you became while everybody thought you were okay.
Repent.
Believe.
Step into the light.
And discover that the hands capable of exposing your sin are also the hands that were pierced to save sinners.
The secret you thought would become the final sentence of your story may become the very place where Jesus begins writing redemption.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “LET HER BREASTS SATISFY YOU”: Why Would God Put a Sentence Like This in Scripture?
paragraphs: “LET HER BREASTS SATISFY YOU”: Why Would God Put a Sentence Like This in Scripture?
We have spent generations whispering about something the Bible was never embarrassed to say out loud—and Proverbs 5:19 may expose far more than our discomfort with sex.
There are verses people frame and hang on walls.
There are verses printed on coffee mugs.
There are verses whispered beside hospital beds, preached at funerals, written inside wedding cards, and highlighted until the paper nearly tears.
And then there is Proverbs 5:19.
“Let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
Yes.
That is in the Bible.
Not in an ancient piece of erotic literature somebody accidentally slipped between Ecclesiastes and Isaiah.
Not in some modern paraphrase trying to make Scripture provocative.
It is Proverbs.
Wisdom literature.
Holy Scripture.
And perhaps the question is not, “Why would God allow something like that in His Word?”
Perhaps the more uncomfortable question is...
Why does it embarrass us more than it apparently embarrassed God?
Stay with me, because this verse is not permission for lust.
It is almost the exact opposite.

And if you have ever struggled with pornography, adultery, wandering eyes, sexual shame, a wounded marriage, secret fantasy, loneliness, temptation, or the feeling that Christianity treats human desire as something filthy, Proverbs 5 may be far more beautiful—and far more confronting—than you were ever told.
The Hebrew does not sanitize the verse.
It says:
אַיֶּלֶת אֲהָבִים וְיַעֲלַת־חֵן דַּדֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּךָ בְכָל־עֵת בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Ayyélet ahavim veya'alat-chen, daddeha yeravvukha bekhol-et; be'ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
The language is tender, poetic—and unmistakably physical.
The woman is pictured as a loving doe, a graceful deer. Her husband is told to find satisfaction in her breasts and to remain continually captivated, even intoxicated, by her love.
The Hebrew does not apologize.
But neither does it isolate her body from covenant love.
That is where our culture—and sometimes even Christians reading this verse too quickly—can completely miss the point.
Because Proverbs 5:19 did not fall out of heaven as a random sentence about breasts.
Read what comes immediately before it.
“Drink water from your own cistern, and running water out of thine own well.”
Then:
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
And immediately after the famous verse comes the question:
“And why wilt thou, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger?”
Do you see it?
This is not God telling a man to objectify women.
This is a father warning his son not to destroy himself through sexual unfaithfulness.

The chapter begins with warnings concerning forbidden sexual relationships. It describes temptation as something that can initially seem sweet and attractive but eventually become bitter and destructive.
Then Scripture does something remarkable.
It does not merely say:
Don’t.
Don’t desire.
Don’t feel.
Don’t touch.
Don’t enjoy.
Instead, biblical wisdom redirects desire toward covenant.
Rejoice in your wife.
Delight in her.
Be captivated by her.
Remain intoxicated with her love.
In other words, God does not answer destructive desire merely by commanding the death of desire.
He teaches desire where to go.
That changes everything.
Because somewhere along the way many believers absorbed an idea the Bible itself never teaches:
That holiness means becoming almost embarrassed by the body.
Yet the first human body was not invented by pornography.
God invented it.
Sexuality was not created in a nightclub.
God created male and female.
Marriage was not invented by Hollywood.
God established covenant companionship before humanity's fall.
Sin did not create desire.
Sin distorts desire.
And there is an enormous difference.
Pornography takes something capable of covenant intimacy and removes covenant.
Lust takes a person and reduces that person to consumption.
Adultery takes desire outside the boundaries of faithfulness.
Sexual exploitation takes what should involve dignity and turns another human being into an instrument.
But Proverbs 5 paints another picture.
A husband.
A wife.
A covenant.
Exclusive affection.
Joy without betrayal.
Desire without theft.
Intimacy without strangers.
A body cherished within faithful love.
That is why verse 19 cannot honestly be separated from verse 18:
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
And it cannot be separated from verse 20:
Why become captivated by another woman?
The entire contrast is between covenant faithfulness and covenant betrayal.
And then comes a sentence that should sober anyone living a secret sexual life:
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD.”
The browser history nobody knows about.
The conversation you keep deleting.
The emotional affair you keep renaming “friendship.”
The private messages.
The second account.
The fantasies you deliberately feed.
The person at work whose attention you have begun craving.
The marriage you have emotionally abandoned while continuing to occupy the same house.
God sees.
Not because He is some cosmic voyeur waiting eagerly to humiliate you.
He sees because nothing that is destroying you is invisible to Him.
And this is where Proverbs 5 becomes painfully personal.
Maybe the scandal is not that God mentions a woman's breasts.
Maybe the scandal is that we live in a culture drowning in sexual imagery while starving for covenant intimacy.
Bodies everywhere.
Faithfulness becoming rare.
Sex everywhere.
Tenderness disappearing.
Access everywhere.
Intimacy nowhere.
People learning thousands of ways to stimulate themselves while forgetting how to give themselves faithfully to another human being.
And pornography may be one of the clearest examples.
Porn promises intimacy without vulnerability.
Pleasure without covenant.
Bodies without responsibility.
Excitement without faithfulness.
It trains the eyes to consume while Proverbs trains the heart to cherish.
Porn says:
More.
Different.
Next.
Someone else.
Proverbs says:
Rejoice in the wife of your youth.
There is something profoundly countercultural about that.
Biblical sexuality is not built around endless novelty.
It is built around faithful rediscovery.
The same covenant.
The same person.
Years passing.
Bodies changing.
Hair graying.
Scars appearing.
Children coming—or perhaps never coming.
Illness.
Arguments.
Forgiveness.
Ordinary mornings.
Difficult seasons.
And somehow...
“Rejoice.”
That may be more radical than anything our hypersexual culture has imagined.
Because lust asks:
“What can I take?”
Covenant asks:
“How can I love?”
Lust consumes bodies.
Love knows names.
Lust hides.
Covenant remains.
Lust continually needs another image.
Faithful love learns to see the same person more deeply.
And maybe someone reading this already feels the shame rising.
Because you crossed the line.
Maybe years ago.
Maybe last night.
Maybe ten minutes before you found this article.
Perhaps your marriage is wounded because of what you did.
Perhaps nobody knows.
Perhaps everybody knows.
Maybe pornography has become the secret room you enter whenever loneliness becomes unbearable.
Maybe you promised God a hundred times:
“Never again.”
And then again happened.
And again.
And again.
Eventually you stopped making promises because breaking them hurt too much.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not pretending sin does not matter.
Jesus never needed to minimize sin in order to maximize grace.
The cross proves precisely how serious sin is.
But the cross also proves something else.
Your sin does not get the final sentence if you belong to Christ.
There is repentance.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is a Savior who already knew the ugliest chapter before He called your name.
Christianity does not announce:
Clean yourself until Jesus can tolerate you.
The Gospel announces that sinners can come to Christ, repent, believe, be forgiven, and begin becoming new.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
Trust may need rebuilding.
A wounded spouse may need time.
Secret patterns may need confession, accountability, pastoral care, counseling, boundaries, and radical changes in behavior.
Repentance is more than feeling terrible after sin.
Repentance turns around.
But shame says:
Hide.
Jesus says:
Come.
Shame says:
You are what you did.
Grace says:
Christ can make you new.
Shame says:
This chapter ruined the entire story.
Then Jesus walks into stories everybody else thought were finished.
That is the Gospel Warrior message.
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Not because sin is cute.
Not because consequences are imaginary.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps that is why Proverbs 5:19 matters so much.
It reveals a God who is not embarrassed by faithful marital intimacy.
A God who created human beings as embodied creatures.
A God who condemns adultery while honoring covenant delight.
A God whose answer to sexual chaos is not shame but holiness.
Not repression, but rightly ordered love.
Not exploitation, but covenant.
Not secrecy, but truth.
Not endless consumption, but faithful delight.
And ultimately...
not merely behavior modification.
Christ.
Because you can install every filter and still have a heart that wants darkness.
You can throw away your phone and still carry lust inside you.
You can learn religious vocabulary while remaining inwardly enslaved.
We need more than restraint.
We need redemption.
We need new hearts.
We need the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Maybe this article found you while you are fighting something nobody knows about.
Then stop pretending with God.
He already knows.
Bring it into the light.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need to confess, confess wisely.
If you need accountability, seek it.
If you have wounded your spouse, stop defending yourself and begin rebuilding truthfully.

If your marriage has become emotionally cold, do not use Proverbs 5:19 as a demand for sex. The verse is not a weapon for coercing a spouse. Biblical marital intimacy belongs inside love, honor, mutual care, faithfulness, and dignity.
Your spouse is not an entitlement.
Your spouse is a person to love.
And if you are unmarried, this passage is not telling you that you are incomplete.
Christ is not a consolation prize until marriage arrives.
The deepest identity of a Christian is not husband, wife, boyfriend, girlfriend, virgin, divorced, widowed, betrayed, or sexually broken.
It is found in Christ.
Maybe you have spent years believing your sexual past disqualified you from being deeply loved by God.
It does not.
Repentance does not rewrite history.
Jesus redeems sinners within history.
The scars may remain.
But scars are not always evidence that the story ended badly.
Sometimes scars prove the wound did not kill you.
Look at the risen Christ.
Even resurrection did not erase every scar.
And maybe somebody you know desperately needs to hear that.
Send this privately to the friend drowning in pornography.
Send it to the believer carrying sexual shame.
Send it to the marriage trying to rebuild after betrayal.
Because temptation has a strange ability to make us forget in the moment what we knew clearly yesterday.
If this exposed something hidden, you do not need to write the details publicly.

And if Christ has already brought you out of sexual bondage, shame, adultery, pornography, or a broken season, consider leaving a testimony—not to glorify the darkness you escaped, but to tell somebody still trapped inside it that chains really can break.
No performance.
No pretending.
Just truth.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, grow deeper in Christ, confront sin, understand grace, and walk more faithfully with Jesus, stay close.
But hear this clearly:
It does not replace obedience to Christ.
It does not buy blessing.
Scripture says Christian generosity should come from the heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
And sometimes supporting Gospel work is not only financial.
Leave thinking about faithfulness.
About what your eyes belong to.
About what your heart has been feeding.
About the person you promised to love.
About the secrets you need to bring into the light.
About the grace you thought you had exhausted.
About the Savior who still receives repentant sinners.
Because one day the secret tab closes.
The fantasy ends.
The body ages.
The applause disappears.
The temptation that once seemed irresistible becomes dust.
And what remains is the question beneath Proverbs 5 all along:
What kind of person are you becoming when nobody else is watching?
God is not embarrassed by holy desire.
He wants to rescue desire from everything that turns love into consumption and people into objects.
And perhaps tonight, the most intimate thing you can do is not touch another body.
Perhaps it is finally to stop hiding your soul.
Come into the light.
Come back to covenant.
Come back to truth.
Come back to Jesus.
Because the chapter you are most ashamed of may become the place where someone else finally discovers what grace actually means.
The sin that told you to hide may become the scar through which somebody else finally sees the light of Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ROMANS 1 ALSO DESCRIBES MEN BURNING WITH PASSION FOR OTHER MEN—Why Is This Passage So Debated?
paragraphs: ROMANS 1 ALSO DESCRIBES MEN BURNING WITH PASSION FOR OTHER MEN—Why Is This Passage So Debated?

Romans 1:27 says something our generation keeps arguing about. But before you use this verse against someone else, you need to hear what Paul says next—because Romans 1 was never written to give religious people permission to stand above sinners. It was written to bring the whole human race to its knees before the mercy of Jesus Christ.
There are Bible verses people whisper about.
Verses people weaponize.
Verses people avoid because they are afraid of what their friends will think if they believe them.
And then there are verses like Romans 1:27.
Read at a distance, it can become ammunition.
Read carelessly, it can become cruelty.
Ignored completely, it can become another place where Christians quietly decide that modern culture has greater authority than Scripture.
But read in context—slowly, humbly, with Romans 2 and Romans 3 still waiting ahead of us—it becomes something much more unsettling.
Because Paul is not merely talking about them.
Eventually, Paul is coming for all of us.
And that changes everything.
The New Testament was written in Greek, not English, so before debating what Romans 1:27 means, we should at least listen to some of the language Paul actually used:
“οἱ ἄρσενες… ἐξεκαύθησαν ἐν τῇ ὀρέξει αὐτῶν εἰς ἀλλήλους, ἄρσενες ἐν ἄρσεσιν…”
hoi arsenes… exekauthēsan en tē orexei autōn eis allēlous, arsenes en arsenesin…

The language describes males abandoning sexual relations with females and becoming inflamed in desire toward one another—“males with males.” That basic observation is not created by an English translation; it is present in the Greek itself.
One word is especially vivid.
ἐξεκαύθησαν — exekauthēsan.
It carries the imagery of being kindled, inflamed, burning.
And Paul says the desire is εἰς ἀλλήλους — eis allēlous: toward one another.
Then comes the striking expression ἄρσενες ἐν ἄρσεσιν — arsenes en arsenesin: males with males.
So we should not pretend Romans 1:27 says nothing about male same-sex sexual behavior.
It does.

That does not settle every modern question about sexual orientation, psychology, pastoral care, temptation, identity, civil law, or how Christians should speak to LGBTQ people. Paul was writing in the first-century Greco-Roman world, not answering a twenty-first-century questionnaire about every dimension of sexuality.
But neither should historical distance become an excuse for making Paul's actual words disappear.
This is one reason the passage remains so fiercely debated.

Some interpreters have argued that Paul's condemnation should be understood more narrowly against particular ancient practices or cultural circumstances. Others understand Romans 1:26–27 as a general rejection of same-sex sexual relations within Paul's larger Jewish-Christian sexual ethic. The debate involves questions about ancient sexuality, Paul's use of “nature,” the relationship between desire and conduct, and how Paul's argument should be applied today.
Yet whatever disagreements surround its application, the Greek of verse 27 explicitly depicts males desiring other males and engaging in sexual behavior with males.
But now comes the part that is often missed.
Romans 1 did not begin with homosexuality.
It began with worship.
That changes the entire conversation.
Paul's deeper diagnosis appears in Romans 1:25: humanity exchanged God's truth for a lie and worshiped and served created things rather than the Creator.
Before Paul talks about disordered sexuality, he talks about disordered worship.
Before he describes what human beings do with their bodies, he describes what human beings have done with God.
That means the deepest crisis in Romans 1 is not simply, “Some people experience sinful sexual desires.”
The deeper tragedy is:
The creature has taken the Creator's throne.
And suddenly this chapter becomes dangerously personal.
Because you may never have desired another person of the same sex…
but you can worship money.
You can worship approval.
You can worship your reputation.
You can worship your career.
You can worship romance.
You can worship political power.
You can worship pornography.
You can worship your body.
You can worship your church position.
You can even worship the image of yourself as the person who is morally superior to everybody mentioned in Romans 1.
Anything created can become an idol when it occupies the place belonging to the Creator.
And that is why Romans 1 is much bigger than one sexual controversy.
Keep reading.
Paul's catalogue expands into greed, envy, murder, strife, deceit, malice, gossip, slander, arrogance, boastfulness, disobedience to parents, faithlessness and mercilessness.
That list should make the smug Christian uncomfortable.
Imagine holding Romans 1:27 like a spotlight pointed at somebody else's bedroom while quietly stepping over Romans 1:29–31 as though those verses belonged to somebody else.
Paul will not permit it.
And then Romans 2 begins.
This may be one of the most important chapter turns in the entire conversation.
The person listening to Paul's indictment might have been nodding.
“Yes.”
“Exactly.”
“Look how sinful those people are.”
And then Paul turns toward the person doing the judging.
The trap closes.
The moral spectator discovers that he, too, is standing in the courtroom.
And by Romans 3 the verdict becomes universal:
All have sinned.
Nobody gets to swagger toward the cross.
Nobody arrives carrying a résumé.
Nobody walks into Calvary saying, “Jesus, You are fortunate to have me.”
We crawl there empty-handed.
Gay or straight.
Religious or rebellious.
Church-raised or completely lost.
Sexually broken or secretly proud.
Addicted.
Greedy.
Self-righteous.
Bitter.
Lustful.
Jealous.
Dishonest.
Ashamed.
Every one of us needs mercy.
That does not mean every sin is identical in its earthly consequences.
It means every sinner ultimately needs the same Savior.
And this is where Christians can make a catastrophic mistake with Romans 1.
We can defend biblical sexual ethics and somehow forget biblical grace.
Truth without love becomes a weapon.
But what our culture calls “love” cannot require Christians to erase whatever Scripture says simply because obedience becomes socially expensive.
Jesus gives us something better than either cowardice or cruelty.
Grace and truth.
So if you experience same-sex attraction, hear this carefully.
You are not a punchline.
You are not a political talking point.
You are not beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.
And experiencing temptation is not itself permission for another Christian to treat you with contempt.
Christian discipleship calls every believer—not merely one particular group—to bring desires, identities, relationships, ambitions and bodies underneath the lordship of Christ.
For one disciple, surrender may touch sexuality.
For another, pornography.
For another, adultery.
For another, greed.
For another, pride.
For another, resentment that has been fermenting for twenty years.
For another, the desperate addiction to being admired.
Different battles.
Same throne.
The Christian question eventually becomes:
Who gets to be Lord?
That is why the Gospel cannot end with, “Stop sinning.”
If Christianity were merely God shouting moral instructions down from heaven at people incapable of saving themselves, none of us would have hope.
The Gospel announces something infinitely greater.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
The sinless Son of God entered our ruin.
He bore sin.
He endured the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And now forgiveness is not offered to people who successfully pretend they never became dirty.
Forgiveness is offered through Christ to people who repent and believe.
That means the church should be one of the few places on earth where someone can finally stop pretending.
Imagine a man sitting silently in the back of a church.
He has followed Jesus for years.
But there is a struggle he has never told anyone about.
He is terrified.
Not merely because of what he feels.
Because he knows what Christians sometimes do with confessions.
So he sings.
He smiles.
He shakes hands.
He says, “I'm doing good.”
And inside he is exhausted.
Maybe your hidden battle is completely different.
But you understand the sentence:
“If they really knew me…”
If they knew what you watched.
If they knew what you wanted.
If they knew what happened.
If they knew how angry you were.
If they knew what you did after midnight.
If they knew how many times you promised God it was the last time.
If they knew how empty your marriage feels.
If they knew what your mind has been entertaining.
If they knew how far you wandered.
Listen.
The Gospel does not say your sin is imaginary.
It says your sin does not have to write the final chapter.
That is radically different.
Jesus does not save us by convincing us darkness is light.
He saves us by entering our darkness and bringing us into His light.
Repentance is therefore not God saying, “Clean yourself up enough and maybe I'll love you.”
Repentance is the sinner finally releasing the thing that is killing him because he has discovered Someone infinitely better.
Jesus.
This is why we cannot rewrite Romans 1 to make Christianity easier.
But neither can we stop at Romans 1 and pretend condemnation is the climax of Paul's Gospel.
Keep reading Romans.
There is justification.
Peace with God.
Grace.
Freedom from condemnation.
Adoption.
The Spirit.
Hope.
Mercy.
Transformation.
And eventually that staggering promise that nothing can separate God's people from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
The Bible's story is not:
“Look at those disgusting sinners.”
It is:
Look at the holiness of God. Look at the rebellion of humanity. And then look at the astonishing mercy of Jesus Christ.
That is where Romans 1 should eventually drive us.
Not toward hatred.
Toward the cross.
Not toward self-congratulation.
Toward repentance.
Not toward pretending sin does not matter.
Toward the Savior who died because it matters terribly—and who rose because sin and death do not get the final word.
So perhaps the most dangerous way to read Romans 1:27 is to read it thinking only about somebody else.
Maybe your struggle is not theirs.
Fine.
What is yours?
What desire have you been protecting from Jesus?
What relationship have you declared off-limits to His authority?
What secret appetite keeps negotiating with your conscience?
What idol would devastate you if Christ asked you to surrender it?
What sin have you renamed because repentance would cost too much?
Don't answer publicly unless you genuinely want to.
But answer God.
Because there is a frightening difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
Somebody reading this has been fighting privately for months.
Maybe years.
You fell again.
You prayed again.
You wondered whether Jesus was tired of hearing your voice.
And perhaps tonight you need to remember:
The answer to your shame is not better hiding.
It is coming into the light of Christ.
Repentance does not mean you will never experience another battle.
It means you have stopped calling the enemy your king.
So come home.
Not when you become impressive.
Now.
Come with trembling hands.
Come ashamed.
Come exhausted.
Come confused.
Come carrying the parts of your story you wish could be erased.
Jesus already knows what is in the room.
And the cross is still standing.
Not because a comment saves anyone.
Christ saves.
But sometimes the first crack in hiding is finally admitting that you need Him.
Someone else reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only Christian fighting a private war.
If someone came to mind while you were reading this, don't use this article as a weapon against them.
Love them.
Pray for them.
And if sharing it would genuinely help them encounter Scripture and the Gospel rather than merely make them feel targeted, send it with compassion.

But voluntary support of Gospel ministry is biblical. Paul himself speaks appreciatively of believers partnering with him in giving and receiving, and the New Testament repeatedly presents Christian generosity as willing rather than coerced.
You cannot purchase God's favor.
You cannot donate enough to erase yesterday.
Salvation is not merchandise.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone searching for answers.
Because somewhere tonight there is another person staring at a screen while fighting a battle nobody knows exists.
Maybe this article reaches them because you shared it.
Maybe they finally pray.
Maybe they finally confess.
Maybe they finally open Romans and discover that the chapter they thought existed merely to condemn somebody actually belongs to a letter announcing God's power to save sinners.
And maybe, eventually, they discover the truth every redeemed person must discover:
The worst chapter of your life does not have to become the last chapter of your life.
Because when Jesus takes the pen, even the chapter you were ashamed to let anyone read can become the place where grace begins writing something new.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID JUDAS NEED TO IDENTIFY JESUS WITH A KISS?
paragraphs: WHY DID JUDAS NEED TO IDENTIFY JESUS WITH A KISS?

They came with lanterns, weapons, and enough men to arrest a dangerous criminal. Yet Judas told them to watch for something strangely intimate: a kiss. Why? The answer takes us beyond the darkness of Gethsemane and frighteningly close to our own hearts.
There is something about the betrayal of Jesus that becomes more disturbing the longer you look at it.
It wasn't merely that Judas betrayed Him.
It was how.
He could have pointed.
He could have shouted, “There He is.”
He could have approached the soldiers beforehand and described Jesus.
He could have stood at a distance and indicated which man they wanted.
Instead, Judas walked through the darkness toward the Man whose feet he had followed for years.
Toward the Rabbi whose miracles he had witnessed.
Toward the One who had fed the hungry, touched lepers, confronted demons, raised the dead, washed His disciples' feet—and only hours earlier had shared a table with him.
And Judas came close enough to kiss Him.
That raises a haunting question.
Why?
Why did Judas need to identify Jesus at all?
And why with a kiss?
Mark preserves the chilling arrangement Judas had made beforehand:
“Ὃν ἂν φιλήσω αὐτός ἐστιν· κρατήσατε αὐτόν…”

Literally, in context: “Whomever I kiss, He is the one; seize Him…” Mark 14:44. The Greek text describes the kiss as a σύσσημον (syssēmon)—an agreed or distinguishing signal. Judas had arranged the sign in advance.
That detail matters.
The kiss wasn't spontaneous emotion.
It was a signal.
An act normally associated with affection became the mechanism of betrayal.
Think about that.
Judas weaponized intimacy.
And perhaps that is why this scene still feels so painfully modern.
Some of the deepest wounds you will ever carry will not come from enemies who hated you openly.
They will come from people who knew how to get close.
People who knew where you were vulnerable.
People who knew your routines.
People who knew what mattered to you.
People whose voices once made you feel safe.
A stranger can attack your reputation.
But only someone close can betray your trust.
And Judas knew where Jesus would be.
John tells us something easy to overlook: Judas knew the garden because Jesus had often gathered there with His disciples.
Read that again emotionally.
Judas used his knowledge of Jesus' place of prayer to help His enemies find Him.
A place associated with fellowship became the location of betrayal.
He knew where Jesus went because he had been there before.
This wasn't merely information.
It was access.
And suddenly Judas becomes much more uncomfortable to read about, because the story begins asking questions we would rather ask about somebody else.
How close can a person get to Jesus without actually surrendering to Jesus?
Apparently...
terrifyingly close.
Judas had traveled with Christ.
He had heard teaching from the mouth of the Son of God.
He had witnessed what generations before him had longed to see.
He belonged outwardly to the Twelve.
People looking at the group would have counted Judas among the followers of Jesus.
Yet proximity to Christ was not the same thing as surrender to Christ.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still conceal rebellion.
You can know worship songs and still protect a secret idol.
You can carry a Bible and refuse to let the Bible confront you.
You can know where Jesus is discussed without wanting Jesus to rule you.
You can even look like a disciple while slowly negotiating with the very things that are pulling your heart away from Him.
That is why Judas should never merely become the villain we stare at from a safe distance.
His story is a warning.
But we still haven't answered the original question.
Why was identification necessary?

The Gospel accounts tell us that Judas arrived with an armed group. Mark says the people accompanying him came with swords and clubs from the chief priests, scribes, and elders. John adds that the arresting party arrived carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons.
Mark explicitly tells us that Judas had already arranged a signal identifying the intended man: the one he kissed was the one they were to seize and lead away securely.
The text therefore gives us the central answer without requiring speculation:
The kiss was a prearranged arrest signal identifying Jesus.
Why choose such a signal?

The Gospels do not explicitly give Judas' private reasoning, so we should not pretend Scripture tells us more than it does. In the nighttime setting, among Jesus and His disciples, a close-range signal would provide an unmistakable identification for members of the arresting party who needed to know precisely whom Judas meant. Judas, unlike them, knew Jesus personally.
But then John adds something extraordinary.
When the group arrived, Jesus did not hide behind Peter.
He did not disappear into the trees.
He did not wait helplessly for Judas to expose Him.
Jesus stepped forward.
John says Jesus knew what was coming and went out to meet them.
“Whom are you seeking?”
“Jesus of Nazareth.”
Jesus answered:
“ἐγώ εἰμι.”
“I am.”
English translations commonly render the statement in context as “I am he.” John then says the arresting party drew back and fell to the ground.
Now the scene becomes even more remarkable.
Judas had arranged the kiss as identification.
But Jesus was not ultimately captured because Judas managed to outsmart Him.
Jesus identified Himself.
He stepped forward.
The traitor arrived with a signal...
and the Savior walked toward His captors.
That changes the emotional center of Gethsemane.
Jesus wasn't wondering what Judas was doing.
He wasn't caught by surprise.
John explicitly says He knew what was coming.
The tragedy of the kiss, therefore, is not that Judas successfully revealed something Jesus desperately wanted hidden.
The horror is that a disciple turned an expression of relationship into an instrument of betrayal.

Mark 14:45 says Judas approached Jesus, called Him “Rabbi,” and kissed Him. The Greek uses κατεφίλησεν (katephilēsen), a form that can carry the sense of kissing warmly or earnestly, though we should be careful not to build more theology on the verb than the context warrants.
Still, the narrative itself is devastating enough.
“Rabbi.”
A kiss.
Then arrest.
His mouth performed affection while his actions delivered betrayal.
And this is where Gethsemane stops being ancient history.
Because there is a kind of Christianity that still knows how to kiss Jesus without surrendering to Jesus.
We can call Him “Lord” while refusing His authority.
We can sing about surrender while negotiating with sin.
We can post Scripture while harboring bitterness.
We can defend Christianity publicly while neglecting Christ privately.
We can lift our hands in worship and use those same hands to hide what we hope nobody discovers.
We can look close to Jesus...
without belonging wholly to Jesus.
That should disturb us.
Not so we become obsessed with whether somebody else is a Judas.
So we examine ourselves.
The most dangerous question this story produces is not:
“Who around me might betray me?”
It is:
“Jesus, is there anything in me that claims intimacy with You while secretly resisting You?”
That question reaches deeper.
Maybe your kiss is religious appearance.
Maybe yours is a hidden addiction you keep promising God you will eventually surrender.
Maybe it is money.
Maybe resentment.
Maybe pride.
Maybe sexual sin.
Maybe unforgiveness.
Maybe you know exactly how to appear spiritually healthy while your private life is collapsing.
Maybe everybody thinks you are close to God because they see what you post.
But only you know how long it has been since you spoke honestly with Him.
No performance.
No audience.
No pretending.
Just you and Christ.
And perhaps the most frightening part of Judas' story is that betrayal did not begin when his lips touched Jesus.
The kiss revealed something that had already been happening in his heart.
That is how spiritual collapse often works.
Long before people see the public fall, there have been private compromises.
Tiny permissions.
Quiet negotiations.
Secret rationalizations.
Things once resisted become tolerated.
Things tolerated become defended.
Things defended eventually become chains.
And then one day everyone asks:
“How did this happen?”
But heaven saw the road long before the world saw the wreckage.
If something hidden in you is slowly pulling you away from Jesus, do not wait until your private compromise becomes your public catastrophe.
Bring it into the light now.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is an invitation to stop running toward destruction and come home.
And this is where Judas' story becomes even more heartbreaking.
Because while Judas was betraying Jesus...
Jesus was moving toward the cross for sinners.
The hands about to be bound would soon be pierced.
The face Judas kissed would soon be struck.
The Teacher he called “Rabbi” would be mocked.
The One being arrested like a criminal would bear the judgment sinners deserved.
And He would do it willingly.
That is the scandal.
And then comes grace.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that decent people can make themselves acceptable to God.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners need a Savior—and that Jesus Christ died and rose again.
The cross exposes how serious sin really is.
Grace reveals how astonishing God's mercy really is.
And maybe you need to hear this tonight:
Your story does not have to end where your worst chapter began.
Your secret does not have to become your identity.
Your failure does not possess greater authority than the blood of Christ.
Your shame does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
But grace is not permission to continue hiding.
Grace calls us out of hiding.
Christ does not merely offer us a better public image.
He calls us to repentance, forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a transformed life.
So stop pretending.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need to confess sin to God, confess it.
If you have wounded someone and restitution is possible and appropriate, begin making things right.
If you have drifted from Christ, return.
You do not need another religious kiss.
You need surrender.
Maybe that is why this story hurts so deeply.
Judas reminds us that a person can stand astonishingly close to Jesus and still have a heart moving away from Him.
But the rest of the Gospel reminds us of something greater:
Jesus went willingly toward the cross to save sinners.
Be honest.
You don't have to explain everything publicly. God already knows the whole story.
Not as religious decoration.
Someone may need to discover tonight that Christianity is not about pretending to have no scars.
It is about bringing sinners to the Savior who was wounded for them.
There may come a night when the person who needs to reread it is you.
The purpose is simple: keep placing biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ where people can encounter it.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Jesus already paid the price we never could.
Your financial support helps.
Your prayers help.
Your comments help this message reach people.
Your shares help.
But never confuse supporting Gospel Warrior with supporting Jesus Himself.
Give freely, prayerfully, cheerfully, and without compulsion. Support your local church and faithful Gospel work as God leads you.
Because ultimately this article isn't about Judas' lips.
It is about our hearts.
The question is not merely why Judas needed a kiss to identify Jesus.
The deeper question is whether our outward affection for Christ matches the inward allegiance of our lives.
Judas came close enough to kiss Him.
But closeness without surrender was not discipleship.
So don't settle for appearing close to Jesus.
Know Him.
Trust Him.
Repent when you fall.
Run toward Him when shame tells you to run away.
Receive the grace you cannot earn.
Follow the Savior who knew exactly what waited for Him in that garden...
and stepped forward anyway.
They came looking for Jesus with lanterns because the night was dark.
But they were arresting the Light of the world.
And the darkness would not have the final word.
The cross was coming.
The tomb was coming.
But so was Sunday.
And if Christ can take history's most infamous betrayal and place it inside the story of redemption, imagine what He can do with the chapter of your life you thought could never be redeemed.
Your darkest chapter may know your name—but it does not get to write your ending when your life is surrendered to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ABIMELECH LOOKED THROUGH A WINDOW AND REALIZED ISAAC AND REBEKAH WERE DEFINITELY NOT ACTING LIKE BROTHER AND SISTER
paragraphs: ABIMELECH LOOKED THROUGH A WINDOW AND REALIZED ISAAC AND REBEKAH WERE DEFINITELY NOT ACTING LIKE BROTHER AND SISTER

One glance through a window exposed the lie Isaac had been living—and Genesis 26 may be asking what would happen if somebody looked through the window of your life long enough to discover what fear has made you hide.
There was a window.
There was a king.
There was a husband who had been calling his wife his sister.
And then there was one ordinary moment when the truth could no longer remain hidden.
Genesis does not tell us that Abimelech launched an investigation.
It does not say somebody betrayed Isaac.
It does not describe spies following him through Gerar.
Abimelech simply looked through a window.
And what he saw changed everything.
The Hebrew text of Genesis 26:8 reads:
“וַיְהִי כִּי אָרְכוּ־לוֹ שָׁם הַיָּמִים וַיַּשְׁקֵף אֲבִימֶלֶךְ מֶלֶךְ פְּלִשְׁתִּים בְּעַד הַחַלּוֹן וַיַּרְא וְהִנֵּה יִצְחָק מְצַחֵק אֵת רִבְקָה אִשְׁתּוֹ׃”
